E-10-2026-003871.t: EU Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation
qt: to the Commission Kathleen Funchion (The Left) Subject:

The EU Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation contains a phased implementation timetable, with strict requirements for recyclability, recycled content, minimisation, empty space, reuse and specific packaging bans. There is deep anxiety among smaller businesses and distributors, particularly in relation to whether or not they will be required to register an authorised representative in each of the 27 Member States. The Commission’s failure to properly communicate the new rules to businesses has led to some reporting a cessation in some of their services due to the lack of clarity. 1.
Can the Commission outline what businesses, if any, are exempt from this new regulation?
Is it necessary for all businesses to register an authorised representative in each EU Member State?
Will the Commission consider a derogation for smaller businesses?

E-10-2026-003870.t: Electronic consignment note is a burden on small producers
qt: to the Commission Emmanouil Fragkos (ECR) Subject:

The Greek Government now requires producers who sell their goods at farmers’ markets to use electronic consignment notes even when they are transporting exclusively their own produce from their farm to the farmers’ market. According to the Independent Authority for Public Revenue (AADE) this requirement comes under phase two of the electronic monitoring of goods and will enter into force on 12 October 2026. These producers are already required to record their farming activity, stay on top of licensing and record retail sales electronically. Additional digitalisation requirements place a significant and unfamiliar burden particularly on small producers who frequently transport perishable products and return unsold quantities. The Commission has recognised the administrative burden on small farmers in particular and, as part of its efforts to simply the common agricultural policy, is pushing for a reduced administrative burden and the once-only principle to streamline data submission through interoperable digital systems. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

Does it believe that requiring small producers to comply with additional digital obligations concerning data that is already available to national authorities, is consistent with its policy of simplifying farmers’ obligations and with the once-only data reporting principle?
Does it intend to encourage Member States to provide for simplification and exceptions in such cases, without undermining the effectiveness of tax controls?

E-10-2026-003869.t: Alleged misappropriation of European funds by the PSOE and the credibility of European institutions
qt: to the Commission Jorge Buxadé Villalba (PfE) Subject:

According to various media reports, the European Public Prosecutor’s Office has requested information from Spain’s national high court (Audiencia Nacional) on the possible use of EU funds to finance party political advertising in the European elections campaign of the Spanish Socialist Workers’ Party (PSOE), and even for alleged illegal espionage, media pressure, blackmail and threats linked to the court case known as the Leire case12. Teresa Ribera, who headed the Socialist candidacy at the time, is now Executive VicePresident of the Commission; Iratxe García, also of the PSOE, chairs the S&D Group. These allegations, if confirmed, go beyond Spanish politics. In view of the above: 1.
What is the Commission’s assessment of these revelations in connection with its monitoring of the rule of law in Spain?

Does the Commission consider that, if illegal funding of the PSOE’s campaign is proven, the political legitimacy of the European officials who benefited from it would be compromised, including the credibility of the Commission’s own Executive VicePresident?
If the allegations under investigation are confirmed, is there a risk that, in accordance with Regulation 2020/2092, disbursements of EU funding to Spain may be suspended?

https://theobjective.com/espana/tribunales/2026-09-25/denunciante-leire-ue-sanchez-desvio-fondos/. https://www.rtve.es/noticias/20260924/fiscalia-europea-solicita-informacion-sobre-caso-leire-por-sihubo-pagos-perjudicaron-a-intereses-union/17239054.shtml. 1 2

E-10-2026-003868.t: Continuing deterioration of the high-speed train service between Lille and Brussels
qt: to the Commission Majdouline Sbai (Verts/ALE) Subject:

The high-speed link between Lille and Brussels has been in steady decline for almost a decade. In 2015, commuters still had four direct trains departing from Brussels after 18:00. In January 2026, the last direct train of the day was brought forward to 18:00 (since then it has temporarily been pushed back to 18:09). This situation makes it extremely difficult, if not impossible, to commute for work between the two cities. Most importantly, according to a calculation tool made available by the French Agency for Ecological Transition (ADEME), the Lille-Brussels route is about fifty times less polluting by train than by petrol/diesel car1. 1.

What action does the Commission intend to take in response to this deterioration in order to maintain the quality of service objectives in connection with the TEN-T Regulation, the recommendations of the Letta report on reducing the border effect and European climate objectives?
What resources does it intend to devote to enhancing the connection between Brussels and Lille, the city that has been chosen as the headquarters of the European Union Customs Authority?
What technical or regulatory solutions could the Commission put in place to reinstate a proper stop in Lille for Eurostar services between Brussels and London?
https://impactco2.fr/outils/transport.

E-10-2026-003867.t: Drastic cuts in cod bycatch and the future of Baltic fishers
qt: to the Commission Piotr Müller (ECR) Subject:

In August 2026, the Commission presented a proposal for Baltic fishing quotas in 2027. It provides for cuts in the bycatch limits for cod of 88% and 51% and an increase in the limits for sprat of 44%. In light of the above: 1.

Why does the Commission consider it proportionate and reasonable to further mechanically tighten restrictions on the fishing sector, given that the bans in force since 2019 have not led to the recovery of cod stocks and that factors not linked to fishing are having a significant impact on the situation?

When proposing to increase the catch limit for sprat by 44%, how did the Commission take into account the requirement to apply an ecosystem-based approach and the key importance of this species in the diet of cod?

How has the Commission assessed the risk that setting bycatch limits on the basis of the bycatch reported in 2025, in the absence of a level set by ICES, will lead to the premature closure of mixed fisheries and drastically impact the coastal fleet?

E-10-2026-003865.t: Safeguarding fawn and wildlife rescue under new EU drone rules
qt: to the Commission Sander Smit (ECR), Jessika van Leeuwen (ECR) Subject:

The Commission’s Action Plan on Drone and Counter-Drone Security announces new rules extending operator registration and direct remote identification requirements to all drones above 100 g1. This could significantly expand the number of drones and operators subject to registration requirements, including thermal-imaging drones used by farmers and volunteers to locate and rescue fawns and other wildlife before mowing. Such operations are time-critical and often rely on existing equipment. At the same time, the Commission has announced ‘regulatory simplification and flexibility for certain operations’. 1.

Has the Commission assessed the additional registration costs and administrative burden resulting from lowering the threshold to drones above 100 g, in particular for farmers, volunteers and organisations carrying out fawn and wildlife rescue operations?
Will existing rescue drones above 100 g without direct remote identification be allowed to continue operating without mandatory replacement or disproportionate retrofitting?

Will the Commission explicitly provide simplified registration rules, transitional arrangements or exemptions for time-critical fawn and wildlife rescue operations, including where Beyond Visual Line of Sight (BVLOS) flights are necessary?

Commission communication of 11 February 2026 entitled ‘Action Plan on Drone and Counter Drone Security’ (COM(2026)0081); in Section 2.2.1 the Commission announces a Drone Security Package extending registration and identification requirements to all drones above 100 g; the Key Actions specify mandatory operator registration and direct remote identification for smaller drones above 100 g. 1

E-10-2026-003841.t: Review of the adequacy decision for the Republic of Korea – impact on negotiation of the security of information agreement
qt: to the Commission César Luena (S&D) Subject:

The adequacy decision concerning the Republic of Korea recently underwent its first review, which was concluded on 23 July 2026. The review found that the Republic of Korea provides an adequate level of protection for personal data transferred from the European Union to bodies in the Republic of Korea subject to the Personal Information Protection Act. Closer cooperation on digital matters and increased data flows between the European Union and the Republic of Korea broaden the benefits of existing agreements between the parties, in particular the Free Trade Agreement and the Digital Trade Agreement. Given that safeguards are in place, to what extent will negotiations on a security of information agreement be fast-tracked to make it easier for classified information to be exchanged and pave the way for closer cooperation, including in areas related to security and defence?

E-10-2026-003840.t: Lack of resources to combat drug trafficking in southern Spain
qt: to the Commission Juan Ignacio Zoido Álvarez (PPE), Alma Ezcurra Almansa (PPE), Dolors Montserrat (PPE), Maravillas Abadía Jover (PPE), Carmen Crespo Díaz (PPE) Subject:

According to recent reports from the Spanish State Public Prosecutor’s Office and the Ministry of the Interior – in its Annual National Security Report – and as acknowledged by the European Commission, southern Europe is a rapidly growing entry point for drug trafficking and illegal immigration. However, the material resources available to the Civil Guard are insufficient to curb this rise in crime. The officers policing the entire Almería coastline (200 km long) do not have a single helicopter and must make do with a measly three patrol boats. Furthermore, various police sources claim that the Costa Tropical of Granada and Almería has become a ‘refuelling point’ for drug traffickers, and the Almería Public Prosecutor’s Office notes that cocaine trafficking has soared by 325 per cent in two years. In light of the above: 1.
Has the Spanish Government informed the Commission of the uptick in drug and human trafficking on the Costa Tropical of Granada and Almería in recent months?
Can Spain make use of any Commission mechanism or programme to provide the Civil Guard with additional material resources to bolster its work in the area? Has it requested such assistance?

E-10-2026-003839.t: Free legal aid for child victims of serious non-sexual crimes
qt: to the Commission Dolors Montserrat (PPE) Subject:

The ‘Bolaños Law’ in Spain has done away with the automatic granting of legal aid to child victims of certain serious non-sexual crimes, instead forcing them to prove they cannot afford legal assistance. The Spanish Public Prosecutor’s Office has warned that this new arrangement may lead to people being left without assistance and has called for protection to be restored. In the light of Directive 2012/29/EU, which requires the best interests of the child to be a primary consideration and guarantees victims access to legal aid under the conditions established in national law: 1.
Does the Commission consider it compatible with EU law for child victims of serious crime to be left without specialised legal assistance if it cannot be proved that they cannot afford it themselves?
Has the Commission assessed whether this reform really protects the child’s best interests and prevents unjustified differences in how child victims are protected depending on the crime?

Does the Commission intend to request information from the Spanish authorities or take any action to ensure that Spanish legislation is fully consistent with the obligations arising from Directive 2012/29/EU?

E-10-2026-003836.t: Pluralism in the public audiovisual sector and the consultation of ‘civil society’
qt: to the Commission Catherine Griset (PfE) Subject:

Under pressure and following a strike against his arrival at France Inter, journalist Charles Sapin eventually decided not to join this public media outlet. The act of censoring a journalist like this, whether for his actual or perceived political views, further tarnishes the image of the public audiovisual sector, which is increasingly and openly being monopolised by the left. Among the trade unions behind this act of censorship is the National Union of Journalists (SNJ)1. And yet, the Commission is consulting this extremist trade union, skilfully presented as a member of ‘civil society’, on topics such as freedom of the press2. 1.
Does the Commission publish a precise account of the requests and contributions made by this trade union or the European network to which it belongs3?
Does it intend to maintain relations with this far-left organisation, which is openly opposed to media pluralism and freedom of expression?

https://snj.fr/france-inter-et-valeurs-actuelles-la-strategie-du-paillasson/2693. In its 2022 Rule of Law Report (Chapter France), the Commission cites the National Union of Journalists in the official list of organisations met to assess the media situation and the transparency of the sector: https://commission.europa.eu/publications/2022-rule-law-report-communication-and-countrychapters_en. 3 https://europeanjournalists.org/about-efj/. 1 2

E-10-2026-003834.t: Indicating the origin of frozen fruit and vegetables
qt: to the Commission Benoit Cassart (Renew) Subject:

Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011 lays down the general framework for the provision of food information to consumers. It stipulates, in particular, that the country of origin or place of provenance must be indicated whenever its absence is likely to mislead consumers. However, this requirement does not apply as a general rule to frozen fruit and vegetables. Consequently, unlike certain fresh products that are subject to specific rules on the indication of origin, consumers may not have clear information on the origin of frozen fruit or vegetables. This raises questions regarding transparency and consumer information, given that the origin of products can play a key role in consumers’ purchasing choices. 1.
Why is the rule on indication of origin not applied in general to frozen fruit and vegetables?

Does the Commission intend to amend Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011 or the applicable sectoral rules to make it compulsory to indicate the ‘EU’ or ‘non-EU’ origin of frozen fruit and vegetables for the final consumer?

E-10-2026-003833.t: Commission’s statements on the establishment of a European Security Council
qt: to the Commission Barbara Bonte (PfE) Subject:

In her 2026 State of the Union Address, Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced that ideas will be set out to make a European Security Council a reality, in a leaders’ format that could also involve third countries such as Ukraine, the United Kingdom, Norway and Canada. However, the EU Treaties make no provision for such a body. In accordance with Articles 24 and 26 TEU, the Common Foreign and Security Policy is defined and implemented within the institutional structure laid down in those articles. 1.
What is the Treaty basis for the Commission President’s proposal to establish a European Security Council?
What are its intended legal status, composition and powers?
How do these relate to the powers of the European Council and the Council pursuant to Articles 24 and 26 TEU?

E-10-2026-003832.t: Commission’s statement on relations with Canada
qt: to the Commission Barbara Bonte (PfE) Subject:

In her 2026 State of the Union Address, Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced the intention to take relations with Canada to a new level. In addition to an ‘Alliance for the Future’, a common prosperity and economic security space and further cooperation on technology and defence, she proposed to open ‘the door for Canada to be the first associate member of the EU’. The Commission also subsequently included this ambition in its State of the Union official initiatives. However, the current EU Treaties make no provision for the status of associate member of the EU. 1.
On what Treaty basis can Canada acquire the status of first ‘associate member of the EU’, as announced by the Commission President?
What rights and obligations would this new status comprise?

E-10-2026-003831.t: 28th company law regime: harmonisation or new regime
qt: to the Commission Barbara Bonte (PfE) Subject:

On 18 March 2026 the Commission presented its proposal for EU Inc., an optional 28th company law regime that will stand alongside the existing national legal forms. The Commission is basing its proposal on Article 114 TFEU and is therefore treating it as a measure that contributes to the harmonisation of the internal market. In its judgment in Case C-436/03, Parliament v Council, the Court of Justice ruled, however, that introducing a new European legal form alongside the existing national legal forms could not be regarded as a harmonisation measure under what was then Article 95 of the EC Treaty, now Article 114 TFEU. In that case the Court accepted what was then Article 308 EC, now Article 352 TFEU, as a legal basis. The Commission is therefore, at the very least, creating the impression of trying to circumvent the principle of unanimity in the Council. How does the Commission justify the choice of Article 114 TFEU as the legal basis for EU Inc., in the light of judgment C-436/03, and why does it believe that Article 352 TFEU — which requires unanimity in the Council — does not apply in this case?

E-10-2026-003830.t: Access to UBO registers and protection of privacy
qt: to the Commission Barbara Bonte (PfE) Subject:

In its judgment in the cases WM and Sovim v Luxembourg Business Registers (C-37/20 and C-601/20), the Court of Justice of the European Union ruled that open public access to information on ultimate beneficial owners (UBOs) constitutes a serious breach of the rights to respect for private and family life and to protection of personal data, as protected by Articles 7 and 8 of the Charter. Directive (EU) 2024/1640 reintroduces access for persons with a ‘legitimate interest’. For certain categories, including journalists and civil-society organisations, such an interest is assumed to apply and a link to the legal entity concerned does not have to be demonstrated. The Directive also stipulates that UBOs will not be informed about which journalist or civilsociety organisation has consulted their personal data. 1.

How is the Commission guaranteeing that access based on an assumed ‘legitimate interest’, for which no concrete link to the entity concerned has to be demonstrated, complies with the requirements of necessity and proportionality highlighted by the Court in the Sovim judgment?
In the Commission’s view, how is the right of UBOs to the protection of their personal data guaranteed if they cannot find out which journalist or civil-society organisation has consulted their data?
How can a UBO verify retrospectively whether data was actually consulted within the framework of a ‘legitimate interest’?

E-10-2026-003828.t: European investment in Latin America in a changing geopolitical landscape
qt: to the Commission Sebastian Kruis (PfE) Subject:

Under the European Union-Latin America and the Caribbean (EU-LAC) Global Gateway Investment Agenda, Team Europe has committed over EUR 45 billion to Latin America and the Caribbean for the period until 2027. Meanwhile, the United States is rapidly expanding its economic and strategic footprint in Latin America, in sectors ranging from critical raw materials and nearshoring to ports and digital infrastructure. This is a competitive risk, but also an opportunity. Where US capital and corporate networks are already moving, EU investors can gain speed and scale by plugging into those flows rather than simply building parallel structures. EU companies, especially small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), still report difficulties in identifying bankable projects and accessing support with project preparation in the region. 1.
How does the Commission assess the effect of intensified US investment in the region on delivery of the EU-LAC Global Gateway Investment Agenda, and where does it see possibilities for cooperation?
Which instruments allow EU investors and SMEs to access project pipelines, technical assistance and co-financing through regional development banks, such as the InterAmerican Development Bank?

Is the Commission willing to launch a pilot with the Inter-American Development Bank and existing business platforms in the Western Hemisphere to develop a joint pipeline of bankable projects, and under what conditions could such a facility operate from outside the EU?

E-10-2026-003826.t: Fragmented local regulations affecting holders of the European Parking Card for people with disabilities
qt: to the Commission Brigitte van den Berg (Renew) Subject:

The UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities requires accessibility and personal mobility. The European Parking Card for people with disabilities is intended to facilitate the recognition of equal access and treatment across Member States. In the Netherlands, however, the practical treatment of cardholders varies between local authorities. Different local regulations and digital systems may apply to low-traffic, car-free or emission-free zones. Cardholders may have to consult local regulations or risk fines and de facto exclusion. Directive (EU) 2024/28411 harmonises the new card but not the parking rights attached to it. Consequently, differences in the practical application of parking rights may persist at local level, limiting the card’s effectiveness. This fragmentation creates uncertainty and restricts equal mobility. In the light of the foregoing: 1.
Does the Commission recognise fragmented local application of parking rights as an emerging issue deserving greater attention at EU level?
How does the Commission ensure that foreign cardholders are treated under the same conditions as local cardholders, pending the implementation of Directive (EU) 2024/2841 in 2028?
Does the Commission intend to support or undertake research into this issue, assessing its prevalence, impact, and implications for greater consistency or minimum standards across Member States?

Directive (EU) 2024/2841 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 23 October 2024 establishing the European Disability Card and the European Parking Card for persons with disabilities (OJ L, 2024/2841, 14.11.2024, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2024/2841/oj). 1

E-10-2026-003823.t: Public consultation on the Dutch restoration plan before and after submission
qt: to the Commission Sander Smit (ECR) Subject:

The Netherlands submitted its draft restoration plan on 25 August 2026 via Reportnet; the submission is restricted, whilst Sweden’s submission was made public1. In its answer to written question E-001684/20262, the Commission confirmed that its comments under Article 17 would be made public and emphasised transparent preparation and public consultation. A six-week public consultation on a public version of the draft has been announced for October; the plan’s environmental impact assessment will follow in the autumn. A previous formal public consultation concerned the methodology of the environmental impact assessment. 1.

On what grounds is the Dutch submission restricted, and will the Commission, or the EEA as the relevant authority, make the submitted draft, together with its annexes and amended versions, available to the public upon request pursuant to Regulation (EC) No 1049/2001 and Regulation (EC) No 1367/2006, having regard to Article 6(1) of Regulation (EC) No 1367/2006?
What type of public participation and justification are required under Article 14(20) and Article 15(3)(w) prior to submission?

In accordance with Article 17, what consequences does the Commission attach to the absence of information on public participation or to discrepancies between the version submitted and the version made available for inspection, and what additional consultation or renewed public participation is required prior to the adoption of the final plan?

Reportnet 3, dataflow/1906, ‘Draft National Restoration Plans – 2026’, accessed on 18 September 2026: Netherlands, submitted on 25 August 2026 at 17.17. 2 https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/E-10-2026-001684-ASW_EN.html. 1

E-10-2026-003821.t: Prostitution of minors online from Switzerland: what are Brussels and Paris doing about it?
qt: to the Commission Virginie Joron (PfE) Subject:

In its article of 20 September 2026, Le Point describes a mother’s struggle to secure the closure of Sexemodel, now Meslibertines, an escort ad platform established in Switzerland, suspected of having allowed her then 13-year-old daughter to be sexually exploited on three occasions1. The Paris Public Prosecutor’s Office has opened an investigation and the High Commissioner for Children has notified the site to the French Regulatory Authority for Audiovisual and Digital Communication to have it shut down, without success to date. This case reveals the lack of clarity as to the jurisdiction applicable to platforms accessible from but established outside the European Union. 1.

The Digital Services Act requires any platform accessible from but established outside the European Union to appoint a legal representative in a Member State (Article 13). Which authority is competent to sanction the foreign platform: the Commission or the competent authorities of a Member State?
Has the Commission contacted the Swiss authorities to penalise the platform?
What procedure and specific means does it use, alone or alongside the competent national Digital Services Coordinator, to block access from the European market to foreign child pornography websites?
Émilie Trevert, ‘Prostitution des mineurs: l’incroyable combat d’une mère pour obtenir une enquête’, Le Point, 20 September 2026, https://www.lepoint.fr/societe/fleau-VO66DN25PJBBHADUUVID75DMQI/. 1

E-10-2026-003819.t: European monitoring and reporting of GNSS interference, following on from P-002590/2026
qt: to the Commission Bart Groothuis (Renew) Subject:
European monitoring and reporting of GNSS interference, following on from P002590/2026

In its answer to written question P-002590/20261, the Commission states that the Galileo Reference Centre (GRC) is not responsible for monitoring, detecting or localising interference affecting GNSS other than Galileo and also does not have any reporting mandate. This contradicts the EUSPA’s mission statement, which describes the GRC’s mandate as follows: ‘[to] perform independent service performance monitoring and assessments of Galileo and also other GNSS’2. The Commission also refers to the Joint Research Centre (JRC), which has analysed GNSS interference in preparation for a future RFI alerting service, not as an ongoing monitoring task. Lastly, reference is made to an action plan, which is not expected until the end of this year, and an alerting service, the feasibility of which is yet to be determined. Against the background of the war in Ukraine and Russia’s increasing capabilities to disrupt GNSS, Europe cannot afford the luxury of investigating the need for monitoring. Europe must know when, where and which GNSS signals are being interfered with. 1.

Does the Commission acknowledge that the mandate of the GRC, as described by the EUSPA, also includes monitoring and assessments of GNSS other than Galileo? If not, how does it explain this mission statement and which EU body does hold this mandate?
Why are existing capacities of the GRC and JRC not already being used for the systematic monitoring of GNSS interference?
From what point will the European Union have access to systematic, continuous monitoring of GNSS interference, including reporting of such interference?
https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/P-10-2026-002590_EN.html. https://www.euspa.europa.eu/eu-space-programme/galileo/galileo-reference-centre.

E-10-2026-003815.t: Triggering a special support clause for electricity and fuel
qt: to the Commission Georgios Aftias (PPE) Subject:

Based on the communications issued by the Commission in 2026, there is fiscal space for actions to address high fuel and energy prices. Targeted subsidies for vulnerable households and support for businesses that have been especially hard hit by the energy crisis should be key tools in addressing this problem. The Commission has already allocated EUR 14.5 billion for measures to address the 2026 energy price shock. At the same time, the new European fiscal framework provides for the possibility of triggering an escape clause, which would allow for a temporary deviation from the agreed fiscal requirements in exceptional circumstances when there is a severe impact on public finances, provided that there is no threat to debt sustainability. Europe cannot be a passive bystander. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

Does it intend, in view of persistent rising prices and high energy costs, to allow additional budgetary flexibility for Member States so that they can provide energy subsidies and direct payments to households, pensioners and small and medium-sized enterprises?
Is it considering triggering a special fiscal clause to address high prices and the energy crisis if high prices persist?

E-10-2026-003812.t: Robotisation, artificial intelligence and labour shortages
qt: to the Commission Mathilde Androuët (PfE) Subject:

In its communication entitled ‘Labour and skills shortages in the EU: an action Plan’ (COM(2024) 131 final) of 20 March 2024, the Commission states that the response to labour shortages must first be to mobilise the untapped potential of the EU labour force (increasing the activity rate, upskilling, improving working conditions and intra-EU mobility), but points out that attracting talent from third countries must also be part of the solution. At the same time, the communication entitled ‘Demographic change in Europe: a toolbox for action’ (COM(2023) 577 final) of 11 October 2023 stresses that higher productivity, the digital transition and technological developments are key levers in addressing the ageing of the population and safeguarding European competitiveness. In view of the above: 1.

What quantitative assessments has the Commission carried out to determine the potential impact of robotisation, artificial intelligence and productivity gains on labour shortages compared with the impact of increased legal migration?

Does it intend to set European targets that prioritise automation, robotisation and greater use of artificial intelligence in sectors under pressure, before resorting to increased migration from third countries?

E-10-2026-003811.t: The Mecca Joint Defence Agreement between Türkiye, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia
qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Nikolas Farantouris (S&D) Subject:

The Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, which was signed on 7 August 2026, is currently the most important diplomatic development in the Middle East, as it militarily ‘unites’ Türkiye, a country that works with the Euro-Atlantic institutions, with Pakistan, the only Muslim state in possession of nuclear weapons, and Saudi Arabia, the most powerful force in the Gulf. The agreement is worthy of special attention, as it signals an effort to pursue new and independent diplomatic action in the region. Although the exact content of the agreement has not been made public, certain key aspects have been made known, e.g. that it contains a mutual military assistance clause and promotes common military and industrial projects. However, many question marks remain. Despite these question marks, press reports have portrayed the Commission’s reaction to the agreement as ‘positive’1. In view of the above, can the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy answer the following: 1.
What is the Commission’s official stance on the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement?
What is the exact content and what are the expected consequences of the agreement, given the concerns it raises about its impact on the balance in the Eastern Mediterranean?
Are the clauses of the agreement in line with the EU’s new security and defence architecture?

E-10-2026-003809.t: Low-emission zones: automactic fines being imposed by Belgian towns and cities on French and European cars
qt: to the Commission Virginie Joron (PfE) Subject:

French motorists are being fined between EUR 150 and 350 euros in Antwerp, Belgium, even if their vehicles run on modern, compliant fuel (Euro 6), as the cameras in place apparently cannot read data from foreign number plates. According to Antwerp’s Deputy Mayor for the Environment, Karim Bachar, ‘we cannot tell [from our cameras] what kind of vehicle a French driver is entering our city in, or whether it meets the standards. That is why, if you have a vehicle registered in France, you must register it in advance. If this is not done, a fine is imposed’1. Antwerp has imposed fines totalling more than EUR 7 million. Antwerp also charges a nonrefundable fee of EUR 75 to register a compliant car when the fine is issued. Across Europe, hundreds of towns and cities are imposing such an extortion scheme on a town-by-town basis, which is reminiscent of the medieval practice of multiple tolls. 1.

Does the Commission consider it compatible with the free movement of goods and EU law2 for a Member State to authorise its towns and villages to automatically impose fines on all vehicles registered in another European country?
Does the Commission consider that a fine of between EUR 150 and 350 and a registration fee of EUR 75 are proportionate for a compliant vehicle and an automated online procedure?
What measures is the Commission taking to prohibit these fines being imposed on compliant European vehicles on the sole pretext of a failure to register a car administratively?
https://www.vrt.be/vrtnws/fr/2026/04/21/plus-de-4-conducteurs-francais-sur-10-ecopent-dune-amende-

dans-l/. The rules of the internal market should be transparent, simple, consistent and effective, thereby ensuring legal certainty and clarity in the interests of businesses and consumers. 2
to the Commission Barry Andrews (Renew) Subject:

Handmade craft goods are a vital part of European culture and innovation. Many European craft makers and designers feel very strongly that the addition of 23 % VAT on original handmade craft goods is excessive. It is almost a quarter of the value of an item which has taken hours of labour done by talented people. Also, in light of the flood of imported mass produced goods from China in recent years, reducing the VAT on European-made craft would help to level the playing field. Finally, it is important to note the difference in treatment of craft versus paintings, which only carry 13.3 % VAT. Will the Commisison consider proposing an update to Directive 2006/112/EC1 to reduce the VAT for handmade craft goods to assist European craftsmen and women?

E-10-2026-003806.t: Risk of discontinuation of treatment for people living with HIV in Romania
qt: to the Commission Nicolae Ștefănuță (Verts/ALE) Subject:

On 16 September 2026, the Romanian Ministry of Health announced the reallocation of RON 56 million from a number of national health programmes, including the national HIV/AIDS programme. According to the Ministry, as of December the programmes concerned will no longer have funding. Romania’s National Union of Organisations of People Affected by HIV/AIDS (UNOPA) has warned that if additional funds are not allocated, a large number of people living with HIV could be left without treatment as of 1 November and in some cases even as early as 15 October. The continuity of antiretroviral treatment is crucial to patients’ health, in preventing the virus from spreading and in achieving the aim of eliminating AIDS as a public health threat by 2030. 1.
Is the Commission aware of the situation and the risks involved in discontinuing access to antiretroviral treatment in Romania?
Does the Commission intend to ask the Romanian authorities for information on the measures in place for guaranteeing continuity of treatment?
What EU tools can be deployed to support Romania, including strategic reserves of medicines, joint procurement mechanisms and European solidarity mechanisms in case of medicine shortages?

E-10-2026-003804.t: Review of existing markets under stress in light of proposal for a regulation 2026/0268 (COD) (Affordable Housing Act)
qt: to the Commission Borja Giménez Larraz (PPE) Subject:
Review of existing markets under stress in light of proposal for a regulation 2026/0268 (COD) (Affordable Housing Act)

In its proposal for a regulation 2026/0268 (COD), the Commission recognises that the lack of common, objective criteria for assessing housing-related measures creates legal uncertainty and hinders the consistent application of EU law. However, Article 14 stipulates that the regulation will not apply to measures adopted prior to its entry into force, even though it affords the competent authorities the opportunity to review such measures under the regulation. A number of Spain’s autonomous communities have designated areas as zones of housing stress (ZHS) and have put in place specific measures based on Law 12/2023. 1.

What would be the added value of establishing an EU framework to harmonise criteria if measures already in place prior to the regulation fall outside its scope and reviews are left to the discretion of the competent authorities?

Does the Commission envisage a mechanism to require Spanish authorities to reassess the measures already in place taking account of the non-discrimination, necessity, proportionality and transparency criteria laid down in the new framework?

If, following a possible review, some measures do not meet the applicable requirements, what legal consequences will it entail, and can two ZHS schemes exist side by side, only one of which is in line with the new requirements?

E-10-2026-003803.t: Legal safeguards and limits to restrictions on private property and the internal market in the light of proposal for a regulation 2026/0268 (COD)
qt: to the Commission Borja Giménez Larraz (PPE) Subject:

The culture of home ownership is a pillar of economic and financial stability in European society and is particularly important in Member States such as Spain. Under Article 5 of the proposal for a regulation, the competent authorities may impose restrictions on the purchase or use of second homes which are not intended as a main place of residence. Experience in a number of European countries – such as France and Switzerland – shows that restrictions of this kind can have a negative impact on economic activity and employment but offer no guarantee that the properties affected will go into the long-term residential rental market. 1.

What legal safeguards does the proposal contain to ensure restrictions on the purchase or use of second homes are consistent with the right to private property, and what mechanisms is it considering to provide legal certainty to affected owners?

The proposal does not place a uniform limit on the scale of the measures that can be taken by the competent authorities, allowing Member States to regulate without restriction. What mechanisms does the Commission envisage to prevent the principle of the internal market from being undermined?
Does it consider that the vast array of measures that could be adopted in the regulation might pose a risk to long-term family savings?

E-10-2026-003802.t: Scope of Protocol No 32 in view of the proposal for a regulation on the Affordable Housing Act (2026/0268 (COD))
qt: to the Commission Borja Giménez Larraz (PPE) Subject:
Scope of Protocol No 32 in view of the proposal for a regulation on the Affordable Housing Act (2026/0268 (COD))

Protocol No 32 annexed to the Treaty allows Denmark to maintain its existing legislation on the acquisition of second homes, by way of derogation from the Treaty provisions on the free movement of capital. Danish legislation imposes restrictions on the purchase of summer and second homes by individuals who do not meet certain criteria regarding their connection to Denmark. In view of this specific derogation: 1.
How would the above-mentioned proposal for a regulation (2026/0268 (COD)) be applied to the Danish restrictions on the purchase of second homes, as protected under Protocol No 32?
Would such measures be subject to the requirements of necessity and proportionality set out in the proposal or would the specific protection granted to Denmark under Protocol No 32 prevail?

If the proposal for a regulation establishes common criteria for assessing restrictions on second homes, could those criteria affect the future application of Danish law? In the event of a conflict between the two instruments, how should their relationship be interpreted and which legal regime would prevail?

E-10-2026-003800.t: Risk of extraterritorial application of the Digital Services Act because of VPN use
qt: to the Commission Adam Bielan (ECR) Subject:

Alarmingly, some governments have sought to apply their online safety laws extraterritorially because the use of VPNs and similar circumvention technologies enables users to bypass such laws. Given this, I request a clear answer from the Commission to the following question: Does the Digital Services Act1, Commission guidance or any EU law require or encourage platforms to implement compliance measures beyond geo-blocking illegal content in the relevant EU jurisdiction, such as removing content globally, because some EU users use a VPN?

E-10-2026-003799.t: Liquidation of Viridian Lithium and difficulties with the financing of strategic projects under the Critical Raw Materials Act
qt: to the Commission Julie Rechagneux (PfE), Aleksandar Nikolic (PfE), André Rougé (PfE), France Jamet (PfE), Valérie Deloge (PfE), Marie-Luce Brasier-Clain (PfE), Séverine Werbrouck (PfE), Pierre Pimpie (PfE), Marie Dauchy (PfE), Claudiu-Richard Târziu (ECR), Christophe Gomart (PPE), Julien Sanchez (PfE), Guillaume Peltier (ECR) Subject:

On 25 March 2025, the Commission recognised the Viridian Lithium refinery in Lauterbourg (France) as a strategic project under Regulation (EU) 2024/1252, with a view to it producing 28 500 tonnes of lithium hydroxide per year. On 9 March 2026, the company was placed in compulsory liquidation as it had failed to secure the EUR 295 million it needed to finance its project. France had granted it a tax credit of EUR 118.9 million, as well as EUR 12.4 million under the France 2030 scheme. According to Viridian Lithium’s former director of development, the fact that European support for the project did not materialise contributed to its failure. In August 2026, 23 of the 60 strategic projects sent ‘urgent calls for action’ to the Commission, complaining that commitments on financing, market access and authorisations had not been met. 1.
What EU funding was actually offered or granted to Viridian Lithium before it was liquidated?
How many of the 60 strategic projects have received EU funding, and what was the total amount disbursed?
What immediate measures does the Commission intend to take to prevent the scrapping of other strategic projects that are facing financing difficulties?
Supporter1
This question is supported by a Member other than the authors: Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE).

E-10-2026-003796.t: EU involvement in CERD General Recommendation No. 40 on slavery reparations
qt: to the Commission Tom Vandendriessche (PfE) Subject:

On 25 August 2026, the Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination (CERD) adopted General Recommendation No. 40 on reparatory justice for slavery and colonialism. Its public consultation process included calls for input and a half-day general discussion in Geneva. In footnote 70, the recommendation cites Parliament’s resolution of 26 March 20191 among examples of regional action on reparatory justice. 1.
Did the Commission, the European External Action Service or the EU Delegation in Geneva follow or participate in the drafting process, and did any of them submit or otherwise contribute input?

Does the Commission consider that paragraphs 69 to 71 of the recommendation, which envisage legislative, administrative and policy measures concerning non-state actors including banks, insurers and other undertakings, fall wholly or partly within Union competence?
Does the Commission intend to propose, support or fund any Union measure giving effect to those recommendations?
European Parliament resolution of 26 March 2019 on fundamental rights of people of African descent in Europe (OJ C 108, 26.3.2021, p. 2). 1

E-10-2026-003793.t: A ‘year of simplification’ and EU regulatory overreach
qt: to the Commission Marieke Ehlers (PfE) Subject:

11 Member States have called for a 12-month pause on new EU legislation, in what they are calling a ‘year of simplification’. Their message is straightforward: Brussels cannot keep piling new rules on citizens, businesses and national administrations while existing legislation is still being implemented, reviewed and enforced. The Commission has repeatedly promised ‘better regulation’ and simplification, yet the flow of new legislation has continued. This raises the more fundamental question of whether the problem is not simply excessive red tape, but a Commission culture of regulatory overreach. 1.
What assessment has the Commission made of the proposal for a year of simplification by this blocking minority in the Council?

Does the Commission recognise that the sheer volume and cumulative effect of EU legislation has itself become a problem, and is it prepared to conduct an honest selfreflection on its own role in creating regulatory overreach, including by identifying areas where it has proposed legislation without a sufficiently demonstrated need for action at EU level?

Which legislative proposals currently under preparation does the Commission consider unnecessary, duplicative or suitable for postponement or withdrawal, and will it commit to putting them on hold during a year of simplification?

E-10-2026-003792.t: Greece’s deviation from European antimicrobial resistance targets
qt: to the Commission Nikolaos Anadiotis (NI) Subject:

The latest data held by the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) shows that Greece is worryingly far off from the targets set for 2030. Since 2019, bloodstream infections with MRSA have increased by 20.7 %, resistant E. coli infections by 109 % and carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae infections by 14.1 %. Corresponding European targets require a reduction or no increase. Just 43 % of the total consumption of antibiotics in humans belongs to the ‘Access’ group of antibiotics when the target is 65 %1. Recommendation 2023/C 220/01 calls on Member States to implement updated national One Health plans, with sufficient resources, measurable targets and regular evaluation2. The Commission is required to monitor implementation and submit a report in 2027. Greece's National Strategy for Quality of Care 2025-2030 states that no infection prevention and control programme is implemented at national level3. As of June 2025, the National Public Health Organisation (EODY) has been executing a related action with the help of NextGenerationEU funding4. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
How does it assess Greece's progress in achieving the agreed 2030 targets and what specific gaps did it identify?
Does it have any proof that Greece is implementing an updated national antimicrobial resistance plan with measurable indicators and sufficient resources?
How does it assess the results so far of EODY’s EU-funded action and what additional measures or technical support does it intend to propose?

E-10-2026-003791.t: Self-building primary residences on small islands in need of population growth
qt: to the Commission Nikolaos Anadiotis (NI) Subject:

The ‘My Home II’ housing programme funded by the Recovery and Resilience Facility provides for loans for the purchase of a primary residence but not for self-building a new home1. This poses a major problem for small Greek islands such as Megisti/Kastellorizo, Symi, Chalki, Tilos and Kasos where available eligible housing stock is limited. The mayors of these islands have asked for the possibility for funding to be given to beneficiaries who own land on which to build their primary residence2. Article 174 TFEU requires particular attention to be paid to island regions facing severe and permanent natural or demographic handicaps3. In addition, the EU strategy for islands calls on Member States to increase the supply of affordable housing with targeted measures for islands4. Commission Recommendation (EU) 2026/2069 provides for locally adapted measures, accelerated construction and the use of EU financial instruments in areas under housing stress5. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Does it consider that specific funding programmes for the construction of a primary residence on privately owned land on small islands are compatible with the current EU framework?
Does it intend to explicitly provide for such a possibility through the new European funding tools for affordable housing?
Will it encourage Greece to establish a special housing facility for small islands in need of population growth?

to the Commission Gilles Pennelle (PfE), Pierre Pimpie (PfE), Valérie Deloge (PfE), Séverine Werbrouck (PfE), Jorge Martín Frías (PfE), António Tânger Corrêa (PfE), Mireia Borrás Pabón (PfE) Subject:

Agricultural trade between the EU and Morocco is governed by the EU-Morocco Association Agreement, expanded in 2012 to further liberalise agricultural trade. During the 2024/2025 season, Morocco exported around 570 000 tonnes of tomatoes to the EU, representing 70 % of EU imports from third countries, up 8 % over a year. This competition is expected to intensify further: in Dakhla, a new plot of 5 200 hectares, irrigated by desalinated sea water, is set to be primarily used to grow vegetables, in particular tomatoes, mostly for export. This model raises serious environmental concerns, owing to the desalination process and transport to Europe in particular, as well as social concerns, because of the working conditions and differences in labour costs. For years, however, the worries of European producer organisations about this unfair competition have fallen on deaf ears in the Commission. When will the Commission finally react and take real measures to protect European producers from this competition, which is destroying their industries and jobs? Supporter1
This question is supported by a Member other than the authors: Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE).

E-10-2026-003788.t: Golden visas and the Oliville Halkidiki complex
qt: to the Commission Nikolaos Anadiotis (NI) Subject:

Oliville Halkidiki, a residential complex being built in the village of Yerakini in Chalkidiki, comprises 175 villas that are being marketed partly as an investment that qualifies for a golden visa1. A circular issued by the Ministry of Migration sets a minimum investment threshold of EUR 400 000 and stipulates that the investment must be limited to one property and, for built properties or properties with a building permit, the habitable floor area must be at least 120 sq m2. According to published data, there are instances of homes being split into two separate apartments with separate deeds, raising the question of whether every property used to obtain a residence permit fulfils all the legal requirements. The Commission has recognised that residence-by-investment schemes pose risks to security, money laundering and the Schengen area3. Directive (EU) 2024/1640 lays down a special risk management framework4. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

Does it intend to ask the Greek authorities for evidence that the golden visa permits granted under the Oliville Halkidiki project are issued exclusively for individual properties that meet national requirements?
Does it not think that systematically granting residence permits for split properties may affect the credibility of the control system and the Schengen area?
Will it address this issue in the context of the implementation of Directive (EU) 2024/1640 and the supervision of residence-by-investment schemes?

On 1 September 2026, the Greek Government announced the completion of the physical implementation of 123 milestones and targets that will be included in the final payment request, amounting to EUR 6.7 billion1. However, in May, Greece requested a further revision of the recovery and resilience plan (RRP), stating that part of it was no longer achievable. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
What differences in physical and financial scope – overall and broken down by measure – are there between Greece’s initial and final RRP?
Given the aforementioned reductions in scope, is it possible to present the initially approved RRP as complete?
It the Commission’s view, which of the 123 milestones were unfulfilled by 31 August 2026, and which corresponding funding reduction will be applied under Article 24 of Regulation (EU) 2021/2414?

E-10-2026-003786.t: Substantial assessment of e-EFKA’s digital transformation
qt: to the Commission Nikolaos Anadiotis (NI) Subject:

The digital transformation of Greece’s Electronic National Social Security Entity (e-EFKA), which was financed with significant resources from the Recovery and Resilience Facility, includes, among other things, the digitisation of insurance history and the development of a new integrated information system. The relevant milestone (134a) stipulates the delivery of the projects – confirmed with an acceptance report from the relevant monitoring committee – as a criterion for completion, with completion scheduled by the end of 20251. Regulation (EU) 2021/241 links disbursements to the satisfactory fulfilment of agreed milestones and targets2. However, key subsystems of the new integrated information system became operational in summer 20263,4, raising a legitimate question: is the formal delivery of an IT project sufficient to assess its successful implementation, or is it also necessary to examine its actual operational functioning and effectiveness? With this in mind, can the Commission say: 1.
Beyond the delivery report, what substantive and qualitative criteria will it use to assess the full implementation of milestone 134a?
Will it check whether the new system was actually put into operation and provided the intended services by the milestone’s scheduled completion date?
Does it assess, prior to disbursement, measurable outcomes such as a reduction in processing times, backlogs and service issues affecting insured persons?

E-10-2026-003785.t: Implementation of Article 32 of Regulation (EU) 2025/40 on packaging and packaging waste
qt: to the Commission Danuše Nerudová (PPE), Wouter Beke (PPE), Dolors Montserrat (PPE), Tomáš Zdechovský (PPE), Stefan Köhler (PPE), Ingeborg Ter Laak (PPE), Massimiliano Salini (PPE), Jan Farský (PPE) Subject:
Implementation of Article 32 of Regulation (EU) 2025/40 on packaging and packaging waste

Article 32 of Regulation (EU) 2025/40 provides that, from 12 February 2027, final distributors in the hotel, restaurant and catering (HORECA) sector offering take-away sales of hot and cold beverages and ready-to-eat meals must allow consumers to bring their own containers to be filled. The provision does not, however, specify how this obligation is to be applied in practice. In particular, it remains unclear under what circumstances a container may be refused on hygiene or safety grounds, where liability lies in the event that food served in a consumerprovided container subsequently gives rise to a food safety incident, whether the obligation to allow consumer-provided containers extends to delivery orders, and whether this obligation is limited to the HORECA sector notwithstanding the fact that certain other establishments also sell food for immediate consumption. In the absence of clarification, Member States and economic operators risk adopting divergent interpretations. In the ligh of the above: 1.

Does the Commission intend to issue guidance or an update Frequently Asked Questions document on the application of Article 32 prior to its date of application on 12 February 2027 and, if so, by when?
What measures does the Commission intend to take to ensure the uniform application of Article 32 across Member States, in view of the divergent national approaches that are emerging?

E-10-2026-003784.t: Who cut us off from gas – Russia or the EU?
qt: to the Commission Erik Kaliňák (NI) Subject:

In her State of the Union address, the Commission President stated: ‘When Russia cut us off from gas, we fought back.’ This claim is a political fiction. As recently as 2025, the EU imported 36 billion m³ of gas from Russia, representing approximately 12.5 % of its total imports. Subsequently, the EU itself adopted Regulation (EU) 2026/261, which legally banned the remaining imports of Russian pipeline gas and LNG in accordance with a set timetable. If, therefore, Russia has indeed ‘cut off the EU’s gas supply’, it is strange that the EU was still importing Russian gas as recently as 2025 and that it was the EU itself which adopted the legislation to bring these imports to an end. In light of the foregoing: 1.

Does the Commission consider it appropriate to mislead citizens by claiming that ‘Russia has cut us off from gas’, when the EU was still importing gas from Russia as late as 2025 and subsequently imposed a legal ban on the remaining imports itself?

If the consequences of its own energy decisions can simply be attributed to Russia, does the Commission take the view that the Green Deal, the ETS and the accelerated phaseout of fossil fuels in the EU were also ‘imposed by Russia’?
Is the Commission prepared to take political responsibility for the costs and consequences of its own decisions, or will it continue to shift the blame for its own failures onto external actors?

E-10-2026-003782.t: Safeguarding the EU’s fire-fighting capacity in the face of increasing climate-related forest and vegetation fires
qt: to the Commission Joachim Streit (Renew) Subject:
Safeguarding the EU’s fire-fighting capacity in the face of increasing climaterelated forest and vegetation fires

According to Eurostat, the number of professional firefighters in the EU fell by 18 200 to 372 400 in 2025 – the worst year for forest fires in the EU’s history to date. Member States subject to the EU’s excessive deficit procedure, such as Poland (-9 000) and France (-4 100), are particularly affected. On 16 July 2025, as part of its proposal for the Multiannual Financial Framework 2028–2034 (MFF), the Commission presented a new sectoral programme on the Union Civil Protection Mechanism (UCPM), aimed at implementing the European Preparedness Union Strategy and strengthening rescEU. 1.

How does the Commission assess the timing of national deficit procedures with regard to staff cuts in professional fire services, and does it plan to address this conflict of objectives between fiscal rules and climate adaptation in the ongoing MFF negotiations?

Will the new UCPM sector programme provide targeted funding to maintain the infrastructure of voluntary fire brigades in rural, structurally disadvantaged regions such as Rhineland-Palatinate, which bear a growing share of the operational burden?
Does the Commission plan to present an EU-wide legal framework or a recommendation on the protection and recognition of the status of volunteer firefighters?

E-10-2026-003781.t: Russian propaganda operatives residing and operating in the EU
qt: to the Commission Tomáš Zdechovský (PPE) Subject:

According to recent media reports1, the Czech authorities detained and subsequently expelled two Russian nationals linked to Russian propaganda structures. One of them, Vitaliy Chashchukhin, reportedly resides legally in Germany and works for Russian media outlets, including Izvestia and REN TV, whose broadcasting activities in the EU are subject to EU restrictive measures. Despite being expelled from Czechia, he was reportedly able to return to Germany, from where he has been operating and travelling within the Schengen area. 1.
Is the Commission aware that individuals working for Russian media outlets subject to EU restrictive measures are legally residing in and operating from Member States, including Germany?
How does the Commission assess the enforcement of EU sanctions in cases where individuals provide services to sanctioned Russian media while residing in the EU?

Does the Commission consider the current coordination and information exchange between the Member States sufficient to prevent the EU and the Schengen area from being used as a base for Russian propaganda operations?

E-10-2026-003768.t: Systematic destruction of books by AI companies
qt: to the Commission Tiemo Wölken (S&D), Jens Geier (S&D), Per Clausen (The Left), Pernando Barrena Arza (The Left), Marta Temido (S&D), Birgit Sippel (S&D), Lena Schilling (Verts/ALE), Erik Marquardt (Verts/ALE), Thomas Bajada (S&D), Chloé Ridel (S&D), Elisabeth Grossmann (S&D), René Repasi (S&D), Krzysztof Śmiszek (S&D), Tomislav Sokol (PPE), Pierre Jouvet (S&D), Alexandra Geese (Verts/ALE), Jean-Marc Germain (S&D), Thomas Pellerin-Carlin (S&D), Joanna Scheuring-Wielgus (S&D), Kristian Vigenin (S&D), Dimitris Tsiodras (PPE), Marc Angel (S&D), Veronika Cifrová Ostrihoňová (Renew), Maria Noichl (S&D), Matjaž Nemec (S&D), Robert Biedroń (S&D), Radan Kanev (PPE), Laurence Farreng (Renew), Vlad Vasile-Voiculescu (Renew), Matthias Ecke (S&D), Emma Rafowicz (S&D) Subject:

Recent news reports suggest that major AI companies are buying, scanning and then destroying large quantities of antique and modern books to train their AI systems, thus destroying cultural heritage to train their AI models. An internal paper from Anthropic even explicitly states the objective of ‘destructively scanning all the books in the world’. The main purpose of this ‘destructive scanning’ of books appears to be to circumvent copyright issues, as it may be covered by the fair use provisions of US copyright law. However, there are also reports that EU booksellers have been approached to supply books for this purpose, with the books being shipped and destroyed overseas. Can the Commission: 1.

Outline which measures it is considering to prevent the potential circumvention of EU copyright law and the destruction of EU cultural heritage through the international shipping of books from the EU to non-EU countries for the purpose of ‘destructive scanning’?
Confirm whether it will address this issue in its forthcoming initiative on AI and copyright?

E-10-2026-003764.t: Baltic Sea fishing quotas for 2027 – a threat to Polish fishermen
qt: to the Council Piotr Müller (ECR) Subject:

On 26‑27 October 2026, the Council will decide on the Baltic Sea fishing quotas for 2027. The Commission’s proposal provides for drastic cuts to cod by-catches (by 88 % and 51 %) and an increase in sprat limits (by 44 %), which is causing serious concern within the sector. In light of the foregoing: 1.

How does the Council intend to modify the proposed reductions of 88 % and 51 % in cod by‑catches so that the EU-wide limits set out in the regulation do not lead to the complete shutdown of mixed fisheries?
How does the Council intend to take into account the negative socio-economic impacts on small-scale fleets and coastal communities when setting the final catch limits?

How does the Council assess the compatibility of the proposed 44 % increase in sprat catch limits with the obligation to apply an ecosystem-based approach and the overarching objective of rebuilding cod stocks?

E-10-2026-003763.t: New customs duty on parcels from outside the EU – protecting European businesses from unfair competition
qt: to the Commission Piotr Müller (ECR) Subject:

From 1 July 2026, a temporary flat-rate customs duty of EUR 3 will apply, levied on each product category in parcels from outside the EU with a value of up to EUR 150. This measure is intended to protect European businesses from unfair competition from non-EU e-commerce platforms. However, its effectiveness depends on the strict and uniform enforcement of the rules across all Member States. In light of the foregoing: 1.

What preliminary data does the Commission currently have regarding the number and value of parcels subject to the new customs duty since 1 July 2026, and when does it intend to publish this data, broken down by individual Member States, including Poland?

What measures is the Commission taking, in cooperation with the customs authorities of the Member States, to detect attempts to circumvent the duty, in particular through the artificial splitting of orders with an actual value exceeding EUR 150, undervaluation or incorrect tariff classification of goods?

Has the Commission identified any differences in the operational readiness of Member States’ customs systems to handle the new customs duty, and what measures is it taking to ensure its uniform enforcement across the Union?

E-10-2026-003755.t: A moratorium on EU enlargement to the Western Balkans for 10 years
qt: to the Commission Charlie Weimers (ECR), Beatrice Timgren (ECR), Dick Erixon (ECR) Subject:

The EU is facing hybrid threats, migration pressures, organised crime and persistent rule-oflaw challenges. Several candidate countries in the Western Balkans are themselves affected by foreign interference. The Commission has acknowledged that a larger EU could require additional resources, complicate decision-making and produce unintended consequences1. Against this background: 1.
Does the Commission consider that further accession negotiations with candidate countries in the Western Balkans should be suspended for at least 10 years?

If not, what objective evidence supports the Commission’s assessment that the EU currently has the institutional, financial and security capacity to admit additional Member States without weakening its internal stability, border management or ability to take decisions?

Under what security-related circumstances would the Commission recommend the suspension or reversal of accession negotiations, particularly where a candidate country does not exercise effective control over its territory or borders or is particularly vulnerable to foreign interference and organised crime?
Commission communication of 20 March 2024 on pre-enlargement reforms and policy reviews (COM(2024)0146). 1

E-10-2026-003754.t: The migration, border and security implications of enlargement
qt: to the Commission Charlie Weimers (ECR), Beatrice Timgren (ECR), Dick Erixon (ECR) Subject:

The Commission has acknowledged that enlargement would create new external borders and new challenges for their protection and control. The Commission stresses the need for candidate countries to strengthen their border-management capacity and migration and asylum systems and improve their alignment with EU visa policy1. Against this background: 1.
How does the Commission assess the potential effects of possible future EU membership for the Western Balkan candidates on the EU’s external borders, migration pressures and internal security?

What mechanisms or transitional arrangements is the Commission considering regarding the free movement of persons and the implementation of the EU asylum acquis in connection with enlargement to the Western Balkans?

Has the Commission estimated the additional budgetary resources that would be required by Frontex, Europol and the EU Agency for Asylum as a result of enlargement to the Western Balkans, and will it publish country-specific risk and impact assessments?
Commission communication of 20 March 2024 on pre-enlargement reforms and policy reviews (COM(2024)0146). 1
to the Commission Charlie Weimers (ECR), Dick Erixon (ECR), Beatrice Timgren (ECR) Subject:

On 14 July 2026, the EU held accession conferences with Montenegro and Albania. For Montenegro, the parties provisionally closed negotiations on competition and customs union, meaning that, in total, 18 out of 33 negotiating chapters have been provisionally closed. As regards Albania, the parties provisionally closed negotiating chapters on science and research, education and culture, and external relations. Albania has now opened all negotiating chapters and provisionally closed three of them1. Against this background: 1.

Given the varying degrees of reform progress between the two countries, how does the Commission ensure that the opening of thematic clusters and the provisional closure of chapters are based exclusively on merit and full compliance with the Copenhagen criteria, particularly regarding the rule of law and the fight against corruption and organised crime?
Does the Commission consider that the current accelerated pace of negotiation risks lowering accession standards?
Will the Commission commit to recommending the reopening of closed chapters if it is shown that the candidate countries have not achieved adequate progress in their respective accession chapters?
