E-10-2026-003752.t: Reuse obligations and effective recycling systems under the Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation
qt: to the Commission Elsi Katainen (Renew) Subject:

The aim of the Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (PPWR) is to promote the reuse of packaging, reduce packaging waste and promote a circular economy. However, those objectives need to take into account the different waste management systems in place in the Member States, as well as the environmental and economic impact of existing return and recycling systems. Finland’s deposit and return system works very efficiently and packaging recycling rates are high. Finland has also mostly switched from washable glass bottles to lighter aluminium and PET packaging, which is less energy-intensive when it comes to transport and recycling. Life‑cycle assessments of packaging show that reusable packaging is therefore not automatically a better option for the environment. The reuse obligations set out in the PPWR may result in significant new investment and logistics costs for businesses, and SMEs in particular, for example in the form of wash lines and heavier packaging. Existing and effective return and recycling systems should be taken into account. Under Article 29(18) of the PPWR, exemptions can be assessed in situations where existing arrangements are more environmentally and economically efficient. With the above in mind: 1.
How will the Commission ensure that the reuse obligations under the PPWR take into account effective deposit and return systems in place and high recycling rates in the Member States?

On the basis of what scientific, environmental and economic criteria does the Commission assess the exemptions under Article 29(18) so that more efficient recycling solutions are not replaced by more cumbersome and more energy-intensive reuse arrangements?

E-10-2026-003750.t: Combating serophobia and the European regulatory framework against HIV-related discrimination
qt: to the Commission Anthony Smith (The Left) Subject:
Combating serophobia and the European regulatory framework against HIVrelated discrimination

On 24 August 2026, Christophe Paco, who is HIV-positive and had been harassed by his neighbours for more than a year, began a hunger strike in Reims to call for a law recognising serophobia as his complaints had been dismissed. Joined by influencer Nicolas Aragona, who received online death threats, he took his action as far as Paris. After nine days on hunger strike, the pair were received by Deputy Minister Aurore Bergé, who pledged to strengthen the fight against discrimination. While discrimination based on health status is already prohibited, serophobia is not specifically identified or penalised anywhere. According to the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control, one in eight people living with HIV is denied access to care in the EU due to stigma. More than 50% of the population say they hold discriminatory attitudes towards people living with HIV, and 20% of people living with HIV have experienced verbal harassment because of their HIV status. In light of the above: 1.

Does the Commission intend to require Member States to explicitly recognise serophobia in their anti-discrimination legislation and to incorporate the fight against serophobia – through funding under the EU4Health programme – into its strategy on sexual and reproductive health?
Does it intend to relaunch the Equal Treatment Directive that has been blocked in the Council since 2008?
What measures does it plan to take to improve training for healthcare professionals on non-transmission of HIV, given that 39% are still unaware of this?

E-10-2026-003749.t: Recognition in Member States of driving licences issued in the United Kingdom before the end of the transition period (Brexit)
qt: to the Commission Kosma Złotowski (ECR) Subject:

I have been receiving reports from Polish citizens regarding cases of potential breaches of the principle of mutual recognition of driving licences obtained in the United Kingdom while it was a Member State of the European Union. This concerns situations in which EU citizens obtained driving licences of specific categories there in accordance with the applicable rules and procedures while the UK was an EU Member State. Directive 2006/126/EC introduced the principle of mutual recognition of driving licences issued by Member States. However, following the United Kingdom’s withdrawal from the EU and the end of the transition period, problems are arising with the recognition of such driving licences by the authorities of Member States, even though these licences were granted while the United Kingdom was a Member State of the EU and in accordance with the laws in force in the United Kingdom at the time of their issue. In this connection: 1.

How does the Commission interpret the obligations of Member States regarding the recognition of driving licences issued by the United Kingdom during its membership of the EU when the holders apply for their recognition or exchange after the end of the transition period?
Can a refusal to recognise driving licence categories granted in accordance with UK law in force at the time of issue be consistent with EU law?
Is the Commission monitoring Member States’ practices in this regard, and, if the problem is widespread, does it plan to take action to ensure a uniform approach to such cases?

E-10-2026-003746.t: Security rights of pledgees and mortgagees in EU Inc. insolvency proceedings
qt: to the Commission Ton Diepeveen (PfE) Subject:

The Commission’s proposal for the EU Inc. appears to take insufficient account of the position of pledgees and mortgagees in the event of insolvency. Under the proposal, they would be unable to lodge a separate claim against the insolvent EU Inc., and their rights as preferential creditors would not be safeguarded, or would be inadequately safeguarded. This could undermine legal certainty for lenders and make it more difficult for EU Inc. companies to access finance. 1.
Can the Commission confirm exactly what rights pledgees and mortgagees have under the proposed insolvency proceedings, and how their existing security rights would be protected?

How does the Commission ensure that the proposed regime does not lead to a situation in which banks and other lenders regard EU Inc. companies as posing a greater risk than companies incorporated as national legal forms, particularly in Member States where pledgees and mortgagees enjoy specific preferential rights?

Is the Commission prepared to amend the proposed insolvency rules to ensure that pledgees and mortgagees can fully exercise their security rights and that EU Inc. companies do not suffer a competitive disadvantage vis-à-vis national company forms?

E-10-2026-003745.t: Directors’ liability and the EU Inc. governance model
qt: to the Commission Ton Diepeveen (PfE) Subject:

The Commission’s proposal for the EU Inc. appears to depart from the stakeholder-driven corporate model (Rhineland model) that exists in several Member States and to align more closely with a US-style shareholder-driven model. For instance, directors no longer appear to be required to assess decisions of the shareholders’ general meeting which go against the interests of the company before implementing them. This may be relevant, for example, where shareholders decide to distribute funds whilst the company’s financial position does not permit this. Accordingly, a discrepancy could result between the legal standards against which directors of an EU Inc. and directors of national companies are assessed. This could reduce legal certainty and the predictability of directors’ liability, particularly for individuals who are simultaneously directors of an EU Inc. and of a company governed by national law. 1.
Why is the Commission moving away from the stakeholder-driven governance model and opting for the shareholder-driven governance model?
What standard should national courts apply when assessing the lawfulness and any liability of directors of an EU Inc., and how does this relate to the various national governance models?
How will the Commission ensure legal certainty for individuals who hold directorships in both an EU Inc. and in companies governed by national law?

E-10-2026-003744.t: Exclusion of legal persons as directors of an EU Inc.
qt: to the Commission Ton Diepeveen (PfE) Subject:

Under the Commission’s proposal, only natural persons may be appointed as directors of an EU Inc. In several Member States, however, it is possible for legal persons to act as directors of a company. By excluding this possibility for the EU Inc., legal persons who, under national law, are directors of a company incorporated under national law are excluded from holding a comparable directorship in an EU Inc. This raises questions about the compatibility of this restriction with the aim of establishing the EU Inc. as an attractive and legally neutral alternative to national company forms. 1.
Why has the Commission chosen to categorically exclude legal persons from acting as directors of an EU Inc., even though this is permitted in several Member States?
How does the Commission assess the risk that this restriction will lead to unequal treatment of companies or legal persons which, under national law, are permitted to act as directors?

Is the Commission prepared to amend the proposed rules so that legal persons may also be appointed as directors of an EU Inc., provided that appropriate rules on representation, responsibility and liability are put in place?

E-10-2026-003736.t: We have ended our dependence. Are we competitive yet?
qt: to the Commission Erik Kaliňák (NI), Katarína Roth Neveďalová (NI) Subject:

The EU presents the reduction in dependence on Russian gas as a means of strengthening energy security. According to the Commission, the share of Russian gas in EU imports has fallen from 45 % in 2021 to 12 % in 2025, with LNG already accounting for 45 % of gas imports into the EU1. However, this has also created a strong price dependency on the global LNG market. The Commission itself notes that the switch to LNG has increased Europe’s exposure to global price shocks2. On 15 September 2026, the European TTF was trading at around 82 EUR/MWh, whilst the US Henry Hub was trading at 2.97 USD/MMBtu (approximately 8.6 EUR/MWh)3. Although the Henry Hub is the US wholesale benchmark and LNG imports into Europe involve additional costs, the price difference remains significant. 1.

Does the Commission consider a situation where the wholesale price of gas in the EU is several times higher than in the US to be compatible with the objective of ensuring affordable energy and the competitiveness of European industry?
What specific measures does the Commission plan to take to significantly reduce the price difference between the EU and its main competitors?
What level of difference between gas prices in the EU and the US does the Commission consider to be sustainable in the long term without further damaging the EU’s competitiveness?

E-10-2026-003735.t: Extended producer responsibility obligations and cross-border sales by micro-enterprises
qt: to the Commission Anna Bryłka (PfE) Subject:
Extended producer responsibility obligations and cross-border sales by microenterprises

The Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (PPWR) aims, among other things, to create business opportunities for small businesses and innovators. However, micro-enterprises selling very small quantities to consumers in other Member States may face separate extended producer responsibility (EPR) registration, reporting and fixed compliance costs in each destination country, often before making their first sale. Such costs may be disproportionate to the scale of sales and discourage the smallest businesses from testing demand and benefiting from the EU internal market. In the light of this: 1.

Does the Commission consider that the EPR costs and administrative obligations imposed on micro-enterprises making very small-scale cross-border sales are proportionate and compatible with the effective functioning of the EU internal market?
Does the Commission plan to introduce EU-level de minimis thresholds or other simplifications for micro-enterprises handling very small volumes of packaging?

Could the Commission establish a centralised EU-level registration and reporting system, such as an EPR one-stop shop, to reduce fixed compliance costs and the need for separate procedures in each Member State?

E-10-2026-003734.t: Consideration of small and medium-sized enterprises in the evaluation of the tobacco control framework
qt: to the Commission Alexandr Vondra (ECR) Subject:

The Commissioner for Health previously promised that the effects on small and mediumsized enterprises (SMEs) would be taken into account when assessing the evaluation criteria for the Tobacco Products Directive12. However, the published evaluation report only refers to SMEs once and does not include a dedicated SME test, despite a four-year evaluation process3. The Commission further indicated that simplification for economic operators in the tobacco sector was not considered, as this could conflict with public health objectives. While public health protection is a priority, the ‘better regulation’ principles require balanced consideration of regulatory impacts, including those on SMEs, to ensure that actions are targeted, achieve their objectives and do not add unnecessary costs. In this context, could the Commission clarify the following: 1.
Why were the effects on SMEs not duly taken into account when assessing the evaluation criteria?
Does the omission of an SME test indicate that the Commission is disregarding or discriminating against the interests of EU SMEs operating in the tobacco sector?
How does the Commission intend to ensure that ‘better regulation’ tools 21, 23, 58 and 59 will be adequately reflected in any future legislative revisions or proposals in this area?

Directive 2014/40/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 3 April 2014 on the approximation of the laws, regulations and administrative provisions of the Member States concerning the manufacture, presentation and sale of tobacco and related products and repealing Directive 2001/37/EC (OJ L 127, 29.4.2014, p. 1, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2014/40/oj). 2 2 October 2023, https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/P-9-2023-002459-ASW_EN.html. 3 Commission staff working document of 3 April 2026 entitled ‘Evaluation of the Tobacco Products Directive (2014/40/EU), the Tobacco Advertising Directive (2003/33/EC) and other related tobacco control policies across the EU’ (SWD(2026)0112). 1

E-10-2026-003733.t: Representation of women at the 23 June 2026 meeting with the Taliban
qt: to the Commission Cynthia Ní Mhurchú (Renew) Subject:
Representation of women at the 23 June 2026 meeting with the Taliban

On 23 June 2026, representatives of the Commission and 15 EU Member States participated in a meeting with representatives of the Taliban. In the light of the EU’s stated commitment to women’s participation and representation in its external relations: 1.
Can the Commission confirm which of its officials and which 15 EU Member States were represented at the meeting, and provide the names and institutional roles of the participants?
How many women were among the Commission and Member State representatives present, and does the Commission maintain an official record of the gender composition of participants at such meetings?

If no women were present among the European participants, can the Commission explain why, and can it also explain what measures it takes to ensure appropriate representation of women in high-level meetings with the Taliban?
to the Commission Dick Erixon (ECR) Subject:

Rising interest costs risk making the EU an even greater burden on Member States and their citizens. The European Court of Auditors warns that outstanding EU borrowing could exceed EUR 900 billion by 20271. It also points out that interest on the NextGenerationEU recovery debt could cost around double the EUR 14.9 billion set aside for 2021-2027, and that interest rates rose significantly after the borrowing began. In early September 2026, government bond yields in Germany and France reached 15-year highs2. 1.
What is the Commission’s latest estimate of total NextGenerationEU interest costs, and how much higher is it than originally planned?
Does the Commission plan to cut other EU spending to cover these costs, so that neither taxes nor Member States’ contributions have to rise?

European Court of Auditors, ‘2024 EU audit in brief – Introducing the 2004 annual reports of the European Court of Auditors’, October 2025. 2 Euronews, ‘European government bond yields surge to 15-year highs as sell-off deepens’, 1 September 2026, https://www.euronews.com/business/2026/09/01/european-government-bond-yields-surge-to-15-yearhighs-as-sell-off-deepens. 1

E-10-2026-003729.t: Horizon Europe, or when science ends and a political project begins
qt: to the Commission Erik Kaliňák (NI) Subject:

The EU is funding projects under the Horizon Europe programme focusing on conducting research into far-right, identity-based and nationalist movements. For example, the YOUDARE project has received nearly EUR 3 million and, according to the CORDIS database, is not intended to be limited to research alone. It also envisages political recommendations and local pilot initiatives aimed at reducing the appeal of far-right views on gender among young people. This approach raises many questions. In light of the above: 1.

What criteria does the Commission use to distinguish legitimate scientific research into political extremism from activities aimed at influencing citizens’ political attitudes funded by the EU budget?

How does the Commission ensure that such projects do not lead to lawful views on gender, migration, the family or national sovereignty – which form part of democratic political discourse – being labelled as extremist or anti-democratic?

In the Commission’s view, is it compatible with the political neutrality of EU funding for the Horizon Europe programme to finance interventions whose stated aim is to reduce the appeal of a specific ideological or political current?

E-10-2026-003728.t: Checks on EU funds in contracts awarded by Pedro Sánchez’s government
qt: to the Commission Jorge Buxadé Villalba (PfE) Subject:

The Spanish Civil Guard’s Central Operational Unit (UCO) has obtained a file from public company ADIF on a contract awarded to Levantina Ingeniería y Construcción SL (B97016125) as part of corruption investigations into the Sánchez Government (Koldo case). The file contains suspected payments linked to contracts awarded by the Directorate-General for Roads1. Between 2021 and 2023, the company was awarded at least three contracts by the government worth EUR 4.4 million for works funded by the ERDF or under NextGenerationEU2. Given that former senior government officials are in prison for bribery, embezzlement and influence peddling in relation to public contracts: 1.
Will the Commission investigate whether alleged corrupt practices linked to former senior officials in the Sánchez government also involved EU-funded contracts, such as the Levantina contracts?
Will it require Spain to repay the EU funds disbursed for each contract, including the company’s share in joint ventures if wrongdoing is detected?
Following all the cases of corruption surrounding Pedro Sánchez, has the Commission launched specific audits to ensure that EU funds allocated by the Spanish Government have not been misappropriated?

https://www.larazon.es/espana/uco-irrumpe-adif-recabar-datos-obrasospecha_202609156aa96879d8ec24478baa591c.html. 2 AI-81, Avilés: file 254213362600 (https://www.boe.es/boe/dias/2022/05/24/pdfs/BOE-B-202216405.pdf?utm_source); A-42, Getafe: file 254222814750 (https://www.boe.es/diario_boe/txt.php?id=BOE-B2023-12687&utm_source); Shed 5, port of Melilla: file A-2021-00020 (https://transparencia.gob.es/serviciosbuscador/contenido/contratolicitacion.htm?fcAct=Fri+Feb+14+04%3A33%3A45+CET+2025&id=Licitacion_2f 11582f3c2f1bb20f9a95f4a3611e6cb730538a&lang=es&utm_source); walkway at San Ignacio pier, port of Santa María: 31/2022 (https://contrataciondelestado.es/wps/portal/plataforma/buscadores/detalle/!ut/p/z1/hY9LD4IwEIR_kelSYJEjj1K KICAPpRdCYmJIeBhjP0Ww1XZ22S_mZ0lktyInLqlf3Tvfp66QelGYmuw1POCkMKx0H2gsV9VGK6Skppc9xCp1vBjHFB-UVM3TPqqM6wEBxAhIEfV5oJnOIG_MloVAerdWqWO8LWIXUvqkOUJWXGqQaApJrm16jKdas_s6WgTQ2tVE3EM3NzjkIzeVgaKezD5hZLGJ5uV7YsT_HwBaHZmyT0vkAo6liwQ!!/dz/d5/L2dBISEvZ 0FBIS9nQSEh/). 1

E-10-2026-003727.t: Protecting workers from asbestos at Kilkis General Hospital
qt: to the Commission Maria Zacharia (NI) Subject:

Complaints have been lodged about the presence of materials containing asbestos in seven points of Kilkis General Hospital, including in parts of the medical emergency service where healthcare and other staff work on a daily basis. The competent Greek authorities have been contacted by the workers’ union. In an official reply to a complaint lodged by the union, the competent department of the Region of Central Macedonia stated that there is no obligation to remove materials containing asbestos if they are intact and that they only pose a health risk when they are worn or disturbed. However, there was no mention of any previous on-site check or evidence-based assessment of the current state of the materials and the risk of workers being exposed to asbestos fibres. Directive 2009/148/EC, as amended by Directive (EU) 2023/2668, lays down stringent requirements for the protection of workers from asbestos. In view of this, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Is the above practice of the Greek authorities in line with the risk prevention and assessment obligations under EU law?
Does it intend to ask the Greek authorities for information on the implementation of the relevant provisions and the measures to protect workers at the hospital in question?

What measures can the Commission take, including making use of available EU funding instruments, to ensure the safe and permanent removal of materials containing asbestos from Kilkis Hospital and from public health infrastructure in general?

E-10-2026-003726.t: Illegal use of driftnets by Moroccan vessels in the Alboran Sea and EU waters
qt: to the Commission Carmen Crespo Díaz (PPE) Subject:

The Alboran Sea is a particularly important area for Mediterranean fisheries and a key corridor for highly migratory species between the Mediterranean and the Atlantic. Moroccan vessels’ continued use of driftnets – despite a ban under the applicable legislation – has been documented. The risk of by-catch when fishing with driftnets is high. What is more, products caught using banned gear could end up on the EU market. In view of the above: 1.
Is the Commission aware of Moroccan vessels’ use of driftnets in the Alboran Sea, particularly the cases documented in waters under Spanish jurisdiction?
Is the Commission assessing, within the framework of the IUU Regulation, the extent of Morocco’s compliance and cooperation and is there cause to initiate a yellow-card procedure?

With a view to preventing products obtained by illegal fishing from entering the European market, is the Commission considering, in cooperation with Spain and through the European Fisheries Control Agency, bolstering fisheries control, inspection and surveillance in the Alboran Sea, and stepping up controls on imports from those fisheries?

E-10-2026-003725.t: Standardisation of battery interfaces for power tools and garden equipment
qt: to the Commission Kateřina Konečná (NI) Subject:

Battery-powered hand tools and garden equipment are sold in the EU in dozens of mutually incompatible formats. Fully functioning battery packs containing critical raw materials end up as waste simply because the user switches to a machine from a different brand. This incompatibility also generates costs associated with changing suppliers, which puts smaller European manufacturers at a disadvantage. Recital 37 of Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 classifies batteries for gardening and cordless power tools as portable batteries incorporated into appliances, and delegates the setting of specific requirements to implementing acts on ecodesign. The Ecodesign Working Plan 2025-2030 does not include either of these product groups. 1.

The Commission was required to assess, by 1 January 2025, the introduction of harmonised standards for a common charger for rechargeable batteries incorporated into certain categories of appliances under Directive 2012/19/EU. Has this assessment already been completed and published, and does the Commission consider removable battery packs for power tools and garden equipment to come under this definition?

Why were these product groups not included among the priorities of the Ecodesign Working Plan 2025-2030, and on what data regarding the market share of interoperable products within the Union does the Commission base its view that voluntary industry initiatives are sufficient?

Is the Commission considering, pursuant to Article 10 of Regulation (EU) 1025/2012, calling on CEN and CENELEC to draw up a European standard for the interfaces of removable battery packs for these machines?

E-10-2026-003724.t: Eligibility of bioenergy technologies for the Innovation Fund 2026 (IF26) heat auction
qt: to the Commission Katri Kulmuni (Renew) Subject:

On 22 May 2026, the Commission’s Directorate-General for Climate Action published the draft terms and conditions for the upcoming IF26 heat auction. The draft terms and conditions exclude biomass use for heat production from the technologies that are eligible for auction. Different types of bioenergy options, such as solid biomass fuels, biogas and biomethane, are considered renewable energy sources under the Renewable Energy Directive (RED). Their use in industrial heat applications can provide cost-effective decarbonisation solutions, particularly where electrification or other renewable energy technologies are not technically possible or economically competitive. Meanwhile, around 75 % of the heat used for industrial processes still comes from fossil fuels, highlighting the scale of the decarbonisation efforts required. 1.
What is the Commission’s justification for excluding viable technologies such as bioenergy from the auction and disregarding the principle of technology neutrality?
Why does the Commission not consider making bioenergy technologies eligible for the IF26 heat auction, provided that the sustainability requirements of the RED are met?

How does the Commission justify excluding a cost-competitive suite of solutions that could, in certain cases, deliver CO2 savings at a lower cost (EUR/t) than other options in a public auction scheme?
to the Commission Gilles Pennelle (PfE), André Rougé (PfE) Subject:

The seed sector is of vital importance to the European Union’s food sovereignty and food security. France is Europe’s foremost producer (and the world’s second-largest exporter) of seeds of all kinds, including those used for arable and fodder crops. However, Ukrainian exports are increasingly undermining this sector’s competitiveness. The years 2017-2021 and 2022-2025 saw Ukraine’s seed exports increase their share of the EU market and the country’s total maize seed exports grow by 450 %, while French maize seed sales on the Ukrainian market fell by 40 % during the same period. Given the above, maintaining the EU’s seed production capacity becomes a food sovereignty and food security issue. 1.
Could the Commission share its assessment of Ukrainian seed production and export trends and their impact on the European and French seed sectors?
Will the Commission introduce measures to protect the internal market and ensure that the European seed sector can continue to compete with Ukrainian and, more generally, international stakeholders?
Supporter1
This question is supported by a Member other than the authors: Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE).

E-10-2026-003722.t: Climate insurance and adaptation financing alliance
qt: to the Commission César Luena (S&D) Subject:

In her State of the Union address of 16 September, President von der Leyen announced the creation of a climate insurance alliance to address the growing gap between climate risks and insurance coverage. Currently, only around 25 % of climate-related economic losses in the EU are covered by insurance. The Commission has announced this initiative – which will bring together insurers, investors, public authorities and other actors – at a time when it is working on a new European climate resilience framework. 1.

How will the new climate insurance alliance be integrated into the upcoming European climate resilience framework and what concrete tools does the Commission envisage to reduce the climate risk protection gap?

What will the Commission do to ensure that growing climate risks do not leave the citizens, businesses and territories most exposed to these threats in a position where they have no coverage options or cannot afford insurance?

Does the Commission hold that improving insurance cover should go hand-in-hand with new European instruments and own resources (an example being a tax on oil and gas company profits) that are specifically designed to finance investments in climate adaptation and risk reduction?

E-10-2026-003721.t: Member State delays in submitting national restoration plans
qt: to the Commission César Luena (S&D) Subject:

Though the Nature Restoration Regulation set 1 September 2026 as the deadline for Member States to submit their draft national restoration plans (NRPs), only eight countries have done so to date. Upon receiving an NRP, the Commission has six months to provide an assessment and feedback, after which the Member State in question has another six months to submit its final plan. In view of the above: 1.
When does the Commission expect to receive the remaining 19 draft NRPs, and what information has it received from the Member States in question?
What action is the Commission taking with regard to the Member States that have failed to meet this deadline?
How will the Commission ensure that these delays do not adversely affect the Regulation’s implementation timeline or compromise its targets for 2030?

E-10-2026-003720.t: New EU water initiative and Water Framework Directive
qt: to the Commission César Luena (S&D) Subject:

In her September 2026 State of the Union address, President von der Leyen announced a new EU water initiative, noting growing water scarcity and water’s importance for agriculture, energy, industry and food security. The announcement comes a year after the European water resilience strategy was adopted. The strategy sets out over 50 actions to improve water management and places implementation of the Water Framework Directive among its top priorities. What is more, the Commission had already announced its intention to revise the Water Framework Directive, despite the findings of its previous fitness check. 1.
What will be the goal, scope and added value of this initiative in comparison with the 2025 water resilience strategy and existing EU water legislation?
How will the initiative relate to the announced revision of the Water Framework Directive?

If the Commission sees a need for a new EU initiative to tackle water scarcity, how has it determined that the problem lies in the current water legislation framework rather than implementation, investment and enforcement gaps?

E-10-2026-003719.t: Revision of the Water Framework Directive and complaint to the European Ombudsman
qt: to the Commission César Luena (S&D) Subject:

On 8 September 2026, five organisations lodged a complaint with the European Ombudsman questioning the procedure the Commission followed to revise the Water Framework Directive. They point out that the decision to revise the directive was announced in December 2025, under RESourceEU, in order to, among other things, improve access to critical raw materials. The announcement came before a targeted evaluation or public consultation were carried out. They also recall that the 2019 fitness check concluded that the directive was fit for purpose. 1.

What specific evidence and analysis formed the basis for the announcement that the directive would be revised? What evidence does the Commission have that the directive’s provisions are hampering the development of critical raw material projects?
What are the Commission’s reasons for taking the political decision to revise the directive before completing an evaluation or consulting stakeholders?
Can the Commission guarantee that any future proposal will fully maintain the current objectives and levels of water protection set by the directive?

E-10-2026-003718.t: Ideological profiles of journalists, press freedom and democratic quality in Mexico
qt: to the Commission Dolors Montserrat (PPE) Subject:

The Mexican Government has compiled reports on the digital ‘ecosystem’, publicly naming journalists and media outlets that are critical towards government policies. This is at a time when there are concerns about press freedom and pluralism and in a country that ranks among the most dangerous for journalists. This is similar to the dossier put together by the Spanish Ministry of the Interior on journalists and their political ideologies. The compilation of the reports coincides with reforms to the Mexican electoral system and other state institutions, which call into question the independence of electoral bodies, the separation of powers and the quality of Mexican democracy. 1.

Is the Commission aware that the Mexican authorities have put together reports on journalists, including information on their political opinions, which constitutes a breach of the rule of law and the European Media Freedom Act and coincides with the negotiation of the modernised Global Agreement between the European Union and Mexico?
How does the Commission assess the evolution of the rule of law in Mexico, especially in light of the contested reforms that are being passed?
In this regard, what steps is the Commission willing to take within the framework of these bilateral relations?

E-10-2026-003717.t: The Aznalcóllar mining project and protecting the Doñana National Park in accordance with EU law
qt: to the Commission César Luena (S&D), Lina Gálvez (S&D) Subject:

UNESCO has sent out another warning about the state of conservation of the Doñana National Park and, in particular, about the potential impact of the new Aznalcóllar mining project (Mina Los Frailes). The World Heritage Committee has once again voiced its concerns about the lack of sufficient information to assess the potential effects of the project and has requested a specific assessment of its potential impact, including the effects of mining waste discharge on water quality. The project, whose environmental assessment is the responsibility of the regional government of Andalucía, involves actions that may affect water bodies and discharge into the Guadalquivir River, in an area of exceptional ecological value protected by EU legislation. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Has it assessed the project’s compatibility with the obligations under the Water Framework Directive, the Habitats Directive and the Birds Directive?

Does it consider that the environmental assessment conducted sufficiently guarantees that the discharges and other actions associated with the project will not damage the water bodies of the Doñana National Park or affect its protected ecosystems?

In light of the warnings issued by UNESCO, will the Commission ask the regional government of Andalusia for information on the environmental assessment and the measures taken to ensure full compliance with EU environmental law?
to the Commission Hanna Gedin (The Left) Subject:

The new EU rules on packaging responsibility (PPWR and EPR) came into force on 12 August. They have raised widespread concerns among microenterprises, who fear that they will render their activities unprofitable. The new rules, which set the same thresholds and impose the same administrative and fee requirements on individual artists as they do on e‑commerce giants such as Amazon, may end up driving microenterprises and sole traders out of business. We are essentially in favour of the Packaging Regulation imposing tighter requirements on businesses and setting ambitious environmental targets, but we are concerned that the fact that the legislation is not proportional will hit small-scale operators – who are already using sustainable alternatives to mass production – the hardest, and could stifle unique, local creativity. 1.
Does the Commission think it would be appropriate to introduce an exemption for microenterprises with regard to administration and fees?
How does the Commission intend to strengthen the conditions and opportunities for micro- and small-business owners operating in the EU?

E-10-2026-003714.t: Persecution and violence against LGBTI+ persons in Türkiye
qt: to the Commission Isabel Serra Sánchez (The Left), Irene Montero (The Left) Subject:

On 13 September 2026, the Turkish authorities launched a coordinated police crackdown on LGBTI+ organisations, activists and individuals in several of the country's cities, with searches, arrests, seized electronic devices and blocking of websites and social media. The attack is a serious escalation of institutional harassment against the LGBTI+ community, a worrying setback for democracy and a violation of fundamental rights in a country that is a candidate for accession to the EU. Currently, the central pillar of EU-Türkiye relations is the millions in funding that the country receives to act as EU border police. It is unacceptable for the EU to keep handing over public money to a regime that not only systematically violates the rights of migrants, but also persecutes the LGBTI+ population and undermines the rule of law. In view of the above: 1.
What urgent measures will the Commission take to demand that Türkiye end oppression, release detainees and put a stop to LGBTI+ censorship?
Will the Commission offer international protection and asylum to LGBTQI+ people persecuted in Türkiye?
Will the Commission suspend EU funding to a regime that violates the rights of migrants and brutally represses LGBTI+ people?

E-10-2026-003712.t: Low European gas stocks, high energy prices and opportunities to boost the EU’s energy supply and domestic gas production
qt: to the Commission Asger Christensen (Renew) Subject:

European gas stocks are at historically low levels for this time of the year, and a number of experts are extremely concerned about the price of energy this coming winter. These high prices can undermine the competitiveness of European companies, as well as put ordinary people’s finances under pressure, especially among lower earners. There is therefore a need to establish energy policy security that can provide greater economic stability and ensure that Europeans are not exposed to energy poverty. With the above in mind: 1.
What concrete action does the Commission intend to take to deal with the current situation of low European gas stocks and to counter the high energy prices expected this winter?
Will the Commission encourage and support extensions and expansions of European gas extraction to increase Europe’s gas production for the benefit of European citizens and businesses this winter?

Does the Commission have proposals for further action to help European citizens cope with the coming winters and high energy prices, and is the Commission considering measures to step up the production of energy via nuclear power and biogas?
to the Commission Kristoffer Storm (ECR) Subject:

The Danish mussel industry is currently facing significant challenges in the wake of the implementation of the revised Fisheries Control Regulation. According to the Danish authorities, the previous sampling scheme can no longer be used, and yet a new sampling plan – which needs to be approved by both the Danish Environmental Protection Agency and the European Commission – is not expected to be in place until 2027. This situation is causing significant uncertainty for fishers and processing firms, with shutdowns and job losses on the cards as a result of an administrative vacuum. 1.

Was it the Commission’s intention for the implementation of the revised Fisheries Control Regulation to result in a transitional period during which the existing sampling scheme can no longer be used, and no new scheme can yet be approved and implemented?

Since some of the new control provisions were enforced only as of 10 July 2026, what is the Commission’s justification for the fact that the previous scheme cannot be maintained until a new sampling plan can enter into force?
Will the Commission bring in a temporary transitional solution or other flexible approach to allow mussel fishing to continue without unnecessary administrative obstacles?

E-10-2026-003709.t: Danish national deck-height rules and fair competition in cross-border animal transport
qt: to the Commission Kristoffer Storm (ECR) Subject:

Danish legislation introducing specific deck-height requirements for the transport of weaner pigs weighing under 40 kg raises important questions regarding EU law and cross-border animal transport. The rules would require operators to replace their vehicles with four-deck vehicles, reducing transport capacity and increasing the number of vehicles and journeys needed to transport the same volume of animals. This risks increasing transport costs and creating unequal competitive conditions for businesses operating in or from Denmark. Such effects are particularly relevant in crossborder transport, where predictability and equal market access are essential for the internal market. The measure also raises concerns under Council Regulation (EC) No 1/2005, and in particular Article 1(3) thereof. Unilateral requirements may contribute to regulatory fragmentation, higher compliance costs and legal uncertainty for operators. 1.
Does the Commission consider that the Danish deck-height requirements are compatible with Council Regulation (EC) No 1/2005, and in particular Article 1(3) thereof?

Does the Commission agree that such national rules risk distorting competition and undermining fair and equal market conditions for transport businesses operating across borders within the internal market?

Considering the ongoing revision of EU animal transport rules, what action will the Commission take to prevent legal uncertainty, market fragmentation and unnecessary compliance costs resulting from unilateral national measures?

E-10-2026-003707.t: Gender gap in cardiovascular health and clinical research
qt: to the Commission Elena Nevado del Campo (PPE) Subject:

Cardiovascular diseases continue to be the leading cause of death for women in Europe. However, for years, it has been approached from predominantly male-focused paradigms. Many women are still being underdiagnosed and misdiagnosed as a result. What is more, their under-representation in cardiovascular research and clinical trials continues to limit data quality and perpetuates structural biases. These differences affect separate stages of the care cycle, from prevention to diagnosis, treatment and clinical follow-up, and they are acknowledged in the gender equality strategy 2026-2030 and the healthy hearts plan. At the same time, the 10th framework programme and the role played by the European Medicines Agency provide an opportunity to step up prevention, early diagnosis, personalised medicine and the generation of more accurate clinical evidence. In the light of the above: 1.
How will the Commission ensure that the precise and measurable targets introduced in the healthy hearts plan reduce the cardiovascular gap between women and men?
What steps will it take to secure balanced participation for women in cardiovascular clinical trials?
How will it ensure that gender- and sex-specific considerations are systematically included in cardiovascular research and clinical trials?

E-10-2026-003706.t: Scope under EU law for reduced VAT on new homes purchased by first-time buyers
qt: to the Commission Regina Doherty (PPE) Subject:
What flexibility do Member States have under existing EU law to use VAT and other fiscal measures to reduce the cost of newly constructed housing for first-time buyers?

Can the Commission clarify whether Directive 2006/112/EC1, as amended by Directive (EU) 2022/542, permits a Member State to apply a reduced VAT rate of 9 % to the supply or construction of new residential properties where the property is purchased by a first-time buyer as their principal private residence, whether such a reduced rate may be targeted specifically at first-time buyers and/or owner-occupiers, rather than applying to all purchasers of new residential property, and whether a targeted VAT reduction of this nature, together with an exemption from residential stamp duty and a reduction in or cap on development contributions, would raise concerns under EU State aid rules?
Council Directive 2006/112/EC of 28 November 2006 on the common system of value added tax, (OJ L 347, 11.12.2006, p. 1, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2006/112/oj). 1

E-10-2026-003705.t: Development of an international protocol for responding to incidents involving frontier AI models
qt: to the Commission Regina Doherty (PPE) Subject:

Will the Commission propose the development of an international protocol for responding to incidents involving frontier AI models, and seek to place this issue on the agenda of the G7, the G20 and the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, with a view to reaching agreement with international partners, including the United States and China?

E-10-2026-003704.t: Possibility of zero VAT on new homes purchased by first-time buyers
qt: to the Commission Regina Doherty (PPE) Subject:

Can the Commission clarify whether current EU VAT legislation permits Ireland to apply a 0 % VAT rate to the purchase of a newly constructed home by a first-time buyer, where that property will be used as the purchaser’s principal private residence and, if a 0 %VAT rate cannot be targeted specifically at first-time buyers, whether Ireland could apply a 0 % or super-reduced VAT rate to a defined category of affordable owner-occupied housing, subject, for example, to a maximum property value, income threshold or requirement that the property remain the purchaser’s principal residence for a specified period?
What conditions would have to be satisfied for such a measure to qualify as the provision of housing ‘as part of a social policy’ for the purposes of the VAT Directive?
If a 0 % rate is not permissible, what is the lowest VAT rate Ireland could lawfully apply to such newly constructed homes under the current EU VAT framework?
to the Commission Siegbert Frank Droese (ESN) Subject:

A digital catch certificate system for all fishery products entering the EU, known as CATCH, came into force on 10 January 2026. The ambitious system replaced the previous paper-based process and is considered central to EU efforts to tackle illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing, help protect marine biodiversity and contribute to the EU’s broader efforts to simplify administrative procedures. Will the Commission please list all persons and organisations (e.g. non-governmental organisations, trade organisations, logistics experts and non-EU exporters) that were consulted in any way during the development of the CATCH system?
to the Commission Siegbert Frank Droese (ESN) Subject:

A digital catch certificate system, known as CATCH, for all fishery products entering the EU came into force on 10 January 2026. The ambitious system replaced the previous paper-based process and is considered central to EU efforts to tackle illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing, help protect marine biodiversity and contribute to the EU’s broader efforts to simplify administrative procedures. 1.
How much did the CATCH system cost to develop?

What was this money spent on (e.g. consultation and planning, information infrastructure, programming or testing)? The Commission is asked to itemise the amounts over the entire period of development.

E-10-2026-003701.t: Recent statements of French President Macron
qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Siegbert Frank Droese (ESN) Subject:

What is the opinion of the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy concerning French President Macron’s creation of an ‘anti-ballistic coalition’ against Russia?
Does the Vice-President / High Representative agree with Macron’s statement that Europe must defend itself ‘if necessary with blood’?

E-10-2026-003697.t: Improvement of the child protection system
qt: to the Commission Sandra Gómez López (S&D) Subject:

Child protection is an essential obligation of Member States and a fundamental principle guiding EU action, as stated in Article 3(3) of the Treaty on European Union and Article 24 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights. It is estimated that more than 750 000 children in the EU live under some form of protection measure1, a growing figure that highlights the need for robust, rights-based systems that prioritise family-based care and guarantee the best interests of the child. To understand the scope of this reality and design effective policies, it is essential to have common data and indicators. The Fundamental Rights Agency (FRA)2 notes that protection systems are complex and that no common understanding currently exists among states. Meanwhile, the Commission, through Recommendation (EU) 2024/1238, formulated key guidelines to promote integrated child protection systems and advance deinstitutionalisation. Therefore: 1.
How does the Commission intend to monitor these recommendations?
Does it plan to submit any proposal to improve data availability?

UNICEF, Children in alternative care: Comparable statistics to monitor progress on deinstitutionalisation across the European Union, 2021: https://www.unicef.org/eca/media/19756/file/UNICEFDataCare%20Policy%20Brief.pdf. 2 FRA, Mapping Child Protection Systems in the EU – Update 2023: https://fra.europa.eu/en/publication/2024/mapping-child-protection-systems-eu-update-2023. 1

E-10-2026-003695.t: Refusal of third countries to provide geolocation data and its implications for the implementation of the EU Deforestation Regulation
qt: to the Commission Angelika Niebler (PPE) Subject:

The EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) requires market operators to provide precise geolocation data for each area in which the raw materials concerned are produced and to submit the data via an information system. Major producer countries including Indonesia and Malaysia have pointed out that, under their national data protection and security laws, the geolocation data required is considered protected cannot be readily disclosed to the EU. 1.

What view does the Commission take of a situation in which the governments of producer countries (Indonesia and Malaysia), citing national data protection and security legislation, refuse to provide or release – or significantly restrict the provision or release – of geolocation data for areas covered by the EUDR, and what conclusions does the Commission draw from this as regards the applicability of the regulation to market operators who rely on raw materials from the countries concerned?

Does the Commission agree that companies must not suffer any disadvantages as a result of the situation described above, and does the Commission intend to come up with any additional guidance, transitional arrangements or relief measures?

Does the Commission intend to enter into binding bilateral or multilateral agreements with the third countries concerned on the provision or reciprocal exchange of geodata in order to prevent the emergence of barriers to market access that are effectively equivalent to an import ban, and in that context, how does the Commission assess the risk of lost turnover and a permanent shift in trade flows away from the EU?

E-10-2026-003694.t: Will Brussels make households pay for its electrification policy?
qt: to the Commission Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE) Subject:

In its Electrification Action Plan of 17 July 20261, the Commission notes that electricity is on average two and a half times more expensive than gas for EU households. It wants to see the electricity-to-gas price ratio for households brought down to a maximum of 2.5 by 2030 and announces a provision regarding their tax differential. It also plans to propose the phasing-out of fossil fuel subsidies. Yet many households – especially rural and low-income households – are still dependent on gas boilers or vehicles with internal combustion engines, and cannot afford to immediately buy a heat pump, renovate their home or buy an electric vehicle. The plan itself acknowledges that the upfront costs of such equipment remain high. Can the Commission guarantee that the proposed tax to rebalance electricity and gas prices and the phasing-out of fossil fuel subsidies will not push up the price of gas or fuel, or, more broadly, the energy bills of households that cannot afford the equipment imposed by this transition?
https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:52026DC0595.

E-10-2026-003693.t: The use of AI in production processes and administration
qt: to the Commission Aldo Patriciello (PfE) Subject:

The increasingly frequent use of artificial intelligence in production processes and administration highlights the need to bridge the digital divide among small and medium-sized enterprises and public administration by leveraging automation and analytics tools. The absence of structured training pathways could hamper the competitiveness and efficiency of public services, thereby harming the European economic fabric. The failure to promptly implement coordinated measures is likely to exacerbate territorial and technological disparities, thereby preventing small companies from accessing global markets and keeping up with modern digital efficiency standards. In the light of the above, could the Commission clarify whether it will develop funded training programmes and common guidelines to support the secure uptake of AI by SMEs and public administration?

E-10-2026-003692.t: Post-COVID recovery fund how much remains to be paid to France?
qt: to the Commission Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE) Subject:

The Recovery and Resilience Facility, created in response to the crisis caused by the COVID19 pandemic, is coming to an end. In accordance with the applicable regulation, Member States must have completed all reforms and investments set out in their national plans by 31 August 2026. The last payment requests can be submitted until 30 September, with payments to be made before 31 December 2026. According to the Commission’s scoreboard, France has received around EUR 34 billion of the EUR 40 billion planned and is meeting 83% of the milestones and targets set. As a result, nearly EUR 6 billion remains to be disbursed with just a few days until the deadline. Against the backdrop of a particularly dire budgetary situation, it is essential to be aware of any potential failures on the part of the French government and the financial consequences those failures might entail. Can the Commission state: 1.
the exact amount still to be paid to France and the part likely to be definitively lost?
the milestones, targets, reforms or investments that have not yet been achieved?
the French projects concerned and the reasons which might lead the Commission to suspend or refuse all or part of the last payments?

E-10-2026-003691.t: Massive data thefts: why is France still delaying transposing of the NIS2 Directive?
qt: to the Commission Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE) Subject:

Since 2024, France has experienced a succession of massive data breaches: 33 million people affected at Viamedis and Almerys, up to 43 million at France Travail, 24 million contracts at Free, 1.2 million bank accounts in the National Register of Bank and Similar Accounts, and recently 678 000 individuals and professionals affected by a breach of the system of the Directorate-General for Public Finance (DGFiP). On 10 November 2022, Members of the Rassemblement National voted in favour of the NIS2 Directive, arguing that the increase in the number and sophistication of cyber-attacks called for appropriate responses and better protection for public and private organisations. This Directive imposes enhanced risk management measures on central and regional administrations. However, France has still not transposed it. On 8 July 2026, the Commission referred the matter to the Court of Justice of the European Union. Can the Commission clarify: 1.
what stage has been reached in this procedure and what penalties is France facing?
whether the DGFiP and France Travail should be deemed essential entities subject to NIS2?
whether these repeated violations reveal a structural deficiency in French cybersecurity and what measures could address it?
to the Commission Aldo Patriciello (PfE) Subject:

A growing number of dwellings in the EU are being occupied by squatters, whose actions are undermining property rights and fuelling social insecurity. The absence of a rapid response from the authorities leaves owners feeling completely vulnerable, a state of affairs that is detrimental to social cohesion and trust in state institutions. In addition, the resulting lengthy legal proceedings and unaffordable fees are a heavy burden that is exacerbating the financial plight of owners and paralysing the housing market. In the light of the above: 1.
Is the Commission aware of the economic and social impact of squatting?
Will it put forward a European action plan that introduces accelerated eviction procedures and protects the owners affected?

E-10-2026-003689.t: Administrative burdens on small businesses and harmonisation of registration and reporting requirements for packaging under the Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation
qt: to the Commission Asger Christensen (Renew) Subject:

The intention of the Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (PPWR) – i.e. to harmonise packaging rules across the EU’s internal market – is not always obvious to smaller companies that are facing major challenges in complying with the legislation. Companies are finding that complying with the rules across countries is an extremely complicated business, with different national registration and reporting systems in place, for example, as well as different administrative requirements. Companies selling their wares across the EU can be saddled with major administrative and financial burdens that hamper their business opportunities. 1.

How will the Commission ensure that, in practice, the PPWR creates uniform rules across Member States so that small businesses do not have to devote a disproportionate amount of resources to navigating a plethora of different national systems?

In this context, will the Commission establish a common EU solution whereby companies can report packaging data via a single platform, along the lines of the onestop shop, so that companies selling across the EU do not have to deal with separate national systems and reporting arrangements?

E-10-2026-003688.t: Ineffectiveness of EU sanctions: European components and technologies continue to flow into the Russian arms industry
qt: to the Commission Michał Dworczyk (ECR) Subject:

Despite successive sanctions packages, the latest information from Ukrainian intelligence reveals that the problem of components, technologies and production equipment from EU companies in Russian weapons systems1 remains unresolved. Of particular concern is the fact that foreign components manufactured in 20262 have been identified in Russian weaponry, indicating that the issue cannot be explained solely by the use of stocks dating from before the sanctions were imposed. The problem remains relevant despite the EU’s further tightening of restrictions on dual-use goods and technology, including under the 20th and 21st sanctions packages. In light of the above: 1.
How many actors in such supply chains are subject to export sanctions or restrictions in general, and how many under the 20th and 21st sanctions packages?

What further measures does the Commission intend to take to monitor end-users more effectively and prevent the re-export to Russia of dual-use components that are of particular importance to the Russian arms industry?
https://war-sanctions.gur.gov.ua/en/components. https://www.president.gov.ua/en/news/yevropejskim-poslam-prodemonstruvali-inozemni-komponentiz-r-104637?utm. 1 2

E-10-2026-003687.t: Supporting the Greek fur industry and the economy of Western Macedonia
qt: to the Commission Emmanouil Kefalogiannis (PPE) Subject:

The Greek fur industry is an outward-looking production sector with a long tradition, and it is inextricably linked to the economic and social life of Western Macedonia, in particular the regional units of Kastoria, Florina, Kozani and Grevena. The sector supports an important network of medium and small-sized businesses, skilled professionals and family businesses while preserving valuable know-how built up over generations. By way of illustration, according to industry data, the sector comprises 2 000 businesses and employs 35 000 people in the area of Kastoria alone. Keeping production within the EU, where strict standards apply, provides employment and contributes to regional cohesion and competitiveness while preventing the transfer of production and added value to non-EU countries where standards are lower. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
What specific measures does it intend to take to support the competitiveness, outwardlooking approach and long-term sustainability of the Greek fur industry?
How does it intend to ensure the preservation of jobs, know-how and the productive in Western Macedonia, a region that is already facing significant economic and development challenges?

E-10-2026-003685.t: Decision-making process and evidence base behind the exclusion of French Guiana from Regulation (EU) 2023/1115 (EU Deforestation Regulation)
qt: to the Commission Alexander Bernhuber (PPE) Subject:

The explanatory memorandum to Commission communication COM(2026)0661 states that unnamed ‘stakeholders have warned’ about the impact of the EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) in French Guiana, yet provides no impact assessment and no data on forest loss, trade flows or compliance costs. 1.

What figures does the Commission hold on (a) annual forest loss in French Guiana since 2020, (b) the area of agricultural clearing planned until 2040, (c) the volume of EUDR commodities traded with Brazil and Suriname, and (d) the volume shipped to the rest of the EU? If it holds none, on what factual basis was the proposal drafted?

What annual compliance costs and how many due diligence statements did the Commission estimate for operators in French Guiana, and how do these figures compare with the costs imposed on farmers and forest owners in low-risk Member States?

France already uses a derogation under the Renewable Energy Directive allowing biomass from forest clearing in French Guiana to bypass sustainability criteria. Has the Commission assessed the combined effect of this derogation and the EUDR exclusion on deforestation, and if not, why not?

E-10-2026-003684.t: Does Article 16 of Directive (EU) 2023/1791 require a specific remote reading technology?
qt: to the Commission Erik Kaliňák (NI) Subject:

Article 16 of Directive (EU) 2023/1791 requires the remote reading of meters and heat cost allocators, but does not specify a particular technology. In blocks of flats, however, a single specific technical solution may be promoted, even though there may be other, less costly ways of ensuring remote reading. In this connection: 1.
In the Commission’s view, does Article 16 of the Directive requires a specific technology, such as radio data transmission, to meet the remote reading requirement?
Does the Commission consider that, where several technically suitable solutions exist, flat owners and occupants may use a less costly solution that meets the requirements of the Directive?
How, in the Commission’s view, should a Member State ensure that consumers do not bear disproportionate costs for remote meter reading if the expected energy savings do not justify such costs?

E-10-2026-003683.t: Cost-efficiency of remote reading of existing meters and heat cost allocators pursuant to Article 16(2) of Directive (EU) 2023/1791
qt: to the Commission Erik Kaliňák (NI) Subject:

Directive (EU) 2023/1791, Article 16(2), stipulates that meters and heat cost allocators already installed but which are not remotely readable must be rendered remotely readable or replaced by 1 January 2027, unless a Member State demonstrates that this is not cost-efficient. In blocks of flats, this may mean replacing devices that are still in working order before the end of their operational life, with the costs potentially being passed on to flat owners and occupants. In light of the foregoing: 1.
What criteria, in the Commission’s view, should Member States apply when assessing the cost-efficiency of introducing remote meter reading for existing meters and heat cost allocators?
In the Commission’s view, does Article 16(2) of the Directive allow the burden of proving that remote meter reading is not cost-efficient to be shifted onto individual flat owners and occupants?

Does the Commission consider that, when assessing cost-efficiency, account should be taken of the total costs of installation, operation, maintenance and replacement of equipment in relation to the energy savings that can realistically be achieved?

E-10-2026-003682.t: Potential withdrawal of EU funding for Saxony-Anhalt and political interference in democratic election results
qt: to the Commission Irmhild Boßdorf (ESN), Mary Khan (ESN) Subject:

Following the AfD’s resounding election victory in the Saxony-Anhalt Landtag elections, in which it received around 44 % of votes, a public debate has begun on withdrawing EU funding or freezing payments if the AfD forms part of the government1. Saxony-Anhalt receives around EUR 2.95 billion in EU funding from the current 2021-2027 EU budget, for investments in schools, nurseries, sports facilities and medical infrastructure, among other things. Against this background, a particular question arises regarding to what extent and under what conditions the Commission could take measures against an individual German federal state and directly or indirectly affect its access to EU funding, and where the limits of political influence by way of EU financial instruments lie. 1.

What EU legal instruments could allow the Commission to suspend, freeze or otherwise restrict EU funding to an individual federal state within a Member State, and who would have the legal authority to make such a decision?

What specific circumstances would have to be in place for such a measure to be lawfully adopted in the case of a German federal state? To what extent would there have to be a direct link between the infringement established and the EU funds concerned?
Has the Commission already suspended, frozen or otherwise restricted funding allocated to a specific region or sub-national authority in a Member State for similar reasons?

E-10-2026-003681.t: National implementation of the Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation creating barriers within the single market
qt: to the Commission Bruno Tobback (S&D) Subject:

Regulation (EU) 2025/40 on packaging and packaging waste (PPWR) establishes a common European framework for packaging and extended producer responsibility. However, producers must first register and comply with extended producer responsibility obligations separately in each Member State where they make packaging or packaged products available. Micro-enterprises selling to consumers across the EU may therefore have to navigate up to 27 national systems with different procedures, reporting requirements, contributions and authorised-representative costs. This multiplication can make entering another national market, or shipping to the EU, economically unviable, especially for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and micro-enterprises. This hinders businesses’ ability to scale across borders and fragments the single market. 1.

Has the Commission assessed whether cumulative national registration, reporting and payment obligations constitute a disproportionate barrier to cross-border trade for companies, particularly SMEs and micro-enterprises?

Will the Commission propose an EU one-stop shop providing a single channel for registration, harmonised reporting and payments for extended producer responsibility contributions? If so, will the Commission organise or oversee its governance and functioning? If not, does it envisage another means of harmonisation and cross-border recognition of registrations across Member States?
What measures will the Commission take, and when, to prevent national implementation of the PPWR from creating (further) barriers within the single market, in line with the single market strategy?
to the Commission Kathleen Funchion (The Left) Subject:

The insurance market for thatched roofing in Ireland has seen steep increases in quote amounts for new applicants since the disruption caused by Brexit and difficulties for EU firms entering the market. What is the Commission doing to improve the situation of the insurance market for thatched roofing in Ireland?

E-10-2026-003678.t: Member States’ assessment obligations and food security, strategic autonomy and sustainable production considerations in relation to the Water Framework Directive
qt: to the Commission Asger Christensen (Renew) Subject:

Does the Commission take the view that, where a project or activity falls within the scope of Article 4(7) of the Water Framework Directive, for example as a ‘sustainable human development activity’, the Member State is required to assess whether the exemption applies, and to state why it does or does not apply?

Does the Commission take the view that the EU’s objectives as regards strategic autonomy, security of supply, food security, reducing dependence on third countries and maintaining and developing sustainable production capacity in the Union may, following a specific assessment, be regarded as considerations that fulfil the conditions for overriding public interest or sustainable development under Article 4(7) of the WFD?

E-10-2026-003677.t: Egnatia motorway: full toll fees are being charged despite limited operation of tunnels
qt: to the Commission Nikolaos Anadiotis (NI) Subject:

According to reports and public statements, the tunnel safety certification required under EU law has not been completed for a significant number of tunnels longer that 500 metres along the Egnatia motorway. This is resulting in the introduction of traffic control measures, lane restrictions and two-way traffic in twin-tube tunnels, as well as causing delays12. The problem seems to be mainly in parts of Western Macedonia and Epirus, such as Kastania, the Metsovo area and the section after Ioannina, going towards Igoumenitsa3. Egnatia is a key part of the trans-European road network and a great deal of national and EU funding has gone into it. Despite this, drivers are paying toll fees to use a motorway that is not fully functional at certain critical points and tunnels are an essential part of the service covered by toll fees. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Has it asked the Greek authorities for a complete list of tunnels along the Egnatia motorway that do not meet the requirements of Directive 2004/54/EC4, along with a binding timetable for compliance?
How does it view the fact that full toll fees are being charged while key sections of the motorway are operating with limited capacity or two-way traffic arrangements?
Will it look into whether the situation calls for temporary toll fee reductions, transparency towards users and remedial measures until tunnels are fully certified?
