E-10-2026-003676.t: Protecting farmed animals from extreme heat under the EU livestock strategy
qt: to the Commission Thomas Waitz (Verts/ALE) Subject:

The summer of 2026 confirmed that extreme heatwaves are now a major threat to the welfare of farmed animals. In June, a heatwave exceeding 40 °C killed 3 million poultry in western France, including around 6 600 tonnes of poultry in Brittany alone according to ANVOL, the French national association for the poultry supply chain. In Belgium and Italy, dairy production losses of up to 10 % were reported, increasing animal suffering alongside direct economic costs for farmers. A study published in Poultry Science, covering 146 million broiler chickens, found that the rate of mortality on arrival is 16.9 times higher when loading temperatures exceed 30 °C. A 2026 study published in Nature projects that by 2050, between 11 % and 21.6 % of the current EU and UK cattle population could face at least 15 additional heatwave days compared with today. 1.

Will the Commission make climate resilience and heat protection an explicit, measurable and enforceable objective of the EU livestock strategy and the forthcoming animal welfare legislation (for broiler chickens, laying hens and pigs)?

Does it intend to introduce science-based temperature and humidity thresholds for animal transport, with mandatory suspension of journeys in dangerous conditions, in line with the European Food Safety Authority’s recommendations?

E-10-2026-003675.t: Alleged EU competence in the field of housing
qt: to the Commission Marieke Ehlers (PfE), Rachel Blom (PfE) Subject:

During his interview on the Brussels Playbook Podcast on 10 September 2026, EU Commissioner Jørgensen stated that housing is partly a matter of EU competence because certain aspects of it relate to the free movement of services – including through short-term lettings – and to the free movement of capital, due to investments in the property market. However, this line of reasoning appears to stretch the division of competences under the Treaties considerably. After all, the free movement of services and capital cannot automatically mean that the Union acquires general competence over matters falling exclusively within national competence, simply because there are points of overlap with the freedom of movement within those areas of competence. If that were true, any tradable good or service would fall within EU competence, irrespective of the division of competences under the Treaties in the area concerned. 1.

Does the Commission acknowledge that the existence of a cross-border aspect, such as short-term lettings or cross-border property investments, does not in itself entail general EU competence in the field of housing, and that measures relating to spatial planning, housing supply, rent control and social housing fall, in principle, within the competence of the Member States?
Can the Commission indicate where, in its view, the legal boundary lies between measures to protect the internal market and de facto harmonisation of national housing policy?

Which competences, which are not currently regulated at EU level, does the Commission intend to regulate in future under the guise of general provisions such as the free movement of services and capital?

E-10-2026-003674.t: Legal classification of e-money tokens fully backed by central bank money in the CSDR reform
qt: to the Commission Siegbert Frank Droese (ESN) Subject:

The reform of the Central Securities Depositories Regulation (CSDR) is expected to enable the use of certain e-money tokens (EMTs) compliant with the Regulation on markets in crypto-assets (MiCA) for the settlement of the cash leg of securities transactions. Article 40 CSDR provides, in principle, for settlement in central bank money where practical and available. A matter that has not yet been expressly addressed is the issue, by a supervised intermediary, of an EMT that is fully backed by central bank deposits in a TARGET account. In such instances, the token is privately issued, but its reserves are 100 % central bank money. 1.
Under Article 40 CSDR, would the use of such an EMT constitute settlement in central bank money or EMTs?
If the latter, what is the regulatory significance of full backing by central bank money, particularly as regards de-risking, insolvency protection and the delivery-versuspayment link?

Does the Commission intend to expressly clarify the legal classification of EMTs fully backed by central bank money as part of the ongoing CSDR reform, whether in the legal text, in the recitals, or through the issue of technical standards or guidelines from the European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA) or the European Banking Authority (EBA)?

E-10-2026-003673.t: Common security and defence policy mission to Lebanon
qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Lynn Boylan (The Left), Kathleen Funchion (The Left), Mimmo Lucano (The Left), Matjaž Nemec (S&D), Arash Saeidi (The Left), Danilo Della Valle (The Left), Benedetta Scuderi (Verts/ALE), Rudi Kennes (The Left), Manon Aubry (The Left), Cecilia Strada (S&D), Giorgos Georgiou (The Left), Rima Hassan (The Left) Subject:

The Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy (VP/HR) is proposing a common security and defence policy (CSDP) mission to Lebanon with the goal of training and supporting the Lebanese Armed Forces. This proposal comes as the UN Interim Force in Lebanon’s (UNIFIL) mandate expires. The end of UNIFIL’s mandate at the end of the year comes as Israel’s violations of Lebanese sovereignty and the UN Charter continue without any real accountability. Israeli forces now occupy much of southern Lebanon and have displaced more than one-fifth of Lebanon’s population. UNIFIL’s key mandate is to confirm the withdrawal of Israeli forces from southern Lebanon and to help the Lebanese Government ensure the return of its effective authority in the area. The public commentary surrounding the proposed CSDP mission would suggest that a similar mandate is not envisaged for it. 1.
Will the VP/HR outline the rationale for effectively ignoring the role of Israel in Lebanon’s deteriorating security situation?
Will she outline what actions the EU has taken to prevent UNIFIL’s mandate from expiring?
Will she propose real measures to end Israeli aggression against Lebanon, including the imposition of sanctions and a two-way arms embargo?

E-10-2026-003672.t: Support for effective multilateralism and activation of Blocking Statute to protect the ICC
qt: to the Commission Thijs Reuten (S&D), Chloé Ridel (S&D), Barry Andrews (Renew), Tineke Strik (Verts/ALE), Catarina Vieira (Verts/ALE) Subject:

We note the ‘Declaration by the EU and its Member States in support of effective multilateralism’ (2 September 2026). While welcoming the commitments outlined in the declaration, we see a persistent gap in the actions of the Commission regarding the International Criminal Court (ICC). Specifically, the Declaration ‘underlines […] the need to preserve and protect [the ICC’s] independence, impartiality and effective functioning free from pressure, intimidation or interference’, therefore implicitly recognising threats to these principles. The United States administration has sanctioned the ICC, several of its judges, the Chief Prosecutor, and ICC staff, as well as non-governmental organisations that support the ICC’s work, and has launched a whole-of-government campaign to dismantle it. The Declaration gives the EU a mandate to act. The Parliament has repeatedly called for the Blocking Statute1 to be activated. However, the Commission has neither taken appropriate action to help protect the ICC, nor responded adequately to the Parliament’s questions and resolutions on this matter. 1.
Does the Commission consider that the United States’ sanctions and threats affect the ICC’s independence, impartiality and effective functioning?
If so, what action has the Commission taken in response, and if it has not acted, why not?
If not, what would need to occur to meet the threshold for the ICC to be considered affected?

Council Regulation (EC) No 2271/96 of 22 November 1996 protecting against the effects of the extraterritorial application of legislation adopted by a third country, and actions based thereon or resulting therefrom (OJ L 309, 29.11.1996, p. 1, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/1996/2271/oj). 1

E-10-2026-003671.t: Urgent measures to bolster museum security to protect cultural heritage that has been abandoned by the State
qt: to the Commission Catherine Griset (PfE) Subject:

Since the spectacular Louvre heist, France has been hit by a growing wave of museum breakins, the latest victim being the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer (Alpes-Maritimes Department)1. Incapable of running the country and grappling with an economic crisis, the French Government has also failed to protect our museums and stop the proliferation of heists targeting our cultural heritage. 1.
Is the Commission aware of the French Government’s lethargic reaction to the spate of thefts targeting the country’s museums?

Could the AgoraEU programme be used to fund efforts to improve the security arrangements of French museums so that we can salvage what we can at a time when law and order in the country have collapsed?

https://www.franceinfo.fr/faits-divers/quatre-tableaux-voles-dont-deux-retrouves-dans-le-jardin-neufmillions-d-euros-de-prejudice-ce-que-l-on-sait-du-cambriolage-au-musee-renoir-de-cagnes-surmer_8182817.html. 1

E-10-2026-003669.t: Improving road safety by making ABS a requirement for all new motorcycles placed on the EU market
qt: to the Council Elena Kountoura (The Left) Subject:

Nearly 3 500 motorcyclists die on European roads each year1. This highlights the urgent need for additional measures to be taken to improve the safety of motorcyclists, including by raising vehicle safety standards. In this context, Article 79 of Regulation (EU) No 168/2013 requires the Commission to consider extending the mandatory installation of anti-lock brake systems (ABS) on category L3e-A1 motorcycles (up to 125 cubic centimetres) and to consider presenting a legislative proposal to that effect2. A study published in 2020 concluded that ABS should be a requirement for all new motorcycles placed on the European market3 because of the significant role it plays in reducing the frequency and severity of collisions. In addition, ABS systems have been proven to reduce road accident involvement by around 30 %, making a decisive contribution to saving human lives4. However, six years after the publication of the study in question, the Commission’s planned legislative proposal has not yet been presented. In view of the above, can the Council answer the following: 1.
How does it assess the Commission’s six-year delay in presenting the envisaged legislative proposal, despite clear scientific evidence of the significant benefits of ABS for road safety?

Does it intend to invite the Commission to present a targeted legislative proposal to extend the mandatory installation of ABS to category L3e-A1 motorcycles, irrespective of the broader revision of Regulation (EU) No 168/2013?

European Commission (2025). Road Traffic Fatalities in the EU in 2023. Collision Matrix (https://tinyurl.com/5dzwuayd). 2 This regulation makes ABS mandatory in the EU as of 2016 only for motorcycle categories over 125 cubic centimetres (categories L3e-A2 and L3e-A3) but not for category L3e-A1 motorcycles (up to 125 cubic centimetres). E-10-2026-003668.t: Improving road safety by making ABS a requirement for all new motorcycles placed on the EU market
qt: to the Commission Elena Kountoura (The Left) Subject:

Nearly 3 500 motorcyclists die on European roads each year1. This highlights the urgent need for additional measures to be taken to improve the safety of motorcyclists, including by raising vehicle safety standards. In this context, Article 79 of Regulation (EU) No 168/2013 requires the Commission to consider extending the mandatory installation of anti-lock brake systems (ABS) on category L3e-A1 motorcycles that are placed on the market and to consider presenting a legislative proposal to that effect2. A study published in 2020 concluded that ABS should be a requirement for all new motorcycles placed on the European market3. Bearing in mind that ABS systems have been proven to reduce road accident involvement by around 30 %, making a decisive contribution to saving human lives4, and that six years after the publication of the study in question, the Commission’s planned legislative proposal has not yet been presented, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Why has it not yet submitted a legislative proposal for the mandatory installation of ABS on new L3e-A1 category motorcycles, despite the clear conclusions of the 2020 study?
Does it intend to propose a targeted amendment to Regulation (EU) No 168/2013 to that effect?
Alternatively, does it intend to extend the mandatory installation of ABS to all new motorcycles placed on the market in the context of a forthcoming revision of Regulation (EU) No 168/2013?
