E-10-2026-003600.t: Strengthening EU measures to address thefts of cultural property in Member States
qt: to the Commission Leire Pajín (S&D), Sandra Gómez López (S&D), Juan Fernando López Aguilar (S&D), Marcos Ros Sempere (S&D), Laura Ballarín Cereza (S&D) Subject:

The robbery from the Villena Treasury on 27 August 2026 came at a time of growing concern over thefts of cultural property from museums in various European Member States. A recent Europol report warns of more aggressive methods targeting high-value objects. Although the Union has instruments such as Directive (EU) 2014/60 on the return of unlawfully held cultural objects, Directive (EU) 2018/1673 on combating money laundering and Directive (EU) 2024/1260 on asset recovery and confiscation, there remain shortcomings in prevention, early warning and cooperation in response to acts of theft in the Union. Does the Commission believe it necessary to review and strengthen the EU framework with a view to: 1.
establishing minimum standards for risk assessment, identification and protection of cultural property, backed by EU funding, particularly for cash-strapped local and regional museums;
setting up a permanent European early-warning system, thereby improving cooperation between national authorities, Europol and INTERPOL;

more aggressively prosecuting these offences at European level as organised crime, not least the laundering and sale of stolen cultural heritage, including on online sales platforms, thus safeguarding the common cultural heritage of all European citizens?

E-10-2026-003597.t: Applying the Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation to the wholesale fruit and vegetable sector: manufacturer status, compliance checks and reusable packaging
qt: to the Commission Salvatore De Meo (PPE) Subject:

Applying Regulation (EU) 2025/40 on packaging and packaging waste (PPWR) poses significant challenges for the wholesale fruit and vegetable sector. Firstly, businesses that purchase standardised packaging – designed, manufactured and certified by specialist firms – can be classed as ‘manufacturers’ simply by displaying their name or logo on it. This customisation, which is necessary for product identification and traceability, can neither alter the characteristics of the packaging nor justify liability for the compliance thereof. The regulation further fails to specify the frequency of or methodology governing the mandatory compliance tests for maximum levels of PFAS and heavy metals set out in Article 5. Lastly, a draft study ordered by the Commission has proposed that reusable fruit and vegetable crates must be used at least 50 times, with scant regard for hygiene and food-safety requirements. Therefore, in the spirit of the simplification which the Commission is endorsing, can the Commission say: 1.

Whether it intends to clarify that the affixing of a name or trademark does not automatically confer the status of ‘manufacturer’, and what methodology and frequency does it consider appropriate for the checks provided for in Article 5?
What scientific evidence is there to confirm that fruit and vegetable crates that have been reused at least 50 times are hygienic?
Does it intend to establish criteria for their early withdrawal when compliance with hygiene and food-safety standards is no longer guaranteed?

E-10-2026-003594.t: Evaluation of the impact of the Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (PPWR) on SMEs
qt: to the Commission Aura Salla (PPE) Subject:

The PPWR1 came into force on 12 August 2026. The regulation imposes obligations on businesses, placing a disproportionate burden on small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and micro-enterprises. European companies are at a disadvantage when competing against operators such as Temu. The impact assessment evaluating EU legislation on packaging and packaging waste (SWD(2022)0384) recognised the need to ensure that the impacts on SMEs remain proportionate. This principle is referred to in the PPWR, stating that attention should be paid to facilitating micro-enterprises and SMEs in complying with the PPWR. The regulation does not provide measures to ensure requirements are proportionate to the capacity of SMEs. The SME test should be used as part of an evaluation of the regulation. The Commission should assess the impact of the PPWR on SMEs and whether additional measures are needed to ensure proportionality. Considering this: 1.
Will the Commission commit to reviewing and evaluating the regulation immediately, as it recognises serious problems that pose a threat to SMEs?
Will the Commission carry out an SME test specifically assessing the actual impacts of the regulation on SMEs?
What steps is the Commission taking to ensure that SMEs and micro-enterprises are not burdened with regulatory obligations that could adversely affect their competitiveness?

Regulation (EU) 2025/40 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 19 December 2024 on packaging and packaging waste, amending Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 and Directive (EU) 2019/904, and repealing Directive 94/62/EC (OJ L, 2025/40, 22.1.2025, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2025/40/oj). 1

E-10-2026-003593.t: Public procurement reform: Higher bills for councils and backroom negotiations?
qt: to the Commission Ioan-Rareş Bogdan (PPE) Subject:

The Commission is proposing a root-and-branch overhaul of the public procurement market which would see the existing directives replaced by a directly applicable regulation. The proposal does away with the traditional lowest-price criterion and introduces mandatory “quality” criteria with weightings of up to 50 % and direct negotiations between authorities and firms. In practice, these mechanisms could make local projects hugely more expensive and public spending less transparent. 1.

How will the Commission financially offset the inevitable rise in costs for local authorities in less developed regions due to the requirement to introduce social and environmental criteria with weightings of at least 30-50 %?

What specific corruption control mechanisms does the new framework introduce to prevent backroom deals, against the backdrop of the legalisation of direct negotiations between contracting authorities and certain tenderers?

What economic data did the Commission rely on when it concluded that the restriction of competition through the “European preference” clause would not lead to an increase in the end prices paid by taxpayers for large-scale infrastructure projects?

E-10-2026-003591.t: Denmark’s unequal treatment of EB students with regard to grade conversion and Bonus A in comparison with STX and IB students
qt: to the Commission Morten Løkkegaard (Renew) Subject:

In 2021, the Commission criticised the Danish conversion model for the European Baccalaureate (EB), in response to which Denmark changed its practice. However, according to Danish parents’ representatives at the European School, the Danish conversion model for EB students still places them at a disadvantage compared with both Danish upper secondary (STX) students and International Baccalaureate (IB) students when applying for higher education, owing, among other things, to the grade conversion and lack of access to an individual ‘Bonus A’ grading adjustment scheme. With the above in mind, and in the light of the attached note1: 1.

Does the Commission take the view that the current Danish grade conversion model for the European Baccalaureate ensures genuine equal treatment and is in line with Denmark’s obligations under the Convention defining the Statute of the European Schools of 21 June 1994?
What practical action will the Commission recommend that Denmark take to ensure that it fully delivers on its commitments?

Does the Commission think that the fact that EB students are not eligible for an individual Bonus A adjustment could put them at a disadvantage compared with Danish STX students, thus constituting discrimination in breach of the Convention defining the Statute of the European Schools of 21 June 1994?
Note: https://www.ft.dk/samling/20252/almdel/EUU/bilag/157/3159215.pdf

E-10-2026-003586.t: Spanish Ministry of the Interior breaches EU law and attacks the freedom of the press
qt: to the Commission Dolors Montserrat (PPE) Subject:

The Spanish Ministry of the Interior has produced an internal dossier with individualised files on dozens of active journalists, including photographs and assessments of their political orientation and ideology, affinity with the government and left-wing or right-wing positions. These facts raise serious questions in light of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR), Article 9 of which provides for enhanced protection of data revealing political opinions, and Regulation (EU) 2024/1083 (European Media Freedom Act). 1.

Does the Commission consider it compatible with EU law (in particular with Articles 5, 6 and 9 of the GDPR and Articles 7, 8 and 11 of the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights) for a government to collect, classify and keep ideological profiles on journalists without their permission?

Does the Commission think that creating or using those profiles could constitute interference that is incompatible with the freedom, editorial independence and pluralism of the media that is protected by Regulation (EU) 2024/1083, especially when the authority responsible deals with media relations and institutional advertising?

Will it ask the Spanish Government for explanations and, if it is confirmed that EU law has been violated, what specific action – including, where appropriate, opening infringement proceedings under Article 258 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union – will it take?

E-10-2026-003584.t: Why is Brussels funding projects in the North Pole, when Romania has the available graphite and infrastructure?
qt: to the Commission Ioan-Rareş Bogdan (PPE) Subject:

The European Commission has announced a Global Gateway package of EUR 200 million for Greenland and the intention to double support to EUR 530 million in the upcoming Multiannual Financial Framework. I welcome any effort by the Union to secure critical resources in the face of global competition and the eagerness to reduce dependence on China! However, while the Commission wants to massively finance the creation of infrastructure from scratch under extreme polar conditions, Member States such as Romania already possess strategic graphite deposits and transport networks, as well as the energy and workforce needed for immediate integration into the European industrial chain. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

Why is the Commission granting financial priority to external mining projects in the Arctic instead of making use of graphite deposits in Member States such as Romania, where these deposits can be readily exploited and where the basic infrastructure is already in place?
Are there any contractual clauses obliging mining companies benefiting from EU support in Greenland to prioritise the delivery of the extracted raw materials to industry in the Member States?
How are the Union’s resource exploitation rights guaranteed in the long term in the event that Greenland declares its full independence from Denmark?

E-10-2026-003581.t: Drinking water losses and funding for island water networks
qt: to the Commission Galato Alexandraki (ECR) Subject:

The European Water Resilience Strategy aims to reduce leaks and modernise infrastructure. Under Article 4(3) of Directive 2020/2184 water leakage levels must be assessed and the results notified to the Commission by 12 January 2026. For the Greek islands, we need to know how much water is being lost and prioritise repairing the networks. Small-scale suppliers also require technical assistance so that they can prepare and implement projects with the help of funding. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Did Greece submit the assessment within the deadline? What are the results for the suppliers covered in the assessment, especially those who supply islands?
What Eu-funded projects are being implemented on the Greek islands to reduce leakages, what is the budget and what are the specific water saving targets?
How will it help small island suppliers record water loss and prepare investor-ready projects, even when they do not fulfil the Directive’s minimum requirements for mandatory assessment?

E-10-2026-003580.t: Delayed environmental projects and the investment gap in Greece
qt: to the Commission Galato Alexandraki (ECR) Subject:

The 2025 Environmental Implementation Review found that Greece was experiencing serious delays in urban wastewater projects, a continued reliance on waste landfilling and systemic failures in complying with EU Court of Justice rulings. The overall environmental investment gap is estimated at EUR 2.3 billion a year. The report warns that the overcapacity of residual waste treatment facilities is not helping Greece’s transition to the circular economy. Resources need to go into infrastructure that works and meets the country’s needs. Clear answers need to be given regarding the delayed projects. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
What corrective measures and timelines have been agreed with the Greek authorities for the most major outstanding waste and urban waste water issues identified in the report?
Which EU-funded projects relating to waste and wastewater are experiencing delays, and what is the funding, implementation stage and expected date of entry into operation for each of these projects?
How does it check that Greek investments meet actual needs and cover separate collection, without creating oversized residual waste facilities?

E-10-2026-003577.t: Greece’s delayed implementation of EU rules on protecting against asbestos exposure
qt: to the Commission Galato Alexandraki (ECR) Subject:

On 8 July 2026, the Commission sent a reasoned opinion to Greece for failing to fully transpose Directive (EU) 2023/2668 on the protection of workers from exposure to asbestos. The deadline for implementing most of the provisions expired on 21 December 2025. The directive reduces the permissible exposure limit from 0.1 to 0.01 fibres per cubic centimetre. The delay is especially serious for those working on demolition and renovation sites and in old public buildings, where the presence of asbestos could endanger their health. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
What provisions has Greece not yet transposed and what is its timetable for compliance?
How is the implementation of the new exposure limit in Greek workplaces currently being monitored?
Does it intend to require specific checks to be carried out on EU-funded renovation and energy retrofit projects?

E-10-2026-003576.t: Incomplete implementation of EU rules on transparent and predictable working conditions in Greece
qt: to the Commission Galato Alexandraki (ECR) Subject:

On 8 July 2026, the Commission opened an infringement procedure against Greece for failing to fully align national legislation with Directive (EU) 2019/1152 on transparent and predictable working conditions. The directive enshrines the right of workers to receive timely information on key conditions such as working hours, pay and job stability. It also provides for protection against unpredictable working hours and last-minute assignments and establishes that mandatory training must be free of charge. Shortages particularly affect seasonal and precarious workers. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
What specific provisions of the Greek law does it consider to be incompatible with the directive?
Which categories of workers does it consider to be insufficiently protected?
What measures will it take if Greece fails to promptly remedy existing shortcomings, in particular in the tourism and catering sectors?

E-10-2026-003574.t: Delayed procurement of medical devices and transfer of cost outside of the Recovery Fund
qt: to the Commission Galato Alexandraki (ECR) Subject:

Under the original Greek Recovery Plan, medical equipment was meant to be delivered to 80 hospitals by June 2026. On 18 June 2026, the project in question, which had an initial budget of around EUR 80 million, was excluded from the Recovery Fund and the corresponding target was removed from the revised plan. On 31 August 2026, the Minister of Health stated that the project had not been cancelled but had been included in the sectoral development plan on 14 July and that it was due to be delivered within the year. This delay meant that the cost was transferred from the European programme to national resources. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
On what basis did it approve the removal of this target from the Greek Recovery Plan?
What amount of European funding was ultimately not used for the procurement of the medical equipment and where was it reallocated?
How will it check that the equipment will actually be delivered to all the hospitals it was originally intended for at no additional cost to Greek taxpayers?
to the Commission Hanna Gedin (The Left) Subject:

In December 2025, the Commission presented a revision to the State aid rules, which aimed to facilitate investments in social and affordable housing across Europe by designating them as services of general economic interest (SGEIs). Sweden does not have social housing, but has a large share of public housing, with over half of all renters living in public housing in Sweden. At the same time, Sweden is facing a housing shortage crisis, and it is more difficult than ever to build at a cost that ordinary people can afford. Is it the Commission’s intention that Swedish public housing can be included in these new revised State aid rules by being designated as SGEIs?
to the Commission Galato Alexandraki (ECR) Subject:

According to the Commission, the AI Omnibus entered into force on 27 July 2026. The rules on high-risk systems set out in Annex III will apply from 2 December 2027 and from 2 August 2028 for the respective systems that have been integrated into products. Clear information is needed on the aspects that are already in place to protect citizens and what will come into force later on. It is therefore considered necessary to provide practical guidance for the human review of adverse decisions. The human review should be carried out by trained officials who are best placed to reject an algorithmic recommendation. Before public authorities use such systems, I would suggest establishing common standards for independent checks and publishing a brief risk assessment that is easy to understand, with personal data protection. Small and medium-sized businesses need easy-to-use compliance tools. Likewise, providers must provide sufficient documentation and not pass their responsibilities on to small users in a non-transparent way. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
When will uniform practical guidance be given on reporting, human review and explaining decisions, depending on the applicable regime?
How are citizens affected by the systems in Annex III protected during the transition period?
What tools will be given to SMEs to exercise compliance and check the documentation of their suppliers?

E-10-2026-003571.t: Lack of reciprocity of standards in the EU-Mercosur agreement
qt: to the Commission Anna Maria Cisint (PfE) Subject:

In addition to raising serious doubts about the ability of Mercosur countries to ensure full compliance with EU standards on antimicrobial use and animal traceability, the recent suspension of imports of beef, poultry, eggs and honey from Brazil also shows there is a real problem: the reciprocity of standards is now reduced to a principle written in the Treaties and ignored in practice. It is unacceptable to require European farmers to incur very high costs to comply with environmental, health, animal welfare and antibiotic use standards, while allowing the entry of products from production systems that are subject to different requirements or insufficient controls: the health of European citizens is also at stake here. In light of the above: 1.
Will the Commission impose additional safeguards on Mercosur countries in order to ensure genuine reciprocity in the standards of imported products?
How does it intend to verify compliance with EU standards throughout the entire life cycle of animals?

E-10-2026-003568.t: New follow-up question to written question E-000437/2026 (Concerns about funding of the NGO ECPS)
qt: to the Commission Auke Zijlstra (PfE) Subject:

On 17 July, Commissioner Zaharieva replied to my follow-up question E-001557/20261, which followed on from my original question E-000437/2026(ASW)2. In her reply, she stated, amongst other things, the following: ‘Proposals received under Horizon Europe are evaluated solely by independent experts, and proposals submitted to the CERV programmes are evaluated by the Commission assisted by independent external experts. Only the highest ranked proposals that best align with the objectives of the programmes are selected for funding.’ In light of this reply, I have the following follow-up questions: 1.
Can the Commission explain how these ‘independent experts’ are selected, what their background is (especially their political background), and what (legal) relationship they have with the Commission?

Can the Commission explain the precise criteria used to identify ‘the highest ranked proposals’? What criteria – political, in particular – underpin this, perhaps drawing an analogy with the current European public procurement criteria?

Can the Commission state, in detail and in concrete terms, whether it considers ‘confronting the rise of populism’ to be so important that it wishes to finance this effort through an NGO such as ECPS?

to the Commission Morten Løkkegaard (Renew) Subject:

Where no accountable EU-based operator or seller can be traced by authorities, will the Commission ensure that the online platform facilitating the sale assumes responsibility for compliance with applicable EU product rules in order to protect children and businesses in the EU?

E-10-2026-003564.t: Training on ‘queer youth and allies: building inclusive youth work’ in Vienna
qt: to the Commission Alexander Jungbluth (ESN) Subject:

From 8 to 12 June 2026 in Vienna, an Erasmus+ training course was held on ‘queer youth and allies: building inclusive youth work’, for 30 youth workers to discuss ‘intersectionality’ and how to create ‘more inclusive spaces for queer young people’. 1.
What specific objectives and measurable outcomes did the Commission aim to achieve by funding this course, and to what extent are these in line with the core objectives of EU youth policy?
What was the total cost of this course, including the contributions made by Erasmus+ and the European Solidarity Corps towards accommodation, meals, travel and organisation?

Which organisations and individuals (please provide names) from which countries of origin took part in the course as participants, trainers or cooperation partners (including OeAD, SALTO, WienXtra and Q:WIR), or were involved in shaping its content?
to the Commission Alexander Jungbluth (ESN) Subject:

Students were invited to take part in make-up workshops, queer discussion groups and, lastly, a drag show. This initiative was organised by Erasmus+, among other organisations. 1.
What specific objectives and measurable outcomes did the Commission aim to achieve by funding this show, and to what extent are these in line with the core objectives of EU youth policy?
What was the total amount of EU support for this event, whether direct or indirect?

Which organisations and individuals (please provide names) from which countries of origin took part in the show as participants, trainers or cooperation partners or were involved in shaping its content?

E-10-2026-003561.t: Fragmentation and interoperability of electric vehicle charging services in the EU
qt: to the Commission Antonín Staněk (PfE) Subject:

The fragmentation of the European electric vehicle charging market continues to create significant difficulties for consumers, particularly when travelling across Member States. Drivers may face different prices for the same charging session depending on whether they use an operator’s RFID card, a mobile application, a QR code or a bank card. At the same time, Plug and Charge technology based on ISO 15118, which could considerably simplify charging by enabling automatic vehicle authentication and payment, remains insufficiently interoperable in practice. Moreover, some vehicle manufacturers appear to restrict Plug and Charge functionality to their own charging or mobility services, potentially limiting consumer choice and disadvantaging competing providers. In this context: 1.

How does the Commission assess whether significant price differences between payment methods comply with the requirements of Regulation (EU) 2023/18041 concerning reasonable, transparent, comparable and non-discriminatory prices?

What further measures will the Commission take to ensure that Plug and Charge is genuinely operational and interoperable across the EU, rather than merely technically supported by charging infrastructure?

Will the Commission consider measures preventing vehicle manufacturers from restricting Plug and Charge to proprietary charging or payment services, so as to ensure consumers can freely choose their preferred mobility service provider?

Regulation (EU) 2023/1804 of 13 September 2023 on the deployment of alternative fuels infrastructure, and repealing Directive 2014/94/EU (OJ L 234, 22.9.2023, p. 1, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2023/1804/oj). 1

E-10-2026-003558.t: Lignite phase-out in Western Macedonia and its damaging consequences for the people
qt: to the Commission Lefteris Nikolaou-Alavanos (NI) Subject:

In recent days, the Greek Prime Minister visited businesses in Western Macedonia, such as greenhouse and district heating projects which are underway following the closure of lignitefired power plants. The Nea Dimokratia Government made an insulting promise to make up for a fraction of the jobs lost. The blasting of lignite excavators was an emblematic snapshot of the criminal lignite phase-out and there is still more to come. New investment, which has meant that corporate groups have been enjoying generous subsidies paid out by the Recovery and Resilience Facility, has called into question a system that had consistently provided local towns and cities with heating for decades. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

What view does it take of the fact that, with its ‘just transition’ programmes and generous RRF funding, the EU has financed a plan that has had disastrous consequences for the people in the light of the lignite phase-out, worsening energy poverty and unemployment, since the new jobs do not even come close to replacing the ones lost, while energy prices continue to skyrocket, with monopolistic corporate groups emerging as the only winners?

What view does the Commission take of the people’s legitimate demand, in support of local trade unions and grassroots organisations, not only for lignite power stations and mines to remain open, but also for compensation to be given for the damage and adverse consequences they have faced and for the stations and mines to reopen after receiving an environmental upgrade, for the abolition of harmful trade in pollutants and the abolition of the energy exchange, all of which is unsustainable for the people in the context of the EU’s ‘green’ strategy, which leaves ordinary people in a serious predicament and plunges them into energy poverty?

E-10-2026-003557.t: Government and EU responsibilities for the spread of the West Nile virus
qt: to the Commission Lefteris Nikolaou-Alavanos (NI) Subject:

The West Nile virus is spreading in Greece, with cases in 66 municipalities, 39 of which in Attica. So far, there have been 290 cases and 24 deaths. The Nea Dimokratia Government has failed to take any measures to protect public health even though circulation of the virus has been common knowledge for years. In appealing to ‘individual responsibility’, it is once again shifting responsibility onto the people. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

What view does it take of the fact that it is the EU’s overall strategy – and in particular Directives 2014/23/EU and 2014/24/EU – that sets the scene for the municipal services of regions and municipalities to be privatised by awarding contracts to private individuals, i.e. by establishing public-private partnerships?

What view does it take of the fact that the policy of contracting and privatising essential public health services, such as spraying, provided for in the above-mentioned directives, on the one hand leads to the underfunding of these services and the deterioration of their quality, as they are subject to ‘cost-benefit’ criteria, ultimately also leading to increased costs for the people and risks to their health, while on the other hand securing huge profits for business groups?

What view does it take of the fact that, at a time when billions are being pumped into the war economy and doled out to EU and national governments to support corporate group profitability, the competent regional directorates for health control and public health are being condemned to tragic understaffing and underfunding?

E-10-2026-003556.t: Protecting viticulture in Ribeira Sacra – derogations from the prohibition on aerial spraying
qt: to the Commission Ana Miranda Paz (Verts/ALE) Subject:

Article 9 of Directive 2009/128/EC prohibits the aerial spraying of plant protection products, although it provides for derogations where there are no viable alternatives or where aerial application presents clear advantages for human health and the environment over land-based methods, provided that safety and control conditions are met. France has put this derogation into practice through specific legislation. The topic is particularly relevant in Ribeira Sacra, an area with mountain viticulture, smallholdings and steep slopes, where conventional mechanisation is practically impossible and the regulated use of drones to apply pesticide treatments could both be a tool for modernisation that is compatible with landscape preservation, and foster generational renewal. 1.

Does the Commission consider that the specific characteristics of the area – terraces, small-scale farming and extremely steep slopes – justify applying the derogations, provided that EU legislation is complied with?

What action will it take to ensure that the application of EU legislation on aerial spraying does not create competitive disadvantages between wine-growers from different regions and that it makes it possible to take advantage, in a safe and controlled manner, of new precision application technologies, such as drones?
Does it consider that the use of such technologies can help retain agricultural activity in disadvantaged areas and preserve landscapes with a high cultural and environmental value?

E-10-2026-003555.t: Spain’s violation of Regulations (EU) 2021/1153 and (EU) 2024/1679 in the core railway network in Asturias
qt: to the Commission Susana Solís Pérez (PPE) Subject:
Spain’s violation of Regulations (EU) 2021/1153 and (EU) 2024/1679 in the core railway network in Asturias

The railway between Gijón, Oviedo, Pola de Lena and León is part of the trans-European transport network’s Atlantic Corridor. The Spanish Government is undertaking works on the Pola de Lena-Oviedo and Oviedo-Gijón sections, as well as on the line that passes through Villabona. However, those works are essentially designed to improve the C-1 Cercanías suburban line and do not meet the requirements laid down for the corridor in Regulations (EU) 2021/1153 and (EU) 2024/1679. The consultations on information studies, projects and calls for tenders currently being pursued do not comply with fundamental aspects of the requirements for the core network laid down in Articles 16 to 20 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1679. Instead, they appear to be in line with the standards specific to the comprehensive network that are established in Article 15 of the regulation. The plans mean that, in practice, the railway section in question will be excluded from the European core network and, therefore, from the Atlantic Corridor. Furthermore, the plans do not adequately address the needs of freight traffic and the connections with Asturian ports and the Zalia logistics centre. In view of the above: In the Commission’s opinion, will the works planned by Spain ensure that the León-Gijón railway line fulfils, by the established deadlines, the requirements applicable to the core network under Regulations (EU) 2021/1153 and (EU) 2024/1679 and, if not, does it intend to require Spain to meet those requirements?

E-10-2026-003554.t: Autonomous AI-enabled cyberattacks and the protection of European critical infrastructure
qt: to the Commission Andi Cristea (S&D) Subject:

In July 2026, during security evaluations of advanced AI models, several models reportedly bypassed safeguards intended to isolate them from the internet, gained external network access and compromised third-party infrastructure. They allegedly exploited vulnerabilities, obtained credentials without authorisation and accessed external systems without explicit instruction, in what was subsequently described as an unprecedented cyber incident. This raises serious concerns about the ability of increasingly capable AI systems to autonomously engage in harmful cyber activities beyond controlled testing environments, posing risks to critical infrastructure and essential services, particularly in Member States such as Romania, which faces heightened cyber and hybrid threats on the EU’s eastern flank. In this context: 1.

Does the Commission consider that the existing EU framework, consisting of the Artificial Intelligence Act1, NIS 2 Directive2 and Cyber Resilience Act3, adequately ensures the mandatory reporting and investigation of incidents involving advanced AI systems autonomously bypassing safeguards and compromising third-party systems?

Will the Commission, together with the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA) and national authorities, assess EU preparedness for autonomous AI-enabled cyberattacks, including attacks in Romania and other eastern-flank Member States?

Does the Commission consider additional safeguards necessary, including mandatory independent safety and security testing, stronger controls on external network access during evaluations and mandatory reporting of serious AI-related security incidents?

Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 of 13 June 2024 laying down harmonised rules on artificial intelligence (OJ L, 2024/1689, 12.7.2024, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj). 2 Directive (EU) 2022/2555 of 14 December 2022 on measures for a high common level of cybersecurity across the Union (OJ L 333, 27.12.2022, p. 80, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2022/2555/oj). 3 Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 of 23 October 2024 on horizontal cybersecurity requirements for products with digital elements (OJ L, 2024/2847, 20.11.2024, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/2847/oj). 1
to the Commission Regina Doherty (PPE) Subject:

There are concerns that the European Banking Authority’s Q&A 2022_6336 adopts a narrow interpretation of the contractual relationship between issuers and merchants, and of the transfer of e-money to merchants, which may not take sufficient account of the way in which four-party payment schemes and other e-money arrangements function and, if applied to such schemes/arrangements, could prevent such products from continuing to operate. In view of the above: 1.

How does the Commission consider the interpretation set out in the European Banking Authority’s Q&A 2022_6336, in particular the requirement for the transfer of e-money to the merchant, to be compatible with the E-Money Directive1 and the relevant caselaw?

Is the Commission considering clarifying that e-money products operating through fourparty payment schemes and other e-money arrangements should not be regarded as falling within the scope of Q&A 2022_6336?

What assessment has the Commission made of the potential impact of this interpretation on existing prepaid card programmes, financial inclusion initiatives and other established e-money products if they were to be reclassified outside of the e-money framework?

Directive 2009/110/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 16 September 2009 on the taking up, pursuit and prudential supervision of the business of electronic money institutions amending Directives 2005/60/EC and 2006/48/EC and repealing Directive 2000/46/EC (OJ L 267, 10.10.2009, p. 7, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2009/110/oj). 1

E-10-2026-003552.t: Concerns at the safety of Chinese-manufactured vehicles owing to short development times
qt: to the Commission Elena Donazzan (ECR) Subject:

In China, new vehicles are now being brought to market in around two years and the Chinese automotive industry has claimed that artificial intelligence could bring this down to under 18 months. In the West, development times range from three to five years, a fact that also compromises industrial competitiveness. China’s reduced development times, at the whim of their car manufacturers, has raised serious concerns even amongst Beijing’s own regulatory authorities as to the possible ramifications for vehicle safety and durability. Given that Chinese-manufactured occupy a growing share of the European market: 1.

Does the Commission believe the current European type-approval and surveillance system to be adequate to identify any risks related to the precipitous reduction in vehicle development cycles in China?

In what way is the long-term durability of Chinese vehicles on the EU market verified? Furthermore, given the concerns that have emerged in China, does the Commission intend to consider more stringent checks to ensure the safety of European consumers?
How does the Commission intend to address this issue, which, as well as being a safety concern, also places European industries at a competitive disadvantage?

E-10-2026-003551.t: Effectiveness of EU funding for Russian civil society organisations and independent media
qt: to the Commission Michał Dworczyk (ECR) Subject:

EU financial support for Russian civil society organisations and independent media should be systematically reviewed to assess not only the implementation of the planned measures but also whether they are actually effective and achieve results. This is particularly important with projects whose aim is to reach Russian society and to support independent access to information at a time when repression and censorship are ramping up in the Russian Federation. In light of the above: 1.

What result indicators does the Commission use to assess projects supporting Russian civil society and independent media, and do they cover actual reach and audience impact within the territory of the Russian Federation or solely project outputs, such as the number of training sessions, conferences, publications or people trained?

Since 2022, has it identified any cases where the funded activities failed to yield a single measurable outcome in Russia; if so, how many such cases were found and what consequences were brought to bear?
How many projects supporting Russian civil society and independent media have undergone ex-post evaluation since 2022, and can the Commission make available the findings of these evaluations?

E-10-2026-003550.t: Justification for and oversight of support for the ‘Thermal Hotel Wrello’ under the EU recovery and resilience plan
qt: to the Commission Irmhild Boßdorf (ESN) Subject:

On 28 August 2026, the Croatian business news site ‘Poslovni.hr’ reported the opening of ‘Thermal Hotel Wrello’ in Stubičke Toplice (Croatia), which was almost entirely funded by EU funds. The four-star wellness hotel, with its covered pool and wellness complex and restaurant with capacity for 100 diners, has cost around EUR 17.4 million in total, with 94.4 % of this covered by EU funds under Croatia’s recovery and resilience plan12. The exceptionally high financing rate and the blatant touristic/commercial nature of the project give rise to serious questions as to whether this was a justifiable, efficient and proportionate use of European taxpayers’ money. 1.

On what specific basis under EU law and on what grounds was a four-star hotel with a restaurant and a pool and wellness complex deemed eligible for EU support at a financing rate of 94.4 %, despite being a tourist facility that is at least partly intended for commercial use?

With a project of this magnitude, precisely what control mechanisms are in place to ensure that the private operator reaps no undue financial benefit, and which body bears ultimate responsibility for this?

If the funding is found to be insufficiently justified or incompatible with the relevant EU rules, will the Commission ask that a correction be made or funds recovered, and what specific criteria will it apply in making this decision?

E-10-2026-003549.t: Extension of the Digital Services Act to ChatGPT, Reddit and Roblox, and the associated ongoing recruitment drive
qt: to the Commission Mary Khan (ESN) Subject:

On 31 August, the Commission announced that it would classify ChatGPT, Reddit and Roblox as very large online platforms (VLOPs) under the Digital Services Act (DSA).1 The US companies now have until January 2027 to comply with the new requirements and to submit regular reports to the Commission. If the companies behind these online services fail to comply with the EU requirements, they face fines running into millions, up to 6 % of their global annual turnover. This turn of events is deeply worrying as while, across the globe, countries and companies are once again allowing greater freedom of expression and distancing themselves from excessive censorship, the EU is bucking the trend and centralising more control with the Brussels thought police. This increasingly begs the question as to whether this apparatus is not being beefed up with ever more staff to form a politically controlled censorship machine that drains ever more funds and resources. 1.
How many staff members are currently employed in DSA enforcement, and how many additional posts are to be created by 31 December 2026?

In view of the increasing number of companies falling under the DSA, does the Commission plan to recruit even more staff in 2027 for tasks relating to DSA enforcement, and what total staff costs does it anticipate for this?

Given the increasing number of companies to be monitored, why is the Commission not making greater use of synergies, existing structures and efficiency gains, rather than continuously ramping up its workforce and, consequently, its costs?

https://germany.representation.ec.europa.eu/nachrichten-undveranstaltungen/pressemitteilungen/gesetz-uber-digitale-dienste-einstufung-von-chatgpt-reddit-und-roblox-202608-31_de?prefLang=en&etrans=en. 1

E-10-2026-003548.t: Personal connections between InnoEnergy, Northvolt and Stegra
qt: to the Commission Dick Erixon (ECR), Beatrice Timgren (ECR), Charlie Weimers (ECR) Subject:

The Swedish former minister and Social Democrat Ibrahim Baylan was appointed as a special adviser at EIT InnoEnergy in 20231. The financial newspaper Dagens industri later reported that Baylan was apparently an EU lobbyist for Harald Mix’s investment company Vargas, which was behind a number of outfits including Northvolt and H2 Green Steel, now known as Stegra2. Meanwhile, Bo Normark has been the head of industrial strategy at EIT InnoEnergy and an adviser at Vargas3. With the above in mind: 1.
Has the Commission looked into whether the overlapping roles at InnoEnergy, Vargas, Northvolt and Stegra have given rise to conflicts of interest or otherwise influenced decisions on EU funding?

Does the Commission take the view that it would be reasonable to exclude a company from EU funding when its managers or staff in other key positions have previously contributed – through negligence, mismanagement or irregularities – to the loss of EU or other public funds?

How does the Commission ensure that people who have been central to failed projects in receipt of large amounts of public funding are not able, without an in-depth review, to move on to new companies and projects that once again receive support or guarantees from EU taxpayers?

Nordic Projects, https://www.nordiskaprojekt.se/2023/02/28/eit-innoenergy-utser-ibrahim-baylan-tillny-särskild-rådgivare-2/. 2 Dagens Industri, https://www.di.se/nyheter/forre-s-toppen-blir-eu-lobbyist-at-harald-mix/. 3 Impact Loop, https://impactloop.se/artikel/decade-vaxer-med-nya-rekryteringar---tar-in-tunga-vargasrådgivaren. 1
to the Commission Dick Erixon (ECR), Charlie Weimers (ECR), Beatrice Timgren (ECR) Subject:

InnoEnergy’s former CEO Diego Pavia and financial director Bart de Beer received more than EUR 9.2 million in remuneration from the company1. Between 2010 and 2024, InnoEnergy received up to EUR 760 million in EU grants, and in its first decade, EU funding accounted for between 60 and 90 % of the company’s revenue2. In addition, former employees have described staff meetings where 150-200 employees were flown in from Europe and the US, and where the evenings included food, entertainment and what a source described as basically unrestricted access to alcohol3. With the above in mind: 1.
Were EU funds used to finance the trips in question, staff expenses or other entertainment costs?
How does the Commission ensure that public funding does not indirectly facilitate the payment of excessive remuneration or entertainment costs?
In the light of the above, does the Commission take the view that InnoEnergy continues to be a suitable recipient for EU funding?

E-10-2026-003546.t: Millions granted to InnoEnergy despite clear failings
qt: to the Commission Dick Erixon (ECR), Charlie Weimers (ECR), Beatrice Timgren (ECR) Subject:

InnoEnergy was awarded EUR 10 million in EU support for the training and reskilling of workers in the European battery sector1. The company subsequently announced that more than 100 000 people had been trained. A review shows, however, that the figure was based on certificates issued rather than on the number of individuals, meaning that one person could be counted several times over. Certificates could be obtained even with a score of 0 % in a test, and around 10 % of the reported participants came from a Minecraft-based educational game aimed at children2. Although InnoEnergy is currently being investigated by the European Public Prosecutor’s Office for suspected grant and VAT fraud, the EU has already granted an additional EUR 9 million to InnoEnergy to set up a similar academy for the solar energy sector3. With the above in mind: 1.
Why has InnoEnergy been awarded additional grants despite ongoing investigations into grant and VAT fraud?
Why has InnoEnergy been awarded additional grants despite the extensive accounting shortcomings described above?
Will the Commission seek recovery of the funds concerned if it finds that EU grants have been misused, and will additional EU funding be suspended?

E-10-2026-003545.t: Grant-focused entrepreneurs cashing in on the EU’s investment policy
qt: to the Commission Dick Erixon (ECR), Beatrice Timgren (ECR), Charlie Weimers (ECR) Subject:

InnoEnergy, an EU-funded venture capital company, has received EU grants to the tune of EUR 760 million1. The European Public Prosecutor’s Office has now opened an investigation into the company in response to a report of suspected financial irregularities. The allegations relate to grant and VAT fraud2. With the above in mind: 1.

Does the Commission take the view that its policy of channelling capital towards the green transition through tax revenues risks distorting the market and attracting operators whose business model relies heavily on obtaining public funds, rather than allowing the market to determine which technologies and companies are competitive?
How does the Commission assess the risk that the EU’s funding model means that although taxpayers bear a significant share of the risk, any financial gains fall into private hands?
In the light of the large number of failed investments made as part of the ‘green transition’, will the Commission stop subsidising so-called welfare entrepreneurs?
