E-10-2026-003544.t: The disappearance of CD players from newly produced vehicles
qt: to the Commission Fernand Kartheiser (NI), Irmhild Boßdorf (ESN), Diana Iovanovici Şoşoacă (NI) Subject:

While CD sales are currently showing signs of growth, many consumers have expressed frustration at the disappearance of CD players from new vehicles. At the same time, the European automotive market appears to be moving towards the full digitalisation of music and entertainment media. In addition to cultural disadvantages, including discrimination of smaller languages, limited access to rarer titles and potentially lower incomes for artists, this development also raises legitimate road safety concerns, as navigating through infotainment system touchscreens may cause greater visual and cognitive distraction than operating the vehicle controls. Against this backdrop, concerns have been raised about the unintended consequences of the EU General Safety Regulation II (GSR II). In particular, its implementation has contributed to the discontinuation of certain equipment, including CD players, affecting the marketability of vehicles still equipped with such systems. 1.
Does the Commission intend to assess whether, and to what extent, GSR II has contributed to the disappearance of CD players from new vehicles?
Was this an intended or foreseeable consequence of GSR II?
Does the Commission intend to ensure that consumers can retain a CD player as an optional feature when acquiring a new vehicle, including by amending GSR II?

E-10-2026-003542.t: National enforcement of the EU Batteries Regulation
qt: to the Commission Eero Heinäluoma (S&D) Subject:

The batteries of electric vehicles (EVs) account for the largest single share of an EV’s price. To increase the number of EVs in use and decrease emissions from the transport sector, it is essential to ensure that EVs can be repaired at a reasonable cost. As a new battery for a used EV can cost well more than the market price of the vehicle, the only solution, in many cases, is to repair used batteries. This also decreases the life-cycle emissions of EVs, as battery manufacturing forms a major part of their emissions. In Finland, the enforcement of Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 (the Batteries Regulation) has posed challenges to the affordable repair of EV batteries. In particular, repairing existing batteries can cause disproportionate administrative and financial burdens, as the repairer risks becoming a remanufacturer, with related requirements. For instance, in accordance with national instructions, if the battery undergoes a small repair without official manufacturer instructions (which are not always available), the repairer becomes a remanufacturer, with related requirements. Our concern is that this will make EV battery repair excessively difficult and expensive. Against this background, we ask the Commission: 1.
Does it consider the national enforcement of the Batteries Regulation to be in line with the goals and requirements of the regulation?
What steps does it aim to take to ensure that affordable solutions exist for repairing and refurbishing EV batteries?

E-10-2026-003541.t: Ensuring direct support for beekeepers and a special funding envelope in the new programming period 2028-2034
qt: to the Commission Elena Kountoura (The Left), Konstantinos Arvanitis (The Left) Subject:

Following a previous question1 on the need to support Greek and European beekeeping, the situation facing the sector remains critical and European support remains inadequate. In its reply2, the Commission referred to the existing support tools that are available through the 2023-2027 CAP and stated that it would continue to work with Member States and industry representatives to consider further support measures. However, the new funding structure for the 2028-2034 CAP, which will be delivered through the National and Regional Partnership Plans, raises legitimate concerns among industry representatives3 about maintaining the current distinct European financial framework for beekeeping4. It seems that, from now on, the support offered will be at the discretion of each Member State, with no European guarantees and guaranteed minimum allocations. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Does it intend to support the preservation of the special funding envelope for beekeeping with sufficient and guaranteed financial support within the new 2028-2034 CAP funding structure?

What measures does it intend to take under the new CAP to support the granting of annual subsidies for individual beehives for pollination services and to ensure both that they are adequately funded and that beekeepers from all Member States have equal access?
What initiatives will it take to support the beekeeping sector in Greece, where the effects of climate change are particularly acute?

https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/E-10-2024-002941_EN.html. https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/E-10-2024-002941-ASW_EN.html. 3 In a letter, the European Beekeeping Association warns that if the special beekeeping envelope is abolished, the sector risks taking a significant hit. It calls on the European Institutions to preserve and strengthen the envelope in the new CAP, underlining the importance of beekeepers for pollination, agricultural production, biodiversity and food security (https://ebaeurope.eu/eba-executive-board-endorses-letter-to-eu-institutions-onthe-beekeeping-envelope/). 4 As has been the case so far under Article 55 of Regulation (EU) 2021/2115, which, among other things and in accordance with paragraph 4 thereof, provides for a guaranteed EU co-financing rate of 50 %. 1 2

E-10-2026-003540.t: Consultation on the possible inclusion of Asparagopsis taxiformis seaweed in the list of invasive alien species of Union concern
qt: to the Commission Adrián Vázquez Lázara (PPE) Subject:

In recent months, the Spanish scientific and fishing community has become increasingly concerned about the extension of the seaweed Asparagopsis taxiformis towards the coasts of southern Galicia. Although it is already a common species in southern Spain, its arrival in new areas could significantly alter the Galician marine ecosystem, not only by displacing native species, but also by changing entire ecological communities and ultimately affecting local fishing activities. As it stands, Asparagopsis taxiformis is not on the list of invasive alien species of Union concern, pursuant to Regulation (EU) No 1143/2014. Can the Commission provide information on: 1.
Whether it is considering revising that list to include Asparagopsis taxiformi, given the risk it poses to marine biodiversity?

Regardless of whether that species is included in the catalogue, the EU measures or financial instruments that could be taken to control its expansion and mitigate its impact on the Galician ecosystem?

E-10-2026-003539.t: Chatbots directing women with unwanted pregnancies to anti-abortion websites
qt: to the Commission Kim Van Sparrentak (Verts/ALE), Marit Maij (S&D), Sandro Gozi (Renew), Sirpa Pietikäinen (PPE), Brando Benifei (S&D), Chloé Ridel (S&D), Carla Tavares (S&D), Elio Di Rupo (S&D), Birgit Sippel (S&D), Alessandra Moretti (S&D), Elisabeth Grossmann (S&D), Idoia Mendia (S&D), Katarina Barley (S&D), Marc Angel (S&D), Maria Noichl (S&D), Joanna Scheuring-Wielgus (S&D), Marko Vešligaj (S&D), Robert Biedroń (S&D), Emma Rafowicz (S&D), Heléne Fritzon (S&D), Evin Incir (S&D), Marianne Vind (S&D), Kathleen Van Brempt (S&D), Karin Karlsbro (Renew), Benoit Cassart (Renew), Sigrid Friis (Renew), Olivier Chastel (Renew), Veronika Cifrová Ostrihoňová (Renew), Raquel García Hermida-Van Der Walle (Renew), Yvan Verougstraete (Renew), Lucia Yar (Renew), Markéta Gregorová (Verts/ALE), Marie Toussaint (Verts/ALE), Villy Søvndal (Verts/ALE), Rasmus Nordqvist (Verts/ALE), Sara Matthieu (Verts/ALE), Tineke Strik (Verts/ALE), Anna Cavazzini (Verts/ALE), Alexandra Geese (Verts/ALE), Kai Tegethoff (Verts/ALE), Nela Riehl (Verts/ALE), Anna Strolenberg (Verts/ALE), Katrin Langensiepen (Verts/ALE), Ana Miranda Paz (Verts/ALE), Lena Schilling (Verts/ALE), Saskia Bricmont (Verts/ALE), Benedetta Scuderi (Verts/ALE), Catarina Vieira (Verts/ALE), Majdouline Sbai (Verts/ALE), Maria Ohisalo (Verts/ALE), Mélissa Camara (Verts/ALE), Pernando Barrena Arza (The Left), Carolina Morace (The Left), Kathleen Funchion (The Left), Manon Aubry (The Left), Estrella Galán (The Left), Luke Ming Flanagan (The Left), Hilde Vautmans (Renew), Hanna Gedin (The Left), Rudi Kennes (The Left), Leila Chaibi (The Left), Lynn Boylan (The Left), Anja Hazekamp (The Left), Ilaria Salis (The Left), Damien Carême (The Left), Mohammed Chahim (S&D), Thijs Reuten (S&D), Reinier Van Lanschot (Verts/ALE) Subject:

According to reports by AlgorithmWatch1, general-purpose AI chatbots across Europe blur the line between official health information and anti-abortion advocacy, directing users seeking information in cases of unwanted pregnancy to anti-abortion content without clearly identifying sources, including by failing to distinguish between official health authorities and anti-abortion organisations, making it difficult for users to assess the provenance and reliability of the information. A team of female journalists tested ChatGPT-5 (OpenAI), Gemini 3 (Google), Grok 4.3 (xAI) and Claude Sonnet 4.8 (Anthropic). In Italy and the UK, official sources were not consistently included in chatbot responses, while in Germany recommendations for help even misdirected people to anti-abortion ‘counselling’, despite the fact that official consultations with healthcare professionals are required locally for an abortion. 1.

Does the Commission agree that reliable healthcare information on abortion from official sources is essential to protect the health, safety and fundamental rights of people in Europe and, if so, does it agree that the general-purpose AI chatbots could pose a systemic risk under the AI Act and, in the case of ChatGPT, under the Digital Services Act?
Is the Commission aware of the AlgorithmWatch report? If so, what steps has it taken to investigate and address this issue?
https://algorithmwatch.org/en/chatbots-abortion-ai/.
What other steps is the Commission taking to address the reliability of information given by chatbots and even possible foreign influence via chatbots?

E-10-2026-003536.t: Supporting the adoption of new technologies by small and medium-sized enterprises in less developed Member States
qt: to the Commission Claudiu-Richard Târziu (ECR) Subject:

Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in Member States such as Romania are particularly exposed to high energy and administrative costs and have more limited access to finance, digital skills and qualified personnel. These constraints can make it difficult for them to adopt advanced technologies, including artificial intelligence. 1.

How will the Commission ensure that its simplification agenda produces measurable benefits for SMEs in Member States with less developed economies and does not disproportionately favour larger companies?
Will the Commission consider strengthening the ‘SME first’ principle by systematically assessing the administrative and financial impact of new EU legislation on SMEs?

What concrete financial, training and technical support does the Commission plan to provide to SMEs in countries such as Romania to accelerate the adoption of artificial intelligence and other advanced technologies?

E-10-2026-003535.t: Energy security, electricity prices and the role of the European Union Agency for the Cooperation of Energy Regulators in Romania
qt: to the Commission Claudiu-Richard Târziu (ECR) Subject:

Romania faces significant challenges regarding the security and adequacy of its electricity system, including insufficient generation capacity, delays in developing new capacity, limited storage, and infrastructure constraints. At the same time, high and volatile electricity prices are placing pressure on Romanian households and industry. 1.

What measures does the Commission expect the European Union Agency for the Cooperation of Energy Regulators (ACER) to take to support better integration of regional electricity markets and stronger interconnections, while ensuring that the benefits of the internal energy market are effectively passed on to consumers and industry in Member States such as Romania?

How does the Commission intend to address persistent differences in electricity costs between EU producers and their competitors outside the EU, particularly where high energy prices undermine the competitiveness of European industry?

In the Commission’s view, which of the following should have priority for investment in Romania, to improve system adequacy and reduce price volatility: cross-border interconnections, electricity storage, additional generation capacity or demand-side flexibility?

E-10-2026-003534.t: Why is Panama still on the EU tax blacklist?
qt: to the Council Sebastian Kruis (PfE), Ton Diepeveen (PfE) Subject:

Panama’s banking system is smaller than a single Belgian retail bank, and the foreign money held there comes mainly from Latin America, not Europe. Panama left the financial action task force (FATF) grey list in 2023, was removed from the EU list of high-risk third countries in 2025, and adopted economic substance rules in May 2026, which will enter into force on 1 January 2027. It nonetheless remains on Annex I to the EU list of non-cooperative jurisdictions for tax purposes. With billions of dollars in canal-terminal, water and railway contracts set to be awarded over the coming year, Panamanian President José Raúl Mulino has barred European companies from public tenders while the listing remains in place. 1.
Why does Panama remain on Annex I, and which specific criteria are still unmet?
Does the Council accept the fact that the tax listing now costs European companies more than it changes anything in Panama?

Will the Council consider the strategic geopolitical perspective and remove Panama from Annex I during the October 2026 revision of the list, so that European firms can compete for important international contracts in Panama?

E-10-2026-003533.t: Progress on Panama’s yellow card on fisheries
qt: to the Commission Sebastian Kruis (PfE), Ton Diepeveen (PfE) Subject:

Panama has held a yellow card, the EU’s formal warning that a country is not doing enough to stop illegal fishing, since December 2019. Panama says it has rewritten its fisheries law, hired inspectors, opened a monitoring centre and tightened controls at ports and processing plants. At this stage, one of Panama’s main priorities is the completion and implementation of its traceability system. Its implementation is taking longer than expected owing to the technical, administrative and budgetary requirements associated with a system of this scope. Panama is no small partner: it runs the Panama Canal, flags more ships than other countries, and sits in a region the EU should have closer ties with. 1.
Will the Commission set out a clear timeline and the criteria that Panama still has to meet, and will it give the country the time it needs to finish its work on the traceability system?
What help can the Commission offer a country under a yellow card, and will it offer that help to Panama, so that this becomes a dialogue more about support and cooperation than about cards?
How does the Commission weigh this process against the EU’s strategic and trade interests in Panama and Latin America, while other global powers move into the region?

E-10-2026-003532.t: Revision of EU legislation on healthcare abroad
qt: to the Commission Mihai Tudose (S&D) Subject:

Fifteen years on from the entry into force of the directive regulating access to cross-border healthcare in the EU, the time has come to take stock and act for the benefit of the citizens. As outlined in a recent study carried out by the European Parliamentary Research Service, European patients still face bureaucratic and financial obstacles when seeking treatment in another Member State. This is primarily due to patients not being well-informed about their rights and to prior authorisation and cost reimbursement procedures being overly complex. This calls for improved coordination of national public health systems and their interoperability, including through the European Health Data Space (EHDS). This space should be up and running in the next five years, in accordance with the EHDS Regulation, which came into force last year. 1.
We are currently in a transition period and in March next year the Commission needs to present a set of detailed implementing rules. At what stage is the preparation of these rules?
More broadly, is the Commission considering a revision of the directive to fully ensure equitable access to healthcare and the free movement of health services and medicines?

E-10-2026-003528.t: Transparency in the banking market and possible breach of the passivity rule in the Intesa Sanpaolo-MPS case
qt: to the Commission Gaetano Pedulla' (The Left), Pasquale Tridico (The Left) Subject:

Intesa Sanpaolo’s complaint to Consob – Italy’s financial markets regulatory and supervisory authority – contesting the correctness of the announced Monte dei Paschi di Siena (MPS) exchange offer for Banco BPM and Banca Generali highlights serious problems in the application of EU legislation on financial markets1. Specifically, the transaction raises serious doubts as to compliance with Article 9 of Directive 2004/25/EC (the Takeover Directive) in relation to the passivity rule (the obligation of management bodies to refrain from defensive actions that could run counter to the objectives of the offer) and with the obligations of timely disclosure of inside information laid down in Regulation (EU) No 596/2014 (the Market Abuse Regulation – MAR). In addition to undermining financial stability, such conduct risks breaching the principles of investor protection and transparency set out in the MiFID II Directive (2014/65/EU), to the detriment of small savers. In view of the above: 1.
Does the Commission consider MPS’s conduct to be a circumvention of the passivity rule within the meaning of Article 9 of Directive 2004/25/EC?
How does it intend to ask the European Securities and Markets Authority to confirm whether there have been breaches of the MAR (Regulation (EU) No 596/2014) rules on correct market information?
What urgent steps will it take to strengthen MiFID II safeguards to protect small shareholders exposed to potential market distortion manoeuvres?

https://www.corriere.it/economia/finanza/26_agosto_26/intesa-sanpaolo-esposto-alla-consob-sulleoperazioni-annunciate-da-mps-dopo-l-opas-dc786b43-2f6b-43a7-8143-9b57c5698xlk.shtml; https://www.ansa.it/sito/notizie/economia/2026/08/21/intesa-sanpaolo-valuta-esposto-alla-consob-sumps_14b84922-cb20-4ca7-b3cd-06f3c121a703.html. 1

E-10-2026-003527.t: Temporary closure of the Bay of Biscay
qt: to the Commission Oihane Agirregoitia Martínez (Renew) Subject:

After three consecutive years (2024, 2025 and 2026) of the bay being closed temporarily for four weeks in February, with pair trawling (and other types of fishing) banned to reduce the number of cetaceans being stranded on the coast of France (Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/3089), we would like to ask: 1.
In view of the lack of information, after three consecutive years, what effect has the measure adopted had on the decline in cetacean numbers?
What economic and social impact has the measure had?
If there are no clear conclusions on the social, economic and environmental impact, would the Commission consider reviewing or scrapping the measure, since its economic and social impact is clear?

E-10-2026-003524.t: EU Commission confirms wind turbines are harmful for health and the environment
qt: to the Commission Gerald Hauser (PfE) Subject:

In its response to written question 002323/20261 from Gerald Hauser MEP, the EU Commission confirms that microplastics are harmful for both the environment and health. Whilst it claims that ‘plastic emissions from wind turbines are much lower than from other sources’, it does not refute the studies cited by Gerald Hauser MEP, according to which one wind turbine can shed up to 62 kg of microplastics annually. Furthermore, the European Commission states that ‘assessment of the environmental impacts of offshore wind [has] also [been] addressed under Horizon Europe’. The EU project HORIZON-HLTH-2026-01-DISEASE-03, cited by the European Commission, focuses, amongst other things, on the long-term health effects of certain environmental and exposure factors. The European Commission thus confirms, in an official document, a link between wind turbines and adverse health effects. Other EU projects also focus on further research into the massive impact of micro- and nanoplastics on human health, as well as environmental damage caused by offshore wind farms. 1.
Why has the Commission thus far studied only microplastic emissions from offshore wind farms, but not from onshore wind farms?
Why has the Commission so far failed to inform the public that wind turbines are causing massive microplastic pollution?
Why has the Commission so far failed to inform the public that wind turbines can have significant adverse impact on health?
https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/E-10-2026-002323-ASW_EN.html.

E-10-2026-003523.t: Local warming effects and the impact of wind turbines on soil moisture and droughts
qt: to the Commission Gerald Hauser (PfE) Subject:

Scientific studies show that wind turbines can impinge on the local climate. The 2018 Harvard study ‘Climatic Impacts of Wind Power’ by Lee M. Miller and David W. Keith calculated that generating all of the country’s electricity with wind turbines would warm the continental USA by 0.24°C.1 At night, local warming of up to 1.5°C was simulated. The researchers chiefly attribute this to the wind turbines’ mixing air with the near-surface atmosphere. Their model further determined that in the first century of use, the direct warming effect of wind power during would exceed the cooling effect of the avoided emissions. This poses questions, particularly in respect of ever-increasing heatwaves and droughts. 1.
What information does the Commission have on the local warming effects of wind turbines?
Has the Commission investigated the extent to which wind farms in the EU are already influencing local temperatures, and, if so, what conclusions has it drawn?
What consequences does the Commission expect the further expansion of wind power to have on local temperatures, soil moisture and the frequency and intensity of dry spells and droughts in the EU?
https://news.harvard.edu/gazette/story/2018/10/large-scale-wind-power-has-its-down-side/.

E-10-2026-003522.t: Perpetuation of gender stereotypes in a new school textbook in Greece
qt: to the Commission Elena Kountoura (The Left) Subject:

In recent months there has been scathing criticism of a new textbook titled ‘Social and Political Education’1. The textbook, which is to be used as of 2027, is intended for pupils attending the final year of lower secondary school. The criticism centres around passages on gender roles and gender-based violence that perpetuate gender stereotypes and shift the burden of protection from abuse onto the potential victim. According to the book, the woman’s role in the family is to ‘bring up children and take care of the household’, while the man’s role is to perform ‘heavy chores, handyman tasks and take care of things outside of the home’. Moreover, instead of clearly articulating the fundamental principle that responsibility for any form of abuse rests solely with the offender, the chapter on abuse advises girls to follow ‘practical advice’, which includes ‘avoiding unsafe situations’ and ‘violent, aggressive and manipulative’ men2. Given that Directive (EU) 2024/1385 on combating violence against women requires Member States to take measures to prevent the perpetuation of harmful gender stereotypes and to carry out awareness-raising campaigns aimed, inter alia, at children3, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

Does it consider the perpetuation of such stereotypes in a school textbook to be consistent with the obligations arising from Directive (EU) 2024/1385 on the prevention and elimination of harmful gender stereotypes?
How does it intend to ensure that the correct transposition of the Directive is not undermined by practical or educational material perpetuating the very stereotypes that it seeks to combat?

Social and Political Education - School textbook for pupils of the final year of lower secondary school Ministry of Education, Religious Affairs and Sports, Institute of Educational Policy (https://ebooksdl.cti.gr/view?item=20.500.14040/30230). 2 Directive (EU) 2024/1385 on combatting violence against women and domestic violence, Chapter 5 ‘Prevention and early intervention’, Article 34 ‘Preventive measures’ and Article 35 ‘Specific measures to prevent rape and to promote the central role of consent in sexual relationships’ (https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legalcontent/En/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202401385). The Greek Government has failed to fully transpose Directive (EU) 2024/1385 into Greek law. 3 It should be noted that gender-based violence is still on the rise in Greece. In 2026, 14 femicides have been recorded in Greece within a period of nine months and according to EIGE’s Equality Index for 2025 the rate of gender-based violence in Greece is above the EU average (https://eige.europa.eu/gender-equalityindex/2025/domain/violence/EL). 1

to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Céline Imart (PPE), François-Xavier Bellamy (PPE), Nicolas Bay (ECR), Ilia Lazarov (PPE), Christophe Gomart (PPE), Aleksandar Nikolic (PfE), Andrey Kovatchev (PPE), Julien Leonardelli (PfE), Michalis Hadjipantela (PPE), Sebastian Tynkkynen (ECR) Subject:

For nearly 40 years, the Polisario Front has been implicated in numerous attacks targeting civilians, including Europeans. The most recent attack, on 5 May 2026 in Es-Smara, left one person injured and was condemned by the European Union, France and the United States. Meanwhile, the EU allocates EUR 9 million of humanitarian aid per year to the Tindouf camps, which are administered by the Polisario Front, while the UN Office of the High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) is not permitted to carry out an independent census of the camps’ residents, despite the UN’s repeated requests for such a census. Furthermore, on 2 October 2025, the EU indicated its intention to increase this aid. This situation raises questions about the traceability of EU funds benefiting, even indirectly, an organisation that employs terrorist methods. In this context: 1.

Does the Commission intend to make any increase in humanitarian aid for the Tindouf camps conditional on an independent registration of beneficiaries by the UNHCR, in order to guarantee the transparency and sound management of EU funds?

Given the repeated attacks targeting the civilian population, has the Commission assessed, or does it intend to assess, the situation of the Polisario Front against the criteria applicable for inclusion on the EU’s list of terrorist organisations?
to the Commission Catherine Griset (PfE), André Rougé (PfE), Marie-Luce Brasier-Clain (PfE), Valérie Deloge (PfE), Séverine Werbrouck (PfE), Pierre Pimpie (PfE) Subject:

While major fires have been breaking out across France and Europe, the existing Canadair fleets are ageing and no longer fit for purpose. On top of that, the Canadairs that have been ordered won’t be arriving anytime soon – the earliest batch will be arriving in 2028 and the later orders in 2032. Further to these new acquisitions, French and European companies (Positive Aviation, Kepplair Evolution, Hynaero, etc.) are working on innovative water bomber aircraft1, converting, for example, used ATR 72 aircraft into amphibious FF72 capable of scooping up 8 000 litres of water at half the cost. These projects would also reduce operating costs by 40 %. The idea of creating water-bombing drones is also being looked at, including by converting existing and decommissioned aircraft into drones. 1.
Is the Commission financing or is it prepared to finance the purchase of these new water-bombing planes or drones?
At the same time, would it be possible to obtain a licence to build Canadair in Europe?
Supporter2
https://x.com/AlexXplore/status/2080954114326876556?s=20. This question is supported by a Member other than the authors: Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE).
to the Commission Aldo Patriciello (PfE) Subject:

Can the Commission say what political, institutional and administrative discussions, if any, have taken place in relation to infringement procedure INFR (2026)4004, and could it clarify the nature of the arguments and opinions put forward by representatives of the Italian State? Specifically, has the Italian State cited political expediency, budgetary constraints or a desire to curb spending in support of its stance? If this is indeed the case, to what extent (if at all) will the Commission take these arguments into account when assessing the compatibility with EU law of Italy’s regulations governing the economic, welfare and social rights of the tax judges concerned?

E-10-2026-003518.t: Bolstering Facebook and Instagram’s child safeguards in the light of Meta’s US settlement
qt: to the Commission Sandro Ruotolo (S&D), Nicola Zingaretti (S&D) Subject:

Meta has agreed to a USD 16.7 billion settlement in a lawsuit brought against the company by a number of US states that had accused Facebook and Instagram of harming the well-being and mental health of underage users. This settlement has shed light on a situation of the utmost concern. Meta employees and witnesses revealed during the proceedings that the company kept certain underused protective measures in place and elected not to implement more effective alternatives because it did not want teenage users to spend less time on its platforms. This evidence only strengthens concerns that Meta is putting profits ahead of child safety. In the light of these developments and given that the Commission itself opened proceedings against Meta in May 2024 over child protection concerns, we ask the Commission: 1.
Over two years since it launched this investigation, how far along are its enquiries, and what conclusions have they reached so far?

Does the Digital Services Act give the Commission the power to compel Meta to introduce measures similar to the ones it has pledged to enforce in the US (time limits, night-time blocks et al), or would new legislation be needed to achieve this?

E-10-2026-003517.t: Effects of the F-gas Regulation on village shops in sparsely populated areas and rural vitality
qt: to the Commission Elsi Katainen (Renew) Subject:

In order to comply with F-gas Regulation (EU) 2024/573, many village shops will need to modernise their refrigeration equipment in the coming years. In Finland, the average amount that will need to be invested is estimated to be around EUR 190 000 per shop. Many shops in sparsely populated areas, which are already not very profitable, are unable to afford the investment needed and may be forced out of business. The closure of village shops would undermine services in rural areas and could mean that people have to travel unreasonably far to do their shopping. A deterioration in services has an adverse effect on regions’ vitality, and, at worst, forces people to leave their home regions. This is at odds with the Right to Stay strategy, the aim of which is to ensure that Europeans have the opportunity to remain and build their future in the place they call home, rather than being forced to relocate because they cannot earn a living or access essential services. In rural areas in particular, the situation is compounded by the fact that services are already under pressure owing to long distances and rising logistics costs, among other factors. The significant additional investment required under the F-gas Regulation may therefore make it even more difficult to keep local services going. Local shops offer a wide range of services, and if they close down it may also mean the end for pharmacy, postal and parcel services. With the above in mind: 1.
Has the Commission assessed what impact the implementation of the regulation will have on keeping grocery shops and other local services going in sparsely populated areas?

Is the Commission intending to prepare targeted exemptions, financial instruments or other support measures to ensure that the significant investment burden caused by the regulation does not lead to shops being closed, the deterioration of services and people having to travel unreasonably far to do their shopping?

E-10-2026-003516.t: Access criteria for transnational club competitions following Case C-333/21
qt: to the Commission Aodhán Ó Ríordáin (S&D) Subject:

In Case C-333/21, the Court of Justice of the European Union held that UEFA’s rules on the prior approval of interclub competitions infringe Articles 101 and 102 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union where they are not subject to substantive criteria and procedural rules ensuring transparency, objectivity, precision, non-discrimination and proportionality. UEFA’s Authorisation Rules Governing International Club Competitions (Edition 2024) do not state whether an authorised transnational club competition – including one situated above national leagues, with promotion, relegation and solidarity payments – would carry places in the UEFA Champions League, Europa League or Conference League, how many such places, at what stage of qualification they would enter, or by reference to what criteria this would be determined. Article 51bis of the UEFA Statutes devolves decisions on access to European club competitions to each national association. 1.

Does the Commission consider the absence of published criteria governing access to UEFA club competitions for an authorised transnational competition to be compatible with the judgment in Case C-333/21?
Does the Commission consider that devolving that decision to the national associations affected satisfies the requirement of non-discrimination?

Given the Commission’s support for the European sport model and its principles of openness and sporting merit, will the Commission examine whether the allocation of guaranteed access within UEFA’s club competitions is consistent with those principles, particularly as regards smaller member associations?

E-10-2026-003515.t: Protecting children in Ceuta during the border crisis
qt: to the Commission Alvise Pérez (NI) Subject:

According to the Department of Education, Culture and Youth, the Government of Ceuta has decided that Nuestra Señora de Africa and Juan Carlos I nursery schools will not open until 28 September, rather than 8 September, when they were originally scheduled to open. Ceuta estimates that the invasion of 30 July 2027 saw more than 80 000 people enter the territory illegally. The European Parliament resolution of 10 June 2021 (2021/2747 (RSP)) condemned Morocco’s use of minors in Ceuta. Article 1(4)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1359 provides a definition of instrumentalisation, Article 24 of the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights protects the best interests of the child and COM(2023)0298 sets out the EU’s approach to mental health. 1.

Will the Commission ask Spain to provide information on how the crisis has affected children, including data on absenteeism, schooling, safety and psychological care? Will it recommend an independent assessment and a contingency plan with public indicators?

Will it ensure that those affected receive emergency assistance under the Asylum, Migration and Integration Fund, in accordance with Article 31 of Regulation (EU) 2021/1147, and support under the Citizens, Equality, Rights and Values programme and EU4Health?

Will it assess whether the funds the EU gave Morocco for migration and border management were used in line with the existing agreement and the conditionality it requires, and will it suspend funding in the event of non-compliance?

E-10-2026-003514.t: Administrative burden on micro and small enterprises in cross-border online trade as a result of the application of the Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation
qt: to the Commission Željana Zovko (PPE) Subject:

Regulation (EU) 2025/40 on packaging and packaging waste introduces key obligations to ensure that producers help pay for the management of packaging waste. However, the application of Articles 44 and 45 risks creating a disproportionate administrative burden for tradespeople and micro and small enterprises involved in cross-border B2C online trade. 1.

Does the Commission intend to perform a targeted assessment of the impact of Articles 44 and 45 on tradespeople and micro and small enterprises occasionally selling crossborder B2C or placing very small quantities of packaging on the market of another Member State, encompassing cumulative fixed administrative costs in more than one Member States?

How does it intend to ensure that registration fees and the costs associated with mandatory authorised representation are proportionate and based on actual costs, particularly for producers placing very small quantities of packaging on the market of a single Member State?

Is it considering the possibility of establishing a harmonised, simplified regime or a de minimis threshold for very small quantities of packaging and occasional cross-border sales, as well as a single European registration and reporting system, modelled on the VAT One Stop Shop scheme, while maintaining the obligation on producers to help pay for the management of packaging waste in the country of destination?

E-10-2026-003512.t: Possible designation of Spotify as a very large online platform under the Digital Services Act
qt: to the Commission Konstantinos Arvanitis (The Left) Subject:

Spotify provides access to podcasts, audiobooks, public playlists and associated text, images and video supplied by users and professional creators. It recommends and disseminates that content through algorithmic systems and monetises user attention through subscriptions and advertising. Spotify itself treats Spotify Main, Spotify for Creators, Spotify for Artists and Spotify for Authors as intermediary services under the Digital Services Act (DSA). Its latest figures report 751 million monthly active users globally, with growth in Europe. Nevertheless, Spotify is absent from the Commission’s list of designated very large online platforms (VLOPs). Under Articles 3(i), 3(p) and 33 DSA, services disseminating recipient-supplied information to the public must be designated as VLOPs when they have at least 45 million average monthly active recipients in the EU. Given Spotify’s scale, recommender systems and capacity to amplify podcasts and other content affecting public discourse, consumer protection and fundamental rights: 1.
Has the Commission assessed whether Spotify’s relevant intermediary services constitute online platforms and exceed the Article 33 threshold?
Has it requested service-specific EU recipient data from Spotify under Article 24(3) DSA, including recipients exposed to creator-uploaded content through Spotify Main?
If the conditions are satisfied, will the Commission designate the relevant Spotify services as VLOPs, and if not, will it publish its legal and quantitative reasons for not doing so?

E-10-2026-003511.t: Under-representation of Poland and Central and Eastern European countries in EEAS staff, in particular in management positions
qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Michał Dworczyk (ECR) Subject:

The under-representation of Central and Eastern European countries, including Poland, among the staff of the European External Action Service is structural and is particularly evident in management positions and among EU Heads of Delegation. I already drew attention to this issue back in 20241. In response to my question, the VicePresident of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy gave an assurance that she was working towards a more balanced representation of the Member States that have joined the EU since 2004, and was monitoring the geographical balance in the EEAS2. However, the latest appointments made by the VicePresident / High Representative as part of the EEAS rotation exercise suggest the opposite. Among the 33 nominated EU Ambassadors and the seven Deputy Heads of Delegation, there are no Polish nationals, despite 13 candidates having applied. Moreover, of the 40 new appointments, only a small proportion were given to nationals of the countries that have joined the EU since 2004. In this connection: 1.

Why is there no one from Poland among the latest appointments, especially considering the country’s size, its location on the eastern border of the EU and its particular role in EU security, as well as the fact that 13 Polish candidates applied?
Since providing an answer to question E-003067/2024, what action has the EEAS taken to improve the geographical balance of the representatives of the countries that have joined the EU since 2004?

Since December 2024, how many special events and information sessions on opportunities for employment and career progression at the EEAS have been either held in Poland or targeted at potential candidates from Poland?
https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/E-10-2024-003067_EN.html. https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/E-10-2024-003067-ASW_EN.html.
to the Commission Christine Anderson (ESN) Subject:

Following the mass entry of migrants into Ceuta on 30-31 July 2026, Commission Executive Vice-President Virkkunen stated on 7 August – while organisers and circumstances remained unknown – that Meta and TikTok must act decisively, increase monitoring and strengthen cooperation with fact-checkers1. On 10 August, she announced Digital Services Act-linked crisis protocols and an ad hoc fact-checking mechanism to ‘stifle criminal networks selling false promises’2. Spain’s National Centre for Immigration and Borders.(CENIF) did not submit its report to the Audiencia Nacional until 31 August 2026 (made public on 1 September)3. It describes a sophisticated, planned operation, highlights permissiveness and active guidance by Moroccan security forces, excludes local criminal organisations as capable organisers and does not identify those ultimately responsible for directing the operation4. Social media was therefore an instrument used by third parties, while the facts needed to assess contemporaneous claims only emerged weeks later. 1.

What evidence did the Commission have at the time concerning Meta’s and TikTok’s conduct, as distinct from that of users or organisers, and, if it had none, why did it publicly demand increased monitoring and fact-checking?
Which specific claims were classified as false, and on what contemporaneous evidence, and were any subsequently confirmed or materially qualified by the CENIF report?

Regarding the Commission-coordinated mechanism, what content or accounts were flagged, on what legal basis and with what moderation outcome, and will the Commission publish this audit trail and safeguards protecting lawful or subsequently verified information?

Henna Virkkunen, statement on X, 7 August 2026, https://x.com/HennaVirkkunen/status/2085807830074904693. 2 Henna Virkkunen, statements on X, 10 August 2026, concerning the crisis protocols and fact-checking mechanism and the stated aim of ‘stifling criminal networks’ https://x.com/HennaVirkkunen/status/2086905875889832362 and https://x.com/HennaVirkkunen/status/2086905877433389465. 3 El Español, 1 September 2026, https://www.elespanol.com/espana/tribunales/20260901/policiainforma-juez-invasion-ceuta-guiada-gendarmes-marroquies-ordenes-agentes-paisano-fin-distintomigratorio/1003744369590_0.html. 4 Spanish National Police/CENIF, Report on the irregular mass entry into Ceuta, particularly pp. 10, 16– 17, 34 and 47–50; see also the detailed account in El País, 2 September 2026, https://elpais.com/espana/2026-0902/el-informe-de-la-policia-apunta-que-agentes-marroquies-guiaron-la-entrada-de-migrantes-a-ceuta.html. 1

E-10-2026-003506.t: Regulatory perimeter of ChatGPT’s designation as a very large online search engine
qt: to the Commission Christine Anderson (ESN) Subject:

Following the designation of ChatGPT as a very large online search engine (VLOSE), questions arise as to how Articles 34 and 35 of the Digital Services Act (DSA) apply where the designated online search functionality and non-search conversational functionality rely on shared technical systems. 1.

Where an algorithmic system, model, memory or personalisation system is shared between the designated online search service and a functionality falling outside that service, does Article 34 DSA require an assessment of risks attributable to its use only within the designated service, and what legal criterion does the Commission use to establish that attribution?

Could mitigation measures under Article 35 DSA require changes to such a shared model or system whereby those changes necessarily also alter non-search functionality outside the designated service? if so, what limits prevent Article 35 from indirectly regulating that non-designated functionality?

Can the fact that an algorithmic system is technically shared with the designated VLOSE, by itself, bring risks arising exclusively from its use in non-designated functionality within Articles 34 and 35 DSA, and the Commission is asked to answer yes or no and to identify the legal basis for its answer.

E-10-2026-003505.t: European register of looted cultural goods
qt: to the Commission Arkadiusz Mularczyk (ECR) Subject:
European register of looted cultural goods

On 3 September 2026, the Register of Damage for Ukraine launched categories B2 and C2 for the registration of claims in respect of the damage, destruction or loss of objects and buildings of cultural value. The mechanism covers museums, archives, libraries, religious buildings, works of art, archaeological finds and collections, as well as the costs of the search for, recovery, restitution, conservation and protection of heritage. The Council of Europe recognises that damage encompasses not only the value of the destroyed or looted object, but also the costs of its identification and recovery. The mechanism concerns the Russian aggression of 24 February 2022 and sets a new standard which should be applied to victims of looting during World War II – including Poland, whose works of art remain abroad, mainly in Germany. Given that the EU is party to/a participant in the register for which categories B2 and C2 were launched on 3 September 2026: 1.
Does the Commission also recognise the costs of the search for and restitution of Ukrainian cultural goods as compensable damage?
Does the Commission take the view that the costs of the search for, identification and restitution of cultural goods looted by Germany in World War II similarly form part of the compensable damage?

Will it consider setting up a European register of looted cultural goods, encompassing the value of objects looted by Germany during World War II, as well as legal expenses and the costs of identification and restitution?

E-10-2026-003504.t: Inhumane living conditions at the Sintiki refugee facility in Serres
qt: to the Commission Kostas Papadakis (NI) Subject:

On 22 and 29 August, incidents and complaints by refugees and migrants were noted at the Controlled Access Facility for the Temporary Reception of Asylum Seekers in Sintiki. The facility is bursting at the seams, there are problems with the water supply, there is no air conditioning despite heatwave-like conditions, a lack of basic hygiene measures and cruel treatment by the police. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

Where does it stand on the request to immediately close the prison-like facility in Sintiki, Serres, along with all corresponding structures in Greece, to stop the prolonged detention and imprisonment of migrants and refugees and to ensure humane reception and living conditions for asylum seekers in open temporary accommodation spaces, with asylum examination procedures based on the Geneva Convention relating to the Status of Refugees and safe travel to their intended countries of destination?

Where does it stand on the fact that events such as those witnessed at Sintiki are caused by the provisions of the ‘EU Pact on Migration and Asylum’, which provides for fasttrack asylum rejection procedures for applicants at the border and their subsequent lockin in their first host country, while retaining the criterion of responsibility of the first country of entry, as well as the arrangements for the barbaric deportation of asylum seekers to third countries, also known as ‘return hubs’?

Where does it stand on the fact that the ‘Pact’s’ fake ‘solidarity mechanism’, has been proven to involve the shared repression of uprooted people, with funding as ‘compensation’ to Member States for entrapment in prison structures, the provision of equipment for border crackdowns, and the strengthening of Frontex-style repressive mechanisms?

E-10-2026-003503.t: Public control in electricity transmission systems
qt: to the Commission Bruno Gonçalves (S&D) Subject:

As a consequence of recent international developments, security of energy supply has regained a central role in public policy. This is substantiated, inter alia, by the decision of NATO partners to set 1.5 % of GDP as a target for investment in critical infrastructure. Against this backdrop, the Portuguese Government has announced the acquisition of a 13.7 % stake in REN (the company responsible for the electricity and gas grids in mainland Portugal). This position raises the following questions, also in relation to the competences of the European Commission in this area: 1.
What view does the Commission take of public control in transmission system operators (TSOs) with regard to the EU priority of energy security?
Does it think EU sovereignty is more secure if Member States have majority stakes in these operators?
Thank you for shedding light on this matter.

E-10-2026-003500.t: Poland shut out of measures and investments under the European semiconductor strategy
qt: to the Commission Maciej Wąsik (ECR) Subject:

The EU’s strategy on the development of the semiconductor industry was touted as a quantum leap for the whole Union. It appears increasingly apparent, however, that rather than boosting the competitiveness of Europe as a whole, the strategy is entrenching the dominant position of a handful of major economies, at the expense of countries such as Poland. The information available shows that flagship investments, public support and key technology partnerships are concentrated in certain western European countries. Central and eastern European companies have been left on the sidelines, despite having the skills, technical facilities and ambition to play a role in this strategic sector1. Such a policy goes against the principle of equal treatment of Member States and undermines trust in EU industrial initiatives. In light of the above, could the Commission answer the following: 1.
Why, in practice, are the measures and investments under the European semiconductor strategy concentrated in a few of the largest Member States, excluding countries such as Poland?
What will it do to counter the fact that central and eastern European companies are being shut out of strategic technology projects?
Does it see a risk that the top-down, centralised implementation of this strategy will prove its undoing; if so, what concrete steps does it intend to take to prevent this?

E-10-2026-003499.t: Suspension of Instagram accounts of Albanian opposition figures and protest activists
qt: to the Commission Sandro Gozi (Renew) Subject:

On 3 September 2026, Albanian media reported that at least 23 Instagram accounts1 linked to opposition figures and participants in ongoing anti-government protests had been suspended. Independent MP Marjana Koçeku claimed that more than 200 pages had been affected. Confirmed cases include opposition MP Agron Shehaj, leader of Mundësia, and activist Gent Progni2. Meta has so far provided no public explanation3. No evidence4 currently establishes government involvement5. However, the scale and timing of the suspensions raise serious concerns about freedom of expression, political pluralism and possible coordinated abuse of platform reporting or moderation systems. Albania is an EU candidate country subject to Commission monitoring on democracy, fundamental rights and media freedom. The Commission has already noted increasing digital threats and online harassment in Albania. 1.
Will the Commission urgently seek clarification from Meta on the reasons for these suspensions and whether coordinated mass-reporting or automated enforcement played a role?
Will it examine this incident in the context of Albania’s accession and rule of law monitoring?
Will it assess whether Meta’s safeguards against coordinated manipulation of moderation systems are adequate, including where comparable risks may affect political speech within the EU?

Banned accounts mentioned in the parliamentary question: https://www.instagram.com/agronshehaj_?stkn=Z2p4bnJkM3MwbjVw; https://www.instagram.com/gent.progni?stkn=MTN6OW9uN3dvOTdvbw==; Euronews Albania https://www.instagram.com/euronews_albania?stkn=NWZ0MTc5MXZmaWR2. 2 Activists who have spoken out: https://www.instagram.com/ari_shady?stkn=MW12a2k3aGZrc2I4bw==; https://www.instagram.com/alesiaburnazi?stkn=bzR2aXR3eXhmcDhz. 3 Citizens.al has also been targeted on Meta. In this case, its Facebook page became inaccessible following a series of reports of impersonation (https://www.facebook.com/share/1DSuYxEAGc/?mibextid=wwXIfr). 4 This investigation reports at least 100 confirmed cases: https://www.reprouncensored.org/casesblog/albania. 5 WIRED, perhaps the most authoritative international publication on the subject, has also reported on this: https://www.wired.com/story/metas-copyright-system-is-being-weaponized-against-albanian-protesters/. 1

E-10-2026-003497.t: Extension of Meta’s new child-safety protections to users in the European Union
qt: to the Commission Nina Carberry (PPE) Subject:

Meta has reached an agreement in the United States to introduce a package of new protections for children and teenagers. The measures include a default two-hour daily time limit, restrictions on access during the night, the blocking of notifications during school hours and stronger parental supervision controls. These measures are welcome, but Meta has not confirmed whether the complete package will also be introduced for children and teenagers in Ireland and across the EU. In the light of the above: 1.
Has the Commission sought a formal commitment from Meta confirming whether it will extend the complete package of US child-safety protections to the EU?
If Meta does not introduce the complete package voluntarily, will the Commission seek to make equivalent or stronger protections legally binding?
How will the Commission ensure that the implementation and effectiveness of these measures are independently assessed?

E-10-2026-003496.t: Romania’s RRF-funded strict-protection mapping and Milestone 34
qt: to the Commission Thomas Waitz (Verts/ALE) Subject:

Project C2.I3.2 under the Romanian Recovery and Resilience Plan, which is funded (RON 23.49 million) through the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF), was designed to identify potential strict-protection areas for implementation of the EU Biodiversity Strategy for 2030. Romania’s methodology states that it contributes to the EU objective of strictly protecting 10 % of the country’s land and sea area. However, the draft catalogue published in August 2026 covered only 2.54 % of Romania; analysis of the Ministry’s spatial data shows that over 90 % overlaps with existing protected areas and only about 0.25 % lies outside them. The final catalogue was adopted on 31 August 2026, but the complete expert mapping outputs, including excluded areas, have not been made public. The Ministry stated that Milestone 34 carries a maximum financial correction of EUR 25.69 million. 1.
Before deeming Milestone 34 fulfilled, will the Commission assess the substantive conservation outcome, not merely the adoption of a legal act?
Will it obtain and assess all RRF-funded mapping outputs, including expert-identified areas excluded from the catalogue, and require their publication?

If the milestone is not satisfactorily fulfilled, will the Commission apply Article 24 of Regulation (EU) 2021/241, including suspension or proportionate reduction of funding, and require corrective measures?
at: (English version) to the Commission Thomas Waitz (Verts/ALE) (3 September 2026) Subject: Romania’s RRF-funded strict-protection mapping and Milestone 34 Project C2.I3.2 under the Romanian Recovery and Resilience Plan, which is funded (RON 23.49 million) through the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF), was designed to identify potential strict-protection areas for implementation of the EU Biodiversity Strategy for 2030. Romania’s methodology states that it contributes to the EU objective of strictly protecting 10% of the country’s land and sea area. However, the draft catalogue published in August 2026 covered only 2.54% of Romania; analysis of the Ministry’s spatial data shows that over 90% overlaps with existing protected areas and only about 0.25% lies outside them. The final catalogue was adopted on 31 August 2026, but the complete expert mapping outputs, including excluded areas, have not been made public. The Ministry stated that Milestone 34 carries a maximum financial correction of EUR 25.69 million. 1. Before deeming Milestone 34 fulfilled, will the Commission assess the substantive conservation outcome, not merely the adoption of a legal act? 2. Will it obtain and assess all RRF-funded mapping outputs, including expert-identified areas excluded from the catalogue, and require their publication? 3. If the milestone is not satisfactorily fulfilled, will the Commission apply Article 24 of Regulation (EU) 2021/241, including suspension or proportionate reduction of funding, and require corrective measures? (2 October 2026) Article 24(3) of the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF) Regulation (1) requires the Commission to assess the fulfilment of milestones and targets as set out in the Council Implementing Decision (2). Milestone 34 of the Romanian recovery and resiliency plan (RRP) (3) requires the entry into force of a legal act for the designation of strictly protected areas identified in Natura 2000 protected areas and in additional areas. A specific outcome of this designation is not explicitly included in the milestone description. Milestone 34 is included in the fifth payment request submitted by Romania on 15 August 2026 and is currently under assessment by the Commission. Notwithstanding a result of the ongoing Commission assessment of Milestone 34, Romania is obligated to comply with all relevant EU acquis relating to conservation. The Commission will obtain and assess all evidence necessary to determine whether Milestone 34 has been satisfactorily fulfilled. The methodology for Identifying Priority Areas for Biodiversity was published in the Official Gazette, Part I, No 468bis on 3 June 2026 (4). Should the Commission conclude that the milestone is not satisfactorily fulfilled, this will indeed lead to a proportionate reduction of funding as set out in Article 24 of the RRF Regulation and according to the procedure detailed in the Guidelines for Member States on operational aspects related to the final phase and closure of the RRF (5) published by the Commission on 30 April 2026.
