E-10-2026-003495.t: Cultural heritage status to preserve Coimbra’s student community houses
qt: to the Commission Catarina Martins (The Left) Subject:

With their centuries-old tradition of self-management, solidarity and civic participation, Coimbra’s repúblicas, or student community houses, are a unique embodiment of the city’s academic and cultural life. They are more than mere student residences: these vibrant communities are woven into the academic history of Coimbra, rooted in the area classified as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The threat of eviction currently hanging over the República das Marias do Loureiro and the República Baco as a result of the university’s construction plans is just one example of a wider problem. Other repúblicas face similar threats to their continued existence and so to the preservation of this tangible and intangible cultural heritage. 1.
Is the Commission aware of this situation and of the cultural and patrimonial value of Coimbra’s repúblicas?
Does it think that EU financial instruments could be deployed to support the restoration of these buildings and, at the same time, to ensure the survival of the communities bringing them to life?
Is the Commission prepared to identify or make available EU funds for the safeguarding of this cultural heritage?

E-10-2026-003493.t: 21 rounds of sanctions behind us – number 22 on the way. What exactly have the sanctions against Russia achieved so far?
qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Erik Kaliňák (NI) Subject:

The EU adopted its 21st round of sanctions against Russia on 23 July 2026. Just a few weeks later, Kaja Kallas had already announced a further extensive expansion of sanctions, including some 1 600 new additions. Sanctions packages are coming one after another. While the Commission is working on the next one, there is still no convincing answer to the fundamental question: what exactly have the previous 21 achieved? 1.
In the Commission’s view, what measurable results had the 21 previous sanctions packages achieved before it began work on the next one?
If the previous sanctions were as effective as the Commission claims, why, after four years, is a 22nd package – and a further 1 600 or so additions – now necessary?
In the Commission’s view, is there a point at which it will admit that further sanctions are no longer yielding results, or will the response to every failure simply be yet another package?

E-10-2026-003492.t: Latvia is asking for an additional EUR 7 billion. Will the cost of cutting ties with Russia be borne by the EU’s common budget?
qt: to the Commission Erik Kaliňák (NI) Subject:

Latvia is seeking an additional allocation of approximately EUR 7 billion in the next EU budget. This is intended to cover higher defence spending and the economic consequences of severing ties with Russia. The cost of the policy of cutting ties with Russia is thus beginning to be shifted onto the common European budget. 1.
Does the Commission regard Latvia’s request as an admission that the policy towards Russia is already costing Member States so much that they are unable to bear the costs themselves?
Does the Commission actually intend to give Latvia those EUR 7 billion?
Does the Commission consider it sustainable for every further tightening of policy towards Russia to result in a new request for money from Brussels?

E-10-2026-003491.t: Even Iceland has said ‘no’ to the EU. When a developed European country remains outside the EU, is there a problem in Brussels as well?
qt: to the Commission Erik Kaliňák (NI) Subject:

In a referendum, Icelanders rejected the resumption of negotiations on EU accession. Iceland is one of the most developed countries in Europe, it is part of the single market through the EEA, and it is in the Schengen area. Most voters nevertheless opted for cooperation without membership. If a democratic and prosperous European country prefers to remain outside the Union, it is fair to ask whether the problem is not with the EU itself. 1.

Does the Commission regard the result of the Icelandic referendum as a sign that the EU is on the wrong track, given that even a developed European country does not feel that full membership offers enough advantages?
Does the Commission see a link between the result of the referendum and the extent to which legislation and powers are being transferred from Member States to the EU level?

E-10-2026-003490.t: Blank cheque first, details to follow. Why should the EU approve billions when it does not know what they will be spent on?
qt: to the Commission Erik Kaliňák (NI) Subject:

The Commission wants to earmark up to EUR 100 billion for Ukraine in the 2028-2034 budget, while itself admitting that the country’s future needs cannot be predicted. Even so, it is requesting a huge margin for further expenditure in advance. This EUR 100 billion is in addition to the Global Europe instrument, which is already generous in its own right. 1.
Why is the Commission requesting up to EUR 100 billion when it itself admits that it cannot predict Ukraine’s needs?
What is preventing the Commission from proposing a specific amount only once it is able to say what the money will be spent on?
In the Commission’s view, is there a ceiling on support for Ukraine, or should every further bill be paid regardless of the amount?

E-10-2026-003489.t: EUR 200 billion for Global Europe, EUR 100 billion for Ukraine. And at home, new levies on businesses and households
qt: to the Commission Erik Kaliňák (NI) Subject:
EUR 200 billion for Global Europe, EUR 100 billion for Ukraine. And at home, new levies on businesses and households

In the next seven-year budget, the Commission wants to allocate EUR 200 billion to the Global Europe instrument. This is intended to fund assistance to countries outside the Union, support for accession candidates and foreign projects such as Global Gateway. On top of that, EUR 15 billion is to go into a reserve. Separately, outside this budget framework, it is proposing up to another EUR 100 billion for Ukraine. Altogether, this amounts to hundreds of billions of euros that will flow out of the EU. At the same time, the Commission says there is not enough money for matters within the Union and is demanding new levies from businesses and citizens. 1.
Why does the Commission say that there is not enough money in the Union while at the same time sending hundreds of billions beyond its borders?
Why, according to the Commission, should taxpayers in the Member States pay for this when public resources in Europe are supposedly insufficient even for domestic priorities?
Why is the Commission seeking new levies instead of significantly cutting expenditure outside the Union?

E-10-2026-003488.t: The largest EU budget in history. And on top of that, hidden EU-wide taxes for businesses and households.
qt: to the Commission Erik Kaliňák (NI) Subject:

In its proposal for the 2028–2034 Multiannual Financial Framework, the Commission is proposing the highest level of expenditure to date, together with new own resources from the ETS, the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, a tobacco levy, an e-waste levy and a corporate contribution. For businesses and consumers, this means further compulsory financial burdens benefiting the EU budget. It is a new form of EU-wide taxation, even though the Commission calls it “own resources”. Such an approach is unacceptable. The Commission should first rein in its spending and only then reach into the pockets of EU citizens for new revenue. Decisions on the tax burden borne by citizens and businesses should primarily be made by the Member States, not the Commission. 1.
Why is the Commission pushing for new EU-wide levies when decisions on the tax burden should primarily be made by the Member States?
What cumulative impact does the Commission estimate these measures will have on industry and final prices in smaller economies, such as Slovakia?
Why is the Commission seeking additional revenue rather than cutting expenditure that it cannot cover from existing resources?

E-10-2026-003487.t: Member States and businesses have to comply with increasingly stringent rules. When drafting those rules, however, the Commission itself abandons its own principles
qt: to the Commission Erik Kaliňák (NI) Subject:

The Commission is currently putting forward several packages of so-called omnibus measures, which it presents as tools for tackling excessive bureaucracy. In several proposals, however, citing urgency, it is restricting consultations and impact assessments that it itself requires under the Better Regulation framework. Simplifying legislation must not be used as a pretext for the Commission to change the rules before their consequences can be properly assessed. 1.
Why is the Commission restricting consultations and impact assessments if it labels its proposal urgent?

Why, according to the Commission, should Member States and businesses comply with increasingly stringent EU regulation when the Commission itself does not follow its own Better Regulation principles when proposing legislation?
Why is the Commission using omnibus packages to “repackage” rules that it itself introduced, instead of abolishing unnecessary obligations?

E-10-2026-003486.t: The Commission is reaching for household savings. Who will bear the losses when it channels them into political projects?
qt: to the Commission Erik Kaliňák (NI) Subject:

The Commission openly speaks of the need to mobilise approximately EUR 10 trillion in European household savings and direct private capital towards the EU’s strategic priorities. Such an approach is unacceptable. Private savings are not Brussels’ reserve fund for the green transition, defence or competitiveness. They are the property of citizens who have put this money aside and who will also bear any potential losses. The Commission has the nerve to talk about ‘mobilising’ other people’s money before admitting that its own spending policy has failed. 1.
On what mandate does the Commission presume to speak of mobilising private household savings?
Who will bear the losses if citizens’ savings are channelled through tax, regulatory or securitisation instruments into politically determined investments?
Why does the Commission want to mobilise citizens’ savings instead of first drastically reducing its own expenditure?

E-10-2026-003484.t: Sustainability and manageability at municipal level of the New European Bauhaus following the ‘From vision to implementation’ communication
qt: to the Commission Joachim Streit (Renew) Subject:

With communication COM(2025)1026 and the recommendation adopted by the Council on 11 May 2026, the Commission has taken the New European Bauhaus (NEB) into a new phase of implementation. The Committee of the Regions (CoR) adopted an opinion on 22 June 2026, calling in particular for more stable funding, capacity-building and the targeted involvement of smaller municipalities. 1.

Is the Commission planning reduced co-financing rates or derogations for NEB funding programmes for structurally weak and rural municipalities, for which existing own contributions are often the key barrier to entry?

Given that the technical support required for integrating NEB principles into calls for funding – at programme management level, not individual project funding – can currently only be provided by 10-15 selected managing authorities across the EU, is the Commission planning to extend this programme so that authorities in less structural regions such as Rhineland-Palatinate also receive a similar level of technical support?

Will it come forward with specific, multi-annual funding commitments as part of its implementation steps announced for autumn 2026, or will funding continue to depend on one-off calls of limited duration called for by the NEB Facility, especially in view of the fact that the CoR opinion of 22 July 2026 calls for more stable, long-term funding for the NEB?

E-10-2026-003483.t: Immediate termination of funding to Morocco
qt: to the Commission Jorge Buxadé Villalba (PfE) Subject:

In response to a recent parliamentary question, Commissioner Brunner acknowledged in July that the Commission plans to disburse EUR 160 million to Morocco until 2027 to support its national immigration and asylum strategy. This figure adds to the almost EUR 10 billion transferred by the EU – according to the OECD and the Commission’s own sources – in direct grants, plus EUR 11.5 billion in favourable EIB loans and measures such as trade agreements. However, Morocco continues to behave like a hostile actor against EU interests. Most recently, it carried out a hybrid attack against Spain, participating – according to police sources – in the invasion of the city of Ceuta, where there have been sexual and physical assaults against the civilian population. In the light of this act of war: 1.
Can the Commission confirm that all budget lines, including those under the migration strategy, destined for Morocco have been cancelled?
What legal mechanisms can the Commission rely on to recover funds already disbursed that clearly do not meet EU funding objectives?
What sanctions affecting special visas, trade policy and cooperation are being considered?

E-10-2026-003482.t: ChatGPT’s safety mechanisms regarding suicide-related content in different language versions
qt: to the Commission Veronika Cifrová Ostrihoňová (Renew) Subject:

On 2 September 2026, an anonymous member of the public alerted me to a test of the large language model ChatGPT, operated by OpenAI, in which the chatbot, in response to a prompt regarding a school essay, generated a suicide note in the Slovak language. When the test was repeated, the chatbot’s responses varied depending on whether the user was logged in, with contact details for a crisis helpline only being offered to the user when logged out. Although the chatbot refused to provide instructions or a plan for suicide in subsequent tests, it did not put a definitive end to the inappropriate thread, so it was possible to continue attempting to obtain further harmful content. This is not merely a hypothetical risk. In the widely publicised case of 16-year-old Adam Raine, his parents claim that ChatGPT continued to engage in conversations about suicide for months, despite repeated signs of imminent danger.1 1.

How will the Commission examine whether the differing levels of protection for logged-in and logged-out users, and the ability to continue a high-risk thread across different language versions, pose systematic risks to minors?
Will the Commission require OpenAI to provide frequent links to crisis support and to put an stop to the distribution of further harmful content?

Following the designation of ChatGPT as a VLOSE under the Digital Services Act of 31 August 2026, how will the Commission use its powers to verify and enforce effective measures to mitigate these risks, including independent testing of safeguards for minors?
https://www.cbsnews.com/sanfrancisco/news/ai-guardrails-california-adam-raine/.
to the Commission Anna Bryłka (PfE) Subject:

Since mid-July, the Black Sea has been blockaded due to Russian attacks on merchant ships. According to information from Ukraine, consultations are ongoing with frontline countries and the EU regarding the transit of agricultural goods and increasing exports to the EU market. In this connection: Is the Commission consulting frontline countries regarding the import of agricultural goods from Ukraine, with a view to preventing a grain crisis such as the one we faced in 2022 and 2023?
to the Commission Anna Bryłka (PfE) Subject:

Since mid-July, the Black Sea has been blockaded due to Russian attacks on merchant ships. According to information from Ukraine, consultations are ongoing with frontline countries and the EU regarding the transit of agricultural goods and increasing exports to the EU market. In this connection: 1.

Is the Commission conducting or planning to launch consultations with Ukraine on revising the DCFTA/Association Agreement or on increasing duty-free tariff quotas for imports of agricultural goods from Ukraine?

How does the Commission monitor and verify the process of aligning Ukrainian production standards with the EU’s stringent requirements, which is a fundamental condition for maintaining fair competition in the single market?
Does the Commission envisage mobilising financial or other instruments to mitigate the effects of the Black Sea blockade?

E-10-2026-003479.t: Enforcement of outstanding traffic fines from users of leased vehicles in the Czech Republic
qt: to the Commission Kosma Złotowski (ECR) Subject:

For several years now, legislation has been in force in the Czech Republic which allows the vehicle owner to be held liable for a traffic offence where the actual driver cannot be identified. This measure is intended to facilitate the enforcement of fines for offences recorded by automated traffic enforcement systems. However, this leads to a problem in the case of leased vehicles. In such cases, if the actual driver cannot be identified, the fine may be charged to the lessor’s account. If a leasing company has a large number of vehicles and many unpaid fines, this can result in a significant debt. During a roadside check, the Czech police may demand payment not only of the driver’s outstanding fines, but also of any arrears attributed to the account of the operator of the vehicle being checked (the lessor). If the arrears are not settled on the spot, the authorities may impound the number plates. In light of the above: 1.
Is the Commission aware of this mechanism, and does it feel that it could restrict EU rights and freedoms, in particular the free movement of persons and services?

Is the procedure whereby an EU citizen, using a leased car and subject to a roadside check in the Czech Republic, may be required to pay outstanding fines for traffic offences which they did not commit – on the grounds that these fines have been attributed to the lessor’s account – compatible with the principles of proportionality and individual liability?
Do provisions involving the enforcement of outstanding debts against the user of a vehicle on account of liabilities attributed to the lessor fall within the scope of Directive 2015/413?

E-10-2026-003477.t: Falling milk prices and the suitability of EU intervention tools
qt: to the Commission André Franqueira Rodrigues (S&D) Subject:

In recent months, milk producers in the Azores have been facing further reductions in the price they are paid, while production costs remain high. The falls announced for September exacerbate already small margins, hinder future investments and have led to signs of abandonment or conversion of holdings. At the same time, the current reference thresholds used in public intervention for butter and skimmed milk powder maintain levels set more than 15 years ago, despite the profound change in production costs and market conditions. In light of the above: 1.

Will the Commission ask the milk market observatory and AFCO for an analysis of price transmission, costs and distribution of margins in the Azores, including persistent regional differences, in relation to the functioning of the internal market?
What immediate steps can the EU take to boost the income, liquidity and bargaining position of Azorean producers?

Does the Commission consider the existing reference thresholds for public intervention in the dairy sector to be suitable, and will it push for them to be updated based on current costs and market conditions?

E-10-2026-003476.t: EU funding for the protection and support of Graviera Kritis PDO
qt: to the Commission Emmanouil Kefalogiannis (PPE) Subject:

Graviera Kritis PDO cheese is one of the most emblematic Cretan agri-food products. It has a direct link with sheep and goat farming, the economic viability of mountainous areas and the preservation of Crete’s food-producing tradition and cultural identity. The establishment of an inter-branch organisation involving producers and manufacturers opens up significant prospects for better coordination of the chain, stronger protection of the designation, more effective marketing of the product and support for livestock farmers. Strengthening the bargaining position of producers through producer organisations, associations and inter-branch organisations is a key priority of the common agricultural policy (CAP). The creation of the inter-branch organisation for Graviera Kritis PDO is an opportunity to strengthen the collective organisation of the sector, in view also of the new CAP. In light of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

What possibilities for financial and technical support can be leveraged for the introduction, recognition and operation of the inter-branch organisation for Graviera Kritis PDO, for designation protection and marketing actions?
Does it intend, in the context of the new CAP, to strengthen incentives and funding for producer organisations and inter-branch organisations, particularly in countries with a less structured setup?

What European collective organisation practices in the dairy and cheese sector could be leveraged to strengthen the position of Cretan livestock farmers and give the Graviera Kritis PDO even more visibility on the markets?

E-10-2026-003474.t: Greece’s purchase of Israeli air defence systems and compatibility with SAFE and other EU instruments
qt: to the Commission Catarina Martins (The Left) Subject:

On 31 August 2026, Greece signed an agreement (dubbed ‘Achilles’ Shield’) with Israel worth around EUR 3 billion for the purchase of an integrated anti-missile and anti-drone defence system, produced by Rafael and Israel Aerospace Industries, plus EUR 26 million for an additional anti-drone system. This is the largest defence contract between the two countries. Greece is a beneficiary of the SAFE instrument (Regulation (EU) 2025/1106), which imposes eligibility requirements regarding the origin of contractors and components. It should also be kept in mind that Israel is subject to genocide proceedings before the International Court of Justice and that several Member States have suspended trade in military material with Israel. In light of the above: 1.

Is the purchase of ‘Achilles’ Shield’ fully or partially financed, co-financed or otherwise supported by SAFE, the European Defence Industry Programme, the European Defence Fund or any other EU instrument?
Has the Commission checked that the SAFE eligibility requirements, including the limit for components originating from third countries, were met in the Greek contracts covered by the instrument?
What monitoring mechanisms ensure that EU funds or loans are not used, directly or indirectly, for purchasing material from Israeli companies?

E-10-2026-003472.t: Drone deliveries to prisons and attacks on emergency services
qt: to the Commission Virginie Joron (PfE) Subject:

In Strasbourg, the use of drones to deliver illicit items to a remand centre led to a ban being introduced from the end of July 20261 on night landings for emergency services helicopters at the hospital. Patients have already had to be diverted. The same phenomenon has been documented in other countries too. Regulation (EU) 2019/947 regulates the use of unmanned aircraft systems2, but does not lay down specific provisions on the neutralisation of a hostile drone flying over a prison. Article 15 of that regulation establishes that to the Member States are responsible for setting the geographical areas in which overflight by drones is restricted or banned. Bearing in mind that the Commission is planning to publish a drone package towards the end of 20263: 1.

Does it intend to include penal establishments among the sites eligible for the voluntary initiative to deploy counter-drone systems and to enable funding to be provided, under domestic security programmes, for nets and drone detection and neutralisation systems?

Has it carried out a security assessment4 of drone intrusions into prisons and identified best practices in Europe (metal nets, staff procedures and powers, jammers, etc.) in cooperation with the European Union Aviation Safety Agency, Europol, the European Organisation of Prison and Correctional Services, and the Member States?
Will the planned recommendation for law enforcement agencies give specific details on the role of prison staff and procedures for intercepting drones flying over a prison?

E-10-2026-003471.t: Public disclosure of sensitive personal data in the Slovak Business Register
qt: to the Commission Tomáš Zdechovský (PPE) Subject:

Following recent changes to the Slovak Business Register, documents in its online collection of deeds are reportedly publicly accessible without the need for authentication. These documents may contain national identification numbers, identity document numbers, full residential addresses and handwritten signatures, creating a serious risk of identity theft and misuse of personal data. The Slovak data protection authority has already raised concerns regarding this practice. It raises serious questions concerning the principles of data minimisation and data protection by design and by default under Articles 5 and 25 of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), as well as Articles 7, 8 and 52 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union. 1.
Does the Commission consider unrestricted online access to documents containing such personal data compatible with the GDPR and the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union?

Is the Commission assessing the relevant Slovak legislation and practice, and is it prepared to take action, including infringement proceedings, should systemic noncompliance with EU law be established?

Has the development or modernisation of the Slovak Business Register received funding under the Recovery and Resilience Facility or other EU instruments and, if so, will the Commission verify whether EU data protection requirements and safeguards were respected?

E-10-2026-003470.t: Different treatment of Apple Siri AI and Google Gemini under the DMA
qt: to the Commission Tomáš Zdechovský (PPE) Subject:

Apple has announced that Siri AI will not be available in the EU with iOS 27, citing interoperability requirements under Article 6(7) of the Digital Markets Act (DMA)1. Apple claims it proposed an 18-month transition period to implement interoperability, while the Commission states this amounted to a request for an exemption from the DMA. In its July 2026 decision concerning Google, the Commission acknowledged that Gemini benefits from access to Android functionalities unavailable to competing AI assistants. Nevertheless, Google may continue offering Gemini while implementing interoperability measures progressively, with deadlines extending to August 2027 and, for certain functionalities, August 2028. Both cases concern Article 6(7) DMA, yet the approaches and transition periods appear substantially different. 1.
What specific legal, technical or factual differences between Apple/Siri AI and Google/Gemini justify these different approaches under the same DMA provision?
Why can Google continue offering Gemini while implementing interoperability requirements until 2027–2028, whereas Apple’s proposed 18-month transition period for Siri AI was rejected?
What objective criteria does the Commission use to determine whether gradual implementation under Article 6(7) DMA is acceptable, and how were they applied differently in these cases?

Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 September 2022 on contestable and fair markets in the digital sector and amending Directives (EU) 2019/1937 and (EU) 2020/1828 (Digital Markets Act) (OJ L 265, 12.10.2022, p. 1, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/1925/oj). 1

E-10-2026-003469.t: Repair and reuse of electric vehicle batteries
qt: to the Commission Anna-Maja Henriksson (Renew) Subject:

A Finnish citizens’ initiative1 has criticised new Finnish authority guidelines2 linked to the Batteries Regulation (EU) 2023/1542. The instigators behind the initiative are warning that the guidelines make battery repairs more expensive and the reuse of batteries and battery components from scrapped or wrecked vehicles more difficult. There is a risk that workshops will face unreasonable demands and that functioning batteries will be discarded unnecessarily instead of being reused. This may limit competition in the internal market, hinder the circular economy and impede the transition from fossil fuel-powered vehicles to electric vehicles as repairs become more expensive. The criticisms raised by the citizens’ initiative include that, under the guidelines, work carried out without the manufacturer's repair instructions must be deemed preparation for reuse or remanufacturing, and not repair. Thus, there is a risk that ordinary repairs will impose manufacturer obligations on the repairer, even when the criteria set out in the Regulation for remanufacturing are not met. 1.
How is the Commission responding to the new guidelines from the Finnish authorities and the criticisms that the workshop enterprises have put forward in the citizens’ initiative?
Is the absence of the manufacturer’s repair instructions sufficient for a repair to be deemed preparation for reuse or remanufacturing?

How will the Commission ensure that qualified, independent workshops throughout the EU can repair electric and hybrid vehicle batteries and reuse functioning batteries and battery components from scrapped or wrecked vehicles?

https://www.kansalaisaloite.fi/fi/aloite/17856. https://lvv.fi/documents/242146171/255610641/Ohje-ajovoima-akkujen-k%C3%A4sittelyyn-jauudelleenk%C3%A4ytt%C3%B6%C3%B6n-03072026.pdf/4b430f72-c5b9-622b-ba26ed38b5bb901e?t=1783317752069. 1 2

E-10-2026-003468.t: Withdrawal of cancer medicines in Greece and the need to ensure equal access for all European citizens to appropriate cancer treatments
qt: to the Commission Elena Kountoura (The Left) Subject:

The recent decision to pull the cancer drug Trodelvy1 from the Greek market triggered strong reactions and caused concern among patients and in the medical community as this is the fourth cancer medicine to be pulled from Greece in recent months. The decision is linked to very high clawbacks imposed in the context of Greek pharmaceutical expenditure, which, reports say, even exceed 100 % of the relevant expenditure2. Bearing in mind: – the letter from the Hellenic Society of Medical Oncology3 calling for structural solutions to ensure the continued availability of the most effective cancer treatments for patients; – the cancer plan for Europe, which aims to ensure that all citizens, regardless of where they live, have equal access to essential cancer treatments; – the European Parliament’s recent resolution4, which stresses the need to ensure equal, timely and affordable access to cancer medicines for all European patients, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Is it aware of the recent withdrawals of cancer medicines from the Greek market, which are linked to the national pricing and reimbursement system?

What existing funding or other tools does it intend to harness to prevent national pricing and reimbursement systems from leading to poor and unequal patient access to approved cancer treatments and medicines?
Does it intend to propose new European tools to prevent similar cancer medicine withdrawals in the future?

On 23 July 2026, the National Organisation for Medecine's Committee on Medicines for Human Use adopted a favourable opinion modifying the terms of the marketing authorisation for Trodelvy and adding a new therapeutic indication for patients with triple negative breast cancer. 2 A clawback is when pharmaceutical companies are obliged to return to the State money that has already been paid, when pharmaceutical expenditure exceeds the limit set in the budget. 3 The Hellenic Society of Medical Oncology (EOPE) had warned about the risk of pulling oncology medicines and had stressed that the current framework for financing innovative cancer treatments, with the increasing cost of clawbacks, poses serious risks to their sustainable availability (https://healthdaily.gr/2026/08/27/epistoli-eope-ston-ypourgo-ygeias-gia-aposyrseis-ogkologikon-farmakon/). 4 The resolution on World Cancer Day notes with concern the persistent inequalities in patients’ access to cancer medicines in EU Member States. 1

E-10-2026-003466.t: Implications for Union law of the amendments to the Slovak Citizenship Act
qt: to the Commission Loránt Vincze (PPE) Subject:

The most recent amendments to the Slovak Citizenship Act entered into force on 15 July, making it easier for certain people with Slovak ancestry to acquire Slovak citizenship. Many of those affected live in countries other than EU Member States, and the amendments mean that applicants will gain Union citizenship as well as Slovak citizenship under a simplified procedure. At the same time, the amendments to the Act do not solve the problem previously pointed out by the Commission, namely that acquisition of the citizenship of another Member State, such as Hungarian citizenship, would automatically result in the loss of Slovak citizenship other than in the small number of cases defined in the Act. In 2024, the Commission asked the Slovak authorities (including in connection with a petition) whether they intended to amend the Slovak Citizenship Act to enable the consequences of losing Slovak nationality to be assessed in a manner consistent with the case-law of the Court and, if so, to enable the person affected to retain their citizenship or have it restored to them in a manner consistent with the case-law of the Court. 1.

Has a response been received from the authorities, and are the Slovak legal rules, whereby they give preferential treatment to one group while revoking ex lege the citizenship of citizens living on its territory when they acquire another citizenship, consistent with the principle of proportionality?

What legal risks could the aforementioned simplified procedure have in terms of Union citizenship in cases where a citizen of a third country outside the Union acquires Union citizenship at the same time?

E-10-2026-003465.t: Maintenance of Russian LNG tankers in Denmark despite EU sanctions and Russia’s ongoing aggression against Ukraine
qt: to the Commission Tomáš Zdechovský (PPE) Subject:

Despite Russia’s ongoing aggression against Ukraine, European services and infrastructure continue to play a significant role in facilitating Russian fossil fuel exports. The Danish Fayard shipyard continues to carry out maintenance on specialised Arc7 tankers that transport LNG from Russia’s Yamal project. According to the Urgewald organisation, the Boris Davydov tanker is currently charting a course to the shipyard. Since its last maintenance at Fayard in 2023, the tanker has transported 50 cargoes of Russian LNG with an estimated value of EUR 1.91 billion. According to available information, Fayard is the last shipyard in the EU still servicing these specialised tankers. Their operation is, however, crucial for maintaining Russian LNG exports from the Arctic and the providing revenue that Russia can use to finance its aggression against Ukraine. 1.

How does the Commission explain that companies in Member States may continue to provide maintenance and other key services to vessels that enable Russia to continue exporting and deriving substantial revenue from LNG?

Does the Commission consider it acceptable for European companies to service these vessels until new restrictions come into force, and thus to effectively extend their ability to transport Russian LNG in the coming years?

Does the Commission intend to propose the immediate closure of the remaining loopholes in the sanctions regime so that EU companies cannot provide servicing, repairs, insurance or other maritime services to vessels involved in the export of Russian oil and LNG?

E-10-2026-003464.t: Commission’s basis for publicly attributing the drone incident at Leipzig/Halle Airport to Russia
qt: to the Commission Friedrich Pürner (NI) Subject:

In a public statement1 on the drone incident of 4 August 2026 at Leipzig/Halle Airport, Commission President Ursula von der Leyen described the incident as an attack by Russia and expressed the European Union’s solidarity with Germany. 1.
On the basis of what specific facts, evidence or findings did the Commission publicly attribute the incident to Russia?

From which sources does this information stem, and to what extent is it based on the Commission’s own findings or on information or assessments provided by German authorities and intelligence services?
https://x.com/VonDerLeyen.

E-10-2026-003463.t: Equal protection of freedom of religion in the EU and conscientious objection in the workplace
qt: to the Commission Arkadiusz Mularczyk (ECR) Subject:

Article 10 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union guarantees freedom of thought, conscience and religion, and recognises the right to refuse to act contrary to one’s own conscience, in accordance with national legislation. Article 21 prohibits discrimination on grounds including religion or belief. The Commission has developed instruments and strategies to combat anti-Semitism and hatred towards Muslims. At the same time, there is no comparable, systematic mechanism for monitoring acts of hatred, discrimination and violence against Christians. This therefore raises the question of ensuring an equal standard of protection for all religious communities. 1.

Does the Commission intend to establish a systematic mechanism for monitoring and countering acts of hate, violence and discrimination against Christians, comparable to the instruments in place for other religious communities? If not, why not?

Does the Commission consider that Directive 2000/78/EC provides sufficient protection for employees invoking conscientious objection, in particular in the medical professions and other situations where professional duties may come into conflict with religious beliefs?

Does the Commission plan to issue guidelines or take other measures to ensure an appropriate balance between the principle of non-discrimination and freedom of conscience and religion in the workplace?

E-10-2026-003462.t: Basis for the Vice-President / High Representative’s public statements on the drone incident at Leipzig/Halle Airport
qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Friedrich Pürner (NI) Subject:

In connection with the drone incident on 4 August 2026 at Leipzig/Halle Airport, the VicePresident of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy, Kaja Kallas, stated that the incident bore ‘all the hallmarks of state-sponsored terrorism’. She also referred to indications of Russian involvement. 1.
On what specific evidence is the VP/HR’s assessment based that the incident bears ‘all the hallmarks of state-sponsored terrorism’?
What specific information or evidence did the VP/HR have at her disposal when she publicly referred to Russia’s involvement in the incident?
Are these assessments based on findings obtained directly by European Union bodies, or on assessments and evaluations provided to her by Member State authorities?

E-10-2026-003461.t: Conditionality of EU aid to Africa and respect for freedom of religion
qt: to the Commission Arkadiusz Mularczyk (ECR) Subject:

The EU-Africa Partnership and the substantial funds allocated by the Union to development cooperation should also serve to effectively protect fundamental human rights. Violence, discrimination and persecution on the grounds of religion or belief occur in some African countries. Religious minorities, including Christian communities and their children, are particularly vulnerable. This phenomenon takes the form of physical violence, abductions, forced displacement, restrictions on access to education and impunity for perpetrators, among other things. The EU, as one of Africa’s most important financial and development partners, has instruments at its disposal to link support to respect for fundamental rights, including freedom of religion or belief. 1.

Is the Commission prepared to make the allocation or disbursement of part of EU funds conditional upon genuine progress in the area of freedom of religion or belief, in particular the effective protection of persecuted minorities and children?

Does the Commission intend to use specific, measurable indicators, including the scale of religiously motivated violence, the prosecution of perpetrators, the protection of places of worship and children’s access to education?

What financial consequences does the Commission envisage for states that systematically violate religious freedom or fail to fulfil their obligation to protect persecuted minorities, and is it possible to reduce, suspend or redirect part of the aid directly to organisations supporting victims?

E-10-2026-003460.t: Flight safety in the Nicosia FIR and Türkiye’s compliance with European and international law
qt: to the Commission Costas Mavrides (S&D) Subject:

The issue of flight safety at the Nicosia FIR was brought to the fore again by the Cyprus Air Traffic Controllers’ Association, following an incident in which a Turkish military aircraft failed to respond to calls from the Nicosia Control Centre and deviated from its course, approaching another civil aircraft. Immediate action is needed to address the recurrent issue of flight safety. This issue is partly due to the continued operation of the illegal airport in occupied Tymbou and in particular the risks to those using it, given that its operation is based on illegal procedures and reduced radar range. Despite the high level of safety ensured in Cypriot airspace thanks to the experience and operational readiness of Cyprus Civil Aviation personnel, Türkiye’s refusal to cooperate with the Republic of Cyprus and comply with international rules is in breach of the law and poses real risks for aviation safety. These serious risks have also been highlighted at European level, including by the European Union Aviation Safety Agency and the International Federation of Air Line Pilots’ Associations, and documented in Commission and Parliament reports, which call on Türkiye to comply. In view of the above: What specific steps does the Commission intend to take to ensure that Türkiye complies with international and European law and aviation safety rules, with regard to the safety of intra-EU flights?

E-10-2026-003459.t: Alleged irregularities concerning the use of Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF) funds in Poland
qt: to the Commission Arkadiusz Mularczyk (ECR) Subject:

Mariusz Haładyj, President of the Supreme Audit Office (NIK), stated in an interview with WNP.pl in March 2026 that approximately 90 % of the RRF funds had been used primarily to manage the liquidity of the public finance sector, rather than for direct investment. This was reportedly due to delays in project implementation and pre-financing, including by the Polish Development Fund (PFR). At the same time, the Polish Government reported that 96.5 % of allocations1 had already been committed. The NextGenerationEU/RRF instrument was intended to support post-COVID-19 recovery, investments and reforms aimed at increasing resilience, not to plug gaps in the budget. The Ministry of Development Funds and Regional Policy claims that every zloty is being used to finance RRF projects. However, there is a divergence between the programme’s aims and the practice of liquidity management. In light of the above: 1.

Is the Commission monitoring whether RRF funds in Poland are being allocated in accordance with the Instrument’s approved plan and objectives, rather than being used on a temporary basis for budget liquidity management?
What control mechanisms and potential corrective measures does the Commission apply in the event of significant investment delays and a predominance of pre-financing settlements?
Does the Commission plan to carry out an independent review of the Polish RRF’s compliance with the principle of additionality and the earmarking of funds for postCOVID-19 recovery?

E-10-2026-003457.t: Infringements of fishing rules and sovereign rights in the Aegean by Turkish vessels and protection of Greek fishers
qt: to the Commission Nikolas Farantouris (S&D) Subject:

On 17 August 2026, Turkish fishing vessels were found to be sailing and, according to reports1, fishing within the Alonnisos-Northern Sporades National Marine Park, near the island of Piperi. Piperi is an important habitat for the Mediterranean monk seal (Monachus monachus) and there is a special protection regime in place, which includes a ban on any vessel approaching within three nautical miles of the island. The incident prompted the coast guard to intervene, but by that point the Turkish vessels had already sailed away from the area2. This cannot be treated as an isolated incident. It adds to the repeated nuisance being caused by Turkish fishing vessels in the Aegean and to a broader Turkish practice aimed at creating faits accomplis and challenging Greek sovereign rights. At the same time, illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing directly affects lawful fishers and marine ecosystems, as the Commission itself recognises. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
What specific measures does it intend to take to protect Greek fishers from repeated illegal activities by Turkish fishing vessels in the Aegean?

Does it intend to systematically include the issue of compliance with European fisheries rules and respect for sovereign rights in discussions on the deepening and modernisation of the EU-Türkiye customs union, given that the Commission is already considering further strengthening economic and trade relations with Türkiye?

https://www.naftemporiki.gr/politics/2152322/toyrkika-alieytika-entopistikan-sto-thalassio-parkoalonnisoy/. 2 https://www.kathimerini.gr/society/564416101/toyrkika-alieytika-sto-thalassio-parko-alonnisoy-tianaferei-to-limeniko/. 1

to the Commission Thomas Pellerin-Carlin (S&D), Nora Mebarek (S&D), Aurore Lalucq (S&D), Raphaël Glucksmann (S&D), Pierre Jouvet (S&D), Jean-Marc Germain (S&D), Chloé Ridel (S&D), Emma Rafowicz (S&D), Murielle Laurent (S&D) Subject:

Climate change is increasing the frequency and intensity of extreme heatwaves in the EU. This resulted in May 2026 becoming the hottest May on record in France. Workers in environments that are highly exposed to heat, such as agriculture, construction, industry, logistics and the maintenance of public spaces, face growing health and safety risks. According to the International Labour Organization, heat-related deaths in the workplace have increased by 42 % since 2000. While Directive 89/391/EEC imposes a general obligation on employers to protect the health and safety of their workers, it does not establish specific provisions with regard to the risks from extreme heatwaves. In light of the above: 1.
In the short term, what steps does the Commission intend to take?
Will the European framework law on adaptation to climate change require plans for the adaptation of working conditions to be established at sector and company level?
Will the Quality Jobs Act impose binding measures concerning the adaptation of working conditions in the event of extreme heatwaves?
to the Commission Tomislav Sokol (PPE), Marjan Šarec (Renew), Thomas Waitz (Verts/ALE) Subject:

Recent developments in Montenegro raise serious concerns regarding political stability, security and respect for European values in an EU candidate country. Prime Minister Milojko Spajić stated that there is serious security intelligence indicating that Montenegro is facing coordinated hybrid action involving officials from at least two countries in the region, without identifying those countries. At the same time, serious threats have been made against a senior member of the government, while public glorification of Ratko Mladić, a proven war criminal responsible for war crimes in Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia, continues. 1.
Is the Commission monitoring these developments, and does it consider that they could jeopardise Montenegro’s political stability, European values and progress in the accession negotiations?

Will the Commission request an institutional investigation into the Prime Minister’s allegations of coordinated hybrid action, or does it consider that unverified claims of such gravity may constitute dangerous political populism, equally destabilising for Montenegro’s European path?

How does the Commission assess the glorification of the proven war criminal Ratko Mladić, and what steps will it take to make clear that glorification of war criminals is unacceptable in an EU candidate country?

E-10-2026-003454.t: Better protection of minors online through the introduction of an EU-wide minimum access age for social media
qt: to the Commission Dimitris Tsiodras (PPE) Subject:

Meta’s recent settlement with 29 US states to resolve lawsuits regarding child safety on social media obliges the company to pay up to USD 16.68 billion and implement specific rules to deal with the impact on the mental health of children and young people. The settlement came a few weeks after the Commission’s preliminary finding that the addictive design of the company’s services is a breach of the Digital Services Act. In view also of the forthcoming 2026 State of the Union speech, can the Commission say: 1.

Does it intend to present stricter measures to protect minors online, including the introduction of an EU-wide minimum access age for social media, as a follow-up to the European Parliament’s report on the matter?
How will it ensure that the age of minors is reliably verified and how will it address social media functions that cause addiction among young people?

How will it oblige companies to comply with European legislation and take their responsibility seriously to ensure that their services are safe for children and young people, without placing a disproportionate burden on parents?

E-10-2026-003453.t: The thousands of children without nursery places and the anti-educational ‘neighbourhood nannies’ programme
qt: to the Commission Kostas Papadakis (NI) Subject:

Every year, thousands of workers find themselves in a tight spot due to the shortages of places at nurseries. The Hellenic Agency for Local Development and Local Government (EETAA) granted EUR 158 009 in vouchers for the period 2026-2027, of which EUR 106 133 was for nurseries, while the rest was for state-supported after-school activity centres for children (KDAP). Applications for after-school activity centres and after-school activity centres for children with disabilities were not covered, resulting in 41 129 children being rejected. Existing nurseries are shrinking despite the confirmed shortages of places. The European ‘neighbourhood nannies’ programme is anti-educational and is being used as a substitute for an improved pedagogical approach. In view of this, where does the Commission stand on: 1.

parents’ long-standing call and need for all children to be admitted, without exception and selection criteria, to free and modern nurseries staffed by full-time carers rather than carers on ‘on-demand contracts’ (Directive 2019/1152)?

the fact that, in order to increase the number of women entering the labour market, to secure corporate profit-making, anti-educational care programmes, such as the ‘neighbourhood nannies’ one, are being implemented on the basis of the European Child Guarantee and Recommendation (EU) 2021/1004?

the urgent need for the billions of euros that the EU and national governments are pumping into the war industry and into supporting the profitability of corporate groups to go towards meeting the needs of ordinary people, through the establishment, for instance, of all the much-needed free, modern and upgraded nurseries, fully-staffed with qualified professionals, so that all needs are universally met under updated terms?

E-10-2026-003451.t: Follow up on EU-funded lie detector for use at the border
qt: to the Commission Raquel García Hermida-Van Der Walle (Renew) Subject:

In its answer to written question E-002623/20261 on ‘EU-funded lie detector for use at the border’, the Commission denies that EU funds have been used to fund projects on ‘lie detectors’. However, in earlier responses, the Commission acknowledged that research on ‘deception detection’ was funded2. 1.
Can the Commission indicate what specific EU funding has gone to research on either lie detectors or deception detection?

Can the Commission provide an overview of EU-funded projects on research on ‘deception detection’ or similar concepts, both past and present? The Commission states that ‘[i]n this specific case, EU funded research allowed a better understanding of the limitations and reliability of the technologies in question and to draw policy conclusions.’
Can the Commission outline which understanding of the limitations and reliability of the technologies in question was obtained, and which policy conclusions were drawn?
