E-10-2026-003450.t: Adhering to the timeline for the European Disability Card
qt: to the Commission Marie Dauchy (PfE), André Rougé (PfE), Catherine Griset (PfE), Marie-Luce BrasierClain (PfE), Rody Tolassy (PfE), Anne-Sophie Frigout (PfE), Antonín Staněk (PfE), Pál Szekeres (PfE), Diana Iovanovici Şoşoacă (NI), Aleksandar Nikolic (PfE), Mélanie Disdier (PfE) Subject:

The Directive establishing the European Disability Card and the European Parking Card for persons with disabilities lays down a clear timeline (notification of contact points by June 2025, transposition by June 2027 and application from June 2028), but some crucial delegated acts are still in the process of being adopted. In the meantime, national card holders are met with refusals to recognise their cards and are given unjustified fines in other Member States. Can the EU ensure that the deadline is met and that there is a smooth transition of rights for persons with disabilities?

E-10-2026-003449.t: GNSS signal interference and spoofing in the Baltic Sea Region
qt: to the Commission Magdalena Adamowicz (PPE) Subject:

The Baltic Sea region has experienced an increase in signal interference incidents in the Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS), including jamming and spoofing. Jamming blocks satellite navigation signals, while spoofing sends false signals that can provide incorrect positioning information. These disruptions create growing concerns for maritime safety, as ships rely on GNSS systems such as the Global Positioning System (GPS) and Galileo for navigation. The consequences of these incidents can include increased risks of maritime accidents, disruption to international trade and supply chains, as well as wider security concerns affecting critical infrastructure. 1.
Does the Commission consider the current EU maritime safety framework sufficient to address the increasing risks caused by GNSS interference in the Baltic Sea region?
What actions is the Commission taking to support the development of alternative or backup navigation systems to ensure safe maritime operations when GNSS signals are disrupted?
Does the Commission intend to increase investment in resilient navigation and communication technologies to strengthen EU maritime security?

E-10-2026-003448.t: PPWR compliance costs for micro and small enterprises
qt: to the Commission Sunčana Glavak (PPE) Subject:

Under Regulation (EU) 2025/40, producers operating across borders may be subject to registration, reporting and Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) obligations in each Member State concerned. For micro and small enterprises with occasional or low-volume sales, these fixed compliance costs can exceed the value of their sales in that market. Although the Regulation refers to the principle of proportionality and provides for simplified reporting below certain thresholds, it does not establish a genuine de minimis exemption from the registration obligation, nor a single EU-wide registration procedure. 1.

Has the Commission assessed the fixed annual compliance costs, broken down by Member State, borne by micro and small enterprises? If so, in how many cases were these costs found to exceed the value of their annual turnover in that Member State?

Will the Commission consider establishing a single EU access point or a ‘once-only’ registration system and a genuine de minimis regime, including reduced, limited or abolished fixed fees for very small-scale cross-border sales?
Given the delay in adopting the implementing act laid down in Article 44(14), how will the Commission ensure legal certainty and proportionate implementation?

E-10-2026-003446.t: Non-inclusion of the planned rent subsidy in the Greek Social Climate Plan
qt: to the Commission Sakis Arnaoutoglou (S&D) Subject:

On 27 August 2026, the Commission adopted the Greek Social Climate Plan 2026–2032, totalling approximately EUR 4.77 billion. The Greek draft that was put out for public consultation in 2025 included action E1.2 in relation to a rent subsidy to approximately 5 500 public officials, in particular health workers, teachers and police officers serving in remote, island and disadvantaged areas, as well as to approximately 8 000 energy-vulnerable households with no possibility of homeownership. This specific action had even been publicly presented by the Greek government as a measure of the Social Climate Fund. However, the action is not included in the final approved Plan and only the heating allowance is provided for as direct income support. Given that Greece submitted the Plan on 27 March 2026, a revised version on 9 July and a final version on 7 August, and that Regulation (EU) 2023/955 provides for special consideration of the needs of island, mountainous and remote areas, the Commission is asked: 1.
Was action E1.2 included in the versions of 27 March and/or 9 July and, if so, at what stage was it removed, for what reason and at whose initiative?
Did the Commission raise an eligibility objection regarding the rental subsidy and, if so, which one exactly?
How are the specific housing needs of vulnerable households and public servants in island, mountainous and remote areas now being met?

E-10-2026-003444.t: Competitiveness of the European chemicals industry in the face of rising energy costs and regulatory burdens
qt: to the Commission Tobiasz Bocheński (ECR) Subject:

For several years now, the European chemicals industry has been warning of a steady decline in its competitiveness vis-à-vis producers from third countries. Industry organisations argue that high energy prices, rising operating costs and ever-increasing regulatory obligations are leading to a reduction in investment and production capacity, and the relocation of some operations outside the EU. This trend raises serious concerns about the future of one of this vital sector of the European economy and the security of strategic supply chains. This issue is of particular concern for Poland, which is one of the largest producers of chemical products in Central and Eastern Europe. The chemicals industry plays a crucial role in the production of fertilisers, plastics, pharmaceuticals, construction materials and many other products used by many other sectors of industry. The declining competitiveness of chemical companies may have a negative impact on both employment and the EU’s economic and food security. 1.

Has the Commission carried out an assessment of the impact of existing and planned environmental and chemical regulations, including amendments to the REACH Regulation, on the competitiveness of the European chemicals industry and on the risk of production being relocated outside the EU?

Does the Commission have at its disposal any analyses regarding the number of investments, production facilities or jobs lost in the chemicals sector as a result of rising energy costs and regulatory burdens?

What specific measures does the Commission intend to adopt to prevent the further deindustrialisation of the European chemicals industry and to ensure that companies from Member States, including Poland, are able to compete on a level playing field with producers outside the EU?

E-10-2026-003443.t: Impact of the planned extension of the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) on the competitiveness of European industry and SMEs
qt: to the Commission Tobiasz Bocheński (ECR) Subject:

CBAM has been portrayed as an instrument designed to prevent carbon leakage and level the playing field between producers from the EU and third countries. At the same time, European industrial representatives are increasingly pointing out that the planned extension of CBAM’s scope to downstream product groups may lead to higher operating costs, more red tape and a decline in the competitiveness of businesses operating within the single market. Particular concerns are being raised by companies acting as links in complex European supply chains, which are warning of the risk of rising costs for components and semi-finished products used in manufacturing. This issue is also of significant importance to Poland, which is one of the largest producers of industrial goods in Central and Eastern Europe and a major exporter of steel, aluminium, automotive parts, machinery and household appliances. For many SMEs, additional reporting obligations could mean a significant increase in operating costs. In light of the foregoing: 1.

Has the Commission carried out an impact assessment of the planned extension of CBAM on the competitiveness of SMEs and on the functioning of European supply chains, particularly in countries such as Poland?
Does the Commission have any analyses at its disposal regarding the anticipated increase in administrative and production costs for enterprises covered by the extended scope of CBAM?
Is the Commission considering introducing simplifications or transitional periods for SMEs in order to reduce the risk of losing competitiveness vis-à-vis non-EU producers?

E-10-2026-003442.t: Competitiveness of the European automotive industry and the impact of EU regulatory policy on Polish manufacturers and suppliers
qt: to the Commission Tobiasz Bocheński (ECR) Subject:

The European automotive industry, including the commercial vehicle sector, has for many months been raising the alarm about its deteriorating competitiveness vis-à-vis manufacturers from third countries. Organisations representing manufacturers and social partners point to mounting problems arising from high energy prices, rising operating costs, the rapid pace of implementation of new climate and environmental regulations, and insufficiently developed infrastructure to support the sector’s transition. At the same time, European manufacturers must compete with companies from outside the EU, which often operate under different regulatory and cost conditions. This is of particular concern for Poland, which is one of the EU’s largest manufacturers of buses, automotive parts and components, and a key link in European supply chains. Tens of thousands of people are employed in this sector, and many companies are heavily dependent on the state of the wider European automotive market. In light of the foregoing: 1.

Has the Commission carried out an analysis of the impact of existing and planned climate and environmental regulations on the competitiveness of the European automotive industry, in particular on manufacturers and suppliers from Central and Eastern European countries, including Poland?
Does the Commission have data on the relocation of production, reduced investment or job cuts in the automotive sector which may be linked to costs arising from EU regulations?

E-10-2026-003441.t: Scope of the judicial cooperation between Eurojust and the Iraqi National Centre for International Judicial Cooperation
qt: to the Commission Saskia Bricmont (Verts/ALE) Subject:

On 30 June 2026, Eurojust and the Iraqi National Centre for International Judicial Cooperation signed a working arrangement to strengthen cooperation in the fight against terrorism, organised crime and international crimes. According to Eurojust, working arrangements allow the exchange of strategic information and facilitate judicial cooperation, without providing a basis for the sharing of personal operational data. In light of the above: 1.

What specific type of judicial cooperation does the Commission envisage between the Member States, Eurojust and the Iraqi authorities, in particular as regards the transfer of information, evidence or files that could be used in proceedings in Iraq, and what procedural guarantees and safeguards for fundamental rights would form part of that cooperation?

Is the working arrangement likely to facilitate the transfer of EU citizens detained in Iraq to their country of nationality to be prosecuted there, including based on evidence gathered by the Iraqi authorities?
Could the cooperation also include the transfer of people convicted in Iraq to a Member State to serve there a sentence handed down by an Iraqi court?

E-10-2026-003440.t: The need to create a permanent financing instrument after the Recovery Fund reaches its end
qt: to the Commission Georgios Aftias (PPE) Subject:

The Recovery and Resilience Facility was an important funding tool that helped boost the European economy and the growth of EU Member States. However, its end marks the need to ensure sufficient and stable resources for Member States, so that they can meet their evergrowing needs. Europe faces major and persistent challenges in the areas of competitiveness, energy, housing, critical infrastructure, defence and security, regional development and the demographic problem. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Is it considering setting up a permanent European financing instrument to fill the gap left by the Recovery Fund, through the multiannual financial framework for 2028-2034?
How will major and common European projects continue to be funded so that national budgets do not have to endure the cost?

E-10-2026-003439.t: Direct financing of low-interest loans to small and medium-sized enterprises from the Social Fund
qt: to the Commission Georgios Aftias (PPE) Subject:

Small and medium-sized enterprises are the backbone of the European economy. In my home country, Greece, there are approximately 680 000 small and medium-sized enterprises. Despite their key role in creating new jobs and boosting competitiveness, they face difficulties in accessing bank loans and microcredit. There is an urgent need to move immediately and decisively towards strengthening small and medium-sized enterprises, which have essentially been excluded from bank lending. These enterprises have outstanding liabilities. Immediate European intervention and support are required. Such an initiative will give them breathing space, as due to their structural problems they cannot secure financing from the banking sector and are looking for a way to cover their financial obligations. In Greece, the Microcredit Fund is financed by the European Social Fund and the NSRF ‘Competitiveness’ programme (2021-2027). The initial objective is to support over 3 500 small businesses across the country. However, economic conditions have deteriorated due to the war in the Persian Gulf. Therefore, increasing the funds available and strengthening the financial instruments are imperative. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Will it increase the microcredit financial instruments to support small and medium-sized enterprises?
Will it enable Member States to take decisive action to support small and medium-sized enterprises effectively?

E-10-2026-003436.t: Violations of Greek airspace by Türkiye in the Alexandroupoli area
qt: to the Commission Yannis Maniatis (S&D) Subject:

On Friday 28 August, a Turkish drone embarked on a flight over the Thracian Sea lasting several hours. It flew in the wider area of Alexandroupoli and Samothrace and very close to Alexandroupoli airport. This dangerous violation by a Turkish drone marks yet another incident confirming the increase in Turkish provocations in the Aegean. It is telling that there were more than 247 instances of Turkish aircraft violating Greek airspace up to and including July this year compared to 225 during the whole of 2025. In fact, on 18 August, Turkish aircraft violated Greek national airspace 25 times, with Greek and Turkish F-16 armed fighter jets getting involved. In view of the ever-increasing violations of Greek airspace by Turkish fighter jets and drones, can the Commission say: 1.
What measures will it take, including potential sanctions against Türkiye, to protect Greek sovereign rights from Turkish provocation?

Does the Commission intend to propose the creation of a Southern Border Watch similar to the one foreseen for the eastern border, which would also include airspace violations, or to extend the implementation of the Eastern Flank Watch to Greece?

E-10-2026-003435.t: New liquid drugs and the evolving narcotics market in the EU
qt: to the Commission Paolo Inselvini (ECR), Carlo Fidanza (ECR), Stefano Cavedagna (ECR), Nicola Procaccini (ECR), Francesco Torselli (ECR), Mariateresa Vivaldini (ECR) Subject:

At Bologna airport on 6 July 2026, as part of Operation Black Poison, the Guardia di Finanza and Italy’s Customs Agency seized over 130 litres of ‘Monkey Tail’ – a home-made liquid psychoactive mixture from Nigeria – transported in over 40 bottles supposedly containing alcohol. The two individuals involved had been in regular transit through Bologna for about six months. The case highlights the evolution of the narcotics market, characterised by the spread of new psychoactive substances, mixtures of variable composition and new methods of concealment. According to the European Union Drugs Agency (EUDA), in 2025, there were 50 new psychoactive substances recorded for the first time in Europe and 55 tonnes were reported to the EU Early Warning System. The EU drugs strategy also recognises criminal organisations’ growing capacity to adapt substances, routes and methods of trafficking. In light of the above: 1.
Is the Commission aware of ‘Monkey Tail’ and its spread in the EU or similar liquid psychoactive mixtures or any other seizures?
How does it intend to adapt EU monitoring and warning tools to the rapid evolution of substances, mixtures and methods of concealment?
How can it strengthen cooperation between the EUDA, Europol, customs authorities, Member States and third countries to identify new substances, routes and trafficking methods in a timely manner?

E-10-2026-003434.t: Access to electronic vehicle systems for vehicles adapted for persons with disabilities
qt: to the Commission Vivien Costanzo (S&D), Gabriele Bischoff (S&D) Subject:

The implementation of cybersecurity requirements for motor vehicles under Regulation (EU) 2019/2144 and UNECE Regulation No 155 is giving rise to more and more secured or closed vehicle architectures (e.g. CAN bus systems). If vehicle manufacturers do not open access to these systems for converters – for example through encrypted or closed CAN bus architectures – adaptations are harder to carry out technically or are possible only at a significantly higher cost. There is currently no explicit EU obligation for vehicle manufacturers to provide access to vehicle systems for the purpose of disability-inclusive adaptations. 1.
Is the Commission planning legislative measures or delegated acts to oblige vehicle manufacturers to provide secure, standardised access to electronic vehicle systems for authorised converters?
What measures does the Commission intend to take to ensure that cybersecurity requirements do not lead to disproportionate barriers or additional costs for people with disabilities?

Is the Commission aware of vehicle manufacturers that already provide converters with secure access to the vehicle features necessary for disability-inclusive conversions? Will it instate a harmonised EU standard for such an interface?

E-10-2026-003433.t: US measures against the European tech collective Autistici/Inventati
qt: to the Commission Per Clausen (The Left) Subject:

On 26 August, the US designated the 25-year-old Italian tech collective Autistici/Inventati as a “specially designated global terrorist”1; as a result, the organisation is now also subject to extraterritorial sanctions. The implication of this appears to be a shutdown2, which would be a severe consequence for a European organisation if the designation is incorrect. In light of the above, could the European Commission answer the following questions: 1.

Does the European Commission agree with the US’s classification of the Italian tech collective Autistici/Inventati as a “global terrorist”, and is it aware of any similar classification from any EU Member State, or does it otherwise consider that this tech collective poses a serious threat to security?

If this is not the case, what measures would the Commission consider taking to prevent US extraterritorial sanctions from effectively forcing a European technology organisation such as Autistici/Inventati to close down?

Does the European Commission know how many European companies and organisations have had their existence threatened, or have been forced to close, as a result of extraterritorial sanctions imposed by countries outside the EU?

https://www.state.gov/releases/office-of-the-spokesperson/2026/08/designation-of-autistici-inventati-asa-specially-designated-global-terrorist. 2 https://www.rainews.it/articoli/2026/08/le-sanzioni-americane-al-collettivo-italiani-autisticiinventati586c570a-033e-4d24-a595-dbf2da57d844.html. 1

E-10-2026-003432.t: Google’s forthcoming Android lockdown for independent app developers
qt: to the Commission Per Clausen (The Left) Subject:

At a time when the focus is on both Europe’s digital sovereignty and the need for innovation, both are threatened by what many describe as Google’s de facto lockdown of the Android system for independent app developers1 (including, potentially, European public authorities). Among other things, these changes mean all developers – even those who do not distribute their programmes via Google’s tools, or who create apps for their own use – MUST register with Google and pay a fee to the company. Moreover, these changes mean that phones running on a system that was marketed as open will no longer be open; instead, Google will have ultimate control and the ability to lock down applications and decide what people are allowed to install on their own devices. In light of the above, could the European Commission answer the following questions: 1.
Google’s plans can only harm innovation and competition in the app market, so what steps will the Commission take in response?
If Google can lock down public applications, does the Commission not consider this to be a potential security risk?
https://arstechnica.com/gadgets/2026/03/with-developer-verification-googles-apple-envy-threatens-todismantle-androids-open-legacy/. 1

E-10-2026-003431.t: Baiting of aquatic birds in the vicinity of Natura 2000 areas
qt: to the Commission Maria Ohisalo (Verts/ALE) Subject:

In Finland, numerous small ponds have been dug out and are being used for the baiting and hunting of aquatic birds in the immediate vicinity of aquatic-bird areas that form part of the Natura 2000 network (including the Liminganlahti and Kempeleenlahti bays).1 This practice puts hunting pressure on the very birds that nest in these protected areas and set off for their migrations from there, including seriously declining species. Only a small proportion of hunters use this method, but it has a disproportionate impact on the total number of birds caught. 1.

Does the Commission consider that baiting on the periphery of a protected area and the consequent concentration of hunting might constitute disturbance of a protected species contrary to Article 6(2) of the Habitats Directive or Article 7(4) of the Birds Directive (sustainable use)?

Does the Commission have the means to ensure that no EU funding has been used for the construction of ponds and wetlands like these (e.g. the Rural Development Fund or LIFE) in a manner inconsistent with the Natura 2000 objectives, and does such aid require an impact assessment in cases like these?

In the stress tests used in practice under the Birds Directive and the Habitats Directive, and when streamlining regulation, is the Commission ensuring that the protection against non-selective catch methods under Article 8/Annex Iv(a) and the ban on the deterioration of natural habitats under Article 6(2) are not being eroded, and are such practices taken into account when assessing this?
https://www.kaleva.fi/kansalaisaloite-vaatii-vesilintujen-houkutusruokin/13609972 (in Finnish).

E-10-2026-003430.t: Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation and its red tape on small businesses
qt: to the Commission Cynthia Ní Mhurchú (Renew) Subject:

Given the Commission’s responsibility and stated commitment to reducing unnecessary administrative burdens and red tape for businesses, and given that competitiveness is a key priority of the Irish Presidency of the Council, what action will the Commission take to address the disproportionate administrative and financial burden imposed by the Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation on small and micro-enterprises, particularly those engaged in cross-border and e-commerce trade?

In particular, why are small businesses required to register separately and pay compliance fees in each Member State in which they sell or ship products, often incurring the same fixed compliance costs as significantly larger companies?

Will the Commission consider introducing simplified, proportionate and EU-wide compliance arrangements, including exemptions or reduced obligations for microenterprises, in order to prevent small businesses from being forced to scale back crossborder trade or withdraw from the EU market altogether?

E-10-2026-003429.t: Delays with the Navarro Corridor and completion of the Trans-European Transport Network’s core network
qt: to the Commission Borja Giménez Larraz (PPE) Subject:

The Navarro high-speed rail corridor is part of the Trans-European Transport Network (TENT), falling within the Atlantic Corridor and the TEN-T core network, which is to be completed by 2030. It connects Plasencia de Jalón in Zaragoza with the ‘Y Vasca’ railway line and is strategic for European rail transport. At 213.9 km long and with a planned investment of EUR 1.8425 billion, it strengthens the rail connection with Europe and its main logistics hubs. However, considerable delays are piling up. Construction has still not started on the ZaragozaCastejón section (82.3 km), despite the fact that the tender for the informative study was awarded in 2018. On the Castejón-Pamplona section (65.2 km), 50 % of the track bed has been finished, 30 % is under construction and studies are being carried out for the remaining 20 %. Construction has yet to start on either the Campanas-Zuasti (24 km) or Zuasti-Y Vasca (42.4 km) sections, and there are still two possible route options for the Zuasti-Y Vasca section. Altogether, construction has not started on three of the four sections. In light of the above: 1.
Does the Commission consider this level of implementation to be compatible with the 2030 deadline for completing the TEN-T core network?
What timeline, milestones and funding has Spain announced for the completion of the 213.9 km in question?
What action does the Commission intend to take to ensure compliance with Regulation (EU) 2024/1679 and to prevent the delays from compromising the continuity of the Atlantic Corridor?

E-10-2026-003428.t: Legal basis for tax provisions relating to electricity and natural gas
qt: to the Commission Barbara Bonte (PfE) Subject:

On 17 July 2026, the Commission proposed COM(2026) 600, amending Regulation (EU) 2019/943 on the internal market for electricity. The legal basis cited by the Commission is Article 194(2) TFEU, which renders the ordinary legislative procedure and qualified majority voting by the Council applicable. However, the proposed Article 18c obliges Member States to apply a tax differential between electricity and natural gas, whereby electricity must not be taxed more heavily than natural gas. The Commission recognises that the proposal contains fiscal measures, but it regards these as secondary to the energy targets. Article 194(3) TFEU, on the other hand, provides that measures that are primarily of a fiscal nature require adoption by the Council by a unanimous decision. 1.
On the basis of what legal criteria does the Commission conclude that Article 18c is not primarily of a fiscal nature within the meaning of Article 194(3) TFEU?
How does the Commission reconcile this direct interference in the taxation of electricity and natural gas with the fiscal powers of Member States?
Why does the Commission consider that Article 194(3) TFEU and the unanimity requirement laid down in it do not apply to Article 18c?

E-10-2026-003427.t: Level playing field with increased import quotas for Ukrainian poultry meat and eggs
qt: to the Commission Barbara Bonte (PfE) Subject:

On 29 October 2025, the revised trade arrangement between the EU and Ukraine entered into force under the Deep and Comprehensive Free Trade Area (DCFTA), with greater tariff-free quotas for various sensitive agricultural products. The annual quota for poultry meat was increased from 90 000 to 120 000 tons, and for eggs from 6 000 to 18 000 tons. The additional market access is accompanied by a gradual alignment of Ukraine with EU production standards, including in relation to animal welfare. In its declaration regarding the Council Decision, Belgium stressed that the current differences in animal welfare standards should not continue beyond 2028 and called on the Commission to monitor imports of sensitive products, particularly poultry and eggs, closely and to activate the safeguard clause immediately if necessary. 1.
Does the Commission share Belgium’s view that the differences between the EU and Ukraine regarding animal welfare standards must be eliminated by 2028, at the latest?
How is the Commission actually monitoring Ukraine’s compliance with its obligations regarding alignment with EU standards?

What objective criteria and thresholds is the Commission applying for activation of the safeguard clause if the increased imports of poultry meat or eggs put pressure on the European market or producers?

E-10-2026-003426.t: Pluralism in advisory bodies representing young people?
qt: to the Commission Catherine Griset (PfE) Subject:

As part of the implementation of the EU Youth Strategy 2019-2027, it appears that a significant number of advisory bodies have been set up to represent young people in EU and national institutions. This is the case for the long-term secretariat of the EU Youth Dialogue, for the Commission Youth Network of youth correspondents in each directorate-general, for the network of young professionals inside and outside the Commission, for the EU Youth Stakeholders Group and for the national youth councils. The role of those advisory bodies is to mainstream youth in the EU’s various policies. However, for such bodies to represent young people, they still need to resemble the youth demographic and not exclude one section of that population. 1.
How are the members of those various networks and councils recruited?
Is that recruitment conditional on the plurality of political views and the diversity of social and geographical origin?
If not, has the Commission ensured that those advisory bodies will not interfere with electoral processes in the various Member States?

E-10-2026-003425.t: AMIF funding for the new Dublin centre in Belgium
qt: to the Commission Barbara Bonte (PfE) Subject:

Version 5.2 of the Belgian Asylum, Migration and Integration Fund (AMIF) programme, approved by Implementing Decision C(2026)6201 of 22 July 2026, provides that the new Dublin centre is to be funded using the resources remaining in the general AMIF envelope and the national budget. Compared to version 4.0, this means an increase in the indicative Union contribution to reception conditions from EUR 18.93 million to EUR 49.76 million and in the target for newly created reception places from 0 to 320. The announced centre in Nazareth-De Pinte will have around 300 places and will be set up in rented private hotel facilities. 1.

In Belgium’s reasoned request for amendment under Article 24(1) of Regulation (EU) 2021/1060, what justification did it provide for the increase in resources for reception conditions, and what amount was envisaged for the funding of the new Dublin centre?
Does the increase in the target from 0 to 320 reception places relate entirely or partially to this centre?

On what legal basis under Regulation (EU) 2021/1147 did the Commission consider the AMIF funding for this centre to be compatible with the Fund, and under what conditions are rental costs for such private facilities eligible for AMIF funding?

E-10-2026-003424.t: Publication of government censorship requests on social media
qt: to the Commission Catherine Griset (PfE) Subject:

On 15 August 2026, Elon Musk announced that, on his X platform, any government-imposed censorship would now be ‘clearly visible’1. As a result, changes to the algorithm resulting from government requests will be made public. This public information is likely to increase the accountability of states that do not respect freedom of expression and would enable people to better understand X’s recommendations. The practice could also promote more transparent and fair electoral processes. 1.
Is the Commission aware of this step that X has taken?
If so, does it intend to encourage all competing platforms to also publish government censorship requests?
https://x.com/elonmusk/status/2088445767673369044?s=20.

E-10-2026-003423.t: Irregularities and possible unlawful favourable treatment of Real Madrid
qt: to the Commission Estrella Galán (The Left), Jaume Asens Llodrà (Verts/ALE), Vicent Marzà Ibáñez (Verts/ALE) Subject:

Madrid City Council is processing a change to Real Madrid FC’s plot DO-190 in Valdebebas that increases the area of buildable land from 360 000 m² to 532 550 m², allows the land to be used for profit-making purposes and increases the value of the land to EUR 360.1 million. Real Madrid competes with European clubs, but the public advantages granted by Madrid can distort that competition, a scenario covered by Articles 107 and 108 TFEU. There has already been – in 2016 – an investigation by the Commission into Real Madrid’s tax privileges and a municipal urban planning project. In question E-002668/20231, Manu Pineda, a former Member of the European Parliament from The Left Group, denounced the contracts that were awarded for the Bernabéu car parks. The Commission claimed ignorance and did not investigate. Subsequently, the courts rendered null and void the tender and the award of the contracts and found that the transaction benefited the club, not the general interest. That precedent supports the core of Pineda’s complaint and should guide how the Valdebebas matter is examined. In light of the above: 1.
Will the Commission investigate whether the reclassification of Valdebebas grants Real Madrid a selective advantage contrary to Article 107 TFEU?
Has it taken note of the decisions bearing out the warnings about the case involving the car parks, and will it apply that precedent to the examination of the Valdebebas matter?

Will it request that full clarification be provided and an independent assessment be carried out, and will it call for the reclassification to be suspended while it investigates that reclassification’s compatibility with EU law?
https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/E-9-2023-002668_EN.html.

E-10-2026-003422.t: Evaluation of national committees of inquiry and transparency of EU pandemic policy
qt: to the Commission Friedrich Pürner (NI) Subject:

Reports on the work of committees of inquiry on the COVID-19 pandemic in Member States, such as Germany1, show that key decisions were prepared by confidential discussions during the COVID-19 pandemic. The Commission also worked with expert panels and national authorities on procurement and safeguards. 1.

Were representatives of the Commission or EU agencies (e.g. ECDC, EMA) involved in confidential meetings at Member State level, and does the Commission have any documents or minutes regarding such meetings?

What steps is the Commission taking to make the decision-making basis for EU pandemic policy fully accessible ex post, and will it fully disclose the relevant documents, minutes, opinions, communications and other documents at the request of the European Parliament or the public?
How does the Commission evaluate the results of Member States’ committees of inquiry to review its own policies and procurement strategies?
https://www.berliner-zeitung.de/article/geheime-sitzungen-corona-enquete-10314463.

E-10-2026-003421.t: Dutch penalties for the unintended EU ban on catching poultry by the legs
qt: to the Commission Bert-Jan Ruissen (ECR) Subject:

On 21 July 2026, the Dutch Trade and Industry Appeals Tribunal (CBb), one of the Netherlands’ highest administrative courts, ruled that catching poultry by the legs is prohibited under Regulation (EC) No 1/2005. Dutch operators must discontinue this practice by 1 January 2027, after which non-compliance may result in penalty payments of up to EUR 60 000. The prohibition is not enforced in other Member States. Moreover, the UK Government concluded that Regulation 1/2005 was not intended to prohibit lifting poultry by the legs and considered the failure to exempt poultry an ’inadvertent drafting error’. The UK consequently amended legislation in 2025 to permit twoleg catching. The Commission’s proposal for a new Animal Transport Regulation likewise explicitly allows birds to be caught, lifted and carried by both legs under specified conditions. 1.

Does the Commission agree that the current Dutch enforcement, including penalty payments, is inappropriate considering the apparent lack of an original intention to prohibit this practice, the lack of similar enforcement in other Member States, and the Commission’s proposal to explicitly allow this practice?
What action can the Commission take to ensure this enforcement is no longer required, and is it willing to take such action before 1 January 2027?

E-10-2026-003416.t: Proposed sale of Everllence to Bain Capital and preservation of European industrial sovereignty
qt: to the Commission Thomas Pellerin-Carlin (S&D) Subject:

The Volkswagen Group intends to transfer a 51 % stake in Everllence to the US investment fund Bain Capital. Everllence is a major player in energy, in nuclear, in marine propulsion and in critical industrial technologies. More than 80 nuclear power plants in 18 countries and several buildings belonging to the French navy are equipped with the Pielstick engines that Everllence produces in France. The sale raises a number of questions in view of the European Union’s objectives of industrial sovereignty and strategic autonomy. According to several reports, an EU solution had also been considered, through a Swedish investment fund. In light of the European economic security strategy, the European industrial strategy and the goal to reduce dependencies in critical sectors: 1.
Has the Commission been informed of this proposed sale and is it assessing the potential consequences for the EU’s strategic interests?
Does it intend to issue an opinion under Regulation (EU) 2019/452 establishing a framework for the screening of foreign direct investments into the Union?
What steps does it intend to take so that the critical industrial capacities and technologies affected by the sale are encouraged to remain in the EU?

E-10-2026-003414.t: Availability of Commission information in Dutch
qt: to the Commission Gerolf Annemans (PfE) Subject:

Regulation No 1/1958 and Article 24 TFEU guarantee the use of the official languages of the Union. At the same time, the Commission recognises that specialised, urgent or short-term web content is not always available in all 24 official languages and that all content is published at least in English. As a result, information may be available in English before it is available in Dutch. 1.
Does the Commission systematically monitor the time lag between the publication of English and Dutch versions of public information?
What objective criteria does the Commission apply when publishing public information in only a limited number of official languages?
Does the Commission regard machine translation as a fully-fledged alternative to a Dutch-language version that has been checked for accuracy?

E-10-2026-003413.t: Serious statements by Markus Lammert regarding the expulsion of unaccompanied children and persons in need of international protection in Ceuta
qt: to the Commission Estrella Galán (The Left), Vicent Marzà Ibáñez (Verts/ALE), Elisabeth Grossmann (S&D), Isabel Serra Sánchez (The Left), Irene Montero (The Left), Murielle Laurent (S&D), Ilaria Salis (The Left), Erik Marquardt (Verts/ALE), Ana Miranda Paz (Verts/ALE), Catarina Martins (The Left), Rima Hassan (The Left), Tineke Strik (Verts/ALE), Per Clausen (The Left), Damien Carême (The Left), Martin Günther (The Left), Jaume Asens Llodrà (Verts/ALE) Subject:

On 18 August 2026, Markus Lammert, the Commission spokesperson for home affairs, made concerning statements encouraging the expulsion of people who had arrived in Ceuta, including unaccompanied minors and persons in need of international protection, who are entitled to legal safeguards regardless of their migration status. It is particularly serious that the Commission would encourage a Member State to act in breach of international and European law, while also failing to ensure individual assessments, access to the asylum procedure, the principle of non-refoulement and the best interests of the child, as well as obligations arising from EU fundamental rights and under international conventions. In this context: 1.
What is the Commission’s priority in responding to the crisis in Ceuta: expulsions or ensuring humanitarian assistance, fundamental rights protection and effective access to international protection?

Under what legal framework did Mr Lammert propose the expulsion of minors and persons who have expressed their intention to apply for international protection, and does the Commission consider his statements as being compatible with this legal framework?

Given that Ceuta is an external border of the EU, will the Commission provide extraordinary financial assistance to Spain and investigate Morocco’s possible role in this crisis, and if geopolitical interference in EU and Spanish sovereignty is established, what measures will it take against the countries responsible?

E-10-2026-003412.t: Administrative obstacles to the recognition of professional qualifications and the mobility of doctors in the EU
qt: to the Commission Loucas Fourlas (PPE) Subject:

Free movement of professionals and mutual recognition of professional qualifications are fundamental principles of the European Union. However, a specific case of a European doctor who moved to Belgium to specialise in obstetrics and gynaecology raises serious questions about the administrative obstacles that health professionals who wish to practise their profession in another Member State still face. This case raises serious questions about the effectiveness and transparency of national procedures applied to health professionals within the EU. In view of the above: 1.

Does the Commission consider it compatible with EU law that a European doctor may, due to lengthy and complex administrative procedures for the recognition of professional qualifications, be denied the possibility of continuing to practise a specialism?

What measures does the Commission intend to take to ensure that Member States implement procedures to recognise professional qualifications that are transparent and completed within reasonable and predictable time limits?
What protection does EU law provide for European citizens who have obtained their professional qualifications in the United Kingdom, in particular after Brexit?

E-10-2026-003411.t: Continued business presence of EU companies in Russia and implications for sanctions policy and competition
qt: to the Commission Loucas Fourlas (PPE) Subject:

Following the Russian invasion of Ukraine, many European companies withdrew from the Russian market, in line with the European Union's sanctions policy. However, some companies still maintain a significant business presence in Russia, continuing to generate revenue and make payments to the Russian state. This situation raises questions as to the coherence of the Union's sanctions policy, and may create an uneven playing field vis-à-vis companies that have withdrawn from the Russian market and borne the associated financial costs. In view of the above: 1.
How does the Commission assess the continued business activity of EU companies in Russia in the light of the Union's sanctions policy?
Does the Commission consider that this situation may distort competition in the single market?
Will the Commission consider additional measures, in particular regarding the transparency of the financial activities of EU companies in Russia, in order to ensure a level playing field?

E-10-2026-003409.t: The use of AI for threats and terrorist purposes
qt: to the Commission Loucas Fourlas (PPE) Subject:

In light of the terrorist act at Berlin’s Brandenburg Gate, the terrorist attack or assassination attempt in the Principality of Monaco, the recent threats made to the political leadership of the US using AI-generated videos and the growing concerns about an anarchic international environment, in which citizens and state officials are at risk, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Where does it stand on terrorist attacks and acts of terrorism and what measures are being taken at EU level?
Is there an EU mechanism and commonly accepted terminology for clearly distinguishing between an attempted assassination and an act of terrorism?
Does it intend to take further measures to protect European citizens and how does it plan to tackle terrorist threats made through AI?
to the Commission Loucas Fourlas (PPE) Subject:

According to Eurostat data, in Member States such as Cyprus, Greece and Romania, the share of utilised agricultural area managed by farms using precision farming technologies was very low, i.e. below 10 %. By contrast, Member States such as Luxembourg, Finland and Estonia recorded rates upwards of 75 %. In view of the above: In what ways and with what concrete measures does the Commission intend to reduce the gap between Member States in terms of use of precision technologies in agriculture?

E-10-2026-003406.t: Cross-border sabotage of peat production in Sweden
qt: to the Commission Beatrice Timgren (ECR), Charlie Weimers (ECR), Dick Erixon (ECR) Subject:

At Grimsås in Sweden, peat production by the Finnish, state-owned company Neova has been subjected to repeated sabotage and actions by radical activist groups. In the summer of 2026, machines were blocked, ditches were filled in and seeds spread on peat surfaces. The damage caused by this sabotage could amount to around SEK 100 million.1 The organisers have themselves stated that the actions that took place during 2026 brought together participants from Finland, Germany, Norway, France, Poland, Belgium, the United Kingdom and elsewhere.2 Previously, Swedish and Finnish activists have also carried out joint actions against the Finnish Parliament with the aim of drawing attention to Neova’s peat operations.3 In light of the above: 1.
Does the Commission consider that organised cross-border actions that result in damage to lawful commercial activity raises the issue of the EU’s collaboration against crossborder criminality?

Is the Commission prepared to facilitate information and police collaboration between the Member States affected when national authorities request it in order to combat sabotage against peat-producing enterprises?
What other measures does the Commission intend to implement to strengthen the protection for lawful strategic production from damage and production stoppages?

Tidningen Näringslivet, Aktivisterna klättrar upp på maskiner – polisen kan inte avvisa dem: ”Upptrappning på helt ny nivå”, https://www.tn.se/naringsliv/48681/aktivisterna-klattrar-upp-pa-maskinerpolisen-kan-inte-avvisa-dem-upptrappning-pa-helt-ny-niva/. 2 Återställ Våtmarker, We’re going to stop their machines, https://aterstallvatmarker.se/en/press/we-regoing-to-stop-their-machines. 3 Yle, Environmental protesters splatter Parliament House pillars with red paint, https://yle.fi/a/7420113835. 1

E-10-2026-003405.t: Rewetting of peatlands – impact on preparedness and food security
qt: to the Commission Beatrice Timgren (ECR), Dick Erixon (ECR), Charlie Weimers (ECR) Subject:

The Nature Restoration Regulation requires the restoration of drained peatlands in agricultural use, but permits flexibility when rewetting would have considerable negative consequences for, inter alia, infrastructure, climate adaptation and other public interests.1 A Swedish government report refers to the importance of peat as a growing medium and states that horticultural peat is the dominant raw material for the production of forest plants and that satisfactory substitute materials are not yet available in the volumes and quality that are required for all applications.2 At the same time, the Commission’s own preparedness strategy stresses that disruption in the supply chains for energy, food and critical raw materials can have serious consequences for the Union.3 In light of the above: 1.
How will the Commission ensure that Sweden's restoration plan will not disproportionately reduce the availability of domestically produced horticultural and energy peat?
Does the Commission consider that food supply, energy preparedness and domestic value chains can be covered by ‘other public interests’ in Article 11.4?
Will the Commission take account of the effects on competitiveness, energy preparedness and food chains when it submits views on national measures?

Nature Restoration Regulation, Article 11.4, OJ L, 2024/1991, 29.7.2024. SOU 2026:18 Odlingstorv och klimatet, p. 38. 3 European Commission, JOINT COMMUNICATION TO THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT, THE EUROPEAN COUNCIL, THE EUROPEAN ECONOMIC AND SOCIAL COMMITTEE AND THE COMMITTEE OF THE REGIONS on the European Preparedness Union Strategy, https://eurlex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52025JC0130. 1 2

E-10-2026-003404.t: Scientifically neutral use of the term ‘sustainability’ for growing media
qt: to the Commission Beatrice Timgren (ECR), Dick Erixon (ECR), Charlie Weimers (ECR) Subject:

The EU’s Ecolabel criteria for growing media categorically state that a product may not contain intentionally added peat.1 However, a scientific article dating from 2026, with researchers from NIBIO, SLU and elsewhere, stresses that sustainability is not an inherent characteristic of an individual material, but must be assessed at system level and encompass environmental, economic and social consequences.2 Therefore, the fact that a product is ‘peat‑free’ does not in itself show that its overall sustainability is better. In light of the above: 1.
What scientific basis justifies the categorical exclusion of peat from the EU Ecolabel, rather than it being assessed on the basis of actual life-cycle performance?
In light of new research, does the Commission intend to review the approach where ‘peat-free’ is used as an indirect indicator of sustainability?

Going forward, will the Commission distinguish more clearly between responsibly produced horticultural peat and energy peat, and take into account function, transport, resource consumption and the environmental impact of the alternatives?

Commission Decision (EU) 2022/1244 establishing the EU Ecolabel criteria for growing media and soil improvers, Annex, criterion 1, OJ L 190, 19.7.2022. 2 Aurdal et al., The challenge of defining ‘sustainable growing media’: why the term is used incorrectly and what needs to be done about it, doi: 10.3389/fhort.2026.1800902. 1

E-10-2026-003403.t: The cumulative impact of EU rules on European peat production
qt: to the Commission Beatrice Timgren (ECR), Charlie Weimers (ECR), Dick Erixon (ECR) Subject:

The Commission’s vision for agriculture and food emphasises food security, resilience and reduced import dependency.1 In its action plan for fertilizer, the Commission has also stressed the need for the domestic production of important intermediate goods, predictable deliveries and emergency preparedness.2 At the same time, there is a risk that ecosystem restoration, climate reporting, ecolabelling and national policy instruments will collectively have a negative impact on the investment conditions for European horticultural peat. A Swedish government report refers to the risk of reduced Swedish production being replaced by imports and emissions being transferred abroad as a result, known as carbon leakage.3 1.
How does the Commission assess the cumulative effect of the EU’s various policy areas on the availability of European horticultural peat and the risks of carbon leakage?
Does the Commission consider that strategic autonomy is desirable with regard to the question of peat as a growing medium?
What measures does the Commission intend to implement to ensure that EU rules do not lead to the discontinuation of lawful production and increased import dependency?

European Commission, COMMUNICATION FROM THE COMMISSION TO THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT, THE COUNCIL, THE EUROPEAN ECONOMIC AND SOCIAL COMMITTEE AND THE COMMITTEE OF THE REGIONS, A Vision for Agriculture and Food Shaping together an attractive farming and agri-food sector for future generations, COM/2025/75 final. 2 European Commission, Ensuring availability and affordability of fertilisers, https://agriculture.ec.europa.eu/common-agricultural-policy/agri-food-supply-chain/ensuring-availability-andaffordability-fertilisers_en. 3 SOU 2026:18 Odlingstorv och klimatet, p. 164 pp. 1

E-10-2026-003402.t: Approval of Bulgaria’s accession to the euro area and reliability of the Commission’s budgetary forecasts
qt: to the Commission Stanislav Stoyanov (ESN) Subject:

According to Eurostat data, Bulgaria’s budget deficit increased to 3.5 % of GDP in 2025, compared with 2.0 % in 2023 and 3.0 % in 2024. Over the same period, government debt rose from 22.9 % to 29.9 % of GDP. Despite this deterioration, the European Commission concluded in its June 2025 Convergence Report that Bulgaria meets the budgetary requirements for joining the euro area. The Commission based its conclusion on forecasts indicating that the deficit for 2025 would decline to 2.8 %. This raises serious questions regarding the reliability of the assessment and the consistent application of Article 126 TFEU, which requires the Commission to monitor compliance with budgetary discipline. 1.
How does the Commission assess its decision to approve Bulgaria’s accession to the euro area on the basis of forecasts that subsequently proved to be materially inaccurate?

Does the Commission have rules or procedures for reviewing approval to join the euro area where the forecasts underpinning that approval subsequently prove materially inaccurate and, if not, does it consider such rules necessary?
How does the Commission ensure that budgetary requirements are applied consistently across all Member States, and can it provide specific examples to substantiate this?
to the Commission Oihane Agirregoitia Martínez (Renew) Subject:

Recent journalistic investigations have revealed that AI-generated YouTube and Instagram accounts that have millions of followers and have been verified by Meta pretend to be real doctors or healers and spread health disinformation. A high percentage of those accounts also promote supplements, despite the fact that in Spain it is illegal to advertise products ‘with a purported health purpose ... that purport to have testimonials from health professionals’. The Digital Services Act requires large platforms to mitigate the risks of illegal content being disseminated and harm being done to public health via their services. In light of the above: 1. Has the Commission assessed whether the existence of such AI-generated accounts reveals potential shortcomings in the risk mitigation measures that very large online platforms are required to implement to mitigate potential negative effects on public health, as provided for in Articles 34 and 35 of the Digital Services Act? 2. Does the Commission intend to initiate additional investigations or take further enforcement action when platforms verify, through paid subscriptions such as Meta Verified, AI-generated profiles that do not represent real people? 3. Has the Commission considered asking Amazon for information about its Associates Program and the systemic risks this could pose with regard to the financing of creators who spread health disinformation?

E-10-2026-003400.t: Regulation on packaging and packaging waste: registration requirements and extended producer responsibility obligations
qt: to the Commission Oihane Agirregoitia Martínez (Renew) Subject:

Regulation (EU) 2025/40 introduces registration requirements and extended producer responsibility obligations for those who market packaging or packaged products in different Member States. Those who sell small volumes online in the EU have expressed concerns about the cumulative administrative and economic burden resulting from the registration requirements and extended producer responsibility obligations in each Member State, including the appointment of authorised representatives. For businesses that make only a limited number of cross-border shipments every year, those fixed costs could be disproportionate to the actual volume of packaging waste generated and constitute a barrier to accessing the single market. The Commission’s impact assessment accompanying the regulation envisaged specific treatment for micro-, small and medium-sized enterprises to ensure that the regulation’s impact would be proportional. 1.

How did the Commission assess the specific administrative and economic impact of the extended producer responsibility obligations on microenterprises and self-employed individuals that carry out a low volume of cross-border e-commerce?
How will it monitor whether Member States’ effective implementation of Articles 44 and 45 results in disproportionate costs or barriers to the single market for such companies?

If disproportionate impacts are identified, will the Commission consider additional simplification, harmonisation or de minimis measures for microenterprises and sellers with low volumes of cross-border shipments?

E-10-2026-003399.t: Packaging: the Commission tells the Member States not to apply its Regulation on packaging and packaging waste the day after the regulation’s official date of application
qt: to the Commission Virginie Joron (PfE) Subject:

Regulation (EU) 2025/40 on packaging and packaging waste became applicable on 12 August 2026. The following day, at a press conference, a senior official at the Commission told the German daily newspaper Die Welt: ‘We encourage Member States not to apply the new rules and not to impose penalties’, calling the text ‘clearly disproportionate’1. At the same time, French ecommerce microenterprises have warned about the red tape, including as regards apostilles and the costs imposed2 for representation in each country. Those costs can exceed EUR 600 – and even EUR 2 000 – per country per year for companies with minimal turnover, forcing them to cease operations in several European countries. On 24 June 2026, due to the lack of a majority, the Council supposedly abandoned the proposal to suspend Article 45(3) of the regulation. An exemption for small businesses will be debated in the European Parliament in October3. 1.

Can the Commission confirm that the ‘pragmatic approach’ recommended by the Commission official means that no fines should be imposed and clarify whether the instructions to not apply the regulation have been formalised in writing to the national supervisory authorities?

Has the Commission made written representations to major intermediaries, such as Amazon, to confirm that this ‘pragmatic approach’ is actually applied in their dealings with small European businesses?

https://audiovisual.ec.europa.eu/en/media/video/I-293384?language=EN&start=2664&end=2750; https://brusselssignal.eu/2026/08/commission-tells-member-states-to-ignore-its-own-new-packaging-rules-andskip-penalties/. 2 Article 45(3) of the Regulation on packaging and packaging waste. 3 https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/press/press-releases/2026/06/24/simplification-council-agreesnegotiating-stance-to-simplify-and-streamline-environmental-rules/; https://expra.eu/2026/06/29/parliamenttakes-a-more-targeted-approach-to-the-epr-authorised-representative-suspension/. 1

E-10-2026-003398.t: The application of the ‘artificially created conditions’ clause in respect of agricultural producer groups in Poland
qt: to the Commission Anna Bryłka (PfE) Subject:

In Poland, the ARiMR payment agency is challenging aid granted to agricultural producer groups, citing ‘artificially created conditions’, including personal, family, organisational or economic links between producers. In some cases, the structures in question had previously been operating with the authority’s knowledge, and the aid was granted following an inspection. In its Judgment of 12 September 2013 in Case C-434/12, Slancheva sila EOOD, the CJEU stated that a finding of artificially created conditions requires consideration of both objective and subjective elements and an assessment of all the circumstances of the specific case. 1.

Can legal, economic, functional or personal links, including family ties, be sufficient in themselves to establish that the conditions for obtaining aid were artificially created, without demonstrating both the objective and subjective elements required by the caselaw of the CJEU?

Does EU law permit – and under what conditions – the recovery of aid previously granted and paid out, where an authority subsequently makes a different assessment of the same circumstances of which it was already aware at the time the aid was granted, without demonstrating that the beneficiaries’ primary objective was to obtain an advantage contrary to the purpose of the support scheme?
What is the significance, in such cases, of the principles of legal certainty, the protection of legitimate expectations, proportionality and the individual assessment of the case?

E-10-2026-003397.t: Misuse of Interpol red notices to target dissidents and journalists
qt: to the Commission Raquel García Hermida-Van Der Walle (Renew) Subject:

Non-democratic states such as Russia, Türkiye and Serbia continue to use Interpol red notices to target political dissidents and journalists1. Some police authorities in EU countries still execute such arrest requests, essentially allowing autocracies to target innocent citizens in the EU, while other police authorities acknowledge that such requests involve political misuse of red notices. Targeted individuals cannot access information about their red notice, leaving them in a state of great uncertainty. Since 2021, the EU and Interpol have been negotiating a cooperation agreement. The European Search Portal, which began operating in June 2026, enables people to query Interpol databases. 1.

Does the Commission agree that different law enforcement practices in different EU countries regarding red notices on political targets and journalists significantly impact these people’s freedom of movement within the EU? If it agrees, what action will it take to address this issue? If it does not agree, then why not?
How is the Commission using the negotiations to pressure Interpol to take firmer action against any political activities by non-democratic regimes, such as the misuse of red notices?

Will the Commission propose EU-wide rules on dealing with Interpol red notices, such as judicial checks on red notices, the granting of a specific status to people who receive abusive red notices following judicial checks, and appeal mechanisms?
https://www.amnesty.org/en/latest/news/2026/01/global-misuse-of-interpol-red-notices-to-targetdissidents-a-grave-institutional-failure/. 1
to the Commission Nicolás González Casares (S&D) Subject:

On 3 June 2026, the Commission put forward its European technological sovereignty package. However, the legislative package did not include an associated proposal on data centre energy efficiency, including the new rating scheme and sustainability labels. According to Commission sources, this new regulation, which will establish sustainability benchmarks and new transparency rules for data centres, will be published ‘by early 2027 at the latest’. In light of the above: 1.
For what reasons has the Commission delayed the file in question?

The President of the European Data Centre Association (EUDCA) has expressed concerns about the sustainability requirements for the industry1 and has stated that Europe might need to turn to fossil fuels to achieve its AI infrastructure goals2. How will the Commission ensure that environmental principles and renewable energy continue to be a priority?

The Commission is promoting tripartite agreements between data centre operators, energy-related parties and public authorities3. What specific measures will be included in those agreements and what role will the EUDCA play in that cooperation?

E-10-2026-003395.t: Establishing whether there are any EU initiatives to combat insurance fraud in recreational boating
qt: to the Commission Stefano Cavedagna (ECR) Subject:

Sectoral operators claim that the recreational boating community as a whole is still very vulnerable to insurance fraud because the competent authorities, surveyors and insurers are not communicating in real time and because the transnational accident database needed to promptly cross-check accident data has yet to be created. The recreational boating insurance market has been hit hard by fraudsters, whose go-to scams include bogus theft and shipwreck claims and ‘double-dipping’, a practice in which policy holders collect benefits from two or more insurance companies for the same loss or damage. Given the cross-border nature of these scams, the Union could, by taking a proactive stance, make a key contribution to bolstering cooperation and data interoperability among the Member States. In the light of the above, could the Commission clarify: 1.

Whether the EU already has (or is in the process of setting up) any initiatives, programmes or databases designed to tackle insurance fraud in recreational boating, or whether it has made funding available to any projects akin to the above?
Whether it will establish a harmonised regulatory framework for the cross-border sharing of maritime accident information which also complies with the EU’s personal data protection legislation?
Which EU regulations could serve as a basis for the establishment of an interoperable and EU-wide maritime insurance fraud prevention system?

E-10-2026-003393.t: The PPWR and existing reusable packaging schemes
qt: to the Commission Marcin Sypniewski (ESN) Subject:

In many sectors, particularly in the drinks industry, schemes for the reuse of glass bottles, crates, kegs and other packaging have been in operation for years. However, businesses are warning of uncertainty regarding the application of the new PPWR requirements to packaging already in circulation and the method for recording the number of times it has been reused. Individually marking and tracking millions of items of packaging could require costly technical changes, while withdrawing packaging that is still usable would lead to the generation of additional waste. In light of the above: 1.

Will the Commission confirm that reusable packaging placed on the market before the new labelling requirements enter into force may remain in circulation until the end of its natural life without the need for modernisation?

Can compliance with the requirements regarding the number of circulation cycles be demonstrated on the basis of reliable statistical and operational data, without the need to track each item of packaging individually?
Will existing reuse schemes be deemed compliant with the PPWR without the need to redraft documentation and demonstrate compliance with Annex VI?

E-10-2026-003392.t: Transmission of information on the 11 May 2026 incident to Frontex Situation Centre teams and national contact points
qt: to the Commission Özlem Demirel (The Left) Subject:
Transmission of information on the 11 May 2026 incident to Frontex Situation Centre teams and national contact points

On 11 May 2026, Frontex observed, including by using a long-range drone, a maritime emergency that took place around 55 nautical miles north of Tripoli, as Sea-Watch 5 rescued 90 people from a vessel in distress. Aerial surveillance footage was later leaked to media outlets in France and Italy without authorisation. It is unclear which of the Frontex teams or Eurosur national contact points previously had access to this material. 1.
What videos of the incident were sent on 11 May 2026 or later to which teams in Frontex or Italy?

Which communication and reporting networks, such as NAVTEX, Eurosur, Mediterranean Border Cooperation Centre and Seahorse Mediterranean in particular, were used by Frontex or the Italian liaison officer at the Frontex Situation Centre to share information about the incident, and when?

How does Frontex explain that recordings of this incident were later posted by conservative media in France and Italy? What measures were taken to investigate this possible unauthorised transfer of Frontex material?

E-10-2026-003391.t: Frontex’s aerial observation of the maritime emergency on 11 May 2026
qt: to the Commission Özlem Demirel (The Left) Subject:
Frontex’s aerial observation of the maritime emergency on 11 May 2026

On 11 May 2026, Frontex observed, including by using a long-range drone, a maritime emergency around 55 nautical miles north of Tripoli, during which the Sea-Watch 5 rescued 90 people from a vessel in distress. Heron 1 departed from Malta but flew back to Valletta before Libyan gunmen fired at the rescue vessel. It is also unclear how Frontex became aware about the maritime emergency. 1.
How did Frontex become aware of the maritime emergency? Which Frontex aircraft then provided information, including any satellite data?

In which Frontex structures or operations were these units deployed, especially if this took place under Joint Operation Italy 2026, Eurosur, Multipurpose Aerial Surveillance or Frontex Aerial Surveillance?
To the best of Frontex’s knowledge, which other vessels or aircraft from neighbouring third countries, such as Libya, were involved in the observing or monitoring the incident?

E-10-2026-003390.t: Classification of the maritime emergency observed by Frontex on 11 May 2026
qt: to the Commission Özlem Demirel (The Left) Subject:
Classification of the maritime emergency observed by Frontex on 11 May 2026

On 11 May 2026, the crew of civilian sea-rescue vessel Sea-Watch 5 saved 90 people from an overcrowded double-deck wooden boat with no adequate life-saving equipment in international waters around 55 nautical miles north of Tripoli. Under the relevant maritime conventions (e.g. SOLAS, SAR), the circumstances constituted an acute maritime emergency. Frontex observed the boat at times using a long-range drone stationed in Malta, but did not take any further action. 1.
What information did Frontex have about the situation on board – the condition people were in, the situation below deck or the availability of life-saving equipment before the Sea-Watch 5 arrived?

What criteria or conventions do Frontex and Frontex aerial surveillance pilots use when sighting a vessel and afterwards, to assess whether a maritime emergency is at hand, and what measures are then taken?
Did Frontex or the Airbus pilot of the long-distance drone classify the observed vessel as being in a maritime emergency, did it take measures, or not, and on what grounds?

E-10-2026-003389.t: Involvement of Libyan authorities in communication on the maritime emergency of 11 May 2026
qt: to the Commission Özlem Demirel (The Left) Subject:
Involvement of Libyan authorities in communication on the maritime emergency of 11 May 2026

On 11 May 2026, Sea-Watch 5 rescued 90 people from a vessel in distress off the Libyan coast. During the rescue operation, the crew were confronted by masked, armed men who threatened to throw people into the water. The EU’s Mediterranean countries have been cooperating with Libyan authorities on migration control for years, including through the Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre (MRCC) in Tripoli. It is unclear to what extent and how these or other Libyan bodies were informed of the maritime emergency or even received footage from Frontex. 1.

Which Libyan bodies were involved in communication by Frontex, including the Italian liaison officer at the Frontex Situation Centre, about the maritime emergency on 11 May 2026? What type of information was sent to them in each case?

When and through which channels were those Libyan bodies informed by Frontex or the Italian liaison officer at the Frontex Situation Centre on 11 May 2026 that masked, armed persons were on board the boat and that the boat had turned back towards Libya?

With which Libyan authorities did Frontex or Italy, including the Italian liaison officer at the Frontex Situation Centre, exchange information following the maritime emergency? What information was transmitted?

E-10-2026-003388.t: Labelling of animal-derived ingredients in medicines
qt: to the Commission Seán Kelly (PPE) Subject:

The use of animal-derived ingredients in medicines is common, yet EU residents often cannot identify these components due to inconsistent or unclear labelling practices. For ethical, religious, medical or dietary reasons many patients require transparency in order to make informed choices. Given that EU consumer legislation already provides for clear labelling in other sectors, improved disclosure in medicinal products would strengthen patient rights and trust while imposing minimal burden on industry. 1.

In the light of the issues faced by millions of consumers, can the Commission indicate whether it intends to propose legislation requiring mandatory and standardised labelling on packaging and patient information leaflets of all animal-derived ingredients used in medicinal products?
Additionally, can the Commission state whether it will consider establishing a centralised, publicly accessible database listing such ingredients for authorised medicines marketed in the EU?

E-10-2026-003387.t: Availability of Siri AI in the EU and Commission engagement with Apple
qt: to the Commission Seán Kelly (PPE) Subject:

Apple has announced that certain Siri AI features will not be made available to iPhone and iPad users in the EU, citing the interoperability requirements of the Digital Markets Act (DMA). The Commission has stated that nothing in the DMA prevents Apple from introducing these services in the EU and that it remains in discussions with Apple on a safe and DMAcompliant solution. It has also stated that Apple has not yet presented a concrete interoperability proposal beyond requesting an exemption from the relevant requirements for more than 18 months. In this context: 1.

What engagement has taken place between the Commission and Apple since the announcement of the delayed EU rollout of Siri AI, and has Apple subsequently presented any concrete technical proposal for DMA-compliant interoperability?

Does the Commission consider that a solution can be found which enables the timely rollout of Siri AI in the EU while ensuring both effective interoperability and appropriate safeguards for users’ privacy and security?
What further steps does the Commission envisage to facilitate such a solution and avoid EU consumers facing a prolonged delay in accessing these services?

E-10-2026-003386.t: Radical NGO distributes weapons to illegal immigrants
qt: to the Commission Jorge Buxadé Villalba (PfE) Subject:

On 28 August 2026, the residents of Ceuta protested against the Moroccan Government’s invasion of the city through the coordinated influx of tens of thousands of Maghrebi people. During the protests, some of the illegal immigrants threw chemical devices/explosive weapons at the Ceutan residents who were defending their right to live in safety. According to media reports1, the weapons were made by NGO No Name Kitchen, an organisation seeking to destroy ‘Europe’s racist and violent borders’, and distributed to illegal immigrants to use against EU citizens. Although No Name Kitchen criticises the EU and states that it does not receive funds from the bloc, there are reports linking the organisation with Open Society Foundations2, an entity that does receive EU funding. In view of the above: 1.
Can the Commission confirm that No Name Kitchen has never received EU funding?
Does the Commission consider it appropriate to withdraw EU funding from Open Society Foundations since it is associated with radical groups that facilitate and encourage violence against Europeans?

Does the Commission consider that, in light of the evidence that No Name Kitchen is involved in organised criminal activities, it should support No Name Kitchen’s inclusion in Europol’s and INTERPOL’s criminal network databases?
