E-10-2026-003385.t: The General Data Protection Regulation and procurement payment data
qt: to the Commission Cynthia Ní Mhurchú (Renew) Subject:

In Ireland, the Office of Government Procurement (OGP) ceased collecting procurementaddressable expenditure data from public bodies following legal advice relating to obligations under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). The Irish Government has stated that the OGP has ‘no legal basis or ability’ to access such data and that data protection issues remain under examination1,2. Public procurement payment data is essential to determine how much public bodies actually paid, to whom, for what purpose, and whether expenditure can be linked to the procurement process that authorised it. 1.

Does the Commission consider that the GDPR prevents a Member State, or a central public authority within a Member State, from collecting and processing public procurement payment data for the purposes of reviewing, analysing and managing public expenditure?

Does the Commission agree that, as a general principle, public authorities must be able to process the expenditure data necessary to discharge their ordinary public financial management, audit, transparency, fraud-risk monitoring and policy functions, subject to appropriate data protection safeguards?
Does the Commission consider that the GDPR should be interpreted in a way that prevents public authorities from maintaining effective oversight of public expenditure?
https://www.oireachtas.ie/en/debates/question/2025-06-24/337/. https://www.oireachtas.ie/en/debates/question/2026-03-18/492/#pq_492.

E-10-2026-003384.t: EU cooperation on personal mobility devices and off-road motorcycles
qt: to the Commission Cynthia Ní Mhurchú (Renew) Subject:

The unsafe and antisocial use of e-scooters, scramblers and quad bikes is creating challenges for road safety and public spaces across Member States. Available figures include 754 escooter, 94 scrambler and 17 quad-bike seizure or detention incidents in Ireland in the first quarter of 2026, 11 944 injury collisions involving e-scooters in Germany in 2024 and a 55 % increase in e-scooter injury collisions in Belgium during the first half of 2025. Although road-use rules and enforcement are primarily national matters, inconsistent definitions, data collection and regulatory approaches hinder comparison and the identification of effective measures. The Commission’s 2024 study on personal mobility devices identified a need for greater EU-level harmonisation. 1.

Will the Commission establish a workstream within the High-Level Group on Road Safety to exchange best practice on topics such as enforcement, seizure, vehicle identification, age restrictions, protective equipment, anti-tampering and public awareness?
Will it develop common EU definitions and a comparable data framework for collisions, injuries, offences and seizures?

E-10-2026-003383.t: Relationship between the Short-Term Rental Regulation and Irish planning restrictions
qt: to the Commission Cynthia Ní Mhurchú (Renew) Subject:

How will the Commission ensure that the EU framework for short-term accommodation rental data collection and sharing1 is implemented in a way that supports evidence-based policymaking and transparency, while ensuring that Member States, including Ireland, do not introduce disproportionate market access (planning) restrictions that go beyond the objectives of improving data availability and regulatory cooperation?

Regulation (EU) 2024/1028 of 11 April 2024 on data collection and sharing relating to short-term accommodation rental services and amending Regulation (EU) 2018/1724 (OJ L, 2024/1028, 29.4.2024, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1028/oj). 1

E-10-2026-003382.t: Does Ireland’s planning-linked STR registration constitute an EU Services Directive authorisation scheme?
qt: to the Commission Cynthia Ní Mhurchú (Renew) Subject:

Given that Ireland’s proposed short-term rental (STR) framework makes access to the national STR registration system conditional upon compliance with planning requirements, does the Commission consider that such a framework may constitute an authorisation scheme within the meaning of Articles 9 and 10 of the Services Directive1?
If so, what criteria would Ireland need to demonstrate are fulfilled to ensure that such restrictions are justified, proportionate, transparent and non-discriminatory?
Directive 2006/123/EC of 12 December 2006 on services in the internal market (ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2006/123/oj). 1

E-10-2026-003381.t: Procurement data as a strategic public-sector capability
qt: to the Commission Cynthia Ní Mhurchú (Renew) Subject:

Public procurement represents a major share of public expenditure across the EU. However, procurement data remains fragmented across contracting authorities, platforms and financial systems, limiting the ability of public authorities to aggregate demand, compare prices, assess supplier performance and identify emerging risks. 1.
Does the Commission consider procurement and expenditure data to be a strategic public-sector asset for improving public financial management and administrative capacity?
Will the Commission assess whether fragmented procurement data limits Member States’ ability to benchmark costs, aggregate demand, manage suppliers and secure value for money?
In the context of the future public procurement act, will the Commission consider measures to help Member States develop more interoperable procurement data systems?

E-10-2026-003380.t: Benchmarking public procurement costs across Member States
qt: to the Commission Cynthia Ní Mhurchú (Renew) Subject:

Public authorities often procure comparable goods, services and works, but the data needed to compare prices, contract values, variations and final expenditure is not consistently available or interoperable. This limits the ability of Member States to identify abnormal costs, weak scoping, inefficient purchasing or recurring overruns. 1.
Does the Commission consider that better procurement data could support cost benchmarking across comparable public contracts in Member States?
Will the Commission assess whether current procurement data standards are sufficient to allow comparison of planned contract values, modified contract values and final expenditure?
Will the Commission consider supporting EU-level guidance or tools to help public authorities benchmark procurement costs and identify areas where public spending efficiency could be improved?

E-10-2026-003379.t: Procurement transparency and SME access to public contracts
qt: to the Commission Cynthia Ní Mhurchú (Renew) Subject:

The Commission has repeatedly emphasised the importance of improving access to public procurement for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). However, limited transparency on purchasing patterns, repeat awards, contract aggregation and supplier concentration may make it harder to assess whether procurement markets are genuinely open to smaller firms. 1.
Does the Commission consider that better procurement data could help identify barriers to SME’s participation in public contracts?
Will the Commission assess whether Member States collect sufficient data on supplier size, repeat awards, contract lots and market concentration to evaluate SME access?
In the future Public Procurement Act, will the Commission consider measures to improve transparency on whether public procurement markets remain accessible to SMEs and new entrants?

E-10-2026-003378.t: Data-driven oversight by national procurement review bodies
qt: to the Commission Cynthia Ní Mhurchú (Renew) Subject:

Under the EU procurement remedies framework, enforcement of procurement rules in nationally funded procurement largely depends on Member State review bodies. However, many oversight systems remain complaint-led and may not have access to structured data needed to identify systemic risks, recurring breaches or patterns of non-compliance. 1.

Does the Commission consider that national procurement review and oversight bodies should have access to structured procurement data to support systemic monitoring, not only individual complaint handling?
Will the Commission assess whether the current remedies framework is adequate for modern, data-driven oversight of procurement compliance?
In the context of the future public procurement act, will the Commission consider whether national oversight bodies need stronger data access, analytical capacity and reporting obligations?

E-10-2026-003377.t: National preparation of national and regional partnership plans
qt: to the Commission Elsi Katainen (Renew) Subject:

Work on the national and regional partnership (NRP) plans referred to in the Commission’s proposal for an NRP regulation (COM(2025)0565) is under way in the Member States, while negotiations on the EU’s future financial framework are ongoing. Under the proposal for a regulation, Member States have to organise and implement comprehensive partnerships, with a balanced representation of, for example, regional and local authorities, the economic and social partners, and civil society. The partnership must operate in accordance with the principle of multi-level governance and a bottom-up approach, and the partners must be involved in the preparation, implementation and evaluation of the plan. In addition, the implementation of the partnership must comply with the Commission’s code of conduct on partnership. Not all the Member States have yet started drawing up regional partnership plans, which raises the question of whether territoriality can be achieved within the target time frame. 1.

How will the Commission ensure that the preparation and implementation of the NRP plans are in line with the final text of the regulation, and that due account is taken of the specific characteristics of regions and the involvement of relevant stakeholders?
What action does the Commission intend to take if the preparation or implementation of a Member State’s NRP plan does not comply with the requirements of the regulation?

E-10-2026-003375.t: Availability of assistive technology for blind and visually impaired people
qt: to the Commission Biljana Borzan (S&D) Subject:

Citizens complain about the increasingly limited availability of advanced digital and AI functionalities in certain Member States, particularly for smaller languages such as Croatian. Certain devices and services – including assistive technologies of crucial importance for blind and visually impaired people – offer a significantly wider range of features in some Member States than in others. However, this practice leads to unequal access to technologies and potential discrimination against citizens based on their language and place of residence, which contradicts the EU’s fundamental principles of equality and inclusion. Can the Commission clarify whether it considers such a practice to be compliant with EU law and whether it plans to issue additional guidance to ensure equal access to digital and AI solutions, particularly assistive technologies, for all EU citizens, regardless of language?

E-10-2026-003374.t: Disclosure of the species of origin for animal-derived excipients in human medicines
qt: to the Commission Biljana Borzan (S&D) Subject:

Article 59 of Directive 2001/83/EC1 requires the package leaflet to list excipients, while Article 54 requires certain excipients to be listed on the outer packaging. However, neither provision requires disclosure of the species from which the product is derived. Excipients such as gelatine, stearates or lactose may be animal- or plant-derived, but this is not specified. In correspondence with a citizen (Ares(2025)10521900; Ares(2026)1090942), the Commission confirmed that EU law does not require disclosure of species origin, while acknowledging the importance of informed patient choice based on ethical, cultural or religious considerations. This lack of transparency affects citizens who follow dietary restrictions related to animal products (e.g., halal, kosher, Hindu, vegetarian or vegan diets). Unlike food labelling rules, EU pharmaceutical legislation provides no mechanism to identify the origin of excipients, despite manufacturers already holding this information for quality and supply-chain purposes. Other jurisdictions have taken steps in this direction: Switzerland requires disclosure for certain excipients, and the American Medical Association supports such transparency. 1.
Does the Commission plan to amend Directive 2001/83/EC or introduce other measures to require disclosure of the species from which excipients originate?
Has it assessed integrating this information into digital product information or eleaflets?
What costs does it foresee, given that this information is already available to manufacturers?
Directive 2001/83/EC of 6 November 2001 on the Community code relating to medicinal products for human use (ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2001/83/oj). 1

E-10-2026-003373.t: Construction of solar power station in Thessaly despite potential violations of EU environmental law and protection of Natura 2000 areas
qt: to the Commission Afroditi Latinopoulou (PfE) Subject:

A solar power station with a capacity of 400 MW is being promoted in Antichasia, in the regional unit of Trikala. The total designated area covers around 1 550 hectares, of which 600 hectares will be taken up by the power station buildings and equipment. From the information I have been provided with, it looks as though the entire area is located within a Natura 2000 Special Protection Area (SPA) and approximately 220 hectares also fall within a Special Area of Conservation (SAC). The site is located just 215 metres from the edge of a settlement and another power station is being developed less than 8 km away. The environmental impact study was submitted hastily and just eight months after the producer authorisation was issued. Potential consequences of the project include the destruction of habitats, flooding, species displacement, water pollution, reduction of land for crop cultivation and livestock farming and permanent visual degradation. In view of this, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

How does it check full compliance with all applicable EU procedures (Directives 2011/92/EU, 92/43/EEC and 2009/147/EC), including the appropriate assessment of Article 6 of the Habitats Directive for projects within Natura areas?
Does it intend to take the necessary steps to protect the environment and ecosystem, which is clearly at risk?
Will it consider the possibility of a breach of procedure and ask for the immediate suspension of permitting procedures until full compliance is ensured?

E-10-2026-003372.t: Credibility of the excessive deficit procedure in relation to France
qt: to the Commission Piotr Müller (ECR) Subject:

France remains subject to the excessive deficit procedure, and the deadline for bringing its deficit below 3 % of GDP on a long-term basis expires in 2029. However, in response to Question E-003433/20251, the Commission concluded that the deviation from the recommended net expenditure growth was small and did not take any further procedural steps. Meanwhile, the Commission’s spring forecast projects a French deficit of 5.1 % of GDP in 2026 and 5.7 % in 2027, with debt rising to over 120 % of GDP. A report commissioned by the French Ministry of Finance, however, warns that without reforms, the deficit will reach 5.9 % in 2027 and almost 7 % in 2030. In this connection: 1.
In the light of these forecasts, does the Commission still consider that France has taken effective action within the meaning of Article 126 TFEU?

Will the Commission recommend to the Council that a failure to take effective action be determined and that the procedure continue to the next stages if France’s 2027 budget does not result in a credible correction of the deficit by 2029?
How does the Commission intend to demonstrate that it applies the same criteria and consequences to France as it does to the other Member States?
https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/E-10-2025-003433_EN.html.

E-10-2026-003371.t: Mercosur and Brazil’s failure to meet EU food safety standards
qt: to the Commission Piotr Müller (ECR) Subject:

Just a few weeks after the EU-Mercosur agreement came into force, the Commission decided to suspend imports from Brazil – including beef and poultry – as of 3 September due to shortcomings in the monitoring of the use of antimicrobials. The problem is particularly serious in the case of beef: the Commission requires proof of compliance with EU standards throughout the animal’s lifetime, and according to experts, full compliance with this condition may not be possible until 2028 or 2029. At the same time, Brazil accounts for around a quarter of the EU’s beef and poultry imports. In this connection: 1.

How can the Commission continue to claim that the EU–Mercosur agreement does not lower standards of protection for European consumers and farmers, when, even after its entry into force, it itself states that the Brazilian monitoring system does not guarantee compliance with EU requirements?
Why did the Commission allow the agreement to enter into force before ascertaining whether or not one of its largest food-exporting partners actually met EU standards?

Will the Commission acknowledge that the case of Brazilian meat demonstrates that European farmers are expected to compete with imports from countries where equivalence of standards exists more in political declarations than in practice?

E-10-2026-003370.t: Concrete measures to reduce the EU’s trade dependence on Türkiye
qt: to the Commission Emmanouil Fragkos (ECR) Subject:

Greece and Cyprus uphold the law while, for Türkiye, money is what speaks. Türkiye continues to challenge the sovereign rights of Greece and Cyprus, including through the illegal Turkish-Libyan Memorandum, planned energy links with the occupied territories of the Republic of Cyprus and the unilateral designation of ‘marine parks’ beyond Turkish territorial waters, in areas where Greece and Cyprus exercise sovereign rights. Meanwhile, Ankara requires European companies participating in the Greek-Cypriot electricity interconnection project to obtain authorisation from Türkiye to carry out works in areas where it has no such jurisdiction. In its answer to question E-000223/20251, the Commission stated that it aims ‘to diversify supply sources and mitigate dependencies’ and reduce excessive dependencies in key sectors. However, in 2025, the value of EU imports of goods from Türkiye totalled EUR 103.3 billion. The scale of this economic relationship makes it necessary to assess the risk of trade dependency turning into a means of political pressure. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
What specific financial, trade and industrial tools can Member States use to replace imports from Türkiye with production or supplies sourced within the EU?
Will it map the dependencies on Türkiye by strategic sector, setting measurable targets, with a timetable for diversification?
Can Greece and Cyprus formally request a specific European plan to gradually reduce these dependencies and, if so, through which specific procedure and EU mechanisms?
https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/E-10-2025-000223_EN.html.

E-10-2026-003368.t: Accelerating the establishment of a system for compensation and for holding Russia accountable for its aggression against Ukraine
qt: to the Commission Arkadiusz Mularczyk (ECR) Subject:

The Register of Damage Caused by the Aggression of the Russian Federation against Ukraine has already received over 180 000 claims, of which approximately 58 000 have been formally registered. Nine further categories of damage have been opened, bringing the total to 21 categories. The Convention establishing an International Claims Commission for Ukraine has been signed by 40 entities; however, 25 ratifications are required for it to enter into force. To date, seven states and the European Union have ratified the convention. At the same time, 36 states and the EU have declared their readiness to participate in the Special Tribunal for the Crime of Aggression against Ukraine. Europe is therefore creating a comprehensive framework encompassing a register of damages, a commission to determine claims, a source of funding and criminal liability for leaders. This also sets an important precedent for the wider debate on reparations and the enforcement of state accountability. 1.

What is the anticipated timetable for the launch of the International Claims Commission for Ukraine, and what specific measures does the Commission intend to take to secure the 17 additional ratifications of the Convention required for it to enter into force?

How does the Commission plan to make use of frozen Russian assets to finance compensation payments under the international compensation mechanism, taking into account the scale of registered claims and the categories of damages covered?

What steps does the Commission intend to take to ensure the effective functioning of the Special Tribunal for the Crime of Aggression against Ukraine, supported by 36 states and the EU, in particular with regard to funding, the appointment of judges and the enforcement of criminal liability of leaders regardless of the perpetrator’s consent?

E-10-2026-003367.t: Strengthening the protection of freedom of religion or belief in the EU’s external policy
qt: to the Commission Arkadiusz Mularczyk (ECR) Subject:

In a statement dated 21 August 2026, the High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy recalled that almost two-thirds of the world’s population live in countries where there are serious violations of freedom of religion or belief. In light of this, the Commission has appointed a new Special Envoy for the Promotion of Freedom of Religion or Belief, whose role is to engage in cooperation with third countries and to raise global awareness regarding religious discrimination and persecution. 1.

What specific mandate and resources have been granted to the Commission’s new Special Envoy for the Promotion of Freedom of Religion or Belief, and how will their activities be coordinated with EU delegations in third countries?

Does the Commission intend to present an action plan comprising measurable criteria for assessing progress in the protection of religious freedom, dedicated funding for organisations defending persecuted religious communities, and a regular mechanism for documenting cases of violence against Christians (who are the most widely persecuted religious community) and other religious groups?

E-10-2026-003366.t: Türkiye’s military preparations, the risks to the Republic of Cyprus and the credibility of the European Union
qt: to the Commission Geadis Geadi (ECR) Subject:

In an official reply to the Grand National Assembly of Türkiye, the Turkish Ministry of Defence states that the necessary work is being carried out and measures are being taken against possible ‘crises, tensions and war’. The classified document which was revealed by the Nordic Monitor and is dated 10 August 2026 and signed by the Turkish Minister of Defence, Yaşar Güler1, is of particular interest to Cyprus. The official acknowledgement by Türkiye’s Ministry of National Defence that it is taking measures in preparation even for war, constitutes a particularly worrying escalation of Türkiye’s aggressive rhetoric. In view of this, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
How does it view Türkiye’s official acknowledgement that it is taking steps to prepare for various scenarios, including war, in Cyprus and more broadly in the Eastern Mediterranean?
What specific measures does it intend to take in the event that Türkiye implements its plans and attacks the Republic of Cyprus?

How can the EU claim international credibility and geopolitical authority when it fails to take meaningful action against a candidate country that is illegally occupying the territory of one of its Member States and is now openly talking about the possibility of war?
https://cdn.sigmalive.com/uploads/280/DDLFK_1787723653.png.

E-10-2026-003365.t: Türkiye is playing with human lives, putting commercial flights and passengers at risk
qt: to the Commission Geadis Geadi (ECR) Subject:

Türkiye is continuing with flagrantly dangerous military actions in the airspace of EU Member States, with the safety of civil aviation now also at risk. On 19 August, Turkish military aircraft TUAF770, which was flying in the Nicosia FIR, failed to respond to calls from the Nicosia Area Control Centre, having deviated from its designated course, and proceeded to move towards the same flight level as passenger Boeing 737-800. A few days later, a Turkish UAV violated Greek airspace, its presence in the Alexandroupoli area affecting the flight path of a commercial flight and triggering the deployment of F-16 fighter jets. In view of this, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
How does it intend to respond to repeated Turkish actions that undermine the safety of civil aviation?
Will the systematic disregard for air traffic rules by a candidate country and actions that threaten the safety of commercial flights and passengers in the EU continue to be accepted?
When will Türkiye face concrete consequences and sanctions for this dangerous behaviour?

E-10-2026-003363.t: The Council of State’s decision not to reinstate 13th and 14th salaries based on EU law
qt: to the Commission Lefteris Nikolaou-Alavanos (NI) Subject:

The decision of the Council of State Plenary to reject public sector workers’ legitimate demands for the reinstatement of the 13th and 14th salaries is unacceptable. It confirms that the so-called ‘rule of law’ and the ‘fundamental rights’ touted by the EU are nothing more than a ‘fig leaf’ for a frontal attack on labour/ordinary people's rights. In the light of Directive (EU) 2022/2041 on the so-called ‘decent standard of living’, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Where does it stand on the fact that the adequate minimum wage directive ultimately defines ‘adequacy’ in terms of corporate profitability, trampling over workers’ labour rights?

Where does it stand on the fact that EU ‘rule of law’ exists only to safeguard the interests of monopolies, rejecting workers’ claims for meaningful wage and pension increases and for measures to support people’s needs as a whole?

Where does it stand on the fact that the fiscal resilience invoked by the government is determined on the basis of the European Semester, the country-specific recommendations, the Euro Plus Pact and the revised Stability Pact, among other EU ‘tools’, which, on the one hand, channel large sums of money towards corporate groups and the war economy, while, on the other are used as ‘caps’ on people’s needs?

E-10-2026-003362.t: Increase in bank debts of Nea Dimokratia and PASOK and the need to keep political influence in check
qt: to the Commission Emmanouil Fragkos (ECR) Subject:

Bank profits in Greece are much higher than the European average because lending rates are extremely high while deposit rates are extremely low. Balance sheets for 2025 show that Nea Dimokratia and PASOK owe around EUR 593 and EUR 560 million respectively. In 2018, the combined debt of both parties stood at EUR 533 million, which means that the debt has more than doubled in seven years. The Commission had already confirmed in 2014 that the vast majority of relevant party loans had been non-performing since January 2013. Meanwhile, the monitoring trustees appointed to oversee the recapitalised Greek banks monitored party loans to make sure that commercial criteria were applied and that there was no political interference. Bearing in mind that the banks were recapitalised through State aid financed with taxpayers’ money, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
How does it explain the fact that not only have loans that were already largely nonperforming in 2013 not been reduced but they have, in fact, more than doubled since 2018?

Will it ask the competent supervisory authorities to examine whether the management, restructurings and capitalisation of interest actually meet the required commercial and arm’s-length criteria or whether they in fact give an economic advantage to Nea Dimokratia and PASOK, allowing them to go on making big profits?

Will there be checks to verify whether the creditor banks used the same means of recovery they would have used against individuals or businesses and what action will it take if preferential treatment or political influence is detected?

E-10-2026-003361.t: Turkish ‘marine parks’ violate every tenet of international law
qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Emmanouil Fragkos (ECR) Subject:

On 16 August the disgraceful Turkish regime announced the designation of two ‘marine parks’ in the marine area between Makri (‘Fethiye’) and Antiphellos (‘Kaş’), surrounding the Kastellorizo archipelago, and between Samothrace and Limnos. These actions are part of plans to deliver the Turkish regime’s expansionist ‘Blue Homeland’ strategy on the ground. The relevant Turkish maps clearly ignore the rights of the Greek islands under the International Law of the Sea and present Türkiye as having jurisdiction beyond Turkish territorial waters. It should be noted that the University of Seville has illustrated the legal status of the area in a map of European maritime zones based on the UNCLOS. Türkiye’s move comes after the country submitted the relevant maps to UNESCO and is part of a bold policy of calling into question Greek sovereignty and sovereign rights in the Aegean and Eastern Mediterranean, in the absence of any meaningful response (i.e. sanctions). The EU simply cannot separate Euro-Turkish relations from Türkiye’s unilateral actions against a Member State, especially while it is considering deepening cooperation between the EU and Türkiye. In view of the above, can the High Representative / Vice-President answer the following: 1.

Assuming she condemns Türkiye’s use of environmental ‘marine parks’ to make unilateral maritime claims against Greece, what policies will she adopt, beyond simply issuing statements, to deter Türkiye from persisting with its illegal actions?
What trade sanctions can she apply right away against the terrorist state?
What clear steps should Greece take for sanctions to be implemented against Türkiye?

E-10-2026-003360.t: Russia’s ‘air shadow fleet’ in Africa and EU financial support
qt: to the Commission Tomáš Zdechovský (PPE) Subject:

According to an analysis by C4ADS1, between January 2025 and July 2026, the Russian ‘air shadow fleet’ carried out at least 75 flights transporting personnel and military equipment for the Africa Corps in Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger. Some of the operators involved have not yet been sanctioned by the EU. At the same time, the EU is channelling significant funds to these countries – between 2021 and 2024, this amounted to EUR 151 million for Mali, EUR 283 million for Burkina Faso and EUR 382.34 million for Niger, even though certain forms of cooperation have been suspended. 1.

Is the Commission investigating and preparing targeted restrictive measures against airlines, aircraft, their owners and operators involved in the transport of personnel or military equipment for Russia’s Africa Corps?

Is the Commission investigating whether countries in receipt of EU funds are allowing their territory, airports or other infrastructure to be used to provide logistical support for Russia’s Africa Corps or to circumvent EU sanctions?

Does the Commission consider it acceptable for the EU to continue providing significant financial support to countries which also allow Russia to use their territory or infrastructure to support Russian military operations, and is it prepared to suspend this support or make it conditional on demonstrable cooperation by these countries in preventing the activities of the Russian ‘air shadow fleet’ and the circumvention of EU sanctions?
https://c4ads.org/commentary/africa-corps-flight-tracking-sahel.

E-10-2026-003359.t: Closure of Eurocentres in the Czech Republic and informing the public about the EU
qt: to the Commission Tomáš Zdechovský (PPE) Subject:

On 17 August 2026, the Czech Government approved the repeal of the existing Strategy for Providing Information on European Affairs and the drafting of a new strategy. This is also set to include the closure of the network of regional Eurocentres in its current form. For more than 20 years, Eurocentres have been maintaining contact with the public in the regions, cooperating with schools, libraries, universities and governments, and organising around 1 300 events per year. The Government is justifying the change on the grounds of modernising communication and making greater use of digital tools. However, it is not yet clear how their regional and educational activities will be replaced, even though steps have already been taken to end the current network. Furthermore, in Liberec, Karlovy Vary and Jihlava, the Eurocentres are directly linked to EUROPE DIRECT centres, whose activities for the period between 2026 and 2030 are largely funded by the Commission. 1.

Is the Commission monitoring the situation with regard to the Czech Government’s decision to close the Eurocentre network and its possible effects on the availability of information on the EU for Czech citizens, especially in the regions, and how does it assess this decision?

Was the Commission or its Representation in the Czech Republic consulted by the Czech Government before this decision was adopted, and did the Czech Government inform the Commission of the specific system it intends to use to replace the Eurocentres’ existing regional information and education activities?

What repercussions might the closure of the Eurocentres have for the operations and funding of the EUROPE DIRECT centres in Liberec, Karlovy Vary and Jihlava, and how does the Commission intend to ensure the continuity of their activities during the 2026‑2030 financial period?

E-10-2026-003358.t: IACS 2026 – Making the most of the possibility of earlier advance payments
qt: to the Commission Sakis Arnaoutoglou (S&D) Subject:

Regulation (EU) 2026/1768, which came into force on 22 July 2026, gives Member States the option, specifically for claim year 2026, to pay direct payment advances of up to 75 %, including before 16 October. The provision is aimed at giving a timely liquidity boost to farmers facing increased production costs. However, in Greece, the submission process for the 2026 single aid application via the myAGRO app only started on 4 August. According to the Independent Authority for Public Revenues (AADE), for applications submitted by 15 September, advance payments may be made by 31 October, while for applications submitted between 16 September and 16 October, advance payments may be made by 30 November. The late start and the limited time available to complete the necessary checks, raise questions about whether Greece is able to benefit from the advance payment option introduced by the EU. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Have the Greek authorities informed it about whether they intend to avail themselves of the possibility of paying advances of up to 75 % before 16 October and what the timeframe for this will be?
Does it believe that the late start to the 2026 single aid application process could deprive Greek producers of the possibility of prompt payment?
How does it plan to help ensure that all necessary checks are completed in time and that this European opportunity is seized fully?

E-10-2026-003357.t: Assassination of a former Member of the European Parliament: how are the European institutions responding to far-left terrorism?
qt: to the Commission Catherine Griset (PfE) Subject:

On 9 July 2026, Ann Widdecombe, a former British minister and former Member of the European Parliament, was murdered at her home having been struck 21 times with a hammer1. The investigation has been handed over to the counter-terrorism police, who have described the murder as a planned and targeted attack. The suspect who was arrested has been described by Nigel Farage as a left-wing extremist: ‘I have it on good authority that the murder suspect was a hard-Left activist. He attended various marches and hated anyone with an opposing view. He had expressed his hatred of me on more than one occasion. He was an intolerant individual obsessed with Soviet communism. He may also have been known to the authorities’2. As part of this investigation, the counter-terrorism police have also reopened an investigation into an attempted burglary and arson attack at a property linked to Nigel Farage. 1.
Is the Commission aware of this case and of the current status of the investigation into the murder of our former fellow Member of the European Parliament?
Do the Commission and its agencies, Europol and Eurojust, anticipate a wave of far-left terrorism, given the ongoing radicalisation of certain sections of our societies?

E-10-2026-003356.t: Summer 2026: the summer of cultural censorship by far-left extremists
qt: to the Commission Catherine Griset (PfE) Subject:

In early July, a concert by DJ Barbara Butch in Grenoble was disrupted by pro-Palestinian activists ‘responding to a call for a boycott backed by LFI’1. In late July, an exhibition by the painter Bruno Chauvierre was cancelled by venue’s management on the grounds that the artist had been a Deputy of the French National Assembly for the National Front in 1986. The artist refers to ‘possible pressure exerted on the event organiser by activists claiming to represent La France insoumise’2. The two artists’ profiles are different, but they have one thing in common. The far left is attempting to ban their performances because of their past or present political views, whether real or imagined. 1.
Is the Commission, which is spearheading the fight against discrimination, aware of these events?
Could it ask the competent French authorities to provide an assessment of the current state of affairs as regards violent extremist groups exerting pressure to censor artistic expression?
Can the AgoraEU programme provide funding for measures to support artists threatened by far-left extremist groups?
