E-10-2026-003354.t: PFAS contamination and the protection of mothers
qt: to the Commission Ufuk Kâhya (Verts/ALE) Subject:
PFAS contamination and the protection of mothers

While the Committee for Socio-Economic Analysis (SEAC) of the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA) continues to assess over 3 500 submissions received during the consultation on the proposed restriction on per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), new evidence continues to demonstrate the scale and persistence of PFAS contamination. For instance, the Dutch National Institute for Public Health and the Environment (RIVM) recently detected PFAS in all breast milk samples analysed from 1 629 women. In 18 % of cases, concentrations exceeded the health-based guidance value, suggesting exposure levels that may negatively affect health. RIVM has warned that excessive PFAS exposure in infants may impair immune system function. 1.

Does the Commission recognise that each additional derogation from a PFAS restriction prolongs contamination of Europe’s water, soil and food chains, while imposing the costs of remediation and related health and environmental impacts on society rather than on polluters?

When considering derogations, will the Commission ensure that the costs associated with PFAS pollution and the resulting impacts, including any necessary remediation, are borne by polluters, in line with the ‘polluter pays’ principle and consistent with the approach reflected in the Urban Wastewater Treatment Directive?
While the restriction process is ongoing, what further measures will the Commission take to protect pregnant women, infants and other vulnerable groups from continued PFAS exposure?

E-10-2026-003353.t: Call for proposals BG16FFPR003-4.004, financed under Bulgaria's 2021–2027 Regional Development Programme through the Just Transition Fund
qt: to the Commission Andrey Novakov (PPE) Subject:

According to the published results, a significant number of project proposals received positive evaluation, with many others placed on reserve lists due to limited available funding. According to the information available to us, an extraordinary audit is being carried out on account of concerns regarding irregularities in the evaluation process. The cancellation of the call in its entirety could adversely affect applicants who have acted in good faith and could undermine investment, job creation and economic diversification in the regions concerned. In this context, the following questions are addressed to the Commission: 1.

Where irregularities are identified in the evaluation of project proposals for EU funding, does the principle of proportionality allow corrective measures to be taken, including reevaluation or re-ranking of the proposals, instead of cancelling the entire call?
Are such corrective measures compatible with the principle of sound financial management where applicants unaffected by the irregularities can be protected?
Are there any deadlines at EU level or specific commitments under the programme requiring this call to be contracted or completed by a certain date?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.10.2026) 1. EU cohesion policy is implemented under shared management. The selection of operations under calls for proposals is the responsibility of the national programme authorities. National authorities are also primarily responsible for taking appropriate corrective measures. If irregularities are detected in an evaluation, the national programme authorities are responsible for assessing their seriousness and deciding on the corrective measures that are proportionate and ensure equal treatment of applicants, transparency and non-discrimination. Possible measures can range from targeted corrective action, such as re-evaluating proposals, to cancelling the entire call. If the irregularities are systemic or impossible to disentangle, and confidence in the whole evaluation process is undermined, cancelling the entire call may be lawful and proportionate. 2. In line with the principles of sound financial management, corrective measures need to be taken where expenditure declared or to be declared to the Commission has been made in breach of the applicable law. Corrective measures must be adequate and proportionate. It is primarily for the national programme authorities to assess the facts and determine the appropriate follow-up. The Commission monitors compliance with applicable law and sound financial management. 3. At EU level, there are no specific deadlines requiring that a particular call for proposals be completed by a given date. However, the general regulatory framework and timing applicable to the 2021-2027 programmes must be respected, including the eligibility period for expenditure, the decommitment deadlines (n+3 mechanism) and the deadlines for submitting the programme closure documents.

E-10-2026-003352.t: New hydrocarbon extraction in the Arctic and EU policy
qt: to the Commission César Luena (S&D) Subject:

Norway has announced it will continue to develop new oil and gas resources in the Barents Sea, as it seeks to secure its contribution to European energy security. The EU’s 2021 Arctic policy, however, sets out a commitment to push for oil, coal and gas to remain in the ground, including in the Arctic, and to explore a multilateral obligation to prevent the development of new hydrocarbon reserves in the region. Given that the Commission is currently updating this policy in the new geopolitical and geoeconomic context: 1.

What view does the Commission take of Norway’s plans to develop new oil and gas reserves in the Arctic in light of the EU’s current Arctic policy and its climate goals, including climate neutrality by 2050?
Does it consider replacing dependence on Russian fossil fuels with new investments that prolong Europe’s dependence on other hydrocarbons to be compatible with those goals?
When reviewing the EU’s Arctic policy, will the Commission continue to oppose the development of new hydrocarbon reserves in the region?

E-10-2026-003351.t: Urgent enhancement of maritime surveillance, European cooperation to tackle the use of high-powered vessels by criminal human and drug trafficking networks
qt: to the Commission Dolors Montserrat (PPE), Juan Ignacio Zoido Álvarez (PPE), Javier Zarzalejos (PPE) Subject:

Following the recent invasion by immigrants in Ceuta, further arrivals on the Spanish coast on fast boats used by criminal networks to illicitly carry people and drugs from North Africa show that migratory pressure and mafia activity continue. Sánchez’s government has been unable to provide an impactful response. Over summer 2026, landings have occurred on beaches in Murcia and Andalusia, even in busy areas and in the middle of the day. Mostly coming from the Algerian coast, the vessels are equipped with high-powered engines, reach the Spanish coast in a few hours, land and then go back, making them difficult to detect and intercept. Representatives of agents on the ground have reported weaknesses in the Spanish maritime surveillance systems. These situations raise obvious questions about the Spanish Government’s ability to properly protect an EU external border and deliver on its commitments under the European Pact on Migration and Asylum. In view of the above: 1.
What does the Commission make of Spain’s management and the resources it has deployed?
Does it believe that the Spanish Government should urgently ramp up its capacities?
How does the Commission intend to demand and support a response that works?

E-10-2026-003350.t: The EU’s deadly anti-racism ideology: the death of Henry Nowak
qt: to the Commission Tom Vandendriessche (PfE), András László (PfE), Elisabeth Dieringer (PfE), Dominik Tarczyński (ECR), Tomasz Froelich (ESN), Petra Steger (PfE), Roman Haider (PfE), Irmhild Boßdorf (ESN), Marc Jongen (ESN), Gerolf Annemans (PfE), Silvia Sardone (PfE), Barbara Bonte (PfE), Roberto Vannacci (ESN), Mary Khan (ESN), Fabrice Leggeri (PfE), Anna Bryłka (PfE), Mélanie Disdier (PfE), Milan Uhrík (ESN), Volker Schnurrbusch (ESN), Branko Grims (NI), Ondřej Knotek (PfE), Jaak Madison (ECR), Tiago Moreira de Sá (PfE) Subject:

The EU anti-racism strategy 2026–2030 is built on the death of George Floyd and the Black Lives Matter movement. That origin matters, as it imports an American racial narrative into EU policy: racism flows in one direction only, with minorities as victims and white citizens as perpetrators. That double standard is written into the strategy itself. It names anti-Black racism, antigypsyism, antisemitism, anti-Asian racism and anti-Muslim hatred. White Europeans as potential victims: absent. By design. This asymmetry is not theoretical. It is deadly. The Henry Nowak case shows where this logic ends: a white student fatally stabbed, then handcuffed after his attacker falsely invoked racism. The accusation overruled reality. A doctrine designed to fight discrimination produced the opposite: unequal credibility before the law, at the cost of a life. 1.
What empirical evidence demonstrates that EU-supported anti-racism training does not create credibility presumptions based on skin colour?
Will the Commission include safeguards against weaponised racism accusations in its upcoming policing compendium?
Will the Commission revise the EU anti-racism strategy 2026–2030 to guarantee equal protection for all citizens regardless of skin colour?

E-10-2026-003348.t: Will the Commission pursue its investigations in the face of Chinese pressure concerning JD.com’s acquisition of Ceconomy?
qt: to the Commission Yvan Verougstraete (Renew) Subject:

Can Beijing prevent Europe from conducting investigations? On 19 August 2026, the Chinese authorities ordered organisations and individuals under their jurisdiction not to cooperate with some parts of the Commission’s investigation into the proposed acquisition of Ceconomy by the Chinese group JD.com. Beijing said that the investigation constituted ‘unlawful extraterritorial jurisdiction measures’ and threatened the EU with countermeasures. In its investigation, the Commission is focusing in particular on potential Chinese subsidies that may have distorted competition in the context of the acquisition. 1.
Does the Commission take the view that the measures taken by the Chinese authorities are likely to hinder its investigation in practice?

What legal and practical action can the Commission take to pursue its investigation effectively when the authorities of a third country order companies and individuals under their jurisdiction not to cooperate?

Does the Commission believe that the EU Foreign Subsidies Regulation provides it with the means it needs to act in situations like these, and is it considering tightening up the regulation if necessary?

E-10-2026-003347.t: Administrative burdens on SMEs and importers arising from the PPWR
qt: to the Commission Marcin Sypniewski (ESN) Subject:

Regulation (EU) 2025/40 on Packaging and Packaging Waste (PPWR) imposes a number of obligations on importers concerning, among other things, the verification of packaging compliance, technical documentation and declarations of conformity. For small businesses importing goods from outside the EU, particularly in the e-commerce sector, these obligations may cover hundreds or thousands of products and overlap with national record-keeping systems, such as Poland’s BDO. In light of the above: 1.

Has the Commission carried out an assessment of the actual administrative costs arising from the PPWR for micro, small and medium-sized importers, in particular businesses importing a large number of different products from outside the EU?
How does the Commission intend to prevent the duplication of registration, recordkeeping and reporting obligations arising from the PPWR and existing national systems, such as Poland’s BDO?

Is the Commission considering further simplifications, de minimis thresholds or simplified documentation and reporting standards for SMEs, in particular importers who have no real influence over the design of packaging by non-EU manufacturers?

E-10-2026-003346.t: Verification of EU financial support for Russian civil society and independent media
qt: to the Commission Michał Dworczyk (ECR) Subject:

The management of EU funds requires not only formal checks on their proper use, but also verifying whether the beneficiaries’ activities comply with the conditions and objectives of the funding that has been granted and with the Union policies which the funds are intended to support. In the context of the Russian Federation’s war of aggression against Ukraine, the EU’s support for Russian civil society organisations and independent media must be subject to strict scrutiny, including those applied to entities operating outside the territory of the Russian Federation. In this connection: 1.

How many times since 2022 has the Commission carried out a review of the activities of Russian civil society organisations and independent media that are beneficiaries of EU funding – including those operating within the Union – to assess their compliance with the objectives of the funding and with EU policies, going beyond the beneficiaries’ own declarations?

Has the Commission identified any instances of beneficiaries’ activities being inconsistent with the objectives of the funding granted or with EU policies as a result of such checks, and if so, how many such instances were identified?
In how many cases did the irregularities identified result in the termination of the contract, the suspension of funding or the initiation of a recovery procedure?

E-10-2026-003345.t: Action by the Commission to ensure that Türkiye complies with the judgment of the European Court of Human Rights on Osman Kavala’s immediate release
qt: to the Commission Emmanouil Kefalogiannis (PPE) Subject:

The European Court of Human Rights has ordered Türkiye to release Osman Kavala ‘at the earliest possible date’, judging his conviction to life imprisonment to be ‘null and void’. The Court also ordered Türkiye to pay Osman Kavala more than EUR 110 000 in compensation. The judgment of the European Court of Human Rights highlights serious breaches in the judicial process and finds that Ankara’s refusal to release Osman Kavala, ignoring the Court's previous rulings, not only undermines citizens’ and society’s trust in the rule of law but also compromises the constitutional order. In light of the above: 1.
What are the Commission’s views in this regard?
Does it intend to raise the issue with Türkiye, which is a candidate country?

E-10-2026-003343.t: The right of EU citizens to give preferential treatment to domestic products
qt: to the Commission Mihai Tudose (S&D) Subject:

A recent EU-wide opinion poll shows that consumers prefer products from their own countries. This survey comes at a time when the Commission’s proposed Industrial Accelerator Act is putting forward the idea of applying the European preference mechanism to public procurement. It is a good idea to support European companies given that public procurement accounts for around 17 % of the EU’s economic output. Member State governments have called for the European preference mechanism to focus on the products themselves, and not on the countries involved. However, EU citizens have made their feelings known, calling for public funds to prioritise products made in their own countries rather than goods from other Member States. Is the Commission planning to uphold the right to national preference and, if so, how will it go about this?

E-10-2026-003342.t: Use of monensin in cattle from Mercosur countries and compliance with EU import requirements
qt: to the Commission Paolo Inselvini (ECR), Carlo Fidanza (ECR) Subject:

Regulation (EU) 2019/61 prohibits the use of antimicrobials to promote growth or increase yield, and Article 118 and Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/9052 extend this principle to animals and products of animal origin imported into the EU. In Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay, monensin is registered as a coccidiostat. However, studies and information from the livestock sector indicate that, in commercial cattle production systems, it may be being administered continuously throughout the fattening cycle, and for 110 to 305 days, to improve feed efficiency and production performance. This suggests a potential discrepancy between the product’s regulatory classification and its actual use; this is particularly relevant in the light of increased beef imports and the EUMercosur agreement. 1.
How does the Commission verify that, where monensin is used in animals intended for export to the EU, its use is exclusively for therapeutic or preventive purposes and not as a growth promoter?
Does it consider the certification and controls provided for under Regulation (EU) 2023/905 sufficient for checking actual antimicrobial use throughout the production cycle?
In cases of prolonged use which is incompatible with the declared purposes, does the Commission intend to suspend imports originating in the farms concerned?
http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2019/6/oj. http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg_del/2023/905/oj.

E-10-2026-003341.t: US sanctions against International Criminal Court President Judge Tomoko Akane and senior trial lawyer Abdoulaye Seye
qt: to the Commission Raquel García Hermida-Van Der Walle (Renew) Subject:

On 19 August 2026, the United States imposed sanctions under Executive Order 14203 on International Criminal Court (ICC) President Judge Tomoko Akane and senior trial lawyer Abdoulaye Seye, bringing the number of sanctioned court officials to 13. The measures can exclude them from payment systems, banking, insurance, cloud and telecommunications services, including services from EU operators. European organisations have called for EU action. Under Article 1 of Regulation (EC) No 2271/961 (the Blocking Statute), the Commission can adopt a delegated act adding third-country legislation with extraterritorial effects to the regulation’s annex. Parliament has repeatedly called for the Blocking Statute to be used to protect the ICC and the EU has reiterated its support for the court. 1.
Has the Commission concluded that Executive Order 14203 meets the criteria under Article 1; if not, what legal or factual threshold remains unmet?
Will it adopt a delegated act adding Executive Order 14203 to the annex, thereby covering the designations based on it, and, if so, when?

What immediate measures will the Commission take to protect the ICC and its officials from the denial of essential services by EU operators, and what guidance and enforcement coordination will it put in place once Executive Order 14203 has been added to the annex?

Council Regulation (EC) No 2271/96 of 22 November 1996 protecting against the effects of the extraterritorial application of legislation adopted by a third country, and actions based thereon or resulting therefrom (OJ L 309, 29.11.1996, p. 1, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/1996/2271/oj). 1

E-10-2026-003340.t: Automatic review of EU legislation and zero-based regulation
qt: to the Commission Charlie Weimers (ECR) Subject:

In 2019, administrative rules in Idaho ceased to be automatically reauthorised, meaning that the authorities have to actively justify and reissue any regulations that are to be maintained. The model was subsequently formalised as ‘zero-based regulation’, involving regular reviews of the rules and regulations in place. By the end of 2024, around 3 235 pages of rules had been abolished, representing around 38 % compared with 20181. As part of the competitiveness agenda, the Commission has set targets to cut red tape by 25 % for businesses in general and by 35 % for SMEs, for example using Omnibus packages, REFIT and the ‘one in, one out’ approach2. The Draghi report also points out that the regulatory burden is an obstacle to Europe’s competitiveness3. 1.
Has the Commission studied Idaho’s model or other systems with automatic sunset clauses and mandatory reviews of existing legislation?
Does the Commission intend to propose or pilot a mechanism whereby parts of the EU’s regulatory framework will have to be regularly reassessed and actively justified in order to remain in force?

What specific steps does the Commission intend to take to move from the simplification of individual rules to a real zero-based or regulatory budgeting approach for all the rules and regulations in place in the EU?

According to the Idaho Governor’s Office and a subsequent assessment of zero-based regulation, 3 235 pages of rules had been abolished by the end of 2024, around 38 % compared with 2018. 2 The Commission’s competitiveness and simplification agenda includes targets of cutting red tape by at least 25 % for businesses in general and by 35 % for SMEs. The Commission’s current ‘one in, one out’ approach offsets costs but does not automatically repeal existing legislation. 3 The Draghi report, ‘The Future of European Competitiveness’, section on the simplification of rules. 1

E-10-2026-003339.t: The need to speed up the presentation of legislative proposals and establish clear restrictions on social media access for minors
qt: to the Commission Ştefan Muşoiu (S&D) Subject:

In recent years, the exposure of minors to social media has become an increasingly serious issue with regard to public health, the protection of minors and digital safety. Algorithms that favour engaging content, extensive data collection and addiction-inducing mechanisms can amplify the risks to child and teen development through exposure to harmful content, online harassment, manipulation and social pressure. For these worrying reasons, which are having an ever greater impact on our daily lives, the Union should act quicker to protect minors and establish clear rules on social media access for minors. I would like to ask the Commission to clarify whether it intends to put forward a unified European legislative framework that would include setting an EU-wide common minimum age, to ensure children are equally protected across all Member States and to strengthen platform responsibility with regard to compliance with these rules.

E-10-2026-003337.t: The position of Russian entities receiving EU funding on the Russian Federation’s war of aggression against Ukraine
qt: to the Commission Michał Dworczyk (ECR) Subject:

Article 21 of the Treaty on European Union sets out the principles and objectives which should guide the Union’s external action, including the promotion of democracy, the rule of law, human rights and respect for international law. Where the EU provides funding to Russian civil society organisations, human rights organisations and independent media, it is of essential importance that they adopt a genuine and unequivocal stance on Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine. In this connection: 1.

Does the Commission require beneficiaries of EU funding to take an unequivocal stance on Russia’s aggression against Ukraine – recognising it as an illegal war of aggression by the Russian Federation – and to support Ukraine’s territorial integrity within its internationally recognised borders, and does it verify their public statements in this regard?

Has the Commission identified any beneficiaries who, during the funding period, avoided unequivocally condemning the invasion, questioned Crimea’s status as part of Ukraine, opposed sanctions against Russia or arms supplies to Ukraine, or called for negotiations at the expense of Ukraine’s territorial integrity, and if so, what consequences have been brought to bear?

In the Commission’s view, is the provision of funding from EU public funds to an entity which does not explicitly oppose Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine compatible with Article 21 of the TEU and with the Union’s policy towards Ukraine?

E-10-2026-003336.t: Shortcomings in the implementation of Directive 2011/70/Euratom on the management of radioactive waste
qt: to the Commission Luděk Niedermayer (PPE) Subject:

Commission reports on the implementation of Directive 2011/70/Euratom1 indicate that most Member States lack the necessary financial resources – and often even reliable cost estimates – for the final disposal of high-level radioactive waste. In its 2019 report, the Commission stated: ‘Almost two thirds of Member States provided information on cost estimates for their national programmes, but these estimates vary significantly in terms of methodology, assumptions, data completeness, scope, and timeframes.’ (SWD(2019)0436, p. 53). 1.
In the next evaluation report, does the Commission intend to publish comparable and verifiable data on estimated costs and the actual funding status in individual Member States?

Will the Commission support the requirement for Member States to set the nuclear levy per megawatt-hour (MWh) based on a transparent methodology that is regularly reviewed in the light of changes in estimated costs?

Council Directive 2011/70/Euratom of 19 July 2011 establishing a Community framework for the responsible and safe management of spent fuel and radioactive waste (OJ L 199, 2.8.2011, p. 48, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2011/70/oj). 1

E-10-2026-003334.t: Termination of the novel food procedure for lithium orotate dihydrate (NF/2024/30250)
qt: to the Commission Gerald Hauser (PfE) Subject:

On 27 March 2026, the Commission issued C(2026)1964, terminating the procedure for authorising lithium orotate dihydrate (NF/2024/30250) as a novel food, without updating the Union list. The specific justification for this has not been published on the Commission’s website. The information available to us suggests that the procedure was not terminated on the basis of a final scientific assessment, but because the application did not contain the full information requested as regards the identity of the novel food, the production process, the exact composition of the novel food and the scientific evidence demonstrating its safety. In 2025, Aron et al. reported in ‘Lithium deficiency and the onset of Alzheimer’s disease’, Nature 645, 712-721, that lithium homeostasis is already disrupted in the human brain in cases of mild cognitive impairment and Alzheimer’s. Experimental lithium deficiency exacerbated pathology and cognitive deficits in mouse models of Alzheimer’s disease; low‑dose lithium orotate prevented or reduced several of these changes. 1.
What specific information regarding identity, the production process, composition and safety was deemed to be missing or insufficient?
What were the scientific safety concerns – if any – about lithium orotate dihydrate, irrespective of any lack of completeness from a formal or documentation-related point of view?

Was the Nature paper by Aron et al. (‘Lithium deficiency and the onset of Alzheimer’s disease’) taken into account? If not, is the Commission or EFSA intending to take it into account if the application is resubmitted, in particular the effects of very low doses of lithium orotate in the Alzheimer’s mouse model that are reported in the paper?

E-10-2026-003333.t: Digital Services Act and cross-border content moderation
qt: to the Commission Adam Bielan (ECR) Subject:
Citizens in democracies must be able to freely debate important political topics online. In this context, I call on the Commission to answer the following questions: 1.

Does the DSA, Commission guidance, or any instruments thereunder require platforms to pre-emptively moderate political speech outside of the EU simply because their content may spill over into the EU?

Does the DSA, Commission guidance, or any instruments thereunder require or encourage platforms to remove or moderate political content, such as criticism of government officials or policies, scientific debate, statistical facts, or interviews of public officials or candidates for public office?

Designated very large online platforms state that their respective content moderation policies apply globally. Does the DSA, Commission guidance, or any instruments thereunder require them to substantially modify their content moderation policies? If so, how?

E-10-2026-003332.t: ChatGPT advertisements across EU countries: transparency, profiling and consumer protection
qt: to the Commission Sandro Gozi (Renew) Subject:

Since 24 August 2026, OpenAI has begun showing advertisements in ChatGPT across 31 European countries. These advertisements have reportedly been selected based on conversation context and displayed alongside AI-generated responses. OpenAI states that advertisers cannot access conversations, ads are clearly labelled and separate from responses, and advertising does not influence answers. This raises concerns about transparency, profiling, and consumer protection, particularly where commercial content may be selected using sensitive information disclosed during a conversation, and where the conversational format may blur the line between AI recommendations and paid promotion. Can the Commission clarify: 1.

Whether it has assessed this development’s compatibility with relevant provisions of the General Data Protection Regulation1, the Digital Services Act2, the AI Act3, and the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive4?

Whether the existing EU legal framework ensures users can clearly distinguish AI output from paid content, and prevents targeting based on sensitive information disclosed during AI interactions or exploitation of user trust?
Whether, if gaps in the legal framework exist, it will take measures to address the risks from such practices, including the designation of ChatGPT as a very large online search engine (VLOSE)?

Regulation (EU) 2016/679 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 April 2016 on the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free movement of such data, and repealing Directive 95/46/EC (General Data Protection Regulation) (OJ L 119, 4.5.2016, p. 1, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj). 2 Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 19 October 2022 on a Single Market For Digital Services and amending Directive 2000/31/EC (Digital Services Act) (OJ L 277, 27.10.2022, p. 1, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/2065/oj). 3 Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 June 2024 laying down harmonised rules on artificial intelligence and amending Regulations (EC) No 300/2008, (EU) No 167/2013, (EU) No 168/2013, (EU) 2018/858, (EU) 2018/1139 and (EU) 2019/2144 and Directives 2014/90/EU, (EU) 2016/797 and (EU) 2020/1828 (Artificial Intelligence Act) (OJ L, 2024/1689, 12.7.2024, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj). 4 Directive 2005/29/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 11 May 2005 concerning unfair business-to-consumer commercial practices in the internal market and amending Council Directive 84/450/EEC, Directives 97/7/EC, 98/27/EC and 2002/65/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council and Regulation (EC) No 2006/2004 of the European Parliament and of the Council (‘Unfair Commercial Practices Directive’) (OJ L 149, 11.6.2005, p. 22, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2005/29/oj). 1

E-10-2026-003331.t: Pre-frontier intelligence in EU border management
qt: to the Commission Jan-Christoph Oetjen (Renew), Veronika Cifrová Ostrihoňová (Renew), Michael McNamara (Renew), Sophie Wilmès (Renew), Lucia Yar (Renew) Subject:

When Commissioner Brunner spoke at the meeting of Parliament’s Committee on Civil Liberties, Justice and Home Affairs of 6 August 2026 about measures that need to be taken in order to enhance EU border management, he mentioned that he aims to ‘improve our prefrontier intelligence’, ‘step up Frontex’s vulnerability assessments’ and overall strengthen the support Frontex offers to non-EU countries. 1.
Exactly what improved or additional pre-frontier intelligence measures is the Commission envisaging?
In what way will the Commission step up Frontex’s vulnerability assessments?

Did the common pre-frontier intelligence picture and Eurosur framework fail either before or during the surge of irregular arrivals in Ceuta at the end of July? If so, why, and what conclusions will the Commission draw from this failure regarding binding obligations for non-EU countries on border management cooperation?

E-10-2026-003330.t: Management of catering waste from international flights and the circular economy
qt: to the Commission César Luena (S&D) Subject:

Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 classifies catering waste from means of transport operating internationally as Category 1 material, which means it is subject to strict disposal rules for biosecurity reasons. However, this category can also include unconsumed, sealed food and beverages from flights from third countries. According to industry data, these types of products account for more than 18 % of airline cabin waste worldwide. Treating them along with higher-risk waste can limit the prevention, reuse and recycling options, and have environmental repercussions that could have been avoided. In view of the above: 1.
Does the Commission have any data on the composition and the health and environmental risks of the different types of catering waste from international flights?
Would it consider carrying out a scientific risk assessment to determine whether certain unconsumed, low-risk products could be managed separately, while fully preserving biosecurity guarantees?
How will it ensure that the implementation of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 is compatible with the EU’s objectives in terms of waste prevention, the circular economy and efficient use of resources?

E-10-2026-003329.t: Settler violence in the West Bank and protecting Christian communities
qt: to the Commission Paolo Inselvini (ECR), Carlo Fidanza (ECR) Subject:

Palestinian civilians in the West Bank are the target of escalating violence, intimidation and attacks at the hands of Israeli settlers. A particular flashpoint is Taybeh, a Christian majority village, where incidents of violence and intimidation have played out on land and property close to residential homes and places of worship. Cardinal Pierbattista Pizzaballa and other representatives of the Church have visited the community and called on the authorities to ensure its security. Serious incidents have also been reported in and around Qusra, where acts of settler aggression, property incursions and violence against Palestinian residents attest to the declining security situation and the danger of local communities being forced to abandon their homes. Civil protection, religious freedom and respect for fundamental rights are among the principles guiding EU external action under Article 21 of the Treaty on European Union. Can the Commission answer the following: 1.
What steps will it take to counter settler violence and protect civilians in the West Bank, including in Taybeh and Qusra?
What instruments will it use specifically to protect the Christian communities, their property and places of worship?
Does it intend to leverage EU-Israel relations to compel the Israeli authorities to take concrete action against the violence and ensure that local communities are able to stay?

E-10-2026-003328.t: Deaths caused by extreme heat and future European climate resilience framework
qt: to the Commission César Luena (S&D) Subject:

Europe has experienced four consecutive record-breaking heatwaves over the summer of 2026. Preliminary data indicates at least 35 000 excess deaths, although the figures available cover only around half the continent and do not yet include all the data for August. The data demonstrates that extreme heat is a growing threat to public health. The Commission is currently preparing the upcoming European climate resilience and risk management framework, which should strengthen the Union’s capacity to anticipate and manage growing climate risks. In view of the above: 1.
How will the Commission incorporate the rising death rate linked to extreme heat into the future European climate resilience and risk management framework?
Will the framework contain specific measures to reduce exposure and vulnerability to heat and especially to protect the most vulnerable individuals and groups?
How will the Commission ensure that the future framework establishes an effective European response to the health risks posed by extreme heat, beyond new planning and assessment obligations?

E-10-2026-003327.t: African swine fever (ASF) restrictions remain in place despite no new cases
qt: to the Commission Marcin Sypniewski (ESN) Subject:

ASF-related restrictions remain in force in some municipalities and districts in Poland, even though no new cases of ASF have been recorded there for some time. One example is the municipality of Przystajń in Kłobuck County, which remains within Restricted Zone I, even though, according to information provided by local farmers, no case of ASF has been detected in wild boar there for over a year. Keeping such restrictions in place has significant economic repercussions for farmers and the local agricultural sector. With the above in mind: 1.

What epidemiological criteria and risk assessment findings does the Commission apply when deciding to continue classifying specific Polish municipalities and districts as areas subject to ASF restrictions, particularly in cases where no new infections have been recorded for over 12 months?

Can the Commission indicate what specific grounds justify the continued imposition of restrictions in the case of municipalities such as Przystajń, and whether the competent Polish authorities have requested a change in the status of these areas?

E-10-2026-003326.t: EUDR: availability of soy for animal feed in the EU
qt: to the Commission Asger Christensen (Renew) Subject:

Soy is a crucial resource in animal feed production and therefore a key component of European livestock production. However, for the third year in a row, stakeholders in the EU soy value chain have signalled that they have been unable to source sufficient soy products. This is because the European Union Deforestation Regulation1 (EUDR) is entering into force imminently, and exporters of soy to the EU have been withholding their offers due to underlying legal uncertainty. If this situation persists, EU livestock farmers might not have enough feed for their animals. 1.

Is the Commission aware of the market disruption experienced by EU soy importers because of the EUDR, and what will the Commission do to ensure that after 30 December 2026 purchases of soybean products for animal feed use are not unduly blocked because of the EUDR?
What concrete measures will the Commission take to provide exporters and importers with sufficient legal certainty to ensure that soybean products continue to be offered and traded on the EU market?

If the EUDR risks restricting access to essential feed ingredients in practice, how will the Commission ensure that European livestock farmers do not end up paying the price for the legal uncertainty surrounding the regulation?

Regulation (EU) 2023/1115 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 31 May 2023 on the making available on the Union market and the export from the Union of certain commodities and products associated with deforestation and forest degradation and repealing Regulation (EU) No 995/2010 (OJ L 150, 9.6.2023, p.206, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2023/1115/oj). 1

E-10-2026-003325.t: Protection of sites commemorating the crimes of Nazi Germany – commercial development on the site of a former subcamp of the Mauthausen concentration camp in Leobersdorf (Austria)
qt: to the Commission Arkadiusz Mularczyk (ECR) Subject:

According to press coverage and reports from the Comité International de Mauthausen (International Mauthausen Committee -– CIM), commercial development is under way on the site of a former subcamp of the Mauthausen concentration camp complex in Leobersdorf, Austria, where a supermarket and a logistics centre are being built. Between 1944 and 1945, around 400 women and girls were imprisoned there and forced into slave labour; many of them subsequently perished during the death march to Mauthausen. The CIM stresses that the traces of these crimes are being destroyed and buried under layers of gravel, steel and concrete. The Mauthausen concentration camp complex held around 190 000 prisoners, of whom almost 90 000 perished1. In response to Question P-002018/20242, the Commission stated that ‘[t]he Commission has supported the Member States to maintain memorial sites of former Nazi concentration and death camps through EU funds’ and that the Commission ‘will continue to do so’. The commercial development of a site where victims suffered stands in blatant contradiction to this commitment and to the EU’s policy on European remembrance. Within the framework of its powers under Article 167 TFEU, what specific measures is the Commission taking, or does it intend to take, to encourage the Member State (Austria) to protect this memorial site from commercial development?
https://www.mauthausen-memorial.org/en/News/Developments-on-the-site-of-the-former-Hirtenbergconcentration-camp. 2 https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/P-10-2024-002018_EN.html. 1

E-10-2026-003323.t: Governance of EU funds allocated to water services, transparency of concessionaires and monitoring of investments co-financed by the European Union
qt: to the Commission Giuseppe Antoci (The Left) Subject:

Through cohesion policy, the Recovery and Resilience Facility and other financial instruments, the European Union supports action to improve water infrastructure, reduce network losses and boost network resilience. In several Member States, including Italy, some of these investments involve concessionaires of the integrated water service, who are called upon to implement investment programmes financed, in whole or in part, with EU resources. In light of the principles of transparency, sound financial management and protection of the EU’s financial interests, it is essential to ensure that those resources produce verifiable results and are used in compliance with the obligations under the funding programmes. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

In the context of the EU-financed programmes, have audits or checks been carried out on the actual implementation of the co-financed investments and on compliance with the obligations under the programmes?

Does it use or intend to develop common indicators at EU level to assess the effectiveness of co-financed investments, with particular reference to reduction of network losses, to service quality and to infrastructure resilience?

E-10-2026-003322.t: Using properties seized from those involved in organised crime to provide housing for people and families in financial hardship in southern European cities
qt: to the Commission Giuseppe Antoci (The Left) Subject:

Access to decent and affordable housing is a prerequisite for the effective exercise of the right to have somewhere to live and to social inclusion, with the latter enshrined in the EU treaties and the European Pillar of Social Rights. In numerous southern European cities, an increasing number of people in economic poverty face mounting difficulties in finding affordable housing, and this situation is playing a major role in driving up housing poverty and weakening social cohesion. At the same time, in some Member States, including Italy, there are significant property assets that have been definitively seized from those involved in organised crime and could be given over to the wider community, contributing to urban regeneration and the fight against widespread economic poverty. In light of the above: 1.
Will the Commission push for action to encourage the reuse of properties seized from those involved in organised crime for housing for people in moderate to severe financial hardship?

Does the Commission think EU resources could be allocated or complemented, including through cohesion policy funds, InvestEU, the European Social Fund Plus or other financial instruments, to support the recovery and refurbishment of these properties?

Will it draw up guidelines or promote the exchange of best practices between Member States on the social reuse of seized properties, as a means of combating organised crime and responding to growing economic poverty?

E-10-2026-003321.t: Leaving home should not mean leaving democracy behind: guaranteeing the voting rights of citizens living away from home as a means of bolstering EU citizenship and territorial cohesion
qt: to the Commission Giuseppe Antoci (The Left) Subject:

The ability to effectively exercise one’s right to vote is crucial to European citizenship and democratic participation. However, thousands of students, researchers and workers who are temporarily residing in Italian councils other than the ones in which they are registered are encountering significant voting barriers. Individuals hailing from Sicily, Sardinia and other parts of southern Italy are more likely to find themselves in this predicament. The absence of established mechanisms enabling citizens living away from home to vote1 is a drain on the latter’s finances, undermines democratic participation and is exacerbating the plight of island and peripheral regions that are already affected by youth mobility and depopulation. This state of affairs is very much at odds with the economic, social and territorial cohesion objectives set out in Article 174 TFEU2. In the light of the Union’s objectives of bolstering democratic participation and European citizenship3, can the Commission answer the following questions: 1.

Does it not agree that the absence of instruments that can effectively uphold the voting rights of citizens who are temporarily living outside the municipalities in which they are registered could prevent the EU from achieving its economic, social and territorial cohesion objectives, particularly in island regions?
Will it promote, while respecting the competences of the Member States, discussions and exchanges of good practices with a view to making it easier for citizens living away from home to vote?

Decree-Law No 196 of 28 December 2025 laying down urgent provisions for the holding of elections and referenda on 22 and 23 March 2026 does not include provisions enabling voters living away from home to exercise their right to vote in a municipality other than the one in which they are registered. See https://www.giustiziainsieme.it/articolo/3817-il-voto-fuori-sede%C3%B9. 2 Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU), OJ C 202, 7.6.2016, p. 127, Article 174. 3 Directive (EU) 2025/1788 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 15 July 2025 laying down detailed arrangements for the exercise of the right to vote and stand as a candidate in elections to the European Parliament in the Member State of residence (recast), in OJEU L, 2025/1788, 12 August 2025. 1

E-10-2026-003320.t: Measures and regulations governing access to the Silvestri Craters, in Natura 2000 special area of conservation (SAC) ITA070009, Mount Etna
qt: to the Commission Giuseppe Antoci (The Left) Subject:

According to information published in October 20251, access regulation systems – including marked trails and other infrastructure to manage tourist flows – may have been introduced in the area around the Silvestri Craters, which are in special area of conservation (SAC) ITA070009, Fascia altomontana dell'Etna, part of the Natura 2000 network established under Directive 92/43/EEC. The area in question is also inside Etna Park and part of the Mount Etna UNESCO World Heritage Site. To date, no information is publicly available on whether the impact assessment provided for in Article 6(3) of the Habitats Directive has been carried out or whether any further environmental and landscape permits have been issued. In the light of the above: 1.
Is the Commission aware of those measures and changes to the access regulations?

Is the construction of delineated paths, barriers or other access management infrastructure in a Natura 2000 site one of the measures that may require a prior assessment under Article 6(3) of Directive 92/43/EEC?
Will it ask the Italian authorities for clarification regarding compliance with the EU legislation applicable to sites in the Natura 2000 network?

https://aic.camera.it/aic/scheda.html?core=aic&numero=4/06103&ramo=CAMERA&leg=19.https://ww w.lasicilia.it/news/cronaca/3000640/ticket-di-5-euro-per-visitare-i-crateri-silvestri-sull-etna-ed-e-polemica.html.

E-10-2026-003319.t: Increasing the maximum age for enlistment in the armed forces and law enforcement agencies in the light of EU’s equal treatment principles
qt: to the Commission Giuseppe Antoci (The Left) Subject:

Italy’s declining population and shrinking 18-25 cohort – the main demographic applying for public jobs – have exposed a systemic vulnerability in the recruitment system used by Italy’s armed forces and law enforcement agencies. One committee1 advocates raising the maximum enlistment age for certain military and law enforcement jobs to 40, with a view to broadening the pool of candidates and harnessing the physical and mental fitness, aptitude and professional skills of older recruits2. Article 707 of Legislative Decree No 66/20103 sets restrictive age limits, only accepting candidates between the ages of 23 and 26. Such an approach should to be assessed in the light of Article 21 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the EU and Directive 2000/78/EC, which prohibits discrimination on grounds of age unless justified by legitimate aims and pursued by appropriate and proportionate means. I therefore have the following questions for the Commission concerning Legislative Decree No 58/20064: 1.
Does it agree that the current enlistment-related age limits should be reviewed in the light of demographic and labour market changes?

Does it agree that recruitment procedures should, in order to be considered proportionate, take the physical and mental fitness, aptitudes and professional skills of candidates into account, and avoid excluding applicants solely on the basis of their age?

Does Directive 2000/78/EC enable Member States to exercise some discretion in adjusting the aforementioned limits without falling foul of the principles of proportionality, equal treatment and non-discrimination?

Committee for Raising Age Limits in the Armed Forces and Law Enforcement (Comitato Innalzamento Limiti d'Età, Forze dell'Ordine e Armate). 2 See the technical dossier entitled ‘Increasing the Maximum Military and Law Enforcement Enlistment Age’, which specifies the job categories concerned and outlines the applicable social security framework. See also the technical and regulatory dossier entitled ‘Structural Amendment and Extension of the Maximum Age for Recruitment in the Military, Law Enforcement and Emergency Services’, which highlights the discrepancy between current regulations and Italy’s demographic, educational and employment trends. 3 See the draft law on raising the age limit for access to competitions in the armed forces and law enforcement. 4 Legislative Decree No 58 of 2 April 2026, ‘Reforming the national military apparatus pursuant to Article 2 (1) of Law No 201 of 28 November 2023 with a view to improving the recruitment and operational capacity of the armed forces’. 1

E-10-2026-003318.t: Implementation of Directive 2008/98/EC as regards the separate collection of textile waste in Sicily
qt: to the Commission Giuseppe Antoci (The Left) Subject:

Since 1 January 2025, under Article 11(1) of Directive 2008/98/EC on waste, as amended by Directive (EU) 2018/851, Member States have been required to use separate collection systems for textile waste. There are still significant problems in Sicily regarding the collection and management of used textiles. Sicily’s regional waste management plan highlights the need to improve separate collection, increase the number of drop-off points, and develop the textile reuse and recycling chain. These issues risk undermining the effective implementation of Article 11 of Directive 2008/98/EC and the objectives of the circular economy. In view of the above: 1.
Does the Commission believe that the textile waste management problems in Sicily are compatible with the requirements laid down in Article 11 of Directive 2008/98/EC?

Will it verify whether Italy has put in place all the necessary measures – including adequate collection and treatment capacities – to ensure that Directive 2008/98/EC is properly implemented throughout Italy?

What steps will it take to support Member States and regions with inadequate textile waste management capacities to ensure that they comply with EU legislation and achieve the objectives of the circular economy?

E-10-2026-003317.t: Legal accountability and preventive measures for cybersecurity breaches caused by autonomous AI systems
qt: to the Commission Fabio De Masi (NI) Subject:
Legal accountability and preventive measures for cybersecurity breaches caused by autonomous AI systems

Recent incidents involving highly capable AI systems have demonstrated that autonomous systems may identify and exploit vulnerabilities, access external systems and cause cybersecurity breaches in ways that were not explicitly designed or anticipated by their developers123. In such circumstances, it appears that European regulation has so far been inadequate in identifying legal responsibilities and preventing such incidents. In this respect, Article 2(8) of Regulation (EU) 2024/16894 excludes from the scope of the AI Act research, testing and development activities concerning AI systems or AI models prior to their being placed on the market or put into service. In the light of the above, we pose the following questions to the Commission. 1.
Do any of the activities involved in the OpenAI and Anthropic incidents, as described above, fall outside the scope of the AI Act under Article 2(8)?
What supervisory action has the Commission taken, or what action does it intend to take, in response to these incidents under its existing powers?

Does the Commission consider that the existing EU legal framework provides sufficiently clear rules establishing responsibility and liability where an autonomous AI system, during research, testing or development, independently exploits a cybersecurity vulnerability and causes damage to a third party?

https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cz7dl7w8y7po. https://edition.cnn.com/2026/08/04/tech/ai-anthropic-openai-security-breach-intl-hnk. 3 https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c2el319vzr3o. 4 Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 June 2024 laying down harmonised rules on artificial intelligence and amending Regulations (EC) No 300/2008, (EU) No 167/2013, (EU) No 168/2013, (EU) 2018/858, (EU) 2018/1139 and (EU) 2019/2144 and Directives 2014/90/EU, (EU) 2016/797 and (EU) 2020/1828 (Artificial Intelligence Act) (OJ L, 2024/1689, 12.7.2024, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj). 1 2

E-10-2026-003316.t: Is Seahorse Advanced replacing the SIVE network on West Africa’s Atlantic coast?
qt: to the Commission Özlem Demirel (The Left) Subject:

Part of the EU-funded Seahorse Mediterranean project, a Mediterranean border cooperation centre (MEBOCC) was intended to connect North African partner states and Eurosur in the Mediterranean Sea, as the central node of the Seahorse Network. It was supposed to receive liaison officers from third countries and serve as an international coordination centre for joint patrols with Frontex. The Commission has now announced that NDICI-Global Europe funds will be used to extend the Seahorse Network to countries on the Atlantic coast of West Africa. This new Seahorse Advanced (A) project is being implemented in close connection with Frontex and Eurosur. It remains unclear how this project relates to Spanish surveillance and communication system SIVE, which has already been in place for two decades along the Atlantic route and upon which Seahorse Mediterranean was originally based. 1.
How does Seahorse Advanced (A) relate to the existing Spanish SIVE system on the Atlantic coast of West Africa, and to what extent does the SIVE system still exist?

What technical infrastructure is being built or upgraded under Seahorse Advanced (A), and what role is being played by similar coordination centres for the national coastguards of the EU Mediterranean states?

What does the Commission or Frontex know about the progress and implementation of the previously planned EU-funded MEBOCC or similar coordination centres in the Mediterranean, and which non-EU coastguards are involved?

E-10-2026-003315.t: Shortage of early childhood services and the employment of women in Sicily
qt: to the Commission Giuseppe Antoci (The Left) Subject:

The EU gender equality strategy and European care strategy recognise access to early childhood services as key to increasing women’s participation in the labour market and promoting social inclusion. According to the Italian National Institute of Statistics’ data on the provision of early childhood education services and the Italian National Social Security Institute’s gender report, Sicily continues to have one of the lowest female employment rates in Italy and childcare coverage significantly below the EU’s targets. This makes it harder for women to strike a balance between work and family life, and increases their risk of unemployment and economic exclusion. Despite the resources made available through the European Social Fund Plus (ESF +) and cohesion policy, significant differences between regions in access to early childhood education services persist. In view of the above: 1.
Would the Commission say that the EU funds allocated to Sicily have been effectively used to expand early childhood services?
Will it further promote initiatives to support the regions that are lagging furthest behind on the EU’s targets for female employment and educational services?
What tools will it use to monitor the effectiveness of EU funding in reducing the gender gap in the labour market and improving people’s work-life balance?

E-10-2026-003314.t: Greek restrictions on repopulation of livestock holdings and their compatibility with EU law
qt: to the Commission Nikos Pappas (The Left) Subject:

For many years now, Greece has faced serious zoonotic diseases that have had devastating consequences, especially for sheep and goat farming. Following the mass culls in the wake of the sheep and goat pox outbreak, thousands of holdings have been left with no productive livestock and the sector is unable to recover. Regulation (EU) 2020/687 provides for a monitoring period of 21 days for the repopulation of a holding after a pox outbreak, subject to certain health conditions. However, the Greek authorities are saying that, in Greece, repopulation is allowed six months after the last outbreak recorded in the country. Prolonged restrictions entail a risk of permanent abandonment of the sector, as well as making it virtually impossible to establish new holdings and include new livestock farmers in the Young Farmers programme. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

To what extent is the horizontal restriction of six months for the repopulation or establishment of new livestock holdings compatible with EU law, in particular when it is enforced without individual epidemiological assessments being carried out and goes beyond the requirements laid down in Regulation (EU) 2016/429 and the relevant EU framework?
How far can the national authorities go in imposing additional or stricter measures than those provided for in EU law?

Does it intend to ask the Greek authorities to review the existing framework and the application of a proportionate and science-based protocol for safe repopulation that takes individual epidemiological circumstances into account while ensuring the protection of young livestock farmers and beneficiaries of the Young Farmers programme?

E-10-2026-003313.t: Compatibility of retrospective appropriate assessment, public participation, peatland drainage and substitute consent mechanisms
qt: to the Commission Ciaran Mullooly (Renew) Subject:

Can an appropriate assessment conducted after significant environmental degradation has already taken place satisfy the requirements of Article 6(3) of Directive 92/43/EEC (Habitats Directive), which requires prior assessment of plans or projects likely to have significant effects on protected sites?

Does the Commission consider that public participation requirements under the Aarhus Convention and Directive 2003/35/EC are fulfilled where local communities were not effectively consulted at the earliest stages of decision-making, particularly in cases involving retrospective applications?

Is the continued drainage and degradation of peatlands, pending decisions on retrospective consent, consistent with the EU’s climate objectives, including emissions reduction commitments and peatland restoration targets under relevant EU policies, and is the Commission aware of, and does it have concerns regarding, any potential systematic reliance by Ireland on retrospective planning mechanisms (such as substitute consent) in sectors including peat extraction, and their compatibility with EU environmental law?

E-10-2026-003312.t: Retrospective environmental impact assessment (EIA) procedures and the use of substitute consent mechanisms
qt: to the Commission Ciaran Mullooly (Renew) Subject:

Does the Commission consider it compatible with the requirements and objectives of Directive 2011/92/EU (as amended) concerning EIA for Member States to regularise long-standing, large-scale industrial activities through retrospective assessment procedures, rather than ensuring assessment prior to development consent?

Does the Commission consider that the use of substitute consent mechanisms risks undermining the preventative and precautionary principles underpinning EU environmental law, particularly where an EIA and appropriate assessment were not carried out before works commenced?
Are Member States required under EU law to ensure that any unlawful environmental damage is fully remedied before considering or granting any form of retrospective or substitute consent?

E-10-2026-003311.t: Protection of Catholic religious sites in Bosnia and Herzegovina
qt: to the Commission Željana Zovko (PPE), Dolors Montserrat (PPE), Nicolás Pascual de la Parte (PPE), Loránt Vincze (PPE), Miriam Lexmann (PPE), Reinhold Lopatka (PPE) Subject:

In the light of the recent appalling act of vandalism targeting the Catholic pilgrimage site of Medjugorje, including the desecration of statues of the Blessed Virgin Mary and the destruction of a place of prayer, as well as a series of previously documented attacks on Catholic churches, shrines and places of worship across Bosnia and Herzegovina, how does the Commission, through the EU Delegation to Bosnia and Herzegovina, intend to contribute to the protection of Catholic religious sites and the effective safeguarding of freedom of religion or belief, which is a fundamental right and a core value of the European Union?

Furthermore, how is the Commission addressing the repeated targeting of Christian religious heritage in Bosnia and Herzegovina in the context of the country’s EU accession process and its obligations to uphold fundamental rights, protect religious communities and combat religiously motivated intolerance?

E-10-2026-003310.t: The Ceuta migration crisis: potential jihadist infiltrations, securing Europe’s external borders and safeguarding the Schengen area
qt: to the Commission Letizia Moratti (PPE), Massimiliano Salini (PPE), Flavio Tosi (PPE), Salvatore De Meo (PPE), Giusi Princi (PPE), Marco Falcone (PPE), Caterina Chinnici (PPE), Fulvio Martusciello (PPE) Subject:

The Ceuta migrant crisis has brought a number of key issues to the fore, namely the management of irregular migrant flows, the security of Europe’s external borders and the functioning of the Schengen system. Press reports indicate that the Spanish Audiencia Nacional is verifying whether any people with links to jihadist terrorism – including extremists who are known to the authorities and individuals who have previously been deported for their radical inclinations – have crossed the border into Spain. The Ceuta migration crisis is clear proof that uncontrolled flows can facilitate the entry of people who pose a security risk. One cannot rule out the involvement of criminal networks or the possibility that external actors could be weaponising these migration flows. In this regard, any uncertainty or grey area in the management of migrant flows could cause issues not just for the two countries involved, but for Europe as a whole. As a result, Europe needs to test how effective the Entry/Exist system (which recently became fully operational) and the EU’s other border management tools are in emergency situations. In the light of the above: 1.

Does the Commission know whether any high-risk individuals have managed to enter the EU through Ceuta, and could it specify the nature of the checks that have been carried out by Europol, the SIS, Interpol and national authorities?

What measures will be taken to promptly step up border identification and screening procedures and bolster database interoperability with a view to preventing any breaches in the Schengen security architecture?

What urgent steps will be taken to introduce stricter conditions in the EU’s agreements with third countries with a view to supporting the Member States exposed to these migration flows and preventing the latter from being used as a geopolitical tool?

E-10-2026-003309.t: The Ceuta migration crisis: potential jihadist infiltrations, securing Europe’s external borders and safeguarding the Schengen area
qt: to the Council Letizia Moratti (PPE), Massimiliano Salini (PPE), Flavio Tosi (PPE), Caterina Chinnici (PPE), Salvatore De Meo (PPE), Giusi Princi (PPE), Fulvio Martusciello (PPE), Marco Falcone (PPE) Subject:

E-10-2026-003308.t: The ‘escape clause’ gives corporate groups a leg up while ordinary people struggle under the yoke of high prices
qt: to the Commission Lefteris Nikolaou-Alavanos (NI) Subject:

The Greek Government is asking for the ‘national escape clause’ to be extended to include corporate groups involved in energy infrastructure projects. The aim is to promote EUR 1.5 billion in investments for the three-year period from 2026 to 2028, which means more fast cash for corporate groups, stolen from the people's coffers. While energy corporations in Greece made a record profit of EUR 2 billion in 2025, households have been seeing a steady increase in electricity prices since 2021. In view of the above, where does the Commission stand on the following: 1.

The fact that the ‘escape clause’ will free up more large sums of money from Member States’ coffers in order to incentivise investments in big energy corporations, with the people having to foot the bill at a time when they are struggling under the yoke of high prices?

The fact that the EU’s energy policy consists of support and funding measures such as ‘pass’ subsidies – aimed at securing profits for energy corporations (also known as ‘green birds of prey’) and energy infrastructure giants –, which essentially perpetuate the high prices borne by ordinary people and secure profits for big corporate groups?

The fact that the energy policy of the EU and the national governments is sending energy prices and poverty rates through the roof, while ordinary people are subjected to decrepit and unsafe infrastructure in an ancient network where corporate groups only promote investment if they are able to secure conditions that will maximise their profit, meaning that the people will continue to foot the hefty bill multiple times over?

E-10-2026-003307.t: Reports of verbal and physical harassment within the European Commission
qt: to the Commission Sander Smit (ECR), Jessika van Leeuwen (ECR) Subject:

POLITICO1 has recently revealed that almost 1 000 written complaints have been received by the European Commission’s confidential counsellors since 2024. These reports cover topics including verbal and physical harassment by managers, humiliation, high workload and fear of repercussions when submitting complaints. However, the counsellors themselves have no authority to investigate. This raises questions about the internal administrative culture within the European Commission and how complaints are followed up. The EU is founded on democracy, equality and respect for human dignity. It is therefore very important that these values are respected and protected within the European institutions too. 1.
What concrete measures is the Commission taking to systematically combat verbal and physical harassment and abuse of power by managers?
Is the Commission willing to report annually and transparently on the nature of the reports, and what guarantees are there of diligent and independent follow-up?

What is the Commission’s assessment of the risk that reports of verbal and physical harassment, abuse of power and inadequate handling of complaints could harm the confidence that European citizens have in the European institutions and the credibility of the EU?

Starcevic S., 1,000 complaints made to European Commission’s anti-harassment team, POLITICO, 6 August 2026, https://www.politico.eu/article/1000-complaints-european-commissions-anti-harassment-team/. 1

E-10-2026-003304.t: Is the EU paving the way for widespread digital surveillance?
qt: to the Commission Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE) Subject:

At the informal meeting of EU Justice Ministers on 17 and 18 July 2026, a broad consensus was reached in favour of developing new EU rules on data retention for law enforcement purposes. The initiative was presented as essential to investigations, particularly in crossborder cases involving serious and organised crime. However, the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) has repeatedly held that general and indiscriminate retention of traffic and location data constitutes very serious interference with the fundamental rights to privacy and to personal data protection. What is more, it is the Member States that are primarily responsible for tackling crime. In view of the above: 1.
How will the Commission ensure that its future legislative proposal fully abides by CJEU case-law?

What points can it put forward to demonstrate that the adoption of a new EU framework would offer real added value compared with the existing national arrangements and mechanisms for judicial and police cooperation between Member States?

Does it intend to leave the Member States sufficient discretion to determine for themselves data storage arrangements that are compatible with their constitutional traditions, their security requirements and the principle of subsidiarity?

E-10-2026-003303.t: Emergency powers: can the Commission bypass the European Parliament?
qt: to the Commission Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE) Subject:

In certain ‘exceptional’ situations, the Commission may propose measures that are then decided by the governments of the Member States, without the European Parliament being fully involved in their adoption. This emergency mechanism should not become a standard way of excluding the representatives elected by the citizens. In recent years, using exceptional instruments in areas such as health, energy, the internal market and defence has led to an increased use of derogation procedures. While these mechanisms may be justified in certain circumstances, they should not lead to long-term weakening of the European Parliament’s role in EU policy-making or to making trivial use of exception procedures. 1.

In what specific situations does the Commission consider that it can propose a measure without going through the normal legislative procedure involving the European Parliament, and what objective criteria make it possible to characterise an emergency that warrants use of such a procedure?

Does the Commission undertake to explain publicly, for each emergency measure, why Parliament cannot be involved in the decision, by publishing a detailed statement of reasons demonstrating that use of that procedure is necessary and proportionate?
Does it agree that these measures should always be limited in time and subject to rapid scrutiny by the European Parliament?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (29.9.2026) 1. Article 122 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU) sets out the conditions under which this provision can be used as a legal basis. In her political guidelines for 2024-2029, the President of the Commission pledged to ensure that the Commission uses this tool only in exceptional circumstances. This commitment is reflected in point 52 of the revised Framework Agreement on relations between the European Parliament and the European Commission1. It provides that, without prejudice to any other procedures provided for in the Treaties, recourse to Article 122 TFEU is only possible on an exceptional basis and under the strict conditions set out in that Article. 2. In line with the commitment in the political guidelines, point 52 of the Framework Agreement also states that the Commission commits to provide without delay comprehensive justification and information on the exceptional and emergency cases where the proposals by the Commission are based on Article 122 TFEU. 3. In addition, point 52 of the Framework Agreement provides that, at the earliest three months after the entry into force of the legal act based on Article 122 TFEU, and at appropriate intervals thereafter, the Member of the Commission responsible shall, at the request of the President of European Parliament, report on the implementation of the legal act concerned, including an assessment of the legal act.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/agree_interinstit/2026/1050/oj/eng.

E-10-2026-003302.t: European elections: does the EU want to impose the same rules on all Member States?
qt: to the Council Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE) Subject:

The European elections are still mainly organised in accordance with each Member State’s own rules. However, a proposed reform would further harmonise the organisation of the elections, including by creating transnational electoral lists and an EU electoral authority to coordinate part of the elections. The reform could enter into force only with the unanimous agreement of the Member States and after each country approves it in accordance with its own constitutional requirements. Transnational lists are not the only thing on the agenda; discussions are also focusing on further harmonising a number of different aspects of the European elections, such as eligibility conditions, campaign procedures, certain rules on political funding and the coordination of election monitoring. Those developments raise questions about the maintenance of the Member States’ powers with regard to the holding of elections. 1.
Does the Council support the creation of transnational lists, with citizens voting for EUwide candidates rather than for candidates in their country alone?
Is it in favour of the creation of an EU electoral authority and the imposition of common rules on voting ages, candidacies, election campaigns and voting methods?
Can it confirm that new electoral rules will only be imposed on a Member State with that Member State’s agreement and in accordance with its national constitutional procedures?

E-10-2026-003301.t: From ‘calm waters’ to new storms after Türkiye declares marine parks, violating the Law of the Sea
qt: to the Commission Geadis Geadi (ECR) Subject:

The publication in the Turkish Government Gazette of presidential decrees with which Ankara proceeded to declare marine parks in two areas, in the North Aegean, between Lemnos and Samothrace, and in the Eastern Mediterranean, where Kastellorizo is cut off from Rhodes, demonstrates the escalation of Türkiye’s revisionist agenda. In the North Aegean, Türkiye is essentially reinstating its position on determining the median line on the basis of the mainland coasts, ignoring the influence of the Greek islands. Correspondingly, in the Eastern Mediterranean it is isolating Kastellorizo from the rest of the Greek island area, restricting its influence on the demarcation of maritime zones. In view of the above: 1.
How will the Commission react if Türkiye imposes restrictions on fishing, research or shipping within these areas, in violation of the International Law of the Sea?
How does the Commission intend to prevent the enactment of the ‘Blue Homeland’ legislation, discussion of which in the Turkish parliament is, according to Turkish media, imminent in October?
Does the Commission intend to review its policy towards Türkiye to date, recognising that this has not prevented – but conversely encouraged – the escalation of its revisionist claims?

E-10-2026-003300.t: Canadair planes: why has Brussels failed to purchase any for 10 years, when it has managed to find EUR 27 million in four months to upgrade sewers in Seychelles?
qt: to the Commission Virginie Joron (PfE) Subject:
Canadair planes: why has Brussels failed to purchase any for 10 years, when it has managed to find EUR 27 million in four months to upgrade sewers in Seychelles?

France saw that its fleet of firefighting aircraft needed upgrading back in 20031. In 2017, after the fires in Portugal in 2016, the Commission noted that ‘the entire French fleet of forest fire fighting planes ... was out of service’2. At that juncture, Emmanuel Macron announced that a European force3 of around 20 Canadair-type water bombers would be in place by 2022. Almost 10 years on, those planes were very much missed this summer. The EU is providing funding to the tune of EUR 600 million to kick-start the manufacture of 12 new planes in Canada, but they will not be ready for delivery until 2029-2030. The European Court of Auditors has reported that ‘although there have been efforts to purchase rescEU reserves jointly, we found that these efforts had produced results in only one case4’. By way of comparison, EUR 27 million in EU funding was authorised in four months for sewers in Seychelles (a European Investment Bank loan made in 2011). The French Development Agency provided a loan of EUR 10 million and the Commission provided a EUR 7 million grant5. 1.
Why is the funding procedure quicker when it comes to sewers in Seychelles than it is for Canadair planes in Europe?
What is the Commission going to do to speed up the delivery of Canadair planes?
Why did it not make the development of a European water bomber a priority?
