E-10-2026-003298.t: Framework and support for small-scale EU coastal fishers in relation to emerging bluefin tuna stocks in the North Sea
qt: to the Commission Willemien Koning (PPE), Sander Smit (ECR), Jeannette Baljeu (Renew) Subject:

Through sustainable fisheries partnership agreements (SFPAs), the EU facilitates access for EU fleets to tuna stocks in the waters of non-EU countries. Concurrently, the recovering eastern stock of Atlantic bluefin tuna is returning to the North Sea. Small-scale EU coastal fishers cannot benefit from this recovery, as national quota allocations rely on historical catch records rather than the current distribution of species. The absence of by-catch arrangements forces them to discard incidental catches, thus undermining the landing obligation. Meanwhile, the UK, having acquired a quota share, has opened a tuna fishery to small-scale vessels. Although quota allocation remains a national competence, Article 17 of the Common Fisheries Policy Regulation requires the Member States to apply socio-economic and environmental criteria when allocating fishing opportunities. 1.

How does the Commission assess the policy imbalance whereby the EU extensively supports international tuna fishing, yet provides no active framework to assist smallscale North Sea fishers in benefiting from locally returning stocks of Atlantic bluefin tuna?

In the light of its vade mecum on Article 171 and the upcoming simplification package, how will the Commission monitor and support Member States in applying this guidance to grant small-scale fishers access to emerging stocks via by-catch or trial quotas?

How does the Commission intend to address, at the upcoming annual meeting of the International Commission for the Conservation of Atlantic Tunas (ICCAT), the geographical scope of artisanal quota provisions in relation to northern EU waters?
http://data.europa.eu/eli/C/2025/6227/oj.

E-10-2026-003297.t: Early harvesting and illegal trade of Greek kiwi fruit – need to protect their quality and reputation in EU markets
qt: to the Commission Sakis Arnaoutoglou (S&D) Subject:

Greek kiwi fruit is one of the country’s most dynamic agricultural export products, with a significant presence in the single market and in non-EU countries. However, there have been recurring complaints about early harvesting and trade of kiwi fruit that do not meet the required maturity and quality characteristics. According to representatives of producers and exporters, Greek kiwi fruit have been found in European markets at a particularly low degree of maturity. Such practices not only harm consistent producers and exporters, but may also undermine the reputation of Greek kiwi fruit and the confidence of European consumers. Despite the existing national and European framework for the marketing of fruit and vegetables, issues arise regarding the effectiveness of controls, traceability and cross-border cooperation between the competent authorities. In view of the above: 1.

How does the Commission assess the application of European marketing and control rules with regard to the trading of kiwi fruit that do not meet the required standards and what is the responsibility of the Member States?

Does the Commission intend to strengthen coordination and information exchange between the Member States' oversight authorities, so that illegal or non-compliant consignments are detected not only in the country of production but also at their final destination?

Is the Commission considering establishing or strengthening a European traceability and maturity control system, from field to market, in order to protect consistent producers, consumers and the international reputation of quality European agricultural products such as Greek kiwi?

E-10-2026-003296.t: Burden of the EU ETS on the production of fertilisers for export
qt: to the Commission Piotr Müller (ECR) Subject:

European agriculture and industry are directly affected by the imposition of ETS costs on fertiliser production. Fertilisers are an essential input for agricultural production, and artificially increasing their costs through EU climate policy translates into higher food production costs, harms the competitiveness of European farms and increases the EU’s dependence on imports. It is even more difficult to justify applying the same burden to fertilisers produced in the EU for export. European producers bear the costs of the ETS and then compete on global markets with companies from third countries that are not burdened with a comparable emissions price. In practice, the EU is itself worsening the competitive position of its own producers, making it easier for competitors to take over export markets and increasing the risk of shifting production outside the EU. Furthermore, this does not lead to a reduction in global emissions, only to European production being replaced by production in countries with lower environmental standards. In light of the above: 1.
How does the Commission justify the application of ETS costs to fertilisers produced in the EU for export when their foreign competitors do not bear comparable burdens?
How does the Commission assess the impact of this measure on exports, employment and the preservation of fertiliser production in the EU?
When will the Commission present an effective mechanism to eliminate the cost of ETS from EU fertiliser exports and ensure a level playing field for European producers?

E-10-2026-003295.t: Funding foreign carbon credits rather than modernising Europe
qt: to the Commission Piotr Müller (ECR) Subject:

The Commission is proposing that, from 2036 onwards, carbon credits from third countries be eligible under the ETS. This would mean channelling European funds into projects outside the EU, at a time when European industry is grappling with high energy prices, insufficient grid capacity and energy storage shortfalls, not to mention the huge costs of decarbonisation. It is difficult to square this proposal with the proclaimed goal of reindustrialising Europe. Instead of using funds to upgrade Europe’s steelworks, chemical plants and power stations, the EU may end up paying to bring down emissions outside the EU (where reductions are often difficult to verify), with no infrastructure, technology or jobs created in Europe. In light of the above: 1.
Why is the Commission proposing to spend funds from Europe’s ETS outside the EU, rather than allocating them in full to modernising Europe’s industry, grids and energy storage facilities?
How will it ensure that foreign credits deliver real, additional and lasting emissions reductions and are not the subject of double-counting?

In whose interest is it proposing the transfer of European funds to third countries for the purchase of carbon credits, given that this solution brings no long-term benefit in terms of investment to European industry but risks supporting economies and businesses in direct competition with EU producers?

E-10-2026-003294.t: Protecting gender minorities in the face of increasingly repressive LGBTI-phobic laws
qt: to the Commission Emma Fourreau (The Left) Subject:

UK legislation now prohibits transgender people from accessing non-gender-mixed facilities, thereby excluding women from certain essential facilities, such as toilets or specialised shelters. In Senegal, the recent tightening of laws, modelled on Uganda’s anti-LGBTI policies, has led to a crackdown on queer people, punishing them with prison sentences, forcing them into exile and placing them in danger. In the face of this rise in LGBTI-phobia, the EU must be at the forefront of defending the rights of gender minorities. However, the Commission has refused to ban conversion therapy. At the same time, the EU is stepping up its support for Senegal to intercept people fleeing to Europe, notably through the second phase of the Joint Operational Partnership programme and Frontex’s monitoring of Senegal’s Search and Rescue (SAR) zone. 1.

What measures does the Commission intend to adopt to encourage Member States to ban conversion therapy and to comply with the request made by the one million signatories to the European Citizens’ Initiative?
What does it intend to do to protect the rights of LGBTI people in the face of threats from anti-gender movements?
Has the Commission or the European Union Agency for Asylum asked Member States to take into account the increasing levels of persecution in several third countries when assessing asylum applications?

E-10-2026-003293.t: Major tourism projects in protected natural areas and compliance with EU nature protection legislation
qt: to the Commission Emma Fourreau (The Left) Subject:

For several months, a number of coastal regions in southern Europe – including Puglia, Sardinia, the Balearic Islands and the Setúbal region of Portugal – have seen people mobilising against tourist complex mega-projects that threaten sensitive coastal ecosystems, echoing the ‘Flamingo Revolution’ in Albania. These projects raise concerns about protecting biodiversity, land take, privatisation of the coast and land grabbing to the benefit of private interests. In several Member States, public authorities are watering down environmental protections to facilitate such projects, such as in Mallorca, or relying on derogation arrangements, such as special economic zones in Italy. This development calls into question compliance with EU law on nature protection, particularly when it concerns protected natural areas. 1.
Does the Commission consider authorising major tourism projects in protected natural areas to be in compliance with obligations under EU nature protection legislation?

How does the Commission intend to ensure that EU nature protection legislation is applied when national or regional authorities relax environmental protections in order to facilitate the implementation of major tourism projects?

E-10-2026-003292.t: Türkiye’s designation of two marine parks in violation of international law and Greek sovereign rights in the Aegean and Eastern Mediterranean
qt: to the Commission Yannis Maniatis (S&D), Nikolas Farantouris (S&D), Nikos Papandreou (S&D), Sakis Arnaoutoglou (S&D) Subject:

On 16 August, Türkiye issued two presidential decrees establishing two so-called ‘national marine parks’, one in the area between Fethiye and Kaş excluding the entire marine area around the Kastellorizo archipelago and the other in the marine area between Samothrace and Limnos. These marine parks, which are based on the illegal Turkish doctrine of the ‘Blue Homeland’, do not recognise the legal status of the Greek islands of Kastellorizo, Samothrace and Limnos, as provided for in international law and the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, which is part of the European acquis. The marine parks extend beyond Turkish territorial waters, violating Greek sovereign rights since they include areas of the Greek continental shelf and EEZ, and even territorial waters to which the Greek Aegean and Eastern Mediterranean islands are entitled under UNCLOS. The announcement about the establishment of the two ‘marine parks’ came after Türkiye submitted the relevant maps to the Intergovernmental Oceanographic Commission of UNESCO around this time last year. These along with other new acts of provocation challenge Greece’s sovereign rights in the Aegean and Eastern Mediterranean and constitute a further escalation, effectively nullifying the ‘calm waters’ policy. In view of this: What measures does the Commission intend to take to provide practical support to Greece against Türkiye's unilateral and illegal actions?

E-10-2026-003291.t: EU-funded home renovations: a worthy initiative, but ineffective at delivering energy savings
qt: to the Commission Mihai Tudose (S&D) Subject:

A recent European Court of Auditors report has found that the post-COVID home renovation works funded by the Recovery and Resilience Facility have delivered lower-than-expected energy savings. According to the audit, the funds involved were primarily allocated to projects that were easy to complete, rather than to endeavours that would have significantly improved energy ratings and resulted in major energy savings. Speed was prioritised over a strategic, long-term approach. As a result, not enough attention was paid to ensuring that these projects were cost-effective. In the light of the above, is the Commission considering prioritising major renovations that can result in substantial energy savings, and does it intend to take into account the Court of Auditors’ findings concerning the need to use specific criteria to rank projects according to their expected impact on energy consumption?

E-10-2026-003290.t: Türkiye’s illegal announcement concerning the establishment of ‘marine parks’, in violation of Greek and European sovereign rights
qt: to the Commission Emmanouil Kefalogiannis (PPE) Subject:

Yet another illegal action by Türkiye has seen the publication of the Presidential Decrees of 15 August establishing two marine parks in the Aegean and Eastern Mediterranean. These parks encroach on areas of Greek sovereign rights and Greece’s continental shelf. The Presidential Decrees establish two marine parks: One stretching between Limnos and Samothrace and another in the Eastern Mediterranean, which cuts Kastellorizo off from Rhodes completely. With this move, Türkiye continues to assert the illegal position that the islands have no rights beyond a six nautical mile limit and insists on drawing a median line between the mainland coasts of the two countries. By establishing these marine parks, supposedly to protect the marine environment, Türkiye is seeking to enforce its claims against Greece and to enshrine in law the so-called ‘Blue Homeland’ doctrine, a doctrine that has been condemned by the European Parliament. In view of this, can the Commission answer the following: What action will it take against Türkiye in response to the illegal act of declaring ‘Turkish marine parks’ in areas extending beyond Türkiye’s territorial waters, with these parks violating Greek and European sovereign rights since they include areas of the Greek continental shelf and EEZ, and even territorial waters over which the Greek islands have jurisdiction under UNCLOS?

E-10-2026-003289.t: Halting funding to Türkiye as long as it persists in threatening Greece and Europe
qt: to the Commission Georgios Aftias (PPE) Subject:

Türkiye has gone ahead and unilaterally announced the establishment of marine parks that encroach on areas beyond its territorial waters, i.e. on the North Aegean and Kastellorizo. In doing so, it is attempting to create faits accomplis against the sovereign rights of my homeland, Greece, a Member State of the European Union, and by extension against the European Union itself. The Commission must do more than issue mere statements. It must act and it must immediately halt all EU funding to Türkiye. I trust that the Commission will take prompt action as it has done in the past with other non-EU countries when they have threatened EU Member States. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Can a candidate country challenge the sovereign rights of a Member State and, at the same time, expect European funding and a privileged relationship with the EU?

What specific economic measures does it intend to take to make it clear to Türkiye that environmental initiatives cannot be used as a tool to challenge the sovereign rights of a Member State or to create a fait accompli in the Aegean and Eastern Mediterranean?
Does it consider these unilateral actions to be compatible with European law and the principle of good neighbourly relations?

E-10-2026-003287.t: Are digital platforms’ advertising revenues taxed where the value is created?
qt: to the Commission Yvan Verougstraete (Renew) Subject:

Accounts published by Meta’s Belgian subsidiary show that Meta paid only around EUR 1 million in tax in Belgium for the 2025 financial year, despite the group’s dominant position in the Belgian digital advertising market. A significant portion of advertising services sold to Belgian companies are invoiced through the group’s Irish entity. The scheme, while in line with current rules, raises questions about how tax revenues are distributed between Member States and about the fairness of the internal market. In light of the above: 1.
Does the Commission have an estimate of the tax revenues that Member States do not receive because of large digital platforms’ advertising revenues being positioned in other Member States?
How will it ensure that the profits of large digital platforms are taxed more heavily in the Member States where revenue and economic value are actually created?

Does it intend to speed up work on ‘Business in Europe: Framework for Taxation’ (BEFIT) or propose other instruments to limit distortions of competition resulting from differences in taxation between Member States?

E-10-2026-003286.t: Holy Monastery of Saint Catherine on Mount Sinai: rule of law and EU-Egypt relations
qt: to the Commission Nikolas Farantouris (S&D), Yannis Maniatis (S&D), Nikos Papandreou (S&D), Sakis Arnaoutoglou (S&D) Subject:

The Holy Monastery of Saint Catherine on Mount Sinai, a UNESCO World Heritage site and one of the oldest continuously used Christian monasteries in the world, is facing legal and administrative proceedings that raise serious concerns about the recognition of its legal personality, the recognition of its archbishop and abbot by the Egyptian Government, its ability to exercise legal representation before the courts and the protection of its property rights, which are protected by international law. This is happening just as the Egyptian Court of Cassation is about to deliver its final ruling on the case and as the EU deepens its partnership with Egypt. In light of Articles 21, 3(5)2 and 213 of the TEU and Decision (EU) 2025/1267 providing macro-financial assistance to the Arab Republic of Egypt, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Were the above developments taken into account in the recent positive assessment of Egypt and in the decision to continue providing financial assistance to the country?
Are the above developments in line with Egypt’s obligations concerning religious freedoms, effective access to justice and the protection of religious institutions?

E-10-2026-003285.t: Recognition of professional qualifications and obstacles to accessing permanent employment in the Slovenian-Italian cross-border area
qt: to the Commission Matjaž Nemec (S&D) Subject:

The European Union promotes the development and attractiveness of cross-border regions and the efficient functioning of the cross-border labour market by removing administrative barriers and strengthening the free movement of workers. However, Slovenian teachers and professors working or wanting to work in Italy still face additional administrative requirements when trying to access permanent employment. According to individuals and organisations affected, once their professional qualification has been recognised they can work as teachers on the basis of fixed-term contracts but need to go through an additional procedure to determine the equivalence of their academic title in order to be employed on a permanent basis. This practice can make access to permanent employment in a cross-border context more difficult. While the problem is currently most acute in the area of education, other regulated professions may face similar barriers. 1.
Is such practice compatible with Directive 2005/36/EC and Article 45 TFEU?
Does the Commission intend to verify whether such requirements constitute a disproportionate obstacle to the effective functioning of the cross-border labour market and the free movement of workers?
Will the Commission, together with the Italian authorities, encourage the removal of administrative barriers that limit equal access to permanent employment in border regions?
at: (English version) to the Commission Matjaž Nemec (S&D) (17 August 2026) Subject: Recognition of professional qualifications and obstacles to accessing permanent employment in the Slovenian-Italian cross-border area The European Union promotes the development and attractiveness of cross-border regions and the efficient functioning of the cross-border labour market by removing administrative barriers and strengthening the free movement of workers. However, Slovenian teachers and professors working or wanting to work in Italy still face additional administrative requirements when trying to access permanent employment. According to individuals and organisations affected, once their professional qualification has been recognised they can work as teachers on the basis of fixed-term contracts but need to go through an additional procedure to determine the equivalence of their academic title in order to be employed on a permanent basis. This practice can make access to permanent employment in a cross-border context more difficult. While the problem is currently most acute in the area of education, other regulated professions may face similar barriers. 1.
Is such practice compatible with Directive 2005/36/EC and Article 45 TFEU?

2. Does the Commission intend to verify whether such requirements constitute a disproportionate obstacle to the effective functioning of the cross-border labour market and the free movement of workers? 3. Will the Commission, together with the Italian authorities, encourage the removal of administrative barriers that limit equal access to permanent employment in border regions? (24 September 2026) Directive 2005/36/EC lays down rules on the recognition of professional qualifications acquired in one Member State for the purpose of pursuing the same profession in another Member State where access to, or pursuit of, that profession is regulated by qualifications. Once recognition has been granted, professionals are entitled to practise the profession under the same conditions as nationals. National authorities cannot impose an additional recognition procedure depending on the manner in which professionals intend to exercise the profession. This is without prejudice to the right of the private or public employers to organise competitive recruitment procedures, potentially entailing writing and oral tests; such competitive recruitment procedures do not constitute additional recognition procedures and they fall under the competence of Member States, as long as these procedures comply with EU law which prohibits discrimination based on nationality between workers of the Member States as regards employment, remuneration and other conditions of work and employment. The Commission will contact the Italian national coordinator for Directive 2005/36/EC to obtain further information on the issue raised by the Honourable Member.

E-10-2026-003283.t: Compatibility with EU law of cumulative penalties resulting in the automatic loss of judicial protection for borrowers
qt: to the Commission Maria Zacharia (NI) Subject:

On the basis of Articles 130-142 of Law 5221/2025, Joint Ministerial Decision 42483/2026 was published on 11 August 2026, during the judicial vacations, setting 1-30 September 2026 as the first timeframe for submitting applications for the rescheduling of court hearings on oppositions to payment orders and enforcement orders. The decision establishes the mandatory rescheduling of hearings on opposition to payment order and enforcement order cases pending at first instance on 15 July 2026 and scheduled for hearing on 17 September 2027: (a) without the submission of an electronic application to reschedule a hearing, the opposition is deemed to have never been filed and the suspension is automatically revoked; (b) the application must be filed within 30 days, otherwise it is deemed to have never been filed; (c) the lawyer who had submitted the opposition is notified, without ensuring that they continue to represent or communicate with the debtor. For the consumer, this means that an auction could take place before the claim or the unfair terms are checked. Based on judgments C-415/11 Aziz, C-34/13 Kušionová and C-725/19 Impuls Leasing, Directive 93/13/EEC requires effective protection and interim measures to prevent irreversible consequences. With this in mind, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

Does it consider the cumulative penalties, which could potentially result in the dismissal of a consumer’s punctually filed judicial opposition, to be proportionate in the light of Articles 6 and 7 of Directive 93/13/EEC and Articles 7, 17 and 47 of the Charter?

Is effective temporary judicial protection guaranteed when the suspension is automatically revoked and can an auction be concluded before a decision is issued on the opposition to a payment or enforcement order and before any unfair terms have been examined?
Will it ask Greece for information and examine the compatibility of the regulations with EU law in order to prevent homes or property from being irreversibly lost?
to the Commission Anna Bryłka (PfE) Subject:

As a result of recent hostilities and the blockade of the Black Sea following Russia’s attacks on merchant ships, the export of Ukrainian grain via this route is now impossible. One possible alternative route runs through Europe’s frontline countries. In recent years, the uncontrolled so-called ‘transit’ transport of Ukrainian agricultural goods has destabilised domestic agricultural markets (e.g. in Poland) and caused significant losses to Member States’ agricultural sectors. 1.

Is the Commission considering introducing a special mechanism to allow the transit of Ukrainian grain through frontline states under the same conditions as apply to existing quotas for these agricultural products?
How does the Commission intend to ensure that Ukrainian grain does not remain on the market of the transit country, given that in recent years this has prompted interventions by Member States?
Does the Commission foresee dedicated financial measures to assist European farmers should agricultural markets in certain Member States be destabilised again?

E-10-2026-003280.t: European funding to upgrade the electricity grid and prevent wildfires in Greece
qt: to the Commission Sakis Arnaoutoglou (S&D) Subject:

Measure 16900 of the Greek Recovery and Resilience Plan provided for an upgrade of the electricity distribution network in forest areas, involving the replacement of bare wires, the installation of insulation, and undergrounding or power line relocation. In its 2024-2028 Network Development Plan, the Hellenic Electricity Distribution Network Operator (DEDDIE) states that the measure involves works across 2 086 kilometres of power lines and a budget of EUR 149.8 million. However, while in previous EU documents measures 16900 and 16901 appear as two separate entries with a budget of EUR 40 million and EUR 60 million respectively, SWD(2026)252 shows measure 16900 as ‘HEDNO network upgrades’ with a budget of EUR 100 million and a broader scope. Meanwhile, the Greek press, citing the arson investigation unit as its source, has published information on megafire cases that are being investigated because of their potential link to power grid problems, without holding anyone accountable prematurely. In view of this, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
What is the exact current physical and financial scope of measure 16900 and has measure 16901 been fully or partially incorporated into it?
How many kilometres of network have been completed and put into operation, for each intervention category and geographical area, and what documentation was used to certify this milestone?

What criteria were used to select the specific intervention areas and, during their selection, assess the risk of the electricity grid causing or spreading forest fires, so that interventions could prioritise higher risk areas?

E-10-2026-003279.t: The Lovable case and SEF funds: protecting EU public resources and preventing capital flight
qt: to the Commission Fulvio Martusciello (PPE) Subject:

Managed by the EQT Group and funded to the tune of EUR 1 billion by the Commission, the Scaleup Europe Fund (SEF) is a EUR 5 billion partnership that was launched to support highpotential EU companies and therefore encourage ‘the best of Europe to choose Europe’. However, SEF recently took part in Lovable’s Series C funding round, even though the Swedish company had already transferred its registered office, voting rights, intellectual property and tax base to Delaware in the US. In other words, by deploying resources from Series B onwards, the EU is funding companies that have already relocated. Another issue is that the SEF’s resources are a drop in the ocean compared to the investments made by US tech giants. In the light of the fact that EU venture capital funds should not finance US companies – and thus undermine Europe’s technological sovereignty, tax base and ability to regulate these companies’ activities – I ask the Commission: 1.
Will it make public fund disbursement conditional on companies maintaining their registered offices and tax bases in the European Union?

What structural changes will it make to the start-up/scaleup strategy so that the EU can invest at an earlier stage and prevent strategic companies from feeling like they have to relocate to the US in order to raise capital?

E-10-2026-003278.t: Vaccination of pregnant women against COVID-19: risks, data and EU responsibility
qt: to the Commission Gerald Hauser (PfE) Subject:

Pregnant women have been considered a particularly vulnerable group since the Thalidomide scandal. Yet, despite this, COVID-19 vaccines have already been administered without this group being included in the initial marketing authorisation studies. Meanwhile, there are reports of possible risks to pregnancy and fertility. An analysis from Czechia found significantly lower rates of successful pregnancies in women vaccinated before conception1. Anthony Fauci also discussed a risk of miscarriage after vaccination in the first trimester as early as January 20212. The frequently cited miscarriage rate of 82 % comes from an analysis by Thorp et al. and was also discussed in the US Senate34. 1.
Since when have the Commission, the EMA and the ECDC been aware of possible risks of COVID-19 vaccinations for pregnancy, miscarriage and fertility?
With the lack of data available early on, why were pregnant women encouraged/recommended to get vaccinated?

Why have all precautionary measures in place for pregnant women since the Thalidomide scandal been overridden for the COVID-19 vaccinations and pregnant women been vaccinated up until now, and who bears political responsibility for this decision at EU level?

E-10-2026-003276.t: Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation creating additional red tape and legal uncertainty for businesses, especially SMEs
qt: to the Commission Benoit Cassart (Renew) Subject:

The entry into force of the Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation on 12 August 2026 is imposing a crippling administrative burden on businesses, especially SMEs. Due to the lack of clarity caused by the delay in the explanatory guidelines and lack of implementing acts, economic operators are having to move ahead without any direction. This situation directly penalises honest entrepreneurs, undermining our SMEs and e-commerce. Given the current technical uncertainty and the fact that some implementing acts are not yet operational, does the Commission intend to ask the Member States to relax the transition conditions by granting an official moratorium on penalties in order to protect our companies, in particular our SMEs?

E-10-2026-003275.t: Impact of AI on reading and interest in books in Europe
qt: to the Commission Ioan-Rareş Bogdan (PPE) Subject:

The way in which Europeans access information has changed rapidly in recent years, with the increasing use of digital tools and artificial intelligence.1 In 2025, 32.7 % of EU citizens aged between 16 and 74 had used AI tools. Meanwhile, the consumption of e-books and audiobooks has grown, showing a transformation in the way Europeans access written content. The development of AI provides fast access to information and can be an aid to learning but the frequent use of tools that provide instant information and responses can influence the way in which people, especially young people, approach long texts and in-depth reading. 1.

Is the Commission considering monitoring the effects of using artificial intelligence on the reading habits of Europeans, especially children and young people, and assessing its impact on in-depth reading, the ability to concentrate and text comprehension?
What steps is the Commission taking to encourage reading and the development of lasting relationships with books in an environment where instant access to information is becoming ever more present?
https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-eurostat-news/w/ddn-20251216-3.

E-10-2026-003274.t: High toll fees on roads co-financed by the EU and European territorial cohesion
qt: to the Commission Sakis Arnaoutoglou (S&D) Subject:

The EU finances the development of the Trans-European Transport Networks with the aim of enhancing mobility, territorial cohesion and the free movement of people and goods. However, the particularly high toll fees on some co-financed motorways raise questions as to whether these objectives are being met. On a recent car journey from Belgium to Greece, toll fees up to Evzonoi totalled EUR 40.96 and then another EUR 41.05 from Evzonoi to Athens. This situation places a disproportionate burden on people living outside big cities, workers, farmers, small and medium-sized enterprises and professional drivers, limiting actual access to infrastructure that was built with European funding. At the same time, there are issues with the proportionality of the charges, the transparency of concessions and the use of toll revenues. In view of this, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

How does it assess the impact of high toll fees charged on co-financed motorways on territorial and social cohesion, on free movement and on the competitiveness of regional economies, in particular at the Union’s external borders?
Does it intend, when financing new or reviewing existing TEN-T projects, to set conditions so that toll charges are proportionate, socially fair and do not limit real accessibility for citizens?
How does it ensure that concessions and toll revenues in co-financed projects serve cohesion policy objectives and enhance their transparency and monitoring?

E-10-2026-003273.t: Reducing the energy costs of producers in the Philippi marshes
qt: to the Commission Emmanouil Fragkos (ECR) Subject:

Farming in the Philippi marshes is heavily dependent on electricity-powered borehole drilling, pumping stations and irrigation, drying and storage systems. The increase in electricity costs places a disproportionate burden on producers of maize, sunflower and other energy-intensive crops, limiting agricultural income and the region’s competitiveness. The production of energy for self-consumption, the collective production of energy by cooperatives and local land reclamation organisations, as well as energy upgrades in agricultural facilities could permanently reduce production costs. However, high upfront costs, the lack of available hosting capacity, connection delays and procedural complexity put off many small and medium-sized producers from harnessing these solutions. The CAP Strategic Plans can fund productive investments and renewable energy sources and EU State aid rules allow support for investment in farms, subject to conditions. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Which CAP and cohesion policy instruments can fund collective self-production and energy storage projects for farmers, cooperatives and land reclamation organisations in the Philippi marshes?
Can priority grid connections and increased aid intensity be envisaged for farmer-led energy communities in agricultural areas with high productivity?
Does it intend to encourage a specific intervention in the Greek CAP Strategic Plan to reduce the energy costs of primary production?

E-10-2026-003271.t: Protection of the Geraneia Mountains and compliance with the EU’s environmental obligations
qt: to the Commission Emmanouil Fragkos (ECR) Subject:

In the Geraneia Mountains, which comprise Natura 2000 areas and a wildlife reserve, plans to install 57 wind turbines that are up to 180 metres high, accompanied by electrochemical energy storage plants, have been put to public consultation. According to the studies carried out, the project involves extensive excavations, including new road excavations, large quantities of concrete and extensive cabling networks. In addition, part of the works are to take place in areas already affected by major wildfires in recent years. The area also hosts important protected fauna species and is a flyway of European importance. Meanwhile, local communities as well as the regional councils of Attica and the Peloponnese have voiced their objections. In view of this, can the Commission answer the following: Does it intend to examine whether special measures are needed to protect recently burnt Natura 2000 areas before authorisation is given for new extensive technical works to go ahead?

E-10-2026-003270.t: Restrictions on the establishment of private roadworthiness inspection centres in Greece and their compatibility with EU law
qt: to the Commission Emmanouil Fragkos (ECR) Subject:

Article 34(2) of Law 2963/2001, as amended by Article 73 of Law 4850/2021, lays down restrictions on the location of private roadworthiness inspection centres (KTEO), forbidding or substantially limiting their establishment in areas within the town/city limits. There have been complaints about these restrictions artificially reducing the availability of suitable real estate, about them making it harder for new businesses to enter the market and about them favouring existing businesses. Meanwhile, the need for these restrictions has not been substantiated. The fact that the services provided by modern roadworthiness inspection centres are lownuisance and that they can operate under strict technical and environmental requirements, calls into question the compatibility of the contentious restrictions with Articles 49 and 56 TFEU, as well as with Articles 14 and 15 of Directive 2006/123/EC on services, which forbid unjustified geographical restrictions and require national restrictions to be necessary and proportionate. In view of this, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Does it consider these provisions to be compatible with Directive 2006/123/EC and the fundamental freedoms of the internal market?
Has it assessed whether these restrictions are necessary and proportionate?
Does it intend to examine whether the application of Greek legislation constitutes an infringement of EU law and does it intend to initiate the applicable procedures if necessary?

E-10-2026-003268.t: Road safety on Highway 7’s Matera-Ferrandina section, which is part of the comprehensive TEN-T network
qt: to the Commission Valentina Palmisano (The Left) Subject:

The Matera-Ferrandina section of Italy’s Highway 7 links the Murgia area and Pollino National Park and is a road of some importance to the EU, seeing as Italian ministerial documents rank it among the country’s most important highways and state that it is part of the TEN-T comprehensive network. Though it is the main road serving Matera (a city that is also a UNESCO site), handles more than 13 000 vehicles on a daily basis and has been the site of a number of accident this year, the Matera-Ferrandina stretch is still a single carriageway. According to Directive 2008/96/EC (which was updated in 2019), Member States have to rank the most hazardous road sections, carry out regular inspections and draw up lists of priority remedial works. In addition, the EU Road Safety Policy Framework 2021-2030 aims to reduce road deaths and serious injuries by 50% by 2030 – a milestone to achieving the ‘Vision Zero’ objective (zero road deaths) by 2050. In the light of the above, I ask the Commission: 1.
Is it aware of the safety issues and accident rate of this section of the TEN-T comprehensive network?

How is it going about verifying Italy’s compliance with the obligations laid down by Directive 2008/96/EC, particularly those concerning the ranking of dangerous road network sections and the drawing up of lists of priority remedial works for important transport links like the one mentioned above?

What cohesion policy funds and other EU instruments could be used to finance works that can make the Matera-Ferrandina section safe and enable the EU to meet its goal of halving the total number of road fatalities and serious injuries by 2030?
to the Commission Jörgen Warborn (PPE) Subject:

Regulation (EU) 2025/401 (PPWR) applies from 12 August 2026 and was presented as harmonisation for the single market. For the smallest businesses the effect seems to be the opposite. A company sending a parcel to a consumer in another Member State is treated as a producer there. It must register in that country’s producer register, specify the packaging materials used, report quantities and pay fees, separately in each Member State. These costs are largely fixed and do not scale with turnover, so a seller shipping a few parcels a year faces broadly the same administrative overhead as a large retailer. Swedish small businesses have publicly announced that they are closing their online stores to customers in other Member States as of 12 August, because compliance is not viable at their volumes. 1.
Has the Commission assessed the risk that micro-enterprises will stop selling across borders as a result of these obligations?
Has the Commission assessed the cumulative administrative cost borne by a microenterprise registering in several Member States?
Will the Commission examine an exemption from producer registration for SMEs, regardless of the volume of packaging placed on the market?
Regulation (EU) 2025/40 of 19 December 2024 on packaging and packaging waste (ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2025/40/oj). 1

E-10-2026-003266.t: Strengthening EU legal framework and enforcement against fake online reviews
qt: to the Commission Jeannette Baljeu (Renew) Subject:

Consumers must be able to trust that online reviews reflect genuine experiences. In recent years, the EU has stepped up efforts to combat fake reviews, prohibiting them under the revised Unfair Commercial Practices Directive and classifying them as illegal content under the Digital Services Act. However, according to a 2024 Commission report, the problem continues to grow. New technological developments are making it cheaper and easier to produce convincing fake reviews at scale, which underlines the need for stronger enforcement to keep pace, protect consumer trust and preserve fair competition in the single market. 1.
Does the Commission consider the current legal framework effective in addressing the current scale of fake reviews?
What action does the Commission regard as most appropriate to counter the growing prevalence of fake reviews?
What further steps will the Commission take to safeguard a level playing field by tackling business models built around the production and sale of fake reviews at scale?

E-10-2026-003265.t: AfD members being excluded from local elections in Germany
qt: to the Commission Alexander Jungbluth (ESN) Subject:

Following the exclusion of several AfD members from local elections in Rhineland-Palatinate and North Rhine-Westphalia, a large number of AfD candidates have now been prevented from running in the local elections on 13 September 2026 by the electoral committees in Lower Saxony. The candidates in question are Member of the Lower House of the German Parliament Martin Sichert (Friesland council election), Member of the State Parliament Thorsten Moriße (Wilhelmshaven mayoral election), Justin Vogel (Herzberg am Harz mayoral election) and Reinhild Goes (Nörten-Hardenberg mayoral election). What’s different about the situation in Lower Saxony is that the decision has been made on the basis of the new local election law adopted in April 2026 by the SPD–Green state government, which provides that, in cases of doubt regarding loyalty to the constitution, recommendations from the Office for the Protection of the Constitution and the Ministry of the Interior may be taken into account – although the AfD has not been banned. 1.

Does the Commission consider the exclusion of democratically elected party representatives from local elections solely based on the fact that they are part of the AfD to be a possible violation of fundamental democratic principles of the EU?

What does it make of this case, considering that it effectively constitutes an exclusion of a party through the back door, when such a decision should be the sole responsibility of the Federal Constitutional Court?
In view of the above, will it consider initiating a procedure under Article 7 of the Treaty on European Union (TEU) against Germany?
at: (English version) to the Commission Alexander Jungbluth (ESN) (12 August 2026) Subject: AfD members being excluded from local elections in Germany Following the exclusion of several AfD members from local elections in Rhineland-Palatinate and North Rhine-Westphalia, a large number of AfD candidates have now been prevented from running in the local elections on 13 September 2026 by the electoral committees in Lower Saxony. The candidates in question are Member of the Lower House of the German Parliament Martin Sichert (Friesland council election), Member of the State Parliament Thorsten Moriße (Wilhelmshaven mayoral election), Justin Vogel (Herzberg am Harz mayoral election) and Reinhild Goes (Nörten-Hardenberg mayoral election). What’s different about the situation in Lower Saxony is that the decision has been made on the basis of the new local election law adopted in April 2026 by the SPD-Green state government, which provides that, in cases of doubt regarding loyalty to the constitution, recommendations from the Office for the Protection of the Constitution and the Ministry of the Interior may be taken into account — although the AfD has not been banned. 1. Does the Commission consider the exclusion of democratically elected party representatives from local elections solely based on the fact that they are part of the AfD to be a possible violation of fundamental democratic principles of the EU? 2. What does it make of this case, considering that it effectively constitutes an exclusion of a party through the back door, when such a decision should be the sole responsibility of the Federal Constitutional Court? 3. In view of the above, will it consider initiating a procedure under Article 7 of the Treaty on European Union (TEU) against Germany? (2 October 2026) It is the Member States’ competence to lay down the specific conditions for the conduct and organisation of local elections, in accordance with their constitutional and legislative rules, subject to EU law and their international obligations. German competent authorities and courts are primarily responsible for ensuring compliance with these rules and addressing any potential irregularities, in accordance with their well-established procedures. The Commission does not comment on individual decisions taken by national authorities, such as local election committees, regarding the disqualification of candidates from standing in elections.

E-10-2026-003264.t: The Commission is cutting back on the promotion of European food while opening up the market to imports from third countries
qt: to the Commission Piotr Müller (ECR) Subject:

The Commission is considering drastically cutting funding for the promotion of European food under the ‘Enjoy, it’s from Europe’ scheme, including a reduction in funding for the MULTI campaign from EUR 60 million to EUR 20 million. At the same time, despite opposition from some Member States, including Poland, the Commission is consistently opening up the EU market to ever-increasing imports of agri-food products from Ukraine and Mercosur countries. European farmers are forced to comply with some of the most stringent and costly production standards in the world, while cheaper products manufactured without a comparable system of requirements, controls and traceability are entering the EU market. In the case of imports from Ukraine, serious concerns regarding the quality and testing of certain products, as well as market destabilisation, have been raised repeatedly by Member States and farmers. In light of the above: 1.
Why is the Commission cutting funding for the promotion of European food while increasing access to the EU market for cheaper products from third countries?

Why is the Commission ignoring the objections of some Member States and concerns regarding the quality and testing of imported food rather than protecting producers who meet the EU’s stringent standards?

Is the Commission’s policy intended to create a situation in which European farmers bear the costs of EU regulations while their place in the market is taken by cheaper food produced to lower standards?

E-10-2026-003263.t: EU legal framework for organised mass border-crossing situations
qt: to the Commission Mika Aaltola (PPE) Subject:

The events in Ceuta in July 2026 confirmed a pattern. The mass storming of an external border is no longer a spontaneous event. It is organised, timed and aimed at the seams of European law. It constitutes a third type of instrumentalisation, alongside coercive state action and corrosive grey zone pressure. Member States have been left to improvise. Finland adopted an emergency law because the EU had not written any rules. Spain applies a different framework. Twenty-seven national emergency fixes are not a system. They are 27 court cases waiting to happen, and every divergence is a seam our adversaries will test. 1.

Will the Commission bring forward a legislative package establishing a single EU legal category and a single border procedure for organised mass storming situations, which is fast, lawful, and applicable at all external borders?
How does the Commission assess the fragmentation risk that divergent national emergency laws pose to the Schengen area and to uniform fundamental rights protection?
What is the Commission’s timetable for closing this legislative gap within the current mandate?

E-10-2026-003262.t: Increasing number of illegal flights by Turkish fighter jets in Nicosia FIR
qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Geadis Geadi (ECR) Subject:

According to recent press reports, there has recently been an increased presence of Turkish F16 fighter jets within the Nicosia Flight Information Region (FIR), particularly in areas near the Green Line1. It should be recalled that in March 2026 Türkiye deployed six F-16 jets in the occupied territories, to which the EU turned a blind eye, displaying a provocatively unacceptable level of tolerance. Increased military aviation activity raises legitimate security and stability concerns in the already tense region of the Middle East, but especially in the Eastern Mediterranean, and particularly as it originates from a candidate country and is directed towards a Member State of the European Union. The Vice-President / High Representative is asked: 1.
Is she aware of the increased number of illegal flights by Turkish fighter jets in the Nicosia FIR and what is her assessment of this development?

For how much longer does the EU intend to tolerate Türkiye’s escalating military provocation against a Member State, without any specific consequences, and how does she justify further deepening EU-Türkiye relations in these circumstances?
What specific measures does she intend to take to safeguard the security of a Member State and prevent actions that undermine regional stability?

E-10-2026-003261.t: The need for a modern European Natural Disaster Response Fund
qt: to the Commission Fredis Beleris (PPE) Subject:

The devastating forest fires experienced by Greece, Cyprus, France and Spain, directly affect citizens’ quality of life and confirm the need for a fully-fledged European response and reconstruction fund. Europe seeks, through the rescEU mechanism, to support Member States that need help with fighting fires but the frequency of the disasters is such that the budget of the EU Solidarity Fund, which provides financial support for infrastructure reconstruction, is unable to provide sufficient funding. Restoring property, infrastructure and forest ecosystems is a necessary condition for protecting the quality of life of European citizens. The European Solidarity Fund needs to evolve into a new European Natural Disaster Response Fund with a guaranteed, independent and sufficient budget in the new MFF 2028-2034, to protect forests and water resources, prevent soil erosion, make infrastructure more resilient and support citizens in the areas affected. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Does it intend to set up a new European Natural Disaster Response Fund with guaranteed funding and common standards and monitoring and evaluation mechanisms?
Does it intend to create a new framework of European assistance to compensate citizens affected by natural disasters?
Does it intend to take steps to introduce a special point-awarding system for local and regional authorities affected by natural disasters when direct funding is given by the European Commission?

E-10-2026-003260.t: EU situational awareness and early warning during the Ceuta crisis
qt: to the Commission Veronika Cifrová Ostrihoňová (Renew), Lucia Yar (Renew), Anna-Maja Henriksson (Renew), Jan-Christoph Oetjen (Renew), Malik Azmani (Renew) Subject:

The EU has significant capabilities for monitoring developments at its external borders through Frontex, the European border surveillance system (EUROSUR), pre-frontier intelligence, risk analysis and open-source and social-media monitoring. Nevertheless, the online and physical mobilisation of migrants to enter Ceuta developed into an unprecedented mass crossing within a short period. 1.
When did the Commission and Frontex first detect indications of online mobilisation, movement towards the border or increasing migratory pressure around Ceuta?
How was this information assessed, when and through which channels was it shared with the Spanish authorities and relevant EU bodies, and what preventive action followed?

Has the Commission conducted an operational review of whether the information was detected, shared and acted upon sufficiently quickly, and what improvements to earlywarning systems, inter-agency information-sharing and social-media monitoring have since been identified or introduced?

E-10-2026-003259.t: Application of the Digital Services Act following the Ceuta crisis
qt: to the Commission Veronika Cifrová Ostrihoňová (Renew), Lucia Yar (Renew), Anna-Maja Henriksson (Renew), Malik Azmani (Renew) Subject:

Public reporting indicates that misleading claims, instructions on how to cross the border and videos of successful arrivals circulated widely on major online platforms before and during the mass arrivals in Ceuta in late July 2026. However, the reach, amplification patterns and possible coordination of this content remain unclear. Articles 34 and 35 of the Digital Services Act1 require very large online platforms (VLOPs) to assess and mitigate systemic risks, including risks to public security. Article 40 provides for mechanisms enabling the Commission and vetted researchers to access platform data, while Article 36 establishes a crisis-response mechanism for extraordinary circumstances that lead to a serious threat to public security. 1.
What action has the Commission taken to secure and examine relevant platform data and facilitate access for vetted researchers?
Has it assessed whether the platforms adequately identified and mitigated the associated systemic risks, and, if so, what were its findings?
Was activation of the Article 36 crisis-response mechanism considered and what measures will the Commission take to improve platform preparedness and accountability during comparable future crises?
Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 of 19 October 2022 on a Single Market For Digital Services and amending Directive 2000/31/EC (Digital Services Act), (ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/2065/oj). 1

E-10-2026-003258.t: Ceuta carnage: the deadly reality of the Pact of suppression, deportation and savage exploitation
qt: to the Commission Kostas Papadakis (NI) Subject:

Following the Melilla massacre, EU governments have now commended the Spanish Government for the latest deadly incident in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, which saw 99 displaced people lose their lives and left dozens missing. This is further proof that the barbarity of the provisions under the awful Pact on Migration and Asylum and the EU’s reactionary migration policy are not managed in a ‘progressive’ way at all. Opening and closing the migration tap to secure cheap labour through transnational slave trade agreements is a common strategy shared by all bourgeois governments. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

Where does it stand on the fact that the Spanish Government proceeded with a crackdown, which left people dead or missing, with immediate mass pushbacks of refugees and migrants, with the full support of EU institutions and governments, without a prior review of asylum claims and without other basic reception procedures being followed, in violation of the Geneva Convention on Refugees?

Where does it stand on Nea Dimokratia’s preposterous proposal to essentially completely abolish the right to asylum, citing yet another ‘emergency’ caused by the mass movement of refugees and migrants, which could in future be classed as a ‘hybrid attack’?

What exactly is involved in the measures it announced to further strengthen the mandate of the repressive mechanisms Frontex and Europol at the borders, given that Schengen already has a system of mass surveillance in place which governments sometimes decide to reinforce with additional border controls, violating the rights of citizens, as well as refugees and migrants?

E-10-2026-003257.t: Animal welfare in Uganda in the context of EU development cooperation
qt: to the Commission Sebastian Everding (The Left), Anja Hazekamp (The Left) Subject:

Recent media reports1 have highlighted cases of alleged deliberate abuse and injury of dogs in Uganda, with videos of their suffering shared on social media to solicit donations. While the alleged perpetrators have reportedly been arrested, concerns have also been raised that some of the confiscated animals have subsequently been euthanised due to insufficient shelter capacity, veterinary care and financial resources. Animal welfare is closely linked to public health, sustainable development, food security and the One Health approach. Article 13 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union recognises animals as sentient beings and requires the EU to pay full regard to animal welfare requirements in the formulation and implementation of its policies. 1.
Is the Commission aware of these reports and has it raised these concerns with the Ugandan authorities?

Does the Commission support, directly or indirectly, projects in Uganda that strengthen animal welfare protection, including through veterinary services, shelter capacity, humane dog population management and the enforcement of animal welfare legislation?

Will the Commission consider further integrating animal welfare into its development cooperation with Uganda, including by strengthening the capacity of the competent authorities and civil society organisations to rescue, rehabilitate and protect animals that are subjected to cruelty?

to the Commission Asger Christensen (Renew) Subject:

The Commission is expected to highlight the importance of supporting the development of plant-based food value chains. Denmark has already introduced a Danish action plan for plant-based food, accompanied by a dedicated plant-based food grant, which supports farmers, businesses and innovation across the value chain. The scheme has proven important in helping farmers diversify their production while stimulating demand and creating markets for European-grown legumes, vegetables and other protein crops. In this context, could the Commission clarify whether it will consider including references in the protein action plan to concrete funding mechanisms that Member States can use to support the development of plant-based food value chains, for example by highlighting successful national initiatives such as the Danish plant-based food grant?

E-10-2026-003253.t: Restrictions on the use of church bells and freedom of religion
qt: to the Commission Marcin Sypniewski (ESN) Subject:

In Poland, noise protection rules also apply to church bells, which are treated in case law as installations capable of causing noise emissions. This may lead to restrictions on the use of bells used directly in connection with religious service and ceremonies. Bells are an integral part of religious practice, as well as being part of the traditional soundscape and cultural heritage of Polish local communities. In many towns and villages, they also serve the long-established function of indicating the time. Directive 2002/49/EC establishes a framework for the assessment and management of environmental noise. When applying EU law, Member States are bound by the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, Article 10 of which protects the freedom to manifest religion. Given the above: 1.

In the Commission’s view, must national legislation and decisions concerning noise, adopted or applied within the scope of EU law, take into account the specific liturgical, cultural and transient nature of the sound of church bells?

Does the Commission consider that applying the same criteria to bells used directly in the context of religious worship as are applied to long-term sources of industrial noise may infringe the principle of proportionality and Article 10 of the Charter?
Does the Commission intend to issue guidelines on taking fundamental rights, including freedom of religion, into account in the national implementation of EU regulations relating to noise?
at: (English version) to the Commission Marcin Sypniewski (ESN) (11 August 2026) Subject: Restrictions on the use of church bells and freedom of religion In Poland, noise protection rules also apply to church bells, which are treated in case law as installations capable of causing noise emissions. This may lead to restrictions on the use of bells used directly in connection with religious service and ceremonies. Bells are an integral part of religious practice, as well as being part of the traditional soundscape and cultural heritage of Polish local communities. In many towns and villages, they also serve the long-established function of indicating the time. Directive 2002/49/EC establishes a framework for the assessment and management of environmental noise. When applying EU law, Member States are bound by the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, Article 10 of which protects the freedom to manifest religion. Given the above: 1.

In the Commission’s view, must national legislation and decisions concerning noise, adopted or applied within the scope of EU law, take into account the specific liturgical, cultural and transient nature of the sound of church bells?

Does the Commission consider that applying the same criteria to bells used directly in the context of religious worship as are applied to long-term sources of industrial noise may infringe the principle of proportionality and Article 10 of the Charter?
Does the Commission intend to issue guidelines on taking fundamental rights, including freedom of religion, into account in the national implementation of EU regulations relating to noise?

(23 September 2026) The Environmental Noise Directive (1) aims to establish a common EU approach to avoid, prevent or reduce the harmful effects of exposure to environmental noise primarily caused by transport traffic, as well as from industrial activities listed in Annex I of the Industrial Emissions Directive (2). Pursuant to its Article 2(2), the directive does not apply to noise that is caused by the exposed person himself, noise from domestic activities, noise created by neighbours, noise at workplaces or noise inside means of transport or due to military activities in military areas. Every five years, Member States are required to establish strategic noise maps and adopt action plans for major roads (3), major railways (4), major airports (5) and large agglomerations (6). These obligations do not concern noise from other sources, such as noise from neighbours, noise from domestic or leisure activities, including noise associated with the church bells, leaving these areas subject to the regulation and protection under the domestic law (taking into account national, regional and local circumstances). The Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union (7) applies to Member States only when they are implementing EU law. As mentioned above, the directive does not apply to noise associated with church bells. In such situation, it is for Member States to ensure that fundamental rights are protected in accordance with their domestic laws and international human rights obligations.

E-10-2026-003252.t: In the EU, 8.3 times more people die from the cold than from heatwaves.
qt: to the Commission Gerald Hauser (PfE) Subject:
In the EU, 8.3 times more people die from the cold than from heatwaves.

In 2024, the European Commission’s Joint Research Centre published data showing that, on average, 363 809 people die each year in Europe as a result of the effects of the cold and around 43 729 people as a result of the effects of heatwaves. There are, therefore, 8.3 times as many cold-related deaths as heat-related ones per year. Cold weather is thus the greatest temperature-related health problem in the EU. Nonetheless, the EU Mission on Adaptation to Climate Change focuses mainly on heat, droughts, heavy rain and floods. There is, however, no specific strand dealing exclusively or primarily with the health effects of cold temperatures. What is more, experts are concerned that the EU’s energy and climate policies, as well as the sanctions against Russia and the war in Iran, could lead to energy shortages in the coming autumn and winter, which could in turn create massive problems for the heating of homes. 1.
What measures will the Commission take to finally reduce the catastrophic number of cold-related deaths?
Why are there no comparable emergency plans to prevent cold-related deaths, as there are for heatwaves?
What measures will the Commission take to prevent a further increase in the number of cold-related deaths in the EU in the face of an impending energy shortage this autumn?

E-10-2026-003251.t: Shortcomings in the application of the Digital Services Act in cases where disinformation goes viral pose a risk to citizens’ safety
qt: to the Commission Ioan-Rareş Bogdan (PPE) Subject:

The viral spread of videos on TikTok containing serious disinformation poses a threat to public order. In recent days, an urban legend about a ‘black ambulance that abducts children’ led to an ambulance crew being attacked in Romania. While very large online platforms are obliged under Articles 34 and 35 of Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 to assess and mitigate systemic risks, current reactive moderation systems are proving slow and unable to stop public panic from spreading within a matter of hours. In view of this lack of effectiveness, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

Does the Commission intend, through practical guidelines or delegated acts, to clarify binding time standards for human moderation and the removal of content inciting violence against essential public services?

Bearing in mind that recommendation algorithms are clearly partly to blame in that they actively amplify disinformation for engagement, what specific measures is the Commission considering to force the temporary shutdown of profiling-based feeds in areas affected by public psychosis?

Is the Commission considering a proposal to revise the regulation in order to stamp out these shortcomings after presenting an assessment of the practical limits of the Digital Services Act in stopping high-speed disinformation?

E-10-2026-003248.t: Contradiction of strengthening the trade partnership with Baku while Armenian hostages and prisoners continue to be detained in Azerbaijan
qt: to the Commission Marina Mesure (The Left) Subject:

On 1 July 2026, Commission President Ursula von der Leyen visited Baku to ‘deepen the EUAzerbaijan partnership’ and boost energy cooperation and investment in the South Caucasus. Shortly thereafter, on 6 August 2026, Azerbaijan’s Court of Appeal ruled that it would uphold the harsh sentences given to Armenian prisoners and hostages in sham trials. This arbitrary detention is in direct contradiction with the position of the European Parliament, which called in its resolution of 13 March 2025 for the 2022 memorandum of understanding in the field of energy to be suspended and insisted that any future partnership agreement with Baku be conditional on the release of Armenian prisoners and hostages. In view of the above: 1.
How does the Commission justify strengthening trade and energy partnerships with Azerbaijan when this approach directly contradicts the position adopted by the European Parliament?
What specific measures will it take to ensure that international law is observed and the Armenian prisoners and hostages are immediately and unconditionally released?
at: (English version) to the Commission Marina Mesure (The Left) (10 August 2026) Subject: Contradiction of strengthening the trade partnership with Baku while Armenian hostages and prisoners continue to be detained in Azerbaijan On 1 July 2026, Commission President Ursula von der Leyen visited Baku to ‘deepen the EU-Azerbaijan partnership’ and boost energy cooperation and investment in the South Caucasus. In view of the above: 1.
How does the Commission justify strengthening trade and energy partnerships with Azerbaijan when this approach directly contradicts the position adopted by the European Parliament?

(17 September 2026) EU engagement with Azerbaijan remains instrumental in promoting peace, stability and prosperity in the South Caucasus through regional cooperation, including in the context of the normalisation process between Armenia and Azerbaijan. Moreover, the EU is committed to phasing out its energy dependency on Russia, including through efforts to diversify the supply of energy imports. Azerbaijan plays an important role in these diversification efforts. The EU has closely followed the trials of Karabakh Armenians in Azerbaijan and has emphasised the importance of ensuring due process, the right to a fair trial and adequate detention conditions, in line with Azerbaijan’s international obligations. The EU has also encouraged Armenia and Azerbaijan to address all outstanding humanitarian issues in the context of their bilateral normalisation process, including through confidence-building measures. Following the initialling of the bilateral peace treaty between Armenia and Azerbaijan on 8 August 2025, the parties have made important progress towards achieving lasting peace. This progress has already resulted in several tangible steps to the benefit of both counties, including the release of detainees and the lifting of trade and transit restrictions. The EU strongly supports this process and remains ready to continue assisting both parties in their efforts.

E-10-2026-003247.t: Criteria for exemptions from extended producer responsibility under the Urban Waste Water Treatment Directive
qt: to the Commission Piotr Müller (ECR) Subject:

Directive (EU) 2024/3019 establishes a system of extended producer responsibility in relation to the costs of removing micropollutants from urban waste water. These new obligations may entail significant costs for cosmetics manufacturers, and the method for determining biodegradability criteria is also particularly important for consumer chemicals sectors, including the detergents industry, which have for years been developing and assessing substances in terms of their behaviour in the environment. Article 9 of the Directive provides for exemptions from the EPR scheme if a producer demonstrates that no micropollutants are generated or that the substance is rapidly biodegradable. Recital 22 requires the Commission to take into account the existing criteria set out in Regulation (EC) 1272/2008, available scientific knowledge and relevant international standards. The implementing criteria should therefore ensure legal certainty and effective opportunities to benefit from the exemptions provided for by the legislator. Given the above: 1.
How will the Commission ensure that the criteria concerning micropollutants and rapid biodegradability fully reflect the requirements of recital 22 of the Directive?
How will the Commission take into account the behaviour of substances in waste water and in the environment when assessing rapid biodegradability?

How will the Commission ensure that the implementing measures do not, in practice, narrow the scope of the exemptions provided for in Article 9, nor introduce additional conditions not derived from the Directive?

E-10-2026-003246.t: Uneven playing field for EU farmers
qt: to the Commission Piotr Müller (ECR) Subject:

The Commission is imposing increasingly costly environmental, climate and animal welfare requirements on EU farmers. At the same time, it is steadily opening up the EU market to imports of agricultural products from third countries whose producers are not subject to comparable standards. Successive trade agreements, including with the Mercosur countries and Australia, as well as trade liberalisation with Ukraine are increasing price pressure on European producers. Given the above: 1.
Why is the Commission continuing to conclude and implement agreements that increase imports of cheaper food produced to lower standards, while increasing the operating costs of EU farmers?

Has the Commission carried out a comprehensive assessment of the impact of imports from Ukraine and of agreements with Mercosur, Australia and other partners on the prices, incomes and competitiveness of EU agricultural producers?

Will the Commission support mandatory mirror clauses in all EU trade agreements, or does it intend to continue to tolerate a situation where an EU farmer adheres to strict standards and then has to compete with imports produced without comparable obligations?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (30.9.2026) Trade agreements (FTAs) are carefully designed to open markets for EU exports, diversify supply chains, strengthen partnerships, and improve food-system resilience. The EU agri-food sector is a strong exporter and has benefited from such agreements. EU farmers apply high standards concerning food safety, animal and plant health, animal welfare, and the environment. All imports placed on the EU market must comply with the relevant EU rules, especially sanitary and phytosanitary requirements – with no exception made to FTA partners. Sensitive sectors are protected via the use of tariff-rate quotas, transition periods, safeguards, or other protections. The Commission regularly carries out impact assessments on trade and agriculture1. It also monitors markets closely. In the case of Ukraine, it has paid particular attention to impacts on neighbouring Member States and sensitive sectors. As regards the Mercosur and Australia free trade agreements, assessments, stakeholders’ inputs and Member States’ consultations have informed decisions, with special attention to sensitive farm products. The Vision for Agriculture and Food2 focuses on the global level playing field. The Commission engages globally to promote higher standards, and under the Union domestic framework, the Commission will pursue, in line with international rules, a stronger alignment of production standards applied to imported products, notably on pesticides and animal welfare.
1 https://policy.trade.ec.europa.eu/analysis-and-assessment/impact-assessments_en. 2 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:52025DC0075.

E-10-2026-003245.t: Putting an end to AdBlue-related fire engine breakdowns
qt: to the Commission Mathilde Androuët (PfE), Pierre Pimpie (PfE), France Jamet (PfE), Valérie Deloge (PfE), Laurent Castillo (PfE), Aleksandar Nikolic (PfE), Gilles Pennelle (PfE), Fabrice Leggeri (PfE), Julien Leonardelli (PfE), Catherine Griset (PfE), Marie Dauchy (PfE), Marie-Luce Brasier-Clain (PfE), Mélanie Disdier (PfE), André Rougé (PfE) Subject:

Due to the EU emission standards for heavy-duty vehicles, many fire engines are using selective catalytic reduction systems that operate using AdBlue. Several French departmental fire and rescue services have reported that their vehicles have lost power, broken down or been unable to restart, with the cause being connected to those systems. Such breakdowns can occur while they are responding to emergencies, including forest fires, directly compromising the effectiveness of emergency operations and the safety of firefighters and communities. Since the purpose of emergency vehicles is to save lives, it is unacceptable that constraints resulting from EU regulations can slow down or prevent their emergency response. 1.

Does the Commission intend to propose an explicit exemption for fire and rescue service vehicles, so that, when they are responding to an emergency, they cannot ever be slowed down, immobilised or prevented from restarting because of AdBlue?
Does it intend to exempt fire engines in general from such pollution control constraints when those constraints compromise the fire engines’ ability to respond to emergencies?

E-10-2026-003244.t: Interpretation of Directive (EU) 2023/970 on pay transparency, especially Article 4 and the concept of equal value
qt: to the Commission Kira Marie Peter-Hansen (Verts/ALE) Subject:
In the light of relevant case-law, and recitals 16 and 20-29 and Articles 4 and 19 of Directive (EU) 2023/9701, how would the Commission interpret the directive as regards the following: 1.

Two jobs or positions at the same employer have been assessed as being of equal value under the directive. The two jobs or positions are different in nature and require different levels of education. Should the two be placed in the same category according to the directive?

Where two jobs at the same employer are deemed work of equal value, is it required that those jobs can be compared for the purposes of ensuring equal pay, irrespective of whether they belong to different job categories or are covered by different collective agreements?

Would it be appropriate to interpret ‘work of equal value’ as meaning that comparisons may be made only between workers in the same job or group of jobs established by a collective agreement, thereby excluding comparisons across different jobs or groups of jobs, even where the work may be of equal value?
