E-10-2026-003241.t: Keeping a check on property purchases made by non-EU countries in cross-border areas
qt: to the Commission Georgios Aftias (PPE) Subject:

The aggressive purchase of land and real estate through the massive inflow of capital from non-EU countries, has intensified in recent years according to news reports and accounts given by residents in many EU Member States. The phenomenon is particularly noticeable in cross-border areas of major economic and national importance. The European Commission should strengthen transparency mechanisms for tracing the source of the money and the ownership purpose and structure. It should also investigate the corporate structure, especially where there are shell companies facilitating tax evasion or where there are other economic activities involved. Lastly, in areas of strategic importance, sales should be subject to stricter controls and approval by the competent authorities of each state when national issues arise. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Will it allow for strict controls in Member States, especially in cross-border areas?
Will it check the type of investment and the source of the money?
Will it check the feasibility of setting up a company?

E-10-2026-003238.t: Safety, European Union Aviation Safety Agency certification and industrial sovereignty in EU-funded aerial firefighting capabilities
qt: to the Commission Grégory Allione (Renew) Subject:

Recently, Sikorsky UH-60 Black Hawk firefighting helicopters were deployed under the rescEU mechanism to fight a fire in the Drôme department of France. However, those helicopters are US-designed military aircraft and are not covered by the civil certification scheme of the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA), which applies to comparable European aircraft. This raises questions about the consistency of EU requirements for aviation safety and fair competition. In its reply of 25 June 2026 to a previous parliamentary communication, the Commission itself pointed out that the lack of harmonisation of aircraft certification rules could lead to operational difficulties, restrictions on cross-border operations and fragmentation of the EU market. EASA certification ensures a high level of safety, continued airworthiness, operational interoperability and maintenance, while also creating a level playing field between EU manufacturers and non-EU suppliers. In light of the above: 1.
What specific initiatives does the Commission intend to implement to encourage Member States to make use of the mechanism provided for in Article 2(6) of Regulation (EU) 2018/1139?
What steps does it intend to take to strengthen the European industrial base and reduce the EU’s dependence on aerial capabilities from outside the EU to fight forest fires?

E-10-2026-003237.t: Transparency of claims managed by credit management companies and protection of borrowers
qt: to the Commission Maria Zacharia (NI) Subject:

Directive (EU) 2021/2167 requires credit purchasers and servicers to act in good faith, fairly and professionally and to provide borrowers with clear, non-misleading and specific information on the amounts owed. For the effective verification of a claim, it is crucial to be able to ascertain how it is structured, in particular as regards the capital, interest and other charges, and whether all payments made to the original creditor before the transfer have been taken into account. Accuracy and verifiability of data are particularly important when the claim is the basis for enforcement measures. The Commission is asked: 1.

Is it sufficient, under Article 10 of Directive (EU) 2021/2167, to disclose the total amount and its breakdown into capital, interest, fees and other charges, or must the information and calculations allowing full verification of the claim, including the full history of payments taken into account, be provided upon request?

Is it consistent with the obligations of good faith and fair dealing and transparency under Article 10 for a credit purchaser or servicer to continue with collection or enforcement actions where the borrower has requested but has not received the information necessary to verify the amount claimed?
If the directive does not guarantee a full right of verification before enforcement measures, does the Commission intend to propose its introduction?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (15.9.2026) Directive (EU) 2021/21671 (the Non-Performing Loans Directive (NPLD)) is a minimum harmonisation directive. The NPLD does not expressly entitle a borrower to obtain a complete payment history from the credit servicer/purchaser. It nevertheless requires the provision of certain information2 concerning the amounts due by the borrower, detailing what is due as capital, interests, fees and other permitted charges and a receipt or a letter of discharge for each payment received by a credit servicer3. Additional requirements may be set out under national legislation transposing the NPLD. The NPLD sets out requirements on how credit servicers/purchasers should act in their dealings with borrowers but does not provide for any automatic suspension of collection or enforcement of claims in the case of non-compliance. The responsibility for the assessment of the credit servicer/purchaser’s conduct against the requirements of good faith, fairness, professional diligence and transparency rests with national competent authorities. Under Articles 30 and 31 of the NPLD, the Commission is required to evaluate the functioning of the Directive and, where appropriate, consider whether further measures may be needed, including concerning communications with borrowers.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2021/2167/oj. 2 Article 10(2)(g) of Directive (EU) 2021/2167. 3 Article 6(2)(d) of Directive (EU) 2021/2167.

E-10-2026-003236.t: Transitional application of Article 45(3) of the Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation to small businesses
qt: to the Commission Ivaylo Valchev (ECR) Subject:
Transitional application of Article 45(3) of the Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation to small businesses

From 12 August 2026, Article 45(3) of Regulation (EU) 2025/40 will require producers established in the EU who sell directly to end-users in another Member State to appoint an authorised representative for extended producer responsibility in that Member State. Fixed costs and administrative burdens may prove disproportionate for craftspeople and micro-producers who sell small quantities abroad, including through online platforms. This will apply even when they are registered with the relevant national schemes and comply with obligations to report and pay contributions. COM(2025) 982 proposes that the application of this provision be suspended, but only from the date on which the amending regulation enters into force. If it is adopted after 12 August, businesses may be forced to hire representatives temporarily, only to terminate their contracts shortly afterwards. 1.
How does the Commission intend to prevent the provisional application of this requirement and the resulting unnecessary costs?
Would it support the suspension of the measure, with effect from 12 August 2026, at least for micro and small enterprises established in the EU?

Until the amendment enters into force, will the Commission coordinate with the Member States to ensure a proportionate and consistent approach to enforcement, without prejudice to other obligations arising from extended producer responsibility?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (25.9.2026) To minimise administrative burdens and costs for small businesses, the Commission proposed, in December 2025, in its Environmental Omnibus1, to suspend the obligation for producers to appoint an authorised representative when they sell packaged products directly to consumers in Member States other than the one where they are located. The Commission has repeatedly called upon the European Parliament and the Council to adopt the proposal as quickly as possible and stands ready to work on it as a matter of urgency. In the meantime, the Commission has invited Member States to take a constructive and pragmatic approach and to avoid disproportionate enforcement. To support an easy and smooth transition to the new rules, the Commission is working closely with stakeholders and Member States to ensure a practical implementation. As part of the Circular Economy Act2, the Commission is assessing a broader reform of extended producer responsibility schemes, focusing on simplification, harmonisation and digitalisation.
1 https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_25_2997. 2 https://environment.ec.europa.eu/strategy/circular-economy_en.

E-10-2026-003235.t: Unpublished emergency plans for military bases
qt: to the Commission Cristina Guarda (Verts/ALE) Subject:

Military use of nuclear technologies falls outside the competences of the Euratom Treaty; however, standards for preparedness for radiological emergencies are laid down in the Euratom Directive (up-to-date plans and information for the public1) and in Directive 2003/4/EC (mandatory active dissemination of information on environmental and health risks2). A number of EU Member States have military bases equipped with NATO nuclear weapons, but the Upper Adriatic has as many as four sensitive sites (Aviano3, Ghedi and the ports of Trieste in Italy and Koper in Slovenia, through which nuclear-powered vessels pass) where the emergency plans – although in place – are not up to date and have not been published, nor is safety information disclosed to the public, as required by the directives. In the light of the above: 1.
Does the Commission consider the provisions on health protection and environmental monitoring also applicable in areas adjacent to infrastructure with nuclear weapons or delivery systems?
What is its assessment of the implementation of the obligation to provide information and ensure transparency vis-à-vis the local population?
What action will it push for to ascertain that the plans protect public health and the environment?

E-10-2026-003234.t: Preventing the abuse of INTERPOL channels for transnational financial repression under the EU-INTERPOL agreement
qt: to the Commission Davor Ivo Stier (PPE), Karlo Ressler (PPE) Subject:

The Commission is negotiating an EU-INTERPOL cooperation agreement. Parliament’s 5 July 2022 recommendation requested purpose limitation, transfer limits, independent oversight and judicial redress. Parliament’s resolution of 16 June 20261 and the 8 July 2026 Hague resolution of the OSCE Parliamentary Assembly2 warn that sanctioned states weaponise INTERPOL notices, together with asset freezes, against those states’ critics in exile. Comprehensive sanctions do not prevent a state from accessing INTERPOL and other interstate channels. The Assembly identified a Russian method to extract funding abroad for its war economy: structures acting for the state, reportedly including Alfa-Bank, combined INTERPOL notices and civil claims with asset freezes in order to bring about the takeover of Baltic Bank and the detention of Andrei Isaev in France in 2020 on an INTERPOL request, whose claims European courts executed even after Alfa-Bank was sanctioned in 2022. 1.
How will the Commission give binding effect to the 5 July 2022 safeguards, and will it require an additional review of requests from sanctioned states such as Russia, or their proxies?
Will it apply the source-based approach under Regulation (EU) 2024/31923 to refuse, by default, cooperation on the basis of requests from states systematically engaged in transnational repression?
Will it create an EU-level appeal mechanism against abusive notices, publish notice statistics by issuing state, and guarantee redress, including banking access?

E-10-2026-003233.t: Public interest in Galicia in accessing documents in the infringement procedure concerning the AP-9 motorway
qt: to the Commission Ana Miranda Paz (Verts/ALE) Subject:

In July 2025, the Commission issued a reasoned opinion in infringement procedure INFR(2021)4052, requesting Spain to comply with EU rules on public procurement, including concession contracts. The Spanish Government had extended the duration of the concession for the AP-9 motorway by 25 years and sold it without initiating a tendering procedure. According to Directive 2014/24/EU and the principles of equal treatment and transparency underlying EU public procurement rules, such an extension constitutes a substantial modification equivalent to the award of a new concession and requires a competitive tendering procedure. Spain had two months to respond and rectify the situation. However, it has not carried out a competitive tendering procedure, has rejected the Commission’s position and has refused to comply with the reasoned opinion. The Supreme Court has now requested the Commission to clarify whether access to the reasoned opinion is legally permissible. This raises questions regarding transparency and access to the documents exchanged between the Commission and Spain during the procedure. 1.

Can the Commission provide access to the response submitted by the Spanish Government to the reasoned opinion, in particular the document in which it rejected or declined to comply with the Commission’s request?
What is the current status of the infringement procedure and what further steps does the Commission intend to take in response to Spain’s refusal to comply with the reasoned opinion?
at: (English version) to the Commission Ana Miranda Paz (Verts/ALE) (8 August 2026) Subject: Public interest in Galicia in accessing documents in the infringement procedure concerning the AP-9 motorway In July 2025, the Commission issued a reasoned opinion in infringement procedure INFR(2021)4052, requesting Spain to comply with EU rules on public procurement, including concession contracts. (16 September 2026) As indicated in the reply to Written Question E-003666/2025 (1) raised by the Honourable Member, the Commission is bound to maintain the confidentiality of the content of an ongoing infringement procedure and cannot share details about it, with a view to attaining an appropriate solution. This obligation applies to all the documents in an ongoing infringement procedure, including the replies from the Member State concerned. Taking into account this obligation and based on the objective of protecting the purpose of the investigation under Regulation 1049/2001/EC (2), the Commission has refused granting public access to the documents pertaining to infringement procedure INFR(2021)4052 (3) following several requests lodged under that regulation. To date, the Commission has not received any request from the Supreme Court regarding infringement procedure INFR(2021)4052. A request from a judicial authority of a Member State to gain privileged access, as opposed to public access, to documents held by the EU institutions is in principle to be treated pursuant to the principle of sincere cooperation laid down in Article 4(3) of the Treaty on European Union (4).

E-10-2026-003232.t: The ‘nuclear doctrine’ being formed in the EU at great danger to the people
qt: to the Commission Kostas Papadakis (NI) Subject:

81 years after the crime of atomic bombs being dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki by the USA, the people are closer than ever to the possibility of a new nuclear catastrophe. This is evidenced by the intensive preparation of all imperialist powers in an environment of escalating antagonism between them and the fronts in Ukraine/the Middle East heading towards merger, as threats of the use of nuclear weapons are intensifying amid the collapse of the New Start agreement between the USA and Russia. The EU is advancing the process of launching armaments and the goal of so-called ‘strategic autonomy’. At the last NATO summit, it was decided to ‘adjust’ nuclear policy, with the deployment of nuclear warheads in European countries. At the same time, EU plans to form a ‘European nuclear pillar’, increase the nuclear arsenal, create a nuclear infrastructure in Member States and for joint exercises and enhanced nuclear planning are progressing, beyond the alreadyinstalled American nuclear plants in a number of Member States (Germany, the Netherlands, Belgium, Italy, etc.). What is the Commission's position on the fact that, 81 years after the crime of nuclear bombs being dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, the risk to the people is increasing with the escalation of the imperialist war and the ever stronger possibility of the use of nuclear weapons being more visible than ever, based on the nuclear doctrine being shaped by the EU as well as the involvement of Member States both in individual nuclear plans between states and within the framework of NATO?
at: (English version) to the Commission Kostas Papadakis (NI) (8 August 2026) Subject: The ‘nuclear doctrine’ being formed in the EU at great danger to the people 81 years after the crime of atomic bombs being dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki by the USA, the people are closer than ever to the possibility of a new nuclear catastrophe. This is evidenced by the intensive preparation of all imperialist powers in an environment of escalating antagonism between them and the fronts in Ukraine/the Middle East heading towards merger, as threats of the use of nuclear weapons are intensifying amid the collapse of the New Start agreement between the USA and Russia. The EU is advancing the process of launching armaments and the goal of so-called ‘strategic autonomy’. At the last NATO summit, it was decided to ‘adjust’ nuclear policy, with the deployment of nuclear warheads in European countries. At the same time, EU plans to form a ‘European nuclear pillar’, increase the nuclear arsenal, create a nuclear infrastructure in Member States and for joint exercises and enhanced nuclear planning are progressing, beyond the alreadyinstalled American nuclear plants in a number of Member States (Germany, the Netherlands, Belgium, Italy, etc.). What is the Commission's position on the fact that, 81 years after the crime of nuclear bombs being dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, the risk to the people is increasing with the escalation of the imperialist war and the ever stronger possibility of the use of nuclear weapons being more visible than ever, based on the nuclear doctrine being shaped by the EU as well as the involvement of Member States both in individual nuclear plans between states and within the framework of NATO? (2 October 2026) Since the adoption of its Strategy against the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction in 2003, the EU has been actively promoting and supporting relevant international non-proliferation and disarmament instruments regarding such weapons — be they nuclear, chemical or biological. The Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (1)(NPT), in force since 1970, is the cornerstone of the global nuclear non-proliferation regime, the essential foundation for the pursuit of nuclear disarmament according to its Article 6, and an important element in developing nuclear energy applications for peaceful purposes. The EU strongly supports the balanced and full implementation of all provisions of the NPT, including its Article 6 whereby states parties undertake ‘to pursue negotiations in good faith on effective measures relating to cessation of the nuclear arms race at an early date and to nuclear disarmament’. The EU shares the ultimate goal of total elimination of nuclear weapons, and actively promotes initiatives consistent with this goal, such as the immediate commencement and early conclusion of negotiations of a treaty banning the production of fissile material for use in nuclear weapons or other nuclear explosive devices and the promotion of universal adherence to and the entry into force of the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty. There is an ongoing debate among NATO allies and some Member States about the European dimension of nuclear deterrence, around proposals for new arrangements on a bilateral basis. The EU does not have a nuclear deterrence policy. Under Common Foreign Security Policy/Common Security and Defence Policy, the development of such a policy would require unanimity among Member States.

E-10-2026-003230.t: Transparency and control of European funding for Turkish Cypriots
qt: to the Commission Geadis Geadi (ECR) Subject:

Significant European Union funds are allocated to support Turkish Cypriots, under Council Regulation (EC) No 389/2006. Given the need for full transparency, sound financial management and effective control of the use of European funds, can the Commission say: 1.
What is the total amount of funds allocated to Turkish Cypriots since 2006?
Who are the final beneficiaries of this funding?

How does the Commission ensure that this funding does not result, directly or indirectly, in the strengthening or consolidation of the illegal structures of the occupation regime in the illegally Turkish-occupied territories of the Republic of Cyprus and which bodies are accountable for compliance with the relevant controls?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (25.9.2026) Since 2006, the EU has allocated EUR 794.6 million to the aid programme for the Turkish Cypriot community under Council Regulation (EC) No 389/2006 (‘Aid Regulation’)1. The objective of the Aid Regulation is to facilitate the reunification of Cyprus by promoting the socio-economic development of the Turkish Cypriot community; supporting infrastructure development; fostering reconciliation and confidence-building measures, strengthening civil society; improving contacts between the two communities and with the EU; and preparing for the implementation of the acquis upon a final settlement of the Cyprus issue. Ultimately, the programme benefits all Cypriots, who stand to gain from the reunification of their country. The Commission does not conclude any contracts with representatives of the non-recognised Turkish Cypriot entity. Under the Aid Regulation, the granting and implementation of assistance shall not imply recognition of any public authority in Cyprus other than the Government of the Republic of Cyprus. The Commission implements the assistance through direct and indirect management in compliance with the EU Financial Regulation2, thus ensuring protection of the financial interests of the EU. The relevant contracts provide for audit rights for the Commission and the European Court of Auditors, including document-based and on the spot checks, over contractors and subcontractors who have received EU funds. The programme is also subject to external evaluations, close monitoring on the ground, and budgetary scrutiny by the European Parliament.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2006/389/oj/eng. 2 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/2509/oj/eng.

E-10-2026-003229.t: Securing a status for agricultural workers
qt: to the Commission Arash Saeidi (The Left) Subject:

On 29 April 2026, Eurostat published a report on the performance of the agricultural sector, which stated that, in the EU, the sector comprises 7.4 million full-time equivalent workers. Of those, non-salaried workers – farm managers and their families – amount to 5 million. Behind the figures lie realities. Family workers are primarily women, the farm managers’ wives. Their work is often unsalaried, which means they have no social rights, including those relating to unemployment and pensions. Salaried labour, on the other hand, is largely provided by seasonal workers who, by definition, face a very high level of job insecurity. In light of this: 1.
Does the Commission intend to impose social clauses in quality labels and contractual conditions?
Does the Commission intend to create an intermittent agricultural worker status enabling such workers to continue to receive wages out of season?
Does the Commission intend to take steps to ensure that non-salaried labour performed by farm managers’ families is recognised?

E-10-2026-003228.t: Repeated recycling plant and landfill fires and dangerous exposure to toxic carcinogens
qt: to the Commission Lefteris Nikolaou-Alavanos (NI) Subject:

The third fire in a recycling plant in a year broke out in Thessaloniki, while the fire that started in the landfill on Paros was devastating. This unacceptable situation is a direct consequence of EU policy, which serves the profitability of business groups that make a fortune from waste. In view of the above: 1.

What is the Commission’s position on the fact that destructive fires are constantly breaking out in landfills, as well as yet another in a recycling plant, given that the necessary protective measures to prevent fires or other natural disasters, with the necessary personnel and infrastructure, are not being observed, while these plants operate near residential areas, creating additional risks of pollution and contamination?

What is the Commission’s position on the fact that there is an urgent need to fund epidemiological studies and imaging tests on the population for cancers, respiratory and other diseases, so that there is a thorough investigation of the consequences on the health and life of the residents of the areas adjacent to these units, as well as in the wider region?

What is the Commission’s position on the fact that the ‘green’ declarations of the EU, such as Directive (EU) 2024/2881 and Directive 2006/118/EC, and those of governments, are proven not to be aimed at protecting the environment, but on the contrary legitimise this unacceptable situation, as, among other things, no substantive measures are being taken and there is no established mechanism for the immediate restoration of polluted land in order to avoid contamination of the aquifer, the groundwater of the area and the air?

E-10-2026-003226.t: Discrimination against migrant children in care in Aragon and compatibility with EU law
qt: to the Commission Isabel Serra Sánchez (The Left) Subject:

The Government of Aragon has announced that it is axing the weekly EUR 17 allowance for unaccompanied foreign minors, while continuing to pay the sum to all other minors in care. The allowance forms part of the socio-educational projects of state-contracted centres and government-funded services. This difference in treatment based on the child’s origin or status as a foreign minor is incompatible with Article 2 of the Treaty on European Union and Articles 1, 21 and 24 of the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights. For minors in the international protection system, the measure may affect compliance with Directive (EU) 2024/1346 on reception conditions. In view of the above: 1.
Does it think that it is compatible with EU law for only foreign minors in care to be excluded from a benefit that is part of the socio-educational project of a public protection service?

Does it intend to collect information from the Spanish authorities and verify whether the centres are in receipt of EU funding, in particular from the Asylum, Migration and Integration Fund, and assess the measure in accordance with Directive (EU) 2024/1346?
What action can it take to guarantee fundamental rights, non-discrimination and the best interests of the child in the face of minors in care being treated differently based on their origin?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (2.10.2026) Under the Reception Conditions Directive1, all asylum-seekers, including unaccompanied minors, are entitled to receive material reception conditions, including a daily expenses allowance, which should allow them to enjoy a minimum degree of autonomy. Based on a case-by-case assessment, Member States may only reduce or withdraw material reception conditions – including the daily expenses allowance – in specified situations, including for example in cases of absconding, not complying with procedural obligations, or failure to take part in integration activities2, after having taken an individual decision for each beneficiary. For unaccompanied minors, such sanctions should be applied taking into account the best interests of the child. In addition, Member States may grant less favourable treatment to applicants compared with nationals when providing material reception conditions in the form of financial allowances or vouchers3. These EU rules are relevant only for asylum-seekers. However, very few migrant unaccompanied minors arriving to Spain apply for protection4. The Commission does not hold information as to whether the children concerned by the Honourable Member’s inquiry are asylum-seekers, or as to whether Asylum and Migration and Integration Fund (‘AMIF’) funding has been or is being disbursed to child protection facilities in Aragon. This information could be requested from the competent Spanish authorities. The Commission monitors compliance with EU legislation, and it can take action where there is consistent evidence of systematic breach of the EU rules, be it by the administrative practice or concerning the transposition of EU law, while ensuring that all measures falling under EU competence comply with the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights.
1 Directive (EU) 2024/1346 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 May 2024 laying down

standards for the reception of applicants for international protection, OJ L, 2024/1346, 22.5.2024. See in particular Recital 8 and Articles 2(7), 2(8) and 19 thereof. 2 See Article 23 of the abovementioned Directive. 3 See Art. 19(7) of the same Directive. 4 This occurs for a variety of reasons that are beyond the scope of this exchange. See e.g. https://asylumineurope.org/reports/country/spain/asylum-procedure/guarantees-vulnerable-groups/legalrepresentation-unaccompanied-children/.

E-10-2026-003225.t: Use of RRF-supported clean vehicles in Lithuania
qt: to the Commission Virginijus Sinkevičius (Verts/ALE) Subject:

Lithuania has introduced support schemes funded by the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF) for the acquisition of clean and low-emission commercial vehicles in categories N2, N3, M2 and M3. The relevant RRF target requires supported vehicles to be purchased and registered in Lithuania. However, Lithuania’s national financing conditions additionally require these vehicles to be used only for domestic transport operations. This domestic-use-only condition may prevent Lithuanian operators from using cleaner vehicles for cross-border freight or passenger transport, including transport linked to Lithuanian export and import flows within the single market. Considering the above: 1.

Does the Commission consider that a national requirement limiting the use of EUsupported clean and low-emission vehicles exclusively to domestic transport operations is compatible with EU law, in particular the freedom to provide cross-border transport services and the principles of the internal market?
Does the Commission consider such an absolute territorial restriction proportionate to the environmental objectives of the scheme?

Will the Commission assess whether Lithuania should amend or clarify this condition to allow supported vehicles to be used for cross-border operations while remaining registered in Lithuania and contributing to the scheme’s climate objectives?

E-10-2026-003224.t: Protection of the Holy Monastery of St. Catherine on Mount Sinai and respect for the rule of law in EU-Egypt relations
qt: to the Commission Emmanouil Fragkos (ECR) Subject:

The Holy Monastery of St. Catherine on Mount Sinai, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, appears to be facing a series of judicial and administrative developments that raise concerns regarding its legal personality, the recognition of its canonical ecclesiastical leadership, its effective judicial representation and the protection of its historic property rights. These issues do not only concern a property dispute, but may be linked to respect for the rule of law, religious freedom and international law. Given that the EU is deepening its strategic partnership with Egypt and providing significant financial support, while the Treaties require its external action to be based on respect for human rights and the rule of law: 1.
Did the Commission take the above developments into account in its recent assessment of Egypt for EU funding?
What actions does the Commission intend to take to ensure respect for the religious freedom, institutional autonomy and property rights of the Monastery?
Does the Commission intend to examine whether these developments affect Egypt's compliance with the commitments arising from the strategic partnership with the European Union?

E-10-2026-003223.t: Equal access of rural areas to natural disaster prevention measures
qt: to the Commission Emmanouil Fragkos (ECR) Subject:

The Agricultural Cooperative of Pangaio points out that, despite the large concentration of perennial and tree crops, the area of Pangaio has not been included in the aerial anti-hail protection programme. The area is an important export centre for produce such as table grapes, kiwis, olives and almonds, which contribute substantially to the agricultural economy of Eastern Macedonia and to Greek agricultural exports. Producers report that the absence of preventive measures increases their exposure to risks associated with the increasingly frequent occurrence of extreme weather events. The repeated hailstorms that have been recorded in recent years in various regions of Greece have caused extensive damage to tree crops and vineyards, highlighting the need to strengthen preventive measures. At the same time, other Member States are implementing broader risk prevention and management systems, through national or co-financed EU programmes. The EU, through the CAP and in particular Regulation (EU) 2021/2115, encourages investments that contribute to risk prevention and to strengthening the resilience of agricultural holdings. The Commission is asked: 1.
Has the Commission assessed whether prevention investments receive sufficient support under the national CAP strategic plans?
Does the Commission intend to further strengthen European support for prevention measures, given that the cost of repairing damage from extreme weather events is constantly on the rise in the EU?

E-10-2026-003222.t: Protection of the PGI ‘Kato Nevrokopi Potato’ from misleading practices in the market and strengthening traceability
qt: to the Commission Emmanouil Fragkos (ECR) Subject:

Potato cultivation is a key pillar of the economy of the Kato Nevrokopi basin and the main source of income for hundreds of family farms in the border area. The name ‘Kato Nevrokopi Potato’ is registered as a Protected Geographical Indication (PGI), recognising the special quality characteristics and the link of the product with its place of production. However, according to complaints from producers and cooperatives, the availability of imported potatoes or those originating from other regions with unclear or misleading indications of origin makes it difficult to distinguish the authentic product, squeezes producer prices and undermines the added value of the PGI. Regulation (EU) 2024/1143 strengthens the protection of geographical indications by providing for official controls and obliging the competent authorities to prevent and stop illegal or misleading uses of protected names. Accordingly: 1.

Does the Commission intend, in cooperation with the Greek authorities, to strengthen official controls on the marketing of fresh potatoes in order more effectively to prevent any abusive or misleading use of the name ‘Kato Nevrokopi Potato’?
Is the Commission considering measures to further strengthen the traceability of fresh agricultural products, so that the country and region of production can be directly verified?
Can digital traceability and PGI promotional activity be financed through the CAP or other EU programmes for the benefit of local producers?

E-10-2026-003221.t: Ensuring the continued operation of the MERE chain in Greece and protecting employees, suppliers and consumers
qt: to the Commission Emmanouil Fragkos (ECR) Subject:

The recent suspension of the operation of the MERE chain outlets in Greece, as a consequence of the imposition of restrictive measures against the group's main shareholder, has left approximately 170 employees out of work, created serious uncertainty for hundreds of Greek suppliers and deprived thousands of consumers of access to a chain with particularly competitive prices. MERE had developed a low-cost retail model, offering particularly competitive prices in a period of increased cost of living, which makes the effects of its suspension of operations all the more intense for consumers. According to publicly available information, the suspension is not related to any problem with the Greek company but to the effects of sanctions on its corporate control.1 The EU has repeatedly stated that sanctions must be targeted and avoid disproportionate collateral consequences for innocent workers, businesses and citizens. Can the Commission answer the following: 1.
What legal corporate or administrative actions could allow MERE’s swift reopening in Greece, without violating the current sanctions regime?

Does the Commission intend to provide guidance or other assistance to the Greek authorities and the company, in order to protect jobs, supplier contracts and the smooth functioning of the market, until the company reopens?
Does the Commission envisage, since the impact of the sanctions provided for is against Greek society, expedited screening procedures?

E-10-2026-003220.t: Radical Islamism: threat to the LGBT+ community and the need to protect public safety in the EU
qt: to the Commission Susanna Ceccardi (PfE), Silvia Sardone (PfE), Anna Maria Cisint (PfE), Raffaele Stancanelli (PfE), Paolo Borchia (PfE), Aldo Patriciello (PfE) Subject:

The Berlin Pride attack of July 2026, which German authorities believe may be ascribable to Islamic extremism, has once again shed light on the growing threat posed by radical Islam to LGBT+ people and the fundamental values of the EU1. Reports suggest that the prime suspect was already known to the authorities owing to a history of involvement with Islamic extremism and his attempts to join Islamic State. While the Commission is launching a slew of strategies, campaigns and funding initiatives to promote LGBT+ rights, it seems curiously loathe to acknowledge that one of the main threats to the safety of LGBT+ people is radical Islamism, an issue generally broached with reluctance lest one be accused of ‘Islamophobia’. This attitude risks undermining the credibility of the EU’s efforts to protect fundamental rights. Given the above: 1.
Would the Commission agree that Islamic extremism is one of the main threats to the safety of LGBT+ people in the EU?

Does the Commission deem it necessary to monitor and even suspend EU funding for multicultural associations that tolerate or espouse values at odds with the fundamental rights enshrined in the treaties?

Does the Commission have any data available on the number of incidents of violence, threats or incitement to hatred against LGBT+ people which may be put down to Islamic extremism? If not, will it take steps to systematically collect this information?

E-10-2026-003219.t: Failure of the EU’s policy towards the authoritarian regime in Morocco
qt: to the Commission Stanisław Tyszka (ESN) Subject:
Failure of the EU’s policy towards the authoritarian regime in Morocco

The EU has made Morocco the guardian of its external border. As part of this policy, it disbursed EUR 234 million from the EUTF between 2015 and 2021 and allocated approximately EUR 193 million from the regional migration envelope between 2021 and 2023. In January 2026, Kaja Kallas and the Moroccan Minister of Foreign Affairs Nasser Bourita described the relationship as a ‘privileged strategic partnership’ and confirmed that Morocco remains the main recipient of EU funding in North Africa. Between 30 and 31 July, over 50 000 people crossed from Morocco into Ceuta. Regardless of whether Rabat lost control of the border or deliberately failed to protect it, the crisis demonstrated the ineffectiveness of the EU-funded model. 1.

Will the Commission immediately suspend all outstanding funds for migration cooperation with Morocco, and if not, why should European taxpayers continue to fund a policy that has failed to ensure the protection of the EU’s border?

Will the Commission introduce a rule whereby the effective prevention of irregular migration and the readmission of migrants will be a condition for the disbursement of funds and the granting of other benefits to Morocco, and failure to fulfil these obligations will result in their automatic suspension?

E-10-2026-003218.t: Loss of control over the border in Ceuta and Spain’s exclusion from the Schengen area
qt: to the Commission Stanisław Tyszka (ESN) Subject:
Loss of control over the border in Ceuta and Spain’s exclusion from the Schengen area

According to the Spanish Ministry of the Interior, 72 000 migrants crossed into Ceuta from Morocco from 30 to 31 July 2026. This unprecedented border breach has laid bare the consequences of the policies pursued by the Sánchez government, which has just carried out the mass regularisation of illegal migrants’ residence status, strengthening the pull factor. Italy has reinstated checks on people arriving from Spain by air and sea, whilst France has stepped up controls at the Spanish border. A letter from 22 EU leaders, spearheaded by Italy and Denmark in the wake of the crisis and calling for the removal of factors encouraging illegal migration, demonstrates a loss of confidence in Spain’s policies and its ability to protect the Schengen area. Articles 13 and 15 of the Schengen Borders Code call for effective border surveillance and the deployment of adequate staff and resources. 1.

Will the Commission immediately call on the Council, pursuant to Article 29 of the Schengen Borders Code, to reinstate border controls with Spain, which would de facto exclude it from the Schengen Area until an EU inspection confirms that Spain has permanently secured the border and prevented such a crisis from recurring?
Will the Commission guarantee that no migrant will be admitted to the mainland Schengen area without their identity having been established and them having undergone security checks?

What mandatory corrective measures will the Commission propose to the Council to prevent such a crisis from recurring, and what consequences will the Sánchez government face if it fails once again to protect the border?

E-10-2026-003217.t: Protection of Daniel Arcuri Rivas after confirmation of his custody while the criminal trial for alleged ill-treatment continues
qt: to the Commission Irene Montero (The Left), Isabel Serra Sánchez (The Left) Subject:

The Italian Court of Cassation has confirmed that custody of Daniel is to be granted to Francesco Arcuri, convicted in Spain of violence against the child’s mother, Juana Rivas. The decision comes while the criminal trial against Arcuri for alleged physical and psychological ill-treatment of Daniel and his brother continues in Italy. Daniel is thus in the custody of someone who is being tried for allegedly mistreating him. Juana Rivas complains that she has not been able to communicate with her son for a year and that he has no contact with her family either. In May 2025, the Commission recognised that the best interests of the child, as enshrined in Article 24 of the Charter, should guide decisions affecting them and that children exposed to domestic violence are victims. In view of the above: 1.

Does the Commission consider that this situation infringes Article 24 of the Charter, Regulation (EU) 2019/1111 as regards parental responsibility and Directive (EU) 2024/1385 on combating violence against women and domestic violence?
In this context, does it maintain that there are no indications that EU law is being implemented incorrectly?
What concrete measures will it take to prevent re-victimisation and to guarantee Daniel’s safety and rights?

E-10-2026-003214.t: Invasion of Ceuta and infiltration by Moroccan intelligence agents
qt: to the Commission Alvise Pérez (NI) Subject:

Ceuta, an external border of the European Union, is facing mass irregular entries from Morocco. Around 72 000 people entered in a single week1, overwhelming reception resources. The President of Ceuta requested a declaration of a national emergency and establishment of a single command, while the parties represented in the city called for deployment of the armed forces. The Spanish Government rejected this mechanism, arguing that immigration does not constitute a risk covered by civil-protection legislation. Recent developments have aggravated the situation. The Guardia Civil has reportedly identified agents of the Moroccan intelligence services among those who took part in last week’s invasion. Their infiltration across an EU external border raises concerns beyond migration: foreign interference, instrumentalisation of migratory pressure and collection of information on Spanish security deployments. It also calls into question Morocco’s reliability as an EU-funded security partner. The security of the EU is directly affected. 1.

Will the Commission urgently request information from Spain and, with Europol and Frontex, assess whether this infiltration constitutes state-sponsored instrumentalisation of migration and a threat to EU internal security and the Schengen area, and take or propose measures available under EU law?

Will the Commission immediately review EU-funded cooperation with Morocco and, if effective cooperation is not restored, suspend the relevant payments and propose that the Council freeze the corresponding cooperation arrangements?

at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (2.10.2026) The EU is closely following developments on the situation in Ceuta and is fully engaged to ensure the security of the EU’s borders and avoid loss of human lives. On 9 September 2026, the Commission decided to provide Spain with EUR 114.7 million in emergency assistance to help manage the situation in Ceuta1. This financial support builds on the Commission's immediate response from the first day, when it offered Spain both financial and operational assistance. The Commission also coordinated and facilitated the mobilisation of support from the EU agencies: the European Border and Coast Guard Agency, the EU Agency for Law Enforcement Cooperation (Europol) and the EU Agency for Asylum responded positively to Spain's request for operational support, further strengthening the assistance available. The EU is in constant contact with Member States and with Europol regarding the situation in Ceuta. It is for the Spanish and Moroccan authorities to establish the facts and get the full picture of what happened; an investigation is ongoing. Morocco is an important partner, notably on migration and border management. EU financial support to Morocco aims to strengthen border management and the capacity to counter migrant smuggling. This cooperation has delivered tangible results with a significant reduction in illegal arrivals. The EU funding is conditional and consistently monitored through robust accountability mechanisms, including regular reporting, programme evaluations, verification missions and indicators linked to disbursement. The Commission is discussing with the Moroccan authorities how to further develop cooperation on migration, in particular on return and readmission, also as part of the negotiations of a comprehensive and strategic partnership.

E-10-2026-003213.t: Recovery and Resilience Facility: assessing the effectiveness of funded forest fire prevention measures in Greece
qt: to the Commission Nikolaos Anadiotis (NI) Subject:

This year, Greece is once again battling widespread forest fires1, with serious environmental, social and economic repercussions and a heavy toll that includes the loss of life of people fighting the flames. Since 2022, the Recovery and Resilience Facility2 has been used to finance forest fire prevention measures, including the AntiNERO3 programme, in order to manage flammable forest material, establish and maintain firebreaks and improve the forest road network. EU funding is governed by the principle of sound financial management (Article 317 TFEU and Regulation (EU, Euratom) 2024/2509) and the Recovery and Resilience Facility is rooted in the achievement of concrete results. With this in mind, can the Commission say: 1.
Does it assess whether the funded preventive actions are achieving/have achieved the objective of reducing the risk and spread of forest fires in Greece?
Does it intend to assess, in cooperation with the Greek authorities, the implementation and effectiveness of the funded projects, the absorption of funds and their compliance with EU law?
Has it envisaged, in the next multiannual financial framework, the establishment of mandatory effectiveness indicators for the financing of forest fire prevention projects?

at: (English version) to the Commission Nikolaos Anadiotis (NI) (5 August 2026) Subject: Recovery and Resilience Facility: assessing the effectiveness of funded forest fire prevention measures in Greece This year, Greece is once again battling widespread forest fires (1), with serious environmental, social and economic repercussions and a heavy toll that includes the loss of life of people fighting the flames. Since 2022, the Recovery and Resilience Facility (2) has been used to finance forest fire prevention measures, including the AntiNERO (3) programme, in order to manage flammable forest material, establish and maintain firebreaks and improve the forest road network. EU funding is governed by the principle of sound financial management (Article 317 TFEU and Regulation (EU, Euratom) 2024/2509) and the Recovery and Resilience Facility is rooted in the achievement of concrete results. With this in mind, can the Commission say: 1.
Does it assess whether the funded preventive actions are achieving/have achieved the objective of reducing the risk and spread of forest fires in Greece?
Does it intend to assess, in cooperation with the Greek authorities, the implementation and effectiveness of the funded projects, the absorption of funds and their compliance with EU law?
Has it envisaged, in the next multiannual financial framework, the establishment of mandatory effectiveness indicators for the financing of forest fire prevention projects?

(22 September 2026) Greece’s Recovery and Resilience Plan (1) (RRP) supports reforestation and fire-prevention actions under measure 16849, with the objective of restoring ecosystems, protecting biodiversity and contributing to carbon regulation. Under the Facility, the Commission disburses funds to Member States only after verifying that the milestones and targets linked to the reforms and investments have been satisfactorily fulfilled. Under measure 16849, Greece has fulfilled two milestones relating to the award of contracts for reforestation, nursery modernisation, and anti-erosion and anti-flood works. The final milestone on the completion of these works will be assessed by the Commission under Greece’s ninth payment request. Without prejudice to the Commission’s role as guardian of the Treaties, Member States are responsible for ensuring that RRP measures comply with EU and national law, including environmental acquis. It is thus for Greek authorities to ensure compliance with applicable EU legislation. The Commission monitors such compliance and may take legal action should Greece fail to implement EU law. An independent ex post evaluation of the Facility and effectiveness of RRP measures is planned for the end of 2028, including analytical studies on reforms and investments and cross-Member State spillovers. For the Multiannual Financial Framework 2028-3034, the Commission proposed a single methodology to monitor EU budget spending through the Performance Regulation (2). Annex I to the proposed Regulation, which is currently subject to adoption by the co-legislators, shows the list of intervention fields (IF) and related output and result indicators, including IF 38, IF 276 and IF 503 which address forest fire prevention and management.

E-10-2026-003212.t: Legal status of the Holy Monastery of St. Catherine on Mount Sinai and Egypt’s obligations regarding religious and cultural protection
qt: to the Commission Nikolaos Anadiotis (NI) Subject:
Legal status of the Holy Monastery of St. Catherine on Mount Sinai and Egypt’s obligations regarding religious and cultural protection

According to a recent report, the Holy Monastery of St. Catherine on Mount Sinai is facing serious challenges to the historical, legal and institutional status under which it has operated for fifteen centuries1,2. Judicial, administrative and political actions are said to be restricting the autonomy of the Monastery, the status of its property and the continuity of the monastic community. The Monastery of St. Catherine is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the oldest functioning Christian monastic sites in the world3. At the same time, the EU and Egypt have upgraded their relations to a strategic and comprehensive partnership, which includes commitments to human rights, fundamental freedoms and respect for international obligations4. In light of the above: 1.
Has the Commission raised with the Egyptian authorities the issue of protecting the historical legal status and monastic continuity of the Monastery of St. Catherine?
How does the Commission assess the developments in the light of freedom of religion, the protection of Christian communities and Egypt's obligations as a State Party to UNESCO?
Will the Commission link the issue to the EU-Egypt political dialogue and European financial cooperation, requesting clear guarantees for the Monastery, its property and its community?

at: (English version) to the Commission Nikolaos Anadiotis (NI) (5 August 2026) Subject: Legal status of the Holy Monastery of St. Catherine on Mount Sinai and Egypt’s obligations regarding religious and cultural protection According to a recent report, the Holy Monastery of St. Catherine on Mount Sinai is facing serious challenges to the historical, legal and institutional status under which it has operated for fifteen centuries (1), (2). Judicial, administrative and political actions are said to be restricting the autonomy of the Monastery, the status of its property and the continuity of the monastic community. The Monastery of St. Catherine is a Unesco World Heritage Site and one of the oldest functioning Christian monastic sites in the world (3). At the same time, the EU and Egypt have upgraded their relations to a strategic and comprehensive partnership, which includes commitments to human rights, fundamental freedoms and respect for international obligations (4). In light of the above: 1.
Has the Commission raised with the Egyptian authorities the issue of protecting the historical legal status and monastic continuity of the Monastery of St. Catherine?
How does the Commission assess the developments in the light of freedom of religion, the protection of Christian communities and Egypt's obligations as a State Party to Unesco?
Will the Commission link the issue to the EU-Egypt political dialogue and European financial cooperation, requesting clear guarantees for the Monastery, its property and its community?

(24 September 2026) The EU welcomes the efforts by Greece and Egypt to work towards safeguarding the rights of Saint Catherine’s Monastery and closely follows developments after the Ismailia Court of Appeals issued a ruling in 2025 linked to the legal status of the Saint Catherine’s Monastery in Sinai. In 2025, the Egyptian authorities informed the European ambassadors that the government remains fully committed to preserving the monastery’s religious, historical, and spiritual status, emphasising that the court ruling formally protects the site for the first time. The EU will continue to follow the matter and the commitments made by the government of Egypt, in close coordination with Greece, insisting on the necessity to preserve the monastery’s religious, historical, and spiritual status, in accordance with the Unesco’s World Heritage Convention. Broadly speaking, the EU prioritises freedom of religion or belief as an important issue within its external human rights policy, aiming to promote tolerance and combat persecution globally. Through EU guidelines adopted in 2013 (1), the EU engages with religious actors, monitors violations, and supports interfaith initiatives, raising issues of concern in its human rights dialogues and sub-committees.

E-10-2026-003211.t: Tax transparency and public procurement in relation to Palantir
qt: to the Commission Kathleen Van Brempt (S&D) Subject:

According to a recent report by the Centre for International Corporate Tax Accountability and Research (CICTAR)1, supported by the European Federation of Public Service Unions (EPSU), Palantir generates significant revenues from public contracts in several Member States while allegedly shifting profits outside Europe and making extensive use of stockbased compensation to minimise its corporate tax liabilities. The report estimates a substantial gap between taxes paid and taxes that would have been due had profits been taxed where economic activity takes place. Given the EU’s increasing reliance on digital providers in sensitive sectors such as defence, healthcare and public administration: 1.

Is the Commission aware of the findings of the CICTAR report and does it consider these tax practices compatible with the objectives of the Anti-Tax Avoidance Directive and the EU’s efforts to ensure fair corporate taxation?

In the ongoing revision of the Public Procurement Directives, is the Commission considering measures to make compliance with corporate tax obligations and tax transparency a condition for participation in public procurement?

How does the Commission reconcile the awarding of strategic public contracts to companies alleged to engage in aggressive tax avoidance with the EU’s objectives on economic security and technological sovereignty?

E-10-2026-003210.t: Fires: The ‘costed’ shortage of personnel and infrastructure leaves ordinary people in Greece and the EU unprotected
qt: to the Commission Lefteris Nikolaou-Alavanos (NI) Subject:

Fifteen people dead, including firefighters, three of them in Greece, dozens injured, hundreds of homes and properties destroyed and 4.3 million acres of torched land is the toll of the fires in France, Spain, and Greece, so far. In Greece, enormous destruction was caused in Rethymno, Boeotia, Paros, and Poikilo Oros in Attica. Both here and throughout the EU, unified firefighting planning with a primary focus on prevention is an ‘unknown concept’. As for the much-vaunted rescEU, in practice it legitimises and perpetuates the shortage of personnel, firefighting equipment and infrastructure. In view of the above: 1.

What is the Commission’s position on the request for the victims of the fires in Greece, Spain, France and other countries to be compensated immediately – for 100% of the damage they suffered – from the EUSF, bypassing the unacceptable conditions that exclude them?

What is the Commission’s position on the fact that the rescEU mechanism aims to recycle a minimum of fire-fighting equipment from country to country, since covering needs at national level is ruled out on the basis of the cost-benefit criterion?

What is the Commission’s position on the fact that the development of a unified fire protection plan with an emphasis on prevention, the organisation of ground forces within the framework of integrated forest management and protection and firefighting and the staffing of Fire Brigades and Forest Services with all the required personnel are considered unnecessary costs – and therefore not prioritised – within the framework of EU policy that endangers people, public property and the environment?

E-10-2026-003209.t: Coherence of EU policies on nature restoration, vineyard restructuring and forest fire prevention
qt: to the Commission Mélanie Disdier (PfE), Catherine Griset (PfE), Valérie Deloge (PfE), Gilles Pennelle (PfE), Julie Rechagneux (PfE), André Rougé (PfE) Subject:

Under Articles 4 and 12 of the Nature Restoration Regulation, Member States are required to restore terrestrial and forest ecosystems. At the same time, recent developments in the common organisation of the market in wine make it possible for support to be provided for the permanent grubbing-up of vineyards under national programmes. In Mediterranean regions, vineyards, agricultural land and pastoral areas act as natural firebreaks, limiting the spread of fires. However, their removing or abandoning them may encourage the continuous growth of combustible vegetation. With megafires on the rise in Southern Europe, the coherence of EU policies must be ensured. 1.

Has the Commission assessed the cumulative effects of the Regulation, the wine sector restructuring measures – including permanent grubbing-up – and the decline in pastoral activities on the risk of wildfires in the Mediterranean regions?
If not, how can it ensure that the combination of these policies will not lead to an increase in combustible biomass, the disappearance of mosaic landscapes and an increased risk of megafires?

Does it intend to systematically incorporate objectives relating to fire prevention, the maintenance of agricultural and pastoral activities, and the preservation of mosaic landscapes into the implementation of these policies?

E-10-2026-003207.t: Proportionality in the digital product passport for handcrafted textiles
qt: to the Commission Christine Singer (Renew) Subject:

On the basis of Regulation (EU) 2024/1781, the Commission is preparing a delegated act for textiles and clothing products, including a digital product passport (DPP). A draft study that the Joint Research Centre has carried out as part of preparations for the delegated act concludes that SMEs, including many micro-enterprises, account for the vast majority of companies in the European textile supply chain and found that many of them do not have the digital infrastructure they need. The study does not, however, lay down any specific rules concerning bespoke products, one-off handcrafted pieces or small production runs. Imposing a one-size-fits-all DPP could place a disproportionate burden on tailors, milliners and other micro-enterprises in the craft sector in particular. Their durable, repairable and regionally manufactured products cannot be compared with industrially mass-produced items. 1.
What exemptions, transitional arrangements or simplified DPP requirements is the Commission considering for bespoke products, one-off handcrafted pieces and small production runs?
What criteria should be used to distinguish between handcrafted, bespoke products or items produced via small production runs and industrially mass-produced items?

What methodology and data does the Commission intend to use in the impact assessment to assess the one-off and recurring costs of the DPP requirements for microenterprises, and to ensure that they are not subject to a disproportionate administrative burden within the meaning of Article 5(11)(f) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1781?

E-10-2026-003205.t: Ecological risk in Basilicata, breach of EU directives and use of cohesion funds
qt: to the Commission Danilo Della Valle (The Left), Valentina Palmisano (The Left) Subject:

Basilicata, Europe’s main onshore drilling hub, is at risk of an environmental overload with a number of applications relating to 15 new fossil fuel wells (as documented by Cova Contro). These procedures are ongoing despite the fact that the region’s Water Protection Plan has not been updated for many years (subject to the 2008 adoption, under Regional Executive Decision No 142/2024) and the landscape procedure has been at a standstill for two years, preventing the application of the SEA Directive (2001/42/EC) on cumulative impacts. Furthermore, the downgrading of Lake Pertusillo (from A2 to A3) violates the ‘nondeterioration principle’ of the Water Directive (2000/60/EC). At the same time, the national costs of access to administrative justice are prohibitive, which is in breach of the principle of non-excessive costs (Article 9(4) of the Aarhus Convention; Article 11 of Directive 2011/92/EU). Given that cohesion funds require compliance with enabling conditions and the ‘do no significant harm’ principle, can the Commission answer the following questions: 1.
Does it consider the authorisation of projects involving outdated planning and deteriorated waters to be in breach of the ‘enabling conditions’, thus blocking EU funds?
Will it launch an infringement procedure against Italy for disproportionate costs of access to administrative justice (Directive 2011/92/EU)?
What opinion will it give (under Article 19 of the EIB Statute) to prevent financing for energy projects in areas without up-to-date protection plans?

E-10-2026-003204.t: Temu’s obstruction of an investigation into foreign subsidies
qt: to the Commission François Kalfon (S&D) Subject:

Regulation (EU) 2022/2560 on foreign subsidies (FSR)1, in force since 2023, fills a loophole under which subsidies from third countries were not subjected to any scrutiny while intra-EU state aid was. On 14 July 2026, the Commission published its review report, in which it declared the Regulation to be fit for purpose and announced adjustments to the procedural setup. On 31 July 2026, the Commission served a statement of objections on PDD Holdings and its subsidiary WhaleCo Technology (Temu) for obstructing an inspection conducted in Dublin in December 2025 by refusing to provide information on the organisation of its operations, IT systems and certain records. Under Article 17 of the FSR, such an infringement is punishable by a fine of up to 1 % of the group’s global turnover. 1.

Given that this company has consistently demonstrated its willingness to circumvent European law on digital matters, consumer protection and state aid, will the Commission confirm that it will fully apply the penalties provided for under the FSR if the alleged obstruction is proven?
Given that the FSR is due to be revised in the near future, will the Commission draw lessons from this case to tighten up compliance and penalty procedures?
ELI: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/2560/oj.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (24.9.2026) Companies operating in the internal market are legally obliged to submit to an inspection ordered by a decision of the Commission pursuant to Article 14 of the Foreign Subsidies Regulation (FSR)1. In the present case, the Commission takes the preliminary view that Temu has obstructed the inspection conducted at its premises last December, by refusing to submit to the inspection and by not providing the required books or other records in a complete form. Should the investigation confirm those preliminary findings, the Commission may impose a fine of up to 1% of Temu’s aggregate turnover of the previous financial year. In accordance with Article 17(6) FSR, when setting the amount of a fine, the Commission has regard to the nature of the identified infringements, their gravity and duration, taking due account of the principles of proportionality and appropriateness. Compliance with FSR provisions and possible breaches are examined under the FSR, and separately from compliance with other EU or national legislations. In July 2026, the Commission published the results of its first review of the FSR, from which it found that the regulation is fit for purpose to address distortions in the internal market caused by foreign subsidies, while acknowledging certain concerns about complexity and administrative burden. The Commission is envisaging targeted adjustments to the FSR procedural framework2.
1 Regulation (EU) 2022/2560 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 December 2022 on foreign
subsidies distorting the internal market, OJ L 330, 23.12.2022, p. 1. 2 https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_26_1606.

E-10-2026-003202.t: Moroccan authorities instrumentalising migration against Spain
qt: to the Commission Geadis Geadi (ECR) Subject:

The recent invasion of irregular migrants in Ceuta, Spain, has sparked serious concern and anxiety across European society. Videos circulating online over the last few days suggest that this situation may be part of a hybrid war being waged by the Moroccan authorities against Spain. A telling example is a video reportedly showing irregular migrants arriving in Ceuta in trucks accompanied by Moroccan police forces and being shown the way. With this in mind, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
How does it intend to react to these incidents?
Is it prepared to impose sanctions on Morocco and suspend any active trade, economic or other agreements between the European Union and Morocco?

Have the Spanish authorities or Frontex been asked to investigate these allegations and the audiovisual material reportedly showing the Moroccan authorities’ involvement in the transportation of irregular migrants to Ceuta?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.10.2026) The EU’s new approach to migration and asylum is delivering results, leading to a sustained drop in illegal arrivals: illegal border crossings in 2025 were under half the total recorded in 2023 and at the lowest level since 2021. The Commission is working with Spain on the effective use of the instruments of the Pact on Migration and Asylum1 to ensure the swift return of those illegally staying, while strengthening the protection of the external borders. Spain has requested additional support to handle the situation in Ceuta from the European Border and Coast Guard Agency, the European Union Agency for Law Enforcement Cooperation, the European Union Agency for Asylum. The agencies are working on the operational response. The Commission welcomes the close cooperation between Spain and Morocco to respond to the situation in Ceuta and ensure the swift return of those who do not have the right to remain. The Commission will step up efforts in five key areas, as outlined in the letter of 3 August 2026 from the Commission President to the Prime Minister of Spain, namely: preventing irregular immigration by strengthening cooperation with the EU’s partners; further strengthening EU external borders; developing joint EU-partner early warning systems; dismantling smuggling networks; reinforcing returns. Morocco is an important partner of the EU, including in managing migration. Cooperation and EU-funded programmes with Morocco are subject to robust accountability mechanisms, including regular reporting, periodic programme evaluations, on-the-spot verification missions and indicators tied to disbursement in the case of budget support. This cooperation has delivered results: irregular border crossings along the Western Mediterranean and Atlantic route combined decreased by 42% in 2025 compared to 2024. They further decreased by 34% in the first 6 months of 2026, compared to the same period in 2025.
1 https://home-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies/migration-and-asylum/pact-migration-and-asylum_en.

E-10-2026-003201.t: Aggressive actions against the president of a Member State and an MEP
qt: to the Commission Geadis Geadi (ECR) Subject:

Last Saturday, 1 August 2026, in my capacity as an MEP, I attended the Municipality of Famagusta’s annual anti-occupation event, in order to denounce the grim anniversary of the Turkish invasion. The event was also attended by the President of the Republic of Cyprus, as well as MPs and other officials. During the event, Ottoman marches could be heard from the occupied areas, as the occupying authorities chose to turn the loudspeakers’ volume to maximum as an act of provocation. However, this was not the end of the provocations. There were repeated violations of the buffer zone by unmanned aerial vehicles (drones)1, which took off from the occupied areas and flew over the site of the anti-occupation event in the Municipality of Famagusta and over the heads of officials. In view of the above, can the Commission say: 1.
How does it intend to react to this latest Turkish provocation?
Does it intend to impose sanctions on Türkiye, as it does in similar cases against the Russian Federation?

E-10-2026-003200.t: Mass illegal entry of around 49 000 migrants into Ceuta
qt: to the Commission Geadis Geadi (ECR) Subject:
Mass illegal entry of around 49 000 migrants into Ceuta

According to estimates from the Spanish Ministry of the Interior, around 49 000 irregular immigrants illegally crossed from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta within 24 hours. This was a massive violation of an EU external border and a direct provocation challenging the integrity of the Schengen area. The incident raises serious questions about the effectiveness of Spain’s border control policy, the operational readiness of the Commission and Frontex and the EU’s ability to address the instrumentalisation of migration as a means of applying political pressure. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Does it consider that the mass illegal entry of around 49 000 irregular immigrants into Ceuta constitutes a serious failure to protect the EU’s external border?

Will it assess Morocco’s role in the incident, as a matter of urgency, and consider whether funding should be made strictly conditional on the country's effective cooperation in preventing illegal departures and accepting readmissions?

If Spain cannot or is not willing to guarantee effective control of the EU’s external borders, will the Commission consider all available legal consequences, including measures such as Spain’s exit from Schengen?

E-10-2026-003199.t: Putting fundamental rights into practice for all citizens in the European Union
qt: to the Commission Geadis Geadi (ECR) Subject:

Recently, there has been increased diplomatic momentum with regard to the Cyprus issue, with UN Secretary-General António Guterres visiting Cyprus with the aim of resuming negotiations, which have remained at a standstill since the breakdown of the Crans-Montana talks. The European Union and the European acquis are founded on the principles of equality, nondiscrimination and respect for human rights for all people, as enshrined in the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union. At the same time, the Charter of the United Nations, and in particular Article 1(3) thereof, provides for the promotion of ‘respect for human rights and for fundamental freedoms for all without distinction as to race, sex, language, or religion’. Could the Commission accept any form of racially based division of the island, in breach of the European acquis and the principles of the UN Charter?

E-10-2026-003197.t: The dangerous working conditions of digital platform workers and the need to sign a collective agreement
qt: to the Commission Kostas Papadakis (NI) Subject:

The recent fatal workplace accident involving a 20-year-old Wolt delivery worker adds to the long list of occupational accidents in the courier and digital platform industries1. These tragic events constitute employer crimes, as large digital platforms are expanding forms of work that transfer the cost of labour and the responsibility for protecting the worker onto workers themselves. In view of the above: 1.

What is the Commission’s position on the fact that Directive (EU) 2024/2831, despite its claims to ‘improve working conditions’, does not abolish the status of bogus selfemployment and contract work, nor does it universally guarantee stable employment relationships and full employment and social security rights for all platform workers, leaving Member States free to adapt this framework to the needs of the competitiveness and profitability of business groups?

What is the Commission’s position on the fact that the EU’s policy on ‘flexible’ working and the competitiveness of businesses, as also reflected in the regulations on digital platforms, has contributed to undermining collective agreements and perpetuating forms of employment that lack stability and full rights?

What is the Commission’s position on the fact that the recent law in Greece on collective agreements is part of the same anti-worker framework of the European guidelines on the ‘competitiveness’ and ‘flexibility’ of the labour market, as reflected, among others, in Directive (EU) 2022/2041 on so-called ‘adequate minimum wages’ and in Directive (EU) 2019/1152 on ‘transparent and predictable working conditions’ in the EU?
