at: (English version) to the Commission Kostas Papadakis (NI) (4 August 2026) Subject: The dangerous working conditions of digital platform workers and the need to sign a collective agreement The recent fatal workplace accident involving a 20-year-old Wolt delivery worker adds to the long list of occupational accidents in the courier and digital platform industries (1). These tragic events constitute employer crimes, as large digital platforms are expanding forms of work that transfer the cost of labour and the responsibility for protecting the worker onto workers themselves. In view of the above: 1.

What is the Commission’s position on the fact that directive (EU) 2024/2831, despite its claims to ‘improve working conditions’, does not abolish the status of bogus self-employment and contract work, nor does it universally guarantee stable employment relationships and full employment and social security rights for all platform workers, leaving Member States free to adapt this framework to the needs of the competitiveness and profitability of business groups?

What is the Commission’s position on the fact that the EU’s policy on ‘flexible’ working and the competitiveness of businesses, as also reflected in the regulations on digital platforms, has contributed to undermining collective agreements and perpetuating forms of employment that lack stability and full rights?

What is the Commission’s position on the fact that the recent law in Greece on collective agreements is part of the same anti-worker framework of the European guidelines on the ‘competitiveness’ and ‘flexibility’ of the labour market, as reflected, among others, in Directive (EU) 2022/2041 on so-called ‘adequate minimum wages’ and in Directive (EU) 2019/1152 on ‘transparent and predictable working conditions’ in the EU?

(28 September 2026) 1. Directive (EU) 2024/2831 (1) facilitates the determination of the correct employment status of persons performing platform work (PPPW), including through a rebuttable presumption of an employment relationship. It will help false selfemployed platform workers to gain access to the correct employment status and to enjoy relevant labour rights deriving from Union law, national law and collective agreements. The directive establishes minimum standards across the EU and Member States may introduce provisions which are more favourable to PPPW. 2. The Commission does not share the premise that EU policies on flexibility and competitiveness undermine collective agreements. The European Pillar of Social Rights explicitly recognises the right to secure and adaptable employment and the importance of social dialogue. Directive (EU) 2024/2831 ensures that the flexibility and innovation of the platform economy do not come at the expense of the rights of PPPW by addressing misclassification and strengthening fairness and the rights of representatives in algorithmic management. The Commission has likewise provided guidelines (2) to facilitate collective bargaining for the solo self-employed. 3. Directive (EU) 2019/1152 (3) sets out minimum requirements to improve working conditions by promoting more transparent and predictable work for workers in all sectors. Directive (EU) 2022/2041 (4) promotes collective bargaining on wage-setting, which is important for ensuring adequate minimum wage protection and a decent standard of living. The Commission will examine the compatibility of the Greek Law 5278/2026 with the provisions of Directive (EU) 2022/2041 in the context of the compliance assessment of the transposition.

E-10-2026-003196.t: Extension of the EU ETS to international flights
qt: to the Commission Piotr Müller (ECR) Subject:

Subsequent proposals to extend the EU ETS are justified by analyses from climate organisations that downplay the economic and social risks to the European aviation sector. The International Council on Clean Transportation argues that including flights between the EU and third countries in the scheme will induce passengers to choose routes via transfer airports outside the EU to a minimal degree. On this basis, it concludes that the risk of European airlines and airports losing traffic should not prevent the extension of the ETS. European carriers and trade unions, however, warn of a shift in traffic to hubs in third countries, job losses and a further weakening of the competitiveness of the EU’s aviation sector. NGOs may participate in the public debate, but they lack a democratic mandate and bear no responsibility for the consequences of the rules that they propose. Their models, assumptions and financial interests cannot replace the Commission’s independent and comprehensive impact assessment. In light of the above: 1.
Is the Commission considering extending the ETS to international flights without first carrying out a full assessment of the impact on European airlines, airports and employment?
Will the Commission review the funding and potential conflicts of interest of the organisations whose analyses it uses when preparing such changes?
Why would the Commission seek to increase the cost of flights from the EU, risking a shift of passengers and traffic to hubs outside the Union?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (2.10.2026)

On 17 July 2026, the Commission adopted its proposal for the revision of the Directive on the EU Emissions Trading System1 (ETS). It includes the extension of the ETS geographical scope to emissions from flights from airports in the European Economic Area (EEA) landing in third country airports located within 5,000 km of the largest aerodrome in the geographical centre of the EU. All parts of the proposal are based on a rigorous impact assessment2 in line with rules in force for policy-making and legal drafting. The impact assessment was published on the same day as the legislative proposal. It includes impacts on airports, airlines and employment. According to the above-mentioned assessment, the Commission’s proposal is expected to cause a minor increase in plane ticket prices, while financing a strengthened support to decarbonise the sector and addressing a larger share of EU aviation’s climate impact. The extension also helps mitigating the risk of shift to non-EEA hubs, which may be caused by a variety of factors, beyond climate policies like the ETS. In its work, the Commission takes into account the input and feedback of a broad range of stakeholders. This includes Member States and competent authorities, industry associations, companies, civil society organisations (including non-governmental organisations), and other interested parties. A public consultation on the revision of the ETS Directive took place last year, providing all stakeholders with the opportunity to express their views.

E-10-2026-003195.t: International child abduction and application of the 1980 Hague Convention
qt: to the Commission Ignazio Roberto Marino (Verts/ALE) Subject:

In April 2024, a Russian citizen left Italy with her two-and-a-half-year-old daughter without the consent of her Italian father. As a result, a criminal case for international child abduction is pending before the Court of Turin. The father filed a report and initiated the procedure laid down in the 1980 Hague Convention to secure the child’s return. According to the same sources, the application was rejected by the Russian courts at two instances. As a result, the father can only maintain contact with his daughter if he travels to Russia. The Hague Convention, applicable between Italy and the Russian Federation, aims to secure the prompt return of children who are wrongfully removed or retained and to ensure that children can maintain contact with both parents. In view of the above: 1.
Is the Commission aware of this case and of the difficulties EU citizens encounter when trying to ensure that the Convention is properly implemented in the Russian Federation?
What cooperation instruments can be used to assist Member States and citizens caught up in international child abduction cases involving third countries?
What is its view of the way in which the Russian Federation implements the Convention and has it encountered repeated difficulties in that regard?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (21.9.2026) The Commission is not aware of the individual case referred to in the question. Relationships between an EU Member State and a third country that are both parties to the 1980 Hague Child Abduction Convention1 are governed by that Convention, not by EU law. Italy and Russia are both Contracting Parties to this Convention, which seeks to protect children from wrongful removal and retention across borders by securing their prompt return and ensuring the protection of rights of access. The application of the Convention is monitored by the Hague Conference on Private International Law (HCCH), not the Commission. EU citizens can ask for assistance from their Central Authority responsible for the application of the Hague 1980 Child Abduction Convention. In Italy, the Ministry of Justice acts as the Central Authority2.

E-10-2026-003194.t: Award procedure for the Rome-Latina intermodal corridor and the promoter’s pre-emption right
qt: to the Commission Ignazio Roberto Marino (Verts/ALE) Subject:

In its judgment of 5 February 2026 in case C-810/24 (Urban Vision), the Court of Justice of the European Union ruled that the mechanism enabling the promoter of a project financing procedure to adjust its offer to match the top offer, in order to be awarded the contract, was incompatible with Article 3(1) of Directive 2014/23/EU. The Italian Council of State applied those principles in judgment No 3805 of 14 May 2026. By way of public notice issued on 29 May 2025, the Italian Ministry of Infrastructure launched the concession procedure for the Rome-Latina intermodal corridor (between Tor de’ Cenci and Latina Borgo Piave). On the basis of paragraph 7, if the promoter is not awarded the contract, it may nevertheless exercise a pre-emption right and be awarded the contract, provided it complies with the same terms as the successful tenderer. On 4 June 2026, the matter was put to the Italian Chamber of Deputies in a question for immediate reply. In view of the above: 1.
Is the Commission aware of this procedure and the conditions benefiting the promoter?
In light of judgment C-810/24, does it deem this procedure compatible with Article 3(1) of Directive 2014/23/EU?
Will it seek clarification from the Italian authorities and, if necessary, take steps to ensure full application of the judgment?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (24.9.2026) As a general rule, the Commission does not examine the details of individual procedures, such as the one referred to by the Honourable Member, as Member States are better placed to investigate individual tendering procedures. The Commission notes that national courts and review bodies referred to in the directives on remedies in public procurement1 are primarily responsible to assess whether, according to the relevant legal and factual circumstances of each individual case, contracting authorities and contracting entities respected their obligations under EU law. Nonetheless, the Commission refers back to its reply to written question P-001533/20262 and recalls that as confirmed by the Court of Justice of the European Union in the judgment cited by the Honourable Member, the provision of a pre-emption right in favour of the promoter such as the one that was foreseen in the national legislation at stake is contrary to the principles of non-discrimination and equal treatment, as enshrined in the EU public procurement rules, and that preliminary rulings are binding both on the referring court and on all courts in Member States. However, it is primarily for the authorities of the Member State concerned to take the general or specific measures necessary to ensure that EU law is complied with within that State.
1 Directive 89/665/EEC and Directive 92/13/EEC, as amended by Directive 2007/66/EC and Directive
2014/23/EU. 2 https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/P-10-2026-001533_EN.html.

E-10-2026-003191.t: Safeguards against perceived conflicts of interest in appointments to the CJEU
qt: to the Council Marc Botenga (The Left) Subject:

Recent reporting by Investigate Europe1 and partner media2 has raised concerns about the appearance of impartiality at the Court of Justice of the European Union, including declared financial interests of Members of the Court and situations where judges may sit in cases involving the Member State that nominated them. Given that judges and advocates general are appointed, by common accord, by the governments of the Member States after consulting the panel set up under Article 255 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU): 1.

Does the Council consider that the current appointment and reappointment procedure adequately examines candidates’ financial interests, previous governmental functions, and links to the nominating Member State?
Has the Council discussed asking the panel set up under Article 255 TFEU to assess perceived conflicts of interest more systematically before appointments or reappointments?
Will the Council consider publishing clearer safeguards on how perceived conflicts identified during the appointment process are assessed, while fully respecting judicial independence?

E-10-2026-003190.t: Unequal treatment of sika deer, wolves and bears under EU species conservation law
qt: to the Commission Markus Buchheit (ESN) Subject:

Native to East Asia, where hunting has driven population numbers right down, the sika deer (Cervus nippon) has been kept and bred in cages in Europe since the 19th century. The species was added to the EU list of invasive alien species by means of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/1422, thereby prohibiting rearing, breeding and reproduction, albeit with a transition period until 2027 for existing establishments. Meanwhile, wolves and bears roaming freely in densely populated parts of central Europe kill tens of thousands of grazing animals every year – a figure that also encompasses high-profile cases such as the death of the Commission President’s pony, Dolly, which was killed in a wolf attack. And yet there is no comparable obligation to eradicate these species. What criteria does the Commission apply to distinguish between the sika deer on the one hand and wolves and bears on the other when deciding which species is/are unmanageable/no longer manageable in densely populated regions of central Europe?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (17.9.2026) The inclusion of sika deer on the list of invasive alien species (IAS) of Union concern under the IAS Regulation1 follows a dedicated risk assessment2 endorsed by the Scientific Forum of Member State experts and supported by a clear majority of Member States when Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/1422 was adopted3. That assessment identified serious environmental, economic and health risks, including damage to forestry and agriculture, impacts on transport, hybridisation with native red deer and the potential transmission of diseases. Unlike wolves and bears, the sika deer is an alien species in Europe. While there is no obligation to eradicate it, particularly where it is already widespread, its inclusion on the list of Union concern gives rise to an obligation to manage it. The wolf, the bear and other large carnivores are part of the native European fauna and biodiversity heritage. As predators at the top of the food chain, they play an important ecological role, contributing to the health and balance of ecosystems, for example through regulation of prey species (roe deers, red deers, or wild boars), and of other predators (foxes, jackals), as well as contribution to natural control of diseases through selective predation. Large carnivores have therefore been listed as species of Community interest under the Habitats Directive4, which means that their favourable conservation status must be achieved or maintained. A recent amendment5 of the Habitats Directive has changed the protection status of the wolf from ‘strictly protected’ to ‘protected’, which gives additional flexibility to Member States in managing their local wolf populations, as long as their favourable conservation status is maintained.
1 Regulation (EU) No 1143/2014 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 22 October 2014 on the

prevention and management of the introduction and spread of invasive alien species, OJ L 317, 4.11.2014, p. 3555. 2 https://circabc.europa.eu/ui/group/98665af0-7dfa-448c-8bf4-e1e086b50d2c/library/5891b3af-e561-4750-86cc709857e88c94?p=1&n=10&sort=modified_DESC. 3 Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/1422 of 17 July 2025 amending Implementing Regulation (EU) 2016/1141 to update the list of invasive alien species of Union concern, 17.7.20125. 4 Council Directive 92/43/EEC of 21 May 1992 on the conservation of natural habitats and of wild fauna and flora, OJ L 206, 22.7.1992, pp. 7–50. 5 Directive (EU) 2025/1237 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 17 June 2025 amending Council Directive 92/43/EEC as regards the protection status of the wolf (Canis lupus), OJ L, 2025/1237, 24.6.2025.

E-10-2026-003188.t: Delays in rolling out the future railway mobile communication system across the EU
qt: to the Commission Markus Buchheit (ESN) Subject:

Since the guidelines for developing a Trans-European Transport Network (TEN-T) were adopted in 1996, the Commission has been working towards the related objectives. The standardisation of the future railway mobile communication system (FRMCS) – which is to be based on 5G technology instead of the outdated GSM-R standard – began in 2015, and the requirements specification was completed in 2020. Despite this preparatory work having started years ago, the FRMCS remains at the pilot and testing stage across the EU. There are no plans for seamless, full-scale operation in any Member State before 2028; in several cases, not before 2035. 1.
How does the Commission explain the fact that, ten years after the start of standardisation work, the FRMCS is still not operational across the EU?
By when exactly does it expect the FRMCS to operate seamlessly and uniformly throughout the EU? Which Member States would it say are currently lagging behind?

E-10-2026-003187.t: Europe’s widening gap in the development of cutting-edge AI
qt: to the Commission Piotr Müller (ECR) Subject:

A report prepared for the European Commission suggests that the EU has just one or two years to take effective action before its ability to close the gap in the development of cuttingedge AI is further diminished. Europe accounts for only around 5 % of global computing power, whilst US companies dominate in the development of frontier AI models and in access to the infrastructure necessary for training them. At the same time, European companies are grappling with high energy prices, limited access to capital, protracted investment procedures and growing regulatory obligations. The Commission is today being warned by its own experts of the risk of Europe becoming permanently dependent on non-European suppliers of the most advanced AI systems. In this connection: 1.

How does the Commission assess its AI policy to date, and does it recognise that the insufficient prioritisation of computing power, energy, investment and business scaling – whilst focusing on new regulatory obligations – has contributed to Europe’s current lag behind the global leaders?
What specific barriers to investment in computing power, data centres and the development of the most advanced AI models does the Commission intend to remove over the next two years?

Will the Commission reassess existing and planned regulatory burdens relating to AI where these may further limit the ability of European businesses to scale up their operations and compete on the global market?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (24.9.2026) At the start of the mandate, the Commission set the objective of making the EU an AI Continent. This translated into policy attention on a number of key dimensions: computing infrastructures, high-quality data, AI adoption, talent and skills, and regulatory simplification. This has led, among others, to the launch of several initiatives including the Apply AI Strategy1, aimed at supporting the integration of AI in strategic sectors and strengthening competitiveness of European businesses. Building on the AI Continent Action Plan2, the Commission proposed the AI Omnibus3 and supported its negotiations by the co-legislators, which introduced targeted simplifications to lower the compliance burden for companies. The Commission also launched its most ambitious initiative to date to expand the EU’s AI computing capacity: a call for tenders to establish AI Gigafactories4 in the EU, which is expected to mobilise at least EUR 30 billion in public and private investment. More broadly, the EU needs to reinforce its capacity across the entire AI stack. This is the goal of the recent Tech Sovereignty Package5. Among others, the Cloud and AI Development Act6 aims to encourage investment in computing capacity by addressing existing barriers, while also supporting the development of frontier, physical and industrial AI. Furthermore, the Strategic Roadmap for Digitalisation and AI in the energy sector7 introduced a strategic initiative where EU grid operators and solutions providers are developing sovereign AI models for planning and managing electricity grids. At the same time, maintaining Europe’s competitiveness in this field will require sustained efforts and investment from all actors in the EU, notably its leading industrial companies.

E-10-2026-003186.t: EU age limit for children’s access to social media
qt: to the Commission Piotr Müller (ECR) Subject:

The Commission is considering introducing a uniform EU age limit for access to social media, citing the recommendations of an expert panel it has set up. Protecting children online is essential; however, the views of academics on the impact of social media, appropriate age limits and the role of parental control remain divided. Member States have differing experiences, education systems and approaches to parents’ rights and responsibilities. Setting a single age limit across the EU is not merely a technical issue concerning the functioning of the internal market, but direct interference in decisions regarding the upbringing of children. In light of the above: 1.
Why does the Commission consider the recommendations of a single panel of experts to be a sufficient basis for proposing a uniform age limit across the EU?

How does the Commission intend to take into account the experiences of Member States, the principle of subsidiarity and the fundamental responsibility of parents for decisions regarding their children’s use of social media?

On what legal basis does the Commission intend to harmonise the age limit, and does it consider Article 114 TFEU to be appropriate for regulating a matter that goes beyond the removal of barriers to the internal market?

E-10-2026-003185.t: Impact of the evaluation of the Nitrates Directive on European agriculture and livestock farming
qt: to the Commission Piotr Müller (ECR) Subject:

In its published evaluation of the Nitrates Directive, the Commission recognised that the current limit of 170 kg of nitrogen from natural fertilisers per hectare remains appropriate and did not propose any fundamental reform of this limit. At the same time, the Commission points out that in regions with a high concentration of livestock production, reducing the number of animals reared could be a solution to the problem of nitrate pollution. This approach raises serious concerns given the high costs of mineral fertilisers, the growing competitive pressure on European farmers and the need to reduce the EU’s dependence on imported inputs. Particularly incomprehensible is the Commission’s assertion that the Directive has not fundamentally affected the competitiveness of the livestock sector. In this connection: 1.
On what basis does the Commission consider that the rules and limits established in 1991 still correspond to the current economic, technological and climatic realities of European agriculture?

Why does the Commission point to a reduction in livestock numbers as a solution to the problem of nutrient surpluses, rather than prioritising support for the processing of manure, biogas plants, precision fertilisation technologies and the transport of nutrients between regions?

How does the Commission justify its assertion that the Nitrates Directive has not affected the competitiveness of the livestock sector, and will it provide a detailed assessment of its cumulative costs to farms?
at: (English version) to the Commission Piotr Müller (ECR) (31 July 2026) Subject: Impact of the evaluation of the Nitrates Directive on European agriculture and livestock farming In its published evaluation of the Nitrates Directive, the Commission recognised that the current limit of 170 kg of nitrogen from natural fertilisers per hectare remains appropriate and did not propose any fundamental reform of this limit. At the same time, the Commission points out that in regions with a high concentration of livestock production, reducing the number of animals reared could be a solution to the problem of nitrate pollution. This approach raises serious concerns given the high costs of mineral fertilisers, the growing competitive pressure on European farmers and the need to reduce the EU’s dependence on imported inputs. Particularly incomprehensible is the Commission’s assertion that the directive has not fundamentally affected the competitiveness of the livestock sector. In this connection: 1.
On what basis does the Commission consider that the rules and limits established in 1991 still correspond to the current economic, technological and climatic realities of European agriculture?

Why does the Commission point to a reduction in livestock numbers as a solution to the problem of nutrient surpluses, rather than prioritising support for the processing of manure, biogas plants, precision fertilisation technologies and the transport of nutrients between regions?

How does the Commission justify its assertion that the Nitrates Directive has not affected the competitiveness of the livestock sector, and will it provide a detailed assessment of its cumulative costs to farms?

(16 September 2026) The evaluation of the Nitrates Directive (1) (ND) published on 15 July 2026 (2) shows that the directive remains effective and relevant in the current economic, technological and climatic context, including the limit on manure application in nitrate vulnerable zones. It also identifies opportunities to simplify implementation and reduce burdens on farmers (3). Reducing livestock numbers can be a solution in regions where excessive manure production represents a challenge for the protection of ground and surface waters, but it is not the focus of the Commission’s policy. The Fertiliser Action Plan (4) of 19 May 2026 aims to promote better nutrient management. To boost circularity and cut emissions, the Commission will support the development and uptake of organic fertilisers and alternatives to conventional inorganic fertilisers, in particular bio-based fertilisers. For example, it will explore the potential for extending the recovered Nitrogen from manure (5) rules under the ND to certain digestates, which can act as alternative to synthetic fertilisers. Furthermore, the Livestock Strategy (6) of 7 July 2026 lays down a dedicated roadmap to enable a more efficient and sustainable circulation of nutrients across the EU. The evaluation of the ND includes an assessment of costs and benefits associated with the directive’s implementation. Intensive livestock producers in certain regions with very high livestock density carry significant costs associated with the management of excess manure, but the ND is not the determining factor in shaping the industry's overall development. This conclusion is supported by international competitiveness indicators as well as an econometric analysis.

E-10-2026-003183.t: Extraordinary measures needed to support the Italian shellfish farming industry
qt: to the Commission Anna Maria Cisint (PfE), Paolo Borchia (PfE) Subject:

The mussels, clams and other bivalve molluscs that the Italian shellfish farming industry relies upon so heavily have been dying in droves due to the unusually high temperatures recorded over the summer. Heat waves in July caused sea temperatures to rise as high as 32 degrees Celsius, starving the shellfish of oxygen. The death toll has been particularly high along the Upper Adriatic and Sardinian coasts. Shellfish farmers estimate that 100 tonnes of PDO mussels were lost in the Sacca degli Scardovari area (Province of Rovigo), and that only 10 % of the Goro Lagoon’s clam harvest has survived. Trieste, another area renowned for its mussels, has also been hit hard. According to trade association estimates, the Italian shellfish farming sector is looking at losses of EUR 200 million. In the light of the above, we ask the Commission: Will it take urgent and exceptional measures to support the Italian shellfish farming sector, which has been hit hard by this year’s abnormal weather patterns?
at: (English version) to the Commission Anna Maria Cisint (PfE), Paolo Borchia (PfE) (31 July 2026) Subject: Extraordinary measures needed to support the Italian shellfish farming industry The mussels, clams and other bivalve molluscs that the Italian shellfish farming industry relies upon so heavily have been dying in droves due to the unusually high temperatures recorded over the summer. Heat waves in July caused sea temperatures to rise as high as 32 degrees Celsius, starving the shellfish of oxygen. The death toll has been particularly high along the Upper Adriatic and Sardinian coasts. Shellfish farmers estimate that 100 tonnes of PDO mussels were lost in the Sacca degli Scardovari area (Province of Rovigo), and that only 10% of the Goro Lagoon’s clam harvest has survived. Trieste, another area renowned for its mussels, has also been hit hard. According to trade association estimates, the Italian shellfish farming sector is looking at losses of EUR 200 million. In the light of the above, we ask the Commission: Will it take urgent and exceptional measures to support the Italian shellfish farming sector, which has been hit hard by this year’s abnormal weather patterns? (7 September 2026) The Commission acknowledges the serious difficulties described for the Italian shellfish farming sector due to the severe weather conditions over the summer. The European Maritime, Fisheries and Aquaculture Fund (EMFAF) (1) provides support to strengthen the competitiveness of the aquaculture sector, while ensuring its long-term sustainability. The implementation of the EMFAF Programme is primarily the responsibility of the Member State concerned under shared management. The Italian EMFAF Programme (2) includes the possibility to support various measures aimed at improving the competitiveness, resilience and development of the aquaculture sector, including through diversification, innovative and experimental projects, and actions to increase the added value of aquaculture products. In addition, the Italian EMFAF Programme may support measures to protect and stabilise the income of aquaculture operators, by means of compensations or insurance schemes. In this respect, Italy may activate the Programme’s measures to support the Italian shellfish farming sector. For example, in 2025 Italy activated EMFAF support for aquaculture companies to compensate for income loss and additional costs resulting from the temporary cessation of activities caused by exceptional climate events during 2024, such as the exceptional increase in sea temperature (3). Beyond EMFAF, Member States may also consider other national support measures, subject to compliance with the applicable EU State aid rules for the fisheries and aquaculture sector.

E-10-2026-003182.t: Repeated mass illegal crossings into Ceuta
qt: to the Commission Mary Khan (ESN) Subject:

Recent reports indicate that thousands of illegal migrants have reached the Spanish exclave of Ceuta in recent days, with a majority reportedly swimming from Moroccan beaches into this territory1. Far from being an isolated incident, this is just the latest in a series of major migration crises affecting Ceuta in recent years. These repeated incidents call into question the effectiveness of the EU’s migration cooperation with Morocco, which has received hundreds of millions of euro through EU funding for migration management, border control and the fight against migrant smuggling. 1.

In the light of these repeated mass illegal crossings, does the Commission consider that Morocco is fulfilling its commitments to prevent and significantly reduce illegal departures from its territory and to combat migrant smuggling?
Will the Commission make future financial assistance conditional upon Morocco delivering measurable reductions in illegal departures towards the EU?
What specific measures will the Commission take to strengthen the external border in Ceuta?
https://www.reuters.com/world/europe/thousands-migrants-cross-into-spains-ceuta-foot-efe-reports2026-07-30/. 1
at: (English version) to the Commission Mary Khan (ESN) (31 July 2026) Subject: Repeated mass illegal crossings into Ceuta Recent reports indicate that thousands of illegal migrants have reached the Spanish exclave of Ceuta in recent days, with a majority reportedly swimming from Moroccan beaches into this territory (1). Far from being an isolated incident, this is just the latest in a series of major migration crises affecting Ceuta in recent years. What specific measures will the Commission take to strengthen the external border in Ceuta?

(25 September 2026) The EU’s new approach to migration and asylum is delivering results, leading to a sustained drop in illegal arrivals (1): illegal border crossings in 2025 were under half the total recorded in 2023 and at the lowest level since 2021. Morocco is an important partner, notably on migration and border management. EU financial support to Morocco aims to strengthen border management and the capacity to counter migrant smuggling. This cooperation has delivered tangible results with a significant reduction in illegal arrivals over the years. The EU funding is conditional and consistently monitored through robust accountability mechanisms, including regular reporting, programme evaluations, verification missions and indicators linked to disbursement. The Commission is discussing with the Moroccan authorities how to further develop cooperation on migration, in particular on return and readmission, also as part of the negotiations of a strategic and comprehensive partnership. The Commission is committed to working closely with Member States to further strengthen external borders. Upon Member States’ request, the EU can provide financial and technical assistance, as well as operational support, including deployments of personnel and equipment, notably through European Border and Coast Guard Agency (Frontex). Work is currently ongoing on a proposal to strengthen the mandate of Frontex, as announced in the political guidelines of the President of the Commission.

E-10-2026-003181.t: Need to adapt the conditions for granting coupled aid in the event of extreme weather events
qt: to the Commission Emmanouil Fragkos (ECR) Subject:

According to representatives of the agricultural associations of Eastern Macedonia, the extreme temperatures and prolonged drought of 2024 caused significant losses in maize production, putting many producers at risk of not meeting the minimum production thresholds required to receive coupled aid. They argue that the loss of production is solely due to extreme weather events and not the fault of farmers. Regulation (EU) 2021/2115 provides Member States with flexibility in the implementation of direct payments, while Article 3 of Regulation (EU) 2021/2116 recognises the concept of force majeure and exceptional circumstances. Maintaining agricultural production and producers’ income is critical for food security and the viability of rural areas. In view of this, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Does it consider that Member States have sufficient flexibility to derogate from the minimum production thresholds for the granting of coupled payments in cases of proven extreme weather events?
Does it intend to issue additional guidelines for the uniform application of the concept of force majeure in the context of the CAP?
Does it intend to consider further flexibilities under the CAP to ensure that coupled payments are maintained in areas systematically affected by adverse weather conditions?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (2.10.2026) Member States may recognise severe meteorological events as force majeure where abnormal and unforeseeable circumstances beyond the beneficiary’s control, despite the exercise of all due care, prevent compliance with the relevant Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) requirements – whether stemming from EU regulations or specific national conditions. This is thus also applicable to coupled income support (CIS). The recognition of cases of force majeure is to be decided by the competent national authority, normally on a case-by-case basis. Where an event gravely affects a well-determined area, EU law1 allows the Member State to consider the whole area gravely affected. Force majeure does not, as such, modify or derogate from applicable requirements. However, under Article 59(5) of the same Regulation, where non-compliance is due to force majeure or exceptional circumstances, no penalty is imposed and the beneficiary retains the right to receive the aid. The Commission Communication COM(2024) 2252 provides comprehensive clarification on the application of force majeure under the CAP. Additional guidelines are therefore not needed. The current rules give the Member States flexibility in designing CIS interventions to address sectors or specific types of farming that are facing structural difficulties and are important for socio-economic or environmental reasons, with support conditions adapted to national, regional or local needs. This approach is maintained in the proposal for the CAP post-2027. It would allow Member States to adjust or propose new support options, where needed, to adapt to evolving needs on the ground, but CIS is not a tool to address income losses due to (recurring) crisis events.

E-10-2026-003180.t: Adequacy of existing European tools for supporting farmers in the face of increasingly frequent extreme weather events
qt: to the Commission Emmanouil Fragkos (ECR) Subject:

Farmers in the regional unit of Kavala report that in recent years they have repeatedly suffered severe production losses due to prolonged heatwaves, drought, insufficient rainfall and extreme temperatures. Specifically, in 2024, losses in crops such as maize, sunflower, soya, vines and almonds were estimated at between 60 % and 100 % in some cases. The increasing frequency of extreme weather events and the increasing volatility of weather conditions call into question the adequacy of the existing risk management mechanisms of the common agricultural policy as provided for in Regulation (EU) 2021/2115, in particular as regards mutual funds, insurance tools and the agricultural crisis reserve. Ensuring the sustainability of our agriculture and food security is becoming increasingly important. In view of this, can the Commission answer the following: Does it, in the context of the future CAP, intend to strengthen the risk management and support tools available to producers in order to safeguard the sustainability and income of our primary sector?

In view of this, can the Commission answer the following: Does it, in the context of the future CAP, intend to strengthen the risk management and support tools available to producers in order to safeguard the sustainability and income of our primary sector? (2 October 2026) Both the current Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) (1) and the proposed CAP measures in the future National and Regional Partnership Plans (NRPP) for 2028-2034 (2), provide Member States with a range of tools supporting farmers to prevent the worst effects of climate change-related crises and build up medium and long-term resilience. Investing in farm climate resilience in the period 2028-2034 will be key for the long-term future of farming in the EU. This is why the Commission proposals for 2028-2034 aim to further strengthen the resilience of the sector and its adaptation to climate change, while maintaining targeted public support when major crisis occur. The Commission is proposing a layered approach combining income support, obligatory risk management tools, crisis payments and preventive measures, including agri-environment-climate measures and a new targeted farm transition scheme, to help farmers in the transition to resilient production systems and overcome financial barriers in a holistic way. To increase the uptake of risk management tools like insurances, mutual funds and income stabilisation tools and to help to increase the capacity to absorb negative impacts and compensate farmers for severe production or income losses, the Commission is proposing for the period 2028-2034 that Member States will have to provide support through their NRPP for such schemes if no national systems exist. The Commission will step up its work with the Member States on resilience, risk management and mapping of the insurance gap.

E-10-2026-003179.t: Support for wine growers in Kavala in light of weather-related disasters and plant health pressures
qt: to the Commission Emmanouil Fragkos (ECR) Subject:

Wine growers in the regional unit of Kavala report that during the 2025 growing season they faced a dramatic drop in the commercial production of table grapes. According to producers, prolonged rainfall and increased humidity over many months have led to the widespread development of fungal diseases, with the result that a significant proportion of crops remains unharvested or has deteriorated in quality to such an extent that it is not marketable. Producers are saying that the economic viability of many holdings is now being called into question. Under Regulation (EU) No 1308/2013 on the common organisation of the markets in agricultural products, the Union can adopt specific support measures in cases where there is serious market disturbance or where there are losses resulting from adverse events. With this in mind, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Is it monitoring the impact of extreme weather events on the European wine-growing sector and in particular on Mediterranean wine-producing regions?
Does it intend to consider exceptional support measures for wine-growing areas affected by recurrent extreme weather events and associated plant damage from pests and diseases?
Is it considering strengthening the existing risk management tools for the wine-growing sector in the context of the future CAP reform?

(14 September 2026) The Commission is closely monitoring the wine market. It prepares and publishes dashboards with key wine market data (1) and discusses the various factors impacting the production and sale of wine with delegates from Member States’ administrations and with the sector experts participating in the Market Observatory. Both the current Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) (2) and the support proposed under the National and Regional Partnership Plans (NRPPs) in the period 2028-2034 (3), provide Member States with a range of tools supporting farmers in crisis situations following natural disasters, adverse climatic events or catastrophic events including ensuing plant pests and diseases. Apart from crisis payments for farmers severely impacted by those events, support is also available for the restoration of agricultural production potential. The CAP also provides a specific toolbox of instruments to help farmers manage risks. This includes support for insurance schemes, mutual funds and income stabilisation tools. These instruments are designed to help farmers cope with severe income shocks and production losses. The overall objective for the future is to shift towards a more preventive and structured approach, while maintaining targeted public support when major crises occur. E-10-2026-003177.t: The death of work-free Sundays is rooted in the EU’s anti-labour legislation
qt: to the Commission Kostas Papadakis (NI) Subject:

A provision included in a draft law that allegedly ensures ‘equal pay for men and women for equal work’ extends the working week to include Sundays and public holidays and adds new industry sectors to the list exceptions to compulsory Sunday rest. The new provision is another link in the long-standing policy of abolishing the observance of Sunday as a day of rest. This policy began under the PASOK and Nea Dimokratia coalition Government and was expanded on under the SYRIZA law. This attack, which the Nea Dimokratia Government is escalating, is part of the policy that endorsed the 13-hour workday, the system of adjustable working time arrangements, flexible employment arrangements and the undermining of collective agreements. The huge profits of large corporate groups rely on wage stagnation, intensification of work, flexible forms of employment and the continuous extension of working time. In view of this, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

Where does it stand on the fact that European guidelines and the relevant legislation on the organisation of working time, including Directive 2003/88/EC, constitute the institutional framework that is used by Member State governments to extend work to Sundays and public holidays, deregulate fixed working time and intensify the exploitation of workers?

Where does it stand on the fact that the ever-growing list of exemptions from compulsory Sunday rest, from retail to an increasing number of industry sectors, is the result of implementing an EU strategy according to which production and businesses function based on the competitiveness and profitability needs of corporate groups and not on the needs of workers for fixed working time and rest?

Where does it stand on the fact that the ever-growing list of exemptions from compulsory Sunday rest, from retail to an increasing number of industry sectors, is the result of implementing an EU strategy according to which production and businesses function based on the competitiveness and profitability needs of corporate groups and not on the needs of workers for fixed working time and rest?

(25 September 2026) Directive 2003/88/EC (1) sets out minimum requirements for the protection of the health and safety of workers, in particular limits to working time (not more than 48 hours a week on average, including overtime), minimum daily and weekly rest (at least 11 consecutive hours of daily rest and 35 hours of uninterrupted weekly rest), paid annual leave (at least four weeks per year) and extra protection for night workers. While requiring minimum weekly rest of 35 hours, the directive leaves it to the Member States to determine whether it must include a Sunday. When transposing the directive into national law, Member States must ensure that workers receive at least the protections provided by the directive, but they may adopt or maintain more favourable provisions for workers. Member States have therefore some flexibilities in how they implement the rules and regulate the practical organisation of working time at national level but cannot reduce the minimum rights guaranteed under the directive. Choices on Sunday work for certain sectors are therefore primarily matters of national law and policy, including collective bargaining, but must always comply with the directive’s minimum standards to ensure the objective of health and safety. Upholding workers’ rights is a central element of fair and competitive labour markets. The Commission has recently renewed its commitment to fostering quality jobs in a competitive econom y (2) and reaffirmed that it remains committed to strengthening social dialogue at all levels (3).

E-10-2026-003176.t: Delays caused by the entry/exit system in summer 2026
qt: to the Commission Özlem Demirel (The Left) Subject:

The 2026 summer holidays got off to a rocky start as the biometric entry/exit system (EES) led to lengthy delays at many of the EU’s external borders. According to media reports, outof-order scanners, failed software updates and overloaded self-service kiosks meant hour-long waits in several Member States. Stressing that it was up to the Member States to remedy such issues, the Commission has rejected calls to suspend the checks to ease the pressure. A political solution remains evasive at land borders with the Western Balkans too. 1.

In summer 2026, which Member States have reported which specific technical or organisational problems with the EES (such as equipment failures, failed software updates or bottlenecks) to the Commission?
In light of these reports, has the Commission taken steps to temporarily relax or lift the EES checks or empowered the Member States to that end; if so, what steps and at which border crossings?

If no such relief has been granted, why has the Commission refrained from taking such steps despite the issues documented by air travel and transport associations, and what criteria would need to be met for a suspension to occur?
at: (English version) to the Commission Özlem Demirel (The Left) (30 July 2026) Subject: Delays caused by the entry/exit system in summer 2026 The 2026 summer holidays got off to a rocky start as the biometric entry/exit system (EES) led to lengthy delays at many of the EU’s external borders. According to media reports, out-of-order scanners, failed software updates and overloaded self-service kiosks meant hour-long waits in several Member States. Stressing that it was up to the Member States to remedy such issues, the Commission has rejected calls to suspend the checks to ease the pressure. In light of these reports, has the Commission taken steps to temporarily relax or lift the EES checks or empowered the Member States to that end; if so, what steps and at which border crossings? 3. If no such relief has been granted, why has the Commission refrained from taking such steps despite the issues documented by air travel and transport associations, and what criteria would need to be met for a suspension to occur? (11 September 2026) The Entry/Exit System (EES) records non-EU citizens when they cross EU borders, when they enter and exit the EU, and it does not apply to EU citizens. It has already proven its value by registering, since its launch in October 2026, 185 million border crossings and nearly 64 000 refusals of entry, including almost 1 700 cases concerning individuals considered a security threat to the EU. The Commission is close contact with Member States on the implementation of the EES and offers support where needed. Certain technical and other adjustments at national level remain ongoing, as often occurs in the operational deployment of large-scale IT systems. Regulation (EU) 2025/1534 (1) provides for the possibility to partially suspend the EES by not registering biometrics in the system until 6 September 2026, in certain circumstances, such as longer waiting times. Member States have used this flexibility, when needed, to manage increased passenger flows during the first summer of the EES operation. It should be underlined that the EES is, first and foremost, a border management system that contributes to the safety of EU citizens and the security of the Schengen area.

E-10-2026-003171.t: VAT – collecting social security contributions via the VAT scheme
qt: to the Commission Benoit Cassart (Renew) Subject:
In certain Member States, social security contributions are collected, fully or in part, via the VAT scheme. Is it necessary for the Commission to give prior authorisation for this?
In the Commission’s view, does this authorisation have a positive impact on the determination of own resources allocated to the EU institutions?
at: (English version) to the Commission Benoit Cassart (Renew) (30 July 2026) Subject: VAT — collecting social security contributions via the VAT scheme 1. In certain Member States, social security contributions are collected, fully or in part, via the VAT scheme. Is it necessary for the Commission to give prior authorisation for this? 2. In the Commission’s view, does this authorisation have a positive impact on the determination of own resources allocated to the EU institutions? (17 September 2026) Article 153(4) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union preserves the right of Member States to define the fundamental principles of their social security systems and requires that EU measures must not significantly affect the financial equilibrium of those systems. Accordingly, the organisation and financing of national social security systems, including collection of social security contributions, remain primarily matters for Member States, subject to compliance with applicable EU law. The collection of the mentioned contributions via a VAT scheme is not regulated by the VAT Directive (1). The decision to do so is under the sole responsibility of the concerned Member State. No prior authorisation is required. Such a collection method should, however, not have any impact on the amount of own resources to be allocated to the EU institutions. Moreover, the use of a VAT scheme in certain Member States to calculate and collect social security contributions would not have a positive impact on VAT-OR, as it would not alter the method of collection or the amount of VAT receipts in the Member State concerned. The VAT scheme would simply serve as an administrative tool for the calculation and/or collection of social security contributions. The collection of social security contributions via a general VAT scheme neither requires prior authorisation by the Commission under Regulation (EC) 883/2004 on coordination of social security systems (2). In principle, such contributions do not qualify as social security contributions under that regulation. Tax levies are only qualified as such if there is a direct and sufficiently relevant link with the legislation on social security benefits listed in that regulation (3).

qt: to the Commission Benoit Cassart (Renew) Subject:

The statement in the minutes of the Council meeting on Directive 77/388/EEC of 17 May 1977 on the harmonisation of the laws of the Member States relating to turnover taxes establishes the following in the relative part of Article 4 (‘Taxable Persons’): ‘the Council and the Commission declare that Member States may consider as not liable to value added tax individuals engaged in honorary activities as well as managers, directors, [members of the supervisory board] and company liquidators in their relations with the companies to the extent that they form a part of such companies’. 1.

Does the Commission conclude, in line with that statement, that, today, a Member State is not required to consider the services provided by directors who are natural persons as falling within the scope of VAT?

If so, does the Commission consider that such directors who are natural persons may be exempted from any administrative obligations in terms of VAT in their Member State of residence, including when they hold an appointment in a company established in another Member State which does not apply this exclusion from the scope of VAT in the same way?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (16.9.2026) Under Article 9(1) of Council Directive 2006/112/EC1 (the value-added tax (VAT) Directive), any person who, independently, carries out in any place any economic activity, whatever the purpose or results of that activity, is regarded as a taxable person. Whether the activity of a company director who is a natural person falls within the scope of the VAT Directive must be assessed in the light of that provision and the relevant case-law of the European Court of Justice, in particular as regards the condition of independent economic activity. The Court has clarified that a member of the board of directors of a public limited company does not carry out an economic activity independently, within the meaning of Article 9(1) of the VAT Directive, where that person does not act on his or her own behalf or under his or her own responsibility, and does not bear the economic risk linked to the activity2. The assessment depends on the factual circumstances of the activity concerned. Where a director, as a natural person, resides in one Member State but holds a position in a company established in another Member State, the VAT treatment is assessed by the Member State where the taxation of the activity takes place according to the place of supply rules in the VAT Directive. If this Member State considers the director’s activity to be an independent taxable service, this will result in VAT obligations to occur in that Member State in connection with that supply. The director may be allowed under certain conditions to apply the small businesses VAT exemption scheme3, available since 1 January 2025, also in Member States where they are not established.
1 Council Directive 2006/112/EC of 28 November 2006 on the common system of value added tax, OJ L 347,
11.12.2006, pp. 1–118. 2 Judgment of 21 December 2023, TP v Administration de l’enregistrement, des domaines et de la TVA, C‑288/22, EU:C:2023:1024. 3 See https://sme-vat-rules.ec.europa.eu/index_en.

at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (23.9.2026) Compliance with the Do No Significant Harm (DNSH) principle is a prerequisite for a measure to be included in a recovery and resilience plan (RRP). E-10-2026-003168.t: Urgent measures to tackle religious extremism and protect EU citizens
qt: to the Commission Anna Maria Cisint (PfE) Subject:

The recent raft of Islamist attacks on symbolic European cities and the numerous arrests of radicalised subjects across various Member States highlight the need for a coordinated EU response. A number of Member States have already raised the alarm: Germany’s intelligence service has, for example, released a report which highlights how jihadist organisations view the country as a priority target. Meanwhile, the Austrian authorities have published a document which stated that the number of jihadist terror attacks and offences attributable to Islamic extremists increased by 42.3 % between 2024 and 2025. Given that protecting people from violent acts carried out by religious fundamentalists and ideological extremists is an essential prerequisite for the full exercise of the freedoms enshrined in the Treaties, I ask the Commission: 1.
What action will it take to combat Islamist radicalism and jihadist terrorism at EU level?
Does it think that the Union’s current immigration and anti-radicalisation policies are fit for the purposes of keeping European citizens safe and upholding the EU’s fundamental values?

E-10-2026-003167.t: Mandate and coordination of the Security College Secretariat
qt: to the Commission José Cepeda (S&D) Subject:

On 22 July 2026, the Commission announced that a Security College Secretariat would be set up to provide integrated analysis on developments in the strategic environment. The decision is a response to the EU’s need for intelligence capabilities to compile information, detect patterns and build a common picture of hybrid threats. However, the announcement raises a number of questions: 1.

What is the legal basis for its detailed mandate, the sources of information – including classified information – it will be able to use, the authorised recipients of its products and the rules applicable to classification, protection, access and disclosure of such information?

How will the Commission ensure that its duties do not overlap with those of the Single Intelligence Analysis Capacity (SIAC) – which is defined as a single entry point for intelligence contributions from the Member States – in order to prevent the European External Action Service (EEAS) from being weakened, stop public resources being fragmented and ensure information is not scattered?

What involvement will Member States and their intelligence services have, what powers will they retain over the information provided and what specific products, capabilities or operational benefits will they receive?

E-10-2026-003166.t: Territorial scope of the amended EU-Morocco Agreement for scientific and technological cooperation concerning Morocco’s participation in PRIMA
qt: to the Commission Andreas Schieder (S&D), Oihane Agirregoitia Martínez (Renew), Vladimir Prebilič (Verts/ALE), Per Clausen (The Left), Ruth Firmenich (NI), Irene Montero (The Left), Elisabeth Grossmann (S&D), Jaume Asens Llodrà (Verts/ALE), Hannes Heide (S&D), Günther Sidl (S&D), Estrella Galán (The Left), Diana Riba i Giner (Verts/ALE), Evelyn Regner (S&D), Matjaž Nemec (S&D), Udo Bullmann (S&D), Martin Günther (The Left), Pernando Barrena Arza (The Left), Vicent Marzà Ibáñez (Verts/ALE), Sebastian Tynkkynen (ECR) Subject:

The proposed amendment to the Agreement for scientific and technological cooperation between the European Union and the Kingdom of Morocco establishes the conditions for Morocco’s participation in the Partnership for Research and Innovation in the Mediterranean Area (PRIMA). In its judgments concerning EU-Morocco agreements, the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) has consistently held that Western Sahara is a territory that is separate and distinct from Morocco under international law. Consequently, agreements concluded between the EU and Morocco cannot apply to Western Sahara unless this is expressly provided for and subject to the applicable requirements under international law. In the light of the above: 1.

What legal and administrative safeguards has the Commission put in place to ensure that no projects, funding, research activities or infrastructure financed under PRIMA are implemented in Western Sahara through the participation of Morocco?

If research entities established in or operating in Western Sahara were to seek participation in projects financed under the Agreement, how would the Commission ensure compliance with the case-law of the CJEU and the EU’s obligations under international law?

Has the Commission carried out a legal assessment of the territorial scope of the amended Agreement in the light of the CJEU’s judgments concerning the applicability of EU-Morocco agreements to Western Sahara, and if so, will it make that assessment available to Parliament?

E-10-2026-003165.t: Temporary VAT exemptions for those affected by forest fires
qt: to the Commission Jorge Buxadé Villalba (PfE) Subject:

Recent forest fires in Spain have destroyed homes, farms, businesses and essential goods. Victims will have to pay VAT for a second time when they repair or rebuild their homes and replace goods on which they have already paid tax. Article 101a of Directive 2006/112 (Directive on the common system of value added tax) allows for exemptions for certain goods intended for disaster victims. What is more, point 10 of Annex III allows for reduced rates to be applied to the repair and reconstruction of dwellings. However, Article 52 of Directive 2009/132 specifically excludes materials and equipment intended for rebuilding from VAT exemptions. In view of the above: 1.
Does the Commission consider a temporary VAT exemption restricted to certain geographical areas for reconstruction of the homes affected by the fires in Spain to be compatible with Article 98?
Has Spain requested an extraordinary temporary derogation to allow zero VAT to be applied to the reconstruction and replacement of essential goods destroyed in the fires?
Will the Commission consider it necessary to amend Article 101a to expressly cover reconstruction efforts following major natural disasters?

(28 September 2026) Ahead of the wildfire season, Spain has proactively activated the Union Civil Protection Mechanism (UCPM) with the request to preposition groundfire teams. During summer 2026, the Commission’s Emergency Response Coordination Centre (ERCC) coordinated support to Spain including firefighting planes, ground forest firefighting teams and deployment of the rescEU aerial assets. Copernicus Rapid Mapping Mode has also activated several times during the same period. Article 101a of Directive 2006/112/EC (1) was introduced as part of the 2022 reform of the value added tax (VAT) rates framework (2). It provides for a mechanism to grant certain tax exemptions in exceptional situations. Where the Commission has authorised a Member State, pursuant to Article 53 of Directive 2009/132/EC (3) to exempt from VAT certain goods imported for the benefit of disaster victims, that Member State may extend the exemption, under the same conditions, to intra-Community acquisitions and supplies of those goods and related services. Such an authorisation can however not extend to materials and equipment intended for reconstruction, in view of the express exclusion laid down in Article 52 of that directive. The Commission has not received from Spain a request for authorisation under Article 53 of Directive 2009/132/EC. Directive 2006/112/EC however allows Member States to apply reduced value-added tax (VAT) rates to the renovation, alteration, demolition, reconstruction and repair of housing and private dwellings (4). Against this background, the Commission does not currently envisage proposing an amendment to Article 101a.

E-10-2026-003163.t: EU funding and environmental and safety concerns regarding the reconversion of the former Winchester site in Anagni (Italy)
qt: to the Commission Cristina Guarda (Verts/ALE) Subject:

This project received support under the EU’s Act in Support of Ammunition Production (ASAP).1 However, although project applications were required to be submitted in complete form by December 2023, key documents, including the fire brigade risk assessment and the technical report, appear to be dated October and December 2024.2 In the light of the above: 1.

Is the Commission aware of this project and has it assessed its compliance with EU environmental, public health and industrial safety legislation, including the adequacy of remediation measures and environmental monitoring requirements?

How does the Commission explain the apparent discrepancy between the ASAP application deadline and the later dates of essential technical and safety documentation, and were these documents available during the evaluation and funding process?

at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (14.9.2026) As recalled in the Commission’s Report on the implementation of Regulation (EU) 2023/1525 on supporting ammunition production (ASAP)1, ASAP involves handling sensitive and classified information. In particular, the technical parts of the proposals were classified, in line with applicable security requirements. The Commission therefore cannot disclose implementation details beyond what has been made public. The Commission confirms that all ASAP proposals are selected in line with the eligibility, selection and award criteria laid down in the Regulation (EU) 2023/1525. The evaluation results obtained the positive opinion of the ASAP Programme Committee on 13 March 2024 and were published on 15 March 20242. ASAP funding does not exempt its beneficiaries from respecting any applicable national, including EU-derived, legislation on environment, public health and safety. Competent authorities are responsible for ensuring compliance. Although Member States may resort to potentially applicable defence exemptions, the ASAP Regulation recalled that these should not compromise the environment, health and safety. Selection of proposals under competitive calls is based on information submitted at the application deadline. Following selection, the Commission and the Coordinator of the awarded consortia carried out the standard Grant Agreement Preparation (GAP) process to finalise the technical, financial and administrative elements of the grant in accordance with the Financial Regulation3.

E-10-2026-003162.t: Public participation in and publicity of SEZ proceedings: compatibility with EU law
qt: to the Commission Cristina Guarda (Verts/ALE) Subject:

Article 15(1) of Italian Decree-Law No 124/2023 governing the Single Special Economic Zone (SEZ) for Southern Italy provides for the application for a single authorisation to be submitted to the SEZ Digital One-Stop Shop for technical documentation. There is no provision requiring the publication of a notice of submission of the application on the municipal noticeboards of the municipalities concerned, nor in local newspapers, nor by displaying it at the site where works will take place. Article 6 of the Aarhus Convention requires ‘timely and effective’ public information in environmental decision-making; the Court of Justice of the European Union has also clarified that this information must actually reach the public concerned (C-535/18, 7 November 2019) and that the public concerned must enjoy wide access to environmental justice (C-243/15, 16 April 2015, Article 11 of Directive 2011/92/EU). In its judgment in Case C-243/15 of 8 November 2016, the Court of Justice of the European Union reiterated that Article 6(1)(b) of the Aarhus Convention grants environmental organisations the right to participate in decision-making procedures with environmental impacts and to obtain effective judicial protection of that right. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following question: Is a piece of legislation compatible with EU law if, by providing for the possibility of implementing a change in urban planning, it does not provide for an appropriate system of publicity around the administrative procedure so that environmental organisations and individual citizens can participate in decision-making procedures relating to projects likely to have effects on the environment?
at: (English version) to the Commission Cristina Guarda (Verts/ALE) (29 July 2026) Subject: Public participation in and publicity of SEZ proceedings: compatibility with EU law Article 15(1) of Italian Decree-Law No 124/2023 governing the Single Special Economic Zone (SEZ) for Southern Italy provides for the application for a single authorisation to be submitted to the SEZ Digital One-Stop Shop for technical documentation. There is no provision requiring the publication of a notice of submission of the application on the municipal noticeboards of the municipalities concerned, nor in local newspapers, nor by displaying it at the site where works will take place. Article 6 of the Aarhus Convention requires ‘timely and effective’ public information in environmental decision-making; the Court of Justice of the European Union has also clarified that this information must actually reach the public concerned (C535/18, 7 November 2019) and that the public concerned must enjoy wide access to environmental justice (C-243/15, 16 April 2015, Article 11 of Directive 2011/92/EU). In its judgment in Case C-243/15 of 8 November 2016, the Court of Justice of the European Union reiterated that Article 6(1) (b) of the Aarhus Convention grants environmental organisations the right to participate in decision-making procedures with environmental impacts and to obtain effective judicial protection of that right. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following question: Is a piece of legislation compatible with EU law if, by providing for the possibility of implementing a change in urban planning, it does not provide for an appropriate system of publicity around the administrative procedure so that environmental organisations and individual citizens can participate in decision-making procedures relating to projects likely to have effects on the environment? (23 September 2026) Urban planning is a Member States’ competence. However, the adoption or authorisation of urban planning plans, programmes or projects must comply with all applicable EU law, including the rules on transparency and public participation under the Strategic Environmental Assessment Directive (1) and the Environmental Liability Directive (2). Moreover, where a specific project is likely to have significant effects on the environment, Member States must inform the public timely and effectively and allow participation at an early stage in the decision-making process. This follows, among others, from Article 6 of the Aarhus Convention (3) and Articles 6 and 11 of the Environmental Impact Assessment Directive (4). The case law of the Court of Justice of the EU (5) has clarified that information must be organised in such a way that it can genuinely reach the public concerned and allow the public to exercise their rights effectively. It has also confirmed that environmental organisations are entitled to participate in relevant procedures and benefit from effective judicial protection of those rights. Italian legislation, including Article 15(1) of Decree-Law No 124/2023 referred to by the Honourable Member, must be read in light of the above-mentioned EU legislation. In any case, the rights provided for under relevant EU legislation must be granted under national law.

E-10-2026-003161.t: Determining whether, under EU law, Italy’s SEZ mission structure can postpone the EIAs of the Ostuni and Loiri Porto San Paolo tourist resort projects
qt: to the Commission Cristina Guarda (Verts/ALE) Subject:

Despite the local and regional authorities’ opposition1 to the construction of two luxury tourist resorts in Ostuni (Province of Brindisi) and Loiri Porto San Paolo (Province of Gallura NorthEast Sardinia), Italy’s Special Economic Zone (SEZ) mission structure has intervened by issuing single authorisations No 423/20252 (which approved an amended version of Ostuni Council’s development plan for the Mogale district) and No 74/2026 (which, though it gave the go-ahead to the Tavolara Bay project in Loiri Porto San Paolo, has since been revoked as a result of the local council’s decision to withdraw its authorisation). The notices published by the Official Gazette of the Apulia Region (BURP) specify that, in addition to definitively giving the green light to the amended Mogale district development plan, single authorisation No 423/2025 also deferred the related environmental impact assessment (EIA) to the final design phase (which precedes the issuing of the building permit), even though it had already confirmed that the project’s building type complied with regulations and endorsed the resort’s site and massing provisions and its aesthetic and construction arrangements3. Article 2(1) of Directive 2011/92/EU requires projects that are likely to have a significant impact on the environment to be assessed prior to approval. Article 2(2) states that EIAs can be integrated into national procedures, but not in such a way as to deprive them of their preventive function. In the light of the above, I ask the Commission to clarify: 1.
Whether postponing the EIA of a project whose essential layout and related townplanning variants have already been approved is an approach that is in line with Directive 2011/92/EU?
Whether SEZ proceedings have the power to amend urban planning arrangements before the completion of the related EIA?

Retrieved from the Official Gazette of the Apulia Region (BURP) No 91, 13 November 2025, pp. 91131-91133 (particularly p.91132, see https://burp.regione.puglia.it/documents/20135/2703581/ATTI_OSTUNI.pdf/e6e7085a-1b1c-492e62e8-ad045a43a820?version=1.0&t=1763042279573). 3 See Ibid, p. 91132, where it is stated that single authorisation No 423/2025 ‘constitutes final approval of the amended development plan’ and defers the EIA to the ‘subsequent executive planning stage’ of a private project whose ‘aesthetic and construction arrangements, site and massing provisions and building type’ have already been approved. 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (23.9.2026) Any project falling within the scope the Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) Directive1 and likely to have significant effects on the environment by virtue, inter alia, of its nature, size or location, shall be made subject to an assessment before authorisation2. Where Member States chose to apply a streamlined (joint or coordinated) procedure for assessments of the environmental impacts of a given project arising from two or more Directives, such a procedure shall comply with the obligations under these Directives. In addition, the Court of Justice of the EU has clarified that Article 2(1) of the EIA Directive requires an environmental impact assessment to be carried out if, in the case the granting of development consent comprises more than one stage, it becomes apparent, in the course of the second stage, that the project is likely to have significant effects on the environment by virtue inter alia of its nature, size or location3. Urban planning is a Member States’ competence. Nevertheless, the adoption or authorisation of any plans, programmes or projects related to urban planning must comply with the provisions of all applicable EU legislation, including those of the Strategic Environmental Assessment Directive4. It is primarily for the national administrative and judicial authorities to ensure that EU environmental law is correctly applied. In its role as guardian of the Treaties, the Commission will monitor the application of the provisions of EU law and may decide to take appropriate action if systemic problems arise5.

E-10-2026-003160.t: PFAS in Veneto – denial of access to environmental data and food safety at risk
qt: to the Commission Cristina Guarda (Verts/ALE) Subject:

In 2021, the Veneto Regional Administrative Court found in favour of Greenpeace and the Mamme No PFAS association, accepting their appeals against the Region of Veneto’s refusal to hand over complete data on analyses of PFAS in food.1 More recently, journalist Marco Milioni reported that, rather than provide full documentation, the region only partially responded to his request for access to documents concerning PFAS in the areas around the Pedemontana Veneta motorway. What is more, many requests for access to documents have been made by regional councillors, including me, which have never been answered. These incidents point to a systematic failure to provide access to information of clear public interest, and they have been taking place while the EU framework has been updated to incorporate the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) opinion from 2020, which set a new tolerable weekly intake of 4.4 ng per kilo of body weight2. Regulation (EU) 2022/2388 also introduced maximum limits for those substances in a number of foods of animal origin, including eggs, meat, fish, crustaceans and molluscs. In view of the above: 1.
Given this systematic denial of access to data, does the Commission intend to look into whether Directive 2003/4/EC on access to environmental information has been breached?
Does it consider it appropriate for food safety assessments to be based on data or thresholds predating the 2020 EFSA opinion?
