E-10-2026-003159.t: Safeguards, transparency and accountability of EU economic interests in Colombia
qt: to the Commission Cristina Guarda (Verts/ALE) Subject:

According to Colombia’s Ombudsman’s Office1, 81 human rights defenders were killed in the first five months of 2025, while the UN reports2 that nearly 100 are killed each year. More than 70 % of Colombian territory is affected by the presence of non-state armed actors exercising varying degrees of social control, in some areas completely undermining the autonomy of local authorities and Indigenous, Afro-descendant and peasant communities. According to Transparency for Colombia, among member countries of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, Colombia ranks among the lowest in terms of corruption perception, surpassing only Mexico and Türkiye. Many of these areas host European companies, receive European investments, or produce goods exported to the EU. 1.

What transparency requirements and accessible mechanisms are available to enable civil society to monitor, oversee and obtain information about the implementation of these safeguards, particularly with regard to business and human rights?

What specific action do the Commission and the EU Delegation to Colombia take when they become aware of alleged human rights or environmental violations linked to European companies or economic interests, and what follow-up and remedial measures are available to ensure accountability?

E-10-2026-003158.t: Transparency, human rights safeguards and public oversight of Global Gateway projects in Colombia
qt: to the Commission Cristina Guarda (Verts/ALE) Subject:

Civil society organisations have reported a lack of transparent and accessible information regarding planned or ongoing projects within the framework of the Global Gateway strategy. The Commission’s website mentions five project areas in Colombia, including green hydrogen production and renewable energy. However, taking into account the current risks related to human and environmental rights in Colombia, where more than 70 % of the national territory is affected by the presence of nonstate armed actors, free, prior and informed consultation faces enormous challenges. 1.

E-10-2026-003157.t: Spectrum renewal in Portugal – compatibility with the Digital Networks Act and the Draghi report
qt: to the Commission Paulo Cunha (PPE) Subject:

The Draghi report1 highlights the need to deepen the internal market and recommends doubling the length of spectrum licences to mitigate investment risk and encourage the allocation of capital to new technologies. This idea was covered in the Digital Networks Act (DNA) proposal2, which establishes telecommunications spectrum usage rights that are indefinite or last for at least 40 years and renew automatically. The Portuguese regulator, ANACOM, has approved a draft decision3 which includes renewals lasting only 6 to 14 years. This divergence from EU guidelines could create regulatory uncertainty and asymmetries between Member States, which would likely have a negative impact on 5G and 6G investment and resilience, digital sovereignty and the single market. ANACOM’s public consultation4 on this matter is open until 27 August 2026. In light of the above: 1.
To what extent does the Commission see national deadlines of 6 to 14 years as being consistent with EU telecoms policy objectives – particularly those in the DNA?
What tools does it plan to make available to national regulators to promote convergence with the Draghi report?
What impact could this uncertainty have on investment in telecommunications, in view of the 5G technological sovereignty and security agenda?

E-10-2026-003156.t: The impact of the benchmark-based design of CBAM pricing on EU metalworking SMEs
qt: to the Commission Svenja Hahn (Renew) Subject:

Despite innovative, patented products and processes, EU small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in the metalwork industry are suffering from unfair competition, particularly from China and other non-EU countries. Of particular concern is the benchmark-oriented approach used to price CO₂ emissions embedded in foreign steel imports under the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM). The ZEW – Leibniz Centre for European Economic Research’s policy brief No. 26-10/2026 clearly identifies disadvantages of this approach. The CBAM’s design, combined with regional subsidies for metalworking companies outside the EU, has damaged EU competitiveness and contributed to significant job losses in the sector, particularly among SMEs. 1.

Will the Commission consider revising the benchmark-based methodology for CBAM pricing, e.g. to base it on average steel production values, including the energy sources used, which would reduce both distortions and administrative burden?

Can the Commission confirm that the CN codes 93052000, 87089499, 87089997, 84339000 and 84799070 fall unambiguously within the scope of the CBAM rules, and if not, what steps will it take to close this gap?

What measures does the Commission plan to take to address the competitive disadvantage and resulting job losses suffered by EU metalworking SMEs due to CBAM circumvention, unfair competition from non-EU countries and subsidised foreign production, pending any revision of the CBAM’s design?
at: (English version) to the Commission Svenja Hahn (Renew) (28 July 2026) Subject: The impact of the benchmark-based design of CBAM pricing on EU metalworking SMEs Despite innovative, patented products and processes, EU small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in the metalwork industry are suffering from unfair competition, particularly from China and other non-EU countries. Of particular concern is the benchmark-oriented approach used to price CO 2 emissions embedded in foreign steel imports under the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM). The ZEW — Leibniz Centre for European Economic Research’s policy brief No. 2610/2026 clearly identifies disadvantages of this approach. The CBAM’s design, combined with regional subsidies for metalworking companies outside the EU, has damaged EU competitiveness and contributed to significant job losses in the sector, particularly among SMEs. 1. Will the Commission consider revising the benchmark-based methodology for CBAM pricing, e.g. to base it on average steel production values, including the energy sources used, which would reduce both distortions and administrative burden? 2. Can the Commission confirm that the CN codes 93052000, 87089499, 87089997, 84339000 and 84799070 fall unambiguously within the scope of the CBAM rules, and if not, what steps will it take to close this gap? 3. What measures does the Commission plan to take to address the competitive disadvantage and resulting job losses suffered by EU metalworking SMEs due to CBAM circumvention, unfair competition from non-EU countries and subsidised foreign production, pending any revision of the CBAM’s design? (23 September 2026) From 2026 to 2034, the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) obligation is adjusted by the equivalent amount of free allocation that EU producers receive for the same goods. This adjustment is based on CBAM benchmarks reflecting the performance of the best installations in the EU. No revision of this methodology is currently foreseen. This approach ensures an equivalent carbon price for domestic and imported goods, thereby addressing the risk of carbon leakage and reducing market distortions. The CBAM currently applies to a limited set of mostly basic material goods, listed in Annex I of the CBAM Regulation (1). The Commission proposed in December 2025 (2) to extend the scope of the CBAM to steel and aluminium-intensive downstream goods. These goods were selected based on clear and objective criteria (3). The legislative proposal is currently under discussion by the co-legislators. The Council adopted its general approach on 12 June 2026 (4), which includes the proposal to add Combined Nomenclature codes 87089499, 87089997 and 84799070 to the CBAM scope. The European Parliament adopted its position on the Commission proposal on 15 September 2026. (5) To ensure an effective implementation of the CBAM, the Commission, in collaboration with national authorities, will continuously monitor reported emissions and corresponding trade, to identify practices of circumvention and non-compliance with the CBAM Regulation and secondary legislation. The Commission proposal of December 2025 includes a wide set of further measures aimed at addressing the risk of circumvention and avoidance of CBAM obligations, including strengthened reporting requirements for high-risk goods or origins.

E-10-2026-003155.t: Dangerous delays in the completion and operation of critical safety infrastructure on the Greek railway network
qt: to the Commission Elena Kountoura (The Left) Subject:

According to recent statements by the CEO of Hellenic Railways1, the European signalling and automatic braking system (ETCS) is still not fully operational on the Greek railway network three and a half years after the criminal railway disaster at Tempi, despite repeated commitments by the Greek Government2. At the same time, according to railway sector representatives, there are still signalling ‘dead spots’ and significant delays in completing critical infrastructure projects, making it impossible to keep to the given timeline3. What is more, the Regulatory Authority for Railways (RAS) has found that a significant number of Hellenic Train vehicles do not meet the requirements for the proper functioning of the ETCS4. These developments raise serious questions as to the respect of the timeline set out in the action plan submitted by the Greek Government to the Commission, as well as the effectiveness of the ongoing infringement procedure for the protection of passengers on the Greek railway network. With this in mind, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
What view does it take of the fact that, three and a half years after the Tempi accident, the ETCS is still not fully operational on the Greek railway network, despite the obligations under EU law?
When should the ETCS be fully operational in line with the action plan?

What measures does it intend to take in the context of the infringement procedure, given that the full operation of the ETCS is still delayed, despite repeated commitments by the Greek Government, undermining the safety of passengers?

On 23 July, the CEO of Hellenic Railways stated before the competent parliamentary committee that ‘the ETCS is not currently operational’, while Hellenic Railways clarified that its operation would only start once the certification and licensing procedures had been completed. 2 The Prime Minister had promised that the ETCS would be operational by November 2025, after which the Deputy Transport Minister announced that the Athens-Thessaloniki line would have fully operational safety systems by the end of August 2026. 3 According to the head of the OSE workers’ union, ‘... there is no prospect of the infrastructure projects being completed within the next six months. It is therefore difficult to make electronic safety systems fully operational as well’. 4 The RAS has identified that 100 vehicles (approximately 70 trains) belonging to Hellenic Train do not meet the European technical specifications for the proper functioning of the ETCS, with dozens lacking documentation. 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (21.9.2026) The Commission is aware of the difficulties faced by Greece with the European Rail Traffic Management System (ERTMS) deployment, which are common in many Member States. Given the complexity of this process, the European Union Agency for Railways, at the request of Greece, is supporting the Greek stakeholders in developing an effective ERTMS deployment plan taking into account the applicable deadlines set out in the revised trans-European transport network (TEN-T) Regulation1. Greece is currently preparing the above-mentioned ERTMS deployment plan which will be formally notified to the Commission in the coming months. The plan is expected to include dates by which ERTMS will be put into operation on specific lines. The infringement proceeding case INFR (2023)20362 concerns failure to comply with the requirements of the Rail Safety Directive3. The deployment of European Train Control System (ETCS), key part of ERTMS, is not in the scope of this proceeding. The Commission also notes that although deployment of ETCS on the network contributes to the improvement of rail safety, it is possible for the railway system to operate safely without it, provided that appropriate alternative risk control measures are implemented.
1 Regulation (EU) 2024/1679 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 June 2024 on Union

guidelines for the development of the trans-European transport network, amending Regulations (EU) 2021/1153 and (EU) No 913/2010 and repealing Regulation (EU) No 1315/2013, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1679/oj. 2 Press release: https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/inf_24_6006. 3 Directive (EU) 2016/798 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 11 May 2016 on railway safety (recast), ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2016/798/oj.

E-10-2026-003154.t: Protection of Spanish greyhounds used for hunting against ill-treatment and abandonment
qt: to the Commission Yvan Verougstraete (Renew) Subject:

For a number of years, animal welfare associations have been speaking out in the media about the mistreatment of Spanish greyhounds. Reared for hunting, these greyhounds are often mistreated, locked up in poor conditions, and then abandoned as soon as they are no longer useful. At the end of the season, the least effective dogs may be subjected to violence, abandoned or be put down. Despite the work of grassroots associations, the structural problem remains: as long as hunting with greyhounds is allowed, these abuses and acts of cruelty will continue. 1.
What specific action can the EU executive take as part of its pet welfare strategy (dogs and cats)?
Does the Commission intend to take action to improve the protection of greyhounds used for hunting, in particular to protect them against being abandoned, ill-treated and put down?

E-10-2026-003153.t: Compatibility of lethal police operations with Article 2 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union and investigation transparency standards
qt: to the Commission Friedrich Pürner (NI) Subject:
Compatibility of lethal police operations with Article 2 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union and investigation transparency standards

The deployment of a special police unit in Berlin (Federal Republic of Germany) resulted in the fatal shooting of a citizen, Abdul B. Article 2 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, read in conjunction with Article 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR), requires Member States to limit any use of lethal force by state bodies to what is strictly necessary and to ensure an effective, independent and transparent investigation. 1.

What legal framework and administrative guidelines exist at EU level to monitor compliance with the principle of proportionality in the context of special police unit operations in the framework of Article 2 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights?

What are the Commission’s minimum requirements for transparency and access to information held by public authorities regarding investigation files (operational protocols, autopsy and ballistic reports) in relation to deaths linked to the use of state force in the Member States?

Does the Commission see a need for reform with regard to uniform standards for independent investigation and public information in the event of the lethal use of firearms by security authorities in the European Union?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (21.9.2026) Maintenance of law and order is a national competence. However, as the Commission set out in its reply to written question E-004924/20251, any use of force by law enforcement authorities should always be exercised in a proportionate manner. Article 2 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union2 states that everyone has the right to life. However, the Charter applies to Member States only when they are implementing EU law3. It is the responsibility of national authorities and courts to ensure that national measures adhere to fundamental rights as provided for in their constitutional order, and in line with their European and international human rights obligations. In the case referred to by the Honourable Member, it is therefore for the German authorities to conduct independent investigations.
1 https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/E-10-2025-004924-ASW_EN.html. 2 https://www.europarl.europa.eu/charter/pdf/text_en.pdf. 3 Please see footnote 2.

E-10-2026-003149.t: Guaranteeing access to drinking water as a human right
qt: to the Commission Nikolas Farantouris (S&D) Subject:

In 2010, the UN General Assembly recognised the right to safe drinking water and sanitation as a human right1. The European Citizens’ Initiative ‘Right2Water’ and the European Parliament Resolution of 2015 on the follow-up to this initiative called on the Commission to enshrine this right in law2. The recast Directive on drinking water (Directive (EU) 2020/2184) improved access to water, especially for vulnerable groups3 and the European Water Resilience Strategy of 2025 explicitly recognises access to clean and affordable water as a human right. However, the right has not yet been enshrined in EU primary law. In view of this, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

Does it intend to take legislative or other steps (including a possible proposal to amend the Charter of Fundamental Rights or strengthen existing directives) to fully guarantee access to drinking water as a human right?
What additional measures is it planning as part of the Water Resilience Strategy to ensure the universal and effective exercise of this right, especially for vulnerable groups?
https://digitallibrary.un.org/record/687002?v=pdf. https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/TA-8-2015-0294_EN.html https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2020/2184/oj.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (29.9.2026) The EU legal framework has been strengthened through the recast Drinking Water Directive1, which requires Member States to improve or maintain access to water intended for human consumption for all, with particular attention to vulnerable and marginalised groups. This Directive needs to be implemented in accordance with the fundamental rights and principles recognised by the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union2 by ensuring full respect for, inter alia, the right to dignity (Article 1) or the right to life (Article 2) and the EU's commitment to a high level of environmental protection (Article 37). Under the European Water Resilience Strategy3, access to clean and affordable water is presented as a human right and a public good. As part of this Strategy, the Commission is focusing on effective implementation of EU law, support for investment in water infrastructure, reduction of pollution, improved water efficiency and resilience, and better protection of water resources. The Commission will continue to promote access to safe drinking water, with particular attention to vulnerable groups.
1 Directive (EU) 2020/2184 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 16 December 2020 on the quality

of water intended for human consumption (recast), OJ L 435, 23.12.2020, p. 1–62. 2 https://www.europarl.europa.eu/charter/pdf/text_en.pdf. 3 https://commission.europa.eu/topics/environment/water-resilience-strategy_en.

E-10-2026-003148.t: Compatibility of the suspension of Hungarian public service media news services with EU law
qt: to the Commission Tamás Deutsch (PfE), Kinga Gál (PfE), Enikő Győri (PfE), András Gyürk (PfE), Viktória Ferenc (PfE), György Hölvényi (PfE), Csaba Dömötör (PfE), András László (PfE), Ernő Schaller-Baross (PfE), Pál Szekeres (PfE) Subject:

Article 11 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union guarantees everyone the right to freedom of expression, including the freedom to receive and impart information and ideas without interference by public authority. Furthermore, EU media legislation requires public service media to operate independently and impartially, with their management selected through transparent, objective and non-discriminatory procedures. The European Media Freedom Act also aims to protect media freedom and editorial independence from political and economic interference. Following the Hungarian Government’s decision to suspend the news services of Hungary’s public service television, radio and online news portal: 1.

Does the Commission consider that this decision is compatible with Article 11 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights, which guarantees the right to receive and impart information without interference by public authority?

Does the Commission consider that the suspension of public service media news services and the Government’s intervention in their operation are compatible with the EU rules safeguarding the independence and impartiality of public service media, including the European Media Freedom Act?
at: (English version) to the Commission Tamás Deutsch (PfE), Kinga Gál (PfE), Enikő Győri (PfE), András Gyürk (PfE), Viktória Ferenc (PfE), György Hölvényi (PfE), Csaba Dömötör (PfE), András László (PfE), Ernő Schaller-Baross (PfE), Pál Szekeres (PfE) (28 July 2026) Subject: Compatibility of the suspension of Hungarian public service media news services with EU law Article 11 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union guarantees everyone the right to freedom of expression, including the freedom to receive and impart information and ideas without interference by public authority. Furthermore, EU media legislation requires public service media to operate independently and impartially, with their management selected through transparent, objective and non-discriminatory procedures. The European Media Freedom Act also aims to protect media freedom and editorial independence from political and economic interference. Following the Hungarian Government’s decision to suspend the news services of Hungary’s public service television, radio and online news portal: 1.

Does the Commission consider that this decision is compatible with Article 11 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights, which guarantees the right to receive and impart information without interference by public authority?

Does the Commission consider that the suspension of public service media news services and the Government’s intervention in their operation are compatible with the EU rules safeguarding the independence and impartiality of public service media, including the European Media Freedom Act?

(21 September 2026) The Commission notes that amendments to the Hungarian Media Act, adopted in June 2026, brought about the termination of the previous Public Service Foundation and the establishment of a new Independent Public Media Board. The legislation establishes new rules regulating the composition of the new Board, nominations thereto, the termination of office and its respective tasks, powers and remuneration of office holders thereof as well as rules governing the public service media provider itself, including the appointment of the provider’s Chief Executive Officer, its financing and management. A key requirement of the European Media Freedom Act (EMFA) (1) is that Member States shall ensure that public service media providers are editorially and functionally independent and provide in an impartial manner a plurality of information and opinions to their audiences. The Commission understands that the suspension of broadcasts was a temporary step in the context of the above-mentioned reform, with the above-mentioned goals in mind and that the service has resumed. The Commission will continue exchanges with the Hungarian authorities in the context of the enforcement of the EMFA.

Regulation (EU) 2024/1083 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 11 April 2024 establishing a common framework for media services in the internal market and amending Directive 2010/13/EU (European Media Freedom Act).

E-10-2026-003147.t: France’s use of EMSA drones in the English Channel
qt: to the Commission Özlem Demirel (The Left) Subject:

Since 2020, the European Maritime Safety Agency (EMSA) has been deploying unmanned helicopters (Schiebel Camcopter S100), supplied by Nordic Unmanned, from Cap Gris-Nez in France to measure sulphur and nitrogen oxide emissions from ships in Emission Control Area (ECA) covering the North Sea and English Channel. The drones are operated by the French Directorate-General for Maritime Affairs. They are also used for general coast guard functions. This includes preventing migration to the UK. 1.

What costs were incurred by EMSA and France for the deployment of EMSA’s remotely piloted aircraft systems in the English Channel between 2020 and 2026, broken down by framework contract with Nordic Unmanned and services actually performed, and how many flight hours have been completed by the Schiebel Camcopter S100 drones in each year since 2020?

In each of these years of operation, what proportion or number of flight hours was apportioned to emissions monitoring as opposed to complementary tasks such as maritime security, fisheries surveillance or migration control, and in how many maritime emergencies was the Camcopter100 used in each of these years?

Where is the collected surveillance data streamed to, and to what extent are EMSA, Frontex or France’s neighbouring countries also given access, and in what way are the UK authorities involved in the operational coordination of the missions?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (2.10.2026) The European Maritime Safety Agency (EMSA) may provide Remote Piloted Aviation Systems services to Member States for the purposes they define. Flights are multipurpose as laid out by the European coast guard cooperation1: once deployed, the unmanned aerial vehicle can be used for emissions monitoring, general surveillance, search and rescue and fisheries control. Member States have operational and planning control of the unmanned aerial vehicle, as responsible coastal or port State. The EMSA Work Programme sets out the number of deployment days (days that the drone is available on site) as performance indicator. The table below shows statistics for 2020-25 for sulphur oxides emission measurements, while those for 2026 are not yet available. Costs cover EMSA’s specific contracts. EMSA does not hold data on costs incurred by French authorities. The Schiebel Campocter S-100 has been used throughout. Emissions monitoring data is provided to Member States and streamed into the EU port State control reporting tool (THETIS) for dissemination to Port State Control authorities. Access rights are defined in THETIS for authorised users.
1 Regulation (EU) 2025/2434 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 26 November 2025 on the
European Maritime Safety Agency and repealing Regulation (EC) No 1406/2002 (Text with EEA relevance), article 12.

E-10-2026-003146.t: Transparency and evaluation of EU funding for reconstruction in northern Evia following the 2021 fires
qt: to the Commission Maria Zacharia (NI) Subject:

Five years after the fires in northern Evia in 2021, considerable funding has been announced for the region’s reconstruction from the Recovery and Resilience Facility, the Cohesion Funds, the NSRF and other EU funding instruments. However, no comprehensive report has been published setting out, by project and funding instrument, the amounts approved, contracted and disbursed, the implementation rate and the physical progress achieved. This shortcoming raises questions regarding transparency, accountability and the evaluation of the effectiveness of the interventions. In accordance with Article 317 TFEU and the Financial Regulation (EU, Euratom) 2018/1046, the Commission is responsible for the implementation of the Union budget in accordance with the principles of sound financial management. With this in mind, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

Does it have a consolidated overview of EU funding for northern Evia, broken down by funding instrument; project; amounts approved, contracted and disbursed; implementation rate and physical progress? If not, how is the transparency of EU funds ensured?
What indicators did it use to assess whether the funded interventions strengthened the region’s resilience?
Does it intend to carry out or request a comprehensive audit of the use of EU funding in northern Evia?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (24.9.2026) 1. Under the regional programme ‘Sterea Ellada 2021-2027’ co-financed by the EU Cohesion policy, the regional authorities approved a EUR 13 million Integrated Territorial Investment strategy for Northern Evia on 24 July 2025, which includes actions for the reconstruction and resilience of the region1. A call for proposals was launched on 1 November 2025 and closes on 30 September 20262. While selection and implementation of projects fall under the responsibility of the national and regional authorities, project data and progress are publicly available through national portals3. Under Greece’s Recovery and Resilience Plan (RRP), more than 5 000 hectares of degraded forest ecosystems in Attica, Thessaloniki and northern Evia are being restored with the aim to repair forest ecosystems and biodiversity, enhance infrastructure and create job opportunities. In addition, based on information provided by the Greek authorities, the North Evia Reconstruction Plan with EUR 390 million of national funds and private donations is put in place4. 2. Resilience is measured through programme indicators focusing on environmental restoration, social cohesion and development, such as population benefiting from flood protection and access to green infrastructure5. 3. Cohesion as well as Recovery and Resilience policy funds are implemented under a robust multi-level control framework, including audits by national bodies, which provide assurance on their regularity and transparency. The Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF) is a performance-based instrument, and the Commission releases funds after it has assessed that the milestones/targets linked to RRP reforms and investments have been satisfactorily fulfilled.

1 https://www.stereaellada.gr/basiki-selida/ohe. 2 https://www.stereaellada.gr/proskliseis/ylopoiisi-draseon-tis-stratigikis-ohe-boreias-eyboias. 3 https://www.espa.gr/el/pages/default.aspx; https://greece20.gov.gr/. 4 https://evoia-meta.gov.gr/. 5 Reporting of indicators is publicly available at

E-10-2026-003145.t: Professional exclusion of life scientists in Greece and compliance with EU law
qt: to the Commission Maria Zacharia (NI) Subject:

Life sciences graduates in Greece, particularly graduates in biology and related fields, have always faced serious inequality when it comes to the recognition of professional qualifications. They have significantly restricted or no access to professional activities that are available to graduates of equivalent faculties in other Member States. This issue appears to be linked to the continued existence of closed professions or fragmented laws governing professions with no clear proportionality assessment, in spite of the requirements of Directive (EU) 2018/958 on a proportionality test before adoption of new regulation of professions, and the principles of free movement of workers and freedom of establishment. This situation is creating real distortions in the labour market and could lead to the unequal treatment of graduates with equivalent qualifications within the Union. In view of this, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

Has it looked into whether the existing restrictions faced by life sciences graduates in Greece with regard to accessing regulated professions are compatible with Directive (EU) 2018/958 and the principles of proportionality and non-discrimination under EU law?
Does it consider that continued exclusion from regulated professions without a substantiated proportionality assessment may constitute an infringement of Articles 45 and 49 TFEU?
Does it intend to ask the Greek authorities for information/data on the comparative treatment of life sciences graduates in Greece and other Member States?

E-10-2026-003144.t: Rail safety in Greece and delays in the operation of the ETCS system
qt: to the Commission Yannis Maniatis (S&D) Subject:

During a committee hearing in the Greek Parliament, the CEO of the Hellenic Railways Organisation (OSE) revealed that the centralised traffic control and automatic braking system, ETCS, is not yet operational anywhere along the Greek railway network, despite the Prime Minister’s announcements in April 2025 that it would be operational by September 2025 at the latest. It is worth remembering that the first contract for the installation of the ETCS system was signed in 2014 and the installation should have been completed by 2016. As acknowledged by the special committee set up to investigate the Tempi train crash in 2023, if the system had been operational, the collision of the two trains would have been avoided. Since the installation of the ETCS was financed by the European Union, and its operation is an essential prerequisite for transport safety, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

Has the Greek Government informed the Commission about when the ETCS system is expected to operate properly and fully, and has it provided an explanation for the threeyear delay following the Tempi tragedy and the constant government announcements?
Is Greece meeting its rail safety obligations even though the ETCS is not operational?
What measures will the Commission take to ensure the safety of rail transport in Greece?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (15.9.2026) The Commission remains in contact with the Greek authorities in relation to the modernisation and reform of its railway sector, including deployment of the European Railway Traffic Management System (ERTMS). The Commission is aware of the ambitious ERTMS roll-out plans. Given the complexity of this process, the European Union Agency for Railways (ERA), at the request of Greece, is supporting stakeholders in developing an effective ERTMS deployment plan. Railway safety can be achieved through a combination of different technical and organisational measures. The deployment on the rail network of European Train Control System (ETCS), a key component of ERTMS, contributes to the improvement of safety of the railway system; however, railway networks can also safely operate without ETCS, provided that appropriate alternative risk control measures are implemented. On 16 December 2024, the Commission opened infringement proceedings (INFR(2023)20361) against Greece for failure to comply with the requirements of the Rail Safety Directive2. The infringement case addresses several long-standing systemic shortcomings in the implementation of the Safety Directive in Greece, also identified during an audit by ERA. In response to the audit report, the Greek authorities have prepared in 2024 an Action Plan to address these shortcomings, which is being implemented, and the Commission is monitoring progress on the basis of regular reports received from Greece.

E-10-2026-003143.t: Beach concessions: calling on the Commission to close the infringement proceeding against Italy in the light of the Court of Justice’s declaration that it is for Member States to determine the scarcity of natural resources
qt: to the Commission Roberto Vannacci (ESN) Subject:

On 10 July 2026, the Court of Justice of the European Union issued an order in Case C574/25 (Balneari Rimini II) regarding concessions on state-owned coastal land used for tourism and recreational purposes. The Court ruled that the obligation laid down in Article 12 of the Bolkestein Directive (2006/123/EC) to hold tendering procedures for concessions applies to cases in which the number of authorisations available is limited by the scarcity of the natural resource in question, and that the latter should be determined by ‘the competent national authority... subject to review by a national court’. In other words, it is for Italy to check whether its beaches are in short supply, not the Commission. On 6 October 2023, the Italian Government issued a Council Presidency note in which it determined, on the basis of general, proportionate and non-discriminatory criteria, that the country’s beaches were not a scarce resource. Yet, under the the infringement proceeding (INFR(2020)4118) it had opened by means of letter of formal notice of 3 December 2020, the Commission issued a reasoned opinion on 16 November 2023 in which it rejected the Italian Government’s findings and threatened to take Italy to the Court of Justice under Article 258 TFEU. Given the CJEU’s recent ruling on beach concessions, will the Commission act with all haste to close the related infringement proceeding against Italy?
at: (English version) to the Commission Roberto Vannacci (ESN) (27 July 2026) Subject: Beach concessions: calling on the Commission to close the infringement proceeding against Italy in the light of the Court of Justice’s declaration that it is for Member States to determine the scarcity of natural resources On 10 July 2026, the Court of Justice of the European Union issued an order in Case C-574/25 (Balneari Rimini II) regarding concessions on state-owned coastal land used for tourism and recreational purposes. The Court ruled that the obligation laid down in Article 12 of the Bolkestein Directive (2006/123/EC) to hold tendering procedures for concessions applies to cases in which the number of authorisations available is limited by the scarcity of the natural resource in question, and that the latter should be determined by ‘the competent national authority… subject to review by a national court’. In other words, it is for Italy to check whether its beaches are in short supply, not the Commission. On 6 October 2023, the Italian Government issued a Council Presidency note in which it determined, on the basis of general, proportionate and non-discriminatory criteria, that the country’s beaches were not a scarce resource. Yet, under the the infringement proceeding (INFR(2020)4118) it had opened by means of letter of formal notice of 3 December 2020, the Commission issued a reasoned opinion on 16 November 2023 in which it rejected the Italian Government’s findings and threatened to take Italy to the Court of Justice under Article 258 TFEU. Given the CJEU’s recent ruling on beach concessions, will the Commission act with all haste to close the related infringement proceeding against Italy? (15 September 2026) The Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) order in Case C-574/25 (1) confirms the CJEU case-law (2), which clarified that the Services Directive (3) applies to situations such as the Italian ‘beach concessions’: authorisations that are limited, due to a scarcity of available natural resources, are to be granted for a limited duration, through non-discriminatory tenders and may not be open to automatic renewal. The infringement procedure INFR(2020)4118 (4) is fully based on such legal principles. As regards the scarcity assessment, the CJEU has already clarified that, while Member States can choose the best approach to conduct such assessment, it is crucial that the criteria ‘are based on objective, non-discriminatory, transparent and proportionate factors’ (5). Moreover, the assessment has to refer to the actual ‘land available for economic exploitation’ (6) and consider that such authorisations are granted at a municipal level. Taking positive note of the significant and growing number of Italian municipalities where open tendering procedures have already been organised, the Commission is expecting the completion of such procedures across the entire national territory by 30 September 2027, as required by Law 166/2024 and its implementation, following the extensive discussions and the mutual understanding with the Italian authorities.

The CJEU gives its ruling by way of order, rather than judgment, where the answer may be clearly deduced from existing case-law. E-10-2026-003142.t: Impact of weather conditions on the production of exportable agricultural products and on the Union’s food security
qt: to the Commission Emmanouil Fragkos (ECR) Subject:

The regional unit of Kavala is an important agricultural area with a strong focus on exports, producing table grapes, kiwis, olives, almonds, asparagus and other fruit and vegetables. However, local producers report that the frequency and intensity of extreme weather events, such as heatwaves, prolonged drought and extreme rainfall, lead to significant production losses and lower the quality of the produce. These developments affect not only producers’ income but also the competitiveness of local/Greek agricultural products on international markets. The Union’s food security and strategic autonomy depend to a great extent on maintaining the productive capacity of European rural areas, as is also highlighted in the Commission’s Vision for Agriculture and Food. In addition, Regulation (EU) 2021/2115 provides for interventions that contribute to the resilience and sustainability of the agricultural sector. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Does it have any estimates regarding the effects of extreme weather phenomena on our export crops?
Does it intend to further increase financing for investments aimed at preventing and responding to damage from extreme weather events under the next CAP?
How does it intend to ensure the maintained production capacity of strategic EU agricultural areas, which make an essential contribution to our food security and selfsufficiency?

How does it intend to ensure the maintained production capacity of strategic EU agricultural areas, which make an essential contribution to our food security and self-sufficiency?

(18 September 2026) 1. The Commission constantly monitors agricultural production in the EU as well as the effects of extreme weather events on agricultural production. No specific monitoring of the situation of products intended for export is taking place. 2. Both the current Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) (1) and the proposed National and Regional Partnership Plans (NRPP) for 2028-2034 (2), provide Member States with a range of tools supporting farmers to prevent climate change related crises and build up medium and long-term resilience. The overall objective for the future is to shift towards a more preventive and structured approach, while maintaining targeted public support when major crises occur. This is why for the post-2027 CAP, the Commission proposes a layered approach combining income support, risk management tools, crisis payments and prevention measures, including new targeted farm transition action plans under the agri-environmental and climate actions, to help farmers in the transition to resilient production systems. 3. Maintaining agricultural production capacity is a central objective of the CAP. The CAP helps farmers to adapt by providing support for investments and knowledge and training, but also by helping them mitigate the economic effects of climate related damages by providing support for risk management. The EU also invests substantially in research, innovation and knowledge exchange to increase the resilience of the agriculture sector, with over EUR 1.8 billion allocated over a fiveyear period from 2021-2025 (3).

E-10-2026-003141.t: Compensation for agricultural damage caused during aerial firefighting operations
qt: to the Commission Emmanouil Fragkos (ECR) Subject:

Producers in the regional unit of Kavala report that aerial firefighting operations caused significant damage to vineyards, as Erickson helicopters scooped water in areas where there were established crops. Those affected are calling for compensation for the damage incurred, pointing out that it was caused in the context of natural disaster response operations. Given that the Union Civil Protection Mechanism, established by Decision 1313/2013/EU, strengthens Member State cooperation in responding to natural disasters, will the Commission say: 1.
Are there European guidelines or best practices on compensation for damage caused unintentionally during civil protection operations?
Does it collect data on collateral damage that may be caused to farms during aerial firefighting operations?
Does it consider that further European coordination or an exchange of best practices is needed in order to ensure swift compensation for such damage in the Member States?

E-10-2026-003140.t: Reducing irrigation-related energy costs through energy communities in the agricultural sector
qt: to the Commission Emmanouil Fragkos (ECR) Subject:

Farmers in the regional unit of Kavala, Greece, point out that the high cost of energy for the abstraction and distribution of irrigation water is one of the most significant factors undermining farms’ competitiveness. Reliance on boreholes, combined with the reduced availability of water resources, leads to increased energy needs and a further burden on rural incomes. The revised Directive (EU) 2023/2413 on the promotion of energy from renewable sources (RED III) recognises the role of energy communities and encourages the participation of citizens and local actors in the production and consumption of energy from renewable sources. With this in mind, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
How does it assess the uptake of energy communities by the agricultural sector in the Member States to date?
Does it intend to propose additional financial incentives for the creation of energy communities by producer groups and agricultural cooperatives?
Does the future CAP envisage special measures to reduce irrigation-related energy costs in areas affected by water scarcity and with increased water abstraction needs?

(28 September 2026) The Commission recognises the key role that citizens can play in the energy transition and the potential of renewable energy to help reduce energy prices. It has promoted the development of energy communities through legislative (1) and non-legislative measures (2), and recognises that there is still untapped potential. To further support the development of energy communities in rural areas, the Commission launched the Rural Energy Community Advisory Hub (3). It helped identify best practices and provided technical assistance to rural energy communities. Today, the European Energy Community Facility (4) provides financial support, in the form of lump sum grants, to emerging energy communities across Europe. The Citizen Energy Advisory Hub (5) provides technical assistance to set up sustainable energy projects, including to rural energy communities and farmers. The future Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) (6) will continue to support water resilience in agriculture which can have a positive impact on irrigation-related energy costs. The proposed new CAP identifies ‘environment and climate priority areas’, including climate change adaptation and water resilience, for which Member States must provide support to farmers, through interventions under Agri-Environmental and Climate Actions. Member States will design these interventions in their National and Regional Partnership Plans taking account of their specific needs and circumstances, as well as the Commission’s CAP national recommendations.

E-10-2026-003139.t: Completing the Marmara dam in Kavala and strengthening the resilience of rural areas
qt: to the Commission Emmanouil Fragkos (ECR) Subject:

Pangaio in Kavala is a very important Greek agricultural area with a strong focus on exporting products such as table grapes, kiwis, olives, asparagus and almonds. However, producers are facing increasing pressures due to water scarcity and increasingly frequent extreme weather events. The Marmara dam, a project of strategic importance for the region, has been left unfinished for decades, depriving farmers of critical irrigation and weather adaptation capabilities. The EU refers to the sustainable management of water resources as a ‘key priority’, including through the Water Framework Directive (2000/60/EC), aiming at the protection and sustainable use of water, as well as in the European strategy on adaptation to climate change. Regulation (EU) 2021/1060 on common provisions for cohesion funds envisages investment that contributes ‘to climate adaptation, risk prevention and strengthening the resilience of regions’. Bearing in mind that Regulation (EU) 2021/2115 on CAP strategic plans provides for ‘support for investments that contribute to resilience, sustainable water management and adaptation to climate change’, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
What European funding tools can be used to complete the Marmara dam and the accompanying irrigation networks?

Does it intend to encourage Greece to integrate or revise relevant projects under the CAP strategic plans or other funds, especially in light of the increasing water scarcity and the need to strengthen the resilience of the agricultural sector?

(15 September 2026) The Commission recognises the growing impact of water scarcity and drought on agriculture in Greece. Several EU funding instruments can support investments to improve water resilience and agricultural adaptation. Under Greece’s Common Agricultural Policy Strategic Plan 2023-2027, the European Agricultural Fund for Rural Development (EAFRD) provides for up to EUR 310 million in support of irrigation-related investments (1). As EAFRD support is implemented under shared management, responsibility for the implementation and progress of the project lies with the Greek authorities. The updated (2) Greek Recovery and Resilience Plan (3) provides for the adoption of a National Water Strategy for the protection and sustainable management of water resources. In addition, under Horizon Europe work programmes (4), Greek entities may participate in research and innovation actions relating to water-smart agriculture, efficient irrigation technologies, reuse, desalination, remote sensing and climate resilience. The LIFE Programme (5) can support pilot, demonstration and best-practice projects in the fields of water, nature, climate adaptation and circular water use.

E-10-2026-003138.t: Closure of the transitional shelter for psychoactive substance users and the dissolution of treatment structures
qt: to the Commission Kostas Papadakis (NI) Subject:

The closure of the transitional shelter for psychoactive substance users – the only temporary accommodation structure for homeless drug addicts in Athens – is yet another dangerous development for people with substance misuse problems. This is another consequence of the implementation of EU guidelines, which the Nea Dimokratia Government is enforcing – as did SYRIZA before it – with the recent law on the ‘completion of the Psychiatric Reform’. There has already been a push to end treatment programmes and break the continuum of care (advice-treatment-social reintegration) through the establishment of the National Organisation for Preventing and Combating Addiction (EOPAE). Facilities were brutally deprived of experienced staff following a wave of unexpected staff transfers last year. No provision is made for people with a dual diagnosis of drug dependence and mental illness to be able to join a Therapeutic Community. The fatal blow to Therapeutic Communities came with the 24-hour shifts imposed on the staff, which essentially turned these environments into ‘first aid stations’, bringing about a detrimental change in the working conditions of staff. Given the need to take substantial measures to prevent drug addiction, for comprehensive, public, free addiction services and to support and expand ‘dry’ addiction programme units, what is the Commission’s position regarding the fact that EU policy – which is based on socalled ‘harm reduction’ and substitution treatments and which every single bourgeois government has implemented over the years on the basis of the ‘cost-benefit’ criterion, including in the field of detoxification – deliberately perpetuates drug dependence, with no meaningful measures being taken to address the issue effectively and help users and their families?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.10.2026) Protecting public health and addressing drug-related harms are key pillars of the EU Drugs Strategy1, adopted by the Commission in December 2025 and endorsed by the Member States in March 20262. The Strategy lays down measures aimed at reducing drug use, providing accessible treatment for everyone, and supporting the recovery and social reintegration of people with drug use disorders. The Strategy notably encourages Member States to step up universal and environmental health prevention and develop and implement evidence-based prevention activities specifically designed for groups in vulnerable situations, as well as to strengthen the availability of evidence-based treatment options integrated in a continuum of care. Across the EU, harm reduction interventions are supported by an extensive body of scientific evidence demonstrating their effectiveness in reducing drug-related harms. These are recognised at both European and international levels, including through successive EU Drugs Strategies and relevant United Nations resolutions. Mental health is also a priority for the Commission. In 2023, the Commission adopted a Communication on a Comprehensive Approach to Mental Health3, with 20 ambitious flagships linked to almost EUR 1.3 billion in funding opportunities, and with a focus on supporting vulnerable groups.

E-10-2026-003137.t: Dissemination of animal torture videos on Telegram and application of Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 (Digital Services Act)
qt: to the Council Sebastian Everding (The Left) Subject:

Since 2023, organised criminal networks – documented by international investigative journalism1 – have been producing and selling commissioned videos of domestic animal torture, primarily targeting cats, for up to USD 1 300 per video on Telegram23. Minors have been documented within these distribution networks. Does the Council intend to: 1.

confirm that animal torture videos disseminated on a platform registered under the Digital Services Act4 (DSA) – where such content is illegal under applicable animal protection laws in one or more Member States – constitute illegal content within the meaning of Article 3(h) of the DSA, and indicate what measures it envisages to ensure effective and durable removal by Telegram within the timeframes set by the DSA;

support or initiate a verification procedure of the monthly active user figures declared by Telegram in the EU5 and consider revisiting the 45-million-user designation threshold for very large online platforms to ensure that platforms posing a systemic risk – particularly for illegal content involving vulnerable individuals or minors – are subject to enhanced obligations;

coordinate action with national Digital Services Coordinators and Europol to initiate formal DSA compliance proceedings against Telegram, given the transnational, organised and commercial nature of these networks and the documented involvement of minors?

CNN, May 2025; Franceinfo, September 2025; Le Temps. Telegram is registered under Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 (DSA) with a legal representative in the Union (EDSR SA, Brussels). The dissemination of animal cruelty footage constitutes illegal content under the laws of several Member States. However, Telegram has not been designated a very large online platform under Article 33 of the DSA, as it declares fewer than 45 million monthly active users in the Union, significantly reducing its moderation obligations. Despite repeated civil society reports, dedicated groups systematically reappear following each removal. 3 Over 12 000 such videos have been catalogued in three years by the Feline Guardians and Les Gardiens des Félins collectives. Between June 2024 and February 2025, this content increased by 500 % across monitored Telegram groups. E-10-2026-003136.t: Israel’s registration requirements imposed on NGOs and the EU adequacy decision for transfer of data to Israel
qt: to the Commission Raquel García Hermida-Van Der Walle (Renew) Subject:

In 2025, Israel adopted Guidelines for the Registration of Organizations and Issuance of Recommendations for Their Foreign Employees, which require non-governmental organisations (NGOs) providing humanitarian aid in the Palestinian Territories to provide a significant amount of personal data to the competent authorities in Israel1. Since 2011, Israel has benefited from an adequacy decision under the EU’s data protection legal framework (currently pursuant to Article 45 of the General Data Protection Regulation2 (GDPR)), which requires the Commission to ‘monitor developments … that could affect the functioning’ of such adequacy decisions. NGOs subject to the GDPR need to comply with the rules and conditions set out in the GDPR. 1.

Does the Commission acknowledge that these guidelines pose problems for NGOs, such as: (a) the requirement to ensure the proportionality, necessity and transparency of such processing activities; (b) the need for a valid legal basis for such processing activities, as imposed by the GDPR; and (c) the need to ensure that data subjects may exercise their rights?

Does the Commission consider that such data flows from NGOs to competent authorities in Israel would fall within the scope of the adequacy decision adopted for Israel? If so, does it consider that these guidelines undermine the adequacy decision?
If so, will the Commission suspend the adequacy decision until Israel fully complies with all the conditions set out in the adequacy decision? If not, why not?

Including personal data of their staff, their spouses and children, and a list of their donors, including their ‘background’ information. 2 Regulation (EU) 2016/679 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 April 2016 on the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free movement of such data, and repealing Directive 95/46/EC (General Data Protection Regulation) (OJ L 119, 4.5.2016, p. 1, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj). 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (30.9.2026) The EU has been unequivocal that the international non-governmental organisations (‘INGO’) registration framework cannot be implemented in its current form, as reiterated in a joint statement issued by the High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy and the Commissioners for Equality Preparedness and Crisis Management, and for the Mediterranean, on 6 January 20261. The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) applies to the processing of personal data in the context of the activities of a controller or processor established in the EU. Accordingly, the processing of personal data by INGOs carried out to comply with Israeli rules may be covered by the GDPR, if and to the extent it is taking place in the EU. In this context, it is for the data protection authorities and courts of the EU Member States to assess if such processing complies with the GDPR. INGOs subject to the GDPR also need to comply with the rules and conditions for the transfer of personal data to third countries set out in Chapter V. Transfers of personal data from the EU to private and public entities in Israel can be based on the Commission’s adequacy decision for Israel of 31 January 2011. The Commission monitors all developments that may affect the level of protection guaranteed in Israel for personal data received from the EU and has mechanisms at its disposal to respond should the level of protection no longer be deemed adequate.
