E-10-2026-003135.t: Providing assistance following the outbreak of war on 24 February 2024 and the implications for businesses
qt: to the Commission Michał Kobosko (Renew) Subject:
Providing assistance following the outbreak of war on 24 February 2024 and the implications for businesses

This question concerns businesses which, between 2022 and 2024, provided assistance to refugees from Ukraine as part of a scheme that was organised by public authorities, with the conditions and remuneration being set by the state. Several years later, the tax authorities began to question the method used to account for the VAT on the services concerned, even though the businesses had provided them in accordance with the rules governing the organisation of the aid. 1.

Does the Commission take the view that the provisions of the VAT Directive and the general principles of EU law – legal certainty, the protection of legitimate expectations and proportionality – preclude the practice of recovering VAT several years down the line from businesses which, between 2022 and 2024, provided accommodation and food under a scheme organised by the public authorities to assist people fleeing the war in Ukraine?

In the Commission’s view, is such a practice compatible with the requirements of Directive 2006/112/EC and with the principles of EU law on the predictability of the application of tax law, in particular where there are serious doubts as to interpretation, as demonstrated by the fact that a national court (the provincial administrative court in Wrocław, ref.: I SA/Wr 1/26) has referred questions to the Court of Justice of the European Union for a preliminary ruling?

Does the Commission intend to issue a position or any guidelines on the application of VAT rules to services provided by businesses as part of a publicly organised humanitarian aid scheme, in order to ensure the uniform application of EU law and the protection of the legitimate expectations of operators acting in good faith?
at: (English version) to the Commission Michał Kobosko (Renew) (27 July 2026) Subject: Providing assistance following the outbreak of war on 24 February 2024 and the implications for businesses This question concerns businesses which, between 2022 and 2024, provided assistance to refugees from Ukraine as part of a scheme that was organised by public authorities, with the conditions and remuneration being set by the state. Several years later, the tax authorities began to question the method used to account for the VAT on the services concerned, even though the businesses had provided them in accordance with the rules governing the organisation of the aid. 1. Does the Commission take the view that the provisions of the VAT Directive and the general principles of EU law — legal certainty, the protection of legitimate expectations and proportionality — preclude the practice of recovering VAT several years down the line from businesses which, between 2022 and 2024, provided accommodation and food under a scheme organised by the public authorities to assist people fleeing the war in Ukraine? 2. In the Commission’s view, is such a practice compatible with the requirements of Directive 2006/112/EC and with the principles of EU law on the predictability of the application of tax law, in particular where there are serious doubts as to interpretation, as demonstrated by the fact that a national court (the provincial administrative court in Wrocław, ref.: I SA/Wr 1/26) has referred questions to the Court of Justice of the European Union for a preliminary ruling? 3. Does the Commission intend to issue a position or any guidelines on the application of VAT rules to services provided by businesses as part of a publicly organised humanitarian aid scheme, in order to ensure the uniform application of EU law and the protection of the legitimate expectations of operators acting in good faith? (23 September 2026) Council Directive 2006/112/EC (‘value-added tax (VAT) Directive’) stipulates that VAT applies to the supply of services for consideration within the territory of a Member State by a taxable person acting as such. According to Article 73 of the VAT Directive the consideration may be paid by the customer or by a third party (for instance a public authority) and this includes subsidies directly linked to the price of the supply. The VAT Directive and the general principles of EU law do not in principle preclude the practice of recovering VAT several years after the relevant supplies took place. The collection of VAT and the control on the correct application is the responsibility of Member States. According to the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) every Member State is under an obligation to take all legislative and administrative measures appropriate for ensuring collection of all the VAT due on its territory. In case of doubts as how to interpret particular legal situation (like in this case, providing support to Ukrainian refugees), a national court may refer questions to the CJEU. In this particular case eight detailed questions have been referred to the CJEU by the Polish Provincial administrative Cour t (1). The Commission will therefore wait for the ruling of the CJEU in this case. The Commission recognises the importance of the uniform application of EU law, as well as the need to safeguard the legitimate expectations of operators acting in good faith. At present, however, the Commission does not intend to issue specific guidance on this matter especially having in mind that the case will be addressed now by the CJEU.
WSA in Wrocław, ref.: I SA/Wr 1/26.

E-10-2026-003134.t: Digital centralisation, EU gold-plating and companies’ competitiveness
qt: to the Commission Mathilde Androuët (PfE) Subject:

The study ‘Interplay between the AI Act and the EU digital legislative framework’1 highlights the growing entanglement of the GDPR, the Data Act, the Digital Services Act, the Digital Markets Act, the NIS2 Directive, the Cyber Resilience Act and the Artificial Intelligence (AI) Act. The study emphasises legal uncertainty, growing compliance costs for businesses – particularly SMEs – and the expansion of the European AI Office as a supranational oversight centre. These developments raise concerns on two fronts: technocratic centralisation, which undermines Member States’ sovereignty in civil liberties, security and public services; and weaker European competitiveness, potentially benefiting large non-EU platforms, which are better equipped to absorb the increasing regulation. Can the Commission clarify: 1.
What is the legal and democratic basis for its intention to extend the powers of the European AI Office?
What guarantees are in place to ensure that Member States remain in control of decisions affecting civil liberties?
Does it recognise that increasing regulation in this way primarily penalises European SMEs? Will it commit to conducting a comprehensive simplification audit before any new AI initiative?

European Parliament, ITRE Committee, ‘Interplay between the AI Act and the EU digital legislative framework’, study published on 25 October 2025. https://www.europarl.europa.eu/RegData/etudes/STUD/2025/778575/ECTI_STU(2025)778575_EN.pdf. 1

E-10-2026-003133.t: Substantiated misgivings about the effectiveness of EU spending on housing energy efficiency upgrades
qt: to the Commission Mathilde Androuët (PfE) Subject:

In a special report published on 7 July 2026, ‘Energy efficiency in residential buildings – Recovery funding has delivered only moderate energy savings’, the European Court of Auditors found that the EUR 43 billion released under the Recovery and Resilience Facility were frequently used for one-off interventions producing limited energy savings rather than truly effective global refurbishment. These findings add to criticism expressed in the European Parliament, particularly by PfE Members, of a policy that is based on uniform targets, growing regulatory obligations and massive spending, but does not sufficiently take account of differences between building stocks, energy mixes and households’ financial resources. In France, EU renovation standards risk putting further burdens on owners, tenants and public finances with no guarantee of commensurate results. Can the Commission clarify: 1.
Given the results observed, what is the Commission’s justification for maintaining costly obligations?
Does it intend to prioritise voluntary measures that target the most energy-intensive homes and provide the best value for money?
Does it acknowledge that the priorities for energy efficiency upgrades and choice of energy mix are primarily matters for Member States?

E-10-2026-003131.t: Tackling the low birth rate and demographic challenges in the EU with binding European measures and adequate funding
qt: to the Commission Elena Kountoura (The Left) Subject:

The EU is facing an acute and ever-worsening demographic crisis, with birth rates below the required population replacement level for many years1. The increased cost of living, economic uncertainty, precarious employment, the difficulty of securing stable and quality employment, the inability to balance work and family life, and the ever-increasing cost of raising children are important factors that dissuade young people from having children and make it difficult to create and support young families. The problem is more pronounced in certain Member States such as Greece2, as well as in island, mountainous and remote areas, where declining births and an ageing population, combined with an increasing number of permanent residents who are leaving, especially young people, are all factors that are accelerating demographic decline and leading to depopulation3. With this in mind, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Does it plan to propose a European action plan to support families, in particular large families, single-parent families and those in vulnerable situations, as requested by the European Parliament?

How does it intend to support the response to demographic challenges in the provinces, islands, mountainous and remote areas of the Member States with the lowest birth rates and the highest risk of depopulation?
Does it plan to put forward a holistic European strategy to tackle the demographic problem, with mandatory measures, measurable targets and adequate funding?

According to Eurostat figures, the fertility rate in Europe fell to 1.34 children per woman in 2024, which is well below the 2.1 rate considered to be the population replacement level, and the number of births dropped to 3.55 million, the lowest recorded in recent decades. 2 Specifically, Greece has one of the lowest fertility rates among the EU Member States, with 1.24 births per woman and it has the fourth oldest population in the EU, with a median age of 47.2. What is more, according to the OECD’s ‘Health at a Glance 2025’ report, in 2050 Greece is expected to be the oldest country in the EU (https://www.oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/publications/reports/2025/11/health-at-a-glance2025_a894f72e/8f9e3f98-en.pdf). 3 In Greece, at least 51 islands have become depopulated since 1950 and more are expected to meet the same fate over the next 20 years (https://www.naftemporiki.gr/society/1795599/dimografiko-apo-to-1950erimosan-51-mikra-nisia-ti-empodizei-tin-epistrofi-ton-neon-kai-to-paradeigma-tis-tiloy/). 1

E-10-2026-003130.t: A European strategy for tackling infertility and supporting assisted reproduction in the EU
qt: to the Commission Elena Kountoura (The Left) Subject:

Infertility is a serious and urgent public health problem1 that affects millions of citizens in the Union and is directly linked to the demographic crisis and the falling birth rates recorded in recent years. Despite this, access to infertility prevention, diagnosis and treatment, including assisted reproduction, remains uneven across Member States and is rarely supported by national health systems2. In view of the severe demographic crisis in Europe and the historically low fertility rate of 1.34 children per woman in the EU3, the high financial cost of treatments, which – combined with the rising cost of living, job insecurity and the imbalance between work and family life – acts as a disincentive for couples wishing to have children, and taking into account the global guideline issued by the WHO in November 2025 on the prevention, diagnosis and treatment of infertility4, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

Does it plan to propose a new European strategy for the prevention, diagnosis and treatment of infertility, in line with WHO recommendations, and to make the infertility challenge a priority of European public health and demographic policies?

Does it intend to support a specific funding mechanism in the new Multiannual Financial Framework to support the fertility and assisted reproduction sector in the Member States, as well as to reduce the financial and mental burden of fertility treatments on citizens?

The WHO defines infertility as a disease of the reproductive system and it is estimated that around one in six people of reproductive age worldwide experience infertility at some point in their lifetime. 2 Βλ. https://www.europarl.europa.eu/RegData/etudes/STUD/2023/757504/IPOL_STU(2023)757504_EN.pdf. 3 https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Fertility_statistics. 4 The guideline includes 40 recommendations covering the whole spectrum of prevention, diagnosis and treatment of infertility and advocates for their integration into the national health systems of all states (https://www.who.int/news/item/28-11-2025-who-issues-first-global-guideline-on-infertility). 1

E-10-2026-003129.t: Need for a European strategy on menopause and the integration of menopause into EU health and employment policies with dedicated funding
qt: to the Commission Elena Kountoura (The Left) Subject:

Menopause is a natural life stage affecting millions of women and has a major impact1 on their physical and mental health, working life2 and overall quality of life. In spite of this, menopause care is still not sufficiently integrated into the EU’s public health and employment policies3. Between the Member States, there are significant discrepancies in early diagnosis, information, training of health professionals, access to appropriate health services and support for women in the workplace. Only some have developed national menopause policies, while others, such as Greece, do not have a framework on this particular matter. In view of the need for a more systematic integration of the gender aspect into health and employment policies, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Does it plan to propose the development of a European strategy on menopause care?
What measures does it intend to take to help women in the workplace during premenopause, menopause and post-menopause, with a view to supporting them and preventing discrimination?

Does it intend to propose dedicated funding for research and innovation, the inclusion of menopause in EU public health programmes, combating menopause poverty, improving information and awareness and collecting comparable data on the impact of menopause on women’s health and employment and on health systems?

According to the European Institute of Women’s Health and surveys of post-menopausal women, up to 90 % reported having experienced symptoms at some point during the menopausal transition, with approximately half considering their symptoms bothersome (https://eurohealth.ie/wpcontent/uploads/2023/11/Menopause-Policy-Brief.pdf). 2 Menopausal women are the fastest growing group in the labour force, currently accounting for 11 % of the labour force in the G7 countries alone, a figure that is expected to increase in the coming years as the population ages (https://podcast.ilo.org/episode/is-the-menopause-a-workplace-issue). 3 The transition to menopause is associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular, metabolic and neurological diseases, but EU prevention strategies rarely address these links in a systematic manner (see European Parliament 2025 Report on Gender Inequalities in Medical Research, Drug Development and Access to Care). 1

E-10-2026-003128.t: Uneven application of Regulation (EC) No 561/2006 and possible malpractices in checks on road transport operators
qt: to the Commission Ştefan Muşoiu (S&D) Subject:
Uneven application of Regulation (EC) No 561/2006 and possible malpractices in checks on road transport operators

The Federation of Romanian Transport Operators has informed me of certain administrative practices where there is an uneven application of Article 8(8a) of Regulation (EC) No 561/2006, as amended by Regulation (EU) 2020/1054. Every four weeks, the French and Hungarian control authorities apparently ask for proof, at the roadside, concerning the organisation of drivers’ returns and impose penalties if the requested documentation is not presented. However, Article 8 establishes the obligation of an undertaking to organise its work in such a way that the driver returns to their place of residence or to the operational centre. Furthermore, it is not the driver’s responsibility to keep documentation on board the vehicle but the employer’s. In addition, the interpretative guidelines on Mobility Package I state that compliance with the relevant obligations is verified by checking documentation kept at the transport undertaking’s premises for administrative controls. 1.
Could the Commission therefore confirm whether Article 8 establishes or not the obligation to present documentation on a driver's return during roadside checks?

Can the Commission clarify whether the practice of some national authorities of applying penalties for simply failing to produce documents during roadside checks, is compatible with Regulation (EC) No 561/2006 and with the obligation to ensure the uniform application of EU law?
Furthermore, does the Commission intend to adopt further measures to standardise control practices and prevent divergent interpretations of Article 8 in the Member States?
to the Commission François-Xavier Bellamy (PPE), Isabelle Le Callennec (PPE), Christophe Gomart (PPE) Subject:

On 13 July 2026, the Commission authorised France to provide up to EUR 63 billion for the installation of 11 GW in offshore wind capacity on the French coast through the AO10 call for tenders. No further inquiries were made. This huge amount of public aid raises obvious questions regarding the unprecedented amount of funding involved, the limited maturity of the technology and its impact on the environment. It also raises democratic issues: rushing to commit the country to massive, long-term spending that benefits private actors in the run-up to a presidential election – especially at a time of extreme budgetary pressure – creates a clear rule-of-law problem. The unconditional validation in this case stands in stark contrast to the in-depth investigation into France’s new European Pressurised Reactor that the Commission decided to launch on 31 March 2026. 1.

Given France’s surplus, decarbonised electricity output, does the Commission believe that handing over EUR 63 billion in public money to private companies for intermittent overcapacity in the run-up to a major election is justifiably urgent under State aid rules?
Does it consider this support for wind power to better meet energy security, environmental protection and competitiveness aims than new nuclear power?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.9.2026) On 13 July 2026, the Commission approved, under the Clean Industrial Deal State Aid Framework (CISAF)1, the French scheme SA.120604 supporting 11 offshore wind farms which will contribute to the EU’s energy and climate objectives. The Commission’s role is to assess the compatibility of notified State aid measures with the internal market under the State aid rules. This assessment does not cover Member States’ choices concerning their energy mix, which remains a national competence. Nor does it consider the political timing of national decisions or electoral considerations. For this scheme, France demonstrated that the aid, granted through an open and non-discriminatory competitive tender, complies with the CISAF requirements. The scheme’s budget constitutes an estimated maximum aid amount over the duration of the scheme, but the final aid granted will depend on the auction result and electricity prices over time. Since the aid is granted in the form of two-way contracts for difference, when electricity prices exceed the contract price set through the tender, the offshore developers will have to pay the difference to the French state, thereby avoiding windfall profits. The Commission assesses aid measures on a case-by-case basis, under the applicable legal framework. Support for nuclear power generation is usually granted directly to an individual beneficiary, and raises distinct legal, economic and technical considerations. The opening of an in-depth investigation reflects the Commission’s duty, where necessary, to gather all information required to complete its assessment; it does not prejudge the final outcome, nor does it imply unequal treatment between technologies.
1 Communication from the Commission of 25 June 2025 on the framework for State aid measures to support the
Clean Industrial Deal (Clean Industrial Deal State Aid Framework), OJ C/2025/3602, 4.7.2025.

E-10-2026-003126.t: Follow-up to Parliament’s resolution of 17 June 2026 on Albania, Narta-Sazan and Chapter 27
qt: to the Commission Thomas Waitz (Verts/ALE) Subject:
Follow-up to Parliament’s resolution of 17 June 2026 on Albania, Narta-Sazan and Chapter 27

Following Parliament’s 17 June 2026 call to repeal the protected areas amendments and impose a moratorium on new development in protected areas, will the Commission act on that call and incorporate it into Albania’s Chapter 27 closing benchmarks, or does it consider the Albanian Government’s 15 June assurances sufficient?

Which concrete and verifiable steps, such as the denial of construction permits, the repeal of the relevant laws in the official gazette, an enforced moratorium, and an independent, published environmental impact assessment evaluated against the Birds Directive and the Habitats Directive, will the Commission require before registering any progress on Chapter 27?

If the announced environmental impact assessment is not conducted independently, or if permits are issued while the area’s protected status remains under review, what consequences would this carry for the Chapter 27 closing benchmark?

This pins the Commission to Parliament’s own position and creates a citable paper trail on implementation. We are glad to provide first-hand information, and the text can, of course, be adapted as the office sees fit.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.9.2026) The Commission is closely monitoring Albania’s progress in aligning with the EU acquis and has taken good note of the Parliament’s resolution of 17 June 2026 on Albania regarding the Vjosa-Narta protected area and Chapter 27 (Environment and Climate Change). Under Chapter 27, Albania has to align its legislation with the EU environmental acquis, including the Environmental Impact Assessment1 and the Strategic Environmental Assessment2 Directives, as well as the Birds3 and Habitats4 Directives. Furthermore, the closing benchmarks, which were formally adopted by the Member States at an Intergovernmental Conference on 16 September 2025 explicitly require Albania to align with the EU nature protection acquis, including by repealing incompatible provisions introduced through amendments to the Law on Protected Areas and terminating the 2015 legislation on Strategic Investments. They also require Albania to demonstrate adequate capacity to manage future Natura 2000 sites and to ensure effective conservation measures preventing habitat and species deterioration. The Commission is in continuous contact with the Albanian authorities and civil society regarding the Narta-Sazan area and conveyed its expectation for a full environmental impact assessment to be carried out in line with European environmental standards.
1 Directive 2011/92/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 December 2011 on the assessment

of the effects of certain public and private projects on the environment, OJ L 26, 28.1.2012, pp. 1–21. 2 Directive 2001/42/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 June 2001 on the assessment of the effects of certain plans and programmes on the environment, OJ L 197, 21.7.2001, pp. 30–37. 3 Directive 2009/147/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 30 November 2009 on the conservation of wild birds, OJ L 20, 26.1.2010, pp. 7–25. 4 Council Directive 92/43/EEC of 21 May 1992 on the conservation of natural habitats and of wild fauna and flora, OJ L 206, 22.7.1992, pp. 7–50.

E-10-2026-003125.t: Plans for dangerous antimony mining in Chios
qt: to the Commission Lefteris Nikolaou-Alavanos (NI) Subject:

Amid staunch opposition from Chios’ grassroots organisations, the Nea Dimokratia Government – together with the EU – is pursuing an investment in antimony mining that is dangerous both for public health and the environment. It is telling that antimony mining had stopped for decades. A large number of studies have noted the negative effect of antimony on the water table. The Greek Government and the EU are prioritising support for corporate groups serving the war and renewable energy industries etc., providing subsidies through the Act on so-called ‘critical raw materials’. As a result, the environment and the health of local residents are being crushed in a stampede by European monopolistic groups, China and the US to make a profit. Local residents have set up a coordinating committee and are continuing to mobilise and protest, supported by more than 100 local entities, as well as others such as the Greek Miners’ Federation. In view of this, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

Where does it stand on the calls from residents and entities for a definitive end to all planning and actions linked to the antimony mining project in Chios, which poses a risk to the health of local residents and the environment?

Where does it stand on the fact that the EU’s Critical Raw Materials Act (CRMA), aimed at boosting the EU’s competitiveness and profitability vis-à-vis its rivals, involves mining activities that are harmful to people’s health and destructive towards the environment?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (8.9.2026) As regards the antimony mining plans referred to by the Honourable Member, the Commission has been made aware of them by written questions E-002085/20241, The Commission would like to remind that mining projects fall under the scope of Directive 2011/92/EU5. Depending on their size, they are either subject to an assessment of the environmental effects or a determination if such an assessment is necessary, based on a caseby-case analysis or by setting specific criteria (such as the location, size or type of project) before their authorization. Where an assessment is required, Members States shall therefore take into account the impacts of the projects on cultural heritage or environmental aspects and the opinion of the concerned public to ensure sustainable development. Without prejudice to the Commission’s role as guardian of the Treaties, it is primarily the responsibility of the Greek authorities to ensure that projects are developed in full compliance with EU environmental legislation. The Critical Raw Materials Act (CRMA)6 was designed to strengthen and diversify the EU’s supply of strategic raw materials while fully maintaining the EU’s high standards for public health, environmental protection and public participation. The CRMA does not lower existing environmental safeguards. Any mining project in the EU must continue to comply with the full body of applicable EU legislation, including requirements relating to environmental impact assessment, water protection, nature conservation, industrial emissions and public consultation.

1 https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/E-10-2024-002085_EN.html. 2 https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/E-10-2024-002980_EN.html. 3 https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/E-10-2025-000429_EN.html. 4 https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/E-10-2025-001718_EN.html. 5 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02011L0092-20140515. 6 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02024R1252-20240503.

E-10-2026-003124.t: Hazardous conditions in the overcrowded port of Rafina
qt: to the Commission Lefteris Nikolaou-Alavanos (NI) Subject:

Due to the decisions of the Greek Government and the Council of Coastal Transportation (SAS), passenger ferries are making increased use of the port of Rafina, which is already operating above capacity on the basis of the guidelines laid down in Regulation (EU) 2024/1679 on the TEN-T network. Reduced staffing levels, heavier workloads, repeated breaches of working time and rest period requirements – which are compatible with Directive 2009/13/EC, as they are not prohibited – and the practice of keeping ships overnight at unsafe anchorages outside the port and ‘races’ between competing ferry companies recently led to an accident whereby a ferry collided with the port jetty. In view of this, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

What is its position on the plans of the Greek Government and the Council of Coastal Transportation, which – in serving the profit-making needs of shipowners, in the name of capital competitiveness and the profitability of business groups – are putting passengers, seafarers and residents at risk in the port of Rafina, despite fierce backlash from seafarers’ unions and local organisations?

What is its position on the justified demand to increase the size of crews on ships, to stop the violation of seafarers’ working hours and rest periods and to ensure the implementation of collective bargaining agreements?

What is its position on the urgent need to take immediate and effective measures to eliminate the risks to marine navigation, passengers, crews and local residents from the dramatically ramped-up schedules that result in ships staying or spending the night outside the port of Rafina in unsafe conditions, given the lack of a tugboat to respond to emergencies?

E-10-2026-003123.t: Definition of ‘manufacturer’ under the PPWR in the context of private-label models
qt: to the Commission Wouter Beke (PPE) Subject:

The application of the definition of ‘manufacturer’ under Article 3(13) of the Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (PPWR) appears unclear in the context of private-label business models. In such models, one undertaking produces and packages a product, while another places it on the market under its own name or trademark. This creates uncertainty regarding the distribution of obligations between the economic operators concerned. 1.
In a private-label model, which entity should be considered the manufacturer within the meaning of Article 3(13) PPWR?

Whose contact details must be indicated on packaging pursuant to Article 15(6) of the regulation, and may the details of another economic operator acting on behalf of the manufacturer be provided instead of those of the manufacturer?
Does the Commission intend to discuss this issue within the Expert Group on Waste or issue guidance to ensure consistent application of the PPWR across the EU?
at: (English version) to the Commission Wouter Beke (PPE) (24 July 2026) Subject: Definition of ‘manufacturer’ under the PPWR in the context of private-label models The application of the definition of ‘manufacturer’ under Article 3(13) of the Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (PPWR) appears unclear in the context of private-label business models. In such models, one undertaking produces and packages a product, while another places it on the market under its own name or trademark. This creates uncertainty regarding the distribution of obligations between the economic operators concerned. 1.
In a private-label model, which entity should be considered the manufacturer within the meaning of Article 3(13) PPWR?

2. Whose contact details must be indicated on packaging pursuant to Article 15(6) of the regulation, and may the details of another economic operator acting on behalf of the manufacturer be provided instead of those of the manufacturer? 3. Does the Commission intend to discuss this issue within the Expert Group on Waste or issue guidance to ensure consistent application of the PPWR across the EU? (14 September 2026) Ahead of the general application of the Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (PPWR) (1) and in order to support the effective and timely implementation thereof by economic operators and Member States, the Commission has issued a Guidance document on the PPWR as well as a Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ) document (2). These documents clarify that under Article 3(1), point 13(a) of the PPWR, if a packaging bears a name or trademark, it is the economic operator under whose name or trademark the packaging is placed on the market that will be considered the ‘manufacturer’. This also applies even if another economic operator is responsible for physically carrying out the manufacturing or filling of that packaging. Pursuant to Article 15(6) of the PPWR, the contact details of the operator considered to be the ‘manufacturer’ must be indicated on the packaging. This obligation cannot be fulfilled by any other economic operator. The Commission is committed to ensuring a pragmatic implementation of the PPWR, and to closely involving stakeholders in this process, including in the context of the Waste Expert Group. Given that stakeholders expressed a strong need for further clarification on the definition of the manufacturer, the Commission provided this at a meeting of the Waste Expert Group on 1 July 2026. Following this request, to ensure a consistent application, the Commission updated the FAQ for the PPWR accordingly. Further information can be found in Section 2 of the above-mentioned Guidance document on the PPWR, as well as Chapter II of the FAQ.

Regulation (EU) 2025/40 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 19 December 2024 on packaging and packaging waste, amending Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 and Directive (EU) 2019/904, and repealing Directive 94/62/EC, OJ L, 2025/40, 22.1.2025. https://green-forum.ec.europa.eu/packaging-and-packaging-waste-regulation-implementation_en.

E-10-2026-003122.t: Practical transitional arrangements for horticulture under the Packaging Regulation
qt: to the Commission Christine Singer (Renew), Joachim Streit (Renew), Engin Eroglu (Renew) Subject:

From 12 August 2026, Regulation (EU) 2025/40 on packaging and packaging waste (PPWR) will oblige manufacturers to indicate their name and postal address on packaging. The related Commission guidance document C/2026/3084, published on 10 June 2026, makes clear that many flowerpots and plant pots are also to be classified as packaging. In horticulture, however, pots are often procured several years in advance, with some plants occupying the same pot for more than a year before being placed on the market. That would therefore mean returning to millions of pots that had previously been planted up or put in storage and labelling them one by one. What is more, pots containing field-grown crops are often muddy, meaning that subsequent labelling requires considerable human, financial and material resources. 1.
Does the Commission concede that retroactively labelling flowerpots that have already been put in storage or planted up entails particular practical challenges?

In view of the environmental objectives of the PPWR, what does the Commission have to say about the fact that the retroactive labelling of flowerpots that have already been planted up or put in storage will mean additional materials and resources?

Where it can be demonstrated that pots were procured or used for plant cultivation prior to 12 August 2026, does the Commission intend to propose transitional arrangements, such as a transition period of four years?
at: (English version) to the Commission Christine Singer (Renew), Joachim Streit (Renew), Engin Eroglu (Renew) (24 July 2026) Subject: Practical transitional arrangements for horticulture under the Packaging Regulation From 12 August 2026, Regulation (EU) 2025/40 on packaging and packaging waste (PPWR) will oblige manufacturers to indicate their name and postal address on packaging. The related Commission guidance document C/2026/3084, published on 10 June 2026, makes clear that many flowerpots and plant pots are also to be classified as packaging. In horticulture, however, pots are often procured several years in advance, with some plants occupying the same pot for more than a year before being placed on the market. That would therefore mean returning to millions of pots that had previously been planted up or put in storage and labelling them one by one. What is more, pots containing field-grown crops are often muddy, meaning that subsequent labelling requires considerable human, financial and material resources. 1. Does the Commission concede that retroactively labelling flowerpots that have already been put in storage or planted up entails particular practical challenges? 2. In view of the environmental objectives of the PPWR, what does the Commission have to say about the fact that the retroactive labelling of flowerpots that have already been planted up or put in storage will mean additional materials and resources? 3. Where it can be demonstrated that pots were procured or used for plant cultivation prior to 12 August 2026, does the Commission intend to propose transitional arrangements, such as a transition period of four years? (17 September 2026) Flowerpots that have not been placed on the market by 12 August 2026, but sit in stock, do not have to be destroyed, remanufactured or re-labelled. To meet the requirements under the Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (1) (PPWR), Articles 15(5) and 15(6), which establish that packaging must bear a unique identification as well as the manufacturer’s name and address, it is possible to provide the required information by means of an accompanying document. This is explained in the Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ) (2) for the PPWR, under section X. The FAQ also explains that, for packaging that is manufactured after the 12 August 2026, an accompanying document can be used when it is not possible to affix the unique identification and the name and address directly on the packaging. Packaging that has been placed on the market before 12 August 2026 can remain on the market, even if it is non-compliant with PPWR.

Regulation (EU) 2025/40 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 19 December 2024 on packaging and packaging waste, amending Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 and Directive (EU) 2019/904, and repealing Directive 94/62/EC, OJ L, 2025/40, 22.1.2025. https://green-forum.ec.europa.eu/packaging-and-packaging-waste-regulation-implementation_en.

E-10-2026-003121.t: Azerbaijan’s erasure of Armenian cultural heritage from Nagorno-Karabakh
qt: to the Commission Marina Mesure (The Left) Subject:

Since the forced exodus of more than 100 000 Armenians from Nagorno-Karabakh in September 2023, the region’s Armenian cultural heritage has been systematically destroyed by Azerbaijan’s authoritarian regime. The Caucasus Heritage Watch initiative (led by archaeologists from Cornell and Purdue universities), which uses satellite imagery to monitor 500 sites that are now inaccessible to independent observers, documented a 75 % rise in the number of sites destroyed between autumn 2023 and spring 2024, and a 29 % rise in the number of sites at risk (churches, monasteries, cemeteries and khatchkars). This pattern mirrors that of Nakhitchevan, where almost all Armenian monuments (108 out of 110) have been razed to the ground since the late 1990s. Meanwhile, by means of its order of 7 December 2021, the International Court of Justice has instructed Azerbaijan to prevent and punish any act of vandalism against that heritage. In the light of the above: 1.
Has the Commission officially protested to Baku about its failure to comply with this order?
Does it intend to make the EU-Azerbaijan energy and trade partnership conditional on compliance with the order of the International Court of Justice of 7 December 2021?
What measures will it support to preserve this common good of humanity and secure displaced people’s right to return?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (21.8.2026) The respect for international law and the protection of human rights are among the core principles that underpin the European Union’s relationship with Azerbaijan, which is based on the EU–Azerbaijan Partnership and Cooperation Agreement1. The EU continues to strongly support the normalisation of relations between Armenia and Azerbaijan. The EU has also consistently made clear that cultural heritage of all communities needs to be effectively protected and that the right to return for displaced persons and refugees needs to be respected. The EU has encouraged Armenia and Azerbaijan to address all outstanding humanitarian issues in the context of their bilateral normalisation process and has offered its support in this regard. The EU-funded European Heritage Hub supported civil society projects in Armenia and Azerbaijan, including a cross-border project. These projects focused on cultural heritage preservation, emergency preparedness in conflict areas, and the role of heritage in peacebuilding. A second call for applications is open until 7 September 2026, supporting initiatives that empower heritage stakeholders in strengthening civil society capacity; strengthen democracy, the rule of law and fundamental rights; build peace and stability, through intercultural and interreligious dialogue and reconciliation. Following the initialling of the bilateral peace treaty between Azerbaijan and Armenia on 8 August 2025, the parties have made important progress towards achieving lasting peace. This progress has already resulted in several tangible steps to the benefit of both countries, including the release of several detainees and the lifting of trade and transit restrictions.

E-10-2026-003120.t: Compliance with the law at the ‘suitable premises’ temporarily holding non-EU nationals subject to a return decision
qt: to the Commission Brando Benifei (S&D) Subject:

In April 2026, Italy’s National Ombudsman for the Rights of Persons Deprived of their Personal Freedoms presented its annual report for 2024 on developments in the areas under its remit, including the ‘various suitable facilities’ placed at the disposal of the Public Security Authority as a back-up (in the event that the specialised detention facilities are at capacity) for the temporary holding of non-EU nationals subject to a return decision. The Ombudsman also highlighted other settings – such as border facilities and crossing points or reception centres for unaccompanied minors – where the de facto deprivation of liberty was a possibility, stressing that the lack of a formal framework governing such sites called for round-the-clock monitoring and stronger safeguards protecting fundamental rights. In the absence of an up-to-date publicly accessible map locating these facilities and with only patchy information available on the way in which they operate and respect the legal rights of the detained, there is much concern about the ‘suitable premises’ and the detention conditions they offer. Particularly in light of the new Return Regulation, can the Commission clarify whether it has any information on the suitable premises in the Member States, whether it intends to publish this information, and whether it deems these facilities and detention practices to be compatible with Union law?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (11.9.2026) The detention of third-country nationals for the purpose of return is currently governed by the Return Directive1, which lays down common standards and procedures for return and detention, including requirements concerning the grounds for detention, judicial oversight, detention conditions, and the protection of fundamental rights. Under the EU legal framework, Member States are responsible for organising and managing detention facilities and for ensuring that any deprivation of liberty complies with EU law, including the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union2. The Commission does not keep any inventory of all facilities that may be used by Member States for the temporary holding or detention of third-country nationals pending return. Consequently, the Commission is not in a position to provide such information. The Commission monitors compliance with the Schengen acquis related to the return of thirdcountry nationals through the Schengen Evaluation and Monitoring Mechanism3. Italy’s last periodic Schengen evaluation took place in June and July 2021, including visits of preremoval detention facilities. During a monitoring visit to some of these specialised detention facilities in April 2026, the evaluation team noted some improvements, while further efforts to improve detention conditions are still required.

E-10-2026-003119.t: Direct funding to address water scarcity and ensure safe drinking water in the outlying island of Ereikoussa
qt: to the Commission Sakis Arnaoutoglou (S&D) Subject:

Ereikoussa, a small outlying island forming part of the Diapontian Islands, is facing a serious problem with the availability and quality of drinking water. Its water supply depends on private wells and boreholes, while the salinisation and overextraction of the underground aquifer compound the issue. The lack of a sewerage system increases the risks to public health and the environment. Although a comprehensive study is in place and ready for implementation to provide a permanent solution to the problem, the local authority’s repeated requests to the national authorities have not been met with a substantive response. The lack of safe water limits the prospects for permanent residence, increases the risk of depopulation and undermines territorial cohesion on an extremely remote and outlying island. In the light of the European water resilience strategy and the new EU strategy for islands, can the Commission say: 1.
Through which EU funding tools can the implementation of this turnkey project be directly supported?
Does it intend to request an update from the Greek authorities with regard to its funding path?
How will it ensure that access to safe water is a priority for small and outlying islands at risk of desertification?

E-10-2026-003118.t: Compatibility with EU law of legislative measures adopted by the Parliament of the Autonomous Community of Valencia with regard to ‘national priority’
qt: to the Commission Leire Pajín (S&D), Sandra Gómez López (S&D), César Luena (S&D), Hana Jalloul Muro (S&D), José Cepeda (S&D), Juan Fernando López Aguilar (S&D), Javi López (S&D), Rosa Serrano Sierra (S&D), Cristina Maestre (S&D), Elena Sancho Murillo (S&D), Marcos Ros Sempere (S&D), Alicia Homs Ginel (S&D), Lina Gálvez (S&D), Nacho Sánchez Amor (S&D), Nicolás González Casares (S&D), Laura Ballarín Cereza (S&D), Idoia Mendia (S&D) Subject:

This week, the Parliament of the Autonomous Community of Valencia adopted a legislative amendment introducing the so-called ‘national priority’ principle and criteria concerning people’s connection to the region, in order to access certain public aid and housing programmes1. Implementing this measure may affect EU citizens and other persons with equal treatment rights recognised by EU law, and – should it come in reach of programmes financed in whole or in part by EU funds – it also raises doubts as to the correct application of EU law. 1.

Does the Commission consider access criteria based on the ‘national priority’ principle to be compatible with Articles 18, 20 and 21 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, Articles 20 and 21 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights, and the principles of equal treatment and non-discrimination?

(15 September 2026) The Commission is aware of the developments referred to by the Honourable Members. Every EU citizen may rely on Article 18 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, which prohibits any discrimination on grounds of nationality in situations falling within the scope of EU law (1). That principle, given specific expression in Article 24 of Directive 2004/38/EC (2), regarding EU citizens exercising free movement, prohibits not only direct discrimination on grounds of nationality but also all indirect forms of discrimination which, by the application of other criteria of differentiation, lead in fact to the same result (3). Indirect discrimination can be justified only if it is based on objective considerations independent of the nationality of the persons concerned and proportionate to the legitimate objective of the national provisions (4). The EU legal migration Directives (5) provide for equal treatment between Member States’ nationals and third-country nationals to the extent covered by those Directives, including, where applicable, regarding social security and access to goods and services made available to the public, including housing. The scope of equal treatment varies between the directives and, in certain areas, Member States may apply the specific limitations or conditions expressly provided for therein. The EU asylum acquis similarly provides for rights as regards access to accommodation, social security and social assistance (6).

E-10-2026-003117.t: Risks of new electrification targets on infrastructure and citizens
qt: to the Commission Ioan-Rareş Bogdan (PPE) Subject:

The Commission’s plan to double electricity use so that it accounts for 46 % of total energy by 2040 puts disproportionate pressure on Eastern European Member States and ignores the economic and structural reality on the ground. 1.

To make the switch to heat pumps and electric vehicles viable, the Commission is proposing an electricity-to-gas price ratio that should not exceed 2.5:1 for households and 2:1 for industry. In the current context, how does the Commission intend to ensure that these ratios are achieved and maintained in countries where the price of electricity is already prohibitive relative to purchasing power, without generating a massive wave of energy poverty or bankrupting national budgets through subsidies?

At the same time, doubling the share of electricity in final consumption requires radical modernisation of transmission and distribution networks, which are already at saturation point. What direct and targeted funding mechanisms is the Commission making available for critical infrastructure in Eastern Europe, given that the storage target of 200 GW by 2030 is unrealistic for these budgets?

Finally, despite the rhetoric about the ‘war on bureaucracy’, the Commission is setting rigid sectoral targets. How does this regulatory fragmentation square with the promise to simplify and reduce the administrative burden for SMEs and citizens?

E-10-2026-003116.t: The Commission’s fractured reality I: redefining democracy beyond the Treaties
qt: to the Commission Christine Anderson (ESN) Subject:

At the meeting of the Special Committee on the European Democracy Shield of 16 July 2026, the Commission’s Joint Research Centre (JRC) presented its report entitled ‘Fractured reality: how democracy can win the global struggle over the information space’. It stated that democracy requires ‘pluralistic, evidence-informed debates’ and that the ‘integrity of the information space guarantees a shared foundation’. It also referred to citizens living in ‘different realities’ and to ‘distorted reality’. Liberal democracy is certainly not limited to majority rule. In the Treaties, however, its substantive content is expressed through representative democracy, pluralism, fundamental rights, political accountability, participation and the rule of law. These guarantees principally protect citizens and political opposition against the misuse of public power. 1.
Does the Commission endorse the JRC’s view that ‘information integrity’, a ‘shared foundation’ and ‘evidence-informed debate’ are constitutive requirements of democracy?
Precisely which provisions of primary EU law establish those concepts as elements of the EU’s democratic order?
Does the Commission accept that these concepts are policy or analytical concepts rather than autonomous legal criteria by which the democratic legitimacy of lawful political debate may be assessed?
at: (English version) to the Commission Christine Anderson (ESN) (23 July 2026) Subject: The Commission’s fractured reality II: information integrity, lawful disagreement and EU competence The Joint Research Centre’s presentation of its report on fractured reality describes democracy as dependent on the ‘integrity of the information space’, a ‘shared foundation’ and ‘evidence-informed’ debate, while referring to ‘distorted reality’ and citizens living in ‘different realities’. This appears to move beyond the traditional liberal-democratic model, under which pluralism includes the freedom to reject institutional opinion, dispute expert claims, distrust public authorities and advance minority interpretations. It risks replacing limits on public power with institutional supervision of how political opinions are formed. 1. How does the Commission define ‘information integrity’, ‘shared foundation’, ‘evidence-informed debate’ and ‘distorted reality’ for the purposes of its policies and programmes? 2. Which authority or actor is entitled to determine when lawful political, scientific or factual disagreement ceases to constitute pluralism and instead threatens the integrity of the information space? 3. Joint answer given by Ms Zaharieva on behalf of the European Commission (23 September 2026) The Commission is committed to protecting and promoting democratic resilience and information integrity online. In its reply to Written Question E-003273/2025 (1), the Commission explained its multifaceted approach to foreign information manipulation and interference and disinformation comprised of regulatory and non-regulatory approaches, each with their respective definitions and legal scope.
https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/E-10-2025-003273-ASW_EN.html.

As set out in the European Democracy Shield, these initiatives strengthen the transparency, accountability and integrity of the information space to ensure that people’s voices are heard and to empower them to be active citizens. Accessing reliable and trustworthy information empowers citizens to exercise their democratic rights and engage meaningfully with institutions. As stated in the pre-amble to the ‘Fractured Reality’ report, its contents do not necessarily reflect the position or opinion of the Commission. The Joint Research Centre provides independent, evidence-based knowledge and science to support EU policy making. The report is intended to inform the Commission’s reflection on ways to strengthen democratic resilience, while fully respecting fundamental rights including freedom of expression, pluralism and democratic accountability. Article 2 of the Treaty on European Union sets out the common values on which the EU is founded. For any EU initiative, the legal basis is determined in the light of the objective and content of the envisaged action.

to the Commission Regina Doherty (PPE) Subject:

The revised electronic Identification, Authentication and Trust Services Regulation (eIDAS Regulation)1 establishes the framework for the European Digital Identity (EUDI) Wallet. Given that the EUDI Wallet will be used to store and present highly sensitive personal identity credentials, cybersecurity and user protection are of paramount importance. Strong customer authentication, including multi-factor authorisation, is widely recognised as an effective safeguard against unauthorised access, identity theft and fraud. At the same time, the implementation of the regulation is progressing at different speeds across the Member States, raising questions about the timetable for the availability and interoperability of EUDI Wallets throughout the EU. In the light of the above: 1.

Why did the Commission not require phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication and hardware-backed security as mandatory minimum security requirements for access to and use of all EUDI Wallets under the revised eIDAS framework and its implementing acts?

Does the Commission consider the current security requirements sufficient to protect users against sophisticated cyber threats and is it considering introducing mandatory multi-factor authentication requirements in future implementing acts or legislative revisions?

Which Member States are on track to meet the applicable deadlines, which have yet to complete the necessary legislative or technical preparations, and how will Commission ensure timely and consistent implementation?

Regulation (EU) 2024/1183 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 11 April 2024 amending Regulation (EU) No 910/2014 as regards establishing the European Digital Identity Framework (OJ L, 2024/1183, 30.4.2024, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1183/oj). 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (8.9.2026)

The security requirements for European Digital Identity Wallets follow a security-by-design approach and provide a high level of protection against sophisticated cyber threats. Wallets must be certified at the high level of assurance as set in Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2015/15021, which requires multi factor authentication. Wallets also rely on strong cryptographic authentication, robust device-bound protections and state-of-the-art encryption. Article 5f(2) of Regulation (EU) No 910/20142 requires private service providers in various sectors to accept European Digital Identity Wallets where strong online user authentication is required. The Commission considers the existing framework to provide an appropriate level of security and is not considering introducing additional requirements. It will, however, continuously monitor technological developments and the evolving cybersecurity threat landscape. Member States are under a legal obligation to provide at least one certified EU Digital Identity Wallet to its citizens by 24 December 2026. The Commission has called on Member States to prioritise wallet issuance preparations in order to meet the regulatory deadline. To support Member States, the Commission has made available a set of tools, including a complete version of the Architecture and Reference Framework, the wallet template, and upcoming testing specifications3. The Commission will also organise an interoperability testing event in October 2026.

E-10-2026-003112.t: Hybrid threats and foreign-controlled charging infrastructure
qt: to the Commission Christine Anderson (ESN) Subject:

On 24 February 2026, the partly publicly-owned German energy company EnBW concluded a multiannual agreement with XCharge for high-power charging stations. EnBW operates more than 8 000 fast-charging points and plans to expand its network to up to 20 000 by 2030. XCharge was founded in Beijing. According to its US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) filings, its chief executive officer (CEO) and its chair/chief technology officer (CTO) control approximately 81.9 % of the voting power through Class B shares, while holding approximately 31.2 % of the share capital. Operators of recharging points are expressly covered by the energy provisions of the Network and Information Systems (NIS 2) Directive, subject to its scope criteria. The Commission has also identified strategic dependencies, unauthorised access to operational data and remotely triggered disruptions as risks arising from connected energy equipment. It has restricted EU funding for projects using solar inverters from high-risk suppliers. 1.

Beyond the general cybersecurity and supply-chain obligations under the NIS 2 Directive, does EU law require the assessment of suppliers’ ultimate control, thirdcountry legal obligations, data access and remote software-update or maintenance capabilities?

Can charging equipment comply with the EU cybersecurity framework where persons exercising decisive control over the supplier retain remote-access or update capabilities and are subject to the laws of a third country presenting elevated security risks?

Will the Commission apply supplier-security and funding restrictions to networked charging infrastructure equivalent to those applied to solar inverters, or explain why charging networks should be treated differently?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (2.10.2026) The proposal for revision of the Cyber Security Act1, currently under negotiation by colegislators, sets out an objective and risk-based framework to address risks related to foreign interference and dependencies in the ICT Supply Chain in NIS 2 sectors2. For charging infrastructure specifically, the Risk Assessment on Connected and Automated Vehicles (CAV3) recommends that Member States apply the ICT Supply Chain Security Toolbox to ‘CAVs and related charging infrastructure’, including assessment of critical suppliers, multi-vendor strategies, reducing dependencies on high-risk suppliers and, where appropriate, restricting or excluding high-risk suppliers from critical supply chains. Risk assessments are legally of non-binding nature. The proposal for revision of the Cyber Security Act4 sets out that the high-risk suppliers, as defined in the proposed act, shall not be entitled to participate in any activities under EU funding programmes and instruments implemented in direct and indirect management in accordance with Article 136 Regulation (EU, Euratom) 2024/2509 and EU sector-specific rules as well as in any EU funding activities implemented in shared management in relation to the provision of ICT components or components that include ICT components to be used in key ICT assets as identified in accordance with the Regulation.

1 https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/proposal-regulation-eu-cybersecurity-act. 2 https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/news/ict-supply-chain-security-eu-adopts-toolbox-mitigate-risks. 3 https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/toolbox-improve-ict-supply-chain-security. 4 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex:52026PC0011.

E-10-2026-003111.t: Application of the EU Methane Regulation to imports from non-EU countries during a possible suspension of sanctions from 1 January 2027
qt: to the Commission Anja Arndt (ESN) Subject:
Application of the EU Methane Regulation to imports from non-EU countries during a possible suspension of sanctions from 1 January 2027

E-10-2026-003110.t: Libya’s repeated unilateral maritime claims against EU Member States
qt: to the Commission Nikolas Farantouris (S&D), Yannis Maniatis (S&D) Subject:

What specific initiatives does it intend to take to protect the sovereign rights and legitimate interests of EU Member States against Libya’s recurrent unilateral claims?

E-10-2026-003109.t: The disproportionate impact of the temporary customs duty on low-value mixed consignments
qt: to the Commission Kathleen Van Brempt (S&D) Subject:

Under Council Regulation (EU) 2026/382, from 1 July 2026 until 1 July 2028 a customs duty of EUR 3 is applicable per tariff sub-heading in consignments whose intrinsic value does not exceed a total of EUR 150. The objectives of fairer competition and improved customs controls are justified. However, there are indications that the levy per tariff sub-heading is making mixed orders disproportionately expensive. In one of the reported cases, an order for electronic components worth EUR 26.81 incurred EUR 14.52 in additional customs charges. This may affect hobbyists, repairers, researchers and small businesses, particularly where specialised components are concerned and which are not available within the EU. 1.

Is the Commission aware of the potentially disproportionate impact of the levy per tariff sub-heading, and does it intend to examine the impact on consumers, looking, amongst other things, at the relationship between the levy and the intrinsic value of consignments?

Is the Commission considering applying targeted adjustments, such as a maximum amount per consignment, a minimum threshold or a broader grouping of closely related tariff sub-headings, with appropriate safeguards to prevent circumvention?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (7.9.2026) The Commission underlines that the temporary EUR 3 customs duty is intended as a transitional solution until the EU Customs Data Hub for e-commerce becomes operational on 1 July 2028, at which point customs duties will be calculated based on the product’s tariff classification, origin and value. The EUR 3 customs duty is applied per declaration line (item) irrespective of the quantity, as every customs duty is today applied per item. The Guidance on implementation of the EUR 3 duty1 provides several examples on how to declare goods. The Commission has further clarified2 that economic operators must be encouraged to use one declaration line per goods sharing tariff classification in H7. It is currently not envisaged to apply any changes or adjustments. Goods can benefit from reduced or zero duty in case of preferential trade and customs EU agreements3. Regarding the ‘customs charges’, consumers buying online are not legally responsible for paying the EUR 3 customs duty to the customs authorities. The debtor is the platform or seller or any other business involved in the sale and transport of the imported goods; it can be the carrier or any authorised representative. The business decision of charging the EUR 3 duty and additional charges to consumers stays with the relevant sellers/platforms. As concerns the impact of the measure, the Commission will have to assess, by 1 October 20264 whether a diversion of trade flows occurs following the introduction of the temporary EUR 3 duty and, if needed, whether to extend the scope of the EUR 3 to all items in consignments not exceeding EUR 150.
1 https://taxation-customs.ec.europa.eu/document/download/053e5b4e-f0be-4f20-9a23-

3e3b659a6676_en?filename=Customs%20Guidance%20on%20EUR%203%20customs%20duty.pdf, see Part 3.3.1. Definition of item. 2 https://taxation-customs.ec.europa.eu/document/download/8350b1aa-935a-4b80-a349385b36292fbe_en?filename=Questions%20and%20answers%20on%203%20EUR%20Guidance%20MS%20and %20Economic%20operators_clean15062026.pdf on the implementation of the EUR 3 customs duty. 3 See Part 3.3.3 of the Guidance. 4 As provided for in Article 3 of Council Regulation (EU) 2026/382.

qt: to the Commission Gerald Hauser (PfE) Subject:

Surrogacy is a medically complex process that can entail a number of risks and side effects. Before the pregnancy can begin, hormonal treatment and artificial insemination are required. Both of these procedures can also be associated with significant side effects. The psychological, ethical, legal, financial and emotional implications of surrogacy should also be emphasised. Just recently, the UN Special Rapporteur on violence against women called for a global ban. The EU has already included the exploitation of surrogacy in its anti-trafficking directive – alongside slavery, sexual exploitation, illegal adoption and forced marriage. It referred to the need to care for victims, including through the provision of medical treatment and psychological and psychiatric assistance. Nevertheless, according to media reports, Germany’s Commissioner of the Federal Government for Drug Policy and the country’s former Health Minister both recently used companies organising surrogacy in the US to have a child, as – unlike in the US – surrogacy is prohibited in Germany. Some media outlets have described their actions as ‘baby buying’. 1.
What is the Commission’s position on the medical, psychological, ethical, financial and legal implications of surrogacy?
Does the Commission intend to take measures to put a stop to this form of human trafficking in general?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (11.9.2026) The Commission is committed to upholding children and women’s rights, in full respect of its competences. Substantive family law, including rules on surrogacy, falls within the competence of the Member States. Each Member State decides its policy and legal position as regards surrogacy, including its medical, psychological, ethical, financial and legal implications. The exploitation of surrogacy is included as a form of exploitation in the Anti-Trafficking Directive1. The Directive targets those who coerce or deceive women into acting as surrogate mothers, without prejudice to national rules on surrogacy, including criminal and family law.
1 Directive 2011/36/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 5 April 2011 on preventing and

combating trafficking in human beings and protecting its victims, and replacing Council Framework Decision 2002/629/JHA (https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2011/36/oj/eng), amended by Directive (EU) 2024/1712 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 June 2024 amending Directive 2011/36/EU on preventing and combating trafficking in human beings and protecting its victims (https://eurlex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2024/1712/oj/eng).

E-10-2026-003106.t: EU external relations and asserting the right of return of Armenians displaced from Nagorno-Karabakh
qt: to the Commission Marina Mesure (The Left) Subject:

Following Azerbaijan’s military offensive in September 2023, more than 100 000 Armenians were forced to flee their historic homeland of Nagorno-Karabakh. During an official trip to Armenia, I met displaced families, including children, who are living in exile in extremely precarious conditions. On 17 November 2023, the International Court of Justice ruled that Azerbaijan must allow the safe and unconditional return of the people displaced from Nagorno-Karabakh, and ensure that the Armenians who remained there are protected. To date, insufficient guarantees have been given as regards the implementation of the international obligation on which the Court’s order is based. At a time when the European Union is forging a closer partnership with Armenia: 1.
What political and legal initiatives does the Commission intend to take to ensure that the international obligations concerned are actually implemented?
Does the Commission intend to make upholding the right of return of the Armenians of Nagorno-Karabakh one of the guiding principles of its political and economic relations with Azerbaijan?

Does it intend to make upholding the right of return of the Armenians of NagornoKarabakh part of its political and diplomatic action in the region, in accordance with the orders of the International Court of Justice?
at: (English version) to the Commission Marina Mesure (The Left) (23 July 2026) Subject: EU external relations and asserting the right of return of Armenians displaced from Nagorno-Karabakh Following Azerbaijan’s military offensive in September 2023, more than 100 000 Armenians were forced to flee their historic homeland of Nagorno-Karabakh. During an official trip to Armenia, I met displaced families, including children, who are living in exile in extremely precarious conditions. On 17 November 2023, the International Court of Justice ruled that Azerbaijan must allow the safe and unconditional return of the people displaced from Nagorno-Karabakh, and ensure that the Armenians who remained there are protected. To date, insufficient guarantees have been given as regards the implementation of the international obligation on which the Court’s order is based. At a time when the European Union is forging a closer partnership with Armenia: 1.
What political and legal initiatives does the Commission intend to take to ensure that the international obligations concerned are actually implemented?
Does the Commission intend to make upholding the right of return of the Armenians of Nagorno-Karabakh one of the guiding principles of its political and economic relations with Azerbaijan?

Does it intend to make upholding the right of return of the Armenians of Nagorno-Karabakh part of its political and diplomatic action in the region, in accordance with the orders of the International Court of Justice?

(2 September 2026) The respect for international law and the protection of human rights are among the core principles that underpin the EU’s relationship with Azerbaijan, which is based on the EU-Azerbaijan Partnership and Cooperation Agreement (1). The EU continues to strongly support the normalisation of relations between Armenia and Azerbaijan. The EU has also consistently made clear that the right of return for displaced persons and refugees, which applies to all concerned people, needs to be respected. The EU has encouraged Armenia and Azerbaijan to address all outstanding humanitarian issues in the context of their bilateral normalisation process, including through confidence-building measures, and has offered its support in this regard. Following the initialling of the bilateral peace treaty between Azerbaijan and Armenia on 8 August 2025, the parties have made important progress towards achieving lasting peace. This progress has already resulted in several tangible steps to the benefit of both countries, including the release of several detainees and the lifting of trade and transit restrictions. The EU strongly supports this process and remains ready to continue assisting the parties in their efforts.
