E-10-2026-003104.t: Phytosanitary, regulatory-reciprocity and trade risks posed by greater citrus imports from third countries
qt: to the Commission Vicent Marzà Ibáñez (Verts/ALE) Subject:

Data from the Commission’s Directorate-General for Agriculture and Rural Development show that, in May 2026 the EU imported 134 923 tonnes of mandarins, clementines and oranges and 50 973 tonnes of lemons and limes (a record high for that month), chiefly from Egypt and South Africa. Bodies representing farmers, such as La Unió Llauradora i Ramadera, have drawn attention to the greater prevalence of verified cases of black spot (Phyllosticta citricarpa), a quarantine pest not present in the EU, in consignments of South African produce. The Commission should ensure that the uptick in these imports does not compromise either plant health or the level playing field for European producers. Given these circumstances: 1.
Why has the increase in cases of black spot detected not led to a precautionary suspension of imports, as provided for in EU phytosanitary regulations on quarantine pests?
Why does the Commission allow third countries to export to the EU without being subject to the same traceability and residue-oversight requirements as those imposed on EU producers?
Is the Commission willing to acknowledge that the trade agreements with Egypt, South Africa and Mercosur are compromising the competitiveness of the European citrus sector?

E-10-2026-003102.t: Possible breaches of Directive (EU) 2020/2184 on the quality of water intended for human consumption and Regulation (EU) No 305/2011 laying down harmonised conditions for the marketing of construction products in the water supply network in  Xàtiva (Valencia)
qt: to the Commission Vicent Marzà Ibáñez (Verts/ALE) Subject:

Possible breaches of Directive (EU) 2020/2184 on the quality of water intended for human consumption and Regulation (EU) No 305/2011 laying down harmonised conditions for the marketing of construction products in the water supply network in Xàtiva (Valencia)

The audit made by the Valencian Community’s audit office (Sindicatura de Comptes) (in 2019, covering financial years 2015–2017) found that the municipality of Xàtiva (Valencia) has a water efficiency rate of 20 per cent and loses around 4 million m³ of drinking water each year in leaks. Seventy per cent of the network (68 km) is made of fibre-cement pipes, and some independent analyses have detected lead and asbestos microfibres in drinking water. The audit office’s report confirms that the municipal council is systematically in breach of its obligations regarding self-monitoring and data reporting, and has not replaced a single kilometre of the network during the period covered by the audit. In view of the above: 1.
Is the Commission aware of this case, in which prohibited materials (fibre-cement and lead) have been found in drinking-water-supply infrastructure in the EU?
Is the Commission of the opinion that a local authority’s prolonged failure to engage in self-monitoring and data-reporting constitutes a breach of Directive (EU) 2020/2184?

How does the Commission intend to check whether Spain is meeting the deadlines for the transposition and effective implementation of Directive (EU) 2020/2184 in local municipalities where proven health risks are present?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (30.9.2026) In EU water supply systems, asbestos-cement pipes were widely used up to the 1980s. Although still present in Member States’ water supply systems, these pipes are progressively phased out. Under the recast Drinking Water Directive (DWD)1, Member States are required to assess potential health risks and, where necessary, take measures to eliminate such risks. To ensure the protection of human health, Member States must ensure that the level of lead in drinking water does not exceed the limit values for lead set out in the recast DWD. The DWD requires Member States to ensure that drinking water is monitored, risks are assessed and managed, and the required data is made available to the European Environmental Agency2 and the Commission. The Commission does not routinely check local monitoring and data collection, as primary responsibility lies with Member States’ competent authorities. However, where there are indications of non-compliances, the Commission can request clarifications, launch targeted fact-finding, and, if necessary, pursue infringement action. The deadline for transposing the DWD in national law was 12 January 2023. The Commission is assessing the transposition conformity in all Member States. In this context, the Commission has launched an infringement procedure INFR(2025)20263 for non-conform transposition against Spain. While the Commission has no indication of any drinking water quality compliance issues in the area concerned, it will continue to monitor the annually updated drinking water quality data provided by Spain. If the Commission identifies shortcomings in water quality compliance, it may take appropriate follow-up action, including infringement proceedings specifically related to such shortcomings.
1 Directive (EU) 2020/2184 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 16 December 2020 on the quality

of water intended for human consumption (recast), OJ L 435, 23.12.2020, p. 1–62. 2 https://www.eea.europa.eu/en. 3 https://ec.europa.eu/implementing-eu-law/search-infringementdecisions/?langCode=EN&version=v1&typeOfSearch=byDecision&refId=INFR(2025)2026&page=1&size=10 &order=desc&sortColumns=decisionDate.

E-10-2026-003101.t: Clarification on the scope of ‘consumer products’ in the proposed restriction of PFAS
qt: to the Commission Flavio Tosi (PPE), Massimiliano Salini (PPE), Letizia Moratti (PPE), Salvatore De Meo (PPE), Susana Solís Pérez (PPE), Stefan Köhler (PPE), Pietro Fiocchi (ECR), Céline Imart (PPE), Christophe Gomart (PPE), Nadine Morano (PPE), François-Xavier Bellamy (PPE) Subject:

The Commission has announced its intention to further restrict the use of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) in consumer products under the REACH Regulation and related policy initiatives. At the same time, questions remain regarding the regulatory scope and practical interpretation of the notion of ‘consumer products’, particularly in relation to products with different lifecycles, uses and technical requirements. In this context, it is important to ensure legal certainty, proportionality and consistency with the EU’s industrial, circular economy and competitiveness objectives. Particular attention has been drawn to the distinction between short-life consumer applications, for which alternatives may already be available, and durable applications that rely on fluoropolymers to meet safety, performance, durability and resource-efficiency requirements. This raises questions regarding how different categories of consumer products, including durable and short-life applications, should be considered in the future regulatory approach. In the light of the above: 1.
Is the Commission considering a clearer definition or categorisation of ‘consumer products’ in the context of the proposed restriction of PFAS?

How does the Commission intend to ensure a proportionate and evidence-based approach that takes into account differences between product categories, including product durability, the availability and life-cycle impact of alternatives, circular economy objectives and the competitiveness of EU industry?
at: (Versione italiana) Interrogazione con richiesta di risposta scritta E-003101/26 alla Commissione Flavio Tosi (PPE), Massimiliano Salini (PPE), Letizia Moratti (PPE), Salvatore De Meo (PPE), Susana Solís Pérez (PPE), Stefan Köhler (PPE), Pietro Fiocchi (ECR), Céline Imart (PPE), Christophe Gomart (PPE), Nadine Morano (PPE), François-Xavier Bellamy (PPE) (23 luglio 2026) Oggetto: Chiarimenti sull'ambito di applicazione del concetto di «prodotti di consumo» nelle future restrizioni relative ai PFAS La Commissione ha annunciato l'intenzione di limitare ulteriormente l'uso dei PFAS nei prodotti di consumo ai sensi del regolamento REACH e delle iniziative politiche correlate. Allo stesso tempo, permangono interrogativi in merito all'ambito di applicazione normativo e all'interpretazione pratica della nozione di «prodotti di consumo», in particolare in relazione ai prodotti con cicli di vita, usi e requisiti tecnici diversi. In tale contesto, è importante garantire la certezza del diritto, la proporzionalità e la coerenza con gli obiettivi dell'UE in materia di industria, economia circolare e competitività. È stata prestata particolare attenzione alla distinzione tra le applicazioni a breve termine per i consumatori, per le quali possono già essere disponibili alternative, e le applicazioni durevoli che si basano su fluoropolimeri per soddisfare i requisiti di sicurezza, prestazione, durabilità ed efficienza delle risorse. Ciò solleva interrogativi sul modo in cui le diverse categorie di prodotti di consumo, comprese le applicazioni durevoli e di breve durata, dovrebbero essere prese in considerazione nel futuro approccio normativo. Alla luce di quanto precede: 1.
la Commissione sta valutando la possibilità di definire o classificare in modo più chiaro i «prodotti di consumo» nel contesto della futura restrizione sui PFAS?

In che modo intende la Commissione garantire un approccio proporzionato e basato su dati concreti che tenga conto delle differenze tra le categorie di prodotti, tra cui la durabilità dei prodotti, la disponibilità e l'impatto sul ciclo di vita delle alternative, gli obiettivi dell'economia circolare e la competitività dell'industria dell'UE?

Presentazione: 23.7.2026 Risposta del Vicepresidente esecutivo Stéphane Séjourné a nome della Commissione europea (25 settembre 2026) Come indicato nel suo piano d'azione per l'industria chimica europea (1), la Commissione affronterà sia l'uso industriale che quello da parte dei consumatori nella sua proposta di restrizione relativa alle sostanze pe — e polifluoroalchiliche (PFAS) Restrizione universale delle PFAS. Tale proposta fornirà le pertinenti definizioni operative della terminologia utilizzata nel testo giuridico, tenendo conto anche delle definizioni esistenti di cui al regolamento concernente la registrazione, la valutazione, l'autorizzazione e la restrizione delle sostanze chimiche (2), come avviene per altre restrizioni e come richiesto per garantire la necessaria certezza del diritto. Il fascicolo di restrizione è attualmente ancora allo studio dell'Agenzia europea per le sostanze chimiche (ECHA). In tale contesto, i diversi tipi di usi, la disponibilità di alternative alle PFAS e gli impatti socioeconomici delle opzioni di restrizione sono valutati dal comitato per l'analisi socioeconomica (SEAC) dell'ECHA. I pareri definitivi dell'ECHA costituiranno la base per l'elaborazione della proposta di restrizione della Commissione, tenendo conto di tutte le informazioni pertinenti, compresi obiettivi quali l'economia circolare e la competitività dell'industria dell'UE. La Commissione si impegna a presentare una proposta equilibrata di restrizione REACH, con l'obiettivo generale di ridurre al minimo le emissioni di PFAS, sostenendo nel contempo la resilienza e l'autonomia strategica dell'UE. Qualora non siano disponibili alternative adeguate in termini di prestazioni e sicurezza, la prosecuzione dell'uso delle PFAS nelle applicazioni industriali critiche può essere consentita, nel rispetto di condizioni rigorose fino a quando non saranno trovati sostituti accettabili.
https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/IT/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:52025DC0530. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/IT/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02006R1907-20260622.

E-10-2026-003099.t: Are the national parliaments still able to defend their countries’ competences?
qt: to the Commission Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE) Subject:

Under the principle of subsidiarity enshrined in the EU’s Treaties, national parliaments have the right to point out instances of a European project unnecessarily encroaching upon the Member States’ competences. They only have eight weeks to react, however, and their objections rarely oblige the Commission to withdraw its text. The early warning mechanism provided for in Protocol No 2 to the Treaty on European Union aims to ensure compliance with the principle of subsidiarity by directly involving national parliaments in the scrutiny of EU legislative proposals. In practice, despite the fact that this ‘yellow card’ mechanism has been used on a number of occasions, it has very rarely led to a Commission proposal being substantially amended or withdrawn. This raises questions as how effective the mechanism actually is. 1.
Is the Commission in favour of giving national parliaments more time to scrutinise proposed EU legislation so that they can fully exercise the subsidiarity check provided for in the Treaties?

Will it agree to a mandatory review of a proposal when a significant number of national parliaments take the view that the EU is reaching beyond its remit, and to provide a detailed statement of the reasons behind any decision to maintain its proposal despite those objections?
Would it support a mechanism that allows the national parliaments to have a proposal for EU legislation withdrawn when a majority of the national parliaments object to it?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (14.9.2026) 1. The deadline of eight weeks for national Parliaments’ subsidiarity check of proposed EU legislation is set in Article 6 of Protocol No 21 to the Treaties. To facilitate national Parliaments’ scrutiny during recess periods, the Commission excludes the periods from 1 to 31 August and from 20 December to 10 January of the following year from the calculation of the eight weeks. Any change of the eight weeks deadline would require a Treaty revision, in which the European Parliament and the Member States play a key role. 2. The thresholds for triggering a review by the Commission of a draft legislative act are described in Article 7(2) of Protocol No 22. After a review, the Commission may decide to maintain, amend or withdraw the draft. Reasons must be given for this decision. Further than that, the Commission has committed to provide a detailed and comprehensive ‘aggregated response’ to the subsidiarity concerns expressed by a significant number of national Parliaments even if the number of their reasoned opinions does not reach the relevant thresholds for triggering a review set in Protocol No 2. 3. Article 7(3) of Protocol No 2 gives to the European Parliament and the Council, as the Union legislator, the right to decide whether a legislative proposal shall be given further consideration after a majority of national Parliaments has considered it as being in breach with the subsidiarity principle but the Commission decided to maintain it. Giving the same right to national Parliaments would require a Treaty change.
1 Protocol (No 2) on the application of the principles of subsidiarity and proportionality, https://eur-

lex.europa.eu/LexUriServ/LexUriServ.do?uri=CELEX:12008M/PRO/02:EN:HTML. 2 Reasoned opinions on a draft legislative act's non-compliance with the principle of subsidiarity representing at least one third of the votes allocated to national Parliaments, or one quarter for proposals in the area of freedom, security and justice based on Article 76 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union.

E-10-2026-003098.t: EU support for the Global Partnership for Education ahead of the 2026 Replenishment Conference
qt: to the Commission Marco Tarquinio (S&D), Barry Andrews (Renew), Sandro Ruotolo (S&D), Giuseppe Lupo (S&D), Elisabetta Gualmini (Renew), Mimmo Lucano (The Left), Erik Marquardt (Verts/ALE), Hana Jalloul Muro (S&D) Subject:

The Global Partnership for Education (GPE) is the leading multilateral fund for strengthening education systems in low-income countries. Its Replenishment Conference will take place in New York on 23 September 2026, at a time when international funding for education is contracting following cuts by several major donors. Against this backdrop, the number of children out of school has risen for the seventh consecutive year, reaching 273 million. This trend risks undermining the right to education and jeopardising the achievement of UN Sustainable Development Goal 4. However, education remains a strategic investment for inclusive growth, gender equality, resilience, peace and stability. A further reduction in financial support would risk reversing decades of progress, particularly in conflict-affected countries. The EU is a long-standing partner of the GPE and its second-largest donor, having allocated EUR 700 million for the period 2021-2027. However, its orientations for the next funding cycle remain unclear. In the light of the above: 1.
What position will the Commission take ahead of the GPE Replenishment Conference?
Will it commit to maintaining at least the current level of support for the GPE?
How will it ensure that education remains a priority of EU external action and the future multiannual financial framework?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (31.8.2026) The EU has long been a steadfast and reliable partner of the Global Partnership for Education (GPE), and this close cooperation remains essential in reinforcing and complementing EU support to partner countries. President of the European Commission pledged EUR 700 million to GPE for the period 2021–20271, and the Commission remains fully committed to honouring that pledge. This represents an average contribution of EUR 100 million per year and already covers 2026 and 2027, the first two years of GPE’s next financing cycle. Education remains a longstanding priority of the EU’s external action and a key pillar of the Global Gateway strategy2. Continued support for education and skills development in partner countries — including vocational education and training, within a lifelong learning approach — will therefore remain of central importance. With regard to the next funding cycle, however, the Commission cannot prejudge the outcome of the negotiations and programming decisions under the Multiannual Financial Framework 2028-2034 and is therefore not in a position, at this stage, to make commitments beyond 2027.
1 https://international-partnerships.ec.europa.eu/news-and-events/news/education-eu-increases-its-commitment-

E-10-2026-003097.t: Cutro shipwreck, tragedies at sea and the right of vicitms’ families
qt: to the Commission Leoluca Orlando (Verts/ALE), Estrella Galán (The Left), Benedetta Scuderi (Verts/ALE), Cecilia Strada (S&D), Rudi Kennes (The Left), Elisabetta Gualmini (Renew), Murielle Laurent (S&D), Mélissa Camara (Verts/ALE), Merja Kyllönen (The Left), Cristina Guarda (Verts/ALE), Per Clausen (The Left), Ignazio Roberto Marino (Verts/ALE), Damien Carême (The Left), Leila Chaibi (The Left), Erik Marquardt (Verts/ALE), Danilo Della Valle (The Left), Ilaria Salis (The Left), Giuseppe Lupo (S&D), Tineke Strik (Verts/ALE), Rima Hassan (The Left), Majdouline Sbai (Verts/ALE), Brando Benifei (S&D), Annalisa Corrado (S&D), Pasquale Tridico (The Left) Subject:

Following the meeting in Brussels with family members of some of the victims of the Cutro shipwreck which occurred in late February 2023, accountability and measures to prevent such tragedies are still lacking in Italy and at European level. At least 94 people drowned in Italian territorial waters near Steccato di Cutro, Calabria, as the vessel sank just metres from the Italian shoreline. At the time, the government had restricted the response to maritime distress calls involving migrants. While not an isolated case, this tragedy is significant as it could have been prevented. Moreover, it highlights the lack of rights afforded to the family members of the deceased and leaves both the families and the deceased as victims of this tragedy. Therefore, we ask: 1.
Is the Commission ready to establish a clear framework for providing both psychological and legal support to the families of those who died in the Mediterranean Sea?
Will the Commission consider opening a humanitarian corridor to Europe for the victims’ family members to enable them to be present for potential legal proceedings?
Will the Commission ask the Italian Government to provide concrete support for the families and ensure accountability for what happened in February 2023 as it had promised?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.9.2026) The Commission deeply regrets the tragic loss of lives in the shipwreck off Cutro in February 2023. Rendering assistance to persons in distress at sea is a duty and an obligation under international law for the Member States. Migrant deaths at sea underline the need for a comprehensive approach to migration management and the fight against migrant smuggling. Under international maritime law, responsibility for coordinating search and rescue operations lies primarily with the competent national authorities. It is for the competent national authorities, including judicial authorities where appropriate, to establish the facts and assess compliance with the applicable legal framework. The Commission continues to monitor developments within the limits of its competences under the Treaties. The Commission has no competence to request an independent assessment of an individual search and rescue operation carried out by a Member State. The Commission continues to support Member States in strengthening search and rescue, including through the Search and Rescue Contact Group, which brings together Member States, EU agencies to exchange operational experience and support the effective implementation of the applicable legal framework. The Victims’ Rights Directive1, revised in 20262, provides for a comprehensive set of rights for victims of crime and their family members3. It is for national authorities to ensure their application in the circumstances raised by the Honourable Members, in line also with the principle of access to justice under Article 47 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the EU4. The examination and issuance of visas fall within the competence of the Member States, as laid down in applicable EU law.

E-10-2026-003096.t: Ensuring cybersecurity, privacy and system integrity safeguards in DMA interoperability requirements for agentic AI
qt: to the Commission Emil Radev (PPE) Subject:

Recent developments in agentic AI have highlighted concerns about the security and privacy risks associated with its development and deployment. Notably, the cybersecurity agencies of Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the UK and the US have issued joint guidance on the adoption of agentic AI, highlighting the need for robust legal, technical and platform-level safeguards. Such safeguards are crucial in the context of the Digital Markets Act (DMA), which may require developers to provide third parties with interoperability access to mobile operating system functionalities relevant to agentic AI. Such obligations must not weaken the privacy, security and integrity protections built into operating systems by design. Against this background: 1.

How does the Commission assess whether DMA safeguards suffice to ensure that interoperability obligations preserve privacy, security and system integrity protections embedded in mobile operating systems?

Will the Commission undertake a more comprehensive assessment of privacy and cybersecurity risks associated with agentic AI-related interoperability requirements, and reflect the findings in future DMA guidance and reviews?

Will the Commission consider establishing a formal role for data protection, cybersecurity and consumer protection authorities in DMA implementation and enforcement to ensure that interoperability measures are assessed across competition, privacy, security and consumer protection objectives?

Notably, the cybersecurity agencies of Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the UK and the US have issued joint guidance on the adoption of agentic AI, highlighting the need for robust legal, technical and platform-level safeguards. Such safeguards are crucial in the context of the Digital Markets Act (DMA), which may require developers to provide third parties with interoperability access to mobile operating system functionalities relevant to agentic AI. Such obligations must not weaken the privacy, security and integrity protections built into operating systems by design. Against this background: 1.

Will the Commission undertake a more comprehensive assessment of privacy and cybersecurity risks associated with agentic AI-related interoperability requirements, and reflect the findings in future DMA guidance and reviews?

Will the Commission consider establishing a formal role for data protection, cybersecurity and consumer protection authorities in DMA implementation and enforcement to ensure that interoperability measures are assessed across competition, privacy, security and consumer protection objectives?

(17 September 2026) AI presents critical and urgent opportunities for Europe. The Commission seeks to unlock them by fostering innovation and diversification while protecting users and fundamental rights. The Digital Markets Act (DMA) (1) interoperability obligation supports this objective by preventing gatekeepers from reserving operating system (OS) features for their own services. The Commission is aware of the risks linked to agentic AI and ensures that they are duly considered in the DMA implementation. Gatekeepers can and must implement the necessary OS safeguards to manage those risks, and the DMA allows them to determine their exact technical implementation. But those risks cannot be used as a pretext to exclude alternative providers — especially as those might offer more secure and privacy-friendly AI services. The Commission recently adopted a decision that provides guidance on how Google Android must interoperate with AI services (2). In developing this guidance, the Commission engaged in extensive technical discussions with Alphabet, including its technical experts and engineers, and allowed Alphabet to implement strong mitigations to preserve privacy, security and system integrity on Android devices (3). Other EU rules — including the Cyber Resilience Act (4), the AI Act (5), the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) (6), the NIS2 Directive (7), and the Digital Services Act (8) — still apply in full to both gatekeepers and third parties.

E-10-2026-003095.t: Israel’s destruction of the Gazan fisheries sector
qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Emma Fourreau (The Left), Rima Hassan (The Left) Subject:

Since October 2023, 238 fishermen have been murdered by Israel in Gaza, including after the ceasefire agreement1. While around 110 000 Gazans depended on the fishing sector before the genocide began, the industry is now at risk: vessels and fishing infrastructure have been destroyed by Israel, materials needed to repair vessels have been subject to a blockade, access to the sea is strictly limited and fishermen are systematically targeted by Israeli gunfire2. Catches of fish – a vital source of protein for Gazans – have fallen to an all-time low. The 15 tonnes that could once be caught in a single day now take more than a month to reel in3. The destruction of the fisheries sector is starving the Palestinian people, driving their economy to collapse and completely eroding their resilience. With this in mind: 1.

What action does the Commission intend to take to support the Gazan fisheries sector, including by providing financial support for the acquisition of the necessary equipment and ensuring safe access to the sea, in order to continually ensure the Gazan people’s right to food?
What action does the Commission intend to take to stop the Israeli blockade, which, in particular, deprives Palestinians of the materials needed to repair and maintain fishing vessels?

E-10-2026-003094.t: Compliance with EU air quality requirements and compatibility of Italy’s ‘Ferrobus’ programme
qt: to the Commission Matteo Ricci (S&D) Subject:

The EU’s sustainable mobility strategy has set the target of growing rail freight transport by 50 % by 2030. With a rail modal share of around 11 %, Italy is already the subject of adverse judgments and infringement procedures for exceeding the EU limit values for PM10, NO2 and PM2.5. Italy’s ‘Ferrobonus’ programme, cited in the national air quality action plan for 2025-2027 as a key measure in the modal shift, implies an ‘increase’ in resources; yet the national budget shows that what we are really seeing is a repackaging of previously allocated funds rather than a genuine increase. After the programme was suspended and the accounts subsequently adjusted, the actual capacity of the programme for the period October 2025-October 2026 has reportedly been cut by 80 %, falling from EUR 50 to 10 million per year. In light of the above: 1.
Is the Commission aware of this cut and the impact it will have on Italy’s compliance with Directive 2008/50/EC?
How does it check that measures in the national plans are backed by actual financial resources and not legacy funds?
In view of ongoing infringement procedures, will it ask Italy for assurances that it is has sufficient funds to cover the modal shift to rail transport?

(11 September 2026) The Ambient Air Quality Directive (1) requires compliance with EU air quality standards, with the aim to protect human health and the environment. It is for Member States to determine the appropriate measures to achieve them and adopt air quality plans to ensure that any exceedance period can be kept as short as possible. The Commission has taken enforcement action on air quality in Italy opening several infringement procedures, currently ongoing (2). In two of these, Italy was referred to the Court of Justice of the EU, that found it in breach of the directive (3), (4). In March 2024, the Commission sent a letter of formal notice (5) to Italy for continued failure to comply with the judgment in Case C-644/18 regarding the exceedance of particulate matter 10 (PM10) limit values. Moreover, in December 2025, the Commission sent a letter of formal notice (6) to Italy for failure to comply with the limit values set for nitrogen dioxide in the agglomerations of Naples and Palermo. From 2030, stricter limit values for pollutants under the revised Air Quality Directive (7) will apply. Where air quality reporting indicates that limit values are exceeded, the Commission assesses whether air quality plans have been adopted and whether the measures part of air quality plans are appropriate, including their financing.

E-10-2026-003093.t: Transparency of environmental, social and governance data
qt: to the Commission François-Xavier Bellamy (PPE), Christophe Gomart (PPE) Subject:

The implementation of the Regulation on sustainability‑related disclosures in the financial services sector (SFDR) is based on environmental, social and governance (ESG) data that enables financial market participants to fulfil their transparency and classification requirements for financial products. Increasing the thresholds at which companies are required to make non‑financial disclosures, while necessary, will nevertheless increase the financial sector’s dependence on external ESG data providers, which are often based outside the EU. While Regulation (EU) 2024/3005 establishes a framework for rating activities, shortcomings in the transparency of the methods used by ESG data providers remain. A lack of transparency over data sources and quality control mechanisms can be detrimental to the comparability, legal certainty and credibility of disclosures, and raises the issue of EU sovereignty when it comes to ESG data. In addition, the ongoing revision of the SFDR seems to establish a difference in treatment between data published by financial actors and data supplied from unregulated data providers. 1.
Is the Commission planning to revise Regulation (EU) 2024/3005 to ensure the SFDR’s effective implementation?
Is it considering including transparency requirements for providers of ESG data used by financial actors operating on the EU market?
at: (English version) to the Commission François-Xavier Bellamy (PPE), Christophe Gomart (PPE) (22 July 2026) Subject: Transparency of environmental, social and governance data The implementation of the regulation on sustainability-related disclosures in the financial services sector (SFDR) is based on environmental, social and governance (ESG) data that enables financial market participants to fulfil their transparency and classification requirements for financial products. Increasing the thresholds at which companies are required to make nonfinancial disclosures, while necessary, will nevertheless increase the financial sector’s dependence on external ESG data providers, which are often based outside the EU. While Regulation (EU) 2024/3005 establishes a framework for rating activities, shortcomings in the transparency of the methods used by ESG data providers remain. A lack of transparency over data sources and quality control mechanisms can be detrimental to the comparability, legal certainty and credibility of disclosures, and raises the issue of EU sovereignty when it comes to ESG data. In addition, the ongoing revision of the SFDR seems to establish a difference in treatment between data published by financial actors and data supplied from unregulated data providers. 1.
Is the Commission planning to revise Regulation (EU) 2024/3005 to ensure the SFDR’s effective implementation?

2. Is it considering including transparency requirements for providers of ESG data used by financial actors operating on the EU market? (8 September 2026) Regulation (EU) 2024/3005 on the transparency and integrity of Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) rating activities (1) (ESG Rating Regulation) includes a review clause (Article 52). The review clause concerns the assessment of whether the scope of the regulation should be extended to ESG data providers. To this aim the Commission would first need to assess the evidence and follow the required procedures before proposing any such change. Such an assessment would require careful analysis of the market and of the distinctions between ESG ratings and other ESG data services and take stock of the review of the Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation (SFDR ) (2). It would also need to take account of stakeholder feedback as well as the need for an appropriate impact assessment. The ongoing revision of the SFDR ensures that financial market participants remain responsible for their sustainability disclosures under the SFDR even when they rely on ESG external providers data. It also clarifies the regulatory expectations as regards the use of data and estimates by financial market participants, no matter whether they rely on external providers.

E-10-2026-003092.t: Maintaining strong producer organisations as a driving force for cooperation
qt: to the Commission Hilde Vautmans (Renew) Subject:

The European fruit and vegetable sector regards producer organisations as a success story. They strengthen the position of farmers, consolidate supply and enable investment in quality, sustainability and innovation. Within the fruit and vegetable sector, there is concern that the new proposal could weaken this role, as European objectives become less clear and other types of producer organisations from other sectors may gain access to the same framework. Questions to the Commission: 1.

Does the Commission intend to ensure that recognised producer organisations and associations of producer organisations continue to play a central role in the fruit and vegetable sector? If so, how does it intend to achieve this?

Will support in this sector continue to be prioritised for recognised producer organisations that actually pool production and organise sales? If not, what specific changes will take place to the detriment of the recognised producer organisations concerned?

Does the Commission intend to explicitly retain the current European objectives for operational programmes, such as production planning, market strengthening, quality, innovation, the environment and climate?

(25 August 2026) Producer organisations (PO) in fruit and vegetables continue to play a critical role in bringing farmers together, to aggregate the supply of its members, strengthen the bargaining power of farmers in the supply chain and connect them to market demand. The Commission clearly recognises this critical role played by producer organisations. This is precisely why it did not modify in its proposals certain exemptions from competition rules for the producer organisations recognised under the common market Organisation (CMO) and the sector specific obligation of supply for PO have not been modified. According to Article 30(2) of the CMO proposal (1), EU support to the fruit and vegetables sectoral interventions would remain mandatory in Member States where producer organisations are recognised for fruit and vegetables products. Objectives of sectoral interventions are covered by the specific objectives of the Fund as spelled out in Article 3(d) of the National and Regional Partnership Plans (NRPP) proposal (2). Finally, the Commission’s CMO and NRPP proposals are currently under discussion with co-legislators, and their provisions may be subject to change in the course of legislative process.

E-10-2026-003091.t: A level playing field for producer organisations in the fruit and vegetable sector
qt: to the Commission Hilde Vautmans (Renew) Subject:

The current CAP offers Member States greater scope to implement policy through tailored measures. All the signs suggest that the next CAP, after 2027, will continue this trend. However, the fruit and vegetable sector warns of a potentially counterproductive effect should the pendulum swing too far. More specifically, there is concern that the new CAP proposal for the period 2028–2034, through the expansion of national flexibility and co-financing, could lead to significant disparities between Member States. This could disrupt the level playing field, particularly for transnational producer organisations in which growers from different Member States work together. Questions to the Commission: 1.

How will the Commission prevent intervention measures at Member State level – resulting from insufficient national co-financing – from leading to distortions of competition between producer organisations in different Member States?
Does the Commission recognise the risk that growers will join producer organisations in Member States with more favourable intervention measures and conditions for aid?
What European minimum rules does the Commission intend to use to ensure a level playing field in the internal market?

What European minimum rules does the Commission intend to use to ensure a level playing field in the internal market?

(1 September 2026) The Commission has proposed that national financial support for sectoral interventions has to be compulsory (see Article 35(8) and (9) of the National and Regional Partnership (NRP) proposal (1)), including for interventions implemented by producer organisations in the fruit and vegetables sector. According to Article 35(8), first subparagraph, of the NRP proposal, the contribution from Member States shall amount to at least 30% of the public eligible expenditure of the operational programmes. Therefore, it is obligatory for Member States to contribute to the financing of operational programmes. It is up to each producer organisation to decide whether to join forces with producer organisations in another Member State by setting-up a transnational producer organisation. Already, under the current strategic plans, operational programmes implemented by transnational producer organisations are possible in accordance with the national rules of the Member State where the headquarter of the transnational producer organisation is located and the organisation is recognised. That Member State is also responsible for establishing the necessary administrative cooperation with the other Member States in which the members are located. Minimum rules ensuring a level playing field in the internal market are captured by Article 35(8) of the NRP proposal. Finally, the Commission proposal referred to above is currently being discussed by the legislators including the financing of fruit and vegetables operational programmes and the transfer of articles from the proposed NRP regulation to the two proposals (2), (3) concerning the Common Agriculture Policy.

E-10-2026-003090.t: Alleged transfer of persons by people-smugglers in the Sea-Watch 5 case and implications for EU migration policy
qt: to the Commission Elisabeth Dieringer (PfE) Subject:

According to a Le Figaro report1 dated 17 July 2026, on 11 May 2026 a Frontex aircraft filmed the transfer of 90 people from a fast boat equipped with two 300-PS engines to the Sea-Watch 5’s rubber dinghies, approximately 45 nautical miles north-east of Tripoli. It further stated that the boat was being operated by five masked men in paramilitary uniforms, who distributed life jackets to the migrants, coordinated the transfer and then sped off towards the Libyan coast. The video footage has been submitted to the Brindisi Public Prosecutor’s Office, and the captain of the Sea-Watch 5, Anne van Dam, is thus under investigation on suspicion of aiding and abetting illegal immigration under aggravating circumstances. The case raises questions as to the oversight of private sea-rescue organisations in the Mediterranean, any EU funding they may receive and the role of Frontex intelligence material in national criminal cases. 1.
Is the Commission aware of the incident of 11 May 2026 and the video footage recorded by Frontex, and has it been informed of it by Frontex or by the Italian authorities?

In view of the repeatedly documented pattern of such incidents, does the Commission intend to propose a binding code of conduct for private sea-rescue organisations in the Mediterranean, for example regarding the sharing of vessel positions or the coordination of operations for the transfer of persons at sea?

Does the Commission believe the existing legal framework under the SAR, SOLAS and Palermo Conventions to be sufficient to distinguish between genuine emergencies at sea and organised people-transfer operations carried out by people-smugglers, or does it see a need for any changes to be made?

at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (15.9.2026) The Commission is aware of the reports concerning the alleged incident of 11 May 2026 involving the vessel Sea-Watch 5 and related judicial proceedings in Italy. Preventing migrant smuggling while protecting life at sea remains a key priority. Assistance to persons in distress at sea is an obligation under international law, and suspected criminal conducts must be investigated. Under international maritime law, coordination of search and rescue operations are a responsibility of the competent national authorities. The international legal framework, including the International Conventions on Maritime Search and Rescue, Safety of Life at Sea and Transnational Organised Crime, together with relevant EU legislation, provides the basis for search and rescue activities and the fight against migrant smuggling. The Commission has also proposed new rules to improve the investigation and prosecution of smuggling networks and reinforce European Union Agency for Law Enforcement Cooperation’s (Europol) role, and more recently, a new EU sanctions regime to freeze smugglers’ assets, restrict their movements and cut off their profits. These efforts are complemented by the Global Alliance to Counter Migrant Smuggling, which strengthens cooperation with third countries and international organisations. The Commission continues to work with Member States through the Search and Rescue (SAR) Contact Group1 and engages with other stakeholders carrying out search and rescue operations. At present, the Commission is not planning to propose a binding EU code of conduct for private vessels.
1 The SAR Contact Group aims at enhancing cooperation and information exchange between Member States, as
well as with other relevant stakeholders, in the field of search and rescue. The last meeting of the SAR Contact Group took place in May 2026.

E-10-2026-003089.t: Anti-dumping investigation AD746 concerning imports of silico-manganese steel wire
qt: to the Commission Mirosława Nykiel (PPE) Subject:

Pursuant to Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/297, imports of silicomanganese steel wire covered by anti-dumping investigation AD746 have been subject to mandatory registration since 11 February 2026. This measure is causing considerable uncertainty for importers and companies using this product as a key raw material, particularly in the construction, automotive and heavy industry sectors. Of particular concern is the possibility of the retroactive collection of duties, which could jeopardise the liquidity of SMEs and affect the continuity of supply. With the above in mind: 1.

How does the Commission assess the likelihood of anti-dumping duties being imposed retroactively for the period covered by mandatory registration, and what criteria will determine the application of this measure?
When will investigation AD746 be concluded and any interim measures published?

How does the Commission intend to weigh, in the Union interest test, the impact of any duties on the competitiveness of EU industry and the situation of SMEs that depend on stable supplies of welding wire?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.9.2026) To apply duties retroactively, the Commission is bound by Article 10(4) of the basic Antidumping Regulation1. There should be a further substantial rise in imports in addition to the level of imports which caused injury during the investigation period which, in the light of its timing and volume and other circumstances, is likely to seriously undermine the remedial effect of the definitive anti-dumping duty to be applied. The provisional measures were published on 10 August 20262. Pre-disclosure of the level of intended provisional measures has been communicated to parties on 13 July 2026. At the initiation of the investigation, the Commission invited all known users of welding wire to cooperate in the investigation. Until now, no user came forward. However, users can still register as interested party in the investigation and submit comments at a later stage. If no users cooperate, findings with regard to the EU interest will be based on the complaint and information obtained at EU producers, exporting producers, and unrelated importers.

E-10-2026-003088.t: Wording of labour provisions in trade and sustainable development (TSD) chapters and implications regarding their enforceability
qt: to the Commission Saskia Bricmont (Verts/ALE) Subject:

In 2019, the Commission initiated dispute settlement proceedings against South Korea, alleging that it had failed to fulfil its obligations concerning International Labour Organization (ILO) conventions under the bilateral free trade agreement (FTA). The dispute focused on the provision requiring the parties to ‘make continuous and sustained efforts towards the ratification’ of the fundamental ILO conventions. In its report of 20 January 20211, the Panel of Experts issued several recommendations. It stressed that this obligation was not enforceable ‘in the absence of explicit targets or at least any informal understanding on expected milestones towards ratification’ (paragraphs 276 and 278). Since then, the European Parliament2 and the Council3 have recommended adopting ‘detailed, time-bound implementation roadmaps’ as a useful tool to achieve the desired results. Nevertheless, subsequent FTAs have retained the same contentious wording in their TSD chapters. 1.
Why has the Commission not incorporated the Panel of Experts’ findings into subsequent FTAs?
Why has it not used the TSD Committee to agree on implementation roadmaps with partner countries? (If it has, what was the outcome?).

E-10-2026-003087.t: Development of Ukrainian drone technologies in the European defence industry
qt: to the Commission Piotr Müller (ECR) Subject:

The Commission and Ukraine have signed a letter of intent to combine Ukraine’s drone experience with Europe’s industrial potential. This cooperation is to be based on a clear division in which Ukraine provides technologies, combat experience and know-how, while further development, standardisation, certification and essential production takes place on EU territory, involving companies from all Member States. Any production in Ukraine should be limited and ancillary. This arises from considerations of security of supply, protection of intellectual property, control of EU funds and the high risk of corruption and non-compliance by Ukraine. The case of the Polish company operating in Kyiv whose favourable ruling in an arbitration case has not been implemented by the Ukrainian side shows that, without hard guarantees, European companies may be deprived of real legal protection. Given the above: 1.
Will the Commission ensure that the bulk of technology development, production, licensing and transfer takes place in the EU?
How will the Commission ensure equal and non-discriminatory access to these technologies for all Member States and eligible companies?
What mechanisms for audits, anti-corruption, enforcement of arbitration awards and recovery will be established?

(14 September 2026) The Letter of Intent signed on 15 July 2026 by the President of the European Commission and the President of Ukraine reflects a political commitment to develop a strategic defence-industrial partnership and, together with the Member States, to establish an EU-Ukraine Defence Industrial Pact. The partnership will be mutually beneficial and support the gradual integration of Ukraine’s defence technological and industrial base into the EU’s defence industrial ecosystem. It will promote joint production, co-production, joint ventures and stronger industrial capacity in the EU and Ukraine. However, it does not establish a general right of access to technologies or intellectual property owned by other undertakings. Licensing, technology transfers and intellectual property sharing will remain subject to the consent of the parties concerned and to applicable intellectual property, security and export-control rules. Participation in EU-supported activities will follow transparent and non-discriminatory eligibility and selection criteria of the relevant EU instruments and procurement procedures. EU programmes supporting the Pact will be implemented in full compliance with their legal bases, eligibility and control requirements, and with the EU Financial Regulation (1). The Ukraine Support Loan Instrument (2) includes a dedicated control system and cooperation with relevant audit bodies to ensure the proper use of funds throughout the implementation chain, from disbursement to delivery to final users. The Letter of Intent also identifies procurement integrity, regulatory alignment, reciprocal market access, and the protection and transfer of intellectual property rights as key elements of the future partnership.

E-10-2026-003086.t: EU takeover of proceeds from national spectrum auctions
qt: to the Commission Piotr Müller (ECR) Subject:

The President of the Eurogroup has publicly floated the idea of channelling 75 % of proceeds from national spectrum auctions to the EU’s multiannual budget and the remaining 25 % to a fund managed by the European Investment Bank. Rather than creating new resources, such a mechanism would redirect existing revenues from national budgets to the Union level. It would mean further fiscal centralisation, limiting the freedom of Member States to manage their own revenues and encroaching hugely on an area that, to date, has remained a national responsibility – and all without solving the underlying problem of the high cost of spectrum access. Making auction proceeds a permanent source of funding for the EU budget risks entrenching incentives to maximise public revenues at the expense of operator investments in developing the network. In this connection: 1.
Is the Commission considering laying claim to all or some of the proceeds from national spectrum auctions in the context of the Digital Networks Act, the EU budget for 20282034 or new own resources?

On what legal basis could the Commission deprive the Member States of these revenues, and how would such a mechanism be consistent with the principles of conferral, subsidiarity and budgetary sovereignty?

Does the Commission share the view that making national proceeds from spectrum auctions an EU own resource would unjustifiably redirect revenues and budgetary powers from the Member States to the Union level, and can it rule out proposing such a measure?

E-10-2026-003085.t: Methane Regulation and risks to the EU’s gas supply over winter
qt: to the Commission Piotr Müller (ECR) Subject:

As of January 2027, importers of oil and gas will be subject to new monitoring, reporting and verification requirements under Regulation (EU) 2024/1787 on the reduction of methane emissions. 17 Member States have reportedly warned that unclear compliance requirements and short deadlines for implementing these may lead suppliers to divert cargo outside the European Union. The new obligations will come into effect during winter, when demand for gas and security of its supply are particularly important. The Commission was to suggest that, in the event of a threat to security of supply, Member States may temporarily refrain from imposing penalties while the legal obligations themselves remain in force. In view of this, I ask: 1.

Has the Commission assessed the risk of uncertainty associated with the new methane requirements coming into force in January 2027 leading to a reduction or redirection of gas supplies to the EU during the winter of 2026-2027, and what are the results of this assessment?
How does the Commission intend to ensure legal certainty for importers if obligations remain binding, while allowing Member States to refrain from imposing penalties for infringements?
Will the Commission consider postponing the application of the relevant import requirements until clear, enforceable and uniform compliance and verification rules are adopted?

E-10-2026-003084.t: Seizure of private aircraft with non‑EU registrations
qt: to the Commission Sophia Kircher (PPE) Subject:

There have been reports since 2021 that the Italian customs administration and the Guardia di Finanza have been seizing private aircraft registered in non‑EU countries that are permanently based in the European Union. The Italian authorities are basing these seizures on national customs legislation (Article 36(4), Presidential Decree No 43/1973), which states that transferring an aircraft’s registration to a non-EU country causes it to lose its EU goods status, resulting in a new import duty obligation once the six‑month temporary importation period has elapsed. On the grounds of smuggling, which is categorised as a continuing offence, these aircraft are being seized after being hangared in the EU for decades without complaint. A proof of customs clearance dating from the time of import offers no protection. This practice bases the loss of status purely on national registration status, even when the aircraft never physically leaves the customs territory of the EU. This can create friction with the Union Customs Code as laid down in Regulation (EU) No 952/2013, as well as with the primacy of EU law. 1.

Does the Commission share the view that EU goods which have been duly released for free circulation should only lose this status if they are actually removed from the customs territory, and not because their registration has merely been transferred to a non-EU country while they remain within the customs territory?
Is the Commission aware of this practice, and if so, what is its position on the matter?
Is the Commission planning to consider measures to address this?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (16.9.2026) According to Article 153(1) Union Customs Code1, all goods in the customs territory of the EU are presumed to have the customs status of EU goods, unless it is established that they are not EU goods. Ιn principle, means of transport located in the EU or released for free circulation therein are deemed to be EU goods. The flag, plate or any other means of registration of the means of transport is irrelevant to determine the customs status of means of transport. The establishment of a non-EU status of the goods can only be assessed effectively by the competent national authorities, based on the information and documentation available to them. To this respect, the processes and conditions for a change from an EU registration of a means of transport to a non-EU registration, which are established by other-than-customs legislation, may affect the assessment on the customs status of the means of transport. If the non-EU status of an aircraft is established, while it is in the EU, then the aircraft must be placed under a customs procedure in the EU or be re-exported. Unless the aircraft is released for free circulation in the EU, the temporary admission procedure is the procedure allowing the (non-EU) aircraft to be used in the EU, under certain conditions. The Commission is not aware of any relevant national practices in Italy breaching the provisions of the Union Customs Code. Regarding the seizures of the private aircrafts, the establishment of such measures, their scope and conditions are decided at national level.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A02013R0952-

E-10-2026-003081.t: Decommissioning of wind turbines and covering dismantling costs
qt: to the Commission Marcin Sypniewski (ESN) Subject:

In many Member States, the development of wind energy is based on long-term land lease contracts between property owners and the companies carrying out the projects concerned. However, once the turbines reach the end of their operational life, problems may arise when it comes to dismantling them and restoring the site concerned, particularly if the entity responsible for carrying out those obligations ceases to exist or becomes insolvent. In such cases, there is a risk of costs being passed on to landowners or public authorities. With the above in mind: 1.
Has the Commission looked into the risks of wind turbines being decommissioned in the Member States without funding being secured to dismantle them and to restore the sites concerned?

Does EU law as it stands, in particular the provisions relating to renewables and environmental protection, allow Member States to require investors to provide financial security (e.g. a bank guarantee, a deposit or a fund) to cover the costs of decommissioning facilities?

Is the Commission considering bringing forward guidelines or a legislative initiative establishing minimum standards for investors’ financial liability for dismantling wind turbines and restoring land so that it can continue to be used?
at: (English version) to the Commission Marcin Sypniewski (ESN) (22 July 2026) Subject: Decommissioning of wind turbines and covering dismantling costs In many Member States, the development of wind energy is based on long-term land lease contracts between property owners and the companies carrying out the projects concerned. However, once the turbines reach the end of their operational life, problems may arise when it comes to dismantling them and restoring the site concerned, particularly if the entity responsible for carrying out those obligations ceases to exist or becomes insolvent. In such cases, there is a risk of costs being passed on to landowners or public authorities. With the above in mind: 1.
Has the Commission looked into the risks of wind turbines being decommissioned in the Member States without funding being secured to dismantle them and to restore the sites concerned?

Does EU law as it stands, in particular the provisions relating to renewables and environmental protection, allow Member States to require investors to provide financial security (e.g. a bank guarantee, a deposit or a fund) to cover the costs of decommissioning facilities?

Is the Commission considering bringing forward guidelines or a legislative initiative establishing minimum standards for investors’ financial liability for dismantling wind turbines and restoring land so that it can continue to be used?

(24 September 2026) The Commission takes note of the concerns raised regarding the dismantling and site-restoration costs of wind turbines at the end of their operational life and is aware of the risks especially where the responsible operator ceases to exist or becomes insolvent. Member States may require investors to provide financial security to cover the future costs of decommissioning renewable energy installations, including wind turbines, provided that the requirement complies with the general principles of EU law, such as proportionality, non-discrimination, legal certainty, and, where applicable, State aid and internal market rules. Therefore, the organisation of such safeguards is, in principle, a matter of national competence, and it is often part of the business plan and assessed in the general permitting procedure There is no planned initiative concerning possible guidance or legislation establishing minimum standards for investors’ financial liability for dismantling wind turbines and restoring land as EU law is broadly compatible with this objective, with the directive (1) governing environmental assessment requiring Member States to consider the environmental impacts of projects throughout their lifecycle, including, where relevant, decommissioning and restoration.

E-10-2026-003078.t: Payment authorisations facilitating unlicensed online gambling in the EU
qt: to the Commission Sabine Verheyen (PPE), Ralf Seekatz (PPE) Subject:

A recent investigation by Investigate Europe1 has found that Soft2bet, a company based in Cyprus and Malta, operates nearly 150 illegal online casinos that are blacklisted by regulators across the Member States. The scheme reportedly generated EUR 600 million over four years, with funds allegedly also being processed through EU-regulated electronic money institutions. This investigation further alleges that a payment company associated with the scheme obtained authorisation from Visa and Mastercard to process card payments and that Paysafe may be processing deposits from these platforms. 1.
Is the Commission aware of allegations that card networks may be authorising payment companies linked to operators blacklisted by gambling regulators in Member States?

What steps is the Commission taking to ensure that card networks and payment service providers carry out adequate due diligence against national gambling blacklists before authorising merchants or processing payments?

In the light of these allegations, does the Commission consider that current legislation, such as Regulation (EU) 2024/1624, is sufficient to prevent payment service providers from facilitating unlicensed online gambling?
https://www.investigate-europe.eu/posts/payment-firms-handled-millions-for-companies-linked-tounlicensed-gambling-network. 1
at: (English version) to the Commission Sabine Verheyen (PPE), Ralf Seekatz (PPE) (22 July 2026) Subject: Payment authorisations facilitating unlicensed online gambling in the EU A recent investigation by Investigate Europe (1) has found that Soft2bet, a company based in Cyprus and Malta, operates nearly 150 illegal online casinos that are blacklisted by regulators across the Member States. The scheme reportedly generated EUR 600 million over four years, with funds allegedly also being processed through EU-regulated electronic money institutions. This investigation further alleges that a payment company associated with the scheme obtained authorisation from Visa and Mastercard to process card payments and that Paysafe may be processing deposits from these platforms. 1. Is the Commission aware of allegations that card networks may be authorising payment companies linked to operators blacklisted by gambling regulators in Member States? 2. What steps is the Commission taking to ensure that card networks and payment service providers carry out adequate due diligence against national gambling blacklists before authorising merchants or processing payments? 3. In the light of these allegations, does the Commission consider that current legislation, such as Regulation (EU) 2024/1624, is sufficient to prevent payment service providers from facilitating unlicensed online gambling? (8 September 2026) The Commission has taken note of the allegations. However, it does not have any investigatory powers in relation to such individual cases. Any assessment of wrongdoing in specific cases is a matter for competent authorities at national level, including regulators, supervisors and law enforcement authorities. Payment service providers, e-money institutions, as well as providers of gambling services established in the EU are subject to the EU anti-money laundering framework, which requires obliged entities to apply risk-based customer due diligence (CDD), including in relation to the nature of the business and the risk profile of the customer and to conduct ongoing monitoring of the business relationship. The rules include an obligation to cease a business relationship where full compliance with CDD requirements is not possible. Under Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 of the European Parliament and of the Council on the prevention of the use of the financial system for the purposes of money laundering or terrorist financing (1), which will apply from 10 July 2027 and will be directly applicable across all Member States, those obligations are strengthened and harmonised. The Commission considers that regulation (EU) 2024/1624 substantially strengthens the EU's framework to prevent the financial system, including payment service providers and electronic money institutions, from being misused to facilitate illicit activity. The Commission and the EU Anti-Money Laundering Authority will continue to monitor emerging risks in relation to payment services and unlicensed gambling.

E-10-2026-003077.t: Crisis in the French lavender industry
qt: to the Commission Marina Mesure (The Left) Subject:

The French lavender industry, which accounts for over 10 000 direct jobs, is navigating a serious structural crisis: plummeting prices, market saturation and unfair competition from within and outside the EU. The current rules penalise the most responsible producers: the States that have rightly banned certain phytosanitary products and laid down minimum social requirements are the only ones bearing the cost of this admirable transition, while the competition gains a direct competitive advantage. Transitions towards agroecology, while necessary, have been encouraged without the conditions of their implementation being harmonised at EU level. This means that the most responsible perfume, aromatic and medicinal plant (PAMP) sectors – including that of France in particular– are being exposed to unfair intra‑European competition, while their competitors benefit from less restrictive phytosanitary and social standards. 1.
What corrective action does the Commission intend to take, including through ecoschemes and subsidies from the European Agricultural Fund for Rural Development, to address this situation?

Faced with PAMP imports produced without equivalence of standards, particularly from Asia, and in the absence of any ecological or social protectionism mechanisms at the EU borders, what instruments does the Commission plan to use to ensure a level playing field – be it sector safeguard measures, bolstered import checks or enhanced traceability?

Does it intend to facilitate access to protected designation of origin (PDO) certification and protected geographical indications (PGI) for small farms, while providing technical support for collective applications and helping to partially cover the costs of certification?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (7.9.2026) The Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) Strategic Plans Regulation includes a variety of types of interventions that Member States can programme to support farmers improving the competitivity of their farms. Lavender producers can be supported through direct payments; investments; agri-environmental commitments, including conversion to organic farming; and voluntary eco-schemes. All products placed on the EU market, whether they are produced domestically or imported, are required to comply with EU health and safety standards. These requirements apply regardless of the origin and of possible trade agreements concluded with non-EU countries. Besides, the Vision for Agriculture and Food1 stipulates that the Union will ensure that ambitious EU standards do not lead to economic, environmental and social leakages, and that the European agri-food sector is not put at a competitive disadvantage without corresponding reciprocity. The Commission will pursue, in line with international rules, a stronger alignment of production standards applied to imported products, notably on pesticides. To this end, a study2 aimed at informing an Impact Assessment was published on 11 August 2026. Trade defence instruments can also be deployed where there is evidence of practices such as dumping that cause injury to the EU industry. The Commission provides guidance on the application procedure for registration of geographical indications. Information is available on its website, including through a dedicated toolkit3for applicant groups, which small farmers may join. Under their CAP Strategic Plans, Member States may provide support for cooperation and participation in Union quality schemes, including support for certification costs.
1 Communication from the Commission to the European Parliament, the Council, the European Economic and

Social Committee and the Committee of the Regions: “A Vision for Agriculture and Food - Shaping together an attractive farming and agri-food sector for future generations”, 19.2.2025 COM(2025) 75 final. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex%3A52025DC0075. 2 https://publications.jrc.ec.europa.eu/repository/handle/JRC147659. 3 https://agriculture.ec.europa.eu/farming/geographical-indications-and-quality-schemes/registration-name-giproduct_en.

E-10-2026-003076.t: Protecting workers against extreme heatwaves in the European Union
qt: to the Commission Marina Mesure (The Left) Subject:

Several Member States have recorded temperatures in excess of 40°C, and such heatwaves are set to become more frequent as a result of climate change. Workers, particularly those in the construction, civil engineering, agriculture, logistics and delivery sectors, are especially at risk of workplace accidents and fatal heatstroke. Directive 89/391/EEC states that workers must stop work and move to a safe place in the event of serious and imminent danger. However, EU law lacks any explicit conditions enabling the immediate exercise of the right to withdraw from work. Can the Commission therefore say: 1.

Whether it intends to propose a stricter EU worker-protection framework by laying down minimum obligations governing work during periods of extreme heat (such as adjusted working hours, compulsory breaks, access to water and the suspension of certain activities once the thresholds set have been exceeded)?

Whether it plans to promote and enshrine the right to meaningful protection against heat at work in legislation on health and safety at work, and to guarantee workers a high level of protection against the heatwave-related risks?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (21.8.2026) The human cost of extreme temperatures for workers can be severe. Heat at work can contribute to fatal and non-fatal occupational accidents and diseases, while also generating significant adverse economic effects. The EU has strong rules addressing all occupational safety and health (OSH) risks. The Framework Directive on Safety and Health at Work1 requires employers to assess and address all OSH risks, including heat-related risks. Other directives, such as those concerning the workplace, construction sites, extractive industries and fishing vessels2, contain more detailed provisions, including related to indoor and work-area temperatures and protection against inclement weather conditions. In addition, the Commission and the European Agency for Safety and Health at Work (EUOSHA) provide guidance and practical tools to support the implementation of EU OSH legislation, including measures to address heat at work3. EU-OSHA's guidance Heat at Work Guidance for Workplaces covers the adaptation of working hours; the organisation of rest breaks and access to hydration. It also recommends that workers in hot environments be encouraged to set their own work and rest schedules. In the context of the ongoing work and social partner consultation on the Quality Jobs Act, the Commission is considering, among other issues, possible further EU action to address occupational safety and health risks, including risks related to heat at work. In December 2025, the EU Advisory Committee on Safety and Health at Work recommended stronger EU action on heat-exposure indicators, workers' acclimatisation to heat at work, hydration and work organisation. However, the Committee did not reach a consensus on whether such measures should be binding or non-binding.
