E-10-2026-003075.t: Compliance of ongoing German war-related compensation schemes with EU non-discrimination law
qt: to the Commission Arkadiusz Mularczyk (ECR) Subject:
Compliance of ongoing German war-related compensation schemes with EU nondiscrimination law

In the judgments of the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) in the Tas-Hagen (C192/05) and the Nerkowska (C-499/06) cases, the CJEU held that war-victim benefits fall within Member State competence, which must nonetheless be governed in compliance with EU law. Germany continues to pay out this compensation under a law known as Sozialgesetzbuch (Social Code Book) XIV, a successor to the Bundesversorgungsgesetz (Federal War Victims Relief Act), including across borders to other Member States. The authors Karl Heinz Roth and Hartmut Rübner (2022) document that victims of Nazi persecution from Germany received on average EUR 34 628 each, whereas Polish victims received EUR 190.90 – 0.55 % of the amount for German victims – with eligibility partly conditional on the ethnic ‘German language and culture area’ criterion. The same schemes, including under the Bundesversorgungsgesetz, paid out EUR 306 billion (from 1949 to 2000) to recipients the authors classify as the Nazi dictatorship’s military-political personnel (Wehrmacht, WaffenSS and National Socialism officials) – almost six times the total received by all victims. 1.

Can the Commission confirm that Member State competence over war-victim compensation must be exercised in accordance with EU law, including Article 18 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union and Directive 2000/43/EC on equal treatment between persons irrespective of racial or ethnic origin, as regards social protection?
Will the Commission, as guardian of the Treaties, assess whether ethnicity-based eligibility criteria in ongoing German compensation schemes comply with EU law?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (18.9.2026) In the cases referred to by the Honourable Member, the Court of Justice ruled that, as EU law stands, a benefit intended to compensate civilian victims of war or repression for physical or mental harm which they have suffered falls within the competence of the Member States. However, Member States must exercise that competence in accordance with EU law1. Article 18 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union prohibits discrimination on grounds of nationality for matters that fall within the scope of EU law. In view of the caselaw, there are no indications that the situation referred to by the Honourable Member falls within the scope of EU law. As far as Council Directive 2000/43/EC (‘Racial Equality Directive’)2 is concerned, that Directive prohibits discrimination on the grounds of racial or ethnic origin in certain welldefined fields, including social protection. However, the Racial Equality Directive does not cover discrimination based on nationality3. The Court of Justice clarified that a person’s nationality cannot, in itself, give rise to a presumption of belonging to a particular ethnic group4.
1 Judgment of the Court of Justice of 22 May 2008, Nerkowska, C-499/06, EU:C:2008:300, paragraphs 23-24

and case-law cited. 2 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2000/43/oj/eng. 3 Recital 13 and Article 3(2) of the Racial Equality Directive. 4 Judgment of the Court of Justice of 18 December 2025, Slagelse Almennyttige Boligselskab, Afdeling Schackenborgvænge, C-417/23, ECLI:EU:C:2025:1017, paragraph 81.

E-10-2026-003074.t: Short-stay travel visa requirements within the Schengen area
qt: to the Commission Barry Andrews (Renew) Subject:

Non-EU nationals legally residing in an EU Member State are subject to different short-stay travel requirements within the Schengen area depending on whether their Member State of residence is part of Schengen. As a result, legally resident non-EU nationals in non-Schengen Member States such as Ireland and Cyprus are generally required to obtain Schengen visas for short stays in other Member States, despite having already undergone immigration and security checks by their country of residence. In this context: 1.
Has the Commission assessed whether the current framework creates disproportionate administrative burdens for legally resident non-EU nationals in non-Schengen Member States?

Has the Commission considered mechanisms for facilitated short-stay mobility based on mutual recognition of residence permits issued by Member States, without affecting free movement rights or residence rights within the EU?
Would the Commission be open to exploring options to reduce administrative barriers for short-term travel for legally resident residents, while maintaining current Schengen security standards?
This proposal is strictly limited to short-stay mobility and does not concern free movement rights or residence rights within the EU.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (10.9.2026) Under the current legal framework, certain third-country nationals legally residing in the Member States that do not, or do not yet fully apply the Schengen acquis are required to obtain a short-stay visa when traveling to the Schengen area for short stay1. In this respect, the applicable framework reflects the legal architecture of the Schengen acquis and the need to ensure a uniform application of external border, visa and security rules. However, existing EU law on short-stay visas already contains elements facilitating mobility for certain categories of legally residing third-country nationals, notably rules on issuing multiple-entry visas of progressively longer validity in the Visa Code2, which also apply to third-country nationals legally residing in Member States that do not yet fully apply the Schengen acquis. These rules can also be adapted to take account of local circumstances, subject to an assessment conducted within local Schengen cooperation in those Member States that do not (yet) fully apply the Schengen acquis. An assessment conducted within local Schengen cooperation in those jurisdictions would be duly examined as per the rules of the Visa Code. Any further consideration of this issue, including any form of broader mutual recognition of residence permits as a basis for short stay travel to the Schengen area, would need to be carefully assessed, including to take account of the applicable Treaty framework and of the specific status of the Member States concerned. The Commission remains attentive to practical difficulties encountered by third-country nationals legally residing in a Member State.
1 Regulation (EU) 2016/399 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 9 March 2016 on a Union Code

on the rules governing the movement of persons across borders (Schengen Borders Code); Regulation (EU) 2018/1806 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 November 2018 listing the third countries whose nationals must be in possession of visas when crossing the external borders and those whose nationals are exempt from that requirement. 2 Regulation (EC) No 810/2009 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 July 2009 establishing a Community Code on Visas (Visa Code).

E-10-2026-003073.t: EU support for the International Criminal Court (ICC)
qt: to the Commission Mieke Andriese (PfE) Subject:

The US Government has recently announced its intention to further dismantle the International Criminal Court (ICC). At the same time, the European Union continues to support the court politically, legally and financially, despite recent integrity issues within the institution. 1.

In light of the recent announcements by the US Government and their implications for transatlantic relations, is the Commission prepared to reconsider or terminate cooperation between the European Union and the ICC? If not, why not?

How does the Commission assess the credibility of the ICC in light of the recent integrity issues surrounding former Chief Prosecutor Karim Khan, and is it prepared to commission an independent evaluation of the way in which the ICC has handled this matter and of the implications for the continuation of EU political, legal and financial support? If not, why not?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.8.2026) 1. The EU stands firm in its support for the International Criminal Court (ICC) and the principles set out in the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court. The EU considers that attacks or threats against the ICC, elected officials, personnel and those cooperating with the ICC are not acceptable. The EU’s unwavering support for the international criminal justice system, including the ICC, has been most recently reaffirmed in the statement issued by the High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy and Vice-President of the European Commission on behalf of the EU on 16 July 2026, to mark the International Criminal Justice Day1. 2. The EU is committed to preserving the ICC’s independence and integrity. The EU take note of the decision2 of the Assembly of State Parties to the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court following the disciplinary proceedings involving the ICC Chief Prosecutor. The EU have no further comments on this decision. The EU also note that the Deputy Prosecutors have been in charge of managing the Office of the Prosecutor since 2025, ensuring business continuity of the ICC.
1 https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/press/press-releases/2026/07/16/international-criminal-justice-day-
statement-by-the-high-representative-on-behalf-of-the-european-union/. 2 https://asp.icc-cpi.int/sites/default/files/asp_docs/ICC-ASP-S-2-SC-24July2026-ENG.pdf.

E-10-2026-003072.t: Incompatibility of Catalan legislation with Directive 2006/123/EC on services in the internal market (Services Directive) – Forced expiry of pre-existing permanent licences
qt: to the Commission Borja Giménez Larraz (PPE) Subject:

Decree-Law 3/2023 brought in authorisation arrangements putting an end to indefinite licences for short-term leases after five years. What is more, the granting of new licences is now subject to provisions of town-planning instruments, which municipalities such as Barcelona refuse to accept, thus placing a de facto obstacle in the way of the approval of such licences. This undermines the legal certainty of investments and raises a barrier to the internal market. I therefore ask the Commission: 1.

Whether it can it confirm that the authorities are restricting the internal market on the basis of sound scientific evidence demonstrating a causal link between short-term leases and housing shortages, or whether it supports the authorities’ discretion to restrict the free movement of services without any empirical justification?

Whether it believes these restrictions to be in compliance with the principles of ‘last resort’, proportionality, legal certainty and legitimate expectations, as well as with Articles 9, 10, 11 and 15 of the Services Directive?

Whether it considers that putting an end to existing licences after five years and making new licences contingent upon town-planning authorisations to be compatible with the freedom to provide services and EU case-law?

E-10-2026-003071.t: Incompatibility of Catalan legislation with Directive 2006/123/EC on services in the internal market (Services Directive) – De facto suspension arrangements
qt: to the Commission Borja Giménez Larraz (PPE) Subject:

Catalonia’s Decree-Law 3/2023 introduced an authorisation scheme and a de facto temporary ban on short-term leases. The authorities maintain that this curtailing of the freedom to provide services is justified by an overriding public-interest reason. These restrictions, however fly in the face of the principle of proportionality, which requires that measures be appropriate and not exceed what is necessary to achieve the objective pursued. In particular, the authorities have: (i) Failed to show a causal link between short-term leases and the housing crisis; (ii) imposed restrictions that disproportionately affect tourist accommodation for an equally disproportionate period of five years; and (iii) failed to consider less restrictive measures. Given these circumstances: 1.
What view does the Commission take of these measures given Articles 10, 14(5), 15(3)(c) and 16(1)(c) of the Services Directive and the Commission’s guidelines1?
Does the Commission consider that Decree-Law 3/2023 might infringe EU law by imposing restrictions that could go beyond what is necessary to achieve the intended objective?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (21.9.2026) Decree-law 3/2023, adopted by the Catalonian government on 7 November 2023, was notified to the Commission pursuant to the Services Directive1 and using the Internal Market Information System (‘the IMI’). This Decree-law made dwellings of touristic use in Catalonia subject to a prior urban planning permission, valid for five years and extendable for subsequent periods of five years, in municipalities that fulfilled certain conditions, which at the time of its adoption amounted to 262 of them. On 18 December 2023, the Commission services issued comments on the notified Decree-law, focusing on the assessment of the suitability of the restrictions to attain the objective of fighting housing shortage and, more broadly, their proportionality on account of their wide geographical scope. The Catalonian Government submitted its reply, via the IMI, on 18 January 2024. The Commission is currently assessing restrictions on short-term accommodation rentals in several Spanish autonomous communities and cities, including Catalonia and Barcelona, and Member States other than Spain. Any decisions will follow a consistent approach, considering the objectives of the European Affordable Housing Plan2 and the recently tabled Commission’s proposal for an Affordable Housing Act3, which seeks to provide legal certainty on justified and proportionate measures that authorities can take to temporarily protect housing markets.
1 Directive 2006/123/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 12 December 2006 on services in the

internal market – https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:32006L0123. 2 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A52025DC1025&qid=1779808979085#. 3 https://housing.ec.europa.eu/document/35c4d242-60cb-408e-8a96-6ddf8ad18a70_en.

E-10-2026-003069.t: State of play in the tripartite dialogue on Brenner-related issues in the run-up to the high-level meeting with Commissioner Tzitzikostas
qt: to the Commission Roman Haider (PfE) Subject:

The Commission has often moderated or supported trilateral talks and discussions between Italy, Austria and Germany. These ad hoc discussions on Brenner-related issues (transport, the Brenner Base Tunnel and transport restrictions), initiated by the Commission and overseen by the transport ministries of the three Member States and the federal states of Tyrol and Bavaria and the South Tyrol/Trentino region, have so far failed to bear fruit. Since these talks have yielded no major results in years, one may be forgiven for thinking that the Commission is using this as a pretext to avoid taking more effective measures – such as opening infringement proceedings against Germany for the ongoing delays in upgrading the northern access route. Italy has already taken action and initiated legal proceedings against the Republic of Austria for this reason. 1.
Is there any formal mandate, agreement or established working procedure governing this tripartite dialogue (e.g. regular meetings at technical or ministerial level)?
Which specific stakeholders are involved (ministries, the federal states of Tyrol and Bavaria and the South Tyrol/Trentino region, EU coordinators and other interested parties)?
What specific results have been achieved and what measures taken to date, and are there any final documents, agreements or progress reports?

E-10-2026-003068.t: Freedom of expression and the arrest of Hungarian influencer István Szakács
qt: to the Commission Tamás Deutsch (PfE), Csaba Dömötör (PfE), Enikő Győri (PfE), András László (PfE), Pál Szekeres (PfE) Subject:

According to publicly available information, Hungarian influencer István Szakács was arrested on suspicion of preparing a terrorist offence after publishing a video in which he stated that, if former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán were arrested, up to 500 000 people would march to secure his release.1 The case has raised concerns about the protection of freedom of expression. Article 2 of the Treaty on European Union (TEU) establishes the EU’s values, including democracy, the rule of law and respect for human rights. Article 11 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union guarantees freedom of expression, and Article 52(1) thereof requires that any limitation on fundamental rights be lawful, necessary and proportionate. In the light of these provisions: 1.
Has the Commission assessed whether the arrest and prosecution of István Szakács are compatible with Article 11 of the Charter and Articles 2 and 6 TEU?

Does the Commission consider the use of terrorism-related charges in response to political speech, in the absence of clear evidence of incitement to or preparation of imminent violence, compatible with Article 52(1) of the Charter?
If criminal law is being used disproportionately to restrict freedom of expression, what measures will the Commission take to ensure compliance with EU fundamental rights standards?

https://mandiner.hu/belfold/2026/07/het-rendor-jelent-meg-szakacs-istvan-hazanal-elvittek-azegyenruhasok-a-jobboldali-bloggert https://europeanconservative.com/articles/news/authoritarianism-inhungary-conservative-influencer-arrested/. 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (24.9.2026) Freedom of expression is protected by Article 11 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the EU1 and the Commission is committed to ensuring its respect within the remit of its competences. However, the Commission does not intervene in individual cases. It is for Member States, including their judicial authorities, to ensure that fundamental rights are effectively respected and protected, in accordance with their national law and international human rights obligations. The Commission is therefore not in a position to assess or comment on the individual case described.
1 Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, OJ C 326, 26.10.2012, pp. 391–407.

E-10-2026-003067.t: New collaboration between Frontex, Bosnia and Herzegovina and EUFOR Althea
qt: to the Commission Özlem Demirel (The Left) Subject:

On 3 June, the Executive Director of Frontex, Hans Leijtens, and the Ministry of Security of Bosnia and Herzegovina signed two transfer agreements in Sarajevo for the provision of IT equipment to the country’s border police. The agreements pertain to the National Coordination Centre and the conduct of border controls. A letter of intent had already been signed on 2 June between Frontex and the EU military mission EUFOR Althea. This is intended to pave the way for closer practical cooperation between the two organisations. 1.
What specific IT equipment from which manufacturers will be supplied to the Bosnia and Herzegovina Border Police under the two transfer agreements, and what will it be used for?
What forms of data exchange with Frontex are provided for in the agreement with the border police?

What specific areas and forms of cooperation are set out in the letter of intent between Frontex and EUFOR Althea, in particular with respect of the exchange of information, shared situational awareness, operational coordination and possible joint operations or support services?
at: EN E- 003067/2026 on behalf of the European Commission (11.9.2026) As the questions fall under the responsibility of the European Border and Coast Guard Agency (Frontex), the Commission has asked the Agency to provide a response to the questions raised by the Honourable Member. The Commission will send the Agency’s reply to the Honourable Member as soon as possible.

E-10-2026-003066.t: Urgent EU action to protect Naâma Asfari and Sahrawi prisoners
qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Ana Catarina Mendes (S&D) Subject:

Detained in deplorable conditions in a Moroccan prison since 2010, Sahrawi human rights defender Naâma Asfari has been held in isolation for the past few days. As a form of protest, he began an indefinite hunger strike at least six weeks ago and has already lost ten kilos. Along with 17 other activists for the Sahrawi cause, Asfari is facing a lengthy prison sentence for taking part – alongside thousands of Sahrawis – in peaceful protests. According to the defence lawyers, the convictions are based on confessions extracted under torture. The Moroccan authorities are unmoved by Asfari’s pleas to transfer prisoners to Western Sahara, where they can receive family visits – something that has been blocked since 2019. It has been at least two days since there was any news from Naâma Asfari, who has not made his usual weekly telephone call. In light of international humanitarian law and the human rights that the Moroccan State is bound to uphold, and given the EU’s international and economic ties with the Kingdom of Morocco, what urgent steps are being taken to save Naâma Asfari’s life and enforce the rights of Sahrawi prisoners?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (21.8.2026) The EU reiterates the importance of upholding and protecting all human rights, while defending their universality. The EU recalls in particular the UN Standard Minimum Rules for the Treatment of Prisoners1, which is an essential component of the rule of law and protection of human dignity worldwide. Respect for democratic principles and fundamental rights is an essential element of the EUMorocco Association Agreement2, which forms the foundation of EU-Morocco relations. Questions regarding human rights, including individual cases, are addressed in the framework foreseen under the Association Agreement, including a dedicated sub-committee, and other regular exchanges with the Moroccan authorities. In addition, the EU conducts a regular dialogue with civil society and non-governmental organisations that closely monitor human rights issues. The EU Delegation to Morocco also regularly coordinates locally with Member States as well as like-minded states on human rights issues. As regards Western Sahara, the EU continues to support the United Nations-led process, in line with UN Security Council resolution 2797(2025)3, and the efforts of the UN Secretary-General and his Personal Envoy to advance a just, lasting and mutually acceptable political solution.

1 https://www.unodc.org/documents/justice-and-prison-reform/Nelson_Mandela_Rules-E-ebook.pdf. 2 (Article 2) https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/FR/ALL/?uri=CELEX%3A22000A0318%2801%29. 3 https://docs.un.org/en/s/res/2797(2025).

E-10-2026-003065.t: Data on Frontex multipurpose aerial surveillance in the Mediterranean
qt: to the Commission Özlem Demirel (The Left) Subject:

The European Border and Coast Guard Agency (Frontex) operates extensive multipurpose aerial surveillance (MAS) missions in the Central Mediterranean, detecting thousands of migrant boats annually. However, comprehensive data on these operations – sightings, alerts issued and outcomes – is not publicly available. In the light of the above: 1.

How many sightings of migrant boats have occurred annually during Frontex MAS missions in the Central Mediterranean since 2019, and how many mayday relays or maritime distress alerts were issued by Frontex surveillance aircraft in relation to these sightings?

How many communications (emails, calls, or written correspondence) with geolocation or vessel identification data on migrant boat sightings have been sent annually by Frontex to the Libyan Coast Guard or other Libyan authorities since 2019, and how many of these sightings resulted in interception and return to Libya?

How many communications (emails, mayday relays, or other alerts) containing information about migrant boat sightings have been sent annually by Frontex to search and rescue non-governmental organisations operating in the Central Mediterranean since 2019?

E-10-2026-003064.t: Implementation of the recommendations of the Commission’s Special Panel on children in the digital world
qt: to the Commission Maria Guzenina (S&D), Biljana Borzan (S&D), Maria Grapini (S&D), Mario Furore (The Left), Manuela Ripa (PPE), Magdalena Adamowicz (PPE), Stéphanie Yon-Courtin (Renew), Dimitris Tsiodras (PPE), Caterina Chinnici (PPE), Heléne Fritzon (S&D), Evin Incir (S&D), Adnan Dibrani (S&D), Sofie Eriksson (S&D), Johan Danielsson (S&D) Subject:

On 13 July 2026, the Commission’s Special Panel on protecting and empowering minors in the digital world presented its report to President von der Leyen. Its recommendations address key areas including age-appropriate design, digital literacy, platform accountability, support for parents and educators, children’s participation and the governance of digital services. Despite progress under the Digital Services Act, AI Act and Better Internet for Kids Strategy, children navigate an evolving ecosystem of platforms, social media, messaging, gaming, immersive environments and AI-powered services. This raises the question whether the EU framework is sufficiently coherent and future-proof to address the full range of risks and opportunities affecting children online. In the light of the above: 1.

Which recommendations in the Special Panel’s final report does the Commission intend to translate into concrete legislative and non-legislative initiatives, and what is the envisaged timeline for their implementation?

Is the Commission considering proposing a dedicated legislative instrument establishing a comprehensive framework for the protection, empowerment and participation of children in the digital ecosystem?

Does the Commission intend to develop a more holistic and future-proof approach to children’s digital rights, ensuring that legislation addresses the full digital ecosystem shaping children’s lives – including online platforms, messaging services, gaming environments, AI systems, immersive technologies and future digital services, among others – rather than regulating individual sectors in isolation?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (11.9.2026) On 13 July 2026, the President of the Commission received the final report of the Co-Chairs of the Special Panel on Child Safety Online1. The report highlights the critical challenges faced by children online and sets out recommendations for better protecting and empowering them, as well as for an age-appropriate use of social media and other digital services. The report confirms that the EU has already established an ambitious and comprehensive framework for the protection of minors online, notably through the Digital Services Act2 and its Guidelines on the Protection of Minors Online3, the AI Act4, the General Data Protection Regulation5, the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive6, and the Better Internet for Kids strategy7. Complementing this framework, the Commission continues to support the colegislators in the ongoing negotiations on the proposed Regulation laying down rules to prevent and combat child sexual abuse8. The report of the Co-Chairs of the Special Panel advocates for a robust safety-by-design framework, as well as making sure that minors have access to age-appropriate digital spaces. The report also reflects a broad debate in Europe on issues such as age assurance, minimum age approaches for digital services, and the possibility of phased, age-appropriate access to specific functionalities. The Commission is now carefully assessing the report and its recommendations and will come forward with a proposal after the summer. In parallel, the Commission is preparing an action plan on the protection of children from crime, which will also follow up on relevant recommendations from the report.
1 Report from the Special panel on child safety online, https://commission.europa.eu/topics/digital-economy-and-

society/special-panel_en. 2 Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 on a Single Market For Digital Services, https://eurlex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/2065/oj/eng. 3 Guidelines on measures to ensure a high level of privacy, safety and security for minors online, pursuant to Article 28(4) of Regulation (EU) 2022/2065, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legalcontent/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:C_202505519. 4 Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 laying down harmonised rules on artificial intelligence, https://eurlex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj/eng. 5 Regulation (EU) 2016/679 on the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free movement of such data. 6 Directive 2005/29/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 11 May 2005 concerning unfair business-to-consumer commercial practices in the internal market. 7 The new European strategy for a better internet for kids, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legalcontent/EN/TXT/?uri=COM:2022:212:FIN. 8 Proposal for a Regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council laying down rules to prevent and combat child sexual abuse, COM(2022) 209 final, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legalcontent/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52022PC0209.

qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Pernando Barrena Arza (The Left), Cristina Guarda (Verts/ALE), Evin Incir (S&D), Ana Miranda Paz (Verts/ALE) Subject:

Following the election of the new government in Colombia, information received by human rights organisations warns of an increased risk of criminalisation, stigmatisation and threats against human rights defenders, social leaders and those engaged in the application of the Peace Agreement. As examples, we can cite the campaign against former Commissioner for Peace Danilo Rueda, the threats directed at former National Electoral Council magistrate Luis Guillermo Pérez, and the attempted assassination and physical surveillance of Cleiner Almanza of the National Network of Women Searchers. These dynamics could undermine the progress made on peace and jeopardise the safety of key regional figures. With this in mind: 1.

How do the European Commission and the European External Action Service assess the current security situation for human rights defenders and peace activists in Colombia following the change of government?
What specific measures do they intend to take to ensure the protection of these people and to support the comprehensive implementation of the Peace Agreement?
Does the EU intend to strengthen its political dialogue with the Colombian authorities in order to prevent criminalisation and ensure respect for fundamental rights?

E-10-2026-003061.t: AI agents: designating gatekeepers under the DMA without delay
qt: to the Commission Stéphanie Yon-Courtin (Renew) Subject:

In its opinion of 17 July 2026, the French Competition Authority considered the AI agents sector to be already highly concentrated, with Google, OpenAI and Anthropic accounting for over 80 % of usage, and shielded by barriers to entry (computing power, energy, data) and expansion (user access, limited portability and interoperability). It warns of disintermediation, given that as these agents become the main gateway to digital services, they will displace other gateways, hitting publishers and retailers and reducing the diversity of supply. Although virtual assistants already feature on the list of core platform services in Article 2(2) of the Digital Markets Act (DMA), the DMA review declined to address AI services. 1.

Is the Commission prepared to open, without delay, a market investigation under Article 17 DMA to designate providers of AI agents meeting the Article 3 DMA criteria as being gatekeepers, including where the quantitative thresholds are not met?
Will it open a market investigation under Article 19 DMA with a view to proposing the addition of AI agents and marketplaces distributing AI models to the core platform services list, and when?

How will it guarantee freedom of choice, portability and interoperability between AI agents, applying Article 14 DMA to monitor gatekeepers’ acquisitions in competing agents, and Articles 101 and 102 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union to their partnerships?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (24.9.2026)

The Commission is closely monitoring the platform economy under the Digital Markets Act (DMA)1, including the rapid development of AI services and assistants. It is actively gathering information from market participants on the types of AI services available, how they function, and their role for business and end users in the EU. On the basis of this fact-finding, the Commission will decide on further steps. At the same time, ensuring contestability and fairness for AI service providers is a key DMA enforcement priority. In July 2026, the Commission concluded two proceedings2 providing measures to improve access to Google Search data for third-party search services, including AIenabled services, and requiring interoperability on Android so that alternative AI assistants can be easily invoked and access relevant device functionalities on equal terms with Google’s own services. Information received under Article 14 DMA confirms gatekeepers’ strong interest in AI markets, reflected in most of their acquisitions in 2025. The Commission shares this information with Member States to support national merger review or possible referrals. The Commission will continue applying the DMA as well as competition law in a complementary way, where relevant and opportune.
1 Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 September 2022 on contestable

and fair markets in the digital sector and amending Directives (EU) 2019/1937 and (EU) 2020/1828 (Digital Markets Act) https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/1925/oj/eng. 2 https://digital-markets-act.ec.europa.eu/commission-provides-guidance-google-ai-interoperability-android-andsharing-google-search-data-under-2026-07-16_en.

E-10-2026-003060.t: The importance of mandatory origin labelling in creating added value in the livestock sector
qt: to the Commission Elsi Katainen (Renew) Subject:

In July, the Commission published the EU’s strategy for the livestock sector. The strategy contains many good initiatives to improve the difficult situation in the livestock sector at farm level, as well as measures to improve the food chain. As stated in the strategy, meat produced in Europe responsibly and to high production standards is a key component of European competitiveness and the vitality of rural areas. The strategy emphasises how important local and regional chains and consumer expectations for production are. It also highlights the fact that European production creates value in the chain through good practices, quality, sustainability and responsibility, rather than competing on the basis of the lowest possible price. It is good that the role of origin labelling is also highlighted as a key measure in the strategy. The importance of origin labelling and the Buy European Food campaign was also outlined by President von der Leyen in her State of the European Union address in Strasbourg in September 2025. Every European has the right to eat meat produced in Europe and the right to a transparent production chain that makes it easy to trace the origin of food. A transparent and traceable food chain also prevents and helps combat food fraud. With the above in mind: 1.

What specific steps does the Commission intend to take to make origin labelling for meat and meat products clearer and more transparent for consumers than it is at present, including country-of-origin labelling?
Does the Commission intend to extend the requirement for origin and country labelling to processed meat products where meat is the main ingredient?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (31.8.2026) In the Vision for Agriculture and Food1, published in February 2025, the Commission announced its intention to extend country-of-origin labelling, taking into account sectorspecific characteristics and the rules of the Single Market. The Livestock Strategy2, published in July 2026, also recognises that greater transparency across the food chain, including clearer information and labelling, is essential. This commitment is reflected in the post-2027 multiannual financial framework package, notably in the proposal to amend Regulation (EU) No 1308/20133 establishing the common organisation of the markets (CMO Regulation), presented in July 2025 and currently under negotiation by the European Parliament and the Council. The proposal clarifies that marketing standards may include requirements relating to the ‘place of farming and/or origin’ and extends the scope for such standards to additional sectors, including protein crops, beef, pigmeat, sheepmeat and goatmeat. This would provide the Commission with an appropriate legal basis to develop, where justified, proportionate and supported by consumer interest, sector-specific EU rules on origin labelling. In addition, the co-legislators have already advanced this objective through the recent amendment of the CMO Regulation4, which introduces such a possibility for poultrymeat. The Livestock Strategy also proposes to enable, through optional reserved terms in the CMO Regulation, an identifiable ‘European excellence’ term on a voluntary basis. This would be supported by clear specifications to valorise the excellence of the EU’s production of animal products. 2. As the envisaged legal basis is Article 75 of the CMO Regulation, any future Commission measure under that framework could only concern products falling within that Article’s scope.

Regulations (EU) No 1308/2013, (EU) 2021/2115 and (EU) 2021/2116 as regards the strengthening of the position of farmers in the food supply chain.

E-10-2026-003059.t: Difficulties in interpreting Regulation (EC) No 561/2006 resulting from the concept of ‘week’
qt: to the Commission Julien Leonardelli (PfE), Mathilde Androuët (PfE), Pierre Pimpie (PfE), Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE), Mélanie Disdier (PfE), André Rougé (PfE), Diana Iovanovici Şoşoacă (NI), Fernand Kartheiser (NI) Subject:
Difficulties in interpreting Regulation (EC) No 561/2006 resulting from the concept of ‘week’

A letter from a trainer in road transport sent to several Members draws attention to recurrent difficulties regarding interpretation of Regulation (EC) No 561/2006. The letter’s author states that use of the word ‘week’ in Articles 4 and 6 leads to misunderstandings in practice and problematic situations during inspections – particularly the distinction between a calendar week and a working week. 1.

Can the Commission confirm whether it is aware of these enforcement troubles, which appear to have a real impact on road transport drivers, particularly those in the perishable goods transport and passenger transport sectors?
Does it intend to clarify how it interprets ‘week’ to ensure the text is properly applied in all Member States or propose a targeted amendment to the regulation to remove any ambiguity?
at: (English version) to the Commission Julien Leonardelli (PfE), Mathilde Androuët (PfE), Pierre Pimpie (PfE), Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE), Mélanie Disdier (PfE), André Rougé (PfE), Diana Iovanovici Şoşoacă (NI), Fernand Kartheiser (NI) (20 July 2026) Subject: Difficulties in interpreting Regulation (EC) No 561/2006 resulting from the concept of ‘week’ A letter from a trainer in road transport sent to several Members draws attention to recurrent difficulties regarding interpretation of Regulation (EC) No 561/2006. The letter’s author states that use of the word ‘week’ in Articles 4 and 6 leads to misunderstandings in practice and problematic situations during inspections — particularly the distinction between a calendar week and a working week. 1. Can the Commission confirm whether it is aware of these enforcement troubles, which appear to have a real impact on road transport drivers, particularly those in the perishable goods transport and passenger transport sectors? 2. Does it intend to clarify how it interprets ‘week’ to ensure the text is properly applied in all Member States or propose a targeted amendment to the regulation to remove any ambiguity? (7 September 2026) Pursuant to the definition laid down in point (i) of Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 561/2006 (1) ‘a week’ means the period of time between 00.00 on Monday and 24.00 on Sunday. With reference to the provisions included in Article 6 of the same Regulation, the above-mentioned definition of ‘week’ applies as the temporal limit for the maximum daily driving time of 10 hours (first paragraph), for the maximum weekly driving time of 56 hours (second paragraph), for the maximum accumulated driving time of 90 hours during any two consecutive weeks (third paragraph), and for the weekly driving time of all driving time in the territories of both the Union and third countries (fourth paragraph). Reference to this calendar week, rather than to each driver’s personal schedule, makes enforcement consistent and predictable across all drivers. As regards Directive 2002/15/EC (2), point (g) of its Article 3 lays down the same definition of ‘week’ as the above-mentioned definition laid down in Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 561/2006: ‘week’ shall mean the period between 00.00 hours on Monday and 24.00 hours on Sunday. Please see the enforcement guidance document Trace 2 — Efficient and harmonised enforcement of Mobility Package 1, published by the Commission (3).

E-10-2026-003056.t: EU-funded Latvian sexuality-education project – non-discrimination compliance and risk of further replication
qt: to the Commission Joanna Scheuring-Wielgus (S&D), Emma Rafowicz (S&D), Elisabeth Grossmann (S&D), Marc Angel (S&D), Mélissa Camara (Verts/ALE), Raquel García Hermida-Van Der Walle (Renew) Subject:

The University of Latvia implemented a project entitled ‘Strengthening values-based family literacy and sexuality education in the Latvian education system’1 with funding from the Recovery and Resilience Facility. Although the grant has closed, the final policy report was presented on 17 March 2026 to the Demography, Family and Children Affairs Subcommittee of the Saeima (Latvian parliament), where its authors called on legislators to incorporate its recommendations into national education standards and guidelines, although no formal decision has yet been taken2. The recommended materials, based on an abstinence-centred programme also active in other Member States, describe extramarital sexual relations as ‘abuse of the body and person’ and call for fostering ‘a critical attitude towards any sexual activity that is not holistic/complete (including homosexual behaviour)’. Latvian civil-society organisations and clinical psychologists have questioned the scientific basis for these materials3. 1.

Did the Commission verify this project’s compliance with Article 5(2) of Regulation 2021/241 and Article 21 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union when assessing the related milestone, and was it satisfactorily fulfilled?

Will the Commission examine whether EU funding is being used to introduce discriminatory or scientifically unsupported sexuality-education materials into Latvian schools, and, if necessary, require corrective measures, including recovery of funds and conditions for any future related funding?

E-10-2026-003055.t: Impact of the Energy Performance of Buildings Directive on construction and housing prices
qt: to the Commission Christian Ehler (PPE) Subject:

The Commission’s recent infringement procedures against all 27 Member States for failing to implement the Energy Performance of Buildings Directive (EPBD) on time highlight the challenges of enforcing EU legislation in a cost-efficient, effective, and non-burdensome way. Many Member States face challenges with rising housing prices, and additional EU requirements could exacerbate this trend. 1.
What are the Commission’s estimates for each Member State’s investments in their building stock in order to comply with the requirements of the EPBD?

What are the Commission’s estimates on the effect of these investments on the average construction price of residential and non-residential buildings in the EU and per Member State, in EUR per square metre, and what are the estimates for the effect on rental and purchasing prices per square metre?
How does the Commission monitor such price effects and developments in the Member States?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (24.9.2026) The Energy Performance of Buildings Directive (EPBD)1 requires Member States to prepare National Building Renovation Plans (NBRPs), covering their associated investment needs. While the Commission aggregates the EU-level investment needs to achieve energy and climate objectives2, Member States are better placed to assess their needs based on their national specificities. On 14 July 2026, the Commission published its assessment3 of the 16 submitted draft NBRPs, which include investment estimates and show a strong commitment to improve the building stock. The Commission has not produced estimates of the impact of Member States’ EPBD-related investments on building construction costs or on purchase and rental prices. Housing prices and rents depend on many factors beyond construction costs, including land and local market values as well as financing conditions. The effects of individual legislative measures are therefore difficult to single out. Housing affordability should also be assessed considering operating costs, including energy expenditure. Better energy performance reduces energy bills and limits exposure to energy price volatility. The EPBD requires Member States to set minimum energy performance requirements with a view to achieving cost-optimal levels over the economic lifecycle of buildings. In the context of the European Semester, the Commission is monitoring housing market development including housing supply, housing and constructing prices, but not the price effect of specific EU legislation. The European Strategy for Housing Construction4, which strengthens the competitiveness and capacity of the construction ecosystem aims to address supply bottlenecks and unnecessary cost pressure.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2024/1275/oj/eng. 2 As for instance most recently in the Clean Energy Investment Strategy (COM(2026) 116 final), https://eur-

lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A52026DC0116&qid=1773310237995. 3 https://energy.ec.europa.eu/news/national-building-renovation-plans-commissions-first-assessment-2026-0714_en. 4 https://webgate.ec.europa.eu/circabc-ewpp/d/d/workspace/SpacesStore/a85e53d8-a82b-47f9-a247f0819f20466d/download.

E-10-2026-003054.t: Inappropriate design of public consultation on European Partnerships
qt: to the Commission Christian Ehler (PPE), Andrea Wechsler (PPE), René Repasi (S&D) Subject:

The open public consultation on the Single Basic Act for Joint Undertakings (JUs) and thematic priorities for the European Partnerships portfolio in Horizon Europe 2028-2034 will inform the accompanying impact assessment. The questionnaire presents five ‘areas for improvement’ as findings the Commission ‘has identified’ and which ‘will have to be addressed by the future Treaty-based partnerships’. Respondents are asked only whether they agree. The mandatory objectives (group 3) and measures (group 4) mirror those five areas one-to-one; a respondent who considers there to be no problem must still rate its causes and remedies. A footnote states the areas ‘do not necessarily pertain to all existing JUs, but are relevant to some JUs to varying extent’ – as worded, the propositions cannot be disagreed with. Every open field is optional and additive, asking only for ‘other problems’, ‘other key factors’, ‘other objectives’ or ‘other measures ... not included above’. 1.
In which recorded field can a respondent state that one of the five areas is not a problem at all?
Will the impact assessment assess options that are not derived from these five areas?
Will disagreement with an area be reported separately from ‘cannot say’ in the quantative data reporting?

E-10-2026-003053.t: Basic methodological mistakes in European Partnerships public consultation
qt: to the Commission Christian Ehler (PPE), Andrea Wechsler (PPE), René Repasi (S&D) Subject:

The open public consultation on the Single Basic Act for Joint Undertakings1 and thematic priorities for the European Partnerships portfolio in Horizon Europe 2028-2034 will inform the accompanying impact assessment. Several mandatory items depart from standard survey practice and from the Better Regulation toolbox. Some questions require a single answer to what are really two (or more) separate questions. Respondents must rate in one answer whether partnerships support ‘development, uptake and/or deployment … by EU industry and society’ or whether ‘membership, participation, and funding access’ are ‘hard to understand and navigate’. Respondents are also asked to rate the effectiveness of something without specifying what they are effective at, e.g. ‘redesign rules for non-cash contributions’, ‘minimum size (budget) of call for proposals’, and even ‘other measures to improve flexibility in programming’. The scale runs from ‘extremely effective’ to ‘not effective’, with no option to say that a measure would actually be counterproductive. Joint Undertakings and Article 185 TFEU initiatives are grouped together throughout the survey, even though they have different governance and funding structures. Even if respondents reject a premise they must still rate its causes and remedies. 1.
Who methodologically validated this questionnaire before launch?
How will the Commission correct for these design effects when reporting results?
Will the microdata and the coding frame for open answers be published?
Council Regulation (EU) 2021/2085 of 19 November 2021 establishing the Joint Undertakings under Horizon Europe (ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2021/2085/oj). 1

E-10-2026-003052.t: Solidarity between Member States during periods of low water levels
qt: to the Commission Bert-Jan Ruissen (ECR) Subject:

Water levels in rivers are unusually low due to the heat and drought1. Low water levels are expected to occur more frequently in the future. It is precisely during periods of drought that demand for water is high. As upstream countries retain more water, the situation in downstream countries, such as the Netherlands, becomes even more acute2. The water needs of different EU countries are set to increasingly come into conflict with one another. The integrated framework for European climate resilience and risk management offers opportunities to bolster international solidarity. 1.

How does the Commission safeguard the position of downstream countries during periods of water scarcity, and does the Commission agree that greater solidarity between Member States is needed to ensure the availability of water for downstream countries in the future?

Is the Commission prepared to promote agreements between Member States on solidarity in the event of unusually low water levels, and to incorporate the promotion of such agreements into the integrated framework for European climate resilience and risk management (ECRRM)3?
Does the Commission see any added value in strengthening the mandate of river commissions to promote cooperation in international river basins, including crossborder regional rivers?

https://nos.nl/artikel/2622907-rivieren-staan-uitzonderlijk-laag-voor-juli-ik-schrik-ervan. https://nos.nl/artikel/2622942-waterschappen-willen-europese-regels-zodat-we-niet-alleen-restjerivierwater-krijgen. 3 https://climate.ec.europa.eu/eu-action/adaptation-and-resilience-climate-change/european-climateresilience-and-risk-management-integrated-framework_en. 1 2
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (25.8.2026) Solidarity and open cooperation are key in transboundary water management. Article 13 of the Water Framework Directive1 (WFD) requires Member States sharing an international river basin to coordinate their river basin management plans, including measures to address water abstraction and ensure enough water flows to achieve good ecological status. Moreover, as Parties to the UN Economic Commission for Europe Water Convention2, Member States must ensure ‘exchange of information on existing and planned uses of water and related installations that are likely to cause transboundary impact’. Article 12 of the WFD3 also allows a Member State to notify the Commission and the other Member States concerned if it faces a water management issue that it cannot resolve alone, and to propose recommendations for addressing it. The WFD does not specify which form the cooperation between Member States should take when addressing water scarcity. In practice, Member States use a range of bilateral or multilateral agreements, which the Commission regularly assesses. However, low flows issues are not addressed consistently4. In its recent assessment of the WFD implementation5, the Commission thus recommended Member States to improve transboundary cooperation, including in the context of the river commissions on quantitative aspects of water management through relevant international cooperation mechanisms and bodies. The integrated framework for European climate resilience and risk management6, will help Member States and the EU strengthen preparedness for future climate conditions. This will be an important contribution to improving water resilience and security, including across shared river basins and in other transboundary contexts.
1 Directive 2000/60/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 23 October 2000 establishing a

framework for Community action in the field of water policy, OJ L 327, 22.12.2000. 2 Convention on the Protection and use of Transboundary Watercourses and International Lakes. 3 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=OJ:L_202600805. This article was recently amended and strengthened by making this cooperation mandatory. 4 An overview is available in the report ‘Assessment of the third River Basin Management Plans under the Water Framework Directive – Assessment of international cooperation under the Water Framework Directive – International River Basins’ (February 2025), available on CIRCABC: https://circabc.europa.eu/ui/group/9ab5926d-bed4-4322-9aa7-9964bbe8312d/library/3bb909f7-04c8-4e1e-9a37337a575239d8/details. 5 Report from the Commission to the Council and the European Parliament on the implementation of the Water Framework Directive (2000/60/EC) and the Floods Directive (2007/60/EC) – Third river basin management plans – Second flood risk management plans, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legalcontent/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:52025DC0002. 6 Scheduled for adoption in the fourth quarter of 2026.

E-10-2026-003050.t: Bot networks on X and Instagram – Russian-linked campaign for the election of far-right parties in Europe
qt: to the Commission Alexandra Geese (Verts/ALE), Erik Marquardt (Verts/ALE), Svenja Hahn (Renew), Jutta Paulus (Verts/ALE), Anna Cavazzini (Verts/ALE), Katarina Barley (S&D) Subject:

On 12 July 2026, Spiegel Online1 ran a piece on large-scale bot networks active mainly on X and Instagram. With Russian-based actors pulling the strings, the bots are programmed to spread disinformation about German politicians, taking aim at all democratic parties, with the exception of politicians from the AfD and the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance. According to media reports2, what we are witnessing is a continuation of the Russian-led ‘Matryoshka’ campaign which, records show, began in 2023 at the latest. 1.

Against this background and in view of the upcoming state elections in Germany, not to mention the elections coming up in various EU Member States in 2027, is the Commission checking whether the very large online platforms (VLOPs) concerned are operating in accordance with the Digital Services Act (DSA) and taking down unlawful content bearing counterfeit media logos in a timely manner?

What specific action has the Commission taken against the VLOPs to date in order to effectively disable coordinated bot networks that pose a systemic threat to public discourse and elections, pursuant to Article 34 DSA?
What has it done to verify compliance with, and enforce, the bot network guidance in its DSA elections toolkit, and is it considering introducing any further enforcement measures?

Der Spiegel, „Wladimir Putin: So wirbt der russische Präsident für AfD und BSW“ [‘Vladimir Putin: how the Russian President is throwing his weight behind AfD and BSW’], 2026. https://www.spiegel.de/wissenschaft/mensch/wladimir-putin-so-wirbt-der-russische-praesident-fuer-afd-undbsw-kolumne-a-60288130-2d29-4dd2-b3b6-5ac10cb62fdd. 2 FAZ, „Prorussisches Bot-Netz greift in Landtagswahl ein“ [‘Pro-Russian bot network meddles in state parliament elections’], 2026. https://www.faz.net/aktuell/politik/ausland/prorussisches-bot-netz-greift-inlandtagswahlkampf-ein-200994855.html. 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (14.9.2026) The Commission is closely monitoring reports concerning coordinated inauthentic behaviour and foreign interference. Under the Digital Services Act (DSA)1, very large online platforms (VLOPs) must identify, assess and mitigate systemic risks linked to their services, including risks to electoral processes, civic discourse, and inauthentic or automated use. They must also act diligently against illegal content, including counterfeit material infringing intellectual property, when aware of it, and are subject to annual independent audits. The Commission is supervising whether VLOPs such as X and Meta comply with these obligations, including on notice-and-action mechanisms, transparency reporting, data access and mitigation of risks linked to deceptive use of media identities and logos where this may breach EU or national law. The Commission uses the full range of DSA tools, including requests for information, scrutiny of risk assessments and mitigation measures, and investigations where appropriate. Formal proceedings have been opened against X2 and Meta3 in areas relevant to electoral integrity and civic discourse: X concerning information manipulation on the platform, and Meta concerning deceptive advertisements and coordinated inauthentic behaviour in the EU4. The Commission also monitors the implementation of the 2025 DSA Elections Guidelines5. Together with the Code of Conduct on Disinformation6 and its voluntary Rapid Response System7, this supports election preparedness and cooperation. As announced in the Democracy Shield8, the Commission, with national Digital Services Coordinators and the European Cooperation Network on Elections, will update the DSA Elections Toolkit9 and develop an incident and crisis protocol under the DSA. 1 Regulation (EU) 2022/2065, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/2065/oj/eng. 2 Overview of DSA enforcement actions – X, https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/list-designated-

vlops-and-vloses#ecl-inpage-twitter. 3 Overview of DSA enforcement actions – Meta, https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/list-designatedvlops-and-vloses#ecl-inpage-metaplatforms. 4 Commission opens formal proceedings against X under the Digital Services Act, https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_23_6709; Commission opens formal proceedings against Facebook and Instagram under the Digital Services Act, https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_24_2373. 5 Communication from the Commission – Commission Guidelines for providers of Very Large Online Platforms and Very Large Online Search Engines on the mitigation of systemic risks for electoral processes pursuant to Article 35(3) of Regulation (EU) 2022/2065, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A52024XC03014&qid=1714466886277. 6 The Code of Conduct on Disinformation, https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/code-conductdisinformation. 7 Defending democratic values in the digital age, https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/democracydigital. 8 European Democracy Shield and EU Strategy for Civil Society pave the way for stronger and more resilient democracies, https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_25_2660. 9 https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/news/commission-presents-new-best-practice-election-toolkit-digitalservices-act.

E-10-2026-003049.t: Water management in Greece and implementation of the European Water Resilience Strategy
qt: to the Commission Galato Alexandraki (ECR) Subject:

The Commission has highlighted water resilience as a European priority, emphasising the need to protect the water cycle, reduce leakages, modernise infrastructure and improve water efficiency. In parallel, a specific technical support project was approved for 2026 to modernise the management of water services in Greece. In view of this, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
How will it monitor whether Greece is using EU technical support to achieve genuine water management reform and not to make purely formal administrative changes?
Does it intend to ask the Greek Government for quantitative targets for leakage reduction, water reuse, groundwater protection and support for rural areas affected by drought?
Will it link future water funding to measurable results and transparency in the way water providers operate?
at: (English version) to the Commission Galato Alexandraki (ECR) (17 July 2026) Subject: Water management in Greece and implementation of the European Water Resilience Strategy The Commission has highlighted water resilience as a European priority, emphasising the need to protect the water cycle, reduce leakages, modernise infrastructure and improve water efficiency. In parallel, a specific technical support project was approved for 2026 to modernise the management of water services in Greece. In view of this, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
How will it monitor whether Greece is using EU technical support to achieve genuine water management reform and not to make purely formal administrative changes?
Does it intend to ask the Greek Government for quantitative targets for leakage reduction, water reuse, groundwater protection and support for rural areas affected by drought?
Will it link future water funding to measurable results and transparency in the way water providers operate?

(11 September 2026) The Commission will monitor EU technical support to Greece through standard Technical Support Instrument governance (1), including the Log Frame Approach with outcome/impact indicators. Greece remains subject to EU water acquis obligations. The Commission will follow implementation closely with Greek authorities and partners to ensure operational, not merely administrative, improvements. The aim is to strengthen the governance, functioning and efficiency of water services. Under the recast Drinking Water Directive (2), Member States reported leakage assessments by January 2026; the Commission will propose a leakage threshold via delegated act by January 2028. The Water Reuse Regulation (3) sets no mandatory targets and will be evaluated by June 2028. The Water Framework Directive (4) requires good quantitative groundwater status by 2027. Under the Water Resilience Strategy (5), guidance on drought management and drought indicators will be published in 2026. Under the Cohesion Policy 2021-2027 (6), water sector performance is monitored via output/result indicators, with reimbursement conditional on the applicable thematic enabling condition (7). The next Multiannual Financial Framework (8) proposal includes water investment fields, with a performance framework for transparent monitoring of EU financial support.

E-10-2026-003048.t: Prison conditions exacerbated by the heatwave in Europe
qt: to the Commission Anthony Smith (The Left) Subject:

In France, the prison occupancy rate stood at an average of 140 % as at 1 July, rising to as high as 170 % in remand centres. Conditions being such, prisoners are forced to share cells measuring around ten square metres with three or even four other inmates. During the heatwave, temperatures in some of these cells rose to nearly 57 °C, as was notably the case in Nimes. Whilst prisoners are forced by law to serve a prison sentence, the appalling conditions in which they are being held are not part of that sentence. The European Convention on Human Rights prohibits inhuman or degrading treatment and sets out minimum standards of detention. However, nothing is being done at European level to ensure these minimum standards of detention are being met. In light of the above: 1.
Does the Commission intend to take the necessary measures to ensure respect for human rights in European prisons through the establishment of a framework setting out minimum conditions for detention?
Does it intend to put in place the necessary measures to monitor whether human rights in European prisons are being respected?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (25.9.2026) Detention issues fall primarily within the responsibility of the Member States. To complement and support Member States’ policies, on 8 December 2022, the Commission adopted the Recommendation on the procedural rights of suspects and accused in pre-trial detention and on material detention conditions1. On the basis of the Recommendation, Member States should ensure that detainees are treated with respect and dignity and in line with human rights obligations, including the prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment as laid down in Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights and Article 4 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union. Moreover, the Recommendation provides specific guidance on the minimum standards to be followed by Member States for material detention conditions, including in relation to accommodation, healthcare, nutrition and time spent outside the cell and outdoors. By the end of 2026, the Commission will publish a comprehensive report assessing the national measures taken by the Member States to follow-up to the Recommendation. The Commission will then be able to evaluate how each Member State is performing and, where implementation falls short, will be better placed to consider how to address any remaining issues.

E-10-2026-003047.t: Transparency and effectiveness in the Greek support scheme for energy-intensive companies
qt: to the Commission Galato Alexandraki (ECR) Subject:

On 18 May 2026, the Commission approved a EUR 405 million Greek State aid scheme to cut electricity levies for energy-intensive companies. The Commission’s aim is to avoid relocating production activities outside the EU and to protect competitiveness. In view of this, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
What will be done to ensure that the Greek scheme genuinely supports production and employment, rather than functioning as a horizontal subsidy with no measurable outcome?
Will Greece be required to publish the beneficiaries, the amounts and the selection criteria in a transparent manner?
Is the Commission looking into whether such solutions can cover smaller production businesses, food processing and agricultural cooperatives, which are also facing pressure from energy costs?
at: (English version) to the Commission Galato Alexandraki (ECR) (17 July 2026) Subject: Transparency and effectiveness in the Greek support scheme for energy-intensive companies On 18 May 2026, the Commission approved a EUR 405 million Greek state aid scheme to cut electricity levies for energyintensive companies. The Commission’s aim is to avoid relocating production activities outside the EU and to protect competitiveness. In view of this, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
What will be done to ensure that the Greek scheme genuinely supports production and employment, rather than functioning as a horizontal subsidy with no measurable outcome?
Will Greece be required to publish the beneficiaries, the amounts and the selection criteria in a transparent manner?
Is the Commission looking into whether such solutions can cover smaller production businesses, food processing and agricultural cooperatives, which are also facing pressure from energy costs?

(8 September 2026) In its decision of 18 May 2026 (1), the Commission authorised this scheme under EU State aid rules, considering the Guidelines on state aid for climate, environmental protection and energy 2022 (CEEAG) (2). Under Section 4.11 of the CEEAG, reductions in certain electricity levies may be granted for eligible sectors that are particularly exposed to international trade and electricity costs, where paying the full levies would increase the risk of relocation outside the EU. The impact assessment report accompanying the CEEAG elaborates further in this respect (3). As stated in Section 3.3.3.8 of the decision, Greece will ensure compliance with the transparency requirements laid down in the CEEAG. These include an obligation to publish, in the Commission’s transparency award module or on a comprehensive state aid website, the full text of the approved scheme and information on each individual award granted under an approved scheme exceeding EUR 100 000. In addition, Greece will have to submit reports to the Commission and maintain records as required for all aid measures under EU State aid rules. While this scheme concerns levies reduction for energy-intensive companies in particular, the EU State aid rules allow, in general, Member States to introduce schemes to alleviate energy cost pressures on companies, including small and mediumsized enterprises. Such support can be provided under various applicable frameworks, including the de minimis Regulation (4), the General Block Exemption Regulation (5), the Clean Industrial Deal State Aid Framework (6), and the Middle East Crisis Temporary State Aid Framework (7).
