E-10-2026-003046.t: Reshoring of the flax sector: industrial and strategic challenges for the EU
qt: to the Commission Valérie Deloge (PfE), Marie-Luce Brasier-Clain (PfE), Aleksandar Nikolic (PfE), André Rougé (PfE), Anne-Sophie Frigout (PfE), Rody Tolassy (PfE), Séverine Werbrouck (PfE), Céline Imart (PPE), Julie Rechagneux (PfE) Subject:

The European Union is today the world’s largest producer of flax. France alone accounts for around 60% of global production. This crop is a strategic asset for our agriculture and for many rural areas. We have recognised know-how in this sector. However, a significant proportion of this flax (95% in France) is exported to China, where it is spun and processed before being re-imported into the European market in the form of finished products, in particular clothing, household linen, composite materials and insulation panels. Much of the added value and jobs associated with processing are thus lost to European producers and industrial firms. At a time when the European Union is consistently expressing its ambition to strengthen its industry and reshore certain strategic production: 1.
Has the Commission assessed the economic and industrial losses associated with exporting of a significant proportion of European flax to China for processing?
How does it explain the fact that the EU remains dependent on processing capacities located in China for a fibre for which the Member States account for the bulk of global production?
What measures does it intend to take to encourage the development of artisanal and industrial flax spinning and processing activities within the EU?
Supporter1
This question is supported by a Member other than the authors: Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE).
at: (English version) to the Commission Valérie Deloge (PfE), Marie-Luce Brasier-Clain (PfE), Aleksandar Nikolic (PfE), André Rougé (PfE), Anne-Sophie Frigout (PfE), Rody Tolassy (PfE), Séverine Werbrouck (PfE), Céline Imart (PPE), Julie Rechagneux (PfE) (17 July 2026) Subject: Reshoring of the flax sector: industrial and strategic challenges for the EU The European Union is today the world’s largest producer of flax. France alone accounts for around 60% of global production. This crop is a strategic asset for our agriculture and for many rural areas. We have recognised know-how in this sector. However, a significant proportion of this flax (95% in France) is exported to China, where it is spun and processed before being re-imported into the European market in the form of finished products, in particular clothing, household linen, composite materials and insulation panels. Much of the added value and jobs associated with processing are thus lost to European producers and industrial firms. At a time when the European Union is consistently expressing its ambition to strengthen its industry and reshore certain strategic production: 1.
Has the Commission assessed the economic and industrial losses associated with exporting of a significant proportion of European flax to China for processing?
How does it explain the fact that the EU remains dependent on processing capacities located in China for a fibre for which the Member States account for the bulk of global production?
What measures does it intend to take to encourage the development of artisanal and industrial flax spinning and processing activities within the EU?

Supporter (1) (3 September 2026) The Commission has not carried out a dedicated assessment on the economic and industrial impact associated with flax exports. The EU represents 75-80% of the global long flax fibre production, but its flax spinning capacity declined over recent decades due to higher production costs and global competition. It still retains about 8% of the global capacity. In the period 2023-2025, the average yearly EU exports were 136 000 tonnes, out of which 108 000 tonnes went to China. However, demand for high quality natural textile fibres is growing, offering opportunities for the EU flax and linen sector and supporting the return of spinning capacity in the EU. The development of additional flax spinning and processing capacity in the EU will depend primarily on the emergence of competitive business models and private investment. In this context, the Commission encourages Member States and regions to make full use of available EU instruments to support innovation, skills, modernisation and value-chain integration. The future Multiannual Financial Framework post-2027 will offer new opportunities to scale up the competitiveness of European industry, in particular through the proposed European Competitiveness Fund. The European Regional Development Fund may support regional industrial development. TCLF SkillBridge is a European initiative funded under the Single Market Programme. The aim is to establish and strengthen Regional Skills Partnerships across Europe in the textile, clothing, leather and footwear sectors.
This question is supported by a Member other than the authors: Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE).

In addition, funding is provided through Horizon Europe to innovative textiles via the European Partnership ‘Textiles for the Future’ for the period 2025-2027. The Commission will dedicate EUR 30 million to actions within the scope of the Partnership, while private partners’ contribution will match the Union contribution.

E-10-2026-003045.t: Infringement procedure against all Member States for failure to transpose the Energy Performance of Buildings Directive
qt: to the Commission Anna Maria Cisint (PfE), Susanna Ceccardi (PfE), Silvia Sardone (PfE), Isabella Tovaglieri (PfE), Raffaele Stancanelli (PfE), Paolo Borchia (PfE), Aldo Patriciello (PfE) Subject:

The Commission has launched infringement procedures against all 27 Member States for failing to transpose the EPBD on ‘green homes’. The fact that no Member State has met the transposition deadline raises questions about the practical feasibility of the regulatory framework adopted. If all the Member States have encountered difficulties severe enough to prevent them from meeting the deadline, it is fair to wonder whether the directive is properly tailored to the different economic, social and housing conditions in the EU, particularly in countries such as Italy, which has a vast private and historical property stock. Rather than merely launching infringement procedures against all Member States, the Commission should assess whether this state of affairs shows that the directive’s design needs to be reconsidered, with a view to preventing disproportionate economic and property effects for citizens and property owners. In the light of the above: 1.
Does the Commission think that the Member States’ collective failure to transpose the directive calls for an overhaul of the directive or an assessment into whether it should be repealed?

How does it justify launching infringement proceedings against all Member States, rather than fostering a dialogue to identify changes that would make implementation more realistic, sustainable and effective?

E-10-2026-003044.t: Commission funding for Euronews and compatibility with the European Media Freedom Act
qt: to the Commission Sabine Verheyen (PPE), Bogdan Andrzej Zdrojewski (PPE), Hannes Heide (S&D), Laurence Farreng (Renew), Nela Riehl (Verts/ALE) Subject:

For years, Euronews has received substantial annual financial support from the Commission, which is now allocated through a competitive public tender process. Serious concerns have emerged regarding Euronews’s editorial independence since control passed in 2021 to Pedro Vargas David, whose firm’s ties to former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán have been documented. Recently, a senior journalist from Euronews alleged editorial interference ahead of Hungary’s April 2026 elections, claiming management removed an article on declining stock valuations of companies linked to the Fidesz government. The journalist described this as a ‘clear breach of editorial integrity’ and raised concerns about ownership-related conflicts of interest.1 The European Media Freedom Act (EMFA), which has been fully applicable since August 2025, prohibits interference in editorial decisions and requires safeguards for editorial independence. In the light of this: 1.
What obligations relating to editorial independence are attached to Commission funding for Euronews and how is compliance verified?
Is the Commission investigating these allegations?
How does continued Commission funding for Euronews align with EMFA obligations?
https://www.euractiv.com/news/euronews-accused-of-clear-breach-of-editorial-integrity-overhungarian-elections/. 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (11.9.2026) Euronews receives EU support through open calls under the Multimedia Actions budget line, funding professional reporting on EU affairs. All beneficiaries operate with full editorial independence, underpinned by an Editorial Charter, and must uphold the highest editorial standards and abide by strict contractual obligations. Beneficiaries of Commission funding must also comply with applicable EU, international and national law, including the European Media Freedom Act (EMFA).1 In particular, Article 6(3)(b) of the EMFA requires media service providers to take measures to disclose any actual or potential conflicts of interest that may affect the provision of news and current affairs content. The Commission checks compliance through regular monitoring of contractual deliverables, independent annual content analyses and periodic evaluations of the Multimedia Actions.2 Allegations, including the one mentioned by the Honourable members, are part of the Commission assessments. If contractual obligations are not met, it can reject costs, reduce grants, suspend payments or terminate the grant agreement in accordance with the relevant rules of Regulation (EU, Euratom) 2024/2509 (Financial Regulation).3 As part of its regular reporting obligations, Euronews also submits the results of independent editorial audits, including for its Hungarian service, which so far indicate a high level of journalistic quality and editorial independence. Based on the information currently available, the Commission has found no evidence of contractual non-compliance by Euronews. It has therefore no grounds to conclude that Euronews’ continued funding is incompatible with the applicable contractual or legal requirements.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1083/oj/eng. 2 https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/multimedia-actions. 3 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/2509/oj/eng.

E-10-2026-003043.t: Regulation (EU) 2023/2055 for industrial downstream users of plastics: distinction between producers and processors
qt: to the Commission Elena Donazzan (ECR), Carlo Fidanza (ECR), Nicola Procaccini (ECR), Antonella Sberna (ECR), Pietro Fiocchi (ECR), Michele Picaro (ECR), Mariateresa Vivaldini (ECR), Alberico Gambino (ECR), Daniele Polato (ECR), Stefano Cavedagna (ECR) Subject:
Regulation (EU) 2023/2055 for industrial downstream users of plastics: distinction between producers and processors

Regulation (EU) 2023/2055, which amends Annex XVII to REACH, prohibits the placing on the market of synthetic polymer microparticles ‘intentionally present [...] to confer a soughtafter characteristic’ and imposes annual reporting obligations on ECHA. Among the entities obliged to follow that rule, paragraph 11 of the annex includes ‘industrial downstream users’, which also formally includes thermoplastic polymer processors. However, the regulation does not distinguish between entities that produce intentionally added microplastics and those such as processors who buy and process already compliant raw materials without adding any microparticles. In this scenario – where microplastics are not ‘intentionally present [...] to confer a sought-after characteristic’ – it is unclear whether the reporting requirements apply. Neither ECHA nor the national authorities have provided operational guidance, exposing SMEs to the risk of formal non-compliance or to consultancy fees that are disproportionate to their actual responsibility in the dispersion of microplastics. In the light of the above, can the Commission clarify whether the obligations laid down in paragraph 11 of the annex to Regulation (EU) 2023/2055 apply to processing companies that buy raw materials that are already compliant, without intentionally adding microparticles? If they do, with which operational tools other than those designed for chemical producers?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.9.2026) Entry 78 of Annex XVII to the Regulation on the Registration, Evaluation, Authorisation and Restriction of chemicals (REACH)1 (“the microplastics restriction”) allows synthetic polymer microparticles (“microplastics”) to be placed on the market for industrial use by the derogation under paragraph 4(a). This means that industrial users may buy these microplastics as raw materials for their own production in compliance with the restriction. However, using these derogated microplastics in industrial production triggers the reporting obligation under paragraph 11 of the same entry. In contrast, if the raw material does not contain any microparticles, then the restriction, including the reporting obligations, does not apply. To support implementation of the microplastic restriction, the Commission has published a specific Explanatory Guide2. It explains in simple terms the provisions and the intended implementation of the restriction, including for reporting. In addition, questions on REACH implementation, including the microplastics restriction, can be addressed to the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA)3 or the REACH national helpdesks4. Detailed operational instructions on how to report estimated microplastics emissions to ECHA are published on the ECHA website5.

20232055-restriction-microplastics-intentionally-added-products_en. 3 https://www.echa.europa.eu/support; https://comments.echa.europa.eu/comments_cms/Contact_REACH.aspx 4 https://echa.europa.eu/support/helpdesks. 5 Guidelines for the reporting requirements set by the REACH restriction of synthetic polymer microparticles (microplastics): https://echa.europa.eu/documents/10162/17246/rest_microplastics_reporting_guidelines_en.pdf/69fe1946-37294d21-0d85-cdc72d05e870?t=1764055280171. E-10-2026-003042.t: Official recognition of a European Day in Remembrance of the Victims of Accidents at Work
qt: to the Commission Anthony Smith (The Left) Subject:

According to Eurostat, nearly 3 300 people died as a result of an accident at work in the EU in 2023. Occupational diseases claim even more lives: the Commission estimates that workrelated cancers cause around 100 000 deaths per year. Although the EU has set itself a ‘zero deaths’ target (‘Vision Zero’) in its strategic framework on health and safety at work 2021-27, it has never designated a specific date to honour the memory of these victims. In its resolution of 21 May 2026, adopted by a large majority, the European Parliament called for the establishment of a European Day in Remembrance of the Victims of Accidents at Work and for the Protection and Dignity of Workers, to be marked each year on 8 August. As that resolution is not binding, it falls on the Commission to make this day a reality. 1.
Does the Commission intend to act on this call by officially designating 8 August as the European Day in Remembrance of the Victims of Accidents at Work?
If not, would it consider dedicating 28 April, the World Day for Safety and Health at Work, to the remembrance of these victims?
What timeframe and arrangements does it envisage for this purpose?
at: (English version) to the Commission Anthony Smith (The Left) (17 July 2026) Subject: Official recognition of a European Day in Remembrance of the Victims of Accidents at Work According to Eurostat, nearly 3 300 people died as a result of an accident at work in the EU in 2023. Occupational diseases claim even more lives: the Commission estimates that work-related cancers cause around 100 000 deaths per year. Although the EU has set itself a ‘zero deaths’ target (‘Vision Zero’) in its strategic framework on health and safety at work 2021-27, it has never designated a specific date to honour the memory of these victims. In its resolution of 21 May 2026, adopted by a large majority, the European Parliament called for the establishment of a European Day in Remembrance of the Victims of Accidents at Work and for the Protection and Dignity of Workers, to be marked each year on 8 August. As that resolution is not binding, it falls on the Commission to make this day a reality. 1. Does the Commission intend to act on this call by officially designating 8 August as the European Day in Remembrance of the Victims of Accidents at Work? 2. If not, would it consider dedicating 28 April, the World Day for Safety and Health at Work, to the remembrance of these victims? 3.
What timeframe and arrangements does it envisage for this purpose?

(21 August 2026) The Commission has taken due note of the European Parliament resolution of 21 May 2026 calling for European Day in Remembrance of the Victims of Accidents at Work and for the Protection and Dignity of Workers, to be observed annually on 8 August. It has also taken note of similar calls made by several Member States at the Council meeting of employment and social affairs ministers on 29 June 2026. In response, the Commission proposes that, together with the European Parliament and the Council, an annual ‘European Day in remembrance of the victims of accidents at work’ is established, to be observed on 8 August each year. The Day of Remembrance is intended to provide an annual occasion for commemoration and for joint awareness-raising on the importance of safety and health at work. Further details regarding the timing and the related preparatory activities will be determined in due course in cooperation with the European Parliament and the Council.

E-10-2026-003041.t: Development of a European cloud to strengthen European cooperation
qt: to the Commission Nadine Morano (PPE) Subject:

Article 4(2) of the Treaty on European Union points out that national security is the sole responsibility of Member States. However, the digital transformation, especially the increasing use of AI, has profoundly changed how criminal networks operate – they are now exploiting digital technology to develop ever more sophisticated and international activities. To respond to these developments, the Commission is preparing a set of reforms for Europol, Eurojust and the European Public Prosecutor’s Office. Those reforms include the creation of a ‘European police cloud’, which is meant to improve Europol’s exchange of information, operational cooperation and analysis capabilities, in order to step up the fight against crossborder crime and cybercrime. At the same time, the Commission stresses that the new tools must respect fundamental rights and Member States’ powers as regards national security. In view of the above: 1.

How does the Commission intend to ensure that the future European police cloud will enable operational data to be shared between national authorities in a manner that is sufficiently comprehensive and homogeneous, while respecting Member States’ prerogatives under Article 4(2) of the Treaty on European Union?
Does it intend to define a minimum set of information that must be shared, in order to ensure that this new European infrastructure is operationally effective?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.9.2026) In its proposal for a new European Union Agency for Law Enforcement Cooperation (Europol) Regulation1, the Commission proposes establishing a Police Shared Data Space to make operational data exchange between national authorities faster and more efficient. It would let Member States open joint operational analysis cases (JOACs)2: secure collaborative environments where Member States, Europol and trusted partners would work simultaneously on the same data3, using Europol’s analytical tools4. To ensure comprehensive and homogeneous exchange, the Commission will adopt implementing acts defining the Police Shared Data Space’s functionalities and the modalities to ensure interoperability5. According to the Commission’s proposal, each Member State may decide whether to open a JOAC6, fully respecting their prerogatives7. Currently Member States are obliged to provide Europol with the information necessary for the Agency to fulfil its tasks8. The Commission’s proposal aims at facilitating compliance with that obligation through mandatory data loaders9, which are automated technical means enabling the systematic, structured uploading of relevant information from national case management systems10. According to the Commission’s proposal, competent authorities of the Member States may refrain from uploading data, including where sharing data would harm national security interests or an ongoing investigation11. The sovereignty of cloud infrastructure and services used in the future to deploy the Police Shared Data Space will be ensured in compliance with the requirements of the Cloud and Artificial Intelligence Development Act12, which puts in place appropriate safeguards to protect highly critical public sector activities and systems deployed in the cloud.

E-10-2026-003040.t: European strategy for sustainable cooling of buildings in the face of intensifying heatwaves
qt: to the Commission Nadine Morano (PPE) Subject:

The heatwave that has affected Europe since June 2026 illustrates the worsening risks associated with climate change. According to the World Health Organisation, it had already caused more than 1 000 deaths by 30 June 20261. Eurostat figures show that annual household energy consumption for cooling has almost doubled in the EU since 2015. While cooling still accounted for only 0.8% of the EU’s final energy consumption in 20242, heatwaves are driving up electricity demand, putting increasing pressure on energy grids and markets. As Europe gets hotter, air conditioning is becoming less and less about comfort and more a public health issue of protecting the most vulnerable. As a consequence, we need to adapt buildings to cope with heatwaves, encourage the installation of efficient, energy-saving airconditioning systems – alongside passive cooling solutions – and ensure that the electricity infrastructure can meet the growing demand for cooling. Does the Commission intend to support Member States in developing sustainable airconditioning solutions and adapting electricity grids to meet the foreseeable increase in cooling needs?

https://euractiv.csom/fr/news/un-cauchemar-climatise-pour-le-reseau-electrique-de-lue/. https://www.euronews.com/business/2026/06/30/how-europes-growing-need-for-cooling-is-reshapingelectricity-demand. 1 2

E-10-2026-003039.t: Stepping up capacity to build water-bomber aircraft in the EU
qt: to the Commission Anthony Smith (The Left) Subject:

Forest fires are on the increase in Europe as a result of climate change. The fires are becoming more intense, more frequent and more widespread. In 2022, 837 212 hectares were burnt in the EU, including almost 72 000 hectares in France. Although the EU has stepped up its response capacity through the rescEU civil protection mechanism, including Canadair-type water-bomber planes, it is still dependent on a limited number of manufacturers and does not have enough industrial capacity to quickly renew and strengthen its fleet. This dependence is posing major challenges for civil security and the strategic autonomy of the EU in the face of heightened climate risks. With the above in mind: 1.
What action is the Commission intending to take to develop EU manufacturing capacity for Canadair-type water-bomber planes or equivalent aircraft?
What EU funding is the Commission planning to deploy to support research and development in this area, as well as the manufacturing of these strategic aircraft?
What measures is it planning to propose with a view to stepping up cooperation, pooling of resources and solidarity among Member States in the face of natural disasters?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (28.8.2026) The Commission shares the concerns about the increasing frequency and intensity of wildfires linked to climate change and is preparing a new EU Integrated Framework on Climate Resilience. It will aim to establish a more anticipatory, comprehensive and coherent approach to climate preparedness and resilience at EU and Member State level, including for EU economy. Since 2019, the EU has started developing the future permanent rescEU1 fleet, financing the acquisition of 12 new firefighting airplanes and five helicopters. While the technical specifications of assets remain under the responsibility of Member States, the Commission is working with them and with the industry to identify and closely monitor the development of potential new suitable European projects. The Commission will continue to mobilise relevant EU programmes, including Horizon Europe, InvestEU and the Cohesion Policy funds, to support research, innovation and, where eligible, industrial investments contributing to develop an EU manufacturing of water-bomber aircraft. The Commission will also continue to strengthen cooperation among Member States through the Union Civil Protection Mechanism2 by expanding rescEU capacities, improving interoperability, promoting joint training and exercises, and reinforcing prevention, preparedness and solidarity. In the context of the negotiations on the next Multiannual Financial Framework (2028–2034) and on the Commission proposal for a Regulation on the Union Civil Protection3, the support of the European Parliament will be essential to ensure the effective implementation of activities aiming at building a more resilient and better-prepared Europe.

E-10-2026-003037.t: Case No 14.724 before the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights
qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Catarina Vieira (Verts/ALE) Subject:

In 1981, during El Salvador’s armed conflict, Jorge Alberto Rodríguez Romero and Francisco Milton Romero Sequeira were forcibly disappeared by government forces. Forty-five years later, their family still awaits the truth about their fate and the return of their remains. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights adopted Merits Report No 262/23, finding El Salvador responsible and issuing recommendations on investigation, search and reparation, with which the government has not complied. The case parallels Cuéllar Sandoval et al. (Inter-American Court, 2024), arising from the same conflict, and falls within the scope of the EU Guidelines on Enforced Disappearances. 1.

Is the Commission/European External Action Service (EEAS) aware that El Salvador, an EU partner under the EU-Central America Association Agreement, has failed to comply with binding recommendations of an international human rights body regarding a 1981 enforced disappearance?

Will the Commission/EEAS raise this case with the Salvadoran authorities through its human rights dialogue and the EU-Central America Association Agreement, urge compliance and a genuine search for the victims’ remains?
Will the Commission/EEAS encourage El Salvador to accede to the Inter-American Convention on Forced Disappearance of Persons?

The case parallels Cuéllar Sandoval et al. (Inter-American Court, 2024), arising from the same conflict, and falls within the scope of the EU Guidelines on Enforced Disappearances. 1. Is the Commission/European External Action Service (EEAS) aware that El Salvador, an EU partner under the EUCentral America Association Agreement, has failed to comply with binding recommendations of an international human rights body regarding a 1981 enforced disappearance? 2. Will the Commission/EEAS raise this case with the Salvadoran authorities through its human rights dialogue and the EUCentral America Association Agreement, urge compliance and a genuine search for the victims’ remains? 3. (15 September 2026) The EU regularly recalls, in its contacts with the Salvadoran authorities, the importance of cooperating fully with international and regional human rights mechanisms and of giving appropriate follow-up to their recommendations. The EU will continue to raise human rights, the rule of law and accountability in its dialogue with El Salvador. The EU does not comment publicly on confidential exchanges concerning individual cases. The EU fully respects the independence of the Inter-American human rights system and supports effective cooperation by States with its institutions.

E-10-2026-003036.t: Procedural urgency in Case No. 14.724 (deadline 16 August 2026)
qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Catarina Vieira (Verts/ALE) Subject:
Procedural urgency in Case No. 14.724 (deadline 16 August 2026)

In Case No. 14.724, concerning the 1981 enforced disappearance of two civilians by Salvadoran State forces, the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights (IACHR) granted El Salvador a final extension, expiring on 16 August 2026, to comply with Merits Report No. 262/23. Should El Salvador remain non-compliant, the case may be referred to the InterAmerican Court of Human Rights, as the petitioners have formally requested, having also submitted a full reparation proposal. El Salvador has used successive extensions to delay rather than cooperate in good faith, a pattern relevant to the EU’s broader engagement on human rights and the rule of law in Central America. 1.
Is the European External Action Service following the imminent 16 August 2026 deadline in Case No. 14.724?
Will the EU convey to the Salvadoran authorities the importance of complying in good faith with the IACHR’s recommendations before that date?
Will the EU support the referral of Case No. 14.724 to the IACHR by diplomatic means should El Salvador fail to comply?
at: (English version) to the Vice-President of the Commission/High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Catarina Vieira (Verts/ALE) (17 July 2026) Subject: Procedural urgency in Case No 14.724 (deadline 16 August 2026) In Case No 14.724, concerning the 1981 enforced disappearance of two civilians by Salvadoran State forces, the InterAmerican Commission on Human Rights (IACHR) granted El Salvador a final extension, expiring on 16 August 2026, to comply with Merits Report No 262/23. Should El Salvador remain non-compliant, the case may be referred to the InterAmerican Court of Human Rights, as the petitioners have formally requested, having also submitted a full reparation proposal. El Salvador has used successive extensions to delay rather than cooperate in good faith, a pattern relevant to the EU’s broader engagement on human rights and the rule of law in Central America. 1.
Is the European External Action Service following the imminent 16 August 2026 deadline in Case No 14.724?

2. Will the EU convey to the Salvadoran authorities the importance of complying in good faith with the IACHR’s recommendations before that date? 3. Will the EU support the referral of Case No 14.724 to the IACHR by diplomatic means should El Salvador fail to comply? (18 September 2026) The European External Action Service closely follows the human rights and rule of law situation in El Salvador, including issues of transitional justice and accountability for serious human rights violations committed during the armed conflict. The EU regularly recalls, in its contacts with the Salvadoran authorities, the importance of cooperating fully with international and regional human rights mechanisms and of giving appropriate follow-up to their recommendations. The EU will continue to raise human rights, the rule of law and accountability in its dialogue with El Salvador. The EU does not comment publicly on confidential exchanges concerning individual cases. The decision whether to refer a case to the Inter-American Court of Human Rights falls within the independent mandate of the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights, in accordance with the American Convention on Human Rights and the InterAmerican Commission’s Rules of Procedure (1). The EU fully respects the independence of the Inter-American human rights system and supports effective cooperation by States with its institutions.

E-10-2026-003035.t: Constitutional coup by Péter Magyar’s government
qt: to the Commission Tamás Deutsch (PfE), Kinga Gál (PfE), Mieke Andriese (PfE), Gerolf Annemans (PfE), Paolo Borchia (PfE), Mireia Borrás Pabón (PfE), Irmhild Boßdorf (ESN), Zsuzsanna Borvendég (ESN), Anna Bryłka (PfE), Jorge Buxadé Villalba (PfE), Petr Bystron (ESN), Margarita de la Pisa Carrión (PfE), Elisabeth Dieringer (PfE), Csaba Dömötör (PfE), Viktória Ferenc (PfE), Carlo Fidanza (ECR), Juan Carlos Girauta Vidal (PfE), Enikő Győri (PfE), András Gyürk (PfE), Roman Haider (PfE), György Hölvényi (PfE), Paolo Inselvini (ECR), Patryk Jaki (ECR), Alexander Jungbluth (ESN), Ondřej Knotek (PfE), Sebastian Kruis (PfE), András László (PfE), Afroditi Latinopoulou (PfE), Jorge Martín Frías (PfE), Georg Mayer (PfE), Tiago Moreira de Sá (PfE), Jana Nagyová (PfE), Jacek Ozdoba (ECR), Gilles Pennelle (PfE), Ernő Schaller-Baross (PfE), Antonín Staněk (PfE), Petra Steger (PfE), Pál Szekeres (PfE), António Tânger Corrêa (PfE), Hermann Tertsch (PfE), Tom Vandendriessche (PfE), Harald Vilimsky (PfE), Auke Zijlstra (PfE) Subject:

On 22 June 2026, Péter Magyar’s government submitted a proposal for the 17th amendment to the Fundamental Law.1 The proposed changes violate the most fundamental democratic and constitutional principles. Unprecedented in Europe, the changes would remove with immediate effect the legitimately elected President of the Republic years before the end of his term through ad hominem legislation. The proposal also restricts citizens’ electoral rights by forbidding anyone who has previously served as a member of the National Assembly for at least 12 years from running as a candidate in elections. The proposal also terminates the mandates of all Constitutional Court members who have reached the age of 70. This constitutes retroactive and ad hominem legislation, resulting in the early termination of four constitutional judges’ mandates, including the President of the Constitutional Court. For over a decade, the Commission has closely monitored the measures taken by the Hungarian Government. 1.
Why is the Commission silent now when a government is blatantly violating European constitutional principles?
Does the Commission not consider these changes to be contrary to basic democratic principles?

qt: to the Commission Kathleen Funchion (The Left) Subject:

The Irish Government has a reduced VAT rate of 9 % for hairdressers but has left the VAT rate at 13.5 % for beauty salons. There has been a consistent lack of clarity throughout the process on why beauty salons have been excluded from the reduced VAT rate enjoyed by hairdressers and that have been applied in other EU Member States to similar businesses. Many of these businesses are SMEs that have been put under severe pressure by energy price shocks and are struggling to remain open. 1.
Does Directive 2006/112/EC prohibit lowering the VAT rate for beauty salons?
If so is the Commission monitoring the impact on the beauty industry of this prohibition in certain Member States that are particularly susceptible to high costs, such as Ireland?
at: (English version) to the Commission Kathleen Funchion (The Left) (16 July 2026) Subject: VAT rates for beauty professionals The Irish Government has a reduced VAT rate of 9% for hairdressers but has left the VAT rate at 13.5% for beauty salons. There has been a consistent lack of clarity throughout the process on why beauty salons have been excluded from the reduced VAT rate enjoyed by hairdressers and that have been applied in other EU Member States to similar businesses. Many of these businesses are SMEs that have been put under severe pressure by energy price shocks and are struggling to remain open. 1.
Does Directive 2006/112/EC prohibit lowering the VAT rate for beauty salons?

2. If so is the Commission monitoring the impact on the beauty industry of this prohibition in certain Member States that are particularly susceptible to high costs, such as Ireland? (25 August 2026) When the Council of the EU adopted the major value-added tax (VAT) rate reform in 2022 (1), Member States unanimously agreed that hairdressing (2) should remain the only body care service eligible for reduced rates. According to Council Directive 2006/112/EC, applying VAT rates lower than the standard rate to other services, such as those supplied by beauty salons, is not permitted. Reduced VAT rates typically have little impact on prices due to the low pass-through effect. This is because shops are not legally required to pass on any savings from reduced VAT rates to their customers by reducing their prices. Consequently, the Commission does not see a need to monitor the impact that VAT rates may have on the beauty industry in specific Member States.

Council Directive (EU) 2022/542 of 5 April 2022 amending Directives 2006/112/EC and (EU) 2020/285 as regards rates of value added tax, OJ L 107, 6.4.2022, p. 1. E-10-2026-003033.t: Transport access for people with disabilities
qt: to the Commission Kathleen Funchion (The Left) Subject:

Various reports suggest that Irish infrastructure projects often run past deadlines and over budget. The Irish Fiscal Advisory Council last year also released figures to show that Irish productivity in the construction sector falls below the EU average. Many parts of Ireland are also over-reliant on roads for transport, and when necessary works are carried out on infrastructure bottlenecks, they can cause significant delays. Such delays result in massive disruption, particularly for people with disabilities, who find themselves cut off from vital services for the duration of the works. With this in mind has the commission monitored Ireland’s provision of adequate alternatives for people with disabilities under Directive 2024/2841? If so, what was the opinion of the Commission?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (29.9.2026) Transport is a policy area of shared competence between the EU and the Member States1. However, the primary responsibility for planning, financing, procuring and developing transport infrastructure lies with the Member States. Directive 2024/28412 is intended to ensure that persons with disabilities, when visiting or travelling to another Member State, can access the special conditions and preferential treatment available in the host country, on equal terms and conditions as its residents. By 5 June 2027, Member States shall adopt and publish the laws, regulations and administrative provisions necessary to comply with this Directive. They shall apply those measures from 5 June 2028. The EU and all its Member States, including Ireland, are parties to the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (UNCRPD)3. In line with its Article 9, State Parties shall identify and eliminate obstacles and barriers to accessibility in, inter alia, the built environment, including buildings, roads, transportation and other indoor and outdoor facilities. Furthermore, in May 2026, the Commission adopted the Communication ‘Enhancing the Strategy for the rights of persons with disabilities’4, in which it put forward a Flagship initiative ‘Better access to transport for persons with disabilities’, covering various means of transport.

qt: to the Commission Kathleen Funchion (The Left) Subject:

Ireland currently has over 11 000 cases of skin cancer a year and it is becoming increasingly clear that one of the contributory factors is the unregulated and unlicensed use of sunbeds and tanning medication such as Melanotan tanning injections and nasal sprays. Furthermore, in 2023 the Health Service Executive found that one third of operators were non-compliant with the applicable legislation, and recent reporting suggests that one in twenty users are under the age of 18, often with access to unregulated, privately owned sunbeds. 1.
What measures is the Commission taking to tackle the influx of illegal tanning medication into the European market?
What measures is the Commission taking to ensure that tanning products legally on the market are being used in a safe and correct manner?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (11.9.2026) The Commission attaches great importance to ensuring that only compliant products are placed on the EU market. The Commission intends to address the growing influx of non-compliant products, including tanning cosmetics and sunbeds, in the context of the ongoing revision of the Market Surveillance Regulation1, as part of the wider European Product Act proposal. The aim is to strengthen enforcement, notably by enhancing the accountability and traceability of EU-based economic operators acting on behalf of third-country manufacturers, and by reinforcing cooperation and information exchange between Member States’ authorities. In the immediate term, market surveillance authorities can make use of a recently launched digital tool that detects potentially non-compliant products offered online before they enter the EU market2. As regards tanning cosmetics, products placed on the EU market must comply with the safety requirements of the Cosmetic Regulation3, including a mandatory safety assessment, appropriate labelling and instructions for safe use, and, where relevant, ingredients restrictions. The Commission also continuously reviews the scientific evidence and updates the regulatory framework. As regards sunbeds placed on the EU market, they must comply with the health and safety requirements of Directive 2014/35/EU4. At the same time, a distinction should be made between the requirements applicable to sunbeds as products and the rules governing their use. EU product legislation sets the requirements that sunbeds must meet when they are placed on the EU market. By contrast, the conditions under which sunbeds may be used remain primarily a matter for Member States. These conditions may therefore vary from one Member State to another.

1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02019R1020-20260812. 2 https://single-market-economy.ec.europa.eu/single-market/goods/building-blocks/market-surveillance_en. 3 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02009R1223-20260501. 4 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A02014L0035-20260530.

E-10-2026-003031.t: Ensuring the continued operation of the Blue Flag Programme under Directive (EU) 2024/825
qt: to the Commission Yannis Maniatis (S&D), Sandra Gómez López (S&D), Sakis Arnaoutoglou (S&D), Ştefan Muşoiu (S&D), Juan Fernando López Aguilar (S&D), Bruno Tobback (S&D), Alicia Homs Ginel (S&D), Marcos Ros Sempere (S&D), Idoia Mendia (S&D), Lina Gálvez (S&D), Nikolas Farantouris (S&D), Marta Temido (S&D), Eric Sargiacomo (S&D), Matjaž Nemec (S&D), Costas Mavrides (S&D), Daniel Attard (S&D), Michalis Hadjipantela (PPE), Sirpa Pietikäinen (PPE), Regina Doherty (PPE), Maravillas Abadía Jover (PPE), Wouter Beke (PPE), Loucas Fourlas (PPE), Hristo Petrov (Renew), Cynthia Ní Mhurchú (Renew), Barry Andrews (Renew), Nikola Minchev (Renew), Vladimir Prebilič (Verts/ALE), Jutta Paulus (Verts/ALE), Rasmus Nordqvist (Verts/ALE), Per Clausen (The Left) Subject:

Founded in 1987, the Blue Flag Programme has become one of Europe’s most recognised environmental initiatives, operating at around 3 800 sites across 22 Member States and contributing to the implementation of EU policies on bathing water quality, environmental management, sustainable tourism, accessibility and environmental education. However, concerns have been raised that the application by September 2026 of Directive (EU) 2024/825, which was designed primarily for commercial products rather than dynamic environments such as beaches, could create disproportionate administrative burdens and costs for participating municipalities and programme operators, potentially undermining participation in the scheme. While the programme is already supported by a multi-level system of independent assessment, international verification and compliance-monitoring arrangements, in line with the spirit of the Directive, questions remain regarding the continued operation of these mechanisms under the framework established by Directive (EU) 2024/825. Against this background and given the significant environmental, educational and tourism benefits delivered by the Blue Flag Programme, we would like to ask the following question: Is the Commission considering providing the necessary legal certainty, practical guidance or other implementation arrangements to ensure that the programme can continue to operate effectively while remaining compliant in principle with Directive (EU) 2024/825?

E-10-2026-003030.t: Possible breaches of EU law in EU-financed measures in the Ríos Guadalhorce, Fahalas and Pereilas special area of conservation
qt: to the Commission Jaume Asens Llodrà (Verts/ALE) Subject:

In 2023, the Regional Government of Andalusia approved, drawing on EU financing, a restoration project in the Ríos Guadalhorce, Fahalas and Pereilas special area of conservation (SAC). However, it included measures involving using heavy machinery in the riverbed, presented as ‘cleaning’ work, without sufficient assessment of their effects on the Natura 2000 network. Since May 2026, excavators contracted by the regional Ministry of Agriculture have been destroying river habitats in a number of hectares in the municipality of Cártama (Málaga), at the height of breeding season for some endangered species. The measures are affecting species of Community interest and vulnerable species, such as the southern Iberian spined loach, southern straight-mouth nase, the orange-spotted emerald dragonfly (Oxygastra curtisii), the squacco heron and the osprey, all of which are listed in the SAC management plan. Those events could constitute an infringement of the EU directives on environmental assessment, habitats, water, flood risks and bird conservation. Given this state of affairs: 1.
What urgent measures will the Commission take to prevent irreversible damage?
Will the Commission consider launching an infringement procedure against Spain?
Was EU financing conditional on ensuring that habitats and species were protected and that a proper environmental assessment was carried out?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (15.9.2026) The Commission takes note of the concerns about the potential impact of the project on the Ríos Guadalhorce, Fahalas y Pereilas1 Natura 2000 site protected under the Habitats2 and Birds3 Directives. Under the Habitats Directive, projects not directly linked to site management must be subject to an assessment to ensure they do not adversely affect the integrity of the site4. Depending on their nature and scale, they may also fall under the Environmental Impact Assessment Directive5 and require assessment before development consent6. Member States are responsible for these assessments, which may be organised through joint or coordinated procedures. Without prejudice to its role as guardian of the Treaties, it is primarily for Member States to ensure compliance with EU law. In line with its strategic enforcement approach7, the Commission focuses its action on systemic and structural issues. Individual alleged cases of non-compliance, like this one, are more effectively addressed through national means, including national courts. Based on the available evidence, the Commission could not identify a breach of EU law in this particular case. As regards EU funding, all supported projects must comply with applicable EU and national law, including the EU environmental law8. If a project supported by the European Regional Development Fund (ERDF)9 may affect the environment or a Natura 2000 site, it must be subject to relevant procedures10. After consulting the Managing Authority of the ERDF in Spain, the Commission was informed that the projects have not received such support. As for

E-10-2026-003029.t: Urgent appeal for the release of Dr Hussam Abu Safiya
qt: to the Commission Annalisa Corrado (S&D), Per Clausen (The Left), Kateřina Konečná (NI), Sandro Ruotolo (S&D), Ana Miranda Paz (Verts/ALE), Marco Tarquinio (S&D), Marta Temido (S&D), Rudi Kennes (The Left), Alessandra Moretti (S&D), Mounir Satouri (Verts/ALE), Maria Zacharia (NI), Marc Botenga (The Left), Laura Ballarín Cereza (S&D), Ilaria Salis (The Left), Brando Benifei (S&D), Cecilia Strada (S&D), Barry Andrews (Renew), César Luena (S&D) Subject:

Palestinian paediatrician Dr Hussam Abu Safiya, former director of Kamal Adwan Hospital in Gaza, has been arbitrarily detained by the Israeli authorities since 27 December 2024, without charge or trial. According to his lawyer, Amnesty International1 and the United Nations2, he has been subjected to prolonged solitary confinement, torture, ill-treatment and deprivation of medical care. His current condition has raised serious concerns for his survival. The UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention has called for his immediate release. His case forms part of the broader context of the Israeli Government’s grave violations of international humanitarian law. The latest report3 of the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry documents systematic violence against children in the Gaza Strip, with more than 20 000 children deliberately killed between 7 October 2023 and 7 October 2025, corroborating concerns repeatedly raised by Dr Abu Safiya himself. In view of the above, could the Commission clarify: 1.
What initiatives it has undertaken to secure the immediate release of Dr Abu Safiya and ensure respect for his fundamental rights?

Whether it intends to urge the Council to implement the suspension of the EU-Israel Association Agreement and support an embargo on arms exports to Israel in light of the violations documented by the United Nations?

at: (English version) to the Commission Annalisa Corrado (S&D), Per Clausen (The Left), Kateřina Konečná (NI), Sandro Ruotolo (S&D), Ana Miranda Paz (Verts/ALE), Marco Tarquinio (S&D), Marta Temido (S&D), Rudi Kennes (The Left), Alessandra Moretti (S&D), Mounir Satouri (Verts/ALE), Maria Zacharia (NI), Marc Botenga (The Left), Laura Ballarín Cereza (S&D), Ilaria Salis (The Left), Brando Benifei (S&D), Cecilia Strada (S&D), Barry Andrews (Renew), César Luena (S&D) (16 July 2026) Subject: Urgent appeal for the release of Dr Hussam Abu Safiya Palestinian paediatrician Dr Hussam Abu Safiya, former director of Kamal Adwan Hospital in Gaza, has been arbitrarily detained by the Israeli authorities since 27 December 2024, without charge or trial. According to his lawyer, Amnesty International (1) and the United Nations (2), he has been subjected to prolonged solitary confinement, torture, ill-treatment and deprivation of medical care. His current condition has raised serious concerns for his survival. The UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention has called for his immediate release. His case forms part of the broader context of the Israeli Government’s grave violations of international humanitarian law. The latest report (3) of the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry documents systematic violence against children in the Gaza Strip, with more than 20 000 children deliberately killed between 7 October 2023 and 7 October 2025, corroborating concerns repeatedly raised by Dr Abu Safiya himself. In view of the above, could the Commission clarify: 1.

Whether it intends to urge the Council to implement the suspension of the EU-Israel Association Agreement and support an embargo on arms exports to Israel in light of the violations documented by the United Nations?

(2 September 2026) The EU has been following closely the case, and it has been raised with the Israeli authorities and called on Israel to ensure full respect for fair trial guarantees and prisoners’ rights in the case of Dr Abu Safiya and other detained Palestinians, including detained medical personnel. The EU acknowledges Israel's legitimate security concerns and its right to investigate credible allegations of involvement with terrorist organisations, while recalling that such investigations should be conducted in full compliance with Israel's obligations under international humanitarian law and international human rights law, including with regard to the treatment of detainees and due process guarantees. The decision on a possible suspension of the EU-Israel Association Agreement (1) requires unanimity in the Council. In light of the situation in Gaza and the West Bank discussions have continued in the Council among Member States on possible options. The competent authorities of Member States take final decision whether to authorise or deny an individual export or transit license of military equipment, in accordance with the said legal frameworks. Member States are solely responsible to ensure compliance with applicable laws, including the Common Position and the ATT.

E-10-2026-003028.t: The EU’s strategic partnership with Azerbaijan: compatibility with EU Treaty obligations
qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Maria Zacharia (NI) Subject:

Articles 2, 3(5), 18 and 21 of the Treaty on European Union (TEU) establish binding obligations requiring the EU’s external action to be guided by human rights, the rule of law and consistency between its values and external policies. Under Article 18 TEU, the VicePresident of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy (VP/HR) must ensure that the common foreign and security policy (CFSP) complies with those obligations. Nevertheless, the EU continues to deepen its strategic partnership with Azerbaijan through cooperation in energy, transport and Global Gateway connectivity, while Armenian detainees, including former political representatives of Nagorno-Karabakh, remain imprisoned amid concerns regarding arbitrary detention, fair trial guarantees and fundamental rights. The strengthening of EU-Azerbaijan relations, without any suspension, restriction, conditionality or concrete consequence linked to those detentions, raises serious questions as to whether the EU’s external action complies with the Treaties. 1.

On what legal basis does the VP/HR consider that the continuation and deepening of the EU’s strategic partnership with Azerbaijan is compatible with the obligations laid down in Articles 2, 3(5), 18 and 21 TEU?

What restrictive measure, suspension, conditionality or concrete consequence has the EU imposed on Azerbaijan in response to the continued detention of Armenian prisoners? If none, how is that consistent with the Treaties?
Has the VP/HR sought or obtained a formal legal assessment confirming that the EU’s policy towards Azerbaijan complies with those obligations? If so, will she make it public?
at: (English version) to the Vice-President of the Commission/High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Maria Zacharia (NI) (16 July 2026) Subject: The EU’s strategic partnership with Azerbaijan: compatibility with EU Treaty obligations Articles 2, 3(5), 18 and 21 of the Treaty on European Union (TEU) establish binding obligations requiring the EU’s external action to be guided by human rights, the rule of law and consistency between its values and external policies. Under Article 18 TEU, the Vice-President of the Commission/High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy (VP/HR) must ensure that the common foreign and security policy (CFSP) complies with those obligations. Nevertheless, the EU continues to deepen its strategic partnership with Azerbaijan through cooperation in energy, transport and Global Gateway connectivity, while Armenian detainees, including former political representatives of Nagorno-Karabakh, remain imprisoned amid concerns regarding arbitrary detention, fair trial guarantees and fundamental rights. The strengthening of EU-Azerbaijan relations, without any suspension, restriction, conditionality or concrete consequence linked to those detentions, raises serious questions as to whether the EU’s external action complies with the Treaties. 1. On what legal basis does the VP/HR consider that the continuation and deepening of the EU’s strategic partnership with Azerbaijan is compatible with the obligations laid down in Articles 2, 3(5), 18 and 21 TEU? 2. What restrictive measure, suspension, conditionality or concrete consequence has the EU imposed on Azerbaijan in response to the continued detention of Armenian prisoners? If none, how is that consistent with the Treaties? 3. Has the VP/HR sought or obtained a formal legal assessment confirming that the EU’s policy towards Azerbaijan complies with those obligations? If so, will she make it public? (25 August 2026) The principle of the rule of law and the protection of human rights form an integral part of the EU’s relationship with Azerbaijan, which is based on the EU-Azerbaijan Partnership and Cooperation Agreement (1). The EU regularly raises these issues with the Azerbaijani authorities, including in discussions on the future development of the relationship. The EU has closely followed the trials of Karabakh Armenians in Azerbaijan and has emphasised the importance of ensuring due process, the right to a fair trial and appropriate detention conditions, in line with Azerbaijan’s international obligations. The EU has also encouraged Azerbaijan and Armenia to address all outstanding humanitarian issues in the context of their bilateral normalisation process, including through confidence-building measures. Following the initialling of the bilateral peace treaty between Azerbaijan and Armenia on 8 August 2025, the parties have made important progress towards achieving lasting peace. This progress has already resulted in several tangible steps to the benefit of both countries, including the release of detainees and the lifting of trade and transit restrictions. The EU strongly supports this process and remains ready to continue assisting the parties in their efforts.

E-10-2026-003027.t: Humanitarian situation of Sahrawi refugees, inadequate EU humanitarian assistance and the growing water crisis in the refugee camps
qt: to the Commission Pernando Barrena Arza (The Left), Isabel Serra Sánchez (The Left), Irene Montero (The Left), Catarina Martins (The Left), Martin Günther (The Left), Jaume Asens Llodrà (Verts/ALE), Estrella Galán (The Left), Diana Riba i Giner (Verts/ALE), Jonas Sjöstedt (The Left), Vicent Marzà Ibáñez (Verts/ALE), Vladimir Prebilič (Verts/ALE), Oihane Agirregoitia Martínez (Renew), Per Clausen (The Left), Rudi Kennes (The Left), Ana Miranda Paz (Verts/ALE), Andreas Schieder (S&D), João Oliveira (The Left), Lynn Boylan (The Left), Merja Kyllönen (The Left), Cecilia Strada (S&D), Leire Pajín (S&D), Hannes Heide (S&D), Ilaria Salis (The Left) Subject:

For nearly five decades, around 170 000 Sahrawi refugees in the Tindouf camps have relied entirely on humanitarian assistance while facing worsening food insecurity, inadequate access to essential services and a growing water crisis. Despite increasing humanitarian needs, the Commission’s funding has remained largely unchanged since 2016, and significant funding gaps continue to prevent humanitarian organisations from meeting basic needs. In light of the above: 1.

How does the Commission assess the current humanitarian situation in the Sahrawi refugee camps, and does it intend to strengthen EU humanitarian assistance, including funding for food security, nutrition, healthcare and sustainable access to safe drinking water infrastructure, in order to address the growing needs of, and ensure adequate support for, the refugee population?

How does the Commission intend to ensure that the protracted humanitarian crisis affecting the Sahrawi refugees receives adequate and sustained attention within the EU’s humanitarian response and international donor coordination efforts?

Does the Commission intend to renew the agreement between its Directorate-General for European Civil Protection and Humanitarian Aid Operations and the World Food Programme to ensure the continuation of essential food assistance for Sahrawi refugees?
at: (English version) to the Commission Pernando Barrena Arza (The Left), Isabel Serra Sánchez (The Left), Irene Montero (The Left), Catarina Martins (The Left), Martin Günther (The Left), Jaume Asens Llodrà (Verts/ALE), Estrella Galán (The Left), Diana Riba i Giner (Verts/ALE), Jonas Sjöstedt (The Left), Vicent Marzà Ibáñez (Verts/ALE), Vladimir Prebilič (Verts/ALE), Oihane Agirregoitia Martínez (Renew), Per Clausen (The Left), Rudi Kennes (The Left), Ana Miranda Paz (Verts/ALE), Andreas Schieder (S&D), João Oliveira (The Left), Lynn Boylan (The Left), Merja Kyllönen (The Left), Cecilia Strada (S&D), Leire Pajín (S&D), Hannes Heide (S&D), Ilaria Salis (The Left) (16 July 2026) Subject: Humanitarian situation of Sahrawi refugees, inadequate EU humanitarian assistance and the growing water crisis in the refugee camps For nearly five decades, around 170 000 Sahrawi refugees in the Tindouf camps have relied entirely on humanitarian assistance while facing worsening food insecurity, inadequate access to essential services and a growing water crisis. Despite increasing humanitarian needs, the Commission’s funding has remained largely unchanged since 2016, and significant funding gaps continue to prevent humanitarian organisations from meeting basic needs. In light of the above: 1.

How does the Commission assess the current humanitarian situation in the Sahrawi refugee camps, and does it intend to strengthen EU humanitarian assistance, including funding for food security, nutrition, healthcare and sustainable access to safe drinking water infrastructure, in order to address the growing needs of, and ensure adequate support for, the refugee population?

How does the Commission intend to ensure that the protracted humanitarian crisis affecting the Sahrawi refugees receives adequate and sustained attention within the EU’s humanitarian response and international donor coordination efforts?

Does the Commission intend to renew the agreement between its Directorate-General for European Civil Protection and Humanitarian Aid Operations and the World Food Programme to ensure the continuation of essential food assistance for Sahrawi refugees?

(27 August 2026) The EU has been a leading humanitarian donor to the Sahrawi refugee population in Algeria since 1993. It continues to provide humanitarian assistance based on needs and in line with humanitarian principles, addressing essential sectors, including food assistance, nutrition, health, water, sanitation and hygiene. The Commission is pursuing a strategic approach that combines immediate humanitarian relief with efforts to strengthen resilience and reduce vulnerabilities over time, including support for more sustainable water solutions, improved service delivery, while fully respecting the humanitarian character of the response. The Commission will continue to monitor the humanitarian situation closely and to adapt its assistance, within available resources, according to evolving needs and the operational assessments of its humanitarian partners and its teams on the ground. The level and scope of EU support are decided through annual humanitarian programming and remain subject to identified needs, partner capacity and budgetary availability. As regards sustained attention to this protracted crisis, the Commission remains engaged with key humanitarian partners, including UN agencies, international organisations and non-governmental organisations, as well as with Member States and other donors. It also continues to advocate for adequate and predictable funding for forgotten and underfunded crises. The Commission values the longstanding role of the World Food Programme (WFP) in delivering food assistance in the camps and will consider support for WFP food assistance within its regular humanitarian decision-making, alongside efforts to promote the continuity of life-saving assistance for Sahrawi refugees.

E-10-2026-003026.t: EU response to United Arab Emirates’ support to the Rapid Support Forces in Sudan
qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Catarina Vieira (Verts/ALE), Marit Maij (S&D), Nela Riehl (Verts/ALE), JanChristoph Oetjen (Renew) Subject:

In addition to evidence of the role of the United Arab Emirates (UAE) in providing weapons and military equipment to the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in Sudan, several credible sources1, including a recent Human Rights Watch (HRW) report2, have reported that UAEbased businesses are involved in hiring and transporting Colombian private military contractors. HRW documented their transit via UAE military facilities and presence in ElFasher, during which these forces conducted a campaign which bore ‘hallmarks of genocide’3. 1.

Has the European External Action Service (EEAS) documented the role of UAE-based company Global Security Services Group (GSSG) and its CEO Mohamed Hamdan alZaabi and other entities in hiring and transporting foreign fighters to support the RSF, with a view to proposing to the Council their listing under its Sudan sanction regime?

What is the EEAS and Commission’s assessment of the UAE’s or UAE-based entities’ role in the provision of weapons and military equipment4 to the RSF – including Bulgarian-made ammunitions5 and French-made equipment6?

Has the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy assessed whether the UAE’s actions are in breach of criteria under the EU Common Position 2008/944/CFSP with a view to proposing an EU arms embargo on the UAE or any other appropriate action?

https://thesentry.org/reports/sudan-mercenaries-rsf-uae-bureaucrat/. https://www.hrw.org/report/2026/05/25/from-bogota-to-el-fasher/the-uaes-role-in-the-deployment-ofcolombian-fighters. 3 https://www.ohchr.org/en/documents/thematic-reports/ahrc6177-sudan-hallmarks-genocide-el-fasherreport-independent. 4 provision of weapons and military equipment. 5 https://www.france24.com/en/africa/20250417-investigation-european-weapons-sudan-part-1-mortarshells-bulgaria. 6 https://www.amnesty.org/en/latest/news/2024/11/sudan-french-manufactured-weapons-systemidentified-in-conflict-new-investigation/. 1 2
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (18.8.2026) The EU has reiterated on multiple occasions that the primary responsibility for ending the conflict in Sudan lies with the leadership of both the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), and those supporting these entities. The EU has addressed the situation in Sudan during its political dialogues and exchanges with the United Arab Emirates (UAE) at various levels. The EU has raised concerns about the reported UAE support to the RSF and will continue engaging with the UAE, which is a member of the Quad (together with United States of America, Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and Egypt) on Sudan, to reach a sustainable ceasefire and a peaceful resolution of the conflict. Enhanced political dialogue is a key tenet of the future Strategic Partnership Agreement, reflecting the shared commitment to promoting regional stability and prosperity. The EU is closely monitoring the actions of all parties to the conflict. The High Representative/Vice President will continue to engage with Member States on the available options under the EU restrictive measures (sanctions). The EU has urged all external actors to take necessary measures to end the sale or supply of arms and related material to all parties as per the arms embargo established by the UN Security Council Resolutions 1556 (2004) and 1591 (2005). The EU has transposed the UN embargo by prohibiting the sale, supply, transfer or export of arms and related materiel of all types to the entire territory of Sudan. The implementation is the responsibility of Member States. In the Council Conclusions on Sudan of October 2025, the EU urged all external actors directly or indirectly supplying arms, financial support or support of any other kind to the warring parties to immediately cease such support1.

E-10-2026-003024.t: Driver monitoring systems and the risk of privacy protections being circumvented
qt: to the Commission Stanisław Tyszka (ESN) Subject:

From 7 July 2026, most new cars, buses and lorries sold in the EU must be fitted with a driver distraction warning system. This system typically uses a camera to monitor the driver’s face and gaze. Article 6(3) of Regulation (EU) 2019/2144 requires that the data used for the warning function must remain within the vehicle, must not be transferred to other entities and must be deleted without delay. However, the Commission has clarified that this protection applies only to the warning function. The same camera may be used for other functions, provided they comply with the GDPR (Q&A on ADDW, document 64714). 1.
Can a manufacturer circumvent these safeguards by using the same data for another function, and does the Commission intend to close this loophole?

Before a new model is authorised for sale, checks are carried out to ensure that the system correctly alerts the driver. Who checks, and how, that the images and other data from the camera are not recorded or transmitted to the manufacturer or other parties?

Does the legislation require a further independent inspection in the event that the manufacturer introduces new ways of using the camera or transmitting data via a remote update after the vehicle has been sold? If not, how does the Commission intend to protect drivers from changes to the rules after they have purchased a car?
at: (English version) to the Commission Stanisław Tyszka (ESN) (16 July 2026) Subject: Driver monitoring systems and the risk of privacy protections being circumvented From 7 July 2026, most new cars, buses and lorries sold in the EU must be fitted with a driver distraction warning system. This system typically uses a camera to monitor the driver’s face and gaze. Article 6(3) of Regulation (EU) 2019/2144 requires that the data used for the warning function must remain within the vehicle, must not be transferred to other entities and must be deleted without delay. However, the Commission has clarified that this protection applies only to the warning function. The same camera may be used for other functions, provided they comply with the GDPR (Q&A on ADDW, document 64714). 1. Can a manufacturer circumvent these safeguards by using the same data for another function, and does the Commission intend to close this loophole? 2. Before a new model is authorised for sale, checks are carried out to ensure that the system correctly alerts the driver. Who checks, and how, that the images and other data from the camera are not recorded or transmitted to the manufacturer or other parties? 3. Does the legislation require a further independent inspection in the event that the manufacturer introduces new ways of using the camera or transmitting data via a remote update after the vehicle has been sold? If not, how does the Commission intend to protect drivers from changes to the rules after they have purchased a car? (7 September 2026) Under Regulation (EU) 2023/2590 (1), Advanced Driver Drowsiness and Warning systems may share hardware components with other vehicle functions. However, the regulation prohibits using systems that would enable the unique identification of the driver or the processing of biometric data. To prevent any circumvention of these safeguards, the system is required to operate as a closed-loop system. This means that data may be processed exclusively for the purpose of detecting driver drowsiness or inattention, must be deleted immediately thereafter, and must not be made accessible to manufacturers or other third parties. National type-approval authorities and the technical services verify compliance with these privacy safeguards in the context of the type-approval process. This assessment is based on a mandatory technical documentation package to be submitted by the manufacturer, which must describe the system architecture, the relevant inputs and the metrics used by the system. The manufacturer is required to notify the approval authority of any significant change made after market introduction. Manufacturers must also comply with the requirements laid down in UN Regulation No 156 (2) on software updates. Continued compliance is monitored by market surveillance authorities, which may carry out checks and require corrective measures.
