E-10-2026-003023.t: Chat Control: scanning of private messages
qt: to the Commission Stanisław Tyszka (ESN) Subject:

On 9 July 2026, Parliament failed to reject the Council’s position extending the ‘Chat Control 1.0’ system, established by Regulation (EU) 2021/1232, until 2028. It adopted amendments excluding end-to-end encrypted communications. The scanning of all other communications was retained on a voluntary basis for the provider, but not for the user, whose communications are analysed without any suspicion of a crime. In Opinion 7/2026 concerning this system, the European Data Protection Supervisor highlighted the lack of a clear legal basis and safeguards against blanket scanning. ‘Chat Control 2.0’ (COM(2022) 209) -– which will feature orders to detect content – is currently in the pipeline. 1.

How does the Commission explain the compatibility of scanning the communications of persons not under suspicion with Articles 7, 8 and 52(1) of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, as well as the case-law of the CJEU concerning the limits of general and indiscriminate interference with the confidentiality of communications – in particular the Digital Rights Ireland and La Quadrature du Net judgments – especially given that the scanning covers the content of messages?

On what evidence does the Commission base the effectiveness and proportionality of Chat Control 1.0, given that in report COM(2025) 740 it acknowledged that the data do not provide grounds to determine whether the system strikes a balance between combating child sexual exploitation and protecting users’ rights?

Will the Commission withdraw or amend the Chat Control 2.0 proposal so as to rule out the mass scanning of the communications of persons not under suspicion, interference with end-to-end encryption and the scanning of messages on the user’s device before they are encrypted?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (18.9.2026) The Commission Proposal for a Regulation to prevent and combat child sexual abuse1 (‘the proposal’) is equipped with numerous specific protections and safeguards for the fundamental rights of the affected individuals. The proposal relies on a thorough and publicly available impact assessment2, demonstrating that it strives to achieve a fair balance in the protection of the rights to respect privacy and protection of personal data and the rights of the child. In particular, detection orders are envisaged as measures of last resort when prevention measures are insufficient. They are targeted only at services that are at risk, and at specific users or groups of users, where possible, and are issued by a judicial or independent administrative authority balancing all the rights at stake and following a thorough assessment of their necessity and proportionality. The proposal neither requires nor allows the indiscriminate scanning of private communications. The implementation report3 finds that voluntary detection under Regulation (EU) 2021/12324 made a significant contribution to child protection: available data show that thousands of children were identified and millions of images and videos were removed from circulation, reducing secondary victimisation. The Commission considers that the evidence supports the proportionality of the temporary and strictly limited regime, which remains justified to avoid legal gaps while negotiations on the proposed long-term Regulation continue. The Commission will continue to support interinstitutional negotiations. The legislative process has advanced substantially, and the Commission is not aware of any reasons that would warrant withdrawing the proposal.

1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex:52022PC0209. 2 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A52022SC0209. 3 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex:52025DC0740. 4 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2021/1232/oj/eng.

E-10-2026-003022.t: European Health Data Space – patient protection and implementation costs
qt: to the Commission Stanisław Tyszka (ESN) Subject:

Regulation (EU) 2025/327 on the European Health Data Space provides for the extensive use of medical data, including for research, statistics and the development of new technologies. At the same time, its implementation will require significant investment in national IT systems, cybersecurity and administration. With that in mind: 1.

How will the Commission ensure that patients’ right to object to the secondary use of their data is simple, effective and easily accessible, and that exceptions to this right do not lead to restrictions being effectively imposed on it?

Does the Commission have a detailed estimate of the costs of implementing the European Health Data Space (EHDS) for Poland, including the costs incurred by hospitals, clinics and public administration, and what proportion of these expenses can be covered by EU funds?

Why is a comprehensive evaluation of the functioning of the Regulation not foreseen until 2035, and does the Commission intend to carry out an earlier evaluation covering costs, the effectiveness of data protection, security incidents and the impact of the new obligations on national healthcare systems?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (24.9.2026) Under Article 71 of Regulation (EU) 2025/327 on the European Health Data Space, (EHDS)1, Member States must provide ‘accessible and easily understandable’ mechanisms for natural persons to exercise their right to opt out from having their personal electronic health data being made available for secondary use. Member States may provide for exceptions to the right to opt out under limited circumstances restricted to cases where data access is requested by public bodies for critical public interest (e.g., health threats) and rigorous justification is required. These exceptions must in particular be necessary and proportionate, maintaining all safeguards of Chapter IV of the EHDS Regulation like re-identification prohibitions. The Commission has provided EU-wide cost estimates in the EHDS impact assessment accompanying its proposal2. While no estimate specific to Poland is available, implementation costs are expected to broadly scale with population, with some economies of scale (i.e. degressive costs). EU funding may support implementation through relevant Union programmes, such as the EU4Health programme, subject to their conditions. Pursuant to Better Regulation guidelines3, ex-post evaluation requires data on the application of the legislation over a period of at least three to four years, as results and impacts take time to materialise. Given the application timelines of the EHDS, an overall review is scheduled for 2035, and a targeted review, including on the opt out for secondary use mechanism, for 2033, in accordance with Article 102 of the EHDS Regulation.

E-10-2026-003021.t: Appointments of CREA Scientific Directors and compatibility with European research policies and merit-based recruitment principles
qt: to the Commission Nicola Zingaretti (S&D), Camilla Laureti (S&D) Subject:

Seventeen of Italy's most eminent researchers, including Nobel laureate Parisi, have signed a letter1 criticising the appointment of twelve scientific directors at CREA centres (Council for Agricultural Research and Economic Analysis) following a selection procedure, highlighting a lack of coherence between the selected candidates’ profiles and the research areas of the centres concerned, notably in the case of the Centre for Genomics and Bioinformatics. CREA receives extensive EU resources from Horizon Europe. It is also a holder of the HR Excellence in Research Award and has therefore undertaken, vis-à-vis the Commission, to apply the OTM-R principles set out in the European Charter for Researchers and the Code of Conduct for the Recruitment of Researchers, which the legislative act on the European Research Area (ERA) – due to be introduced in 2026 – aims to reinforce in a legally binding manner. In the light of the above, we ask the Commission: 1.

Does it consider that a selection procedure for the scientific leadership that results in the appointment of a candidate whose profile is not related to the centre’s field of activity is compatible with the OTM-R principles?

Will it take this issue into account in the forthcoming external evaluation of CREA under the Human Resources Strategy for Researchers (HRS4R), calling on CREA to address this issue in its OTM-R action plan?
Does it intend to check whether the scientific governance of the CREA centres involved in Horizon Europe projects guarantees adequate standards for the use of EU funds?
https://www.scienzainrete.it/articolo/crea-rischia-grave-perdita-di-autorevolezza-scientifica/2026-07-
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (25.9.2026) The appointment of a candidate whose profile does not correspond directly to the centre’s field of activity is not, in itself, incompatible with the Open, Transparent and Merit-Based Recruitment (OTM-R) principles under the European Charter for Researchers and the HR Excellence in Research Award1. OTM-R requires open, transparent and merit-based procedures, with clear and proportionate criteria applied objectively. Where these requirements are met, including publication of the criteria, a fair and documented assessment and a reasoned decision, such an appointment may be compatible with OTM-R, even if the candidate’s background differs from the centre’s traditional disciplinary focus. Individual recruitment cases fall outside the scope of the HR Excellence in Research Award assessment2. However, if the issues raised point to broader shortcomings, assessors may recommend measures in CREA’s3 OTM-R, action plan, and its internal HRS4R4. This would not constitute a judgement on an individual appointment but would aim to strengthen CREA’s alignment with OTM-R principles and the Award requirements. 1 OTM-R (Open, Transparent and Merit-Based Recruitment) is a key part of the HR Excellence in Research

Award and, since 2018, a compulsory element of the process. It is embedded in the European Charter for Researchers (Annex II to Council Recommendation of 18 December 2023 on a European framework to attract and retain research, innovation and entrepreneurial talents in Europe, OJ C, C/2023/1640 https://eurlex.europa.eu/eli/C/2023/1640/oj/eng), especially Pillar 2, and it promotes fair, inclusive and merit-based recruitment. OTM-R requires transparent and objective assessment in both recruitment and career progression, without discrimination based on gender, age, ethnic origin, disability, religion, sexual orientation or social background. In line with the Charter, evaluation should consider not only publications and traditional academic metrics, but also diverse career paths, mobility, interdisciplinary experience, teaching, supervision, open science, teamwork, and societal impact. During the assessment phase in the frame of the HR Excellence in Research process, assessors review the organisation’s OTM-R policy and wider institutional approach, not individual recruitment cases. 2 The European Charter for Researchers sets out 20 principles defining the roles, responsibilities and entitlements of researchers, as well as those of their employers and funders. Organisations may voluntarily endorse the Charter and implement its principles in order to obtain and retain the HR Excellence in Research Award. The award recognises efforts to align human resources policies with the Charter, and regular assessments by experienced, independent experts help ensure continuous improvement. It is important to emphasise that the Charter is a non-binding EU recommendation under Article 288 TFEU. It sets out best practices but does not create legal obligations. This is true both for the original 2005 Charter & Code 2005/251/EC , OJ L 75, 22.3.2005 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:32005H0251 and for the updated 2023 version (Council Recommendation C/2023/1640 of 18 December 2023). Although recommendations allow EU institutions to suggest a course of action and influence national legislation and practice, they are not legally binding on those to whom they are addressed. In addition, while Open, Transparent and Merit-based Recruitment (OTM-R) is an explicit requirement in the documentation to be assessed, evaluators examine the organisation’s OTM-R policy and broader institutional approach, rather than individual recruitment cases. 3 Council for Agricultural Research and Economic Analysis (Consiglio per la ricerca in agricoltura e l'analisi dell'economia agraria) https//www.crea.gov.it. 4 Until 2024, the ’Human Resources Strategy for Researchers’ (HRS4R) referred to the process for implementing the European Charter for Researchers and the Code of Conduct for the Recruitment of Researchers (also known as the ‘Charter & Code’), which could lead to the HR Excellence in Research Award. Since 2024, the name of the process has been aligned with the name of the award, and the term HRS4R is no longer used to refer to the process; it is now called the HR Excellence in Research process. Today, HRS4R refers exclusively to an organisation’s internal HR strategy, setting out its plan for implementing the principles of the European Charter for Researchers.

Beneficiaries in Horizon Europe (HE) projects must comply with the HE legal framework as set out in the HE Framework Programme5 and the respective HE grant agreement6. This includes, inter alia, compliance with the highest standards of ethical principles and research integrity and any relevant EU, national and international law (see Art. 19 of the HE Regulation). Under the grant agreement, the granting authority may, where appropriate, conduct checks, reviews, audits and investigations and take appropriately action if noncompliance is established.
5 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2021/695/oj/eng. 6 Horizon Europe Model Grant Agreement, in particular Annex 5, https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-
tenders/opportunities/docs/2021-2027/common/agr-contr/general-mga_horizon-euratom_en.pdf.

E-10-2026-003020.t: Imports of microchips that are vital for AI development
qt: to the Commission Fernand Kartheiser (NI) Subject:

In January 2025, the US decided to restrict its exports of microchips that are essential for AI development. The decision applied to a number of countries, including Luxembourg, Poland and Portugal, and is therefore having an adverse effect on the smooth functioning of the internal market. It looks likely that similar decisions will be taken against Spain, for political reasons. 1.

How does the Commission respond to such decisions with a view to safeguarding the internal market and the interests of all the Member States, and what is the current state of play regarding microchips?
What stage is the EU at both industrially (investment in microchips, and manufacturing facilities in particular) and with regard to legislation (implementation of the Chips Act)?
How is the Commission intending to secure Europe’s supply of the rare earths that are vital in this area, in particular germanium and gallium?
at: (English version) to the Commission Fernand Kartheiser (NI) (16 July 2026) Subject: Imports of microchips that are vital for AI development In January 2025, the US decided to restrict its exports of microchips that are essential for AI development. The decision applied to a number of countries, including Luxembourg, Poland and Portugal, and is therefore having an adverse effect on the smooth functioning of the internal market. It looks likely that similar decisions will be taken against Spain, for political reasons. 1. How does the Commission respond to such decisions with a view to safeguarding the internal market and the interests of all the Member States, and what is the current state of play regarding microchips? 2. What stage is the EU at both industrially (investment in microchips, and manufacturing facilities in particular) and with regard to legislation (implementation of the Chips Act)? 3. How is the Commission intending to secure Europe’s supply of the rare earths that are vital in this area, in particular germanium and gallium? (7 September 2026) The Commission engaged with the US at political and technical levels on the US AI Diffusion Rule (1) and, more broadly, the EU’s exposure to third-country measures affecting access to advanced semiconductors and AI technologies. Following the rescission of the Rule in May 2025, the Commission continues to monitor broader challenges in this area. The Commission is taking actions to reduce strategic dependencies, strengthen industrial capacity, and address distortions through policy actions such as those under the Economic Security Strategy (2) and the Foreign Subsidies Regulation (3). The Chips Act (4) has been successful and has delivered concrete results such as over EUR 52 billion in public and private investments across the semiconductor value chain. To date, 18 State aid measures to support manufacturing capacity have been approved. The EU has launched five pilot lines to support the development and industrial deployment of next-generation chips. Competence centres have been established in all Member States to give companies access to expertise, training, testing and experimentation facilities. The Commission has recently proposed the Chips Act 2.0 (5) to further strengthen the EU’s semiconductor ecosystem, notably by reinforcing design capabilities and expanding capacities for mature and advanced semiconductors. The Critical Raw Materials Act (CRMA) (6) sets 2030 benchmarks for strategic raw materials, such as germanium and gallium, to secure and diversify their supply, among other actions, by selecting strategic projects (7). The RESourceEU Action Plan (8) further accelerates the achievement of the CRMA objectives.

E-10-2026-003019.t: Cumulative burden of CBAM and steel tariffs, and lack of transparency regarding quotas
qt: to the Commission Fernand Kartheiser (NI) Subject:

With regard to the Commission’s reply of 26 May 2026 (E-001234/20261): it is clear that the EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) and steel tariffs are two distinct measures. However, the significant additional burden on small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) arises from the simultaneous application of CBAM and steel tariffs. This was precisely the focus of my question, rather than the legal purpose of the individual instruments. 1.
Given this cumulative effect on the same import transaction, what specific mechanism does the Commission intend to use to avoid the double burden of CBAM and steel tariffs on SMEs?
In the light of this combined burden and the specific proposals submitted to the Commission to avoid it, why do SMEs remain subject to this burden, rather than being explicitly exempted from it?

The new country-specific quotas2 have led to significant cuts for some origins and products; in some cases, only 25 % of the quantities still available under the safeguard measure remain. Why have cuts in some categories been so disproportionate that they correspond neither to the 2013 level nor to the market share for 2022-2024?
https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/E-10-2026-001234_EN.html. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202601457.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.9.2026) The EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM)1 and Regulation (EU) 2026/1384 (‘the Steel Regulation’)2 are two distinct measures with different policy objectives and legal basis. Hence, these two instruments apply independently from one another to EU companies, including small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). The Commission is closely monitoring the implementation of both the Steel Regulation and CBAM. Please note that the CBAM simplification provides that importers with annual CBAMcovered imports of up to 50 tonnes will fall outside the scope of CBAM. Hence, the vast majority of EU small importers will not be subject to CBAM obligations. At the same time, as SMEs represent a significant share of EU operators active in the steel sector, it is not possible to exempt them from the application of the Steel Regulation. This would otherwise undermine the effectiveness of the Steel Regulation. The tariff-rate quotas (TRQs) made available in the EU steel market by the Steel Regulation were calculated by taking as a reference the market shares of the imports into the EU in 2013 for the overall consumption in the EU steel market in 2024. 2024 was the latest year for which complete data was available. The total TRQs volumes was then subdivided in 30 product categories based on the share of imports of each product category over the period 2022-2024. The TRQs for specific countries were calculated on the basis of a common methodology rooted in several criteria, including the average 2022-2024 imports and additional TRQs made available to preferential partners of the EU. This explains the different levels of TRQs across different countries compared to average 2022-2024 imports.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2023/956/2025-10-20. 2 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2026/1384/oj/eng.

E-10-2026-003018.t: European presence in the field of artificial intelligence
qt: to the Commission Fernand Kartheiser (NI) Subject:

The European Union’s Artificial Intelligence (AI) Act has been heavily criticised for the legal constraints it places on free scientific research. As a result, there is a lack of investment in AI in the EU, and qualified AI personnel are leaving in droves, particularly to the United States. 1.
Is the Commission willing to review AI regulations to provide more flexibility for European research?
In view of the massive AI investment programmes being pursued by the US and China, how will the Commission make sure the EU once again becomes a key, indispensable technology player?
Given the significant amounts of stable and affordable energy needed to develop AI infrastructure, does the Commission intend to massively promote the deployment of nuclear energy in Europe?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (7.9.2026) The AI Act1 does not apply to AI systems or models developed and used exclusively for scientific research and development2, nor to AI research, testing or development activities before they are placed on the market or put into service3. The Commission is developing guidelines clarifying the scope of the exclusion. While the AI Omnibus recently entered into force4, the Digital Omnibus5 further aims to support scientific research and responsible AI development in the EU. The Commission considers AI as a strategic area for the EU’s competitiveness and technological sovereignty and launched several initiatives for the development of frontier AI models and systems as strategic assets for the EU and to support AI Science and the applications of AI in scientific domains6. The Commission continues to support the development and uptake of AI through EU-level actions on research, innovation, digital infrastructure and skills. The Commission recognises that AI infrastructure requires secure and affordable electricity and supports all zero- and low-carbon solutions that can help meet this need, including nuclear7, as reflected in the Small Modular Reactors Strategy8. For Member States choosing nuclear, the Commission’s role is to support the conditions under which it can contribute to common European objectives, notably decarbonisation, competitiveness and security of supply. EU AI policy also prioritises energy-efficient, sustainable data centres and their integration into the energy system9. Alongside clear incentives for the data centre sector to transition to a clean energy system, the proposal for the Cloud and AI Development Act10 also promotes data centres’ on-site generation and storage of clean energy.

1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj/eng. 2 Article 2(6) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689. 3 Article 2(8) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689. ‘Such activities shall be conducted in accordance with applicable

Union law. Testing in real world conditions shall not be covered by that exclusion’. 4 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex:52025PC0836. 5 https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/digital-omnibus-regulation-proposal. 6 European Frontier AI Initiative, European Strategy for AI in Science, and the Resource for AI Science in Europe (RAISE). 7 https://energy.ec.europa.eu/topics/nuclear-energy/nuclear-investment-needs_en. 8 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex:52026DC0117. 9 https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/cloud-and-ai-development-act. 10 https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/proposal-cloud-and-ai-development-act-cada.

qt: to the Commission Fernand Kartheiser (NI) Subject:

Artificial intelligence opens up many opportunities, though it brings with it new risks for our societies. The ethical aspect of the relationship between humans and AI must be at the forefront of technical and legal concerns. Several documented cases show that AI has been able to manipulate people, in order to achieve an expected result. 1.
Does the Commission intend to propose legislation to ensure that decisions made by AI always remain subject to human oversight?
Will it be established that humans will always be held responsible for decisions made with the help of AI?
How can legislation ensure that AI respects the common good and is free from any political or ideological bias?
at: (English version) to the Commission Fernand Kartheiser (NI) (16 July 2026) Subject: AI ethics Artificial intelligence opens up many opportunities, though it brings with it new risks for our societies. The ethical aspect of the relationship between humans and AI must be at the forefront of technical and legal concerns. Several documented cases show that AI has been able to manipulate people, in order to achieve an expected result. 1. Does the Commission intend to propose legislation to ensure that decisions made by AI always remain subject to human oversight? 2.
Will it be established that humans will always be held responsible for decisions made with the help of AI?
How can legislation ensure that AI respects the common good and is free from any political or ideological bias?

(7 September 2026) On 1 August 2024, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (the AI Act) (1) entered into force. The AI Act establishes harmonised rules to ensure a consistent, high level of protection of health, safety and fundamental rights in relation to AI in the EU. The AI Act follows a risk-based approach. AI systems considered particularly harmful or abusive, such as AI systems that deploy subliminal or purposefully manipulative or deceptive techniques or those that exploit vulnerabilities due to age, disability, or a specific social or economic situation, are prohibited. AI systems intended to be used in certain contexts which pose risks, amongst others, to health, safety or fundamental rights are classified as high-risk and subject to strict requirements, including human oversight and data quality enabling the detection, prevention and mitigation of bias. As regards the potential for political or ideological biases, providers of high-risk AI systems are required to detect, prevent and mitigate such biases if they are likely to affect the health, safety or fundamental rights of persons. Finally, certain AI systems are subject to transparency obligations, such as AI chatbots interacting with natural persons and AI systems that generate or manipulate content. The AI Act is designed as safety legislation, meaning that AI is treated as a product and only safe products are placed on the market or put into service; the AI Act does not establish a liability framework. Human oversight is a compliance requirement, not a liability rule, for providers of high-risk AI systems. The liability rules for products, including AI, are regulated by Member State law, which is required to transpose the Product Liability Directive (2).

E-10-2026-003016.t: Protecting consumers and competition during the transition to exclusively digital distribution of PlayStation console games
qt: to the Commission Tomáš Zdechovský (PPE) Subject:

Sony Interactive Entertainment has announced that, as of January 2028, it will cease production of physical discs for newly released PlayStation games. New titles will be available exclusively in digital format from the PlayStation Store. This move raises questions regarding consumer protection. Unlike a physical copy, which can be kept or resold, with digital games the consumer usually acquires only a licence. Access to the game may therefore be restricted under the terms of the licence or at the discretion of the platform operator. At the same time, the phasing out of physical games may restrict the second-hand market and competition among retailers, whilst strengthening Sony’s control over prices and distribution within a closed ecosystem. This situation is also the focus of the European Citizens’ Initiative ‘Stop Destroying Videogames’, to which the Commission has responded by stating that it does not currently plan to introduce an obligation to keep games playable after support has ended, and that it favours dialogue and voluntary standards. 1.
Does the Commission feel that the current EU rules provide sufficient protection for consumers purchasing digital games?
Will the Commission assess whether this distribution model could restrict competition or lead to the abuse of a dominant position?

How will it ensure that a voluntary approach guarantees consumers clear information on licensing, the duration of support and continued access to the game, and when will it consider introducing binding legislation?
at: (English version) to the Commission Tomáš Zdechovský (PPE) (16 July 2026) Subject: Protecting consumers and competition during the transition to exclusively digital distribution of PlayStation console games Sony Interactive Entertainment has announced that, as of January 2028, it will cease production of physical discs for newly released PlayStation games. New titles will be available exclusively in digital format from the PlayStation Store. This move raises questions regarding consumer protection. Unlike a physical copy, which can be kept or resold, with digital games the consumer usually acquires only a licence. Access to the game may therefore be restricted under the terms of the licence or at the discretion of the platform operator. At the same time, the phasing out of physical games may restrict the second-hand market and competition among retailers, whilst strengthening Sony’s control over prices and distribution within a closed ecosystem. This situation is also the focus of the European Citizens’ Initiative ‘Stop Destroying Videogames’, to which the Commission has responded by stating that it does not currently plan to introduce an obligation to keep games playable after support has ended, and that it favours dialogue and voluntary standards. 1.
Does the Commission feel that the current EU rules provide sufficient protection for consumers purchasing digital games?

2. Will the Commission assess whether this distribution model could restrict competition or lead to the abuse of a dominant position? 3. How will it ensure that a voluntary approach guarantees consumers clear information on licensing, the duration of support and continued access to the game, and when will it consider introducing binding legislation? (15 September 2026) EU consumer law does not prescribe how digital providers should supply their products, such as video games, which can be online or on a tangible data carrier. It protects consumers in all these supply modes. Digital content or service must be in conformity with the contractual stipulations and the consumer’s reasonable expectations, including as regards its continuity (1). Digital providers must also provide consumers with clear information before the conclusion of the contrac t (2). These EU instruments are transposed into national laws. Member States’ authorities and courts deal with their enforcement. The Commission has observed the changes in the distribution model of Sony Interactive Entertainment and is actively monitoring the market. Articles 101 and 102 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union prohibit anti-competitive agreements and the abuse of a dominant position. The application of these provisions depends on the specific facts and circumstances of each individual case. The Commission cannot, at this stage, take a position on whether investigative steps will be taken in this case. In its communication on the European Citizens’ Initiative Stop Destroying Videogame s (3), the Commission indicated that it does not envisage new legislation and explained the reasons, notably, the existing EU rules protecting consumer’s economic interests and providers’ intellectual property rights. The announced stakeholder exchanges towards a self-regulatory code of conduct will aim at improving the management of video games’ end-of-life and transparency to consumers, without prejudice to the application of the above-mentioned EU consumer rights.

Directive (EU) 2019/770, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2019/770/oj. Directive 2011/83/EU, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2011/83/oj. https://ec.europa.eu/transparency/documents-register/detail?ref=C(2026)4110&lang=en.

E-10-2026-003015.t: Venezuelan disaster: call for solidarity that delivers
qt: to the Commission Tiago Moreira de Sá (PfE), Kinga Gál (PfE), Hermann Tertsch (PfE), Jorge Martín Frías (PfE), Enikő Győri (PfE), Diana Iovanovici Şoşoacă (NI), Ľuboš Blaha (NI), Fernand Kartheiser (NI) Subject:

On 24 June 2026, two devastating earthquakes hit Venezuela, triggering a humanitarian disaster of great magnitude. With 119 Portuguese nationals and people of Portuguese descent already confirmed among the dead, not to mention those still missing, Europe’s response must be swift, robust and commensurate with the sheer scale of the disaster and the way in which it is unfolding on the ground. The Commission has activated the EU Civil Protection Mechanism and deployed the Copernicus emergency mapping service, but has announced just EUR 5 million in humanitarian aid to top up the EUR 52 million in regular aid already planned prior to the disaster. In light of the above: 1.

Can the Commission say precisely what emergency support the Commission has already mobilised for Venezuela, indicating the financial, human, logistical and technical resources deployed, and whether the EUR 5 million pledged are deemed sufficient given the scale of the disaster?

What type of assistance – for example, search-and-rescue operations, medical support, temporary accommodation, telecommunications, emergency mapping services and protection of the most vulnerable – is being provided on the ground?

What additional measures is the Commission planning, in cooperation with the Member States, to step up the humanitarian response and support the communities affected, and does it undertake to provide regular updates on the actual implementation and the transparent use of the aid deployed?
Supporters1
This question is supported by Members other than the authors: Nora Junco García (ECR), Diego Solier (ECR), Alvise Pérez (NI). 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (7.9.2026) In the immediate aftermath of the disaster, the EU Civil Protection Mechanism1 (UCPM) was activated on 25 June 2026, following the request for assistance from Venezuela. The Commission’s Emergency Response Coordination Centre (ERCC) coordinated with Member States and the Venezuelan authorities the delivery of assistance2. Around 750 responders and tonnes of relief items have been mobilised from 19 countries. This includes search and rescue, emergency medical teams, a telecommunication module, a structural engineering team, medicines, shelters among others. Final deliveries under the UCPM are being planned, after which the operation is expected to conclude3. The EU’s Copernicus satellite service4 provided emergency mapping to support operations on the ground. Under ReliefEU5, five Humanitarian Air Bridge flights have carried over 214 tonnes of emergency supplies, of which 57 tonnes were donated from EU stockpiles6. On 15 July 2026, the EU announced EUR 20 million in support for the earthquake response in Venezuela7. This adds to the EUR 5 million life-saving assistance already approved at the end of June 2026, and to the EUR 52 million allocated at the beginning of the year to respond to the humanitarian consequences of the socio-economic crisis in Venezuela8. EU-funded humanitarian assistance is needs-based and channelled through humanitarian partners, in accordance with the humanitarian principles. It is delivered within the framework of the established humanitarian coordination architecture, under the leadership of UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)9. The Commission will continue to keep the Member States and European Parliament updated.

1 https://civil-protection-humanitarian-aid.ec.europa.eu/what/civil-protection/eu-civil-protection-mechanism_en. 2 A European Civil Protection Team was deployed to strengthen coordination efforts on the ground - 10 experts,

1 ERCC Liaison Officer and 1 Rapid Response Coordinator. 3 UCPM assistance from Portugal and Greece. 4 https://mapping.emergency.copernicus.eu/activations/EMSR884/. 5 https://civil-protection-humanitarian-aid.ec.europa.eu/what/humanitarian-aid/reliefeu_en. 6 In addition, one information management officer, two logistics officers and one emergency medical team have been deployed with support from ReliefEU. 7 Comprising EUR 10 million in additional humanitarian funding to help the most affected communities and EUR 10 million, subject to approval by the Budgetary Authority, including to support the search and rescue, medical and other expert teams’ operation, as well as in-kind assistance; https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/mex_26_1621. 8 EUR 52 million represent the EU’s humanitarian response both inside and outside Venezuela. 9 The UN Humanitarian Coordinator and the internationally mandated coordination body.

qt: to the Commission Jonas Sjöstedt (The Left), Hanna Gedin (The Left) Subject:

The General Court of the European Union ruled in June 2026 that the manufacture of private jets cannot be excluded from a list of activities deemed to be environmentally sustainable, annulling the Commission’s 2023 decision to exclude aircraft for private or commercial business aviation from the sustainable finance taxonomy list, based on CO2 emissions per passenger kilometre compared with other modes of transport. The General Court stated that the Commission could not base its assessment on the criterion of the CO2 footprint per passenger kilometre, as this is not provided for in the Taxonomy Regulation and relates to the operation of aircraft rather than their manufacture. 1.
Does the Commission intend to appeal this ruling?
Is the Commission planning to update the Taxonomy Regulation to enable assessments to also be based on the operation of private jets, such as the CO2 footprint per passenger kilometre?
What other alternatives does the Commission have to close the loophole in the Taxonomy Regulation which has now been created through this ruling?
at: (English version) to the Commission Jonas Sjöstedt (The Left), Hanna Gedin (The Left) (16 July 2026) Subject: EU taxonomy and private jets The General Court of the European Union ruled in June 2026 that the manufacture of private jets cannot be excluded from a list of activities deemed to be environmentally sustainable, annulling the Commission’s 2023 decision to exclude aircraft for private or commercial business aviation from the sustainable finance taxonomy list, based on CO 2 emissions per passenger kilometre compared with other modes of transport. The General Court stated that the Commission could not base its assessment on the criterion of the CO2 footprint per passenger kilometre, as this is not provided for in the Taxonomy Regulation and relates to the operation of aircraft rather than their manufacture. 1.
Does the Commission intend to appeal this ruling?

2. Is the Commission planning to update the Taxonomy Regulation to enable assessments to also be based on the operation of private jets, such as the CO2 footprint per passenger kilometre? 3. What other alternatives does the Commission have to close the loophole in the Taxonomy Regulation which has now been created through this ruling? (7 September 2026) In the light of the sound reasoning of the General Court in its judgmen t (1), the Commission considers that an appeal would most probably not be successful. The judgment does not mean that private jets are automatically classified as environmentally sustainable under the EU Taxonomy. By annulling Section 3.21 of Annex I to Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2139 (2), the General Court removed the legal basis for reporting aircraft-manufacturing activities under that Section. The Commission will aim to reintroduce a new Section 3.21 as part of the ongoing revision of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2139 in a manner that complies with the General Court’s judgment and ensures that the criteria remain robust and consistent with the objectives of the Taxonomy Regulation. E-10-2026-003013.t: Fatal accidents at work as a result of the heatwave
qt: to the Commission Jonas Sjöstedt (The Left), Hanna Gedin (The Left) Subject:

Throughout Europe, records for high temperatures are being broken time and again, and many people are feeling the severe effects of the heat. It is a particular problem for those who have to work in the heat. Figures from the European Trade Union Confederation show that the number of deaths in European workplaces is rising in line with the increase in temperatures. Accidents at work increase by 7% when the temperature exceeds 30 degrees and by 15% at temperatures over 38 degrees. The Commission has adopted a ‘vision zero’ approach to workrelated deaths. This is a central plank of the EU’s strategic framework on health and safety at work for 2021-2027, which aims to eliminate fatal accidents at work in the EU. 1.
How is the Commission’s work on vision zero affected by the fact that more people are now dying at work in these hotter conditions?
What specific measures is the Commission taking to ensure that Member States achieve vision zero now that deaths are on the increase with extreme temperatures of over 38 degrees?

This is not a short-term problem: it will continue to get worse as greenhouse gas emissions change our climate. What is the Commission doing to ensure that Member States make efforts not only to cut emissions but also to mitigate the consequences of a hotter climate?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (26.8.2026) The data collection ‘The European Statistics on Accidents at Work’1 compiled by Eurostat, shows that the incidence rate of fatal work accidents in the EU-27 fell by nearly 30% between 2010 and 20232, the latest year for which data are currently available, although several of the final years of this period were among the hottest on record in Europe3. The EU has strong rules for addressing occupational safety and health (OSH) risks. In particular, the Framework Directive on Safety and Health at Work requires employers to assess and address all OSH risks, including heat-related risks4. In addition, the Commission and the European Agency for Safety and Health at Work provide guidance and practical tools to support the implementation of EU OSH legislation, including measures to address heat at work5.All policy activities of the Commission in the field of OSH contribute to the objective of zero work-related deaths, as set out in the EU Strategic Framework on Health and Safety at Work 2021–20276. The EU has put in place an ambitious legislative framework to reduce its net greenhouse gas emissions7. In addition, the Commission is currently developing a new European framework to strengthen climate resilience and preparedness across all levels of government and policy areas, which it expects to adopt during the 4th quarter of 2026. qt: to the Commission Francisco José Millán Mon (PPE), Gabriel Mato (PPE) Subject:

The Commission has recently acknowledged the lack of harmonised welfare rules for aquatic animals in the EU1. At the same time, ongoing work through the European Union Reference Centre for Animal Welfare for Aquatic Animals (EURCAW Aqua) and other scientific initiatives continues to advance technical knowledge on fish welfare indicators and assessment systems. In recent years, collaborative initiatives in several EU countries involving aquaculture stakeholders, scientists and other relevant actors have developed practical welfare guidelines2 and assessment tools for farmed fish. In Spain and Greece for example, multi-stakeholder welfare guidelines have provided valuable technical experience that could help inform future EU approaches in this field. We acknowledge that welfare needs vary across individual species, production systems and farm sizes. With this in mind: 1.

Does the Commission envisage further work towards the development and harmonisation of species-specific welfare indicators and welfare assessment criteria for farmed fish across the EU?
How will the Commission ensure that future trade relations with third countries do not disadvantage EU producers already investing in higher welfare standards?

At the same time, ongoing work through the European Union Reference Centre for Animal Welfare for Aquatic Animals (EURCAW Aqua) and other scientific initiatives continues to advance technical knowledge on fish welfare indicators and assessment systems. In recent years, collaborative initiatives in several EU countries involving aquaculture stakeholders, scientists and other relevant actors have developed practical welfare guidelines (2) and assessment tools for farmed fish. (24 August 2026) The Commission is focusing on improved implementation of the rules applicable to aquatic animals (1). The EU Reference Centre for Animal Welfare on aquatic animals supports Member States in carrying out official controls and work on animal welfare assessments. An external ongoing study on animal welfare indicators aims to develop a cohesive set of operational animal welfare indicators, with consensus from stakeholders. These indicators could be used to monitor animal welfare at farm, transport and slaughter and may be used for policy formulation, evaluation or operators’ own use. In addition, the European Partnership on Animal Health and Welfare (EUPAHW) (2), is advancing technologies and methods to improve animal welfare. ‘Good Husbandry Practices for aquaculture’ (3) and a ‘Code of good practices on fish welfare and fish welfare indicators’ (4) were developed, implementing the ‘Strategic guidelines for a more sustainable and competitive EU aquaculture for the period 2021 to 2030’ (5). The future policy agenda for aquaculture will continue action on aquatic animal welfare. Animal welfare is reflected in the EU’s trade policy, through dialogues and cooperation with trading partners, and where applicable animal-welfare related import requirements in full respect of EU’s international obligations. In its recent trade agreements, the EU has sought to include discipline on trade and sustainable management aquaculture, under which each Party commits to promoting the development of sustainable and responsible aquaculture, including in accordance with the Food and Organisation’s Guidelines for Sustainable Aquaculture.

E-10-2026-003010.t: Preventing the unwarranted classification of linear and logistic regression models as AI systems
qt: to the Commission Arba Kokalari (PPE), Axel Voss (PPE), Markus Ferber (PPE) Subject:

We are writing following continued discussions on whether linear and logistic regression models may be classified as AI systems under the AI Act. These models have been widely used in financial services for decades, are generally explainable and already subject to extensive financial services, consumer protection and data protection rules. Classifying linear and logistic regression models as AI would extend the scope of the AI Act to established statistical methods that do not carry the same risks, creating additional compliance and supervisory burdens without clear benefits. The Commission’s June 2025 Guidelines indicate that linear and logistic regression models fall outside the definition of an AI system. This is consistent with the positions taken by the European Central Bank and the European Insurance and Occupational Pensions Authority, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) approach with which the AI Act is aligned and the view supported by Member States in the AI Board subgroup on financial services. How will the Commission ensure that any future guidance remains consistent with its guidelines, established supervisory practice and the OECD approach?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (17.9.2026) Article 3(1) of the AI Act1 defines an AI system in a manner aligned with the approach of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development. Recital 12 of the AI Act clarifies that techniques that enable inference while building an AI system include machine learning (ML) approaches that learn from data how to achieve certain objectives. Systems based on linear or logistic regression use ML techniques. Their parameters are learned from their training data. The Commission considers these systems to fall outside the definition of an AI system where they meet the narrow conditions outlined in points 42 to 45 of the Guidelines on the AI system definition2. If such systems permit adjustments of their decision-making models in an intelligent way, they fall within that definition. For the financial sector, the AI Act classifies as high-risk AI systems that fall within the two use cases listed in point 5(b) and (c) of Annex III of the AI Act3. Such systems are subject to requirements under the AI Act regarding, inter alia, their design and use to mitigate potential risks to fundamental rights4. Nevertheless, no high-risk AI system placed on the market5 before 2 December 2027 will be subject to these requirements unless its design is significantly changed after this date. The Commission´s public consultation6 on the draft guidelines on the classification of highrisk AI systems included specific questions on the need to remove, adapt or add high-risk use cases to the list in Annex III of the AI Act. Findings will be published in a report pursuant to Article 112(1) of the AI Act. The Commission is working towards a simplified and proportionate approach for the application of the AI Act’s requirements to high-risk AI systems based on linear or logistic regression used in the financial sector that properly reflects those systems’ transparent and explainable nature.
1 Regulation (EU) 2024/1689. 2 C(2025) 5053 final. 3 That classification has been done even if the use cases in practice largely relied on systems based on linear or

logistic regression given their dependency on data and risks of biases. 4 In particular the right to non-discrimination, especially when trained on biased data sets. 5 The same applies to high-risk AI systems put into service before 2 December 2027. 6 https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/consultations/targeted-consultation-draft-guidelines-classification-highrisk-artificial-intelligence-systems.

E-10-2026-003009.t: Reforming European venture capital funds (EuVECA) to finance Europe’s start-ups and scale-ups
qt: to the Commission Arba Kokalari (PPE) Subject:
Reforming European venture capital funds (EuVECA) to finance Europe’s startups and scale-ups

European competitiveness is under pressure. The EU continues to lag behind the United States and China in economic growth, innovation financing and investment. The sense of urgency is especially acute for European start-ups and scale-ups, which too often lack access to the capital they need to grow, commercialise innovation and remain in Europe. Venture capital is essential to addressing these financing gaps and to completing the savings and investments union. The European venture capital market nevertheless remains far smaller than it could potentially be. This potential can be unlocked through a more integrated and proportional regulatory framework. The upcoming review of the European Venture Capital Fund (EuVECA) Regulation must therefore deliver meaningful reform. This should include substantially raising the threshold for qualifying EuVECA managers and indexing it to prevent its future irrelevance. The review should also simplify reporting and compliance requirements, remove unnecessary administrative burdens, and harmonise the treatment of non-EU country investments with the Alternative Investment Fund Managers Directive. What, then, are the Commission’s overall policy objectives for the EuVECA review, and will it commit to an ambitious reform that strengthens the role of venture capital in financing European growth by expanding access to capital for start-ups and scale-ups?
at: (English version) to the Commission Arba Kokalari (PPE) (16 July 2026) Subject: Reforming European venture capital funds (EuVECA) to finance Europe’s start-ups and scale-ups European competitiveness is under pressure. The sense of urgency is especially acute for European start-ups and scale-ups, which too often lack access to the capital they need to grow, commercialise innovation and remain in Europe. Venture capital is essential to addressing these financing gaps and to completing the savings and investments union. The European venture capital market nevertheless remains far smaller than it could potentially be. This potential can be unlocked through a more integrated and proportional regulatory framework. The upcoming review of the European Venture Capital Fund (EuVECA) Regulation must therefore deliver meaningful reform. This should include substantially raising the threshold for qualifying EuVECA managers and indexing it to prevent its future irrelevance. The review should also simplify reporting and compliance requirements, remove unnecessary administrative burdens, and harmonise the treatment of non-EU country investments with the Alternative Investment Fund Managers Directive. What, then, are the Commission’s overall policy objectives for the EuVECA review, and will it commit to an ambitious reform that strengthens the role of venture capital in financing European growth by expanding access to capital for start-ups and scaleups? (8 September 2026) The Commission fully subscribes to the Honourable Member’s diagnosis of a structural startup and scaleup financing gap and its implications for EU competitiveness. Addressing this gap is a priority for the Commission under the Savings and Investments Union strategy (1) and other policy initiatives. A more integrated and proportionate regulatory framework including a European venture capital funds review would contribute to improving the EU venture capital ecosystem. The Commission is committed to enabling fund managers to more effectively operate across the EU single market, reach greater scale and finance more EU startups and scaleups as they grow. Acting on the regulatory framework for investment funds alone would not be sufficient, as other factors play an important role in developing the EU venture capital ecosystem. The Commission hence has delivered other relevant initiatives such as measures mobilising institutional investors towards equity investments (2), the Scaleup Europe Fund (3) and a proposal on the 28th regime corporate legal framework (‘EU Inc’ proposal) (4). Together, these measures are expected to enable venture and growth capital funds to provide more capital to EU companies, including startups and scaleups in strategic sectors.

E-10-2026-003008.t: One year since Portuguese citizen and pro-democracy Macao activist Au Kam San’s arrest
qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Francisco Assis (S&D) Subject:

Under the ‘one country, two systems’ principle, the Basic Laws of Hong Kong and Macao enshrine respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms. In spite of that formal recognition, deterioration of those rights is getting worse and the repression of civil society is clear. On 30 July 2025, former Macao MP and Portuguese national Au Kam San was taken into custody for alleged ‘collusion with foreign anti-China forces’ – a scheme repeatedly used to weaken democratic dissent and which has already put hundreds of activists behind bars. Au Kam San was one of the organisers of the public vigils to mark the date of the Tiananmen massacre, until the new National Security Law was adopted. One year on, Au Kam San is still unable to communicate with the outside world, including his own family, and has no access to legal assistance. On 2 August 2025, the EU condemned the arrest and acknowledged the erosion of fundamental freedoms in the Macao Special Administrative Region. Given that the situation of Au Kam San has not changed since that date: What action is the EU taking to secure the rapid release of this EU citizen?
at: (English version) to the Vice-President of the Commission/High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Francisco Assis (S&D) (16 July 2026) Subject: One year since Portuguese citizen and pro-democracy Macao activist Au Kam San’s arrest Under the ‘one country, two systems’ principle, the Basic Laws of Hong Kong and Macao enshrine respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms. In spite of that formal recognition, deterioration of those rights is getting worse and the repression of civil society is clear. On 30 July 2025, former Macao MP and Portuguese national Au Kam San was taken into custody for alleged ‘collusion with foreign anti-China forces’ — a scheme repeatedly used to weaken democratic dissent and which has already put hundreds of activists behind bars. Au Kam San was one of the organisers of the public vigils to mark the date of the Tiananmen massacre, until the new National Security Law was adopted. One year on, Au Kam San is still unable to communicate with the outside world, including his own family, and has no access to legal assistance. On 2 August 2025, the EU condemned the arrest and acknowledged the erosion of fundamental freedoms in the Macao Special Administrative Region. Given that the situation of Au Kam San has not changed since that date: What action is the EU taking to secure the rapid release of this EU citizen? (21 August 2026) The EU closely follows the human rights situation in the Macao Special Administrative Region and has repeatedly expressed concern about the continued erosion of fundamental freedoms, political pluralism and civic space, including in the context of the application of national security legislation. Following the arrest of former legislator and EU citizen Au Kam San on 30 July 2025, the EU publicly condemned his arrest and called on the Macao authorities to uphold the rights and freedoms guaranteed under Macao’s Basic Law and international human rights law (1). The Office of the EU in Hong Kong and Macao continues to follow his case closely. The EU raises his case and concerns surrounding his prolonged detention in exchanges with the relevant authorities, including at senior level, and liaises with the Portuguese authorities. These concerns include his conditions of detention, restrictions on contact with his family and his access to independent and effective legal representation. The EU calls for the immediate and unconditional release of Au Kam San and, pending his release, for full respect for his procedural rights, including prompt and unhindered access to a lawyer of his choice and family visits.

qt: to the Commission Céline Imart (PPE), Gilles Pennelle (PfE), Cristina Maestre (S&D), Daniele Polato (ECR), Sarah Knafo (ESN), Volker Schnurrbusch (ESN), Isabelle Le Callennec (PPE), Christophe Gomart (PPE), Valérie Deloge (PfE) Subject:

Following an application submitted by Guinea, in January 2026 the Commission published a Traditional Speciality Guaranteed (TSG) registration for ‘Fleur de Sel’. This TSG appears highly problematic, as it is based on a specification that is not shared by all existing or pending Protected Geographical Indications (PGIs), such as ‘Fleur de Sel de Camargue’, nor by the national rules of several Member States regulating flower of salt. These products are clearly identified by consumers, fully comply with the chemical and organoleptic characteristics that distinguish fleur de sel from coarse salt, and are rooted in local practices determined by their specific environments. Furthermore, the creation of an overarching TSG would weaken the legal protection afforded to PGIs for fleur de sel by encouraging the use of generic designations that run counter to the very purpose of the PGI system and would conflict with national rules of several Member States. In this context: 1.
How does the Commission intend to safeguard the integrity of existing PGIs and those currently undergoing the registration process?

Should the Commission not reclassify the TSG application as an application for the PGI ‘Guinean Fleur de Sel’, thereby ensuring recognition of the specific characteristics of its own production method?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (26.8.2026) The registration and protection of geographical indications (GIs) and traditional specialities guaranteed (TSG) are governed by Regulation (EU) 2024/11431, which lays down distinct conditions and procedures for each scheme. The Commission applies those rules in a manner that preserves the integrity of each scheme and the protection of registered names. It examines each application carefully, including possible conflicts with earlier rights and compliance with the relevant rules. TSG applications are examined taking into account the protection of registered Protected Geographical Indications (PGIs) and Protected Designations of Origin (PDOs), as well as any pending PGI or PDO applications, in accordance with the applicable legal requirements. The application to register ‘Fleur de sel/Flor de sal/Solni cvet’ as a TSG was published in the registration but opened the opposition procedure, allowing interested parties to submit an opposition under the applicable rules. The Commission is examining the application under the relevant legal framework. The Commission cannot unilaterally reclassify a TSG application as a PGI application. The two schemes are legally distinct and subject to different requirements and procedures. It is for the applicant to decide under which scheme an application is submitted. Any application to register a name such as ‘Guinean Fleur de Sel’ as a PGI would need to be submitted separately and would have to demonstrate compliance with Regulation (EU) 2024/1143, including the required link between a given quality, reputation or other characteristic of the product and the defined geographical area.
1 Regulation (EU) 2024/1143 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 11 April 2024 on geographical
indications for wine, spirit drinks and agricultural products, as well as traditional specialities guaranteed and optional quality terms for agricultural products.

E-10-2026-003006.t: IOC decision to lift the suspension of the Russian Olympic Committee
qt: to the Commission Tomáš Zdechovský (PPE) Subject:

The International Olympic Committee has provisionally lifted the suspension of the Russian Olympic Committee, potentially paving the way for Russian athletes to take part in qualifying competitions and team sports ahead of the 2028 Summer Olympic Games in Los Angeles. This decision comes at a time when the Russian Federation continues to wage a war of aggression against Ukraine, committing atrocities on a daily basis against Ukrainian civilians and systematically violating international law. Russian sport has long been used as a tool of state propaganda, and any return of Russian athletes and institutions to international competitions therefore risks being exploited by the Kremlin as a sign of the normalisation of relations. In this connection: 1.

Does the Commission intend to coordinate its approach with the Member States and use diplomatic or political channels to call on the International Olympic Committee and the relevant international sports federations to reconsider this decision, or, where appropriate, to tighten the conditions for the return of Russian athletes and sports institutions?

Is the Commission considering adopting stricter EU measures against Russian sports organisations, officials or athletes linked to the Russian state, the army, security services or propaganda structures, including a possible expansion of the EU sanctions lists?

What specific steps could the Commission take to prevent the Russian Federation from abusing Russian athletes’ participation in international competitions for propaganda purposes as it seeks to legitimise its aggression against Ukraine or undermine the EU’s unified stance in support of Ukraine?

E-10-2026-003005.t: Application of EU law to national legislation on debts managed by credit servicing companies
qt: to the Commission Maria Zacharia (NI) Subject:

Article 126 of Greek Law 5313/2026, which was adopted following Decision No 6/2026 of the plenary of the Supreme Court, provides that amounts unduly paid by borrowers under Law 3869/2010 must be refunded only against active repayment arrangements, while for arrangements that have been closed or have lapsed, these sums ‘shall not be recovered’ (paragraph 5). At the same time, paragraph 6 provides for a special financial settlement mechanism between credit institutions and entities acquiring debts through securitisations under Law 4649/2019. The Commission has repeatedly stated that Directive (EU) 2021/2167 aims to ensure that the transfer and management of loans does not undermine borrowers’ rights. With this in mind, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

Does it consider that Article 126 of Law 5313/2026, in so far as it also applies to debts managed by credit management companies and credit purchasers, falls within the scope of EU law, in particular Directive (EU) 2021/2167?

If so, has it examined whether paragraph 5, read in conjunction with paragraph 6, is compatible with Articles 17, 38 and 47 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights and with the obligation to ensure a high level of consumer protection?
If no such assessment has been carried out, does it intend to do so in its capacity as guardian of the Treaties?

E-10-2026-003004.t: Restrictions on issuing documents to Belarusian nationals living in the EU
qt: to the Commission Ana Miguel Pedro (PPE) Subject:

Since the fraudulent 2020 presidential elections in Belarus, which have been followed by a systematic and prolonged repression, hundreds of thousands of Belarusian nationals have sought refuge in the European Union. Eurostat figures show that more than 750 000 Belarusians obtained residence permits in the EU between 2022 and 2024. In September 2023, the Lukashenka regime passed Decree No 278, which prevents Belarusians abroad from accessing consular services, including acquiring or renewing passports or obtaining legally certified documents. As a result, thousands of legal residents in the EU find themselves unable to obtain documents, making it difficult for them to formalise their stay or gain access to employment or basic services. Some Member States, such as Spain, have started to adopt national solutions to resolve this problem, and the majority of Belarusian citizens are fully integrated, contribute legally and respect European values. Can the Commission say: 1.
Are solutions being considered to provide a coordinated EU response to Belarusian nationals’ inability to renew their documents?
Are alternative European mechanisms being considered?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (11.9.2026) The Commission follows closely the situation in Belarus and strongly condemns measures introduced by Decree No 278, restricting the issuance of passports and other consular services to Belarusians abroad. This is a form of transnational repression which punishes Belarusians perceived as hostile by the regime while creating security risks for Member States. The Commission recognises the importance of ensuring that Belarusians in the EU have access to identity and travel documents, despite the lack of access to consular services. Together with the European External Action Service, it promotes exchanges with Member States on national best practices to help identify appropriate solutions for Belarusian citizens in the EU. Member States are encouraged to draw on the flexibility offered by EU and national migration and residence rules to facilitate the legal entry and stay of affected persons. Any third country national in the EU who cannot obtain a passport from their country of origin should primarily seek a travel document – such as an aliens’ passport – from the Member State they are resident in1. EU and national frameworks may provide for flexibility in the assessment of residence permit applications and of cases where the conditions for entry and stay are no longer formally met due to absence of a valid passport. The EU reiterates its commitment to continue supporting people-to-people contacts between Belarus and the EU, inter alia by supporting mobility, in line with the principles included in the Council Conclusions of 2020 and 20242. Since 2020, the EU has mobilised EUR 200 million to support the people of Belarus, which has included providing mobility opportunities for Belarusian students, researchers, artists and professionals.
1 Member States already issue passports and other identity documents to third country nationals that cannot

acquire those from their own government, according to national law. 2 https://www.consilium.europa.eu/media/46076/council-conclusions-on-belarus.pdf; and https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-6737-2024-INIT/en/pdf.

E-10-2026-003003.t: Foreign influences in Brussels: who is paying to sway EU decisions?
qt: to the Commission Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE) Subject:

Non-EU governments can use consultancies, lobbyists or other intermediaries to defend their interests, or to influence or destabilise the EU institutions. The EU is currently discussing new transparency rules for influence activities carried out on behalf of non-EU countries. However, certain activities, including diplomatic, media, legal or academic ones, would not be included in the proposed arrangements. At the same time, it has been highlighted, in various investigations and through other parliamentary work, that intermediary structures – consultancies, think tanks, nongovernmental organisations, law firms and academic institutions – are increasingly being used to act, directly or indirectly, on behalf of foreign interests, without the real principals always being clearly identified. 1.
Does the Commission support the creation of a single public register indicating which foreign governments are seeking to influence EU decisions, through which intermediaries and for what sums?
Will it publish the list of meetings between the representatives of those foreign interests and Commissioners, their cabinets and senior Commission officials?

How will it prevent the exceptions for certain activities from being used to hide influence operations, especially those conducted through consultancies, nongovernmental organisations, think tanks or academic institutions?

How will it prevent the exceptions for certain activities from being used to hide influence operations, especially those conducted through consultancies, non-governmental organisations, think tanks or academic institutions? (14 September 2026) To increase transparency and democratic accountability of activities impacting EU decision-making processes, the Commission presented, in December 2023, a proposal for a directive on interest representation carried out on behalf of third countries (1). The proposed harmonised transparency requirements rely on a framework of national registers and would apply to entities carrying out interest representation on behalf of third countries, regardless of their legal form. The proposed directive concerns economic activities in the internal market, which could cover activities carried out in the context of research and education, such as the dissemination by think tanks of papers recommending or favouring the adoption of a specific public policy. It contains limited exceptions, in particular with regard to activities connected to the exercise of official authority, including the exercise of diplomatic relations or the provision of legal and other professional advice during legal proceedings. The proposal is currently being discussed by the co-legislators. Pursuant to the Interinstitutional Agreement on the Transparency Register (2), legal entities (such as public affairs consultancy, law firms), offices or networks without diplomatic status or intermediaries representing public authorities of third countries are eligible to register in the Transparency Register. As stated in the Transparency Register guidelines (3), information relating to such interest representation activities is to be duly reported. The Commission applies strict rules on its contacts with interest representatives (4). Information on and minutes of those meetings are published in accordance with Commission Decisions (EU) 2024/3081 (5) and 2024/3082 (6).

E-10-2026-003002.t: Will Parliament really be able to scrutinise the Commission’s decisions?
qt: to the Commission Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE) Subject:

Under the new agreement governing its relations with Parliament, the Commission pledges to comply with more stringent information-sharing obligations, particularly as regards document transparency and transmission, while Commissioners will have to make themselves more available for (and attend a greater number of) hearings, committee debates and other proceedings involving MEPs. The new agreement also aims to enhance the follow-up to Parliament’s legislative requests by laying down clearer deadlines and requiring the Commission to issue more structured replies. A number of recent proceedings have highlighted that Parliament is struggling to obtain specific preparatory documents, legal opinions and information held by the Commission within a timeframe that would enable the EP to effectively exercise its powers of scrutiny. 1.

What specific measures will the Commission take to ensure that it complies with the allotted deadlines for sending the confidential and other documents that Parliament needs to scrutinise its decisions?
Will it publish a register of Parliament’s legislative requests that includes the Commission’s answers, response times and the reasons given to justify any refusals?

How will it ensure that its members respond to Parliament’s invitations and report to MEPs over the progress they have achieved in fulfilling their commitments – particularly those made at their respective confirmation hearings and before the relevant parliamentary committees?
at: (English version) to the Commission Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE) (16 July 2026) Subject: Will Parliament really be able to scrutinise the Commission’s decisions? (7 September 2026) The revised Framework Agreement on Relations between the European Parliament and the Commission (1), was signed by the Presidents of both institutions on 28 April 2026. This agreement enhances cooperation amongst the Commission and the European Parliament, strengthens representative democracy, improves dialogue and ensures greater transparency. In Annex II of the framework Agreement, on the forwarding of confidential information to the European Parliament, both institutions commit to act in accordance with their mutual duties of sincere cooperation. The Commission commits to share with the European Parliament confidential information, in a timely manner, enabling it to exercise its role under the Treaties. In practice, this means that the Commission will share, with all due despatch, any confidential information required for the exercise of European Parliament’s prerogatives and competences. The Commission commits to giving prompt and detailed consideration to the European Parliament’s legislative initiative reports under Article 225 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union. This includes replying to such requests within three months, stating the intended follow-up, in full respect of the principles of proportionality, subsidiarity and better regulation. The Commission commits to coming forward with a legislative proposal, normally after one year. In case the Commission does not intend to submit a proposal, it shall inform the European Parliament of the reasons. The framework Agreement provides for annual meetings between the Conference of Presidents and the Conference of Committee Chairs and the College of Commissioners, to discuss relevant issues, including the preparation and implementation of the Commission Work Programme. Moreover, Commissioners commit to attending plenary debates or parliamentary committee meetings to discuss issues related to specific files, or to provide information on matters of concern to the committee.
