E-10-2026-003001.t: EU agencies: who chooses their directors and according to what criteria?
qt: to the Commission Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE) Subject:

EU agencies take decisions that can have direct consequences for citizens and businesses. The European Parliament has recently strengthened its scrutiny procedures for certain appointments, while the new agreement between Parliament and the Commission provides for candidate hearings for director roles at regulatory agencies. 1.
When the Commission takes part in a selection procedure, does it undertake to publish the criteria chosen, the number of applications received and the reasons for the choice of candidates proposed?
Does it intend to make it compulsory for candidates to submit a declaration of interests and undergo an independent check of risks of conflicts of interest before they are nominated?
Will it propose common rules, for all the agencies concerned, that ensure a transparent, competency-based appointment process that is subject to meaningful parliamentary scrutiny?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (8.9.2026) 1. The rules for the selection of directors of decentralised agencies are specified in the legal bases regulating each agency. Where, according to those legal bases, the Commission is in charge of making proposals or adopting shortlists for appointment, it carries out selection processes for agency directors in accordance with its policy for the selection and recruitment of senior managers, namely the Compilation Document on Senior Officials Policy1. The eligibility and selection criteria for each post are integral parts of the vacancy notices, which are published. The number of candidates, as well as the reasons for the choice of candidates proposed, are recorded in the documents of the selection procedure. These documents are not made public as they contain sensitive personal data of candidates and information on the deliberations of selection panels, which are confidential. 2. Pursuant to Article 11 of the Staff Regulations2, before recruitment, the Appointing Authority, which, for regulatory agencies, is usually the management board, must examine whether the candidate has any personal interest such as to impair their independence or any other conflict of interest. The requirement for a declaration of interest is also provided for by the legal basis of certain agencies and is, in such cases, consequently included in the vacancy notices for agency directors and the analysis of that declaration is made at the appropriate stage, according to that legal basis. 3. Where the legal basis delegates the selection to the Commission, that process uniformly applies the same selection rules, while taking into account the specific requirements of the agencies’ legal bases.

E-10-2026-003000.t: Dire situation of young people in the EU
qt: to the Commission Gerald Hauser (PfE) Subject:

In 2025, around 15 % of young people in Europe were classified as NEETs, meaning that they were not in education, employment or training.1 Lockdown and school closure policies during the COVID-19 pandemic compounded this problem, hindering access to education and reducing young people’s employment opportunities. Already in 2021, the World Bank spoke of a ‘lost generation’ as a result of learning losses and the loss of social interaction.2 NEETs do not contribute to tax revenues and often rely on social benefits. The cost to European countries is estimated at around EUR 153 billion per year. This represents around 1.2 % of the gross domestic product of the entire EU.3 Against a backdrop of demographic change, persistent economic weakness, rising unemployment, as well as advancing digitalisation, including artificial intelligence, this situation presents a ticking time bomb. 1.
What specific measures will the Commission take to solve this problem, which has so far been downplayed?
How will these millions of children and young people be integrated into training programmes and the labour market?
What percentage of NEETs in the EU are young people with a migrant background?

https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-eurostat-news/w/ddn-20260528-2?utm_source=chatgpt.com. https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/press-release/2021/12/06/learning-losses-from-covid-19-couldcost-this-generation-of-students-close-to-17-trillion-in-lifetime-earnings?utm_source=chatgpt.com. 3 https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/103971468187482224/pdf/98665-WP-P148191Box393178B-PUBLIC-Understanding-Out-of-Work-and-Out-of-School-Youth-in-ECA-Mauro-Mitra-WorkingPaper-final2015.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com. 1 2
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.9.2026) The main EU policy framework to support young people’s labour market integration and address the NEET (Not in education, employment or training) phenomenon is the Youth Guarantee. Created in 2013, it was reinforced in 20201 to respond to the rising youth unemployment figures caused by the COVID-19 crisis. Since 2013, the Youth Guarantee has helped more than 63 million young people in Europe. Member States implement the Youth Guarantee through a variety of measures. The Commission supports them in these efforts, e.g. by monitoring the implementation and facilitating the exchange of best practices. As announced in the Anti-Poverty Strategy, by 2027, the Commission will develop a toolkit to strengthen the links between the Child and Youth Guarantees. EU funds and other EU initiatives related to education, training and upskilling – e.g. the Union of Skills, Erasmus+, the European Solidarity Corps, the European Alliance for Apprenticeships, the ALMA initiative – also support young people in building skills and confidence and gaining work experience. As regards young people with a migrant background, the Action Plan on Integration and Inclusion 2021-20272 complements mainstream youth policies by addressing barriers to participation in education, training and employment. The 2025 mid-term3 review confirms that, despite progress, migrant young people continue to face disadvantages, including a higher risk of early school leaving and difficulties in accessing employment matching their skills. In 2025 the NEET rate4 (15-29) stood at 11%5. The trend has been decreasing since 2013 (16.1%) apart from a peak during the COVID-19 pandemic (13.8% in 2020). In 20246, the percentage of NEETs with a migrant background7 was approximately 16%.

content/EN/TXT/?uri=uriserv%3AOJ.C_.2020.372.01.0001.01.ENG&toc=OJ%3AC%3A2020%3A372%3ATO C. 2 European Commission, Action Plan on Integration and Inclusion 2021-2027, COM(2020) 758. 3 European Commission, Mid-term review of the Action Plan on Integration and Inclusion 2021-2027. 4 https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/edat_lfse_20/default/table?lang=en. 5 Ranging from 5% in the Netherlands to 19% in Romania. 6 Directorate-General for Employment, Social Affairs & Inclusion own calculation, based on the latest available Eurostat Labour Force Survey microdata. 7 Individuals with a migrant background are born in a non-EU country.

E-10-2026-002999.t: EU funds possibly earmarked for a contract with a Cuban state-owned company
qt: to the Commission Jorge Buxadé Villalba (PfE) Subject:

The Consular Digitalisation Plan of the Spanish Ministry of Foreign Affairs, European Union and Cooperation has been granted EUR 115 million in NextGenerationEU funds under component 11 of Spain’s Recovery, Transformation and Resilience Plan (RTRP). The ministry has linked the digitalisation in question to its capacity to process applications for citizenship under what is known as the grandchildren’s law1. In addition, the Border Management and Visa Instrument (BMVI) provides EUR 30 million in EU funding to support consular offices and Schengen visa points. At the same time, the Spanish consulate in Havana has concluded a contract worth EUR 1 131 295.68 (plus VAT) with Palco, a Cuban state-owned company, subcontracting it to provide between 88 and 107 workers who, according to press reports, could access sensitive personal data relating to those applying for Spanish nationality under the grandchildren’s law. In view of the above: 1.
Can the Commission confirm whether the reinforcement of the consulate staff by Cuban company Palco is funded, directly or indirectly, under component 11 of the RTRP or under the BMVI?
Has Spain established before the Commission that the NextGenerationEU funds linked to consular digitalisation do not pay for functions carried out by the staff of a non-EU state entity?
If EU funds have been earmarked for this contract, what action does the Commission intend to take?

E-10-2026-002998.t: Awarding of a contract by the Spanish Government to a Cuban state-owned company
qt: to the Commission Jorge Buxadé Villalba (PfE) Subject:

Spain’s Under-Secretariat of Foreign Affairs, the European Union and Cooperation awarded file 2024SWs0014, for EUR 1 131 295.68 (plus VAT), to Cuban state entity PALCO for staff reinforcements at the Spanish consulate in Havana for the processing of citizenship applications in application of what is known as the ‘grandchildren’s law’1. According to press reports, the contract was awarded through a restricted procedure with a single tender and no reduction in the budget. Cuba is not a party to the WTO Agreement on Government Procurement, and the Political Dialogue and Cooperation Agreement between the EU and Cuba does not integrate Cuba into the European public procurement market, nor does it provide for equivalent reciprocal opening of the market. In addition, a Cuban stateowned company may have received foreign financial contributions within the meaning of Regulation (EU) 2022/2560. In light of the above: 1.
Did Spain inform the Commission about this contract, in accordance with the duty of sincere cooperation (Article 4(3) of the Treaty on European Union ) and Regulation (EU) 2022/2560?

Does the Commission view the absence of an EU-Cuba public procurement agreement as precluding the presumption of reciprocity for the purposes of Article 68 of Spain’s Public Sector Contracts Law (LCSP)?
What view does the Commission take of employees of a state company of the Cuban regime having access to applicants’ sensitive personal data?
Eighth additional provision of Spanish Law 20/2022 of 19 October 2022 on democratic memory: https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2022-17099. 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (7.9.2026) Spain’s Under-Secretariat of Foreign Affairs did not inform the Commission of the award of file 2024SWs0014 (the contract). Under Article 28(1)(a) of the Foreign Subsidies Regulation (FSR)1, a foreign financial contribution in public procurement is notifiable where the estimated contract value, net of Value Added Tax, is at least EUR 250 million. The contract did not reach that threshold. Therefore, no notification was required under Article 29 of the FSR, and, consequently, none was required pursuant to Article 4(3) of the Treaty on European Union2 either. Cuba is neither a Party to the World Trade Organization Agreement on Government Procurement3 – which would otherwise apply to the case mentioned by the Honourable Member – nor does it have any bilateral agreement with the EU on public procurement. Therefore, national contracting authorities are still allowed to award contracts to Cuban bidders, since there is currently no EU provision forbidding it. Indeed, according to the principles established in the Kolin judgment of the Court of Justice of the EU4, it is for the individual contracting authority, and not its Member State, to decide whether or not third country bidders can participate in a procurement procedure in the absence of any international agreement guaranteeing that right. Transfers of personal data to third countries may be carried out only in compliance with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)5. The GDPR sets a governance system which tasks national supervisory authorities to ensure its monitoring and enforcement. Thus, the Spanish data protection authority would seem the competent one to ensure compliance with it, including the processing of applicants’ sensitive personal data.
1 Regulation (EU) 2022/2560 of 14 December 2022 on foreign subsidies distorting the internal market,

E-10-2026-002997.t: Flights between the European Union and Western Sahara
qt: to the Commission Irene Montero (The Left) Subject:

On 8 July 2026, the European Parliament approved the Protocol amending the EuroMediterranean Aviation Agreement between the European Community and its Member States, of the one part, and the Kingdom of Morocco, of the other part (EU-Morocco aviation agreement), to take account of the accession of Croatia. The agreement does not cover the separate and distinct territory of Western Sahara. However, European airlines are currently operating the Paris-Dajla route, on Transavia, Madrid-Dajla, on Ryanair, and Las Palmas de Gran Canaria-El Aaiún, on Binter. As these connections are not covered by the EU-Morocco aviation agreement: 1.
What is the legal and administrative basis for operating the mentioned routes and which bilateral agreements or national authorisations cover them?
Have France and Spain informed the Commission of these agreements or authorisations, in accordance with Regulation (EC) No 847/2004?

Has the Commission assessed their compatibility with EU law and, in particular, with the judgments of the Court of Justice of 4 October 2024, which confirm the separate and distinct status of Western Sahara and the need for the consent of the Sahrawi people in order for an international agreement to apply to that territory?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (2.9.2026) As rightly pointed out by the Honourable Member, in accordance with the case law of the Court of Justice, the Euro-Mediterranean aviation agreement between the EU and Morocco does not apply to routes from the territory of an EU Member State to the territory of the Western Sahara. The legal basis for operating the mentioned routes is established by the bilateral agreements concluded by the Member States from whose territories these routes are operated. The bilateral agreements concerned have been notified under Regulation (EC) No 847/20041. The agreement between France and Morocco was concluded in 1957 and was notified to the Commission on 23 September 2004. The agreement between Spain and Morocco was concluded in 1970 and was notified to the Commission on 16 July 2004. The Commission assessed their compatibility with EU law as established in Regulation (EC) No 847/2004.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2004/847/oj/eng.

E-10-2026-002996.t: Use of NextGenerationEU funds to finance the Benasque-Cerler cable car project ruled illegal by the Spanish courts
qt: to the Commission Isabel Serra Sánchez (The Left) Subject:

The territorial plans for sustainable tourism at Spanish destinations are included in Spain’s Resilience and Recovery Plan under measure C14.I1, ‘Transformation of the tourism model towards sustainability’. The measures calls for projects to follow the ‘do no significant harm’ principle and national and EU environmental legislation. The Huesca Single Administrative Court has declared the cable car between Benasque and the ski resort of Cerler to be unlawful. The judgment identified serious irregularities: the terminal’s location in an area prone to flooding from the River Ésera, shortcomings in the geotechnical studies and the lack of an economic viability report. In response to a previous question12 from this Member, the Executive Vice-President for Cohesion and Reforms, Raffaele Fitto stated that the Spanish authorities could replace that project with another as long as it met the selection criteria under targets 217, 218 and 219. Nevertheless, as of 1 July 2026, when the implementation period for NextGenerationEUfunded projects ended, there was no evidence that the Spanish authorities had reallocated the funds. In view of the above: Does the Commission intend to claim the funds for the Benasque-Cerler cable car back from Spain, given that a judgment has found serious legal breaches and potential environmental damage that could be evidence that EU funds have been misused?

qt: to the Commission Moritz Körner (Renew) Subject:

Should the Strait of Hormuz remain blocked for a prolonged period of time, considerable amounts of oil and gas from the Gulf region could be withdrawn from the global market. At the same time, there is a risk that the US Government may impose export restrictions on US oil and gas to lower domestic energy prices. As a result, Europe could end up in a situation where supplies from the Gulf region are insufficient and supplies from the United States are limited. In the light of the above: 1.

What is the Commission’s assessment of the risk of simultaneous disruption or curtailment of oil and gas supplies from Russia, the Gulf region and the United States? What specific contingency and crisis plans are in place for such a scenario?

What strategic oil and gas reserves does the European Union have? For how long could those reserves meet European needs? What alternative countries, transport routes and energy sources could be brought into play for supplies at short notice?

Is the Commission engaged in discussions with the US administration on possible export restrictions on oil and LNG? What measures are planned to prevent massive price increases, production losses and social strain in Europe in the event of a crisis?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (17.9.2026) The Commission is closely monitoring the developments on the gas and oil markets. At this stage, there is no supply disruption in Europe. Past efforts, especially the work to diversify gas supplies as reinforced by REPowerEU, have paid off in this respect. Moreover, Regulation (EU)1938/2017 on security of gas supply1 requires Member States to develop preventive action plans and emergency plans at national and regional level. They set out measures to prevent, mitigate and respond to supply disruptions. These tools, together with the close coordination through the Gas Coordination Group, have already proven effective during the last crises. Under Directive 2009/119/EC on emergency oil stocks2, in addition to building emergency stocks, Member States have to prepare contingency plans to mitigate the impact of security of supply incidents. The Commission also coordinates actions with Member States and industry and other actors through the Oil Coordination Group. EU gas storage capacity is around 100 billion cubic meters, which corresponds to one-third of the overall winter gas consumption needs. EU gas storage levels are being refilled in preparation for next winter, which was ca. 57% full as of 31 July 2026. For oil, Member States have to hold emergency stocks of crude oil and petroleum products equivalent to 90 days of net imports or 61 days of consumption, whichever amount is higher. The global oil market is liquid, and the EU supply is diversified. Beyond the US and the Middle East, the EU oil imports come mostly from Norway, Kazakhstan, Africa and Latin America. The Commission has regular discussions with the US administration on security of supply matters.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2017/1938/oj/eng. 2 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2009/119/oj/eng.

to the Commission Moritz Körner (Renew) Subject:

Gross domestic product (GDP) per capita in the United States sits well above the European Union average. Over an extended period, the EU has exhibited markedly weaker growth in economic performance per capita relative to the United States. This difference can be largely attributed to lower productivity growth in Europe. 1.
How does the Commission explain the fact that the US has experienced significantly more real GDP per capita and productivity growth than the EU?
Can the Commission say what it and the Member States should have done differently, and when, in order to experience GDP growth similar to that of the US?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (28.9.2026) Over the past 20 years, US productivity has grown faster than in the EU. This was highlighted in the Draghi report, which identified the EU-US productivity growth lag as a main reason for the widening the gap competitiveness. As shown in that report, key reasons for the EU-US productivity gap is a lower investment in the EU in the years after the 2008 financial crisis and especially lower growth in so-called total factor productivity, reflecting slower innovation, weaker adoption of new technologies, and less economic dynamism. Differences between the EU and the US performance were particularly visible in the Information and Communication Technology and digital sector, with EU young innovative firms not in the position to achieve the sufficient scale to compete on a global scale. The Commission has addressed the concerns raised in the Draghi report in its Competitiveness Compass agenda published in January 2025, which aims to strengthen innovation, decarbonisation and economic security by cutting red tape, removing single market barriers, promoting investment financing and skills, and improving policy coordination. The Commission has been delivering at record speed detailed action plans and legislative proposals on most items of the agenda. However, action at EU level only cannot be the only solution to the productivity problem. Whereas the regulatory and incentives framework can be spurred by EU-level action, a concerted effort between EU institutions, Member States and the private sector is needed to bring the changes necessary to boost European competitiveness, as highlighted in the Draghi report, the Competitiveness Compass and the One Europe, One Market roadmap.

COVID-19 not only causes acute illness, but has also triggered a growing wave of chronic diseases, which continue to affect millions of people and are the source of mounting socioeconomic costs. Alongside long COVID or post-COVID syndrome, ME/CFS (Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome) has also long been thought to cause considerable societal costs. Can the Commission indicate the number of people living with ME/CFS or long COVID and the cost of those diseases in the EU?
at: (English version) to the Commission Moritz Körner (Renew) (15 July 2026) Subject: Impact of COVID-19 COVID-19 not only causes acute illness, but has also triggered a growing wave of chronic diseases, which continue to affect millions of people and are the source of mounting socioeconomic costs. Alongside long COVID or post-COVID syndrome, ME/CFS (Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome) has also long been thought to cause considerable societal costs. Can the Commission indicate the number of people living with ME/CFS or long COVID and the cost of those diseases in the EU? (24 September 2026) Myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS) is a serious chronic and complex multi-system disease characterised by symptoms such as post-exertional malaise, fatigue, cognitive impairment and pain. Diagnosis is based on international consensus criteria, and no curative treatment is available (1). A recent 2025 scoping review on burden of disease in ME/CFS continues to highlight the uncertainty related to the number of affected people, giving a European prevalence range of 0.1-2.2% (2). Recent estimates indicate that long COVID affected around 5% of the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) population on average in 2021, corresponding to around 75 million people, with direct healthcare costs estimated at USD 53 billion. While prevalence has since declined, long COVID is projected to affect 0.6-1.0% of the OECD population between 2025 and 2035, with direct healthcare costs estimated at around USD 11 billion annually. Indirect economic costs related to reduced workforce participation and productivity are expected to be higher, with projected losses of 0.1-0.2% of gross domestic product (3). The Network of Expertise on long COVID (4), supported under the EU4Health programme (5) brings together national centres of expertise on long COVID to exchange experiences on diagnosis, treatment, and management.

A recent OECD report estimates for the prevalence of long COVID to remain below 1% from 2025 to 2035 (affecting 0.6-1.0% of the OECD and EU population). https://www.oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/publications/reports/2026/03/addressing-the-costs-and-care-for-long-covid_e203e3d0/87a0c171-en.pdf. With its judgment of 29 June 2026, the US Supreme Court removed the statutory protection of members of the Federal Trade Commission against politically motivated dismissal. This undermines a key assumption underpinning the adoption of the adequacy decision (EU) 2023/1795, i.e. that compliance by U.S. companies with data protection obligations is monitored and enforced by an independent and effective supervisory authority. An authority whose management can be removed at any time by the US President can hardly be considered independent from the executive. Nevertheless, the Commission continues to enable large-scale transfers of personal data to the US, even though the GDPR requires the Commission to monitor relevant developments without delay and to suspend or repeal an adequacy decision as soon as an equivalent level of protection is no longer ensured. 1.

Does the Commission maintain that the FTC meets the requirements for independent and effective oversight if its members are subject to the direct political control of the US President?

Will the Commission revoke the adequacy decision and warn controllers not to continue relying on the data protection framework, or is it knowingly prepared to accept a third defeat before the Court of Justice of the European Union?

to the Commission Moritz Körner (Renew) Subject:

Companies such as ASML Holding N.V. and Carl Zeiss SMT possess technologies that are vitally important for manufacturing cutting-edge semiconductors and for which there is no easy substitute in the short term. Europe therefore occupies a strategically important position in the global semiconductor supply chain. At the same time, there is a risk that third countries could restrict the access of European companies, research institutes and public authorities to the latest AI models, supercomputers, cloud services or other key digital technologies. Such measures could significantly undermine Europe’s technological competitiveness and further exacerbate existing dependencies. 1.

What knowledge does the Commission have of any restrictions that the US government or US-based companies are planning to introduce that would deny European users simultaneous and non-discriminatory access to the latest and most powerful AI models, cloud services or other strategic technologies?

Is the Commission considering introducing an automatic European reciprocity mechanism under which any such access restrictions imposed by third countries would immediately trigger the review, suspension or restriction of European export licences for critical semiconductor technologies, systems, components, software and patents, in particular within the framework of the EU Dual-Use Regulation, the Anti-Coercion Instrument and other trade defence instruments?

Does the Commission intend, together with Member States and strategically relevant European companies such as ASML Holding N.V. and Carl Zeiss SMT, to prepare specific measures under which production capacities within the European Union would be prioritised when making cutting-edge European semiconductor technologies available, and exports to third countries would be restricted for as long as European companies, research institutes and public authorities do not enjoy equal access to the latest AI models and similar key technologies?
at: (English version) to the Commission Moritz Körner (Renew) (15 July 2026) Subject: AI dependency Companies such as ASML Holding N.V. and Carl Zeiss SMT possess technologies that are vitally important for manufacturing cutting-edge semiconductors and for which there is no easy substitute in the short term. Europe therefore occupies a strategically important position in the global semiconductor supply chain. At the same time, there is a risk that third countries could restrict the access of European companies, research institutes and public authorities to the latest AI models, supercomputers, cloud services or other key digital technologies. Such measures could significantly undermine Europe’s technological competitiveness and further exacerbate existing dependencies. 1. What knowledge does the Commission have of any restrictions that the US government or US-based companies are planning to introduce that would deny European users simultaneous and non-discriminatory access to the latest and most powerful AI models, cloud services or other strategic technologies? 2. Is the Commission considering introducing an automatic European reciprocity mechanism under which any such access restrictions imposed by third countries would immediately trigger the review, suspension or restriction of European export licences for critical semiconductor technologies, systems, components, software and patents, in particular within the framework of the EU Dual-Use Regulation, the Anti-Coercion Instrument and other trade defence instruments? 3. Does the Commission intend, together with Member States and strategically relevant European companies such as ASML Holding N.V. and Carl Zeiss SMT, to prepare specific measures under which production capacities within the European Union would be prioritised when making cutting-edge European semiconductor technologies available, and exports to third countries would be restricted for as long as European companies, research institutes and public authorities do not enjoy equal access to the latest AI models and similar key technologies? (1 September 2026) The Commission is closely monitoring developments in third countries’ policies that may affect the EU’s access to strategic digital technologies, including advanced AI models, cloud services, high-performance computing resources and other critical inputs that underpin Europe’s innovation capacity and competitiveness. The Commission remains in regular contact with Member States, relevant stakeholders and international partners to monitor possible restrictions or discriminatory measures affecting European companies, research organisations, and public authorities. In this context, the Commission will continue to carefully assess any information concerning actual or envisaged measures by a third country government or by third country-based providers that could limit timely, effective and non-discriminatory access to such technologies for European users. The Commission is committed to strengthening the EU’s technological and industrial base in line with the objectives of Europe’s tech sovereignty agenda. In the recently proposed Tech Sovereignty Package (1), the Commission is taking forward measures to reinforce the security of supply, reduce strategic dependencies and support the development and scaling-up of critical technologies and production capacities in Europe, including in sectors of strategic importance such as advanced semiconductors. The Chips Act 2.0 proposal (2) sets out such measures for the semiconductor domain.

qt: to the Commission Moritz Körner (Renew) Subject:

In Germany, around 9.38 terawatt-hours (TWh) of electricity from renewable sources had to be curtailed due to redispatching interventions in 2025. Operators of the plants concerned received approximately EUR 434.5 million in financial compensation as a result. 1.
What was the scale and cost of renewable energy curtailment in the other Member States? The Commission is asked to provide data on all Member States for 2025.
How does the Commission assess the scale of renewable energy curtailment and the associated compensation payments in Germany?

In the Commission’s view, how is a system under which operators are also compensated for curtailed electricity and electricity not fed into the grid expected to create effective incentives to develop grid infrastructure as needed?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (2.10.2026) The Commission agrees it is important to monitor renewable energy sources (RES) curtailment levels. There is currently no consistent EU-wide definition of curtailment, making it difficult to measure in a consistent manner. Realised curtailment levels are heterogeneously reported by national system operators with varying methodologies and definitions. It is estimated that in 2024 the cost of curtailment amounted to over EUR 6 bn in six countries1 and over 10 TWh of electricity from RES could not be used in the EU due to grid congestion and insufficient availability of cross-border capacity2. Whilst a certain level of curtailment may help manage overall system costs, high levels of curtailment can be an indicator of system failures limiting the integration of renewable electricity. Developing a common EU wide definition of RES curtailment could increase transparency, support a more coherent approach to curtailment monitoring, and improve locational investment signals for grid development, flexibility and RES generation. The power sector in the EU is unbundled: power plant operators receive redispatching compensation while grid expansion is carried out by system operators. Effective incentives for grid development are provided through the regulatory framework; including grid planning obligations, cost-recovery rules, performance-based regulation and public oversight. The Connecting Europe Facility (CEF) also funds cross-border energy infrastructure, and the Commission has proposed a five-fold increase (EUR 29.9 bn) in its budget for CEF-Energy in the next Multiannual Financial Framework. Finally, support mechanisms must be welldesigned to avoid grid congestion curtailment being compensated for through redispatching3.
1 Costs refer to country-specific curtailment payments, re-dispatch and/or counter-trading costs. Combined

estimate for France, Finland, Germany, Hungary, Poland and Spain: https://beyondfossilfuels.org/wpcontent/uploads/2025/05/REPORT_FINAL.pdf. 2 ACER Market Monitoring Report, 2025: https://www.acer.europa.eu/monitoring/cross-zonal-electricity-trade2025. 3 See e.g. for guidance on design principles for two-way contracts for difference: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legalcontent/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A52025XC06701&qid=1767881386609.

qt: to the Commission Moritz Körner (Renew) Subject:

In January, the Chinese owner of TikTok, ByteDance Ltd., concluded an agreement to establish a majority US-owned joint venture. This averted a ban in the US on the short video app, which is popular with more than 200 million Americans. 1.
How does the Commission assess the solution found in the US with regard to security concerns?
Does this mean that the data of US citizens is better protected than that of EU citizens?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.9.2026) The Commission does not comment on agreements concluded between digital services providers and third-country governments. EU citizens are protected online by a robust legal framework. In particular, the General Data Protection Regulation1 sets strict requirements for the processing and international transfer of personal data, including transfers to third countries such as China. In addition, the Digital Services Act (DSA)2 establishes unprecedented obligations for online platforms operating in the EU in terms of transparency and accountability. The Commission is enforcing its laws firmly and fairly throughout the EU. In this respect, TikTok is designated as a very large online platform under the DSA and is therefore obliged to diligently assess and mitigate systemic risks stemming from its service. This includes risks related to the dissemination of illegal content, the protection of fundamental rights, civic discourse, and electoral processes. When platform providers fail to meet their obligations, the Commission acts. The Commission opened several investigations into TikTok and preliminarily found breaches of the DSA for its failure to publish an advertisement repository3 , its addictive design4 and its failure to ensure safe accounts for minors5. Following extensive engagement with the Commission, TikTok submitted binding commitments to withdraw the rewards programme6, which could have stimulated addiction-like behaviour, and to address the Commission’s concerns about TikTok’s ad repository, measures which are already having a positive impact for users in the EU.
1 Regulation (EU) 2016/679 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 April 2016 on the protection of

natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free movement of such data, and repealing Directive 95/46/EC (General Data Protection Regulation). 2 Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 on a Single market for digital services and amending Directive 2000/31/EC (Digital Services Act), https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/2065/oj/eng. 3 Commission preliminarily finds TikTok's ad repository in breach of the DSA, https://digitalstrategy.ec.europa.eu/en/news/commission-preliminarily-finds-tiktoks-ad-repository-breach-digital-services-act. 4 Commission preliminarily finds TikTok's addictive design in breach of the DSA, https://digitalstrategy.ec.europa.eu/en/news/commission-preliminarily-finds-tiktoks-addictive-design-breach-digital-servicesact. 5 Commission preliminary finds TikTok in breach of the DSA for failing to ensure safe accounts for minors, https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/news/commission-preliminary-finds-tiktok-breach-digital-services-actfailing-ensure-safe-accounts-minors. 6 TikTok commits to permanently withdraw TikTok Lite Rewards programme from the EU to comply with the DSA, https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/news/tiktok-commits-permanently-withdraw-tiktok-lite-rewardsprogramme-eu-comply-digital-services-act.

to the Commission Moritz Körner (Renew) Subject:

The European private credit market has grown considerably in recent years. A significant share of the financing provided to European companies comes from funds based outside the EU or from globally active fund groups. At the same time, there are deep interconnections with European banks, insurance companies and pension funds, for example through credit lines, holdings, derivatives and risk transfers. 1.
What is the Commission’s current assessment of the systemic risks posed by the private credit sector to the financial stability of the European Union?

What proportion of private credit financing of EU companies is provided by non-EU funds, and what risks does this entail for European financial stability and the continued financing of the real economy?
What would be the impact of a simultaneous increase in credit losses, value adjustments and refinancing costs in the private credit sector on banks, institutional investors and companies in the EU?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (8.9.2026) Available evidence suggests that EU private credit (PC) markets do not pose immediate financial stability risks, while exposure to US PC markets needs to be monitored. The Commission is working with the European Supervisory Authorities (ESAs), European Systemic Risk Board (ESRB) and European Central Bank (ECB) to improve our understanding of the characteristics of PC markets, identify potential data gaps and enhance granular risk monitoring. This is essential to monitor interconnections and concentration and to properly assess leverage and valuation practices. Private Credit enhances financial diversification and stability by increasingly becoming a source of funding for the economy in the EU. Non-bank credit to non-financial corporations (NFCs) reached 21% of total credit in the EU1. Euro area (EA) NFCs receive around 70% of PC funding from non-EA PC funds2. PC investments are limited to roughly 6% of EU alternative investment funds’ assets under management, based on preliminary evidence (upper-bound estimate). In a scenario of a shock originating from non-EU PC markets, impacts would vary across the EU financial system. Potential direct losses would be limited for EA banks, given limited direct exposures. Second-round market valuation effects could be larger. They could especially affect certain insurers due to concentrated and less senior private credit and equity exposures, and pension funds, though the latter have less exposure to PC and more equity holdings3. Notwithstanding those risks and noting this may differ at the individual level, EU banks, insurance companies and pension funds on aggregate are well positioned to absorb a severe shock4.

1 2025 ESRB Non-bank Financial Intermediation (NBFI) Monitor. 2 ECB Financial Stability Review May 2026. 3 European Insurance and Occupational Pensions Authority (EIOPA) Financial Stability Report December 2025. 4 ECB Financial Stability Review May 2026.

qt: to the Commission Moritz Körner (Renew) Subject:

In a June 2023 NewsNation interview, then US Senator Marco Rubio said that several current or former government personnel had approached the US Senate Intelligence Committee with what he called ‘firsthand knowledge or firsthand claims’ concerning matters related to unidentified anomalous phenomena (UAP). He added that many had held high-level security clearances and senior government positions. The current US Government has been regularly releasing tranches of documents on this issue. 1.
Has the Commission verified the documents and the statements of its US counterparts on this issue?
Does the Commission consider the publications of the US administration to be at all serious?
Does the Commission rule out the existence of UAP/UFOs?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (25.8.2026) The area of unidentified anomalous phenomenon (UAP) is considered a competence of the Member States, allowing them to address these phenomena according to the national security needs. For example, France has established the Unidentified Aerospace Phenomena Research and Information Group (GEIPAN). Therefore, the Commission is not in a position to verify any document or make any consideration regarding publications on this topic. The Commission and the High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy/Vice President remain dedicated to collaborating with stakeholders to ensure the safety and security of the space environment.

qt: to the Commission Moritz Körner (Renew) Subject:

Since July 2024, it has been the case that certain single-use drinks containers holding up to three litres may only be placed on the market in the EU if the plastic cap stays attached to the container during its intended use. Could the Commission please list all the benefits of this rule that it knows about on the basis of practical experience thus far?
at: (English version) to the Commission Moritz Körner (Renew) (15 July 2026) Subject: Bottles Since July 2024, it has been the case that certain single-use drinks containers holding up to three litres may only be placed on the market in the EU if the plastic cap stays attached to the container during its intended use. Could the Commission please list all the benefits of this rule that it knows about on the basis of practical experience thus far? (25 August 2026) The tethering requirement for caps of single-use plastic (SUP) beverage containers under the SUP Directiv e (1) was introduced as caps were found to be littered more than twice as often on EU beaches than containers. In combination with the separate collection targets for SUP beverage bottles, it aims to reduce littering and increase recycling of the caps. Member States provide data on beach litter via the Marine Strategic Framework Directive (2), which the Joint Research Centre (JRC) of the Commission (3) analyses for trends. In 2025, a JRC report (4) showed that marine SUP litter on EU beaches decreased by 40%. While an assessment of an EU-wide litter trend specifically for caps is not available to date, a report from the Netherlands indicates a significant decrease of littered caps (5). In addition to the above data on environmental benefits, the Commission published a call for evidence and an open public consultation (6) related to the upcoming evaluation of the SUP Directive (due 3 July 2027), inviting all interested stakeholders to share their experience with the different measures of the directive. Feedback on the tethered caps design requirement was mixed. Benefits for people with disabilities were identified as the tethering prevents the bottle caps from being misplaced (7), (8).

(17 September 2026) The Commission assesses blackout risks and their impacts on a systemic basis through several instruments, including EU disaster scenarios (1) and the Risk-Preparedness Regulation (2). It uses the Blackout Simulator (3) to estimate economic losses, while risk assessments remain the basis for estimating potential fatalities and health impacts. Consequences depend on season, location and weather: impacts are greater in summer in southern Member States due to cooling needs and in winter in northern Member States due to heating demand. The regulation (4) on serious cross-border health threats would apply if needed. The Commission follows up on the recommendations from the Expert Panel investigations (5) and lessons identified by affected Member States (6). With Member States and stakeholders, it is considering measures to strengthen electricity system resilience and security, feeding into the ongoing revision of the EU energy security framework and updates to the Network Codes. No fixed annual probability can be assigned to large-scale blackouts, as risks, particularly from malicious acts, depend on the evolving security environment. Strengthening security and resilience is a key priority with emphasis on cross-border connectivity (see mid-term review of the Cohesion Policy (7), (8)), and emergency preparedness. Under the next Multiannual Financial Framework support will come through the National and Regional Partnership Plans, the Connecting Europe Facility, and the European Competitiveness Fund.

(14 September 2026) Beside the banking sector, non-bank financial intermediaries (NBFIs) play a role in contributing to the competitiveness of the financial services sector and in driving deeper market integration in the EU. The Commission acknowledges that the growing presence of NBFIs could become a source of vulnerabilities, including from various interconnectedness links, noting that NBFIs are heterogeneous entities differing in size, activities, and leverage, amongst others. In January 2024, the Commission published a risk assessment, followed by a targeted consultation to seek stakeholders’ views on the adequacy of the macroprudential framework for NBFIs. A feedback statement was published in March 2025 (1). In its risk assessment, the Commission called for a more holistic and well-coordinated oversight framework to improve the early identification and assessment of systemic risks (2). In support of this, the Commission is closely following national system-wide stress test exercises as they provide key intakes with regard to EU financial stability. Furthermore, the Commission, in cooperation with the European Supervisory Authorities, the European Systemic Risk Board and national competent authorities, continuously monitors systemic risks in relation to NBFIs, including in the repo market, where there are strong links between banks and NBFIs involving sovereign bond markets. Regarding those risks, the Commission notes that the regulatory framework already contains relevant instruments, including the option to restrict the use of leverage by alternative investment fund managers (3). Finally, the Commission engages within the Financial Stability Board as well as other international organisations to promote a common approach to risk monitoring and data sharing.

E-10-2026-002973.t: Decision of the Supreme Court of Bulgaria regarding the Euroins Romania case
qt: to the Commission Rada Laykova (ESN) Subject:

The Bulgarian Supreme Court of Cassation recently confirmed the legality of the reinsurance agreement that existed between EuroinsRomania and EIG.Re in 2023 when the Romanian Financial Supervisory Authority (ASF) withdrew EuroinsRomania’s operating licence. The Supreme Court ruling is in line with the position taken in 2023 by the Bulgarian Regulator (FSC), which argued against ASF’s position on Euroins. It is also aligned with the position taken by the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (ERBD), which pointed out in 2023 that EuroinsRomania was solvent and had no capital gap, and that its reinsurance contracts met all Solvency II requirements. It is in line with leading actuarial consultants who communicated with, but were ignored by, ASF, the European Insurance and Occupational Pensions Authority (EIOPA) and the Commission. The Court decision also confirms the International Arbitration Court ruling of 2 July 2024 on the case. Given the mounting evidence that the position taken by ASF in 2023 was wrong and that the judgment exercised in relation to EuroinsRomania by EIOPA was questionable: 1.
Has the Commission reviewed EIOPA’s assessment of EuroinsRomania?

If so, what conclusions has it reached and will it grant immediate access to its analysis? If not, does the Commission agree to immediately commence an open and comprehensive review of the EuroinsRomania case with particular emphasis on the performance of EIOPA?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.9.2026) Under the current EU supervisory framework, national supervisory authorities (NSAs) are solely responsible for the supervision of insurance undertakings within their jurisdiction, ensuring compliance with Solvency II1. NSAs operate independently in line with their mandates, including ensuring compliance with applicable rules, safeguarding consumer protection, and taking corrective measures when necessary. It was the responsibility of the Romanian Financial Supervisory Authority (ASF) to assess whether Euroins Romania was solvent and take appropriate supervisory action. The Bulgarian supervisor and other competent authorities were consulted as part of an exceptional supervisory college on Euroins. The Commission understands that prudential concerns were confirmed by a separate assessment of the valuation of technical provisions of Euroins undertaken by the European Insurance and Occupational Pensions Authority (EIOPA). Article 1(6) of the EIOPA Regulation2 sets out that EIOPA will act independently, objectively and in the interests of the EU. The Commission did not have access to, and therefore cannot comment on, either the conclusions of the independent assessment by EIOPA, or on the outcome of the actuarial analysis conducted by a private consulting firm which was mandated by Euroins Insurance Group, with the support of the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development which is a minority shareholder of the Group. EIOPA and the national supervisory authorities are independent authorities and have the expertise to make objective assessments. EIOPA is accountable to the European Parliament and the Council, both of which can exercise their prerogatives. Finally, the Commission does not comment on national court decisions.

and pursuit of the business of Insurance and Reinsurance, OJ L 335, 17.12.2009, p. 1–155. 2 Regulation (EU) No 1094/2010 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 24 November 2010 establishing a European Supervisory Authority (European Insurance and Occupational Pensions Authority), OJ L 331, 15.12.2010, pp. 48–83

(10 September 2026) The Global Gateway (GG) supports sustainable quality investments with high social, environmental and governance standards. All GG projects apply a human rights-based approach as requested by the Neighbourhood, Development and International Cooperation Instrument — Global Europe (NDICI-GE) instrument regulation (1). In 2025, the Commission also strengthened contractual provisions on human rights and introduced an internal complaints procedure for external actions to support right holders in claiming their rights. Regular dialogue with partners, project visits and monitoring help ensure safeguards are respected. Under GG, the Commission works in indirect management with development finance institutions that are pillar-assessed under the EU Financial Regulation (2). Pillar assessment is a review by the Commission of the systems and procedures of entities to check if they fulfil the criteria to be entrusted with budget implementation. Pillar 7, for instance, covers entities’ capacity to detect situations that would exclude recipients from access to funding such as fraud, corruption or human trafficking. It is important to distinguish between corporate due diligence as set out in the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD) (3), and the requirements for investments under GG. The CSDDD goes beyond a specific investment project. It requires large companies to identify and address adverse human rights and environmental impacts in their own operations and those of their subsidiaries and to engage continuously with their business partners.

E-10-2026-002969.t: Implications of the reclassification of SILTAC for plant protection and farms
qt: to the Commission Anna Zalewska (ECR) Subject:

In agricultural practice, plant protection relies on stable access to tried-and-tested tools to control pests while minimising the use of chemical plant protection products. SILTAC is a product with active physical effects that has been used by farmers in various Member States for many years as an alternative to conventional chemicals. Its availability has enabled professional users to plan crop protection in a predictable way, in line with the principles of sustainable farming. In January 2024, as part of the SCoPAFF Committee’s work, SILTAC was reclassified in the Commission’s working document entitled ‘Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 – scope and borderline issues’. It was placed into the category of plant protection products. This reclassification took place without a transition period. In practice, it has brought about a risk that farmers in some Member States might suddenly lose access to SILTAC as a tool, without being able to replace it with equivalent solutions. With the above in mind: 1.
Has the Commission looked into whether farmers have alternatives to SILTAC with a comparable profile and level of effectiveness?
What action does the Commission plan to take to prevent the loss of available tools to support plant protection in similar cases in the future?

E-10-2026-002967.t: Servicing Russian Arc7-class LNG icebreakers and the effectiveness of the EU’s sanctions policy
qt: to the Commission Michał Dworczyk (ECR) Subject:

The European Union has repeatedly stated its intention to phase out Russian fossil fuels entirely and to curb the Russian Federation’s revenues from energy exports. However, even though successive rounds of sanctions have been adopted, there are still sectors and economic activities that have not been subject to appropriate restrictions, enabling Russia to generate further revenue. A particular cause for concern are media reports about a European shipyard providing repair and maintenance services for Arc7-class LNG icebreakers, which are crucial to the operation of Russia’s Yamal LNG project1. These vessels are the cornerstone of Russia’s Arctic LNG exports. Carrying out maintenance work in 2026 will extend the life of the vessels concerned by several more years, enabling Russia to continue exporting LNG and financing the war against Ukraine. In the light of the foregoing: 1.

Does the Commission take the view that the provision by EU companies of repair and maintenance services for vessels that are a key part of Russia’s LNG export infrastructure is in line with the objectives of the EU’s sanctions policy?

Does the Commission intend to propose, as part of the next round of sanctions, an amendment to Regulation (EU) No 833/2014 by removing the transition period for the provision of technical, repair and certification services for Arc7-class LNG icebreakers, in order to prevent Russia from prolonging its ability to export LNG from the Arctic?
https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-shipyard-races-to-service-russia-vladimir-putin-lng-fleet-beforesanctions-bite/. 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (24.8.2026) The Commission remains fully committed to the EU’s restrictive measures (‘sanctions’) imposed in response to Russia’s illegal war of aggression against Ukraine. The 21 EU sanctions packages on Russia, with the last one adopted on 23 July 2026, include a broad range of measures in the field of energy, e.g. import ban on oil and measures targeting Russian liquified natural gas (LNG). In addition, the EU adopted, as part of the 20th sanctions package on 23 April 20261, a prohibition on maintenance services for Russian LNG tankers and icebreakers. This prohibits – after relevant wind-down periods – EU operators’ support to Russian LNG exports and further constrains Russia’s ability to maintain its seaborne assets. EU operators are prohibited since April 2026 to provide technical or financial assistance, which also covers maintenance and repairs, to Russian owned, managed, flagged or operated ice-breaker vessels and LNG tankers. The prohibition to provide services to any LNG tankers used in Russia applies from 1 January 2027. The Council may decide, in unanimity, on the possible extension of any restrictive measures, including limiting the transition period. Restrictive measures are established via Council decisions in the area of Common Foreign and Security Policy and Council regulations giving effect to those decisions in EU law. Member States are responsible for the effective implementation and enforcement of sanctions, and the Commission is closely monitoring and supporting the Member States in those tasks.

E-10-2026-002966.t: Application of the life cycle CO₂ emissions exemption under Article 11(2) of Regulation (EU) 2024/573
qt: to the Commission Wouter Beke (PPE) Subject:
Application of the life cycle CO₂ emissions exemption under Article 11(2) of Regulation (EU) 2024/573

Heat pumps are widely recognised as a key technology for achieving the EU’s energy security and decarbonisation objectives. Regulation (EU) 2024/573 (F-gas Regulation) introduces market prohibitions on certain refrigerants in heat pump equipment from 2027 onwards. However, alternative refrigerants are not yet available for all applications. The Regulation therefore provides exemptions to ensure a balanced and realistic transition. Article 11(2) states that certain placing-on-the-market prohibitions do not apply where the life cycle CO₂ equivalent emissions of the equipment are lower than those of equivalent equipment meeting the relevant ecodesign requirements. However, the Commission has not yet clarified the methodology to calculate these life cycle emissions, and the current ecodesign regulations do not provide a clear reference. Without such clarity, manufacturers cannot apply the exemption consistently or with sufficient legal certainty, while market surveillance authorities may face difficulties in verification and enforcement. Can the Commission clarify what concrete steps are being taken to develop and integrate an appropriate life cycle CO₂ emissions calculation methodology into the relevant ecodesign regulations before the market prohibition comes into force, so that the Article 11(2) exemption can be applied and verified consistently across the EU, taking into account the provisions of recital 23 of the F-gas Regulation?
at: (English version) to the Commission Wouter Beke (PPE) (15 July 2026) Subject: Application of the life cycle CO2 emissions exemption under Article 11(2) of Regulation (EU) 2024/573 Heat pumps are widely recognised as a key technology for achieving the EU’s energy security and decarbonisation objectives. Regulation (EU) 2024/573 (F-gas Regulation) introduces market prohibitions on certain refrigerants in heat pump equipment from 2027 onwards. However, alternative refrigerants are not yet available for all applications. The regulation therefore provides exemptions to ensure a balanced and realistic transition. Article 11(2) states that certain placing-on-the-market prohibitions do not apply where the life cycle CO 2 equivalent emissions of the equipment are lower than those of equivalent equipment meeting the relevant ecodesign requirements. However, the Commission has not yet clarified the methodology to calculate these life cycle emissions, and the current ecodesign regulations do not provide a clear reference. Without such clarity, manufacturers cannot apply the exemption consistently or with sufficient legal certainty, while market surveillance authorities may face difficulties in verification and enforcement. Can the Commission clarify what concrete steps are being taken to develop and integrate an appropriate life cycle CO 2 emissions calculation methodology into the relevant ecodesign regulations before the market prohibition comes into force, so that the article 11(2) exemption can be applied and verified consistently across the EU, taking into account the provisions of Recital 23 of the F-gas Regulation? (1 September 2026) The Commission agrees that heat pumps are a key technology to achieve the EU’s electrification, decarbonisation and energy security objectives. Article 11(2) of the F-gas Regulation (1) is meant to ensure that there are no trade-offs between efforts to reduce the direct (Fgas Regulation) and indirect (Eco-design for Sustainable Products Regulation (ESPR)) (2) emissions of equipment using fluorinated gases such as heat pumps. It requires that a clear methodology is set under ESPR rules. ESPR rules are developed at the product level, e.g. for space heaters or air conditioners and comfort fans, and regularly updated. During that process of updating, extensive technical work is undertaken. If it becomes evident during that process that the rules of the F-gas Regulation would force a move towards refrigerants that would result in lower efficiency, an appropriate life cycle CO 2 methodology could be included to avoid such outcomes. While Article 11(2) has been part of the F-gas Regulation since 2015 (it is identical in the previous Regulation (EU) No 517/2014) (3), no such cases have yet been identified.

E-10-2026-002965.t: Illegal drug websites are making a comeback via foreign domain names
qt: to the Commission Malik Azmani (Renew), Hilde Vautmans (Renew), Raquel García Hermida-Van Der Walle (Renew), Sophie Wilmès (Renew) Subject:

In April 2026, the Netherlands Food and Consumer Product Safety Authority (NVWA) took action to remove websites offering harmful and prohibited substances, including addictive designer drugs and illegal medicines. The use of these substances can be dangerous. However, recent investigations have revealed that eight of these websites have since reappeared after relocating their domain names to servers abroad. This not only undermines the enforcement efforts of national judicial authorities but also makes these activities significantly more difficult to tackle. This demonstrates that criminal networks are highly adaptive and continue to exploit crossborder loopholes faster than authorities can respond, with consequences for the whole EU. On the basis of these findings: 1.

Is the Commission aware of the reported cases in which illegal drug websites reappear shortly after national enforcement measures by relocating to foreign domains or hosting providers and as a result, illegal drugs can once again be sold throughout the EU?

Does the Commission agree that the current framework for cross-border enforcement is insufficient in cases where national authorities are unable to ensure the effective removal of websites selling illegal drugs?

Which existing EU instruments can be used to improve the removal of websites offering illegal drugs and is the Commission considering additional legislative or operational measures to strengthen cross-border enforcement?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (16.9.2026) The EU rules on the fight against drug trafficking1 also apply to drug trafficking online. In line with the EU Drugs Strategy2 and Action Plan against drug trafficking3, the Commission is assessing whether these rules remain fit for purpose and contribute to effective cross-border cooperation. The findings of the evaluation are expected in 2026. The Action Plan addresses digitally enabled drug trafficking, including expanding the Europol’s4 operational support to Member States to monitor online drug markets. The Commission is working with technology companies within the EU Internet Forum5 to include measures against drug trafficking in their terms of reference and content moderation processes. The Knowledge Package on Combating Drugs Sales Online helps online platforms and law enforcement authorities moderate and remove drug-related content online. The Digital Services Act (DSA)6 requires providers of hosting services to have notice-andaction mechanisms for suspected illegal content. If found to be illegal under applicable national or EU law, the platform must act expeditiously to remove such content. The Commission is enforcing these rules to address the online sale and promotion of drugs and other illicit products7. A temporary ban of an online platform in the EU is possible as a last resort ordered by a national court, following a thorough investigation demonstrating the provider’s continued breach of the DSA. As a last resort and under strict conditions, the DSA allows national courts to leverage temporary suspensions or restrictions. To fight falsified medicines sold online, the EU Falsified Medicines Directive8 introduced safety features on medicine packs and stricter controls across the supply chain and requires common rules for legal online pharmacies9.
1 Council Framework Decision 2004/757/JHA of 25 October 2004 laying down minimum provisions on the

constituent elements of criminal acts and penalties in the field of illicit drug trafficking, OJ L 335, 11.11.2004. 2 COM(2025) 743 final. 3 COM(2025) 744 final. 4 European Union Agency for Law Enforcement Cooperation. 5 https://home-affairs.ec.europa.eu/networks/european-union-internet-forum_en. 6 Regulation 2022/2065 on a Single Market For Digital Services (Digital Services Act); https://eurlex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/2065/oj/eng. 7 For example, in March 2026 it opened proceedings against Snapchat over concerns including the promotion of illegal drugs to minors – Commission investigates Snapchat's compliance with child protection rules under the Digital Services Act, https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/news/commission-investigates-snapchatscompliance-child-protection-rules-under-digital-services-act. 8 Directive 2011/62/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 8 June 2011 amending Directive 2001/83/EC on the Community code relating to medicinal products for human use, as regards the prevention of the entry into the legal supply chain of falsified medicinal products, OJ L 174, 1.7.2011. 9 For instance the EU-wide logo that helps citizens identify authorised sellers of medicines on the internet.

E-10-2026-002964.t: Reducing administrative burdens and improving legal clarity on EUDR implementation
qt: to the Commission Katri Kulmuni (Renew) Subject:

The Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) currently creates significant administrative burdens and legal uncertainty for the European sawmill industry. Compliance requires substantial investments, while providing no direct revenue or competitiveness benefits. A major challenge is the lack of legal clarity in the regulation and the Commission’s interpretations. A more streamlined approach would focus EUDR obligations at the start of the supply chain, allow flexibility in the management of due diligence references, exempt low-risk by-products from reporting obligations, and recognise Finland’s forest-use notification system as a due diligence mechanism in low-risk countries. 1.

When will the Commission provide legally binding clarifications on the definitions of ‘operator’ and ‘placing on the market’, as well as on the obligations regarding the transfer of due diligence statement reference numbers, and how will it ensure that the aggregation and bundling of due diligence statements can be implemented flexibly and broadly across the different timber procurement models used at national level?

Does the Commission intend to exclude low-risk sawmill by-products, such as wood chips, sawdust and bark, from the scope of EUDR obligations to reduce disproportionate administrative burdens in low-risk supply chains?
Could Finland’s current forest monitoring system be recognised as fulfilling EUDR due diligence requirements in low-risk countries in order to reduce administrative burden?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.9.2026) On 4 May 2026, the Commission published a report on simplifying the EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR)1 and a set of new measures to provide additional clarity and ensure legal stability and predictability2. All simplification measures adopted since the EUDR entered into force in 2023 are expected, taken together, to reduce annual compliance costs for companies subject to EUDR obligations by 75% compared to the original EUDR. The simplification package includes updated Guidance and Frequently Asked Questions providing further clarifications, including on the definitions of ‘operator’ and ‘placing on the market’, and on obligations concerning the transfer of due diligence statement reference numbers, in line with customs legislation and legislation governing the EU single market. In particular, these documents explain that EUDR obligations focus on the first placer on the market. They were developed together with Member States and therefore constitute an important implementation tool. On 13 July 2026, a Delegated Act updating the EUDR product scope was adopted3, taking into account input received during the four-week public feedback period. The suggestion to remove wood residues and sawmill by-products was not accommodated as these products are already regulated under the EU Timber Regulation4. The request also lacked support from the relevant industry sectors. The Delegated Act is now subject to scrutiny by the European Parliament and the Council. As regards Member States’ national forest monitoring systems or databases, these can play an important role in facilitating EUDR compliance, especially of micro or small primary operators, in accordance with Article 4a(4) EUDR.
1 Regulation (EU) 2023/1115 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 31 May 2023 on the making

available on the Union market and the export from the Union of certain commodities and products associated with deforestation and forest degradation and repealing Regulation (EU) No 995/2010, OJ L 150, 9.6.2023, p. 206–247. 2 https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/api/files/document/print/en/ip_26_941/IP_26_941_EN.pdf. 3 https://environment.ec.europa.eu/news/commission-updates-product-scope-and-tools-support-eudr-2026-0713_en. 4 Regulation (EU) No 995/2010 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 20 October 2010 laying down the obligations of operators who place timber and timber products on the market, OJ L 295, 12.11.2010, pp. 23– 34.

E-10-2026-002963.t: Risk of access being suspended to the most advanced AI models, to the detriment of EU businesses
qt: to the Commission Catherine Griset (PfE) Subject:

On 15 June 2026, the US administration ordered Anthropic to block foreign nationals, including those living in the US, from accessing its best AI models: Mythos 5 and its restricted version, Fable 5. However, since Anthropic could not determine the nationality of its users with any certainty, it decided to disable its models for all customers1. Collateral victims of this decision, European companies and users have thus been put in a difficult position, revealing our dependence on the policy decisions of non-EU countries that are much more advanced with regard to digital technology. That dependence could increase in light of recent developments in China, which also has plans to limit global access to its most advanced AI models2. 1.
Given the risk of EU companies being cut off at any moment from the world’s leading AI models, is the Commission ready to boost the development of European AI models, which are few and far between?
Will there be priority access for European AI in public procurement in the EU?
Will the requirement to process EU data within our internal market be gradually implemented?

https://www.radiofrance.fr/franceculture/podcasts/un-monde-connecte/ia-blocage-d-anthropic-auxetrangers-son-patron-dario-amodei-pompier-pyromane-pris-a-son-propre-jeu-2380545. 2 https://siecledigital.fr/2026/07/14/pourquoi-la-chine-pourrait-bientot-limiter-lacces-mondial-a-sesmodeles-dia-les-plus-avances/. 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (7.9.2026) The Commission is committed to strengthening the development of European AI models. Through the AI Continent Action Plan1 and the InvestAI initiative2, it supports European AI developers and the infrastructure they require. Recently, it launched a call for tenders for AI Gigafactories, supported by up to EUR 10 billion in public funding and expected to unlock at least EUR 20 billion in private investment for developing advanced AI models on European infrastructure3. The European Frontier AI Initiative complements these efforts to enhance the Union’s competitiveness, sovereignty and security in frontier AI. The Cloud and AI Development Act (CADA)4, proposed by the Commission as part of the Tech Sovereignty package5, promotes sovereign services and EU added value. It obliges contracting authorities to include criteria in the procurement of cloud computing services and AI systems rewarding local innovation and supply chain resilience. Furthermore, CADA introduces a single EU-wide sovereignty framework for cloud computing services based on four assurance levels. Highly critical public sector activities will have to rely on the suitable assurance levels. The highest assurance levels are easier to attain for EU AI providers as it is more straightforward for them to demonstrate conformity with several of the sovereignty requirements, notably the absence of third-country influence. Every EU assurance level under the CADA proposal requires customer data to in principle remain exclusively within the EU. This requirement applies to all cloud computing services supplied to public sector bodies.
