E-10-2026-002893.t: Risks of organised crime infiltrating the main agri-food hubs in the European Union – the case of Vittoria fruit and vegetable market
qt: to the Commission Giuseppe Antoci (The Left) Subject:

The fruit and vegetable market in Vittoria (Sicily) is one of the main European hubs for the marketing of fruit and vegetables and plays a strategic role for the EU’s agri-food sectors. Over the years, investigative and judicial activities have highlighted the risk of organised crime infiltrating the fruit and vegetable sector, transport and logistics. Recent information has also highlighted the possible use of commercial and logistical networks related to this hub for transnational illicit trafficking, including drug trafficking1. In the light of the European Union’s objective of combating organised crime and protecting the integrity of the internal market and EU financial interests: 1.

Is the Commission aware of the risks of organised crime infiltrating the main European agri-food hubs, with particular reference to the Vittoria market, and does it consider it appropriate to assess the impact on the internal market?

Does it consider the monitoring tools and conditionality instruments to be up to the job of ensuring EU funds, in particular those under the common agricultural policy and cohesion policy, are not paid out to businesses affected by disqualifications or infiltrated by organised crime?

Will it consider taking further EU initiatives to prevent this infiltration, by strengthening cooperation between the Member States, Europol, Eurojust and the European Public Prosecutor’s Office and checks on the traceability of supply chains and the security of commercial logistics?

If these risks materialised, there would be serious consequences for competition, the protection of honest economic operators, the safety of agri-food chains and the protection of the EU’s financial interests. 1

E-10-2026-002892.t: Mobilisation of precarious researchers at the National Research Council’s Palermo and Catania institutes and implementation of the European framework for research careers
qt: to the Commission Giuseppe Antoci (The Left) Subject:

Precarious researchers and technologists working at the Palermo and Catania institutes of Italy’s National Research Council are mobilising in protest at the failure to open pathways to permanent employment and the insufficient resources allocated to recruitment. Many of these professionals have been working in research for years, including on projects funded by the EU. Persistent precariousness risks affecting the ability of public research institutions to attract and retain talent, as well as ensure the continuity of scientific activities, thus making it harder to achieve the objectives pursued in Council Recommendation C/2023/1640 and the European Research Area. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following questions: 1.

Does it consider the systematic and prolonged use of precarious employment contracts in public research bodies to be consistent with the objectives of Recommendation C/2023/1640 and of the European Research Area?
How does it check whether the entities receiving EU funding apply the principles of the European framework for research careers, particularly with regard to the working conditions of researchers?

Does it believe that the persistent precariousness of staff working also on EU-funded projects could undermine the objectives of the European Research Area and, if so, what steps does it intend to take?

How does it check whether the entities receiving EU funding apply the principles of the European framework for research careers, particularly with regard to the working conditions of researchers?

Does it believe that the persistent precariousness of staff working also on EU-funded projects could undermine the objectives of the European Research Area and, if so, what steps does it intend to take?

(24 September 2026) The Commission considers that the systematic and prolonged use of precarious contracts for research staff is not in line with Council Recommendation C/2023/1640 and European Research Area (ERA) objectives (1). The recommendation, annexing the revised European Charter for Researchers (2), calls for open, transparent and stable career paths and identifies persistent precariousness as an obstacle to attracting and retaining talent and ensuring continuity of scientific work. The recommendation is not a legally binding instrument. The Commission monitors voluntary uptake of Charter and Code principles through the HR Strategy for Researchers and the HR Excellence in Research awar d (3), held by 22 Italian organisations, including the University of Palermo. Adherence is also a condition of participation in the Marie Skłodowska-Curie Actions. EU law permits fixed-term employment contracts, but Clause 5 of the framework Agreement on fixed-term work (Annex to Directive 1999/70) (4) requires Member States to adopt effective measures preventing misuse of successive fixed-term contracts, including for researchers. Enforcement remains a Member State responsibility. The Commission agrees that persistent precariousness undermines the ERA's objectives of attracting and retaining talent and supports Member States’ efforts to improve research careers. Under the ERA Policy Agenda 2025-2027 (5), all Member States committed to a structural policy on research careers, cocreating guidelines to implement the recommendation and reduce precarity. The Commission is also preparing the ERA Act, a legislative instrument to further develop the European Research Area and therefore improve research careers.

Case C-326/19, Ministero dell'Istruzione, dell'Università e della Ricerca — MIUR and Others (Academic Researchers), Judgment of the Court (Seventh Chamber) of 3 June 2021, ECLI:EU:C:2021:438. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:62019CJ0326. https://euraxess.ec.europa.eu/system/files/2025-12/EC-European%20Charter%20for%20Researchers%20FINAL_WEB.pdf. https://euraxess.ec.europa.eu/hrexcellenceaward. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:31999L0070. https://european-research-area.ec.europa.eu/era-policy-agenda-2025-2027.

E-10-2026-002891.t: Use of local public resources to finance public transport for asylum seekers and compatibility with EU law
qt: to the Commission Anna Maria Cisint (PfE) Subject:

The Metropolitan City of Bologna uses its own public resources to finance public transport passes for asylum seekers hosted at contingency reception centres. Thus, local authorities are using public resources for a specific category of beneficiaries – asylum seekers, while many Italian and EU citizens who live in the same area do not receive the same treatment, raising questions about compliance with the principles of proportionality, equal treatment and sound financial management referred to in EU law. In the light of the above: 1.

Does the Commission consider it compatible with EU law to go beyond the standards laid down in EU legislation on reception by using local authorities’ own resources to provide free local public transport for asylum seekers?

Given that a large share of Italian and EU citizens who live in that area pay for this service, is this choice compatible with the principles of proportionality, nondiscrimination and sound financial management?

Will the Commission check that the use of local public resources for those purposes does not lead to unjustified preferential treatment over other categories of citizens and is consistent with the EU’s regulatory framework on reception and integration?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (2.10.2026) Under Directive (EU) 2024/13461 Member States may grant more favourable conditions to applicants for international protection, insofar as compatible with the Directive. Using financial resources to provide free public transport passes to applicants for international protection is a responsibility of the competent national, regional or local authority. Differentiated access to local benefits must comply with EU primary law, including the principles of equal treatment and non‑discrimination enshrined in the Treaties and in the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the EU, as well as with any applicable secondary legislation. Distinctions between groups of beneficiaries need an objective and proportionate justification linked to legitimate public policy aims. Under EU law, Member States remain competent to determine how national resources are used, subject to compliance with national law and applicable EU law. As noted in the first paragraph, EU law does not prevent more favourable conditions to applicants for international protection. E-10-2026-002888.t: Lab-grown meat – unanswered questions on health and consumer protection
qt: to the Commission Gerald Hauser (PfE) Subject:

Mindful to protect consumer health and preserve traditional food production, Italy has spoken out against the production and marketing of lab-grown meat. At EU level, meanwhile, discussions are still underway about authorising novel foods. Serious doubts abound as to whether the health effects of lab-grown meat have been sufficiently probed. In particular, there are no long-term findings on the likely consequences of regular consumption. Unanswered questions include those concerning the stability and safety of the cell lines used, possible production residues, the use of growth factors and culture media, possible microbial contamination, and potential allergenic or other previously insufficiently investigated effects on the human body. In line with the precautionary principle, food should only be authorised for widespread use once its safety has been fully established through scientific evidence. 1.
Why does the Commission not follow Italy’s lead and advocate an EU-wide ban on labgrown meat?
What long-term scientific studies form the basis of the Commission’s assumption that the regular consumption of lab-grown meat poses no risk to consumer health?

In view of the scientific misgivings that exist and the precautionary principle, does the Commission consider it prudent to authorise lab-grown meat, or will it decline to grant such an authorisation in order to protect EU public health?
at: (English version) to the Commission Gerald Hauser (PfE) (13 July 2026) Subject: Lab-grown meat — unanswered questions on health and consumer protection Mindful to protect consumer health and preserve traditional food production, Italy has spoken out against the production and marketing of lab-grown meat. At EU level, meanwhile, discussions are still underway about authorising novel foods. Serious doubts abound as to whether the health effects of lab-grown meat have been sufficiently probed. In particular, there are no long-term findings on the likely consequences of regular consumption. Unanswered questions include those concerning the stability and safety of the cell lines used, possible production residues, the use of growth factors and culture media, possible microbial contamination, and potential allergenic or other previously insufficiently investigated effects on the human body. In line with the precautionary principle, food should only be authorised for widespread use once its safety has been fully established through scientific evidence. 1.
Why does the Commission not follow Italy’s lead and advocate an EU-wide ban on lab-grown meat?

2. What long-term scientific studies form the basis of the Commission’s assumption that the regular consumption of labgrown meat poses no risk to consumer health? 3. In view of the scientific misgivings that exist and the precautionary principle, does the Commission consider it prudent to authorise lab-grown meat, or will it decline to grant such an authorisation in order to protect EU public health? (7 September 2026) Lab-grown meat is regulated in the EU under Regulation (EU) 2015/2283 (1) on novel foods. That regulation requires prior authorisation following a stringent scientific risk assessment carried out by the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) for any new novel food that an applicant wishes to place on the EU market. It is for the applicant to demonstrate the safety of its product through a comprehensive dossier covering, among others, the production process and compositional, nutritional and toxicological data, including, where necessary, data on longer-term consumption (2). To date, two applications for cell-based meat have been submitted to the Commission under Regulation (EU) 2015/2283 — for one EFSA is conducting the scientific risk assessment, while for the other further information is awaited to complete the application dossier. The Commission must apply the procedures laid down in the regulation when an application is submitted, while ensuring a high level of health protection and the proper functioning of the internal market. The Commission is aware of the societal debate surrounding cell-based meat, including ethical, socioeconomic and environmental considerations. Other legitimate factors than food safety may also, where appropriate, be taken into account in the decision-making process. However, the Commission cannot prejudge the outcome of that process, in which the protection of public health will remain the primary consideration.

E-10-2026-002887.t: Contamination by PFAS from wind turbines
qt: to the Commission Gerald Hauser (PfE) Subject:

Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are water-, fat- and heat-resistant chemicals and are found in many everyday products. They do not break down easily and therefore accumulate over time in soil, water, plants, animals and ultimately in humans. These ‘forever chemicals’ are highly toxic to humans and the environment. Among other things, they have an effect on hormones, damage the immune system, impair fertility and can cause cancer. Wind farms continually contaminate their surroundings with PFAS. These are found, inter alia, in the coatings of the blades, which are exposed to abrasion, as well as in transmissions, storage systems, lubricants, hydraulic fluids and cable insulation. As a result, more than 200 chemicals, including PFAS, are released from wind turbines into the air, soil, gardens, surface water and groundwater. Denmark and Sweden have recognised the risk and introduced significantly stricter limits than the European Union for certain PFAS – these limits being 25 and 50 times lower, respectively. 1.
What does the Commission intend to do to finally ban PFAS?
What does the Commission intend to do to stop the ongoing contamination of humans, animals and the environment by PFAS from wind turbines?
What is the Commission’s position regarding the numerous statements by environmental experts and doctors that the current EU limits for PFAS are far too high?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.9.2026) A restriction proposal covering all per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) was submitted by five national authorities1 under the Regulation concerning the Registration, Evaluation, Authorisation and Restriction of Chemicals (REACH)2 in 2023. This proposal, universal in its scope (i.e. covering all PFAS), is currently being assessed by the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA). Wind turbines are one of the sub-uses under the energy sector assessed in detail during this process in terms of risk, availability of alternatives and socioeconomic impacts3. However, the risk assessment is carried out per (sub)use and not necessarily per individual technology. Once finalised, ECHA’s Committees’ final opinions will be the basis for the Commission to prepare a restriction proposal for the placing on the market and use of PFAS, taking into account all relevant information. While waiting for ECHA’s final scientific assessment, the Commission cannot anticipate how the use of PFAS in wind turbines will be addressed. Nonetheless, as announced in the Chemicals Industry Action Plan4, the Commission is fully committed to minimising PFAS emissions and addressing the pollution caused by PFAS to protect the health of EU citizens and the environment. Where adequate alternatives in terms of performance and safety are not available, the continued use of PFAS in industrial applications may be allowed for critical applications, under specific conditions until acceptable substitutes are found. Possible derogations for uses of PFAS will need to be accompanied by requirements to reduce emissions at all lifecycle stages to limit the release of pollutants into the environment and by clear incentives to innovate towards finding alternatives.
1 Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden. 2 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02006R1907-20260511. 3 https://chem.echa.europa.eu/api-activity-
list/v1/restrictionProcess/documents?name=90261f0ec4fde13102704a507698a6e6_rest_pfas_12_energy_rac_en. pdf. 4 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:52025DC0530.

E-10-2026-002886.t: Consistency between EU industrial decarbonisation funding and the EU’s restrictive measures: the case of ROCKWOOL
qt: to the Commission Anthony Smith (The Left) Subject:

The ROCKWOOL Group continued to operate four factories in Russia following the invasion of Ukraine, until they were decreed to be under external administration in January 2026. According to its accounts, in 2025 its Russian operations made a turnover of EUR 261 million and an operating profit of EUR 78 million. Investigations by journalists have revealed that ROCKWOOL products have been supplied, via distributors, to 31 Russian ships and submarines, and that they are present in occupied Ukrainian territories, including Mariupol. At the same time, a project to build a ROCKWOOL facility in France is receiving EUR 10.6 million in public funding under the ‘decarbonisation of industry’ scheme, itself co-funded to the tune of 40 per cent from by the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF). 1.

Does the Commission run checks to ensure that recipients of decarbonisation aid reimbursed by the RRF comply with the Union’s restrictive measures and have no links with the Russian war economy or the development of the occupied territories?
Does it consider that such a company should, in the interests of consistency in policy, be eligible for European funding, and what conditions govern the use of these funds?
Does it intend to publish guidelines to rule out EU industrial and decarbonisation funding for companies linked to the Russian war economy or the development of occupied territories?

E-10-2026-002885.t: Reassessment of the scope of the EU Deforestation Regulation in light of new scientific evidence
qt: to the Commission Sebastian Kruis (PfE) Subject:

A recent peer-reviewed study published in Nature Food (Singh and Persson, 2026)1 provides new evidence on commodity-driven deforestation and associated carbon emissions. The study concludes that, between 2001 and 2022, the overwhelming majority of commodity-driven deforestation is linked to cattle meat (42 %), oil palm and soy (16 %) and forest plantations (14 %). By contrast, stimulant and aromatic crops, mainly cocoa and coffee, account for 2 % and 1 % respectively of global commodity-driven deforestation. At the same time, the EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) imposes significant compliance, traceability and administrative burdens on producers, small and medium-sized enterprises, importers and consumers, including partner countries closely tied to the EU through trade agreements. 1.
Will the Commission reassess whether the current product scope of the EUDR remains proportionate to the real drivers of global deforestation?

How does the Commission justify maintaining cocoa and coffee within the scope of the Regulation when the latest scientific evidence indicates that their contribution to global deforestation is negligible compared with that of other commodities?

Does the Commission still intend to proceed with the implementation of the EUDR? If so, will it consider removing low-impact commodities such as coffee and cocoa from the scope to reduce unnecessary economic and political burdens on European consumers and partner countries?
https://www.nature.com/articles/s43016-026-01305-4.
at: (English version) to the Commission Sebastian Kruis (PfE) (13 July 2026) Subject: Reassessment of the scope of the EU Deforestation Regulation in light of new scientific evidence A recent peer-reviewed study published in Nature Food (Singh and Persson, 2026) (1) provides new evidence on commoditydriven deforestation and associated carbon emissions. The study concludes that, between 2001 and 2022, the overwhelming majority of commodity-driven deforestation is linked to cattle meat (42%), oil palm and soy (16%) and forest plantations (14%). By contrast, stimulant and aromatic crops, mainly cocoa and coffee, account for 2% and 1% respectively of global commodity-driven deforestation. At the same time, the EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) imposes significant compliance, traceability and administrative burdens on producers, small and medium-sized enterprises, importers and consumers, including partner countries closely tied to the EU through trade agreements. 1. Will the Commission reassess whether the current product scope of the EUDR remains proportionate to the real drivers of global deforestation? 2. How does the Commission justify maintaining cocoa and coffee within the scope of the regulation when the latest scientific evidence indicates that their contribution to global deforestation is negligible compared with that of other commodities? 3. Does the Commission still intend to proceed with the implementation of the EUDR? If so, will it consider removing lowimpact commodities such as coffee and cocoa from the scope to reduce unnecessary economic and political burdens on European consumers and partner countries? (25 August 2026) The list of relevant commodities covered by the EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) (1) was defined through the impact assessment accompanying the original EUDR proposal (2). The list of commodities, which was endorsed and expanded by the European Parliament and the Council during the legislative negotiations, was based on literature review and an efficiency analysis which compared the hectares of deforestation linked to EU consumption with the average value of EU imports. Article 34(2) mandates the Commission to carry out a general review of the EUDR by 30 June 2030 and at least every five years thereafter and present a report to the European Parliament and the Council accompanied, if appropriate, by a legislative proposal. The first of these reports shall include an evaluation of change in trade patterns of relevant commodities and the impact of those commodities on deforestation and forest degradation. The Commission will therefore assess the list of relevant commodities covered by the EUDR in this context. With less than five months before the entry into application of the EUDR, the Commission’s priority is to ensure a stable and predictable legal framework for all stakeholders in order to safeguard the public and private investments made so far to ensure compliance. In this regard, the Commission published in May 2026 the Simplification Review of the EUDR (3), in line with Article 34(1a). The Review contains a report on the simplification of the EUDR and a set of further measures for a smooth implementation, including a Delegated Act with simplifications and targeted changes to the EUDR product scope. The Delegated Act was adopted by the Commission on 13 July 2026, and it is now with the European Parliament and the Council for the two months scrutiny period.

E-10-2026-002884.t: Possible road toll discrimination in Belgium
qt: to the Commission Auke Zijlstra (PfE), Sebastian Kruis (PfE) Subject:

According to the business newspaper De Tijd, the Belgian Government intends to introduce tolls on the road network via a digital tax disk from 1 May 2027.1 Belgian citizens will be compensated through a reduction in road tax, meaning that, in reality, only foreign drivers will be affected by this proposal. In 2017, Dutch Minister Van Nieuwenhuizen took the matter to the Court of Justice of the European Union to challenge similar discriminatory toll plans by Germany.2 In view of this: 1.
What is the Commission’s position on this proposal by the Belgian Government?
Does the Commission consider this proposal to be compatible with the European single market?

Should this plan be implemented, does the Commission intend to bring a case before the Court of Justice of the European Union on behalf of the Member States and/or to take measures against the Belgian Government to have this plan annulled?

at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.9.2026) 1 and 2. Tolls and user charges (the latter also commonly known as ‘vignettes’) are regulated in the EU under Directive 1999/62/EC on the charging of vehicles for the use of road infrastructures1. The Belgian government intends to levy a new user charge on light-duty vehicles, including passenger cars, starting next year. While Article 7h of the Directive requires Member States to notify in advance new tolls for heavy-duty vehicles, this notification requirement does not apply to the present case as light-duty vehicles are not in scope of this notification requirement. Directive 1999/62/EC does not prevent by itself reforms of other national legislation at the same time as the implementation of a new road charge. However, all national legislation must comply with the EU treaties, including Article 18 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union on non-discrimination on grounds of nationality. 3. The Commission may assess the compliance of the new charging system with EU law and, should a breach of EU law be identified, it may initiate the necessary steps to ensure that it complies with EU law, including with the principle of non-discrimination.

E-10-2026-002883.t: Transparency obligation and minimum remuneration rates for staff serving in Luxembourg
qt: to the Commission Fernand Kartheiser (NI) Subject:

On 17 June 2026, the General Court of the Court of Justice of the European Union reaffirmed the principle that any administrative decision affecting the rights of a staff member must be reasoned in a clear, precise and transparent manner and ordered the European institutions to comply with that principle (Case T-121/25, Asma Gharbi v European Commission). 1.
Following the transparency obligation imposed by the General Court, how will the Commission implement it in its relations with its agents?

Does the Commission intend to adjust the remuneration of its staff serving in Luxembourg so that it is at least equal to the minimum social wage applicable to qualified workers in that Member State, as is already the case in the European Parliament and the Court of Justice?
If so, will it also ensure that its method of calculating remuneration is indexed to the inflation rate in force in Luxembourg?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (8.9.2026) 1. Before accepting an offer of employment, prospective Commission staff are informed about their financial rights, social measures and working conditions in Luxembourg. Following Case T-121/25, the Commission has strengthened its communication on individual financial entitlements and eligibility for non-statutory social assistance measure for staff earning below the statutory minimum wage in Luxembourg. 2. The Commission Decision on a payment of social assistance to some Commission staff members employed in Luxembourg (C(2015)4907) already ensures that no staff member receives a net remuneration below the corresponding statutory minimum wage in Luxembourg. More precisely, the Commission compares its staff members’ individual net remuneration with the net remuneration that the same person would hypothetically receive under Luxembourgish law, taking into account their personal situation (e.g. family situation). Hence, the Commission’s legal framework addresses in a targeted and efficient manner the situation of staff members in Luxembourg whose remuneration could be inferior to the statutory minimum wage in Luxembourg. 3. The social assistance in the above-mentioned Commission Decision is subject to a yearly review, ensuring that Commission staff members in Luxembourg always receive a net remuneration corresponding to the statutory minimum wage for a qualified worker as defined under the Luxembourg Labour Code. The Commission scheme takes into account the possibility for Luxembourg to increase the minimum level of salaries for qualified workers (e.g. to address the evolution of the cost of living in Luxembourg). The net payments granted to staff members are adjusted accordingly.

E-10-2026-002880.t: Drone attacks against civilians in Western Sahara
qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Isabel Serra Sánchez (The Left), Estrella Galán (The Left), Jaume Asens Llodrà (Verts/ALE), João Oliveira (The Left), Catarina Martins (The Left), Jussi Saramo (The Left), Oihane Agirregoitia Martínez (Renew), Martin Günther (The Left), Vladimir Prebilič (Verts/ALE), Lynn Boylan (The Left) Subject:

Since the resumption of hostilities in Western Sahara in November 2020, there has been a documented increase in the number of drone attacks carried out by the Moroccan Armed Forces against civilians east of the Berm. According to the Sahrawi Mine Action Coordination Office, 129 attacks and more than 310 victims, including women and minors, were recorded between 2021 and 2025. Those affected include travellers, herders and other people engaged in civilian activities, many of whom were attacked hundreds of kilometres away from combat zones. The updated report estimates that 63 % of the victims were killed. The report also documents forced displacement, the destruction of vehicles and livelihoods, and serious psychological consequences, and raises concerns about possible violations of the principles of distinction, proportionality, precaution and military necessity. Western Sahara remains a non-self-governing territory pending decolonisation. 1.

Will the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy (VP/HR) call for an international, independent and impartial investigation into these attacks?

Does the VP/HR consider the maintenance of trade agreements with Morocco to be compatible with the repeated allegations of violations of human rights and international humanitarian law in Western Sahara?

What measures will the VP/HR take to ensure that no technology, components, funding or military cooperation from the EU or its Member States contribute directly or indirectly to attacks against the Sahrawi civilian population?

E-10-2026-002879.t: Explosion in Aspropyrgos injures 11 people – another warning sign of a large-scale industrial accident
qt: to the Commission Lefteris Nikolaou-Alavanos (NI) Subject:
Explosion in Aspropyrgos injures 11 people – another warning sign of a largescale industrial accident

Eleven people in the hospital, some with very severe burns – this is the result of an explosion and fire that took place at a scrap metal plant in Aspropyrgos, Attica. Thousands of local residents live with the risk of inhaling dangerous substances, as they share their neighbourhood with refineries, LPG plants and other such sites. This incident is the latest in a long series of fires at industrial facilities – an issue that residents and organisations have repeatedly raised – yet no protection measures have been put in place, as they are regarded as a cost by business groups. The EU and the Nea Demokratia Government, like its predecessors, have left ordinary people in the region unprotected, refusing to implement basic protective measures and to draw up a comprehensive plan to prevent and respond to a potential large-scale industrial accident. With this in mind, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

What view does it take of the fact that, although the risks of a large-scale industrial accident in Western Attica have been repeatedly highlighted and that accidents continue to occur, no response plan has been drawn up, even though the Thriasio Plain area is home to many industrial facilities that fall under the provisions of the Seveso Directive?

What view does it take of the fact that, under the Seveso III Directive (2012/18/EU), the risk posed by substances and the assessment of the consequences of accidents on people and the environment are based primarily on self-assessments by the business groups involved, that is to say, by those responsible for the accidents?

(26 August 2026) The Seveso Directive (1) (SD) covers establishments where dangerous substances may be present in quantities above certain thresholds. According to the Commission’s information (2), the plant referred to by the Honourable Member is not a Seveso establishment. Thus, it is not subject to the obligations set out in the SD. Other establishments in Aspropyrgos are indeed Seveso establishments. For those, the SD requires operators to take necessary measures to prevent accidents and limit their consequences (3). It is for the competent authorities to enforce such measures and to conduct thorough risk assessments and evaluations, based on operators’ inputs (4), considering also effects coming from non-Seveso plants. The SD requires that safety information and measures be communicated to local authorities (5) and the public (6). It stresses the importance of preparing and implementing major-accident prevention policies (7). In addition to the SD, other EU occupational safety and health Directives also set out preventive and protective measures (8). The Commission regularly evaluates the implementation by Member States of EU legislatio n (9). However, the primary responsibility for implementing EU legislation lies with national authorities. Likewise, national courts are best placed for applying EU law effectively in cases citizens would challenge the liability of operators for the damages created by such accidents. E-10-2026-002878.t: The EU Biotech Act – implications for competitiveness and healthcare systems
qt: to the Commission Stanisław Tyszka (ESN) Subject:

The Commission has portrayed the European Biotech Act as an instrument that will strengthen the competitiveness of the European biotechnology sector by streamlining procedures, supporting strategic projects and improving access to funding. The proposal covers, amongst other things, clinical trials, advanced therapies, biological and biosimilar medicines and incentives for investment and production within the EU. At the same time, it may have implications for competition, public expenditure and the geographical distribution of investment. In light of the above: 1.

Why did the Commission not present, alongside the proposal, a standard, comprehensive impact assessment reviewed by the Regulatory Scrutiny Board, despite its potentially significant impact on competition, Member States’ budgets, medicine prices and administrative burdens, and why was the analytical supporting document only published after the legislative procedure had begun?

How does the Commission intend to prevent the concentration of funding, strategic projects and biotechnology investments in a handful of the most developed Member States, and to ensure the genuine involvement of companies and research centres from Central and Eastern Europe, including Poland?

How does the Commission intend to ensure that the development of new and often very costly biotechnology therapies does not widen the gap in access to treatment between wealthier and less affluent Member States?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (24.9.2026) The President of the Commission announced in her Political Guidelines of July 2024 a Biotech Act by 20251. The need to act swiftly was highlighted in the Draghi Report2 and echoed by stakeholders given the strong economic, social and public health potential of the health biotech sector. The Commission extensively consulted a broad range of stakeholders and commissioned several supporting studies. This resulted in two well-grounded, evidencebased proposals3 (collectively referred to as the ’Biotech Act’) and a Staff Working Document4, prepared in line with Better Regulation rules, that brings together all the evidence and assesses the expected impacts of the proposal. The industrial policy measures included in the proposed Biotech Act foster, with a specific focus on health, food and feed, multi-country cooperation and information sharing, thus building on the capabilities of all Member States. The measures also provide for the establishment of a European Health Biotechnology Steering Group5 where all Member States would be represented and, together with the Commission coordinate their implementation. The proposed Biotech Act includes measures to accelerate and streamline the assessment of clinical trial applications, which support the development of health treatments and medicines and are an opportunity to give patients early access across the EU. Moreover, other initiatives, like the reform of the EU pharmaceutical legislation6, the Critical Medicines Act7 and the Health Technology Regulation8 aim to improve availability of medicines in the EU. In addition, the European Reference Networks9 facilitate cross-border exchange of expert knowledge to improve the diagnosis and treatment of rare and complex diseases across the EU.

E-10-2026-002877.t: Meta’s new AI tool, Muse Image, exploits the content of public accounts
qt: to the Commission Sandro Gozi (Renew) Subject:

According to several press reports, Meta has launched Muse Image, a generative AI tool that would allow public content published on Instagram and Facebook by users with public profiles to be used for generating or modifying images, unless the user explicitly objects. The fact that a profile is public cannot, on its own, be equated with explicit consent for the person’s image to be used to create AI-generated content. That practice raises serious questions in light of the General Data Protection Regulation, the Digital Services Act and Article 50 of the AI Act, which impose transparency obligations for artificially generated or manipulated content, including deepfakes. 1.

Does the Commission consider that, under EU law, Meta Image can use an opt-out mechanism or option to collect consent for using a picture of an identifiable individual to generate realistic content with AI?
Will it ask Meta to clarify whether Muse Image is or will be available in the EU and what safeguards will be put in place in relation to consent, transparency and withdrawal?
What action will it take to prevent platforms from reusing publicly available content to generate deepfakes or other AI-manipulated content without an appropriate legal basis or explicit consent?

(16 September 2026) Meta announced on 10 July 2026 that the functionality allowing users to reference public Instagram accounts in image generation prompts is no longer available (1). Under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) (2), consent is one of the six lawful grounds for personal data processing. Another ground is the pursuit of a legitimate interest under Article 6(1)(f) of the GDPR, provided all conditions are met (3). When assessing whether the legitimate interest of the controller or a third party does not override the rights and interests of the data subject, his or her reasonable expectations should also be considered. Data subjects are more likely to reasonably expect the processing of their personal data held in open profiles (4). Data subjects have a right to object to such processing on grounds relating to their situation. The enforcement of the GDPR in individual cases lies with the national competent data protection authorities and the courts (5). As designated very large online platforms (VLOPs) under the Digital Services Act (DSA ) (6), Facebook and Instagram must assess and mitigate systemic risks, which may include prominently marking generated or manipulated content resembling real persons. The Commission monitors the roll-out of generative AI functionalities in VLOPs and may require information under Article 67 of the DSA or open proceedings. E-10-2026-002876.t: Resilience of Commission buildings to heatwaves and coherence with EU policies
qt: to the Commission Stanisław Tyszka (ESN) Subject:

According to Politico, on 26 June 2026, air conditioning on floors one through seven was switched off in one of the Commission's main buildings, while air conditioning on higher floors continued to operate. Trade unions representing the staff of EU institutions, including U4U, are also drawing attention to wider air-conditioning problems in Commission buildings and the impact this has on working conditions. The Commission promotes adapting infrastructure and public administration to heatwaves and assessing climate risks, and also highlights the leading role that the public sector plays in energy efficiency. EU institutional buildings should therefore lead by example in combining climate resilience, energy efficiency and adequate working conditions. 1.
What technical or organisational criteria have led to air conditioning only operating on some floors of this building?
Has the Commission carried out an assessment of the resilience of its buildings and their cooling systems to increasingly frequent heatwaves?

How does the Commission ensure that the management of its own buildings remains consistent with the climate resilience, energy efficiency and public administration preparation standards it promotes vis-à-vis the Member States?

The Commission promotes adapting infrastructure and public administration to heatwaves and assessing climate risks, and also highlights the leading role that the public sector plays in energy efficiency. EU institutional buildings should therefore lead by example in combining climate resilience, energy efficiency and adequate working conditions. 1.
What technical or organisational criteria have led to air conditioning only operating on some floors of this building?

2. Has the Commission carried out an assessment of the resilience of its buildings and their cooling systems to increasingly frequent heatwaves? 3. How does the Commission ensure that the management of its own buildings remains consistent with the climate resilience, energy efficiency and public administration preparation standards it promotes vis-à-vis the Member States? (18 September 2026) 1. Due to technical reasons, the air conditioning system in the Berlaymont building had to progressively switch off on Friday 26 June 2026 afternoon, floor by floor. Before the end of the day, the entire building was without cooling system. This was done to prevent the cooling system from stalling, which could have led to more long-lasting consequences. 2. The Commission carries out climate vulnerability and risk assessments for all new buildings and continuously assesses the fitness of its buildings. These assessments can lead to technical adjustments or renovation of older buildings to improve energy performance and increase climate resilience. 3. The Commission integrates the climate resilience and energy efficiency standards it promotes externally in its internal buildings policy, with measures such as passive cooling, shading and improved insulation forming an integral part of its renovation and maintenance programmes.

qt: to the Commission Alexander Jungbluth (ESN) Subject:

The official line on the rule of law mechanism is that it is based on objective criteria, four standardised pillars for analysis, the annual rule of law cycle (comprising reports, focused dialogues and country visits) and the requirements of Regulation (EU, Euratom) 2020/2092. Nevertheless, its practical application in procedures against individual Member State casts considerable doubt on just how objective and consistent the mechanism really is. 1.
How does the Commission make sure that decisions on which Member States to prioritise in the annual visit schedules and dialogues are purely objective and free from political influence?
When taking decisions on the introduction and intensity of measures, to what extent is it ensured that a uniform and comparable approach is adopted for all Member States facing similar challenges?
What safeguards are in place to ensure that Article 7 measures are lifted only if specifically agreed reforms have been carried out, rather than as a result of shifting political influences?
at: (English version) to the Commission Alexander Jungbluth (ESN) (13 July 2026) Subject: Rule of law mechanism The official line on the rule of law mechanism is that it is based on objective criteria, four standardised pillars for analysis, the annual rule of law cycle (comprising reports, focused dialogues and country visits) and the requirements of Regulation (EU, Euratom) 2020/2092. Nevertheless, its practical application in procedures against individual Member State casts considerable doubt on just how objective and consistent the mechanism really is. 1. How does the Commission make sure that decisions on which Member States to prioritise in the annual visit schedules and dialogues are purely objective and free from political influence? 2. When taking decisions on the introduction and intensity of measures, to what extent is it ensured that a uniform and comparable approach is adopted for all Member States facing similar challenges? 3. What safeguards are in place to ensure that Article 7 measures are lifted only if specifically agreed reforms have been carried out, rather than as a result of shifting political influences? (17 September 2026) The Commission’s annual Rule of Law Cycle (1), with the Rule of Law Report at its centre, is an instrument for monitoring and dialogue, aiming to prevent rule of law challenges from emerging or deepening. The report is based on a transparent and objective methodology (2), the result of close collaboration and dialogue with national authorities and relies on input from a variety of sources. The Commission conducts virtual or in-person country visits in all Member States every year, which include meetings with national authorities, independent bodies and stakeholders, ensuring the respect of equal treatment and proportionality. The regulation on a general regime of conditionality (3) can be applied in case of breaches of the principles of the rule of law which affect or seriously risk affecting the sound financial management of the EU budget or the protection of the financial interests of the EU in a sufficiently direct way. It can be applied only if no other EU law instruments protect the EU budget more effectively. When identifying and assessing breaches of the principles of the rule of law that may be relevant for the application of the general regime of conditionality, the Rule of Law report is one of the sources of information the Commission takes into account. Measures under the regulation are enacted and lifted by a Council decision (taken by qualified majority), based on a proposal by the Commission. As regards the procedure enshrined under Article 7 of the Treaty on European Union, the Commission notes that it is separate from the annual Rule of Law Cycle. Under that procedure, it is exclusively the Council that may decide to vary or revoke measures imposed on the Member State subject to that procedure.

France was recently shaken by a case of violent child sexual abuse that resulted in the victim’s death. The case exposed systemic failures and illustrates the need for a rapid, coordinated and victim-centred response to sexual violence. In Belgium, ten sexual assault centres provide an integrated model of care, offering medical, psychological and legal support under one roof, including emergency nursing care, case management and the possibility of a police interview at a single location. Such multidisciplinary centres can contribute to the earlier detection of sexual violence, improved collection of forensic evidence, and coordinated follow-up between healthcare and judicial services, thereby reducing the risk of further escalation and repeat victimisation. Directive (EU) 2024/1385 on combating violence against women and domestic violence1 requires Member States to provide victims of sexual violence with access to free medical and forensic examinations through coordinated support centres. The deadline for transposition is 14 June 2027. 1.

E-10-2026-002871.t: Taking account of the outermost regions’ specific characteristics in the revision of State aid for air transport
qt: to the Commission Marie-Luce Brasier-Clain (PfE), Mathilde Androuët (PfE), Volker Schnurrbusch (ESN), Valérie Deloge (PfE), Catherine Griset (PfE), António Tânger Corrêa (PfE), Alvise Pérez (NI), Jorge Martín Frías (PfE), Julie Rechagneux (PfE), Margarita de la Pisa Carrión (PfE), Pierre Pimpie (PfE) Subject:

The Commission has launched a revision of the guidelines on State aid in the air transport sector to take account of decarbonisation goals in particular. The outermost regions (ORs), recognised under Article 349 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, continue to grapple with permanent structural constraints as a result of their remoteness, insularity and reliance on air transport. Air transport is essential to ensuring they remain connected to the mainland and have access to care, education, employment and local economic development. In view of the above: 1.

How does the Commission intend to ensure that the revision of the guidelines and decarbonisation objectives does not result in fewer air connections or higher travel costs for residents in the outermost regions?

Does it intend to maintain or adapt support mechanisms for strategic air links serving the ORs, including links with nearby third countries, as those links help open up those territories, keep them connected to the mainland and contribute to their economic development?

How does the Commission intend to take into account the complementary nature of certain airport infrastructure located in the ORs when that infrastructure specific access and resilience needs in those regions?
Supporter1
This question is supported by a Member other than the authors: Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE).
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (2.9.2026) The draft Air Transport guidelines1, as recently published for public consultation from 11 May 2026 – 11 June 2026, specifically address the constraints faced by remote regions, including outermost regions. For example, they provide for a bonus for investment aid projects and when it comes to the designation of outermost regions airports as Services of General Economic Interest. In the parallel, as part of the revision of the General Block Exemption Regulation2 the Commission proposes to raise the notification threshold for operating and investment aid to airports from 200,000 to 500,000 passengers per year, which will considerably simplify the granting of aid to many airports, including in the outermost regions. The Commission is currently assessing the feedback to the public consultation. This will feed into the revision, and the Commission will ensure that both the special situation of outermost regions and all relevant EU objectives such as territorial and social cohesion, regional development and decarbonisation are duly considered. When it comes to safeguarding essential air services at affordable terms, the existing State aid framework allows Member States to impose public service obligations pursuant to Regulation (EC) No 1008/2008 (intra-EU routes) or rely on social aid (in principle also for routes connecting an EU airport to a non-EU airport). These possibilities remain unaffected by the ongoing revision.

E-10-2026-002870.t: Risk of extinction of the Pityusan wall lizard (Podarcis pityusensis) due to the spread of invasive snakes, and the adequacy of current quarantine measures
qt: to the Commission Jaume Asens Llodrà (Verts/ALE), César Luena (S&D), Irene Montero (The Left), Javi López (S&D), Alicia Homs Ginel (S&D), Sandra Gómez López (S&D), Leire Pajín (S&D), Lena Schilling (Verts/ALE), Rosa Estaràs Ferragut (PPE), Jutta Paulus (Verts/ALE), Manuela Ripa (PPE) Subject:

The Pityusan wall lizard (Podarcis pityusensis), an endemic species of Ibiza and Formentera listed in Annexes II and IV of the Habitats Directive (92/43/EEC) and reclassified in 2024 by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) as ‘endangered’, faces a direct threat from the spread of invasive snakes (Hemorrhois hippocrepis), whose main pathway of introduction is the transport of large ornamental olive trees and other ornamental trees from the Iberian Peninsula, which are intended for gardening and landscaping. According to the IbizaPreservation foundation and herpetologists at the University of Salamanca, the current quarantine measures are proving insufficient to halt the spread of invasive snakes, with documented cases of local extinction on several islets. 1.
What measures does the Commission intend to adopt to ensure the effective protection of this species?
Has the Commission assessed whether the current quarantine measures are effective and compatible with the strict protection obligations under Article 12 of Directive 92/43/EEC?
at: DE Antwort von Jessika Roswall im Namen der Europäischen Kommission (1.9.2026) Der Kommission sind die Bedenken hinsichtlich des Erhaltungszustands der PityusenEidechse1 bekannt, einer auf Ibiza, Formentera und den umliegenden Inseln endemischen Art, die gemäß der Habitat-Richtlinie streng geschützt2 und auch in zwölf Natura-2000-Gebieten geschützt3 ist. Der Kommission ist auch die von der invasiven Schlangenart ausgehende Bedrohung bewusst. Mit der Richtlinie wird ein Rahmen für die Erhaltung von Arten und Lebensräumen von EU-weiter Bedeutung geschaffen, und die Mitgliedstaaten sind verpflichtet, die erforderlichen Maßnahmen zu ergreifen, um die Ziele der Richtlinie zu verwirklichen. Daher fallen die Gestaltung und Umsetzung von Artenschutzstrategien, einschließlich Maßnahmen zur Bekämpfung invasiver Arten, weiterhin in erster Linie in die Zuständigkeit der einschlägigen nationalen und regionalen Behörden. Um die Mitgliedstaaten bei dieser Aufgabe zu unterstützen, hat die Kommission häufig gestellte Fragen dazu veröffentlicht, wie die Verordnung über invasive gebietsfremde Arten4 mit den EU-Naturschutzrichtlinien5 zusammenwirkt. Die spanischen und balearischen Behörden haben legislative, administrative und praktische Maßnahmen ergriffen, um der Bedrohung der Pityusen-Eidechse entgegenzuwirken6. Im Rahmen des EU-Programms für Umwelt- und Klimapolitik unterstützt die Kommission diese Bemühungen durch das spezifische, von der EU kofinanzierte Projekt: „LIFE Reptiles“7. Die Kommission unterhält überdies fachliche Dialoge mit den spanischen Behörden, um Unterstützung anzubieten und Herausforderungen und Lösungen bei der Umsetzung zu erörtern.
1 Podarcis pityusensis. 2 Richtlinie 92/43/EWG des Rates vom 21. Mai 1992 zur Erhaltung der natürlichen Lebensräume sowie der wild

lebenden Tiere und Pflanzen (ABl. L 206 vom 22.7.1992, S. 7). 3 https://biodiversity.europa.eu/species/768. 4 Verordnung (EU) Nr. 1143/2014 des Europäischen Parlaments und des Rates vom 22. Oktober 2014 über die Prävention und das Management der Einbringung und Ausbreitung invasiver gebietsfremder Arten (ABl. L 317 vom 4.11.2014, S. 35). 5 https://circabc.europa.eu/ui/group/3f466d71-92a7-49eb-9c63-6cb0fadf29dc/library/dc8502c3-6028-45f9-b2bf6600cb267d61/details. 6 https://www.miteco.gob.es/es/biodiversidad/temas/conservacion-de-especies/especies-exoticas-invasoras/ceeei-catalogo.html. https://www.caib.es/webgoib/w/el-govern-destina-gaireb%C3%A9-dos-milions-d-euros-de-l-its-per-controlarles-esp%C3%A8cies-invasores-a-les-piti%C3%BCses-i-per-construir-un-centre-de-recuperaci%C3%B3-defauna-a-eivissa. https://vlex.es/vid/decreto-ley-1-2023-934314266. https://www.caib.es/pidip2front/ficha_convocatoria.xhtml?lang=es&urlSemantica=el-govern-supera-las-4400capturas-de-serpientes-invasoras-en-las-pitiusas-y-refuerza-el-dispositivo-para-proteger-a-la-lagartija-pitiusa-. 7 Im Rahmen des LIFE-Programms wurden 4 921 282,45 EUR zur Kofinanzierung eines sechsjährigen Projekts mit einem Gesamtbudget von 8 202 137,43 EUR für den Artenschutz bereitgestellt. Mit dem Projekt wurde am 1. Juli 2026 begonnen, und es befasst sich außerdem mit vier weiteren streng geschützten endemischen Eidechsenarten auf den Balearen und Grand Canaria, die von invasiven Schlangenarten bedroht sind.

Unbeschadet der Rolle der Kommission als Hüterin der Verträge tragen die Mitgliedstaaten die Hauptverantwortung für die ordnungsgemäße Umsetzung der oben genannten Bestimmungen. Die strategische Durchsetzungspolitik der Kommission konzentriert sich auf systemische und strukturelle Probleme8.

(C(2016) 8600, ABl. C 18 vom 19.1.2017, S. 10) und in der Mitteilung vom 13. Oktober 2022 „Durchsetzung des EU-Rechts für ein Europa, das greifbare Ergebnisse liefert“ (COM(2022) 518 final) dargelegt.

E-10-2026-002869.t: Brutal crackdown on popular protests against the NATO Summit in Türkiye
qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kostas Papadakis (NI) Subject:

This year’s NATO Summit, in which very dangerous decisions were taken to the detriment of ordinary people, took place in Ankara, Türkiye. The Turkish Government quickly put on a show of power, responding to the anti-NATO protests with a brutal crackdown. Dozens were injured and arrested by the Turkish police, who spared neither members of parliament nor journalists from their sights. In fact, dozens of members of Türkiye’s Communist Party were arrested. In view of the above, can the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy say: 1.
What view does she take of the brutal crackdown on peaceful protesters by Turkish police forces and the fact that people were arrested even inside their homes to be taken into custody?

What view does she take of the calls not to prosecute protesters – both Turkish and foreign nationals – who had been arrested for expressing their opposition to NATO’s plans, which pose a danger to ordinary people?

What view does she take of the unacceptable restriction of the right to demonstrate and protest, which is regularly applied wherever the NATO Summit is organised, in this case in Ankara and throughout Türkiye?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (17.9.2026) The Commission has reiterated on numerous occasions that citizens’ participation, including through peaceful protest, is essential to the functioning of an open and democratic society. As regards individuals arrested in connection with demonstrations, the Commission has consistently called for the full respect for due process, access to legal assistance, and an individual assessment of each case on the basis of credible evidence. Peaceful protest must not in itself lead to prosecution or punitive measures. The Commission recalls that Türkiye, as a candidate country, a member of the Council of Europe and a party to the European Convention on Human Rights, is expected to uphold the highest democratic standards and to ensure an enabling environment in which people can express their opinions freely and without fear of repression. While the authorities have a duty to ensure public order and safety, any intervention by law enforcement must be strictly proportionate, based on the rule of law, and respectful of human dignity and fundamental freedoms. As noted in the 2025 enlargement report on Türkiye1, legislation governing the right to assembly and demonstration, along with its practical implementation, remains inconsistent with European standards. The Council of Europe’s Committee of Ministers had urged the authorities to amend the Law on demonstrations and meetings in line with the case law of the European Court of Human Rights and the Constitutional Court.
1 https://enlargement.ec.europa.eu/turkiye-report-2025_en.

E-10-2026-002868.t: Missing and runaway children as an indicator of violence, abuse and grooming
qt: to the Commission Magdalena Adamowicz (PPE), Ewa Kopacz (PPE), Kamila Gasiuk-Pihowicz (PPE), Bartłomiej Sienkiewicz (PPE), Marta Wcisło (PPE), Andrzej Buła (PPE), Maria Walsh (PPE), Łukasz Kohut (PPE), Rasa Juknevičienė (PPE), Javier Zarzalejos (PPE), Lukas Mandl (PPE), Caterina Chinnici (PPE), Bogdan Andrzej Zdrojewski (PPE), Malik Azmani (Renew), Jeroen Lenaers (PPE), Krzysztof Brejza (PPE) Subject:

According to Missing Children Europe’s 2025 Figures and Trends report, published in June 2026, runaway children accounted for 58 % of cases reported to Europe’s 116 000 hotline network for missing children in 2025. Missing Children Europe, AMBER Alert Europe and other watchdog organisations warn that running away is often the final result of violence, including bullying, both online and offline, and of grooming. Bullying and grooming increasingly occur online. While very large online platforms (VLOPs), especially Facebook, Instagram, Snapchat and TikTok, are well-known channels, the misuse of chat and messaging features within online multiplayer games for the purpose of grooming remains less known, documented and addressed. 1.
Will the Commission promote use of return home interviews and standardised indicators across Member States to identify whether grooming or violence preceded a child’s disappearance?
How does the Commission intend to use existing instruments, especially the Digital Services Act, to improve the early detection of violence that may lead to children going missing or running away?

Does the Commission intend to assess how online grooming, including through chat and messaging features within online multiplayer games, contributes to cases involving missing or runaway children and identify the main channels involved?

E-10-2026-002866.t: Increase in the bioethanol blending rate under the Fuel Quality Directive
qt: to the Commission Marion Maréchal (ECR), Nicolas Bay (ECR), Laurence Trochu (ECR), Guillaume Peltier (ECR), Christophe Gomart (PPE), Anne-Sophie Frigout (PfE), Waldemar Buda (ECR), Fabrice Leggeri (PfE), Diana Iovanovici Şoşoacă (NI) Subject:

In a recent letter reported in the press (April 2026), Ursula von der Leyen indicated that the Commission was in favour of revising the Fuel Quality Directive, which, notably, imposes a 10 % limit on the incorporation of bioethanol in petrol (E10) sold to consumers. This limit hinders the development of vehicles compatible with petrol with higher incorporation rates (E20, for example). Increasing this limit would strengthen the European biofuel sector and its agricultural and industrial jobs, encourage manufacturers to adopt these alternative solutions, and contribute to the security of energy supply in Europe. However, this potential revision has not yet been the subject of any official communication from the Commission. The Commission is therefore invited to answer the following questions: 1.
Does it intend to present a proposal amending the Fuel Quality Directive in the near future? If so, according to what timetable?

Given that the Renewable Energy Directive III stipulates that up to 29 % of the energy in transport fuels must come from renewable sources by 2030, what additional measures is it planning to take to develop ethanol production and achieve this ambitious target?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.9.2026) The Fuel Quality Directive1 sets minimum quality requirements for petrol and diesel fuels placed on the EU market with the aim to establish a single fuel market. Currently, the maximum permitted ethanol content in petrol is set at 10% (E10). The Commission acknowledges the role that higher biofuel blends can play to decarbonise the existing vehicles fleets. In the context of the revision of the fuels-related policy framework, the Commission will look into the possibility to enable the higher blends, E20 for example, taking into account possible issues related to engines compatibility as well as the need to incentivise investments in advanced biofuels. Under the Renewable Energy Directive2, it is for Member States, in line with the principle of subsidiarity, to decide how to meet the 2030 transport target. The Commission continues to support all renewable transport solutions, such as certified biofuel feedstocks, advancing electrification and strengthening the overall framework for renewable energy in transport.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2009/30/oj/eng. 2 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2023/2413/oj/eng.

qt: to the Commission Regina Doherty (PPE) Subject:

Presented in September 2022, the European care strategy set out to improve the availability, affordability and quality of care services, to strengthen the working conditions and rights of formal and informal carers and to boost investment in the sector. It remains essential to the well-being of citizens and the resilience of our societies, particularly in the context of an ageing population and persistent staff shortages across the care sector. As the strategy approaches its fourth anniversary, it is important to seek a clear and updated account of its implementation. Can the Commission provide an update on the concrete progress made in implementing the European care strategy since its adoption, including the state of play regarding Member States’ uptake of the recommendations, the main achievements delivered so far and the challenges that remain in reaching its original objectives?
at: (English version) to the Commission Regina Doherty (PPE) (10 July 2026) Subject: European care strategy Presented in September 2022, the European care strategy set out to improve the availability, affordability and quality of care services, to strengthen the working conditions and rights of formal and informal carers and to boost investment in the sector. It remains essential to the well-being of citizens and the resilience of our societies, particularly in the context of an ageing population and persistent staff shortages across the care sector. As the strategy approaches its fourth anniversary, it is important to seek a clear and updated account of its implementation. Can the Commission provide an update on the concrete progress made in implementing the European care strategy since its adoption, including the state of play regarding Member States’ uptake of the recommendations, the main achievements delivered so far and the challenges that remain in reaching its original objectives? (11 August 2026) The European Care Strategy (1) aims to ensure high quality, affordable and accessible care services while supporting formal and informal carers. The Council Recommendation on access to affordable high-quality long-term care (2) (LTC) sets out a policy framework for investments and reforms. In the national implementation plans (3), workforce and availability of LTC are at the top of the reform agenda. The recommendation is monitored through an indicator-based framework (4). This analysis feeds in the European Semester, with 21 Country-Specific Recommendations on LTC issued in 2026. The Commission will report on the implementation of the recommendation to the Council in 2027. EU-level actions include a self-assessment toolkit (5) for Member States, an online training course for informal carers (6) and evidence packages on adequacy of social protection for LTC (7), LTC workforce (8), labour mobility and enforcement challenges in the LTC sector (9) and LTC settings (10). The creation of a European social dialogue committee for social services, which produced a Joint Framework of Action on Staff Retention and Recruitment in the sector (11), and the launch of a large-scale skills partnership for LTC under the Pact for Skills (12) further strengthened the professionalisation of workforce. These are complemented by mutual learning, policy dialogues and EU funding, notably through the European Social Fund Plus (13), the Recovery and Resilience Facility (14) and the Technical Support Instrument (15).

E-10-2026-002861.t: Voluntary commitment over consumer protection – Commission response to the European Citizens’ Initiative ‘Stop Destroying Videogames!’
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (29.9.2026)

The Commission’s intention to initiate, by the end of 2026, stakeholder exchanges on an industry code of conduct1 is without prejudice to the consumer rights conferred by the Digital Content Directive2 as regards digital content and services and, as regards goods with digital elements, to the seller’s obligation under the Sale of Goods Directive3 to provide updates necessary to keep such goods in conformity, thereby safeguarding their continued functioning. In addition, Directive 2024/825/EU4 strengthens protection against misleading practices related to durability, such as withholding information about updates that negatively affect goods and promoting goods with known durabilitylimiting features, while the Regulation (EU) 2024/17815 contributes to the durability of goods by enabling product-specific requirements, including mandatory software update availability obligations6, preventing premature obsolescence7, and ensuring non-discriminatory access for professional repairers to any software or firmware needed for repair8. Finally, copyright and consumer law pursue different objectives. The former aims at ensuring that consumers enjoy products conforming with the contract and their reasonable expectations, whilst the latter’s purpose is to stimulate and protect creativity. The purchase of games does not necessarily entail a transfer of ownership, as modern video game distribution models are typically based on licensing. Although their terms and conditions may differ between vendors, the licenses acquired are not perpetual, nor are they mandated to be under EU copyright law. Nevertheless, the fact that a product is supplied under a licence does not exempt traders from complying with applicable consumer law obligations. 1 Communication from the Commission on the European Citizens’ Initiative (ECI) ‘Stop Destroying
