E-10-2026-002860.t: MiFID II – Personal recommendations,  suitability statement and allocation of responsibility for investment advice provided by various different professionals or automated systems
qt: to the Commission Sibylle Berg (NI) Subject:
MiFID II – Personal recommendations, suitability statement and allocation of responsibility for investment advice provided by various different professionals or automated systems

Under Directive 2014/65/EU on markets in financial instruments (MiFID II) investment advice is defined as personal recommendations to a client in respect of transactions relating to financial instruments. In parallel, responsibility for carrying out the suitability assessment and providing the suitability statement lies with the investment firm. In practice, personal recommendations, suitability assessments, documentation and technical preparatory work for the suitability statement are sometimes carried out by several different staff members or semiautomated systems. 1.

Under EU law, is the determining factor in establishing whether investment advice has been provided – and by whom – the identity of the person who actually gives or conveys the personalised recommendation to the client, even if the statement of suitability is prepared, technically generated or transmitted by other individuals or systems?

Under EU law, is the statement of suitability as laid down in Article 25 of MiFID II and Article 54 of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2017/565 to be understood as documentation and justification of a recommendation that has already been made?

For the purposes of the provision of investment advice under EU law, must the individual providing or conveying the personalised recommendation be the self-same person who also technically generates, approves or transmits the suitability statement, or does the attribution of responsibility remain unaffected if system and documentation records do not appear under that person’s identifier, even though they conducted the client meeting and explained the recommendation?
at: (English version) to the Commission Sibylle Berg (NI) (10 July 2026) Subject: MiFID II — Personal recommendations, suitability statement and allocation of responsibility for investment advice provided by various different professionals or automated systems Under Directive 2014/65/EU on markets in financial instruments (MiFID II) investment advice is defined as personal recommendations to a client in respect of transactions relating to financial instruments. In parallel, responsibility for carrying out the suitability assessment and providing the suitability statement lies with the investment firm. In practice, personal recommendations, suitability assessments, documentation and technical preparatory work for the suitability statement are sometimes carried out by several different staff members or semi-automated systems. 1. Under EU law, is the determining factor in establishing whether investment advice has been provided — and by whom — the identity of the person who actually gives or conveys the personalised recommendation to the client, even if the statement of suitability is prepared, technically generated or transmitted by other individuals or systems? 2. Under EU law, is the statement of suitability as laid down in Article 25 of MiFID II and Article 54 of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2017/565 to be understood as documentation and justification of a recommendation that has already been made? 3. For the purposes of the provision of investment advice under EU law, must the individual providing or conveying the personalised recommendation be the self-same person who also technically generates, approves or transmits the suitability statement, or does the attribution of responsibility remain unaffected if system and documentation records do not appear under that person’s identifier, even though they conducted the client meeting and explained the recommendation? (8 September 2026) Pursuant to Article 4(1)(4) and Article 25(2) of Directive 2014/65/EU (the Markets in Financial Instruments Directive (MiFID) II) (1), a person acting for the investment firm is regarded as giving investment advice when he or she delivers a personal recommendation to a client in respect of one or more transactions relating to financial instruments that is tailored to the client’s knowledge and experience, financial situation, investment objectives, and risk tolerance. The individual who communicates the personalised recommendation is the advice-giver, irrespective of who prepares the underlying suitability assessment. The suitability statement referred to in Article 25(6) of MiFID II is a documentary record that specifies the advice given and explains how the advice meets the preferences, objectives and other characteristics of the retail client. Article 21 of Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2017/565 (2) obliges the investment firm to maintain documented procedures with clear reporting lines and allocation of functions and responsibilities.
OJ L 173, 12.6.2014, pp. 349-496, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2014/65/oj. OJ L 87, 31.3.2017, pp. 1-83, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg_del/2017/565/oj.

E-10-2026-002859.t: MiFID II – Distinction between supervised investment advice and independent advice in cases of divided responsibilities or system-assisted delivery
qt: to the Commission Sibylle Berg (NI) Subject:
MiFID II – Distinction between supervised investment advice and independent advice in cases of divided responsibilities or system-assisted delivery

In the practice of investment firms, it is not uncommon for one employee to conduct the client meeting, determine the client’s personal circumstances and explain a specific recommendation, while another employee or a semi-automated system carries out the suitability assessment, grants approval or prepares the suitability statement. 1.

What criteria under EU law are to be used to assess whether, in such a case, the employee who conducts the client meeting and explains the recommendation is already providing investment advice to the client or is merely acting under supervision?

For the purposes of that distinction, is it decisive who gives or communicates the content of the personal recommendation to the client or who carries out the suitability assessment, grants the approval or technically prepares or transmits the suitability statement?

What are the requirements under Directive 2014/65/EU on markets in financial instruments (MiFID II) and Delegated Regulation (EU) 2017/565 for a clear, transparently documented and unambiguously attributable allocation of responsibilities if the meeting, personal recommendation, suitability assessment and suitability statement are divided among several persons or systems within the relevant institution?
at: (English version) to the Commission Sibylle Berg (NI) (10 July 2026) Subject: MiFID II — Distinction between supervised investment advice and independent advice in cases of divided responsibilities or system-assisted delivery In the practice of investment firms, it is not uncommon for one employee to conduct the client meeting, determine the client’s personal circumstances and explain a specific recommendation, while another employee or a semi-automated system carries out the suitability assessment, grants approval or prepares the suitability statement. 1. What criteria under EU law are to be used to assess whether, in such a case, the employee who conducts the client meeting and explains the recommendation is already providing investment advice to the client or is merely acting under supervision? 2. For the purposes of that distinction, is it decisive who gives or communicates the content of the personal recommendation to the client or who carries out the suitability assessment, grants the approval or technically prepares or transmits the suitability statement? 3. What are the requirements under Directive 2014/65/EU on markets in financial instruments (MiFID II) and Delegated Regulation (EU) 2017/565 for a clear, transparently documented and unambiguously attributable allocation of responsibilities if the meeting, personal recommendation, suitability assessment and suitability statement are divided among several persons or systems within the relevant institution? (8 September 2026) Pursuant to Article 4(1)(4) of Directive 2014/65/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council (the Markets in Financial Instruments Directive II) (1), ‘investment advice means the provision of personal recommendations to a client, either upon its request or at the initiative of the investment firm, in respect of one or more transactions relating to financial instruments’. According to Article 9 of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2017/565 (2), ‘a personal recommendation shall be considered a recommendation that is made to a person in his capacity as an investor or potential investor, or in his capacity as an agent for an investor or potential investor. That recommendation shall be presented as suitable for that person, or shall be based on a consideration of the circumstances of that person … A recommendation shall not be considered a personal recommendation if it is issued exclusively to the public.’ Acting ‘under supervision’ means providing the relevant services to clients under the responsibility of a staff member who has both appropriate qualifications and appropriate experience. The attribution of the recommendation, not the performance of the suitability assessment, is decisive. The individual who communicates the personal recommendation to the client is deemed to be the advice-giver. The suitability assessment may be delegated to other staff or to a semi-automated system. Article 21 of Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2017/565 requires that the investment firm ‘establish[es], implement[s] and maintain[s] decision-making procedures and an organisational structure which clearly and in documented manner specifies reporting lines and allocates functions and responsibilities’.

Directive 2014/65/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 15 May 2014 on markets in financial instruments and amending Directive 2002/92/EC and Directive 2011/61/EU, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2014/65/oj. Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2017/565 of 25 April 2016 supplementing Directive 2014/65/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council as regards organisational requirements and operating conditions for investment firms and defined terms for the purposes of that directive, http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg_del/2017/565/oj.

E-10-2026-002858.t: Drug and firearms trafficking along the Balkan route
qt: to the Commission Anna Maria Cisint (PfE) Subject:

The Frontex Annual Risk Analysis (ARA) for 2026/2027 states that criminal organisations operating along the Western Balkans route have bolstered their operational capacity by consolidating their physical presence in drug-producing countries and stepping up cocaine, heroin and cannabis smuggling operations into the European Union. The ARA also highlights that the ever-growing flow of illegal firearms from Türkiye and the Western Balkans is fuelling the rise of increasingly organised, sophisticated and violent criminal networks that are often involved in migrant smuggling. Frontex’s findings are borne out by recent events in Italy, where a sting coordinated by the Milan District Anti-Mafia Directorate succeeded in dismantling a transnational organisation involved in drug and weapons trafficking along the Balkan route. In the light of the above, I ask the Commission: 1.

What additional measures – potentially involving Frontex and Europol, as well as enhanced cooperation with countries in the Western Balkans – need to be implemented to tackle cross-border drug and firearms trafficking along the Balkan route?

What tangible results have been achieved by Frontex’s operations against the criminal networks that use the Balkan route, and how could the Agency step up its support to Member State border and customs authorities with a view to enhancing efforts to detect and combat the smuggling of drugs, firearms and other illicit goods?
at: (English version) to the Commission Anna Maria Cisint (PfE) (9 July 2026) Subject: Drug and firearms trafficking along the Balkan route The Frontex Annual Risk Analysis (ARA) for 2026/2027 states that criminal organisations operating along the Western Balkans route have bolstered their operational capacity by consolidating their physical presence in drug-producing countries and stepping up cocaine, heroin and cannabis smuggling operations into the European Union. The ARA also highlights that the ever-growing flow of illegal firearms from Türkiye and the Western Balkans is fuelling the rise of increasingly organised, sophisticated and violent criminal networks that are often involved in migrant smuggling. Frontex’s findings are borne out by recent events in Italy, where a sting coordinated by the Milan District Anti-Mafia Directorate succeeded in dismantling a transnational organisation involved in drug and weapons trafficking along the Balkan route. In the light of the above, I ask the Commission: 1.

What additional measures — potentially involving Frontex and Europol, as well as enhanced cooperation with countries in the Western Balkans — need to be implemented to tackle cross-border drug and firearms trafficking along the Balkan route?

What tangible results have been achieved by Frontex’s operations against the criminal networks that use the Balkan route, and how could the Agency step up its support to Member State border and customs authorities with a view to enhancing efforts to detect and combat the smuggling of drugs, firearms and other illicit goods?

(1 September 2026) The Commission is aware of the situation and the findings of the European Border and Coast Guard Agency (Frontex) Annual Risk Analysis on serious cross-border crime along the Western Balkans route. Here, Frontex provides operational support to Member States through joint operations and its role in the European Multidisciplinary Platform Against Criminal Threats (EMPACT) (1). The European Union Agency for Law Enforcement Cooperation (Europol) supports Member States in combating illicit firearms and drug trafficking. Together with Member States and Western Balkan partners, both agencies execute joint operational actions against organised crime and exchange intelligence to maintain a shared situational picture at EU borders. In 2025, Frontex joint operations with EMPACT led to seizures of 191 firearms and 104 000 kg of illicit drugs. The EU supports capacity building, criminal intelligence and prevention across the Western Balkans. For example, via EU4FAST (with Frontex), it fights migrant smuggling, trafficking in human beings and organised crime. The Commission proposed a new Directive to fight illicit firearms trafficking (2) in 2026, introducing EU-wide criminal penalties and establishing mandatory cross-border intelligence sharing. Under the EU Drugs Strategy (3) and Action Plan (4), the Western Balkans is a priority region for cooperation to disrupt trafficking routes. The EU also continues supporting the Western Balkan partners in implementing the regional Small Arms and Light Weapons Roadmap (5). The Commission and the High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy have recently proposed a new EU sanctions regime (6) to tackle migrant smuggling, trafficking in human beings and other forms of organised crime.

E-10-2026-002857.t: Protecting EU consumers from non-compliant sun creams being sold on e-commerce platforms
qt: to the Commission Laura Ballarín Cereza (S&D), Nicolás González Casares (S&D) Subject:
Protecting EU consumers from non-compliant sun creams being sold on ecommerce platforms

On 8 July 2026, the organisation Que Choisir Ensemble published the results of an analysis of the quality of sun creams sold on the AliExpress, Shein and Temu e-commerce platforms. The results are concerning: of the 10 products analysed, three contained banned substances, six provided significantly less sun protection than that indicated and only one offered acceptable levels of protection, but it contained an endocrine disruptor that is dangerous to health. Under the Digital Services Act, AliExpress, Shein and Temu are classified as very large online platforms and are therefore subject to greater obligations, such as the requirements to assess systemic risks (Article 34) and to put measures in place to mitigate those risks (Article 35). However, the investigations opened into these e-commerce platforms are still ongoing and have not yet resulted in final decisions. In light of the above: 1.
Will the Commission take this data into account in the ongoing investigations?
Pending the conclusion of the investigations, what urgent action does it intend to take to stop dangerous products from being sold in the EU?
What additional legislative and enforcement measures will it adopt to effectively protect the health of EU consumers?
at: (English version) to the Commission Laura Ballarín Cereza (S&D), Nicolás González Casares (S&D) (9 July 2026) Subject: Protecting EU consumers from non-compliant sun creams being sold on e-commerce platforms On 8 July 2026, the organisation Que Choisir Ensemble published the results of an analysis of the quality of sun creams sold on the AliExpress, Shein and Temu e-commerce platforms. The results are concerning: of the 10 products analysed, three contained banned substances, six provided significantly less sun protection than that indicated and only one offered acceptable levels of protection, but it contained an endocrine disruptor that is dangerous to health. Under the Digital Services Act, AliExpress, Shein and Temu are classified as very large online platforms and are therefore subject to greater obligations, such as the requirements to assess systemic risks (Article 34) and to put measures in place to mitigate those risks (Article 35). However, the investigations opened into these e-commerce platforms are still ongoing and have not yet resulted in final decisions. In light of the above: 1.
Will the Commission take this data into account in the ongoing investigations?
Pending the conclusion of the investigations, what urgent action does it intend to take to stop dangerous products from being sold in the EU?
What additional legislative and enforcement measures will it adopt to effectively protect the health of EU consumers?

(7 September 2026) The Commission takes the concerns raised very seriously and assures that the enforcement of the Digital Services Act (1) remains a priority. Providers of very large online platforms and very large online search engines are required to diligently identify, analyse, assess and mitigate systemic risks stemming from the design, functioning or use made of their services, including the risk of dissemination of illegal content. The Commission initiated proceedings against the providers of AliExpress (2), Temu (3) and Shein (4) concerning their assessment and mitigation measures regarding the systemic risk of dissemination of illegal products. On 28 May 2026, Temu was fined EUR 200 million for insufficiently assessing such risk (5). The investigation is ongoing regarding other aspects such as the obligation of the provider of Temu to put in place measures to mitigate the systemic risk of dissemination of illegal products. Additionally, on 20 July 2026, the Commission fined AliExpress EUR 550 million for failing to properly assess and mitigate the risk of dissemination of illegal products (6). The Commission is coordinating joint actions, including on cosmetics, to address non-compliance comprehensively. Authorities can resort to a recently launched proactive web crawler to detect non-compliant goods online before they enter the EU market. The Commission will tackle the influx of non-compliant products through the ongoing revision of the Market Surveillance Regulation (7), within the European Product Act proposal.

E-10-2026-002855.t: Precautionary principle and lack of EU standards on siting large-scale energy storage facilities
qt: to the Commission Arkadiusz Mularczyk (ECR) Subject:

In its response to question E-001873/20261, the Commission confirmed that it supports accelerating the granting of permits to large-scale energy storage facilities, while noting that it does not envisage introducing rules on minimum distances between such facilities and housing, leaving spatial planning issues at the discretion of the Member States. Article 191(2) TFEU stipulates that Union policy on the environment shall be based on the precautionary principle and ensure a high level of protection for the health of people and the environment. In light of the above: 1.

Does the Commission consider that accelerating the granting of permits to large-scale energy storage facilities, in the absence of common EU standards for their siting relative to residential development, aligns with the precautionary principle as set out in Article 191(2)?

On the basis of which scientific analyses or risk assessments did the Commission consider that the absence of minimum standards for the siting of such installations would not adversely affect the safety of residents and the high level of protection of health and the environment in the EU?
https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/E-10-2026-001873_EN.html.
at: (English version) to the Commission Arkadiusz Mularczyk (ECR) (9 July 2026) Subject: Precautionary principle and lack of EU standards on siting large-scale energy storage facilities In its response to Question E-001873/2026 (1), the Commission confirmed that it supports accelerating the granting of permits to large-scale energy storage facilities, while noting that it does not envisage introducing rules on minimum distances between such facilities and housing, leaving spatial planning issues at the discretion of the Member States. Article 191(2) TFEU stipulates that Union policy on the environment shall be based on the precautionary principle and ensure a high level of protection for the health of people and the environment. In light of the above: 1.

Does the Commission consider that accelerating the granting of permits to large-scale energy storage facilities, in the absence of common EU standards for their siting relative to residential development, aligns with the precautionary principle as set out in Article 191(2)?

On the basis of which scientific analyses or risk assessments did the Commission consider that the absence of minimum standards for the siting of such installations would not adversely affect the safety of residents and the high level of protection of health and the environment in the EU?

(17 September 2026) Supporting the acceleration of permit-granting procedures for large-scale energy storage facilities should go hand in hand with safeguards relating to the siting of projects and their environmental and other assessments, as necessary. The precautionary principle, as referred to in Article 191(2) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU), applies where a risk to human health or the environment has been identified. Its application must be based on a case-by-case assessment, best available scientific evidence and in accordance with the principles of proportionality and non-discrimination. While Member States have the discretion to lay down national planning, safety and public health rules, siting and permitting of such facilities remain subject to the relevant provisions of Union law, in particular Directives 2001/42/EC (1), 2011/92/EU (2), 2000/60/EC (3), 92/43/EEC (4) and 2009/147/EU (5) where applicable. The absence of harmonised EU siting standards does not in itself imply incompatibility with Article 191(2) TFEU, provided that permitting decisions are based on an adequate risk assessment and comply with the applicable legal framework. Setting minimum standards for the siting of large-scale installations such as minimum distances is the responsibility of Member States in line with national and regional specificities. This does not mean that there is a lower level of protection for health and the environment, but rather that each Member State has the discretion to define appropriate safeguards. The same applies to wind installations, for instance (6).

E-10-2026-002853.t: The incinerator in Rome and safeguarding drinking water resources
qt: to the Commission Dario Tamburrano (The Left), Ignazio Roberto Marino (Verts/ALE) Subject:

The site that the Roman municipal authorities have earmarked for the capital’s new incinerator had, until 18 November 20221, been off-limits to waste treatment plants because it had been included2 in the Lazio Region’s environmental restrictions system3 as part of the process of drawing the boundaries of the protection area for the Laurentino water wells (which provide drinking water to the town of Ardea4). In March 2025, the Lazio Region decided to call off the Laurentino protection area mapping procedure5. The decision was taken at the request of ACEA, a multi-utility company which manages the water network and is controlled by the municipal authorities6. ACEA cited the 20167 discovery of chlorine-based pollutants in the Laurentino aquifer and the possibility of switching to other (as-yet-unspecified) sources of water as being the reasons behind its decision. The Laurentino wells9 will continue to supply Ardea8 on an indefinite basis. ACEA’s request does nothing to address the damage that has already been done to the Laurentino wells and could, in fact, expose the aquifer to new sources of pollution. It could, additionally, constitute a conflict of interest, as ACEA heads the consortium responsible for building the Rome incinerator10. Having regard for infringement procedures INFR (2025) 2207 and INFR (2026) 2038 and two cases similar to the one in question – namely the recent measures authorising the construction on the outskirts of Rome of the Salone and Casal Selce11 biodigesters, the latter of which is the subject of an ongoing appeal before the Court of Justice of the European Union12 – could the Commission clarify whether, in relation to the matter at hand, Italy is correctly applying the Water Framework Directive? at: (English version) to the Commission Dario Tamburrano (The Left), Ignazio Roberto Marino (Verts/ALE) (9 July 2026) Subject: The incinerator in Rome and safeguarding drinking water resources The site that the Roman municipal authorities have earmarked for the capital’s new incinerator had, until 18 November 2022 (1), been off-limits to waste treatment plants because it had been included (2) in the Lazio Region’s environmental restrictions system (3) as part of the process of drawing the boundaries of the protection area for the Laurentino water wells (which provide drinking water to the town of Ardea (4)). In March 2025, the Lazio Region decided to call off the Laurentino protection area mapping procedure (5). The decision was taken at the request of ACEA, a multi-utility company which manages the water network and is controlled by the municipal authorities (6). ACEA cited the 2016 (7) discovery of chlorine-based pollutants in the Laurentino aquifer and the possibility of switching to other (as-yet-unspecified) sources of water as being the reasons behind its decision. The Laurentino wells (9) will continue to supply Ardea (8) on an indefinite basis. ACEA’s request does nothing to address the damage that has already been done to the Laurentino wells and could, in fact, expose the aquifer to new sources of pollution. It could, additionally, constitute a conflict of interest, as ACEA heads the consortium responsible for building the Rome incinerator (10). Having regard for infringement procedures INFR (2025) 2207 and INFR (2026) 2038 and two cases similar to the one in question — namely the recent measures authorising the construction on the outskirts of Rome of the Salone and Casal Selce (11) biodigesters, the latter of which is the subject of an ongoing appeal before the Court of Justice of the European Union (12) — could the Commission clarify whether, in relation to the matter at hand, Italy is correctly applying the Water Framework Directive? (2 September 2026) The Water Framework Directive (WFD) (1) requires Member States to prevent the deterioration of status of water bodies and to carry out a prior assessment of the potential impacts of a new project if it may pose a risk in this respect. The assessment can be combined with an environmental impact assessment (EIA) or other assessments required under EU or national law. Article 7 WFD requires Member States to identify and monitor the water bodies used for abstracting drinking water, and to ensure the necessary protection to avoid deterioration, including through the possible establishment of safeguard zones. This Article requires that the resulting water meets the minimum quality standards set by the Drinking Water Directive (DWD) (2). Under the DWD, Member States must ensure that, by July 2027, a risk assessment and risk management is carried out in catchment areas for abstraction points, in relation to hazardous events that potentially cause harm to human health.

E-10-2026-002852.t: Specific measures provided for in the Safe Hearts Plan to tackle obesity and promote the Mediterranean diet
qt: to the Commission Carlo Ciccioli (ECR), Carlo Fidanza (ECR), Michele Picaro (ECR), Ruggero Razza (ECR) Subject:

In December 2025, the Commission adopted the EU cardiovascular health plan (Safe Hearts Plan). More than half of adults in the EU are overweight and obesity is now one of the main drivers of cardiovascular disease, diabetes and cancer, acting through hypertension, insulin resistance and systemic inflammation. The childhood obesity crisis is accelerating (around 1 in 4 children aged 7 to 9 are overweight and 1 in 10 obese), compounding long-term cardiovascular risk from childhood. In the light of the above: 1.

What specific, educational and binding measures are already provided for in the Safe Hearts Plan and what steps does the Commission plan to take to address the root causes of cardiovascular diseases, in particular obesity and, most importantly, childhood obesity?
Does the Commission agree that obesity is the main cause of heart disease?
What specific action is it planning with a view to addressing obesity and promoting the traditional Mediterranean diet effectively?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (21.8.2026) In line with Article 168(7) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU1, the Union complements national policies and encourages cooperation across Member States in the field of public health. Therefore, the Commission is supporting Member States in addressing noncommunicable diseases and their risk factors, including obesity, through the ‘Healthier Together’ initiative2. Actions funded under the EU4Health Programme3 include PreventNCD4, Health4EUkids5 and stakeholder-led projects6, such as PODiaCar7. The Safe Hearts Plan8 builds on these actions for young people under its prevention pillar. Through the aforementioned initiatives, this Plan addresses obesity as one of the main contributing factors in the development of heart disease. The Safe Hearts Plan addresses lifelong prevention, including obesity, through existing actions and those newly funded under the EU4Health work programme, such as a Joint Action on lifelong prevention9 funded with EUR 5 million and supported technically by the World Health Organization and the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development. Two flagships of the Plan specifically address ultra-processed foods, toward healthier diets. The plan makes it clear that the Commission intends to continue to provide EU funding to support physical activity, including its crucial role in prevention, through programmes such as Erasmus10 and EU4Health. Furthermore, obesity is addressed through the Council Recommendation on health-enhancing physical activity11, the European Week of Sport12 and the #BeActive campaign13. The Mediterranean diet is recognised as a model for healthy living in the EU Strategy for Adriatic and Ionian Vision for 203014.

E-10-2026-002851.t: Mental health of young people in the EU and the need for a coordinated European response
qt: to the Commission Elena Kountoura (The Left) Subject:

According to recent OECD and Commission data, the rates of adolescents and young people reporting mental health problems in the EU have increased significantly1 due to social isolation, reduced physical activity and increased exposure to problematic internet and social media use and cyberbullying. Cases of anxiety, depression and other mental disorders have worsened and increased and the fact that suicide is ranked as the main cause of death among young people aged between 15 and 29 is particularly concerning2. Meanwhile, one in four countries lacks community mental health services for children, highlighting significant gaps in prevention, early diagnosis and cross-border cooperation on addressing mental health disorders3. According to the OECD, major depression disorders, generalised anxiety disorders and alcohol use disorders will reduce healthy life expectancy in the EU by 2.5 years over the next 25 years, corresponding to around 28 000 premature deaths per year4. With this in mind, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Does the Commission intend to propose a European strategy on the mental health of young people or, alternatively, a dedicated action plan with clear and measurable objectives for the Member States?
Does it plan to adopt a psychosocial approach and include mandatory mental health impact assessments in employment, housing and education policies?
What additional steps does it intend to take to strengthen prevention, education and regulation of exposure to the internet, social media and online bullying?

According to the report ‘Health at a Glance: Europe 2024: State of Health in the EU Cycle’, the proportion of 15-year-olds in the EU reporting multiple physical and psychological problems, rose from 42 % in 2017-2018 to 52 % in 2021-2022, with this rate reaching 68 % among 15-year-old girls. 2 Eurofound - Mental health: Risk groups, trends, services and policies, https://www.eurofound.europa.eu/en/publications/all/mental-health-risk-groups-trends-services-and-policies. According to a WHO survey on children’s mental health in the EU, one in seven children live with a mental health condition. 3 It is estimated that 67.5 % of people in need of mental health care in the EU do not have access to treatment. 4 On 20 June 2025, the Council called for greater efforts to protect the mental health of children and adolescents in the digital era, through the safe and healthy use of digital tools and the creation of a healthier, safer and more age-appropriate digital environment. 1

E-10-2026-002850.t: Document fraud in extraordinary regularisation processes and protecting the integrity of the Schengen area
qt: to the Commission Alma Ezcurra Almansa (PPE), Dolors Montserrat (PPE), Javier Zarzalejos (PPE), Juan Ignacio Zoido Álvarez (PPE) Subject:

The Commission considers document fraud to be a threat to EU security and is tackling the problem through the FADO system and cooperation between Frontex and Europol1, given document fraud’s close ties with organised crime and migrant smuggling23. The risk is particularly great during national regularisation processes, where insufficient checks on documents can leave the door open to fraud or secondary movements. Recent police operations45 and reports by the Spanish National Police6 have warned of an increase in fake documents to obtain residence permits. In the light of the above: 1.

Does the Commission agree that insufficient checks on documents during national regularisation processes can compromise the integrity of the Schengen area and strengthen the business model for migrant smuggling networks?
Does the Commission believe cooperation needs to be ramped up between Member States, Frontex and Europol to prevent document fraud in those processes?

What best practices does the Commission recommend to Member States to prevent and detect document fraud in national procedures for granting residence permits, including extraordinary regularisation processes, and avoid risks to the integrity of the Schengen area?

E-10-2026-002849.t: Mass granting of Spanish citizenship by descent, document authenticity and governance of the Schengen area
qt: to the Commission Alma Ezcurra Almansa (PPE), Dolors Montserrat (PPE), Javier Zarzalejos (PPE), Juan Ignacio Zoido Álvarez (PPE) Subject:

The eighth additional provision of Spanish Law 20/20221 has created an extraordinary procedure for acquiring Spanish nationality by descent. As of March 2026, the authorities had approved 545 000 files out of a total of 2.45 million applications2. The Commission has pointed out that – without prejudice to the division of competences established by the EU Treaties – national decisions may have consequences for Member States and the EU and must be implemented in accordance with the principle of sincere cooperation3. Given that nationality of a Member State implies EU citizenship, free movement within the Schengen area and exercising electoral rights: 1.
Has Spain informed the Commission of the scope, effects and estimated number of beneficiaries of this extraordinary procedure for acquiring nationality?

Does the Commission agree that insufficient document verification processes may affect mutual trust between Member States and the principle of sincere cooperation laid down in Article 4(3) of the Treaty on European Union?
Does the Commission believe these processes should incorporate enhanced document verification assurances and promote common standards, given their impact on EU citizenship and the Schengen area?

at: (Versión española) Pregunta con solicitud de respuesta escrita E-002849/26 a la Comisión Alma Ezcurra Almansa (PPE), Dolors Montserrat (PPE), Javier Zarzalejos (PPE), Juan Ignacio Zoido Álvarez (PPE) (9 de julio de 2026) Asunto: Concesión masiva de nacionalidad española por descendencia, integridad documental y gobernanza del espacio Schengen La disposición adicional octava de la Ley 20/2022 (1) ha dado lugar a un procedimiento extraordinario de adquisición de la nacionalidad española por descendencia. A marzo de 2026, las autoridades habían aprobado 545 000 expedientes de un total de 2,45 millones de solicitudes (2). La Comisión ha señalado que —sin perjuicio del reparto de competencias establecido por los tratados de la UE— las decisiones nacionales pueden tener consecuencias para Estados miembros y la Unión y deben aplicarse conforme al principio de cooperación leal (3). Dado que la nacionalidad de un Estado miembro implica la ciudadanía de la Unión, la libre circulación en el espacio Schengen y el ejercicio de derechos electorales: 1.
¿Ha informado España a la Comisión del alcance, efectos y número estimado de beneficiarios de este procedimiento extraordinario de adquisición de la nacionalidad?

¿Comparte la Comisión que unos controles insuficientes de verificación documental pueden afectar a la confianza mutua entre los Estados miembros y al principio de cooperación leal previsto en el artículo 4.3 del Tratado de la Unión Europea?

¿Considera la Comisión que estos procedimientos deben incorporar garantías reforzadas de verificación documental y promover estándares comunes, habida cuenta de sus efectos sobre la ciudadanía de la Unión y el espacio Schengen?

Presentación: 9.7.2026 Respuesta del Sr. McGrath en nombre de la Comisión Europea (15 de septiembre de 2026) Los Estados miembros no están obligados a notificar a la Comisión los cambios en su legislación sobre adquisición y pérdida de la nacionalidad. No obstante, la Comisión está al corriente de la legislación a que se refieren sus señorías. Según reiterada jurisprudencia del Tribunal de Justicia de la Unión Europea, si bien corresponde a cada Estado miembro establecer, teniendo debidamente en cuenta el Derecho internacional, las condiciones para la concesión y la pérdida de la nacionalidad de un Estado miembro, dicha competencia debe ejercerse teniendo debidamente en cuenta el Derecho de la Unión (4). De esta jurisprudencia se desprende que la definición de los requisitos de concesión de la nacionalidad de un Estado miembro no es competencia de la Unión, sino de cada Estado miembro, que dispone de un amplio margen de apreciación para decidir los criterios que hayan de aplicarse, siempre que esos criterios se apliquen respetando el Derecho de la Unión (5).

E-10-2026-002848.t: The Commission’s social media strategy and use of W Social
qt: to the Commission Alexandra Geese (Verts/ALE) Subject:

The Commission recently announced its presence on W Social shortly after publishing its strategy on the future of virtual worlds and web technologies, while maintaining accounts on ActivityPub-based services. At the same time, concerns have been raised regarding the Commission’s promotion of specific commercial social media platforms and the absence of a coherent approach to digital public infrastructure. In this context: 1.

Why did the Commission choose to establish a presence on the closed-source platform W Social immediately after publishing a strategy that emphasises openness, rather than operating its own Atmosphere servers as it does for its ActivityPub presence?

Does the Commission intend to publish a comprehensive social media strategy addressing both its communications objectives and its approach to European technological sovereignty, including whether it will prioritise open digital infrastructure and interoperable ecosystems over dependence on proprietary platforms?

Does the Commission consider it appropriate, in the light of the applicable ethics rules in the Code of Conduct, for the Commission President to publish content on her Instagram account that could reasonably be perceived as promoting specific commercial social media companies?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (11.9.2026) Establishing presence on the European social media platform W is part of the Commission’s continued approach to diversify its presence on social media and to reach out to as many Europeans as possible. The content posted on the Commission’s account on W is fully accessible to the public through the interoperable Authenticated Transfer Protocol as well as through the web. The Commission continues to provide strong policy and implementation support for interoperability and open digital ecosystems, including open standards, open source solutions and European digital public infrastructures. This commitment is reflected in a range of concrete initiatives, such as sovereign cloud procurement1, code.europa.eu, and the EU Open Source Solutions Catalogue2, which facilitates the publication, discovery and reuse of open source solutions across the EU public sector. The recently adopted Open Source Strategy3 provides that the Commission will seek to strengthen the open source media space by supporting open and decentralised social media solutions and platforms. Posts on corporate accounts aim to promote the presence and activities on social media and do not imply endorsement of any commercial service or business model.

1 https://commission.europa.eu/news-and-media/news/sovereign-cloud-framework-explained-2026-06-01_en. 2 https://interoperable-europe.ec.europa.eu/eu-oss-catalogue. 3 https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/factpages/eu-open-source-strategy.

E-10-2026-002847.t: Crisis in mental health services in Cyprus and possibilities for European support
qt: to the Commission Geadis Geadi (ECR) Subject:

Cyprus is experiencing serious and persistent mental health shortages. According to the PanCyprian Association for Mental Health Organisations, the number of psychiatric beds is exceedingly low – 18 beds per 100 000 inhabitants – compared to the European average of 73. Athalassa Hospital is experiencing overcrowding, understaffing, a shortage in medicines and a lack of adequate treatment programmes and psychosocial programmes. Specifically, it has been reported that wards with sufficient staff for and designed to accommodate 60 patients are currently hosting around 120 patients, with some sleeping on mattresses on the floor. Despite the preparation of a three-year national strategy for the period 2025-2028, community care remains inadequate, with shortages in sheltered accommodation facilities, day centres, support for families/carers, etc. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

What funding and technical support options are available to the Republic of Cyprus for the completion of the new Athalassa Hospital, the development of community mental health infrastructure and, in general, the implementation of actions proposed in the National Action Plan?

Is there a European institution that could follow the content of the treatment programme that is in place in voluntary and involuntary hospitalisation facilities and advise/complement/provide training in therapeutic approaches other than medication, e.g. psychosocial support programmes or other approaches recommended by modern psychiatry?

(7 September 2026) Under its Recovery and Resilience Plan, Cyprus is implementing a broad package of reforms and investments to strengthen the resilience, quality and accessibility of its healthcare system. This includes Investment C1.1I5, which finances construction works and new equipment for Cyprus State Hospitals, including the Mental Health Hospital. The broader healthcare package also includes reforms and investments supporting evidence-based clinical practice, quality assurance, digital health and value-based healthcare. The target related to the Mental Health Hospital has already been positively assessed by the Commission in the context of Cyprus' previous payment requests under the Recovery and Resilience Facility (1). All milestones and targets need to be implemented by 31 August 2026. Furthermore, the Commission is currently focusing on the implementation of the 2023 Communication on a comprehensive approach to mental health (2), that supports Member States in reinforcing mental health systems through 20 flagship initiatives and almost EUR 1.3 billion in funding opportunities. Examples of flagships are the EUR 11 million support to the World Health Organisation to provide tailored support to Member States through policy dialogues and capacity building, and the multidisciplinary capacity building programme for health professionals EU-PROMENS (3) (EUR 9 million). Cyprus was partner in the former joint action ImpleMENTAL (4), that finished in autumn 2024, which supported Member States with EUR 4,5 million in transferring the Belgian best practice on community mental health reform.

Further information on the already positively assessed milestones and targets is available on the Commission's country page dedicated to Cyprus' Recovery and Resilience Plan: https://reforms-investments.ec.europa.eu/recovery-and-resilience-facility-1/country-pages/cyprus-recovery-and-resilienceplan_en#documents. https://health.ec.europa.eu/document/download/cef45b6d-a871-44d5-9d62-3cecc47eda89_en?filename=com_2023_298_1_act_en.pdf. https://eu-promens.eu/eu-promens. https://implemental.org/.

E-10-2026-002846.t: Submission of national restoration plans under the Nature Restoration Regulation (2024/1991)
qt: to the Commission Wouter Beke (PPE) Subject:

Under Regulation (EU) 2024/1991 on nature restoration (the Nature Restoration Regulation), Member States must submit their draft national restoration plans to the Commission by 1 September 2026 at the latest. These plans may have significant implications for the granting of permits, as well as for agriculture, infrastructure, businesses and investment. At the same time, there is still insufficient clarity regarding the funding of the measures required to achieve the regulation’s objectives, which will come in addition to existing instruments such as the CAP. Moreover, various simplification processes are underway in the context of EU environmental policy, which include the stress test under the Birds and Habitats Directives. Given that the Nature Restoration Regulation builds on the Habitats Directive, legal certainty for Member States, citizens and businesses is essential. 1.
Does the Commission recognise that national restoration plans may have significant implications for the granting of permits, for businesses and for investment in the Member States?
Is the Commission prepared to consider postponing the submission of national restoration plans?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (2.9.2026) The Commission recognises that the preparation and implementation of national restoration plans (NRP) may have practical implications in Member States, including for land-use choices, sectoral planning and, depending on national implementation, for permitting processes, businesses and investment. However, the Nature Restoration Regulation (NRR)1 does not create a new permitting regime. It leaves to Member States to align the implementation of the Regulation with existing frameworks, including the Environmental Impact Assessment Directive2 and the Birds and Habitats Directives3, as well as with existing national tools and procedures, including permitting. The NRR also requires Member States to involve stakeholders in NRP preparation, to ensure it fits local circumstances and to support affected stakeholders if relevant. This should allow Member States to integrate restoration obligations in a coherent manner while reducing administrative burden. The NRR provides for a stepwise process. After submission of a draft NRP by 1 September 2026, the subsequent assessment of the draft by the Commission4 and its observations are intended to support a constructive dialogue with Member States and may lead to further refinements of the NRP before its finalisation by September 2027. NRPs may also be reviewed thereafter5. In this context, the Commission does not intend to extend the deadline for submitting draft NRP but will continue to support Member States in finalising and implementing them as committed in its communication Simplifying for sustainable competitiveness6. Nature restoration is an urgent but continuous process thus it is in the interest of the resilience and competitiveness of the EU not to delay it further.
1 Regulation (EU) 2024/1991 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 24 June 2024 on nature

restoration and amending Regulation (EU) 2022/869, OJ L, 2024/1991, 29.7.2024. 2 Directive 2011/92/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 December 2011 on the assessment of the effects of certain public and private projects on the environment, OJ L 26, 28.1.2012, p. 1–21, as amended by Directive 2014/52/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 16 April 2014, OJ L 124, 25.4.2014, p. 1–18. 3 Directive 2009/147/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 30 November 2009 on the conservation of wild birds, OJ L 20, 26.1.2010, p. 7–25.; and Council Directive 92/43/EEC of 21 May 1992 on the conservation of natural habitats and of wild fauna and flora, OJ L 206, 22.7.1992, p. 7–50. 4 In accordance with Article 17 of the Nature Restoration Regulation. 5 In accordance with Article 19 of the Nature Restoration Regulation. 6 https://environment.ec.europa.eu/publications/simplification-administrative-burdens-environmentallegislation_en.

E-10-2026-002845.t: Effective exercise by the ECA of its audit rights in relation to Pillar II of the Ukraine Facility
qt: to the Commission Barbara Bonte (PfE) Subject:

The Ukraine Investment Framework constitutes Pillar II of the Ukraine Facility and is implemented through indirect management by international financial institutions and other implementing partners. In Opinion 03/2023, the European Court of Auditors (ECA) highlighted risks relating to the effective exercise of its audit rights in the context of indirect management. It also referred to previous cases in which international organisations had restricted or refused access to documentation. Various guarantee and financing agreements have now been concluded under Pillar II. 1.

Has the ECA already been able to effectively exercise its audit rights under Pillar II with regard to implementing partners, financial intermediaries or final beneficiaries, and have any cases been identified in which access to data, documents, systems or premises have been restricted or refused?

What contractual escalation, corrective and sanction mechanisms – including suspension of payments, financial corrections, recovery, contractual termination or exclusion from future operations – apply when implementing partners, financial intermediaries or final beneficiaries fail to comply with their audit or informationrelated obligations vis-à-vis the Commission, OLAF, the EPPO or the ECA?
What are the Commission’s conclusions and further recommendations with regard to the second pillar and does it propose any compensatory supervisory measures in that regard?
at: (English version) to the Commission Barbara Bonte (PfE) (9 July 2026) Subject: Effective exercise by the ECA of its audit rights in relation to Pillar II of the Ukraine Facility The Ukraine Investment Framework constitutes Pillar II of the Ukraine Facility and is implemented through indirect management by international financial institutions and other implementing partners. In Opinion 03/2023, the European Court of Auditors (ECA) highlighted risks relating to the effective exercise of its audit rights in the context of indirect management. It also referred to previous cases in which international organisations had restricted or refused access to documentation. Various guarantee and financing agreements have now been concluded under Pillar II. 1. Has the ECA already been able to effectively exercise its audit rights under Pillar II with regard to implementing partners, financial intermediaries or final beneficiaries, and have any cases been identified in which access to data, documents, systems or premises have been restricted or refused? 2. What contractual escalation, corrective and sanction mechanisms — including suspension of payments, financial corrections, recovery, contractual termination or exclusion from future operations — apply when implementing partners, financial intermediaries or final beneficiaries fail to comply with their audit or information-related obligations vis-à-vis the Commission, OLAF, the EPPO or the ECA? 3. What are the Commission’s conclusions and further recommendations with regard to the second pillar and does it propose any compensatory supervisory measures in that regard? (25 August 2026) The Commission is not aware of any difficulties faced by the European Court of Auditors (ECA) in accessing documents when auditing expenditure under indirect management in Ukraine, notably in the context of the implementation of Pillar II (Ukraine Investment Framework (1)) of the Ukraine Facility (2). The Commission is committed to supporting the ECA in performing its audits. Implementing partners must comply with transparency requirements which are contractually enacted in the agreements signed with the Commission for the implementation of operations under the Ukraine Investment Framework. In compliance with the existing rules and regulations, the framework Agreement for the implementation of EU funding under the Ukraine Facility establishes Ukraine’s obligation to ensure that the European Anti-Fraud Office (OLAF), the European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO) and the ECA may freely exert their rights and have full access to carry out reviews, checks, audits and investigations (3). The Commission considers that the existing control system for indirect management with entrusted entities is efficient. The Commission follows up on errors identified by the ECA and by the Commission’s own audits and verifications, and recovers ineligible expenditure, or applies suspensions/reductions of payments, when appropriate and in accordance with the applicable legal framework.

E-10-2026-002843.t: Extreme heatwaves, energy poverty and protecting vulnerable people in Sicily and Mediterranean regions
qt: to the Commission Giuseppe Antoci (The Left) Subject:

With record temperatures in multiple areas of the Mediterranean, and particularly in Sicily, the recent heatwaves in many Member States have had serious repercussions on health and society. In areas with high summer temperatures and significant levels of poverty, single elderly people, homeless people, people with chronic conditions and households living in energy poverty are among the most exposed to the effects, often unable to access adequate cooling systems. This situation highlights how the effects of climate change exacerbate social inequalities, so we need to strengthen EU coordination across climate policy, health policy and social policy, including through the instruments provided for by the Social Climate Fund. In the light of the above: 1.
Will the Commission promote specific measures to support Member States in protecting the most vulnerable during extreme heatwaves?
Will it promote, including through EU funding, the setting up of air-conditioned spaces for the public and assistance services for the most vulnerable groups?
Will it adopt common guidelines to combat the effects of extreme heat and energy poverty, with a particular focus on Mediterranean regions, such as Sicily?
at: (English version) to the Commission Giuseppe Antoci (The Left) (8 July 2026) Subject: Extreme heatwaves, energy poverty and protecting vulnerable people in Sicily and Mediterranean regions With record temperatures in multiple areas of the Mediterranean, and particularly in Sicily, the recent heatwaves in many Member States have had serious repercussions on health and society. In areas with high summer temperatures and significant levels of poverty, single elderly people, homeless people, people with chronic conditions and households living in energy poverty are among the most exposed to the effects, often unable to access adequate cooling systems. This situation highlights how the effects of climate change exacerbate social inequalities, so we need to strengthen EU coordination across climate policy, health policy and social policy, including through the instruments provided for by the Social Climate Fund. In the light of the above: 1.
Will the Commission promote specific measures to support Member States in protecting the most vulnerable during extreme heatwaves?
Will it promote, including through EU funding, the setting up of air-conditioned spaces for the public and assistance services for the most vulnerable groups?
Will it adopt common guidelines to combat the effects of extreme heat and energy poverty, with a particular focus on Mediterranean regions, such as Sicily?

(1 September 2026) 1. The Commission helps Member States to protect those most vulnerable from heatwaves. Examples include guidance for national climate adaptation strategies and plans (1); for heat health action plans (from the European Climate and Health Observatory) (2); for employers and workplaces to implement EU legal obligations (3); and for improving prevention, preparedness and response planning under the regulation on Serious Cross-Border Threats to Health (4). The impact of extreme temperatures on workers is taken into account in the preparation of the upcoming Quality Jobs Act. It is, however, for the (sub)national authorities to choose the most appropriate heat protection measures, in line with the subsidiarity principle and the local heating and cooling plans as foreseen by Article 25(6) of the Energy Efficiency Directive (5). The Commission is also developing a new European framework to strengthen overall climate resilience and preparedness across all levels of government and policy areas, which it expects to adopt during the fourth quarter of 2026. 2. Member State authorities have the possibility of using EU funds for the purpose of setting up air-conditioned spaces for the public and assistance services for the most vulnerable groups. The Commission considers air conditioning an important heat protection measure for vulnerable groups. It also supports a comprehensive approach enhancing the performance of buildings for the summer (6), the micro-climate around buildings as well as the urban heat island effect through urban planning (7). 3. The Commission’s 2023 Recommendation on energy poverty (8) and guidance document (9). will soon be updated with specific focus on summer energy poverty, affecting notably the Mediterranean regions.

E-10-2026-002842.t: Arbitrations under the Energy Charter Treaty brought against the EU by entities linked to sanctioned individuals
qt: to the Commission Raphaël Glucksmann (S&D) Subject:

In 2025, two arbitrations were brought against the EU under the Energy Charter Treaty (ECT): one by sanctioned individual Aleksandra Melnichenko, and the other by TerraBrown AG, of which she is the final beneficiary. In December 2025, the General Court ruled that the sanctions imposed on Mr and Ms Melnichenko did not extend to TerraBrown. The 18th package of sanctions prohibits the recognition or enforcement of certain arbitration awards linked to sanctions. The recitals would appear to include within the scope entities owned or controlled by sanctioned individuals. However, in their current form, the operative provisions target only sanctioned corporations and those who own or control them. 1.

Do the operative provisions of the 18th package of sanctions cover awards rendered in favour of an entity that is not sanctioned but is owned or controlled by a sanctioned individual? If not, what is the Commission’s planned schedule for reviewing infringement complaints lodged under Article 258 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union?
Is it aware of any analogous arbitrations, and on what basis does the Commission justify the non-disclosure of the notices of arbitration received?
Does it consider the continuation of bilateral investment treaties with Belarus to be compatible with EU policy?
at: (English version) to the Commission Raphaël Glucksmann (S&D) (8 July 2026) Subject: Arbitrations under the Energy Charter Treaty brought against the EU by entities linked to sanctioned individuals In 2025, two arbitrations were brought against the EU under the Energy Charter Treaty (ECT): one by sanctioned individual Aleksandra Melnichenko, and the other by TerraBrown AG, of which she is the final beneficiary. In December 2025, the General Court ruled that the sanctions imposed on Mr and Ms Melnichenko did not extend to TerraBrown. The 18th package of sanctions prohibits the recognition or enforcement of certain arbitration awards linked to sanctions. The recitals would appear to include within the scope entities owned or controlled by sanctioned individuals. However, in their current form, the operative provisions target only sanctioned corporations and those who own or control them. 1. Do the operative provisions of the 18th package of sanctions cover awards rendered in favour of an entity that is not sanctioned but is owned or controlled by a sanctioned individual? If not, what is the Commission’s planned schedule for reviewing infringement complaints lodged under Article 258 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union? 2. Is it aware of any analogous arbitrations, and on what basis does the Commission justify the non-disclosure of the notices of arbitration received? 3.
Does it consider the continuation of bilateral investment treaties with Belarus to be compatible with EU policy?

(17 September 2026) In its judgments of December 2025 (1), the General Court stressed that its review was limited to the listings of the natural persons and did not pronounce itself on whether TerraBrown AG is subject to EU sanctions. Article 11(1) of Regulation 833/2014 (2) and Article 11(1) of Regulation 269/2014 (3) prohibit the satisfaction of any claim in connection with a contract or transaction which is affected by EU sanctions. This prohibition includes the satisfaction of such claims in arbitral proceedings as well as the recognition and enforcement of arbitral awards resulting from such proceedings in the EU. Article 11(2a) of Regulation 833/2014 further specifies that Member States are not to recognise or enforce non-EU court judgments, arbitral awards or administrative decisions issued pursuant to or derived from investor-State dispute settlement proceedings against a Member State, which could lead to the satisfaction of any claim linked to EU restrictive measures, when these are invoked by, inter alia, listed persons or entities, or by legal persons, entities or bodies established outside the EU whose proprietary rights are directly or indirectly owned for more than 50% by sanctioned persons or entities. This provision could extend to those invoked by a non-listed entity, which is owned or controlled by a listed person or entity. The Commission is aware of arbitration proceedings initiated under Member States’ bilateral investment treaties (BITs). Any request for access to related documents is examined in accordance with Regulation (EC) 1049/2001 (4). Member States’ BITs are grandfathered by Regulation No 1219/2012 (5). The Commission continues to monitor the compatibility of Member States’ BITs with the EU investment policy, including those with Belarus.

E-10-2026-002840.t: Condition of the barrels of radioactive waste in the Atlantic trench and their impact on the Galician coast
qt: to the Commission Ana Miranda Paz (Verts/ALE) Subject:

The area off the Galician coast known as the Atlantic trench was the dumping ground for 220 000 drums of nuclear waste. The Commission has admitted in answers to previous questions1 that it is not in possession of any up-to-date studies and that it did not carry out the relevant monitoring included in the verification mission programme for 2030. The Commission has clearly failed to act with regard to this serious issue. In its investigations, France’s NODSSUM expedition, led by the French National Centre for Scientific Research, found 3 550 radioactive barrels off the Atlantic coast and discovered that they had cracks, showed signs of advanced deterioration and were leaking, with the area having higher-than-expected levels of radionuclides. In view of the above: Having received this scientific evidence regarding the condition of the barrels of radioactive waste, will the Commission finally carry out a rigorous investigation into the impact their condition is having?

to the Commission Jessica Polfjärd (PPE) Subject:

Both the Industrial Accelerator Act and the proposed revision of the CO2 standards for cars and vans refer to ‘low-carbon steel’ without defining it. In both cases, the definition is left to future delegated acts under the Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation. 1.
Will the Commission ensure a single, coordinated definition of low-carbon steel for both laws, and, if so, by when?
How will the Commission avoid the application of two different definitions at the same time?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (21.8.2026) Article 14 of the proposal for the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA)1 ensures the necessary coherence between the CO2 standards provisions and the IAA provisions on public procurement and incentives concerning the low carbon definition. For both purposes, a single definition of low-carbon steel will be developed by the Commission in a delegated act on iron and steel products under the Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation2, currently foreseen for the second quarter of 2027. The Commission is aware of the need to prevent legal uncertainty and market fragmentation that could result from parallel or divergent definitions. This will be avoided by adopting a single definition of low carbon steel in the said delegated act under the Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation.

E-10-2026-002838.t: Protecting people living in the immediate vicinity of regional airport runways
qt: to the Commission Maria Zacharia (NI) Subject:

Many regional airports in the European Union operate in the immediate vicinity of residential areas, schools and tourist facilities. In Greece, a typical example is Rhodes International Airport, where a significant number of locals live below the flight paths of approaching and departing planes. While EU law does not provide for a single minimum distance between aerodromes and residential areas, Regulation (EU) 2018/1139, the implementing acts adopted pursuant to it and the international standards of ICAO, in particular Annex 14 (Aerodromes), require the systematic assessment of the risks associated with the operation of aerodromes as well as safety management. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
What are the obligations under EU law to assess and manage the risks faced by residents living in the immediate vicinity of regional airport runways?

Does the certification and oversight framework for aerodromes, in accordance with Regulation (EU) 2018/1139 and the relevant EASA requirements, include a thirdparty/ground risk assessment, in particular when there are residential areas or other sensitive uses below flight paths?

Does it intend to examine whether additional EU guidelines or legislative initiatives are needed to better protect residents living in the immediate vicinity of regional airports, particularly in island and tourist regions with high levels of seasonal air traffic?
at: (English version) to the Commission Maria Zacharia (NI) (8 July 2026) Subject: Protecting people living in the immediate vicinity of regional airport runways Many regional airports in the European Union operate in the immediate vicinity of residential areas, schools and tourist facilities. In Greece, a typical example is Rhodes International Airport, where a significant number of locals live below the flight paths of approaching and departing planes. While EU law does not provide for a single minimum distance between aerodromes and residential areas, Regulation (EU) 2018/1139, the implementing acts adopted pursuant to it and the international standards of ICAO, in particular Annex 14 (Aerodromes), require the systematic assessment of the risks associated with the operation of aerodromes as well as safety management. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
What are the obligations under EU law to assess and manage the risks faced by residents living in the immediate vicinity of regional airport runways?

Does the certification and oversight framework for aerodromes, in accordance with Regulation (EU) 2018/1139 and the relevant EASA requirements, include a third-party/ground risk assessment, in particular when there are residential areas or other sensitive uses below flight paths?

Does it intend to examine whether additional EU guidelines or legislative initiatives are needed to better protect residents living in the immediate vicinity of regional airports, particularly in island and tourist regions with high levels of seasonal air traffic?

(22 September 2026) Regulation (EU) 2018/1139 (1) and Commission Regulation (EU) No 139/2014 (2) regulate aerodrome safety. The application of Article 2, paragraph 1 (f)) of Regulation (EU) 2018/1139, as it applies to aerodromes within its scope, is ‘without prejudice to Union and national law on environment and land-use planning, the safeguarding of surroundings’. The aviation safety requirements related to the aerodrome surroundings therefore do not override or replace existing Union or national laws on environmental protection or land-use planning. The aerodromes’ safety certification and oversight framework does not include an explicit requirement for a third-party or ground risk assessment, including assessments of residential areas or other sensitive land uses beneath flight paths. Responsibility for assessing and managing risk to people on the ground remains with Member States in line with applicable Union and national planning, environmental, and public safety legislation. Based on safety data available, analysis and follow-up of occurrences in civil aviation, there is not sufficient evidence that such an initiative would be warranted.

E-10-2026-002836.t: Interim EUR 3 flat-rate customs duty applied to printed books and magazines
qt: to the Commission Aodhán Ó Ríordáin (S&D) Subject:
Interim EUR 3 flat-rate customs duty applied to printed books and magazines

From 1 July 2026, an interim flat-rate customs duty of EUR 3 per declaration line applies to low-value e-commerce consignments entering the EU, under Council Regulation (EU) 2026/382 of 11 February 20261, as implemented by Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/1200 of 5 June 20262. This measure targets fast fashion and non-compliant goods, not culture and education. Printed books (CN/TARIC 4901 99 00) carry a 0 % most-favoured nation (MFN) customs duty, reflecting the EU’s commitment to safeguarding literature and academic material. However, Article 2 of Council Regulation (EU) 2026/382 applies the EUR 3 duty to all qualifying consignments regardless of tariff classification, with no exemption for books. A book is charged the same EUR 3 duty as any other item, irrespective of heading. In Ireland, constituents report that book shipments via An Post’s clearance portal, correctly identified as ‘books’, are still charged the EUR 3 duty plus a EUR 6.95 handling fee. 1.
Was the Commission aware, when implementing Council Regulation (EU) 2026/382, that it would apply uniformly to books otherwise carrying 0 % MFN duty?
Does the Commission consider it compatible with the EU’s cultural and educational objectives for this duty to apply indiscriminately to books?
Will the Commission bring forward a carve-out for CN 4901 goods, or clarify how one can be introduced before the measure ends on 1 July 2028?

OJ L, 2026/382, 18.2.2026, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2026/382/oj (http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2026/382/oj). 2 OJ L, 2026/1200, 8.6.2026, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg_impl/2026/1200/oj (http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg_impl/2026/1200/oj). 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (8.9.2026) Council Regulation (EU) 2026/3821 abolishes the EUR 150 threshold-based customs duty exemption and imposes, from 1 July 2026 until 1 July 2028, a temporary EUR 3 customs duty per item in consignments valued at up to EUR 150 and sold in distance sales. This in principle includes books and magazines. However, imported goods can benefit from existing duty exemptions or preferential treatment if they fulfil the relevant conditions. Books and magazines printed in third countries and meeting the rules of origin with those third countries for which the EU has preferential trade agreements can benefit from preferential duty rates, if the appropriate proof of origin is provided when required to customs. If the preferential treatment applies, it must be claimed by declaring the goods using a normal (H1) customs declaration. The simplified (H7) declaration cannot be used for preferential treatment, as it does not contain the data elements necessary to claim preferential origin. Pursuant to the Duty Relief Regulation2, the duty-free import of certain educational, scientific and cultural materials will still be possible, provided that certain conditions are met. For example, it will be possible to import duty-free microfilms of books, children’s picture books or colouring books, maps, scientific charts and diagrams, if the advertising contained therein does not cover more than 25 % of the surface. The Commission will, by 1 October 2026, assess the impact of the temporary EUR 3 customs duty on possible diversions of trade flows and unintended consequences for specific categories of goods, such as books and magazines. If appropriate, the Commission will consider submitting a proposal to amend Council Regulation (EU) 2026/382.

E-10-2026-002834.t: Türkiye’s refusal to admit an LGBTQ+ cruise ship
qt: to the Commission Kathleen Van Brempt (S&D), Hilde Vautmans (Renew), Sara Matthieu (Verts/ALE) Subject:

On 5 July 2026, the Scarlet Lady, carrying 2 000 LGBTQ+ passengers, was denied entry to the Turkish port of Kuşadası, with local authorities stating that the group’s presence did not ‘align with the structure of our society and our moral values’. This is part of a broader pattern: Istanbul Pride has been banned every year since 2015, and senior Turkish officials have repeatedly described LGBTQ+ people as a threat to society. The EU maintains active cooperation with Türkiye, and Türkiye remains an EU candidate country. The promotion of human rights and non-discrimination is a core principle of the EU’s external action under Article 21 of the Treaty on European Union. 1.

Does the Commission, together with the European External Action Service, intend to raise this incident with the Turkish authorities as part of the EU’s political dialogue on human rights, and if so, how?
How is the Commission ensuring that respect for LGBTQ+ rights and nondiscrimination is systematically integrated into the EU’s broader relationship with Türkiye?
What will the Commission do to help protect the rights of LGBTQ+ EU citizens travelling to Türkiye, given the risk of discriminatory treatment such as this?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.9.2026)

The European Commission is aware of the denial of entry to the Scarlet Lady in Kuşadası. It has underlined on numerous occasions, including in its last enlargement report on Türkiye1, that the protection of fundamental rights of LGBTIQ+ people in Türkiye remains a major concern. The Commission regularly raises human rights issues with the Turkish authorities. This includes concerns related to the protection of LGBTIQ+ people’s rights. The Commissioner for Enlargement has met members of the LGBTIQ+ community during her recent visits to Türkiye to discuss the situation. As an EU candidate country and member of the Council of Europe, Türkiye is expected to uphold the highest democratic standards and to ensure the respect of fundamental rights for all, including visitors, without discrimination, including on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity. These issues are taken into account in the assessment of the country’s alignment with EU values and standards. The Commission will continue to support civil society and human rights defenders through its financial assistance in Türkiye, including organisations that promote and defend the rights of LGBTIQ+ people. The Commission will also continue to raise these issues in all relevant contacts with the Turkish authorities, including in the context of the sub-committee covering this area, established under the Association Agreement with Türkiye2.
