E-10-2026-002832.t: New climate and environmental labels for textiles and clothing
qt: to the Commission Jessica Polfjärd (PPE) Subject:

As part of ongoing work concerning textiles and clothing, the Joint Research Centre and the Commission are proposing new carbon and environmental footprint labels. More labels risk confusing consumers rather than helping them, while at the same time increasing red tape for businesses. In addition, it remains unclear whether the labels will be voluntary or mandatory. Experts in the Commission’s own Ecodesign Forum have pointed out that the scientific basis is weak and, in a worst-case scenario, labels risk contributing to greenwashing, as they are not life-cycle based. 1.
How do the new labels benefit consumers compared to already established and trusted voluntary labels on the market, such as the EU Ecolabel and the Nordic Swan Ecolabel?

How does the introduction of new labels relate to the simplification agenda and the Commission’s own ambition to tidy up the labelling jungle, as set out in the Directive on empowering consumers for the green transition (Directive (EU) 2024/825)?
at: (English version) to the Commission Jessica Polfjärd (PPE) (8 July 2026) Subject: New climate and environmental labels for textiles and clothing As part of ongoing work concerning textiles and clothing, the Joint Research Centre and the Commission are proposing new carbon and environmental footprint labels. More labels risk confusing consumers rather than helping them, while at the same time increasing red tape for businesses. In addition, it remains unclear whether the labels will be voluntary or mandatory. Experts in the Commission’s own Ecodesign Forum have pointed out that the scientific basis is weak and, in a worst-case scenario, labels risk contributing to greenwashing, as they are not life-cycle based. 1. How do the new labels benefit consumers compared to already established and trusted voluntary labels on the market, such as the EU Ecolabel and the Nordic Swan Ecolabel? 2. How does the introduction of new labels relate to the simplification agenda and the Commission’s own ambition to tidy up the labelling jungle, as set out in the directive on empowering consumers for the green transition (Directive (EU) 2024/825)? (25 August 2026) The Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation (1) is a key instrument to promote a circular economy and responds to requests from stakeholders including businesses to have common requirements on this matter within the single market. The form and shape of Ecodesign requirements (performance and/or information) for apparel textiles will be determined during the ongoing impact assessment process. The Ecodesign Forum will discuss the draft measures with stakeholders, and the Commission will publish a Call for Evidence and a public consultation on the ‘Have Your Say’ portal. In particular, information requirements under the Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation aim to function as an incentive for sustainable consumption. Therefore, the introduction of labelling provisions in the delegated act will be considered if the impact assessment demonstrates that a label would clearly contribute to this goal. Labels harmonised at EU level also replace the need to comply with multiple, differing national schemes, making it easier for businesses to market products across Member States without having to adapt to separate national requirements, reducing administrative complexity and compliance costs. This thorough process will ensure that any information requirements are not disproportionate and in line with the Commission’s simplification objectives. While Directive (EU) 2024/825 (2) does not apply to mandatory labels required under Union law, the Commission will also take into account the interaction of requirements under the Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation with existing EU rules.

Regulation (EU) 2024/1781 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 June 2024 establishing a framework for the setting of ecodesign requirements for sustainable products, amending Directive (EU) 2020/1828 and Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 and repealing Directive 2009/125/EC, OJ L, 2024/1781, 28.6.2024. E-10-2026-002831.t: Commission action to address the consequences of the climate crisis and the impact of phenomena such as water scarcity on islands
qt: to the Commission Dimitris Tsiodras (PPE) Subject:

Both water scarcity and water-related risks are being exacerbated as a result of the climate crisis, as rising temperatures throw the entire water cycle out of kilter. Water scarcity is not only a major challenge for islands and their inhabitants; it also presents a major obstacle to their economic development. While its water resilience strategy refers to the need to reduce leaks and improve water storage and efficiency, the Commission – beyond its commitment to support innovation in the field of sustainable desalination – does not propose specific measures for island regions. It is worth noting that the European Commission estimates that the water management investment gap stands at EUR 23 billion per year. In view of the forthcoming European climate adaptation plan, can the Commission say: 1.
What steps will it take to mitigate climate change and ensure sufficient water supply on islands?

Does it intend to create specific financial tools to meet the investment needed to modernise infrastructure and address leaks, as well as to fund the research and development of new technologies to address the problem?
How will it ensure that any measures taken will meet the needs of islands?

(1 September 2026) The European Integrated Framework for Climate Resilience (1), to be adopted by the end of 2026, will set out a strengthened, comprehensive and coherent EU approach to climate resilience and preparedness to become better prepared for and more resilient to the inevitable impacts of climate change, including on islands. The proposal for the next Multiannual Financial Framework (2) stipulates that at least 35% of the EU budget should contribute to climate and environmental objectives, including water resilience. The proposed National and Regional Partnership Plans will contribute to ensuring sustainable prosperity, maintaining quality of life across the Union, and addressing specific needs of islands and coastal areas, feature a climate and environmental contribution of at least 43% (3). The European Competitiveness Fund (4) may also support water resilience and transition to a water-smart economy under its ‘Clean Transition and Industrial Decarbonisation’ window. The EU strategy for islands (5) recognises that islands face water-related challenges and recommends that Member States prioritise investments in water infrastructure to improve water services and distribution networks and increase water saving and water reuse, while restoring natural water retention. The mid-term review of cohesion policy encouraged Member States to increase investments in sustainable water management, increased water efficiency, secure access to water and measures enhancing water resilience, resulting in the reallocation of EUR 1.6 billion to islands through cohesion policy programmes, including EUR 158 million for water-related investments.

E-10-2026-002830.t: Protecting workers’ rights during medical absences
qt: to the Commission Idoia Mendia (S&D), Alicia Homs Ginel (S&D), Leire Pajín (S&D), Nicolás González Casares (S&D) Subject:

Measures to reduce workers’ wages or benefits during periods of sick leave or justified absence are being considered in the public debate in some countries. These proposals present illness as a cost or abuse, without differentiating between fraudulent cases, recognised temporary incapacity, legitimate leave, caring for family members or mental health issues. Directive 89/391/EEC requires that the safety and health of workers be ensured in every aspect related to their work. Article 31 of the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights recognises the right of every worker to conditions which respect his or her health, safety and dignity. In light of the above: 1.
Does the Commission consider it compatible with the European acquis on health and safety at work to penalise workers financially during duly recognised sick leave?

Does it agree that imposing financial penalties for medical absences, including those resulting from ordinary circumstances, can put pressure on workers to return to work before they are fully recovered, putting their physical and mental health at risk and weakening the effective protection of their health at work?
Will it ensure that the Quality Jobs Act promotes an approach based on prevention, mental health, workplace adaptation and social dialogue, rather than punitive measures in response to illness?
to the Commission Bert-Jan Ruissen (ECR), Carmen Crespo Díaz (PPE) Subject:

On 15 April 2026, the Commission reported to Parliament’s Committee on Fisheries that only three Member States, representing a small minority of total eel stock, had notified it regarding their updated Eel Management Plans (EMPs) under Council Regulation (EC) No 1100/2007 (the Eel Regulation). In order to improve the regulation’s governance and to ensure regular updates to EMPs, Parliament has recommended the creation of an eel-specific expert group to advise the Commission on implementation, to provide feedback to Member States on their EMPs and to evaluate progress. The joint special group set up under the marine action plan brings together fisheries and environment ministries, but lacks a specific focus on eel. Given the eel’s marine and freshwater life cycle, an eel-specific subgroup would be a cost-efficient and coherent way to address all impacts on eel. 1.
Will the Commission consider creating a subgroup under the joint special group that would be dedicated to improved governance of the Eel Regulation?
How would the Commission involve representatives from commercial and recreational fishers, water managers, hydro-power companies, civil society and other relevant parties in such a subgroup?
How will the Commission ensure the viability and competitiveness of the eel fisheries sector taking into consideration its socio-economic impact?

(24 August 2026) The Commission created in 2023 the Joint Special Group under the EU Marine Action Plan (1) as a forum to exchange on matters pertaining to the implementation of this Action Plan. This also covers actions related to improving the protection of European eel. The Joint Special Group includes representatives of the Member States’ fisheries and environmental administrations, as well as observers representing various stakeholder groups, including fisheries sector, environmental non-governmental organisations, advisory councils. This Special Group last met on 30 June 2026. Issues related to the governance and implementation of the Eel Regulation, and to the eel matters more generally, can be and are already being discussed under the existing structure of the action plan and in other fora at the EU, regional and international levels. For instance, upon request from the Special Group, the Commission organised in April 2024 a dedicated intersessional technical workshop on eels (2). The creation of a dedicated subgroup on eels is therefore not considered necessary. The conservation and management of critically endangered European eel require a comprehensive approach, taking into consideration fisheries, environmental and socioeconomic impacts. Existing measures at EU level allow fishing for eels in accordance with EU law (3). In that respect, it should be noted that the European eel is the only fish stock with a zero-catch advice issued by the International Council for the Exploration of the Sea (4) for which targeted fishing is allowed to continue.

E-10-2026-002828.t: Protecting minors from generative artificial intelligence systems in the context of the digital omnibus measures simplifying the AI Act
qt: to the Commission Şerban Dimitrie Sturdza (ECR) Subject:

The Commission proposed the digital omnibus with the aim of simplifying some obligations under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on artificial intelligence and thus reducing the administrative burden on European businesses and strengthening competitiveness. Generative AI systems are accessible to minors and can create or recommend text, images, audio and videos. These systems pose risks to children, including exposure to unsuitable content, behavioural manipulation, the creation of harmful content and effects on mental development. The protection of children in the digital environment is guaranteed by Articles 24 and 14(3) of the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights, which enshrine the right of the child to protection and the right of parents to ensure that children are educated according to their convictions. 1.

How will the Commission ensure that the simplification of the AI Act through the digital omnibus does not lower the level of protection of minors from generative artificial intelligence systems, in particular with regard to exposure to age-inappropriate content?
What concrete support is the Commission offering to allow parents to effectively exercise their right to control and consent to the exposure of their young children to these types of systems?

How will consistency be ensured between the simplification measures and the obligations already provided for in the Digital Services Act with regard to the protection of minors, so that no regulatory gaps emerge?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.9.2026) The AI Act1 protects children by introducing safeguards for the development and use of AI systems. It prohibits AI systems that manipulate, deceive or exploit children’s vulnerabilities with the objective or the effect of materially distorting children’s behaviour in a manner likely to lead to significant harm2. AI systems used in education are high-risk and must comply with requirements on, among others, risk management, transparency and human oversight. The AI Omnibus does not undermine the high level of protection that the AI Act provides. It strengthens children’s protection by prohibiting AI systems that generate child sexual abuse material and non-consensual intimate content3. The Digital Services Act (DSA)4 sets harmonised rules for a safe, predictable and trusted online environment, including for children, and is unaffected by the AI Omnibus. Article 28 DSA requires providers of online platforms accessible to minors to put in place appropriate and proportionate measures to ensure a high level of privacy, safety and security of minors, on their service. The Commission Guidelines on the protection of minors5 set out measures that, in the Commission’s view, providers should implement to comply with that obligation. The AI Act and DSA are complementary and together ensure a high level of child protection in the EU6. The Commission also fosters media literacy and digital learning through the European strategy for a Better Internet for Kids7 (BIK+), the Safer Internet Centres and the BIK platform8. These support children and young people in, among others, building critical digital skills and using social media and AI responsibly. They also equip parents, caregivers, teachers and educators with the knowledge and tools to support children online.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj/eng. 2 https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/commission-publishes-guidelines-prohibited-artificial-

intelligence-ai-practices-defined-ai-act. This prohibition is applicable since 2 February 2025. 3 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202601744. This prohibition will be applicable as of 2 December 2026. 4 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/2065/oj/eng. 5 https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/commission-publishes-guidelines-protection-minors. 6 In due compliance with children’s rights as enshrined in the Charter of fundamental rights of the European Union. 7 https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/strategy-better-internet-kids. 8 https://better-internet-for-kids.europa.eu/en.

E-10-2026-002826.t: Meta’s failure to moderate fraudulent advertisements under the DSA
qt: to the Commission Kathleen Van Brempt (S&D) Subject:

Recent investigations, including those by the VRT programme Pano1 and AI Forensics2 reveal that Meta continues to profit from fraudulent advertisements, including scams impersonating public figures and journalists and more than 46 000 health-related advertisements featuring unapproved drugs, deepfakes and false medical claims, viewed 292 million times by EU users since the Digital Services Act (DSA) entered into force. Internal Meta documents reportedly estimate that scam advertisements generate around 10 % of its annual revenue, far exceeding likely fines for non-compliance. On 21 May 2026, the European Consumer Organisation (BEUC) and 29 member organisations filed formal complaints with the Commission against Meta over its systematic failure to remove fraudulent financial advertisements. Meanwhile, victims report that national police often lack the resources to investigate such cases, particularly when servers are hosted outside the EU or when the fraud involves less than EUR 5 000. 1.
Is the Commission aware of these findings and has it engaged with Meta on this systemic non-compliance?
Is the Commission considering a formal investigation into Meta under the DSA regarding this issue?

How will the Commission ensure effective follow-up and redress for victims, given that national authorities often cannot act on complaints below certain thresholds or when servers are hosted outside the EU?
https://aiforensics.org/uploads/meta_health.pdf. https://aiforensics.org/uploads/meta_health.pdf.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (14.9.2026) The Commission takes the concerns raised very seriously. The Commission is aware of the complaints and reports regarding the dissemination of deceptive advertising on Meta’s platforms. In April 2024, the Commission initiated proceedings against the provider of Facebook and Instagram, including in relation to the suspicion that the provider does not comply with obligations related to addressing deceptive advertisements, including financial scam advertisements1. On 24 October 2025, the Commission preliminarily found the provider of Facebook and Instagram in breach of its obligations to put in place user-friendly and easily accessible mechanisms to allow recipients to notify content considered to be illegal and to provide users with an internal complaint-handling system that allows them to effectively challenge content moderation decisions taken by the provider2. The case in relation to financial scam advertisements is ongoing, and the Commission cannot comment on the status of ongoing investigations. Recipients of intermediary services may lodge a complaint against a provider of those services alleging an infringement of the Digital Services Act (DSA)3. Complaints must be submitted to the Digital Services Coordinator (DSC)4 of the Member State where the recipient of the service is located or established. The Commission remains in close contact with competent national authorities through the DSCs to ensure the effective fulfilment of DSA obligations. The revised Victims’ Rights’ Directive5 (June 2026) enhances the rights, protection, and access to justice for victims of crime, including of online frauds. An EU Action Plan on digital frauds and a Strategy on victims’ rights are forthcoming and will contain measures to support victims of online fraud.

E-10-2026-002825.t: Requirement for an expert ballistics report when slaughtering livestock at the farm of origin
qt: to the Commission Veronika Vrecionová (ECR) Subject:

Regulation (EC) No 1099/2009 sets forth requirements for the protection of animals at the time of killing, including the use of firearms with free projectiles, particularly with regard to the professional competence of the person performing the slaughter, the selection of ammunition and ensuring the immediate and effective stunning of the animal. In the Czech Republic, however, the slaughter of farm animals at the farm of origin requires a site plan of the shooting location, accompanied by an expert ballistics report. This report is drafted at the farmer’s expense, is valid for three years, and must be redrafted if the conditions under which the permit was issued change. Can the Commission answer the following questions: 1.

Does the obligation to submit a site plan for the shooting location and an expert ballistics report stem directly from EU legislation or from Commission guidelines or recommendations, or is this a decision by a Member State that goes beyond the scope of the Regulation?

Does the Commission feel that additional national requirements not expressly provided for in Union law may constitute a disproportionate administrative or financial burden for small family farms, mobile or regional slaughterhouses and the development of short supply chains?
Is the Commission considering issuing guidelines or examples of best practices to promote a proportionate and more uniform application of the rules on on-farm slaughter in the Member States?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (24.8.2026) Regulation (EC) No 1099/20091 establishes rules for the protection of animals at the time of killing. These rules include the obligation to prevent animals from experiencing any avoidable pain, distress or suffering. Where firearms using free projectiles are used, Regulation (EC) No 1999/2009 specifies the conditions but does not explicitly require a site plan or an expert ballistics report. A site plan and a ballistic report can help to demonstrate that the shooting location is safe for both the animal and persons present, and the firearm is working properly. Responsibility for implementing and enforcing the obligations laid down in Regulation (EC) No 1999/2009 lies primarily with Member States, through their competent authorities. Regulation (EC) No 853/20042 lays down the food safety rules applicable during slaughter. It includes the possibility to allow slaughter on farm with the aim to avoid animal welfare issues during transport. National rules may be adopted and must be notified to the Commission and to the other Member States that must express their agreement. For that reason, the Commission does not feel that they may constitute a disproportionate administrative or financial burden for small family farms, mobile or regional slaughterhouses. To support harmonised application of the possibilities laid down by Regulation (EC) No 853/2004 across the EU, the Commission has published a Guidance document on the implementation of certain provisions of this Regulation on the hygiene of food of animal origin3. The Commission also published a series of factsheets4 intended to help farmers and workers in small slaughterhouses apply EU animal welfare rules.
1 Council Regulation (EC) No 1099/2009 of 24 September 2009 on the protection of animals at the time of

killing (OJ L 303, 18.11.2009, pp. 1–30), p. 1, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2009/1099/oj). 2 Regulation (EC) No 853/2004 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 29 April 2004 laying down specific hygiene rules for food of animal origin (OJ L 139, 30.4.2004, p. 55, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2004/853/oj). 3 https://food.ec.europa.eu/document/download/ce8efc9d-8750-4b75-9563-7427da889666_en. 4 https://food.ec.europa.eu/animals/animal-welfare/eu-animal-welfare-legislation/slaughter-stunning/2018factsheets_en.

E-10-2026-002824.t: Application of rules on the handling of blood during the slaughter of farm animals at the farm of origin
qt: to the Commission Veronika Vrecionová (ECR) Subject:

According to Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 and related EU legislation on hygiene, blood resulting from the slaughter of farm animals is subject to the rules governing animal byproducts. This also applies to the one-time slaughter of an animal on the farm of origin under EU rules, where the blood must be handled in a controlled manner. In contrast, when hunting wild game, the blood can typically remain in the wild, even though the meat is also intended for human consumption. Strict hygiene protocols are entirely understandable in large slaughterhouses or intensive livestock operations. However, for family farms that slaughter one or two animals a year out in the open, the question arises as to whether these requirements are proportionate. Can the Commission answer the following questions: 1.
On the basis of what scientific or hygiene findings is blood from the one-time slaughter of a farm animal subject to stricter rules than blood from hunted wild game intended for human consumption?
Did the Commission assess the proportionality of these requirements in relation to small family farms that only occasionally slaughter livestock when drafting the legislation?

As part of a future revision of rules on hygiene or animal by-products, is the Commission considering the creation of a more proportionate regime for small farms without compromising food safety, animal health or environmental protection?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (21.8.2026) Wild game hunting is inherently unpredictable, and blood dispersal in such cases is typically minimal. In contrast, the on-farm slaughter of farmed animals can be planned under controlled hygienic conditions, enabling systematic risk mitigation such as preventing pathogen transmission to humans or other animals through blood. EU food hygiene rules do not apply to the on-farm slaughter of farmed animals for private domestic consumption. When blood is intended for human consumption, it must be handled under strict hygiene conditions according to Regulation (EC) No 853/20041. If these requirements cannot be met, the blood must be excluded from the food chain. Only then Regulation (EC) No 1069/20092 on animal by-products not intended for human consumption starts to apply regarding the collection and disposal of blood. The principle of proportionality was integral to the development of the EU rules, which recognise that even occasional on-farm slaughter must adhere to core hygiene standards to prevent disease spread and safeguard human health. The Commission regularly reviews EU legislation on food hygiene and on animal by-products to improve practicality without compromising safety. Additionally, Member States may adapt certain EU food hygiene requirements to preserve traditional methods of food production or accommodate businesses in regions with specific geographic constraints. Such adaptations must be notified to the Commission in advance and must not pose a risk to public health.
1 Regulation (EC) No 853/2004 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 29 April 2004 laying down

specific hygiene rules for food of animal origin (OJ L 139, 30.4.2004, pp. 55–205). 2 Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 21 October 2009 laying down health rules as regards animal by-products and derived products not intended for human consumption and repealing Regulation (EC) No 1774/2002 (Animal by-products Regulation) (OJ L 300, 14.11.2009, pp. 1–33).

E-10-2026-002823.t: Impact of the recent US Supreme Court ruling on the EU–US Data Privacy Framework and European data sovereignty
qt: to the Commission Aura Salla (PPE), Mika Aaltola (PPE), Pekka Toveri (PPE), Alexandra Mehnert (PPE), Andrea Wechsler (PPE), Maria Guzenina (S&D), Maria Grapini (S&D), Lucia Yar (Renew), Sophie Wilmès (Renew), Kai Tegethoff (Verts/ALE), Anna Strolenberg (Verts/ALE), Per Clausen (The Left), Merja Kyllönen (The Left), Leila Chaibi (The Left), Sirpa Pietikäinen (PPE), Wouter Beke (PPE), Axel Voss (PPE), Michael McNamara (Renew), Kim Van Sparrentak (Verts/ALE), Nela Riehl (Verts/ALE), Reinier Van Lanschot (Verts/ALE), Emil Radev (PPE) Subject:

A recent ruling by the Supreme Court of the United States weakens the independence of key federal oversight bodies and may undermine the legal assumptions underpinning the EU–US Data Privacy Framework. As the stability of transatlantic data transfers depends on effective and independent oversight in the United States, this development highlights the EU’s continued exposure to external legal and political developments and the need to strengthen European digital sovereignty. Considering this: 1.
Will the Commission urgently assess the implications of the ruling for the validity and stability of the EU–US Data Privacy Framework?
What steps is the Commission taking to strengthen European data sovereignty and reduce the EU’s dependence on non-EU data transfer mechanisms?
Is the Commission preparing contingency measures, including an orderly transition, should the current framework become legally unsustainable?
at: (English version) to the Commission Raquel García Hermida-Van Der Walle (Renew) (25 June 2026) Subject: EU-US biometric data-sharing agreement and US data protection practice Negotiations between the EU and the United States on the framework agreement regarding the exchange of personal data, including biometric data, for the purpose of screening and identity verification of travellers (1), are expected to be concluded soon. According to the Commission, in this context ‘ensur[ing] respect of the EU’s standards on the protection of personal data’ is a ‘key priority’ (2). This should not only be the case prior to signing an agreement, but also afterwards, in practice. The EU-US Umbrella Agreement, in force since 2017 and intended to improve the overall level of data protection in EU-US law enforcement cooperation, was supposed to be jointly reviewed by 2020. However, six years later, a joint review report has yet to be published. 1. Why was no joint review of the EU-US Umbrella Agreement published, despite the legal requirement to do so (3)? If the data protection requirements of that agreement cannot be reviewed or assessed because there are no results to review, and noting the worrying developments in the US regarding the protection of personal data, how does the Commission expect EU citizens to have trust in the US authorities as regards the safety of their transferred biometric data? 2. Will the Commission ensure that the draft agreement fully incorporates the standards set by the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) in relevant case law (4), and if so, is it convinced that the envisaged agreement would hold up in court? Priority question for written answer P-002741/26 to the Commission Raquel García Hermida-Van Der Walle (Renew) (2 July 2026) Subject: Validity of EU-US Data Privacy Framework following US Supreme Court judgment In 2023, the Commission issued an adequacy decision in line with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) for data transfers to the United States, implemented under the EU-US Data Privacy Framework. In this adequacy decision, the Commission relied on the US Federal Trade Commission as an ‘independent’ supervisory authority with the power to monitor and enforce compliance with the data protection rules (1). On 29 June 2026, the US Supreme Court ruled that independent executive authorities in the United States are unconstitutional (2), which raises questions regarding the validity of the Commission’s adequacy decision, leaving both citizens and companies in legal uncertainty. In 2015 and 2020, earlier adequacy decisions for data transfers to the US were invalidated by the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU), because of a lack of adequate data protection in the United States.

Also known as the Enhanced Border Security Partnership. Article 23 of the EU-US Umbrella Agreement, (OJ L 336, 10.12.2016, p. 3-13 ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/agree_internation/2016/2220/oj). In the field of (transatlantic) data exchange, including, but not limited to, the CJEU’s opinion on the envisaged EU-Canada PNR agreement and judgments in the Safe Harbour and Privacy Shield cases. Commission Implementing Decision EU 2023/1795 of 10 July 2023 pursuant to Regulation (EU) 2016/679 of the European Parliament and of the Council on the adequate level of protection of personal data under the EU-US Data Privacy Framework (notified under document C(2023)4745), http://data.europa.eu/eli/dec_impl/2023/1795/oj. https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/25pdf/25-332_qn12.pdf.

1. Does the Commission share the concerns regarding the Supreme Court judgment, and by which date does the Commission plan to publish an assessment of whether or not this affects the validity of its adequacy decision? 2. Will the Commission reach out and discuss this matter with the US authorities on a political level, to ensure that they are fully aware that independent supervision is a condition for the continuation of the EU-US Data Privacy Framework? 3. Will the Commission be more proactive in safeguarding EU citizens’ data protection, or will it wait for a possible third invalidation of an adequacy decision by the CJEU? to the Commission Aura Salla (PPE), Mika Aaltola (PPE), Pekka Toveri (PPE), Alexandra Mehnert (PPE), Andrea Wechsler (PPE), Maria Guzenina (S&D), Maria Grapini (S&D), Lucia Yar (Renew), Sophie Wilmès (Renew), Kai Tegethoff (Verts/ALE), Anna Strolenberg (Verts/ALE), Per Clausen (The Left), Merja Kyllönen (The Left), Leila Chaibi (The Left), Sirpa Pietikäinen (PPE), Wouter Beke (PPE), Axel Voss (PPE), Michael McNamara (Renew), Kim Van Sparrentak (Verts/ALE), Nela Riehl (Verts/ALE), Reinier Van Lanschot (Verts/ALE), Emil Radev (PPE) (8 July 2026) Subject: Impact of the recent US Supreme Court ruling on the EU-US Data Privacy Framework and European data sovereignty A recent ruling by the Supreme Court of the United States weakens the independence of key federal oversight bodies and may undermine the legal assumptions underpinning the EU-US Data Privacy Framework. As the stability of transatlantic data transfers depends on effective and independent oversight in the United States, this development highlights the EU’s continued exposure to external legal and political developments and the need to strengthen European digital sovereignty. Considering this: 1.

to the Commission Catherine Griset (PfE) (13 July 2026) Subject: Urgent need to develop European cloud service providers The US Supreme Court has paved the way for the President of the United States to dismiss the commissioners of the Federal Trade Commission, the agency responsible, amongst other things, for protecting the personal data of Europeans when it is processed by US tech firms (1). Since 1935, the independence of these commissioners had been based on protection against politically-motivated dismissal: the President of the United States could appoint them, but could not remove them from office. This agreement was in fact conditional upon the existence of independent supervisory authorities in the United States. E-10-2026-002822.t: European funds allocated to fighting period poverty
qt: to the Commission Saskia Bricmont (Verts/ALE), Mélissa Camara (Verts/ALE), Kim Van Sparrentak (Verts/ALE), Martin Hojsík (Renew), Joanna Scheuring-Wielgus (S&D), Katrin Langensiepen (Verts/ALE), Ana Miranda Paz (Verts/ALE), Marie Toussaint (Verts/ALE), Anthony Smith (The Left), Mounir Satouri (Verts/ALE), Diana Riba i Giner (Verts/ALE), Raquel García Hermida-Van Der Walle (Renew), Murielle Laurent (S&D), Veronika Cifrová Ostrihoňová (Renew), Manon Aubry (The Left), Majdouline Sbai (Verts/ALE), Rudi Kennes (The Left), Christophe Clergeau (S&D), Leoluca Orlando (Verts/ALE), Lucia Yar (Renew), Tilly Metz (Verts/ALE), Gabriela Firea (S&D), Estelle Ceulemans (S&D), Aodhán Ó Ríordáin (S&D), Anja Hazekamp (The Left), Cristina Guarda (Verts/ALE), Marit Maij (S&D), Catarina Martins (The Left), Nicolae Ștefănuță (Verts/ALE), Emma Rafowicz (S&D), Leila Chaibi (The Left), Marc Angel (S&D), Lynn Boylan (The Left), Maria Guzenina (S&D), Lena Schilling (Verts/ALE), Aurore Lalucq (S&D), Cecilia Strada (S&D) Subject:

The 2026-2030 gender equality strategy, adopted by the Commission on 5 March 2026, acknowledges for the first time that menstrual and menopause poverty affect many women across the EU. In the strategy, the Commission referenced the 2022 revision of the VAT Directive, which enabled Member States to apply a reduced or zero rate to menstrual products, and proposed organising an exchange of best practices between EU Member States regarding measures to combat menstrual and menopause poverty at national level. However, VAT reduction alone does not guarantee the accessibility of menstrual products. According to estimates, in 2024 and 2025, 42 % of European women experienced period poverty at least once1. This figure highlights the limitations of current measures and raises questions about what further steps could be taken at EU and national level to address the issue more effectively. 1.

In addition to the exchange of best practices, what EU budget mechanisms does the Commission intend to mobilise to support Member States in facilitating access to menstrual products, including, for example, the European Social Fund Plus, which already supports measures targeting poverty and social exclusion?
Will the Commission issue guidance to the Member States on the eligibility of such measures under current funding programmes?
European Survey entitled ‘Règles Élémentaires’, OpinionWay Healthcare, 2025.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (2.10.2026) As acknowledged by the Honourable Members, the Roadmap for Women’s Rights1 and the Gender Equality Strategy 2026-20302 recognise that tackling menstrual poverty and improving access to affordable menstrual products are important for gender equality. The Strategy also notes that, on top of the 2022 revision of the VAT Directive, other measures, such as providing menstrual products free of charge or organising free distribution for specific groups, may in some cases offer a more targeted way of supporting those most in need. In this context, Member States may use European Social Fund Plus (ESF+)3 to support basic material assistance, including hygiene products, where this supports social inclusion and addresses material deprivation. As announced in the Strategy, the Commission will also fund a study on the macro- and micro-economic and societal benefits of closing the women’s health gap related to certain conditions over the life course, including menopause. Furthermore, the EU Anti-Poverty Strategy aims to tackle the causes of poverty while improving access to affordable, high-quality social and essential services. The Commission will track progress towards the reduction of poverty, strengthen monitoring, and propose new affordability indicators. The existing regulatory framework, including the ESF+, already provides possibilities for supporting measures aimed at reducing poverty and social exclusion, where such measures fall within the scope of the relevant specific objectives and national or regional programmes. The Commission will continue to provide clarification and support to Member States, where needed, in the context of programme implementation and exchanges of good practices.
1 Communication from the Commission to the European Parliament, the Council, the European Economic and

Social Committee and the Committee of the Regions ‘A Roadmap for Women's Rights’, COM(2025)97 final. 2 Communication from the Commission to the European Parliament, the Council, the European Economic tnd Social Committee and the Committee of the Regions ‘Gender Equality Strategy 2026-2030’, COM(2026)113 final. 3 https://european-social-fund-plus.ec.europa.eu/en.

E-10-2026-002821.t: EU-UAE trade negotiations in light of new evidence concerning UAE support to the RSF in Sudan
qt: to the Commission Aodhán Ó Ríordáin (S&D) Subject:

A new investigation by Lighthouse Reports, Evident and Sudan War Monitor has found that Rapid Support Forces (RSF) fighters are being trained in Libyan camps by the Libyan National Army and mercenaries contracted by the United Arab Emirates (UAE), using UAEsupplied weapons. These findings come as the UN Security Council warns of an imminent risk of mass atrocities in El Obeid, and as the EU prepares its next round of trade negotiations with the UAE. MEPs have questioned whether concluding such an agreement with a state accused of prolonging a conflict involving serious crimes under international law is compatible with the EU’s obligations under Article 21 of the Treaty on European Union (TEU). In light of the above: 1.

Does the Commission consider the continuation of EU-UAE trade negotiations to be compatible with Article 21 TEU and the EU’s commitments on atrocity prevention and arms-export control, given mounting evidence of UAE support to the RSF?

Will the Commission propose suspending EU-UAE trade negotiations until allegations of UAE support to the RSF and other actors implicated in atrocity crimes in Sudan are clarified, including via independent investigation and cooperation with UN mechanisms?

What steps is the Commission taking to ensure that any future EU-UAE trade agreement is conditional on the UAE ending all military, logistical or financial support to parties in Sudan’s conflict, and on full compliance with the Darfur arms embargo and international humanitarian law?

E-10-2026-002820.t: France’s invocation of the European Globalisation Adjustment Fund for Displaced Workers
qt: to the Commission Anthony Smith (The Left) Subject:

In 2007 the EU established the European Globalisation Adjustment Fund (EGF) to support workers affected by mass redundancies in Europe, primarily in the regions and sectors most at risk of job losses. With a maximum annual endowment of EUR 210 million euros for 2021– 2027, it helps laid-off workers find new employment or start a new business, by providing financial support for training, reskilling and reintegration into the labour market. Since its creation, the EGF has disbursed a total of some EUR 700 to 800 million in support for several hundred thousand workers made redundant across the European Union, although this is considerably under what it could theoretically provide, because Member States have been loath to use the EGF to its fullest extent. In France there are as yet no precise figures on the use of this scheme. Can the Commission therefore state: For what reasons, if any, have France and the workers laid off in large-scale redundancy schemes not been able to benefit from this fund?
at: (English version) to the Commission Anthony Smith (The Left) (8 July 2026) Subject: France’s invocation of the European Globalisation Adjustment Fund for Displaced Workers In 2007 the EU established the European Globalisation Adjustment Fund (EGF) to support workers affected by mass redundancies in Europe, primarily in the regions and sectors most at risk of job losses. With a maximum annual endowment of EUR 210 million euros for 2021-2027, it helps laid-off workers find new employment or start a new business, by providing financial support for training, reskilling and reintegration into the labour market. Since its creation, the EGF has disbursed a total of some EUR 700 to 800 million in support for several hundred thousand workers made redundant across the European Union, although this is considerably under what it could theoretically provide, because Member States have been loath to use the EGF to its fullest extent. In France there are as yet no precise figures on the use of this scheme. Can the Commission therefore state: For what reasons, if any, have France and the workers laid off in large-scale redundancy schemes not been able to benefit from this fund? (1 October 2026) Since the European Globalisation Adjustment Fund for Displaced Workers (EGF) began operations in 2007, it has been mobilised 12 times following applications from France, with a total allocation of EUR 123 million to offer support to 21 687 workers. Considering only the 2021-2027 period, EUR 23 million has been mobilised to offer support to 2 243 workers, following three applications. France is the Member State that has received the largest amount of EGF funding, at three times the average amount. Should the Honourable Member wish to obtain further details, the Commission refers the Honourable Member to the report from the Commission to the European Parliament and the Council on the activities of the European Globalisation Adjustment Fund for Displaced Workers (EGF) in 2023 and 2024 (1).

E-10-2026-002819.t: Protection of European analogue cultural heritage against destructive scanning and circumvention of AI Act obligations by AI developers
qt: to the Commission Andreas Schwab (PPE) Subject:

Press reports1 indicate that artificial intelligence (AI) developers are using shell companies to execute automated bulk purchases of rare, out-of-print physical books from European secondhand bookshops. These books undergo ‘destructive scanning’, where bindings are destroyed for high-speed digitisation, and are subsequently shredded. This predatory practice permanently removes rare books from secondary markets, exploiting an analogue loophole to mask data provenance. Under Article 53 of the AI Act2, general-purpose AI (GPAI) providers must comply with EU copyright law, respect text and data mining opt-outs under Directive (EU) 2019/7903, and publish detailed training data summaries, regardless of whether sources are digital-native or physically digitised. 1.

What concrete enforcement actions will the Commission take to ensure that GPAI providers utilising physical-to-digital pipelines fully disclose these works in transparency summaries, preventing the masking of data provenance following physical acquisition?

Does the Commission agree that digitising legally purchased books for commercial AI training without a licence constitutes unauthorised reproduction under EU law, regardless of the physical original’s destruction?
What initiatives will the Commission introduce to help libraries and second-hand bookshops protect out-of-print regional heritage from commercial buyouts and physical destruction?

https://www.swr.de/kultur/literatur/kaufen-ki-firmen-massenhaft-antiquariatsbuecher-auf-100.html. Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 June 2024 laying down harmonised rules on artificial intelligence and amending Regulations (EC) No 300/2008, (EU) No 167/2013, (EU) No 168/2013, (EU) 2018/858, (EU) 2018/1139 and (EU) 2019/2144 and Directives 2014/90/EU, (EU) 2016/797 and (EU) 2020/1828 (Artificial Intelligence Act) (OJ L, 2024/1689, 12.7.2024, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj). 3 Directive (EU) 2019/790 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 17 April 2019 on copyright and related rights in the Digital Single Market and amending Directives 96/9/EC and 2001/29/EC (OJ L 130, 17.5.2019, p. 92, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2019/790/oj). 1 2
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (16.9.2026) The Commission observes that Section 2.6 of the template for the public summary of training data, published in July 2025, requires a general, narrative description of the ‘other sources of data’, which include self-digitised media1. General Purpose AI model providers are required to use the template in accordance with Article 53(1)(d) of the AI Act2. The Commission is monitoring the publication of summaries and has engaged with providers on the adequacy of their published summaries. Where no summaries are published or they appear deficient, the Commission will consider appropriate enforcement action. The Directive on the harmonisation of certain aspects of copyright and related rights in the information society (InfoSoc Directive)3 grants authors the exclusive right to authorise or prohibit the reproduction of their works, by any means and in any form, in whole or in part. The digitisation of books protected by copyright, including books lawfully acquired in analogue form, constitutes an act of reproduction requiring the rightsholder’s prior authorisation unless a relevant exception or limitation provided for under EU law and implemented in national law applies. As the text and data mining exceptions only apply to text and data in digital form, they do not cover the digitisation of works in physical format4. Directive (EU) 2019/790 established, in Articles 8 to 11, a framework intended to facilitate the use of out-of-commerce works by cultural heritage institutions, while seeking to support the digitisation and dissemination of Europe’s cultural heritage while ensuring appropriate safeguards for rightsholders. The Commission is currently preparing the review of the Directive and will assess the impacts of these provisions on the availability of out-of-commerce works.

E-10-2026-002818.t: Application of the ‘continuous, systematic and grave human rights violations’ standard under the EU-Colombia-Ecuador-Peru Trade Agreement
qt: to the Commission Martin Günther (The Left) Subject:

In its reply to written question E-003764/202512, the Commission stated that the suspension of the EU-Colombia-Ecuador-Peru Trade Agreement could be considered in cases of ‘continuous, systematic and grave human rights violations’, while concluding that this threshold had not been met in Ecuador. Since then, reports from the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, the InterAmerican Commission on Human Rights (IACHR), Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International have documented serious concerns, including prolonged states of emergency, increased militarisation of internal security operations and allegations of enforced disappearances, arbitrary detention, excessive use of force and extrajudicial killings. The UN has raised concerns regarding the conduct of security operations. The IACHR has issued precautionary measures concerning alleged enforced disappearances during military operations under states of emergency. Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International have reported patterns of arbitrary detention, enforced disappearances and excessive use of force linked to the security strategy. In this context: 1.
What criteria does the Commission use to assess whether violations are ‘continuous, systematic and grave’, and what weight does the Commission attach to findings from UN bodies and the IACHR?
On what factual basis does the Commission maintain that the threshold has not been met in Ecuador?
What factual circumstances would lead the Commission to conclude that the threshold is met and to initiate consultations or consider suspension under the essential elements clause?

(21 August 2026) Respect for democratic principles, human rights, and the rule of law constitutes an essential element of the Trade Agreement between the European Union and Colombia, Peru and Ecuador (3). Violations of the Agreement’s essential elements clause, including the respect of human rights, can trigger the right of the parties to take ‘appropriate measures’, including the possible suspension in whole or in part of the agreement. As stated in the reply to Written Question E-003764/2025 (4), the suspension of the Agreement is a last-resort measure. Before taking such a step, the EU typically looks at other measures that can be applied in a proportionate manner, calibrating its actions in a way that is seen as the most conducive to respond to the situation in a specific country. The EU’s preference is to maintain engagement and dialogue as long as possible, since suspension in part or in full of an agreement may have significant detrimental effects on the population of the partner country, notably the most vulnerable. It is important to note that the EU raises these matters directly with the authorities on a regular basis, both on concrete cases and in a generic manner. In its monitoring of the situation, the Commission uses the findings, reports, and rulings of independent international and regional human rights mechanisms such as UN bodies and the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights. Because these bodies provide rigorous analysis, their findings frequently trigger EU diplomatic demarches, inform Council conclusions, and serve as components in determining EU policy shifts or restrictive measures toward partner countries.

E-10-2026-002817.t: Withdrawal of funding for the Seine-Nord Europe canal
qt: to the Commission Emma Fourreau (The Left) Subject:

The Seine-Nord Europe canal is one of the largest transport infrastructure projects co-funded by the European Union. Its construction will have significant environmental consequences, increasing land take and reducing biodiversity. Those environmental issues are compounded by significant delays and skyrocketing costs, which call into question the viability of the project. According to a recent report by the European Court of Auditors1, the project is estimated to cost a total of EUR 5.1 billion – and might even end up costing more than that. For its part, the French Court of Auditors now estimates the project cost to be between EUR 8.38 billion and EUR 10.53 billion before tax2. The project is heavily reliant on EU funding, which currently amounts to around 40 % of the eligible expenditure. In fact, several people in charge of the project have stressed that ‘Europe is the project’s life insurance’3. Given the environmental impact, the budget overruns observed and the project’s dependence on EU funding, does the Commission intend to stop providing financial support for the SeineNord Europe canal?

at: (English version) to the Commission Emma Fourreau (The Left) (8 July 2026) Subject: Withdrawal of funding for the Seine-Nord Europe canal The Seine-Nord Europe canal is one of the largest transport infrastructure projects co-funded by the European Union. Its construction will have significant environmental consequences, increasing land take and reducing biodiversity. Those environmental issues are compounded by significant delays and skyrocketing costs, which call into question the viability of the project. According to a recent report by the European Court of Auditors (1), the project is estimated to cost a total of EUR 5.1 billion — and might even end up costing more than that. For its part, the French Court of Auditors now estimates the project cost to be between EUR 8.38 billion and EUR 10.53 billion before tax (2). The project is heavily reliant on EU funding, which currently amounts to around 40% of the eligible expenditure. In fact, several people in charge of the project have stressed that ‘Europe is the project’s life insurance’ (3). Given the environmental impact, the budget overruns observed and the project’s dependence on EU funding, does the Commission intend to stop providing financial support for the Seine-Nord Europe canal? (10 September 2026) The Commission takes note of the Honourable Member’s concerns regarding the Seine-Nord Europe canal. The Seine-Escaut cross-border global project, mainly on the North Sea-Rhine-Mediterranean European Transport Corridor, aims to complete a wide-gauge inland waterway link between France, Belgium and the Netherlands to better connect their sea and inland ports. It has the potential to improve inland waterway transport thus reducing emissions of air pollutants and noise of transport. The Seine-Escaut project was included in the annexes on pre-identified projects on the Trans-European Transport network (TEN-T) core network of the Connecting Europe Facility (CEF) 2014-2020 and CEF 2021-2027 Regulations — adopted by the European Parliament and the Council. The project is making solid progress and its promoters in France and Belgium are working together closely under the coordination of France’s Ministère de la Transition Écologique. Up until the present date, approximately EUR 528 million has been invested in this project under CEF 2014-2020 (at a 43% cofinancing rate) and EUR 1,083 billion are allocated under CEF 2021-2027 (at a 50% co-financing rate). The Commission included the Seine-Escaut project in the indicative list of projects of common interest with cross-border dimension under the CEF 2028-2034 proposal. This is now being negotiated by the co-legislators. In line with current practice, the CEF 2028-2034 proposal envisages direct management by the Commission based on competitive calls for proposals.

E-10-2026-002816.t: EU enlargement: will the people get to have their say?
qt: to the Commission Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE) Subject:

The European Union is considering the accession of a number of new countries. Such an enlargement could change the number of representatives from each Member State in the European Parliament, the weighting of each country’s vote in intergovernmental votes, the composition of the Commission and the distribution of the EU budget. The European Parliament itself considers that significant institutional reform will be necessary before any further enlargements. In particular, it is looking at reviewing the functioning of the Council, the composition of the institutions and certain voting rules. 1.
Does the Commission take the view that the EU can bring in new Member States and profoundly alter its functioning without consulting EU citizens directly?
Does it plan to organise a public consultation across the EU and to recommend that Member States consult their citizens before any major institutional reform relating to enlargement?

Before each new accession, will it publish a clear study indicating the impact on each Member State, including in terms of its clout in EU decision-making, the number of MEPs representing it and its contribution to the EU budget?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (28.8.2026) Enlargement is a geostrategic investment in peace, security, stability and prosperity for the EU1. Decisions on enlargement are taken unanimously by the Member States’ representatives in the Council, who represent their citizens at national and European level. For the EU to enlarge, the European Parliament also needs to give its consent. In addition, any future Accession Treaty would have to be ratified by all Member States, and by the acceding country, in accordance with their respective constitutional requirements, which in some cases may include a referendum. In that sense, enlargement and any related changes to the EU’s functioning are anchored in democratic legitimacy through both representative democracy and national ratification processes. The Commission is currently preparing pre-enlargement policy reviews as part of the EU’s wider work to ensure that the EU is politically, institutionally and financially prepared for a larger membership, while taking into account that the Treaties already offer ways of ensuring the continued efficient functioning of the EU that could prove particularly useful in view of an enlarged EU. The Commission remains fully committed to transparency, public debate and democratic accountability as discussions on enlargement and the EU’s preparedness move forward.
1 European Council conclusions, 19 December 2024; https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/press/press-
releases/2024/12/19/european-council-conclusions-19-december-2024/.

qt: to the Commission Fernand Kartheiser (NI) Subject:

According to a recent Eurobarometer survey, nearly half of Europeans believe the EU should have greater financial means given its political objectives, while more than four in ten consider current resources adequate1. However, respondents were unable to answer whether the EU budget should be decreased. Similar methodological weaknesses in Eurobarometer surveys have been highlighted in academic studies2. Other weaknesses include suggestive wording of questions, overly complex or hypothetical questions, an aggregation of results at EU level that obscures national differences in favour of a purported ‘European’ opinion and the removal of questions that previously presented negative perceptions of the EU. Moreover, Eurobarometer surveys residents of a Member State, but not necessarily its citizens, so it cannot claim to reflect the perspective of that country’s citizens. Considering these concerns: 1.
Is the Commission concerned about the biases inherent in the Eurobarometer survey methodology?
How relevant are the Eurobarometer surveys given that, at considerable cost, they fail to genuinely represent citizens’ opinions?
What steps will the Commission undertake to prevent biased Eurobarometer data from misleading policy recommendations and spreading misinformation?

(7 September 2026) Eurobarometer surveys are an important tool measuring and analysing public opinion trends across the Union and beyond, both at national and subnational level. They provide comparable data over time and between countries. All Eurobarometer survey data, including country-specific results, are publicly available on the Eurobarometer Public Opinion website (1). The Commission attaches great importance to the methodological quality and rigour of Eurobarometer surveys. Their design, sampling, fieldwork and analysis follow established research practices and are subject to quality assurance. Contractors are requested to comply fully with the professional and ethical code of the European Society for Opinion and Market Research (ESOMAR) and the World Association for Public Opinion Research (WAPOR). This contributes to ensuring that surveys are conducted in line with the highest applicable standards and requirements in the field of opinion polling. The Commission also continues, where appropriate, to improve survey design and implementation. The Commission is committed to ensuring that Eurobarometer surveys are conducted according to rigorous methodological principles. This includes designing questionnaires that are clear, neutral and accessible, understandable to respondents of different ages, educational backgrounds, occupations and cultural backgrounds, and that are submitted in the respondents’ respective languages.

E-10-2026-002813.t: Gas storage levels ahead of winter
qt: to the Commission Fernand Kartheiser (NI) Subject:

Gas storage, particularly underground gas storage, is essential for ensuring the security of the EU’s gas supply. It provides strategic reserves during periods of high demand and accounts for more than one quarter of the gas consumed during winter periods1. Successive economic sanctions affecting Russian gas have deprived the EU of a major source of supply. Simultaneously, the crisis in the Middle East, including the Strait of Hormuz blockade, has further constrained global gas supplies, causing prices to skyrocket. Moreover, extreme weather events, such as severe cold in winter and heatwaves in summer, increase energy consumption and underline the need to ensure that the EU can withstand supply and demand shocks. In the light of the above: 1.
What is the current level of gas storage across the EU, and does the Commission consider the present injection trajectory sufficient to meet storage targets ahead of the winter season?
How is the Commission working to ensure continuity of supply should another source encounter delivery problems?
What measures is the Commission taking to secure gas imports at the most competitive prices possible?

E-10-2026-002812.t: Possible breach of EU environmental law in the Modern Eco Village urban development project
qt: to the Commission Diana Riba i Giner (Verts/ALE) Subject:

In the municipality of Planes (comarca of el Comtat, Autonomous Community of Valencia), the Modern Eco Village mega-development – comprising up to 500 luxury homes on rural land, next to the River Serpis and the Beniarrés reservoir – is going ahead in an area partially included in the Natura 2000 network. The project could double or triple the local population and has prompted concerns about its environmental, water and public participation effects. In the light of Directive 2011/92/EU, the Water Framework Directive (2000/60/EC) and the Habitats Directive (92/43/EEC): 1.
Has the Commission received any information on Spain’s compliance with the environmental assessment requirements for this project?

Given the projected population increase (115 % – 215 %) in an area where water stress is a recurrent problem, does the Commission believe that Spain is complying with Article 4 of the Water Framework Directive, in particular the principle of nondeterioration, and has it checked the conduct of the Confederación Hidrográfica del Júcar (the Júcar river basin authority)?
What measures could the Commission take to help to secure effective public participation in line with the Aarhus Convention?

E-10-2026-002811.t: Addressing obesity as a chronic disease: recognition, prevention and treatment at EU level
qt: to the Commission Elena Kountoura (The Left) Subject:

Obesity is one of the most serious public health problems in Europe. Around 51 % of the EU population over the age of 16 is overweight, while 17 % is obese1. Obesity significantly increases the risk of cardiovascular disease and diabetes, and is considered to be responsible for at least 13 types of cancer. At the same time, stigma and fatphobia take a toll on patients’ mental health. Bearing in mind that obesity is the fourth-leading cause of premature death worldwide, that the socio-economic impact on European health systems amounts to EUR 70 billion per year2, that EASO has expressed concern that obesity is not fully addressed as a chronic disease in the Commission’s Safe Hearts plan3, that around one in three children in Greece is overweight or obese4, and that the European Parliament resolution explicitly recognises obesity as an NCD and calls on the Commission to propose a new, comprehensive action plan for obesity with measurable indicators and mechanisms to monitor results5, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Does it intend to recognise obesity as a chronic disease?
Does it intend to propose a new European action plan for obesity and specific financial tools to strengthen early diagnosis, research and equitable access to obesity treatments?

Does it intend to support the Member States in developing targeted public information and awareness-raising activities, combating stigma and integrating obesity education into the curricula of healthcare professionals?

See: EPRS, Obesity in the EU: An ongoing epidemic, March 2025, https://www.europarl.europa.eu/RegData/etudes/ATAG/2025/769510/EPRS_ATA(2025)769510_EN.pdf. 2 See: https://knowledge4policy.ec.europa.eu/health-promotion-knowledge-gateway/obesity_en. 3 EASO, Safe Hearts Plan: EASO responds to the European Commission Cardiovascular Health Plan, February 2026, https://easo.org/safe-hearts-plan-easo-responds-to-the-european-commission-cardiovascularhealth-plan/. 4 According to the WHO, Greece is among the countries with the highest prevalence rates, ranking second in obesity and third in overweight, https://www.who.int/europe/publications/i/item/WHO-EURO-202511788-51560-78769. 5 See: European Parliament resolution of 13 December 2023 on non-communicable diseases (NCDs), https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/TA-9-2023-0467_EN.html#def_1_17. 1

(3 September 2026) The World Health Organisation is responsible for the International Classification of Diseases (1) (ICD-11). In line with Article 168(7) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU (2) (TFEU), the EU complements national policies and encourages cooperation in public health across Member States. The Commission supports Member States in addressing non-communicable diseases and their risk factors, including obesity, through the ‘Healthier Together’ initiative (3), joint actions PreventNCD (4) and Health4EUkids (5) and stakeholder-led projects (6). The Safe Hearts Plan (7) builds on these actions under its prevention pillar. Obesity is addressed through the Council Recommendation on health-enhancing physical activity (8) and initiatives such as the European Week of Sport (9) and the #BeActive campaign. Horizon Europe will continue to fund research on evidence-based prevention, diagnosis, and treatment strategies. Under Article 165 TFEU, Member States are responsible for the content of teaching and the organisation of their education systems, including decisions on whether and how to integrate obesity education into curricula.

E-10-2026-002810.t: Inadequate implementation of the AFIR and excessively high, non-transparent public charging rates for electric vehicles in the EU
qt: to the Commission Elena Kountoura (The Left) Subject:

A recent study1 carried out for Parliament’s TRAN Committee found that public charging is still significantly more expensive than charging at home or at work and often appears unreasonably high, non-transparent, complex and not user-friendly2, undermining the transition to e-mobility and the cost reasoning behind buying a car, especially for citizens for whom home charging is not an option. In addition, the same charging session often leads to different final costs depending on the provider, app, card or payment method used by the consumer and price information is often not available for consumers before charging starts3. Although Article 5 of the AFIR stipulates that public charging prices must be reasonable, easily and clearly comparable, transparent and non-discriminatory, its implementation and enforcement remain incomplete, fragmented and uneven. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
What measures does it intend to take to address excessively high, non-transparent and insufficiently justified charging prices for electric vehicles in the EU?

Does it intend to revise the AFIR and propose minimum EU requirements to improve price transparency, such as the mandatory display of the total charging price before charging begins, including all surcharges, as well as the mandatory display, before charging, of both the MSP price and the ad hoc charging price?

See https://www.europarl.europa.eu/RegData/etudes/STUD/2026/759345/CASP_STU(2026)759345_EN.pdf. 2 Average AC charging prices through mobility service providers range from EUR 0.27/kWh to EUR 0.65/kWh, while for DC charging the range is even wider, from EUR 0.32 to EUR 0.85, with the highest prices exceeding EUR 1.00/kWh in some markets. Even at the same charging station, the difference between the highest and lowest price usually ranges from EUR 0.40 to EUR 1.00 and in extreme cases can reach EUR 1.40/kWh. 3 According to the study, price information is often not displayed before charging starts, the price calculation method is difficult for consumers to understand and the final price depends to a large degree on whether the user pays ad hoc via a charge point operator (CPO) or a mobility service provider (MSP/roaming), sometimes including hidden charges. 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (28.8.2026) Regulation (EU) 2023/1804 on the deployment of alternative fuels infrastructure1 (AFIR) sets clear rules on how operators of recharging points and mobility service providers must make price information available to consumers. Article 5 of the Regulation requires that prices charged by operators of publicly accessible recharging points and by mobility service providers must be reasonable, easily and clearly comparable, transparent and non-discriminatory. The regulation equally requires that those operators must make available all relevant price information prior to the start of the recharging session. Article 5(6) also requires Member States to monitor the recharging market in particular with regards to those price transparency provisions. The Commission is currently reviewing Regulation (EU) 2023/1804 in accordance with Article 24 of the Regulation. This review addresses, among others, user aspects, including on price transparency and enforcement aspects. The study commissioned by the Parliament’s Committee on Transport and Tourism (TRAN Committee) will serve as one input to the ongoing impact assessment. As announced in the Commission Communication COM (2025) 95 final2 the Commission plans to adopt a proposal for the revision of AFIR by the end of this year.

deployment of alternative fuels infrastructure, and repealing Directive 2014/94/EU, OJ L 234, 22.9.2023, pp. 1– 47. 2 Communication from the Commission to the European Parliament, the Council, the European Economic and Social Committee and the Committee of the Regions Industrial Action Plan for the European automotive sector, COM/2025/95 final.

E-10-2026-002809.t: RAI’s independence and financial viability in Europe’s pluralistic media landscape
qt: to the Commission Gaetano Pedulla' (The Left), Carolina Morace (The Left), Dario Tamburrano (The Left), Pasquale Tridico (The Left), Valentina Palmisano (The Left), Mario Furore (The Left), Giuseppe Antoci (The Left) Subject:

RAI, the Italian state broadcaster, is going through a phase of major institutional and financial turmoil. Its parliamentary supervisory board has resigned1, after almost two years of being mired in a deadlock brought on by the majority’s obstructive actions. Speaking in a parliamentary hearing, Minister of Economy Giorgetti insisted that he should appoint two members of the board of directors2, contrary to the European Media Freedom Act (EMFA), which seeks to shield public services from government influence. Italy’s most recent draft budget foists a funding cut of EUR 10 million on the broadcaster. As board members Natale and Di Majo have pointed out3, this is liable to limit the public service’s capacity to fulfil its mission. Directive (EU) 2018/1808 and the EMFA oblige Member States to guard the independence of public media from political and financial interference. Given that Forza Italia, a partner in the current government majority, maintains close ties4 with the Berlusconi family, which owns RAI’s main private broadcasting competitor, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Is it examining the comments made by the Italian Minister of Economy and Finance on RAI’s governance for a possible EMFA breach?
Does it consider the cuts made to RAI to be in line with EU standards on the adequate funding of public services?
What action will it take if it is established that RAI’s editorial independence has been compromised?
Supporter5

https://www.ilsole24ore.com/art/vigilanza-rai-dimissioni-massa-i-consiglieri-opposizione-AIXkBwyD. https://www.juorno.it/rai-giorgetti-frena-la-riforma-il-mef-non-puo-perdere-il-ruolo-sullamministratoredelegato/. 3 https://www.articolo21.org/2026/06/natale-cda-rai-la-subalternita-sta-soffocando-il-servizio-pubblico/. 4 https://www.ilpost.it/2026/04/22/perche-forza-italia-comandano-berlusconi/. 5 This question is supported by a Member other than the authors: Danilo Della Valle (The Left). 1 2
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.9.2026) The European Media Freedom Act (the EMFA)1 sets out targeted safeguards for the independent functioning of public service media. These include rules for transparent and effective appointments of heads of management or members of management boards, and rules on funding procedures to guarantee adequate, sustainable and predictable financial resources. The EMFA does not prescribe specific governance and funding models, and Member States retain discretion on how to organise these in line with their national specificities. It also does not affect the competence of Member States to provide for the funding of public service media providers, as enshrined in Protocol No 292. The 2026 Rule of Law Report on Italy considered the reform of Radiotelevisione italiana (RAI) governance and funding rules and took note of the concerns expressed by stakeholders regarding the impact on RAI’s financial stability and predictability of the EUR 10 million reduction in its public funding for 2026, which the Government indicated as intended to rationalise RAI’s operating costs3. Exchanges are ongoing between the Commission and all Member States, including Italy, to ensure the effective and correct implementation of the EMFA. As a regulation, the EMFA is directly applicable and can be litigated before national courts, where relevant. The Commission is monitoring the state of implementation in all Member States and may make use of its powers to bring infringement procedures. The Commission will also continue to monitor closely the state of media pluralism and media freedom in all Member States, including Italy, in the context of its annual Rule of Law Report.
