European Union, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/treaty/tfeu_2016/pro_29/oj/eng. 3 https://commission.europa.eu/publications/2026-rule-law-report-communication-and-country-chapters_en.

E-10-2026-002808.t: Increasing Frontex resources and a real operational presence at the EU’s external borders
qt: to the Commission Stanisław Tyszka (ESN) Subject:

In accordance with Regulation (EU) 2019/1896, the standing corps of the European Border and Coast Guard is to reach a target capacity of 10 000 staff by 2027, comprising 3 000 officers employed directly by Frontex and 7 000 officers seconded by Member States. At the same time, Frontex reported 2 545 occupied posts at the end of 2024 and in June 2026 some 3 800 officers stationed at the EU’s external borders. In light of the above: 1.

What is the current numerical breakdown of Frontex staff between standing corps officers who are actually deployed on operational activities, officers undergoing training or on standby, and staff carrying out administrative, analytical, training, logistical and fundamental rights monitoring tasks?

In which Member States, Schengen associated countries and third countries are standing corps officers currently deployed, how many officers perform tasks directly related to border protection and how many to return activities?

How does the Commission intend to ensure that the further increase in Frontex staff to 10 000 will translate first and foremost into a more effective presence of officers at the EU’s external borders and more effective returns, rather than an expansion of the Agency’s administration?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (31.8.2026) As sub-questions one and two fall under the responsibility of the European Border and Coast Guard Agency (Frontex), the Commission has asked the Agency to provide a response to the questions raised by the Honourable Member. The Commission will send the Agency’s reply to the Honourable Member as soon as possible. The European Border and Coast Guard standing corps of 10 000 consist of statutory staff employed by Frontex (category 1), operational staff seconded by Member States for long-term deployments (category 2) and operational staff made available by Member States for shortterm deployments. The standing corps, including the Agency’s statutory staff, is expected to carry out operational tasks primarily as members of the teams in line with the Agency’s core activities. The Commission, as a member of the Management Board, monitors the Agency’s regular reporting on both operational and administrative staff.

E-10-2026-002807.t: Availability of air conditioning in the context of heatwave-related deaths
qt: to the Commission Stanisław Tyszka (ESN) Subject:

The World Health Organization (WHO) says that the heatwave that began on 21 June 2026 is responsible for more than 1 300 excess deaths and warns that heat claims more than 175 000 lives annually in the WHO European Region. The 2022 report of the Lancet Countdown estimates that, in 2019 alone, access to air conditioning averted around 195 000 heat-related deaths globally among over-65s. Around 20 % of European households are fitted with AC units, versus over 90 % in the United States, Japan and South Korea. According to Euronews, despite declining to pick a side in the AC debate on 30 June, the Commission conceded on 2 July that air conditioning was a ‘very necessary tool’ but that its widespread use would push up bills at a time of high energy prices. The price of CO₂ emission allowances under the EU ETS is approximately EUR 80/tonne. This inflates electricity generation costs, driving up household bills. 1.
Has the Commission assessed the extent to which EU ETS costs are limiting households’ access to health-protecting and life-saving air conditioning during heatwaves?
Will the Commission broaden its impact assessment of the EU ETS review in 2026 to cover the impact of energy prices on air-conditioning availability?
With heatwaves raging, does the Commission consider it acceptable that EU ETS costs have been driving up the price of AC use in homes, schools, hospitals and care homes?
at: (English version) to the Commission Stanisław Tyszka (ESN) (7 July 2026) Subject: Availability of air conditioning in the context of heatwave-related deaths The World Health Organisation (WHO) says that the heatwave that began on 21 June 2026 is responsible for more than 1 300 excess deaths and warns that heat claims more than 175 000 lives annually in the WHO European Region. The 2022 report of the Lancet Countdown estimates that, in 2019 alone, access to air conditioning averted around 195 000 heat-related deaths globally among over-65s. Around 20% of European households are fitted with AC units, versus over 90% in the United States, Japan and South Korea. According to Euronews, despite declining to pick a side in the AC debate on 30 June, the Commission conceded on 2 July that air conditioning was a ‘very necessary tool’ but that its widespread use would push up bills at a time of high energy prices. The price of CO2 emission allowances under the EU ETS is approximately EUR 80/tonne. This inflates electricity generation costs, driving up household bills. 1. Has the Commission assessed the extent to which EU ETS costs are limiting households’ access to health-protecting and life-saving air conditioning during heatwaves? 2. Will the Commission broaden its impact assessment of the EU ETS review in 2026 to cover the impact of energy prices on air-conditioning availability? 3. With heatwaves raging, does the Commission consider it acceptable that EU ETS costs have been driving up the price of AC use in homes, schools, hospitals and care homes? (31 August 2026) The Commission agrees that during periods of dangerous heat, air conditioning is part of the measures and technologies that can help maintain thermal comfort, safety and productivity. Air conditioners are often inverse heat pumps, that in winter can heat homes, while emitting less greenhouse gas than fossil fuel heating appliances. By putting a price on carbon, and generating revenues that are reinvested in clean energy, the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) will directly promote the deployment of heat pumps, and thus in part also air conditioning, in regions in the EU where heating needs are still the primary driver to install such technologies. Regarding the impact of the ETS on electricity prices, on average the largest driver of high and volatile electricity prices is the EU’s exposure to imported fossil fuels. The next largest drivers are grid charges and taxes and levies. On 17 July 2026, the Commission presented an Electrification Action Plan which tackles drivers of electricity costs (1). It includes measures to make better use of electricity grids, reduce network charges, encourage smarter electricity consumption, and better align energy taxation to make sure that electricity is not taxed more heavily than gas. The review of the ETS, also presented on 17 July 2016, did not look at the contribution of ETS costs to the affordability of air conditioning specifically. However, the ETS provides an effective contribution towards EU climate goals since it is technologically neutral and lets markets find ways to reduce emissions at the lowest cost. The direct ETS contribution to electricity prices, which is already lower than the components mentioned above, will decrease with a cleaner generation mix.

E-10-2026-002806.t: Impact of Court ruling on Hungarian anti-LGBTI propaganda law on similar law in Bulgaria
qt: to the Commission Raquel García Hermida-Van Der Walle (Renew), Valérie Hayer (Renew), Sophie Wilmès (Renew), Fabienne Keller (Renew), Billy Kelleher (Renew), Malik Azmani (Renew), Hilde Vautmans (Renew), Veronika Cifrová Ostrihoňová (Renew), Lucia Yar (Renew), Dainius Žalimas (Renew), Irena Joveva (Renew), Anna-Maja Henriksson (Renew), Brigitte van den Berg (Renew), Pina Picierno (Renew), Oihane Agirregoitia Martínez (Renew), Olivier Chastel (Renew), Jan-Christoph Oetjen (Renew), Lukas Sieper (Renew), Anouk Van Brug (Renew) Subject:

In April 2026, the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) ruled that the anti-LGBTI amendments to the Hungarian Public Education Law, adopted under the Orbán regime, breach EU law by impeding exercise of the right to free movement of services with regard to remuneration for external service providers hired by schools or remuneration for services outside the public education system. Unfortunately; Bulgaria also has an ‘anti-LGBTI propaganda’ law, which has been in place since August 2024 and bans the promotion of ideas and views related to ‘non-traditional’ sexual orientation and determination of gender identity ‘other than biological’ in education. Unlike in the case of Hungary, the Commission has not launched infringement proceedings against Bulgaria concerning LGBTI rights. 1.

Does the Commission agree that the CJEU’s reasoning in its judgment on the ‘antiLGBTI propaganda’ law in Hungary also applies to the current ‘anti-LGBTI propaganda’ law in Bulgaria, and specifically regarding the field of education?

If so, as a guardian of the Treaties, what action will the Commission take against the Bulgarian Government to ensure that Bulgarian LGBTI youth and teachers are no longer discriminated against by their own government, and when will it launch infringement proceedings, as it did against Hungary?
If not, how does the Commission consider this rampant discrimination against LGBTI people in Bulgaria to be in line with EU law, the Treaties and the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the EU?

Unfortunately; Bulgaria also has an ‘anti-LGBTI propaganda’ law, which has been in place since August 2024 and bans the promotion of ideas and views related to ‘non-traditional’ sexual orientation and determination of gender identity ‘other than biological’ in education. Unlike in the case of Hungary, the Commission has not launched infringement proceedings against Bulgaria concerning LGBTI rights. 1. Does the Commission agree that the CJEU’s reasoning in its judgment on the ‘anti-LGBTI propaganda’ law in Hungary also applies to the current ‘anti-LGBTI propaganda’ law in Bulgaria, and specifically regarding the field of education? 2. If so, as a guardian of the Treaties, what action will the Commission take against the Bulgarian Government to ensure that Bulgarian LGBTI youth and teachers are no longer discriminated against by their own government, and when will it launch infringement proceedings, as it did against Hungary? 3. If not, how does the Commission consider this rampant discrimination against LGBTI people in Bulgaria to be in line with EU law, the Treaties and the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the EU? (1 September 2026) The Commission welcomes the landmark ruling of the Court of Justice of the European Union in the so-called Hungarian ‘Child Protection Law’. As reaffirmed by this ruling, the Commission firmly believes that the protection of children and the safeguarding of the fundamental rights of LGBTIQ+ (1) people are not mutually exclusive. The Commission remains fully committed to addressing inequality and discrimination, as outlined in the renewed LGBTIQ+ Equality Strategy 2026-2030 (2). Furthermore, the Commission, as guardian of the Treaties, is committed to ensuring the proper application of EU law, including fundamental rights under the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union (3) and relevant judgments of the Court of Justice. Concerning the so-called ‘anti-Propaganda law’ in Bulgaria, the Commission has been engaging with Bulgarian authorities and reporting on the situation, including in the context of the 2025 and 2026 Rule of Law Reports. As reported in the 2026 Rule of Law Report, national procedures with the Bulgarian Ombudsman are ongoing with the view to challenge the constitutionality of this law.

On 19 June 2026, EUObserver reported1 that Israel had bombed and bulldozed at least EUR 150 million worth of EU-funded infrastructure in the West Bank and Gaza without ever paying back any of the money. recover the funds by deducting them from sources of EU funding enjoyed by Israel?

E-10-2026-002804.t: Exclusion of the Republic of Cyprus by the Turkish COP31 Presidency
qt: to the Commission Geadis Geadi (ECR) Subject:

The Turkish Presidency of COP31 allegedly excluded the Republic of Cyprus from preparatory briefings on the UN summit and is refusing requests for bilateral meetings submitted by Nicosia. The Republic of Cyprus was not invited by the Turkish Presidency to attend preparatory meetings at the UN headquarters in New York and faced objections even when it participated as a member of the EU delegation. (21 August 2026) In line with the EU position, the Commission considers that the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) process must be inclusive, transparent and open to all Parties to the UNFCCC and Paris Agreement, with full respect for their rights. E-10-2026-002801.t: Closure of Renfe’s hauled stock maintenance depot in Miranda de Ebro
qt: to the Commission Estrella Galán (The Left) Subject:

The European Union is encouraging the growth of rail freight with the European Green Deal, the Sustainable and Smart Mobility Strategy, Regulation (EU) 2024/1679 and the Clean Industrial Deal. Accordingly, Spain has committed to having 10 % of its freight transported by rail by 2030. The recent closure of Renfe’s hauled stock maintenance depot in Miranda de Ebro is therefore worrying, as a piece of public infrastructure located at a strategic hub in the Trans-European Transport Network (TEN-T). In view of the above: 1.

Does the Commission consider closure of the Miranda de Ebro depot to be in line with the objective of Regulation (EU) 2024/1679 (TEN-T) to build up the EU rail system’s capacity, resilience and competitiveness?

Is maintaining the goal of boosting the share of rail freight transport compatible with closing strategic public facilities such as the Miranda de Ebro depot, which are essential for ensuring rolling stock is available?

In the Commission’s view, could the closure go against the Clean Industrial Deal’s goal of preserving industrial capacity, and will the Commission ask the Spanish Government information on how the decision is in line with the EU’s priorities?

(2 September 2026) 1. The Commission takes note of the relocation of maintenance activities from Renfe’s hauled stock depot in Miranda de Ebro to the adjacent Material Motor facility (1). Given the operational consolidation and planned investments, this change does not necessarily conflict with trans-European transport network Regulation (EU) 2024/1679 (2), which prioritises efficient and resilient infrastructure. However, full alignment depends on ensuring no reduction in maintenance capacity for freight rolling stock and uninterrupted service during the transition. The relocation must also comply with EU Regulation 2017/2177 (3), which requires non-discriminatory and transparent access to rail facilities. 2. The consolidation of public service facilities is not incompatible with the target of transporting 10% of freight by rail in Spain by 2030, provided the Material Motor depot can absorb the workload without delays. The Commission takes positive note of Renfe’s planned enhancements to maintenance operations in Miranda de Ebro, as detailed in their recent announcement (4). 3. The Clean Industrial Deal underscores the importance of preserving industrial capacity and green jobs in strategic sectors, including rail. The modernisation investments outlined in the Spanish government’s plans regarding the reallocation of rail freight rolling stock maintenance capacities in Miranda de Ebro (5) do not seem to contradict the goal of sustaining industrial capacity. The repurposing of part of the site for a digital competences centre is in line with EU priorities.

E-10-2026-002799.t: Enforcing the ban on medium-chain chlorinated paraffins (MCCPs) and ensuring a level playing field in the internal market
qt: to the Commission Salvatore De Meo (PPE), Marco Falcone (PPE), Fulvio Martusciello (PPE), Letizia Moratti (PPE), Giusi Princi (PPE), Massimiliano Salini (PPE), Flavio Tosi (PPE) Subject:

New restrictions on medium-chain chlorinated paraffins (MCCPs) will enter into force as of 16 December 2026. MCCPs feature in many industrial processes and, because they are used in a plethora of applications, are found in PVC products, electric cables and building materials. Though they agree with the new measures’ environmental and health protection objectives, a number of industrial operators are concerned that these restrictions will result in disparities that will give third-country producers an edge over their European competitors. Because detecting the presence of MCCPs requires complex analytical techniques – and is generally too tall an order for routine inspections – these sectoral stakeholders are concerned that thirdcountry products containing MCCPs – which are not subject to equivalent checks – could continue to enter the EU market. In the light of the above, we ask the Commission: 1.
What measures will it implement to ensure that restrictions on MCCPs and thirdcountry finished products containing these paraffins are effectively enforced?
Will it introduce specific certification, traceability or due diligence requirements for operators placing these products on the EU market?
How will it ensure a level playing field between the European and non-EU producers concerned while also protecting the internal market from distortions and warding off the threat of delocalisation?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (25.8.2026) The Commission attaches the highest importance to ensuring that the internal market and European citizens are protected from hazardous chemicals that should not be in the products. A level playing field between EU and non-EU producers is ensured by the fact that the prohibitions introduced under the regulation on persistent organic pollutants (POPs Regulation)1 apply in the same way both to products manufactured in the EU and to those imported. Member States have the primary responsibility to monitor the application of the POPs Regulation and ensure compliance with EU law, including for imported products. Enforcement issues are regularly discussed with industry and the Member States in the relevant expert group for the POPs Regulation, as well as in the dedicated instance for enforcement purposes established in the Regulation on Registration, Evaluation, Authorisation and Restriction of Chemicals (REACH)2, the Forum for Exchange of Information on Enforcement. Where problems are flagged, the Commission ensures follow up. The Commission does not intend to introduce specific certification or due diligence requirements as regards the possible presence of medium-chain chlorinated paraffins (MCCPs) in products placed on the EU market, as this would unduly increase costs for EU businesses.
1 Regulation (EU) 2019/1021 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 20 June 2019 on persistent

organic pollutants (recast), OJ L 169, 25.6.2019, p. 45-77. 2 Regulation (EC) No 1907/2006 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 18 December 2006 concerning the Registration, Evaluation, Authorisation and Restriction of Chemicals (REACH), OJ L 396, 30.12.2006.

E-10-2026-002798.t: Developments in Romania as a precedent for halting further EU enlargement
qt: to the Commission Mieke Andriese (PfE) Subject:

Romania, an EU Member State since 2007, is once again in the throes of a deep political crisis. A government is not expected to be formed before September, and the country is failing to implement the reforms required to access approximately EUR 5.1 billion in recovery funds. Almost twenty years after accession, Romania is still grappling with political instability, weak institutions and corruption. Membership has not resolved these problems, but has instead imported them into the Union, whilst at the same time recovery funds are being paid for by EU taxpayers. Nevertheless, the Commission is pressing ahead with negotiations with Moldova: following the opening of the first cluster on 15 June 2026, it intends to open all remaining clusters before the summer recess. However, Moldova’s institutional and economic situation is even worse than Romania’s was at the same point in time. The following questions thus arise: 1.
How does the Commission assess its enlargement policy, given the ongoing governance and institutional problems in Romania twenty years after accession?
On the basis of which criteria does the Commission conclude that Moldova meets the Copenhagen criteria and does not pose comparable risks to the Union’s absorption capacity?

Is the Commission prepared to suspend accession negotiations until it has been demonstrated that further enlargement will not entail any new administrative, institutional or financial risks for the Union and its taxpayers? If not, why not?
at: (English version) to the Commission Mieke Andriese (PfE) (7 July 2026) Subject: Developments in Romania as a precedent for halting further EU enlargement Romania, an EU Member State since 2007, is once again in the throes of a deep political crisis. A government is not expected to be formed before September, and the country is failing to implement the reforms required to access approximately EUR 5.1 billion in recovery funds. Almost twenty years after accession, Romania is still grappling with political instability, weak institutions and corruption. Membership has not resolved these problems, but has instead imported them into the Union, whilst at the same time recovery funds are being paid for by EU taxpayers. Nevertheless, the Commission is pressing ahead with negotiations with Moldova: following the opening of the first cluster on 15 June 2026, it intends to open all remaining clusters before the summer recess. However, Moldova’s institutional and economic situation is even worse than Romania’s was at the same point in time. The following questions thus arise: 1.
How does the Commission assess its enlargement policy, given the ongoing governance and institutional problems in Romania twenty years after accession?
On the basis of which criteria does the Commission conclude that Moldova meets the Copenhagen criteria and does not pose comparable risks to the Union’s absorption capacity?

Is the Commission prepared to suspend accession negotiations until it has been demonstrated that further enlargement will not entail any new administrative, institutional or financial risks for the Union and its taxpayers? If not, why not?

(19 August 2026) EU enlargement policy is guided by a merit-based process and the assessment of any candidate country, including Moldova, is based on its own progress in delivering the required reforms, particularly on the so-called ‘fundamentals’ — democracy, the rule of law, fundamental rights, public administration reform and the economic criteria — in line with the 2020 revised enlargement methodology (1). This framework provides for continuous monitoring and allows for reversibility where progress stalls or backsliding occurs. This ensures that negotiations remain closely linked to tangible and sustained reform outcomes. To ensure that new Member States continue to safeguard and maintain their track-record on the rule of law, democracy and fundamental rights, the Commission considers that future Accession Treaties should contain stronger safeguards against backsliding on commitments made during the accession negotiations. Enlargement will continue to advance based on the pace of reforms in candidate countries while taking into account the EU’s capacity to integrate new members effectively. The Commission is currently preparing pre-enlargement policy reviews, to be presented in the autumn, as part of the EU’s wider work to ensure that the EU is politically, institutionally and financially prepared for a larger membership.

Communication from the Commission to the European Parliament, the Council, the European Economic and Social Committee and the Committee of the Regions: Enhancing the Accession Process — A Credible EU Perspective for the Western Balkans, COM(2020) 57 final, Brussels, 5 February 2020.

E-10-2026-002797.t: Climate emergencies and protection of EU funds from mafia infiltration
qt: to the Commission Giuseppe Antoci (The Left) Subject:

Given that climate change continues to get worse – extreme events such as forest fires, heatwaves and prolonged periods of drought are growing in frequency – EU-financed emergency measures will be called on increasingly frequently for support. Article 191 TFEU establishes that combating climate change is a key objective of EU environmental policy1, and the 2021 strategy on adaptation to climate change highlights the rising impact of the economic costs of climate change2. In particularly vulnerable areas, such as Sicily, which has recently been hit by extreme weather events3 and benefits from substantial public investment and infrastructure projects, increasing the resources used in emergencies may raise the risk of infiltration by criminal organisations4. Europol’s reports on environmental crime5 and the joint Europol-OLAF report on NextGenerationEU6 shine a spotlight on how criminal organisations exploit crisis contexts and regulatory failings to make a profit at the expense of the EU7. In the light of the above: 1.
Does the Commission believe that the growing use of EU financing for climate emergencies could raise the risk of infiltration by organised crime?
Will it step up cooperation between Europol, OLAF and the EPPO to prevent and combat mafia fraud and infiltration?
Will it introduce further monitoring, transparency and control tools in the use of those resources, particularly in the areas most exposed to the risk of criminal infiltration?

at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (7.9.2026) Protecting the EU financial interests is essential in the design, implementation and monitoring of EU funding instruments. The Commission works with the Member States and competent Union bodies including the European Anti-Fraud Office, the European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO), Europol, Eurojust and the EU Authority for Anti-Money Laundering and Countering the Financing of Terrorism (AMLA), to prevent, detect and investigate illegal activities affecting the EU budget. The investigation and prosecution of organised crime remain primarily the responsibility of the EPPO, where competent, and national prosecution authorities. With the 2025 White Paper1, the Commission launched the review of the EU Anti-Fraud Architecture (AFA), to strengthen cooperation and coordination among the EU anti-fraud actors and protect the EU budget across all spending areas, including climate funds. The next Multiannual Financial Framework aims to better monitor and control EU funds, notably through the parallel revision of the AFA. The Commission will present the AFA review results in a Communication by end of 2026. This may, where appropriate, be accompanied by legislative proposals concerning the EU anti-fraud framework. The Commission remains committed to protecting EU funds from fraud, corruption and organised crime, ensuring all spending complies with Union law. Member States hold primary responsibility for preventing, detecting, and correcting irregularities under shared management and the Recovery and Resilience Facility.

E-10-2026-002796.t: Activating EU instruments in the face of wildfire emergencies in southern Europe
qt: to the Commission Dolors Montserrat (PPE) Subject:

The wildfire that broke out on 3 July 2026 in the Gavarres massif in Girona has burned over 2 300 hectares, most of which was of high forest and environmental value. The fire has resulted in thousands of people having to stay indoors, residential areas having to be evacuated and an extensive emergency operation having to be deployed. Given the rising impact of extreme wildfires in southern Europe, the European Union needs to be able to quickly mobilise all available financial and solidarity instruments to support the recovery of affected areas, restore damaged ecosystems and increase resilience to future fires. 1.

What financial instruments does the Commission think could be mobilised to support the economic, social and environmental recovery of the areas affected by the Gavarres fire, including forest restoration efforts and work to rebuild damaged infrastructure?

Has the Commission been in contact with the Spanish or Catalan authorities to assess the scale of the damage and look into possibly activating EU support mechanisms (including, if applicable, the European Union Solidarity Fund) if the requirements are met?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (21.8.2026) 1. Under the Common Agriculture Policy (CAP), Member States have a large set of interventions1 at their disposal which can be mobilised in their CAP Strategic Plans. The Spanish CAP Strategic Plan already supports investments for restoring agricultural or forestry potential following natural disasters. The regional programme of Catalonia 2021-2027 and the Pluri-regional programme of Spain 2021-2027, both funded by the European Regional Development Fund, already include an amount of EUR 205 million and EUR 165 million respectively, to finance investments related to the prevention and management of climate change risks, including forest fires. The implementation of these investments is ongoing and closely followed by the Commission. Beyond financial assistance, Spain may request help through the Union Civil Protection Mechanism (UCPM), including aerial firefighting assets and ground teams, and may activate Copernicus mapping. On 24 July 2026, Spain activated the UCPM for wildfires in Ávila and Madrid, requesting four firefighting planes. To date, the operation is ongoing and the Emergency Response Coordination Centre remains in close contact with Spain. 2. The Commission is also in contact with the Spanish authorities regarding a potential application for the EU Solidarity Fund (EUSF). The EUSF can only be activated at the request of Spain which has a deadline of 12 weeks as from the date when the first damage occurred, demonstrating that the total direct damage exceeds the thresholds specified in Article 2 of Regulation (EC) 2012/20022. The EUSF may cover a part of the costs for emergency and recovery operations incurred by public authorities3. The Commission stands ready to assist Spain should they request support.
1 These include inter alia risk management schemes, support for appropriate investments and replanting and

restocking aimed at preventing, mitigating, and repairing the impact of natural disasters and adverse weather events on agricultural production. 2 Council Regulation (EC) No 2012/2002 of 11 November 2002 establishing the European Union Solidarity Fund (OJ L 311, 14.11.2002, p. 3) as amended by Regulation (EU) No 661/2014 of the European Parliament and the Council of 15 May 2014 (OJ L 189, 27.6.2014, p. 143) and by Regulation (EU) 2020/461 of the European Parliament and the Council of 30 March 2020 (OJ L 99, 31.3.2020, p. 9: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legalcontent/EN/TXT/?uri=celex:32002R2012). 3 This means, for example, the recovery of essential infrastructure, provision of temporary accommodation to the population, cleaning-up operations, and protection of the cultural heritage.

E-10-2026-002794.t: COVID-19 vaccination recommendations with no medical justification
qt: to the Commission Gerald Hauser (PfE) Subject:

Austria was the only country in the EU to make COVID-19 vaccinations compulsory, as publicly called for by Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. The following population groups, amongst others, were exempted by law from the vaccination requirement on medical grounds: Pregnant women, as well as people with autoimmune diseases, severe inflammatory conditions, severe chronic illnesses, and people for whom ‘a sufficient immune response to a COVID-19 vaccination cannot be expected for medical reasons’ (e.g. following organ transplants, in cases of immunosuppression, active and currently treated or metastatic cancers, and other severe medical conditions). However, current vaccination guidelines in Austria and the EU1 now recommend regular COVID-19 vaccination for the groups mentioned. This is completely incomprehensible from a medical point of view and cannot be justified. By way of comparison, in the USA, general COVID-19 vaccination recommendations have been withdrawn. 1.

What are the grounds given by the Commission and the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) for recommending COVID-19 vaccination specifically for the above-mentioned groups of people, contrary to medical and legal standards?
Why are the vulnerable groups mentioned above, of all people, being exposed to the risk of vaccine failure and serious side effects, including death?
What purpose do European COVID-19 vaccination recommendations serve at all, now that the US has withdrawn all COVID-19 vaccination recommendations?

at: (English version) to the Commission Gerald Hauser (PfE) (6 July 2026) Subject: COVID-19 vaccination recommendations with no medical justification Austria was the only country in the EU to make COVID-19 vaccinations compulsory, as publicly called for by Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. The following population groups, amongst others, were exempted by law from the vaccination requirement on medical grounds: Pregnant women, as well as people with autoimmune diseases, severe inflammatory conditions, severe chronic illnesses, and people for whom ‘a sufficient immune response to a COVID-19 vaccination cannot be expected for medical reasons’ (e.g. following organ transplants, in cases of immunosuppression, active and currently treated or metastatic cancers, and other severe medical conditions). However, current vaccination guidelines in Austria and the EU (1) now recommend regular COVID-19 vaccination for the groups mentioned. This is completely incomprehensible from a medical point of view and cannot be justified. By way of comparison, in the USA, general COVID-19 vaccination recommendations have been withdrawn. 1. What are the grounds given by the Commission and the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) for recommending COVID-19 vaccination specifically for the above-mentioned groups of people, contrary to medical and legal standards? 2. Why are the vulnerable groups mentioned above, of all people, being exposed to the risk of vaccine failure and serious side effects, including death? 3. What purpose do European COVID-19 vaccination recommendations serve at all, now that the US has withdrawn all COVID-19 vaccination recommendations? (24 August 2026) The Commission did not call for vaccination to be mandatory. The organisation and delivery of health services and medical care is a national competence (1). As such, decisions about vaccines, including who they are recommended for or whether they are compulsory, are the sole responsibility of the Member States. Real world data has shown that vaccines are as safe in special populations, such as people with underlying medical conditions, immunocompromised patients and pregnant women, as they are in the general population. Vaccination of these groups is strongly recommended because they are at higher risk of complications from COVID-19. Vaccination during pregnancy protects both the mother and the baby. Vaccines against COVID-19 are safe and have been widely used, with more than 13 billion doses administered worldwide (2). It is the largest vaccination programme in history. Estimates indicate that millions of lives have been saved by COVID-19 vaccination (3). Regulators have an unprecedented amount of data to confirm the safety and efficacy of COVID-19 vaccines. National authorities and the European Medicines Agency (EMA) continuously monitor the safety of COVID-19 vaccines to ensure any possible risks are detected and managed as early as possible (4).

E-10-2026-002793.t: Labour market integration and access to family-related social benefits
qt: to the Commission Christine Anderson (ESN) Subject:
The Court of Justice of the European Union has repeatedly referred in its case-law to the requirement of a genuine link or integration in the labour market. 1.
What criteria does the Commission consider relevant for determining whether there is sufficient labour market integration?
Does the Commission consider that, when granting certain social benefits, Member States may take into account the duration and stability of employment relationships?
To what extent are Member States permitted to distinguish between short-term employment and sustainable labour market integration?
at: (English version) to the Commission Christine Anderson (ESN) (6 July 2026) Subject: Labour market integration and access to family-related social benefits The Court of Justice of the European Union has repeatedly referred in its case-law to the requirement of a genuine link or integration in the labour market. 1. What criteria does the Commission consider relevant for determining whether there is sufficient labour market integration? 2. Does the Commission consider that, when granting certain social benefits, Member States may take into account the duration and stability of employment relationships? 3. To what extent are Member States permitted to distinguish between short-term employment and sustainable labour market integration? (31 August 2026) According to the case law of the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU), a sufficient link of integration of a mobile EU worker with the society of a Member State is, in principle, created by participation in the employment market of a Member State (1). This link of integration arises, in particular, from the fact that, through the taxes and social security contributions which EU mobile and frontier workers pay in the host Member State by virtue of their employment there, they also contribute to the financing of the social policies of that State. In view of this contribution, the CJEU underlined the importance of ensuring mobile workers receive equal treatment as regards family benefits and tax and social advantages in the Member State of work (2). In accordance with the CJEU case law on free movement of workers, the term ‘worker’ covers any person who undertakes genuine and effective work for which he is paid under the direction of someone els e (3). This might include activities such as part-time work, traineeships, au pairing, volunteering and students’ work. However, activities carried out on such a small scale as to be regarded as marginal or ancillary do not fall within that term. It is the responsibility of the national authorities to undertake, in the light of that definition, a case-by-case evaluation to establish whether those criteria are met. Moreover, it is the responsibility of Member States to design labour market policies and determine eligibility to social protection systems e.g. duration of employment for accessing some social security benefits.

E-10-2026-002792.t: Protection of national social security systems under EU law
qt: to the Commission Christine Anderson (ESN) Subject:
The Court of Justice of the European Union has recognised in several judgments that Member States may seek to safeguard the financial stability of their social security systems. 1.
How does the Commission currently assess the relationship between the freedom of movement under EU law and the fiscal sustainability of national social security systems?
Does the Commission consider that Member States retain sufficient scope for action to limit disproportionate burdens arising from the coordination of social security benefits across borders?
Is the Commission considering additional safeguards against the abusive or disproportionate use of family-related social security benefits?
at: (English version) to the Commission Christine Anderson (ESN) (6 July 2026) Subject: Protection of national social security systems under EU law The Court of Justice of the European Union has recognised in several judgments that Member States may seek to safeguard the financial stability of their social security systems. 1. How does the Commission currently assess the relationship between the freedom of movement under EU law and the fiscal sustainability of national social security systems? 2. Does the Commission consider that Member States retain sufficient scope for action to limit disproportionate burdens arising from the coordination of social security benefits across borders? 3. Is the Commission considering additional safeguards against the abusive or disproportionate use of family-related social security benefits? (4 August 2026) Pursuant to rules on the determination of applicable legislation laid down in Article 11 of Regulation (EC) No 883/2004 (1), economically active persons are covered by the social security scheme of the Member State where they pursue their professional activity whereas economically non-active persons are covered by the social security scheme of the Member State where they have their habitual residence. These rules ensure that insured persons contribute to the financing of the social policies of the competent Member State through the social security contributions and tax which they pay in that State by virtue of their employment or residence there. At the same time, the rules ensure that the free movement of workers does not undermine the financial sustainability of national social security schemes. For example, to avoid disproportionate burdens, the CJEU held that Member States can require economically non-active citizens residing in their territory to pay a proportionate fee when joining the national sickness insurance scheme of the host State (2). The Commission is not considering additional measures against any abusive or disproportionate use of family benefits as it is the responsibility of Member States to ensure that the rules on social security are correctly implemented and followed.

E-10-2026-002791.t: Management and control mechanisms for family-related social benefits
qt: to the Commission Christine Anderson (ESN) Subject:
Member States continue to face administrative challenges when checking eligibility conditions for family-related social benefits in cross-border situations. 1.
To what extent can Member States beef up control mechanisms regarding the habitual residence, schooling, gainful employment or actual residence of dependent children?
Does the Commission support an expansion of digital administrative cooperation and cross-border data cross-checks on this matter?
Has the Commission identified shortcomings in the current framework of administrative cooperation under Regulation (EC) No 883/2004?
at: (English version) to the Commission Christine Anderson (ESN) (6 July 2026) Subject: Management and control mechanisms for family-related social benefits Member States continue to face administrative challenges when checking eligibility conditions for family-related social benefits in cross-border situations. 1. To what extent can Member States beef up control mechanisms regarding the habitual residence, schooling, gainful employment or actual residence of dependent children? 2. Does the Commission support an expansion of digital administrative cooperation and cross-border data cross-checks on this matter? 3. Has the Commission identified shortcomings in the current framework of administrative cooperation under Regulation (EC) No 883/2004? (13 August 2026) The principle of equal treatment laid down in Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 883/2004 (1) on the coordination of social security systems prohibits Member States from imposing on EU mobile workers who have applied for family benefits any additional requirements which are not imposed on their own nationals. The Commission promotes digitalisation and the electronic exchange of information to facilitate the correct application of the EU social security coordination rules. The Electronic Exchange of Social Security Information system supports such cross-border exchanges in the field of family benefits. Furthermore, within the framework of the Fair Labour Mobility Package (2), the Commission intends to propose additional measures, notably the European Social Security Pass, to facilitate exchanges of social security information via digital means in view of a proper application and enforcement of the social security coordination rules. Pursuant to Article 76 of the above-mentioned Regulation, national authorities and institutions shall lend one another their good offices and have the duty of mutual information and cooperation to ensure the correct implementation of the regulation. The Commission is not aware of systematic shortcomings related to administrative cooperation between institutions in the field of cross-border applications for family benefits.

qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Elissavet Vozemberg-Vrionidi (PPE), Georgios Aftias (PPE), Vangelis Meimarakis (PPE), Fredis Beleris (PPE), Eleonora Meleti (PPE), Emmanouil Kefalogiannis (PPE), Dimitris Tsiodras (PPE) Subject:
EU-Türkiye meeting of 30 June 2026

In the joint statement issued following the meeting of 30 June 2026 in Ankara between the Minister of Foreign Affairs of Türkiye, Hakan Fidan, the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the EU for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy, Kaja Kallas, the Commissioner for Enlargement, Marta Kos, and the Commissioner for Internal Affairs and Migration, Magnus Brunner, the EU side stressed that Türkiye’s accession progress hinged on strengthening the rule of law, protecting fundamental rights and ensuring high democratic standards. However, the joint statement and the discussions made no reference to the recommendations contained in the European Parliament’s report condemning Türkiye’s ongoing casus belli against Greece, its continued violation of the sovereignty and sovereign rights of Greece and Cyprus, its obstructions to projects of common European interest, its reactions to the Greek marine park in the Aegean and the increase in illegal fishing by Turkish vessels in Greek territorial waters. In view of the above, can the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy say: 1.
Why was no reference made to the recommendations and conclusions of the European Parliament report of 17 June 2026?
How does the Commission ensure that the European Parliament’s recommendations form an integral part of the political framework of the EU’s foreign policy?
at: (English version) to the Vice-President of the Commission/High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Elissavet Vozemberg-Vrionidi (PPE), Georgios Aftias (PPE), Vangelis Meimarakis (PPE), Fredis Beleris (PPE), Eleonora Meleti (PPE), Emmanouil Kefalogiannis (PPE), Dimitris Tsiodras (PPE) (6 July 2026) Subject: EU-Türkiye meeting of 30 June 2026 In the joint statement issued following the meeting of 30 June 2026 in Ankara between the Minister of Foreign Affairs of Türkiye, Hakan Fidan, the Vice-President of the Commission/High Representative of the EU for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy, Kaja Kallas, the Commissioner for Enlargement, Marta Kos, and the Commissioner for Internal Affairs and Migration, Magnus Brunner, the EU side stressed that Türkiye’s accession progress hinged on strengthening the rule of law, protecting fundamental rights and ensuring high democratic standards. However, the joint statement and the discussions made no reference to the recommendations contained in the European Parliament’s report condemning Türkiye’s ongoing casus belli against Greece, its continued violation of the sovereignty and sovereign rights of Greece and Cyprus, its obstructions to projects of common European interest, its reactions to the Greek marine park in the Aegean and the increase in illegal fishing by Turkish vessels in Greek territorial waters. In view of the above, can the Vice-President of the Commission/High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy say: 1.
Why was no reference made to the recommendations and conclusions of the European Parliament report of 17 June 2026?
How does the Commission ensure that the European Parliament’s recommendations form an integral part of the political framework of the EU’s foreign policy?

(13 August 2026) The EU’s relations with Türkiye are guided by the European Council’s conclusions, the Council’s established positions, the relevant Commission enlargement reports, and the EU’s broader strategic interest. The joint statement (1) issued following the meeting of 30 June 2026 was intended to reflect the main points discussed at that occasion and was not designed to provide an exhaustive account of all issues and documents that shape the EU’s position towards Türkiye. The absence of an explicit reference to specific elements of the European Parliament’s resolution of 17 June 2026 does not in any way imply that the concerns raised therein are disregarded. The High Representative/Vice-President and the Commission attach great importance to the views expressed by the European Parliament, including those relating to respect for the sovereignty and sovereign rights of Member States, regional stability, good neighbourly relations, and alignment with the EU’s common foreign and security policy objectives, are taken into account in the EU’s ongoing assessment of relations with Türkiye. As regards the role of the European Parliament’s recommendations in the political framework of the EU’s foreign policy, the High Representative/Vice-President and the Commission ensure close and regular engagement with the European Parliament, including through debates in plenary, committee exchanges, written replies, and the consideration of the European Parliament’s reports and resolutions in policy preparation and implementation. The European Parliament’s views form an important element of the institutional dialogue underpinning the EU’s external action, in full respect of the institutional balance laid down in the Treaties.

E-10-2026-002787.t: Question about an immediate stop to prosecution of academics at the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki
qt: to the Commission Lefteris Nikolaou-Alavanos (NI) Subject:

The president and members of the Board of Directors of the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki Faculty Union are facing legal charges on the basis of unfounded accusations, because they expressed their support for the fair demands and the protests of students living in halls of residence. This is the first instance of the Nea Dimokratia Government's unacceptable disciplinary framework for public servants (Law 5224/25) being applied. Government and administrations are intensifying efforts to silence universities through a series of repressive measures, so that anti-educational policies that undermine labour and education rights can be pursued without any hinderance. In the same context, Law 5224/25 is using Regulations (EU) 2019/945 and (EU) 2019/947 on drones, with ‘safety’ as the pretext. All this demonstrates the perennial downside to public and free higher education, the underfunding of academic institutions, their transformation into incubators for war research, working predominantly on EU war programmes (European Defence Fund (EDF) and NATO's DIANA ) as well as Horizon-funded programmes for research into dual-use products. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

Where does it stand on the fact that, in the name of ‘academic freedom’, the implementation of the guidelines of the European Higher Education Area ensures the business operation of institutions by increasingly allowing war research to infiltrate universities, while measures are taken to suppress protestation and limit industrial action, with a view to allowing the unhindered promotion of the European strategy and the interests of monopolies in higher education and research?
How does it view the legitimate calls from the academic community for an end to the prosecution of students, professors and university workers?
at: (English version) to the Commission Lefteris Nikolaou-Alavanos (NI) (6 July 2026) Subject: Question about an immediate stop to prosecution of academics at the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki The president and members of the Board of Directors of the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki Faculty Union are facing legal charges on the basis of unfounded accusations, because they expressed their support for the fair demands and the protests of students living in halls of residence. This is the first instance of the Nea Dimokratia Government's unacceptable disciplinary framework for public servants (Law 5224/25) being applied. Government and administrations are intensifying efforts to silence universities through a series of repressive measures, so that anti-educational policies that undermine labour and education rights can be pursued without any hinderance. In the same context, Law 5224/25 is using Regulations (EU) 2019/945 and (EU) 2019/947 on drones, with ‘safety’ as the pretext. All this demonstrates the perennial downside to public and free higher education, the underfunding of academic institutions, their transformation into incubators for war research, working predominantly on EU war programmes (European Defence Fund (EDF) and NATO's DIANA ) as well as Horizon-funded programmes for research into dual-use products. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

Where does it stand on the fact that, in the name of ‘academic freedom’, the implementation of the guidelines of the European Higher Education Area ensures the business operation of institutions by increasingly allowing war research to infiltrate universities, while measures are taken to suppress protestation and limit industrial action, with a view to allowing the unhindered promotion of the European strategy and the interests of monopolies in higher education and research?
How does it view the legitimate calls from the academic community for an end to the prosecution of students, professors and university workers?

(26 August 2026) The Commission does not comment on the legal charges, which fall exclusively within the competence of the Member State concerned. Education remains a Member States’ competence, including for the content of teaching. At the same time, the Commission remains firmly committed to academic freedom and the freedom of scientific research, in line with Article 13 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union (1). The Commission will continue to promote these principles across all its policies and interactions with higher education institutions and public authorities. The Commission also participates actively to the European Higher Education Area as a full member of the Bologna Follow-Up Group (2), alongside all Member States including Greece. The Tirana Communiqué (2024) (3) reaffirmed that academic freedom is one of six fundamental academic values, next to academic integrity, institutional autonomy, student and staff participation in higher education governance, public responsibility for higher education and public responsibility of higher education, and that these values must be implemented as a coherent whole. Nonetheless, Council recommendations (4) emphasise the importance of external quality assurance conducted in line with the Standards and Guidelines for Quality Assurance in the European Higher Education Area and by independent quality assurance agencies registered with the European Quality Assurance Register (5) to protect the interests of students and staff.

E-10-2026-002786.t: PFAS contamination in food and lack of monitoring by the Veneto Region
qt: to the Commission Dario Tamburrano (The Left), Cristina Guarda (Verts/ALE), Leoluca Orlando (Verts/ALE), Ignazio Roberto Marino (Verts/ALE), Gaetano Pedulla' (The Left), Carolina Morace (The Left), Danilo Della Valle (The Left) Subject:

Exposure to perfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) occurs mainly through the food chain, with contamination originating from the soil and agricultural run-off. Given the presence of PFAS in the environment1 and their potential for bioaccumulation, these substances, which are harmful to human health, need to be monitored. The Veneto Region’s PFAS monitoring plan2 proposes measures to monitor the agri-food supply chain and the products offered for sale in the region. Can the Commission therefore say: 1.

In accordance with the precautionary principle and in light of the obligations arising from Recommendation (EU) 2022/14313 and Regulation (EU) 2022/2388, why are the results of the PFAS Monitoring Plan for agri-food products in the red and orange zone not yet available to the public, and when are they expected to be published?

What measures is ARPAV4 required to take under Commission Delegated Regulation (UE) 2022/9315, and do the failure to publish results, the lack of tracking and the limited range of products analysed pose risks of further food contamination within the meaning of Regulation (EU) 2023/915?

Given the critical levels of PFAS in food and groundwater documented by ARPAV and the absence of public data on food inspections, does the Commission believe Italy and the Veneto region to be fulfilling the consumer-risk-assessment obligations incumbent upon them under Annex I, paragraph 3(c) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/931?

Panieri, E., Baralic, K., Djukic-Cosic, D., Buha Djordjevic, A., & Saso, L. (2022), PFAS Molecules: A Major Concern for the Human Health and the Environment, Toxics, 10(2), 44, https://doi.org/10.3390/toxics10020044. 2 PFAS Monitoring Plan for agri-food products in the red and orange zones: alimenti vegetali, Regione Veneto, https://bur.regione.veneto.it/BurvServices/pubblica/DettaglioDgr.aspx?id=520082. 3 Commission Recommendation (EU) 2022/1431 of 24 August 2022 on the monitoring of perfluoroalkyl substances in food: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reco/2022/1431/oj. 4 Veneto Regional Environmental Protection Agency. 5 Annex I, point 3(c) thereof. 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.9.2026) Regulation (EU) 2023/9151 has established maximum levels (MLs) for perfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) in certain foods of animal origin, with a view of ensuring a high level of human health protection and those foods must comply with these MLs, when placed on the EU market. According to Recommendation (EU) 2022/14312, Member States should have monitored PFAS in a wide range of foods between 2022 and 2025. However, this is not a legal obligation. The data collected under this Recommendation were to be submitted to the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) by June 2026. EFSA is currently compiling the data, which are expected to be available by October 2026. These data will be used for discussions with the Member States on the possible need to set new or revised MLs for PFAS in food. Under Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/9313, Member States are required to draw up national control plans on contaminants in food. These plans should include the monitoring of certain persistent organic pollutants in foods for which MLs are established, such as PFAS in foods of animal origin. The control plans must be risk-based; however, the Regulation does not specify the number of samples that need to be taken specifically for PFAS, nor does it set specific sampling requirements for certain regions within a Member State. Neither the Recommendation nor the Regulation includes requirements to publish monitoring results. Aggregated data may be requested from EFSA4; however; these data are not necessarily available for a specific region within a Member State. So far, the Commission has no indication that Italy did not comply with the requirements of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/931.

1 http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2023/915/oj. 2 http://data.europa.eu/eli/reco/2022/1431/oj. 3 http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg_del/2022/931/oj. 4 By submitting a request to: data.collection@efsa.europa.eu.

E-10-2026-002785.t: Compensation for fishers affected by silver-cheeked toadfish
qt: to the Commission Georgios Aftias (PPE) Subject:

Silver-cheeked toadfish (Lagocephalus sceleratus) were first detected in Greece in 2005. Within a span of 23 years, the fish can now be found not only in Greek waters, but also in those of Italy and Spain. Recently, the damage they have caused to Greek fishers and their property has been extensive. They destroy their marketable catch and fishing gear, reducing their production capacity. This directly affects the Greek fishing industry – a productive mainstay of the Greek economy. Coordinated European action is therefore required, as is compensation for fishers affected by silver-cheeked toadfish. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Will it provide compensation to fishers affected by silver-cheeked toadfish?
Will it take measures to address similar future risks?
In the context of drafting the new EU multiannual financial framework for 2028-2034, will it allocate additional resources to strengthen the resilience of the Greek fishing fleet?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (21.8.2026) 1. Member States can use the European Maritime, Fisheries and Aquaculture Fund (EMFAF) to fund targeted management actions and support fishers affected by non-indigenous species (NIS). Greece has recently launched a relevant action, in a pilot phase, focusing on Lagocephalus and aiming to protect marine biodiversity through targeted fisheries management measures, scientific monitoring and remuneration to participating coastal fishers for targeted catching and landing. It is for the Member States to design and implement such measures within their national EMFAF programmes. 2. The Commission announced a dedicated policy initiative within the Ocean Pact1 to address the issue of NIS. In addition, through collaboration and financial support to the General Fisheries Commission for the Mediterranean, the EU has been supporting work on NIS through research programmes and establishment of a regional NIS observatory to enhance knowledge and share best practices in tackling NIS. 3. For fisheries, the Commission proposal foresees a ring-fenced amount of EUR 2 billion for certain activities under the Common Fisheries Policy (CFP), ensuring a minimum level of support for key CFP objectives, including sustainability, conservation of marine biological resources, innovation and the Common Market Organisation. Member States will be able to complement this dedicated amount from the overall envelope of their national and regional partnership plans to address additional needs related to fisheries, aquaculture, coastal communities, the wider blue economy and the ocean.
1 Communication of the Commission on the European Ocean Pact, COM(2025) 281 of 5.6.2025.

E-10-2026-002784.t: Business and human rights in Colombia – the Jericó 11
qt: to the Commission Cristina Guarda (Verts/ALE), Isabel Serra Sánchez (The Left), Evin Incir (S&D) Subject:

AngloGold Ashanti, a global gold-mining company with European investment, has been conducting prospecting and mining exploration in Jericó, in the Antioquia region of Colombia, since 2002. The company aims to establish a mining district to extract copper, gold, silver and their concentrates. Numerous small-scale farmers and their families live and work in the area intended for the mining project, growing coffee, avocados and other foods for their own sustenance. Since the announcement of the mining project in the region, those who have voiced criticism of it have been subjected to stigmatisation tactics and disinformation campaigns aimed at intimidating them. The situation escalated when AngloGold Ashanti filed a criminal complaint in 2025 against 11 peasant leaders, accusing them of kidnapping, aggravated theft and personal injury, simply for exercising their right to peaceful protest. The next hearing will take place in August 2026. In this context we would like to ask the Commission: 1.
Does the EU Delegation in Bogotá have any plans to visit the affected communities to ensure that the company is complying fully with European standards on due diligence and human rights?
How does the EU Delegation intend to monitor the legal proceedings against the farmers, in line with its obligations under the guidelines on human rights defenders and the Anti-SLAPP Directive?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (13.8.2026) The EU Delegation to Colombia closely follows the situation in Jericó, including through the project ‘The Right to Defend Rights’, under which one of its implementing partners, the Corporación Jurídica Libertad, has provided legal defence to the farmers facing criminal proceedings and conducted advisory and support visits to the affected community. As part of the project, a podcast episode is also being prepared to raise awareness of the situation in Jericó. Officials of the European External Action Service also met with the Coordinator of the Mesa Ambiental de Jericó in June 2026, during his visit to Brussels to participate in a meeting of the European Parliament delegation for relations with the countries of the Andean Community, entitled ‘Voices of Human Rights Defenders in Andean Communities – Technical perspective, international framework and testimonies’. The EU, including its Delegation in Bogotá, will continue to maintain regular dialogue with civil society organisations and implementing partners of EU-funded initiatives to stay informed about developments on the ground.

E-10-2026-002782.t: EIB-financing of transport investments in Morocco
qt: to the Commission Stanisław Tyszka (ESN) Subject:

The European Investment Bank has announced EUR 365 million in financing for the transport sector in Morocco – a third country that is not an EU Member State. Funds will go to the motorway network and railway system, with the latter also benefiting from a non-repayable grant of EUR 15 million. The EIB’s non-EU operations under Union external mandates are usually backed by EU budgetary guarantees. The Draghi report highlights that the EU needs EUR 750-800 billion in additional investments per year, while the European Court of Auditors, in special report 02/2026, finds further delays and cost increases in EU transport infrastructure projects. The Commission also points out that regional differences persist in Poland, including between big cities and rural areas. In this connection: 1.
Are EIB operations in the Moroccan transport sector backed by the EU budget, including EFSD+ guarantees, and if so, at what rate and with what amount set aside in the EU budget?

According to what criteria and under what procedure was Morocco – a country that is neither an EU Member State nor a candidate country – singled out as a priority for EU support, and what measurable benefits are expected to ensue for the EU?
In view of the urgent investment needs of Member States, including Poland, how does the Commission justify allocating grants and budgetary guarantees to transport infrastructure in Morocco?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (25.9.2026) EU relations with Morocco encompass a broad range of issues, including security, trade, investment, economic cooperation and migration. Support to the Moroccan transport sector aims to contribute to sustainable economic development, regional connectivity and the green transition, while also promoting higher safety, environmental and governance standards. The transport sector also offers opportunities for leading EU companies to invest, sell advanced technologies and contribute their expertise. Such cooperation is part of the EU’s broader partnership with Morocco and is consistent with the EU’s interest in stable, secure and prosperous neighbouring countries in the southern Mediterranean. The European Investment Bank’s (EIB) operations in the Moroccan transport sector are supported through a mix of EIB own funds and EU grants and guarantees under the European Fund for Sustainable Development Plus, within the legal framework established by the Neighbourhood, Development and International Cooperation Instrument – Global Europe (NDICI–GE) jointly agreed by the co-legislators. Since 2022, the EU budget has supported two EIB investment operations in Morocco’s transport sector through a blending grant of EUR 15.4 million and guarantee cover on EIB loans totalling EUR 550 million. The total amount committed from the EU budget for these two operations is EUR 64.9 million, comprising the grant contribution and the provisioning for the guarantee coverage. It should be underlined that EU budget allocations for external action, including those concerning Morocco, are distinct from the resources earmarked for Member States and they represent around 8% of the overall current Multiannual Financial Framework. The EU supports the urgent investment needs of Member States through dedicated internal instruments and programmes such as Cohesion Policy, the Recovery and Resilience Facility and InvestEU. External financing instruments such as NDICI–GE pursue, among others, the complementary objective of fostering stability and prosperity in the EU’s neighbourhood, thereby contributing to the EU’s broader strategic interests and benefiting the EU as a whole.

E-10-2026-002781.t: Revision of the data centre sustainability rating system
qt: to the Commission Nicolás González Casares (S&D) Subject:

According to recent news reports1, the ongoing revision of the delegated act on the sustainability rating of data centres drastically reduces the sustainability criteria required from operators. The Commission seems prepared to yield to the requests of Big Tech, with new reporting requirements that do not cut actual emissions and remove incentives to acquire additional renewable energy. This poses a risk to Europe’s energy security, price affordability and climate goals by allowing dependence on fossil fuels rather than encouraging new local renewable energy production. In view of the above: 1.

Will the Commission ensure that the final text includes criteria that reflect the actual sustainability of a data centre with conditions requiring additional renewable sources and for production to be made nearby and at the right time for demand, rather than allowing emissions to be offset?
How will the Commission ensure that revision of the delegated act does not compromise energy security, affordability for consumers or binding EU climate targets?

Has the Commission carried out an assessment to ensure that the new rating system will prevent against the risk of increased marginal generation at peak times using natural gas as a result of the higher electricity demand from data centres?
https://www.ft.com/content/21358a9a-b93b-443c-8a68-6fed89c8b3a6?sharetype=blocked&syn25a6b1a6=1. 1
at: (English version) to the Commission Nicolás González Casares (S&D) (3 July 2026) Subject: Revision of the data centre sustainability rating system According to recent news reports (1), the ongoing revision of the delegated act on the sustainability rating of data centres drastically reduces the sustainability criteria required from operators. The Commission seems prepared to yield to the requests of Big Tech, with new reporting requirements that do not cut actual emissions and remove incentives to acquire additional renewable energy. This poses a risk to Europe’s energy security, price affordability and climate goals by allowing dependence on fossil fuels rather than encouraging new local renewable energy production. In view of the above: 1.

Will the Commission ensure that the final text includes criteria that reflect the actual sustainability of a data centre with conditions requiring additional renewable sources and for production to be made nearby and at the right time for demand, rather than allowing emissions to be offset?
How will the Commission ensure that revision of the delegated act does not compromise energy security, affordability for consumers or binding EU climate targets?

Has the Commission carried out an assessment to ensure that the new rating system will prevent against the risk of increased marginal generation at peak times using natural gas as a result of the higher electricity demand from data centres?

(27 August 2026) The upcoming rating scheme for data centres has been developed based on the reporting obligations established in line with the Energy Efficiency Directive (1). It intends to address the need for data centres to better substantiate claims that their energy use is ‘green’ or ‘carbon-neutral’, including by linking clean energy production more closely to the physical location and timing of data centre consumption, while avoiding undue market distortions, respecting technology neutrality, and overall promoting clean energy generation and smarter energy uses. Following the public consultation, the Commission is carefully assessing the feedback received, including on this matter, and will ensure that the final text does not compromise the Union’s objectives of competitiveness, energy security, affordability and decarbonisation. In addition, the Commission will consider an early review clause to ensure that implementation results, and environmental, technological and market developments can be addressed, if necessary. Concerning increased marginal generation at peak times, the rating scheme does not rule on how electricity is generated and priced, and does not promote electricity generation using natural gas, but rather new clean energy generation capacity and smarter energy uses.

E-10-2026-002780.t: Extreme heatwaves and bolstering health resilience and civil protection in the EU
qt: to the Commission Ruggero Razza (ECR), Alberico Gambino (ECR), Chiara Gemma (ECR), Giuseppe Milazzo (ECR), Daniele Polato (ECR), Francesco Torselli (ECR), Mariateresa Vivaldini (ECR) Subject:

According to the World Health Organization, extreme temperatures have caused more than 1 300 excess deaths in Europe since 21 June, confirming the escalating impact of heatwaves on public health and health and social care systems. They are also increasingly affecting Mediterranean Member States, including Italy, Spain, Greece and Portugal, where they are growing in frequency and length, causing ramifications for the health of society’s most vulnerable, and for electricity grids, water resources, farming, forest fires and civil protection. In the light of the above: 1.

Will the Commission, together with the Member States, support follow-up to the preventive measures and social and health assistance taken during the summer period to protect the elderly and the most vulnerable?
Does it believe that the European preparedness and resilience strategy gives sufficient priority to the risk posed by extreme heat waves?
Does it think that the current Union civil protection mechanism is sufficient for the increase in extreme weather events or will it propose that the mechanism be strengthened?
at: (English version) to the Commission Ruggero Razza (ECR), Alberico Gambino (ECR), Chiara Gemma (ECR), Giuseppe Milazzo (ECR), Daniele Polato (ECR), Francesco Torselli (ECR), Mariateresa Vivaldini (ECR) (3 July 2026) Subject: Extreme heatwaves and bolstering health resilience and civil protection in the EU According to the World Health Organisation, extreme temperatures have caused more than 1 300 excess deaths in Europe since 21 June, confirming the escalating impact of heatwaves on public health and health and social care systems. They are also increasingly affecting Mediterranean Member States, including Italy, Spain, Greece and Portugal, where they are growing in frequency and length, causing ramifications for the health of society’s most vulnerable, and for electricity grids, water resources, farming, forest fires and civil protection. In the light of the above: 1.

Will the Commission, together with the Member States, support follow-up to the preventive measures and social and health assistance taken during the summer period to protect the elderly and the most vulnerable?
Does it believe that the European preparedness and resilience strategy gives sufficient priority to the risk posed by extreme heat waves?
Does it think that the current Union civil protection mechanism is sufficient for the increase in extreme weather events or will it propose that the mechanism be strengthened?

(20 August 2026) The Union Civil Protection Mechanism (UCPM) (1) coordinates disaster response and supports Member States in implementing prevention and preparedness activities. To address growing wildfires, fuelled by heatwaves, the Commission proposed an integrated wildfire risk management approach (2), covering prevention, preparedness, response and recovery; and reinforced UCPM capacities. The Preparedness Union Strategy (3) adopts an all-hazards approach. This includes strengthening resilience to heatwaves through early warning, prevention, resilient infrastructure, healthcare preparedness and community action, with particular attention to vulnerable populations’ needs. The Commission is exploring further heatwave preparedness actions to complement Member State efforts. The European integrated framework for climate resilience (4), which will include a legal proposal and a communication, will prioritise heatwave risks. It will address all major climate risks identified in the European Climate Risk Assessmen t (5). Heat stress is a top ranked risk, requiring action. The European Climate and Health Observatory (6) provides evidence on adapting to climate change-induced health impacts. Its partner, World Health Organisation Europe, published guidance on heat-health action plans (7), covering preparedness, warning, populations at risk, health system resilience, etc. The regulation on Serious Cross-Border Threats to Health (8) strengthens prevention, preparedness and response planning, also for climate-related threats such as extreme heat. The Commission’s UCPM/HER Proposal (9) aims to strengthen the UCPM to tackle extreme weather events by improving coordination, forward planning, crisis monitoring and cross-sectoral preparedness.
