E-10-2026-002779.t: Illegal implementation of the cable car construction project on the archaeological site of Monemvasia without a building permit and funded by the RRF
qt: to the Commission Konstantinos Arvanitis (The Left) Subject:

In the context of cooperation between the Municipality of Monemvasia, the Region of Peloponnese and the Greek Ministry of Culture, construction works are being carried out to install a cable car at Monemvasia Castle, an archaeological site and a potential UNESCO cultural heritage site, with a budget of EUR 6 800 360 from the Recovery and Resilience Fund. However, the project is being carried out amid serious arbitrariness and irregularities, including the failure to publish a geological stability study, the failure to issue the required building permit for the construction of the station and the accompanying infrastructure of the cable car, and the lack of adequate explanations from the competent urban planning department. The above-mentioned shortcomings are at odds with Directive 2011/92/EU on environmental impact assessment (EIA), European legislation on the protection of cultural heritage, as well as EU funding eligibility rules. With this in mind, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Is it aware that the project is being carried out without the required planning permits, approved geological studies and using methods (rock excavation) that contradict the original approvals?

Does the start of construction of a public building on a national road and within an archaeological zone, without a building permit, constitute a breach of EU environmental standards and the principles of the rule of law?

Given that the project is financed by the RRF with a strict deadline for completion in September 2026, does the Commission intend to check the legality of the disbursement of funds due to a breach of sound financial management rules and, if applicable, suspend the relevant funding as a precautionary measure?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (5.8.2026) Measure 16735 of the Greek Recovery and Resilience Plan (RRP)1 aims to improve physical access to cultural venues, including for older people and persons with disabilities. According to Decision 185395 of 19 December 20222, the construction of the Monemvasia lift was integrated into the Greek RRP under measure 16735 to ensure access for persons with mobility constraints to the upper town of Monemvasia, to speed up access in case of emergency, and to transfer materials for the preservation of monuments. The Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF) Regulation3 provides that no measure included in a RRP should do significant harm to environmental objectives within the meaning of Article 17 of Regulation (EU) 2020/8524. Decision 185395 of 19 December 2022 sets out that the installation of the lift should be carried out with due regard to the landscape and environment, and that the project should comply with the RRF Regulation including the ‘do no significant harm’ principle. The published call for tender also requires that the project should comply with EU and national environmental and other rules5. The granting of building permits and the supervision of construction works fall primarily within the competence of the national authorities. The siting of the project was approved, in accordance with archaeological legislation, by Decision 452351 of 23 September 2021 of the Minister of Culture following the unanimous opinion of the Central Archaeological Council. The RRF is a performance-based financing instrument. Therefore, the Commission releases funds to Member States only after it has assessed the satisfactory fulfilment of the agreed milestones and targets that are linked to the reforms and investments under the RRP. Payment requests related to this measure have not been submitted by Greece and thus have not yet been assessed by the Commission.

and-resilience-plan_en. 2 https://greece20.gov.gr/wp-content/uploads/575.-Anavatorio_Kastro_Monemvasias_5198124.pdf. 3 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:32021R0241. 4 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2020/852/oj/eng. 5 https://monemvasia.gov.gr/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/2024-04-08_diaxirisi_anavatorio_kastrou-diakiriksi.pdf.

E-10-2026-002778.t: Follow-up to the European Citizens’ Panel on Preparedness
qt: to the Commission Pascal Arimont (PPE), Joachim Streit (Renew), Thomas Pellerin-Carlin (S&D), Matej Tonin (PPE), Grégory Allione (Renew), Liesbet Sommen (PPE), Olivier Chastel (Renew), Vladimir Prebilič (Verts/ALE), Aurelijus Veryga (ECR), Christophe Clergeau (S&D) Subject:

The recently concluded European Citizens’ Panel on Preparedness brought together 150 randomly selected citizens from across all 27 Member States and resulted in 20 recommendations to strengthen the EU’s capacity to prevent and respond to crises. These recommendations address, among other issues, risk and crisis communication, warning systems, information integrity, inclusion, citizens’ self-sufficiency, volunteering and education on preparedness. In view of the Commission’s stated intention to incorporate these recommendations into the implementation of the Preparedness Union Strategy: 1.
Will the Commission publish a structured follow-up setting out which recommendations will be taken forward, by which services and within what time frame?
How does the Commission intend to follow up on recommendation 5.1 of the panel concerning volunteering and the strengthening of volunteer work?
How does the Commission assess the proposal to establish a European Preparedness Week as part of the follow-up to the citizens’ panel and the implementation of the Preparedness Union Strategy?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (21.8.2026) The Commission will publish a follow-up to the recommendations from the Citizens’ Panel on Preparedness in a Citizens’ Report. It will outline how it intends to respond to the recommendations, and in what time frame. The response will be prepared by the concerned Commission services. It is expected to be published before the Civil Protection Forum in November 2026. The Commission takes note of recommendation 5.1 (to strengthen volunteer work). The European Solidarity Corps offers cross-border volunteering activities and is identified as a key instrument for building a culture of preparedness. Through Action 30 of the Preparedness Union Strategy1, preparedness is now a formal priority within EU youth funding. The Commission is working on a set of guidelines for Member States on preparedness education for schools (Action 29), which could help to promote preparedness and volunteering (for example through activities with local organisations and emergency responders). The Commission is currently considering the rest of the suggestions proposed in the recommendations and will provide a response in the Citizens’ Report. The Commission welcomed the citizens’ recommendations on the European Preparedness Week, which aligns very well with the spirit of the Preparedness Union Strategy (in particular Action 27). In this context, the EU will propose an annual EU Preparedness Day to raise awareness on the topic. This is expected to be announced at the Civil Protection Forum (34 November 2026), with the first edition being held in 2027, at a date to be confirmed.
1 https://commission.europa.eu/topics/preparedness_en.

E-10-2026-002777.t: Proportionate implementation of EU short-term rental registration rules
qt: to the Commission Cynthia Ní Mhurchú (Renew) Subject:

The Irish Government has announced plans to introduce what it describes as the ‘most stringent’ short-term rental (STR) regulations in the EU, including linking registration to planning compliance, before reliable data on the sector has been collected and assessed. Given that the EU STR Regulation on data collection for short-term accommodation rentals has just been enforced and is intended to improve transparency and support evidence-based policymaking, and given concerns that many small-scale hosts, rural communities and tourism businesses could be disproportionately affected without demonstrable benefits for housing supply: 1.

How can the Commission ensure that Member States allow sufficient time to collect and analyse registration data before introducing restrictive enforcement measures, in line with the principles of proportionality and better regulation?

How will the upcoming Affordable Housing Act, which intends to fine-tune the existing framework that addresses the proportionality of local legislation, address measures that do not have demonstrable benefits for housing supply but impact the local economy in a disproportionate way?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (8.9.2026) Short-term rentals (STR) offer many benefits. However, in some cities and tourist hotspots, limited housing supply growth combined with the rapid expansion of STR as well as speculative investment practices may be intensifying competition for limited housing stock.1 The Regulation (EU) 2024/10282, aims to increase transparency by harmonising registration systems including regular transmission of activity data from platforms to competent authorities. These data are intended to support evidence‑based and proportionate policymaking. The Commission takes note of concerns that restrictive measures might be introduced by the Member States without sufficient use of these data. In exercising its role as guardian of the Treaties and in line with the Directive 2006/123/EC3, it assesses national measures against single market rules and the principles of proportionality and may engage with Member States where doubts arise. The Commission is finalising its proposal for an Affordable Housing Act4. This initiative is envisaged to enable public authorities, in line with subsidiarity, to take measures to safeguard housing availability and affordability while providing for legal certainty. In this context, the Commission is assessing how a common framework could help ensure that housing-related measures are evidence-based and proportionate, considering both their contribution to housing objectives and their wider economic impacts.

E-10-2026-002776.t: European Investment Bank funds Morocco’s road and rail networks
qt: to the Commission Jorge Buxadé Villalba (PfE), Hermann Tertsch (PfE), Jorge Martín Frías (PfE), Juan Carlos Girauta Vidal (PfE), Mireia Borrás Pabón (PfE), Margarita de la Pisa Carrión (PfE) Subject:

On 30 June 2026, the European Investment Bank (EIB) announced that it was investing EUR 365 million to strengthen Morocco’s road and rail networks. Over the years, the EIB has mobilised more than EUR 12 billion for the Kingdom of Morocco. The EIB’s decision comes five months after the rail accident in Adamuz, Córdoba, which killed 46 people and took place on a section of track that had been reported for technical issues. EU resources are being earmarked for foreign transport while investment is seriously lacking for the road and rail networks in Spain and other Member States. In addition, the funding recently announced by the EIB does not appear to be linked to any reciprocal action by the Kingdom of Morocco in areas such as unfair competition, fraudulent labelling and the exploitation of immigration as a hybrid threat. In light of the above: 1.
Does the Commission consider it appropriate to be funding Moroccan railways while the road and rail networks in Spain and the EU are seriously under-maintained?
What reciprocal action is required of Morocco in return for the funding in question?
Does the Commission consider that such actions can strengthen international relations that are based on blackmail and pressure from hybrid threats?

E-10-2026-002775.t: Recycled aluminium supply chains for beverage packaging
qt: to the Commission Angelika Winzig (PPE) Subject:

Packaging represents the second largest source of aluminium scrap at global level1, while 76 % of aluminium beverage cans are recycled in Europe. Beverage companies are a key supply-side driver of recycled aluminium, providing cheaper secondary raw material that uses up to 95 % less energy than primary production2. Meanwhile, given the reuse targets for beverage packaging under Article 29 of the Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation, operators may be required to invest simultaneously in largescale reused packaging materials, diverting from the aluminium-made format, and in highperforming recycling systems, even where the latter alone delivers better outcomes. Given the foregoing: 1.

In Austria, rules exempt beverage containers with a capacity below 0.5 litres from reuse obligations, while mandating a 90 % collection and recycling rate. Is the Commission considering generalising the Austrian model across the EU via a delegated act to exempt aluminium beverage packaging from reuse targets?
Can the Commission clarify whether operators using aluminium packaging could be excluded from the re-use obligation?
Such schemes contribute to secure access to strategic raw materials. Will these factors be taken into account when developing the guidelines under Article 29(8)?

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0921344916301604. https://european-aluminium.eu/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/EA-MPE-BevCan-2023-RecyclingResults-Press-Release-17-February.pdf. 1 2
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (21.9.2026) The harmonised reuse targets set out in the Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation1 (PPWR) ensure that economic operators must only apply one set of rules instead of 27 national ones. The beverages that fall within the scope of the reuse targets for beverages in Article 29(6) will be specified in guidelines to be published by 12 February 2027. These guidelines are being prepared in consultation with Member States and other relevant stakeholders. The guidelines cannot provide exemptions that are not already included in the PPWR, such as for smaller beverage packaging or for specific materials. As specified in the Commission’s Guidance Notice2 on the PPWR, point 24, Member States may, under certain conditions, exempt materials from the reuse targets in the PPWR. For example, if the recycling target for aluminium is exceeded in a Member State, final distributors could be allowed to deduct beverages sold in aluminium cans from the products within the scope of the obligation to sell 10% of the beverages in reusable packaging. By 1 January 2034, the Commission shall present a report reviewing the implementation of the 2030 targets, also taking into account the evolution of the state of the art of technology and the practical experience gained by economic operators and Member States. In that regard, access to strategic raw materials could also be considered.
1 Regulation (EU) 2025/40 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 19 December 2024 on packaging

and packaging waste, amending Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 and Directive (EU) 2019/904, and repealing Directive 94/62/EC, OJ L, 2025/40, 22.1.2025. 2 https://green-forum.ec.europa.eu/packaging-and-packaging-waste-regulation-implementation_en.

E-10-2026-002774.t: End of right to veto: will Member States be forced to comply?
qt: to the Commission Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE) Subject:

A number of proposals for EU reform aim to replace the unanimity rule – which requires unanimous agreement from all Member States – with qualified majority voting in particularly sensitive areas like foreign policy, taxation and certain defence issues. In practice, this means that a decision could be adopted even if multiple Member States are opposed to it, provided that a majority of Member States, representing a significant proportion of the EU population, are in favour. This change would profoundly alter the current balance between the Member States and the European institutions. A country could thus be forced to apply a decision that it had in fact rejected, including in areas that directly affect its essential national interests. 1.
Does the Commission wish to abolish Member States’ right to veto in certain areas and, if so, which areas?

Can it guarantee that no Member State will be deprived of its right to veto without an official amendment to the Treaties and without the agreement of the Member States in accordance with their national laws?
Before any reforms are made, will it publish a clear study explaining the powers that each Member State will lose and the decisions which could then be imposed on them?
at: (English version) to the Commission Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE) (3 July 2026) Subject: End of right to veto: will Member States be forced to comply? A number of proposals for EU reform aim to replace the unanimity rule — which requires unanimous agreement from all Member States — with qualified majority voting in particularly sensitive areas like foreign policy, taxation and certain defence issues. In practice, this means that a decision could be adopted even if multiple Member States are opposed to it, provided that a majority of Member States, representing a significant proportion of the EU population, are in favour. This change would profoundly alter the current balance between the Member States and the European institutions. A country could thus be forced to apply a decision that it had in fact rejected, including in areas that directly affect its essential national interests. 1.
Does the Commission wish to abolish Member States’ right to veto in certain areas and, if so, which areas?

2. Can it guarantee that no Member State will be deprived of its right to veto without an official amendment to the Treaties and without the agreement of the Member States in accordance with their national laws? 3. Before any reforms are made, will it publish a clear study explaining the powers that each Member State will lose and the decisions which could then be imposed on them? (9 September 2026) 1. The Commission’s longstanding position, reiterated by the President of the Commission in her State of the Union address in September 2025 (1), is that, if the EU wants to act quickly, efficiently, and therefore strategically, unanimity voting ought to be reconsidered in certain policy areas. These include tax policy, social policy, energy and climate policy and aspects of the Common Foreign and Security Policy. 2. The move away from unanimity can be achieved through Treaty change or the activation of the passerelle clauses provided for in the EU Treaties. In any case a move away from unanimity depends on the agreement of all Member States. 3. The Commission has already set out detailed considerations in Communications from 2018 (2), 2019 (3) and 2024 (4). The Commission believes it is possible to move away from unanimity without putting at risk Member States strategic interests. This can be done by combining the activation of passerelle clauses with appropriate and proportionate safeguards to accommodate strategic national interests.

E-10-2026-002773.t: Montenegro’s accession: the EUR 3.2 billion cost to EU citizens
qt: to the Commission Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE) Subject:
Montenegro’s accession: the EUR 3.2 billion cost to EU citizens

The Commission estimates that Montenegro’s accession on 1 January 2028 would result in approximately EUR 3.2 billion in additional EU spending between 2028 and 2034. This sum would fund, among other things, the country’s economic and regional development, gradual access to EU agricultural subsidies, border controls, security and competitiveness. The Commission also envisages an additional EUR 442 million in additional administrative spending for the EU institutions. This is the estimate at a point when only 16 of the 33 chapters in the accession negotiations have been provisionally closed. 1.
What would be the real net cost of this accession, after deducting Montenegro’s future contribution to the EU budget and the pre-accession assistance that it would no longer receive?
Would this additional spending be funded by raising Member States’ contributions, by reducing the funding currently allocated to Member States, or through new EU resources?

Before negotiations conclude, will the Commission publish a study detailing the impacts of this accession on the budget of each Member State, the composition of the European Parliament, the votes in the Council and institution staffing levels?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (24.9.2026) The Commission communication1 sets out the gross budgetary impact of Montenegro’s prospective accession. The net cost will depend on Montenegro’s future contribution to the EU budget, to be set once EU acquis’ Chapter 33 (Financial and Budgetary Provisions)2 negotiations close. To partially offset the additional expenditure, the Commission proposes to transfer Montenegro’s allocation under the proposed Europe Pillar of the Global Europe instrument3, between budget headings, within its proposal for the next Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) 2028–20344. The package ensures that Member States are not negatively impacted, so the additional expenditure is not intended to be met by reducing the funding foreseen for the EU-27. The introduction of new own resources would strengthen the sustainability of revenues needed to support key EU priorities, all without adding undue burden onto Member States contributions. These priorities include not only the funding of a larger EU but also other key priorities such as security and competitiveness. The Commission is preparing pre-enlargement policy reviews to ensure the EU is politically, institutionally and financially prepared for a larger membership, taking into account that the Treaties already offer possibilities to adapt its governance to an enlarged EU. Definitive figures cannot be provided at this stage, pending the outcome of negotiations on the next MFF and the Own Resources Decision5.

E-10-2026-002772.t: Implementation of the new European anti-corruption agenda in Greece
qt: to the Commission Galato Alexandraki (ECR) Subject:

In May 2026, the new Directive on combating corruption entered into force and the Commission also opened a consultation on the first European anti-corruption strategy. The Commission rightly brings together prevention, penalties, public procurement, the protection of the EU’s financial interests and asset recovery. With this in mind, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Will it ask Greece to incorporate into its new national approach specific measures against corruption relating to European funds, agricultural aid and public procurement?
How will it be assessed whether Greece’s preventive mechanisms are working in practice and not only on paper?
Does the Commission intend to propose common European indices for imputation, recovery of funds, conflicts of interest and the protection of whistle-blowers?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.9.2026) Preventing and combating corruption remains a key political priority of the Commission. The entry into force of Directive (EU) 2026/10211 on combatting corruption in May 2026 marks a significant milestone in strengthening the EU’s legal framework against corruption. The Directive notably harmonises the definition of corruption offences and criminal penalties across the EU and establishes minimum common standards for preventive measures, which are particularly relevant to the Honourable Member's question. Member States have up to 24 months to transpose most of the provisions of the Directive into national law2. As with all directives, the Commission will support Member States in the transposition and will closely monitor this process. The timely and correct transposition of the Directive into national law will be assessed after the transposition period has expired. The Commission will continue to monitor the anti-corruption framework of Member States, including Greece, in the context of its annual Rule of Law report3. The EU Anti-Corruption Strategy, to be adopted in 2026, will build upon the Directive and support its effective implementation. The overall objective of the Strategy is to support a more comprehensive and coherent approach to preventing and combating corruption, while ensuring complementarity with relevant action at EU, national and international level. It will aim to strengthen trust in public institutions by promoting transparency, integrity and accountability, while safeguarding democracy, the rule of law and fair competition across the EU. In preparation of the Strategy, the Commission has conducted extensive consultations, including of the European Parliament.
1 Directive (EU) 2026/1021 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 29 April 2026 on combatting

corruption, replacing Council Framework Decision 2003/568/JHA and the Convention on the fight against corruption involving officials of the European Communities or officials of Member States of the European Union and amending Directive (EU) 2017/1371 of the European Parliament and of the Council. 2 Except for adopting and publishing a national strategy on preventing and combatting corruption as well as a risk assessment, for which Member States have 36 months. 3 2026 Annual Rule of Law report - https://commission.europa.eu/publications/2026-rule-law-reportcommunication-and-country-chapters_en.

E-10-2026-002771.t: Making the most of the European strategy for islands and coastal communities
qt: to the Commission Galato Alexandraki (ECR) Subject:

On 10 June 2026, the Commission presented the first dedicated EU strategies for islands and coastal communities, recognising that these regions face particular pressures when it comes to transport, energy, housing, climate resilience and access to services. The initiative is a move in the right direction, especially for Greece, where insularity is not an exception but a key element of national cohesion. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Does it intend to ask the Greek Government for a comprehensive national plan for the implementation of the strategy for the Greek islands, with clear projects, a timeline and result indicators?
How will it ensure that European funding is not limited to piecemeal projects, but supports permanent needs such as health, water, coastal shipping, energy and housing?
Will special care be taken to ensure that island development does not turn into a tourism monoculture to the detriment of residents, fishers and producers?
at: (English version) to the Commission Galato Alexandraki (ECR) (3 July 2026) Subject: Making the most of the European strategy for islands and coastal communities On 10 June 2026, the Commission presented the first dedicated EU strategies for islands and coastal communities, recognising that these regions face particular pressures when it comes to transport, energy, housing, climate resilience and access to services. The initiative is a move in the right direction, especially for Greece, where insularity is not an exception but a key element of national cohesion. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Does it intend to ask the Greek Government for a comprehensive national plan for the implementation of the strategy for the Greek islands, with clear projects, a timeline and result indicators?
How will it ensure that European funding is not limited to piecemeal projects, but supports permanent needs such as health, water, coastal shipping, energy and housing?
Will special care be taken to ensure that island development does not turn into a tourism monoculture to the detriment of residents, fishers and producers?

(19 August 2026) The EU strategy for islands (1) establishes a coordinated policy framework, through EU actions and recommendations to better steer EU support and national policies for islands. The strategy does not require Member States to submit implementation plans. However, the Commission will maintain a dialogue with the competent authorities to support reflecting the needs of islands in the implementation of relevant EU policies at national and regional levels. The strategy foresees continuation of the support to Member States and island authorities through the Technical Support Instrument, TAIEX-REGIO Peer2Peer, the European Urban Initiative, the Clean Energy for EU Islands, and regular technical dialogues to facilitate simplification and exchange of good practices and reduce administrative burden. The Commission will support Member States in tailoring and implementing reforms and investments addressing the needs of islands in the future National and Regional Partnership Plans (2). In Greece, in the programming period 2021-2027 the regional programmes (3) allocate significant resources to integrated territorial strategies in island areas, combining investments in sustainable resource management, climate change adaptation, urban mobility and social actions. The GR-eco islands initiative in particular, which is explicitly referred to in the strategy, supports the energy transition and sustainable development of small islands ensuring that island development does not turn into a tourism monoculture.

E-10-2026-002770.t: Institutional shortcomings in addressing the high prices of everyday essentials in Greece
qt: to the Commission Galato Alexandraki (ECR) Subject:

According to reports, the Greek Government is calling a meeting with big market players to bring down prices on essential items. This development raises serious questions about the effectiveness of institutional market control mechanisms, especially when consumer protection appears to depend on informal government negotiations with powerful economic operators. EU competition law, notably Articles 101 and 102 TFEU, prohibits concerted practices and the abuse of a dominant position. In addition, transparency and the possibility of effective price comparison are requirements of the consumer protection framework. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Is it monitoring whether there is sufficient competition in the Greek essential goods market or whether instead it shows signs of overconcentration and unjustified price increases?
Does it consider a policy of informal pricing agreements between the Government and big businesses to be compatible with EU law?
Does it intend to ask the Greek authorities for proof of the effectiveness of market controls and consumer protection?
at: (English version) to the Commission Galato Alexandraki (ECR) (3 July 2026) Subject: Institutional shortcomings in addressing the high prices of everyday essentials in Greece According to reports, the Greek Government is calling a meeting with big market players to bring down prices on essential items. This development raises serious questions about the effectiveness of institutional market control mechanisms, especially when consumer protection appears to depend on informal government negotiations with powerful economic operators. EU competition law, notably Articles 101 and 102 TFEU, prohibits concerted practices and the abuse of a dominant position. In addition, transparency and the possibility of effective price comparison are requirements of the consumer protection framework. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Is it monitoring whether there is sufficient competition in the Greek essential goods market or whether instead it shows signs of overconcentration and unjustified price increases?
Does it consider a policy of informal pricing agreements between the Government and big businesses to be compatible with EU law?
Does it intend to ask the Greek authorities for proof of the effectiveness of market controls and consumer protection?

(21 August 2026) The Commission and the competition authorities of the Member States apply EU competition rules in close cooperation within the European Competition Network, in compliance with the principles of subsidiarity and procedural autonomy. In principle, the Greek authorities are well placed to monitor the Greek food and groceries market whereas the Commission is competent to investigate practices in that sector which affect several Member States, as it did for instance for the cartel on food delivery services (1) and market partitioning by Mondelez in the chocolate, biscuits and coffee sectors (2). The Commission closely monitors the evolution of consumer goods prices across Member States , as well as matters that may affect consumer protection. In this context, it may, on its own initiative or acting on the basis of complaints by interested third parties or of market information, examine measures that risk undermining the functioning of the internal market or the uniform application of EU competition rules. A Member State may convene operators to discuss market developments to the extent that it does not infringe the obligation of sincere cooperation of Member States under Article 4(3) of the Treaty on European Union, in conjunction with the prohibition of anti-competitive agreements under Article 101 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union. For instance, such discussions should not lead to agreements on prices between operators. If appropriate, the Commission may confer with the Greek authorities regarding the measures they plan to adopt.

E-10-2026-002769.t: Revision of Directive 92/83/EEC to exempt traditional sugar cane spirits produced on a small scale
qt: to the Commission Sérgio Gonçalves (S&D) Subject:

Directive 92/83/EEC1 allows the application of reduced taxes or full exemptions for regional or traditional alcohol-based products. However, this derogation applies only to products derived from fruits. This excludes many traditional products obtained from other local crops. In the Autonomous Region of Madeira, the production of spirits from sugar cane is historically linked to local agricultural practices and to Madeira’s cultural heritage. Such spirits are often produced on a small scale from cane grown on small plots. Despite this, they do not benefit from conditions equivalent to those applicable to fruit spirits. 1.
Has the Portuguese Government already engaged with the Commission on this topic?
Would the Commission consider revising Directive 92/83/EEC to allow equivalent exemptions for spirits produced on a small scale from agricultural raw materials other than fruits, such as sugar cane?

Council Directive 92/83/EEC of 19 October 1992 on the harmonization of the structures of excise duties on alcohol and alcoholic beverages (OJ L 316, 31.10.1992, p. 21, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/1992/83/oj). 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (26.8.2026) Portugal can apply a reduced rate of excise duty in the autonomous region of Madeira on locally produced and consumed rum and liqueurs which may be lower than the minimum rate of excise duty set by Council Directive 92/84/EEC1, but not more than 75% lower than the standard national excise duty on alcohol. This is based on Council Decision (EU) 2020/1790 of 16 November 20202 authorising Portugal to apply a reduced rate of excise duty on certain alcoholic products produced in the autonomous regions of Madeira and Azores. The rum covered by this Council Decision is defined as ‘a spirit drink produced exclusively by the distillation of the product obtained by the alcoholic fermentation of molasses or syrup produced in the manufacture of cane sugar or of sugar-cane juice itself’3. The Council Decision is based on Article 349 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU, which establishes a special legal regime for the EU’s outermost regions, allowing specific measures to address their structural, economic and geographic challenges. Directive 92/83/EEC lays down the structures of excise duties on alcohol and alcoholic beverages, including certain specific provisions and exemptions applicable to particular categories of products. The current framework reflects long-standing policy choices and seeks to ensure the proper functioning of the Internal Market. At this stage, the Commission is not planning a revision of this Directive. Nevertheless, the Commission continues to monitor the implementation and application of the existing rules and remains attentive to developments in the sector, including any evidence provided by stakeholders and Member States regarding the functioning of the current framework.
1 Council Directive 92/84/EEC of 19 October 1992 on the approximation of the rates of excise duty on alcohol and

alcoholic beverages (OJ L 316, 31.10.1992, p. 29). 2 Council Decision (EU) 2020/1790 of 16 November 2020 authorising Portugal to apply a reduced rate of taxation to alcohol produced in the autonomous region of Madeira, OJ L 402, 1.12.2020, p. 21. 3 See Article 3(1)(a) of Council Decision (EU) 2020/1790 in conjunction with point 1(a) of Annex I to Regulation (EU) 2019/787 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 17 April 2019, OJ L 130, 17.5.2019, pp. 1–54, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2019/787/oj.

E-10-2026-002768.t: Shortcomings in Greece’s transposition of the Money Laundering Directive
qt: to the Commission Galato Alexandraki (ECR) Subject:

As part of its June 2026 infringements package, the Commission sent a letter of formal notice to Greece for failing to correctly transpose provisions of the Directive on combating money laundering, in particular as regards offences and penalties. The Directive aims to strengthen the criminal law response to financial crimes and cooperation between Member States. With this in mind, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
What specific shortcomings did it identify in Greek legislation with regard to money laundering offences and penalties?
Does it consider that these shortcomings can affect the effective investigation of cases linked to European funds, public procurement or organised financial fraud?
If Greece does not comply within the given deadline, does the Commission intend to issue a reasoned opinion straight away?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (31.8.2026) The Commission is currently assessing this matter. In order to preserve a climate of mutual trust, indispensable to build a constructive exchange with Member States concerning the issues identified in the national legislation, the details of ongoing infringement procedures are protected under the principles of confidentiality and fair cooperation and can therefore not be made public. While the Commission cannot share information on the specific infringement case against Greece, the correct transposition of the Directive on combating money laundering by criminal law1 by Member States is key to facilitating investigations and prosecutions in this area, as well as cross-border cooperation. Shortcomings in transposition by the Member States could affect the effective investigation and prosecution of money laundering, including where it involves the proceeds of fraud affecting European funds, public-procurement related offences or organised financial fraud. The Commission reiterates the importance of transposing the Directive on combating money laundering by criminal law into national legislation. If the Commission deems national measures not to be in line with the Directive, it can continue to follow the stages of infringement proceedings.
1 Directive (EU) 2018/1673 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 23 October 2018 on combating
money laundering by criminal law, PE/30/2018/REV/1, OJ L 284, 12.11.2018, pp. 22–30.

E-10-2026-002767.t: Illegal Turkish fishing in the Aegean and the need for a European protection mechanism
qt: to the Commission Galato Alexandraki (ECR) Subject:

The Parliament study titled ‘Cross-border cooperation in fisheries management: Best practices from the Western Waters’, which was conducted by the Committee on Fisheries (PECH) and published on 29 June 2026, highlights that the management of shared fish stocks requires formally established cross-border cooperation, scientific data, the involvement of fishers and the coordinated implementation of rules. Looking at the examples of the Iberian sardine and the Bay of Biscay anchovy, the study shows that cooperation between states can protect stocks and fishing communities. In the Aegean, however, repeated cases of illegal Turkish fishing, as well as complaints about the presence of the Turkish Coast Guard close to the Greek islands, show that the issue also concerns the protection of the EU’s external sea borders. In May 2026, Greece officially asked the EU to intervene in the light of instances of illegal fishing and violations of the law of the sea by Turkish fishers. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Will it set up a dedicated European mechanism for recording and monitoring illegal fishing in the Aegean?
How will it make use of the EFCA, Frontex, EMFAF and satellite surveillance to protect Greek fishers?

E-10-2026-002764.t: Mandatory ceilings for data centre water consumption and impact of AI infrastructure
qt: to the Commission Ioan-Rareş Bogdan (PPE) Subject:

Under the Energy Efficiency Directive and Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1364, data centres are subject to mandatory Water Usage Effectiveness (WUE) reporting. However, data collection does not ensure the preservation of resources. EU law fails to set mandatory maximum consumption ceilings and to prohibit the use of drinking water for cooling in waterstressed regions. Meanwhile, the expansion of AI is exponentially increasing the water footprint due to the high thermal density of new chips. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following three questions: 1.
Does it intend to introduce binding maximum water consumption limits (WUE ceilings) for data centres, going beyond the phase of simply monitoring and reporting?
Is it considering banning the use of drinking water for cooling new facilities, obliging operators in vulnerable areas to use only dry, immersion cooling or industrial waste water technologies?

How will it review the European sustainability rating scheme to introduce restrictive criteria tailored to the specific water impact of new infrastructure dedicated exclusively to artificial intelligence?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (26.8.2026) The Commission, based on the Energy Efficiency Directive1, will introduce a rating scheme for data centres2, in the form of a label showcasing the energy efficiency and sustainability performance of facilities. With the Electrification Action Plan3, the Commission announced to introduce minimum performance standards for data centres4, to ensure that new or retrofitted facilities meet sustainability criteria, including on water consumption. In this framework, it should be recalled that the Water Framework Directive5 requires Member States to protect and, where necessary, restore water bodies to reach good status, and prevent deterioration. Replying to the specific questions of the Honourable Member: 1. At this stage, the Commission cannot prejudge whether minimum performance standards for data centres, would take the form of binding maximum water-use ceilings. 2. As regards the use of drinking water, the Commission recognises that water stress varies significantly across regions. The forthcoming rating scheme (label) is intended to provide easily comparable information on freshwater consumption, while allowing competent local and regional authorities to set context-specific requirements or thresholds considering local water availability and use. 3. The Commission intends to propose an early review clause for the features of the data centre label to ensure that implementation results, and environmental, technological and market developments can be reflected, if necessary.
1 Directive (EU) 2023/1791 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 September 2023 on energy

efficiency and amending Regulation (EU) 2023/955 (recast): http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2023/1791/oj. 2 https://energy.ec.europa.eu/news/rating-scheme-data-centres-eu-commission-launches-call-feedback-2026-0327_en. 3 COM/2026/595 final: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A52026DC0595 4 https://energy.ec.europa.eu/topics/energy-efficiency/energy-efficiency-targets-directive-and-rules/energyefficiency-directive/energy-performance-data-centres_en#next-steps. 5 https://environment.ec.europa.eu/topics/water/water-framework-directive_en.

E-10-2026-002763.t: Safeguards for operational neutrality and protection of Romania’s strategic economic interests
qt: to the Commission Ioan-Rareş Bogdan (PPE) Subject:

I welcome the European Commission’s new legislative package aimed at strengthening Europol and Eurojust to fight cross-border crime. However, the principles of subsidiarity and national sovereignty must be respected when expanding Eurojust’s mandate to act on its own initiative and establishing local Europol offices. To prevent economic exploitation or asymmetric bottlenecks, can the Commission clarify the following: 1.

What explicit safeguards are in place to prevent the risk of Eurojust’s new owninitiative powers being used in cross-border commercial competition or interfering with strategic investment projects being carried out by Member States in cooperation with international partners?

How will the Commission guarantee that autonomous actions by EU agencies will not be used to freeze or prematurely delay major energy or national infrastructure projects before national courts have made a definitive ruling?

E-10-2026-002762.t: Will the Commission’s new omnibus proposals simplify rules for Romanian businesses or saddle them with hidden costs?
qt: to the Commission Ioan-Rareş Bogdan (PPE) Subject:

The Commission believes that it will substantially reduce administrative costs for businesses by means of its two new omnibus proposals of 25 June 2026, which set ambitious targets for cutting red tape by 2029. However, regulatory relief measures tend not to have a uniform impact on Member States because the latter have distinct economic characteristics. I therefore ask the Commission: 1.

What support mechanisms or transitional periods do these omnibus proposals provide for producers and retailers in Romania, where estimated savings could be offset in the short-term by the cost of complying with the new labelling schemes’ technical standards?

How will it ensure that these ‘simplified tax rules’ do not lead to the covert establishment of harmonised tax arrangements, which would harm the competitiveness of states that use tax incentives to attract investment?

What are the estimated net savings that these omnibus proposals – which are expected to cut administrative costs by EUR 18 billion across the board – will generate for companies registered in Romania?
at: (English version) to the Commission Ioan-Rareş Bogdan (PPE) (3 July 2026) Subject: Will the Commission’s new omnibus proposals simplify rules for Romanian businesses or saddle them with hidden costs? The Commission believes that it will substantially reduce administrative costs for businesses by means of its two new omnibus proposals of 25 June 2026, which set ambitious targets for cutting red tape by 2029. However, regulatory relief measures tend not to have a uniform impact on Member States because the latter have distinct economic characteristics. I therefore ask the Commission: 1.

What support mechanisms or transitional periods do these omnibus proposals provide for producers and retailers in Romania, where estimated savings could be offset in the short-term by the cost of complying with the new labelling schemes’ technical standards?

How will it ensure that these ‘simplified tax rules’ do not lead to the covert establishment of harmonised tax arrangements, which would harm the competitiveness of states that use tax incentives to attract investment?

What are the estimated net savings that these omnibus proposals — which are expected to cut administrative costs by EUR 18 billion across the board — will generate for companies registered in Romania?

(21 September 2026) Omnibus XII on energy and tyre labelling aims to simplify and clarify rules set in existing Regulations. It does not create any technical standards. Overall, we expect important benefits and cost reductions for producers and retailers, but these benefits are not expected to be substantially different in Romania from any other Member States. The Omnibus on taxation (Omnibus XI) aims to simplify the EU direct tax Directives to keep them fit for purpose, while preserving existing safeguards and the level of protection. It does not lower tax (good governance) standards, or mitigate measures to fight tax fraud, avoidance and evasion. The Commission remains fully committed to retaining these high standards and objectives. At the same time, the omnibus will help businesses operate more easily across the EU, supporting a level playing field and a well-functioning internal market, boosting investment, growth and competitiveness. The proposal is expected to significantly cut tax compliance costs for EU taxpayers, including companies registered in Romania. The accompanying Impact Assessment estimates a lower administrative burden that translates into savings of around EUR 6.6 billion, of which about EUR 2 billion in recurring, annual compliance costs on an annual basis.

E-10-2026-002761.t: Recent visit of the Vice-President / High Representative and Commissioners to Türkiye
qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Nikolas Farantouris (S&D) Subject:

On 30 June, the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy visited Ankara together with the Commissioner for Enlargement and the Commissioner for Migration and Home Affairs. The meeting was followed by a joint press release issued together with the Turkish Foreign Minister. The press release underlines the ‘strategic value’ of EU-Türkiye relations in promoting regional stability, security and economic resilience1. However, there is no mention of Türkiye persistent attempts to undermine the sovereign rights and legitimate interests of EU Member States, such as challenging the maritime zones of Greece and Cyprus, preparing the upcoming ‘Blue Homeland’ law, obstructing the European project to connect the power grids of Greece and Cyprus and excluding Cyprus from the COP31 meetings. In view of the above, can the Vice-President / High Representative answer the following: 1.

Did she, during the meeting with the Turkish leadership, raise the issues of the casus belli, the challenges to the sovereign rights of Greece and Cyprus, the Kasos incident, and Türkiye’s ongoing revisionist policy ?

How does the recognition of Türkiye as a strategic partner square with the persistent challenges to the sovereign rights of Member States and what specific conditions does the EU intend to lay down to make the further deepening of EU-Türkiye relations conditional on full respect for international law and the good neighbourliness principle2?
Can EU foreign policy be decoupled from full respect for the sovereign rights of EU Member States?

https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_26_1495 It should be noted that in a recent answer she gave, the Vice-President / High Representative underlined the unwavering commitment to defending the sovereign rights and interests of the Member States and the need for Türkiye to fully respect international law, the Law of the Sea and good neighbourly relations (https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/E-10-2026-002001-ASW_EN.html). 1 2
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (28.8.2026) The EU remains committed to defending its interests and those of its Member States, as well as to upholding regional stability. The sovereignty and sovereign rights of all EU Member States must be respected. In this context, the EU has consistently underlined that Türkiye is expected to make an unequivocal commitment to good neighbourly relations, international agreements and the peaceful settlement of disputes, in accordance with international law and the UN Charter. The EU continues to follow developments in the Aegean and the Eastern Mediterranean closely and will raise matters of concern with Türkiye through the appropriate channels. An unequivocal commitment to international law, including the Law of the Sea, international agreements and the UN Charter, remains essential, as does abstaining from unilateral actions which violate international law and the sovereign rights of Member States. These are essential requirements to ensure a stable and secure environment in the Eastern Mediterranean and the development of a cooperative and mutually beneficial relationship between the EU and Türkiye. As stated in the joint press release1 issued following the visit to Ankara on 30 June 2026, the EU and Türkiye acknowledged the strategic value of their relationship in promoting regional stability, security and economic resilience. They also reaffirmed the shared determination to take steps that would further enhance the cooperative and mutually beneficial relationship and agreed on the importance of regional stability and good neighbourly relations. At the same time, such engagement continues to be based on the relevant European Council conclusions, including the need for sustained de-escalation and a constructive approach by Türkiye.
1 https://enlargement.ec.europa.eu/news/joint-press-release-turkiyes-fm-hakan-fidan-hrvp-kaja-kallas-and-eu-
commissioners-marta-kos-and-2026-06-30_en.

E-10-2026-002760.t: Red tape and late transposition of Directive (EU) 2023/970
qt: to the Commission Christine Anderson (ESN) Subject:
Red tape and late transposition of Directive (EU) 2023/970

According to a reply from the German Federal Government to a parliamentary question, preparations for the transposition of Directive (EU) 2023/970 are still ongoing and substantial transposition issues remain unresolved. At the same time, the Federal Government explicitly emphasises the need for ‘implementation with minimal red tape’, referring to the considerable administrative burden associated with the Directive.1 1.
How many Member States have not yet fully transposed Directive (EU) 2023/970 into national law?

On what basis does the Commission consider the administrative burden associated with the Directive to be proportionate, in particular for small and medium-sized enterprises, also in the light of the concerns expressed by the German Federal Government regarding implementation with minimal red tape?

Has the Commission carried out, or does it intend to carry out, an updated impact assessment on administrative and compliance costs, in particular in view of the fact that the content of the final adopted text of the Directive can deviate significantly from the Commission’s original proposal in the course of the legislative process?

As the Commission noted in its reply to Written Question E-001576/2026, the Pay Transparency Directive (2) provides proportionate pay transparency obligations and delayed reporting according to the size of companies (3). It also provides flexibility concerning methodologies to guide the assessment of work of equal value by employers (4) and allows the use of administrative data to assist companies in fulfilling their pay reporting obligations (5). The Commission does not plan to carry out an updated impact assessment. The Commission examines implementation costs through implementation reviews and evaluations after adoption. However, it will submit a report to the European Parliament and to the Council by 7 June 2033 (6) and will, if necessary, propose any legislative amendments based on that report.

E-10-2026-002759.t: Member States’ freedom to exceed minimum standards for periodic roadworthiness testing of motor vehicles
qt: to the Commission Kris Van Dijck (ECR) Subject:

Article 1 of Directive 2014/45/EU on periodic roadworthiness tests for motor vehicles states that this Directive establishes minimum requirements. Under the Directive, Member States may require vehicles to undergo additional tests if, for example, ownership is transferred, a high mileage is reached or a vehicle could present an increased safety risk (Article 5(4) and Article 8(4)). The revision of the roadworthiness package is currently the subject of negotiations. Within this context, the Commission and Parliament are focusing on further updating and reinforcing the testing requirements, including for electric vehicles and advanced driver assistance systems. Against this background, questions are being raised about the discretion that Member States have to adopt or retain additional national testing measures. 1.

Can the Commission confirm that Directive 2014/45/EU does not require Member States to water down existing, stricter national testing measures, but actually gives them the freedom to retain or introduce additional safety tests, provided that they are compatible with Union law?

Can the Commission clarify whether a future revision of the roadworthiness package could contain new obligations requiring additional transposition or the amendment of national regulations by Member States?
at: (English version) to the Commission Kris Van Dijck (ECR) (2 July 2026) Subject: Member States’ freedom to exceed minimum standards for periodic roadworthiness testing of motor vehicles Article 1 of Directive 2014/45/EU on periodic roadworthiness tests for motor vehicles states that this directive establishes minimum requirements. Under the directive, Member States may require vehicles to undergo additional tests if, for example, ownership is transferred, a high mileage is reached or a vehicle could present an increased safety risk (Article 5(4) and Article 8(4)). The revision of the roadworthiness package is currently the subject of negotiations. Within this context, the Commission and Parliament are focusing on further updating and reinforcing the testing requirements, including for electric vehicles and advanced driver assistance systems. Against this background, questions are being raised about the discretion that Member States have to adopt or retain additional national testing measures. 1. Can the Commission confirm that directive 2014/45/EU does not require Member States to water down existing, stricter national testing measures, but actually gives them the freedom to retain or introduce additional safety tests, provided that they are compatible with Union law? 2. Can the Commission clarify whether a future revision of the roadworthiness package could contain new obligations requiring additional transposition or the amendment of national regulations by Member States? (22 September 2026) As noted by the Honourable Member, Article 1 of Directive 2014/45/EU states that it “establishes minimum requirements for a regime of periodic roadworthiness tests of vehicles used on public roads”. The 4th recital further explains that Member States should be allowed to set higher standards, provided of course that such national measures are indeed compatible with Union law, including the Treaties. It is premature at this time to speculate on the scope of any possible future Commission proposals to further amend the provisions of the Roadworthiness Package. However, the Commission would note that a directive, by its very nature, establishes rules which Member States are legally obliged to transpose into their national law.

E-10-2026-002758.t: Stepping up protection of the EU’s external borders along the Balkan route
qt: to the Commission Anna Maria Cisint (PfE) Subject:

In recent months, urban decay and problems connected with migratory movements along the Balkan route have continued to plague the border towns and cities of Friuli Venezia Giulia, particularly Gorizia and Trieste. Despite the cooperation instruments that the EU has already put in place – including Frontex operational support and the cooperation agreements signed with the Western Balkan countries – the local authorities are reporting a rise in makeshift settlements in public spaces, with growing repercussions on safety and the urban landscape. In light of these persistent problems: 1.

Given that the measures currently in place along the Balkan route seem to fall short of offering effective protection of the EU’s external borders, will the Commission issue calls to further step up Frontex’s operational deployment and cooperation with partner countries, including Bosnia and Herzegovina?

Will it adopt further measures – and, if so, which ones – to reduce irregular crossings and support the frontline Member States, so that situations such as those facing Gorizia and Trieste can be addressed in an effective and lasting manner?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (11.9.2026) Irregular border crossings along the Western Balkan route have decreased significantly in recent years, including by 41% in 2025 compared to 2024. This reflects stronger border management, close operational cooperation with Western Balkan partners, and EU measures under the Action Plan on the Western Balkans1. The Commission takes note of the concerns raised regarding Gorizia and Trieste. Under Regulation (EU) 2019/18962, the European Border and Coast Guard Agency (Frontex) already supports Member States and Western Balkan partners through joint operations and standing corps deployments based on existing status agreements, including with Bosnia and Herzegovina. Work is ongoing to revise Frontex mandate, with the aim of strengthening cooperation with third countries, while fully respecting Member States’ primary responsibility for border control. Efforts to reduce irregular crossings rely on range of tools: including the Global Alliance to Counter Migrant Smuggling, the European Union Agency for Law Enforcement Cooperation (Europol)’s European Centre Against Migrant Smuggling3, the European Multidisciplinary Platform Against Criminal Threats (EMPACT)4, and Frontex deployments. Visa policy alignment and effective border management, supported by the Instrument for Pre-accession Assistance III and other EU instruments, remain key elements of both the Western Balkans Action Plan and to accession-related conditionality. Support to frontline Member States, including Italy, is provided through Frontex operations, European Union Agency for Asylum roadmaps, and targeted funding for border management and migration systems. These measures aim to help national and local authorities address migratory pressure while upholding fundamental rights and complying with EU obligations.

E-10-2026-002757.t: Review report on Regulation (EU) 2024/1747 on the electricity market
qt: to the Commission Nicolás González Casares (S&D) Subject:
Review report on Regulation (EU) 2024/1747 on the electricity market

Regulation (EU) 2024/1747 as regards improving the Union’s electricity market design set 30 June 2026 as the deadline for the Commission to review that design, assessing, among other matters, the functioning of short-term electricity markets and their potential inefficiencies, including crisis and emergency situations, the EU legal and funding framework for distribution networks, and the potential for EU-wide power purchase agreement (PPA) market platforms. That deadline has now passed, but the Commission has yet to send the report to Parliament and the Council. Taking into account the urgent need to harness the full potential of the electricity market to make electricity more affordable for European consumers and increase resilience in crisis situations: 1.
When does the Commission intend to publish the review report and, if necessary, the corresponding legislative proposal?

Will the Commission ensure that the review fully addresses the effectiveness of the current market structure, possible remedies in crisis situations and the adequacy of the existing framework for distribution networks and PPAs, as required by the Regulation?
at: EN E- 002757/2026 on behalf of the European Commission (27.8.2026) The Commission attaches high political importance to the proper functioning of the EU’s electricity market. In this context, the implementation of the electricity market design reform adopted in 2024 is a key priority. In addition, the Commission is currently finalising the report reviewing the functioning of short-term electricity markets, the legal and funding framework for distribution networks, and the potential for EU-wide power purchase agreement market platforms. E-10-2026-002756.t: Combating the production and online dissemination of animal torture videos
qt: to the Commission Sebastian Everding (The Left), Anja Hazekamp (The Left) Subject:

Investigations by international media and animal welfare organisations have documented networks that are producing and distributing videos that depict the torture and brutal killing of cats and other animals, with many reports identifying operators based in China.12 These videos continue to circulate on online platforms accessible within the EU, thereby exposing users, including minors, to content depicting real acts of extreme violence. Their continued circulation raises concerns regarding animal welfare, the protection of minors and the enforcement of the Digital Services Act (DSA). 1.
What steps is the Commission taking to ensure that online platforms effectively detect and remove content depicting animal cruelty, in line with their obligations under the DSA?

Will the Commission, in its dialogue with the Chinese authorities and other thirdcountry authorities, encourage the adoption and effective enforcement of comprehensive national animal welfare legislation, including criminal sanctions against animal abusers?
https://edition.cnn.com/2025/05/30/asia/china-cat-deleters-torture-intl-hnk-dst. https://felineguardians.org/.
at: (English version) to the Commission Sebastian Everding (The Left), Anja Hazekamp (The Left) (2 July 2026) Subject: Combating the production and online dissemination of animal torture videos Investigations by international media and animal welfare organisations have documented networks that are producing and distributing videos that depict the torture and brutal killing of cats and other animals, with many reports identifying operators based in China. (1) (2) These videos continue to circulate on online platforms accessible within the EU, thereby exposing users, including minors, to content depicting real acts of extreme violence. Their continued circulation raises concerns regarding animal welfare, the protection of minors and the enforcement of the Digital Services Act (DSA). 1. What steps is the Commission taking to ensure that online platforms effectively detect and remove content depicting animal cruelty, in line with their obligations under the DSA? 2. Will the Commission, in its dialogue with the Chinese authorities and other third-country authorities, encourage the adoption and effective enforcement of comprehensive national animal welfare legislation, including criminal sanctions against animal abusers? (7 September 2026) The Commission understands the concerns raised by the Honourable Members and reiterates the EU’s firm commitment to ensuring high animal welfare standards across the EU. The Digital Services Act (DSA) (1) obliges online platforms to put in place ‘notice and action’ mechanisms for users to notify suspected illegal content in an easy and accessible way. Online platforms are required to process such notices in a timely and diligent manner. Should a platform not expeditiously remove content it knows to be illegal, it may be held liable for it. Whether specific content is considered illegal content must be assessed on a case-by-case basis pursuant to applicable European and national law. The DSA does not establish a general monitoring obligation, but rather requires platforms to have appropriate mechanisms and, where appropriate, to adopt proportionate mitigation measures addressing identified risks. The Commission works closely with the National Digital Services Coordinators and the European Board for Digital Services to support the consistent enforcement of these rules. In addition, under the DSA, the providers of very large online platforms are required to identify, assess and mitigate the systemic risks stemming from the design and functioning of their services, including risks relating to the dissemination of illegal content. Furthermore, the Audiovisual Media Services Directive (2) requires video-sharing platform providers to take appropriate measures to protect in particular minors from programmes and user-generated videos that may impair their physical, mental or moral development. The most harmful content, such as gratuitous violence, shall be subject to the strictest measures.

E-10-2026-002755.t: Influence of Russian fur revenue on European policymaking
qt: to the Commission Anja Hazekamp (The Left) Subject:

Research by Politico reveals that the International Fur Federation has funded its European policy work through a Liechtenstein trust fund that also received money from Russian auctions1. The 2023 financial statements of the lobbying organisation show that EUR 223 870 came from the Russian fur auction house Sojuzpushnina, based in St. Petersburg, of which EUR 216 000 was allegedly used to pay the lobbyist of the International Fur Federation in Brussels. In 2025, the European Commissioner for Animal Welfare held another lobbying meeting with the International Fur Federation and Fur Europe, the lobbying organisation into which the Federation has since merged, to discuss the European Citizens’ Initiative ‘Fur Free Europe’2. 1.

Can the Commission confirm that the revenues received by the International Fur Federation from the Russian fur auction house are covered by EU sanctions and are therefore in violation of EU sanctions against Russia?
Does the Commission agree that lobbying organisations receiving Russian revenues should not be able to influence EU policies?

When will the Commission introduce a European ban on keeping and killing animals for fur production and on importing fur, as requested by more than 1.5 million EU citizens in the European Citizens’ Initiative ‘Fur Free Europe’3?

Council Regulation (EU) No 833/2014 of 31 July 2014 concerning restrictive measures in view of Russia's actions destabilising the situation in Ukraine (1), Article 5n, prohibits EU-based firms from providing a range of services. This includes public relations services (lobbying) for the Government of Russia or any legal person, entity or body established in Russia. This may affect registrants of the Transparency Register. E-10-2026-002754.t: Agricultural plastics and the forthcoming Circular Economy Act
qt: to the Commission Benoit Cassart (Renew) Subject:

The Commission is expected to present its Circular Economy Act in the third quarter of 2026. Agricultural plastics are vital production tools that contribute to food production, water efficiency and climate resilience. Several Member States have already set up successful collection and recycling schemes, demonstrating that targeted collection and recycling schemes for agricultural plastics strengthen the circular economy while reducing the risks of plastic dispersal in agricultural soils. 1.

Can the Commission explain why agricultural plastics no longer seem to be covered by the future Circular Economy Act, despite the sector having shown that it is committed to the circular economy and several Member States having already set up national collection and recycling schemes?

If agricultural plastics are not actually included in the initial proposal for the Circular Economy Act, how will the Commission support the rapid development of circular systems to manage this vital flow of agricultural products?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.8.2026) Based on a thorough impact assessment, the Circular Economy Act1 will set out solutions to address fragmentation of the Single Market, market failures and misaligned economic and technological incentives hindering the take-up of circular practices, and insufficient separate collection and recycling of different waste streams. The aim is to strengthen the business case for circular business models, and boost synergies with the existing EU rules to make sure the EU has a comprehensive framework for circularity that promotes prevention, reuse and recycling of materials. This should help strengthen Europe's resilience, competitiveness and strategic autonomy. The work on the Circular Economy Act proposal is ongoing, and the Commission cannot prejudge the final content of the proposal at the current juncture. However, the Circular Economy Act should make a business case for circularity across various sectors. In parallel, the Commission will continue to build on the existing EU framework supporting circularity, promoting separate collection, recycling and markets for secondary raw materials. Where farmers use plastic as packaging as defined under the Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation2, this packaging must comply with the requirements therein, including, if applicable, provisions on recyclability and for extended producer responsibility to ensure that it is properly collected and recycled.
1 https://environment.ec.europa.eu/strategy/circular-economy_en. 2 Regulation (EU) 2025/40 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 19 December 2024 on packaging
and packaging waste, amending Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 and Directive (EU) 2019/904, and repealing Directive 94/62/EC, OJ L, 2025/40, 22.1.2025.

E-10-2026-002753.t: Concerns regarding the application of Regulation (EU) 2020/1054 to the non-commercial transport of rescued animals
qt: to the Commission Sebastian Everding (The Left) Subject:
Concerns regarding the application of Regulation (EU) 2020/1054 to the noncommercial transport of rescued animals

Under Regulation (EU) 2020/1054, which amends Regulation (EC) No 561/2006 and Regulation (EU) No 165/2014, as from 1 July 2026, light commercial vehicles used for international transport, i.e. those weighing between 2.5 and 3.5 tonnes, will be obliged to install intelligent tachographs and comply with driving and rest times. This weight class involves vehicles used by animal welfare organisations for the transport of adopted pets. While the rules are primarily intended for the international transport of commercial goods, animal welfare organisations warn that applying them to the noncommercial transport of rescued cats and dogs for cross-border adoptions would impose disproportionate costs and longer journey times, undermining animal welfare during transport and reducing adoption opportunities. 1.
Is the Commission aware of the problems that result from the application of Regulation (EC) No 561/2026 to non-profit organisations transporting rescued animals for adoption between Member States?

Will the Commission consider introducing a specific exemption or an adapted legal framework for the non-commercial transport of rescued companion animals, taking into account the objectives of animal welfare during transport, including under Regulation (EC) No 1/2005?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (2.9.2026) 1. The Commission has been informed by non-profit organisations of difficulties arising from the application of Regulation (EC) No 561/20061 to the transport of rescued animals for adoption between Member States. 2. At this stage, the Commission is not considering the introduction of any specific exemption or an adapted legal framework for the transport of rescued companion animals. The extension of the tachograph and driving and rest time rules to light commercial vehicles was introduced by Regulation (EU) 2020/10542 with the aim of ensuring a high level of protection for professional drivers, enhancing road safety by reducing fatigue-related risks, and promoting fair competition across the EU road transport sector. The Commission recognises that the new rules may give rise to important operational and financial challenges for those concerned in ensuring compliance with all applicable legal obligations. Nevertheless, the protection of drivers’ working conditions and well-being, as well as road safety, cannot be compromised. In respect of Regulation (EC) 1/20053, on 7 December 2023 the Commission adopted a proposal to revise EU legislation on welfare of animals during transport4. Work is currently ongoing in the European Parliament and in the Council ahead of the interinstitutional negotiations. The Commission proposal includes several improvements of provisions on protection of dogs and cats in transport in the context of an economic activity. In addition, one of the main goals of the revision is to reduce administrative burden and to facilitate the enforcement of the requirements through more modern tools.
