E-10-2026-002751.t: The compatibility with EU law of approaches that do not open hydropower concessions in Italy’s autonomous regions up to the free market
qt: to the Commission Gaetano Pedulla' (The Left) Subject:

The rigid legal framework governing Italy’s major hydroelectric diversions is ill-suited to the country’s regional diversity, hydrogeological features and socio-historic background. Because a one-size-fits-all approach at national level is likely to overlook the manifold vulnerabilities of Italy’s mountainous areas, it is vital to equip the country’s autonomous regions with a specific legal framework – an approach that is in keeping with these entities’ autonomous statutes and the principles of subsidiarity and proximity. Water management in these regions must prioritise territorial security, infrastructure resilience and the needs of local communities – all objectives which the free market and competing private actors cannot achieve in full. In the light of the above: 1.

What is the Commission’s view of the compatibility with EU law of alternative management models – examples of which include ‘in-house’ production approaches that are geared towards public safety and multi-purpose water use, as well as publiccollective partnership schemes which, in line with the Green Deal, promote the involvement of energy communities and cooperatives in the governance of energy sales and distribution – if we understand these models to be instruments that are indispensable to ensuring the implementation of social cohesion, environmental protection and sustainable water management objectives?
What guarantees do models like the above need to put in place in order to ensure compliance with the competition, transparency and water resource protection requirements laid down by EU law?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (14.8.2026) 1. The Commission duly recognises and respects the autonomy of the Member States and their public authorities in the organisation and provision of public services, including through their own resources. Under EU law, Member States and competent public authorities remain free to decide how public services are organised and delivered, including whether to provide them directly, through in-house arrangements, through public-public, public-collective or public-private partnerships, or through other forms of organisation, provided that the applicable EU rules are respected, including the rules on the internal market, public procurement, including concessions, and competition, where applicable. 2. Any assessment of the above-mentioned management models would depend on the specific circumstances of the case and would need to be carried out in accordance with the applicable legal framework. Member States and competent national authorities are under a duty to ensure that specific projects or governance models are designed and implemented in compliance with EU law.

E-10-2026-002750.t: Compatibility of regional legislation in Trentino-Alto Adige/Südtirol with Directive 2003/4/EC on access to environmental information
qt: to the Commission Gaetano Pedulla' (The Left) Subject:

Question No 5/04076 of 10 June 20251 to the Italian Chamber of Deputies and question No 218/XVII of 8 June 20262 to the Regional Council of Trentino Alto Adige/Südtirol highlighted possible issues with the application of Regional Law No 10/2014, which eases the requirements on the region’s municipalities to proactively publish environmental information. In the context of the PFAS contamination in the municipality of Storo, brought to light by the Trentino-based association Più Democrazia3, the ombudsperson of the autonomous province of Trento has raised concerns regarding the transparency of environmental information and is calling for the regional legal framework to be aligned with requirements under national and EU law. In light of Directive 2003/4/EC and European environmental transparency principles, does the Commission believe it would be a good idea to ask for clarification from the relevant regional and Italian authorities and to check whether the rules in force are compatible with EU law?

at: (English version) to the Commission Gaetano Pedulla' (The Left) (2 July 2026) Subject: Compatibility of regional legislation in Trentino-Alto Adige/Südtirol with Directive 2003/4/EC on access to environmental information Question No 5/04076 of 10 June 2025 (1) to the Italian Chamber of Deputies and question No 218/XVII of 8 June 2026 (2) to the Regional Council of Trentino Alto Adige/Südtirol highlighted possible issues with the application of Regional Law No 10/2014, which eases the requirements on the region’s municipalities to proactively publish environmental information. In the context of the PFAS contamination in the municipality of Storo, brought to light by the Trentino-based association Più Democrazia (3), the ombudsperson of the autonomous province of Trento has raised concerns regarding the transparency of environmental information and is calling for the regional legal framework to be aligned with requirements under national and EU law. Although institutional consultations with the National Anticorruption Authority (ANAC) have been underway for years, a roadmap for aligning the regional legislation has yet to be drawn up. In light of Directive 2003/4/EC and European environmental transparency principles, does the Commission believe it would be a good idea to ask for clarification from the relevant regional and Italian authorities and to check whether the rules in force are compatible with EU law? (26 August 2026) Access to environmental information is an important element of the environmental rule of law and the Aarhus Convention (1). The EU and Italy are both parties to the Convention. According to Article 7(1) of Directive 2003/4/EC (2) on public access to environmental information, ‘Member States shall take the necessary measures to ensure that public authorities organise the environmental information which is relevant to their functions and which is held by or for them, with a view to its active and systematic dissemination to the public, in particular by means of computer telecommunication and/or electronic technology, where available’. However, in accordance with Article 7(5) of the directive, certain exceptions apply. Therefore, national authorities can reject a request for environmental information provided that the exceptions provided for in Article 4 of the directive apply. Addressing non-conformity of national or regional legislation with EU law is an enforcement priority for the Commission (3). The Commission will assess whether the relevant legislation of Trentino-Alto Adige/Südtirol complies with EU law and, if necessary, raise the matter with the Italian authorities.

E-10-2026-002748.t: Announcement of restructuring at Volkswagen Group due to rising costs of e-mobility and competition from China
qt: to the Commission Kosma Złotowski (ECR) Subject:
Announcement of restructuring at Volkswagen Group due to rising costs of emobility and competition from China

According to media reports, the Volkswagen Group is preparing a restructuring process and considering making up to a hundred thousand workers redundant, including at four sites in Germany: Hanover, Zwickau, Emden and Neckarsulm. The need to cut staff had already been communicated, but on a scale close to half that. The Volkswagen Group is saying the scale of these planned job cuts is necessary because of the problems facing the European car industry, including the rising costs of the transition to electromobility, competition from Chinese manufacturers and the overall slowdown in the market. However, the crisis in the automotive sector does not affect the Volkswagen Group alone – both electromobility and the increasing pressure of competition from China pose challenges, and in many cases even a threat, to most car manufacturers. In light of the above: 1.

How does the Commission assess the impact of EU climate policy and electromobility regulations, in particular the ban on the sale of combustion-engine cars from 2035, on the competitiveness of the European automotive industry?

Is the Commission considering taking action, including possibly proposing changes to the pace or method of implementing climate targets, which could reduce the risk of further job losses in the European automotive sector?
What instruments does the Commission plan to implement to strengthen the competitiveness of the European automotive industry in the face of increasing pressure from Chinese manufacturers?

(15 September 2026) The competitiveness of the European automotive industry is currently being challenged by a combination of factors, including low sales volumes on the EU market, high energy prices, supply chain vulnerabilities, and increased competition from China. These structural challenges affect all vehicle technologies (including the traditional internal combustion engine). In this context, it remains crucial to support the European automotive industry by setting a clear long-term signal on the scale of the technological transformation needed, ensuring 2050 climate neutrality and strategic independence, as well as innovation and competitiveness. The proposed revision of the CO2 emission standards for cars and vans (1) aims to enhance technology neutrality and to provide more flexibility to vehicle manufacturers, while providing predictability for the industry and maintaining a strong market signal towards zero-emission vehicles. The proposal is currently being discussed at the European Parliament and the Council. Since the beginning of this mandate, the Commission has been working to build a proactive approach to keep automotive manufacturing in the EU competitive — through the Strategic Dialogue launched by the President of the Commissio n (2), the Industrial Action Plan for the European automotive sector (3), the Automotive Package from December 2025 (4), and the proposal for an Industrial Accelerator Act (5), including EU content requirements for vehicles and their components in public procurement and public financial support.

E-10-2026-002747.t: Sale of assets confiscated from opponents by the Ortega and Murillo regime in Nicaragua
qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Leire Pajín (S&D), Hana Jalloul Muro (S&D), Nacho Sánchez Amor (S&D), Alicia Homs Ginel (S&D), José Cepeda (S&D), Juan Fernando López Aguilar (S&D), Rosa Serrano Sierra (S&D) Subject:

Since 2018, and particularly since 2023, the Ortega and Murillo regime has been pursuing a systematic policy of confiscating assets from opponents, journalists, human rights defenders, civil society organisations and persons stripped of their nationality and forced into exile. The United Nations Group of Human Rights Experts on Nicaragua (GHREN) has confirmed that these confiscations form part of a deliberate strategy of transnational repression. According to press investigations, the confiscated goods are currently being sold, let or transferred to private individuals, regime sympathisers and public institutions, thereby compounding their plundering and use for the purposes of personal and political enrichment. This is in breach of the right to property and effective redress, whilst also creating legal uncertainty for third-party purchasers. Given this situation: 1.

What measures does the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union propose to put an end to transnational repression and confiscations, and to return this property to its rightful owners?
Does the VP/HR intend to propose extending the Union’s sanctions to encompass people who order, carry out or personally benefit from these confiscations?
Does the Commission plan to issue guidance to European companies and investors on the legal risks of acquiring or exploiting assets arbitrarily confiscated in Nicaragua?
at: (English version) to the Vice-President of the Commission/High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Leire Pajín (S&D), Hana Jalloul Muro (S&D), Nacho Sánchez Amor (S&D), Alicia Homs Ginel (S&D), José Cepeda (S&D), Juan Fernando López Aguilar (S&D), Rosa Serrano Sierra (S&D) (2 July 2026) Subject: Sale of assets confiscated from opponents by the Ortega and Murillo regime in Nicaragua Since 2018, and particularly since 2023, the Ortega and Murillo regime has been pursuing a systematic policy of confiscating assets from opponents, journalists, human rights defenders, civil society organisations and persons stripped of their nationality and forced into exile. The United Nations Group of Human Rights Experts on Nicaragua (GHREN) has confirmed that these confiscations form part of a deliberate strategy of transnational repression. This is in breach of the right to property and effective redress, whilst also creating legal uncertainty for third-party purchasers. Given this situation: 1.

What measures does the Vice-President of the Commission/High Representative of the Union propose to put an end to transnational repression and confiscations, and to return this property to its rightful owners?
Does the VP/HR intend to propose extending the Union’s sanctions to encompass people who order, carry out or personally benefit from these confiscations?
Does the Commission plan to issue guidance to European companies and investors on the legal risks of acquiring or exploiting assets arbitrarily confiscated in Nicaragua?

(7 August 2026) The EU remains very concerned about the situation of political rights and fundamental freedoms in Nicaragua and has publicly condemned the practices of the Nicaraguan authorities in relation to deportations, stripping of nationality, and the confiscation of properties and assets, as well as the pressures exerted on civil society and the repression of dissenting voices and political opposition, including beyond Nicaragua’s national borders. The EU continues to strongly promote democratic values and fundamental rights in Nicaragua. On every pertinent occasion, the High Representative/Vice-President (HR/VP) reiterates deep concern to the Nicaraguan authorities, including on potential consequences for investments. Furthermore, the HR/VP keeps calling for inclusive and serious intra-Nicaraguan dialogue towards a democratic and peaceful solution to the current political stalemate. In parallel, the EU imposes restrictive measures (‘sanctions’) in view of the situation in Nicaragua, with 21 individuals and 3 entities current subject to the asset freeze measures and the prohibition to make funds or economic resources available to them. In addition, the listed individuals are subject to a travel ban into the EU. The listings include Ortega family members (including Co-President Murillo) as well as members of the National Police. The measures are reviewed at regular intervals, and at least every 12 months. The last review of the sanctions adopted in view of the situation in Nicaragua was concluded in September 2025, when they were extended until 15 October 2026. The implementation and enforcement of sanctions are the primary responsibility of Member States. Furthermore, any decision on sanctions, including on potential changes, remains with the Council and requires the unanimity of the 27 Member States.

E-10-2026-002746.t: EU anti-corruption strategy and the fight against corruption in EU institutions
qt: to the Commission Mariusz Kamiński (ECR) Subject:

While the anti-corruption directive provides a definition of a ‘Union official’, in practice, it does not address the problem of corruption within the EU institutions themselves, as if this problem did not exist. The reality is quite the reverse: European public opinion is constantly being shaken by successive corruption scandals involving leading EU politicians and officials. The Qatargate scandal remains unresolved, with further details still emerging. In recent days, the media have reported that Belgian investigators intend to request the arrest of former Commissioner Dimitris Avramopoulos. There is also the case of former Commissioner for Justice Didier Reynders, accused of money laundering during his time at the Commission. This is compounded by allegations against former High Representative Federica Mogherini and investigations related to the Huawei scandal. EU citizens have had enough of this farce and are expecting strong anti-corruption measures. Regular surveys on the perception of corruption in the EU institutions, which need new, viable and effective anti-corruption mechanisms, should return. The strategy should include an obligation to submit, under penalty of criminal liability, public and verifiable asset declarations. Senior officials and commissioners should disclose their assets and the sources of these. The current discretionary declarations of conflicts of interest are clearly insufficient. Illegal lobbying should also be drastically reduced and revolving doors, which undermine citizens’ trust in the European institutions, should be effectively eliminated. Will the Commission’s anti-corruption strategy include specific actions on corruption in the EU institutions, including measures to address the problems I have identified here?

(3 September 2026) Preventing and combating corruption remains a key political priority of the Commission. The entry into force of Directive (EU) 2026/1021 (1) marks a significant milestone in strengthening the EU’s legal framework against corruption. National criminal law also applies to EU staff and members of EU institutions. The Staff Regulations and its implementing rules contain the obligations incumbent on EU officials, including regarding situations of conflict of interest and the engagement in another occupation during and after leaving the service. With respect to lobbying, the Commission applies strict transparency rules. As regards Commissioners, the EU Treaties state that they must refrain from any action incompatible with their duties. They are subject to strict rules governing conflicts of interest and must declare any interests or assets which might create a conflict of interest in the performance of their duties. The EU Anti-Corruption Strategy, to be adopted by the end of 2026, will build upon the directive (EU) 2026/1021 and support its effective implementation. It will aim to further strengthen integrity, transparency and accountability at EU and national level. The overall objective of the strategy will be to foster a culture of integrity, raise public awareness while strengthening the role of civil society. The Commission has consulted key stakeholders, including the European Parliament, in the preparation of the strategy.

E-10-2026-002744.t: EU financing instruments for the deployment of fusion energy infrastructure
qt: to the Commission Matej Tonin (PPE), Bart Groothuis (Renew), Vladimir Prebilič (Verts/ALE), Elena Donazzan (ECR), Ondřej Krutílek (ECR), Kris Van Dijck (ECR), Inese Vaidere (PPE), Christophe Grudler (Renew), Nicola Procaccini (ECR), Andrea Wechsler (PPE), Angelika Niebler (PPE), Pascal Arimont (PPE), Zala Černilec Tomašič (PPE), FrançoisXavier Bellamy (PPE) Subject:

Rising pressure on Europe’s energy security, competitiveness and resilience underscores the strategic importance of fusion as a clean, reliable and scalable energy. European companies are progressing toward commercialisation, with plans for pilots, demonstration facilities, and first-of-a-kind plants in the 2030s. However, these projects require substantial upfront investment and effective risk sharing. While the EU’s Clean Energy Investment Strategy highlights the need to mobilise finance and de-risk innovative projects, concrete instruments remain unclear. Existing funding is not tailored to supporting large-scale fusion infrastructures. Moreover, the EU still lacks a dedicated Fusion Strategy. In this context, and in view of the upcoming Fusion Strategy: 1.

How would the Commission ensure that EU-level funding instruments are available to support the construction of fusion demonstration facilities and first-of-a-kind power plants in Europe, including through instruments such as the Innovation Fund or other mechanisms for large-scale clean energy projects?

Does the Commission plan to establish dedicated EU-level financing or risk-sharing mechanisms, such as milestone-based funding schemes, or contracts for difference to mobilise both public and private capital for fusion deployment?
What measures would the Commission take to ensure that the EU remains globally competitive in financing and deploying fusion as a strategic energy technology?

(14 September 2026) The upcoming EU Fusion Strategy will aim to set out a clear vision and a coordinated framework and concrete actions to enable the industrial deployment of fusion power plants in Europe, including through enhanced coordination of relevant EU funding instruments (1). The Commission has allocated EUR 242 million for indirect actions on fusion Research and Development (R&D) under the Euratom Research and Training Programme for 2026-2027 (2). In March 2026, fusion was included in the scope of an InvestEU top-up of EUR 200 million until 2028, currently being considered and implemented in cooperation with the European Investment Bank (EIB) (3). In the context of the next Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF), it has proposed a new Euratom Research and Training Programme with an EUR 6.68 billion budget for 2028-2032 (4), including the EU's contribution to ITER. The Commission is also exploring other financial and de-risking mechanisms to support EU fusion startups and companies (5) to facilitate the development of pilot and commercial fusion power plants in Europe as part of the upcoming EU Fusion Strategy. Once adopted, the Commission counts on a strong commitment and engagement of all actors, including Member States, industry, EU startups, the fusion supply chain, research organisations and financing institutions to implement the EU Fusion Strategy and continue its support for the timely construction and operation of ITER and for closing the research and technological gaps towards commercial power plants. Upon adoption of the strategy, the Commission stands ready to engage with the European Parliament on its implementation.

E-10-2026-002743.t: Clarification regarding the legality and proportionality of the SUPD Guidelines
qt: to the Commission Beatrice Timgren (ECR) Subject:

Wet wipes are an essential product for millions of consumers. They provide hygiene solutions for families, infants, elderly people and persons with disabilities. This sector plays an important role in the European economy, supporting manufacturing, innovation and thousands of jobs. The guidelines on the costs of cleaning up litter under the Single-Use Plastics Directive (SUPD) suggest that the scope of litter clean-up costs may include the cleaning of waste water infrastructure. The guidelines, which should merely interpret legislation and not extend its scope, go beyond the SUPD, which never refers to such costs. This document creates uncertainty for national authorities and economic operators, while imposing costs on industries and families that were never subject to an impact assessment. Can the Commission clarify the following: 1.
Did the Commission conduct an impact assessment of the impact of the guidelines on industry and on the affordability of essential hygiene products, particularly for families with young children?
Did the Commission assess the proportionality of the measure, considering that infrastructure maintenance costs exist regardless of wet wipes?
How do these guidelines align with the current Commission’s simplification agenda?

Did the Commission assess the proportionality of the measure, considering that infrastructure maintenance costs exist regardless of wet wipes?
How do these guidelines align with the current Commission’s simplification agenda?

(25 August 2026) The Single-Use Plastics Directive (SUPD) (1) aims to prevent and reduce the impact of certain single-use plastic products on the environment and human health. Article 8 requires Member States to establish extended producer responsibility (EPR) schemes in line with the polluter-pays principle. For wet wipes, these cover litter clean-up costs. The Guidelines (2) do not amend the SUPD but clarify its application. As such, no impact assessment additional to that of the SUPD (3) is required. Member States were consulted. The Guidelines consider ‘littering’ to include indirect disposal into air, land or water where there is a risk of pollution. Sewer systems are not closed systems: overflows and leakages can release wet wipes into rivers and seas. Flushing them is an indirect pathway of littering, and their removal constitutes litter clean-up. As regards proportionality, producers have to cover only costs attributable to littered wet wipes, not ordinary maintenance. National EPR schemes assess and allocate these costs using representative data. Fewer flushed or littered wipes should therefore reduce costs covered by EPR-fees. Waste operators (4) report that the wipes require staff time and resources beyond normal maintenance. Without EPR, these additional costs would ultimately be borne by the public. Their coverage by producers reflects the polluter pays principle. |(⸱1|)∙ |(⸱2|)∙ |(⸱3|)∙ |(⸱4|)∙

Directive (EU) 2019/904 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 5 June 2019 on the reduction of the impact of certain plastic products on the environment, OJ L 155, 12.6.2019. E-10-2026-002742.t: Proportionality and effectiveness of periodic CPC training for professional drivers
qt: to the Commission Beatrice Timgren (ECR) Subject:

Article 3(1)(b) of Directive (EU) 2022/2561, read together with Article 8 and Annex I, Section 4, requires periodic certificate of professional competence (CPC) training for drivers within its scope, consisting of 35 hours every five years1. In Sweden, Transportstyrelsen, the Swedish Transport Agency, states that a CPC (Yrkeskompetensbevis) is valid for five years and that its renewal requires 35 hours of continuing training2. Compliance with the recurring training requirement entails mandatory time away from work, course attendance and associated administrative requirements. Questions have been raised as to whether these obligations remain proportionate, particularly for experienced drivers. In the light of the EU’s objectives on road safety, competitiveness, better regulation and addressing the driver shortage: 1.
What evidence does the Commission have on the road-safety impact and costeffectiveness of the 35-hour periodic training requirement every five years?

Will the Commission evaluate whether more proportionate alternatives could be allowed, including risk-based or needs-based training, greater use of digital training, practical assessment, or exemptions for drivers with long experience and a clean safety record?
What flexibility do Member States currently have to reduce the burden while maintaining road-safety standards?
https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2022/2561/oj/eng. https://www.transportstyrelsen.se/sv/vagtrafik/yrkestrafik/yrkesforarkompetens/for-forare/fortbildning/.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (7.9.2026) Well-trained drivers are generally safer drivers, and there is a clear link between the education and training of drivers and road safety1. However, the qualification and training of bus and lorry drivers is not only intended to improve road safety but also the safety of the driver, including during operations carried out by the driver while the vehicle is stopped. Moreover, it enables the driver to meet the demands of the road transport market. The periodic training is intended to assist drivers in remaining up to date in the skills and knowledge of matters which are essential for their profession. The requirement of 35 hours of periodic training every five years, i.e. on average one seven-hour period per year, does not appear disproportionate in a professional environment that is rapidly evolving. The periodic training should be relevant for the driver and take his or her specific training needs into account. Experienced drivers should also be able to benefit from it. Member States have several ways to reduce the burden on drivers. A third of periodic training (up to 12 hours) can already today be given as e-learning, i.e. in a digital way. Moreover, Member States may include the completed specific training as required under other Union legislation for up to one (in exceptional cases two) of the stipulated seven-hour periods2. The Commission plans to hold an implementation dialogue in November 2026 to discuss any difficulties encountered in the implementation of Directive (EU) 2022/25613, in particular as regards the diverging needs of drivers, and any possibilities of simplification of the training framework.

E-10-2026-002740.t: Agricultural land grabbing in the EU and the appropriation of CAP funds by foreign interests
qt: to the Commission Gilles Pennelle (PfE), Julien Sanchez (PfE), Mathilde Androuët (PfE), Pierre Pimpie (PfE), Marie Dauchy (PfE), Aleksandar Nikolic (PfE), Séverine Werbrouck (PfE), André Rougé (PfE), Mélanie Disdier (PfE), Laurent Castillo (PfE), Marie-Luce BrasierClain (PfE), Valérie Deloge (PfE), Virginie Joron (PfE), Anne-Sophie Frigout (PfE) Subject:

A number of recent investigations have highlighted a rise in mass acquisitions of EU agricultural land by foreign groups, sovereign wealth funds and large international agroindustrial structures. This sometimes entails the appropriation of substantial subsidies under the common agricultural policy (CAP), despite the fact that these farms are likely to be supplying markets outside the European Union. At a time marked by mounting pressure on farm incomes, the announced – unacceptable – reduction to the CAP budget and the planned integration of the CAP into a broader common budgetary fund, this development raises a key question of food sovereignty and the proper use of EU funds. Can the Commission therefore answer the following: 1.
Does it have an accurate overview of the final beneficiaries of CAP subsidies, including in cases where farms are held by foreign groups, sovereign funds or complex legal structures?
How does it plan to ensure that EU funds are primarily used to support European farmers, family farms and food production intended for the European market?
Supporter1
This question is supported by a Member other than the authors: Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE).
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (18.8.2026) Information about beneficiaries of the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) and their identification is made public by Member States as required by the Regulation (EU) 2021/21161. The identification of ultimate beneficial owners is not required by the current Regulation. For the 2028-2034 Multiannual Financial Framework, the Financial Regulation in combination with the proposed sector-specific rules, would require the collection of information on beneficial owners2. For the future CAP rules, the Commission considers that support should go to the farmers whose principal activity is agriculture. In the Commission’s proposal for the CAP, in addition to the eligibility linked to the agricultural activity, the total annual amount of degressive area-based income support would be reduced for payments exceeding EUR 20 000 and capped at EUR 100 000 per year. These provisions, as proposed, address the risk that income support goes to entities whose principal business activity is not farming. The proposal is currently under negotiation by colegislators.

E-10-2026-002738.t: Engine damage caused by biofuel in inland shipping
qt: to the Commission Bert-Jan Ruissen (ECR) Subject:

In a few countries, inland navigation fuel is now blended with biological components, under the Fuel Quality Directive (FQD) and the Renewable Energy Directive (RED III). The switch should not, in theory, cause problems for engines. However, concerns persist among some in the sector. The Algemeene Schippers Vereeniging ASV, a Dutch inland shipping association, advised its members in May to bunker only unblended diesel. The organisation warned ‘that widely used biofuels, in particular FAME (Fatty Acid Methyl Ester), are causing technical problems’1. A boatmaster told me that he suspects that fuel containing animal fats damages engines, in particular the fuel pump and injectors. Others, however, consider these concerns to be unjustified. 1.
Does the Commission have any information indicating that fuel which fully complies with EN 590 and EN 14214 causes structural damage to engines under normal conditions of use?
Is the Commission prepared to standardise fuel and blending (HVO/FAME) for inland shipping in the same way as for road transport?

E-10-2026-002737.t: Increase in administrative costs for EU institutions and rationalisation of infrastructure expenditure
qt: to the Commission Stanisław Tyszka (ESN) Subject:

In view of the increasing pressure on the European Union budget – caused by the increase in the number and cost of EU programmes and the need to repay the debt stemming from the NextGenerationEU instrument – it is particularly important that efficient and economical management of the funds allocated to the Union’s administration be ensured. One important element of this expenditure is the costs of maintaining, modernising, renting and managing the buildings used by the EU institutions, bodies and agencies. In light of the above: 1.

Does the Commission have an aggregated analysis of the evolution of the administrative costs borne by the Commission, its bodies and agencies between 2014 and 2025, or any other longer period, detailing expenditure on salaries, property maintenance, rent, renovation, security and energy consumption?

Has the Commission carried out an assessment of the extent to which buildings owned by the Commission and its agencies have been used, in particular now that hybrid working has become more widespread, and have any cost-saving options through the consolidation of office space, the sale of unused property or the abandonment of part of rental contracts been identified?

Does the Commission intend to present to Parliament a comprehensive strategy for the rationalisation of administrative costs, including measurable targets for reducing expenditure on buildings and increasing their efficient use?

E-10-2026-002736.t: Impact of the upgraded EU-Ukraine DCFTA on border countries
qt: to the Commission Stanisław Tyszka (ESN) Subject:

The upgraded EU-Ukraine DCFTA increases access for selected Ukrainian products to the EU market. At the same time, the agreement provides for mechanisms for administrative cooperation, control of irregularities, approximation of sanitary and phytosanitary standards and application of safeguard measures. Border states, including Poland, face specific costs from the liberalising of trade with Ukraine, especially in sensitive sectors: cereals, sugar, poultry, eggs, honey and dairy products. The problem is often regional rather than EU-wide, as imports and transit are concentrated in a few Member States. 1.
What specific indicators, thresholds and data does the Commission use to assess whether imports from Ukraine cause serious market disturbances in one or more Member States?
Will the Commission publish regular data on imports from Ukraine, broken down by product, Member State, volume, price and transit status?

Will the Commission commit not to propose further increases in quotas for sensitive products without a full impact assessment for border countries and the confirmed alignment of Ukraine with EU standards?
at: (English version) to the Commission Stanisław Tyszka (ESN) (1 July 2026) Subject: Impact of the upgraded EU-Ukraine DCFTA on border countries The upgraded EU-Ukraine DCFTA increases access for selected Ukrainian products to the EU market. At the same time, the agreement provides for mechanisms for administrative cooperation, control of irregularities, approximation of sanitary and phytosanitary standards and application of safeguard measures. Border states, including Poland, face specific costs from the liberalising of trade with Ukraine, especially in sensitive sectors: cereals, sugar, poultry, eggs, honey and dairy products. The problem is often regional rather than EU-wide, as imports and transit are concentrated in a few Member States. 1. What specific indicators, thresholds and data does the Commission use to assess whether imports from Ukraine cause serious market disturbances in one or more Member States? 2. Will the Commission publish regular data on imports from Ukraine, broken down by product, Member State, volume, price and transit status? 3. Will the Commission commit not to propose further increases in quotas for sensitive products without a full impact assessment for border countries and the confirmed alignment of Ukraine with EU standards? (19 August 2026) The Commission relies on the statistics declared by Member States, including Poland, to Eurostat. Each Member State is responsible for surveillance and communication of relevant data. Eurostat and the Commission surveillance allow monitoring of the most recent data on imports, while still subject to review. EU import data are accessible and publicly available underTariff quota consultation (1), Agri-food data portal (2) and EasyComext (3). In 2026, data so far show that imports into the EU are within the limits established by the reviewed EU-Ukraine Deep and Comprehensive Free Trade Area (DCFTA) for the most sensitive agri-food products and are well below previous years' levels. The only exception is eggs, where imports have remained high, including under erga omnes quotas and out-of-quota. This is explained by most-favoured-nation duties allowing competitive imports beyond the preferential tariff rate quota under the DCFTA. Current imports of eggs are also the result of avian influenza cases recorded within the EU and increased consumers’ demand for cheaper protein sources, leading to high EU egg prices. EU-Ukraine trade relations are governed by the reviewed DCFTA, which entered into force on 29 October 2025 and replaced the previous, exceptional EU autonomous trade measures, which remained in force until 5 June 2025. The reviewed DCFTA represent the balanced result of negotiations, as agreed at EU level. It also includes Ukraine’s commitment to complying with certain EU standards by the end of 2028, as well as the rules applying in case of non-compliance.

E-10-2026-002735.t: Justification for continuing to implement the migration pact in its current form
qt: to the Commission Stanisław Tyszka (ESN) Subject:

The Pact on Migration and Asylum has been in force since 12 June 2026 as a package of acts including border, asylum and return procedures, responsibility rules and a solidarity mechanism. From the start of its application, fundamental problems have been apparent: deep differences in public support for a common migration policy, political opposition from some Member States, doubts about operational readiness, and actions that could increase migratory pressure, such as the mass regularisation by the Pedro Sánchez government in Spain. 1.

Is the Commission considering revising, suspending or withdrawing the current migration pact if its application in practice confirms the ineffectiveness of the solidarity mechanism or the unwillingness of Member States to implement the new obligations?

Does the Commission consider the mass regularisation of migrants’ residence status carried out by a Member State to be consistent with the objectives of the migration pact, and does it not undermine the rationale of the solidarity mechanism?

In view of these issues, does the Commission envisage an earlier evaluation of the functioning of the pact, rather than waiting for the first review, which is not due until 1 February 2028, and the overall assessment of the regulation, which is not due until 1 July 2031?

(29 September 2026) Any suspension, withdrawal or substantive revision of the Pact on Migration and Asylum (1), including the solidarity mechanism under the Asylum and Migration Management Regulation (2), would require a proposal under the Treaties and agreement by the co-legislators. As indicated in the European Asylum and Migration Management Strategy (3), the review scheduled for 2027 of the Asylum and Migration Management Regulation and the Asylum Procedure Regulation (4) will be the opportunity for a first evaluation of how the new rules are working in practice, and whether further adjustments are needed. Notwithstanding the distribution of competences defined by the EU legal framework, policies and individual decisions to regularise the status of illegally staying third-country nationals should not affect the correct application of the EU migration and asylum rules. A national residence permit gives authorisation only to live and work in the Member State that issued it. National decisions regarding the regularisation measures do not alter the applicability of the Pact’s responsibility and solidarity rules. The Commission continuously monitors the application of the Pact, including operational readiness in all Member States. The legal acts establishing the Pact contain clauses and deadlines for the reviews to be complied with. The Commission is regularly reporting on the implementation of the Pact and is available to exchange with the European Parliament when needed.

E-10-2026-002734.t: Effectiveness of the NDICI at curbing migratory pressure from North Africa
qt: to the Commission Stanisław Tyszka (ESN) Subject:

One of the aims of the Neighbourhood, Development and International Cooperation Instrument (NDICI) – Global Europe is to curb irregular migration from North Africa by funding border management, the fight against human smuggling, and return and reintegration in Tunisia, Egypt, Mauretania, Morocco and Libya. Frontex data, however, shows that smuggling gangs are adapting and shifting operations between routes. In the first 11 months of 2025, more than 63 000 crossings were detected along the Central Mediterranean route, mainly from Libya to Italy, with Libya responsible for more than 90 %, while the number of crossings from Libya to Crete grew by over 260 % year on year. In the first five months of 2026, the number of crossings detected along the Central Mediterranean route fell by around 49 % year on year; at the same time, the Western Mediterranean route from Algeria to Spain saw an upturn of 46 %. 1.
How much NDICI funding for 2021-2025, broken down by country, has been earmarked for migration management action in Tunisia, Egypt, Mauretania, Morocco and Libya?
Are the NDICI funding mechanisms sufficiently flexible to keep pace with rapidly evolving migratory routes, or are they late to respond?

Does the Commission have any evidence that NDICI funding has brought about a permanent reduction in irregular border crossings into the EU from North Africa, rather than simply shifting migratory pressure to other routes?

Frontex data, however, shows that smuggling gangs are adapting and shifting operations between routes. In the first 11 months of 2025, more than 63 000 crossings were detected along the Central Mediterranean route, mainly from Libya to Italy, with Libya responsible for more than 90%, while the number of crossings from Libya to Crete grew by over 260% year on year. In the first five months of 2026, the number of crossings detected along the Central Mediterranean route fell by around 49% year on year; at the same time, the Western Mediterranean route from Algeria to Spain saw an upturn of 46%. 1. How much NDICI funding for 2021-2025, broken down by country, has been earmarked for migration management action in Tunisia, Egypt, Mauretania, Morocco and Libya? 2. Are the NDICI funding mechanisms sufficiently flexible to keep pace with rapidly evolving migratory routes, or are they late to respond? 3. Does the Commission have any evidence that NDICI funding has brought about a permanent reduction in irregular border crossings into the EU from North Africa, rather than simply shifting migratory pressure to other routes? (2 September 2026) As part of the whole-of-route approach to migration (1), the Neighbourhood, Development and International Cooperation Instrument — Global Europe (NDICI-GE) funding supports, among others, migration management, return and reintegration, combats smuggling and trafficking, promotes protection and legal pathways. These priorities guide cooperation with partner countries, with 2021-2025 funding amounting approximately EUR 290 million and EUR 250 million in Libya and Tunisia; in Egypt, EUR 250 million; EUR 115 million in Mauritania; and around EUR 235 million and the upcoming EUR 160 million budget support for the implementation of the migration strategy in Morocco, especially important after the Ceuta crisis. The impact of NDICI-GE-funded actions is assessed against the specific objectives and indicators set for each action under applicable rules, while migratory movements are shaped by multiple external factors. The Commission monitors developments across migratory routes and uses the instrument’s flexibility to adapt to changing circumstances and act effectively when needed. Detections of irregular border crossings at the EU’s external borders fell by 26% in 202 5 (2) and continued to decline in the first six months of 2026, with all detections being 37% lower than the same period in 202 5 (3). This is the result of strengthened approach to migration, including cooperation with partner countries.

E-10-2026-002732.t: The Erasmus+ ‘Spark’ project and the use of EU funds for sexual education programmes
qt: to the Commission Paolo Inselvini (ECR), Jadwiga Wiśniewska (ECR), Ivaylo Valchev (ECR), Sergio Berlato (ECR), Bert-Jan Ruissen (ECR), Chiara Gemma (ECR), Marco Squarta (ECR), Carlo Ciccioli (ECR), Lara Magoni (ECR) Subject:

With an EU contribution of approximately EUR 400 000, the Erasmus+ Spark project aims to train school leaders, teachers and parents in how to provide comprehensive sexuality education. An approach which, as stated on the project website, involves the ‘whole school community’. Allocating European funds to teach sexual education to children, or to train those who are supposed to pass it on to them, seems quite absurd. Children have the right to receive a solid education in fundamental skills from their school, whereas regarding sensitive issues such as sexuality, the primary role and responsibility belong to parents. Can the Commission clarify: 1.
What specific content will be developed and disseminated within the framework of the Spark project, which is financed with approximately EUR 400 000 of Erasmus+ funds?

How does it intend to ensure full respect for the right of parents to be involved and to ensure that the education and teaching of their children is in conformity with their own convictions, as enshrined in Article 14(3) of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, and whether an explicit informed consent mechanism is planned?

Does it consider it appropriate to continue funding, with EU resources, projects that promote ideologically divisive approaches to sexual education, in an area which the Treaties reserve primarily to the responsibility of the Member States?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (19.8.2026) SPARK1 is an ongoing three-year cooperation project between organisations active in the field of school education, led by the Dublin City University and seven partners from Ireland, Cyprus, Greece, Italy and Portugal. It has been selected by the Irish National Agency further to a call for proposals and on the basis of the criteria set out in the call. SPARK’s main objective is to develop and implement Comprehensive Sexuality Education (CSE) courses across five countries. Using the European approach to micro-credentials, CSE expertise will be exchanged across the partners. The project aims to provide school leaders and teachers with the skill set needed to deliver meaningful CSE lessons, with parental cooperation. Respect for parental rights under Article 14(3) of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union2 is ensured within the distribution of competences established by the EU Treaties. Responsibility for school curricula, teaching arrangements and any consent mechanisms for participation in sexuality education remains with Member States and the competent educational authorities3. Within the competences of the EU, the Commission contributes to the development of quality and inclusive education by encouraging cooperation between Member States and by supporting and supplementing their action. Beneficiaries of Erasmus+ must ensure full respect for and compliance with the values and rights enshrined in the EU Treaties and in the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union.

1 https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/projects/search/details/2024-1-IE01-KA220-SCH-000245697. 2 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/treaty/char_2012/oj/eng. 3 According to Article 165 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union.

E-10-2026-002731.t: The granting of Spanish nationality to Cuban regime-linked individuals and Schengen security risks under Spain’s ‘ Ley de Nietos ’
qt: to the Commission Alvise Pérez (NI) Subject:
The granting of Spanish nationality to Cuban regime-linked individuals and Schengen security risks under Spain’s ‘Ley de Nietos’

According to press reports1, the US Department of State is examining the granting of Spanish nationality under Spain’s Democratic Memory Law (’Ley de Nietos’) to individuals linked to the Cuban regime and allegedly connected to Caribbean drug trafficking and transnational organised crime. Spanish judicial reporting2 has also stated that the Ministry of Justice granted nationality to former Venezuelan deputy minister Nervis Villalobos, amid alleged pressure linked to a corruption network, as investigated by the Guardia Civil’s central operational unit. At the same time, Portugal has moved in the opposite direction, tightening access to nationality, and is considering its withdrawal in cases involving certain serious crimes. This creates a serious regulatory asymmetry in the Iberian Peninsula: a person rejected in Portugal may obtain access to the EU through Spain. Spanish nationality automatically confers EU citizenship and free movement rights within the Schengen area. The contrast with Portugal’s nationality law reform raises concerns about divergent national screening standards affecting the EU’s internal security. 1.
How does the Commission assess the Schengen security impact when a Member State grants nationality to persons allegedly linked to drug trafficking, money laundering or transnational organised crime?
Will the Commission examine whether Spain’s screening procedures are compatible with loyal cooperation and Schengen security obligations?
Will the Commission propose EU-level safeguards to prevent nationality procedures from becoming an entry route for organised crime into the Schengen area?

at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (17.9.2026) According to settled case-law of the Court of Justice of the European Union, it is for each Member State, having due regard to international law, to lay down the conditions for the grant and loss of the nationality of a Member State, while its powers must be exercised having due regard to EU law1. Where a Member State awards nationality, the person concerned automatically becomes an EU citizen in accordance with Article 9 of the Treaty on European Union2 and Article 20(1) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union3. EU citizens enjoy the right to move and reside within the territory of the Member States as enshrined in the EU Treaties and further regulated in Directive 2004/38/EC4. Directive 2004/38/EC allows Member States to restrict the freedom of movement and residence of EU citizens on grounds of public policy, public security or public health, provided that the restrictive measures comply with the principle of proportionality and are based exclusively on the personal conduct of the individual concerned, which must represent a genuine, present and sufficiently serious threat affecting one of the fundamental interests of society.

E-10-2026-002730.t: A common EU framework for Tempo 100 approval of caravans and light trailers
qt: to the Commission Johan Danielsson (S&D) Subject:

In several European countries, including Germany, Denmark and Norway, certain caravans and light trailers may be approved for speed limits of up to 100 km/h under so-called Tempo 100 schemes. These are not general speed-limit increases, but are based on technical and roadworthiness requirements, including brakes, tyres, stabilisation equipment, weight ratios and periodic inspection. However, there is no common EU framework for such approvals. Citizens travelling across borders with caravans or light trailers may therefore need separate national stickers or certificates, even where technical requirements are similar. Since March 2024, Denmark and Norway have recognised each other’s Tempo 100 approvals, showing that mutual recognition can reduce administrative burden while preserving national control over speed limits. Against this background: 1.
Does the Commission see scope for a common EU framework or certificate for Tempo 100 approval of caravans and light trailers?
Would the Commission consider EU-wide mutual recognition of such approvals, while leaving Member States competent to decide whether and where 100 km/h driving is permitted?

Will the Commission assess whether such a certificate could reduce the administrative burden for cross-border travellers, while ensuring that higher speed limits are only authorised for vehicle combinations meeting strict safety requirements?

(7 September 2026) The maximum speed at which vehicles and combinations of vehicles can be used on the road and the conditions under which vehicles or combinations of vehicles can be driven at a certain speed are regulated at national level. There is currently no harmonisation at international level neither of the conditions for the use of a combination of a passenger car and a caravan or light trailer at a certain speed nor of the general speed limits for the use of such combinations (1). In the absence of international rules on this matter, Member States may recognise each other’s approval schemes and also those of third countries on a bilateral basis, as exemplified by the Danish and Norwegian Tempo 100 schemes. If further steps towards harmonising rules at international level were to be taken, the Commission considers that, due to its wider reach, the Global Forum for Road Traffic Safety at the United Nations Economic Commission for Europe (UNECE ) (2) would be the most appropriate forum for discussions on this matter.

E-10-2026-002729.t: Enforcement of EU sanctions against financial networks linked to the Iranian regime
qt: to the Commission Hannah Neumann (Verts/ALE) Subject:

Investigative reporting has alleged that individuals linked to the Iranian ruling elite have used complex corporate structures, nominee shareholders, offshore companies and real-estate investments across Europe to conceal beneficial ownership and maintain access to European markets despite sanctions imposed by partner countries1. 1.

How does the Commission assess the risk that existing EU sanctions may be circumvented through complex ownership structures involving family members, trustees, nominee shareholders or companies established in third countries?

What action has the Commission taken to support Member States in identifying and freezing assets that are ultimately controlled by sanctioned or regime-linked Iranian individuals through the use of indirect ownership structures?

Does the Commission consider the current EU framework on anti-money laundering, beneficial ownership transparency and sanctions enforcement sufficient to detect and prevent such practices, or is it assessing the need for further legislative or enforcement measures?

https://www.bloomberg.com/news/features/2026-01-28/how-iran-supreme-leader-khamenei-s-son-builta-global-property-empire, https://www.iranintl.com/en/202602123979, https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2024-12-30/iran-oil-how-to-get-inside-the-western-financial-system. 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (24.8.2026) The Commission attaches great importance to the effective implementation and enforcement of EU restrictive measures (sanctions). It is aware that complex ownership and control structures – including the use of family members, trustees, nominee shareholders and entities established in third countries – may be used to circumvent sanctions. Under EU sanctions, assets freezes and prohibition on making economic resources available do not apply to listed persons and entities only, but also to entities owned or controlled by them. In the case of Iran, EU sanctions cover situations involving indirect ownership or control used for circumvention. The assessment of such situations must be carried out on a case-by-case basis. The Commission continues to support Member States by issuing guidance, promoting exchanges through the Freeze and Seize Task Force as well as cooperation with international partners. In addition, and in accordance with Recital 105 of the Anti-Money Laundering Regulation1, the Commission is working on guidelines to set out how rules for identifying the beneficial owners in different scenarios, including in the case of complex corporate structures, are to be applied. The use of examples aims to help obliged entities identify beneficial owners. In parallel, the Commission is working on a methodology to conduct a risk assessment at EU level, as referred to in Article 7 of the Anti-Money Laundering Directive 2014/16402, where the risk of non-implementation or evasion of targeted financial sanctions will be thoroughly reported. Furthermore, Directive (EU) 2024/12263 requires Member States to criminalise the circumvention of EU sanctions, including through concealment of ownership or control of assets or economic resources.

E-10-2026-002728.t: The Cutro shipwreck and compliance with European obligations regarding search and rescue
qt: to the Commission Mimmo Lucano (The Left) Subject:

The shipwreck that took place on 26 February 2023 at Steccato di Cutro resulted in the deaths of at least 94 people, including numerous children. Witness reports from survivors, media reports and judicial developments have raised questions regarding the timeliness of the rescue operation and the coordination between relevant authorities. The victims’ families are calling for truth and justice, a full investigation into who was responsible, guarantees that they will be able to participate in the legal proceedings – including through the issuance of the necessary visas – and measures to ensure that such tragedies do not happen again. In the light of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union and international obligations regarding search and rescue at sea, the Commission is asked: 1.
Does it consider that the obligations arising from EU and international law regarding search and rescue were complied with in the Cutro case?
Does it intend to call for an independent assessment of the operational coordination and any shortcomings that may have emerged?

What measures could it take to help ensure that the victims’ families are guaranteed effective access to justice, including by facilitating the issuance of the necessary visas to enable them to participate in legal proceedings in the Member States?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (14.9.2026) The Commission deeply regrets the tragic loss of lives in the shipwreck of Steccato di Cutro. Rendering assistance to persons in distress at sea is a moral duty and a legal obligation under international law. Migrant deaths at sea are a tragic reminder of the need for a comprehensive approach to migration management and countering migrant smuggling. Under international maritime law, responsibility for coordinating search and rescue operations lies primarily with the competent national authorities. It is for the competent national authorities, including judicial authorities where appropriate, to establish the facts and assess compliance with the applicable legal framework. The Commission continues to monitor developments within the limits of the competences conferred by the Treaties. The Commission has no competence to request an independent assessment of an individual search and rescue operation carried out by a Member State. The Victims’ Rights Directive1, revised in June 20262, provides for a comprehensive set of rights for victims of crime and their family members3. It is for national authorities to ensure their application in the specific circumstances raised by the Honourable Member, in line also with the principle of access to justice as enshrined in Article 47 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union4. The examination and issuance of visas fall within the competence of the Member States, as laid down in applicable EU law5.

E-10-2026-002727.t: Draft delegated act updating the minimum training requirements for midwives under Directive 2005/36/EC
qt: to the Commission Marc Angel (S&D) Subject:

The Commission has published a draft delegated act updating the minimum training requirements for midwives under Directive 2005/36/EC1. Midwives play a central role in supporting women, newborns and families throughout pregnancy, childbirth and the postnatal period. As the quality of midwifery education directly influences the care received by millions of women across the EU, this revision represents an important opportunity to ensure that training requirements remain aligned with current scientific evidence, evolving professional practice and the healthcare needs of women and families. In recent years, international organisations such as the World Health Organization and the International Confederation of Midwives have updated their educational standards and competency frameworks to reflect developments in areas including evidence-based care, continuity of care, perinatal mental health, neonatal care, and sexual and reproductive healthcare. Given that Directive 2005/36/EC empowers the Commission to update minimum training requirements in the light of generally acknowledged scientific and technical progress: 1.
How were these international standards, competency frameworks and the evidence underpinning them assessed and taken into account in preparing the draft delegated act?
Has the Commission assessed whether further updates, supported by broad professional consensus and established international standards, could be incorporated before the act is finalised?

Directive 2005/36/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 7 September 2005 on the recognition of professional qualifications (OJ L 255, 30.9.2005, p. 22, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2005/36/oj). 1
at: (English version) to the Commission Marc Angel (S&D) (1 July 2026) Subject: Draft delegated act updating the minimum training requirements for midwives under Directive 2005/36/EC The Commission has published a draft delegated act updating the minimum training requirements for midwives under Directive 2005/36/EC (1). Midwives play a central role in supporting women, newborns and families throughout pregnancy, childbirth and the postnatal period. As the quality of midwifery education directly influences the care received by millions of women across the EU, this revision represents an important opportunity to ensure that training requirements remain aligned with current scientific evidence, evolving professional practice and the healthcare needs of women and families. In recent years, international organisations such as the World Health Organisation and the International Confederation of Midwives have updated their educational standards and competency frameworks to reflect developments in areas including evidence-based care, continuity of care, perinatal mental health, neonatal care, and sexual and reproductive healthcare. Given that directive 2005/36/EC empowers the Commission to update minimum training requirements in the light of generally acknowledged scientific and technical progress: 1.
How were these international standards, competency frameworks and the evidence underpinning them assessed and taken into account in preparing the draft delegated act?
Has the Commission assessed whether further updates, supported by broad professional consensus and established international standards, could be incorporated before the act is finalised?

(11 September 2026) Directive 2005/36/EC (1) facilitates free movement of professionals in the internal market by setting the rules for mutual recognition of professional qualifications. Certain professions, including midwives, benefit from automatic recognition based on minimum training requirements set out in the directive. The directive does not aim to fully harmonise training requirements. In line with Articles 165, 166 and 168(7) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, Member States are responsible for the organisation of their education and training systems, as well as for the definition of their health policy and the delivery of health services and medical care. To ensure that the minimum training requirements set in the directive remain fit for purpose, the Commission may adopt delegated acts to update them in light of generally acknowledged scientific and technical progress. The delegated directive updating minimum training requirements for midwives is based on the results of a study (2) published in July 2025, which was preceded by a thorough mapping of education and training requirements across the EU and broad stakeholder consultations. In 2026, the Commission also consulted Member States via the Group of Coordinators established under Directive 2005/36/EC and launched a public feedback period via Have Your Say website (3). Therefore, while the delegated directive indeed aims to reflect the broad professional consensus and established international standards, it must also remain within the delegated powers granted to the Commission under the directive, i.e., it must set out the minimum training requirements based on the requirements which are currently part of the midwifery training programmes in the majority of Member States.

E-10-2026-002726.t: Rents for NRRP student halls outprice local market
qt: to the Commission Valentina Palmisano (The Left) Subject:

Target M4C1-30 of the Italian national recovery and resilience plan (NRRP) aspires1 to create at least 30 000 new sleeping accommodation units. The Council implementing decision specifies that 30 % of those units must be reserved for students facing socio-economic difficulties and that rents must be at least 15 % below local prices. The same conditions apply to the Student Housing Fund, endowed with EUR 599 million2. According to an investigation by Chora Media3 and Will Media4, in many Italian regions (and particularly in the south), average rents for NRRP-backed accommodation are higher than those for privately rented rooms. What is more, at equal demand, procuring sleeping accommodation units in existing buildings rather than creating new housing capacity limits the increase in supply and ensuing decrease in market prices. These points raise concerns about compliance with the conditions attached to the measures. Can the Commission answer the following: 1.

What data and methodology will it use to check, in accordance with Article 24 of Regulation (EU) 2021/241, that the 15 % reduction relates to the prices actually charged on the local market rather than fees resulting from a ministerial simulation?
Are non-compliant sleeping accommodation units able to be counted towards the M4C1-30 target and eligible to benefit from the fund?
Prior to any assessment, will it ask Italy for data (broken down by structure) on rents, benchmarks, beneficiaries, and units set aside for ‘right to study’ cases, and publish that data?

to the Commission Esther Herranz García (PPE), Elena Nevado del Campo (PPE), Dolors Montserrat (PPE), Raúl de la Hoz Quintano (PPE) Subject:

Monacolins derived from red yeast rice have been used safely in the EU for over 30 years to treat mild to moderate increases in cholesterol. However, the Commission is moving towards a total ban in food supplements under the procedure of Article 8 of Regulation (EC) No 1925/2006, a proposal which received a favourable opinion from the Standing Committee on Plants, Animals, Food and Feed on 13 May 2026. This measure raises doubts about its proportionality, given that Regulation (EU) 2022/860 already imposes mandatory labelling warnings. New scientific evidence and an analysis of its impact on public health are expected shortly. In view of the above: 1.
Why did the Commission decide to put the final decision to a vote before this new evidence was published, rather than wait for the new evidence?

Does it consider that a zero-risk approach, such as the one applied to monacolin K, benefits heart health, how does it fit in with the safe Hearts Plan and how does the Commission justify the proportionality of a total ban?

Given that the ban on hydroxyanthracene derivatives, imposed through the same procedure, was annulled by the General Court, and that a ruling from the CJEU is pending, why would the Commission choose to vote to ban monacolin K now rather than wait for that ruling?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (2.10.2026) The draft Regulation1 referred to in the question aims to prohibit the use of monacolins from red yeast rice following a period of Union scrutiny during which interested parties could submit scientific evidence to demonstrate their safety in accordance with Article 8(4) of Regulation (EC) No 1925/20062. It is based on the European Food Safety Authority`s (EFSA) scientific opinion3 of 29 January 2025, which concluded that safety of monacolins could not be established based on the data submitted. The Commission is not aware of any new scientific evidence on the safety of monacolins to be expected shortly. The Commission, in close consultation with the Member States, took into account EFSA’s scientific opinions, other legitimate factors and the objective of the Article 8 procedure in deciding how to proceed. Given the severe adverse health effects, identified by EFSA in its opinion of 3 August 20184 and reiterated in its opinion of 29 January 2025, namely that exposure to monacolins at intake levels as low as 3 mg/day could lead to severe adverse effects on the musculoskeletal system and the liver, less restrictive measures, such as continuing to allow monacolins under certain conditions of use, would not adequately protect consumers’ health. This is consistent with the Safe Hearts Plan, which is built on evidencebased screening and access to properly authorised treatment pathways for cardiovascular risk factors, and considering the food supplements should not be relied upon to prevent or treat disease. The ongoing court cases concern solely Commission Regulation (EU) 2021/4685. Under Article 8(5) of Regulation (EC) No 1925/2006, the Commission is legally obliged to act following the expiry of a scrutiny period related to the safety of a substance.
1 PE-E1-PRAC-SANTE/1575/2025 - COMMISSION REGULATION (EU) …/… of XXX amending Annex III

to Regulation (EC) No 1925/2006 of the European Parliament and of the Council as regards monacolins from red yeast rice. 2 Regulation (EC) No 1925/2006 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 20 December 2006 on the addition of vitamins and minerals and of certain other substances to foods, OJ L 404, 30.12.2006, p. 26, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2006/1925/oj. 3 Scientific opinion on additional scientific data related to the safety of monacolins from red yeast rice submitted pursuant to Article 8(4) of Regulation (EC) No 1925/2006, EFSA Journal; 2025;23: e9276. 4 EFSA ANS Panel (EFSA Panel on Food Additives and Nutrient Sources added to Food), Aggett, P., Aguilar, F., Crebelli, R., Dusemund, B. et al., Scientific opinion on the safety of monacolins in red yeast rice, EFSA Journal; 2018;16(8):5368. 5 Commission Regulation (EU) 2021/468 of 18 March 2021 amending Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 1925/2006 of the European Parliament and of the Council as regards botanical species containing hydroxyanthracene derivatives, C/2021/1670, OJ L 96, 19.3.2021, p. 6., ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2021/468/oj.

E-10-2026-002724.t: Calculation of relevant turnover for State aid for shellfish farms affected by warming of waters
qt: to the Commission Giuseppe Lupo (S&D) Subject:

In recent years, the unprecedented rise in Mediterranean sea temperatures has seriously damaged shellfish farms, particularly those producing oysters and other shellfish, causing heavy financial losses. In note Ares(2011)666348 of 21 June 2011, concerning aid scheme No 618/2009 relating to adverse weather conditions that occurred in August 2008 in the Gulf of Olbia, the Commission clarified that, for the purposes of the 30 % threshold laid down in the guidelines on State aid in the fisheries and aquaculture sector, the term ‘annual turnover’ was to be interpreted as referring to the total annual turnover of the undertaking in question, and not just to the turnover from the product affected by the event. In the light of the developments in the regulatory framework governing State aid for fisheries and aquaculture, and the increasing frequency with which climate change is affecting aquaculture farms: 1.
Does that interpretation still apply?

Does the Commission believe that, in cases where climate damage affects only a specific aquaculture product, the 30 % threshold should continue to be calculated on the basis of the company’s total turnover?
Will it consider updating the guidelines to take account of the specific characteristics of shellfish farming and the growing impact of warming sea waters on businesses?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (26.8.2026) 1. The interpretation that the 30% threshold refers to the total annual turnover of the undertaking still applies. Aid to make good the damage caused by adverse climatic events which can be assimilated to a natural disaster is covered by Section 1.2. of the 2023 Guidelines for State aid in the fishery and aquaculture sector (the ‘Fishery Guidelines’)1. These provide, in point (163)(a), that ‘the damage caused by the adverse climatic event which can be assimilated to a natural disaster must amount to more than 30 % of the average annual production […]’. The 2008 Guidelines for the examination of State aid to fisheries and aquaculture2, which applied in 2011, provided, in their Section 4.4., that aid can be deemed compatible ‘if the level of damages caused by the event concerned reaches the threshold of 30 % of the average annual turnover […]’. The switch from a reference to average annual turnover to a reference to average annual production created consistency between the wording of Guidelines in the agricultural and fisheries sectors3. In both areas the concept refers to the total annual production rather than just the production affected by the adverse climatic event, in particular due to the intention to limit aid to undertakings that have been particularly affected by the event. 2. The Commission interprets point (163)(a) of the Fishery Guidelines as referring to the 30% of the company’s total production, even in cases where climate damage affects only a specific aquaculture product’. 3. At the time of the revision of the fisheries and aquaculture State aid rules, the Commission will assess the specific characteristics of the sector, including the shellfish farming and the growing impact of warming sea waters on businesses.
