E-10-2026-002695.t: Exports of European military material to Türkiye and implementation of Common Position 2008/944/CFSP
qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Nikolaos Anadiotis (NI) Subject:

Common Position 2008/944/CFSP lays down common criteria for exports of military technology and equipment, including Criterion Four on the preservation of regional peace, security and stability1. Nonetheless, Türkiye continues to occupy 37 % of the Republic of Cyprus2, has maintained since 1995 a threat of war against Greece if it exercises its legitimate sovereign rights in the Aegean3, and has a military presence or involvement in Syria, Iraq and Libya4. Notwithstanding the above, EU Member States are either authorising or considering military exports or defence partnerships with Türkiye, including through programmes such as Eurofighter and related European defence partnerships5. In light of the above, I would like to ask the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy the following: 1.
How does she assess the compatibility of exports of military material to Türkiye with Criterion Four of Common Position 2008/944/CFSP?
Does she intend to ask Member States to review export authorisations to Türkiye, given that there is a risk of equipment being used against Member States or in destabilising operations?

Will she propose a coordinated European stance calling for the suspension of exports of military material to Türkiye until the country withdraws its casus belli and fully respects the sovereignty of Greece and Cyprus?

(27 August 2026) The control of arms exports by Member States is subject, inter alia (1), to Council Common Position (CP) 2008/944/CFSP (2). Under Article 2(5)(b), when assessing export licence applications, they must consider the risk of use of the items against their forces or those of other Member States, as well as friendly and allied countries. This also includes the potential export of the Eurofighter, which is subject to the unanimous approval of state participants of the project. The Commission has no mandate to influence Member States’ decisions in individual cases regarding their arms export authorisation. Member States work within the Common Foreign and Security Policy framework to promote convergence in arms exports. The Council’s Working Party on Conventional Arms Export continues to examine arms exports to Türkiye. The EU has repeatedly stressed that Türkiye must respect the sovereignty and sovereign rights of all Member States. The High Representative/Vice-President reiterated this message in the press conference of the Foreign Affairs Council on 13 July 2026 (3). The EU also underlined its expectations that Türkiye fully respects international law, to de-escalate tensions in the interest of regional stability in the Eastern Mediterranean, and to promote good neighbourly relations in a sustainable way (4). E-10-2026-002694.t: Is the EU complicit in the US war of aggression against Iran?
qt: to the Commission Marc Botenga (The Left) Subject:

The Commission condemned Belarus’ decision to make its territory available to Russia for the latter’s aggression against Ukraine. The President of the Commission described Belarus as ‘the other aggressor’, in particular because it had granted Russian forces access to its territory. The European Union subsequently sanctioned Belarus1. During the United States’ illegal war on Iran, which began on 28 February 2026, a number of European countries have also made military bases, airports and other infrastructure located in their territory available to US forces. According to the NATO Secretary‑General, Italy has allowed 500 US aircraft to take off from its soil to take part in military operations. Romania is reported to have authorised tanker aircraft to take off from its civilian airports. Ramstein Air Base in Germany has been used to direct and coordinate this war of aggression. 1.

In the context of the illegal war on Iran, does the Commission take the view that making territory, infrastructure and airspace available to the United States means that the countries concerned are complicit in this aggression?
If so, what action does it propose to ensure that the EU and its Member States respect international law, as the Treaty requires?
If not, why does it consider Belarus to be complicit in Russia’s aggression, but does not view the countries concerned as being complicit in the US aggression?

E-10-2026-002693.t: No impact assessment when regions align roadworthiness tests with the minimum laid down in Directive 2014/45/EU
qt: to the Commission Benoit Cassart (Renew) Subject:
No impact assessment when regions align roadworthiness tests with the minimum laid down in Directive 2014/45/EU

Directive 2014/45/EU lays down minimum requirements for how often roadworthiness tests must be carried out, but competent authorities may set higher test standards. However, some of them could drop their requirements to the EU minimum by doing away with roadworthiness tests upon the resale of a vehicle and by increasing the intervals at which older vehicles and vehicles for the carriage of persons are subject to testing. Such a development could take place without an independent road safety impact assessment, even though the Commission is, in fact, proposing to increase the minimum requirements (COM(2025)0180). 1.

In light of its own impact assessment accompanying its proposal for a directive (COM(2025)0180), does the Commission consider that a prior road safety assessment needs to be carried out when a Member State or region reduces the frequency of its tests to the EU minimum?

What is its view of the fact that a Member State can align itself with the minimum required at a time when the Commission is working to increase that minimum? Does it have any means at its disposal to take this into account in the ongoing revision of the directive?

However, some of them could drop their requirements to the EU minimum by doing away with roadworthiness tests upon the resale of a vehicle and by increasing the intervals at which older vehicles and vehicles for the carriage of persons are subject to testing. Such a development could take place without an independent road safety impact assessment, even though the Commission is, in fact, proposing to increase the minimum requirements (COM(2025)0180). 1. In light of its own impact assessment accompanying its proposal for a directive (COM(2025)0180), does the Commission consider that a prior road safety assessment needs to be carried out when a Member State or region reduces the frequency of its tests to the EU minimum? 2. What is its view of the fact that a Member State can align itself with the minimum required at a time when the Commission is working to increase that minimum? Does it have any means at its disposal to take this into account in the ongoing revision of the directive? (7 September 2026) Regarding road safety assessments in the Member States, the Commission would note that whilst it may be advisable, it is not a requirement under EU law that such an assessment is carried out when a Member State is considering reducing the frequency of periodic technical inspections to align its existing rules with the minimum requirements under EU law. If the minimum requirements are amended as a result of the current negotiations between the legislators, or in the future, Member States will have to adapt to comply with any change in EU law.

E-10-2026-002692.t: China’s dominant position in Latin America and the possible emergence of further threats to the EU’s supply of raw materials
qt: to the Commission Alberico Gambino (ECR), Carlo Fidanza (ECR), Mariateresa Vivaldini (ECR), Francesco Torselli (ECR), Daniele Polato (ECR), Stefano Cavedagna (ECR), Francesco Ventola (ECR), Paolo Inselvini (ECR), Chiara Gemma (ECR), Sergio Berlato (ECR), Alessandro Ciriani (ECR), Michele Picaro (ECR) Subject:

Global demand for copper is set to grow in the coming years as a result of the energy transition, e-mobility and digitalisation. Chinese companies are expanding their presence in key extraction projects in Latin America, and are even investing in the extraction infrastructure required. Beijing’s strategy is to increase its control over global critical raw material value chains, from the extraction phase to the processing stage. Itself no stranger to relying on external suppliers for critical resources in key sectors, Europe could, as a result of the green and digital transition, once again find itself in a vulnerable economic and geopolitical position. Given the foregoing: 1.

How does the Commission assess the risk that China’s increasingly tight grip over the copper industry and the supply chains of other critical raw materials could undermine the Union’s strategic autonomy?

How will the Commission strengthen the EU’s economic and industrial presence in Latin America with a view to ensuring more secure and diversified supply chains that are less dependent on Chinese operators?

Has it conducted an assessment of the geopolitical and industrial impact of the potential concentration of critical raw material supply chains in the hands of operators linked to the People’s Republic of China?
at: (English version) to the Commission Alberico Gambino (ECR), Carlo Fidanza (ECR), Mariateresa Vivaldini (ECR), Francesco Torselli (ECR), Daniele Polato (ECR), Stefano Cavedagna (ECR), Francesco Ventola (ECR), Paolo Inselvini (ECR), Chiara Gemma (ECR), Sergio Berlato (ECR), Alessandro Ciriani (ECR), Michele Picaro (ECR) (29 June 2026) Subject: China’s dominant position in Latin America and the possible emergence of further threats to the EU’s supply of raw materials Global demand for copper is set to grow in the coming years as a result of the energy transition, e-mobility and digitalisation. Chinese companies are expanding their presence in key extraction projects in Latin America, and are even investing in the extraction infrastructure required. Beijing’s strategy is to increase its control over global critical raw material value chains, from the extraction phase to the processing stage. Itself no stranger to relying on external suppliers for critical resources in key sectors, Europe could, as a result of the green and digital transition, once again find itself in a vulnerable economic and geopolitical position. Given the foregoing: 1.

How does the Commission assess the risk that China’s increasingly tight grip over the copper industry and the supply chains of other critical raw materials could undermine the Union’s strategic autonomy?

How will the Commission strengthen the EU’s economic and industrial presence in Latin America with a view to ensuring more secure and diversified supply chains that are less dependent on Chinese operators?

Has it conducted an assessment of the geopolitical and industrial impact of the potential concentration of critical raw material supply chains in the hands of operators linked to the People’s Republic of China?

(19 August 2026) The Commission is aware of China’s increasing refining capacity and the involvement of Chinese companies in many copper mining operations outside China. As copper demand in the EU is projected to grow by over 50% by 2050, the Commission designated several copper projects as ‘strategic projects’ under the Critical Raw Materials Act (1), including 11 in the EU (2) and one in Norway. These projects should contribute to strengthening the EU’s strategic autonomy in the sector, including by boosting recycling. The Commission is strengthening the EU’s economic and industrial presence in Latin America through strategic partnerships, trade agreements and targeted investment to build secure, resilient and diversified supply chains. It has concluded Memoranda of Understanding (MoU) on critical raw materials with Chile and Argentina — a similar MoU is under negotiation with Brazil — and dedicated roadmaps to deliver projects. The conclusion of the EU-Mercosur Partnership Agreement (3) will improve market access and predictability for EU firms. The Commission continuously assesses supply chain vulnerabilities and geopolitical risks, including risks linked to market concentration and the role of operators from third countries. This work feeds into the EU’s broader approach on economic security, resilience and risk management. The Commission’s assessment is that excessive concentration at any stage of the value chain — whether in extraction, processing, transport, recycling or technology ownership — can create industrial and geopolitical vulnerabilities for the EU.

OJ L, 2024/1252, 3.5.2024; https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1252/oj/eng. https://single-market-economy.ec.europa.eu/sectors/raw-materials/areas-specific-interest/critical-raw-materials/strategic-projects-under-crma/selectedprojects_en. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A22026A00186&qid=1772192739535.
Thus, the Commission is pursuing a policy based on diversification, domestic capacity-building, circularity, sustainability, strategic partnerships and increased risk monitoring.

E-10-2026-002689.t: Scrutiny of hunting trophy imports into the EU
qt: to the Commission Tilly Metz (Verts/ALE), Maria Ohisalo (Verts/ALE), Sebastian Everding (The Left), César Luena (S&D), Lynn Boylan (The Left), Sirpa Pietikäinen (PPE), Gerben-Jan Gerbrandy (Renew), Anja Hazekamp (The Left), Manuela Ripa (PPE) Subject:

The EU is the world’s second-largest importer of hunting trophies, yet the overwhelming majority of trophies entering the EU, i.e. most species listed in Annex B to Council Regulation (EC) No 338/97, do not require import permits, despite the fact that permits are required when the same species are imported for other purposes. As import permits are the only mechanism for assessing whether trade is detrimental to species survival, the Scientific Review Group cannot conduct non-detriment assessments for most hunting trophy imports, limiting a key safeguard of the EU wildlife trade control system. The need for greater scrutiny of trophy imports is recognised in the EU Action Plan against Wildlife Trafficking1 and Parliament’s resolution on CITES CoP202, which calls for import permits to be extended to all Annex B trophies. In this context: 1.
What is the scientific rationale for excluding most Annex B hunting trophies from import permit requirements?
How does the Commission ensure effective scrutiny where permits are not required, and is it open to extending permit requirements to all Annex B trophies? If not, why not?
What are the Commission’s plans for assessing additional species, beyond those under discussion, for possible inclusion in Annex XIII to Commission Regulation (EC) No 865/2006?

Commission communication of 9 November 2022 entitled ‘Revision of the EU action plan against wildlife trafficking’ (COM(2022)0581). 2 European Parliament resolution of 23 October 2025 on the EU strategic objectives for the 20th meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES), to be held in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, from 24 November to 5 December 2025 (OJ C, C/2026/2102, 29.4.2026, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/C/2026/2102/oj). 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (25.8.2026) The EU applies a risk-based approach to hunting trophy imports under the EU Wildlife Trade Regulations1. Trophies imported for non-commercial purposes are generally treated as personal effects. However, stricter requirements apply to the first introduction into the EU of trophies from 12 Annex B-listed species included in Annex XIII to the Implementing Regulation (EC) No 865/20062. These species require a non-detriment finding by the scientific authority of the Member State of destination. Applying the same requirements to all Annex B species would not reflect different conservation situations and risks. Where import permits are not required, imports remain subject to the EU Wildlife Trade Regulations and the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora framework. The Commission, supported by the Scientific Review Group (SRG)3, monitors conservation status and trade patterns based on scientific information. The revised EU Action Plan against Wildlife Trafficking4 lays down measures for increased scrutiny for additional Annex B species. The SRG is currently examining available evidence, but no decision has been taken yet. The Commission and the scientific authorities of the Member States assess scientific and trade information for possible amendments to Annex XIII. Any future inclusion of species would rely on evidence concerning conservation status, trade sustainability and illegal trade risks, in line with the precautionary, risk- and science-based approach of the EU Wildlife Trade Regulations.
1 https://environment.ec.europa.eu/topics/nature-and-biodiversity/wildlife-trade_en. 2 Commission Regulation (EC) No 865/2006 of 4 May 2006 laying down detailed rules concerning the

implementation of Council Regulation (EC) No 338/97 on the protection of species of wild fauna and flora by regulating trade therein, OJ L 166, 19.6.2006, pp. 1–69. 3 https://ec.europa.eu/transparency/expert-groups-register/screen/expertgroups/consult?lang=en&do=groupDetail.groupDetail&groupID=365. 4 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:52022DC0581.

E-10-2026-002688.t: Community of Madrid’s new hunting and fisheries law: compliance with EU biodiversity rules
qt: to the Commission César Luena (S&D), Hana Jalloul Muro (S&D), José Cepeda (S&D) Subject:

The Assembly of Madrid has adopted a hunting and fishing law that includes population control plans for species with surplus animals – which can also be used outside normal hunting periods – expands the use of certain hunting technologies and amends the rules for various huntable species. A number of scientific and environmental organisations have questioned the scientific basis of some of these measures and have raised concerns about their potential impact on biodiversity. As wildlife management must comply with the Birds and Habitats Directives, could the Commission answer the following: 1.

Does it consider that measures like these should be based on up-to-date scientific information on the conservation status of the species concerned, which would provide justification for their necessity, proportionality and compatibility with the conservation objectives set out in both Directives?

What obligations under those Directives must be fulfilled when adopting rules that expand, or change the purpose of, hunting for wild species, such as authorising population control outside normal hunting periods or expanding the tools used to that end?
How does the Commission verify whether this type of regional legislative reform is compatible with the EU’s species and habitats conservation objectives?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.8.2026) The Birds1 and the Habitats2 Directives require that hunting and fishing and any population management of wild species covered by these Directives respect the objective of maintaining or restoring favourable conservation status. The case-law of the Court of Justice of the European Union underscores the importance of using the best available scientific information as a basis for implementing the Directives. Hunting and fishing regimes as well as population control measures must be aligned with the Directives’ protection systems3. Species listed in Annex V of the Habitats Directive and Annex II of the Birds Directive may be hunted and subject to management measures, if this is compatible with their being maintained at a favourable conservation status, and following the provisions set under the Directives. Any derogations from the general provisions, including for strictly protected species, must satisfy the strict and cumulative conditions set out under Article 9 of the Birds Directive and Article 16 of the Habitats Directive (including that there is no other satisfactory solution, that the measure pursues a permitted derogation objective, and that it is subject to strict supervision, selective application and to the other safeguards required by those provisions). The primary responsibility for ensuring that national hunting and fisheries law complies with the applicable EU law lies with the Member States’ competent authorities and judiciary system. In order to assist them, the Commission has adopted several guidance documents4. The Commission, as guardian of the Treaties, monitors the implementation of the EU legislation in EU Member States and may take actions to address systemic non-compliance, when appropriate.
1 Directive 2009/147/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 30 November 2009 on the

conservation of wild birds, OJ L 20, 26.1.2010, p. 7–25. 2 Council Directive 92/43/EEC of 21 May 1992 on the conservation of natural habitats and of wild fauna and flora, OJ L 206, 22.7.1992, p. 7–50. 3 Articles 12 to 16 of the Habitats Directive and Article 7 to 9 of the Birds Directive. 4 Guidance to sustainable hunting under the Birds Directive https://circabc.europa.eu/ui/group/3f466d71-92a749eb-9c63-6cb0fadf29dc/library/c899b11c-90f6-4aad-95c5-aac35e4c1e38/details; Guidance document on the general system of protection of bird species - Article 5 and Article 9 of the Birds Directive https://environment.ec.europa.eu/publications/guidance-document-general-system-protection-birdspecies-article-5-and-article-9-birds-directive_en; Commission notice Guidance document on the strict protection of animal species of Community interest under the Habitats Directive https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=PI_COM:C(2021)7301; https://environment.ec.europa.eu/news/commission-adopts-guidance-natura-2000-and-fishing-2025-10-17_en.

E-10-2026-002687.t: Apple Inc. statement that Siri AI won’t be available to EU users on iOS 27 and iPadOS 27 due to the Digital Markets Act
qt: to the Commission Fernand Kartheiser (NI), Friedrich Pürner (NI), Alexander Jungbluth (ESN), Alvise Pérez (NI) Subject:

According to Apple Inc.’s statement1 on Monday 8 June 2026, the company will not make its new Siri AI available to EU users on iOS 27 and iPadOS 27 due to the Digital Markets Act (DMA). Apple says EU regulators rejected its proposed solutions for enabling Siri AI while continuing to safely support third-party virtual assistants. These proposals included a ‘Trusted System Agent’ intermediary, which Apple claims is designed to protect user privacy and security. 1.

Can the Commission confirm whether its interpretation and application of the DMA is preventing Apple from offering Siri AI on iPhones and iPads in the EU? If so, what are the Commission’s specific motives and legal basis?

Does the DMA require Apple to grant any third-party AI operator the same system-level access to user data, device functions and personal information as Siri AI, and if so, does that threaten user controls or privacy safeguards that could increase risks of data theft or misuse?

Did the Commission reject Apple’s ‘Trusted System Agent’ proposal? If so, what were the reasons, and what alternative compliance solutions does the Commission propose to enable secure roll-out of advanced AI assistants in the EU?
https://www.apple.com/newsroom/2026/06/due-to-dma-siri-ai-delayed-in-eu-for-ios-27-and-ipados-27/.
at: (English version) to the Commission Fernand Kartheiser (NI), Friedrich Pürner (NI), Alexander Jungbluth (ESN), Alvise Pérez (NI) (29 June 2026) Subject: Apple Inc. statement that Siri AI won’t be available to EU users on iOS 27 and iPadOS 27 due to the Digital Markets Act According to Apple Inc.’s statement (1) on Monday 8 June 2026, the company will not make its new Siri AI available to EU users on iOS 27 and iPadOS 27 due to the Digital Markets Act (DMA). Apple says EU regulators rejected its proposed solutions for enabling Siri AI while continuing to safely support third-party virtual assistants. These proposals included a ‘Trusted System Agent’ intermediary, which Apple claims is designed to protect user privacy and security. 1. Can the Commission confirm whether its interpretation and application of the DMA is preventing Apple from offering Siri AI on iPhones and iPads in the EU? If so, what are the Commission’s specific motives and legal basis? 2. Does the DMA require Apple to grant any third-party AI operator the same system-level access to user data, device functions and personal information as Siri AI, and if so, does that threaten user controls or privacy safeguards that could increase risks of data theft or misuse? 3. Did the Commission reject Apple’s ‘Trusted System Agent’ proposal? If so, what were the reasons, and what alternative compliance solutions does the Commission propose to enable secure roll-out of advanced AI assistants in the EU? (2 September 2026) Article 6(7) of the Digital Markets Act (DMA) requires Apple to grant third parties the same interoperability with iOS and iPadOS that its own services enjoy, preventing it from disadvantaging rivals. Apple may implement security and privacy safeguards, provided they comply with EU law and are non-discriminatory. It cannot impose stricter requirements on third parties than on its own services. Where appropriate, users should decide which services they trust and allow to access their devices. Apple chose not to launch Siri AI in the EU despite being aware of its DMA obligations during development. Rather than proposing a compliant interoperability solution, it requested a temporary exemption, which would have delayed interoperable AI features by 2-3 years. Apple later referred to a ‘trusted system agent’, but presented only a high-level concept without technical details or evidence that it would provide access comparable to Siri. The EU remains an important market for Apple, and launching Siri AI in the EU would offer significant opportunities to improve the product through EU users. The Commission continues technical discussions with Apple, but under the DMA it is Apple's responsibility to propose a compliant solution without restricting user choice or delaying compliance.
https://www.apple.com/newsroom/2026/06/due-to-dma-siri-ai-delayed-in-eu-for-ios-27-and-ipados-27/.

E-10-2026-002686.t: Future integration of the CRCF into the EU climate architecture and its implications for forest management and the bioeconomy
qt: to the Commission Katri Kulmuni (Renew) Subject:
There are indications that the Commission may be planning to integrate the Carbon Removal Certification Framework (CRCF) into the post-2030 EU climate architecture. In this context: 1.

Can the Commission clarify how it justifies linking a voluntary framework to future climate policy obligations, given that the instrument was negotiated and agreed as voluntary and that its overall effectiveness has not yet been evaluated? At present, there remains considerable uncertainty as to whether the delegated acts and draft methodologies will meaningfully contribute to enhancing carbon sinks or product-based carbon storage.

Moreover, how does the Commission intend to avoid creating de facto regulatory obligations for forest management practices and biomass sustainability through the implementation of the CRCF? Such a development would appear to go against the Commission’s simplification objectives as well as the Member States’ competence in the field of forest policy.

Finally, if the integration of the CRCF into the EU climate architecture is being considered, does the Commission envisage a comprehensive reassessment of the delegated acts to ensure that they are fit for purpose, proportionate and aligned with the objective of promoting a competitive bioeconomy, including the availability of raw wood material?
at: (English version) to the Commission Katri Kulmuni (Renew) (29 June 2026) Subject: Future integration of the CRCF into the EU climate architecture and its implications for forest management and the bioeconomy There are indications that the Commission may be planning to integrate the Carbon Removal Certification Framework (CRCF) into the post-2030 EU climate architecture. In this context: 1.

Can the Commission clarify how it justifies linking a voluntary framework to future climate policy obligations, given that the instrument was negotiated and agreed as voluntary and that its overall effectiveness has not yet been evaluated? At present, there remains considerable uncertainty as to whether the delegated acts and draft methodologies will meaningfully contribute to enhancing carbon sinks or product-based carbon storage.

Moreover, how does the Commission intend to avoid creating de facto regulatory obligations for forest management practices and biomass sustainability through the implementation of the CRCF? Such a development would appear to go against the Commission’s simplification objectives as well as the Member States’ competence in the field of forest policy.

Finally, if the integration of the CRCF into the EU climate architecture is being considered, does the Commission envisage a comprehensive reassessment of the delegated acts to ensure that they are fit for purpose, proportionate and aligned with the objective of promoting a competitive bioeconomy, including the availability of raw wood material?

(19 August 2026) The Commission is committed to promoting a circular bioeconomy as an important enabler for the EU’s transition towards climate neutrality. Healthy soils and forests will be essential to secure sustainable, long-term access to biomass and biogenic carbon, in particular in the face of the increasing impacts of climate change. In the context of reviewing the role for national targets for the post-2030 framework the Commission is therefore also considering how to further promote investments in carbon removals and improving the resilience of the EU land sector, including by promoting the voluntary Carbon Removal and Carbon Farming (CRCF) market. The amended EU Climate Law underlines the need for enhanced flexibility within and across sectors and instruments to support the achievement of the 2040 target in a simple and cost-effective way. The Commission is working towards a proposal for national climate targets in the fourth quarter of 2026, which will be accompanied by a thorough impact assessment. The Commission will also assess opportunities for simplification and reduced administrative burden, including on implementing and delegated acts. The aim of a voluntary CRCF market is to mobilise additional investments into improved land management practices as well as carbon storage in products and permanent removals. To date, methodologies for the certification of permanent removals and carbon farming activities (e.g. rewetting of peatlands and afforestation) have been adopted, building on current EU legislation and best practice. These contain provisions on monitoring and reporting obligations, sustainability as well as quantification of carbon removed and stored.

E-10-2026-002685.t: Imports of meat from Brazil – consumer safety and regulatory restrictions
qt: to the Commission Ewa Zajączkowska-Hernik (PfE) Subject:

The decision to restrict imports of meat from Brazil and information emerging about the possible use of substances not authorised on the EU market raise questions about consumer safety and the transitional period before the entry into force of the new restrictions. Reports of Salmonella being detected in consignments of meat placed on the Greek market raise additional concerns, underlining the importance of effective food safety monitoring and transparent communication by EU authorities. 1.
Has the Commission assessed the potential impact of meat imported from Brazil on the health safety of EU consumers, and will the results of any such analyses be published?
Why are restrictions on the import and sale of meat covered by the new rules set to enter into force only on 3 September, and what consumer protection measures will be in place until then?
at: (English version) to the Commission Ewa Zajączkowska-Hernik (PfE) (29 June 2026) Subject: Imports of meat from Brazil — consumer safety and regulatory restrictions The decision to restrict imports of meat from Brazil and information emerging about the possible use of substances not authorised on the EU market raise questions about consumer safety and the transitional period before the entry into force of the new restrictions. Reports of Salmonella being detected in consignments of meat placed on the Greek market raise additional concerns, underlining the importance of effective food safety monitoring and transparent communication by EU authorities. 1. Has the Commission assessed the potential impact of meat imported from Brazil on the health safety of EU consumers, and will the results of any such analyses be published? 2. Why are restrictions on the import and sale of meat covered by the new rules set to enter into force only on 3 September, and what consumer protection measures will be in place until then? (21 August 2026) The new entry conditions related to the use of certain antimicrobials, applying from 3 September 2026, are unrelated to detections of salmonella or other incidents and are therefore addressed through different regulatory approaches. Goods of animal origin imported from Brazil are subject to the highest frequency of border checks compared to any other third country, based on the past record of compliance with EU legislation, data and information collected through TRACES and the Rapid Alert System for Food and Feed (RASFF), and the findings of controls carried out by Commission experts in third countries. Specifically, in the last six months, 75% of consignments have undergone physical checks while 30% have been subjected to laboratory testing. Despite these stringent controls, only 1% (152 out of 15 197 consignments) of the consignments of goods of animal origin exported by Brazil to the EU since the beginning of 2026 were found non-compliant. This rate is in line with the average rate of non-compliance observed for the rest of third countries. Those non-compliant consignments were intercepted by the competent authorities and were not placed on the EU market. Furthermore, the Commission carries out regular on-spot audits to assess Brazilian control system. All the audit reports are publicly available (1). The Commission had extensive discussions with all relevant actors, in particular the European Parliament and the Council, including on the timing to apply the prohibition of use of certain antimicrobial medicinal products in food producing animals or products of animal origin exported from third countries into the EU. The Commission considers that the application date of this measure does not pose a risk to the health of EU consumers.
https://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/audit-report.

E-10-2026-002684.t: Consistency between EU climate policy and trade policy
qt: to the Commission Ewa Zajączkowska-Hernik (PfE) Subject:

Reducing greenhouse gas emissions and promoting local and sustainable food production remains a priority for the European Union. However, the EU also supports imports of agricultural products from Mercosur countries. The transportation of these products to Europe generates additional emissions related to intercontinental logistics, while the production process itself is often linked to deforestation. 1.

Has the Commission carried out an analysis comparing the actual carbon footprint of EU-produced meat with that of meat imported from Mercosur countries, taking into account transport and land-use change emissions?
If a breach of EU environmental standards is identified, does the Commission intend to suspend imports of agricultural products from Mercosur countries into the European Union?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (19.8.2026) The Commission has performed several analytical assessments prior to the signature of the EU-Mercosur Partnership Agreement (EMPA)1 and the Interim Trade Agreement (ITA)2, which has been provisionally applied since 1 May 2026. These include the Sustainability Impact Assessment3 and the Economic Analysis of the Negotiated Outcome of the EMPA4, which evaluate impacts across key sectors, with particular attention to sensitive sectors such as agriculture. The economic analysis concluded that the overall impact of the agreement on global greenhouse gas emissions would be negligible. However, the Commission has not carried out a direct comparative assessment of the carbon footprint of EU-produced meat and Mercosur imports. More generally, the EMPA and the ITA contain a chapter on sustainable development with discipline on trade and climate change including the obligation for the Parties to effectively implement the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change and the Paris Agreement, and the Paris Agreement on Climate Change is an ‘essential element’ of the agreements. All products placed on the EU market must comply with applicable EU legislation. An example is the EU Deforestation Regulation5, under which relevant commodities must be deforestation-free, legal according to the laws of the country of production and covered by a due diligence statement or a simplified declaration. Products that do not meet those requirements cannot be placed on the EU market.

Negotiations-between-the-EU-and-Mercosur-Exec-Summary-EN.pdf. 4 https://op.europa.eu/en/publication-detail/-/publication/6f1a741f-677e-11f0-bf4e-01aa75ed71a1. 5 Regulation (EU) 2023/1115 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 31 May 2023 on the making available on the Union market and the export from the Union of certain commodities and products associated with deforestation and forest degradation and repealing Regulation (EU) No 995/2010: https://eurlex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2023/1115/oj/eng.

E-10-2026-002683.t: Possible influence of pharmaceutical interests on EU policies on menopause
qt: to the Commission Irmhild Boßdorf (ESN) Subject:

In June 2026, there was an article entitled ‘From Silence to Strategy: Rethinking Menopause as a European Priority’ in the Media Partner section of ‘The Parliament’ magazine1. In this article, the Members of the European Parliament Maria Walsh (EPP), Veronika Cifrová Ostrihoňová (Renew), Billy Kelleher (Renew) and Christophe Clergeau (S&D), among others, argued that menopause should to a greater extent be seen as a European health, economic and societal challenge. The article was supported by the pharmaceutical company Besins Healthcare (transparency register number: 7859633100766-19). The company describes menopause as a policy area where significant health and economic potential could be unlocked through prevention, awareness raising, improved access to treatment and early intervention. Besins Healthcare is an international pharmaceutical group that specialises in hormonal therapies and claims to be the world leader in this field. 1.

Has the Commission assessed the financial impact of extending or increasing public reimbursement for hormone replacement therapies and other menopause treatments, including the resulting market opportunities for pharmaceutical companies?

How does the Commission ensure that menopause policy initiatives are not influenced by the economic interests of companies which market such treatments and at the same time support campaigns, events or media contributions on the issue?

Has the Commission analysed whether and to what extent industry-supported communication and lobbying activities on the issue of menopause have influenced policy priorities at EU level, in particular in the context of the FEMM report 2025/2074(INI)?

E-10-2026-002682.t: Rescue ship ‘Ocean Viking’ shot at by so-called Libyan coastguard
qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Özlem Demirel (The Left) Subject:

On 24 August 2025, the so-called Libyan coastguard opened fire on the civil rescue ship ‘Ocean Viking’. The so-called Libyan coastguard claimed to have merely fired warning shots and accused the non‑governmental organisation of collaborating with traffickers. In a meeting with the EU Ambassador, representatives from the Libyan Tripoli Government claimed that the shooting was compliant with the rules in place. The incident was discussed in the framework of the memorandum of understanding between Italy and the Libyan Tripoli Government on the supply and deployment of ships. The Libyan Tripoli Government stated that an investigation had been launched and, at the insistence of EU representatives, indicated that it would announce the results ‘soon’. 1.
When and how were these ‘soon’ to be announced results of the Libyan Tripoli Government’s investigation into this incident communicated to the EU, and what do they indicate?

How is the EU monitoring compliance with the human rights obligations laid out in the memorandum of understanding between Italy and the Libyan Tripoli Government, and what penalties does the agreement provide for in the event of non-compliance?

What ‘technical meetings’ have taken place with representatives of the Libyan Tripoli Government and the so‑called Libyan coastguard to discuss the shots fired at ‘Ocean Viking’, what was the outcome of these meetings and to what extent has the frequency of ‘technical meetings’ increased in comparison to the first three quarters of 2025?

The so-called Libyan coastguard claimed to have merely fired warning shots and accused the non-governmental organisation of collaborating with traffickers. In a meeting with the EU Ambassador, representatives from the Libyan Tripoli Government claimed that the shooting was compliant with the rules in place. The incident was discussed in the framework of the memorandum of understanding between Italy and the Libyan Tripoli Government on the supply and deployment of ships. The Libyan Tripoli Government stated that an investigation had been launched and, at the insistence of EU representatives, indicated that it would announce the results ‘soon’. 1. When and how were these ‘soon’ to be announced results of the Libyan Tripoli Government’s investigation into this incident communicated to the EU, and what do they indicate? 2. What ‘technical meetings’ have taken place with representatives of the Libyan Tripoli Government and the so-called Libyan coastguard to discuss the shots fired at ‘Ocean Viking’, what was the outcome of these meetings and to what extent has the frequency of ‘technical meetings’ increased in comparison to the first three quarters of 2025? (3 September 2026) The EU has not yet received formally the final findings of internal investigations concerning the incident referred to by the Honourable Member. The competent national authorities remain in contact with the flag state of the vessel concerning any legal outcomes and possible implications. The memorandum of understanding between Italy and the Libyan Tripoli Government (1) is a bilateral arrangement between Italy and the Libyan authorities. The Commission is not a party to that memorandum and therefore it is neither responsible for monitoring compliance with its provisions nor for any enforcement or penalty mechanisms it may contain. More generally, in the context of the EU's engagement with Libya, the Commission services and the European External Action Service regularly raise issues relating to human rights and international law with the Libyan authorities. EU support is provided in line with the applicable legal framework and is subject to appropriate monitoring arrangements and safeguards. The incident was discussed during the EU's regular technical exchanges with the Libyan authorities, the latest of which took place in early July 2026. The EU reiterated the importance of conducting maritime operations in full compliance with international law and requested information on the investigation and any follow-up. Additional technical exchanges are held in Tripoli on the basis of operational needs and policy priorities.

E-10-2026-002680.t: Protecting minors online from manipulation, bullying and grooming
qt: to the Commission Magdalena Adamowicz (PPE), Borys Budka (PPE), Bogdan Andrzej Zdrojewski (PPE), Ewa Kopacz (PPE), Robert Biedroń (S&D), Bartłomiej Sienkiewicz (PPE), Seán Kelly (PPE), Tomas Tobé (PPE), Eleonora Meleti (PPE), Maria Walsh (PPE) Subject:

The resolution adopted by Parliament on the need for targeted criminal law provisions and enhanced platform responsibility to address online bullying and harassment highlights the growing risks faced by minors in digital environments. Parliament calls for cyberbullying to be classified as a particularly serious crime with a crossborder dimension and stresses the need to effectively enforce platforms’ obligations under the Digital Services Act (DSA), in particular Article 28 thereof, including those relating to ingame chat and voice communication tools where minors may be exposed to manipulation, exploitation, bullying and grooming. Stakeholders and watchdog organisations warn about the links between online platforms and such risks. The regulatory gap resulting from the pending negotiations on the Child Sexual Abuse Regulation (CSAR) continues to limit detection and prevention mechanisms. 1.
Does the Commission intend to build on Parliament’s resolution and, if so, what additional measures does it envisage to strengthen the safety and protection of minors online?
Does the Commission consider the existing obligations under the DSA sufficient to address the systemic risks faced by minors online, particularly in relation to manipulation, bullying and grooming?
Is the Commission considering additional targeted legislative or enforcement measures aimed at protecting minors online from such risks?
at: (English version) to the Commission Magdalena Adamowicz (PPE), Borys Budka (PPE), Bogdan Andrzej Zdrojewski (PPE), Ewa Kopacz (PPE), Robert Biedroń (S&D), Bartłomiej Sienkiewicz (PPE), Seán Kelly (PPE), Tomas Tobé (PPE), Eleonora Meleti (PPE), Maria Walsh (PPE) (29 June 2026) Subject: Protecting minors online from manipulation, bullying and grooming The resolution adopted by Parliament on the need for targeted criminal law provisions and enhanced platform responsibility to address online bullying and harassment highlights the growing risks faced by minors in digital environments. Parliament calls for cyberbullying to be classified as a particularly serious crime with a cross-border dimension and stresses the need to effectively enforce platforms’ obligations under the Digital Services Act (DSA), in particular Article 28 thereof, including those relating to in-game chat and voice communication tools where minors may be exposed to manipulation, exploitation, bullying and grooming. Stakeholders and watchdog organisations warn about the links between online platforms and such risks. The regulatory gap resulting from the pending negotiations on the Child Sexual Abuse Regulation (CSAR) continues to limit detection and prevention mechanisms. 1. Does the Commission intend to build on Parliament’s resolution and, if so, what additional measures does it envisage to strengthen the safety and protection of minors online? 2. Does the Commission consider the existing obligations under the DSA sufficient to address the systemic risks faced by minors online, particularly in relation to manipulation, bullying and grooming? 3. Is the Commission considering additional targeted legislative or enforcement measures aimed at protecting minors online from such risks? (11 September 2026) The Commission takes good note of the resolution. The protection of minors online is addressed under the existing legal and policy framework. Under the Digital Services Act (DSA) (1), providers of online platforms accessible to minors are required to ensure a high level of privacy, safety and security of minors. The Commission also adopted the Guidelines on the protection of minors (2), which set out a non-exhaustive list of measures that the Commission considers that providers of online platforms may implement to comply with these obligations. In addition, very large online platforms must also assess and mitigate systemic risks on their services, including those affecting minors. The Commission is enforcing these rules. In March 2026, for example, the Commission opened formal proceedings against Snapchat. Beyond the DSA, the Commission has adopted the action plan against Cyberbullying (3), focused on protection, awarenessraising, reporting and support. Concerning the classification of cyberbullying as a serious crime, the EU acquis already provides important safeguards and criminal law measures against cyberviolence (4), while additional measures are considered against online public incitement to violence or hatred (5). As regards further action, the Commission will assess the recommendations of the final repor t (6) presented on 13 July 2026 by the co-chairs of the Special Panel on Child Safety Online, with a view to further strengthening children’s safety and participation online. |(⸱1|)∙ |(⸱2|)∙ |(⸱3|)∙ |(⸱4|)∙ |(⸱5|)∙ |(⸱6|)∙

E-10-2026-002679.t: Evasion of European sanctions through Türkiye in the case of machinery produced in Member States for the Russian military supply chain
qt: to the Commission Pina Picierno (Renew), Lucia Yar (Renew), Oihane Agirregoitia Martínez (Renew), Ľubica Karvašová (Renew), Sandro Gozi (Renew), Elisabetta Gualmini (Renew), Lukas Sieper (Renew), Malik Azmani (Renew), Bart Groothuis (Renew), Veronika Cifrová Ostrihoňová (Renew) Subject:

An investigation by IrpiMedia and The Kyiv Independent has revealed that the Turkish company Redwing Metal shipped dual-use machinery produced in Italy and six other EU Member States to Russia in 2023 and 2024, with a total value of nearly EUR 6 million, in violation of the EU sanctions regime1. The goods were delivered to two Russian metallurgical companies in the military sector, AMR and SMK, which produce components for missiles and fighter jets. Sanctions experts agree that the transit of goods through Türkiye constitutes evasion of EU sanctions. Under the strict liability rules introduced in June 2024, European producers are directly responsible for the final destination of their goods. Considering the above, the Commission is asked the following questions: 1.

Does it intend to open an investigation into Redwing Metal’s activities assessing the application of the sanctions provided for under Regulation (EU) No 833/2014 against individuals and entities involved in the evasion of the sanctions regime, including through third countries?

Does it consider that the strict liability rules introduced in 2024 are being sufficiently enforced by Member States against national producers whose goods reach Russia via third countries, and what measures does it intend to adopt to strengthen their enforcement?
What initiatives does it intend to promote to prevent Türkiye and other third countries from continuing to serve as platforms for the evasion of European sanctions?
https://irpimedia.irpi.eu/macchinari-italiani-europei-per-missili-caccia-russi-redwing-metal/.
at: (English version) to the Commission Pina Picierno (Renew), Lucia Yar (Renew), Oihane Agirregoitia Martínez (Renew), Ľubica Karvašová (Renew), Sandro Gozi (Renew), Elisabetta Gualmini (Renew), Lukas Sieper (Renew), Malik Azmani (Renew), Bart Groothuis (Renew), Veronika Cifrová Ostrihoňová (Renew) (29 June 2026) Subject: Evasion of European sanctions through Türkiye in the case of machinery produced in Member States for the Russian military supply chain An investigation by IrpiMedia and The Kyiv Independent has revealed that the Turkish company Redwing Metal shipped dualuse machinery produced in Italy and six other EU Member States to Russia in 2023 and 2024, with a total value of nearly EUR 6 million, in violation of the EU sanctions regime (1). The goods were delivered to two Russian metallurgical companies in the military sector, AMR and SMK, which produce components for missiles and fighter jets. Sanctions experts agree that the transit of goods through Türkiye constitutes evasion of EU sanctions. Under the strict liability rules introduced in June 2024, European producers are directly responsible for the final destination of their goods. Considering the above, the Commission is asked the following questions: 1.

Does it intend to open an investigation into Redwing Metal’s activities assessing the application of the sanctions provided for under Regulation (EU) No 833/2014 against individuals and entities involved in the evasion of the sanctions regime, including through third countries?

Does it consider that the strict liability rules introduced in 2024 are being sufficiently enforced by Member States against national producers whose goods reach Russia via third countries, and what measures does it intend to adopt to strengthen their enforcement?
What initiatives does it intend to promote to prevent Türkiye and other third countries from continuing to serve as platforms for the evasion of European sanctions?

(21 August 2026) The Commission takes very seriously allegations of circumvention of EU restrictive measures (‘sanctions’), which is now a crime under EU law (1) when carried out in the EU. Enforcement of sanctions falls primarily under the responsibility of Member States. Article 12 of Regulation (EU) No 833/2014 (2) prohibits, knowingly and intentionally, the circumvention of sanctions. This complements other measures (3), which require Union operators to contractually prohibit re-exportation to Russia and reexportation for use in Russia of certain sensitive goods and technology. Tackling sanctions circumvention, including through third country jurisdictions, is among the Commission’s key priorities. The Commission monitors trade flows, especially goods on the Common High Priority (4) (CHP) and Economically Critical Goods (5) (ECG) lists, from the EU to third countries considered to be at high risk of being used as a platform for circumvention, and from these countries to Russia. Dual-use goods can be used in military applications or to enhance Russia’s industrial capabilities, which is why in its outreach the EU urges third countries to ban their re-export to Russia. The International Special Envoy for the Implementation of EU Sanctions has visited Türkiye on five occasions. Türkiye has banned the re-export of EU-origin CHP items.

E-10-2026-002678.t: Deterioration of Elene Khoshtaria’s health condition and political persecution in Georgia
qt: to the Commission Pina Picierno (Renew), Nathalie Loiseau (Renew), Lucia Yar (Renew), Dainius Žalimas (Renew), Ľubica Karvašová (Renew), Elisabetta Gualmini (Renew), Dan Barna (Renew), Lukas Sieper (Renew), Malik Azmani (Renew), Veronika Cifrová Ostrihoňová (Renew), Marie-Agnes Strack-Zimmermann (Renew) Subject:

On 24 March 2026, the Tbilisi Court sentenced Elene Khoshtaria, leader of the opposition party Droa, to 18 months’ imprisonment for defacing election posters of the ruling Georgian Dream party as an act of protest in solidarity with an activist who had been arrested for the same action. Amnesty International has described the conviction as politically motivated1. Khoshtaria’s legal team has reported a serious deterioration in her health condition, including severe joint pain, increasing difficulty in moving and an inability to write2. The European Parliament has already acknowledged this situation and the need for specialised medical care in its resolution3, however the Georgian authorities continue to ignore requests for an adequate treatment plan. In the light of the above, can the Commission clarify: 1.

Whether it intends to exert formal pressure on the Georgian authorities to ensure that Khoshtaria receives adequate specialised medical care, in accordance with Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights;

Whether it considers that the sentence imposed on Khoshtaria for a symbolic act of protest constitutes a violation of the right to freedom of expression as protected by the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights;

What concrete measures it intends to take to secure the release of Khoshtaria and other political prisoners, including within the framework of the EU-Georgia dialogue and the instruments provided for under the EU-Georgia Association Agreement.

https://www.amnesty.org/en/latest/news/2026/03/georgia-opposition-politician-elene-khoshtaria-givenpolitically-motivated-prison-sentence-for-graffiti/. 2 https://oc-media.org/jailed-georgian-opposition-politician-khoshtarias-health-deteriorating-lawyersays/. 3 https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/TA-10-2026-0083_EN.html. 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (5.8.2026) The Commission and the European External Action Service (EEAS) have kept Georgia high on their agenda amid democratic backsliding and the deterioration of human rights. The Commission and the EEAS held frequent discussions with Member States in the Foreign Affairs Council. The EU consistently recalls that Georgia must respect, protect and fulfil human rights and fundamental freedoms under international law. In March 2026, the EU suspended visa-free travel for holders of Georgian diplomatic, service, official passports due to persistent breaches of the fundamental rights benchmarks of the EU-Georgia visa-free regime. A technical meeting with the authorities took place on 11 June 2026. Failure to address the 2024–2025 Visa Suspension Mechanism recommendations may lead to further measures. Efforts by the EEAS to resume the Human Rights Dialogue with Georgia have so far not materialised. The Commission condemns the repression of opposition leaders, journalists and civil society and expresses solidarity with all those arbitrarily detained, ill-treated or imprisoned, including Elene Khoshtaria. The Commission appreciates the European Parliament's efforts to keep Georgia’s human rights situation under scrutiny, including through the urgency debate on Ms Khoshtaria's case in March 2026. The EU expects the authorities to ensure adequate medical care in line with Article 3 European Convention on Human Rights and will continue to monitor and raise her case together with those of other arbitrarily detained persons.

E-10-2026-002677.t: The Commission’s shortcomings in implementing the rescEU reserve
qt: to the Commission Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE) Subject:

The European Court of Auditors’ Special Report No 17/2026 on rescEU1 – the EU’s civil protection reserve of strategic assets and stockpiles for when national capacities fall short – highlights several weaknesses in the planning, governance and assessment of EU-funded capacities. In light of this: 1.

How does the Commission justify funding new rescEU capacities without a harmonised methodology that enables the prior assessment of existing national capacities and prevents duplication with national civil protection schemes?

What performance indicators does it intend to put in place in order to objectively assess the cost, mobilisation time and operational added value of rescEU stockpiles, in comparison with the direct mobilisation of assets held by Member States?

Does it intend to make any future development of rescEU conditional on a prior demonstration of its economic and operational effectiveness, in accordance with the recommendations of the European Court of Auditors, in order to ensure the proper use of EU funds and compliance with the principle of subsidiarity?
https://www.eca.europa.eu/ECAPublications/SR-2026-17/SR-2026-17_EN.pdf
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (21.8.2026) The Commission, together with the Member States and participating states of the Union Civil Protection Mechanism (UCPM), undertakes a comprehensive capacity gap analysis, also in relation to existing national capacities1. A common methodology, adapted to the specificities of the different sectors, is applied for such a gap analysis, by gathering data shared by Member States and participating states, as they consider it possible based on the sensitivity of the information. In addition, the Commission continuously analyses the response to the requests for assistance under the UCPM to further assess possible gaps. If new rescEU2 capacities are deemed essential to address these gaps, in agreement with Member States and participating states, the Commission establishes a strategy – in line with the EU Stockpiling Strategy3 – and allocates funds for their development. rescEU's performance is assessed through key indicators, which include timely mobilisation, as well as identification of capacity gaps and critical needs where Member States' capacities are unavailable or insufficient. Mobilisation timelines4 are tailored to the assistance’s nature, with associated costs covered by the Commission5. The economic and operational effectiveness of the existing capacities is a key condition for the future development of rescEU. To ensure that the standards of performance are preserved and further strengthened, the Commission fully acknowledges the added value of the European Court of Auditors’ recommendations. These insights will be given due consideration for future actions, jointly with Member States and participating states.
1 Including those pre-committed to the European Civil Protection Pool in line with the Regulation (EU)

E-10-2026-002676.t: Meeting between the Commission and a Taliban delegation in Brussels
qt: to the Commission Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE) Subject:

On 23 June 2026, the Commission, together with several Member States, welcomed a Taliban delegation in Brussels to discuss migration issues, notably the return of Afghan migrants to their home country. The Commission explained that these were merely technical discussions. It also points out that the EU does not formally recognise the Taliban regime and continues to condemn the numerous violations of fundamental rights, especially the restrictions on women and girls. 1.
What concrete results were achieved at that meeting, in particular as regards the return of Afghan nationals subject to a return decision?

Does the continuation of these discussions depend on Afghanistan’s de facto authorities cooperating fully with a view to readmitting Afghan nationals subject to return decisions and combating illegal migration networks?
What steps is the Commission taking to ensure that these contacts are not perceived as being a formal recognition or political legitimisation of the Taliban regime?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (10.8.2026) 1. On 23 June 2026, Commission and Sweden, on behalf of interested Member States, cochaired a technical meeting in Brussels with representatives of the de facto authorities of Afghanistan responsible for return and readmission. The meeting followed a letter sent in October 2025 by 20 Ministers from Member States and Schengen associated countries who asked the Commission to coordinate at EU level technical contacts on return and readmission to Afghanistan, with a focus on persons who pose a threat to public order and national security. The discussion contributed to clarifying technical aspects of the different stages of the readmission procedure. 2. There are no concrete plans at this stage for further engagement on this topic with the Afghan de facto authorities at EU level. 3. When the Taliban returned to power in August 2021, the EU adopted a policy of principled engagement with them, as ratified by Council conclusions of September 20211 and March 20232. The EU maintains diplomatic presence in Kabul and speaks to the Afghan de facto authorities in a principled way, without recognising or legitimising them in any manner, on issues pertaining to its key values and interests. The aforementioned technical meeting on returns was within the parameters of the EU’s principled engagement policy. It implies no change in the EU’s policy of not recognising and not legitimising the Afghan de facto authorities.
1 https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/press/press-releases/2021/09/21/afghanistan-council-conclusions-set-out-
the-eu-s-position-and-next-steps/. 2 https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/press/press-releases/2023/03/20/afghanistan-council-approvesconclusions-on-afghanistan/.

E-10-2026-002674.t: Recall of infant formula due to cereulide toxin
qt: to the Commission Lynn Boylan (The Left) Subject:
Early 2026 saw multi-country recalls of infant formula after the toxin cereulide was detected in batches of multiple international brands. In response to these recalls: 1.

Have all Member States classified food poisoning caused by cereulide as a notifiable disease, and have they ensured that notification and guidance have been provided to frontline healthcare professionals, parents and caregivers?

Have all Member States adopted a clinical pathway for investigating and testing cases, including a retrospective analysis of gastrointestinal illness data, and will the Commission publish a consolidated EU-wide epidemiological assessment based on national investigations?

Given that 21 of the 23 Rapid Alert System for Food and Feed (RASFF) notifications related to this incident were classified as ‘potentially serious’, with two issued on 1 May 2026 reclassified as ‘serious’, can the Commission comment as to the reasons for this escalation in risk classification, the additional steps taken in response to the reclassification, and whether it considers the existing RASFF classification framework adequate for incidents involving a product that is the sole source of nutrition for vulnerable infants?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (20.8.2026) 1. At the time of publication of the joint Rapid Outbreak Assessment (ROA) by the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) and the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) on 19 February 2026, which consolidated the available evidence, food poisoning caused by cereulide was not a notifiable disease in most EU/EEA1 countries. The organisation of national disease notification systems and communication of public health guidance are the responsibility of Member States. The ECDC supported Member States by facilitating information exchange through EpiPulse, publishing a European outbreak case definition on 6 March 2026, and providing scientific support. 2. Clinical pathways, diagnostic procedures, and retrospective analyses fall within Member States’ competences. The Commission does not systematically collect information on these measures. At the time of publication of the ROA, cereulide toxin testing in human (faecal) samples was not routinely available in clinical laboratories across Member States. The ECDC supported Member States by providing access to such testing through a contracted laboratory. 3. RASFF2 notifications 2026.38623 and 2026.38634 were submitted by Ireland as alert notifications with a ‘serious risk’ classification. This was a decision of the Irish authorities. These notifications were handled like previous cereulide notifications. All Alert notifications require rapid action by the network.

1 European Economic Area. 2 Rapid Alert System for Food and Feed. 3 https://webgate.ec.europa.eu/rasff-window/screen/notification/841471. 4 https://webgate.ec.europa.eu/rasff-window/screen/notification/841474.

E-10-2026-002673.t: Potential clash between RED II and Italy’s rules governing incentives for renewable energy communities
qt: to the Commission Dario Tamburrano (The Left), Valentina Palmisano (The Left), Cristina Guarda (Verts/ALE) Subject:
Potential clash between RED II and Italy’s rules governing incentives for renewable energy communities

In 2021, Italy transposed Directive (EU) 2018/2001 by means of Legislative Decree No 199/20211. Article 3(2)(b) of the Italian Ministry for the Environment and Energy Security’s2 2024 decree establishing the national incentive scheme for renewable energy communities (RECs) references Articles 30-32 of Legislative Decree No 199/2021, which state that an REC can include completed facilities, including those that were built before its formal establishment. Having been granted the power to lay down the operating rules governing RECs by Article 11 of the aforementioned MASE decree, GSE3 has determined that, provided that they applied for state incentives before 22 June 20244, facilities can join an REC even though they were completed and operational before the latter’s establishment as a legal entity. This means that facilities that were operational before the establishment of their respective RECs that missed the 22 June deadline are not entitled to these incentives. In the light of the above: 1.
Does the Commission not think that the GSE policy outlined above runs counter to the principles of transparency and non-discrimination enshrined in Article 21(6)(e) and Article 22(4)(i) of RED II?
Does the Commission not agree that fostering the growth of RECs (an objective of the Citizens Energy Package) requires the removal of all the administrative barriers that are hampering this process?

at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (26.8.2026) The Commission understands that the Honourable Members are referring to a situation in which a renewable energy source (RES) facility owned by an individual self-consumer is made available to a renewable energy community in view of entering a contract with Gestore Servici Energitici (GSE)1 to benefit from a national incentive scheme for energy sharing within renewable energy communities. However, from a general perspective, it is the Commission’s view that Article 21 (6) e) applies to self-consumers and not to renewable energy communities. Article 22 (4) i) refers to members of renewable energy communities in their role as consumers and not to members of renewable energy communities who are producers/owners of a renewable energy facility. Article 22 of the Renewable Energy Directive (RED) II lays down the obligations for Member States in relation to the promotion of renewable energy communities through rights as well as an enabling framework, including the removal of unjustified regulatory and administrative barriers to renewable energy communities. E-10-2026-002672.t: Revision of Regulation (EU) 2020/1201 on Xylella fastidiosa in the light of new scientific evidence
qt: to the Commission Michele Picaro (ECR) Subject:
Revision of Regulation (EU) 2020/1201 on Xylella fastidiosa in the light of new scientific evidence

Xylella fastidiosa’s epidemiological picture has changed dramatically since the bacterium was first detected in Europe more than a decade ago. Monitoring efforts in the EU have identified a number of Xylella subspecies and genotypes which attack different host plants and are characterised by a range of aggression and risk profiles. An example is the situation in Italy, where the impact of certain Xylella fastidiosa variants on agriculture is minor – if not downright negligible – compared to the devastation wrought on the Salento area’s olive crops by subspecies pauca Sequence Type 53. Yet the measures implemented under Regulation (EU) 2020/1201 continue to push a one-size-fits-all approach that is not sufficiently tailored to the different subspecies, strains and areas concerned. Given that the Commission gave EFSA until the end of this year to update its risk assessment for Xylella fastidiosa, I ask the Commission: 1.
Will it, in the light of new scientific findings, revise Regulation (EC) No 2020/1201?
Will it adopt measures that are tailored to individual Xylella subspecies and strains, as well as to their established risk profiles?

Is it considering introducing a more flexible model whereby national plant health authorities can, in coordination with the Commission, adopt strategies that are proportionate to the gravity of individual outbreaks and whose economic repercussions do not outweigh the actual plant health risks involved?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.9.2026) The Commission confirms that it mandated the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) to update the risk assessment for Xylella fastidiosa (M-2024-000291). It explicitly requested from EFSA to update the risk assessment by subspecies of Xylella fastidiosa present in the EU, as well as to consider different scenarios and relevant risk reduction options. The output of EFSA in response to this mandate is expected by the end of 2026. On the basis of the information provided by EFSA, the Commission intends to open a discussion with Member States at the Standing Committee on Plants, Animals, Food and Feed as regards the phytosanitary measures implemented under Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2020/12012, including whether these measures can be more closely tailored to the risk profiles of individual subspecies and strains, and whether further flexibility is warranted to allow for measures that are proportionate to the severity of individual outbreaks.

E-10-2026-002671.t: Allowing advanced practice nurses to renew or adapt treatments
qt: to the Commission Christophe Clergeau (S&D) Subject:

EU Member States are increasingly using advanced practice nurses to address challenges in access to care, continuity of care and the management of chronic diseases. In some Member States, questions remain as to whether these professionals, where provided for in their national legislation, are able to renew or adapt treatments covered by a marketing authorisation granted under the EU centralised procedure. However, according to Article 168 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, the organisation and delivery of health services, and the definition of the competences of health professionals, are primarily the responsibility of the Member States. 1.

Does the Commission consider that Regulation (EC) No 726/2004 and Directive 2001/83/EC preclude a Member State from authorising advanced practice nurses, within the framework of their national competences, to renew or adapt treatments with a centralised marketing authorisation?
Does it intend to clarify this point to ensure uniform application of EU law and promote continuity of care in the Member States?
at: (English version) to the Commission Christophe Clergeau (S&D) (29 June 2026) Subject: Allowing advanced practice nurses to renew or adapt treatments EU Member States are increasingly using advanced practice nurses to address challenges in access to care, continuity of care and the management of chronic diseases. In some Member States, questions remain as to whether these professionals, where provided for in their national legislation, are able to renew or adapt treatments covered by a marketing authorisation granted under the EU centralised procedure. However, according to Article 168 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, the organisation and delivery of health services, and the definition of the competences of health professionals, are primarily the responsibility of the Member States. 1. Does the Commission consider that regulation (EC) No 726/2004 and Directive 2001/83/EC preclude a Member State from authorising advanced practice nurses, within the framework of their national competences, to renew or adapt treatments with a centralised marketing authorisation? 2. Does it intend to clarify this point to ensure uniform application of EU law and promote continuity of care in the Member States? (21 August 2026) The EU pharmaceutical legislation, in particular Regulation (EC) No 726/2004 (1) and Directive 2001/83/EC (2), does not preclude a Member State, acting within the framework of its national competences, from allowing advanced practice nurses to renew or adjust treatments involving a medicinal product that has a centralised marketing authorisation. The aforementioned EU legislative acts govern the authorisation, supervision and placing on the market of medicinal products and do not regulate the activities of healthcare professionals. The proposed reform of the EU pharmaceutical legislation (3), which is expected to enter into force by the end of 2026, is designed to complement the current authorisation framework by strengthening the generation and use of real-world evidence throughout the lifecycle of medicines, thereby supporting treatment optimisation while maintaining the high standards of quality, safety and efficacy of medicinal products. At the same time, by clarifying regulatory obligations and reinforcing the common EU framework, the new pharmaceutical legislation will help ensure the uniform application of EU legislation. However, continuity of care and the organisation of healthcare services, including prescribing and treatment renewal practices, remain primarily the responsibility of the Member States.

E-10-2026-002669.t: Renewal of the Manfredonia fisheries’ transparent goby management plan
qt: to the Commission Michele Picaro (ECR) Subject:

Transparent goby fishing is a traditional and seasonal endeavour that is particularly important to the economy of the Gulf of Manfredonia. According to reports, the scientists tasked with reviewing the proposed transparent goby management plan hold that the new scheme is an improvement over current arrangements, though they have also requested that DG MARE carry out further assessments. The failure to renew the management plan would be a further blow to jobs in the area and the local economy, and would have a direct bearing on the livelihoods of more than 120 fishers and on the future of around 60 vessels and a number of related businesses. In the light of the new data gathered by Italian researchers, including as regards fishing methods, and given the seasonal nature of transparent goby fishing, I ask the Commission: 1.
Will its assessment also take into account the important socio-economic role that transparent goby fishing plays for Manfredonia’s community and maritime economy?
What additional technical conditions or management measures does the management plan for 2025-2028 need to include in order to ensure that it is renewed?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (2.9.2026) The Commission is aware of the socio-economic importance of the transparent goby fishery for Manfredonia’s community and maritime economy. However, the Commission may grant a derogation from the prohibition to use towed gears set out in Article 13(1) of Regulation (EC) No 1967/2006 only if a number of the conditions set out in Article 13(5) and (9) are fulfilled. Based on the latest Scientific, Technical and Economic Committee for Fisheries (STECF) scientific evaluation1 of 2025, the Commission considers it necessary that a revised management plan addresses the concerns of STECF communicated through previous evaluations. The ongoing experimental fishery, notified by Italy and aimed at collecting more information, could help address the outstanding technical points raised by STECF. In addition, the revised management plan should provide sufficient monitoring, control and surveillance to ensure that the fishing operations concerned are conducted exclusively with boat seines, as defined in Article 2.1(ii) of Regulation (EC) No 1967/2006. The Commission may ask STECF to carry out a further evaluation of an updated management plan containing the main missing elements and management measures identified above.
