E-10-2026-002668.t: The Polish Government’s sluggishness in implementing EU measures on the collection and sharing of data on short-term rentals
qt: to the Commission Piotr Müller (ECR) Subject:

Regulation (EU) 2024/1028 of the European Parliament and of the Council on data collection and sharing relating to short-term accommodation rental services entered into force on 20 May 2026, introducing a harmonised legal framework to make the sector more transparent throughout the European Union. Because Donald Tusk’s government has not yet drafted or implemented the relevant alignment legislation, Poland currently has no statutory regulations of its own to bring these EU measures into force. 1.
Is the Commission monitoring the delays in implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/1028 in Poland and the current lack of legislative action on the part of the Polish authorities?

If the required national legislation is not implemented on time, does the Commission plan to initiate proceedings against Poland for failing to fulfil its obligations as a Member State (infringement procedure)?
What consequences does the Polish Government’s inaction in this area have when it comes to the coherence of the internal market and the effectiveness of data-sharing with online platforms?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (21.8.2026) Regulation (EU) 2024/10281 (the Short-Term Rental (STR) Regulation) establishes a harmonised framework for the exchange of data between STR platforms and the competent authorities of the Member States. The data collected under the Regulation are intended to support Member States in designing appropriate and proportionate measures concerning the STR Regulation. The Regulation harmonises registration schemes and for data-sharing requirements concerning online STR platforms, where Member States decide to put in place such schemes or requirements. However, Member States remain free not to request data from platforms, for example where they do not intend to adopt legislation regulating or restricting the provision of short-term rental services. In light of the specific nature of the STR Regulation, which has been into effect since 20 May 2026, the Commission is monitoring its implementation to ensure the establishment of a harmonised and interoperable system enabling Member States' competent authorities to receive reliable and complete data while allowing platforms to comply with a single legal framework. However, the Commission has no power to require Member States that do not impose registration requirements to make use of the Regulation or to initiate infringement proceedings. That said, to promote the coherence of the internal market and ensure the effectiveness of the data-sharing framework established by the STR Regulation, the Commission continues to encourage all Member States to implement and make effective use of the Regulation.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=OJ:L_202401028.

E-10-2026-002667.t: Abolition of the Hungarian Constitutional Court’s power to issue preliminary opinions on EU-related matters
qt: to the Commission Enikő Győri (PfE), Tamás Deutsch (PfE), Kinga Gál (PfE), Csaba Dömötör (PfE), András László (PfE), Pál Szekeres (PfE), Annamária Vicsek (PfE), Viktória Ferenc (PfE), András Gyürk (PfE), Ernő Schaller-Baross (PfE), György Hölvényi (PfE) Subject:

The Tisza Party’s parliamentary majority has adopted a legislative package which, according to the Hungarian Government, was necessary for Hungary to unlock EU funds currently being withheld. The law repeals Section 1(c) and Subtitle 16/A of Act CLI of 2011, which empowered the Constitutional Court to issue preliminary interpretative opinions under the Fundamental Law on Hungary’s constitutional order, sovereignty, national identity, constitutional traditions and fundamental rights. During a session of the Hungarian Parliament’s Committee on European Affairs, the Parliamentary State Secretary for Justice stated that all amendments in the package resulted from consultations with the Commission. Given that this repeal directly affects Hungary’s constitutional order, while its link to the protection of the EU’s financial interests remains unclear: 1.

Did the Commission, during negotiations with the new Hungarian Government, request the repeal of Section 1(c) and Subtitle 16/A of Act CLI of 2011, or make the disbursement of EU funds conditional, in any way, on such a repeal?

If it did, what is the legal basis in EU law for such a request and what is the direct link between this requirement, the protection of the EU’s financial interests and the conditions for access to EU funds?
If not, how does the Commission assess the Hungarian Government’s claim?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (7.9.2026) In the spirit of sincere cooperation, the Commission has exchanged with the Hungarian government. The technical discussions concerned open issues in various domains, including procedures to protect the EU’s financial interests from rule of law breaches and corruption risks. As announced on 29 May 20261, the Commission and the Hungarian authorities agreed on a robust architecture to ensure that Hungary addresses corruption and rule of law concerns to access Union funding currently on hold under different procedures. The Hungarian government is treating the reforms needed as a top priority. It is for Hungary to submit (i) a written notification under the Conditionality Regulation2, (ii) a first payment request under the Resilience and Recovery Fund Regulation3 and (iii) its positive self-assessment on the fulfilment of the Charter horizontal enabling condition of the Common Provisions Regulation4, for the Commission to assess the reforms under the respective legal frameworks and, in the case of the Conditionality procedure, the Council to lift the measures. The Commission does not comment on Member States’ internal legislative processes or negotiations, including the dialogue between the government and the parliament.

E-10-2026-002666.t: Granting pre-accession benefits to candidate countries and compatibility with the Treaties
qt: to the Commission Stanisław Tyszka (ESN) Subject:

According to Politico, the Commission is currently preparing a ‘gradual integration’ framework for candidate countries. This mechanism would allow selected economic benefits to be granted to candidate countries even before they formally accede. More specifically, this would include access to certain EU funding programmes, trade preferences and partial access to the single market. This may be particularly relevant in the case of Ukraine, whose accession process may take many years. Article 49 TEU sets out the Treaty procedure for accession to the Union, requiring the unanimous agreement of the Member States and ratification in accordance with their constitutional requirements. Granting candidate countries, especially Ukraine, benefits similar to membership outside this procedure could represent a significant departure from the current system and have serious legal, budgetary and economic implications. 1.

What specific legal basis in the Treaties does the Commission consider sufficient to grant candidate countries, especially Ukraine, partial access to the single market, EU programmes and EU funds before accession?
How will the Commission ensure that ‘gradual integration’ does not lead to a circumvention of Article 49 TEU or to a de facto predetermination of Member States’ decisions on Ukraine’s accession?
Will the Commission publish a legal assessment of the compatibility of this framework with the Treaties before presenting specific measures?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (13.8.2026) The Commission considers Article 217 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union to provide the legal basis for concluding association agreements with third countries, including candidate countries, establishing reciprocal rights and obligations, common action and special procedures. In Ukraine’s case, the Association Agreement1, in force since 2017, already provides the basis for access to parts of the single market, subject to strict conditions, such as alignment with the EU acquis indicated in the Agreement. One example is Ukraine’s access to the EU-Roam-Like-at-Home area as of January 2026. In addition, there are several cases in which EU law already provides for the sectoral opening of the single market on the basis of specific third-country regimes, subject to the conditions laid down in the EU acquis. As regards EU funds and programmes, participation is based on bilateral agreements with the candidate countries. Under Article 49 of the Treaty on European Union (TEU), accession remains a single, comprehensive process based on full acceptance of the rights and obligations of membership. Any pre-accession sectoral integration serves only to support convergence and preparation, in the EU’s interest; it neither replaces nor prejudges accession. The process remains fully governed by Article 49 TEU, with Member States in the Council deciding unanimously on each key step, including the opening of clusters, the closing of chapters and, ultimately, accession itself. Any specific gradual integration measure will be assessed in accordance with the applicable legal regime and considering the conditions set out therein. Where a measure requires a bilateral agreement, the legal basis will be set out in that agreement with the enlargement partner.
1 Consolidated text: Association Agreement between the European Union and the European Atomic Energy
Community and their Member States, of the one part, and Ukraine, of the other part; http://data.europa.eu/eli/agree_internation/2014/295/2025-10-29.

E-10-2026-002665.t: Mass regularisation of migrants in Spain, Schengen and the migration pact
qt: to the Commission Stanisław Tyszka (ESN) Subject:

Spain has launched a procedure to regularise the stay of third-country nationals illegally staying in its territory. The procedure runs until the end of June 2026. People who receive a Spanish residence permit will be able to move within the Schengen area on a short-term basis and apply for EU long-term resident status after five years of legal residence. During a debate in the European Parliament on 10 February 2026, Commissioner Magnus Brunner pointed out that regularisation is a national competence, but that decisions by one country must not be to the detriment of other Member States. Regulation (EU) 2024/1351, a key element of the migration pact, establishes a mandatory solidarity mechanism covering relocations, financial contributions and other measures. 1.

How will the Commission reconcile Commissioner Brunner’s position with the scale of the regularisation in Spain, which, a few days before the procedure ended, had risen to more than 900 000 applications, far exceeding the Sánchez government’s original estimate of around 500 000, and which may have significant implications for the entire Schengen Area?
Does the Commission have an estimate of how many beneficiaries of this procedure can obtain EU long-term resident status and move to other Member States?

Why should the unilateral mass regularisation of migrants in Spain be treated as a national matter, when countries that refuse to relocate migrants or make financial contributions under the migration pact are deemed by the Commission to be not acting in solidarity?
at: (English version) to the Commission Stanisław Tyszka (ESN) (26 June 2026) Subject: Mass regularisation of migrants in Spain, Schengen and the migration pact Spain has launched a procedure to regularise the stay of third-country nationals illegally staying in its territory. Regulation (EU) 2024/1351, a key element of the migration pact, establishes a mandatory solidarity mechanism covering relocations, financial contributions and other measures. 1. Does the Commission have an estimate of how many beneficiaries of this procedure can obtain EU long-term resident status and move to other Member States? 3. Why should the unilateral mass regularisation of migrants in Spain be treated as a national matter, when countries that refuse to relocate migrants or make financial contributions under the migration pact are deemed by the Commission to be not acting in solidarity? (11 September 2026) The Commission refers to its replies to the questions: E-000366/2026 (1); E-000405/2026 (2); E-000522/2026 (3); and E001628/2026 (4). In these replies, the Commission explained that decisions to regularise third-country nationals illegally staying in a Member State are a national competence. E-10-2026-002664.t: Glorification of the UPA and European values in Ukraine’s accession process
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (19.8.2026) The EU is founded on the values set out in Article 2 of the Treaty on European Union, including respect for human dignity, human rights, democracy, equality and the rights of persons belonging to minorities. These values also underpin the accession process. The Commission assesses compliance of Ukraine with the accession criteria on the basis of the established framework, including the political criteria relating to the stability of institutions guaranteeing democracy, the rule of law, human rights and respect for and protection of minorities. The Commission reports regularly on Ukraine’s progress in the context of the enlargement process. Issues pertaining to historical interpretation, remembrance policies and commemorative practices are first and foremost matters under national competence to be addressed in a spirit of dialogue, responsibility and good relations with neighbours. In this context, the Commission encourages all efforts aimed at dialogue, reconciliation, and the respectful commemoration of all victims. The Commission will continue to assess Ukraine’s overall compliance with the accession criteria, in line with the established methodology for enlargement.

E-10-2026-002663.t: Risk of an Member State contributions increasing in the future MFF
qt: to the Commission Stanisław Tyszka (ESN) Subject:

In July 2025, the Commission put forward a proposal for the 2028-2034 multiannual financial framework (MFF) worth almost EUR 2 trillion. The next MFF is expected to tackle the repayment period of NextGenerationEU (NGEU) debt, pressure to establish new own resources and the possible further enlargement of the European Union. This entails a risk of a permanent increase in the EU’s budget, further transfers of funds from Member States to the Commission, and a reduction in the budgetary sovereignty of nation states. In connection with the above: 1.

Has the Commission prepared an alternative 2028-2034 MFF to finance EU priorities without creating new own resources and without increasing Member States’ contributions, in particular by reducing or reallocating existing expenditure?

Has the Commission included the possibility of Ukraine joining the EU in 2028-2034 in the draft MFF and, in particular, the impact of this on common agricultural policy and cohesion policy expenditure?

What are the Commission’s estimates of the costs of servicing and repaying NGEU debt over the 2028-2034 MFF period, and does the Commission envisage covering them by reducing EU spending instead of through new own resources or higher contributions from Member States?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (17.8.2026) The Commission’s proposal for the next Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) 2028-2034 steers funding to EU political priorities, delivering results that national budgets cannot achieve alone. Moreover, the EU must adopt a modern and diversified revenue stream, funding its priorities while limiting national contributions to the EU budget. Compared to 2027, average annual national contributions over 2028-2034 at the EU level (in 2025 prices) are expected to remain stable due to the proposed new own resources package (NOR)1. The Commission cannot prejudge the timeline of enlargement, which is merit-based and depends on each candidate's progress. The proposed MFF ensures the EU is ready for future geopolitical challenges and enlargement. This includes reinforced external action funding through Global Europe2 and unwavering support for Ukraine. In the event of EU accessions, the MFF shall be revised in accordance with the relevant Accession Treaties to reflect the related expenditure needs. Repayment of the liabilities related to the financing of NextGenerationEU (NGEU) nonrepayable support will start in 2028. The Own Resources Decision3 requires that it is fully repaid by 2058. The Commission proposed a fixed annual amount of EUR 24 billion in current prices for the debt service of NGEU affecting the EU budget, between 2028-2034, including both the interest and the principal. Future refinancing costs will set the exact split between interest and principal repayment. This approach ensures predictability for budgetary planning and for Member States’ contributions to the EU budget. As foreseen in the 2020 Interinstitutional Agreement4, NOR aim to repay the NGEU borrowing without placing undue burden on Member States’ national contributions.

E-10-2026-002662.t: Copenhagen economic criteria and Ukraine’s EU accession
qt: to the Commission Stanisław Tyszka (ESN) Subject:

One of the Copenhagen criteria is the existence of a functioning market economy and the capacity to cope with competitive pressure in the EU. The Commission’s assessment its 2025 report was that Ukraine was merely ‘at some level of preparation’ in establishing a functioning market economy and between ‘an early stage of preparation’ and ‘having some level of preparation’ to cope with competitive pressure on the EU market. At the same time, Ukraine is still operating under wartime conditions, with high deficits, growing debt, a dependency on external financing, currency restrictions and problems with competition, state ownership and the influence of large economic groups. In light of the above: 1.
What measurable criteria must Ukraine meet for the Commission to recognise it as a functioning market economy fit for EU membership?
Does the Commission consider it acceptable to proceed with accession while Ukraine’s budget remains structurally dependent on external grants, loans and the EU’s extraordinary financial instruments?

(17 August 2026) For the existence of a functioning market economy, Ukraine should demonstrate continued macroeconomic stability, notably by preserving monetary and exchange-rate stability while gradually easing foreign-exchange restrictions. E-10-2026-002656.t: Eliminating double taxation for EU investors
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.8.2026) The FASTER Directive (EU) 2025/501 resolves practical obstacles within the EU by standardising and making more efficient and fraud-proof withholding tax refund procedures, thereby attracting investment to and within the EU and reinforcing the Savings and Investments Union. Member States will have an option to maintain their existing comprehensive relief-at-source system for dividends on publicly traded shares in place, provided their market capitalisation ratio is below 1.5%. In the light of this, the Commission currently does not envisage the introduction of a standardised or largely automated EU-wide ‘relief-at-source’ procedure before 2030. Regarding further measures the Commission has recently proposed the Taxation Omnibus Directive2 to abolish withholding taxes on cross-border payments of dividends, interest and royalties between EU companies. This measure will strengthen the Single Market, enhance the competitiveness of European businesses, and support the development of the Savings and Investments Union by improving the free movement of capital across the EU. In addition, the scope of the Parent-Subsidiary Directive will be extended to pension institutions, enabling them to benefit from withholding tax exemptions on dividends received from other Member States. Finally, in 2025, the Commission issued a Recommendation on Savings and Investment Accounts3, which promotes tax simplification to boost investment accessibility.

E-10-2026-002654.t: Consistent rail passenger rights across the EU
qt: to the Commission Sophia Kircher (PPE) Subject:

Regulation (EU) 2021/782 has further harmonised and strengthened rail passengers’ rights in the European Union. It lays down passengers’ rights in the event of delays and train cancellations, including requirements for railway undertakings to provide information as well as support services such as meals and, where necessary, accommodation. While these rules are applicable throughout the EU, there are significant differences when it comes to their practical implementation in the Member States, particularly with regard to the scope and provision of passenger support services. 1.

How does the Commission view the implementation and enforcement of this regulation in the Member States, particularly as regards the interpretation of the terms ‘practically available’ and ‘where practically possible’, and what is being done to ensure that railway undertakings document extraordinary circumstances coherently in accordance with Article 19(10) (‘force majeure’), to ensure that passengers can scrutinise any rejection of their compensation claims?

How does the Commission plan to ensure consistency in national implementation and interpretation practices for this regulation, particularly given the existing exceptions for regional and suburban services in individual Member States?

In the Commission’s view, what are the minimum requirements for passenger care and support in the event of prolonged service disruptions or emergencies, particularly as regards the provision of food, drinking water and emergency packs on trains – which some Member States and rail undertakings already do?

While these rules are applicable throughout the EU, there are significant differences when it comes to their practical implementation in the Member States, particularly with regard to the scope and provision of passenger support services. 1. How does the Commission view the implementation and enforcement of this regulation in the Member States, particularly as regards the interpretation of the terms ‘practically available’ and ‘where practically possible’, and what is being done to ensure that railway undertakings document extraordinary circumstances coherently in accordance with Article 19(10) (‘force majeure’), to ensure that passengers can scrutinise any rejection of their compensation claims? 2. How does the Commission plan to ensure consistency in national implementation and interpretation practices for this regulation, particularly given the existing exceptions for regional and suburban services in individual Member States? 3. (13 August 2026) 1. It is for the Member States and in particular their National Enforcement Bodies (NEBs ) (1) to closely monitor compliance with Regulation (EU) 2021/782 (2) and to take the measures necessary to ensure that the rights of passengers are upheld, including with regard to Article 19(10) of the regulation. With a view to a harmonised implementation and enforcement of the regulation, the Commission organises expert group meetings, where NEBs of all Member States exchange their experiences on enforcement practices, emerging issues and possible solutions. At the same time, if NEBs and Member States do not correctly implement and apply the EU rules on passenger rights the Commission may decide to take appropriate action. 2. In its recent Report on the implementation and the results of this regulation (3), the Commission found that the pattern of exemptions has become more structured and more limited than under the previous Regulation. While derogations do still exist, especially for urban, suburban and regional services, they are now more often targeted, time-limited and specific to certain provisions. This indicates a gradual narrowing of exemptions and a corresponding expansion of the regulation’s effective scope in practice. 3. The Commission would like to refer to Article 20 of the regulation, which defines the minimum requirements for passenger care in the form of refreshments, meals and accommodation, as well as support in the event of major disruptions.

qt: to the Commission Dimitris Tsiodras (PPE) Subject:

The number of low-value packages imported in 2025 stood at around 6 billion, making checks thereon practically impossible. The lion’s share of these packages were purchased through non-EU platforms and a large portion of them may not comply with EU rules. This poses a significant threat to the health and safety of consumers, who are confronted with imported products such as dangerous toys for children and articles containing dangerous metals. Indeed, 2025 saw the highest number of alerts (4 671) for unsafe products in the European Rapid Alert System. What steps will it take until the hub becomes operational and how will it contribute to increasing the use of artificial intelligence to make the management of these packages more effective?

(24 September 2026) 1. Addressing the challenges of non-compliant products imported from third countries via e-commerce is a key objective of the Commission, which continues to implement the actions set out in the communication on e-commerce (1). On 1 July 2026 (2), the EU abolished the EUR 150 duty exemption and introduced a temporary EUR 3 customs duty to low value e-commerce items. This is a transitional solution until the EU e-commerce Data Hub is operational, after which customs duties will be calculated on the product’s tariff classification, origin and value. From November 2026, an EU handling fee will apply to address the scaling costs of supervising the large amounts of e-commerce parcels. The EU e-commerce Data Hub that will operate under EU Customs Authority as of July 2028 will centralise (customs) data for all imports within a secure EU sovereign space accessible to other enforcement authorities and will use AI tools. The Commission has also made available to market surveillance authorities new AI that detect dangerous products already listed in the Safety Gate and perform automated searches for potentially non-compliant products on online marketplaces. 2. A key component of the forthcoming Single Market and Customs Programme is strengthening market surveillance. The Commissions plans to enhance cooperation between national market surveillance and customs authorities through coordinated enforcement, improved information exchange, shared digital tools and closer operational links, enabling authorities to target high-risk consignments more effectively.

E-10-2026-002650.t: The unacceptable ban on Soviet and anti-fascist symbols in Germany and the Baltic states
qt: to the Commission Kostas Papadakis (NI) Subject:

The authorities in Germany and the Baltic states banned the ‘display’ and posting of Soviet and anti-fascist symbols during the 9 May celebrations to mark Victory Over Fascism Day. The flawed reasoning behind the decision hinges on the ‘law on freedom of assembly’, a right eradicated by this very ban. Based on unfounded claims, this reasoning attempts to equate capitalist Russia with the Soviet Union, where a different socioeconomic system had been achieved. The use of Soviet symbols is interpreted in a completely arbitrary manner as a sign of support for Russia’s ‘expansionist military ambitions’. At a time when the EU is taking billions from the pockets of the people and pumping it into the war economy, anticommunism and the distortion of History are being exploited to the full. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

What view does it take of the unacceptable ban, in its Member States (namely Germany and the Baltic States), on the use of Soviet and anti-fascist symbols at events held around the world to mark Victory Over Fascism Day?

How does it view the distortion of historical truth for the sake of serving war propaganda, in which the EU also plays an active role, and getting the people to take sides in the imperialist slaughterhouse against the peoples in Ukraine?

Where does it stand on the urgent need to protect the historical monuments of the peoples’ anti-fascist struggle , which are currently in imminent danger from vandalism and other unacceptable acts of desecration by fascist gangs, encouraged by unacceptable bans such as the one in question?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (28.9.2026) Freedom of assembly and association is a fundamental right enshrined in the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights (the Charter). Together with freedom of expression and information, it is a cornerstone of a free and democratic society. In line with its Article 51(1), the Charter applies to Member States only when they are implementing EU law. As regards events related to commemorating victory over Nazi Germany on 8 or 9 May, the rules fall primarily within the competence of the Member States, which should exercise this competence in conformity with their international human rights obligations, notably the European Convention on Human Rights. Compliance with the Convention is assessed by national courts and, ultimately, by the European Court of Human Rights. Regarding cultural heritage, the Commission considers the safeguarding of all forms of cultural heritage with the utmost importance. However, the EU has no specific competence in this field. The preservation, conservation and promotion of all forms of cultural heritage are primarily the responsibility of the Member States.

E-10-2026-002649.t: AI models and digital advertising: protecting media publishers’ revenues
qt: to the Commission Laurence Farreng (Renew), Sabine Verheyen (PPE) Subject:

The rise of AI-powered interfaces is radically transforming the digital advertising landscape. OpenAI entered the advertising market in February 2026 and announced this week, at the Cannes Lions festival, that it is now ‘clearly established in the advertising sector’. Google has stated its intention to integrate advertisements into Gemini in 2026. These developments come at a time when media publishers are facing substantial traffic losses. According to Chartbeat data cited by the Reuters Institute, traffic from Google to media publishers fell by 17 % in Europe between 2024 and 2025. The emergence of AI appears to be accelerating the shift in advertising revenue away from media publishers and towards online platforms. 1.

Does the Commission intend to adopt specific regulatory measures governing the entry of AI models into the advertising market, in particular to ensure transparency and prevent a further erosion of advertising revenue at the expense of media publishers?

The review of the Audiovisual Media Services Directive (AVMSD) is scheduled to take place by the end of 2026. Does the Commission plan to use this review to introduce specific provisions ensuring that media publishers can recoup advertising revenue lost to digital platforms and AI?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (6.8.2026) The Commission has launched a call for evidence1 to examine the challenges arising from the use of copyright-protected content, including press publications, by AI models for training and output generation. The call seeks to determine whether further measures are needed to strengthen transparency, licensing and enforcement, fully taking into account the existing EU acquis, including the copyright-related transparency obligations under the AI Act2, as well as the Copyright Directive3 which provides for text and data mining exceptions relevant to AI and harmonises the legal protection for press publications. The call will seek stakeholder views on whether possible transparency gaps in the AI context exist in order to ensure fair remuneration for creators and support access for AI developers to high-quality data and AI innovations. The Commission is evaluating the Audiovisual Media Services Directive (AVMSD)4 and is preparing a proposal for its review. As part of this process, the Commission aims to further support the economic viability of the EU media sector, notably by strengthening the prominence of media services of general interest and modernising advertising rules to support the sector’s sustainability.

E-10-2026-002647.t: Special fishing arrangements for Iceland in the event of EU accession
qt: to the Commission Emmanouil Fragkos (ECR) Subject:

Iceland is set to hold a referendum on 29 August 2026 on the resumption of negotiations for its accession to the European Union. The fisheries sector is of vital strategic and economic importance to Iceland, and the country has historically insisted on maintaining full sovereign control over its EEZ and fisheries resources. In accordance with Article 49 TEU, any European State seeking to accede to the Union must accept and fully implement the Union acquis. In this context, Chapter 13 (‘Fisheries’) of the accession negotiations requires, in principle, full alignment with the common fisheries policy, unless specific transitional arrangements are agreed during the accession negotiations. Can the Commission confirm that the full implementation of the common fisheries policy is a condition of Iceland’s accession to the European Union and that, at present, no permanent exemptions, special arrangements or opt-outs are envisaged with regard to the implementation of that policy?
at: (English version) to the Commission Emmanouil Fragkos (ECR) (25 June 2026) Subject: Special fishing arrangements for Iceland in the event of EU accession Iceland is set to hold a referendum on 29 August 2026 on the resumption of negotiations for its accession to the European Union. The fisheries sector is of vital strategic and economic importance to Iceland, and the country has historically insisted on maintaining full sovereign control over its EEZ and fisheries resources. In accordance with Article 49 TEU, any European State seeking to accede to the Union must accept and fully implement the Union acquis. In this context, Chapter 13 (‘Fisheries’) of the accession negotiations requires, in principle, full alignment with the common fisheries policy, unless specific transitional arrangements are agreed during the accession negotiations. Can the Commission confirm that the full implementation of the common fisheries policy is a condition of Iceland’s accession to the European Union and that, at present, no permanent exemptions, special arrangements or opt-outs are envisaged with regard to the implementation of that policy? (21 August 2026) On 29 August 2026, the citizens of Iceland will decide, by referendum, whether their country should resume accession negotiations with the European Union. There are currently no discussions with Iceland on fisheries in the context of their possible accession to the EU. A treaty of accession may provide for certain derogations from EU rules applicable to a new Member State. However, pending the outcome of the referendum and any decision to resume accession negotiations, it is premature to comment on any related aspects that might be agreed upon in the context of Iceland’s possible accession to the EU.

E-10-2026-002646.t: EU assistance following the earthquakes in Venezuela
qt: to the Commission Leire Pajín (S&D) Subject:

Two earthquakes – with magnitudes of 7.2 and 7.5 and separated by just 39 seconds – shook northern Venezuela this Wednesday and were also felt in Caracas. The Venezuelan authorities have declared a state of emergency, in the light of collapsed buildings, damage to critical infrastructure, disruption to transport and a possible rise in the number of casualties. A number of countries in the region and Spain have already offered assistance. In view of this situation: 1.
What type of humanitarian, medical or logistical support does the Commission plan to send or fund to help those affected by the earthquakes in Venezuela?

Is the Commission prepared to activate the EU Civil Protection Mechanism if Venezuela so requests to make sure EU assistance reaches the country in a swift, effective and coordinated manner and responds to needs on the ground?

How is the Commission coordinating with the Member States to deliver humanitarian aid to meet the population’s needs arising from the emergency, such as temporary accommodation, food distribution, and health and hygiene measures to prevent the spread of diseases?
at: (English version) to the Commission Leire Pajín (S&D) (25 June 2026) Subject: EU assistance following the earthquakes in Venezuela Two earthquakes — with magnitudes of 7.2 and 7.5 and separated by just 39 seconds — shook northern Venezuela this Wednesday and were also felt in Caracas. The Venezuelan authorities have declared a state of emergency, in the light of collapsed buildings, damage to critical infrastructure, disruption to transport and a possible rise in the number of casualties. A number of countries in the region and Spain have already offered assistance. In view of this situation: 1.
What type of humanitarian, medical or logistical support does the Commission plan to send or fund to help those affected by the earthquakes in Venezuela?

Is the Commission prepared to activate the EU Civil Protection Mechanism if Venezuela so requests to make sure EU assistance reaches the country in a swift, effective and coordinated manner and responds to needs on the ground?

How is the Commission coordinating with the Member States to deliver humanitarian aid to meet the population’s needs arising from the emergency, such as temporary accommodation, food distribution, and health and hygiene measures to prevent the spread of diseases?

(12 August 2026) The Union Civil Protection Mechanism (UCPM) was activated on 25 June 2026 following Venezuela’s request. Through the UCPM, around 750 responders and experts, as well as relief items, have been mobilised from 18 countries. This includes rescue teams, medicines, shelter and a satellite telecommunication platform. The EU’s Copernicus (1) satellite service also provided emergency mapping to support operations on the ground. A European Civil Protection Tea m (2) was deployed to strengthen coordination efforts on the ground. On 15 July 2026, the Commission announced an additional emergency funding of EUR 20 million (3) to support the response to this crisis, in the week that the Commissioner for Equality, Preparedness and Crisis Management visited Venezuela to show EU solidarity. This adds to the EUR 5 million (4) life-saving assistance already approved at the end of June, and to the EUR 52 million allocated at the beginning of the year to respond to the humanitarian consequences of the socioeconomic crisis in Venezuela (5). The Commission is ensuring that ongoing cooperation projects strengthen the humanitarian-development nexus in the current post-earthquake context. Also, three EU Humanitarian Air Bridge flights brought nearly 150 tonnes of essential supplies. Additional flights are planned for the coming weeks. EU humanitarian aid is channelled through partners including United Nations agencies and international non-governmental organisations, within the established humanitarian coordination architecture led by the United Nations Humanitarian Coordinator. For UCPM support, the Commission’s Emergency Response Coordination Centre coordinates with Member States and the Venezuelan authorities to facilitate the delivery of assistance.

E-10-2026-002645.t: Attacks on the memory of the victims of dictatorship in Argentina
qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Anthony Smith (The Left) Subject:

The ‘Our Children Cultural Space’ (ECuNHi – Espacio Cultural Nuestros Hijos), founded by the Mothers of Plaza de Mayo association in Buenos Aires, is an important space dedicated to remembrance, culture and protection of human rights in Argentina. It helps preserve the memory of the victims of Argentina’s military dictatorship and promote truth and justice. For several months, public remembrance policies in Argentina have become weaker, as public funding cuts hit institutions and initiatives dedicated to preserving the memory of crimes committed during the dictatorship. The challenges ECuNHi is facing are part of this worrying trend orchestrated by the revisionist far right that is currently in power. The challenges also come shortly after the death of Taty Almeida, an emblematic figure in the Mothers of Plaza de Mayo association and a tireless human rights activist. In the light of the above: 1.
Does the Vice-President / High Representative condemn any direct or indirect attack on the memory of the victims of the Argentinian dictatorship?

Does the Vice-President / High Representative intend to address this issue in the political dialogue between the EU and Argentina and to recall the importance of preserving sites, institutions and initiatives dedicated to remembrance, truth and justice?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (13.8.2026) The EU is following developments in Argentina closely and has taken note of the current government’s financing decisions in the context of its broader policy of reducing public expenditures and achieving a balanced budget. These decisions have also affected statesponsored policies and activities related to transitional justice and to ‘memory, truth and justice’. The EU strongly promotes the rights to truth and justice as core human rights and reiterates the crucial role of civil society and victims’ organisations in this regard. The EU has also supported several projects addressing truth seeking, justice and memory, including with the Abuelas de Plaza de Mayo. As Argentina marks in 2026 the 50th anniversary of the 1976 military coup, the EU Delegation, together with the embassies of EU Member States, commemorated this date through a joint visit to the Park of Remembrance (Parque de la Memoria) in Buenos Aires on 20 March 2026. The visit paid tribute to the victims of repression, many of them Europeans, while highlighting EU support for democracy, human rights and accountability. The EU remains committed to engaging with all stakeholders through the regular EU-Argentina Human Rights dialogue. This serves as an effective and constructive platform for raising specific concerns, monitoring developments, and supporting the promotion and protection of human rights in the country. The next meeting is planned before the end of the year.

E-10-2026-002644.t: Attacks on the memory of the victims of the dictatorship in Argentina
qt: to the Commission Anthony Smith (The Left) Subject:

The ‘Our Children Cultural Space’ (ECuNHi – Espacio Cultural Nuestros Hijos), set up by the Mothers of Plaza de Mayo association in Buenos Aires, is an important space dedicated to remembrance, culture, education and the promotion of human rights in Argentina. For decades, ECuNHi has helped to preserve the memory of the victims of the military dictatorship and to run cultural and civic activities open to society as a whole. However, following the ideological budget cuts imposed by the Argentinian far-right government, which particularly affect human rights organisations, ECuNHi is currently facing serious financial difficulties. The situation is exacerbated by the worrying condition of the building, which requires urgent infrastructure work to ensure users remain safe and its work can carry on. In view of this, can the Commission say whether EU financial instruments, particular in the fields of culture, historical memory, civil society and fundamental rights, can be accessed by an organisation like ECuNHi?

E-10-2026-002640.t: Transparency and use of EU funds earmarked for safety measures at the former I.A.O. site in Giardinetto Agro (Troia, Foggia)
qt: to the Commission Valentina Palmisano (The Left), Mario Furore (The Left) Subject:

The former Industria Ambientale Organizzata (I.A.O.) site in Giardinetto Agro, in the municipality of Troia (Foggia), is one of the biggest environmental emergencies in Puglia. According to publicly available data, the site covers around 40 hectares, allegedly contains over 300 000 tonnes of waste, and benefits from public funding of around EUR 49 million, including EUR 19.85 million from Italy’s national recovery and resilience plan (NRRP)1. According to recent press reports and tip-offs from the public2, the emergency safety works would seem to have been substantially slowed down or halted since the end of 2025. Despite the considerable use of public money, up-to-date information on the state of progress of the works, how much they are costing and whether they are running to schedule is not easily accessible. In view of the above: 1.
Does the Commission have any information on the progress of the emergency safety works and the reasons for the possible slowdowns or suspensions of activity reported since the end of 2025?
What checks have been carried out on the use of EU and NRRP resources allocated to the project and the reporting thereof?
Does the Commission intend to ask the competent Italian authorities for an updated public report on the state of play, the resources used and the expected timeframe for completing the project?

at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (11.8.2026) The Commission monitors the implementation of the Italian national recovery and resilience plan (RRP) based on the legal requirements outlined in the Annex to the Council Implementing Decision on the approval of the assessment of Italy’s RRP1. Regarding the investment on the remediation of ‘orphan-sites soil’, target M2C4-25 of Italy’s RRP will be assessed in the context of the tenth payment request, expected to be submitted by Italy in September 2026. The target concerns the issuance of certificates of soil remediation2 for 70% of the surface of orphan sites listed in the Action Plan3. The former Industria Ambientale Organizzata site in Giardinetto Agro, in the municipality of Troia (Foggia), is divided into lots. According to the latest Action Plan5, only interventions for lot 2.a are financed by the Italian RRP, for a total of EUR 19.85 million. This lot has a surface of 74 000 square metres. In line with the applicable legal framework of the Recovery and Resilience Facility, Member States must meet all milestones and targets by 31 August 2026, and the Commission must make the final payments by 31 December 2026. Should the Commission assess that any milestone or target is not satisfactorily met, it can take action in line with Article 24 of Regulation (EU) 2021/2416. E-10-2026-002639.t: Development of EU standards for artificial intelligence
qt: to the Commission Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE) Subject:

The 2025 annual report of the European Ombudsman, Teresa Anjinho1, mentions an inquiry being opened into the development of EU standards for artificial intelligence. That inquiry raises questions about the creation of the standards and the people working on them. With the technical standards developed as part of implementing the AI Act being likely to have significant consequences for French and EU businesses, administrations and citizens, the rules in question must surely be developed in a clear manner to increase public trust. In view of the above: 1.

How does the Commission ensure transparency in the process of developing EU standards for artificial intelligence, particularly as regards access to information on participants and their contributions?
How does it make sure there is balanced representation of the different stakeholders participating in the work, including SMEs, researchers, civil society organisations and Member States?
Does it think that the rules could slow down the development of AI in the EU and increase its dependence on the US and China?
https://www.ombudsman.europa.eu/en/publication/en/223854
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.9.2026) European Standardisation Organisations (ESOs) are bound by the provisions on transparency of the Regulation on Standardisation1. If these provisions are not met, the Commission can decide not to cite offered harmonised standards in the Official Journal. There are however no legal requirements on ESOs to disclose to the public information on participants and their contributions, but this information is available for participants of the respective technical committee. Sharing information on specific contributions goes beyond the reporting obligations of ESOs to the Commission. The Commission’s request to the ESOs to develop harmonised standards for the AI Act2 contains, in line with the Regulation on Standardisation3, requirements to facilitate the appropriate representation and effective participation of relevant stakeholders. The ESOs are required to report on the fulfilment of this and other requirements to the Commission every three months. The AI Act lays down a single set of rules for AI in the EU, creating a level playing field for all companies that want to do business in the EU. Only AI systems classified as high-risk AI need to fulfil the requirements for high-risk AI systems. Standards play a key role to provide technical solutions to providers to ensure compliance with the AI Act, to promote innovation as well as competitiveness and growth in the single market. All companies that aim to develop trustworthy AI can benefit from using these standards. Standards will thus help the development of AI in the EU.

E-10-2026-002638.t: Unavailability of EUvsDisinfo in some of the EU’s official languages
qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Tomáš Zdechovský (PPE) Subject:

As part of the fight against foreign information manipulation and disinformation campaigns, the European External Action Service (EEAS) is implementing the EUvsDisinfo project, which aims to identify and counter disinformation spread primarily by actors linked to Russia and China. Although this project is funded by the EU and its stated goal is to strengthen European society’s resilience to disinformation, the EUvsDisinfo website is not available in a number of official EU languages, including Czech and Slovak. Conversely, it offers versions in languages such as Russian, Armenian and Kazakh. 1.
What is the target audience of the EUvsDisinfo project, and on what criteria was the decision to select the website’s language versions based?

How does the Commission assess the fact that citizens of some Member States do not have access to the project’s content in their native language, even though they are one of the main target groups of foreign disinformation campaigns?

Shouldn’t the Commission, in cooperation with the EEAS, ensure that the project is available in all official EU languages so that it can effectively fulfil its stated purpose and reach European citizens who are the targets of disinformation operations?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (10.8.2026) 1. EUvsDisinfo1 is a website that provides information and analysis concerning Russia’s foreign information manipulation and interference (FIMI) activities for a broad audience, including citizens of the EU and the EU's Eastern neighbourhood, as well as policymakers, journalists, researchers and civil society organisations. With this aim, the current language coverage comprises several of the most widely spoken official EU languages, together with languages of the EU's Eastern neighbourhood. 2. The European External Action Service (EEAS) attaches importance to ensuring that awareness of FIMI activities reaches audiences across the EU. The EEAS continues to examine ways of further enhancing the accessibility of the EUvsDisinfo website, including by considering AI-assisted translation technologies, which may enable the gradual expansion of language availability. 3. The EEAS supports efforts to maximise the accessibility and reach of communication on FIMI, both through the languages used, as well as the formats and platforms on which EUvsDisinfo content is made available. In addition, cooperation with authorities and partners in certain Member States has successfully helped extend the reach of EUvsDisinfo content in local languages. Opportunities to further expand the linguistic coverage of EUvsDisinfo, including through AI-assisted translation, are currently under assessment.
1 https://euvsdisinfo.eu/.

E-10-2026-002637.t: Oversight of Recovery and Resilience Facility funding for digitalisation projects in Slovakia
qt: to the Commission Tomáš Zdechovský (PPE) Subject:

Several projects financed under Slovakia’s recovery and resilience plan have recently raised concerns regarding the selection and monitoring of beneficiaries by the Ministry of Investments, Regional Development and Informatization (MIRRI). Media reports1 have highlighted several grants in particular including approximately EUR 1.3 million for an inactive advertisement portal, EUR 1.2 million to Forecast AI and EUR 1.2 million to Biape, as well as funding awarded to other entities including Respilon Slovakia and Foaf. Questions have been raised regarding the operational capacity of beneficiaries, their ownership structures, their arrangements for implementing projects, and their ability to achieve project objectives. In addition, a EUR 90 million project to upgrade the public e-government portal Slovensko.sk has reportedly been suspended following public scrutiny. In the light of the Commission’s responsibility to protect the EU’s financial interests: 1.
Is the Commission aware of these cases and has it assessed whether the relevant projects comply with the requirements of the Recovery and Resilience Facility and the applicable EU financial rules?
Has the Commission identified any red flags, weaknesses in project selection, or risks of irregularities in MIRRI’s management of these funds?
What audits, verifications, corrective measures or financial recoveries are planned or currently being conducted in relation to these projects?

E-10-2026-002636.t: The Baltic Sea as an urgent priority in the European Ocean Pact, one year after the UN Ocean Conference
qt: to the Commission Sofie Eriksson (S&D), Heléne Fritzon (S&D) Subject:

The Baltic Sea is facing not just one challenge, but several interconnected ones: industrial fishing, climate change and nutrient pollution, as well as growing security threats linked to the Russian shadow fleet, unsafe shipping and violations of maritime law. The reality of this threat is illustrated by recent incidents off the coast of Skåne in southern Sweden. Swedish authorities have boarded several vessels suspected of belonging to the shadow fleet, and two ships remain anchored outside Trelleborg. The seafarers on board – numbering in the dozens – are in acute need of basic assistance, including food and water. At the same time, critical underwater infrastructure is increasingly exposed to hybrid threats, cyber risks and sabotage, while unexploded ordnance on the seabed continues to threaten ecosystems and infrastructure. In the European Ocean Pact, the Commission commits to strengthening maritime surveillance, coast guard cooperation, the protection of critical infrastructure, and action to address unexploded ordnance. The question is: what actions have already been taken, and how will the Commission ensure that these commitments are turned into concrete action in the Baltic Sea, with Member States receiving the coordination and technology needed to respond to these multiple threats together?
at: (English version) to the Commission Sofie Eriksson (S&D), Heléne Fritzon (S&D) (25 June 2026) Subject: The Baltic Sea as an urgent priority in the European Ocean Pact, one year after the UN Ocean Conference The Baltic Sea is facing not just one challenge, but several interconnected ones: industrial fishing, climate change and nutrient pollution, as well as growing security threats linked to the Russian shadow fleet, unsafe shipping and violations of maritime law. (13 August 2026) The Commission is consulting Member States and stakeholders in view of preparing an EU Strategy for the safe remediation of unexploded ordnance (UXO) in European Seas. This initiative builds on the results of EU-funded projects, including the ongoing Pilot Project ‘CAMMera ’ (1) and ‘MMineSweeper’ (2), funded by the European Union. These projects are contributing to advancing knowledge, mapping, risk assessment, testing technologies and sharing best practices for safe management of UXO. Moreover, the EU funds several initiatives on innovation in maritime security surveillance technologies, such as ongoing projects ‘SEAGUARD’ (3), ‘BorderForce’ (4), MARCONNECT (5) and ‘CROSSMARE’ (6). On 23 June 2026, the Commission approved two proposals by Member States setting up Regional Cable Hubs (7) in the Baltic and Mediterranean. The Baltic Sea hub received EUR 2.5 million to reinforce national and cross-border operation centres, enhance surveillance, information-sharing, and response capabilities to protect critical maritime infrastructure. Future calls for regional cable hubs will support the establishment of new hubs, reinforce those already launched, and ensure a swift and effective response in emergency situations. On 3 July, the Commission proposed (8) five European Defences Projects of Common Interest (EDPCI) for Council approval. Of these, the ‘Integrated Maritime and Seabed Defence’ project focuses on protecting and monitoring the maritime domain and seabed infrastructure, while ‘Drone and Counter-Drone European Resolve’ will enhance aerial surveillance and protection against unmanned threats.

E-10-2026-002635.t: The Baltic Sea as a priority under the European Ocean Pact and the forthcoming negotiations on fishing quotas
qt: to the Commission Sofie Eriksson (S&D), Heléne Fritzon (S&D) Subject:

The Baltic Sea was identified as an urgent priority in the European Ocean Pact and the Commission organised the high-level ‘Our Baltic’ event in 2025. This event was presented as the starting point for a renewed and more holistic approach to addressing the serious challenges facing the Baltic Sea, including ecosystem degradation, pollution from land and sea and the need for more sustainable fisheries management. Since the ‘Our Baltic’ event, Parliament has adopted its own-initiative report on the Baltic Sea, thereby making its ambitions and expectations of the Commission very clear. However, it remains unclear what concrete next steps the Commission intends to take. 1.
What concrete actions does the Commission intend to take going forward to address ecosystem challenges, pollution, and fisheries management in the Baltic Sea?

In the light of the recently published advice of the International Council for the Exploration of the Sea (ICES), does the Commission intend to advocate for lower fishing quotas in the Baltic Sea next year? Please answer yes or no.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (6.8.2026) 1. The Commission is cooperating with Member States to improve the implementation of the EU environmental legislation, notably the Marine Strategy Framework Directive1 to achieve good environmental status. Within the Helsinki Convention for the Baltic the European Union supports regional commitments to achieve the same goal. The Commission also reinforces the EU’s zero-pollution agenda by targeting nutrient pollution, hazardous chemicals and marine litter, focussing on enforcing rules to reduce pollution at source, as through the evaluation of the Nitrate Directive2 and the revised Urban Wastewater Treatment Directive3. In parallel, the Commission is strengthening the science and knowledge base for action by improving ocean research, data and knowledge through initiatives like OceanEye4. This is intended to support better-informed decisions on pollution, biodiversity and climate, alongside work on an Ocean and Water Research and Innovation Strategy. As regards fisheries management, with the ‘Baltic project’ the International Council for the Exploration of the Sea, its partners and the Commission services work on further improving the scientific advice by widening the considerations covered. A first concrete step is a threeyear research project which aims to build the scientific and operational foundation for ecosystem-based fisheries management in the western Baltic Sea. Moreover, the Commission is committed to continue the rebuilding trajectories for the fishers. 2. For its proposal on the Baltic fishing opportunities for 2027, the Commission will consider all relevant aspects, including ecosystem-based approach to fisheries management, as set out in Article 2 of the Regulation establishing the Common Fisheries Policy5.

E-10-2026-002634.t: EU-US biometric data-sharing agreement and US data protection practice
qt: to the Commission Raquel García Hermida-Van Der Walle (Renew) Subject:

Negotiations between the EU and the United States on the framework agreement regarding the exchange of personal data, including biometric data, for the purpose of screening and identity verification of travellers1, are expected to be concluded soon. According to the Commission, in this context ‘ensur[ing] respect of the EU’s standards on the protection of personal data’ is a ‘key priority’2. This should not only be the case prior to signing an agreement, but also afterwards, in practice. The EU-US Umbrella Agreement, in force since 2017 and intended to improve the overall level of data protection in EU-US law enforcement cooperation, was supposed to be jointly reviewed by 2020. However, six years later, a joint review report has yet to be published. 1.

Why was no joint review of the EU-US Umbrella Agreement published, despite the legal requirement to do so3? If the data protection requirements of that agreement cannot be reviewed or assessed because there are no results to review, and noting the worrying developments in the US regarding the protection of personal data, how does the Commission expect EU citizens to have trust in the US authorities as regards the safety of their transferred biometric data?

Will the Commission ensure that the draft agreement fully incorporates the standards set by the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) in relevant case law4, and if so, is it convinced that the envisaged agreement would hold up in court?

E-10-2026-002632.t: GTA VI physical edition with no disc (video game)
qt: to the Commission Kosma Złotowski (ECR) Subject:
GTA VI physical edition with no disc (video game)

GTA (Grand Theft Auto) is an action-adventure video game series developed by Rockstar Games. It is one of the most successful video game franchises, with GTA V having sold nearly 230 million copies. According to information released by the developer, GTA VI, scheduled for release in November 2026, will cost EUR 79.99. The physical edition will reportedly not contain a game disc, but only a code enabling the digital download of the game. Once activated, the code will be linked to a single user account and cannot be reused or transferred. As traditional physical editions contain a disc that allows both installation and resale of the game, this model would effectively prevent the secondary sale of legally purchased copies. In practice, the so-called physical edition would function as a digital edition, as consumers would be required to register the code and download the game online. This raises concerns regarding consumer rights and ownership of digital products. In the light of the above: 1.
Is the Commission aware of such practices and, if so, what is its position on them, and does it consider this model to raise concerns regarding consumer rights or consumer protection legislation?
Does the Commission have any legal or regulatory instruments to address situations where a product marketed as a physical edition is, in practice, a digital edition?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (2.10.2026) EU consumer law does not prescribe how digital providers should supply their products, which can be online or on physical/tangible data carrier. EU consumer law protects the consumers of digital content and services, such as video games, in all their supply modes. In particular, the consumer is entitled to enjoy a digital content or service, including a video game, that is in conformity with the contractual stipulations and with the consumer’s reasonable expectations as regards its functionality (Directive (EU) 2019/7701). Providers of digital content and services must provide consumers with clear information about the main characteristics and functionality of their products (Directive 2011/83/EU2). Misleading information or omission of material information that consumers need for taking informed transactional definitions is prohibited (Directive 2005/29/EC3). Subject to case-bycase assessment, misleading marketing of the distribution mode of a game could amount to an infringement. The relevant EU instruments are transposed into national laws. Member States authorities and courts deal with the enforcement. Under EU copyright law, rightholders enjoy exclusive rights over their creations, such as videogames which are complex works comprising other elements beyond the computer program4. In practice, rightholders may allow third parties to exercise certain rights in respect of their protected works by way of licence, unless an exception or limitation applies or the principle of exhaustion applies. The principle of exhaustion may apply in certain circumstances to the distribution in electronic or digital form of a computer program5.

1 http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2019/770/oj. 2 http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2011/83/oj. 3 http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2005/29/oj. 4 CJEU case C-355/12, Nintendo. 5 CJEU case C-128/11, UsedSoft v Oracle.

E-10-2026-002631.t: Foetal alcohol spectrum disorder: EU action on recognition, diagnosis, and support across Member States
qt: to the Commission Cynthia Ní Mhurchú (Renew) Subject:
Foetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD) is estimated to affect millions of European citizens and Europe has been identified as having the highest prevalence of FASD globally. In the light of this: 1.
What action is the Commission taking to support greater recognition of FASD across Member States and to promote more consistent approaches to diagnosis, data collection and prevalence monitoring?

How is the Commission supporting the inclusion of people living with FASD within the objectives of the European Disability Rights Strategy 2021–2030 and the implementation of the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, including access to appropriate health, education, employment, disability and social supports?

Does the Commission intend to consider further EU-level guidance or policy measures, including the explicit recognition of FASD within future disability and public health initiatives, to address inequalities in the recognition of and support for people living with FASD across the EU?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (24.9.2026) Foetal alcohol spectrum disorder is classified as rare disease (ORPHA 1915). Since 2017, the Commission has been funding the European Reference Networks for Rare Diseases (ERNs), which enable specialists in Europe to discuss cases of patients affected by rare, lowprevalence and complex diseases, providing advice on the most appropriate diagnosis and the best treatment available. Foetal alcohol spectrum disorder in particular is covered by the ERN for Rare Malformation Syndromes and Rare Intellectual and Neurodevelopmental Disorders (ITHACA). The Strategy for the Rights of Persons with Disabilities 2021-2023 further supports selfdetermination, autonomy and participation. It covers persons with different kinds of disabilities equally. Rare diseases often lead to disabilities and thus the Strategy in its health area focuses on fostering research and innovation on rare diseases. The Pharma Package also intends to make orphan drugs against rare diseases more accessible1. The Commission is currently implementing the current actions of the Strategy. On different occasions, including the meetings of the Disability Platform, it discusses progress on implementation, which can help define new needs to be integrated into the Strategy and feed into future policy measures.
1 https://commission.europa.eu/document/ab0bcea9-6b3a-48c1-875c-1cc687fba6d0_en.

E-10-2026-002630.t: Commission communication: A Simpler, Clearer and Better Enforced EU Rulebook
qt: to the Commission Ton Diepeveen (PfE) Subject:

In its communication ‘A Simpler, Clearer and Better Enforced EU Rulebook’, the Commission proposes a new simplification platform to support the action plan for a comprehensive regulatory review. According to the communication, this platform focuses exclusively on the following policy priorities: goods and services, financial services, customs, taxation, health and food safety, agriculture, transport, energy, climate, environment, digital, housing and permitting. 1.

If this list is exhaustive, why does the Commission focus only on these policy areas and not on other key policy areas where simplification is urgently needed, such as: competition policy (State aid, mergers and acquisitions), the common commercial policy with regard to non-EU countries, economic policy (e.g. the European Semester), employment and social policy (e.g. labour law, working conditions and social inclusion), consumer protection and justice and home affairs (e.g. judicial cooperation, cooperation in civil and criminal matters and police and security cooperation)?

Does the Commission consider these policy areas not to be a priority? This question is all the more pertinent since the Union’s Treaty-based competences in areas such as common commercial policy and competition policy are considerably broader than its limited competences in areas such as customs, taxation and housing.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (8.9.2026) The Commission communication ‘A Simpler, Clearer and Better Enforced EU Rulebook’1 states that a key action will be ‘setting up a new high-level expert group – the Simplification Platform – to support simplification and burden reduction efforts.’ The communication does not state that the Platform will limit itself to any specific area of EU law or policy in its works. According to the Commission communication, the Platform will support the regulatory deep cleaning efforts, but these efforts will not be its exclusive focus. As explained in the communication, the Regulatory Deep Cleaning Action Plan focuses on 12 priority areas, selected based on internal analysis of implementation challenges and on stakeholder input, including in implementation dialogues and reality checks.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex:52026DC0380.

E-10-2026-002629.t: Interaction between CBAM and the EU ETS: impact of free allowances on competition and decarbonisation
qt: to the Commission Cynthia Ní Mhurchú (Renew) Subject:

The Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) and the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) are designed to operate in a complementary manner, ensuring coherence between carbon pricing for domestic production and imports. While the revision of CBAM is ongoing and the EU ETS is scheduled for further review on 15 July 2026, questions arise regarding the interaction between these instruments in practice. In particular, the existence of accumulated free allowances under the EU ETS in certain sectors may create differing capacities among market participants to absorb carbon-related costs. This could potentially lead to distortions of competition between operators that have historically benefited from free allocations and those that have not, including importers subject to CBAM obligations. Given that free allowances are intended to support the decarbonisation of energy-intensive industries, the accumulation of significant unused stocks also raises questions regarding their effective use and their impact on market dynamics. Against this background: 1.
How does the Commission assess the potential impact of accumulated free allowances on competition and the level playing field in sectors covered by the CBAM?
Does the Commission envisage measures, in the context of the upcoming reviews, to address possible imbalances arising from such situations?
How does the Commission ensure that free allowances under the EU ETS effectively contribute to the decarbonisation objectives in the sectors concerned?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.9.2026) The Commission’s proposal to revise the European Union Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) was adopted on 17 July 20261. It has a strong focus on clean investment, providing further support and incentives to industry, and establishing a predictable and pragmatic emissions reduction pathway to support the business case for investment in Europe. As part of this, it proposes to modernise free allocation by linking continued support beyond 2030 to investing in decarbonisation in the EU. As part of the proposal, free allocation will continue to be phased out gradually (by 2038) in step with the phase-in of the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM). The Market Stability Reserve (MSR) is the main EU ETS tool for dealing with historical surplus of allowances. The proposal also modernises the MSR for the post-2030 period, building on a separate proposal presented by the Commission in April 20262. In keeping with previous assessments, the Commission focused on a predictable, rule-based forward approach and does not consider retroactive adjustments of private allowance holdings.
1 https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_26_1596. 2 https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_26_666.

E-10-2026-002628.t: Billions into the grid, but who pays the bill? Industry and households are facing the prospect of paying the bill for the EU’s green transition
qt: to the Commission Erik Kaliňák (NI) Subject:

The EU is anticipating a significant increase in electricity consumption as a consequence of the electrification of transport, heating and industry. However, several Member States are also warning of the need for extensive modernisation of transmission and distribution networks. 1.

In the Commission’s view, is the current pace of electrical grid modernisation sufficient to meet electrification targets, or is there a risk that these targets will remain dead letters due to outdated grids?
Which parts of the energy infrastructure does the Commission feel are at the greatest risk of failure during implementation of the electrification strategy over the next decade?
How does the Commission intend to prevent industry and households from having to pay for the billions in grid investments through higher energy prices?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.8.2026) The Commission acknowledges the present challenges facing Europe’s electricity grids, which relate to permitting bottlenecks, insufficient investment, low efficiency in the use of existing grids, supply-chain pressures, and shortages of skilled workers. Distribution grids are particularly vulnerable because they must absorb rising decentralised generation and demand, while being refurbished and adapted to climate risks. To accelerate network development in line with electrification objectives while mitigating pressure on energy bills, the Commission has adopted the Grids Action Plan1, the electricity market design reform2, and the European Grids Package3 which contain measures aimed at better using existing infrastructure and accelerating the rollout of the grids needed for the energy transition. As part of the 2028-2034 multiannual financial framework, the Commission has proposed a five-fold increase of the Connecting Europe Facility’s energy budget from EUR 5.84 billion to EUR 29.91 billion, to deliver direct financial support4. The Electrification Action Plan will further support the existing framework needed to accelerate progress5. The Proposal to future-proof electricity bills6 aims at bringing down electricity costs for all consumers by designing network charges that incentivise a system-friendly use of the grid and integration of generation and loads. The Commission also adopted a Clean Energy Investment Strategy7 to help mobilise significant additional private investment for clean energy.
