E-10-2026-002627.t: The EU’s green dream is turning into a nightmare: massive transfer of car production to China and layoffs in Europe?
qt: to the Commission Erik Kaliňák (NI) Subject:

The automotive industry is one of the most important industrial sectors in the EU. At the same time, competition is growing from manufacturers in third countries, particularly China, which are gradually increasing their share of the European electric vehicle market. 1.
Does the Commission truly believe that its current regulatory framework will enable European car manufacturers to keep production in Europe competitive in the face of Chinese competition beyond 2030?
Which Member States and industrial regions does the Commission consider to be most at risk of a decline in production and job losses in the automotive industry?
What specific measures does the Commission plan to take to ensure that the transition to zero-emission mobility does not result in the relocation of production and investment outside the EU?
at: (English version) to the Commission Erik Kaliňák (NI) (25 June 2026) Subject: The EU’s green dream is turning into a nightmare: massive transfer of car production to China and layoffs in Europe? The automotive industry is one of the most important industrial sectors in the EU. At the same time, competition is growing from manufacturers in third countries, particularly China, which are gradually increasing their share of the European electric vehicle market. 1. Does the Commission truly believe that its current regulatory framework will enable European car manufacturers to keep production in Europe competitive in the face of Chinese competition beyond 2030? 2. Which Member States and industrial regions does the Commission consider to be most at risk of a decline in production and job losses in the automotive industry? 3. What specific measures does the Commission plan to take to ensure that the transition to zero-emission mobility does not result in the relocation of production and investment outside the EU? (11 August 2026) The automotive industry is a cornerstone of Europe’s industrial base, innovation and employment. However, it is currently facing major challenges, including lower sales on domestic and global markets, high energy prices, supply chain vulnerabilities and rising competition from Chinese manufacturers across all powertrains. The severity of the impact of production decline and job losses for certain Member States or regions depends on several factors, including energy prices, share of employment in the automotive value chain and capacity of the industry to adapt. Through cohesion policy, targeted territorial support is offered, including productive investments in industrial modernisation, innovation and re- and upskilling of workers. Under this mandate, the Commission has been working on a proactive approach to keep automotive manufacturing in the EU competitive through the Industrial Action Plan for the European automotive sector (1), the Automotive Package from December 2025 (2) and the Industrial Accelerator Act proposal (IAA) (3). The IAA introduces EU origin requirements for the automotive industry with a substantial share of vehicle components (4) to be sourced or produced within the EU (or partner countries) when public money (5) is spent. This measure is expected to boost production and investment across the entire EU automotive value chain. The measure will also re-level the playing field with third countries, thereby reducing the risk of job losses in the automotive industry. Finally, in the context of investments in zero-emission mobility supported under the Social Climate Fund (6), the Commission is encouraging Member States to ensure a sustainable supply chain, as outlined in the Net Zero Industry Act (7) and the IAA (8).

E-10-2026-002626.t: Green renovations at the price of debt? The Commission must explain who will pay – owners, tenants or the middle class?
qt: to the Commission Erik Kaliňák (NI) Subject:
The Commission has repeatedly stressed the need to improve buildings’ energy efficiency. At the same time, housing prices in several Member States have been rising faster than household incomes. 1.
How does the Commission respond to concerns that further tightening of building requirements could drive up housing prices and rents?
Does the Commission see a risk that some owners will be unable to finance the required renovations without going into debt?
Does the Commission consider it acceptable for the costs of meeting climate targets in the building sector to be borne mainly by property owners and tenants?
at: (English version) to the Commission Erik Kaliňák (NI) (25 June 2026) Subject: Green renovations at the price of debt? The Commission must explain who will pay — owners, tenants or the middle class? The Commission has repeatedly stressed the need to improve buildings’ energy efficiency. At the same time, housing prices in several Member States have been rising faster than household incomes. 1. How does the Commission respond to concerns that further tightening of building requirements could drive up housing prices and rents? 2. Does the Commission see a risk that some owners will be unable to finance the required renovations without going into debt? 3. Does the Commission consider it acceptable for the costs of meeting climate targets in the building sector to be borne mainly by property owners and tenants? (27 August 2026) Building energy requirements (1) are set by Member States. According to the Energy Performance of Buildings Directiv e (2), they must be at least cost-optimal (3). This framework ensures that building requirements establish a balance between construction, installation and running costs. Member States, at their discretion, may set more ambitious requirements. Energy efficiency is key to ensuring that housing remains affordable, given that energy costs are an important part of overall housing costs. A variety of EU funds is available to support renovation of buildings. Although public financing for renovation has grown significantly since 2021, more than 80% of the investments needed must be mobilised from private capital. The Commission is supporting Member States to develop comprehensive national building renovation plans to channel private and public investment for renovation. As announced in the European Affordable Housing Plan (4), the Commission is developing partnerships for better homes to overcome at local level practical barriers to delivering finance for renovations and achieving scale. In March 2026 the Commission adopted a support package for financing energy efficiency (5).

This includes minimum requirements at building level (kWh/m 2 year). It may also include minimum requirements at building element level (e.g. wall or roof insulation, or window performance). https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=OJ:L_202401275. The Cost optimal framework (set in Article 5 of the Energy Performance of Buildings Directive (EPBD) recast in 2010), requires Member State to carry out an assessment on the energy performance of buildings and building elements over their lifetime. The assessment takes into consideration, amongst others, minimum levels of air quality and comfort, multiple building measures and technologies, climate, construction and installation costs, running costs, and finance. The assessment also considers inflation and changes in energy prices. https://housing.ec.europa.eu/european-affordable-housing-plan_en. The support package comprised a report (COM/2026/118), and two Commission Recommendations (EU) 2026/536 and (EU) 2026/537.

E-10-2026-002625.t: The EU’s AI dream could turn into a nightmare – without energy, the US and China will overtake us and we’ll end up paying more for electricity!
qt: to the Commission Erik Kaliňák (NI) Subject:

Developing AI is one of the EU’s top priorities. At the same time, the number of data centres is growing, and significant amounts of electricity and new investments in energy grids are required to keep them running. In some Member States, grid operators are already warning of increasing problems with connecting new capacity. 1.

Does the Commission believe that Europe currently has sufficient energy and modern grids at its disposal to fulfil its AI ambitions, and that the development of AI will not drive up electricity prices for industry and households?

Does the Commission see a real risk that delays in the development of energy infrastructure will hinder the European AI sector and further increase the Union’s dependence on technologies and services from third countries?

What specific measures does the Commission intend to take to ensure that data centres do not consume energy while depriving the rest of European industry and households of access to energy at competitive prices?
at: (English version) to the Commission Erik Kaliňák (NI) (25 June 2026) Subject: The EU’s AI dream could turn into a nightmare — without energy, the US and China will overtake us and we’ll end up paying more for electricity! Developing AI is one of the EU’s top priorities. At the same time, the number of data centres is growing, and significant amounts of electricity and new investments in energy grids are required to keep them running. In some Member States, grid operators are already warning of increasing problems with connecting new capacity. 1. Does the Commission believe that Europe currently has sufficient energy and modern grids at its disposal to fulfil its AI ambitions, and that the development of AI will not drive up electricity prices for industry and households? 2. Does the Commission see a real risk that delays in the development of energy infrastructure will hinder the European AI sector and further increase the Union’s dependence on technologies and services from third countries? 3. What specific measures does the Commission intend to take to ensure that data centres do not consume energy while depriving the rest of European industry and households of access to energy at competitive prices? (27 August 2026) The Commission acknowledges that data centres demand is expected to significantly grow in line with the ambition to triple their computing capacity in the next five to seven years to ensure EU technological sovereignty (1). The Cloud and Artificial Intelligence (AI) Development Act (2) proposed measures to accelerate deployment of sustainable cloud and data centre infrastructure. To contribute to sustainable data centres grid integration, the European Grids package (3) proposed cross-sectorial network planning with involvement of stakeholders, accelerated permit-granting procedures and priority emphasis on grid efficiency in planning. Under the Strategic Roadmap for Digitalisation and AI in the Energy Sector (4), as well as under AI Factories and the AI Gigafactories initiative (5), the Commission is working with energy and digital industries to develop a model tripartite agreement for the sustainable integration of data centres (6). The proposal to future-proof electricity bills (7) aims at bringing down electricity costs by designing network charges that incentivise a flexible, system-friendly use of the grid and integration of generation and loads, as well as by ensuring smart and efficient electricity grids and efficient network access.

https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/eu-tech-sovereignty. https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/proposal-cloud-and-ai-development-act-cada. https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_25_2945. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A52026DC0501. Environmental sustainability is embedded directly into the core of the AI Factories and the AI Gigafactories initiative. During the AI Gigafactories selection process, all proposals will be rigorously evaluated against strict sustainability criteria. This includes assessing a facility’s overall energy and water efficiency, its commitment to utilizing renewable energy sources, and its ability to integrate into the local energy system sustainably. For example, the LUMI EuroHPC supercomputer gets all of its electricity from 100% renewable hydroelectric power. In addition, the waste heat produced by LUMI will be utilised in the district heating network of Kajaani (the town where Lumi is located), which means that its overall carbon footprint is negative. The waste heat produced by LUMI will provide 20% of Kajaani’s annual demand for district heat. Furthermore, according to the latest top 500 list, which was published ISC High Performance 2026 in Hamburg, the EuroHPC supercomputer JUPITER at Forschungszentrum Jülich remains one of the world’s most powerful supercomputers, ranking fifth worldwide while it ranks first as the most energy-efficient computer in the exascale class. https://digitalstrategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/ai-factories; https://commission.europa.eu/topics/competitiveness/competitiveness-coordination-tool-projects/aigigafactories_en. The model will lay down actions on improved information for grid planning, and data centre sitting, ensure addressing of speculative grid connection requests of data centres, use of power purchase agreements by data centre operators, deliver additional generation of clean energy, deliver solutions for data centre flexibility and support the use of waste heat. The model can be subsequently adapted and piloted in Member States and regions. COM(2026) 600 final.

The Commission is also working on a Data Centre Energy Efficiency Package (8) to introduce a rating scheme (9) for the energy efficiency of data centres. The Commission will also launch a public consultation for possible minimum performance standards for data centres.

https://energy.ec.europa.eu/topics/energy-efficiency/energy-efficiency-targets-directive-and-rules/energy-efficiency-directive/energy-performance-datacentres_en#next-steps. https://energy.ec.europa.eu/news/rating-scheme-data-centres-eu-commission-launches-call-feedback-2026-03-27_en.

E-10-2026-002624.t: Pollution in the River Paiva threatening Portugal’s natural resources
qt: to the Commission Ana Miguel Pedro (PPE) Subject:

Pollution in the River Paiva poses a threat to the environmental, ecological, tourism and economic resources in the municipality of Arouca. Recurring episodes of water quality deterioration in the River Paiva and some of its tributaries have been recorded for a number of years and have given rise to several complaints to the competent authorities. The situation has grown worse in recent weeks, as evidenced by increased water turbidity, the presence of significant amounts of whitish foam and intense and unpleasant odours. On 10 June 2026, signs of pollution appeared once again in the parishes of Canelas and Espiunca, in the municipality of Arouca, warranting further investigation. 1.
Is the Commission aware of the above?

Does the Commission consider that the situation could constitute a breach of the obligations laid down in Directive 2000/60/EC, particularly as regards protection of the quality of surface water bodies in the River Paiva river basin?
Is the Commission in a position to urge the relevant municipal authorities to investigate and, where appropriate, take immediate corrective action to ensure EU environmental legislation is followed?
at: (English version) to the Commission Ana Miguel Pedro (PPE) (25 June 2026) Subject: Pollution in the River Paiva threatening Portugal’s natural resources Pollution in the River Paiva poses a threat to the environmental, ecological, tourism and economic resources in the municipality of Arouca. Recurring episodes of water quality deterioration in the River Paiva and some of its tributaries have been recorded for a number of years and have given rise to several complaints to the competent authorities. The situation has grown worse in recent weeks, as evidenced by increased water turbidity, the presence of significant amounts of whitish foam and intense and unpleasant odours. On 10 June 2026, signs of pollution appeared once again in the parishes of Canelas and Espiunca, in the municipality of Arouca, warranting further investigation. 1.
Is the Commission aware of the above?

2. Does the Commission consider that the situation could constitute a breach of the obligations laid down in Directive 2000/60/EC, particularly as regards protection of the quality of surface water bodies in the River Paiva river basin? 3. Is the Commission in a position to urge the relevant municipal authorities to investigate and, where appropriate, take immediate corrective action to ensure EU environmental legislation is followed? (12 August 2026) The Commission has not received any information on the observations of water turbidity, whitish foam and odour formation on River Paiva reported by the Honourable Member and is therefore not in a position to assess whether the situation is caused by a breach of obligations under the Water Framework Directive (WFD) (1). According to the relevant third River Basin Management Plan, the River Paiva, at its passage through Canelas and Espiunca, was reported to be in good ecological and chemical status, indicating compliance with the WFD’s goals for good surface water status (2). Without prejudice to the Commission’s role as guardian of the Treaties, Member States are primarily responsible to ensure compliance with EU law, including verifying individual cases of potential breach of the relevant rules. Consequently, it is for the competent authorities of the Member State concerned to establish appropriate monitoring programmes, maintain effective inspection mechanisms to detect unauthorised discharges, and apply the necessary enforcement measures when environmental standards are not met. In line with its strategic approach on enforcement action the Commission focuses on systemic non-compliance (3).

Commission Directive 2014/101/EU of 30 October 2014 amending Directive 2000/60/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council establishing a framework for Community action in the field of water policy, OJ L 311, 31.10.2014, p. 32-35. Surface water body status can be viewed here: https://discomap.eea.europa.eu/wise-freshwaterviewer/. Communication from the Commission — EU law: Better results through better application, OJ C 18, 19.1.2017, p. 10-20, and Communication from the Commission — Enforcing EU law for a Europe that delivers, 13.10.2022, COM(2022) 518 final.

E-10-2026-002623.t: EU-funded lie detector for use at the border
qt: to the Commission Raquel García Hermida-Van Der Walle (Renew) Subject:

Research by Dutch investigative journalists has revealed that the Dutch research institute TNO and technology company Vicarvision have developed a lie detector that could assist border guards in determining whether an individual is telling the truth. The AI-driven tool, funded under Horizon Europe, looks for non-verbal cues in individuals being questioned, such as whether the person being checked blinks, makes hand movements, leans forwards or backwards and how they laugh. Dutch and Greek border guards are reported to have experimented with this lie detector between 2018 and 2021. TNO itself acknowledged that the lie detector was not reliable and therefore insisted that the framing of the project should be positive1. There had previously been significant criticism of a similar project, iBorderCtrl. 1.
Why did the Commission fund projects involving lie detectors for border checks, despite large-scale research showing that detecting lies is virtually impossible?
Can it provide an overview of EU-funded projects developing lie detectors for use in border checks, both past and present?
Will it withdraw funding from ongoing projects? If not, does it dispute the widely shared consensus that lie detectors are unreliable?

Investico in samenwerking met De Groene Amsterdammer, Trouw en Argos (https://www.platforminvestico.nl/onderzoeken/wie-is-migrant-wie-is-crimineel-eu-onderzoekt-ai-toepassingen-voor-grenstechnologie en https://www.trouw.nl/verdieping/leugendetectie-verboden-niet-voor-criminelen-en-migranten~b65443f0/). 1
at: (English version) to the Commission Raquel García Hermida-Van Der Walle (Renew) (25 June 2026) Subject: EU-funded lie detector for use at the border Research by Dutch investigative journalists has revealed that the Dutch research institute TNO and technology company Vicarvision have developed a lie detector that could assist border guards in determining whether an individual is telling the truth. The AI-driven tool, funded under Horizon Europe, looks for non-verbal cues in individuals being questioned, such as whether the person being checked blinks, makes hand movements, leans forwards or backwards and how they laugh. Dutch and Greek border guards are reported to have experimented with this lie detector between 2018 and 2021. TNO itself acknowledged that the lie detector was not reliable and therefore insisted that the framing of the project should be positive (1). There had previously been significant criticism of a similar project, iBorderCtrl. 1. Why did the Commission fund projects involving lie detectors for border checks, despite large-scale research showing that detecting lies is virtually impossible? 2. Can it provide an overview of EU-funded projects developing lie detectors for use in border checks, both past and present? 3. Will it withdraw funding from ongoing projects? If not, does it dispute the widely shared consensus that lie detectors are unreliable? (6 August 2026) Investing in European civil security research helps European authorities to have effective, trustworthy and compliant EU technologies to protect the EU and its citizens. Funding research does not imply their deployment. In this specific case, EU funded research allowed a better understanding of the limitations and reliability of the technologies in question and to draw policy conclusions. While the Commission has not funded and is not funding projects specifically developing ‘lie detectors’ for use in border checks, EU funds are used to support research for Member States authorities to effectively and efficiently implement the obligations set out in, among others, the Schengen Borders Code (1). All funded research projects undergo ethics screening and review by independent experts, are bound by obligations on compliance with the applicable law and are monitored until the completion of their research. Whilst AI systems intended to be used as polygraphs, or similar tools intended to be used by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities, are not prohibited under the Artificial Intelligence Act (2), they are classified as high risk requiring them to comply with stringent safeguards to mitigate any risks to fundamental rights, health and safety.

Investico in samenwerking met De Groene Amsterdammer, Trouw en Argos (https://www.platform-investico.nl/onderzoeken/wie-is-migrant-wie-is-crimineeleu-onderzoekt-ai-toepassingen-voor-grenstechnologie en https://www.trouw.nl/verdieping/leugendetectie-verboden-niet-voor-criminelen-enmigranten~b65443f0/). E-10-2026-002622.t: Implementation of the Urban Wastewater Treatment Directive and costs of quaternary treatment
qt: to the Commission Piotr Müller (ECR) Subject:

In a resolution adopted in June 2026, Parliament highlighted the risks associated with implementing the provisions on the quaternary treatment of wastewater and the extended producer responsibility (EPR) scheme for the pharmaceutical and cosmetics industries. Parliament stressed the need for a new assessment of the impact of these provisions on the availability of medicinal and cosmetic products, business competitiveness, the stability of supply chains and the costs incurred by consumers and patients. In light of the above: 1.

Does the Commission intend to perform a new impact assessment verifying the costs of implementing quaternary wastewater treatment or the impact of the EPR scheme on the pharmaceutical and cosmetics industries?

What up-to-date data does it have to illustrate the actual contribution of the pharmaceutical and cosmetics industries to the release of the micropollutants covered by the directive, and does this data justify saddling these industries with the brunt of the costs?

What steps will it take to ensure that the achievement of environmental objectives does not push up prices, hobble production in the EU or reduce the availability of medicinal and cosmetic products on the EU market?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (11.9.2026) An update study on the cost of quaternary treatment published by the Joint Research Centre in 2025, taking into account updated cost data, the provisions of the final Urban Wastewater Treatment Directive (UWWTD)1 compared to the Commission proposal and inflation2 concluded that the impact assessment estimates on extended producer responsibility (EPR) costs remain valid. Work on the assessment of substances in urban wastewater has been part of the preparatory work accompanying the Commission proposal for a revised UWWTD3. The evaluation of the Directive, due by 2033, will consider ‘improved knowledge on the presence of micropollutants in urban wastewater, their impacts (…), as well as data resulting from the new monitoring obligations on micropollutants’4. In line with recital 21 of the recast Directive, Member States should take into consideration the possible impacts of the application of the EPR on the accessibility, availability and affordability of products at national level. The Commission will continue its close cooperation with the European Parliament, Member States and stakeholders on the pragmatic implementation of the recast Directive and will monitor its impact on the accessibility, availability and affordability of products at national level, in particular medicines.
1 Directive (EU) 2024/3019 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 November 2024 concerning

urban wastewater treatment (recast), OJ L, 2024/3019, 12.12.2024. 2 Joint Research Centre (2025) - Updated estimation of the costs of quaternary wastewater treatment in the EU: https://publications.jrc.ec.europa.eu/repository/handle/JRC144745. 3 Joint Research Centre (2022): https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0048969722042218?via%3Dihub; Commission impact assessment accompanying the proposal for a Directive of the European Parliament and of the Council concerning urban wastewater treatment (recast) SWD(2022) 541 final. 4 Article 30 of Directive (EU) 2024/3019.

E-10-2026-002620.t: Commission’s knowledge of cetacean hunts in the Faroe Islands and parliamentary scrutiny
qt: to the Commission César Luena (S&D), Jutta Paulus (Verts/ALE), Sebastian Everding (The Left) Subject:

During the exchange of views between Commissioner Roswall and Parliament’s Environment, Climate and Food Safety (ENVI) Committee on 1 June 2026 on the implementation of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, several Members raised concerns about the recent killing of hundreds of dolphins in the Faroe Islands. The Commissioner stated that, although she knew the Faroe Islands from previous responsibilities, she was not familiar with this issue and that Members would soon receive a reply to the letter sent on the matter. 1.

Given that the hunting of dolphins and other cetaceans in the Faroe Islands is a longstanding and widely documented practice that has attracted international attention for decades, what assessment has the Commission made of this issue and its implications for biodiversity conservation and animal welfare?

How does the Commission ensure that concerns raised repeatedly by Members of Parliament on matters related to biodiversity conservation are adequately reflected in its engagement with relevant international partners and stakeholders?

What procedures are in place to ensure that Commissioners and their services are sufficiently briefed on issues that have been raised by Parliament in advance of committee exchanges, and how were these procedures applied in relation to the concerns regarding cetacean hunts in the Faroe Islands?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.8.2026) The Commission acknowledges the strong public concern regarding the hunting of dolphins and other cetaceans in the Faroe Islands. It attaches importance to cetacean conservation and animal welfare and raises these concerns with the Faroese authorities, including through annual consultations under the Memorandum of Understanding on Enhanced Cooperation between the EU and the Government of the Faroe Islands1. The Commission is committed to continuing a constructive dialogue with the European Parliament and to ensuring that concerns raised by the European Parliament and its Members are taken duly into account, also through welcoming Members of the European Parliament as observers in the delegations to the relevant international conventions. The Commission will also continue to engage with all partners, exchange scientific knowledge and promote cooperation to advance shared biodiversity conservation objectives in bilateral dialogues and relevant multilateral fora, including on the issues mentioned above. In line with the Commission's 2024 Working Methods2, Commissioners, their Cabinets and the relevant services maintain regular exchanges of information to ensure that Commissioners are appropriately briefed for their engagement with the European Parliament. This includes the sharing of accurate and up-to-date information on issues raised by Members of the European Parliament, including in committee activities and parliamentary questions. These arrangements were applied in preparation for the Commissioner's exchange of views with the European Parliament’s Environment, Climate and Food Safety Committee.
1 https://www.eeas.europa.eu/sites/default/files/documents/2024/20240321 Signed MoU.pdf. 2 https://commission.europa.eu/document/download/4b958a25-a16a-4ac2-bda8-
c14a18bd117c_en?filename=Working%20Methods%20of%20the%20European%20Commission.PDF.

E-10-2026-002619.t: Accessibility of public services for individuals with learning disabilities
qt: to the Commission Barry Cowen (Renew) Subject:

Many citizens with learning disabilities, including dyslexia, can face barriers when accessing public services that are increasingly delivered through digital channels. Ensuring that information is presented in an accessible and understandable format is essential to guaranteeing equal access to public services across the European Union. 1.
How does the Commission monitor Member States’ compliance with EU accessibility requirements in relation to public services and digital platforms operated by national administrations?

Are accessibility measures for individuals with learning disabilities, including dyslexia, considered as part of any EU auditing, compliance, evaluation or monitoring procedures relating to Member State administrations, including those responsible for agriculture and fisheries?
What steps is the Commission taking to promote best practice among Member States in ensuring that public services are accessible and understandable for individuals with learning disabilities?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (18.8.2026) Directive (EU) 2019/882 (European Accessibility Act, EAA)1 sets mandatory accessibility requirements for certain products and services. Where public sector bodies provide such services, they must comply with those requirements. Regarding services, the EAA is enforced by national authorities responsible for the compliance of services. To establish cooperation among those authorities and gain a common understanding of the situation, an informal Commission expert group on the EAA was created under Article 28 of the Act. Directive (EU) 2016/2102 (Web Accessibility Directive, WAD)2 regulates public sector bodies’ websites and mobile applications by setting obligations for the Member States to set minimum harmonisation accessibility requirements3. Article 8 of WAD obliges the Member States to monitor the compliance of the public sector websites and mobile applications with the accessibility requirements and submit a report every three years to the Commission. The Member States’ reports are then published45. The Commission WAD expert group is a forum for Member States to exchange best practices concerning WAD, including its accessibility requirements and reporting obligations. The accessibility requirements of the EAA and WAD6 address a wide range of disabilities including learning disabilities such as dyslexia. Since 2022, the Commission launched a European resource centre, AccessibleEU7, designed, inter alia, to support the implementation of EU accessibility legislation. Moreover, the abovementioned EAA expert group brings together market surveillance authorities, industry experts, and organisations of persons with disabilities to exchange best practices.
1 Directive (EU) 2019/882 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 17 April 2019 on the accessibility

requirements for products and services (OJ L 151, 7.6.2019, PP.70-115, ELI: https://eurlex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2019/882/oj). 2 Directive (EU) 2016/2102 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 26 October 2016 on the accessibility of the websites and mobile applications of public sector bodies (OJ L 327, 2.12.2016, pp. 1–15, ELI: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2016/2102/oj). 3 Public sector bodies cover e.g. public bodies responsible for agriculture and fisheries. However, there are some exceptions in the applicable scope as stated in Article 1 WAD. For example, Member States have the option of excluding websites and mobile applications of schools, nurseries, and kindergartens from the applicable scope in situations where the content is not related to essential online administrative functions. 4 https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/news/web-accessibility-directive-monitoring-reports-2022-2024. 5 See, e.g., Web Accessibility Directive – Monitoring reports 2022-2024, https://digitalstrategy.ec.europa.eu/en/news/web-accessibility-directive-monitoring-reports-2022-2024. 6 Accessibility requirements of WAD are linked to the harmonised European standard EN 301 549, which refers to a large extent to the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG). 7 https://accessible-eu-centre.ec.europa.eu/index_en.

E-10-2026-002617.t: Transparency regarding the use of instant messaging services
qt: to the Commission Fabio De Masi (NI) Subject:

The European Ombudsman is currently conducting an inquiry into the Commission’s handling of requests for access to text messages1. This concerns, inter alia, a group chat between Commission President Ursula von der Leyen (‘Washington Group’) with a number of Heads of State or Government. In this connection, the question arises as to how the rights to access documents under Regulation (EC) No 1049/2001 are effectively safeguarded also with regard to informal communication channels. 1.

How does the Commission ensure that text messages and other forms of electronic communication containing information related to the institution’s activities, competences or decisions are identified, registered and, where appropriate, stored, so that the right of access to documents enshrined in Regulation (EC) No 1049/2001 is not undermined by the use of informal or ephemeral means of communication?

Can the Commission confirm that text messages or other electronic messages between the President of the Commission and Heads of State or Government of Member States or of third countries – in so far as they serve the purposes of policy coordination, the preparation of decisions or the performance of institutional tasks – are as a rule subject to an assessment regarding registration and record-keeping obligations and are not automatically excluded from the documentation and transparency requirements from the outset solely as a result of the means of communication used or of any automatic deletion functions activated?
https://www.ftm.eu/articles/european-ombudsman-opens-investigation-into-text-messages-von-der-
leyen.
at: (English version) to the Commission Fabio De Masi (NI) (24 June 2026) Subject: Transparency regarding the use of instant messaging services The European Ombudsman is currently conducting an inquiry into the Commission’s handling of requests for access to text messages (1). This concerns, inter alia, a group chat between Commission President Ursula von der Leyen (‘Washington Group’) with a number of Heads of State or Government. In this connection, the question arises as to how the rights to access documents under Regulation (EC) No 1049/2001 are effectively safeguarded also with regard to informal communication channels. 1. How does the Commission ensure that text messages and other forms of electronic communication containing information related to the institution’s activities, competences or decisions are identified, registered and, where appropriate, stored, so that the right of access to documents enshrined in Regulation (EC) No 1049/2001 is not undermined by the use of informal or ephemeral means of communication? 2. Can the Commission confirm that text messages or other electronic messages between the President of the Commission and Heads of State or Government of Member States or of third countries — in so far as they serve the purposes of policy coordination, the preparation of decisions or the performance of institutional tasks — are as a rule subject to an assessment regarding registration and record-keeping obligations and are not automatically excluded from the documentation and transparency requirements from the outset solely as a result of the means of communication used or of any automatic deletion functions activated? E-10-2026-002616.t: CAP subsidies received by the UAE royal family and transparency of ultimate beneficiaries
qt: to the Commission Ilaria Salis (The Left), Rudi Kennes (The Left), Jonas Sjöstedt (The Left), Arash Saeidi (The Left), Anja Hazekamp (The Left), Maria Noichl (S&D), Martin Günther (The Left), Estrella Galán (The Left), Claire Fita (S&D), Chloé Ridel (S&D), Eric Sargiacomo (S&D) Subject:

Recent investigations1 have reported that members of the royal family of the United Arab Emirates (UAE) – a country with a human rights record that Parliament has formally condemned2 – received more than EUR 71 million in common agricultural policy (CAP) subsidies between 2019 and 2024, through 110 payments traced to companies and subsidiaries controlled by the Al Nahyan family, for landholdings in Romania, Italy and Spain. Under existing disclosure requirements, only direct recipients of subsidies are named, making it difficult to identify the ultimate beneficiaries. This raises concerns about whether these payments comply with the eligibility and management control requirements of Regulation (EU) 2021/21163. 1.

Does the Commission consider this situation an infringement of Regulation (EU) 2021/2116, and what measures will it take to prevent CAP funds from benefiting ultrawealthy beneficiaries from non-EU countries through complex corporate structures?

What tracing mechanisms exist at EU level to identify the ultimate beneficiaries of CAP funds, and would the Commission consider introducing mandatory beneficial ownership disclosure as part of the 2028 CAP reform, and commit to publishing such data in a complete and accessible format?

Where CAP payments have been obtained through opaque structures or arrangements contrary to CAP objectives, will the Commission investigate and seek recovery of unduly paid funds under Regulation (EU) 2021/2116?

https://www.desmog.com/2026/05/06/gulf-royal-family-banks-over-e70-million-in-eu-farming-funds/. European Parliament resolution of 16 September 2021 on the case of human rights defender Ahmed Mansoor in the United Arab Emirates (OJ C 117, 11.3.2022, p. 109). 3 Regulation (EU) 2021/2116 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 2 December 2021 on the financing, management and monitoring of the common agricultural policy and repealing Regulation (EU) No 1306/2013 (OJ L 435, 6.12.2021, p. 187, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2021/2116/oj). 1 2
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (10.9.2026) Current rules on the eligibility of direct payments from the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) require CAP beneficiaries to be active farmers, but do not contain provisions at EU level excluding beneficiaries referred to in the question. Under shared management, the Commission is not involved in payments to final beneficiaries. This is the Member States’ role and responsibility. Member States have to put in place management and control systems. The Commission assesses whether these systems function properly. Information about beneficiaries of the CAP and their identification is made public by Member States as required by Regulation (EU) 2021/21161. The identification of beneficial owners is not required by the current Regulation. Under the proposed 2028-2034 Multiannual Financial Framework, the Financial Regulation, in combination with the proposed sector-specific rules, would require the collection of information on beneficial owners2. For such future CAP rules3, the Commission considers that support should go to farmers whose principal activity is agriculture. In addition to the eligibility linked to agricultural activity, the Commission’s proposal for the next CAP states that the total annual amount of degressive area-based income support would be reduced for payments exceeding EUR 20 000 and capped at EUR 100 000 per year. These provisions, as proposed, address the risk that income support goes to entities whose principal business activity is not farming. The proposal is currently under negotiation by the co-legislators. In a shared management system such as the CAP financing, national authorities should ensure that the CAP funds are distributed in line with the applicable legislation. The Commission has tools to protect the Union’s financial interests if irregularities have not been adequately addressed. When the Commission becomes aware of any suspected case of fraud, corruption or illegal activity affecting the EU budget, it informs the European Anti-Fraud Office and/or the European Public Prosecutor’s Office in accordance with applicable EU legislation.
1 Article 59 (4) and Article 98 of Regulation (EU) 2021/2116 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-

content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02021R2116-20260101. 2 This is included in the proposal for National and Regional Partnership (NRP) Regulation. 3 Article 4(3)(c)(i) of proposal for the NRP Regulation (COM(2025)565. Article 63(1)(iv).

E-10-2026-002615.t: EU food additive rules and their impact on reformulation and sugar reduction
qt: to the Commission Barry Cowen (Renew) Subject:

The Vision for Agriculture and Food and the Safe Hearts Plan, presented by the Commission in 2025, highlight the importance of promoting the reformulation of food and drink products, while ensuring a high level of consumer protection and public health. However, the food and feed safety omnibus of 16 December 2025 does not include specific measures to support further innovation in this area. The ‘30 % energy-reduction rule’ in the Food Additives Regulation (Regulation (EC) No 1333/2008) allows the use of low- or no-calorie sweeteners only where the final product has at least 30 % lower energy content than a comparable product. Stakeholders have raised concerns that this threshold may limit manufacturers’ ability to pursue incremental sugar-reduction strategies, particularly where significant reductions have already been achieved. 1.

How does the Commission assess whether the 30 % energy-reduction threshold remains appropriate in light of its objectives to support public health through sugar reduction, while also promoting innovation and competitiveness?
Does the Commission intend to review Article 7(a) of the Food Additives Regulation to assess whether the threshold remains proportionate and fit for purpose?
What scientific and policy rationale underpins the threshold and has the Commission assessed its impact on incremental reformulation efforts and product innovation?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (24.9.2026) A food additive may be included in the Union lists of Authorised additives1 only if it does not pose a safety concern to the health of the consumer, there is a reasonable technological need that cannot be achieved by other economically and technologically practicable means, its use does not mislead the consumer and it has advantages and benefits for the consumer. For food additives belonging to the functional class of sweeteners, additional specific conditions2 must be met. Among those additional conditions, the ‘30 % energy-reduction threshold’3 referred to by the Honourable Member was included in the Food Additives Regulation4 to ensure a significant energy-reduction and thus clear benefits from replacing sugars by sweeteners in foods. This guarantees a meaningful reformulation that provides a legitimate nutritional advantage by comparison with foods containing sugars. The restriction also ensures that the use of sweetener food additives is limited to certain products within specific food categories, as set out in Annex II of the Food Additives Regulation. The Commission considers that the rationale underpinning this restriction remains relevant and does not intend to review Article 7(a) of the Food Additives Regulation. In the broader context of improving dietary habits, the Commission supports efforts to reduce sugar consumption, including through the food industry-led EU Code of Conduct on Responsible Food Business and Marketing Practices and through Food 20305, as well as support to national reformulation initiatives6 The Annex on Added Sugars of the 2015 EU Framework for National Initiatives for Selected Nutrients7 indicates as preferred outcome that the reduction of added sugars also leads to a reduction of the sweet taste.
1 In Annexes II and III to Regulation (EC) No 1333/2008 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 16

December 2008 on food additives (OJ L 354, 31.12.2008, p. 16). 2 A food additive may be included in the Union list in Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 1333/2008 for the functional class of sweetener only if it serves one or more of the following purposes: (a) replacing sugars for the production of energy-reduced food, non-cariogenic food or food with no added sugars; or (b) replacing sugars where this permits an increase in the shelf-life of the food; or (c) producing food intended for particular nutritional uses as defined in Article 1(2)(a) of Directive 89/398/EEC. 3 Article 3(2) f of Regulation (EC) No 1333/2008 defines ‘energy-reduced food’ as a food with an energy value reduced by at least 30 % compared with the original food or a similar product. 4 Regulation (EC) No 1333/2008 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 16 December 2008 on food additives OJ L 354, 31.12.2008, pp. 16–33. 5 the research and innovation policy framework deployed under the Horizon Europe programme. 6 European Commission, Communication on an EU cardiovascular health plan: the Safe Hearts Plan, COM(2025) 1024 final, 16 December 2025. 7 Available at https://health.ec.europa.eu/publications/added-sugars-annex-eu-framework-national-initiativesselected-nutrients_en.

E-10-2026-002614.t: Regulating new genomic techniques: protecting Europe’s agricultural biodiversity and safeguards for small farms
qt: to the Commission Giuseppe Antoci (The Left) Subject:

The EU acts as the custodian of Europe’s agricultural biodiversity heritage – one of the most important in the world, built over centuries through the work of millions of farmers who have handpicked, conserved and promoted native varieties closely connected with the local area. Products bearing the PDO, PGI, DOC and DOCG labels form a pillar of Europe’s agri-food economy. Small and medium-sized farms and family businesses play a key role in protecting the rural landscape, conserving biodiversity and looking after inland areas. The revision of the EU’s rules on new genomic techniques (NGT)1 unlocks major opportunities for the farming sector to innovate, but also raises questions as regards the impact on biodiversity, farmers’ freedom of choice, product traceability and the increasingly concentrated seed market. In light of the above: 1.

What steps will the Commission take to ensure that the future NGT rules do not endanger Europe’s agricultural biodiversity or undermine the conservation of native varieties and the protection of certified PDO, PGI, DOC and DOCG products?
In the interests of transparency, freedom of choice for consumers and safeguards for farmers, how will it ensure effective traceability mechanisms for NGT products?
What initiatives will it promote to strike the right balance between scientific innovation, protecting Europe’s genetic heritage and the economic viability of farms?
https://www.europarl.europa.eu/news/en/press-room/20260611IPR45215/new-genomic-techniques-forplants-to-boost-innovation-in-sustainable-agriculture 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.9.2026) Regulation (EU) 2026/13881, adopted on 17 June 2026 by the European Parliament and the Council, creates an enabling regulatory framework for plants obtained by New Genomic Techniques (NGT) so that breeders can diversify plant reproductive material to find solutions for pressing challenges that farmers face today, such as crops more resilient to climate change or requiring less fertilisers and pesticides. As set out in the Regulation, the Commission will monitor the impacts of NGT plants, including as regards the issues raised by the Honourable Member. The Regulation distinguishes two situations on traceability. Category 1 NGT plants, considered equivalent to conventional plants and their products, do not require traceability or specific labelling. Transparency is ensured through seed labelling, a public register of NGT plants, and information in plant variety catalogues. Category 2 NGT plants and products, featuring more complex modifications, remain subject to the traceability and labelling of the Genetically modified organisms regulatory framework. The Commission will support the proper implementation of these new rules as set out in its implementation strategy2. Geographical Indications, through their legal specifications, help producers obtain fair value for their products and support rural employment, thereby safeguarding the economic viability of farmers. They also preserve traditions, while allowing producers to innovate, provided the product keeps its essential link to its origin and recognised characteristics. Various EU-funded projects are advancing innovation in agriculture, including in the area of NGTs while addressing technical, socio-economic and other dimensions.

E-10-2026-002613.t: Retention of capped funds under the National and Regional Partnership Fund (NRP Fund) and the new CAP from 2028
qt: to the Commission Marion Walsmann (PPE) Subject:

The Commission’s proposal to reform the common agricultural policy (CAP) from 2028 and introduce the National and Regional Partnership Fund (NRP Fund) provides for capping and degressivity of direct payments. Under the current design of the CAP, funds freed up as a result of capping remained within the respective region and corresponding support area and could still be used there for agricultural policy purposes. Under the new governance structure of the National and Regional Partnership Plans (NRPs), there are questions as to how the geographical and administrative distribution of funds will work in the future. 1.
Do funds freed up as a result of capping direct payments also remain within the same region under the NRP funds?

How does the Commission define the term ‘region’ in this context? Does it refer to the Member State as a whole, to regional administrative units (e.g. the Länder in Germany) or to other land divisions?
If the funds no longer necessarily remain within the same region, what are the criteria for redistribution within the respective NRP Plan in the future?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (28.8.2026) 1. Funds freed up as a result of degressivity and capping remains at Member State level within the budget ring-fenced for certain agricultural interventions. According to the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) legislative proposal of July 20251, Member States have a large flexibility to re-allocate these funds. Accordingly, a Member State can decide that funds freed up as a result of degressivity and capping remain within the same area or region. 2. Because of the large flexibility regarding the geographical distribution, as referred above, the Commission proposal does not define ‘region’ in the context of degressive area based income support. 3. There are no criteria set at EU level for the targeting of funds freed up as a result of capping and degressivity. Member States may decide to reallocate such funds to income support interventions such as coupled income support, climate and agri-environment actions or investments, in line with their policy priorities as defined in national and regional partnership plans.

E-10-2026-002612.t: Cross-border drone flights to transport medical supplies in border regions
qt: to the Commission Pascal Arimont (PPE) Subject:

Research is ongoing under the Interreg EDEN-Medical project1 on the cross-border use of drones in medical logistics, for instance for transporting medicines, laboratory samples or medical equipment between hospitals. A recent study by the Institute for Transnational and Euregional cross-border cooperation and Mobility2 highlights major legal and administrative obstacles, including separate authorisation procedures in a number of Member States, divergent national aviation practices, an absence of harmonised geo-zones, outstanding issues in operations beyond the visual line of sight (BVLOS) and ad hoc operations, liability, insurance, health data and reimbursement. 1.
Is the Commission planning legislative or other measures to facilitate cross-border drone flights for medical logistics, as well as for fire brigades and other emergency services?
Will the Commission consider introducing a uniform application procedure or mutual recognition of national authorisations for cross-border drone operations, particularly in border regions?

How does the Commission intend to integrate the lessons learned from the EDENMedical project into its work on crisis preparedness, civil protection, digital health and advanced air mobility solutions?
https://www.interregmeuserhine.eu/en/projects/eden-medical/ https://crossborderitem.eu/wp-content/uploads/EDEN-Medical-Concept-Paper-1.pdf
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.9.2026) The EU regulatory framework for Unmanned Aerial Systems (UAS) is based on an operationcentric and risk-based approach, allowing operations to be authorised according to their level of risk. This framework already enables UAS beyond visual line of sight (BVLOS) operations, including medical logistics use cases, to the extent these operations are not excluded from European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) Basic Regulation coverage (Regulation (EU) 2018/11391) and its implementing rules as provided by Article 2(3)(a). The need for separate authorisation procedures in each Member State is largely due to the diverging approaches used to assess and mitigate air risk. As part of the continuous regulatory monitoring and review process, EASA has proposed an amendment to the U-space framework that aims to establish common procedures to address the lack of mutual recognition of operational authorisations among the different Member States. The Commission will continue to assess whether further action is needed in the context of the implementation of the EU drone framework, the roll-out of the U-space framework, and the follow-up to the Drone Strategy 2.0. As regards a uniform application procedure or mutual recognition of national authorisations, the Commission will continue, with EASA and Member States, to encourage convergence in administrative practices, facilitate the exchange of lessons learned including EU funded projects and to identify whether additional measures could further simplify cross-border procedures, while preserving safety oversight, responsibilities and sovereignty of national competent authorities.

E-10-2026-002611.t: Cross-border exchange of patient information during emergency service interventions
qt: to the Commission Pascal Arimont (PPE) Subject:

In border regions such as the Meuse-Rhine Euroregion, emergency services cooperate regularly and in a structured manner across borders. In practice, however, the exchange of necessary patient information between coordination centres, emergency services, hospitals and cost bearers is often hampered by diverging interpretations of the General Data Protection Regulation and national data protection rules. This can lead to situations where interventions cannot be properly documented or charged to insurers, as the insurance-related data cannot be fully shared between the participating Member States. The costs thus left uncovered often place a particularly heavy burden on local authorities in border regions. 1.

What specific legal bases and guidelines does the Commission envisage for the exchange of necessary patient and intervention data between rescue centres, emergency services, hospitals and cost bearers in cross-border emergencies?
How does the Commission ensure that EHDS and MyHealth@EU cover such emergency scenarios in practice, including with regard to billing and medical records?
Does the Commission plan to draw up model agreements, guidelines or pilot projects for border regions in order to prevent local authorities from having to shoulder the costs?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (24.9.2026) Regulation (EU) 2025/327 on the European Health Data Space1 (EHDS Regulation) establishes the rules on the cross-border exchange (including in emergency situations) of certain categories of electronic health data for the provision of healthcare, including relevant reimbursement services. The reimbursement of costs of cross-border healthcare is addressed by Directive 2011/24/EU on the application of patients’ rights in cross-border healthcare2. It is complemented by Regulation (EC) No 883/20043 which coordinates national social security schemes and gives persons insured within one Member State’s public health scheme the right to receive necessary health care during a stay in another Member State. The European Health Insurance Card (EHIC) provides the necessary legal basis for patient data to be exchanged and for billing the competent institution for the cost of the healthcare provided. Under the Interreg Specific Objective 1, 2021-27 Interreg programmes can support activities improving cooperation governance, such as removing barriers preventing border regions citizens benefiting from for e.g. cross-border emergency care. It has been used for instance by the Estonian Latvian Interreg programme in the Valga-Valka (twin city) where patients from Valka (LV) can access some medical assistance at the Valga hospital (EE). It is also recommended for Member States to take full advantage of BRIDGEforEU4, an instrument that can facilitate the resolution of cross-border obstacles.
1 Regulation (EU) 2025/327 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 11 February 2025 on the European

Health Data Space and amending Directive 2011/24/EU and Regulation (EU) 2024/2847, OJ L, 2025/327, 5.3.2025, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2025/327/oj. 2 Directive 2011/24/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 9 March 2011 on the application of patients’ rights in cross-border healthcare, OJ L 88, 4.4.2011, pp. 45–6, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2011/24/oj. 3 Regulation (EC) 883/2004 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 29 April 2004 on the coordination of social security systems: OJ L 66, 30.4.2004,ELI: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2004/883/oj/eng. 4 Regulation (EU) 2025/925 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 7 May 2025 on a Border Regions’ instrument for development and growth - https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legalcontent/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32025R0925&qid=1789569120297.

E-10-2026-002610.t: Mandatory disclosure and portability of cloud control servers for connected products on the single market
qt: to the Commission Markéta Gregorová (Verts/ALE) Subject:

A growing share of products on the EU market rely on cloud control centres operated through mobile applications, including solar inverters, robotic vacuum cleaners, smart home devices and connected toys. Auditing every such product is neither feasible for Member States nor proportionate for manufacturers, and software updates may alter a product’s behaviour. A targeted, low-cost measure would address part of this gap. Manufacturers and importers could be required to document all application programming interfaces (APIs) and control server addresses used by a product, including those used by future software versions, in the declaration of conformity and to ensure the control server can be changed by the operator. Such a measure would expose hidden functions, allow control centres to be switched where a manufacturer becomes unreliable, keep products working after insolvency and enable third party integration across brands. 1.

Do existing instruments, such as the Cyber Resilience Act or delegated acts under the Radio Equipment Directive, already require disclosure of control server addresses and APIs? If not, will the Commission assess the introduction of such a requirement?
Will the Commission examine mandating control server portability to extend product lifespan and reduce lock-in?
How will the Commission address the risks posed by software updates that introduce new control endpoints after placement on the market?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (17.9.2026) The Cyber Resilience Act (CRA)1, applying in full from 11 December 2027, requires manufacturers of products with digital elements2 to keep up-to-date technical documentation at least during the product’s support period. That documentation shall include, where applicable, a description of the system architecture explaining how software components build on or feed into each other and integrate into the overall processing. This may include identifying relevant application programming interfaces (APIs) and control server addresses. Furthermore, where a product is substantially modified as defined in Article 3(30) of the CRA after placement on the market, it is required to undergo a new conformity assessment. The Radio Equipment Directive3 does not specifically require the manufacturer to disclose control server addresses and APIs. It requires manufacturers to draw up a technical documentation, which, where appropriate, should include versions of software or firmware affecting compliance with relevant essential requirements set out in that Directive. In the framework of the Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation4 and the 2025-2030 Work Programme5, the Commission has been working on the ecodesign of servers and data storage products, as well as on addressing, where relevant, aspects linked to software, durability and upgradability. Finally, the proposed revision of the Cybersecurity Act6 puts forward a framework to address strategic Information and Communication Technologies (ICT) supply chain risks and monitor dependencies in several critical ICT supply chains including cloud services. Within this framework, a range of targeted and proportional derisking measures, also transparencyrelated, could be taken.
1 Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 23 October 2024 on horizontal

cybersecurity requirements for products with digital elements and amending Regulations (EU) No 168/2013 and (EU) 2019/1020 and Directive (EU) 2020/1828 (Cyber Resilience Act) (Text with EEA relevance), OJ L, 2024/2847, 20.11.2024, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/2847/oj. 2 A product with digital elements includes its remote data processing solutions, in accordance with Article 3(1). 3 Directive 2014/53/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 16 April 2014 on the harmonisation of the laws of the Member States relating to the making available on the market of radio equipment and repealing Directive 1999/5/EC (Text with EEA relevance), OJ L 153, 22.5.2014, pp. 62–106, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2014/53/oj. 4 Regulation (EU) 2024/1781 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 June 2024 establishing a framework for the setting of ecodesign requirements for sustainable products, amending Directive (EU) 2020/1828 and Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 and repealing Directive 2009/125/EC (Text with EEA relevance), OJ L, 2024/1781, 28.6.2024, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1781/oj. 5 Communication from the Commission ‘Ecodesign for Sustainable Products and Energy Labelling Working Plan 2025-2030’, https://environment.ec.europa.eu/document/download/5f7ff5e2-ebe9-4bd4-a139db881bd6398f_en?filename=FAQ-UPDATE-4th-Iteration_clean.pdf. 6 COM/2026/11 final.

at: (English version) to the Commission Dan-Ştefan Motreanu (PPE) (24 June 2026) Subject: Mobilising private investment for critical minerals projects On 10 June 2026, the French G7 Presidency announced that 39 European and international companies, financial institutions and trade federations had presented a joint statement calling for greater investment in the resilience and diversification of critical minerals value chains. E-10-2026-002607.t: Regulatory fragmentation and uptake of 5G standalone across Member States
qt: to the Commission Dan-Ştefan Motreanu (PPE) Subject:

Recent analysis has revealed that, despite early harmonisation of key 5G pioneer bands, the EU is failing to translate spectrum policy into high-performance network deployment, with 5G standalone (5G SA) coverage available to only 2 % of consumers in the EU, in contrast to 80 % in China, 52 % in India and 24 % in the United States. Moreover, the roll-out of 5G SA networks remains highly uneven across Member States, with many still relying on nonstandalone solutions that deliver inferior speeds and higher latency. Such fragmentation collectively suppresses investment incentives and acts as a constraint on the transition towards 6G. In the light of this, what measures is the Commission exploring to tackle regulatory fragmentation across the Member States and accelerate the uptake of 5G standalone within the EU?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.9.2026) Accelerating the deployment of high-performance 5G Standalone (5G SA) networks is essential for Europe's digital transformation, industrial competitiveness and the future development of 6G. Despite progress in assigning the harmonised 5G pioneer bands, the deployment of 5G SA remains uneven across the EU. This reflects still-emerging demand for advanced 5G services, fragmented national spectrum regulation, heterogeneous authorisation conditions and high investment costs of network upgrades. The Commission proposal for a Digital Networks Act1 (DNA) aims to address these barriers by promoting a more coherent and investment-friendly regulatory framework. The DNA proposes more consistent and investment-friendly conditions for radio spectrum assignment, including indefinite licence durations and facilitated renewal, more efficient use of spectrum, through mainstreaming spectrum sharing, where technically feasible and in line with competition law, and reinforced ‘use it or share it’ obligations, more predictable spectrum awards, through an ex-ante spectrum Single Market mechanism to prevent market distortion, and long-term spectrum planning, and spectrum availability for key services and technologies, through the establishment of a Union Radio Spectrum Strategy and roadmap. By improving investment conditions and reducing regulatory fragmentation, the DNA will accelerate network upgrades and the transition to 5G SA, paving the way for future 6G deployment.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A52026PC0016.

E-10-2026-002606.t: Addressing barriers to the recycling of critical raw materials
qt: to the Commission Dan-Ştefan Motreanu (PPE) Subject:

In order to address Europe’s import dependency on critical raw materials, the Critical Raw Materials Act (CRMA) mandated that at least 25 % of the EU’s strategic raw materials should be sourced from recycled resources by 2030. Nonetheless, 7 out of the 26 materials required for the green transition have recycling rates of between 1 % and 5 %, while 10 of those materials are not recycled at all. Additionally, overly broad recycling targets fail to incentivise the recovery of harder-to-extract materials, while high processing costs continue to undermine the competitiveness of European recyclers. In the light of this: Does the Commission plan to introduce material-specific recycling targets or incentives for particularly strategic and hard-to-recover materials, such as rare earth elements?
at: (English version) to the Commission Dan-Ştefan Motreanu (PPE) (24 June 2026) Subject: Addressing barriers to the recycling of critical raw materials In order to address Europe’s import dependency on critical raw materials, the Critical Raw Materials Act (CRMA) mandated that at least 25% of the EU’s strategic raw materials should be sourced from recycled resources by 2030. Nonetheless, 7 out of the 26 materials required for the green transition have recycling rates of between 1% and 5%, while 10 of those materials are not recycled at all. Additionally, overly broad recycling targets fail to incentivise the recovery of harder-to-extract materials, while high processing costs continue to undermine the competitiveness of European recyclers. In the light of this: Does the Commission plan to introduce material-specific recycling targets or incentives for particularly strategic and hard-torecover materials, such as rare earth elements? (11 September 2026) The Critical Raw Materials Act (1) (CRMA) addresses the importance of significantly increasing the recycling of strategic raw materials in the EU through both an overall recycling-capacity benchmark and more targeted measures. By 2030, the EU’s recycling capacity should be able to produce at least 25% of the EU’s annual consumption of strategic raw materials, while also ensuring a significant increase in the amounts of each strategic raw material recycled from waste. This objective will be further supported by the forthcoming Circular Economy Act, to be adopted in the fourth quarter of 2026. The CRMA also recognises that a broad, aggregate benchmark alone may not sufficiently incentivise the recovery of individual materials, particularly those that are technologically more difficult or costly to recycle. Article 5(3) of the CRMA therefore requires the Commission to establish, by 1 January 2027, additional recycling-capacity benchmarks for strategic raw materials contained in relevant waste streams by means of delegated acts. These benchmarks will take into account the existing EU recycling capacity, the technological and economic feasibility of recovering individual materials, and relevant recycling and recovery targets under other EU legislation.

E-10-2026-002605.t: Extension of the Prüm II Regulation to non-EU countries
qt: to the Commission Dan-Ştefan Motreanu (PPE) Subject:

In the light of increased cooperation between Member States’ enforcement authorities and non-EU countries, including the United Kingdom, Ukraine and Canada, the Commission recently announced its aim to extend the scope of the Prüm II Regulation1. The regulation provides a framework for the automated exchange of biometric and identification data between Member States, and the Commission now seeks to bring non-EU countries within its scope in order to combat the fragmentation that might arise from the current approach. Therefore, given that non-EU countries are not subject to the same data protection standards as the EU Member States, what measures is the Commission exploring to ensure that data exchanges under the extended framework meet an adequate level of protection?

Regulation (EU) 2024/982 of 13 March 2024 on the automated search and exchange of data for police cooperation, and amending Council Decisions 2008/615/JHA and 2008/616/JHA and Regulations (EU) 2018/1726, (EU) No 2019/817 and (EU) 2019/818 of the European Parliament and of the Council (the Prüm II Regulation) (OJ L, 2024/982, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/982/oj). 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (31.8.2026) The so-called Prüm International initiative aims at strengthening information exchange for law enforcement purposes with key trusted non-EU countries. The Commission will explore the measures available under EU law for such exchanges, as indicated also in the call for evidence1. Directive (EU) 2016/6802 applies to exchange of data between competent authorities of Member States for the purposes of prevention, investigation, detection or prosecution of criminal offences or execution of criminal penalties. The Directive also provides for specific measures concerning the transfer of personal data to third countries, particularly the existence of an adequacy decision with the third country (Article 36) or appropriate safeguards (Article 37). With the Prüm International initiative, the Commission will aim to ensure that the information exchange for law enforcement purposes with key trusted non-EU countries will meet high EU standards on data security and fundamental rights, including data protection, with clear purpose limitation and national oversight over operational decisions.
