E-10-2026-002604.t: Over-regulation and lack of impact assessments
qt: to the Commission Jorge Buxadé Villalba (PfE) Subject:

According to the Regulatory Scrutiny Board’s Annual Report 2025, in 2025 the Commission adopted a total of 116 legislative proposals and 741 delegated and implementing acts. Only 38 legislative proposals had an impact assessment. The Regulatory Scrutiny Board itself, an internal and independent body of the Commission, did not give a single positive opinion among the 25 impact assessments it analysed at first instance, recording a negative opinion rate of 56 % and classifying the average quality of the reports as ‘weak’ or ‘unsatisfactory’. The Board also found that many impact assessments lacked adequate quantification of costs and benefits. This situation shows that the European Union legislates extensively, poorly and without taking into account the socio-economic realities or the views of its own quality control body. In view of the above: 1.
Does the Commission believe that regulating massively benefits companies, families and workers?
Is the Commission aware that its over-regulation is leading to a transfer of income from the productive economy to the compliance industry?
Does the Commission agree that failing to carry out impact assessments shows that it is driven by its own political agenda and interests, and not by the problems facing Europeans?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (24.8.2026) Competitiveness and making business easier and faster in Europe are key priorities for this Commission. Its better regulation and regulatory tools (impact assessments, evaluations and stakeholders’ engagement) support designing evidence-based policies and laws that achieve their objectives in the most effective and efficient way, responsive to the needs of EU citizens, businesses, and civil society. Impact assessments provide evidence-based answers to key questions regarding the expected impact of a new initiative. They include an estimation of benefits and quantification of costs, including all compliance costs where this is feasible and proportionate. The Commission proposes laws and regulations where the benefits outweigh the associated costs. The Better Regulation Guidelines1 set several criteria to determine when an initiative needs an impact assessment. The main ones are that there must be a political choice and significant impacts to consider. Further to the Communication ‘A Simpler, Clearer and Better Enforced EU Rulebook’2 more initiatives are to be accompanied by an impact assessment, including targeted or urgent initiatives, where feasible. Cases of exceptional urgency may require derogations. Moreover, several legislative proposals could be accompanied by one single impact assessment. The Commission is pursuing ambitious simplification to lighten the EU regulatory burden, while maintaining high regulatory standards. Burden reduction targets (to lower the administrative burden by at least 25% for all businesses and by at least 35% for small and medium-sized enterprises) contribute to this ambition. To create a more cohesive and efficient single market, the Commission will ensure that new legislative proposals avoid regulatory complexity and fragmentation.
1 https://commission.europa.eu/system/files/2021-11/swd2021_305_en.pdf. 2 COM(2026) 380 final – Communication from the Commission to the European Parliament, the European

Council, the Council, the European Economic and Social Committee and the Committee of the Regions - A Simpler, Clearer and Better Enforced EU Rulebook’ - https://eurlex.europa.eu/resource.html?uri=cellar:e3002437-4314-11f1-809501aa75ed71a1.0001.02/DOC_1&format=PDF.

qt: to the Commission Jorge Buxadé Villalba (PfE) Subject:

Between 2019 and 2024, the EU issued more than 13 000 new regulations. In the financial sector, EU regulatory output has grown by more than 700 % in three decades, reaching around 1 629 documents – some 95 500 pages – across the banking and capital markets regulatory framework. More than 60 % of European companies identify regulation as an obstacle to investment, and 55 % of SMEs point to the regulatory and administrative burden as their biggest challenge. In the European Round Table for Industry survey for the second half of 2025, only 8 % of the CEOs consulted planned to increase investment in Europe, while 45 % expected to invest more than expected in the US. Does the Commission: 1.
understand that the complexity and quantity of its regulation – especially in the energy, financial, food and transport sectors – is creating regulatory chaos and discouraging investments?
agree that European companies are increasingly dedicating resources to compliance and reporting rather than investing in technology, employment or innovation?
consider itself responsible for the gradual loss of competitiveness, industrial capacity and quality of life in Europe?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (10.8.2026) Regulatory complexity can affect competitiveness. This is why the Commission is pursuing modernisation and simplification of European legislation and is effectively reducing the administrative burdens for companies. The Commission has a target to lower the administrative burden by at least 25% and at least 35% for small and medium-sized enterprises. To this end, it has so far proposed 12 omnibus packages and other simplification proposals, with net recurrent cost savings of some EUR 18 billion. Half of the proposals for the Commission work programme 2026 are simplification proposals. Looking ahead, the recent Communication ‘A Simpler, Clearer and Better Enforced EU Rulebook’1 contains a Regulatory Deep Cleaning Action Plan with 12 policy areas, including the energy, financial, food and transport sectors mentioned in the question. It will tackle inconsistencies, outdated, overlapping or redundant provisions, or overly complex rules that hinder competitiveness and innovation. The Communication also includes simplicity by design as a new way of making legislation. The Commission is acting decisively and swiftly to address EU loss of competitiveness. It is a shared responsibility with co-legislators to make this ambition a concrete deliverable.

E-10-2026-002602.t: Use of payment data by payment service providers and the purpose limitation principle of Article 5 GDPR
qt: to the Commission Auke Zijlstra (PfE), Marieke Ehlers (PfE) Subject:
Use of payment data by payment service providers and the purpose limitation principle of Article 5 GDPR

Banks hold large amounts of personal data resulting from the use of payment accounts and other financial services. There are indications that such payment data is used for purposes for which customers have not given their explicit consent. For example, data on spending in other Member States are apparently being used to develop policy positions and lobbying national governments1. In addition, data relating to, inter alia, the number of cars, credit cards, minor children and mortgage payments are apparently being used to assess the creditworthiness of customers and determine whether they can take on further debt2. Article 5(1)(b) of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) provides that personal data may be processed only for specified, explicit and legitimate purposes (purpose limitation principle). 1.
Does the Commission consider such processing to be compatible with the principle of purpose limitation, as laid down in Article 5 GDPR?
Does the use of payment data for shaping policy, lobbying or profiling for credit decisions require explicit consent from the persons concerned?
What measures is the Commission taking to ensure that banks do not process payment data for purposes incompatible with the original purpose for which they were collected?

E-10-2026-002601.t: Continuous revisions of the Greek Recovery and Resilience Plan (‘Greece 2.0’) and impact on the achievement of its initial targets
qt: to the Commission Sakis Arnaoutoglou (S&D) Subject:

The National Recovery and Resilience Plan ‘Greece 2.0’ has been subject to repeated revisions since its adoption in 2021. According to a recent comparative assessment of the plan in its original and current form, a significant number of measures have been substantially modified, reduced in their physical or financial scope or completely withdrawn. Among the projects allegedly withdrawn or significantly changed are interventions related to water infrastructure, civil protection, rail, 5G networks, telecommunication infrastructure, childcare facilities, research and innovation, irrigation projects, energy storage and just transition areas. Bearing in mind that the RRF was created with the aim of supporting reforms and investments with high added value for sustainable growth and the green and digital transitions and strengthening the social and economic resilience of the Member States, can the Commission say: Does it have an assessment of whether project modifications or withdrawals affect the achievement of the original strategic objectives of the Greek RRP?
at: (English version) to the Commission Sakis Arnaoutoglou (S&D) (24 June 2026) Subject: Continuous revisions of the Greek Recovery and Resilience Plan (‘Greece 2.0’) and impact on the achievement of its initial targets The National Recovery and Resilience Plan ‘Greece 2.0’ has been subject to repeated revisions since its adoption in 2021. According to a recent comparative assessment of the plan in its original and current form, a significant number of measures have been substantially modified, reduced in their physical or financial scope or completely withdrawn. Among the projects allegedly withdrawn or significantly changed are interventions related to water infrastructure, civil protection, rail, 5G networks, telecommunication infrastructure, childcare facilities, research and innovation, irrigation projects, energy storage and just transition areas. Bearing in mind that the RRF was created with the aim of supporting reforms and investments with high added value for sustainable growth and the green and digital transitions and strengthening the social and economic resilience of the Member States, can the Commission say: Does it have an assessment of whether project modifications or withdrawals affect the achievement of the original strategic objectives of the Greek RRP? (7 September 2026) Greece’s Recovery and Resilience Plan (RRP) was amended several times since its adoption, most recently in July 2026, based on Article 21 of the regulation (EU) 2021/241 establishing the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF) Regulation (1). Article 21 allows for amendments if the Plan, particularly its milestones and targets, becomes partly or wholly unattainable due to objective circumstances, such as unexpected technical challenges, delays related to public procurement procedures, lowerthan-expected demand, or force majeure. The Commission is assessing each amendment against the criteria in Article 19(3) and in accordance with Annex V of the RRF Regulation, before proposing the amendment to the Council. These assessments consistently confirmed that the revised plans continue to meet all the criteria set out in the RRF Regulation. The share of the plan supporting climate objectives has risen from 37.5% in the original plan to 39.8% in the latest amended RRP’s total allocation, while the digital tagging stands at 25.2%, both above the required thresholds. Moreover, revisions have also allowed the plan to address emerging needs, in line with the RRF legal basis, such as the reconstructions following storms Daniel and Elias. On this basis, the Commission considers that the revised plans remain conducive to achieving the RRF’s strategic objectives.

E-10-2026-002600.t: Sheep and goat pox-related transhumance restrictions in Greece and the need for EU support for livestock farmers
qt: to the Commission Sakis Arnaoutoglou (S&D) Subject:

Transhumance is a long-established pillar of rural Greece's production and environment, particularly in mountainous and disadvantaged areas. It helps preserve biodiversity and prevent rural depopulation and contributes to sustainable pasture management and the production of high-added-value products, such as Feta PDO. In Greece, tough restrictions have been introduced on the movement of herds to summer pastures, as a result of the sheep and goat pox epidemic. While the protection of animal health is absolutely necessary, livestock farmers practising seasonal transhumance are facing serious practical and financial challenges, namely high feed costs, difficulty in accessing pastures, additional transport and biosecurity costs, as well as uncertainty about the adequacy and speed of compensation. The issue is especially important given that the UN has declared 2026 as the International Year of Rangelands and Pastoralists, recognising the crucial role of pastoralism in food security, the resilience of rural communities and the protection of ecosystems. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Is it monitoring the impact of sanitary restrictions on transhumance in Greece, particularly in mountainous and disadvantaged areas?
What European funding tools can be used right away to cover the increased costs of feed, transport, biosecurity and loss of access to pasture?
Does it intend to consider dedicated European initiatives, within the framework of the CAP and the International Year of Rangelands and Pastoralists 2026, to support and maintain transhumance?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (28.8.2026) 1. The Commission monitors the application of the Animal Health Law1 and remains in contact with the Greek authorities who are responsible for the implementation of sanitary restrictions. The Commission is also attentive to the broader effects that such restrictions may have on livestock farming systems, including transhumance practices. However, assessments of the socio-economic impact of these measures, including grazing activities, fall primarily within the competence of the Member States. 2. Support may be provided through the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP)2 Strategic Plans (CSP) including risk management and sectoral or investment-related measures3. In addition, exceptional measures are provided under Regulation (EU) No 1308/20134, to be funded by the agricultural reserve5. Support can also be granted by the national authorities to compensate for the costs of the prevention, control and eradication of animal diseases under the Agricultural de minimis Regulation6, the Agricultural Block Exemption Regulation (ABER)7 or the Agricultural state aid Guidelines8, provided that all relevant conditions are met. 3. Interventions for transhumance may be included in the CSPs notably as eco-schemes9. The Greek CSP provides for such an intervention10. The Commission will continue supporting awareness-raising and policy dialogue on sustainable agriculture, including transhumance, by

E-10-2026-002599.t: Personal protective equipment for rescue and emergency services
qt: Anfrage zur schriftlichen Beantwortung E-002599/2026 an die Kommission Artikel 144 der Geschäftsordnung Mika Aaltola (PPE) Betrifft:
Persönliche Schutzausrüstung für Rettungs- und Notfalldienste

In den EU-Rechtsvorschriften über persönliche Schutzausrüstungen (PSA) besteht eine Lücke. Artikel 2 Absatz 2 Buchstabe a der Verordnung (EU) 2016/425 sieht eine Ausnahmeregelung für PSA vor, die speziell zur Verwendung durch Streit- oder Ordnungskräfte entworfen wurden. Diese Ausnahmeregelung erstreckt sich jedoch nicht auf Rettungs- und Notfalldienste. Der derzeitige Rahmen sollte überarbeitet werden, damit den Einsatzgegebenheiten der Rettungs- und Notfalldienste angemessen Rechnung getragen wird. Die Lehren aus dem Konflikt in der Ukraine haben gezeigt, dass Rettungskräfte und Notfalleinsatzkräfte ähnlichen Gefahren wie Streit- und Ordnungskräfte ausgesetzt sind. Infolge der derzeitigen Regelungslücke sind die Mitgliedstaaten daran gehindert, geeignete Schutzausrüstungen für Rettungsdienste zu erwerben und zu lagern. Daher wären Klarstellungen zu mehreren Sachverhalten wünschenswert. 1.
Ist der Kommission diese Regelungslücke bekannt, und hat sie eine Bewertung ihrer Auswirkungen auf die Einsatzbereitschaft der Rettungs- und Notfalldienste in den Mitgliedstaaten vorgenommen?

Beabsichtigt die Kommission, einen Vorschlag zur Änderung der Verordnung (EU) 2016/425 vorzulegen und die bestehende Ausnahmeregelung auf PSA auszuweiten, die speziell zur Verwendung durch Rettungs- und Notfalldienste entworfen wurden?
Unterstützer1 Eingang: 24.6.2026

Diese Anfrage wird von Mitgliedern unterstützt, die nicht mit dem Verfasser bzw. der Verfasserin identisch sind: Tomáš Zdechovský (PPE), Dan-Ştefan Motreanu (PPE), Ville Niinistö (Verts/ALE), Pekka Toveri (PPE), Katri Kulmuni (Renew), Merja Kyllönen (The Left), Tomas Tobé (PPE), Ana Miguel Pedro (PPE), Radan Kanev (PPE), Sirpa Pietikäinen (PPE), Ondřej Krutílek (ECR), Sebastian Tynkkynen (ECR), Maria Guzenina (S&D), Elisabeth Dieringer (PfE), Maria Ohisalo (Verts/ALE), Malika Sorel (NI), Lena Düpont (PPE), Petras Auštrevičius (Renew), Grégory Allione (Renew), Emil Radev (PPE), Maria Grapini (S&D), Michalis Hadjipantela (PPE), Sabine Verheyen (PPE), Matej Tonin (PPE), Kosma Złotowski (ECR), Sebastian Everding (The Left), Michał Dworczyk (ECR). 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (11.8.2026) Personal protective equipment (PPE) designed for the armed forces has operational and security requirements (e.g. integration with weapons, communications and other military systems, camouflage, defence-specific conformity assessment processes, confidentiality of sensitive information) that are distinct from the PPE used by emergency service workers and civilians in general. Moreover, defence PPE is closely linked to national defence and security interests, which remain the sole responsibility of each Member State1. Regulation (EU) 2016/4252 is aimed at PPE placed on the EU market for civilian use and covers all physical, chemical and biological hazards to which emergency service workers can be exposed, including bullet wounds and knife stabs. PPE for emergency service workers was already covered by former Directive 89/686/EEC3 and the risk of bullet wounds and knife stabs was reclassified during the revision4 of the Directive. To guarantee that PPE does not present a risk for emergency workers, it is necessary to continue ensuring compliance with Regulation (EU) 2016/425. The Commission has thus no intention to amend Regulation (EU) 2016/425 to exclude these products from its scope. In the area of safety and health at work, equipment used by emergency and rescue services, as well as PPE worn or used by the military, the police and other public order agencies, is excluded from the minimum requirements of Directive 89/656/EEC on the use of PPE by workers at the workplace. Member States are however free to adopt more stringent protective measures compatible with the Treaties5.

qt: to the Commission Elena Nevado del Campo (PPE) Subject:

In 2023, the European Commission published ‘A comprehensive approach to mental health’, recognising the need to address mental health in EU institutions and Member States, and taking into account areas that go far beyond health, such as education, employment, digital policy, social inclusion and justice. However, the current framework has limitations, such as the fact that Member State participation is voluntary, that temporary projects are relied on to respond to systemic challenges, and that there are no guarantees of continuity beyond 2026. New initiatives are also needed to promote an approach based on prevention, community care, integration of mental health into all policy and stable funding for civil society and people with lived experience. What steps will the Commission take to integrate mental health into employment, education, youth, digitalisation and social policy?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (24.8.2026) Promoting good mental health across all policy areas is supported through the 2023 Communication on a comprehensive approach to mental health1. Under the flagship ‘Children Health 360’, a prevention toolkit is developed with UNICEF. The focus is currently on the implementation of the Communication, including related joint actions, such as MENTOR2 and PRISM3. The Commission will focus on addressing the impact of digitalisation on youth mental health. On 16 June 2026, it published a flash Eurobarometer4 that informed the work of Commission President’s Special Panel on child safety online5. The co-Chairs’s recommendations6, published on 13 July 2026, are currently being reviewed. Under the Digital Services Act7, very large online platforms and very large online search engines are obliged to assess and mitigate systemic risks, including risks to mental well-being. Research and innovation in this area are supported through a Horizon Europe call8. As part of the envisaged Quality Jobs Act, the Commission is considering the area of occupational health and safety risks in the workplace, including psychosocial ones. The European Agency for Safety and Health at Work will carry out a campaign on mental health and psychosocial risks at work in 2026-2028. Further support is provided through the EU Youth Strategy, Erasmus+ Youth, the European Solidarity Corps, the 2022 Council Recommendation on Pathways to School Success9 and the 2024 Wellbeing Guidelines10. Support is also provided through sport via #BeActive, the European Week of Sport, and through a planned Open Method of Coordination Group on mental health in sport.

E-10-2026-002596.t: Timeline and scope of the forthcoming simplification package on fisheries legislation to support the competitiveness of the EU fleet
qt: to the Commission Carmen Crespo Díaz (PPE), Isabelle Le Callennec (PPE), Paulo do Nascimento Cabral (PPE), Fredis Beleris (PPE), Niclas Herbst (PPE), Marco Falcone (PPE), Željana Zovko (PPE), Jessica Polfjärd (PPE), Susana Solís Pérez (PPE), Magdalena Adamowicz (PPE), Bartosz Arłukowicz (PPE), Francisco José Millán Mon (PPE), Javier Zarzalejos (PPE), Willemien Koning (PPE) Subject:

On 16 June 2026, during the plenary debate in Strasbourg on simplification and competitiveness, European Commissioner for Economy and Productivity; Implementation and Simplification Valdis Dombrovskis announced that the Commission is working on a ‘simplification package’ for the fisheries sector. The European fisheries and aquaculture sectors have repeatedly called for a reduction in administrative burdens and a simplification of the regulatory framework. The recent evaluation of the common fisheries policy also identified opportunities to simplify existing legislation and improve its implementation. Given the urgency of these concerns and the need to provide legal certainty and boost the competitiveness of the fisheries sector, we ask the Commission: 1.
What is the indicative timetable for presenting the forthcoming fisheries simplification package?

It is important to clarify whether the Commission envisages reviewing the common fisheries policy (including the landing obligation), the Fisheries Control Regulation1, the Common Market Organisation Regulation2, the multiannual management plans, the Deep-Sea Access Regulation3, and the framework for the European Maritime, Fisheries and Aquaculture Fund. Which legislative instruments does it intend to include in this package?

Given the importance of these reforms for the sector’s viability, what timeline does the Commission contemplate for the subsequent legislative process with the European Parliament and the Council, and how will it ensure that the package is adopted before the end of the current term?

(20 August 2026) The Commission is working on simplifying and reducing administrative burden in the area of fisheries and aquaculture. qt: to the Commission Joachim Streit (Renew) Subject:

In 2023, the European Union Drugs Agency (EUDA) recorded a new all-time high for the seizure of drug precursors essential for the production of synthetic drugs. Under EU legislation, the legal trade in drug precursors is regulated through requirements for transparency, registration and authorisation. In order to circumvent statutory obligations, known drug precursors are slightly modified chemically. The Commission aims to counter the increasingly frequent use of such drug precursors via a new drugs strategy. The strategy aims to close legal loopholes and improve the identification of these substances. A crackdown on drug laboratories is also to be prioritised, as drug precursors are increasingly being processed into end products in Europe and existing substances chemically modified, resulting in new derivatives such as nitazenes or fentanyl derivatives. 1.

To what extent does the strategy take into account ensuring that innovative actors in the development of chemical products are not exposed to accusations of developing drug precursors – and that what is known as the deterrent effect does not come into play?

How does the Commission ensure that research into new, legitimate applications and innovation remains possible, despite the prohibition under Article 16 of the Commission’s legislative proposal on the possession and use of drug precursors and on performing intermediary activities involving them?

How does the Commission assess the added value of EU measures to combat production within Member States, compared to the actions of individual Member States, given that synthetic drugs are increasingly being manufactured within Member States?

How does the Commission assess the added value of EU measures to combat production within Member States, compared to the actions of individual Member States, given that synthetic drugs are increasingly being manufactured within Member States? (14 September 2026) Action on drug precursors is a key element of the EU Drugs Strategy and Action Plan against drug trafficking (1). However, many precursors are chemicals with an essential role for legitimate industrial production, such as in pharmaceuticals, batteries, cosmetics or food additives. The Commission Proposal for a regulation on monitoring and controlling drug precursors (2) aims to address the challenge of preventing the use of drug precursors in the illicit manufacture of drugs, while simplifying rules and procedures for legitimate trade. The proposed Regulation will set out conditions for legitimate trade of these substances, thus providing for legal certainty to legitimate actors. The proposal also acts specifically on designer precursors, i.e. substances with no known legitimate use only developed to circumvent the regime applicable to scheduled substances. For these chemicals, the proposal contains provisions to safeguard their use for research and innovation purposes, either in small quantities via prior notification or by requesting a licence. The EU Drugs Agency would also help businesses and authorities identifying the substances coming under the scope of the control measures by setting up an information repository on drug precursors. The Impact Assessment supporting the proposal concluded that EU wide action benefits businesses, national authorities and society, ensuring the good functioning of the internal market and reducing administrative burden, while taking a harmonised and stringent approach across all Member States on fighting illicit drug production. Framework Decision 2004/757/JHA (3) further allows a common approach to fight drugs and precursors trafficking by establishing minimum rules relating to these offences.

qt: to the Commission Catarina Martins (The Left), Ana Miranda Paz (Verts/ALE) Subject:

New outbreaks of cyanobacterial blooms and eutrophication in the Lindoso (Portugal) and As Conchas (Galicia) reservoirs on the River Lima pose serious risks to public health and ecosystems, affecting the Peneda-Gerês National Park. The Spanish Supreme Court recently upheld a landmark ruling finding the Regional Government of Galicia (Xunta de Galicia) and the Minho-Sil River Basin Authority guilty of failure to act, holding these public bodies responsible for infringing the public’s rights to health and to a healthy environment. This international river basin is regulated by the Albufeira Convention, which requires Portugal and Spain to coordinate measures to prevent pollution and achieve ‘good status’ for the waters, in line with the Water Framework Directive (Directive 2000/60/EC). In view of the continuing cross-border environmental degradation, the following questions arise: 1.
Is the Commission aware of these incidents of pollution and of the court rulings finding the Spanish authorities guilty of failing to act to protect this ecosystem?

Does the Commission consider that this situation constitutes a continuing failure by the Member States concerned to fulfil their obligations under the Water Framework Directive and the Nitrates Directive?

What steps or requests for clarification does the Commission intend to take or submit with regard to Portugal and Spain to ensure the effective implementation of European Union environmental law in this cross-border body of water?
at: (English version) to the Commission Catarina Martins (The Left), Ana Miranda Paz (Verts/ALE) (24 June 2026) Subject: Pollutants in the River Lima New outbreaks of cyanobacterial blooms and eutrophication in the Lindoso (Portugal) and As Conchas (Galicia) reservoirs on the River Lima pose serious risks to public health and ecosystems, affecting the Peneda-Gerês National Park. The Spanish Supreme Court recently upheld a landmark ruling finding the Regional Government of Galicia (Xunta de Galicia) and the Minho-Sil River Basin Authority guilty of failure to act, holding these public bodies responsible for infringing the public’s rights to health and to a healthy environment. This international river basin is regulated by the Albufeira Convention, which requires Portugal and Spain to coordinate measures to prevent pollution and achieve ‘good status’ for the waters, in line with the Water Framework Directive (Directive 2000/60/EC). In view of the continuing cross-border environmental degradation, the following questions arise: 1.
Is the Commission aware of these incidents of pollution and of the court rulings finding the Spanish authorities guilty of failing to act to protect this ecosystem?

Does the Commission consider that this situation constitutes a continuing failure by the Member States concerned to fulfil their obligations under the Water Framework Directive and the Nitrates Directive?

What steps or requests for clarification does the Commission intend to take or submit with regard to Portugal and Spain to ensure the effective implementation of European Union environmental law in this cross-border body of water?

(1 September 2026) The Commission is aware of cyanobacterial blooms affecting the Lindoso and As Conchas reservoirs, as well as of the rulings of the High Court of Justice of Galicia and — subsequently — of the Spanish Supreme Court, concerning the failure of the competent authorities to act. Under the Water Framework Directive (1), Member States must prevent deterioration and achieve good status of water bodies, including through proper identification of pressures and appropriate programmes of measures. Under the Nitrates Directive (2), Member States must designate as Nitrates Vulnerable Zones all land which drains into the waters identified as polluted and reinforce action programmes where pollution from diffuse agricultural sources persists. Determining whether a particular situation constitutes a continuing failure to fulfil these obligations requires an assessment in accordance with the applicable procedures and on the basis of sufficient evidence. The Commission will continue to closely monitor developments, notably in the context of the upcoming fourth River Basin Management Plans (due by December 2027) and the 2024-2027 reporting cycle under the Nitrates Directive. The Commission will also follow the action (or lack thereof) undertaken by the competent authorities in response to the rulings of the High Court of Justice of Galicia and the Spanish Supreme Court and decide on any appropriate follow-up in its role as guardian of the Treaties. Moreover, to address the growing risk of toxic algal blooms, the Commission’s Joint Research Centre, is presently conducting a pilot study, commissioned by the European Parliament, on a near-real-time monitoring system for harmful algal blooms across European waters.

E-10-2026-002593.t: Deterioration in the situation of European industry as regards ferro-alloys and silicon metal, which are of recognised strategic importance for the European Union’s economic security
qt: to the Commission Bogdan Andrzej Zdrojewski (PPE) Subject:

The ferro-alloy and silicon metal industry plays a key role in European value chains in connection with the production of steel, aluminium, batteries and semiconductors, and also in relation to energy technologies and the defence sector. At the same time, however, the sector is under heavy import pressure, primarily from China. A matter of particular concern is the fact that silicon metal, which has been recognised by the European Union as a strategic and critical raw material, has not been granted protection of the sort accorded to certain ferroalloys. As a result, EU production has been virtually eliminated. Silicon metal is increasingly being used as a substitute for ferro-silicon in certain industrial applications. The silicon metal currently being imported – primarily from China and Angola – is placed on the EU market at such low prices that industrial users use it in preference to ferro-silicon. This undermines the effectiveness of the entire safeguard mechanism in place for ferro-alloy production. In view of the deteriorating situation of the European ferro-alloy and silicon metal industry, I would like to put the following questions to the European Commission: 1.
Has the European Commission analysed the phenomenon whereby silicon metal is used as a substitute for ferro-silicon, rendering ineffective the safeguards put in place for ferro-silicon?
How does the Commission intend to take into consideration the status of silicon metal as a strategic and critical raw material when developing the EU’s industrial and commercial policy?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.9.2026) The European Commission has imposed definitive safeguard measures on imports of certain ferroalloys into the EU on 18 November 2025. A comparison of import data of January to April 2025 with January to April 2026 shows a decrease of import volumes and fluctuating import prices. In order to thoroughly analyse the effectiveness of the measure, the Commission will initiate a review no later than November 2026. As regards silicon metal, there are anti-dumping measures in place on imports from China since 1990, which have been continued following several reviews which have extended the measures before they expired. The Commission is committed to ensuring the effectiveness of measures in place and may initiate a review to reexamine the measures where there is evidence to suggest that they may no longer be sufficient to counteract the negative effects of dumped imports. The Commission engages with the EU industry requesting to review the existing measures to ensure that the correct evidentiary standards are met. If these standards are met, an investigation is initiated to examine the circumstances with a view to adapting the measures if necessary. The Commission considers carefully the designation of strategic and critical raw materials when developing commercial and industrial policies. Relatedly, promoting the recycling of strategic and critical raw materials in general in the EU is also of important consideration in these.

E-10-2026-002592.t: Delays in payments to Olive Producer Organisations’ programmes in Greece
qt: to the Commission Sakis Arnaoutoglou (S&D) Subject:

Serious disruption has been caused to the Greek olive production sector due to the long delay in the payment of aid for the programmes of Olive Producer Organisations (OEFs). According to industry representatives, approximately 65 olive grower organisations and OEFs, representing more than 20 000 olive producers across the country, have already implemented approved actions and met their obligations, without however receiving the expected funding. These are programmes that are financed by resources derived from deductions from olive growers and returned to them through actions that enhance competitiveness, quality, education, innovation and sustainability in the Greek olive sector. These delays create conditions of economic strangulation, an inability to plan future activities, a risk of disruption to the organisations’ operations and have serious consequences for workers, producers and local economies. In view of the above: 1.
Is the Commission monitoring the proper and timely implementation of OEF programmes in Greece, in particular with regard to the payment of planned aid?
Does the Commission intend to ask the Greek authorities for a clear schedule of repayment to OEFs?
What measures can the Commission take to ensure that payment delays do not undermine the operation of OEFs and support for olive producers?

(1 September 2026) The Commission closely monitors the proper and timely implementation of the operational programmes for olive oil and table olives in Greece. Therefore, it is aware of delays affecting both the implementation of the programmes and the disbursement of the aid provided for thereunder. It has accordingly reminded the Greek authorities of their obligation to ensure that payments are made without undue delay. Under shared management, Greece is primarily responsible for ensuring the correct and timely payment of Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) support under the operational programmes for olive oil and table olives, in line with Regulation (EU) 2021/2116 (1). The Commission may request information from the Greek authorities, assess whether national management as well as control systems comply with Union rules and maintain close follow-up with the national authorities, including technical support where appropriate. The Commission will continue to remain in close contact with the Greek authorities regarding the delays affecting the implementation of these programmes and the related payments.

E-10-2026-002588.t: Opening of AKP representative office in occupied Nicosia, in a historic building that is purportedly a cultural heritage monument
qt: to the Commission Giorgos Georgiou (The Left) Subject:

According to reports, the ruling party of Türkiye (AKP) has opened a representative office in occupied Nicosia, in a historic building that is purportedly a cultural heritage monument, without the required permits and without a clear legal framework for the operation of foreign political parties in the occupied areas. This development raises concerns about Türkiye’s growing political and administrative influence in the occupied areas of the Republic of Cyprus, as well as about the protection of cultural heritage and respect for the sovereignty of an EU Member State. In view of the above: 1.

Does the Commission agree that the operation of an office of the ruling party of Türkiye in the occupied areas constitutes further political and administrative interference in the territory of an EU Member State, and does the Commission intend to make a statement or take diplomatic action in relation to this?
What measures does the Commission intend to take to monitor and protect cultural heritage monuments in the occupied areas, especially in cases of the possible unauthorised use of listed buildings?
Does the Commission intend to raise the issue in the context of Euro-Turkish relations, calling on Türkiye to respect the relevant UN resolutions and the sovereignty of the Republic of Cyprus?

E-10-2026-002586.t: Costs, objectives and evaluation of the EU campaign ‘Protect what matters: our democracy’
qt: to the Commission Martin Sonneborn (NI) Subject:

From 20 April to 21 June 2026, the Commission ran the campaign ‘Protect what matters: our democracy’ (with the involvement of the agencies Havas Paris, Havas Play, Havas Media, Prose on Pixels), securing over 75 440 outdoor advertising spaces in 3 650 cities across all 27 Member States. In statements to the media, the European Commission representation in Estonia quoted figures of approximately EUR 3 million for content creation and production and EUR 30 million for media placement, adding that a breakdown by Member State would not provide a complete picture. 1.
Can the Commission confirm or correct the sums quoted and can it indicate the budget line used, with a breakdown by type of expenditure and by Member State?

E-10-2026-002585.t: The number of illegal immigrants in France, according to the Government and Eurostat: a methodological error or wilful blindness?
qt: to the Commission Fabrice Leggeri (PfE), Mathilde Androuët (PfE), Pierre-Romain Thionnet (PfE), André Rougé (PfE), Séverine Werbrouck (PfE), Marie-Luce Brasier-Clain (PfE), Aleksandar Nikolic (PfE), Angéline Furet (PfE), Julie Rechagneux (PfE), Pierre Pimpie (PfE), Valérie Deloge (PfE), Marie Dauchy (PfE), Mélanie Disdier (PfE) Subject:

On 12 May 2026, a post on the Eurostat website stated that 719 395 people were illegally present in the European Union in 2025, including 159 460 in France1. In October 2025, Laurent Nunez, the French Minister for the Interior, estimated that there were 700 000 illegal immigrants in France, a figure very similar to that reported by Eurostat for the European Union as a whole. As early as 2021, Gérald Darmanin, then Minister for the Interior, announced that there were between 600 000 and 700 000 illegal immigrants on French soil. While discrepancies arising from a different calculation method are understandable, the one observed here appears to be particularly significant. If we assume that the differences are of the same magnitude across the whole of the Union, this would suggest that the number of undocumented foreign nationals in the Union could exceed three million. The significant discrepancies between these figures contribute to confusion regarding the actual number of people residing in the Union illegally. For the sake of clarity, could the Commission: 1.
explain the 1:4 discrepancy between the figures provided by the French Minister for the Interior and those from Eurostat for France?
consider using a different statistical category or method in order to better reflect the estimates produced by the national authorities of the Member States?

While discrepancies arising from a different calculation method are understandable, the one observed here appears to be particularly significant. The significant discrepancies between these figures contribute to confusion regarding the actual number of people residing in the Union illegally. For the sake of clarity, could the Commission: 1.

Supporters (2) (31 August 2026) Eurostat, the statistical office of the European Union, publishes official and verified statistics based on a common methodology and data provided by the Member States. Accordingly, when it comes to illegally staying third-country nationals, the Eurostat data is based on reporting by the national statistical authorities, in this case the French authorities. Furthermore, Eurostat data undergoes quality verifications and validations. The Eurostat indicator in question refers to the number of third-country nationals illegally staying in the country who were detected by France during the whole calendar year of 2025. It includes persons who were apprehended to be illegally present in the territory of France and who do not fulfil, or no longer fulfil, the conditions for stay or residence in this country (1). The figure mentioned by the French Minister for the Interior seems to be an estimation of the total absolute number of thirdcountry nationals illegally staying in the country (not only those detected). The Commission does not have any information about the source, the methodology or the relevant reference period or reference date that underlie the figure mentioned by the French Minister for the Interior and is referred to by the Honourable Member.

E-10-2026-002584.t: Harmonised charging and battery systems for light means of transport (LMTs)
qt: to the Commission Manuela Ripa (PPE) Subject:

The use of LMTs, such as e-bikes and e-scooters, is steadily increasing across the EU. However, market fragmentation caused by a multitude of manufacturer-specific charging ports, chargers and battery systems hinders interoperability, imposes unnecessary costs on consumers and generates avoidable electronic waste. Taking into account Recital 41 of Regulation (EU) 2023/15421 concerning batteries and waste batteries (Batteries Regulation), the interoperability of chargers is a key instrument for waste prevention. Recital 41 states that the regulation should require the Commission to assess how harmonised standards can be introduced for common chargers, specifically for LMT batteries. As no concrete proposals have been submitted so far, we ask the Commission the following questions: 1.
Since the entry into force of the Batteries Regulation, what concrete steps has the Commission taken to assess or prepare harmonised charging or battery systems for LMT batteries?
Does the Commission intend to introduce EU-wide mandatory standards or interoperability requirements for the charging interfaces of light electric vehicles, and if so, what is the expected timeline?
How does the Commission assess the impact of non-interoperable charging and battery systems on e-waste generation, consumer costs, and the development of public charging infrastructure across the EU?

Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 12 July 2023 concerning batteries and waste batteries, amending Directive 2008/98/EC and Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 and repealing Directive 2006/66/EC (OJ L 191, 28.7.2023, p. 1, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2023/1542/oj). 1

However, market fragmentation caused by a multitude of manufacturer-specific charging ports, chargers and battery systems hinders interoperability, imposes unnecessary costs on consumers and generates avoidable electronic waste. Taking into account Recital 41 of Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 (1) concerning batteries and waste batteries (Batteries Regulation), the interoperability of chargers is a key instrument for waste prevention. Recital 41 states that the regulation should require the Commission to assess how harmonised standards can be introduced for common chargers, specifically for LMT batteries. As no concrete proposals have been submitted so far, we ask the Commission the following questions: 1.
Since the entry into force of the Batteries Regulation, what concrete steps has the Commission taken to assess or prepare harmonised charging or battery systems for LMT batteries?
Does the Commission intend to introduce EU-wide mandatory standards or interoperability requirements for the charging interfaces of light electric vehicles, and if so, what is the expected timeline?
How does the Commission assess the impact of non-interoperable charging and battery systems on e-waste generation, consumer costs, and the development of public charging infrastructure across the EU?

(1 September 2026) As the Commission stated in its reply to Written Question E-004909/25 (1), it has been monitoring the situation of charging interoperability of light means of transport (LMT) since the adoption of the Batteries Regulation (2). Following an obligation in Article 94(6) of the regulation, a study (3) on this topic was published in 2024. The study revealed that while the LMT market is fragmented in terms of charging interoperability, there are different use cases which require different approaches. At the same time, the study acknowledged that different chargers to operate rechargeable LMT are associated with environmental and social costs from resource consumption during production and waste generation at end of life. In recent years, a number of industry-led initiatives have been emerging which hold the potential to improve the interoperability of LMT across different brands. These include solutions based on the market implementation of open international charging standards, although with different business models. The uptake of these solutions is promising but so far limited. At this stage, considering ongoing market developments, it would be premature to launch regulatory and/or standardisation activities around the charging interoperability of LMTs, including the potential mandate of a single charging plug interface. The Commission services will continue to monitor the market situation closely.

E-10-2026-002583.t: Albania’s accession process: rule of law, transparency and protected areas
qt: to the Commission Sandro Gozi (Renew) Subject:

Following the 2024 amendments to Albania’s Law on Protected Areas, a major real estate project is being developed in the Vjosa-Narta protected lagoon, including initial construction and site fencing. The project, which is linked to foreign investors who were granted preferential access, raises serious concerns over transparency, governance and the use of public assets. It has triggered large peaceful protests, now on their 24th consecutive day, and is reportedly under investigation by Albania’s Special Prosecution Office against Corruption and Organised Crime (SPAK). The Commission has indicated that it is monitoring the situation closely and has urged Albania to act without delay to safeguard progress under Chapter 27 of the EU accession process. In this context: 1.

How does the Commission assess these developments against Albania’s obligations on the rule of law, transparency and public procurement, notably under the ‘fundamentals’ cluster of negotiating chapters and the Copenhagen criteria?
Are Albania’s 2024 legislative amendments and the ongoing works in the Vjosa-Narta area compatible with the EU environmental acquis and the Chapter 27 benchmarks?
What actions will the Commission take to ensure transparent decision-making, sound environmental assessments with effective public participation and respect for the right to peaceful protest?

Are Albania’s 2024 legislative amendments and the ongoing works in the Vjosa-Narta area compatible with the EU environmental acquis and the Chapter 27 benchmarks?
What actions will the Commission take to ensure transparent decision-making, sound environmental assessments with effective public participation and respect for the right to peaceful protest?

(25 August 2026) The Commission is closely following Albania’s progress in aligning with the EU acquis. More generally, respect for the rule of law remains at the heart of the EU accession process and this work needs to continue in Albania to meet the closing benchmarks set under the fundamentals cluster of accession negotiations. Chapter 27, ‘Environment and climate change’, is assessed in Albania’s accession negotiations and reported on in the Commission’s annual report. Under this chapter Albania is expected to align its legislation with the EU environmental acquis, including the Environmental Impact Assessment Directive (1), the Strategic Environmental Assessment Directive (2), and the Birds (3) and Habitats Directives (4). The closing benchmarks also require Albania to repeal incompatible provisions introduced through amendments to the law on Protected Areas and terminating the 2015 legislation on strategic investments. Albania must also demonstrate adequate capacity to manage future Natura 2000 sites and ensure effective conservation measures preventing habitat and species deterioration. The Commission is in continuous contact with the Albanian authorities and civil society regarding the developments in the Pishë Poro-Nartë area. It has encouraged the Albanian authorities to continue taking steps to fulfil of the closing benchmarks and coming to decisions in a transparent, accountable and inclusive manner.

qt: to the Commission Auke Zijlstra (PfE) Subject:

On 18 June 2026, the Commission sent information to Parliament’s Committee on Budgets concerning an undertaking given during the G7 summit to provide EUR 75 million towards the restoration of the New Safe Confinement, the Chornobyl sarcophagus. The Committee on Budgets has already indicated that this is contrary to paragraph 39 of the new Framework Agreement on relations between the European Parliament and the European Commission1. With this in mind: 1.
Is it common for the Commission to take a decision before consulting Parliament in accordance with the rules in force?
Was the Commission in a hurry in this particular case, or did its President come under any pressure from the G7 to reach this decision?2
Does the Commission still see the value in interinstitutional consultation and in following official procedures?

at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (19.8.2026) On 14 February 2025, a Russian drone strike hit and severely damaged the New Safe Confinement (NSC) at the Chornobyl Nuclear Power Plant that covers the damaged unit 4. The damage poses serious risks to nuclear safety with potential consequences in Ukraine and beyond, including in the EU. In order to mitigate the risk of radioactive contamination, urgent repairs to the NSC must be implemented as soon as possible. Further work is also required to establish and implement long term repairs, which will ensure nuclear and radiation safety from within the NSC and enable safe decommissioning of the damaged unit 4. In the context of this urgency, the Commission has thus pledged EUR 75 million in grant funding as its contribution to nuclear safety, preparedness, environmental protection and international cooperation and is urging European and G7 partners to follow suit. The Commission values the cooperation with the European Parliament, which is why the Commission sent information to European Parliament’s Committee on Budgets regarding this undertaking, in line with usual arrangements.

E-10-2026-002581.t: European Digital Identity Wallet: economic reliability and preventing mafia infiltration
qt: to the Commission Giuseppe Antoci (The Left) Subject:

The EU is preparing to introduce the European Digital Identity Wallet, scope for which is provided under Regulation (EU) No 910/2014 (eIDAS), as amended by Regulation (EU) 2024/1183. The measure is designed to simplify the digital interactions between businesses and public authorities across the EU and make them more secure. The proposal forms part of a series of Commission reforms devised in line with the Beneficial Ownership Registers Interconnection System (BORIS), which was established pursuant to the Anti-Money Laundering Directive ((EU) 2015/849)1. The proposal will provide an interoperable environment in which legal persons and professionals can exchange data and official documents across the EU, store certified credentials, and make use of qualified electronic signatures. It is in line with the ‘once only’ principle2. Given the strategic importance of the European Digital Identity Wallet and the risk of economic identity takeover in digital administrative and economic procedures in the EU: 1.
What steps will the Commission take to stop the European Digital Identity Wallet from becoming susceptible to criminal infiltration, money laundering and malpractice?
In the context of EU tender procedures and other public funding schemes, could the European Digital Identity Wallet be used as an official tool for digital identification and certification purposes?
Will the Commission consider introducing EU red flag mechanisms in order to combat the fraudulent use of digital identities on the part of organised crime?

The measure is designed to simplify the digital interactions between businesses and public authorities across the EU and make them more secure. The proposal forms part of a series of Commission reforms devised in line with the Beneficial Ownership Registers Interconnection System (BORIS), which was established pursuant to the Anti-Money Laundering Directive ((EU) 2015/849) (1). The proposal will provide an interoperable environment in which legal persons and professionals can exchange data and official documents across the EU, store certified credentials, and make use of qualified electronic signatures. It is in line with the ‘once only’ principle (2). Given the strategic importance of the European Digital Identity Wallet and the risk of economic identity takeover in digital administrative and economic procedures in the EU: 1.
What steps will the Commission take to stop the European Digital Identity Wallet from becoming susceptible to criminal infiltration, money laundering and malpractice?
In the context of EU tender procedures and other public funding schemes, could the European Digital Identity Wallet be used as an official tool for digital identification and certification purposes?
Will the Commission consider introducing EU red flag mechanisms in order to combat the fraudulent use of digital identities on the part of organised crime?

(7 September 2026) Regulation (EU) 2024/1183 (1) introduced the European Digital Identity Wallets (EUDIWs). Although not itself an anti-money laundering instrument, EUDIWs will contribute to the prevention of fraudulent uses of digital identities by enabling secure digital identification. The EUDIWs will be provided under an electronic identification scheme certified against Level of Assurance high requirements, making them a reliable alternative to less robust identification solutions. EUDIWs will be secure-by-design, and the regulation establishes advanced security features to protect against identity and other data theft, denial of service and other cyber threats. Those security features include state-of-the-art encryption and storage methods that are accessible and decryptable only by the user and end-to-end encrypted communication with other EUDIWs and relying parties. The regulatory framework does not provide a legal basis for introducing functionalities such as a red flag mechanism. However, Wallets will use strong cryptographic authentication and robust device-bound protections to ensure credentials cannot be easily duplicated, tampered with, or misused, even by highly capable attackers. The Commission has also proposed the regulation on the European Business Wallets (2) to complement the EUDIWs in digital identification, interactions and procedures for economic operators. The Commission intends to propose revised public procurement legislation this year. The digitalisation of procurement is an essential feature of the revision, and the Commission is considering all possible avenues for its secure implementation. The Business Wallets shall be accepted for any administrative procedure that requires identification.

E-10-2026-002580.t: Potential health risks of glycerol (E422) in slushy drinks and the adequacy of EU food safety and labelling rules for child protection
qt: to the Commission Biljana Borzan (S&D) Subject:

Recent warnings by the European Food Safety Authority have highlighted potential health risks associated with the consumption of slushy drinks containing glycerol, particularly by young children, including reported cases of acute illness and hospitalisation. In the light of the above: 1.
Is the Commission considering the introduction of mandatory, clear and visible warning labels on products such as slushy drinks containing glycerol, especially given their appeal to children?
Does the Commission plan to assess the need for age-related sales restrictions for such products, in line with the precautionary principle?
What concrete steps does the Commission intend to take to ensure better protection of vulnerable groups, particularly children, in the light of emerging scientific evidence on this issue?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (20.8.2026) Food additives are subject to a premarket safety assessment and may be authorised only if, based on the available scientific evidence, their proposed use does not raise a safety concern for consumer’s health and the other conditions1 laid down in the legislation2 are met. Authorised additives are kept under continuous observation, and their safety is re-evaluated whenever necessary in light of changing conditions of use and new scientific information. In addition, the Commission set up a programme for the re-evaluation of the safety of food additives that were already permitted in the Union before 20 January 20093. The safety of glycerol (E 422) was confirmed by the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) in 20174 within this re-evaluation programme. Nevertheless, in 2024 and 2025, some Member States reported an acute exposure concern in relation to the use of glycerol in slush ice drinks. In response to a request from the Commission, EFSA assessed the safety of acute exposure to glycerol (E 422) from beverages taking into account new information on the use of glycerol (E 422) in slush ice drinks5 and published its opinion6 on 5 May 2026. Against this background, in June 2026 the Commission launched discussions with Member States on reviewing the authorisation conditions for glycerol (E 422) in light of the recent EFSA opinion. The aim, in line with the applicable legislation, is to assure that the use levels of glycerol as a food additive do not pose safety concerns for any population group, including young children. In this context, the Commission is not considering restrictions on the sale of slush ice drinks or additional labelling requirements.
1 There is a reasonable technological need that cannot be achieved by other economically and technologically

practicable means; its use does not mislead the consumer; and there are advantages and benefits for the consumes. There are additional specific conditions for food additives used as sweeteners and colours. 2 Regulation (EC) No 1333/2008 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 16 December 2008 on food additives (OJ L 354, 31.12.2008, p. 16). 3 Commission Regulation (EU) No 257/2010 of 25 March 2010 setting up a program for the re-evaluation of approved food additives in accordance with Regulation (EC) No 1333/2008 of the European Parliament and of the Council on food additives (OJ L 80, 26.3.2010, p. 19). 4 https://efsa.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.2903/j.efsa.2017.4720. 5 The use levels in slush ice drinks presented in 2024 and 2025 were significantly higher than the use levels accounted for flavoured drinks in the EFSA 2017 opinion. 6 https://efsa.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.2903/j.efsa.2026.10057.

E-10-2026-002579.t: Directors of general and administrative services in Italy: working conditions and proper recognition
qt: to the Commission Danilo Della Valle (The Left), Valentina Palmisano (The Left), Carolina Morace (The Left) Subject:

In Italy, directors of general and administrative services (DGSAs) perform highly complex and independent roles in helping to oversee how schools and their accounts are managed. Although DGSAs have a senior level of responsibility and need to be highly specialised, those in equivalent positions in the Italian civil service enjoy better standards of remuneration and legal status – an unfair disparity. DGSAs receive a variable managerial allowance, but it is based on indicators from 2007 and a statutory number of teaching staff, not how many teachers are actually employed at their school. Worse still, their pay is not performance-related, they receive no overtime pay, and they are not eligible to transition to managerial roles in other departments. This state of affairs would appear to be at odds with the fifth principle of the European Pillar of Social Rights, which upholds the right to equal treatment and the proper recognition of professional skills. Furthermore, the absence of a dedicated career path for these professionals risks undermining efficient administration, a key objective of Italy's recovery and resilience plan. Given all this: 1.
Does the Commission believe that the pay and regulatory disparity outlined above is in line with the principles of fairness and equal treatment enshrined in the European Pillar of Social Rights?

As part of its efforts to monitor the country’s recovery and resilience plan, will the Commission call on Italy to remove restrictions on professional mobility and ensure that DGSAs are given a proper chance to transition to managerial roles?
What steps will the Commission take to ensure fairer recognition for senior roles in Europe’s public education sector?
at: (English version) to the Commission Danilo Della Valle (The Left), Valentina Palmisano (The Left), Carolina Morace (The Left) (23 June 2026) Subject: Directors of general and administrative services in Italy: working conditions and proper recognition In Italy, directors of general and administrative services (DGSAs) perform highly complex and independent roles in helping to oversee how schools and their accounts are managed. Although DGSAs have a senior level of responsibility and need to be highly specialised, those in equivalent positions in the Italian civil service enjoy better standards of remuneration and legal status — an unfair disparity. DGSAs receive a variable managerial allowance, but it is based on indicators from 2007 and a statutory number of teaching staff, not how many teachers are actually employed at their school. Worse still, their pay is not performance-related, they receive no overtime pay, and they are not eligible to transition to managerial roles in other departments. What steps will the Commission take to ensure fairer recognition for senior roles in Europe’s public education sector?

(13 August 2026) EU labour law establishes minimum requirements on working conditions, such as working time, health and safety and equal treatment on protected grounds. It does not harmonise the remuneration or legal status of comparable categories of public employees nor does it require performance-related or overtime pay or regulate access to particular career paths. The organisation of national public administrations, including the definition of career structures, access to managerial positions, and professional mobility within the public sector, falls within the competence of Member States. Similarly, pursuant to Article 153(5) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, the EU’s competence in the field of social policy does not extend to pay. The European Pillar of Social Rights provides a framework for promoting fair and well-functioning labour markets. The Pillar is legally non-binding. Its principles do not extend the EU’s competences or create directly enforceable obligations but rather serve as a guiding framework for Member States to coordinate their policies. Italy’s recovery and resilience plan (RRP) includes reforms of public employment and of the school network, requiring the entry into force of legislation setting the criteria for the organic contingent of dirigenti scolastici and directors of general and administrative services (now funzionari di elevata qualificazione) and its regional distribution. The Commission assesses the implementation of the RRP against the implementation of milestones and targets, in line with the Council Implementing Decision (1). The organisation of civil servants remains primarily the responsibility of Member States, in line with applicable national and EU law.

E-10-2026-002578.t: Protecting fundamental rights at major international sporting events
qt: to the Commission Carolina Morace (The Left), Mario Furore (The Left), Valentina Palmisano (The Left), Danilo Della Valle (The Left), Gaetano Pedulla' (The Left) Subject:

Major international sporting events have a considerable impact on fundamental rights, including workers’ rights, freedom of expression, freedom of the press, non-discrimination, gender equality and the safety of LGBTIQ+ people. In recent years, a number of international competitions have prompted concerns over a disregard for human rights, both during and in the run-up to the events. Given the critical nature of this issue: 1.
Will the Commission support the creation of a permanent EU mechanism to monitor respect for human rights at major international sporting events?
Will it urge FIFA, UEFA and the International Olympic Committee to adopt compulsory minimum standards on fundamental rights, which should apply before events are awarded?

Does it believe that all EU funding in this context should be contingent on verifiable criteria designed to safeguard human rights, guard against discrimination and protect the safety of those involved?

E-10-2026-002576.t: Commission-Moderna contract: unanswered questions surrounding liability and effectiveness
qt: to the Commission Gerald Hauser (PfE) Subject:

Moderna CEO Stéphane Bancel publicly stated in 2023 that his company already knew about the 2020 pandemic in 2019 and was preparing to produce billions of vaccine doses1. On 4 December 2020, Stéphane Bancel (Moderna) and Stella Kyriakides (EU Commission and EU Member States) signed the Moderna mRNA COVID-19 vaccine contract (SANTE/2020/C3/054 – SI2.838958). The signatories acknowledged that Moderna could under no circumstances warrant or assume any liability that the mRNA gene-based vaccine would produce the desired results or be free from ‘unacceptable side effects’ as a result of the ‘accelerated timelines’ for the development, production and delivery of the mRNA genebased vaccine. Moderna has been exempted from any liability for vaccine damage in the event of death, physical, mental or emotional injury, illness or disability, or in the event of fear of physical, mental or emotional injury, illness or disability, property loss or damage to property or business interruption of a vaccinated person. Member States took on those risks, as they did the case of the BioNTech/Pfizer mRNA gene-based vaccine2. 1.
Why did the Commission accept the risk that Moderna’s gene-based vaccination could be ineffective and have ‘unacceptable side effects’?
Why has Moderna been released from any liability for vaccine damage?
Did the Commission know in 2019 that there would be a pandemic in 2020, requiring billions of vaccine doses?

haben/. 2

at: (English version) to the Commission Gerald Hauser (PfE) (23 June 2026) Subject: Commission-Moderna contract: unanswered questions surrounding liability and effectiveness Moderna CEO Stéphane Bancel publicly stated in 2023 that his company already knew about the 2020 pandemic in 2019 and was preparing to produce billions of vaccine doses (1). On 4 December 2020, Stéphane Bancel (Moderna) and Stella Kyriakides (EU Commission and EU Member States) signed the Moderna mRNA COVID-19 vaccine contract (SANTE/2020/C3/054 — SI2.838958). The signatories acknowledged that Moderna could under no circumstances warrant or assume any liability that the mRNA gene-based vaccine would produce the desired results or be free from ‘unacceptable side effects’ as a result of the ‘accelerated timelines’ for the development, production and delivery of the mRNA gene-based vaccine. Moderna has been exempted from any liability for vaccine damage in the event of death, physical, mental or emotional injury, illness or disability, or in the event of fear of physical, mental or emotional injury, illness or disability, property loss or damage to property or business interruption of a vaccinated person. Member States took on those risks, as they did the case of the BioNTech/Pfizer mRNA gene-based vaccine (2). 1. Why did the Commission accept the risk that Moderna’s gene-based vaccination could be ineffective and have ‘unacceptable side effects’? 2.
Why has Moderna been released from any liability for vaccine damage?
Did the Commission know in 2019 that there would be a pandemic in 2020, requiring billions of vaccine doses?

(21 August 2026) The Commission did not know in 2019 that there would be a pandemic in 2020. In 2020, due to unprecedented circumstances created by the unfolding COVID-19 pandemic, to preserve and protect the health of the population, the EU, similarly to other parts of the world, invested in the ramping up of development and production of vaccines against COVID-19. Crucially, this investment was done before knowing whether any of these vaccines would prove successful. These decisive actions taken at risk paid off and the development of vaccines has been successful, allowing a faster launch of a mass vaccination campaign in the EU. The Commission and Member States considered early introduction of the vaccine to be in the interest of public health (1). Member States indicated their willingness to reduce manufacturers’ risks linked to liability for adverse effects, in order to provide sufficient incentives to the manufacturers to enter the market. The terms of the COVID-19 vaccine (advance) purchase agreements, including indemnification clauses, concluded with the pharmaceutical companies, were negotiated by a joint negotiation team and endorsed by the Member States representatives. Under the contractual terms, legal responsibility for the damages lies with the vaccine manufacturers. However, Member States in principle indemnify vaccine manufacturers for the compensation of damages and legal costs on the condition that the claim is successful, except in cases where the damages result from wilful misconduct, gross negligence, or failure to comply with EU good manufacturing practices by the vaccine manufacturers.
