E-10-2026-002575.t: Low ratio of storage capacity to installed capacity of Renewable Energy Sources (RES) in Greece
qt: to the Commission Yannis Maniatis (S&D) Subject:

According to reports, despite the significant penetration of RES, Greece has only 0.22 GW of installed battery capacity (storage adequacy index – 2 % RES SAI), in contrast to neighbouring countries such as Bulgaria (3.5 GW / 52 % RES SAI). This year’s European Semester report for Greece acknowledges that increasing energy storage will reduce curtailments and increase the use of green electricity, and that Greece has made limited progress in implementing the 2025 recommendation (CSR) to develop flexibility solutions that include storage and contribute to making electricity prices more affordable. It also notes the significant and rapidly increasing curtailments and uncertainty, which are forcing smaller RES producers to exit the market. Finally, it calls on Greece to improve the design of support schemes with a view to adding smaller battery storage systems connected to RES installations. The Commission is asked: 1.
What are the Greek storage measures (investments and reforms) that were initially included in the Recovery Fund and have not yet been implemented?
How many MW of storage have been financed by the Recovery Fund and how many have been connected to the electricity system to date?
Can the annual cost to Greek energy prices from the delay in the implementation of projects be estimated?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (9.9.2026) Since its inception, the Greek Recovery and Resilience Plan (RRP) has included Measure 16926 (‘Support of the installation of storage systems to enhance renewable energy sources (RES) penetration’) which covers battery energy storage systems and the construction of a pumped hydro storage system in Amfilochia. The measure was revised due to objective circumstances, including the extended time needed for the electrification of the battery storage systems and supply bottlenecks affecting the timely delivery of equipment needed for the Amfilochia Pumped Hydro Storage facility. The final milestone 16 of Measure 16926 will be assessed as part of the ninth and final payment request that Greece is expected to submit in September 2026. The milestone requires: (i) the installation of battery energy storage projects with a total capacity of 700 megawatts (MW); and (ii) the completion of the civil engineering works for the Amfilochia Pumped Hydro Storage Station. The Commission has not carried out any analysis of the exact impact on electricity prices resulting from Greece’s lack of grid scale battery storage capacity. However, a lack of flexibility can generally contribute to greater price volatility and higher system costs. The factsheet1 published by the Commission in March 2026 provides additional information on how the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF) is supporting Greece’s transition away from polluting energy sources toward cleaner alternatives, such as wind and solar power.
1 https://reforms-investments.ec.europa.eu/document/download/ca8dd927-d7fb-47a0-84db-
adcf48530877_en?filename=Factsheet%20RRF%20Greece%20March%2026%20V5.pdf

E-10-2026-002574.t: Evaluation and revision of the Biocidal Products Regulation to improve EU health preparedness and innovation
qt: to the Commission Aurelijus Veryga (ECR) Subject:

The Commission recognises that biocidal products play an important role in EU citizens’ daily lives, for example, helping to protect against vector-borne diseases (e.g. malaria, dengue fever or chikungunya), food-borne diseases (e.g. salmonellosis, listeriosis) and hospitalacquired infections (e.g. methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus – MRSA). However, more than 10 years since its entry into application, significant shortcomings in the Biocidal Products Regulation1 (BPR), including lengthy approval and authorisation timelines, complex procedures and high compliance costs, create investment uncertainty and negatively impact businesses’ performance, particularly for small and medium-sized enterprises. These challenges hinder innovation and highlight the need for a revision of the BPR to ensure it becomes fit for purpose and supports the EU’s preparedness for future health crises. 1.

Can the Commission provide a clear timeline for the completion of the BPR evaluation, including the expected adoption of its conclusions and any subsequent steps towards a much-needed legislative revision?

How will the Commission address delays and improve harmonisation and predictability in authorisation processes to strengthen the EU’s crisis preparedness, and does the Commission intend to address these challenges through a revision of the BPR, following its evaluation?
What measures does the Commission envisage to strengthen the European biocidal sector, and create a favourable environment for innovation?

Regulation (EU) No 528/2012 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 22 May 2012 concerning the making available on the market and use of biocidal products (OJ L 167, 27.6.2012, p. 1, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2012/528/oj). 1
at: (English version) to the Commission Aurelijus Veryga (ECR) (23 June 2026) Subject: Evaluation and revision of the Biocidal Products Regulation to improve EU health preparedness and innovation The Commission recognises that biocidal products play an important role in EU citizens’ daily lives, for example, helping to protect against vector-borne diseases (e.g. malaria, dengue fever or chikungunya), food-borne diseases (e.g. salmonellosis, listeriosis) and hospital-acquired infections (e.g. methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus — MRSA). However, more than 10 years since its entry into application, significant shortcomings in the Biocidal Products Regulation (1) (BPR), including lengthy approval and authorisation timelines, complex procedures and high compliance costs, create investment uncertainty and negatively impact businesses’ performance, particularly for small and medium-sized enterprises. These challenges hinder innovation and highlight the need for a revision of the BPR to ensure it becomes fit for purpose and supports the EU’s preparedness for future health crises. 1. Can the Commission provide a clear timeline for the completion of the BPR evaluation, including the expected adoption of its conclusions and any subsequent steps towards a much-needed legislative revision? 2. How will the Commission address delays and improve harmonisation and predictability in authorisation processes to strengthen the EU’s crisis preparedness, and does the Commission intend to address these challenges through a revision of the BPR, following its evaluation? 3. What measures does the Commission envisage to strengthen the European biocidal sector, and create a favourable environment for innovation? (25 September 2026) The evaluation of the regulation (EU) No 528/2012 on biocidal products (BPR) (1) is ongoing and will assess the functioning of the BPR, including its effectiveness in improving the functioning of the EU single market and ensuring a high level of protection for human health, animal health, and the environment. Ahead of the completion of the evaluation, and based on the implementation report (2) submitted to the European Parliament and the Council in 2021 and further discussion with stakeholders, the Commission has already made some proposals for simplification as part of the Food and Feed Safety Simplification Package (3), with a view to address the substantial delays in the completion of the work programme for the approval of existing active substances and the authorisation of all biocidal products placed on the EU market according to harmonised rules. Other proposals may be put forward by the Commission, if considered appropriate and depending on the findings of the evaluation. Such proposals would be supported by an impact assessment that would follow the evaluation. The creation of an environment favourable for innovation does not depend solely on the legislation. The Commission has recently taken new action in order to foster innovation for the biocides sector under the Horizon Europe framework (4). E-10-2026-002572.t: Ensuring that people with hearing and visual impairments can access the information provided in emergency communications
qt: to the Commission Sirpa Pietikäinen (PPE) Subject:

Under Article 9 of the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, as ratified by the European Union, States Parties are to ensure that persons with disabilities have access to information, communications and other services, including electronic services and emergency services. The human rights of people with hearing and visual impairments should therefore be upheld by ensuring that they too receive emergency communications that are sent to the public. The vulnerability of people with hearing and visual impairments when it comes to receiving emergency communications has become more of an issue in recent years owing to the general security situation and to geopolitical conditions. This raises questions as to how people with hearing and visual impairments are taken into account in the design of emergency communications and the tools used to send them, and what practical solutions exist to ensure that people with hearing and visual impairments can access information and assistance in crisis situations. With that in mind: 1.
What steps does the Commission intend to take to ensure that people with hearing or visual impairments receive information on an equal footing with other EU citizens in crisis situations?

In the implementation of the forthcoming regulation on the EU civil protection mechanism, how does the Commission intend to ensure that people with hearing and visual impairments are also able to receive, in full, the emergency communication actions defined in the regulation?

(7 September 2026) Civil society organisations (CSOs) are non-governmental, non-profit and independent entities acting in the public interest. As recognised by the EU Strategy for Civil Society (1) and the Digital Services Act (DSA) (2), they perform legitimate roles, including researching systemic risks such as the spread of illegal content or risks to fundamental rights online. The Commission's enforcement of the DSA is evidence-based and respects due process. Its assessments may draw on information from providers of online platforms and search engines, competent authorities, CSOs and other stakeholders, and such evidence is gathered in respect of the fundamental rights (3). In its investigation into X, the Commission assessed all relevant evidence, considered the arguments presented by the provider of X, gave that provider the opportunity to respond to the Commission’s preliminary findings (4), and considered that response when adopting a final decision (5). The provider of X has challenged the non-compliance decision before the European General Court. The Commission does not fund CSOs for DSA enforcement. The EU may provide funding to CSOs through transparent procedures such as open calls under programmes including Digital Europe or Citizens, Equality, Rights and Values subject to clear criteria and public scrutiny. The censorship allegations in the referenced report are unfounded. The DSA strengthens accountability for intermediary services in the EU, while protecting freedom of expression by giving users recourse when content is removed or restricted. By way of illustration, since the DSA became fully applicable, 30% of appealed moderation decisions adopted by online platforms (6) have been reversed.

E-10-2026-002570.t: Will remuneration for press publishers from digital platforms really be fair?
qt: to the Commission Catherine Griset (PfE) Subject:

In its judgment of 12 May 20261, the Court of Justice of the European Union ruled that legislation requiring digital platforms to compensate press publishers for using their content is in line with EU law. The decision also confirms that: – such remuneration is to be negotiated between platforms and publishers; – content is to be kept visible while negotiations proceed; – platforms must provide the data necessary to determine the amount of compensation; – press publishers have the right to allow their content to be used free of charge or refuse such use. The decision is a decisive step forward for media financing. Nevertheless, national regulatory authorities, such as Arcom in France, will be responsible for mediating disputes between platforms and publishers. 1.

Will their decisions have to comply with the principle of proportionality and be based on data provided by digital platforms so each publisher is remunerated fairly in proportion to the number of views its articles receive?
Can the Commission guarantee that no press publisher will be excluded from such remuneration as a result of its political positions?
https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:62023CJ0797.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.9.2026) While Article 15 of the Directive on Copyright in the Digital Single Market1 (DSM Directive) introduces an exclusive right for press publishers for the online use of their publications by information society service providers (ISSPs), it does not require Member States to introduce any mediation mechanism to support negotiations between the parties or to empower a national authority in this respect. In its judgement in case C-797/23 (Meta/AGCOM)2, the Court of Justice of the European Union confirmed that Member States enjoy a broad discretion in the implementation of Article 15. The Court stated that national rules imposing on ISSPs who use or intend to use online publications of press publishers, exploiting them economically, the obligation to negotiate, not reduce visibility during negotiations, and to provide necessary information to publishers and a public authority are compatible with EU law where such obligations comply with the principle of proportionality, preserve the publishers’ right to refuse to authorise the use of their publications or to authorise such use free of charge, and do not impose on the ISSPs any payment obligation unrelated to the use of such publications. This framework has to be taken into account by Member States when introducing measures to support the implementation of Article 15. Article 15 of the DSM Directive does not introduce any obligations to use press publications. If they want to use online such publications, ISSPs shall obtain an authorisation from press publishers and remunerate them accordingly. Article 15 applies irrespective of the content of the press publication, therefore, the remuneration paid by ISSPs in return for the authorisation is neutral as regards the press publication used.
1 Directive (EU) 2019/790. 2 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex:62023CJ0797.

Supporter (2) (18 August 2026) Ensuring beneficiaries receive correct information on the origin of Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) support and that the Union’s role is duly acknowledged is of the utmost importance. Under the CAP legal framework, Member States and paying agencies are subject to information, publicity and visibility obligations concerning the European agricultural guarantee fund (EAGF) and the European agricultural fund for rural development (EAFRD) financing. E-10-2026-002568.t: Range of electric cars: is the Commission endorsing information that is misleading consumers?
qt: to the Commission Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE) Subject:

As a result of regulatory pressure from Brussels and national tax arrangements designed to put people off internal combustion engines, consumers are being encouraged to buy electric vehicles. Such purchases are, however, often made on the basis of the range established via the Worldwide Harmonised Light Vehicles Test Procedure (WLTP)1. That range is obtained from tests conducted in a wind- and rain-free laboratory at a temperature of 23 °C, with a fully charged, conditioned battery. The testing cycle includes in-town, open road and motorway driving, but does not take into account wintry conditions, extended periods of motorway driving or the use of heating or air conditioning. The Netherlands Organisation for Applied Scientific Research (TNO)2 looked at the testing of some 45 000 electric vehicles and noted that the average gap between the WLTP range and the actual range increased from 13 % in 2020 to 22 % in 2024. The ADAC3, Germany’s automobile association, tested 14 family cars whose WLTP range was at least 500 km: at a temperature of 0 °C on a simulated journey of 582 km, most had to stop at least twice. Italy’s competition and markets authority4 has demanded that Stellantis, Tesla, BYD and Volkswagen clarify the information provided on actual range, battery depletion and warranties. 1.
Does the Commission think that it is misleading for consumers if only the WLTP range is used commercially?
Will the Commission make it mandatory to provide a realistic range for winter and motorway driving?
Will it request an overhaul of the WLTP for electric vehicles?

(25 August 2026) The Commission is committed to ensuring consumers receive transparent, accurate and comparable information on electric vehicle performance. To this end, it is revising the Car Labelling Directive (1) to provide potential consumers with relevant, accessible information by adding electric energy consumption and zero-emission electric range to the label. This will help consumers make informed purchase decisions. The Worldwide Harmonised Light Vehicles Test Procedure (WLTP) provides a realistic and rigorous assessment of vehicle emissions and electric range. However, as a laboratory-based type-approval test, its main purpose is to compare models on a standardised, fair and reproducible basis. The framework cannot replicate every driving style, payload or local weather condition. To monitor the gap between type-approval tests and real-world performance, the Commission analyses real-world energy consumption data collected via on-board fuel and energy consumption monitoring devices installed in new vehicles. The regulatory framework for light-duty vehicles is also evolving to address low-temperature range. Under the Euro 7 Regulation (2), Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/1764 incorporates the latest provisions of UN Regulation No 154 (3), including a new cold ambient range testing procedure requiring activation of heating and air conditioning systems, ensuring a more accurate reflection of energy consumption in wintry conditions. qt: to the Commission Lena Düpont (PPE) Subject:

Is the Commission aware of reports that mandatory driver assistance systems can interfere with emergency-response driving?

at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (6.8.2026) Regulation (EU) 2018/858 on the approval and market surveillance of motor vehicles1 applies optionally to vehicles designed and constructed or adapted for use by civil protection, fire services and forces responsible for maintaining public order2. Ambulances are defined as special purpose vehicles and specific requirements are provided for them in Annex II, Part III, Appendix 1 to this Regulation. Ambulances are not exempted from the advanced safety systems mandated by the General Safety Regulation (EU) 2019/21443 like advanced emergency braking, emergency lanekeeping, intelligent speed assistance and driver drowsiness and attention warning systems, as they can still benefit from the safety potential of the systems when driven outside the emergency-response regime. qt: to the Commission Reinier Van Lanschot (Verts/ALE), Anna Strolenberg (Verts/ALE), Kai Tegethoff (Verts/ALE), Nela Riehl (Verts/ALE) Subject:

The Commission is currently engaged in pre-notification consultations with the Dutch authorities regarding the proposed measure. The civil society organisation Advocates for the Future has submitted observations outlining concerns about the compatibility of the aid with EU State aid rules, in particular under the climate, environmental protection and energy aid guidelines (CEEAG). The Commission is asked to clarify the process and its considerations regarding the assessment of this State aid measure under the CEEAG: 1.
When does the Commission intend to conclude the pre-notification phase and initiate the formal assessment of the proposed aid, and what is the expected timeline for this assessment?

How will the Commission verify that the proposed State aid fulfils the additionality requirement under the CEEAG, given that TSN may already be subject to existing legal obligations to reduce emissions?
How will the Commission assess whether the aid is proportionate, in particular in the light of concerns that up to 40 % of the investment costs may be publicly funded?

(26 August 2026) The Commission is in pre-notification contact with the Netherlands regarding the proposed measure, however it cannot comment on ongoing cases neither on substance nor timing. In general, when a Member State submits files which are not sufficiently clear, the Commission sends requests for information. This is a standard step in a state aid assessment, which also determines the timeline of such assessment. That timeline therefore differs from case to case. One of the conditions that need to be assessed to see whether environmental aid can be considered compatible with the internal market is whether the aid has an incentive effect, as set out in Section 3.1.2 of the Climate Environmental protection and Energy Aid Guidelines (CEEAG) (1). This means that the aid incentivises the beneficiary to change its behaviour to engage in additional economic activity or in more environmentally-friendly economic activity, which it would not do without the aid. Therefore, aid cannot be granted to merely cover the cost of adapting to EU standards. The CEEAG sets out in Section 3.2.1.3 that aid is considered to be proportionate if the aid amount per beneficiary is limited to the minimum needed for carrying out the aided project. The aid therefore needs to correspond to the net extra cost necessary to meet the objective of the aid measure, compared to the counterfactual scenario in the absence of aid. The determination of these net extra costs depends on the aid granting process (competitive bidding or not) and on the type of aid granted.
Communication from the Commission — Guidelines on state aid for climate, environmental protection and energy 2022 (OJ C 80, 18.2.2022, p. 1).

E-10-2026-002565.t: Effectiveness of EU funds and the impact of bureaucracy on rail modernisation in Śląskie Province
qt: to the Commission Marcin Sypniewski (ESN) Subject:

In connection with the summer revision of the train timetable introduced on 14 June 2026 (in force until 29 August 2026) and the ongoing infrastructure investments in Śląskie Province, could the Commission answer the following questions: 1.

As part of its monitoring of railway investments in Śląskie Province co-financed by the EU, does the Commission have any information regarding delays that have occurred and to what extent these may be attributable to administrative, environmental or technical procedures relating to the requirements for the implementation of EU-funded projects?

How does the Commission, as part of its oversight of the use of EU funds for infrastructure investments in regions undergoing the energy transition, such as Śląskie Province, assess the impact of such investments on the accessibility and reliability of public transport, as well as the administrative burden associated with securing and utilising these funds?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (30.9.2026) 1. Rail investments in Poland are financed by the Cohesion Policy Funds and by Connecting Europe Facility. The Cohesion Policy funds, including the European Regional Development Fund and the Cohesion Fund, are implemented under shared management between the Commission and Member States1. Member States prepare and implement programmes and projects, while the Commission monitors implementation, including transport investments. Consequently, administrative, environmental and technical procedures for individual projects are primarily the responsibility of national and regional authorities. Regarding Connecting Europe Facility projects, some of them have been delayed in the region due to complex studies and works, lengthy tendering procedures, appeals by unsuccessful bidders, difficult ground conditions linked to legacy coal mining, collisions with undocumented cable infrastructure, and, in some cases, lengthy power connection agreements. These delays are not attributable to EU requirements. 2. For the Commission sustainable and accessible transport remains a priority. The Commission closely monitors the implementation and performance of the EU Funds through regular reporting, Monitoring Committees, Annual Performance Reviews and audits. The reporting includes indicators such as upgraded railway infrastructure, increased network capacity and improved benefits for passengers and other users. Efforts also continue to reduce administrative burden through simplification, capacity-building, clearer guidance and digitalisation, while preserving transparency, competition, environmental protection and financial accountability.
1 Under Article 7 of Regulation (EU) 2021/1060: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2021/1060/oj/eng.

E-10-2026-002564.t: SCoPAFF’s reclassification of plant protection products
qt: to the Commission Adam Jarubas (PPE), Krzysztof Hetman (PPE) Subject:

The EU’s single market operates on the premise that EU law is applied uniformly and consistently in all Member States. This is particularly relevant when it comes to the regulatory qualification of commercial products, since divergent approaches among national authorities lead to distortions of competition and legal uncertainty. In January 2024, as part of the work of the Standing Committee on Plants, Animals, Food and Feed (SCoPAFF), SILTAC was reclassified in Commission working document ‘Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 – scope and borderline issues’. It was categorised as a plant protection product (PPP), despite having previously spent years on the EU market as a non-PPP. This change has been implemented to varying degrees and in different ways by the national authorities of the individual Member States, leading to disparate market effects depending on the country. In light of the above: 1.
Is the Commission monitoring the way in which the Member States are applying SILTAC’s reclassification arising from the SCoPAFF working document?
Is it aware of the national authorities’ divergent approaches to this reclassification and their impact on the functioning of the EU internal market?
What action is it taking or planning to take in order to prevent market fragmentation as a result of the non-uniform application of the qualification of a specific product?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (25.9.2026) The Commission refers the Honourable Members to the replies to E-001536/261 and E000469/262, which explain in detail the procedure followed to determine whether SILTAC falls within the scope of Regulation (EC) No 1107/20093, the role of the Standing Committee on Plants, Animals, Food and Feed, Section Phytopharmaceuticals – Legislation (‘SCoPAFF’), and of the related scope document4, as a coordination tool between Member States and the Commission, aimed at supporting a coherent and harmonised application of the existing legal framework in technically complex or borderline situations. The Commission is not aware of market fragmentation as regards the product SILTAC, as all Member States agree that the product is within the scope of Regulation (EC) No 1107/20095. It has discussed with Member States possibilities for leniency in enforcement provided that the manufacturer takes the necessary steps to seek approval of the active substance(s) and authorisation of the product under that Regulation, thereby regularising its legal situation. The manufacturer could approach a Member State willing to become the rapporteur for the initial risk assessment for advice, including the Member State where the manufacturer is based (Poland). However, at the meeting of SCoPAFF on 29-30 June 20266, the Member States informed that so far none of them had been contacted by the manufacturer of SILTAC with a view to submitting an application for the approval of the active substance(s) and the subsequent authorisation of the product. The Commission will continue to work with Member States towards a coherent and uniform application and enforcement of the provisions of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 to prevent fragmentation of the internal market.

E-10-2026-002563.t: Sacred art under attack – fraud, plagiarism and unfair competition from outside the EU
qt: to the Commission Jorge Buxadé Villalba (PfE) Subject:

Since the Middle Ages, Spanish artisans have passed down techniques of embroidery, goldsmithing, carving, restoration and painting from one generation to the next, and these traditions are still preserved in many Spanish cities. These are trades that continue to generate employment and cultural wealth, dedicating their magnificent works to the devotion of the faithful and to our Christian identity. Spanish sacred art is one of the world’s richest historical and artistic heritages; the Seville Trade Association for Sacred Art has condemned the growing influx of products from Pakistan and India that are being sold on the EU market, evading customs controls and the payment of duties, and committing fraud through the misappropriation of images and designs. In light of the above: 1.

Is the Commission going to take measures to protect those Spanish artisans who, through their work, preserve and enrich traditions, against commercial interference from third countries whose sole aim, moreover, is to undermine our Christian identity and everything associated with it?
How does the Commission account for the fact that products from third countries are entering the single market via international couriers, thereby circumventing customs controls and duties?
Will the Commission investigate these organised networks from third countries?
at: (English version) to the Commission Jorge Buxadé Villalba (PfE) (22 June 2026) Subject: Sacred art under attack — fraud, plagiarism and unfair competition from outside the EU Since the Middle Ages, Spanish artisans have passed down techniques of embroidery, goldsmithing, carving, restoration and painting from one generation to the next, and these traditions are still preserved in many Spanish cities. These are trades that continue to generate employment and cultural wealth, dedicating their magnificent works to the devotion of the faithful and to our Christian identity. Spanish sacred art is one of the world’s richest historical and artistic heritages; the Seville Trade Association for Sacred Art has condemned the growing influx of products from Pakistan and India that are being sold on the EU market, evading customs controls and the payment of duties, and committing fraud through the misappropriation of images and designs. In light of the above: 1.

Is the Commission going to take measures to protect those Spanish artisans who, through their work, preserve and enrich traditions, against commercial interference from third countries whose sole aim, moreover, is to undermine our Christian identity and everything associated with it?
How does the Commission account for the fact that products from third countries are entering the single market via international couriers, thereby circumventing customs controls and duties?
Will the Commission investigate these organised networks from third countries?

(4 September 2026) The Commission is seriously invested in the protection of EU traditional crafts products. Among others, the EU recently adopted the regulation on the protection of geographical indications for craft and industrial products (1) (CIGI Regulation) which establishes an EU wide system of protection for traditional names linked to a particular geographical area. The directive on the Enforcement of intellectual property rights (2) complements this regime, setting a harmonised standard in the EU for the enforcement of all intellectual property rights, including CIGIs. This enables preventing the unauthorised sale of products using a protected name without meeting the necessary requirements, including being manufactured outside the protected area. Since the goods in question seem to be contemporary copies of European handicrafts, they are outside the scope of Regulation (EU) 2019/880 on the introduction and the import of cultural goods (3). The Commission supports Member States through the EU customs risk management framework, cooperation mechanisms, customs information exchange and risk analysis, and works to strengthen the EU's capacity to combat customs fraud. Goods entering the EU are subject to customs legislation and controls including those carried by express or postal operators. Where there are indications that organised networks are involved in customs fraud or the evasion of customs duties, it is for the competent customs and, where appropriate, law enforcement authorities of the Member States to investigate such cases. In case of suspected fraud or other illegal activities affecting the EU budget, the Commission informs the European Anti-Fraud Office (OLAF) and, where applicable, the European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO).

E-10-2026-002562.t: Measures to prevent and mitigate exceptionally early heatwaves in the Autonomous Community of Valencia (Spain)
qt: to the Commission Leire Pajín (S&D), Sandra Gómez López (S&D) Subject:

The summer has just officially begun and some Mediterranean areas of the European Union, such as Alicante in the Autonomous Community of Valencia (Spain), are already expected to experience a sweltering succession of tropical nights (temperatures remaining above 20 °C). This is not the usual westerly wind we experience, but a period of sustained atmospheric stability caused by a heat dome that will spread over much of western Europe. The most worrying aspect is that it has come extremely early: it is unusual to have such intense heat at this stage of the year. Spain’s meteorological agency, AEMET1, is warning that the average temperatures for the period from 22 to 26 June for the Autonomous Community of Valencia could reach record levels on each of those dates, at least since comparable records exist (1950). In view of the above: 1.
What early warning systems to anticipate heatwaves and their impact at European and global level are being developed by the Commission?
When will it adopt its climate resilience framework?
What measures will be introduced under this framework to make it more ambitious and comprehensive in the face of the climate risks and repercussions affecting Mediterranean areas in particular?
https://x.com/AEMET_CValencia/status/2067213365244510606.
at: (English version) to the Commission Leire Pajín (S&D), Sandra Gómez López (S&D) (22 June 2026) Subject: Measures to prevent and mitigate exceptionally early heatwaves in the Autonomous Community of Valencia (Spain) The summer has just officially begun and some Mediterranean areas of the European Union, such as Alicante in the Autonomous Community of Valencia (Spain), are already expected to experience a sweltering succession of tropical nights (temperatures remaining above 20 °C). This is not the usual westerly wind we experience, but a period of sustained atmospheric stability caused by a heat dome that will spread over much of western Europe. The most worrying aspect is that it has come extremely early: it is unusual to have such intense heat at this stage of the year. Spain’s meteorological agency, AEMET (1), is warning that the average temperatures for the period from 22 to 26 June for the Autonomous Community of Valencia could reach record levels on each of those dates, at least since comparable records exist (1950). In view of the above: 1.
What early warning systems to anticipate heatwaves and their impact at European and global level are being developed by the Commission?
When will it adopt its climate resilience framework?
What measures will be introduced under this framework to make it more ambitious and comprehensive in the face of the climate risks and repercussions affecting Mediterranean areas in particular?

(1 September 2026) The 2024 European Climate Risk Assessment (EUCRA) (1) assessed all climate change-related longer-term risks and ranked heat as a priority, notably because of the identified projected severe impacts on human health and energy systems. A second EUCRA is expected to be published in 2028. The European Network of National Meteorological Services EUMETNET operates the MeteoAlarm early warning dissemination system (2), which aggregates, visualises, and accessibly provides information from 44 European National Meteorological and Hydrological Services regarding short-term risks. Moreover, under the Copernicus Emergency Management Services (CEMS), the Commission has developed the European and the Global Drought Observatories (EDO/GDO) to help monitor and forecast drought conditions and heatwaves, both at European and global levels. New heatwave-related indicators have been added to help monitor and forecast their duration and intensity across Europe and at global levels. The Commission expects to adopt the new EU climate resilience framework during the fourth quarter of 2026. The Commission set out possible elements of the framework in its Open Public Consultation (3), including common climate reference scenarios, more harmonised risk assessments, strengthened planning and implementation, more effective monitoring, reporting and evaluation, and simplification of existing legal obligations. The accompanying impact assessment helps determine the appropriate mix of measures, including legislative instruments and support mechanisms, to ensure that the framework delivers the necessary ambition and impact.

E-10-2026-002561.t: Increased use of fossil fuels: wind energy underperformance particularly to blame
qt: to the Commission Mathilde Androuët (PfE) Subject:

According to the Ember think tank, the EU upped its production of electricity from fossil fuels by 7 % in the first half of 2025 – to 368.46 TWh from 343.28 TWh in 2024. This rise, which led to a 5 % increase in power sector emissions, cannot explained by electricity demand, which grew by only 0.7 %. Instead, it stems from the increased use of gas to compensate for the fall in wind energy production (-8.5 %, -21 TWh) and hydropower production (-17 %, -33 TWh)1. This development is at odds with the European Green Deal’s climate and decarbonisation objectives2. It lays bare the limits and risks of an energy policy based on intermittent sources, to the detriment of dispatchable capacities, in particular stored nuclear and hydraulic energy. These risks became apparent during Spain’s blackout in April 20253. 1.
How does the Commission explain this contradiction with its commitments to reduce emissions4 and increase the share of renewable energy5?
Does it intend to shift the balance of EU energy policy in favour of stable and dispatchable sources to reduce dependence on fossil fuels and strengthen our energy security?

Contexte, Tuesday 7 October 2025. COM(2019)0640 (European Green Deal). 3 ‘Red Eléctrica hopes to be able to use renewable energy to control electrical voltage from the first quarter of 2026’, Sandra Acosta, 8 October 2025, https://elperiodicodelaenergia.com/red-electrica-espera-poderactivar-que-las-renovables-controlen-la-tension-a-partir-del-primer-trimestre-de-2026. 4 Regulation (EU) 2021/1119 – target of reducing emissions by at least 55 % by 2030. 5 Directive (EU) 2023/2413 concerning the share of renewable energy (Renewable Energy Directive, RED III). 1 2
at: (English version) to the Commission Mathilde Androuët (PfE) (22 June 2026) Subject: Increased use of fossil fuels: wind energy underperformance particularly to blame According to the Ember think tank, the EU upped its production of electricity from fossil fuels by 7% in the first half of 2025 — to 368.46 TWh from 343.28 TWh in 2024. This rise, which led to a 5% increase in power sector emissions, cannot explained by electricity demand, which grew by only 0.7%. Instead, it stems from the increased use of gas to compensate for the fall in wind energy production (-8.5%, -21 TWh) and hydropower production (-17%, -33 TWh) (1). This development is at odds with the European Green Deal’s climate and decarbonisation objectives (2). It lays bare the limits and risks of an energy policy based on intermittent sources, to the detriment of dispatchable capacities, in particular stored nuclear and hydraulic energy. These risks became apparent during Spain’s blackout in April 2025 (3). 1. How does the Commission explain this contradiction with its commitments to reduce emissions (4) and increase the share of renewable energy (5)? 2. Does it intend to shift the balance of EU energy policy in favour of stable and dispatchable sources to reduce dependence on fossil fuels and strengthen our energy security? (26 August 2026) The Commission is fully committed to a decarbonised, secure and affordable energy system. Renewables have developed significantly over the last years, reducing fossil fuel share in the electricity generation, with positive impacts on energy security. However, the EU's electricity system remains affected by inefficiencies due to insufficient development of flexibility sources, grid capacities and market integration, leading to curtailment of renewable energy. This prevents a fully efficient use of the clean electricity produced. In 2024 alone, over 10 TWh (1) of electricity from renewable energy sources could not be used in the EU due to grid congestion and insufficient capacity being available for cross-border trade (2). Expensive fossil technologies therefore had to be activated to cover the difference in spite of cheaper electricity available elsewhere. To better integrate renewables into the European electricity system, further effort towards market integration and developing non-fossil flexibility is key to fully reap the benefits of renewable energy generation. The electricity market design reform adopted in 2024, will enable Member States to derive indicative objectives and further develop non-fossil flexibility, such as demand response and storage (pumped hydro, batteries etc.). Furthermore, recent Commission initiatives such as the Tripartite Agreement for Energy Storage (3), the Grids Package (4) and the legislative proposal to future-proof electricity bills (5) amending Regulation (EU) 2019/943 aim to boost flexibility and make the most efficient use of existing grids.

E-10-2026-002560.t: Measures to prevent, prepare for and respond to the effects of the El Niño climate phenomenon
qt: to the Commission Leire Pajín (S&D) Subject:

The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) has noted a significant increase in water temperatures in the Pacific since May 2026, with measurements exceeding the average by over 6 °C. According to the WMO, the El Niño climate phenomenon is 80 % likely to take place between June and August 2026, with a 90 % likelihood of lasting until November. As stated by UN Secretary-General António Guterres, this is an urgent climate warning as there would be an increased chance of extreme weather events in the coming months and, therefore, an increased risk of extreme rainfall, floods, fires, heatwaves, intensified droughts and increased cyclone activity, both in Europe and around the world. Given this situation: 1.

What measures is the Commission taking to prevent, prepare for and respond to this potential El Niño episode, which may lead to an increase in natural disasters in Europe and around the world in the coming months?
Given the increased risk of fires, has the Commission extended the rescEU reserve, in line with the EU’s fire strategy?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (11.8.2026) The Commission is actively monitoring the new El Niño phase, among others through Copernicus Climate Change Service1, by publishing reports on plausible scenarios and its impacts2, and stands ready to support any potentially affected country via the Union Civil Protection Mechanism (rescEU). Flexible, early and anticipatory action is a critical element of effective crisis management. To support this approach, the humanitarian funding framework includes crisis modifiers (CM) which enable humanitarian partners to rapidly reallocate resources from ongoing actions to respond to newly emerging shocks. It is designed to address immediate, life-saving needs arising from rapid-onset crises or deteriorating situations, particularly when no other response mechanisms are yet in place. The Emergency Response Coordination Centre mapped its ongoing humanitarian aid projects where CM might be activated to address new needs3. In response to the increasing frequency and intensity of wildfires, the Commission created rescEU in 2019 and developed its aerial forest firefighting fleet. In 2023, the number of rescEU aerial firefighting assets was doubled. In addition, grants have been awarded to six Member States for the procurement of 12 medium amphibious aircraft, which will become operational from 2028 onwards, and to three Member States for the procurement of five helicopters. The Commission promotes a holistic and integrated approach to wildfire risk management, as outlined in its recent Communication4 on the subject. In line with the latter, the Commission intends to maintain the current level of ambition for the rescEU aerial firefighting fleet, while retaining the possibility of procuring additional aircrafts if needed.

1 https://climate.copernicus.eu/. 2 https://publications.jrc.ec.europa.eu/repository/handle/JRC147365. 3 Several CM have already been activated in response to El Niño, notably in Central America: The Commission

allocated of EUR 2.6 million to humanitarian partners to cover the basic food needs of more than 13 200 vulnerable individuals in Guatemala and Honduras. A crisis modifier was activated for a German Red Cross project in Guatemala. Around 250 families will receive a one-off cash transfer of USD 150 per household. In Belize, the World Food Programme has activated drought anticipatory action payouts, delivering early cash assistance to 419 pre-identified rain-fed smallholder farmers for investment in drought-tolerant seeds and water storage during the pre-impact window, to reduce crop losses and safeguard livelihoods. 4 COM(2026) 330 final.

E-10-2026-002559.t: Application of the Digital Services Act (DSA – Regulation (EU) 2022/2065) to reverse proxy services
qt: to the Commission Leire Pajín (S&D) Subject:
Application of the Digital Services Act (DSA – Regulation (EU) 2022/2065) to reverse proxy services

As recognised by Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 itself, new technologies and services have emerged in recent decades ‘that improve the availability, efficiency, speed, reliability, capacity and security of systems for the transmission, ‘findability’ and storage of data online, leading to an increasingly complex online ecosystem’. Doubts sometimes arise as to the legal nature of such services for the purposes of their qualification as ‘intermediaries’ in the area of digital services regulation and, therefore, as to their obligations to collaborate with the relevant authorities on removing or blocking illegal content, their place under the exemptions from liability and subjection to the DSA itself. In light of the various judicial and administrative rulings in the Member States in application of the DSA and, where applicable, with the information included in the data-sharing platform between Digital Services Coordinators and the Commission (AGORA): 1.
Does the Commission consider that reverse proxy services would qualify as intermediary services under Regulation (EU) 2022/2065?
If so, under which category regulated by Regulation (EU) No 2022/2065 would they fall?

E-10-2026-002558.t: Using the AGORA platform to share data on orders to act against illegal content
qt: to the Commission Leire Pajín (S&D) Subject:

Article 9(4) of Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 (Digital Services Act) provides that Member States’ Digital Services Coordinators shall, without undue delay, transmit a copy of each order to act against illegal content that is issued by judicial or administrative authorities. Two years after the adoption of the implementing regulation establishing the data-sharing platform between Member States and the Commission (AGORA) as a secure and reliable information exchange system between Digital Services Coordinators: 1.
Are national Digital Services Coordinators complying with the obligations of Article 9(4) by transmitting the relevant information to the data-sharing platform?
If so, which Member States are not complying with this obligation?

Depending on the analysis of the information shared on the data-sharing platform, has the Commission planned any measures to facilitate the protection of the fundamental rights most affected by unlawful conduct?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (7.9.2026) The Commission cooperates with Digital Services Coordinators (DSCs) in the framework of the European Board for Digital Services (the Board) Working Group on orders and criminal issues1. DSCs use the AGORA2 information-sharing platform, established under Article 85 of the Digital Services Act (DSA)3, to facilitate the transmission of orders received from national authorities to all other DSCs under Article 9(4) of the DSA. The Commission is also working to enhance the user experience of AGORA and to strengthen its interoperability with national IT systems, with the aim of facilitating more efficient information exchange. The protection of fundamental rights is at the core of the DSA and of the related enforcement work. Most recently, the Board, in cooperation with the Commission, has published its second annual report on systemic risks under the DSA4, which identifies systemic risks, such as the spread of illegal content or threats to fundamental rights, occurring on very large online platforms and gives an overview of the mitigation measures taken by platforms to counter such risks.

https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/dsa-board-working-groups. 2 https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/news/dsa-agora-data-sharing-platform-between-digital-servicescoordinators-and-commission-ready. 3 Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 on a Single Market for Digital Services, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/2065/oj/eng. 4 Second report on systemic risks on very large online platforms and search engines under the DSA, https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/second-report-systemic-risks-very-large-online-platforms-andsearch-engines-under-digital-services.

E-10-2026-002555.t: Application of the Digital Services Act (DSA – Regulation (EU) 2022/2065) to domain name resolution (DSN) services
qt: to the Commission Leire Pajín (S&D) Subject:
Application of the Digital Services Act (DSA – Regulation (EU) 2022/2065) to domain name resolution (DSN) services

As recognised by Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 itself, new technologies and services have emerged in recent decades ‘that improve the availability, efficiency, speed, reliability, capacity and security of systems for the transmission, ‘findability’ and storage of data online, leading to an increasingly complex online ecosystem’. Doubts sometimes arise as to the legal nature of such services for the purposes of their qualification as ‘intermediaries’ in the area of digital services regulation and, therefore, as to their obligations to collaborate with the relevant authorities on removing or blocking illegal content, their place under the exemptions from liability and subjection to the DSA itself. In light of the various judicial and administrative rulings in the Member States in application of the DSA and, where applicable, with the information included in the data-sharing platform between Digital Services Coordinators and the Commission (AGORA): 1.
Does the Commission consider domain name resolution services to qualify as intermediary services under Regulation (EU) 2022/2065?
Which category would they fall under in Regulation (EU) 2022/2065, if any?

E-10-2026-002554.t: Israel’s expulsion of Greek trade union delegation and criteria for reviewing compliance with Article 2 of the EU-Israel Association Agreement
qt: to the Commission Maria Zacharia (NI) Subject:
Israel’s expulsion of Greek trade union delegation and criteria for reviewing compliance with Article 2 of the EU-Israel Association Agreement

On 21 June 2026, the Israeli authorities refused entry to and expelled a Greek trade union delegation travelling to Ramallah at the invitation of Palestinian organisations. The incident prompted the Greek Ministry of Foreign Affairs to make a formal complaint. This adds to a series of complaints concerning restrictions against members of civil society, yet the Commission is still not recommending activating the clause in Article 2 of the EUIsrael Association Agreement, despite acknowledging that this Article – which provides that relations between the parties must be based on respect for human rights and democratic principles – constitutes an essential element of the Agreement. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

What specific legal, factual and institutional criteria does it apply to assess compliance with Article 2 of the EU-Israel Association Agreement and to determine the conditions for activating the relevant clause?
Are these criteria included in internal opinions, compliance assessments or other Commission documents and, if so, why are they not made public and communicated to the European Parliament?

Does it consider that the expulsion of an EU Member State’s citizens on account of their trade union and political activity is an element that is taken into account when assessing compliance with Article 2 and, if not, why not?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.8.2026) The High Representative/Vice-President conducted – with the support of a majority of Member States – a review of Israel’s compliance with its obligations under Article 2 of the EU-Israel Association Agreement1 in May 2025. The review concluded that there are indications that Israel would be in breach of its obligations. Discussions continue in the Council on the package of measures presented by the Commission following the review. Suspension of the entire agreement would require unanimity of all 27 Member States. The assessment was carried out by the European External Action Service, in coordination with the services of the Commission, relying in particular on factual reports by relevant international and United Nations organisations.
1 https://eeas.europa.eu/archives/delegations/israel/documents/eu_israel/asso_agree_en.pdf.

E-10-2026-002553.t: Distortion of competition to the detriment of Greek businesses providing ship supply services
qt: to the Commission Elena Kountoura (The Left) Subject:

European legislation1 provides for exemptions from duties, excise duty and VAT for Member States on goods intended for the supply of international ships, without distinction as to the invoiced party. In Greece, under national regulations2, exemptions are granted only when the goods are invoiced directly to the ship owner or operator, excluding catering companies and concessionaires operating on ships. Exemptions also do not apply to entire categories of vessels, such as professional pleasure boats on international voyages, international ferry liners and seagoing vessels. No such restrictions appear to be in place in the other Member States. This means that Greek products and businesses providing ship supply services lose a significant share of the relevant market and that ship supply services in Greek ports are outsourced to businesses in other Member States3, leading to a distortion of competition to the detriment of Greek businesses. Since the memoranda of the sectors concerned have not remedied the problem, can the Commission say: 1.
Does it consider that the above restrictions in Greece are compatible with EU law, the principle of equal treatment and the level playing field in the internal market?
What is its assessment of the link between exemptions and invoiced parties, when this is not explicitly provided for in EU law?
What steps does it intend to take to ensure the proper and uniform application of the exemptions in all Member States?

See Article 132 of Regulation (EC) No 1186/2009, which gives Member States the option of adopting provisions on exemptions, as well as Directive 2006/112/EC on VAT and Directive (EU) 2020/262 on excise duty, which provide for the possibility of exempting all products from the relevant taxes. 2 See Article 36(3) of Law 5222/2025 and Article 32(1) of Law 5144/24 on the exemption from duties, excise duty, tax on consumption and VAT respectively, of goods intended for the supply of ships, including food supplies, drinks, fuel and lubricants, etc. 3 Sectoral stakeholders already sent a memorandum to the Independent Authority for Public Revenue (AADE) in 2025 (see https://libertypress.gr/efodiasmos-ploivn-aade/). 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (25.8.2026) Article 148(a) of Council Directive 2006/112/EC (the VAT (value-added tax) Directive)1 provides that supplies of goods for the fuelling and provisioning of vessels used on the high seas are to be exempt from VAT. The exemption applies only to vessels used for navigation on the high seas and carrying passengers for reward or used for commercial, industrial or fishing activities, as well as to vessels used for rescue or assistance at sea or for inshore fishing, with the exception, in the case of the latter, of ships’ provisions. The Court held that the exemption applies only to the supply of goods to a vessel operator who will use those goods for fuelling and provisioning and cannot be extended to the supply of those goods effected at a previous stage in the commercial chain2. Therefore the fact that the exemption is granted only when the goods are invoiced directly to the ship owner or operator does not seem to be in breach of EU Law. As regards excise duties, Article 13 of Council Directive (EU) 2020/262 allows Member States to exempt excise goods supplied on board a ship during the sea-crossing to a third territory or a third country. Member States must take the measures necessary to prevent any possible evasion, avoidance or abuse. The production, processing, holding and storage of excise goods is covered by Chapter III of this Directive, whereas the movement of excise goods under suspension of excise duty is governed in Chapter IV thereof. Regarding customs duties, according to the Union Customs Code, no such duties apply to ship supplies, except for cases of non-compliance with the obligations regarding the customs supervision, movement, or exit of the goods out of the customs territory of the EU.
1 Council Directive 2006/112/EC of 28 November 2006 on the common system of value added tax (OJ L 347,

11.12.2006, p. 1). 2 Judgment of 26 June 1990, Velker International Oil Company Ltd NV, C-185/89, EU:C:1990:262; paragraph 22; Judgment of 14 September 2006, Elmeka NE, Joined cases C-181/04 to C-183/04, EU:C:2006:563, paragraph 25; Judgment of 3 September 2015, UAB "Fast Bunkering Klaipėda“, C-526/13, EU:C:2015:536, paragraph 29.

E-10-2026-002552.t: Personal protective equipment (PPE) for emergency service workers
qt: to the Commission Sebastian Tynkkynen (ECR) Subject:

Violence against rescue and emergency workers has risen sharply in recent years. Interventions in high-risk areas are increasingly dangerous, and emergency workers are often required to respond to attacks such as shootings, stabbings and bombings. This raises serious concerns for the safety of our emergency service providers. Russia’s aggression against Ukraine has further exposed these risks, with emergency responders being deliberately targeted. These circumstances require them to wear bulletproof vests and helmets to perform their duties. Regulation (EU) 2016/4251 sets out the current EU-level requirements for PPE. A derogation is provided for PPE designed for use by the armed forces or in the maintenance of law and order. The reason for the derogation is that PPE designed for these purposes might not include the CE marking required by this regulation. However, rescue and emergency workers are not included in the derogation. This limits the possibilities for protecting workers in this field. Can the Commission therefore clarify: 1.
Whether it intends to amend Regulation (EU) 2016/425 to extend the derogation to cover PPE designed for use by rescue and emergency services?
What the time frame will be for this urgent update to the existing regulation?

Regulation (EU) 2016/425 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 9 March 2016 on personal protective equipment and repealing Council Directive 89/686/EEC (OJ L 81, 31.3.2016, p. 51, http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/425/oj). 1

E-10-2026-002551.t: High microfibre emissions from synthetic textiles and the need for product-specific regulation
qt: to the Commission Martin Günther (The Left) Subject:
High microfibre emissions from synthetic textiles and the need for productspecific regulation

In the light of growing evidence1 that certain synthetic textiles, in particular polyester fleece, release disproportionately high quantities of microfibres throughout their life cycle, including during production, washing, drying and wear, and noting that fabric construction (e.g. brushed surfaces) significantly increases fibre shedding, and that current EU policy does not differentiate between textile products based on their microfibre emission intensity: 1.
Does the Commission recognise that specific textile types, such as fleece, represent disproportionately large sources of microplastic pollution compared to other materials?
How does the Commission intend to address microfibre shedding at product design level under existing or forthcoming legislation, including the Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation?

Is the Commission considering the introduction of requirements or restrictions for highshedding textile products, including design standards, material choices or performance thresholds for fibre release, such as minimum durability requirements and measurable limits on fibre shedding for textiles placed on the EU market?

Novotna J, Tunak M, Militky J, Kremenakova D, Wiener J, Novakova J, Sevcu A., ‘Release of Microplastic Fibers from Polyester Knit Fleece during Abrasion, Washing, and Drying’, ACS Omega, 31 March 2025; 10(14):14241-14249. doi: 10.1021/acsomega.5c00258. PMID: 40256517; PMCID: PMC12004151. 1
at: (English version) to the Commission Martin Günther (The Left) (22 June 2026) Subject: High microfibre emissions from synthetic textiles and the need for product-specific regulation In the light of growing evidence (1) that certain synthetic textiles, in particular polyester fleece, release disproportionately high quantities of microfibres throughout their life cycle, including during production, washing, drying and wear, and noting that fabric construction (e.g. brushed surfaces) significantly increases fibre shedding, and that current EU policy does not differentiate between textile products based on their microfibre emission intensity: 1.
Does the Commission recognise that specific textile types, such as fleece, represent disproportionately large sources of microplastic pollution compared to other materials?
How does the Commission intend to address microfibre shedding at product design level under existing or forthcoming legislation, including the Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation?

Is the Commission considering the introduction of requirements or restrictions for high-shedding textile products, including design standards, material choices or performance thresholds for fibre release, such as minimum durability requirements and measurable limits on fibre shedding for textiles placed on the EU market?

(25 August 2026) The Commission recognised the environmental impacts of the shedding of microplastics from synthetic textiles in the EU Strategy for Sustainable and Circular Textiles (1). In view of the broader environmental impacts of this sector, the Ecodesign for Sustainable Products and Energy Labelling Working Plan 2025-2030 (2) prioritised the preparation of ecodesign requirements for textile apparel. The aim of the requirements is to make products more sustainable and circular by removing the worst performing products from the market, and by driving sustainable consumption through provision of information on product environmental impacts. A preparatory study by the Joint Research Centre is ongoing and aims to identify feasible measures that will be further considered in an impact assessment. This study will include an analysis on the fragmentation of textile into microfibres. In parallel, the Commission is working on a revision of Environmental Footprint methods (3) for modelling, calculating, and reporting the life cycle environmental impacts of products, such as textiles. Among other aspects, this revision is expected to integrate methods to address the release of microplastics.

E-10-2026-002550.t: Structural and operational problems at the Hellenic Post Office (ELTA)
qt: to the Commission Yannis Maniatis (S&D) Subject:

According to recent reports in the Greek press, the Hellenic Post Office (ELTA), despite repeated restructuring and the significant public funding it has received for the provision of universal postal services in Greece, is now facing insurmountable structural and operational problems. There are documented reports of egregious delays in the delivery of mail and basic utility bills, branch closures, network shrinkage and staff shortages, while at the same time it is alleged that even administrative employees have been asked to assist voluntarily in the distribution of parcels. Given that the universal postal service is an obligation arising from EU law and is crucial for territorial and social cohesion, particularly in remote and island regions: 1.

Has the Commission assessed the extent to which the provision of the universal postal service in Greece by ELTA complies with the requirements of the relevant Directive 2008/6/EC with regard to the full accomplishment of the internal market of Community postal services?

Does the Commission monitor the effectiveness of European and national aid or compensation granted for the provision of this universal service, which is estimated to have exceeded EUR 300 million over the last decade?

Does the Commission intend to examine whether the continuing shortcomings in the quality and reliability of ELTA's postal services affect the rights of Greek citizens to equal access to essential services throughout the territory?
at: (English version) to the Commission Yannis Maniatis (S&D) (20 June 2026) Subject: Structural and operational problems at the Hellenic Post Office (ELTA) According to recent reports in the Greek press, the Hellenic Post Office (ELTA), despite repeated restructuring and the significant public funding it has received for the provision of universal postal services in Greece, is now facing insurmountable structural and operational problems. There are documented reports of egregious delays in the delivery of mail and basic utility bills, branch closures, network shrinkage and staff shortages, while at the same time it is alleged that even administrative employees have been asked to assist voluntarily in the distribution of parcels. Given that the universal postal service is an obligation arising from EU law and is crucial for territorial and social cohesion, particularly in remote and island regions: 1.

Has the Commission assessed the extent to which the provision of the universal postal service in Greece by ELTA complies with the requirements of the relevant Directive 2008/6/EC with regard to the full accomplishment of the internal market of Community postal services?

Does the Commission monitor the effectiveness of European and national aid or compensation granted for the provision of this universal service, which is estimated to have exceeded EUR 300 million over the last decade?

Does the Commission intend to examine whether the continuing shortcomings in the quality and reliability of ELTA's postal services affect the rights of Greek citizens to equal access to essential services throughout the territory?

(2 September 2026) The Postal Services Directive (1) (hereafter the directive) establishes the regulatory framework for postal services across the European Union. The directive requires Member States to ensure a permanent universal service at all points of the territory at affordable prices and of a certain quality. In Greece, this legal obligation has been entrusted to the Hellenic Post Office (ELTA) and is to be supervised by the national regulatory authority (EETT). Should EETT not fulfil its obligations under the directive, in its role as guardian of the Treaties, the Commission monitors the situation and may decide to take appropriate action. Any state aid granted to ELTA for discharging the universal service obligation must be notified under Article 108(3) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU (2) and comply with the requirements of the directive and with Services of General Economic Interest rules (3). It is primarily the responsibility of EETT to monitor ELTA. The Commission is currently working on a proposal aimed at the modernisation of the postal regulatory framework, and particularly the universal service. The proposal is expected to be finalised in the first quarter of 2027.

E-10-2026-002549.t: Coéns mine: new mining project near a population centre and a protected area
qt: to the Commission Ana Miranda Paz (Verts/ALE) Subject:

The Coéns mining project (Laxe) is located less than 40 metres from a rural settlement. This open-cast mine would aim to produce 9 000 tonnes of kaolin per year, with residents already expressing their grave concern over kaolin mining and its serious impact on health. The potential public health impact is on a par with the negative environmental impact this mine would have. The mine is close to the Redondela lagoon, which is listed in the Galician inventory of wetlands. Plataforma Contra a Mina de Coéns believes that the simplified environmental impact study shows that the mine will have an unacceptable impact and calls for the mine project to not go ahead due to the serious consequences it could have for residents and on the wetlands of Redondela. 1.
Is the Commission aware that, in Galicia, there are plans to carry out an open-cast mining project using explosives a mere 20 metres from residential houses?

Does the Commission consider the opening – or reopening, as is the case of Coéns – of mines near population centres to be a model to follow in order to achieve sovereignty in European critical materials?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (28.8.2026) The Commission is not aware of the plans referred to by the Honourable Member. Under the principle of subsidiarity1, spatial planning and land-use management are in principle within the remit of Member States. EU law establishes a harmonised framework of ex-ante procedural obligations to identify and evaluate the environmental and public health risks of projects such as the one in question. These assessment requirements are governed inter alia by the Environmental Impact Assessment2, Extractive Waste3 and Water Framework4 Directives, which Member States may implement via a joint or coordinated procedure. Furthermore, national authorities must guarantee public participation and ensure that the public concerned has access to a review procedure to challenge the substantive or procedural legality of any development consent granted in breach of these obligations. The Commission is committed to fostering sustainable and resilient raw material value chains for strategic sectors. The Critical Raw Materials Act5 introduces projects which are designated as strategic projects by the Commission. To be designated as strategic project, projects have to fulfil environmental, social and governance aspects. This includes the prevention and minimisation of socially adverse impacts using socially responsible practices. The Commission notes that, according to the available information, the project referred to by the Honourable Member has not been designated as strategic under the Critical Raw Materials Act6.
1 Enshrined in Article 5(3) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union. 2 Directive 2011/92/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 December 2011 on the assessment

of the effects of certain public and private projects on the environment. OJ L 26, 28.1.2012, p. 1–21, as amended by Directive 2014/52/EU of 16 April 2014 - OJ L 124, 25.4.2014, p. 1–18. Point 2 a) of Annex II of the EIA Directive refers to ‘Open-cast mining’. 3 Directive 2006/21/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 15 March 2006 on the management of waste from extractive industries and amending Directive 2004/35/EC - Statement by the European Parliament, the Council and the Commission, OJ L 102, 11.4.2006, p. 15–34. 4 Directive 2000/60/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 23 October 2000 establishing a framework for Community action in the field of water policy - OJ L 327, 22.12.2000, pp. 1–73. 5 Regulation (EU) 2024/1252 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 11 April 2024 establishing a framework for ensuring a secure and sustainable supply of critical raw materials and amending Regulations (EU) No 168/2013, (EU) 2018/858, (EU) 2018/1724 and (EU) 2019/1020 (Text with EEA relevance) - OJ L, 2024/1252, 3.5.2024. 6 Regulation (EU) 2024/1252 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 11 April 2024 establishing a framework for ensuring a secure and sustainable supply of critical raw materials, OJ L, 2024/1252, 3.5.2024.

E-10-2026-002548.t: TikTok Shop and the protection of young consumers and the internal market
qt: to the Commission Dirk Gotink (PPE) Subject:

On 15 June 2026, ByteDance launched TikTok Shop in the Netherlands and Belgium. An inapp button allows users to buy products without leaving the app – thereby removing the last barrier to impulse purchases. On 6 February 2026, the Commission already concluded that TikTok’s addictive design violates the DSA. 31 % of users are between 18 and 24 years old, a group particularly prone to social media addiction and indebtedness. In China, 85 % of purchases on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, do not result from a search but from the timeline. Consumers buy what the algorithm shows. Moreover, products offered do not always comply with EU safety standards and it is unclear how data collected is processed. TikTok has been designated as a gatekeeper under the DMA; TikTok Shop is therefore also covered by this Regulation. 1.
How will the Commission ensure that TikTok and TikTok Shop comply with DMA obligations, including fair competition and transparency for business users?
What measures is the Commission taking to protect young consumers from shopping addiction and debts resulting from Tik Tok’s addictive design combined with its in-app payment function?
How does the Commission ensure that personal data collected through TikTok Shop remain within the EU and are not used for purposes that undermine the EU’s digital sovereignty?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (31.8.2026) ByteDance is bound by all obligations that apply to online social networking services1 under the Digital Markets Act (DMA)2. These obligations ensure fairness and transparency for business users. The Commission uses all tools at its disposal to ensure gatekeepers comply with the DMA, including compliance monitoring, regulatory dialogue and enforcement tools if necessary. Article 28 of the Digital Services Act (DSA)3 requires providers of online platforms accessible to minors to ensure a high level of privacy, safety and security of minors. The Commission considers, as set out in its Guidelines on the protection of minors4, that providers are to put in place measures that prevent minors from being exposed to excessive volumes of commercial content and to increase the transparency of economic transactions. Advertising should be clearly marked as such. While, according to the information available to the Commission, access to TikTok Shop should be limited to users above 18 years of age, it will continue to monitor the potential impact of TikTok Shop on the identification, analysis and assessment of the risks of negative effects on minors and whether the mitigation measures proposed by TikTok are sufficient. The DSA also sets out rules applicable to providers of online marketplaces. The Commission, in cooperation with Digital Services Coordinators, will continue to supervise the evolution of such features in the EU, including compliance with the rules applicable to online marketplaces. In accordance with the GDPR5, companies may transfer personal data to third countries provided the data controller ensures compliance with the rules in Chapter V of the GDPR. National supervisory authorities are competent to assess whether TikTok Shop is in violation of the GDPR’s rules on international data transfers.

E-10-2026-002547.t: Ban the butt: it is time to stub out cigarette filters
qt: to the Commission Mohammed Chahim (S&D), Jeannette Baljeu (Renew), Gerben-Jan Gerbrandy (Renew), Marta Temido (S&D), Sebastian Everding (The Left), Anja Hazekamp (The Left), Christophe Clergeau (S&D), Ingeborg Ter Laak (PPE), Thomas Pellerin-Carlin (S&D), Tilly Metz (Verts/ALE) Subject:

A recent documentary from Dutch broadcaster HUMAN1 has raised concerns about the severe environmental impact of cigarette filters, which release microplastics and toxic chemicals into water, soil and ecosystems. At the same time, scientific consensus (including from the World Health Organization) increasingly demonstrates that cigarette filters do not provide any health benefits to smokers and may even increase certain health risks. 1.

How does the Commission assess the findings of the World Health Organization2, the Dutch National Institute for Public Health and the Environment3, and the consultancy CE Delft4 regarding the environmental and health impacts of cigarette filters?

How could the Commission revise the Single-Use Plastics Directive or utilise alternative legislative frameworks such as REACH and the Tobacco Products Directive to implement a ban on cigarette filters?

The initial impact assessment of the Single-Use Plastics Directive concluded that no viable alternatives to cigarette filters existed, thereby ruling out a ban. Given the definitive scientific evidence that filters offer no health benefits, does the Commission now agree that a filterless cigarette constitutes a viable alternative?
