at: (English version) to the Commission Mohammed Chahim (S&D), Jeannette Baljeu (Renew), Gerben-Jan Gerbrandy (Renew), Marta Temido (S&D), Sebastian Everding (The Left), Anja Hazekamp (The Left), Christophe Clergeau (S&D), Ingeborg Ter Laak (PPE), Thomas Pellerin-Carlin (S&D), Tilly Metz (Verts/ALE) (19 June 2026) Subject: Ban the butt: it is time to stub out cigarette filters A recent documentary from Dutch broadcaster HUMAN (1) has raised concerns about the severe environmental impact of cigarette filters, which release microplastics and toxic chemicals into water, soil and ecosystems. At the same time, scientific consensus (including from the World Health Organisation) increasingly demonstrates that cigarette filters do not provide any health benefits to smokers and may even increase certain health risks. 1. How does the Commission assess the findings of the World Health Organisation (2), the Dutch National Institute for Public Health and the Environment (3), and the consultancy CE Delft (4) regarding the environmental and health impacts of cigarette filters? 2. How could the Commission revise the Single-Use Plastics Directive or utilise alternative legislative frameworks such as REACH and the Tobacco Products Directive to implement a ban on cigarette filters? 3. The initial impact assessment of the Single-Use Plastics Directive concluded that no viable alternatives to cigarette filters existed, thereby ruling out a ban. Given the definitive scientific evidence that filters offer no health benefits, does the Commission now agree that a filterless cigarette constitutes a viable alternative? (3 September 2026) The assessments of the Commission draw, among others, on scientific reports, surveys and other analyses. The Commission acknowledges that several components of tobacco products are toxic and that cigarette filters are a major source of waste generated by the tobacco industry and its products. The Single-Use Plastics Directive (SUPD) (1) seeks to limit the negative impact of certain plastic products, including tobacco filters containing plastic, on the environment. Due to the ongoing evaluation of the SUPD, which is expected to be completed by July 2027, it is premature to conclude if the SUPD measures applicable to filters should be changed or if the focus should be on improving their effectiveness. The Commission intends to propose by the end of 2026 a revision of the legislative framework on tobacco control (2). The Commission is committed to guaranteeing that the EU tobacco control legislation facilitates the smooth functioning of the internal market, while ensuring a high level of protection of human health, especially for young people.

E-10-2026-002546.t: The grave impact of the dirty war by the US and Israel against Iran on energy prices and the responsibilities of the EU and the Government
qt: to the Commission Lefteris Nikolaou-Alavanos (NI) Subject:

The escalation of the war in the Middle East is driving up energy and fuel prices, robbing the working-class family, while energy groups and shipowners are cashing in. Nea Dimokratia and the other bourgeois parties that have put their stamp on the coformulation and promotion of the EU's anti-working class energy strategy and the country's involvement in this crime bear heavy responsibility. In view of this: 1.

What is the Commission’s position on the fact that the Commission, within the framework of the toolkit of fuel and energy measures, is even considering fuel rations for ordinary households, travel restrictions and other measures against the people, confirming that the EU is targeting and blaming the needs of the people, who have long been condemned to energy poverty, while through its policy it is supporting the profitability of energy groups and refineries?

What is the Commission’s position on ‘fuel pass’ subsidies and other forms of ‘coupons’ and other token gestures, since they boost the profitability of energy and fuel groups by keeping prices high, instead of real relief measures, such as the abolition of excise duties on fuel and energy, caps on fuel prices and on the wholesale energy market, the abolition of VAT on consumer goods and substantive increases in wages with a full reinstatement of collective bargaining agreements?

What is the Commission’s position on the request for the abolition of the European Union institutional framework that turns energy into a stock market product and a gamble for business groups, such as the adjustment clause, the energy exchange and the special fee for the reduction of greenhouse gas emissions?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (8.9.2026) The conflict in the Middle East has led to volatile and increased oil and gas prices worldwide. As a continent that is still dependent on fossil fuel imports, these developments have negatively affected businesses and citizens in the European Union. The Commission will continue monitoring the situation in view of the continued disruptions. The Commission has supported Member States in facilitating a coordinated response to manage this situation. Whilst no physical supply disruptions at consumer level occurred, some Member States took national action to protect households and business consumers from the higher energy prices. The Commission prepared a repository of these measures1, and published a catalogue of national practices to help reduce costs whilst strengthening energy resilience2. This catalogue included energy-specific measures like targeted income support schemes, energy vouchers and social leasing schemes, lowering taxes and excise duties on electricity for vulnerable households; and measures to promote the deployment of renewable energy sources and to accelerate the electrification of the economy to address vulnerabilities linked to fossil fuel dependencies. The Commission continues to support the development of transparent and open EU energy markets as the most effective means to ensure competitive and affordable energy for the endconsumers, whilst introducing important safeguards for ensuring energy security, addressing energy poverty, and reducing greenhouse gas emissions.

E-10-2026-002545.t: Support for healthcare workers suffering from Long Covid and access to adequate social protection
qt: to the Commission Ciaran Mullooly (Renew) Subject:

Healthcare and social care workers who contracted COVID-19 at work continue to experience Long Covid, with severe impacts on their health, work capacity and financial security. In its resolution on the COVID-19 pandemic: lessons learned and recommendations for the future, the European Parliament called on EU countries to provide adequate support to people suffering from Long Covid, including by extending sickness allowances and facilitating access to social benefit schemes, and called for the recognition of Long Covid as an occupational disease for those workers. In this context and in view of the situation of healthcare workers who have exhausted sickness benefits and face a sudden drop in income while still unfit for work: What assessment has the Commission made of the extent to which Member States are giving practical effect to Parliament’s 2023 recommendations on adequate support for people with Long Covid, including access to sickness allowances and social protection schemes?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (26.8.2026) The design and management of social protection systems, including eligibility to sickness benefits and their duration, remains fundamentally the responsibility of the Member States (Article 153 (4) Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union). The Commission supports Member States through facilitating exchange of experience, analysis and policy guidance. The summary report of the 2024 mutual learning on access to social protection1 with focus on health, sickness, accidents at work and occupational diseases shows that most measures implemented as a response to the COVID-19 pandemic were only temporary and, in some cases, structural reforms were postponed. The Commission Recommendation (EU) 2022/2337 calls on Member States to recognise COVID-19 as an occupational disease, including when caused by work in health and social care2. Eurostat’s survey on the possibility of recognising COVID-19 as being of occupational origin3 shows that, in most countries, COVID-19 can be linked to work-related activities. However, the form of recognition varies between countries. The Commission recognises the significant medical and socioeconomic consequences of Long COVID and remains committed to supporting effective responses across these areas. The Network of Expertise on Long COVID4, supported from the EU4Health programme5 and carried out in collaboration with international organisations, aims to strengthen EU and national-level responses, including a training programme for healthcare professionals.

E-10-2026-002543.t: Mass redundancies in Upper Silesia and the Just Transition Fund
qt: to the Commission Marcin Sypniewski (ESN) Subject:

The Commission has announced that the energy transition will protect jobs and create new, high-quality jobs in coal and industrial regions. However, despite over EUR 2 billion being allocated from the Just Transition Fund (JTF) to Silesia to create jobs, the region is experiencing mass layoffs. In May 2026, Jastrzębska Spółka Węglowa announced a redundancy programme for up to 4 248 employees, while the Stellantis factory in Tychy laid off 740 people as a result of EU emission standards. The current transition process therefore does not appear to be protecting the local labour market and is not creating sustainable alternatives at a sufficient pace. In light of the above: 1.

Does the Commission plan to carry out an independent audit of the effectiveness of the JTF in Silesia in order to realistically assess whether the funds spent actually created a sufficient number of sustainable jobs?
Is the Commission investigating the phenomenon of accelerated deindustrialisation in JTF regions and the direct impact of EU climate policy on mass redundancies in key workplaces?
Does the Commission envisage reorienting the priorities of the JTF and making its budget more flexible in order to save regional economic potential and to effectively tackle structural unemployment?

(21 August 2026) 1. The Commission closely monitors the implementation and performance of the Just Transition Fund (JTF) through regular reporting, Monitoring Committees, Annual Performance Reviews and audits. Managing Authorities are required to report on programme indicators, enabling the Commission to assess progress against the objectives set out in the Territorial Just Transition Plans (TJTPs), prepared by Member States and regions in partnership with local stakeholders. The JTF programme for Silesia is the largest in the EU, with an allocation of EUR 2.2 billion. By March 2026, 85% of this allocation had already been committed to selected operations (1). 2. The TJTPs identify the challenges and risks of deindustrialisation in the territories in transition and job creation is a central objective of the JTF. E-10-2026-002542.t: Proportionality of the EU Deforestation Regulation in the light of the Commission’s own cited scientific evidence
qt: to the Commission Asger Christensen (Renew), Benoit Cassart (Renew), Katri Kulmuni (Renew) Subject:

On 4 May 2026, the Commission published its simplification review of the EU Deforestation Regulation1 (EUDR). The report cites Singh and Persson2 and states that seven EUDR commodities account for over 4 million hectares of deforestation annually, which amounts to approximately 70 % of agriculture-driven deforestation. The same study, however, gives a more differentiated commodity-level picture: deforestation footprints vary considerably among the EUDR commodities, while staple crops like maize, rice and cassava – currently out of the regulation’s scope – collectively account for about 11 % of global deforestation, exceeding cocoa (2 %), coffee (1 %) and rubber (1 %). The study provides valuable new insights for EUDR risk benchmarking and regulatory scope, showing that both country and commodity dynamic shifts are critical for the regulation’s success in achieving its ambition while preserving competitiveness and enhancing global supply chain resilience. In the light of the above: 1.
How does the Commission assess the apparent divergence between the study’s commodity-level findings and the current EUDR commodity scope?
How will the Commission incorporate the study’s full findings in future scoping, benchmarking or review exercises?
What safeguards will the Commission apply to ensure that the EUDR remains riskbased, proportionate and focused on the commodities and supply chains with the greatest deforestation risk?

M., 2026, Global patterns of commodity-driven deforestation and associated carbon emissions. Nature Food, 7(2), 138-151. 1
at: (English version) to the Commission Asger Christensen (Renew), Benoit Cassart (Renew), Katri Kulmuni (Renew) (19 June 2026) Subject: Proportionality of the EU Deforestation Regulation in the light of the Commission’s own cited scientific evidence On 4 May 2026, the Commission published its simplification review of the EU Deforestation Regulation (1) (EUDR). The report cites Singh and Persson (2) and states that seven EUDR commodities account for over 4 million hectares of deforestation annually, which amounts to approximately 70% of agriculture-driven deforestation. The same study, however, gives a more differentiated commodity-level picture: deforestation footprints vary considerably among the EUDR commodities, while staple crops like maize, rice and cassava — currently out of the regulation’s scope — collectively account for about 11% of global deforestation, exceeding cocoa (2%), coffee (1%) and rubber (1%). The study provides valuable new insights for EUDR risk benchmarking and regulatory scope, showing that both country and commodity dynamic shifts are critical for the regulation’s success in achieving its ambition while preserving competitiveness and enhancing global supply chain resilience. In the light of the above: 1.
How does the Commission assess the apparent divergence between the study’s commodity-level findings and the current EUDR commodity scope?
How will the Commission incorporate the study’s full findings in future scoping, benchmarking or review exercises?
What safeguards will the Commission apply to ensure that the EUDR remains risk-based, proportionate and focused on the commodities and supply chains with the greatest deforestation risk?

(25 August 2026) The EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) (1) aims to address the EU's contribution to global deforestation. In that context, it is important to distinguish between global deforestation attributable to a commodity and deforestation linked specifically to EU consumption of that commodity. The relevance of a commodity under the EUDR depends not only on its overall deforestation footprint but also on the extent to which EU demand drives that footprint. This explains why commodities such as cocoa, of which a substantial proportion of global production is exported to the EU market, are included within the EUDR despite their relatively modest contribution to global deforestation, and cassava is not. At the same time, agricultural production systems, international trade patterns, and consumer preferences evolve over time. Recognising this dynamic, the EUDR includes a review clause which requires the Commission to present a review of the regulation and its scope no later than 30 June 2030.

E-10-2026-002540.t: Integration of digital identity systems for identification and access procedures in the digital euro
qt: to the Commission Siegbert Frank Droese (ESN) Subject:

The legal framework for the digital euro increasingly provides for the integration of digital identity systems for identification and access procedures. While digital identity can be a useful optional tool, there are concerns that, as its uptake grows, it could gradually become the only means of access used in practice, effectively displacing national forms of identification and other traditional means of access. How does the Commission intend to ensure that access to the digital euro remains possible through national forms of identification, including national identity cards, and that digital identity does not become the only practical means of identification or access in the long term?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.9.2026) Article 5a (15) of Regulation (EU) No 910/2014 of the European Parliament and of the Council1 establishes that the use of the EU Digital Identity Wallets is voluntary. It states that access to public and private services, access to the labour market and freedom to conduct business shall not in any way be restricted or made disadvantageous to natural or legal persons that do not use EU Digital Identity Wallets and that it shall remain possible to access public and private services by other existing identification and authentication means. In addition, Regulation (EU) 2024/1183 of the European Parliament and of the Council2, which amended Regulation (EU) No 910/2014, does not foresee a discontinuation of national identification systems in the context of the deployment of the EU Digital Identity Wallets. For the digital euro, this means that the EU Digital Identity Wallets are a voluntary option that citizens can use, if they wish, for identification, onboarding and authorising payments with the digital euro. In order to enable this option for users, Article 25 of the Commission proposal provides that front-end services shall be interoperable with, or integrated into, the EU Digital Identity Wallets. It also provides that on request by digital euro users, payment service providers distributing the digital euro shall ensure that those users can rely on the functionalities of their EU Digital Identity Wallets.
1 Regulation (EU) No 910/2014 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 23 July 2014 on electronic

identification and trust services for electronic transactions in the internal market and repealing Directive 1999/93/EC (OJ L 257, 28.8.2014, p. 73, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2014/910/oj). 2 Regulation (EU) 2024/1183 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 11 April 2024 amending Regulation (EU) No 910/2014 as regards establishing the European Digital Identity Framework (OJ L, 2024/1183, 30.4.2024, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1183/oj).

E-10-2026-002539.t: Legal basis for the digital euro
qt: to the Commission Siegbert Frank Droese (ESN) Subject:

The legal basis used for the digital euro is Article 133 TFEU, which concerns measures necessary for the use of the euro as the single currency. However, the legal framework for the digital euro may include elements that go beyond classic monetary policy measures, such as mandatory acceptance requirements, the integration of digital identity systems, and more farreaching interventions in payment market structures. Against this background, there are doubts as to whether the scope of Article 133 TFEU could already have been exceeded. 1.
Does the Commission nevertheless consider that Article 133 TFEU alone constitutes a sufficient legal basis for the entire legal framework of the digital euro?
In the Commission’s view, where are the limits of Article 133 TFEU in relation to the digital euro and what types of measures or functions would go beyond the scope of Article 133 TFEU?
at: (English version) to the Commission Siegbert Frank Droese (ESN) (18 June 2026) Subject: Legal basis for the digital euro The legal basis used for the digital euro is Article 133 TFEU, which concerns measures necessary for the use of the euro as the single currency. However, the legal framework for the digital euro may include elements that go beyond classic monetary policy measures, such as mandatory acceptance requirements, the integration of digital identity systems, and more far-reaching interventions in payment market structures. Against this background, there are doubts as to whether the scope of Article 133 TFEU could already have been exceeded. 1. Does the Commission nevertheless consider that Article 133 TFEU alone constitutes a sufficient legal basis for the entire legal framework of the digital euro? 2. In the Commission’s view, where are the limits of Article 133 TFEU in relation to the digital euro and what types of measures or functions would go beyond the scope of Article 133 TFEU? (7 August 2026) In accordance with the case-law, the choice of legal basis for a EU measure must rest on objective factors that are amenable to judicial review, including the aim and content of the measure (1). Article 1 of the proposal for a digital euro Regulation (2) makes clear that its aim is to adapt the euro to technological changes and to ensure its use as a single currency. To that end, the regulation lays down rules concerning the legal tender status of the digital euro, its distribution, use, and essential technical features. The aim and content of the proposal fall within the scope of Article 133 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, which allows the EU legislature to lay down measures necessary for the use of the euro as the single currency. According to the case law of the Court of Justice, the concept of monetary policy is not limited to its operational implementation by the European System of Central Banks but also entails a regulatory dimension (3). The proposal remains within the limits of that dimension. Its provisions ensure that the euro will be used effectively as a single currency in the euro area. In particular, the mandatory acceptance of the digital euro is necessary to ensure the effective use of the euro as a single currency since it will lead to a sufficiently uniform level of acceptance throughout the euro area. The other measures of the regulation pursue the same objectives and are necessary to ensure the effective use of the euro as the EU’s single currency.

See, for example, judgment of 3 December 2019, Czech Republic v European Parliament and Council of the European Union, C-482/17, EU:C:2019:1035, paragraphs 31 and 32. COM(2023) 369 final. E-10-2026-002537.t: New Caledonian nickel industry and Europeans’ strategic autonomy
qt: to the Commission André Rougé (PfE), Christophe Bay (PfE), Valérie Deloge (PfE), France Jamet (PfE), Fabrice Leggeri (PfE), Gilles Pennelle (PfE), Alexandre Varaut (PfE), Marie-Luce Brasier-Clain (PfE), Aleksandar Nikolic (PfE), Julie Rechagneux (PfE) Subject:

The energy transition and the European defence industry depend on nickel. Our 27 Member States are 80 % reliant on Chinese or Indonesian production, while for refined nickel, the figure reaches 90 %. New Caledonia, a French overseas territory, remains the world’s largest source of nickel, possessing some 25 % of the world’s lateritic nickel reserves. However, the New Caledonian nickel sector is in crisis, with production shut down at two out of three industrial sites and uncertainty about the future of the Eramet group, which includes the French State among its shareholders. There are reports of Chinese buyers. At a time when Europe is aiming to secure its supplies with the Critical Raw Materials Act, no plan has been put forward to make New Caledonia the natural and secure source of nickel for Europeans. In comparison, Chinese dominance in the battery and rare earth sectors demonstrates that mining groups cannot thrive without the support of their governments. 1.

To prevent the Critical Raw Materials Act from becoming a dead letter, will the Commission support the New Caledonian nickel sector, including through strategic stockpiling and support for industrial projects?
Are steps being taken to oppose Indonesian nickel produced without compliance with environmental, social and governance criteria?

However, the New Caledonian nickel sector is in crisis, with production shut down at two out of three industrial sites and uncertainty about the future of the Eramet group, which includes the French State among its shareholders. There are reports of Chinese buyers. At a time when Europe is aiming to secure its supplies with the Critical Raw Materials Act, no plan has been put forward to make New Caledonia the natural and secure source of nickel for Europeans. In comparison, Chinese dominance in the battery and rare earth sectors demonstrates that mining groups cannot thrive without the support of their governments. 1. Are steps being taken to oppose Indonesian nickel produced without compliance with environmental, social and governance criteria? (7 August 2026) In an increasingly volatile geopolitical context and amid intensifying international competition, the Commission is stepping up its efforts to diversify and secure the EU’s supply of critical minerals. In this context, cooperation with Overseas Countries and Territories (OCT) that are endowed with critical minerals, such as New Caledonia, is of particular relevance. New Caledonia holds significant nickel resources and industrial processing capacities that make it an important actor in global nickel value chains. It also has potential for copper, zinc, manganese, platinum, antimony, magnesium and bismuth. Given the importance of nickel for energy transition and defence-related industry ecosystems, New Caledonia’s nickel sector, its broader mineral potential as well as its privileged position as an OCT in the Indo-Pacific, the Commission recognises the value in promoting closer integration of New Caledonia into European critical raw materials value chains. Among the Strategic Projects announced by the Commission (1) the CaledoNi project in New Caledonia will help boost nickel production, address existing environmental disturbances, create both direct and indirect jobs, and generate local value creation. The Commission is therefore actively working to advance its Strategic Projects, including CaledoNi, to strengthen the EU’s security of supply. The Commission continues to support responsible sourcing. It will continue to use relevant EU instruments to promote sustainable production and to reduce strategic dependencies, including where concerns arise regarding environmental, social and governance conditions in third-country production.

E-10-2026-002536.t: Use of European Social Fund Plus resources to finance abortion, and the definition of healthcare

In its reply to Written Question E-000928/20261, the Commission stated that Member States may allocate European Social Fund Plus (ESF+) resources to abortion-related services, referring to the ESF+’s objective of improving access to healthcare services. However, this interpretation raises serious concerns regarding both the original objectives of the ESF+ and the very notion of healthcare. Article 3(a) of Directive 2011/24/EU on the application of patients’ rights in cross-border healthcare2 defines healthcare as services provided to patients ‘to assess, maintain or restore their state of health’. It is therefore controversial to equate with this definition a practice that deliberately brings an end to a human life at the prenatal stage. Can the Commission clarify the following: 1.

In the absence of specific pathological conditions or particular medical prescriptions, does it consider a pregnant woman to be in a situation in which it is necessary ‘to assess, maintain or restore’ her state of health?
How does it reconcile its interpretation of abortion as a healthcare service with the definition of healthcare set out in Article 3(a) of Directive 2011/24/EU?
In the light of the above, does it intend to amend its communication C(2026)32253, issued on 26 February 2026 in response to the European Citizens’ Initiative ‘My Voice, My Choice’?

(24 September 2026) The Commission has clarified that Member States may use the European Social Fund Plus (ESF+) under their national or regional programmes as a way to contribute to the objectives of the ‘My Voice, My Choice’ initiative, as ‘enhancing equal and timely access to quality, sustainable and affordable services’, including healthcare services (1), is one of the objectives that may be supported by the ESF+ as set out in Article 4(1)(k) of the ESF+ Regulation (2). E-10-2026-002535.t: Inclusion of surrogacy in the new EU strategy to combat trafficking in human beings
qt: to the Commission Paolo Inselvini (ECR), Kosma Złotowski (ECR), Sergio Berlato (ECR), Arkadiusz Mularczyk (ECR), Bert-Jan Ruissen (ECR), Mariateresa Vivaldini (ECR), Nora Junco García (ECR), Laurence Trochu (ECR), Daniele Polato (ECR), Aurelijus Veryga (ECR), Carlo Ciccioli (ECR), Claudiu-Richard Târziu (ECR), Margarita de la Pisa Carrión (PfE), Sander Smit (ECR), Nicolas Bay (ECR), Şerban Dimitrie Sturdza (ECR), Jadwiga Wiśniewska (ECR), Geadis Geadi (ECR), Stephen Nikola Bartulica (ECR), Diego Solier (ECR) Subject:

During the joint hearing of 3 June 2026 of Parliament’s Committees on Civil Liberties, Justice and Home Affairs and on Women’s Rights and Gender Equality concerning the forthcoming strategy to combat trafficking in human beings, the Commission’s EU Anti-Trafficking Coordinator, Diane Schmitt, stated that surrogacy would not be included in the strategy. This statement is surprising, given that Directive (EU) 2024/17121, which amended Directive 2011/36/EU on preventing and combating trafficking in human beings, expressly included surrogacy among the forms of exploitation that Member States must classify as trafficking in human beings. Furthermore, in its news article of 12 July 2024 on the entry into force of the new anti-trafficking rules2, the Commission itself highlighted that the exploitation of surrogacy is one of the new forms of exploitation covered by the legislative revision. Can the Commission clarify: 1.
whether it considers surrogacy to constitute a form of trafficking in human beings within the meaning of Directive (EU) 2024/1712?
whether it intends to explicitly include measures to combat surrogacy in the forthcoming EU strategy to combat trafficking in human beings?
what concrete initiatives it intends to adopt to tackle transnational criminal networks involved in cross-border surrogacy arrangements and the sale of children?

(4 August 2026) As the Commission noted in its reply to Written Question P-003805/2025, the exploitation of surrogacy, among others, is included as a form of exploitation in the Anti-Trafficking Directive, modified by Directive (EU) 2024/1712 of 13 June 2024 (1). It targets those who coerce or deceive women into acting as surrogate mothers, without prejudice to the national rules on surrogacy, including criminal and family law. Rules on surrogacy fall exclusively within the competence of the Member States. As regards cross-border operational cooperation, the European Multidisciplinary Platform Against Criminal Threats (EMPACT) has a dedicated operational action on illegal commercial surrogacy and the exploitation of illegal adoption, through which Member States exchange operational intelligence and cooperate on concrete cross-border trafficking cases.

E-10-2026-002534.t: Online gambling: protecting EU citizens, promoting the integrity of the single market and safeguarding tax fairness
qt: to the Commission Bruno Gonçalves (S&D), Laura Ballarín Cereza (S&D) Subject:

In recent years, the gambling sector has become increasingly digital. Despite the cross-border nature of such services, online gambling remains primarily regulated at national level. This fragmentation fails to address spillover effects, given that companies can establish themselves in jurisdictions with lenient regulations while providing services across the EU. The current situation creates an uneven playing field and can undermine both consumer protection and taxation laws. Furthermore, lack of regulation enables aggressive marketing of these services, posing a risk to consumers, particularly young people, while potentially leading to addiction and rapid debt accumulation. 1.

Does the Commission recognise the need for a harmonised regulatory framework for online gambling at EU level to address cross-border spillover effects and ensure a level playing field for all enterprises?
What specific issues can be addressed at EU level to strengthen consumer protection, notably by restricting aggressive advertising and preventing gambling-induced addiction and debt accumulation?
How can the taxation of cross-border digital gambling operators be improved to ensure that they pay a fair share of taxes in the Member States where their consumers are located?
at: (English version) to the Commission Bruno Gonçalves (S&D), Laura Ballarín Cereza (S&D) (18 June 2026) Subject: Online gambling: protecting EU citizens, promoting the integrity of the single market and safeguarding tax fairness In recent years, the gambling sector has become increasingly digital. Despite the cross-border nature of such services, online gambling remains primarily regulated at national level. This fragmentation fails to address spillover effects, given that companies can establish themselves in jurisdictions with lenient regulations while providing services across the EU. The current situation creates an uneven playing field and can undermine both consumer protection and taxation laws. Furthermore, lack of regulation enables aggressive marketing of these services, posing a risk to consumers, particularly young people, while potentially leading to addiction and rapid debt accumulation. 1. Does the Commission recognise the need for a harmonised regulatory framework for online gambling at EU level to address cross-border spillover effects and ensure a level playing field for all enterprises? 2. What specific issues can be addressed at EU level to strengthen consumer protection, notably by restricting aggressive advertising and preventing gambling-induced addiction and debt accumulation? 3. How can the taxation of cross-border digital gambling operators be improved to ensure that they pay a fair share of taxes in the Member States where their consumers are located? (3 September 2026) While there is no sector-specific EU legislation on gambling, Member States have established national rules, including on restricting gambling advertising and the European Court of Justice has recognised their right to restrict online gambling services where necessary (1). The Commission supports Member States in their efforts to modernise their online gambling legal frameworks and facilitate cooperation between regulators. Moreover, the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive (2) (UCPD) may be relevant in this context as it prohibits misleading or aggressive advertising affecting consumers’ transactional decisions and may consider that such advertising targets vulnerable consumers, including minors. The protection of minors is also a priority under the upcoming Digital Fairness Act (3). Users can notify gambling advertisements they believe are illegal, under applicable national laws or the UCPD using the notice and action mechanism of the Digital Services Act (DSA) (4). DSA guidelines (5) recommend preventing access to age-restricted content (including gambling) and exposure to practices encouraging addictive behaviour. The Commission continues to raise awareness of Member States to enhance administrative cooperation between tax authorities, such as exchange of tax information and use of the Central Electronic System of Payment Information (6) for Value Added Tax purposes. Finally, taxation entails different collection models across the supply chain. How these operate in the internal market is under examination, and a dedicated study is planned.

See e.g Judgment of the Court (Sixth Chamber) of 28 February 2018 in Case C-3/17, ECLI:EU:C:2018:130, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/? qid=1529074281898&uri=CELEX:62017CJ0003. http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2005/29/oj. E-10-2026-002533.t: Procedural irregularities surrounding the case of the ‘Ulm 5’ activists in Germany
qt: to the Commission Jaume Asens Llodrà (Verts/ALE), Özlem Demirel (The Left), Erik Marquardt (Verts/ALE), Hana Jalloul Muro (S&D), Ciaran Mullooly (Renew), Benedetta Scuderi (Verts/ALE), Estrella Galán (The Left), Mounir Satouri (Verts/ALE), Cecilia Strada (S&D), Catarina Martins (The Left), Ana Miranda Paz (Verts/ALE), Marc Botenga (The Left), Majdouline Sbai (Verts/ALE), Martin Sonneborn (NI), Isabel Serra Sánchez (The Left), Rudi Kennes (The Left), Sibylle Berg (NI), Emma Fourreau (The Left), Kathleen Funchion (The Left), Branislav Ondruš (NI), Danilo Della Valle (The Left) Subject:

The German state is prosecuting five European citizens before the higher regional court in Stuttgart in proceedings marked by procedural irregularities: the accused appear in court handcuffed and confined to a glass cage, despite having no criminal records or prior disciplinary incidents; the trial is being held in a special courtroom, surrounded by barbed wire; the presiding judge has repeatedly rejected defence arguments without giving reasons; and the accused have been held in pre-trial detention for months for acts limited to property damage. The European Court of Human Rights established in Svinarenko and Slyadnev v Russia1 that confinement in restraint structures during trial constitutes degrading treatment under Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR), and in Jiga v Romania2 that presenting accused persons in handcuffs without individual justification violates Article 6(2). The fact that the accused are being prosecuted for opposing an Israeli defence company’s operations in Gaza compounds these concerns and points to proceedings bearing the hallmarks of political persecution. 1.
Are the procedural conditions described compatible with Article 47 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union and Directive 2016/343/EU3?
If not, does the Commission intend to open a formal dialogue with German authorities regarding compliance with these guarantees?

Judgment of the European Court of Human Rights of 17 July 2014, Svinarenko and Slyadnev v Russia, application nos 32541/08 and 43441/08. 2 Judgment of the European Court of Human Rights of 16 March 2010, Jiga v Romania, application no 14352/04. 3 Directive (EU) 2016/343 of 9 March 2016 on the strengthening of certain aspects of the presumption of innocence and of the right to be present at the trial in criminal proceedings (ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2016/343/oj). 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (2.9.2026) The Commission places great importance on ensuring respect for the procedural rights of suspects and accused persons in criminal proceedings. Directive (EU) 2016/3431, which contributes to safeguarding the right to a fair trial and the rights of defence set out in Article 6 of the European Convention of Human Rights and in Articles 47 and 48 the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the EU, requires Member States to ensure that suspects or accused persons are not presented as being guilty, whether in court or in public, through the use of measures of physical restraint. Such measures may only be used where justified by case-specific reasons, relating to security or to the prevention of suspects or accused persons from absconding or from having contact with third persons. The Commission is closely monitoring the transposition and application of this Directive. Where specific non-conformity issues arise, the Commission will take every appropriate measure to ensure the compliance of national legislation with the Directive. Detention issues fall primarily within the responsibility of the Member States. On 8 December 2022, the Commission adopted the Recommendation on the procedural rights of suspects and accused in pre-trial detention and on material detention conditions2. By the end of 2026, the Commission will publish a report assessing the national measures taken by the Member States to implement the Recommendation.
1 Directive (EU) 2016/343 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 9 March 2016 on the strengthening

of certain aspects of the presumption of innocence and of the right to be present at the trial in criminal proceedings, OJ L 65, 11.3.2016, pp. 1–11. 2 Commission Recommendation (EU) 2023/681 of 8 December 2022 on procedural rights of suspects and accused persons subject to pre-trial detention and on material detention conditions, C/2022/8987, OJ L 86, 24.3.2023, p. 44–57.

E-10-2026-002532.t: Human trafficking and human rights violations through recruitment of non-Russian nationals, in particular from Africa, for Russia’s war of aggression in Ukraine
qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Marit Maij (S&D), Thijs Reuten (S&D), Sergey Lagodinsky (Verts/ALE), Urmas Paet (Renew), Robert Biedroń (S&D), Sander Smit (ECR), Barry Andrews (Renew), Villy Søvndal (Verts/ALE), Merja Kyllönen (The Left), Carla Tavares (S&D), Marie-Agnes Strack-Zimmermann (Renew), Raphaël Glucksmann (S&D), Veronika Cifrová Ostrihoňová (Renew), Catarina Vieira (Verts/ALE), Thomas Waitz (Verts/ALE), Nathalie Loiseau (Renew), Joanna Scheuring-Wielgus (S&D), Rihards Kols (ECR), Hannes Heide (S&D), Thomas Pellerin-Carlin (S&D), Per Clausen (The Left), Tineke Strik (Verts/ALE), Hilde Vautmans (Renew), Marc Angel (S&D), Maria Guzenina (S&D), Heléne Fritzon (S&D), Erik Marquardt (Verts/ALE), Anja Hazekamp (The Left) Subject:
Human trafficking and human rights violations through recruitment of nonRussian nationals, in particular from Africa, for Russia’s war of aggression in Ukraine

In its illegal war of aggression against Ukraine, Russia is employing deceptive tactics and coercion to recruit thousands of foreign nationals from African states. Recruited under false promises of employment, education and citizenship and then stripped of their identity documents, they are forced to serve at the frontline in Ukraine, where they are often used as mere cannon fodder. Recruited women are tricked into working in factories under dangerous and exploitative conditions. These recruitment schemes are enabled through state-linked (paramilitary) companies, intermediaries, military structures and embassy officials. Parliament has called for the EU and the Member States to support efforts to tackle human trafficking, impose targeted sanctions and facilitate release and repatriation. Recently, the United Kingdom has imposed targeted sanctions to counter these illicit recruitment schemes. 1.

What concrete measures are the Commission and the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy (VP/HR) undertaking to dismantle illicit recruitment networks, combat human trafficking and address the Russian disinformation practices that enable it?
Is the Commission or the VP/HR initiating, or considering initiating, targeted sanctions similar to those imposed by the United Kingdom?

What specific measures are the Commission or the VP/HR taking, or planning to take, to ensure the repatriation of trafficked individuals, and what financial and operational support will be made available to that end?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (6.8.2026) The EU strongly condemns Russia’s deceitful and coercive recruitment of third country citizens, including Africans, to fight in its war against Ukraine and to work in its military industry. The High Representative/Vice-President and EU representatives have raised this issue in diplomatic and political contacts with countries affected and have invited them to warn their citizens against this threat, against signing up for job or training opportunities in Russia. Furthermore, the European External Action Service has been raising awareness on this issue through public diplomacy and strategic communication campaigns, including through the network of EU Delegations, notably in Africa. The High Representative/Vice-President has also discussed with the leadership of Ukraine possible specific measures to be implemented, given the varying circumstances of the foreign national individuals in question. Any additional restrictive measures on individuals and entities are decided by the Council by unanimity.

E-10-2026-002531.t: Future of air transport in northern Germany
qt: to the Commission David McAllister (PPE) Subject:

A key sector in northern Germany, air transport ensures industrial value creation, innovation and employment and is also integral to the international competitiveness of Germany’s export-driven economy. It plays a vital role in the mobility of people and goods. At the intersection of science, industry and transport, it is also a key driver of innovation and technological progress, and is pivotal to global connectivity, local competitiveness and economic dynamism. 1.
How does the Commission plan to further deepen European cooperation in air transport, in order to boost the efficiency, competitiveness and sustainability of the European air transport system?
How does it plan to reduce the regulatory burden and foster a level playing field in the EU?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (18.8.2026) 1. The Commission plans to deepen European cooperation in air transport through the forthcoming Aviation Strategy, which is expected to be adopted before the end of 2026. It should address major challenges linked to efficiency, competitiveness and sustainability, notably by advancing the Single European Sky to reduce fragmentation and improve air navigation, promoting digital and AI technologies, strengthening supply chains, access to critical materials, research and innovation and infrastructure modernisation, and accelerating the green transition through low- and zero-emission propulsion and sustainable aviation fuels. More broadly, the Strategy should aim to reinforce the sector’s resilience, strategic autonomy and global leadership, while maintaining high safety, social and environmental standards and ensuring that European aviation remains fit for future challenges. 2. The Commission continues to advance initiatives that provide benefits to citizens and businesses, upholding the Union’s standards. These efforts include simplifying EU laws, minimising compliance burden, addressing inconsistencies and implementation challenges. As announced in the ‘A Simpler, Clearer and Better Enforced EU Rulebook’1, the Commission will notably simplify ReFuelEU Aviation2 by clarifying and streamlining obligations, improving transparency and reducing complexity, while preserving the policy’s ambition and predictability for investments into Sustainable Aviation Fuels. The revision of the Air Services Regulation3 will modernise the framework for EU air services to reinforce the internal market and make EU airlines more competitive in global aviation markets.

E-10-2026-002530.t: EU-US cooperation in the fight against hunger
qt: to the Commission Lukas Mandl (PPE) Subject:

As humanitarian crises intensify, hunger is on the rise, with serious consequences for children and adults alike, as well as for global developments migration to radicalisation. Contributions from key development cooperation partners to the UN World Food Programme have decreased in recent times. The United Nations’ contribution fell from around UD 4.44 billion in 2024 to around USD 2.06 billion in 2025. Contributions also decreased in Europe. Those of the EU decreased from around EUR 550.3 million in 2024 to around EUR 520.1 million in 2025. Member States’ contributions decreased from around EUR 1.65 billion to around EUR 1.09 billion. 1.
Since the reply to the 2025 question1, what concrete steps has the Commission taken to deepen cooperation with the United States on food security, addressing root causes of migration and support?
Does the European Union already have a coordinated strategy with the United States to combat hunger?

In light of the decline in contributions from key development cooperation partners, what steps are being taken to ensure that the World Food Programme remains operational in humanitarian crises and to strengthen Europe’s role in ensuring global food security?
https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/E-10-2025-001091_EN.html.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.8.2026) The European Commission shares the concern over the worsening global food security situation and the impact of declining funding on the most vulnerable populations. Cooperation with the US on food security has traditionally been smooth and conducted through relevant multilateral fora, including the G7, G20, the Global Network Against Food Crises or the Food Assistance Convention, which provide channels for exchanging on priorities and coordinated action. The Commission continues to welcome cooperation with the US on humanitarian action. The EU’s response is guided by humanitarian needs and adapted to each crisis context. Depending on needs, local capacities, market conditions and operational constraints, assistance may include food or cash support, nutrition interventions, and measures to protect livelihoods and strengthen resilience. Between 2022 and 2025, the Commission provided more than EUR 3.1 billion for humanitarian food and nutrition assistance. In recent years, the World Food Programme (WFP) has consistently been the largest recipient of Commission humanitarian funding, reflecting its central role in delivering life-saving assistance. Through its regular Strategic Dialogue with WFP, the Commission discusses shared priorities, operational challenges and ways to strengthen cooperation. This close engagement helps safeguard life-saving operations and promote timely, flexible and predictable funding, while supporting preparedness, anticipatory action and, where appropriate, resilience building.

qt: to the Commission Lukas Mandl (PPE) Subject:

The need for grain-oriented electrical steel (GOES) has increased significantly in recent years owing to the expansion of renewable energy sources, in particular through decentralised generation facilities such as photovoltaic plants, and the associated increasing need for transformers and grid infrastructure. The Union market is too uncompetitive and at the same time dependent on other parts of the world. 1.
Imports: What measures does the Commission plan to take to ensure the supply of highquality grain-oriented electrical sheet to EU industries from reliable markets?

Production: What initiatives is the Commission taking to strengthen the competitiveness and production capacity of the EU’s electrical sheet industry in the face of increasing demand through energy transition, grid expansion and transformer production, and to thus reduce strategic dependencies?

Future: What concrete steps does the Commission plan to take to promote research, innovation and quality improvements in the production of grain-oriented electrical sheet in the EU, so that EU producers can also meet the high technical requirements of modern, efficient transformers in the future?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (13.8.2026) A safeguard investigation on grain-oriented electrical steel (GOES) was initiated on 27 March 2026. If the investigation finds that an increase in imports has caused serious injury to the EU industry, the Commission can propose temporary protective measures that will allow the EU industry to make the necessary adjustments to remain competitive in the future. As part of its analysis, the Commission is closely assessing the needs of all stakeholders, including EU companies that imports high-grade GOES. The Commission supports research and innovation activities on high quality steel, such as GOES, through the Research Fund for Coal and Steel (RFCS)1 and the Horizon Europe framework programme for research and innovation2. The RFCS invests EUR 81 million per year to support steel research, partly through bottomup annual calls for proposals and partly through ‘Big Ticket’ calls focusing on large pilot and demonstration projects. A reform of the RFCS was adopted by the Council of the EU on 29 June 2026. The reform secures higher funding of up to EUR 87 million per year for steel research until 2034. Advanced steel grades and applications, such as GOES, remain eligible to the programme. Under Horizon Europe, research on quality steels and applications is performed under the Clean Steel Partnership (CSP)3, a co-programmed public-private partnership in Cluster 4 ‘Digital, Industry and Space’ launched in 2021 and covering the period 2021-2027. For example, in 2024 a topic implementing the CSP supported projects addressing ‘innovative steel applications for low CO2 emissions, with an overall budget of EUR 20 million.

calls/research-fund-coal-and-steel-rfcs_en. 2 https://research-and-innovation.ec.europa.eu/funding/funding-opportunities/funding-programmes-and-opencalls/horizon-europe_en. 3 https://single-market-economy.ec.europa.eu/industry/sustainability/net-zero-industry-act/net-zeronavigator/list-instruments/clean-steel-partnership-horizon-europe-partnership_en.

E-10-2026-002528.t: Rule of law in Ukraine in relation to EU investments
qt: to the Commission Lukas Mandl (PPE) Subject:

The Commission has sent monitors to observe hearings in two ongoing civil suits1 that have brought the Ukrainian subsidiary of the insurance group UNIQA before the Ukrainian courts2. Proceedings have been adjourned several times and an appeal judgment3 in UNIQA’s favour has been overturned by the Supreme Court. Two Ukrainian state banks stand to benefit handsomely from the disputed insurance payment/payout. 1.
What has the Commission learned from its monitoring of the hearings in Case No 910/10742/23, and what are its thoughts on proceedings so far with regard to/in light of rule-of-law standards?
How is it factoring cases with alleged procedural delays or other irregularities into its overall assessment of Ukraine’s progress in the rule of law?
What instruments and measures does it envisage to bolster legal certainty for EU businesses that are active or investing in Ukraine?

https://court.opendatabot.ua/companies/37390074?judgment_code=3. https://court.opendatabot.ua/companies/39374562?judgment_code=3. https://opendatabot.ua/court/135000484-91be8a60c74cd7cc48fc74d2aac11435.
at: (English version) to the Commission Lukas Mandl (PPE) (18 June 2026) Subject: Rule of law in Ukraine in relation to EU investments The Commission has sent monitors to observe hearings in two ongoing civil suits (1) that have brought the Ukrainian subsidiary of the insurance group UNIQA before the Ukrainian courts (2). Proceedings have been adjourned several times and an appeal judgment (3) in UNIQA’s favour has been overturned by the Supreme Court. Two Ukrainian state banks stand to benefit handsomely from the disputed insurance payment/payout. 1. What has the Commission learned from its monitoring of the hearings in Case No 910/10742/23, and what are its thoughts on proceedings so far with regard to/in light of rule-of-law standards? 2. How is it factoring cases with alleged procedural delays or other irregularities into its overall assessment of Ukraine’s progress in the rule of law? 3. What instruments and measures does it envisage to bolster legal certainty for EU businesses that are active or investing in Ukraine? (10 August 2026) The Commission assesses Ukraine’s progress on the rule of law on the basis of a broad range of sources and indicators. These include developments concerning judicial independence, efficiency, accountability and anti-corruption, as well as the practical implementation of reforms. Information on procedural delays or irregularities in individual cases may be relevant where they point to wider structural shortcomings. The Commission takes systemic issues into account in its overall monitoring and in its assessment of Ukraine’s accessionrelated reform track. However, the Commission cannot comment on individual cases and court proceedings. The Commission follows closely the functioning of judicial and anti-corruption institutions, the transparency and predictability of judicial procedures, and the capacity of the authorities. This all to ensure effective remedies and legal certainty. These elements are reflected in the Commission’s regular reporting. The Commission also supports the strengthening of legal certainty for EU businesses active or investing in Ukraine. In particular, support under the Ukraine Facility is subject to the precondition that Ukraine continues to uphold and respect effective democratic mechanisms, the rule of law and human rights (1). The Commission monitors the fulfilment of that precondition before any disbursement is made. The Ukraine Facility also links financial support to the implementation of agreed reform steps, including in the areas of rule of law and the business environment. The Commission further supports measures aimed at improving the investment climate, promoting transparent and predictable regulation, and reinforcing safeguards for property rights, contract enforcement and dispute resolution. Through this combination of policy dialogue, conditional financial support, technical assistance programmes and systematic monitoring, the Commission continues to encourage reforms. These are essential both for Ukraine’s accession path and for a more stable and predictable framework for economic operators, including EU businesses.

E-10-2026-002527.t: Anti-dumping complaint against Chinese imports of 6-aminopenicillanic acid, a key ingredient for producing amoxicillin
qt: to the Commission Majdouline Sbai (Verts/ALE), Marie Toussaint (Verts/ALE), Mélissa Camara (Verts/ALE), David Cormand (Verts/ALE), Mounir Satouri (Verts/ALE), Tilly Metz (Verts/ALE) Subject:

On 28 May 2026, the pharmaceuticals company Sandoz lodged an anti-dumping complaint concerning Chinese imports of 6-aminopenicillanic acid, a key ingredient in the production of amoxicillin, the world’s most widely used antibiotic1. Commissioner Ribera has stated that: ‘The Critical Medicines Act is about improving a secure supply of vital medicines in Europe.’2 With the trilogue agreement expected to be adopted shortly, we call on the Commission to act without delay to protect our amoxicillin producers from Chinese competition. The Commission’s respect for confidentiality obligations from the moment the complaint is received, even before any investigation may be opened is laudable. 1.

E-10-2026-002525.t: Systemic risks arising from developments in the EU ETS market and the financial exposure of companies subject to compliance obligations
qt: to the Commission Paolo Inselvini (ECR), Stefano Cavedagna (ECR), Carlo Fidanza (ECR) Subject:

The European Union Emissions Trading Scheme (EU ETS) is a synthetic EU policy instrument. In recent years, EU emission allowances have fluctuated widely in value, while the expansion of the scheme and the gradual reduction in the number of available allowances have pushed up the financing needs of companies subject to compliance obligations. Many industrial operators rely on bank financing, derivatives and other transactions to purchase ETS allowances. Against a backdrop of high energy costs, tighter credit conditions and possible future interest rate rises, further increases in the price of allowances could lead to liquidity problems and exert financial strain on the most vulnerable sectors. The growing participation of financial operators in the carbon market raises questions about the risk of speculation and misalignments between the value of allowances and economic fundamentals. In the light of the above: 1.
Does the Commission have an updated contingency plan to address risks arising from potential price shocks in the carbon market and, if so, what does it entail?
Does the Commission believe that the current structure of the EU ETS market contains elements liable to give rise to speculative behaviour or financial bubbles?
Does it have any instruments to mitigate the systemic risks arising from high financial leverage in the EU ETS market?

(2 October 2026) The EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) is a market-based climate policy instrument that helps reduce emissions in a costeffective manner. Most ETS compliance entities indeed buy or sell their allowances through financial intermediaries, which play a key role in the carbon market by providing carbon financing and risk management options, while contributing to liquidity in the market so that prices are more predictable. The ETS is equipped with important safeguards to address the risks of potential price shocks in the carbon market, such as the measure in case of excessive price fluctuations and the Market Stability Reserve (MSR) in case of scarcity, both of which contain rule-based triggers to inject extra allowances in the market. The Commission has proposed this year a revision of the MSR (1), which includes a wider assessment of market stability going forward. The EU carbon market is governed by the same, robust EU financial legislation and oversight (2) that applies to other financial markets such as shares and bonds. Moreover, under its mandate in the ETS Directive the European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA) regularly monitors and reports annually on the EU carbon market. The latest ESMA report confirms that the EU carbon market is healthy and functions normally, in line with market fundamentals, and that financial firms play a central role (3). Therefore, the Commission has not proposed additional measures regarding participation of financial actors in the market.

E-10-2026-002524.t: Shortcomings in the functioning of the CATCH system
qt: to the Commission Francisco José Millán Mon (PPE) Subject:

The CATCH system aims to be a key tool to strengthen the traceability of fishery products and prevent catches from illegal fishing from entering the EU market. However, almost six months after its implementation, there are still technical issues, delays in the processing of certificates and operational difficulties that are seriously impacting European operators and ports. These shortcomings are causing significant disruption in key European ports, such as the Port of Vigo, the EU’s main fishing port. The industry reports delays in processing imports, logistical backlogs and additional costs (up to EUR 3 000/container) that harm its competitiveness in relation to non-EU operators12. Reports also indicate that the system is not being evenly implemented across Member States, which would compromise the level playing field on the internal market. 1.

E-10-2026-002523.t: Recent study shows wind turbine infrasound can be harmful to health
qt: to the Commission Gerald Hauser (PfE) Subject:

Infrasound is sound with a frequency below the lower limit of human hearing. Widely occurring in nature (for example, in earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, etc.), it is also artificially generated by wind turbines. Since infrasound propagates over vast distances with virtually no losses, it can affect the whole body, disrupting cellular processes in humans and animals. As a result, it can also be used as a weapon.1 A recent study from the infrasound working group at the Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz found that areas where wind energy has expanded massively are experiencing a markedly higher rate of newly diagnosed cardiovascular disease (heart arrhythmias, cardiac insufficiency).2Infrasound can cause balance disturbances, dizziness, nausea, sleep disorders, changes to blood flow, an increase in blood pressure, and damage to lungs and internal organs. There can also be adverse psychological effects, particularly reduced concentration.3 In the meantime, three judgments have been handed down by courts in Belgium and France4, awarding local residents compensation for wind-turbine-induced health problems.5 1.

What is its view of the court judgments from Belgium and France acknowledging health problems caused by wind turbines?

E-10-2026-002519.t: Charging stations for e-vehicles – uniform and transparent price display standards
qt: to the Commission Aldo Patriciello (PfE) Subject:

The rise in the number of charging stations for electric vehicles available for use in the EU has not been accompanied by uniform and transparent price display standards. Unlike users of traditional fuels, for which prices must be clearly displayed on fuel price boards visible from a distance, e-vehicle users have no physical signage to go on, and rates are often only accessible via digital applications or QR codes. This lack of information and rate fragmentation creates uncertainty among consumers, leading to a significant imbalance that hampers the development of sustainable mobility and restricts free competition in the internal market. The absence of a requirement for prices to be displayed physically, as they are for traditional petrol pumps, raises serious transparency problems. In the light of the above: 1.
Will the Commission push for the introduction of a standardised obligation for operators to display prices, as is the case for fossil fuels?
Does it believe that the current fragmentation violates consumers’ rights to transparency?

What steps does it plan to take within the framework of the Alternative Fuels Infrastructure Regulation to ensure that clearly comparable prices are available to customers before they use the charging stations?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (6.8.2026) Regulation (EU) 2023/1804 on the deployment of alternative fuels infrastructure1 sets clear rules on how operators of recharging points and mobility service providers must make price information available to consumers. Article 5(4) of the Regulation requires that the operator of a publicly accessible recharging point with a power output at or above 50kW must show full price information on the ad hoc price and any possible occupancy fee at the recharging point. However, for recharging points below 50kW, this information must be made available, for example on an app, but its display at the recharging point is not required. The Commission is currently reviewing Regulation (EU) 2023/1804 in accordance with Article 24 of the Regulation. This review addresses, among others, user aspects, including on price transparency issues. The Commission plans to adopt a legislative proposal for the amendment of the Regulation by the end of 2026.

E-10-2026-002518.t: Dynamic pricing for major sporting and cultural events
qt: to the Commission Adnan Dibrani (S&D), Laura Ballarín Cereza (S&D), Andreas Schieder (S&D), Yvan Verougstraete (Renew), Erik Marquardt (Verts/ALE), Rasmus Andresen (Verts/ALE), Bruno Gonçalves (S&D), Heléne Fritzon (S&D), Johan Danielsson (S&D), Evin Incir (S&D), Sofie Eriksson (S&D), Nikola Minchev (Renew), Christel Schaldemose (S&D), Hannes Heide (S&D), René Repasi (S&D), Matjaž Nemec (S&D), Emma Rafowicz (S&D), Marc Angel (S&D), Pierfrancesco Maran (S&D), Diana Riba i Giner (Verts/ALE), Elisabeth Grossmann (S&D), Tonino Picula (S&D), Biljana Borzan (S&D), Elena Sancho Murillo (S&D), Lara Wolters (S&D), Maria Grapini (S&D), Daniel Attard (S&D), Hanna Gedin (The Left), Sakis Arnaoutoglou (S&D), Katarina Barley (S&D), Sérgio Gonçalves (S&D), Anna Cavazzini (Verts/ALE), Gordan Bosanac (Verts/ALE), Niels Fuglsang (S&D), Carolina Morace (The Left), Lídia Pereira (PPE) Subject:

Ticket sales for the 2026 FIFA World Cup have renewed concerns about dynamic pricing, with some tickets reaching prices of USD 30 000. Media sources have described it as the most expensive World Cup in football history. Dynamic pricing relies on algorithms that adjust prices in real time based on demand. Such practices risk undermining transparency, consumer trust and fair access to major sporting and cultural events. When prices are changed continuously by algorithms that consumers cannot scrutinise, markets risk becoming opaque and unfair. In the light of the upcoming 2030 FIFA World Cup in Spain, Portugal and Morocco and the growing use of dynamic pricing across the live events sector: 1.

Does the Commission consider the current EU framework to be sufficient to protect consumers from excessive and unpredictable price increases caused by dynamic pricing, or will it propose additional transparency requirements and consumer safeguards?

Will the Commission investigate whether the use of dynamic pricing by dominant ticketing platforms could distort competition or constitute an abuse of a dominant position under Article 102 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union?

Ahead of the 2030 World Cup, will the Commission take action on dynamic pricing for major sporting and cultural events, including by considering restricting or, where necessary, prohibiting such practices?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (15.9.2026) EU consumer protection rules do not prevent price changes by market operators, including in the event ticketing sector and when implemented via dynamic pricing. Consumers are protected by the transparency requirements of the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive1 (UCPD) and the Consumer Rights Directive2 (CRD). Furthermore, the UCPD prohibits misleading practices. EU consumer law directives are transposed into national law. Member States’ authorities and courts are responsible for enforcement in individual cases, including as in the context of major sporting and cultural events. The Commission may propose in the upcoming Digital Fairness Act3 additional rules regarding price marketing. Dynamic pricing by dominant undertakings can fall within the scope of Article 102 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union if it amounts to the imposition of excessive prices. However, whether pricing is excessive depends on the relationship between a dominant undertaking’s costs and profits rather than on pricing mechanisms. The Commission has in the past investigated excessive pricing by dominant undertakings including in the pharmaceutical and energy sectors4. The Commission remains vigilant as regards possible excessive pricing abuses and stands ready to intervene in appropriate cases also in light of its priorities5. Through policies and programmes including Erasmus+, the Commission promotes a European Sport Model grounded in values such as fairness and solidarity. The upcoming Commission Communication on ‘A Strategic Vision for Sport in Europe: Reinforcing the European Sport Model’ aims to strengthen good governance principles, notably stakeholder representation including fans6.

1 Directive 2005/29/EC, http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2005/29/oj. 2 Directive 2011/83/EU, http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2011/83/oj. 3 Subject to the impact assessment, the Commission plans to propose the Digital Fairness Act in the fourth

quarter of 2026, for more information: https://ec.europa.eu/info/law/better-regulation/have-yoursay/initiatives/14622-Digital-Fairness-Act_en. 4 Case AT.40394 - Aspen; and case AT. 39816 - Upstream gas supplies in Central and Eastern Europe. In both cases, the Commission accepted commitments by the dominant undertaking that allowed bringing prices to lower, competitive levels. 5 For completeness, the Commission has received a complaint by Euroconsumers and Football Supporters Europe, which alleges that the Fédération Internationale de Football Association (FIFA) abused its dominant position by imposing excessive ticket prices as well as opaque and unfair purchasing conditions on European fans ahead of the 2026 World Cup. The Commission is examining the complaint in line with the applicable rules and cannot comment on ongoing cases. 6 For more information: https://ec.europa.eu/info/law/better-regulation/have-your-say/initiatives/14741-Astrategic-vision-for-sport-in-Europe-reinforcing-the-European-Sport-Model/public-consultation_en.

E-10-2026-002517.t: Public statements on the management of migrant arrivals and Member States' compliance with EU law
qt: to the Commission Nikos Pappas (The Left) Subject:

Recent public statements by senior government officials in Greece regarding the treatment of boats carrying migrants have raised concerns about their compatibility with obligations to protect human life at sea and those seeking international protection.1 The EU is founded on respect for human dignity and human rights (Article 2 TEU). Articles 1, 2, 18 and 19 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights guarantee human dignity, the right to life, the right to asylum and the prohibition of refoulement. Furthermore, Article 78 TFEU, the new Pact on Migration and Asylum (Regulations (EU) 2024/1348, 2024/1356 and 2024/1358), the 1951 Geneva Convention, Article 98 of UNCLOS, as well as the SOLAS and SAR Conventions require the protection of human life and respect for international search and rescue obligations at sea. Accordingly: 1.
How does the Commission assess public statements by state officials that may be perceived as incompatible with the above obligations and with the principle of nonrefoulement?

What measures can the Commission take to ensure that public statements do not encourage practices that may endanger human life at sea or undermine the implementation of European immigration and refugee law?
https://www.ethnos.gr/Politics/article/410929/thathboyliaxoymethbarkasalosapotisdhloseistoyboridhgiat oysmetanastes.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (14.9.2026) The Commission does not comment on individual public statements. Member States are required to implement EU asylum and migration legislation in full compliance with EU law, including the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, the principle of nonrefoulement as enshrined in Article 19 of the Charter, and the applicable obligations under international law. The Commission contributes to the consistent implementation of the EU legal framework through dialogue with Member States, cooperation with the relevant EU agencies and, where appropriate, the provision of guidance. In Greece, such dialogue is continuous at technical and political level. When it comes to cooperation with EU agencies, the European Union Agency for Asylum (EUAA) and the European Border and Coast Guard Agency (Frontex) have significant presence in Greece and are providing assistance and guidance on the implementation of the relevant legal framework. Where there are indications that practices implemented by a Member State deviate from the applicable framework, the Commission assesses all relevant information and, where appropriate, makes use of the instruments available under the Treaties to ensure compliance with EU law.

E-10-2026-002516.t: Recognition of obesity as a chronic disease under EU public health policy
qt: to the Commission Magdalena Adamowicz (PPE), Adam Jarubas (PPE), Elżbieta Katarzyna Łukacijewska (PPE), Kamila Gasiuk-Pihowicz (PPE), Jagna Marczułajtis-Walczak (PPE), Borys Budka (PPE), Bogdan Andrzej Zdrojewski (PPE), Dariusz Joński (PPE), Michał Wawrykiewicz (PPE), Ewa Kopacz (PPE), Krzysztof Śmiszek (S&D), Robert Biedroń (S&D), Joanna Scheuring-Wielgus (S&D), Emil Radev (PPE), Isilda Gomes (S&D), Manuela Ripa (PPE), Andrzej Buła (PPE), Marta Wcisło (PPE) Subject:

At the international level, the World Health Organization (WHO), followed by the American Medical Association in 2013, have already recognised obesity as a chronic disease. According to Eurostat, over half of adults in the EU (50.6 %) are overweight, with 17 % suffering from obesity. According to the 2022 WHO European Regional Obesity Report, obesity has been linked to at least 13 types of cancer, diabetes, cardiovascular and musculoskeletal disease, as well as mental health disorders. The Blueprint for Action to Address Obesity estimates the annual cost of obesity at approximately EUR 70 billion. Despite the European Association for the Study of Obesity (EASO) advocating for the recognition of obesity at the EU level and Parliament calling on the Commission to align with the 11th Revision of the International Classification of Diseases (ICD-11) in its resolution of December 20231, the recognition, diagnosis, and treatment of obesity remain fragmented across the EU. 1.
Does the Commission intend to recognise obesity as a chronic disease under European public health policy, and through which policy instruments and, if so, on what timeframe?
How does the Commission intend to support Member States in improving the recognition, research, and treatment of obesity?
Does the Commission intend to address the discrimination against persons suffering from obesity, particularly children affected by bullying, both offline and online?
Resolution of 13 December 2023 on non-communicable diseases (NCDs) (ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/C/2024/4171/oj). 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (24.8.2026) Under Article 168(7) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU1, Member States are responsible for organising and delivering their health services. The Commission supports Member States in addressing non-communicable diseases (NCDs) and their risk factors, including obesity, through the ‘Healthier Together’ EU NCD initiative2. The EU4Health Programme3 funds actions that address obesity, such as the joint actions PreventNCD4 and Health4EUkids5, and stakeholder-led projects such as PODiaCar6. The Safe Hearts Plan7 builds on these actions under its prevention pillar. The Health Promotion and Disease Prevention Knowledge Gateway8 provides information on primary prevention programmes and policy recommendations related to obesity prevention. Through the Horizon Europe programme9 over EUR 2.7 billion have been invested in research and innovation related to obesity, diabetes and nutrition. The EU Funding and Tenders Portal10 includes information about open and upcoming funding opportunities for related research. In February 2026, the Commission adopted the Action Plan against cyberbullying11. It sets out complementary measures to address abusive behaviour online through protection, prevention, support for victims and improved reporting mechanisms, including appearance-related cyberbullying affecting children and young people. In line with the Commission Recommendation on integrated child protection systems12, it calls for national comprehensive anti-bullying plans. The World Health Organization is responsible for the International Classification of Diseases13 (ICD-11). The Commission has no role in this process.
