E-10-2026-002515.t: Systematic sexualised torture against Palestinian detainees
qt: to the Commission Rima Hassan (The Left), Mounir Satouri (Verts/ALE), Anthony Smith (The Left), David Cormand (Verts/ALE), Estrella Galán (The Left), Annalisa Corrado (S&D), Mélissa Camara (Verts/ALE), Jaume Asens Llodrà (Verts/ALE), Özlem Demirel (The Left), Manon Aubry (The Left), Catarina Vieira (Verts/ALE), Leila Chaibi (The Left), Maria Ohisalo (Verts/ALE), Hanna Gedin (The Left), Jonas Sjöstedt (The Left), Danilo Della Valle (The Left), Cecilia Strada (S&D), Arash Saeidi (The Left), Nikos Pappas (The Left), Daniel Attard (S&D), Benedetta Scuderi (Verts/ALE), Sara Matthieu (Verts/ALE), Emma Fourreau (The Left), Pernando Barrena Arza (The Left) Subject:

A recent article in The New York Times1 compiles heart-rending interviews with Palestinians recounting a pattern of widespread sexual violence by Israeli settlers, soldiers, prison guards and Shin Bet interrogators against men, women and children. Testimonies describe rape, rape with objects, gang rape, beatings of genitals, sexual abuse involving dogs, and the taking of photographs during assaults to coerce cooperation, followed by threats after release. These allegations reflect a systemic pattern of violence and dehumanisation, rather than isolated acts. They corroborate findings documented by organisations such as Euro-Med Human Rights Monitor2 and B’Tselem3, and a United Nations4 report concluding that Palestinians are ‘systematically’ subjected to sexualised torture with at least implicit encouragement from senior civilian and military leaders. Israel has rejected calls to investigate abuses against Palestinians. Since October 2023, Israel has detained over 20 000 Palestinians in the West Bank, largely without charging them, and has denied these detainees access to basic rights. 1.
Does the Commission condemn these practices?
Will these practices be considered a further breach of Article 2 of the EU-Israel Association Agreement5, justifying its suspension?
What could the Commission do to help ensure that the International Committee of the Red Cross has full and immediate access to all detention facilities holding Palestinian detainees?

at: (English version) to the Commission Rima Hassan (The Left), Mounir Satouri (Verts/ALE), Anthony Smith (The Left), David Cormand (Verts/ALE), Estrella Galán (The Left), Annalisa Corrado (S&D), Mélissa Camara (Verts/ALE), Jaume Asens Llodrà (Verts/ALE), Özlem Demirel (The Left), Manon Aubry (The Left), Catarina Vieira (Verts/ALE), Leila Chaibi (The Left), Maria Ohisalo (Verts/ALE), Hanna Gedin (The Left), Jonas Sjöstedt (The Left), Danilo Della Valle (The Left), Cecilia Strada (S&D), Arash Saeidi (The Left), Nikos Pappas (The Left), Daniel Attard (S&D), Benedetta Scuderi (Verts/ALE), Sara Matthieu (Verts/ALE), Emma Fourreau (The Left), Pernando Barrena Arza (The Left) (17 June 2026) Subject: Systematic sexualised torture against Palestinian detainees A recent article in The New York Times (1) compiles heart-rending interviews with Palestinians recounting a pattern of widespread sexual violence by Israeli settlers, soldiers, prison guards and Shin Bet interrogators against men, women and children. Israel has rejected calls to investigate abuses against Palestinians. Since October 2023, Israel has detained over 20 000 Palestinians in the West Bank, largely without charging them, and has denied these detainees access to basic rights. 1.
Does the Commission condemn these practices?

2. Will these practices be considered a further breach of Article 2 of the EU-Israel Association Agreement (5), justifying its suspension? 3. (12 August 2026) The EU is concerned by reports of sexual violence and other forms of ill-treatment against Palestinian detainees. All prisoners and detained persons must be treated with dignity, in line with international humanitarian law and international human rights law. The EU has reiterated consistently that there must be accountability for violations of international law (1). The EU continues to support independent investigations into all alleged violations and abuses of international humanitarian law, with a view to ending impunity for crimes committed by all parties to the conflict. E-10-2026-002513.t: Coordinated consultation campaigns and the integrity of stakeholder input in the revision of the Tobacco Products Directive
qt: to the Commission Tilly Metz (Verts/ALE), Nicolás González Casares (S&D) Subject:

The Commission’s public consultation on the revision of the Tobacco Products Directive (2014/40/EU) is a key element of the evidence-gathering process supporting future EU tobacco control policy and the objectives of Europe’s Beating Cancer Plan. The ‘Fix the Flaws’ platform1 has deployed a digital tool designed to systematically generate automated, pre-formulated responses to this public consultation. Such campaigns raise broader questions about the distinction between genuine individual participation and coordinated mobilisation efforts designed to amplify specific policy positions. Given the EU’s obligations under Article 5.3 of the World Health Organization (WHO) Framework Convention on Tobacco Control (FCTC), which requires public health policies to be protected from the commercial and other vested interests of the tobacco industry: 1.
How does the Commission assess and account for coordinated or pre-formulated consultation submissions when analysing the results of public consultations?
What safeguards are in place to ensure that organised campaigns do not distort the perceived balance of stakeholder views or undermine the quality of evidence used in impact assessments?

How is the Commission ensuring that its preparations for the future revision of the Tobacco Products Directive remain consistent with the transparency and public health objectives underpinning Article 5.3 WHO FCTC?

E-10-2026-002511.t: Compatibility of Spanish banking practices with EU law on freedom of movement, non-discrimination and consumer protection
qt: to the Commission Tineke Strik (Verts/ALE) Subject:

In accordance with the Bank of Spain’s Compendium of best banking practice criteria, when assessing solvency, banks are entitled to use a stricter approach to mortgage credit in relation to nationals of other EU Member States resident abroad and Spanish nationals resident abroad. This stricter approach may conflict with EU law on the free movement of EU citizens, non-discrimination and consumer protection. 1.

Is it compatible with EU law for a bank to impose more stringent requirements on nationals residing in another Member State, and is the criterion of residence in the territory of a Member State, leading to less favourable conditions in solvency assessments and mortgage offers, compatible with Directive 2004/381 and Articles 21, 26, and 45 of the Charter?

Do banks have an obligation to prevent mortgage offers to nationals residing in another Member State from including conditions that do not respect the proportionality principle set out in Directives 2023/22252 and 2014/173?

What safeguards should banks apply to prevent conditions in the creditworthiness assessment and mortgage offers from causing indirect harm to or penalties for Spanish nationals simply for having exercised their rights of free movement, and to prevent unequal treatment or discrimination in this regard?

Directive 2004/38/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 29 April 2004 on the right of citizens of the Union and their family members to move and reside freely within the territory of the Member States (ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2004/38/oj). 2 Directive (EU) 2023/2225 of 18 October 2023 on credit agreements for consumers (ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2023/2225/oj). 3 Directive 2014/17/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 4 February 2014 on credit agreements for consumers relating to residential immovable property (ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2014/17/oj). 1
at: (English version) to the Commission Tineke Strik (Verts/ALE) (17 June 2026) Subject: Compatibility of Spanish banking practices with EU law on freedom of movement, non-discrimination and consumer protection In accordance with the Bank of Spain’s Compendium of best banking practice criteria, when assessing solvency, banks are entitled to use a stricter approach to mortgage credit in relation to nationals of other EU Member States resident abroad and Spanish nationals resident abroad. This stricter approach may conflict with EU law on the free movement of EU citizens, nondiscrimination and consumer protection. 1. Is it compatible with EU law for a bank to impose more stringent requirements on nationals residing in another Member State, and is the criterion of residence in the territory of a Member State, leading to less favourable conditions in solvency assessments and mortgage offers, compatible with Directive 2004/38 (1) and Articles 21, 26, and 45 of the Charter? 2. Do banks have an obligation to prevent mortgage offers to nationals residing in another Member State from including conditions that do not respect the proportionality principle set out in Directives 2023/2225 (2) and 2014/17 (3)? 3. What safeguards should banks apply to prevent conditions in the creditworthiness assessment and mortgage offers from causing indirect harm to or penalties for Spanish nationals simply for having exercised their rights of free movement, and to prevent unequal treatment or discrimination in this regard? (13 August 2026) In order to prevent irresponsible lending practices and over-indebtedness and safeguard financial stability, both Directive 2014/17/EU (1) and Directive (EU) 2023/2225 (2) require creditors to carry out a thorough creditworthiness assessment before providing a credit. The creditworthiness assessment needs to be carried out on the basis of information on the consumer’s income and expenses and other financial and economic circumstances, ensuring that such information is necessary, sufficient and proportionate. In the case of mortgages, the residence of the consumer can only be relevant as far as it has an impact on the prospect of the consumer to meet the debt obligation resulting from the credit agreement. Even if the creditworthiness assessment for a mortgage credit is positive, banks are in principle free to decide whether they provide a mortgage and, if so, under which conditions. The Commission would however like to recall that the fundamental freedoms of the Treaty, including the free movement of capital, services and persons, bind the authorities of the Member States and generally prohibit discriminations and restrictions, whatever their form, unless they are objectively justified and proportionate to an overriding reason of public interest.

E-10-2026-002510.t: Protection of young people and educational freedom of families at Pride events involving children
qt: to the Commission Anna Maria Cisint (PfE) Subject:

Article 6 of the Treaty on European Union states that the rights guaranteed by the European Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (ECHR) constitute general principles of the Union’s law. Under Article 24 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, in all actions relating to children, the child’s best interests must be a primary consideration. Article 2 of Protocol No 1 to the ECHR protects the right of parents to ensure the education and teaching of their children in accordance with their own religious and philosophical beliefs, while the protection and welfare of children are the primary objectives of the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child. In view of the above: 1.

Does the Commission consider that the organised involvement of children and young people in public events of a political, ideological or identity-based nature – as recently see in Budrio – are compatible with these principles1?
Does it plan to adopt guidelines to ensure full respect for the best interests of the child, the educational freedom of families and the fundamental principles of European law?
https://lanuovabq.it/it/pdf/gender-per-grandi-e-piccini-il-baby-pride-fa-tappa-a-budrio.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (14.8.2026) Under the Treaties, child protection, education, parental rights, and the regulation of public events fall primarily within Member States’ competences. Against this background, the EU Strategy on the Rights of the Child1, the LGBTIQ2+ Equality Strategy3 and the Commission Recommendation on integrated child protection systems4 promote a rights-based and participatory approach. They also provide a policy framework to support Member States in adopting appropriate measures to ensure that children are treated at all times in a manner that protects their dignity, while duly taking into account their personality, best interests, and special needs, and involving all actors, including families as primary carers.

E-10-2026-002509.t: Scientific basis for the Commission’s policy references to ‘transgender youth’ following its evasive reply to E-000395/2026
qt: to the Commission Christine Anderson (ESN), Sebastian Kruis (PfE), Marieke Ehlers (PfE) Subject:

Question E-000395/20261 asked whether the Commission accepts the findings of recent independent evidence reviews concerning medical transition in minors, including the Cass Review in the United Kingdom. The Commission’s reply, submitted more than four months after the question was tabled and well after the normal deadline for written questions, did not address this issue. Instead, it referred to Member State competences in healthcare and to the principles of equality and nondiscrimination. However, the question did not concern the division of competences between the EU and the Member States. It concerned the scientific evidence on which the Commission relies when developing and implementing EU policies referring to ‘transgender youth’. 1.
Does the Commission accept, reject or partially accept the conclusions of the Cass Review regarding the evidential bases for puberty blockers and cross-sex hormones in minors?
If the Commission does not accept those conclusions, which specific systematic reviews, evidence assessments or clinical guidelines does it consider more authoritative?

Given the considerable delay in replying to E-000395/2026, can the Commission explain why it was unable to provide a direct answer to the scientific question originally asked, and when it intends to do so?
https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/E-10-2026-000395_EN.html.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.8.2026) As mentioned in the Commission’s reply to written question E-000395/2026, healthcare policy, including the development of clinical guidelines and the assessment of evidence supporting treatments, remains the responsibility of Member States and their competent scientific and health authorities. Where relevant to EU action, the Commission relies on expertise from relevant EU agencies and scientific bodies acting within their respective mandates. The Commission’s reply to written question E-000395/2026 addressed the aspects falling within the Commission's responsibilities under the Treaties. The scientific assessment of clinical interventions on minors falls outside the Commission's competence. The Commission has, accordingly, no position on related scientific reviews.

E-10-2026-002508.t: Establishment of a mechanism to restrict or tax copper waste and scrap exports to third countries
qt: to the Commission Thomas Pellerin-Carlin (S&D) Subject:

The energy and digital transition is ramping up Europe’s copper requirements, as it is vital for electricity grids, renewable energy, electric vehicles and digital infrastructure. However, the EU is still exporting large volumes of copper waste and scrap to third countries, despite it being a resource that is essential for Europe’s industrial autonomy. In France, the fibre roll-out will, by 2030, lead to the gradual dismantling of the old ADSL network, estimated at almost 1 million kilometres of cables. The recycling of those cables should benefit European industry first and foremost. The Commission is aware of the risks of this metal scrap leakage from the EU and, on 23 July 2025, it activated a surveillance system to monitor imports and exports of metal waste, including copper, to assess their impact on supplies for EU industries. In view of the above: 1.

Is the Commission planning to propose a mechanism to restrict or tax copper waste and scrap exports to third countries in order to ensure that EU industries have an adequate supply of copper for recycling?
Can it provide a timetable for any binding legislative initiatives or additional measures being considered in the wake of this surveillance?
at: (English version) to the Commission Thomas Pellerin-Carlin (S&D) (17 June 2026) Subject: Establishment of a mechanism to restrict or tax copper waste and scrap exports to third countries The energy and digital transition is ramping up Europe’s copper requirements, as it is vital for electricity grids, renewable energy, electric vehicles and digital infrastructure. However, the EU is still exporting large volumes of copper waste and scrap to third countries, despite it being a resource that is essential for Europe’s industrial autonomy. In France, the fibre roll-out will, by 2030, lead to the gradual dismantling of the old ADSL network, estimated at almost 1 million kilometres of cables. The recycling of those cables should benefit European industry first and foremost. The Commission is aware of the risks of this metal scrap leakage from the EU and, on 23 July 2025, it activated a surveillance system to monitor imports and exports of metal waste, including copper, to assess their impact on supplies for EU industries. In view of the above: 1.

Is the Commission planning to propose a mechanism to restrict or tax copper waste and scrap exports to third countries in order to ensure that EU industries have an adequate supply of copper for recycling?
Can it provide a timetable for any binding legislative initiatives or additional measures being considered in the wake of this surveillance?

(29 July 2026) In the European Steel and Metals Action Plan (1), the Commission recognises the necessity to ensure sufficient availability of scrap for EU producers and outlines actions across different policy areas, including trade. In this context, in July 2025, the Commission has introduced surveillance of imports and exports of steel, aluminium, and copper scrap. In December 2025, this has been further strengthened in the RESourceEU Action Plan (2), with a commitment to propose targeted measures on aluminium scrap, and similar measures for copper if this proves necessary. The copper waste and scrap exports for the period January to May 2026 have registered a small increase of 10.8% in volume terms versus those of the same period last year. Such an increase has not so far warranted a trade measure or any other legislative initiative for copper waste and scrap. The Commission continues to monitor the situation and stands ready to act if necessary.

E-10-2026-002507.t: Geographical balance in recent EEAS appointments and the absence of Polish nationals among newly appointed senior officials
qt: to the Commission Adam Bielan (ECR) Subject:

The recent appointments of EU Heads of Delegation and senior European External Action Service (EEAS) officials, announced by the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy (VP/HR), Kaja Kallas, did not include any Polish nationals, despite Poland being one of the EU’s largest Member States, but did include a Maltese national. Given that the VP/HR acts in her capacity as a Member of the Commission, and in the light of the principle of geographical balance laid down in Article 27 of the Staff Regulations of Officials of the European Union: 1.

Does the Commission consider the current level of representation of Polish nationals in senior management and ambassadorial positions within the EEAS to be consistent with Article 27 of the Staff Regulations, which provides for recruitment on the broadest possible geographical basis, and with the requirement under Council Decision 2010/427/EU1 for ‘a meaningful presence of nationals from all the Member States’?

How does the Commission, within its collective responsibility for EU external action, justify the persistent under-representation of Polish nationals among Heads of Delegation, Deputy Heads of Delegation, and EEAS Directors-General, and what institutional steps will it take to ensure that geographical balance is respected?

Was an assessment of the impact of the recent appointments on geographical balance within the EEAS conducted prior to the nominations? If so, what were its conclusions regarding the representation of Polish nationals?
Council Decision of 26 July 2010 establishing the organisation and functioning of the European External Action Service (OJ L 201, 3.8.2010, p. 30, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dec/2010/427/oj). 1

E-10-2026-002506.t: Lviv authorities’ failure to comply with arbitration decisions in favour of Polish company Control Process S.A.
qt: to the Commission Adam Bielan (ECR) Subject:

Since 2021, Polish company Control Process S.A. has been carrying out a contract worth over EUR 36 million to construct a mechanical biological treatment plant for municipal waste in Lviv. In March 2026, the Lviv authorities unilaterally terminated the contract even though the investment was around 95 % complete. The company won all FIDIC arbitration proceedings and obtained a ruling from the International Chamber of Commerce (ICC) in Paris on 16 May 2026 confirming the unlawfulness of the Ukrainian side’s actions. Despite these arbitration decisions, the Lviv authorities are continuing to refuse to pay what the company is owed, estimated to be around EUR 17-18 million, and are failing to implement binding arbitration decisions and stopping representatives of the company and the Polish Consulate General from accessing the investment site. 1.

Will the Commission, in assessing Ukraine's compliance with the rule of law and foreign investment protection standards as part of the accession process, take into account cases in which local authorities fail to enforce binding arbitration awards against EU investors, including the case of Control Process S.A. and the ICC ruling of 16 May 2026?

How is the Commission monitoring Ukraine’s compliance with foreign investment protection standards and the principles of the rule of law and legal certainty in the context of the accession process, in particular as regards the enforcement of binding arbitration decisions?

What action does the Commission intend to take to ensure that EU funds for the reconstruction of Ukraine do not reach public or municipal entities that do not implement final and binding arbitration decisions?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.9.2026) The Commission follows closely the capacity of the Ukrainian authorities to ensure effective remedies and legal certainty, including the effective protection of investors’ rights. While the Commission cannot comment on individual cases and court proceedings, it takes systemic issues into account in its regular monitoring and assessment of Ukraine’s EU accessionrelated reforms. Information on delays or irregularities in individual cases may be relevant where they point to wider structural shortcomings. The Commission supports the strengthening of legal certainty for EU businesses active or investing in Ukraine by leveraging its financial conditionality, technical support and regular engagement with the Ukrainian authorities. Support under the Ukraine Facility links disbursements to the implementation of agreed reform steps, including in the areas of rule of law and business environment. The Commission further supports measures aimed at improving the investment climate, promoting transparent and predictable regulation, and reinforcing safeguards for property rights, contract enforcement and dispute resolution. The Commission will continue monitoring developments in these areas, while consistently underlining the importance of a stable and predictable legal framework for economic operators.

E-10-2026-002504.t: Future expansion of the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism to include processed products
qt: to the Commission Pierre Jouvet (S&D) Subject:

The Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) currently covers raw steel and aluminium, but not the processed products that use them. This asymmetry penalises EU manufacturers, which have to bear the carbon cost of their inputs, unlike imported finished products that avoid it. Two specific examples: in heating and cooling systems, the additional CBAM upstream cost can account for between 5 % and 10 % of the final price of equipment (heat pumps and ventilation), according to manufacturers; in the tyre sector, steel wire rods used in tyres manufactured in Europe are subject to the CBAM, yet tyres imported from China are not, which directly reduces the price competitiveness of European manufacturers. 1.
Has the Commission assessed the impact of this asymmetry on the competitiveness of manufacturing sectors that process steel or aluminium?
Does it intend to expand the scope of the CBAM to include processed products, and if so, when?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (25.8.2026) The Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) aims to address the risk of carbon leakage, by ensuring that imports are subject to a carbon price equivalent to that faced by domestic producers under the EU Emission Trading System. CBAM was initially designed with a limited scope, including basic goods that are most carbon intensive and exposed to the risk of carbon leakage. On 17 December 2025, the Commission adopted a proposal to amend the CBAM Regulation, among others, by extending CBAM’s scope to certain downstream products. The proposed date of entry into force for the downstream extension is 1 January 2028. The selection of goods in the Commission’s proposal was carried out to minimise the carbon leakage risk, while keeping the related administrative burden limited. Based on this analysis, the Commission proposed the extension of the CBAM scope to 180 downstream CBAM goods. This selection includes, among others, parts for refrigerating or freezing equipment and heat pumps (Combined Nomenclature (CN) 8418 99 90), as well as various cords and wires made of iron or steel (CN codes from the 4-digit heading 7312). The Commission's proposal is currently being discussed by the co-legislators. On 12 June 2026, the Council, at its Economic and Financial Affairs Council (ECOFIN) meeting, reached a General Approach on the proposal for revising the CBAM Regulation. The General Approach extends the list of goods for downstream extension by another 200 CN codes, which includes heat pumps (CN 8418 61 00). The Commission proposal is still under discussion at the European Parliament.

qt: to the Commission Olivier Chastel (Renew) Subject:

The development of online shopping has led to a significant increase in order returns, sometimes encouraged by free or very flexible return policies. While these practices make it easier to shop online, they also increase logistics flows, generate additional packaging and, in some cases, lead to new or usable products being devalued, resold at a loss or destroyed. 1.
Has the Commission specifically assessed the environmental impact of online returns, particularly in terms of transport, packaging and the management of returned products?

Does it plan to take any measures to encourage online platforms and retailers to reduce the environmental footprint of returns, for example through better consumer information, reusable packaging or more sustainable logistics?
at: (English version) to the Commission Olivier Chastel (Renew) (17 June 2026) Subject: Impact of online returns The development of online shopping has led to a significant increase in order returns, sometimes encouraged by free or very flexible return policies. While these practices make it easier to shop online, they also increase logistics flows, generate additional packaging and, in some cases, lead to new or usable products being devalued, resold at a loss or destroyed. 1. Has the Commission specifically assessed the environmental impact of online returns, particularly in terms of transport, packaging and the management of returned products? 2. Does it plan to take any measures to encourage online platforms and retailers to reduce the environmental footprint of returns, for example through better consumer information, reusable packaging or more sustainable logistics? (28 August 2026) The Commission is aware of the environmental impacts associated with online sales and returns, including transport emissions linked to shipping products and the additional packaging associated with returns. To reduce the amounts of single-use packaging and the growing quantities of packaging waste generated in the EU, Article 24(1) of the Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (PPWR) (1), establishes that by 1 January 2030 e-commerce packaging must be designed so that the maximum empty space ratio is reduced by 2030. Furthermore, certain transport packaging formats, as specified in Article 29(1) of the PPWR, must be reusable when shipped within a Member State or between different sites where a company carries out its activities. In other situations, 40% of these packaging formats must be reusable. Moreover, producers placing packaging on the market are subject to extended producer responsibility, which means that they must pay a fee to cover its end-of-life treatment. Online platforms must ensure that the producer comply with this obligation. Providers of online platforms are also subject to other sector-specific laws on product requirements, with a view to protect EU consumers, and are subject to fines if they do not comply with those rules. Lastly, as indicated in the 2030 Consumer Agenda (2), the Commission will explore the need for a recommendation on ‘green by design’ features in e-commerce to further tackle the environmental impact of this sector. This could cover aspects such as the availability of sustainability filters, greener delivery options, and sustainable returnmanagement policies.

Regulation (EU) 2025/40 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 19 December 2024 on packaging and packaging waste, amending Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 and Directive (EU) 2019/904, and repealing Directive 94/62/EC, OJ L, 2025/40, 22.1.2025. COM (2025) 848 final.

E-10-2026-002502.t: Protecting children from violent and sexual content in video games
qt: to the Commission Olivier Chastel (Renew) Subject:

Video games are becoming an increasingly popular pastime among young Europeans, and they can be accessed in many different ways, including via consoles, computers, smartphones and online platforms. While age rating systems already exist, there are still concerns around children’s exposure to violent, sexual or inappropriate content, especially when there is a lack of information for parents or when parental controls are barely used or difficult to set. 1.
Does the Commission consider that the current age rating and consumer information mechanisms properly protect children from exposure to violent or sexual content in video games?

Does it intend to tighten up, at EU level, the requirements for platforms, developers and distributors in terms of clearly indicating sensitive content and providing simple, harmonised and effective parental controls?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.9.2026) While the Audiovisual Media Services Directive (AVMSD)1 does not apply to online videogames as such, the Digital Services Act (DSA)2 applies to videogames that qualify as intermediary services. Under the DSA, providers of online platforms are required to ensure a high level of privacy, safety, and security for minors, in line with the protection of minors’ online guidelines3. Moreover, the protection of minors in videogames is currently carried out on the basis of selfregulatory mechanisms such as the Pan-European Game Information (PEGI) age and content rating system. This system aims to empower parents by providing relevant information allowing them to make informed choices. It has been recently updated to reflect emerging risks related to online games such as loot boxes or in-game communications4. While the Commission acknowledges the contribution of the PEGI system and the overall efforts by the industry to provide a safer online gaming environment for consumers, notably for vulnerable groups such as minors, it will continue to assess whether further measures may be appropriate in this area, in particular in the light of the recommendations of the Special Panel on child safety online5. The Commission is fully committed to upholding children’s rights online as off-line, ensuring their protection, safety and well-being.
1 Directive 2010/13/EU on the coordination of certain provisions laid down by law, regulation or administrative

action in Member States concerning the provision of audiovisual media services in view of changing market realities. 2 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/EN/legal-content/summary/digital-services-act.html. 3 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:C_202505519. 4 https://pegi.info/news/pegi-expands-age-rating-criteria-interactive-risk-categories. 5 https://commission.europa.eu/document/download/d833504d-5ec3-4fac-945f38e7d0bd5326_en?filename=Special-panel-report.pdf.

E-10-2026-002501.t: Humanitarian and security situation in Ethiopia’s Tigray region
qt: to the Commission Nicolas Bay (ECR), Marion Maréchal (ECR), Christophe Gomart (PPE), Waldemar Tomaszewski (ECR), Ondřej Krutílek (ECR) Subject:

The situation in the Tigray region continues to be extremely concerning. The conflict that took place there is considered one of the deadliest of the 21st century, with hundreds of thousands killed and millions displaced. The populations affected are predominantly Christian, belonging primarily to the Ethiopian Orthodox Church. According to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, more than 20 million people in Ethiopia are still in need of humanitarian assistance, many of whom are in the northern regions, including Tigray, demonstrating that a major crisis is still ongoing. Despite the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement signed in November 2022, concerns over the safety of civilians, humanitarian access and respect for fundamental rights remain. Tensions also continue to exist between the forces involved, in particular over disarmament and the withdrawal of foreign troops. In view of the above: 1.
Can the Commission clarify the current state of EU humanitarian aid in the Tigray region and what the obstacles are to its delivery?
What action does it intend to take to ensure that the peace agreement is complied with and civilians are protected?
Does it intend to support the mechanisms for investigating human rights violations committed during the conflict?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (5.8.2026) The overall humanitarian situation in Ethiopia remains fragile, affected by a combination of violence, insecurity and the impact of natural events. Against this background, the EU has allocated EUR 43 million for Ethiopia in 2026 to provide life-saving assistance to the most vulnerable, including in post-conflict areas of Tigray where people continue to suffer the consequences of the conflict. Aid delivery is nonetheless constrained by insecurity and bureaucratic impediments, including limits on data collection. The EU continues to call for unimpeded humanitarian access and for a joint information management system, transparently reflecting the reality of humanitarian needs in the country. The EU follows closely the developments in Tigray, remains concerned by the displacement, insecurity and human rights violations reported in Tigray and wider Ethiopia, and has repeatedly1 expressed concerns over rising tensions and breaches of the Pretoria Agreement. The EU will continue to encourage the resumption of talks and to support the African Unionled mediation efforts, while reiterating the importance of accountability, protection of civilians and respect for international humanitarian law and human rights laws. Finally, the EU supports accountability efforts and credible investigations, including through relevant international and regional human rights mechanisms. This includes ongoing support to the Ethiopian Human Rights Commission as well as society organisations to enable a transparent, accountable, inclusive, participatory, survivor-centred and inclusive transitional justice process.
1 European External Action Service, ‘Statement by the Spokesperson on the latest developments in Tigray’, 30

April 2026, https://www.eeas.europa.eu/eeas/ethiopia-statement-spokesperson-latest-developments-tigray_en; EU Delegation to Ethiopia, ‘EU Delegation to Ethiopia on the situation in Tigray’, 29 June 2026, https://www.facebook.com/eudelethiopia/posts/eu-delegation-to-ethiopia-on-the-situation-in-tigray-concernedabout-the-tense-s/1348408380816486.

E-10-2026-002500.t: Revision of the EU Emissions Trading System – provisions for aviation
qt: to the Commission Johan Van Overtveldt (ECR) Subject:

The Commission is preparing its revision of the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS), including provisions for aviation. At its high-level stakeholder workshop on 12 May 2026, the Commission’s Directorate-General for Climate Action (DG CLIMA) indicated that the proposal may extend the aviation ETS to outbound flights from the European Economic Area (EEA) to non-EEA countries. The current scope of application of the ETS for aviation is intra-EEA, in line with the ‘stopthe-clock’ derogation for aviation under Article 28(a)(2) of Directive 2003/87/EC1, which expires at the end of 2026. Unless further action is taken, the ETS would automatically apply to both inbound and outbound flights between the EEA and non-EEA countries before the colegislators have reached a decision on the Commission’s forthcoming proposal. 1.
How does the Commission intend to address the expiry of the derogation while the revision of the EU ETS is still being negotiated?

Does the Commission recognise that an automatic extension to all flights between the EEA and non-EEA countries will negatively impact commitments under the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA), and may also create tensions with international partners and risk causing trade disputes that might severely affect the entire European industry – including aeronautics – before the EU will have finalised the ETS revision?

Directive 2003/87/EC of 13 October 2003 establishing a scheme for greenhouse gas emission allowance trading within the Community and amending Council Directive 96/61/EC (ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2003/87/oj). 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (14.8.2026) The Commission is aware of the expiry of the derogation under Article 28a(1) point (a) of the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) Directive1. Its proposal for the revision of the ETS Directive addresses airlines’ compliance with their ETS obligations. Aircraft operators must surrender their allowances for emissions from 2027 by end of September 2028. According to the ‘One Europe, One Market’ roadmap, the Council, the Parliament and the European Commission, have set the first quarter of 2027 as target for agreeing on the review of the EU ETS. The EU ETS and the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA) have coexisted for years, with high ETS compliance from EU and non-EU airlines. The EU implemented CORSIA early on in a legally binding manner. The ETS already ensures airlines only pay once for their emissions. The Commission published its proposal on the revision of EU ETS on 17 July 20262, together with an impact assessment and it does not affect the EU’s unwavering commitment to a global solution to address international aviation emissions. While the proposal expands the scope of the ETS to departing flights from European Economic Area airports landing in third country airports located within 5000 km of the geographical centre of the EU3, CORSIA continues to apply on these routes. However, airlines will be able to use the ETS deduction mechanism to avoid double pricing with CORSIA. In addition, the proposal expands the support to Sustainable Alternative Fuels and technologies to all departing flights as from 2029, to the benefit of EU and non-EU operators. The Commission and Member States will continue having an active role in the work of the International Civil Aviation Organization, including on environmental matters.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A02003L0087-20240301. 2 https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_26_1596. 3 i.e. Frankfurt’s airport.

E-10-2026-002499.t: EU-Mercosur agreement, farming prices and benefits for consumers
qt: to the Commission Mathilde Androuët (PfE) Subject:

The Commission regularly presents trade liberalisation as a way to improve economic efficiency to benefit European consumers. The study ‘Growth narrative debunked, inequalities uncovered’1 disputes such claims. The study points out that lower agricultural producer prices do not necessarily mean lower prices for consumers, particularly in highly concentrated food chains. The authors consider that the gains from lower agricultural prices are likely to be captured by processors and retailers, rather than passed on to consumers (p. 3 and p. 8). The study also points out that, despite a fall in producer prices in 2024, consumer food prices continued to rise, albeit more slowly (p. 8). In view of this: 1.
Can the Commission still maintain and show that the agreement will cut food prices for European consumers?
Has the Commission assessed how much of the gains could be captured by intermediaries?
How does the Commission justify undermining European producers without any guarantee of benefits for consumers?

‘New Economic Study on the EU-Mercosur Trade Agreement: Growth Narrative Debunked, Inequalities Uncovered’, Orsola Costantini and Alex Izurieta, https://caneurope.org/app/uploads/2026/04/economic-study-eu-mercosur-trade-agreement.pdf. 1
at: (English version) to the Commission Mathilde Androuët (PfE) (17 June 2026) Subject: EU-Mercosur agreement, farming prices and benefits for consumers The Commission regularly presents trade liberalisation as a way to improve economic efficiency to benefit European consumers. The study ‘Growth narrative debunked, inequalities uncovered’ (1) disputes such claims. The study points out that lower agricultural producer prices do not necessarily mean lower prices for consumers, particularly in highly concentrated food chains. The authors consider that the gains from lower agricultural prices are likely to be captured by processors and retailers, rather than passed on to consumers (p. 3 and p. 8). The study also points out that, despite a fall in producer prices in 2024, consumer food prices continued to rise, albeit more slowly (p. 8). In view of this: 1.
Can the Commission still maintain and show that the agreement will cut food prices for European consumers?
Has the Commission assessed how much of the gains could be captured by intermediaries?
How does the Commission justify undermining European producers without any guarantee of benefits for consumers?

(10 August 2026) The Commission remains confident that, overall, trade agreements, including the EU-Mercosur Interim Trade Agreement (ITA), will translate to lower consumer prices in the stores. The study cited in the question, on the other hand, bases itself on three studies, two of which are over 60 years old. The remaining one investigates a confined phenomenon, namely price increases during the COVID-19 pandemic and the role that market concentration plays. The Commission has not specifically quantified how gains resulting from the agreement would be distributed along the supply chain. Price transmission along the agri-food chain depends on several factors, including market structure, costs and contractual relations. The Commission is addressing imbalances in the agri-food chain through Directive (EU) 2019/633 (1), which prohibits unfair trading practices imposed by stronger buyers on weaker suppliers. Following its evaluation (2), the Commission is examining how the framework could be further strengthened, in particular to better protect farmers and other weaker suppliers. In parallel, the EU Agri-food Chain Observatory intended to improve transparency and the understanding of how value is shared among the different operators, including whether changes in agricultural prices are transmitted further along the chain. The Commission does not agree with the statement that the ITA is undermining European producers. The degree of tariff liberalisation for EU sensitive agricultural products is limited to a very small volume in order not to expose vulnerable producers to excessive competition. Therefore, the impact for those specific goods is by construction expected to be very limited.

‘New Economic Study on the EU-Mercosur Trade Agreement: Growth Narrative Debunked, Inequalities Uncovered’, Orsola Costantini and Alex Izurieta, https://caneurope.org/app/uploads/2026/04/economic-study-eu-mercosur-trade-agreement.pdf. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2019/633/oj/eng. Commission Staff Working Document — Evaluation of the directive (EU) 2019/633 on unfair trading practices in business-to-business relationships in the agricultural and food supply chain — accompanying the report from the Commission to the European Parliament, the Council, the European Economic and Social Committee and the Committee of Regions — Evaluation of the Unfair Trading Practices Directive, SWD(2025) 405 final, 1 December 2025, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:52025SC0405 .

E-10-2026-002498.t: Animal welfare and beef imports from Mercosur
qt: to the Commission Mathilde Androuët (PfE) Subject:

In its Farm to Fork Strategy, the Commission recognised that animal welfare is a key aspect of a sustainable EU food system1. It also maintains that the EU‑Mercosur agreement upholds the EU’s standards on animal health and promotes reinforced cooperation on animal welfare2. However, images recorded by the Animal Welfare Foundation between August 2025 and March 2026 in Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay3 show cattle intended for the EU market in particular being reared in feedlots, confined to open‑air pens and subjected to artificial diets based primarily on grains and soybeans to accelerate weight gain before slaughter. These practices appear to be directly at odds with the commitments made by the European Union. In light of the above: 1.
Has the Commission verified this information with the Brazilian, Argentinian and Uruguayan governments?
Can it guarantee the that beef imported into the EU is not a product of these practices?

Communication COM(2020) 381 final of 20 May 2020, ‘A Farm to Fork Strategy for a fair, healthy and environmentally‑friendly food system’, in which the Commission commits to revising the animal welfare legislation in order to ‘ensure a higher level of animal welfare’. 2 European Commission, Directorate‑General for Trade and Economic Security, ‘Factsheet: EU‑Mercosur partnership agreement – Respecting Europe’s health and safety standards’, https://policy.trade.ec.europa.eu/eu-trade-relationships-country-and-region/countries-and-regions/mercosur/eumercosur-agreement/factsheet-eu-mercosur-partnership-agreement-respecting-europes-health-and-safetystandards_en. 3 ‘Images of cattle feedlots in Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay reveal animal suffering, NGO reports’, Contexte, 4 May 2026. 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (21.8.2026) The Commission recognises that animal welfare is an important component of sustainable food systems. It also recalls that the EU‑Mercosur Interim Trade Agreement (ITA) does not lower EU rules and preserves each Party’s right to regulate, including in areas linked to food safety, animal health and animal welfare. The ITA, which has been provisionally applied between the EU and the Mercosur Signatory Parties since 1 May 2026, also provides for cooperation and dialogue on animal welfare with Mercosur partners. Current EU legislation on the protection of animals at the time of slaughter applies to imports. However, the same principle does not currently apply to EU rules on the welfare of animals at farm. Over the last two years, welfare of animals at slaughter has been checked during audits conducted in Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay. Although not all audit reports are published yet, the outcomes of such checks were satisfactory. As announced in the Livestock Strategy1 of 7 July 2026, the Commission intends to propose by the end of 2026 a targeted revision of animal welfare rules for laying hens and broilers, and in 2027, a similar proposal aims to address pig welfare. These proposals aim to follow-up on the Citizens’ Initiative ‘End the cage age’ and also aim to provide an opportunity to introduce equivalent animal welfare requirements for imported products specifically in those sectors. At this stage, no legislative proposal on the welfare of beef cattle is planned. There is no specific EU animal welfare legislation applicable to beef cattle. Only the general rules of Directive 98/58/EC apply2, which do not prohibit open‑air pens or feeding practices provided health and weather protection are ensured, and nutritional needs are satisfied.
1 Commission Communication « EU strategy on livestock », COM(2026) 576 final. 2 Council Directive 98/58/EC of 20 July 1998 concerning the protection of animals kept for farming purposes,

E-10-2026-002497.t: Albania: defending ecosystems against Trump family mega-projects
qt: to the Commission Emma Fourreau (The Left), Marc Botenga (The Left), Danilo Della Valle (The Left), Sebastian Everding (The Left), Hanna Gedin (The Left), Anja Hazekamp (The Left), Marina Mesure (The Left), Arash Saeidi (The Left), Ilaria Salis (The Left), Jonas Sjöstedt (The Left), Anthony Smith (The Left) Subject:

In Albania, there is currently a popular movement opposing tourism development projects on Sazan Island and within the Vjosa-Narta protected area financed by Jared Kushner’s investment fund. These demonstrations reflect the view that Albania should not be sold off piecemeal for the benefit of the private interests of the ultra-rich and the imperial ambitions associated with the Trump family. These hotel developments pose risks to protected coastal and marine ecosystems and biodiversity, as well as to the habitats of threatened species. Sazan Island is located within the Karaburun-Sazan Marine National Park, which is designated as a Specially Protected Area of Mediterranean Importance (SPAMI). These projects therefore raise questions regarding their compatibility with Albania’s commitments under its EU accession process, particularly with regard to alignment with the EU environmental acquis. 1.

How does the Commission assess the compatibility of real estate investments linked to the family of a non-EU head of state with the standards of transparency and good governance expected from countries seeking accession to the EU?

Given the concerns already expressed by the EU regarding the 2024 amendments to Albania’s law on protected areas, what measures does the Commission intend to take to ensure that these mega-projects do not undermine Albania’s alignment with the EU environmental acquis?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (13.8.2026) The Commission is closely following Albania’s progress in aligning with the EU acquis. Foreign investments can bring benefits, provided they are transparent and in line with national and EU rules. Developments in the area of environment and nature protection are assessed in the context of Albania’s accession negotiations. Under Chapter 27 – Environment and climate change, Albania has to align its legislation with the EU environmental acquis, including the Environmental Impact Assessment1 and the Strategic Environmental Assessment2 Directives, and the Birds3 and Habitats4 Directives. Furthermore, the closing benchmarks explicitly require Albania to align with the EU nature protection acquis, including by repealing incompatible provisions introduced through amendments to the law on Protected Areas and terminating the 2015 legislation on strategic investments. They also require Albania to demonstrate adequate capacity to manage future Natura 2000 sites and to ensure effective conservation measures preventing habitat and species deterioration. The Commission is in continuous contact with the Albanian authorities and civil society regarding the project in the Pishë Poro - Nartë area. This project, like all ongoing projects in Albania, will need to comply with the benchmarks set under Chapter 27. The Commission has encouraged the Albanian authorities to continue taking steps supporting the fulfilment of the closing benchmarks and move forward on its EU path and it will monitor closely such fulfilment. The Government of Albania is assuring that a full environmental impact assessment will be carried out and that European environmental standards will be respected.

E-10-2026-002494.t: Transparency of Visa and Mastercard fees – the case for a European reporting framework to protect merchants
qt: to the Commission Aurore Lalucq (S&D) Subject:

A recent study by the UK’s Payment Systems Regulator reveals that fees charged to merchants by Visa and Mastercard have risen by 30 % over the past five years, largely enabled by the opacity surrounding their pricing practices. Across the European Union, merchants are subject to unilateral and unpredictable fee increases, as well as penalties applied in an arbitrary and non-transparent manner. 1.
Does the Commission share the assessment that the pricing opacity of Visa and Mastercard exposes European merchants to unjustified cost increases and arbitrary billing practices?

While Article 31(a) of the proposed Payment Services Regulation (PSR) will introduce new transparency rules and a future delegated act, how does the Commission intend to enforce compliance by international card schemes, and shield merchants from noncompliance?

Beyond mere transparency, and given the direct impact on European consumers’ purchasing power, is the Commission considering a regulatory framework to actively cap scheme fees that circumvent the Interchange Fee Regulation?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (26.8.2026) The Commission is continuously monitoring the payments market and actively investigating when relevant. It is conducting a preliminary investigation into an alleged lack of transparency of card scheme and processing services that Visa and Mastercard charge to acquirers in the European Economic Area. Since it is ongoing, no further information can be provided at this stage. Under the upcoming Payment Services Regulation (PSR)1, card schemes and processing entities have to ensure that the fees levied on acquirers are categorised and disclosed transparently, allowing for the comparability of billing categories. Acquirers will have to ensure that their information vis-à-vis merchants has the same level of transparency. Authorities designated by Member States will enforce those requirements. The Commission will prepare a report on the practices of card schemes, processing entities, and acquirers, covering, inter alia, these transparency requirements. Formal adoption by the co-legislators is expected in Q4 2026. Scheme fees charged to acquirers are not covered under the interchange fee caps of the Interchange Fees Regulation (IFR)2, which nevertheless foresees detailed rules addressing possible circumvention of caps through alternative flows of monies. The 2020 Report3 on the application of the IFR, supported by a comprehensive Study4, found that interchange fees had declined and that ‘Scheme fees, which are not within the scope of the IFR, appear to have increased to a limited extent’ (2020 Report p.5). A follow-up Study in 2024 largely aligns with the previous Study on fees aspects5 (2024 Study p.83-84 and 95).

transactions, Commission Staff Working Document of 29.6.2020 SWD(2020) 118. https://competitionpolicy.ec.europa.eu/document/download/d8055968-b4c2-424b-b281c4c6959df19b_en?filename=IFR_report_card_payment.pdf. 4 Study on the application of Interchange Fee Regulation, 2020, prepared by Ernst&Young and Copenhagen Economics, available at https://op.europa.eu/en/publication-detail/-/publication/79f1072d-d6c2-11ea-adf701aa75ed71a1. 5 https://competition-policy.ec.europa.eu/document/65d4f65a-6b23-49c7-91cb-e5cd166a19ed_en.

E-10-2026-002493.t: Follow-up to the Interchange Fee Regulation – European Court of Auditors report
qt: to the Commission Aurore Lalucq (S&D) Subject:

In its 2024 special report, the European Court of Auditors (ECA) concluded that the Commission had not conducted a sufficiently rigorous evaluation of the application of the Interchange Fee Regulation (IFR)1, adopted in 2015. The court notably found that evaluation work is significantly overdue, and that several Member States are not correctly implementing the interchange fee caps, to the detriment of European merchants. 1.
What concrete measures does the Commission intend to take in response to the ECA’s findings regarding the shortcomings in the implementation of the IFR, and according to what timeline?

Does the Commission plan to carry out a new, thorough and independent evaluation of the application of the IFR across all Member States, in order to ensure effective compliance with interchange fee caps – and if so, within what timeframe?
Regulation (EU) 2015/751 of 29 April 2015 on interchange fees for card-based payment transactions (ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2015/751/oj). 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (7.8.2026) The 2020 Report1 to the European Parliament and the Council on the impact of the Interchange Fee Regulation (IFR) 2015/751 (‘the Regulation’), the underlying study2 to the 2020 Report and the 2024 study – the latter focusing in particular on areas for further monitoring and reinforced data gathering identified in the 2020 Report3, all concluded that the Regulation is working well, including the caps on interchange fees across the EU. As highlighted in the Commission’s replies to the European Court of Auditors’ (ECA) Report4, the 2024 study suggested that merchant service charges may be on the rise for debit cards transactions while charges for credit card transactions may be decreasing, based on a limited merchant survey (2024 study page 95). In addition, it is worth noting that the current caps on interchange fees for consumer debit and credit cards under the Regulation are low compared to other jurisdictions5. The Commission reviewed the application of the Regulation in line with its review clause under the 2020 Report, concluding in particular that it was too early ‘to decide on the necessity of a legislative proposal to review the IFR’. While at this stage another study is not envisaged, the Commission is in regular contact with the national competent authorities to foster consistent implementation, closely monitors developments in retail payment markets and actively investigates when relevant.

E-10-2026-002492.t: EU-produced alumina exports to Russia and the integrity of EU sanctions
qt: to the Commission Tomáš Zdechovský (PPE) Subject:

EU sanctions are intended to restrict Russia’s access to strategic industrial inputs relevant to its war economy. However, Aughinish Alumina in Ireland, owned by Russia’s Rusal, continues to export significant volumes of alumina to Russia. In 2024, exports of alumina from Ireland to Russia reached approximately USD 376 million, up from USD 243 million in 2022, making Russia Ireland’s largest alumina export market. The plant itself accounts for around 30 % of EU alumina output. A substantial share of the exported material is shipped to and processed at Rusal’s Krasnoyarsk smelter in Siberia, where it is converted into aluminium and enters downstream production chains, including those with reported links to Russia’s defence sector. 1.

How does the Commission ensure the effectiveness of EU sanctions when EU-produced strategic inputs controlled by Russian-linked entities continue to enter Russia’s industrial supply chains, including aluminium production linked to Rusal?

What assessment has the Commission made of the risk that strategic inputs originating in the EU may indirectly contribute to Russia’s military-industrial capacity, and of the implications this has for the credibility of the EU sanctions regime?
at: (English version) to the Commission Tomáš Zdechovský (PPE) (17 June 2026) Subject: EU-produced alumina exports to Russia and the integrity of EU sanctions EU sanctions are intended to restrict Russia’s access to strategic industrial inputs relevant to its war economy. However, Aughinish Alumina in Ireland, owned by Russia’s Rusal, continues to export significant volumes of alumina to Russia. In 2024, exports of alumina from Ireland to Russia reached approximately USD 376 million, up from USD 243 million in 2022, making Russia Ireland’s largest alumina export market. The plant itself accounts for around 30% of EU alumina output. A substantial share of the exported material is shipped to and processed at Rusal’s Krasnoyarsk smelter in Siberia, where it is converted into aluminium and enters downstream production chains, including those with reported links to Russia’s defence sector. 1. How does the Commission ensure the effectiveness of EU sanctions when EU-produced strategic inputs controlled by Russian-linked entities continue to enter Russia’s industrial supply chains, including aluminium production linked to Rusal? 2. What assessment has the Commission made of the risk that strategic inputs originating in the EU may indirectly contribute to Russia’s military-industrial capacity, and of the implications this has for the credibility of the EU sanctions regime? (31 July 2026) The EU has adopted a wide range of restrictive measures (‘sanctions’) on Russia, including far-reaching trade restrictions in several economic sectors. The measures in place reflect a careful balance between the EU’s determination to impact Russia’s ability to finance its war and usage of aggression against Ukraine and to limit to the extent possible negative impacts on Member States and industry. This assessment is conducted with even greater care when it concerns critical raw materials that are subject to supply shortages. EU sanctions are regularly reviewed. Any decision to amend the existing sanctions is for the Council to take by unanimity. Potential measures targeting aluminium oxide (‘alumina’) exports need to take into account global market conditions, supply diversification and potential impacts on EU operators in international value chains and their EU customers. Taking these considerations into account, alumina is not subject to EU export restrictive measures (i.e. an export ban). However, as a general observation, it should be noted that indirect economic support to listed Russian arms manufacturers is prohibited. The High Representative/Vice-President and the Commission continue to work to further close loopholes and find ways to prevent Russia from sustaining its military industrial complex. The Member States are, first and foremost, responsible for the implementation of EU sanctions and investigating potential circumvention of prohibitions under EU sanctions. The Commission is monitoring the implementation and enforcement of EU sanctions across all Member States. In the case at hand, the Irish authorities are responsible for investigating the allegations and the Commission is in contact with them on this matter.

E-10-2026-002491.t: Illicit trade and the EU enlargement agenda
qt: to the Commission Tomáš Zdechovský (PPE) Subject:

Illicit trade remains a significant challenge for public revenue and in the fight against organised crime across Europe. It includes illicit trade in goods that can be excised, including alcohol or tobacco products, as well as counterfeit goods and other forms of illegal commerce. Beyond its economic impact, illicit trade undermines fair competition, weakens institutional effectiveness, and creates opportunities for criminal networks to operate across borders. As the European Union continues to deepen cooperation with candidate and partner countries, such as Ukraine, and support their economic integration, strengthened customs cooperation, enforcement capacity and market transparency remain an important element of broader efforts to promote economic resilience, governance and the rule of law. In this context: 1.
How does the Commission assess the role of combating illicit trade in terms of supporting economic resilience, market integrity and rule of law reforms in candidate and partner countries?

What measures is the Commission taking to support candidate and partner countries in strengthening customs cooperation, enforcement capacity and inter-agency coordination, in order to address illicit trade?

How can the Commission further support candidate countries in promoting transparent trade, fair competition and a predictable business environment, as part of their integration into the EU single market?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.9.2026) For EU candidate countries, aligning with the EU acquis is key to tackling illicit trade. This includes alignment with the customs union, notably on controls of counterfeit and pirated goods, as well as with the EU anti-money laundering framework. Together, these measures help prevent and detect the financial flows linked to illicit trade. In accession negotiations, candidate countries must also prepare a rule of law roadmap covering organised crime, other serious cross-border crime and border management, of which illicit trade is a part. One concrete measure supporting the fight against illicit trade is EMPACT, the EU Multidisciplinary Platform Against Criminal Threats. As the EU framework for addressing serious and organised crime, it enables the Commission to support the participation of nonEU countries in operational actions against excise and customs fraud, as well as intellectual property crime and the counterfeiting of goods or currencies, which are identified as priorities for the current cycle 2026-2029. Trade facilitation, fair competition and a predictable business environment are key to the stability of candidate countries. Through targeted financial and technical support under the Instrument for Pre-Accession, the Commission can strengthen administrative capacity, improve enforcement and support reforms that increase market transparency. This helps candidate countries integrate gradually into the EU single market and creates a more stable and attractive environment for investment and growth. The Commission remains engaged, as appropriate, in accompanying reform efforts and in encouraging progress in areas of particular importance for the accession process.

E-10-2026-002490.t: Failure to transpose the Pay Transparency Directive and its impact on gender equality
qt: to the Commission Heléne Fritzon (S&D) Subject:

The deadline for transposing Directive (EU) 2023/970 on pay transparency expired on 7 June 2026. Nevertheless, only a small number of Member States have confirmed that they have transposed the provisions of the directive in full. The Directive is not perfect, but the failure to implement this landmark legislation delays progress towards gender equality and prevents workers from benefiting from rights already adopted at EU level. It aims to tackle pay discrimination, increase workplace transparency and strengthen enforcement of equal pay for equal work and work of equal value. Every delay risks allowing discriminatory pay structures to remain hidden, unchallenged and uncorrected. It also means that women continue to bear the long-term consequences of unequal pay, including lower earnings, reduced pension rights and greater economic insecurity later in life. The limited progress in implementation raises serious concerns regarding the level of political commitment in some Member States to fully comply with their obligations. In light of this: 1.
What measures does the Commission intend to take against Member States that have failed to comply with their obligations?
How will the Commission ensure the swift and effective implementation of the Directive across the EU so that women can benefit from the rights it establishes without further delay?

(18 August 2026) The Commission is committed to ensure the full and effective transposition of the Pay Transparency Directive by all Member States and is currently assessing Member States’ notifications of their transposition measures. Where a Member State fails to transpose the directive within the prescribed deadline, the Commission may take appropriate measures, including initiate infringement proceedings. To further support the implementation of the directive, the Commission will continue to assist Member States and stakeholders. For instance, it has held implementation workshops with Member States and social partners, covering all of the directive’s provisions. It will continue with mutual learning exercises and engage in dialogue with Member States and stakeholders. The Commission has also made funding available in the 2024 and 2026 Citizens, Equality, Rights and Values programmes to support employers with pay reporting (1). Furthermore, the Commission and the European Institute for Gender Equality published an EU-wide toolkit to aid employers when carrying out gender-neutral job evaluations and classifications (2).

E-10-2026-002488.t: Control and enforcement of EU requirements for imports of animal products from third countries
qt: to the Commission Christine Singer (Renew), Engin Eroglu (Renew), Joachim Streit (Renew) Subject:

The Commission has decided to remove Brazil from the list of third countries authorised to export certain animals and products of animal origin to the EU as of 3 September 2026. The decision was made as a result of inadequate guarantees of compliance with certain EU requirements for the production of animal products. As parliamentarians, we have received numerous questions from the public about whether the agreed EU standards are actually checked and enforced when goods are imported from third countries. The case raises fundamental questions about the effectiveness of import controls and the timing of the measures. 1.
For how long has the Commission had evidence or knowledge that Brazil may not fully comply with agreed standards for animals and products of animal origin?
Why was authorisation not revoked and corresponding imports not halted sooner?

What measures is the Commission taking to ensure that future breaches of agreed standards – for example on prohibited substances, traceability and control systems – are detected earlier and prevented more effectively in the case of imports from third countries?
at: (English version) to the Commission Christine Singer (Renew), Engin Eroglu (Renew), Joachim Streit (Renew) (17 June 2026) Subject: Control and enforcement of EU requirements for imports of animal products from third countries The Commission has decided to remove Brazil from the list of third countries authorised to export certain animals and products of animal origin to the EU as of 3 September 2026. The decision was made as a result of inadequate guarantees of compliance with certain EU requirements for the production of animal products. As parliamentarians, we have received numerous questions from the public about whether the agreed EU standards are actually checked and enforced when goods are imported from third countries. The case raises fundamental questions about the effectiveness of import controls and the timing of the measures. 1. For how long has the Commission had evidence or knowledge that Brazil may not fully comply with agreed standards for animals and products of animal origin? 2.
Why was authorisation not revoked and corresponding imports not halted sooner?

3. What measures is the Commission taking to ensure that future breaches of agreed standards — for example on prohibited substances, traceability and control systems — are detected earlier and prevented more effectively in the case of imports from third countries? (21 August 2026) As part of the EU’s broader efforts against antimicrobial resistance, a major global public threat, all imports of animals or products of animal origin intended for human consumption must comply with EU rules banning the use of antimicrobials for growth promotion and yield increase, and antimicrobials reserved for human infections. The detailed provisions on these requirements and date of application were set in 2023, following discussions between the European Parliament, the Council and the Commission. In accordance with these provisions, the entry conditions related to the requirements on the use of antimicrobials do not apply before 3 September 2026. This is without prejudice to the obligation for products entering the EU before that date to comply with other applicable EU requirements (e.g. animal health, food hygiene or residue limits). As announced on 9 December 2025 (1), several measures have been introduced to maintain EU’s highest food safety and public health standards. These include a 50% increase in audits in non-EU countries over the next two years and a 33% increase in audits of EU border control posts. A taskforce has also been set up to strengthen imports controls, bringing together Member States authorities and Commission’s experts. Furthermore, every year the Commission evaluates third countries’ residue control plans and regularly audits their implementation. The EU system is designed to respond swiftly and effectively whenever a risk emerges.

E-10-2026-002487.t: Compatibility of Germany’s internal border controls with the Schengen Borders Code
qt: to the Commission Pascal Arimont (PPE) Subject:

In September 2024, I put a question to the Commission on the controls that Germany had reinstated at internal borders (E‑001719/2024). In its answer, the Commission said that it was assessing the necessity and proportionality of the measures on the basis of the information it had received from Germany. On 2 June 2026, the Commission issued an opinion on Germany’s maintenance of internal border controls1. It stresses that internal border controls are only permitted as a last resort, points to available alternatives and calls on Germany to work towards phasing out the controls. 1.
What specific conclusions did the Commission reach on the necessity and proportionality of the internal border controls that Germany has kept in place?
What specific action does it expect Germany to take as it phases out the controls as requested, and within what time frame?
What steps will it take if Germany clings onto its controls and refuses to comply with the request in the opinion of 2 June 2026 to phase them out?
https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_26_1223.
at: (English version) to the Commission Pascal Arimont (PPE) (17 June 2026) Subject: Compatibility of Germany’s internal border controls with the Schengen Borders Code In September 2024, I put a question to the Commission on the controls that Germany had reinstated at internal borders (E001719/2024). In its answer, the Commission said that it was assessing the necessity and proportionality of the measures on the basis of the information it had received from Germany. On 2 June 2026, the Commission issued an opinion on Germany’s maintenance of internal border controls (1). It stresses that internal border controls are only permitted as a last resort, points to available alternatives and calls on Germany to work towards phasing out the controls. 1. What specific conclusions did the Commission reach on the necessity and proportionality of the internal border controls that Germany has kept in place? 2. What specific action does it expect Germany to take as it phases out the controls as requested, and within what time frame? 3. What steps will it take if Germany clings onto its controls and refuses to comply with the request in the opinion of 2 June 2026 to phase them out? (30 July 2026) In its Opinion issued on 2 June 2026 (1), the Commission acknowledges the serious threats invoked by Germany due to the complex security and migration situation it is confronted with. The Commission stresses that internal border controls must remain a temporary measure of last resort as required by the Schengen Borders Code (2). The Commission has recommended that Germany work towards the gradual lifting of internal border controls, based on a tailor-made approach per part of the internal border and per threat, making full use of the available alternative measures as laid out in Commission adopted Recommendation (EU) 2024/268 (3) on cooperation between the Member States with regard to serious threats to internal security and public policy in the area without internal border controls, and the possibilities under the revised Schengen Borders Code. The Commission, with the support of its Schengen Coordinator, has now initiated a new round of consultations with all Member States concerned by the reintroduction of internal border control. It is also in close contact with the German authorities to ensure that an appropriate follow-up is given to the recommendations made in the Commission’s Opinion. It notes that important progress has already been made, for instance at the German-Luxembourg border, where static controls have been replaced by mobile checks.
