E-10-2026-002486.t: EU funding for sustainable timber construction in the 2028-2034 multiannual financial framework
qt: to the Commission Pascal Arimont (PPE) Subject:

The European Union participates, through national funding programmes, in various timberbased residential construction projects co-financed by EU funds. Such projects create added value in many ways: they enhance regional added value, promote sustainable forest management, support rural areas and contribute to the decarbonisation of the construction sector. Under the multiannual financial framework (MFF) for 2028-2034, the Commission is proposing a new funding architecture, which raises questions about the continuity of such cofinancing projects. 1.
What EU funding instruments will be able to support sustainable timber construction projects under the 2028-2034 MFF, particularly in rural areas?

How does the Commission intend to ensure that successful funding models under the current MFF remain accessible and viable for local actors, municipalities, small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and forestry companies under the next one?
Is the Commission planning to draw up specific guidelines to target the promotion of sustainable timber construction as part of European construction culture?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.9.2026) The National and Regional Partnership Plans (NRPP) and the European Competitiveness Fund (ECF) proposed by the Commission could support sustainable timber construction projects under the 2028-2034 Multiannual Financial Framework. The NRPP would be implemented in shared management, under which Member State authorities are able to programme resources in line with their specific needs and priorities. The NRPP include relevant specific objectives, such as making territories more attractive, strengthening sustainable manufacturing, promoting the bioeconomy, and boosting the competitiveness of small and medium-sized enterprises. Within these objectives, Member States and regions may choose to support projects related to sustainable timber construction. The NRPP can also support sustainable forest management to provide the quality wood required for construction. The ECF includes a policy window on ‘Health, Biotech, Agriculture and Bioeconomy’, which aims to foster competitiveness, sustainability, resilience and fairness of agriculture, fisheries, aquaculture, forestry sectors and rural and coastal areas. The concrete scope and activities that this window will support will be defined in the context of the dedicated work programme(s). The Commission will not promote specific construction materials, including timber. It follows a technology- and material-neutral approach, setting sustainability goals while leaving material choices to market operators and Member States. The revised Construction Products Regulation (EU) 2024/31101 supports this by improving harmonised environmental information for transparent, informed choices without favouring any material.

E-10-2026-002485.t: Acoustic turning warning systems for the protection of vulnerable road users
qt: to the Commission Pascal Arimont (PPE) Subject:

The efforts of the EU and its Member States to protect vulnerable road users are most welcome. Due to their size and wide turning circle, turning lorries are a risk factor. Modern turning assistance systems can detect people in the lateral danger area and warn the driver. In some Member States, acoustic warnings are used. These also alert pedestrians and cyclists to the danger when a vehicle is turning. Since July 2024, Regulation (EU) 2019/2144 has provided for mandatory turning assistance systems for newly registered lorries to enhance protection of vulnerable road users. 1.
What is the Commission’s assessment of the use of external acoustic turning signals on lorries and buses as a complementary measure to protect pedestrians and cyclists?
Is the Commission examining whether acoustic blind-spot assistance systems could be made mandatory across the EU, including with regard to retrofit solutions for existing fleets?
Is the Commission planning to introduce other measures to minimise the number of accidents between turning vehicles and vulnerable road users?
at: (English version) to the Commission Pascal Arimont (PPE) (17 June 2026) Subject: Acoustic turning warning systems for the protection of vulnerable road users The efforts of the EU and its Member States to protect vulnerable road users are most welcome. Due to their size and wide turning circle, turning lorries are a risk factor. Modern turning assistance systems can detect people in the lateral danger area and warn the driver. In some Member States, acoustic warnings are used. These also alert pedestrians and cyclists to the danger when a vehicle is turning. Since July 2024, Regulation (EU) 2019/2144 has provided for mandatory turning assistance systems for newly registered lorries to enhance protection of vulnerable road users. 1. What is the Commission’s assessment of the use of external acoustic turning signals on lorries and buses as a complementary measure to protect pedestrians and cyclists? 2. Is the Commission examining whether acoustic blind-spot assistance systems could be made mandatory across the EU, including with regard to retrofit solutions for existing fleets? 3. Is the Commission planning to introduce other measures to minimise the number of accidents between turning vehicles and vulnerable road users? (6 August 2026) Regulation (EU) 2019/2144 (1) mandates from July 2024 all new trucks and buses to be equipped with advanced safety systems capable of detecting vulnerable road users in proximity — blind spot information (2) and collision warning (3) systems alert drivers of the risk of collision when turning. In addition, from January 2029 all new trucks and buses must provide enhanced direct visibility of vulnerable road users from the driver seat. The new Driving Licence Directive (4) also mandates more focused testing of candidate drivers of heavy-duty vehicles. In 2027, the Commission will evaluate the effectiveness of the safety measures and any legislative proposal for additional mandatory requirements will be based on a comprehensive cost-benefit analysis and impact assessment. E-10-2026-002484.t: Proportionality of EU CATCH requirements for legal raw fish
qt: to the Commission Piotr Müller (ECR) Subject:

The Commission is presenting EU CATCH as a tool for digitalisation, harmonising controls and reducing the administrative burden. In practice, however, the system may have the opposite effect on legal raw fish from lowIUU-risk fisheries if the documentation requirements do not take the specificities of supply based on aggregated catches into account. This includes wild Pacific salmon, which can be an important raw material for EU and Polish processing plants. One lot may include fish from multiple small vessels and multiple fishing days, which may require a very large number of records to be manually reported. I therefore ask: 1.
Does the Commission consider the current EU CATCH requirements proportionate for low-IUU-risk fisheries, where catches are aggregated prior to being delivered to processing plants?
How will the Commission address the allegation that the current requirements may create a de facto administrative barrier to the legal raw material needed for EU processing?
Does the Commission intend to introduce simplifications for fisheries with a high level of aggregated catches?
at: (English version) Priority question for written answer P-002480/26 to the Commission Piotr Müller (ECR) (16 June 2026) Subject: EU CATCH transition period and wild salmon fishing season The new EU CATCH requirements come into effect at a particularly delicate time for wild Pacific salmon supplies to the EU fish processing industry. The six-month transition period ends on 10 July 2026, in the middle of a short fishing season. The existing simplified administrative arrangements between the EU and the US are coming to an end and exporters need to adapt to the new documentation requirements. The issue is not the legality of catches or the risk of IUU fishing, but the risk of disruption of supplies to EU processors due to the system not being adapted to the catch aggregation model. Industry representatives warn that a lack of swift action could prevent a significant share of catches from the 2026 season from reaching Europe, hitting not only processing companies, but also industry workers and consumers. I therefore ask: 1.

Has the Commission carried out an analysis of the impact of the transition period ending on 10 July 2026 on the continued supply of legal raw material to the EU fish processing industry, including on business competitiveness, jobs and consumer prices?

Does the Commission envisage urgent measures to prevent supply disruptions during the 2026 fishing season, in particular for fisheries based on aggregated catches, in order to avoid losing part of the legal supply of raw material to the EU?
Is the Commission considering extending the transitional period beyond 10 July 2026 to ensure continuity of supply to EU processors?

to the Commission Piotr Müller (ECR) (16 June 2026) Subject: Impact of EU CATCH on Polish and EU fish processors The EU CATCH system aims to combat illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fishing and improve the traceability of fishery products. There are no doubts as to the aim of the EU CATCH system. However, the practical implementation of the new requirements for legal raw material from heavily regulated fisheries used by EU importers and fish processors, including those in Poland, is of concern. For example, one lot of wild salmon from Alaska may consist of catches from multiple small vessels and multiple fishing days, which are then pooled before being delivered to the processing plant. The transition period ends on 10 July 2026 — in the middle of a short fishing season, which risks disrupting supply. I therefore ask:
Has the Commission assessed the impact of EU CATCH on Polish and EU fish processors using legal raw fish from fisheries where catches are aggregated before processing?
Will the Commission consider introducing alternative means of demonstrating compliance with EU CATCH requirements for such fisheries, with full traceability and monitoring of the legality of catches?
Will the Commission extend the transitional period beyond 10 July 2026 to avoid disrupting the supply during the fishing season?

Joint answer given by Mr Kadis on behalf of the European Commission (3 August 2026) Member States and third countries’ authorities were informed of the amendments to the illegal, unreported, and unregulated (IUU) fishing Regulation (1) almost two years before the application of the revised catch certificate template and the obligatory use of CATCH for EU importers and EU authorities as of 10 January 2026. The Commission considers that two years should have been sufficient time for all administrations to prepare their industry and adapt for the initial application date of 10 January 2026. Nevertheless, to ease the digital transition for stakeholders, the Commission introduced flexibility in CATCH to avoid that new requirements would block submissions of importer declarations. The rules are applied in a non-discriminatory manner towards third countries exporting to the EU. The Commission has therefore no intentions of excluding certain fisheries (e.g. where catches are aggregated before processing) from providing the data required in the catch certificate. The Commission has carefully listened to the EU industry who has pointed out possible supply issues during summer and early autumn of 2026 for wild salmon and American lobster.

Council Regulation (EC) No 1005/2008 of 29 September 2008 establishing a Union system to prevent, deter and eliminate illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing, amending Regulations (EEC) No 2847/93, (EC) No 1936/2001 and (EC) No 601/2004 and repealing Regulations (EC) No 1093/94 and (EC) No 1447/1999.

The Commission has therefore decided to prolong the flexibilities for the former administrative arrangement third countries (2) by allowing submission into CATCH of the old templates up to and including 30 November 2026. The flexibilities will end after 30 November. The Commission continues therefore to encourage the EU processing industry to engage fully with third country suppliers to ensure adequate and uniform implementation of CATCH.

E-10-2026-002483.t: Visa ban for (ex-)combatants of armed forces implicated in serious violations
qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Mounir Satouri (Verts/ALE), Benedetta Scuderi (Verts/ALE), Mélissa Camara (Verts/ALE), Villy Søvndal (Verts/ALE), Ana Miranda Paz (Verts/ALE), Majdouline Sbai (Verts/ALE), Cristina Guarda (Verts/ALE), Jaume Asens Llodrà (Verts/ALE), Catarina Vieira (Verts/ALE), Maria Ohisalo (Verts/ALE), Marie Toussaint (Verts/ALE), David Cormand (Verts/ALE), Marc Botenga (The Left), Rudi Kennes (The Left), Cecilia Strada (S&D), Matjaž Nemec (S&D), Marco Tarquinio (S&D), Hanna Gedin (The Left), Danilo Della Valle (The Left), Manon Aubry (The Left), Chloé Ridel (S&D), Barry Andrews (Renew), Annalisa Corrado (S&D), Thijs Reuten (S&D) Subject:

On 9 June 2026, presenting the proposed 21st package of sanctions against Russia, the Commission announced a comprehensive visa ban for Russia’s (ex-)combatants, who should not be authorised to enter EU territory1. The Office of the EU Special Representative for Human Rights, in its note of 20 June 20252, documented serious international humanitarian law (IHL) and international human rights law (IHRL) violations attributable to Israeli forces. Even since the ‘ceasefire’ in Gaza, violations have continued, including with the intensification of the colonisation in the West Bank3 and the indiscriminate bombing campaign in Lebanon coupled with ethnic cleansing4. French5 and Italian6 prosecutors have also opened ‘war crime’ and ‘torture’ probes over Israel’s treatment of Gaza flotilla activists. Therefore, 1.

What justification underpins the proposed visa ban for (ex-)combatants of the Russian armed forces? Is this criterion transposable to Israeli (ex-)soldiers? If not, on what objective grounds is the distinction drawn?

Does the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy (VP/HR) consider that the radicalisation and desensitisation to violence of Israeli soldiers, resulting from the commission of war crimes listed in the aforementioned note, pose a security risk if they are present on EU territory?

at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (30.7.2026) The EU has a clear position that international law must be upheld in all circumstances. There is no hierarchy of victims of human rights violations and abuses. They all deserve justice and accountability. The EU’s stance on Ukraine, the Middle East, and beyond demonstrates that the EU defends the rules, not rule-breakers. Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine is a flagrant violation of the UN Charter, with serious consequences for international security and the rules based international order. The gravity of the situation has called for an unprecedented EU engagement. Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine has had widespread implications, including an aggravation of the risks and threats faced by the EU. Their presence constitutes a threat to the values, interests and security of the EU as a whole, as well as to the public policy or to the internal security or international relations of one or more Member States or of the EU as a whole. E-10-2026-002482.t: Impact of the ban on exports of sheep from Romania
qt: to the Commission Ioan-Rareş Bogdan (PPE) Subject:

Implementing Decision (EU) 2026/1217, which was motivated by isolated outbreaks of sheep pox, places a total ban on movements and exports of live sheep from Romania to the single market. Although protecting animal health is a legitimate aim, this measure is contrary to the principle of proportionality. In similar crises within the EU, the Commission has applied surgical regionalisation, isolating the affected areas. The collective penalisation of the whole of Romania is distorting competition, leaving production at a standstill and directly favouring competitors in the rest of the EU. The ban on transportation by land is forcing Romanians to bear asymmetrical logistical costs for third markets, pushing family farms towards bankruptcy. This artificial collapse in producer prices is solely benefiting large industrial slaughterhouses, which are imposing monopoly prices. At the same time, the elimination of the biggest exporter of live sheep will cause an inflationary shock in the consumer markets of importing Member States. 1.
What technical justifications underlie the refusal to apply the principle of strict regionalisation for Romania, by contrast with the procedures applied in western countries?
How does the Commission plan to mitigate the market abuse perpetrated by large processors against Romanian farmers, who are being forced to sell at prices below their production costs?
Will the Commission activate mechanisms of direct compensation from the agricultural crisis reserve to prevent this strategic sector from going bankrupt?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (21.8.2026) At EU level, Regulation (EU) 2016/4291 and Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/6872 regulate sheep pox and goat pox. In Romania, Implementing Decision (EU) 2026/11083 introduced additional temporary emergency measures including a restriction on the movement of sheep and goats from the entire territory of Romania to other Member States or third countries, considering that the disease situation is uncertain and deteriorating. Preliminary surveillance results in May-June 2026 identified seropositive establishments outside the currently existing restricted zones, indicating possible wider circulation of the disease. The Commission works with Romania on further eradication measures, including emergency vaccination. The EU has introduced several tools to strengthen the farmers position in the food chain. Regulation (EU) No 1308/20134 reinforces written contracts, cost-based price formulas and mediation. Directive (EU) 2019/6335 on unfair trading practices is being revised, to address cases where farmers are forced to systematically sell below production costs, while maintaining the Common Agricultural Policy market orientation. The Commission may adopt exceptional support measures for market losses due to restrictions imposed for disease control. Under Regulation (EU) 2021/21156, countries may amend their CAP Strategic Plans to provide crisis payment and support investments to restore agricultural production after animal disease outbreaks, and grant aid in line with EU State aid rules.

E-10-2026-002478.t: Implementation of the Forced Labour Regulation and risks related to DPRK-linked products
qt: to the Commission César Luena (S&D), Danuše Nerudová (PPE), Hanna Gedin (The Left), Nikola Minchev (Renew), Vladimir Prebilič (Verts/ALE) Subject:
Implementation of the Forced Labour Regulation and risks related to DPRKlinked products

The Democratic People’s Republic of North Korea (DPRK)1 operates a system of stateimposed forced labour that is well documented. Reports2 have found forced labour institutionalised across multiple sectors. Estimates3 indicate that over 100 000 North Korean nationals work overseas under state control. Investigations have traced the products of this labour into global supply chains, many relabeled as Chinese-made products before export and processed in facilities supplying EU markets, including the European Parliament’s cafeteria. The Commission is due to finalise the implementation guidelines for the Forced Labour Regulation4 and a forced labour risk database by the end of June 2026. State-imposed forced labour in the DPRK presents distinct due diligence challenges, as the coercive mechanism is the state itself. This raises questions as to whether the implementation of the regulation adequately addresses the risks. In this context: 1.
How will the Commission reflect the documented risk profile of the DPRK in the forced labour risk database in the light of the fact that related products are entering EU supply chains?

How will the Commission ensure that evidence on forced labour supply chains not covered by the regulation’s specified sources can be considered, including where such findings are validated by eligible bodies?
How can the Commission financially support non-governmental organisations documenting the situation of forced labour in the DPRK?

Reports (2) have found forced labour institutionalised across multiple sectors. Estimates (3) indicate that over 100 000 North Korean nationals work overseas under state control. (19 August 2026) As recognised in recent UN General Assembly (1) and UN Human Rights Council (2) resolutions, the use of forced labour in and by the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK) has become institutionalised and includes the exploitation of workers sent abroad, often for the purpose of generating income for the DPRK government. The database of forced labour risks established under Article 8 of the Forced Labour Regulation (3) will include an indicative and non-exhaustive list of forced labour risks and products in specific geographic areas. If eligible sources confirm the existence of forced labour risks connected to overseas workers from a particular country, the database will take into account the specific country or region where the products are produced or made. The Commission is responsible for establishing, maintaining and updating the risk database. In line with the requirements of the regulation, the risk database will rely exclusively on evidence-based, verifiable and independent information that has been made publicly available by international organisations, institutional organisations or research and academic organisations. The Commission will assess and decide on a case-by-case basis inclusion of specific sources taking into account those eligibility criteria. As part of the implementation of the regulation, the Commission and Member States may consider the development of cooperation initiatives and accompanying measures to support the efforts of relevant stakeholders, including civil society organisations, to tackle forced labour.

E-10-2026-002477.t: Ramifications of the fraud scandal at the German Agency for International Cooperation (GIZ) in Yemen
qt: to the Commission Marc Jongen (ESN) Subject:

According to media reports, since 2022 the German Agency for International Cooperation (GIZ) has been investigating allegations of fraud in projects in Yemen. These are said to have involved such offences as currency manipulation and falsified fuel expense claims; 24 staff members have already been suspended. Insiders estimate the potential losses to run into the tens of millions. Although initial indications emerged several years ago and the relevant ministry states it has been aware of the matter since 2023, the investigations are still ongoing1. The case raises fundamental questions about the oversight of development funds in fragile states, particularly as the EU intends to continue providing substantial funding for development projects under the ‘NDICI/Europe in the World’ instrument. 1.
How many cases of fraud, embezzlement or other serious financial irregularities have been detected in EU-funded development projects since 2016, and what was the total amount of losses in each case?
What new, binding control, audit and early-warning arrangements are being introduced under the ‘NDICI/Europe in the World’ instrument, and how do they differ from the procedures currently in place?
Does the Commission intend to temporarily or permanently exclude organisations or contractors from EU funding in the event of serious control failures in the future?

E-10-2026-002476.t: Promoting ‘freedom to stay’ for the completion of the single market for a more resilient Europe and a locally anchored industrial policy
qt: to the Commission Camilla Laureti (S&D), Alexandra Mehnert (PPE), Benedetta Scuderi (Verts/ALE), Maravillas Abadía Jover (PPE), Thomas Bajada (S&D), Stefano Bonaccini (S&D), Gabriele Bischoff (S&D), Aurore Lalucq (S&D), Elisabetta Gualmini (Renew), Nora Mebarek (S&D), Giorgio Gori (S&D), Pierre Jouvet (S&D), Giuseppe Lupo (S&D), Annalisa Corrado (S&D), Thomas Waitz (Verts/ALE), Pasquale Tridico (The Left), Pierfrancesco Maran (S&D), Branislav Ondruš (NI) Subject:

The Letta Report underscores the need to further deepen the single market by strengthening its resilience and ensuring that economic activity remains rooted across all regions. It stresses that the single market should enable citizens to prosper wherever they live, rather than pushing them to relocate in search of opportunities. In this context, forging stronger connections between the single market, industrial policy and territorial cohesion is essential. Services of General Interest (SGI) play a crucial role in sustaining local economic ecosystems and supporting industrial development. In light of the above: 1.
How does the Commission plan to integrate the ‘freedom to stay’ as a guiding objective in the next MFF, ensuring that territorial cohesion, social resilience and competitiveness are strengthened?
Does the Commission intend to create a ‘freedom to stay’ indicator, designed to complement the European Semester, translating cohesion and SGI objectives into measurable outcomes?
What follow-up actions does the Commission plan to take to implement Letta’s proposal for developing an action plan on high-quality SGIs in Europe?

It stresses that the single market should enable citizens to prosper wherever they live, rather than pushing them to relocate in search of opportunities. In this context, forging stronger connections between the single market, industrial policy and territorial cohesion is essential. Services of General Interest (SGI) play a crucial role in sustaining local economic ecosystems and supporting industrial development. In light of the above: 1.
How does the Commission plan to integrate the ‘freedom to stay’ as a guiding objective in the next MFF, ensuring that territorial cohesion, social resilience and competitiveness are strengthened?
Does the Commission intend to create a ‘freedom to stay’ indicator, designed to complement the European Semester, translating cohesion and SGI objectives into measurable outcomes?
What follow-up actions does the Commission plan to take to implement Letta’s proposal for developing an action plan on high-quality SGIs in Europe?

(4 September 2026) 1. The Commission proposal for the European Fund (1) for the period 2028-2034 mentions ‘fostering the attractiveness of territories to support the right to stay’ under specific objective ‘support the Union’s prosperity among regions’ (Article 3(1)(a) (1)). Strengthening territorial cohesion, social resilience and competitiveness require integrated and place-based approaches across many areas to support the conditions communities need to prosper. The future National and Regional Partnership Plans will provide a coherent and simplified framework to support business opportunities, employment and skills, connectivity, innovation, access to services and infrastructure, thus ensuring that territories experiencing depopulation and economic challenges remain attractive places to live and work. 2. The Commission is now analysing the 704 contributions, including best practices and possible ways to support the ‘Right to Stay’. 3. Action is needed across many areas: fostering economic development, boosting competitiveness, and ensuring access to services. The availability and quality of services such as healthcare, education, childcare, public transport, digital infrastructure, directly influence individuals and families' residential decisions. E-10-2026-002475.t: Non-compliance with trans law in Spain
qt: to the Commission Irene Montero (The Left) Subject:

The Spanish Government approved Law 4/2023 of 28 February ensuring the real and effective equality of trans people and guaranteeing the rights of LGBTI+ people. Article 50 regulates changes of name and sex in identity documents for foreigners residing in Spain. The nineteenth final provision empowers the government to adopt any provisions necessary to roll out and implement this law, which it must do within one year of its entry into force. In addition, also within one year of entry into force, the government should have, by means of regulations, authorised procedures for the adaptation of documents issued to foreigners. Three years have passed and the government has not made the relevant changes to ensure that foreigners residing in Spain have this right. 1.
Will the Commission require the Spanish Government to implement the law to guarantee fundamental rights to foreign nationals – often citizens of other Member States – residing in Spain?
What action will the Commission take in the case that non-compliance continues?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (11.8.2026) Equality and non-discrimination are founding values of the EU enshrined in the Treaty on European Union, the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union and the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union1. National authorities are responsible to determine the conditions and procedures for legal gender recognition, in compliance with fundamental rights and in accordance with their constitution and the obligations arising under international instruments’ obligations. The Commission’s LGBTIQ+ Equality Strategy 2026-20302 aims at fighting discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual, trans, intersex and queer (LGBTIQ+) people to build a true Union of Equality. Among other things, it outlines that the Commission will facilitate exchanges of best practices among Member States for legal gender recognition based on selfdetermination. The Commission will continue to closely monitor the situation of LGBTIQ+ people across the EU within the limits of its competences, and to use all the instruments at its disposal to uphold EU law in Member States.

E-10-2026-002473.t: Delay and lack of transparency in the publication of the supporting study underpinning the SWD evaluation of the Tobacco Products Directive
qt: to the Commission Mariateresa Vivaldini (ECR), Daniele Polato (ECR), Sergio Berlato (ECR), Stefano Cavedagna (ECR), Chiara Gemma (ECR), Pietro Fiocchi (ECR), Denis Nesci (ECR) Subject:

The Commission’s staff working document evaluating the Tobacco Products Directive (SWD(2026)0111) states that the evaluation ‘draws on a broad and diverse evidence base, including a supporting study conducted by an external contractor’. A review of the SWD reveals that the 2025 study conducted by Open Evidence entitled ‘Study supporting the Evaluation of the Tobacco Control Acquis’ is referenced throughout the document, including in footnotes 92, 143, 148, 212, 221, 250 and 262, among others. Given the frequency and nature of these references, the study appears to constitute one of the primary evidentiary pillars of the evaluation. However, the study did not appear to be publicly available immediately after the publication of the SWD’s conclusions. Meaningful scrutiny of the SWD’s conclusions necessarily requires immediate and easy access to the evidence on which those conclusions rest. The unavailability of this study has significantly impacted the ability to assess the robustness, completeness and objectivity of the evaluation. 1.
Can the Commission provide an explanation for the delay in the immediate release of Open Evidence’s supporting study, and confirm that it is now fully accessible?

Does the Commission consider this procedure consistent with its Better Regulation commitments and transparency obligations, given that an evaluation of the SWD relies heavily on an external study that was not made publicly available at the same time of the publication of the conclusions?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.9.2026) The evaluation1 of the Tobacco Products Directive2 and the Tobacco Advertising Directive3 was carried out in full compliance with the better regulation framework. The data sources, methodologies, and analytical approaches underpinning the evaluation are described in the accompanying Commission Staff Working Document and its Annexes4, ensuring transparency regarding the evidence used. Following the publication of the Staff Working Document, the Commission also published all supporting documents that were not yet publicly accessible at the time of its publication, including the external study referred to in the question. These documents are now fully accessible on the Commission's webpage on the evaluation of the legislative framework for tobacco control5. The short interval between the publication of the Staff Working Document and that of the supporting study reflected the time required to complete the Commission’s internal publication process for the study.

E-10-2026-002472.t: Ensuring fair treatment of cultural goods in EU customs reform
qt: to the Commission Ernő Schaller-Baross (PfE), Enikő Győri (PfE) Subject:

Within the framework of the EU’s customs reform, the exemption from customs duties for consignments valued below EUR 150 will be abolished. However, the framework does not appear to introduce any meaningful distinction between product categories, meaning that fastfashion items from non-EU countries, books, or press products may all fall under the same customs duties and related fees. As a result, situations may arise in which even low-value newspapers or magazines are subject to the same flat-rate charge and handling fee as other imported goods of similar value. Given that cultural goods – in particular books, newspapers and periodicals – are essential for access to information, media pluralism and cultural diversity, it is questionable whether the current design of the rules adequately reflects the specific nature and societal value of these products. I would therefore like to ask the Commission the following: 1.
Does it intend to consider any measures for cultural and educational goods – particularly books and newspapers – in relation to handling and administrative fees affected by the Customs Union reform?
Has the Commission taken into account existing global practices that provide customs or fee exemptions or reductions for cultural goods, in particular books and press products?
at: (English version) to the Commission Ernő Schaller-Baross (PfE), Enikő Győri (PfE) (16 June 2026) Subject: Ensuring fair treatment of cultural goods in EU customs reform Within the framework of the EU’s customs reform, the exemption from customs duties for consignments valued below EUR 150 will be abolished. However, the framework does not appear to introduce any meaningful distinction between product categories, meaning that fast-fashion items from non-EU countries, books, or press products may all fall under the same customs duties and related fees. As a result, situations may arise in which even low-value newspapers or magazines are subject to the same flat-rate charge and handling fee as other imported goods of similar value. Given that cultural goods — in particular books, newspapers and periodicals — are essential for access to information, media pluralism and cultural diversity, it is questionable whether the current design of the rules adequately reflects the specific nature and societal value of these products. I would therefore like to ask the Commission the following: 1.
Does it intend to consider any measures for cultural and educational goods — particularly books and newspapers — in relation to handling and administrative fees affected by the Customs Union reform?
Has the Commission taken into account existing global practices that provide customs or fee exemptions or reductions for cultural goods, in particular books and press products?

(12 August 2026) Within the context of the EU Customs Reform, Council Regulation (EU) 2026/382 abolishes the EUR 150 threshold-based customs duty exemption and imposes, from 1 July 2026 until 1 July 2028, a temporary EUR 3 customs duty per item in consignments valued up to EUR 150 and sold in distance sales. This in principle includes books and newspapers. However, imported goods, including books and newspapers, can benefit from existing duty exemptions or preferential treatment if they fulfil the relevant conditions. Books and newspapers printed in third countries and meeting the rules of origin with those third countries for which the EU has preferential trade agreements can benefit from preferential duty rates, if the appropriate proof of origin is provided when required to the customs authorities. Pursuant to the Duty Relief Regulation (1), the duty-free import of certain educational, scientific and cultural materials will still be possible, provided that certain conditions are met. For example, it will be possible to import duty-free microfilms of books, children’s picture books or colouring books, maps, and scientific charts and diagrams, as long as the advertising contained therein does not cover more than 25% of the surface. Regulation (EU) 2019/880 regulates more widely the introduction and import of cultural goods into the EU but it generally applies to goods with a minimum value threshold of EUR 18000 and it is therefore not relevant for goods to which the temporary EUR 3 duty applies.
Regulation (EC) No 1186/2009.

E-10-2026-002471.t: Privatisation of SATA Internacional and SATA Handling and protecting the Azores’ transport links
qt: to the Commission Catarina Martins (The Left) Subject:

The decision to grant aid to the SATA Group was approved by decisions C(2022) 3816 and C(2025) 9277, with the privatisation of SATA Internacional and SATA Handling forming part of the plan. However, moving Azores Airlines’ liabilities to the national balance sheet may be tantamount to an economic advantage qualifying as new State aid within the meaning of Article 107 TFEU, in the event that it changes the authorised conditions or distorts competition. What is more, the sale of 100 % of SATA Handling in an island market that is reliant on regional public services is cause for serious concern. In view of this: 1.
Does the Commission consider that the full privatisation of SATA Handling in a small, island market that has no real competition could lead to a de facto private monopoly on ground handling services?

Is the Commission willing to study a review of the plan, which includes divestment of 100 % of SATA Handling, if the Member State puts forward an alternative that keeps the activity in the public sphere on continuity of service grounds?

Is the Commission willing to assess alternatives to the ongoing privatisation model for the two companies if there is proof of significant shortcomings, a risk of further aid or a threat to territorial continuity?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (26.8.2026) The Commission’s Decision of 2022 authorised a EUR 453 million aid to bring SATA Air Açores (‘SATA')1 back to viability in line with the Guidelines for rescuing and restructuring undertakings in difficulty (the ‘Guidelines’)2. To ensure that distortions of competition remained limited whilst securing return to viability of SATA, Portugal committed that SATA would divest activities that are not central to its regional airline business, such as ground handling in some airports and airfields. Indeed, the Commission Decision considers the divestment of non-core activities as necessary also for the credibility of SATA’s financial projections3. Hence, after restructuring, SATA should only discharge public service obligations and services of general economic interest to the benefit of the Azorean community. To prevent abuses in ground-handling, Portugal has both regulatory and competition law instruments. Under the Guidelines4 a Member State may request changes to the restructuring plan, but the revised plan must still show a return to viability within a reasonable timescale and, if the restructuring costs are increased, the own contribution must also increase. Furthermore, if the proposed measures to limit distortions of competition are more limited, the amount of aid must be reduced, as was the case in the amending decision adopted by the Commission at Portugal’s request in 2025 to extend the timeline for divestments5. The initial Commission decision already considered that SATA could not withstand further divestments or withdrawals of capacity without impairing its return to viability6.

E-10-2026-002470.t: Use of budgetary headroom for the EUR 90 billion support loan to Ukraine
qt: to the Commission Tom Vandendriessche (PfE) Subject:
Use of budgetary headroom for the EUR 90 billion support loan to Ukraine

According to the Commission and the Council, the debt servicing costs of the EUR 90 billion support loan to Ukraine – including interest, issuance and liquidity costs – are borne by the EU budget. At the same time, the 2026 draft budget shows that NextGenerationEU interest costs are already putting pressure on the margins available under the current MFF, requiring the mobilisation of additional instruments over and above the MFF ceilings. How does the Commission justify the use of the same budgetary margins and emergency instruments for additional joint EU debt issuance, when in fact the existing NGEU debt service already leaves no budgetary headroom within the current MFF margins?
at: (English version) to the Commission Tom Vandendriessche (PfE) (16 June 2026) Subject: Use of budgetary headroom for the EUR 90 billion support loan to Ukraine According to the Commission and the Council, the debt servicing costs of the EUR 90 billion support loan to Ukraine — including interest, issuance and liquidity costs — are borne by the EU budget. At the same time, the 2026 draft budget shows that NextGenerationEU interest costs are already putting pressure on the margins available under the current MFF, requiring the mobilisation of additional instruments over and above the MFF ceilings. How does the Commission justify the use of the same budgetary margins and emergency instruments for additional joint EU debt issuance, when in fact the existing NGEU debt service already leaves no budgetary headroom within the current MFF margins? (4 August 2026) To address Ukraine’s immediate needs for continued financing in 2026 and 2027, the 2021- 2027 Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) Regulation (1) was amended to enable the new Ukraine Support Loan of EUR 90 billion (2). This will provide Ukraine with urgently needed military assistance to strengthen its defence capabilities (EUR 60 billion) and budget support (EUR 30 billion). To provide concessional support to Ukraine and contribute to ensuring the continued sustainability of Ukraine’s public finances, the EU budget will cover the debt service costs. In 2027, the debt service costs to cover the related borrowing operations are expected to amount to EUR 1.15 billion. In line with the requirements set out in the new Article 10c of the MFF Regulation (3), in the draft budget of 2027 the Commission has proposed to finance these costs through budgetary availabilities under the ceilings (notably savings from excess provisioning of the European Fund for Sustainable Development (4) in heading 6) and existing special instruments (availabilities in the Single Margin Instrument and Flexibility Instrument (5)). As a result, it would not be necessary to mobilise the new Ukraine Support Loan Instrumen t (6), nor cut any existing programmes, thereby leaving almost half a billion euro in margins under the MFF ceilings for 2027. For the period 2028-2034, the ongoing negotiations take into account the need to finance the debt service costs of the Ukraine Support Loan. The Commission closely monitors EU’s contingent liabilities and their budgetary implications. The Commission will publish an updated assessment of the headroom in the annual report in line with Article 256 of the Financial Regulation (7). The 2026 edition of the report will be published in the autumn 2026.

E-10-2026-002469.t: EU support for municipalities neighbouring Kraków-Balice Airport and other strategic TEN-T network airports
qt: to the Commission Arkadiusz Mularczyk (ECR) Subject:

The agreement on stronger air passenger rights confirms how important air transport is to citizen mobility and the functioning of the European Union’s single market. However, the dynamic development of airports also generates significant social, environmental and infrastructure costs, largely borne by local authorities. One example is Jan Paul II Kraków-Balice Airport, Poland’s second-largest airport and one of the fastest growing airports in Central Europe. The municipality of Zabierzów, the municipality of Liszki and the city of Kraków are facing increasing costs related to aircraft noise, necessary expansions of the road and public transport systems, environmental protection and spatial planning constraints resulting from the operation of infrastructure that is important at both national and European scale. 1.
Has the Commission analysed the impact that large airports have on the financial situation and quality of life of neighbouring municipalities?

Does the Commission intend to propose a dedicated financial mechanism or programme under the future EU Multiannual Financial Framework 2028–2034 to support municipalities and regions bearing above-average operating costs of the TEN-T network’s aviation infrastructure, particularly through financing investments to reduce noise, improve public transport, develop road infrastructure and protect the environment? This mechanism would allow for a fairer distribution of the costs and benefits of developing European transport infrastructure and would strengthen public acceptance for further development of strategic airports.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (28.8.2026) The Commission has not undertaken such analyses. The effects that airports may have on their surroundings are, however, reflected in several strands of EU legislation. This includes Directive 2002/49/EC on environmental noise1, Regulation (EU) No 598/2014 which sets rules and procedures with regard to the introduction of noise-related operating restrictions at Union airports2 and a growing body of air quality, environmental assessment and nature legislation. This allows the Commission to monitor environmental and infrastructure-related impacts of airport activity. The detailed assessment of local social, planning and budgetary consequences for municipalities remains, under the principle of subsidiarity, primarily a matter for national, regional and local authorities. In any event, several studies show that air connectivity enabled by airports is key for growth, jobs, social cohesion and vital for EU regions3. In 2025, a report on the impact of Polish airports on regions found that Kraków-Balice airport had a direct impact of PLN 470,7 million on the Małopolska region’s economy and an induced impact of PLN 240 million and 1.700 jobs, bringing a gross value added of PLN 1,56 billion to the Polish economy4. The Commission has not proposed a dedicated financial mechanism for this purpose. Under the next multiannual financial framework, support for such investments may be available through different EU funding programmes in line with the objectives and rules of the relevant funds. Any supported project will need to comply with relevant EU environmental legislation.

E-10-2026-002468.t: Risk to residents and the environment from the wind farm in a Natura area on Mount Othrys
qt: to the Commission Kostas Papadakis (NI) Subject:

A wind farm with 21 wind turbines 249 meters high is to be built around the Gerakovouni peak of Mount Othrys, which is otherwise part of the Natura 2000 network. Due to the promotion of RES, the people continue to pay extremely expensive bills. The claim that RES will contribute to reducing prices has not been confirmed anywhere, given that in Greece almost half of the electricity demand is now covered by RES (46 %) and prices are skyrocketing. In view of the above: 1.

What is the Commission's position regarding the demand by residents and mass organisations to immediately stop the plans that are detrimental to the interests of residents and the environment, as a result of the ‘Green Deal’, which dictates investments in RES with the sole criterion of increasing the profitability of ‘green business groups’?

What is the Commission’s position regarding the fact that the designation of an area as Natura not only does not protect it from business exploitation, but – on the contrary – signals the rush of business groups in order to make a profit, destroying the wider region’s last remaining natural lungs, such as Mount Othrys, one of the areas of rare natural beauty with rich vegetation, herbs, etc.?

What is the Commission’s position regarding the fact that ordinary working-class people will not only feel no benefit from this development, but that the impasses they experience, including energy poverty, will be exacerbated as a result of the ‘green transition’ itself and energy liberalisation?

E-10-2026-002467.t: Exclusion of EU accession prospects for Armenia as a matter of principle
qt: to the Commission Mieke Andriese (PfE) Subject:

The recent elections in Armenia point towards the adoption of a pro-Western policy. In the past, however, we have seen how the Commission has sought to exploit such situations to push through hasty, activist enlargement agendas. The fast-track procedures concerning Ukraine’s and Moldova’s candidacy for membership, prompted by geopolitical shifts, are clear examples of this. We urgently need to learn from this – geopolitical changes should never be used as a justification for European expansion or top-down centralisation from Brussels. The EU should primarily focus on its core economic mission and respect the sovereignty of European nations. 1.

Does the Commission share the view that, given its fundamentally European character, the European Union must adhere to clear geographical boundaries, and that the prospect of Armenia’s accession should therefore be definitively ruled out?

Is the Commission willing to officially confirm that the Union has no intention of offering Armenia, now or in the future, the prospect of accession or a pre-accession process, in order to avoid raising false expectations?

How will the Commission ensure that current and future cooperation with Armenia is limited solely to regular diplomatic, economic and trade relations and does not serve as a stepping stone towards political unification or institutional integration?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (28.7.2026) The Commission has taken note of the recent elections in Armenia and welcomes the country's continued interest in deepening its relations with the European Union. The law on launching the European Union accession process, adopted by the Armenian Parliament in March 2025, is an important symbolic step and reflects Armenia's political aspirations. However, it does not constitute a formal application for membership. Under Article 49 of the Treaty on European Union1, accession to the European Union is governed by the procedures and conditions laid down in the Treaties. The accession process begins with the submission of a formal application, which Armenia has not submitted to date. Any decision to admit a new Member State requires the unanimous agreement of all Member States and consent of the European Parliament. The European Union and Armenia continue to deepen their partnership through the implementation of the Comprehensive and Enhanced Partnership Agreement2, which provides the framework for extensive cooperation. The Strategic Agenda for the EU-Armenia Partnership3, agreed in December 2025, further reinforces this cooperation by setting out more ambitious joint priorities across a broad range of areas.
1 Article 49 of the Treaty on European Union: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/EN/legal-content/summary/treaty-on-

european-union-joining-the-eu.html. 2 EU-Armenia Comprehensive and Enhanced Partnership Agreement: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legalcontent/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:22018A0126(01). 3 Strategic Agenda for the EU-Armenia Partnership: https://enlargement.ec.europa.eu/document/download/131d04c9-dc44-4484-b7cffcf8e621593a_en?filename=Strategic%20Agenda%20for%20the%20EU-Armenia%20Partnership.pdf.

E-10-2026-002466.t: Escalating neo-Ottoman rhetoric by the Turkish Interior Minister Mustafa Çiftçi and threats against the State of Israel
qt: to the Commission Geadis Geadi (ECR) Subject:

With this question I would like to condemn the recent statements by Turkish Interior Minister Mustafa Çiftçi, who expressed the wish to one day become ‘Jerusalem’s Governor’ and suggested that the city would eventually return to Ottoman rule. He further declared that, just as Türkiye witnessed the so-called ‘liberation’ of Damascus, Aleppo and Nagorno-Karabakh, it may also witness the ‘liberation of Jerusalem’.1 These remarks form part of a broader pattern of revisionist and neo-Ottoman rhetoric emanating from senior Turkish officials, challenging the sovereignty and territorial integrity of neighbouring states and contributing to instability across the Eastern Mediterranean and the Middle East. Such statements are particularly alarming given Türkiye’s continued military occupation of part of the Republic of Cyprus and its persistent threats against the sovereign rights of EU Member States. In the light of the above: 1.
Does the Commission condemn these statements by the Turkish Minister of the Interior?

Given that Türkiye continues to receive substantial EU financial assistance, does the Commission intend to examine whether repeated revisionist claims and threats to the sovereignty of third states should have consequences for EU funding and political engagement with Türkiye?
https://www.dailysabah.com/politics/turkish-interior-minister-hopes-for-liberation-of-jerusalem/news
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (14.8.2026) The EU has stated repeatedly its deep concern about such statements, expressing its expectation by Türkiye to de-escalate tensions in the interest of regional stability in the Eastern Mediterranean1. In particular, the Commission has underlined in the 2025 enlargement report on Türkiye that the latter is expected to make an unequivocal commitment to good neighbourly relations, international agreements and the peaceful settlement of disputes having recourse, if necessary, to the International Court of Justice2.
1 https://www.consilium.europa.eu/media/57442/2022-06-2324-euco-conclusions-en.pdf. 2 https://enlargement.ec.europa.eu/document/download/4bb4ddd1-4f20-4ee0-92db-

E-10-2026-002465.t: Volkswagen Group prevents users from accessing free, real-time charging data from their electric cars
qt: to the Commission Bruno Tobback (S&D) Subject:

Since 27 May 2026, Volkswagen Group has been making it impossible for VW owners/users to retrieve recharging data from their electric car in real time and free of charge. Volkswagen is said to be invoking cybersecurity as a reason for blocking the data. However, Volkswagen Group offers the same data for a fee. On eu-data-act.drivesomethinggreater.com, Volkswagen provides the owner only with a limited amount of data, and with a delay; this is therefore not an equivalent alternative. This is not in line with the EU Data Act, which requires that data must be made available to users and/or a third-party service provider of their choice easily, securely, free of charge, continuously and in real time, with the same quality as the data available to the data holder. Not only does this change by Volkswagen Group prevent owners from accessing their own data free of charge and in real time, it also hinders the development and use of tools designed to utilise this data to devise optimal charging scenarios that benefit individual users, the efficient use of renewable energy and the stability of the electricity grid. 1.
Is the Commission aware of this practice by Volkswagen Group?
Does it consider it to be in breach of Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 (Data Act)?
If so, what action will the Commission take to monitor and enforce the correct application of the EU Data Act and to address the potential infringement?
at: (English version) to the Commission Bruno Tobback (S&D) (16 June 2026) Subject: Volkswagen Group prevents users from accessing free, real-time charging data from their electric cars Since 27 May 2026, Volkswagen Group has been making it impossible for VW owners/users to retrieve recharging data from their electric car in real time and free of charge. Volkswagen is said to be invoking cybersecurity as a reason for blocking the data. However, Volkswagen Group offers the same data for a fee. On eu-data-act.drivesomethinggreater.com, Volkswagen provides the owner only with a limited amount of data, and with a delay; this is therefore not an equivalent alternative. This is not in line with the EU Data Act, which requires that data must be made available to users and/or a third-party service provider of their choice easily, securely, free of charge, continuously and in real time, with the same quality as the data available to the data holder. Not only does this change by Volkswagen Group prevent owners from accessing their own data free of charge and in real time, it also hinders the development and use of tools designed to utilise this data to devise optimal charging scenarios that benefit individual users, the efficient use of renewable energy and the stability of the electricity grid. 1.
Is the Commission aware of this practice by Volkswagen Group?
Does it consider it to be in breach of Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 (Data Act)?

3. If so, what action will the Commission take to monitor and enforce the correct application of the EU Data Act and to address the potential infringement? (31 August 2026) The Commission is aware of reports on changes in Volkswagen’s method of disseminating to users relevant information about their electric vehicle, namely about the state of charge of the battery. The Data Act (1) (‘DA’) allows manufacturers to use different technical means to make available data in scope. Where the Data Act requires continuous and real-time data access, the technical means should enable this. While access is free of charge for users, reasonable compensation may be asked from third parties. Specifically for electric vehicles, Art. 20a (2) of the Renewable Energy Directive (3) (‘RED’) obliges Member States to require that vehicle manufacturers make available the data points in question in real time, under non-discriminatory terms and at no cost, in accordance with the data protection rules. Commission guidance (4) provides helpful input to Member States in how to implement the provision. The transposition check of the rules under RED is ongoing, with several Member States having already fully transposed that provision. Without prejudice to the Commission’s role as guardian of the Treaties, the monitoring and enforcement of EU law lies primarily with the competent national authorities and courts. Under the DA, users of electric vehicles can enforce their rights directly against the data holder before the national courts, in line with national procedural rules. In addition, natural and legal persons have the right to lodge a complaint with a national competent authority, if they consider their rights under the DA have been infringed. |(⸱1|)∙ |(⸱2|)∙

Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 December 2023 on harmonised rules on fair access to and use of data and amending Regulation (EU) 2017/2394 and Directive (EU) 2020/1828 (Data Act), OJ L, 2023/2854 of 22.12.2023. Article 20a(3), second subparagraph RED: ‘Member States shall adopt measures to require that vehicle manufacturers make available, in real-time, in-vehicle data related to the battery state of health, battery state of charge, battery power set point, battery capacity, and, where appropriate, the location of electric vehicles, to electric vehicle owners and users, as well as to third parties acting on the owners’ and users’ behalf, such as electricity market participants and electromobility service providers, under non- discriminatory terms and at no cost, in accordance with the data protection rules, and in addition to further requirements with regard to type approval and market surveillance laid down in Regulation (EU) 2018/858 of the European Parliament and of the Council’. Directive (EU) 2018/2001 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 11 December 2018 on the promotion of the use of energy from renewable sources, OJ L, 328/82 of 21.12.2018, as amended by Directive (EU) 2023/2413. Commission notice on the application of requirements for battery-related data sharing under the revised Renewable Energy Directive, OJ C, 2025/4104 of 25.07.2025.

Given the relevance of the continuous availability of battery data in the context of the transition towards a greater use of renewable energy resources, the Commission will closely monitor the situation and interact with relevant competent authorities.

E-10-2026-002464.t: IMEC corridor prospects and impact of competing regional transport and connectivity projects
qt: to the Commission Nikolas Farantouris (S&D) Subject:

The IMEC corridor is a strategically important connectivity project, supported by the European Union, the United States, India, Saudi Arabia and the UAE, with the aim of strengthening trade, energy and transport networks between Europe, the Middle East and the Indo-Pacific1. However, according to recent official statements by Turkish and Saudi Arabian government officials, the two countries plan to develop a rail link in competition with IMEC2, creating new data regarding the strategic architecture of connectivity corridors in the wider region. Given that IMEC has been presented as a project of high geoeconomic and geopolitical importance for European competitiveness, energy security and the diversification of trade routes: 1.
Does the Commission still consider IMEC strategically and economically viable in light of the Ankara-Riyadh initiative?
How does the Commission assess the participation of candidate countries, such as Türkiye, in projects competing with initiatives supported by the European Union and its strategic partners?

What specific measures does the Commission intend to take to ensure the implementation and geoeconomic effectiveness of IMEC, as well as to strengthen the Member States that are investing in this strategic route and expect significant economic, energy and geopolitical benefits from its operation?

https://global-gateway-forum.ec.europa.eu/news/global-gateway-forum-accelerating-digitaltransformation-through-imec-eu-africa-india-digital-2025-10-10_en. 2 https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/turkey-saudi-arabia-aim-build-rail-link-with-jordan-syriaminister-says-2026-06-14/. 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.9.2026) The Commission considers the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC) a strategically important initiative. Its core objective is to strengthen connectivity between Europe, the Middle East and the Indo-Pacific, and support resilient, efficient and sustainable links in the areas of transport, energy and digital infrastructure. Recent events, notably the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, have made IMEC more relevant than ever, reinforcing the need for diversified supply routes. This is fully acknowledged by IMEC signatories who regularly meet at senior officials’ level. The Commission, alongside other IMEC signatories, considers IMEC to be a ‘network of corridors’ which can extend beyond the initial route envisaged in the Memorandum of Understanding. In this context, IMEC is envisaged as a broader and more flexible network. The EU sees IMEC as part of a set of diverse but interconnected initiatives that improve connectivity between Europe, the Middle East and India, promoting inclusiveness, complementarity and flexibility rather than competition. This applies to the Ankara–Riyadh initiative and to other routes under development in the region. The Commission will continue to work with IMEC signatories and relevant stakeholders to advance viable projects and collectively support the broader objective of diversified, resilient and efficient connectivity, therefore maximising the geoeconomic effectiveness of IMEC.

E-10-2026-002462.t: Regional autonomy when implementing the 2028-2034 MFF via national and regional partnership plans
qt: to the Commission Barbara Bonte (PfE) Subject:

The Commission is proposing that various funds under shared management, including cohesion and agricultural funds, are brought together under national and regional partnership plans. This raises questions for federal Member States such as Belgium, where important powers relating to cohesion, agriculture and regional economic policy have been constitutionally assigned to the regions. Analyses by the European Parliament also highlight risks to territorial cohesion, multi-level governance and the role of regions. 1.

How will the Commission guarantee that the NRPP structure remains in line with the principles of subsidiarity and proportionality, in particular in federal Member States where powers in the areas of cohesion and agriculture have been constitutionally assigned to the regions, and what formal safeguards will it put in place for these competent regional governments?

Can the Commission approve a national and regional partnership plan if competent regional governments within a federal Member State formally object to the proposed distribution or governance of the funds?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (5.8.2026) 1. Member States are responsible for designing their National and Regional Partnership Plans (NRPPs) and for setting up their governance arrangements in line with their administrative, institutional and legal framework. As set out in Article 6 of the Commission’s proposal1, NRPPs must be prepared and implemented in partnership with regional, local, urban, rural authorities and stakeholders in accordance with the multi-level governance principle and a bottom-up approach. The proposal enables regional chapters as part of the NRPPs. The Commission’s President proposed in November 2025 additional clarifications to reinforce the role of regions in the design, implementation and evaluation of the Plans, including safeguards to prevent significant decrease in allocations to transition and more developed regions (unless justified based on objective criteria). The governance model for the NRPPs can be built on the existing implementation structures. 2. After the Member State’s submission of a NRPP, the Commission will need to assess whether the Plan complies with all applicable requirements, notably Article 22 of the proposal, including how the partnership principle in the preparation and implementation of the Plan is respected, and compliance with the European code of conduct on partnership. As part of its assessment, the Commission may make observations to Member States and request additional information.
1 COM(2025) 565 final/2 : https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-
content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX%3A52025PC0565R%2801%29.

E-10-2026-002461.t: Rushed introduction of reporting obligations under the EU Methane Regulation
qt: to the Commission Barbara Bonte (PfE) Subject:

According to recent sectoral analyses, the implementation requirements that will apply from 2027 under the EU Methane Regulation could mean that a significant portion of the EU’s existing oil and gas imports can no longer be declared compliant, due to a lack of reporting, certification and verification mechanisms at suppliers outside the EU. These analyses warn of higher energy prices, supply problems and additional pressure on European industry. 1.

Why has the Commission decided to bring the reporting, certification and verification obligations into force from as early as 2027 when, according to sectoral analyses, only a limited number of third countries will be able to meet these requirements from a technical and administrative perspective?
What are the results of any research that the Commission has carried out relating to the impact of this rushed introduction on energy security, supplies and the competitiveness of European industry?
Is the Commission prepared to postpone the introduction of these obligations until an adequate, internationally operational reporting and verification framework is in place?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (26.8.2026) The EU Methane Regulation1 and its obligations and deadlines are the result of an agreement between the co-legislators. The Commission’s initial proposal did not contain an obligation for importers to demonstrate Monitoring, Reporting and Verification (MRV) equivalence for their imports (Article 28); this obligation and its deadline were introduced in the ordinary legislative procedure. However, it is now the Commission’s duty to support and ensure its implementation. Compliance with these provisions can be demonstrated by achieving reporting equivalent to Level 5 of the voluntary Oil and Gas Methane Partnership 2.0 (OGMP) framework, complemented by independent verification of the reports. OGMP covers ca. 45% of global oil and gas production. Based on their assessment, by 2027 ca 70% of OGMP production would reach Level 5. Following the Parliament’s 2021 resolution calling on the Commission to make all fossil fuel imports into the Union conditional on compliance with EU rules on MRV, Leak Detection and Repair (LDAR) and on venting and flaring applicable to the entire supply chain2, the Commission examined options for mandatory MRV measures applicable to imports in the Impact Assessment3 accompanying the 2021 proposal. Based on the assessment, the Commission decided not to include such measures in its proposal. The Commission has no empowerment to postpone these obligations. Nevertheless, the Commission is providing support for companies and competent authorities to comply with them, notably through a recommendation on compliance solutions and public questions and answers. The Commission has also adopted a recommendation on a temporary suspension of penalties for non-compliance, reflecting the current security of supply context.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1787/oj/eng. 2 2021/2006(INI). 3 https://ec.europa.eu/transparency/documents-register/detail?ref=SWD(2021)459&lang=en (p.77-80).

E-10-2026-002460.t: Measurable results of reducing the administrative burden for companies
qt: to the Commission Barbara Bonte (PfE) Subject:

During a conference in Brussels, MIT research scientist Andrew McAfee1 stated that Europe is not suffering from a shortage of talent or innovation, but rather from an excess of bureaucracy and regulation. He pointed to European companies’ declining share in global value creation and warned that overregulation inhibits innovation and entrepreneurship. The Commission has committed to reducing the administrative and reporting burden by 25 % for companies and by 35 % for SMEs. However, companies say that they are still having to contend with increasing reporting, compliance and licensing requirements. 1.
What concrete, measurable reductions in the administrative burden has the Commission actually achieved for companies and SMEs since taking office?
What methodology forms the basis for measuring and independently verifying these burden reductions?
In euro, how much has actually been saved on annual compliance and reporting costs to date?

Andrew McAfee, speaking at the New Insights conference organised by De Tijd and L’Echo in Brussels, 9 June 2026. See: “Andrew McAfee (MIT): ‘Le problème de l’Europe, c’est vraiment la régulation’”, L’Echo, 9 June 2026. 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (19.8.2026) The European Commission is pursuing an ambitious simplification agenda to lighten the EU regulatory burden, while maintaining high regulatory standards. To achieve this, the Commission introduced burden reduction targets, a new small and medium-sized enterprise (SME) check and a reinforced competitiveness check, the stress testing of existing legislation, regulatory deep cleaning of the acquis and new consultation tools (implementation dialogues and reality checks). The Commission has put a target to lower the administrative burden by at least 25% for all businesses and by at least 35% for SMEs. This target requires cutting recurring administrative costs by EUR 37.5 billion over the Commission’s mandate. The 12 Omnibus and other simplification proposals put forward by the Commission by mid-2026 will translate in more than EUR 18 billion of annual administrative cost savings for companies of all sizes. In particular the SMEs would benefit from significant savings, for instance through the digital omnibus (EUR 860 million of administrative burden reduction) or through the proposed targeted revision of the EU rules for medical devices and in vitro diagnostics (EUR 1.5 billion of administrative burden reduction). The evidence and methodology for these estimates are laid out in Impact Assessments or Staff Working Documents accompanying the Commission’s proposals. The Regulatory Scrutiny Board, an independent body, provides central quality control and support for the Commission Impact Assessments. In April 2026 the Commission adopted its Communication ‘A Simpler, Clearer and Better Enforced EU Rulebook’1, which will result in more quality control being performed on a wider range of assessments supporting policy proposals.
1 COM(2026) 380 final: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/resource.html?uri=cellar:e3002437-4314-11f1-8095-
01aa75ed71a1.0001.02/DOC_1&format=PDF.

E-10-2026-002459.t: Securing the EU’s climate targets in the aviation sector
qt: to the Commission César Luena (S&D) Subject:

Major representatives of the aviation industry have recently acknowledged that reaching netzero emissions by 2050 is becoming increasingly unlikely due to delays in the production of sustainable aviation fuels (SAF), difficulties in the deployment of international emission reduction mechanisms and delays in the deployment of more efficient technologies. Given that a significant part of the European aviation industry’s decarbonisation strategy is based on these instruments and technologies, these statements raise doubts as to the credibility of the sector’s current emissions reduction trajectories. 1.
What is the Commission’s view of recent statements within the aviation industry1 on the feasibility of reaching climate neutrality by 2050?
Does the Commission consider current forecasts for SAF availability to be sufficient to meet the EU’s climate targets for the aviation sector?

If certain technological or market solutions are not developed at the expected pace, what additional measures does the Commission envisage to ensure that the aviation sector fully contributes to the EU’s climate targets without making them less ambitious?
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2026/jun/08/airline-industry-chiefs-willie-walsh-2050-netzero-unlikely 1
at: (English version) to the Commission César Luena (S&D) (15 June 2026) Subject: Securing the EU’s climate targets in the aviation sector Major representatives of the aviation industry have recently acknowledged that reaching net-zero emissions by 2050 is becoming increasingly unlikely due to delays in the production of sustainable aviation fuels (SAF), difficulties in the deployment of international emission reduction mechanisms and delays in the deployment of more efficient technologies. Given that a significant part of the European aviation industry’s decarbonisation strategy is based on these instruments and technologies, these statements raise doubts as to the credibility of the sector’s current emissions reduction trajectories. 1. What is the Commission’s view of recent statements within the aviation industry (1) on the feasibility of reaching climate neutrality by 2050? 2. Does the Commission consider current forecasts for SAF availability to be sufficient to meet the EU’s climate targets for the aviation sector? 3. If certain technological or market solutions are not developed at the expected pace, what additional measures does the Commission envisage to ensure that the aviation sector fully contributes to the EU’s climate targets without making them less ambitious? (14 August 2026) The Commission takes note of the statements made by some stakeholders and sees the transition of aviation towards climate neutrality as a major priority. The Commission is committed to implementing EU actions that are already in place, notably the ReFuelEU Aviation Regulation (1), the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) (2), and support for research and innovation. The Commission also reiterates its support to the global implementation of CORSIA (3). Sustainable aviation fuels (SAF) are today the leading technology to decarbonise aviation. ReFuelEU Aviation gives the longterm certainty to scale up SAF production and uptake. Current market developments indicate that SAF availability is on track to support the EU’s climate goals (4). SAF supply exceeded the 2% mandate in 2025, showing that ReFuelEU Aviation works. Its long-term predictability is essential for investments. Global SAF production has also ramped up in recent years (5). While SAF ramp-up is a reality, more investments are needed for synthetic fuels (eSAF). The Commission presented in 2025 the Sustainable Transport Investment Plan notably to stimulate eSAF production, by de-risking investments and facilitating offtake (6). It reconfirms the targets and is expected to mobilise at least EUR 2.9 billion by end of 2027. The EU ETS also saves 20 million allowances to support SAF and eSAF uptake in 2024 — 2030. The recent EU ETS review proposal adds an extra 110 million allowances for this purpose until 2040. Yet, SAF alone will not be enough to decarbonise aviation. It is therefore key to invest in disruptive technologies (electric, hybrid-electric, hydrogen aircraft), modernise and digitalise air traffic management and continue developing economic incentives to encourage airlines to decarbonise.
