E-10-2026-002458.t: Construction of a photovoltaic park in Preveza endangers residents, the environment and historical monuments for the profits of ‘green’ business groups
qt: to the Commission Lefteris Nikolaou-Alavanos (NI) Subject:

Residents, livestock breeders, farmers and grassroots organisations are protesting and expressing their strong opposition to the construction of a 1 000-acre photovoltaic park, with 141 791 monocrystalline silicon photovoltaic panels, in Kamarina, Preveza. The proposed site for the location of the photovoltaic park is even visible from the aforementioned monuments of major significance, such as the heroic rock of Zalongos, an historically preserved landmark, and Zongolopoulos’s sculpture-monument commemorating the Souliote heroines, as well as the archaeological park. Its construction and operation will have an impact on surface and groundwater and cause drastic changes in soil fertility. Accordingly: 1.

What is the Commission's position on the residents' demand to stop the installation of photovoltaic panels, which is harmful to residents, the environment and emblematic historical monuments, as a consequence of the implementation of the ‘Green Deal’, which dictates investments in RES with the sole criterion of increasing the profitability of ‘green business groups’?

What is the Commission's position on the fact that ordinary working-class people will not only feel no benefit from this development, but will be further afflicted by the impasses they are experiencing, including energy poverty and the unacceptable conditions imposed by energy groups, having the European Union directives of the ‘green transition’ itself and energy liberalisation (e.g. Directive (EU) 2019/944) as an ally for their profitability?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (19.8.2026) The European Green Deal accelerates renewable energy because it serves both citizens and the environment: it reduces greenhouse gas emissions, improves air and environment quality to the benefit of citizens’ health and safety, lowers dependence on imported fossil fuels and strengthens Europe’s energy security. Renewable energy projects can benefit local communities by creating local jobs, generating municipal revenues and providing direct benefits to nearby residents. The Renewable Energy Directive (RED)1 includes an obligation for Member States to promote public acceptance of renewable energy projects by means of direct and indirect participation of local communities. In December 2025, the Commission proposed the European Grids Package2 which includes sectorial measures on the authorisation procedures for large scale energy infrastructures and new public participation requirements under RED, including in relation to benefit-sharing. Renewable energy deployment also moderates electricity prices3. Renewables have very low operating costs and, when they enter the market, their cheaper production is sold before more polluting and expensive power generation means like gas. In Spain, for example, wind and solar growth has reduced the influence of expensive fossil generators on the electricity price by 75% since 20194. This is particularly beneficial for vulnerable and energy poor households. The assessment and authorisation of individual projects, including their location and possible environmental or cultural heritage impacts, is primarily a competence of the national authorities, in line with EU law on environmental assessment and public participation.

Directive (EU) 2018/2001, Regulation (EU) 2018/1999 and Directive 98/70/EC as regards the promotion of energy from renewable sources, and repealing Council Directive (EU) 2015/652, OJ L, 2023/2413, 31.10.2023. 2 https://energy.ec.europa.eu/topics/infrastructure/european-grids_en. 3 ACER 2026 Monitoring Report, available at https://www.acer.europa.eu/monitoring/electricity-gas-keydevelopments-2026. See also European Environmental Agency: ‘Renewables, electrification and flexibility - For a competitive EU energy system transformation by 2030’, available at https://www.eea.europa.eu/en/newsroom/news/renewables-lower-energy-prices. 4 https://ember-energy.org/latest-insights/decoupled-how-spain-cut-the-link-between-gas-and-power-pricesusing-renewables/.

E-10-2026-002457.t: EU ports strategy: investments, priorities and role of Member States
qt: to the Commission David McAllister (PPE) Subject:

The EU ports strategy provides a solid basis for the continued development of maritime ports in the German state of Lower Saxony. What matters now is backing the measures announced with adequate funding, providing effective support for investments, speeding up planning and permitting procedures and better coordinating the various infrastructure projects. 1.

What does the Commission make of concerns that the broad and partly non‑binding nature of the EU ports strategy and the large number of promised initiatives, alliances and support instruments harbour the risk of policy fragmentation, potentially making effective prioritisation more difficult?

How does it plan to meet the high investment needs of EU ports, particularly with regard to small and medium-sized enterprises, smaller shipyards and regional stakeholders, who are key to the strategy’s implementation?

As the strategy is developed further and put into effect, how does the Commission intend to ensure that national and regional interests are duly considered and that the different starting points of EU ports are sufficiently taken into account?
at: (English version) to the Commission David McAllister (PPE) (15 June 2026) Subject: EU ports strategy: investments, priorities and role of Member States The EU ports strategy provides a solid basis for the continued development of maritime ports in the German state of Lower Saxony. What matters now is backing the measures announced with adequate funding, providing effective support for investments, speeding up planning and permitting procedures and better coordinating the various infrastructure projects. 1. What does the Commission make of concerns that the broad and partly non-binding nature of the EU ports strategy and the large number of promised initiatives, alliances and support instruments harbour the risk of policy fragmentation, potentially making effective prioritisation more difficult? 2. How does it plan to meet the high investment needs of EU ports, particularly with regard to small and medium-sized enterprises, smaller shipyards and regional stakeholders, who are key to the strategy’s implementation? 3. As the strategy is developed further and put into effect, how does the Commission intend to ensure that national and regional interests are duly considered and that the different starting points of EU ports are sufficiently taken into account? (26 August 2026) The Commission refers to its reply to E-000595/2026. The EU Ports Strategy is conceived as a framework that establishes common priorities and brings together existing and new initiatives, funding principles and guidance to align transport, energy, security and cohesion policies affecting ports rather than create parallel, uncoordinated or fragmented strands of action. On investment needs, the strategy identifies ports as a priority within the trans-European transport network and underlines the role of current and future EU funding programmes (1). It includes a specific roadmap for competitive small and medium-sized ports, which can benefit small and medium enterprises (SMEs) and smaller shipyards indirectly through improved infrastructure, innovation support and advisory services. The European Investment Bank and national promotional banks, alongside private investors, will also have an important role in meeting the investment needs of ports. The EU Ports Strategy does not set out a one-size-fits-all solution but reflects the diversity of EU ports, in full respect of subsidiarity. National and regional interests remain central, as port ownership, land-use planning, permitting fall within Member State and regional competences. Through trans-European transport network governance, cohesion programming and the future national and regional partnership plans, Member States and regions participate in defining priorities and ensuring that different starting points of ports, including those in Lower Saxony, are reflected when designing and implementing projects consistent with the strategy.
E.g. the Connecting Europe Facility, cohesion policy funds, Horizon Europe, the Innovation Fund and the instruments of the future Multiannual Financial Framework.

E-10-2026-002456.t: Ensuring a variety of raw materials in EU feed industry
qt: to the Commission Christine Singer (Renew) Subject:

According to feed industry sources, during the regular update of the EU Catalogue of feed materials under Regulation (EU) No 68/2013, as well as the clean‑up of the EU Feed Materials Register, an increasing number of entries are being reviewed and deleted. It seems that plant products that have until now been used as animal feed materials – such as liquorice, biochar, roots and herbs – are also affected. There is concern within the EU feed industry that this will limit the range of feed feedstocks available. This could have a negative effect on product variety, the development of new nutritional approaches and the competitiveness of EU companies. 1.

What criteria form the basis for the review and potential removal of existing feed materials from the EU Catalogue and for the clean‑up of the EU Feed Materials Register, particularly where these products are not intended as feed additives?

What regulatory goal is the Commission pursuing by deleting these products from the EU Catalogue or the EU Register, and what legal or regulatory pathway does it envisage for such products, so that they can continue to be available as feed feedstocks to the feed industry, without triggering disproportionate authorisation procedures?
What does it see as the potential implications of this development for innovation, product variety and the competitiveness of the EU feed industry?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (20.8.2026) Pursuant to Art. 24(6) of Regulation 767/20091, the first time a Feed Business Operator (FBO) places a new feed material on the market, it must notify this to the Feed Chain Task Force (EUFCTF), which is required to publish and update a register of these notifications. As a consequence, the Register is a list of notifications to the EUFCTF by FBOs that certain substances are placed on the market as feed materials, but the Register itself does not grant such status. The Commission, the Member States and the EUFCTF are currently verifying some Register entries in order to identify those that are not feed materials but other substances, such as feed additives. The misclassification of additives as feed materials can allow companies to bypass the required authorisation procedure, granting an unfair advantage over compliant competitors. This procedure is not intended to remove genuine feed materials from the Register, but only substances erroneously entered as such. Notifiers of questionable entries are given the opportunity to clarify the status and use of the substances concerned, and as a rule the removal occurs only with the notifier's agreement. Regarding the Catalogue of Feed Materials2, the ongoing revision is mostly aimed at adding new entries, rather than removing them; the only few that could be removed are substances on which all involved parties agree that they are not feed materials. This verification measure prioritises innovation and competitiveness by preventing substances from circumventing the procedures laid down by law, to the detriment of compliant companies.
1 ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2009/767/oj. 2 Commission Regulation (EU) No 68/2013 of 16 January 2013 on the Catalogue of feed materials (ELI:
http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2013/68/oj).

E-10-2026-002455.t: Proportionality of the plant passport regime for local exchange systems in horticulture
qt: to the Commission Christine Singer (Renew) Subject:

The plant passport under Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 is a vital tool for plant health and traceability, and is subject to the control and enforcement provisions in Regulation (EU) 2017/625. In practice, however, difficulties are arising with small‑scale local exchange arrangements between horticultural businesses, which often help each other out short term with small quantities of plants – for example, within local delivery networks. These transactions are currently subject to the same bureaucratic requirements as cross‑border trade. 1.

Has the Commission looked into whether the current requirements for local and smallscale transfers of ornamental plants are proportionate, and what does it have to say about businesses with distinct production and sales arms which effectively have to issue themselves plant passports?
Does it see any scope for a simplified regime for short‑term regional exchange arrangements between horticultural businesses, without compromising the goals of plant health?
Does it intend to review the plant passport regime for small and medium-sized horticultural businesses as part of ongoing simplification initiatives?
at: (English version) to the Commission Christine Singer (Renew) (15 June 2026) Subject: Proportionality of the plant passport regime for local exchange systems in horticulture The plant passport under Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 is a vital tool for plant health and traceability, and is subject to the control and enforcement provisions in Regulation (EU) 2017/625. In practice, however, difficulties are arising with small-scale local exchange arrangements between horticultural businesses, which often help each other out short term with small quantities of plants — for example, within local delivery networks. These transactions are currently subject to the same bureaucratic requirements as cross-border trade. 1. Has the Commission looked into whether the current requirements for local and small-scale transfers of ornamental plants are proportionate, and what does it have to say about businesses with distinct production and sales arms which effectively have to issue themselves plant passports? 2. Does it see any scope for a simplified regime for short-term regional exchange arrangements between horticultural businesses, without compromising the goals of plant health? 3. Does it intend to review the plant passport regime for small and medium-sized horticultural businesses as part of ongoing simplification initiatives? (24 August 2026) According to Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 (1), plant passports are not required for the supply of plants, plant products and other objects to final users, except in the case of sales via distance contracts. For the movement of plants from business to business, the regulation does not provide for exemptions for local or small-scale businesses. Nevertheless, that regulation includes the possibility of the plant passport to be issued by the competent authorities, as a derogation from the general rule of being issued by the authorised professional operator. Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/66 (2) already provides for the possibility to reduce the frequency of controls when risk management plans have been implemented by the operators. The Commission is currently discussing with Member States how to better implement these provisions, in order to reduce controls for operators that pose a lower risk. Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 was amended in 2024 (3) and two simplification provisions were introduced, in relation to plant passports: 1) for derogations for the attachment of the plant passport to the trade unit; and 2) for the use of plant passport for final users on sales via distance contracts. At this stage, no other revision has been foreseen.

E-10-2026-002454.t: Proportionality of mandatory use of EPPO codes in horticulture
qt: to the Commission Christine Singer (Renew) Subject:

The mandatory use of codes from the European and Mediterranean Plant Protection Organization (EPPO) in plant protection documentation places an additional administrative burden on small and medium-sized horticultural businesses in particular. In the ornamental plant and shrub sector especially, many businesses work with a wide range of species and varieties. Meanwhile, a globally recognised botanical nomenclature with Latin genus and species names already exists, and is used both in teaching and in practice. 1.

What additional technical or phytosanitary function does the mandatory use of EPPO codes serve compared with existing botanical nomenclature, and has the Commission examined the practical implications of this obligation for small and medium-sized horticultural businesses?

Does the Commission see any scope for allowing simplified generic terminology or other real‑world solutions in the ornamental plant sector in particular, without compromising the goals of plant health and traceability?
As part of ongoing simplification initiatives, is the Commission planning to review these documentation requirements for proportionality?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (11.9.2026) The European Parliament and the Council set out the obligation to record the use of plant protection products (PPP) by professional users and the scope of that information in Article 67(1) of Regulation (EC) No 1107/20091. Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/5642 harmonises the content and format of those records. As set out in Article 1 of this Regulation and in the Annex thereto, the crop names, situations and land uses should be recorded using the common names and not the European and Mediterranean Plant Protection Organization (EPPO) codes and the Member States should provide those common names in national languages corresponding to EPPO codes. This simplifies the task of the users compared with the direct use of EPPO codes or botanical nomenclature. In the particular case of ornamental plants, this corresponds to a small number3 of common names instead of many scientific names. The EU legislation on plant health4 and on plant reproductive material5 do not prescribe the use of codes from the EPPO for the description of a plant. Under both legal frameworks, plants are identified using the scientific nomenclature based on genus and species names. Operators, including small and medium-sized horticultural businesses, may continue to rely on this scientific nomenclature for this purpose, without any need to refer to EPPO codes. This approach applies similarly to the ornamental plant and shrub sector. Thus, no additional burden for the businesses concerned will occur.
1 Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 21 October 2009 concerning

the placing of plant protection products on the market and repealing Council Directives 79/117/EEC and 91/414/EEC, OJ L 309, 24.11.2009, p. 1, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2009/1107/oj. 2 Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/564 of 10 March 2023 as regards the content and format of the records of plant protection products kept by professional users pursuant to Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 of the European Parliament and of the Council, OJ L 74, 13.3.2023, p. 4, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg_impl/2023/564/oj. 3 https://gd.eppo.int/search?k=ornamental. 4 Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 of the European Parliament of the Council of 26 October 2016 on protective measures against pests of plants, amending Regulations (EU) No 228/2013, (EU) No 652/2014 and (EU) No 1143/2014 of the European Parliament and of the Council and repealing Council Directives 69/464/EEC, 74/647/EEC, 93/85/EEC, 98/57/EC, 2000/29/EC, 2006/91/EC and 2007/33/EC, OJ L 317, 23.11.2016, p. 4, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/2031/oj. 5 Council Directives 66/401/EEC, 66/402/EEC, 68/193/EEC, 98/56/EC, 1999/105/EC, 2002/53/EC, 2002/54/EC, 2002/55/EC, 2002/56/EC, 2002/57/EC, 2008/72/EC and 2008/90/EC.

E-10-2026-002453.t: Risks of increased food and packaging waste under the Empowering Consumers for the Green Transition Directive (ECGT)
qt: to the Commission Stefano Cavedagna (ECR) Subject:

Directive (EU) 2024/8251, which will apply from 27 September 2026, aims to combat greenwashing and provide consumers with accurate sustainability information. However, under the Commission’s current interpretation, businesses may be required to relabel, repackage or discard products already placed on the market that were compliant with the rules in force at the time of production. In sectors such as food and fast-moving consumer goods, this could generate significant food and packaging waste, contrary to the objectives of the Waste Framework Directive and the EU’s broader circular economy commitments, particularly given that the Commission only published its FAQs in November 2025. In this context: 1.
What measures is the Commission taking to prevent unnecessary food and packaging waste resulting from the application of the ECGT requirements to legacy stock already placed on the market?

How does the Commission intend to ensure that the implementation of the ECGT does not discourage food manufacturers from investing in sustainability initiatives while allowing them to continue communicating genuine sustainability commitments to consumers?

Directive (EU) 2024/825 of 28 February 2024 amending Directives 2005/29/EC and 2011/83/EU as regards empowering consumers for the green transition through better protection against unfair practices and through better information (ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2024/825/oj). 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (31.7.2026) The Commission endeavours to ensure that the application of Directive (EU) 2024/825 will not lead to unnecessary food or packaging waste. Under Regulation (EU) 2025/401, Member States shall reduce packaging waste generated per capita by 5% by 2030, 10% by 2035, and 15% by 2040, compared with 2018 levels. The Commission has published a Question & Answers document reflecting the main questions raised by traders and other stakeholders, including on ‘old stock’ situations. This document is a support tool and does not replace the traders’ own responsibility to prepare for the rules adopted in early 2024. The Commission remains in regular contact with stakeholders at EU and national level as well as national authorities to support a coherent application across the EU. In addition, the Commission facilitated exchanges within the Consumer Protection Cooperation (CPC) Network concerning such ‘old stock’ situations. The CPC authorities have published a Common Understanding on the matter of old stock to support a coherent and proportionate enforcement approach across the EU. According to that CPC document, national authorities plan to take into account genuine transitional difficulties and practical constraints concerning old stock situations in their enforcement actions2. The Directive does not prevent food business operators from communicating genuine sustainability efforts. Businesses are encouraged to continue to communicate about their sustainability efforts, provided they are clear, accurate and not misleading. The new rules should strengthen consumer trust and support a level playing field for businesses.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=OJ:L_202500040. 2 https://commission.europa.eu/topics/consumers/consumer-rights-and-complaints/enforcement-consumer-
protection/coordinated-actions/sustainable-consumption-actions_en.

E-10-2026-002452.t: Mobiles as critical endpoints for citizens’ cybersecurity and European digital resilience
qt: to the Commission José Cepeda (S&D) Subject:

Mobile phones are regularly used to access essential public services, e-government facilities, digital credentials, professional communication systems and corporate systems. However, while frameworks such as the NIS2 directive, DORA and the Cyber Resilience Act strengthen the risk management, operational resilience and security of products with digital elements, mobiles still only appear indirectly within the European regulatory ecosystem. This situation can create uncertainty for citizens, businesses and administrations as to what minimum security standards should be required from mobile devices, especially when they act as endpoints connected to critical services or contain sensitive credentials, such as biometric profiles. With this in mind: 1.

Is the Commission planning to request that the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA) provide a specific guide on the protection of mobile devices as endpoints, including risk management, updates, encryption, authentication, applications and BYODs?
How will the Commission ensure that the review of the Cyber Resilience Act adequately covers risks linked to mobile phones, operating systems, pre-installed applications and update cycles?

Will the Commission, along with ENISA, the European Data Protection Supervisor and the European Data Protection Board, develop common guidelines that reconcile mobile cybersecurity, data protection and users’ rights?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (7.9.2026) The Cyber Resilience Act1 (CRA) establishes essential cybersecurity requirements for products with digital elements, including mobile phones, operating systems and mobile applications, aimed at strengthening protection from cyber threats for users of such products. In order to support the implementation of the CRA, the Commission requested to the European standardisation organisations the development of a number of harmonised standards2, including one for operating systems3. The EU Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA) is also supporting the implementation of the CRA through a range of technical guidance documents for manufacturers4. Furthermore, the CRA establishes obligations for distributors, including the need to act with due care in relation to the requirements of the Regulation and to withdraw and recall, if appropriate, products with digital elements that are not in conformity with the essential cybersecurity requirements set out in the CRA. In addition, the NIS2 Directive5 requires providers of public electronic communication networks and of publicly available electronic communication services to take cybersecurity risk management measures to protect their services. More recently, the trusted information and communication technologies (ICT) supply chain framework in the revised Cybersecurity Act6 proposes measures to ensure the security of the ICT supply chain of electronic communications networks and protect them from strategic cybersecurity risks notably linked with high-risk suppliers. Finally, the ePrivacy Directive7 protects the integrity of mobile endpoints by making access to such endpoints and the processing of information stored on such endpoints in principle subject to consent of the user.
1 Regulation (EU) 2024/2847. 2 C(2025) 618 final. 3 Products with digital elements that have the core functionality of operating systems will need to apply that

harmonised standard or be subject to a more stringent conformity assessment procedure, in accordance with Article 32(2). 4 ENISA Secure by Design and Default Playbook https://www.enisa.europa.eu/publications/enisa-secure-bydesign-and-default-playbook or ENISA Technical Advisory for Secure Use of Package Managers https://www.enisa.europa.eu/publications/enisa-technical-advisory-for-secure-use-of-package-managers. 5 Directive (EU) 2022/2555 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 December 2022 on measures for a high common level of cybersecurity across the Union, amending Regulation (EU) No 910/2014 and Directive (EU) 2018/1972, and repealing Directive (EU) 2016/1148 (NIS 2 Directive). 6 COM(2026) 11 final. 7 Directive 2002/58/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 12 July 2002 concerning the processing of personal data and the protection of privacy in the electronic communications sector (Directive on privacy and electronic communications).

E-10-2026-002450.t: Ensuring tripartite governance and meaningful participation on the EU-OSHA Management Board
qt: to the Commission Konstantinos Arvanitis (The Left) Subject:

The European Agency for Safety and Health at Work (EU-OSHA) operates on the basis of the tripartite participation of governments, employers’ organisations and workers’ organisations. Tripartite governance is a key element of the legitimacy and effective functioning of the Agency. The EU-OSHA Management Board unanimously decided in January 2024 to continue meetings in a hybrid format, in order to ensure the maximum possible active participation of members, while saving resources and limiting travel. However, the Commission is reportedly pushing for a revision of the current model, which could limit the meaningful participation of Management Board members and in practice weaken the active tripartite dialogue within the Agency1. The Commission is asked: 1.
What objectives does this unexpected change, which directly contradicts the recent decision of the Agency's Management Board on the way it meets and makes decisions, serve?

Has the Commission assessed the impact of such a change on the active participation of the social partners and the government side and, consequently, on the effective functioning of the Agency and the purpose it serves? What does the Commission intend to do to ensure that any changes to the way the Board meets do not lead to a deterioration in the democratic, tripartite and participatory functioning of EU-OSHA?
https://www.osetee.gr/article.php?id=1017.
at: (English version) to the Commission Konstantinos Arvanitis (The Left) (15 June 2026) Subject: Ensuring tripartite governance and meaningful participation on the EU-OSHA Management Board The European Agency for Safety and Health at Work (EU-OSHA) operates on the basis of the tripartite participation of governments, employers’ organisations and workers’ organisations. Tripartite governance is a key element of the legitimacy and effective functioning of the Agency. However, the Commission is reportedly pushing for a revision of the current model, which could limit the meaningful participation of Management Board members and in practice weaken the active tripartite dialogue within the Agency (1). The Commission is asked: 1.
What objectives does this unexpected change, which directly contradicts the recent decision of the Agency's Management Board on the way it meets and makes decisions, serve?

Has the Commission assessed the impact of such a change on the active participation of the social partners and the government side and, consequently, on the effective functioning of the Agency and the purpose it serves? What does the Commission intend to do to ensure that any changes to the way the Board meets do not lead to a deterioration in the democratic, tripartite and participatory functioning of EU-OSHA?

(24 July 2026) According to Article 28 of Regulation (EU) 2019/126 establishing the European Agency for Safety and Health at Work (EUOSHA) (1), the Commission is required to carry out an evaluation of the Agency every five years. One of the recommendations put forward by the evaluation completed in 2024 invited EU-OSHA to examine whether EUOSHA’s governance arrangements could be further optimised, at the same time acknowledging that its tripartite nature offers significant advantages in terms of representation, strategic direction, expertise, knowledge sharing and dissemination of the Agency’s work. At its June 2026 meeting, the EU-OSHA Management Board examined the different options put forward by the Agency. It concluded that the current governance arrangements of EU-OSHA, as they stand, are efficient and effective and respond to the needs and ambitions of tripartism. To this end, the Management Board agreed that it should continue to meet twice a year, in June and December.

E-10-2026-002449.t: Consistency in the application of sporting boycotts
qt: to the Commission Lynn Boylan (The Left) Subject:

The Commissioner responsible for sport, Glenn Micallef, set a standard for the intersection of international law and sport when stating in relation to Russia on X that: ‘Sport unites when it stands on principle. It divides when it compromises them’1 and ‘sport cannot reward aggression’2. While the Commission has consistently been in favour of isolating Russian athletic delegations, a striking discrepancy exists concerning Israel whose athletes and fans continue to enjoy unfettered access to European sporting arenas despite multiple provisional measures issued by the International Court of Justice (ICJ) warning of plausible acts of genocide. 1.

Does the Commission agree that ‘sport cannot reward aggression’ by Israel, which has launched wars of aggression on neighbouring countries and, if so, what measures does it propose to take to prevent Israel from being rewarded?
What criteria does the Commission apply to ensure that the principles are applied universally and without political double standards?
https://x.com/GlennMicallef/status/2024064875249484105, 18 February 2026. https://x.com/GlennMicallef/status/2044470991103864875, 15 April 2026.
at: (English version) to the Commission Lynn Boylan (The Left) (15 June 2026) Subject: Consistency in the application of sporting boycotts The Commissioner responsible for sport, Glenn Micallef, set a standard for the intersection of international law and sport when stating in relation to Russia on X that: ‘Sport unites when it stands on principle. It divides when it compromises them’ (1) and ‘sport cannot reward aggression’ (2). While the Commission has consistently been in favour of isolating Russian athletic delegations, a striking discrepancy exists concerning Israel whose athletes and fans continue to enjoy unfettered access to European sporting arenas despite multiple provisional measures issued by the International Court of Justice (ICJ) warning of plausible acts of genocide. 1. Does the Commission agree that ‘sport cannot reward aggression’ by Israel, which has launched wars of aggression on neighbouring countries and, if so, what measures does it propose to take to prevent Israel from being rewarded? 2. What criteria does the Commission apply to ensure that the principles are applied universally and without political double standards? (12 August 2026) The Commission recalls that sport should uphold fundamental values, including respect for international law. It should never be weaponised for propaganda or to normalise acts of aggression. Sport organisations are autonomous, but with this autonomy comes the responsibility to ensure good governance and to uphold the integrity and values of sport. The Commission’s position on Russia is consistent with the EU’s restrictive measures adopted in response to Russia’s unprovoked and unjustified war of aggression against Ukraine. As the circumstances underlying the EU’s position on Russia remain unchanged, and with Russian attacks on civilian infrastructure continuing, there is no basis for changing the current approach. Reversing it would risk undermining the coherence of the EU’s response and could be exploited for propaganda purposes. The Commission notes that, in the case of Russia, sporting organisations took autonomous decisions within their respective competences against the backdrop of the broad restrictive measures adopted by the EU and many international partners. This contributed to a coherent international response. While decisions on participation in sporting competitions remain the responsibility of the competent sporting organisations, the Commission considers that, where the international community adopts restrictive measures in response to serious breaches of international law, it is appropriate for those organisations to consider whether their approach remains consistent with the fundamental values of sport.
https://x.com/GlennMicallef/status/2024064875249484105, 18 February 2026. https://x.com/GlennMicallef/status/2044470991103864875, 15 April 2026.

qt: to the Commission Sarah Knafo (ESN), Adrian-George Axinia (ECR), Nikola Bartůšek (ECR), Markus Buchheit (ESN), Petr Bystron (ESN), Christophe Gomart (PPE), Fernand Kartheiser (NI), Kateřina Konečná (NI), Ondřej Krutílek (ECR), Alvise Pérez (NI), Katarína Roth Neveďalová (NI), Volker Schnurrbusch (ESN), Georgiana Teodorescu (ECR), Auke Zijlstra (PfE) Subject:

On 3 June 2026, the Commission presented the EU’s Cloud and AI Development Act, which aims to triple the EU’s data centre capacity. Article 4(1)(e) explicitly identifies small modular reactors as an energy source to power these facilities. Meanwhile, Article 11 requires that data centres deployed in acceleration zones apply the performance indicators specified in Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1364. These include the renewable energy factor, which puts facilities powered by nuclear energy at a disadvantage, despite them being carbon‑free. On 26 May 2026, ten Member States, including France, wrote to the Commission condemning this departure from the principle of technological neutrality and demanding that nuclear power be recognised as sustainable in the same way as solar and wind power. 1.

How does the Commission justify promoting nuclear power to supply data centres in Article 4 of the EU’s Cloud and AI Development Act, while including indicators in Article 11 which specifically penalise data centres powered by that same energy source?

Does the Commission intend to recognise nuclear power as a sustainable energy source in future labelling of data centres, in line with the principle of technological neutrality and the request of the ten Member States that signed the letter of 26 May 2026?
at: (English version) to the Commission Sarah Knafo (ESN), Adrian-George Axinia (ECR), Nikola Bartůšek (ECR), Markus Buchheit (ESN), Petr Bystron (ESN), Christophe Gomart (PPE), Fernand Kartheiser (NI), Kateřina Konečná (NI), Ondřej Krutílek (ECR), Alvise Pérez (NI), Katarína Roth Neveďalová (NI), Volker Schnurrbusch (ESN), Georgiana Teodorescu (ECR), Auke Zijlstra (PfE) (15 June 2026) Subject: Nuclear power and data centres On 3 June 2026, the Commission presented the EU’s Cloud and AI Development Act, which aims to triple the EU’s data centre capacity. Article 4(1)(e) explicitly identifies small modular reactors as an energy source to power these facilities. Meanwhile, Article 11 requires that data centres deployed in acceleration zones apply the performance indicators specified in Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1364. These include the renewable energy factor, which puts facilities powered by nuclear energy at a disadvantage, despite them being carbon-free. On 26 May 2026, ten Member States, including France, wrote to the Commission condemning this departure from the principle of technological neutrality and demanding that nuclear power be recognised as sustainable in the same way as solar and wind power. 1. How does the Commission justify promoting nuclear power to supply data centres in Article 4 of the EU’s Cloud and AI Development Act, while including indicators in Article 11 which specifically penalise data centres powered by that same energy source? 2. Does the Commission intend to recognise nuclear power as a sustainable energy source in future labelling of data centres, in line with the principle of technological neutrality and the request of the ten Member States that signed the letter of 26 May 2026? (4 August 2026) The data centre rating scheme was developed based on the reporting obligations for data centres under the Energy Efficiency Directive (1). Following the open public consultation on the draft act, the Commission is considering the feedback received from Member States and stakeholders to include the use of nuclear power in the labelling of data centres, in line with the principle of technological neutrality. Article 4 of the proposed Cloud and AI Development Act (2) lays down the proposed operational objectives of the Cloud and AI Leadership Initiatives. Article 4(1)(e) of the proposal recognises small modular reactors (SMRs) as one possible energy source for data centres in that context. Separately, Article 11(1) of the proposal only refers to letters (a) to (n) and does not reference the metrics that concern renewable energy consumption (letters (o) to (r)), which preserves technological neutrality when sustainability requirements are established for data centres in acceleration zones. This approach enables competent authorities to assess projects based on their overall energy performance rather than favouring specific energy generation technologies. Therefore, Article 11 does not penalise data centres powered by SMRs or nuclear in general.

E-10-2026-002447.t: Compensation for additional costs resulting from new animal transport rules
qt: to the Commission Daniel Buda (PPE) Subject:

The modernisation of the European rules on animal welfare during transport pursues a legitimate aim, but the introduction of new requirements entails significant logistical, technological and operational adjustments for farmers and transporters. Without adequate support, these additional costs could affect scrupulous operators in particular and widen the gaps between Member States in terms of their implementation capacity. In order for the high welfare standards to be complied with in practice, they must be accompanied by instruments that make the transition economically viable. Otherwise, there is a danger that the financial pressure will be shifted onto producers who are already vulnerable, particularly in outlying areas or in regions where logistical distances are greater. Good regulation must also be enforceable, not just ambitious. Does the Commission intend to provide for a European financial support mechanism to help the sector adapt to the new animal transport rules so that the compliance costs do not disproportionately affect farmers and operators in logistically disadvantaged regions?

Without adequate support, these additional costs could affect scrupulous operators in particular and widen the gaps between Member States in terms of their implementation capacity. In order for the high welfare standards to be complied with in practice, they must be accompanied by instruments that make the transition economically viable. Otherwise, there is a danger that the financial pressure will be shifted onto producers who are already vulnerable, particularly in outlying areas or in regions where logistical distances are greater. Good regulation must also be enforceable, not just ambitious. Does the Commission intend to provide for a European financial support mechanism to help the sector adapt to the new animal transport rules so that the compliance costs do not disproportionately affect farmers and operators in logistically disadvantaged regions? (21 August 2026) As indicated in Commission’s answer to the Parliamentary Question E-004663/2025 (1), the impact assessment (2) accompanying the proposal on the protection of animals at the time of transport (3) distinguishes between costs borne by farmers and those borne by transporters and other sectors. Specific costs for vehicle improvements, space allowance and weather-dependent logistical planning, are primarily borne by transporters. To mitigate the impacts, the proposal includes transition periods. As the most important economic impacts identified relate to space allowance requirements, the Commission looks forward to discussing with the co-legislators in the context of the interinstitutional negotiations of the proposal how the final rules can best balance animal welfare improvements with their economic impacts. There are various EU funds that are relevant, which include, among others, the Common Agricultural Policy for farmers. Nevertheless, existing EU funding and financing instruments may support investments where relevant. In particular, support for farmers can be provided under the common agricultural policy, for investments in infrastructure and equipment facilitating compliance with the proposal’s requirements. Furthermore, in the framework of the recently published EU Livestock Strategy (4), the Commission will explore the possibility of a potential dedicated financial instrument for the livestock sector including for animal welfare measures.

E-10-2026-002446.t: Creation of a European rapid response mechanism to restore productive capacity following natural disasters
qt: to the Commission Daniel Buda (PPE) Subject:

An increasing number of European agricultural regions are experiencing natural disasters that not only result in crop losses in a single season, but also affect infrastructure, soils, livestock numbers and production capacity for several years. In such situations, one-time support is useful but often insufficient to truly relaunch agricultural activity. The recent mobilisation of exceptional support for farmers affected by natural disasters shows that the Union can intervene, but these responses remain largely reactive and contextdependent. A clearer and faster mechanism that is focused not only on compensation but also on effective restoration of productive potential is needed. Is the Commission considering establishing a European rapid response mechanism for agriculture affected by natural disasters which would combine emergency compensation with support for the restoration of agricultural infrastructure, biological capital and productive capacity in the medium term?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (5.8.2026) Both the current Common Agricultural Policy (CAP)1 and the support proposed under the National and Regional Partnership Plans in the period 2028-20342, provide Member States with a range of tools supporting farmers in crisis situations following natural disasters, adverse climatic events or catastrophic events. Apart from crisis payments for farmers severely impacted by those events, support is also available for the restoration of agricultural production potential. The Commission's priority is not only to increase the availability of crisis support but also to improve the overall architecture of risk and crisis management. The overall objective is to shift towards a more preventive and structured approach, while maintaining targeted public support when major crises occur. This is why for the post-2027 CAP3 the Commission proposes a layered approach combining income support, risk management tools, crisis payments and prevention measures, including a new targeted farm transition scheme, to help farmers in the transition to resilient production systems and overcome financial barriers in a holistic way. To enhance overall resilience to climate impacts across the Union and the Member States, the forthcoming European Integrated Framework for Climate Resilience aims to significantly step up efforts, including by providing greater support to public and private actors to better anticipate and manage climate risks.

E-10-2026-002445.t: European framework for payments to farmers who provide measurable ecosystem services
qt: to the Commission Daniel Buda (PPE), Dan-Ştefan Motreanu (PPE) Subject:

Increasingly often, European farmers are required to contribute to environmental and climate goals through practices that reduce emissions, protect soil, conserve water, preserve agricultural landscapes and support biodiversity. In many cases, however, the costs of adaptation are immediate, whereas the economic benefits for farms remain uncertain, insufficient, or difficult to access because of bureaucracy. For the ecological transition to be credible and accepted, farmers must be viewed not solely as targets of obligations, but also as suppliers of quantifiable public goods. In the absence of a clear, simple and predictable mechanism of payments for ecosystem services, there is a risk that green policies will be perceived as an additional burden rather than as an economic opportunity for rural areas. 1.

Does the Commission intend to propose a European legal framework for payments for ecosystem services provided by farmers, over and above the Carbon Farming Framework, based on measurable indicators and simplified procedures, so that the contribution made by agriculture to environmental and climate goals is recognised and fairly compensated?
What are the interim results of the actions announced in the Roadmap towards Nature Credits?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (28.8.2026) 1. The Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) supports eco-schemes and environmental, climate-related and management commitments that contribute to the achievement of EU environmental and climate goals. Programmed and reported measurable indicators aim at monitoring the implementation of these interventions. Schemes can be based on achievements, to reward the results. The Commission proposal for future CAP includes incentive payments for agri-environmental-climate actions. Moving from compensation to incentives opens the way to reward environmental services. The Carbon Removals and Carbon Farming Regulation (CRCF)1 can support a results-based eco-scheme for farmers by establishing a voluntary EU certification framework by which farmers are rewarded for the carbon removed. The CRCF requires carbon farming activities to generate co-benefits for biodiversity, ecosystems, soil, water and climate adaptation. CRCF methodologies covering agriculture, agroforestry, rewetting of peatlands, and afforestation have been adopted on 9th July 2026. 2. The Commission adopted the Roadmap towards Nature Credits2. A dedicated Expert Group3 is advancing discussions on methodologies and metrics, governance and integrity, market readiness and finance, policy coherence, and international cooperation. Monitoring, reporting and verification will be developed under ongoing pilots that test the feasibility of a market for nature credits of nature positive actions for various ecosystems at EU scale.

1 Regulation (EU) 2024/3012 - https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=OJ:L_202403012. 2 https://green-forum.ec.europa.eu/green-business/nature-credits_en. 3 The Expert Group met in December 2025, March 2026 and 18 June 2026.

E-10-2026-002444.t: An integrated European approach to water security in agriculture
qt: to the Commission Daniel Buda (PPE) Subject:

Climate change is making droughts more frequent and increasing hydrological imbalances and pressure on water resources in many agricultural regions of the Union. For many farmers, access to water is no longer just a technical factor of production, but a strategic issue of economic survival and food security. Recent water resilience initiatives in rural areas show that examples of good practice and innovative solutions exist, but they remain scattered and are not adequately supported by a coherent European architecture. Without accelerated investment in storage, secondary infrastructure, efficiency and local governance of water, regional disparities could widen. 1.

Does the Commission intend to propose an integrated European framework for water security in agriculture based on a map of areas affected by water scarcity and vulnerable areas, which would include dedicated funding for sustainable, smart irrigation, water retention, water reuse and digitalisation of consumption, as well as differentiated support for regions that are most exposed to drought and desertification?

Will the Commission develop a roadmap or other measures to ensure water security in agriculture, including sharing of water resources in crisis situations to ensure stable continuity of agricultural production?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (24.7.2026) 1. The Commission is monitoring the effects of climate change on water availability, including for the farming sector. In its Vision for Agriculture and Food1, the Commission highlights the importance of sufficient and clean water for a thriving agri-food sector. The European Water Resilience Strategy (WRS)2 provides a comprehensive framework for enhancing water resilience in agriculture. In addition, the forthcoming European Integrated Framework for Climate Resilience aims to step up assistance to Member States in better anticipating and managing climate risk. The Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) provides a range of tools to increase water resilience in agriculture, including support for farming practices that improve soil health and water retention, investments to enhance water efficiency, circularity, water reuse and storage solutions, as well as climate resilient crops. This is complemented by support for innovation, knowledge sharing3 and advice. In their CAP Strategic Plans4 Member States are responsible for targeting support to the areas most affected by water scarcity and droughts. 2. In line with the Water Framework Directive (WFD)5, the responsibility for integrated water management, which includes climate resilience6, rests with Member States. The Commission recommended7 ‘that Member States ensure appropriate governance for water management by ensuring in particular transparent, secure, inclusive, fair and predictable mechanisms for water allocation, providing certainty on allocation priorities between categories of uses in case of scarcity, while safeguarding vulnerable and marginalised groups’ access to affordable drinking water and water for sanitation’.

E-10-2026-002443.t: Rebuilding local agri-food processing capacities in vulnerable regions
qt: to the Commission Daniel Buda (PPE) Subject:

In many regions of the Union, farmers produce raw materials, but the added value is captured elsewhere due to the disappearance or underdevelopment of local processing capacities. This disconnect particularly affects vulnerable rural areas, where logistical distances drive up costs, reduce producers’ margins and limit their bargaining power within the food supply chain. In the absence of nearby collection and processing facilities, farmers remain exposed to volatile markets and excessive intermediation. The problem is not only economic, but also strategic. A resilient European agriculture sector needs shorter food supply chains that are more regionally rooted and capable of sustaining jobs in rural areas. If the Union wants cohesion, competitiveness and food security, then rebuilding local processing infrastructure must be treated as a common industrial and agricultural priority and not merely as a regional issue. Can the Commission clarify whether it intends to propose a European instrument dedicated to rebuilding and modernising local agri-food processing capacities, especially in vulnerable rural regions, so that farmers can retain a bigger share of the added value generated by their production?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (5.8.2026) A key principle of the proposal for a National and Regional Partnership Plans (NRPP)1 Regulation for the programming period 2028–2034 is to strengthen synergies and complementarities between different sources of EU funding and make them work together more effectively, including in rural areas. The ring-fenced amount for agricultural income provides for supporting on-farm investments and for the setting up of businesses in the farming sector and in other sectors of the rural economy. In addition, sectoral interventions supports actions such as processing and marketing of agri-food products. Beyond the ring-fenced amount Member States may support business development, innovation and investments including in food and bioeconomy, both from the NRPP fund and the European Competitiveness Fund. Place based strategies shall be employed to make best use of regional advantages. The recently adopted EU livestock strategy proposes developing locally integrated livestock value chains and a dedicated roadmap to foster low-capacity and mobile slaughterhouses in rural areas, supported by investments in local processing infrastructure and legislative simplification. In November 2025, the President of the Commission put forward a rural spending target of 10% of the budget allocation of each NRPP beyond amounts ringfenced for agricultural and fisheries income support. This would be used to support a consistent agenda of measures to address rural needs, building synergies across policy domains. In this context, Member States would be encouraged to invest in local and wider territorial value chains contributing to rural prosperity, including processing of local food products2.

E-10-2026-002442.t: Protecting European agriculture from excessive speculation in raw materials
qt: to the Commission Daniel Buda (PPE) Subject:

The prices of agricultural products and essential inputs are influenced not just by realities on the ground, but also by financial dynamics that can artificially increase volatility. When markets are dominated by disproportionate speculative movements, farmers face additional instability without having the tools they need to protect themselves effectively. This pressure affects production decisions, investment planning and the ability of farms to remain competitive. Agriculture cannot be left at the mercy of fluctuations that are disconnected from the real economy, especially in a context where European producers are already subject to high compliance costs and growing climate risks. The Union must ensure that markets retain their legitimate economic function without becoming an additional destabilising factor for food producers. Does the Commission intend to consider, together with the competent institutions, additional measures to limit excessive speculative effects on agricultural markets and to protect European farmers from financial volatility that does not reflect actual production and supply conditions?
at: (English version) to the Commission Daniel Buda (PPE) (14 June 2026) Subject: Protecting European agriculture from excessive speculation in raw materials The prices of agricultural products and essential inputs are influenced not just by realities on the ground, but also by financial dynamics that can artificially increase volatility. When markets are dominated by disproportionate speculative movements, farmers face additional instability without having the tools they need to protect themselves effectively. This pressure affects production decisions, investment planning and the ability of farms to remain competitive. Agriculture cannot be left at the mercy of fluctuations that are disconnected from the real economy, especially in a context where European producers are already subject to high compliance costs and growing climate risks. The Union must ensure that markets retain their legitimate economic function without becoming an additional destabilising factor for food producers. Does the Commission intend to consider, together with the competent institutions, additional measures to limit excessive speculative effects on agricultural markets and to protect European farmers from financial volatility that does not reflect actual production and supply conditions? (7 August 2026) The Commission shares the view that market developments should be driven by underlying supply and demand fundamentals. As part of the Fertiliser Action Plan (1), the Commission is working to improve transparency in fertiliser markets, within the limits of EU competition rules, to support informed market decisions and reduce the risk of distortions that could amplify price volatility for farmers. The action plan also considers exploring the role of financial risk-management tools, to help fertiliser market participants hedge against price volatility. Such instruments are intended to improve price certainty for farmers, rather than to encourage speculative activity or influence market fundamentals. Finally, the Fertiliser Market Observatory is one of the Commission's sectoral market observatories, which together enhance transparency and provide timely market intelligence across key agricultural sectors. It plays a key role in monitoring developments in the fertiliser market, serving as the Commission's main platform for exchanging information on market conditions, enabling farmers and other stakeholders to share their views and raise concerns. Representatives from several Commission Directorates-General participate in the Observatory, ensuring a coordinated and cross sectoral approach to monitoring market developments and addressing emerging challenges.

E-10-2026-002441.t: Supporting European production of essential agricultural inputs and reducing external dependencies
qt: to the Commission Daniel Buda (PPE) Subject:

The competitiveness of European agriculture depends not only on farmers’ performance, but also on the Union’s ability to ensure stable and affordable access to essential inputs: fertilisers, seed material, plant protection products, precision technology, and equipment. Recent crises have shown how vulnerable the sector is when external supply chains are disrupted and costs increase sharply at a critical time in the agricultural calendar. In the absence of an industrial strategy aligned with agricultural policy, farmers are expected to achieve European-level performance with tools that are increasingly expensive or hard to find. This disconnect between production requirements and actual supply capacity weakens the Union’s strategic autonomy and may increase dependence on third markets precisely in sectors that are essential to food security. Can the Commission indicate whether it is preparing a European strategy focused on critical agricultural inputs that includes stimulation of domestic production, support for industrial capacities in the Member States and rapid response mechanisms for situations where supply is disrupted, in order to protect European farmers from external shocks?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (6.8.2026) The Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) plays a key role in supporting European farmers in the transition towards more resilient and sustainable farming practices. This will also continue in the future programming period 2028-2034. In addition, the Commission addresses the dependency of agricultural inputs in several ways, such as a proposed dedicated preparedness framework in the amended Common Market Organisation Regulation (EU) 1308/20131, operationalising in the agri-food sector the aims of the Preparedness Union Strategy2 and the EU Stockpiling Strategy3 to ensure continuity of supply during severe crises and emergencies. In the same context, the Commission has established an Agri-Food Chain Observatory4 with a view to monitoring the developments of costs of inputs such as fertilisers. In 2024, the EU has put forward ambitious measures in the Critical Raw Materials Act5. and to accelerate implementation the Commission adopted the REsourceEU communication6 mobilising a large spectrum of policy tools. As of 29 May 2026, the Internal Market Emergency and Resilience Act7 applies, helping to enhance the resilience of the internal market and address the vulnerabilities as highlighted by recent crises Furthermore, the recently adopted Fertilisers Action Plan8, aims to strengthen EU’s own production capacity, including by promoting bio-based fertilisers, recycled nutrients and reducing dependency on fossil fuels. The European Emission Trading Scheme in combination with the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), will steer production, such as fertiliser production, towards decarbonisation, thus helping to shield European farmers from external shocks.

qt: to the Commission Nikolaos Anadiotis (NI) Subject:

In its answer of 4 June 2026 to question E-000653/2026, the Commission referred generally to inclusive education, minority rights and monitoring Albania's accession process1. Has the Commission examined the specific excerpts and maps from Albanian school textbooks referred to in question E-000653/2026?
Will the Commission explicitly include the issue of irredentist school textbook content in Albania’s accession dossier and subsequent evaluation reports?
Will the Commission request from Albania a specific review of the disputed school textbooks with the participation of independent experts?

(18 August 2026) The Commission has taken note of the concerns raised in Question E-000653/2026 regarding specific excerpts and maps in certain Albanian school textbooks. qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Nikolaos Anadiotis (NI) Subject:

According to reports, Ethiopia’s Christian heritage is under increasing pressure, through attacks on Christian communities, churches, clergy and believers, as well as through ethnoreligious violence and a policy of impunity1 https://www.opendoors.org/en-US/persecution/countries/ethiopia/. https://www.eeas.europa.eu/eeas/freedom-religion-or-belief_en. In parallel, international organisations record ongoing attacks in regions such as Oromia and Amhara, where churches have been burned, looted or destroyed, and believers and communities are being forcibly displaced2. The EU has stated that the promotion and protection of freedom of religion or belief is a key priority of its foreign policy3. In view of the above: 1.

How does the Vice-President of the Commission/High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy assess the situation of Christian and other religious communities in Ethiopia, in particular in areas where attacks on places of worship, worshippers and religious symbols are recorded?

Does the Vice-President of the Commission/High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy intend to raise the issue of the protection of religious freedom and cultural heritage in the EU-Ethiopia political dialogue?

Will the Vice-President of the Commission/High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy call for an independent investigation into attacks on Christian and other religious communities and for those responsible to be held accountable, in particular where inaction or complicity of state authorities is alleged?

(3 August 2026) The EU is deeply concerned by the conflict situations ongoing in Ethiopia, including reports of attacks on religious and cultural heritage in the Oromia and Amhara regions. Intentionally attacking places of worship is a crime under international humanitarian law. The vast majority of Ethiopians care deeply about religion, and respect for religious diversity is crucial to the country’s unique character. The promotion and protection of freedom of religion or belief is a key priority of EU foreign policy, as set out in the EU Action Plan on Human Rights and Democracy (1) and in the EU Guidelines on the promotion and protection of freedom of religion or belief (2). All persons have the right to practise their faith free from violence, intimidation or discrimination, and persons who change or leave their religion or belief should be equally protected. The EU condemns all acts of violence targeting religious communities and their places of worship and calls on Ethiopian authorities to investigate incidents thoroughly, bring perpetrators to justice, and end the culture of impunity. The EU closely monitors the situation on the ground and engages regularly with Ethiopia on human rights issues, including through political dialogue at senior level, as most recently demonstrated by the European External Action Service Political Director’s visit in early 2026. The protection of freedom of religion or belief, intercommunal tolerance, and the rule of law are standing elements of that dialogue.

E-10-2026-002438.t: Impact of sanctions against Russia on the historic fur industry in Kastoria
qt: to the Commission Nikolaos Anadiotis (NI) Subject:

The fur industry has been a historical pillar of the economic and social life of Kastoria for more than five centuries, forming part of the region’s traditional expertise and cultural heritage1. Both the EU sanctions against Russia and the absence of a specific just transition plan for Kastoria had devastating consequences for the industry, as up to 90 % of exports were lost, leading to business closures, job losses and a chain reaction of economic and demographic decline in the region. Despite European policies to protect traditional crafts and historic professions, there does not seem to be any particular concern for the preservation of fur trade in Kastoria2. In light of the above: 1.
Has the Commission assessed the economic and social impact of the sanctions on the historic fur trade in Kastoria?
Does the Commission intend to consider specific support measures to preserve local expertise and production activity?
Is there a possibility of special transitional arrangements for areas suffering serious economic damage due to the sanctions?

https://www.moneyreview.gr/business-and-finance/business/84110/apelpisia-stin-kastoria-oi-kyroseiskata-tis-rosias-katastrefoyn-toys-goynarades/. 2 https://greekreporter.com/2026/03/30/russia-ukraine-war-ravaged-fur-trade-greece-city-kastoria/. 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (21.8.2026) The decision to impose EU restrictive measures (‘sanctions’) on Russia in the context of its illegal aggression against Ukraine, is taken unanimously by all Member States in the Council. These measures are carefully targeted, proportionate and temporary, set with the view to increase pressure on Russia and its war economy, supporting efforts to end the brutal war of aggression. Sanctions are regularly reviewed and the EU can calibrate, ease or lift them if the EU’s objectives or meaningful steps towards them, are achieved. The EU’s sanctions are carefully calibrated to limit unintended effects on the EU and partner countries, maintaining an appropriate balance between effectiveness of sanctions as a foreign and security policy tool and broader economic impacts. The Commission closely monitors the economic impact of the EU’s sanctions against Russia, including on sectors that have historically relied on exports to the Russian market. Within its competences, the Commission also supports Member States in implementing EU restrictive measures. The Commission encourages Member States to design specific support measures aimed at preserving local expertise and facilitating the adaptation of economic activities to new market conditions. Unrelated to sanctions alignment, enterprises in Western Macedonia may benefit from support under the European Regional Development Fund1 as well as from the Just Transition Fund2. Both programmes have allocated financial resources to support entrepreneurship, business competitiveness and economic diversification in the region. E-10-2026-002437.t: Risk of accelerated deindustrialisation: EU regulations versus financial incentives in the USA
qt: to the Commission Ioan-Rareş Bogdan (PPE) Subject:

In its answer1 to the question for written answer with the title ‘European production moved to USA‘2, the Commission acknowledges that industrial subsidies in third countries and energy prices are putting huge pressure on European companies, but points to the ‘Clean Industrial Deal’ and new quality job rules as solutions. I see a major strategic asymmetry: while the USA attracts European capital through direct fiscal stimuli, cheap energy and measures such as the IRA (Inflation Reduction Act), the EU responds with new layers of regulation, bureaucracy and strict climate targets which increase compliance costs for producers. 1.

How will the Commission ensure that the ‘Clean Industrial Deal’ does not speed up relocation to the USA, given that it adds new administrative costs rather than providing direct cost reductions or compensation for the energy price gap?
Does the Commission have a quantitative impact study assessing how many companies in energy-intensive sectors could choose subsidies in the USA over the new compliance schemes proposed by the EU?

at: (English version) to the Commission Ioan-Rareş Bogdan (PPE) (13 June 2026) Subject: Risk of accelerated deindustrialisation: EU regulations versus financial incentives in the USA In its answer (1) to the question for written answer with the title ‘European production moved to USA‘ (2), the Commission acknowledges that industrial subsidies in third countries and energy prices are putting huge pressure on European companies, but points to the “Clean Industrial Deal” and new quality job rules as solutions. I see a major strategic asymmetry: while the USA attracts European capital through direct fiscal stimuli, cheap energy and measures such as the IRA (Inflation Reduction Act), the EU responds with new layers of regulation, bureaucracy and strict climate targets which increase compliance costs for producers. 1. How will the Commission ensure that the “Clean Industrial Deal” does not speed up relocation to the USA, given that it adds new administrative costs rather than providing direct cost reductions or compensation for the energy price gap? 2. Does the Commission have a quantitative impact study assessing how many companies in energy-intensive sectors could choose subsidies in the USA over the new compliance schemes proposed by the EU? (4 August 2026) The Clean Industrial Deal (1) is designed to strengthen the business case for decarbonisation and competitiveness in Europe, by reinforcing Europe’s industrial base, and, as a result, reducing the risk of relocation. It aims to support decarbonisation while improving the business environment for industry through better access to affordable energy, investment, materials and skilled labour. Many of its measures are already adopted or in implementation, including short-term support provided through the Clean Industrial Deal State Aid Framework (2). The proposed European Competitiveness Fund (3) and the Industrial Accelerator Act (4) are intended to strengthen the case for producing and investing in the EU, by accelerating permitting procedures, supporting industrial scale-up and creating lead markets for European and low-carbon industrial products and technologies. Meanwhile, the Commission is pursuing an ambitious simplification agenda to reduce the administrative burdens on companies. While a quantitative study predicting potential company choices to opt for subsidies in the US versus EU compliance schemes has not been performed by the Commission, the Commission closely monitors the impact of global subsidies on European energy-intensive industries and is implementing policy measures aiming at mitigating such impact by supporting investments in European industrial capacities.

E-10-2026-002436.t: Discriminatory treatment of dual citizens in the university admission process
qt: to the Commission Pascal Arimont (PPE) Subject:

In border regions in particular, transnational mobility plays a key role in the daily life of the population. This also applies to the mobility of young people for the purposes of learning and study. In the context of the common objective of free movement of Union citizens, the following matter has arisen and needs to be assessed: The author of this question was recently made aware of a case involving a young prospective student holding dual citizenship of two Member States of the Union (Belgium and Germany), who, prior to commencing studies at a German university, is required to have his Belgian school leaving qualification (Abitur) recognised by the competent administration of the German Land concerned. What is particularly remarkable about this additional administrative burden is that the applicant’s German citizenship is the decisive factor here: If he did not hold German citizenship (but only that of Belgium), the German university would, paradoxically, accept his Belgian qualification as sufficient for admission even without prior German recognition. A citizen of the Union is thus placed at a disadvantage by virtue of his dual nationality, with an additional administrative burden in one of his two home States, which he would be spared if he did not hold the corresponding nationality. 1.
Does the Commission consider that such admission procedures comply with EU law?
What is the Commission’s assessment of such admission practices in the light of the concept of the single market and cross-border educational mobility?
To what extent does the Commission plan to address this aspect in the forthcoming ‘Skills Portability Initiative’?

What is particularly remarkable about this additional administrative burden is that the applicant’s German citizenship is the decisive factor here: If he did not hold German citizenship (but only that of Belgium), the German university would, paradoxically, accept his Belgian qualification as sufficient for admission even without prior German recognition. A citizen of the Union is thus placed at a disadvantage by virtue of his dual nationality, with an additional administrative burden in one of his two home States, which he would be spared if he did not hold the corresponding nationality. 1.
Does the Commission consider that such admission procedures comply with EU law?
2. What is the Commission’s assessment of such admission practices in the light of the concept of the single market and cross-border educational mobility? 3.
To what extent does the Commission plan to address this aspect in the forthcoming ‘Skills Portability Initiative’?

(28 July 2026) In relation to this case, the Commission does not have sufficient information (in particular regarding the specific Land or university concerned) to carry out a full assessment at this stage. The Commission would suggest inviting the citizen concerned to submit a complaint (Make a complaint | European Union (1)), which the Commission stands ready to examine and, if warranted, to take appropriate action. In the spirit of further promoting mobility in all fields of study and actively removing obstacles to mobility in education, the Skills Portability Initiative to be soon announced by the Commission will help further improve the transparency, recognition and transferability of skills and qualifications across Member States. Announced as part of the Union of Skills in March 2025 and forming part of the Fair Mobility Package, the initiative seeks to enable skilled workers to move more easily within Europe, while supporting employers in hiring across borders. It will focus primarily on professional qualifications and their cross-border recognition to enhance labour mobility, rather than on the recognition of secondary education for entrance to universities.
