E-10-2026-002435.t: Disproportionate administrative spending and lack of control over value for money in the 2027 EU draft budget
qt: to the Commission Alvise Pérez (NI) Subject:

The Commission’s 2027 draft budget amounts to EUR 199.9 billion in commitments and EUR 212 billion in payments. It is presented as a budget for competitiveness, housing, defence, Ukraine, the energy transition and agriculture. However, the figures raise serious questions about priorities and value for money. The European public administration alone receives EUR 13.659 billion, more than four times the EUR 3.066 billion allocated to security and defence, and significantly more than migration and border management and security and defence combined. At a time when European families, workers and companies are facing inflation, housing pressure, high taxation and weak competitiveness, the EU cannot justify ever-expanding administrative costs, politically convenient subsidies or external spending without strict audits, while funding allocations to core priorities such as defence, borders and productivity remain comparatively limited. 1.
Will the Commission explain why the European public administration is being allocated more than four times as much funding as security and defence?
Will the Commission publish a detailed value-for-money assessment of administrative expenditure and subsidy-based programmes in the 2027 draft budget?
Will the Commission identify which budget lines can be reduced to prioritise competitiveness, border control, defence and tax relief for citizens?

E-10-2026-002434.t: State-linked intimidation of an MEP in Spain and the Commission’s double standards on the rule of law
qt: to the Commission Alvise Pérez (NI) Subject:

On 11 June 2026, I submitted a court filing in Spain in Preliminary Proceedings 150/2025 asking to be admitted as victim and private prosecutor. The filing states that I was allegedly targeted because of my political activity, my work as an information analyst and my denunciations of corruption. It refers to an alleged ‘Leire Díez agenda’ monitoring my activity, an alleged coordinated media smear campaign and alleged surveillance around my home and family environment by agents linked to information or intelligence departments. Without prejudging national criminal proceedings, if state-linked or politically connected structures were used to monitor, intimidate or discredit an elected Member of the European Parliament, this would affect democratic pluralism, the free exercise of my mandate and the values enshrined in Article 2 of the Treaty on European Union. The Commission’s Rule of Law Report assesses justice systems, anti-corruption frameworks, media pluralism and institutional checks and balances. 1.
In its Rule of Law Report will the Commission assess possible misuse of Spanish public authorities’ or state resources against an MEP?
Will it reflect these allegations in the report’s country chapter on Spain if they are deemed to affect democratic pluralism or the free exercise of my mandate?
What objective criteria will the Commission apply to ensure that possible rule-of-law breaches in Spain are scrutinised with the same rigour as in other Member States?

The Commission’s Rule of Law Report assesses justice systems, anti-corruption frameworks, media pluralism and institutional checks and balances. 1. In its Rule of Law Report will the Commission assess possible misuse of Spanish public authorities’ or state resources against an MEP? 2. Will it reflect these allegations in the report’s country chapter on Spain if they are deemed to affect democratic pluralism or the free exercise of my mandate? 3. What objective criteria will the Commission apply to ensure that possible rule-of-law breaches in Spain are scrutinised with the same rigour as in other Member States? (4 September 2026) The 2026 Rule of Law Report presents developments and recommendations concerning the situation of the rule of law in all 27 Member States, including Spain, across four pillars: the justice system, the anti-corruption framework, media freedom and pluralism, and other institutional issues related to checks and balances. The report provides a qualitative assessment carried out by the Commission with a focus on a synthesis of significant developments in full respect of the principle of equality of Member States. The Commission generally does not comment on individual cases or ongoing national court proceedings. The investigation and, where appropriate, prosecution of such cases fall, in general, within the competence of the national authorities. The Commission applies the same objective methodology to all Member States, ensuring consistent and comparable scrutiny while fully respecting national competences. This methodology is published on the Commission’s website.

E-10-2026-002433.t: EU engagement with democratic actors in Türkiye
qt: to the Commission Erik Marquardt (Verts/ALE), Hannah Neumann (Verts/ALE) Subject:

On 6 February 2026, the Commissioner for Enlargement, Marta Kos, visited Ankara and met exclusively with Turkish government officials, namely the Vice‑President, Minister of Trade, Minister of Foreign Affairs, and Minister of Treasury and Finance. The visit took place while Ekrem İmamoğlu, the twice‑elected Mayor of Istanbul and leading opposition candidate, has been in detention since March 2025 following proceedings widely criticised by international bodies as politically motivated, together with numerous municipal officials and civil society actors. In this context: 1.

What considerations led the Commissioner during her one and only visit in February 2026 not to meet with civil society organisations or leaders of the opposition parties or visit the Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality?

How does the Commission intend, going forward, to ensure balanced political engagement with Türkiye, including systematic dialogue with civil society, opposition actors and democratically elected local authorities as part of the enlargement framework?

Is the Commission planning a follow‑up visit to Türkiye that would include meetings beyond government representatives, and does it intend to seek direct contact with detained elected representatives, including the Mayor of Istanbul?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (7.8.2026) Türkiye is a candidate country and key partner for the EU. As reiterated by the Council and the European Council1, the EU has a strategic interest in a stable and secure environment in the Eastern Mediterranean and in the development of a cooperative and mutually beneficial relationship with Türkiye. The Commission engages with Türkiye in areas of joint interest, while also addressing concerns over the deterioration of the rule of law and democratic standards in the country, as noted in the 2025 Enlargement Report on Türkiye2. The Commission has expressed concerns regarding the imprisonment of politicians, journalists, business people and civil society activists in Türkiye, including the arrest of Istanbul Mayor3. During the Commissioner for Enlargement visit to Ankara in February 2026, these concerns were raised in meetings with authorities and engaged with Members of the Grand National Assembly of Türkiye, including representatives from the opposition. The Commissioner also met civil society representatives during the February and June 2026 visits. While time constraints precluded parliamentary meetings in June, Directors from the Directorate-General for Enlargement and the Eastern Neighbourhood and the European External Action Service had engaged with Members of Parliament from all major political groups only days before the visit. As an EU candidate country and long-standing member of the Council of Europe, Türkiye is expected to apply the highest democratic standards and practices and the Commission addresses these issues in all relevant contacts with Turkish authorities, including within the context of the sub-committee covering this area, established under the Association Agreement with Türkiye. The Commission will continue to engage with a wide variety of stakeholders in its outreach to candidate countries.

E-10-2026-002431.t: Letter of concern from Nordic NGOs to the Executive Secretary of the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD)
qt: to the Commission Rasmus Nordqvist (Verts/ALE), Isabella Lövin (Verts/ALE) Subject:

On 11 June 2026, the President of the Commission received a copy of a letter of concern sent by Nordic nature conservation societies to the Executive Secretary of the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD). The letter raises deep concern about unsustainable fishing quotas and destructive fishing practices in protected marine areas – issues linked to several specific articles of the Convention – as well as to specific targets of the Global Biodiversity Framework adopted under the Kunming-Montreal Agreement. The letter considered that although ‘the EU is committed to the full and swift implementation of the Global Biodiversity Framework’1 it is neither fulfilling obligations within the Convention itself, nor ensuring sufficient progress in reaching the relevant Kunming Montreal targets: 1.

How will the Commission change fisheries and ocean management using an ecosystem approach to guarantee that the EU can meet the obligations under the CBD to halt biodiversity loss and restore ocean health?
How will the Commission guarantee that destructive bottom-trawl fishing will not take place in Natura 2000 areas in the future, so obligations and targets under the CBD can be met?
https://environment.ec.europa.eu/topics/nature-and-biodiversity/global-biodiversity_en.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (20.8.2026) The Commission is fully committed to achieving the EU’s marine biodiversity objectives to contribute to the implementation of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework as can be seen in the Convention on Biological Diversity online reporting tool. The EU implements the ecosystem-based approach through the Birds1, Habitats2, Marine Strategy Framework3 and the Maritime Spatial Planning4 Directives, the Common Fisheries Policy (CFP)5, the Nature Restoration Regulation6 and the Biodiversity Strategy7. The Commission regularly assesses progress in achieving marine protection and sustainable fisheries objectives under EU law. The recently launched OceanEye8 will support the development of a strong evidence base for sustainable marine management. Under the Habitats Directive, Member States must prevent deterioration of protected habitats and species and adopt conservation objectives and measures for each Natura 2000 site. They must assess, case by case, whether fishing activities, including mobile bottom-contacting gears, are compatible with the corresponding conservation objectives. Under the Marine Action Plan9 the Commission sets out its vision on how to best preserve marine biodiversity and increase the resilience and sustainability of fisheries, exploiting synergies between the CFP and the environmental legislation. It issued a guidance on Natura 2000 and fishing10. The European Ocean Pact11 addresses sustainability and protecting and restoring ocean health. Under the Nature Restoration Regulation, Member States are required to restore degraded marine habitats, which may involve restrictions on mobile bottom fishing. Member States are due to submit their first national restoration plans in September 2026.

E-10-2026-002430.t: Moroccan drone strikes, human rights violations and trade agreements in Western Sahara
qt: to the Commission Catarina Martins (The Left) Subject:

On 7 June 2026, Lehbib Mohamed Abdelaziz, a commander of the Polisario Front, was killed by a Moroccan drone strike. This assassination, which took place in the context of a war that Morocco instigated but has never acknowledged, is exacerbating the situation in Western Sahara, with the Commission a complicit party. In October 2024, the Court of Justice annulled two agreements between the EU and Morocco on the grounds that Sahrawis had not given their consent. In spite of this, the Commission then produced a revised agreement in late 2025, having excluded a legitimate partner from the process and turned a blind eye to increasing repression. One of the victims of the Moroccan crackdown is Naâma Asfari, who has been in prison for 16 years following an unlawful trial. He is currently on hunger strike in an attempt to draw attention to the plight of Sahrawi political prisoners. All EU trade agreements contain strict human rights safeguard clauses which are legally binding on both parties. The violation of Sahrawis’ right to self-determination, the perpetration of violence, and the assassination of political and military leaders all constitute a flagrant violation of these fundamental principles, thereby further undermining the legitimacy of the EU-Morocco trade agreements. In the light of the foregoing: 1.
What steps will the Commission take in response to this drone strike and Morocco’s human rights violations?
Will the Commission trigger the suspension clauses of the trade agreement over a breach of international law?
How can the Commission justify maintaining an agreement that excludes a legitimate representative recognised by the Court of Justice?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (10.8.2026) The EU recalls that now is the time for dialogue and negotiations and that any military escalation runs counter to this effort and should be avoided. The EU continues to support fully the United Nations-led process, in line with UN Security Council resolution 2797(2025)1, and the efforts of the UN Secretary-General and his Personal Envoy to advance a just, lasting and mutually acceptable political solution. The EU remains committed to upholding human rights and international law in all its external action. Article 2 of the EU-Morocco Association Agreement2 enshrines respect for democratic principles and human rights as the foundation of the EU-Morocco partnership. Regarding the Agreement in the form of an Exchange of Letters signed on 3 October 2025, this new agreement replaces the earlier arrangement concerning tariff preferences for products originating in Western Sahara. It applies provisionally pending completion of the procedures required for its conclusion by the EU. The agreement includes provisions reflecting the requirements set out by the Court of Justice of the European Union.

E-10-2026-002429.t: Clearcutting in Ovar pine forest (Portugal) and the destruction of Priority Habitat 2270*
qt: to the Commission Catarina Martins (The Left) Subject:
Clearcutting in Ovar pine forest (Portugal) and the destruction of Priority Habitat 2270*

The Ovar forest perimeter is home to Priority Habitat 2270* (present condition: ‘unfavourable-poor’) and encompasses two special areas of conservation (SACs): PTCON0014 and PTCON0006. Since Ovar is designated as a ‘shaded area’ that falls within the scope of the Natura 2000 network, the Portuguese Nature Conservation and Forests Institute (ICNF) is enacting a forest management plan (2020-2038) without the need for a strategic environmental assessment (SEA). 363 hectares of mature pine forest are being cleared. These activities contravene the norms and practices of the ICNF, which has prohibited just such operations in a similar SAC in Mira (PTCON0055). In the light of the case law of the Court of Justice (judgments in Cases C-117/03, Dragaggi and C-244/05, Bund Naturschutz): 1.
Does the Commission deem Portugal to be in breach of its obligation to conserve the ‘shaded area’ in Ovar by authorising such destructive clearcutting?

By designating clearcutting as a ‘forestry operation’ that is exempt from an environmental impact assessment (EIA) and organising the project in such a way that plots of land are divided up into fewer than 10 hectares each, could these actions be construed as an attempt to obviate legal requirements designed to prevent the assessment of cumulative impacts, and hence be in breach of Directives 2001/42/EC and 2011/92/EU?

Will the Commission ascertain the facts of the matter and launch infringement proceedings against Portugal pursuant to Article 258 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU for breaches of Directives 2001/42/EC (SEA), 2001/92/EU (EIA) and 92/43/ECC (Habitats)?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (25.8.2026) Priority Habitat 2270* is protected in 20 sites in Portugal, including near the Ovar region in the Special Area of Conservation (SAC) Ria de Aveiro (PTCON0061). Under Article 6(3) of the Habitats Directive1, any plan or project likely to have a significant effect on a Natura 2000 site must undergo an appropriate assessment, whether located inside or outside the site. National authorities may authorise such plans or projects only after establishing that they will not adversely affect the integrity of the site, without prejudice to Article 6(4) of the same Directive. Member States are responsible for ensuring that these requirements are complied with. Certain ‘forestry operation’ projects may fall under the scope of the Environmental Impact Assessment Directive2; however, there is no automatic obligation to carry out an environmental impact assessment. For such projects3, Member States must determine if an assessment is required, taking into account relevant selection criteria4. Forestry plans and programmes fall under the scope of the Strategic Environmental Assessment Directive5 and must be assessed, provided that certain conditions are fulfilled6. As stated in its Communication ‘EU Law: Better Results through Better Application’7, the Commission prioritises enforcement action in cases indicating a systematic breach of EU law in a Member State and considers national means of redress the most effective way to address individual alleged cases of non-compliance.
1 Council Directive 92/43/EEC of 21 May 1992 on the conservation of natural habitats and of wild fauna and

flora. E-10-2026-002428.t: Risk of full dependency on China for vitamins and potential implications for food and health security
qt: to the Commission Stefan Köhler (PPE), Herbert Dorfmann (PPE), Norbert Lins (PPE), Alexander Bernhuber (PPE), Andreas Schwab (PPE) Subject:

Vitamins are essential micronutrients that play a crucial role in human nutrition and health. Supplementation is frequently necessary, particularly for vulnerable population groups, and some vitamins are on the EU list of critical medicines. Additionally, vitamins are a key component of infant formula. In agriculture, vitamins are key to supporting animal health, productivity and reproduction, thereby ensuring a stable supply of animal proteins through the meat, dairy, eggs and fish consumed daily by EU citizens. The EU is highly dependent on vitamin imports from China. The remaining EU production capacity is at risk of irreversible loss due to global price distortions driven by structural overcapacity in China. Given the complex technical expertise and high capital investment required, once lost, this capacity will be extremely difficult to rebuild. The EU therefore faces a risk of irreversible dependency, threatening its food and health security. 1.
How does the Commission assess the importance of vitamins as critical molecules for European health and food security?
Is it aware of the risk of the irreversible loss of EU vitamin production and its implications for the EU’s food and health security?
Is it planning measures to reduce dependency and support production in the EU?
at: (English version) to the Commission Stefan Köhler (PPE), Herbert Dorfmann (PPE), Norbert Lins (PPE), Alexander Bernhuber (PPE), Andreas Schwab (PPE) (12 June 2026) Subject: Risk of full dependency on China for vitamins and potential implications for food and health security Vitamins are essential micronutrients that play a crucial role in human nutrition and health. Supplementation is frequently necessary, particularly for vulnerable population groups, and some vitamins are on the EU list of critical medicines. Additionally, vitamins are a key component of infant formula. In agriculture, vitamins are key to supporting animal health, productivity and reproduction, thereby ensuring a stable supply of animal proteins through the meat, dairy, eggs and fish consumed daily by EU citizens. The EU is highly dependent on vitamin imports from China. The remaining EU production capacity is at risk of irreversible loss due to global price distortions driven by structural overcapacity in China. Given the complex technical expertise and high capital investment required, once lost, this capacity will be extremely difficult to rebuild. The EU therefore faces a risk of irreversible dependency, threatening its food and health security. 1.
How does the Commission assess the importance of vitamins as critical molecules for European health and food security?
2. Is it aware of the risk of the irreversible loss of EU vitamin production and its implications for the EU’s food and health security? 3.
Is it planning measures to reduce dependency and support production in the EU?

(29 July 2026) Vitamins are essential to ensure the nutritional adequacy of several food categories regulated under Regulation (EU) No 609/2013 (1). They are also used as ingredients in food supplements and fortified foods, providing European consumers the choice to supplement their dietary vitamin intakes. The Commission acknowledges the importance of ensuring food security for European citizens and, to this end, the EU has adopted the European Preparedness Union Strategy (2) and established the European Food Security Crisis preparedness and response Mechanism (3). The Commission continues to work with Member States and stakeholders to monitor dependencies on imports of agricultural inputs and developments of agri-food supply chains, as part of the EU's preparedness efforts. The latest State of Food Security in the EU report (4) identifies highly concentrated imports for several feed additives, including vitamins. While these dependencies warrant attention, they have not resulted in disruptions affecting their overall availability in the EU. The European Council of 30 June 2023 called for reducing critical dependencies and for de-risking, not decoupling, from China. Since then, the EU has intensified diversification and resilience efforts through the European Economic Security Strategy (5), and cooperation with reliable partners. The EU Protein Action Plan (6) and other resilience and competitiveness initiatives under the Vision on Agriculture and Food (7), further assess strategic dependencies and identify measures to strengthen resilience.

E-10-2026-002427.t: The western Black Sea in the EU’s new strategy
qt: to the Commission Ioan-Rareş Bogdan (PPE) Subject:

The new Coastal Communities Strategy adopted by the Commission on 10 June is a welcome step towards protecting the EU’s 70 000 kilometres of coastline. However, the western Black Sea region suffers from two vulnerabilities: firstly, severe coastal erosion exacerbated by specific hydrographic dynamics, and secondly, significant geopolitical and economic pressure on port infrastructure and communities close to the Danube Delta. The Black Sea Member States, including Romania, are making major efforts to develop the offshore renewable (wind) energy sector, but face high costs of connecting and adapting critical coastal infrastructure. 1.

How will the Commission ensure that the funding mechanisms for the new strategy will reflect the characteristics and risks specific to the Black Sea basin, which has different dynamics from the Atlantic or Mediterranean basins?

What specific financial instruments will be made available from ‘blue carbon’ credits or innovation funds to help Black Sea ports to adapt infrastructure to accept offshore green energy and simultaneously combat erosion?

What specific measures does the strategy include for coastal communities in areas with special environmental protection regimes (such as the Danube Delta), where economic diversification is severely restricted by environmental regulations?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (7.8.2026) The EU Coastal Communities Strategy1 promotes a place-based approach to coastal development. It encourages Member States to use the flexibility of the future National and Regional Partnership Plans under the funding period 2028-2034, to address the strategy’s objectives and local needs, in cooperation with national, regional and local authorities. The Common Maritime Agenda2 can support regional cooperation and provide a basin-level forum for regional actions specific to the Black Sea. The Communication on the EU’s eastern border regions3 set out an overarching plan for more secure, resilient and attractive places. Future carbon farming activities in coastal ecosystems may be certified4 for CO2 removals thanks to the conservation, restoration, or management of these ecosystems, including by ports5. Any credits accrued may then be sold on the carbon market to offset emissions. The Commission is also working on a regulated nature credits market through the Roadmap towards Nature Credits.6 The Strategy acknowledges that despite substantial protection efforts coastal and marine ecosystems remain under pressure, which risks undermining also the blue economy sectors. In areas under strict environmental protection regimes, economic resilience relies on diversifying towards low-impact activities. The Commission highlights the diversification of sustainable blue economy models (including pesca-tourism), community initiatives, local value chains, blue bioeconomy clusters, nature-based solutions and co-management partnerships (including fishers) for protected areas as possible solutions. EU funding7 is available for biodiversity, climate resilience, sustainable water management and circular economy.

establishing a Union certification framework for permanent carbon removals, carbon farming and carbon storage in products. 5 Such as mangrove forests, tidal marshes and seagrass meadows. 6 COM(2025) 374 final. The roadmap has a timeline for implementation until 2027. 7 Cohesion Policy funds, European Maritime, Fisheries, and Aquaculture Fund (EMFAF) and LIFE programme.

E-10-2026-002426.t: Use of EU funds for the new railway bridge over the Adda River between Paderno and Calusco and the project’s compliance with EU sustainable mobility objectives
qt: to the Commission Gaetano Pedulla' (The Left) Subject:

Rete Ferroviaria Italiana (RFI) is planning to build a new railway bridge over the Adda on the Carnate-Ponte San Pietro line1. The Italian infrastructure manager claims that this is a ‘sustainable mobility’ project that is in keeping with the provisions of Regulation (EU) 2021/1058 on the ERDF and the Cohesion Fund – two instruments which finance transport infrastructure in line with the EU’s 2021-2027 cohesion policy, the Green Deal and the Union’s climate neutrality objective. However, a study commissioned by the Milan Metropolitan Area’s Intercommunal Programming Research Center2 estimates that the number of vehicles using the new road and rail bridge on a daily basis will increase by 90 % to around 14 700 (including 2 000 trucks) and that neighbouring municipalities will experience a spike in traffic and pollution – a scenario that is at odds with the ‘do no significant harm’ (DNSH) principle referred to in Regulation (EU) 2021/1058 and in the EU’s climate legislation. I therefore ask the Commission: 1.
Have any ERDF, Cohesion or other EU funds already been requested for, or allocated to, the Adda bridge project?
Did the relevant eligibility assessment take the new bridge’s expected impact on traffic, air quality and noise pollution into account, in line with the DNSH principle?

What instruments for monitoring funds and withdrawing or redirecting resources could be deployed if it transpires that an EU-funded infrastructure project is at odds with the Union’s sustainable mobility and emission reduction objectives?

E-10-2026-002425.t: Urgent need for EU action regarding the spread of  Lagocephalus sceleratus  in popular coastal tourist destinations in Greece
qt: to the Commission Sakis Arnaoutoglou (S&D), Thomas Bajada (S&D), Giuseppe Lupo (S&D), André Franqueira Rodrigues (S&D) Subject:
Urgent need for EU action regarding the spread of Lagocephalus sceleratus in popular coastal tourist destinations in Greece

Despite repeated scientific warnings and previous representations to the Commission concerning the spread of the toxic silver-cheeked toadfish (Lagocephalus sceleratus) in the Eastern Mediterranean, recent media reports and scientific evidence indicate that the species has now reached the Saronic Gulf, one of Greece’s most densely populated coastal areas and a major tourist destination. Incidents involving bathers, including cases requiring medical treatment, have already been reported, given that this particular species contains tetrodotoxin, one of nature’s most powerful neurotoxins. The situation now raises serious concerns not only for marine ecosystems and fisheries, but also for public safety, public health and the tourism economy of Mediterranean coastal areas, particularly at a time when millions of citizens and visitors are entering the summer bathing season across the Mediterranean. The Commission is asked: 1.

Does it consider that the presence of Lagocephalus sceleratus in heavily frequented tourist areas and popular bathing sites constitutes a risk to public safety, public health and the economic activity of coastal areas?
What immediate measures could it take to help to protect citizens and fishers, as well as to inform visitors about the risks associated with this species?

Does it intend to urgently support and fund actions to limit the population of Lagocephalus sceleratus and assist Mediterranean Member States in addressing a problem that simultaneously threatens biodiversity, fisheries, citizens’ safety and the tourism economy?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (21.8.2026) 1. The Commission recognises that the spread of Lagocephalus sceleratus presents challenges for public health, marine ecosystems and coastal communities. The species contains tetrodotoxin, which can cause severe poisoning if consumed, highlighting the importance of preventing its entry into the food chain. It may also affect coastal fisheries through damage to fishing gear and catches, with potential consequences for the economic activity of communities that depend on fisheries. 2. The Commission announced a dedicated policy initiative within the European Ocean Pact1 to address the issue of Non-Indigenous Species (NIS) threatening fisheries and aquaculture. The Commission also works with the General Fisheries Commission for the Mediterranean (GFCM), through an EU-funded GFCM pilot on NIS in the Eastern Mediterranean. This pilot is gathering fisheries-dependent and independent data and establishing a NIS observatory to enhance knowledge and share best practices in tackling the spread of these species. The EU assists Member States through the European Maritime, Fisheries and Aquaculture Fund (EMFAF), which can support a range of actions, including raising public awareness on the risks associated with the species. 3. The EMFAF provides support to Member States to adopt measures to prevent the further spread of this species and mitigate its impacts. The Greek EMFAF Managing Authority has launched a call, which includes a pilot environmental management measure for Lagocephalus in cooperation with scientific institutions. It provides fees to participating fishers for the targeted catching, landing and destruction of the species. A similar scheme is already in place in Cyprus.
1 Communication of the Commission on the European Ocean Pact, COM(2025) 281 of 5.6.2025.

E-10-2026-002424.t: European measures to manage health and trade risks caused by the confirmation of an atypical BSE case in Ireland
qt: to the Commission Daniel Buda (PPE) Subject:

Given the recent confirmation of an atypical case of bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE) in Ireland, and the swift reactions of trade partners, including the suspension of imports of beef by South Korea, this situation raises serious concerns with regard to both market stability and the confidence of consumers and external partners. Against this backdrop: 1.

What immediate measures does the Commission intend to take to prevent the spread of health risks and to maintain confidence in food chain safety at EU level, and what tools is the Commission considering to limit the impact on European beef exports and avoid disproportionate reactions by third countries?
Given that there is currently no effective treatment or widely available vaccine for BSE, what prevention and control measures are being prioritised at European level to reduce future risks?
Is the Commission considering stepping up investments in research and innovation, including the development of a possible vaccine or advanced disease diagnosis and control methods?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (21.8.2026) Prevention, control and eradication measures for bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE) are laid down in Regulation (EC) No 999/20011. Ensuring the effective implementation of these measures remains a priority for the Commission. To this end, the Commission has monitored the situation in cooperation with the competent authorities of the Member States to ensure that following the confirmation of a BSE case, whether classical or atypical, all measures under that Regulation were implemented to mitigate any health risk. Detection of an atypical case of BSE does not affect a country's negligible risk status under the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) and does not justify restrictions on international trade. The co-funded European Partnership on Animal Health and Welfare (EUPAHW)2 was launched in 2024 with an overall budget of EUR 354 million for 10 years. Under priority 2, it supports research and innovation for animal health and welfare. The EraBSE project3, launched in December 2025 for 36 months, aims to develop tools for surveillance, epidemiological investigation and control of future cases of animal prion diseases.

E-10-2026-002422.t: Impact of egg price rises on food security and the transition to alternative rearing systems
qt: to the Commission Daniel Buda (PPE) Subject:

Given that the price of eggs in the EU is now about 37 % higher than the average over the last five years and rose by 12 % over the last six months, with most of the Member States being affected, this development raises serious concerns about the affordability of basic food items. A key short-term factor is outbreaks of avian influenza, which have affected production significantly. At the same time, new animal welfare proposals which could include phasing out cage rearing systems for laying hens are being prepared at EU level. In this context, the transition to alternative systems entails additional costs and, in many cases, a reduction in production capacity, which can increase the pressures on prices and the risks of shortages. 1.
Does the Commission intend to reconsider the timeframe for the phase-out of cage rearing systems or its scale in the context of the current pressures and the risks to food security?
What specific measures is the Commission considering to support producers in the transition to alternative systems so as to avoid significant decreases in production and further price rises?
How does the Commission intend to ensure a balance between welfare objectives and the need to keep prices affordable for consumers?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (21.8.2026) As announced in the Livestock Strategy1, the Commission aims to present legislative proposals on the revision of the existing EU animal welfare legislation on laying hens and broilers at farm by the end of 2026. Based on the impact assessment and stakeholder consultations, the Commission aims to propose proportionate rules, with a gradual approach, species-specific transition periods, and adequate time and support for farmers to adapt. Any cumulative impact on farmers will also be carefully considered in this process and taken into account when preparing an upcoming proposal. The practical experience of farmers that have already undergone a transition process into cage free farming is of particular importance for this exercise and has been carefully considered in the process. The impact assessment will consider both the potential positive effects and the potential costs of modernised and harmonised rules, such as greater long-term regulatory stability for farmers’ investments, reduced market fragmentation, enhanced consumer confidence, and opportunities for innovation.
1 COM/2026/576 final.

E-10-2026-002420.t: Forced sterilisation of women with disabilities – data and safeguards in institutional settings
qt: to the Commission Katrin Langensiepen (Verts/ALE), Merja Kyllönen (The Left), Marie Toussaint (Verts/ALE), Jagna Marczułajtis-Walczak (PPE), Marc Angel (S&D), Kathleen Funchion (The Left), Sirpa Pietikäinen (PPE), Gabriella Gerzsenyi (PPE) Subject:

The EU and its Member States are bound by the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, which guarantees free and informed consent, bodily integrity and protection from violence, prohibiting practices such as forced sterilisation. Reports by the European Disability Forum and other stakeholders indicate that forced sterilisation of women with disabilities persists in the EU, particularly in institutional settings. 1.

How is the Commission planning to address the widespread issue of forced sterilisation of women with disabilities – for instance, is it planning to adopt its anticipated recommendation on the prevention of harmful practices against women and girls, or other policy measures to prevent and end forced sterilisation?

What data does the Commission collect on cases of forced sterilisation of persons with disabilities, in particular women, including in institutional settings, and does it plan to establish EU-wide monitoring or data collection on this issue?

What steps is the Commission taking, including in the context of Directive (EU) 2024/13851, to ensure that all Member States explicitly prohibit and criminalise forced sterilisation in line with the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities?

Directive (EU) 2024/1385 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 May 2024 on combating violence against women and domestic violence (OJ L, 2024/1385, 24.5.2024, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2024/1385/oj). 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.9.2026) Forced sterilisation is a grave violation of fundamental rights. The Commission, through the Enhanced Disability Strategy1, is committed to upholding the rights of persons with disabilities, including women and girls. Under the EU4Health Programme (2021-2027), detailed guidelines have been published to improve access to healthcare for persons with disabilities, including on informed consent and the prohibition of forced sterilisation2. Data on forced sterilisation is currently limited at EU level, as there is no harmonised or comparable reporting of such cases across Member States from which EU-wide data could be derived. However, the Commission will launch a study on violence against women with disabilities in the EU, including forced sterilisation. With the World Health Organization, the Commission will also explore ways to improve the quality and accessibility of women’s physical and mental healthcare. In October 2023, the EU acceded to the Council of Europe Convention on preventing and combating violence against women and domestic violence (the so-called Istanbul Convention3). It requires its State Parties to criminalise forced sterilisation. Forced sterilisation, insofar as criminalised, is also partially covered by Directive (EU) 2024/13854, which requires Member States to provide specific support to victims, including accessibility, and to issue guidelines for professionals on how to address the specific needs of victims experiencing intersectional discrimination. The Commission is supporting Member States in their transposition of the Directive, which is due by 14 June 2027.

E-10-2026-002419.t: EU-funded deinstitutionalisation reforms in Romania and implementation of person-centred financing
qt: to the Commission Katrin Langensiepen (Verts/ALE), Merja Kyllönen (The Left), Marie Toussaint (Verts/ALE), Jagna Marczułajtis-Walczak (PPE), Marc Angel (S&D), Kathleen Funchion (The Left), Sirpa Pietikäinen (PPE), Gabriella Gerzsenyi (PPE), Katarina Barley (S&D) Subject:

The EU is committed to advancing deinstitutionalisation and independent living through the European Disability Strategy 2021-2030 and the Commission’s 2024 guidance on independent living for persons with disabilities, both of which support the transition from institutional to community-based care. In the context of EU-funded deinstitutionalisation reforms in Romania, including the PIRIS (individualised support planning) system, serious concerns arise regarding the lack of effective implementation at local level. Although PIRIS is designed to ensure person-centred financing on the basis of individual needs, community-based, licensed social services are often not financed. Authorities instead rely on public procurement procedures and cite budgetary constraints, leading to the exclusion of qualified providers and continued reliance on institutional or legacy systems. Reports by German non-profit association Agape e.V.1 have identified gaps between the design of such systems and their practical implementation at local level. This contradicts Article 19 of the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities and the principle that EU funds should complement, not replace, national public expenditure. How does the Commission assess: 1.
the compatibility of procurement-based financing with PIRIS;
the obligation of authorities to fund services once needs are established; and
the risk that EU funds replace, rather than complement, national responsibilities?

Agape e.V., Memorandum on the Implementation of Community-Based Social Services in Romania in the Context of EU-Funded Deinstitutionalisation Policies (PIRIS) See also Agape e.V.: https://agape-kinder.de/. 1
at: (English version) to the Commission Katrin Langensiepen (Verts/ALE), Merja Kyllönen (The Left), Marie Toussaint (Verts/ALE), Jagna MarczułajtisWalczak (PPE), Marc Angel (S&D), Kathleen Funchion (The Left), Sirpa Pietikäinen (PPE), Gabriella Gerzsenyi (PPE), Katarina Barley (S&D) (11 June 2026) Subject: EU-funded deinstitutionalisation reforms in Romania and implementation of person-centred financing The EU is committed to advancing deinstitutionalisation and independent living through the European Disability Strategy 2021-2030 and the Commission’s 2024 guidance on independent living for persons with disabilities, both of which support the transition from institutional to community-based care. In the context of EU-funded deinstitutionalisation reforms in Romania, including the PIRIS (individualised support planning) system, serious concerns arise regarding the lack of effective implementation at local level. Although PIRIS is designed to ensure person-centred financing on the basis of individual needs, community-based, licensed social services are often not financed. Authorities instead rely on public procurement procedures and cite budgetary constraints, leading to the exclusion of qualified providers and continued reliance on institutional or legacy systems. Reports by German non-profit association Agape e.V. (1) have identified gaps between the design of such systems and their practical implementation at local level. This contradicts Article 19 of the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities and the principle that EU funds should complement, not replace, national public expenditure. How does the Commission assess: 1.
the compatibility of procurement-based financing with PIRIS;
the obligation of authorities to fund services once needs are established; and
the risk that EU funds replace, rather than complement, national responsibilities?

(1 September 2026) The organisation and financing of social services, including for persons with disabilities, fall primarily within Member State competence under Articles 4 and 153 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union. The EU provides guidance and monitoring, but the design and enforcement of specific measures remain a national responsibility. Romania is responsible for how these services are delivered and financed, in compliance with EU law. EU law does not prohibit Member States from financing social services exclusively via public procurement where a personcentered system such as PIRIS exists. Directive 2014/24/EU contains a specific regime for social and other services and allows Member States to select providers based on the best price-quality ratio, taking account of quality and sustainability criteria. Any obligation to finance services once individual needs have been established is a matter of national law and does not derive from EU law. Where Directive 2014/24/EU (1) applies, contracts for relevant social services above the threshold in Article 4(d) must respect its rules. The Commission closely monitors the implementation of EU funds via annual review processes, dedicated missions, the European Semester and audits. Where legal requirements are not respected, the Commission may require corrective action, interrupt or suspend payments, and apply financial corrections.

Agape e.V., Memorandum on the Implementation of Community-Based Social Services in Romania in the Context of EU-Funded Deinstitutionalisation Policies (PIRIS) See also Agape e.V.: https://agape-kinder.de/. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2014/24/oj/eng.

The Commission’s guidance on independent living (2) recalls that EU funds should support community-based services and complement national funding, guided by partnerships with all relevant stakeholders.

E-10-2026-002418.t: Instrumentalisation of migration flows and political coercion of Member States
qt: to the Commission Mieke Andriese (PfE), Marieke Ehlers (PfE) Subject:

Third countries are increasingly instrumentalising migratory flows as a strategic tool to exert pressure against the EU, with disruptive consequences. Although the Commission identified a firm return policy as an absolute priority1, it appears that in 2025 only 28 % of those subject to expulsion orders actually left the territory of the EU2. This structural failure is inherent in the centralised approach that frames migration as a shared responsibility. Indeed, this European dogma deprives sovereign Member States of the necessary policy leeway and diplomatic tools to act effectively in their own right, lest they incur EU sanctions. The following questions thus arise: 1.
How does the Commission explain the gap between the promised 100 % commitment and the actual 28 % expulsion rate?

Does the Commission recognise national sovereignty, and is it prepared – given the failure of the European approach – to return migration policy competences to the Member States, which can regulate it more effectively, without using EU sanctions as a sword of Damocles?

Is the Commission prepared to include strict return clauses in trade agreements, which automatically lead to the freezing of preferential trade agreements in the event of noncompliance, and to provide more effective diplomatic room for manoeuvre for Member States to respond to the cries for help from the indigenous population, which is suffering under the strain of disruptive mass migration?
https://commission.europa.eu/priorities-2024-2029/security-and-defence_nl. https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_26_1222.

(16 September 2026) With swifter, simpler and more effective procedures across the EU, when in force, the Return Regulation (1) will give Member States better tools to address these shortcomings in full respect of fundamental rights. In parallel, the Commission, together with Member States, is continuing to work with third countries to increase cooperation on readmission. Pursuant to the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, the immigration policy is a shared competence between the Member States and the EU. The European Parliament and the Council have agreed to reform the return policy and to legislate with a regulation. The regulation aims at increasing the efficiency of returns and will complement the Pact on Migration and Asylum (2) that is applicable since 12 June 2026. The EU is developing a comprehensive toolkit of leverages to incentivise better cooperation on readmission of partner countries. Under visa policy (3), the mechanism under Article 25a of the Visa Code (4) has proven its effectiveness to enhance third countries’ cooperation on readmission. The new Generalised Scheme of Preferences (GSP) (5), effective from 2027, introduces the possibility of suspending trade benefits for countries that fail to cooperate on readmission.

E-10-2026-002417.t: EU funding for institutional care – data and safeguards
qt: to the Commission Katrin Langensiepen (Verts/ALE), Tomáš Zdechovský (PPE), Merja Kyllönen (The Left), Marie Toussaint (Verts/ALE), Ciaran Mullooly (Renew), Jagna MarczułajtisWalczak (PPE), Marc Angel (S&D), Kathleen Funchion (The Left), Sirpa Pietikäinen (PPE), Gabriella Gerzsenyi (PPE), Catarina Martins (The Left) Subject:

The EU and its Member States are bound by the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (UN CRPD), notably Article 19, as well as the Charter of Fundamental Rights and the European Disability Strategy 2021–2030, promoting the transition to community-based care. In its 2025 concluding observations, the United Nations Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities expressed concern about the continued use of EU funds for investments not fully aligned with the Convention, including those that may support institutionalisation. 1.

How many ESF+ and ERDF-funded projects in the 2014–2020 and 2021–2027 programming periods involve residential or institutional care settings and what is the total EU funding allocated to these projects? Please provide a breakdown by Member State.

E-10-2026-002416.t: Will merging Erasmus+ and the Solidarity Corps programme also include actions in support of migrants and refugees?
qt: to the Commission Catherine Griset (PfE) Subject:

Under the proposal for a Regulation establishing the Erasmus+ programme for the period 2028–2034, and repealing Regulations (EU) 2021/817 and (EU) 2021/8881 the European Solidarity Corps will merge with the Erasmus+ programme2. The European Voluntary Humanitarian Aid Corps would therefore also be included3. Although merging these programmes makes sense due to their complementarity and in order to reinforce their overall effectiveness, it should be borne in mind that the European Solidarity Corps, which funds voluntary missions for young people aged 18–30, is also designed to support migrants and refugees4. 1.
Will the new Erasmus+ programme, which includes the European Solidarity Corps, also fund support actions for migrants and refugees?
During the 2021–2027 budget period, how much was spent on supporting migrants and refugees under the European Solidarity Corps?

Could the European Voluntary Humanitarian Aid Corps, deployed exclusively in third countries, carry out missions to support third countries that have agreed to receive migrants on behalf of a Member State for the purpose of processing their asylum applications, as illustrated by the agreement between Albania and Italy?

at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (13.8.2026) The Commission proposal for the 2028-2034 Erasmus+ programme, including the European Solidarity Corps, keeps a strong emphasis on inclusion, notably through targeted measures aimed at supporting persons with fewer opportunities. While it is not designed to function as a dedicated instrument for asylum- or migration-related support, volunteering projects in the future programme are expected to contribute to addressing societal or humanitarian challenges, which might include challenges experienced by migrants and refugees. Since 2021, 1 229 projects of the European Solidarity Corps out of 13 924 have selected ‘reception and integration of refugees and migrants’ as one topic for their activities, out of several topics that can be tackled in the same project. As there is no budgetary split by topic within an activity, it is not possible ultimately to assign a precise spending on projects addressing any selected topic. Article 2(6) of the Commission proposal for a Regulation establishing the Erasmus+ programme for the period 2028–20341 provides that “the ‘European Voluntary Humanitarian Aid Corps’ refers to volunteering activities that […] include actions that aim to reinforce disaster preparedness and disaster risk reduction, link relief, rehabilitation and development and contribute towards strengthening the resilience and capacity of vulnerable or disasteraffected communities to cope with and recover from crises”. Volunteering missions in support of third countries that have agreed to receive migrants on behalf of a Member State for the purpose of processing their asylum applications that do not include actions described in this definition would not be eligible for funding under the European Voluntary Humanitarian Aid Corps.

E-10-2026-002415.t: EU support for the Libyan authorities in the wake of the reported attack on the ‘Sea-Watch 5’
qt: to the Commission Özlem Demirel (The Left) Subject:

On 11 May 2026, units of the Libyan coastguard opened fire on the civilian rescue vessel ‘Sea-Watch 5’ – which had just performed a rescue operation in international waters – and threatened to tow it to Libya. The incident occurred despite earlier assurances from the Commission that it had stepped up monitoring and dialogue mechanisms in the wake of the attack on the rescue vessel ‘Ocean Viking’ in August 2025. Reports of severe violence against migrants in Libya at the hands of civilian, state and quasi-state actors are currently on the rise. 1.

Under which framework (EU-funded programmes, cooperation frameworks or EUbacked bilateral agreements) did the EU supply, retrofit, maintain, co-finance or otherwise support the vessels involved in the incident (patrol boats 101, 662 ‘Murzuq’ and 648 ‘Ras Jadir’)?

What specific steps has the Commission taken since the attack on the ‘Ocean Viking’ in August 2025 to bolster its monitoring and dialogue mechanisms with the Libyan authorities, what incidents have been dealt with and what consequences ensued?

What criteria does the Commission use to decide whether incidents warrant the suspension, cutting or discontinuation of EU funding, training, equipment support or operational cooperation, and does it consider the aforementioned incident to be an escalation that necessitates changes to the current approach?

E-10-2026-002414.t: Exclusion of EU manufacturers from public procurement based on ownership structure
qt: to the Commission Sofie Eriksson (S&D), Adnan Dibrani (S&D) Subject:

In Article 11 of the draft Industrial Acceleration Act1 (hereinafter IAA), the Commission proposes that companies established and operating in the European Union, but controlled by entities from third countries that do not have an agreement on market access with the EU, should be excluded from public procurement procedures in strategic sectors such as electric vehicles. This would mean that public authorities could be prohibited from procuring electric vehicles produced in Europe by European workers, due to the tenderers’ ultimate ownership structure and regardless of their contribution to the EU economy. 1.

Is it the Commission’s intention that companies manufacturing in the EU, employing European workers, making substantial investments and undertaking research and development in Europe, and contributing to Europe’s industrial base should be excluded from public tenders solely on the basis of their ultimate ownership structure?

How does the Commission assess the impact of the proposed ownership control requirement in Article 11 of the IAA on the companies and European workers that will be affected by it, including in terms of the number of jobs at risk in the concerned sectors?

Has the Commission assessed whether an ownership-based approach could undermine the objectives of strengthening European competitiveness and industrial capacity by excluding companies that contribute significantly to the European economy?

Commission proposal of 4 March 2026 for a regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council establishing a framework of measures for the acceleration of industrial capacity and decarbonisation in strategic sectors (COM(2026)0100). 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (7.8.2026) The proposal for the Industrial Accelerator Act1 seeks to establish a framework of measures to accelerate industrial capacity and decarbonisation in strategic sectors, while strengthening the EU’s long-term resilience and prosperity. Article 11 requires contracting authorities and entities, for the specific procurement procedures covered by the Industrial Accelerator Act, to exclude from procurement procedures falling within its scope tenders submitted by economic operators owned or controlled by an entity established in a third country that has not concluded an international agreement with the EU guaranteeing such access. The provision is targeted and does not constitute a general exclusion from the EU market or from public procurement outside the scope of Article 11. It seeks to ensure reciprocity, avoid circumvention through EU-based subsidiaries and support resilient industrial capacity in strategic sectors. The Commission assessed the economic and social impacts of the proposal as a whole. The Commission recognises the contribution of foreign-owned companies to EU employment, investment and innovation. It considers that a limited ownership-based requirement in strategic procurement can support competitiveness by addressing asymmetric market access and strategic dependencies. The proposal remains subject to negotiations by the European Parliament and the Council.
1 https://single-market-economy.ec.europa.eu/publications/industrial-accelerator-act_en.

E-10-2026-002413.t: Sales of counterfeit medicines online: beefing up checks in the EU to combat organised crime and protect EU citizens

The Italian environmental protection and consumer rights network (Codacons) has revealed that a growing number of websites and e-commerce platforms are illegally selling counterfeit medicines and health products that contravene EU health regulations. Will the Commission strengthen the implementation of Directive 2011/62/EU on falsified medicinal products and the Digital Services Act by making use of joint monitoring and cooperation arrangements between the Member States, Europol, the European Medicines Agency and the competent national authorities?

How exactly will the Commission require online marketplaces, social networks and digital messaging services to swiftly take down content and advertising pertaining to the illegal sales of counterfeit medicines and goods?

Will the Commission promote EU-wide campaigns in an effort to forestall and raise awareness of this problem among consumers and to tackle the profits realised by organised crime across the EU as a result of the illegal trafficking of pharmaceuticals?

(14 September 2026) The Commission fully recognises the serious public health threats identified. Directive 2011/62/EU (1) harmonises safeguards to prevent falsified medicinal products from entering the legal supply chain and restricts online sale of medicines to suppliers authorised by national law. The common EU logo helps consumers identify legally operating online retailers. The Commission provided Member States with a toolkit for national campaigns promoting the logo, as the primary enforcers against falsified medicines. Cooperation between national enforcement authorities is facilitated at EU level, including through the Working Group of Enforcement Officers, the Board of Digital Services Coordinators or Europol. The Digital Services Act (DSA) (2) requires providers of online platforms to put in place mechanisms to notify suspected illegal content, including illegal advertisements or counterfeit or illegal medicines. E-10-2026-002412.t: German humanitarian payments to Polish victims of Nazi crimes – political decision pending by 17 June 2026
qt: to the Commission Arkadiusz Mularczyk (ECR) Subject:
German humanitarian payments to Polish victims of Nazi crimes – political decision pending by 17 June 2026

An open letter of 18 May 2026, signed by Poland’s main victim associations and the board of the Foundation for Polish-German Reconciliation1, calls for a German political decision by 17 June 2026 – the 35th anniversary of the conclusion of the Polish-German Treaty of Good Neighbourliness – to resume humanitarian payments to Polish victims of Nazi German crimes, with disbursements commencing in July 2026. Payments ceased in 2006. Fewer than 50 000 eligible survivors remain in Poland and this number is declining by approximately 800 per month. On 28 April 2026, Germany’s Ambassador to Poland, Miguel Berger, confirmed that the pending decision is purely political, not legal or operational2. The Joint Declaration of the Polish-German Intergovernmental Consultations of 1 December 2025 records Germany’s commitment to examine possibilities of providing additional support to Polish victims. Germany already applies humanitarian mechanisms to other surviving Nazi victim groups. 1.
Will the Commission use its stated facilitation role to encourage Germany to honour its commitment of 1 December 2025, given that its Ambassador has confirmed that no legal obstacle exists?
Does the exclusion of Polish victims from mechanisms applied to other Nazi victim groups comply with Article 21 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union?
With 800 victims dying monthly, does the Commission consider a further delay to be compatible with the right to effective remedy under Directive 2012/29/EU?

at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (16.9.2026) Questions concerning the consequences of historical events, including reparations or compensation between Member States, are primarily the responsibility of the Member States concerned and fall outside the competences conferred upon the Commission by the EU Treaties1. Within the limits of its competences, the Commission remains firmly committed to support preserving the memory of the victims of the Second World War, promoting reconciliation, and fostering historical remembrance, dialogue and mutual understanding across the EU, in particular through relevant programmes such as the call on remembrance under the Citizens, Equality, Rights and Values (CERV) programme2. According to Article 51(1) of the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights3, the Charter is applicable to Members States only when they are implementing EU law. As regards specifically the access to reparation of Polish World War II victims and their families for harm caused during the war, there are no applicable EU rules on this matter. The Commission also recalls its replies to written parliamentary questions P-000819/20254 and P-002838/20245.

E-10-2026-002411.t: Revising the criteria for determining the non-preferential origin of agricultural products and foodstuffs
qt: to the Commission Danilo Della Valle (The Left), Carolina Morace (The Left), Gaetano Pedulla' (The Left), Dario Tamburrano (The Left) Subject:

Article 60 of the Union Customs Code (Regulation (EU) No 952/2013 or UCC) establishes that the country in which a product that is made entirely from raw materials sourced in other states undergoes its last substantial and economically justified processing is that product’s country of origin. This provision undermines the transparency of information concerning the actual origin of ingredients, and is therefore blatantly at odds with the aims of Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011, which regulates the provision of food information to consumers. By paving the way for ‘Italian-sounding’ goods and distorting competition, the UCC is penalising the industries that are behind Europe’s outstanding agri-food products, examples of which include the Campania Region’s PDOs and PGIs and its 610 traditional agri-food products (PAPs). We therefore ask the Commission: 1.
Will it propose a revision of Regulation (EU) No 952/2013 with a view to ensuring that the last substantial transformation criterion does not apply to agri-food products?
What steps will it take to bring the UCC’s country-of-origin provisions in line with the definition of ‘place of provenance’ set out in Article 2(2)(g) of Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011?
What measures will it take to protect certified local products from the distortions arising from EU customs law?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.9.2026) The last substantial transformation as set out in Article 60(2) of the Union Customs Code (UCC)1 is the underlying principle for the determination of the country of non-preferential origin, for products where more than one country or territory is involved in their production. The principle is anchored in the World Trade Organisation’s Agreement on Rules of Origin and has been confirmed by European Court of Justice jurisprudence. The Commission is currently evaluating the UCC non-preferential rules of origin to assess whether they are still fit for purpose, though any adaptations will not deviate from the concept of the last substantial transformation. Therefore, no proposals are envisaged to remove agri-food products from that scope. ‘Place of provenance’ in Regulation (EU) No 1169/20112 is distinct from ‘country of origin’. While the latter is determined by reference to the UCC legal framework and is used to determine the tariff treatment upon import, the former refers to any place where the food is indicated as coming from and not the country of origin (such as a region or the EU). Geographical indications registered in the EU enjoy a high level of protection. Protected designations of origin and protected geographical indications are governed by the specific rules of Regulation (EU) 2024/11433, which also lay out specific enforcement actions to prevent or stop the use of names that contravene this protection. The Commission has not identified any distortions stemming from EU customs legislation which would affect the protection of geographical indications registered in the EU.

E-10-2026-002409.t: Ebola: the next pandemic that wasn't
qt: to the Commission Gerald Hauser (PfE) Subject:

Ebola is, without a doubt, one of the most dangerous viral diseases. While its mortality rate can be extremely high, its rate of transmission is comparatively low. Almost 40 Ebola outbreaks have been recorded in Africa since the 1970s. Although some of these outbreaks had dramatic local outcomes, none evolved into a global pandemic.1 Recently, however, the topic of Ebola has been played up.2 The timing is no coincidence: only recently did the scaremongering about Hantavirus come to nothing.3 What is more, Moderna received an additional EUR 50 million to speed up the production of the experimental mRNA-Ebola vaccine.45 However, the WHO has now had to back-pedal on Ebola and, just recently, revise the number of suspected cases significantly downwards.6 This is probably due to the strong resistance from local communities in Africa, who reject the authority of the WHO and its nongovernmental organisations. 1.
How does the Commission actually assess the risk of an Ebola pandemic in the EU?
Does the Commission intend to declare a public health emergency now that the WHO has already declared a public health emergency of international concern?

To what extent is the Commission involved in supporting the rapid deployment of Moderna’s experimental Ebola vaccine through its participation in the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (CEPI)7?

(24 September 2026) The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) currently assesses the overall risk of Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) very low for the EU. A public health emergency of international concern, which was declared by the World Health Organisation (WHO) on 17 May 2026 (1), does not automatically trigger the recognition of a public health emergency (PHE) at Union level. The WHO also stated that the outbreak does not meet the criteria of a ‘pandemic emergency’, as the risk at the global level is low (2). The Union-level recognition of the PHE requires that the threat endangers public health in the EU/EEA. The Commission may, after considering any expert opinion issued by the ECDC, any other relevant Union agencies or bodies or of the Advisory Committee on Public Health Emergency, formally recognise a PHE at Union level. The situation is continuously monitored by the ECDC, by health experts from the Directorate-General for European Civil Protection and Humanitarian Aid Operations, and by staff of the EU Health Task Force deployed on the ground to support the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, and so far the risk assessment for the Union remains unchanged. The Commission supports the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (CEPI) through the Horizon Europe (HE) Programme. For the current BVD outbreak, the Commission has earmarked EUR 73.7 million under the HE 2026 Work Programme for CEPI. CEPI has committed up to USD 50 million to Moderna for preclinical work, Phase I trials and parallel manufacturing for potential future trials.

At the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) summit on 10 March 2026, Commission President Ursula von der Leyen acknowledged that it was a strategic mistake for Europe to turn its back on nuclear energy and announced an additional temporary InvestEU top-up of EUR 200 million until 2028 to support private investment in innovative nuclear technologies1. On the same day, the Commission adopted a strategy for the development and deployment of small modular reactors (SMRs) in Europe2, with the objective of making this new technology operational in Europe by the early 2030s. While this strategy marks an important shift in the Commission’s approach to nuclear energy, concrete measures will now be essential to ensure European leadership in the development of SMRs. 1.
What concrete actions does the Commission intend to take to implement the objectives set out in the SMR strategy, and what timeline does it foresee for these measures?
How does the Commission intend to operationalise the EUR 200 million InvestEU support announced and how much private investment does it expect to mobilise?

Will the Commission propose a legislative initiative to facilitate pre-licensing and licensing processes for SMRs, guarantee wide access to financing, including the multiannual financial framework (MFF), and ensure technological neutrality in existing legislation?

(20 August 2026) The small modular reactors (SMR) Strategy (1) sets out concrete actions to support the strategic objective of the deployment of first SMRs in Europe in the early 2030s. The timely completion of the actions will depend on a strong commitment and engagement of all actors, including Member States, nuclear safety authorities, industry, research organisations and financing institutions (2). It supports a stronger European industrial ecosystem, including a competitive supply chain, a fleet approach, a focus on a limited number of the most promising designs, and the development of industrial standards, modular manufacturing and ‘SMR Valleys’ to support serial production (3). The Commission is working with the European Investment Bank (EIB) on the announced InvestEU top-up of EUR 200 million with a view to support the initial commercial units of innovative nuclear technologies (4) within the Union (5). The aim is to make it possible for the EIB to invite applications from eligible projects later this year and in due course support the de-risking of such concrete investments in innovative nuclear technologies and to crowd in further private funding.

The European Industrial Alliance on SMRs, launched in February 2024 and coordinated by the Commission, which chairs the Alliance’s Governing Board, operates through eight technical working groups that provide tailored support to identified SMR projects and work on establishing long-term enabling conditions for their development. Its Strategic Action Plan 2025-2029, endorsed in 2025, identifies top ten targeted actions which will be delivered by the Alliance through the technical working groups, in collaboration with the project working groups, over the next five years. See: https://webgate.ec.europa.eu/circabc-ewpp/d/d/workspace/SpacesStore/d5970517-ec7c-4aa6-af5a-77fc8dde33a9/download . Access to financing will be a key enabler for the deployment of SMRs. Member States considering SMRs as part of their energy strategies are encouraged, where appropriate, to develop coordinated financing and de-risking approaches to support the mobilisation of private investment at scale. Including light-water SMRs, advanced modular reactors (AMRs), microreactors and fusion. The top-up (loan guarantee) to the InvestEU programme from the EU Innovation Fund will be directed to support innovative nuclear energy projects to address financing challenges by enabling additional EIB venture debt operations.

Since the EIB finances at most 50% of the investment costs of any given project, it will unlock at least an equal amount of further investment from other sources (6). The Commission promotes and supports — including via a dedicated grant scheme — closer regulatory cooperation through joint early reviews between national nuclear safety regulators, regulatory sandboxes and a regulatory coalition of willing countries (7), to achieve greater convergence and regulatory efficiency while maintaining the highest nuclear safety standards. It does not foresee a specific legislative initiative exclusively for SMRs.

Separately, the upcoming Scaleup Europe Fund (as a new compartment of the European Innovation Council (EIC) Fund) could also help innovative nuclear technologies to achieve faster deployment. In addition, the Commission is working closely with Member States on the design of the IPCEI ( Important Project of Common European Interest) candidate for innovative nuclear technologies, which is currently in its design phase. Support through the Euratom Research and Training Programme is also available: five Euratom research projects related to light-water SMRs and AMRs were launched in 2024 with a total value of EUR 30 million, and the Commission expects to continue funding research on the safety of SMRs with EUR 15 million in 2026-27. In which the countries involved could align their licensing procedures or mutually recognise each other’s licensing decisions.

E-10-2026-002407.t: Zero and super-reduced VAT on assistive technology
qt: to the Commission Emmanouil Fragkos (ECR) Subject:

There is a clear trend in the OECD towards reducing/zero-rating VAT on assistive technology products for people with disabilities According to the OECD Consumption Tax Trends 2024, around 20 OECD countries apply reduced rates or special exemptions for disability equipment. The United Kingdom maintains a zero VAT regime for products specifically designed for people with disabilities. Malta issued new guidelines for zero VAT on disability aids and rehabilitation devices in 2024. Spain applies super-reduced rates – as low as 4 % – for some disability aids, while Belgium, Germany, France, the Netherlands and South Korea maintain reduced VAT on wheelchairs, hearing aids and assistive medical devices. At the same time, European legislation (Directive 2006/112/EC) now allows rates as low as 0 % for assistive technology and accessibility equipment, reflecting the gradual treatment of aids not as simple consumer goods but as tools for social inclusion, education and equal access. Accordingly: 1.
Does the Commission intend to encourage Member States more actively to apply zero or super-reduced VAT rates to assistive technology products and accessibility aids for people with disabilities?
On the basis of comparative data for countries that currently apply reduced or zero VAT rates to disability equipment, are the results of zero taxation supported?
Is the Commission considering issuing guidelines on the tax facilitation of assistive technologies, including digital tools and accessibility software for daily living and work?

(26 August 2026) Reduced value added tax (VAT) rates typically have little impact on prices due to the low pass-through effect. This is because shops are not legally required to pass on any savings from reduced VAT to their customers by reducing their prices. Therefore, the Commission does not expect reduced or zero VAT rates to have significant effects on the price of sales of disability equipment nor does it consider issuing related guidelines on tax facilitation. When the Council of the EU adopted the major VAT rate reform in 2022 (1), Member States unanimously agreed on revised wording for the category relating to goods for persons with disabilities (2). As part of this hard-fought political compromise, Member States retained the discretion to apply and set reduced or zero VAT rates, based on the provisions of the VAT Directive (3). The Commission respects the fiscal policy decisions taken by Member States and does not generally encourage them to apply zero or super-reduced VAT rates, including for assistive technologies. As announced in the communication ‘Enhancing the strategy for the rights of persons with disabilities up to 2030 ’ (4) adopted in May 2026, the Commission will seek to promote better knowledge and strengthen the single market for assistive technologies and AI applications as part of its flagship initiative. The aim is to identify and remove bottlenecks that prevent persons with disabilities from benefiting from accessible and affordable technologies.
