E-10-2026-002406.t: ‘Recent incidents’ involving drones in the context of the Action Plan on Drone and Counter-Drone Security
qt: to the Commission Fabio De Masi (NI) Subject:

In response to our Written Question E‑001142/2026 about ‘recent incidents’ involving drones in the context of the Action Plan on Drone and Counter-Drone Security1, the Commission stated that ‘attribution of responsibility for individual incidents is not within the Commission’s competence’2. 1.

Without prejudice to the question of which authority is formally responsible for investigating or attributing individual incidents, what information does the Commission possess regarding the actors believed to be responsible for the drone incidents referred to in the action plan?

In particular, has the Commission received information from any Member States, EU agencies or other competent authorities concerning the likely perpetrators, their affiliations, or the origin of these incidents, and if so, what conclusions has it drawn from that information?
https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/E-10-2026-001142_EN.html. https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/E-10-2026-001142-ASW_EN.html.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.9.2026)

Operational incident response is the responsibility of Member States, given the strong link with national security and defence matters. However, coordinated actions at EU level can support Member States in the deployment of counter-drone capacities and solutions. There is no formal reporting obligation in EU legislation for Member States concerning drone security incidents, unless the incident falls within the scope of the Critical Entities Resilience Directive (CER)1 or Directive (EU) 2022/2555 (NIS 2 Directives2), amongst other relevant instruments. Those requirements do not mandate the sharing of the origin of the incident and the affiliation of perpetrators behind the incident with the Commission. Information sharing between Member States and the Commission for drone-security-related incidents has taken place on a voluntary basis. The Action Plan on Drone and Counter-Drone Security3 fosters cross-border information sharing between Member States to improve lessons learnt from previous incidents and establish a clear situational picture. The Action Plan considers supporting initiatives from willing Member States to enhance information sharing, for instance at regional level.

E-10-2026-002405.t: Reliability of recycling data and the double financial burden on Spanish consumers
qt: to the Commission Alvise Pérez (NI) Subject:

The Spanish packaging system presents a paradox: citizens and businesses bear the burden of taxes, costs built into product prices and local authority charges under the promise of effective recycling, while doubts remain as to how much is actually recycled. Ecoembes claimed to have recycled 1 560 404 tonnes of household packaging in 2024, representing 76.3 % of the packaging placed on the market by its clients. However, the European Environment Agency warns that Spain reports packaging recycling rates higher than the target, but possibly overestimated; and the Ministry revised downwards to 41.3 % the separate collection of plastic bottles, which Ecoembes had put at 73.4 %. This is not about imposing more regulation or presenting new deposit schemes as a priority solution, but about demanding transparency: if citizens pay for waste management at the point of purchase, through local taxes and via public expenditure, they must know whether actual recycling is taking place or whether an opaque system of intermediaries, campaigns and inflated statistical results is being funded. 1.
Will the Commission verify the reliability of the Spanish recycling data reported under European regulations?

Will it assess whether Spain’s implementation of EU extended producer responsibility rules ensures transparent cost allocation and prevents consumers or taxpayers from bearing costs that should be covered by producers?
Will it demand verifiable traceability of packaging right through to its actual recycling?

(27 August 2026) The Commission and Member States work together in accordance with the principle of sincere cooperation, as laid down in Article 4(3) of the Treaty on EU. Member States are required to ensure the reliability and accuracy of packaging recycling data reported to the Commission (1). They must verify and cross-check the amounts of packaging waste generated and inform the Commission of such verification carried out and, where appropriate, of any significant inconsistencies identified and corrective measures planned or taken. Based on Article 56 of the Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (2) (PPWR), the Commission will update the rules for calculation, verification and submission of recycling data to the Commission to ensure better data quality. As regards plastic packaging, the Commission carries out inspection visits to verify the data provided by Member States for the calculation of the own resource based on non-recycled plastic packaging waste (3). An extended producer responsibility (EPR) fee shall reflect the actual costs and not exceed the costs that are necessary to provide waste management services in a cost-efficient way. As established in Article 6(4) of the PPWR, the Commission will also set up a harmonised framework for the eco-modulation of EPR fees based on packaging’s recyclability. Finally, as part of the Circular Economy Act (4), the Commission is assessing how to simplify and harmonise EPR rules.

E-10-2026-002404.t: Risk of European industrial decline due to delays in software, AI and digitalisation
qt: to the Commission Alvise Pérez (NI) Subject:

Europe is facing a decisive industrial transformation. While China and the United States are making strides in artificial intelligence, robotics, digital platforms and software-defined vehicles, much of European industry remains stuck in a 20th century model: namely powerful factories with limited in-house capabilities for coding, data management, automation and digital integration. The German case is particularly worrying. Germany, the EU’s industrial powerhouse, ranks only mid-table in terms of digitalisation and lags far behind in digital administration. In the automotive sector, Volkswagen’s need to partner with Rivian or XPeng highlights that even Europe’s major industrial champions are increasingly reliant on third parties for critical software technologies. Industrial strength in the 21st century is no longer decided solely by assembly lines, but by AI, operating systems, data, chips, the cloud, robotics and speed of execution. This technology lag will not be resolved by more abstract public plans, but rather by unlocking private investment, reducing energy costs, simplifying regulations and allowing European companies to compete. 1.
Does the Commission recognise that this technology lag in terms of software, AI and digitalisation threatens the EU’s industrial competitiveness?
Will the Commission assess the cumulative impact of bureaucracy, regulation and energy costs on investment in technology in the EU?
What specific measures will it take to accelerate private investment, regulatory simplification and digital industrialisation in the EU?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.9.2026) The Commission agrees on the need for substantial investment in critical digital technologies for the EU’s competitiveness. A clear-eyed assessment of the EU’s reliance on foreign software, products, AI models and digital infrastructure is the starting point of the recent Communication on Tech Sovereignty Package1, designed to boost the EU’s capacity to develop and deploy such technologies and curb strategic dependencies that affect competitiveness. The Strategic Roadmap for Digitalisation and AI in the Energy Sector2 advocates for a digitalised, interconnected energy system increasing electrification and clean energy integration to face high energy prices. The package also calls for the urgent mobilisation of private risk capital to address the gap in high-risk financing for EU deep-tech firms and large-scale infrastructure, against investment need estimated more broadly at up to EUR 450 billion by 2036, and the injection of considerable resources into strategic technologies by other economies. In parallel, the Commission is looking to increase AI uptake in EU strategic sectors through the AI Continent Action Plan3 and the Apply AI Strategy4. It is also undertaking a regulatory ‘deep cleaning’ as part of the Digital Simplification Package5. The AI Omnibus clarifies the application timelines of the AI Act6, and the proposal for a Digital Omnibus aims to unlock data and provide legal certainty for AI training. To gauge the cumulative impact of digital rules, the 2027 Digital Fitness Check7 will assess whether governance delivers a predictable, harmonised rulebook.

E-10-2026-002403.t: Mass regularisation in Spain versus the Nordic model of migration control and effective returns
qt: to the Commission Alvise Pérez (NI) Subject:

While several Member States are tightening their migration policies in response to integration problems, pressure on public services and difficulties in coexistence, the Spanish Government has approved an extraordinary regularisation scheme for undocumented migrants. The measure acts as an incentive for further illegal arrivals, undermines the credibility of European return rules, and shifts additional costs onto housing, healthcare, education, social welfare and the labour market. Sweden, after years of generous reception policies, has opted to require longer residence, selfsufficiency, good conduct and knowledge of the language and society in order to gain citizenship. Spain, by contrast, appears to be moving towards a model of mass regularisation without a transparent European assessment of its impact on Schengen, genuine integration and the sustainability of the welfare state. The EU cannot call for border control and effective returns while tolerating national decisions which, in practice, reward illegal entry and generate pull effects across the entire common area. 1.
Has the Commission assessed the impact of Spain’s extraordinary regularisation on Schengen and on returns, and whether it is consistent with the European Pact on Migration and Asylum?
Will the Commission request data from Spain on costs, actual labour market integration, access to benefits and the background of the beneficiaries?
Does the Commission consider this type of mass regularisation to be compatible with a credible European policy on illegal migration?

E-10-2026-002402.t: Digital euro acceptance requirements in the corresponding Commission proposal
qt: to the Commission Rada Laykova (ESN) Subject:
The Commission proposal on the digital euro provides for mandatory acceptance requirements for certain market participants. 1.
What makes the Commission believe that these mandatory acceptance requirements still fall within the scope of Article 133 TFEU as measures necessary for the use of the euro as the single currency?
In this context, where does the Commission see the clear line of demarcation between conventional monetary policy and broader interference in market and contractual structures?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.8.2026) The Commission proposal1 grants the digital euro, as a new, digital form of the single currency, legal tender status. This is similar to the legal tender status of euro banknotes and coins, which also entails mandatory acceptance. The mandatory acceptance of the digital euro is necessary to ensure the effective use of the euro as the EU's single currency, which is the very objective of Article 133 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU). The mandatory acceptance will allow the digital euro to enjoy a sufficiently uniform level of acceptance throughout the euro area. In the absence of this acceptance requirement, there would be a risk that the digital euro is accepted only selectively, leading to a fragmented usability of the digital euro, which stands in contrast to the aim of Article 133 TFEU. According to the case law of the Court of Justice, the concept of monetary policy is not limited to its operational implementation by the European System of Central Banks, but also entails a regulatory dimension intended to guarantee the status of the euro as the single currency. The legal basis for that purpose is Article 133 TFEU, with the aforementioned objective2. Any impact of the acceptance requirements on market- and contractual structures is therefore an inherent consequence of the monetary law provisions. In that context, it should also be highlighted that the proposal provides for duly justified and proportionate exceptions to the general acceptance obligation, for instance for small merchants that only accept euro banknotes and coins. Furthermore, it is worth underlining that the contractual freedom is not unduly affected by the digital euro’s acceptance requirements, as payer and payee can agree on a different means of payment.

E-10-2026-002398.t: Combating the Muslim Brotherhood’s spread in the EU and Italy
qt: to the Commission Anna Maria Cisint (PfE) Subject:

A report published by the Israeli Ministry of Diaspora Affairs states that a number of organisations believed to be part of the Muslim Brotherhood’s network (namely the Union of Islamic Communities in Italy, the Young Muslims of Italy, the Islamic Alliance of Italy and Association of Palestinians in Italy) are active in my country. These conclusions corroborate the findings of a May 2025 French secret service report entitled ‘The Muslim Brotherhood and Political Islam in France’. E-10-2026-002397.t: Effects of the ETS on European industrial competitiveness
qt: to the Commission Anna Maria Cisint (PfE) Subject:

The current Emissions Trading System (ETS) is imposing growing costs on European industry, which are exacerbated by the high volatility of the CO2 price, the increasing presence of financial actors in the allowance market and the progressive disappearance of free allocations for the sectors most exposed to international competition. It also seems necessary to adapt the allowance reduction rate to what is really technologically possible for companies to achieve in terms of decarbonisation, limit the effects of the ETS on energy prices and combat speculative practices that risk altering the original objectives of the system. In addition, the application of the ETS to maritime transport is of particular concern in the absence of alternative fuels available on competitive terms, with the risk of encouraging the relocation of traffic to non-EU ports. In the light of the above: 1.

Is the Commission aware that the current ETS is contributing to deindustrialisation processes in the European Union, and will it therefore propose a radical overhaul of the system, taking action on the allowance price setting mechanisms and on the participation of financial actors?

Will it suspend application of the ETS to the maritime sector until economically viable technological and energy alternatives are available and its effects on European competitiveness have been fully assessed?

(1 September 2026) The EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) contains numerous measures to protect industry against carbon leakage, including free allocation of allowances, dedicated state aid guidelines (1) and financial support from ETS revenues. On 17 July 2026, the Commission put forward a comprehensive review of the ETS, including proposals for the future of these elements beyond 2030. The proposal also revises the emissions reduction pathway consistent with the 2040 climate target as established in the European Climate Law (2). This means that the decarbonisation pathway to 2040 will be more gradual than the one applicable today. The review also proposes to reform the Market Stability Reserve to keep the carbon market stable, rules-based, and aligned with technological and economic realities, building on a complementary proposal made on 1 April 2026 (3). As regards financial actors, the latest annual report of the European Securities and Markets Authority reconfirmed that EU carbon markets operate in line with market fundamentals and found no issue in their integrity or transparency (4). The Commission does not intend to suspend the application of ETS to maritime. Decarbonisation of the sector is needed for its long-term competitiveness and energy independence, and the Commission is actively monitoring the impact of the ETS extension to maritime. In line with the EU Industrial Maritime Strategy (5), the ETS review includes measures to strengthen the sector’s competitiveness, including a new mechanism to directly support shipping companies with ETS allowances to boost the uptake of sustainable fuels and zero-emission propulsion technologies, alongside the objectives to address concerns on evasion risks, connectivity and level playing field.

E-10-2026-002396.t: Extraterritorial sanctions against Cuba and the EU’s Blocking Statute
qt: to the Commission Per Clausen (The Left) Subject:

The latest extraterritorial sanctions from the US targeting Cuba have already led to many European companies, large and small, having to quickly abandon business in Cuba, in what the press has described as their fleeing the island1. This clearly means that US sanctions are already resulting in both direct and indirect costs for numerous European companies. Fortunately the EU has an instrument – the Blocking Statute23 – which can be used (and indeed has been used in the past) for exactly this type of situation. It is important that this, and other tools, be employed to counter US actions. In this regard: 1.

What specific actions is the European Commission planning to take to counter or mitigate the impact on European companies, following the latest US sanctions against Cuba and their extraterritorial nature?

Does the Commission have an estimate of the potential monthly losses, both direct and indirect, that European businesses – and by extension the European economy – might incur as a result of these sanctions, and if not, when will one be produced?
When will the EU’s Blocking Statute be triggered in response to this situation, as it was with the 1996 US sanctions?

at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (7.8.2026) The Commission has consistently maintained that the extra-territorial application of secondary sanctions is incompatible with international law and that sanctions must comply with the UN Charter, international humanitarian law and due process. Where the new executive orders can be considered as an action based on or resulting from an act specified in the Annex of Regulation 2271/96 (Blocking Statute)1, including the Helms Burton Act, then the latter regulation already protects the EU operators by prohibiting compliance with that executive order. Information obtained under the Blocking Statute Regulation pertains to the effects of the laws, regulations and other legislative instruments included in its Annex. E-10-2026-002395.t: Large-scale development plans with no strategic environmental assessment in Torri del Benaco
qt: to the Commission Cristina Guarda (Verts/ALE) Subject:

On 20 November 2025, the Municipality of Torri del Benaco (Province of Verona) adopted a development plan (P.I. 3.1) which provides for further expansion and land take in an area that is saturated with tourism and speculative development and includes two sites of Community importance (SCIs)1. The development plan identifies measures for the transformation of the area in line with the local land-use plan (PAT). The current PAT2 is subject to specific environmental requirements, such as ‘environmental improvement with a view to strengthening or enhancing landscape features of primary importance for species of Community interest, taking account of ecological and functional connectivity with areas of the Natura 2000 network3’. It is crucial, therefore, that the plan’s cumulative effects on the environment and land use are looked into. However, of the roughly 320 building works provided for in P.I. 3, only 50 were included in P.I. 3.14, which suggests that attempts are being made to bypass the strategic environmental assessment (SEA) or its screening procedure. In the light of the above, and to prevent the carving up of this excessive development and ensure that the overall environmental impacts of Torri del Benaco town planning instruments are properly assessed, could the Commission investigate whether the SEA legislation has been complied with?

The current PAT (2) is subject to specific environmental requirements, such as ‘environmental improvement with a view to strengthening or enhancing landscape features of primary importance for species of Community interest, taking account of ecological and functional connectivity with areas of the Natura 2000 network (3)’. It is crucial, therefore, that the plan’s cumulative effects on the environment and land use are looked into. However, of the roughly 320 building works provided for in P.I. 3, only 50 were included in P.I. 3.1 (4), which suggests that attempts are being made to bypass the strategic environmental assessment (SEA) or its screening procedure. (28 July 2026) According to Article 3 of the Strategic Environmental Assessment Directive (SEAD) (1), an environmental assessment shall be carried out for plans and programmes which are likely to have significant environmental effects. This includes plans and programmes which are prepared for tourism or land use and plans or programmes that have been determined to require an assessment pursuant to the Habitats Directive (2). Moreover, based on Article 3 (4) of SEAD, Member States shall determine whether plans and programmes that set the framework for future development consent of projects are likely to have significant environmental effects. It would seem that the planning instrument referred to would set the framework for future projects listed in Annex II of the Environmental Impact Assessment Directive (3), namely apartment projects (depending on their size and scale) and could be covered by point 10(b) of Annex II and be subject to a screening. As pointed out by the Honourable Member, it would seem that there was an assessment procedure carried out, including public consultation. Furthermore, it seems that the municipality is in the process of preparing a new urban planning amendment and might still opt for further screening and/or environmental assessment as appropriate. Therefore, at this stage, the Commission cannot establish that there is a breach of EU law.

E-10-2026-002393.t: Transposition deficit of the Pay Transparency Directive ((EU) 2023/970) ahead of the 7 June 2026 deadline
qt: to the Commission Angelika Winzig (PPE) Subject:

To date, only a tiny minority of Member States have fully transposed the Pay Transparency Directive, while the vast majority face significant delays. For instance, Germany does not even have a first draft bill, delaying entry into force until late 2026 or early 2027. Similarly, ‘gold-plating’ debates have slowed France’s legislative process, and Belgium has formally requested a six-month extension. Given that the deadline expires in a few days, we request the following information: 1.

Does the fact that large Member States are going to miss the 7 June deadline change the Commission’s stance on enforcement and a ‘stop-the-clock’ mechanism, and how does it plan to handle the imminent harmonisation gap across the single market?
How does the Commission intend to protect companies and cross-border workers from legal uncertainty in those Member States that have not transposed the Pay Transparency Directive on time?

Does the Commission consider the transposition obligations to have been substantially met by Member States such as Austria, where sector-wide collective agreements already guarantee transparent, non-discriminatory pay structures covering the entire workforce? If not, what additional benefit does the Pay Transparency Directive provide in such systems?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (24.8.2026) The Commission remains committed to ensuring the full and correct implementation of the Pay Transparency Directive1. It is currently assessing the state of transposition in the Member States and will consider all appropriate measures to follow up, including the launch of infringement proceedings. To ensure legal certainty for companies and workers, the Commission is closely monitoring transposition, answers daily to complaints received from citizens and continues to support Member States to transpose the directive correctly. The Commission organised five implementation workshops, together with European social partners and relevant national stakeholders. In March 2026, the Commission published together with the European Institute for Gender Equality a step-by-step toolkit to facilitate the implementation of the Directive for micro, small and medium-sized and large employers. The Commission is also providing technical support bilaterally to Member States having requested it. The principle of equal pay for equal work or work of equal value applies to all employers, including where pay is set through collective bargaining2. The Directive complements national collective agreements with common EU minimum standards, individual transparency rights, tools to detect pay discrimination, and strong enforcement measures. While collective agreements can be a powerful tool to achieve equal pay, the Directive does not foresee a presumption of compliance on their basis.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2023/970/oj/eng. 2 See cases Royal Copenhagen C-400/93 and Defrenne v Sabena C-43/75.

E-10-2026-002392.t: Energy policy implications of the United Arab Emirates’ withdrawal from OPEC and OPEC+
qt: to the Commission Angelika Winzig (PPE) Subject:

The United Arab Emirates’ (UAE) withdrawal from OPEC and OPEC+, effective as of 1 May 2026, begs the question as to how the EU can leverage it in terms of energy policy. For European companies and end consumers, affordable energy prices, security of supply and stable trade routes are of key importance. In this context, the UAE could become a more important player as a stable, capable voice in the Gulf – not only as an energy supplier, but as a partner that ensures security of supply and provides infrastructure and regional resilience. Closer cooperation must not, however, give rise to new fossil fuel dependencies, but should rather combine diversification, resilience and transformation. In the short term, oil products, LNG (liquefied natural gas) and supply flexibility could be of use. In the medium term, infrastructure, storage and industrial cooperation will become more relevant, while, in the long term, hydrogen, ammonia and synthetic fuels will be the order of the day. At the same time, de-escalation in the Gulf, open sea lanes – particularly the Strait of Hormuz – and the protection of civilian energy infrastructure remain key prerequisites for stable markets. 1.
Is the Commission considering forging a strategic energy partnership with the UAE to ensure security of supply, competitive prices and diversification?
How does the Commission intend to integrate secure maritime trade and energy routes in the Gulf more closely into its energy and foreign policy?
What measures is the Commission planning to weave decarbonisation, hydrogen, ammonia, synthetic fuels and European industrial competitiveness into such a partnership?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (8.9.2026) As of today, the bulk of the United Arab Emirates (UAE)’s energy exports are destined to Asian markets. At the same time, the UAE is an important regional energy actor and investor in the energy transition, including in Africa, the Middle East and the EU. Its clean-tech and energy market remains comparatively less open to European companies, and there is scope to improve market access and investment conditions for EU companies. The EU is currently negotiating a Free Trade Agreement (FTA) with the UAE. This is a strategic priority and covers the energy, raw materials, and inter alia, sustainable development. It provides the appropriate framework for cooperation on energy and clean technologies, including renewables and critical raw materials, in line with the EU’s policy objectives on energy security, competitiveness, diversification and decarbonisation. With the European Council, the Commission stresses the need to respect freedom of navigation and maritime security in line with international law and the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea. It welcomes efforts announced by Member States and partners to ensure such freedom in the Strait of Hormuz. The Commission recognises the strategic importance of secure and resilient maritime trade and energy routes in the Gulf and Middle East for European supply chains and energy security. It will continue to support more diversified and resilient transport and logistics connections between Europe and the Gulf, including through development of existing and complementary sustainable, multimodal transport links and corridors, through initiatives such as India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC), among other, and in line with the Global Gateway strategy.

E-10-2026-002391.t: Impact of the proposed PFAS restriction on the availability of critical medical devices in the EU
qt: to the Commission Tomislav Sokol (PPE) Subject:

Evidence submitted by stakeholders in the medical technology sector to the European Chemicals Agency consultation on the proposed restriction on PFAS (per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances) highlights that fluoropolymers play a critical role in numerous key medical devices, including vascular grafts, catheters, guidewires and surgical meshes. These materials are used because of their unique properties such as biocompatibility, durability, and resistance to degradation, which are essential to ensuring clinical performance and patient safety. The current Annex XV restriction dossier acknowledges that, for many of these applications, no technically and clinically viable alternatives to fluoropolymers exist. The potential for substitution is considered to be low. Concerns have been raised that the proposed restriction could lead to reduced availability of established therapies, increased reliance on more invasive procedures that carry higher risks for patients, and higher healthcare costs due to complications, longer hospital stays or repeat interventions. In this context: 1.

What actions is the Commission taking to comprehensively assess the impact of the proposed PFAS restriction on the availability, safety and performance of critical medical devices and their role in clinical pathways?
If the Commission identifies a risk to the availability of such medical devices, what regulatory or policy measures does it intend to take to prevent disruption to patient access?
What steps will the Commission take to ensure the long-term availability of these essential medical technologies in the EU?

Medical devices is one of the sectors assessed in detail during this process (1). In that context, the availability of alternatives to PFAS and the socioeconomic impacts of the restriction options are evaluated by ECHA’s Committee for Socio-Economic Analysis (SEAC). qt: to the Commission Isabel Serra Sánchez (The Left) Subject:

According to a press source1, Zaragoza City Council reportedly allocated EUR 152 012.06 to the ‘Plan de medios y difusión del proyecto Huerva Ríos’ (Media and communications plan for the River Huerva project), an institutional campaign partly financed by NextGenerationEU and intended to raise awareness of the renaturalisation of the River Huerva. qt: to the Commission Mireia Borrás Pabón (PfE) Subject:

Under EU rules, using antimicrobials for promoting the growth or increasing the yield of livestock is prohibited, as is using antimicrobials reserved for human infections to treat animals. What percentage of imports from Mercosur countries are currently being subject to physical and analytical border checks?

E-10-2026-002387.t: Health risks in imports from Mercosur
qt: to the Commission Mireia Borrás Pabón (PfE) Subject:

The Commission was aware, prior to the signing of the EU-Mercosur Agreement, that some signatory countries, such as Brazil, permitted the use of substances banned in the EU because of their risks to human health, including certain antimicrobials and growth hormones in meat production. Furthermore, new cases of food contamination have been detected in recent weeks, including Salmonella in Brazilian poultry products. Given this situation: 1.
How does the Commission justify the signing and provisional application of the Agreement despite having prior knowledge of these health risks and the existing regulatory divergences?

Before the Agreement was signed, did the Commission have detailed reports or assessments warning of the health and food safety risks arising from the liberalisation of imports of meat products from Brazil?
at: (English version) to the Commission Mireia Borrás Pabón (PfE) (10 June 2026) Subject: Health risks in imports from Mercosur The Commission was aware, prior to the signing of the EU-Mercosur Agreement, that some signatory countries, such as Brazil, permitted the use of substances banned in the EU because of their risks to human health, including certain antimicrobials and growth hormones in meat production. Furthermore, new cases of food contamination have been detected in recent weeks, including Salmonella in Brazilian poultry products. Given this situation: 1.
How does the Commission justify the signing and provisional application of the Agreement despite having prior knowledge of these health risks and the existing regulatory divergences?

Before the Agreement was signed, did the Commission have detailed reports or assessments warning of the health and food safety risks arising from the liberalisation of imports of meat products from Brazil?

(10 August 2026) Article 6.6(1) of the EU-Mercosur Interim Trade Agreement (ITA) (1) provides that products exported from a Party shall meet the applicable sanitary or phytosanitary (SPS) requirements of the importing Party. Products placed on the EU market, including from Mercosur or from any other countries, must continue to comply fully with all EU import rules. This includes requirements on animal health, residue controls, and the prohibition of substances not authorised in the EU, such as certain growth promoters. Imports of products of animal origin are subject to approval of exporting countries and establishments, residue monitoring, audits and border controls. Before its conclusion, the Commission considered the effects of the Agreement. The Sustainability Impact Assessment (2) provides an examination of the potential economic, social, human rights and environmental impact of the trade component of an Agreement between the EU and Mercosur. Separately, food and animal health risks linked to imports were assessed and managed through established procedures, including Commission audits, residue-control requirements, Rapid Alert System for Food and Feed (3) notifications, and country- and establishment-approval procedures. When deficiencies in operators or control systems were identified, including in relation to certain Brazilian meat establishments, they were addressed through various measures, including more audits. The ITA therefore does not require the EU to lower its SPS standards, and any market access remains conditional on continued compliance with EU law, with the EU retaining full power to monitor, restrict or suspend imports where necessary and regardless of the existence of a trade agreement with the trade partner in question.

E-10-2026-002386.t: Digital sovereignty stress test: Who will foot the bill for the EU’s technological ambitions?
qt: to the Commission Ioan-Rareş Bogdan (PPE) Subject:

The European Technological Sovereignty Package acknowledges major dependence, with the EU spending EUR 264 billion a year on third-party software and cloud products, and proposes that data centre capacity be trebled. At the same time, the objectives of the Cloud and AI Development Act and the Chips Act 2.0 put huge financial and logistical pressure on the Member States. 1.

Through which financial mechanisms will the Commission support startups and local authorities in redirecting part of the EUR 264 billion to the European open-source ecosystem, preventing the funds from being absorbed once again by large international integrators?

How will the Commission ensure the fair distribution and EU co-financing of the massive costs of modernising national electricity grids, given the logistical burden that the trebling of data centre capacity will place on the Member States?

How will the Commission reconcile the implementation of the ‘cloud and AI sovereignty assessment framework’ with the promise to keep the market open to likeminded partners without creating operational bottlenecks or major compliance costs for EU SMEs?
at: (English version) to the Commission Ioan-Rareş Bogdan (PPE) (10 June 2026) Subject: Digital sovereignty stress test: Who will foot the bill for the EU’s technological ambitions? The European Technological Sovereignty Package acknowledges major dependence, with the EU spending EUR 264 billion a year on third-party software and cloud products, and proposes that data centre capacity be trebled. At the same time, the objectives of the Cloud and AI Development Act and the Chips Act 2.0 put huge financial and logistical pressure on the Member States. 1. Through which financial mechanisms will the Commission support startups and local authorities in redirecting part of the EUR 264 billion to the European open-source ecosystem, preventing the funds from being absorbed once again by large international integrators? 2. How will the Commission ensure the fair distribution and EU co-financing of the massive costs of modernising national electricity grids, given the logistical burden that the trebling of data centre capacity will place on the Member States? 3. How will the Commission reconcile the implementation of the ‘cloud and AI sovereignty assessment framework’ with the promise to keep the market open to like-minded partners without creating operational bottlenecks or major compliance costs for EU SMEs? (1 September 2026) Strengthening tech sovereignty requires sustained financial funding. Discussions on the Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) 2028-2034 are ongoing, including on funding EU competitiveness through instruments like the future European Competitiveness Fund (1). Procurement promoting open standards and reusable solutions can also help local authorities buy from Europe’s open-source ecosystem and reduce reliance on large international providers (2). The European Parliament has a key role in achieving this ambition, notably in the MFF and Tech Sovereignty Packag e (3) negotiations. Increased data centre (DC) capacity will require major grid investments. To increase grid capacity in a cost-effective manner, the Commission has taken action including through the Grids Action Plan (4), the European Grids package (5) and the Connecting Europe Facility (6) to make better use of existing infrastructure, reinforce cross-border coordination and crosssectoral planning, and accelerate permit-granting procedures and access to funding. In addition, the proposal to future-proof electricity bills (7) aims to lower electricity costs through efficient network charges and smart electricity grid and network access. The sovereignty framework under the proposed Cloud and AI Development Act (8) is risk-based and proportionate, with requirements increasing where justified by the sensitivity of the service. Under the proposal, procurement of cloud and AI services remains open to like-minded partners that meet security, transparency and control requirements. A single EU framework is expected to reduce fragmentation, costs and bottlenecks. Small and medium-sized enterprises would benefit from simpler procedures and improved access to public procurement for cloud services.

qt: to the Commission Olivier Chastel (Renew) Subject:
Reports from a number of Member States and the European Court of Auditors have revealed that tens of billions of euros in e-commerce VAT and customs duties have gone uncollected. 1.

Does the Commission have an up-to-date estimate of the shortfall for the EU budget caused by major types of customs fraud for low-value and high-value business-toconsumer distance sales flows, as well as for business-to-business e-commerce flows where goods are sold after their arrival on EU soil?

Given the practical difficulties for national customs administrations to physically check millions of parcels every day, how does the Commission plan to modernise the reporting method applicable to business-to-consumer distance sales flows and to business-to-business e-commerce flows? What is the timetable for this?

To what extent does the Commission plan to integrate source-based data certification technologies to ensure that the amounts collected by online sales platforms actually correspond to the financial transactions carried out and to ensure the accuracy of customs declarations for all types of flows – including business-to-business e-commerce flows?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.9.2026) The Commission annually publishes the value-added tax (VAT) Gap study, which estimated the EU VAT compliance gap for 2023 at EUR 128 billion. The methodology does not identify specific fraud types. Work with Member States is ongoing to develop methods to estimate VAT losses linked to e-commerce fraud. For customs duties, the Commission has no estimate of the shortfall in the EU budget. Further to the introduction of the EUR 3 temporary customs duty, the Commission shall assess by 1 October 2026 whether a diversion of trade flows occurs If needed the Commission can extend the scope of this duty to all goods with a value not exceeding EUR 150. Under the upcoming EU Customs Reform, operators will submit data to a new EU Customs Data Hub instead of separate national systems. Its first phase, covering e-commerce business-toconsumer supplies, is expected to start on 1 July 2028. This should improve data management and customs controls. The full Hub should be used by Trust and Check traders1 from March 2031 and by all operators from February 2034. From 1 July 2026, items in parcels worth up to EUR 150 sent from a third country to an EU consumer are subject to a temporary EUR 3 customs duty. In parallel, the Commission, together with e-commerce stakeholders and Member State experts, is developing a fast-track solution to strengthen the security of the Import One Stop Shop. From 1 November 2026, all distance sales will also be subject to an EU handling fee. The Commission also supports Eurofisc in using data from payment service providers to detect inconsistencies between payment flows and VAT declarations.
1 Customs authorities can grant this status to economic operators considered as highly trustworthy, because they

fulfil stricter criteria of legal, digital and operational compliance. These traders may enjoy specific benefits, e.g. no customs intervention to release or control the goods (‘green lane’), supervision by their Member States of establishment and no obligation to put the goods in transit.

E-10-2026-002383.t: Migration via the Algeria–Balearic Islands route II
qt: to the Commission Christine Anderson (ESN) Subject:

Recent reports indicate a substantial increase in illegal arrivals on the Balearic Islands from Algeria. While these arrivals take place on Spanish territory, questions arise on the subsequent distribution of these migrants within the European Union, and on whether this occurs through official mechanisms or through onward movements. 1.

Have migrants who initially entered the European Union via the Algeria–Balearic Islands route been relocated or transferred to other Member States under EU solidarity mechanisms, voluntary relocation schemes or comparable arrangements, and if so, in what numbers and to which Member States?

Does the Commission possess data, estimates or assessments concerning subsequent secondary movements of migrants arriving via this route to other Member States, and if so, which Member States are identified as the principal destinations?

Taking into account both relocations and secondary movements, how does the Commission assess the overall impact of the Algeria–Balearic Islands route on migration pressures in Member States other than Spain, and what effect does it expect the Migration and Asylum Pact to have on these movements?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (31.7.2026) With the Asylum and Migration Management Regulation (AMMR)1, which entered into application on 12 June 2026, a permanent and flexible solidarity mechanism is in place. Following the Commission's assessment covering the period July 2024 – June 20252, Spain was identified as a Member State under migratory pressure and is eligible to benefit from the Solidarity Pool agreed by the Council in December 20253. The solidarity mechanism does not operate on the basis of specific migratory routes. Information on the implementation of solidarity measures will be reported by Member States to the EU Solidarity Coordinator in accordance with Article 60(6) of the AMMR. The second Annual Report that the Commission will adopt in October 2026 will present the state of implementation of the Pact on Migration and Asylum, including the solidarity mechanism4. The Commission regularly monitors secondary movements and, when assessing whether a Member State is under migratory pressure, at risk thereof or facing a significant migratory situation, takes into account a range of indicators, including asylum applications, outgoing take back requests as well as outgoing take charge requests based on illegal entry and stay5. The Commission has no specific information on secondary movements from the Balearic Islands to other Member States.
1 Regulation (EU) 2024/1351 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 May 2024 on asylum and

migration management, amending Regulations (EU) 2021/1147 and (EU) 2021/1060 and repealing Regulation (EU) No 604/2013. 2 Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2025/2323 of 11 November 2025 pursuant to Article 11 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1351 of the European Parliament and of the Council. 3 Council Implementing Decision (EU) 2025/2642 of 22 December 2025 on the establishment of the Annual Solidarity Pool for 2026. 4 https://home-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies/migration-and-asylum/pact-migration-and-asylum/implementingpact-migration-and-asylum_en. 5 Commission Staff Working Document, SWD(2025) 792 final, Methodology for the purposes of Commission implementing decision pursuant to Article 11 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1351 of the European Parliament and of the Council; https://home-affairs.ec.europa.eu/document/download/80637837-e569-4896-98f22e8b92abf66e_en?filename=Methodology_en.pdf.

E-10-2026-002382.t: Monitoring of public funds used for the rescue of Plus Ultra during the COVID-19 crisis
qt: to the Commission Christine Anderson (ESN) Subject:

During the COVID-19 pandemic, the Spanish airline Plus Ultra received EUR 53 million in public support through Spain’s SEPI strategic rescue fund. Subsequent reports have linked the company to ongoing investigations concerning alleged money laundering, corruption and financial transactions involving persons connected to the so-called Zapatero affair. In this context: 1.

Did the Commission assess whether the public resources used for the rescue of Plus Ultra originated, directly or indirectly, from EU-funded COVID-19 instruments, including the Recovery and Resilience Facility, REACT-EU, SURE or other EUsupported measures?

Following the approval of the rescue under the applicable State aid framework, did the Commission, OLAF or any other Union body conduct or request any ex post verification regarding the ultimate use of the funds received by Plus Ultra?

If no such verification was carried out, how does the Commission ensure that public funds mobilised during the COVID-19 crisis were not exposed to fraud, corruption, money laundering or other forms of misuse after their disbursement?
at: (Deutsche Fassung) Anfrage zur schriftlichen Beantwortung E-002382/26 an die Kommission Christine Anderson (ESN) (10. Juni 2026) Betrifft: Überprüfung der zur Rettung von Plus Ultra während der COVID-19-Krise eingesetzten öffentlichen Mittel Während der COVID-19-Pandemie erhielt die spanische Fluggesellschaft Plus Ultra öffentliche Zuwendungen in Höhe von 53 Mio. EUR aus dem strategischen Rettungsfonds der spanischen SEPI. In späteren Berichten wurde das Unternehmen mit laufenden Ermittlungen wegen mutmaßlicher Geldwäsche, Korruption und Finanztransaktionen im Umfeld von in die Zapatero-Affäre verwickelten Personen in Verbindung gebracht. 1. Hat die Kommission geprüft, ob die für die Rettung von Plus Ultra verwendeten öffentlichen Mittel direkt oder indirekt aus EU-finanzierten COVID-19-Instrumenten, einschließlich der Aufbau- und Resilienzfazilität, REACT-EU, SURE oder anderer von der EU unterstützter Maßnahmen, stammten? 2. Hat die Kommission, das OLAF oder eine andere Einrichtung der EU nach der Genehmigung der Rettungsbeihilfe gemäß dem geltenden Rechtsrahmen für staatliche Beihilfen eine Ex-post-Überprüfung hinsichtlich der letztendlichen Verwendung der von Plus Ultra erhaltenen Mittel durchgeführt oder um diese ersucht? 3. Falls keine solche Überprüfung durchgeführt wurde: Wie stellt die Kommission sicher, dass öffentliche Mittel, die während der COVID-19-Krise mobilisiert wurden, nach ihrer Auszahlung nicht Gegenstand von Betrug, Korruption, Geldwäsche oder anderweitigem Missbrauch wurden? Eingang: 10.6.2026 Antwort von Valdis Dombrovskis im Namen der Europäischen Kommission (24. September 2026) Die Kommission verfügt über solide Verfahren zur Verhinderung und Aufdeckung von Betrug bei der Verwaltung von EU-Mitteln (1). Dazu gehören Verfahren gemäß der Haushaltsordnung, die für alle EU-Mittel gilt, darunter Mittel aus SURE, NextGenerationEU und der Kohäsionspolitik. Die Mitgliedstaaten müssen Unregelmäßigkeiten und Betrug verhindern, aufdecken und korrigieren. Darüber hinaus führt die Kommission Systemprüfungen durch und meldet Verdachtsfälle dem Europäischen Amt für Betrugsbekämpfung (OLAF), und bei Bedarf ermittelt die Europäische Staatsanwaltschaft. Der spanische Rettungsfonds „Fondo de Apoyo a la Solvencia de Empresas Estrategicas“, aus dem Plus Ultra finanzielle Unterstützung erhalten hat, war mit keinem Etappenziel oder Zielwert im geltenden Durchführungsbeschluss des Rates zum Aufbau- und Resilienzplan Spaniens verknüpft (2). Die kohäsionspolitischen Fonds, darunter REACT-EU, waren ebenfalls nicht betroffen. Im Rahmen von SURE wurden den Mitgliedstaaten Darlehen zur Finanzierung von Kurzarbeitsregelungen und ähnlichen Maßnahmen zur Verfügung gestellt.

Artikel 36 und 63 der Haushaltsordnung: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/DE/TXT/PDF/?uri=OJ:L_202402509. Durchführungsbeschluss des Rates zum Aufbau- und Resilienzplan Spaniens, mitsamt Änderungen (COM(2026) 257): https://eur-lex.europa.eu/resource.html?uri=cellar:56ce2369-5451-11f1-b3e2-01aa75ed71a1.0002.02/DOC_1&format=PDF.

E-10-2026-002381.t: Migration via the Algeria–Balearic Islands route I
qt: to the Commission Christine Anderson (ESN) Subject:

According to recent media reports, the number of illegal migrants arriving on the Balearic Islands from Algeria has increased significantly. Several boats carrying dozens of migrants have reportedly reached Mallorca and Formentera within a short period of time, adding to a broader rise in arrivals via this route. 1.

What is the Commission’s assessment of the current scale and development of the Algeria–Balearic Islands migration route, including the nationalities of those arriving and the risks posed to the EU’s external borders?

What operational activities is Frontex currently carrying out in relation to this route, and what support is being provided to Spain regarding border surveillance, registration procedures and return operations?
How many persons arriving via this route have, to the Commission’s knowledge, been effectively returned to Algeria or other countries of origin or transit during the last three years?
at: (English version) to the Commission Christine Anderson (ESN) (10 June 2026) Subject: Migration via the Algeria-Balearic Islands route I According to recent media reports, the number of illegal migrants arriving on the Balearic Islands from Algeria has increased significantly. Several boats carrying dozens of migrants have reportedly reached Mallorca and Formentera within a short period of time, adding to a broader rise in arrivals via this route. 1. What is the Commission’s assessment of the current scale and development of the Algeria-Balearic Islands migration route, including the nationalities of those arriving and the risks posed to the EU’s external borders? 2. What operational activities is Frontex currently carrying out in relation to this route, and what support is being provided to Spain regarding border surveillance, registration procedures and return operations? 3. How many persons arriving via this route have, to the Commission’s knowledge, been effectively returned to Algeria or other countries of origin or transit during the last three years? (27 July 2026) According to the data collected by the European Border and Coast Guard Agency (Frontex) (1), illegal border crossings (IBCs) to Spain along the Western Mediterranean and the Atlantic routes combined decreased in the first four months of 2026 (-45%, 7 726) compared to the same period in 2025. Along the Western Mediterranean route alone, IBCs increased between January and April 2026 (+57%, 5 394) compared to the same period in 2025. The main nationalities along the Western Mediterranean route in the first four months of 2026 were Algerians, Moroccans, Sudanese, Malians and Guineans. Frontex is supporting Spain and other Member States in the region through operational activities at sea, including maritime surveillance, pre-frontier aerial surveillance and at key ports of entry. Frontex currently deploys around 200 standing corps officers to support the Spanish authorities, with the majority stationed along Spain’s Mediterranean coast. The EU also engages with Algeria on migration governance, protection of migrants and refugees, and capacity-building, notably through the regional programmes such as Himaya and the Regional Development and Protection Programme for North Africa. Available statistics on returns are not disaggregated by migration route of arrival. According to Eurostat dat a (2), in the past three years, 6 105 (2024), 5 705 (2025) and 1 545 (2026) third-country nationals having received an order to leave have been returned by Spain. At EU level, 3 590 (2024), 2 695 (2025), and 575 (2026) Algerian nationals were returned to Algeria.

https://www.frontex.europa.eu/what-we-do/monitoring-and-risk-analysis/migratory-map/. The data can be disaggregated by nationality: https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/migr_eirtn/default/table? lang=en&category=migr.migr_man.migr_eil.

E-10-2026-002380.t: Strengthening prevention, mental well-being and healthy ageing through improved hearing health
qt: to the Commission Manuela Ripa (PPE), Tomáš Zdechovský (PPE), Dan-Ştefan Motreanu (PPE), Liudas Mažylis (PPE), Eleonora Meleti (PPE), Jagna Marczułajtis-Walczak (PPE), Elena Nevado del Campo (PPE), Alex Agius Saliba (S&D), Vytenis Povilas Andriukaitis (S&D), Ondřej Krutílek (ECR), Elisabetta Gualmini (Renew), Ciaran Mullooly (Renew), Majdouline Sbai (Verts/ALE), Mounir Satouri (Verts/ALE), Sebastian Everding (The Left), Merja Kyllönen (The Left) Subject:

At a time when the EU is facing growing mental health challenges and increasing pressure on healthcare systems, hearing health remains insufficiently integrated into prevention and mental well-being strategies. Yet untreated hearing loss affects more than 57 million EU citizens and is closely linked to social isolation, depression and cognitive decline. Hearing loss is also considered the leading modifiable risk factor for dementia, with the potential to reduce individual dementia risk by up to 8 %. Despite the availability of effective and affordable solutions, many people requiring hearing care remain untreated. Strengthening prevention, early detection and access to care could therefore play an important role in supporting healthy ageing, improving quality of life and reducing the long-term burden on healthcare systems across the EU. In the light of the ‘Healthier Together’ initiative, can the Commission clarify the following: 1.
How does the Commission plan to strengthen prevention and early detection of hearing loss across Member States?
What actions will the Commission take under EU4Health and related initiatives to improve access to hearing care and reduce environmental factors contributing to hearing loss?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (21.8.2026) 1. The Commission supports Member States and stakeholders in the prevention and management of non-communicable diseases (NCDs) via the 2022 ‘Healthier Together’ EU NCDs initiative1, which recognises hearing loss as a factor contributing to dementia. In May 2026, the Commission adopted a communication Enhancing the Strategy for the Rights of Persons with Disabilities up to 2030, which reinforces its commitment to building a Union where the rights and dignity of persons with disabilities are fully realised. The strategy pays attention to accessibility as an enabler of rights2. In December 2025, the Commission proposed the revision of the EU legislative framework for medical devices, which also applies to hearing aids3. The revision will simplify procedures while maintaining patient safety and public health protection. 2. The Commission has provided financial support on dementia from the EU4Health programme4 to support collaborative work between Member States and stakeholder-led projects. Under the joint action PreventNCD5 (EUR 76 million), Member States collaborate on developing and implementing prevention policies on NCDs and their risk factors. The joint action JADE-Health6 (EUR 4,5 million) aims to reduce the burden of dementia and other neurological disorders by transferring best practices from the EU Best Practice Portal on Public Health7. The project Care4Elders8 (EUR 450 000) works on transforming dementia through innovative, digital, and person-centred approaches. Through the European Research Council the Commission also funds research in hearing and audio-based diagnostics. READIHEAR project9 funded under Horizon Europe10 aims to set the basis for a new generation of 1 https://health.ec.europa.eu/document/download/d843d53e-c1c1-4664-b31e-febf618d011a_en?filename=eu-

ncd-initiative_publication_en_0.pdf. 2 https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/policies/justice-and-fundamental-rights/disability/unionequality-strategy-rights-persons-disabilities-2021-2030_en. 3 Proposal for a regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council amending Regulations (EU) 2017/745 and (EU) 2017/746 as regards simplifying and reducing the burden of the rules on medical devices and in vitro diagnostic medical devices, and amending Regulation (EU) 2022/123 as regards the support of the European Medicines Agency for the expert panels on medical devices and Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 as regards the list of Union harmonisation legislation referred to in its Annex I: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legalcontent/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52025PC1023. 4 https://health.ec.europa.eu/funding/eu4health-programme-2021-2027-vision-healthier-european-union_en. 5 https://www.preventncd.eu/. 6 https://jadementia.eu/. 7 https://webgate.ec.europa.eu/dyna/bp-portal/. 8 https://care4elders.eu/. 9 https://cordis.europa.eu/project/id/101044753. 10 https://research-and-innovation.ec.europa.eu/funding/funding-opportunities/funding-programmes-and-opencalls/horizon-europe_en.

E-10-2026-002378.t: Application of tachograph rules in short-haul delivery transport and penalties for human error in record-keeping
qt: to the Commission Merja Kyllönen (The Left), Katri Kulmuni (Renew), Sebastian Tynkkynen (ECR), Maria Ohisalo (Verts/ALE) Subject:

The EU rules on driving time, rest periods and the tachograph system are designed to improve road safety, curb fatigue and prevent the manipulation of working hours. Practical experience has shown, however, that the application of the rules to short-haul delivery transport has raised concerns about their proportionality and appropriateness. Where distribution is concerned, frequent daily stops require constant changes to be made to the tachograph, and this increases the risk of human error in record-keeping. In practice, individual unintentional failures to mark the correct space could be treated in the same way as intentional breaches of driving times and rest periods. This could result in disproportionate penalties, such as an increase in the risk rating and the threat of a transport licence being withdrawn, even if the actual driving time and workload were well within safe limits. Furthermore, the current system does not fully take into account the specific characteristics of delivery transport, where work consists of short trips, frequent stops and load handling. 1.

How suitable does the Commission think the tachograph system and the current rules on driving times and rest periods are for short-haul delivery transport, where stops are more frequent and work is more intermittent than in long-haul transport?

Does the Commission take the view that the current rules and the practices in place to enforce them draw enough of a distinction between intentional infringements and human errors in record-keeping, and is the Commission willing to assess the need to clarify or fine-tune the rules with a view to establishing proportionate enforcement practices for short-haul delivery transport?

Does the Commission intend to look into whether current tachograph technology, and the ways in which it is used, are sufficiently compatible with the ways in which modern urban and delivery transport actually operate?
at: (English version) to the Commission Merja Kyllönen (The Left), Katri Kulmuni (Renew), Sebastian Tynkkynen (ECR), Maria Ohisalo (Verts/ALE) (9 June 2026) Subject: Application of tachograph rules in short-haul delivery transport and penalties for human error in record-keeping The EU rules on driving time, rest periods and the tachograph system are designed to improve road safety, curb fatigue and prevent the manipulation of working hours. Practical experience has shown, however, that the application of the rules to short-haul delivery transport has raised concerns about their proportionality and appropriateness. Where distribution is concerned, frequent daily stops require constant changes to be made to the tachograph, and this increases the risk of human error in record-keeping. In practice, individual unintentional failures to mark the correct space could be treated in the same way as intentional breaches of driving times and rest periods. This could result in disproportionate penalties, such as an increase in the risk rating and the threat of a transport licence being withdrawn, even if the actual driving time and workload were well within safe limits. Furthermore, the current system does not fully take into account the specific characteristics of delivery transport, where work consists of short trips, frequent stops and load handling. 1. How suitable does the Commission think the tachograph system and the current rules on driving times and rest periods are for short-haul delivery transport, where stops are more frequent and work is more intermittent than in long-haul transport? 2. Does the Commission take the view that the current rules and the practices in place to enforce them draw enough of a distinction between intentional infringements and human errors in record-keeping, and is the Commission willing to assess the need to clarify or fine-tune the rules with a view to establishing proportionate enforcement practices for short-haul delivery transport? 3. Does the Commission intend to look into whether current tachograph technology, and the ways in which it is used, are sufficiently compatible with the ways in which modern urban and delivery transport actually operate? (21 August 2026) The Commission takes note of the concerns raised regarding the application of Regulation (EC) No 561/2006 (1) and Regulation (EU) No 165/2014 (2) to short-haul delivery transport. These acts aim to improve road safety and fair working conditions across all professional road transport, while allowing certain exemptions and derogations which Member States may use for specific categories of local operations under Article 13 of Regulation (EC) No 561/2006. Under Article 19 of Regulation (EC) No 561/2006 and Article 41 of Regulation (EU) No 165/2014, Member States lay down rules on penalties, which must be effective, proportionate, dissuasive and non-discriminatory. Directive 2006/22/EC (3), including its Annex III, frames the seriousness of infringements. National authorities are responsible for risk-rating systems and for distinguishing between manipulations of the tachograph and inadvertent mistakes, subject to those EU-level requirements. The Commission monitors the implementation of the social rules and tachograph legislation through regular reports, expert dialogue and the Tachograph Forum, and adopts and continues to review detailed technical specifications for smart tachographs under Regulation (EU) No 165/2014, including features intended to ease use, improve accuracy and support enforcement. At this stage, however, the Commission has not been made aware, in this context, of particular issues arising from short-haul delivery transports, which are usually carried out by vehicles below 3.5 tonnes and therefore fall outside the scope of the relevant EU rules when undertaken in domestic transport.

E-10-2026-002377.t: Protection of Italian citizen Nessy Guerra and her daughter, a minor, in Egypt
qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Ilaria Salis (The Left), Benedetta Scuderi (Verts/ALE), Brando Benifei (S&D), Mimmo Lucano (The Left), Giuseppe Lupo (S&D), Cecilia Strada (S&D), Alessandra Moretti (S&D), Mélissa Camara (Verts/ALE), Mounir Satouri (Verts/ALE), Marco Tarquinio (S&D), Leoluca Orlando (Verts/ALE), Nikos Papandreou (S&D), Annalisa Corrado (S&D), Georgia Tramacere (S&D), Alessandro Zan (S&D), Pina Picierno (Renew), Ignazio Roberto Marino (Verts/ALE), Chloé Ridel (S&D), Malika Sorel (NI), Dario Tamburrano (The Left), Danilo Della Valle (The Left), Gaetano Pedulla' (The Left), Pasquale Tridico (The Left), Valentina Palmisano (The Left) Subject:

Italian citizen Nessy Guerra has been sentenced on appeal in Egypt in proceedings concerning alleged adultery following a complaint lodged by her former husband. The sentence includes a six-month prison term and compulsory prison labour. Ms Guerra had previously reported situations of domestic violence, threats and coercive behaviour by her former husband. Serious concerns also arise regarding the situation of her daughter, a minor, who is reportedly subject to a travel ban imposed by Egyptian authorities preventing her return to Italy. In the light of the above: 1.

Is the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy (VP/HR) aware of this case and of the concerns relating to the protection of the fundamental rights of Ms Guerra and her daughter, and in contact with the Italian and/or Egyptian authorities?

What concrete steps is the VP/HR taking, in coordination with the Italian authorities and the EU Delegation to Egypt, to monitor further judicial proceedings and ensure respect for fair trial standards and the protection and rights of women victims of violence?
What actions are the VP/HR and the European External Action Service currently taking or could they take to support Ms Guerra and ensure the protection and best interests of her daughter?
Supporter1
This question is supported by a Member other than the authors: Cristina Guarda (Verts/ALE).
at: (English version) to the Vice-President of the Commission/High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Ilaria Salis (The Left), Benedetta Scuderi (Verts/ALE), Brando Benifei (S&D), Mimmo Lucano (The Left), Giuseppe Lupo (S&D), Cecilia Strada (S&D), Alessandra Moretti (S&D), Mélissa Camara (Verts/ALE), Mounir Satouri (Verts/ALE), Marco Tarquinio (S&D), Leoluca Orlando (Verts/ALE), Nikos Papandreou (S&D), Annalisa Corrado (S&D), Georgia Tramacere (S&D), Alessandro Zan (S&D), Pina Picierno (Renew), Ignazio Roberto Marino (Verts/ALE), Chloé Ridel (S&D), Malika Sorel (NI), Dario Tamburrano (The Left), Danilo Della Valle (The Left), Gaetano Pedulla' (The Left), Pasquale Tridico (The Left), Valentina Palmisano (The Left) (9 June 2026) Subject: Protection of Italian citizen Nessy Guerra and her daughter, a minor, in Egypt Italian citizen Nessy Guerra has been sentenced on appeal in Egypt in proceedings concerning alleged adultery following a complaint lodged by her former husband. The sentence includes a six-month prison term and compulsory prison labour. Ms Guerra had previously reported situations of domestic violence, threats and coercive behaviour by her former husband. Serious concerns also arise regarding the situation of her daughter, a minor, who is reportedly subject to a travel ban imposed by Egyptian authorities preventing her return to Italy. In the light of the above: 1.

Is the Vice-President of the Commission/High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy (VP/HR) aware of this case and of the concerns relating to the protection of the fundamental rights of Ms Guerra and her daughter, and in contact with the Italian and/or Egyptian authorities?

What concrete steps is the VP/HR taking, in coordination with the Italian authorities and the EU Delegation to Egypt, to monitor further judicial proceedings and ensure respect for fair trial standards and the protection and rights of women victims of violence?
What actions are the VP/HR and the European External Action Service currently taking or could they take to support Ms Guerra and ensure the protection and best interests of her daughter?

Supporter (1) (7 August 2026) The High Representative/Vice-President is well aware of this case, and the EU Delegation in Cairo remains in contact with the Italian Embassy. According to the Italian Embassy in Cairo, the citizen has appealed her conviction before the Egyptian Court of Cassation at the end of June 2026 and no hearing date has yet been communicated. With respect to the custody proceedings concerning her daughter, the appeal hearing, initially scheduled for 3 June 2026, has been postponed and is currently expected to take place on 6 August 2026. The Italian authorities, which are providing consular assistance, have not requested support from the EU, and the persons concerned have likewise not sought EU assistance. Consequently, the EU Delegation does not currently plan to observe the custody proceedings and, at this stage, considers the matter primarily to fall within the remit of Italian consular protection. The EU remains committed to promoting respect for human rights, including the rights of women and children and the right to a fair trial, in its dialogue with Egypt. The EU will continue to follow developments in this case, remain in contact with the Italian authorities, and stand ready to provide support, should this be requested.

E-10-2026-002376.t: The Spotify-Universal Music Group (UMG) AI music deal and its impact on competition and culture
qt: to the Commission Nicola Zingaretti (S&D) Subject:

Though the deal struck by Spotify (whose 761 million users make it the world’s biggest audio streaming platform) and global music industry leader UMG concerning AI-generated covers and remixes could bring about some positive developments (including as regards consent, credits and remuneration), it still raises serious competition and cultural diversity concerns. I therefore ask the Commission: 1.

Does it hold that this exclusive agreement between two of the world’s biggest music industry stakeholders could undermine competition and close off the market to indie music, non-UMG artists, small labels and independent producers, and does it therefore intend to open a formal investigation into the matter?

Does it agree that the ‘turning one song into ten thousand’ model will drive down artist incomes and systematically penalise originality by devaluing and disincentivising creativity and by undermining financial support and prospects for artists? If so, what measures will it adopt?
Are Directive (EU) 2019/790 and its compensation mechanisms applicable to business models such as the one described above and, if not will the Commission propose a regulatory revision to this effect?

(14 September 2026) The Commission is closely monitoring the music streaming sector, including any relevant impact of AI-related developments. The Commission may initiate a competition investigation where there are reasonable indications of either anti-competitive agreements (Article 101 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU)) or the abuse of a dominant position (Article 102 of the TFEU) affecting trade between Member States. While the Commission is not conducting a competition investigation at the present stage, it remains committed to ensuring the full respect for EU competition law in this sector. The Commission notes the possibility to create remixes or covers, including through the use of AI, but all such uses should take place in compliance with applicable EU copyright rules including any relevant exception. Chapter 3 of Directive (EU) 2019/790 (1) (Fair remuneration in exploitation contracts of authors and performers) applies to the relationships entered into by authors or performers and the parties to whom they have licensed or transferred their rights, with the aim of strengthening transparency, contractual balance and fair remuneration. Therefore, Chapter 3 is not confined to a particular form of exploitation. As required under Article 30 of the directive, the Commission has started a review process to examine the impact of the directive on the relevant stakeholders (2).
OJ L 130, 17.5.2019, pp. 92-125. Call for evidence, https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/news/commission-seeks-views-review-eu-copyright-rules.

E-10-2026-002374.t: Concerns regarding the transposition of the Pay Transparency Directive in Slovakia
qt: to the Commission Veronika Cifrová Ostrihoňová (Renew) Subject:

Slovakia has recently adopted legislation intended to transpose the Pay Transparency Directive1. Concerns have been raised about the compatibility of several provisions of the national legislation with the directive. These relate to the exclusion of certain categories of senior public officials and statutory office holders from the legislation’s scope, the postponement of workers’ access to pay information rights beyond the transposition deadline, and the transposition of criteria for assessing work of equal value. These provisions may limit the protection provided by the directive and affect its uniform application across the EU. 1.

Does the Commission consider the exclusion of state servants holding public office, statutory office holders, and other senior public-sector officials appointed by the Slovak Parliament, President or Government or members of the Slovak Government from the scope of the national legislation to be compatible with Article 2 of the directive?

Does the Commission consider it compatible with Article 4(4) of the directive to replace the concepts of ‘skills’ and ‘effort’ with narrower national definitions, and to reduce the requirement that relevant soft skills ‘shall not be undervalued’ to merely taking them into account?

Does the Commission consider the postponement of workers’ access to pay information rights beyond 7 June 2026 to be compatible with Articles 7 and 34, given that the directive does not appear to provide for such a transitional period?

Directive (EU) 2023/970 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 10 May 2023 to strengthen the application of the principle of equal pay for equal work or work of equal value between men and women through pay transparency and enforcement mechanisms (OJ L 132, 17.5.2023, p. 21, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2023/970/oj). 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (20.8.2026) In line with the Better Regulation framework1, the Commission assesses transposition in two stages: a completeness check to verify that all necessary national measures have been notified; and a conformity check to assess whether those measures fully comply with the Directive. The Commission is currently examining Member States’ notifications. Where a Member State fails to transpose the Directive by the deadline, the Commission may initiate infringement proceedings under Article 258 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union. As regards the substance of national implementing measures, including the Slovak legal provisions referred to by the Honourable Member, the Commission will, in accordance with established procedures, carry out a detailed assessment of their compliance with the Directive, as part of its conformity review of all implementing measures in all Member States, thereby helping to ensure consistent implementation across the EU. Such assessment will take place once the transposition review is completed, as it requires a comprehensive examination of relevant national labour, civil and procedural law provisions.
