E-10-2026-002373.t: Article 6(11) of the Digital Markets Act – privacy risk assessment, anonymisation standards and compliance oversight for search data sharing
qt: to the Commission Cynthia Ní Mhurchú (Renew) Subject:

Article 6(11) of the Digital Markets Act1 (DMA) provides that search engines are required to provide certain query, click and view data to qualifying competitors. This provision is intended to promote contestability and competition in digital markets. At the same time, the sharing of large-scale search-related datasets raises important questions regarding data protection, anonymisation standards and safeguards against re-identification. Regulatory certainty in this area is important both for effective DMA implementation and maintaining public trust in the protection of users’ personal data. In this context, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

With regard to risk assessment, what methodologies has the Commission used, or does it intend to use, to assess potential privacy and data protection risks arising from the mandatory sharing of search-related datasets under Article 6(11)?

Regarding anonymisation standards, what technical criteria, benchmarks or guidance does the Commission consider appropriate to ensure that data shared pursuant to Article 6(11) is effectively anonymised and cannot reasonably be used to identify individual users?

Regarding monitoring and enforcement, what oversight, auditing or compliance mechanisms will be used to verify that data recipients and providers comply with these safeguards and that the risk of re-identification remains adequately mitigated over time?

Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 September 2022 on contestable and fair markets in the digital sector and amending Directives (EU) 2019/1937 and (EU) 2020/1828 (Digital Markets Act) (OJ L 265, 12.10.2022, p. 1, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/1925/oj). 1
at: (English version) to the Commission Cynthia Ní Mhurchú (Renew) (9 June 2026) Subject: Article 6(11) of the Digital Markets Act — privacy risk assessment, anonymisation standards and compliance oversight for search data sharing Article 6(11) of the Digital Markets Act (1) (DMA) provides that search engines are required to provide certain query, click and view data to qualifying competitors. This provision is intended to promote contestability and competition in digital markets. At the same time, the sharing of large-scale search-related datasets raises important questions regarding data protection, anonymisation standards and safeguards against re-identification. Regulatory certainty in this area is important both for effective DMA implementation and maintaining public trust in the protection of users’ personal data. In this context, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

With regard to risk assessment, what methodologies has the Commission used, or does it intend to use, to assess potential privacy and data protection risks arising from the mandatory sharing of search-related datasets under Article 6(11)?

Regarding anonymisation standards, what technical criteria, benchmarks or guidance does the Commission consider appropriate to ensure that data shared pursuant to Article 6(11) is effectively anonymised and cannot reasonably be used to identify individual users?

Regarding monitoring and enforcement, what oversight, auditing or compliance mechanisms will be used to verify that data recipients and providers comply with these safeguards and that the risk of re-identification remains adequately mitigated over time?

(22 July 2026) The issue of compliance with the obligation pursuant to Article 6(11) of the Digital Markets Act (DMA) (1) to share ranking, query, click and view data, currently arises in the context of the Commission’s specification case regarding Alphabet in case DMA.100209. In that case, the envisaged anonymisation approach is being developed in collaboration with internal and external privacy experts. It follows established anonymisation practices in line with the risk-based logic of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) (2). Conscious of the importance of keeping strict standards to protect privacy, the Commission and the European Data Protection Board (EDPB) have drafted joint guidance on how to implement the DMA in coherence with the GDPR (3). The anonymisation approach being developed by the Commission’s DMA team is in line with these guidelines to ensure a robust protection of user privacy while pursuing the important public interest of increasing contestability of the online search market in line with the obligation pursuant to Article 6(11) DMA. The anonymisation approach gives a prominent role to technical measures that are complemented by contractual measures to anonymise search data. The data will only be shared with online search engines that must meet strict eligibility criteria. Recipients of the search data are also subject to strict contractual measures. These contractual measures include segregation of the search data, limitation of the purpose of use, and data governance and integrity and confidentiality measures.

Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 September 2022 on contestable and fair markets in the digital sector and amending Directives (EU) 2019/1937 and (EU) 2020/1828 (Digital Markets Act) (OJ L 265, 12.10.2022, p. 1, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/1925/oj). https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/1925/oj/eng. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj/eng.

E-10-2026-002372.t: Strengthening the effectiveness of EU-funded measures to tackle youth unemployment
qt: to the Commission Nikolas Farantouris (S&D) Subject:

Tackling youth unemployment by creating quality jobs remains a challenge for many Member States. Since 2014, the EU has allocated around EUR 25 billion from Cohesion Policy to this end. However, many of the funded measures do not focus on the long-term integration of young people into the labour market, the European Court of Auditors (ECA)1 finds. The ECA makes recommendations to strengthen the monitoring and evaluation of EU funding, improve the effectiveness of funded incentives for hiring young people and provide targeted support to economically inactive young people. Strengthening the effectiveness of EU-funded measures is all the more necessary for countries such as Greece, which has one of the highest youth unemployment rates in the EU, while quality jobs with decent wages and good working conditions remain a challenge. Given that the Commission has accepted the ECA recommendations and has identified weaknesses in the labour market in Greece2: 1.
What specific measures does the Commission intend to take to enhance the effectiveness of the funded measures to tackle youth unemployment?
What measures does it intend to take to provide targeted assistance to countries, such as Greece, which continue to face major challenges in tackling youth unemployment and creating quality jobs?
https://www.eca.europa.eu/en/publications/SR-2026-15. https://economy-finance.ec.europa.eu/economic-surveillance-eu-member-states/country-pagesincluding-country-reports/country-report-greece_en. 1 2
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (31.7.2026) To tackle youth unemployment, full implementation of the Youth Guarantee by all Member States is key. In line with European Court of Auditors (ECA) findings, measures that could enhance the effectiveness of EU-funded initiatives under the European Social Fund + (ESF+), include the strengthening of monitoring and evaluation frameworks to ensure long-term labour market integration of young people. The Commission will also engage with Member States to exchange knowledge and best practices on how to design and implement effective youth employment measures targeting, inter alia, inactive young people. ESF+ funding could be used to support vocational training to address skills mismatches while expanding childcare and long-term care services to improve labour market participation1. To provide targeted assistance to Greece, where ESF+ allocations for youth unemployment amount to approximately EUR 700 million (2021-2027), the Commission is aligning ESF+ interventions with the country-specific recommendations, which highlight structural labour market weaknesses, including skills mismatches and precarious employment conditions. Enhanced collaboration with Greek authorities under the European Semester framework will prioritise quality job creation, particularly in sectors with growth potential, such as the green and digital transitions. The Just Transition Fund allocation of EUR 1.63 billion for Greece will further support regional employment initiatives in areas most affected by economic shifts. Technical support instruments could also be used to strengthen Greece’s administrative capacity to absorb EU funds efficiently, ensuring compliance with ECA guidelines on sustainable youth integration.
1 Particularly for women and vulnerable groups.

qt: to the Commission Mihai Tudose (S&D) Subject:

The latest Eurobarometer shows that 46 % of SMEs in the EU report difficulties in finding employees with adequate skills. The survey highlights companies’ complaints about bureaucratic obstacles in the process of recruiting workers from outside the EU. The fact that European SMEs are seeking workers outside the Union for construction, healthcare, cleaning, public catering and transport is a warning sign. Before we boost international recruitment, it would make more sense to prioritise education for young people and retraining for adults in the Member States as a solution to the skills shortage. The European Commission’s 2025 report on the labour market and the social situation shows that we have 51 million citizens who are unemployed even though they are of working age. There are 13 million unemployed people in Europe. Nearly 1 in 10 young people drops out of school, with a sad record in Romania – 15.5 %. These figures reflect European human resource potential that should not be overlooked. Especially since these people are among the 93 million European citizens at risk of poverty and social exclusion. What measures is the Commission considering to solve the problem of the EU labour and skills shortage by mobilising the European workforce?

(12 August 2026) Maximising the potential of the EU workforce is a top priority for the Commission. The Union of Skills Communication (1) addresses mismatches via human capital development, from basic skills to lifelong learning. The recommendation on Human Capital (2) urges Member States to closer align education and labour market needs (3). The forthcoming Education Package envisages supporting basic skills, European school alliances, and the EU Teachers and Trainers Agenda. The Commission will consult social partners on the possible direction of EU action to support the activation of persons excluded from the labour market and gender equality regarding labour market opportunities (4). The European Network of Public Employment Services facilitates exchanges of best practices and uses bench learning to help improve the functioning of such services, which are important in supporting access to employment (5). It is envisaged that the upcoming Fair Labour Mobility Package will provide for improvement in information access and support for mobile workers, modernise EURopean Employment Services (EURES) and remove barriers related to skills and qualifications (6). Under the European Social Fund+ (ESF+), the EU and Member States are investing EUR 139.1 billion (7) in 2021-2027 to strengthen the EU’s employment, social, education and skills policies (8). In Romania, EUR 4 billion is invested in the labour market, education and skills, and preventing school dropouts. While the EU's shrinking working-age population means that recruiting non-EU workers for key shortage occupations might be necessary (9), the Commission encourages Member States to prioritise skills development and training, support EU workers outside the labour market, and improve working conditions.

E-10-2026-002369.t: Planned ban on PFAS chemicals and impact on the food processing industry
qt: to the Commission Stefan Köhler (PPE), Christine Singer (Renew), Angelika Niebler (PPE), Christian Doleschal (PPE) Subject:

At the end of March 2026, the two scientific committees of the European Chemicals Agency announced their support for restricting the PFAS substance group, with targeted exemptions. The PFAS substance group contains more than 10 000 different chemicals. They include fluoropolymers, which play a key role in the food processing industry. They reduce the adhesion of biofilms, simplify cleaning processes and ensure high, modern hygiene standards. A ban in the near future is being discussed even though the chemicals cannot yet be replaced in some key industrial sectors, such as the chemical, pharmaceutical or food industries. There is ambiguity with regard to this development and the expected consequences of a sweeping PFAS ban for the food industry. 1.
Does the Commission plan to introduce exemptions to the ban on the use of PFAS in industry? What criteria could be used for such exemptions?
What is the Commission’s assessment of the risk that a possible PFAS ban and a lack of alternatives in food production could lower EU food safety standards?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (31.7.2026) The Commission recognises that regulatory changes of the magnitude of the restriction on perand polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), proposed under the Regulation concerning the Registration, Evaluation, Authorisation and Restriction of Chemicals (REACH)1 warrant serious attention and that their potential impacts, including on the food processing industry need to be carefully assessed. The Commission is fully committed to address the pollution caused by PFAS to protect the health of EU citizens and the environment. The European Chemicals Agency (ECHA)’s scientific committees have been assessing the restriction proposal submitted by five national authorities2 in January 2023. The Commission expects to receive the final opinions of ECHA by the end of 2026 and has committed to presenting its proposal for amendment of Annex XVII to the REACH Regulation as soon as possible thereafter. As indicated in the European Chemicals Industry Action Plan3, where adequate alternatives in terms of safety and performance are not available, the continued use of PFAS in industrial applications may be allowed for critical applications, accompanied by requirements to reduce emissions at all lifecycle stages to limit the release of pollutants into the environment and by clear incentives to innovate, until acceptable substitutes are found.
1 Regulation (EC) No 1907/2006 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 18 December 2006

concerning the Registration, Evaluation, Authorisation and Restriction of Chemicals (REACH), establishing a European Chemicals Agency, amending Directive 1999/45/EC and repealing Council Regulation (EEC) No 793/93 and Commission Regulation (EC) No 1488/94 as well as Council Directive 76/769/EEC and Commission Directives 91/155/EEC, 93/67/EEC, 93/105/EC and 2000/21/EC. 2 Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden. 3 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex:52025DC0530.

E-10-2026-002368.t: Crisis in the extra virgin olive oil sector and protecting EU producers’ competitiveness
qt: to the Commission Valentina Palmisano (The Left), Mario Furore (The Left) Subject:

According to sector organisations, the extra virgin olive oil sector is experiencing a period of severe economic difficulty. The Calabria and Puglia regions have requested an urgent debate on the crisis in the sector, in order to highlight to the Italian Government the challenges faced throughout this area of the economy1. In addition to falling profitability, there are rising production costs, price volatility and growing concerns about competition from third-country imports. In this context, a number of producers are speaking out about the risk of a progressive loss of competitiveness in EU olive growing and insufficient producer remuneration. In the light of the above: 1.

Is the Commission aware of the crisis affecting the extra virgin olive oil sector in various regions of the EU, and what assessments has it made of the economic impact of the crisis on producers’ incomes?

Will it adopt or consider adopting extraordinary support measures or crisis management instruments under the common agricultural policy to safeguard the sector’s competitiveness and economic sustainability?

What checks and inspections are carried out to ensure that imports of olive oil from third countries meet standards equivalent to those required of EU producers from an environmental, phytosanitary and social point of view, and does the Commission agree that the principle of reciprocity in this area should be strengthened?

(3 August 2026) The Commission is fully aware of the concerns mentioned by the Honourable Member. Production recovery in Spain and Italy, after years of drought and record prices, together with faltering demand, are putting pressure on olive oil prices. In the meantime, record harvests in third countries and geopolitical events add uncertainty and higher input costs. Regulation (EU) No 1308/2013 (1) provides tools to address market volatility, such as Article 167a allowing Member States to regulate supply, improve and stabilise the olive oil market. The Commission may, in case of severe imbalance, activate private storage aid for olive oil. The continued income support from the Common Agricultural Policy through direct payments plays an important role for farmers. In terms of costs, the Commission is aware of high input and energy costs and has taken measures to address them (2). Finally, the promotion policy is available for the sector, co-funding campaigns to promote consumption both in the EU and third countries. Food products from third countries must comply with import requirements laid down in EU legislation. Member States must carry out risk-based official controls on products from non-EU countries (3). The Commission performs audits in Member States to verify the application of substantive and control rules. The Commission also performs audits in third countries to ensure that goods intended for export comply with EU rules and control systems are capable of ensuring it (4).

E-10-2026-002367.t: Lack of standardised cross-border postage rates in the single market
qt: to the Commission Markus Buchheit (ESN) Subject:

It took general post director Heinrich von Stephan just a few years to standardise postage rates in the newly federally constituted German Empire; what is more, in founding the Universal Postal Union in 1874, he established a cross-border tariff system for a number of sovereign states. By contrast, the EU, in its 70 years or so of integration – and despite claiming to have a completed single market – has managed nothing of the sort. For example, sending a standard letter from Belgium to Germany via bpost currently costs EUR 3.07 – almost 2.5 times more than the EUR 1.25 Deutsche Post charges in the other direction. 1.
How does the Commission explain the persistence of such blatant tariff asymmetry for comparable cross-border correspondence within the single market?
Does it intend to bring in an initiative to harmonise or standardise cross-border postage rates; if so, when will it do so?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.8.2026) 1. The Postal Services Directive1 establishes the regulatory framework for postal services across the EU. The Postal Services Directive requires Member States to ensure a permanent universal service at all points of the territory at affordable prices. This concerns most notably letters and includes cross-border services. Prices shall also be cost oriented. However, there is no legal obligation for uniform tariffs between domestic and cross border universal service letters. Asymmetric tariffs may have their reasons in different volumes, agreements and coststructures. 2. In the Single Market Strategy2 of May 2025, the Commission announced the intention to propose an EU Delivery Act to modernise the postal regulatory framework and in particular the universal service. The aim of the EU Delivery Act would be to ensure that citizens and businesses can receive deliveries throughout the EU at affordable prices, while promoting fair competition on delivery markets and increasing consumer protection. The proposal is planned for the first quarter of 2027.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:01997L0067-20080227. 2 https://single-market-economy.ec.europa.eu/publications/single-market-our-european-home-market-uncertain-
world_en.

E-10-2026-002366.t: Staffing and value for money of press operations at Commission representations in German-speaking countries
qt: to the Commission Markus Buchheit (ESN) Subject:

According to the available information, the Commission representation in Berlin alone has a six-strong press and public relations team; on top of this, there is another position at each of the regional representations in Bonn and Munich and two positions at the representation in Vienna. These decentralised media operations exist in parallel with a generously staffed Spokesperson’s Service and DG COMM, which reports directly to the President; they communicate the Commission President’s messages straight to the accredited media in Brussels. 1.

How many press and media positions have been allocated to the representation in Berlin, the regional representations in Bonn and Munich and the representation in Vienna – broken down by full-time/part-time status and by employment category (officials, other staff, contract personnel)?

What tangible, measurable added value do these decentralised press operations bring with respect to the central communication apparatus made up of the Spokesperson’s Service and DG COMM, and based on what criteria – e.g. reach, media output, independent content – is this added value determined?

How does the Commission square this duplication of centralised and decentralised communication structures with the budgetary principles of economy and efficiency (Article 33 of the Financial Regulation)?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (13.8.2026) The Commission’s Representations in the Member States operate under the guidance of the Directorate-General for Communication. They ensure communication activities at national level and engage with citizens, media and stakeholders on EU policies, in the national context. The press team of the Commission’s Representation and regional offices in Germany comprises one official, one temporary agent, five contract agents and one local agent. Of these, three posts are full-time and five are part-time. The team in the Representation in Austria comprises one official and two contract agents, all full time. The Commission’s Spokespersons’ Service (SPP) and the Representations’ press teams have distinct and complementary roles, in line with the Commission’s Working Methods1. The SPP is the contact point for the Brussels-based press corps. The Representations’ press teams support the media in the Member States, providing tailored information that facilitates coverage by locally based journalists on EU policies with relevance for citizens and communities. Daily close coordination between SPP and Representations ensures that media professionals in the Member States receive relevant information adapted to the national context, enabling them to better inform citizens about the EU. The division of tasks enables the Commission to reach its communication objectives better and in a cost-effective way, in line with the Working Methods and the budgetary principles of the Financial Regulation2.
1 https://commission.europa.eu/document/download/4b958a25-a16a-4ac2-bda8-
c14a18bd117c_en?filename=Working%20Methods%20of%20the%20European%20Commission.PDF. 2 https://op.europa.eu/en/publication-detail/-/publication/990fe2a6-8f52-11ef-a130-01aa75ed71a1/language-en.

E-10-2026-002365.t: Restoring nature in outdoor areas and greening of Commission buildings
qt: to the Commission Markus Buchheit (ESN) Subject:

Until the 1990s, the Berlaymont building was surrounded by thriving Japanese cherry trees. During the process to remove asbestos from the building, the trees were felled and replaced by uninterrupted bare paving. The Commission itself has advanced the Nature Restoration Law (the Nature Restoration Regulation). 1.
When does the Commission intend to break up the paving in front of the Berlaymont building and replace it with new trees, in line with its nature restoration regulation?
Which patios and roofs of its other buildings in Brussels and Luxembourg and those of its agencies and delegations does it intend to green? By when and what are the estimated costs?
at: (English version) to the Commission Markus Buchheit (ESN) (9 June 2026) Subject: Restoring nature in outdoor areas and greening of Commission buildings Until the 1990s, the Berlaymont building was surrounded by thriving Japanese cherry trees. During the process to remove asbestos from the building, the trees were felled and replaced by uninterrupted bare paving. The Commission itself has advanced the Nature Restoration Law (the Nature Restoration Regulation). 1. When does the Commission intend to break up the paving in front of the Berlaymont building and replace it with new trees, in line with its nature restoration regulation? 2. Which patios and roofs of its other buildings in Brussels and Luxembourg and those of its agencies and delegations does it intend to green? By when and what are the estimated costs? (22 September 2026) The Commission is committed to integrating greenery and restoring nature (1) where feasible. The redevelopment in front of Charlemagne strengthens the esplanade’s green character by introducing more vegetation and landscaping to improve the microclimate, reduce heat, and enhance overall environmental quality. A native garden was developed in 2022 near the Berlaymont visitors’ entrance and nearly 1 000 m 2 were then transformed into a distinctive biodiverse garden. Tree planting in front of the Berlaymont building is however currently not foreseen due to security, technical and spatial constraints including insufficient soil depth, risk of water leakage, and the need to maintain safe access for firefighters. The Commission has developed biodiversity plans for its sites that aim to develop green areas in urban sites (Brussels, Luxembourg and Seville) and to manage its green areas in non-urban sites (2). In Brussels, the latest biodiversity initiatives were implemented at the Berlaymont, Loi 41, Belliard 28, Charlemagne (including a green roof), Tervueren 211, Cour Saint Michel and Mérode buildings. The playground design for the Grand Clovis building also promotes urban biodiversity. Since 2023, around EUR 360 000 have been allocated to these projects (3). In Luxembourg, biodiversity actions are in place or under implementation at the Euroforum, CPE3, CPE5, Mercier-Post, Foyer and T2 buildings. Since 2023, around EUR 40 000 have been allocated to these projects. The JMO2 design achieved the highest rating for longterm impact on biodiversity under the Building Research Establishment Environmental Assessment Method (BREEAM) with, for example, around 9 000 m2 of planted surfaces. The JMO2 biodiversity related costs are currently estimated at EUR 620 000 and are included in the overall construction costs.

Under the Commission’s Communication on Greening, 2022: https://commission.europa.eu/about/service-standards-and-principles/modernising-europeancommission/greening-european-commission_en. These include the Joint Research Centres and the Directorate-General for Health and Food Safety at Grange, Ireland as reported in the EMAS Environmental Statement: https://op.europa.eu/webpub/hr/ec-environmental-statement-2025/index.html. Feasibility studies for further projects are ongoing. The Commission plans green spaces to promote biodiversity in all its new buildings in Brussels.

E-10-2026-002364.t: Gender pay gaps in top jobs at the Commission
qt: to the Commission Markus Buchheit (ESN), Elisabeth Dieringer (PfE) Subject:

The Commission regularly stresses its commitment to transparency and to closing the gender pay gap. The salaries of members of the Commission are not uniform, but rather graded according to function: The President, the Vice-Presidents and the other Commission members receive different basic salaries, plus a housing or residence allowance for each of them. 1.

Is the Commission, which is committed to transparency, in a position to disclose the pay gap at the very top of its own organisation, specifically the salary – including the housing allowance – of the President and her Vice-Presidents on the one hand, and the majority of Commission members on the other?
What view does the Commission take of this internal, role-based pay scale in light of its own demands for equal pay and the elimination of the gender pay gap?
at: (English version) to the Commission Markus Buchheit (ESN), Elisabeth Dieringer (PfE) (9 June 2026) Subject: Gender pay gaps in top jobs at the Commission The Commission regularly stresses its commitment to transparency and to closing the gender pay gap. The salaries of members of the Commission are not uniform, but rather graded according to function: The President, the Vice-Presidents and the other Commission members receive different basic salaries, plus a housing or residence allowance for each of them. 1. Is the Commission, which is committed to transparency, in a position to disclose the pay gap at the very top of its own organisation, specifically the salary — including the housing allowance — of the President and her Vice-Presidents on the one hand, and the majority of Commission members on the other? 2. What view does the Commission take of this internal, role-based pay scale in light of its own demands for equal pay and the elimination of the gender pay gap? (12 August 2026) The salaries and allowances of the Members of the European Commission, including the differences between the salaries of the President, Vice-Presidents and Members, are transparent as they are set in Council Regulation (EU) 2016/300 of 29 February 2016 determining the emoluments of EU high-level public office holders which is published in the Official Journal of the European Union (1). The differences in remuneration between the President, Vice-Presidents and Members of the Commission reflect differences in institutional roles and responsibilities established by the Treaties and the applicable Council Regulation. They do not constitute unequal pay for equal work, or a gender pay gap.

E-10-2026-002363.t: Small-scale EU projects – organised crime’s favourite way of circumventing OLAF and the EPPO
qt: to the Commission Markus Buchheit (ESN) Subject:

A recently published study suggests that the Italian Mafia has adapted its scams to skim money off the EU budget. It further states that EU projects worth less than EUR 150 000 are specifically targeted, as the European Anti-Fraud Office (OLAF), the European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO) and other Commission departments do not see cases of this size to be worth prosecuting1. Organised crime is thus deliberately exploiting thresholds and de minimis limits to operate under the radar of watchdogs and law enforcement. 1.

Is the Commission willing to corroborate the findings of this study, namely that organised crime favours EU projects worth less than EUR 150 000 because OLAF, the EPPO and other Commission departments consider such cases to be too insignificant to prosecute?
What conclusions does the Commission intend to draw from these findings, particularly with regard to existing de minimis and minor offence thresholds in the fight against fraud?
https://www.euractiv.com/news/how-italys-mafia-learnt-to-think-small-with-eu-cash/.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (7.9.2026) Regulation (EU, Euratom) 883/20131 does not establish a financial threshold for the opening of an investigation by the European Anti-Fraud Office (OLAF). In its independent investigations, OLAF assesses each case individually based on the criteria set out in Article 5(1) of Regulation (EU, Euratom) 883/2013 and not only based on its possible financial impact. The European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO) investigates and prosecutes – in full independence from the Commission and all other EU institutions, bodies, offices and agencies – crimes affecting the EU’s financial interests (Protection of the European Union’s Financial Interests – PIF crimes), including organised crime when the focus of the activity of criminal organisations is to commit PIF crimes. The 2025 EPPO Annual Report2 demonstrates the key role played by the EPPO in dismantling criminal organisations. In 2025, organised crime cases accounted for about 15% of the total EPPO cases (529 out of 3 602). The threshold of EUR 150 000 referred to in the text of the question does not affect the competence of the EPPO or OLAF to open or conduct investigations.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2013/883/oj/eng. 2 https://www.eppo.europa.eu/assets/annual-report-2025/pdfs/EPPO_Annual_Report_2025_en.pdf.

E-10-2026-002362.t: The housing crisis on EU islands and the need for targeted European policies for social and affordable housing
qt: to the Commission Elena Kountoura (The Left) Subject:

Housing is a fundamental human right and a prerequisite for social and economic well-being. However, it has become one of the most significant social crises facing the EU today. The housing crisis particularly affects island regions, where structural and geographical constraints, an unchecked increase in short-term rentals, limited land availability, increased housing construction costs1 and a lack of adequate public housing exacerbate the situation2, dramatically limiting the availability of housing for residents, students, seasonal workers and public sector workers such as teachers, doctors, nurses, firefighters and police officers. In view of the forthcoming European strategy for islands, can the Commission say: 1.

How will the European affordable housing plan address the specific housing needs of island communities and ensure that the challenges of island regions are taken into account in every European policy, mechanism and financial tool on housing?

Does it intend to propose a ‘Statute of the EU Islands’ and an ‘Islands Pact’, as called for by the European Parliament3, to recognise insularity as a differential feature and address the additional housing costs it entails4?

Will it support the creation of a dedicated funding line in the new multiannual financial framework to support social and affordable housing on islands facing significant pressure from tourism, with a view to meeting the housing needs of residents, public officials and seasonal workers?

According to Commission data, the cost of building new dwellings increased by 56 % between 2010 and 2024. 2 According to the recent OECD report ‘Policy Pathways Beyond the Shoreline: Enhancing Resilience and Innovation in Island Economies’, on some islands, housing costs can be 75 % to 130 % higher than in mainland areas. 3 See paragraph 9 of the report of 24 February 2026 on the housing crisis in the European Union with the aim of proposing solutions for decent, sustainable and affordable housing. 4 For example, the revised Energy Performance of Buildings Directive sets ambitious targets for renovations and zero-emission buildings, but does not sufficiently take into account the increased construction and renovation costs on islands resulting from their insularity. Without targeted financial support, its implementation may slow down renovations and exacerbate housing poverty, rather than contributing to a just green transition. 1
at: (English version) to the Commission Elena Kountoura (The Left) (9 June 2026) Subject: The housing crisis on EU islands and the need for targeted European policies for social and affordable housing Housing is a fundamental human right and a prerequisite for social and economic well-being. However, it has become one of the most significant social crises facing the EU today. The housing crisis particularly affects island regions, where structural and geographical constraints, an unchecked increase in short-term rentals, limited land availability, increased housing construction costs (1) and a lack of adequate public housing exacerbate the situation (2), dramatically limiting the availability of housing for residents, students, seasonal workers and public sector workers such as teachers, doctors, nurses, firefighters and police officers. In view of the forthcoming European strategy for islands, can the Commission say: 1.

How will the European affordable housing plan address the specific housing needs of island communities and ensure that the challenges of island regions are taken into account in every European policy, mechanism and financial tool on housing?

Does it intend to propose a ‘Statute of the EU Islands’ and an ‘Islands Pact’, as called for by the European Parliament (3), to recognise insularity as a differential feature and address the additional housing costs it entails (4)?

Will it support the creation of a dedicated funding line in the new multiannual financial framework to support social and affordable housing on islands facing significant pressure from tourism, with a view to meeting the housing needs of residents, public officials and seasonal workers?

(28 July 2026) The European Affordable Housing Plan (EAHP) recognises that territories face different housing challenges: urban areas and tourist destinations face housing shortages and unaffordability, while rural and remote areas experience demographic decline. The EAHP also recognises the ‘right to stay’ by supporting the renovation and upgrading of local housing in places with economic potential alongside investments in essential infrastructure and services. The EAHP includes ten actions where the EU can support Member States, including islands (1). The European Housing Alliance also facilitates cooperation on housing challenges, potentially including islands, among Member States, regional and local authorities and stakeholders. In addition, the Commission adopted the strategy for Islands (2), recognising the distinct characteristics and challenges of these territories and seeking to better reflect their needs across EU policies including through concrete actions. The Statute of the EU Islands and Island Pact are not among the actions proposed by the communication. The EU has already mobilised at least EUR 43 billion housing-related investment under the current Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) through Cohesion Policy Funds, InvestEU, LIFE, the Single Market Programme and Horizon Europe as well as through NextGenerationEU. The Mid-Term review also enabled Cohesion policy funding to be reprogrammed towards housing. Island regions have access to these programmes and funds.

According to Commission data, the cost of building new dwellings increased by 56% between 2010 and 2024. According to the recent OECD report ‘Policy Pathways Beyond the Shoreline: Enhancing Resilience and Innovation in Island Economies’, on some islands, housing costs can be 75% to 130% higher than in mainland areas. See paragraph 9 of the report of 24 February 2026 on the housing crisis in the European Union with the aim of proposing solutions for decent, sustainable and affordable housing. For example, the revised Energy Performance of Buildings Directive sets ambitious targets for renovations and zero-emission buildings, but does not sufficiently take into account the increased construction and renovation costs on islands resulting from their insularity. Without targeted financial support, its implementation may slow down renovations and exacerbate housing poverty, rather than contributing to a just green transition. For example, the Affordable Housing Act in 2026 will provide a framework to support authorities to identify areas under housing stress and to protect and promote affordability in these areas, in full respect of subsidiarity. COM(2026) 520 final.

Social and affordable housing is among the specific objectives proposed for the future (3). Negotiations on the next MFF are ongoing, therefore final funding possibilities will depend on the co-legislators.

E-10-2026-002361.t: Need to institutionalise an integrated multi-level governance framework and strengthen the administrative capacity of island authorities
qt: to the Commission Elena Kountoura (The Left) Subject:

The effective implementation of the upcoming European strategy for islands requires an integrated, functional multi-level governance framework, which will ensure coordination between the European, national, regional and local levels, as well as the substantive participation of island authorities and local bodies in the formulation, implementation and monitoring of the strategy. Taking into account the proposal to create a ‘European Coordination Platform’ for islands, which will operate as a permanent mechanism for political dialogue, coordination and monitoring of the strategy with the participation of the Commission, Member States, island authorities and economic and social partners1; the fact that the limited administrative and technical capacity of many island administrations constitutes a significant obstacle to the use of available European financial instruments and the implementation of projects2; the fact that an implementation plan for the strategy is required per island, on the basis of the specific characteristics and challenges it faces; and the need to provide specialised administrative and technical assistance, simplify procedures and create ‘one-stop-shop’ mechanisms to facilitate access to EU funding for island entities and businesses3: 1.
Does the Commission intend to establish a European Coordination Platform for islands, to coordinate, monitor and evaluate the implementation of the strategy?

Does the Commission plan to provide for specific mechanisms for technical assistance and strengthening of the administrative capacity of island authorities and bodies, including the creation of ‘one-stop-shops’ on the islands for better access to European financial instruments, support in bringing projects to fruition and simplification of administrative procedures?

See CPMR Islands Commission, Contribution to the Future EU Strategy for Islands. The fragmentation of EU instruments and funding flows creates administrative complexity, which disproportionately affects islands with limited institutional capacity. This limits accessibility to resources and knowledge and weakens the overall effectiveness of EU support. 3 According to the Cyclades Chamber of Commerce and Industry, a typical small business in the Cyclades is faced simultaneously with complex regulatory requirements from multiple authorities and access to financial instruments from different levels of governance, while having to deal with administrative procedures designed for businesses with specialised staff. This reality often leads to the de facto exclusion of smaller island SMEs from available financing, even when they meet the formal eligibility criteria. 1 2
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (17.7.2026) 1. The Commission adopted its first strategy for EU islands1 on 10 June 2026, recognising the distinct characteristics and specific challenges of these territories. As the forward-looking action, the strategy foresees the organisation of a biennial Islands Forum to promote dialogue between the Commission and island stakeholders, facilitate the exchange of experience and good practices, and take stock of progress in implementing the strategy. 2. The strategy recognises that the effective implementation of EU policies requires sufficient administrative capacity at national, regional and local level. In light of this, the strategy foresees continuation of the support to Member States and island authorities through the Technical Support Instrument2, TAIEX-REGIO Peer2Peer3, the European Urban Initiative4, the Clean Energy for EU Islands5, and regular technical dialogues to facilitate simplification, facilitate the exchange of good practices and reduce administrative burden. Furthermore, the Commission will also continue supporting Member States in tailoring and implementing reforms and investments addressing the needs of islands, including in the context of future National and Regional Partnership Plans.

instrument_en#documents. 3 https://ec.europa.eu/regional_policy/policy/how/improving-investment/regio-peer-2-peer_en. 4 https://www.urban-initiative.eu/capacity-building. 5 https://clean-energy-islands.ec.europa.eu/assistance.

E-10-2026-002360.t: Need for a legally binding definition of islands and introduction of a mandatory ‘island clause’ in the future EU strategy for islands
qt: to the Commission Elena Kountoura (The Left) Subject:

Although Article 174 TFEU explicitly recognises islands as areas with permanent natural or demographic handicaps, EU law still lacks a legally binding definition of ‘islands’ and ‘island regions’. Its absence is a barrier to the effective implementation of Article 174 TFEU. In this context, the future strategy should establish a systematic approach that integrates the island dimension into EU policies and redresses injustices against islands1. Island status must be enshrined as a horizontal parameter, integrated from the outset into the design of every European policy, legislative initiative and financial instrument through an operational model of ‘island-proofing by default’ in legislation and programmes. Taking into account that mandatory impact assessments for European initiatives affecting islands could be integrated into existing Better Regulation tools2: 1.

Will the Commission propose a legally binding definition of ‘islands’ and a typology of island regions on the basis of objective, multidimensional criteria3 and support their integration into the new MFF 2028-2034 for differentiated funding by island type?

How will the Commission ensure that the strategy produces a functional model of ‘island-proofing by default’ in European legislation and programmes, with the island dimension taken into account from the outset?

Does the Commission intend to introduce a mandatory ‘island clause’ in key sectors with significant territorial impact, through mandatory island impact assessments incorporated into tools such as territorial impact assessments?

The vast majority of island stakeholders who participated in the public consultation on the introduction of an ‘island clause’ into key policy areas, such as cohesion policy, transport, energy, digital infrastructure, CAP, fisheries, water/waste management and state aid. 2 Such assessments could be integrated into existing Better Regulation tools, such as territorial impact assessments. 3 The typology could be based on the OECD (2026) study ‘Policy Pathways Beyond the Shoreline: Enhancing Resilience and Innovation in Island Economies’, which introduces a hybrid territorial approach to classification based on multidimensional criteria, such as for example size, isolation, fragmentation, seasonality and dependence on external resources, and recommends functional typologies that capture the real interconnections of movement and services, especially for archipelagos like the Aegean. 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (30.7.2026) The Commission adopted its first Islands Strategy1 on 10 June 2006, recognising the distinct characteristics of these territories. The Commission considers that existing legal and statistical frameworks already provide definitions and classifications that cover islands and are tailored to the objectives of the relevant policy areas. For example, Eurostat applies a statistical definition of island regions. The Commission will continue to assess whether existing definitions remain fit for purpose in their respective policy areas. Any future proposals would need to be considered in the context of the relevant sectoral legislation and impact assessments. The Commission applies an integrated approach to Better Regulation2 when preparing new initiatives. The Better Regulation Guidelines3 and Toolbox4 provide for the assessment of territorial impacts, including those affecting islands, where these are relevant and proportionate to the initiative concerned. Such analysis can help identify place-based risks, distributional effects and possible mitigation measures where impacts may affect islands differently from other territories. Under the new Multiannual Financial Framework (2028-2034) islands will continue to receive EU support. The Commission considers that territorial impacts affecting islands can be addressed through existing Better Regulation tools and procedures. In this context, it does not consider introducing further island specific mandatory impact assessments.
1 COM(2026) 520 final. 2 COM/2021/219 final. 3 SWD(2021) 305 final. 4 https://commission.europa.eu/document/download/9c8d2189-8abd-4f29-84e9-
abc843cc68e0_en?filename=BR%20toolbox%20-%20December%202025.pdf.

E-10-2026-002359.t: Need for European mechanisms to compensate the permanent costs of island living in the context of the forthcoming European strategy for islands
qt: to the Commission Elena Kountoura (The Left) Subject:

Following a previous question1 on the need to strengthen the connectivity and territorial cohesion of islands, the Commission responded that it ‘is not proposing a separate financial mechanism or measures exclusively for the connectivity of islands’. Its position fails to address the permanent and structural nature of the handicaps recognised by Article 174 TFEU.2 Taking into account that the permanent additional costs of island living constitute a form of structural market failure and justify the adoption of specific, permanent compensatory mechanisms and fiscal instruments (such as reduced VAT and the transport equivalent) and adapted state aid rules for all islands, and that the implementation of European measures to decarbonise air and maritime transport (ReFuelEU aviation and ETS) may disproportionately burden island regions, increasing transport costs and limiting their connectivity in the absence of appropriate transitional and compensatory measures: 1.

Does the Commission intend to propose specific European compensation mechanisms to address the permanent additional costs of island living,3 in particular in the areas of transport, energy and the provision of essential public services?

Does the Commission plan to adapt the EU state aid framework, including the de minimis rule, the General Block Exemption Regulation and regional aid rules, to take sufficient account of the permanent structural handicaps and increased operating costs of island economies?
Does the Commission intend to introduce specific measures to offset the impact of decarbonisation policies for air and maritime transport on island regions?4

See E-000173/2026 https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/E-10-2026-000173_EN.html. The state of being an island creates structural problems of dependence on maritime and air transport, which constitute a public service on which the daily life of European citizens living on islands depends, with additional costs for the import and export of goods and raw materials, mainly for energy and consumer products, as well as for the transport of passengers. 3 These mechanisms should include specific financial instruments and adapted regulatory frameworks to address the additional costs related to transport, maritime and air connections, energy, market access and the provision of public services. 4 Such as, for example, protecting accessible and reliable connectivity, maintaining public service obligations and using ETS revenues to support island transport systems. 1 2
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (23.7.2026) The EU’s State aid frameworks1 give Member States the possibility to provide islands with tailored support in view of the structurally higher costs they face. The proposals for the General Block Exemption Regulation2 (GBER) and the Air Transport Guidelines3 continue to support island airports. Among the provisions under discussion in the GBER revision is an increase in the eligibility threshold for airport aid from 200 000 to 500 000 yearly passengers. Airports located on islands can also benefit from higher aid intensities for their investments. In addition, the proposals for the GBER and the Air Transport Guidelines explicitly consider the complexity of maritime connections between islands and the mainland. The ongoing reviews of the relevant State aid frameworks provide an opportunity to assess comments, as appropriate, on the need to cater for island specificities. Public Service Obligations4 (PSOs) facilitate maritime connections and can help offset some of the additional costs that islands face as a result of their insularity. For example, in Greece, the PSO in the electricity sector provides a subsidy mechanism that spreads the extra cost of supplying non-interconnected islands across all consumers, helping to keep island electricity prices lower. The EU is also investing in island interconnections to reduce those costs over time and support decarbonisation. To reduce costs, the Emissions Trading System5 and FuelEU Maritime6 allow Member States to exempt voyages servicing small islands from their scope. Finally, the EU strategy for islands7, sets out a forward-looking action for the Commission to launch an in-depth analysis of the cost of insularity and best practice measures to mitigate it, notably in the transport sector.

E-10-2026-002358.t: Addressing the lack of reliable and comparable data on islands in the context of the upcoming European strategy for islands
qt: to the Commission Elena Kountoura (The Left) Subject:

The persistent lack of reliable, comparable and sufficiently detailed data on islands limits the possibility of evidence-based policymaking and proper assessment of the territorial impact of European policies1. The effective implementation of the upcoming European strategy for islands depends on the systematic collection, analysis and exploitation of reliable and comparable data reflecting island realities2. In view of the upcoming European strategy for islands, the need to create an ‘island dashboard’ with indicators on connectivity costs, access to basic services, energy dependence and related costs, water pressure, the seasonality of employment and tourism, administrative capacity and demographic trends, and the fact that the current administrative geography, NUTS, insufficiently reflects the true ‘island situation’, especially when islands are part of wider regions with a predominantly mainland character, which leads to an underestimation of their real needs3, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Does it intend to propose a comprehensive EU framework to enhance the availability, comparability and interoperability of data on islands?

Does it plan to develop a European island dashboard, with reliable, comparable indicators that capture the specific economic, social, demographic and environmental situations of island regions to support the impact assessment of EU policies?
Does it intend to address the current limitations of the NUTS classification through functional typologies and complementary, spatially disaggregated data at lower geographical levels?

This issue has been highlighted on several occasions by the European Parliament, the Committee of the Regions and the EESC, and has also been confirmed by the recent OECD report, which highlights persistent gaps in the availability, comparability and territorial analysis of data on island regions at EU level and the implications thereof for the creation of evidence-based public policies (https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/policy-pathways-beyond-the-shoreline_1aedeacb-en/full-report.html). 2 European islands – while facing common challenges – have various geographical features and institutional setups, which mean it is crucial to adopt flexible solutions that take into account these specificities; 3 The complementary use of functional and thematic approaches is therefore necessary, as is the improved availability of spatially disaggregated data at lower geographical levels. 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (15.7.2026) The Commission acknowledges that there is scope to further improve the availability and granularity of statistical data on islands in order to support a more comprehensive assessment of their economic, social, demographic and environmental conditions. In particular, the current Nomenclature of Territorial Units for Statistics (NUTS) classification does not always allow islands to be distinguished from the wider regions to which they belong, which may limit the availability of island-specific data and analyses. The importance of improving the availability of data on islands has been highlighted by EU institutions and island stakeholders in their opinions and position papers, as well as in the contributions submitted during the call for evidence1 launched in the context of the preparation of the EU strategy for islands2. To address these challenges, the strategy sets out action to promote the use of existing data on the economic and social conditions of islands, as well as the production of more granular data, with a view to improving the understanding of island specificities. At this stage, it would be premature to determine how the results of these efforts may be presented, or whether they may require broader changes to the existing statistical framework.
1 Call for evidence - Ares(2026)2435909: https://ec.europa.eu/info/law/better-regulation/have-your-
say/initiatives/16992-EU-strategy-for-islands_en. 2 COM(2026) 520 final (adopted on 10 June 2026).

E-10-2026-002357.t: Tackling water scarcity and strengthening water resilience in island regions in the context of the European strategy for islands
qt: to the Commission Elena Kountoura (The Left) Subject:

Island regions are particularly exposed to the threat of water scarcity.1 The limited water resources are under pressure due to the impacts of the climate crisis, intensifying periods of drought, outdated water supply networks and significant seasonal population increases due to tourism.2 On most islands, which are popular tourist destinations, natural water reserves are insufficient, leading to costly and energy-intensive solutions, such as reliance on water imports and conventional desalination plants. Taking into account the Parliament's position on water resilience, which calls for special treatment of islands due to their vulnerability and for the removal of barriers to access to financial support for local and regional investments in water management and infrastructure,3 the need for integrated rainwater collection and storage systems, modern desalination plants with renewable energy sources, smart water management networks with real-time leakage detection, wastewater reuse systems for irrigation and smart demand management systems,4 as well as the need for enhanced participation of island authorities in decision-making on infrastructure planning: 1.

Does the Commission intend to recognise addressing water scarcity on islands as a strategic priority and to incorporate a specific pillar on water security and resilience in the forthcoming European strategy for islands?

Does the Commission intend to support the creation of a new specific financial instrument in the new MFF for investments in sustainable, resilient solutions and infrastructure for integrated water management on islands?

Water scarcity is becoming a systemic phenomenon and a significant limiting factor for economic development. 2 According to official data, approximately 30 % of the European population lives in areas with permanent water stress and up to 70 % in areas with seasonal stress during the summer period (https://www.eea.europa.eu/en/analysis/indicators/use-of-freshwater-resources-in-europe-1). Notably, in Greece last year, dozens of island municipalities were placed in a state of emergency due to water scarcity, while today many islands are in this situation already. Seven Greek islands are already in a state of emergency due to water scarcity. 3 https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/TA-10-2025-0091_EL.html. 4 See e.g. the INSULEUR proposals, https://ec.europa.eu/info/law/better-regulation/have-yoursay/initiatives/16992-Στρατηγικη-της-ΕΕ-για-της-ΕΕ-για-τα-νησια/F33386921_el. 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (31.7.2026) The EU strategy for islands1 recognises that islands face water-related challenges and recommends that Member States prioritise investments in water infrastructure to improve water services and distribution networks and increase water saving and water reuse, while restoring natural water retention. Cohesion policy supports such investments by strengthening water resilience and sustainable water management. Reflecting the growing importance of water resilience, the mid-term review of cohesion policy2 encouraged Member States to increase investments in sustainable water management, increased water efficiency, secure access to water and measures enhancing water resilience, resulting in the reallocation of EUR 1.6 billion to islands through cohesion policy programmes, including EUR 158 million for water-related investments. The proposal for the next Multiannual Financial Framework3 provides that at least 35% of the EU budget should contribute to climate and environmental objectives, including water resilience, while continuing to support research and innovation projects that accelerate the green transition. Water resilience is also reflected in the main funding programmes, in shared management, under the EU’s proposed next long-term budget. It is an important element of the National and Regional Partnership Plans, with a climate and environmental contribution of at least 43%, which aim to ensure sustainable prosperity across all regions and maintain quality of life across the EU4. The European Competitiveness Fund5 will also support water resilience and the transition to a water-smart economy, through its clean Transition and Industrial Decarbonisation window.

review-2025_en.pdf. 3 https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/eu-budget/long-term-eu-budget/eu-budget-2028-2034_en. 4 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legalcontent/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A52025PC0565R%2801%29&qid=1753697054840. 5 https://commission.europa.eu/publications/european-competitiveness-fund_en.

E-10-2026-002356.t: Establishing specific financial and regulatory tools to support small and medium-sized island enterprises under the European strategy for islands
qt: to the Commission Elena Kountoura (The Left) Subject:
Establishing specific financial and regulatory tools to support small and mediumsized island enterprises under the European strategy for islands

Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), including micro-enterprises, are the backbone of the Union's island economies. However, they operate under particularly unfavourable conditions due to geographical isolation, higher transport and logistics costs, the limited size of local markets, dependence on seasonal activities and demand, lack of skilled personnel and limited access to finance1. At the same time, they face significant obstacles or are excluded from the use of European financial instruments, as the complex administrative requirements, minimum eligible budget limits and co-financing requirements do not correspond to the liquidity of island businesses with seasonal turnover2. Considering that the existing rules and funding programmes are mainly designed with larger businesses and mainland markets in mind and taking into account the need to create a specific competitiveness strand and targeted support for island SMEs within the framework of key EU funds and financing programmes3: the Commission is asked: 1.

Does it intend to create a specific competitiveness strand for small, medium-sized and micro-enterprises on islands within the framework of EU financial instruments, cohesion policy and the new MFF, with adapted eligibility criteria, lower minimum investment thresholds and increased aid rates for island regions?
Does it plan to simplify the procedures for accessing European funding, so that they better reflect the limited administrative and financial resources of the enterprises in question?
Is it aiming to provide adequate technical and financial support to island businesses in critical areas of resilience4 and in human resource specialisation?

Without targeted support, these constraints hinder scaling up, innovation and integration into higher value chains. 2 In particular, many funding programmes were designed for businesses with administrative structures that do not exist in island businesses of one to three people. Furthermore, the minimum budget limits de facto exclude micro-businesses, while the high mandatory co-financing rates are not feasible for businesses with liquidity concentrated in the few months of the tourist season (https://ec.europa.eu/info/law/betterregulation/have-your-say/initiatives/16992-EU-strategy-for-islands/F33386921_en). 3 Including the ERDF, ESF+, Horizon Europe, CEF and LIFE. 4 Sectors and cutting-edge fields that are of critical importance – especially in island regions – include green energy, water, the circular economy, agri-food, sustainable tourism, green transport and digital services. 1

(31 July 2026) 1. The Commission has no current plans to set up a dedicated central instrument. However, Member States will be encouraged, throughout the future plan negotiations, to dedicate resources, including through financial instruments, to address the challenges of islands. 2. Implementation mechanisms under the National and Regional Partnership Plans will be simpler, enabling easier access to EU support for small businesses. 3. The EU strategy for islands (1) establishes a coordinated policy framework, through EU actions and recommendations to steer EU support and national policies for islands. It includes actions to help reduce the cost of insularity and strengthen the competitiveness of island businesses. For example, it proposes extending technical assistance though the Clean Energy for EU Islands (2) initiative until 2030, supporting the energy transition, helping to reduce energy costs and improve the competitiveness of island businesses. It will also consider issues affecting islands in the upcoming reviews of the EU Emissions Trading System (3) and FuelEU Maritime Regulation (4) and the ongoing reviews of the EU State aid framework, with potential benefits for the competitiveness of small and medium enterprises. 4. Under InvestEU (5), the Commission is supporting microfinance programs for financially excluded people, where microcredits, business development services, mentoring and other services are provided. E-10-2026-002355.t: Recognising renewable bio-based materials as circular solutions
qt: to the Commission Katri Kulmuni (Renew) Subject:

Based on the available information regarding the Commission’s upcoming proposal for a circular economy act, the act will focus heavily on secondary raw materials and less on biobased materials. Renewable and bio-based materials should qualify as circular materials in the same way as recycled materials when developing measures to boost demand for circular materials and products. This would also provide an important link between the circular economy act and the EU’s bioeconomy strategy. I see a risk that the two main initiatives are being developed in silos, where the circular economy act focuses only on waste and secondary raw materials and the bioeconomy strategy, including the forthcoming biotech act II, focuses on bio-based inputs. With the above in mind: 1.
How will the Commission take renewable bio-based materials and products into account in the upcoming EU initiatives, especially in the circular economy act?
How will the Commission ensure that renewability and renewable bio-based materials are specifically considered in the Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation1?

How is the Commission ensuring that the Product Environmental Footprint methodology development is aligned with the bioeconomy strategy, including the crediting of carbon removal and storage for bio-based materials and products containing biogenic carbon, and in contrast to fossil-based alternatives?

The Commission is implementing this framework through different initiatives, including the upcoming Biotech Act II (2), the Circular Economy Act (CEA) (3), and dedicated work on bio-based plastics under the Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (4). These initiatives will support the uptake of bio-based materials where they offer the best environmental and economic performance, and will also improve the collection, treatment and use of biowaste. Ensuring that products placed on the EU market become more sustainable over their whole life cycle is a core objective of the Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation (ESPR) (5). The Commission will carry out an impact assessment for each priority product (6) and propose the most effective and proportionate set of measures for the ESPR 2025-2030 work programme. Aspects concerning sustainable sourcing and circularity could be included where relevant. E-10-2026-002354.t: Implementation of Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 on machinery: shortcomings in the technical framework and risks to Europe’s industrial competitiveness
qt: to the Commission Elena Donazzan (ECR), Alessandro Ciriani (ECR), Pietro Fiocchi (ECR), Mariateresa Vivaldini (ECR), Carlo Ciccioli (ECR), Nicola Procaccini (ECR) Subject:

Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 on machinery is due to enter into force on 20 January 2027. With just a few months to go, the Commission is yet to publish its implementation guide and the harmonised standards. This is depriving businesses and duly authorised bodies of the tools necessary to ensure compliance, legal certainty and display the CE marking correctly. The new requirements, on safety components, artificial intelligence-based systems and digital architectures, necessitate structural overhauls that cannot be completed in the current timeframe in the absence of clear technical guidance. This affects strategic sectors such as aerospace, defence, energy and advanced engineering and the automotive industry, thus directly jeopardising skilled employment and the Union’s industrial sovereignty. Can the Comision therefore say: 1.
When it plans to publish the application guide and harmonised standards?
Whether it intends to adopt transitional measures to enable businesses to comply fully with the new requirements?
Whether it has assessed the socio-economic impact of the technical delay on the industrial sectors concerned?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (6.8.2026) The Machinery Regulation1 was adopted in 2023 and applies as of 20 January 2027, meaning that stakeholders have had significant time to prepare. It sets out the Essential Health and Safety Requirements (EHSRs) that products must comply with. While cited harmonised standards help provide a presumption of conformity, they are not mandatory. Though machinery and related products must comply with the EHSRs, it is possible to comply with the latter without harmonised standards being applied. The Commission fully recognises the importance of harmonised standards. Consequently, it has planned for the majority of harmonised standards currently cited in support of the Machinery Directive2 to be re-cited under the Regulation, to ensure a smooth transition. Those harmonised standards will again be providing the presumption of conformity insofar as they cover relevant EHSRs. The adoption by the Commission and citation in the Official Journal of the EU is planned for the fourth quarter of 2026. An updated guide to the application of the machinery legislation is due to be made available around the same time. On cybersecurity and Artificial Intelligence elements3, the relevant new harmonised standards, once offered by the European Standardisation Organisations (ESOs) and if positively assessed by the Commission, will be listed. Such new standards have not yet been delivered by the ESOs. Note that the deadlines for delivery were set out in the relevant Commission standardisation request4. Nonetheless, the preparation of the standard covering cyber-safety has been prioritised and the Commission expects the ESOs to offer it soon. As mentioned above, it is possible to comply with the EHSRs, without harmonised standards being applied.
1 Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 of the European Parliament and of the Council. 2 Directive 2006/42/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council; harmonised standards are cited in

support of that Directive via Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2023/1586. 3 More specifically, safety components incorporating Artificial Intelligence with fully or partially self-evolving behaviour. 4 Phase 1: 20 January 2026: C(2025) 129 final.

E-10-2026-002353.t: Religious freedom training for EU diplomats
qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Bert-Jan Ruissen (ECR), Malika Sorel (NI), Aurelijus Veryga (ECR), Nikos Papandreou (S&D), Davor Ivo Stier (PPE), Lukas Mandl (PPE), Tomislav Sokol (PPE) Subject:

Religious freedom is a fundamental human right, enshrined in most constitutions, as well as in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union. Many conflicts across the globe have a religious component and Christians are especially heavily persecuted. Open Doors estimates that 388 million Christians worldwide are persecuted because of their faith. It is therefore paramount that the EU is fully equipped to engage in dialogue with stakeholders outside of the EU on the freedom of religion or belief. The European Parliament called on the European External Action Service (EEAS) to train EU diplomats in this respect in its discharge resolutions of 2023 and 2024. Various tools to address this are available and have been used in the past for training, such as the Freedom of Religion or Belief (FORB) learning platform. 1.
How does the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy (VP/HR) plan to implement Parliament’s call for training?
How does the VP/HR ensure that all EEAS staff are equipped to engage in dialogue on religious freedom and how are tools such as the FORB learning platform used?
What staff and budget resources are allocated to prioritise this issue?
at: (English version) to the Vice-President of the Commission/High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Bert-Jan Ruissen (ECR), Malika Sorel (NI), Aurelijus Veryga (ECR), Nikos Papandreou (S&D), Davor Ivo Stier (PPE), Lukas Mandl (PPE), Tomislav Sokol (PPE) (9 June 2026) Subject: Religious freedom training for EU diplomats Religious freedom is a fundamental human right, enshrined in most constitutions, as well as in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union. Many conflicts across the globe have a religious component and Christians are especially heavily persecuted. It is therefore paramount that the EU is fully equipped to engage in dialogue with stakeholders outside of the EU on the freedom of religion or belief. The European Parliament called on the European External Action Service (EEAS) to train EU diplomats in this respect in its discharge resolutions of 2023 and 2024. Various tools to address this are available and have been used in the past for training, such as the Freedom of Religion or Belief (FORB) learning platform. 1. How does the VP/HR ensure that all EEAS staff are equipped to engage in dialogue on religious freedom and how are tools such as the FORB learning platform used? 3.
