(29 July 2026) The European External Action Service regularly provides dedicated training on religion-related aspects of foreign policy and diplomacy, including freedom of religion or belief. Recent annual courses addressed religion and geopolitics, religion in Africa, and religious nationalism, with a particular focus on religious literacy, human rights, conflict prevention and practical tools for diplomatic engagement. Freedom of religion or belief is also addressed through cooperation with the Directorate-General for International Partnerships of the Commission on the EU learning package on freedom of religion or belief, including the e-learning courses ‘Freedom of Religion or Belief for All’ and ‘Freedom of Religion or Belief and Gender Equality’, complemented by webinars and practical guidance. In May 2026, an EU-wide training on practical resources to address freedom of religion or belief was offered to staff in Headquarters and EU Delegations. The course ‘Religious nationalism and the evolving geo-political reality’ is organised on annual basis with approximately 40 participants. Human rights trainings are integrated into broader diplomatic training, including international human rights law in the Essential EU Diplomatic Training. These activities are implemented within existing human and financial resources and in cooperation with relevant Commission services.

E-10-2026-002352.t: Competitiveness of Europe’s video games sector and the forthcoming Digital Fairness Act
qt: to the Commission Katri Kulmuni (Renew) Subject:

The video games sector is one of Europe’s most innovative cultural and creative sectors. It employs talented, highly skilled people and promotes technological progress, digital skills and cross-border growth. There are some 5 900 games studios in Europe, many of which are SMEs or independent developers. The European Parliament and the Council have recognised how strategically important the sector is for innovation, cultural diversity and the creative economy. The sector’s growth has been supported by innovative business models, in particular the freeto-play model, where games are free and revenues are based on in-game currencies such as coins, diamonds and precious stones. These can either be earned through playing the game or purchased with real money. Operators in the industry have expressed concern that the Digital Fairness Act (DFA) currently under consideration could require the price of virtual products to be displayed in euro every time they are used. This could lead to price confirmations being shown repeatedly during the same gaming session, undermine the user experience and make European gaming companies less competitive on the global market. 1.
How does the Commission intend to ensure that, in practice, the DFA does not make the pay-to-play model unworkable or undermine the competitiveness of the sector?

How does the Commission intend to ensure that future regulation is proportionate, evidence-based and compatible with existing EU legislation, in particular in the light of the Regulatory Scrutiny Board’s negative assessment of the way in which preparations for the DFA are being made?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (11.9.2026) EU consumer legislation1 requires traders to ensure price transparency towards consumers. The Commission considers that price transparency requirements apply also in cases where traders, such as video games providers, introduce in-game currencies as intermediate means that consumers must use for purchasing in-game virtual items2. Member States’ consumer authorities acting within the Consumer Protection Co-operation (CPC) network have also endorsed this interpretation of EU law in the CPC Network’s Key Principles on In-game Virtual currencies. Enforcement of existing EU consumer legislation being a priority, the Commission continues to facilitate discussions between the CPC Network and the video game industry to uphold existing EU consumer rights3. The upcoming Digital Fairness Act4 (DFA) will address identified consumer protection gaps and problematic features in digital products and services5, including video games. The impact assessment examines if action is needed on specific topics, including clarification of the existing price transparency rules when virtual currencies are deployed, e.g. through indicating the price both in virtual and real currency. It assesses various approaches, including coregulation, to frame possible measures. The impact assessment process includes an examination by the Regulatory Scrutiny Board. By clarifying consumer protection rules, the DFA will facilitate enforcement, provide greater legal certainty, a more level playing field and more harmonisation for traders. It will also include important simplification elements, such as reduction of consumer information requirements for contracts concerning in-app purchases, whilst maintaining the price transparency principle.
1 See Articles 5 and 6 of Directive 2011/83/EU on consumer rights,

http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2011/83/oj; Article 7 of Directive 2005/29/EC on Unfair Commercial Practices, http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2005/29/oj. 2 See Section 4.2.9 of Commission Notice – Guidance on the interpretation and application of Directive 2005/29/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council concerning unfair business-to-consumer commercial practices in the internal market, OJ C 526, 29.12.2021, pp. 1–129. 3 https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_25_831. 4 https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/consultations/commission-launches-open-consultation-forthcomingdigital-fairness-act. 5 See Commission Staff Working Document ‘Fitness Check of EU consumer law on digital fairness’ of 3.10.2024, SWD(2024) 230 final.

E-10-2026-002351.t: Austria Power Grid’s plans for a 380 kV overhead power line between East Tyrol and south-east Carinthia
qt: to the Commission Elisabeth Dieringer (PfE) Subject:
Austria Power Grid’s plans for a 380 kV overhead power line between East Tyrol and south-east Carinthia

Austria Power Grid (APG) is planning a 380 kV overhead power line spanning approximately 180 km from Lienz (East Tyrol) to Völkermarkt (south-east Carinthia), which is to pass straight through highly sensitive Alpine forest areas. The plan involves pylons up to 90 m high, resting on concrete foundations with an area of 20 x 20 m. In addition to the health impacts feared by local residents and the impairment to quality of life and housing, there are risks of significant land take, soil compaction, adverse effects on native flora and fauna and their biodiversity, as well as long-term and large-scale deforestation and permanent disfigurement of the natural scenery. The project is therefore in flagrant contradiction with the objectives of the Alpine Convention and with the requirements of EU law on the protection of forests and the restoration of nature. 1.
What is the Commission’s assessment of the project’s compatibility with the Alpine Convention and the relevant provisions of EU law?

As guardian of the Treaties, what measures does the Commission intend to take to urge the APG to adopt a less harmful approach that protects the landscape and nature, namely the laying of underground or underwater cables?
at: (English version) to the Commission Elisabeth Dieringer (PfE) (9 June 2026) Subject: Austria Power Grid’s plans for a 380 kV overhead power line between East Tyrol and south-east Carinthia Austria Power Grid (APG) is planning a 380 kV overhead power line spanning approximately 180 km from Lienz (East Tyrol) to Völkermarkt (south-east Carinthia), which is to pass straight through highly sensitive Alpine forest areas. The plan involves pylons up to 90 m high, resting on concrete foundations with an area of 20 x 20 m. In addition to the health impacts feared by local residents and the impairment to quality of life and housing, there are risks of significant land take, soil compaction, adverse effects on native flora and fauna and their biodiversity, as well as long-term and large-scale deforestation and permanent disfigurement of the natural scenery. The project is therefore in flagrant contradiction with the objectives of the Alpine Convention and with the requirements of EU law on the protection of forests and the restoration of nature. 1. What is the Commission’s assessment of the project’s compatibility with the Alpine Convention and the relevant provisions of EU law? 2. As guardian of the Treaties, what measures does the Commission intend to take to urge the APG to adopt a less harmful approach that protects the landscape and nature, namely the laying of underground or underwater cables? (12 August 2026) The EU has not ratified the Alpine Convention protocols on Nature Protection and Landscape Conservatio n (1), and on Mountain Forests (2), which could be relevant for the case, although they apply in Austria. By contrast, the Convention’s Energy Protocol (3) was ratified by the EU in 2006 and forms part of both Austrian and Union law. Its Articles 2, 10 and 12 contain relevant provisions on power lines. The Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) Directive (4) requires an EIA for projects likely to have significant environmental effects, including overhead electricity lines above 220 kV and longer than 15 km (5). The project, which is currently in the planning phase (6), appears to fall within that scope and therefore requiring an EIA, which must examine all likely environmental effects, including under the Birds Directive (7) and the Habitats Directive (8), (9). On top of the public engagement which is compulsory for projects with a status of a Project of Common Interest, the EIA Directive also ensures public participation. Member States are therefore primarily responsible for assessing these projects and ensuring their compliance with Union energy and environmental law and the Alpine Convention and its Energy, Nature Protection and Landscape Conservation, and Mountain Forests protocols, also when only in force in the specific Member State. In addition, the Convention has its own compliance mechanism (10).

The Commission is closely following project’s progress, and the inclusion on the Union list of PCIs is also linked with an obligation to provide detailed information on planned project implementation and public involvement (https://ec.europa.eu/energy/infrastructure/transparency_platform/map-viewer/main.html). |(⸱7|)∙ Directive 2009/147/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 30 November 2009 on the conservation of wild birds, OJ L 20, 26.1.2010, p. 7-25. |(⸱8|)∙ Council Directive 92/43/EEC of 21 May 1992 on the conservation of natural habitats and of wild fauna and flora, OJ L 206, 22.7.1992, p. 7-50. |(⸱9|)∙ Under Article 6(3) of the Habitats Directive, any plan or project likely to significantly affect a Natura 2000 site, either alone or in combination with other plans or projects, must undergo an appropriate assessment of its implications in view of the site's conservation objectives. Authorisation may be granted only if the site’s integrity is not adversely affected, or exceptionally, if no alternative exists, there is overriding public interest, and compensatory measures are implemented. E-10-2026-002350.t: Compatibility of ‘zero-log’ AI systems with EU digital legislation – case of WhatsApp Meta AI incognito mode
qt: to the Commission Veronika Cifrová Ostrihoňová (Renew), Sandro Gozi (Renew), Anna-Maja Henriksson (Renew), Nathalie Loiseau (Renew), Oihane Agirregoitia Martínez (Renew), Michael McNamara (Renew), Dan Barna (Renew) Subject:

On 13 May 2026, WhatsApp announced the launch of an ’incognito’ mode for its integrated Meta AI chatbot1. This feature operates on a ‘zero-log’ infrastructure, meaning that past conversations disappear instantly and no logs are stored on servers. According to cybersecurity experts, this lack of data retention creates an accountability vacuum. Concerns have been raised that the absence of retained interaction data may create challenges for accountability, incident investigation, auditing and enforcement where harmful outputs or unlawful activities are involved, particularly in relation to minors2. In the light of these concerns: 1.

Is the Commission aware of WhatsApp’s ‘incognito’ Meta AI feature, and has it assessed whether ‘zero-log’ AI architectures are compatible with relevant EU digital legislation, particularly regarding consumer protection, child safety and platform accountability?

How does the Commission intend to ensure effective compliance monitoring and regulatory oversight where AI interactions are not retained and may therefore not be available for audits, investigations or incident reporting?
https://about.fb.com/news/2026/05/incognito-chat-whatsapp-meta-ai/. https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c99lmyr1dnxo.
at: (English version) to the Commission Veronika Cifrová Ostrihoňová (Renew), Sandro Gozi (Renew), Anna-Maja Henriksson (Renew), Nathalie Loiseau (Renew), Oihane Agirregoitia Martínez (Renew), Michael McNamara (Renew), Dan Barna (Renew) (8 June 2026) Subject: Compatibility of ‘zero-log’ AI systems with EU digital legislation — case of WhatsApp Meta AI incognito mode On 13 May 2026, WhatsApp announced the launch of an ‘incognito’ mode for its integrated Meta AI chatbot (1). This feature operates on a ‘zero-log’ infrastructure, meaning that past conversations disappear instantly and no logs are stored on servers. According to cybersecurity experts, this lack of data retention creates an accountability vacuum. Concerns have been raised that the absence of retained interaction data may create challenges for accountability, incident investigation, auditing and enforcement where harmful outputs or unlawful activities are involved, particularly in relation to minors (2). In the light of these concerns: 1.

Is the Commission aware of WhatsApp’s ‘incognito’ Meta AI feature, and has it assessed whether ‘zero-log’ AI architectures are compatible with relevant EU digital legislation, particularly regarding consumer protection, child safety and platform accountability?

How does the Commission intend to ensure effective compliance monitoring and regulatory oversight where AI interactions are not retained and may therefore not be available for audits, investigations or incident reporting?

(27 July 2026) The Commission is aware of WhatsApp’s ‘Incognito Chat’ Meta AI feature (1). The AI Act (2) requires the automated recording and storage of logs only for AI systems classified as high-risk (3). Thus, for other AI systems, the AI Act does not explicitly rule out the possibility of ‘zero-log’ AI architectures. However, the Act obliges providers of the most advanced general-purpose AI models to assess and mitigate systemic risks stemming from their models and their use, and to keep track of relevant information about serious incidents (4). ‘Zero-log’ AI architectures make it more difficult to assess and mitigate risks associated with model use and reduce the availability of relevant incident information. Therefore, providers may need to implement additional safeguards and reporting channels to keep risks at an acceptable level and ensure that relevant information is recorded. The assessment of whether the new feature would fall within the scope of the Digital Services Act (DSA) (5) ultimately depends on the specific design and functionalities, and the legal qualification of the feature. In cooperation with Coimisiún na Meán, the Irish Digital Services Coordinator (6), the Commission will continue to monitor the provider of WhatsApp’s compliance with all the applicable obligations under the DSA. Under EU digital legislation, the Commission can request relevant information on compliance in the absence of visibility into user logs via several channels. The Commission is monitoring the situation and the need for regulatory intervention regarding ‘zero-log’ AI architectures.

E-10-2026-002349.t: Access to Temporary Protection Directive provisions in Belgium for babies born after 24 February 2022
qt: to the Commission Saskia Bricmont (Verts/ALE), Estelle Ceulemans (S&D), Kathleen Van Brempt (S&D), Elio Di Rupo (S&D), Hilde Vautmans (Renew), Sara Matthieu (Verts/ALE), Bruno Tobback (S&D) Subject:
Access to Temporary Protection Directive provisions in Belgium for babies born after 24 February 2022

Since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, the EU Temporary Protection Directive1 has provided essential protection to displaced persons across the EU. Serious concerns have nevertheless arisen regarding children born in Ukraine after 24 February 2022 to mothers benefiting from temporary protection in Belgium. According to the information received, these children are not granted temporary protection or an equivalent residence status in Belgium, despite their mothers being lawfully present under the temporary protection regime. After 90 days, many reportedly remain without a secure residence status, health insurance or effective access to basic rights. Families are instead directed towards family reunification procedures. This situation appears inconsistent with the objectives of Council Implementing Decision (EU) 2022/3822, notably recital 11, which highlights the importance of preserving family unity and avoiding diverging statuses within the same family, and recital 14, which allows Member States to extend protection to additional categories of persons. 1.
Is the Commission aware of this situation, and has it assessed the compatibility thereof with EU temporary protection rules?
Does the Commission consider this approach to be compatible with family unity and the best interests of the child?
What action will the Commission take to ensure a consistent approach across Member States?

Council Directive 2001/55/EC of 20 July 2001 on minimum standards for giving temporary protection in the event of a mass influx of displaced persons and on measures promoting a balance of efforts between Member States in receiving such persons and bearing the consequences thereof (OJ L 212, 7.8.2001, p. 12, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2001/55/oj). 2 Council Implementing Decision (EU) 2022/382 of 4 March 2022 establishing the existence of a mass influx of displaced persons from Ukraine within the meaning of Article 5 of Directive 2001/55/EC, and having the effect of introducing temporary protection (OJ L 71, 4.3.2022, p. 1, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dec_impl/2022/382/oj). 1
at: (English version) to the Commission Saskia Bricmont (Verts/ALE), Estelle Ceulemans (S&D), Kathleen Van Brempt (S&D), Elio Di Rupo (S&D), Hilde Vautmans (Renew), Sara Matthieu (Verts/ALE), Bruno Tobback (S&D) (8 June 2026) Subject: Access to Temporary Protection Directive provisions in Belgium for babies born after 24 February 2022 Since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, the EU Temporary Protection Directive (1) has provided essential protection to displaced persons across the EU. Serious concerns have nevertheless arisen regarding children born in Ukraine after 24 February 2022 to mothers benefiting from temporary protection in Belgium. According to the information received, these children are not granted temporary protection or an equivalent residence status in Belgium, despite their mothers being lawfully present under the temporary protection regime. After 90 days, many reportedly remain without a secure residence status, health insurance or effective access to basic rights. Families are instead directed towards family reunification procedures. This situation appears inconsistent with the objectives of Council Implementing Decision (EU) 2022/382 (2), notably Recital 11, which highlights the importance of preserving family unity and avoiding diverging statuses within the same family, and Recital 14, which allows Member States to extend protection to additional categories of persons. 1. Is the Commission aware of this situation, and has it assessed the compatibility thereof with EU temporary protection rules? 2.
Does the Commission consider this approach to be compatible with family unity and the best interests of the child?
What action will the Commission take to ensure a consistent approach across Member States?

(31 August 2026) The Commission is aware of the situation and is in contact with the relevant Belgian authorities with a view to getting a better understanding of the situation and supporting them in the correct implementation of the Temporary Protection Directive (Directive 2001/55/EC) (1). Member States must pay particular attention to the objectives of preserving family unity, under Article 15 of Directive 2001/55/EC (2) and Recital 11 of Implementing Decision 2022/382 (3), as well as to the requirements of the Charter of Fundamental Rights, notably Articles 7 and 24 on respect for family life and the child’s best interests, and Article 21 on nondiscrimination. The implementation of the directive has not been without challenges across the EU, but due to the continued efforts of the EU institutions and Member States, it continues to offer protection for millions of displaced persons fleeing Russia’s war of aggression. The Commission will continue to work closely with Member States’ authorities to ensure the most effective implementation of the Temporary Protection Directive and to address any emerging challenges in this context.

E-10-2026-002348.t: Sardinia and Sicily: sharp increase in freight traffic costs and impact on businesses and consumers
qt: to the Commission Marco Falcone (PPE), Caterina Chinnici (PPE), Salvatore De Meo (PPE), Fulvio Martusciello (PPE), Letizia Moratti (PPE), Giusi Princi (PPE), Flavio Tosi (PPE), Massimiliano Salini (PPE) Subject:

Maritime transport is vital to ensuring the territorial continuity of Sardinia and Sicily and to integrating their production and logistical chains in the European single market. Sectoral operators report that the unilateral introduction by certain shipping companies of summer freight surcharges – which took effect on 1 June 2026 and are as high as 50 % for routes that are not subject to public service obligations – has driven up operating costs. These hikes come at a time when the ETS’ extension to include the maritime sector has resulted in increased costs and burdens for the whole supply chain. The very survival of road haulage companies and of the Sicilian and Sardinian productive sectors is at stake, inasmuch as these surcharges could exacerbate the structural disadvantages specific to island regions, reduce competitiveness and even drive up the price of consumer goods and weaken the purchasing power of citizens. Having regard for the economic, social and territorial cohesion principles enshrined in Articles 174-175 TFEU, we ask the Commission: 1.
What initiatives will it take to increase the transparency, fairness and sustainability of maritime freight rates?
Will it promote measures to manage or mitigate the impact of ETS costs on freight transport with a view to preventing inflation?
Does it agree that it should bolster the mechanisms that safeguard the territorial continuity of island regions, potentially by including a dedicated fund in the EU budget?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (26.8.2026) The Commission recognises the importance to address the challenges impacting the economic sustainability and quality of life of the EU islands. In this context, the EU strategy for islands1 adopted in June 2026 sets out a coordinated approach to support islands and unlock their longterm potential. The Commission is aware of the recent rise in freight rates. Rates for commercial maritime transport services are set by market operators and are not governed by EU legislation. Shipping companies must nonetheless comply with the relevant EU competition rules, including bans on anti-competitive agreements and the abuse of a dominant position. The Emissions Trading System (ETS) review proposes changes that also reduce compliance costs for shipping companies, including administrative simplifications and a dedicated EU mechanism to support shipping companies with ETS allowances for the uptake of sustainable fuels and clean propulsion technologies. The current multiannual financial framework (MFF) allows for support tailored to the specific needs of islands, notably through the European Regional Development Fund, the Cohesion Fund and the Connecting Europe Facility. The Commission proposal for the next MFF fully supports the objectives set out in Article 174 of the Treaty to promote economic, social and territorial cohesion in the EU, including by addressing the needs of areas facing severe natural or demographic handicaps, such as islands. The accompanying national and regional partnership proposal provides Member States with flexibility to address structural challenges while setting out the requirement to allocate resources in a manner that considers, inter alia, the specific needs and constraints of islands and outermost regions.
1 https://ec.europa.eu/regional_policy/sources/policy/themes/islands/EU_strategy_for_islands.pdf.

E-10-2026-002347.t: Transposition of the directive on the protection of the environment through criminal law
qt: to the Commission Saskia Bricmont (Verts/ALE), Marie Toussaint (Verts/ALE), Sirpa Pietikäinen (PPE) Subject:

The EU directive on the protection of the environment through criminal law1 is an essential tool for combating environmental crimes, which are often linked to organised crime and cause serious damage to biodiversity and significant risks to public health. Although the transposition deadline was 21 May 2026, the majority of Member States have not yet finalised the adoption of the necessary national measures. It is, however, crucial that the implementation of this directive be ambitious and be backed by sufficient human, financial and judicial resources as well as enhanced cooperation between national authorities, European agencies and civil society. In this context, it is essential that the Commission fully exercise its role as the guardian of the Treaties in order to prevent persistent delays, divergences in application and ensure the protection of environmental defenders. 1.
What is the current status of the transposition of this directive in the Member States?
According to what timetable and methodology will the Commission assess the effectiveness of the national measures adopted?
What further initiatives does the Commission intend to take to ensure uniform implementation, in particular with regard to Article 23 on statistical data?
Directive (EU) 2024/1203 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 11 April 2024 on the protection of the environment through criminal law (ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2024/1203/oj). 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (20.7.2026) The Commission attaches great importance to the complete and timely transposition of the Directive (EU) 2024/1203 on the protection of the environment through criminal law (’the Directive’) by the Member States. In order to support Member States, the Commission organised three transposition workshops, provided a detailed guidance document and held bilateral meetings with Member States to address specific issues, upon their request. On 21 May 2026, the deadline for Member States to implement the Directive expired. As of June 2026, the Commission received notifications of national transposition measures from nine Member States of which only two indicated a full transposition. The Commission is closely following the transposition process, and will take appropriate steps, as relevant. In accordance with Article 25 of the Directive, the Commission will assess the Member States’ compliance with the Directive by 2028, carry out an evaluation of the impact of the Directive by 2031 and submit the respective reports to the European Parliament and the Council. In accordance with Article 24 of the Directive, the Environmental Crimes Data Committee was set up to establish a standard format for transmitting statistical data to the Commission, as provided under Articles 22-23 of the Directive. Two Committee meetings have already been held, and a third one is foreseen in September 2026.

E-10-2026-002346.t: Jean Monnet Actions European funding of universities and promotion of the federalist project
qt: to the Commission Catherine Griset (PfE), André Rougé (PfE), Mélanie Disdier (PfE), Antonín Staněk (PfE), Ondřej Knotek (PfE), Pascale Piera (PfE), Marie Dauchy (PfE), Pál Szekeres (PfE), Zsuzsanna Borvendég (ESN) Subject:

Created by the Commission in 1989, Jean Monnet Actions fund chairs, university courses and research on the European Union in more than a thousand universities. The Commission itself states that these programmes aim to support decision-makers and strengthen the dialogue around European policies. However, this funding raises questions about respect for academic neutrality. By exclusively supporting teaching on European integration, they can help to promote a vision that is essentially favourable to European policies, to the detriment of more critical approaches that emphasise the sovereignty of the Member States. 1.
Can the Commission clarify what safeguards are in place to ensure the academic rigour of programmes funded through Jean Monnet Actions?
Is the funding granted subject to an assessment to ensure that it is not used to promote a uniquely federalist vision of European integration?
Does the Commission intend to publish an independent assessment of the political and ideological impact of Jean Monnet Actions on European higher education?
Supporter1
This question is supported by a Member other than the authors: Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE).
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (24.7.2026) The Jean Monnet Actions (JMA), part of Erasmus+, foster teaching, research and debate about the EU to deepen understanding while nurturing open dialogue, critical thinking and democratic engagement. Rooted in EU rights and values1, including academic freedom, the JMA support higher education institutions in academic teaching and research projects in the field of EU studies. The JMA support academic research, teaching and inquiry that critically examines EU policies and institutions. Projects cover diverse topics that reflect societal challenges, scientific priorities and policy-relevant research, and may explore critical or underrepresented viewpoints. Higher education institutions retain full autonomy throughout their projects. Several robust safeguards underpin academic rigour. The mandatory evaluations under Article 24 of the Erasmus+ Regulation2 provide independent assessments. The selection procedure is open and competitive, following excellence and merit principles to guarantee fairness and equal opportunities for all applicants. Impartial external experts assess the projects against predefined criteria published in the Programme Guide3. Funding decisions thus reflect expert evaluations and a rigorous selection procedure. Transparency and accountability are ensured through clear criteria, documented procedures, sound financial management and oversight mechanisms. The Commission safeguards procedural fairness and never interferes with the projects’ content. Beneficiaries remain fully responsible for delivering activities in line with their projects.
1 Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, OJ C, C 326, 26.10.2012,

ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/treaty/char_2012/oj; Council Recommendation on https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legalcontent/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32018H0607%2801%29, OJ C, C 195, 7.6.2018., 6(a-d); Council conclusions on the contribution of education and training to strengthening common European values and democratic citizenship, OJ C, C/2023/1339, 29.11.2023, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/C/2023/1339/oj. 2 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2021/817/oj. 3 https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/erasmus-programme-guide.

E-10-2026-002345.t: Ensuring sufficient accredited verifier capacity for CBAM compliance
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (30.7.2026) Enabling authorised Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) declarants to declare embedded emissions on the basis of actual verified values is a priority of the Commission. Following the adoption of the implementing legislation on the calculation and verification of embedded emissions and on accreditation, it is now for Member States’ national accreditation bodies (NABs) to accredit legal persons to be CBAM verifiers. The Commission is in regular contact with NABs and with the European cooperation for Accreditation (EA). According to the information which they provided, CBAM accreditation is currently open in eleven Member States and 23 EU NABs will offer CBAM accreditation services. Third-country applicants may apply in four Member States and a total of seven NABs will offer this service. It is expected that more NABs will start providing accreditation services soon, including to third-country verifiers. The first CBAM verifiers should be accredited by September 2026, after which they must register in the CBAM registry. Following their registration, the Commission will publish the list of accredited CBAM verifiers. It is necessary to ensure that there will be sufficient verification capacity in 2027, and in time for the submission of the first CBAM declarations by 30 September 2027. Importers of CBAM goods should ensure that suppliers established in a third-country monitor and calculate embedded emissions in accordance with the CBAM Regulation.

E-10-2026-002343.t: Support for European university alliance projects through the future European Competitiveness Fund
at: (English version) to the Commission Mihai Tudose (S&D) (8 June 2026) Subject: Support for European university alliance projects through the future European Competitiveness Fund Alliances of European universities are increasingly creating academic projects with an impact on cohesion and competitiveness within the EU. These university alliances will continue to receive European support through the Erasmus+ programme under the future multiannual financial framework 2028-2034. This is a heartening decision by the Council. However, beyond the realm of academic cooperation and mobility, there is a major socioeconomic component: the impact on research, innovation and competitiveness. This is why, at a time when ways of boosting European businesses in this regard are being sought, there is a need for solid, predictable, long-term support for inter-university projects that have an impact on the economy. Does the Commission plan to include funding for European university alliance projects in the future European Competitiveness Fund and the Horizon Europe research programme? (6 August 2026) European Universities alliances are primarily supported under the Erasmus+ programme (1), which provides funding for longterm structural cooperation between higher education institutions. Horizon Europe (2), as a competitive, excellence-based programme, does not provide direct institutional funding to European Universities alliances, but entities participating in European Universities alliances may apply for funding, where their activities are relevant to objectives and topics set out in the programme. The next Horizon Europe 2028-2034 (3) will aim to continue supporting research and innovation through competitive calls. As specified in recital (21) of the European Competitiveness Fund (ECF) Regulation proposal (4), the Fund should support skills intelligence, upskilling and reskilling, and foster public-private cooperation. Wherever in line with the Fund's objectives and priorities, European Universities alliances could apply for support under the ECF, also in cooperation with their associated partners such as local businesses, with the objective of strengthening their contribution to innovation and development of skills and talent in support of Europe’s competitiveness. European Universities alliances are encouraged to make use of the ECF, Erasmus+, Horizon Europe and other EU instruments and programmes which will aim to provide complementary funding opportunities, thereby also incentivising national and regional contributions to the alliances.

E-10-2026-002342.t: Health-sector preparedness as a component of EU security and defence
qt: to the Commission Aurelijus Veryga (ECR), Vytenis Povilas Andriukaitis (S&D), Vlad Vasile-Voiculescu (Renew), Reinis Pozņaks (ECR), Tomislav Sokol (PPE) Subject:

The Maastricht criteria require Member States to keep their annual government deficits below 3 % of GDP. In response to the deteriorating security environment, the EU has introduced temporary fiscal flexibility to allow increased defence spending and strengthen military capabilities. However, another essential pillar of resilience risks being overlooked: the health sector. In the event of a military conflict or other large-scale crisis, civilian healthcare systems would be expected to support both civilian and military needs. Hospitals, emergency services, medical supply chains, specialised equipment and healthcare professionals are indispensable for ensuring societal resilience and operational readiness. Strengthening these capacities requires substantial investments in infrastructure, workforce training, emergency preparedness, stockpiling and specialised medical capabilities. While NATO members have committed to increasing defence-related spending and recognise the importance of broader resilience measures, some Member States remain constrained by the EU fiscal framework when investing in healthcare preparedness. Ensuring that healthcare systems can withstand and respond effectively to security threats is a matter of strategic importance for the EU as a whole. In this context, is the Commission considering allowing temporary deviations from fiscal requirements for investments aimed at strengthening health-sector preparedness for security and defence purposes in order to provide Member States with greater flexibility to enhance healthcare resilience and contribute to the EU’s overall preparedness objectives?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (31.7.2026) The reform of the Stability and Growth Pact put in place a balanced framework that accommodates spending on common priorities of the EU while maintaining sound and sustainable public finances in Member States. Regulation 2024/1263 indicates that social and economic resilience is a common priority in the EU1. As a result, investments in health-sector preparedness and resilience may be put forward in Member States’ medium-term fiscal-structural plans within a package of investments and reforms that underpin a more gradual fiscal adjustment, up to seven years instead of four years. This provides for an important incentive for Member States to implement reforms and investments in the area of health-sector preparedness and resilience. The national escape clause has been activated in March 2025 due to the urgent need to step up defence capabilities. This limited and temporary flexibility has been duly framed in scope in order to preserve fiscal sustainability. Concretely, eligible expenditure is limited to increases in expenditure under classification of the functions of government (COFOG) division 02. More generally, within its supporting role2, the Commission encourages health system preparedness and resilience. The EU Recovery and Resilience Facility has provided largescale financial support to strengthen and build resilient health systems in the EU, including investments and structural reforms worth EUR 42 billion3. More recently, the EU Preparedness Union Strategy4 recognises that investing in resilient health care systems, especially in hospital services and enhanced stockpiling of critical medical equipment, medicines and other medical materials, can help protect Europe in the event of health and other emergencies5.

E-10-2026-002339.t: Biodigester in Colle Monfortani (Rome) and protecting potable groundwater
qt: to the Commission Dario Tamburrano (The Left), Mario Furore (The Left) Subject:

Lazio Region has given the green light for a private biodigester, ‘Salone’, to be built in Rome (via Prenestina, Colle Monfortani),1 with an annual processing capacity of 75 000 tonnes of organic waste. The proposed site is a few hundred metres from the organic farm attached to the Sereni agricultural school2, whose wines include Vinitaly award winners3. The biodigester is expected to cause an increase in heavy vehicle traffic along the narrow via Prenestina, which is already congested on account of traffic from the nearby major waste treatment facilities in Rocca Cencia (Ama4 and Porcarelli5). Authorisation documents give the express go-ahead6 for the facility to be located in groundwater protection areas from which drinking water is drawn, and state that ‘no restrictions shall be placed on activities to be carried out in these areas’. This implies that there is no prohibition on building a waste treatment facility – or indeed on activities of any kind – in an aquifer protection area that feeds an aqueduct. In light of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Is Italy correctly applying the Water Framework Directive in the case of the ‘Salone’ biodigester; if not, what action does the Commission intend to take?
Is it considering including this case in EU Pilot Procedure (2019)9541 on waste management in Lazio?

(25 August 2026) The Water Framework Directive (WFD) (1) requires Member States to prevent the deterioration of the status of water bodies and to carry out a prior assessment of the potential impacts of a new project if this may pose a risk in this respect. Such an assessment can be combined with an environmental impact assessment (EIA) or other assessments required under EU or national law. The WFD also set out restrictive conditions under which an exemption according to Article 4(7) of the WFD can be invoked to authorise a project even if it would result in the deterioration of the status of the body of water concerned (2). Based on the information available, the competent national authorities have assessed the potential impact of the project on water as part of the EIA and no objections or positive opinions with conditions were issued by the Autorità di Bacino Distrettuale dell’Appennino Centrale and the Dipartimento III ‘Ambiente e Tutela del Territorio’ of the Rome Metropolitan City. The Commission has therefore in this case no basis to conclude that the WFD has not been correctly applied by Italy. In its role as guardian of the Treaties, the Commission monitors Member States’ compliance with EU law, focusing its enforcement action on systemic issues of non-compliance (3). National courts are competent to verify compliance with EU law for individual cases.

E-10-2026-002338.t: Sponsored media events and circumvention of European transparency rules
qt: to the Commission Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE) Subject:

According to an investigation published by Euractiv1 on 3 June 2026, several specialist media outlets are organising dinners, round-table discussions and conferences in Brussels sponsored by companies and trade associations, thus giving them access to EU Commissioners, their staff and officials. It refers to 1 102 media events between 2019 and 2025 covered by sponsorship packages costing up to EUR 85 000, as well as table placements offering lobbyists the opportunity to engage directly with European decision-makers on sensitive issues. The transparency register covers meetings, conferences or events aimed at influencing European decision-making, but excludes ad hoc or private/social gatherings. 1.

Does the Commission consider a sponsored media event, when it organises or facilitates targeted access to European decision-makers, in particular Commissioners, to constitute a lobbying activity that should be declared?
How many Commissioners, members of their staff or directors-general have taken part in such sponsored events since 2019, and have details of these meetings been made public?
What changes will the Commission propose to address this shortcoming?
https://www.euractiv.com/news/pay-to-play-in-brussels-how-media-events-became-the-new-lobbyingfrontier et https://www.euractiv.com/news/rapporteur-how-eu-media-became-events-businesses 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.8.2026) Organising conferences, events or communication campaigns with the objective of influencing the formulation or implementation of policy or legislation, or the decision-making process of the EU institutions, are interest representation activities covered by the Interinstitutional Agreement on the Transparency Register1, pursuant to its Article 3. Interest representatives which are registered in the Transparency Register are required to declare in their registrations those activities, as well as the related financial information, including any sponsorship received or provided. The Commission publishes information on, and minutes of, all meetings held between Members of the Commission, their members of Cabinet or Commission staff holding management functions and interest representatives in accordance with Commission Decisions (EU) 2024/30812 and 2024/30823. These publication rules do not apply to the participation of Members of the Commission, members of their Cabinets or Commission staff holding management functions in public events, including conferences or other public sponsored media events, since information on such occurrences is already in the public domain. In order to ensure transparency, the Commission does however require publishing information on closed-door events, as well as on any meetings held with interest representatives in the margins of such events, pursuant to the publication rules of the above-referenced Commission Decisions.

E-10-2026-002336.t: Spanish bureaucratic obstacles to critical minerals and European industrial autonomy
qt: to the Commission Alvise Pérez (NI) Subject:

The Critical Raw Materials Act1 sets targets for industrial self-sufficiency in critical raw materials by 2030. These include extracting at least 10 % of annual consumption of strategic raw materials within the EU, processing 40 % of strategic raw materials in the EU, and reducing dependence on any single non-EU country to below 65 %. The Commission has identified strategic projects in Spain in Extremadura, Galicia, Andalusia and Castile-La Mancha for lithium, copper, nickel, cobalt and tungsten extraction. However, Spain remains hamstrung by a Mining Act dating from 1973, more than half a century old, with slow authorisation processes, administrative opposition and a ‘no to everything’ culture that deters private investment. Deposits in Jaén, Cáceres, Ciudad Real and other regions could bolster European industry, defence, the automotive sector, permanent magnets and the value chain for neodymium, monazite, tungsten, copper and strontium. Added to this is the Spanish ban on new concessions for radioactive minerals, including uranium, despite their strategic importance. The answer cannot be to create inefficient stateowned mining companies, but rather to unlock private investment under clear rules, binding deadlines and legal certainty. 1.
Does the Commission consider that Spain is properly applying the deadlines and operating one-stop shops (single points of contact) as provided for in the Critical Raw Materials Act?
Will the Commission assess whether Spanish regulations are hindering European objectives of strategic autonomy?
Will the Commission support pro-investment reforms over inefficient state-run models?

Regulation (EU) 2024/1252 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 11 April 2024 establishing a framework for ensuring a secure and sustainable supply of critical raw materials (ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1252/oj). 1

(23 July 2026) Spain has nominated single points of contact (SPOCs) for permitting as set out in the Critical Raw Materials Act (CRMA) (1) at a regional level (2). The Commission is aware of ongoing collaboration between the SPOCs and the designated strategic projects in Spain. For extraction projects, the permitting timeline for strategic projects are 27 months from the acknowledgment of completeness of the permit applications. For already ongoing permit-granting procedures the timeline is 24 months. Since the first strategic projects were designated on 25 March 2025, this deadline has not yet been reached. Potential regulatory changes at national or regional level to ensure the meeting of the objectives and legal requirements under the CRMA are to be assessed at the respective governance level. E-10-2026-002335.t: Türkiye’s instrumentalisation of fisheries and environmental protection in the context of the ‘Blue Homeland’
qt: to the Commission Nikolas Farantouris (S&D) Subject:

The Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry of Türkiye is implementing a new action plan to protect marine resources and harmonise policies with UN Food and Agriculture Organization standards1. However, this plan is directly linked to strengthening Türkiye’s alleged ‘sovereign rights’ to its continental shelf and Exclusive Economic Zones, effectively integrating fisheries policy and environmental surveillance mechanisms into the broader revisionist doctrine of the so-called ‘Blue Homeland’.2 This development is a cause for legitimate concern, as Türkiye is using issues of fisheries, marine environment protection and natural resource management to promote unlawful unilateral claims in maritime areas where EU Member States, in particular Greece and Cyprus, have sovereign rights and legitimate interests. Accordingly: 1.

How does the Commission assess the connection between Türkiye's policy to combat illegal fishing and unlawful claims based on the ‘Blue Homeland’ doctrine that challenge the sovereign rights of EU Member States under the International Law of the Sea?

Does the Commission consider it acceptable to instrumentalise environmental protection and natural resource management to promote revisionist geopolitical aspirations to the detriment of EU Member States?

What specific measures does the Commission intend to take to protect the sovereign rights of Greece and Cyprus and the EU's strategic interests in the Eastern Mediterranean against illegal unilateral actions by Türkiye?

(30 July 2026) The Commission is aware of the implementation of a new action plan by the Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry of Türkiye to protect marine resources and harmonise policies with UN Food and Agriculture Organisation standards. These issues are assessed on an annual basis in the context of the enlargement reports on Türkiye. Türkiye must avoid threats and actions that damage good neighbourly relations and respect the sovereignty of all Member States over their territorial sea and airspace as well as all their sovereign rights, including the right to explore and exploit natural resources in accordance with EU and international law, in particular the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea. E-10-2026-002334.t: Harassment of European defence ministers by occupying authorities in Cyprus
qt: to the Commission Yannis Maniatis (S&D) Subject:

According to reports, the planes transporting the defence ministers of the Netherlands, France and Greece to Cyprus for the informal meeting of defence ministers were harassed on their approach through radio interference from the illegal Tymbou airport in the Turkish-occupied area of Cyprus. What is more, a pair of Turkish F-16 fighter jets took off from the Occupied Territories, although they kept a distance from the planes transporting the three European defence ministers. This incident – which is particularly serious as it took place in the margins of an informal meeting of European defence ministers in the context of the Cypriot Presidency – constitutes yet another provocation by Türkiye’s occupying forces and a violation of Cyprus’s sovereign rights. Moreover, it was also only recently that Türkiye excluded Cyprus from the preliminary negotiations ahead of COP31 in Antalya. With this in mind, can the Commission say: 1.
Is it aware of this incident?
How will it ensure aviation safety in the face of the harassment from Türkiye’s illegal airport in the Occupied Territories?
What assurances has it received from Türkiye and the United Nations that Cyprus will participate in all relevant meetings and negotiations, as well as in the COP31 meetings themselves in Antalya?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (10.8.2026) The EU is aware of the reports and remain in contact with its counterparts in the Republic of Cyprus. The EU has a strategic interest in a stable and secure environment in the Eastern Mediterranean and in the development of a cooperative and mutually beneficial relationship with Türkiye. In this context, Türkiye is expected to respect international law, as well as the sovereignty and territorial integrity of all Member States. It is also of paramount importance that Türkiye commits to and actively contributes to a fair, comprehensive and viable settlement of the Cyprus issue, including its external aspects. These are key elements for upholding regional stability in the Eastern Mediterranean. The EU and its Member States are of the firm view that United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) process has to be inclusive, transparent and open to all parties to UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement, in observance of their full rights. This includes that conditions must be met for all Parties to UNFCCC and to the Paris Agreement to participate in the United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) and to be invited in any international meeting or event hosted or organised by Türkiye in its COP31 Presidency capacity. This also includes access to all relevant documentation and information, as is the case for all other UN Member States. The EU has therefore made it clear to the incoming COP Turkish presidency, at all relevant levels, that the exclusion of a UN Member State from the preparation process of COP31 is not acceptable. The same message was conveyed to the UN Secretariat and the incoming Australian presidency of COP31 negotiations. The Commission will continue to strongly advocate for the full inclusiveness of the UNFCCC process.

(English version) to the Commission Markéta Gregorová (Verts/ALE) (8 June 2026) Subject: Euronet ATM dark patterns Regular reports from independent users of Euronet ATMs have shown that the company has been using dark patterns to deceive consumers into making choices that are less financially sound. Does the Commission consider these practices to be in line with the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive (4), particularly Articles 5, 6 and 7 thereof, with regard to the information provided and how it is displayed? 2. Does the Commission consider that changing pre-defined withdrawal amounts depending on the card and not allowing euro withdrawals from euro accounts could distort the behaviour of a specific group of consumers, as set out in Article 5(2) (b) of the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive? 3. Does the Commission consider that the information on the fees charged is sufficiently clear and accessible, as required by the Cross-Border Payments Regulation (5)? (18 September 2026) The directive 2005/29/EC (1) prohibits misleading practices by traders, including misleading actions or omissions about the price or the manner in which the price is calculated. It is transposed in national laws and Member States authorities and courts deal with its enforcement regarding specific traders, considering all the circumstances and the impact of specific commercial practice on the average consumer’s transactional decision. Directive 2005/29/EC acts as a safety net complementing more detailed requirements provided in sectoral EU law. Specifically, Article 4 of the Cross-Border Payments Regulation (CBPR) (2) requires providers of currency conversion services at an automated teller machine (ATM) to express the total currency conversion charges as a percentage mark-up over the latest available euro foreign exchange reference rates issued by the European Central Bank. This information must be clearly displayed at the ATM before the transaction is initiated. It is for the national competent authorities and courts to enforce these rules. The forthcoming revised legislative framework on payment services (3) aims to improve the effective supervision of independent ATM deployers and the application of transparency requirements, by requiring those deployers to register with the national competent authorities where the cash withdrawal services are provided. The new rules will also bring greater detail to the transparency obligations with which these operators must comply. In addition, the Commission is working on a proposal for a Digital Fairness Act, which aims at strengthening consumer protection in the digital environment, including as regards so-called ‘dark patterns’.

E-10-2026-002331.t: Harmonisation of maximum levels of vitamins and minerals in food supplements and fortified food products
qt: to the Commission Barbara Bonte (PfE) Subject:

More than 20 years after the entry into force of Directive 2002/46/EC, maximum levels have still not been set at EU level. Since 2023, the European Food Safety Authority has published revised scientific opinions concerning the Tolerable Upper Intake Levels (ULs) for vitamin B6, vitamin D, folic acid (folate), and selenium, among others; it is currently undertaking further revisions to the ULs for vitamins A and E, beta-carotene, iron, and manganese. At the same time, industry organisations have expressed concern about the modelling approach made public in January 2025, which in their view could lead to significantly stricter dosages than currently allowed in various Member States, resulting in changes to product formulations and the withdrawal of products from the market. 1.
What is the current state of play regarding the setting of harmonised maximum levels for vitamins and minerals in food supplements and fortified food products?
To what extent is the variability in consumption patterns between Member States and population groups, such as athletes, taken into account?
Which nutrients will be included in the first set of maximum levels?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.7.2026) Based on scientific advice, preparatory and technical work has been undertaken with a view to setting harmonised maximum levels for vitamins and minerals in food supplements and foods to which vitamins and minerals are added. In this context, the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) has updated the safe consumption levels for more than ten vitamins and minerals, Member States’ technical experts have contributed technical expertise, and all Member States have engaged in preparatory discussions, which are still on-going. These exchanges also make it possible to take account of national experience in setting maximum levels, including existing national rules and guidance where applicable. A Call for Evidence to collect initial public and stakeholder feedback is intended to be launched in the second half of 2026. The general approach chosen to derive maximum levels will be based on the specific detailed legal requirements for setting maximum amounts in the relevant EU legal acts, namely Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 1925/2006 on fortified foods1 and Article 5 of Directive 2002/46/EC on food supplements2, while also taking into account relevant case law by the Court of Justice of the European Union. Both legal acts stipulate that maximum levels shall be set considering, among others, upper safe levels of vitamins and minerals established by scientific risk assessment based on generally accepted scientific data, taking into account, as appropriate, the varying degrees of sensitivity of different consumer groups. Currently, all vitamins and minerals authorised for use in fortified foods and in food supplements are examined for the purpose of setting maximum levels.
1 Regulation (EC) No 1925/2006 on the addition of vitamins and minerals and of certain other substances to
foods, OJ L 404, 30.12.2006, pp. 26–38. 2 Directive 2002/46/EC on the approximation of the laws of the Member States relating to food supplements , OJ L 183, 12/07/2002 P. 51-57.

E-10-2026-002329.t: GSP status of Cuba in light of the systematic torture of 1 260 political prisoners
qt: to the Commission Barbara Bonte (PfE) Subject:
GSP status of Cuba in light of the systematic torture of 1 260 political prisoners

Cuba enjoys preferential market access to the European Union under the Generalised Scheme of Preferences (GSP). However, the Prisoners Defenders report describes how the Cuban regime abuses and mistreats thousands of political prisoners, including through prolonged solitary confinement, sleep deprivation, forced postures, physical abuse and the systematic denial of medical care. Of the 1 260 political prisoners, 128 are women and 32 were arrested as minors. 1.

Is the Commission aware of the report by Prisoners Defenders documenting a record high of 1 260 political prisoners in Cuba, as well as systematic torture, sexual violence and death threats as routine practices of the regime?
Does the Commission agree that the torture and ill-treatment of political prisoners, of which there are more and more, is a violation of the conditions laid down in the GSP scheme?

Is the Commission considering opening a formal investigation procedure that could lead to the temporary suspension of Cuba from the GSP scheme, in accordance with Article 19 of Regulation (EU) No 978/2012, as long as the regime continues to torture its political prisoners and uses them as forced labourers for the production of export goods destined for the EU?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.8.2026) The Commission is aware of the report by Prisoner Defenders to which reference is made in the question. As recalled the intervention1 of High Representative/Vice-President of the Commission at the plenary of the European Parliament on 19 May 2026, Cuba urgently needs to make fundamental political, economic and democratic reforms, respecting the human rights and fundamental freedoms of the Cuban people and releasing political prisoners and all individuals who have been arbitrarily detained. The EU including through its Delegation in Havana and its Special Representative for Human Rights regularly raises individual cases of political prisoners with the Cuban authorities calling for their immediate release. The EU has regularly called the Cuban authorities to ensure that all persons deprived of their liberty are treated in full compliance with international human rights standards. Cuba is not a beneficiary of the EU generalised scheme of preferences nor of any EU preferential trade regime, hence the premise underlying questions 2 and 3 does not apply.

E-10-2026-002328.t: Financing jobs in North Africa: how does it help the EU with borders and returns?
qt: to the Commission Dick Erixon (ECR) Subject:

The EU is putting EUR 15 million into the EUR 80 million Social Entrepreneurship Fund (SEF), which includes a EUR 35 million debt fund and funds start-ups in non-EU countries in North Africa and the southern Mediterranean1. The fund is part of the Pact for the Mediterranean, which also covers migration, yet the announcement of its launch says nothing about border control, returns or readmission2. 1.

How does this sum of EUR 15 million, and any further EU exposure that may arise from the debt fund and possible defaults, serve the EU’s interest in protecting its external borders and securing the return of people who have no right to stay in the EU?
Is disbursement under the SEF in any way conditional on the partner countries cooperating on readmission and returns, and if not, why not?
Is investing in start-ups in non-EU countries the most effective way to achieve the EU’s objectives in the region, which include reducing illegal migration to the EU?

at: (English version) to the Commission Dick Erixon (ECR) (8 June 2026) Subject: Financing jobs in North Africa: how does it help the EU with borders and returns? The EU is putting EUR 15 million into the EUR 80 million Social Entrepreneurship Fund (SEF), which includes a EUR 35 million debt fund and funds start-ups in non-EU countries in North Africa and the southern Mediterranean (1). The fund is part of the Pact for the Mediterranean, which also covers migration, yet the announcement of its launch says nothing about border control, returns or readmission (2). 1. How does this sum of EUR 15 million, and any further EU exposure that may arise from the debt fund and possible defaults, serve the EU’s interest in protecting its external borders and securing the return of people who have no right to stay in the EU? 2. Is disbursement under the SEF in any way conditional on the partner countries cooperating on readmission and returns, and if not, why not? 3. Is investing in start-ups in non-EU countries the most effective way to achieve the EU’s objectives in the region, which include reducing illegal migration to the EU? (7 August 2026) The Social Entrepreneurship Fund (SEF) (1) is a joint initiative of the EU with the KfW development bank and is anchored in the Pact for Mediterranean (2) as it delivers jointly on Pillar I (People: driving force for change, connections and innovation) and Pillar II (Stronger, more sustainable and integrated economies). By supporting socially and environmentally driven innovation in the region, the EU contribution serves the EU’s broader strategic interest in promoting stability, economic opportunity and resilience in the EU’s neighbourhood. Cooperation on migration, including readmission and returns, is pursued through dedicated policy dialogues, partnerships and instruments that are specifically designed for that purpose. By creating decent jobs and supporting the digital and green transition the SEF helps address socioeconomic challenges in partner countries and so contributes to redressing the structural drivers that can contribute to irregular migration.

What is the Commission’s assessment from the point of view of international law (Agreement Governing the Activities of States on the Moon and Other Celestial Bodies, Treaty on Principles Governing the Activities of States in the Exploration and Use of Outer Space, including the Moon and Other Celestial Bodies) of NASA’s announcement that it will establish a permanent base on the Moon and demarcate territory using drones? (31 August 2026) The Commission is not in a position to comment on the activities of the US National Aeronautics and Space Administration, as the EU does not engage in Human Spaceflight activities, which are the purview of the intergovernmental European Space Agency. The Commission recalls, however, that any activities on the Moon must be conducted in accordance with the applicable international legal framework. In this respect, relevant principles include the non-appropriation of outer space and celestial bodies, their use for peaceful purposes, and the obligation to conduct activities with due regard to the corresponding interests of other States. The Commission remains fully committed to the peaceful, safe and sustainable use of outer space in full respect of international law. In view of the increasing risks linked to the militarisation of space, the EU is pursuing both regulatory and operational measures. These include the proposed EU Space Act (1) aiming at strengthening the safety, resilience and environmental sustainability of space activities and the work of the EU Space Surveillance and Tracking (2) part of the EU Space Programme (3), which has for the past 10 years enhanced the protection of space infrastructures of Member States and the global community at large, free of charge. The EU strongly supports the rules-based international system, with the UN at its core, and the multilateral approach to international affairs including cooperation on outer space issues. The UN, through its dedicated bodies, remains the unique international platform for international cooperation in the peaceful uses of outer space and space security.

E-10-2026-002325.t: Alleged forced labour at the BYD construction site in Szeged, Hungary: follow-up
qt: to the Commission Raphaël Glucksmann (S&D), Kathleen Van Brempt (S&D), Klára Dobrev (S&D) Subject:

The Commission’s answer to E-001437/20261 confirms its awareness of the allegations of labour rights violations at the BYD construction site and notes that the European Labour Authority (ELA) has offered support to the Hungarian authorities. Three concerns remain unaddressed. 1.

First, the Commission references the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD) as a relevant instrument. However, following the Omnibus I amendments (Directive (EU) 2025/794), the threshold for net EU turnover has been raised to EUR 1.5 billion for non-EU companies. Can the Commission confirm whether BYD currently falls within the scope of the CSDDD?

Second, the Forced Labour Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2024/3015) applies to products placed on the EU market. As the alleged violations concern a construction site – not a product – the regulation appears to be inapplicable to this case. Does the Commission share this assessment and does it identify a legal gap?

Third, ELA’s lack of investigative powers, confirmed in the Commission’s reply, illustrates a structural weakness as more non-EU companies establish operations in the EU. Does the Commission intend to propose strengthening ELA’s mandate to enable proactive cross-border labour inspections?
https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/E-10-2026-001437_EN.html.
at: (English version) to the Commission Raphaël Glucksmann (S&D), Kathleen Van Brempt (S&D), Klára Dobrev (S&D) (5 June 2026) Subject: Alleged forced labour at the BYD construction site in Szeged, Hungary: follow-up The Commission’s answer to E-001437/2026 (1) confirms its awareness of the allegations of labour rights violations at the BYD construction site and notes that the European Labour Authority (ELA) has offered support to the Hungarian authorities. Three concerns remain unaddressed. 1. First, the Commission references the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD) as a relevant instrument. However, following the Omnibus I amendments (Directive (EU) 2025/794), the threshold for net EU turnover has been raised to EUR 1.5 billion for non-EU companies. Can the Commission confirm whether BYD currently falls within the scope of the CSDDD? 2. Second, the Forced Labour Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2024/3015) applies to products placed on the EU market. As the alleged violations concern a construction site — not a product — the regulation appears to be inapplicable to this case. Does the Commission share this assessment and does it identify a legal gap? 3. Third, ELA’s lack of investigative powers, confirmed in the Commission’s reply, illustrates a structural weakness as more non-EU companies establish operations in the EU. Does the Commission intend to propose strengthening ELA’s mandate to enable proactive cross-border labour inspections? (22 July 2026) 1. While data availability will improve by the time the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD) (1) becomes applicable and enforceable on 26 July 2029, currently available data suggest that the ultimate parent company of the European BYD subsidiaries will fall under the scope of the directive. 2. The fact that regulation (EU) 2024/3015 (2) is focused on products does not imply that a legal gap exists. The regulation is only one of the instruments at the disposal of the Commission and Member States to combat forced labour and must be understood as complementary to other instruments that can be used to address situations of forced labour in Member States, such as national labour and criminal laws. 3. The European Labour Authority (ELA) plays a supporting and coordinating role in relation to concerted and joint inspections. It does not replace national labour inspectorates or carry out inspections independently; rather, it helps Member States cooperate in enforcing EU rules on labour mobility and social security coordination. As part of the already announced Fair Labour Mobility Package, the Commission is currently working on a legislative proposal aimed at strengthening the mandate of ELA, including with regard to cross-border labour inspections. The content and scope of the Commission proposal are currently under preparation.

E-10-2026-002324.t: New surge in illegal immigration on the Libya-Crete-Gavdos route
qt: to the Commission Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE), Fabrice Leggeri (PfE), Matthieu Valet (PfE) Subject:

On 27 and 28 May 2026, several press releases1 from the Hellenic Coast Guard reported numerous search and rescue operations south of Crete and the neighbouring island of Gavdos that involved more than 700 migrants. Several boats reportedly left Tobruk in Libya in return for payment to smuggling networks. The press releases mention Frontex support and disembarkations in Gavdos, Souda, Kaloi Limenes, Agia Galini and Heraklion. In light of the fact that the Libyan route to Crete and Gavdos is putting increasing pressure on the EU’s southern external border: 1.
What immediate operational measures does the Commission intend to support, with Frontex and the Greek authorities, to prevent illegal departures from Libya and to dismantle the smuggling networks?

E-10-2026-002323.t: Environmental and health effects of microplastics shed from wind turbines
qt: to the Commission Gerald Hauser (PfE) Subject:

In 2021, the Commission adopted an action plan to achieve a zero pollution target by 2050.1 In 2025, Regulation (EU) 2025/2365 on reducing microplastic pollution was passed.2 Microplastics are harmful to the environment and human health.3 When large wind turbines move at high rotor speeds of well over 300 km/h, rain, wind, hail and airborne sand from the Sahara have a sandpaper‑like effect.4 A Norwegian study has found that one wind turbine can shed up to 62 kg of microplastics annually5, with harmful effects on the air, water bodies, soil and oceans, as well as microorganisms, plants, animals and, ultimately, humans.6This means that, over the years, wind turbines release tonnes of microplastics and countless environmental pollutants.7 The exact amount varies and depends primarily on a wind turbine’s size, its location and the prevailing weather conditions.8 1.
Why is the Commission keeping silent about the environmental pollution caused by microplastics wearing off wind turbines?
How does it intend to achieve its 2050 zero pollution target with the mass expansion of wind energy set to continue?
Is the Commission’s priority safeguarding public health and conserving the environment, or is it more concerned about clinging to the narrative of ‘safe’ and ‘harmless’ wind power?

https://germany.representation.ec.europa.eu/news/kommission-legt-plan-fur-null-schadstoff-ziel-bis2050-vor-2021-05-12_de. 2 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=OJ:L_202502365. 3 https://www.umweltbundesamt.de/themen/gesundheit/umwelteinfluesse-auf-den-menschen/chemischestoffe/mikroplastik#fragen-und-antworten-zu-mikroplastik. 4 https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0960148121000501. 5 https://docs.wind-watch.org/Leading-Edge-erosion-and-pollution-from-wind-turbineblades_5_july_English.pdf. 6 https://www.agrarheute.com/energie/abrieb-windraedern-fuer-hohe-pfas-werte-wildschweinenverantwortlich-633135. 7 https://www.energy.gov/cmei/systems/articles/research-led-sandia-reveals-leading-edge-erosionsignificantly-reduces-wind. 8 https://www.agrarheute.com/energie/strom/windraeder-verschmutzen-umwelt-mikroplastik-feinstaubwahrheit-fake-639724. 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (12.8.2026) The Commission is fully aware of the environmental challenges posed by microplastics, both those intentionally added to products and those unintentionally released into the environment. As highlighted in the Commission's brochure EU Action against Microplastic1, the main sources of unintentional microplastic releases include paints and coatings, tyre wear, plastic pellets, synthetic textiles, geotextiles and, to a lesser extent, detergent capsules. The Commission has already taken action to address several of these sources. In particular, the Regulation on Plastic Pellets2 was adopted to reduce microplastic pollution arising from pellet handling and transport. The remaining sources of unintentional microplastic releases are being assessed and will continue to be addressed through the measures and initiatives outlined in the Commission's publication, including actions relating to tyres, synthetic textiles, paints, geotextiles and other relevant sources. The Commission has also adopted restrictions on intentionally added microplastics under the Regulation on Registration, Evaluation, Authorisation and Restriction of Chemicals3. Research indicates that plastic emissions from wind turbines are much lower than from other sources4. Assessment of the environmental impacts of offshore wind was also addressed in a recent call under Horizon Europe5.

E-10-2026-002322.t: Plight of Alain‑Claude Bilie‑By‑Nze in Gabon
qt: to the Commission Thierry Mariani (PfE) Subject:
Plight of Alain‑Claude Bilie‑By‑Nze in Gabon

Alain-Claude Bilie-By-Nze, the former Prime Minister of the Gabonese Republic, was arrested in Libreville on 15 April 2026 and taken into custody the next day after being implicated in a debt case dating back to 2008. His legal representatives have raised questions about the limitation period of this case under Gabonese law. Bilie-By-Nze, who stood in the April 2025 presidential election, is a leading political figure in Gabon’s post‑transition landscape. Against this background, and given the EU’s interest in strengthening the rule of law and in smooth democratic transitions in central Africa: 1.

Has the Commission been made aware of this matter by its services or the EU Delegation in Libreville? Has it had the opportunity to liaise with the Gabonese authorities on compliance with procedural safeguards in this case?
Via which preferred channels of dialogue will it ensure that Bilie-By-Nze’s right of defence is fully respected, in line with Gabon’s international commitments?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (20.7.2026) The EU Delegation in Libreville and the resident EU Member States Embassies are closely monitoring developments concerning the case of former Prime Minister of the Republic of Gabon and political opponent, Alain-Claude Bilie-By-Nze and are regularly reporting to their respective headquarters. Since his arrest, the EU has met with representatives of his party, Ensemble pour le Gabon, members of his family and members of the Gabonese civil society to discuss his case. Human rights issues are regularly raised with the Gabonese authorities, most recently during the EU-Gabon Partnership Dialogue on 8 June 20261. During this dialogue, the EU conveyed concerns regarding arbitrary detentions and other human rights issues, referring also to the perceptions of international Non-Governmental Organisations and the reputational consequences for the country. The EU will continue engaging with the Gabonese authorities on human rights issues, including alleged cases of arbitrary detention and the right of due process.
