E-10-2026-002321.t: Privacy and safety implications of AI-enabled smart glasses and wearable recording devices
qt: to the Commission Veronika Cifrová Ostrihoňová (Renew), Abir Al-Sahlani (Renew), Yvan Verougstraete (Renew) Subject:

Recent media reports have highlighted concerns regarding AI-enabled smart glasses and other wearable devices capable of surreptitiously recording images and audio in public spaces. Particular concerns have been raised by women who report being unknowingly filmed and whose images may subsequently be shared online. The rapid development of wearable devices combining cameras, microphones and AI raises important questions regarding privacy, data protection, transparency and public safety. While current EU legislation, specifically the General Data Protection Regulation and the AI Act, provides safeguards, the practical application of these rules to consumer AI wearables may require further clarification. In this context: 1.
How does the Commission assess the compatibility of AI-enabled smart glasses and similar wearable devices with current EU data protection, privacy and consumer protection legislation?

How is the Commission assessing the impact of such technologies on women, including risks related to gender-based harassment, non-consensual recording and the online dissemination of images, as well as the impact on women’s sense of safety and participation in public spaces?

Does the Commission intend, in cooperation with the European Data Protection Board and other relevant authorities, to issue guidance on the use of AI-enabled wearable devices and the processing of personal data collected from non-users?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (24.9.2026) The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)1 requires that personal data processing is fair, transparent and lawful2 and in line with data protection by design and by default3. Smart glasses are not a new technology, and the data protection authorities have previously examined their compliance with the GDPR and recommended measures to increase transparency towards individuals4. The impact on privacy and data protection of individuals is also discussed by the European Data Protection Board5. In addition to data protection requirements, these products must fully comply with EU product safety legislation6. Depending on their primary function, they may also fall under sectoral rules. The use of such technologies may also raise concerns about technology-facilitated genderbased violence (TF-GBV). Such concerns should be considered when applying the existing legal framework, including Directive (EU) 2024/1385 on combating violence against women and domestic violence (VAW Directive)7 which requires the criminalisation of the most widespread forms of TF-GBV by 14 June 2027. The covert use of AI-enabled wearable devices to record and subsequently disseminate images online may fall within the scope of the VAW Directive’s framework. The Gender Equality Strategy 2026-20308 also reaffirms the Commission’s commitment to preventing and combating all forms of violence against women, including TF-GBV. This includes addressing emerging digital and AI-enabled risks that may disproportionately affect women and girls. Member State competent authorities and courts have a primary responsibility to monitor the application of the relevant legal provisions and to take the necessary steps for enforcement, without prejudice to the competences of the Commission as guardian of the Treaties.
1 Regulation (EU) 2016/679 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 April 2016 on the protection of

natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free movement of such data, and repealing Directive 95/46/EC (General Data Protection Regulation), OJ L 119, 4.5.2016, pp. 1–88. 2 Article 5 GDPR. 3 Article 25 GDPR. 4 Statement Irish data protection authority: https://www.dataprotection.ie/en/news-media/latest-news/dataprotection-commission-statement-concerning-facebook-view-glasses; Data Protection Commission Annual report 2023 (p. 75) https://www.dataprotection.ie/sites/default/files/uploads/2026-02/DPC EN_AR 2023_Final_ACO1.pdf#Glasses. 5 https://www.politico.eu/article/new-privacy-frontier-europe-eyes-crackdown-smart-glasses/. 6 Regulation (EU) 2023/988 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 10 May 2023 on general product safety, amending Regulation (EU) No 1025/2012 of the European Parliament and of the Council and Directive (EU) 2020/1828 of the European Parliament and the Council, and repealing Directive 2001/95/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council and Council Directive 87/357/EEC, OJ L 135, 23.5.2023, pp. 1–51. 7 Directive (EU) 2024/1385 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 May 2024 on combating violence against women and domestic violence, OJ L, 2024/1385, 24.5.2024. 8 Communication from the Commission to the European Parliament, the Council, the European Economic and Social Committee and the Committee of the Regions, Gender Equality Strategy 2026-2030, COM(2026) 113 final.

E-10-2026-002320.t: Emissions from the Livarna Gorica foundry and cross-border repercussions in the Gorizia-Nova Gorica area
qt: to the Commission Alessandro Ciriani (ECR) Subject:

For years, residents of Montesanto and the northern part of Gorizia, near the border with Solkan (Nova Gorica), have been reporting unpleasant odours and serious environmental issues caused by the Livarna Gorica foundry, located close to the Italian border in Slovenia. According to ARPA FVG (Friuli Venezia Giulia Regional Environmental Protection Agency), the reports of odours have increased significantly since May 2025 and their nature suggests that they are emanating from the foundry’s activities. In all, 140 reports were registered in September 2025, 96 in November 2025, 109 in February 2026 and 93 in March 2026, with a high proportion coming from the Montesanto area. This issue has a clear cross-border dynamic and may require action to verify compliance with Directive 2010/75/EU on industrial emissions, with best available techniques and with requirements for Member States to cooperate with one another. In view of the above: 1.
Is the Commission aware of this situation and does it intend to ask the competent Slovenian authorities for further information?
Does it consider it necessary to verify whether the plant is operating in line with Directive 2010/75/EU and the relevant best available techniques (BAT)?
Will it promote stable and transparent cross-border monitoring of air quality in the Gorizia-Nova Gorica area?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (17.7.2026) The Commission is aware of cross-border odour emissions from the industrial facility Livarna Gorica d.o.o and understands that exchanges have been initiated between Italian and Slovenian local authorities. The Commission therefore does not intend to intervene at this stage. In its role as guardian of the Treaties, the Commission monitors the application of EU law and may decide to take appropriate action, in line with its enforcement priorities1. On 6 December 2024, Commission implementing decision on Best Available Techniques conclusions for the smitheries and foundries industry2 was published and permits of existing installations must be updated within four years to comply with these norms, including on odour. In addition, Article 26 of the Industrial Emissions Directive3 requires cooperation between neighbouring Member States to limit the consequences for the environment and human health of installations’ operations. This includes consultation of the other Member State during the permitting procedure. Under the Air Quality Directive4, where exceedances of air quality limit or target values are significantly affected by pollution transported from another Member State, Member States should notify the Commission and cooperate with concerned Member States to address the exceedances. Based on the latest available data reported to the Commission – for 2024 – there have been no exceedances of air quality standards in Gorizia nor Nova Gorica for particulate matter, nitrogen dioxide or benzo(a)pyrene.
1 Communication from the Commission - EU law: Better results through better application, OJ C 18, 19.1.2017,

p. 10–20, and Communication from the Commission - Enforcing EU law for a Europe that delivers, 13.10.2022, COM(2022) 518 final. 2 Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2024/2974 establishing the best available techniques (BAT) conclusions under the Industrial Emissions Directive for the smitheries and foundries industry: https://eurlex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A02024D2974-20241206. 3 Directive (EU) 2024/1785 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 24 April 2024 amending Directive 2010/75/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council on industrial emissions (integrated pollution prevention and control) and Council Directive 1999/31/EC on the landfill of waste, OJ L, 2024/1785, 15.7.2024. 4 Article 21 of Directive (EU) 2024/2881 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 23 October 2024 on ambient air quality and cleaner air for Europe (recast), OJ L, 2024/2881, 20.11.2024.

to the Commission Gabriel Mato (PPE), Francisco José Millán Mon (PPE) Subject:

In the negotiations on the free trade agreement between the EU and the Philippines, special attention should be paid to a sector as sensitive as the European tuna processing industry, which is a strategic sector and very important to a number of coastal communities. It is labour-intensive, creates a large number of jobs and processes some 340 000 tonnes a year. The Philippines is a very competitive player in the global tuna sector and has the potential to get significantly stronger. It is currently the chief Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) exporter of canned tuna to the EU. Granting trade preferences to the Philippines – on top of those already granted or provided for in other agreements – would increase pressure on the European processing industry, in a market where imports already account for around 50% of consumption. Against this backdrop, and taking into account that the Commission is aware of the importance of this sector: 1.
Is the Commission considering maintaining tuna’s status as a sensitive product in the negotiations with the Philippines?
Has it carried out or does it intend to carry out an assessment on the impact of liberalising imports of preserved Filipino tuna into the European processing industry?
Would an assessment take account of the cumulative effects of other agreements – such as the one recently concluded with Mexico – and preferential arrangements?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (16.7.2026) The negotiations for a Free Trade Agreement (FTA) with the Philippines are ongoing. So far, six rounds of negotiations have taken place. The Commission aims for an ambitious, comprehensive and modern agreement that can create opportunities for EU businesses while carefully handling sensitivities and potential impacts on particular sectors. Throughout the negotiations, the Commission shares with the co-legislators all the EU’s text proposals and market access offers and maintains regular contacts with stakeholders. The Philippines is a beneficiary of the Generalised Scheme of Preferences + arrangement, under which it has enjoyed duty-free, quota-free access for tuna products for over a decade, with stable export volumes over that period. Therefore, the FTA would not open a new flow into the EU market but, at most, consolidate an existing one. Tuna remains sensitive in the negotiations, and the Commission is handling it accordingly. The Commission will take into account the interests of the EU fleet and processing industry, the current and potential impact of imports, and the cumulative effect on the EU market of preferential access granted under other agreements and arrangements, in order to achieve a balanced outcome.

E-10-2026-002317.t: Revision of Regulation (EC) No 1099/2009 and phase-out of CO₂ stunning of pigs
qt: to the Commission Tilly Metz (Verts/ALE), Petras Auštrevičius (Renew), David Cormand (Verts/ALE), Anja Hazekamp (The Left), Manuela Ripa (PPE), Krzysztof Śmiszek (S&D), Sebastian Everding (The Left), Sigrid Friis (Renew), Ville Niinistö (Verts/ALE), Marianne Vind (S&D), Niels Fuglsang (S&D), Emma Fourreau (The Left), Sirpa Pietikäinen (PPE) Subject:

Each year, over 150 million pigs in the EU are stunned with CO₂ before slaughter. The method causes pain, fear, aversion and severe respiratory distress before loss of consciousness. In opinions from 2004 and 2020, the European Food Safety Authority identified CO₂ stunning as a serious animal welfare concern, concluding that the suffering is inherent and cannot be mitigated by technical improvements. The Commission has acknowledged, including in replies to Written Questions E-003066/20251 and alternatives in Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 1099/20093. No timeline has been provided for revising or phasing out CO₂ stunning. The expectation that the sector will voluntarily transition is not supported by evidence, including PigStun’s finding that slaughterhouses are unlikely to abandon established systems because of cost, reliability and competitiveness concerns. When will the Commission present the revision of Regulation (EC) No 1099/2009?

E-10-2026-002316.t: Vehicle type approval divergence and the Northern Ireland vehicle market
qt: to the Commission Barry Cowen (Renew) Subject:

Recent regulatory divergence between EU and Great Britain (GB) vehicle type approval regimes risks creating barriers for the automotive market in Northern Ireland. Since the end of 2025, vehicles placed on the GB market have required GB national type approval, while Northern Ireland continues to apply EU type approval rules under the Windsor Framework. Industry representatives warn that this divergence could reduce vehicle choice, increase costs and distort competition between retailers in Northern Ireland and Great Britain. The sector supports approximately 17 600 jobs and brings GDP 3 billion in annual revenues to Northern Ireland. In the light of these concerns: 1.

What assessment has the Commission made of the impact of the divergence between EU and GB vehicle type approval regimes on the availability and affordability of vehicles in Northern Ireland, and on profitability and investment in the sector?

Has the Commission examined whether the Windsor Framework could allow vehicles approved under the GB national type approval regime to be registered in Northern Ireland while maintaining the integrity of the single market?

What engagement has the Commission had with representatives of the Northern Ireland motor industry on this issue, and does it intend to explore solutions to ensure consumer choice and fair competition?
at: (English version) to the Commission Barry Cowen (Renew) (4 June 2026) Subject: Vehicle type approval divergence and the Northern Ireland vehicle market Recent regulatory divergence between EU and Great Britain (GB) vehicle type approval regimes risks creating barriers for the automotive market in Northern Ireland. Since the end of 2025, vehicles placed on the GB market have required GB national type approval, while Northern Ireland continues to apply EU type approval rules under the Windsor Framework. Industry representatives warn that this divergence could reduce vehicle choice, increase costs and distort competition between retailers in Northern Ireland and Great Britain. The sector supports approximately 17 600 jobs and brings GDP 3 billion in annual revenues to Northern Ireland. In the light of these concerns: 1.

What assessment has the Commission made of the impact of the divergence between EU and GB vehicle type approval regimes on the availability and affordability of vehicles in Northern Ireland, and on profitability and investment in the sector?

Has the Commission examined whether the Windsor Framework could allow vehicles approved under the GB national type approval regime to be registered in Northern Ireland while maintaining the integrity of the single market?

What engagement has the Commission had with representatives of the Northern Ireland motor industry on this issue, and does it intend to explore solutions to ensure consumer choice and fair competition?

(7 August 2026) 1. Under the Windsor Framework, the UK Government is responsible for implementing the limited set of EU rules that apply in Northern Ireland. It is therefore for the UK Government to assess whether there is any divergence between EU and Great Britain vehicle type approval regimes impacting the availability and affordability of vehicles in Northern Ireland. That said, the latest updates in the EU-UK Trade and Cooperation Agreement Automotive Working Group show a strong degree of alignment between EU and Great Britain vehicle type approval regimes. 2. In accordance with the Windsor Framework, vehicles can be registered in Northern Ireland if they are EU or UK(NI) type approved (1). Vehicles approved only in Great Britain cannot therefore be registered in Northern Irelan d (2). This is required to continue to ensure Northern Ireland’s unique access to the EU Single Market, the protection of the EU Single Market and the avoidance of a hard border on the island of Ireland. 3. The Commission engages extensively with Northern Ireland stakeholders. On the specific matter of vehicle type approval, clarifications to concerns raised by Northern Ireland businesses were also brought jointly by the EU and the UK in their regular engagement with Northern Ireland stakeholders in the margins of the Specialised Committee on the Windsor Framework.

UK(NI) type approval is subject to the same rules as in the EU, with UK authorities involved in the assessment process. Vehicles in Northern Ireland may however have a dual EU and Great Britrain type approval.

at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (31.7.2026) The Commission is fully aware of and takes into serious consideration the adverse effects of possible accidents related to oil and gas exploitation in the Arctic, including in the Barents Sea. The Commission draws on capability assessments from international bodies, including the Arctic Council’s Emergency Prevention, Preparedness and Response and Protection of the Arctic Marine Environment Working Groups, and the European Maritime Safety Agency’s supplementary response mechanisms. Also, the Offshore Safety Directive1 aims to reduce the likelihood of major offshore oil and gas accidents and limit the consequences for workers, the environment and coastal communities, by mandating a strict Report on Major Hazards and climate-specific risk testing. The Commission continues to engage with the European Economic Area, the European Free Trade Association States for the latter to incorporate this Directive. In the event of a disaster that exceeds a State’s national capacity, assistance can be requested through the EU Civil Protection Mechanism (UCPM)2. This enables the Emergency Response Cooperation Centre3 to mobilise support from Member States and UCPM Participating States, such as specialised equipment and response teams. The Commission remains committed to the approach set out in the 2021 Joint Communication on the EU Arctic Policy4. Addressing climate change and environmental degradation and supporting sustainable economic development remain valid objectives. The Commission has taken note of the different perspectives received during the public consultation and does not comment on media reports. E-10-2026-002312.t: Use of Anti-Coercion Instrument against Trump in Cuba
qt: to the Commission Emma Fourreau (The Left), Leila Chaibi (The Left), Anthony Smith (The Left), Manon Aubry (The Left), Irene Montero (The Left), Catarina Martins (The Left), Dario Tamburrano (The Left), Martin Günther (The Left), Rudi Kennes (The Left), Jaume Asens Llodrà (Verts/ALE), Vladimir Prebilič (Verts/ALE), Benedetta Scuderi (Verts/ALE), Marco Tarquinio (S&D), Giuseppe Lupo (S&D), Ilaria Salis (The Left) Subject:

Since January 2026, the administration of Donald Trump has further escalated sanctions against Cuba by threatening retaliatory tariffs against countries supplying oil to the island. On 1 May 2026, a new US executive order introduced sanctions targeting third-country operators maintaining economic relations with Cuba, particularly in the energy, security and financial sectors1. US extraterritorial laws are having severe consequences for Cuba and risk significantly affecting European companies. In practice, these measures may compel European operators to abandon activities that are lawful under EU law, not as a result of free commercial decisions, but because of coercive pressure arising from US sanctions. Council Regulation (EC) No 2271/96 (the Blocking Statute) has so far proven insufficient to counter the Trump administration’s imperialist offensive. To protect its economic sovereignty and the activities of European companies, the European Union could consider activating the Anti-Coercion Instrument in order to establish a credible deterrent framework vis-à-vis the US. 1.
Will the Commission condemn the illegal blockade imposed by Donald Trump on the Cuban people?
What measures does the Commission intend to take to ensure enforcement of the Blocking Statute and to give European operators the option of maintaining relations with Cuba?
Does the Commission intend to activate the Anti-Coercion Instrument in response to Trump’s economic and commercial pressure on Cuba?
https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2026/05/imposing-sanctions-on-those-responsible-forrepression-in-cuba-and-for-threats-to-united-states-national-security-and-foreign-policy/. 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.8.2026) The Commission has consistently maintained that the extra-territorial application of secondary sanctions is incompatible with international law and that sanctions must comply with the UN Charter, international humanitarian law and other international law and due process. Recently, the High Representative/ Vice-President has stressed ‘Cuba's economic crisis is really reaching a breaking point. Cuban people deserve opportunity and freedom, not more control and isolation’1. The assessment of third-country extraterritorial sanctions on Cuba should be framed also within the EU’s commitment to safeguard legitimate trade and investment. Where the new Executive orders can be considered as an action based on or resulting from an act specified in the Annex of Regulation 2271/96 (Blocking Statute)2, including the Helms Burton Act, then the latter regulation already protects the EU operators by prohibiting compliance with that executive order. Regulation (EU) 2023/2675 (the ‘Anti-Coercion Instrument’, ACI)3 allows responding to cases where a third country applies or threatens to apply a measure affecting trade or investment in order to prevent or obtain the cessation, modification or adoption of a particular act by the EU or a Member State, thereby interfering in the legitimate sovereign choices of the EU or a Member State. Conversely, and without prejudice to the qualification of the US measures in a specific context, the ACI cannot be activated in response to economic coercion by a third country towards another third country.

E-10-2026-002311.t: Delays and vagueness in the Commission’s replies to parliamentary questions
qt: to the Commission Marcin Sypniewski (ESN) Subject:

In accordance with Parliament’s Rules of Procedure and the official guidelines published on Parliament’s parliamentary questions page (‘must be answered’, ‘is three weeks’), the Commission is required to reply to written questions within the following deadlines: six weeks for ordinary questions and three weeks for priority questions. However, reviewing the last 40 answers to my questions reveals a systemic failure to comply with those obligations. The average delay is currently 31 days and, in extreme cases, the delay has reached 94 days (E-001545/2024)1. Moreover, the quality of the answers given is alarming. Only 10 % of responses were fully comprehensive. The remaining 90 % were only partial replies, in which the Commission often used vague language, avoided difficult topics and, in 7 cases, completely ignored at least one of the questions asked. Given the above: 1.
What systemic or administrative problems within the Commission cause such extensive and regular delays in answering written questions?
What immediate action does the Commission intend to take to ensure that replies are provided within the deadlines set out in the Rules of Procedure?

Does the Commission have internal guidelines for formulating vague answers and ignoring specific questions posed by Members of the European Parliament? If not, how can it be forced to improve the quality of its answers?

E-10-2026-002310.t: Scandal surrounding the naming of a Ukrainian military unit ‘Heroes of the UPA’ – the accession process and EU support for Ukraine
qt: to the Commission Marcin Sypniewski (ESN) Subject:

Recently, a Ukrainian military unit was named ‘Heroes of the UPA’ (Ukrainian Insurgent Army). UPA was an armed formation directly responsible for a genocide of citizens of the Second Republic of Poland, known as the Volhynia Massacre, in which over 100 000 Poles were cruelly murdered in 1943 and 1944. Glorifying formations responsible for ethnic cleansing and mass atrocities clearly goes against the fundamental values of the European Union, such as respect for human dignity, human rights and the pursuit of historic truth and reconciliation. As a candidate country to the European Union and recipient of unprecedented financial and military assistance from EU institutions, Ukraine should be required to comply with European standards, including stopping the national idolisation of criminals. Given the above: 1.
Is the Commission monitoring cases of institutional glorification of a formation responsible for a genocide against Poles, and does it intend to officially respond to this scandal?

Will the Commission consider the issue of historical revisionism, including the idolisation of UPA and the blocking of the exhumation of murdered Poles, in its assessment of Ukraine’s compliance with the political criteria necessary for membership of the European Union?

Is the Commission considering introducing conditionality mechanisms that would make the disbursement of further instalments of macro-financial assistance to Ukraine conditional on stopping the idolisation of individuals and organisations responsible for the genocide of citizens of current EU Member States?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.8.2026) The Commission assesses compliance of Ukraine with the accession criteria on the basis of the established framework, including the political criteria relating to the stability of institutions guaranteeing democracy, the rule of law, human rights and respect for and protection of minorities. The Commission reports regularly on Ukraine’s progress in the context of the enlargement process. EU budget support and macro-financial assistance to Ukraine are governed by Regulations (EU) 2026/4671 and 2024/7922, requiring the fulfilment of a political precondition on upholding democracy, rule of law, and human rights, including those of persons belonging to minorities. Ukraine Facility disbursements also depend on the fulfilment of Ukraine Plan steps, including reforms to align with EU rules, values and standards. Issues pertaining to historical interpretation, remembrance policies and commemorative practices are matters to be addressed in a spirit of dialogue, responsibility and good relations with neighbours. The Commission encourages all efforts aimed at dialogue, reconciliation, and the respectful commemoration of all victims. As regards exhumations and related bilateral matters, the Commission encourages continued cooperation and dialogue between Ukraine and Poland, with a view to achieving tangible progress based on mutual respect and historical reconciliation.

enhanced cooperation on the establishment of the Ukraine Support Loan for 2026 and 2027: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2026/467/oj. 2 Regulation (EU) 2024/792 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 29 February 2024 establishing the Ukraine Facility: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/792/2026-02-27.

According to Spanish press reports, campaign expenses for the 2024 European Parliament election are being investigated because they may actually have been used to buy recordings made, in an effort to obtain information, in saunas run by the Prime Minister’s father-in-law. at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (25.9.2026) The conduct and organisation of elections are the responsibility of the Member States, in accordance with their constitution and national laws, in line with EU law and their international obligations. The Commission closely monitors developments pertaining to the rule of law in all Member States, including in the context of the Rule of Law Report. The rule of law is one of the values enshrined in Article 2 of the Treaty on European Union on which the EU is founded. The 2026 edition of the Report was published on 17 July 20261.

E-10-2026-002308.t: Guarantees for vulnerable consumers in Romania in the application of the Energy Performance of Buildings Directive
qt: to the Commission Ioan-Rareş Bogdan (PPE) Subject:

The entry into force on 30 May 2026 of the revised Energy Performance of Buildings Directive imposes decarbonisation objectives to be achieved by 2050. However, the structure of building stock differs from country to country. Romania is a unique case. The rate of private home ownership exceeds 95 %, largely medium- and low-income families or pensioners who are already at risk of energy poverty. In addition, the transition from heating based on natural gas – a strategic resource in which massive investment has been made – to fully electrified systems is putting pressure on low-voltage distribution networks, which require long-lasting modernisation. 1.

How does the Commission anticipate that Romania will be able to raise the capital needed for major renovations without causing a credit crunch or excluding citizens who are ineligible for private co-financing?

Given the strategic investments in regional security (such as the gas fields in the Black Sea), what margin of flexibility will the Commission allow when assessing National Plans for countries that decide to use hybrid systems (gas-hydrogen or gas-heat pump) beyond the standard time limits for phasing out fossil fuel boilers?

In rural areas where centralised infrastructure or smart electricity networks do not allow for the installation of heat pumps, will the Commission agree to the use of highefficiency biomass (wood) stoves as a solution consistent with emissions reduction objectives, without penalising Member States?
at: (English version) to the Commission Ioan-Rareş Bogdan (PPE) (4 June 2026) Subject: Guarantees for vulnerable consumers in Romania in the application of the Energy Performance of Buildings Directive The entry into force on 30 May 2026 of the revised Energy Performance of Buildings Directive imposes decarbonisation objectives to be achieved by 2050. However, the structure of building stock differs from country to country. Romania is a unique case. The rate of private home ownership exceeds 95%, largely medium- and low-income families or pensioners who are already at risk of energy poverty. In addition, the transition from heating based on natural gas — a strategic resource in which massive investment has been made — to fully electrified systems is putting pressure on low-voltage distribution networks, which require long-lasting modernisation. 1. How does the Commission anticipate that Romania will be able to raise the capital needed for major renovations without causing a credit crunch or excluding citizens who are ineligible for private co-financing? 2. Given the strategic investments in regional security (such as the gas fields in the Black Sea), what margin of flexibility will the Commission allow when assessing National Plans for countries that decide to use hybrid systems (gas-hydrogen or gasheat pump) beyond the standard time limits for phasing out fossil fuel boilers? 3. In rural areas where centralised infrastructure or smart electricity networks do not allow for the installation of heat pumps, will the Commission agree to the use of high-efficiency biomass (wood) stoves as a solution consistent with emissions reduction objectives, without penalising Member States? (26 August 2026) The Commission acknowledges the investment needs for renovation and the necessary support to the most vulnerable EU citizens. This is reflected in the budgetary allocation through EU Funds, European Investment Bank instruments and other initiatives (1). In its recovery and resilience plan (2), Romania had EUR 2.9 billion allocated for energy-efficiency renovation and seismic consolidation of residential and public buildings. Other EUR 2.3 billion are allocated for the period 2021-2027 from the Cohesion funds for investment in improving the energy performance of residential and public buildings, renewables and smart energy systems. To further mobilise private financing for energy efficiency, improve citizens’ access to finance and de-risk investments, the Commission is working together with the EU Member States, financial institutions and industry within the European Energy Efficiency Financing Coalition (3). Directive (EU) 2024/1275 on the Energy Performance of Buildings (EPBD) (4) requires for a trajectory for progressive renovation of the residential building stock and not of each building. National building renovation plans are the tool foreseen to draw up measures adapted to specific national conditions, estimate investment needs and identify financing sources. Romania has submitted its draft plan in December 2025. It is possible to install hybrid heating systems, in line with specific conditions provided by the Commission guidanc e (5), (6). While the EPBD obliges Member States to set out policies and measures with view of a complete phase-out of fossil fuel boilers, the date (2040) is an indicative target. The use of sustainable biomass in high-efficient heating systems is compliant with the EU energy legislation. There is no obligation to install heat pumps.

qt: to the Commission Lynn Boylan (The Left) Subject:

Recent reports1 reveal that Article 5(5) of Delegated Act (EU) 2024/1364 was transposed almost verbatim from lobbying documents submitted by Microsoft and DigitalEurope. (19 August 2026) The Energy Efficiency Directive (EED) (1) distinguishes between publicly available and non-public data, as well as the respective obligations of the Commission and Member States. The Commission is required to establish a European database on data centres with data publicly available on an aggregated level. This obligation has been fulfilled through the creation of the European database (2) and a public dashboard (3). Member States are required to define which specific data, data centres in their territory shall make publicly available. The Commission is examining whether Member States have correctly transposed the relevant EED provisions. Delegated Regulation 2024/1364 (4) was prepared in line with Better Regulation rules and included transparent consultations of Member States and stakeholders. The final text respects the EED legal base as well as the clear request by several Member States and stakeholders to ensure security and privacy of the reported data. In the Commission’s view, the confidentiality of the data in the European database complies with EU law and the Aarhus convention.

at: (English version) to the Commission Fabio De Masi (NI) (4 June 2026) Subject: OLAF and Mandelson in the context of priority Question P-000829/2026 On 27 February 2026, I submitted priority Question P-000829/2026 (1) to the Commission for written answer. I asked whether the Commission or any other competent authority (e.g. Europol) was independently and systematically examining the Epstein files in order to identify links to individuals such as former EU Trade Commissioner Peter Mandelson. On 11 May 2026, 10.5 weeks later, I received an answer. However, on 25 April 2026, a German news webiste, SPIEGEL Online (2), reported that the European Anti-Fraud Office (OLAF) was investigating Mandelson, thereby effectively providing an answer to my parliamentary question. How does the Commission justify the delay of 7.5 weeks in answering my question? (8 September 2026) The Commission attaches great importance to parliamentary questions as a political scrutiny tool and integral part of the special partnership with the European Parliament. To guarantee the quality of its answers, the Commission ensures that every reply is subject to an internal validation procedure, so that all relevant policy aspects are taken into account before the College adopts it. In this particular case, several parliamentary questions on the same or closely related issues were received within a short period. Additional time was therefore required to carry out the necessary internal coordination and consultations and to ensure consistent replies, reflecting the latest state of play. Article 230 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union requires the Commission to reply to questions from Members but does not establish binding time limits. The timelines set by the European Parliament in its Rules of Procedure are not legally binding on the Commission. Nevertheless, the Commission has continued to do its utmost to reply to all parliamentary questions (between 4000 and 6000 annually) taking into account the timelines set by Parliament. In 2025, the average response time was approximately 39 working days for normal questions and 30 working days for priority questions, compared with European Parliament’s indicative timelines of 30 and 15 working days, respectively. The Commission constantly works to streamline its internal processes to ensure pertinent and timely replies.

qt: to the Commission Fabio De Masi (NI) Subject:
In a letter to EU leaders dated 18 May 2026, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz pitched the idea of ‘associate membership’ for Ukraine. What does the Commission make of this bid?
at: (English version) to the Commission Fabio De Masi (NI) (4 June 2026) Subject: ‘Associate membership’ for Ukraine In a letter to EU leaders dated 18 May 2026, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz pitched the idea of ‘associate membership’ for Ukraine. What does the Commission make of this bid? (30 July 2026) The Commission has received the letter by the Federal Chancellor of Germany and welcomes the fact that Member States are actively reflecting on how to bring Ukraine closer to the EU, where Ukraine’s future lies. For the Commission, this discussion shows the strong commitment across the EU to make enlargement a reality. At the same time, any innovative ideas must be assessed carefully, including from a legal and institutional point of view, and they must remain anchored in the merit-based accession process. The objective is not to create a substitute for membership, or a secondclass status, but to support Ukraine on its path towards full EU membership. The Commission’s immediate focus therefore remains clear: to advance Ukraine’s accession negotiations, support reform implementation, and ensure that the enlargement process remains credible, fair and fit for purpose for Ukraine and for all candidate countries. On 15 June 2026, following a unanimous decision by Member States, the EU formally opened accession negotiations on Cluster 1 (Fundamentals) with Ukraine and Moldova. This long-awaited step is a well-deserved recognition of Ukraine’s commendable reform efforts, a powerful signal of support and a demonstration that the current enlargement methodology works. This was followed by the opening of Cluster 6 (External relations) on 14 July 2026. Formalising decisions on the remaining clusters without further delay must remain a priority, as it will reaffirm the merit-based and credible character of the accession process, and clearly and transparently define milestones to be achieved.

E-10-2026-002302.t: Unrealistic CO<sub>2</sub> emission rates for coke production and risk of deindustrialisation
qt: to the Commission Marcin Sypniewski (ESN) Subject:
Unrealistic CO2 emission rates for coke production and risk of deindustrialisation

The Commission’s proposal to reduce the emission rate for coke production to 0.143 Mg CO2/t is technologically unattainable for European plants. This indicator was calculated statistically, with reference installations’ data not provided, preventing operators from implementing appropriate low-carbon techniques. At the same time, the sector does not receive a sufficient number of allowances, while non-EU coke can circumvent the CBAM mechanism. Given the above: 1.

Will the Commission publish a list of the top 10% of installations that are least carbon intensive on the basis of which the new benchmark was calculated, including details of the processes, raw materials processed and low-carbon technologies used?

How does the Commission reconcile the immediate imposition of these technologically unattainable indicators with the principles of the IED, given the absence of updated BREF documents or BAT conclusions on emissions reductions in the coking sector?

Does the Commission plan to allocate 100 % free emission allowances for coke production or to include it in the CBAM mechanism to prevent the deindustrialisation of the European coke sector and dependence on imports from third countries?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.8.2026) The Commission cannot disclose the identity of the installations forming the 10% most efficient group for reasons of business confidentiality surrounding the data. But to increase transparency, the Commission intends to publish a document including benchmark curves and key parameters of the benchmark exercise, as the one published in October 20211. The benchmark update methodology is set in the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) Directive2 and is based on the actual performance of the most efficient installations rather than Best Available Techniques conclusions under the Industrial Emissions Directive3, which do not include levels for emissions of greenhouse gases covered by the ETS. Indeed, the data submitted by the Member States to the Commission of the performance of installations includes verified data on emissions and heat flows, but not feedstock and technology used. In the case of coke, however, it should be noted that the greenhouse gas intensity of the 10% best-performing installations is lower than the 2026-2030 benchmark level, which indicates that the most efficient installations should still receive sufficient free allocation to cover their emissions. The Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) review report4 required by the CBAM Regulation5 includes an assessment of a potential extension of CBAM to more goods and precursors based on carbon leakage risk and technical feasibility. Several sectors have been considered in the analytical work, such as organic chemicals and polymers, as highlighted by the Regulation, but also refinery products, among others. These materials have been prioritised for further assessment. It is therefore too early to say whether coke would be included in any future CBAM scope extension.

E-10-2026-002301.t: Accumulation of free carbon allowances and risks of competition being distorted under the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism
qt: to the Commission Julie Rechagneux (PfE), Aleksandar Nikolic (PfE), André Rougé (PfE), Céline Imart (PPE), Valérie Deloge (PfE), Marie Dauchy (PfE), Séverine Werbrouck (PfE), Roman Haider (PfE), Marie-Luce Brasier-Clain (PfE), Pierre Pimpie (PfE), France Jamet (PfE), Volker Schnurrbusch (ESN), Mélanie Disdier (PfE), Rody Tolassy (PfE), Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE) Subject:

The Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) and the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) are designed to work together to ensure that EU and imported products are subject to comparable carbon constraints. However, while the CBAM is being revised and a further reform of the EU ETS is expected, concerns remain about the interaction between the two mechanisms. Some EU companies still have significant stocks of free carbon allowances that they have accumulated over the years. Those reserves can make absorbing carbon costs easier for them than it is for those who have not received such allowances, including importers subject to the CBAM. This could distort competition in the sectors concerned. In addition, free allowances were initially intended to support the decarbonisation of the most heavily affected industries. The fact that there are a large number of unused allowances therefore raises questions as to their effective use and their impact on the market. In view of the above: 1.
What is the Commission’s assessment of the impact of the accumulated free allowances on competition in CBAM sectors?
Does it intend to introduce measures in future revisions to address any imbalances resulting from such situations?
Does it ensure that free allowances granted under the EU ETS contribute effectively to the decarbonisation objectives of the sectors concerned?
at: (English version) to the Commission Julie Rechagneux (PfE), Aleksandar Nikolic (PfE), André Rougé (PfE), Céline Imart (PPE), Valérie Deloge (PfE), Marie Dauchy (PfE), Séverine Werbrouck (PfE), Roman Haider (PfE), Marie-Luce Brasier-Clain (PfE), Pierre Pimpie (PfE), France Jamet (PfE), Volker Schnurrbusch (ESN), Mélanie Disdier (PfE), Rody Tolassy (PfE), Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE) (4 June 2026) Subject: Accumulation of free carbon allowances and risks of competition being distorted under the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism The Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) and the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) are designed to work together to ensure that EU and imported products are subject to comparable carbon constraints. However, while the CBAM is being revised and a further reform of the EU ETS is expected, concerns remain about the interaction between the two mechanisms. Some EU companies still have significant stocks of free carbon allowances that they have accumulated over the years. Those reserves can make absorbing carbon costs easier for them than it is for those who have not received such allowances, including importers subject to the CBAM. This could distort competition in the sectors concerned. In addition, free allowances were initially intended to support the decarbonisation of the most heavily affected industries. The fact that there are a large number of unused allowances therefore raises questions as to their effective use and their impact on the market. In view of the above: 1.
What is the Commission’s assessment of the impact of the accumulated free allowances on competition in CBAM sectors?
Does it intend to introduce measures in future revisions to address any imbalances resulting from such situations?
Does it ensure that free allowances granted under the EU ETS contribute effectively to the decarbonisation objectives of the sectors concerned?

(1 September 2026) The Emissions Trading System (ETS) Directive (1) includes the provision of free allowances to certain installations as a measure to prevent carbon leakage in those sectors. As free allocation is determined based on benchmarks and the activity level of the respective installations, it is possible that certain installations have received more free allowances than they have reported emissions. Successive reforms of the EU ETS have introduced measures to ensure that free allocation is better targeted and that the overallocation of allowances is avoided. These include making sure that benchmark levels better reflect the performance of the top 10% installations, that free allocation is adjusted to account for changes in activity levels of installations, or the exclusion of installations that use over 95% biomass as their fuel. Free allocation in excess of the emissions reported by an installation can also be an indicator of operators of installations having successfully invested in reducing emissions. The resulting surplus of free allocation can cover part of the cost of such decarbonisation investments. The Commission proposal for the revision of the ETS Directive, adopted on 17 July 2026 (2), includes further reforms to the free allocation regime designed to provide a balance between carbon leakage protection and ensuring that installations invest in reducing their emissions.

E-10-2026-002300.t: Stray animals in Greece: EU-wide comparison and public safety implications
qt: to the Commission Nikolaos Anadiotis (NI) Subject:

With around 3 million stray dogs and cats1, Greece has one of the most serious stray animal problems in the European Union. This number corresponds to a very high stray-to-inhabitant ratio, although the absence of a single European registration mechanism does not allow for a full comparison across Member States. There are estimated to be more than 100 million stray animals on the streets of Europe as a whole2, with a number of countries having systematically developed tools for registering, tagging, and preventing abandonment. In Greece, the problem concerns animal welfare, road accidents and – most importantly – the public safety of citizens. Especially in the area of Pylaia (Thessaloniki)3, there are frequent incidents involving threatening dogs. One even resulted in the death of a 65-year old individual, a case in which the municipality was found liable by the court4. With this in mind, can the Commission say: 1.

Does it intend to promote a common European framework for the registration of dogs and cats in order to reliably assess the situation in each Member State and to enhance the detection of animal abandonment and the accountability of owners?
Will it specifically examine the link between the problem of stray animals and public safety issues, such as attacks on citizens, aggressive packs and road accidents?
https://www.mdpi.com/2813-9372/2/1/1. https://linkly.link/2iBrJ. https://linkly.link/2iBqH. https://linkly.link/2iBrv.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (21.8.2026) 1. The Regulation on the welfare of dogs and cats and their traceability1 will establish an EUwide traceability system for the identification and registration of dogs and cats. This system will consist of national databases that are interoperable across the Union. It will be developed in a stepwise manner and will become fully operational within five years from the entry into force of the Regulation. From four years from the entry into force of the Regulation, operators of breeding and selling establishments, shelters and foster homes will be required to ensure that dogs and cats are identified by means of a microchip and registered in a national database. The same obligation will apply to pet owners from ten years from entry into force in the case of dogs, and from fifteen years from entry into force in the case of cats. These measures are expected to discourage the abandonment of dogs and cats and strengthen accountability in relation to such acts. 2. The management of stray dog and cat populations, including considerations related to public safety, falls and will continue to fall within the exclusive competence of the Member States, in accordance with the principle of subsidiarity and in line with the relevant international standards of the World Organisation for Animal Health.

E-10-2026-002298.t: Lack of traceability and oversight of EU funds mobilised for Ukrainians displaced by the war
qt: to the Commission Jorge Buxadé Villalba (PfE) Subject:

When the war between Russia and Ukraine started, the EU made EUR 193.3 billion available to Ukraine, of which EUR 17 billion supposedly went to Member States to support those fleeing the war. The latter figure is three times the amount Spain receives annually under the common agricultural policy. However, although the funds were made available, that did not mean that the abovementioned amount was granted directly; instead, Member States were allowed to reallocate that sum for the purpose in question from sources such as the cohesion policy funds for the 2014-2020 period and REACT-EU funds. In light of the above: 1.
How much of those EU funds has Spain certified that it reallocated between 2022 and 2025 for measures to help Ukrainians displaced by the war?
What amounts have the Member States reallocated from the above EU funds for the purpose in question?
What traceability mechanisms has the Commission applied to monitor the destination of the funds?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (31.7.2026) 1-2. Cohesion policy supports a broad range of migration-related measures. With the approval of a set of Regulations for refugees in Europe1, funding flexibility was increased, for example through additional liquidity (amounting to about EUR 13.7 billion overall, out of which about EUR 1.8 billion for Spain2). This mainly served to take pressure off Member States’ national budgets negatively impacted by the Russian military aggression. In addition, 18 Member States and the UK3 mobilised EUR 1.4 billion4 in cohesion policy programmes, out of which EUR 0.26 billion allocated by Spain to support displaced people from Ukraine by providing accommodation, healthcare, employment orientation, medical, social and psychological support. 3. Measures relevant to migration-related policies were subject to the Commission’s regular monitoring based on programme data reported by Member States, including common output indicators. Additionally, in their final implementation report on 2014-20205, Member States had to explain how some CARE6-related requirements were fulfilled. An ex post evaluation7 which covered expressly the Ukrainian refugee crisis was also conducted.

E-10-2026-002296.t: Regulation (EU) 2025/40 on packaging and packaging waste
qt: to the Commission Krzysztof Śmiszek (S&D), Joanna Scheuring-Wielgus (S&D), Robert Biedroń (S&D) Subject:
Regulation (EU) 2025/40 on packaging and packaging waste

Regulation (EU) 2025/40 on packaging and packaging waste rightly exempts the packaging of medicinal products from mandatory recycling requirements to ensure the security of medicine supply and patient safety. However, this results in the mass generation of polyvinyl chloride (PVC) waste that is not recycled. Member States cannot implement regulation on their own due to the full harmonisation of the pharmaceutical market in the EU. Given the general interest, environmental protection and the EU’s circular economy objectives, we ask: 1.

Is the Commission planning to take legislative action or revise pharmaceutical legislation with a view to a systemic shift away from PVC in medicine packaging towards safe and recyclable alternatives?

Does the Commission intend, in cooperation with the European Medicines Agency (EMA), to implement simplified registration procedures for manufacturers switching packaging material to greener solutions?
Is EU financial or research support planned for the development of innovative, immediate green packaging technology in the pharmaceutical industry?
at: (English version) to the Commission Krzysztof Śmiszek (S&D), Joanna Scheuring-Wielgus (S&D), Robert Biedroń (S&D) (4 June 2026) Subject: Regulation (EU) 2025/40 on packaging and packaging waste Regulation (EU) 2025/40 on packaging and packaging waste rightly exempts the packaging of medicinal products from mandatory recycling requirements to ensure the security of medicine supply and patient safety. However, this results in the mass generation of polyvinyl chloride (PVC) waste that is not recycled. (21 August 2026) 1. The Commission has funded various projects for more sustainable medical packaging (1). Funding for innovations in this area would be possible in the future under the Commission’s proposal for a European Competitiveness Fund. Indeed, packaging of medicinal product is an integral part of the market authorisation of medicines, with patient safety at the core of the authorisation. Therefore, they are exempted from the recyclability and recycled-content obligations under the packaging and packaging waste Regulation (2). The Commission will by 2035 review, whether the exemptions from the recyclability requirements, including those for medicinal products, should be revised. 2. The current EU pharmaceutical legislation (3) already provides mechanisms for the European Medicines Agency to assess post-authorisation changes, according to their nature and potential impact on the medicinal product. The Commission continues to monitor developments in this area and remains attentive to possible approaches that reconcile sustainability objectives with the regulatory requirements applicable to medicinal products. 3. Horizon Europe (4) has funded projects addressing sustainability and circularity challenges, including packaging, digital solutions, alternatives to single-use tools and modular construction. DICE (5) is bringing these approaches to a high technology readiness level and testing them in real healthcare settings. SolRec2 (6) (7) developed prototypes and recycling strategies for epaper labels, pharma blister packs and laminate packaging waste. Support for novel packaging materials, including biobased solutions, has also been provided across sectors, and is proposed under the framework programme for research and innovation Horizon Europe 2028-2034.

E-10-2026-002295.t: Ensuring a robust support framework for the wine sector under the new multiannual financial framework for 2028-2034
qt: to the Commission Dimitris Tsiodras (PPE) Subject:

The European Commission’s proposal for the new multiannual financial framework for 20282034 and the reform of programmes such as the common agricultural policy are raising concerns about a possible weakening of the specific support framework for the wine sector. The challenges faced by the sector, such as climate change and the impact of the volatile geopolitical context on exports, as well as its vital contribution to the EU economy and society, create a need to maintain a stable, coherent and effective support framework for the sector under the next EU budget for 2028-2034. In light of the above, can the Commission say: 1.

Is it committed to maintaining the separate and ring-fenced financial envelope for wine under the next EU budget, as well as the common European framework, to prevent the creation of inequalities between Member States?
Does it intend to maintain and strengthen the recent wine package and, if so, how?
Is it considering the possibility of setting up a specific mechanism to insure against climate change-related risks?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (5.8.2026) 1. On 16 July 2025, the Commission made a proposal1 aiming at granting Member States more flexibility across a simpler and more streamlined budget. Member States will propose the allocation for their wine sectoral intervention and for other measures they deem necessary to achieve objectives in the sector. The wine sectoral intervention is proposed to be financed from the financial envelope of EUR 293.7 billion, the wine sector may also benefit from the EUR 6.3 billion for the Unity Safety Net. Finally, wine sectoral interventions linked to research and innovation or environment and climate may benefit, if decided by Member States, from a maximum support rate of up to 95% of the total eligible cost of the intervention concerned, which is higher than the general support rate of maximum 75%. 2. The proposals for the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) were made before the conclusion of the discussions on the wine package. These proposals are now in the hands of the colegislators who will ultimately decide on the elements they wish to adapt or align. The provisions in the wine package included in the Regulation for a Common Organisation of the Markets (CMO) in agricultural products2 are not affected by these proposals. 3. The legal proposals of the Commission contain a robust toolbox that allow setting up risk management tools under Article 12 of the CAP Proposal3 or Article 31 of the CMO4.

E-10-2026-002294.t: The conflict in the Middle East has made energy more expensive. How much has this cost Slovak industry, and what is Brussels doing about it?
qt: to the Commission Erik Kaliňák (NI) Subject:

Several Member States, including Slovakia, have repeatedly warned that the sharp rise in energy prices following the outbreak of the conflict between Iran and its opponents at the turn of February and March 2026 has significantly increased pressure on European industry. They also referred to this reality when rejecting any further restriction of free emission allowances. 1.
How does the Commission assess the impact of the escalation of the conflict between Iran and its adversaries on the competitiveness of energy-intensive industries in the EU?

How does the Commission assess the impact of rising energy prices on the competitiveness of European industry, and which industrial sectors does it consider to be the most vulnerable to further increases in energy prices?
Is the Commission preparing emergency measures to protect energy-intensive undertakings from further increases in energy prices?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (13.8.2026) The Commission has closely monitored the Gulf crisis and its impact on EU industries. The crisis triggered an energy price shock affecting all sectors, especially energy-intensive industries (EIIs), as well as disruptions to supply chains and increase in commodity price volatility. Renewed escalations between the US and Iran have pushed energy prices higher, reversing much of the relief seen during the ceasefire. Commission assessments show that impacts vary across industrial sectors, with basic metals being among the most affected. In response, the Commission launched AccelerateEU1, combining targeted, short-term actions with structural measures. These include speeding up the shift to homegrown clean energy by introducing an EU electrification target improving the gas to fossil fuel price ratio by reducing network charges, electricity taxation and accelerating the roll out of clean energy generation as well as addressing other electrification barriers, coordinated gas storage filling and oil stock releases, and fast-tracking the EU Grids Package2. Furthermore, under the Middle East crisis Temporary State aid Framework (METSAF)3, Member States have the possibility to provide temporary electricity and fuel price relief to businesses and raise the maximum aid intensity under the Clean Industrial Deal State Aid Framework (CISAF). In July 2026, the Commission approved Slovakia’s amended scheme4 to compensate EIIs for their indirect CO2 in electricity prices, increasing its budget to EUR 710 million until 2030. In parallel, the Industrial Accelerator Act5 will further support EIIs by creating lead markets for European low-carbon products and streamlining permitting for EII projects.

Social Committee and the Committee of the Regions – AccelerateEU – Energy Union: Affordable and Secure Energy through Accelerated Action, COM(2026) 370 final, 22 April 2026. 2 Communication from the Commission to the European Parliament, the Council, the European Economic and Social Committee and the Committee of the Regions – European Grids Package, COM(2025) 1005 final, 10 December 2025. 3 Communication from the Commission - Middle East Crisis Temporary State Aid Framework, C/2026/2593, 5 May 2026. 4 https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/mex_26_1709. 5 Proposal for a Regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council Establishing a Framework of Measures for the Acceleration of Industrial Capacity and Decarbonisation in Strategic Sectors and Amending Regulations (EU) 2018/1724, (EU) 2024/1735 and (EU) 2024/3110, COM(2026) 100 final, 4 March 2026.

E-10-2026-002293.t: Only a few per cent of migrants are actually deported. Will the new regulation finally change this?
qt: to the Commission Erik Kaliňák (NI) Subject:

On 1 June 2026, a political agreement was reached on the return regulation, which is intended finally to speed up and significantly increase the number of deportations of illegally staying migrants from third countries, including through the use of return centres outside the EU. Despite the EU’s long-standing dysfunctional migration policy and the low rate of returns, illegal migration continues to exert pressure on several Member States. 1.
Does the Commission consider the enforcement of return decisions in the individual EU Member States to be adequate?
What financial costs does the Commission anticipate for the establishment and operation of return centres outside the territory of the EU?
What specific measurable targets has the Commission set for increasing the return rate, expressed as percentages, in the first 12 and 24 months after the new regulation enters into force?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (16.9.2026) In the explanatory memorandum of its proposal for a Return Regulation1, the Commission noted the low share of third-country nationals that actually leave the EU compared to those ordered to leave and identified a number of shortcomings that are addressed in the proposed regulation to improve the effectiveness of the return system. The application of EU rules on return by Member States is assessed under the Schengen evaluation and monitoring mechanism2, and, where shortcomings are identified, specific recommendations are set out in country reports. The future Return Regulation will allow Member States to establish return hubs, subject to specific conditions and safeguards. It is for Member States to assess the potential financial costs of the specific initiative they take. The Commission will regularly monitor the application of the Return Regulation, including through the Schengen evaluation mechanism. The Commission will report on the implementation of the new Regulation in five years after its entry into force pursuant to Article 48 of the future Return Regulation.

E-10-2026-002291.t: EUR 150 billion for EU defence. How much of this will the Slovak defence industry actually receive?
qt: to the Commission Erik Kaliňák (NI) Subject:
EUR 150 billion for EU defence. How much of this will the Slovak defence industry actually receive?

Last year, the Council of the EU approved the SAFE instrument, with a maximum volume of EUR 150 billion, to support joint defence procurement and the development of the European defence industry. In connection with this instrument, I would like to ask: 1.
What volume of funding from the SAFE instrument does the Commission estimate could realistically be directed to Slovak companies and the Slovak defence industry?

What specific conditions must Slovak firms meet in order to participate fully in projects and consortia financed from the SAFE instrument, for example requirements relating to cooperation, technological standards and security clearances?

What proportion of production and supplies under projects financed by SAFE will have to be carried out in EU Member States, and what proportion may be carried out outside the Union, including in third countries?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (7.8.2026) The Commission does not estimate the share of Security Action for Europe (SAFE)1 financing accruing to an individual Member State’s industry, as loans are granted to Member States, not to companies. Slovakia is itself a beneficiary. Moreover, contractors and subcontractors established in Slovakia are eligible to take part in any procurement supported by SAFE, including common procurements conducted by other Member States. The value Slovak undertakings may obtain is therefore not limited to Slovakia’s allocation but depends on their competitiveness across all SAFE supported procurements. Under Article 16 of SAFE, contractors and subcontractors must be established and have their executive management structures located in the EU, the European Economic Area (EEA) – European Free Trade Association (EFTA) or Ukraine, and must not be controlled by a third country, save where guarantees approved by the Member State apply. For defence products related to category two, contractors must also have the ability to decide, without restrictions imposed by third countries, on the definition, adaptation and evolution of the design of the defence product procured, including the legal authority to substitute or remove components subject to such restrictions. These conditions apply uniformly to all participating Member States. The SAFE Regulation does not require any proportion of production to be placed outside the EU. It sets a ceiling: for each end product, the cost of components originating outside the EU, the EEA-EFTA states, and Ukraine may not exceed 35% of the estimated cost of the components. This is a maximum threshold applied per procurement, not a target or a guaranteed share; in practice production takes place predominantly within the EU, the EEAEFTA states and Ukraine.

E-10-2026-002290.t: Thousands of jobs in energy-intensive industries under pressure from Brussels. The Commission’s response?
qt: to the Commission Erik Kaliňák (NI) Subject:

Six Member States, including Slovakia, reject the proposal for a further significant reduction in free emission allowances for industrial enterprises. They warn that this measure risks causing a massive shift of production outside the EU (carbon leakage) loss of competitiveness and the deindustrialisation of Europe. In light of the foregoing: 1.

What serious negative economic impacts does the Commission expect following a significant reduction in the volume of free emission allowances, in particular in terms of rising energy prices, loss of competitiveness and a decline in investment in energyintensive sectors?

Has the Commission assessed the real risk of plant closures and the relocation of production to third countries with lower environmental standards, and what are its estimates of the scale of this carbon leakage?

What specific and effective measures does the Commission plan to introduce to protect European industry, in order to prevent further deindustrialisation and the massive relocation of jobs outside the Union?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.9.2026) Under the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS), free allocation supports competitiveness during the transition while maintaining incentives to cut emissions and rewarding efficiency rather than simply subsidising emissions. On 17 July 2026 the Commission adopted a proposal to review the ETS1. Accompanying this proposal is a Staff Working Document2, which includes an evaluation of the functioning of the ETS and an impact assessment3 of different policy options for the future. These assessments have concluded that, so far, the carbon leakage protection has been effective and that the reforms introduced continue to reduce carbon leakage risks and improve the competitiveness of European industry. Conscious that a reduction in free emissions allowances can create short-term pressure on energy-intensive, carbon-leakage exposed sectors, the review includes other carbon leakage prevention measures as well as a significant increase in the support for investments in the decarbonisation of the EU, in particular through the Industrial Decarbonisation Bank and the Investment Booster. Furthermore, the Commission is taking multiple measures to support industry in the current energy crisis affecting supply of imported fossil fuels, including under the Affordable Energy Action Plan, AccelerateEU4 and the Electrification Action Plan5.

E-10-2026-002289.t: Millions of euros for sanctions and aid to Ukraine, while the EU is becoming poorer. How much longer can we afford to pay for sanctions against Russia?
qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Erik Kaliňák (NI) Subject:

In April 2026, the European Union adopted the 20th package of sanctions against the Russian Federation, and the Member States are already discussing a further sanctions package. At the same time, EU expenditure on support for Ukraine continues to rise. Against this background, the EU is facing slowing growth, increasing budgetary pressure and deteriorating competitiveness. I would therefore like to ask: 1.
What specific measurable indicators does the European External Action Service use when assessing the effectiveness of sanctions?

What results has the 20th sanctions package produced in terms of the Russian Federation’s revenue from energy exports? I am not interested in claims that ‘sanctions are working’; I want to know how and to what benefit, in figures.
Has the EEAS carried out, or commissioned, an analysis of the economic impact of the sanctions on the individual Member States, including the Slovak Republic?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (13.7.2026) In response to Russia’s unprovoked and unjustified military aggression against Ukraine, the EU has imposed unprecedented restrictive measures against Russia. Those measures are designed to reduce the Kremlin’s ability to finance the war, impose clear economic and political costs on Russia’s political elite, while increasing the long-term economic costs of its aggression. Russia’s economy is showing increasing signs of strain. In the first quarter of 2026, real gross domestic product (GDP) contracted by 0.2%, while the key interest rate remains very high (currently at 14.25%), keeping the cost of capital elevated and constraining investment and growth. Outstanding corporate loan debt in Russia has nearly doubled since the start of the war, heightening credit risks in the banking sector and adding to broader macroeconomic fragility. At the same time, despite rising defence expenditure and higher oil prices, Russia’s fiscal position has deteriorated sharply. By end May 2026, the budget deficit reached 6 trillion RUB, equivalent to 2.6% of GDP. This is more than the deficit recorded for the whole 2025 and already 50% above the entire deficit planned for 2026. Furthermore, Russian fossil fuel revenues are almost one third lower than pre-invasion levels. EU sanctions are designed to maximise pressure on Russia while minimising unintended consequences for the EU and the rest of the world. Restrictive measures are regularly reviewed, amended and renewed by the Council by unanimity, in the light of political developments on the ground.

E-10-2026-002288.t: Recognition of malignant neoplasms in firefighters as occupationally related diseases
qt: to the Commission Afroditi Latinopoulou (PfE) Subject:

In 2022, the World Health Organization’s International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) classified occupational exposure of firefighters in Group 1 (‘carcinogenic to humans’). The relevant IARC Monographs Volume 132 extensively documents the association of the firefighting profession with an increased risk of developing many types of cancer. At the same time, several countries have already made specific arrangements to recognise cancers as occupational diseases of firefighters. Given that firefighters are exposed daily to carcinogens in the performance of their duties: 1.
Will the Commission consider updating the European list of occupational diseases to recognise cancers associated with the firefighting profession?
Does the Commission intend to propose guidelines or European initiatives to Member States on the prevention, monitoring and compensation of occupational malignancies in firefighters?
Does the Commission have data on occupationally related cancers and deaths of firefighters in the EU Member States?
at: (English version) to the Commission Afroditi Latinopoulou (PfE) (3 June 2026) Subject: Recognition of malignant neoplasms in firefighters as occupationally related diseases In 2022, the World Health Organisation’s International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) classified occupational exposure of firefighters in Group 1 (‘carcinogenic to humans’). The relevant IARC Monographs Volume 132 extensively documents the association of the firefighting profession with an increased risk of developing many types of cancer. At the same time, several countries have already made specific arrangements to recognise cancers as occupational diseases of firefighters. Given that firefighters are exposed daily to carcinogens in the performance of their duties: 1.
Will the Commission consider updating the European list of occupational diseases to recognise cancers associated with the firefighting profession?
Does the Commission intend to propose guidelines or European initiatives to Member States on the prevention, monitoring and compensation of occupational malignancies in firefighters?
Does the Commission have data on occupationally related cancers and deaths of firefighters in the EU Member States?

(7 July 2026) 1. The recommendation on the European schedule of occupational diseases (1) does not focus on specific occupations, but it covers specific diseases caused by specific hazardous substances. Substances of concern to firefighters, such as benzene, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, formaldehyde, asbestos, chromium and heavy metals like lead and mercury, are covered by the recommendation, which was recently updated with further asbestos-related diseases. 2. Under EU legislation (2), employers must assess all safety and health risks that their workers face as a result of their work and take the necessary preventive and protective measures. Member States must ensure that workers receive health surveillance appropriate to the risks they incur at work, including from exposure to carcinogens and other chemicals. Moreover, in 2025, the Commission adopted guidelines for managing asbestos-related health and safety risks at wor k (3). They include a chapter addressed specifically to firefighters and other emergency services. In addition, the European Agency for Safety and Health at Work provides information and tools (4), as well as a case study (5) on protecting the health of firefighters. Matters related to the recognition of and compensation for occupational diseases fall under the competence of the Member States. 3. Under EU legislation on EU statistics on health and safety at work (6), Member States are not obliged to provide data on accidents at work that are subject to confidentiality rules under national legislation, including as regards such accidents suffered by firefighters and in fire service activities (7). European occupational diseases statistics (EODS) (8) data do not allow for a breakdown of occupational cancer cases reported by occupation for firefighters.
