E-10-2026-002287.t: Inadequate external border controls and lifting Italian-Slovenian border checks
qt: to the Commission Anna Maria Cisint (PfE) Subject:

The European Commission has recently recommended that Schengen States phase out all internal border checks, a stance that is blatantly at odds with the new Schengen Borders Code. One of the areas affected would be the Italian-Slovenian border, where checks were reintroduced in 2023 as a result of the major influx of migrants travelling along the Balkan Route. Yet, at the same time, the Union’s efforts to protect its external borders continue to be beset by major shortcomings, while the Balkan Route is still one of the main corridors used by irregular migrants heading for Europe and remains a major security concern for the regions where Italy, Austria and Slovenia share bi-national borders. Given the situation, it is completely illogical to ask Member States to stop using an instrument that has enabled national authorities to beef up checks and step up their efforts to tackle the criminal networks involved in migrant trafficking. In the light of the above: 1.
Does the Commission not think that asking Italy to divest itself of an effective control instrument is illogical, given that the Union remains incapable of fully securing its external borders?
What further measures could the Commission take to combat new illegal migration flows and criminal organisations operating along the Balkan route?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (29.7.2026) The Commission Opinion on the necessity and proportionality of the reintroduction of border control by Italy of 2 June 20261 stresses that the reintroduction of internal border control must remain a temporary and exceptional measure of last resort, subject to the rules of the revised Schengen Borders Code2. The European Border and Coast Guard Agency (Frontex) shows a steady decline in detected unauthorised border crossings, including along the Western Balkans Route3. Moreover, the use of alternative measures, such as cross-border police cooperation and information exchange are an efficient and effective means to ensure a high level of security. The Commission continues to work on the reinforcement of the management of the external borders, through the upcoming revision of the Frontex Regulation and the entry into application of the Pact on Asylum and Migration, which includes the screening of third country nationals at the external borders4. Member States along the Western Balkans route continue to strengthen their operational cooperation under a ‘whole of route-approach’. Member States should fully use existing mechanisms to enhance security and operational law enforcement cooperation. The European Multidisciplinary Platform Against Criminal Threats (EMPACT) has two Operational Action Plans dedicated to Migrant Smuggling and Human Trafficking5. The European Union Agency for Law Enforcement Cooperation (Europol) continues to target migrant smuggling along the Western Balkans route. The recently established European Centre Against Migrant Smuggling within Europol further strengthens EU-level operational and analytical support for Member States in dismantling high-risk migrant smuggling networks.

E-10-2026-002286.t: Transboundary pollution of the River Evros by the Ergene and protection of the Evros Delta
qt: to the Commission Nikolaos Anadiotis (NI) Subject:

The River Evros is a transboundary water system of Greece, Türkiye and Bulgaria, with an important ecological, agricultural and economic role for the Evros border region.1 The Turkish River Ergene, part of the same basin, passes through heavily industrialised areas, and scientific publications record serious pollution by heavy metals and other chemicals, with potential impacts on public health and ecosystems.2 Given that the Evros Delta is part of the Natura 20003 network and that Directive 2000/60/EC imposes good water status objectives and cooperation in transboundary basins,4 the possible transfer of pollutants via the Ergene to the Evros is a matter of European interest. On the basis of the above: 1.
Does the Commission have data or an assessment of the possible transfer of industrial or chemical pollution by the Ergene to the Evros and the Evros Delta?
How does the Commission monitor the implementation of Directive 2000/60/EC in transboundary basins involving a non-EU country, such as Türkiye?
Does the Commission intend to support a permanent, transparent and publicly accessible water quality monitoring system in the Evros, in cooperation with Greece, Bulgaria and Türkiye?

(25 August 2026) Türkiye is not an EU Member State and there is no Water Framework Directive (WFD) (1) reporting obligation on the Turkish side. An ad hoc joint committee on Evros cooperation has been in place since 2010 and recently Greece and Türkiye have decided to reactivate it as part of a broader effort to deepen cooperation on sustainable water management in the Meriç/Evros River Basin. Under Article 3(5) of the WFD, for international river basin districts extending beyond EU borders, the Member States concerned shall endeavour to establish appropriate coordination with the relevant non-Member States. Under Article 13, Member States sharing an international river basin with non-Member States shall endeavour to produce a single river basin management plan (RBMP) and, where this is not possible, to have a plan for the portion of the river basin district lying within their own territory. Transboundary cooperation is assessed by the Commission as part of its assessment of Member States’ RBMPs. For transboundary river basins involving Türkiye, the Commission does not monitor Türkiye directly under the WFD. Instead, Türkiye reports on its alignment with the EU water acquis through the Instrument for Pre-accession Assistance programme’s (2) monitoring and annual reporting as part of the enlargement process (Chapter 27). In 2013 Türkiye has adopted a 15-point Ergene River Protection Action Plan, leading to different investments. In 2019 Türkiye has also adopted the RBMP for Meriç-Ergene Basin. Turkish authorities are monitoring the water quality in Ergene and note significant improvement.

E-10-2026-002285.t: Violence, harassment and psychosocial risks in the school environment in Greece - Protection of teachers
qt: to the Commission Nikolaos Anadiotis (NI) Subject:

The death of English-language teacher Sofia Christidou in Thessaloniki, following a haemorrhagic stroke, has sparked public debate over alleged complaints of bullying by pupils and the way in which the educational authorities handled her case. According to reports, the Sworn Administrative Inquiry is examining 16 documents, complaints and the teacher's referral to a health committee, while relatives attribute the deterioration of her health to behaviour and institutional inaction12. The incident highlights a broader issue of protecting teachers from violence, harassment and psychosocial risks in the workplace, which fall within the scope of health and safety at work under Directive 89/391/EEC34. In light of the above: 1.
Does the Commission have comparable data on incidents of violence, harassment or intimidation against teachers in Member States?
How does the Commission assess the implementation of Directive 89/391/EEC on the prevention of psychosocial risks and violence by third parties in public education?
Does the Commission intend to propose guidelines or a European mechanism for recording and preventing such incidents and supporting teachers who encounter them?

at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (20.7.2026) The Commission (Eurostat) collects data on reported non-fatal and fatal accidents at work. In the education sector in Greece, no fatal1 accidents were reported for 2014-2023, while the number of non-fatal cases2 rose from 42 in 2021 to 54 in 2023. According to the 2024 European Survey of Enterprises on New and Emerging Risks (ESENER) survey3, 85% of respondents in the education sector in Greece reported having to deal with difficult customers, patients or pupils. The Commission is working with stakeholders to find solutions for this complex topic. The Framework Directive on Safety and Health at Work4 covers all occupational risks and applies to all sectors of activity, including education, and it is up to Member States to properly and effectively transpose it. The Commission regularly undertakes a review to assess the practical implementation at the national level of this and 23 related EU directives. The results of the latest review, covering the period 2018 to 2022, are expected to be published later in 2026. As part of the envisaged Quality Jobs Act, the Commission is carrying out a review of the Workplace Directive5 and Display Screen Directive6. Possible EU action would strive to reconcile the need to improve worker protection in light of the digital transition, while avoiding unnecessary burden on companies and simplifying the legislation. Issues to be addressed would include better addressing the psychosocial risks, including in education. The Commission supports teacher safety by promoting safe, inclusive school environments and whole-school measures to prevent school violence, bullying and harassment7. The envisaged EU Teachers and Trainers Agenda announced in the Union of Skills would also cover teachers’ working conditions.

What specific measures does the Vice-President of the Commission/High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy intend to take to ensure that no Member State participates in future in military activities of non-EU countries that threaten the security of the EU? Are there relevant guidelines and an institutional framework for dealing with similar incidents?

(27 July 2026) Decisions relating to the participation of Member States in military exercises with third countries fall within the responsibility of the Member States concerned. The EU has no prerogatives in this area. In addition, there is no specific EU legal instrument governing Member States’ participation in military exercises organised by third countries. The High Representative/Vice-President remains in close contact with Member States on developments related to European security and defence. In more general terms, the EU has repeatedly made clear that Türkiye is expected to make an unequivocal commitment to good neighbourly relations, international agreements and the peaceful settlement of disputes, in accordance with the United Nations Charter. This position has been consistently endorsed by the Council and the European Council (1) and has been underlined in all relevant contacts with Turkish authorities, including on recent visits by the High Representative/Vice-President and the Commissioner for Enlargement to Ankara (2).

E-10-2026-002283.t: Ukraine’s glorification of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army criminals and the EU accession process
qt: to the Commission Ewa Zajączkowska-Hernik (PfE), Tomasz Buczek (PfE), Anna Bryłka (PfE), Tomasz Froelich (ESN), Milan Uhrík (ESN), Petar Volgin (ESN), András László (PfE), Irmhild Boßdorf (ESN) Subject:

On 26 May 2026, the President of Ukraine signed Decree No 440/2026, granting a military unit the name ‘Heroes of the UPA’ (Ukrainian Insurgent Army). This formation was responsible for mass crimes against the Polish population, including the genocide in Volhynia, with approximately 100 000–120 000 victims. This decision has been regarded as promoting the cult of perpetrators of murders of civilians, including women and children, and as evidence of Ukraine’s moral unpreparedness for EU membership. At the same time, the President of the Commission has recently announced ‘decisive steps’ in Ukraine’s accession process. The glorification of the chauvinistic and criminal ideology of Banderism stands in clear contradiction to the values set out in Article 2 of the Treaty on European Union (TEU). In view of the above: 1.
Does the Commission consider that the official commemoration by a candidate state of a formation responsible for genocide is incompatible with the EU values enshrined in Article 2 TEU?
Does the Commission intend to officially condemn the resurgence of Ukrainian chauvinism and make further negotiations conditional upon Kyiv completely ceasing the glorification of war criminals?
Does the Commission still seek the rapid accession of Ukraine to the EU in a situation where its historical policy strikes at deep sensitivities and the remembrance of victims in Member States?
at: (English version) to the Commission Ewa Zajączkowska-Hernik (PfE), Tomasz Buczek (PfE), Anna Bryłka (PfE), Tomasz Froelich (ESN), Milan Uhrík (ESN), Petar Volgin (ESN), András László (PfE), Irmhild Boßdorf (ESN) (3 June 2026) Subject: Ukraine’s glorification of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army criminals and the EU accession process On 26 May 2026, the President of Ukraine signed Decree No 440/2026, granting a military unit the name ‘Heroes of the UPA’ (Ukrainian Insurgent Army). This decision has been regarded as promoting the cult of perpetrators of murders of civilians, including women and children, and as evidence of Ukraine’s moral unpreparedness for EU membership. At the same time, the President of the Commission has recently announced ‘decisive steps’ in Ukraine’s accession process. The glorification of the chauvinistic and criminal ideology of Banderism stands in clear contradiction to the values set out in Article 2 of the Treaty on European Union (TEU). In view of the above: 1.
Does the Commission consider that the official commemoration by a candidate state of a formation responsible for genocide is incompatible with the EU values enshrined in Article 2 TEU?
Does the Commission intend to officially condemn the resurgence of Ukrainian chauvinism and make further negotiations conditional upon Kyiv completely ceasing the glorification of war criminals?
Does the Commission still seek the rapid accession of Ukraine to the EU in a situation where its historical policy strikes at deep sensitivities and the remembrance of victims in Member States?

(14 August 2026) The EU is founded on the values set out in Article 2 of the Treaty on European Union, including respect for human dignity, human rights, democracy, equality and the rights of persons belonging to minorities. These values also underpin the accession process. The Commission assesses compliance of Ukraine with the accession criteria on the basis of the established framework, including the political criteria relating to the stability of institutions guaranteeing democracy, the rule of law, human rights and respect for and protection of minorities. The Commission reports regularly on Ukraine’s progress in the context of the enlargement process. Issues pertaining to the massacres of Polish civilians in Volhynia and Eastern Galicia, as well as related questions of historical memory, remembrance policies and commemorative practices should be addressed in a spirit of dialogue, responsibility and good neighbourly relations. In this context, the Commission encourages and supports all efforts aimed at genuine reconciliation, and at the dignified and respectful commemoration of the Polish victims. The Commission will continue to assess Ukraine’s overall compliance with the accession criteria in line with the established methodology for enlargement.

E-10-2026-002282.t: Air quality around schools and backsliding on sustainable mobility in Logroño
qt: to the Commission César Luena (S&D) Subject:

A report1 on air quality around 34 schools in Logroño, Spain, concludes that 97 % of the schools tested exceed the WHO recommendations for NO₂, while more than 45 % exceed the new limits for 2030 set by Directive (EU) 2024/2881. The study highlights a close link between the intensity of motorised traffic and the levels of pollution recorded around schools. These findings come against the backdrop of recent decisions to reduce sustainable mobility infrastructure in the city and remove cycle lanes, even though the Commission has highlighted the role active mobility has to play in improving urban air quality. 1.
What is the Commission’s view of the results of this study, taking the new European objectives on air quality and the protection of children’s health into account?
In the Commission’s view, is removing active and sustainable mobility infrastructure in urban environments that have problems with air pollution compatible with these objectives?

What measures will the Commission take to foster healthy environments for schools and to support local authorities that focus on reducing motorised traffic, increasing active mobility and improving air quality?
https://www.ecologistasenaccion.org/365706/.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.8.2026) The Commission takes note of the referenced study aimed to serve the Spanish authorities in their implementation of the revised Ambient Air Quality Directive1. Given the division of responsibilities under the Directive, it is up to the Member States’ authorities to decide on the relevance of different inputs, in their decision-making process. The Directive introduces stricter EU air quality standards, including for nitrogen dioxide (NO2), to be attained by 2030. Where from 2026 until 2029 the levels of air pollutants are higher than air quality standards, authorities need to adopt roadmaps establishing measures to reach these. The Directive also improves the rules on air quality monitoring, requiring authorities to consider, to the extent possible, sensitive population and vulnerable groups – such as children – when deciding where to measure at hotspot locations. While the Directive establishes an indicative list of measures to be considered2, including measures to encourage a modal shift towards active mobility and less polluting forms of transport, the final choice of measures is up to the Member States. Active mobility infrastructure plays an important role, in urban areas, in line also with the New EU Urban Mobility Framework3 and the European Declaration on Cycling4. In addition, the Commission highlights relevant EU urban initiatives that provide targeted support to local authorities, notably the European Mobility Week5 and the Green City Accord6.
1 Directive (EU) 2024/2881 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 23 October 2024 on ambient air

quality and cleaner air for Europe (recast), OJ L, 2024/2881, 20.11.2024. 2 Annex VIII of Directive (EU) 2024/2881. 3 COM(2021) 811 final; https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex:52021DC0811. 4 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=OJ:C_202402377. 5 https://mobilityweek.eu. 6 https://environment.ec.europa.eu/topics/urban-environment/green-city-accord_en.

E-10-2026-002281.t: Insufficient electrification along the Aalborg-Hirtshals/Frederikshavn section of the TEN-T network
qt: to the Commission Per Clausen (The Left) Subject:

Unfortunately, a number of governments in Denmark have failed to take the necessary action to ensure the electrification of relevant parts of the rail network with a view to establishing the kind of climate-friendly, coherent rail corridor that the EU’s TEN-T network is supposed to provide. If nothing is done about this now, then not only might the goals set for 2040 be impossible to achieve, but it would also reduce the scope that local and regional authorities have to take action to secure transport options in the future. With the above in mind: 1.
What would the potential consequences for Denmark be if no efforts are made to electrify the Aalborg-Hirtshals/Frederikshavn section of the TEN-T network before 2040?
Can the use of battery-powered trains be seen as a satisfactory replacement for the actual electrification of the Aalborg-Hirtshals/Frederikshavn section?
What possibilities are there for EU co-financing of the electrification of the AalborgHirtshals/Frederikshavn rail section of the TEN-T network?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.8.2026) The Aalborg-Hirtshals/Frederikshavn section is an integral part of the trans-European transport (TEN-T) core network for passenger and freight transport and of the ScandinavianMediterranean European Transport Corridor. According to Article 16.6 of the TEN-T Regulation1 the lines shall be electrified by 31 December 2030. The Commission monitors the development of the Danish network regarding its compliance with the TEN-T Regulation. Article 16.11 of the Regulation grants Member States the possibility to request exemptions from the requirements on grounds of specific geographical or significant physical constraints, negative result of socio-economic cost-benefit analysis or significant negative impacts on environment or biodiversity. Any such request shall be substantiated with sufficient justification. The Commission shall assess the request in the light of the justification provided as well as in terms of its significant impact on interoperability and continuity of the railway network, where relevant. In case of an exemption, Article 20 (h) of the regulation calls for the development and deployment of innovative alternative fuels technologies for railways, such as hydrogen or battery powered trains for sections and rail access routes that are exempted from the electrification requirement. Depending on the outcome of the negotiations on the next multiannual financial framework, the electrification of railway lines on the TEN-T network could be co-funded under the Connecting Europe Facility or under the National and Regional Partnership Plans.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32024R1679.

E-10-2026-002280.t: Equivalence requirements for imported animal products and timeline for Commission action
qt: to the Commission Saskia Bricmont (Verts/ALE) Subject:

In its Vision for Agriculture and Food, the Commission committed to proposing rules that set the same animal welfare and animal production standards for imported products as those applying to EU farmers. Since then, this intention has been publicly and repeatedly reaffirmed. This commitment has garnered broad support, with farmers’ organisations and civil society groups across the EU calling for mirror clauses, as a matter of competitive fairness and ethical consistency. The current asymmetry undermines EU farmers, who must meet standards that their foreign competitors can ignore while accessing the single market. This also risks triggering an animal welfare leakage effect, ultimately undermining the EU’s animal welfare and environmental objectives. Legal pathways exist within the World Trade Organization framework, notably under GATT Article XX(a) on public morals and Article XX(b) on human and animal health, provided that measures are designed in a proportionate and non-discriminatory manner. Can the Commission clarify: 1.
What concrete legislative steps it next intends to take, and by when, in order to materialise its commitment?

How will it coordinate across its relevant directorates-general, including the Directorate-General for Trade, the Directorate-General for Agriculture and Rural Development, the Directorate-General for Health and Food Safety and the DirectorateGeneral for International Partnerships?
How will it inform and cooperate with trade partners regarding the future legislation so as to prevent allegations of ‘protectionism’?
at: (English version) to the Commission Saskia Bricmont (Verts/ALE) (3 June 2026) Subject: Equivalence requirements for imported animal products and timeline for Commission action In its Vision for Agriculture and Food, the Commission committed to proposing rules that set the same animal welfare and animal production standards for imported products as those applying to EU farmers. Since then, this intention has been publicly and repeatedly reaffirmed. This commitment has garnered broad support, with farmers’ organisations and civil society groups across the EU calling for mirror clauses, as a matter of competitive fairness and ethical consistency. The current asymmetry undermines EU farmers, who must meet standards that their foreign competitors can ignore while accessing the single market. This also risks triggering an animal welfare leakage effect, ultimately undermining the EU’s animal welfare and environmental objectives. Legal pathways exist within the World Trade Organisation framework, notably under GATT Article XX(a) on public morals and Article XX(b) on human and animal health, provided that measures are designed in a proportionate and non-discriminatory manner. Can the Commission clarify: 1.
What concrete legislative steps it next intends to take, and by when, in order to materialise its commitment?

How will it coordinate across its relevant directorates-general, including the Directorate-General for Trade, the Directorate-General for Agriculture and Rural Development, the Directorate-General for Health and Food Safety and the Directorate-General for International Partnerships?
How will it inform and cooperate with trade partners regarding the future legislation so as to prevent allegations of ‘protectionism’?

(28 July 2026) As announced in the EU Vision on Agriculture and Food (1), the Commission is preparing revision of the existing EU animal welfare legislation through a sector-by-sector approach. To support this work, a Call for Evidence (2) was launched in June 2025, from which follows that the option of requiring equivalent animal welfare standards to apply at imports is being reflected upon by the Commission as part of this exercise. As further announced in the Livestock Strategy (3) of 7 July 2026, by the end of 2026, the Commission intends to propose a targeted revision of animal welfare rules for laying hens and broilers, and by the second quarter of 2027, a similar proposal will address pig welfare. These proposals aim to follow-up on the Citizens’ Initiative ‘End the cage age’ and will also provide an opportunity to introduce equivalent animal welfare requirements for imported products in those sectors, in line with the World Trade Organisation rules. For any legislative proposal the coordination between relevant Directorates-general (DGs) of the Commission is ensured by discussions in the framework of the Interservice Coordination Group, which includes all concerned DGs. Together with the formal Interservice Consultation which precedes all legislative proposals, it ensures coordination between services in the preparation of legislative initiatives adopted jointly by the College of Commissioners. During the preparation of the legislative proposal the Commission is consulting all relevant stakeholders, including international trading partners, supported by an external study, published with the proposals, which also includes certain case studies on impacts for third countries.

E-10-2026-002279.t: Commission’s position on EU-Philippines relations following the Toboso massacre
qt: to the Commission Marc Botenga (The Left) Subject:

On 19 April 2026, 19 people were killed in an operation conducted by the Philippine armed forces. In addition, more than 650 people living in the village of Toboso were forcibly displaced as a result of that operation. Several human rights organisations consider the operation to have violated international humanitarian law and to have seemingly targeted community organising work and solidarity activities. They therefore call for an independent investigation123. The EU and the Philippines are negotiating a free trade agreement, in which respect for human and labour rights is a prerequisite. However, the Philippine Government continues to violate those rights, including through arbitrary arrests, extrajudicial killings and red-tagging. In light of the above: 1.
Has the Commission suspended negotiations for a free trade agreement with the Philippines?

Will it call for an independent international investigation into the Toboso massacre, as well as for those responsible for the massacre, along with the perpetrators of extrajudicial killings, abductions and arbitrary detentions, to be brought to justice?
Given that participation in the Generalised Scheme of Preferences Plus is conditional on respect for human and labour rights, does the Commission intend to suspend the Philippines from the scheme?

at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (28.7.2026) The Commission and the High Representative/Vice-President (HR/VP) are committed to continue engaging with the Filipino authorities on human rights. The engagement of the EU with the Philippines on human rights is underpinned by the Framework Agreement on Partnership and Cooperation (PCA)1. A Subcommittee Meeting on Good Governance, Rule of Law, and Human Rights was held on 6 October 2025, the next is planned in the last quarter of 2026. The EU and the Philippines reaffirmed a strong commitment to advancing good governance, the rule of law and human rights, and agreed on concrete follow-up in key areas2 and to intensify cooperation. The Commission, jointly with the HR/VP engages with Filipino authorities on human rights in the context of the EU’s Special Incentive Arrangement for Sustainable Development and Good Governance of the Generalised Scheme of Preferences (GSP+). The most recent GSP+ monitoring mission took place in March 2025 and the next GSP monitoring report is forthcoming this July 2026. The PCA will constitute the political framework for a future Free Trade Agreement (FTA), which is currently under negotiation, and for which the Commission is pursuing strong sustainability provisions. The Sustainability Impact Assessment in support of FTA negotiations concluded that an FTA could have overall positive impacts on the human rights situation3. The Commission provides targeted support to human rights under the thematic programme for Human Rights and Democracy and has also supported the Commission on Human Rights of the Philippines to carry out its mandate to protect civil and political rights and enhance human rights promotion.

E-10-2026-002278.t: EPBD and the conservation of Podhale’s wooden architecture – flexibility of requirements and exceptions for heritage
qt: to the Commission Marcin Sypniewski (ESN) Subject:

Member States were required to transpose the revised Energy Performance of Buildings Directive (EPBD) by 29 May 2026. In Polish public debate, including in Podhale, there are concerns that future energy efficiency requirements could lead to pressure to make changes to traditional wooden architecture (Zakopane-style log houses) that would put aesthetic and cultural heritage values at risk. At the same time, the Commission indicates that the directive allows for exemptions for, among other things, historical buildings and that Member States are free to choose renovation measures that suit their national context. In connection with the above: 1.

How does the Commission interpret the scope of permitted exemptions/derogations for buildings that are protected due to their historical or architectural value – especially when an unacceptable change in appearance would be required to meet the standards?
Is the Commission planning to publish (or has it already published) guidelines for the practical reconciliation of the EPBD with heritage conservation in regions with specific building traditions?

When assessing the transposition of the EPBD, will the Commission consider national solutions that more broadly protect regional heritage (e.g. Podhale’s wooden buildings) compatible with the directive through exemptions or less stringent requirements?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.8.2026) For residential buildings, the recast Energy Performance of Buildings Directive (EPBD)1 does not require mandatory improvements to individual buildings but imposes an average improvement at national level. Member States have flexibility as regards which part of their building stock they focus on, while at the same time prioritising the worst-performing ones. For non-residential buildings, Member States may exclude protected ones from the obligation to achieve minimum levels of energy performance. In doing so, Member States are responsible for defining the protected status according to national rules and the level of exemptions granted to such buildings. In 2025, the Commission adopted a support package2 offering guidance to help EU countries implement and transpose the EPBD including on exemptions for protected buildings3. Many renovation measures can be applied without compromising architectural or historical merits thanks to technological innovations. Some EU-supported practical resources are available.4 In assessing transposition, the Commission will verify compliance with the Directive, while considering the flexibility allowed to develop tailor-made solutions reflecting local building characteristics. The Commission supports efforts to protect the cultural heritage value of buildings.

E-10-2026-002277.t: ETS2 and historic tenement buildings: risk of disproportionate heating costs and lack of possibilities for thermal modernisation
qt: to the Commission Marcin Sypniewski (ESN) Subject:

Under ETS2, fuels used for, among other things, heating buildings are to be subject to a carbon price. In many Polish cities, especially in Silesia, there are thousands of tenement buildings on the register of monuments, with conservators restricting or prohibiting the insulation of facades and other key thermal modernisation measures. In practice, residents often have no real possibility to switch to electric or low-emissions heating without drastic increases in expenditure (due to high levels of heat loss). At the same time, ETS2 will increase the costs of heating with gas and other fossil fuels, which may lead to permanent and disproportionate financial penalties for tenants of historic buildings, despite the fact that barriers to modernisation stem from the system protecting historical monuments. The Commission states that the Social Climate Fund aims to mitigate the effects of ETS2. In connection with the above: 1.

Does the Commission allow mechanisms for historic buildings (e.g. compensation solutions or specific treatment) in the application of the ETS2 to avoid disproportionate heating costs when full thermal modernisation is not possible?

Does the Commission recommend that Member States include dedicated instruments for tenants and communities in historic buildings (e.g. support for alternative technologies: high-temperature heat pumps, modernisation of internal installations, internal insulation) in their National Social and Climate Plans?

Is the Commission considering guidelines (or a legislative initiative) to better reconcile climate objectives with heritage conservation – so that conservation legislation does not prevent reasonable efficiency measures in historic buildings?
at: (English version) to the Commission Marcin Sypniewski (ESN) (3 June 2026) Subject: ETS2 and historic tenement buildings: risk of disproportionate heating costs and lack of possibilities for thermal modernisation Under ETS2, fuels used for, among other things, heating buildings are to be subject to a carbon price. At the same time, ETS2 will increase the costs of heating with gas and other fossil fuels, which may lead to permanent and disproportionate financial penalties for tenants of historic buildings, despite the fact that barriers to modernisation stem from the system protecting historical monuments. (14 July 2026) EU law includes safeguards to avoid hardship for households living in protected buildings. Under the Energy Performance of Buildings Directive (EPBD) (1), Member States may exempt protected non-residential buildings from minimum energy performance requirements where compliance would unacceptably alter their character or appearance. The EPBD does not require mandatory improvements to individual residential buildings but requires Member States to improve the building stock at the national-level with flexibility on which part of the building stock they focus on, while prioritising the worst-performing ones. Many renovation measures can be applied without compromising architectural or historical merits thanks to technological innovations (2). The Social Climate Fund supports Member State action to address social impacts of the new carbon pricing for buildings and road transport (ETS2) by assisting the most vulnerable households, who disproportionately live in the worst-performing buildings including historic buildings. The Social Climate Fund provides Poland an opportunity to finance renovations, heating replacement and advisory services. The Commission encourages Member States to adapt their plans to specific national circumstances to address such issues. There are also opportunities resulting from the decarbonisation of Silesian district heating infrastructure. Households connected to large district heating systems (>20 megawatt) are not directly affected by ETS2. Under the existing EU-ETS, until 2030 operators of these systems in Poland are eligible for additional free allocation of emissions allowances, limiting price rises, based on implementation of climate neutrality plans.

E-10-2026-002276.t: Possibility of introducing a shortcut for the recognition of midwives’ professional qualifications in the context of Directive 2005/36/EC
qt: to the Commission Marcin Sypniewski (ESN) Subject:
Possibility of introducing a shortcut for the recognition of midwives’ professional qualifications in the context of Directive 2005/36/EC

Poland is seeing the progressive closure of obstetric and gynaecological units, leading to thousands of highly qualified midwives losing their jobs. At the same time, the Polish healthcare system is suffering from chronic shortages of nursing staff. Midwives have extensive skills acquired during their studies and many years of professional practice, including in the departments of surgery, general medicine, anaesthetics and intensive care, and have also completed postgraduate courses in surgical and anaesthetic nursing. Nevertheless, they face barriers to these qualifications being recognised in other branches. In connection to this: 1.

Is the Commission considering the possibility of amending Article 31 of Directive 2005/36/EC by adding an additional shortened training route (bridge studies) enabling midwives to obtain a qualification as a nurse responsible for general care, taking into account ECTS credits and professional experience?

What action is the Commission taking to facilitate the recognition of partial qualifications and professional experience acquired in the health sector, particularly in the context of staff shortages in the Member States?
Does the Commission plan to carry out an analysis of the impact that possible changes to the directive may have on patient safety and the professional mobility of healthcare professionals?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.7.2026) Directive 2005/36/EC1 sets minimum training requirements for accessing the profession of nurse responsible for general care across the EU. Under the Directive2, bridges between different health professional careers paths can be set at national level for equivalent training in terms of content and level to the ones required for nurse training. Health workforce shortages are a major challenge, requiring action in line with the division of competences in the EU. The organisation of education systems3 and the management of health services4, including adequate staffing, are Member States’ responsibility. EU acquis56 aims to facilitate mobility by ensuring recognition of EU professional qualifications7 and by harmonising minimum training requirements for five health professions8. Under the Directive, Member States may grant full or partial exemption on the basis of a case-by-case assessment via academic recognition to professionals wishing to change or evolve in their professional career path. The upcoming Skills Portability Initiative9 aims, under its Actions 2 and 3, at modernising and speeding up the processes for recognition of professional qualifications for EU citizens and introducing common rules on recognition to attract talent from third countries10. An impact assessment will accompany those initiatives to quantify its impact, notably on the mobility of professionals and how it will be facilitated. However, under these initiatives, the Commission does not intend to modify any of the minimum training requirements for health professions which are provided under the Directive.
1 Directive 2005/36/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 7 September 2005 on the recognition

E-10-2026-002275.t: Proposed merger between Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery: a threat to Europe’s film ecosystem
qt: to the Commission Emma Rafowicz (S&D), Joanna Scheuring-Wielgus (S&D) Subject:

The Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger will create an entity with strong market positions in film production, distribution and streaming. This may lead to price increases, pressure on theatrical exclusivity windows and a reduction in the number and diversity of films released, with implications for audience choice and cultural diversity. The merger may affect European independent producers and creators through fewer commissioning editors and reduced access to financing and distribution, undermining film diversity for European audiences and the viability of Europe’s creative industries. Based on the above: 1.

How will the Commission assess the merger’s impact on competition in the EU’s audiovisual sector, particularly regarding market concentration, the number and diversity of films released, and bargaining power vis-à-vis cinemas and independent producers?
Does the Commission intend to request the opinion of the European Board for Media Services under Article 23 of the European Media Freedom Act?

Will the Commission ensure that the parties offer commitments to address the risks of worsening commercial terms, reduced theatrical exclusivity, loss of cultural diversity and reduced sustainability of the European film ecosystem and does it consider that, if adequate remedies cannot be secured, the merger should be blocked?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (7.8.2026) On 22 July 2026, the proposed acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery by Paramount Skydance Corporation was approved by the Commission subject to conditions. The Commission thoroughly assessed the impact of the proposed acquisition in the EU from all possible angles, including but not limited to: (i) the production of films for cinema release, (ii) the distribution of films for cinema release; (iii) the distribution of television channels and (iv) streaming services. The assessment revealed that the concentration would lead to competition concerns in the European Economic Area (EEA) countries where Paramount currently distributes films to cinemas under the joint venture United International Pictures (‘UIP’) with Universal. Therefore, the Commission accepted remedy measures proposed by the parties that ensure the termination of Paramount’s stake in UIP in the EEA. The primary way for the European Board for Media Services (the Board) to draw up its opinions concerning media market concentrations is under Article 22 of the European Media Freedom Act (EMFA)1, where a media market concentration is likely to affect the functioning of the internal market for media services and upon consultation by the national regulatory authority or body concerned. Drawing up an opinion under Article 23 of the EMFA is conditional on the absence of an assessment or a consultation by the national regulatory authority or body concerned. At this stage, the Commission does not intend to request the opinion of the Board under Article 23 of the EMFA. In the event that the Commission’s assessment under the EU Merger Regulation does not align with a future opinion of the Board or any national media authority, the Commission’s assessment is without prejudice to the assessment that is carried out by the relevant media authorities.2
1 Regulation (EU) 2024/1083 of the European Parliament and of the Council establishing a common framework
for media services in the internal market and amending Directive 2010/13/EU (European Media Freedom Act), OJ L 2024/1083, 17.4.2024, p. 1. 2 Article 22(1) EMFA.

E-10-2026-002274.t: Housing and short-term rentals in tensioned areas
qt: to the Commission Jaume Asens Llodrà (Verts/ALE) Subject:

The housing crisis in Europe is being worsened by the pressure of short-term tourist rentals on the residential stock, reducing the supply available to residents and driving up access costs; in cities such as Barcelona, thousands of tourist rental licences have been withdrawn to return homes to residential use. 1.

Given that the Commission is preparing the first European housing plan in the light of the new EU regulation on short-term accommodation rentals, does the Commission intend to include in that plan binding measures on tourist rentals in ‘tensioned areas’ – areas officially designated as experiencing significant pressure in the housing rental market, including high housing costs relative to local incomes – which would allow Member States and cities to limit them with legal certainty and EU support?

If so, what concrete coordination and support mechanisms does the Commission intend to provide to support cities that are already regulating or restricting tourist rentals in areas facing a housing crisis?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (28.7.2026) Short-term rentals offer many benefits: greater choice, and a boost to tourism, incomes and jobs. While the shortage of affordable housing can mainly be attributed to other structural factors, increases in short term rental activity have been associated with higher rental and sale prices in several European cities.1 In December 2025, the Commission adopted the European Affordable Housing Plan2 setting ten key areas of action where the EU can add value and support Member States in addressing the housing crisis. Among these actions, the Commission will propose an Affordable Housing Act in 2026, to help public authorities identify areas under housing stress, using publicly available data, and enable them, in line with subsidiarity, to take proportionate measures to safeguard housing availability and affordability in those areas. The Commission is currently assessing different policy options to support local decision-making and to increase legal certainty, while fully respecting the competence of authorities in the Member States in matters of housing policy. Moreover, the Regulation on Short-term Rentals3 which has been applicable since 20 May 2026 will bring more transparency and help public authorities to design appropriate policies by providing for harmonised rules on the registration of hosts and sharing of activity data between digital platforms and national authorities.

1 Commission Staff Working Document accompanying the EAHP “Understanding the Housing Crisis”. 2 The European Affordable Housing Action Plan. COM (2025) 1025 final. 3 Regulation (EU) 2024/1028 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 11 April 2024 on data collection
and sharing relating to short-term accommodation rental services and amending Regulation (EU) 2018/1724 OJ L, 2024/1028, 29.4.2024.

E-10-2026-002272.t: Urgent steps to protect consumers from residues of banned pesticides in food imported from third countries
qt: to the Commission Anna Maria Cisint (PfE) Subject:

A recent report by the organisation Foodwatch has shed light on a serious problem affecting the food safety of European citizens. Residues of pesticides banned in the EU have been found in 14 foodstuffs sold in France, Germany and Austria, including a well-known brand of Thai rice. This is yet more evidence of need for an overhaul of our monitoring system and the fallibility of our safeguard mechanisms, undermining the principle of reciprocity. Instead, the Commission would be well advised to change its approach and instead ensure the automatic alignment of maximum residue levels (MRLs) for imported products, granting limited derogations in exceptional cases, subject to compliance with food-safety criteria. Can the Commission therefore say: 1.
How it intends to prioritise the need to protect European rice, by means of the monitoring system and the measures set out in the ‘food and feed safety’ omnibus package currently under negotiation.

Whether it considers it useful, pending the final revision of the rules, to implement a system for verifying alternative substances which, in the interests of ensuring genuine sustainability, is compatible with safeguarding the potential yield and strategic role of agricultural districts, such as those that produce rice.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.9.2026) Pesticide residues in food placed on the EU market, whether produced in the EU or imported, are subject to strict rules, including the setting of maximum residue levels (MRLs)1, and are systematically monitored by the Member States’ competent authorities. The results are summarised in annual reports by the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA). EFSA’s latest report2 shows a 98.2% compliance rate with MRLs based on 86,449 samples analysed across a wide range of products in the Member States. When non-compliances are detected, Member State authorities take measures that are proportionate to the risk for consumers. Noncompliant goods are either stopped at the border and not allowed on the EU market or withdrawn from it. In addition to the current EU monitoring and enforcement framework, the Commission launched in January 2026 a Task Force on Import Controls3 to improve the harmonised implementation of import controls across the EU, including for pesticide residues, and to ensure that food placed on the EU market is safe. The Food and Feed Simplification Package4 aims to stimulate innovation and accelerate market access for new biocontrol substances and plant protection products (PPPs) containing them while ensuring that farmers have access to essential PPPs for which alternatives are not available, especially when a serious danger to plant production is identified5. The Commission has also proposed that Member States can grant longer grace periods for distribution and use of existing stocks of PPPs when their authorisations must be withdrawn. During the negotiation of the proposed Package, the Commission and the Member States remain bound by the current legislative framework.
1 Regulation (EC) No 396/2005 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 23 February 2005 on

maximum residue levels of pesticides in or on food and feed of plant and animal origin and amending Council Directive 91/414/EEC, OJ L 70, 16.3.2005. 2 https://efsa.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.2903/j.efsa.2026.10054. 3 Import controls of food and feed Q&As - Food Safety: https://food.ec.europa.eu/horizontal-topics/officialcontrols-and-enforcement/import-controls-food-and-feed-qas_en. 4 https://food.ec.europa.eu/horizontal-topics/simplification-legislation_en. 5 For this purpose, the Commission has proposed amendment to Article 4(7) of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009.

E-10-2026-002271.t: EU-funded literary prizes and the interests of taxpayers
qt: to the Commission Dick Erixon (ECR) Subject:

The Commission has announced the winners of the 2026 European Union Prize for Literature1. The winner of the Grand Prix receives EUR 10 000 and financial support for two translations. The two special mention recipients receive EUR 5 000 each and support for one translation each. In addition, the other shortlisted authors receive support for one translation, and all shortlisted authors are promoted at major book fairs in Europe. The prize is an annual part of the Creative Europe programme. In this context: 1.

Can the Commission provide an account of the total budgetary impact of the 2026 literature prize and a full list of all other prizes awarded by the institution, including the budget impact of each prize (total cost of the prize, including the production of awards/diplomas/medals and, for prize ceremonies, logistical support, award panel or jury costs, promotional costs and any other costs)?
How does the Commission justify EU taxpayers financing these types of action while their cost of living is increasing?
https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/mex_26_1216.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (9.9.2026) The Commission is committed to supporting European artists and Europe’s cultural heritage at a time when platforms are becoming ever more powerful and tend to promote nonEuropean culture. This makes it more difficult for European artists and heritage to remain visible to European citizens. One important way of strengthening the visibility of European culture is through the various cultural prizes awarded by the EU. These prizes are co-funded by the Creative Europe Programme. In practice, the Programme supports the prizes through lump-sum grants awarded to the organisations and consortia responsible for managing them. This support is set out in the annual work programmes. For the year 2026, the total amounts corresponding to the awards are: - EU Prize for Popular and Contemporary Music: EUR 600 000 - EU Prize for Contemporary Architecture: EUR 500 000 - European Union Prize for Literature (EUPL): EUR 600 000 - EU Prize for Cultural Heritage: EUR 450 000 - EU Prize for Jewish Cultural Heritage: EUR 300 000 The total amount of co-financing for prizes for 2026 is EUR 2.45 million, representing 0.64% of the Creative Europe budget for that year. The Creative Europe Programme amounts to about 0.23% of the total EU budget for 2021–2027. The prizes are implemented by organisations active in the respective sectors, helping to ensure that prize activities serve the interests of the artists and cultural stakeholders concerned. They are also accompanied by promotion and market-development efforts. For example, winners and nominated authors of the EU Prize for Literature are actively promoted at major book fairs, helping to secure translation rights and broaden international visibility.

E-10-2026-002270.t: Temporary Decarbonisation Fund and impact of EU climate policy on industry
qt: to the Commission Mathilde Androuët (PfE), Marie-Luce Brasier-Clain (PfE) Subject:

The Temporary Decarbonisation Fund proposed by the Commission1 aims to support certain carbon‑intensive sectors, including steel, aluminium and fertilisers, that are at risk of carbon leakage during the phase‑out of free allocation under the EU emissions trading system (ETS) and the gradual introduction of the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM). However, Opinion 13/2026 of the European Court of Auditors2 stresses that this fund is based on retroactive payments linked to production taking place in 2026 and 2027, with funds only disbursed in 2028 and 2029. The Court also notes that this type of payment limits the influence of the awarding authority over the actions that are actually funded and poses risks to sound financial management. In view of the above: 1.
Does the Commission acknowledge that this fund corrects the negative impact on European industry created by its own ETS and CBAM architecture?
How can retroactive payment serve as a genuine reindustrialisation and decarbonisation strategy?
Does the Commission intend to slow down the phase-out of free allowances for strategic sectors, such as fertilisers, in order to safeguard European industrial and agricultural sovereignty?

Proposal for a Regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council establishing the Temporary Decarbonisation Fund, COM(2025) 990 final, 17 December 2025, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legalcontent/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52025PC0990. 2 Opinion 13/2026 (pursuant to Article 322, TFEU) concerning the proposal for a regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council establishing the Temporary Decarbonisation Fund, COM(2025) 990 final, https://www.eca.europa.eu/en/publications/op-2026-13. 1
at: (English version) to the Commission Mathilde Androuët (PfE), Marie-Luce Brasier-Clain (PfE) (3 June 2026) Subject: Temporary Decarbonisation Fund and impact of EU climate policy on industry The Temporary Decarbonisation Fund proposed by the Commission (1) aims to support certain carbon-intensive sectors, including steel, aluminium and fertilisers, that are at risk of carbon leakage during the phase-out of free allocation under the EU emissions trading system (ETS) and the gradual introduction of the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM). However, Opinion 13/2026 of the European Court of Auditors (2) stresses that this fund is based on retroactive payments linked to production taking place in 2026 and 2027, with funds only disbursed in 2028 and 2029. The Court also notes that this type of payment limits the influence of the awarding authority over the actions that are actually funded and poses risks to sound financial management. In view of the above: 1.
Does the Commission acknowledge that this fund corrects the negative impact on European industry created by its own ETS and CBAM architecture?
How can retroactive payment serve as a genuine reindustrialisation and decarbonisation strategy?
Does the Commission intend to slow down the phase-out of free allowances for strategic sectors, such as fertilisers, in order to safeguard European industrial and agricultural sovereignty?

(22 July 2026) The Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) (1) addresses carbon leakage risks on the EU internal market, but not the remaining carbon leakage risk on third-country markets. If agreed by the co-legislators, the Temporary Decarbonisation Fund will provide temporary decarbonisation support to EU producers of certain CBAM goods to reduce their exposure to a remaining carbon leakage risk. This addresses the competitiveness loss in third-country markets where EU goods might be supplanted by cheaper, more emission-intensive alternatives, potentially increasing global emissions. The Commission stands ready to support co-legislators in finding a swift agreement on the proposed fund. The earlier this agreement is reached, the earlier eligible operators can factor this support into their investment decisions. This will contribute to planning certainty, which is key for avoiding carbon leakage and fostering decarbonisation. The Commission has been consulting stakeholders on its upcoming review of the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) (2). The review will address, among other things, the effectiveness of the ETS Directive (3) as a whole, including all relevant parameters of its functioning such as free allocation in promoting reductions of greenhouse gas emissions in a cost-effective and economically efficient manner. This covers CBAM sectors, including fertilisers.

Proposal for a regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council establishing the Temporary Decarbonisation Fund, COM(2025) 990 final, 17 December 2025, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52025PC0990. Opinion 13/2026 (pursuant to Article 322, TFEU) concerning the proposal for a regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council establishing the Temporary Decarbonisation Fund, COM(2025) 990 final, https://www.eca.europa.eu/en/publications/op-2026-13. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2023/956/oj .

E-10-2026-002269.t: Cost of AccelerateEU for households, small and medium-sized enterprises and rural areas
qt: to the Commission Mathilde Androuët (PfE) Subject:

The Commission has announced, as part of AccelerateEU1, an electrification action plan for industry, transport and buildings, which covers heat pumps, electric vehicles, heat networks, hydrogen, sustainable fuels, charging points, storage and electrified industrial equipment. It is presented as a response to the energy price crisis. However, it risks piling more costs on households, craftsmen, farmers, fishers, hauliers, small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and rural areas, which will have to pay for additional equipment, standards, connections and adaptations. In view of the above: 1.
Has the Commission assessed the total cost of this accelerated electrification for an average household, an SME and a farm?
How does it justify responding to a cost-of-living crisis with new requirements for equipment and investment?
Does it intend to abandon any measure that would force people to replace their vehicles, boilers or professional tools prematurely?

Communication from the Commission to the European Parliament, the Council, the European Economic and Social Committee and the Committee of the Regions, ‘AccelerateEU – Energy Union: Affordable and Secure Energy through Accelerated Action’, COM(2026)0370, Brussels, 22 April 2026. 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (19.8.2026) The Commission adopted the Electrification Action Plan1 on 17 July 2026 to accelerate the electrification of the EU economy. There are clear benefits of increased electrification for consumers: for example, driving a battery-electric vehicle can save up to 78% compared to an equivalent fossil-fuelled car2, and switching from gas boilers to heat pumps cuts the average EU household's heating bill by up to 60%3. However, barriers to widespread adoption, which the Electrification Action Plan aims to address remain. The Plan does not propose obligations for consumers. Instead, it focuses on reducing the price gap between electricity and fossil energy costs and on incentivising the uptake of cleaner, electricity-based technologies such as heat pumps, electric vehicles and batteries, among others, across Europe. The Action Plan also seeks to level the playing field between electricity and gas. Their price differential often discourages the shift to more efficient options such as heat pumps, electric vehicles and electric industrial processes.
1 https://energy.ec.europa.eu/topics/eus-energy-system/electrification_en. 2 Depending on the Member State. The website https://evroutes.com uses residential prices to calculate savings
from the use of electricity compared to oil. 3 https://energy.ec.europa.eu/news/5-things-you-should-know-about-heat-pumps-2025-12-05_en.

E-10-2026-002268.t: Funding for grids, storage and decarbonisation under AccelerateEU
qt: to the Commission Mathilde Androuët (PfE) Subject:

The Commission1 estimates that the investment needs of the energy transition total EUR 660 billion a year until 2030. To that end, it wants to mobilise EU funds, institutional investors, banks, insurers, State aid and revenue from the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS). It has also announced the creation of an industrial decarbonisation bank, endowed with EUR 100 billion and including an investment booster financed by EUR 400 million in ETS allowances. At the same time, it wants to accelerate grids, interconnections, smart meters and storage capacities, with the aim of increasing storage capacity from the current 55 GW to 200 GW by 2030. The announcements raise a key question: who will pay? In view of the above: 1.
Can the Commission specify how much of those costs will be borne by consumers, taxpayers and businesses in the Member States?
Does it recognise that the ETS acts as an indirect carbon tax that pushes up the price of European energy?
How can it claim to protect European industry while increasing costs relating to decarbonisation, the grid and flexibility?

Communication from the Commission to the European Parliament, the Council, the European Economic and Social Committee and the Committee of the Regions, ‘AccelerateEU – Energy Union: Affordable and Secure Energy through Accelerated Action’, COM(2026)0370, Brussels, 22 April 2026. 1
at: (English version) to the Commission Mathilde Androuët (PfE) (3 June 2026) Subject: Funding for grids, storage and decarbonisation under AccelerateEU The Commission (1) estimates that the investment needs of the energy transition total EUR 660 billion a year until 2030. To that end, it wants to mobilise EU funds, institutional investors, banks, insurers, State aid and revenue from the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS). It has also announced the creation of an industrial decarbonisation bank, endowed with EUR 100 billion and including an investment booster financed by EUR 400 million in ETS allowances. At the same time, it wants to accelerate grids, interconnections, smart meters and storage capacities, with the aim of increasing storage capacity from the current 55 GW to 200 GW by 2030. The announcements raise a key question: who will pay? In view of the above: 1.
Can the Commission specify how much of those costs will be borne by consumers, taxpayers and businesses in the Member States?
Does it recognise that the ETS acts as an indirect carbon tax that pushes up the price of European energy?
How can it claim to protect European industry while increasing costs relating to decarbonisation, the grid and flexibility?

(26 August 2026) The clean energy transition is vital for Europe’s strategic autonomy and competitiveness. Significant investments are necessary to modernise our energy system, and secure affordable energy for all Europeans, while ensuring that costs are allocated fairly and vulnerable consumers are protected. The long-term benefits will more than offset the costs. A number of Member States are already reaping the benefits of the energy transition. Member States with a high share of clean energy in their electricity mix, a flexible system and sufficient grid capacity benefit from lower electricity prices and are better protected from fossil fuel supply shocks. The Commission estimates that an accelerated transition can lead to annual savings in the EU’s fossil fuel import bill up to EUR 260 billion by 2040 (1). The Grids Package (2) and the proposal on network charges (3) aim at optimising the planning and the use of the grid infrastructure, contributing to reduce energy prices and import dependence. By accelerating the energy transition, the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) is a key tool to improve energy security and independence. Thanks also the ETS, Europe reduced fossil fuel consumption by 25% between 2010 and 2024, improving resilience to geopolitical crises. The ETS has generated more than EUR 250 billion since 2013. These revenues supported decarbonisation investments and measures to reduce electricity prices for industry.

Communication from the Commission to the European Parliament, the Council, the European Economic and Social Committee and the Committee of the Regions, ‘AccelerateEU — Energy Union: Affordable and Secure Energy through Accelerated Action’, COM(2026)0370, Brussels, 22 April 2026. Estimate based on the energy modelling the Commission developed for the 2040 Climate Target plan. See also: https://commission.europa.eu/newsand-media/news/new-action-plan-save-eu260-billion-annually-energy-2040-2025-02-26_en . https://energy.ec.europa.eu/topics/infrastructure/european-grids_en . https://energy.ec.europa.eu/publications/communication-future-proof-network-charges-reduced-energy-system-costs_en .

A key aim in the EU ETS Review, adopted by the Commission on 17 July 2026, is to accelerate support for industrial decarbonisation and the buildout of clean energy, including also an obligation to invest 50% of national ETS revenues to industrial decarbonisation and the creation of a EUR 100 billion Industrial Decarbonisation Bank.

E-10-2026-002267.t: Influence of foreign-funded think tanks on shaping the European Green Deal
qt: to the Commission Mathilde Androuët (PfE) Subject:

According to an article published by Euractiv on 12 May 20261, US-based think tank Regulatory Assistance Project (RAP) ‘quietly shaped’ the European Green Deal’s ‘energy efficiency first’ principle and is now considering a merger with German think tank Agora Energiewende, an important player in European climate policy. These structures would benefit from significant funding from mainly American foundations and philanthropic organisations. In view of the above: 1.
Can the Commission clarify the exact nature of RAP and Agora’s contributions to the development of European climate policies, in particular in relation to the ‘energy efficiency first’ principle?

Has the Commission verified the possible existence of direct or indirect links between these funders and foreign economic, industrial or state interests that could influence European climate policies?

Does the Commission consider it legitimate for structures that are largely financed from abroad to have a significant influence on strategic choices with major consequences for Member States’ industry, energy prices and economic sovereignty?
‘Europe’s most influential energy think tanks to merge’, Euractiv, 12 May 2026, Nikolaus J. Kurmayer, https://www.euractiv.com/news/europes-most-influential-energy-think-tanks-to-merge/. 1
at: (English version) to the Commission Mathilde Androuët (PfE) (3 June 2026) Subject: Influence of foreign-funded think tanks on shaping the European Green Deal According to an article published by Euractiv on 12 May 2026 (1), US-based think tank Regulatory Assistance Project (RAP) ‘quietly shaped’ the European Green Deal’s ‘energy efficiency first’ principle and is now considering a merger with German think tank Agora Energiewende, an important player in European climate policy. These structures would benefit from significant funding from mainly American foundations and philanthropic organisations. In view of the above: 1.

Does the Commission consider it legitimate for structures that are largely financed from abroad to have a significant influence on strategic choices with major consequences for Member States’ industry, energy prices and economic sovereignty?

(27 August 2026) The energy efficiency first principle is defined in Article 2(18) of Regulation 2018/1999 (1), which was adopted by the colegislators. The need to treat energy efficiency as an energy source in its own right resulted from internal reflection in the Commission and had not been inspired by any particular external actor. Already in 2015, the Commission encouraged Member States to give energy efficiency primary consideration in their policies (2). Its subsequent development into legal requirements and guidance was supported by several research projects and consultancy contracts, which provided expertise and collected opinions, as part of standard procedures. The Regulatory Assistance Project (RAP) was part of the consortia of eight projects funded by Horizon Europe, five by Horizon 2020 and six by LIFE, and one study contract, which informed the policy development (3). The Commission adheres strictly to its transparency obligations by publishing information on funding recipients in the Financial Transparency System (4) and proactively disclosing the objectives and outcomes of funded projects on the Funding and Tenders Portal (5). The Commission also uses the Transparency Register (6) as a source of information on interest representatives carrying out influencing activities at EU level. Under the Agreement, registrants not representing commercial interests must declare their overall budget, funding sources, and any individual contribution above EUR 10 000 that represents more than 10% of their total annual budget, including the contributor’s name.

E-10-2026-002266.t: An appropriate regulatory regime for investment firms
qt: to the Commission Anouk Van Brug (Renew), Billy Kelleher (Renew) Subject:

In October 2025, the European Banking Authority (EBA) and the European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA) published their technical advice for the Commission, which suggested targeted revisions to simplify the prudential framework for investment firms, such as liquidity providers and market makers. In the context of the savings and investments union (SIU) goals, these amendments would help EU investment firms play a role in the development of European markets. As the Commission is currently looking at banks’ competitiveness, the EBA/ESMA advice is a reminder that the prudential regime for investment firms in the EU is more stringent and complex than in other jurisdictions. The application of the Investment Firms Directive1 (IFD) and the Investment Firms Regulation2 (IFR), their extraterritorial impact and lack of proportionality, has already had a negative impact on EU-based investment firms. This runs counter to the goal of having strong, diverse and autonomous capital markets. Strategic functions for capital markets (such as market making) should be strengthened in order to increase the attractiveness of the EU’s capital markets. 1.
What is the Commission’s assessment of the advice published by the EBA and ESMA?
How is the Commission planning to integrate the EBA/ESMA recommendations into its legislative agenda supporting the SIU?
Will the Commission propose adjustments in the context of a review of the IFD/IFR, in order to ensure that EU-based market makers continue to provide liquidity on European exchanges?

E-10-2026-002265.t: Violations of property rights of the Greek National Minority in Albania and their connection to the closing benchmarks of Chapter 23
qt: to the Commission Nikolaos Anadiotis (NI) Subject:
Violations of property rights of the Greek National Minority in Albania and their connection to the closing benchmarks of Chapter 23

According to a recent report, violent incidents occurred in Albania during residents’ reactions to tourist development, with members of the Greek National Minority among the injured, and the protesters raising the issue of protection of property rights12. At the same time, similar protests by residents against beach fencing, restricted access, contested land use and lack of transparency in licensing have been recorded on the Albanian coastline.3 Following the recent intergovernmental Conference of 26 May 2026 and the adoption of the Interim Benchmark Assessment Report (IBAR),4 Albania entered the final phase of accession negotiations, with Cluster 1 ‘Fundamentals’ including the rule of law, fundamental rights, functioning of democratic institutions and public administration. The protection of property, access to justice and transparency in land expropriations or concessions are directly linked to the accession criteria. In view of the above: 1.
How does the Commission assess the allegations of infringement of property rights and lack of transparency in tourism development in Albania?
Does the Commission intend to include the property issue and the related allegations explicitly in Albania's accession dossier and evaluation reports?
Will the Commission ask the Albanian authorities to conduct an independent investigation into the incidents of violence and the licensing of the projects in dispute?

at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.8.2026) The Commission is closely monitoring developments in Albania as part of its EU accession process. The quality and efficiency of the judiciary, and the respect and protection of fundamental rights, including the right to property and rights of persons belonging to minorities, are crucial components of the benchmarks under Cluster 1 – Fundamentals of the accession negotiations. To assess Albania’s progress on its EU accession path, the Commission rigorously monitors all developments and continuously engages with the national authorities in all areas of the negotiations, including on the rights of persons belonging to minorities, property rights, freedom of association, access to justice and due process. All ongoing projects in Albania must comply with the applicable legal framework and with the relevant accession negotiations benchmarks. Albania is expected to ensure effective judicial follow-up in any cases of alleged violence.
