E-10-2026-002264.t: Non‑commercial movement of pet animals from non-EU countries
qt: to the Commission Sebastian Everding (The Left) Subject:

According to EU law1, for the movement of a pet animal to be considered as non-commercial, the pet animal must be accompanying its owner and the purpose of the movement must not be its sale or transfer of ownership. If the movement is carried out by an authorised person, it must take place within five days of the owner’s journey2. At the same time, the Commission is empowered to provide for derogations to this deadline3. 1.

On what up-to-date scientific risk assessment does the Commission base the assumption that the same properly vaccinated and documented pet from a listed non-EU country should be treated differently under animal health legislation if the five‑day deadline has been exceeded, compared to movement within this deadline (even though the animal health requirements remain unchanged), and does the Commission consider it proportionate that only private deferred transports – for example in cases of illness, flight cancellations or other force majeure – are, after a period of five days, effectively subject to the import regime including BCPs/TRACES?

Is the Commission considering proactively asking countries for applications in accordance with Article 13 of Regulation (EU) No 576/2013, and will the Commission make use of its empowerment to propose derogations or an extended deadline, for example 30 days, for cases that can be proven to be private and involve no transfer of ownership?
Article 4, point (14), of Regulation (EU) 2016/429. Article 245(2). Article 245(3) point (b)
at: (English version) to the Commission Sebastian Everding (The Left) (3 June 2026) Subject: Non-commercial movement of pet animals from non-EU countries According to EU law (1), for the movement of a pet animal to be considered as non-commercial, the pet animal must be accompanying its owner and the purpose of the movement must not be its sale or transfer of ownership. If the movement is carried out by an authorised person, it must take place within five days of the owner’s journey (2). At the same time, the Commission is empowered to provide for derogations to this deadline (3). 1. On what up-to-date scientific risk assessment does the Commission base the assumption that the same properly vaccinated and documented pet from a listed non-EU country should be treated differently under animal health legislation if the five-day deadline has been exceeded, compared to movement within this deadline (even though the animal health requirements remain unchanged), and does the Commission consider it proportionate that only private deferred transports — for example in cases of illness, flight cancellations or other force majeure — are, after a period of five days, effectively subject to the import regime including BCPs/TRACES? 2. Is the Commission considering proactively asking countries for applications in accordance with Article 13 of Regulation (EU) No 576/2013, and will the Commission make use of its empowerment to propose derogations or an extended deadline, for example 30 days, for cases that can be proven to be private and involve no transfer of ownership? (22 July 2026) The non-commercial movement scheme was introduced in the EU legislation (1) to facilitate private movements of citizens with their pet animals. To prevent misuse of this scheme, specific criteria must be complied with for a movement to qualify as non-commercial. A key criterion is that the pet animal must accompany its owner. When the non-commercial movement cannot be carried out by the owner and an authorised person travels with the animal instead, it was deemed proportionate to require that the pet animal movement remains close in time to that of the owner and no more than five days before or after that of the owner. This requirement was originally established under Regulation (EU) No 576/2013 (2) and remains unchanged under Regulation (EU) 2016/429 (3) and Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/131 (4). The Commission does not plan to use the empowerment provided by Article 245(3), point (b), of Regulation (EU) 2016/429 to propose an extended period. Finally, the Commission does not proactively ask non-EU countries to apply for listing under former Article 13 of Regulation (EU) No 576/2013 and now Article 17 of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/131.

E-10-2026-002262.t: Online gambling: a new EU tax on a national competence?
qt: to the Commission Dick Erixon (ECR), Charlie Weimers (ECR), Beatrice Timgren (ECR) Subject:

In its resolution of 28 April 20261, Parliament called for exploring an EU own resource based on online gambling. However, gambling is currently excluded from the Services Directive2, which means it is regulated by the Member States rather than under common EU rules. In 2017, the Commission also closed all gambling cases, taking the view that such matters could be handled more efficiently at national level3. The Commission is now reported to be forecasting significant budgetary revenue from such a levy4. 1.

On what grounds is taxing online gambling at EU level consistent with the principle of subsidiarity and the principle of conferral, given that the EU has never been given taxation power by the Member States5?

In what way would financing the EU budget through a gambling levy be more beneficial for EU citizens than a direct contribution from the Member States, given that both ultimately draw on the same economy?
Will the Commission assess the cost of removing tax competition between the Member States that the harmonising of gambling tax rates would entail?

European Parliament resolution of 28 April 2026 on the proposal for the multiannual financial framework for 2028-2034 (interim report, 2025/0571R(APP)). 2 Directive 2006/123/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 12 December 2006 on services in the internal market (OJ L 376, 27.12.2006, p. 36, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2006/123/oj), Article 2(2)(h), excluding gambling from its scope. 3 European Commission, press release IP-17-5109, ‘Commission closes infringement procedures and complaints in the gambling sector’, 7 December 2017. 4 Sorgi, G., ‘EU forecasts €13B budget return from new gambling tax’, Politico, 28 May 2026. 5 Articles 5(2) and 5(3) of the Treaty on European Union (principles of conferral and subsidiarity). 1
at: (English version) to the Commission Dick Erixon (ECR), Charlie Weimers (ECR), Beatrice Timgren (ECR) (3 June 2026) Subject: Online gambling: a new EU tax on a national competence? In its resolution of 28 April 2026 (1), Parliament called for exploring an EU own resource based on online gambling. However, gambling is currently excluded from the Services Directive (2), which means it is regulated by the Member States rather than under common EU rules. In 2017, the Commission also closed all gambling cases, taking the view that such matters could be handled more efficiently at national level (3). The Commission is now reported to be forecasting significant budgetary revenue from such a levy (4). 1. On what grounds is taxing online gambling at EU level consistent with the principle of subsidiarity and the principle of conferral, given that the EU has never been given taxation power by the Member States (5)? 2. In what way would financing the EU budget through a gambling levy be more beneficial for EU citizens than a direct contribution from the Member States, given that both ultimately draw on the same economy? 3. Will the Commission assess the cost of removing tax competition between the Member States that the harmonising of gambling tax rates would entail? (30 July 2026) As stated in Articles 113 and 115 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU), the EU has competence to harmonise legislation in the area of taxation for the smooth functioning of the internal market. According to Article 311 TFEU, the EU shall provide itself with own resources to finance its policies. Own resources are, by nature, an exclusive competence of the EU. Article 311(3) TFEU empowers the Council to establish new categories of own resources. This Article neither defines own resources nor limits the form they may take. The own resources decision fully respects Member States’ tax sovereignty. It is adopted with unanimity in the Council after consultation of the European Parliament and must be approved by Member States according to their constitutional requirements. The Commission proposed in July 2025 five new own resources (1) to reduce reliance on contributions from gross national income and Value Added Tax and diversify revenue streams in line with EU policies. The Commission stands by the proposed package as it meets the principles of fairness, efficiency, and feasibility. It generates adequate revenue, ensuring the EU’s capacity to deliver on its shared needs and ambitions. Should it be decided to propose a levy on online gambling revenues, the Commission would, in line with the interinstitutional agreement on better regulation, assess all aspects of the issue. The Commission would also like to draw attention of the Honourable Members to its official reply to the European Parliament’s resolution of 28 April 2026 on the proposal for the multiannual financial framework for 2028-2034 that was transmitted on 19 June 2026.

E-10-2026-002261.t: EU support for the healthcare systems of the EU’s outermost regions
qt: to the Commission Sérgio Gonçalves (S&D) Subject:

The Commission’s 2022 strategy for the EU’s outermost regions (ORs) recognised that, while their healthcare systems vary, these regions are generally characterised by lower healthcare capacity and fewer healthcare professionals than national and EU averages. ORs also have, on average, lower life expectancy rates and particularly high infant mortality rates, as well as a greater risk of tropical disease outbreaks and pollution-related illnesses. In the 2022 strategy, the Commission outlined measures it would take to address these issues, such as improving the accessibility, quality and sustainability of the healthcare systems of the ORs through the European Social Fund Plus and the European Regional Development Fund, and addressing the ORs’ specific vulnerabilities in the work programmes of the Commission’s Health Emergency Preparedness and Response Authority. In view of the forthcoming renewed strategy for the ORs, could the Commission clarify the following: 1.
How does it assess the implementation and results of health-related measures announced in the 2022 strategy?
How does it assess current access to healthcare, medical capacity and availability of medicine in the ORs?
Will the forthcoming strategy include further measures to support the healthcare systems of the ORs?
at: (English version) to the Commission Sérgio Gonçalves (S&D) (3 June 2026) Subject: EU support for the healthcare systems of the EU’s outermost regions The Commission’s 2022 strategy for the EU’s outermost regions (ORs) recognised that, while their healthcare systems vary, these regions are generally characterised by lower healthcare capacity and fewer healthcare professionals than national and EU averages. ORs also have, on average, lower life expectancy rates and particularly high infant mortality rates, as well as a greater risk of tropical disease outbreaks and pollution-related illnesses. In the 2022 strategy, the Commission outlined measures it would take to address these issues, such as improving the accessibility, quality and sustainability of the healthcare systems of the ORs through the European Social Fund Plus and the European Regional Development Fund, and addressing the ORs’ specific vulnerabilities in the work programmes of the Commission’s Health Emergency Preparedness and Response Authority. In view of the forthcoming renewed strategy for the ORs, could the Commission clarify the following: 1.
How does it assess the implementation and results of health-related measures announced in the 2022 strategy?
How does it assess current access to healthcare, medical capacity and availability of medicine in the ORs?
Will the forthcoming strategy include further measures to support the healthcare systems of the ORs?

(15 July 2026) The Commission remains fully committed to supporting the outermost regions (ORs), including in the area of health. The assessment of the implementation of the 2022 strategy for the ORs is presented in the Commission Staff Working Document published in October 2024 (1). This assessment takes stock of progress made across the strategy’s priorities, including actions relevant to health, and confirms the continued need for tailored support that addresses the specific challenges of the ORs. The Commission has supported health-related action in the ORs through several EU instruments, including cohesion policy funds, EU4Health (2) and Horizon Europe (3). Support at EU levelcomplements Member States’ efforts to render health systems more resilient and accessible and to reduce inequalities, while respecting Member States’ primary responsibility for the organisation and delivery of healthcare. These instruments contribute to strengthen resilience, access to care, prevention, workforce capacity and innovation in the ORs. The forthcoming strategy for the ORs will also take into account the specific situation and needs of these regions. It is expected to also address health both as a fundamental need for citizens and as a key policy priority for ensuring the resilience of the outermost regions facing external shocks.

E-10-2026-002260.t: ‘Miracle of tourism’ means gains for corporations and the war economy but cuts and abuses of workers’ rights in the tourism sector
qt: to the Commission Lefteris Nikolaou-Alavanos (NI) Subject:

‘Tourism development’ and the ‘economic miracle’ of the tourism sector are based on the profound exploitation of workers through low wages, intensification of work, exhausting hours, insufficient rest time and the erosion of any labour and insurance rights that remain, with reduced protection for the seasonally unemployed, the writing off of specialisms – such as cooks, maids and pot washers – other than the heavy-duty and unsanitary ones, and the shrinkage of gains such as lump sum payments for hotel employees. An example is the local sectoral collective agreement signed by the Hotel Employees Union and the Rhodes Labour Centre with catering employers, by which they are forcing workers – through a ‘solemn declaration’ that they themselves will sign – to work seven days. Accordingly: 1.

What is the Commission’s position on the fact that while it constantly invokes ‘budgetary restrictions’ with regard to meeting workers’ basic needs, such as supporting the seasonally unemployed, restoring labour and insurance rights and strengthening health and safety measures in the workplace, at the same time it promotes the provocative subsidisation of business groups in the sector and the launch of military spending, allocating billions for armaments programmes in the context of the EU’s war preparations and NATO commitments?

What is the Commission’s position on the promotion and implementation of anti-labour legislation through EU guidelines and directives (2022/2041, 2019/1152, 2019/1158, 2003/88/EC), which have been incorporated into national law over time by all governments and by Nea Dimokratia, leading to further weakening of collective bargaining agreements, the expansion of flexibility with inhumane, exhausting working hours and wage compression?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (18.9.2026) The Commission does not set national wage levels, unemployment benefits or defence budgets. Under the Treaties, these are primarily matters for Member States, while EU social legislation establishes minimum standards and supports social dialogue. The Commission rejects any abuse of workers’ rights. EU law requires Member States to ensure minimum protection on working time1, transparent and predictable working conditions2, work-life balance3, and adequate minimum wage frameworks4, in line with Directive 2003/88/EC, Directive (EU) 2019/1152, Directive (EU) 2019/1158 and Directive (EU) 2022/2041. These instruments are intended to improve workers’ protection, not reduce it. Their application and enforcement, including in tourism and seasonal work, are the responsibility of national authorities, courts and labour inspectorates. Collective agreements must comply with applicable national and EU law. Any national measures or agreements must respect EU rules on daily and weekly rest, maximum working time and fair working conditions. Regarding funding priorities, EU support for tourism or defence is grounded in distinct legal bases and serves different policy objectives decided by the co-legislators. The Commission encourages Member States to use available EU instruments, including the European Social Fund Plus, to support employment, education and skills, and healthy and well-adapted working environments that address health risks, including for seasonal workers.

aspects of the organisation of working time, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2003/88/oj. 2 Directive (EU) 2019/1152 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 20 June 2019 on transparent and predictable working conditions, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2019/1152/oj. 3 Directive (EU) 2019/1158 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 20 June 2019 on work-life balance for parents and carers and repealing Council Directive 2010/18/EU, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2019/1158/oj. 4 Directive (EU) 2022/2041 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 19 October 2022 on adequate minimum wages in the European Union, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2022/2041/oj.

E-10-2026-002258.t: Violence against Greeks and attempted seizure of assets belonging to the Greek ethnic minority in Albania
qt: to the Commission Afroditi Latinopoulou (PfE) Subject:

The recent violent attack on the officially recognised Greek ethnic minority in Zvërnec, Albania – carried out by a private security company, no less – comes on top of a series of serious allegations of criminal and authoritarian practices in Albania. For a number of years, there have been allegations of pressure, contestation and encroachment on the property rights of Greeks in Northern Epirus, and this latest incident raises serious questions about respect for the rule of law and fundamental rights in a candidate country. Bearing in mind that respect for the rule of law, minorities and property is a basic condition for accession to the European Union, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
How does it assess the recurring incidents targeting the Greek ethnic minority in Albania?
Does it consider that the allegations of violations of property rights and intimidation practices are in line with the criteria for EU accession?
Does it consider that discussions on Albania’s accession to the EU can continue if the safety of the Greek ethnic minority is not ensured?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (7.8.2026) The Commission is closely monitoring developments in Albania in the context of its EU accession process. The respect for the rule of law and the protection of fundamental rights, including property rights and the rights of persons belonging to minorities, are at the core of the accession negotiations under Cluster 1 - Fundamentals and they are thoroughly monitored by the Commission to assess Albania’s progress in these areas. Albania is notably expected to ensure due process, effective judicial follow-up, and compliance with the relevant closing benchmarks. The Commission will continue to engage with the Albanian authorities to uphold the highest standards of rule of law and to ensure the protection of fundamental rights. Albania’s progress will be assessed at every step of the accession process.

E-10-2026-002256.t: Revision of the Tobacco Products Directive to address new nicotine products and protect young people
qt: to the Commission Christel Schaldemose (S&D) Subject:

In February 2026, the Nordic Cancer Union (NCU) called for a revision of the Tobacco Products Directive1 (TPD). Their recommendations also reflect concerns raised in the European Parliament, including in its draft report on the implementation of the Europe’s Beating Cancer Plan. The use of new nicotine products among young Europeans has risen in recent years, driven by targeted marketing, including via product design, social media, choice of flavours and packaging. The evaluation of the EU tobacco control framework2 underscores the need to adapt current legislation to new tobacco and nicotine risks. I would like to ask about how the Commission will ensure that the revision moves forward. 1.
How will the Commission take the NCU’s recommendations into account in preparing for the upcoming revision of the TPD?

Given the market development of harmful tobacco and nicotine products, how will the Commission ensure that the Member States will be, under the revised directive, fully able to prohibit certain categories of tobacco, nicotine and related products in order to protect public health, as is currently the case under Article 24(3) of the TPD?

How will the Commission ensure a transparent and timely revision process, and one that is protected from tobacco industry interference, according to its obligations under Article 5(3) of the World Health Organization Framework Convention on Tobacco Control?

Directive 2014/40/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 3 April 2014 on the approximation of the laws, regulations and administrative provisions of the Member States concerning the manufacture, presentation and sale of tobacco and related products and repealing Directive 2001/37/EC (OJ L 127, 29.4.2014, p. 1, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2014/40/oj). 2 https://health.ec.europa.eu/tobacco/evaluation-legislative-framework-tobacco-control_en. 1
at: (English version) to the Commission Christel Schaldemose (S&D) (3 June 2026) Subject: Revision of the Tobacco Products Directive to address new nicotine products and protect young people In February 2026, the Nordic Cancer Union (NCU) called for a revision of the Tobacco Products Directive (1) (TPD). Their recommendations also reflect concerns raised in the European Parliament, including in its draft report on the implementation of the Europe’s Beating Cancer Plan. The use of new nicotine products among young Europeans has risen in recent years, driven by targeted marketing, including via product design, social media, choice of flavours and packaging. The evaluation of the EU tobacco control framework (2) underscores the need to adapt current legislation to new tobacco and nicotine risks. I would like to ask about how the Commission will ensure that the revision moves forward. 1. How will the Commission take the NCU’s recommendations into account in preparing for the upcoming revision of the TPD? 2. Given the market development of harmful tobacco and nicotine products, how will the Commission ensure that the Member States will be, under the revised directive, fully able to prohibit certain categories of tobacco, nicotine and related products in order to protect public health, as is currently the case under Article 24(3) of the TPD? 3. How will the Commission ensure a transparent and timely revision process, and one that is protected from tobacco industry interference, according to its obligations under Article 5(3) of the World Health Organisation Framework Convention on Tobacco Control? (17 July 2026) Following the evaluation of the Tobacco Products Directive and Tobacco Advertising Directive (1), the Commission is conducting an impact assessment and consultation activities, in full compliance with the Better Regulation framework. For example, a call for evidence on the revision of the EU tobacco control rules was published on 18 May 2026 (2) and a public consultation (3) on 22 May 2026, enabling citizens and stakeholders to share their views. All feedback received will be considered when assessing future policy options. The Commission intends to propose by the end of 2026 a revision of the legislative framework on tobacco control (4). The revision process is carried out in full compliance with Article 5.3 of the World Health Organisation Framework Convention on Tobacco Control (5). E-10-2026-002253.t: Review of the Emissions Trading System – integration of municipal waste-to-energy units
qt: to the Commission Grégory Allione (Renew) Subject:
Review of the Emissions Trading System – integration of municipal waste-toenergy units

The Commission will present its review of the Emissions Trading System (ETS) this summer. The possible integration of municipal waste-to-energy (WtE) units raises questions about the coherence of environmental and energy policies, and the risks of economic distortions. WtE units supply heating networks with locally recovered energy. Around 80 % of their fossil emissions come from non-recyclable plastics, the reduction of which falls under the circular economy. Unlike other ETS sectors, operators have no control over the composition or volume of waste and they lack reduction levers such as fuel substitution. The Circular Economy Act, expected in September, must address these challenges. Legislation to reduce non-recyclable plastics will only enter into force in 2035. 1.

How can coherence be ensured between the ETS and the Circular Economy Act to avoid conflicting price signals and pass the carbon price signal on to producers of nonrecyclable plastics, in line with the polluter pays principle?
Has the Commission assessed the impact on energy security and the risks of distortion of competition between Member States?
How can we prevent a shift towards landfill, given that the EU aims to bury less than 10 % of municipal waste by 2035?
at: (English version) to the Commission Grégory Allione (Renew) (3 June 2026) Subject: Review of the Emissions Trading System — integration of municipal waste-to-energy units The Commission will present its review of the Emissions Trading System (ETS) this summer. The possible integration of municipal waste-to-energy (WtE) units raises questions about the coherence of environmental and energy policies, and the risks of economic distortions. WtE units supply heating networks with locally recovered energy. Around 80% of their fossil emissions come from nonrecyclable plastics, the reduction of which falls under the circular economy. Unlike other ETS sectors, operators have no control over the composition or volume of waste and they lack reduction levers such as fuel substitution. The Circular Economy Act, expected in September, must address these challenges. Legislation to reduce non-recyclable plastics will only enter into force in 2035. 1. How can coherence be ensured between the ETS and the Circular Economy Act to avoid conflicting price signals and pass the carbon price signal on to producers of non-recyclable plastics, in line with the polluter pays principle? 2. Has the Commission assessed the impact on energy security and the risks of distortion of competition between Member States? 3.
How can we prevent a shift towards landfill, given that the EU aims to bury less than 10% of municipal waste by 2035?

(31 August 2026) The Competitiveness Compass (1) and Clean Industrial Deal (2) aim to accelerate decarbonisation and circularity to increase economic security, resilience and competitiveness. In the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) review and Circular Economy Act, the Commission assesses the framework to support those objectives. The ETS review proposes integrating municipal waste incineration into the ETS, as well as measures to promote circular carbon capture and utilisation (CCU) (3), encouraging circular use of carbon in products and incentivising improved sorting of municipal waste. The Commission is assessing how to incentivise and support circularity and decarbonisation across the waste value chain, ensuring a coherent approach between the ETS and the Circular Economy Act, including by strengthening upstream eco-design requirements and Extended Producer Responsibility. The assessment considers all appropriate, feasible and effective mechanisms to promote convergence and reinforce the achievement of the Landfill Directive (4) targets, while avoiding unintended consequences contradicting the waste hierarchy. This could include stronger regulatory and fiscal policies, economic incentives and improved measuring of landfill emissions. Waste-to-energy provides around 1.5% of EU electricity generation and 10% of district heating, contributing to energy independence, resilience and reducing fossil fuel use, while emitting about 40 megatonnes of fossil carbon dioxide equivalent greenhouse gas emissions. The impact assessment considers how to contribute to a level playing field in the energy sector through a harmonised economic incentive, avoiding competitive distortion and accelerating the roll-out of clean and affordable energy.

at: (English version) to the Commission Nikolaos Anadiotis (NI) (2 June 2026) Subject: Increase in new cancer diagnoses in Greece (2020-2024) The available data from international and national bodies (ECIS, OECD, GLOBOCAN, Hellenic Cancer Federation) show that new cancer diagnoses in Greece have increased from 62 000 in 2020 to 68 000 in 2024 (1), (2), (3). At the same time, the international literature includes numerous studies reporting an association of COVID-19 mRNA vaccines with various forms of cancer and blood malignancies, a fact that is extremely worrying (4), (5). This trend clearly burdens the National Health System and creates significant challenges for prevention, diagnosis and treatment. In view of the above: 1.
Is the Commission aware of these aforementioned studies and, if so, what does it intend to do?
If the Commission is not aware, does it intend to request an investigation into a possible causal association with COVID19 vaccines?

(17 July 2026) The Commission wishes to note that European Cancer Information System (ECIS) data is provided by population-based cancer registries and at present, Greece does not have a functioning cancer registry able to provide national incidence data to ECIS (1). Incidence figures currently available are model-based estimates, rather than directly measured data. Such estimates are calculated separately for a given reference year and do not allow for comparisons over time. Consequently, differences between estimates published in successive releases may reflect methodological updates or changes in data availability and completeness, rather than true changes in cancer incidence. It should also be noted that for Greece the most recent incidence estimates in ECIS report 62 234 new cancer cases estimated for 2024 (2). Regarding concerns linked to COVID-19 vaccines, the Commission relies on the European Medicines Agency (EMA) for continuous monitoring and supervision on the safety of medicines and vaccines authorised in the EU (3). To date, EMA has not established any causal association between COVID-19 vaccines and an increase in cancer incidence. T he Commission refers the Honourable Member to the answer to Parliamentary Question E-002078/2025 (4) for more detailed information.

E-10-2026-002250.t: Drift towards authoritarianism and breaches of the rule of law in the Plurinational State of Bolivia
qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Anthony Smith (The Left), Emma Fourreau (The Left), Marina Mesure (The Left) Subject:

For over three weeks, the Bolivian people have mobilised to defend their purchasing power and their sovereignty over the conditions for the exploitation of the country’s raw materials. US multinationals, supported by the Trump administration, are seeking to take the profits of those raw materials for themselves. The repressive will of President Rodrigo Paz, who has been in power for several months, can be seen in the images reaching us. With the arrest warrant issued by the Bolivian Public Prosecutor’s Office against Mario Argollo Mamani, executive secretary of the main trade union, as well as against six other leaders, including Justino Apaza Callisaya, leader of the Federation of Neighbourhood Councils of La Paz, we cannot but be concerned about how the Bolivian President is drifting towards authoritarianism and breaching the rule of law. Will the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy therefore: 1.
condemn the Bolivian Government’s crackdown on the demonstrations, as well as the Bolivian President’s drift towards authoritarianism in his actions against those responsible for the social protest?

reaffirm the people’s right to self-determination by condemning the United States’ interference in the country, as well as in the region more generally, as it seeks to grab the natural resources of South American countries?

reaffirm the people’s right to self-determination by condemning the United States’ interference in the country, as well as in the region more generally, as it seeks to grab the natural resources of South American countries?

(22 July 2026) Eight months ago, Bolivia held exemplary, peaceful, and serene general elections, as witnessed by the Electoral Observation Mission deployed by the EU, resulting in a clear victory of their President. The EU has been following the recent social conflict and blockades closely and it deplores the loss of life and injuries. Bolivia’s social conflict can only be resolved through peaceful dialogue, within the framework of respect for democracy, constitutional order, and the institutions of the state. The EU notes that the government has consistently called for dialogue, a call so far rejected by some of the protesting sectors. To give dialogue a chance, the government has moreover refrained from calling a state of emergency, despite pressures from many parts. Demonstrations and protests must be conducted peacefully. The EU calls on all parties to act with responsibility and restraint, avoiding all forms of violence, incitement to confrontation, or actions that could deepen polarisation and increase the suffering of the population, and ensuring respect for the rule of law and human rights, including the freedoms of expression and association. At the same time, it highlights the need to guarantee the population’s access to essential services, medical care, food, fuel, and other indispensable goods. As regards Bolivia's raw materials, the EU’s position is that this sector should be developed through a sustainable, transparent, and mutually beneficial partnership that creates value inside Bolivia. The EU aims to support investment, technology transfer, local processing, environmental standards, and job creation as part of Bolivia's economic development, particularly in sectors such as lithium and other strategic minerals.

E-10-2026-002248.t: Possible conflict of interest in EU-funded public contracts in Valencia City Council
qt: to the Commission Vicent Marzà Ibáñez (Verts/ALE) Subject:

The Autonomous Community of Valencia’s Agency for the Prevention and Fight against Fraud and Corruption has found that the Valencia city councillor in charge of contracting, José Marí Olano, had signed incorrect declarations of no conflict of interest in tendering procedures partially funded by the European Union. The councillor himself has acknowledged in his statements that he did not abstain when appropriate in at least three procedures involving EU funding. The anti-fraud agency has forwarded its findings to Spain’s National Anti-Fraud Coordination Service (SNCA), a body that works directly with the European AntiFraud Office (OLAF). In view of the above: 1.
Is the Commission aware of the above facts and of the Valencian anti-fraud agency’s decision, and has it received any communication from the SNCA or OLAF in relation to the contracts in question?

What action can the Commission take to ensure that the EU funds allocated to those contracts have been managed in accordance with Regulation (EU) 2018/1046 and the principle of sound financial management?
Should any irregularities be confirmed, does the Commission intend to launch a procedure to recover the funds?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.8.2026) The European anti-fraud office (OLAF) is not in a position to provide details regarding cases which it may or may not be treating. This is in order to protect the confidentiality of any possible investigations and of possible ensuing judicial proceedings, as well as to ensure respect for personal data and procedural rights. In the context of OLAF administrative investigations, where fraud or irregularities are detected, OLAF sends recommendations to the competent Commission Services for their appropriate follow-up. These recommendations may require financial, judicial, administrative or disciplinary follow-up. In case of financial recommendations, Commission Services may recover, suspend of offset the relevant EU funding, according to the relevant provisions of the Financial Regulation.

E-10-2026-002247.t: Waste management of lead gunshot in outdoor shooting ranges
qt: to the Commission Vicent Marzà Ibáñez (Verts/ALE) Subject:

Lead is classified as a hazardous substance under the CLP Regulation. Its systematic dumping in outdoor shooting ranges without certified periodic collection constitutes an uncontrolled dispersal of hazardous waste that is potentially incompatible with the Waste Framework Directive (2008/98/EC), with documented effects on agricultural land, wildlife and aquifers. The ECHA has issued scientific opinions in favour of restricting lead in outdoor ammunition under the REACH Regulation, pending a decision by the Commission. At the same time, the Environmental Liability Directive (2004/35/EC) requires operators responsible for environmental damage to bear the costs of remediation, an obligation which, in practice, is rarely applied to this type of pollution. In view of the above: 1.
What is the current status of the decision regarding the REACH restriction on lead in outdoor ammunition?
Does the Commission have mechanisms in place to verify compliance with the Waste Directive by shooting range operators?
Does the future Soil Directive contain specific provisions on the remediation of agricultural land contaminated by this type of activity?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.8.2026) The proposal to restrict lead in gunshot under the Regulation on Registration, Evaluation, Authorisation and Restriction of Chemicals (REACH)1 was supported by a qualified majority of Member States in the REACH Committee on 25 June 2026. It has been transmitted to the European Parliament and the Council for a 3-month scrutiny. If no objections are raised, the proposal can then be adopted. Discarded lead ammunition may be considered waste to the extent it fulfils the definition of waste laid down in the EU waste legislation. Classification of such waste is subject to the provisions of Annex III to the Waste Framework Directive2 and Commission Decision 2000/532/EC3 (establishing a List of Waste, LoW). It is up to the Member States how to apply and monitor the application of the LoW. Under Article 14.1 of the Soil Monitoring Law4 Member States should systematically identify potentially contaminated sites and establish a list of potentially contaminating activities, which may include shooting ranges. Member States should ensure that those sites are investigated and that, in case of unacceptable risks, the appropriate risk reduction measures are taken. Articles 6 to 11 of the Soil Monitoring Law also require Member States to monitor and assess diffuse soil contamination by heavy metals, like lead, set sustainable targets and operational trigger values, and provide support to improve soil health and resilience.
1 Regulation (EC) No 1907/2006 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 18 December 2006

concerning the Registration, Evaluation, Authorisation and Restriction of Chemicals, OJ L 396 30.12.2006, p. 1. 2 Directive 2008/98/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 19 November 2008 on waste and repealing certain Directives, OJ L 312, 22.11.2008, p. 3–30, as amended by Directive (EU) 2018/851 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 30 May, OJ L 150, 14.6.2018, p. 109–140 and Directive (EU) 2025/1892 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 10 September 2025, OJ L, 2025/1892, 26.9.2025. 3 Commission Decision of 3 May 2000 replacing Decision 94/3/EC establishing a list of wastes pursuant to Article 1(a) of Council Directive 75/442/EEC on waste and Council Decision 94/904/EC establishing a list of hazardous waste pursuant to Article 1(4) of Council Directive 91/689/EEC on hazardous waste (notified under document number C(2000) 1147), OJ L 226, 6.9.2000, pp. 3–24. 4 Directive (EU) 2025/2360 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 12 November 2025 on soil monitoring and resilience (Soil Monitoring Law), OJ L, 2025/2360, 26.11.2025.

E-10-2026-002246.t: Absence of a cumulative impact assessment on European Mediterranean citrus farming
qt: to the Commission Vicent Marzà Ibáñez (Verts/ALE) Subject:

The European citrus sector is having to contend simultaneously with the EU-SADC Agreement with South Africa, the EU-Egypt Agreement and the new EU-Mercosur Agreement. Analysing each of them in isolation obscures the real impact on Mediterranean producers. Citrus imports from South Africa to the EU amounted to approximately 794 500 tonnes per year between 2020 and 2024, and 954 490 tonnes between January and October 2025, coinciding with the most critical months of the European season. Mercosur liberalisation will now push the volume up even further. In light of the above: 1.
Does the Commission have an assessment quantifying the cumulative impact of existing trade agreements on Mediterranean citrus farming?
If not, when does it plan to draw up such an assessment?
What early warning mechanisms will be activated if import volumes reach market disruption levels?
at: (English version) to the Commission Vicent Marzà Ibáñez (Verts/ALE) (2 June 2026) Subject: Absence of a cumulative impact assessment on European Mediterranean citrus farming The European citrus sector is having to contend simultaneously with the EU-SADC Agreement with South Africa, the EUEgypt Agreement and the new EU-Mercosur Agreement. Analysing each of them in isolation obscures the real impact on Mediterranean producers. Citrus imports from South Africa to the EU amounted to approximately 794 500 tonnes per year between 2020 and 2024, and 954 490 tonnes between January and October 2025, coinciding with the most critical months of the European season. Mercosur liberalisation will now push the volume up even further. In light of the above: 1.
Does the Commission have an assessment quantifying the cumulative impact of existing trade agreements on Mediterranean citrus farming?
If not, when does it plan to draw up such an assessment?
What early warning mechanisms will be activated if import volumes reach market disruption levels?

(27 July 2026) The Commission conducts sustainability impact assessments (1) when updating or concluding new free trade agreements. In addition, it makes available cumulative studies on the economic impact of such agreements on agricultur e (2) including the fruit and vegetables sector. In this context, the Commission adopts a holistic and balanced approach across all sectors. With regard to imports, it pays particular attention to sensitive agricultural products by excluding them from liberalisation or granting only partial liberalisation, including through carefully calibrated tariff rate quotas. The trade agreements concluded by the EU generally include bilateral safeguard clauses, which allow appropriate measures to be taken if imports cause or threaten to cause serious injury to EU producers. In addition, where the legal conditions are fulfilled, the Union may make use of trade defence instruments, as well as safeguard measures, as provided for under applicable agreements and World Trade Organisation rules (3). However, no such concerns have been identified for citrus at this stage. The Commission closely monitors the EU citrus market on the basis of trade and production data, including through the Citrus Market Observatory.

E-10-2026-002244.t: Impact of the EU-Mercosur Interim Agreement on the European citrus processing industry
qt: to the Commission Vicent Marzà Ibáñez (Verts/ALE) Subject:

Brazil is structurally dominant in the European juice market, with average annual imports of around 900 000 tonnes and peaks which, in years such as 2023, exceed one million tonnes. From 1 May 2026, the EU-Mercosur Interim Agreement will phase out the 12.20% tariff on Brazilian juice without any quotas or specific safeguards. The European processing industry accounts for around 20% of citrus production, acts as a mechanism for regulating the fresh produce market, and supports employment and economic activity in producing regions. Downward pressure on juice prices could leave hundreds of thousands of tonnes of Mediterranean citrus fruit with nowhere to go each season. In light of the above: 1.
Why has Brazilian orange juice not been classified as a sensitive product in the agreement, despite Brazil accounting for 80% of global production?
Does the Commission intend to introduce automatic safeguard mechanisms that can be activated in the event of a disruption to the European juice market?
at: (English version) to the Commission Vicent Marzà Ibáñez (Verts/ALE) (2 June 2026) Subject: Impact of the EU-Mercosur Interim Agreement on the European citrus processing industry Brazil is structurally dominant in the European juice market, with average annual imports of around 900 000 tonnes and peaks which, in years such as 2023, exceed one million tonnes. From 1 May 2026, the EU-Mercosur Interim Agreement will phase out the 12.20% tariff on Brazilian juice without any quotas or specific safeguards. The European processing industry accounts for around 20% of citrus production, acts as a mechanism for regulating the fresh produce market, and supports employment and economic activity in producing regions. Downward pressure on juice prices could leave hundreds of thousands of tonnes of Mediterranean citrus fruit with nowhere to go each season. In light of the above: 1.
Why has Brazilian orange juice not been classified as a sensitive product in the agreement, despite Brazil accounting for 80% of global production?
Does the Commission intend to introduce automatic safeguard mechanisms that can be activated in the event of a disruption to the European juice market?

(9 July 2026) 1. The classification of products as sensitive in trade negotiations is based on a balanced assessment including overall economic impacts and reciprocal market access objectives. Brazil’s situation as a main global supplier of juice was taken into consideration, but this alone did not justify treating juice as a product subject to other specific measures. Under the EUMercosur Interim Trade Agreement, imports to the EU of citrus juice products are generally subject to tariff reductions phased in over seven to 10 years while for certain products the reduction of both the ad valorem tariff and the specific duty is limited to a maximum of 50%. The Commission continues to monitor the EU juice market through trade and production data and the annual Citrus Market Observatory. EU imports of juice from Brazil have decreased from around 1.3 million tonnes in 2020 to 600,000 tonnes in 2025. 2. According to Article 4 of Regulation (EU) 2026/687 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 11 March 2026 implementing the bilateral safeguard clauses of the EU-Mercosur Partnership Agreement and the EU-Mercosur Interim Trade Agreement for agricultural products (1), the Commission shall constantly and proactively monitor the Union market of sensitive products listed in Annex I to the regulation, in particular as regards import and export trends, production and price developments. Upon a duly justified request by the Union industry concerned, the Commission may extend the scope of the monitoring to any products other than those referred to in the annex.

qt: to the Commission Nikola Minchev (Renew), Dimitris Tsiodras (PPE), Dan Barna (Renew), Veronika Cifrová Ostrihoňová (Renew), Malika Sorel (NI), Hristo Petrov (Renew), Radan Kanev (PPE), Bogdan Andrzej Zdrojewski (PPE), Elena Kountoura (The Left), Tomáš Kubín (PfE) Subject:

With rapid advancements in technology and AI, the tools available to malicious actors to commit fraud and mislead consumers have increased. One clear example is streaming fraud, where fake ‘plays’ of tracks on music-streaming platforms are artificially generated to inflate perceived popularity. These practices divert royalties away from legitimate artists and other contributors to the music economy, and undermine consumer trust in digital services. Streaming fraud can amount to breaches of consumer protection and unfair competition law, and to computer-misuse offences, and may in some cases also be linked to other serious crimes such as money laundering. The Digital Services Act1 (DSA) addresses the risks posed by illegal content online by imposing obligations on intermediaries and online platforms, including very large online platforms (VLOPs) and very large online search engines (VLOSEs), to identify, analyse and mitigate risks related to illegal content, including streaming fraud. In this context: 1.
How is the Commission ensuring that VLOSEs are effectively implementing their obligations under the DSA to prevent their services from being used to support streaming fraud?
Does the Commission consider current measures sufficient, or does it envisage further actions to tackle the problem?

Does the Commission consider current measures sufficient, or does it envisage further actions to tackle the problem?

(31 July 2026) The Digital Services Act (DSA) (1) addresses risks arising from the design, functioning and use of online intermediary services. Practices such as the artificial inflation of streaming or play counts are best understood as a form of manipulation of the service through inauthentic use or automated exploitation; they may also breach providers’ terms of service. The Commission notes that the DSA only covers streaming in respect of those parts that involve storing and making available content uploaded by its users. Providers of designated Very Large Online Platforms (VLOPs) and Very Large Online Search Engines (VLOSEs) must, under Articles 34 and 35 DSA, identify, assess and mitigate the systemic risks stemming from their services. The risk assessment must expressly examine how those risks are influenced by intentional manipulation of the service, including through inauthentic use or automated exploitation, and providers must adopt reasonable and effective mitigation measures. The use of automated tools or AI to generate deceptive activity falls within that exercise. In addition, where such practices are illegal, hosting providers must under Article 16 DSA enable any user to notify them and handle such notices in a timely and diligent manner. As a rule, the Commission does not comment on potential or ongoing proceedings. It stands ready to draw on the full range of its supervisory and enforcement powers, complemented where relevant by the EU consumer protection rules, to address evolving forms of online fraud.

E-10-2026-002242.t: Post-2027 future of EU defence innovation instrument AGILE
qt: to the Commission Engin Eroglu (Renew) Subject:

The Commission’s proposal to set up an instrument for agile and rapid defence innovation (the ‘AGILE’ programme) is an important step in fast-tracking civil and dual-use technologies into defence applications and bolstering the EU’s defence innovation ecosystem. In light of Russia’s continued war of aggression against Ukraine, the urgent need to scale up Europe’s defence industrial capabilities and intensifying technological competition, the rapid operational deployment of disruptive technologies is crucial for Europe’s security and technological sovereignty. At the same time, the proposal currently contains very few provisions on the future of the instrument beyond 2027. Notably absent are a review clause, reporting requirements, a requirement to design a follow‑up instrument and indications as to how successful AGILE mechanisms are to be integrated into future defence instruments. 1.
How does the Commission plan to assess the strategic impact of AGILE, particularly with regard to strengthening the EU’s defence innovation ecosystem?
Does the Commission intend to set up a formal review mechanism or a roadmap to continue or extend AGILE beyond 2027?
How are the lessons learned from AGILE to be taken into account in future EU defence instruments such as the EDF, EUDIS or successor programmes?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (7.8.2026) The proposal for a Regulation establishing the Programme for Agile and Rapid Defence Innovation (AGILE)1 includes clear reporting obligations in line with the Commission’s Better Regulation2 requirements. The explanatory memorandum and the legislative financial and digital statement accompanying the proposal provides for an implementation report and sets out several performance indicators which will support the assessment of AGILE’s results. The Commission recalls that the AGILE programme is designed to be implemented within the current Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF)3. As such, the proposal cannot contain provisions concerning the future of the instrument beyond 2027, which would prejudge discussions in the context of the next MFF. At the same time, the Commission has sought to ensure a legal framework in its proposal for the future European Competitiveness Fund4 that includes a dedicated policy window on ‘Resilience and Security, Defence Industry, and Space’, encompassing activities in support of defence innovation. This would ensure the AGILE-type actions can be supported and potentially scaled up, provided this framework is endorsed by co-legislators, who are currently negotiating the text. The lessons learnt from AGILE will be considered through the above-mentioned implementation, reporting and broader policy preparation work. This will allow the Commission to identify the most effective mechanisms to support defence innovation, informing the implementation of EU defence instruments, including the European Defence Fund5 and the EU Defence Innovation Scheme6, and the design and implementation of possible successor programmes.
1 https://defence-industry-space.ec.europa.eu/eu-defence-industry/programme-agile-and-rapid-defence-

innovation_en. 2 https://commission.europa.eu/law/law-making-process/better-regulation_en. 3 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/EN/legal-content/summary/eu-multiannual-financial-framework-2021-2027.html. 4 https://single-market-economy.ec.europa.eu/access-finance/european-competitiveness-fund_en. 5 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2021/697/oj/eng. 6 https://eudis.europa.eu/index_en.

E-10-2026-002241.t: mRNA COVID-19 vaccines in Europe: transparency in batch testing and adverse reaction reports
qt: to the Commission Gerald Hauser (PfE) Subject:
mRNA COVID-19 vaccines in Europe: transparency in batch testing and adverse reaction reports

Several reports suggest considerable variation in adverse reactions to individual batches of mRNA vaccines. Here are two examples: Schmeling, Manniche and Hansen (2023), ‘Batch-dependent safety of the BNT162b2 mRNA COVID-19 vaccine’, Journal: European Journal of Clinical Investigation1. The authors analysed Danish reporting data on Pfizer/BioNTech (BNT162b2) and found that the number of suspected cases of adverse events varied considerably between batches. They described clusters of batches with different rates of reporting and identified these as a ‘batch‑dependent safety signal’. The authors called for further study on the matter. – Manniche et al. (2024), ‘Reports of Batch-Dependent Suspected Adverse Events of the BNT162b2 mRNA COVID-19 Vaccine: Comparison of Results from Denmark and Sweden’, Journal: Medicines2. This study compared suspected cases in Denmark and Sweden. The authors reported that similar patterns of variation between batches had been observed in both countries. They stressed that the results were preliminary and hypothesis-generating. 1.
Does the Commission know what independent assessments have been carried out on individual batches of mRNA vaccines, and what conclusion was drawn?
Does the Commission know what variation has been observed between batches of mRNA vaccines in quality controls, and is there also variation between EU Member States?
Has the Commission launched investigations into published observations regarding variations in adverse reaction reports between batches?
https://research.regionh.dk/en/publications/batch-dependent-safety-of-the-bnt162b2-mrna-covid-19-
vaccine/. 2
https://research.regionh.dk/en/publications/reports-of-batch-dependent-suspected-adverse-events-of-the-
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.7.2026) Once a COVID-19 vaccine has received approval, each batch can only be released following quality control testing to confirm that the product is in line with the specifications approved as part of the marketing authorisation. For most centrally authorised vaccines, an additional independent control is performed by a Member State Official Medicines Control Laboratory before their release in the EU. The Commission also refers the Honourable Member to the reply to parliamentary question (PQ) E-001537/20231, where this point was addressed. Only batches complying with the approved quality specifications can be released. The Commission does not hold comparative batch-level quality control data by Member State. However, the European Medicines Agency (EMA) has no evidence suggesting that some batches of COVID-19 vaccines caused more, or more serious, side effects than other batches. For Comirnaty, this was already indicated in the reply to PQ P-002990/20242. Furthermore, pharmacovigilance systems are in place to monitor the suspected adverse reactions and detect safety issues potentially related to quality. The EMA and national authorities continuously monitor safety, including EudraVigilance reports, medical literature and product quality issue detection tools3. Analyses performed by the EMA of suspected cases of adverse reactions did not reveal an increased risk of side effects for specific batches. This was also indicated in the answer to PQ E-001537/2023.

The latest edition of ISS World Europe1, a trade fair on intelligence support systems for electronic surveillance, is taking place in Prague from 2 to 4 June 2026. The main sponsor of the event is NSO Group, developer of the Pegasus spyware, which has been used to unlawfully target journalists, activists, opposition politicians and others in several EU Member States. Among the other sponsors and exhibitors are companies linked to the unlawful use of surveillance technologies in various countries around the world. The fair is reportedly being attended by representatives of several EU governments. 1.
Will representatives of the Commission, or of any of its agencies or bodies, attend the ISS World Europe fair in June 2026?
Can the Commission confirm whether any such representatives have attended previous editions of ISS World Europe, and if so, in what capacity and with what outcome?

What internal guidelines, transparency requirements or safeguards govern participation by EU representatives in events involving companies active in the cyber-surveillance and dual-use technology sectors?
Supporter2
https://www.issworldtraining.com/iss_europe/sponsors.html. This question is supported by a Member other than the authors: Cecilia Strada (S&D).
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (21.9.2026) According to the Commission’s mission’s data, no representatives of the Commission, or its services attended the Intelligence Support Systems (ISS) World Europe Fair in June 2026 in Prague, or any previous editions of the ISS World Europe. Decisions are taken by the relevant Commission department considering the purpose of the event, the objectives of the participation, the expected contribution of Commission representatives, and the applicable administrative and budgetary rules. E-10-2026-002239.t: Application of the Early Detection and Exclusion System to companies active in the cyber-surveillance sector, including those involved in spyware
qt: to the Commission Saskia Bricmont (Verts/ALE), Sandro Ruotolo (S&D), Veronika Cifrová Ostrihoňová (Renew), Krzysztof Brejza (PPE), Mounir Satouri (Verts/ALE), Hilde Vautmans (Renew), Estelle Ceulemans (S&D), Martin Hojsík (Renew), Marie Toussaint (Verts/ALE), Majdouline Sbai (Verts/ALE), Lynn Boylan (The Left), Sara Matthieu (Verts/ALE), Cecilia Strada (S&D), Robert Biedroń (S&D), Thomas Waitz (Verts/ALE), Leoluca Orlando (Verts/ALE), Raquel García Hermida-Van Der Walle (Renew), Damien Carême (The Left), Sebastian Everding (The Left), Leila Chaibi (The Left), Hannah Neumann (Verts/ALE), Brando Benifei (S&D), Erik Marquardt (Verts/ALE), Markéta Gregorová (Verts/ALE), Birgit Sippel (S&D), Diana Riba i Giner (Verts/ALE), Nikolas Farantouris (S&D), Marco Tarquinio (S&D), Pernando Barrena Arza (The Left), Matjaž Nemec (S&D), Chloé Ridel (S&D) Subject:

As acknowledged by the Commission, EU funding instruments, including Horizon Europe and the European Defence Fund, have supported companies active in the cyber-surveillance sector, including those in the spyware technology sector, such as Intellexa, Cognyte and Paragon. The European Parliament’s Committee of Inquiry to investigate the use of Pegasus and equivalent surveillance spyware identified serious concerns regarding the misuse of spyware technologies against journalists, political actors and civil society representatives, raising important questions about compliance with EU values, the protection of fundamental rights and oversight mechanisms. The revised Financial Regulation1 introduced an additional Early Detection and Exclusion System (EDES) ground for exclusion concerning entities involved in activities contrary to EU values. The Commission also stated that grave professional misconduct and serious breaches of fundamental rights may justify exclusion from EU funding programmes. In this context: 1.
Has the Commission assessed whether entities operating in the cyber-surveillance sector, including those involved in spyware, may fall within the scope of the revised EDES provisions?

Does the Commission intend to develop specific guidance or risk-assessment criteria regarding access to EU funding for companies implicated in documented breaches of fundamental rights or violations of EU values?
Has EDES previously been applied in relation to entities operating in the dual-use or cyber-surveillance sectors, and if so, for what categories of cases?

Regulation (EU, Euratom) 2024/2509 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 23 September 2024 on the financial rules applicable to the general budget of the Union (OJ L, 2024/2509, 26.9.2024, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/2509/oj). 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (5.8.2026) 1. The Commission considers that existing mechanisms provide sufficient legal tools to prevent EU funds from being awarded to entities that are involved in activities incompatible with EU values, provided that their involvement in such activities is substantiated by concrete, reliable, and admissible evidence and meets the legal requirements laid down in the Financial Regulation1, and notably the early detection and exclusion system (EDES)2 rules. Where such activities constitute grave professional misconduct under the ground of incitement to discrimination, violence or hatred, or any other activities contrary to EU values, such findings must result from a final judgment. In the absence of such a judgment, the ground of exclusion is applicable on a preliminary classification in law by the EDES Panel referred to in Article 145 of the Financial Regulation. In such cases and based on individualised assessments and following adversarial procedures, exclusion from EU funding is mandatory. 2. Breaches of fundamental rights or EU values are considered at different stages of the application for and implementation of EU financial support. The Commission’s data mining and risk-scoring tool Arachne+3 can support the Member States in risk assessment, but no specific risk indicators can currently assess breaches of fundamental rights or values. 3. The information on whether EDES had previously been applied in relation to entities operating in the dual-use or cyber-surveillance sectors is not available, as there is no existing list indicating the sector in which an entity that has been the subject of an EDES proceeding operates. Similarly, for reasons of confidentiality, the Commission is unable to provide information regarding ongoing Panel cases.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/2509/oj/eng. 2 https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/eu-budget/how-it-works/annual-
lifecycle/implementation/anti-fraud-measures/edes_en. 3 https://antifraud-knowledge-centre.ec.europa.eu/useful-tools/what-arachne_en.

E-10-2026-002238.t: Risks associated with tariff quota management system in EU-Mercosur agreement
qt: to the Commission Christophe Bay (PfE), Daniel Obajtek (ECR), Jadwiga Wiśniewska (ECR), Georgiana Teodorescu (ECR), Jan-Peter Warnke (NI), Mariusz Kamiński (ECR), Julie Rechagneux (PfE), Şerban Dimitrie Sturdza (ECR), Claudiu-Richard Târziu (ECR), Valérie Deloge (PfE), Ivan David (ESN), Séverine Werbrouck (PfE), Marie-Luce Brasier-Clain (PfE), Ewa Zajączkowska-Hernik (PfE), Gilles Pennelle (PfE), Enikő Győri (PfE), Mélanie Disdier (PfE), Dominik Tarczyński (ECR), Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE), Waldemar Buda (ECR), Anne-Sophie Frigout (PfE), Nicolas Bay (ECR), André Rougé (PfE) Subject:

Implementing regulation (EU) 2026/888 of 20 April 2026 lays down the management modes for tariff rate quotas on products originating in Mercosur countries. This arrangement marks a significant change by allowing partner countries to notify the allocation of volumes amongst their operators and, in effect, to intervene in the allocation of quotas. The mechanism is a departure from the principle of tariff quotas being managed entirely by the EU via its export licence system. By making access to quotas contingent on approval from export authorities, it poses a real risk of a partial transfer of control to third countries or private companies. This development raises serious concerns about adherence to the principles of open, transparent and non‑discriminatory access to quotas. It could lead to volumes being concentrated in the hands of a limited number of dominant stakeholders, particularly the Brazilian group JBS, putting EU operators and vulnerable agricultural sectors at a disadvantage. It also sets a precedent that could weaken the EU’s commercial sovereignty in the long term. In view of this: 1.
What action does the Commission intend to take to avoid quotas being monopolised by a limited number of dominant operators in Mercosur countries?
Does it plan to introduce a revision clause for this instrument?
Supporter1
This question is supported by a Member other than the authors: Csaba Dömötör (PfE).
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.7.2026) Import Tariff Rate Quotas (TRQs) established under the EU-Mercosur Interim Trade Agreement (ITA) are administered exclusively by the EU, as laid down in Regulation (EU) 2026/9961. This Regulation introduced in Implementing Regulations (EU) 2020/7612 and (EU) 2020/19883 rules for the management of those import TRQs for agricultural products. In accordance with Article 3.30 of the ITA, ‘products exported under tariff rate quotas granted by the EU shall be accompanied by an official document issued by the Signatory Mercosur States’. Such a document is understood to allow Mercosur Signatory States to verify quota allocation among themselves. The model of this document was published in the Official Journal on 14 April 20264. The Commission will closely monitor imports under TRQs. The agreement also provides for consultation and dispute settlement mechanisms. The Commission, in line with Regulation (EU) 2026/6875 will monitor import flows and price trends and will report regularly to the European Parliament and the Council.
1 Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/996 of 29 April 2026 amending Implementing Regulations

(EU) 2020/761 and (EU) 2020/1988 regarding the creation, amendment and management of certain tariff quotas following the Interim Agreement on Trade between the European Union, of the one part, and the Common Market of the South, the Argentine Republic, the Federative Republic of Brazil, the Republic of Paraguay and the Oriental Republic of Uruguay, of the other part (OJ L, 2026/996, 30.4.2026, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg_impl/2026/996/oj). 2 Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2020/761 of 17 December 2019 laying down rules for the application of Regulations (EU) No 1306/2013, (EU) No 1308/2013 and (EU) No 510/2014 of the European Parliament and of the Council as regards the management system of tariff quotas with licences (OJ L 185, 12.6.2020, pp. 24–252, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg_impl/2020/761/oj). 3 Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2020/1988 of 11 November 2020 laying down rules for the application of Regulations (EU) No 1308/2013 and (EU) No 510/2014 of the European Parliament and of the Council as regards the administration of import tariff quotas in accordance with the ‘first come, first served’ principle (OJ L 422, 14.12.2020, pp. 4–136, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg_impl/2020/1988/oj). 4 Notice of the European Commission[2026/874], ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/notice/2026/874/oj. 5 Regulation (EU) 2026/687 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 11 March 2026 implementing the bilateral safeguard clauses of the EU-Mercosur Partnership Agreement and the EU-Mercosur Interim Trade Agreement for agricultural products; OJ L, 2026/687, 19.3.2026, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2026/687/oj.

E-10-2026-002236.t: Transparency on the financial burden on Member States under the 2028–2034 MFF and Own Resources package
qt: to the Commission Dick Erixon (ECR), Charlie Weimers (ECR), Beatrice Timgren (ECR), Kristoffer Storm (ECR) Subject:

In July 2025, the Commission presented its proposals for the 2028–2034 multiannual financial framework (MFF) and the accompanying decision on own resources1. To date, the Commission has not made publicly available a consolidated breakdown of the estimated financial burden attributable to each Member State, including the revenues needed to repay and service NextGenerationEU and any further EU-level borrowing. 1.

Will the Commission publish a single, consolidated and publicly accessible table showing, per Member State, the estimated total revenues to be collected for the EU budget in 2028-2034 across all own resources, existing and those newly proposed, including the share needed to repay and service NextGenerationEU and any other EU borrowing?

Will the Commission disclose, per Member State, a like-for-like comparison between the total estimated revenues to be collected under the 2028-2034 MFF and the corresponding figures under the 2021-2027 MFF?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (14.7.2026) The Commission does not publish Member State specific tables detailing estimates of total EU budget revenues, including own resources or debt servicing, nor comparative tables between the current (2021-2027)1 and proposed (2028-2034) Multiannual Financial Framework (‘MFF’)2. These data remain confidential, as they are based on preliminary calculations and assumptions that may evolve during the legislative process. The Commission’s proposals for the 2028–2034 MFF and own resources provide aggregate EU-level figures, including in the long-term forecast of future inflows and outflows of the EU budget3.

E-10-2026-002235.t: Reports of the Palestinian Authority’s continuing ‘pay-for-slay’ scheme
qt: to the Commission Bert-Jan Ruissen (ECR), Charlie Weimers (ECR), Dick Erixon (ECR), Beatrice Timgren (ECR), Hildegard Bentele (PPE), Rihards Kols (ECR), Tomáš Kubín (PfE), Alice Teodorescu Måwe (PPE), Antonio López-Istúriz White (PPE) Subject:

On 4 May 2026, a Ramallah Court1 ordered the Palestinian Authority (PA) to resume payments under the ‘pay-for-slay’ scheme – officially known as the Martyrs Fund – to the family of a man held in an Israeli prison. This ruling and reports by Reuters2 and The Jerusalem Post3 raise serious questions as to whether the pay-for-slay scheme has been or will be truly abolished as President Abbas claimed during a Fatah conference, when he said that the PA had restructured its payments to no longer reflect the prisoner’s sentences but to distribute the funds in the form of social welfare. Commissioner Šuica explained in an answer to earlier questions that these social welfare allowances are now based on vulnerability criteria4, as requested by the EU5. 1.

How does the Commission respond to this court ruling and the criticism that the PA reforms only amount to cosmetic restructuring designed to satisfy Western donors while preserving the pay-for-slay-scheme domestically?

Since the Commission emphasised ‘democratic, transparent and efficient governance’ as a condition for EU funding, what benchmarks has the PA actually met so far and can the Commission publish the agreed Reform Matrix and milestones?
Can the Commission confirm that no EU funds are used or will be used to support prisoners, terrorists and/or their families?

https://www.timesofisrael.com/ignoring-pay-for-slay-reform-ramallah-court-tells-pa-to-reinstatemoney-for-prisoner/amp/. 2 https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/abbas-revokes-payment-system-financial-allowancesfamilies-palestinian-prisoners-2025-02-10/. 3 https://www.jpost.com/middle-east/article-896389. 4 ‘The draft constitution under public consultation contains references to caring for the families of inter alia martyrs, the wounded and prisoners to meet their humanitarian needs but does not indicate reinstatement of former schemes. Subject to any revisions following the public consultation, the current provisions do not provide a basis for concluding that the abolished prisoners and martyrs scheme will be reinstated within the future Palestinian constitutional framework.’ (https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/E-10-2026-000887ASW_EN.html#ref2). 5 https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/E-10-2025-002057-ASW_EN.html. 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.9.2026) On 10 February 2025, by Presidential decree 4/20251, the Palestinian Authority (PA) abolished the previous prisoners and martyrs’ payment system and established a new social system based exclusively on socio-economic and vulnerability criteria. An independent and international audit contracted by the PA of the new system is ongoing since January 2026. The EU has also launched its own comprehensive system audit to verify that no parallel payment system is in place. This audit is expected to be completed by the end of 2026. The May 2026 court ruling reported by the Times of Israel concerns an individual case arising from the application of the previous legal framework governing prisoners' entitlements. It does not call into question the overall reform currently being implemented. Most funds disbursed by the EU to the PA are linked to its progress on reforms in the areas of fiscal sustainability, including social protection, good governance, private sector development and the provision of public services. The Reform Matrix is a working document attached to the Financing Agreements with the PA of 2025 and 2026-2027, which is not for public dissemination. The Commission has always excluded financial support to the prisoners and martyrs’ payment system. Part of the EU’s funding contributes to the PA’s social allowances to vulnerable individuals and families, allocated on the basis of socio-economic criteria. All financial support is subject to robust controls and safeguards to ensure that EU funds are used only for their intended purposes. The EU applies a strict vetting process to the beneficiaries of its payments and tracks each financial transfer to vetted individuals.

qt: to the Commission Loucas Fourlas (PPE) Subject:

European citizens are faced with ever-increasing charges for basic banking services and digital transactions, at a time when the cost of living remains particularly high. How does the Commission assess the issue of rising bank and digital fees in the European Union?
Does the Commission intend to promote a stricter European framework for transparency and control of related fees?
What measures are being considered to strengthen consumer protection in digital financial services?

Complaints are being registered in several Member States about excessive bank fees, opaque charges for online transactions, and practices by digital platforms that place a disproportionate burden on consumers. Consumer protection and ensuring fair conditions in the single market are fundamental principles of the European Union. However, the rapid digitalisation of financial services creates new challenges in terms of transparency, competition and the protection of citizens from unfair commercial practices. In view of the above: 1.
How does the Commission assess the issue of rising bank and digital fees in the European Union?
Does the Commission intend to promote a stricter European framework for transparency and control of related fees?
What measures are being considered to strengthen consumer protection in digital financial services?

(31 July 2026) The Commission follows closely the developments in the EU banking sector, including on fees and transparency. EU legislation regulates transparency of fees and charges but does not prescribe their level. With regard to transparency, payment service providers are required to present fees for payment accounts in a clear, standardised and comparable manner (1) and to provide information on charges, interest and exchange rates relating to payment transactions (2). The forthcoming Payment Services Regulation (3) will introduce additional transparency on charges applicable to currency conversion, including for domestic ATM withdrawals. Creditors are also required to provide clear information on all costs, charges and the total cost of credit before consumers enter into an agreement (4). Furthermore, EU legislation requires banks to propose payment accounts with basic features to be offered free of charge or for a reasonable fee only (5). It also requires fees for euro instant credit transfers to not be higher than fees for euro regular credit transfer s (6) and, in the area of consumer credits, requires Member States to introduce measures against excessively high borrowing rates, annual percentage rates of charge or total costs of credit, such as caps (7).
