E-10-2026-002203.t: Continuation of support measures for the wine sector after 2027
qt: to the Commission Emmanouil Kefalogiannis (PPE) Subject:

The recent ‘wine package’ constitutes a substantial step towards strengthening and adapting the sector for new circumstances. However, there are legitimate concerns that a possible delay in the adoption of the new Multiannual Financial Framework 2028-2034 could cause a gap in funding and in the continuation of support measures from 2028 onwards. For this reason, the European Parliament supports the need for transitional arrangements to be adopted promptly in order to ensure the seamless continuation of existing support programmes for the wine sector until the new framework is fully implemented. In view of the above: 1.

Does the Commission intend to proceed in a timely manner with the adoption of transitional arrangements to ensure the uninterrupted continuation of support programmes for the wine sector after 2027 and until the full implementation of the new Multiannual Financial Framework?
What initiatives does the Commission intend to take to maintain specific funding for the wine sector in the new financial framework?

How does the Commission intend to strengthen actions relating to climate adaptation, innovation and the sustainability of European wine production in order to ensure the competitiveness of producers and in particular small and medium-sized agricultural holdings in rural areas?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (7.8.2026) 1. As regards wine sectoral interventions implemented via the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) Plans under Regulation (EU) 2021/21151, where part of their implementation is expected to take place after 2027, the National and Regional Partnership (NRP) proposal ensures that expenditure related to legal commitments that continue to be implemented after 2027 remain eligible under the NRP Plans provided that such ongoing interventions are reprogrammed under the NRP Plans in accordance with Article 21(3) of the NRP proposal2. Article 35(10) of the NRP proposal sets out that sectoral interventions fully implemented under the CAP Plans before the end of 2027, but for which payments remain outstanding, can be financed from Member States’ CAP ringfenced allocations for financial year 2028 under the new multiannual financial framework as part of the legacy payments. Ensuring continuation of payments in an orderly and timely manner is a priority for the Commission. Discussions on further arrangements for a smooth transition are ongoing with the co-legislators, particularly in light of the Council’s recent Partial General Approach, while awaiting the Parliament’s position on this issue. 2. Wine sectoral interventions can be financed within the ring-fenced amount of EUR 293.7 billion. Member States have full flexibility to allocate funds to the wine sector from this amount. In addition, Member States can complement this amount from the unallocated part of the NRP Plan budget to design the CAP approach that corresponds to the needs of the wine sector. 3. Wine sectoral interventions linked to research and innovation or environment and climate may benefit, if decided by the Member States, from a maximum support rate of up to 95% of the total eligible cost of the intervention concerned, which is higher than the general support rate of maximum 75%.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2021/2115/oj/eng. 2 Article 21(3) of the Proposal; Article 35a(1) added by the Council in the Partial General Approach - https://eur-
lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52025PC0565R(01).

E-10-2026-002202.t: Encroachment on land and properties of the Greek ethnic minority in Zvërnec, Vlora Region, Albania
qt: to the Commission Fredis Beleris (PPE) Subject:

In the village of Zvërnec, Vlora Region, which is primarily inhabited by members of the Greek ethnic minority, it is alleged that a private company is intervening and encroaching on land and properties that were illegally seized by the communist regime in the 1960s and have not yet been returned to their rightful owners. At the same time, during peaceful protests by residents about the injustice they have suffered, incidents of violence and intimidation by individuals allegedly associated with the company were recorded, even in the presence of police forces. These incidents raise serious questions regarding respect for fundamental freedoms, property rights and the protection of recognised national minorities in a country that is a candidate for accession to the European Union. In view of this: 1.

Is the Commission aware of the allegations of violence and intimidation against residents of Zvërnec during peaceful protests and does it intend to seek clarification from the Albanian authorities on the safeguarding of the right to protest?
What measures is the Commission taking to protect the fundamental rights of recognised ethnic minorities, including their property rights, in the candidate countries?

Given that the Commission is in contact with the Albanian competent authorities, how does it ensure the objectivity of the findings of the Interim Benchmark Assessment Report (IBAR) and annual reports of the Commission?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (18.8.2026) The Commission is closely following developments in Albania and it is aware of the protests referred to by Honourable Member. The Commission also notes that the protests have been largely peaceful. Freedom of assembly and expression are fundamental rights and core European values and should be respected. The Commission monitors closely fulfilment of such fundamentals rights and values, and it is in continuous contact with the Albanian authorities and civil society. In the context of the accession process, the Commission monitors and reports also on property rights and on the rights of persons belonging to minorities in its annual report on Albania. The annual report 2026 is currently being drafted and will reflect the Commission’s assessment of Albania’s progress in these areas since 2025. All documents drafted by the Commission, including the Interim Benchmark Assessment Report, the Interim EU Common Position and the annual reports, follow a precise methodology which requires the very regular consultation of a wide variety of interlocutors other than the Albanian authorities. The insights of international organisations, civil society organisations, independent agencies, monitoring bodies and experts are taken in due consideration when making assessments of Albania’s progress.

E-10-2026-002201.t: European framework for health risks to firefighters and funding for the modernisation of personal protective equipment across Europe
qt: to the Commission Fredis Beleris (PPE) Subject:

Firefighters in all EU Member States – especially in urban and industrial areas – are exposed daily to extremely high occupational risks, such as toxic fumes, carcinogens, asbestos, chemicals from burning materials and extreme temperatures in forest fires, with prolonged physical exhaustion. The World Health Organization (WHO), through the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), which is the competent body for classifying carcinogens, has ranked the profession of firefighter in Group 1 ‘Carcinogenic to humans’, i.e. the highest category of carcinogens, on the basis of sufficient evidence that occupational exposure as a firefighter causes cancer in humans. The EU Strategic Framework on Health and Safety at Work 2021-2027 and Directive 2004/37/EC set as key objectives the prevention of occupational diseases, the protection of workers from hazardous substances and the adoption of the ‘Vision Zero’ approach to workrelated deaths. On the basis of the above: 1.
Will the Commission provide financial support to national, local and regional authorities for the modernisation of personal protective equipment and the decontamination of equipment and uniforms?
Will the Commission provide funding in the 2028-2034 MFF for the implementation of the upcoming updated Directive 2004/37/EC?
Will the Commission include firefighters and rescue workers in the new EU Strategic Framework on Health and Safety at Work 2028-2034?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.7.2026) The Commission supports, through EU funding instruments, preparedness, prevention and response capacities in Member States. It has also supported financially the stockpiling of critical equipment, including personal protective equipment, and measures to strengthen the resilience of health and civil protection systems in emergencies. The co-legislators reached a provisional agreement on 23 June 2026 on the sixth revision of the Carcinogens, Mutagens and Reprotoxic Substances Directive (CMRD1). The next Multiannual Financial Framework and the National and Regional Partnership Plans (NRPPs), encourage Member States to invest in line with European priorities, according to their national, regional and local needs. Measures to support the implementation of an updated CMRD could be part of this if the measures contribute to the objectives of the regulation. The current EU occupational safety and health (OSH) strategic framework2 aims to protect all workers and runs until 2027. The content of a possible strategic framework after 2027 will involve consultations with relevant stakeholders. The Communication on integrated wildfire risk management3, adopted in March 2026, and the Council Recommendation on integrated wildfire risk management4, adopted in June 2026 highlight that firefighters need adequate protection, equipment, training, and assets, in line with OSH standards, underlining that they are exposed to various health risks. These can be mitigated through adequate training, appropriate protective equipment, and accessible health support, among others. By 2028, the Commission intends to launch a study to promote monitoring of firefighters’ exposure to wildfires and possible related long-term health impacts.

E-10-2026-002200.t: Tragic situation in primary health care boosts EU/Government health trade
qt: to the Commission Lefteris Nikolaou-Alavanos (NI) Subject:

Problems such as closures, mergers and transfers of health centres or their constituent parts are being recorded throughout Greece, along with chronic underfunding and understaffing. Despite the – provocative – declarations of New Democracy and the Ministry of Health regarding the ‘upgrading’ of primary health care, reality belies the hype. A decrease in medical staff of 9.8 % has been observed in public primary health care structures over the last four years. The ‘new National Health System’ means an acceleration of the degradation of public structures. Governments and the EU have paved the way for the commodification of health or the privatisation of profitable components, promoting commercial public-private partnerships. The profits of private groups exceeded EUR 2 billion in 2023 (a further increase of around 3 % is expected in 2024-2026). In view of the above: 1.

What is the Commission’s position on the fact that at the same time that health centres are completely understaffed and unable to provide basic primary health care services to patients, energy upgrades and renovations for health centres in Greece are subsidising construction groups in the ‘green transition’ through the EU’s NextGenerationEU funding?

What is the Commission’s position on the fact that according to Eurostat data (2023), 34.3 % of total health expenditure in Greece comprises private spending, i.e. it comes from the pockets of ordinary working-class families, demonstrating that EU policy – as well as that of governments – favours the trade in health?
at: (English version) to the Commission Lefteris Nikolaou-Alavanos (NI) (1 June 2026) Subject: Tragic situation in primary healthcare boosts EU/Government health trade Problems such as closures, mergers and transfers of health centres or their constituent parts are being recorded throughout Greece, along with chronic underfunding and understaffing. Despite the — provocative — declarations of New Democracy and the Ministry of Health regarding the ‘upgrading’ of primary healthcare, reality belies the hype. A decrease in medical staff of 9.8% has been observed in public primary healthcare structures over the last four years. The ‘new National Health System’ means an acceleration of the degradation of public structures. Governments and the EU have paved the way for the commodification of health or the privatisation of profitable components, promoting commercial public-private partnerships. The profits of private groups exceeded EUR 2 billion in 2023 (a further increase of around 3% is expected in 2024-2026). In view of the above: 1.

What is the Commission’s position on the fact that at the same time that health centres are completely understaffed and unable to provide basic primary healthcare services to patients, energy upgrades and renovations for health centres in Greece are subsidising construction groups in the ‘green transition’ through the EU’s NextGenerationEU funding?

What is the Commission’s position on the fact that according to Eurostat data (2023), 34.3% of total health expenditure in Greece comprises private spending, i.e. it comes from the pockets of ordinary working-class families, demonstrating that EU policy — as well as that of governments — favours the trade in health?

(17 July 2026) Under Article 168(7) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (1), Member States are responsible for the organisation and delivery of their health services and medical care. The EU’s role is to support them in strengthening their health systems by encouraging cooperation and exchange of best practices via technical assistance, funding, and policy guidance. Analysis, including under the European Semester, identifies persistent shortages and uneven distribution of health professionals in Greece, hampering access to healthcare (2). Several measures under the Greek recovery and resilience plan can address this: a reform of the primary healthcare system, including the renovation of primary healthcare units, the delivery of medical equipment, training of primary healthcare providers, and a referral mechanism; the reform of the personal doctor; the creation of a national health map that records the demand and supply of services in the health system. In 2023, the share of out-of-pocket payments in Greece’s current health expenditure was about 3 percentage points lower than 10 years earlier. It remains one of the highest in the EU. In the 2020, 2022 and 2023 cycles of the European Semester, Greece received recommendations to ensure adequate and equal access to healthcare. Moreover, the Semester Country Reports systematically stress the high share of out-of-pocket in Greek’s healthcare expenditure, and health workforce challenges. Moreover, the 2026 proposed recommendation to Greece highlights the need to tackle shortages of nurses and doctors, as well as of reducing out-of-pocket payments (3).

qt: to the Commission Yannis Maniatis (S&D) Subject:

The Seta-Manikia dam in Evia has remained unfinished since 2005, despite being a vital project for the water supply of the municipalities of Kymi-Aliveri and Eretria, which have been affected by extremely significant drinking water shortages over time. The completion of the project will significantly improve water supply, irrigation, water resources management and the production of renewable energy, contributing decisively to the climate resilience of the wider region. According to the competent Greek authorities, the project now has updated technical studies and approved environmental conditions, but its financing decision is pending. Public reports link the project’s financing to the Island Decarbonisation Fund, with resources from the auction of 25 million CO₂ emission allowances under the European Emissions Trading System (EU ETS). However, the status of the dam’s inclusion in this financial instrument remains unclear. The Commission is asked: 1.

Has the Greek Government included the ‘Seta-Manikia’ dam in the list of projects of the Decarbonisation Fund and, if so, what are the key details of the investment (works to be financed, budget, timetable)?
In the event that the project is not included in the Decarbonisation Fund, what alternative EU financial instruments or programmes could be used to finance this dam?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (14.7.2026) 1. The Emissions Trading System (ETS) Greek Decarbonisation Fund provides up to 25 million allowances for decarbonisation of the electricity supply of Greek islands. As the decarbonisation project is undergoing assessment by the European Investment Bank (EIB), as per the terms set out in Article 10a(9) of the ETS Directive1, the Commission is not in a position to share information on the project components at this stage. Information on the project components supported under the Greek Decarbonisation Fund will be made publicly available once the project has been confirmed. 2. If the dam project is not financed under the Decarbonisation Fund, other funds could serve as the main EU financing instrument. In fact, EU funding has supported investments in Greece across a range of sectors, including dam infrastructure. For instance, the Recovery and Resilience Facility has supported projects such as the Amfilochia pumped-storage hydropower plant in Western Greece, with an EU contribution of around EUR 250 million2. Moreover, under the 2021-2027 period, approximately EUR 2.1 billion has been allocated under Cohesion Policy funds in Greece to support secure access to drinking water, sustainable water management, and resilient public water supply and wastewater infrastructure. Under Cohesion Policy and in accordance with the principle of shared management, Member States are responsible for the selection and implementation of projects, including water-related investments, in line with programme priorities and Regulations3.
1 Directive 2003/87/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 October 2003 establishing a scheme

for greenhouse gas emission allowance trading within the Community and amending Council Directive 96/61/EC. 2 European Commission, Reforms and Investments: Pumped Storage Hydro Plant in Western Greece (Amfilochia). Additional information available in the link: https://reformsinvestments.ec.europa.eu/projects/pumped-storage-hydro-plant-western-greece-amfilochia_en. 3 Regulation (EU) 2021/1060 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 24 June 2021.

E-10-2026-002196.t: Unacceptable raising of the LGBTQI flag on the Commission building
qt: to the Commission Geadis Geadi (ECR), Georgiana Teodorescu (ECR), Małgorzata Gosiewska (ECR), Roman Haider (PfE), Şerban Dimitrie Sturdza (ECR), Nikolaos Anadiotis (NI), Paolo Borchia (PfE), Paolo Inselvini (ECR), Marc Jongen (ESN), Hermann Tertsch (PfE), Nicolas Bay (ECR), Sebastian Tynkkynen (ECR), Tomasz Froelich (ESN), Milan Mazurek (ESN) Subject:

With this question, we wish to denounce the raising of the LGBTQI flag on the Commission’s premises, as shared on social media, because this constitutes an action that undermines the principle of institutional neutrality and raises legitimate concerns regarding the political and ideological impartiality of the EU institutions. In their operations, the EU institutions are required to display neutrality, respect all European citizens and avoid symbolic actions that may be perceived as politically or ideologically aligned with specific groups or agendas. We call on the Commission to answer the following: 1.
Does the Commission institutionally equate the LGBTQI flag with the flags of recognised sovereign states or with the official flag of the EU?
Has any democratic mandate or approval been sought or obtained from European citizens for the display of such symbols by EU institutions?
Does the Commission intend, in the spirit of equal treatment and institutional neutrality, to raise corresponding flags or symbols on the International Day of Families?
at: (English version) to the Commission Geadis Geadi (ECR), Georgiana Teodorescu (ECR), Małgorzata Gosiewska (ECR), Roman Haider (PfE), Şerban Dimitrie Sturdza (ECR), Nikolaos Anadiotis (NI), Paolo Borchia (PfE), Paolo Inselvini (ECR), Marc Jongen (ESN), Hermann Tertsch (PfE), Nicolas Bay (ECR), Sebastian Tynkkynen (ECR), Tomasz Froelich (ESN), Milan Mazurek (ESN) (31 May 2026) Subject: Unacceptable raising of the LGBTQI flag on the Commission building With this question, we wish to denounce the raising of the LGBTQI flag on the Commission’s premises, as shared on social media, because this constitutes an action that undermines the principle of institutional neutrality and raises legitimate concerns regarding the political and ideological impartiality of the EU institutions. In their operations, the EU institutions are required to display neutrality, respect all European citizens and avoid symbolic actions that may be perceived as politically or ideologically aligned with specific groups or agendas. We call on the Commission to answer the following: 1.
Does the Commission institutionally equate the LGBTQI flag with the flags of recognised sovereign states or with the official flag of the EU?
Has any democratic mandate or approval been sought or obtained from European citizens for the display of such symbols by EU institutions?
Does the Commission intend, in the spirit of equal treatment and institutional neutrality, to raise corresponding flags or symbols on the International Day of Families?

(27 August 2026) Equality and non-discrimination are founding values and fundamental rights enshrined in the EU Treaties and the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union (1). As set out in the Commission’s 2024-2029 political guidelines (2), the Commission is committed to building a union of equality. Each year, on 17 May (the International Day Against Homophobia, Biphobia and Transphobia), the Commission reaffirms its support for the lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and queer (LGBTIQ) community and its commitment to combating all forms of discrimination, hatred and violence against LGBTIQ people, as set out in the LGBTIQ+ equality strategy 2026-2030 (3). This includes the symbolic action of flying the Pride progress flag on 17 May outside the Commission’s Berlaymont headquarters, in coordination with other European institutions and bodies, including the European Parliament, the Council of the European Union and the European External Action Service, among others.

E-10-2026-002195.t: Combating period poverty in the EU
qt: to the Commission Gabriela Firea (S&D) Subject:

The Gender Equality Strategy 2026-2030 recognises period poverty and menopause poverty, which affect millions of women across the European Union, and mentions the need for concrete measures such as free distribution of personal hygiene products and the sharing of best practices between Member States. In Romania, austerity measures to correct the budget deficit have contributed to the rise in the cost of living, increases in medication prices and limitation of access to basic personal hygiene products for hundreds of girls and women, who are experiencing a daily reality that affects their health. 1.

In the context of the budgetary pressures and rising cost of living in some Member States, including Romania, how does the Commission believe it can combat period poverty and menopause poverty in a concrete manner, other than by sharing best practices?

Does the Commission intend to offer support to Member States through a specific programme or through European funds, such as ESF+, so that personal hygiene products can be distributed free of charge in schools, high schools and universities?
How will the Commission monitor the social impact of period poverty and menopause poverty on health, education and women’s participation in the labour market?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (19.8.2026) The Roadmap for Women’s Rights1 highlights the importance of tackling women’s poverty for gender equality. The Gender Equality Strategy2 points to the lack of access to affordable menstrual products. Directive 2022/542, which introduced reforms as regards rates of value added tax3 expanded Member States’ flexibility to apply super-reduced rates, including 0%, to certain goods, such as female hygiene products, where national governments choose to do so. The EU Anti-Poverty Strategy4 promotes people’s access to affordable, quality social and essential services, along with addressing the root causes of poverty. Member States can use European Social Fund Plus5 to support basic material assistance, including hygiene products, where this contributes to social inclusion and addresses material deprivation. In order to deliver effectively on the objectives of the Anti-Poverty Strategy, the Commission will continue to monitor progress towards the reduction of poverty and aims to improve monitoring and put forward new indicators to measure the impact of affordability components on poverty, with a view to having them agreed by 2028. The aim is to improve the timeliness and comprehensiveness of poverty-related data, including by assessing different dimensions of poverty and affordability. Furthermore, the Commission will fund a study on the macroand micro-economic and societal benefits of closing the women’s health gap related to certain conditions over the life course, like menopause.

E-10-2026-002192.t: Recognition of work beyond the five-day period in the Armed Forces
qt: to the Commission Emmanouil Fragkos (ECR) Subject:

The non-recognition of work beyond the five-day period for military personnel of the Armed Forces, in contrast to what applies to personnel of the Law Enforcement Agencies under Article 127 of Law 4472/2017, raises issues of equal treatment, protection of health and safety at work and compliance with the fundamental principles of the European acquis. There is no regulatory framework regulating working time, minimum rest periods and compensation for exceeding the prescribed weekly working time for personnel of the Armed Forces, despite the fact that a 40-hour work week has been established by decision no. Φ.400/163881/Σ.4187/89-2011 of the Ministry of National Defence. Taking into account Directive 2003/88/EC concerning certain aspects of the organisation of working time, as well as Article 31 of the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights on fair and secure working conditions: 1.

Does the Commission consider that the complete exclusion of military personnel from any form of special compensation for work exceeding five days is consistent with the principles of equal treatment and the protection of the health and safety of workers?

How does the Commission assess the absence of a specific regulatory framework for working time and minimum rest periods for Armed Forces personnel in Greece, in light of European case law and Directive 2003/88/EC?
Does the Commission intend to examine the issue in the context of social dialogue and the implementation of European rules on health and safety at work?
at: (English version) to the Commission Emmanouil Fragkos (ECR) (29 May 2026) Subject: Recognition of work beyond the five-day period in the Armed Forces The non-recognition of work beyond the five-day period for military personnel of the Armed Forces, in contrast to what applies to personnel of the Law Enforcement Agencies under Article 127 of Law 4472/2017, raises issues of equal treatment, protection of health and safety at work and compliance with the fundamental principles of the European acquis. There is no regulatory framework regulating working time, minimum rest periods and compensation for exceeding the prescribed weekly working time for personnel of the Armed Forces, despite the fact that a 40-hour work week has been established by decision no. Φ.400/163881/Σ.4187/8-9-2011 of the Ministry of National Defence. Taking into account Directive 2003/88/EC concerning certain aspects of the organisation of working time, as well as Article 31 of the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights on fair and secure working conditions: 1.

Does the Commission consider that the complete exclusion of military personnel from any form of special compensation for work exceeding five days is consistent with the principles of equal treatment and the protection of the health and safety of workers?

How does the Commission assess the absence of a specific regulatory framework for working time and minimum rest periods for Armed Forces personnel in Greece, in light of European case law and Directive 2003/88/EC?
Does the Commission intend to examine the issue in the context of social dialogue and the implementation of European rules on health and safety at work?

(20 July 2026) The Working Time Directive (1), which lays down minimum safety and health requirements for working time, applies to all sectors of activity, public and private. It sets out minimum requirements on minimum uninterrupted weekly rest (2) and other rest periods. The Court of Justice of the EU has held that in principle the directive applies to military personnel; however, it may not apply in relation to its specific activities such as active deployment or initial or operational training (3), and it may be temporarily disapplied for certain activities in circumstances whose gravity and scale are exceptional. When the directive applies, it offers significant flexibilities to establish derogations under certain conditions, notably in the case of activities requiring continuity of service. The directive does not deal with the issue of remuneration (4) and the matter of access to special compensation does not fall within the scope of EU law. EU law does not guarantee that all public sector workers receive identical benefits or compensations. In the area of working conditions, EU law protects against discrimination of part-time or fixed-term workers in comparison to full-time or permanent workers, and against discrimination on grounds of age, sex, disability, ethnic or racial origin, religion or belief, or sexual orientation. In its role of guardian of the Treaties, the Commission monitors compliance with the directive by all Member States, including Greece. Greece explicitly applies the directive to its armed forces (5).

Directive 2003/88/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 4 November 2003 concerning certain aspects of the organisation of working time, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2003/88/oj/eng. Article 5 of Directive 2003/88/EC entitles every worker, per each seven-day period, to a minimum uninterrupted rest period of 24 hours plus 11 hours of daily rest. Article 16(a) of Directive 2003/88/EC allows Member States to lay down a reference period up to 14 days. https://curia.europa.eu/juris/liste.jsf?num=C-742/19. In compliance with Article 153(5) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union which excludes regulation on pay. E-10-2026-002191.t: Transparency and supplier selection in Lisbon metro Foreign Subsidies Regulation case
qt: to the Commission Tomáš Zdechovský (PPE) Subject:

In its decision of 21 April 2026 in Case FSP.103117 concerning the procurement of rolling stock for the Lisbon metro (Metropolitano de Lisboa), the Commission accepted commitments under the Foreign Subsidies Regulation1 (FSR), resulting in the replacement of the Chinese supplier CRRC by the Polish manufacturer PESA. According to publicly available information, the consortium had identified more than one EUbased supplier capable of replacing CRRC. As this was the first remedy procedure to be completed under the FSR, greater clarity is needed regarding the selection process and its implications for future cases. 1.

Was the Commission aware of any alternative FSR-compliant rolling-stock supplier proposed by the consortium, and if so, did it assess that supplier as part of its review; and what was the outcome of that assessment?

Did the Commission’s decision specifically require the appointment of PESA, or did it merely require the replacement of CRRC by an FSR-compliant supplier? If the latter, what factors led to the acceptance of PESA?
Does the Commission intend to publish the non-confidential version of the decision and/or issue guidance on the treatment and selection of replacement suppliers in future FSR remedy procedures?
Regulation (EU) 2022/2560 of 14 December 2022 on foreign subsidies distorting the internal market (ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/2560/oj). 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.7.2026) Pursuant to Article 7(2) of Regulation (EU) 2022/25601 (Foreign Subsidies Regulation (FSR)), ‘the Commission may accept commitments offered by the undertaking under investigation where such commitments fully and effectively remedy the distortion in the internal market’. In this case, the consortium led by Mota-Engil (the Consortium) offered commitments to dispel the concerns the Commission had expressed in the decision opening the in-depth investigation into the case. The Commission conducted a preliminary review of potential alternative subcontractors on the basis of the information submitted by the Consortium for each potential subcontractor. While the Commission can confirm that the Consortium negotiated with several potential subcontractors, the precise number is confidential and cannot be publicly disclosed. Based on the information received, the Commission could confirm that Pojazdy Szynowe PESA Bydgoszcz Spółka Akcyjna (PESA) had not received foreign subsidies. This assessment does not prejudge whether foreign subsidies exist in relation to the other potential subcontractors. In this context, the Consortium committed to replace Portugal CRRC with PESA, and the Commission adopted a decision with commitments under Article 31(1) FSR. This decision does not predetermine the outcome of the award procedure. It is for Metropolitano de Lisboa, the contracting entity, to assess whether the bid of the Consortium complies with all technical and quality requirements set out in the tender documents. The non-confidential version of the Commission’s decision, with any confidential elements redacted, will be published on the Commission’s website dedicated to the FSR in public procurement procedures2 as soon as possible.

E-10-2026-002190.t: Implementing the fifth freedom of movement in the internal market: research, innovation, data and knowledge
qt: to the Commission Lídia Pereira (PPE), Sebastião Bugalho (PPE), Paulo Cunha (PPE), Paulo do Nascimento Cabral (PPE) Subject:

The Letta report1 (April 2024) proposed a fifth freedom of movement in the single market for research, innovation, data, skills and education – an idea already put forward by Jacques Delors in 1989. Two years on and we have yet to achieve this fundamental condition to reverse the slowdown in European competitiveness. Despite initiatives such as Choose Europe for Science and the European Health Data Space, there is still no integrated strategy for the free movement of researchers, knowledge and data. Given that the EU’s share of global patents has been falling and that 90 % of public investment in research and innovation remains national and focused on domestic priorities, this issue is becoming particularly pressing. Can the Commission therefore say: 1.
What legislative or non-legislative initiatives does it intend to pursue, and what the timeline would be, to formally enshrine the fifth freedom of movement in the single market?
Does it envisage setting up a European grant for deep tech, with rules tailored to risk finance?

Does it believe it is the right moment to set up a European Joint Knowledge Centre, in line with the Letta report, based around a centralised digital platform providing access to publicly funded research, data and educational resources?
https://www.consilium.europa.eu/media/ny3j24sm/much-more-than-a-market-report-by-enrico-letta.pdf
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (7.8.2026) As announced in the Competitiveness Compass1 and the One Europe, One Market Roadmap2, the Commission is preparing a legislative proposal for a European Research Area (ERA) Act, targeted for adoption in the second half of 2026. The ERA Act will contribute to implementing the Fifth Freedom by improving framework conditions for research and innovation, notably through measures supporting attractive research careers, mobility, knowledge circulation and open science. The Commission is also advancing these objectives through existing initiatives such as the ERA Policy Agenda3, the ERA Talent Platform4, the Union of Skills5 and Choose Europe for Science6. The European Innovation Council already provides a combination of grants and equity investments for breakthrough innovation and high-risk deep tech. The Commission proposes to reinforce these instruments under the next Multiannual Financial Framework and is also advancing the proposal for a Scaleup Europe Fund to help address financing gaps for strategic European companies. The European Open Science Cloud (EOSC)7 realises the vision of a European Knowledge Commons through the EOSC Federation8, a federated ‘system of systems’ enabling researchers to store, share, process, analyse and reuse Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Reusable (FAIR) research outputs across Europe. Rather than establishing a new centralised structure, EOSC is expanding as an interoperable infrastructure, which addresses the fragmentation and under-exploitation of publicly funded research outputs. It also facilitates cross-border access and collaboration in an open, secure and trusted environment, while developing synergies with other European Common Data Spaces and strategic data initiatives.

9756159ba614_en?filename=one-europe-one-market-roadmap.pdf. 3 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=OJ:C_202503593. 4 https://ec.europa.eu/era-talent-platform/. 5 https://commission.europa.eu/document/download/f0beb292-fe6a-47e8-8570-ce5569f1be5c_en. 6 https://commission.europa.eu/topics/research-and-innovation/choose-europe_en. 7 https://research-and-innovation.ec.europa.eu/strategy/strategy-research-and-innovation/our-digital-future/openscience/european-open-science-cloud-eosc_en. 8 https://eosc.eu/building-the-eosc-federation.

E-10-2026-002189.t: Follow-up to the EIOPA/ESM proposal for a European risk-sharing mechanism for natural disasters
qt: to the Commission Lídia Pereira (PPE), Sebastião Bugalho (PPE), Paulo Cunha (PPE), Paulo do Nascimento Cabral (PPE) Subject:

On 9 April 2026, the European Insurance and Occupational Pensions Authority (EIOPA) and the European Stability Mechanism (ESM) published a joint document1 proposing a European risk-sharing mechanism for natural disasters, based on two pillars: a European insurance pool financed by risk-based premiums and a loan-based backstop for extreme events, with an estimated capacity of between EUR 10 billion and 65 billion. The document estimates that between 50 % and 75 % of economic losses from natural disasters remain uninsured, and it identifies Portugal among the Member States with the biggest protection gaps, particularly in terms of wildfires, floods, heatwaves and earthquake risk. In light of the above: 1.

Does the Commission intend to follow up on the EIOPA/ESM proposal with legislative action and, if so, what would the timeline be, and how would it link to existing national regimes or those under preparation, including the future Fundo de Catástrofes português (‘Portuguese Disaster Fund’)?
How does the Commission intend to complement this supply-driven mechanism with demand-side measures, including risk literacy and investment in prevention and adaptation?
What role does it see for the capital market in strengthening the capacity of the European pool?

https://www.eiopa.europa.eu/document/download/c8be856b-b358-4b68-9c3480672f2e4c28_en?filename=ESM-EIOPA%20Discussion%20Paper%20-%20Sharing%20the%20risk%20%20A%20European%20approach%20to%20natural%20catastrophe%20risk%20management.pdf. 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.7.2026) The Commission’s priority is to engage with insurance distributors and insurance undertakings on the role that they can play in raising household awareness of potential options to increase insurance coverage for climate-related losses. The Commission is of the view that enhanced awareness regarding the increased frequency, and sometimes severity, of climate related losses and, to that end, enhanced financial literacy, will play an essential role in efforts to narrow the climate protection gap in the EU. The Commission is also investigating, together with the European Insurance and Occupational Pensions Authority, whether premium benefits for precautionary action taken by households could play a role in raising awareness of climate risk and reduce its potential impacts. The discussion paper published by the European Insurance and Occupational Pensions Authority and the European Stability Mechanism provides technical input to inform policy discussions on natural catastrophe risk management. Such input, as well as initiatives emerging at national level, as for example Portugal’s recent announcement to establish a national disaster fund, will feed the Commission’s reflections in this area. The Commission aims to strengthen preparedness across society by improving public awareness of risks and how to reduce them. As part of the Preparedness Union Strategy1, particular focus is placed on population preparedness and on improving access to reliable risk information, for example through tools like the Risk Data Hub. In addition, the Commission supports prevention and adaptation through its broader policy and funding framework, including through the adoption of the Preparedness by Design principle.
1 https://commission.europa.eu/topics/preparedness_en.

E-10-2026-002188.t: Cyprus's unacceptable exclusion from COP31 processes
qt: to the Commission Nikolas Farantouris (S&D) Subject:

According to reports,1 Türkiye has excluded Cyprus from a series of informal preparatory meetings ahead of the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31), which will take place from 9-20 November 2026 in Antalya, Türkiye, with Türkiye holding the official presidency and hosting the summit and Australia assuming the presidency of negotiations within the framework of the summit. Türkiye is alleged to have implemented a broader practice of excluding Cyprus from informal processes of the event, not sending invitations to Cypriot authorities for important information meetings and even ignoring requests for bilateral contacts submitted by Cyprus on behalf of the EU as it held the Presidency of the Council of the EU. As the Commission has also stated,2 this exclusion is unacceptable and inconsistent with Türkiye's status as host country of COP31. Given that the above practice by Türkiye violates UN procedures and does not respect Cyprus's status as both an equal member of the UN and as the holder of the Presidency of the Council of the EU: 1.
What specific actions does the Commission intend to take in order to ensure Cyprus's equal and unhindered participation in the COP31 processes?
What measures does the Commission intend to take if new instances or methods of excluding Cyprus are observed?

https://www.politico.eu/article/turkey-freezes-cyprus-out-cop31-climate-summit-preparations/. https://www.politico.eu/article/unacceptable-brussels-rebukes-turkey-for-excluding-cyprus-fromclimate-meetings/. 1 2

What specific actions does the Commission intend to take in order to ensure Cyprus's equal and unhindered participation in the COP31 processes?
What measures does the Commission intend to take if new instances or methods of excluding Cyprus are observed?

(10 August 2026) In line with the EU position, the Commission considers that the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) process must be inclusive, transparent and open to all Parties to the UNFCCC and Paris Agreement, with full respect for their rights. This includes that all Parties to the UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement must be invited to the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) and any international meetings or events hosted or organised by Türkiye in its COP31 Presidency capacity. This also includes access to all relevant documentation and information. The Commission has therefore made it clear to Türkiye, as incoming COP Presidency, that the exclusion of a UN Member State from the preparation process of COP31 is not acceptable. The same message was conveyed to the UN Secretariat and Australia, as incoming President of Negotiations for COP31. The Commission will continue to advocate strongly for a fully inclusive UNFCCC process and will discuss with the EU Member States, on possible further steps if this is not ensured.

E-10-2026-002187.t: Latest inflammatory statements by the Turkish Minister of Defence and the direct challenge to Greek and Cypriot sovereignty
qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Emmanouil Kefalogiannis (PPE) Subject:

In provocative statements, the Turkish Defence Minister stressed the following: ‘Our rights and interests in the Aegean Sea, the Eastern Mediterranean and Cyprus are based on historical, legal and legitimate foundations. It should be well known that we will not remain indifferent to any initiative targeting our sovereign rights, our security and our legitimate rights and interests in our seas.’1 These statements represent a blatant challenge against Member States and mark a return to Türkiye’s revisionist policy. By systematically violating international law, the Turkish Government is attempting to fabricate non-existent sovereignty issues in the Aegean, while continuing to maintain an active casus belli against Greece. Not only do these statements constitute provocative rhetoric, they also undermine regional stability, security and international legitimacy. Greece has an inalienable and legitimate right to bolster its islands’ defences in the face of a country that retains landing capabilities on the coast of Asia Minor. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Does it intend to condemn these statements, which directly target Member States?
How does it view the ongoing threat of war against a Member State, which is incompatible with the fundamental principles, values and obligations of a candidate country?
Does it intend to impose sanctions on Türkiye if its revisionist and aggressive policy against Greece and Cyprus continues?

(20 July 2026) The EU stands collectively, firmly and unequivocally with all Member States in the face of any threat and remains committed to defending its interests and those of its Member States, as well as to upholding regional stability and respect of international law. As emphasised in the 2025 enlargement report on Türkiye (1), the possible extension of Greek territorial waters to 12 nautical miles under Article 3 of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (Unclos) continued to weigh on the relationship. In this context, the 1995 declaration of the Turkish Grand National Assembly that any action by Greece to extend its territorial waters would be considered a casus belli still holds. qt: to the Commission Özlem Demirel (The Left) Subject:

An internal report by Europol’s Data Protection Officer, which was submitted in early 2019 and brought to light by an investigation, described significant security and data protection gaps in the CFN system (‘shadow IT’), which was not subject to oversight at the time. Europol’s own Data Protection Officer warned against a possible ban on the processing of the entire parallel data system, effectively amounting to a complete cessation of Europol’s operational business. Since then, Europol and the European Data Protection Supervisor have been in continuous discussions on measures to address them. Last February, the Data Protection Supervisor informed the Joint Parliamentary Scrutiny Group (JPSG) that, although his inquiry had been concluded, certain issues remained unresolved, in particular in the area of IT security and the logging of data access. Of the 150 recommendations issued, fifteen had not been implemented. 1.

What is the current state of security of Europol’s systems, including as regards ensuring that all operations and processing steps can be properly logged, and what is the breakdown of individual access instances (including privileged access) and access rights by year, system and individual?
Does Europol have full control over who has access to which systems and have the deficiencies in password management been remedied?
How is effective oversight ensured as regards compliance with the code of conduct by all staff, posted liaison officers, and third parties with access to Europol systems?

Europol’s own Data Protection Officer warned against a possible ban on the processing of the entire parallel data system, effectively amounting to a complete cessation of Europol’s operational business. Since then, Europol and the European Data Protection Supervisor have been in continuous discussions on measures to address them. Last February, the Data Protection Supervisor informed the Joint Parliamentary Scrutiny Group (JPSG) that, although his inquiry had been concluded, certain issues remained unresolved, in particular in the area of IT security and the logging of data access. Of the 150 recommendations issued, fifteen had not been implemented. 1. What is the current state of security of Europol’s systems, including as regards ensuring that all operations and processing steps can be properly logged, and what is the breakdown of individual access instances (including privileged access) and access rights by year, system and individual? 2. Does Europol have full control over who has access to which systems and have the deficiencies in password management been remedied? 3. How is effective oversight ensured as regards compliance with the code of conduct by all staff, posted liaison officers, and third parties with access to Europol systems? (22 September 2026) The security of the European Union Agency for Law Enforcement Cooperation (Europol) information systems is framed by the Europol Regulation (1) and the EU data protection framework (2), including independent supervision by the European Data Protection Supervisor (EDPS) (3), with which Europol cooperates closely. Europol is required to keep logs of its processing operations (4), which may be used to verify the lawfulness of processing, selfmonitoring and ensuring data integrity and security, and are available to Europol’s Data Protection Officer and the EDPS for their oversight functions. Europol is also subject to the provisions of Regulation (EU, Euratom) 2023/2841 to ensure a high level of cybersecurity (5). Europol is required to establish the requisite security measures across its information systems to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risks (6). The implementation of these requirements, including as regards access management, is subject to independent supervision by the EDPS. The recent Commission proposal for a new Europol Regulation (7) includes rules on the core services and tools developed and maintained by Europol, to update its framework in response to the evolving security environment and to further strengthen the transparency and accountability of the Agency in the performance of its tasks in this new context. The code of conduct of Europol is available on its website (8). Europol has also a dedicated Internal Investigations Service, which handles suspected misconduct, and which cooperates, where required, with the European Anti-Fraud Office, the European Public Prosecutor’s Office and national competent authorities.

qt: to the Commission Regina Doherty (PPE) Subject:
I would like to ask the following questions in relation to Regulation (EU) 2024/9001 and the upcoming stakeholder review: 1.

What consultation, if any, took place with political parties (as distinct from politicians) at a national level in relation to this regulation, especially considering that the implementation burden falls primarily upon national political parties?
What regulatory impact assessment, if any, was undertaken?

Will the Commission commit, as part of any review of this regulation, to engage with national political parties at an organisational rather than a political level to ensure that any implementing rules are operational?

Regulation (EU) 2024/900 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 March 2024 on the transparency and targeting of political advertising (OJ L, 2024/900, 20.3.2024, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/900/oj). 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.7.2026) Regulation (EU) 2024/9001 provides for EU common standards on transparency of political advertising services. Political parties typically act as sponsors of political ads and as such only have to comply with the obligations applicable to sponsors. In particular, they have to ensure the truthfulness and accuracy of the relevant information provided to providers of political advertising services but are not responsible for labelling of the political advertisements. The legislative proposal was accompanied by an impact assessment, which assessed the impact of the policy measures considered2. To gather evidence and reach out to key stakeholders, the Commission conducted broad consultation activities on issues related to political advertising, as well as bilateral meetings with stakeholders, including political actors at EU level. Details of consultation activities are available in annex 2 of the impact assessment. The preparation of the impact assessment was also supported by an external study which, among others, assessed the impact of the different policy options per relevant actor, including national political parties. The Commission published practical guidelines3 to clarify the rules and obligations. The guidelines, which were drafted based on feedback received by stakeholders including political actors, support all actors under the scope of the regulation to understand and comply with their obligations. The Commission has been actively engaging with relevant stakeholders to provide additional guidance and support as regards the application of the Regulation. The Commission will also organise an implementation dialogue in 2026 to draw insights as necessary from the application of the rules.

E-10-2026-002183.t: Sanctions imposed on the European citizens Saif Abukeshek and Jaldía Abubakra by the United States
qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Irene Montero (The Left), Isabel Serra Sánchez (The Left) Subject:

On 19 May 2026, the US Department of the Treasury imposed sanctions on, among others, the European citizens Saif Abukeshek and Jaldía Abubakra for their participation in the civil society initiative Global Sumud Flotilla and for their links to the Samidoun organisation, respectively. The purpose of these sanctions is to freeze their assets and financial interests located in the United States or under the control of US individuals and companies – including financial transactions – thereby leaving them in a state of vulnerability and defencelessness. These sanctions have been imposed without prior judicial process and are based on ideological assumptions that have not been proven in accordance with due legal guarantees, demonstrating that this is a politically motivated persecution and a violation of their fundamental rights. 1.

Does the Vice-President/High Representative consider that the imposition of sanctions by the United States against European citizens for their participation in initiatives promoting solidarity with Palestine may infringe their fundamental rights, in particular the freedom of expression, association and political participation?
How does the Vice-President/High Representative intend to ensure that the increasing use of sanctions regimes is not employed as an instrument of political repression?

How does the Vice-President/High Representative intend to safeguard the political liberties and fundamental rights of these citizens, who are being persecuted by a foreign country, namely the United States?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (31.7.2026) 1. The EU respects the intention and the right of those on board of the Global Sumud Flotilla ships to draw attention to the humanitarian plight of the population of Gaza. Freedom of expression and freedom of peaceful assembly and association are human rights enshrined in international law, in the European Convention on Human Rights, and in the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights. The EU is firmly committed to protect and support civic space and an enabling environment for civil society everywhere. 2. The EU opposes any legislation, regulation or practices that unduly limit freedom of expression, peaceful assembly and association, and urges States to repeal or amend measures that penalise individuals or civil society organisations for exercising those rights. In this respect, attacks against participants of the Global Sumud Flotilla or reprisals against them constitute a breach of international law, including international human rights law and international humanitarian law. The delivery of humanitarian aid, food, medicine, or other emergency supplies should be exempted from sanctions, as provided in the UN Security Council Resolution 2664 (2022) and transposed by the EU across its sanctions regimes. The EU considers that sanctions, whether adopted by the UN Security Council or autonomously by the EU, must be grounded in international law, targeted, proportionate and accompanied by appropriate procedural safeguards, including respect for the rights of listed persons. 3. The EU supports independent investigations into all alleged violations of international law. The EU uses various tools at its disposal to stand up for human rights around the world, including through bilateral contacts with the United States and other countries.

E-10-2026-002181.t: Ethics of media coverage of suicides and protection of vulnerable groups in the EU
qt: to the Commission Nikos Pappas (The Left) Subject:

Recent cases of suicide committed by minors in the EU, including in Greece, have been the subject of extensive, sensationalist media coverage. Scientific literature warns of the risk of copycat behaviour among vulnerable groups. The EU framework enshrines the freedom of expression and independence of the media through the European Media Freedom Act and Article 11 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, as well as the protection of minors and human dignity through Articles 1 and 24 of the Charter and Article 28 of the Audiovisual Media Services Directive. However, certain journalistic reporting practices appear to raise issues of compatibility with the spirit of the above provisions and the effective protection of minors. In view of the above, can the Commission say: 1.

How does it assess the adequacy of the current framework (Media Freedom Act and Article 28 of the Audiovisual Media Services Directive) in protecting minors from the effects of media coverage of suicidal behaviour?
Does it intend to strengthen the common guidelines for journalistic coverage of suicides, in the interests of public health and preventing copycat behaviour?

How is the balance between press freedom and the protection of minors and vulnerable groups ensured in the context of Articles 11 and 24 of the Charter, the European Media Freedom Act and the Audiovisual Media Services Directive?
at: (English version) to the Commission Nikos Pappas (The Left) (29 May 2026) Subject: Ethics of media coverage of suicides and protection of vulnerable groups in the EU Recent cases of suicide committed by minors in the EU, including in Greece, have been the subject of extensive, sensationalist media coverage. Scientific literature warns of the risk of copycat behaviour among vulnerable groups. The EU framework enshrines the freedom of expression and independence of the media through the European Media Freedom Act and Article 11 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, as well as the protection of minors and human dignity through Articles 1 and 24 of the Charter and Article 28 of the Audiovisual Media Services Directive. However, certain journalistic reporting practices appear to raise issues of compatibility with the spirit of the above provisions and the effective protection of minors. In view of the above, can the Commission say: 1.

How does it assess the adequacy of the current framework (Media Freedom Act and Article 28 of the Audiovisual Media Services Directive) in protecting minors from the effects of media coverage of suicidal behaviour?
Does it intend to strengthen the common guidelines for journalistic coverage of suicides, in the interests of public health and preventing copycat behaviour?

How is the balance between press freedom and the protection of minors and vulnerable groups ensured in the context of Articles 11 and 24 of the Charter, the European Media Freedom Act and the Audiovisual Media Services Directive?

(30 July 2026) Article 6 of the Audiovisual Media Services Directive (AVMSD) (1) requires Member States to ensure that audiovisual media services provided under their jurisdiction respect and protect human dignity. Articles 6a and 28b require that measures are put in place in both audiovisual media services and video-sharing platforms, respectively, in order to protect minors from content that may impair their physical, mental or moral development, as well as to protect the general public from content constituting criminal offences (such as child pornography). In addition, Article 28 of the Digital Services Act (DSA) (2) obliges providers of online platforms accessible to minors to put in place appropriate and proportionate measures to ensure a high level of privacy, safety, and security of minors, on their service. Moreover, the European Media Freedom Act (EMFA) (3) underlines the role of self-regulation in ensuring ethical media coverage, notably regarding the content moderation safeguards laid down in Article 18 of the EMFA. This Article deals with media content on very large online platforms designated as such under the DSA and requires that media service providers declare when they adhere to a widely recognised and accepted co-regulatory or self-regulatory mechanism governing editorial standards in order to benefit from such safeguards. The Commission closely monitors the implementation of the DSA and AVMSD rules in the Member States, including those related to the protection of minors, and will further assess the latter during the upcoming review planned for the third quarter of 2026. On 6 February 2026, the Commission also published guidelines on the protection of media content online under Article 18 of the EMFA (4).

E-10-2026-002177.t: Use of European public funds for institutional campaigns on the ‘free press’
qt: to the Commission Jorge Martín Frías (PfE) Subject:

The Commission has launched a campaign under the slogan ‘Free press. Protect what matters’. A corresponding institutional advertising campaign on street furniture has been launched in the Member States. On the campaign's official page, the Commission states that ‘in the EU, the press is free to ask tough questions, hold those in power accountable and provide reliable information sources’. However, Eurobarometer data shows that only 56 % of Europeans are satisfied with the state of media freedom, independence and pluralism in the EU. In addition, a significant proportion of citizens do not consider the media to provide fully reliable information or a sufficient diversity of perspectives. 1.
What is the total cost of this campaign and what other activities have been financed under this umbrella?
Has funding been earmarked for media? If so, what mechanisms is the Commission using to ensure that the media receiving funding is independent?
Does the Commission consider it satisfactory that only 56 % of Europeans say they are satisfied with the state of media freedom, independence and pluralism in the EU?

E-10-2026-002176.t: Protecting and supporting olive growers’ income in the new common agricultural policy (CAP) in the face of climate crisis consequences
qt: to the Commission Emmanouil Kefalogiannis (PPE) Subject:

The climate crisis is causing volatility in the prices and production levels of olive oil in the Mediterranean, where 95 % of the world’s olive oil is produced. Greece is bearing the brunt of the impact, with producers facing increased irrigation and energy costs, reduced yields and pressure on their incomes. Between 2024 and 2025, the price of extra virgin olive oil on the European market fluctuated, ranging from EUR 3 200 to over EUR 9 000 per tonne. At the same time, production rose by 43 % in Greece and by 21 % in Portugal in the space of a single growing season, highlighting the extreme instability created by the climate crisis in the primary sector. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

How does it intend to address the ever-increasing volatility in olive oil prices and production levels caused by the climate crisis, in order to ensure a sustainable income for Mediterranean producers?
Does it intend to look into the creation of specific support mechanisms or risk management tools for Mediterranean tree crop farming, in particular olive cultivation, under the new CAP?

How will provisions for investment in water management projects, irrigation infrastructure, agricultural research and innovative sustainable farming practices in the Mediterranean regions affected by the climate crisis be incorporated into the new CAP?
at: (English version) to the Commission Emmanouil Kefalogiannis (PPE) (28 May 2026) Subject: Protecting and supporting olive growers’ income in the new common agricultural policy (CAP) in the face of climate crisis consequences The climate crisis is causing volatility in the prices and production levels of olive oil in the Mediterranean, where 95% of the world’s olive oil is produced. Greece is bearing the brunt of the impact, with producers facing increased irrigation and energy costs, reduced yields and pressure on their incomes. Between 2024 and 2025, the price of extra virgin olive oil on the European market fluctuated, ranging from EUR 3 200 to over EUR 9 000 per tonne. At the same time, production rose by 43% in Greece and by 21% in Portugal in the space of a single growing season, highlighting the extreme instability created by the climate crisis in the primary sector. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

How does it intend to address the ever-increasing volatility in olive oil prices and production levels caused by the climate crisis, in order to ensure a sustainable income for Mediterranean producers?
Does it intend to look into the creation of specific support mechanisms or risk management tools for Mediterranean tree crop farming, in particular olive cultivation, under the new CAP?

How will provisions for investment in water management projects, irrigation infrastructure, agricultural research and innovative sustainable farming practices in the Mediterranean regions affected by the climate crisis be incorporated into the new CAP?

(27 July 2026) Tools already exist to tackle market volatility in the olive oil sector. Article 167a of EU Regulation 1308/2013 (1) allows producing Member States to lay down marketing rules to regulate supply and improve and stabilise the operation of the market. Furthermore, in case of severe imbalance, the Commission may agree to activate private storage aid for olive oil, as it was the case in 2019/20. Income support through direct payments, together with crisis payments for natural disasters, adverse climatic or catastrophic events, included in the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), are also designed to help farmers absorb some of the consequences of climate change. The CAP also provides a specific toolbox of instruments to help farmers manage risks. This includes support for insurance schemes, mutual funds and income stabilisation tools. These instruments are designed to help farmers cope with severe income shocks and production losses. These tools will still be available in the CAP post-2027, and Member States will have greater flexibility in implementing and designing them to support the Mediterranean tree crop farming. Under the Commission’s proposal for the CAP for the period 2028 to 2034 (2), support will remain available for on-farm investments that enhance water efficiency and circularity, as well as water resilient farming practices which improve soil management and water retention. Furthermore, the EU CAP network and EIP-AGRI (3) will continue to promote knowledge sharing and innovative solutions in this field.

E-10-2026-002175.t: Border allowances and equal treatment of military personnel in remote areas of Greece
qt: to the Commission Emmanouil Fragkos (ECR) Subject:

The non-granting of the allowance for remote/border areas and category A problematic areas to military personnel, e.g. in the regional unit of Kilkis, constitutes unfair discrimination in relation to other employees transferred to the same area. Although the Prefecture of Kilkis has been classified as a category A problematic area according to Greek law, military personnel are excluded from the relevant status, even when they serve under corresponding geographical, social and economic conditions to those of other public sector employees. This situation acquires particular significance in light of the increasing cost of living in border areas and the need to strengthen the staffing of critical areas of national importance. In light of Article 20 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union on equality before the law, Article 31 on fair working conditions, and the principles of the European Pillar of Social Rights on fair treatment of workers: 1.

Does the Commission consider that the exclusion of military personnel from financial benefits linked exclusively to the geographical and social conditions of a region may create conditions of indirect unequal treatment within the public sector?

How does the Commission assess the possible impact of the failure to provide corresponding incentives on maintaining adequate staffing and operational readiness in border areas of strategic importance?
Does the Commission intend to examine, within the framework of European policies of social cohesion and territorial balance, the discrimination described in social and economic living conditions?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (20.7.2026) The Commission has no relevant information or competence to evaluate whether the exclusion of military personnel from financial benefits linked exclusively to the geographical and social conditions of a region may create conditions of indirect unequal treatment within the public sector. This is for the national authorities, including the judiciary, to determine. Notably, EU law does not guarantee that all public sector workers receive identical financial benefits. In the area of working conditions, EU law protects against discrimination of parttime or fixed-term workers in comparison to the comparable full-time or permanent workers, and against discrimination on grounds of age, sex, disability, ethnic or racial origin, religion or belief, or sexual orientation. The Commission recognises that retention of adequate staffing in remote and border regions may be affected by economic and social conditions including the cost of living. However, the assessment of the operational readiness of the armed forces and of the incentives considered necessary to ensure sufficient personnel in areas of strategic importance remains a matter for the Greek authorities within their national competence. The Commission does not intend to examine the situation described as such under European social cohesion or territorial balance policies, since the measure at issue concerns the remuneration and service conditions of military personnel, which are primarily a national responsibility. More generally, cohesion policy, including the European Social Fund Plus, plays a key role in reducing disparities between EU regions to promote economic, social and territorial cohesion, but it does not harmonise the pay or allowance systems applicable to national armed forces.

E-10-2026-002174.t: Transfer arrangements for military personnel, protection of family life and housing difficulties of members of the armed forces
qt: to the Commission Emmanouil Fragkos (ECR) Subject:

The absence of a specific framework on transfers of armed forces personnel, based on the number of years of actual service, creates serious social, family and financial consequences for members of the armed forces and their families. Frequent transfers, especially to areas with high housing costs and limited availability of longterm housing, place a heavy burden on family income and act as a barrier to the professional and social stability of military families. At the same time, the constant movement of families places a psychological burden on their school-age children, destabilises family life and leads to increased difficulties in adjusting to school and social settings. What is more, this situation appears to contribute to the increasing number of resignations among military personnel, as well as to the decreasing attractiveness of military schools. In light of Article 7 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union on respect for private and family life, Article 33 thereof on the protection of family and professional life, and the European Pillar of Social Rights: 1.
How does it assess the impact of frequent transfers of military personnel on family cohesion, child protection and work-life balance?
Does it consider that specific support policies are needed for personnel serving in areas with particularly high housing costs?
Are there best practices in Member States for long-term stability in the deployment of military personnel after a specific number of years of service?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (29.7.2026) The Commission is aware that frequent geographic mobility of armed forces personnel may weigh on private and family life, including children’s well‑being and work–life balance. However, the principal tasks of the armed forces of the Member States are expressly included among the essential functions of the State which the European Union must respect. Moreover, Member States’ choices of military organisation are not governed, as such by EU law. The Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union applies to Member States only when they implement EU law1. Issues relating to family cohesion and child protection are addressed at EU level through the social policy provisions of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union and instruments such as Directive (EU) 2019/11582 on work‑life balance for parents and carers. These measures promote reconciliation of professional and family responsibilities and a child‑centred approach, which may inform national solutions, including for military families, where Member States so decide. Housing policy largely remains a national and local responsibility. Nevertheless, several Regulations3 allow Member States to design programmes that improve access to affordable housing and services in high‑cost areas, from which mobile families, including those of military personnel, may benefit on a non‑discriminatory basis. The Commission does not regulate deployment stability schemes for armed forces personnel and does not maintain a comparative inventory of such rules. Within its social policy coordination work, including the European Semester and the Social Open Method of Coordination, it promotes exchange of experience on work‑life balance and social protection more broadly, where Member States choose to share relevant practices.
