E-10-2026-002173.t: European money, Chinese contracts – the Global Gateway and the share of subsidised Chinese state-owned enterprises in EU-funded projects
qt: to the Commission Mariusz Kamiński (ECR) Subject:

Although Europe wants to build an alternative to China’s Belt and Road Initiative under the Global Gateway strategy, Beijing-subsidised companies are increasingly crowding out European competitors from key infrastructure projects. There is a parallel Chinese initiative for almost every European flagship project in Africa. Moreover, Chinese companies are winning contracts for EU flagship projects. The current situation concerning a huge contract for buses powered by natural gas in Dakar, Senegal1, is not an exceptional case, but rather a symptom of systemic failure; European taxpayers’ money is financing China’s supply chains, perpetuating Beijing’s technological standards and supporting China’s global ambitions for power. Meanwhile, China’s expansion is heavily subsidised by the state; companies such as CRRC are an instrument of China’s foreign, economic and – through military-civil fusion – security policy, which does not aim for short-term profit but for strategic market access, building long-term dependencies, imposing Chinese technical standards, and entrenching geopolitical influence. This strategy is being implemented globally and consistently, including in Europe. However, the EU has instruments such as the Foreign Subsidies Regulation (FSR) to counteract this, for example, a few weeks ago, CRRC was excluded from a Portuguese tender and the contract went to a Polish company, PESA2. However, EU-funded projects in third countries are not covered by the FSR. 1.

How does the Commission intend to prevent situations such as the one playing out in Senegal – where unequal processes are causing European companies to lose out to, de facto, the Chinese state – from reoccurring?
https://www.euractiv.com/news/outrage-as-chinese-state-owned-company-poised-to-win-e320m-euproject-in-africa/. 2 https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_26_853. 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (29.7.2026) As regards the current procurement rules on eligibility and exclusion and the implementation of strategic procurement under Global Gateway1, the Commission refers to its replies to the European Parliament’s questions for written answers E-001172/2025 of 5 June 20252 and E002457/2025 of 29 September 20253. As regards the tender for buses powered by natural gas in Dakar, the process is ongoing and under European Investment Bank assessment for compliance with its procurement rules; exclusion of state-backed firms is part of the eligibility criteria and is currently being scrutinised. Under the next Multiannual Financial Framework, in the proposal for a Regulation establishing Global Europe4, the Commission proposes to establish a broader legal basis for restricting or extending EU eligibility rules across all award procedures, including when working with implementing partners. The grounds explicitly include EU restrictive measures, situations of economic coercion, lack of reciprocity under the International Procurement Instrument and other EU strategic interests. These decisions are made by the responsible authorising officer, ensuring that adjustments can be made rapidly. Lastly, it is worth noting that eligibility restrictions will apply, as a rule and for security reasons, to ‘high-risk suppliers’5. These changes reflect the need to provide for a broader legal basis to adjust eligibility rules in line with the EU’s interests. When implementing EU funds in third countries, the Commission also supports the inclusion of strategic procurement, promoting price and quality as award criteria, strengthening environmental, social and governance standards and adopting a more strategic approach to project preparation, appraisal and selection, that considers from an early stage the EU partner countries’ objectives and the competitive advantage of EU economic operators.

qt: to the Commission Sophie Wilmès (Renew), Benoit Cassart (Renew), Olivier Chastel (Renew), Hilde Vautmans (Renew), Wouter Beke (PPE), Elisabetta Gualmini (Renew), Maria Grapini (S&D), Ilhan Kyuchyuk (Renew), Michael McNamara (Renew), Ciaran Mullooly (Renew), Jan-Christoph Oetjen (Renew) Subject:

The revision of the Energy Performance of Buildings Directive1 (EPBD) forms part of the EU’s objective to achieve a zero-emission European building stock. While this objective is consistent with the EU’s climate commitments, the ability to achieve it raises important questions, particularly given the diverse building stocks across the Member States. There is a risk of a disconnect between this objective and the efforts required to fulfil it, which could undermine stakeholder support and, ultimately, the achievement of this objective. In the light of this: 1.

Does the Commission intend to establish stronger monitoring and evaluation mechanisms to assess the real feasibility and implementation of national renovation pathways under the EPBD, and based on the use of such strengthened mechanisms, would the Commission envisage a targeted review of the EPBD or would it in any case keep the Directive as it stands to maintain alignment with climate objectives?

Does the Commission envisage introducing greater operational flexibility or countryspecific adaptation mechanisms to reflect the structural disparities between national building stocks and investment capacities?

How does the Commission intend to ensure that the investment trajectory required under the EPBD remains financially sustainable and socially acceptable, particularly as regards the capacity of Member States to support vulnerable households affected by energy poverty?
OJ L, 2024/1275, 8.5.2024, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2024/1275/oj.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (19.8.2026) Under the Energy Performance of Buildings Directive (EPBD)1, Member States are obliged to regularly review the implementation of minimum energy performance requirements and to prepare and regularly review national building renovation plans, including renovation trajectories. The EPBD requires the Commission to conduct a review by the end of 2028, including an assessment of whether its application, in combination with other legislative instruments, delivers sufficient progress towards a fully decarbonised building stock by 2050. The EPBD already provides ample flexibilities, allowing Member States to tailor measures to their specific national context, including allowing for exemptions that can be justified on unfavourable cost-benefit assessment grounds. The EPBD requires Member States to provide appropriate financial measures and technical assistance, in particular for vulnerable households. The Commission’s March 2026 Report on Energy Efficiency Financing2 promotes the increased use of financial instruments and blended financing solutions, and the recommendation on unlocking private investments3 proposes innovative financing schemes. The Social Climate Fund4 supports vulnerable households, including those in energy poverty. Member States must also use national auction revenues for climate or energy measures, including building decarbonisation while prioritising social aspects.

E-10-2026-002169.t: Portugal’s possible objection to the San Juan mine (in A Gudiña, Galicia) strategic project under the Critical Raw Materials Act
qt: to the Commission Catarina Martins (The Left) Subject:

The San Juan open-pit wolfram mine project in A Gudiña, Galicia, is located just 2 km away from the Portuguese border. It poses a direct threat to the ecosystem of the Montesinho Natural Park and the water resources of the River Rabaçal, the drainage basin of which is shared and is used for public water supply in Portugal. The project promoter recently submitted an application to the Commission for the project to be recognised as a ‘strategic project’ under the Critical Raw Materials Act. Article 7(8) of the act provides that a project cannot be considered for recognition as strategic if a substantiated objection is lodged by a Member State whose territory is concerned by that proposed project. Has the Commission notified Portugal of this request to classify the San Juan mine as a strategic European project? If so, when?

Has Portugal formally raised any objection with the Commission concerning the application for this mining project? If so, what grounds did it give and what is the immediate impact on the Commission’s assessment of the application for the project to be recognised as strategic?
If the Commission has not yet received any formal objection, what is the deadline for Portugal to exercise its right to veto in this specific case?

(6 July 2026) The second selection round of Strategic Projects under the Critical Raw Materials Act (1) (CRMA) is ongoing. The Commission cannot comment on whether projects have applied and cannot prejudge possible outcomes of the assessment. In alignment with Article 7 of the CRMA, the Commission transmitted complete applications to the Member States in which the project is located. E-10-2026-002168.t: EU participation in the Special Tribunal for the Crime of Aggression against Ukraine – implications for Polish WWII victims
qt: to the Commission Arkadiusz Mularczyk (ECR) Subject:

On 15 May 2026, the Commission formally joined the Special Tribunal for the Crime of Aggression against Ukraine1 – a mechanism addressing the same category of international crime committed by Nazi Germany against Poland in 1939, which caused the deaths of approximately 5.9 million Polish citizens. The Commission maintains that World War II (WWII) crimes are a bilateral matter, that no EU competence exists to act on historical crimes within Member States, and that transitional justice instruments apply only externally. The Commission’s participation in the Special Tribunal directly contradicts each of these positions. 1.

How does the Commission reconcile its institutional support for accountability for the crime of aggression against Ukraine with its refusal to support equivalent mechanisms for Polish WWII victims, given that both involve the same category of crime under international law?

Does the Commission’s participation in the Special Tribunal constitute a precedent under Article 3(5) of the Treaty on European Union – which commits the EU to strictly observing international law – that could support a dedicated accountability mechanism for WWII crimes against Poland?
https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_26_1087.
at: (English version) to the Commission Arkadiusz Mularczyk (ECR) (27 May 2026) Subject: EU participation in the Special Tribunal for the Crime of Aggression against Ukraine — implications for Polish WWII victims On 15 May 2026, the Commission formally joined the Special Tribunal for the Crime of Aggression against Ukraine (1) — a mechanism addressing the same category of international crime committed by Nazi Germany against Poland in 1939, which caused the deaths of approximately 5.9 million Polish citizens. The Commission maintains that World War II (WWII) crimes are a bilateral matter, that no EU competence exists to act on historical crimes within Member States, and that transitional justice instruments apply only externally. The Commission’s participation in the Special Tribunal directly contradicts each of these positions. 1. How does the Commission reconcile its institutional support for accountability for the crime of aggression against Ukraine with its refusal to support equivalent mechanisms for Polish WWII victims, given that both involve the same category of crime under international law? 2. Does the Commission’s participation in the Special Tribunal constitute a precedent under Article 3(5) of the Treaty on European Union — which commits the EU to strictly observing international law — that could support a dedicated accountability mechanism for WWII crimes against Poland? (10 July 2026) The Commission attaches utmost importance to accountability for violations of international law and to the preservation of the memory of all victims of war and serious crimes committed in Europe. The Commission recognises the immense suffering endured by the Polish people during the Second World War and honours the memory of the millions of victims of the aggression and occupation by Nazi Germany. The EU’s support for the establishment of the Special Tribunal for the Crime of Aggression against Ukraine reflects its longstanding commitment to upholding the principles of the UN Charter and ensuring accountability for violations of international law. The EU’s engagement is based on the specific legal, institutional and geopolitical circumstances arising from the Russian Federation’s ongoing war of aggression against Ukraine and is conducted within the framework of the competences conferred to the EU by the Treaties. The Commission notes that matters relating to the legal and political consequences of historical events, including questions of reparations and accountability for crimes committed during the Second World War, fall primarily within the framework of international law, the relevant treaties and agreements concluded by the states concerned, and the responsibilities of those states. The Commission remains committed to supporting initiatives, remembrance, historical research, and education aimed at preserving the memory of the victims of the Second World War across Europe.

E-10-2026-002166.t: EUR 10 billion of Spanish pensions funded by the country’s European neighbours?
qt: to the Commission Virginie Joron (PfE) Subject:
EUR 10 billion of Spanish pensions funded by the country’s European neighbours?

Spain is the second-largest recipient of EU post-COVID funds: EUR 60.5 billion in grants and EUR 17.3 billion in loans from the EUR 724 billion European recovery package. The Spanish Court of Auditors reported that in 2024, EUR 2.4 billion of ‘surplus appropriations’ from the EU recovery fund were used to meet unavoidable obligations related to civil service pensions. In 2025, the Socialist Government apparently diverted at least another EUR 8.5 billion to fund pensions, minimum income benefits and other social spending1. The Court of Auditors also noted that the legal basis for those transactions should have been better justified2. 1.
Can the Commission confirm whether the Spanish Socialist Government used over EUR 10 billion from EU funds to pay its civil servants’ pensions in 2024-2025?
How much of that EUR 10 billion sum was funded by France and the French people?

Does the Commission authorise the French Government to use EU funds from the postCOVID recovery plan to finance its pensions and social spending, and what would be the deadline for the last application?
https://www.elmundo.es/economia/2026/05/06/69fb8c83fdddffe7128b4586.html. https://www.euractiv.com/news/spain-under-fire-for-using-eu-post-pandemic-fund-to-patch-pension-
deficit/.
at: (English version) to the Commission Virginie Joron (PfE) (27 May 2026) Subject: EUR 10 billion of Spanish pensions funded by the country’s European neighbours? Spain is the second-largest recipient of EU post-COVID funds: EUR 60.5 billion in grants and EUR 17.3 billion in loans from the EUR 724 billion European recovery package. The Spanish Court of Auditors reported that in 2024, EUR 2.4 billion of ‘surplus appropriations’ from the EU recovery fund were used to meet unavoidable obligations related to civil service pensions. In 2025, the Socialist Government apparently diverted at least another EUR 8.5 billion to fund pensions, minimum income benefits and other social spending (1). The Court of Auditors also noted that the legal basis for those transactions should have been better justified (2). 1. Can the Commission confirm whether the Spanish Socialist Government used over EUR 10 billion from EU funds to pay its civil servants’ pensions in 2024-2025? 2.
How much of that EUR 10 billion sum was funded by France and the French people?

3. Does the Commission authorise the French Government to use EU funds from the post-COVID recovery plan to finance its pensions and social spending, and what would be the deadline for the last application? (18 September 2026) The Commission is aware of the observations made by the Spanish Court of Auditors in this report, particularly their finding that the legal grounds for certain internal budgetary transfers ‘should have been more thoroughly justified (1)’. These observations do not call into question the lawful use of the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF) under EU law. Rather, they pertain to procedural requirements under Spanish budgetary law, which are a matter of domestic accountability. Under the RRF Regulation (2), Member States receive EU funds following the achievement of milestones and targets, which reflect progress in carrying out eligible reforms and investments, in line with requirements laid down in Council implementing decisions. In the Spanish Recovery and Resilience Plan, there is no milestone or target related to pension expenditures, since those are ineligible under the RRF. Payments to Member States under the RRF are financed through NextGenerationEU, with the Commission raising funds on capital markets on behalf of the EU. For grant payments, the funds are repaid by 2058 through the EU budget. For loan payments, Member States are responsible for repaying the RRF loans they receive.

E-10-2026-002165.t: Letter from the European Chief Prosecutor to the Commission on the effective and independent functioning of the European Public Prosecutor’s Office in Greece
qt: to the Commission Nikolas Farantouris (S&D) Subject:

On 22 May 2026, the European Chief Prosecutor sent a letter to the Commission1 with regard to an amendment to the Greek Code of Criminal Procedure, which introduces a special procedure for felonies committed by Members of the Greek Parliament, and the refusal of the Hellenic Supreme Judicial Council to recognise the full effect of the decision taken by the College of the European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO) to renew the mandate of three European Delegated Prosecutors for five years. The letter also refers to a negative effect on the EPPO’s ability to effectively investigate and prosecute offences under its competence, a negative effect on the EPPO’s independence in Greece and serious doubts as to the Greek authorities’ compliance with their obligation of sincere cooperation under Article 4(3) TEU. The fact that the letter was sent in accordance with recital 16 of Regulation (EU) 2020/2092 on a general regime of conditionality for the protection of the Union budget2 raises concerns as to the potential triggering of the procedures set out in the Regulation. In the interest of preventing any loss of funds, can the Commission say: 1.
Has it examined the letter from the European Chief Prosecutor?
How does it assess the recent legislative amendments and decisions in Greece referred to in the letter?
What measures does it intend to propose to the Greek Government in order to address the serious concerns raised by the European Chief Prosecutor in her letter?

https://www.eppo.europa.eu/en/media/news/statement-regarding-recent-developments-affectingeffective-and-independent-functioning. 2 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32020R2092. 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (6.7.2026) The Commission attaches great attention to the concerns and issues brought to its attention by the European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO), in particular where the EPPO considers that they may affect its ability to effectively carry out the tasks entrusted to it under the EPPO Regulation1. In the present case, the Commission has monitored the developments closely and is currently assessing all the information available and received, as well as the concerns raised by the EPPO. The Commission will also continue to follow any further developments.

E-10-2026-002164.t: Harmonisation of asbestos identification technologies in the single market
qt: to the Commission Thomas Pellerin-Carlin (S&D) Subject:

Asbestos causes cancer and known serious diseases. Despite being banned in the European Union since 2005, it remains prevalent in existing buildings (schools, hospitals and homes) and new matrices are increasingly being tested for it, particularly when it comes to certain products intended for children. To strengthen worker protection, the Commission has required that electron microscopy be used to identify asbestos, but has left the choice between scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) up to Member States. However, those two techniques do not offer equivalent performance. Only with TEM can the finest fibres be observed and analysed using electron diffraction, which is vital for reliably distinguishing asbestos fibres from interferents, especially at very low concentrations. In other words, when asbestos is in certain forms, it cannot be detected by SEM, even though it is known to be dangerous in those forms. With a view to harmonising the internal market and providing equivalent protection for workers and the public, does the Commission intend to explicitly recommend, or even mandate, the EU-wide use of TEM to identify asbestos?
at: (English version) to the Commission Thomas Pellerin-Carlin (S&D) (27 May 2026) Subject: Harmonisation of asbestos identification technologies in the single market Asbestos causes cancer and known serious diseases. Despite being banned in the European Union since 2005, it remains prevalent in existing buildings (schools, hospitals and homes) and new matrices are increasingly being tested for it, particularly when it comes to certain products intended for children. To strengthen worker protection, the Commission has required that electron microscopy be used to identify asbestos, but has left the choice between scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) up to Member States. However, those two techniques do not offer equivalent performance. Only with TEM can the finest fibres be observed and analysed using electron diffraction, which is vital for reliably distinguishing asbestos fibres from interferents, especially at very low concentrations. In other words, when asbestos is in certain forms, it cannot be detected by SEM, even though it is known to be dangerous in those forms. With a view to harmonising the internal market and providing equivalent protection for workers and the public, does the Commission intend to explicitly recommend, or even mandate, the EU-wide use of TEM to identify asbestos? (2 July 2026) According to Article 7(6) of Directive 2009/148/EC on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos at work (1) as recently amended by Directive (EU) 2023/2668 (2), fibre counting shall be carried out by electron microscopy or by any alternative method that provides equivalent or more accurate results. A detailed description of the analytical methods, including transmission electron microscopy (TEM), can be found in the Guidelines for managing asbestos-related health and safety risks at work recently published by the Commission (3). It is for the Member States to determine the appropriate methods for achieving the objectives and limit values set out in the directive. Directive 2009/148/EC lays down minimum requirements and Member States may apply or introduce measures ensuring greater protection for workers.

E-10-2026-002163.t: Revision of the regulation on CO<sub>2</sub> emissions from cars
qt: to the Commission Thomas Pellerin-Carlin (S&D) Subject:
Revision of the regulation on CO2 emissions from cars

Regulation (EU) 2019/631 and its ongoing revision (COM(2025)0995) establish limits on emissions for vehicle manufacturers and are based on Article 192 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union. The regulation sets identical quantified targets for all manufacturers throughout the European market and ensures their harmonisation. In light of that, can a Member State unilaterally require that manufacturers’ CO2 emissions be 0 g CO2/km; that is, can they impose a more ambitious target and by an earlier date than is required by the regulation?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (15.7.2026) Regulation (EU) 2019/6311 establishes harmonised CO₂ emission performance standards for new light-duty vehicles and sets binding targets for vehicle manufacturers, who are directly responsible for the emissions intensity of their fleets. As part of the EU’s internal market and climate framework, it aims to provide a common regulatory structure across the EU. Article 193 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union allows Member States to maintain or introduce more stringent environmental measures, provided they are compatible with the Treaties and notified to the Commission. Given the detailed harmonisation introduced by Regulation (EU) 2019/631, the compatibility of any national measure concerning CO₂ requirements for new cars and vans would need to be assessed on a case-bycase basis, taking into account its design, proportionality, and consistency with EU law, including internal market rules and the free movement of goods.
1 Regulation (EU) 2019/631 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 17 April 2019 setting CO2

emission performance standards for new passenger cars and for new light commercial vehicles, and repealing Regulations (EC) No 443/2009 and (EU) No 510/2011, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2019/631/2025-07-09.

E-10-2026-002162.t: Possible overlap of initiatives in EU startup policy and the role of the Europe Startup Nations Alliance (ESNA)
qt: to the Commission Carla Tavares (S&D) Subject:

The mandate of the Europe Startup Nations Alliance (ESNA) was granted by a political declaration signed by 26 EU Member States and by Iceland and Ukraine. It was set up to monitor and help implement startup-friendly policies in Europe and encourage aligned national entrepreneurship ecosystems. In July 2024, the European Commission launched a call for tenders worth half a million euros to develop a pilot platform with goals that appear to significantly overlap with those pursued by ESNA. 1.

Given that ESNA has a mandate to develop a platform with similar goals, what consideration was given to ESNA in the Commission’s decision-making process? How will the Commission ensure that the new platform and ESNA – which is entirely funded by EU money – will complement each other to prevent duplication of efforts and make the most efficient use of public resources?

How does the Commission intend to align its initiatives with the political declaration signed by 26 Member States along with Iceland and Ukraine conferring on ESNA the responsibility of monitoring implementation of start-up friendly policies?
How does the Commission make the most of the tools that ESNA has developed, including its data platform, to support evidence-based policy-making rather than duplicating existing efforts?
at: (English version) to the Commission Carla Tavares (S&D) (27 May 2026) Subject: Possible overlap of initiatives in EU startup policy and the role of the Europe Startup Nations Alliance (ESNA) The mandate of the Europe Startup Nations Alliance (ESNA) was granted by a political declaration signed by 26 EU Member States and by Iceland and Ukraine. It was set up to monitor and help implement startup-friendly policies in Europe and encourage aligned national entrepreneurship ecosystems. In July 2024, the European Commission launched a call for tenders worth half a million euros to develop a pilot platform with goals that appear to significantly overlap with those pursued by ESNA. 1. Given that ESNA has a mandate to develop a platform with similar goals, what consideration was given to ESNA in the Commission’s decision-making process? How will the Commission ensure that the new platform and ESNA — which is entirely funded by EU money — will complement each other to prevent duplication of efforts and make the most efficient use of public resources? 2. How does the Commission intend to align its initiatives with the political declaration signed by 26 Member States along with Iceland and Ukraine conferring on ESNA the responsibility of monitoring implementation of start-up friendly policies? 3. How does the Commission make the most of the tools that ESNA has developed, including its data platform, to support evidence-based policy-making rather than duplicating existing efforts? (30 July 2026) The Commission understands that the question refers to the European Startup and Scaleup Scoreboard (1). The EU Startup and Scaleup Strategy (2) announced that the Commission will set up such a Scoreboard to measure, based on a set of indicators, the performance of the European and national startup and scaleup ecosystems. Commission services worked closely with Europe Startup Nations Alliance (ESNA) in the preparation of the Scoreboard, which is complementary to but different from the data platform developed by ESNA. While some indicators of the Scoreboard are based on ESNA data, the Scoreboard is primarily an annual report providing a detailed comparative analysis of startup and scaleup ecosystems in the EU based on 36 indicators grouped across six dimensions, supported by an online visualisation tool with interactive features. The Scoreboard is also a benchmarking tool, as its scores are indexed to the EU average performance and enable to group countries in four performance groups. The Commission welcomes the work of ESNA supporting the monitoring of implementation of start-up friendly policies. This is complementary to the work of the Commission under the European Semester (3), the EU’s annual cycle for coordinating economic, fiscal, and social policies, with the Commission providing analysis, guidance, and country-specific recommendations to Member States. The ESNA’s Startup Nations Standards represents a valuable source of analysis that can be used in the context of the European Semester. The Commission will continue to use a set of relevant tools and data sources to support evidenced-based policy-making supporting startups and scaleups, taking into account the availability, quality and geographic coverage of data.

E-10-2026-002160.t: Alleged ill-treatment of EU citizens detained following Global Sumud Flotilla interception
qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Maria Zacharia (NI) Subject:

After Israeli forces intercepted the Global Sumud Flotilla in international waters, the release and repatriation of the detained participants – numbering around 430 and including citizens of EU Member States, among them 19 Greeks – has finally been completed. According to public statements by the mission’s organisers, as well as international publications (Reuters), a number of those released have been hospitalised with injuries, and at least 15 people have reported sexual assault, including rape, as well as beatings leading to fractures and being shot with rubber bullets at close range. The Israeli authorities deny the allegations. These are extremely serious accusations which, if confirmed, constitute torture and sexual violence within the meaning of international law and call for an immediate, independent and effective investigation. Can the the Vice-President/High Representative answer the following: 1.
Has the EEAS gathered information on the conditions of detention and the treatment of the EU citizens who were participating in the flotilla?

What steps will the Vice-President / High Representative take to ensure that these allegations of ill-treatment and sexual violence are subject to an independent, impartial and effective investigation, in accordance with international standards?
Does the the Vice-President/High Representative consider that, if substantiated, these incidents raise an issue of compliance with Article 2 of the EU-Israel Association Agreement?
at: (English version) to the Vice-President of the Commission/High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Maria Zacharia (NI) (27 May 2026) Subject: Alleged ill-treatment of EU citizens detained following Global Sumud Flotilla interception After Israeli forces intercepted the Global Sumud Flotilla in international waters, the release and repatriation of the detained participants — numbering around 430 and including citizens of EU Member States, among them 19 Greeks — has finally been completed. According to public statements by the mission’s organisers, as well as international publications (Reuters), a number of those released have been hospitalised with injuries, and at least 15 people have reported sexual assault, including rape, as well as beatings leading to fractures and being shot with rubber bullets at close range. The Israeli authorities deny the allegations. These are extremely serious accusations which, if confirmed, constitute torture and sexual violence within the meaning of international law and call for an immediate, independent and effective investigation. Can the the Vice-President/High Representative answer the following: 1.
Has the EEAS gathered information on the conditions of detention and the treatment of the EU citizens who were participating in the flotilla?

What steps will the Vice-President/High Representative take to ensure that these allegations of ill-treatment and sexual violence are subject to an independent, impartial and effective investigation, in accordance with international standards?
Does the the Vice-President/High Representative consider that, if substantiated, these incidents raise an issue of compliance with Article 2 of the EU-Israel Association Agreement?

(31 July 2026) The EU followed the situation of the Global Sumud Flotilla closely, including through its Delegation to the State of Israel that was in touch with human rights organisations representing the flotilla participants. Following the interception of the Global Sumud Flotilla in international waters and the detention of flotilla participants, the High Representative/Vice-President (HR/VP) reached out to Israel’s Foreign Minister urging to ensure their safety and dignity in detention. The EU Member States bear responsibility for consular protection and the security of their citizens at sea. In line with the Consular Protection Directive (1), the EU Delegation has facilitated coordination of EU efforts on the ground for this consular crisis response. Since 7 October 2023, the EU has provided over EUR 674 million in humanitarian assistance for Palestine. The EU understands the goal of the flotilla’s participants to deliver much-needed aid to people in desperate need. However, the EU discourages such initiatives due to the risks to participants’ safety and potential for escalation, and because the best way to deliver humanitarian assistance to Gaza is through established channels. The HR/VP has engaged repeatedly with Israeli counterparts to convey the EU’s positions. The EU will also continue to support efforts towards independent investigations into violations human rights and of international humanitarian law, including through UN human rights mechanisms. In September 2025, the Commission proposed a partial suspension of the EU-Israel Association Agreement (2) on certain trade matters, following a review of Israel’s compliance with Article 2 of the Agreement conducted by HR/VP with the support of a majority of Member States. The conclusion of the review was that there are indications that Israel would be in breach of its obligations.

E-10-2026-002159.t: Extension of the Polish SENT system to clothing and footwear
qt: to the Commission Marcin Sypniewski (ESN) Subject:

On 17 March 2026, Poland extended its electronic transport monitoring system SENT to clothing and footwear. The SENT system was originally designed to monitor sensitive goods such as fuels or excise goods. Subsequently, a regulation introducing partial exemptions from the SENT notification requirement for selected microenterprises selling on markets subject to a market fee entered into force. However, these exemptions are very limited in scope and do not cover a significant part of legal retail trade, including market halls, e-commerce and many forms of mobile sales. Representatives of the SME sector point out that the current rules create disproportionate administrative burdens, obstacles to the domestic trade in goods legally authorised for sale on the EU market, and unequal treatment of businesses engaged in identical economic activities. In this connection: 1.

Does the Commission consider that extending the transport monitoring system, which was established for goods posing a high tax risk, to the ordinary trade in clothing and footwear is compatible with the principle of proportionality and the principle of free movement of goods under Articles 34-36 TFEU?

Does applying different treatment to businesses engaged in an identical activity solely on the basis of where they conduct their sales infringe the principles of the internal market and fair competition in force in the EU?

Does the Commission intend to examine whether the requirements under the Polish SENT system lead to a disproportionate duplication of existing reporting and control obligations in relation to VAT, customs duties and reporting, particularly for micro, small and medium-sized enterprises?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (17.7.2026) The Commission is aware of the use of transport monitoring systems at national level and of its impact on the transport system. These systems aim at fighting value added tax (VAT) fraud and must be examined in light of Article 273 of the VAT Directive1, which (i) allows Member States to impose obligations other than those laid down in the Directive in so far as necessary to ensure the correct collection of VAT and to prevent evasion; and (ii) provides that those obligations must respect the principle of equal treatment between domestic and intra-EU transactions and must not give rise, in intra-EU trade, to cross-border formalities. The Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) has ruled that every Member State is under an obligation to take all legislative and administrative measures appropriate to ensure the collection of the VAT due on its territory. Further, Member States enjoy in that respect a certain measure of latitude2. Article 273 of the VAT Directive therefore grants Member States a margin of discretion in this area. Nevertheless, the CJEU has also ruled3 that Member States must exercise that discretion in compliance with EU law, in particular with the principle of proportionality. A measure intended to combat tax fraud complies with that principle only if it is suitable for achieving that objective, does not go beyond what is necessary and does not impose disadvantages that are disproportionate in relation to the benefits pursued. The Commission intends to engage with Poland in order to ensure that, while remaining effective in fighting fraud, its transport monitoring system also complies with the principle of proportionality.
1 Council Directive 2006/112/EC of 28 November 2006 on the common system of value added tax, OJ L 347,

11.12.2006, pp. 1-118. 2 Judgment of 17 July 2008, Commission vs Italy, C-132/06, EU:C:2008:412, paragraphs 38 et sequentes. 3 Order of 21 October 2021, EuroChem Agro Hungary Kft. v Nemzeti Adó- és Vámhivatal Fellebbviteli Igazgatósága, C-583/20, EU:C:2021:919.

E-10-2026-002158.t: Right to stay strategy and the outermost regions
qt: to the Commission Sérgio Gonçalves (S&D), André Franqueira Rodrigues (S&D) Subject:

The Commission’s forthcoming right to stay strategy aims to ensure that people can remain and build their future in the place they call home. This objective is particularly relevant for the outermost regions, where permanent structural constraints affect employment, education, training, housing, services and connectivity, limiting opportunities and contributing to emigration. These challenges particularly affect the young. Data shows that the rate of young people not in employment, education or training remains above the EU average (11 %) in most outermost regions and exceeds 30 % in the most affected ones. Considering that the Commission is also preparing a renewed strategy for the outermost regions: 1.

How does the Commission intend to develop concrete synergies between both strategies in their implementation and ensure that the monitoring of the right to stay strategy takes into account the specific constraints of the outermost regions?
Will the right to stay strategy include legislative measures, regulatory adaptations or dedicated funding instruments?
Will the right to stay strategy include specific measures for the outermost regions, notably on youth employment, skills, essential services, housing, transport and digital connectivity?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (8.7.2026) The Commission recognises the unique challenges faced by the outermost regions, particularly for young people, and is committed to continuing to address them, with a focus on the right to stay. 1. The forthcoming Right to Stay Strategy1 and Outermost Regions Strategy2 will be closely aligned and reinforce their respective objectives. Both strategies will have a clear focus on addressing key territorial challenges, such as economic development, skills, essential services, transport, and connectivity, and promoting place-based solutions to address them. 2. Both strategies will take the form of a Commission communication. The Right to Stay Strategy will not create new funding streams or legislative proposals. 3. The Right to Stay Strategy will support the attractiveness of territories, with particular focus on those with declining population and socio-economic challenges, including the outermost regions. It will provide guidance for programming and implementing EU funds, leverage existing EU policies and showcase examples of successful policy implementation. The strategy will also assist the concerned Member States and regions in embedding its objectives into their National Recovery and Resilience Plans and translating them into concrete measures, taking into account their structural social and economic situations in accordance with Article 349 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union. The outermost regions strategy will focus on enhancing competitiveness, resilience, regional integration and social fairness in the outermost regions. It will include commitments to support local employment, education and training, address the housing crisis, and encourage economic dynamism and diversification in these regions.

E-10-2026-002155.t: Safeguarding the competitiveness of the Polish and European road transport sectors
qt: to the Commission Arkadiusz Mularczyk (ECR) Subject:

The Polish road transport sector has been at the forefront of international transport in the European Union for many years and is one of the pillars of the functioning of the common market and European supply chains. Polish hauliers carry out a significant proportion of road transport operations within the EU, ensuring the competitiveness of the European economy and the logistical safety of Member States. However, transport companies operating in the EU, in particular in the SME sector, are under strong pressure due to the impact of the war in Ukraine, the economic slowdown in Germany, rising fuel costs, financing, wages and road tolls. The activity of Ukrainian hauliers also poses an additional challenge, since they operate outside the provisions of the mobility package and benefit from lower operating costs, such as for fuel, when entering the EU, including Poland. As of January 2026, 1 234 Polish transport companies have disappeared and hundreds more are on the brink of bankruptcy. This is why hauliers are warning that the Commission needs to act. In connection to the above: 1.
Is the Commission planning additional support programmes for EU hauliers, particularly from border countries?
Does the Commission intend to review the rules on the liberalisation of road transport between the EU and Ukraine, the effects of which contribute to the collapse of Polish and European hauliers?
Does the Commission envisage any safeguarding mechanisms to ensure a level playing field between EU and Ukrainian hauliers?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (12.8.2026) The Commission is well aware of the concerns raised by the Polish haulage companies in relation to the Agreement between the European Union and Ukraine on the Carriage of Freight by Road (‘the Agreement’)1. As indicated in the reply to Question E-002109/2025, any potential abuse or unfair competition is now prevented following modifications to the Agreement made in 2024. Road transport operations from and to Ukraine represent, on average, only a small proportion of the business of EU hauliers. Ukrainian trucks entering the EU must also comply with international road transport regulations and safety standards. Against this background, the Commission has so far not identified any major disturbance on the EU haulage market arising from the rights granted to Ukrainian haulage undertakings under the Agreement. The Commission has launched a study on the impact of the Agreement on the road transport market which will be delivered by 30 November 2026. The Commission is also assessing if satisfactory progress is made on the alignment of Ukrainian legislation with the relevant EU acquis to ensure a level playing field with EU haulage operators. Any decision to further prolong the Agreement after 31 March 2027 will be subject to satisfactory progress made by Ukraine on alignment with the EU acquis and will be informed by the results of the study2. The Commission has approved, under EU State aid rules, a EUR 1.5 billion (PLN 6.4 billion) Polish scheme to provide State-supported reinsurance of insurance for transport on the territory of Ukraine3.
1 Agreement between the European Union and Ukraine on the carriage of freight by road (OJ L 179, 6.7.2022,

p. 4, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/agree_internation/2022/1158/oj), amended by the Agreement between the European Union and Ukraine amending the Agreement between the European Union and Ukraine on the Carriage of Freight by Road of 29 June 2022 (OJ L, 2024/1878, 2.7.2024, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/agree_internation/2024/1878/oj). 2 In accordance with Council Decision (EU) 2025/1997 of 25 September 2025on the position to be taken on behalf of the European Union within the Joint Committee established by the Agreement between the European Union and Ukraine on the carriage of freight by road as regards the continuation of the Agreement (OJ L 2025/1997, 1.10.2025). 3 https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_25_971.

E-10-2026-002154.t: Measures to monitor jet fuel prices and safeguard passenger rights in European air transport
qt: to the Commission Mariateresa Vivaldini (ECR), Sergio Berlato (ECR), Chiara Gemma (ECR), Elena Donazzan (ECR), Paolo Inselvini (ECR), Alberico Gambino (ECR), Daniele Polato (ECR), Carlo Ciccioli (ECR), Michele Picaro (ECR), Francesco Ventola (ECR) Subject:

In light of the recent statements by Commissioner Apostolos Tzitzikostas, according to which any potential flight cancellations would stem from increases in jet fuel prices rather than from an immediate fuel shortage, and considering that the Commission has announced guidance for the transport and tourism sectors in relation to the crisis in the Middle East, the Commission is asked: 1.

What instruments does it intend to activate to monitor trends in aviation fuel prices, identify any speculative or distortive practices, and prevent disproportionate effects on airlines’ operating costs and on the continuity of air connections?

How does it intend to ensure that the rise in jet fuel costs does not result in excessive price hikes for passengers or cancellations based solely on commercial considerations, while safeguarding accessibility, competition, and the protection of travellers’ rights in the European air transport market?

Does it intend to strengthen coordination with Member States, national regulatory authorities, the European Union Aviation Safety Agency and competition authorities to ensure transparency regarding costs, supply availability, and compliance with refund and compensation obligations in the event of cancellations?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.7.2026) 1. While fuel prices have risen in Europe, European carriers have been less impacted than US or Asian carriers due to their fuel hedging policies on at least parts of their supply. Consequently, the effect on airlines’ operating costs is mitigated to some extent, which reduces the likelihood of adverse impacts on the continuity of air connections and the provision of air transport services. 2. As announced in the AccelerateEU Communication1, the Commission issued, on 8 May 2026, guidance on the flexibilities offered by EU aviation legislation to ensure a coordinated response across Member States. This covers amongst other travellers and passenger rights2 where the guidance recalls the strong protection granted under EU law, including concerning the rules on price transparency. If the situation worsens and existing flexibilities no longer suffice, the Commission would consider possible responses and, if appropriate, propose targeted amendments to the legislative framework where justified. To strengthen preparedness, and as announced in the AccelerateEU Communication the Commission established a fuel observatory to monitor EU production, imports, exports and fuel stocks. This has improved visibility over supply and demand, helps detect shortages, track stock levels and supports targeted action such as alternative sourcing or coordinated stock releases in the EU. 3. Based, on these measures, the fuel supply situation is also discussed with the Member State authorities on a recurring basis with the Oil Coordination Group. Furthermore, the Commission is monitoring daily the situation and is working closely with Member States, including through regular meetings with aviation directors and national transport contact points.
1 https://energy.ec.europa.eu/publications/accelerateeu-energy-union-affordable-and-secure-energy-through-
accelerated-action_en. 2 http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2004/261/oj.

E-10-2026-002153.t: EU funds used for financing terrorism
qt: to the Commission Charlie Weimers (ECR), Dick Erixon (ECR), Beatrice Timgren (ECR) Subject:

Islamic Relief Worldwide received EU funding to the tune of more than EUR 34 million between 2007 and 20201. In May 2026, previously withheld reports by the German Federal Court of Auditors became public2. It found that Islamic Relief Germany has forwarded large amounts of funds directly to its partner organisations, where scrutiny, transparency and control is more limited. In one case, EUR 240 000 were transferred in suitcases by plane from Germany to Türkiye. Furthermore, it is stated that Islamic Relief Worldwide supports Hamas, and that German public funds have flowed to Hamas indirectly through these organisations. In light of the above: 1.
Does the Commission assess that any of the tens of millions it has distributed to Islamic Relief Worldwide may have flowed directly or indirectly to Hamas or other terror organisations?
Will the Commission commit to removing Islamic Relief Sweden and Islamic Relief Germany from the list of EU humanitarian partners?
Will the Commission examine whether funds distributed to Islamic Relief and associated organisations have been misused and, if so, will the Commission reclaim these funds?

Gior, Europe and the Global Muslim Brotherhood Part 1: European Governmental Funding, https://www.global-influence-ops.com/reports/european-funding-of-the-global-muslim-brotherhood/. 2 https://www.giordano-brunostiftung.de/sites/gbs/files/abschliessende_pruefungsmitteilung_teil_1_geschwaerzt_final.pdf; https://www.giordano-brunostiftung.de/sites/gbs/files/abschliessende_pruefungsmitteilung_teil_2_geschwaerzt_final.pdf. 1
at: (English version) to the Commission Charlie Weimers (ECR), Dick Erixon (ECR), Beatrice Timgren (ECR) (27 May 2026) Subject: EU funds used for financing terrorism Islamic Relief Worldwide received EU funding to the tune of more than EUR 34 million between 2007 and 2020 (1). In May 2026, previously withheld reports by the German Federal Court of Auditors became public (2). It found that Islamic Relief Germany has forwarded large amounts of funds directly to its partner organisations, where scrutiny, transparency and control is more limited. In one case, EUR 240 000 were transferred in suitcases by plane from Germany to Türkiye. Furthermore, it is stated that Islamic Relief Worldwide supports Hamas, and that German public funds have flowed to Hamas indirectly through these organisations. In light of the above: 1.
Does the Commission assess that any of the tens of millions it has distributed to Islamic Relief Worldwide may have flowed directly or indirectly to Hamas or other terror organisations?
Will the Commission commit to removing Islamic Relief Sweden and Islamic Relief Germany from the list of EU humanitarian partners?
Will the Commission examine whether funds distributed to Islamic Relief and associated organisations have been misused and, if so, will the Commission reclaim these funds?

(31 July 2026) The Commission applies strict legal, financial and operational safeguards to all EU-funded actions to prevent any EU funds from benefiting entities or individuals subject to EU restrictive measures or involved in terrorism. All humanitarian aid implemented under the Commission’s responsibility is subject to robust ex-ante assessments, contractual obligations, monitoring requirements and audit and control mechanisms. EU-funded partners must comply with the applicable EU legal framework. The actions implemented by Islamic Relief in the past have been subject to the standard audit, control and monitoring procedures applicable under EU-funded humanitarian actions. In this context, the Commission has no evidence at present that EU humanitarian funding provided has been diverted to Hamas or to terrorist organisations. The Commission notes that the reports of the German Federal Court of Auditors do not contain direct evidence that funds were transferred to the Muslim Brotherhood or Hamas, or that Islamic Relief used such funds to finance terrorist attacks. As regards the status of Islamic Relief Sweden and Islamic Relief Germany as EU humanitarian partners, the Commission continuously assesses whether partner organisations comply with the conditions required to obtain and keep the EU humanitarian certificate. Any decision affecting the eligibility of a partner would need to be based on substantiated findings following the relevant procedures. The Commission will continue to monitor the implementation of EU-funded actions closely to safeguard the EU budget and ensure that financial assistance reaches people in need in full compliance with EU law and humanitarian principles, including impartiality and neutrality.

E-10-2026-002152.t: Protecting the EU steel market from overproduction from third countries – need to adopt an effective implementing regulation
qt: to the Commission Jadwiga Wiśniewska (ECR) Subject:

The global overproduction of steel and ever-increasing steel imports to Europe limit the competitiveness of the EU’s steel industry, which is unable to compete with cheap imported steel from countries that do not have to comply with the excessive climate standards arising mainly from the EU ETS. Under a regulation protecting the EU’s steel industry from the negative effects of global overcapacity of steel (2025/0726(COD)), the Commission should urgently adopt an implementing regulation that defines quotas for importing steel for third countries. The new EU trade policy tool will only be effective if it is watertight and based on mechanisms that tangibly reduce the influx of steel from outside the EU. 1.

Is the Commission planning to impose tariff rate quotas (TRQs) on third countries in order to tangibly reduce imports from countries that are flooding the EU with cheap imported steel and, if so, how does it plan to do so?

Ukraine exports significant quantities of steel to the EU. Therefore, quotas for steel imports from Ukraine should be based on an objective share of imports to the EU in 2022–2024. Does the Commission plan to apply specific exceptions or derogations to imports of Ukrainian steel?

Does the Commission intend to ensure the credibility and effectiveness of the future instrument by not using the ‘exceptional circumstances’ clause for EU candidate countries as a basis for increasing their allocations?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (30.7.2026) The Regulation (EU) 2026/1384 addressing the negative trade-related effects of global overcapacity on the EU steel market introduces tariff-rate quotas (TRQs) applicable from 1 July 20261. It provides for 18.3 million tonnes of duty-free imports, while imports exceeding the applicable quotas are subject to a 50% duty. It also introduces a ‘melt and pour’ rule to strengthen transparency. On 30 June 2026, the Commission adopted an Implementing Act2, which entered into force on 1 July 2026, establishing the allocation of the TRQs among third countries in accordance with the criteria and procedures laid down in the Regulation, following an objective and fair methodology with a view to ensuring that the instrument effectively addresses the impact of global steel overcapacity while remaining consistent with the EU's international obligations. With regard to Ukraine, the Commission’s Implementing Act applies the provisions of Article 5(1)(i) of Regulation (EU) 2026/2384 and ensures that the quotas take into account the situation of a candidate country facing an exceptional and immediate security situation. The Commission remains committed to ensuring that the new instrument is implemented in an effective, transparent and proportionate manner and provides meaningful protection for the EU steel market.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202601384. 2 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202601457.

E-10-2026-002151.t: Politicians and senior officials’ corruption and incompatibilities within the rule of law in Spain
qt: to the Commission Dolors Montserrat (PPE), Javier Zarzalejos (PPE) Subject:

For seven years, the Commission and GRECO have been calling on Spain to effectively regulate interest groups, be more transparent and tighten the rules on incompatibilities for senior and former policymakers. The absence of a regulatory framework for lobbying has helped create an environment that is institutionally opaque and leads to serious cases such as the current scandal affecting former Prime Minister José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero, which includes alleged oil businesses, trading gold, business with risky companies such as Huawei, as well as the collection of possible kickbacks and money laundering. In light of the above: 1.

In the Commission’s view, does this case reflect risks in terms of institutionalised corruption, transparency and control of political influence that the Commission and GRECO have been highlighting as points of concern for Spain for several years?

Does the Commission intend to step up the specific follow-up on Spain in the next rule of law report in the light of the judicial investigations into the ‘Zapatero case’, particularly as a result of alleged schemes of influence peddling, money laundering and economic considerations linked to third countries with high risks in terms of corruption and democratic standards, such as Venezuela and China?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.9.2026) The Commission does not comment on individual cases. The Commission closely follows the developments in all Member States, including Spain, as regards the rule of law and anti-corruption efforts, notably under the annual Rule of Law Report. The seventh EU Rule of Law report was published on 17 July 20261. Regarding anti-corruption, the Commission concluded in the 2026 Report that Spain has made limited progress on the recommendations on lobbying and on the rules on conflicts of interest and asset declarations of persons in top executive functions, as well as some progress on the recommendation on addressing the length of investigations and prosecutions of high-level corruption. The Commission recommended Spain to continue the ongoing procedure to adopt legislation on lobbying, including the establishment of a mandatory public register of lobbyists, to strengthen rules on conflicts of interest and asset declarations of persons with top executive functions, and to take forward the legislative process to revise the Code of Criminal Procedure to strengthen the framework for investigations and prosecutions in high-level corruption cases, with a view to reducing delays.
1 https://commission.europa.eu/publications/2026-rule-law-report-communication-and-country-chapters_en.

E-10-2026-002149.t: Enhanced due diligence for public officials involved in significant mortgage transactions
qt: to the Commission Alvise Pérez (NI) Subject:

Directive (EU) 2015/849 requires that credit institutions implement enhanced measures regarding politically exposed persons (PEPs), their family members and close associates, including the identification of the source of their assets and funds. Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 confirms this framework, including for occasional transactions. According to public information based on Spanish legal proceedings, an investigation is under way into the possible illicit origin of funds linked to former Prime Minister José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero and his inner circle, including the early repayment of a mortgage of nearly EUR 500 000 from a joint account with his wife. Without assuming criminal liability, the case raises an issue: if an ordinary EU citizen is subject to strict banking controls for minor transactions, a person holding public office in the EU must be subject to enhanced, documented and verifiable controls. 1.

Does the Commission consider that the current framework ensures that credit institutions document the origin of funds used for significant mortgage repayments made by persons holding public office or by those linked to them?
Is the Commission, together with the European Banking Authority and national financial intelligence units, assessing whether suspicious transaction reports function properly for domestic PEPs?
What role does the Commission assign to the future Anti-Money Laundering Authority in the supervision of higher-risk credit institutions in similar cases?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.7.2026) The EU anti-money laundering framework1 requires obliged entities, including credit institutions, to apply enhanced customer due diligence measures in respect of politically exposed persons, their family members and persons known to be close associates. These measures include taking reasonable measures to establish the source of wealth and the source of funds involved in business relationships or transactions. Compliance with these requirements is the responsibility of obliged entities and is checked by supervisors. Ensuring the proper reporting of suspicious transactions by obliged entities is the task of financial intelligence units and supervisors. The Commission continues to monitor the effective implementation of the EU anti-money laundering framework. Under the new EU anti-money laundering package, the Anti-Money Laundering Authority (AMLA)2 will contribute to ensuring consistent and effective supervision across the EU. AMLA will directly supervise selected high-risk cross-border financial sector entities and will coordinate and support the supervisory system as a whole. AMLA will also support cooperation and information exchange among supervisors and financial intelligence units, thereby strengthening the consistent application of EU anti-money laundering rules.
1 https://finance.ec.europa.eu/financial-crime/anti-money-laundering-and-countering-financing-terrorism-eu-
level_en. 2 https://www.amla.europa.eu/index_en.

E-10-2026-002148.t: CAP funding: beneficiary transparency, beneficial ownership and payment concentration
qt: to the Commission Paolo Borchia (PfE) Subject:

Multinational media investigations1 have revealed that companies owned by the Al Nahyan family and Emirati sovereign wealth fund ADQ and registered in Romania, Spain and Italy received CAP payments worth more than EUR 71 million between 2019 and 2024. According to these reports, EUR 10.5 million were paid out in 2024 alone to Romanian company Agricost, a subsidiary of the UAE-based Al Dahra Group that is among the Union’s biggest agribusinesses and controls roughly 57 000 hectares in Romania’s Great Brăila Island. In the light of the above: 1.
Is the Commission aware of this situation?

Does it hold that the EU’s current beneficiary transparency rules and its capping and degressivity tools can ensure the systematic and harmonised mapping of all ultimate beneficial owners, particularly as regards companies that are owned or controlled by actors outside the EU?

Will the Commission’s upcoming CAP-related legislative proposals include harmonised due diligence requirements and impose greater transparency obligations as regards beneficial ownership, and could the Commission potentially even consider limiting access to funds for entities that are controlled by sovereign wealth funds or are based in third countries?
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/may/07/uae-ruling-royal-family-eu-farming-subsidies.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (28.8.2026) Information about beneficiaries of the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) is made public by Member States as required by the Regulation (EU) 2021/21161. The identification of ultimate beneficial owners is not required by the Regulation. For programmes adopted under and financed from the proposed multiannual financial framework 2028-2034, the Financial Regulation2 in combination with the proposed sectorspecific rules, would require the collection of information on beneficial owners3 under all management modes. The Commission proposal for the National and Regional Partnership Plans Regulation4 requires the Member States to collect data on beneficial owners of beneficiaries, including farmers (natural or legal persons). Therefore, data on beneficial owners of farms which are subsidiaries or transnational arrangements would be collected by Member States based on the Commission’s proposal. For the future CAP rules, the Commission considers that support should go to the farmers whose principal activity is agriculture. Under the Commission’s proposal for the CAP, in addition to the eligibility linked to the agricultural activity, the total annual amount of degressive area-based income support would be reduced for payments exceeding EUR 20 000 and capped at EUR 100 000 per farmer per year. These provisions, as proposed by the Commission, address the risk that income support will go to entities whose principal business activity is not farming. The proposal is currently under negotiation by co-legislators.
1 Article 59 (4) and Article 98 of Regulation (EU) 2021/2116 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-

content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02021R2116-20260101. 2 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32024R2509&qid=1782306972219. 3 Beneficial owners are defined in Article 3(6) of the Anti-Money Laundering (AML) Directive (EU) 2015/849 of the European Parliament and of the Council. 4 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A52025PC0565&qid=1781540097949, Article 63(1)(iv).

E-10-2026-002147.t: The Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation and the EU’s preparations for digital financial markets
qt: to the Commission Ilhan Kyuchyuk (Renew) Subject:

With the rapid development of cryptocurrencies, blockchain technologies and decentralised financial services (DeFi), the European Union faces the challenge of ensuring financial stability, consumer protection and the competitiveness of the European economy amid global digital transformation. Following the entry into force of the Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (MiCA) and growing international interest in digital assets, questions are increasingly being raised about future European policies regarding cryptocurrencies, the supervision of crypto markets, investor protection and the potential impact on the banking system and monetary policy. Against the backdrop of growing participation from institutional investors, the development of stablecoins, the tokenisation of assets and discussions surrounding the digital euro, the European Commission needs to present a clear long-term strategy regarding the crypto industry’s place in the European economy. 1.

What additional regulatory measures does the European Commission plan to implement following the adoption of MiCA to ensure transparency, protect consumers and mitigate systemic risks associated with cryptocurrencies and decentralised finance platforms?

Does the Commission plan to establish a pan-European framework for the taxation of crypto-assets and coordinated mechanisms to combat money laundering, market manipulation and unregulated cross-border transactions?

How does the European Commission assess the potential impact of cryptocurrencies, stablecoins and the digital euro on financial stability, the banking sector and the EU’s competitiveness vis-à-vis the United States and Asian markets in the coming years?
at: (English version) to the Commission Ilhan Kyuchyuk (Renew) (27 May 2026) Subject: The Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation and the EU’s preparations for digital financial markets With the rapid development of cryptocurrencies, blockchain technologies and decentralised financial services (DeFi), the European Union faces the challenge of ensuring financial stability, consumer protection and the competitiveness of the European economy amid global digital transformation. Following the entry into force of the Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (MiCA) and growing international interest in digital assets, questions are increasingly being raised about future European policies regarding cryptocurrencies, the supervision of crypto markets, investor protection and the potential impact on the banking system and monetary policy. Against the backdrop of growing participation from institutional investors, the development of stablecoins, the tokenisation of assets and discussions surrounding the digital euro, the European Commission needs to present a clear long-term strategy regarding the crypto industry’s place in the European economy. 1. What additional regulatory measures does the European Commission plan to implement following the adoption of MiCA to ensure transparency, protect consumers and mitigate systemic risks associated with cryptocurrencies and decentralised finance platforms? 2. Does the Commission plan to establish a pan-European framework for the taxation of crypto-assets and coordinated mechanisms to combat money laundering, market manipulation and unregulated cross-border transactions? 3. How does the European Commission assess the potential impact of cryptocurrencies, stablecoins and the digital euro on financial stability, the banking sector and the EU’s competitiveness vis-à-vis the United States and Asian markets in the coming years? (24 July 2026) The Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (MiCA) (1) established a harmonised EU framework for crypto-assets and related services that protects investors, supports innovation, ensures financial stability, and creates consistent rules across all Member States. As regards the potential impact of cryptocurrencies, stablecoins and the digital euro on financial stability and bank intermediation, the Commission’s impact assessments for MiCA (2) and the digital euro (3) — conducted prior to their adoption — identified key risks and proposed adequate measures to mitigate them. Anti-money laundering obligations have been extended to all crypto-assets service providers, who are required to complete all crypto-asset transfers they operate with information on their originators and beneficiaries (4). In addition, the provision and custody of anonymous crypto-asset accounts will be banned in the EU from July 2027 (5), and Member States are required to extend centralised automated mechanisms or registers allowing the identification of persons holding payment accounts to holders of crypto-asset accounts by that same date (6). The recently amended Directive on Administrative Cooperation (7), mandates automated exchange of tax-relevant crypto-asset data among Member States.

Regulation (EU) 2023/1114 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 31 May 2023 on markets in crypto-assets, and amending Regulations (EU) No 1093/2010 and (EU) No 1095/2010 and Directives 2013/36/EU and (EU) 2019/1937, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2023/1114/oj. SWD(2020) 380 final. SWD(2023) 233 final. Regulation (EU) 2023/1113 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 31 May 2023 on information accompanying transfers of funds and certain crypto-assets and amending Directive (EU) 2015/849, http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2023/1113/oj. See Article 79 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 31 May 2024 on the prevention of the use of the financial system for the purposes of money laundering or terrorist financing, http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1624/oj. Directive (EU) 2024/1640 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 31 May 2024 on the mechanisms to be put in place by Member States for the prevention of the use of the financial system for the purposes of money laundering or terrorist financing, amending Directive(EU) 2019/1937, and amending and repealing Directive (EU) 2015/849, http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2024/1640/oj. Council Directive 2011/16/EU of 15 February 2011 on administrative cooperation in the field of taxation and repealing Directive 77/799/EEC, http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2011/16/oj, as amended by Council Directive (EU) 2025/872 of 14 April 2025 amending Directive 2011/16/EU on administrative cooperation in the field of taxation, http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2025/872/oj.

The Commission remains committed to preserving transparency, consumer protection, and systemic risk mitigation in cryptoasset and decentralised finance markets, and is now assessing whether the EU framework needs to be updated with a public and targeted consultation (8) to gather stakeholder input on emerging risks and regulatory gaps. In that context, it is examining whether and how additional measures are necessary to strengthen the EU’s competitiveness in digital finance vis-à-vis major third-country jurisdictions.
https://finance.ec.europa.eu/news/commission-seeks-feedback-functioning-eu-crypto-assets-rules-2026-05-20_en.

E-10-2026-002145.t: The Commission’s letter concerning Italy’s hunting decree-law
qt: to the Commission Annalisa Corrado (S&D), Camilla Laureti (S&D), Irene Tinagli (S&D), Marco Tarquinio (S&D) Subject:

According to several Italian animal welfare associations and press sources1, the Commission sent a formal letter to the Italian Government on 18 December 2025 highlighting a number of issues with Draft Law No 1552, which is supposed to amend Law No 157/1992 on the protection of wild fauna. The Commission has highlighted certain serious infringements of Directives 2009/147/EC (Birds) and 92/43/EEC (Habitats) contained in the draft law, particularly the provisions which extend hunting periods, allow for the use of optical devices for night hunting and lift certain restrictions concerning the use of live decoys – all of which could lead to an uptick in poaching and wildlife trafficking. The formal letter’s biggest concern is the fact that the Draft Law No 1552 is proposing to water down the role played by the Italian Institute for Environmental Protection and Research (ISPRA), whose opinions would no longer be binding. Though these provisions have been flagged as problematic, they have not undergone substantial changes as Draft Law No 1552 continues its passage through the Italian Parliament. In the light of the above, we ask the Commission: 1.
Has the Italian Government formally replied to the queries contained in the Commission’s communication of 18 December 2025 and what clarifications or commitments, if any, has it made?
Does the Commission think that the law in its present form could be at odds with EU law and trigger infringement proceedings?

(25 August 2026) The Italian authorities have replied to the Commission’s queries posed on draft law no. 1552 on hunting and indicated that they are considering proposing amendments to the legislators in light of the Commission’s observations.
