E-10-2026-002144.t: Call for the release of activists from the ‘Global Sumud Maghreb’ international humanitarian land convoy
qt: to the Commission João Oliveira (The Left) Subject:

The goal of the ‘Global Sumud Maghreb’ international humanitarian land convoy is to deliver urgent humanitarian aid to Palestinians in the Gaza Strip, who are being denied access to basic goods required for survival as a result of Israel’s criminal blockade. On 24 May 2026, ten activists from this international humanitarian convoy were stopped and detained in Sirte, in eastern Libya, while negotiating safe passage through a security checkpoint. The 10 activists, including a Portuguese citizen, have been incommunicado ever since and their whereabouts are unknown. In view of the above: 1.

What steps does the Commission intend to take to establish the whereabouts of the Portuguese citizen and ensure her rights and those of the other members of the international humanitarian convoy are respected?
Will it intervene to help secure the release of the Portuguese citizen and the other activists of the humanitarian convoy and request their free passage to Gaza?

What diplomatic steps is it taking to bring an end to Israel’s criminal blockade against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip, put a stop to Israel’s violations of international law and establish the State of Palestine, as UN resolutions have been advocating for decades?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (7.8.2026) Member States authorities are responsible for consular protection and the security of their citizens. The EU can confirm that the ten activists from the international humanitarian convoy, including the Portuguese national who had been detained in Sirte, Libya, since 24 May 2026, have been released. The Commission welcomes this outcome and the fact that they were able to return safely. The humanitarian situation in Gaza is of grave concern, and the EU has been constantly calling on Israel to allow immediate, unimpeded access and sustained distribution of humanitarian assistance at scale into and throughout Gaza as well as to reopen border crossings and comply with international humanitarian law, thereby upholding its obligations under international law. Since 2023, the EU provided over EUR 674 million in humanitarian assistance for Palestine1, working with trusted and certified partners to ensure aid reaches those most in need. The EU understands the goal of the flotilla’s participants to deliver much-needed aid to people in desperate need. At the same time, the EU discourages such initiatives due to the risks to participants’ safety and potential for escalation, and because the best way to deliver humanitarian assistance to Gaza is to do it through established channels. The EU is firmly committed to a lasting and sustainable peace based on the two-state solution. The EU is ready to contribute to all efforts towards this solution and call on all parties to refrain from actions that undermine its viability. The EU will equally continue to work with regional and international partners, including through the Global Alliance.
1 This designation shall not be construed as recognition of a State of Palestine and is without prejudice to the
individual positions of the Member States on this issue.

E-10-2026-002142.t: Israel’s violent and illegal detention of activists supporting the Palestinian people, including Portuguese nationals
qt: to the Commission João Oliveira (The Left) Subject:

The Global Sumud flotilla, carrying humanitarian aid for Palestinians in the Gaza Strip, was attacked by Israeli military forces on 18 May 2026 around 463 km from the Gaza Strip. The attack 430 members of the flotilla being detained, including Portuguese nationals. Images have circulated showing soldiers beating, dragging, pushing and pinning down activists while Israeli minister Ben-Gvir shouts humiliating words at them. The same minister defended the assaults in the Israeli Parliament. Some members of the flotilla have reported acts of violence and physical, psychological and sexual torture. The way they were treated is unacceptable, indecent and inhumane. The attack and the assaults that followed form part of Israel’s systematic violation of international law, including the genocide of the Palestinian people in the Gaza Strip. The EU has an obligation to act to put an end to these atrocities. Staying silent and failing to speak up and condemn this state of affairs is, from a political or moral standpoint, not acceptable. In view of the above: 1.
Will the Commission condemn Israel’s actions? What steps does it intend to take?
What measures will it adopt to ensure urgent humanitarian assistance reaches the Palestinian population in the Gaza Strip?
How does it justify maintaining the EU-Israel Association Agreement given the breaches of the Palestinian people’s rights and the crimes committed by the Israeli authorities?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.7.2026) The EU has followed the situation around the Global Sumud flotilla very closely. The High Representative/Vice-President was in direct contact with Foreign Affairs Minister of Israel regarding the detention of flotilla members and urged him to ensure their safety and dignity in detention. The EU Delegation to Israel has also been following closely their situation on the ground and has been in contact with Member States who have the primary responsibility for consular issues. In response to increasing calls from Member States to sanction extremist Ministers of the Israeli government, discussions are ongoing in the Council. Since October 2023, the EU provided over EUR 674 million in humanitarian assistance for Palestine, working with trusted and principled partners to ensure aid reaches those most in need. The EU respects the intentions of activists to raise awareness about the catastrophic situation in Gaza and shares the same goals: the immediate and essential delivery of humanitarian aid, end of suffering in Gaza, and respect for international humanitarian law. However, the EU encourages the delivery of humanitarian assistance through traditional means, which are more effective and safer. The EU engaged repeatedly with Israeli counterparts to convey the EU’s positions and request to ensure immediate, unimpeded and sustained aid delivery at scale into and throughout Gaza and reopen all border crossings. Any decision to suspend the EU-Israel Association Agreement requires unanimity in the Council.

E-10-2026-002140.t: Risks linked to public contracts awarded to Huawei in Spanish critical infrastructure
qt: to the Commission Dolors Montserrat (PPE) Subject:

As part of the investigation into the alleged corruption scheme, influence peddling and irregular awarding of contracts in the Ministry led by Óscar Puente and around former president José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero, irregularities have now come to light in connection with a public contract of an estimated value of EUR 400 000, awarded to Huawei Technologies by ADIF for railway data networks of the General Railway Network.1 Given the repeated warnings from EU institutions about the risks associated with high-risk technology providers and the need to reduce strategic dependency on third countries such as China, especially on critical infrastructure: 1.
Has the Commission requested information from the Spanish Government on all contracts awarded to Huawei in the strategic transport and telecommunications sectors?

Does the Commission consider it compatible with the European objectives of risk reduction and economic security for public entities responsible for critical infrastructure to continue awarding sensitive technology contracts to suppliers considered to be highrisk?

nt.html
at: (English version) to the Commission Dolors Montserrat (PPE) (26 May 2026) Subject: Risks linked to public contracts awarded to Huawei in Spanish critical infrastructure As part of the investigation into the alleged corruption scheme, influence peddling and irregular awarding of contracts in the Ministry led by Óscar Puente and around former president José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero, irregularities have now come to light in connection with a public contract of an estimated value of EUR 400 000, awarded to Huawei Technologies by ADIF for railway data networks of the General Railway Network. (1) Given the repeated warnings from EU institutions about the risks associated with high-risk technology providers and the need to reduce strategic dependency on third countries such as China, especially on critical infrastructure: 1.
Has the Commission requested information from the Spanish Government on all contracts awarded to Huawei in the strategic transport and telecommunications sectors?

Does the Commission consider it compatible with the European objectives of risk reduction and economic security for public entities responsible for critical infrastructure to continue awarding sensitive technology contracts to suppliers considered to be high-risk?

(10 August 2026) The Commission has not requested information from the Spanish Government on contracts awarded to Huawei in the transport and telecommunications sectors and does not comment on procurement decisions within the remit of national authorities. The Commission’s concerns with respect to high-risk suppliers in the telecommunications sector are clearly expressed in its communication on the implementation of the EU 5G cybersecurity Toolbox (1). The Commission assessed that Huawei (and ZTE) presents materially higher risks than other 5G suppliers. The Commission considered that Member States’ decisions to restrict or exclude these suppliers from 5G networks are justified and compliant with the 5G Toolbox. The Joint Communication on strengthening economic security (2) also recognised the risk of disruption of the EU’s critical infrastructure by foreign actors, outlining among the objectives in this area the limitation of ownership/control/operation by high-risk entities of EU critical infrastructure and the limitation of dependencies on single suppliers or high-risk suppliers. To overcome the diversity of approaches across Member States, the proposal for a revised Cybersecurity Act (3) proposes, among other things, the mandatory de-risking of European mobile and fixed electronic communications networks from highrisk suppliers in key information and communication technology assets, building on the work already carried out under the Toolbox. Through this proposal, the Commission sends a clear and strong signal that the EU can no longer afford to jeopardise its security and the security of its most critical infrastructure by being dependent on untrusted suppliers.

E-10-2026-002139.t: Transparency regarding the final beneficiaries of CAP aid and foreign investment in European agricultural land
qt: to the Commission David Cormand (Verts/ALE), Cristina Guarda (Verts/ALE), Pär Holmgren (Verts/ALE), Tilly Metz (Verts/ALE), Anna Strolenberg (Verts/ALE), Thomas Waitz (Verts/ALE) Subject:

A recent journalistic investigation has revealed that companies linked to sovereign wealth funds and the ruling family of the United Arab Emirates have received tens of millions of euro in EU common agricultural policy (CAP) subsidies through very large agricultural holdings located in several EU Member States. This situation raises questions about transparency regarding the final beneficiaries of EU aid, land concentration and the monitoring of foreign investments in strategic agricultural assets. While the Commission has launched a pilot project for a European Land Observatory, it is asked to answer the following questions: 1.
Does the Commission plan to make it mandatory to identify the final beneficiaries of farms receiving CAP subsidies, including when these are held through subsidiaries or transnational arrangements?
Will the future European Land Observatory be tasked with monitoring foreign investments in large-scale purchases of agricultural land within the EU?
Does the Commission consider that current CAP rules effectively prevent land concentration and the capture of subsidies by very large farms or financial actors?
at: (English version) to the Commission David Cormand (Verts/ALE), Cristina Guarda (Verts/ALE), Pär Holmgren (Verts/ALE), Tilly Metz (Verts/ALE), Anna Strolenberg (Verts/ALE), Thomas Waitz (Verts/ALE) (26 May 2026) Subject: Transparency regarding the final beneficiaries of CAP aid and foreign investment in European agricultural land A recent journalistic investigation has revealed that companies linked to sovereign wealth funds and the ruling family of the United Arab Emirates have received tens of millions of euro in EU common agricultural policy (CAP) subsidies through very large agricultural holdings located in several EU Member States. This situation raises questions about transparency regarding the final beneficiaries of EU aid, land concentration and the monitoring of foreign investments in strategic agricultural assets. While the Commission has launched a pilot project for a European Land Observatory, it is asked to answer the following questions: 1.
Does the Commission plan to make it mandatory to identify the final beneficiaries of farms receiving CAP subsidies, including when these are held through subsidiaries or transnational arrangements?
Will the future European Land Observatory be tasked with monitoring foreign investments in large-scale purchases of agricultural land within the EU?
Does the Commission consider that current CAP rules effectively prevent land concentration and the capture of subsidies by very large farms or financial actors?

(30 July 2026) For programmes adopted under and financed from the proposed multiannual financial framework 2028-2034, the Financial Regulation (1) requires the collection of information on beneficial owners (2) under all management modes. The Commission proposal for the National and Regional Partnership Regulation (3) requires the Member States to collect data on beneficial owners of beneficiaries, including farmers (natural or legal persons). Therefore, data on beneficial owners of farms which are subsidiaries or transnational arrangements would be collected by Member States. The ongoing Pilot Project for an EU Observatory on Farmland will provide the analytical foundation for this future Observatory. Its work includes assessing the data needs, availability, accessibility and gaps, particularly regarding land transactions and transfers of land use rights, price trends and market behaviour, changes in land use, as well as loss of agricultural and natural land. Upon completion, the pilot’s findings will inform decisions on the Observatory’s establishment, shaping its structure and mandate, in full respect of Member States’ competence in land regulation. Any future role in monitoring foreign investments would be defined at a later stage. Land ownership lies within the competence of the Member States. However, concentration of land use currently does lead to high Common Agricultural Policy support amounts going to a small number of beneficiaries. To address this issue, in its proposal for the future Regulation (4) the Commission has proposed the introduction of mandatory degressivity and capping of area-based income support which would in particular concern large beneficiaries which are deemed to profit from economies of scale.

E-10-2026-002137.t: Exportability and indexation of family‑related social benefits
qt: to the Commission Christine Anderson (ESN) Subject:
Regulation (EC) 883/2004 sets out the coordination of social security systems within the European Union, including the exportability of certain family-related benefits. 1.

Does the Commission take the view that Member States retain some leeway in terms of the indexation of exported family-related benefits on the basis of differences in purchasing power or cost of living?
Has the Commission investigated the fiscal impact of the exportability of family-related benefits on individual Member States?
Are reforms to Regulation (EC) 883/2004 in this area currently under discussion?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (6.7.2026) 1. In its judgment of 16 June 20221, the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) stated that national legislation establishing a mechanism for adjusting the amount of family benefits granted to EU mobile workers, who or whose children are residing in another Member State, to the cost of living in the latter State, is not compatible with Article 45 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU (TFEU), Article 7(2) of Regulation (EU) No 492/2011 and Articles 4 and 67 of Regulation (EC) No 883/2004. The CJEU confirmed this case-law in its judgment of 16 April 20262. Consequently, the Commission is of the opinion that Member States do not maintain any leeway to differentiate the amount of family benefits paid depending on the cost of living in the State of residence of EU mobile workers and/or their children. 2. In this case-law, the CJEU relied on the principles of equal treatment and of exportability of family benefits and confirmed that mobile workers, who contribute to the financing of the social policies of the host Member State through the tax and social security benefits they pay in that State by virtue of their employment, must be able to benefit from them under the same conditions as national workers3. Hence, the Commission does not consider it required to investigate the fiscal consequences of exportability of family-related benefits for individual Member States. 3. The provisional agreement to amend EU social security coordination Regulations4, reached by the co-legislators on 22 April 2026, includes amendments to the coordination rules on family benefits. However, these changes do not provide for the possibility to adjust the amount of family benefits to the cost of living in the Member State of residence, which the CJEU considered incompatible with Article 45 TFEU5 and the secondary legislation, as referred-to above.

content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex:62020CJ0328. 2 Case C-642/24, Commission v Germany, EU:C:2026:303 - https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legalcontent/EN/TXT/?uri=celex:62024CJ0642. 3 Case C-642/24, Commission v Germany, EU:C:2026:303, para. 43. 4 Regulation( EC) No 883/2004 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2004/883/oj/eng and its implementing Regulation (EC) No 987/2009 - https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2009/987/oj/eng. 5 Case C-328/20, Commission v Austria, EU :C :2022 :468, para 57.

E-10-2026-002136.t: Equal treatment and economically inactive EU citizens’ access to family-related social benefits
qt: to the Commission Christine Anderson (ESN) Subject:

In its judgements Dano (C‑333/13) and Alimanovic (C‑67/14), the Court of Justice of the European Union acknowledged that economically inactive EU citizens can be excluded from social benefits under certain conditions. 1.

Does the Commission hold the view that Member States may differentiate between economically active and economically inactive EU citizens when granting access to certain family-related social benefits?
What criteria does the Commission consider particularly relevant when assessing such a differentiation under EU law?
To what extent does the Commission consider protecting the financial viability of national social benefit systems to be a legitimate aim under EU law?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (10.7.2026) As stated by the Court of Justice in Dano1, Member States may exclude from social assistance economically inactive nationals of other Member States who – due to insufficient resources – do not fulfil the conditions for residence based on Directive 2004/38/EC. In Commission v UK2, the Court stated that Member States may require economically inactive mobile EU citizens to reside lawfully in their territory based on Directive 2004/38/EC to receive noncontributory family related social benefits falling into the scope of Article 1(z) of Regulation (EC) No 883/2004. In addition, pursuant to Article 24(2) of Directive 2004/38/EC, Member States may limit for certain periods the entitlement to social assistance and maintenance aid referred to in that provision of mobile EU citizens who are not economically active. By contrast, mobile EU citizens who are workers or who are self-employed persons (or those who retain that status following the cessation of an economic activity3) and their family members are entitled to the same social assistance as nationals from the beginning of their stay4. As also mentioned by the Court in Dano5, the exclusion of economically inactive citizens who are not residing lawfully in their territory based on the Directive 2004/38/EC from equal access to social assistance is intended to prevent such EU citizens from using the host Member State’s welfare system to fund their means of subsistence and to ensure that no unreasonable burden is placed on the social assistance systems of the host Member State.

1 Judgment of the Court of Justice of 11 November 2014, Dano, C-333/13, EU:C:2014:2358, paragraph 82. 2 Judgment of the Court of Justice of 16 June 2016, Commission v UK, C-308/14, ECLI:EU:C:2016:436,

paragraph 86. 3 Judgment of the Court of Justice of 15 September 2015, Alimanovic, C-67/14, ECLI:EU:C:2015:597, paragraphs 53 and 54. 4 Judgment of the Court of Justice of 25 February 2016, García-Nieto, C-299/14, ECLI:EU:C:2016:114, paragraph 44. 5 Judgment of the Court of Justice of 11 November 2014, Dano, C-333/13, EU:C:2014:2358, paragraphs 74 and 76.

E-10-2026-002135.t: Minimum residence requirements for family-related social benefits
qt: to the Commission Christine Anderson (ESN) Subject:
Several Member States impose residence-related conditions on social support and familyrelated social benefits. 1.
To what extent can Member States make access to certain family-related social benefits conditional on a minimum period of legal residence?

Does the Commission consider that such residence requirements can be justified by objectives such as effective integration, administrative control interests or the protection of national social benefits systems?
In that regard, what limits under EU law follow, in particular, from the judgments of the Court of Justice in cases Brey (C-140/12) and CG (C-709/20)?
at: (English version) to the Commission Christine Anderson (ESN) (26 May 2026) Subject: Minimum residence requirements for family-related social benefits Several Member States impose residence-related conditions on social support and family-related social benefits. 1. To what extent can Member States make access to certain family-related social benefits conditional on a minimum period of legal residence? 2. Does the Commission consider that such residence requirements can be justified by objectives such as effective integration, administrative control interests or the protection of national social benefits systems? 3. In that regard, what limits under EU law follow, in particular, from the judgments of the Court of Justice in cases Brey (C140/12) and CG (C-709/20)? (9 July 2026) The principle of non-discrimination on grounds of nationality enshrined in Article 18 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union and laid down specifically in respect of EU citizens within the scope of Directive 2004/38/EC in Article 24 thereof, prohibits not only direct discrimination but also all indirect forms of discrimination which, by the application of other criteria of differentiation, lead in fact to the same result (1). A distinction based on residence, which is liable to operate mainly to the detriment of nationals of other Member States, constitutes indirect discrimination on the ground of nationality which is permissible only if it is objectively justified (2). In this context, a justification put forward by a Member State must be assessed considering the specific situation and measure at hand. For this reason, the Commission cannot take a general position on the suitability of such justifications. According to the case-law of the Court of Justice, mobile EU citizens covered by Regulation (EC) No 883/2004 are entitled to family benefits provided under the legislation of the competent Member States under the same conditions as nationals thereof (3). Family benefits granted independently of individual needs and not intended to cover means of subsistence but to meet family expenses do not fall under the concept of ‘social assistance’ within the meaning of Article 24(2) of Directive 2004/38/EC (4). As the judgments in Brey (5) and CG (6) primarily concern questions regarding access to social assistance, they do not appear relevant to the question of non-discrimination as regards family benefits. However, as noted by the Court in Dano, EU citizens who do not meet conditions for legal residence in the host Member State cannot benefit from Article 24 of Directive 2004/38/EC (7).

Judgment of the Court of Justice of 4 October 2012, C-75/11, Commission v Austria, ECLI:EU:C:2012:605, paragraph 49. Judgment of the Court of Justice of 16 June 2022, Commission v Austria, C-328/20, ECLI:EU:C:2022:468, paragraph 99. Judgment of the Court of Justice of 1 August 2022, S v Familienkasse Niedersachsen-Bremen der Bundesagentur für Arbeit, C-411/20, ECLI:EU:C:2022:602 and Judgment of the Court of Justice of 16 June 2022, Commission v Austria, C-328/20, ECLI:EU:C:2022:468 Judgment of the Court of Justice of 1 August 2022, S v Familienkasse Niedersachsen-Bremen der Bundesagentur für Arbeit, C-411/20, ECLI:EU:C:2022:602, paragraphs 47 and 48. Judgment of the Court of Justice of 19 September 2013, Brey, C-140/12, ECLI:EU:C:2013:565, paragraphs 60-62. Judgment of the Court of Justice of 15 July 2021, CG, C-709/20, ECLI:EU:C:2021:602, paragraphs 68-71. E-10-2026-002133.t: Need for a dedicated European industrial strategy in the light of Electrolux’s planned layoffs and the European household appliances sector’s jobs crisis
qt: to the Commission Elena Donazzan (ECR), Stefano Cavedagna (ECR), Carlo Ciccioli (ECR), Alessandro Ciriani (ECR), Daniele Polato (ECR), Mariateresa Vivaldini (ECR) Subject:

Electrolux’s 11 May announcement that it is planning to lay off 1 700 workers in Italy and close a plant in the country is, along with similar decisions made by Bosch and Beko, testament to the serious crisis that the European household appliances sector is currently experiencing. Europe used to be a leader in this sector, boasting as it did an integrated industrial ecosystem predicated on innovation, quality, research and a diversified and highly skilled production chain. The cold chain is of particular strategic importance, as it is crucial for food security, energy efficiency and quality of life. However, the competitiveness and attractiveness of low-cost production chains based outside the EU are progressively eroding European production capacity and know-how. The partnership that Electrolux has entered into with the Midea Group is also a concern, as this joint venture could result in the divestment of strategic assets, as has been the case in other areas of the green transition. In the light of the above: 1.

What will the Commission do to bring about a European industrial policy which specifically targets both the household appliances sector and the cold chain and aims to combat de-industrialisation and bolster the EU’s strategic autonomy?
Will the Commission strengthen certain EU instruments (state aid, investment screening) with a view to protecting Europe’s strategic production capacities?
How will the Commission go about supporting Member States, including the Italian Government, and ensure that goods are actually being produced in Europe?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (20.7.2026) The Commission is committed to strengthening Europe's industrial base and supporting the competitiveness, resilience and sustainability of European manufacturing industry, including energy-related products and their value chains. Through initiatives to boost innovation, skills, circularity and access to affordable clean energy, the Commission seeks to reinforce the EU's strategic autonomy. State aid tools provide many possibilities to support undertakings active in manufacturing. The Commission has expanded the possibilities for Member States to support certain strategic manufacturing capacities with the Clean Industrial Deal State Aid Framework, helping European businesses meet the twin challenge of preserving competitiveness while advancing the clean transition for key strategic products. The revised EU framework for screening foreign investment further strengthens the EU's ability to address risks to security and public order linked to certain foreign investments, while preserving the EU's openness to investment. Furthermore, the Commission has proposed the Industrial Accelerator Act to boost industrial manufacturing capacities, notably in strategic sectors, through European preference and foreign investment conditions. As regards unfair competition from imports, the Commission acts to defend EU industry where it receives complaints with evidence that such imports are harming the industry in Europe. The Complaints Office of Trade Defence Services can be contacted to discuss the procedure1. To further equalize the level playing field between imports and EU-made products, the Commission proposed to extend the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism to downstream products in the steel and aluminium sectors.
1 trade-defence-complaints@ec.europa.eu

E-10-2026-002132.t: The new fire season: Lack of staff, infrastructure and integrated forest management by the EU and national governments make for a highly flammable situation
qt: to the Commission Kostas Papadakis (NI) Subject:

With over 1 million hectares of land burned – including 400 000 hectares in Natura 2000 protected areas and 500 000 hectares in Greece alone – 2025 was the EU’s most destructive wildfire season. This is the result of EU and national policies, which treat environmental protection as a cost. All this at a time when the EU is fully integrating civil protection structures into war preparations by promoting ‘dual-use investments’ and already weakening and diverting even more attention from dealing with natural phenomena based on capabilities and scientific and technological progress. In view of the above: 1.

What is the Commission’s position on the fact that, after last year’s unprecedented scale of destruction to the natural environment, the separation of forest fire prevention and firefighting is set to continue, as well as the lack of integrated forest management as part of which fireproof design could also be effectively addressed?

How does the Commission intend to address the fact that there are still huge shortages of personnel and ground resources, which are also perpetuated by the rescEU mechanism, as it recycles minimal forces and infrastructure from country to country while at the same time the war economy is given a premium?

Why are no modern and science-based measures taken to protect the health and safety of firefighters and, given the carcinogenic nature of firefighting as a profession, why are firefighters still working unacceptable amounts of overtime and unable to take their accumulated leave?
at: (English version) to the Commission Kostas Papadakis (NI) (26 May 2026) Subject: The new fire season: Lack of staff, infrastructure and integrated forest management by the EU and national governments make for a highly flammable situation With over 1 million hectares of land burned — including 400 000 hectares in Natura 2000 protected areas and 500 000 hectares in Greece alone — 2025 was the EU’s most destructive wildfire season. This is the result of EU and national policies, which treat environmental protection as a cost. All this at a time when the EU is fully integrating civil protection structures into war preparations by promoting ‘dual-use investments’ and already weakening and diverting even more attention from dealing with natural phenomena based on capabilities and scientific and technological progress. In view of the above: 1.

What is the Commission’s position on the fact that, after last year’s unprecedented scale of destruction to the natural environment, the separation of forest fire prevention and firefighting is set to continue, as well as the lack of integrated forest management as part of which fireproof design could also be effectively addressed?

Why are no modern and science-based measures taken to protect the health and safety of firefighters and, given the carcinogenic nature of firefighting as a profession, why are firefighters still working unacceptable amounts of overtime and unable to take their accumulated leave?

(6 August 2026) The Commission promotes a holistic, integrated approach to wildfire risk management, as set out in its communicatio n (1), aiming at improving coordination between national, regional and local authorities and across prevention, preparedness, response and recovery. The Commission intends to publish guidance by 2027 on best practices for governance and funding. While Member States remain primarily responsible, this and other proposed actions aim to support coordinated efforts at the EU level. Reflecting a strong political commitment, a Council Recommendation on integrated wildfire risk managemen t (2) was adopted under the Cypriot Presidency. Member States are competent to determine the level of firefighting staff and assets. The Commission’s rescEU (3) capacity acts as a safety net and strengthens crisis response, including for wildfires. It has proved effective in delivering vital assistance to countries in need. Directive 89/391/EEC (4) sets the general EU framework for protecting workers’ safety and health at work and applies to all workers, including firefighters. It is complemented by Directive 2004/37/EC (5), laying down minimum requirements for protecting workers from exposure to carcinogens, mutagens or reprotoxic substances. The Commission tracks scientific and technological developments in occupational safety and health, including the occupational exposure to carcinogens with support from the Advisory Committee on Safety and Health at Work and the European Chemicals Agency.

E-10-2026-002131.t: Destruction of the Lagunas de Ambroz due to the reopening of a sepiolite mine in Madrid
qt: to the Commission Isabel Serra Sánchez (The Left) Subject:

Despite strong public opposition, the Community of Madrid has authorised the Tolsa company to reopen a sepiolite mine in the Lagunas de Ambroz. This will destroy a peri-urban ecosystem that has re-wilded itself. Emptying the large lagoon and clearing its banks goes against the EU’s Nature Restoration Legislation, which requires natural ecosystems and peri-urban green spaces to be protected, conserved and restored. The permits are based on an outdated and deficient environmental impact statement that ignores the presence of new protected species that have recently made the site their home, such as a large colony of sand martins. 1.
Does the Commission consider the authorisation of this operation to comply with the objectives and obligations of Regulation (EU) 2024/1991?

Does the Commission consider an environmental impact statement that does not incorporate recent ecological developments in the area or the presence of new protected species to comply with EU environmental assessment and biodiversity protection requirements?
Will the Commission request information from the Spanish authorities on this authorisation and on the measures to preserve the Lagunas de Ambroz and the protected species found at the site?
at: (English version) to the Commission Isabel Serra Sánchez (The Left) (26 May 2026) Subject: Destruction of the Lagunas de Ambroz due to the reopening of a sepiolite mine in Madrid Despite strong public opposition, the Community of Madrid has authorised the Tolsa company to reopen a sepiolite mine in the Lagunas de Ambroz. This will destroy a peri-urban ecosystem that has re-wilded itself. Emptying the large lagoon and clearing its banks goes against the EU’s Nature Restoration Legislation, which requires natural ecosystems and peri-urban green spaces to be protected, conserved and restored. The permits are based on an outdated and deficient environmental impact statement that ignores the presence of new protected species that have recently made the site their home, such as a large colony of sand martins. 1. Does the Commission consider the authorisation of this operation to comply with the objectives and obligations of Regulation (EU) 2024/1991? 2. Does the Commission consider an environmental impact statement that does not incorporate recent ecological developments in the area or the presence of new protected species to comply with EU environmental assessment and biodiversity protection requirements? 3. Will the Commission request information from the Spanish authorities on this authorisation and on the measures to preserve the Lagunas de Ambroz and the protected species found at the site? (17 July 2026) The Nature Restoration Regulation (1) sets targets at national level to maintain and then increase the total levels of urban green and tree cover. It does not address specific individual planning cases. Lagunas de Ambroz is not in Natura 2000, however, the sand martin is protected under the Birds Directive (2). Therefore, under Article 5, deliberate destruction or damage of nests and eggs, or deliberate disturbance, especially during breeding and rearing, is prohibited where it affects the species’ conservation. Without prejudice to the Commission’s role as guardian of the Treaties, Member States are primarily responsible to ensure compliance with EU law. To support them, the Commission has issued guidance on Article 5 (3), (4), including on extractive activities, related risks and preventive measures. Risks must be assessed case by case, with ongoing monitoring and appropriate site-specific action. The Commission considers that the available national remedies constitute the most appropriate mechanism for the public concerned to exercise their rights and, where appropriate, seek compensation for any damages caused. This avenue is furthermore consistent with the Commission strategic approach to its enforcement policy, focused on systemic issues of non-compliance (5).

E-10-2026-002130.t: Unilateral trade-related measures by Member States targeting Israel and the EU’s exclusive competence in common commercial policy
qt: to the Commission Sebastian Kruis (PfE), Ton Diepeveen (PfE) Subject:

Several Member States, including Spain, Ireland and Slovenia, have recently announced or considered unilateral measures affecting trade relations with Israel or goods originating from Judea and Samaria. At the same time, Article 3(1)(e) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU) provides that the common commercial policy falls under the exclusive competence of the European Union. This raises questions regarding the legal basis of unilateral national measures, their compatibility with EU law, and their impact on the integrity of the internal market. In the light of this: 1.

How does the Commission assess the compatibility of unilateral trade-related measures adopted by individual Member States against Israel or goods from Judea and Samaria with the EU’s exclusive competence in the field of common commercial policy under Article 3 TFEU?
Has the Commission conducted any legal assessment or initiated any procedures regarding Member States that have introduced or announced such unilateral measures, and if so, what were the conclusions?

Does the Commission recognise that allowing Member States to adopt divergent national trade measures against non-EU countries risks undermining the uniformity of EU external trade policy and the functioning of the internal market?
at: (English version) to the Commission Sebastian Kruis (PfE), Ton Diepeveen (PfE) (26 May 2026) Subject: Unilateral trade-related measures by Member States targeting Israel and the EU’s exclusive competence in common commercial policy Several Member States, including Spain, Ireland and Slovenia, have recently announced or considered unilateral measures affecting trade relations with Israel or goods originating from Judea and Samaria. At the same time, Article 3(1)(e) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU) provides that the common commercial policy falls under the exclusive competence of the European Union. This raises questions regarding the legal basis of unilateral national measures, their compatibility with EU law, and their impact on the integrity of the internal market. In the light of this: 1.

How does the Commission assess the compatibility of unilateral trade-related measures adopted by individual Member States against Israel or goods from Judea and Samaria with the EU’s exclusive competence in the field of common commercial policy under Article 3 TFEU?
Has the Commission conducted any legal assessment or initiated any procedures regarding Member States that have introduced or announced such unilateral measures, and if so, what were the conclusions?

Does the Commission recognise that allowing Member States to adopt divergent national trade measures against non-EU countries risks undermining the uniformity of EU external trade policy and the functioning of the internal market?

(30 July 2026) The Commission takes note of the Honourable Member’s question about the legal compatibility with EU law of the measures taken by several Member States, including Spain, Ireland and Slovenia, concerning trade relations with Israel or illegal settlements in occupied Palestinian territories. As explained in the response to the parliamentary Written Question E-002393/2025 (1), the EU has the exclusive competence for the adoption of common commercial policy measures according to Articles 3(1)(e) and 207 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union. However, Article 24 of the Import Regulation (2) sets out the circumstances and conditions in which Member States may adopt certain measures affecting the importation of goods into the EU. In accordance with the case law of the Court of Justice of the European Union, such circumstances must be interpreted narrowly and the Member State concerned is required to substantiate that the conditions for invoking the exception are met. In all cases, Member States have an obligation to notify the Commission if they intend to introduce measures affecting the importation of goods into the EU covered by the common commercial policy. Measures adopted by Member States need to be compliant with the EU’s international commitments and notably be proportionate, designed to meet the objective pursued and not more trade restrictive than necessary.

E-10-2026-002129.t: IMF recommendations, fuel taxation and fiscal sovereignty in Spain
qt: to the Commission Alvise Pérez (NI) Subject:

On 22 May 2026, the International Monetary Fund reportedly urged Spain to phase out broad fuel and energy support measures and to harmonise VAT rates, while recommending targeted protection for vulnerable households. Spain had adopted temporary fuel-tax relief after March 2026 energy price tensions, including a VAT cut on fuels from 21 % to 10 % and a reduction of hydrocarbon duties to EU minimum levels. In normal conditions, taxes accounted for around 50 % of the final petrol price and 43 % of diesel in Spain in 2025. Such measures are socially regressive when millions of workers, self-employed people, rural families and lower-income households have no real alternative to private transport. Removing fuel relief is not a neutral fiscal adjustment; it is an immediate increase in the cost of working, transporting goods and accessing basic services. EU economic governance must not become an instrument for pushing Member States into fiscal harmonisation or indirect tax increases against their citizens. 1.

Does the Commission intend to recommend, request or incentivise Spain, through the European Semester, fiscal surveillance or any EU funding framework, to withdraw fueltax relief or energy-support measures?
Will the Commission rule out linking EU funds, fiscal assessments or country-specific recommendations to VAT harmonisation or higher fuel taxation in Spain?
How will the Commission assess the distributive impact on workers and lower-income households before supporting such measures?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (24.9.2026) 1. In the Recommendation for a Council Recommendation of 3 June 20261, the Commission recommended that Spain act in 2026 and 2027 to ensure that measures addressing higher energy prices are temporary, targeted at addressing the needs of vulnerable households or energy-intensive firms, preserve incentives for energy savings, and remain consistent with the EU fiscal framework. 2. Under Spain’s Recovery and Resilience Plan, agreed measures for tax reform included the entry into force of reforms based on the Committee of Experts’ recommendations or other Ministry of Finance analyses in areas including environmental, corporate, wealth and health taxation, personal income tax on capital income, as well as diesel tax increases. Additionally, where relevant, the European Semester incorporates country-specific policy recommendations on the quality and composition of Member States’ tax systems. 3. With its Affordable Energy Action Plan2 and its AccelerateEU Communication3, the Commission has implemented and assisted Member States in implementing short- and longterm measures to ensure affordable energy and protect consumers from the impacts of the energy crisis, particularly vulnerable households and the most affected sectors. Generally, value-added tax (VAT) rates reduction cannot be targeted to specific users, which makes VAT less efficient in targeting vulnerable consumers. At the same time, Member States have the possibility to, for example, reduce VAT rates as low as 5% to promote electrification. The Commission has assessed the distributional impact of higher fuel prices on households across income groups4.

1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=comnat:COM_2026_0209_FIN. 2 https://energy.ec.europa.eu/strategy/affordable-energy_en. 3 https://energy.ec.europa.eu/strategy/accelerateeu-strengthen-eu-energy-resilience_en. 4 https://op.europa.eu/en/publication-detail/-/publication/21e0877a-7b57-11f1-bf5e-01aa75ed71a1/language-en.

E-10-2026-002128.t: Appointment of the Governor of the Bank of Spain and safeguards for central bank independence
qt: to the Commission Alvise Pérez (NI) Subject:

On 4 September 2024, the Spanish Government announced that José Luis Escrivá, then Minister for Digital Transformation and the Civil Service, would be put forward as Governor of the Bank of Spain. The Bank of Spain’s own website states that he served as a minister between 2020 and 2024 and has been Governor since 2024, while also sitting on the Governing Council and General Council of the European Central Bank. A popular Spanish television channel reported that no serving minister had previously been appointed Governor of the Bank of Spain in democratic Spain. Without questioning the Member States’ formal power to appoint national central bank governors, this immediate transition from the Council of Ministers to a national central bank participating in the Eurosystem and banking supervision framework raises serious concerns about independence, institutional confidence and safeguards against partisan capture. Article 130 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU) requires that national central banks and their decision makers be free from government influence. 1.

Does the Commission consider that appointments without a cooling-off period may undermine the practical effectiveness of Article 130 TFEU and the independence guarantees of the European System of Central Banks?
Will the Commission request information from Spain on the safeguards applied in this appointment?
Will the Commission assess EU-wide minimum standards on cooling-off periods, transparency and conflicts of interest for national central bank appointments?
at: (English version) to the Commission Alvise Pérez (NI) (24 May 2026) Subject: Appointment of the Governor of the Bank of Spain and safeguards for central bank independence On 4 September 2024, the Spanish Government announced that José Luis Escrivá, then Minister for Digital Transformation and the Civil Service, would be put forward as Governor of the Bank of Spain. The Bank of Spain’s own website states that he served as a minister between 2020 and 2024 and has been Governor since 2024, while also sitting on the Governing Council and General Council of the European Central Bank. A popular Spanish television channel reported that no serving minister had previously been appointed Governor of the Bank of Spain in democratic Spain. Without questioning the Member States’ formal power to appoint national central bank governors, this immediate transition from the Council of Ministers to a national central bank participating in the Eurosystem and banking supervision framework raises serious concerns about independence, institutional confidence and safeguards against partisan capture. Article 130 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU) requires that national central banks and their decision-makers be free from government influence. 1. Does the Commission consider that appointments without a cooling-off period may undermine the practical effectiveness of Article 130 TFEU and the independence guarantees of the European System of Central Banks? 2.
Will the Commission request information from Spain on the safeguards applied in this appointment?

3. Will the Commission assess EU-wide minimum standards on cooling-off periods, transparency and conflicts of interest for national central bank appointments? (27 July 2026) Institutional independence is reflected in Article 130 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (1) and Article 7 of the European System of Central Banks (ESCB) and of the European Central Bank Statute (2). The Treaty’s requirement of central bank independence is linked to the primary objective of price stability, which is best served by a fully independent institution with a clearly defined mandate. In this context, institutional independence in relation to Governors of national central banks is a critical component of central bank independence. The Commission would note that these Articles do not provide any specific requirements regarding the appointment of the Governor. Member States are, therefore, competent to set the conditions required for such appointments, provided that they do not conflict with the features of central bank independence, as stated in the Treaty. Notably, once appointed, what needs to be assessed is whether the legal framework and the safeguards in place ensure that the Governor can exercise the mandate independently of any political influence. The Commission, as guardian of the Treaties, will continue to monitor whether the Governors of ESCB central banks exercise their mandate free from political influence.

E-10-2026-002127.t: Plus Ultra rescue, judicial references to Mr Escrivá and safeguards for State aid integrity
qt: to the Commission Alvise Pérez (NI) Subject:

According to press reports, based on an order of Spain’s Audiencia Nacional in the Plus Ultra case, judicial material refers to a meeting on 7 September 2020 between former Prime Minister José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero and José Luis Escrivá, then Minister for Inclusion, Social Security and Migration and now governor of the Bank of Spain. Reports state that Plus Ultra obtained social security certificates saying that it had no overdue debts before it received EUR 53 million from Spain’s SEPI solvency fund, despite later documentation indicating a pre-existing debt of EUR 451 954.79 and a subsequent deferral. This is no longer merely a domestic political controversy. It concerns confidence in State aid controls, institutional independence and the credibility of a national central bank in the Eurosystem. Without presuming criminal liability, the fact that the current governor of the Bank of Spain previously led the ministry whose administration is mentioned in a corruptionrelated judicial investigation raises concerns about conflicts of interest, transparency and due diligence. 1.
Will the Commission ask Spain whether all eligibility conditions and declarations used to grant State aid to Plus Ultra were accurate and compatible with EU State aid rules?
Will the Commission assess whether new judicial information requires a review of Spain’s control mechanisms for SEPI aid?
Will the Commission evaluate EU-level standards for national central bank governors on conflicts of interest/cooling-off periods?

Without presuming criminal liability, the fact that the current governor of the Bank of Spain previously led the ministry whose administration is mentioned in a corruptionrelated judicial investigation raises concerns about conflicts of interest, transparency and due diligence. 1. Will the Commission ask Spain whether all eligibility conditions and declarations used to grant state aid to Plus Ultra were accurate and compatible with EU State aid rules? 2. Will the Commission assess whether new judicial information requires a review of Spain’s control mechanisms for SEPI aid? 3. Will the Commission evaluate EU-level standards for national central bank governors on conflicts of interest/cooling-off periods? (4 August 2026) The Commission does not wish to comment on the ongoing judicial inquiries regarding the airline Plus Ultra. The Commission does not have any information that would justify reopening the case concerning its decision of 31 July 2020 authorising the recapitalisation aid scheme in question, the legality of which under state aid rules has been confirmed by the General Court and the Court of Justice of the European Union (1). The decisions by the relevant administrative bodies to grant individual aid under the recapitalisation aid scheme in question were open to appeal at the time by any interested parties who considered themselves to have been adversely affected. The Spanish scheme in question specifically requires beneficiaries not to have outstanding debts with social security institutions, which, while not a requirement for the aid to be compatible with the single market, is no impediment. The Commission does not intend to take the place of the courts responsible for reviewing the acts of the Spanish administration granting individual aid or the specific involvement of persons holding — or having held — positions within the Spanish administration in connection with the granting of aid to Plus Ultra.

E-10-2026-002125.t: Conclusion of the 10th European Migration Forum (EMF)
qt: to the Commission Marieke Ehlers (PfE) Subject:

At the 10th European Migration Forum (EMF), it was concluded that migrants make a positive economic contribution1. However, this contradicts the facts regarding asylum migration specifically. For example, Statistics Netherlands (CBS) reports an increase in dependency on social assistance among people born outside Europe2. In addition, research by Dr Jan van de Beek (published as ‘Grenzeloze verzorgingsstaat’/‘Borderless Welfare State’) indicates that the average cost to the Treasury per asylum seeker over their lifetime amounts to EUR 800 000 owing to low employment rates and high reliance on the welfare state3. The following questions arise in this regard: 1.
How does the Commission explain the EMF conclusion regarding a ‘positive economic contribution’ in light of the CBS figures on increasing assistance-dependency among non-European migrants?
What is the Commission’s assessment of Van de Beek’s findings that, on balance, each asylum seeker costs Member States EUR 800 000?

Does the Commission acknowledge that, overall, asylum migration does not generate a single cent, but costs the welfare state a considerable amount of money? If not, what specific, independent figures – relating specifically to asylum seekers – can it cite to substantiate the contrary? Is it willing to undertake (further) research to determine the costs incurred per asylum seeker?
Verslag 10e Europees Migratieforum. CBS (2024/48), “Toename bijstand onder mensen geboren buiten Europa”. J. van de Beek, Grenzeloze verzorgingsstaat / Borderless Welfare State.

(31 August 2026) The report of the European Migration Forum (EMF) reflects, among other things, the main take-aways from the EMF roundtable sessions, including that ‘people with migrant backgrounds make a positive economic and social contribution in the EU’. This can refer to EU citizens who are either EU-born but with at least one foreign-born parent, foreign-born EU citizens, or it can also include third-country nationals more broadly. Regarding asylum seekers specifically, the Commission does not comment neither on individual research nor on figures without any reference regarding the estimated fiscal costs respectively benefits per asylum seeker over their lifetime. The recast Reception Conditions Directive (1), which needed to be fully transposed into national law by 12 June 2026, aims to promote self-sufficiency of asylum applicants by providing clear rules on access to labour market. More broadly, the Commission is supporting research on migration via the Horizon Europe 2021-2027 Programme (2) and Eurostat’s work on migrant integration indicators.

qt: to the Commission Georgia Tramacere (S&D), Sandro Ruotolo (S&D), Pina Picierno (S&D), Brando Benifei (S&D) Subject:

Under Italy’s legislation governing digital tickets for shows and amusement parks, online platforms based in other EU countries are also required to obtain prior approval from the Italian Revenue Agency to operate in Italy. In other words, European stakeholders who already have authorisation to operate in other Member States are being saddled with an additional national procedure. According to several sectoral sources, Italy’s legal framework could throw up barriers to ecommerce and limit access to the biggest international online sales platforms for Italy’s amusement parks, thereby putting the latter at a competitive disadvantage compared to their European counterparts. In the light of the above: 1.
Will the Commission formally verify the compatibility of Italy’s relevant legislation with the ‘country of origin’ principle laid down in Directive 2000/31/EC on electronic commerce?
How will the Commission respond if it does indeed transpire that Italy’s laws are at odds with EU legislation, and what measures will it take against Italy?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (28.7.2026) The Commission is aware of the concerns raised regarding the Italian rules applicable to the sale of tickets for amusement parks. On the basis of the information currently available, the Commission has not identified elements suggesting that the measures in question fall within the coordinated field of Directive 2000/31/EC1 on electronic commerce. In particular, the measures appear to regulate certain conditions relating to the purchase and sale of tickets, such as user verification requirements and limitations on the number of tickets that may be purchased, rather than requirements governing the access to, or the pursuit of, an information society service within the meaning of that Directive. The Commission nevertheless continues to monitor the application of EU law by Member States. Should evidence emerge that national measures impose restrictions falling within the scope of Directive 2000/31/EC or otherwise raise concerns under EU law, the Commission may assess their compatibility with the relevant provisions of Union law. The Commission may take appropriate action where it considers that a Member State has failed to comply with its obligations under Union law, including, where appropriate, by initiating infringement proceedings pursuant to Article 258 TFEU2.

E-10-2026-002123.t: Application of the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism
qt: to the Commission Susana Solís Pérez (PPE) Subject:

On 1 January 2026, the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) entered its definitive phase. In the first quarter of 2026, imports from high carbon-intensity countries such as China and India surged significantly. This has raised concerns about whether the full economic liability under CBAM, payable at certificate surrender after the close of the reporting year, will apply to those imports. In particular, a number of importers have questioned whether CBAM obligations apply to goods produced in 2025 but imported on or after 1 January 2026, drawing on interpretations of the Commission Implementing Regulation on the calculation of embedded emissions1. In this context: 1.
Can the Commission clarify whether CBAM obligations are determined solely by the date of import into the EU, regardless of when the goods were produced?

Can the Commission confirm that CBAM certificates must be surrendered, and the corresponding economic liability borne, for all goods imported on or after 1 January 2026, even if produced before that date?
What measures will the Commission take to ensure legal certainty and prevent circumvention of CBAM obligations ahead of the certificate surrender deadline?

Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/2547 of 10 December 2025 laying down rules for the application of Regulation (EU) 2023/956 of the European Parliament and the Council as regards the methods for the calculation of emissions embedded in goods (OJ L, 2025/2547, 22.12.2025, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg_impl/2025/2547/oj). 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (23.7.2026) On 1 January 2026, the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) entered its definitive phase. From 2026 onwards, the CBAM obligations apply for importers which exceed the annual single mass-based threshold. Therefore, importers must request an authorisation and, by 30 September 2027, submit their CBAM declaration and surrender the corresponding number of CBAM certificates for the importation year 2026. For each CBAM good, the CBAM obligations are determined by the date of importation into the EU customs territory. This date corresponds to the date on which the customs declaration is accepted by the national customs authority. In other words: for all relevant goods imported into the EU on or after 1 January 2026, CBAM obligations apply, except where importers remain below the annual single mass-based threshold. In addition to the obligation for importers to get an authorisation, from 1 January 2027 onwards, the quarterly obligation for authorised CBAM declarants to ensure they have a sufficient number of CBAM certificates on their account in the CBAM registry in the course of each importation year will facilitate compliance with the final CBAM financial liability and minimise circumvention risks ahead of the surrender deadline of the CBAM certificates. The Commission, in close cooperation with custom authorities and national competent authorities, is also performing reviews of CBAM declarations in the context of a broader risk management framework. Controls notably include the consistency of CBAM declarations with custom declarations.

E-10-2026-002121.t: Notification and request for clarification: potential non-compliance with the EU rules on association, privacy and the GDPR, reported by 700 NGOs
qt: to the Commission Nicolae Ștefănuță (Verts/ALE) Subject:

On 18 May 2026, the Romanian Senate adopted legislative proposal No L 233/2026 supplementing Government Order No 26/2000 on associations and foundations, which has now passed to the Chamber of Deputies for debate and adoption. Over 700 organisations have flagged up incompatibilities with EU standards in a letter (attached), amid a climate of ever-increasing pressure on civil society. The bill imposes the requirement to publish the identity of donors, along with potentially disproportionate sanctions similar to those assessed in Case C-78/18 (CJEU, 2020). Given its consistent commitment to protecting civil society, can the Commission answer the following questions: 1.

Are the clauses on automatic suspension and dissolution compatible with Articles 12 and 7 of the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights, and might the requirement to publicly disclose a donor’s identity constitute a disproportionate processing of data in the light of Article 5 of the GDPR?
What steps is the Commission planning to take to ensure that this legislative initiative is compliant with the European Democracy Shield and the EU Civil Society Strategy?

Should there be a risk of incompatibility with EU standards, what recommendations would the Commission make to the Romanian authorities to ensure that this legislative act does not unduly restrict civil society activities?

Are the clauses on automatic suspension and dissolution compatible with Articles 12 and 7 of the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights, and might the requirement to publicly disclose a donor’s identity constitute a disproportionate processing of data in the light of Article 5 of the GDPR?
What steps is the Commission planning to take to ensure that this legislative initiative is compliant with the European Democracy Shield and the EU Civil Society Strategy?

Should there be a risk of incompatibility with EU standards, what recommendations would the Commission make to the Romanian authorities to ensure that this legislative act does not unduly restrict civil society activities?

(31 August 2026) The Commission acknowledges the crucial role that civil society plays in vibrant democracies, as underlined in the EU Strategy for Civil Society (1) presented by the Commission in November 2025. In particular, this Strategy puts forward a framework for action at EU and national level to engage with, protect, and support civil society. In this context, the Commission encourages Member States to provide for an open, safe and enabling environment for civil society. As set out in the European Democracy Shield (2), engaged and empowered citizens and an active civil society are the backbone of democracy. The Commission is aware of the Romanian draft legislation referred to by the Honourable Member and of the concerns expressed by a large number of civil society organisations. The Commission is closely monitoring these developments, including when it comes to compatibility with EU law. The Commission also follows the situation regarding the role of civil society organisations as essential checks and balances in the context of the Rule of Law Report. E-10-2026-002119.t: Complaints by consumer associations against very large online platforms for systemic failure to tackle ad-driven financial scams
qt: to the Commission Elena Kountoura (The Left) Subject:

On 21 May 2026, the BEUC, together with 29 consumer associations from 27 Member States, including the Greek associations EKPIZO and KEPKA, submitted1 to the Commission and competent national Digital Services Coordinators formal complaints against very large online platforms, based on Article 53 of the DSA, after an evidence-gathering exercise2, showing their apparent failure to prevent scam ads, deceptive products or prohibited services on their platforms3. According to the evidence gathered between December 2025 and March 2026, nearly 900 advertisements were in breach of EU law. Of these, the platforms only took down 27 % of the ads and rejected or ignored 52 % of the reports. It is claimed that hundreds of financial scams are still ongoing, creating a risk of further financial losses and harm to millions of European consumers4. Considering the upcoming Action Plan on Online Fraud5, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

What steps does it intend to take for an investigation to be conducted into the BEUC’s complaints concerning the compliance of very large online platforms with the obligation to address systemic risks of financial fraud?
What specific enforcement measures does it plan to put in place against platforms that systematically fail to comply with this obligation?

Does it plan to propose tightening the current legislative framework with binding obligations and sanctions for online platforms, in order to prevent, detect more effectively and promptly remove fraudulent ads?

(17 July 2026) According to the EU Value Added Tax (VAT) legislation (1) limited geographical derogations exist for specific territories in Greece (Aegean islands), Portugal (Azores and Madeira), France (Corsica), Spain (Canary Islands, Ceuta, and Melilla), and Austria (Jungholz and Mittelberg). This different treatment was introduced under strict conditions, at the time of adoption of the directive and in line with strict sunset clauses agreed by the Council, tied to insularity, remoteness, or unique geographical constraints. E-10-2026-002117.t: The EU’s unacceptable meeting invitation to the Taliban and the arranged deportation of refugees to Afghanistan
qt: to the Commission Kostas Papadakis (NI) Subject:

Nearly five years after the Taliban returned to Afghanistan with the help of the EU and its allies (i.e. the US), the EU has invited Taliban officials to Brussels for meetings. The purpose of the meeting is to discuss the deportation/‘return’ of Afghan migrants who are forbidden to stay in the EU. The resolution on Afghanistan adopted by the European Parliament in plenary, not only condones the meeting but says nothing about the plan to deport Afghans from the EU and deliver them to the Taliban. In the same context, a few days ago, the EU announced the resumption of the full implementation of the cooperation agreement between the EU and AlSharaa jihadist Syria. In view of the above: 1.

Why is the Commission issuing invitations to representatives of the leadership of the obscurantist Taliban movement and maintaining corresponding relations with Syrian jihadists, whitewashing and financing them to carry out atrocities against the people of Afghanistan and Syria?

What is the Commission’s position on the fact that, by promoting deportations, the EU is prioritising relations and contacts with jihadist gangs such as those in Afghanistan and Syria, which carry out crimes and atrocities against the people of the two countries with a view to terrorising them, while in its Member States they persecute the Palestinian people with unfounded accusations of ‘terrorism’ as they resist Israeli occupation, along with trade unionists who express their solidarity with the people of Palestine?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (12.8.2026) The Commission was asked by 20 Member States and Schengen associated countries in a letter signed by their Ministers in October 2025, to coordinate contacts on returns with the de facto authorities, to ensure a coherent European approach. Their focus is on the return of persons posing a threat to public order or national security. Returns to Afghanistan need to be addressed in a comprehensive and coordinated manner, bearing in mind the challenges arising from the acute humanitarian and human rights situation in Afghanistan. The Commission and Sweden, on behalf of interested Member States, co-chaired a technical-level meeting with representatives of the de facto authorities of Afghanistan responsible for return and readmission, following technical-level discussions in Kabul, in January 2026. The technicallevel meeting aimed to give Member States the opportunity to address practical aspects of the readmission process. 15 Member States participated in the meeting. Operational engagement with the de facto authorities is in line with the Council conclusions of 15 September 20211 and 20 March 20232. It does not constitute nor imply recognition, which remains conditioned upon progress on the EU’s established benchmarks, especially counterterrorism, inclusive governance and human rights, with particular concern for the rights of women and girls. The EU has strongly condemned the systemic violation of human rights. The Commission acts in full respect of the Council conclusions and of its international obligations and will continue its unwavering support to all persons concerned by those violations of human rights. The first high-level political dialogue between the EU and Syria was held in Brussels on 11 May 2026. The dialogue was an opportunity to discuss issues of strategic interest for Syria and the EU, including on migration. The work continues with the authorities and the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees to ensure that the conditions are conducive to safe, dignified and sustainable returns to Syria. The EU is stepping up its work with the Syrian authorities and relevant partners to develop a comprehensive approach to migration and displacement. This means strengthening institutional capacities to address asylum and migration, including returns, and contributing to solutions for internally displaced populations.

E-10-2026-002116.t: Protection of consumers, particularly minors, from predatory practices in mobile video games distributed through major app stores
qt: to the Commission Nicolás González Casares (S&D), Laura Ballarín Cereza (S&D) Subject:

The mobile game Age of Origins allegedly uses manipulative monetisation systems, including dark patterns, misleading advertising and simulated gambling mechanics, to encourage spending by users. Concerns have been raised about inadequate moderation of hate speech and violent threats within the game’s social environment, and inconsistent Pan-European Game Information (PEGI) ratings across platforms. The game also promoted speculative crypto-assets whose collapse caused financial losses to users. Questions arise as to whether Apple and Alphabet (Google Play) fulfilled their responsibilities under EU consumer protection law, namely the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive, the Digital Services Act (DSA) and the Digital Markets Act (DMA). In this context: 1.

Does the Commission consider that very large online platforms under the DSA and app store operators designated as ‘gatekeepers’ under the DMA bear greater responsibility when profiting from harmful or unlawful monetisation and crypto-asset systems targeting minors?

If so, will the Commission consider launching an investigation or coordinated enforcement action into the systemic risks that mobile gaming ecosystems may pose to consumers’ mental health, financial security and fundamental rights?

How will the Commission strengthen EU-wide protection for minors against loot boxes (randomised in-game purchases with unknown rewards), simulated gambling and manipulative monetisation mechanisms in online games through the upcoming Digital Fairness Act and the revision of the Consumer Protection Cooperation Regulation?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (30.7.2026) In recognition of their extensive reach and influence, the Digital Services Act (DSA)1 places additional obligations on designated very large online platforms like Google Play and Apple App Store. Their provider must at least annually diligently identify, assess and mitigate systemic risks on their services, including negative impacts on the wellbeing of minors. The DSA guidelines on the protection of minors2 contain measures to shield minors from certain commercial practices on online platforms that could negatively impact their privacy, safety and security. For example, minors should not be exposed to methods that make financial transactions untransparent or potentially misleading like virtual currencies. The Commission is diligently enforcing the DSA. In September 2025, the Commission asked the Apple App Store and Google Play to provide detailed information on how they assess the presence of fraudulent content and the measures they take to reduce the risks of financial scams, including fraudulent applications imitating legitimate banking, investment or trading apps. In October 2025, the Commission requested information from the Apple App Store and Google Play regarding their measures to ensure that minors are not exposed to harmful apps, like gambling apps, and the effectiveness of their age rating systems. At the national level, for example, the German Bundesnetzagentur is investigating the gaming platform Steam due to possible breaches of the DSA in connection with the Plantation Simulator video game. The ongoing impact assessment for the Digital Fairness Act3 examines if further action is needed to address specific practices like gambling-simulating features (loot boxes) or pay-towin and pay-to-progress features that are widely used in video games. The revision of the Consumer Protection Cooperation Regulation4 will aim to ensure stronger, faster and more deterrent enforcement of EU consumer law, thus also contributing to an enhanced protection of young consumers, including in the digital world.

1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/EN/legal-content/summary/digital-services-act.html. 2 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:C_202505519. 3 https://ec.europa.eu/info/law/better-regulation/have-your-say/initiatives/14622-Digital-Fairness-Act_en. 4 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A02017R2394-20250912.

E-10-2026-002115.t: Prison overcrowding in Italy and violation of prisoners’ fundamental rights
qt: to the Commission Pina Picierno (S&D) Subject:

Overcrowded to the point of 140 % of statutory capacity, Italian prisons are in dire straits. Part of the blame lies with the use of an algorithm which in applying revised criteria for calculating the detention space per prisoner modifies the walkable area of cells in a manner that contravenes case law and allocates non-existent per capita space to inmates. This irregularity was picked up during an inspection of the Regina Coeli prison on 30 September 2025, carried out in the presence of representatives from the NGO Nessuno tocchi Caino (‘Hands Off Cain’), which found that approved cells fell short of minimum standards laid down in Article 35(b) of the Italian Penitentiary Act. The relevant authorities have yet to put forward measures to remedy the situation. In light of the above: 1.

Will the Commission launch a monitoring exercise to gauge the compatibility of detention conditions in Italy with the standards laid down in Article 4 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, with a particular emphasis on the use of algorithmic tools for calculating detention space which alter detention conditions?
Does it consider the failure of the Italian authorities to take regulatory action against established violations to be consistent with the obligations arising from Article 2 TEU?

Will it promote binding, uniform EU-wide standards for calculating prison capacity, in line with recommendation Rec(2006)2 of the Committee of Ministers to Member States on the European prison rules, to prevent methodological differences between countries from being held up as a smokescreen to conceal overcrowding?

To support Member States in this area, on 8 December 2022, the Commission adopted the recommendation on the procedural rights of suspects and accused in pre-trial detention and on material detention conditions (1).
