E-10-2026-002114.t: Tuna fillets in the EU-Indonesia trade agreement
qt: to the Commission Francisco José Millán Mon (PPE), Gabriel Mato (PPE) Subject:

The trade agreement between the EU and Indonesia, particularly the arrangements for tuna fillets, is raising concerns in the European fisheries sector and has recently been drawing extensive media attention from outlets such as La Voz de Galicia1 and ABC2. The agreement fully liberalises tuna fillets, treating them differently from other tuna products, such as tuna loins and canned tuna, which are fortunately still subject to tariff quotas. Fillets are a high value-added segment for the EU fleet, which has also invested heavily to position itself in this niche market and to meet the high health requirements. Given that Indonesia is one of the world’s leading tuna producers: 1.
Has the Commission carried out a specific assessment of the economic impact that could be had on the EU’s tuna fleet due to tariffs on tuna fillets being completely eliminated?

Since it is expected that tuna fillet imports will increase and since they are destined primarily for direct consumption, does the Commission consider the guarantees offered by the standards Indonesian operators are required to meet to be equivalent to those provided by the standards applicable to EU operators, particularly with regard to health and food safety?

https://www.lavozdegalicia.es/noticia/somosmar/2026/05/12/flota-europea-teme-entrada-masiva-filetesatun-indonesio-cumplen-requisitos-ue/0003_202605G12P27992.htm. 2 https://www.abc.es/espana/galicia/flota-atunera-teme-competencia-desleal-acuerdo-comercial20260513201659-nt.html. 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (30.7.2026) Trade in frozen tuna fillets has been fully liberalised, and as of entry into force, in most free trade agreements concluded by the EU to date. No particular concern has been flagged to the Commission in this respect. Throughout the negotiations for the Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement1 (CEPA) with Indonesia, the Commission engaged regularly with stakeholders to identify key interests and sensitivities. It carried out a Sustainability Impact Assessment, looking at potential economic impacts of the agreement, and shared with the co-legislators all the EU tariff offers. In the nine years of CEPA negotiations, the Commission did not receive any indication that a liberalisation of frozen tuna fillets would be disruptive for the EU fleet or industry. The preferential treatment of products identified as sensitive under the CEPA, such as canned tuna and tuna loins, has been carefully handled in the negotiations. The balanced outcome ensures modalities to avoid disruptions for EU industry, through strict rules of origin for all tuna products and tariff-rate quotas calibrated on current trade flows for canned tuna (800 metric tonnes) and for tuna loins (5 000 metric tonnes). For tuna fillets, despite lack of apparent sensitivity, the Commission negotiated a seven-year staging period for the tariff elimination, which provides EU industry with an additional transition period to adjust if necessary. As regards the EU health and food safety rules, the CEPA does not affect their application. Indonesian products placed on the EU market, including frozen tuna fillets, will continue being subject to strict EU rules and related controls.

E-10-2026-002113.t: Acquisition of strategic companies by ‘vulture funds’
qt: to the Commission Anthony Smith (The Left) Subject:

For a number of years, certain buyouts of European strategic companies by investment funds have raised serious concerns about maintaining industrial capacity, employment and strategic sovereignty in the EU. This is the case in France in particular, where a number of acquisitions have recently taken place, including the acquisition of Valdunes, Fonderie de Bretagne and Forges de Tarbes by Europlasma, and of Eurasteel by Syntagma. Owing to a lack of investment and industrial planning, several of these companies are now threatened with closure, even though they specialise in strategic sectors, including defence. These practices can therefore be regarded as part of a ‘vulture fund’ approach, which involves taking control of industrial assets without a long-term industrial strategy, with the sole purpose of appropriating expertise and benefiting from government support. 1.
Does the Commission intend to bolster monitoring and apply the strictest environmental and social standards during acquisitions of strategic companies?
Does it plan to put EU mechanisms in place that require investment and sustained production following acquisitions of strategic companies?
How does it intend to prevent speculative trading that could erode the EU’s industrial sovereignty?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (29.7.2026) Preserving the EU’s industrial sovereignty remains a key priority for the Commission. The Commission also remains committed to ambitious environmental and social conditions in Europe. To contribute to this objective, the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA)1 proposes to impose conditions on certain large foreign direct investments. These conditions are intended to maximise the benefits of such foreign direct investments for the Single Market including by supporting the maintenance and creation of high-quality jobs in the EU. To that end, the IAA requires a minimum employment threshold of 50% EU workers in the context of the foreign direct investment. Moreover, the conditions set out in the proposed IAA also seek to ensure that foreign investors contribute to the EU’s research and development ecosystem by allocating 1% of their investment’s gross annual revenue to such activities. They also promote integration into the EU value chain by introducing as one of the possible conditions that investors endeavour to source inputs from Europe and to publish an investment strategy on their website demonstrating compliance with this obligation. Following the proposal of the Commission of 24 January 2024, the European Parliament and the Council have recently adopted Regulation (EU) 2026/1386 on the screening of foreign investments in the Union and repealing Regulation (EU) 2019/4522. This upgraded framework for the screening of foreign direct investments will contribute to a reinforced and more harmonised protection of the EU’s security and public order.
1 https://single-market-economy.ec.europa.eu/publications/industrial-accelerator-act_en. 2 http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2026/1386/oj.

E-10-2026-002112.t: Europe has an obligation to act quickly on the demographic problem
qt: to the Commission Georgios Aftias (PPE) Subject:

The demographic problem is a major issue that is troubling Greece and the EU as a whole. The time has come to take immediate and decisive measures and initiatives to resolve this issue. The Commission has an obligation to take decisive action. Supporting families with stable work, robust economic growth, easy access to affordable housing, equality in healthcare and education provision and social assistance will help young people to start a family. Economic security must be solid and equal so young people can secure a stable future. In addition, boosting regional development will form the other pillar providing support and effective intervention for the resolution of the demographic problem. Measures to create stable jobs, together with the state care provided to families, are very important factors. The public and private sector can work together to solve the demographic crisis. The demographic problem affects us all. Stability in the finances of young families will help alleviate the problem. In view of the above: 1.
Will the Commission take fresh economic measures to resolve the demographic problem?
Will the Commission support governments’ decisions financially to solve this major problem?

(17 July 2026) Demographic change is impacted by life choices that individuals and families make. Although demographic policies are primarily national competences, the EU supports Member States through policy frameworks and funding. The Demography Toolbox (1) points to EU-supported relevant reforms and investments Member States could implement in their national and regional contexts to address demographic change. The Commission is committed to develop such policies further, also based on their success and interest. Recent initiatives such as the strategy on Intergenerational Fairness (2), the European Affordable Housing Plan (3), the Anti-Poverty Strategy (4) and the Talent Booster Mechanism (5) collectively address diverse consequences of demographic change. The Commission is preparing a dedicated strategy on the Right to Stay, proposing a vision and concrete measures to increase prosperity and quality of life for those regions which are struggling with population decline. The Commission proposal for the next Multiannual Financial Framework (2028-2034) includes addressing demographic change as an objective of both National and Regional Partnership Plans and the European Competitiveness Fund. Member States can already use several financial instruments: —
The European Social Fund Plus (6) (EUR 142 billion for 2021-2027) funds childcare, long-term care, skills development and social innovation.

E-10-2026-002110.t: Recovery fund shortcomings risk taxpayer losses
qt: to the Commission Dick Erixon (ECR), Bert-Jan Ruissen (ECR) Subject:

The European Court of Auditors (ECA) has identified significant shortcomings in the control of the recovery fund1, specifically, that information on final recipients, contractors, subcontractors, actual costs and results achieved is insufficient. Payments are also made on the basis of milestones and targets rather than actual costs. This makes it difficult to assess whether taxpayers’ money has been used efficiently or whether Member States have been able to retain savings when measures turned out to be cheaper than estimated2. Given that the Recovery and Resilience Facility may be the model for future EU spending: 1.
How does the Commission intend to ensure value for money and that the use of taxpayers’ money has not resulted in overfunding, inefficient expenditure or savings that have not been reallocated?

Why does the Commission not systematically request actual cost data per measure when such data is necessary to assess efficiency, especially given that 70 % of Member States already collect this data systematically, which would allow the Commission to benchmark the cost of comparable measures across Member States?
Will the Commission guarantee that future EU instruments will come with binding requirements on full traceability, actual costs and public transparency, the best practices identified by the ECA?

European Court of Auditors’ Special Report 14/2026 on transparency and traceability in the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF), https://www.eca.europa.eu/sv/publications/SR-2026-14. 2 The ECA found that for 15 out of 19 completed measures examined in four Member States, actual costs were lower than estimated, in some cases by up to 25 %. 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.7.2026) The Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF) Regulation1 precludes the Commission from controlling the actual costs incurred by the Member States2. While the Commission has no legal mandate to systematically request information on actual costs, Member States can submit actual cost data when revising their Recovery and Resilience Plans (RRPs). In such situations the Commission duly considers this data and requests clarifications when needed. Where the Commission has been informed of major cost savings under a specific measure, it has requested the respective Member State to address this when revising its RRP. In this context, it should be noted that in its report, the European Court of Auditors has not identified deficiencies in the Commission’s application of the binding RRF legislative framework. The principle of efficiency, among the principles of sound financial management under the Financial Regulation3, requires the best relationship between the resources employed, the activities undertaken and the achievement of objectives. Accordingly, the efficiency of the RRF must be assessed by comparing the payments to the Member States against the achievement of the relevant milestones and targets, and the underlying reforms and investments, as set out and approved by the Council. The recast Financial Regulation4 (adopted in September 2024) widens the scope of the data collection and transparency requirements at EU level. Furthermore, under the Commission’s proposal for future National and Regional Partnership Plans5, information on beneficiaries, recipients, final recipients, contractors and sub-contractors, including the amount of the EU contribution committed, as well as operations, will be collected and published.
1 Regulation (EU) 2021/241 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 12 February 2021 establishing the

Recovery and Resilience Facility, OJ L 57, 18.2.2021, pp. 17–75, http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2021/241/oj. 2 Recital 18 of the RRF Regulation. 3 https://commission.europa.eu/publications/eu-financial-regulation_en. 4 See footnote 3. 5 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52025PC0565.

Spain’s National High Court has indicted former Spanish Prime Minister J. L. Rodríguez Zapatero for the alleged crimes of criminal association, influence peddling, forgery of documents and money laundering in connection with the EUR 53 million public bailout of Plus Ultra, an airline with links to the sanctioned Venezuelan regime. What steps does the Commission intend to take to verify whether the European procedures and obligations relating to transparency, equal treatment, oversight and good administration were violated in providing the bailout?

E-10-2026-002108.t: Liabilities of each participating Member State for the EUR 90 billion EU loan package for Ukraine
qt: to the Commission Fernand Kartheiser (NI), Ondřej Dostál (NI), Georgiana Teodorescu (ECR), Petar Volgin (ESN), Jan-Peter Warnke (NI), Hans Neuhoff (ESN), Diana Iovanovici Şoşoacă (NI), Michael von der Schulenburg (NI), Friedrich Pürner (NI), Fidias Panayiotou (NI), Branislav Ondruš (NI), Milan Uhrík (ESN), Gerald Hauser (PfE) Subject:
Liabilities of each participating Member State for the EUR 90 billion EU loan package for Ukraine

The Council recently adopted the EUR 90 billion loan package for Ukraine covering the years 2026 and 2027. The package is financed through borrowing on the capital markets and is backed by the EU budget. It is being implemented under enhanced cooperation, with three countries having opted out. 1.

What is the legal and financial mechanism, including the contribution key, that determines the liability of each participating Member State for the loan itself and for the associated debt-servicing costs should the loan not be paid back?
What is the estimated or maximum contingent liability for each participating Member State, both in absolute euro amounts and as a percentage of the total package?

If Ukraine does not repay the loan, or if there is any shortfall in the EU budget headroom, how will any additional calls on national budgets be distributed among the participating Member States? Has the Commission carried out an assessment of the impact of these contingent liabilities on the national debt and deficit positions of the participating Member States under the Stability and Growth Pact and the EU’s new fiscal rules?
at: (English version) to the Commission Fernand Kartheiser (NI), Ondřej Dostál (NI), Georgiana Teodorescu (ECR), Petar Volgin (ESN), Jan-Peter Warnke (NI), Hans Neuhoff (ESN), Diana Iovanovici Şoşoacă (NI), Michael von der Schulenburg (NI), Friedrich Pürner (NI), Fidias Panayiotou (NI), Branislav Ondruš (NI), Milan Uhrík (ESN), Gerald Hauser (PfE) (21 May 2026) Subject: Liabilities of each participating Member State for the EUR 90 billion EU loan package for Ukraine The Council recently adopted the EUR 90 billion loan package for Ukraine covering the years 2026 and 2027. The package is financed through borrowing on the capital markets and is backed by the EU budget. It is being implemented under enhanced cooperation, with three countries having opted out. 1. What is the legal and financial mechanism, including the contribution key, that determines the liability of each participating Member State for the loan itself and for the associated debt-servicing costs should the loan not be paid back? 2. What is the estimated or maximum contingent liability for each participating Member State, both in absolute euro amounts and as a percentage of the total package? 3. If Ukraine does not repay the loan, or if there is any shortfall in the EU budget headroom, how will any additional calls on national budgets be distributed among the participating Member States? Has the Commission carried out an assessment of the impact of these contingent liabilities on the national debt and deficit positions of the participating Member States under the Stability and Growth Pact and the EU’s new fiscal rules? (16 July 2026) The amendment of the Multiannual Financial Framework Regulation (1) provides for the coverage of EU debt securities issued to finance the Ukraine Support Loan (2) (UASL) by the EU budget headroom. The contribution key is defined according to the Own Resources Decision (3) and the Making Available Regulation (4). The debt is issued by the EU and the UASL is a contingent liability for the EU. The issuance does not impact Member States’ deficit and debt statistics. In case the contingent liability materialises, the Commission can call for contributions from Member States participating in the enhanced cooperation, to the extent necessary to cover it. The percentage share of each Member State is defined by the gross national income (GNI) key, which is updated annually with the adoption of the annual budget and is available in the financing tables of the annual budge t (5) (Table 5). The actual amount will depend on the applicable GNI key and the financial assistance disbursed under the UASL. In line with the firm support of 25 Heads of State and Government on the margins of the European Council of 18 December 2025 (6) and in accordance with Article 20(2)(j) of Regulation (EU) 2026/467 (7), Ukraine must pay back the loan when it receives war reparations from Russia, or if it (i) no longer fulfils the loan preconditions on effective democratic mechanisms and respect for human rights, or (ii) has engaged in any act of fraud, corruption or any illegal activity detrimental to the financial interests of the EU, for the corresponding value. As for other contingent liabilities backed by the headroom, should they materialise, the Commission will activate all available measures to cover them and protect the financial interests of the EU. The Commission reports annually on the sustainability of contingent liabilities based on Article 256 of the Financial Regulation (8).

E-10-2026-002107.t: Trends in the single-wagon-load services segment of rail freight transport
qt: to the Commission Ondřej Krutílek (ECR) Subject:

Rail freight transport in the European Union has been steadily losing market share for a long time. In many Member States, including the Czech Republic, road transport is now the dominant mode of transport. At the same time, there is a decline in total transport volumes and a significant downturn in the single-wagon-load segment, which is among the fastestdeclining segments of rail freight transport. The Commission should therefore answer the following questions: 1.
How does the Commission assess current developments and the reasons for the decline in rail freight transport in the EU, particularly the decline in the single-wagon-load segment?

What tools and measures does the Commission have at its disposal to strengthen the competitiveness of rail transport vis-à-vis road transport and to support the development of relevant infrastructure, including intermodal terminals and cross-border connections?
Does the Commission take into account the specific characteristics of the single-wagonload segment in its policies, particularly with regard to its economic sustainability?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (17.8.2026) The rail freight market has three main segments. Block trains (coal, metals, chemicals) are declining due to economic change. Intermodal transport (containers and semi-trailers) is growing but not yet enough to compensate for block train losses. Single wagon load faces structural high costs, fragmentation, and empty runs, making it less competitive than road haulage. The Commission is actively strengthening rail freight competitiveness through key initiatives, as outlined in the answer to the Parliamentary question E-003039/20241. One of these initiatives is the pilot deployment of Digital Automatic Coupling. It could make single wagon load more efficient and attractive by making shunting faster, safer and less labour-intensive, since wagons no longer need to be coupled manually. Since the most recent reply to a parliamentary question on this subject in 2025, two new initiatives have entered into force. Firstyl, in March 2026, modernised State aid rules for transport were adopted2. They allow Member States to support actions benefitting freight shippers and rail freight companies. Secondly, in June 2026, the Rail Infrastructure Capacity Regulation entered into force3. It introduces the possibility for short-term capacity allocation, and more reliable train paths for freight.

2024-003039-ASW_EN.html. 2 Communication from the Commission. Guidelines on State aid for land and multimodal transport (C/2026/1656) OJ C, 30.3.2026. 3 Regulation (EU) 2026/1184 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 20 May 2026 on the use of railway infrastructure capacity in the single European railway area, amending Directive 2012/34/EU and repealing Regulation (EU) No 913/2010 (Text with EEA relevance) (OJ L, 2026/1184, 10.6.2026).

In 2025, US investors began talks on acquiring a stake in TurkStream1 and what remains of Nord Stream2. The US’s negotiations with Russia regarding Ukraine also address the role and control of the US in the resumption of Russian gas supplies to the EU3. The head of the Slovak Government recently reported4 that the US was very interested in buying all energy transport infrastructure. The US is expected to become the EU’s main gas supplier this year5. E-10-2026-002105.t: Financing biodiversity conservation and nature restoration
qt: to the Commission César Luena (S&D) Subject:

Environmental degradation and biodiversity loss are increasing the EU’s vulnerability to climate-related and natural disasters, with growing impacts on health, food security and economic resilience. The Nature Restoration Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2024/1991) is a key step towards restoring degraded ecosystems and strengthening Europe’s resilience. However, biodiversity protection and restoration remain largely underfunded, while the Commission appears to place increasing emphasis on market-based instruments such as nature credits. At the same time, concerns persist that harmful subsidies and offset-based projects could continue to undermine EU environmental objectives. 1.

How will the Commission ensure adequate and dedicated funding for the implementation of the Nature Restoration Regulation and broader EU biodiversity objectives under the next multiannual financial framework?
How will the Commission ensure that the development of a nature credits framework complements, rather than replaces, sufficient public funding for nature restoration and biodiversity protection?

With its proposed performance regulation, the Commission aims to mainstream the ‘do no significant harm’ principle across the next EU budget. In the light of this, how will the Commission address environmentally harmful subsidies and prevent nature credits or compensation schemes from undermining the integrity of EU environmental legislation?
at: (English version) to the Commission César Luena (S&D) (20 May 2026) Subject: Financing biodiversity conservation and nature restoration Environmental degradation and biodiversity loss are increasing the EU’s vulnerability to climate-related and natural disasters, with growing impacts on health, food security and economic resilience. The Nature Restoration Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2024/1991) is a key step towards restoring degraded ecosystems and strengthening Europe’s resilience. However, biodiversity protection and restoration remain largely underfunded, while the Commission appears to place increasing emphasis on market-based instruments such as nature credits. At the same time, concerns persist that harmful subsidies and offset-based projects could continue to undermine EU environmental objectives. 1. How will the Commission ensure adequate and dedicated funding for the implementation of the Nature Restoration Regulation and broader EU biodiversity objectives under the next multiannual financial framework? 2. How will the Commission ensure that the development of a nature credits framework complements, rather than replaces, sufficient public funding for nature restoration and biodiversity protection? 3. With its proposed performance regulation, the Commission aims to mainstream the ‘do no significant harm’ principle across the next EU budget. In the light of this, how will the Commission address environmentally harmful subsidies and prevent nature credits or compensation schemes from undermining the integrity of EU environmental legislation? (17 July 2026) The Commission proposals for the 2028-2034 Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) (1) reinforce support to climate and environmental objectives through a legally binding 35% climate and environment spending target covering climate mitigation and adaptation, biodiversity, water, pollution prevention and circular economy. Implementation of the Nature Restoration Regulation (2) is to be supported in particular via the National and Regional Partnership Plans (3), which must be consistent with national restoration plans. The EU facility is set to provide continuity to LIFE activities under the EU programme for the environment and climate action (4) for strategic nature projects, strategic integrated and strategic action projects, environmental governance, enforcement networks and civil society. Innovative tools, including nature credits, may help mobilise private finance and complement public funding, subject to robust safeguards against greenwashing. By rewarding nature positive actions, nature credits may constitute additional revenue streams for land and sea stewards, and retribute the social value of nature restoration and biodiversity protection. Nature credits can be combined with upstream public support to incentivise project holders and derisk investments. An expert group was established to support the Commission’s exploratory work on nature credits, ensuring full alignment with high-level principles such as ecological integrity, transparency and permanence of biodiversity outcomes. The ‘do no significant harm’ principle in the proposed MFF performance framework will be supported by a proportionate guidance to ensure that EU spending does not undermine environmental objectives.

E-10-2026-002104.t: Rejection by the Spanish Parliament of the Agreement between the EU and the United Kingdom in respect of Gibraltar
qt: to the Commission Jorge Buxadé Villalba (PfE) Subject:

On 13 April 2026, the Joint Congress-Senate Committee on the European Union of the Spanish Cortes Generales adopted a resolution urging the Government to reject the EU-UK Agreement in respect of Gibraltar1. The Cortes Generales, which, pursuant to the Constitution, have the power to give or withhold approval for the conclusion of international treaties that are binding upon the State, have rejected the Agreement on the grounds that it runs counter to the Spanish claim of sovereignty over the British colony, which is afforded a much more favourable regime than it enjoyed during the United Kingdom’s membership of the European Union, and indeed than that stipulated under the Treaty of Utrecht. It also condemned the Agreement for failing to equalise taxation between the Gibraltar and Campo de Gibraltar. The Cortes Generales also rejected the Agreement on the grounds that the Government is in breach of the Constitution by not submitting it for prior approval. In light of the above: 1.
Does the Commission still intend to ratify a treaty which has not been approved by the Parliament of the Member State concerned and which holds the title of sovereignty over Gibraltar?
Does it consider that the mere approval by the European Parliament dispenses with the obligation to seek the approval of the national parliament of the State concerned?
https://www.congreso.es/public_oficiales/L15/CORT/BOCG/A/BOCG-15-CG-A-230.PDF#page=2
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.8.2026) 1. The EU-United Kingdom Agreement in respect of Gibraltar represents the last element that completes the legal framework of the relations between the EU and the United Kingdom following Brexit. The legal basis for the conclusion of the EU-United Kingdom Agreement in respect of Gibraltar is Article 217 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU)1, according to which the EU has competence to conclude association agreements with third countries. The procedure for the conclusion of association agreements is foreseen in Article 218 TFEU2. On this basis, the Council takes the decision authorising the signature of the agreement and its provisional application and it is also for the Council to conclude the agreement, after obtaining the consent of the European Parliament. These decisions are adopted by the Council by unanimity. The same procedure was used for the conclusion of the EU-United Kingdom Trade and Cooperation Agreement3. 2. The EU-United Kingdom Agreement in respect of Gibraltar states that it shall be without prejudice to legal positions of Spain and the United Kingdom with regard to sovereignty and jurisdiction and shall not constitute the basis for any assertion or denial of sovereignty including in legal proceedings or otherwise.

qt: to the Commission Jörgen Warborn (PPE) Subject:

‘Think Small First’ has been a guiding principle in EU policy on small businesses for quite some time. It stipulates that the implications for SMEs must be analysed and taken into account at an early stage in the legislative process, and that rules and regulations must be clear, transparent and easy to apply, even for small businesses that do not have access to specialist legal expertise. The Commission communication entitled ‘A Simpler, Clearer and Better Enforced EU Rulebook’ (COM(2026)0380) confirms that the principle should continue to apply and that the needs of SMEs should be taken into account in the drafting of new legislation. Despite this, however, the Commission is still bringing forward highly complex legislative proposals that are often difficult to grasp, with multiple layers of secondary legislation – in the shape of implementing and delegated acts – being laid on top of basic acts that are already inscrutable. With the above in mind: 1.
How does the Commission make sure that the day-to-day concerns of SMEs are taken into account at an early stage in the legislative process?

In addition to the general SME test, what specific mechanisms does the Commission intend to use to prevent disproportionate burdens being placed on SMEs and to ensure that legislation is comprehensible, including for SMEs?

Does the Commission intend to change its approach when it comes to new legislation, so that the situation of SMEs is taken as a starting point, and any additional requirements for larger companies are justified separately?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (30.7.2026) The Commission applies the ‘Think Small First’ principle through tools designed to integrate small and medium-sized enterprise (SME) considerations from the earliest stages of the legislative process. The SME filter1, applied when the Commission publishes its intention to legislate on the ‘Have Your Say’ portal2, identifies which initiatives are relevant for SMEs and thus require a proportionate SME test. The SME test3 assesses the impact of new legislation on SMEs where an impact assessment is required. The SME check, a compulsory annex to impact assessment reports, summarises the key SME test findings for initiatives that are (highly) relevant for SMEs. In addition, targeted SME consultations, including panels supported by the Enterprise Europe Network4, gather direct input on SME challenges. As announced in the 2025 Single Market Strategy5, the Commission is preparing good practice examples of SME-friendly provisions to support EU and national lawmakers in tailoring legislation to SME needs. The Commission presented its approach to designing new legislation which is 'simple-bydesign' in the Communication ‘A Simpler, Clearer and Better Enforced EU Rulebook’6. Future legislation should be simple, designed with implementation in mind from the outset and take into account the needs and capabilities of SMEs. This further reinforces the Commission’s simplification agenda that has a clear target to reduce administrative burdens for SMEs by 35% by the end of the mandate7.

E-10-2026-002102.t: Poultry farms in Poland and their compliance with Directive 2010/75/EU on industrial emissions
qt: to the Commission Tilly Metz (Verts/ALE) Subject:

Media reports1 allege that almost 1 000 poultry farms in Poland are operating without the permits required under Directive 2010/75/EU on industrial emissions (IED). It is further reported that some of these farms have caused environmental damage and water pollution, allegedly in breach of Articles 4, 5 and 14 IED, with negative impacts on the health and wellbeing of local communities. According to reports, Poland’s Chief Inspectorate for Environmental Protection asked all regional inspectorates to review their records and determine how many industrial poultry farms require permits under the IED. It is understood that this exercise found that around 80 % of the farms operating without permits were in fact large enough to require one. In the light of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Is it aware of the scale of non-compliance with the IED by industrial poultry farms in Poland, and can it confirm the findings reported by the Polish authorities?
What assessment has the Commission made of the environmental and public health impact of these alleged breaches?
What action does it intend to take to ensure compliance with EU environmental law and effective enforcement by the Polish authorities?
https://www.thebureauinvestigates.com/stories/2026-03-31/polands-packed-ghost-farms-present-thedanger-of-undetected-disease 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (16.7.2026) The Commission is aware of the allegations1 about non-compliance of poultry farms in Poland with the Industrial Emissions Directive2 (IED) as in March 2026, a complaint on that issue was submitted to the Commission and is currently under analysis. The Commission notes that it is primarily for the Member States to ensure the correct application of and full compliance with EU environmental legislation, including the IED and its provisions on inspections and compliance assurance. The Commission services have reached out to the Polish authorities and asked for further information. Any decisions on the potential follow up and action to be taken will be made once the analysis is finalised. The Commission also notes that, in February 2024, an infringement case for non-conform transposition of some of the IED provisions was opened against Poland3. The case covers ninety grievances and the analysis of the Polish reply to the letter of formal notice is underway. Further steps will be decided after the assessment of the reply is finalised.

E-10-2026-002101.t: Management of foot-and-mouth disease in Cyprus
qt: to the Commission Tilly Metz (Verts/ALE) Subject:

The Republic of Cyprus, as an island Member State, faces specific challenges in managing foot-and-mouth disease (FMD). The Commission confirmed that preventive vaccination cannot be used in disease-free Member States, while emergency vaccination may be applied in affected areas and that Cyprus had notified three FMD outbreaks in Larnaca on 21 February 2026 and received vaccine doses, support from the European Union Veterinary Emergency Team (EUVET) and emergency assistance. In the areas of Cyprus not under the government’s effective control, where the acquis are suspended under Protocol No 10, the EU continues to support animal-health measures, including veterinary assistance and the delivery of 500 000 FMD vaccine doses in February 2026. 1.

Will the Commission urgently request an assessment by the European Food Safety Authority, with input from EUVET and the EU Reference Laboratory for FMD, on the effectiveness and proportionality of emergency vaccination compared with wider culling under Cyprus’s island conditions, and under what timeframe?

Does the Commission intend to examine whether the EU framework on emergency FMD vaccination should be adapted for island Member States, including on recovery periods, movement derogations and recovery arrangements?

Will the Commission strengthen the conditions attached to EU animal-health support in areas not under government control by requiring verifiable FMD-control benchmarks, including surveillance, vaccination records, movement controls, traceability, outbreak reporting and external audit?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.7.2026) The EU legal framework, in particular Regulation (EU) 2016/4291 and Commission Delegated Regulations (EU) 2020/6872, 2020/6893 and 2023/3614 provide the instruments to control and eradicate category A diseases such as foot and mouth disease (FMD). Within this framework, the Commission adopted emergency regionalisation measures5. The Commission has supported Cyprus following its FMD outbreaks via several EUVET deployments6 and 1 029 000 vaccine doses from the EU FMD antigen bank7. The EU Reference Laboratory for FMD, which operates under the Official Controls Regulation8, regularly reviews the testing capacities of national reference laboratories, including Cyprus. The Commission has already requested the European Food Safety Authority to assess control measures for Category A diseases in the framework of the Animal Health Law9, including FMD10. The current framework allows flexibility for emergency vaccination based on risk assessments and foresees a timeframe for lifting the measures and movement derogations. The Commission continues to monitor emergency vaccination implementation in Cyprus and assess whether additional action is needed. In the Turkish Cypriot community, the EU Aid Programme11 finances priority animal-health measures. The Commission applies conditionalities adapted to the island-specific circumstances and the financial support available. It promotes a coordinated and effective disease prevention and response, including by supporting the work of the bicommunal Veterinary Sub-Committee under the Technical Committee for Health. Such response requires both communities to engage. The delegated body Bureau Veritas (Decision 2021/58612) is bound to deliver reliable and independent information on FMD control activities.

E-10-2026-002098.t: Council debate on targeted revision of EU species-protection rules
qt: to the Commission Beatrice Timgren (ECR), Pietro Fiocchi (ECR), Anna Zalewska (ECR), Sander Smit (ECR), Paolo Inselvini (ECR), Alexandr Vondra (ECR) Subject:

Article 8 of the Commission proposal for a regulation on speeding-up environmental assessments1 introduces a population-level and mitigation-based approach: incidental killing or disturbance of protected species would not be considered deliberate where appropriate and proportionate measures prevent significant adverse impacts on the species population. However, key bottlenecks remain outside Article 8, including rules on nests and eggs under the Birds Directive2, breeding sites and resting places under the Habitats Directive3, and protected plant species. These provisions continue to create legal uncertainty, administrative burden and delays for strategic projects even where no significant adverse effects occur at population level. Recent Council discussions, including reported proposals to go beyond Article 8, indicate growing Member State concern that the current framework does not provide sufficient legal certainty for strategic projects4. 1.
Does the Commission agree that Article 8 reflects a broader shift towards populationlevel, mitigation-based species protection?
In the light of the emerging Council debate and the ongoing stress test5, will the Commission assess targeted amendments to the Birds Directive and the Habitats Directive?
Does the Commission consider the current specimen-based approach proportionate for strategic projects where significant population-level impacts are excluded?

https://oeil.europarl.europa.eu/oeil/en/procedure-file?reference=2025/0391(COD). Directive 2009/147/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 30 November 2009 on the conservation of wild birds (ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2009/147/oj). 3 Council Directive 92/43/EEC of 21 May 1992 on the conservation of natural habitats and of wild fauna and flora (ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/1992/43/oj). 4 https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-countries-weigh-letting-industry-kill-more-wildlife/. 5 https://green-forum.ec.europa.eu/nature-and-biodiversity/stress-test-birds-and-habitats-directives_en. 1 2
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (16.7.2026) The provision on protected species in the proposed Regulation on speeding-up environmental assessments1 (RSEA), aimed to provide legal clarity and speed up permits, complements the relevant provisions of the Birds2 and Habitats3 Directives. Specifically, Article 8 provides that when the implementation of a plan or project results in the occasional killing or disturbance of protected species, such killing or disturbance will not be considered deliberate if the plan or project has adopted appropriate and proportionate mitigation measures. When assessing whether these measures are appropriate and proportionate, the Member States’ authorities should consider if significant adverse impacts on the population of the species concerned are avoided, despite the possible negative impacts on individual specimens of these species. Discussions on the proposal in the European Parliament and the Council are ongoing. The stress test aims to identify opportunities for achieving the Directives’ objectives in a more cost-efficient way while maintaining their ambition and high standards of nature protection. The Commission will decide on the appropriate follow up of the stress test, also taking into account the state of play of the legislative process on the RSEA. The Commission proposal sets out a proportionate approach including for strategic projects, aiming to better reconcile the need for species protection with the need to speed up permitting of plans and projects.

E-10-2026-002097.t: Sweden’s compliance with the EU Pay Transparency Directive
qt: to the Commission Hanna Gedin (The Left) Subject:

I am seeking clarification on the Member States’ obligation to take timely action to transpose Directive (EU) 2023/970 of the European Parliament and of the Council on pay transparency, which aims to strengthen the principle of equal pay for equal work or work of equal value and to counter unjustified pay gaps. In the public debate on the issue in Sweden, the government has said it is keen to postpone or reconsider implementation, citing administrative consequences, among other issues. This raises questions about how much scope a Member State has to postpone the implementation of a directive that has already been adopted. 1.
Are the Member States obliged to transpose Directive (EU) 2023/970 before the expiry of the deadline set?
Is it compatible with EU law for a Member State to unilaterally postpone the implementation of an adopted directive pending a possible future renegotiation or amendment?
What steps can the Commission take against Member States that fail to implement a directive within the prescribed time limit?
at: (English version) to the Commission Hanna Gedin (The Left) (20 May 2026) Subject: Sweden’s compliance with the EU Pay Transparency Directive I am seeking clarification on the Member States’ obligation to take timely action to transpose Directive (EU) 2023/970 of the European Parliament and of the Council on pay transparency, which aims to strengthen the principle of equal pay for equal work or work of equal value and to counter unjustified pay gaps. In the public debate on the issue in Sweden, the government has said it is keen to postpone or reconsider implementation, citing administrative consequences, among other issues. This raises questions about how much scope a Member State has to postpone the implementation of a directive that has already been adopted. 1.
Are the Member States obliged to transpose Directive (EU) 2023/970 before the expiry of the deadline set?

2. Is it compatible with EU law for a Member State to unilaterally postpone the implementation of an adopted directive pending a possible future renegotiation or amendment? 3. What steps can the Commission take against Member States that fail to implement a directive within the prescribed time limit? (17 July 2026) The Pay Transparency Directive (1) is instrumental for the full realisation of the right to equal pay for the same work or work of equal value between women and men. The Commission recalls that all Member States must have transposed the directive by the deadline of 7 June 2026 (2). Member States are not allowed to unilaterally postpone the implementation of a directive under any circumstances. The applicable transposition deadline of 7 June 2026 is set in the Pay Transparency Directive. The transposition period for this directive was three years, as agreed between the co-legislators. Member States have a legal obligation to fully transpose the directive by the transposition deadline and to notify the Commission thereof. If a Member State has not notified transposition measures by the deadline, the Commission will assess the situation and may open infringement proceedings under Article 258 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union. The Commission recalls that it remains fully committed to the correct and timely implementation of the Pay Transparency Directive in Member States. As the Commission noted in its reply to Written Question P-001317/2026, the Commission does not envisage to include the directive in any future omnibus regulatory simplification package or a ‘stop-the-clock’ measure (3).

E-10-2026-002096.t: Measures supporting regional airports in the EU
qt: to the Commission Sophia Kircher (PPE) Subject:

Regional airports form an essential part of our EU-wide transport infrastructure. They ensure international connectivity for rural regions, thus boosting their economic development and competitiveness. They also serve as feeder airports serving major international aviation hubs. They are, meanwhile, facing significant challenges, notably limited profitability, high investment- and operating costs for infrastructure, the trend towards ever-larger aircraft, structural dependence on major network carriers and limited opportunities for code-sharing and interline agreements. 1.
What specific policy and financial measures is the Commission pursuing to ensure that the EU’s rural regions remain accessible via regional airports in the long term?

How is the new EU aviation strategy intended to take account of the structural challenges and needs of regional airports, particularly with regard to their weaker position vis-à-vis major network carriers in terms of access to code-sharing and interline agreements?

How does the Commission intend to ensure that the EU’s decarbonisation targets for aviation, particularly those pertaining to the EU Emissions Trading System or sustainable aviation fuel quotas, do not undermine the EU aviation sector’s competitiveness?

They are, meanwhile, facing significant challenges, notably limited profitability, high investmentand operating costs for infrastructure, the trend towards ever-larger aircraft, structural dependence on major network carriers and limited opportunities for code-sharing and interline agreements. 1. What specific policy and financial measures is the Commission pursuing to ensure that the EU’s rural regions remain accessible via regional airports in the long term? 2. How is the new EU aviation strategy intended to take account of the structural challenges and needs of regional airports, particularly with regard to their weaker position vis-à-vis major network carriers in terms of access to code-sharing and interline agreements? 3. How does the Commission intend to ensure that the EU’s decarbonisation targets for aviation, particularly those pertaining to the EU Emissions Trading System or sustainable aviation fuel quotas, do not undermine the EU aviation sector’s competitiveness? (3 August 2026) 1. The EU law allows Member States to support regional airports with investment and operating state aid and to help new connections with start-up aid (1). Member States may also impose a public service obligation (PSO) for scheduled air services between an airport serving a peripheral or development region and other EU airport s (2). They can also subsidise air tickets for residents of remote and outermost regions (3). Several EU instruments offer targeted funding support to airports, e.g., for testing innovative solutions, implementing the green transition, or fostering territorial cohesion, in particular the framework Programmes on research and innovation, the Connecting Europe Facility, the InvestEU programme, the Emissions Trading System (ETS) Innovation Fund, the Cohesion Fund and the European Regional Development Fund. 2. The upcoming Aviation Strategy will highlight the importance of regional airport connectivity, in line with the Fitness Check of airport legislation, the Air Services Regulation (4), and revised state aid guidelines. While code-sharing and interlining are airline business decisions, the strategy will aim to support robust flight connections from regional airports. This will allow airlines to exercise their commercial freedom to engage in these agreements within the wider network. 3. The Commission is aware of the concerns raised by the industry about the potential impact of sustainable aviation fuel mandates or ETS on EU carriers’ competitiveness. The Commission is monitoring evidence on business leakage risks. It will consider this in whether and how to design measures addressing identified distortions, consistently with international obligations and the EU's broader climate and competitiveness agenda.

E-10-2026-002095.t: Review of EU ETS benchmarks and support for a tailored methodology for the European ceramics industry
qt: to the Commission Sandra Gómez López (S&D), Leire Pajín (S&D) Subject:

Following the concerns expressed by the European ceramics industry – including ASCER (the Spanish Ceramic Tile Manufacturer’s Association) – and other industry representatives and regional authorities in the Joint Statement For The Future Of European Ceramics1, as well as the initiatives taken by Spain and other Member States to adapt the EU ETS to the technological reality of energy-intensive sectors that still have limited decarbonisation alternatives, the Commission has noted that it may review the applicable methodology and consider more sector-specific benchmarks. Given the strategic importance of the ceramics industry for regions such as Castellón and for European industrial autonomy: 1.

How does the Commission intend to consider the contributions of Member States and the sectors concerned in order to ensure more realistic benchmarks adapted to the technological constraints of the ceramics industry, and what is the timetable for these new benchmarks to be adopted and to enter into force?

Is the Commission considering setting a specific benchmark for ceramic tiles and related products that better reflects actual production conditions and avoids a disproportionate impact on competitiveness and employment?
What measures will the Commission take to prevent carbon leakage in hard-todecarbonise sectors such as ceramics?

(1 September 2026) To address concerns expressed by a number of Member States and industry, on 17 July 2026 (1) the Commission adopted at the same time as the ETS revision a separate proposal aimed at increasing the free allocation determined on the basis of the fallback benchmarks, which are the most relevant benchmarks for the ceramics sector. This provides additional free allocation in the order of EUR 6 billion for the period 2026-2030. The Commission also confirmed the launching of the ETS Investment Booster, a EUR 30 billion financial support scheme. The aim is to finance decarbonisation projects, facilitating access for small and medium-sized enterprises and targeting certain industrial processes where tailored decarbonisation pathways are needed. The proposal covers allocations relating to the period 2026-2030 and becomes applicable as early as possible if endorsed by the co-legislators. The Commission will work to facilitate an early agreement between co-legislators on this proposal. To better reflect available emissions reduction capacities in different industrial sectors for the longer term, the ETS revision proposal foresees a delegation of power for the Commission to establish sector-specific heat and fuel fallback benchmarks for the period after 2031. The proposal also reduces the maximum update rate of Union-wide benchmarks to ensure predictability. To prevent carbon leakage, the proposal for the 2026-2030 top-up is designed to avoid the application of the cross-sectoral correction factor, which would otherwise trigger a harmonised reduction of free allocation. For the period after 2031, it is proposed to increase the free allocation buffer from 3% to 4% of the total quantity of allowances.

(27 July 2026) In its reply to Written Question E-003543/2025 (1), the Commission emphasised the need for ‘sufficient and effective access to cash’ which is central in the Commission’s proposal on the legal tender of euro banknotes and coins (2) and which introduces specific obligations for Member States to monitor and report on cash access and acceptance levels, and to take appropriate remedial measures where necessary. The Commission is working with the co-legislators to reach a swift agreement on the proposal. Pursuant to principle 8 of the Euro Legal Tender Expert Group (ELTEG III) final report of 6 July 2022 (3), policy measures should be taken at the appropriate level to ensure that euro cash availability and cash lodgements on bank accounts are guaranteed throughout the euro area as services of general interest and cash deposit facilities. The Payment Accounts Directive (PAD) (4) requires credit institutions to offer basic banking services (5), as part of a payment account with basic features (PABF), including cash deposits and withdrawal, to the extent that they already offer those services to consumers holding payment accounts other than a PABF. To ensure sufficient access for consumers to basic banking services, the PAD (6) requires Member States to ensure that all or a sufficient number of credit institutions offer PABFs. The Commission is in contact with the relevant national authorities and, at present, the Commission does not have indications that there would not be a sufficient number of credit institutions offering PABFs and cash deposit and withdrawal services in the relevant region to meet the needs of the consumers.

E-10-2026-002093.t: Forced labour by political prisoners in Cuban cigar production
qt: to the Commission Barbara Bonte (PfE) Subject:

According to recent reports by Prisoners Defenders, the Cuban regime systematically subjects political prisoners to harsh forced labour conditions without any legal protection.1 In prisons such as Quivicán, prisoners work up to 15 hours a day rolling cigars by hand. The Cuban state-owned company Tabacuba itself acknowledged the use of prisoners in cigar production. Regulation (EU) 2024/3015 on forced labour prohibits imports into the European Union of products made by forced labour as of 14 December 2027. 1.
Is the Commission aware of the systematic use of political prisoners in the manufacture of products under forced labour?

Is the Commission considering suspending the Political Dialogue and Cooperation Agreement with Cuba as long as the regime continues to exploit political prisoners for the production of export goods destined for the European market?
Does the Commission consider the use of political prisoners to produce these products, under forced labour, to be a violation of Regulation (EU) 2024/2015 on forced labour?
https://hrwf.eu/cubas-prison-business-60000-prisoners-are-used-as-slave-labor/.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.7.2026) As recalled during the intervention of the High Representative/Vice President at the plenary of the European Parliament on 19 May 2026, Cuba urgently needs to make fundamental political, economic and democratic reforms, respecting the human rights and fundamental freedoms of the Cuban people and releasing political prisoners and all individuals who have been arbitrarily detained. The EU, including through its Delegation in Havana and its Special Representative for Human Rights, regularly raises cases of political prisoners with the Cuban authorities. The Political Dialogue and Cooperation Agreement with Cuba1 establishes a framework for the EU to engage with Cuban authorities, including in areas of divergence such as the detention of political prisoners. Regarding forced labour, the Commission follows closely information about the presence of forced labour in Cuba, including through reports from international organisations, civil society and other relevant stakeholders and takes the allegations very seriously. From the entry into application of Regulation (EU) 2024/3015 in December 20272, the Commission and competent authorities of Member States will be able to investigate products suspected to be made with forced labour, included on the basis of submissions of information made by stakeholders.
1 https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/documents/treaties-agreements/agreement/?id=2016056. 2 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/EN/legal-content/summary/ban-on-forced-labour-products-on-the-eu-market.html.

E-10-2026-002092.t: Including CN code 7317 (nails) within the expanded CBAM scope
qt: to the Commission Markus Buchheit (ESN) Subject:
Including CN code 7317 (nails) within the expanded CBAM scope

Through Regulation COM(2025)0989, the Commission proposed an extension of the scope of the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) to include downstream goods. In addition, the proposal explicitly provides for the possibility of reviewing and expanding the product list within six months of its entry into force. Nails (CN code 7317) are a steelintensive industrial product manufactured by around 30 companies in the EU, employing around 3 000 people, with a yearly production of roughly 300 000 tonnes. In spite of their importance for the economy and supply chains, nails have so far not been included in the scope of the proposed regulation, even though there are already corresponding guidelines in the accompanying documents and an impact assessment has already been undertaken. 1.
Does the Commission intend to include CN code 7317 in the scope of the CBAM during the envisioned review period?
What criteria are used to assess which downstream steel products should be included?
What specific steps can Member States and economic actors take to request an expansion of the product list?
at: (English version) to the Commission Markus Buchheit (ESN) (20 May 2026) Subject: Including CN code 7317 (nails) within the expanded CBAM scope Through Regulation COM(2025)0989, the Commission proposed an extension of the scope of the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) to include downstream goods. In addition, the proposal explicitly provides for the possibility of reviewing and expanding the product list within six months of its entry into force. In spite of their importance for the economy and supply chains, nails have so far not been included in the scope of the proposed regulation, even though there are already corresponding guidelines in the accompanying documents and an impact assessment has already been undertaken. 1.
Does the Commission intend to include CN code 7317 in the scope of the CBAM during the envisioned review period?
What criteria are used to assess which downstream steel products should be included?
What specific steps can Member States and economic actors take to request an expansion of the product list?

(11 August 2026) On 17 December 2025, the Commission adopted a proposal to amend the regulation of the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) (1). The proposal includes, among other, a list of steel and aluminium intensive downstream products to be added into CBAM’s scope. The proposal does include all CN codes belonging to the Harmonised System (HS) heading 7317 (2). This Commission proposal was based on an impact assessment, which details the methodology, as well as the collected data, to select downstream goods that should be included into the CBAM scope (3). The selection methodology takes into account and quantifies the extent of carbon leakage risk, as well as the emission intensity associated with downstream goods. The selection is carried out to minimise the carbon leakage risk, while keeping the related administrative burden limited. The Commission proposal is currently under discussion by the co-legislators, the Council and the European Parliament. The outcome of these discussions will determine the final list of goods to be added into the scope of CBAM.

COM(2025) 989, Proposal for a regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council amending Regulation (EU) 2023/956 as regards the extension of its scope to downstream goods and anti-circumvention measures, 2025/0419 (COD). See Annex I of the proposal. The products of the 7317 family are CN 73170020 Nails of iron or steel wire, in strips or coils; CN 73170060 Nails, tacks, corrugated nails, staples and similar articles, of iron or steel wire (excl. nails in strips or coils, and staples in strips); CN 73170080 Nails, tacks, drawing pins, corrugated nails, staples and similar articles, of iron or steel (excl. cold-pressed from wire, and staples in strips). E-10-2026-002090.t: Unlocking final investment decisions along the carbon capture, utilisation and storage (CCUS) value chain
qt: to the Commission Jeannette Baljeu (Renew) Subject:
Unlocking final investment decisions along the carbon capture, utilisation and storage (CCUS) value chain

Article 23 of the Net-Zero Industry Act1 sets a binding target of 50 Mt CO₂ injection capacity per year by 2030. The Commission has identified CCUS as essential to meeting this target. Achieving this requires final investment decisions (FIDs) across the CCUS value chain in the near term. However, FIDs remain stalled: capture projects depend on transport and storage availability, while storage developers need firm offtake commitments. Without coordinated action, the 50 Mt target will not be met. This is a coordination challenge the market cannot resolve alone. The upcoming proposals concerning CO₂ markets and infrastructure (Q3 2026)2 and the Industrial Decarbonisation Bank (Q2 2026)3 are expected to address this, but concrete mechanisms are still unclear. 1.
What regulatory measures will the Commission propose in the CO₂ Markets and Infrastructure proposal to ensure FIDs in the CCUS value chain, and what is the timeline?

How will the Commission address the risk that emitters bear continued costs for complying with the Emissions Trading System (ETS) during value chain disruptions beyond their control, when capture is operationally unavailable4?

How will the Commission use the Industrial Decarbonisation Bank, alongside other financial de-risking instruments and regulatory measures (e.g. ETS-backed guarantees), to enable and accelerate early FIDs for CCUS projects?

Regulation (EU) 2024/1735 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 June 2024 on establishing a framework of measures for strengthening Europe’s net-zero technology manufacturing ecosystem and amending Regulation (EU) 2018/1724 (OJ L, 2024/1735, 28.6.2024, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1735/oj). 2 Commission Work Programme 2026, ‘Development of CO₂ transportation infrastructure and markets,’ planned for Q3 2026. 3 Clean Industrial Deal (February 2025); proposal for Industrial Decarbonisation Bank planned for Q2 2026, EUR 100 billion envelope. 4 Zero Emissions Platform, response to EU public consultation on CO₂ markets and infrastructure, January 2026. 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (31.7.2026) The Commission is currently preparing a legislative proposal for adoption at the end of 2026 on CO₂1 Markets and Infrastructure. The proposal will include rules for developing an internal market for CO2. In terms of liability, under the Emissions Trading System (ETS) liability for the CO2 under their control is assigned to each value chain actor. For emitters that capture CO2, there is indeed a commercial risk in case CO2 transport and CO2 storage services are not available, that they need to take into account. This risk is expected to reduce with the development of a more diversified, competitive storage market. With the Innovation Fund the Commission is financially de-risking 60 Industrial Carbon Management projects with more than EUR 6 billion in committed grants that cover both investment and operational expenditures for CO2 services. Support to carbon capture, utilisation, and storage (CCUS) projects is also discussed in context of the announced Industrial Decarbonisation Bank.
1 Carbon dioxide.

E-10-2026-002089.t: Future regulation of fur farming in the EU
qt: to the Commission Asger Christensen (Renew) Subject:

There is still a lot of political debate and uncertainty surrounding the future regulation of fur farming in the EU. Several Member States and stakeholders have also emphasised the need to ensure high standards of animal welfare, disease control and traceability in the sectors concerned, which continue to operate under strict regulation in Europe. In the light of the foregoing: 1.

How does the Commission assess the risk that a blanket EU ban on fur farming would lead to production being moved to third countries with lower standards of animal welfare, disease control and traceability?

In its further efforts on this issue, will the Commission consider an approach that is based on common European minimum standards, verifiable animal welfare protocols and strict regulation, rather than a blanket ban at EU level?
Can the Commission provide information on the expected timeline for the forthcoming communication on the future regulation of fur farming in the EU?

(27 July 2026) The Commissioner for Democracy, Justice, the Rule of Law and Consumer Protection was on an official visit to Greece on 12 May 2026. Hearing firsthand perspectives from different stakeholders offered a comprehensive overview of the rule of law situation in the country, both on the progress made and the remaining challenges. Stakeholders brought to the Commissioner’s attention different topics, including the appointments to the leadership of the highest courts, developments surrounding the alleged use of spyware, the independence and effective functioning of independent authorities, public procurement, civic space and the upcoming constitutional revision. E-10-2026-002086.t: Differing national interpretations of the classification of pickup vehicles and their impact on the coherence of the internal market
qt: to the Commission Merja Kyllönen (The Left) Subject:
Differing national interpretations of the classification of pickup vehicles and their impact on the coherence of the internal market

It is clear that vehicle taxation and certain classification issues are matters for the Member States. However, according to recent information, there has been a significant change in the administrative practices in place in Finland when it comes to the classification of certain light commercial vehicles, in particular large pickups such as the Ram 1500. The data reported show that new vehicles in the category concerned are, in practice, no longer approved for registration as light commercial vehicles (classification N1), but the same vehicle can still be registered as a passenger car (classification M1), albeit subject to significantly higher rates of tax. This situation raises questions on the consistency and predictability of regulation and on the equal treatment of operators in the internal market. With the above in mind: 1.

Does the Commission take the view that different interpretations of vehicle classifications by the Member States (N1 versus M1) could lead to distortions in the internal market, particularly in situations where the same vehicle is treated differently depending on its tax rating?

To what extent does EU law allow Member States to apply restrictive interpretation criteria for the classification of light commercial vehicles, particularly where such practices may have a major impact on cross-border trade and market access?

Is the Commission aware of recent changes in national administrative practices in this area, does it intend to assess whether classification criteria need to be more harmonised or clarified so as to ensure legal certainty and predictability, and could it consider the need for guidance or legislative clarification on vehicle classification rules, including with regard to the legislation on the circular economy and end-of-life vehicles?
at: (English version) to the Commission Merja Kyllönen (The Left) (20 May 2026) Subject: Differing national interpretations of the classification of pickup vehicles and their impact on the coherence of the internal market It is clear that vehicle taxation and certain classification issues are matters for the Member States. However, according to recent information, there has been a significant change in the administrative practices in place in Finland when it comes to the classification of certain light commercial vehicles, in particular large pickups such as the Ram 1500. The data reported show that new vehicles in the category concerned are, in practice, no longer approved for registration as light commercial vehicles (classification N1), but the same vehicle can still be registered as a passenger car (classification M1), albeit subject to significantly higher rates of tax. This situation raises questions on the consistency and predictability of regulation and on the equal treatment of operators in the internal market. With the above in mind: 1.

Does the Commission take the view that different interpretations of vehicle classifications by the Member States (N1 versus M1) could lead to distortions in the internal market, particularly in situations where the same vehicle is treated differently depending on its tax rating?

To what extent does EU law allow Member States to apply restrictive interpretation criteria for the classification of light commercial vehicles, particularly where such practices may have a major impact on cross-border trade and market access?

Is the Commission aware of recent changes in national administrative practices in this area, does it intend to assess whether classification criteria need to be more harmonised or clarified so as to ensure legal certainty and predictability, and could it consider the need for guidance or legislative clarification on vehicle classification rules, including with regard to the legislation on the circular economy and end-of-life vehicles?

(20 July 2026) Regulation (EU) 2018/858 on the approval and market surveillance of motor vehicles (1) defines the vehicle categories (2) and sets out harmonised criteria for vehicle categorisation (3). It also provides different requirements for vehicles of categories M 1 (cars) and N1 (vans). To be approved and placed on the market, motor vehicles must meet the criteria for the respective vehicle category and the requirements applicable to that category. In principle, pick-up trucks are categorised and approved as N 1 vehicles. However, the above-mentioned criteria for vehicle categorisation apply for the purpose of vehicle approval and do not necessarily apply to the classification of vehicles for taxation purposes or for tariff classification for customs purposes. Moreover, taxation on motor vehicles remains an area where Member States retain a large discretion. National registration and circulation taxes vary considerably across Member States. Thus, the same vehicle can be taxed differently regardless of its category. Member States are also free to change the level and method of calculation of motor vehicle taxes, provided that the principle of non-discrimination of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU is respected (4). The tariff classification of goods under the EU Combined Nomenclature (5), based on global system developed by the World Customs Organisation, follows its own structure and classification rules. Hence, the Commission adopted specific guidance for pick-up vehicles (6) to ensure uniform classification of goods across the EU.

E-10-2026-002085.t: Procedure for registering Capocollo di Martina Franca as a protected geographical indication (PGI)
qt: to the Commission Valentina Palmisano (The Left) Subject:

Capocollo di Martina Franca is one of the Apulian culinary tradition’s most time-honoured and iconic delicacies. Based on practices that have been handed down over generations in the Valle d’Itria, Capocollo’s artisanal production process is a particularly significant part of the area’s cultural and economic heritage. In February 2024, the Italian authorities sent the Commission a request to recognise Capocollo as a PGI. Further clarification and supporting documents were submitted in 2024 and 2025 as part of the relevant assessment procedure. It should also be noted that the competent Italian administrative court issued a definitive ruling on 30 October 2025 in which it determined that the decision confirming the full legitimacy of Capocollo’s designation procedure had acquired the force of res judicata. In the light of the above: 1.
Is the Commission still in the process of assessing the application to register Capocollo di Martina Franca as a PGI?
What are the next stages that applications like the above typically have to go through as part of the registration process?

Given that, as mentioned above, the relevant additional documentation supporting the application has already been submitted, could the Commission estimate how long it will take to complete this registration procedure and publish the resulting PGI single document in the Official Journal?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (10.7.2026) Following the completion of the Commission’s scrutiny of the application for registration of the name ‘Capocollo di Martina Franca’ as a protected geographical indication (PGI) since, according to the Commission, the application fulfils the conditions referred to in Article 15(1) and (4) of Regulation (EU) 2024/11431, it has been published for opposition in the Official Journal (C series) of the European Union on 22 June 20262. This publication will open a three-month opposition period. If no admissible reasoned statement of opposition is received within this period, the Commission will then launch the adoption procedure for the Commission Implementing Regulation on the registration of the geographical indication and finally publish it in the Official Journal (L series). The completion of the registration process usually takes four to six additional weeks after the end of the publication period.
