E-10-2026-002084.t: EU response to WHO-declared public health emergency of international concern following Ebola outbreak in Central Africa
qt: to the Commission Leire Pajín (S&D) Subject:

The World Health Organization has declared the Ebola outbreak caused by the Bundibugyo virus in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) a public health emergency of international concern. The outbreak has already spread beyond the DRC into Uganda, with suspected and confirmed cases reported in urban and cross-border areas affected by insecurity, humanitarian crises and high population mobility. Given the absence of approved vaccines or treatments for the Bundibugyo strain, the situation poses a serious risk to regional and global health security. 1.

What immediate humanitarian, financial and technical support is the Commission providing to the DRC, Uganda and neighbouring countries to strengthen surveillance, testing and isolation capacities and cross-border coordination?
What measures is the Commission taking, together with international partners, to support research and development on vaccines and treatments for Ebola, and to protect European citizens?
at: (English version) to the Commission Leire Pajín (S&D) (20 May 2026) Subject: EU response to WHO-declared public health emergency of international concern following Ebola outbreak in Central Africa The World Health Organisation has declared the Ebola outbreak caused by the Bundibugyo virus in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) a public health emergency of international concern. The outbreak has already spread beyond the DRC into Uganda, with suspected and confirmed cases reported in urban and cross-border areas affected by insecurity, humanitarian crises and high population mobility. Given the absence of approved vaccines or treatments for the Bundibugyo strain, the situation poses a serious risk to regional and global health security. 1. What immediate humanitarian, financial and technical support is the Commission providing to the DRC, Uganda and neighbouring countries to strengthen surveillance, testing and isolation capacities and cross-border coordination? 2. What measures is the Commission taking, together with international partners, to support research and development on vaccines and treatments for Ebola, and to protect European citizens? (28 July 2026) The Commission is providing immediate support in response to the ongoing Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and Uganda by supporting testing, sequencing, detection and isolations capacities through different projects funded by the EU4Health and Global Europe programmes in Africa. The Commission has already supported the mobilisation of 6.3 tonnes of medical countermeasures and supplies to the DRC through the World Health Organisation (WHO) AFRO Regional Emergency Hub in Dakar, including sample collection kits, viral haemorrhagic fever kits, medications, as well as the deployment of EU Health Task Force expert teams on the ground (1). The Union’s support amounts to EUR 493 million in emergency aid, vaccines, treatment and health security in the Great Lakes and Uganda region, including EUR 84 million in immediate humanitarian aid (2), development and research (3) funding in response to the outbreak. The Commission is working closely with EU Member States to ensure a coordinated Team Europe response. The Commission is supporting the WHO Research and Development blueprint which sponsors the development of recommendations on priority candidate vaccines and therapeutics and the establishment of clinical trials. The Commission is also working with international partners to accelerate research, development, local manufacturing and equitable access to new vaccines and treatments, including via its support to the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness and Innovation through Horizon Europe. Gavi’s First Response Fund has been activated, allocating up to USD 50 million for accelerated vaccine access and outbreak response needs (4).

The EU Health Task Force has been deployed to support the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention in outbreak coordination and operational planning, as well as to assess exit screening measures in place in the DRC and Uganda. Through the EU Humanitarian Air Bridge, the Commission facilitated the transport of over 140 tonnes of medicines, protective equipment, infection-control materials and tents, with additional flights planned. The EU-funded European and Developing Countries Clinical Trials Partnership with Africa is pivoting three Ebola research projects towards validation of treatments, post-exposure prophylaxis, and point-of-care diagnostics. The European Union is the fifth largest donor to Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance and Team Europe is collectively the largest donor.

E-10-2026-002083.t: The EU’s role as a global humanitarian leader in the context of the ‘Humanitarian Reset’
qt: to the Commission Leire Pajín (S&D) Subject:

The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) has announced an additional contribution of USD 1.8 billion by the United States to humanitarian funds aimed at responding to emergencies in specific countries, to be targeted at least 17 countries during 2026. This announcement comes in the context of OCHA’s ‘Humanitarian Reset’ initiative, which seeks to improve the effectiveness, prioritisation and delivery of humanitarian assistance in the face of reduced global humanitarian funding. While the countries selected by the United States to receive additional humanitarian aid will receive additional aid, this will leave many other countries exposed to ever increasing humanitarian needs. 1.
How does the Commission assess the recent additional humanitarian contribution by the US Administration to OCHA’s ‘Humanitarian Reset’ initiative?
Does the Commission intend to present, in 2026, a report on the role and contribution to the ‘Humanitarian Reset’ initiative?
How does the Commission intend to reassert itself as a global humanitarian actor, and contribute to reducing disparities in humanitarian funding between countries and regions?
at: (English version) to the Commission Leire Pajín (S&D) (20 May 2026) Subject: The EU’s role as a global humanitarian leader in the context of the ‘Humanitarian Reset’ The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) has announced an additional contribution of USD 1.8 billion by the United States to humanitarian funds aimed at responding to emergencies in specific countries, to be targeted at least 17 countries during 2026. This announcement comes in the context of OCHA’s ‘Humanitarian Reset’ initiative, which seeks to improve the effectiveness, prioritisation and delivery of humanitarian assistance in the face of reduced global humanitarian funding. While the countries selected by the United States to receive additional humanitarian aid will receive additional aid, this will leave many other countries exposed to ever increasing humanitarian needs. 1. How does the Commission assess the recent additional humanitarian contribution by the US Administration to OCHA’s ‘Humanitarian Reset’ initiative? 2. Does the Commission intend to present, in 2026, a report on the role and contribution to the ‘Humanitarian Reset’ initiative? 3. How does the Commission intend to reassert itself as a global humanitarian actor, and contribute to reducing disparities in humanitarian funding between countries and regions? (30 July 2026) The Commission welcomes the additional humanitarian contribution provided by the US Administration to the Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) pooled funds, extending for a year vital support to 21 crisis contexts. As contributor to OCHA pooled funds, the Commission will continue to advocate that their implementation remains principled, needs-based and in line with localisation objectives. The EU and its Member States are at the forefront of steering an inclusive, sustainable and transformative Humanitarian Reset. Progress will continue to be tracked, in coordination with Member States under Team Europe approach. The Commission stands ready to brief the European Parliament as part of its regular exchanges. The EU is taking decisive strategic action to assert its strategic leadership in shaping a more effective and principles-based global humanitarian system. With the adoption of a Joint Communication on EU Humanitarian Aid on 27 May 2026 (1), the EU commits to reach those most in need efficiently and in a principled manner by reiterating the EU’s commitment to the protection of humanitarian principles, personnel and affected people, by identifying ways to increase cost-effectiveness and reduce humanitarian needs and by promoting more strategic alliances with other donors, peace and development actors, including international financial institutions and the private sector, to address the humanitarian funding gap and ensure a coordinated, sustainable response to crises. In a world where humanitarian needs are outpacing resources, the EU approach is clear: solidarity is not optional, it is a moral duty and a strategic imperative.

E-10-2026-002082.t: Russia’s admission to the Biennale Festival and EU funding
qt: to the Commission Bartłomiej Sienkiewicz (PPE) Subject:

The Venice Biennale Foundation’s decision to allow a Russian delegation to participate in the International Art Exhibition has been deeply controversial at both diplomatic and political level, with public protests taking place and several other national pavilions refusing to participate. The Commission has concluded that this decision did not align with the common Union response to Russia’s aggression. In addition, ministers from 22 EU Member States sent a joint letter to the Biennale Board, requesting that they reconsider their decision. The Commission sought clarification on the arrangements between the foundation and the Russian Government to assess compliance with the EU sanctions regime. In light of the above: 1.
When will the Commission suspend or withdraw EU funding granted to the Venice Biennale Foundation?

If a decision has not yet been taken, what factors justify EU financial support continuing despite this potential non-compliance with EU sanctions policy and the broader diplomatic implications of the foundation’s decision?
Should the Commission not take preventive action at this stage, rather than simply waiting for formal clarification?

(16 July 2026) The Commission does not provide direct funding to the Biennale of Arts. However, the participation of a delegation of artists from the Russian Federation, using a national pavilion and whose participation is funded and promoted by the Russian government at the Biennale of Arts is being assessed for a possible breach of the EU restrictive measures imposed on Russia in the context of its illegal aggression against Ukraine (1). This could entail consequences for existing contracts signed with the Biennale. Hence, the European Education and Culture Executive Agency (EACEA), in cooperation with the Commission, is reviewing a grant action funded under the MEDIA strand of Creative Europe (2) that aims to enhance virtual production and provide network opportunities to audiovisual professionals. The EACEA has formally notified the Biennale Foundation of the Agency’s intention to suspend or terminate the grant if grounds of grave professional misconduct and serious breach of contractual obligations are established, in particular in relation to potential non-compliance with EU sanctions against Russia and disrespect for EU fundamental values. The Biennale Foundation is currently exercising its right to be heard, and a thorough examination of the Foundation’s response will be performed before any decision on final measures is taken. Pending this review, grant-related payments remain suspended. These actions are fully in line with EU law and the principles of sound financial management.

E-10-2026-002081.t: Future of DG REGIO and possible centralisation of EU cohesion policy
qt: to the Commission Valentina Palmisano (The Left), Gaetano Pedulla' (The Left), Mario Furore (The Left), Danilo Della Valle (The Left), Dario Tamburrano (The Left), Carolina Morace (The Left), Pasquale Tridico (The Left) Subject:

According to international media outlets (including Politico)1, the Commission is considering restructuring DG REGIO, either by merging it with SG REFORM or absorbing it into a centralised structure for strategic investments. This decision appears to be part of a shift towards centralised resource management models, which are viewed by some as being quicker at absorbing EU funds. Were the Commission to opt for such a policy, it would be deviating from the commitments made by the EU institutions and Member States alike to maintain cohesion as a priority in the next MFF. It could well be that the stated objective of simplifying administration is merely a ruse, and that the Commission’s real goal is to bolster the defence sector and the competitiveness of European industries, thereby reducing territorial cohesion and its integrated approach (see Articles 174-175 TFEU) to secondary concerns. This shift towards centralisation will curtail the autonomy of local authorities, make multi-level governance a dead letter and exclude civil society from efforts to address regional inequalities. In the light of the above: 1.
Will the Commission confirm that DG REGIO will indeed be either merged or absorbed, thereby downgrading cohesion policy as an EU priority and stripping it of its autonomy?

What are the impact assessments that have led the Commission to believe that a centralised model arising from negotiations that only involved high-level bureaucrats is better at responding to the needs of vulnerable communities than the multi-level governance approach?
How will the Commission ensure that these new arrangements comply with the cohesion principles enshrined in the European Treaties?
https://www.politico.eu/newsletter/brussels-playbook/regio-on-the-rocks/?reg-wall=true.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (7.9.2026) The Commission reaffirms the role of the Directorate-General Regional and Urban Policy (DG REGIO) in promoting balanced regional development, addressing disparities, and strengthening the EU’s engagement with citizens. As every institution, the Commission continuously reflects on how best to organise itself to deliver effectively on its policy objectives. In this context, the President of the Commission tasked the Commissioner responsible for Budget, Anti-Fraud, Public Administration with conducting a large-scale review of the Commission’s organisation and operations. The review is expected to result in a set of actionable recommendations by the end of 2026. The proposals for the 2028–2034 Multiannual Financial Framework1, presented on 16 July 2025, aim to streamline the EU budget structure in order to maximise its impact in the face of the multiple challenges confronting Europe. Regions will continue to play a key role in shaping and implementing strategies and projects tailored to their specific needs, while maintaining direct contact with the Commission. The Commission fully shares the view that cohesion policy must not be reduced to a centralised investment instrument. Its strength lies precisely in its capacity to respond to diverse territorial challenges, from demographic decline in rural areas to ensuring a just transition in industrial regions. Cohesion policy is firmly anchored in the EU Treaties and remains at the heart of the European project. In this context, the expertise of the colleagues working in DG REGIO, the institutional memory, and close cooperation with national, regional, and local stakeholders are important assets for delivering tangible results for citizens across Europe.
1 https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/eu-budget/long-term-eu-budget/eu-budget-2028-2034_en.

E-10-2026-002080.t: Circumvention of EU sanctions against Russia in the aviation sector
qt: to the Commission Petras Auštrevičius (Renew), Bart Groothuis (Renew) Subject:

Recent reporting and documentation suggests that entities linked to Russia’s aviation sector, including S7 Engineering LLC and S7 Airlines, continued to feature after February 2022 in contracts, invoices, freight records and maintenance records involving intermediaries in the United Arab Emirates, Jordan and Kyrgyzstan. Other companies referenced include Golden Falcon Aviation FZE, Casper Aviation Spares Trading FZE, U.C.A Aviation Spares Trading FZE, Aerospace Technical Services, ATS Heavy Equipment and Machinery Spare Parts Trading, Aeroparts AOG, Royal Aircraft Maintenance Company and Sky Asia Technics LLC. In December 2023, the U.S. Department of the Treasury added A T S Heavy Equipment and Machinery Spare Parts Trading to the sanctions list, alleging it had supplied millions of dollars worth of aircraft parts to Russia. Given that under EU sanctions, the export of aviation goods, technology and related maintenance services to Russia or for use in Russia is prohibited: 1.
Will the Commission investigate whether the companies and supply chains identified have enabled the diversion of aviation goods, maintenance services or technical support to Russian operators?
Will the Commission share relevant information with Member State enforcement authorities, the European Anti-Fraud Office (OLAF) and international partners including the US, the UK and Ukraine?
Does the Commission intend to propose further listings, export restrictions or anticircumvention measures targeting aviation supply routes through non-EU countries used by Russian operators?

(16 July 2026) The EU has imposed a broad range of restrictive measures (sanctions) in response to Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine, including a ban on the sale, supply, transfer or export of goods and technology suited for use in aviation to Russia or for use in Russia, as well as a ban on related services (1). Member States are primarily responsible for the implementation and enforcement of EU sanctions, including conducting investigations into possible cases of sanctions circumvention. The Commission supports Member States in the uniform implementation and enforcement of EU sanctions. This includes information exchange with national competent authorities, also in cooperation with the European Anti-Fraud Office, which has a role in preventing, detecting, and investigating cases of sanctions circumvention and cooperates with international partners to exchange information. The Commission continuously monitors developments that may contribute to Russia’s ability to sustain its war of aggression against Ukraine. Where credible information emerges regarding activities that may circumvent or undermine existing EU sanctions, the Commission engages on the matter together with Member States as well as with relevant third countries. The Commission will also not hesitate to propose additional measures where necessary to safeguard the effectiveness of EU sanctions.

E-10-2026-002079.t: Huawei equipment purchased in Spain using NextGenerationEU funds

E-10-2026-002078.t: Inclusion of the alcohol-to-jet sector in the ReFuelEU Aviation Regulation
qt: to the Commission Valérie Devaux (Renew) Subject:

The ReFuelEU Aviation Regulation sets targets for the gradual uptake of sustainable aviation fuels (SAF). Considerable volumes will be required to decarbonise the aviation sector and enable it to become less dependent on fossil kerosene. At this stage, the main SAF production pathway in the EU is hydroprocessed esters and fatty acids. However, given the limited availability of raw materials, the targets set cannot be achieved through that pathway alone. Meanwhile, electro-sustainable aviation fuel is still very expensive. The alcohol-to-jet (AtJ) sector, which uses bioethanol in particular, has great potential for SAF production. Against this backdrop, deploying an AtJ sector would be an important tool for decarbonising air transport, while also generating income for the agricultural sector. It would also help strengthen European energy sovereignty. In the context of the revision of the ReFuelEU Aviation Regulation, does the Commission intend to propose a specific sub-target for AtJ technology, as well as to propose expanding the list of raw materials eligible for SAF production, as is already the case in certain non-EU countries?
at: (English version) to the Commission Valérie Devaux (Renew) (20 May 2026) Subject: Inclusion of the alcohol-to-jet sector in the ReFuelEU Aviation Regulation The ReFuelEU Aviation Regulation sets targets for the gradual uptake of sustainable aviation fuels (SAF). Considerable volumes will be required to decarbonise the aviation sector and enable it to become less dependent on fossil kerosene. At this stage, the main SAF production pathway in the EU is hydroprocessed esters and fatty acids. However, given the limited availability of raw materials, the targets set cannot be achieved through that pathway alone. Meanwhile, electro-sustainable aviation fuel is still very expensive. The alcohol-to-jet (AtJ) sector, which uses bioethanol in particular, has great potential for SAF production. Against this backdrop, deploying an AtJ sector would be an important tool for decarbonising air transport, while also generating income for the agricultural sector. It would also help strengthen European energy sovereignty. In the context of the revision of the ReFuelEU Aviation Regulation, does the Commission intend to propose a specific subtarget for AtJ technology, as well as to propose expanding the list of raw materials eligible for SAF production, as is already the case in certain non-EU countries? (1 July 2026) The Commission supports that deploying diverse technology pathways is essential to meet ReFuelEU Aviation (RFEUA) (1) targets and reduce reliance on fossil kerosene. For instance, the alcohol-to-jet pathway using bioethanol derived from agricultural waste — listed in Part A of Annex IX of the Renewable Energy Directive (2) — is recognised as an advanced biofuel under the EU sustainability framework. Nonetheless, RFEUA remains technologically neutral regarding production pathways. Instead of setting technology-specific sub-targets, it prioritises the total available volumes of sustainable aviation fuels (SAF). Furthermore, to incentivise such pathways, the EU Emissions Trading System Directive (3) provides enhanced financial support by covering a larger share of the price premium for advanced bio-SAF. Regarding the expansion of eligible raw materials, ensuring a sustainable feedstock supply is instrumental for the bio-SAF ramp-up. Delegated Directive (EU) 2024/1405 (4) has already enlarged the eligible list to include intermediate crops and crops grown on severely degraded land. The Commission is also reviewing Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/996 (5) to assess if certification rules should be modified. While biofuels produced from food and feed crop are excluded to count for RFEUA mandates — due to indirect land-use change risks — the eligible feedstock list under RFEUA is not static, it evolves dynamically with the reviews of Annex IX of the Renewable Energy Directive to integrate new sustainable inputs.

E-10-2026-002077.t: Biofuels and e-fuels in road transport
qt: to the Commission Annalisa Corrado (S&D), Thomas Pellerin-Carlin (S&D), César Luena (S&D), Elena Sancho Murillo (S&D), Tiemo Wölken (S&D), Marco Tarquinio (S&D) Subject:

The possibility of expanding the role of sustainable renewable fuels raises serious concerns regarding climate integrity, resource efficiency and investment certainty. Direct electrification remains the most efficient decarbonisation pathway for road transport. A million hectares of photovoltaic panels could power 400 million electric vehicles (EVs) compared with the 32 million hectares currently used for biofuel production to fuel 130 million combustion engine vehicles. Europe’s 8 million EVs have already cut oil imports by 48 million barrels. Alternative fuels are not cost-competitive: hydrotreated vegetable oil costs approximately 79 % more per 100 km than charging an EV; e-fuels are projected to reach EUR 7 per litre by 2030. Recent analysis shows that a biofuel loophole in the Car CO2 Regulation would raise total EU demand to between two and nine times the sustainably available supply, putting it in direct competition with the aviation and maritime sectors, where no mature alternatives exist. The current EU biofuel mix delivers only 20–40% life cycle CO2 savings, and certification fraud, including mislabelling of virgin palm oil as waste-based feedstock, risks erasing even those gains. Finally, unlike EVs, combustion engines emit local air pollutants which, according to the European Environment Agency, cause hundreds of thousands of premature deaths each year in the EU. How does the Commission assess the climate, social and industrial risks of slowing direct electrification in order to accommodate alternatives that are insufficient, unscalable, more expensive and more polluting?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (14.7.2026) The Commission’s proposal amending Regulation (EU) 2019/6311 maintains a strong market signal for zero-emission vehicles, since vehicle electrification is the most efficient pathway to decarbonisation, energy security and independence, and it is the direction in which global markets are moving. This supports continued investment by the EU industrial value chains in the transition and safeguards their competitiveness. At the same time, the proposal enhances technological neutrality by providing manufacturers with more flexibility to achieve their targets. The contribution of renewable fuels is capped and limited to advanced and wastebased biofuels and renewable fuels of non-biological origin (RFNBO) that meet greenhouse gas and sustainability criteria, while other biofuel types, which would raise sustainability and food-competition concerns, are not incentivised, in line with the Renewable Energy Directive2. The impact assessment3 accompanying the proposal provides a comprehensive analysis of the environmental, economic and social impacts of the options considered regarding the role of sustainable renewable fuels. While acknowledging the benefits for the renewable fuels sector, it highlights the need for including appropriate safeguards to avoid that any shift away from electrification would lead to higher emissions, more energy consumption and an increased total cost of vehicle ownership for citizens. This is also to avoid the risk that the limited availability of advanced biofuels and RFNBO hampers the decarbonisation of sectors without technological alternatives, such as aviation and maritime, and the achievement of the climate objectives set out in the European Climate Law.
1 Proposal for a Regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council amending Regulation (EU) 2019/631

as regards CO2 emission performance standards for new light duty vehicles and vehicle labelling and repealing Directive 1999/94/EC, COM/2025/995 final. 2 http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2023/2413/oj. 3 SWD(2025) 1058 final.

E-10-2026-002076.t: Indictment of former Prime Minister Rodríguez Zapatero and possible fraud with regard to Commission-authorised State aid in the Plus Ultra case
qt: to the Commission Nora Junco García (ECR), Diego Solier (ECR) Subject:

On 19 May 2026, Spain’s National High Court charged the former Spanish Prime Minister, José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero, with criminal association, influence peddling, money laundering and forgery of documents in connection with the EUR 53 million public bailout of Plus Ultra Líneas Aéreas in 2021. The aid was granted under a scheme authorised by the Commission (SA.59371, COVID-19 Temporary Framework). The court order states that the beneficiaries acted ‘through mechanisms outside the legally established channels’ and that the airline itself paid for the technical reports supporting its classification as a ‘strategic’ company. In 2024, the Spanish Court of Auditors found that the Spanish state-owned industrial holding company, Sociedad Estatal de Participaciones Industriales, had breached its obligation to provide a report to the Commission on the Solvency Support Fund for Strategic Companies in 2022. In view of the above: 1.

Will the Commission reopen case SA.59371 and require the aid to be fully recovered in accordance with Article 16 of Regulation (EU) 2015/1589 if it is confirmed that it was granted as a result of false information?
Will the Commission refer the case to the European Public Prosecutor’s Office so that it can assess whether it is competent for the matter under Article 22(3) of Regulation (EU) 2017/1939?
Will it open infringement proceedings against Spain for failure to provide information, as identified by the Spanish Court of Auditors?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (23.7.2026) The Commission does not wish to speculate on the ongoing judicial inquiries regarding the airline Plus Ultra. The Commission does not currently have any information that would justify either reopening the case or revoking its decision of 31 July 2020 authorising the recapitalisation aid scheme in question, the legality of which has been confirmed by the General Court and the Court of Justice of the European Union1. The Commission recalls that, in accordance with Article 22 of Regulation (EU) 2017/19392, the material competence of the European Public Prosecutor’s Office is limited to criminal offences affecting the financial interests of the European Union that are provided for in Directive (EU) 2017/1371. The Commission’s decision referred to above specifies that the aid scheme in question has been funded by the Spanish State budget. In these circumstances, the question of whether a criminal offence may have been committed does not seem relevant in light of the ongoing judicial inquiries.
1 State Aid SA.57659(2020/N) - Spain COVID 19 - Recapitalisation fund. OJ C/2020/269, 14.8.2020, p. 8. Cases

T-628/20 EU:T:2021:514 and C-441/21 P, EU:C:2024:447. 2 Council Regulation (EU) 2017/1939 of 12 October 2017 implementing enhanced cooperation on the establishment of the European Public Prosecutor’s Office (the EPPO), OJ L 283, 31.10.2017, p.1.

E-10-2026-002075.t: Outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease in Cyprus
qt: to the Commission Anna Strolenberg (Verts/ALE) Subject:

The recent outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease in Cyprus has exposed structural vulnerabilities in the EU’s biosecurity framework. The disease originated in areas where the EU acquis is suspended under Protocol No 10 on Cyprus annexed to the 2003 Act of Accession and subsequently spread to government-controlled areas, despite containment efforts. In the absence of a regulatory authority, the EU intervened through its Aid Programme for the Turkish Cypriot community, providing vaccines and technical support. However, this raises concerns regarding the effectiveness of financial assistance without enforceable conditionality linked to EU veterinary standards. In this context: 1.

How does the Commission assess the risks posed to EU animal health and the internal market by the inability to ensure the application of EU sanitary standards in areas where the EU acquis is suspended?
Does the Commission intend to strengthen conditionality mechanisms linking EU financial assistance to compliance with EU veterinary and biosecurity protocols?
What additional measures might be envisaged to ensure coordinated and effective disease prevention and response across the entire territory of a Member State under such circumstances?
Supporters1
This question is supported by Members other than the author: Kai Tegethoff (Verts/ALE), Reinier Van Lanschot (Verts/ALE), Nela Riehl (Verts/ALE), Damian Boeselager (Verts/ALE). 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (10.7.2026) The EU legal framework governing animal health protection in the EU is in line with international standards and includes risk-based rules for imports of animals and products thereof into the EU. Relevant international standards have been incorporated into Council Regulation 866/20041 through Commission Decisions, that set out the terms under which goods can cross the line from the areas of the Republic of Cyprus (RoC) in which the RoC Government does not exercise effective control. Pursuant to Protocol No 10 of the 2003 Act of Accession2, the acquis is suspended in the mentioned areas. The Aid Programme for the Turkish Cypriot community aims to improve the socio-economic situation of the Turkish Cypriot community and is implemented in line with EU policies. Regarding the foot-and-mouth disease in Cyprus, support provided through the Aid Programme has contributed to improving animal health in the northern part of the island in recent years. The Commission applies conditionalities adapted to the specific circumstances of the island and the size of the financial support available. It promotes a coordinated and effective disease prevention and response, including by supporting the work of the Veterinary Sub-Committee, under the Technical Committee for Health, established by the leaders of the two communities. An effective, all-island approach requires the engagement of both Greek Cypriot and Turkish Cypriot communities. The Commission reiterates that a comprehensive settlement of the Cyprus issue, in line with the relevant UN Security Council resolutions, is the best path towards lasting and sustainable solutions to challenges affecting the entire island.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A02004R0866-20150831. 2 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/treaty/acc_2003/act_1/pro_10/sign/eng.

E-10-2026-002074.t: Will the Commission encourage a Claims Conference-type mechanism for Polish victims of World War Two
qt: to the Commission Arkadiusz Mularczyk (ECR) Subject:

Germany has, since the early 1950s, negotiated reparations with the Conference on Jewish Material Claims Against Germany (the Claims Conference), a non-governmental representative body. This facilitated bilateral framework requires neither legislation nor a formal treaty, and the Commission has never objected to it, implicitly endorsing it. The Commission has also stated that within its competence it can ‘facilitate the process of remembrance by encouraging discussion and sharing of experiences’.1 Poland formally requested dialogue on reparations in its diplomatic note of 3 October 2022, but Germany declined without substantive justification. 1.

Does the Commission consider that encouraging the establishment of a similar negotiated mechanism between Germany and Poland for Polish victims of World War Two – modelled on the Claims Conference framework which Germany already operates – falls within its stated competence to facilitate dialogue between Member States?

If the Commission can encourage Holocaust remembrance, fund memorial sites, and support civil society engagement with World War Two history, why does it consider it outside its competence to encourage Germany to enter into a dialogue with Poland specifically about victim compensation, given that such a dialogue is already the stated demand of the Polish Government?
Will the Commission use its good offices to encourage Germany to respond substantively to Poland’s diplomatic note of 3 October 2022?
https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/P-10-2024-002838-ASW_EN.html.

Within the scope of its competences, the Commission supports projects and initiatives that contribute to remembrance, historical research, education and dialogue, including through relevant EU programmes such as the call on remembrance under the Citizens, Equality, Rights and Values (CERV) programme.

E-10-2026-002073.t: The differential compensation of Polish forced labourers under the EVZ Foundation and the Commission’s role
qt: to the Commission Arkadiusz Mularczyk (ECR) Subject:

The Foundation Remembrance, Responsibility and Future (EVZ), established in 2000 with contributions from the German Government and German industry, paid approximately EUR 4.4 billion to 1.66 million former forced labourers. However, the payment scheme applied a tiered structure under which forced labourers from Eastern European countries, including Poland, received substantially lower payments than those from Western European countries – despite suffering the same category of crime. EU institutions monitor the EVZ Foundation and its operations1. 1.

Was the Commission involved in any capacity in the design or approval of the EVZ Foundation’s payment structure, and if so, did it raise concerns about the differential payment rates applied to Eastern European, and specifically Polish, forced labourers?

Does the Commission consider that the differential payment structure applied to Polish forced labourers under the EVZ scheme – which resulted in lower compensation for victims from Eastern Europe – was consistent with the principle of equal treatment?
https://www.eurofound.europa.eu/en/publications/all/forced-labour-compensation-scheme-facesdifficulties. 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.9.2026) Within the scope of its competences, the Commission remains committed in assisting Member States to ensure that victims of crime receive fair and adequate compensation. However, EU law does not confer on the Commission a role in supervising or approving the design of arrangements that include compensation, such as the Foundation Remembrance, Responsibility and Future (EVZ). Under EU law, the 2004 Compensation Directive1 obliges Member States to ensure that their national rules provide for the existence of a scheme on compensation to victims of violent intentional crimes committed on their respective territories which guarantees fair and appropriate compensation to victims. The modalities of the national compensation schemes, however, remain the responsibility of the national authorities. Given that the scope of the EVZ differentiates from a national compensation scheme, the Commission is not in a position to assess its payments.
1 Council Directive 2004/80/EC of 29 April 2004 relating to compensation to crime victims, OJ L 261, 6.8.2004,

E-10-2026-002072.t: Ongoing German reparations payments in 2026 and the discriminatory exclusion of Polish victims
qt: to the Commission Arkadiusz Mularczyk (ECR) Subject:

According to publicly available sources, in 2026 Germany continues to make substantial payments connected to harm caused during the Second World War, including approximately EUR 924 million in home care for Holocaust survivors worldwide and annual hardship payments of EUR 1 350 per person to over 128 000 recipients. These payments are negotiated annually between the German Government and the Conference on Jewish Material Claims Against Germany (the Claims Conference). Polish victims of Nazi German aggression, including survivors of mass executions, forced labour and systematic destruction of civilian property, receive no comparable ongoing payments and are excluded from these mechanisms. 1.

Does the Commission consider that the exclusion of Polish victims from these ongoing payment mechanisms, on the basis that they are not covered by the Claims Conference framework, raises issues of equal treatment and non-discrimination under Article 21 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the EU, given that both Jewish and non-Jewish Polish victims suffered?
What could the Commission do to investigate whether this ongoing differential treatment of EU citizens who are victims of the same historical atrocities is compatible with EU fundamental rights law?

E-10-2026-002071.t: Google’s non-compliance with the Digital Markets Act
qt: to the Commission Oihane Agirregoitia Martínez (Renew) Subject:

In March 2025, the Commission published preliminary findings stating that Google had failed to comply with Article 6(5) of the Digital Markets Act (DMA) by ‘self-preferencing’ its vertical search services and breached anti-steering rules on Google Play. A non-compliance decision has yet to be adopted, despite the indicative 12-month deadline established in Article 29 of the DMA Regulation. In its resolution of 23 April 2026, the European Parliament explicitly warned of external political pressures designed to weaken the DMA and called for the ongoing proceedings to be concluded without delay. The IMCO Committee’s DMA working group, chaired by Andreas Schwab MEP and Anna Cavazzini MEP, has repeatedly called for stronger enforcement. In view of the above: 1.
When does the Commission intend to adopt a non-compliance decision and, if appropriate, impose fines under Articles 30 and 31 of the regulation?

What is the Commission’s specific response to the European Parliament resolution? What measures is it taking to ensure that application of the regulation effectively protects the European digital sector from anti-competitive practices by gatekeepers?
at: (English version) to the Commission Oihane Agirregoitia Martínez (Renew) (19 May 2026) Subject: Google’s non-compliance with the Digital Markets Act In March 2025, the Commission published preliminary findings stating that Google had failed to comply with Article 6(5) of the Digital Markets Act (DMA) by ‘self-preferencing’ its vertical search services and breached anti-steering rules on Google Play. A non-compliance decision has yet to be adopted, despite the indicative 12-month deadline established in Article 29 of the DMA Regulation. In its resolution of 23 April 2026, the European Parliament explicitly warned of external political pressures designed to weaken the DMA and called for the ongoing proceedings to be concluded without delay. The IMCO Committee’s DMA working group, chaired by Andreas Schwab MEP and Anna Cavazzini MEP, has repeatedly called for stronger enforcement. In view of the above: 1.
When does the Commission intend to adopt a non-compliance decision and, if appropriate, impose fines under Articles 30 and 31 of the regulation?

What is the Commission’s specific response to the European Parliament resolution? What measures is it taking to ensure that application of the regulation effectively protects the European digital sector from anti-competitive practices by gatekeepers?

(1 July 2026) In March 2025, the Commission preliminarily found that Alphabet was engaging in illegal ‘self-preferencing’ practices on Google Search and ‘anti-steering’ practices on Google Play, in breach of Articles 6(5) and 5(4) of the Digital Markets Act (DMA) (1). The Commission is aware that, in April 2026, the Parliament adopted a resolution expressing concern over political pressure from third countries to weaken the DMA, and calling for ongoing non-compliance proceedings to be concluded ‘without undue delay’. At present, these two Alphabet investigations remain ongoing and they remain a high priority for the Commission. The Commission is conducting these complex investigations with the utmost respect of its duties to carefully review all evidence and to respect Alphabet’s procedural rights, but mindful of the importance of rapid procedures. At the same time, the Commission is engaged in intensive discussions with Alphabet about possible solutions to comply with the DMA, which Alphabet will have to put in place if the Commission ultimately concludes that Alphabet did not comply with its obligations under the DMA. The Commission reaffirms its commitment to the full and effective implementation and enforcement of the DMA, regardless of any geopolitical pressures or uncertainties. The EU lawmakers gave the Commission a clear mandate when adopting the DMA, to ensure that the DMA is fully and effectively applied in order to foster contestability and fairness in digital markets. The Commission continues to advance all ongoing DMA investigations and engages actively with gatekeepers and third parties through regulatory dialogue. It stands ready to take further enforcement action where necessary.

E-10-2026-002070.t: Employment conditions at the Italian National Institute of Astrophysics and protection of EU research funds
qt: to the Commission Nicola Zingaretti (S&D), Sandro Ruotolo (S&D), Irene Tinagli (S&D), Giorgio Gori (S&D), Brando Benifei (S&D), Georgia Tramacere (S&D), Alessandro Zan (S&D) Subject:

In a potential infringement of Directive 1999/70/EC, the Italian National Institute of Astrophysics (INAF) employs some 37 % of its staff on fixed-term contracts. Around 300 workers meet the requirements to be made permanent within the meaning of Article 20 of Legislative Decree No 75/2017 (‘Madia Law’), which expires on 31 December 2026. They are professionals with an average age of 40 who were precariously employed for 8 to 10 years after they received their doctorates. Law No 199/2025 and Ministerial Decree No 195 of 5 March 2026 (Ministry of Universities and Research (MUR) Distribution Decree) allocate only EUR 1.7 million to the recruitment of INAF staff, compared with the EUR 6.5 million proposed by the MUR in June 2025, covering a small proportion of eligible staff. The same provision excludes a significant proportion of longer-term temporary workers who are paid by means of research cheques or non-National Recovery and Resilience Plan funds. Without action, more than 100 researchers – whose training was paid for through NRRP and Horizon Europe funds, among others (Regulation (EU) 2021/695) – will be forced to leave the system by the end of the year. In the light of the above: 1.
Does the Commission consider the levels of precarious employment at INAF compatible with Directive 1999/70/EC?
What steps will it take to prevent EU funds from perpetuating structural precariousness?
Will it make future research disbursements conditional on compliance with fair employment standards, including under the European Pillar of Social Rights?

(3 July 2026) Council Directive 1999/70/EC (1) does not lay down limits on the share of fixed-term contracts in specific sectors but requires Member States to adopt measures to prevent misuse of successive fixed-term employment contracts, in taking account of the needs of specific sectors (2). The Commission is closely monitoring Member States’ compliance, having regard to the case law of the Court of Justice (3). The Commission is committed to ensuring that disbursements of EU research funds under the Recovery and Resilience Fund are conditional on compliance with fair employment standards, in line with the European Pillar of Social Rights. Italy’s national Recovery and Resilience Plan includes reforms aimed at supporting research institutions, as a prerequisite for receiving instalments (4). Likewise, Horizon Europe (5) (HE) promotes attractive and sustainable careers for researchers, including through requirements (6) in line with the European framework for research careers and the principles of the European Charter for Researchers (7).

http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/1999/70/oj. The directive assigns to the Member States the general objective of preventing such abuse, while leaving them discretion as to how to achieve it. The Court of Justice has clarified that the framework Agreement on fixed-term work does not lay down a general obligation on the Member States to provide for the conversion of fixed-term employment contracts into contracts of indefinite duration, confer, e.g., judgment of 8 March 2012, Martial Huet v Université de Bretagne occidentale, C-251/11, EU:2012:133, paragraph 38, https://infocuria.curia.europa.eu/tabs/document? source=document&text=&docid=120125&pageIndex=0&doclang=EN&mode=lst&dir=&occ=first&part=1&cid=3435083. Concerning researchers’ careers in Italy, the Court has for instance ruled that Clause 5 of the framework Agreement on fixed-term work must be interpreted as not precluding national legislation which sets the total duration of the employment contracts that may be concluded by a single researcher, including with different universities and institutes, at 12 years, confer judgment of 15 December 2022, AQ and Others v Presidenza del Consiglio dei ministri and Others, C40/20, EU:C:2022:985, https://juris.curia.europa.eu/juris/document/document.jsf? text=&docid=268607&pageIndex=0&doclang=en&mode=lst&dir=&occ=first&part=1&cid=3381762. Specifically, one key reform focuses on enhancing the stability and transparency of research funding, by establishing a binding legal framework for a threeyear rolling plan that allocates predictable, multi-annual funding for research activities. If Italy fails to implement such reforms adequately, the Commission may withhold payments until corrective measures are taken. https://research-and-innovation.ec.europa.eu/funding/funding-opportunities/funding-programmes-and-open-calls/horizon-europe_en. According to Article 18 of Annex 5 to the Horizon Europe General Model Grant Agreement, beneficiaries must take all measures to implement the principles of the European Charter for Researchers and must ensure that researchers and all participants involved in the action are aware of them. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/C/2023/1640/oj/eng

Moreover, the same framework recommends that Member States counter the phenomenon of precarity and support job security and stability (8). A Mutual Learning Exercise supported by HE allowed Member States to exchange good practices on research careers, including to fight precarity (9). Generally, in the context of funds managed under the shared management principle, such as the European Social Fund plus, the Commission verifies (10) that the managing authority takes the necessary steps to ensure that projects are in line with the objectives of the programme and with the cohesion policy.

E-10-2026-002068.t: Promoting the development and deployment of small modular reactors in the EU
qt: to the Commission Sebastian Tynkkynen (ECR) Subject:

The Commission has adopted a strategy for developing and deploying small modular reactors, which recognises the role that they can play across the wider energy system, not only in generating electricity but also in providing heat. In the current geopolitical context – especially considering Russia’s war of aggression – strengthening Europe’s energy self-sufficiency is a necessity. In this regard, small modular reactors offer a way of increasing stable energy production while reducing the EU’s dependence on external energy sources. Nuclear energy is also clean. However, many of the proposed EU-level actions on this important technology remain quite general. Europe’s energy system would benefit from more concrete actions that would help ensure that these crucial objectives – reducing the EU’s energy dependency and increasing stable production – are actually achieved. In this context: 1.
Will the Commission ensure that the upcoming proposals for the post-2030 energy and climate framework are fully in line with the objectives of this strategy?

What additional financial instruments does the Commission plan to introduce post-2028 to support first-of-a-kind nuclear projects and the scaling-up of commercially viable innovative nuclear technologies?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.8.2026) The Commission’s work towards a more flexible, investment-driven and delivery-focused Energy Union1 in post-2030 build on the actions taken under the Affordable Energy Action Plan, which include the Small Modular Reactors Strategy adopted on 10 March 20262, and the recently adopted AccelerateEU Communication3 and Electrification Action Plan4. For those Member States choosing nuclear energy, the Commission has recognised that nuclear can contribute to decarbonisation, competitiveness, security of supply and strategic autonomy5. In that context, the Commission will continue to uphold the principle of technology neutrality across all policy and legislative initiatives, while fully respecting Member States’ right to determine their energy mix6. The Commission proposal for the next multiannual financial framework (MFF) to apply from 2028 onwards is currently being negotiated with the budgetary authority. The Commission respects the process and does not wish to speculate on its outcomes. In parallel, the Commission works with the European Investment Bank to implement, already in the current MFF, a temporary InvestEU top up of EUR 200 million until 20287 to support innovative nuclear technologies8. Other relevant avenues to fund nuclear investments in the EU already pursued include the prospective Important Projects of Common European Interest (IPCEI) on innovative nuclear technologies9 and the Scaleup Europe Fund10 as well as funding for nuclear research and innovation activities under the Euratom Research and Training Programme.

qt: to the Commission Gerald Hauser (PfE) Subject:

Just as they did with COVID-19, the mainstream media and vaccination advocates have been stoking fears about the hantavirus for several days now. The virus has, however, been known for decades and infects several thousand people in Europe every year without making many waves thus far. Most infections are asymptomatic or harmless, although in rare cases the disease can prove deadly. In a February 2021 report to the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), Pfizer listed hantavirus infections as a possible side effect of the COVID-19 vaccine. As early as 2021, the international vaccine alliance GAVI warned that the ‘next pandemic’ could be caused by the hantavirus. Moderna has been working on an mRNA vaccine for several years now. On 8 May 2026, Austria enacted legislation stipulating that the authorities must be notified of any infections or suspected cases of hantavirus. Recently, military doctors were even parachuted on to an island in the Atlantic. However, the WHO Director-General travelled to Tenerife in person and, surprisingly enough, declared there to be no major danger. The WHO has stated that human-to-human transmission is, I quote, ‘uncommon’. 1.

E-10-2026-002066.t: Award of Horizon Europe grant to the Israel Antiquities Authority (project 101167454) despite Article 2 breaches
qt: to the Commission Matjaž Nemec (S&D) Subject:

In June 2025, the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy carried out a review of Israel’s compliance with Article 2 of the EU-Israel Association Agreement and determined a breach. On 29 July 2025, the Commission proposed the partial suspension of the Association Agreement with Israel and of its participation in Horizon Europe1. However, the Commission has not yet triggered Article14 of the Horizon Europe Grant Agreement in relation to Israel or entities originating from Israel. Despite the review findings, on 19 December 2025 the Commission awarded a grant to a consortium, including the Israel Antiquities Authority (IAA) – a state agency, under Horizon Europe project 101167454, with an estimated EU contribution of EUR 153 7502. The IAA has historically faced criticism for its role in archaeological activities within the occupied Palestinian territory, including East Jerusalem, which Israel de facto annexed, constituting a grave violation of international law. 1.
Why did the Commission award a grant to the IAA despite its own conclusion that Israel is in breach of Article 2 of the EU-Israel Association Agreement?

What specific mechanisms or ‘ethical screenings’ were applied to project 101167454 to ensure that no IAA activities funded by the EU take place in the territories occupied by Israel since 1967, in compliance with Commission Guidelines 2013/C 205/05 and international law, including International Court of Justice advisory opinions on Palestine?

E-10-2026-002065.t: Data security and competitiveness of SMEs in the European Health Data Space
qt: to the Commission Piotr Müller (ECR) Subject:

The European Health Data Space (EHDS) framework currently in the pipeline aims to create an integrated system for exchanging medical information to support innovation and improve healthcare across the EU. At the same time, the organisation and delivery of health services remain the competence of Member States, which raises questions as to the impact of a centralised digital infrastructure on the autonomy of national healthcare systems, the competitiveness of European businesses and the security of strategic health data. There is also a risk of market concentration around the largest global tech players, in particular from countries that do not guarantee democratic standards and data protection equivalent to EU law. In view of this, I ask: 1.
What financial instruments and procedural simplifications does the Commission envisage to ensure that the costs of certifying EHDS systems do not become a barrier for Polish and European SMEs?

What legal and technical mechanisms will be put in place to prevent entities from countries that do not meet democratic and data protection standards equivalent to EU law from using EU citizens’ health data?
Is the Commission monitoring the impact of digitalising health on the exclusion of older people and the risk of increased costs for health services as a result of market concentration?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (28.7.2026) The European Health Data Space (EHDS)1 Regulation establishes provisions for strengthening the single market of electronic health record (EHR) systems, reducing costs and barriers to entry. By harmonising rules for EHR systems, the compliance costs get lower for new entrants, including small and medium-sized enterprises. For example, the Regulation lays down a self-certification procedure for EHR systems limiting certification costs and administrative burdens for EHR systems manufacturers of all sizes, including small and medium-sized enterprises. Regarding use EU citizens’ health data by entities from third countries, the EHDS Regulation sets out a mechanism2 of reciprocal access that will serve to assess the rules in third countries to ensure that only entities from third countries recognised as providing similar rules will be able to apply for access. Transfers of personal data to third countries can only take place subject to the conditions and limitations set out in Chapter V of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)3, notably the need to ensure a level of protection in the third country that is essentially equivalent to the one guaranteed within the EU4. When it comes to risks of digital exclusion among older populations, the EHDS promotes inclusive design usable for all, including older adults, enabling them to exercise their rights under the Regulation.
1 Regulation (EU) 2025/327 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 11 February 2025 on the

European Health Data Space and amending Directive 2011/24/EU and Regulation (EU) 2024/2847, OJ L, 2025/327, 5.3.2025, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2025/327/oj. 2 See Articles 75(5) and 91 EHDS Regulation. 3 Regulation (EU) 2016/679 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 April 2016 on the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free movement of such data, and repealing Directive 95/46/EC (General Data Protection Regulation), OJ L 119, 4.5.2016, p. 1–88. 4 See also recitals 35 and 81 EHDS Regulation.

E-10-2026-002064.t: Impact of EU climate policy on the competitiveness of agriculture and the fertiliser sector
qt: to the Commission Piotr Müller (ECR) Subject:

European farmers are facing ever-increasing production costs linked to energy and fertiliser prices, as well as the increasing regulatory burden of EU climate policy. Meanwhile, the European Commission has also announced further actions to reduce the use of mineral fertilisers, highlighting the development of biogas plants and digestate as an alternative. However, without adequate investment support and safeguarding the competitiveness of European production, these measures could exacerbate the crisis in agriculture, increase the EU’s dependence on imports and further increase food prices. In light of the above: 1.
What impact assessment has the Commission carried out on the effect of EU climate policy on the competitiveness of the European fertiliser sector and costs for farmers?
What specific financial instruments does the Commission intend to mobilise to support the construction of biogas plants and the development of the use of digestate in Member States?
How does the Commission intend to prevent a further reduction in fertiliser production in Europe and a deepening of the crisis in the competitiveness of European agriculture?

(4 August 2026) The Impact Assessment to accompany the revision of the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) Directive (1) has analysed the impact of several elements, including potential measures to prevent the risk of carbon leakage, as well as measures for supporting the decarbonisation of industry via the Industrial Decarbonisation Bank. As part of this process, the Commission took fully into account the provisions relevant to carbon leakage in the revision of the EU ETS Directive. The Fertilisers Action Plan (FAP) (2) notes that Member States can use Cohesion Funds to support sustainable biogas and biomethane production and, in line with AccelerateEU (3), can deploy accelerating measures for Cohesion Funds and Recovery and Resilience Plans. The Common Agricultural Policy also supports bioeconomy and sustainable biogas/methane through interventions, such as rural development funding for investments, cooperation partnerships to achieve economies of scale, training/advisory services. Additionally, the InvestEU programme (4), including through the European Investment Bank and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, supports biogas and bioenergy projects in the EU. The FAP sets out a comprehensive package of measures to strengthen the resilience and competitiveness of the EU fertiliser sector. The Plan aims to support domestic production capacity, accelerate the deployment of low carbon and circular fertiliser solutions, diversify sources of raw materials and feedstocks, improve market transparency, and foster innovation, all while advancing the sector’s decarbonisation.

E-10-2026-002063.t: Risk of restricting access to advanced AI technologies and cybersecurity in the EU
qt: to the Commission Piotr Müller (ECR) Subject:

Debates in Parliament on advanced AI systems used in cybersecurity show the increasing importance of Western countries cooperating on technology in the face of threats from authoritarian states, particularly China. However, there are also concerns that the Commission may try to respond to the development of new technologies primarily through further regulatory or administrative restrictions on providers of advanced digital solutions, including US companies working with European institutions and businesses. In light of the above: 1.
Is the Commission considering introducing new regulatory or administrative restrictions on advanced AI and cybersecurity systems provided by US companies?

How does the Commission intend to ensure that EU regulatory policy does not restrict access for European businesses and public administrations to modern strategic technologies developed by allied countries?

How does the Commission intend to reconcile the development of European technological capabilities with maintaining strong transatlantic cooperation in the area of cybersecurity and artificial intelligence?

(8 September 2026) As advances in frontier AI models offer opportunities as well as novel and heightened risks for cybersecurity, the Commission adopted on 7 July 2026 an Action Plan on Cybersecurity and AI with concrete actions to support Member States and organisations across the EU (1). A key priority of the Commission is to ensure that frontier AI models are safe, accessible and deployable for cybersecurity in Europe. The action plan proposes a Blueprint as a framework for secure access to frontier AI models with cyber capabilities as well as investment for testing and evaluation of such models. Europe must also step up its preparedness and resilience in the face of the cybersecurity risks posed by frontier AI. The Commission considers that this requires, first and foremost, the effective implementation of the EU’s existing legislation, including the NIS2 Directive (2), the Cyber Resilience Act (3), and the AI Act (4) that obliges providers of the most advanced AI models to assess and mitigate systemic risk, including of misuse in the cyber realm. The action plan also prioritises investments in European AI capabilities for cybersecurity, for which existing investments in research and development under the Horizon and Digital Europe Programmes will be complemented by the launch of an EU Grand Challenge on AI-assisted vulnerability remediation. In order to finance Europe’s tech sovereignty ambitions, the communication on European Tech Sovereignty calls for a reflection on the means to boost a European equity capacity at scale in order to establish a portfolio of equity investments in advanced technologies and infrastructure in critical sectors, including AI (5). As the challenges posed by frontier AI are shared and global in nature, it is imperative that the EU works closely with partners at international level.

E-10-2026-002062.t: Analytical basis for the planned regulation of data centres
qt: to the Commission Piotr Müller (ECR) Subject:

The Commission is continuing to work on further initiatives for the sustainable functioning of data centres, including ratings systems and potential minimum environmental performance standards. However, representatives of the technology sector and infrastructure operators have highlighted major methodological shortcomings and limitations of the database used to prepare these initiatives. According to the available information, only some of the entities subject to reporting obligations provided the required data, while some Member States are, in practice, not reporting at all. This raises concerns that the Commission is trying to create far-reaching regulation for strategic digital infrastructure without a sufficient empirical basis, which could negatively affect investment in AI, cloud computing and the development of European technological sovereignty. In light of the above: 1.

How does the Commission justify continuing to work on potential minimum environmental standards for data centres despite the limited level of data reporting and insufficient representativeness of available information?

How will the Commission ensure that the process of preparing new data centre regulations is based on real operational data and infrastructure operators’ experience rather than primarily on external consultants’ analyses?

Is the Commission considering halting the development of new mandatory standards until more complete and reliable data on the energy and environmental performance of European data centres becomes available?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (19.8.2026) The European Union is the first to introduce comprehensive legislation on the energy performance and efficiency of data centres. The EU legislative framework, notably the Energy Efficiency Directive1 and its Delegated Act2 increase transparency significantly in this area. As the report to the European Parliament and the Council on the energy efficiency of data centres in the EU shows that, while data centres in the EU are becoming more sustainable, there is enormous potential for further improvements, especially as part of a better integration with the energy system. The report will be published soon. Since the Commission is assessing the transposition and implementation of the Energy efficiency Directive, including Article 12 and Annex VII, reporting compliance is expected to improve in next cycles as operators adapt to regulatory requirements and benefit from Commission guidance3. Furthermore, the Commission supplements reported data with technical studies4,5, stakeholder consultations, including with Member States, and expert validation. Before possibly proposing any minimum performance standards, the Commission will launch a call for evidence and an open public consultation, followed by an impact assessment. Halting the discussion on possible minimum performance standards when the Commission expects that most of the data centre capacity that will be on the ground in the next 20 years will be designed and be constructed in the next five to seven years, would risk delaying progress toward a sustainable and competitive EU data centre sector.
1 Directive (EU) 2023/1791 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 September 2023 on energy

efficiency and amending Regulation (EU) 2023/955 (recast): http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2023/1791/oj. 2 Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1364 of 14 March 2024 on the first phase of the establishment of a common Union rating scheme for data centres: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg_del/2024/1364/oj. 3 https://energy.ec.europa.eu/topics/energy-efficiency/energy-efficiency-targets-directive-and-rules/energyefficiency-directive/energy-performance-data-centres_en#a-data-base-for-reporting. 4 Technical Assistance in support of implementing Article 12(5) of Directive 2023/1791 on the energy performance and sustainability of data centres, https://www.borderstep.org/projekte/eudcear/. 5 https://energy.ec.europa.eu/resources/preparatory-studies/minimum-performance-standards-eu-data-centres_en.

E-10-2026-002061.t: Facial recognition feature on French police officers’ phones
qt: to the Commission Markéta Gregorová (Verts/ALE), Leila Chaibi (The Left), David Cormand (Verts/ALE) Subject:

The media organisation Disclose has revealed that French police officers were equipped with ‘NEO’ mobile phones containing software that allows for real-time biometric identification. The software can be used for investigations related to crimes, offences and even certain minor offences. The facial recognition feature does not seem to have had any safeguards in place regarding its use: police officers have used the software for mere identity checks. The software connects directly to the ‘TAJ’ database, which is estimated to contain 17 million files regarding suspects and 48 million files regarding victims, with an estimated 9 million facial images1. The database can contain very sensitive information, such as religion, sexual orientation, union membership, etc. The TAJ database has been heavily criticised by the French Data Protection Authority for its lack of accuracy2. 1.

Does the Commission consider the system as being a real-time remote biometric identification system and does it consider that the system complies with the temporal, geographic and personal limitations established under the AI Act?
Does the Commission consider the requirement for prior judicial or independent administrative authorisation to be met?
Does the Commission consider the crimes and offences covered to be compliant with Annex II to the AI Act?

https://disclose.ngo/fr/article/la-reconnaissance-faciale-deployee-a-grande-echelle-sur-les-telephonesdes-forces-de-lordre. 2 https://www.cnil.fr/fr/traitement-dantecedents-judiciaires-la-cnil-rappelle-lordre-deux-ministeres. 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.7.2026) Under the AI Act1, the use of real-time remote biometric identification (RBI) systems in publicly accessible spaces for the purposes of law enforcement is prohibited, unless and in so far as such use is strictly necessary for one of the three objectives specified under Article 5(1)(h) of the AI Act and the Member State law permitting the use of such systems comply with the requirements in Article 5(2)-(7) of the AI Act. The following three objectives are listed in Article 5(1)(h): (i) the targeted search for victims of three specific serious crimes and missing persons, (ii) the prevention of imminent threats to life or physical safety or a genuine threat of terrorist attacks, and (iii) the localisation or identification of suspects and offenders of certain serious crimes as listed in Annex II. According to the requirements in Article 5(2)-(7) of the AI Act, the deployment of a real-time RBI system in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement purposes shall be subject to a prior authorisation granted by a judicial authority or an independent administrative authority whose decision is binding. The prohibition in Article 5(1)(h) of the AI Act started to apply as from 2 February 2025. However, the provisions on the enforcement of the AI Act will only start to apply on 2 August 2026. Therefore, the enforcement of Article 5 of the AI Act cannot be initiated earlier at either national or EU level. The Commission will observe this matter closely.
1 Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 of 13 June 2024 laying down harmonised rules on artificial intelligence,
