qt: to the Council Ana Miranda Paz (Verts/ALE) Subject:

Galician is used every day by thousands of people in Galicia but has still not been accepted as an official language of the European Union, in spite of the Spanish Government’s request to make Galician, Catalan and Basque EU official languages. The fact that the people of my country cannot communicate with the EU in their own language reveals a deficit in legitimacy and democracy that undermines the image of the Union. Galician Literature Day is held on 17 May. Galicians celebrate figures who are important for their language and call for Galician to be used more widely in society. Like every year, the 2026 event saw thousands of people protesting against the removal of Galician from education, culture and public services and a Galician Government that undermines our language. Public opinion is irrefutably against that policy. In view of the above: When will the Council allow Galician and the other official languages of Spain be official languages of the European Union?
at: In 2006, the Council concluded an administrative arrangement with the Kingdom of Spain1 on the official use of additional languages whose status is recognised by the Constitution of the Kingdom of Spain in all or part of its territory, or the use of which as a national language is authorised by law. Based on that arrangement, Spanish citizens may send to and receive from the Council written communication in Galician via the competent body designated for that purpose by the Spanish Government. Spanish representatives may also, under certain conditions, use such languages in speeches at Council meetings. In addition, the Spanish Government may make certified translations into Galician of acts of the European Union adopted under the ordinary legislative procedure and forward them to the General Secretariat of the Council. Such certified translations are added by the Council to its archives. The Council provides copies of such translations on request to any citizen of the Union. Moreover, in accordance with Article 55(2) of the Treaty on European Union, the Kingdom of Spain deposited in September 2011 a certified copy of the EU Treaties translated into Galician.

E-10-2026-002059.t: EU countries’ responsibility for arms transfers to Israel
qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Krzysztof Śmiszek (S&D), Joanna Scheuring-Wielgus (S&D), Robert Biedroń (S&D) Subject:

There is a growing debate about EU countries’ responsibility for arms transfers to Israel in the context of the conflict in Gaza. While export controls are a national competence, governments are bound by the Arms Trade Treaty and the Council Common Position banning supplies where there is a risk of humanitarian law being violated. It is crucial to establish what supervisory tools the EU institutions have at their disposal to respond to possible errors in EU Member States’ licensing procedures. In light of this: 1.

Do the European Commission and the European External Action Service have a mechanism to monitor and report arms exports to Israel when there is a clear risk of their use in violation of the Arms Trade Treaty and the criteria of the Council Common Position?

In the Vice-President / High Representative’s view, do arms transfers from the EU to Israel currently comply with the obligation to refuse export authorisations when countries continue to engage in trade, despite being aware of the real risk of weapons being used for war crimes?

Could the deliberate omission, underestimation or flawed assessment of risks in the licensing process constitute grounds for the EU to initiate investigations, restrict transfers or impose policy measures against non-compliant countries?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (13.7.2026) The control on the export of arms by Member States is subject to national legislation, the Council Common Position 2008/944/CFSP1 and the Arms Trade Treaty2 (ATT). The competent authorities of Member States take final decision whether to authorise or deny an individual export or transit license of military equipment, in accordance with the said legal frameworks. Member States are solely responsible to ensure compliance with applicable laws, including the Common Position and the ATT. The High Representative/Vice-President is not in a position to assess specific export cases against the criteria of the Common Position, nor is mandated, under EU law, to enforce the Common Position or other applicable laws. The Council, through its competent Working Group, works towards increased convergence amongst Member States’ arms export policies. This includes exchanges of views on application of criteria of the Common Position. Specifically, the impact of the conflict in Gaza on national arms exports policies of Member States is continuously on the agenda and Member States confidentially share information about their respective approaches. The EU remains deeply concerned about the catastrophic humanitarian situation in Gaza and continues to urge Israel to improve it. In the context of the Israel/Hamas conflict in Gaza, the EU recognised Israel’s right to defend itself from the beginning, but consistently urges Israel to do so in line with International Law, International Human Rights Law and International Humanitarian Law and to ensure the protection of civilians. The disproportionate use of force against civilians and civilian infrastructure is unacceptable.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex%3A32008E0944. 2 https://old.thearmstradetreaty.org/.

E-10-2026-002058.t: Use of Hungarian public funds for organised activities concerning transnational political influence in the EU democratic space
qt: to the Commission Krzysztof Śmiszek (S&D), Alessandro Zan (S&D), Brando Benifei (S&D), Mounir Satouri (Verts/ALE), Tineke Strik (Verts/ALE), Mélissa Camara (Verts/ALE), Lukas Sieper (Renew), Robert Biedroń (S&D), David Cormand (Verts/ALE), Kim Van Sparrentak (Verts/ALE), Raquel García Hermida-Van Der Walle (Renew), Benedetta Scuderi (Verts/ALE), Joanna Scheuring-Wielgus (S&D) Subject:

Recent statements1 by the new Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar allege that, during the previous government’s term, Hungarian public funds may have been used to finance the Conservative Political Action Conference in Hungary (CPAC Hungary) and related international political networks. The organisations reportedly involved include the Center for Fundamental Rights, the Mathias Corvinus Collegium (MCC) Foundation and associated transnational advocacy networks active at EU and international level, such as the Political Network for Values (PNfV). These allegations raise concerns that public resources in a Member State may have supported partisan international political activity involving actors from other Member States and non-EU countries. 1.

Is the Commission aware of these statements, and will it assess whether EU funds, EUsupported entities, EU co-financed projects, or entities receiving EU funding were directly or indirectly involved in connection with CPAC Hungary or related networks?

Does the Commission consider that such use of public resources, if confirmed, could fall within the scope of EU safeguards related to fraud prevention, anti-corruption, public procurement, the rule of law, political financing or electoral integrity?

Would the Commission consider involving the European Anti-Fraud Office (OLAF), the European Public Prosecutor’s Office where competent, or other relevant EU bodies in the matter, if indications emerge that EU funds or EU electoral processes were affected?

E-10-2026-002057.t: Legislation on borrowers’ rights referred back to legislature
qt: to the Commission Giorgos Georgiou (The Left) Subject:

For years, the Republic of Cyprus has continued to face serious issues of incorrect implementation of Directive 93/13/EEC on unfair terms in consumer contracts, in particular in relation to banking contracts and the effective protection of borrowers. Recently, the Cyprus’s House of Representatives adopted legislation aimed at bringing national law in line with the requirements of this directive, and in particular the right of access to justice, with the aim of suspending foreclosures until a case is heard when unfair terms are alleged or the outstanding amount is contested. However, the President of the Republic of Cyprus has referred this legislation back to the legislature, creating further uncertainty as to the country’s compliance with the EU acquis and effective consumer protection. In light of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
What does the fact that this legislation was referred back to the legislature and its nonimplementation mean for Cyprus’ compliance with EU law?
What will be the consequences of continued non-alignment with European legislation and insufficient consumer protection?
at: (English version) to the Commission Giorgos Georgiou (The Left) (19 May 2026) Subject: Legislation on borrowers’ rights referred back to legislature For years, the Republic of Cyprus has continued to face serious issues of incorrect implementation of Directive 93/13/EEC on unfair terms in consumer contracts, in particular in relation to banking contracts and the effective protection of borrowers. However, the President of the Republic of Cyprus has referred this legislation back to the legislature, creating further uncertainty as to the country’s compliance with the EU acquis and effective consumer protection. In light of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

What will be the consequences of continued non-alignment with European legislation and insufficient consumer protection?

(28 September 2026) Council Directive 93/13/EEC (1) requires Member States to ensure that consumers are not bound by unfair contract terms, including in mortgage contracts. However, procedures applicable to enforcement procedures must be set out in national legislation (2). It is the primary responsibility of the national authorities and courts to ensure the monitoring and enforcement of the application of consumer law in individual disputes and to provide redress where appropriate (3). The Commission opened an infringement procedure against Cyprus (4) concerning the correct application and enforcement of Directive 93/13/EEC and Directive 2005/29/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council (5). Further to changes of the Cypriot legislation in 2021 and 2022 (6), as well as additional data from Cyprus in 2025 on the practice of the consumer protection authorities, the Commission is finalising its assessment of the case to consider next steps. The Commission continues monitoring the situation and may decide to take further action if necessary. Directive (EU) 2021/2167 of the European Parliament and of the Council (7), which regulates credit servicers and credit purchasers, has reinforced borrower protection, in particular by introducing general principles for the conduct of credit servicers and by establishing transparency obligations towards borrowers. Cyprus notified complete transposition of Directive (EU) 2021/2167 on 12 November 2024. The Commission has opened an informal dialogue with Cyprus to seek clarifications on various issues arising from the national transposition.

E-10-2026-002056.t: Retroactive reversal of favourable administrative decisions
qt: to the Commission Hanna Gedin (The Left), Jonas Sjöstedt (The Left) Subject:

The rule of law is a universal principle of governance and is fundamental to international peace, security and political stability. Mindful of the developments taking place with regard to rule of law policy in the EU, the Commission published a communication in 2014 on a new EU framework to strengthen the rule of law. In 2019, further definitions were established with regard to the rule of law, and in December 2020 the EU’s co-legislators codified a legally binding definition as part of the Conditionality Regulation (Article 2). A core element of the rule of law is the principle of legality, according to which the exercise of public powers must be foreseeable, legally certain and clearly regulated by law. In Sweden, a discussion has taken place on the possibility of bringing in a special law that would allow for the blanket revocation of permanent residence permits. The introduction of such a law would mean that administrative decisions that were previously favourable would be retroactively amended, to the detriment of the individuals concerned. Views diverge as to whether this would be in line with EU law. With the above in mind, we should like some guidance from the Commission. 1.

Does the Commission consider the retroactive, blanket revocation of permanent residence permits that have already been granted to be compatible with legal certainty and the fundamental principles of the rule of law?

Does the Commission take the view that the retroactive reversal of previously favourable administrative decisions, to the detriment of the individuals concerned, would be compatible with EU law, the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union and the Treaty on European Union?

qt: to the Commission Regina Doherty (PPE), Seán Kelly (PPE) Subject:

Small and medium-sized enterprises rely on online intermediaries to access markets and reach customers in sectors such as hospitality, retail and media publishing. Repealing the Platform-to-Business (P2B) Regulation would remove safeguards at a time when platform power is increasing and distribution models are becoming more complex through algorithmic and AI-driven ranking and recommendation systems. While the Digital Markets Act plays a role in addressing unfair practices by designated gatekeepers, its scope is limited to a small number of very large platforms designated as gatekeepers. For these relationships, the P2B Regulation remains the only horizontal EU instrument ensuring baseline transparency and fairness. Although the Digital Services Act introduces obligations on transparency and accountability, its primary objective is content moderation and systemic risk management rather than ensuring commercial fairness between platforms and business users. The P2B Regulation has been used by national competition authorities, including in France in July 2025 to challenge Booking.com’s service terms containing clauses deemed unfair to hoteliers. In 2025, the Italian national competition authority identified breaches of the P2B Regulation by Refurbed Marketplace GmbH. In Ireland in 2023, the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission consulted business users of online platforms under the P2B Regulation. How does the Commission reconcile continued support for small and medium-sized enterprises with the repeal of the P2B Regulation?
at: (English version) to the Commission Regina Doherty (PPE), Seán Kelly (PPE) (19 May 2026) Subject: Repealing the Platform-to-Business Regulation Small and medium-sized enterprises rely on online intermediaries to access markets and reach customers in sectors such as hospitality, retail and media publishing. Repealing the Platform-to-Business (P2B) Regulation would remove safeguards at a time when platform power is increasing and distribution models are becoming more complex through algorithmic and AI-driven ranking and recommendation systems. While the Digital Markets Act plays a role in addressing unfair practices by designated gatekeepers, its scope is limited to a small number of very large platforms designated as gatekeepers. For these relationships, the P2B Regulation remains the only horizontal EU instrument ensuring baseline transparency and fairness. Although the Digital Services Act introduces obligations on transparency and accountability, its primary objective is content moderation and systemic risk management rather than ensuring commercial fairness between platforms and business users. The P2B Regulation has been used by national competition authorities, including in France in July 2025 to challenge Booking.com’s service terms containing clauses deemed unfair to hoteliers. In 2025, the Italian national competition authority identified breaches of the P2B Regulation by Refurbed Marketplace GmbH. In Ireland in 2023, the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission consulted business users of online platforms under the P2B Regulation. How does the Commission reconcile continued support for small and medium-sized enterprises with the repeal of the P2B Regulation? (6 July 2026) Since the adoption of the P2B Regulation in 2019 (1), the EU regulatory framework governing online platforms has been strengthened significantly, particularly with the Digital Services Act (DSA) (2) and the Digital Markets Act (DMA) (3). These two acts have introduced effective and far-reaching rules to ensure a safe, predictable and trusted online environment, as well as contestable and fair digital markets. In line with the shared agenda of simplification, repealing the P2B Regulation will make the navigation for online platforms and for business users clearer as an additional layer of regulation will be removed, bringing legal clarity and lower compliance costs. The Commission also noted that the P2B Regulation has been under-applied and under-enforced. With the DSA and the DMA, a much more robust enforcement structure is in place so that rights of business users are effectively protected, not just on paper. Businesses need most protection in asymmetrical relationships where online platforms have considerable economic power or hold a strong negotiation position. While the DMA focuses on gatekeepers and not all online platforms, it goes further than the mere transparency afforded by P2B in that it imposes obligations and prohibitions on those platforms where SMEs might otherwise fear retaliation. Moreover, the DSA applies to online platforms of all sizes, with additional risk-based obligations for Very Large Online Platforms (VLOPs) and Very Large Online Search Engines (VLOSEs), mirroring P2B provisions on terms and conditions, recommender systems, internal complaint-handling mechanism and mediation.

Regulation (EU) 2019/1150 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 20 June 2019 on promoting fairness and transparency for business users of online intermediation services; https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2019/1150/oj. Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 19 October 2022 on a Single Market For Digital Services and amending Directive 2000/31/EC (Digital Services Act); https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/2065/oj. Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 September 2022 on contestable and fair markets in the digital sector and amending Directives (EU) 2019/1937 and (EU) 2020/1828 (Digital Markets Act); https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/1925/oj.
The Commission therefore considers, via the DMA and the DSA, protections for business, including SMEs, are actually strengthened in situations where it matters most.

E-10-2026-002053.t: Regional Activity Centre on Climate Change’s possible involvement in the preparation of Türkiye’s ‘Blue Homeland’ bill
qt: to the Commission Yannis Maniatis (S&D) Subject:

Türkiye is preparing a bill with a view to claiming maritime jurisdiction in parts of the Aegean and Eastern Mediterranean, based on the legally unfounded Turkish claim that the islands cannot have a continental shelf and EEZ, in total contradiction with the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), which is an integral part of the European acquis. The National Center for the Sea and Maritime Law (DEHUKAM)12 of the University of Ankara, whose organisational structure includes the Regional Activity Centre on Climate Change (CC/RAC) of the UN3, has contributed to the bill, while until recently the director of the CC/RAC4 was also the CEO5 of DEHUKAM. According to DEHUKAM6, Türkiye, in cooperation with the EU, presented the proposal to create the CC/RAC, which was unanimously adopted by the Parties to the Barcelona Convention on 6 December 2023. Can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Has it checked whether the CC/RAC contributed to the preparation of this bill?

Can it confirm that no European technical, financial or human resources have been allocated to the CC/RAC, which may have contributed to DEHUKAM’s preparation of Türkiye’s illegal maritime spatial planning?
Does it continue to support the 2023 decision on the CC/RAC, despite its relationship with DEHUKAM, whose positions are publicly at odds with the European acquis, such as UNCLOS?

E-10-2026-002052.t: Cancellation of organic beekeeping and livestock farming programmes in Greece
qt: to the Commission Yannis Maniatis (S&D) Subject:

The Greek authorities recently announced the cancellation of organic beekeeping and organic livestock farming programmes worth a total of EUR 134 million (EUR 19 million and EUR 115 million respectively). The Ministry of Rural Development and Food reached this decision citing widespread irregularities, high rates of non-compliance and serious weaknesses in audit and certification mechanisms. In particular, of 737 audits carried out on the above-mentioned organic farming programmes, 35 % revealed issues and 20.5 % of participants withdrew of their own accord, with the combined rate of issues and withdrawals reaching 55.5 %. The Ministry of Rural Development and Food has announced that financial penalties have already been imposed on six (6) certification bodies and the suspension of operations in a further three (3) cases. Finally, according to the Greek Government, funds that had been earmarked for the cancelled measures are to be redirected towards ‘other priorities’, even though these measures form part of Greece’s strategic plan for the common agricultural policy for 2023-2027 and were designed to support organic production. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Is it aware of the cancellation of these programmes and, if so, how does it assess their management by the Greek authorities?
Does it intend to approve the redirection of the above-mentioned resources towards ‘other priorities’ possibly unrelated to the EU’s objectives on sustainable agriculture and organic production?
How does it intend to protect compliant producers affected by such a blanket decision?

(9 July 2026) Following issues identified by the Commission services concerning the certification of organic production, the Greek authorities decided to cancel the planned interventions for organic beekeeping and organic livestock farming. The Commission is assessing the information provided by the Greek authorities in an ongoing enquiry. Member States have the obligation to protect the financial interests of the Union and to take all the appropriate measures to this effect. In this regard, the cancellation of interventions is at the discretion of the Greek authorities taking into consideration the principle of proportionality and the specific circumstances of each case such as that no beneficiaries have been confirmed. An intervention can be cancelled from the Common Agricultural Policy Strategic Plans and resources under those interventions may be redirected to other interventions following a request for a strategic amendment from the Member State concerned and subject to approval by the Commission (1). The Commission was informed that Greece intends to submit a request for an amendment in September 2026. Following a submission, the Commission will assess the consistency of the strategic amendment with Regulation (EU) 2021/2115 (2) and Regulation (EU) 2021/2116 (3), as well as the delegated and implementing acts adopted pursuant to them, and the effective contribution of the strategic amendment to achieving the specific objectives under Regulation (EU) 2021/2115.

E-10-2026-002051.t: Concern about a new project threatening water, air, health and nature quality in A Laracha (A Coruña)
qt: to the Commission Ana Miranda Paz (Verts/ALE) Subject:
Concern about a new project threatening water, air, health and nature quality in A Laracha (A Coruña)

The planned large-scale biogas plant in A Laracha aims to produce organic fertiliser to generate biomethane by treating 63 500 tonnes of waste. The plant’s location in an area of high environmental and heritage value close to several population centres has led to widespread public opposition to the project, due to potential risks to health and the natural environment, including the Río Anllóns SCI and SAC. The Stop Biogás A Laracha platform called for a mass demonstration and the BNG submitted a complaint before the Galician Parliament. Galicia does not have any legislation on such large-scale plants and, in addition, trails in the number of protected Natura 2000 network areas in both Spain and the EU. This project again shows how protecting the environment is secondary for the Galician and Spanish governments, even in view of the Commission’s infringement procedure for the breach of Directive 92/43/EEC (Habitats Directive) and the mismanagement of the Natura 2000 network in Galicia. In light of the above, 1.
Is the Commission aware of this project and the possible effects on protected natural areas?
Does it have information on what specific measures have been taken by the Galician and Spanish governments to comply with the conservation requirements for these unique areas under threat?
at: (English version) to the Commission Ana Miranda Paz (Verts/ALE) (19 May 2026) Subject: Concern about a new project threatening water, air, health and nature quality in A Laracha (A Coruña) The planned large-scale biogas plant in A Laracha aims to produce organic fertiliser to generate biomethane by treating 63 500 tonnes of waste. The plant’s location in an area of high environmental and heritage value close to several population centres has led to widespread public opposition to the project, due to potential risks to health and the natural environment, including the Río Anllóns SCI and SAC. The Stop Biogás A Laracha platform called for a mass demonstration and the BNG submitted a complaint before the Galician Parliament. Galicia does not have any legislation on such large-scale plants and, in addition, trails in the number of protected Natura 2000 network areas in both Spain and the EU. This project again shows how protecting the environment is secondary for the Galician and Spanish governments, even in view of the Commission’s infringement procedure for the breach of Directive 92/43/EEC (Habitats Directive) and the mismanagement of the Natura 2000 network in Galicia. In light of the above, 1.
Is the Commission aware of this project and the possible effects on protected natural areas?

2. Does it have information on what specific measures have been taken by the Galician and Spanish governments to comply with the conservation requirements for these unique areas under threat? (16 July 2026) At this stage, the information available to the Commission regarding the project to build a biogas plant in A Laracha is limited to what has been transmitted by the Honourable Member and is publicly available. While the Commission does not have specific information on the measures that have been taken by the Galician and Spanish governments to comply with the conservation requirements for SAC Río Anllóns (1) regarding the project at stake, the Commission recalls that under Articles 6(2) and 6(3) of the Habitats Directive (2), any plan or project likely to have a significant effect on a Natura 2000 site must be subject to an appropriate assessment of its implications for the site, and may be authorised only if it is ascertained that it will not adversely affect the site’s integrity, subject to the derogation regime in Article 6(4). These requirements apply to the competent Spanish authorities, which remain responsible for the correct implementation of these provisions. As guardian of the Treaties, the Commission monitors the implementation of EU nature legislation in Spain, including through the ongoing infringement procedure (3) regarding the management of the Natura 2000 network. As a complement to its strategic enforcement policy, focused on systemic and structural issue s (4), the Commission considers that national means of redress are the most effective means to address individual alleged cases of non-compliance, such as the situation described by the Honourable Member.

E-10-2026-002050.t: Potential conflicts of interest for Jyrki Katainen as the EU’s Special Adviser for the Arctic while working as a lobbyist with interests in the region
qt: to the Commission Per Clausen (The Left) Subject:

The appointment of Jyrki Katainen as the EU’s Special Adviser for EU‑Arctic relations1 has raised concerns2 about potential conflicts of interest in many circles. One of the tasks included in his new role will be to update the EU’s Arctic strategy. One of the main sources of concern is the fact that, once he has taken up his new role, Mr Katainen will continue as Head of Group Public & Regulatory Affairs3 at Nordea, a bank. And it is precisely because Nordea has substantial – and potentially escalating – investment interests in, among other things, fossil fuel extraction in the Arctic, that it is difficult to see how this situation cannot be problematic when one of the key issues in the new Arctic strategy is whether the EU should maintain its moratorium on oil and gas extraction in the Arctic. In the light of the foregoing: 1.
What specific consideration has been given to how to both prevent and – not least – address complaints or concerns about specific conflicts of interest related to Mr Katainen’s different roles?
How many other EU special advisers and envoys are there who may have similar conflicts of interest?
Has any action ever been taken against a special adviser or envoy on the basis of suspected potential conflicts of interest?

at: (English version) to the Commission Per Clausen (The Left) (19 May 2026) Subject: Potential conflicts of interest for Jyrki Katainen as the EU’s Special Adviser for the Arctic while working as a lobbyist with interests in the region The appointment of Jyrki Katainen as the EU’s Special Adviser for EU-Arctic relations (1) has raised concerns (2) about potential conflicts of interest in many circles. One of the tasks included in his new role will be to update the EU’s Arctic strategy. One of the main sources of concern is the fact that, once he has taken up his new role, Mr Katainen will continue as Head of Group Public & Regulatory Affairs (3) at Nordea, a bank. And it is precisely because Nordea has substantial — and potentially escalating — investment interests in, among other things, fossil fuel extraction in the Arctic, that it is difficult to see how this situation cannot be problematic when one of the key issues in the new Arctic strategy is whether the EU should maintain its moratorium on oil and gas extraction in the Arctic. In the light of the foregoing: 1.
What specific consideration has been given to how to both prevent and — not least — address complaints or concerns about specific conflicts of interest related to Mr Katainen’s different roles?
How many other EU special advisers and envoys are there who may have similar conflicts of interest?
Has any action ever been taken against a special adviser or envoy on the basis of suspected potential conflicts of interest?

(8 September 2026) The procedure for the designation and appointment of Special Advisers is governed by Commission Decision C(2007)6655 (1). Before the appointment of any Special Adviser, the Commission carries out an ex-ante assessment of potential conflicts of interest based on a declaration of interests submitted by the person concerned. Where appropriate, safeguard measures are put in place to prevent any actual or perceived conflict of interest. In the case referred to by the Honourable Member, the Commission carried out such an assessment prior to the appointment of Mr Katainen, to ensure that there is no conflict of interest between his duties as Special Adviser and his professional activities outside the Commission. Appropriate safeguards have also been put in place and accepted by the Special Adviser. In accordance with applicable data protection rules, the Commission cannot disclose details relating to an individual’s assessment or safeguards. His role is to advise the Commission on the EU's Arctic policy, not to update its strategy. Any update remains the responsibility of the Commission and the High Representative of the European Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy/Vice-President. The complete list of Special Advisers, together with their curricula vitae and declarations, is published on the Commission’s dedicated webpage (2), in accordance with the applicable rules. The Commission assesses each appointment individually based on the applicable legal framework and does not categorise Special Advisers according to potential conflicts of interest. Therefore, it does not maintain a list of Special Advisers who may have ‘similar conflicts of interest’. The Commission applies its conflict of interest rules rigorously. Any concerns are assessed under the legal framework and applicable procedures.

E-10-2026-002049.t: Türkiye’s threats should be met with funding cuts
qt: to the Commission Georgios Aftias (PPE) Subject:

Türkiye is annoyed about the legitimate choices the Greek Government has made to protect Greece. Ankara is bothered by Greece’s relations with Israel, France and the United States. It is deeply annoyed about being excluded from SAFE defence funding. The Turks have even gone as far as to threaten the energy giant Chevron, which operates south of Crete. Meanwhile, Türkiye is peddling the Blue Homeland narrative, which is directed against Greece’s sovereignty, with statements by top officials. In view of the above: 1.
Will the Commission continue to provide EU funds to Türkiye when the latter is threatening an EU country?
When does the Commission plan to apply financial safeguards to funds intended for non-EU countries when they persistently violate international law?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (21.8.2026) Türkiye is a candidate country and key partner for the EU. As reiterated by the Council of the European Union and the European Council1, the EU has a strategic interest in a stable and secure environment in the Eastern Mediterranean, and in the development of a cooperative and mutually beneficial relationship with Türkiye. The Commission engages with Türkiye in areas of joint interest, while also addressing concerns. The accession negotiations with Türkiye have been at a standstill since 2018, due to backsliding on the rule of law. As a result, the EU has reduced pre-accession support to Türkiye and has reoriented funding towards civil society, people-to-people contacts, and EU priorities. In line with European Council conclusions of April 20242, the Commission is pursuing engagement with Türkiye in a phased, proportionate, and reversible manner. The EU has underlined on numerous occasions that Türkiye must avoid threats and actions that damage good neighbourly relations and respect the sovereignty of all Member States over their territorial sea and airspace as well as all their sovereign rights, including the right to explore and exploit natural resources in accordance with EU and international law, in particular the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea. The EU remains committed to defending its interests and those of its Member States as well as to upholding regional stability.

E-10-2026-002048.t: Transparency and integrity of the CRMA strategic project selection process
qt: to the Commission Martin Günther (The Left) Subject:

Following reports on the selection of strategic projects under the Critical Raw Materials Act (CRMA), concerns have emerged regarding transparency and procedural integrity1. Internal documents indicate that several projects – including highly controversial mining projects such as the Barroso lithium project in Portugal and the Jadar Valley project in Serbia – were added between a draft and final list in 2025, despite earlier expert assessments. This raises questions about the consistency and credibility of the selection process. 1.

What steps does the Commission intend to take to ensure full transparency in the CRMA selection process, including publication of draft and final project lists, expert assessments and clear justification for changes introduced between stages, particularly where projects initially failed to meet technical or sustainability criteria?
How does the Commission safeguard the independence and weight of expert evaluations during consultations within the European Critical Raw Materials Board?
How does the Commission ensure that Member State or political considerations do not override prior technical assessments, particularly for projects that are environmentally and socially sensitive?
https://table.media/esg/talk-of-the-town-en/critical-raw-materials-doubts-raised-about-the-eus-projectselection. 1
at: (English version) to the Commission Martin Günther (The Left) (19 May 2026) Subject: Transparency and integrity of the CRMA strategic project selection process Following reports on the selection of strategic projects under the Critical Raw Materials Act (CRMA), concerns have emerged regarding transparency and procedural integrity (1). Internal documents indicate that several projects — including highly controversial mining projects such as the Barroso lithium project in Portugal and the Jadar Valley project in Serbia — were added between a draft and final list in 2025, despite earlier expert assessments. This raises questions about the consistency and credibility of the selection process. 1. What steps does the Commission intend to take to ensure full transparency in the CRMA selection process, including publication of draft and final project lists, expert assessments and clear justification for changes introduced between stages, particularly where projects initially failed to meet technical or sustainability criteria? 2. How does the Commission safeguard the independence and weight of expert evaluations during consultations within the European Critical Raw Materials Board? 3. How does the Commission ensure that Member State or political considerations do not override prior technical assessments, particularly for projects that are environmentally and socially sensitive? (22 July 2026) The selection of Strategic Projects follows the process and requirements set out in the Critical Raw Materials Act (CRMA) (1). The technical assessment is conducted by external experts, who work independently and are coordinated by the Commission. All selected projects were assessed as meeting the criteria set out in Article 6 of the CRMA. In accordance with Article 7 of the CRMA, the Member State whose territory is concerned receives the full application and can veto the recognition of a project as a Strategic Project. The Critical Raw Materials Board is consulted and issues an opinion on whether the proposed projects fulfil the criteria laid down in Article 6(1). The consultation process with Member States and the adoption of the opinion are transparently reported and publicly available on the Critical Raw Materials Board website (2). From the minutes of the relevant Board meetings for the first selection round, it is clear that the results presented on 20 February 2026 were preliminary and that the expert assessment was not finalised for some projects. The Commission has published substantial information on the process, including guidance for applicants, assessment report templates and project factsheets (3). Certain detailed evaluation elements cannot be disclosed where this would undermine the protection of commercially sensitive information or the integrity of the decision-making process.

E-10-2026-002047.t: Rule of law conditionality in respect of EU cooperation funding for El Salvador
qt: to the Commission Per Clausen (The Left) Subject:

The EU-Central America Association Agreement1 establishes respect for democratic principles, human rights and the rule of law as an essential element of the Agreement, and provides for appropriate measures in the event of a serious breach thereof. In its resolution of 8 October 2025, Parliament expressed deep concern over the erosion of democratic principles in El Salvador, including widespread arbitrary detention, torture, forced disappearances, lack of judicial independence, and deliberate circumvention of constitutional safeguards. It is known that the French company POMA receives EU funding to develop an intermodal cable car line (Aeromodal) in El Salvador. However, under the State of Exception, which lacks transparency, the Salvadoran state has not, despite repeated requests, yet provided even the most basic information about the project and its impact. This raises serious questions. In the light of the foregoing, can the Commission confirm: 1.

Whether or not the proposed mass passenger transport cooperation programme for El Salvador and other projects funded by public European investments have been subject to a formal human rights and rule of law conditionality assessment prior to their approval, and, if so, what the findings were.
How it will address the lack of public transparency with regard to EU-funded projects in El Salvador.
https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:22012A1215(01).
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (9.7.2026) The Commission clarifies that POMA1 does not receive EU funding for developing cable car lines in El Salvador. The Commission is financing technical assistance and pre-investment studies to support sustainable transport solutions in the San Salvador Metropolitan Area in benefit of the population. Any future investment operation will be subject to a comprehensive due diligence process. All EU-funded cooperation actions in El Salvador – with a focus on sustainable, inclusive human development, environmental sustainability, digital connectivity, civil society and human rights – are designed and implemented in accordance with EU Regulation2. Human rights, rule of law and governance risks are considered during action design and implementation and are monitored throughout. Transparency is a core principle of the EU’s approach. At country level, EU supports enhanced transparency and public participation and engages with relevant partners, including independent civil society organisations. In El Salvador, the EU-funded pre-investment assistance places particular emphasis on governance, accountability, transparency and public participation, including through engagement with civil society organisations. Upon conclusion of the studies phase, should the bankability of an investment be confirmed, the ensuing EU-supported actions will be subject to appropriate public transparency requirements. The Commission coordinates with its partners to monitor and assess respect for fundamental values, and this coordination feeds into the political and sectoral dialogues with the country. The EU engages regularly with Salvadorian authorities on human rights and rule of law3.

E-10-2026-002046.t: Detection of military unmanned surface vessel (USV) in Lefkada and gaps in European maritime surveillance
qt: to the Commission Nikolaos Anadiotis (NI) Subject:

According to recent reports, an unmanned surface vessel was detected in the maritime area of Lefkada, Greece. It appears to be a Ukrainian Magura V5 fitted with communication equipment, sensors and explosives. The competent authorities are investigating its route and the reason for its presence there12. The incident raises serious questions about the ability to quickly identify small military or potentially dangerous unmanned systems in maritime zones of the Union, the presence of which may result in Member States becoming involved in wars going on elsewhere. The EU has already developed tools to enhance maritime surveillance and information sharing, such as CISE, EUROSUR and the revised European Maritime Security Strategy, to improve situational awareness in the European maritime domain34. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
What is its assessment of the incident in the light of surveillance and the need to identify small unmanned military systems?
Does it intend to strengthen CISE and EUROSUR so that they can respond more effectively to threats from USVs, unmanned vessels and hybrid maritime systems?
Will it consider establishing a European protocol for immediate notification and coordination in such cases?

https://www.kathimerini.gr/politics/amyna/564216031/leykada-to-oykraniko-drone-efialtis-gia-tonrosiko-stolo/ 2 https://gr.euronews.com/my-europe/2026/05/10/zhtountai-apanthseis-thalassio-drone-vrethike-leukada 3 https://oceans-and-fisheries.ec.europa.eu/maritime-security/common-information-sharing-environmentcise_en 4 https://oceans-and-fisheries.ec.europa.eu/maritime-security/maritime-security-strategy_en 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.7.2026) Under the European Defence Fund (EDF) and the European Defence Industry Programme (EDIP), several calls were launched to enhance Member States’ maritime surveillance capabilities, including detection and neutralisation of unmanned threats. EDF-funded projects on maritime domain awareness address such gaps by developing advanced sensors, AI-driven analytics and integrated C21 solutions. The Commission cooperates with Member States to strengthen the Common Information Sharing Environment (CISE), through the development of its classified network in 2026. This will enhance information exchange to address threats such as unmanned surface vessels. CISE improves maritime domain awareness by enabling faster, cross-border coordination between Member States’ civil and military authorities. The Commission is looking into strengthening EUROSUR to better reflect threats at external borders, including hybrid threats and unmanned systems. EUROSUR focuses on situational awareness and information sharing. Any strengthening would mainly concern better reporting, analysis, fusion services and the European situational picture, while national authorities are responsible for operational responses. The Action Plan on Cable Security provides for regional cable hubs to improve monitoring and threat detection near submarine cables, by aggregating relevant data and information. These hubs should be supported by AI-based threat analysis to set a near real-time situational picture and allow faster response to incidents. The EU Action Plan on Drone and CounterDrone Security also addresses undersea and surface drones, building on the capabilities of regional cable hubs and launching pilot action to enhance maritime domain awareness.

E-10-2026-002045.t: Mass regularisation of migrants in Spain and implications for the Schengen area and the internal security of the EU
qt: to the Commission Nikolaos Anadiotis (NI) Subject:

According to recent reports, Spain is putting forward measures to regularise up to 500,000 migrants by granting them legal residency status and access to the labour market1. Since beneficiaries are being granted residency in a Member State within the Schengen area, this development is likely to have a wider impact on secondary movement and on the internal security of the Union. The Schengen area functions based on mutual trust and the uniform application of asylum and migration rules, in particular Directive 2011/95/EU (Qualification Directive), which lays down common criteria for granting international protection2. Significant variations in national policies may put uneven pressure on Member States and affect the system’s cohesion. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Are there indications that such practices affect internal security or the balance between Member States?

Does the Commission intend to ask Spain for specific information on identity, security and public order checks prior to permits being granted, as well as on the monitoring or return to Spain of beneficiaries who may move illegally to other Member States?

(6 August 2026) The Commission refers to its replies to the following parliamentary questions: E-000366/2026 (1), E-000405/2026 (2), E000522/2026 (3) and P-001628/2026 (4). When issuing a residence permit, national authorities are responsible for carrying out an individual assessment of any potential security risks. This include, for example, consulting the Schengen Information System (SIS) to verify whether a person is subject to an alert (5). In addition, since 2023, persons subject to a return decision in a Member State should also be subject to a return alert in SIS (6). In such cases, the SIS can help monitor persons subject to a return decision and moving to another Member State. A national residence permit issued by a Member State does not give authorisation to settle freely around the EU, but only to live and work in the Member State that issued it. If a person holding a national residence permit is found to be illegally staying in another Member State, or if that person applies for asylum in another Member State, that person must go back to the Member State that issued the residence permit. National authorities must act in a spirit of sincere cooperation for this to happen swiftly. As regards the requirement for Spain to provide specific information on identity, security and public order checks carried out prior to the granting of residence permits, there is no EU legal instrument imposing such an obligation. Nevertheless, the new Visa Information System (VIS), once launched, will enable Schengen States to exchange information not only on short-stay visas, but also on long-stay visas and residence permits.

E-10-2026-002043.t: Removal of the ‘Trust your Stars’ project from the Recovery and Resilience Fund
qt: to the Commission Nikolas Farantouris (S&D) Subject:

In 2022, the project ‘Trust your Stars’, with a total budget of EUR 80.6 million, was included in the Greek recovery and resilience plan. The project was presented as a flagship programme to support young researchers, with the aim of harnessing existing scientific potential and implementing research projects with a high impact on the academic community, the economy and society, showcasing Greece’s universities as hubs of excellence and innovation1. However, despite the submission of 1 241 proposals by researchers and research teams2 and amid multiple complaints from the academic community about significant delays3, on 28 April 2026 the decision for the project’s inclusion in the Recovery and Resilience Fund was revoked, due to a revision of the Greek recovery and resilience plan and the removal therefrom of the project in question4. Given that the decision to remove the project leaves hundreds of researchers and research groups in the lurch and constitutes an admission of political and administrative failure in the management of public and European research funds, can the Commission say: 1.
How did the Greek Government justify the removal of this project, which entailed funding of vital importance for the survival of high-level research university teams?
To which projects will the funds that had been earmarked for the ‘Trust your Stars’ project be channelled?
How could it help researchers who have been left in the lurch following the decision for the project’s removal?,

(13 July 2026) The project relates to measure 16289: ‘Strategy for Excellence in Universities & Innovation’ of Greece’s Recovery and Resilience Plan (RRP). Following Greece’s request to revise its RRP, the project ‘Trust Your Stars’ was removed from the RRP as approved by the Council on 17 July 2025 (1). In the supporting evidence justifying the amendment, the Greek authorities indicated that, due to the high number of applications, the submitted proposals were still at the time under evaluation by external evaluators. The authorities concluded that the project was no longer achievable under the RRP considering the limited time available for implementation. The overall modifications of measure 16289 included the removal of three projects (‘Visiting Professors/Researchers’; ‘Industrial PhDs’; ‘Trust Your Stars’) and the addition of a new project (‘Postgraduate Study Programs with Foreign Universities’) (2). As a result, the total estimated cost for measure 16289 was reduced. Finally, the decision for the continuation and financing of projects removed from the RRP lies exclusively with the Greek authorities. The Commission is not responsible for financing decisions of this tenure.

E-10-2026-002042.t: Commission‑funded media outlets reporting on EU news should also mention opposition parties
qt: to the Commission Virginie Joron (PfE), Catherine Griset (PfE) Subject:

On 1 April 2026, the Commission announced a grant of EUR 7.4 million to various media outlets including Agence France‑Presse (AFP) for coverage of EU affairs1. It allocates a total of EUR 21.1 million in support of media pluralism. So AFP2 has apparently received between EUR 9 million and EUR 12 million since 2014. The Commission also subscribes to European press agencies like Contexte and Agence Europe. A number of media outlets financed by the Commission, however, do not report the positions of all of the political groups in the European Parliament, often neglecting to mention the opinions of certain groups. How does it verify that all political groups are actually mentioned?
What amounts have AFP and France Télévision received from the Commission since 2014?

E-10-2026-002041.t: Farming crisis in Sicily: impact of price rises and the geopolitical crisis
qt: to the Commission Giuseppe Antoci (The Left) Subject:

Farming in Sicily is facing a severe crisis, which is being exacerbated by a combination of geopolitical, economic and climate factors that are jeopardising the sector’s productive and social fabric. The ongoing water crisis and the effects of the green transition are being compounded by the fallout from the war in Iran and tensions in the Strait of Hormuz, which are causing a surge in energy, fertiliser and maritime transport costs1. Sicilian farms – at a disadvantage because their island location makes them dependent on sea and air transport for essential supplies and the distribution of agri-food products – are bearing the brunt of these price rises. According to the markets division of the Italian Institute for Agri-Food Market Services, the meat and fruit and vegetable sectors are the hardest hit with production costs climbing by as much as 7 % and 6 %, respectively2. Faced with such dire straits, the Sicilian branch of the Italian farmers’ confederation CIAAgricoltori Italiani has called for ‘urgent drastic measures’ and warns that the closure of Sicilian farms would wreak serious economic, social and environmental consequences, entrenching the dependency on foreign imports3. In light of the above: 1.
What measures will the Commission take to support the Sicilian farms severely hit by the price increases stemming from the geopolitical crisis in the Middle East?
How will it safeguard food sovereignty and the competitiveness of Sicilian agricultural products, including by means of EU funds for 2026?

(27 July 2026) The Commission recognises the pressure farmers face due to high energy, fertiliser and transport costs linked to tensions in the Middle East and is working on multiple fronts to support farmers. On 19 May 2026, the Commission adopted a Fertiliser Action Plan (1), which includes short-term and long-term measures to reduce import dependency, boost domestic production and provide targeted support to farmers, while remaining aligned with the EU’s climate and environmental objectives. In this context, it will soon adopt an exceptional support for farmers facing high input costs funded through the agricultural reserve, amounting to 540 million, out of which Italy gets an important share. This will provide immediate relief ahead of the next production cycle and help sustain agricultural production. To enable Member States to provide additional support, the Commission also adopted on 12 June 2026 a legislative proposal aimed at enabling Member States to maximise support available under the Common Agricultural Policy Strategic Plans (CSP) including through liquidity support, more flexible advanced payments and adjustments of direct payments for 2027. In parallel, work is ongoing on structural solutions to reduce EU dependencies. Also, on 22 April 2026 the Commission adopted AccelerateEU (2), a communication proposing several measures that will directly benefit consumers and businesses, including farmers. On 29 April 2026 it adopted a temporary framework for state aid (3) to support the most exposed sectors, including the primary production of agricultural products.

E-10-2026-002040.t: Impact of the new multiannual financial framework (MFF) 2028-2034 on Sicilian small-scale fisheries
qt: to the Commission Giuseppe Antoci (The Left) Subject:

The fisheries sector in Sicily is strategic to the economy and identity of coastal communities, but it continues to face growing difficulties linked to increased operating costs, environmental changes and administrative burdens. Recent discussions in the European Parliament’s Committee on Fisheries (PECH) have highlighted the need to strengthen the competitiveness of the fisheries sector, while reducing bureaucracy and providing more certainty for operators. Also of concern is the new MFF 2028-2034, which could affect the availability of resources for fisheries and aquaculture in the EU, potentially affecting island regions, such as Sicily. In light of the above: 1.
What steps will the Commission take to support small-scale fishing in island regions?

Under the MFF 2028-2034, are there specific safeguards in place to avoid reductions in resources allocated to small-scale and sustainable fisheries, and what instruments or measures will the Commission provide to strengthen their competitiveness, sustainability and economic resilience in island and peripheral regions?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (6.7.2026) The Commission presented on 10 June 2026 the first-ever EU strategies for islands and coastal communities1 setting out a coordinated EU approach to unlock the long-term potential of these territories. In the Commission proposal for the new multiannual financial framework (MFF) 2028-2034, Member States shall take into account in their National and Regional Partnership (NRP) plans the specific needs of fisheries, aquaculture and coastal communities and in particular of smallscale coastal fishing. Under the NRP plans, for small-scale coastal fisheries, the aid intensity rate granted can reach a maximum of 100% allowing Member States to encourage sustainable fishing practice by giving small-scale coastal fishers preferential treatment. The Common Fisheries Policy will benefit from synergies and additional support within the NRP Plans, with a specific amount ringfenced for certain interventions. Small-scale coastal fishers may also be eligible for support under the Competitiveness Fund, e.g. for decarbonisation of fishing fleets and the energy transition. In addition, there are various tools in place for Member States to support small-scale and coastal fishers in islands and other coastal regions. Member States can use the possibilities provided by Article 17 of the Common Fisheries Policy Regulation2 to allocate fishing opportunities to those segments. In its guidelines seeking to help Member States in supporting small-scale fishers and enhancing transparency and good governance in the allocation of fishing opportunities published in November 20253, the Commission encourages Member States in this regard. Member States can also identify and plan for fishing areas in their maritime spatial planning.

E-10-2026-002039.t: Rising food prices and the inflationary impact on southern Italy’s most vulnerable households
qt: to the Commission Giuseppe Antoci (The Left) Subject:

The problem of rising food prices over the past year remains an open issue, as shown by recent Eurostat data. This is despite the European Central Bank (ECB) forecasting food inflation to slow down in the coming months1. The issue weighs heaviest on the most economically fragile households in Sicily, Sardinia and southern Italy. With these large increases in unavoidable expenditure ongoing, the region is in danger of being rather exposed to any new energy and geopolitical shocks2. As Eurostat’s data show3, annual inflation in the euro area increased by 3 % over the last month compared with the previous month of March. Despite the inflationary slowdown of around 1.5 % in 2025, prices remain particularly high compared to the period before the Ukraine war in 2022, which also had persistent effects on food, leading to a considerable rise in ‘shopping basket’ prices. In view of the above: 1.
What steps will the Commission take to curb food inflation in the most vulnerable regions, particularly Sicily?
Considering the ECB’s analyses, does the Commission intend to adopt specific extraordinary measures for island regions?

https://it.euronews.com/business/2026/02/10/prezzi-alimentari-la-maggioranza-degli-europei-temeaumenti-piu-rapidi-nel-2026. 2 https://www.messinatoday.it/economia/inflazione-dati-spesa-istat-famiglie-costo-vita-crisi-divariosud.html. 3 https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-euro-indicators/w/2-30042026-ap. 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.7.2026) As stipulated in Article 127 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, the mandate of keeping inflation in check rests with the European System of Central Banks. The Commission and Member States support this endeavour with a coherent mix of fiscal and structural policies geared towards stimulating real economic growth without overheating demand. Member States have been alleviating the impact of the recent surge in imported energy prices on the most vulnerable households and firms, while stepping up action to boost energy autonomy. Within the AccelerateEU Package1, the Commission has adopted a State Aid Temporary Framework and committed to assist Member States to make maximum use of cohesion policy funds in order to support their decarbonisation efforts, through renewable energy deployment, energy efficiency and clean technology manufacturing. The EU’s agricultural, fisheries and trade policies also foster the supply of healthy and quality food at reasonable prices, while the cohesion policy helps to tackle possible bottlenecks in value chains, which may also help address increases in local prices. The Commission does not envisage adopting specific measures to curb food inflation in specific regions. It encourages Member States to mitigate the economic and social impact of the energy crisis with measures that are temporary, targeted and fiscally sustainable – particularly in countries with high public debt – and preserve the price incentive to reduce demand for fossil fuels.
1 COM(2026) 370 final of 22 April 2026.

E-10-2026-002038.t: Failure of the evaluation of the tobacco products directive to take into account impact on agriculture and rural areas
qt: to the Commission Anna Zalewska (ECR) Subject:

On 2 April 2026, the Commission published an evaluation of the tobacco products directive (TPD), which will serve as the basis of the planned revision of this legislation. The report shows that the evaluation does not include an analysis of the impact of current rules on raw tobacco producers, employment in rural areas or the functioning of agricultural supply chains. This issue is particularly relevant in the case of Poland, where tobacco cultivation remains a significant sector, accounting for around 12 % of tobacco production in the European Union and involving around 3 500 entities that provide employment for over 20 000 farmers. This shortcoming raises doubts over the completeness of the evaluation carried out and its compliance with the better regulation principles, including the obligation to take into account economic, social and territorial impacts, with a particular focus on rural areas. In light of the above: 1.
Why has the Commission not considered the impact of the directive on raw tobacco producers, especially in Poland, in its evaluation?
How does the Commission justify this omission in the context of its better regulation principles, especially with regard to the territorial and rural impact?
Does the Commission intend to carry out a full impact assessment on agriculture and rural areas before proposing a revision of the directive?

(9 July 2026) The evaluation of the Tobacco Products Directive 2014/40/EU and the Tobacco Advertising Directive 2003/33/EC (1) was conducted in full compliance with the better regulation framework. The consultation activities carried out in the context of the evaluation gathered contributions from a broad range of stakeholders, including economic operators and business associations. All relevant feedback was carefully analysed and taken into account in assessing the extent to which the existing rules of the two Directives remain effective, efficient, relevant, coherent, and have EU added value. On the basis of this evaluation, the Commission will carry out an impact assessment, in full compliance with the better regulation framework. In that context, the Commission has already started wide-ranging consultation activities to support possible future policy measures. A call for evidence on the revision of the EU tobacco control rules was published on 18 May 2026 (2), and a public consultation was published on 22 May 2026 (3), providing all citizens and interested stakeholders with an opportunity to share their views.

qt: to the Commission Luděk Niedermayer (PPE) Subject:

The United States has recently been flooded with a wave of lawsuits related to the online platform Roblox, which is referred to in this context as a paradise for sexual predators. Gradually, the Roblox platform has created an environment where children can encounter all the negative aspects of online life: gambling, theft, bullying, threats, blackmail, violence and sexually explicit content. However, the problem is broader. The problem of predators also exists on Fortnite, Minecraft, and social networks and communication platforms such as Discord. In addition, it often happens that predators move communication with children to less controlled platforms, typically Discord or Snapchat, where conversations are not subject to the filters used by Roblox, however imperfect those filters may be. Considering that all these platforms also operate in the EU, where children are exposed to sexual predators similarly to in the United States, I would like to ask: 1.

How is a higher level of protection for children ensured in the EU than in the United States, so that cases of sexual predation ending in kidnappings and rapes, as have occurred in the United States, cannot happen in the EU?
Does the Commission have an idea of how to increase this protection if it is not efficient and/or sufficient?
at: (English version) to the Commission Luděk Niedermayer (PPE) (18 May 2026) Subject: Child-unfriendly environment on social networks The United States has recently been flooded with a wave of lawsuits related to the online platform Roblox, which is referred to in this context as a paradise for sexual predators. Gradually, the Roblox platform has created an environment where children can encounter all the negative aspects of online life: gambling, theft, bullying, threats, blackmail, violence and sexually explicit content. However, the problem is broader. The problem of predators also exists on Fortnite, Minecraft, and social networks and communication platforms such as Discord. In addition, it often happens that predators move communication with children to less controlled platforms, typically Discord or Snapchat, where conversations are not subject to the filters used by Roblox, however imperfect those filters may be. Considering that all these platforms also operate in the EU, where children are exposed to sexual predators similarly to in the United States, I would like to ask: 1.

How is a higher level of protection for children ensured in the EU than in the United States, so that cases of sexual predation ending in kidnappings and rapes, as have occurred in the United States, cannot happen in the EU?
Does the Commission have an idea of how to increase this protection if it is not efficient and/or sufficient?

(20 July 2026) The Commission takes the concerns related to grooming and sexual exploitation of minors on online platforms very seriously. The Digital Services Act (DSA) (1) requires all platforms accessible to minors to ensure them with a high level of privacy, safety and security. The guidelines on the protection of minors (2) under the DSA set out a non-exhaustive list of measures that platforms can implement to meet this requirement, including measures to tackle online grooming, sextortion and sexual exploitation. For example, platforms should ensure that minors cannot be contacted by unconnected accounts and automatically hide children’s social media posts and activity from unconnected accounts. The Commission is diligently enforcing the DSA’s provisions in this area, and in March 2026 opened proceedings against the provider of Snapchat due to concerns, inter alia, relating to the grooming of minors on their services. Digital Services Coordinators (DSC) in Member States are also enforcing the DSA to ensure a high level of protection for minors. For example, the Dutch DSC has opened an investigation into Roblox, including relating to the grooming of minors on the platform (3). In addition, the special panel on child safety online (4) has examined how to strengthen Europe’s toolbox for protecting minors online, including in relation to video games. The proposed Regulation on preventing and combatting child sexual abuse (5) introduces obligations for providers to prevent and if necessary, to detect, report, remove and block such abuse on their services, while ensuring respect of fundamental rights and the general principles of EU law. The Commission will continue to support the co-legislators in reaching an agreement as soon as possible on the proposal.

E-10-2026-002035.t: Dependency on digital instruments threatening European sovereignty
qt: to the Commission Jonas Sjöstedt (The Left), Hanna Gedin (The Left) Subject:

Many Member States depend on software companies from non-EU countries. One such company is Palantir, which has been identified in UN reports as being complicit in violations of international law in Gaza, and there is concern that countries using Palantir might lose data sovereignty and that sensitive EU data could leak to US authorities or intelligence services. The Swedish police have faced criticism for using Palantir’s tools without being transparent about the risk it entails. Since the software is proprietary, no one can scrutinise how the algorithms weigh data points when identifying an individual’s ‘risk profile’. Despite widespread criticism, Swedish pension funds continue to invest large sums in the company. In April, the company published a manifesto on X1, discussing inter alia ‘cultural hierarchies’ and demanding ‘hard power’. The text confirms the image of a company that prioritises US interests and military dominance over democratic principles and the data sovereignty of other nations. In the UK, Members of Parliament have stated that the manifesto demonstrates that Palantir is fundamentally unsuitable to handle citizens’ sensitive data. Therefore, we would like to ask the Commission: At a time when European sovereignty is a top priority, is it appropriate for Member States to become dependent on these kinds of digital tools?
https://x.com/PalantirTech/status/2045574398573453312?s=20.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.8.2026) The Commission takes seriously the vulnerabilities created by dependencies on digital solutions from non-EU-controlled companies. They may threaten security, data sovereignty and EU-law compliance, and create vendor lock-in. The Commission Roadmap and HighLevel Group report1 confirm these concerns. The Commission does not comment on individual companies or national procurement decisions. Addressing these concerns is central to the Tech Sovereignty Package2. The proposed Cloud and AI Development Act3 would establish a cloud and AI sovereignty framework, enabling evidence-based assessment of sovereignty credentials and helping public administrations use services at the required level for critical services. The Open Source Strategy4 promotes secure, transparent open-source tools for public administrations and stronger European alternatives across the technology stack. The Commission supports development, industrial scale-up and joint procurement of sovereign defence solutions through the European Defence Fund (EDF), the European Defence Industry Programme (EDIP) and the Security Action for Europe (SAFE). Non-discrimination is a core EU value under the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union5. The Commission is committed to ensuring digital solutions respect fundamental rights, rules and values. The AI Act6 sets clear rules for high-risk AI systems, including in law enforcement. Through the European AI Office, the Commission works with national authorities to implement, supervise and enforce it.
