E-10-2026-002034.t: Lack of access to urban green areas in European cities
qt: to the Commission César Luena (S&D) Subject:

A recent study of 862 European cities published in Nature Communications1 concluded that less than 15 % of the European population meets the basic criteria for daily access to urban nature using the 3-30-300 rule (tree visibility, tree canopy cover and proximity to parks). Furthermore, this study highlights a clear socio-economic gap, as higher income areas systematically have more urban green spaces. Article 8 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1991 on nature restoration sets out the obligation to ensure that there is no net loss of green urban space or tree cover in cities by 2030, taking 2024 as the reference year. From 2031 onwards, these areas must increase, incorporating the integration of green areas into buildings and infrastructure. In view of the above: 1.
What measures is the Commission considering to ensure that inequalities in access to green areas between neighbourhoods are reduced in a verifiable manner?
Does the Commission intend to issue guidelines to prioritise investments in neighbourhoods with a greater deficit of urban green areas and prevent ‘green gentrification’?
Is the Commission considering establishing common access indicators to allow for comparable monitoring of cities?

Bertassello, L. E., van der Velde, M., Maes, J. et al., Assessing European cities with the 3-30-300 rule underscores the need for enhanced urban greening efforts, Nature Communications, 2026, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-71523-8 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (17.7.2026) The Commission is not planning direct measures relating to addressing inequalities in access to green areas. However, the Nature Restoration Regulation1 will promote the greening of urban development in the future. Moreover, the Commission has already produced guidance2 on how to develop urban greening plans as called upon by the Biodiversity Strategy3 for all cities with populations over 20 000. Such guidance strongly promotes working with citizens on developing a vision for cities and promotes addressing inequality. No specific guidelines are planned in relation to investments in neighbourhoods with a greater deficit of urban green areas and to prevent ‘green gentrification’. However, the question of how and where to prioritise urban green space will be addressed in discussions on how to establish a ‘satisfactory level’ of green space under the post 2030 rules in the Nature Restoration Regulation. As regards common access indicators to allow for comparable monitoring of cities, EU wide data is already publicly available on green space and tree cover in urban areas4. Furthermore, these data can be combined with population data by Member States or local authorities to study access to green space. In addition, under the Green City Accord5, an EU initiative supporting cities committed to environmental improvement, signatories already report data on urban greenery using standardised indicators: percentage of protected natural areas on public land in a municipality and percentage of tree canopy cover within the municipality.
1 Regulation (EU) 2024/1991 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 24 June 2024 on nature

restoration and amending Regulation (EU) 2022/869, OJ L, 2024/1991, 29.7.2024. 2 https://op.europa.eu/en/publication-detail/-/publication/bdb452c0-901c-11ef-a130-01aa75ed71a1/language-en. 3 https://environment.ec.europa.eu/strategy/biodiversity-strategy-2030_en. 4 https://land.copernicus.eu/en/products/urban-atlas. 5 https://environment.ec.europa.eu/topics/urban-environment/green-city-accord_en.

E-10-2026-002033.t: Use of forensic AI software by the Spanish Tax Agency
qt: to the Commission Alvise Pérez (NI) Subject:

According to press reports, the Spanish Tax Agency has acquired licences for Cellebrite Pathfinder Enterprise, a digital forensic analysis tool reportedly used to process information captured from taxpayers’ electronic devices in tax or judicial proceedings. Experts have warned that the increasing use of artificial intelligence and forensic dataanalysis tools by tax authorities may entail serious risks for privacy, proportionality, the presumption of innocence, the right to an effective remedy and the protection of personal data, particularly where large volumes of private information from electronic devices are processed. In this context: 1.
Is the Commission aware of the Spanish Tax Agency’s acquisition or use of Cellebrite Pathfinder Enterprise or similar forensic AI tools?

Does the Commission consider that the use of such tools by national tax authorities must be subject to prior authorisation, strict proportionality tests, auditability, data minimisation and effective remedies under EU law?

Will the Commission assess whether the use of AI-based forensic tools by national tax authorities complies with the General Data Protection Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2016/679), the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union and the AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689)?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.7.2026) The Commission does not actively monitor the tools deployed by national tax administrations. Currently, there is no obligation under the AI Act1 to notify the Commission of the use of AI systems. As from December 2027, the AI Act will require providers to register high-risk AI systems in the EU database before placing them on the market or putting them into service. A similar duty will apply for public authorities before deploying a high-risk AI system. The correct classification of AI systems is the responsibility of the provider.2 Once the rules start to apply, the oversight whether a system such as that in question qualifies as a high-risk will fall within the competence of the Spanish market surveillance authorities. Pursuant to Article 85 AI Act, natural and legal persons may also lodge a complaint with the competent market surveillance authority where they consider that the AI Act was infringed. If an AI system classifies as high-risk, the system will be subject to strict requirements, including risk management and fundamental rights impact assessment as well as above noted registration. EU data protection law, including the Regulation 2016/6793 and the Directive 2016/6804, sets out the principles and rules to be complied with for processing of personal data, regardless of the technology used. Without prejudice to the role of the Commission as guardian of the Treaties, the enforcement of those rules lies with national data protection supervisory authorities and the courts5.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj/eng. 2 For guidance, see section 6.3 of this document: https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/draft-

commission-guidelines-classification-high-risk-ai-systems. 3 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj/eng. 4 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2016/680/oj/eng. 5 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/treaty/char_2012/oj/eng.

E-10-2026-002032.t: Need to recognise cancers as occupational diseases of firefighters in the European Union
qt: to the Commission Elena Kountoura (The Left), Konstantinos Arvanitis (The Left) Subject:

According to the WHO International Agency for Research on Cancer, occupational exposure as a firefighter is categorised as a Group 1 human carcinogen1, as the performance of duties entails long-term and cumulative exposure to carcinogenic combustion substances, smoke particles and toxic gases, PFAS, as well as other chemicals from protective equipment and firefighting foams2. Research shows that cancer is the primary cause of death related to the profession of firefighter3, with firefighters subject to a 9 % higher cancer risk and 14 % higher death rate compared to the general population. Despite repeated calls by European and national trade unions for the institutional recognition of specific types of cancer as occupational diseases of firefighters and the need to establish a uniform framework for prevention, registration and protection, in many Member States, including Greece, the current institutional framework remains inadequate. Can the Commission therefore answer the following: 1.

Does it intend to update Recommendation (EU) 2022/23374 on the European schedule of occupational diseases in order to strengthen prevention measures and the possibility of compensation for diseases linked to the occupational exposure of firefighters, as proposed by the European Parliament5?

What initiatives does it intend to take to create a common European framework for the protection, registration, prevention and support of firefighters and emergency workers in light of the health risks they face in the performance of their duties?

See https://publications.iarc.who.int/615. Based on international research, the IARC concludes that there is an increased incidence of prostate, testicular, kidney, bladder, lung and laryngeal cancer, as well as melanoma, mesothelioma, leukaemia and lymphoma, among firefighters compared with the general population. 2 As a result, specific risk assessments, adequate protective measures, and targeted medical surveillance are necessary for these high-risk workers. 3 According to IAFF data, from 2002 to 2019, cancer was responsible for 66 % of the deaths of firefighters during their professional careers. 4 Commission Recommendation (EU) 2022/2337 concerning the European schedule of occupational diseases (OJ L 309, 30.11.2022, p.12, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reco/2022/2337/oj). 5 https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/A-10-2026-0100_EN.html 1
at: (English version) to the Commission Elena Kountoura (The Left), Konstantinos Arvanitis (The Left) (18 May 2026) Subject: Need to recognise cancers as occupational diseases of firefighters in the European Union According to the WHO International Agency for Research on Cancer, occupational exposure as a firefighter is categorised as a Group 1 human carcinogen (1), as the performance of duties entails long-term and cumulative exposure to carcinogenic combustion substances, smoke particles and toxic gases, PFAS, as well as other chemicals from protective equipment and firefighting foams (2). Research shows that cancer is the primary cause of death related to the profession of firefighter (3), with firefighters subject to a 9% higher cancer risk and 14% higher death rate compared to the general population. Despite repeated calls by European and national trade unions for the institutional recognition of specific types of cancer as occupational diseases of firefighters and the need to establish a uniform framework for prevention, registration and protection, in many Member States, including Greece, the current institutional framework remains inadequate. Can the Commission therefore answer the following: 1.

Does it intend to update Recommendation (EU) 2022/2337 (4) on the European schedule of occupational diseases in order to strengthen prevention measures and the possibility of compensation for diseases linked to the occupational exposure of firefighters, as proposed by the European Parliament (5)?

What initiatives does it intend to take to create a common European framework for the protection, registration, prevention and support of firefighters and emergency workers in light of the health risks they face in the performance of their duties?

(7 July 2026) The recommendation on the European schedule of occupational diseases (1) does not focus on specific occupations; it covers specific diseases caused by exposure to specific hazardous substances covering all workers in all sectors. Substances of concern to firefighters, such as benzene, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, formaldehyde, asbestos, chromium VI and heavy metals such as lead and mercury are covered by the recommendation pointing to specific diseases resulting from such exposure. It was recently updated with further asbestos-related diseases. Under EU legislation (2), employers are required to assess all safety and health risks that their workers face as a result of their work, and to take the necessary preventive and protective measures. Member States are required to ensure that workers receive health surveillance appropriate to the risks they incur at work, including the risks from exposure to carcinogens and other chemicals that firefighters could face because of their work.

See https://publications.iarc.who.int/615. Based on international research, the IARC concludes that there is an increased incidence of prostate, testicular, kidney, bladder, lung and laryngeal cancer, as well as melanoma, mesothelioma, leukaemia and lymphoma, among firefighters compared with the general population. As a result, specific risk assessments, adequate protective measures, and targeted medical surveillance are necessary for these high-risk workers. According to IAFF data, from 2002 to 2019, cancer was responsible for 66% of the deaths of firefighters during their professional careers. Commission Recommendation (EU) 2022/2337 concerning the European schedule of occupational diseases (OJ L 309, 30.11.2022, p.12, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reco/2022/2337/oj). https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/A-10-2026-0100_EN.html Commission Recommendation (EU) 2025/2609 of 18 December 2025 concerning the European schedule of occupational diseases (C/2025/8593), https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reco/2025/2609/oj. Including in particular Council Directive 89/391/EEC of 12 June 1989 on the introduction of measures to encourage improvements in the safety and health of workers at work (OJ L 183, 29.6.1989, p. 1) (the ‘Framework Directive’), https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/1989/391/2008-12-11, Directive 2009/148/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 30 November 2009 on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos at work (OJ L 330, 16.12.2009, p. 28), https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2009/148/2023-12-20, Council Directive 98/24/EC of 7 April 1998 on the protection of the health and safety of workers from the risks related to chemical agents at work (OJ L 131, 5.5.1998, p. 11), https://eurlex.europa.eu/eli/dir/1998/24/2024-04-08, and Directive 2004/37/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 29 April 2004 on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to carcinogens, mutagens or reprotoxic substances at work (OJ L 158, 30.4.2004, p. 50), https://eurlex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2004/37/2024-04-08.

Moreover, guidelines for managing asbestos-related health and safety risks at work (3) include a chapter addressed specifically at firefighters and other emergency services, whilst the European Agency for Safety and Health at Work provides information and tools (4), as well as a case study (5) on protecting the health of firefighters. In May 2025, the European Chemicals Agency was mandated to produce guidelines for the assessment of the exposure to a combination of chemicals that have similar health effects (6), relevant also for firefighters that are often subject to such exposure. Within 24 months, an interim report on methodologies/tools to drive an assessment will be developed and in the following 24 months practical guidelines will be drafted.

qt: to the Commission Kathleen Van Brempt (S&D) Subject:

Performance-based navigation (PBN) is a requirement across Europe for determining flight paths in order to make air traffic more efficient. However, the implementation of the PBN requirement is in conflict with the health interests of many residents in urban areas. In Brussels, the new RNP-07L route has led to a concentration of noise pollution in several municipalities, severely affecting more than 400 000 people. This is also evident from the ongoing evaluation of the Balanced Approach Regulation1, in which hundreds of people have already pointed out that the noise impact is concentrated and unevenly distributed. Given the planned full roll-out of PBN by 2030, it seems essential that its implementation be evaluated now, specifically regarding the impact on urban areas with high population density. I therefore ask the Commission the following questions: 1.

How does the Commission ensure that PBN routes do not cause disproportionate nuisance in densely populated areas, and is there an operational monitoring mechanism in place to detect and correct negative noise impacts?
How is population density effectively integrated into the application of the Environmental Noise Directive2 and the Balanced Approach Regulation?
Does the Commission already plan to conduct an updated evaluation of the PBN Regulation3 before 2028, so that adjustments can be made before PBN is fully implemented in 2030?

Regulation (EU) No 598/2014 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 16 April 2014 on the establishment of rules and procedures with regard to the introduction of noise-related operating restrictions at Union airports within a Balanced Approach and repealing Directive 2002/30/EC (OJ L 173, 12.6.2014, p. 65, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2014/598/oj). 2 Directive 2002/49/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 25 June 2002 relating to the assessment and management of environmental noise – Declaration by the Commission in the Conciliation Committee on the Directive relating to the assessment and management of environmental noise (OJ L 189, 18.7.2002, p. 12, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2002/49/oj). 3 Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2018/1048 of 18 July 2018 laying down airspace usage requirements and operating procedures concerning performance-based navigation (OJ L 189, 26.7.2018, p. 3, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg_impl/2018/1048/oj). 1
at: (English version) to the Commission Kathleen Van Brempt (S&D) (18 May 2026) Subject: Performance-based navigation Performance-based navigation (PBN) is a requirement across Europe for determining flight paths in order to make air traffic more efficient. However, the implementation of the PBN requirement is in conflict with the health interests of many residents in urban areas. In Brussels, the new RNP-07L route has led to a concentration of noise pollution in several municipalities, severely affecting more than 400 000 people. This is also evident from the ongoing evaluation of the Balanced Approach Regulation (1), in which hundreds of people have already pointed out that the noise impact is concentrated and unevenly distributed. Given the planned full roll-out of PBN by 2030, it seems essential that its implementation be evaluated now, specifically regarding the impact on urban areas with high population density. I therefore ask the Commission the following questions: 1.

How does the Commission ensure that PBN routes do not cause disproportionate nuisance in densely populated areas, and is there an operational monitoring mechanism in place to detect and correct negative noise impacts?
How is population density effectively integrated into the application of the Environmental Noise Directive (2) and the Balanced Approach Regulation?
Does the Commission already plan to conduct an updated evaluation of the PBN Regulation (3) before 2028, so that adjustments can be made before PBN is fully implemented in 2030?

(17 July 2026) 1. The Performance-based navigation (PBN Regulation EU (2018/1048 (1)) requires the publication of PBN procedures in all runways ends by January 2024. However, the PBN regulation does not regulate the design and the use of PBN procedures. The terminal airspace design remains in the remit of the local authorities. The noise impact of PBN procedures is highly dependent on local conditions and can vary immensely. T he local authorities decide about the design and operational use of PBN procedures taking into account local factors. 2. The strategic noise maps, which Member States must regularly prepare for major airports (2) under the Environmental Noise Directive (3), show the population which is affected by air traffic noise in the vicinity of the airport. They are the basis for determining a noise abatement objective under the Balanced Approach Regulation (4) which is usually expressed in terms of reducing the number of people and dwellings within certain noise contour around the airport. 3. Yes, the PBN Regulation is currently subject of review under the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) Rulemaking Task (RMT) 0761 that has started in February 2026. The environmental assessments of PBN procedures are however not part of the PBN Regulation and therefore not included so far in the scope of EASA RMT 0761.

E-10-2026-002030.t: Recent legislative changes in Bosnia and Herzegovina regarding the Southern Gas Interconnection between Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia
qt: to the Commission Gordan Bosanac (Verts/ALE), Thomas Waitz (Verts/ALE), Vladimir Prebilič (Verts/ALE), Tineke Strik (Verts/ALE) Subject:

On 15 April 2026, the House of Peoples of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina (BiH) adopted amendments to the Law on the Southern Gas Interconnection between BiH and Croatia, directly appointing AAFS, a recently formed Trump-linked company with no experience and opaque ownership, as the investor. This took place with no tender, contrary to national rules and through a fast-track procedure without public debate. With gas comprising less than 3 % of BiH’s energy supply (mostly being used for heating in Sarajevo), building major new infrastructure would undermine decarbonisation and increase the country’s dependence on imported liquefied natural gas from the United States. The pipeline would have a capacity six times the country’s annual consumption, either resulting in increased gas lock-in or, more likely, stranded assets. Solutions for Sarajevo’s district heating such as heat pumps and/or geothermal energy would likely be quicker than building a pipeline that may not be ready for a decade. We therefore ask: 1.
What is the Commission’s stance on the new law and has it communicated this to the BiH authorities?
What could the Commission do to assist BiH in developing renewable solutions for Sarajevo’s district heating?

What could the Commission do to assist BiH in developing renewable solutions for Sarajevo’s district heating?

(19 August 2026) With regards to the Law on the Southern Gas Interconnection, the Commission has urged the country to complete the transposition of the EU and Energy Community gas acquis and respect its key requirements in any related legislative initiative. The EU encourages Bosnia and Herzegovina to implement its draft National Energy and Climate Plan that includes its targets for renewable energy in gross final energy consumption and supports the adoption of energy solutions which prioritise renewable sources, including for district heating, through cooperation via the Energy Community. This also includes the transposition and implementation of EU legislation on energy via the Energy Community Treaty, to which Bosnia and Herzegovina is a Contracting Party. The EU is the largest financial provider for Bosnia and Herzegovina's energy transition. As underlined by the President of the Commission on 5 June 2026, the Growth Plan supports this, with the December 2025 approval of Bosnia and Herzegovina’s Reform Agenda unlocking up to EUR 976.6 million under the Reform and Growth Facility. This adds to EUR 1.1 billion provided via the Western Balkans Investment Framework since 2009, EUR 824 million in European Innovation Partnership grants, and a EUR 46 million European Bank for Reconstruction and Development loan in June 2026 for grid modernisation. With regards to infrastructure funding, fossil fuel projects are no longer eligible to EU funding from the Western Balkans Reform and Growth Facility and Investment Framework, nor can they be identified as priority projects under the TransEuropean Networks for Energy (TEN-E) Regulation (1).

E-10-2026-002029.t: Access to reliable clinical performance data and regulatory oversight of CGM systems in the EU
qt: to the Commission András Tivadar Kulja (PPE) Subject:

Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) systems play an essential role in supporting improved glycaemic control, health outcomes, patient education and self-management. As more CGM systems are entering the EU market, clinicians and people living with diabetes have raised concerns about device quality, limited transparency in clinical performance evaluation, and the lack of comparable data on real-world performance. This raises questions about whether notified bodies and regulatory authorities have the tools needed to ensure patient safety and trust in line with the highest performance standards. 1.

Starting from 28 May 2026, EUDAMED will provide digital information on the life cycle of medical devices. However it remains limited in scope, especially for medium to high-risk devices. How does the Commission intend to ensure that healthcare professionals and people living with diabetes can meaningfully benefit from access to transparent, comparable and clinically relevant performance data – including on accuracy, testing conditions and system alignment – to support informed clinical decision-making?
Does the Commission intend to establish common specifications for CGM systems, taking into account stakeholder input?

(17 July 2026) Continuous glucose monitoring systems (CGMs) in the scope of Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on medical device s (1) (MDR) or Regulation (EU) 2017/746 on in vitro diagnostic medical devices (2) (IVDR) on the EU market must comply with the general safety and performance requirements laid down in these Regulations and undergo the relevant conformity assessment procedures, quality and risk management, and clinical studies, to ensure a high level of protection of health and safety of patients. The European database on medical devices (3) provides information to professionals and patients on devices of all classes placed on the EU market, including CGMs, as a major tool for transparency. The first four modules became mandatory to use as of 28 May 2026 (4), while the module on Clinical Investigations and Performance Studies is under development. For CGMs, adding to harmonised standards already available for quality management system s (5), risk management (6) and blood-glucose monitoring systems (7), the Commission is collecting information from stakeholders to update its request to the European standardisation organisations (8) to adopt new harmonised standards for CGMs. In parallel, to provide for a short-term solution, the Commission has raised to the Medical Device Coordination Group the intention to develop device-specific guidance to clarify the implementation of certain requirements and technical solutions for CGMs. The development of harmonised standards and of common specifications for the requirements to be met by CGMs in accordance with MDR/IVDR Article 9, would require a longer timeframe. The Commission is thus considering acting at both levels, proposing guidance and initiating the process for standards and/or common specifications, as necessary.

E-10-2026-002026.t: NGO funding for LGBTIQ+ and DEI actions through European programmes
qt: to the Commission Afroditi Latinopoulou (PfE) Subject:

Through programmes such as Citizens, Equality, Rights and Values (CERV), the European Commission funds a wide range of NGOs and organisations working on LGBTIQ+ and DEI (Diversity, Equity and Inclusion) issues. However, there are concerns in a number of Member States about the political neutrality of certain actions, as well as about the potential indirect funding of political or ideological activity through European funds. Can the Commission therefore say: 1.
What European funds have been allocated in the last five years to NGOs and organisations for LGBTIQ+ and DEI policy-related actions?
What control mechanisms ensure that these funds are not used to promote political parties, political causes, or ideologies?
Does it intend to publish a detailed and fully accessible list of the organisations, amounts and actions funded in each Member State?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (6.7.2026) The objectives of EU funding are defined in funding programmes adopted by the European Parliament and the Council. The Citizens, Equality, Rights and Values (CERV)1 programme, adopted in 2021, aims at protecting and promoting the rights and values enshrined in the EU Treaties. Under the equality, rights and gender equality strand it aims at combating racism, xenophobia and all forms of intolerance, including homophobia, biphobia, transphobia and interphobia. The funding allocated under the EQUAL calls (2021-2025) amounts to EUR 44 million. The programmes are implemented through work programmes approved by representatives of the Member States and open calls for proposals. Proposals are evaluated against preannounced selection and award criteria among which quality and relevance to the objectives of the programme. Only the best ranked proposals are selected for funding. Under the EQUAL calls2 funding to political parties is expressly excluded. Beneficiaries are subject to reporting, monitoring and audits, and the Commission may take appropriate measures, including the recovery of funds, in cases of non-compliance with the grant agreement. Information on recipients of EU funding is available in the Financial Transparency System3 (FTS) of the Commission while information about funded projects can be found on the Funding and Tenders Portal4. On the FTS, information can be filtered and retrieved based on several parameters, including beneficiary type, country, the department responsible for the funding and the name of the programme under which the funding is awarded.

E-10-2026-002025.t: Strategic coherence and urgent need for high-level political dialogue on the CCUS value chain for Europe’s industrial revival
qt: to the Commission Nicola Procaccini (ECR), Carlo Fidanza (ECR), Mariateresa Vivaldini (ECR), Carlo Ciccioli (ECR), Lara Magoni (ECR), Elena Donazzan (ECR), Pietro Fiocchi (ECR), Alessandro Ciriani (ECR), Francesco Torselli (ECR) Subject:

The EU considers carbon capture and storage (CCS) funndamental pillars for the competitiveness of hard-to-abate sectors and the goals of the Net-Zero Industry Act. However, the latest Connecting Europe Facility (CEF Energy) call for proposals excluded CCS projects from the EUR 650 million earmarked for that call, creating deep uncertainty for the industrial sector. While the Innovation Fund provides financing for CO2 capture sites, the paucity of CEF support for transport and storage may undermine investment in CCS, which operators consider the only sustainable way to prevent deindustrialisation. Plans are afoot for a regulatory package for CO2 transport; however, the global market calls for clear political direction and meaningful action. Can the Commission answer the following questions: 1.

Will it acknowledge that the absence of CEF financing for transport and storage is at odds with the value chain approach taken in the Net-Zero Industry Act, and how does it intend to remedy this state of affairs to prevent capital flight?

Apart from a possible increase to the CEF budget or future CO2 regulatory frameworks, what financial instruments will it use to ensure that carbon capture projects that have already received funding have the right infrastructure by 2030?

Does it agree that, with a view to establishing a roadmap that does away with piecemeal financing, CCS should be given priority in high-level political dialogue with Member States and industry leaders, and if so, within what time frame?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (9.7.2026) The Connecting Europe Facility for Energy (CEF-E) provides financing for projects of common interest and projects of mutual interest, including cross-border carbon dioxide transport and storage infrastructure1. The CEF-E award decisions follow a transparent and competitive process assessed by independent external experts and the Commission2. Since 2014, CEF-E has provided financial support in grants amounting to EUR 973 million to Carbon Dioxide (CO2) projects. More than 20 CO2 storage projects are under development in the EU, including three projects that already received storage permits3. Seven additional CO2 storage projects are applying for a permit in the EU. In total, these sites could contribute more than 19 million tonnes per year in CO2 injection capacity. Demand for storage still exceeds the foreseen supply, making it urgent that Member States make full use of the framework established by the Net-Zero Industry Act4 (NZIA) and recognise all projects as Net-Zero Strategic Projects. Member States should also provide streamlined permit-granting and financial support from their emission trading system (ETS) revenues. Without prejudice to the outcome of the negotiations on the next multiannual financial framework, strategic CO2 infrastructure could also be supported through the national regional and partnership plans and the European Competitiveness Fund proposals. The latter also foresees support to net-zero strategic projects and to scale-up net-zero value chains. The Commission is currently implementing and preparing a number of measures seeking to foster improvements to the investment and deployment of Industrial Carbon Management5 value chains. In that context it will engage with Member States and stakeholders.

1 Falling under the energy infrastructure categories set out in point (5) of Annex II of Regulation (EU) 2022/869. 2 In accordance with the CEF Regulation (EU) 2021/1153 which lays down the rules governing how EU

financial support is awarded and managed. 3 The Greensand site in Denmark, the Porthos site in the Netherlands, and the Prinos site in Greece. 4 Regulation (EU) 2024/1735. 5 COM/2024/62 final, Towards an ambitious Industrial Carbon Management for the EU.

E-10-2026-002024.t: Follow up to written question regarding the exclusion of Israel from Most-Favoured Nation treatment under World Trade Organization rules
qt: to the Commission Lynn Boylan (The Left), Majdouline Sbai (Verts/ALE), Rima Hassan (The Left), Rudi Kennes (The Left), Danilo Della Valle (The Left), Manon Aubry (The Left) Subject:
Follow up to written question regarding the exclusion of Israel from MostFavoured Nation treatment under World Trade Organization rules

The Commission was asked in Written Question E-000951/20261 whether it would stop treating Israel as a most-favoured nation within the World Trade Organization (WTO) framework and engage with G7 colleagues to work towards the ending of most-favoured nation treatment for Israel, as was done when Russia illegally invaded Ukraine. The Commission was further asked whether it would advocate at the WTO’s 14th Ministerial Conference in Cameroon for as many countries as possible to collectively stop treating Israel as a most-favoured nation. The Commission’s reply2 does not address the questions that were asked and instead speaks about the measures currently before the Council. The proposal to end Israel’s most-favoured nation treatment would be consistent with the treatment of Russia following its illegal invasion of Ukraine. 1.
While the Commission acknowledges Israel’s most-favoured nation status in its reply, will it commit to stop treating Israel as a most-favoured nation within the WTO framework?
Will the Commission engage with G7 colleagues to work towards the ending of Israel’s most-favoured nation treatment, as was done when Russia illegally invaded Ukraine?
Furthermore, did the Commission engage on this issue at the WTO’s 14th Ministerial Conference in Cameroon?

(4 August 2026) The EU applies the most-favoured nation (MFN) principle and its exceptions in accordance with the applicable World Trade Organisation (WTO) rules. As explained in the response to parliamentary Written Question E-000951/2026 (1), the MFN treatment for imports into the EU of goods originating in Israel was not part of the package announced by the Commission’s President on 10 September 2025 (2). E-10-2026-002023.t: Signs of distortion and concentration in the Greek energy market and the need to verify whether practices are at odds with EU law
qt: to the Commission Maria Zacharia (NI) Subject:

The Greek electricity market is characterised by persistently high prices for households, businesses and agricultural holdings and there have been serious allegations of limited actual competition, significant market concentration and costs being passed on to consumers. Meanwhile, production cuts have also been reported, along with electricity exports during hours when prices are very low or negative, and cost socialisation. Economic benefits seem to be concentrated in the hands of a limited number of powerful players. The available information paints a picture of an oligopoly characterised by excessive profits and heavy burdens on consumers and industry, notably a potential strategy of withholding power and distorting prices in the wholesale market. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

Does it intend to immediately ask the Greek authorities, the national Regulatory Authority for Energy, Waste and Water and ACER for complete information on pricing, profit margins, production cuts, cross-border flows/exports during hours when prices are very low or negative, financing of relevant deficits through public funds or bill charges?

Does it intend to assess, in the light of competition rules, the integrity and transparency of the wholesale energy market, the application of REMIT, whether the functioning of the Greek market shows signs of distortion, manipulation or other practices that are at odds with EU law?

If the above information provides compelling evidence, does the Commission intend to request or initiate, within its remit and in cooperation with ACER and the competent authorities, appropriate audit or investigative procedures?

(9 July 2026) The Commission plays a critical role in overseeing the EU’s internal electricity market, including through monitoring the implementation of EU electricity legislation. In case of non-compliance, the Commission may take legal action against the Member State concerned. At this stage, the Commission has not taken any legal action against Greece for non-compliance with EU electricity legislation and does not have any indications pointing to any potential non-compliance. Hence, the Commission does not intend to request any information from the Greek authorities on that matter. The Commission notes that the Hellenic Competition Commission (HCC) is investigating the Greek electricity sector under EU and national competition rules. As the HCC is well placed to assess these issues, the Commission does not intend to open an investigation, in line with the case allocation rules of the European Competition Network (1). The Commission also notes that regulation (EU) 1227/2011 on Wholesale Energy Market Integrity and Transparency (‘REMIT’) (2) is enforced at national level. Under REMIT, only the national regulatory authorities (‘NRAs’) are competent in taking enforcement measures against market participants for potential market abuse, except for cases with cross-border elements. In those cases, the European Union Agency for the Cooperation of Energy Regulators (‘ACER’) has specific investigatory powers complementing those of NRAs.

E-10-2026-002022.t: Funding of the refugee settlement on Alexandra Avenue through the NSRF and compliance with obligations concerning social inclusion and the avoidance of social displacement
qt: to the Commission Maria Zacharia (NI) Subject:

A development plan to restore the refugee apartment blocks (Prosfygika) on Alexandra Avenue is being funded by NSRF 2021-2027 for the Attica Region (Policy Objective 4: A more social and inclusive Europe). For decades now, there has been an organised community of 400 people living in this refugee settlement, including 50 children and vulnerable groups. There are support structures for cancer patients and their carers, as well as social cultural functions linked to the historic nature of the space as a living heritage. According to reports from residents, no social impact assessment has been presented, there have been no assurances about the avoidance of social displacement or guarantees of a partial temporary relocation where needed for safety reasons, no guaranteed right to return or mechanisms to involve the community in the project design. Bearing in mind that the implementation of cohesion funds triggers the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

Will it ask the Greek authorities for all information showing the project’s compliance with the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights and Article 9 of Regulation (EU) 2021/1060, in particular as regards social inclusion, non-discrimination and avoidance of the social displacement of vulnerable persons?

Has the Commission been sent a social impact assessment and informed of participatory consultation processes, temporary relocation assurances and guarantees concerning the community’s right to return to the space once the project has been completed?

Does the Commission intend to look into whether, in the context of the oversight and monitoring responsibilities attached to the cohesion funds, funding a project that may lead to the removal of an existing vulnerable community without clear social guarantees is compatible with the enabling conditions and social cohesion objectives of the Union?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (29.6.2026) The legal framework and criteria for ensuring respect for fundamental rights in the implementation of cohesion policy funds in the 2021-2027 programming period are set out in the Common Provisions Regulation (CPR)1. Under Article 9 of the CPR, Member States must ensure compliance with the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the EU (‘the Charter’)2 in the implementation of the funds. Programmes under cohesion policy funds should not support actions contributing to the segregation, isolation or exclusion of vulnerable groups. In this regard, housing solutions should also promote socially mixed communities and support the long-term socio-economic inclusion of vulnerable groups. Cohesion policy funds are implemented under shared management3. Therefore, Member States are responsible for selecting projects and overseeing their implementation. Throughout the design and implementation of support, including the selection of operations4, Member States are required to have effective mechanisms5 in place to ensure compliance with the Charter6. Greek authorities have informed the Commission that no call has yet been launched to include the ‘Prosfygika’ project in the regional programme ‘Attica’. As no operation has been selected for EU funding, the Commission has not received project-specific information. Greek authorities have indicated that all applicable EU requirements will be respected to any project proposed for support.
1 Regulation (EU) 2021/1060 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 24 June 2021 laying down

common provisions on the European Regional Development Fund, the European Social Fund Plus, the Cohesion Fund, the Just Transition Fund and the European Maritime, Fisheries and Aquaculture Fund and financial rules for those and for the Asylum, Migration and Integration Fund, the Internal Security Fund and the Instrument for Financial Support for Border Management and Visa Policy, PE/47/2021/INIT, OJ L 231, 30.6.2021, pp. 159706. 2 Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, 2012/C 326/02. 3 In accordance with Article 63 of the Financial Regulation. 4 Article 9 ‘Horizontal principles’ and Article 73 ‘Selection of operations by the managing authority’ of the Common Provisions Regulation. 5 Including (1) arrangements to ensure compliance of the programmes supported by the funds and their implementation with the relevant provisions of the Charter, and (2) reporting arrangements to the monitoring committee regarding cases of non-compliance of operations supported by the Funds with the Charter and complaints regarding the Charter. 6 Article 15 and Annex III of the Common Provisions Regulation.

E-10-2026-002021.t: EU framework for contract work at Hellenic Petroleum and the permanent employment of contract workers
qt: to the Commission Lefteris Nikolaou-Alavanos (NI) Subject:

Contract workers at Hellenic Petroleum (ELPE) are on strike, demanding the signature of a company-level collective agreement, i.e. their direct recruitment as permanent staff by ELPE. The unacceptable system of contract work – integral to the EU’s overall anti-worker framework – prevails in the refinery sector, where it is used to reduce labour costs and perpetuate a state of permanent job insecurity. The just struggle of contract workers is being met with threats and suppression by ELPE and subcontracting firms/intermediaries, while the Nea Demokratia Government – holding 31.18 % of the shares in HELLENiQ ENERGY through the Hellenic Corporation of Assets and Participations (HCAP) – turns a blind eye. At the same time as ELPE workers are demanding health and safety measures, Energy Commissioner Jørgensen is calling on governments to defer refinery maintenance to address shortages in energy reserves due to the US-Israeli military escalation against Iran. Can the Commission answer the following: 1.
What view does it take on the inalienable right to work in a permanent, stable job with full labour rights and the full restoration of collective agreements?

What view does it take of the fact that it is European directives – particularly Directive (EU) 2019/1152 – that have paved the way for the dismantling of permanent, stable employment, legitimising a regime of job insecurity and flexible employment relationships, with the sole condition being that workers are aware of the unacceptable terms under which they will be employed?

What view does it take on the call for the abolition of subcontracting and all kinds of intermediaries so that workers are employed in permanent and stable employment relationships, with collective protection, dignity and guaranteed rights?

(2 July 2026) The Commission has no power to interfere with management decisions on work organisation and contractual relations between workers and employers. Directive 2019/1152 (1) sets out minimum requirements to improve working conditions by promoting more transparent and predictable employment while ensuring labour market adaptability. The directive does not constitute valid grounds for reducing the general level of protection already afforded to workers in Member States and does not prevent Member States from applying national provisions or collective agreements more favorable to workers (2). The directive respects the autonomy of social partners by allowing for different arrangements to be set out in collective agreements as long as these ensure the overall protection of workers (3). All employers, including in subcontracting chains, employing workers in the EU must apply EU labour and health and safety rules. Moreover, on 4 December 2025, the Commission presented the Quality Jobs Roadmap (4), an initiative to improve job quality and create high-quality and future-proof jobs in the EU. It initiated a consultation of EU social partners on an envisaged Quality Jobs Act (5), aiming to ensure protection of workers’ rights while keeping up with technological, economic and societal changes and ensuring competitiveness of the EU economy. |(⸱1|)∙ |(⸱2|)∙ |(⸱3|)∙ |(⸱4|)∙ |(⸱5|)∙

E-10-2026-002020.t: Failings in EU’s internal market information alert mechanism with regard to sanctioned healthcare professionals
qt: to the Commission Grégory Allione (Renew), Olivier Chastel (Renew), Valérie Devaux (Renew) Subject:

Published on 6 May 20261, an investigation by newspaper Le Monde – conducted in cooperation with the Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project (OCCRP), daily De Tijd and France 2 – has revealed that a number of doctors who had been struck off or barred from the profession in France have managed to keep practising in Belgium, and vice versa. This is despite alerts issued via the internal market information system (IMI). Alarmingly, the investigation found that France had consulted none of the over 2 000 IMI alerts analysed between 2021 and 2025, while Belgium had checked fewer than 2 %. This state of affairs highlights major shortcomings in the alert mechanism provided for in Article 56 of Directive 2013/55/EU amending Directive 2005/36/EC on the recognition of professional qualifications. 1.

In light of the above, does the Commission intend to examine the extent to which the relevant Member State authorities consult and follow up on notifications, as well as the uniformity of compliance with the exchange-of-information obligations, in order to gauge the true effectiveness of the EU’s IMI alert mechanism?

In the interests of preventing the circumvention of national decisions and ensuring better protection for patients within the EU, is it also planning to tighten obligations regarding the systematic consultation, confirmation of receipt and traceability of alerts concerning the most serious cases of medical disciplinary action?

Anne Michel, ‘How sanctioned doctors keep practicing across the French-Belgian border’, Le Monde, Les Décodeurs, French original published 6 May 2026 (updated 8 May 2026) Available online at: https://www.lemonde.fr/en/les-decodeurs/article/2026/05/08/how-sanctioned-doctors-kept-practicing-across-thefrench-belgian-border_6753239_8.html 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (13.8.2026) The Alert Mechanism set out in Directive 2005/36/EC1 concerns certain professionals (including doctors) who are prohibited or restricted from pursuing professional activities. Member States are obliged to send alerts in the cases set out in the Directive. However, in line with the division of competencies in this area between the EU and the Member States2, it is for the Member States to decide how to follow up on those alerts. In any case, the Commission continuously monitors compliance by Member States with their obligations to send the alerts and focuses on continuous improvements of the Internal Market Information System and facilitating its use by the national authorities. The new guidelines concerning alerts were published in January 20263 and training sessions were provided to over 500 competent authorities in December 2025 and in March 2026. The Commission has also organised discussions with Member States’ experts to facilitate exchange of best practices concerning legal and operational frameworks to follow up on alerts. New IT developments have also been deployed, improving the search functionality, providing more information about the reasons of alerts, and allowing the Member States to re-evaluate and improve allocation of alert-handling duties to competent authorities. Furthermore, when developing new policy initiatives (the Skills Portability Initiative, Action 2)4, the Commission reflects on further integrating handling of alerts into possible common digital solutions and other related policy measures.

https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A02005L0036-20251029. 2 The definition of health policy, the organisation and delivery of health services and medical care as well as the organisation of education systems, are the responsibilities of Member States. 3 They can be found in the Internal Market Information System Library, https://ec.europa.eu/internal_market/imi-net/library/index_en.htm. 4 https://ec.europa.eu/info/law/better-regulation/have-your-say/initiatives/15894-Fair-labour-mobility-packageSkills-Portability-2-modernise-and-expand-recognition-processes-for-regulated-professions_en.

E-10-2026-002019.t: Another shooting attack by Libyan militias on the humanitarian vessel Sea-Watch 5
qt: to the Commission Cecilia Strada (S&D), Birgit Sippel (S&D), Tineke Strik (Verts/ALE), Estrella Galán (The Left), Sandro Ruotolo (S&D), Brando Benifei (S&D), Sebastian Everding (The Left), Leoluca Orlando (Verts/ALE), Hanna Gedin (The Left), Estelle Ceulemans (S&D), Mounir Satouri (Verts/ALE), Matthias Ecke (S&D), Erik Marquardt (Verts/ALE), Annalisa Corrado (S&D), Ilaria Salis (The Left), Saskia Bricmont (Verts/ALE), Alessandra Moretti (S&D), Pernando Barrena Arza (The Left), Georgia Tramacere (S&D), Marco Tarquinio (S&D), Benedetta Scuderi (Verts/ALE), Irene Tinagli (S&D), Martin Günther (The Left), Matjaž Nemec (S&D), Stefano Bonaccini (S&D), Udo Bullmann (S&D), Alessandro Zan (S&D), Rima Hassan (The Left), Danilo Della Valle (The Left), Camilla Laureti (S&D), Thomas Waitz (Verts/ALE), Damien Carême (The Left) Subject:

On 11 May 2026, a Libyan patrol boat opened fire on the humanitarian vessel Sea-Watch 5, which had just rescued 90 people during an operation in the Mediterranean. This incident is part of a long series of acts in violation of international law and the law of the sea perpetrated by the Libyan coast guard. From 2016 to 2025, over 70 incidents of maritime violence were recorded, with increasingly frequent shootings by Libyan patrol boats targeting vessels carrying civilians. Most of these Libyan boats were reportedly provided by Italian authorities under the Italy-Libya Memorandum of Understanding. This agreement also provides for the transfer of equipment and other forms of financial and logistical assistance, including training. These national schemes are often coordinated with and supplemented by EU funding, totalling around EUR 65 million for border management activities between 2015 and 2021, with an extension planned until 2027. Considering the UN report published on 17 February 2026, which highlights human rights violations and abuses committed by Libyan authorities and entities, could the Commission clarify: 1.
Whether it considers such acts to be contrary to international law?

Whether it intends therefore to propose the suspension of the aforementioned funding, by activating, for instance, the internal procedure for handling human rights complaints in relation to EU-funded projects?

(10 August 2026) The EU continues to closely monitor the human rights situation in Libya, including the treatment of migrants and refugees. The Commission and the European External Action Service (EEAS) consistently raise the existing concerns with the Libyan authorities. The EU continues to support a comprehensive, rights-based approach to migration management, in full respect of international standards and obligations. EU-funded programmes provide capacity-building and training to improve operational procedures and reinforce respect for human rights and international standards. E-10-2026-002018.t: Finance and support for the Libyan coastguard in spite of renewed armed attacks on civilian maritime rescue operations
qt: to the Commission Erik Marquardt (Verts/ALE) Subject:

On 11 May 2026, units of the Libyan coastguard opened fire on the civilian rescue ship Sea‑Watch 5 in international waters, shortly after it had rescued around 90 people in distress. The coastguard fired multiple shots at the ship, threatened to board the vessel and forcibly return all persons on board to Libya, and proceeded to pursue the ship for several hours. There have been repeated reports of serious attacks by Libyan actors on civilian rescue ships in the past. For years, the EU and its Member States have provided financial, logistical and training support to the Libyan Ministry of the Interior and the Libyan coastguard. At the same time, there is well‑documented proof of serious human rights violations against asylum seekers who have been returned to Libya. 1.
What does the Commission know about the attack against Sea‑Watch 5 on 11 May 2026, and how does it assess the incident?

What specific measures is the Commission taking to ensure that EU funds and equipment supplied by Member States are not used by entities involved in attacks on civilian maritime rescue operations or human rights violations?

In light of the repeated acts of violence against civilian rescue ships and the systematic violation of human rights in Libya, does the Commission still consider its support of the Libyan coastguard and the Libyan Ministry of the Interior to be in keeping with EU values and the Charter of Fundamental Rights?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (10.8.2026) The Commission takes note of reports concerning an incident involving the vessel Sea-Watch 5 on 11 May 2026. The EU Delegation in Libya raised the matter with the Libyan authorities and is seeking clarification regarding the circumstances of the incident. The Commission and the European External Action Service (EEAS) consistently raise the existing concerns with the Libyan authorities. The Commission recalls that all parties involved in search and rescue operations must fully respect international law, including international maritime law and human rights obligations. The Commission monitors EU-funded programmes to ensure compliance with human rights obligations. Capacity-building, equipment and training provided under these programmes are used exclusively for their intended purposes and include trainings on human rights and international maritime law. The Commission receives regular reports from implementing partners, conducts verification and monitoring, and relies on annual risk assessments by EU Delegations, including assessments of human rights risks, as per the applicable rules. It has also strengthened its human rights-based approach guidance and formalised internal procedures for handling alleged abuses linked to EU-funded programmes. Since 2024, the Commission maintains a regular technical dialogue with the Libyan authorities on compliance with international law and human-rights and specific incidents. Equipment provided by Member States through bilateral cooperation falls outside the Commission’s responsibility. Respect for international and human rights law, including the principle of non-refoulement, is central to the EU's engagement in Libya. EU support aims to save lives at sea, combat migrant smuggling and trafficking, and strengthen migration governance in line with international law. The Commission considers that continued engagement is necessary to improve protection standards, strengthen accountability and address human rights concerns.

(29 July 2026) As part of its communication, the Commission, like other EU and national institutions, engages with content creators to effectively communicate with citizens at large and foster open and transparent communication. In this context, the Commission shares relevant and tailored public information with such creators based on their interests and audiences. It also occasionally organises visits mostly to important events where they can learn more about the Commission’s priorities and actions. In the latter case, travel and accommodation expenses may be covered. It is important to underline that while attending such events they retain full editorial freedom. In specific cases, content creators are also engaged as part of integrated communication campaigns. Paid partnerships are explicitly labelled as such to ensure transparency. E-10-2026-002015.t: Urgent measures against the threat to European beekeeping of the  Tropilaelaps  mite species
qt: to the Commission Cristina Guarda (Verts/ALE), Thomas Waitz (Verts/ALE) Subject:
Urgent measures against the threat to European beekeeping of the Tropilaelaps mite species

The parasitic mite species Tropilaelaps causes the rapid collapse of honeybee colonies, and its presence has been confirmed in Georgia and southern Russia. Its presence is also suspected in Ukraine and Türkiye, countries from which the EU currently authorises bee imports. In Asia, this parasite has caused losses of 30-90 % of bee colonies. If the parasite spreads, it threatens catastrophic consequences for European beekeeping and agricultural production. While Canada and the United Kingdom have already banned imports from Ukraine, and Poland, Romania, Hungary and Bulgaria have adopted national restrictions, the EU maintains the status quo despite evidence of illegal trafficking documented by the European Anti-Fraud Office and Europol. In the light of this situation: 1.
What comprehensive strategy does the Commission intend to adopt in order to protect the European beekeeping sector from this existential threat?

Is the Commission considering activating some of the immediate preventive measures requested by the sector, such as the precautionary suspension of imports from at-risk countries, molecular analysis of Ukrainian and Turkish honey samples, and the tightening of anti-smuggling controls, or even a complete temporary suspension of bee imports, as an extreme measure, if necessary?

(22 July 2026) The Commission alerted the Member States at the regulatory Committee to the alleged presence of Tropilaelaps spp. in several third countries late last year (1), (2). Since then, the Commission contacted those third countries in writing, financed and co-organised a regional workshop with the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) in the autumn, and ensured that Tropilaelaps is on the agenda on the annual meeting by the EU Reference Laboratory for the National Reference Laboratories of the Member States. Comprehensive EU rules apply for the entry into the EU of honeybee queens (slide 7 of the referred presentation in footnote 1). They are considered proportionate and fit for use, conform to international standards of the WOAH and to science. In this legal framework, the competent authorities of the Member States must implement and enforce the rules, including by carrying out adequate surveillance (3), while operators must undertake surveillance of animals under their responsibility (4).

E-10-2026-002014.t: Antisemitism Case at the University of Coimbra: serious institutional failures, urgent questions about accountability, and EU scrutiny over fundamental rights
qt: to the Commission Tiago Moreira de Sá (PfE), Alice Teodorescu Måwe (PPE), Bert-Jan Ruissen (ECR), Sebastian Kruis (PfE), Paolo Borchia (PfE) Subject:

From late 2023, an Israeli PhD student at the University of Coimbra documented a sustained campaign of antisemitic harassment, including physical assault, explicit death threats, and the proliferation of antisemitic propaganda across university premises. When Bar Harel reported the incidents, the institution invoked ‘freedom of expression’ to justify its inaction. He withdrew from his doctorate and left Portugal in September 2025. In 2026, the Portuguese Ombudsman found that the University of Coimbra had violated fundamental rights and administrative law, characterised the institution’s response as a grave abuse of authority, ordered formal reparations, and recommended adoption of the IHRA working definition of antisemitism. The case remains unresolved, with court proceedings still pending. Given the manifest risks to European values and the fundamental principle of nondiscrimination, we ask: 1.
Does the Commission intend to include this case in its next report on the Rule of law in the EU?
Does the Commission consider that potential breaches of EU law may be at stake, particularly regarding non-discrimination obligations and the protection of students’ fundamental rights?

What concrete mechanisms is the Commission prepared to activate to ensure that higher education institutions in Member States fulfil their duties to prevent, investigate and sanction discriminatory conduct?
Supporter1
This question is supported by a Member other than the authors: Catherine Griset (PfE).

qt: to the Commission Nicola Zingaretti (S&D), Mario Furore (The Left), Carolina Morace (The Left), Sandro Ruotolo (S&D), Benedetta Scuderi (Verts/ALE) Subject:
The proposed Italian performing arts law’s new organisational model and its potential breach of Directive 1999/70/EC

Chapter IV of the proposal for a new performing arts law – which the Italian Government has submitted to the country’s regional authorities and the National Association of Italian Municipalities (ANCI) – establishes a national ballet company for outstanding talents, all of whom would be hired on fixed-term contracts of 36 months – which can be extended by a further 24 months – and also perform in Italy’s most prestigious opera houses. There is a risk that these precarious contracts will become the new norm, as setting up a national company will come at the expense of reconstituting the resident troupes of 10 of Italy’s 14 flagship venues, which would offer stable working conditions to their employees. Having regard to Directive 1999/70/EC on the abuse of fixed-term contracts, the objectives of the cultural compass on decent work, the European Pillar of Social Rights’s principles concerning employment stability and the CJEU’s judgment in case C-331/17 (which found that the misuse of successive fixed-term contracts in Italian operatic and orchestral foundations was unlawful), could the Commission answer the following questions: 1.
Is setting up the aforementioned national ballet company and opting for precarious contracts compatible with EU law and/or EU objectives?

Will the Commission monitor the proposed performing arts law’s legislative process and will it consider activating the relevant procedures laid down in the Treaties if any incompatibilities with EU law arise?
at: (English version) to the Commission Nicola Zingaretti (S&D), Mario Furore (The Left), Carolina Morace (The Left), Sandro Ruotolo (S&D), Benedetta Scuderi (Verts/ALE) (13 May 2026) Subject: The proposed Italian performing arts law’s new organisational model and its potential breach of Directive 1999/70/EC Chapter IV of the proposal for a new performing arts law — which the Italian Government has submitted to the country’s regional authorities and the National Association of Italian Municipalities (ANCI) — establishes a national ballet company for outstanding talents, all of whom would be hired on fixed-term contracts of 36 months — which can be extended by a further 24 months — and also perform in Italy’s most prestigious opera houses. There is a risk that these precarious contracts will become the new norm, as setting up a national company will come at the expense of reconstituting the resident troupes of 10 of Italy’s 14 flagship venues, which would offer stable working conditions to their employees. Having regard to Directive 1999/70/EC on the abuse of fixed-term contracts, the objectives of the cultural compass on decent work, the European Pillar of Social Rights’s principles concerning employment stability and the CJEU’s judgment in case C331/17 (which found that the misuse of successive fixed-term contracts in Italian operatic and orchestral foundations was unlawful), could the Commission answer the following questions: 1.
Is setting up the aforementioned national ballet company and opting for precarious contracts compatible with EU law and/or EU objectives?

Will the Commission monitor the proposed performing arts law’s legislative process and will it consider activating the relevant procedures laid down in the Treaties if any incompatibilities with EU law arise?

(23 June 2026) The Commission notes that the Italian performing arts law is still under discussion. Any assessment of compatibility with EU law, including with Directive 1999/70/EC (1) concerning the framework agreement on fixed-term work, can however only be carried out on the basis of the final text once adopted. Nevertheless, the Commission respectfully recalls that limits on the overall duration of successive fixed-term contracts and limits on the number of renewals are amongst the measures that Member States may adopt, pursuant to Clause 5 of the framework Agreement, to prevent abuse arising from the use of successive fixed-term employment contracts or relationships. Based on the information available, the proposed system appears to provide for employment relationships of 36 months, which can be extended by a further 24 months. Such limits would in principle appear suitable to prevent abusive recourse to successive fixed-term contracts, provided that effective penalties are also in place if abuse nevertheless occurs in practice. The Commission will follow developments concerning the proposed legislation and, where appropriate, will assess its compatibility with EU law in light of the final adopted provisions. The Commission also recalls that improving artists’ working conditions remains an important priority, as recently reaffirmed in the Culture Compass for Europe.

E-10-2026-002012.t: Impact of drone strike in the Akrotiri area on EU security
qt: to the Commission Loucas Fourlas (PPE) Subject:

The recent drone strike on the Akrotiri area, in the context of the broader regional conflict in the Middle East, has raised serious security issues for an EU Member State. This incident shows that escalating tensions in the region are already having a tangible impact on the wider region. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Has it carried out a formal threat assessment regarding the security of the Republic of Cyprus and the Eastern Mediterranean?
Is the strengthening of the EU’s presence or operational cooperation in the region, within the framework of the Common Security and Defence Policy, being considered?

(7 August 2026) EU Intelligence and Situation Centre, in the framework of Single Intelligence Analysis Capacity (SIAC), is assessing the security situation across all regions where the interests of the Member States are concerned. In the context of the war in Middle East, SIAC, as part of its mandate, is providing intelligence-based analysis reports, which focus on capabilities of threat actors, amongst other things. SIAC does not conduct formal threat assessments regarding specific Member States.

E-10-2026-002011.t: Weaponisation of animal cruelty on social network: the Commission stands idly by
qt: to the Commission Virginie Joron (PfE) Subject:

Since early 2026, we have seen a surge in sophisticated scams on social media1. Malicious individuals are circulating staged images of alleged animal cruelty to encourage donations to online fundraising campaigns. This content, which is often fabricated or manipulated, is used for the purposes of scams that have nothing whatsoever to do with animal welfare. The Digital Services Act2, in particular Articles 16, 28, 34, 66 and 67 thereof, lays down due diligence obligations for platforms regarding illegal content and entrusts the Commission with supervisory and sanctioning powers. Given this urgent state of affairs, can the Commission say: 1.
Whether it intends to open investigations or formal proceedings against platforms that fail to comply with their obligation to moderate and remove such manifestly illegal content?

Whether believes the proliferation of these organised scams to constitute a systemic risk within the meaning of Article 34, particularly in respect of to consumer protection and the dissemination of illegal content?
How it can justify prioritising sanctions against symbolic elements3 (such as ‘blue checkmarks’) over fighting criminal networks that are ripping off Europeans?

at: (English version) to the Commission Virginie Joron (PfE) (13 May 2026) Subject: Weaponisation of animal cruelty on social network: the Commission stands idly by Since early 2026, we have seen a surge in sophisticated scams on social media (1). Malicious individuals are circulating staged images of alleged animal cruelty to encourage donations to online fundraising campaigns. This content, which is often fabricated or manipulated, is used for the purposes of scams that have nothing whatsoever to do with animal welfare. The Digital Services Act (2), in particular Articles 16, 28, 34, 66 and 67 thereof, lays down due diligence obligations for platforms regarding illegal content and entrusts the Commission with supervisory and sanctioning powers. Given this urgent state of affairs, can the Commission say: 1.
Whether it intends to open investigations or formal proceedings against platforms that fail to comply with their obligation to moderate and remove such manifestly illegal content?

Whether believes the proliferation of these organised scams to constitute a systemic risk within the meaning of Article 34, particularly in respect of to consumer protection and the dissemination of illegal content?
How it can justify prioritising sanctions against symbolic elements (3) (such as ‘blue checkmarks’) over fighting criminal networks that are ripping off Europeans?

(29 June 2026) Under the Digital Services Act (DSA) (1), when providers of hosting services are made aware of illegal content on their services they must act expeditiously to remove or to disable access to it if their wish to benefit from the exemption from liability provided by the DSA. Article 16 DSA requires providers of hosting services to put in place mechanisms allowing any user to notify content they consider illegal and to process such notices in a timely, diligent and non-arbitrary way. Articles 34 and 35 DSA require providers of very large online platforms (VLOPs) to diligently identify, assess and mitigate systemic risks stemming from the design, functioning or use made of their services, including the dissemination of illegal content and any actual or foreseeable negative effects for the exercise of fundamental rights. The Commission is competent to supervise and enforce compliance with the DSA of VLOPs and of very large online search engines. The Commission will not provide comments on potential or ongoing investigations, but it can confirm that fraudulent schemes are part of the systemic risks within the meaning of Article 34 of the DSA. The two objectives raised in the third question are not in tension. In its first non-compliance decision under the DSA, the Commission found that the provider of X’s use of the ‘blue checkmark’ for ‘verified accounts’ deceives users (2). By allowing users to purchase verified status, it misleads users about authenticity and can itself heighten their exposure to scams and impersonation fraud. Action on deceptive design and action against fraudulent content are therefore mutually reinforcing rather than alternatives and the Commission continues to draw on the full range of its supervisory and enforcement powers.

E-10-2026-002009.t: Living conditions of seasonal farm workers and public health protection in the EU
qt: to the Commission Nikos Pappas (The Left) Subject:

Recent confirmed cases of tuberculosis among farm workers from non-EU countries in West Achaea and Ilia in Greece prompted the health authorities to intervene, triggered epidemiological surveillance and brought to the fore serious concerns about the conditions faced by seasonal workers in terms of housing, hygiene and access to healthcare. Similar cases have been recorded in other Member States, notably in Italy and Spain, suggesting that this is a Europe-wide issue. The Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union enshrines human dignity, health protection and safe working conditions (Articles 1, 31 and 35). Directive 2014/36/EU, in particular Articles 5, 20 and 23, provides for decent housing conditions and the equal treatment of seasonal workers. In addition, Directive 89/391/EEC and the European Pillar of Social Rights provide for a high level of health protection and safety for workers. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Does it have comparative data on the living conditions of seasonal farm workers in the Member States?
How does it assess the application of Directive 2014/36/EU to agricultural production sectors linked to common agricultural policy funding?
Does it intend to look into reinforced oversight mechanisms for the protection of public health and workers’ fundamental rights?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (5.8.2026) The Commission is committed to ensuring dignified working and living conditions for thirdcountry seasonal workers. Directive 2014/36/EU1 provides specific requirements in this regard, including on adequate accommodation, equal treatment as regards working conditions and occupational safety and health, complaint mechanisms, redress and sanctions. While public health surveillance, healthcare organisation and the enforcement of labour, housing and occupational safety and health rules are primarily the responsibility of Member States, the Commission monitors the correct implementation of Directive 2014/36/EU. The Directive applies to third-country nationals admitted for seasonal work, including in agriculture, irrespective of whether the employer receives Common Agricultural Policy funding. The Commission has not harmonised EU-wide comparative data on seasonal farm workers’ living conditions. However, its 2026 implementation report on Directive 2014/36/EU2 confirmed that the Directive remains fit for purpose. It identified persistent challenges in some Member States, notably on adequate accommodation, information provision, change of employer, complaints and redress, monitoring, inspections and sanctions. As for the next steps, the Commission will continue monitoring the correct implementation of the Directive, including via the ongoing infringement procedures, and supporting Member States, including through Asylum, Migration and Integration Fund funding. In the context of the upcoming Fair Labour Mobility Package, the planned revision of the European Labour Authority’s mandate aims, inter alia, to enable it to address abuses affecting third-country nationals, including seasonal workers.
1 Directive 2014/36/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 26 February 2014 on the conditions of

entry and stay of third-country nationals for the purpose of employment as seasonal workers, OJ L 94, 28.3.2014, pp. 375–390. 2 Report from the Commission to the European Parliament and the Council in accordance with Article 27 of Directive 2014/36/EU on the conditions of entry and stay of third-country nationals for the purpose of employment as seasonal workers, 8.5.2026, COM(2026) 261 final.

E-10-2026-002008.t: Strengthening the EU framework to prevent and combat illegal possession of weapons in the EU
qt: to the Commission Nikos Pappas (The Left) Subject:

The illegal possession of firearms remains a critical threat to the internal security of the EU. Recent instances of armed violence in Greece (for example in Crete and in Kallithea, Attica), as well as the increase in crime in countries such as Belgium and Sweden, highlight the crossborder dimension of the phenomenon. The current legal framework is laid down in Directive (EU) 2021/555, which sets out (in Articles 4 to 10) marking and registration obligations as well as tracing mechanisms (Articles 13 to 15). At the same time, the new Regulation (EU) 2024/1392 strengthens checks on imports and transit, with a view to optimising the security of citizens. In view of this, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
How does it assess Member States’ compliance with the marking and informationsharing obligations laid down in Directive 2021/555 regarding the effective tracing of weapons?
What data is available from Europol on illicit arms trafficking routes and their degree of connection to organised crime within the internal market?

Does the Commission intend to further strengthen operational cooperation through the national operational centres (Firearms Focal Points) and the use of new technologies for darknet market surveillance?
