(26 June 2026) The Commission has assessed the transposition of Directive (EU) 2021/555 (1) into national legislation and issued 26 infringements for incorrect transposition (2). These procedures cover a broad range of transposition issues, including the incorrect transposition of the rules on marking and the exchange of information. The details of the ongoing infringements cannot be shared before the end of the procedures. The European Union Agency for Law Enforcement Cooperation (Europol) has established an Analysis Project Weapons and Explosives that focuses on identifying major threats, supply chains, sources and end-users of weapons (3). It supports Member States with operational, analytical and forensic assistance, as well as the identification and tracing of weapons. Moreover, the Commission adopted a proposal for a directive on combating firearms trafficking and other firearmsrelated offences on 26 February 2026 (4). Its objectives cover the registration by Member States of all seized firearms using a minimum dataset and to share this data with Europol. This data collection will improve the identification of trends, new modi operandi, and trafficking routes. The proposal aims to set up a National Firearms Focal Point in each Member State. The proposal also focuses on the prevention of disseminating blueprints which can be used as guidebooks to 3D print firearms, essential components and ammunition. Criminalising the circulation of blueprints makes it illegal content under the Digital Services Act (5). This could be used to tackle the dissemination, including on the darknet.

E-10-2026-002007.t: Managing the hantavirus-related health risk, transparency in EU vaccination policy and safeguards against further emergency backsliding
qt: to the Commission Susanna Ceccardi (PfE), Anna Maria Cisint (PfE), Silvia Sardone (PfE), Isabella Tovaglieri (PfE) Subject:

Recent reports of climbing hantavirus case numbers are fuelling growing public concern. A zoonotic disease carried mainly by wild rodents, hantavirus can, in some cases, lead to severe respiratory or renal complications. During the COVID-19 pandemic, extraordinary measures were adopted to deal with the crisis; these encroached on individual freedoms and people’s right to work and to free movement, with examples including controversial instruments such as the EU digital COVID certificate and strong pressure to get vaccinated. What is more, question marks and concerns still hang over the Commission’s centralised procurement of the COVID vaccines. A case in point is ‘Pfizergate’, which involved Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and sparked questions about the transparency of negotiations with pharmaceutical companies. Today, many fear that future health emergencies could be used as a pretext for further curbs on human rights, without proper safeguards to ensure transparency and proportionality. In light of the above: 1.
What is the current assessment of the health risk associated with hantavirus in the EU?
Has the Commission ruled out introducing similar instruments to the EU digital COVID certificate in future?

Does it consider it appropriate to publish in full all correspondence and documents pertaining to health negotiations in the public interest where EU funds and contracts with pharmaceutical companies are involved?

(9 July 2026) The threat assessment carried by the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) states that the risk to the general population in the EU/EEA (European Economic Area) from the Andes virus spreading from the MV Hondius cruise ship outbreak is very low (1). The virus does not transmit easily between humans, and the close contact required for transmission rarely occurs outside very close personal settings. Furthermore, the rodent species that typically carry this virus are not native to Europe, so sustained animal-to-human transmission is unlikely. A public health response requires tailored, context-specific measures to protect populations during public health emergencies. Under Article 21 of Regulation (EU) 2022/2371 (2), Member States shall consult one another and coordinate within the Health Security Committee (HSC), working in liaison with the Commission, regarding specific response measures. The HSC has issued an opinion on managing and responding to the Andes hantavirus outbrea k (3). The HSC continues to monitor the evolution of the outbreak, while the ECDC’s risk assessment remains unchanged. The Commission is committed to high standards of transparency and accountability and is ensuring the largest possible transparency regarding the use of EU funds. In line with EU transparency rules, requests for access to documents and correspondences are assessed under Regulation (EC) No 1049/2001 (4), ensuring protection of interests under Article 4 where applicable.

E-10-2026-002005.t: Stop tax evasion by means of foreign-plated vehicles: urgent measures to tackle tax and insurance fraud in the single market
qt: to the Commission Fulvio Martusciello (PPE) Subject:

Foreign-plated vehicles (mainly from eastern European countries, such as Poland and Bulgaria) have become alarmingly common on the roads, particularly in metropolitan areas such as Naples, creating a clear mismatch between registration and actual use. This practice makes it possible to systematically circumvent the national tax system by diverting vital resources such as car tax (worth in excess of EUR 6.5 billion per year to regions), the highpowered vehicle tax, contributions to the National Health Service and the provincial tax on motor vehicle liability insurance. Distortion of the insurance and tax market of that kind leads to across-the-board premium increases for law-abiding citizens (with average peaks of more than EUR 1 160 per year in some cities) to compensate for the costs of accidents caused by ‘ghost cars’; in 2022 alone, around 4 500 suspicious accidents involving foreign vehicles were reported, fuelling a system of legal opacity that harms consumers, businesses and European road safety. In view of the above: To prevent the principle of free movement of services from being exploited for the purposes of tax evasion and insurance fraud, does the Commission not believe that action must be taken to harmonise EU legislation on vehicle registration and cross-border movement?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (21.9.2026) Directive 1999/37/EC1 deals with vehicle registration documents for vehicles, while the vehicle registration itself remains a competence of Member States. Directive 1999/37/EC provides inter alia that a Member State must recognise the vehicle registration documents issued by another Member State for a vehicle, for the purposes of that vehicle’s identification in international traffic or for its re-registration in another Member State. However, the way in which Member States regulate circulation on their roads, including the registration of such vehicles and the issuing of vehicle identification plates, is not harmonised by EU legislation and therefore falls within Member States authorities' remit. With regard to insurance, Directive 2009/103/EC (the ‘Motor Insurance Directive’)2 ensures that vehicles circulating within the Union are subject to third party liability insurance in the Member State where they are normally based, which applies throughout the EU, and that injured parties benefit from harmonised minimum amounts of cover, including through mechanisms for cross-border claims handling and compensation. However, matters relating to detection, investigation and sanctioning of insurance fraud, rest with the competent authorities of the Member States. Existing EU frameworks facilitate cooperation between competent national authorities, including police and judicial authorities, in tackling cross-border criminal or fraudulent activities.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/1999/37/oj/eng. 2 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2009/103/oj/eng.

E-10-2026-002004.t: Zervochia, South Pelion: restoration after Storm Daniel, Natura 2000 and legal action against residents
qt: to the Commission Galato Alexandraki (ECR) Subject:
Zervochia, South Pelion: restoration after Storm Daniel, Natura 2000 and legal action against residents

In the village of Zervochia in South Pelion, Greece, there are reports that following damage caused by Storm Daniel in 2023, collapsed stream crossings remain provisionally filled in, old, dilapidated bridges make it dangerous for fire engines to pass, while rural roads and main access routes remain in poor condition even after water supply works were carried out in 2024. Residents, including the elderly, are reportedly forced to take matters into their own hands to restore the basic functioning of roads, calling for safe access, property protection, water and fire safety. At the same time, the Municipal Council of South Pelion reportedly decided on 7 May 2026 to take legal action against residents who protested publicly. What is more, questions have been raised about photovoltaic installations in an area connected to the Pelion Natura 2000 protected area (GR1430008), following a court decision for the annulment of a permit. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Will the Commission request data on the use of EU funds for the restoration of infrastructure following Storm Daniel in the municipality of South Pelion?
Will it examine compliance with Natura 2000 rules and Directive 92/43/EEC in the Zervochia area?
With regard to public participation in environmental matters, what is its view on legal action against residents who report safety, access and environmental protection problems?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (21.8.2026) 1. In 2024, Greece received EUR 101 million of assistance from the EU Solidarity Fund1 for the disaster caused by storm Daniel in November 2023. The Greek Cohesion Policy programmes integrated emergency relief in Greece’s disaster management system to aid households as well as to support workers and firms with job retention subsidies and business reactivation measures. Greece’s Recovery and Resilience Plan2 supports the restoration of Thessaly’s road and railway network. The Commission will assess how EU funds contributed to the recovery efforts based on the evidence which the Greek authorities will provide. 2. According to Article 6(3) of the Habitats Directive3, any plan or project likely to have a negative effect on a Natura 2000 site4 must undergo an impact assessment and can only be approved if they do not compromise the site’s integrity. Exceptions to this obligation may be accepted under the conditions established in Article 6(4) of the Directive. It is primarily Greece’s responsibility to ensure compliance with EU environmental law. 3. Article 3(8) of the Aarhus Convention5, of which the EU and its Member States are party to, requires parties to protect environmental defenders when they make use of their rights, including public participation. The EU partially implements this obligation through Directive (EU) 2024/10696, the transposition period of which expired on 7 May 2026. The Commission will follow up with the Greek authorities on the correct transposition.
1 Council Regulation (EC) No 2012/2002 of 11 November 2002 establishing the European Union Solidarity

Fund (OJ L 311, 14.11.2002, p. 3) as amended by Regulation (EU) No 661/2014 of the European Parliament and the Council of 15 May 2014 (OJ L 189, 27.6.2014, p. 143) and by Regulation (EU) 2020/461 of the European Parliament and the Council of 30 March 2020 (OJ L 99, 31.3.2020, p. 9): https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legalcontent/EN/TXT/?uri=celex:32002R2012. 2 https://reforms-investments.ec.europa.eu/recovery-and-resilience-facility-1/country-pages/greeces-recoveryand-resilience-plan_en?prefLang=es. 3 Council Directive 92/43/EEC of 21 May 1992 on the conservation of natural habitats and of wild fauna and flora, OJ L 206, 22.7.1992, p. 7. 4 Either individually or in combination with other plans or projects. 5 Convention on Access to Information, Public Participation in Decision-Making and Access to Justice in Environmental Matters, 25 June 1998: https://unece.org/environment-policy/public-participation/aarhusconvention/text. 6 Directive (EU) 2024/1069 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 11 April 2024 on protecting persons who engage in public participation from manifestly unfounded claims or abusive court proceedings (‘Strategic lawsuits against public participation’): http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2024/1069/oj.

E-10-2026-002002.t: Distortion of competition in EU trade agreements disadvantaging outermost regions
qt: to the Commission Marie-Luce Brasier-Clain (PfE), Thierry Mariani (PfE), Nicolas Bay (ECR), Marie Dauchy (PfE), Valérie Deloge (PfE), Gilles Pennelle (PfE), France Jamet (PfE), Séverine Werbrouck (PfE), Julie Rechagneux (PfE) Subject:

The farming and agro-industrial sectors in the outermost regions, and the sugar cane and rum sector in La Réunion in particular, are exposed to growing competition from products imported from third countries. Their production costs are often lower and they follow different standards. The state of affairs is made worse by certain trade agreements concluded by the European Union. The agreements can distort competition and harm production in overseas regions, including in their high-end segments. Production in those regions is subject to stricter environmental requirements and faces higher structural costs owing to remoteness, insularity and logistical dependence. At a time when food sovereignty and maintaining local production are strategic challenges for the outermost regions, imbalances of this kind cause lasting damage to the sectors concerned. How does the Commission intend to make sure the principle of reciprocity in the Union’s trade agreements is really upheld and better protect agricultural production in the outermost regions against competition from third countries?
at: (English version) to the Commission Marie-Luce Brasier-Clain (PfE), Thierry Mariani (PfE), Nicolas Bay (ECR), Marie Dauchy (PfE), Valérie Deloge (PfE), Gilles Pennelle (PfE), France Jamet (PfE), Séverine Werbrouck (PfE), Julie Rechagneux (PfE) (13 May 2026) Subject: Distortion of competition in EU trade agreements disadvantaging outermost regions The farming and agro-industrial sectors in the outermost regions, and the sugar cane and rum sector in La Réunion in particular, are exposed to growing competition from products imported from third countries. Their production costs are often lower and they follow different standards. The state of affairs is made worse by certain trade agreements concluded by the European Union. The agreements can distort competition and harm production in overseas regions, including in their high-end segments. Production in those regions is subject to stricter environmental requirements and faces higher structural costs owing to remoteness, insularity and logistical dependence. At a time when food sovereignty and maintaining local production are strategic challenges for the outermost regions, imbalances of this kind cause lasting damage to the sectors concerned. How does the Commission intend to make sure the principle of reciprocity in the Union’s trade agreements is really upheld and better protect agricultural production in the outermost regions against competition from third countries? (3 August 2026) Food products imported into the EU from third countries must comply with the strict food safety import requirements laid down in EU legislation and meet the same high food safety standards as EU products. These apply regardless of Free Trade Agreements (FTA) and are enforced through rigorous border controls and audits of third countries. Agricultural sensitivities of outermost regions are particularly taken care of in trade negotiations. Trade concessions, if any, are mainly granted under the form of limited Tariff-Rate Quotas (TRQs). Moreover, FTAs normally include a specific safeguard provision tailor-made for the outermost regions. A comprehensive study on the cumulative impact of FTA confirmed their positive benefit on the EU agri-food sector (1). The Commission will pursue (2), in line with international rules (3) and based on impact assessment, a stronger alignment of production standards applied to imported products, such as on pesticides and animal welfare. In that respect, the Commission will establish a principle that the most hazardous pesticides banned in the EU for health and environmental reasons are not allowed back into the EU through imported products. EU policies contain numerous provisions recognising the specific situation of the outermost regions, notably POSE I (4), which supports the long-term viability of the agricultural sector, while strengthening food security, competitiveness and resilience.

E-10-2026-002001.t: Turkish bill violating sovereign rights of Greece and Cyprus in the Aegean and the Eastern Mediterranean
qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Yannis Maniatis (S&D), Nikos Papandreou (S&D), Nikolas Farantouris (S&D) Subject:

According to international press reports1, the Turkish Government is preparing to submit a bill to the Turkish National Assembly with a view to claiming maritime jurisdiction over parts of the Aegean and the Eastern Mediterranean. According to the information published, the bill will presumably be based on the legally unfounded Turkish claim that the islands cannot have a continental shelf and EEZ. This is in complete contradiction with the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), which is an integral part of the European acquis, as well as with the case law of the International Court of Justice in The Hague. Is she aware of the Turkish Government’s intention and what is her view on it?
What specific steps will she take to prevent the bill in question from being submitted and adopted?

Does she intend to propose to the Council that penalties be imposed on members of the Turkish Government who put forward a bill that violates the sovereign rights of two EU Member States and is completely contrary to the European acquis and international law?

E-10-2026-002000.t: Spain – possible misappropriation of COVID aid
qt: to the Commission Friedrich Pürner (NI) Subject:

Several media reports123 allege that Spain may have misappropriated around EUR 10 billion in EU funds (COVID recovery programme) to plug holes in its national finances, most notably in its pensions system. If these accounts are found to be true, difficult questions would have to be asked about the regularity of the use of EU funds and scrutiny by the relevant EU bodies and institutions. The proper use of EU funds is crucial for the credibility and effective operation of the EU. 1.
Is the Commission aware of such operations or the suspicions against Spain, and has an audit on the use of the funds concerned already been carried out or got underway?
What control mechanisms are currently in place for the reliable prevention or early detection of the improper use of EU funds by Member States?
What would be the repercussions if the suspicion were found to be true, and is there legal provision for the possible repayment of funds to the EU budget?

(8 July 2026) The Commission is aware of the observations made by the Spanish Court of Auditors in its report, particularly of their finding that the legal grounds for certain internal budgetary transfers ‘should have been more thoroughly justified’ (1). These observations do not call into question the lawful use of the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF) under EU law. Rather, they pertain to procedural requirements under Spanish budgetary law, which are a matter of domestic accountability. Under the RRF Regulation (2), Member States receive EU funds following the achievement of milestones and targets, which reflect progress in carrying out eligible reforms and investments, in line with requirements laid down in Council implementing decisions. In the Spanish Recovery and Resilience Plan there is no milestone or target related to pension expenditures, since those are ineligible under the RRF. Additionally, the Recovery and Resilience framework ensures the protection of the financial interests of the EU through strict checks. In this regard, every payment request has been thoroughly and transparently assessed before the related disbursement, so as to always safeguard the financial interests of the EU.

qt: to the Commission Eleonora Meleti (PPE) Subject:

E-10-2026-001998.t: Obligations under international law regarding the repatriation of irregular Afghans in the EU
qt: to the Commission Pina Picierno (S&D) Subject:

On 12 May 2026, the European Commission confirmed that it is currently engaged in talks with the Taliban regarding the repatriation of undocumented Afghans. This is despite: – the United Nations Spokesperson for Human Rights, Ravina Shamdasani, in July 2025, calling for an immediate halt to the forcible return of all Afghan refugees and asylum seekers, stating that ‘sending people back to a country in which they are at risk of persecution, torture, cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment or other irreparable harm, violates the core international law principle of non-refoulement’1; – the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU), in its judgment C-608/22 and C-609/222, ruling that Afghan women may be granted refugee status solely on the basis of their gender and nationality, without having to demonstrate an individual risk. The Commission is asked: 1.
How does it justify an agreement that, according to the UN, would violate international law?
Whether it intends to provide a clear and uniform definition of the concept of ‘threat to security’ and comply with what has been established by the CJEU;
What procedures and safeguards does it intend to put in place to protect repatriated Afghans from the risk of torture, cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment or punishment, or other irreparable harm?

AH and FN v Bundesamt für Fremdenwesen und Asyl. Requests for a preliminary ruling from the Verwaltungsgerichtshof. References for a preliminary ruling – Area of freedom, security and justice – Common asylum policy – Directive 2011/95/EU – Conditions that must be fulfilled by third-country nationals in order to be granted refugee status – Article 2(d) and (e) – Concept of ‘act of persecution’ – Level of seriousness required – Article 9 – Sufficiently severe accumulation of measures that discriminate against women – Article 9(1)(b) – Types of acts of persecution – Article 9(2) – Assessment of applications for international protection – Article 4(3) – Obligation to carry out an individual assessment – Scope. Joined Cases C-608/22 and C-609/22, ECLI:EU:C:2024:828.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.7.2026) The Council conclusions on Afghanistan of September 20211 and March 20232 strongly condemn the systemic violation of human rights, in particular of women, children, persons belonging to ethnic and religious minorities, LGBTI persons, human rights defenders, journalists and other media workers, former security forces and politicians. The Commission will continue its unwavering support to every person affected by violations of human rights. The Commission is not negotiating an agreement. The Commission is coordinating with Member States to better structure work on returns with the de facto authorities and to ensure a coherent European approach in full compliance with EU and international law, bearing in mind the challenges arising from the acute humanitarian and human rights situation in the country. It is the responsibility of Member States to determine if an individual constitutes a security threat. EU law3 provides for the possibility to apply stricter rules for third-country nationals that represent a serious threat to public policy, public security or national security. All procedures should ensure the full respect of fundamental rights and an individual assessment is to be carried out in all cases. EU law4 foresees that those who have no legal right to stay in the EU must be returned, based on an individual assessment and in full compliance with relevant caselaw and fundamental rights, including the principle of non-refoulement.

E-10-2026-001997.t: EU trade with Israeli settlements, illegal under international law
qt: to the Commission Nacho Sánchez Amor (S&D) Subject:

Recent reports following this week’s Foreign Affairs Council indicate that Member States discussed possible measures concerning EU trade relations with Israel in the light of the situation in the occupied Palestinian territories. Among the options reportedly raised was a proposal by several Member States to introduce tariffs or restrictive trade measures on products originating from illegal Israeli settlements. According to the reports, the Council did not reach a political decision at this stage but tasked the Commission with preparing possible options and scenarios for further discussion. At the same time, trade in products from Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territories contravenes international law and EU case-law. In its 2024 Advisory Opinion – mandatory for the EU and the Member States – the International Court of Justice stated that states and international organisations should refrain from actions that imply recognition of or assistance to the illegal situation arising from the occupation, including economic and trade relations. Against this backdrop, merely discussing tariffs on settlement products risks implicitly accepting the continuation of trade that is in itself illegal. 1.
How can the Commission justify introducing tariffs on products for which trade is illegal under international law? Is this not a way of normalising illegal trade?
Does the Commission intend to fully uphold international law obligations in its trade relations with Israel?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.8.2026) The UN resolutions on the status of the occupied Palestinian territory (oPt) and the Advisory Opinion1 of the International Court of Justice require not to recognise as legal the unlawful presence of Israel in the oPt, not to render aid or assistance in maintaining this situation and to abstain from entering into economic or trade dealings with Israel concerning the oPt which may entrench its unlawful presence in the territory. Therefore, trade with the settlements is not as such illegal under international law. Goods imported from the illegal settlements are subject to the EU Most Favoured Nation tariff rate, which applies by default to all imports of goods into the EU that are not eligible for preferential treatment. As explained in the reply to parliamentary written question E-001713/20242, the EU has a long-standing position of non-recognition of Israel’s sovereignty over the territories occupied by Israel since 1967 and considers Israel’s settlements in the oPt as illegal. EU positions and policies on non-recognition and non-assistance are fully aligned with the obligations under international law. On 17 September 2025, the Commission proposed a partial suspension of the EU-Israel Association Agreement3 on certain trade matters, following a review of Israel’s compliance with Article 2 of the Agreement, which found indications that actions taken by the Israeli government would represent a breach of essential elements relating to respect for human rights and democratic principles. On 13 July 2026, the Member States discussed options for further trade-related measures visà-vis the products originating in the settlements, as presented by the Commission, in accordance with the conclusions of the European Council of June 2026.

E-10-2026-001996.t: Commission to host Taliban in talks on Afghan deportations
qt: to the Commission Nacho Sánchez Amor (S&D) Subject:

As recently confirmed, the Commission is preparing to meet with representatives of the Taliban regime in Brussels to discuss the deportation of Afghan nationals. At the same time, the EU has consistently maintained that it does not recognise the Taliban as the legitimate government of Afghanistan, notably because of the regime’s systematic violations of fundamental rights, especially those affecting women and girls. The ongoing contact with the Taliban – including meetings in Kabul last January – has been driven by political pressure from Member States such as Sweden and Belgium. However, this initiative risks sending a highly damaging political signal, potentially impacting the EU’s credibility, image and consistency in upholding its principles and honouring its international commitments. EU involvement in this matter is not only regrettable but unnecessary, as it could be dealt with by specific Member States. 1.
How does the Commission argue that this contact does not equate to de facto recognition of the Taliban authorities?
What is the added value of the Commission taking such a prominent role rather than leaving possible readmission arrangements to Member States willing to engage with the Taliban bilaterally?
How do these actions reconcile with the EU’s obligation to uphold its values and respect international law, particularly the protection of Afghan women and girls in Europe at risk of deportation?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (30.7.2026) 1. The Commission was asked by 20 Member States and Schengen associated countries in a letter signed by their Ministers in October 2025, to coordinate contacts on returns with the de facto authorities, to ensure a coherent European approach. Their focus is on the return of persons posing a threat to public order or national security. Returns to Afghanistan need to be addressed in a comprehensive and coordinated manner, bearing in mind the challenges arising from the acute humanitarian and human rights situation in Afghanistan. The Commission and Sweden, on behalf of interested Member States, co-chaired a technical-level meeting with representatives of the de facto authorities of Afghanistan responsible for return and readmission, following technical-level discussions in Kabul, in January 2026. The technicallevel meeting aimed to give Member States the opportunity to address practical aspects of the readmission process. Fifteen Member States participated in the meeting. 2. Operational engagement with the de facto authorities is in line with the Council conclusions of 15 September 20211 and 20 March 20232. It does not constitute nor imply recognition, which remains conditioned upon progress on the EU’s established benchmarks, especially counterterrorism, inclusive governance and human rights, with particular concern for the rights of women and girls. 3. The EU has strongly condemned the systemic violation of human rights. The Commission acts in full respect of the Council conclusions and of its international obligations and will continue its unwavering support to all persons concerned by those violations of human rights.
1 https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-11713-2021-REV-2/en/pdf. 2 https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-7264-2023-INIT/en/pdf.

E-10-2026-001995.t: Suspension of the meetings of the EU-India Joint Working Group on Pharmaceuticals, Biotechnology and Medical Devices
qt: to the Commission Ondřej Dostál (NI) Subject:

Since the end of the COVID-19 pandemic, the regular meetings of the EU-India Joint Working Group on Pharmaceuticals, Biotechnology and Medical Devices have been suspended. What is the reason for this suspension?

India, a country with traditional strengths in the pharmaceutical and medical sectors, could help protect EU citizens in the event of a future pandemic through the export of medicines and vaccines. Why are the Indian authorities’ requests for a meeting going unanswered?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (13.7.2026) The Commission recognises India’s importance in global pharmaceutical supply chains, which helps ensuring access to affordable, safe, and effective medicines – a priority for EU citizens. Meetings of the EU-India Joint Working Group on Pharmaceuticals, Biotechnology, and Medical Devices were regularly held until 2020, with discussions covering regulatory alignment, supply chain resilience, and innovation. No further meetings took place during the EU-India Free Trade Agreement (FTA) negotiations, because these negotiations included discussions on pharmaceutical and health-related provisions. With the FTA now concluded, the Commission is further assessing the most effective format to engage with India.

E-10-2026-001993.t: Türkiye’s ‘Blue Homeland’ bill and implications for the Eastern Mediterranean
qt: to the Commission Loucas Fourlas (PPE) Subject:

Türkiye is attempting to formally incorporate its so-called ‘Blue Homeland’ strategy into domestic law, promoting a policy that directly challenges the international law of the sea, the sovereign rights of the Republic of Cyprus and Greece, and stability in the Eastern Mediterranean. This development constitutes a systematic effort to legitimise revisionist and expansionist claims against Member States of the European Union. Ankara is attempting to create a new fait accompli, ignoring the principles of international law. The European Union cannot remain idle in the face of actions against the sovereignty and sovereign rights of its Member States. Can the Commission therefore say: 1.
How does it view Türkiye’s latest attempt to institutionalise the ‘Blue Homeland’ strategy through its domestic legislation?
What specific measures does it intend to take to protect the sovereign rights of the Republic of Cyprus and Greece in the face of the ongoing Turkish provocations in the Eastern Mediterranean?
Does it intend to look into the possibility of political or diplomatic consequences for Türkiye?
at: EN P-002111/2026 on behalf of the European Commission (19.6.2026) The European Commission follows closely the occurring media reports and statements referencing preparations for the submission to the Turkish parliament of draft legislation on maritime jurisdiction areas. The content of this legislation has not been made officially public. The Commission does not comment on media reports. The EU has repeatedly made clear that Türkiye is expected to make an unequivocal commitment to good neighbourly relations, international agreements and the peaceful settlement of disputes. The EU remains committed to defending its interests and those of its Member States as well as to upholding regional stability. In this context, the EU attaches the greatest importance to safeguarding the sovereign rights of all Member States, in full respect of international law. Abstaining from unilateral actions, which violate international law and the sovereign rights of Member States, is an essential requirement to ensure a stable and secure environment in the Eastern Mediterranean and the development of a cooperative and mutually beneficial relationship between the EU and Türkiye.

E-10-2026-001991.t: Threats posed by the digital euro
qt: to the Commission Gerald Hauser (PfE) Subject:

The EU and the European Central Bank are gradually preparing the foundations for the digital euro, including technical pilot phases, legal proposals and the development of a possible infrastructure for issuing and using central bank digital money. Implementation must be halted until major criticisms have been addressed. For many, the particularly problematic points are a weakening of cash as an anonymous means of payment and a possible increase in the traceability of transactions. There are also concerns that the financial structure is shifting and there is a growing dependence on the digital payment system, which could pose risks in the event of crises or technical disruptions. Moreover, it will be technically possible to programme digital money, which could restrict how it is used. 1.
How will the Commission ensure that money in the form of digital euro cannot be programmed (and therefore have its use restricted) under any circumstances?
How will the Commission ensure that money in the form of digital euro will not be affected by blackouts or other crises?
How will the Commission ensure that all shops, institutions and other payees will accept cash?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (16.7.2026) The digital euro will complement and not replace cash. The Commission is determined to safeguard the accessibility and acceptance of euro cash, in line with its legal tender status1. The Commission’s proposal for a Regulation on the legal tender of cash2, which is part of the Single Currency Package3, will ensure that euro cash is widely accepted and accessible across the euro area. Member States will have to monitor the situation and, where necessary, take remedial measures to safeguard the ability of citizens to access and pay with euro cash. In accordance with Article 24(2) of the Commission’s proposal4, ‘The digital euro shall not be programmable money’. This provision is maintained in the Council’s negotiation mandate of 17 December 2025. This means that one digital euro will have full fungibility and can be spent as its holder decides. To promote resilience, the digital euro would be built on European infrastructure and standards, reducing dependence on third-country providers. The European Central Bank (ECB) has announced5 that it has signed agreements with three European standard-setting organisations – the European Card Payment Cooperation, Nexo Standards and the Berlin Group – to reuse these existing open technical and European standards for processing digital euro online payments. The offline functionality of the digital euro enables payments to take place even amidst connectivity outages. Moreover, the Digital Operational Resilience Act6 ensures that digital euro service providers can withstand, respond to, and recover from information and communication technology disruptions, such as cyberattacks or system failures. The Council’s negotiation mandate of 17 December 20257 has added a new chapter on resilience and preparedness of digital euro payments to the draft Regulation on the digital euro.

E-10-2026-001990.t: Detailed criteria, data sources and methodology for Member State classification under the Migration Pact solidarity mechanism (2)
qt: to the Commission Rihards Kols (ECR) Subject:

Each year, under Article 11 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1351, the Commission assesses whether Member States are: (i) under migratory pressure; (ii) at risk thereof; or (iii) facing a significant migratory situation. This determines access to the solidarity pool and calibrated contributions, including relocation, financial and operational contributions. 1.

Are beneficiaries of temporary protection under Directive 2001/55/EC, which was activated in response to Russia’s aggression against Ukraine, including national special measures, included in the indicators for ‘asylum applications received’ and ‘reception capacity’ when calculating migratory pressure?
If they are excluded or adjusted, on what legal basis is this justified under Regulation (EU) 2024/1351 or Directive 2001/55/EC?

How does this inclusion or exclusion affect the resulting solidarity obligations, including relocation, financial and operational contributions, for host states bearing a disproportionate share of temporary protection beneficiaries?
at: (English version) to the Commission Rihards Kols (ECR) (13 May 2026) Subject: Detailed criteria, data sources and methodology for Member State classification under the Migration Pact solidarity mechanism (2) Each year, under Article 11 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1351, the Commission assesses whether Member States are: (i) under migratory pressure; (ii) at risk thereof; or (iii) facing a significant migratory situation. This determines access to the solidarity pool and calibrated contributions, including relocation, financial and operational contributions. 1. If they are excluded or adjusted, on what legal basis is this justified under Regulation (EU) 2024/1351 or Directive 2001/55/EC? 3. How does this inclusion or exclusion affect the resulting solidarity obligations, including relocation, financial and operational contributions, for host states bearing a disproportionate share of temporary protection beneficiaries? (31 July 2026) For the assessment pursuant to Article 11 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1351 (1), an evidence-based methodology on the basis of the elements listed in Article 9, in particular paragraph (3) (a), and Article 10(2) (a) to (k), applies. The aggregation of these elements is explained in a Commission Staff Working Document (2). The number of registrations of beneficiaries of temporary protection under Directive 2001/55/EC (3) is taken into account as an indicator. The quantitative data was provided by the Member States via the Union Agencies and Eurostat, pursuant to Article 9(2) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1351 using a common definition and methodology. Reception data is not yet of an adequate quality that would allow a reliable comparison across Member States, due to significant differences in national reception systems and the lack of key data breakdowns. The Commission is currently working, together with Member States, on improving the data collection related to reception. The methodology was developed in consultation with Member States and is applied consistently across Member States. It provides the basis for the assessment and will continue to be refined including as more robust Eurodac and reception data become available. In accordance with the rules of Regulation (EU) 2024/1351, Member States identified as being under migratory pressure are eligible to receive solidarity, while those identified as facing a significant migratory situation may receive a full or partial deduction of their solidarity contributions.

E-10-2026-001989.t: Possible EU ban on VPN services
qt: to the Commission Dick Erixon (ECR) Subject:

The Commission has urged Member States to accelerate the deployment of online age verification tools. At the Commission press conference on 29 April 2026, a question was raised about whether minors could use VPN services to circumvent such tools. In reply, Commission Executive Vice-President Henna Virkkunen stated that it is difficult to make any technological solution impossible to circumvent. She added that the Commission must ensure the implementation of the rules and will look at preventing circumvention, in particular for high-risk services. VPN services are widely used by businesses, public authorities, journalists, lawyers, doctors and private individuals, including minors, to enhance cybersecurity and privacy when using public Wi-Fi networks. Any EU-level restriction, ban or age limit on VPN services could therefore have significant implications for privacy, security and freedom of communication. 1.
Can the Commission confirm whether any EU-wide ban, restriction, age limit or identification requirement for VPN services is currently being discussed, assessed or prepared?
If such measures are being considered, what is their legal basis?
What safeguards are proposed to protect freedom of communication?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (29.6.2026) The Commission’s work on the protection of minors is grounded in a comprehensive, ambitious, and rights-based EU framework1, which combines strong legislative measures, such as the Digital Services Act2, and rigorous enforcement with targeted policies to foster a safer and more empowering digital environment for children3. This approach strikes a careful balance between protection and empowerment, while fully respecting fundamental rights, including freedom of expression and communication. The Commission is not currently preparing an EU-wide ban, restriction, age limit, or mandatory identification requirement for virtual private network services. Regarding age verification, the Executive Vice-President for Technological Sovereignty, Security and Democracy, has emphasised the need for effective mechanisms to prevent minors from accessing harmful content online. In her statements, she highlighted the limitations of self-declaration systems, particularly in the context of pornographic platforms, where such measures have proven insufficient to shield children from age-inappropriate material. The Commission’s privacy preserving EU-wide age verification system is designed to address this challenge, ensuring that minors are better protected from exposure to harmful or inappropriate content while upholding data protection and privacy safeguards4.

E-10-2026-001988.t: ME/CFS: assessing Horizon Europe funding, uptake gaps and the need for targeted EU research action
qt: to the Commission Verena Mertens (PPE), Pascal Arimont (PPE), Jens Gieseke (PPE), Alexandra Mehnert (PPE), Dimitris Tsiodras (PPE), Sabine Verheyen (PPE), Andrea Wechsler (PPE) Subject:

Myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS) is a severe, chronic and debilitating multisystem disease affecting the nervous, immune and energy metabolism systems. It is characterised by extreme fatigue, cognitive impairment and post-exertional symptom exacerbation. In severe cases, patients are unable to work or leave their homes. Despite affecting an estimated 40 million people worldwide, it remains one of the least researched chronic conditions, with no causal treatments and significant gaps in diagnosis and care. There is increasing evidence and feedback from across the Member States pointing to persistent shortcomings in research, funding uptake and patient care. At the same time, it remains unclear as to what extent existing EU funding instruments are effectively utilised for ME/CFS research. In this context: 1.
What specific funding has been allocated and utilised to date under Horizon Europe for research on ME/CFS or closely related conditions?
What measures is the Commission taking to ensure that Member States and research institutions initiate projects relevant to ME/CFS and make use of existing funding opportunities?
Does the Commission plan to launch specific calls for proposals or programmes to strengthen research on ME/CFS?
at: (English version) to the Commission Verena Mertens (PPE), Pascal Arimont (PPE), Jens Gieseke (PPE), Alexandra Mehnert (PPE), Dimitris Tsiodras (PPE), Sabine Verheyen (PPE), Andrea Wechsler (PPE) (13 May 2026) Subject: ME/CFS: assessing Horizon Europe funding, uptake gaps and the need for targeted EU research action Myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS) is a severe, chronic and debilitating multisystem disease affecting the nervous, immune and energy metabolism systems. It is characterised by extreme fatigue, cognitive impairment and post-exertional symptom exacerbation. In severe cases, patients are unable to work or leave their homes. Despite affecting an estimated 40 million people worldwide, it remains one of the least researched chronic conditions, with no causal treatments and significant gaps in diagnosis and care. There is increasing evidence and feedback from across the Member States pointing to persistent shortcomings in research, funding uptake and patient care. At the same time, it remains unclear as to what extent existing EU funding instruments are effectively utilised for ME/CFS research. In this context: 1.
What specific funding has been allocated and utilised to date under Horizon Europe for research on ME/CFS or closely related conditions?
What measures is the Commission taking to ensure that Member States and research institutions initiate projects relevant to ME/CFS and make use of existing funding opportunities?
Does the Commission plan to launch specific calls for proposals or programmes to strengthen research on ME/CFS?

(15 July 2026) 1. The Commission does not earmark specific funding for research into myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS) under Horizon Europe. However, it proposed in the Horizon Europe Cluster 1 ‘Health’ Work Programme 2025 the call topic ‘Tackling high burden for patients and under-researched medical conditions ’ (1), which is relevant for ME/CFS research. Similar considerations are being made for the call topic: ‘Advancing research on the prevention, diagnosis, and management of post-infection long-term conditions’ (2) from the Horizon Europe Work Programme 2026-2027 for Cluster 1 ‘Health’. Additionally, the Commission supports the recently launched European Partnership for Brain Health which should also cater to the needs of researchers working in the area of ME/CFS (3). 2. The Commission recognises the importance of addressing high burden and under- researched medical conditions, including ME/CFS. It remains committed to funding high-quality proposals across all medical fields, within available budget allocations and in line with strategic priorities agreed together with Member States and associated countries. In this regard, the Commission is also organising dedicated public Horizon Europe ‘Health’ (Cluster 1) info days (4) and supports the National Contact Points Network (5) to raise awareness of funding opportunities under the forthcoming calls in the Cluster Health work programme. 3. Subject to the outcome of negotiations on the next Multiannual Financial Framework, the Commission may consider reflecting on proposing call topics in all medical fields, including under-researched medical conditions such as ME/CFS.

E-10-2026-001987.t: Objectives and participants of the ‘SEAHORSE Atlantic Network’ project
qt: to the Commission Özlem Demirel (The Left) Subject:

The European Union intends to extend the 'SEAHORSE Atlantic Network' project to countries on the West African Atlantic coast, using EUR 3 million from the 'NDICI-Global Europe' instrument. As far as is known, these are Mauritania, Senegal and The Gambia. A previous similar project – the ‘SEAHORSE Mediterranean Network’ – aimed to strengthen the Libyan Coast Guard’s capacity for search and rescue, but failed due to a lack of cooperation from North African states. The ‘SEAHORSE Atlantic Network’ project aims at regional maritime cooperation and combating migrant smuggling and trafficking in human beings. The signing was planned for the first quarter of 2026. 1.
What are the objectives of the ‘SEAHORSE Atlantic Network’ project and how are they to be implemented?
When was the ‘SEAHORSE Atlantic Network’ project agreed and set up, which countries are taking part, and which of their authorities are involved?

Which other countries are to be integrated in the existing multilateral SEAHORSE network, and under what conditions will information be transmitted to the nonparticipating European Border and Coast Guard Agency (Frontex) or the European Border Surveillance System (Eurosur)?
at: (English version) to the Commission Özlem Demirel (The Left) (13 May 2026) Subject: Objectives and participants of the ‘SEAHORSE Atlantic Network’ project The European Union intends to extend the ‘SEAHORSE Atlantic Network’ project to countries on the West African Atlantic coast, using EUR 3 million from the ‘NDICI-Global Europe’ instrument. As far as is known, these are Mauritania, Senegal and The Gambia. A previous similar project — the ‘SEAHORSE Mediterranean Network’ — aimed to strengthen the Libyan Coast Guard’s capacity for search and rescue, but failed due to a lack of cooperation from North African states. The ‘SEAHORSE Atlantic Network’ project aims at regional maritime cooperation and combating migrant smuggling and trafficking in human beings. The signing was planned for the first quarter of 2026. 1.
What are the objectives of the ‘SEAHORSE Atlantic Network’ project and how are they to be implemented?

2. When was the ‘SEAHORSE Atlantic Network’ project agreed and set up, which countries are taking part, and which of their authorities are involved? 3. Which other countries are to be integrated in the existing multilateral SEAHORSE network, and under what conditions will information be transmitted to the non-participating European Border and Coast Guard Agency (Frontex) or the European Border Surveillance System (Eurosur)? (31 July 2026) The upcoming Seahorse Advanced (A) project is part of the Migration and Jobs Package for Western Africa (i.e. Individual measure in favour of Western Africa for 2025 (1)), which seeks to support the vulnerable population of West African countries, by intensifying efforts to improve migration management, addressing the root causes of irregular migration and promoting socioeconomic opportunities. Within this framework, Seahorse A aims to strengthen national and regional maritime surveillance and coordination to complement efforts in countering irregular migration along the Atlantic route. To allow for a comprehensive regional response, the action will cover Senegal, Mauritania, Guinea, The Gambia, GuineaBissau and Cabo Verde to varying degrees according to specific needs and contexts, and in complementarity with other ongoing projects. Competent national authorities responsible for maritime surveillance, counter-smuggling/trafficking activities and prevention of irregular migration, will be involved. There is no ongoing multilateral Seahorse network. Seahorse A is a new project, which will also build on and enhance the results achieved under previous Seahorse initiatives, which have now ended. Close coordination with the European Border and Coast Guard Agency (Frontex) will be ensured (participation to relevant workshops and trainings, timely reporting and information sharing, notably via the European Border Surveillance system (Eurosur) (2)).

E-10-2026-001986.t: Electrolux restructuring in Italy: closure of the Cerreto d’Esi plant and 1 700 redundancies
qt: to the Commission Matteo Ricci (S&D) Subject:
Electrolux restructuring in Italy: closure of the Cerreto d’Esi plant and 1 700 redundancies

On 11 May 2026, the Swedish group Electrolux announced a restructuring plan that provides for some 1 700 redundancies of 4 500 employees in Italy and the definitive closure of the Cerreto d’Esi (Ancona) plant, which employs 170 people. The plan involves all the group’s Italian production sites: Porcia, Susegana, Forlì and Solaro. The trade unions Fim, Fiom and Uilm declared the plan ‘unacceptable’ and announced an open-ended period of industrial action. The workers caught up in the plans will be difficult to relocate in the short term, causing serious economic and social repercussions for the regions in question. In the light of the above: 1.
Does the Commission consider that the conditions have been met for the European Globalisation Adjustment Fund to be mobilised to provide support for those workers and their families?

How will it ensure that Electrolux complies with the obligations laid down in Directive 2002/14/EC and Directive 98/59/EC on collective redundancies that workers must be informed and consulted in advance?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (29.6.2026) The European Globalisation Adjustment Fund for Displaced Workers (EGF) is directed at supporting active labour market policy measures and personalised services that aim to support workers’ job transitions, helping them to reintegrate into decent and sustainable employment. Support through the EGF may be deployed for dismissed workers if the Member State applies and the criteria defined in the Regulation1 are fulfilled. Companies planning to dismiss 200 or more workers can now request EGF co-financing to support these workers through the EGF Managing Authority2 in the EU country where the layoffs will take place, enabling early intervention before dismissals occur. Such requests must be submitted within 14 weeks of notifying workers' representatives about the redundancies. The Commission has no powers to intervene in specific company decisions such as those at issue. However, companies have to respect the body of EU law, which includes directives on information and consultation of employees3 and on collective redundancies4. They lay down minimum requirements for the protection of workers by providing for information and consultation of workers’ representatives on matters affecting workers’ jobs, and when envisaging collective redundancies. Member States must transpose and implement EU Directives, and Italy has transposed both Directives into national law5. It is for the competent national authorities, including the courts, to ensure that an individual employer complies with the relevant national rules transposing the Directives, having regard to the specific circumstances of each case.

E-10-2026-001985.t: The common agricultural policy and protection of European farmers
qt: to the Commission Ilhan Kyuchyuk (Renew) Subject:

Amid the ongoing farmers’ protests in many Member States and the growing dissatisfaction with the administrative burden and uneven distribution of common agricultural policy (CAP) subsidies, increasingly more European farmers are raising concerns over the future of agriculture in the EU after 2027. Small and medium-sized farmers are facing serious financial difficulties, ever more regulatory requirements and a lack of sufficient predictability as regards the future framework for EU funding. 1.

Is the Commission planning to reform the way that EU subsidies are distributed in order to support small and medium-sized farmers more fairly and restrain the disproportionate concentration of funding among large agricultural holdings?
How does the Commission intend to ensure the sustainability and competitiveness of European agriculture without this resulting in additional financial and regulatory pressure for producers?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (9.7.2026) 1. Yes. The Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) and national and regional partnership plan legislative proposals of July 2025 reinforce the targeting of degressive area-based income support to farmers who need it most, in particular to young and new farmers, as well as to areas with natural constraints and small farms. The Commission proposes degressivity and capping of income support for the largest beneficiaries and the differentiation of the support by group of farmers and type of areas on the basis of the farm income needs. This allows ensuring higher income support, for instance: in rural areas with lower competitiveness such as mountain areas, for small and medium farms. Moreover, a higher support per hectare to young farmers is proposed to be mandatory. 2. Agriculture and the agri-food supply chain benefit from a series of Omnibus simplification proposals that the Commission tabled to reduce administrative burden and enhance competitiveness of the European economy. Financial support to improve competitiveness, such as investment support and training continue to be available under the proposed new CAP. This proposal is also designed in a simpler way: the new degressive area-based income support scheme will not be implemented through a complex entitlements system. A simpler payment to small farmers in the form of a lump sum payment replacing several interventions is proposed.

E-10-2026-001984.t: Farmers’ incomes and imbalances in the food supply chain
qt: to the Commission Ilhan Kyuchyuk (Renew) Subject:

European farmers are continuing to see their incomes severely squeezed by rising production costs, inflation and their unequal footing in the food supply chain. At the same time, many large retail chains and intermediaries are making considerable profits, while farmers are often being forced to sell their products at less than cost price. This has created the risk of bankruptcies, a drop in internal production and heightened food insecurity in the EU. 1.
What steps will the Commission take to ensure a fairer distribution of added value throughout the food supply chain and to protect farmers’ incomes?

Is the Commission considering introducing tighter checks on unfair trading practices, binding minimum standards for agreements between producers and retail chains, and new mechanisms for transparency in the setting of food prices?

How does the Commission view the impact of inflation and rising production costs on the competitiveness of European agriculture, and is it planning to take exceptional support measures for that sector in 2026?
at: (English version) to the Commission Ilhan Kyuchyuk (Renew) (13 May 2026) Subject: Farmers’ incomes and imbalances in the food supply chain European farmers are continuing to see their incomes severely squeezed by rising production costs, inflation and their unequal footing in the food supply chain. At the same time, many large retail chains and intermediaries are making considerable profits, while farmers are often being forced to sell their products at less than cost price. This has created the risk of bankruptcies, a drop in internal production and heightened food insecurity in the EU. 1. What steps will the Commission take to ensure a fairer distribution of added value throughout the food supply chain and to protect farmers’ incomes? 2. Is the Commission considering introducing tighter checks on unfair trading practices, binding minimum standards for agreements between producers and retail chains, and new mechanisms for transparency in the setting of food prices? 3. How does the Commission view the impact of inflation and rising production costs on the competitiveness of European agriculture, and is it planning to take exceptional support measures for that sector in 2026? (3 August 2026) Co-legislators have recently adopted measures to strengthen farmers’ position in the food supply chain (1) by improving the functioning of the chain and ensuring a fairer distribution of value. This includes clearer rules to support fair and short supply chains, stronger cooperation possibilities (including on social sustainability objectives) and greater transparency in contracting practices, notably through mandatory cost-related indicators in pricing clauses. Commission services are working on the revision of the directive on Unfair Trading Practices, following up on a first evaluation. They are assessing potential regulatory gaps linked to emerging unfair trading practices not fully covered by the current framework. Any future measures will be based on concrete and robust evidence and an impact assessment. Such measures will remain proportionate, targeted, and consistent with the common agricultural policy’s (CAP) market-oriented approach and the internal market’s functioning. The Commission acknowledges that rising production costs harm farmers’ and European agriculture’s competitiveness. In this context, it adopted on 19 May 2026 a Fertilisers Action Plan which set the basis for two immediate deliverables, namely a targeted exceptional support to farmers facing high input costs through the agricultural reserve amounting to EUR 540 million, and co-legislators have recently adopted measures proposed to allow Member States to reprogramme their national CAP plans in favour of a new liquidity measure and more flexibility in how they manage their funds (2). These two packages will offer immediate relief for farmers ahead of the next production cycle and help sustain agricultural production.

Regulation (EU) 2026/1768 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 July 2026 amending Regulation (EU) 2021/2115 as regards a specific type of intervention to provide exceptional temporary support under the European Agricultural Fund for Rural Development (EAFRD) and the possibility to adapt direct payments allocations for calendar year 2027 and Regulation (EU) 2021/2116 as regards more flexible rules on payments of advances in response to the increased fertiliser prices due to the Middle East crisis, OJ L 21.7.2026. https://www.europarl.europa.eu/news/en/press-room/20260706IPR46307/fertiliser-prices-meps-approve-support-for-farmers; https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/press/press-releases/2026/07/13/council-adopts-targeted-measures-to-support-farmers-facing-high-fertiliser-costs/.

E-10-2026-001983.t: EU and Member State preparedness for a new pandemic
qt: to the Commission Claudiu-Richard Târziu (ECR) Subject:

Given the fresh warnings of the risk of pandemic outbreaks and the major difficulties encountered by Member States in managing the COVID-19 crisis, including the lack of medical equipment, dependence on external suppliers, conflicting measures and the severe impact on the economy and fundamental rights, the question arises as to whether the European Union has actually learned the lessons of that period. 1.
What concrete measures has the Commission taken to assess and bolster the real response capacity of Member States in the event of a new pandemic?

Does the Commission have an up-to-date appraisal of the state of preparedness of national health systems, including strategic stockpiles, medical infrastructure and the availability of specialised staff?

What guarantees can the Commission provide that any future health measures will respect the principles of proportionality, transparency and protection of the fundamental rights and freedoms of EU citizens?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (20.7.2026) While the pandemic demonstrated scope for improvement of the European health security framework, it also showed the importance of coordination to protect people’s health and Member States’ economies. 1. The Commission updated the EU Health security framework to enhance EU-level capacities on prevention, preparedness and response (PPR) to health emergencies. The Health Emergency Preparedness and Response Authority was established, as a Commission service, and the Council adopted an Emergency Framework Regulation1 that can be activated to ensure access and availability to medical countermeasures in times of crisis. Also, a new Regulation on serious cross-border threats to health was adopted2, setting out mechanisms for strengthened coordination and response. Among those, the regulation established a cycle of Member State reporting on PPR capacities3, followed by assessments by the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) on those national capacities4. 2. On the basis of Regulation (EU) 2022/2371, the Commission will adopt later this year the second State of Health Preparedness Report5, based on the reporting by Member States on their national PPR capacities6 and the results of the Public Health Emergency Preparedness Assessments (PHEPAs) carried out by ECDC. This report will cover all aspects of public health preparedness, including management of medical countermeasures, health emergency management and surge capacity. In accordance with Article 168(7) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, Member States retain full responsibility for defining their health policy and organising their health services. It is therefore national authorities that bear primary responsibility for ensuring that measures are guided by the respect for the dignity, human rights and fundamental freedoms.
1 Council Regulation (EU) 2022/2372 of 24 October 2022 on a framework of measures for ensuring the supply

of crisis-relevant medical countermeasures in the event of a public health emergency at Union level, OJ L 314, 6.12.2022, p. 64, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/2372/oj. 2 Regulation (EU) 2022/2371 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 23 November 2022 on serious cross-border threats to health and repealing Decision No 1082/2013/EU, OJ L 314, 6.12.2022, p. 26, ELI: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/2371/oj/eng. 3 Under Article 7. 4 Under Article 8: Public Health Emergency Preparedness Assessments (PHEPAs): https://www.ecdc.europa.eu/en/about-us/what-we-do/public-health-emergency-preparedness-assessments. 5 The first such report, as per Article 9 of the Regulation, was adopted in December 2023: https://health.ec.europa.eu/publications/state-health-preparedness-report-2023_en. 6 Pursuant to Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/1808 of 21 September 2023 setting out the template for the provision of information on prevention, preparedness and response planning in relation to serious cross-border threats to health in accordance with Regulation (EU) 2022/2371 of the European Parliament and of the Council.

E-10-2026-001982.t: Rampant inflation and the risk of stagflation in the EU
qt: to the Commission Ilhan Kyuchyuk (Renew) Subject:

According to the latest economic statistics, inflation in the euro area still stood at 3 % in April 2026, with March 2026 witnessing the sharpest monthly increase since 2022. This trend raises serious concerns over the sustainability of economic growth, the purchasing power of EU citizens, price stability and the competitiveness of the European economy. Against the backdrop of high interest rates, a slowdown in production and continuing pressure on consumer prices, the risk of stagflation in the EU is becoming increasingly real. 1.

What coordinated measures is the Commission planning to curb inflationary pressures and protect the purchasing power of EU citizens, and especially that of vulnerable social groups and the middle class?

Is the Commission planning to introduce temporary anti-inflation mechanisms within the European common market, more flexible budgetary and fiscal rules for Member States and new instruments to support small and medium-sized enterprises in a climate of high costs and limited access to finance?
How does the Commission view the risk of stagflation in the EU in 2026 and will it bring forward an EU-wide investment and productivity stimulus package?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.8.2026) The Middle East conflict has triggered a renewed energy shock. The Commission’s Spring 2026 Forecast projects slower growth and higher inflation. Following the recent US-Iran MoU in June oil prices dropped sharply. Subsequent lower energy inflation led the euro area inflation to fall from 3.2% in May to 2.8% in June. Re-escalation of the conflict, however, could affect the inflation outlook. Significant structural adjustments in the EU that has led to rapid expansion of renewable energy generation help to mitigate the severity of the shock. It is now vital to further accelerate the transition towards a more resilient and less fossil fuel-dependent economy. To ensure coordination, the Middle East crisis Temporary State aid Framework1 will enable Member States to support the most exposed sectors in a targeted and temporary manner. In addition, the AccelerateEU Communication2 has proposed actions and practical examples3 to protect citizen from the energy shock and to accelerate the energy transition. Fiscal measures can provide relief but cannot address the shortfall in energy supply. Member States need to ensure that emergency measures taken to reduce the economic and social impact of the energy crisis on households and businesses are temporary, targeted, timely, proportionate, and fiscally sustainable, and that they do not increase the demand for fossil fuels.4 A more expansionary fiscal stance would fuel inflation and further increase pressures on consumers’ purchasing power.

E-10-2026-001981.t: Possible illegal surveillance of European officials through surveillance of their Greek counterparts
qt: to the Commission Nikolas Farantouris (S&D), Yannis Maniatis (S&D), Nikos Papandreou (S&D), Sakis Arnaoutoglou (S&D) Subject:

The wiretapping scandal has been plaguing the Greek political and social scene since 2020, with the surveillance of Greek politicians, military personnel, journalists, business people, judges, state officials and others through the National Intelligence Service system or the use of illegal Predator software1. In fact, the surveillance by the National Intelligence Service was supposedly carried out for ‘national security reasons’, which have not been disclosed despite the decision of the Council of State that deemed the universal and total prohibition on informing the affected individuals of surveillance completed on them to be unconstitutional2. However, beyond the critical questions that remain unanswered within the country, the surveillance of Greek ministers, senior military and other officials leaves open the possibility that their conversations with other European ministers, senior military and other officials were monitored, both in the context of bilateral contacts (e.g. telephone communications or meetings) and in the context of their participation in meetings of EU institutions and bodies (e.g. EU ministerial meetings, meetings of the EU Military Committee). In view of the above: 1.

How will the Commission help to investigate whether European officials have been victims of surveillance due to their communications with Greek ministers, military or other officials who were monitored by the National Intelligence Service or via Predator?

Does the Commission intend to request information from the Greek authorities and contribute to the full clarification of the wiretapping scandal in Greece in order to investigate the above possibility?

https://www.tovima.gr/2026/03/08/dikaiosyni/ypoklopes-i-lista-menoudakou-sto-fos-oi-stoxoi-toupretador-kai-i-siopi/, https://www.tanea.gr/2024/07/26/greece/skandalo-ypoklopon-o-katalogos-ton-koinonstoxon-eyp-kai-predator/. 2 https://www.kathimerini.gr/politics/562966408/ste-gia-parakoloythiseis-antisyntagmatikos-o-nomosgia-mi-enimerosi-androylaki/. 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (24.7.2026) The Commission takes allegations concerning the unlawful use of spyware and the surveillance of the communications of its staff very seriously. At present, the Commission has no information indicating that its staff were either specifically or incidentally targeted in the context of the reported surveillance of communications referred to by the Honourable Member. Nor has the Commission been requested to assist in any related investigation. Should information emerge suggesting that Commission staff may have been affected, the competent Commission services would take all necessary steps to verify and investigate the matter. More generally, following the 2023 recommendations made by the Committee of Inquiry to investigate the use of Pegasus and equivalent surveillance spyware (PEGA Committee)1, the Commission has further strengthened its security framework and enhanced cooperation with the other EU institutions under the coordination of the Computer Emergency Response Team for the EU institutions, bodies and agencies (CERT-EU).

E-10-2026-001977.t: Regulation introducing provisional anti-dumping duties on imports of polyamide yarn from China
qt: to the Commission Waldemar Buda (ECR) Subject:

The Commission recently published a regulation introducing provisional anti-dumping duties on imports of polyamide yarn from China1, after concluding that China was selling polyamide yarn on the EU market below fair market value, causing material injury. This action, while dealing with one problem, exacerbates issues for European producers in the knitting, weaving and light industry sectors. Introducing anti-dumping duties on polyamide yarn – essential for manufacturing – without addressing the issue of finished products, reduces EU competitiveness, shifts production out of the EU and puts enormous pressure on small and medium-sized enterprises, which form the cornerstone of the EU economy. The fate of around 100 manufacturers employing a large number of people from central and eastern Europe, including Poland, has been left hanging in the balance. In the light of the above: 1.
Did the Commission evaluate the impact of anti-dumping duties on EU manufacturers prior to imposing the duties?
Is the Commission considering anti-dumping duties on finished products from China in order to level the playing field for downstream manufacturing in the EU?

How is the current situation consistent with the EU’s broader objectives of supporting reindustrialisation, preserving manufacturing capacity and protecting employment within its light industry sector?

Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/734 of 26 March 2026 imposing a provisional antidumping duty on imports of yarns of polyamide originating in the People’s Republic of China (OJ L, 2026/734, 27.3.2026, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg_impl/2026/734/oj). 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.7.2026) The impact of anti-dumping measures on the downstream industries is analysed in the context of the EU interest analysis. However, this requires cooperation of the users of polyamide yarns. Upon initiation, 140 users of polyamide yarns identified in the complaint were invited to cooperate. Only three users and one users’ association registered as interested parties. None of them filled in the user questionnaire, but merely provided general comments on the possible negative impact of the measures on the downstream industry, not supported by any evidence or data. In case the downstream industry faces pressure from unfairly priced imports, it can also submit a complaint and request an anti-dumping investigation. In order for the investigation to be initiated, the complaint should contain sufficient evidence of dumping, injury and the causal link between the two. The current investigation has the objective of preserving manufacturing capacity and protecting employment of the yarn industry (being a part of light industry sector), which is directly endangered by unfair dumped imports from China. The Commission will monitor potential changes in the pattern of trade after imposition of anti-dumping duties should the Chinese exporters move their export activity to the downstream industry that is using polyamide yarns.

E-10-2026-001975.t: EU-Mercosur agreement: what guarantees are in place to protect French and European farmers from unfair competition?
qt: to the Commission Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE), Christophe Bay (PfE) Subject:

Since 1 May 2026, the Interim Trade Agreement between the European Union and the Mercosur countries has been provisionally applied with Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay1. The Commission is presenting this agreement as an opportunity for EU exports, including industrial and agri-food exports. However, it also exposes the EU market to sensitive quotas, including 99 000 tonnes of beef at a reduced tariff rate, 180 000 tonnes of poultry, 450 000 tonnes of ethanol for the chemical industry and other agricultural products. For years, French and European farmers have warned of the risk of unfair competition, particularly when imports do not comply with health, environmental and social standards equivalent to those in force in the EU.
