https://trade.ec.europa.eu/access-to-markets/en/news/application-eu-mercosur-interim-trade-agreement-1may-2026
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (29.6.2026) According to Article 4 of Regulation (EU) 2026/687 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 11 March 2026 implementing the bilateral safeguard clauses of the EU-Mercosur Partnership Agreement and the EU-Mercosur Interim Trade Agreement for agricultural products1, the Commission shall constantly and proactively monitor the EU market of sensitive products listed in Annex I to the Regulation in particular as regards import and export trends, production and price developments, with the support of the EU market observatories established under Regulation (EU) No 1308/2013 of the European Parliament and of the Council2. For this purpose, the Commission shall cooperate and exchange data with Member States, the European Parliament and the EU industry on a regular basis. In line with Regulation (EU) 2026/687, the Commission will present a monitoring report to the European Parliament and to the Council at least every six months containing its assessment of the impact of imports of sensitive products benefitting from preferential market access under the Agreement. E-10-2026-001974.t: Impact of the Food and Feed Safety Omnibus
qt: to the Commission Tilly Metz (Verts/ALE), Anna Strolenberg (Verts/ALE), Gerben-Jan Gerbrandy (Renew), Biljana Borzan (S&D), Anja Hazekamp (The Left) Subject:

The Commission has indicated that its intended simplification proposal known as the Food and Feed Safety Omnibus would not have a negative impact on health or the environment. On 5 March 2026, AFP reported that Commissioner Olivér Várhelyi stated that only low-risk substances were eligible for unlimited approvals. However, the current version of the text does not reflect such a restriction. Furthermore, a scientific assessment1 commissioned by the Dutch Parliament concluded that the Commission proposal fails to meet many of its intended objectives. The assessment concludes that the simplification proposal would not reduce administrative workload, risks creating an uneven playing field, could hamper innovation and poses significant risks for human and environmental health protection. 1.

Does the Commission confirm that unlimited approvals should only be granted to lowrisk substances, as defined in Article 22 of the Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 and listed in Annex 1 of Regulation (EU) No 528/2012, and that in its view the proposal should be amended to reflect this?
How does the Commission respond to the main concerns raised in the scientific assessment as described above?
Is the Commission developing its own impact assessment to evaluate these effects?
https://www.tweedekamer.nl/debat_en_vergadering/commissievergaderingen/details?id=2026A02677.
at: (English version) to the Commission Tilly Metz (Verts/ALE), Anna Strolenberg (Verts/ALE), Gerben-Jan Gerbrandy (Renew), Biljana Borzan (S&D), Anja Hazekamp (The Left) (12 May 2026) Subject: Impact of the Food and Feed Safety Omnibus The Commission has indicated that its intended simplification proposal known as the Food and Feed Safety Omnibus would not have a negative impact on health or the environment. On 5 March 2026, AFP reported that Commissioner Olivér Várhelyi stated that only low-risk substances were eligible for unlimited approvals. However, the current version of the text does not reflect such a restriction. Furthermore, a scientific assessment (1) commissioned by the Dutch Parliament concluded that the Commission proposal fails to meet many of its intended objectives. The assessment concludes that the simplification proposal would not reduce administrative workload, risks creating an uneven playing field, could hamper innovation and poses significant risks for human and environmental health protection. 1. Does the Commission confirm that unlimited approvals should only be granted to low-risk substances, as defined in Article 22 of the regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 and listed in Annex 1 of Regulation (EU) No 528/2012, and that in its view the proposal should be amended to reflect this? 2.
How does the Commission respond to the main concerns raised in the scientific assessment as described above?
Is the Commission developing its own impact assessment to evaluate these effects?

(3 July 2026) The Food and Feed Safety Simplification Package proposed by the Commission on 16 December 2025 (1) provides for the possibility of approvals to become unlimited for active substances except for substances that are candidates for substitution, that have been approved despite not meeting all criteria under the derogation in Article 4(7) of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 (2) because there are no alternatives, and those for which the approval, in light of the risk assessment’s outcome, will indicate that they should be re-evaluated after a certain period of time. The Commission proposal contains safeguards to ensure that the current high level of protection of health and environment remains guaranteed, i.e. through periodic identification of active substances for a full or targeted re-evaluation (3), existing ad hoc review mechanisms and the fact that authorisations of plant protection products remain limited in time. The proposal reduces administrative burdens by streamlining procedures, clarifying and harmonising rules and allowing Member States to re-assign limited available resources from renewal procedures to the assessment of innovative substances and products. In line with one of the recommendations in the scientific assessment commissioned by the Dutch Parliament, the proposal precisely intends to achieve a ‘smarter’ reassessment system in order to address the systematic delays by proposing structural changes and recognising that significant resource increases in Member States are unlikely. The simplification proposal does not alter core policy objectives nor introduces significant new obligations, therefore, it is not accompanied by an impact assessment but a staff working document (4) analysing the expected cost savings.

E-10-2026-001973.t: Concern about the increase in gambling addiction among children and young people: stricter regulation needed from public authorities
qt: to the Commission Ana Miranda Paz (Verts/ALE) Subject:

Gambling addiction creates serious mental health and financial problems for a large part of Europe’s population, especially young people. The impact of advertising and the floods of betting adverts are increasing the normalisation of gambling among children and young people. In Spain, gambling addiction is rising among the most vulnerable population aged 1825, with one of the highest addiction rates in Europe, particularly in sports betting. Up to 4.9 % of students aged 14-18 are at risk of gambling addiction because they are regular players and have risk characteristics for mental health issues and debt problems. We deplore the proliferation of these betting shops in many working-class neighbourhoods. Public authorities must provide a strict response to this phenomenon, which needs to be examined. They must also limit the social impact of the laxity that exists towards betting companies by means of stricter regulation. We regret that governments such as the Galician Government are involved in the openings of betting shop companies, as happened recently. What measures is the Commission promoting or will it promote to combat gambling addiction among young people and children?
at: (English version) to the Commission Ana Miranda Paz (Verts/ALE) (12 May 2026) Subject: Concern about the increase in gambling addiction among children and young people: stricter regulation needed from public authorities Gambling addiction creates serious mental health and financial problems for a large part of Europe’s population, especially young people. The impact of advertising and the floods of betting adverts are increasing the normalisation of gambling among children and young people. In Spain, gambling addiction is rising among the most vulnerable population aged 18-25, with one of the highest addiction rates in Europe, particularly in sports betting. Up to 4.9% of students aged 14-18 are at risk of gambling addiction because they are regular players and have risk characteristics for mental health issues and debt problems. We deplore the proliferation of these betting shops in many working-class neighbourhoods. Public authorities must provide a strict response to this phenomenon, which needs to be examined. They must also limit the social impact of the laxity that exists towards betting companies by means of stricter regulation. We regret that governments such as the Galician Government are involved in the openings of betting shop companies, as happened recently. What measures is the Commission promoting or will it promote to combat gambling addiction among young people and children? (24 September 2026) There is no sector-specific EU legislation on gambling. Gambling is regulated by the Member States and national gambling laws often include restrictions on advertising. The Commission supports Member States in their efforts to modernise their online gambling legal frameworks and facilitates cooperation between regulators. In EU consumer law, Directive 2005/29/EC on unfair commercial practices (1) prohibits misleading or aggressive advertising affecting consumers’ transactional decisions, especially when it targets vulnerable consumers, such as minors. In the area of gambling, it serves as a safety net and is without prejudice to national legislation. Furthermore, Article 28 of the Digital Services Act (2) requires providers of online platforms accessible to minors to ensure a high level of privacy, safety and security of minors. The Commission considers, as set out in its Guidelines on the protection of minors (3), that providers are to put in place measures to prevent minors from accessing age-inappropriate content, including gambling content, and to ensure that minors are not exposed to gambling-like commercial practices. The Commission is diligently enforcing these obligations (4). Moreover, the EU-funded Better Internet for Kids platform provides resources addressing responsible online gaming (5).

In October 2025, the Commission requested information from the Apple App Store and Google Play regarding their measures to ensure that minors are not exposed to harmful apps, such as gambling apps. According to press reports1, this investigation concerns networks accused of raising funds in Italy destined, directly or indirectly, for Hamas. (13 August 2026) The EU position on Hamas has been very clear and consistent. The EU condemns in the strongest terms Hamas and its brutal and indiscriminate terrorist attacks across Israel and deeply deplores the loss of lives. Hamas has been listed on the EU terrorist list since 2003 (1). In 2024, the EU established a framework of restrictive measures dedicated to Hamas and the Palestinian Islamic Jihad (2). The EU also recently adopted the third package of listings against Hamas (3). According to Council Regulation (EC) 2580/2001 on specific restrictive measures directed against certain persons and entities with a view to combating terrorism (CR2580) (4), the making available of funds to listed groups, including by EU officials or institutions to Hamas, directly or indirectly, is prohibited. All Commission grantees must uphold fundamental EU values (5) and all contracts involving EU funding worldwide contain provisions that no funds are made available to any listed group. According to CR2580, Member States shall lay down the rules on penalties, including criminal penalties, applicable to infringements of the provisions of that regulation and shall take all measures necessary to ensure that they are implemented (6). Any assessment of possible criminal conduct or alleged links with entities under investigation falls within the competence of the relevant national judicial and law-enforcement authorities of the Member States.

E-10-2026-001971.t: Commissioner Lahbib’s urgent request to MEPs to lobby for abortion in Member States
qt: to the Commission Bert-Jan Ruissen (ECR), Margarita de la Pisa Carrión (PfE), Stephen Nikola Bartulica (ECR), Aurelijus Veryga (ECR), Christophe Gomart (PPE), Matej Tonin (PPE) Subject:

During the exchange of views with Commissioner Hadja Lahbib in Parliament’s Committee on Women’s Rights and Gender Equality on Tuesday 14 April 2026, the Commissioner replied to questions on the state of play on ‘My Voice, My Choice’. She stressed that the Commission has to respect the EU Treaties regarding abortion, that abortion is a national competence and that Member States can now voluntarily use ESF+ funds to pay for abortions. She urged MEPs, however, to lobby and apply pressure in their home countries to do so. 1.

How does the Commission justify funding abortions, given abortion’s exclusion from EU competence as reaffirmed by the Commissioner on 14 April 2026, deliberately breaching core Treaty principles of conferral, subsidiarity and proportionality?

MEPs are not lobbying instruments to be used by the Commission. In this context, on what legal and institutional basis does the Commission justify encouraging MEPs to exert political pressure at national level to advance its policy objectives in an area that lies outside EU competence?
The Commissioner stated that 10 Member States support the Commission’s response to ‘My Voice, My Choice’. Which countries were they?
at: (English version) to the Commission Bert-Jan Ruissen (ECR), Margarita de la Pisa Carrión (PfE), Stephen Nikola Bartulica (ECR), Aurelijus Veryga (ECR), Christophe Gomart (PPE), Matej Tonin (PPE) (12 May 2026) Subject: Commissioner Lahbib’s urgent request to MEPs to lobby for abortion in Member States During the exchange of views with Commissioner Hadja Lahbib in Parliament’s Committee on Women’s Rights and Gender Equality on Tuesday 14 April 2026, the Commissioner replied to questions on the state of play on ‘My Voice, My Choice’. She stressed that the Commission has to respect the EU Treaties regarding abortion, that abortion is a national competence and that Member States can now voluntarily use ESF+ funds to pay for abortions. She urged MEPs, however, to lobby and apply pressure in their home countries to do so. 1. How does the Commission justify funding abortions, given abortion’s exclusion from EU competence as reaffirmed by the Commissioner on 14 April 2026, deliberately breaching core Treaty principles of conferral, subsidiarity and proportionality? 2. MEPs are not lobbying instruments to be used by the Commission. In this context, on what legal and institutional basis does the Commission justify encouraging MEPs to exert political pressure at national level to advance its policy objectives in an area that lies outside EU competence? 3. The Commissioner stated that 10 Member States support the Commission’s response to ‘My Voice, My Choice’. Which countries were they? (29 June 2026) As the Commission has expressed in reply to several similar questions (1) received by the Honourable Members of the Parliament, the Commission’s follow up to the Citizen’s initiative ‘My Voice, My Choice’ falls within the EU’s supportive competence. One of the specific objectives of the European Social Fund+, set out in Article 4(1)(k), is that of enhancing equal and timely access to quality, sustainable and affordable services, including the access to person-centred care including healthcare (2). Therefore, the European Social Fund+ can support initiatives that aim to ensure and enhance equal and timely access to healthcare services, including safe abortions. In her response (3) to the Honourable Members during the Structured Dialogue on 14 April, the Commissioner for Equality; Preparedness and Crisis Management reiterated that, while the Commission has clarified that the Member States can make use of the funds under the European Social Fund+ to support services providing safe abortions, it is now up to them to decide whether and how to make use of that possibility. As mentioned also in the reply (4) to the initiative, the Member States may do so on a voluntary basis. Member States may then submit their amended ESF+ programme to the European Commission for approval. The 10 Member States that support the Commission’s response to ‘My Voice, My Choice’ are Austria, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Luxembourg, Poland, Slovenia, Spain and Sweden.

E-10-2026-001970.t: Impact of firework displays on the biodiversity of the Lago di Sartirana SAC (IT2030007)
qt: to the Commission Gaetano Pedulla' (The Left) Subject:

Established by Regional Law 86/1983, the Lago di Sartirana regional nature reserve in Merate (Province of Lecco) was designated as a Natura 2000 Special Area of Conservation (SAC) and Site of Community Interest (SCI) by a 2016 ministerial decree. The Lago di Sartirana (IT2030007) is a site of great importance for the migration, reproduction and nesting of several species protected by the Birds Directive (2009/147/EC), namely the Ferruginous Duck, Little Bittern, Kingfisher and Marsh Harrier. Every year, a 20-minute firework display is held a mere 400 metres from the reserve’s perimeter to mark the local saint’s feast day in late June, a period in which many birds are in the area and nesting1. A source of bright lights and loud noises, these pyrotechnic shows could be at odds with Article 6 of the Habitats Directive (92/43/EEC), which states that activities disturbing local designated species should be avoided. In the light of the above, we ask the Commission: 1.

Is granting authorisation to hold firework displays in the immediate vicinity of an SAC during the nesting season compatible with the protection obligations laid down by the aforementioned Directives, especially given that no environmental implications assessments have been carried out to rule out any potential harm for local species?
How will the Commission go about involving Member States in efforts to ban the use of fireworks in SCIs and their immediate vicinity?

(10 July 2026) The Habitats Directive (1) requires the establishment of the necessary conservation measures for Special Areas of Conservation (Article 6(1)), where the deterioration of habitats and disturbance of the species for which the site was designated must be avoided, in so far as such disturbance could be significant in relation to the objectives of the directive (2) (Article 6(2)). It also requires that plans or projects not directly connected with or necessary to the management of the site, but likely to have an impact must undergo an appropriate assessment of its implications in view of the site's conservation objectives (Article 6(3)). Any activity likely to have a significant effect on a Natura 2000 site, such as the Lago di Sartirana (IT2030007), is concerned. Under the Birds Directive (3), Member States must also apply a general system of protection for all wild birds present on their territory, by prohibiting certain harmful activities (Article 5). Italy has transposed these provisions in its legislation. It has also adopted national guidelines (4) to improve the application of Article 6(3) across its regions, and Lombardy has also transposed them into its regional legal order (5).

E-10-2026-001968.t: Compliance of CAP payments with environmental conditionality in water-stressed areas
qt: to the Commission Jaume Asens Llodrà (Verts/ALE) Subject:

An international journalistic investigation has documented that companies partly owned by the Emirati sovereign wealth fund ADQ received more than EUR 71 million in common agricultural policy (CAP) subsidies between 2019 and 2024, mainly for alfalfa cultivation in areas of the Ebro Basin classified as being under severe water stress under the Water Framework Directive (Directive2000/60/EC). This crop consumes between 8 000 and 10 000 m³ of water per hectare per year, and 98 % of the production is exported outside the European Union. Has the Commission verified whether CAP payments granted to these farms comply with the environmental conditionality requirements laid down in Regulation (EU) 2021/2115, in particular regarding compatibility with the river basin management plans adopted under the Water Framework Directive in the affected areas?

This crop consumes between 8 000 and 10 000 m3 of water per hectare per year, and 98% of the production is exported outside the European Union. Has the Commission verified whether CAP payments granted to these farms comply with the environmental conditionality requirements laid down in Regulation (EU) 2021/2115, in particular regarding compatibility with the river basin management plans adopted under the Water Framework Directive in the affected areas? (7 July 2026) Eligibility for agricultural direct payments is subject to compliance with the Member States’ obligations relating to good practices as listed in Annex III to Regulation (EU) 2021/2115 (rules on conditionality). This includes the compliance of interventions under the common agricultural policy (CAP) with Directive 2000/60/EC (1), as referred to by the Honourable Member. The guiding principle in the management of the CAP Strategic Plan is the sharing of responsibilities between the Member State and the Commission. Accordingly, it is for the competent authorities of the Member State to ensure compliance with the conditionality requirements. For its part, the Commission is planning compliance audits of these bodies in order to check the governance systems of the EU countries and to assess how effectively those systems protect the EU budget.

E-10-2026-001967.t: Use of AIFMD-regulated investment vehicles for large-scale acquisition of residential housing
qt: to the Commission Jaume Asens Llodrà (Verts/ALE) Subject:

Over the past decade, alternative investment funds and real estate investment vehicles regulated under Directive 2011/61/EU on Alternative Investment Fund Managers (AIFMD) have significantly and demonstrably increased their participation in residential housing markets across several Member States, particularly in high-pressure urban areas in Spain, Ireland, the Netherlands and Germany. This trend was identified by the European Central Bank in its 2022 Financial Stability Review as a systemic risk factor with a direct impact on housing affordability. The Commission holds direct competence for the supervision of financial markets and is currently reviewing the regulatory framework of the AIFMD. Has the Commission assessed whether the large-scale accumulation of residential housing by funds regulated under the AIFMD constitutes a use of such vehicles that is contrary to the general interest, and if so, can it share the conclusions of that assessment?
at: (English version) to the Commission Jaume Asens Llodrà (Verts/ALE) (12 May 2026) Subject: Use of AIFMD-regulated investment vehicles for large-scale acquisition of residential housing Over the past decade, alternative investment funds and real estate investment vehicles regulated under Directive 2011/61/EU on Alternative Investment Fund Managers (AIFMD) have significantly and demonstrably increased their participation in residential housing markets across several Member States, particularly in high-pressure urban areas in Spain, Ireland, the Netherlands and Germany. This trend was identified by the European Central Bank in its 2022 Financial Stability Review as a systemic risk factor with a direct impact on housing affordability. The Commission holds direct competence for the supervision of financial markets and is currently reviewing the regulatory framework of the AIFMD. Has the Commission assessed whether the large-scale accumulation of residential housing by funds regulated under the AIFMD constitutes a use of such vehicles that is contrary to the general interest, and if so, can it share the conclusions of that assessment? (16 July 2026) Private investments play an important role in supplying social infrastructure, including affordable and sustainable housing. At the same time, concerns have been raised about potential market distortions, overvaluation and speculative pressures. Limited data and lack of transparency on ownership and key real estate transactions hamper public authorities from evaluating the validity of such claims and monitoring market developments. The Commission will therefore promote greater transparency in the residential property market and will present in 2026 an analysis of housing price dynamics, including available evidence of speculation patterns, data gaps and economic consequences in full respect of the subsidiarity. As regards financial stability, investment in real assets such as real estate may carry risks due to their typically low liquidity and exposure to price volatility, with the European Central Bank (1) highlighting potential macroprudential risks, including liquidity mismatches between assets and liabilities. It should be noted nonetheless that EU alternative investment funds are subject to the Alternative Investment Fund Managers Directive framework (2). This regime sets high regulatory standards and provides safeguards aiming to mitigate risks, such as independent valuation, liquidity risk management, and supervisory reporting, while national authorities coordinated by the European Securities and Markets Authority monitor compliance; recent reforms have further strengthened liquidity management tools and the macroprudential toolkit.

E-10-2026-001966.t: Stakeholder involvement and evidence-based decision-making regarding the Fur Free Europe citizens’ initiative
qt: to the Commission Maria Ohisalo (Verts/ALE), Ville Niinistö (Verts/ALE), Sirpa Pietikäinen (PPE), Maria Noichl (S&D), Niels Fuglsang (S&D), Sebastian Everding (The Left), Annalisa Corrado (S&D), Martin Hojsík (Renew), Thomas Waitz (Verts/ALE), Michal Wiezik (Renew), Manuela Ripa (PPE), Tilly Metz (Verts/ALE) Subject:

The European citizens’ initiative Fur Free Europe1 calls for a prohibition on fur farming and the placing of fur products on the EU market. The Commission indicated that, taking into account the scientific opinion of the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) and its own assessment, it would communicate by March 2026 whether it intends to propose such a prohibition or alternative measures. The Commissioner for Health and Animal Welfare has also refused to meet the organisers of the citizens’ initiative Fur Free Europe2, although he has met with the fur farming industry. It has also come to our attention that the content of the upcoming communication is maintaining fur farming under revised welfare standards, which contradicts the core objectives of the initiative as well as EFSA scientific opinion3, which calls for a ban on fur farming. Therefore we ask the Commission: 1.
When does it intend to publish its communication on the Fur Free Europe initiative?
How is it ensuring balanced stakeholder involvement and evidence-based decisionmaking without meeting the organisers of the initiative?
How is it ensuring that its response respects the democratic expression of EU citizens and aligns with the scientific evidence?

(9 July 2026) The Commission is preparing the follow-up Communication replying to the European Citizen’s Initiative ‘Fur Free Europe’ (1). qt: to the Commission Moritz Körner (Renew) Subject:

The Spanish Government has allegedly misappropriated over EUR 13 billion from the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF) to pay pensions, minimum income benefits and even contributions to the postal service. Spain has decided to legalise the status of 500 000 people who entered the country illegally. A Spanish residence permit gives those concerned the right to visit other Schengen countries as tourists. Border controls will need to be introduced to monitor this. Furthermore, such mass regularisations are an incentive for more people to enter Europe illegally. Spain wants access to cheap EU SAFE funding, but it does not want to meet NATO’s 5 % defence spending target. Spain uses EU funds – to which Hungary also contributes – to finance a basic income that is twice as high as Hungarian social assistance, while Hungarian citizens lose their unemployment benefits after three months and are required to take part in public work schemes in exchange for significantly lower social benefits. 1.
Since when has the Commission been aware of these misappropriations, and what specific measures has it taken since they came to light? Please list all the measures.

What punitive measures are available to the Commission, and which of those does it intend to impose on Spain to prevent that country or other Member States from effectively stealing money that should be helping European taxpayers?

What specific conclusions is the Commission drawing from Spain’s actions in recent months regarding future European solidarity mechanisms, and what reforms of existing solidarity instruments are planned?
at: EN E-001965/26 on behalf of the European Commission (3.9.2026) The Commission is aware of the Spanish Court of Auditors’ observations that the legal basis for certain internal budget transfers ‘should have been more thoroughly justified’1. These do not call into question the lawful use of Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF) funds under EU law but rather concern procedural requirements under Spanish budgetary law. While Spain’s Recovery and Resilience Plan supported the set up and reform of the national minimum income scheme ‘Ingreso Minimo Vital’ via Reform 5 (C22.R5)2, its management and implementation fall under the responsibility of the Member State, which fiscal aggregates must still comply with the EU’s economic governance framework. Furthermore, under Article 22 of the RRF Regulation3, the Commission may apply corrective measures where fraud, corruption or conflicts of interest in the implementation of the RRF are not corrected by the Member State. Based on current information, these situations do not concur in the instances highlighted by the Honourable Member. Under Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2025/23234, Spain was identified as a Member State under migratory pressure for the first annual cycle of the permanent solidarity mechanism under the Asylum and Migration Management Regulation5. This will give it access to the 2026 Solidarity Pool, upon application of the Pact on Migration and Asylum under Council Implementing Decision (EU) 2025/26426. This is unrelated to Spain’s extraordinary regularisation process. Council Regulation (EU) 2025/11067 establishing the Security Action for Europe Regulation sets conditions for support to defence industry investments and does not link eligibility to NATO spending targets. Loan agreements, signed after each Council Implementing Decision, include required control and audit provisions under Article 223(4) of the Financial Regulation.

E-10-2026-001963.t: Government and EU overseeing the integration of higher educational institutions into Greece's war involvement through war research
qt: to the Commission Kostas Papadakis (NI) Subject:

In a period of adjustment towards the ‘war economy’, the alignment of science and research with the pursuits of the capitalist economy is being strengthened, in order to shield EU capital against the possibility of a generalised imperialist war. In its interim evaluation of ‘Horizon Europe’, the EU allocated a huge amount of money to research aimed at developing ‘dual-use’ technologies, while the strategy will be expanded in the new ‘Horizon Europe 2028-2034’ programme. Greek universities and research centres are being transformed into branches of the war industry: the research centres ‘Demokritos’, ‘CERTH’ and ‘FORTH’ are participating in the NATO DIANA programme; we have the NTUA involved in 21 projects for military purposes funded by the EDF and ‘Horizon Europe’; the ‘UnderSec’ programme in which the University of West Attica and the Hellenic Mediterranean University are collaborating with the Israeli Ministry of Defence; and the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki and Panteion taking on the role of war propagandist. In view of the above: 1.

What is the Commission's position on the fact that the shift to a war economy and the Preparedness Union are turning infrastructure and human knowledge into a pawn of imperialist competition, aligning the funding of research and scientific programmes with the pursuit of strengthening the EU's war industry, while cutting back on research in areas that could substantially improve the living conditions of the people?

What is the Commission’s position on the request to disengage universities and research centres from war preparations, by stopping all military war programmes and ensuring state funding for research focused on the needs of the people?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (7.7.2026) Horizon Europe1 is an over EUR 90 billion programme which covers vast areas of research and innovation, for example in clean transition and decarbonisation, digital transition, health, biotech, agriculture and bioeconomy. The Commission remains strongly committed to the funding of these priorities, through the specific programme implementing Horizon Europe2. This funding is not affected in any way by the support provided by the specific programme for defence research (the European Defence Fund3) which funds only activities with an exclusive focus on defence applications. As outlined in the Preparedness Union4 and ProtectEU Strategies5, reaching defence readiness requires a whole-of-society approach. Accordingly, civilian research institutions can play an important role in the pursuit of civilian preparedness. Furthermore, investments in defence research and development have positive spillover effects for the EU economy, boosting competitiveness, increasing the gross domestic product, and fostering innovation in critical sectors beyond defence, such as healthcare, energy and transport. This is also in the interest of European citizens.

E-10-2026-001962.t: Serious rule of law issues from the decision of the Supreme Court Prosecutor not to reopen the wiretapping case
qt: to the Commission Nikolas Farantouris (S&D), Yannis Maniatis (S&D), Nikos Papandreou (S&D), Sakis Arnaoutoglou (S&D) Subject:

On 26 February 2026, the Single-Member Misdemeanour Court of Athens issued a landmark decision on the wiretapping scandal, finding the defendants guilty and imposing a total prison sentence of 126 years and 8 months1. At the same time, the case file was forwarded again to the prosecutorial authorities due to sufficient evidence of serious criminal acts despite the previous archiving of the case, given the volume of new evidence that emerged. However, on 27 April 2026, the Prosecutor of the Supreme Court (who, as supervising prosecutor of Greece’s national intelligence agency, had signed off the surveillance of eleven individuals who were also targets of Predator2) decided not to retrieve the case from the archive and, therefore, not to order any further investigation3. This decision has provoked strong reactions from society, the political world and the Bar Associations4. Given that, on the basis of the Commission's annual reports on the rule of law, the perceived independence of the judiciary in Greece has been continuously declining in recent years5: 1.
Does the Commission consider that the practices complained of and the absence of a substantive judicial investigation are in line with Greece's obligations under EU law6?

Does the Commission intend to include, in its forthcoming report on the rule of law in Greece, specific findings and recommendations to ensure the independence and impartiality of the prosecution, the effective investigation of the wiretapping scandal and Greece’s full compliance with EU law?

at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.7.2026) The Commission does not comment on investigations and proceedings before national courts in individual cases. In general, as the Commission has stated on numerous occasions, it strongly condemns any illegal access to interpersonal communications. The EU has a strong legal framework for data protection and privacy when the use of spyware falls with the scope of EU law. The Commission’s annual Rule of Law Report monitors and reports on developments, with allegations of illegal use of spyware taken into consideration when relevant under the framework of national checks and balances, the protection of journalists and the safeguarding of media freedom. The Commission continues monitoring the situation of the rule of law in all Member States including Greece in the context of the 2026 Rule of Law Report, which is set for publication in July 2026.

E-10-2026-001961.t: Query concerning RRF flexibility and deadlines for social housing energy efficiency projects in the light of the continued availability of funding and unforeseen global shocks
qt: to the Commission Danilo Della Valle (The Left), Dario Tamburrano (The Left), Leoluca Orlando (Verts/ALE), Brando Benifei (S&D) Subject:

Measure M.7-I.17 of the Italian NRRP1 is crucial for helping vulnerable groups living in social housing (ERP). However, the energy and inflationary shocks brought about by the April 2026 Iran-US conflict have caused the price of materials to rise to unaffordable levels, a scenario that falls under the definition of ‘objective circumstances’ laid down in Article 21 of Regulation (EU) 2021/241. Though the NRRP deadline for finalising financial agreements is 30 June 2026, the resource tracker managed by the Government-owned Gestore Servizi Energetici (Energy Services Operator) shows that significant sums have yet to be used. Local administrations are grappling with feasibility plans, energy service company tenders and other processes that will not be concluded before the NRRP deadline, potentially costing many ERP projects their funding. We therefore ask: 1.

Given the proven existence of unused NRRP funds, will the Commission recognise that the geopolitical crisis and procedural complexities described above do indeed qualify as ‘objective circumstances’ and grant an 18-month extension in which the remaining M.7I.17 resources can be claimed?

What flexibility instruments will the Commission enact to enable the implementation of price adjustment measures with a view to preventing ERP projects from losing their allocations owing to a lack of funding?
Will the Commission ensure that the reallocation of residual NRRP funding towards Italy’s housing plan does not undermine REPowerEU’s energy efficiency objectives and social targets?

at: (English version) to the Commission Danilo Della Valle (The Left), Dario Tamburrano (The Left), Leoluca Orlando (Verts/ALE), Brando Benifei (S&D) (12 May 2026) Subject: Query concerning RRF flexibility and deadlines for social housing energy efficiency projects in the light of the continued availability of funding and unforeseen global shocks Measure M.7-I.17 of the Italian NRRP (1) is crucial for helping vulnerable groups living in social housing (ERP). However, the energy and inflationary shocks brought about by the April 2026 Iran-US conflict have caused the price of materials to rise to unaffordable levels, a scenario that falls under the definition of ‘objective circumstances’ laid down in Article 21 of Regulation (EU) 2021/241. Though the NRRP deadline for finalising financial agreements is 30 June 2026, the resource tracker managed by the Government-owned Gestore Servizi Energetici (Energy Services Operator) shows that significant sums have yet to be used. Local administrations are grappling with feasibility plans, energy service company tenders and other processes that will not be concluded before the NRRP deadline, potentially costing many ERP projects their funding. We therefore ask: 1.

Given the proven existence of unused NRRP funds, will the Commission recognise that the geopolitical crisis and procedural complexities described above do indeed qualify as ‘objective circumstances’ and grant an 18-month extension in which the remaining M.7-I.17 resources can be claimed?

What flexibility instruments will the Commission enact to enable the implementation of price adjustment measures with a view to preventing ERP projects from losing their allocations owing to a lack of funding?
Will the Commission ensure that the reallocation of residual NRRP funding towards Italy’s housing plan does not undermine REPowerEU’s energy efficiency objectives and social targets?

(16 July 2026) Under the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF) legal framework, Member States must meet all milestones and targets by 31 August 2026, and the Commission must make the final payments by 31 December 2026. The concept of ‘unused funds’ does not apply under the RRF Regulation (1) in this context, since RRF support remains strictly subject to the satisfactory fulfilment of the relevant milestones and targets within the applicable deadlines just mentioned. The implementation of the Recovery and Resilience Plan (RRP) remains a shared effort for which the Commission maintains a continuous dialogue with the Italian authorities, including on Measure M.7-I.17. Where an RRP measure is no longer achievable because of objective circumstances, the Member State concerned may make a reasoned request to the Commission for its amendment or replacement. In view of the timeline of the RRF, the Commission communicated in its Guidelines on the closure of the RRF (2) that Member States were expected to make any such requests before the end of May 2026.

E-10-2026-001960.t: Explicit recognition of the function of ‘MEP’ on the ‘EU laissez-passer’
qt: to the Commission Nadine Morano (PPE), Céline Imart (PPE), Isabelle Le Callennec (PPE), Christophe Gomart (PPE), Tomáš Zdechovský (PPE), Andrey Kovatchev (PPE) Subject:

The EU laissez-passer is an additional travel document that facilitates, among other things, the procedures for obtaining visas for professional purposes. It is recognised by Member States’ authorities and may also be recognised by third countries under specific agreements. Its use is strictly limited to the exercise of official duties. In accordance with Protocol (No 7) on the Privileges and Immunities of the European Union and Regulation (EU) No 1417/2013, this document may be issued to Members of the European Parliament and to officials and other servants of the European Union. When MEPs do not have a diplomatic or service passport issued by their Member State, they can apply for a laissez-passer to facilitate their travel when they register for the exercise of their mandate. However, unlike officials, the function of Member of the European Parliament is not explicitly mentioned on page 4, which seems to run counter to the recognition of the official function of Member of the European Parliament. This situation appears all the more paradoxical given that Protocol (No 7) guarantees Members travel facilities equivalent to those granted to senior officials or representatives on official missions. Something therefore needs to be done to address this missing reference to the official function of Member of the European Parliament. When does the Commission intend to address this issue?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (31.8.2026) Article 6 of the Protocol on the privileges and immunities of the European Union (PPI) provides that ‘laissez-passer in a form to be prescribed by the Council, acting by a simple majority, [...] may be issued to members and servants of the institutions of the Union by the Presidents of those institutions’. Annex I to Council Regulation (EU) No 1417/2013 of 17 December 20131 laying down the form of the laissez-passer issued by the European Union requires that the ‘function’ be indicated on page 4 of the laissez-passer. However, no official list of functions to be indicated has been adopted, leaving this matter open to interpretation by each institution. Article 6 of the Protocol states that laissez-passer may be issued by the Presidents of each institution. Therefore, any request to indicate the official function of Member of the European Parliament on the laissez-passer must be addressed to the institution competent to issue them to Members of the European Parliament, namely the European Parliament.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32013R1417.

E-10-2026-001959.t: Is the Council afraid to openly stand up for the postwar order – the end of the Beneš, Bierut and AVNOJ decrees?
qt: to the Council Erik Kaliňák (NI), Judita Laššáková (NI) Subject:

In the context of the recent Hungarian parliamentary elections, the issue of the Beneš decrees has resurfaced, and Parliament plans to address it in a special debate. However, the Beneš Decrees in Czechoslovakia, the Bierut Decrees in Poland and the AVNOJ Decrees in Yugoslavia were the cornerstones of the post-war order in Europe and no longer have any practical legal effect today. As the representative of the Member States, the Council has a responsibility to preserve unity and stability. 1.
Does the Council agree that these three sets of decrees are also an integral and historical part of the post-war European order, upon which today’s European Union itself is founded?

Why has the Council not yet taken a clear stance against any attempts to revise the postwar European order, which would call into question the Beneš Decrees and, inevitably, the Bierut and AVNOJ Decrees?

Does the Council not consider that the Union’s cohesion could be threatened if a discussion were to open regarding the revision of these historic decrees, which could undermine trust among Member States and the stability of the post-war order?

E-10-2026-001958.t: Is the EU risking a new crisis and a loss of trust among Member States over the Beneš Decrees?
qt: to the President of the European Council Erik Kaliňák (NI), Judita Laššáková (NI) Subject:

In the wake of the recent Hungarian parliamentary elections and related political developments, calls to revisit the Beneš Decrees have re-emerged in public discourse (including in the European Parliament). Yet the Beneš Decrees, just like the Bierut Decrees in Poland or the AVNOJ Decrees in the former Yugoslavia, were fundamental pillars of the post-war order in Europe, constituting purely historical legislation and that currently has no practical effect. 1.

Does the President of the European Council agree that these three sets of decrees constitute an enduring historical part of the post-war European order, upon which today’s European Union itself is founded?

Does the President of the European Council not consider that the stability and cohesion of the Union would be seriously undermined if a discussion were to begin at the highest political level regarding the revision of these historical acts, which could undermine legal certainty, historical continuity and mutual trust among Member States?

E-10-2026-001957.t: Is Brussels seeking to revise the Beneš, Bierut and AVNOJ decrees? Will the EU risk destabilising Central Europe over these decrees?
qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Erik Kaliňák (NI), Judita Laššáková (NI) Subject:
Is Brussels seeking to revise the Beneš, Bierut and AVNOJ decrees? Will the EU risk destabilising Central Europe over these decrees?

In the recent Hungarian parliamentary elections, as well as afterwards, the issue of the Beneš Decrees has come to the fore. The European Parliament, for example, intends to address it in a separate debate. Somehow, amid this post-election enthusiasm over Péter Magyar’s rise to power, it is being forgotten that the Beneš Decrees, the Bierut Decrees and the AVNOJ Decrees were key acts in the post-war order of Europe after 1945 and no longer have any practical application today. In its foreign policy, the EU often emphasises stability and respect for historical agreements. 1.
Is the High Representative aware that these three sets of decrees represent a closed historical chapter that ensured post-war stability in Central and Eastern Europe?

Does the High Representative not consider that opening up discussions on the revision of these decrees poses a risk to the Union’s foreign policy, as it could destabilise the historical foundations of the European order in relation to third countries?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (7.8.2026) The so-called Beneš, Bierut and the Anti-Fascist Council for the National Liberation of Yugoslavia (AVNOJ) Decrees are historical acts undertaken by national authorities prior to accession to the EU in a very specific economic and social context. The Commission ensures the respect of EU law, within the remit of its competences.

E-10-2026-001956.t: Is the Commission secretly preparing to repeal the Beneš Decrees? Is postwar Europe at risk of falling apart?
qt: to the Commission Erik Kaliňák (NI), Judita Laššáková (NI) Subject:

In the context of the recent Hungarian parliamentary elections, the issue of the Beneš Decrees of 1945–1946 has resurfaced, and the Commission and Parliament plan to address it in a special debate. This is happening despite the fact that the Beneš Decrees in Czechoslovakia, the Bierut Decrees in Poland and the AVNOJ Decrees in the former Yugoslavia were a fundamental part of the post-war order in Europe, represent historical legislation and are no longer in force today. However, the Commission is engaging in the discussion on the Beneš Decrees without offering a clear and categorical rejection of any efforts to revise them. 1.
How does the Commission view these three sets of decrees, which form an integral historical part of the post-war legal framework upon which today’s Europe is built?
Why has the Commission not categorically rejected any attempts to repeal the Beneš Decrees, and thereby any similar future efforts to challenge the Bierut or AVNOJ Decrees?

Could it be that the Commission perhaps plan to open a discussion on revising these decrees, which could jeopardise legal certainty, historical continuity and the stability of the post-war order throughout Europe?

E-10-2026-001955.t: Lack of legal remedy in the event of failure to make a referral and to comply with the obligation to state reasons pursuant to CILFIT and Remling – follow-up question to E-000611/2026 and E-004470/2025
qt: to the Commission Marion Walsmann (PPE) Subject:

In its answers to questions for written answer E-004470/20251 and E-000611/20262, the Commission did not provide a clear answer to the question of whether the absence of a judicial remedy against a wrongful failure to refer is compatible with Article 19(1) of the Treaty on European Union (TEU) and Article 47 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union (CFR). According to the CILFIT judgment (Case C-283/81), a court of final instance is exempt from the obligation to refer a question for a preliminary ruling under Article 267(3) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU) only in exceptional circumstances. According to the Remling judgment (Case C-767/23), the court must provide specific and concrete reasons for the non-referral. 1.

Does the Commission consider the absence of a legal remedy before a specialised court in the event of a breach of these obligations to be compatible with Article 19(1) TEU and Article 47 CFR, and if so, on what basis under EU law?
If not, what specific requirements does this entail for the Member States?

If the Commission does not systematically record infringements of the obligations to refer and to state reasons for non-referral set out in the CILFIT and Remling judgments, how can it possibly identify any structural deficits or systematic breaches as referred to in its previous replies?
https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/E-10-2025-004470_DE.html. https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/E-10-2026-000611_DE.html.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.7.2026) As provided for in the second subparagraph of Article 19(1) Treaty on European Union, it is for the Member States to establish a system of legal remedies and procedures ensuring compliance with the right to effective judicial protection in the fields covered by EU law. The principle of effective judicial protection is a general principle of EU law stemming from the constitutional traditions common to the Member States, which has been enshrined in Articles 6 and 13 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms, and is reaffirmed in Article 47 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union1. As the Commission explained in its answers to written questions E-000611/2026 and E004470/2025, Article 267 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU) sets up a dialogue between the Court of Justice of the European Union and the courts of the Member States, in which the latter are closely involved in the uniform interpretation and correct application of EU law and the protection of individual rights. It should be reiterated that the Commission monitors structural deficits in the dialogue under Article 267 TFEU. As guardian of the Treaties, the Commission may initiate infringement proceedings under Article 258 TFEU for possible non-compliance with Article 267(3) TFEU when a Member State adopts legislation preventing proper judicial cooperation under that provision, or when evidence points to a systematic breach.
1 Judgment of 11 May 2023, Inspecţia Judiciară, C-817/21, EU:C:2023:391, para. 40; judgment of 21 December
2021, Euro Box Promotion and Others, C‑357/19, C‑379/19, C‑547/19, C‑811/19 and C‑840/19, EU:C:2021:1034, para. 219 and the case-law cited.

E-10-2026-001952.t: Shortage of hormone medication in Sweden
qt: to the Commission Jessica Polfjärd (PPE) Subject:

For several years now, there has been a shortage of oestrogen medication in Sweden, and the situation is now critical. Hundreds of thousands of Swedish women are therefore at risk of serious health problems unless something is done. The Swedish Government has taken steps to address the shortage, and is currently looking into whether there are any EU mechanisms that might be able to provide support to countries with shortages. With the above in mind: 1.
Is the Commission monitoring the serious situation currently facing women who need hormone medicines in Sweden?
What possibilities does the Commission see, within the EU’s remit, to help the hundreds of thousands of Swedish women who could be affected by the shortage?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (9.7.2026) The management of medicines shortages primarily falls under the responsibility of Member States, as national authorities are best placed to assess and address local supply disruptions. When a critical shortage cannot be resolved at the national level, a Member State may report to the European Medicines Agency (EMA), through the Medicine Shortages Single Point of Contact (SPOC) Working Party, for coordination at EU level. The Commission, in close collaboration with the EMA and the Medicines Shortages Steering Group, which includes representatives from all Member States, actively monitors and addresses shortages escalated to the EU level. Regarding the specific case of oestrogen, the Commission is not aware of a serious situation that would require EU-level monitoring or intervention. Currently, there are no critical shortages of oestrogen at Union level that have been notified to the European Medicines Agency or that are subject to coordinated action. Should Sweden, or any other Member State, identify a need for EU-wide coordination on this or any other medicine shortage, the established Single Point of Contact working party and the Medicines Shortages Steering Group provide the mechanisms for escalation, collective assessment, and mitigation.

E-10-2026-001951.t: France’s ban on nicotine pouches and the consequences for EU citizens
qt: to the Commission Jessica Polfjärd (PPE) Subject:

Nicotine pouches (also known as ‘white snus’) have been banned in France since 1 April 2026. France has however gone further than simply banning or regulating the sale of nicotine pouches: under French law, white snus is now categorised as a narcotic, meaning that anyone in possession of it risks a heavy fine or even imprisonment. Smoking cigarettes, however, is still totally fine in France. Snus, including white snus, is an important hallmark of Swedish culture and part of Sweden’s tobacco model. With that in mind: 1.

Does the Commission consider it reasonable that Swedish citizens – including staff working for the EU institutions who regularly travel to France in the course of their duties – could be imprisoned for possession of a product which, for Swedes, has a high cultural value and which, unlike smoking, does not pose any risk to third parties?
Does the Commission take the view that the French rules are consistent with the EU’s principles of free movement and with the EU’s motto, ‘United in diversity’?

Does the Commission take the view that the French rules are consistent with the EU’s principles of free movement and with the EU’s motto, ‘United in diversity’?

(17 July 2026) With regard to products that do not fall under harmonised EU legislation, such as nicotine pouches, measures having equivalent effect to quantitative restrictions within the meaning of Article 34 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU) can be considered justified when falling within one of the exceptions provided for in Article 36 TFEU, which include the protection of health and life of humans and are compliant with the general principles of EU law such as proportionality. Considering the discretion of Member States to determine the level of protection which they wish to afford to public health and the way they want to achieve it, in accordance with the case-law of the Court of Justice of the European Unio n (1), the Commission has not identified sufficient elements indicating that the notified French legislatio n (2) would be unjustified or disproportionate to the need to protect the life and health of the population and particularly of minors. As highlighted by the recent evaluation of the EU tobacco control framework (3), novel tobacco and nicotine products, including nicotine pouches, pose serious health risks and represent a significant public health concern. The enforcement of national legislation falls within the Member States’ competence.

See Case C-198/14, Visnapuu, ECLI:EU:C:2015:751. https://technical-regulation-information-system.ec.europa.eu/en/notification/26692. https://ec.europa.eu/info/law/better-regulation/have-your-say/initiatives/13481-Evaluation-of-the-legislative-framework-for-tobacco-control_en.

E-10-2026-001950.t: Impact of EU digital regulation on competitiveness and achieving digital sovereignty
qt: to the Commission Piotr Müller (ECR) Subject:

The EU’s digital regulatory framework is increasingly acting as a barrier to capital and innovation, undermining the Union’s competitiveness. At the same time, the Commission stresses the need to build ‘digital sovereignty’ given the risks associated with depending on external technologies, especially in the context of China’s growing role and geopolitical tensions. It is undeniable that certain threats – particularly those linked to countries with different regulatory and democratic standards – need to be addressed. However, the answer is not further expanding internal regulations or limiting access to global services, but instead building strong technology partnerships with countries that share our democratic values and creating conditions conducive to innovative development in Europe. The Commission’s current rhetoric appears to focus on external factors to explain the weakness of the EU’s tech sector, despite the fact that complex and rigid EU regulations, often introduced under the guise of user protection, also significantly contribute to this weakness. I therefore ask: 1.
How does the Commission justify its emphasis on external threats while failing to reflect on the impact of its own regulations on the outflow of investment and innovation from the Union?

What guarantees are there that the concept of ‘digital sovereignty’ will be implemented by strengthening cooperation with countries with similar values, rather than by further restricting access to services and technologies in the internal market?
Is the Commission planning a comprehensive review of the existing digital regulations with a view to simplifying them and creating a more favourable environment for European tech companies?

However, the answer is not further expanding internal regulations or limiting access to global services, but instead building strong technology partnerships with countries that share our democratic values and creating conditions conducive to innovative development in Europe. The Commission’s current rhetoric appears to focus on external factors to explain the weakness of the EU’s tech sector, despite the fact that complex and rigid EU regulations, often introduced under the guise of user protection, also significantly contribute to this weakness. I therefore ask: 1.

What guarantees are there that the concept of ‘digital sovereignty’ will be implemented by strengthening cooperation with countries with similar values, rather than by further restricting access to services and technologies in the internal market?
Is the Commission planning a comprehensive review of the existing digital regulations with a view to simplifying them and creating a more favourable environment for European tech companies?

(22 July 2026) The EU cannot be technologically dependent of countries with fundamentally misaligned standards and values, which may translate into products and services used by EU citizens and businesses. Such dependencies pose a potential risk to EU citizens. The Technological Sovereignty Package (1) addresses this, focusing on semiconductors, cloud and AI development, opensource solutions and sustainable energy usage. It aims to reduce critical dependencies and strengthening Europe’s capacity to act — while staying open and engaged with the world, in line with the International Digital Strategy for the EU (2). Supply chains, standards, security and innovation are global and interconnected. They need market openness and international cooperation. The Commission is also assessing the EU’s own digital rulebook very seriously. In 2025, it put forward two Omnibus legislative proposals (3), addressing the areas that affect digital competitiveness the most: AI and data, and cybersecurity. Overall, the proposals are jointly expected to cut at least EUR 5 billion of administrative costs for enterprises by 2029, spurring innovation. Additionally, proposals such as the EU Business Wallets (4) or the Digital Networks Act (5) have simplification as a core dimension.

The Commission is now working on a Digital Fitness Check (6), an analysis of the cumulative effect of digital regulation. This further complements the individual evaluations already completed or planned under the current mandate, such as those of the Digital Markets Act (7) and the Audiovisual Media Services Directive (8) in 2026.

E-10-2026-001949.t: Assessment of the impact of the proposed PFAS restriction on critical medical technologies and continuity of patient care
qt: to the Commission Aurelijus Veryga (ECR) Subject:
Can the Commission clarify: 1.

what methodology the Commission is using to assess the potential impact of the proposed restriction on per-and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) on the availability, safety, clinical performance and continuity of supply of critical Class IIb and Class III medical devices, including implantable and invasive technologies, and whether this assessment includes an analysis of the cumulative impacts arising from Medical Devices Regulation (MDR) transition requirements, capacity constraints of notified bodies and supply chain dependencies;

whether the Commission has assessed the risk that insufficient or narrowly defined derogation periods could result in the withdrawal of clinically established technologies from the EU market before technically and clinically validated alternatives become available, and what specific corrective measures it would consider should such a risk be identified;

what measures the Commission intends to put in place to ensure long-term regulatory certainty and continuity of patient access to essential medical technologies, including consideration of: a material-class-based exemption for fluoropolymers; alignment between the REACH Regulation and MDR classifications and definitions; dedicated exemptions for invasive delivery systems required for implantable therapies; and mechanisms to avoid increased reliance on more invasive procedures associated with higher complication rates, longer hospital stays and increased costs for European healthcare systems?
at: (English version) to the Commission Aurelijus Veryga (ECR) (11 May 2026) Subject: Assessment of the impact of the proposed PFAS restriction on critical medical technologies and continuity of patient care Can the Commission clarify: 1.

what methodology the Commission is using to assess the potential impact of the proposed restriction on per-and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) on the availability, safety, clinical performance and continuity of supply of critical Class IIb and Class III medical devices, including implantable and invasive technologies, and whether this assessment includes an analysis of the cumulative impacts arising from Medical Devices Regulation (MDR) transition requirements, capacity constraints of notified bodies and supply chain dependencies;

whether the Commission has assessed the risk that insufficient or narrowly defined derogation periods could result in the withdrawal of clinically established technologies from the EU market before technically and clinically validated alternatives become available, and what specific corrective measures it would consider should such a risk be identified;

what measures the Commission intends to put in place to ensure long-term regulatory certainty and continuity of patient access to essential medical technologies, including consideration of: a material-class-based exemption for fluoropolymers; alignment between the REACH Regulation and MDR classifications and definitions; dedicated exemptions for invasive delivery systems required for implantable therapies; and mechanisms to avoid increased reliance on more invasive procedures associated with higher complication rates, longer hospital stays and increased costs for European healthcare systems?

(6 July 2026) The restriction dossier submitted to the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA) by five national authorities in 2023 on per-and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), the so-called universal PFAS restriction, is still being assessed by the Agency. Medical devices are one of the sectors assessed in detail during this process (1). In that context, the availability of alternatives to PFAS and the socioeconomic impacts of the restriction options are evaluated by ECHA’s Committee for Socio-Economic Analysis (SEAC). The public consultation on SEAC’s draft opinion has closed and SEAC will finalise its opinion considering the comments received. Once finalised, ECHA’s final opinions will be the basis for the Commission to prepare a restriction proposal, taking into account all relevant information. As announced in the Chemicals Industry Action Plan (2), where adequate alternatives in terms of performance and safety are not available, the continued use of PFAS in industrial applications may be allowed for critical applications, such as health, under strict specific conditions until acceptable substitutes are found.

E-10-2026-001948.t: The compatibility with EU law of the Italian 2026 Security Law’s video surveillance measure
qt: to the Commission Alessandro Zan (S&D), Giuseppe Lupo (S&D), Alessandra Moretti (S&D), Georgia Tramacere (S&D), Pina Picierno (S&D), Sandro Ruotolo (S&D), Irene Tinagli (S&D), Brando Benifei (S&D), Marco Tarquinio (S&D), Camilla Laureti (S&D), Cecilia Strada (S&D), Annalisa Corrado (S&D), Elisabetta Gualmini (Renew), Gaetano Pedulla' (The Left), Leoluca Orlando (Verts/ALE), Ilaria Salis (The Left) Subject:
The compatibility with EU law of the Italian 2026 Security Law’s video surveillance measure

Also known as the 2026 Security Law, Decree-Law No 23/2026 allocates EUR 19 million to the expansion of the interconnected video surveillance networks that are used by municipalities, local police forces, provincial police headquarters (questure) and Italy’s gendarmerie (Carabinieri) and financial police (Guardia di Finanza). The new law does not, however, lay down any minimum IT security requirements (such as strong authentication procedures, centralised access tracking and network segmentation) or data protection measures for these networks which, given the absence of implementing decrees, will not be governed by an appropriate protection and guarantee framework. We believe this surveillance measure to be at odds with Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (particularly Articles 32, 24, 25 and 35 thereof) and also have concerns about the role allocated to the Data Protection Authority1 and the Security Law's compliance with the principles of data security, accessibility and protection. Finally, we fear that DecreeLaw No 23/2026 could turn out to be vague and disproportionate, and that these expanded surveillance systems could therefore be vulnerable to unauthorised access, be complemented by inadequate organisational and technical measures and be used in unjustified profiling initiatives and in other ways that exceed their stated purpose. Having regard to the EU’s cybersecurity framework, the NIS2 Directive and the provisions of Articles 7 and 8 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights, and considering the need to ensure the full implementation of the NIS2 Directive, we ask the Commission: 1.
Is it aware of the 2026 Security Law’s surveillance measure and its inadequate protection and guarantee framework?

Does it consider the provisions outlined above to be compatible with EU law? If not, what further measures does it think are needed to bring this surveillance measure in line with European law and ensure that it fully upholds fundamental rights?
Will it take action to ensure compliance with EU law?

E-10-2026-001947.t: Transparency and traceability of EU fund usage
qt: to the Commission Mihai Tudose (S&D) Subject:

The European Court of Auditors has published the results of the audit on the Recovery and Resilience Facility. One of the main problems identified by the Court of Auditors is the insufficient collection of data to verify the payment history from source to final destination. The audit criticised the European Commission for the lack of clarity in EU data collection regulations. The way things stand at the moment there is a lack of comprehensive information, meaning there is uncertainty about whether funds have been used efficiently and whether they covered real costs. This situation is unacceptable and it is the Commission’s duty to eliminate such shortcomings in the future. What measures is the Commission considering to avoid similar problems in the next multiannual financial framework?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (30.6.2026) The Financial Regulation 20241 introduces enhanced requirements for the collection and publication of data on recipients of EU funding across all budget implementation modes. This means that, as of the next multiannual financial framework 2028-2034, the EU institutions and bodies, Member States, and all persons and entities implementing the EU budget will be required to collect and make available to the Commission information on amounts committed and, where a commitment involves multiple recipients, a breakdown of the amount by recipient, where available. Under the Commission’s proposal for National and Regional Partnership Plans2 the Member States will be required to collect and make available to the Commission information on beneficiaries, recipients, final recipients, contractors, and subcontractors, together with the amount of EU funding committed and information on supported operations. The Commission will publish this information on a centralised website, the Single Gateway3. Concerning the European Court of Auditor’s Special Report on the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF) transparency and traceability4, the Commission notes that the Court has not identified any deficiencies in the Commission’s application of the RRF legislative framework. Under the RRF, the Commission has no legal mandate to systematically request information on actual costs. Nevertheless, Member States can submit such information when revising their Plans. The RRF Regulation5 is based on a robust system to protect the financial interests of the EU and includes the obligation for Member States to take appropriate measures to prevent, detect and correct fraud, corruption, and conflicts of interests6 and to collect and ensure access to data on funds paid under the RRF7.

The Single Gateway will also incorporate the enhanced Financial Transparency System (https://ec.europa.eu/budget/financial-transparency-system/index.html). E-10-2026-001946.t: Greek Government to end the My Home II housing programme early
qt: to the Commission Yannis Maniatis (S&D) Subject:

The Greek Government recently decided to drastically shorten the deadline (from 31 August to 2 June) for signing the loan contracts under the My Home II programme funded by the Recovery Fund. This is despite the fact that, according to the government, there are still EUR 380 million worth of unallocated funds available for the thousands of remaining applicants and many fellow citizens have invested a great deal of time and money in applying for the programme and risk being shut out at the last minute. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Has it agreed to the programme ending early, creating legal uncertainty for citizens and making the EU’s housing policy appear unreliable, when housing is a priority under its current mandate?

Have the consequences been assessed for the thousands of citizens who put their faith in the credibility the EU brought to the programme and who have already advanced money and gone through a number of lengthy and costly preparatory procedures, such as technical/legal checks, regularisation of building irregularities, issuing of required certificates?

Has it assessed whether the My Home I and II programmes – instead of representing policies for the development of public land and vacant housing, the creation of social housing and more generally increasing the housing supply – are in fact effective and do not lead to market distortions, such as a faster increase in the prices of old properties?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (25.6.2026) The ‘My Home II’ programme was designed to provide affordable financing for low-income first-time home buyers with little or no access to mortgage lending at lower than market interest rates. The Greek Recovery and Resilience Plan (RRP)1 allocates EUR 1 billion to the ‘My Home II’ Facility (ID 16400). While ‘My Home II’ is supporting low-income households facing high housing costs and exhibits positive welfare effects, complementary measures in the Greek RRP aim to address elevated house price growth. In this respect, the Greek RRP also includes the adoption of the national housing strategy and the social exchange programme (Koinoniki Antiparochi). The former includes an analysis of the functioning of the housing market, which should set the ground for effective policies in the area of housing in Greece, while the latter’s goal is to directly increase the supply of affordable housing. The Recovery and Resilience Facility Regulation2 provides that all milestones and targets for the implementation of reforms and investments must be completed by 31 August 2026. As such, all payment requests, including supporting evidence necessary for the Commission’s assessment, must be submitted to the Commission by 30 September 2026. In light of these deadlines, it is the responsibility of the Greek authorities to put in place the necessary arrangements, including the signature of financing agreements with final beneficiaries, ensuring that all the relevant evidence demonstrating the fulfilment of the relevant milestones and targets is timely submitted to the Commission.

and-resilience-plan_en. 2 Regulation (EU) 2021/241 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 12 February 2021 establishing the Recovery and Resilience Facility: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2021/241/oj/eng.

qt: to the Commission Barbara Bonte (PfE) Subject:

According to media reports, as part of the ‘#ProtectWhatMatters’ campaign, the Commission is said to have sent promotional kits – including a microphone – to influencers and online content creators to promote the campaign. 1.
Can the Commission confirm that such promotional kits were sent out as part of the ‘#ProtectWhatMatters’ campaign?

(3 August 2026) 1. 55 promotional kits, containing a campaign flyer, two pens, three posters, stickers, a t-shirt, bar coasters, and a microphone, were sent to a limited number of content creators. The material aimed to inspire the participants to visit some of the campaign locations in their respective EU countries and regions and create content showing why democracy matters to them. 2.
