E-10-2026-001944.t: Safety and prescription of SSRIs and SNRIs in the EU, in particular to adolescents and pregnant women
qt: to the Commission Barbara Bonte (PfE) Subject:

The use of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) has increased significantly in the European Union in recent years. A systematic review in 2025 (European Child & Adolescent Psychiatry) in eight EU Member States showed a relative increase in antidepressant use among young people during and after the COVID-19 pandemic ranging from 23 to 52 %. SSRIs were by far the most commonly used category (73.9 to 90.9 %), with a more marked increase among adolescent girls. At the same time, recent publications in the Nature portfolio (Nature Communications, 2025; Nature Mental Health, 2025; Neuropsychopharmacology, 2026) highlight gaps in our understanding of the impact of prenatal SSRI/SNRI exposure on foetal brain development. Moreover, a 2025 systematic review focusing on post-acute withdrawal syndrome (PAWS) reported persistent withdrawal symptoms after discontinuation, whilst the EMA’s latest EUwide safety assessment dates back to 2005. 1.
Does the Commission possess any up-to-date EU-wide data on the prescription of SSRIs and SNRIs to minors and pregnant women?
What conclusions does it draw from the documented increased use among adolescents?

Is the Commission prepared to request that the European Medicines Agency (EMA) initiate a safety reassessment of these medicinal product classes, with a particular focus on long-term use, post-acute withdrawal syndrome, and perinatal exposure?
at: (English version) to the Commission Barbara Bonte (PfE) (11 May 2026) Subject: Safety and prescription of SSRIs and SNRIs in the EU, in particular to adolescents and pregnant women The use of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) has increased significantly in the European Union in recent years. A systematic review in 2025 (European Child & Adolescent Psychiatry) in eight EU Member States showed a relative increase in antidepressant use among young people during and after the COVID-19 pandemic ranging from 23 to 52%. SSRIs were by far the most commonly used category (73.9 to 90.9%), with a more marked increase among adolescent girls. At the same time, recent publications in the Nature portfolio (Nature Communications, 2025; Nature Mental Health, 2025; Neuropsychopharmacology, 2026) highlight gaps in our understanding of the impact of prenatal SSRI/SNRI exposure on foetal brain development. Moreover, a 2025 systematic review focusing on post-acute withdrawal syndrome (PAWS) reported persistent withdrawal symptoms after discontinuation, whilst the EMA’s latest EU-wide safety assessment dates back to 2005. 1. Does the Commission possess any up-to-date EU-wide data on the prescription of SSRIs and SNRIs to minors and pregnant women? 2.
What conclusions does it draw from the documented increased use among adolescents?

3. Is the Commission prepared to request that the European Medicines Agency (EMA) initiate a safety reassessment of these medicinal product classes, with a particular focus on long-term use, post-acute withdrawal syndrome, and perinatal exposure? (8 July 2026) The Commission does not hold EU-wide prescription data for medicines, including serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs). The collection and monitoring of prescription trends fall within the competence of Member States and are not centralised at EU level. All medicines authorised in the EU are subject to continuous and rigorous safety monitoring with cooperation of the national regulatory authorities, the European Medicines Agency and the Commission, to ensure that any possible risks are detected and managed as early as possible. This includes a comprehensive analysis of the benefit-risk balance taking into account new or emerging safety information. These regular reviews include use in children and adolescents. On that basis, the Commission regularly updates the product information of medicines. Where a specific safety concern needs to be investigated further, the marketing authorisation holder may also be required to conduct a post-authorisation safety study (PASS) (1) to identify, characterise or quantify the concern, the results of which are assessed by the Pharmacovigilance Risk Assessment Committee (PRAC) (2) and can lead to regulatory action. Moreover, if new safety concerns emerge, a referral procedure (3) may be started and a scientific assessment by the European Medicines Agency can be requested. Mental health is a priority for the Commission. In 2023, it presented its comprehensive approach to mental healt h (4) to support Member States and stakeholders in the prevention and management of mental health problems, including among young people. The Commission is currently implementing this initiative.

Post-authorisation safety studies (PASS): https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/human-regulatory-overview/post-authorisation/pharmacovigilance-postauthorisation/post-authorisation-safety-studies-pass. E-10-2026-001942.t: Irish authorities’ non-recognition of EU technical certificates for MMC cladding products
qt: to the Commission Ciaran Mullooly (Renew) Subject:

It has been brought to my attention that the Department of Housing and building control authorities in Ireland are refusing to recognise or accept technical certificates for modern methods of construction (MMC) products (specifically cladding) issued by Kiwa, an inspection and certification company accredited in other EU Member States. Despite the products holding valid certification demonstrating compliance with safety and performance standards equivalent to those required by the National Standards Authority of Ireland (NSAI), developers are being forced to undergo redundant, costly and time-consuming national recertification. 1.

Is the Commission aware that local building control authorities in Ireland are effectively disregarding certificates from accredited EU notified bodies, thereby creating a de facto technical barrier to trade?
Does the Commission consider the systematic refusal to accept equivalent certifications from other Member States a violation of Regulation (EU) 2019/515 on the mutual recognition of goods1?
What steps will the Commission take to ensure that Irish authorities comply with the single market rules to prevent the delay of innovative, sustainable MMC products?
OJ L 91, 29.3.2019, p. 1, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2019/515/oj.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.7.2026) The Commission is not aware of any practice of Irish building control authorities of not taking into account certificates issued by notified bodies in other EU Member States. To assess whether there are grounds for an investigation, the Commission would need more information about the products in question. Under Regulation (EU) 3110/20241, if a product is covered by a harmonised technical specification, it must be CE-marked and Member States are required to allow it onto their markets. If a product is not covered by either a harmonised specification or a European technical assessment (ETA), the placing of the product on the market is governed by national frameworks and the principle of mutual recognition. In the case of non-harmonised or partially harmonised products, Regulation (EU) 2019/515 on mutual recognition2 requires the competent authorities of the Member State of destination to take account of test reports and certificates issued by conformity assessment bodies. Competent authorities may not refuse such reports or certificates on grounds related to the competence of the body where it is accredited in accordance with Regulation (EC) No 765/20083 for the relevant assessment activity. The Commission is not aware of instances where Irish authorities systematically fail to give consideration to certificates issued by accredited bodies in other Member States. With the Construction Product Regulation (CPR) Acquis process, the Commission aims to update, by 2033, all harmonised standards developed over the last 25 years and to extend coverage to all relevant product families4. Further details about the process are laid down in the (First) CPR Working Plan for 2026-20295.

E-10-2026-001941.t: Second cyberattack on the European Commission in a single year – the credibility of EU cyber policy
qt: to the Commission Barbara Bonte (PfE) Subject:

On 24 March 2026, the Commission detected a cyberattack on the cloud infrastructure of the Europa.eu platform. According to CERT-EU, approximately 92 GB of data was stolen, including personal data and email content. In addition, data from at least 29 other EU entities may have been concerned. The attack was carried out via a compromised version of the opensource tool Trivy. This was already the second attack on the Commission in 2026, following an earlier hack in February on the Mobile Device Management platform. These incidents are occurring whilst the Commission itself has proposed a new cybersecurity package and is requiring thousands of public authorities and businesses to comply with the NIS2 Directive and the EU Cybersecurity Regulation. 1.
How does the Commission assess the credibility of its own cybersecurity regulations, in the light of the fact that the institution has been compromised twice in the space of a few months?
What lessons is the Commission drawing from the fact that the attack occurred via a compromised open-source tool in the supply chain?
Who within the Commission bears political and operational responsibility for this, and will the internal review be made public?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.7.2026) In the present geopolitical context, the Commission is a high-profile target for cyberattacks. Their scenarios are increasingly complex and deceptive, as threat actors use more advanced techniques, including artificial intelligence. This trend is demonstrated by the two recent significant incidents. Neither of them caused any major disruption to the Commission’s IT systems, proving that cybersecurity measures put in place by the Commission in line with Regulation 2023/28411 – and continuously improved in cooperation with CERT-EU2 – are effective in detecting and containing the attack attempts swiftly, and in reducing their impact. A thorough investigation of the personal data breach dimension of both incidents was conducted, in full respect of the regulatory obligations. The incident involving the cloud infrastructure of the europa.eu platform points to a major and growing risk of software supply-chain attacks. The Commission is reinforcing the measures aiming at verification of software origin and authenticity, tighter controls on third-party and open-source components, continuous monitoring, and defence-in-depth to limit the propagation of attacks. Lessons learned from all incidents are systematically used to improve the Commission’s internal operational protocols. Besides, the Commission proposed a new framework to strengthen the security of information and communications technologies supply chains in the revised Cybersecurity Act 23. The roles and responsibilities in cybersecurity in the Commission are defined in the internal cybersecurity risk-management, governance and control framework4, in full compliance with the provisions of Regulation 2023/2841, in particular with regards to reporting obligations.
1 Regulation (EU, Euratom) 2023/2841 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 December 2023

laying down measures for a high common level of cybersecurity at the institutions, bodies, offices and agencies of the Union, OJ L, 2023/2841, 18.12.2023. 2 The Cybersecurity Service for the Union institutions, bodies, offices and agencies. 3 Proposal for a Regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council on the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA), the European cybersecurity certification framework, and ICT supply chain security and repealing Regulation (EU) 2019/881 (The Cybersecurity Act 2), COM/2026/11 final. 4 Commission Decision (EU, Euratom) 2017/46 of 10 January 2017 on the security of communication and information systems in the European Commission, C/2016/8998.

E-10-2026-001940.t: Pakistan’s GSP+ status and the arbitrary detention of human rights activist Idris Khattak
qt: to the Commission Barbara Bonte (PfE) Subject:

Since 2014, Pakistan has enjoyed privileged market access under the GSP+ scheme. Pakistan is one of the largest beneficiaries under the scheme. However, recent reports point to ongoing violations of GSP+ obligations. The case of Idris Khattak starkly illustrates how Pakistan is flouting these obligations. Khattak is a renowned human rights activist specialising in enforced disappearances, but he himself disappeared in 2019. In June 2020, the Pakistani authorities acknowledged his detention. The UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention has concluded in a recent opinion that his detention is contrary to international law, that his right to a fair trial has been repeatedly violated, and that he is being held because of his work as a human rights defender. 1.
Is the Commission aware of this case and of the recent opinion of the UN Working Group?
Does the Commission share the view that the unlawful detention of Idris Khattak in appalling conditions constitutes a breach of the conditions attached to GSP+ status?

Is the Commission considering initiating a formal investigation procedure that could lead to the temporary suspension of Pakistan from the GSP+ scheme in accordance with Article 19 of Regulation (EU) No 978/2012?
at: (English version) to the Commission Barbara Bonte (PfE) (11 May 2026) Subject: Pakistan’s GSP+ status and the arbitrary detention of human rights activist Idris Khattak Since 2014, Pakistan has enjoyed privileged market access under the GSP+ scheme. Pakistan is one of the largest beneficiaries under the scheme. However, recent reports point to ongoing violations of GSP+ obligations. The case of Idris Khattak starkly illustrates how Pakistan is flouting these obligations. Khattak is a renowned human rights activist specialising in enforced disappearances, but he himself disappeared in 2019. In June 2020, the Pakistani authorities acknowledged his detention. The UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention has concluded in a recent opinion that his detention is contrary to international law, that his right to a fair trial has been repeatedly violated, and that he is being held because of his work as a human rights defender. 1.
Is the Commission aware of this case and of the recent opinion of the UN Working Group?

2. Does the Commission share the view that the unlawful detention of Idris Khattak in appalling conditions constitutes a breach of the conditions attached to GSP+ status? 3. Is the Commission considering initiating a formal investigation procedure that could lead to the temporary suspension of Pakistan from the GSP+ scheme in accordance with Article 19 of Regulation (EU) No 978/2012? (22 July 2026) The High Representative/Vice-President of the EU acknowledges the significance of the concerns raised regarding this case. The EU delegation to Pakistan has been closely monitoring the case. The EU has consistently emphasised the importance of humane treatment, due process, fair trial guarantees and respect for fundamental freedoms in all its dialogues with Pakistan. The EU has taken note of concerns expressed by international human rights actors, including UN Special Rapporteurs, remains attentive to developments and will consider appropriate steps, as necessary, in line with available information. Moreover, this case has been raised by the EU during the eight Strategic Dialogue with Pakistan with Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister of Pakistan Ishaq Dar. In cooperation with international partners, the Delegation will continue to follow this case with attention through diplomatic channels. Broader engagement on human rights, including under the Generalised Scheme of Preferences Plus (GSP+) framework (1), remains an important tenet of the bilateral relationship. As for any GSP+ beneficiary, Pakistan is subject to continuous monitoring of its implementation of 27 international conventions listed in the GSP Regulation (2), including the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. The EU conducted a GSP+ monitoring mission in Pakistan in late 2025. A GSP monitoring report will be issued to the European Parliament and the Council by summer 2026. This will include the EU evaluation, incorporating also findings from UN bodies, civil society, and organisations such as Amnesty International, and will inform the EU’s decision on Pakistan’s future GSP+ status, including in the context of Pakistan’s possible reapplication for GSP+ under the new GSP Regulation, if it wishes to continue benefitting from the scheme.

E-10-2026-001939.t: Shipment of salmonella-contaminated chicken from Brazil
qt: to the Commission Jessika van Leeuwen (ECR), Sander Smit (ECR), Céline Imart (PPE) Subject:

A shipment of Brazilian frozen chicken (3 tonnes) imported into Greece under the trade agreement between the EU and Mercosur – which recently entered into force – was found to be 80 % contaminated with salmonella. The consignment was immediately returned to Brazil. It had previously been pointed out in both the Committee on Environment, Public Health and Food Safety (ENVI) and the Committee on International Trade (INTA) that controls in Brazil are inadequate. The Commission had promised that controls would be tightened up under the trade agreement with Mercosur. 1.
Is the Commission aware of this specific case of salmonella contamination, and how does it explain that such a high contamination rate was possible despite the alleged ‘tighter controls’?

How can the Commission guarantee that Brazilian poultry products comply with strict EU standards, given that Brazil itself acknowledges that it cannot fully guarantee its own control system and that problems with salmonella in Brazilian meat have been reported in the EU for years?

What concrete measures is the Commission taking to prevent such contamination from Mercosur countries reaching the European market and thereby further undermining the confidence of European consumers and the competitive position of European farmers and poultry farmers?

The consignment was immediately returned to Brazil. The Commission had promised that controls would be tightened up under the trade agreement with Mercosur. 1. Is the Commission aware of this specific case of salmonella contamination, and how does it explain that such a high contamination rate was possible despite the alleged ‘tighter controls’? 2. How can the Commission guarantee that Brazilian poultry products comply with strict EU standards, given that Brazil itself acknowledges that it cannot fully guarantee its own control system and that problems with salmonella in Brazilian meat have been reported in the EU for years? 3. What concrete measures is the Commission taking to prevent such contamination from Mercosur countries reaching the European market and thereby further undermining the confidence of European consumers and the competitive position of European farmers and poultry farmers? (22 July 2026) Imported poultry meat must comply with the microbiological criteria for foodstuffs laid down in Regulation (EU) 2073/2005. The authorities in the EU Member States carry out controls at border on imported products. If they detect levels that go beyond those as laid down in that regulation, they are obliged to notify the Commission and the other Member States via the Rapid Alert System for Food and Feed (RASFF system). In 2026, there have been no notifications made by Greece to the RASFF system regarding salmonella contamination in imports of Brazilian poultry meat or products thereof. The EU import control system operates at several levels. It includes audits in third countries to verify that these countries have control systems in place which ensure that consignments of goods exported to the EU comply with the relevant EU requirements or with requirements equivalent thereto. It also provides for mandatory controls at EU border control posts, including risk-based physical checks (which may include laboratory checks), to detect non-compliances upon entry. In addition, Member States must carry out risk-based controls at any stage of production, processing and distribution, including for imported products. Where specific risks are identified, additional measures are adopted, such as intensified official control s (1), or increased frequencies of physical checks for goods from specific third countries (2). Where necessary, the Commission may adopt stricter measures such as restrictions of imports (3).

E-10-2026-001937.t: Increase in irregular crossings in the Western Mediterranean: what measures will be taken against smugglers and migratory pressure?
qt: to the Commission Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE), Fabrice Leggeri (PfE) Subject:

According to Frontex, illegal crossings detected at the EU’s external borders decreased by around 40% in the first quarter of 2026. However, this overall decrease should not hide a worrying development: the Western Mediterranean route is the only major migratory route to record an increase, with around 4 400 crossings detected over the same period, a rise of 66% year-on-year1. This route directly concerns the security of Southern Europe and, in turn, the security of the entire Schengen area. It shows how smuggling networks are quickly able to adapt to the controls and shift flows to points of vulnerability. Can the Commission say: 1.
what additional operational measures will be taken with Frontex to strengthen surveillance in the Western Mediterranean?
whether European resources will be mobilised specifically to combat the networks of smugglers active on this route?

whether it will propose making aid, visas and cooperation agreements with countries of origin and transit more strictly conditional on verifiable results in terms of both preventing departures and readmission?

E-10-2026-001936.t: Improving security at the EU’s southern border in the face of criminal networks
qt: to the Commission Dolors Montserrat (PPE), Juan Ignacio Zoido Álvarez (PPE), Javier Zarzalejos (PPE) Subject:

Another two new Guardia Civil officers have died on duty while pursuing a drug trafficking speedboat in Huelva, at a time of a concerning increase in criminal networks in the Atlantic and the Mediterranean. In recent years, the Guardia Civil and the National Police have warned of the material disadvantage their agents face in combating drug trafficking. Parliament’s PETI Committee adopted a report in November 2025 calling on the Spanish Government to protect agents fighting drug trafficking by providing more resources, legal protection and tougher penalties for criminal organisations. In view of the above: Has the Spanish Government informed the Commission of any progress in strengthening operational capacities, resources at sea or legal protection for law enforcement agencies tackling drug trafficking since Parliament’s report was adopted?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.7.2026) The fight against drug trafficking is a priority of the Commission1. The Commission is working with Member States to effectively implement the EU Drugs Strategy2 and the EU Action Plan to fight drug trafficking in line with the European Council conclusions of 16 June 20263. The EU Action Plan to fight drug trafficking aims to address the misuse of high-speed vessels and foster innovative technologies to detect drugs trafficking in high-risk areas and transport hubs. Maintaining law and order and safeguarding internal security are the responsibility of Member States, in line with Article 72 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union. Under EMPACT 2026–20294, drug trafficking remains a core EU priority. Spain leads the operational action plan on cannabis, cocaine and heroin trafficking and is a Member of the Maritime Analysis and Operations Centre – Narcotics5 funded by the Internal Security Fund. This framework supports coordination, maritime intelligence, port cooperation and action against criminal networks using Atlantic and Mediterranean routes, including the threat of gofast vessels and infiltration of organised crime in ports.

E-10-2026-001935.t: Limiting daily subsistence allowances for people in post-retirement employment and upholding the EU principle of non-discrimination
qt: to the Commission Anthony Smith (The Left) Subject:

Under French law, people in post-retirement employment who are on sick leave are entitled to a maximum of 60 days’ subsistence allowance over their entire working life. However, these employees continue to make contributions at the same rate as other workers, who are entitled to compensation of up to 365 days, renewable annually. This arrangement, which was introduced under the Social Security Financing Act for 2020, affects hundreds of thousands of people in France. It has led to the introduction of a separate compensation scheme for a category of workers defined primarily by their age and retirement status, even though they are working under the same conditions as other employees. Article 21 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union prohibits any discrimination, including on the basis of age. In view of this: 1.
Does the Commission consider this arrangement to be compatible with the EU principle of non‑discrimination on the basis of age?

Does it take the view that, by continuing to apply this specific limitation to people in post-retirement employment, the French Government could be in breach of EU law? Does it intend to engage in dialogue with the French authorities on this matter?

(9 September 2026) Council Employment Equality Directive 2000/78/EC (1) prohibits discrimination based on age in employment and occupation. However, this directive does not apply to payments of any kind made by state schemes or similar, including state social security or social protection schemes. Accordingly, the situation described in the Honourable Member’s question appears to fall outside the scope of the directive. Moreover, the Court of Justice of the European Union clarified that the scope of the directive may not be extended beyond the listed grounds (2). As the differential treatment raised by the Honourable Member focuses on retirement status rather than age, this would not constitute direct discrimination based on age. As regards indirect discrimination based on age, under the directive, Member States may provide that differences of treatment based on age shall not constitute discrimination, if, within the context of national law, they are objectively and reasonably justified by a legitimate aim (including legitimate employment policy, labour market and vocational training objectives), and if the means of achieving that aim are appropriate and necessary. The Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union applies to Member States only when implementing EU law (3), which does not appear to be the case here. The Commission considers that the Employment Equality Directive has been correctly transposed in French national legislation. The Commission monitors the implementation of the directive, and published a report on its application in July 2026 (4).

E-10-2026-001934.t: Towards an EU framework for minimum mirror measures to ensure fair competition
qt: to the Commission Yvan Verougstraete (Renew) Subject:

European producers are subject to particularly strict environmental, health and social standards. Despite this, however, the EU continues to import products made using methods that do not comply with those standards, distorting competition and fuelling a race to the bottom. In a number of sectors, instruments are already in place or under development, for example with regard to imported deforestation and importer accountability. However, these approaches remain fragmented and mainly focus on the characteristics of the end product. In view of this: 1.

Does the Commission plan to bring in a horizontal framework for ‘minimum mirror measures’ that make access to the EU market conditional on compliance with production standards that are equivalent to those applicable in the EU and go beyond criteria that can be measured solely on the basis of the end product?

Does it intend, particularly with regard to the agricultural sector, to systematically introduce production method requirements, including those concerning the use of substances that are banned in the EU, animal welfare, traceability or deforestation?
Is it exploring the possibility of eventually widening the scope of CE marking to include requirements that are linked to production conditions, in addition to product compliance?

(2 July 2026) The Commission’s 2022 report on the application of EU health and environmental standards to imported agri-food product s (1) concluded that, in specific cases and pursuant to a case-by-case assessment, the EU may require imported products to meet certain production standards, in accordance with the EU’s international obligations. The same principles apply to the agricultural sector. The EU already ensures a high level of consumer health protection by requiring all food placed on the EU market to comply with its health and safety standards. In some areas, the EU went even further, by introducing production and processing method requirements applicable to imports, such as those relative to antimicrobials, maximum residue levels for pesticides harmful to bee s (2), and rules on animal welfare (for example, stunning and slaughter). The Commission’s Vision for Agriculture and Food (3) aims, among others, to better align EU and imported products’ standards, especially on pesticides and animal welfare, while respecting international rules and relying on impact assessments. The Commission has proposed and is currently assessing the possibility of introducing new measures on pesticides and animal welfare in a manner consistent with the EU’s international obligations. As regards the question on the possible extension of CE (4) marking to cover to production conditions, it is important to stress that CE marking is the manufacturer’s self-declaration under EU product legislation and should not be considered a guarantee of compliance.

E-10-2026-001933.t: Competition for the same resources between complementary policies in the future MFF
qt: to the Commission Daniel Buda (PPE), Dan-Ştefan Motreanu (PPE) Subject:

The abolition of the 2-pillar structure of the CAP has erased the complementarity and synergies between Pillar 2 and the rural development fund facet of cohesion policy. The EAFRD and the ERDF had separate objectives, and their merger into a single mega-fund in the future programming period will lead to competition for the same resources under the national and regional partnership plans, both between the two funds and between them and other programmes. Without substantial investment in rural areas, these will remain insufficiently attractive to tempt young people or convince them to stay and hence foster generational renewal, placing a question mark over long-term food security. The EUR 47.8 billion proposed as a minimum rural target by the Commission is insufficient if Member States’ ambition remains limited. Moreover, there is a total overlap between the rural target and the target of EUR 218 billion for less-developed regions. 1.

How will the Commission ensure that rural areas receive sufficient funding to guarantee their development and generational renewal, hence reversing demographic decline and eliminating talent development traps?
Has the Commission conducted a study into the impact on rural areas of the dismantling of the EAFRD and the ERDF?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.7.2026) The proposal putting forward a single National and Regional Partnership Plan (NRPP)1 for each Member State (and an additional Interreg Plan) aims to address the current fragmented implementation of resources with a single rulebook approach, thus enhancing synergies between policies, increasing flexibility in resource allocation and use, as well as simplifying access to funding for beneficiaries. The impact assessment2 accompanying the Commission proposal for the NRPPs identified that combining the common agricultural policy, cohesion policy and other EU Funds in a single plan allowed Member States to provide the most effective and comprehensive support to rural areas, provided that appropriate strategies for rural areas are in place. Fostering attractiveness of territories and improving living standards in rural areas feature explicitly in the objectives of the future NRPPs. A rural spending target of 10% of each Member State’s envelope outside ringfenced amounts for the Common Agricultural Policy and the Common Fisheries Policy has been proposed to ensure continuity of investments in the development of rural territories. Member States and regions are expected to build a consistent agenda of measures on the basis of the reference framework set out in Article 22 of the proposal addressing rural areas’ specific needs and challenges and concentrate resources to foster diverse and resilient rural economies and support generational renewal, contributing to the right to stay. The rural spending target should be seen as a tool to ensure a comprehensive approach to address the needs and opportunities of rural areas, including outside less developed regions.

E-10-2026-001932.t: Ensuring a genuine transition period prior to the withdrawal of essential active substances
qt: to the Commission Daniel Buda (PPE) Subject:

The withdrawal of active substances used in agriculture is often portrayed as part of a necessary process of adapting to meet environmental and public health objectives. However, in many cases, farmers are seeing the essential tools they use to protect their crops being removed before any viable, affordable and effective alternatives are widely available. This approach is creating real production difficulties and has exposed farms to significant economic risk. A credible transition cannot be built around premature bans followed by belated solutions. At a time when farmers are being required to produce more sustainably, the Union must ensure they have the necessary technical means to do this in practice, not just theoretically. Without a solid adaptation period, the competitiveness of European agriculture will be affected, with the burden of that adaptation falling disproportionately on producers. Can the Commission state whether it will introduce a binding principle making the withdrawal of essential active substances conditional on there being viable alternatives whose worth has been proven in practice and which farmers in all Member States can afford?

(9 July 2026) In the Vision for Agriculture and Food (1), in response to farmers’ concerns about their ability to ensure production and food security, the Commission announced that it will carefully consider any further ban of pesticides if alternatives are not yet available (2). In that regard, as part of the Food and Feed Safety Simplification Package (3) adopted in December 2025, the Commission has proposed to modify Article 4(7) of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 (4) to clarify its applicability to allow active substances that do not fulfil certain approval criteria to be approved for a period of five years when they are needed to control a serious danger to plant health or plant production, when no equally effective and affordable alternatives are available (chemical or nonchemical). The derogation will not be available for active substances with the most severe hazards for health and the environment and approval of active substances under the derogation must be subject to risk mitigation measures to ensure that exposure of humans and the environment is minimised. The Commission’s proposal also includes the possibility for Member States to grant longer grace periods for the distribution and use of plant protection products (PPPs) containing active substances the approval of which could not be renewed (of up to three years). This would give farmers additional time to find alternative solutions and additional time for Member States to authorise alternative PPPs.

E-10-2026-001930.t: Extension of promotion tools to the benefit of European agri-food products from vulnerable regions
qt: to the Commission Daniel Buda (PPE) Subject:

In an increasingly competitive market under pressure from cheap imports, European agri-food products must not only maintain high standards but also enjoy effective mechanisms which ensure their visibility and differentiation. In the case of vulnerable agricultural regions, the promotion of products on the internal and external market can serve as a genuine means of economic consolidation and support for local added value. The EU’s promotion programme received substantial funding for 2026, but actually accessing that funding remains a problem for many producers and organisations in peripheral areas or ones less well represented at an institutional level. Without a more inclusive approach, there is a risk that the funding available will always go to those who are already in a strong position. Can the Commission state whether it will simplify and extend access to EU promotion programmes for agri-food products from vulnerable regions, including through dedicated criteria, enhanced technical assistance and better representation of small and medium-sized producers?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (19.6.2026) The Commission acknowledges the importance of simplifying and ensuring access to EU funding for promotion programmes for agri-food products from vulnerable regions. The Commission has undertaken several initiatives to this end, such as publishing improved guidelines and frequently asked questions, and strengthening outreach, in particular by organising live-streamed info days in Brussels and encouraging similar initiatives in Member States. The amendment to the relevant Delegated Act1 in 2024 removed the representativeness requirement through membership for agri-food sector bodies. The Commission is considering other changes soon that will further improve support for applicants. These efforts aim to reduce the potential applicants’ concerns about burden and encourage participation from all Member States, including those that have historically been underrepresented. The Commission is also considering measures to strengthen applicants’ ability in these Member States to design and deliver high-quality proposals, including technical support to improve understanding of relevant Union rules for programme development and implementation. Additionally, the Commission recognises the need for better representation of small and medium-sized producers and is exploring ways to improve their access to promotion funding. These measures align with the EU's objectives of enhancing the competitiveness of the agricultural sector and supporting the economic development of vulnerable regions.

E-10-2026-001928.t: Fresh Turkish provocation in the Aegean and the Eastern Mediterranean
qt: to the Commission Elissavet Vozemberg-Vrionidi (PPE) Subject:

Athens has been following the developments of recent days in Türkiye with particular concern, as Ankara has announced that it will submit a bill on the ‘Blue Homeland’. According to Turkish media, Türkiye is preparing a new law that attempts to legitimise its maritime jurisdiction claims in the Aegean and Eastern Mediterranean, ignoring Greek sovereign rights. Specifically, the new legislation will give the Turkish fleet and coastguard rights to intervene and act even in areas that have not been declared as being within the EEZ. In addition, the Turkish President will have the power to unilaterally attribute a special status to a maritime area. In view of the above and taking into account the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea and the basic principles of the International Law of the Sea, can the Commission say: 1.
What is its legal assessment of Türkiye’s actions, which aim to create faits accomplish in the Aegean and Eastern Mediterranean?
How does it intend to pressure Türkiye into finally respecting the sovereign rights of EU Member States, which it deliberately and systematically violates?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.7.2026) The Commission is closely following media reports and statements referring to preparations to submit draft legislation on maritime jurisdiction areas to the Turkish Grand National Assembly. The content of this legislation has not been made public. The Commission does not comment on media reports. The EU has repeatedly made clear that Türkiye is expected to make an unequivocal commitment to good neighbourly relations, international agreements and the peaceful settlement of disputes. The EU remains committed to defending its interests and those of its Member States as well as to upholding regional stability. In this context, the EU attaches the greatest importance to safeguarding the sovereign rights of all Member States, in full respect of international law including the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea. Abstaining from unilateral actions that violate international law and the sovereign rights of Member States is essential to ensure a stable and secure environment in the Eastern Mediterranean. It is also essential for developing a cooperative and mutually beneficial relationship between the EU and Türkiye. The High Representative/Vice-President raised these issues during her visit to Ankara on 30 June 2026, in the meetings both with the President of the Republic of Türkiye and the Foreign Minister. In the joint press release issued after the visit, it is highlighted that both EU and Türkiye agreed on the importance of regional stability and good neighbourly relations1.

E-10-2026-001925.t: Adequacy and effectiveness of monitoring horsepower (kW) and tonnage (GT) under Regulation (EU) No 1380/2013
qt: to the Commission Konstantinos Arvanitis (The Left) Subject:
Adequacy and effectiveness of monitoring horsepower (kW) and tonnage (GT) under Regulation (EU) No 1380/2013

Regulation (EU) No 1380/2013 establishes the framework for the Common Fisheries Policy (CFP) with the aim of sustainable exploitation of marine biological resources. In this context, the monitoring of fishing capacity continues to be implemented through the indicators of horsepower (kW) and gross tonnage (GT). In light of developments in the fisheries sector, technical issues have arisen regarding the application of these indicators. Technological progress in fishing vessels has increased fishing efficiency without a corresponding change in recorded GT and kW. At the same time, there are differences in the practices of recording and certifying engine power between Member States, which affects the comparability of data. Furthermore, the implementation of the relevant provisions varies at national level. Finally, the GT and kW indicators are not directly linked to biological indicators of fish stock management, such as maximum sustainable yield (MSY), but function mainly as administrative tools for fleet control. The Commission is asked: 1.

How does it assess the suitability of the existing GT and kW indicators as tools for monitoring fishing capacity in light of technological developments, and is the use of complementary fishing effort indicators for monitoring fishing capacity being considered?
What measures ensure they are applied uniformly across the EU?
Is there provision for updating the methodologies for measuring and certifying fishing capacity?

(22 July 2026) A recent study on the EU fishing fleet assesses its evolution and current and future challenges, including possible alternative approaches to measuring fishing capacity (1). It highlights challenges linked to the energy transition, safety and welfare, and examines how potential changes to gross tonnage (GT) and engine power (kW) could affect fishing capacity, with a view to better balancing fleet capacity with available fishing opportunities while supporting economic, social and environmental sustainability. The study fed into the evaluation of the Common Fisheries Policy (CFP) Regulation (2). Article 4(1)(24) of the CFP Regulation (3) defines fishing capacity and parameters for fleet capacity management. Member States submit annual reports on the balance between the fishing capacity of their fleets and their fishing opportunities under Article 22 of the CFP Regulation. These are assessed by the Scientific, Technical and Economic Committee for Fisheries (STECF). Member States must comply with capacity ceilings and ensure checks on GT and kW. The Commission has issued technical guidance to support harmonised monitoring and control of engine power. The Fisheries Control Regulation, as amended by Regulation (EU) 2023/2842 (4), empowers the Commission to adopt implementing acts on certification and verification of engine power, including continuous monitoring systems, contributing to improving uniform application. These rules shall be applicable from 10 January 2028. GT and kW measurement methodologies are well established by Regulation (EU) 2017/113 0 (5), and based on accepted technical standards.

https://cinea.ec.europa.eu/document/download/a4685a4b-359c-472e-bc8f-ea2035470a37_en?filename=european%20unions%20fishing%20fleetHZ0126066ENN%20%281%29.pdf. https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_26_938. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2013/1380/oj/eng. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2023/2842/oj/eng. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2017/1130/oj/eng.
There is no evidence to underpin a clear and specific need, nor are there viable alternative standards to support an update of these methodologies.

E-10-2026-001924.t: Commission plans for the second EU Voluntary Review on the implementation of the SDGs
qt: to the Commission Sakis Arnaoutoglou (S&D) Subject:

The EU presented its first Voluntary Review (VR) on the implementation of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) at the 2023 High-level Political Forum on Sustainable Development (HLPF), marking an important step for transparency, accountability and the EU’s commitment to the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. In its conclusions of 27 November 2023, the Council invited the Commission to present a new EU VR on a four‑yearly basis at minimum and by no later than the next SDG summit. It should be prepared using a timely, open, transparent and participatory process involving key stakeholders, the European Parliament and the Council, in line with UN guidance. In this context: 1.
Can the Commission confirm whether it intends to present a second EU VR and, if so, in which year it plans to submit it to the HLPF?
What steps has it taken, or does it plan to take, to organise the preparation of the review, including internal coordination and an indicative timetable for drafting and adoption?

How will it ensure the timely and meaningful participation of civil society, Parliament, the Council, the European Economic and Social Committee and the Committee of the Regions, and how will the findings be integrated into EU policymaking and monitoring frameworks?

(16 July 2026) The EU budget offers many funding opportunities for public and private undertakings in all regions across Europe, to deliver on defined priorities for a common democratic, peaceful, prosperous and competitive future. These EU funds are managed directly by the Commission, in partnership with Member States and/or national agencies depending on intervention areas and funding sources. Within this hybrid framework, the Commission does not centralise information in a way that allows to communicate the total amount of EU funding currently allocated to all beneficiaries in a precisely defined geographical zone, such as Dublin’s local authority areas. For instance, while the Cohesion open data platform (1) offers an overview on budget allocations and financial progress in implementing Cohesion policy funds in Ireland, for the programming period 2021-2027, it is the role of national managing authorities to publish on programmes’ websites more detailed information concerning operations (2). More broadly, the Commission publishes via the Financial Transparency System (3), information on beneficiaries of various funding types managed directly or indirectly, from 2014 to 2024. The tool enables recipients to be filtered by their registered city and postal code, which are assigned to a high-level regional category (Nomenclature of territorial units for statistics — NUTS 2 (4)), as well as by the beneficiary and benefiting country. E-10-2026-001918.t: Dangerous Turkish peppers on the European market
qt: to the Commission Emmanouil Fragkos (ECR) Subject:

A clear and recurring pattern of problems with Turkish pepper imports into the EU, due to excessive or banned pesticides, has been recorded in 2025–2026. In 2025, the RASFF system recorded 27 European alerts for Turkish peppers, of which eight concerned the substance formetanate, a toxic substance not accepted even in Türkiye. In 2026, the serious incidents continued: Bulgaria activated multiple alerts for peppers with abamectin and pirimiphos methyl, while in another case tebufenopyrad was detected at approximately 35 times above the EU limit, resulting in the classification of ‘serious risk’ and the import of the load being prohibited at the border. At the same time, Romania issued a warning about Turkish red kapya peppers due to excess cadmium. These substances are linked to neurotoxicity, cholinesterase inhibition, possible effects on child development, liver toxicity and, in the case of cadmium, long-term carcinogenic effects. Organisations such as PAN Europe and Greenpeace Türkiye are now speaking out about a systemic problem concerning the reliability of Turkish food exports. Unfortunately, the Greek authorities have not reported the detection of contaminated Turkish peppers over the past two years. At the same time, Greece exceeds the EU average in blood cancers, non-Hodgkin lymphomas, leukemia and myelodysplastic syndromes. In view of the above: 1.
Does the Commission consider the current framework for protecting consumers against imports of substances associated with serious haematological and neurotoxic effects to be adequate?
How does the Commission assess the adequacy of the checks carried out by the Greek authorities on imported Turkish fruit and vegetables with repeated RASFF notifications?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (9.7.2026) To ensure compliance with EU food safety requirements, the Member States must carry out risk based official controls and enforcement activities in line with Regulation (EU) 2017/6251. Where food of non-animal origin from third countries poses a risk, the Commission may adopt measures through Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/17932. The results of official controls of consignments of Turkish peppers entering Greece does not raise concerns as regards detection of non-complaint consignments. The Commission performs audits in Member States to verify in particular the application of the substantive rules and of the control rules. Ther Commission also performs audits in third countries to ensure that goods intended for export to the EU comply with the applicable EU rules and that the control system is capable of ensuring it3. An audit of the import control system in Greece is planned in late 2026 which will include the official controls on high-risk imported fruit and vegetables. General monitoring of residues in the EU coordinated multiannual control programme is based on an assessment of European Food Safety Authority which identified 36 products but does not single out Greece or banned substances exclusively. Member States tailor their riskbased sampling programmes. The Commission established a Task Force4 to make import controls more efficient, which will focus e.g. on pesticide residues and will consider coordinated EU action on specific imported products.

1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2017/625/oj. 2 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg_impl/2019/1793/oj. 3 https://food.ec.europa.eu/horizontal-topics/official-controls-and-enforcement/health-and-food-audits-and-
analysis_en. 4 https://food.ec.europa.eu/horizontal-topics/official-controls-and-enforcement/import-controls-food-and-feedqas_en.

E-10-2026-001917.t: Risk of EU overtaxing property and stepping up economic surveillance of citizens
qt: to the Commission Emmanouil Fragkos (ECR) Subject:

Many citizens, in particular the middle class and small and medium-sized entrepreneurs are deeply concerned by recent studies and Commission discussions on the taxation of net wealth, the increase of capital taxes, the interconnection of asset-related data and the use of mechanisms such as exit tax. Behind technocratic terms such as ‘tax justice’ and ‘fighting inequalities’, one gradually begins to discern a broader political direction aiming to strengthen economic control over citizens and centralise tax powers at European level. Greek citizens have already felt on their own skin the effects of overtaxation, the memoranda, property tax (ENFIA) and continuous pressure on ownership and family assets. Of particular concern is the potential creation of interconnected European asset monitoring mechanisms, which could further burden small-scale owners, family businesses and citizens seeking to transfer their tax residence or engage in investment activities. 1.
Does the Commission intend to promote new forms of property taxation or harmonisation of capital taxes at European level?
Is the creation of pan-European mechanisms for the interconnection and monitoring of citizens’ asset-related data being considered?
Does the Commission acknowledge that direct taxation is a national competence that lies exclusively with the Member States?
at: (English version) to the Commission Emmanouil Fragkos (ECR) (8 May 2026) Subject: Risk of EU overtaxing property and stepping up economic surveillance of citizens Many citizens, in particular the middle class and small and medium-sized entrepreneurs are deeply concerned by recent studies and Commission discussions on the taxation of net wealth, the increase of capital taxes, the interconnection of asset-related data and the use of mechanisms such as exit tax. Behind technocratic terms such as ‘tax justice’ and ‘fighting inequalities’, one gradually begins to discern a broader political direction aiming to strengthen economic control over citizens and centralise tax powers at European level. Greek citizens have already felt on their own skin the effects of overtaxation, the memoranda, property tax (ENFIA) and continuous pressure on ownership and family assets. Of particular concern is the potential creation of interconnected European asset monitoring mechanisms, which could further burden small-scale owners, family businesses and citizens seeking to transfer their tax residence or engage in investment activities. 1. Does the Commission intend to promote new forms of property taxation or harmonisation of capital taxes at European level? 2. Is the creation of pan-European mechanisms for the interconnection and monitoring of citizens’ asset-related data being considered? 3. Does the Commission acknowledge that direct taxation is a national competence that lies exclusively with the Member States? (17 July 2026) The Commission published a study on wealth taxation (1) offering an assessment of wealth-related taxes based on empirical evidence, comparative mapping and country case studies. Its findings confirm that there is no one-size-fits-all measure. As set out in the 2025 Affordable Housing Plan (2), the Commission will continue to work with the Member States, including within the European Semester, to support tax reforms that improve housing availability and affordability while efficiently raising tax revenue. The Commission published a study on the use of asset registers to combat tax evasion and money launderin g (3). While the interconnection of such registers is technically feasible, this would need to be assessed against EU law, including the principle of necessity. The directive on Administrative Cooperation (DAC) (4) in direct taxation is an efficient tool that already allows Member States to exchange cross-border information on non-resident owners of immovable property. The Commission currently has no plans to interconnect national asset registers. Instead, the Commission favours the use of the instrument of the DAC and the wider access for tax authorities to national registers, including immovable property registers. Under current EU law, direct taxation remains largely a Member State competence. Where no EU secondary legislation applies, Member States design their own tax systems autonomously, while complying with the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, including the principles of non-discrimination and proportionality.

E-10-2026-001916.t: Increased risks of digital surveillance through age verification and the DSA
qt: to the Commission Emmanouil Fragkos (ECR) Subject:

Recent statements by the Commissioner for Tech Sovereignty, Security and Democracy regarding age verification systems and the Digital Services Act (DSA) and the future integration of these mechanisms into the European Digital Identity Wallet are giving rise to growing concerns among many European citizens about the protection of anonymity and freedom of expression online. Although the Commission has not announced a ban on VPNs, public debates on preventing age verification systems from being bypassed by using VPNs or other technical means are creating the impression of a digital system gradually being built to control internet access. Many citizens fear that mechanisms initially presented as tools to protect minors may in future be used to limit anonymous expression, enhance online censorship and monitor online activity more widely. Meanwhile, cybersecurity experts have already highlighted serious technical weaknesses in relevant prototype age verification systems. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Is it considering measures to restrict or prevent the use of VPNs in the context of age verification systems or the DSA?
How is it ensured that these systems will not lead to the indirect removal of anonymous internet access?
Who is legally and financially accountable in the event of a mass leak of personal data from such digital identification infrastructure?
at: (English version) to the Commission Emmanouil Fragkos (ECR) (8 May 2026) Subject: Increased risks of digital surveillance through age verification and the DSA Recent statements by the Commissioner for Tech Sovereignty, Security and Democracy regarding age verification systems and the Digital Services Act (DSA) and the future integration of these mechanisms into the European Digital Identity Wallet are giving rise to growing concerns among many European citizens about the protection of anonymity and freedom of expression online. Although the Commission has not announced a ban on VPNs, public debates on preventing age verification systems from being bypassed by using VPNs or other technical means are creating the impression of a digital system gradually being built to control Internet access. Many citizens fear that mechanisms initially presented as tools to protect minors may in future be used to limit anonymous expression, enhance online censorship and monitor online activity more widely. Meanwhile, cybersecurity experts have already highlighted serious technical weaknesses in relevant prototype age verification systems. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Is it considering measures to restrict or prevent the use of VPNs in the context of age verification systems or the DSA?
How is it ensured that these systems will not lead to the indirect removal of anonymous Internet access?
Who is legally and financially accountable in the event of a mass leak of personal data from such digital identification infrastructure?

(1 July 2026) The Commission is not planning any measures to restrict the availability of virtual private networks (VPNs) in the EU. It is essential to find a balance between ensuring the privacy of users while also protecting minors online. Age verification measures remain valuable as barriers to easy or accidental access to age-restricted content by minors, even if VPNs could in certain circumstances make it possible to circumvent these age verification measures. The principle of online anonymity, as established in the e-Commerce Directive (1), remains unchanged under the Digital Services Act (2). The EU’s Age Verification Blueprint is privacy-preserving and has been developed in line with guidance from the European Data Protection Board (3). This device-based system does not store any personal data and only generates an anonymous attestation proving that the user is over a certain age threshold. It also uses zero-knowledge proofs, a cryptographic technology that can securely prove that the user has a valid age credential without revealing the credential itself or any other information. This significantly limits the risk of personal data being leaked. In the case of a data breach, the overall liability regime is governed in Article 13 of Regulation (EU) 910/2014 (4), while for identity systems it is Article 11 of Regulation (EU) 910/2014.

See Recital 14 of the e-Commerce Directive, ‘this directive cannot prevent the anonymous use of open networks such as the Internet’, https://eurlex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2000/31/oj/eng. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/2065/oj/eng. https://www.edpb.europa.eu/our-work-tools/our-documents/statements/statement-12025-age-assurance_en. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2014/910/oj/eng.

E-10-2026-001915.t: European framework for protecting firefighters from cancer
qt: to the Commission Emmanouil Fragkos (ECR) Subject:

The World Health Organization's International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) has classified the occupational exposure of firefighters as Group 1 carcinogenic to humans. According to scientific evidence and firefighters' associations, firefighters are systematically exposed to benzene, dioxins, PFAS, formaldehyde, heavy metals, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons and other toxic combustion products, often through long-term and cumulative exposure. This exposure has been associated with an increased risk of leukaemia, Hodgkin and nonHodgkin lymphomas, lung, kidney, bladder and mesothelioma cancers. In addition, several Member States have already recognised specific types of cancer as occupational diseases of firefighters or are considering relevant legislative initiatives. European trade unions are also calling for a strengthening of the EU framework for the prevention of and protection against occupational cancers. 1.
Does the Commission consider that current EU legislation on health and safety at work provides adequate protection for firefighters against cumulative exposure to carcinogens?
Will the Commission consider European guidelines on identifying occupational cancers in firefighters and monitoring their health long-term?
Will the Commission consider further restrictions on PFAS in fire-fighting foams and related equipment under the REACH Regulation?
at: (English version) to the Commission Emmanouil Fragkos (ECR) (8 May 2026) Subject: European framework for protecting firefighters from cancer The World Health Organisation's International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) has classified the occupational exposure of firefighters as Group 1 carcinogenic to humans. According to scientific evidence and firefighters' associations, firefighters are systematically exposed to benzene, dioxins, PFAS, formaldehyde, heavy metals, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons and other toxic combustion products, often through long-term and cumulative exposure. This exposure has been associated with an increased risk of leukaemia, Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphomas, lung, kidney, bladder and mesothelioma cancers. In addition, several Member States have already recognised specific types of cancer as occupational diseases of firefighters or are considering relevant legislative initiatives. European trade unions are also calling for a strengthening of the EU framework for the prevention of and protection against occupational cancers. 1. Does the Commission consider that current EU legislation on health and safety at work provides adequate protection for firefighters against cumulative exposure to carcinogens? 2. Will the Commission consider European guidelines on identifying occupational cancers in firefighters and monitoring their health long-term? 3. Will the Commission consider further restrictions on PFAS in fire-fighting foams and related equipment under the REACH Regulation? (6 July 2026) 1. The EU occupational safety and health (OSH) directives set minimum requirements for the adequate health and safety protection of all workers, including firefighters. Substances of particular concern to firefighters, such as benzene, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, formaldehyde, chromium VI and heavy metals, such as lead and mercury, are covered by the Carcinogens, Mutagens and Reprotoxic Substances Directive (1). This directive requires employers to assess all risks (2) to which workers are or might be exposed, including those arising from cumulative exposure to carcinogens, and to put in place adequate preventive and protective measures. 2. While there are no specific guidelines for firefighters, in May 2025, the European Chemicals Agency was mandated to produce guidelines for the assessment of the exposure to a combination of chemicals that have similar health effects (3). These will be particularly relevant for firefighters that are often subject to such exposure. Within 24 months, an interim report on methodologies/tools to drive an assessment will be developed and in the following 24 months practical guidelines will be drafted. 3. The Commission has adopted a restriction banning the use of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) in firefighting foams (4). The restriction will prevent around 470 tonnes of PFAS emissions every year and drastically reduce the exposure of firefighters to PFAS. Other uses of PFAS will be addressed in the context of the universal restriction proposal, which is currently being assessed by the European Chemicals Agency (5).

http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2004/37/oj. Article 3 paragraph 2. On the basis of Article 2(2), point (b) of Directive (EU) 2024/869, http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2024/869/oj. http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2025/1988/oj. E-10-2026-001914.t: Infringement complaint against France over the A69 motorway
qt: to the Commission Manon Aubry (The Left), Marie Toussaint (Verts/ALE), Emma Fourreau (The Left), Rima Hassan (The Left), Mounir Satouri (Verts/ALE), Mélissa Camara (Verts/ALE), Arash Saeidi (The Left), David Cormand (Verts/ALE), Damien Carême (The Left), Majdouline Sbai (Verts/ALE), Leila Chaibi (The Left) Subject:

On 16 April 2024, the Commission received a complaint from the law firm Huglo Lepage alleging an infringement by the French State and asking for the matter to be referred to the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU). This complaint alleges that France is systematically breaching several European directives by granting environmental permits for major projects that are incompatible with its obligations to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, without offsetting these emissions. The A69 motorway project, in particular, has been granted an environmental permit, and the complainants contest the procedure for assessing its impact on the climate. They also raise the issue of the Commission’s failure to respond to this complaint. In the meantime, the French Government has authorised several road projects, thus concreting over vast tracts of land and undermining efforts to combat climate change. Work on the A69 is not yet complete: a clear response from the Commission would send a strong message that the public has long been waiting for. Can the Commission therefore: 1.
provide a status update on the processing of this complaint and acknowledge receipt of it?
refer the matter to the CJEU?
take all necessary steps to compel Member States, and in particular France, to comply with the aforementioned legislation?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (17.7.2026) The complaint mentioned by the Honourable Members concerns France’s alleged breach of the Environmental Impact Assessment Directive1 through the failure of the French authorities and courts to take full account of the impacts of road projects on climate change. As regards the A69 motorway project, which is mentioned as an example in the complaint and which is referred to by the Honourable Members, the Commission recalls that it has been subject to several court cases and administrative proceedings in France and that the main court case is now pending before the Council of State (Conseil d’Etat), the French supreme administrative court. The complaint is being examined by the Commission services. The complainant has already received an acknowledgement of receipt and will be informed of the next steps. In its role as guardian of the Treaties, the Commission monitors the application of EU law and may decide to take appropriate action, in line with its enforcement priorities2.
1 Directive 2011/92/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 December 2011 on the assessment

of the effects of certain public and private projects on the environment, OJ L 26, 28.1.2012, p. 1-21. 2 Communication from the Commission - EU law: Better results through better application, OJ C 18, 19.1.2017, p. 10–20, and Communication from the Commission - Enforcing EU law for a Europe that delivers, 13.10.2022, COM(2022) 518 final.

E-10-2026-001913.t: Protecting older persons from abuse and neglect
qt: to the Commission Eleonora Meleti (PPE) Subject:

In recent years, several Member States have seen an increase in cases of abuse against older persons either in the form of physical, psychological or verbal violence or neglect by caregivers. This is a serious social problem the European Union is facing and one that is underreported and not highlighted enough. The demographic evolution in the European Union and the ever-increasing need for long-term care services make it necessary to enhance the quality of the services provided through the development of prevention, inspection and reporting systems, as well as to further strengthen the professionalism of the sector, provide ongoing training for carers and ensure safe and decent care conditions for older persons. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
What measures does it intend to take and how does it plan to support Member States in preventing and addressing the mistreatment of older persons in situations of dependency?

Is it considering establishing common European standards for the training, certification, supervision and assessment of carers looking after older people, to ensure the quality and safety of care provided?

Does it intend to promote the collection of comparable data from across the EU concerning cases of abuse of older persons and the quality of long-term care services, as part of the European Care Strategy?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (23.6.2026) The Commission supports Member States to prevent and address the mistreatment of older persons, in line with the European Care Strategy1 and the Council Recommendation on LongTerm Care2 (LTC). This encompasses technical support and EU funds, such as Cohesion funds or the Recovery and Resilience Facility, and mutual learning. In addition, the Commission, in cooperation with the World Health Organisation, supports Member States improve the quality of LTC services across all care settings through mutual learning and compiles data on LTC quality management. The Recommendation on LTC underscores the need for adequate training and working conditions for care professionals. To support this, the Commission has launched the LargeScale Skills Partnership for LTC to equip workers with digital and person-centred care skills. The European Social Fund plus helps reskill and upskill care workers and funds measures to help improve their working conditions. To underpin monitoring efforts, the Commission and the Social Protection Committee developed a Monitoring Framework, which establishes a core set of LTC indicators, including policy levers on LTC quality. The Commission will report to the Council on the implementation of the Recommendation on LTC and put forward a European Care Deal in 2027. In 2023, the Commission proposed a Regulation on the protection of adults in cross-border situations. The Regulation aims to safeguard adults who, due to a disability or health-related limitations, are not in a position to fully protect their own interests in cross-border situations and to ensure that their right to individual autonomy is maintained when they move or reside across Member States3.

Regulation is now being finalized.

E-10-2026-001912.t: The applicability of principles of European law to legal services excluded from the scope of Directive 2014/24/EU
qt: to the Commission Alberico Gambino (ECR) Subject:

Article 10 of Directive 2014/24/EU excludes certain legal services – including legal representation in judicial, arbitration or conciliation proceedings and legal advice closely related to such proceedings – from its scope. By means of Order No 3462 of 4 May 2026, the Italian Council of State (Section V) referred a number of questions for a preliminary ruling to the Court of Justice of the European Union concerning the compatibility with EU law of the Italian legislation governing the awarding of legal service contracts by public authorities. These referrals pertain to whether the legal services referred to in Article 10 should be subject to the principles of transparency, impartiality, non-discrimination and proportionality, as well as to any obligations related to the assignment of tender identification codes and the payment of contributions to ANAC, the National Anti-Corruption Authority. In the light of the above: 1.

What is the Commission’s understanding of the interplay between Article 10 and laws that subject the services covered by the Article to the principles of transparency, impartiality, non-discrimination and proportionality?

Does the Commission think that the applicability of additional national obligations – concerning, among other things, traceability, identifiers and contributions to supervisory authorities – should also be subject to the principle of proportionality and the specific nature of the legal representation and defence services in question?
Does the Commission agree that it should promote the drafting of interpretative guidelines that ensure the uniform and proportionate application of Directive 2014/24/EU?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (30.7.2026) The Commission acknowledges that a preliminary ruling request by a national court is pending and it can confirm that it will submit its written observations to the Court, which has the sole power to ensure the uniform interpretation of EU law across all Member States. The Commission ensures appropriate follow-up of those preliminary rulings where the Court establishes non-compliance of specific national rules under judicial scrutiny with EU law.

E-10-2026-001911.t: Destination and implementation of European Union funds in Nicaragua
qt: to the Commission Jorge Martín Frías (PfE) Subject:

In response to written question E-000104/2026/rev.11, the Commission stated that from January 2021 to January 2026, EUR 22.9 million had been disbursed as part of the European Union’s cooperation programme with Nicaragua2. However, the Commission did not specify the specific destination of these funds or their beneficiaries. 1.

What proportion of these funds has been channelled – whether directly or indirectly – through institutions, public bodies or entities controlled by the Nicaraguan regime, and what oversight and audit arrangements does the Commission apply to ensure that European funds are not used to strengthen structures linked to Daniel Ortega’s regime?
Has the Commission suspended, reviewed or reconsidered any cooperation programme with Nicaragua owing to the deterioration of the democratic situation and human rights in the country?
https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/E-10-2026-000104_EN.html. https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/E-10-2026-000104-ASW_EN.html.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (31.7.2026) EU cooperation in Nicaragua supports actions directly benefiting vulnerable populations, including women, farmers and cooperatives, local and indigenous communities. Sectors of intervention include adaptation to climate change, disaster risk reduction and support to sustainable practices in specific value chains, particularly cocoa and coffee. No EU funds are provided to the government of Nicaragua or as budgetary support to public institutions. EU funding in the country is entirely channelled through non-governmental implementing partners, including EU Member States’ agencies, international organisations and civil society organisations with a solid presence on the ground. All actions are subject to the Commission’s control and monitoring mechanisms, including regular project monitoring, independent audits, and close scrutiny of the eligibility of expenditure and the use of the funds, to ensure EU support directly benefits vulnerable populations. No project has been suspended. However, the strategy and the design of actions has been adjusted to the evolving political and operational context, with a view to maximising support to the communities most affected by poverty, exclusion and vulnerability.

E-10-2026-001910.t: EU funding Abu Dhabi’s royal family
qt: to the Commission Charlie Weimers (ECR), Beatrice Timgren (ECR), Dick Erixon (ECR) Subject:

Several news outlets have reported that subsidiaries controlled by the UAE’s Al Nahyan ruling family and the Emirati sovereign wealth fund, ADQ, received more than EUR 71 million in common agricultural policy (CAP) payments between 2019 and 2024 for farmland in Romania, Spain and Italy1. Agricost, in Romania, which operates the EU’s largest single farm, received EUR 10.5 million in 2024 alone. EU taxpayers finance the EU agriculture budget of EUR 386.6 billion for 2021-2027. In light of the above: 1.
Does the Commission consider it acceptable that CAP funds can benefit one of the world’s wealthiest non-EU ruling families through corporate structures?
Will it publish an EU-wide assessment of CAP payments for which the ultimate beneficial owners are non-EU state-linked entities, sovereign wealth funds or billionaires?
Will it urgently propose caps, ownership-transparency rules and recovery mechanisms to ensure that CAP money reaches EU farmers rather than foreign elites?
