(30 July 2026) 1. The Commission is of the opinion that support should go to genuine farmers whose principal activity is agriculture and has made proposals in this sense for the future Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) rules (see also below under 3). 2. Regulation (EU) 2021/2116 (1) requires that Member States ensure that CAP beneficiaries provide them with the information necessary for their identification. The related information is made public. Categorisation of CAP payments by ultimate beneficial owners is not required. For the 2027-2034 Multiannual Financial Framework, the Financial Regulation requires the collection of information on beneficial owners. The data will feed the information and monitoring system, and support risk assessment for selection, award, financial management, monitoring, investigation, control and audit. 3. According to the Commission’s proposed changes to the CAP (2), farms above a certain size threshold set by Member States would not be eligible for support if agriculture is not their principal activity. The Commission’s proposal also includes a mandatory requirement for Member States to differentiate degressive area-based income support to the benefit of those farmers who need it most. Finally, the total amount of degressive area-based income support would be capped at EUR 100 000 per year and apply to all holdings controlled by the natural or legal person, preventing circumvention of the cap. These provisions will help to mitigate the risk that income support will go to foreign entities whose principal business activity is not farming.

E-10-2026-001908.t: Export of alumina from a Member State entering the Russian military supply chain
qt: to the Commission Pina Picierno (S&D), Elisabetta Gualmini (Renew), Giorgio Gori (S&D), Karin Karlsbro (Renew), Engin Eroglu (Renew), Bruno Gonçalves (S&D), Lukas Sieper (Renew), Vytenis Povilas Andriukaitis (S&D), Ondřej Krutílek (ECR), Ľubica Karvašová (Renew), Sergey Lagodinsky (Verts/ALE), Veronika Cifrová Ostrihoňová (Renew), Rihards Kols (ECR), Sebastian Tynkkynen (ECR), Lucia Yar (Renew), Martin Hojsík (Renew), Reinier Van Lanschot (Verts/ALE), Michael Bloss (Verts/ALE), Heléne Fritzon (S&D) Subject:

An investigation by The Irish Times and Organised Crime and Corruption Reporting Project revealed that the Aughinish alumina refinery in Ireland, owned by the Russian group Rusal, exports growing quantities of alumina to Russian smelters in Siberia1. The material is processed into aluminium and sold to over 100 Russian defence companies, 40 of which are already sanctioned by the EU, that manufacture missiles, tanks and combat jets deployed in the war against Ukraine. The Irish Government has repeatedly lobbied both the US and the EU to keep Rusal exempt from sanctions, citing job protection. It is unacceptable that, while the EU funds Ukraine’s defence, a Russian-owned company operates undisturbed within a Member State, supplying the Kremlin’s military industry. Given the above, we ask the Commission: 1.
whether it will assess the inclusion of alumina among goods subject to export restrictions to Russia, given its documented use in the Russian military industry;
what measures it intends to take to ensure that exemptions from the sanctions regime do not structurally weaken the effectiveness of the EU’s restrictive policies towards Russia;

whether it considers a Member State systematically lobbying to exempt a Russianowned company operating on its territory from European sanctions to be compatible with the principle of sincere cooperation enshrined in Article 4 of the Treaty on European Union.
https://www.irishtimes.com/world/europe/2026/03/24/from-the-shannon-to-siberia-how-alumina-from-alimerick-refinery-enters-russias-weapons-supply-chain/.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (29.7.2026) Since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion, the EU has adopted an unprecedented set of sanctions designed to weaken Russia’s capacity to finance and sustain its aggression. These measures include far-reaching trade restrictions across key sectors alongside targeted individual measures against over 2 700 individuals and entities. In the metallurgical sector, restrictions on aluminium have been progressively tightened on both the export and import side. The Commission is aware of press reports and the calls, including from Members of the European Parliament, for an export ban on aluminium oxide (‘alumina’) to Russia. Potential measures targeting alumina exports need to take into account global market conditions, including supply diversification and potential impacts on EU operators active in international value chains and their EU customers. Alumina is being widely used in the production of many common goods (e.g. food cans), but it is also critical to the EU’s aeronautical and machinery sectors. Taking these various considerations into account, alumina is not subject to EU export restrictive measures. The Commission continues to assess the situation and is engaging with the Irish government. It is important to recall that any further sanctions would require unanimity among all Member States in the Council. The measures that the EU has in place today reflect a careful balance between its determination to undermine Russia’s illegal war against Ukraine as much as possible and to limit – to the extent possible – negative impacts on the Member States, industry and consumers.

E-10-2026-001907.t: Governance and composition of the European Skills High-Level Board under the Union of Skills
qt: to the Commission Nela Riehl (Verts/ALE) Subject:

The Union of Skills communication announced the establishment of the European Skills High-Level Board. Chaired by the Commission, the Board is tasked with providing crosssectoral guidance on skills policy, feeding directly into the European Semester and countryspecific recommendations. Given the Board’s significant advisory influence over EU-wide education, employment and competitiveness policy, transparency regarding its composition and formation is essential to uphold democratic accountability and the principle of participatory democracy enshrined in Article 11 of the Treaty on European Union (TEU). 1.

What criteria, selection procedures and transparency measures does the Commission apply or intend to apply when recruiting members to the Board, and how will it ensure a balanced representation of civil society, social partners, education institutions and the private sector?

How does the Commission intend to fulfil its obligations under Article 11 TEU – including open, transparent and regular dialogue with representative associations – regarding the Board’s ongoing operations, and will the Board’s meetings, agendas and outputs be made publicly accessible?

What accountability mechanisms will ensure that the Board’s recommendations are scrutinised by Parliament’s Committees on Culture and Education and on Employment and Social Affairs, and how will the Commission prevent sectoral or commercial interests from exerting undue influence over the shaping of EU skills and education policy?
at: (English version) to the Commission Nela Riehl (Verts/ALE) (8 May 2026) Subject: Governance and composition of the European Skills High-Level Board under the Union of Skills The Union of Skills communication announced the establishment of the European Skills High-Level Board. Chaired by the Commission, the Board is tasked with providing cross-sectoral guidance on skills policy, feeding directly into the European Semester and country-specific recommendations. Given the Board’s significant advisory influence over EU-wide education, employment and competitiveness policy, transparency regarding its composition and formation is essential to uphold democratic accountability and the principle of participatory democracy enshrined in Article 11 of the Treaty on European Union (TEU). 1. What criteria, selection procedures and transparency measures does the Commission apply or intend to apply when recruiting members to the Board, and how will it ensure a balanced representation of civil society, social partners, education institutions and the private sector? 2. How does the Commission intend to fulfil its obligations under Article 11 TEU — including open, transparent and regular dialogue with representative associations — regarding the Board’s ongoing operations, and will the Board’s meetings, agendas and outputs be made publicly accessible? 3. What accountability mechanisms will ensure that the Board’s recommendations are scrutinised by Parliament’s Committees on Culture and Education and on Employment and Social Affairs, and how will the Commission prevent sectoral or commercial interests from exerting undue influence over the shaping of EU skills and education policy? (8 July 2026) The Union of Skills Communication (1) defines the European Skills High Level Board’s composition, consisting of businesses, education and training providers and social partners. This composition ensures a broad perspective on workforce needs and skills gaps in the EU. Board members were appointed based on selection criteria aligned with the Board’s mandate (point 6 of the published terms of reference (2)): first hand experience and track record in the implementation of impactful, innovative and targeted human capital development strategies at organisational level and in strategic sectors or in the provision of education, training and up- and reskilling in line with evolving trends and needs of the labour market. An overview of the Board objectives, nature and members is publicly available (3). The Board’s meetings, agendas, minutes and conclusions will be published, in line with the highest transparency standards applicable to Commission expert groups. Board members are registered in the Transparency Register, clear rules apply as well as in relation to potential conflict of interests (point 12 of published rules of procedure). The Board provides independent non-binding advice to the Commission. The Commission uses multiple sources to ensure balanced representation of interests and an evidence-based approach. Within its competences, the Commission retains any ultimate decision when it comes to EU legislative proposals or policymaking in this area. The European Parliament retains its scrutiny powers as defined in the Treaties.

E-10-2026-001906.t: Ivermectin was and continues to be permitted for use in the treatment of COVID-19
qt: to the Commission Gerald Hauser (PfE) Subject:
Ivermectin was and continues to be permitted for use in the treatment of COVID19

The Austrian Supreme Administrative Court ruled in a final judgment that ivermectin was and continues to be permitted to be prescribed for the treatment of COVID-191. Doctors are obliged to provide conscientious care to patients. This may even go beyond ‘conventional medical’ knowledge if the patient’s well-being so warrants it. What matters is whether a medicine is necessary. There is extensive scientific literature on ivermectin, as well as clinical experience from doctors, which proves precisely this2. Ivermectin has been successfully and safely used against COVID-19 throughout the world, including in several EU Member States. EMA and WHO recommendations to use ivermectin only in clinical trials are not legally binding. Guidelines cannot replace the treating physician’s expertise and freedom to choose a course of treatment. 1.
Why was ivermectin, which has been on the WHO list of essential medicines for decades, not recommended by the Commission and the EMA for the treatment of COVID-19?
Why was the use of ivermectin even hindered by the Commission and the EMA using all means available?

What conclusions does the Commission draw from the fact that, according to scientific literature, around half of the COVID-19 deaths in the EU could have been prevented if the patients had received ivermectin?

at: (English version) to the Commission Gerald Hauser (PfE) (8 May 2026) Subject: Ivermectin was and continues to be permitted for use in the treatment of COVID-19 The Austrian Supreme Administrative Court ruled in a final judgment that ivermectin was and continues to be permitted to be prescribed for the treatment of COVID-19 (1). Doctors are obliged to provide conscientious care to patients. This may even go beyond ‘conventional medical’ knowledge if the patient’s well-being so warrants it. What matters is whether a medicine is necessary. There is extensive scientific literature on ivermectin, as well as clinical experience from doctors, which proves precisely this (2). Ivermectin has been successfully and safely used against COVID-19 throughout the world, including in several EU Member States. EMA and WHO recommendations to use ivermectin only in clinical trials are not legally binding. Guidelines cannot replace the treating physician’s expertise and freedom to choose a course of treatment. 1. Why was ivermectin, which has been on the WHO list of essential medicines for decades, not recommended by the Commission and the EMA for the treatment of COVID-19? 2.
Why was the use of ivermectin even hindered by the Commission and the EMA using all means available?

3. What conclusions does the Commission draw from the fact that, according to scientific literature, around half of the COVID-19 deaths in the EU could have been prevented if the patients had received ivermectin? (9 July 2026) As the Commission pointed out in its reply to written questions E-004556/2021 and P-003029/2023, evidence during the COVID-19 pandemic showed that no clinical data from appropriately conducted trials were available to support the claim that ivermectin is efficacious to prevent or treat COVID-19, while bearing a significant risk of toxicity at higher than approved doses (which would be required to be effective against SARS-Cov-2). Ivermectin medicines are not authorised for use in COVID-19 in the EU and the European Medicines Agency (EMA) has not received any application for such use either. EMA published a press release (1) in March 2021, explaining why it advised against the use of ivermectin for the prevention or treatment of COVID-19 outside randomised clinical trials. The EMA’s preliminary assessment of the analysis referenced in the footnote of the parliamentary question shows that such analysis does not appear to have been published in a peer reviewed scientific journal. It also shows that the analysis findings are likely subject to significant methodological limitations. In particular, the analysis combines a large number of heterogeneous studies, including those of low quality and, in some cases, potentially biased or unreliable, and merges non-comparable data into a single pooled estimate. Moreover, sufficiently rigorous quality assessment or control measures do not seem to have been applied in the analysis. Taken together, these limitations are likely to bias the analysis towards demonstrating an apparent treatment effect, even where higherquality evidence does not confirm such findings.

E-10-2026-001904.t: Contaminated poultry from Brazil and EU food security
qt: to the Commission Jadwiga Wiśniewska (ECR) Subject:

Following the Commission’s decision to provisionally apply the trade part of the EUMercosur agreement, Greece received its first batch of frozen poultry from Brazil. According to the Panhellenic Federation of Public Geotechnical Engineers, around 80% of the samples tested, totalling three tonnes of meat, were contaminated with salmonella and were immediately withdrawn. At the same time, experts are warning that effective control of millions of tonnes of food imported from outside the EU is not possible in practice, pointing to the inadequacy of the control system and the lack of staff in the veterinary services. This means that the Commission is pushing through trade liberalisation with no real way to ensure food security for EU citizens and without guaranteeing fair competition for European farmers. In this connection: 1.

How does the Commission intend to guarantee the health security of EU citizens in the face of increasing food imports from Mercosur countries given the serious health risks already apparent from the first batches of products?

Is the Commission considering immediately suspending imports of products of animal origin from establishments and countries where food contamination with dangerous pathogens has been detected, and removing these establishments from the list kept in accordance with Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2021/405?

Why is the Commission pushing through trade liberalisation with countries that do not meet EU sanitary standards, putting European consumers at risk while undermining the competitiveness of EU farmers?
at: (English version) to the Commission Jadwiga Wiśniewska (ECR) (8 May 2026) Subject: Contaminated poultry from Brazil and EU food security Following the Commission’s decision to provisionally apply the trade part of the EU-Mercosur agreement, Greece received its first batch of frozen poultry from Brazil. According to the Panhellenic Federation of Public Geotechnical Engineers, around 80% of the samples tested, totalling three tonnes of meat, were contaminated with salmonella and were immediately withdrawn. At the same time, experts are warning that effective control of millions of tonnes of food imported from outside the EU is not possible in practice, pointing to the inadequacy of the control system and the lack of staff in the veterinary services. This means that the Commission is pushing through trade liberalisation with no real way to ensure food security for EU citizens and without guaranteeing fair competition for European farmers. In this connection: 1.

How does the Commission intend to guarantee the health security of EU citizens in the face of increasing food imports from Mercosur countries given the serious health risks already apparent from the first batches of products?

Is the Commission considering immediately suspending imports of products of animal origin from establishments and countries where food contamination with dangerous pathogens has been detected, and removing these establishments from the list kept in accordance with Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2021/405?

Why is the Commission pushing through trade liberalisation with countries that do not meet EU sanitary standards, putting European consumers at risk while undermining the competitiveness of EU farmers?

(10 July 2026) The EU import control system operates at several levels. It includes audits in third countries carried out by the Commission to verify that they have control systems in place preventing non-compliant goods from being exported to the EU. It also provides for mandatory controls carried out by Member States at EU border control posts, including risk-based physical checks (which may include laboratory checks), to detect non-compliances. In addition, Member States must carry out risk-based controls at any stage of production, processing, distribution and use, including for imported products. Where specific risks are identified, additional measures are adopted, such as intensified official control s (1), or increased frequencies of physical checks at EU border control posts for goods from specific third countries (2). Where necessary, the Commission can adopt stricter measures such as restrictions of imports (3). Only third countries which provide guarantees that the animals and goods concerned from that third country comply with the relevant EU requirements are listed in Regulation (EU) 2021/405 (4). This act does not contain lists of establishments authorised to export to the EU. Those lists are elaborated by the authorised third countries. EU food safety rules are the strictest in the world. Furthermore, according to Article 6.6(1) of the EU-Mercosur Agreement (5), products imported into the EU from Mercosur countries must comply with those rules. Also, in line with the Vision for Agriculture and Food (6), the Commission is pursuing a stronger alignment of production standards applied to imports, notably on animal welfare and pesticides. Moreover, a dedicated task force is in place to strengthen import controls.

E-10-2026-001903.t: Application of the Water Framework Directive: the River Tagus and the Albufeira Convention flow regime
qt: to the Commission Catarina Martins (The Left) Subject:

The Commission recently closed a complaint lodged by 31 Portuguese and Spanish organisations regarding the lack of an ecological flow regime defined according to scientific parameters for the River Tagus – particularly for the Cedillo reservoir – despite obligations under the Water Framework Directive. The organisations criticise the incompatibility between the Water Framework Directive and the current Albufeira Convention regime, which is based on a minimum annual flow rate set in 1998 built on political and economic criteria. It is also founded on an understanding that Cedillo’s classification as a ‘heavily modified water body’ means ecological flows do not need to be defined. In light of the above: 1.

Does the Commission consider that a flow regime established before the Water Framework Directive entered into force and that does not have a proper scientific basis can ensure obligations regarding good ecological potential are met?
What legal, technical and scientific grounds underpin the understanding that Cedillo’s classification as a heavily modified water body does away with the need to define ecological flows?
Does the Commission intend to reassess the Albufeira Convention regime’s compatibility with EU law on water and nature conservation?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (25.8.2026) All the elements related to status assessment under the Water Framework Directive1 (WFD) ought to be based on the best available evidence and methodologies. In addition, the Court of Justice of the European Union has held that the environmental objectives of the WFD are binding on Member States, while leaving them a margin of discretion regarding the technical and methodological means of implementation, in particular the assessment and classification of water status and the design of measures to achieve those objectives2. Cedillo’s reservoir is designated as a heavily modified water body3 (HMWB) under the WFD. It is therefore subject to the objective of good ecological potential4 (GEP), instead of good ecological status (GES). Flow conditions consistent with GES of a natural water body are called ‘ecological flow’5, while flow conditions consistent with GEP of an HMWB are called ‘GEP flow’6. This reservoir is subject to the objective of GEP, then by definition to a GEP flow. The WFD requires Member States to strengthen transboundary cooperation in international river basins. The Commission does not have evidence at this stage of the incompatibility of the Albufeira Convention with the WFD provisions. At the same time, the Commission recalls that, under the WFD, hydrological regimes – including flow conditions – should support the achievement of the relevant environmental objectives for the water body concerned. In this regard, the Commission will, during 2026-27, hold structured dialogues with Spain and Portugal – as with all Member States – to ensure that adaptations are made where necessary.
1 Directive 2000/60/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 23 October 2000 establishing a

framework for Community action in the field of water policy, OJ L 327, 22.12.2000, pp. 1–73. 2 Case C-461/13, paragraph 43 (https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:62013CA0461) and Case C-346/14, paragraphs 53-55 and 70 (https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legalcontent/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:62014CA0346). 3 According to WFD article 4.3, such designation is possible only if the changes to the hydromorphological characteristics of the water body which would be necessary for achieving good ecological status would have significant adverse effects on various uses, including inter alia, navigation, hydropower generation, drinkingwater supply, and flood protection. Besides, another necessary condition for the designation as heavily modified water body is that the beneficial objectives served by the artificial or modified characteristics of the water body cannot, for reasons of technical feasibility or disproportionate costs, reasonably be achieved by other means, which are a significantly better environmental option. 4 As defined under WFD annex V. 5 As defined in guidance document n° 31 under the Common Implementation Strategy for the WFD : Ecological flows are considered within the context of the WFD as ‘an hydrological regime consistent with the achievement of the environmental objectives of the WFD in natural surface water bodies as mentioned in Article 4(1)’, https://circabc.europa.eu/ui/group/9ab5926d-bed4-4322-9aa7-9964bbe8312d/library/0c814b98-ee99-4376-93139655d522ef9c/details. 6 As defined in guidance document n° 37 under the Common Implementation Strategy for the WFD, https://circabc.europa.eu/ui/group/9ab5926d-bed4-4322-9aa7-9964bbe8312d/library/e1e6f1c6-5025-4312-92e81e0874ce82b6/details.

E-10-2026-001902.t: Repairs in the wake of Storm Kristin
qt: to the Commission Catarina Martins (The Left) Subject:

Storm Kristin caused damage to essential infrastructure in a number of areas of Portugal. One hundred days later, many households are still missing roofs, have no electricity supply and many more have no access to fixed networks. The companies responsible give no indication of when the problems will be fixed, creating great uncertainty. Even the government has admitted to huge hold-ups in the approval process for the thousands of applications for support, and many households have been forced to find solutions to their problems without any help. The government has also said that it has reallocated roughly EUR 500 million of RRP works that were planned in the areas affected. Given that this is a matter of fundamental rights, such as the right to health and decent housing, I would like to ask the following questions: 1.
Is the Commission monitoring the situation, including the rate at which issues are being resolved?
Has the Portuguese Government provided any information or requested support with regard to progressing with repair work?
Can the Commission confirm that the region will not be deprived of the investment planned under the RRP?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.7.2026) When it comes to EU instruments which can offer support, on 26 January 2026, Portugal activated the Copernicus Emergency Management Service - on demand mapping - to assess the situation during and after the event. Some maps were requested to detect the flooded area, and other products to provide damage assessment. The activation is still ongoing. Beyond the use of EU instruments, it is for the Member State to monitor the situation. On 13 April 2026, Portugal submitted an EU Solidarity Fund (EUSF)1 application regarding several consecutive storms in January and February 2026. In the application, Portugal provided information regarding the direct damages caused by the disaster. The Commission’s assessment of the application is ongoing. Following an amendment request by Portugal according to Article 21 of the Recovery and Resilience Facility regulation2, the Commission adopted on 18 May 2026 a proposal for a Council Implementing Decision amending the recovery and resilience plan (RRP) for Portugal3, which addressed inter alia the impact of natural disasters on the implementation of the RRP. According to this proposal, the overall allocation for the Portuguese RRP would not be modified. This revision of the Portuguese RRP was adopted by the Council on 12 June 2026.
1 Council Regulation (EC) No 2012/2002 of 11 November 2002 establishing the European Union Solidarity

Fund (OJ L 311, 14.11.2002, p. 3) as amended by Regulation (EU) No 661/2014 of the European Parliament and the Council of 15 May 2014 (OJ L 189, 27.6.2014, p. 143) and by Regulation (EU) 2020/461 of the European Parliament and the Council of 30 March 2020 (OJ L 99, 31.3.2020, p. 9); https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legalcontent/EN/TXT/?uri=celex:32002R2012. 2 Regulation (EU) 2021/241 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 12 February 2021 establishing the Recovery and Resilience Facility. 3 COM(2026) 248 final.

E-10-2026-001901.t: Floods in Crosia Municipality and the Calabria Region’s growing vulnerability to hydrogeological events
qt: to the Commission Pasquale Tridico (The Left) Subject:

The Municipality of Crosia and other parts of Calabria have recently been hit by floods that have, according to local authorities, caused damage to public infrastructure, housing and businesses. These extreme weather events are increasingly frequent in Calabria, highlighting the region's inherent vulnerability to hydrogeological events and growing exposure to the impact of climate change. Despite the resources made available by the European Union for hydrogeological risk prevention and climate adaptation measures, the planning and implementation of public initiatives continues to be problematic. I therefore ask: 1.

Can the Commission confirm that, partly as a result of the floods that have hit Crosia and other areas in the vicinity, the Italian authorities have applied for support from the European Union Solidarity Fund?

Given, among other things, the recurring extreme weather events that are hitting Calabria, is the Commission assessing whether EU funds earmarked for the region’s hydrogeological risk prevention and climate adaptation initiatives are being used effectively?

Is the Commission strengthening the monitoring, coordination and support tools for local authorities with a view to improving territorial resilience, prevention capacity and the management of climate emergencies in the areas most exposed to hydrogeological events?

E-10-2026-001899.t: European Union coordination and support to the Canary Islands following the activation of the Civil Protection Mechanism due to the hantavirus outbreak
qt: to the Commission Juan Fernando López Aguilar (S&D) Subject:

The detection of several confirmed cases of hantavirus on a cruise bound for the Canary Islands and the activation of the EU Civil Protection Mechanism have created a logical concern in an outermost territory particularly exposed to international flows. In view of the need to ensure a rapid, coordinated and solidarity-based response for the Canary Islands, as an external border of the European Union, can the Commission answer the following questions: 1.
What concrete assistance is the Emergency Response Coordination Centre coordinating to support Spain and the Canary Islands authorities following the activation of the EU Civil Protection Mechanism?

Does the European Union have – through rescEU or other EU health preparedness instruments – strategic reserves of antivirals, protective equipment or medical equipment that can be quickly mobilised to the Canary Islands if necessary?

Does the Commission intend to adopt specific support and coordination measures for outermost regions, such as the Canary Islands, in the face of health risks associated with international maritime traffic?
at: (English version) to the Commission Juan Fernando López Aguilar (S&D) (7 May 2026) Subject: European Union coordination and support to the Canary Islands following the activation of the Civil Protection Mechanism due to the hantavirus outbreak The detection of several confirmed cases of hantavirus on a cruise bound for the Canary Islands and the activation of the EU Civil Protection Mechanism have created a logical concern in an outermost territory particularly exposed to international flows. In view of the need to ensure a rapid, coordinated and solidarity-based response for the Canary Islands, as an external border of the European Union, can the Commission answer the following questions: 1.
What concrete assistance is the Emergency Response Coordination Centre coordinating to support Spain and the Canary Islands authorities following the activation of the EU Civil Protection Mechanism?

Does the European Union have — through rescEU or other EU health preparedness instruments — strategic reserves of antivirals, protective equipment or medical equipment that can be quickly mobilised to the Canary Islands if necessary?

Does the Commission intend to adopt specific support and coordination measures for outermost regions, such as the Canary Islands, in the face of health risks associated with international maritime traffic?

(6 July 2026) On 6 May 2026, Spain activated the EU Civil Protection Mechanism (UCPM) (1) with a request for medical evacuation and transport support, to ensure the safe and coordinated transfer of passengers and crew members from Tenerife. The Emergency Response Coordination Centre (ERCC) (2) coordinated the organisation of six flights under the UCPM by five Member States and mobilised the rescEU (3) air ambulance hosted by Norway for prepositioning in Tenerife from 9 to 12 May 2026 as a precautionary measure, should any passengers develop symptoms and deteriorate rapidly. An ERCC Liaison Officer was deployed to Tenerife from 9 to 13 May 2026 to coordinate with the relevant authorities and provide on-site support for the UCPM operation. In total, the ERCC coordinated the evacuation of over 70 people, including 43 citizens from Member States and two from UCPM Participating States. The EU maintains strategic medical countermeasures reserves, including certain antivirals, protective equipment, and medical equipment, under rescEU. These could be quickly mobilised in case of health crisis. The ERCC would then assess the precise needs and coordinate the delivery of rescEU or other stockpiles, as necessary. The ERCC stands ready to provide support should any Member State activate the UCPM in need of assistance, including in outermost regions. While there are currently no medicines nor vaccines approved for hantavirus treatment or prevention, the European Medicine Agency considered the benefit/risk balance of favipiravir to be favourable on the basis of available information. The Commission has been in constant contact with Member States to ensure rapid access and secured the delivery of 1 400 tablets of favipiravir at the request of France, Spain and the Netherlands.

E-10-2026-001898.t: Favourable conservation status of the wolf and biogeographical regions
qt: to the Commission Jan-Christoph Oetjen (Renew) Subject:

Wolves pose major challenges for many farmers of grazing livestock in Germany. The wolf population and number of wolf kills are steadily increasing. While a first step has been taken with the lowering of the protection status in the Habitats Directive (FFHD), transposition into national measures is progressing slowly. So far, Germany has requested a favourable conservation status for the wolf in the continental and the Atlantic sub-regions1. According to the FFHD classification, three biogeographical regions in Germany are relevant for the wolf2. In order to ensure legal certainty for any measures, the establishment of favourable conservation status is of key importance. 1.

Is the notification of favourable conservation status for biogeographical sub-regions legally sufficient to introduce wolf population management in those regions, if the Commission confirms the favourable conservation status?
Must a favourable conservation status be established for all three German biogeographical regions before population management is permitted in Germany as a whole?
Is it necessary to establish a favourable reference population in order to be able to carry out interventions with legal certainty?

https://www.bundesumweltministerium.de/pressemitteilung/deutschland-meldet-guenstigenerhaltungszustand-des-wolfs-an-eu-kommission. https://www.bfn.de/daten-und-fakten/biogeografische-regionen-und-naturraeumliche-haupteinheitendeutschlands.
at: (English version) to the Commission Jan-Christoph Oetjen (Renew) (7 May 2026) Subject: Favourable conservation status of the wolf and biogeographical regions Wolves pose major challenges for many farmers of grazing livestock in Germany. The wolf population and number of wolf kills are steadily increasing. While a first step has been taken with the lowering of the protection status in the Habitats Directive (FFHD), transposition into national measures is progressing slowly. So far, Germany has requested a favourable conservation status for the wolf in the continental and the Atlantic sub-regions (1). According to the FFHD classification, three biogeographical regions in Germany are relevant for the wolf (2). In order to ensure legal certainty for any measures, the establishment of favourable conservation status is of key importance. 1. Is the notification of favourable conservation status for biogeographical sub-regions legally sufficient to introduce wolf population management in those regions, if the Commission confirms the favourable conservation status? 2. Must a favourable conservation status be established for all three German biogeographical regions before population management is permitted in Germany as a whole? 3. Is it necessary to establish a favourable reference population in order to be able to carry out interventions with legal certainty? (16 July 2026) Member States are required to submit their science-based assessment of the national biogeographic conservation status of protected species every six years. The Commission does not confirm the conservation status submitted but uses this information to assess data and trends at EU level (1). National biogeographic conservation status assessments are an important element for wolf management decisions. Article 14 of the Habitats Directives (2) requires Member States to take measures to ensure that the taking of Annex V species is compatible with their maintenance at a favourable conservation status. Therefore, population management can only take place where it does not prevent the achievement or maintenance of favourable conservation status. The Court of Justice of the EU has confirmed that the assessment of the conservation status and of the management measures must be made, where appropriate, at local, biogeographical and cross-border levels (3). As a result, if an Annex V species is not in favourable conservation status at these levels, or population management would impact conservation status of that species at these levels, the discretion of Member States to manage populations of Annex V species is restricted, and measures must be taken to improve their status (4). For example, managing a wolf population in the Atlantic biogeographical region in Lower Saxony or Brandenburg would not affect the Alpine biogeographical region in Bavaria because of the large geographical distance. Favourable Reference Population (FRP) is an important part of the parameter ‘population’ in the assessment of the conservation status (5). Consequently, no accurate assessment of conservation status can be made without a FRP.

E-10-2026-001897.t: Possible unlawful use of more than EUR 2 billion in Recovery and Resilience Facility funds by the Government of Spain
qt: to the Commission Dirk Gotink (PPE) Subject:
Possible unlawful use of more than EUR 2 billion in Recovery and Resilience Facility funds by the Government of Spain

On 5 May 2026, the Spanish Court of Auditors1 published a report flagging two budget amendments totalling EUR 2 389.4 million. Appropriations originally earmarked for Spain’s national recovery and resilience plan in the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF) were redirected to civil service pensions, with ‘unavoidable commitments’ cited as a legal basis. The Court found this legal justification insufficient, raising questions over the correct use of RRF funds and taxpayers’ money. 1.

Does the Commission consider that the redirection of RRF funds by Spain to ordinary national expenditure complies with the RRF Regulation, including Article 21 on the amendment of Member States’ RRF plans and Article 22 on the protection of the financial interests of the Union?

Has the Commission been informed of the budget amendments identified by the Spanish Court of Auditors, and has it initiated any verification or follow-up under the RRF Regulation or the applicable audit framework?

What concrete steps will the Commission take in response to the findings of the Spanish Court of Auditors, and what consequences might Spain face if the redirection of RRF funds is found to be incompatible with the conditions of its approved recovery plan?

E-10-2026-001896.t: Interpretation of Annex V (Row 1) to the Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation on grouped packaging and impact on supply chains
qt: to the Commission Tomáš Zdechovský (PPE), Alexandr Vondra (ECR), Sebastian Tynkkynen (ECR), Anna Zalewska (ECR), Diana Iovanovici Şoşoacă (NI), Zala Tomašič (PPE), Merja Kyllönen (The Left), Stefan Köhler (PPE), Ondřej Krutílek (ECR), Jaroslav Bžoch (PfE), Jana Nagyová (PfE), Ondřej Knotek (PfE), Tomáš Kubín (PfE), Mircea-Gheorghe Hava (PPE), Miriam Lexmann (PPE), Kateřina Konečná (NI), Massimiliano Salini (PPE), Jan Farský (PPE) Subject:

Annex V (Row 1) to the Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation1 (PPWR) restricts certain grouped packaging formats while allowing exceptions where packaging is ‘necessary for handling’. However, this concept is not defined, and under the regulation the Commission is not required to provide further clarification before early 2027. This creates immediate legal uncertainty for operators who have to adapt packaging formats ahead of the 2030 deadline. Without clear interpretation, companies cannot determine whether widely used solutions, such as plastic shrink wrap, will remain permitted. In addition, a premature shift away from certain grouped packaging formats may lead to increased use of alternative packaging, potentially resulting in higher packaging volumes and waste, contrary to the environmental objectives of the PPWR. 1.
How does the Commission interpret ‘necessary for handling’ under Annex V (Row 1) to the PPWR?
Given that clarification may only be provided by early 2027, how will the Commission ensure that operators can prepare in time to meet the 2030 requirements?
How will the Commission ensure that implementation of Annex V avoids unintended environmental impacts, including increased packaging waste?

Regulation (EU) 2025/40 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 19 December 2024 on packaging and packaging waste, amending Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 and Directive (EU) 2019/904, and repealing Directive 94/62/EC (OJ L, 2025/40, 22.1.2025, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2025/40/oj).
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (16.7.2026) The Commission fully shares the objective of adopting the guidelines without undue delay and is actively working towards their timely adoption. To support this process, an external contractor has been appointed to assist the Commission with the preparatory work. This preparatory work includes, among others, the development of illustrative examples and further clarification of key concepts, such as ‘necessary to facilitate handling’. The Commission intends to discuss the progress and preliminary outcomes of this work already during 2026, in close dialogue with Member States and stakeholders. This approach aims to provide legal certainty, clarity and predictability for industry and national authorities, while supporting a practical and harmonised implementation of the Regulation across the EU. Annex V focuses on phasing out unnecessary packaging, and the impact assessment accompanying the Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation1 concluded that it contributes significantly to reducing packaging waste overall. The Commission is committed to develop high-quality guidelines to ensure avoidance of unintended increases in packaging waste and has mobilised the necessary technical support to this end. For instance, the involvement of the European Food Safety Authority in developing exemptions from the restriction on the use of single-use plastic packaging for fresh fruit and vegetables weighing less than 1.5 kg ensures a robust scientific basis.
1 Regulation (EU) 2025/40 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 19 December 2024 on packaging
and packaging waste, amending Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 and Directive (EU) 2019/904, and repealing Directive 94/62/EC, OJ L, 2025/40, 22.1.2025.

E-10-2026-001894.t: Integrating the principles of good governance into the EU’s cohesion policy
qt: to the Commission Pasquale Tridico (The Left), Brando Benifei (S&D) Subject:

The 12 principles of good democratic governance – adopted by the Council of Europe and reaffirmed in Recommendation CM/Rec(2023)5 – aim to enhance transparency, accountability, efficiency and participation at local and regional level. The debate on the future of the EU’s cohesion policy has shown, also against the backdrop of the report by the High Level Group set up by the Commission, that quality of governance and administrative capacity have a decisive influence on how efficiently EU funds are used, particularly in less developed regions. In this context, several local governments in the EU have adopted governance quality assurance tools, in line with these principles, in order to help improve administrative performance. In light of the above: 1.
Will the Commission promote the integration of the principles of good governance into post-2027 cohesion policy programmes?
Will it consider introducing reward mechanisms for bodies that adopt recognised standards of good governance?
What steps will it take to strengthen the administrative capacity of local and regional authorities, including through technical support tools and the exchange of good practices?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (13.7.2026) 1. Addressing the need to enhance administrative capacity remains a top priority under the proposal for a National and Regional Partnership Fund1. Under Article 3(1)(e)(III) the proposal includes a specific objective on enhancing the efficiency of public administration and the institutional capacity of public authorities and stakeholders at national, regional and local level. All National and Regional Partnership Plans should contribute to that objective and set out measures to enhance the quality of governance and reinforce the administrative capacity of public administrations. 2. In addition to investments, the plans will incentivise reforms, including for enhancing the quality of governance to address the identified needs and challenges at national, regional and local level. The framework for programming and implementing reforms has incentivising effects through payments for fulfilled milestones and targets including for governanceenhancing measures. 3. Member States are encouraged to use their technical assistance from the funds to enhance the administrative capacity of plan authorities, stakeholders and beneficiaries, which is necessary for the effective implementation of the Plan. The Commission will continue to support EU-wide networks of Member States’ authorities and other relevant stakeholders, including for the purposes of exchanging good practices and promoting good governance. In addition, Member States can request technical support from the EU Facility under the National and Regional Partnership Fund to prepare reforms at national or sub-national level included in their National and Regional Partnership Plans.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex:52025PC0565.

E-10-2026-001893.t: Consequences of the CJEU’s judgment in Case C-796/22 for the Commission’s infringement strategy
qt: to the Commission Marieke Ehlers (PfE) Subject:

Following the judgment in Case C-769/22- Commission v Hungary1, the Court of Justice recognised that Article 2 of the Treaty on European Union (TEU) may function as a selfstanding legal basis in infringement proceedings under Article 258 Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union. This development appears to strengthen the Commission’s capacity to address alleged breaches of EU values through judicial means, complementing the existing political mechanism under Article 7 TEU. 1.

How does the Commission intend to integrate Article 2 TEU as a stand-alone ground in its infringement strategy, and does it intend to prioritise Article 258 proceedings over initiating or advancing Article 7 TEU procedures?

To what extent does the Commission consider that judgments based directly on Article 2 TEU could serve as evidentiary or procedural support in ongoing or future Article 7 TEU proceedings against individual Member States?

How will the Commission ensure that the expanded use of Article 2 TEU in infringement actions respects the principle of conferral and avoids encroaching on Member States’ constitutional identities, without enforcing an ideological agenda on the individual Member States through lawfare?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.7.2026) The Commission has taken note of the landmark judgment of the Court of Justice in the infringement procedure launched by the Commission against Hungary in case C-769/221. In that judgment, the Court of Justice has found, for the first time, a separate infringement of Article 2 of the Treaty on the EU, which lists the values on which the EU is founded and which are common to all the Member States. The Commission, as guardian of the Treaties, will continue to use all the tools at its disposal to promote and uphold the values on which the EU is founded, in accordance with the case law of the Court of Justice. The infringement procedure, which is based on Article 258 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU and the procedure under Article 7 of the Treaty on the EU to which the Honourable Member refers, are separate procedures and rely on different mechanisms. There is no direct influence of the one over the other.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:62022CJ0769.

E-10-2026-001892.t: The presence of lead in tampons and consumer safety in the EU
qt: to the Commission Christel Schaldemose (S&D) Subject:

A recent study by the Norwegian newspaper VG showed that all the tampons it tested from 11 different brands contained traces of lead, a toxic heavy metal. The study also showed that lead can leach out of tampons during use, and that even a minimal level of lead should be regarded as harmful to health. This raises serious questions about consumer safety and whether existing EU regulations, including REACH, adequately protect consumers from exposure to harmful substances in hygiene products. In the light of the foregoing: 1.
Does the Commission acknowledge that the detection of lead in tampons is a problem, and thus poses a threat to the health of EU consumers?
Does the Commission acknowledge that there are shortcomings in the legislation on hygiene products, which are in prolonged contact with mucous membranes and the skin?
What does the Commission intend to do about the problem of lead in hygiene products?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (29.6.2026) Lead is a substance of very high concern (SVHC) due to its hazardous properties as toxic for reproduction. To protect human health and the environment, lead is regulated under the Regulation on the Registration, Evaluation, Authorisation and Restriction of chemicals (REACH)1 in mixtures2 and several consumer products3, as well as in several sectors: batteries4, electronic equipment5, end of life vehicles6 . Consumer products placed or made available on the EU market, including hygiene products, must comply with the General Product Safety Regulation7. The Commission is not aware of the mentioned Norwegian study. However, the Commission takes the safety of consumer products, very seriously. Authorities from the Member States and the European Economic Area (EEA) must notify measures taken against products containing hazardous substances, through the Safety Gate Rapid Alert System8. This system enables the quick exchange of information among authorities and makes relevant information publicly available. The Commission has not planned actions on lead in tampons under REACH. The Commission is open to engaging with researchers, national authorities, and industry stakeholders to assess new evidence and determine appropriate actions to safeguard public health. Ongoing and planned work on REACH restrictions is publicly available in the restriction roadmap9. Member States, and EEA States, have the possibility to propose substances for restriction under REACH if they consider they pose an unacceptable risk to human health or the environment.

E-10-2026-001890.t: EU-Mercosur agreement: exposure of the European market to the JBS Group and the risks of geoeconomic dependence in agricultural supply chains
qt: to the Commission Céline Imart (PPE), Luke Ming Flanagan (The Left), Tomáš Kubín (PfE), Ciaran Mullooly (Renew), Christophe Gomart (PPE), Marko Vešligaj (S&D), Galato Alexandraki (ECR), Georgiana Teodorescu (ECR), Maria Grapini (S&D), Jessika van Leeuwen (ECR), François-Xavier Bellamy (PPE), Krzysztof Hetman (PPE), Nicolas Bay (ECR), Benoit Cassart (Renew), Sander Smit (ECR), Michael McNamara (Renew), Christine Singer (Renew), Zsuzsanna Borvendég (ESN), Petr Bystron (ESN), Marion Maréchal (ECR), Laurence Trochu (ECR), Sebastian Tynkkynen (ECR) Subject:

According to several intelligence and economic analyses1, as well as corroborated journalistic investigations2345, the EU-Mercosur agreement could strengthen the position of actors that are already highly concentrated in the global animal protein market, notably the world’s largest producer, the Brazilian group JBS, whose international expansion has historically benefited from the support of Brazilian public instruments. Serious controversies involving this group have been documented, including the corruption of foreign public officials in the United States, illegal farming on indigenous lands, deforestation, animal welfare violations and judicial settlements with several prosecutorial authorities, against a backdrop of major politico-financial cases involving high-level political figures. These elements raise concerns about the potential use of the agreement as a lever for geoeconomic dependence. 1.
Did the Commission carry out a comprehensive assessment of the risks linked to strengthening such actors during the negotiations on the agreement?

What concrete and verifiable guarantees can the Commission provide to ensure fair competition, in the light of the potential implications for the EU’s food sovereignty and the risk of structural dependence on actors strongly supported by their state of origin?
Does the Commission intend to suspend or reassess the agreement, the provisional application of which began on 1 May 2026?

Les Échos, ‘Après l’incarcération de ses fils, Jose Batista, 84 ans, reprend les rênes du numéro un mondial de la viande’ [Following his son’s imprisonment, 84-year-old Jose Batista is back at the helm of the world’s biggest meat processor], 18 September 2017. The Guardian, ‘How a Brazilian meat tycoon accused of bribery and deforestation became a key player in regional diplomacy’, 16 December 2025.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (18.6.2026) The Commission has performed several analytical assessments prior to the signature of the EU-Mercosur Partnership Agreement (EMPA)1 and the Interim Trade Agreement (ITA)2, which has been provisionally applied since 1 May 2026. These include the Sustainability Impact Assessment3 and the Economic Analysis of the Negotiated Outcome of the EMPA4, which evaluate impacts across key sectors, with particular attention to sensitive sectors such as agriculture. The agreements include provisions to counter corruption and protect the EU market from anticompetitive practices. The EMPA includes provisions to strengthen collaboration on combating corruption through prevention, investigation, prosecution of offenders, and mutual legal assistance. Under the ITA, all parties are required to adopt and enforce comprehensive competition laws that effectively address anti-competitive behaviour. The Agreement also safeguards EU producers of sensitive agricultural products (e.g., beef and poultry) against sudden import surges through tariff-rate quotas and safeguard measures. The EU’s Foreign Subsidies Regulation5 provides an additional layer of protection. If a company receives financial contributions from a third country (i.e. a non-Member State) that are on advantageous terms – such as a government grant – this may constitute a foreign subsidy under the Foreign Subsidies Regulation. The Commission is empowered to assess whether such foreign subsidies distort the internal market and, where appropriate, adopt redressive measures to address such distortion. The Commission currently has no plans to suspend or reassess the ITA. If needed, the Commission can utilise the ITA’s robust safeguard clauses and dispute settlement mechanisms.

E-10-2026-001889.t: Commission actions to deal with the effects of the Middle East conflict on the agri-food sector and strengthen food security
qt: to the Commission Dimitris Tsiodras (PPE) Subject:

The ongoing conflict in the Middle East and geopolitical uncertainty are having a significant impact on the agri-food sector. In addition to the surge in energy costs, according to the Commission, in April 2026, nitrogen fertilisers cost 70 % more compared to 2024 and global supply has been disrupted, as the region accounts for 20-30 % of ammonia and urea exports. These developments translate into increased production costs and a possible increase in food prices, weakening the purchasing power of European consumers. Given the importance of this sector, it is imperative that the European Union take immediate action to ensure food security. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
In view of the forthcoming Fertiliser Action Plan, how will the Commission help towards bringing down the cost of fertilisers so that they are affordable for farmers?
Following the AccelerateEU Communication, what action does it intend to take to ensure affordable energy for the agri-food sector, especially for small and medium-sized enterprises?
Does it have any data on the potential impact of the CBAM and ETS on agricultural prices and how does it intend to address these potential consequences?
at: (English version) to the Commission Dimitris Tsiodras (PPE) (7 May 2026) Subject: Commission actions to deal with the effects of the Middle East conflict on the agri-food sector and strengthen food security The ongoing conflict in the Middle East and geopolitical uncertainty are having a significant impact on the agri-food sector. In addition to the surge in energy costs, according to the Commission, in April 2026, nitrogen fertilisers cost 70% more compared to 2024 and global supply has been disrupted, as the region accounts for 20-30% of ammonia and urea exports. These developments translate into increased production costs and a possible increase in food prices, weakening the purchasing power of European consumers. Given the importance of this sector, it is imperative that the European Union take immediate action to ensure food security. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
In view of the forthcoming Fertiliser Action Plan, how will the Commission help towards bringing down the cost of fertilisers so that they are affordable for farmers?
Following the AccelerateEU Communication, what action does it intend to take to ensure affordable energy for the agrifood sector, especially for small and medium-sized enterprises?
Does it have any data on the potential impact of the CBAM and ETS on agricultural prices and how does it intend to address these potential consequences?

(22 July 2026) The Commission is closely monitoring the impact of geopolitical developments on fertilisers, energy and agricultural markets. To help address rising costs, it has already taken measures, including a temporary suspension of duties for urea, ammonia and other key nitrogen fertilisers within given quotas (excluding imports from Russia and Belarus) (1) and a reduction of the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) default value markup to 1%. The Commission has proposed actions to help Member States protect vulnerable consumers and sectors affected by the Middle East energy crisis. These include targeted and temporary national support measures, supported by the new Middle East Crisis Temporary state aid Framework (METSAF) (2), which allows state aid to some sectors including the primary agricultural production. With Accelerate EU (3), the Commission has established a catalogue of good practices, showcasing national measures to support vulnerable consumers, small and medium-size enterprises and others. The Fertiliser Action Plan (4) also includes short term measures to improve affordability for farmers, including the possibility of targeted support through the agricultural reserve and a legislative package offering additional options under Common Agricultural Policy Strategic Plans, including liquidity support, to be adopted by the co-legislators in July 2026. To strengthen resilience, the Plan sets out actions to increase EU fertiliser production capacity, support decarbonisation, diversify supply, improve market transparency and promote nutrient recycling. The Commission will also assess how CBAM and ETS related costs are reflected in fertiliser prices and food prices.

E-10-2026-001888.t: The NRRP-funded Genoa dam project’s major technical shortcomings and untransparent management
qt: to the Commission Gaetano Pedulla' (The Left) Subject:

Funded to the tune of ca. EUR 1.5 billion (including NRRP resources), Genoa’s new dam project has critical vulnerabilities. It recently transpired1 that tests to determine the foundation’s structural stability could not be completed at a depth of 50 metres because the water pressure had destroyed the piezometers involved. Though project staff have been unable to confirm whether the seabed under the gravel blanket can indeed support the dam, the Extraordinary Commissioner has decided to accept this risk and says that construction will go ahead and be based on real-world data instead of preventive testing. Such an approach could be at odds with the ‘Do No Significant Harm’ (DNSH) principle and the provisions of Regulation (EU) 2021/241. The project could also be in breach of Directive 2003/4/EC on public access to environmental information because management have so far refused to disclose any monitoring data, citing the need to avoid any ‘premature conclusions’. I therefore ask the Commission: 1.

Does it hold that allowing the Genoa dam project to proceed despite the lack of valid test results at a depth of 50 metres is an approach that is in keeping with the Recovery and Resilience Facility’s strict technical safety standards?

What measures will it take to check whether the risk accepted by the project’s commission could indeed violate the DSNH principle by compromising the dam’s longterm stability and harming the local environment?
Does it consider the secrecy surrounding the project’s technical monitoring data to be compatible with the transparency and reporting requirements laid down by EU law?

Does it consider the secrecy surrounding the project’s technical monitoring data to be compatible with the transparency and reporting requirements laid down by EU law?

(23 July 2026) The Commission would like to highlight that the Genoa dam project has been financed by complementary national resources under the National Complementary Fund and is not part as such of the approved National Recovery and Resilience Plan (NRRP) under Regulation (EU) 2021/241 (1). The Do-Not-Significant-Harm principle, as well as technical safety and reporting standards of the Recovery and Resilience Facility, are applicable to the implementation of, inter alia, projects financed under the Italian Recovery and Resilience Plan (PNRR), while it does not apply to projects funded through any national resources, including the National Complementary Fund. Under Article 3(1) of Directive 2003/4/EC (2) ‘Member States shall ensure that public authorities are required, in accordance with the provisions of this directive, to make available environmental information held by or for them to any applicant at his request and without his having to state an interest’. Member States may provide for a request for environmental information to be refused under the exceptions regime laid down IN Article 4 of the same Directive. Without prejudice to the Commission’s role as guardian of the Treaties, Member States are primarily responsible for ensuring that specific financed projects comply with EU and national law.

E-10-2026-001886.t: Serious damage to orchards in Pella and Imathia and need for scientific investigation and support for producers
qt: to the Commission Sakis Arnaoutoglou (S&D) Subject:

Producers of stone fruits in the Regional Units of Pella and Imathia, Greece, have been facing a serious problem in recent years: widespread fruit deformation and gradual tree desiccation in peach orchards – a phenomenon that seems to be spreading to other tree types, such as apricot, plum and cherry. According to local rural actors, the area affected is estimated to have reached around 21 km2, and in several cases production has fallen by as much as 60 %, with serious repercussions for producers’ incomes and the viability of crops. Despite the seriousness of the situation, the exact cause of the phenomenon remains to be clarified, while the Greek Government’s response to date has been limited to insufficient and fragmented compensation, without a comprehensive plan for scientific investigation and addressing the problem. Given the importance of tree crops for the region’s rural economy and for European stone fruit production, can the Commission say: 1.
Is it monitoring this disease phenomenon affecting stone fruit crops in Greece, and can it contribute to the investigation of its causes through European research programmes or scientific networks?
What tools of the common agricultural policy or other European programmes can be used to support producers who suffer significant production losses?
Does it intend to consider measures to prevent and manage similar phytosanitary risks in order to prevent the phenomenon from spreading further to other parts of the EU?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.7.2026) The Commission is aware of this disease phenomenon. As the causal agent remains unidentified, no specific EU plant health obligations currently apply1. A Horizon Europe2 Cluster 63 topic4 on emerging plant pest risks will open early next year for applications. Member States may also use Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) support to support research for instance through EIP-AGRI5 Operational Groups6 for innovative solutions under the CAP. At least 2% of eligible expenditure allocated to research and innovation under operational programmes for recognised fruit and vegetable producer organisations could be used to address such challenges. These recognised producer organisations may also make use of the various risk prevention and management interventions7 being part of their operational programmes. Moreover, when the reduction of the value of marketed production (VMP) determining the EU subsidies for producer organisations is due to a pest and falls by at least 35%8, Member States may take this into account when calculating the final support to mitigate the impact of the VMP reduction. The CAP also offers other tools. Member States introduce in their CAP Strategic Plans crisis payments for farmers affected by plant pests9. Member States can use CAP tools to build medium and long-term resilience10 and address short-term impacts through direct payments, risk management, and investments in restoration of production potential, while also supporting preventive investments.

E-10-2026-001885.t: Risk of Ryanair shutting up shop in Thessaloniki: a new blow to connectivity, tourism and regional cohesion in Northern Greece
qt: to the Commission Sakis Arnaoutoglou (S&D) Subject:

According to reports and information that has been made public, Ryanair has allegedly informed its employees of its intention to close its base at Thessaloniki’s Makedonia Airport, citing a significant increase in airport fees. Such a development would have serious consequences for the international connectivity of Northern Greece, tourism, the local economy, but also hundreds of workers directly or indirectly linked to the operation of the company and the airport. At the same time, it highlights once again the broader European problem of the rising cost of accessing regional airports and the lack of a coherent European strategy to maintain regional air connectivity. Thessaloniki and Northern Greece as a whole cannot become isolated ‘white zones’ in terms of air connectivity, at a time when the EU is talking about cohesion, regional development and equal access opportunities. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Is it following the matter of Ryanair’s possible departure from Thessaloniki and what measures does it intend to take to ensure air connectivity for European regions?
Does it not consider that rising fees at regional airports act as a deterrent for low-cost airlines, which risks harming the regional economy and tourism?
Does it intend to consider creating a European support framework for maintaining strategic air connections in peripheral and less accessible areas of the EU?
to the Commission Bert-Jan Ruissen (ECR), Willemien Koning (PPE), Jeannette Baljeu (Renew), Rachel Blom (PfE) Subject:

Blockades in the Strait of Hormuz are causing global fuel shortages and kerosene is no exception. It is essential for passenger and cargo transport in the EU aviation sector that the remaining kerosene be used as efficiently as possible. However, under EU law, European airlines must operate at least 80 per cent of their flights in order not to lose landing rights. During the coronavirus pandemic, the Commission suspended this rule to prevent inefficient flights and so-called ghost flights. 1.

In view of the exceptional situation in the Middle East, the Commission’s call for fuel economy and the expected long recovery period, is the Commission prepared to temporarily suspend the EU Slot Allocation Regulation once again or to make it more flexible (for example, through an EU slot exemption from the 80-20 rule), so that airlines can use kerosene more efficiently to carry as many passengers and cargo as possible?

Is the Commission prepared to clarify the situation as to whether severe shortages and the high price of kerosene constitute grounds for ‘justified non-use of slots’, and how will harmonised application by slot coordinators be ensured in this regard?
What is the Commission’s take on a temporary suspension of the anti-tankering rules in the ReFuelEU Regulation, so that EU airlines can refuel more outside the EU if necessary?
at: (English version) to the Commission Bert-Jan Ruissen (ECR), Willemien Koning (PPE), Jeannette Baljeu (Renew), Rachel Blom (PfE) (7 May 2026) Subject: Aviation fuel shortage Blockades in the Strait of Hormuz are causing global fuel shortages and kerosene is no exception. It is essential for passenger and cargo transport in the EU aviation sector that the remaining kerosene be used as efficiently as possible. However, under EU law, European airlines must operate at least 80% of their flights in order not to lose landing rights. During the coronavirus pandemic, the Commission suspended this rule to prevent inefficient flights and so-called ghost flights. 1. In view of the exceptional situation in the Middle East, the Commission’s call for fuel economy and the expected long recovery period, is the Commission prepared to temporarily suspend the EU Slot Allocation Regulation once again or to make it more flexible (for example, through an EU slot exemption from the 80-20 rule), so that airlines can use kerosene more efficiently to carry as many passengers and cargo as possible? 2. Is the Commission prepared to clarify the situation as to whether severe shortages and the high price of kerosene constitute grounds for ‘justified non-use of slots’, and how will harmonised application by slot coordinators be ensured in this regard? 3. What is the Commission’s take on a temporary suspension of the anti-tankering rules in the ReFuelEU Regulation, so that EU airlines can refuel more outside the EU if necessary? (15 June 2026) 1. Any suspension of the slot use rules must be underpinned by reliable data and targeted to the needs of the sector. While it is not excluded that disruptions could arise in certain areas, at present there is no immediate threat to the security of fuel supply. The Commission is committed to supporting the aviation sector amid continued uncertainty on the length and severity of the Middle East crisis, when and where justified. 2. On 8 May 2026, the Commission adopted Guidance (1) clarifying that fuel shortages may constitute grounds for the ‘Justified Non-use of Slots’ exception and calling on EU slot-coordinators to adopt a harmonised approach. It also clarified that high kerosene prices cannot constitute grounds for justified non-use of slots under the Slot Regulatio n (2). If the price increases lead to a significant drop in demand, slot relief measures could be considered, as has been the case in previous crises. 3. The interpretative guidelines (3) on Article 5 of the ReFuelEU Aviation Regulation (4) clarify how aircraft operators can be exempted from their refuelling obligation in cases of fuel shortage. The conflict in the Middle East reinforces the need to accelerate the transition towards more diversified energy sources. Maintaining the ambition of ReFuelEU Aviatio n (5) and implementing the Sustainable Transport Investment Plan (STIP) (6) are therefore essential to strengthen Europe’s energy security, strategic autonomy and competitiveness. If the situation worsens and existing flexibilities no longer suffice, the Commission will propose temporary changes to the applicable EU legislative framework, where justified.

E-10-2026-001883.t: Level playing field for agricultural producers in light of the rules on pesticide residues
qt: to the Commission Jadwiga Wiśniewska (ECR) Subject:

The EU has banned a number of active substances in agriculture, such as thiophanate-methyl, carbendazim and benomyl, because of their potentially harmful effects on human health and the environment. At the same time, agricultural products imported from third countries – including fruit and vegetables such as mangoes, papayas, citrus fruits and grapes, as well as other plant products – that may contain residues of these substances continue to enter the EU market. This situation raises serious doubts as to the coherence of EU regulations and the equal treatment of producers. Farmers in the EU are required to comply with strict standards and bear the associated costs, while products produced using substances banned in the EU can compete with them in the single market. In this connection: How does the Commission assess the impact of the current rules allowing imports of products containing residues of substances not authorised in the EU on the competitiveness of EU agricultural producers? The current legal situation undermines the credibility of the EU’s food safety policy, the protection of citizens’ health and the coherence of single market rules.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (20.8.2026) Regulation (EC) No 396/2005 on maximum residues levels (MRLs) of pesticides1 ensures the safety of food and feed products, for both domestically and imported products, through a rigorous, science-based risk assessment process. The Regulation allows setting MRLs for imported agricultural products that contain residues of active substances, but only if these MRLs are safe for EU consumers. This possibility contributes to food and feed security – in particular for commodities for which the EU is not self-sufficient – while ensuring that imported food meets the EU’s high safety standards. As regards the specific substances referred to by the Honourable Member, the Commission has adopted a Regulation on 8 July 2026 to lower all MRLs for carbendazim, benomyl and thiophanate-methyl to the technical zero2. More generally, in the Vision for Agriculture and Food3, the Commission announced that it will establish a principle that the most hazardous pesticides banned in the EU for health and environmental reasons are not allowed back to the EU through imported products. To advance on this, the Commission has launched a study4 that will inform an impact assessment that will consider the impacts on the EU’s competitive position and the international implications and, if appropriate, amendments to the applicable legal framework will be proposed. The Commission has also proposed in the Food and Feed Safety Simplification Package5 to establish the possibility to lower MRLs to the technical zero for the most hazardous substances6 not approved in the EU on a case-by-case basis, if considered appropriate, in the light of the outcome of substance-specific assessments.

E-10-2026-001882.t: Policies to tackle discrimination against the Roma of Thrace
qt: to the Commission Emmanouil Fragkos (ECR) Subject:

Historically, Roma have been one of the most marginalised and culturally prolific population groups in the Balkans, including parts of Bulgaria, Greece and Türkiye. Unfortunately, Roma are subject to intense Turkification efforts by Türkiye, which attacks and belittles their identity, as it does with all non-Turkish identities. Despite the EU’s longstanding commitment to equality, inclusion and the protection of fundamental rights, many Roma communities continue to face persistent structural challenges, such as poverty, social exclusion, insufficient access to education, housing, healthcare and employment, as well as discrimination and limited participation in public life. In some areas, these problems are exacerbated by geographical isolation, weak institutional support and limited access to appropriate educational tools. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Is there funding for the creation of media, such as radio, television or social media, or even some programmes on existing networks?

Given that, in Thrace, a large part of the minority are Roma, does it not consider that it would be more important for there to be a Roma Studies course in Greece rather than a Turkish Studies course?
At the very least, what European tools could be used to support a Museum of Roma Culture in Xanthi?
