(17 September 2026) The Commission is firmly committed to combating antigypsyism and discrimination against Roma. Under the EU Roma Strategic Framework for Equality, Inclusion and Participation 2020-2030, all Member States are encouraged to fight antigypsyism, promote Roma equality, and prevent social and economic exclusion. In 2026, the Commission will adopt its third report on progress made in the implementation of national Roma strategic frameworks. EU funding is provided for media pluralism and news media, including local, regional and community media, through Creative Europe. Cohesion Policy funding supports cultural infrastructure, including museums, and the regional programme for Eastern Macedonia and Thrace allocated around EUR 13 million to cultural investments. The Citizens, Equality, Rights and Values programme, via the calls for proposals on Remembrance, supports commemoration, research and education, including remembrance of Roma victims. Creative Europe supports museums through cooperation projects, exhibitions, learning activities, digital heritage, skills development and inclusion. On Romani studies in Thrace, education content and the organisation of education systems remain Member State competences. The EU has no general power over the use of regional or minority languages, and EU competence does not extend to discrimination based on language or belonging to a national minority.

E-10-2026-001881.t: Protecting coral reefs in European EEZs
qt: to the Commission Emmanouil Fragkos (ECR) Subject:

Coral reefs are ‘tropical forests’ that host 25 % of marine life, protect coastlines and support the global food chain. Although we have the most advanced tools for mapping and monitoring marine ecosystems, such as the Copernicus Marine Service (CMEMS), the MAES initiative and the European Digital Twin Ocean, the Commission stated in 2021 (Ref. E-001607/2021) that mapping of European reefs is incomplete. At the same time, coral reefs continue to deteriorate, while the implementation of the Nature Restoration Law is still ongoing. Given that, in accordance with Article 56 of UNCLOS, Member States exercise sovereign rights within their EEZs for the protection and management of marine resources and that the EU has exclusive competence for their conservation, issues are cropping up in relation to coordination, operational implementation and the use of available tools. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
What specific measures has it taken since 2021 to fully map reefs within Member States’ maritime zones, including their EEZs?
How is it ensured that Member States make use of available Union tools to actively exercise their sovereign rights to protect marine ecosystems?

Does it intend to propose binding measures to strengthen the practical implementation of Member States’ rights and obligations in their EEZs, in particular as regards the protection and restoration of reefs?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (17.7.2026) Member States are required under the Marine Strategy Framework1 and Habitats Directives2 to monitor and protect habitats, including reefs, in the marine waters where they have jurisdiction. The Nature Restoration Regulation3 further introduces binding mapping and restoration targets for marine habitats. Member States’ plans for mapping and restoration of habitats will be shared in their draft national restoration plans by 1 September 2026. As regards fisheries measures, while the EU has exclusive competence to adopt acts on the conservation of marine biological resources under the common fisheries policy4, Member States are responsible for their implementation. To support Member States, the Commission is promoting the use of monitoring, data and modelling tools through technical support and EU funding programmes5. The Copernicus Marine Service6 provides observations of parameters such as sea-surface temperature, ocean currents and acidification; EMODnet7 provides access to marine in-situ data on parameters, including the distribution of coralligenous structures; the future Digital Twin of the Ocean8 will have the capacity to simulate reef ecosystems to inform conservation strategies. The new OceanEye initiative9 provides a strategic framework to reinforce these efforts by strengthening ocean observation capacities, improving access to marine data and intelligence, and fostering cooperation between Member States, research organisations and international partners. The Commission is currently preparing a proposal to revise the Marine Strategy Framework Directive, with the aim to progress towards good environmental status of EU seas10.

E-10-2026-001880.t: Protecting actual Greek farmers from the consequences of the Government scandal at OPEKEPE
qt: to the Commission Emmanouil Fragkos (ECR) Subject:

The scandal under investigation at OPEKEPE is challenging Greek farmers, as it becomes obvious that the weaknesses in the management of European funds are structural, while questions are raised about the adequacy of national control mechanisms, as well as ‘independent authorities’, at a time when the revelations ‘are coming from outside’. Responsibility seems to lie with administrative and political practices, and not with the producers themselves, who are currently faced with delays, aid reductions and increased uncertainty. At the same time, concerns have been expressed that, as a result of the controls and corrective measures, the flow of funding to Greek farmers may be restricted or budgetary corrections may be imposed that will horizontally affect beneficiaries. It is important to note that the real value of agricultural production has been decreasing over the last 15 years. Correspondingly, the real income of farmers is also decreasing. This is outrageous for a country with excellent agricultural products and enormous untapped productive potential. 1.
Does the Commission believe that it is morally right for responsibility that lies with administrative and governmental practices to affect actual Greek farmers who are fighting to survive?
What specific measures does the Commission intend to take to ensure that actual Greek farmers do not suffer the consequences of irregularities for which they are not responsible?
How does the Commission plan to press for the fastest possible investigation and clarification of the case, so as to stop the activity of the outgoing Government from harming Greek farmers?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (29.6.2026) Under the shared management of the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), and with the objective to ensure timely payments to farmers, Member States must set up the aid application systems in line with the applicable rules and ensure that, following sufficient checks, payments are made in full and on time to beneficiaries1. The Commission obtains assurance on the Member States’ management and control systems through the audits of these systems, including by the national Certification Bodies. On specific measures taken, the Commission performed multiple audits of CAP spending in Greece and, in several cases, decided on financial corrections. The national authorities must recover the irregularly spent funds from the beneficiaries who committed the irregularities. In September 2024, the Greek authorities put the paying agency OPEKEPE’s accreditation on probation due to several deficiencies that were identified and designed an action plan to address them. On 12 March 2026, the Greek authorities reported that the accreditation action plan was fully implemented and reinstated the accreditation of the paying agency. The Commission received the report from the competent authority on completion of the action plan. An accreditation audit mission is planned during which the auditors of the DirectorateGeneral for Agriculture and Rural Development will review the effective implementation of the actions included in the accreditation action plan and check whether these actions effectively address the issues at stake. Regarding the European Public Prosecutor’s Office investigations, the Commission cannot comment on ongoing criminal investigations.

E-10-2026-001879.t: Mining activity in a residential area in Achlada, Florina, and implementation of the EU environmental  acquis
qt: to the Commission Maria Zacharia (NI) Subject:
Mining activity in a residential area in Achlada, Florina, and implementation of the EU environmental acquis

In Achlada, Florina, lignite mining activities are continuing in an active residential area – in the immediate vicinity of homes and a school – without residents having been relocated as required. These conditions give rise to serious concerns regarding the exposure of residents – particularly minors – to particulate matter, noise, vibrations and other nuisances, and calls into question the adequacy of environmental licensing practices, the protection of human health and the management of extractive waste. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

Does it consider that the continuation of this kind of mining activity in the immediate vicinity of a residential area and school calls for a specific check on compliance with Directive 2011/92/EU on environmental impact assessments, EU air quality legislation and Directive 2006/21/EC on extractive waste?

Has it requested or does it intend to request from the Greek authorities the relevant data on air quality, noise, vibrations, school protection measures and conditions for the safe continuation of the activity?
If shortcomings are identified in the implementation of EU environmental law, does the Commission intend to consider initiating a procedure under Article 258 TFEU?

(10 July 2026) Open-cast mining where the surface of the site exceeds 25 hectares are listed in Annex I of the Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) Directive (1) and according to Article 4(1) of the same Directive, an environmental impact assessment must be carried out. Other open-cast mining and underground mining are listed in Annex II (points 2.a and 2.b). According to Article 4 (2) of the EIA Directive, prior to granting a consent for such projects, it is up to Member States to determine whether an environmental impact assessment is necessary, based on a case-by-case analysis or by setting specific criteria (such as the location, size or type of project). Such an assessment, if required, should identify and address any significant impacts of such projects on the environment (including, where relevant, impacts related to noise, air pollution) and human health. However, and without prejudice to the Commission’s role as guardian of the Treaties, it is primarily the responsibility of the Greek authorities to ensure that projects are developed and authorised in full compliance with EU environmental legislation.

E-10-2026-001878.t: Compatibility of a Greek draft law with EU environmental law in relation to Natura 2000 sites
qt: to the Commission Maria Zacharia (NI) Subject:
Compatibility of a Greek draft law with EU environmental law in relation to Natura 2000 sites

The Greek Ministry of the Environment and Energy’s law on the modernisation of legislation on the use and production of energy from renewable sources, which ostensibly transposes Directives (EU) 2023/2413 and (EU) 2024/1788 into national law, is not limited to the faithful transposition of those directives, but introduces provisions that go beyond their regulatory framework and distort their objective of ensuring a high level of environmental protection. Specifically, the draft law establishes permitted uses and activities within Natura 2000 sites without making their implementation contingent upon a prior appropriate impact assessment capable of ruling out – on the basis of the best available scientific data – any reasonable doubt as to the deterioration of the protected habitats. This approach raises questions as to the compatibility with Directive 92/43/EEC and Directive 2011/92/EU, as well as with the principles of Articles 11 and 191 TFEU. Furthermore, the public consultation lasted only two weeks, one of which coincided with Holy Week and Easter, which, according to the comments received, undermines meaningful public participation. In light of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Is the above legislative approach in line with Article 6 of Directive 92/43/EEC?
How does it assess the above decoupling of the implementation of activities from the prior appropriate assessment?
Does the consultation process meet the requirements for effective public participation under EU law?

(16 July 2026) The Commission notes that the bill in question has not yet been adopted and cannot thus comment on its content. Any measure communicated by the Member States for the transposition of the directives (EU) 2023/2413 (1) and (EU) 2024/1788 (2) will be assessed by the Commission Services under the relevant transposition exercise. According to Article 6(3) of the Habitats Directive (3) in case a Natura 2000 site is likely to be significantly impacted by a project, then an appropriate assessment of its impact must be carried out and the project can only be authorised if it has been ascertained that it will not significantly impact such a site. Any legislative change should not introduce provisions, that would contradict the above-mentioned provision. Article 7 of the Aarhus Convention (4) requires each Party, ‘to the extent appropriate’, to ‘endeavour to provide opportunities for public participation in the preparation of policies relating to the environment’. However, the more specific public participation requirements under Articles 6 and 7 of the Aarhus Convention (including Article 6(3) requiring reasonable timeframes) apply only to projects, plans and programmes.

E-10-2026-001875.t: Preparedness measures against zoonotic diseases in view of the recent outbreak of hantavirus
qt: to the Commission Leire Pajín (S&D) Subject:

In May 2026, three people died following a suspected hantavirus outbreak on a cruise ship sailing between Argentina and Cabo Verde, according to the World Health Organization. Other suspected cases have been under investigation following this incident. Hantaviruses are a group of rare zoonotic viruses, transmitted mainly through contact with the faeces or urine of infected rodents, and can cause serious diseases such as hantavirus pulmonary syndrome or haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome. There is currently no specific treatment or widely available vaccine, making preparedness crucial for likely future outbreaks of zoonotic diseases with pandemic potential. 1.
What measures is the Commission taking to strengthen epidemiological surveillance of rare but potentially serious zoonoses, including hantaviruses, in the EU and in cooperation with non-EU countries?

What initiatives does the Commission envisage as regards the exchange of scientific data and coordinated preparedness with non-EU countries in order to be ready for possible zoonotic outbreaks in high-risk environments?

What is the Commission doing to strengthen the EU’s preparedness for future zoonotic and emerging infectious disease threats, in particular by supporting the development of antiviral medicines and rapidly adaptable vaccine platforms, including mRNA technologies?

What initiatives does the Commission envisage as regards the exchange of scientific data and coordinated preparedness with non-EU countries in order to be ready for possible zoonotic outbreaks in high-risk environments? 3. What is the Commission doing to strengthen the EU’s preparedness for future zoonotic and emerging infectious disease threats, in particular by supporting the development of antiviral medicines and rapidly adaptable vaccine platforms, including mRNA technologies? (25 August 2026)

The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC), through surveillance activities, identifies outbreaks caused by any novel, unusual and severe pathogen (1). The Commission counts on an early warning and response system (EWRS) for the notification of events (2). Under Regulation (EU) 2022/2371 (3), European Reference Laboratories (4) are established. The EU Health Task Force (5) was mobilised during the Andes virus outbreak. The ECDC is also supporting the African Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) (6) to increase its response capacities. The network of European Public Health Institutes promotes collaboration with non-EU countries, including African countries and their public health institutes and African agencies (including Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention and the African Medicines Agency). It is mobilised for technical assistance, workforce development training and peer to peer cooperation. The Global Health Resilience Initiative (7) is establishing a strategic framework to respond quicker to health threats in an interconnected world. In 2026/2027, the Commission is investing more than EUR 500 million for the development of medical countermeasures, including EUR 225 million for next generation influenza vaccines and EUR 20 million for dengue therapeutics. Under the Medical Countermeasures Strategy (8), the Commission will continue to advance medical countermeasures’ development and strengthen related global health threat intelligence. Hantaviridae were identified as a viral family of high-priority concern for the EU in the Commission’s 2025 Health Threat Prioritisation Assessment (9).

E-10-2026-001873.t: Lack of EU standards on siting large-scale energy storage facilities close to residential buildings
qt: to the Commission Arkadiusz Mularczyk (ECR) Subject:

In the municipality of Lisia Góra (Poland), the authorities are planning to rezone agricultural land for industrial use to accommodate a large-scale energy facility comprising hundreds of thousands of photovoltaic panels, energy storage facilities based on lithium-iron-phosphate batteries, transformer stations and high-voltage infrastructure. In this connection residents are expressing serious concerns about safety and the lack of appropriate regulations. Currently, energy storage facilities are treated in the legislation in the same way as standard industrial facilities, without taking into account their specific features and potential risks. At the same time, there are no clear standards setting minimum distances between this type of infrastructure and residential buildings. In this connection: 1.
Does the Commission plan to introduce uniform EU-wide standards regarding the siting of large-scale energy storage facilities in relation to residential areas?
Do the current EU regulations on energy infrastructure safety take into account the specific features of energy storage facilities based on LFP batteries?
Is the Commission considering legislative initiatives to ensure minimum distances between such installations and residential housing?

(9 July 2026) As recognised by European leaders and reflected in the European Council conclusions of March 2026 (1), it is crucial to accelerate the deployment of renewables and energy storage to reduce dependency on volatile fossil fuel markets and enhance EU security of supply. In that respect, the Commission welcomes initiatives to boost storage facilities. That said, permitting processes for such projects, whether at European, national or local level, should include the assessment of all relevant safety issues and contain a relevant risk assessment, if applicable. Article 12 of Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 (2) sets out the safety requirements for stationary battery energy storage systems placed on the market or put into service, regardless of their chemical composition. The safety parameters are laid out in details in Annex V of the regulation. As part of the legislative proposal in the European Grids Package (currently under discussion by the co-legislators), the Commission has proposed measures to streamline and simplify permit-granting procedures for certain stand-alone storage projects (3). Such streamlining is intended to reduce costs, delays and uncertainty without jeopardising safety and environmental standards. The proposals do not introduce distance rules or other spatial planning requirements, which remain at the discretion of the Member States.

The EU-Canada Digital Partnership aims to promote trustworthy AI and strengthen digital sovereignty, yet some major concerns have yet to be addressed. 1.
Might the Commission’s actions ultimately jeopardise the EU’s push for strategic autonomy by returning it to a state of technological dependence?

at: (English version) to the Commission Benoit Cassart (Renew) (6 May 2026) Subject: EU-Canada Digital Partnership The EU-Canada Digital Partnership aims to promote trustworthy AI and strengthen digital sovereignty, yet some major concerns have yet to be addressed. 1. Might the Commission’s actions ultimately jeopardise the EU’s push for strategic autonomy by returning it to a state of technological dependence? 2.

(29 June 2026) The EU advances a forward-looking vision of digital sovereignty, as outlined in the recently adopted Tech Sovereignty Package, not as protectionism or isolationism, but as the ability to act independently while remaining open and cooperative. In parallel to developing its own technology capacity, the EU is working with like-minded partners like Canada to diversify and increase supply chain resilience and co-create trustworthy and interoperable technology solutions that will reduce reliance on any one company, country or technology. By intensifying research cooperation in emerging and critical technologies like quantum or AI, by advancing regulatory cooperation and the interoperability of technical standards and by enabling joint projects on secure and trusted digital infrastructure such as 5G and digital identities, the EU-Canada Digital Partnership creates framework conditions to build digital ecosystems that serve the needs of our citizens and our businesses, strengthens economic security and avoids overdependencies (1).

E-10-2026-001868.t: EU enterprise losing a EUR 320 million EU-funded public transport contract in Dakar to a Chinese state-backed company
qt: to the Commission Kristoffer Storm (ECR), Sebastian Tynkkynen (ECR), Dick Erixon (ECR) Subject:
EU enterprise losing a EUR 320 million EU-funded public transport contract in Dakar to a Chinese state-backed company

EU public funding should not benefit Chinese state-owned enterprises or companies operating under massive state subsidies. The Global Gateway strategy is intended to be Europe’s answer to China’s Belt and Road Initiative, not a vehicle for indirectly financing it. This case is particularly concerning in the light of previous experiences involving Chinese contractors in similar projects, where aggressively low bids have subsequently led to significant cost overruns and renegotiations. This raises serious doubt as to whether such offers reflect fair competition or strategic underbidding. 1.

Does the Commission not see a fundamental contradiction in presenting Global Gateway as Europe’s strategic answer to China while allowing Chinese state-backed companies to secure flagship EU-supported projects?
Why should European taxpayers accept EU funds being used to favour Chinese statebacked firms?
Will the Commission commit to closing this loophole and ensuring that EU-funded infrastructure projects cannot be awarded to Chinese state-owned or heavily subsidised bidders?

(23 July 2026) The public transport restructuring project aims to cut travel times and pollution by linking Dakar’s peripheral areas to the Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) and Electric Regional Train (TER) corridors. It also seeks to increase ridership of BRT and TER, both operated by European companies (Meridiam and SENTER/SNCF), strengthening the financial sustainability of their concessions while offering affordable, efficient services to the population. The overall project was approved in 2022 (1) and combines EUR 354 million in a Team Europe approach: European Investment Bank (EIB) (EUR 167 million loan), Agence Française de Développement (EUR 100 million loan and EUR 3 million grant), Kreditanstalt für Wiederaufbau (EUR 20 million grant) and the EU (EUR 20 million grant). The management of the EU contribution is entrusted to the EIB. The Senegal-led project follows international rules and covers road infrastructure, depots, rolling stock, and ticketing and passenger information systems via separate tenders. The tender for gas buses is ongoing and under EIB assessment for compliance with its procurement rules; exclusion of statebacked firms is part of the eligibility criteria and is currently being scrutinised. The EIB’s 2025 Strategic Procurement Roadmap globally reinforces sustainability, Environmental Social and Governance (ESG) and quality criteria and helps ensure a level playing field for EU bidders. E-10-2026-001867.t: Compatibility of ‘Diversity Mark’ with EU law on equal treatment, data protection and competition
qt: to the Commission Afroditi Latinopoulou (PfE) Subject:

In Greece, the Government has announced a voluntary business certification scheme (‘Diversity Mark’), which assesses corporate practices regarding gender, age, nationality and sexual orientation. According to public announcements1, the scheme is linked to ESG indicators and probably influences access to funding or other benefits. However, Union law forbids discrimination in the field of employment (Directive 2000/78/EC and Directive 2006/54/EC), allows positive measures only under the strict principle of proportionality (Article 157(4) TFEU and relevant CJEU case law) and Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (General Data Protection Regulation - GDPR) lays down tight restrictions on the processing of sensitive personal data such as sexual orientation and how to prove it. In addition, level playing field issues may arise (Articles 101-107 TFEU) if indirect advantages are granted. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Is such an assessment system compatible with Directives 2000/78/EC and 2006/54/EC, in particular if it indirectly influences recruitment decisions?
How is compliance with the GDPR ensured if the assessment relates to sensitive personal data?
Does linking such certifications to financing or investment advantages constitute a potential distortion of competition?
https://www.esgstories.gr/csr/sima-diaforetikotitas-100-ellinikes-epiheiriseis-oi-protes-stin-koyrsa-pos-thakanete-aitisi.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (15.7.2026) Equality and non-discrimination are founding values enshrined in the EU Treaties, the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights1 and the European Pillar of Social Rights. The Commission reasserted its commitment to diversity and inclusion by renewing its Union of Equality Strategies2, and by continuing supporting organisations in the EU in cooperation with the 27 Diversity Charters. Directive 2000/78/EC does not prevent Member States from maintaining or adopting specific measures to prevent or compensate for disadvantages linked to any of the protected grounds. Directive 2006/54/EC prohibits direct and indirect discrimination on grounds of sex in access to employment, including recruitment, and allows positive action in favour of the underrepresented sex as set out in Article 157(4) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU) and under the conditions of the Court of Justice’s case law. Accordingly, the described voluntary scheme does not appear to contravene either of these Directives. The equality data collection and processing are regulated by anti-discrimination legislation and the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)3. Monitoring and enforcement of the GDPR falls within the competence of national data protection authorities (DPAs) and courts, without prejudice to the Commission’s role as guardian of the Treaties. It is thus for the Greek DPA to examine whether the data processing activities at stake comply with the GDPR. State aid schemes are, by virtue of Article 107 TFEU, distortive for competition and the internal market, therefore subject to compliance with EU’s State aid rules. When designing such schemes, Member States can impose conditions if they are in line with EU law and EU’s international obligations.

E-10-2026-001866.t: Cuts to the CAP in the new MFF and the devastating impact on Greek agriculture
qt: to the Commission Afroditi Latinopoulou (PfE) Subject:

The European Commission has proposed significant cuts and radical restructuring to the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) budget under the next Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF 2028-2034). Although the Commission says certain funds are being ‘protected’, overall funding for agriculture is being reduced significantly in real terms and there will now be strong competition from other EU policy priorities. Bearing in mind that Greek primary production is largely based on direct payments, consists mainly of small and medium-sized farms and depends on sectors such as olive cultivation, livestock farming, fruit and vegetables and on mountainous and island regions facing unique challenges, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

How does it assess the specific effects of the proposed cuts on Greek rural regions, especially in areas with high dependence on the CAP, low competitiveness and increased production costs, and which are strongly affected by climate change?

Does it intend to ensure sufficient and protected funds for Greece that are not reduced in real terms (taking into account inflation and the energy crisis), so that there is no further drop in the income of Greek farmers and livestock farmers?

What specific safeguards does it provide for simplifying bureaucratic procedures, supporting small and medium-sized producers and young farmers in order to prevent further abandonment of Greece’s rural areas and the shrinking of national agricultural production?
at: (English version) to the Commission Afroditi Latinopoulou (PfE) (6 May 2026) Subject: Cuts to the CAP in the new MFF and the devastating impact on Greek agriculture The European Commission has proposed significant cuts and radical restructuring to the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) budget under the next Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF 2028-2034). Although the Commission says certain funds are being ‘protected’, overall funding for agriculture is being reduced significantly in real terms and there will now be strong competition from other EU policy priorities. Bearing in mind that Greek primary production is largely based on direct payments, consists mainly of small and medium-sized farms and depends on sectors such as olive cultivation, livestock farming, fruit and vegetables and on mountainous and island regions facing unique challenges, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

How does it assess the specific effects of the proposed cuts on Greek rural regions, especially in areas with high dependence on the CAP, low competitiveness and increased production costs, and which are strongly affected by climate change?

Does it intend to ensure sufficient and protected funds for Greece that are not reduced in real terms (taking into account inflation and the energy crisis), so that there is no further drop in the income of Greek farmers and livestock farmers?

What specific safeguards does it provide for simplifying bureaucratic procedures, supporting small and medium-sized producers and young farmers in order to prevent further abandonment of Greece’s rural areas and the shrinking of national agricultural production?

(10 July 2026) The future CAP (1) for 2028-2034 aims at improving income support towards those farmers who need it most, particularly smaller and young farmers. Under the proposed multiannual financial framework (MFF) for the period, a minimum of EUR 293.7 billion is ring-fenced under the national and regional partnership (NRP) plans to support farmers’ income. Member States will complement this secured allocation by tapping into the unallocated part of the NRP fund. The Commission also proposed a 10% rural target of Member States’ NRP allocation, beyond the CAP ring-fenced envelope, to strengthen support for rural areas. This translates into EUR 48.7 billion, or over 63.5 billion if the Catalyst Europe loans are included. Member States can access EUR 45 billion from the flexibility amount foreseen for the mid-term review to support measures for farmers and rural areas. For Greece, this means a total amount of approximately EUR 20 billion, if full use is made of the proposed rural spending target and early use of the flexibility amount for its NRP plan, which altogether is slightly higher compared to the current EUR 19 billion. The next MFF introduces a new method to handle inflation at the level of its ceilings. It keeps the annual price adjustment at 2% if EU inflation is between 1% and 3%. If inflation falls below 1% or rises above 3%, the adjustment matches the actual forecast rate. The proposed rules are less burdensome for both farmers and national administrations. Merging of the funds and alignment of the rules allows Member States to design tools for farmers that are more consistent and synergistic. This is accompanied of simplified forms of payments, e.g., for smaller farmers and for investment projects and more proportionate approach to obligations and controls.

E-10-2026-001864.t: Capacity and institutional strengthening of the EU AI Office
qt: to the Commission Fabio De Masi (NI) Subject:

The newly established EU AI Office is tasked with monitoring compliance with the Artificial Intelligence Act but has faced criticism for being inadequately equipped1. According to reports, the office currently has no access to advanced models such as Mythos developed by Anthropic, which is reported to potentially outperform human capabilities in detecting software vulnerabilities and could pose risks to critical infrastructure. While the UK AI Security Institute has already presented a technical analysis, the Commission is not among the organisations that were granted access to the model. Furthermore, the office’s safety unit is reported to be understaffed with around 36 employees and to have a relatively low position within the Commission’s hierarchy. 1.
What specific measures is the Commission taking to strengthen the AI Office in terms of staffing, technical expertise and budget, and what measures does it intend to take in the future?
Does the Commission intend to upgrade the office’s institutional position to ensure that it can act independently and respond in the event of an acute cybersecurity crisis?
What political and diplomatic measures does the Commission intend to take to be able to carry out its own technical analysis of Mythos?
https://www.politico.eu/article/anthropic-hacking-technology-exposes-eu-ai-office-struggles/.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.7.2026) The AI Office is a directorate within the Directorate-General for Communications Networks, Content and Technology (CNECT). The AI Office employs more than 140 staff, including over 40, predominantly technical, staff in the AI Safety Unit, and 35 in the Regulatory and Compliance Unit. There are no plans to change the institutional position of the AI Office within CNECT, which mirrors that of the directorates responsible for enforcing the Digital Services Act1 and the Digital Markets Act2. The Digital Omnibus on AI foresees additional staffing. The next Multiannual Financial Framework, where the Commission has asked for an increase in human resources, will determine staff levels from 2028. On cyber risk, capacity is also located within CNECT’s Directorate for Cybersecurity and the EU Agency for Cybersecurity. Regarding Mythos, Anthropic is a signatory to the EU General-Purpose AI Code of Practice3 and has committed to assess and mitigate systemic risks, including cybersecurity risks, and submit results to the AI Office. As regulator, the AI Office has held technical meetings with Anthropic to support implementation of the Code. The AI Office has unique access to providers’ internal safety practices and is discussing how to improve them. Where appropriate, it may run its own AI evaluations. The Code also requires companies to work with third-party evaluators – organisations that test AI models for capabilities and risks. Once the AI Office’s enforcement powers apply in August 2026, requests for information, and, if necessary, model access will become mandatory. On 9 June 2026, Anthropic made a safeguarded Mythos-class model, Fable 5, publicly available. After US government’s intervention on 12 June 2026, Anthropic withdrew the model.

E-10-2026-001862.t: Administrative fragmentation and environmental assessment of the Escatrón-La Secuita very high voltage power line
qt: to the Commission Vicent Marzà Ibáñez (Verts/ALE) Subject:

Plans for the Escatrón-Els Aubals-La Secuita very high voltage power line – running for around 181 km between Aragon and Catalonia, and with an estimated transmission capacity of 3 000 MW – have been processed in seven separate administrative files, despite being presented as a unitary and interdependent infrastructure. According to various institutional and social complaints, this fragmentation would prevent a full environmental assessment of its cumulative and synergistic effects on the municipalities concerned, Natura 2000 sites, the landscape, agricultural activity and property owners. 1.

Does the Commission consider the administrative fragmentation of a functionally unitary infrastructure to be compatible with EU law, in particular with the Environmental Impact Assessment Act and the Habitats Directive, when this may prevent an integrated assessment of its impacts?

Does the Commission intend to look into whether this project should be subject to a comprehensive environmental assessment that takes into account the line and its associated infrastructure as a whole and its cumulative effects on the areas concerned?
at: (English version) to the Commission Vicent Marzà Ibáñez (Verts/ALE) (6 May 2026) Subject: Administrative fragmentation and environmental assessment of the Escatrón-La Secuita very high voltage power line Plans for the Escatrón-Els Aubals-La Secuita very high voltage power line — running for around 181 km between Aragon and Catalonia, and with an estimated transmission capacity of 3 000 MW — have been processed in seven separate administrative files, despite being presented as a unitary and interdependent infrastructure. According to various institutional and social complaints, this fragmentation would prevent a full environmental assessment of its cumulative and synergistic effects on the municipalities concerned, Natura 2000 sites, the landscape, agricultural activity and property owners. 1. Does the Commission consider the administrative fragmentation of a functionally unitary infrastructure to be compatible with EU law, in particular with the Environmental Impact Assessment Act and the Habitats Directive, when this may prevent an integrated assessment of its impacts? 2. Does the Commission intend to look into whether this project should be subject to a comprehensive environmental assessment that takes into account the line and its associated infrastructure as a whole and its cumulative effects on the areas concerned? (13 July 2026) The purpose of the Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) Directive (1) is to ensure that, before consent is given, projects likely to have significant effects on the environment are made subject to an assessment of their effects. As the Court of Justice of the European Union has consistently held (2), this purpose cannot be circumvented by artificially splitting a project into smaller parts, each falling below the applicable thresholds or criteri a (3), to avoid the requirement for an EIA. Furthermore, the EIA must consider cumulation with other existing, approved, or reasonably foreseeable projects (4). This covers synergistic impacts where combined effects may be significant, even if individual ones are not (5). Under the Habitats Directive (6), projects likely to have significant effects on Natura 2000 require an appropriate assessment prior to authorisation, which is possible only if it is ascertained — also taking into account cumulative effects — that the project in question will not adversely affect the integrity of the sites concerned (7) or, exceptionally, under the strict conditions laid down in the directive (8). Without prejudice to the Commission’s role as guardian of the Treaties, Member States are primarily responsible for the correct implementation of the above provisions. Moreover, the EIA Directive requires Member States to ensure national legal systems make available the appropriate review procedures to interested or impacted parties, which assess compliance with substantive or procedural requirements under the directive. Thus, national means of redress are the most effective to address individual cases of non-compliance and complement the Commission’s strategic enforcement policy focused on systemic and structural issues (9).

E-10-2026-001861.t: Dana in Valencia: ‘build back better’ principle and gaps in RESTORE cohesion mechanisms
qt: to the Commission Vicent Marzà Ibáñez (Verts/ALE) Subject:

The ‘isolated high-altitude depression’ (depresión aislada en niveles altos or dana) in October 2024 caused devastating damage in Valencia. The RESTORE mechanism has made the use of cohesion funds more flexible. However, a recent European Parliament study (PE 776.001) has found that the ‘build back better’ principle has still only been integrated to a limited extent. Some critical gaps remain: a lack of risk-based selection criteria, outdated territorial assessment tools, insufficient monitoring and low community involvement. European funds therefore risk being used to simply restore pre-existing infrastructure without incorporating resilience standards or reducing exposure to extreme events, which will become more common and more intense. In view of the above: 1.

What specific climate resilience and risk reduction indicators does the Commission plan to require from beneficiary states and territories in their monitoring systems to check whether funds produce long-term benefits that go beyond mere restoration?
How will the Commission incorporate the ‘build back better’ principle in its 2028-2034 cohesion regulations in operational terms?

What measures will the Commission take to improve local and territorial institutions’ capacity – particularly in the Valencian Community – and ensure affected communities are truly involved in decisions regarding resilient reconstruction?

(22 June 2026) 1. The European Regional Development Fund (ERDF), in the framework of the RESTORE legislation, supports reconstruction of the areas hit by the DANA through the ERDF national programme of Spain and the ERDF regional programme of the Valencia Region (1). In accordance with RESTORE, national authorities should prioritise operations based on the ‘build back better’ principle. In addition, support to investment in infrastructure is subject to rigorous climate proofing assessment, to guarantee long-term resilience of the infrastructure. 2. Under the Multiannual Financial Framework 2028-2034, support to greener and more resilient communities, infrastructure, economies and natural disaster response will be operationalised via National and Regional Partnership Plans and the EU Facility (2). The Plans should be based on integrated territorial planning and include the obligation to align investments with sustainable development, climate adaptation and disaster resilience. In the event of a natural disaster or another emergency situation, Member States and regions will be able to use different sources of support including under their Plans and the EU Facility. 3. In accordance with Article 8 of Regulation 2021/1060 (3), Member States ensure that key partners, including local authorities, are involved in the design, implementation, monitoring and evaluation of cohesion policy programmes, with support from ERDF technical assistance. This is carried out, among others, through programme monitoring committees involving the Commission. Furthermore, under the ERDF national programme, local authorities, assisted by the Managing Authority, design and implement integrated urban development strategies, including project selection.

E-10-2026-001860.t: Compatibility with EU law of measures based on so-called ‘national priority’
qt: to the Commission Vicent Marzà Ibáñez (Verts/ALE) Subject:

Various initiatives in Member States are introducing criteria for access to public benefits and housing based on the so-called principle of ‘national priority’, via requirements of long-term settlement, continuous residence, or territorial attachment. In some cases, such as Aragon, these criteria have been incorporated into recent government agreements. These measures, although formally neutral, may constitute indirect discrimination within the meaning of Article 2(2)(b) of Directive 2000/43/EC, disproportionately affecting long-term residents protected under Article 11 of Directive 2003/109/EC. According to the case law of the CJEU, indirect discrimination does not require intent but disproportionate effect. Moreover, the explicit designation of ‘national priority’ constitutes a strong indication of a discriminatory objective, incompatible with Articles 20 and 21 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights. In light of the above, 1.
How does the Commission assess the compatibility of these requirements with Article 11 of Directive 2003/109/EC when they may limit the effective exercise of the rights of long-term residents?
Does it consider that policies explicitly aimed at establishing a ‘national priority’ can be compatible with the principles of equality and non-discrimination in EU law?
Does it intend to take action against measures that may constitute indirect discrimination or disproportionate restrictions?
at: (English version) to the Commission Vicent Marzà Ibáñez (Verts/ALE) (6 May 2026) Subject: Compatibility with EU law of measures based on so-called ‘national priority’ Various initiatives in Member States are introducing criteria for access to public benefits and housing based on the so-called principle of ‘national priority’, via requirements of long-term settlement, continuous residence, or territorial attachment. In some cases, such as Aragon, these criteria have been incorporated into recent government agreements. These measures, although formally neutral, may constitute indirect discrimination within the meaning of Article 2(2)(b) of Directive 2000/43/EC, disproportionately affecting long-term residents protected under Article 11 of Directive 2003/109/EC. According to the case law of the CJEU, indirect discrimination does not require intent but disproportionate effect. Moreover, the explicit designation of ‘national priority’ constitutes a strong indication of a discriminatory objective, incompatible with Articles 20 and 21 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights. In light of the above, 1. How does the Commission assess the compatibility of these requirements with Article 11 of Directive 2003/109/EC when they may limit the effective exercise of the rights of long-term residents? 2. Does it consider that policies explicitly aimed at establishing a ‘national priority’ can be compatible with the principles of equality and non-discrimination in EU law? 3.
Does it intend to take action against measures that may constitute indirect discrimination or disproportionate restrictions?

(10 September 2026) EU long-term residents are guaranteed equal treatment with nationals of the host Member State in a number of areas that are exhaustively enumerated in Article 11 of Council Directive 2003/109/EC (1), such as access to social security, social assistance and social protection, and procedures for obtaining housing. In this context, the Court of Justice clarified that Member States cannot unilaterally impose longer residence requirement than the five-year period laid down in Article 4 of that directive (2). A policy establishing a ‘national priority’ for nationals of the Member States needs to comply with the rules of Directive 2003/109/EC that provides for equal treatment between national citizens and holders of the long-term resident status. Council Directive 2000/43/EC (3) prohibits discrimination on the grounds of racial or ethnic origin, but it does not cover differences of treatment based on nationality. It is established case-law that the principle of non-discrimination prohibits not only direct discrimination on grounds of nationality but also all indirect discrimination which, by the application of other criteria of differentiation, leads in fact to the same result (4). Unless justified and proportionate, a provision of national law is indirectly discriminatory if it intrinsically affects nationals of other Member States or third-country nationals more than nationals of the host State, and, as a consequence, places the former in a disadvantaged position. This applies, for example, to a residence condition (5). The Commission understands that the Aragon law is yet to be adopted. The Commission does not comment on draft laws or proposals. Nevertheless, the Commission will continue to monitor the developments to ensure compliance with EU law.

E-10-2026-001859.t: The scenario of non-payment of reparations by Russia and the cost of the loan to support Ukraine
qt: to the Commission Stanisław Tyszka (ESN) Subject:

Under Regulation (EU) 2026/467 of 24 February 2026, Ukraine is required to repay its EUR 90 billion loan within 30 days of Russia’s payment of war reparations. Article 20(2)(l) provides, in turn, that outstanding amounts will remain in place indefinitely in the event of non-payment of reparations. And Article 20(2)(j)(iv) provides for repayment in the event of fraud or corruption on the part of Ukraine. However, the Regulation does not specify a competent authority, and neither OLAF nor the EPPO nor the Court of Auditors have jurisdiction over Ukraine. 1.

Who will be liable for repaying the principal of the loan (EUR 90 billion), and how much, if Russia refuses to pay reparations – will this liability fall on the 24 participating states in proportion to their GNI as a share of the total GNI of the 24 participating states, and when would it become due?
Has the Commission carried out a financial impact assessment for the scenario of Russia not paying reparations, or delaying payment for years, and if so, when will it be made public?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (7.8.2026) Russia – as the aggressor state – is under an obligation to make full reparation for the damage caused by its war of aggression against Ukraine. Council Decision (CFSP) 2022/3351 and Council Regulation (EU) 2022/3342 prohibit transactions related to the management of reserves as well as assets of the Central Bank of Russia, including transactions with any legal person, entity or body acting on behalf of, or at the direction of, the Central Bank of Russia. In its conclusions of 27 June, 17 October and 19 December 2024, the European Council has stated that, subject to EU law, Russia’s assets should remain immobilised until Russia ceases its war of aggression against Ukraine and compensates Ukraine for the damage caused by that war. In that context, the EU has made clear that Russia is responsible for compensating Ukraine for the damage it has caused. The EU has further made clear that Russia’s assets should remain immobilised until Russia, inter alia, compensates Ukraine for the damage caused by that war. Such compensation from Russia will be used by Ukraine to repay the Ukraine Support Loan. Finally, it is noted that the Ukraine Support Loan is a limited-recourse loan, where Ukraine is only due to repay the principal of the loan when Russia pays reparations. Until such time, the principal of the loan will not fall due for payment and – as such – no one will repay the principal of the loan. The Commission closely monitors the EU’s contingent liabilities and their budgetary implications.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dec/2022/335/oj/eng. 2 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/334/oj/eng.

E-10-2026-001858.t: Costs of Poland’s participation in the loan for Ukraine
qt: to the Commission Stanisław Tyszka (ESN) Subject:

Under Regulation (EU) 2026/467 of 24 February 2026, the EU is providing a EUR 90 billion loan to Ukraine, financed through joint EU debt. Repayment of the loan is contingent on the payment of war reparations by Russia. No maturity date has been specified, which basically makes the loan a grant. Pursuant to Article 22 of the regulation, the costs of servicing the loan (interest and administrative costs) can be covered by Ukraine or the EU. Given Ukraine’s financial difficulties, those costs will have to be borne by the EU. Commissioner Serafin has estimated that the costs will amount to around EUR 1 billion in 2027 and around EUR 3 billion per year as of 2028. The costs concerned, as well as any activation of guarantees in the EU budget’s flexibility margin, are to be borne exclusively by the 24 participating countries, depending on the proportion of their GNI in the total GNI of all participating countries. 1.

What is the exact nominal amount, in EUR, which – calculated as a proportion of Poland’s GNI in the total GNI of the 24 participating countries – represents Poland’s full exposure under the guarantee on the capital of this loan?
Exactly how many million euro will the nominal annual cost of servicing the loan amount to for Poland in 2027, and from 2028 onwards?
What interest rate assumptions were made when the costs of servicing the loan were estimated, and how will Poland’s costs change if interest rates rise by one percentage point?
at: (English version) to the Commission Stanisław Tyszka (ESN) (6 May 2026) Subject: Costs of Poland’s participation in the loan for Ukraine Under Regulation (EU) 2026/467 of 24 February 2026, the EU is providing a EUR 90 billion loan to Ukraine, financed through joint EU debt. Repayment of the loan is contingent on the payment of war reparations by Russia. No maturity date has been specified, which basically makes the loan a grant. Pursuant to Article 22 of the regulation, the costs of servicing the loan (interest and administrative costs) can be covered by Ukraine or the EU. Given Ukraine’s financial difficulties, those costs will have to be borne by the EU. Commissioner Serafin has estimated that the costs will amount to around EUR 1 billion in 2027 and around EUR 3 billion per year as of 2028. The costs concerned, as well as any activation of guarantees in the EU budget’s flexibility margin, are to be borne exclusively by the 24 participating countries, depending on the proportion of their GNI in the total GNI of all participating countries. 1. What is the exact nominal amount, in EUR, which — calculated as a proportion of Poland’s GNI in the total GNI of the 24 participating countries — represents Poland’s full exposure under the guarantee on the capital of this loan? 2. Exactly how many million euro will the nominal annual cost of servicing the loan amount to for Poland in 2027, and from 2028 onwards? 3. What interest rate assumptions were made when the costs of servicing the loan were estimated, and how will Poland’s costs change if interest rates rise by one percentage point? (21 August 2026) The Ukraine Support Loan (UASL) provided under Regulation (EU) 2026/467 (1) is a contingent liability for the EU. In line with the firm support of 25 Heads of State and Government in the margins of the European Council of 18 December 2025 (2) and in accordance with Article 20(2)(j) of Regulation (EU) 2026/467, the UASL should be repaid by Ukraine once reparations from Russia are received, and the EU reserves its right to make use of the Russian assets immobilised in the EU to repay the loan, in full accordance with EU and international law. In case the contingent liability materialises, as a last resort, the Commission can call for additional contributions from Member States participating in enhanced cooperation, to the extent necessary to cover it. The share of each Member State would be defined by the gross national income (GNI) key, which is updated annually with the adoption of the annual budget and is available in the financing tables of the annual budget (3). The exact nominal amount in EUR will depend on the applicable GNI key and on the amount of financial assistance disbursed under the UASL. According to Article 22 of Regulation (EU) 2026/467, the EU may provide a borrowing costs subsidy to Ukraine to cover the costs arising from borrowing, if so requested by Ukraine. In accordance with Article 1(2) of Council Regulation (EU) 2026/469 (4), debt service costs are to be covered by the availabilities under the EU budget, first under existing budgetary ceilings and subsequently under other special instruments. If these are not sufficient, the Ukraine Support Loan Instrument may be mobilised over and above the ceilings of the multiannual financial framework in the context of the budgetary procedure. The exact contribution for Poland will depend on the applicable GNI key in the 2027 budget and following years, actual market interest rates and the actual financial assistance disbursed under the UASL. In accordance with Article 332 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, expenditure resulting from implementation of enhanced cooperation, other than administrative costs entailed for the institutions, must be borne by the 24 participating Member States.

E-10-2026-001857.t: Continuity of tertiary education for pregnant women and women with children
qt: to the Commission Giusi Princi (PPE), Antonella Sberna (ECR), Pina Picierno (S&D), Ewa Kopacz (PPE), Eleonora Meleti (PPE), Fulvio Martusciello (PPE), Marco Falcone (PPE), Massimiliano Salini (PPE), Letizia Moratti (PPE), Salvatore De Meo (PPE), Caterina Chinnici (PPE), Flavio Tosi (PPE), Manuela Ripa (PPE), Bogdan Andrzej Zdrojewski (PPE), Niels Geuking (PPE), Elżbieta Katarzyna Łukacijewska (PPE), Loucas Fourlas (PPE), Paulo do Nascimento Cabral (PPE), Gheorghe Falcă (PPE), Andrzej Buła (PPE), Verena Mertens (PPE), Arba Kokalari (PPE), Gabriella Gerzsenyi (PPE), Alessandra Moretti (S&D), Nicola Zingaretti (S&D), Sandro Ruotolo (S&D), Annalisa Corrado (S&D), Sabrina Repp (S&D), Maria Guzenina (S&D), Maria Noichl (S&D), Pasquale Tridico (The Left), Giuseppe Antoci (The Left), Denis Nesci (ECR), Chiara Gemma (ECR), Marco Squarta (ECR), Lara Magoni (ECR), Mariateresa Vivaldini (ECR), Elena Donazzan (ECR), Carolina Morace (The Left), Veronika Cifrová Ostrihoňová (Renew), Lucia Yar (Renew), Jana Toom (Renew), Hristo Petrov (Renew), Leoluca Orlando (Verts/ALE), Catherine Griset (PfE), Cristina Guarda (Verts/ALE), Billy Kelleher (Renew) Subject:

Tertiary education is a key tool for reducing the gender employment gap in the EU, in line with the Gender Equality Strategy 2026–2030. However, progress remains influenced by parenthood: mothers have poorer employment outcomes than women without children, particularly among those with lower levels of education. The challenge concerns not only access to education, but also the continuity and completion of studies, which are often disrupted by pregnancy and motherhood. Ensuring that women can continue their education during these stages is both a matter of social equity and a lever for strengthening women’s participation in skilled employment and enhancing European competitiveness. Some Member States have introduced measures such as childcare services, flexible learning pathways and targeted support, but these remain fragmented. While the EU provides support through programmes such as Erasmus+ and Horizon, a systemic approach that takes parenthood into account in tertiary education policies is still lacking. In the light of the above: 1.
Does the Commission have comparable EU-level data on pregnant students and mothers in tertiary education including data on retention, completion and employment outcomes?
Does the Commission intend to develop a more systemic approach to addressing parenthood in tertiary education policies, including through guidelines or recommendations for Member States?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.7.2026) The Commission does not collect data on pregnant students in higher education as this is considered sensitive health-related information1. Neither does it have comparable EU-level data on students with children in higher education. However, EUROSTUDENT analyses social and economic conditions of student life in Europe. Their latest comprehensive analysis EUROSTUDENT 8 Synopsys of Indicators 2021-20242 studies the characteristics of students with children and some of the challenges they face, such as their chosen type of higher education institution, access route, study intensity and accommodation costs. Ensuring equal and equitable access and opportunities to current and prospective participants from all backgrounds is one of the key horizontal dimensions of the Erasmus+ programme, as stressed in the Programme guide 20263. The programme encourages higher education institutions to prioritise participants with fewer opportunities, such as students with children, when designing mobility projects. It also provides top-up grants for students with fewer opportunities for both long and short-term mobility.
