E-10-2026-001856.t: Practical feasibility of labelling requirements for secondary and tertiary reusable packaging under Articles 12 and 15(8) PPWR
qt: to the Commission Stefan Köhler (PPE), Christian Doleschal (PPE), Norbert Lins (PPE), Alexandra Mehnert (PPE), Michael Gahler (PPE), Sabine Verheyen (PPE), Markus Ferber (PPE), Jens Gieseke (PPE), Angelika Niebler (PPE), David McAllister (PPE), Andrea Wechsler (PPE), Verena Mertens (PPE), Sven Simon (PPE) Subject:

Articles 12 and 15(8) of the Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (PPWR)1 introduce labelling requirements for reusable packaging, including secondary and tertiary packaging such as crates and pallets. However, their application creates a significant challenge for the implementation of the PPWR. Although Article 12 applies to packaging placed on the market after 12 February 2025, items placed before and after that date cannot be distinguished in automated systems. This may lead to a presumption of non-compliance under Article 15(8), effectively requiring retrofitting or withdrawal of large volumes of packaging currently in circulation. Retrofitting appears technologically and logistically unfeasible at scale, with potentially disproportionate costs. This risks penalising well-functioning reuse systems and undermining circular economy objectives. 1.
How does the Commission assess the feasibility of applying Articles 12 and 15(8) to existing secondary and tertiary reusable packaging?
How will the Commission address the inability to distinguish packaging placed on the market before and after 12 February 2025?

Will the Commission consider, in the relevant implementing acts, pragmatic solutions such as targeted derogations or transitional arrangements for existing packaging, where the core objectives of Article 12 are already met?

Regulation (EU) 2025/40 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 19 December 2024 on packaging and packaging waste, amending Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 and Directive (EU) 2019/904, and repealing Directive 94/62/EC (OJ L, 2025/40, 22.1.2025, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2025/40/oj).
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (10.7.2026) Article 12 of the Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation1 (PPWR) introduces harmonised labelling requirements for reusable packaging, including transport packaging. In its guidance document of 30 March 20262, Commission clarified, in point 14, that reusable transport packaging placed on the market before 11 February 2025 does not need to be withdrawn or retrofitted; if it was placed on the market after that date but before the application date of the new labelling requirements, it will have to be retrofitted only in 2032, after the expiry of all the transitional periods to comply with the new harmonised labels. Packaging in open loop reuse systems is exempted from the labelling requirements. The Commission recognises the practical challenges linked to identifying packaging placed on the market before and after 11 February 2025, in particular in automated logistics and reuse systems where packaging circulates for many years. The guidance therefore confirms that the PPWR allows for the provision of information via websites or accompanying documentation in the case of reusable transport packaging in business-to-business situations managed by a system operator in a closed-loop system. The Commission considers that the PPWR should support, and not disrupt, well-functioning reuse systems and circular business models. In preparing the implementing acts under Article 12, the Commission will therefore take account of proportionality, technical feasibility and the need to avoid unnecessary administrative or economic burdens. The Commission will continue engaging with stakeholders and Member States to ensure pragmatic and harmonised implementation solutions, including appropriate transitional approaches where justified.
1 Regulation (EU) 2025/40 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 19 December 2024 on packaging

and packaging waste, amending Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 and Directive (EU) 2019/904, and repealing Directive 94/62/EC, OJ L, 2025/40, 22.1.2025. 2 https://environment.ec.europa.eu/publications/guidance-document-packaging-and-packaging-waste-regulationppwr_en.

E-10-2026-001855.t: Activist exhibition ‘Postcolonial?’ at the House of European History
qt: to the Commission Marieke Ehlers (PfE) Subject:

The House of European History in Brussels is currently hosting the exhibition ‘Postcolonial?’. Instead of offering a nuanced view of history, the museum has opted for an extremely onesided and activist narrative. The focus is solely on ‘brutal oppression’ and the need for a ‘European reckoning’. European citizens are therefore paying to have our own history smeared. This immediately raises questions about the funding of such ideological projects. 1.

Has the Commission contributed (directly or indirectly) to the creation or promotion of the exhibition ‘Postcolonial?’? If so, exactly how much taxpayers’ money was spent on this and from which budget lines?
Does the Commission consider it a good use of European taxpayers’ money to support exhibitions that portray European history in such a one-sided and negative light?

How does the Commission actually ensure that EU-funded cultural projects remain objective, and is it prepared to take measures to ensure that the EU no longer funds this kind of activist project in future?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.8.2026) The Commission does not intervene in the curatorial decisions of the House of European History. The House of European History is an initiative of the European Parliament operating under its administrative and financial responsibility. The Commission’s financial contribution is governed by a Service Level Agreement which expires at the end of the current Multiannual Financial Framework and foresees up to EUR 3 million annually. This amount is not earmarked for any specific exhibition but is a contribution to cover operational costs incurred by the institution.

E-10-2026-001854.t: GBER and the definition of an undertaking in difficulty
qt: to the Commission Anouk Van Brug (Renew) Subject:

The EU needs innovative businesses in order to achieve many of its goals and boost its autonomy. Successful innovative start-ups become scale-ups. However, this does not mean that they have finished developing their product. A business still needs to carry out a lot of research and development (R&D) to become profitable. In this regard, the definition of an undertaking in difficulty within the General Block Exemption Regulation (GBER)1 poses a major obstacle to innovative start-ups and scale-ups achieving success and realising their potential, as public aid will often still be needed for implementing innovative techniques and bringing them to the market. 1.
How will the Commission accommodate innovative scale-ups in the draft revision of the GBER, specifically in the definition of an undertaking in difficulty?
What considerations did the Commission take into account in the revision of the GBER to ensure that innovative businesses are exempted from the definition of an undertaking in difficulty?
Why has the Commission not yet made any adjustments to the definition of ‘own funds’?

Commission Regulation (EU) No 651/2014 of 17 June 2014 declaring certain categories of aid compatible with the internal market in application of Articles 107 and 108 of the Treaty (OJ L 187 26.6.2014, p. 1, http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2014/651/2023-07-01).
at: (English version) to the Commission Anouk Van Brug (Renew) (6 May 2026) Subject: GBER and the definition of an undertaking in difficulty The EU needs innovative businesses in order to achieve many of its goals and boost its autonomy. Successful innovative startups become scale-ups. However, this does not mean that they have finished developing their product. A business still needs to carry out a lot of research and development (R&D) to become profitable. In this regard, the definition of an undertaking in difficulty within the General Block Exemption Regulation (GBER) (1) poses a major obstacle to innovative start-ups and scaleups achieving success and realising their potential, as public aid will often still be needed for implementing innovative techniques and bringing them to the market. 1. How will the Commission accommodate innovative scale-ups in the draft revision of the GBER, specifically in the definition of an undertaking in difficulty? 2. What considerations did the Commission take into account in the revision of the GBER to ensure that innovative businesses are exempted from the definition of an undertaking in difficulty? 3.
Why has the Commission not yet made any adjustments to the definition of ‘own funds’?

(10 July 2026) As a general rule, the General Block Exemption Regulation (GBER) (1) excludes from its scope aid to undertakings in difficulty (UiD). This is because such aid keeps inefficient companies on the market and is particularly distortive of competition. However, there are exceptions to this rule. For example, small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) up to 3 years may receive all types of aid. In addition, start-ups up to 5 years and unlisted SMEs up to 10 years may respectively receive start-up aid (Article 22 GBER) and risk finance aid (Article 21 GBER). The Commission is currently reviewing the GBER with the aim to simplify it. The Commission is aware of the specific growth model of innovative companies and has carefully assessed feedback from the public consultation on this topic. The Commission intends to enable innovative start-ups to receive all types of aid available under the GBER during their early growth phase, including environmental aid and aid with social objectives. The Commission will also clarify the notion of equity, so as to take into account financial instruments absorbing losses on a going concern basis, such as preferred shares, silent participations and convertible bonds. The Commission aims at adopting the revised GBER in December 2026.

Commission Regulation (EU) No 651/2014 of 17 June 2014 declaring certain categories of aid compatible with the internal market in application of Articles 107 and 108 of the Treaty (OJ L 187 26.6.2014, p. 1, http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2014/651/2023-07-01). https://competition-policy.ec.europa.eu/state-aid/legislation/regulations_en .

E-10-2026-001851.t: Human rights and environmental concerns in West Papua under the EU-Indonesia Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement
qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Pernando Barrena Arza (The Left) Subject:

On 23 September 2025, the EU and Indonesia concluded negotiations on a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) and an Investment Protection Agreement, aimed at boosting trade and market access. However, the situation in West Papua does not appear to be adequately reflected in the sustainability impact assessment or the EU’s human rights assessment, despite its importance to Indonesia’s exports of palm oil, liquefied natural gas and metals. This is particularly concerning given the scale of environmental degradation and human rights abuses in the territory. Around 71 % of West Papua’s forest loss has occurred since 2011, with a further 13 % projected by 2036. As of January 2026, 105 878 West Papuans were internally displaced, while access for foreign journalists remains restricted. In 2022, the Commission joined international partners in urging Indonesia to allow a visit by the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights. Indonesia has denied such access since 2018. Given this: 1.
Will the Commission conduct a thorough human rights review of Indonesian rule in West Papua before the CEPA’s ratification?
What steps does the Commission propose to ensure that the Indonesian Government authorises a visit by the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights to West Papua?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (16.6.2026) The EU and Indonesia have had a comprehensive partnership since 2014, including regular dialogue and broad cooperation on human rights. These consultations take place in the framework of the Partnership and Cooperation Agreement1, in which both sides have reaffirmed their commitment to the respect, promotion and protection of democratic principles and fundamental human rights, rule of law, but also respect for the sovereignty, territorial integrity and national unity of the Republic of Indonesia. The EU closely works with Indonesia to defend and deliver on commitments to the protection and promotion of human rights and will continue to do so in close consultation and cooperation with civil society and the National Human Rights Commission in Indonesia. It will continue to urge Indonesia to invite the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights to visit the country. Furthermore, the EU and Indonesia reaffirm, in the Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement2 (whose negotiations concluded in September 2025), their commitment to the Charter of the UN and the principles of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. The Agreement is undergoing legal revision and will next be ratified by both parties.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/EN/legal-content/summary/eu-indonesia-framework-agreement-on-comprehensive-
partnership-and-cooperation.html. 2 https://policy.trade.ec.europa.eu/eu-trade-relationships-country-and-region/countries-and-regions/indonesia/euindonesia-agreements/text-agreements_en.

E-10-2026-001850.t: EU loan of EUR 90 billion to Ukraine: what guarantees are in place for EU taxpayers and industry?
qt: to the Council Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE) Subject:
EU loan of EUR 90 billion to Ukraine: what guarantees are in place for EU taxpayers and industry?

On 23 April 2026, the Council finalised an EU loan of EUR 90 billion to cover Ukraine’s budgetary and defence needs for 2026 and 2027. According to the Council, the loan will be financed through EU borrowing on the capital markets, backed by the EU budget, and is to be repaid by hypothetical war reparations owed by Russia to Ukraine. An indicative amount of EUR 60 billion is to be used to strengthen Ukraine’s capacity to invest in the defence industry. Alongside this, the Security Action for Europe instrument allows up to EUR 150 billion to be loaned to Member States for their defence investments. In view of the above: 1.
What budgetary guarantees are envisaged if Russian reparations do not result in repayment of the loan?
What impact might this have on European taxpayers and on EU budget margins?
What rules are in place to ensure that the orders financed by these instruments will primarily benefit European industry, and French industry in particular, rather than nonEU suppliers?
at: According to Article 24(1) of Regulation (EU) 2026/467, in order to finance assistance under the Ukraine Support Loan, the Commission is empowered, on behalf of the Union, to borrow the necessary funds on the capital markets or from financial institutions under the diversified funding strategy referred to in Article 224 of Regulation (EU, Euratom) 2024/2509. With regard to repayment of the loan, Article 20(2), point (a), of Regulation (EU) 2026/467 establishes that the Ukraine Support Loan is to be a limited recourse loan that becomes due and payable upon the occurrence of any of the repayment triggers defined in point (j), which include the receipt of cash by Ukraine for war reparations, indemnities or any financial settlement from Russia up to the amount of such settlement. Article 1(1) of Council Regulation (EU) 2026/469 makes it possible to mobilise a guarantee for the provision of the financial assistance under Regulation (EU) 2026/467 over and above the ceilings of the multiannual financial framework. The aim of such a guarantee is to ensure that the necessary resources are always available in time to allow the Union to meet all of its financial obligations towards its creditors, as stated in recital 4 of Council Regulation (EU) 2026/469. If the guarantee were to be called in part or in full, contributions from Member States would be provided in accordance with Council Decision (EU, Euratom) 2020/2053 on the system of own resources of the European Union and Council Regulation (EU, Euratom) No 609/2014 on the methods and procedure for making available the traditional, VAT and GNI-based own resources and on the measures to meet cash requirements. In line with Article 4(4) of Regulation (EU) 2026/467, Member States not participating in the enhanced cooperation would be entitled to an adjustment of a call on the guarantee. In this context, whether the guarantee would be called and for how much cannot be determined at this stage.

Finally, Regulation (EU) 2026/467 and Regulation (EU) 2025/1106 set out detailed rules to support the defence industrial capacities of the European Union and Ukraine. For instance, they impose eligibility rules requiring that most of the value of the procured defence products originate in the EU, an EEA-EFTA state or Ukraine. Furthermore, both Regulations provide that, as a rule, legal entities have to be established in the Union, an EEA-EFTA state or Ukraine to be eligible as potential suppliers of defence products. Derogations to the eligibility rules are subject to strict conditions. In the case of the Ukraine Support Loan, procurements from outside the EU, EEAEFTA states or Ukraine are allowed either based on individual derogations adopted by means of a Commission implementing act, where the industries in those countries cannot deliver the required defence products fast enough and/or in sufficient quantities (Article 13(5) of Regulation (EU) 2026/467), or from a third country that has become eligible for that purpose pursuant to a Commission delegated act or to a Council implementing act (Article 13(10) and (11) of Regulation (EU) 2026/467).

E-10-2026-001848.t: Labour inspection: Now even more favourable to big business and its unaccountability
qt: to the Commission Kostas Papadakis (NI) Subject:

The Greek Government (Ν.5297/202611) and the EU recently passed a law promoting a commercialised labour inspection system that is even friendlier towards big business and its unaccountability. By focusing on business profitability it will never fulfil its duty of protecting the lives and safety of workers. In view of the above, where does the Commission stand on the following: 1.

The fact that the guidelines for ‘simplification’ in the name of competitiveness and the reduction of the ‘administrative burden’ lead to employers being informed in advance about inspections, as well as to additional obstacles which hinder inspectors from carrying out their work, the involvement of private individuals against even the 81st Labour Inspection Convention and the dismantling of required health and safety measures, putting workers’ lives at risk?

The fact that employers’ so-called self-compliance and staff cuts in inspection systems – practices which are based on the strategy of ‘independent’ authorities and mechanisms such as the European Labour Authority, and which are being implemented by the governments of the Member States – are contributing to a surge in the number of accidents at work and instances of criminal negligence by employers?

The fact that in the name of competitiveness and the ‘flexibility’ of the 13-hour working day, which only gives workers 11 hours of rest between shifts, as required by EU directives, intensification of work is escalating, retirement age is rising, pensioners are returning to work, the employment of minors is increasing, and explosive conditions are being created, leading to a systematic deterioration in the protection of workers’ lives and health, resulting in an increase in accidents at work and fatal incidents at work?
https://www.e-nomothesia.gr/kat-epikheireseis/nomos-5297-2026.html.

By focusing on business profitability it will never fulfil its duty of protecting the lives and safety of workers. In view of the above, where does the Commission stand on the following: 1.

The fact that the guidelines for ‘simplification’ in the name of competitiveness and the reduction of the ‘administrative burden’ lead to employers being informed in advance about inspections, as well as to additional obstacles which hinder inspectors from carrying out their work, the involvement of private individuals against even the 81st Labour Inspection Convention and the dismantling of required health and safety measures, putting workers’ lives at risk?

The fact that employers’ so-called self-compliance and staff cuts in inspection systems — practices which are based on the strategy of ‘independent’ authorities and mechanisms such as the European Labour Authority, and which are being implemented by the governments of the Member States — are contributing to a surge in the number of accidents at work and instances of criminal negligence by employers?

The fact that in the name of competitiveness and the ‘flexibility’ of the 13-hour working day, which only gives workers 11 hours of rest between shifts, as required by EU directives, intensification of work is escalating, retirement age is rising, pensioners are returning to work, the employment of minors is increasing, and explosive conditions are being created, leading to a systematic deterioration in the protection of workers’ lives and health, resulting in an increase in accidents at work and fatal incidents at work?

(8 July 2026) The EU has not passed a law promoting commercialised labour inspection system. The framework Directive 89/391/EEC (1) and the EU occupational safety and health (OSH) directives (2) set minimum requirements for the protection of workers. They require that the employer safeguards the health and safety of workers in every aspect related to their work, assessing all occupational risks and putting in place the necessary preventive and protective measures. The responsibility for transposing directives and enforcing national legislation lies with Member States. Member States must ensure adequate controls and supervision of the application of the national provisions transposing the EU OSH directives. Member States are competent to decide on the organisation of labour inspectorates and on the nature, frequency, and procedures of such controls. The Commission has not issued guidelines encouraging advance notice of inspection or self-compliance. The Senior Labour Inspectors Committee (SLIC) (3) supports the effective implementation and enforcement of EU OSH legislation at national level. SLIC established a set of EU common principles for OSH labour inspection and produces materials to facilitate the activities of labour inspectors, such as enforcement and awareness raising.

Established by Commission Decision 95/319/EC in 1995 and amended in 2008 (Commission Decision 2008/823/EC).

Directive 2003/88/EC (4) sets out minimum requirements for the protection of the health and safety of workers, including limits to average weekly working time (not more than 48 hours), a right to rest breaks, minimum daily rest (at least 11 consecutive hours) and weekly rest, paid annual leave and extra protection for night workers. It allows a 13-hour working day, under the condition that the average maximum weekly working time of 48 hours is respected.

E-10-2026-001847.t: Funding opportunities for music umbrella organisations in the next MFF
qt: to the Commission Pascal Arimont (PPE) Subject:

In many Member States, regional and national music umbrella organisations represent a central point of contact for amateur music. Through their representative function, numerous opportunities for education and training, public performances and nurturing of young talent, music umbrella organisations make an essential contribution to sustaining and promoting musical and cultural education in the EU. They are also key players in cultural education and potential stakeholders in the wider education system. Article 167 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union states that ‘The Union shall contribute to the flowering of the cultures of the Member States, while respecting their national and regional diversity and at the same time bringing the common cultural heritage to the fore’. The EU’s financial support of cultural organisations plays a key role in fulfilling this commitment. In view of the ongoing negotiations on the multiannual financial framework (MFF) for the period 2028-2034, I would therefore like to submit the following questions on the financial support of music umbrella organisations: 1.
To what extent does the next generation of the Erasmus+ programme for the period 2028-2034 include plans for financial support opportunities for music umbrella organisations?
How does the Commission assess the classification of music umbrella organisations as educational institutions?
What funding opportunities besides Erasmus+ will be available to music umbrella organisations in the forthcoming MFF?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.7.2026) The Commission recognises the important role played by music umbrella organisations in promoting cultural participation, supporting musical education and lifelong learning, nurturing young talent and strengthening social cohesion and cultural diversity across Europe. The Parliament and the Council are currently examining the Commission’s proposal for the Erasmus+ programme 2028-20341. While the future Erasmus+ programme will be accessible to organisations active in the fields of education, training, youth and sport, the criteria for organisations to be considered as eligible will be specified later at the programme implementation stage. The music umbrella organisations will be able to participate in programme calls as long as they meet these eligibility criteria. Pursuant to the EU Treaty, Member States are responsible for the organisation of their education systems, including setting rules on the recognition and definition of educational institutions, and whether or not music umbrella organisations qualify as such, provided that there is no breach of EU law2. The Parliament and the Council are currently also examining the Commission’s proposal for the AgoraEU programme 2028-20343. This proposal builds in particular on the successes of the current Creative Europe programme4. The future culture strand of AgoraEU programme will continue to support the music sector and music organisations.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex:52025PC0549. 2 In line with Article 165 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU), the EU is obliged to

fully respect’ ’the responsibility of the Member States for the content of teaching and the organisation of education systems’. The role of the EU in this particular field is limited to contributing to ‘the development of quality education by encouraging cooperation between Member States and, if necessary, by supporting and supplementing their action’. Finally, it is important to note that Article 165(4) TFEU explicitly excludes any harmonisation of laws and regulations of the Member States in the field of education. 3 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A52025PC0550. 4 https://culture.ec.europa.eu/creative-europe.

qt: to the Commission Jeroen Lenaers (PPE) Subject:

Is a resident of the Netherlands who runs a business as a self-employed person on Belgian territory and is covered by social security in Belgium still entitled to the Flemish childbirth allowance in accordance with Article 18 TFEU in conjunction with Article 49 TFEU and Article 56 TFEU1? In addition to the Flemish initial allowance, supplementary municipal childbirth allowances also exist. Dutch cross-border workers pay their income tax in Belgium, including the surcharge for municipal tax (7 %). The municipality in which the Dutch cross-border worker in question is employed takes the view that such workers are not entitled to the supplementary municipal childbirth allowance. On the basis of Article 7(2) of Regulation (EU) No 492/2011 in conjunction with Article 45 TFEU, is there indirect discrimination in the case referred to above as the Dutch cross-border worker in question is covered by social security in Belgium and, through municipal surcharges – which form part of Belgian income tax – contributes to the financing of the Belgian municipality where he works2?
See judgment of the CJEU of 30 January 1997 in Joined Cases C‑4/95 and C--5/95 Stöber and Pereira v Bundesanstalt für Arbeit. See also Case C‑119/24 [Chefquet].
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (19.6.2026) 1. Articles 49 and 56 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union are not applicable in the present case, since the person concerned is neither hindered nor restricted in pursuing a self-employed activity in Belgium, but is already effectively established and providing services there. The fact that the individual resides in the Netherlands is distinct from the pursuit of an economic activity in Belgium and, accordingly, the grant or refusal of the Flemish childbirth allowance does not, in itself, constitute a restriction on the freedom of establishment or the freedom to provide services within the meaning of the Treaty. 2. With respect to workers who are employed in another Member State, they should in principle enjoy the same social advantages as national workers in the Member State where they work according to Article 7(2) Regulation 492/20111. Two factors should be taken into account: firstly, whether the ‘birth allowance’ granted by local municipalities could be qualified as a social advantage and as such should also be granted to EU mobile workers according to Article 7(2) of Regulation 492/2011 regardless of their place of residence. It is possible that such a residence condition could also be justified by a legitimate aim. Secondly, whether the ‘birth allowance’ granted by local municipalities is to be considered as a family benefit in the meaning of Article 1 (z) of Regulation 883/20042.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/en/ALL/?uri=celex:32011R0492. 2 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2004/883/oj/eng.

qt: to the Commission Gerben-Jan Gerbrandy (Renew) Subject:

I have reviewed the Commission’s reply regarding Written Question P-000703-20261 on the Food and Feed Safety Omnibus, in particular the proposed changes to Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009. I note that Question 3 was not addressed, which leads me to assume that societal costs are not being considered as a parameter for this proposal. In the light of the response provided, I would like to seek clarification on the following points: 1.
The Commission states that the level of protection will increase. On which scientific assessments or criteria is this claim based?

Given the Commission’s recent statement during a Dutch Parliament hearing that ‘the proof is in the pudding’ and thus that it cannot pre-empt conclusions on the proposal’s health and environmental impacts, how does this approach align with the Commission’s claim that the proposal could increase the level of protection, as stated in its answer to Written Question P-00703-2026?

How does it interpret the findings of the scientific assessment commissioned by the Dutch Parliament on the effects of the Food and Feed Safety Omnibus2, and would the Commission be able to provide a written response to this scientific assessment?

I note that Question 3 was not addressed, which leads me to assume that societal costs are not being considered as a parameter for this proposal. In the light of the response provided, I would like to seek clarification on the following points: 1.

Given the Commission’s recent statement during a Dutch Parliament hearing that ‘the proof is in the pudding’ and thus that it cannot pre-empt conclusions on the proposal’s health and environmental impacts, how does this approach align with the Commission’s claim that the proposal could increase the level of protection, as stated in its answer to Written Question P-00703-2026?

How does it interpret the findings of the scientific assessment commissioned by the Dutch Parliament on the effects of the Food and Feed Safety Omnibus (2), and would the Commission be able to provide a written response to this scientific assessment?

(9 July 2026) As outlined in the Staff Working Document (1) accompanying the Food and Feed Safety Simplification Package (2), ‘the current level of protection for human and animal health and the environment will be maintained and can be expected to increase’. In particular, the more agile approach proposed for selecting substances to undergo a full renewal procedure or targeted reassessment is expected to result in an accelerated uptake of new scientific or technical knowledge and a more rapid response to emerging issues. It should also be recalled that in the current system, substantial delays occur in practically all renewal procedures, which therefore also lead to delays in potentially necessary regulatory action. The expected improvements will depend on the outcome of the negotiations between co-legislators and the subsequent implementation. Furthermore, accelerating market access for biocontrol-based plant protection products is expected to lead to the replacement of products containing chemical active substances, improving sustainability and reducing risks from the use of plant protection products. The Commission would like to note that with its proposal it intends to reduce administrative burdens by streamlining procedures, clarifying and harmonising rules and allowing Member States to re-assign limited available resources from renewal procedures to the assessment of innovative solutions. In line with one of the recommendations of the assessment commission by the Dutch parliament, the proposal thus precisely intends to achieve a ‘smarter’ reassessment system to address the systematic delays by proposing structural changes and recognising that significant resource increases in Member States are unlikely.

E-10-2026-001844.t: European capacity for AI-driven large-scale vulnerability research and cybersecurity resilience
qt: to the Commission José Cepeda (S&D), Elio Di Rupo (S&D), Nacho Sánchez Amor (S&D), Sven Mikser (S&D) Subject:

On 7 April 2026, the US company Anthropic announced Claude Mythos Preview, a generalpurpose AI model reportedly capable of autonomously identifying and exploiting large numbers of zero-day vulnerabilities across widely used software systems. This development highlights the growing role of AI in cybersecurity, including both defensive and offensive capabilities, in a context where the EU has identified cyber, AI and electronic warfare as priority capability domains for its security and defence. At the same time, EU cybersecurity policy has so far focused primarily on resilience, risk management and incident response (e.g. the NIS2 Directive1, the Cyber Resilience Act2), rather than on large-scale vulnerability discovery capabilities. Considering this evolving technological landscape: 1.

What measures is the Commission taking to strengthen EU-level capabilities for largescale, AI-assisted vulnerability research, including through the European Cybersecurity Competence Centre, the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity, Digital Europe and Horizon Europe?
How does the Commission assess the risks associated with a potential concentration of advanced vulnerability discovery capabilities in non-EU actors for the security and resilience of the EU?

Does the Commission envisage mechanisms to ensure timely access, sharing and coordinated remediation of critical vulnerabilities identified by advanced AI systems, in particular where they may affect European critical infrastructure?

(12 August 2026) The Commission adopted on 7 July 2026 an Action Plan on Cybersecurity and AI with concrete actions to support Member States and organisations across the EU (1). A key priority is to ensure that Europe steps up its preparedness and resilience in the face of the cybersecurity risks posed by frontier AI. Amongst other things, the action plan proposes concrete actions for the Commission, Member States and the EU Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA) to upgrade existing vulnerability handling processes to be effective in the age of AI-assisted vulnerability discovery. The Commission also tasks ENISA to accelerate patching of vulnerabilities in the area of open source software. A mapping of critical open source components is foreseen under the EU Open Source Strategy (2) and based on a preliminary list informed by agreed criteria, ENISA will pilot a Critical Open Source Resilience Campaign for open source components relevant to critical infrastructure. The action plan also prioritises investments in European AI capabilities for cybersecurity with investments in research and development for homegrown advanced AI-enabled cybersecurity technologies already existing under the Horizon (3) and Digital Europe Programmes (4). It proposes to launch an EU Grand Challenge on AI-assisted vulnerability.

E-10-2026-001843.t: European regulatory gap regarding offensive AI capabilities
qt: to the Commission José Cepeda (S&D), Elio Di Rupo (S&D), Nacho Sánchez Amor (S&D), Sven Mikser (S&D) Subject:

On 7 April 2026, the US company Anthropic announced Claude Mythos Preview, a generalpurpose artificial intelligence (AI) model capable of autonomously discovering and exploiting thousands of zero-day vulnerabilities across major operating systems and web browsers. This case reveals a significant structural gap in the European regulatory framework: Article 2(3) of the AI Act1 expressly excludes from its scope AI systems used for military, defence or national security purposes, regardless of whether the operator is a public or private entity. This means that AI models with state-level offensive capabilities – including those that could potentially be deployed by private actors in defence-related contexts – may operate in a largely unregulated space at EU level. This exclusion creates a regulatory grey area, particularly for dual-use AI systems developed by private actors, whose initial purpose is not military, but which can be integrated into offensive cyber operations or intelligence capabilities. In the light of the above, does the Commission intend to address the gap in Article 2(3) of the AI Act with regard to AI systems with offensive cyber capabilities developed by private actors, in particular when such systems are deployed in decision-making chains affecting the security of the EU and its Member States?

Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 June 2024 laying down harmonised rules on artificial intelligence and amending Regulations (EC) No 300/2008, (EU) No 167/2013, (EU) No 168/2013, (EU) 2018/858, (EU) 2018/1139 and (EU) 2019/2144 and Directives 2014/90/EU, (EU) 2016/797 and (EU) 2020/1828 (Artificial Intelligence Act) (OJ L, 2024/1689, 12.7.2024, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj).
at: (English version) to the Commission José Cepeda (S&D), Elio Di Rupo (S&D), Nacho Sánchez Amor (S&D), Sven Mikser (S&D) (6 May 2026) Subject: European regulatory gap regarding offensive AI capabilities On 7 April 2026, the US company Anthropic announced Claude Mythos Preview, a general-purpose artificial intelligence (AI) model capable of autonomously discovering and exploiting thousands of zero-day vulnerabilities across major operating systems and web browsers. This case reveals a significant structural gap in the European regulatory framework: Article 2(3) of the AI Act (1) expressly excludes from its scope AI systems used for military, defence or national security purposes, regardless of whether the operator is a public or private entity. This means that AI models with state-level offensive capabilities — including those that could potentially be deployed by private actors in defence-related contexts — may operate in a largely unregulated space at EU level. This exclusion creates a regulatory grey area, particularly for dual-use AI systems developed by private actors, whose initial purpose is not military, but which can be integrated into offensive cyber operations or intelligence capabilities. In the light of the above, does the Commission intend to address the gap in Article 2(3) of the AI Act with regard to AI systems with offensive cyber capabilities developed by private actors, in particular when such systems are deployed in decision-making chains affecting the security of the EU and its Member States? (7 July 2026) Pursuant to Article 2(3) of the AI Act (1), the AI Act does not apply to AI systems where and in so far they are placed on the market, put into service, or used with or without modification or where the output is used in the EU exclusively for military, defence or national security purposes, regardless of the type of entity carrying out those activities. Hence, these exemptions apply regardless of whether the deployer is a public or a private entity. Concerning dual-use AI systems, the purpose is not exclusively for military, defence or national security purposes, so the AI Act applies for these systems. This is clarified by Recital 24 of the AI Act: ‘AI systems placed on the market or put into service for an excluded purpose, namely military, defence or national security, and one or more non-excluded purposes, such as civilian purposes or law enforcement, fall within the scope of this regulation and providers […] should ensure compliance with this regulation’. In the Guidelines on Prohibited AI Practices (2), paragraphs 24 and 25 refer to dual-use AI systems falling within the scope of the AI Act and present an example:‘if a company offers a remote biometric identification system for various purposes, including law enforcement and national security, that company […] must ensure its compliance with the requirements in the AI Act’. According to the information available to the Commission, Mythos Preview has been made available to a range of business customers and cyber-defensive organisations in the course of commercial activity and is not placed on the market exclusively for military, defence or national security purposes within the meaning of Article 2(3) AI Act.

E-10-2026-001841.t: Freedom of expression in the EU and lack of transparency in content moderation by online platforms
qt: to the Commission Alexandra Geese (Verts/ALE) Subject:

In recent months, there has been a noticeable trend in which an increasing number of influencers are reporting on their accounts that their content on Instagram is being restricted, their reach reduced or their accounts suspended. The majority of these influencers call out hate speech, share information about sex, women’s health1 and self-determination, or are part of the LGBTQI community2 – such as @sammlungderschande, @klartext_mit_lilly, @womenhelporg in Poland, @stopcryingjosiie and @marieejoan3. They report that their accounts have been subject to reach restrictions or suspended without transparent or reasonable justifications. This situation raises fundamental questions about freedom of expression in the EU. When large, mostly non-European platforms decide what content sees the light of day, it makes it seem that external actors have a significant influence on public discourse in Europe. This affects not only individual users, but democratic debate culture as a whole. Against this background, the question arises as to whether Meta is sufficiently complying with its obligations under the Digital Services Act (DSA), in particular as regards the obligation to provide clear and specific statements of reasons (Article 17), functioning and accessible internal complaint procedures (Article 20) and risk assessment (Article 34). Does the Commission intend to launch formal procedures to assess whether Meta is in breach of these DSA provisions?

at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.7.2026) The Commission is aware of the issue referred to and is in touch with relevant stakeholders. Under the Digital Services Act (DSA)1, providers of very large online platforms (such as Facebook and Instagram) and of very large online search engines, are required to diligently identify, analyse and assess systemic risks stemming from their services and to put in place effective measures to mitigate the identified risks. This includes risks of any actual or foreseeable negative effects for the exercise of fundamental rights such as freedom of expression and of information, including media pluralism, and on electoral processes and civic discourse. In 2024, the Commission initiated proceedings under the DSA against Meta, including in relation to its suspicion that the recommender systems of Facebook and Instagram demote political content and that Meta had failed to put in place an effective internal complainthandling system2. On 24 October 2025, the Commission preliminarily found Meta, inter alia, in breach of its obligation to put in place an effective internal complaint-handling system3. The Commission is not in a position to comment on the details of its investigation, beyond publicly available information. The Commission is continuously monitoring Meta’s compliance with the DSA, engages in regulatory dialogue, and has sent requests for information, including on Meta’s obligations under the DSA regarding the assessment and mitigation of systemic risks, the provision of clear and specific statements of reason, and transparency obligations4. It is Meta’s responsibility to comply with all applicable EU and national laws, including the DSA and other provisions protecting freedom of expression.

E-10-2026-001839.t: Ship safety in the Strait of Hormuz
qt: to the Commission Elissavet Vozemberg-Vrionidi (PPE) Subject:

According to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre, at least two commercial ships, including a Greek vessel, came under fire on 22 April 2026 after coordinated attacks by Iran’s Revolutionary Guards Corps as they were coming through the Strait of Hormuz. This incident raises serious concerns about the safety of shipping and the protection of seafarers amid broader geopolitical unrest, resulting in continued disruption to maritime trade flows and limiting freedom of navigation, in a region that plays a critical role in the global supply chain. Given the crucial role shipping plays in ensuring the EU’s energy security and economic resilience, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
What steps does it intend to take, in coordination with the Member States, to ensure the safety of ships and the protection of crews at sea on trade routes?
How does it intend to ensure the freedom of European shipping and prevent further escalation on maritime routes of strategic importance, such as the Strait of Hormuz?
How does it intend to ensure that European shipping continues to be a pillar of EU energy security, especially in the context of rising geopolitical tensions?

How does it intend to ensure that European shipping continues to be a pillar of EU energy security, especially in the context of rising geopolitical tensions?

(14 August 2026) The Commission is deeply concerned by attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz and strongly condemns any action that puts seafarers at risk. The safety of crews at sea is the priority, and attacks on civilian vessels are unacceptable. The EU works closely with Member States and partners to monitor threats in high-risk areas. The EU supports the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) framework, which sets clear rules on maritime safety and the protection of seafarers. The IMO adopted resolutions calling for the implementation of an evacuation corridor. The Commission works closely with IMO to operationalise it as soon as the security situation allows. The EU is committed to freedom of navigation under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, which sets the framework within which all activities in the oceans and seas must be carried out. The EU calls on all states to refrain from any action that interferes with freedom of navigation in straits used for international navigation in order to avoid escalation. As regards the conditions for the reopening of traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, the Commission opposes any mechanism that would link a transit passage to the payment of a fee or charge, which would constitute a breach of international law and create a precedent hampering global freedom of navigation The EU is conducting the EU Naval Force (EUNAVFOR) operation ASPIDES (1) in the Red Sea and in the Gulf of Aden, where it provides support for merchant vessels. The EU will contribute to international efforts in the Strait of Hormuz when the security situation allows, subject to a decision by the Member States. Any such contributions would support and complement the wider multinational effort.

E-10-2026-001838.t: Systemic corruption scheme within the Slovak Paying Agency (PPA)
qt: to the Commission Tomáš Zdechovský (PPE) Subject:

The Committee on Budgetary Control (CONT) has repeatedly identified serious deficiencies in the management and control of EU agricultural funds in Slovakia, including risks of corruption, conflicts of interest and political interference. The ‘Dobytkár’ case exposed a systemic corruption scheme within the Slovak Paying Agency (PPA), involving bribes of up to 20-25 % of allocated common agricultural policy (CAP) subsidies. Norbert Bödör has been charged in connection with this case. Recent reports indicate new cases in which CAP subsidies have been granted to entities allegedly linked to Bödör, with suggestions that these funds were approved by individuals with personal or business connections to the beneficiaries.1 These developments raise concerns that previously identified networks of influence may still be active. 1.
How does the Commission assess the allocation of EU funds to entities linked to a person charged in a major corruption case involving CAP funds?
Does the Commission consider that these new developments indicate a persistent failure to address conflicts of interest under Article 61 of the Financial Regulation?

What concrete measures will the Commission take to protect the EU budget, including possible financial corrections, suspension of payments or referrals to the European AntiFraud Office and the European Public Prosecutor’s Office?

(7 July 2026) The Commission is assessing the legislative changes adopted by Slovakia on the provision of support in agriculture and rural development. This assessment is currently ongoing. Member States are required to respect EU legislation, including provisions on the management of conflict of interests (1). As guardian of the Treaties, the Commission monitors the situation and may take appropriate action to protect the EU’s financial interests if conflicts of interest have not been adequately addressed. The Commission has taken concrete measures to protect the EU budget. In 2020, the management and control system of the Slovak Paying Agency was found to be gravely deficient, leading to a financial correction of almost EUR 28 million. The Commission is following up on these matters in the framework of ongoing audits, in which it also assesses the compliance of the Paying Agency, responsible for the management and control of Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) payments with accreditation criteria. The Commission is also assessing rule of law developments in Slovakia in its annual Rule of Law report, including as regards Slovakia’s anti-corruption framework. The Rule of Law report has repeatedly identified agriculture to rank among Slovakia’s high-risk corruption areas. When the Commission becomes aware of any suspected case of fraud, corruption or illegal activity affecting the EU budget, it informs the European Anti-Fraud Office (OLAF) and/or the European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO) in accordance with applicable EU legislation.

E-10-2026-001837.t: Loophole in EU sanctions – Irish alumina exports to Russia
qt: to the Commission Arkadiusz Mularczyk (ECR) Subject:

I wish to raise concerns about a significant loophole in the EU’s regime of sanctions against Russia. Irish refinery Aughinish Alumina is still exporting a considerable share of its alumina production (as much as 50-70 %) to Russian giant Rusal. This raw material is then processed to form the aluminium used by Russia’s defence sector to produce missiles, drones and other military equipment used against Ukraine. While Australia banned such exports as far back as March 2022, in the EU this trade is continuing legally and thus shoring up Russia’s war machine. In light of the above: 1.
Is the Commission planning to include alumina exports in the EU’s 21st package of sanctions against Russia, and what is the state of play in this regard?
What is its assessment of the impact of this export on the productive capacity of Russia’s military and industrial complex?
What action has it taken against Ireland to ensure that the Aughinish refinery is not directly supporting the Russian aggression?

(15 July 2026) The EU has adopted a wide range of restrictive measures (‘sanctions’) on Russia, including far-reaching trade restrictions in several economic sectors. The measures in place reflect a careful balance between the EU’s determination to impact Russia’s ability to finance its war of aggression and to limit, to the extent possible, negative impacts on Member States and their industry. This assessment is conducted with even greater care when certain critical raw materials subject to supply shortages are concerned. EU restrictive measures are regularly reviewed. Any decision to amend the existing sanctions is for the Council to take by unanimity. The Commission is aware of allegations in press reports that alumina of EU origin may ultimately feed the Russian militaryindustrial complex. As a general observation, it should be noted that indirect economic support (making economic resources available) to listed Russian arms manufacturers is prohibited. The Member States are, first and foremost, responsible for the implementation of EU restrictive measures and investigation of potential circumvention of prohibitions under EU sanctions. The Irish authorities are responsible for investigating these allegations. The Commission is monitoring the implementation and enforcement of EU sanctions across all Member States.

E-10-2026-001836.t: Circumvention of EU sanctions via Russian-linked ‘shadow airlines’ operating from non-EU countries
qt: to the Commission Tomáš Zdechovský (PPE) Subject:

Recent investigative reporting1 has revealed that Russian-linked ‘shadow airlines’ are allegedly operating from Algeria and conducting covert logistics missions, potentially circumventing EU sanctions and export controls. These activities raise serious concerns regarding the effectiveness of EU restrictive measures, the risk of dual-use goods being transferred, and the broader implications for the credibility of the EU’s security and foreign policy. At the same time, EU agencies such as Eurojust and bodies such as the European Public Prosecutor’s Office warn about the growing complexity and cross-border nature of organised crime and sanctions circumvention, while also facing increasing workloads and resource constraints. 1.
What concrete steps is the Commission taking to monitor and disrupt the use of non-EU hubs, such as Algeria, for the circumvention of EU sanctions by Russian-linked entities?
How does the Commission assess the role of ‘shadow aviation networks’ in facilitating sanctions evasion and potential transfers of dual-use or military-relevant goods?

Does the Commission intend to propose strengthening the mandates and resources of EU agencies and bodies (e.g. Europol, Eurojust and the European Public Prosecutor’s Office) to improve their capacity to investigate and prosecute increasingly sophisticated sanctions circumvention schemes?
https://www.defensenews.com/global/europe/2026/04/30/investigation-russian-shadow-airlines-usealgeria-as-base-for-secretive-missions/. 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (15.7.2026) The Commission is aware of the operation of Russian state-affiliated aircraft flying into various third countries. Whilst these countries are not bound by EU sanctions, the EU Sanctions Envoy, David O’Sullivan, conducts diplomatic outreach to third countries identified as potential hubs for sanctions circumvention to find mutually agreeable solutions to avoid that EU sanctions are circumvented via these jurisdictions. The EU has also reinforced its anti-circumvention toolbox and has also imposed direct sanctions on companies based in third countries, that have been found to circumvent sanctions. The EU sanctions law also contains obligations on EU operators to ensure sanctioned goods are not supplied to Russia via third parties, such as deploying enhanced due diligence when trading in Common High Priority (CHP) items1 or inserting a ‘no re-export to Russia’ clause in their export contracts. EU agencies and bodies such as Europol, Eurojust and the European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO) are already competent to deal with sanctions violation cases, within their respective competences. Their role and cooperation have also been recognised in the Directive on the criminalisation of the violation of EU sanctions2. The Commission is taking due consideration of the reflections of a possible extension of the EPPO’s competence to sanctions violations in the context of the possible revision of the EPPO Regulation3, which the Commission may propose at the end of 2026. The Commission has also adopted a proposal for a revision of the Europol Regulation4 to equip the Agency with new capabilities to enhance its support to Member States’ investigations in targeting criminal assets owned by individuals and legal entities subject to EU sanctions.

E-10-2026-001835.t: Applications that assign values to food products using algorithms
qt: to the Commission Aldo Patriciello (PfE) Subject:

The widespread growth across the EU of applications that assign summary values to food products using algorithms that have not been approved by any European or national health authority, based on standardised parameters relating to 100 grams of the product and without taking into consideration any actual portions and the overall nutritional context, is having potentially harmful and distortive effects on the agri-food industry, and is especially detrimental to high-quality ‘Made in Italy’ products. These simplistic and reductive methods give results that are highly prejudicial to designation of origin products, which can mislead and create alarm among consumers. This poses a real risk of economic and reputational damage being caused to entire EU production chains. The absence of scientific checks and approval raises serious questions over consumer protection, transparency of information and the proper functioning of the internal market. Given the above, can the Commission answer the following questions: 1.
Will it take action to ascertain whether the algorithms used are scientifically reliable and transparent?
Does it consider it acceptable for tools that have not been approved to be allowed to influence consumer choices?
Is it planning to take steps to tackle these potentially deceptive and anti-competitive practices?

(16 September 2026) EU sectoral legislation on food (1) does not apply to digital apps that assign values to food products using algorithms (2). However, traders providing such apps to consumers must respect EU consumer law. Specifically, Directive 2005/29/EC (3) prohibits misleading practices that affect consumer decisions about products. The enforcement of national rules transposing that directive lies with national authorities, which can cooperate within the framework of the Consumer Protection Cooperation Network established by Regulation (EU) 2017/2394 (4). The Commission does not approve individual digital services, such as food apps, nor does it assess the reliability or transparency of their algorithms. Notwithstanding the above, the Commission is fully committed to safeguarding traditional and high-quality food products, particularly those protected as/by geographical indications (GI) (5). Regulation (EU) 2024/1143 (6) provides for protection of GIs against use, misuse, imitation or evocation, and against any other false or misleading indications and any other practice liable to mislead consumers as to the true origin of a product. The enforcement of these rules is the responsibility of Member States.

Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 25 October 2011 on the provision of food information to consumers, amending Regulations (EC) No 1924/2006 and (EC) No 1925/2006 of the European Parliament and of the Council, and repealing Commission Directive 87/250/EEC, Council Directive 90/496/EEC, Commission Directive 1999/10/EC, Directive 2000/13/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council, Commission Directives 2002/67/EC and 2008/5/EC and Commission Regulation (EC) No 608/2004 (OJ L 304, 22.11.2011, p. 18, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2011/1169/2025-04-01). This regulation applies only to ‘food businesses,’ defined as ‘any undertaking, whether for profit or not and whether public or private, carrying out any of the activities related to any stage of production, processing and distribution of food.’ Digital applications that assign summary values to food products using algorithms are usually not owned or managed by food business operators. Directive 2005/29/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 11 May 2005 concerning unfair business-to-consumer commercial practices in the internal market and amending Council Directive 84/450/EEC, Directives 97/7/EC, 98/27/EC and 2002/65/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council and Regulation (EC) No 2006/2004 of the European Parliament and of the Council (OJ L 149, 11.6.2005, p. 22, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2005/29/oj). Regulation (EU) 2017/2394 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 12 December 2017 on cooperation between national authorities responsible for the enforcement of consumer protection laws and repealing Regulation (EC) No 2006/2004 (OJ L 345, 27.12.2017, p. 1, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2017/2394/oj). As set out in Regulation (EU) 2024/1143 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 11 April 2024 on geographical indications for wine, spirit drinks and agricultural products, as well as traditional specialities guaranteed and optional quality terms for agricultural products, amending Regulations (EU) No 1308/2013, (EU) 2019/787 and (EU) 2019/1753 and repealing Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012 (OJ L, 2024/1143, 23.4.2024, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1143/oj). https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1143/oj/eng.

The Commission promotes networks and experience sharing among the competent national authorities in view of raising awareness on misleading practices and making the fight against them more effective. While no specific assessment on food rating apps has been conducted so far, the Commission continuously monitors digital tools that could affect the food supply chain, including their potential impact on competition. Should concrete evidence of anticompetitive practices emerge, the Commission will consider further action under EU competition rules.

E-10-2026-001834.t: Cross-border dissemination of fraudulent online financial advertising and identity theft
qt: to the Commission Paolo Inselvini (ECR), Alessandro Ciriani (ECR), Nicola Procaccini (ECR) Subject:

According to Europol’s Internet Organised Crime Threat Assessment (IOCTA), cybercrime in the European Union causes estimated losses of over EUR 5.5 billion per year. Investment scams are one of the most devastating types of financial fraud, with average losses per victim ranging from EUR 20 000 to EUR 50 000 and double-digit annual growth rates in several Member States. ESMA and national supervisory authorities report a significant increase in fraudulent schemes disseminated via online commercial communications, including advertisements misappropriating the identity of third parties and mimicking editorial content. Such practices are characterised by systematic repetition, a high capacity for algorithmic targeting and a marked cross-border dimension, with critical issues regarding the identification of advertisers, the traceability of financial flows and the timeliness of removal measures. Can the Commission therefore say: 1.
How effective it believes the current EU framework (in particular Directive 2005/29/EC and Directive 2011/83/EU) to be in combating such practices on a cross-border basis?

What operational and coordination tools it intends to strengthen with a view to improving the identification of advertisers and cooperation between competent authorities and financial supervisory authorities?
Whether it believes it necessary to propose further binding measures to ensure the more rapid cessation and prevention of fraudulent online commercial communications?

Investment scams are one of the most devastating types of financial fraud, with average losses per victim ranging from EUR 20 000 to EUR 50 000 and double-digit annual growth rates in several Member States. What operational and coordination tools it intends to strengthen with a view to improving the identification of advertisers and cooperation between competent authorities and financial supervisory authorities?

(17 September 2026) Directives 2005/29/EC and 2011/83/EU protect consumers in business-to-consumer relations. They are enforced by public enforcement authorities and through individual and collective court actions. Cybercrime and investment scams are first and foremost criminal offences tackled by law enforcement bodies. EU consumer legislation requires traders to provide their identity to consumers in every invitation to purchase, including in advertising. Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 on a Single Market For Digital Services and amending Directive 2000/31/EC on Digital Services Act (DSA) (1) requires online platforms to allow the report of illegal content including illegal advertisement. Where providers are made aware of illegal content, they must remove it expeditiously. They must also provide clear information about the person on whose behalf an ad is shown, who paid for it, the targeting parameters and where applicable, how users can modify them. On 30 April 2024, the Commission initiated formal proceedings against Meta, including over concerns that it had failed to diligently assess and mitigate the dissemination of deceptive advertisements, including those facilitating financial scams. In September 2025, it sent requests for information to Google Play and Google Search related to scams and fraudulent content. Subject to final adoption by the co-legislators, a Payment Services Regulation could complement the DSA in tackling online scams involving the fraudulent offer of financial services (2). On 18 November 2025, the European Board for Digital Services launched a coordinated initiative to ensure a long-term, systemic approach to tackling online scams and fraud. The Commission plans to adopt by end of 2026 an action plan against digital fraud focusing on prevention, disruption and cooperation to support and protect victims (3).

E-10-2026-001832.t: Increased support for vaccination in the forthcoming livestock strategy and revision of EU animal welfare legislation
qt: to the Commission Aurelijus Veryga (ECR) Subject:

In the light of the upcoming EU livestock strategy and revision of EU animal welfare legislation, I want to highlight the importance of vaccination. It is a cost-effective way to prevent livestock diseases, improve animal welfare, support farm productivity and protect public health from the risks of zoonotic diseases. Vaccination should therefore be integrated into EU policies, with stronger support for research, funding for vaccination programmes and better access for farmers to the tools and knowledge needed for effective implementation. Therefore, I ask the Commission: 1.
Will it consider increased support for vaccination as a central component of the forthcoming EU livestock strategy and the revision of EU animal welfare legislation?
What measures are being proposed to support farmers in adopting vaccination practices, especially in the light of emerging animal diseases and the need for improved biosecurity?
How does it plan to ensure that vaccination programmes contribute to both the welfare of animals and the protection of public health, particularly in preventing zoonotic diseases?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (10.7.2026) EU legislation on animal health1 recognises that prevention is better than cure. Vaccination is one of the additional tools that Member States can choose to implement under EU legislation to ensure the most efficient prevention or control of certain major listed animal diseases in accordance with the specific EU rules that have been recently revised2, in order to facilitate their use in a more efficient manner. Regarding research and innovation on livestock vaccines, a number of projects were and are funded under the framework programmes for research and innovation Horizon 20203 and Horizon Europe4 (e.g. VAX4ASF5, SAPHIR6, REPRODIVAC7). Furthermore, a European Partnership on Animal Health and Welfare8, bringing together organisations from 19 EU Member States and 5 countries associated to Horizon Europe, aims to develop new vaccines or improving existing vaccines, including adjuvants and immunemodulators. The Partnership has already led to new projects in this area. The EU is technically and financially supporting Member States’ efforts, notably through the Single Market Programme,9 by deploying vaccine banks and co-financing vaccination plans. Furthermore, the Commission is participating in the discussions of the World Organisation for Animal Health in relation to the promotion of vaccination use, including its recently launched ‘Prevent Forum’.10

The Spanish Court of Auditors approved its audit report on the 2024 General State Account, which states that the Government allocated resources from the Recovery and Resilience Facility, NextGenerationEU, to cover current expenditure. at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.7.2026) The Commission is aware of the observations made by the Spanish Court of Auditors in its report, particularly the Court’s finding that the legal grounds for certain internal budgetary transfers ‘should have been more thoroughly justified’. These observations do not call into question the lawfulness of the use of the Recovery and Resilience Fund under EU law. Rather, they pertain to procedural requirements under Spanish budgetary law, which are a matter of national accountability. Under the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF) Regulation1, Member States receive EU funds following the achievement of milestones and targets, which reflect progress in implementing eligible reforms and investments, in line with requirements laid down in Council implementing decisions. E-10-2026-001829.t: Funding for model communities of children with disabilities and their parents
qt: to the Commission Georgios Aftias (PPE) Subject:

Thousands of parents of children with disabilities in Europe and Greece are anxious about their children’s future once they themselves are gone. They seek solutions to the trauma and sense of abandonment which their children will feel. Trusting in your sensitivity, the parents of individuals with disabilities request the following: 1.

Funding for model community centres. Model projects have already been presented to EU governments. Parent and child grow old together with the child participating in the parent’s life right up until the end. Parents sacrifice themselves for their children and the centre guarantees continuity of care.
Funding for the creation of model education centres for parents of children with disabilities.
The introduction of personal assistants for people with disabilities within living centres, Europe-wide, providing the relevant financial support.

Funding for the creation of European villages for children with disabilities, where parents do not just drop their children at the gate but can actually live there with them, as workers, volunteers and/or carers.
The establishment of 14 May as the Europe-wide day celebrating mothers of children with disabilities.
Given the above, can the Commission say: 1.
Will it provide financial support for this profoundly human endeavour?
Will it give the green light for Member States to fund this social need with European funding?

E-10-2026-001828.t: Commission meeting with Taliban on deportations of Afghans
qt: to the Commission Tineke Strik (Verts/ALE), Saskia Bricmont (Verts/ALE), Catarina Vieira (Verts/ALE), Per Clausen (The Left), Raquel García Hermida-Van Der Walle (Renew), Cecilia Strada (S&D), Erik Marquardt (Verts/ALE), Jan-Christoph Oetjen (Renew), Mélissa Camara (Verts/ALE), Hannah Neumann (Verts/ALE), Jana Toom (Renew), Marie-Agnes Strack-Zimmermann (Renew), Damien Carême (The Left), Marie Toussaint (Verts/ALE), Katrin Langensiepen (Verts/ALE), Dainius Žalimas (Renew), Kathleen Van Brempt (S&D), Leoluca Orlando (Verts/ALE), Konstantinos Arvanitis (The Left), Alessandra Moretti (S&D), Pernando Barrena Arza (The Left) Subject:

On 21 April 2026, Euractiv reported1 that the Commission, the European External Action Service and selected Member States intend to host a Taliban delegation for discussions on the deportation of Afghan nationals. 1.

Does the Commission recognise the Taliban as the legitimate government of Afghanistan? If not, with what status or in what capacity will this delegation be received for discussions on the return of Afghan nationals?

Does the Commission consider the guiding principles for future engagement as established by the Council to be fulfilled, particularly with regard to respect for all human rights, including the full enjoyment of the rights of women and girls, as well as respect for the rule of law, freedom of speech and media freedom, with specific attention to human rights defenders? If not, what are the grounds for deviating from these guiding principles, and has the Council given its formal consent?

In the light of Parliament’s competence in the area of justice and home affairs under the Treaties, does the Commission intend to formally provide Parliament with full transparency regarding this meeting, including details of the participating Member States, the agenda and the outcomes?
https://www.euractiv.com/news/exclusive-brussels-to-host-taliban-in-talks-on-afghan-deportations/.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.8.2026) The Commission was asked by 20 Member States and Schengen associated countries in a letter signed by their Ministers in October 2025, to coordinate contacts on returns with the de facto authorities, to ensure a coherent European approach. Their focus is on the return of persons posing a threat to public order or national security. Returns to Afghanistan need to be addressed in a comprehensive and coordinated manner, bearing in mind the challenges arising from the acute humanitarian and human rights situation in Afghanistan. The Commission and Sweden, on behalf of interested Member States, co-chaired a technical-level meeting with representatives of the de facto authorities of Afghanistan responsible for return and readmission, following technical-level discussions in Kabul, in January 2026. The technicallevel meeting aimed to give Member States the opportunity to address practical aspects of the readmission process. 15 Member States participated in the meeting. Operational engagement with the de facto authorities is in line with the Council conclusions of 15 September 20211 and 20 March 20232. It does not constitute nor imply recognition, which remains conditioned upon progress on the EU’s established benchmarks, especially counterterrorism, inclusive governance and human rights, with particular concern for the rights of women and girls. The EU has strongly condemned the systemic violation of human rights. The Commission acts in full respect of the Council conclusions and of its international obligations and will continue its unwavering support to all persons concerned by those violations of human rights. Following a briefing by the Commission and the European External Action Service to the Coordinators of the Committee on Civil Liberties, Justice and Home Affairs (LIBE), the Commissioner for Internal Affairs and Migration held an exchange of views with the LIBE Committee on 14 July 2026 on all aspects of the technical-level meeting.
