E-10-2026-001827.t: Extension of derogations from the stability pact to energy investments and energy cost disparities in the EU
qt: to the Commission Anna Maria Cisint (PfE) Subject:

Lasting energy cost disparities among the Member States continue to seriously hamper the industrial competitiveness of a number of Member States, upsetting the balance between the internal market and the principle of economic cohesion. In particular, some economies appear to be exposed to structurally higher burdens that undermine productive capacity, investment and employment. Against the current backdrop of the energy transition and geopolitical instability, extraordinary and coordinated instruments at EU level need to be adopted increasingly urgently. This is where the proposal put forward by the Minister for the Economy, Giancarlo Giorgetti, comes into play; at the Eurogroup meeting, he argued in favour of extending the derogations from the stability pact – already provided for in strategic sectors such as defence – to the energy sector. In the light of the above: Will the Commission, with a view to recognising their strategic role in EU security and competitiveness, consider extending the stability pact’s flexibility clauses to investments in the energy sector?
at: (English version) to the Commission Anna Maria Cisint (PfE) (5 May 2026) Subject: Extension of derogations from the stability pact to energy investments and energy cost disparities in the EU Lasting energy cost disparities among the Member States continue to seriously hamper the industrial competitiveness of a number of Member States, upsetting the balance between the internal market and the principle of economic cohesion. In particular, some economies appear to be exposed to structurally higher burdens that undermine productive capacity, investment and employment. Against the current backdrop of the energy transition and geopolitical instability, extraordinary and coordinated instruments at EU level need to be adopted increasingly urgently. This is where the proposal put forward by the Minister for the Economy, Giancarlo Giorgetti, comes into play; at the Eurogroup meeting, he argued in favour of extending the derogations from the stability pact — already provided for in strategic sectors such as defence — to the energy sector. In the light of the above: Will the Commission, with a view to recognising their strategic role in EU security and competitiveness, consider extending the stability pact’s flexibility clauses to investments in the energy sector? (31 July 2026) The Commission recognises that Member States might face significant upfront fiscal costs in order to accelerate the implementation of measures that ensure Europe’s long-term energy security. The Commission has been stressing that, in responding to the surge in energy prices recorded after the outbreak of the conflict in the Middle East, it is essential to heed the lessons from the past energy crisis, when Member States incurred large fiscal costs by providing mostly untargeted support, and often distorting the price signals which are important to reduce demand of fossil fuels. It is also crucial to protect the credibility of the EU fiscal framework, which works as a guarantor of public finance sustainability. Against this background, on 3 June 2026, the Commission announced that measures that strengthen the structural resilience of the European energy system and accelerate the transition away from fossil fuels may benefit from the existing flexibility within the fiscal framework. (1) Upon request by the Member States, the scope of the current national escape clause for defence could be broadened to accommodate the measures undertaken since the outbreak of the conflict in the Middle East to reduce the dependence on imported fossil fuels and thereby contribute to Europe’s security and defence. The flexibility allowed for measures aimed at reducing dependency on fossil fuels would be capped at 0.3% per year with a cumulative maximum of 0.6% of gross domestic product until 2028. Existing fiscal sustainability safeguards remain fully in place.

E-10-2026-001826.t: Protection of downstream steel and aluminium-processing industries against combined effects of CBAM, global overcapacity and non-EU country subsidies
qt: to the Commission Susana Solís Pérez (PPE), Esther Herranz García (PPE) Subject:

EU downstream manufacturers using steel and aluminium face a compounding cost crisis. The phase-out of free allowances under the EU’s emissions trading system raises domestic material prices, while the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) and forthcoming steel overcapacity regulation increase import costs. The EU has recognised unfair pricing of these inputs through the placing of anti-dumping duties on Chinese steel and aluminium of up to 50 % and 24.5 % respectively, yet these measures do not extend to finished products made from those same subsidised materials. Non-EU competitors benefit from export tax rebates of up to 10 % on finished products exported to the EU, without facing equivalent charges, undercutting EU producers. The Commission has failed to extend the CBAM to downstream products such as cookware, cutlery and household articles (HS 7615, 7323, 7324, 8211, 8212, 8213, 8214). 1.
How does the Commission intend to protect downstream manufacturers facing rising input costs, while their finished products receive no protection?

Given that trade defence measures protect upstream but not downstream producers, how will the Commission address the competitive distortion amplified by subsidised non-EU exports of finished products, and is it considering an anti-subsidy investigation into these products?
What monetisable compensation does the Commission envisage for downstream producers whose embedded costs originate upstream, and who do not qualify for the decarbonisation fund?
at: (English version) to the Commission Susana Solís Pérez (PPE), Esther Herranz García (PPE) (5 May 2026) Subject: Protection of downstream steel and aluminium-processing industries against combined effects of CBAM, global overcapacity and non-EU country subsidies EU downstream manufacturers using steel and aluminium face a compounding cost crisis. The phase-out of free allowances under the EU’s emissions trading system raises domestic material prices, while the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) and forthcoming steel overcapacity regulation increase import costs. The EU has recognised unfair pricing of these inputs through the placing of anti-dumping duties on Chinese steel and aluminium of up to 50% and 24.5% respectively, yet these measures do not extend to finished products made from those same subsidised materials. Non-EU competitors benefit from export tax rebates of up to 10% on finished products exported to the EU, without facing equivalent charges, undercutting EU producers. The Commission has failed to extend the CBAM to downstream products such as cookware, cutlery and household articles (HS 7615, 7323, 7324, 8211, 8212, 8213, 8214). 1. How does the Commission intend to protect downstream manufacturers facing rising input costs, while their finished products receive no protection? 2. Given that trade defence measures protect upstream but not downstream producers, how will the Commission address the competitive distortion amplified by subsidised non-EU exports of finished products, and is it considering an anti-subsidy investigation into these products? 3. What monetisable compensation does the Commission envisage for downstream producers whose embedded costs originate upstream, and who do not qualify for the decarbonisation fund? (14 July 2026) To address the risk of downstream carbon leakage, the Commission has proposed to extend the scope of the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) to selected steel and aluminium-intensive downstream goods. The proposal includes intermediate goods and final consumer goods. As the CBAM is an environmental measure, the list of goods to be included in its scope needs to be justified on the basis of clear carbon leakage risks. To this end, only products meeting the criteria set for identifying the carbon leakage risk and climate relevance were included in the proposal. The Commission also proposed a Temporary Decarbonisation Fund (1) to address remaining risks of carbon leakage. While targeting operators of EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) installations producing CBAM goods identified as being at increased remaining risk of carbon leakage, the Fund may also decrease associated downstream costs. The proposed Fund is temporary, addressing the production years 2026 and 2027, while a structural solution to remaining carbon leakage risk will be sought as part of the review of the EU ETS (2). The Commission is committed to protecting EU producers from unfairly traded imports and defends EU industry against dumped or subsidised imports that cause injury. There are over 240 measures in place a third of which concern steel, the sector most protected by measures, including a safeguard measure. These cover steel products from rolled steel to ropes and cables to wind towers. Aluminium products are also covered by measures ranging from aluminium extrusions to finished products like road wheels. The Complaints Office of Trade Defence Services can be contacted by any industry in the steel or aluminium value chains to discuss the procedures (3).

Proposal for a regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council establishing the Temporary Decarbonisation Fund, COM(2025)990, accessible at https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A52025PC0990. E-10-2026-001824.t: Provisional application of the trade part of the EU-Mercosur agreement and security of the agricultural sector and transparency of the economic impact
qt: to the Commission Piotr Müller (ECR) Subject:

The agreement (EMPA and iTA) between the EU and Mercosur was signed on 17 January 2026. The trade part of the agreement will be provisionally applied as from 1 May 2026. This is controversial as the European Parliament has suspended final approval of the agreement and referred it to the Court of Justice of the EU. Although the EU has recently adopted legislation which in theory will protect our agricultural sector, fundamental questions remain unanswered. Citizens and farmers still have serious and unresolved concerns about food safety, the hidden costs for the EU budget and the overall impact of the agreement on our agricultural economy. In light of the above: 1.
In view of the Commission’s announcement regarding the strengthening of sanitary and phytosanitary controls, what will be the specific procedures and scope of the new import control task force?

Will the planned EUR 6.3 billion crisis reserve for farmers, provided for under the future CAP budget for 2028-2034, be redeployed from other existing funding lines, and if so, from which ones exactly?

Is the Commission planning to have a comprehensive macroeconomic assessment carried out of the impact that the provisional application of the agreement will have, taking into account the effect on employment in regions dependent on agriculture, as well as on the EU’s GDP and trade balance, and to publish the results before the final vote in the European Parliament?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.6.2026) The Import Control Task Force1 does not replace official controls performed by Member States or create parallel structures, but builds on existing expert and working groups within the framework of import controls (namely, groups on veterinary import controls, food and feed of non-animal origin, plant health, e-commerce and the Official Controls Regulation2), bringing them together in a coordinated and strategic way. Its added value lies in improving harmonised implementation in the EU, identifying gaps or inconsistencies and proposing joint actions where an EU-level approach is best. The Unity safety net3, amounting to EUR 6.3 billion over the 2028-2034 period, will serve as a dedicated tool within the EU Facility to address market disturbances and ensure agricultural market stability. It replaces the current agricultural reserve, doubling its budget and supporting a stronger crisis response for farmers. The funding is integrated into the next Multiannual Financial Framework, without redeploying resources from other EU priorities. The Commission has already conducted an economic analysis of the negotiated outcome of the EU-Mercosur Partnership Agreement4, published in June 2025. This assesses the agreement’s projected impacts on key areas, including gross domestic product, trade flows, employment and sectoral effects, with particular attention to sensitive sectors such as agriculture. No further comprehensive macroeconomic assessment is planned specifically for the phase of the EU-Mercosur Interim Trade Agreement’s provisional application. The existing analysis, alongside ongoing monitoring, will inform stakeholders.

E-10-2026-001822.t: European Scientific Working group on Influenza and EU policy: tasks and spheres of influence
qt: to the Commission Gerald Hauser (PfE) Subject:

The European Scientific Working group on Influenza is a European public health network organisation founded in 1992. Its core objective is reducing the impact of acute respiratory viral infections in Europe. It is financed by EU funds, scientific research funding and pharmaceutical companies (e.g. AstraZeneca, GSK, Sanofi). Alongside the major respiratory viruses (such as influenza, RSV, COVID-19 and hMPV), its areas of focus include vaccination strategies, pandemic preparedness, the monitoring of viruses and health communication. According to ChatGPT, the European Scientific Working group on Influenza has established itself over the years as an important voice in European influenza and pandemic policy, as an interface between science and policy and as a platform for awareness and communication. ChatGPT also states that the organisation’s role was bolstered particularly in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic. 1.
Which tasks are carried out by the European Scientific Working group on Influenza that are not or cannot be performed by the EU administration?
In the past ten years, how much funding has the EU provided each year?
What specific tasks and role did this NGO fulfil during the COVID-19 pandemic and vaccination campaigns?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (24.8.2026) 1. The European Scientific Working Group on Influenza1 (ESWI) is a network organisation that aims to reduce the burden of influenza and other acute respiratory viruses in Europe. It organises conferences, roundtables, webinars, etc. The EU administration proposes and implements laws, manages the EU budget, ensures policies are correctly applied, and represents the EU globally, all tasks that a network of academics cannot do. 2. The ESWI was a participant in the PREPARE project2 under the Seventh Framework programme for Research3. The legal commitment was initially signed in 2013, and the project implementation took place between 1 February 2014 and 31 January 2021. ESWI’s anticipated EU funding under the grant was for an amount of EUR 80,362. 3. The Commission did not entrust any specific task or role to ESWI during the COVID-19 pandemic.

E-10-2026-001821.t: E-fuels, feasibility, regulatory flexibility and geopolitical resilience
qt: to the Commission Beatrice Timgren (ECR) Subject:

The EU’s regulatory framework for reducing CO2 emissions from passenger cars and light commercial vehicles, notably Regulation (EU) 2019/631 as amended by Regulation (EU) 2023/851, sets ambitious targets for the transition to zero-emission mobility. However, key challenges remain, including limited consumer uptake of electric vehicles, insufficient charging infrastructure and high energy costs, raising concerns about feasibility, costeffectiveness and global competitiveness. At the same time, heightened geopolitical tensions, including war-related disruptions and risks to critical energy chokepoints such as the Strait of Hormuz, underline the importance of diversifying energy pathways and strengthening resilience in fuel supply chains. Synthetic fuels (e-fuels) are increasingly discussed as a complementary pathway that could help reduce emissions, leverage existing assets and provide greater flexibility in the transition. 1.

How does the Commission assess the availability and scalability of e-fuels, including from international markets, in contributing to CO2 emissions reduction targets, particularly given geopolitical supply risks?
Is the Commission considering adjusting the regulatory framework to enable a technologically neutral and cost-efficient integration of e-fuels while strengthening resilience to external shocks?
How does the Commission ensure that regulatory conditions do not create unintended barriers to e-fuels, especially where they could support industrial competitiveness and energy security?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (31.7.2026) Accelerating the transition to clean, secure and affordable energy is an economic and security imperative. The Commission considers that renewable and low-carbon fuels including electrofuels (eFuels) play a critical role to decarbonise hard-to-abate sectors such as aviation and maritime transport. However, eFuel production and in particular electro-Sustainable Aviation Fuels (eSAF) production is a nascent technology. Through the Sustainable Transport Investment Plan (STIP)1 and AccelerateEU2, the Commission aims to accelerate investment in renewable and low-carbon fuel production in general with a particular focus on promoting eSAF production in the EU or securing supplies of sustainable transport fuels to the EU, through Clean Trade and Investment Partnerships3, aiming at facilitating investments in third countries. The Commission’s recent proposal to amend the CO2 emission standards for cars and vans4 is aligned with the targets and objectives established in the European Climate Law5. It maintains a strong market signal for zero-emission vehicles, while providing vehicle manufacturers with more flexibility to achieve their targets, including based on the placement on the market of sustainable renewable fuels.

strategic-approach-boost-renewable-and-low-2025-11-05_en. 2 https://energy.ec.europa.eu/strategy/accelerateeu-strengthen-eu-energy-resilience_en. 3 https://policy.trade.ec.europa.eu/news/eu-and-south-africa-sign-first-ever-clean-trade-and-investmentpartnership-ctip-2025-11-20_en. 4 COM/2025/995 final. 5 http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2021/1119/oj.

E-10-2026-001819.t: EU-UK agreement on Gibraltar and safeguards for Spanish sovereignty
qt: to the Commission Alvise Pérez (NI) Subject:

On 11 June 2025, the EU and the United Kingdom announced a political agreement on Gibraltar. The draft treaty was published only months later and establishes a specific framework for the movement of persons and goods, which includes provisions removing controls at the land border and stipulating that Schengen checks are to be carried out at Gibraltar’s port and airport. At the same time, the agreement leaves unchanged the legal positions of Spain and the United Kingdom on sovereignty and jurisdiction, while preserving specific arrangements for British military facilities and personnel. Given that Gibraltar remains outside the EU and Schengen, but would have a stable and exceptional connection to the Schengen area and the European market: 1.

How will the Commission ensure that this arrangement does not amount to the longterm normalisation of Gibraltar’s exceptional economic, fiscal and logistical position, without progress on sovereignty?
What concrete guarantees will Spain retain regarding border, customs, fiscal and security control?
How does the Commission justify special treatment for British military facilities and personnel within a framework designed to facilitate civilian and economic integration?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.7.2026) 1. The EU-UK Agreement in respect of Gibraltar states that it shall be without prejudice to the legal positions of Spain and the UK with regard to sovereignty and jurisdiction and shall not constitute the basis for any assertion or denial of sovereignty including in legal proceedings or otherwise. 2. The Agreement includes strong safeguard measures preserving the integrity of the EU’s Single Market, the Customs Union and the EU’s financial interests as well as the security of the Schengen area. In relation to the movement of persons, Spain will perform full Schengen checks at Gibraltar airport and port, and will be responsible for border surveillance, including in adjacent waters, in line with relevant EU rules. In relation to the movement of goods, the Agreement provides for customs checks and controls to be carried out by Spanish authorities or jointly by the authorities of Spain and the authorities of the UK, in respect of Gibraltar, and for strong cooperation on tax and customs matters, anti-fraud and tobacco provisions with the authorities of the UK, in respect of Gibraltar. 3. In order to ensure the continuation of the proper functioning of the military base in Gibraltar, the Agreement includes rules for the entry and exit of goods as well as for the entry and exit of military personnel, the civilian component and their family members going to the military base.

E-10-2026-001818.t: Alleged misuse of NextGenerationEU funds by the Spanish Government
qt: to the Commission Jorge Buxadé Villalba (PfE) Subject:

According to media reports, the audit of the 2024 national accounts by the Spanish Court of Auditors has led to unprecedented internal dissent – with criticism of a number of directors and a negative vote – due to alleged irregularities in the use of NextGenerationEU funds.1 In particular, funding received from the European Union but not yet allocated may have been redirected to the Treasury’s single account and thus used for ordinary government spending – including pension payments – that has no connection to the investment and reform goals of the Recovery and Resilience Facility. This information compounds existing concerns over how these funds are managed in Spain, with low implementation, a lack of transparency and corruption linked to EU-funded contracts, such as the ‘Koldo case’ or PSOE case. 1.
Does the Commission consider that, if confirmed, these facts could constitute an irregularity in the use of EU funds?
Does it intend to ask the Spanish Government for clarification?
Could these irregularities justify the suspension, reduction or cancellation of future disbursements?

https://www.tcu.es/export/sites/portal/repositorio2/DECLARACION-CUENTA-GENERAL-DELESTADO/2026/I1677.pdf. https://euractiv.com/es/news/espana-en-el-punto-de-mira-por-utilizar-fondos-dela-ue-destinados-a-la-recuperacion-pospandemica-para-cubrir-el-deficit-de-las-pensiones/.

E-10-2026-001817.t: Management of cross-regional wind farms – SPA-SAC site Capanne di Marcarolo
qt: to the Commission Gaetano Pedulla' (The Left) Subject:

Site IT 11800261 is a vital migratory route between Piedmont and Liguria for protected bird species. Although its managing authority rejected a project to install wind turbines, applying the construction ban in the buffer zone provided for in the duly approved site-specific measures – a one-kilometre area from the site’s perimeter along the regional border – Ligurian authorities chose to bypass the environmental impact assessment (EIA) process for that project. Their reasoning was that the Piedmont-approved conservation measures did not apply outside the administrative boundaries and that the buffer zone could not extend into Ligurian territory. The Council of State2 ruled that the site-specific measures were perfectly valid. The Habitats Directive (92/43/EEC) and the Birds Directive (2009/147/EC) mandate protection and ecological integrity in Natura 2000 sites beyond regional borders. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Should special areas of conservation (SAC) measures also be considered binding for neighbouring regions whose territory falls within the buffer zone?
Is the bypassing of the EIA for wind turbines in areas adjacent to protected migration routes – simply because of regional administrative boundaries – a breach of Article 6 of Directive 92/43/EEC?

Does the Commission believe that administrative fragmentation can legitimise the circumvention of EU environmental constraints, making it possible to build infrastructure with an impact on Natura 2000 areas simply by moving projects across a regional border?

Designated by means of Decision 2006/3261/EC. Judgment of the Council of State, Section IV, 7 January 2025, No 68: https://www.studiolegalemescia.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/Consiglio-di-Stato-Sezione-QuartaSentenza-07-gennaio-2025-n.-68.pdf.
at: (English version) to the Commission Gaetano Pedulla' (The Left) (5 May 2026) Subject: Management of cross-regional wind farms — SPA-SAC site Capanne di Marcarolo Site IT 1180026 (1) is a vital migratory route between Piedmont and Liguria for protected bird species. Although its managing authority rejected a project to install wind turbines, applying the construction ban in the buffer zone provided for in the duly approved site-specific measures — a one-kilometre area from the site’s perimeter along the regional border — Ligurian authorities chose to bypass the environmental impact assessment (EIA) process for that project. Their reasoning was that the Piedmont-approved conservation measures did not apply outside the administrative boundaries and that the buffer zone could not extend into Ligurian territory. The Council of State (2) ruled that the site-specific measures were perfectly valid. The Habitats Directive (92/43/EEC) and the Birds Directive (2009/147/EC) mandate protection and ecological integrity in Natura 2000 sites beyond regional borders. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Should special areas of conservation (SAC) measures also be considered binding for neighbouring regions whose territory falls within the buffer zone?
Is the bypassing of the EIA for wind turbines in areas adjacent to protected migration routes — simply because of regional administrative boundaries — a breach of Article 6 of Directive 92/43/EEC?

Does the Commission believe that administrative fragmentation can legitimise the circumvention of EU environmental constraints, making it possible to build infrastructure with an impact on Natura 2000 areas simply by moving projects across a regional border?

(10 July 2026) The Habitats Directive (1) requires the establishment of the necessary conservation measures for Special Areas of Conservation (2), where the deterioration of habitats and disturbance of the species for which the site was designated must be avoided (3). It also requires that plans or projects not directly connected with or necessary to the management of the site, but likely to have an impact on the site must undergo an appropriate assessment of its implications in view of the site’s conservation objectives (4). Member States and regions must therefore not only consider the impacts of plans and projects on sites under their responsibility, but also of those located outside the affected site, including in other regions or Member States, whenever such impacts cannot be excluded due to the nature of the plan or project, the geographic location of the site or the ecological requirements of the habitats and species protected in that site. The Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) Directive (5) covers windfarms projects but this does not imply an automatic obligation for an EIA assessment. Member States must determine if a project should be assessed due to its likely impacts on the environment, considering the relevant selection criteria, including the location of the project (6).

Designated by means of Decision 2006/3261/EC. Judgment of the Council of State, Section IV, 7 January 2025, No 68: https://www.studiolegalemescia.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/Consiglio-di-StatoSezione-Quarta-Sentenza-07-gennaio-2025-n.-68.pdf. Council Directive 92/43/EEC of 21 May 1992 on the conservation of natural habitats and of wild fauna and flora. OJ L 206, 22.7.1992, pp. 7-50. Article 6(1) of the Habitats Directive. Article 6(2) of the Habitats Directive. Article 6(3) of the Habitats Directive. Directive 2011/92/EU, Annex II, point 3(i). For example, in view of impacts on Natura 2000 sites.

Regional or administrative boundaries are not part of the location criterion. Undertaking an appropriate assessment (7) is without prejudice to the requirements under the EIA Directive. Member States are responsible for ensuring the respect of these provisions within their national administrative set up and, as confirmed by consolidated case law (8), administrative allocation of competences within a Member State cannot be used to circumvent EU law and its coherent application.
In accordance with the Habitats Directive. C-96/81, Commission v. Netherlands (1982) ECLI:EU:C:1982:192, para. 12.

E-10-2026-001816.t: Reports on plans for a meeting to establish cooperation between the Afghan Taliban regime, the Commission and EU countries, including Sweden
qt: to the Commission Alice Kuhnke (Verts/ALE), Isabella Lövin (Verts/ALE), Pär Holmgren (Verts/ALE), Abir Al-Sahlani (Renew), Jonas Sjöstedt (The Left), Hanna Gedin (The Left) Subject:

Media reports1 suggest that the Commission, the EEAS and a number of Member States – including Sweden – are planning to host a delegation of representatives of Afghanistan’s Taliban regime in Brussels for talks on deporting more Afghan nationals. Apparently, the Commission had at first been reluctant to organise the meeting on its own initiative, but changed its position after Sweden signalled its support. Johan Forsell, Sweden’s Minister for Migration, claims that the Commission has asked Sweden to host the meeting, citing Sweden’s ‘successful’ work on returns. We firmly believe that the meeting would help legitimise the Taliban regime, and we therefore take these reports very seriously. With that in mind: 1.
What specific role has Sweden played in the Commission’s decision to organise this meeting, and when and on what basis was the decision taken to allow Sweden to host it?

What is the Commission’s justification for holding such a meeting, when the Taliban regime has banned girls and women from accessing education and systematically breaches basic human rights, and has the Council formally approved a departure from the guiding principles of the EU’s engagement with Afghanistan?

Is the Commission considering offering financial support to the Taliban regime in exchange for cooperation on returns, and if so, does the Commission consider the Taliban regime to be a legitimate partner for cooperation?
https://www.euractiv.com/news/sweden-confirms-role-in-eu-outreach-to-taliban-over-afghan-deportations/ https://www.etc.se/inrikes/regeringen-bjuder-in-talibanerna-vill-utvisa-fler-till-afghanistan
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.8.2026) The Commission was asked by 20 Member States and Schengen associated countries in a letter signed by their Ministers in October 2025, to coordinate contacts on returns with the de facto authorities, to ensure a coherent European approach. Their focus is on the return of persons posing a threat to public order or national security. Returns to Afghanistan need to be addressed in a comprehensive and coordinated manner, bearing in mind the challenges arising from the acute humanitarian and human rights situation in Afghanistan. The Commission and Sweden, on behalf of interested Member States, co-chaired a technical-level meeting with representatives of the de facto authorities of Afghanistan responsible for return and readmission, following technical-level discussions in Kabul, in January 2026. The technicallevel meeting aimed to give Member States the opportunity to address practical aspects of the readmission process. 15 Member States participated in the meeting. Operational engagement with the de facto authorities is in line with the Council conclusions of 15 September 20211 and 20 March 20232. It does not constitute nor imply recognition, which remains conditioned upon progress on the EU’s established benchmarks, especially counterterrorism, inclusive governance and human rights, with particular concern for the rights of women and girls. The EU has strongly condemned the systemic violation of human rights. The Commission acts in full respect of the Council conclusions and of its international obligations and will continue its unwavering support to all persons concerned by those violations of human rights. The EU maintains a stable presence in Afghanistan and continues to provide life-saving assistance in Afghanistan through its various funding programmes, supporting vulnerable communities and sustaining essential services. No conditionality is attached to delivering humanitarian aid in Afghanistan.
1 https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-11713-2021-REV-2/en/pdf. 2 https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-7264-2023-INIT/en/pdf.

E-10-2026-001815.t: Treatment of clean terminal equipment under State aid rules
qt: to the Commission Kris Van Dijck (ECR) Subject:

In its reply to Written Question P-004500/20251, the Commission indicated that certain decarbonisation investments in ports can be supported under Articles 36 and 36b of the General Block Exemption Regulation (Regulation (EU) No 651/2014 (GBER)), including through the notion of ‘vehicles’. However, in the draft revised GBER (in which the relevant provisions are now reflected in Article 54), the definition of ‘vehicle’ has been further specified across transport sectors, but does not explicitly include mobile terminal equipment. At the same time, support for port superstructures appears to remain limited, except in cases linked to intermodality under the Land and Multimodal Transport Guidelines and Transport Block Exemption Regulation. This raises questions regarding the treatment of clean mobile terminal equipment where the primary objective is decarbonisation. 1.
Why do the Land and Multimodal Transport Guidelines and the Transport Block Exemption Regulation not cover aid granted solely for clean mobile terminal equipment?
Why does the draft revised GBER, in particular Article 54 thereof, define the notion of ‘vehicle’ across transport sectors in detail, but not include mobile terminal equipment?
https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/P-10-2025-004500_EN.html.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (10.7.2026) The answer to the first question is the legal basis for the Land and Multimodal Transport Guidelines and for the Transport Block Exemption Regulation. The legal basis for the Land and Multimodal Transport Guidelines and the Transport Block Exemption Regulation is Article 93 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (‘aid for the coordination of transport’). The concept of ‘coordination of transport’ implies an intervention by public authorities that is aimed at guiding the development of the transport sector in the common interest. By contrast, aid with a primary environmental objective, such as decarbonisation, is assessed under Article 107 (3) (c) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union. It therefore does not fall within the scope of the Land and Multimodal Transport Guidelines and of the Transport Block Exemption Regulation but is assessed under the Commission’s ‘Guidelines on State aid for climate, environmental protection and energy 2022’, if such aid is not blockexempted under Commission Regulation (EU) No 651/2014. On the second question, the Commission’s review of the General Block Exemption Regulation is ongoing. The outcome of the revision cannot be prejudged at this stage.

E-10-2026-001814.t: Safeguarding press freedom and protecting journalists in the EU
qt: to the Commission Jaume Asens Llodrà (Verts/ALE) Subject:

There are growing signs in the EU of a shrinking civic space, driven by pressures and sanctions that may hinder journalistic work, including surveillance practices, administrative obstacles, and a particularly hostile environment when covering protests, the war in Gaza and other conflicts. Protecting press freedom requires that security measures, sanctions and judicial cooperation fully respect the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union and ensure proportionality, transparency and effective avenues for redress. 1.

How does the Commission assess the deterioration of press freedom in the EU, including the use of sanctions, strategic lawsuits against public participation (SLAPPs), accreditation restrictions, surveillance and the criminalisation of protest coverage, and what concrete measures will it take to prevent reprisals and guarantee effective protection and remedies for journalists?

What actions can the Commission take to help ensure that, in the coverage of armed conflicts, no journalist in the EU is investigated, detained, sanctioned or expelled for their reporting, and to guarantee clear guidelines and safeguards in the application of sanctions and judicial cooperation so as to avoid penalising journalistic work?
at: (English version) to the Commission Jaume Asens Llodrà (Verts/ALE) (4 May 2026) Subject: Safeguarding press freedom and protecting journalists in the EU There are growing signs in the EU of a shrinking civic space, driven by pressures and sanctions that may hinder journalistic work, including surveillance practices, administrative obstacles, and a particularly hostile environment when covering protests, the war in Gaza and other conflicts. Protecting press freedom requires that security measures, sanctions and judicial cooperation fully respect the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union and ensure proportionality, transparency and effective avenues for redress. 1. How does the Commission assess the deterioration of press freedom in the EU, including the use of sanctions, strategic lawsuits against public participation (SLAPPs), accreditation restrictions, surveillance and the criminalisation of protest coverage, and what concrete measures will it take to prevent reprisals and guarantee effective protection and remedies for journalists? 2. What actions can the Commission take to help ensure that, in the coverage of armed conflicts, no journalist in the EU is investigated, detained, sanctioned or expelled for their reporting, and to guarantee clear guidelines and safeguards in the application of sanctions and judicial cooperation so as to avoid penalising journalistic work? (16 July 2026) The European Media Freedom Act (1) provides effective safeguards for media and journalists against political interference and surveillance, protecting their editorial independence and journalistic sources. Provisions on editorial independence, whereby media service providers of news and current affairs must guarantee that editorial decisions are taken freely, apply since February 2025. Those regarding safeguarding journalistic sources apply since August 2025. Its correct implementation is a priority for the Commission. The European Democracy Shield (2) recognises the essential role of free and independent media and journalists as public watchdogs and foresees additional measures for their protection. The Anti-SLAPP Directive (3) protects them from strategic lawsuits against public participation (SLAPPs) in civil cross border cases. The Commission will update the 2021 Recommendation on the safety of journalists (4) and review the impact of the 2022 Recommendation on protecting journalists from manifestly unfounded or abusive court proceedings (5). The former encourages Member States to investigate and prosecute all criminal acts against journalists in an impartial independent, effective, transparent and timely manner, making full use of existing legislation. It also calls for better safety of journalists during protests and demonstrations. The EU restrictive measures are designed and applied in line with the Charter of Fundamental Rights (6). The EU pays particular attention to avoiding unintended effects on legitimate journalistic work. All measures are imposed following unanimous decision by Member States. The implementation and enforcement are principally their responsibility, with a monitoring role for the Commission.

European Democracy Shield: Empowering Strong and Resilient Democracies — https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/? uri=CELEX:52025JC0791. Directive (EU) 2024/1069 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 11 April 2024 on protecting persons who engage in public participation from manifestly unfounded claims or abusive court proceedings (‘Strategic lawsuits against public participation’) — https://eurlex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2024/1069/oj/eng. E-10-2026-001813.t: Use of data analytics software in security and defence: compliance with EU law and fundamental rights
qt: to the Commission Jaume Asens Llodrà (Verts/ALE) Subject:

According to recent reports, several Member States have awarded contracts to companies such as Palantir Technologies for the use of large-scale data analytics software in the fields of security and defence, in some cases through procedures that lack transparency. These technologies raise concerns regarding the protection of personal data and may create situations of technological dependency on external providers. 1.

Does the Commission have information on these contracts, and has it assessed their compliance with Regulation (EU) 2016/679 and Directive (EU) 2016/680, particularly with regard to proportionality, purpose limitation and international data transfers?

Does the Commission intend to adopt measures or guidelines to ensure that the public procurement of artificial intelligence technologies in the field of security fully respects fundamental rights, transparency and the EU’s technological sovereignty?
at: (English version) to the Commission Jaume Asens Llodrà (Verts/ALE) (4 May 2026) Subject: Use of data analytics software in security and defence: compliance with EU law and fundamental rights According to recent reports, several Member States have awarded contracts to companies such as Palantir Technologies for the use of large-scale data analytics software in the fields of security and defence, in some cases through procedures that lack transparency. These technologies raise concerns regarding the protection of personal data and may create situations of technological dependency on external providers. 1. Does the Commission have information on these contracts, and has it assessed their compliance with Regulation (EU) 2016/679 and Directive (EU) 2016/680, particularly with regard to proportionality, purpose limitation and international data transfers? 2. Does the Commission intend to adopt measures or guidelines to ensure that the public procurement of artificial intelligence technologies in the field of security fully respects fundamental rights, transparency and the EU’s technological sovereignty? (16 September 2026) EU data protection law, including Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (1) and Directive 2016/680 (2), sets out the principles and rules to be complied with for the processing of personal data, regardless of the technology used. The enforcement of those rules lies primarily with national data protection supervisory authorities and courts. The EU data protection law does not apply in case of state activities with genuine national security or defence purposes. The AI Act (3) establishes harmonised EU rules for trustworthy AI, but it does not apply to AI systems used exclusively for military, defence, or national security purposes. Where AI systems are also used for other purposes (e.g. law enforcement), the AI Act applies (4), and such systems may be classified as high-risk under the AI Act rules or fall under the prohibitions laid down in Article 5 (e.g. social scoring and predictive policing). For AI systems covered by the AI Act, Article 62(3)(d) requires the AI Office to evaluate and promote the convergence of best practices in public procurement procedures in relation to such systems. To support Member States and businesses in tackling cybersecurity risks and harnessing opportunities related to the development of frontier AI models, the Commission has adopted on 7 July 2026 an Action Plan on Cybersecurity and AI that that offers a structured, coherent and prioritized framework to bolster the preparedness of the EU (5).

Article 2(3) and Recital 24 of the AI Act. https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/eu-action-plan-cybersecurity-and-artificial-intelligence.

E-10-2026-001812.t: Addressing rental affordability and housing insecurity in Spain through the European Semester
qt: to the Commission Jaume Asens Llodrà (Verts/ALE) Subject:

The rental affordability crisis in the EU poses a social and macroeconomic risk. In Spain, 40 % of tenants spend more than 30 % of their income on rent, exceeding the overburden threshold. Without prejudice to national competences in the field of tenancy law, the Commission can guide and coordinate policies based on outcomes through the European Semester and, where appropriate, through the monitoring of EU instruments. In this context: 1.

Does the Commission intend to address rental overburden and housing insecurity in Spain and other severely affected EU countries within the European Semester and to reflect this in its country-specific recommendations?

When does the Commission plan to promote measurable objectives and verifiable indicators (e.g. reducing overburden and preventing residential displacement) to guide national measures aimed at stabilising rental markets?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (28.7.2026) The Commission adopted the first-ever European Affordable Housing Plan (EAHP)1 on 16 December 2025 and works closely with national, regional and local authorities to help tackle the issues identified by the EAHP. Through the European Semester, the Commission aims to help Member States design effective policy measures for affordable and social housing, taking into account the specific context of each country. Housing is analysed extensively in the country reports published as part of the European Semester Spring Package adopted on 3 June 2026. The country reports include for the first time dedicated housing annexes with more detailed analysis on housing for all Member States, including based on the housing cost overburden rate as a headline indicator of the Social Scoreboard as well as severe housing deprivation for owners and renters as secondary indicators. As part of the Spring Package, the Commission adopted a recommendation for a Council Recommendation on the economic, social, employment, structural and budgetary policies of Spain2, covering various topics of housing. Similarly, a broad range of housing-related topics is included in the recommendations for other Member States. Setting concrete policy objectives and relevant indicators for housing remains mainly a responsibility of Member States. EU-level initiatives such as the ones identified by the EAHP and the proposal for a Council Recommendation on Fighting Housing Exclusion encourage Member States to put in place monitoring frameworks, to be taken forward on the basis of national circumstances and housing systems.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52025DC1025. 2 https://reforms-investments.ec.europa.eu/publications-0/2026-european-semester-country-specific-
recommendations-commission-recommendations_en.

E-10-2026-001811.t: Need to protect European silicon producers: case of the plant in Sabón, A Coruña
qt: to the Commission Ana Miranda Paz (Verts/ALE) Subject:

Sabón (A Coruña) is home to the only silicon plant in Spain, which creates jobs in a key sector, as silicon is an essential raw material for both alloys and the photovoltaic industry. However, in recent years, the industry has complained of significant economic losses owing to oversupply from China and Angola of low-cost silicon, which has caused EU prices and market share to nosedive – market share fell to 24 % in 2025 from 38 % in 2019 – despite the safeguard measures the EU took in November 2025. Faced with this challenge and unfair competition, the silicon sector is turning to the production of ferrosilicon; however, the costto-revenue imbalance is leading to significant financial losses, undermining the viability of a key Galician economic sector. How will the Commission tailor the safeguards to the current vulnerability to a workforce restructuring that could threaten jobs at the Sabón plant?
at: (English version) to the Commission Ana Miranda Paz (Verts/ALE) (4 May 2026) Subject: Need to protect European silicon producers: case of the plant in Sabón, A Coruña Sabón (A Coruña) is home to the only silicon plant in Spain, which creates jobs in a key sector, as silicon is an essential raw material for both alloys and the photovoltaic industry. However, in recent years, the industry has complained of significant economic losses owing to oversupply from China and Angola of low-cost silicon, which has caused EU prices and market share to nosedive — market share fell to 24% in 2025 from 38% in 2019 — despite the safeguard measures the EU took in November 2025. Faced with this challenge and unfair competition, the silicon sector is turning to the production of ferrosilicon; however, the cost-to-revenue imbalance is leading to significant financial losses, undermining the viability of a key Galician economic sector. How will the Commission tailor the safeguards to the current vulnerability to a workforce restructuring that could threaten jobs at the Sabón plant? (30 July 2026) The safeguard measures adopted by the Commission in November 2025 (1) were imposed following an investigation carried out in accordance with the applicable EU and World Trade Organisation rules and apply to the specific ferro-alloy products covered by that investigation. Silicon was examined in the course of that investigation but was not included in the safeguard measures, as the legal conditions for its inclusion were not met at that time. The Commission continuously monitors the functioning of the safeguard measures. As provided for in the Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/2351, the Commission will review the measures in the event of a change in circumstances, such as insufficient availability of ferro-alloys or unsustainable price increases for certain downstream users, and, in any event, no later than one year after their entry into force. Any review will be conducted in accordance with the applicable legal framework. The Commission is aware of the difficult circumstances currently faced by the EU silicon industry and of the strategic importance of silicon for a range of industrial applications. While the industry is also facing challenges such as high energy costs and structural overcapacity, the Commission remains available to engage with the industry to explore the possible use of the trade defence instruments available under EU law, where the applicable legal conditions are met.
Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/2351 of 18 November 2025 imposing a definitive safeguard measure with regard to imports of certain ferroalloying elements, OJ L, 2025/2351, 18.11.2025.

E-10-2026-001810.t: Strengthening Europe’s Beating Cancer Plan: from implementation to outcomes and patient-centred policy
qt: to the Commission Cynthia Ní Mhurchú (Renew) Subject:

Will the Commission support strengthening Europe’s Beating Cancer Plan to shift from implementation-based to outcome-based policy, improve patient access and data-driven evaluation, and ensure stronger patient involvement, while recognising cancer as a societal challenge requiring an ’all policies’ approach across all EU frameworks?
at: (English version) to the Commission Cynthia Ní Mhurchú (Renew) (4 May 2026) Subject: Strengthening Europe’s Beating Cancer Plan: from implementation to outcomes and patient-centred policy Will the Commission support strengthening Europe’s Beating Cancer Plan to shift from implementation-based to outcomebased policy, improve patient access and data-driven evaluation, and ensure stronger patient involvement, while recognising cancer as a societal challenge requiring an ‘all policies’ approach across all EU frameworks? (9 July 2026) The Commission continues to implement the Europe’s Beating Cancer Plan (1) and deliver tangible outcomes. The recently published European Court of Auditors report (2) put forward recommendations supporting this work and suggesting to strengthen the related monitoring and evaluation. Existing tools to map outcomes include the Implementation Roadmap and the 2025 Cancer Plan revie w (3). By 2027, the Commission will establish a Cancer Plan-wide monitoring framework, with a comprehensive evaluation planned by 2030. In parallel, the Commission is preparing the mid-term assessment of the five EU Missions, including for the EU Cancer Mission (4). Patient access is a key theme of the Cancer Plan, which is reflected in flagship initiatives such as the new EU Cancer Screening Scheme (5), (6), and the EU Network of Comprehensive Cancer Centres (7) in the areas of early detection, diagnosis, and treatment. Patient involvement is another important pillar of the Cancer Plan, as reflected for example in the inclusion of patients in the expert working groups for the Commission Initiatives on cancer screening and care (8) and the long-term dialogue with adolescents and young adults living with and beyond cancer under the EU Cancer Mission (9).

E-10-2026-001809.t: EU funding for digital civic participation and citizen science initiatives
qt: to the Commission Cynthia Ní Mhurchú (Renew) Subject:

Can the Commission clarify whether any EU funding instruments, including the European Fund for Sustainable Development Plus, currently support digital civic participation and citizen engagement infrastructure, and does it intend to increase support for citizen science and digital democracy initiatives aimed at strengthening public participation and addressing the so-called democracy gap in the EU?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.8.2026) The Commission supports citizen engagement and democratic participation through several EU programmes. Under Horizon Europe1, support includes citizen participation in research and innovation, digital democracy, AI-enabled deliberation tools and 2026-2027 actions on citizen science, youth engagement and scientific literacy. The Commission cooperates with European Research Area (ERA) countries and stakeholders to implement the 2025-2027 ERA policy agenda action on enhancing trust in science through citizen participation and science communication. The Development Education and Awareness Raising in Europe (DEAR) programme2 promotes awareness of global development issues and active engagement for justice, human rights, democracy, gender equality and sustainable development. The Citizens, Equality, Rights and Values (CERV) programme3 supports citizens’ engagement, democratic participation and civil society. Creative Europe and Digital Europe strengthen media literacy and resilience against disinformation. The European Democracy Shield4 supports a European civic tech hub, pilot projects on civic tech and participatory digital tools, national authorities on citizen participation and strengthened media literacy. Under the Multiannual Financial Framework 2028-2034, the proposed AgoraEU programme, notably the CERV+ strand, would support democratic participation, citizens’ engagement, civil society, media freedom and democratic resilience, including through the European Democracy Shield. The proposed Horizon Europe programme would support research and innovation on democratic values, civic engagement, citizen involvement in research and innovation and the integrity of the information and media space.

E-10-2026-001808.t: Investigating Live Nation / Ticketmaster’s control of the EU’s live-event ticketing market
qt: to the Commission Cynthia Ní Mhurchú (Renew) Subject:
Investigating Live Nation / Ticketmaster’s control of the EU’s live-event ticketing market

Will the Commission launch or consider an investigation into Live Nation / Ticketmaster’s alleged monopoly and anti-competitive practices in the EU’s live-event ticketing market, in the light of concerns regarding high market concentration, vertical integration across ticketing, venue ownership and artist management, and exclusive dealing arrangements, and what specific steps is the Commission taking to address these issues and protect consumers, particularly regarding practices such as dynamic pricing, hidden fees, restricted ticket transferability and reduced consumer choice in live-event ticketing across the EU?
at: (English version) to the Commission Cynthia Ní Mhurchú (Renew) (4 May 2026) Subject: Investigating Live Nation/Ticketmaster’s control of the EU’s live-event ticketing market Will the Commission launch or consider an investigation into Live Nation/Ticketmaster’s alleged monopoly and anticompetitive practices in the EU’s live-event ticketing market, in the light of concerns regarding high market concentration, vertical integration across ticketing, venue ownership and artist management, and exclusive dealing arrangements, and what specific steps is the Commission taking to address these issues and protect consumers, particularly regarding practices such as dynamic pricing, hidden fees, restricted ticket transferability and reduced consumer choice in live-event ticketing across the EU? (26 June 2026) There is no ongoing investigation into the alleged behaviour of Live Nation/Ticketmaster. The Commission is closely monitoring the live-event ticketing sector and remains committed to ensuring the full respect for EU competition law. Opening an investigation requires reasonable indications of a likely infringement of EU competition rules. If a transaction occurs in the sector, it may well have to be notified to the Commission or Member States to the extent that this transaction amounts to a concentration, within the meaning of EU or national merger control rules and meets the thresholds at EU or national level. Such notification would enable the Commission or the competent national competition authority to assess the transaction’s potential impact on competition in relevant markets. Consumers are protected against unfair commercial practices, including in relation to the marketing of event tickets, under Directive 2005/29/EC (1). This directive is transposed into national legislation and Member States’ authorities and courts are responsible for enforcement in individual cases. Subject to the outcome of the ongoing impact assessment of the Digital Fairness Act (2), the Commission may propose more specific rules regarding price marketing, such as a prohibition of misleading ‘starting from’ price claims and of hidden fees (‘drip pricing’). The Commission may also propose increased transparency when consumers must wait in a virtual queue for their chance to buy.

E-10-2026-001807.t: Does the release of EU funds to Hungary comply with the rule of law?
qt: to the Commission Catherine Griset (PfE) Subject:

Hungary’s new Prime Minister, Péter Magyar, is calling on the Commission to release EU funds that were frozen during ‘the rule-of-law breaches era’1. However, the Commission should exercise caution following the precedent set in the case of Poland: according to Eulalia Rubio, a researcher for the highly federalist Jacques Delors Institute, ‘there was political bargaining at stake’ in releasing the funds and ‘the measures in Poland were not sufficient’2. 1.
Drawing on this experience, can the Commission specify the conditions that must be met before any EU funds are released to Hungary?

In March 2024, Parliament initiated legal proceedings before the Court of Justice of the European Union to challenge an initial unfreezing of funds for Hungary, on the grounds that its reforms were insufficient. Will the Commission thus risk unlocking additional funds that could be challenged before the same Court?
During his election campaign, Mr Magyar promised rapid access to these funds, so would releasing them not indicate EU interference in the internal election of a Member State?
https://www.euractiv.com/news/hungarys-magyar-wants-eu-cash-back-but-brussels-wont-make-it-easy/. Idem.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.8.2026) Hungary is currently unable to access certain EU funds due to decisions under different instruments: (i) the Conditionality Regulation1, (ii) the Recovery and Resilience Facility2 (RRF) and (iii) the requirements for compliance with the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the EU under the horizontal enabling conditions of the so-called Common Provisions Regulation3 (CPR) The conditions for the concerned funding to be released are public and set in these instruments or specified in published decisions taken by the Commission or the Council. These are also known by Hungary. The Commission will make its assessment and proceed according to the relevant legislation once Hungary has addressed the relevant breaches or met the requirements. Any release of funds will be linked to the fulfilment of legal requirements. The newly elected Hungarian government has given priority to the unblocking of EU funds. On 9 June 2026, Hungary submitted to the Commission a revised Recovery and Resilience Plan. On 19 June, the Commission endorsed the revised plan, which maintains the ambition in terms of protection of the financial interests of the EU and of rule of law related reforms. The Council adopted the revised plan on 10 July4. The Hungarian Parliament also adopted an omnibus law which seeks to increase transparency and establish robust tools to fight corruption and prevent conflict of interest5. Regarding the legal proceeding initiated by the European Parliament on the assessment of the fulfilment of the Charter horizontal enabling condition as regards judicial independence, the Commission awaits the judgment of the European Court of Justice.

E-10-2026-001806.t: Measures for the protection of Portuguese farmers and consumers in the aftermath of storms
qt: to the Commission Catarina Martins (The Left) Subject:

In recent weeks, several storms have hit Portugal, causing a wave of destruction on an unprecedented scale. In addition to causing damage to homes, vehicles, trees, businesses, electricity and communications networks, as well as to the water supply, the gales and floods have devastated the agricultural sector in the regions concerned. For most farmers, in addition to the damage suffered, this means starting again almost from scratch. Beyond this direct impact on farmers, there will be consequences for consumers as a result of reduced or limited agricultural production, whether due to rising food prices or supply shortages. In light of the above: 1.
Will the European Commission take all necessary measures to compensate farmers for the damages they have suffered, and also to support the recovery of their businesses?
What measures does the European Commission intend to take to ensure, in accordance with Article 39 TFEU, the availability of supplies and to ensure that supplies reach consumers at reasonable prices?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (8.7.2026) Under the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), in its 2023-2027 CAP Strategic Plan (CSP), Portugal has programmed support for the restoration of agricultural and forestry potential following natural disasters, adverse climatic events or catastrophic events amounting to EUR 23.6 million of the European Agricultural Fund for Rural Development (EAFRD) available for farmers and forest owners. In addition, following the recent omnibus simplification1, Member States can mobilise CSP funding for crisis payments that compensate for production losses due to such events. The Portuguese authorities can use this option. To provide support to Portugal, the Commission proposed to allocate EUR 30 million from the agricultural crisis reserve, which was endorsed by the Member States. Portugal shall compensate the most affected farmers for their economic losses. Furthermore, Portugal may grant additional national support up to maximum of 200% of the EU emergency financial contribution. The Commission will now adopt its proposal, and it will enter into force the day following its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union. This will allow farmers to receive support as soon as possible. Regarding the impact on the availability of supply and prices to consumers, the EU internal market for agricultural products ensures the free movement of agri-food goods across borders. The CAP integrates the agricultural sector into the broader single market to ensure fair competition, food security, a level playing field for farmers and reasonable prices for consumers.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=OJ:L_202502649.

E-10-2026-001805.t: Decarbonising transport in the outermost regions: the specific challenges and needs of the Canary Islands
qt: to the Commission Juan Fernando López Aguilar (S&D) Subject:

In the last legislative term, we adopted a strong stance in favour of decarbonisation and renewable energy, which are both vital when moving towards a sustainable growth model. However, as an outermost region, the Canary Islands face specific structural challenges. When it comes to the decarbonisation of transport specifically, the islands are hampered by insularity, territorial fragmentation, insufficient charging infrastructure and a high dependence on fossil fuels. This is compounded by the citizens’ reduced financial capacity – the average income was 9.58 % below the national average in 2023, according to Spain’s National Statistics Institute – which makes it difficult to renew an already ageing fleet. In view of the above: 1.
Does the Commission intend to look into differentiated application of the EU emissions framework for the outermost regions, in accordance with Article 349 TFEU?
Which funding instruments could be strengthened to support charging infrastructure, energy storage and grid modernisation?
Is it planning any specific financial support measures to facilitate fleet renewal?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.6.2026) The Commission fully recognises the structural constraints faced by outermost regions such as insularity, territorial fragmentation and dependence on maritime and air links. The EU Emission Trading System1 (ETS) framework already contains targeted derogations for these situations, including a derogation for maritime and air transport until the end of 2030 for routes within outermost regions and to/from the mainland Member State. For air transport, airlines flying from airports in outermost regions to the European Economic Area, Switzerland and the United Kingdom benefit from the highest level of ETS support for the uptake of sustainable aviation fuels. Moreover, emissions from flights under public service obligations are also excluded from the ETS. The 2026 ETS Directive review will assess further connectivity, territorial cohesion and outermost region concerns. As regards road transport, the CO2 standards apply to new vehicles put on the market by manufacturers at the EU level, as such allowing varying regional uptake rates of zero-emission vehicles. Several financial instruments are available to support investments in zero-emission vehicles and charging infrastructure, including the Recovery and Resilience Fund, ETS national auction revenues, the cohesion policy – notably the European Regional Development Fund, as well as the Social Climate Fund, which addresses households and microenterprises vulnerable to transport poverty, and can for instance support schemes to increase the affordability of zero-emission vehicles for such users. In addition, the Alternative Fuels Infrastructure Facility supports the deployment of charging infrastructure along the main road axis and nodes (Trans-European Transport Network).
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A02003L0087-20240301.

E-10-2026-001804.t: Impact of storm Kristin and assessment of damage
qt: to the Commission Catarina Martins (The Left) Subject:

Storm Kristin caused significant damage to several regions of Portugal. A damage-reporting mechanism was subsequently set up to assess the damage and facilitate access to public aid. However, those affected were urged to report the damage at a stage when land and homes were still flooded or under water, particularly in Montemor-o-Velho (Coimbra). This casts doubt on the reliability of the assessments, since much of the damage was not yet known or had not yet been fully assessed. The premature collection of information makes it harder to assess – and may underestimate – damage, and unduly disqualifies those affected from support mechanisms, including those covered by EU instruments. It is important to ensure that the assessment criteria and procedures do not end up restricting access to aid for those in need of it. Can the Commission therefore say: 1.
Whether it is aware of situations where damage was reported before the effects of the events had stabilised?
Whether it considers such practices to be compatible with the principles of good administration and equal access to support?
Which European Union instruments can be mobilised to ensure the reassessment of damage?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (29.6.2026) The Commission provides guidance and support to Member States regarding the damage assessment following a climate-related disaster. However, under the remits of cohesion policy and the Common Agricultural Policy, assessment of damage falls under the Member State’s responsibility as part of the shared management principle governing these funds. In case where initial assessments are found to be incomplete, Portugal may reopen or extend deadlines for damage and adjust the selection criteria to ensure that those affected are not unduly excluded. When it comes to EU instruments which can offer support, on 26 January 2026, Portugal activated the Copernicus Emergency Management Service - on demand mapping - to assess the situation during and after the event. Some maps were requested to detect the flooded area, and other products to provide damage assessment. The activation is still ongoing. Moreover, on 13 April 2026, Portugal submitted an EU Solidarity Fund (EUSF)1 application regarding several consecutive storms in January and February 2026. In its application for EUSF funding, Portugal reported direct damages caused by the disaster that were collected during the 12-week application period2. Due to the nature of the disaster, the EUSF Regulation3 permits national authorities to update or supplement their EUSF application even after the 12-week application deadline, in justified cases, to take account of possible additional damages identified after the initial submission of the application.
1 Council Regulation (EC) No 2012/2002 of 11 November 2002 establishing the European Union Solidarity

Fund (OJ L 311, 14.11.2002, p. 3) as amended by Regulation (EU) No 661/2014 of the European Parliament and the Council of 15 May 2014 (OJ L 189, 27.6.2014, p. 143) and by Regulation (EU) 2020/461 of the European Parliament and the Council of 30 March 2020 (OJ L 99, 31.3.2020, p. 9). 2 The 12-week application period begins on the date the disaster first caused damage. 3 Article 4(1)(a) of Council Regulation (EC) No 2012/2002: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2002/2012/oj/eng.

qt: to the Commission Thierry Mariani (PfE) Subject:

Ethiopia, the global birthplace of arabica, has over five million small-scale producers. These include family farms located in agroforestry areas which are unable to meet the geolocation and traceability requirements of Regulation (EU) 2023/1115 in a timely manner. Coffee represents the country’s primary source of foreign exchange and is a fundamental pillar of its rural economy. Efforts are underway to digitalise the industry, including by issuing producers with individual cards that come with a QR code. However, the institutional and financial capacities required for these to be deployed on a national scale are still insufficient in terms of meeting the deadlines set out in the Regulation. 1.
Does the Commission plan to grant Ethiopia an extended deadline for compliance?

How does it intend to mobilise development aid instruments, including as part of the Global Gateway strategy, to provide practical support to this industry, 30% of whose output is exported to the European Union?
at: (English version) to the Commission Thierry Mariani (PfE) (4 May 2026) Subject: Coffee sector in Ethiopia Ethiopia, the global birthplace of arabica, has over five million small-scale producers. These include family farms located in agroforestry areas which are unable to meet the geolocation and traceability requirements of Regulation (EU) 2023/1115 in a timely manner. Coffee represents the country’s primary source of foreign exchange and is a fundamental pillar of its rural economy. Efforts are underway to digitalise the industry, including by issuing producers with individual cards that come with a QR code. However, the institutional and financial capacities required for these to be deployed on a national scale are still insufficient in terms of meeting the deadlines set out in the regulation. 1.
Does the Commission plan to grant Ethiopia an extended deadline for compliance?

2. How does it intend to mobilise development aid instruments, including as part of the Global Gateway strategy, to provide practical support to this industry, 30% of whose output is exported to the European Union? (10 July 2026) A new, extended deadline for Ethiopia would require to amend Regulation 2023/1115 (1) (EUDR (2)) before it starts applying, which would create further legal uncertainty, undermining the effectiveness of the regulation. The Commission’s focus is on effective implementation of the regulation. Partner countries and companies need legal clarity and predictability. The Commission remains fully committed to finding pragmatic solutions to streamline and simplify the implementation of the EUDR in close dialogue with stakeholders and based on their on-the-ground experience. The Commission has increasingly supported partner countries in making their coffee value chains EUDR-compliant. In the case of Ethiopia, consultations were held with the Ethiopian Coffee and Tea Authority (ECTA) and private operators to clarify requirements, raise awareness, and develop a national compliance strategy and action plan. To support preparedness efforts, technical assistance was mobilised for an ‘EUDR Preparedness Check’ by the European Forest Institute (EFI) to assess the readiness of Ethiopia’s coffee sector and identify gaps and opportunities related to EUDR requirements. Furthermore, the ‘EU-Coffee Action for Ethiopia (3)’ project was repurposed, in collaboration with ECTA, to support government-led compliance work. Further efforts are planned, including to support the rollout of digital traceability systems as well as the expansion of the digital cadastre and second-level rural land certification in coffee-producing areas. Lastly, the EFI has also started cooperation with the Ethiopian Space Science and Geospatial Institute for high-resolution mapping and land-use audits linked to the National Rural Land Administration Information System.
