E-10-2026-001801.t: Greek rice ‘victim’ of EU trade agreements and unscrupulous merchants
qt: to the Commission Lefteris Nikolaou-Alavanos (NI) Subject:

Rice producers in Greece are being hit hard by the policy of the EU and Greek governments. Our country is one of the biggest producers in the EU. For the last two years, Greek farmers have despaired over mass imports of rice from non-EU countries. Merchants and processing groups – exploiting the common agricultural policy – import rice of dubious and inferior quality, often produced with pesticides banned in the EU. The consequences are disastrous. The producer price has fallen to levels that do not even cover production costs. High-quality Greek rice remains unsold. Months after the farmers’ protests, producers have still not received a single euro, as the so-called ‘support’ of the Nea Demokratia Government has not materialised. The situation is the direct result of the ‘free market’ and the CAP. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

What view does it take of the fact that EU trade agreements under the CAP are stifling Greek production, permitting the entry of products that do not even meet the necessary standards adhered to by our farmers?

What is the Commission’s position on the urgent need to immediately and fully compensate Greek rice producers for their lost income, beyond the de minimis amounts, which are insufficient to meet their needs and have not yet been paid out?
at: (English version) to the Commission Lefteris Nikolaou-Alavanos (NI) (4 May 2026) Subject: Greek rice ‘victim’ of EU trade agreements and unscrupulous merchants Rice producers in Greece are being hit hard by the policy of the EU and Greek governments. Our country is one of the biggest producers in the EU. For the last two years, Greek farmers have despaired over mass imports of rice from non-EU countries. Merchants and processing groups — exploiting the common agricultural policy — import rice of dubious and inferior quality, often produced with pesticides banned in the EU. The consequences are disastrous. The producer price has fallen to levels that do not even cover production costs. High-quality Greek rice remains unsold. Months after the farmers’ protests, producers have still not received a single euro, as the so-called ‘support’ of the Nea Demokratia Government has not materialised. The situation is the direct result of the ‘free market’ and the CAP. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

What view does it take of the fact that EU trade agreements under the CAP are stifling Greek production, permitting the entry of products that do not even meet the necessary standards adhered to by our farmers?

What is the Commission’s position on the urgent need to immediately and fully compensate Greek rice producers for their lost income, beyond the de minimis amounts, which are insufficient to meet their needs and have not yet been paid out?

(1 July 2026) The Commission closely monitors the situation of Union rice production, where rising input costs and low prices, similar to other crops, have been increasing. Rice is sensitive in all trade negotiations. Most duty-free rice imports fall under the Everything But Arms arrangement of the Generalised Scheme of Preferences (GSP) (1). As of 2027, under the new GSP (2), a new rice-specific automatic safeguard will be available, in addition to three other safeguards also available to the Union rice sector. All food products on the market, including imported foods, must comply with the same non-negotiable Union standards on safety and health. which are enforced through rigorous import controls, regular audits in countries exporting to the Union, and immediate corrective actions when needed. Where imported rice poses a risk, the Commission may adopt measures under Regulation 2019/1793 (3). Currently, rice from India and Pakistan is subject to increased controls at entry into the Union. Under the Vision for Agriculture and Food, measures will be adopted to ensure the highest level of food safety, including more audits in other countries and more audits of European Border Control Posts. The Commission will also pursue a stronger alignment of production standards applied to imported products. The proposal for the new multiannual financial framework includes an enhanced crisis response in case of market disturbances through the Unity Safety Net, doubling the current crisis reserve and helping farmers when markets are disrupted. Under the promotion policy, EUR 205 million are available to launch programmes and actions in 2026 to boost the Union's agri-food competitiveness and its export market diversification.

E-10-2026-001800.t: Israel’s unacceptable piracy attack on the international solidarity fleet for Gaza
qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Lefteris Nikolaou-Alavanos (NI) Subject:

In the early hours of 30 April 2026, another incident of Israeli State piracy unfolded in international waters near Crete. Hundreds of people participating in the Gaza solidarity flotilla were attacked by Israeli military forces, causing serious damage and leaving the vessels dead in the water. This latest attack by the Israeli State in the Greek search and rescue area of responsibility also demonstrates the serious responsibility borne by the Nea Demokratia Government, which maintains a ‘strategic relationship’ with the occupying State of Israel. It has become clear that the murderous state, emboldened by its international alliances, knows no bounds and tramples on every notion of humanitarian principles as it escalates its aggression in Palestine, Lebanon, Iran and Syria. The EU also bears particular responsibility for the actions of the State of Israel, as it continues to maintain economic, military and political relations with Israel to this day. The Vice-President / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy is asked: 1.

What is her position on the criminal attack perpetrated by the State of Israel in the Greek search and rescue area of responsibility against the flotilla that was transporting humanitarian aid to Gaza, putting the lives of hundreds of people at direct risk?

What is her position on the calls to stop the EU-Israel Association Agreement here and now and to terminate all trade, political and military agreements between the EU and its Member States and the occupying State of Israel?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (5.6.2026) In relation to the Israeli interception of the flotilla on 30 April 2026, the EU has made clear that no attacks or any use of force against the flotilla, including drone strikes or seizures, are acceptable. The EU reiterates its call on Israel to respect international law, including international humanitarian law and international maritime law. The freedom of navigation under international law must be upheld. What the activists wish to achieve is raising awareness about the catastrophic situation in Gaza and delivering much needed aid to a people in desperate need. However, while the EU respects the humanitarian commitment of those aboard the flotilla and recognise the challenges in delivering aid to Gaza, the EU discourages flotillas as a form of aid delivery, as they risk the safety of their participants. The EU, including through outreach by the High Representative/Vice President, remains in regular contact with Member States and with Israel regarding the humanitarian situation in Gaza and reiterates our consistent call for rapid and unimpeded delivery of aid. In light of the catastrophic situation in Gaza and following a review of Israel’s obligations under Article 2 of the EU-Israel Association Agreement1 which the High Representative/Vice President conducted with the support of a majority of Member States, the President of the Commission proposed a package of measures during her State of the Union address in September 2025. Discussions continue in the Council on the package of measures presented by the Commission following the review. Any decision to suspend the Association Agreement requires unanimity in the Council, meaning the agreement of all 27 Member States.
1 https://eeas.europa.eu/archives/delegations/israel/documents/eu_israel/asso_agree_en.pdf.

E-10-2026-001799.t: Meeting students’ needs for free and safe student halls
qt: to the Commission Lefteris Nikolaou-Alavanos (NI) Subject:

As many as 17 cities with a university have no student halls and the cost of a small flat is over two thirds of an average salary. Student housing and rent prices in Europe have gone through the roof. By continuing the policy pursued by SYRIZA, the Nea Dimokratia Government is mocking students and working-class families as it brags about building student accommodation through public-private partnerships (PPPs). It is abolishing free housing and further commercialising the right to housing. This policy is underpinned by the priorities of the EU, which see the right to housing as an opportunity for big construction groups and real estate companies to profit. It is the people who are footing the bill through PPP payments. Meanwhile, working-class families are paying double, since student accommodation will be granted for a fee. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

What view does it take of the fact that the promotion of PPPs does away with free student housing, so that big construction groups can secure huge amounts of money for the construction, reconstruction, maintenance and operation of student halls, with prime pieces of public property being exploited, while workers pay double for student homes by repaying the PPPs through unfair taxation on the one hand and on the other by paying ‘rent’ for the student accommodation in question?
How does it view the fair demands of students and working-class families for safe and free student halls for those studying in cities other than those in which they live?
at: (English version) to the Commission Lefteris Nikolaou-Alavanos (NI) (4 May 2026) Subject: Meeting students’ needs for free and safe student halls As many as 17 cities with a university have no student halls and the cost of a small flat is over two thirds of an average salary. Student housing and rent prices in Europe have gone through the roof. By continuing the policy pursued by SYRIZA, the Nea Dimokratia Government is mocking students and working-class families as it brags about building student accommodation through public-private partnerships (PPPs). It is abolishing free housing and further commercialising the right to housing. This policy is underpinned by the priorities of the EU, which see the right to housing as an opportunity for big construction groups and real estate companies to profit. It is the people who are footing the bill through PPP payments. Meanwhile, working-class families are paying double, since student accommodation will be granted for a fee. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

What view does it take of the fact that the promotion of PPPs does away with free student housing, so that big construction groups can secure huge amounts of money for the construction, reconstruction, maintenance and operation of student halls, with prime pieces of public property being exploited, while workers pay double for student homes by repaying the PPPs through unfair taxation on the one hand and on the other by paying ‘rent’ for the student accommodation in question?
How does it view the fair demands of students and working-class families for safe and free student halls for those studying in cities other than those in which they live?

(22 June 2026) The Commission is aware of the challenges students face to find affordable housing and works closely with national, regional and local authorities to help tackle the issues. In respect of the principle of subsidiarity, the main responsibility for housing — including how project financing takes place — remains within the remit of these authorities. The European Affordable Housing Plan (EAHP) (1) specifically refers to improving access to housing for young people, students, apprentices and trainees. Actions of the EAHP aim to support the development of more student housing by mobilising investments, and helping students, trainees and apprentices find housing on the private rental market. In addition, the Commission intends to launch a pilot scheme under Erasmus+ programme to increase availability of affordable and innovative housing solutions for mobile students from disadvantaged backgrounds. Furthermore, the Commission will work with Member States to encourage the use of European Social Fund+ to further support affordable housing solutions for disadvantaged students. The European Housing Alliance will also help the relevant stakeholders to help ameliorating student housing. Support for projects — including those involving public-private partnerships — through EU funding must comply with the rules governing these programmes. Student housing will remain central in shaping EU recommendations and funding programmes. The Commission is committed to continue its work on student welfare, addressing especially equal access to higher education, student housing and living conditions, and health.

E-10-2026-001798.t: The need for accelerated legislative intervention in the fisheries and aquaculture sector
qt: to the Commission Stephen Nikola Bartulica (ECR) Subject:

The Commission is currently carrying out an evaluation of the common fisheries policy. A lengthy, multi-year reform process that primarily focuses on the revision of the CFP Basic Regulation, while leaving the implementation of certain provisions unresolved, is unacceptable for the fisheries and aquaculture sector. Given the urgent challenges this sector is facing, is the Commission considering proposing a targeted omnibus regulation to simplify and streamline fisheries legislation as soon as possible (including the Fisheries Control Regulation, the Mediterranean Regulation and others)?
at: (English version) to the Commission Stephen Nikola Bartulica (ECR) (4 May 2026) Subject: The need for accelerated legislative intervention in the fisheries and aquaculture sector The Commission is currently carrying out an evaluation of the common fisheries policy. A lengthy, multi-year reform process that primarily focuses on the revision of the CFP Basic Regulation, while leaving the implementation of certain provisions unresolved, is unacceptable for the fisheries and aquaculture sector. Given the urgent challenges this sector is facing, is the Commission considering proposing a targeted omnibus regulation to simplify and streamline fisheries legislation as soon as possible (including the Fisheries Control Regulation, the Mediterranean Regulation and others)? (3 July 2026) The Commission published the evaluation of the Common Fisheries Policy (CFP) Regulation on 30 April 2026 (1). It is a diagnosis setting out what has worked, what has not, and why, based on comprehensive evidence gathered over the evaluation period. On this basis, and after taking into account the views of the co-legislators and stakeholders, the Commission will draw conclusions and decide on the follow-up, including on whether addressing the challenges and shortcomings identified in the evaluation require a revision of existing legislation, and to which extent. Simplification and reduction of red tape are guiding principles in the Commission’s daily policy work, including when preparing the implementing rules supporting the revised Control Regulation (2). The revision was undertaken to streamline, facilitate and simplify procedures for stakeholders and authorities, through digitalisation and the use of technology (3), enhancing efficiency and effectiveness and reducing costs in the long term. The Commission is actively listening to calls from stakeholders on simplification and on possible legislative amendments. In this regard, and in parallel to ongoing discussions on the follow-up to the evaluation of the CFP Regulation, the Commission launched a call for evidence — closed on 23 June 2026 (4) — to gather feedback on the four EU fisheries Multiannual Management Plans and one on the European Fisheries, Maritime and Aquaculture Fund (EMFAF) (5), open until 21 July 2026.

E-10-2026-001796.t: Confidentiality clause curtailing access to environmental impact data for data centres and compliance with EU legislation
qt: to the Commission César Luena (S&D) Subject:

According to various studies, Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1364 on the first phase of the establishment of a common Union rating scheme for data centre included a general confidentiality clause, ‘copied word for word’ from a proposal submitted by Microsoft, which obliges the Commission and Member States to keep the indicators and information for each individual data centre confidential, limiting disclosures to aggregated data1. The experts cited warn that this ‘broad presumption of confidentiality’ could run counter to the requirements for access to environmental information laid down in the Aarhus Convention, Directive 2003/4/EC and Regulations (EC) No 1367/2006 and (EU) 2021/1767. Can the Commission therefore say: 1.

How it can ensure that this clause is compatible with the aforementioned rules, stipulating as they do that exceptions on the grounds of business secrecy may only be granted under strict interpretations of the rules and cannot be invoked to deny access to information relating to emissions into the environment?
Why it has opted for automatic confidentiality rather than a case-by-case assessments when deciding whether to publish, at the very least, the information essential for assessing local impacts?
Whether it intends to review this clause in light of the forthcoming energy efficiency package for data centres to ensure reliability and prevent greenwashing?
Investigate Europe. How Big Tech wrote secrecy into EU law to hide data centres’ environmental toll, 16 April 2026.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.8.2026) The Energy Efficiency Directive (EED)1 requires the Commission to establish a European database on data centres with data publicly available on an aggregated level. The Commission established the European database2 in line with these provisions and has fulfilled its obligation to make publicly available aggregated data via a public dashboard3 that summarises and presents data as soon as they are confirmed by the Member States. The Commission has repeatedly confirmed4 that the confidentiality of the data in the European database is compatible with EU law, as well as the provisions of the Aarhus convention. To increase transparency, the Commission has committed to analysing every year the figures reported to the European database. The analysis for the first year is publicly available5 and the analysis for the second year is being prepared. Member States and not the Commission decide which specific data, data centres in their territory must publish. The Commission, as part of the EED transposition check, is examining whether Member States have transposed and implemented the relevant provisions of the Directive correctly. Similarly, Member States’ authorities can decide, during the permitting or possible local consultation processes, what information they want to disclose about the benefits and impacts of new data centres at the local level. The upcoming Data Centre Energy Efficiency Package is not foreseen to review the EED.
1 Directive (EU) 2023/1791 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 September 2023 on energy

efficiency and amending Regulation (EU) 2023/955 (recast) (OJ L 231, 20.9.2023, p. 1, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2023/1791/oj). 2 Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1364 of 14 March 2024 on the first phase of the establishment of a common Union rating scheme for data centres, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg_del/2024/1364/oj. 3 https://dashboard.tech.ec.europa.eu/qs_digit_dashboard_mt/public/sense/app/940a61c3-bcfe-47d6-a78625d93aa63b85/sheet/ZLWpJa/state/analysis/bookmark/381456a5-1044-4047-92f5-671be7ad92c4. 4 For example, in this confirmatory request: https://ec.europa.eu/transparency/documentsrequest/search/document-details/18424. 5 https://op.europa.eu/en/publication-detail/-/publication/83be4c3e-5c79-11f0-a9d0-01aa75ed71a1/language-en.

E-10-2026-001795.t: Non-compliance with European legislation on farm-animal welfare in pig holdings and state of play regarding the ‘End the Cage Age’ initiative
qt: to the Commission César Luena (S&D) Subject:

According to the press and NGOs1, certain European pig holdings have serious shortcomings with regard to animal welfare (wounded or dying animals not being given appropriate care, cannibalism, lack of hygiene, inadequate carcass management, etc.), thereby jeopardising biosecurity and public health. Moreover, it has come to light that these large-scale farms are supplying products to distributors bearing an ‘animal welfare’ and sustainability seal. This raises questions about the enforcement of EU rules, in particular Directive 98/58/EC (reasonable steps to ensure the welfare of farm animals) and Directive 2008/120/EC (minimum standards for the protection of pigs), as well as Article 13 TFEU and green labelling. All this is happening while the European Citizens’ Initiative ‘End the Cage Age’ (with more than 1.4 million signatories) is still awaiting announced legislative proposals. In light of the above: 1.
What measures does the Commission envisage to strengthen the uniform implementation of Directives 98/58/EC and 2008/120/EC in intensive pig holdings?
What is the state of play regarding the reform resulting from the End the Cage Age initiative?
Is it considering more stringent verification and audit requirements for animal welfare labels/claims to prevent greenwashing?
https://www.eldiario.es/aragon/sociedad/cerdos-enfermos-canibalismo-restos-cadaveres-suelo-granjahorrores-aragon_1_13075016.html.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.7.2026) Member States have the primary responsibility for the implementation, application and enforcement of said Council Directives. Common requirements for official controls to verify compliance with these Directives are laid down in Regulation (EU) 2017/6251. To further ensure harmonisation, the Commission regularly performs audits to verify that Member States control systems fulfil the common requirements. The EU Reference Centre on pig welfare2 provides publicly available guidance, supporting uniform implementation of EU rules. As stated in the EU Vision for Agriculture and Food3, the Commission intends to closely exchange with farmers, the food chain and civil society, and on that basis present proposals on the revision of the existing animal welfare legislation, including its commitment to phase out cages. This work is progressing as planned and a legislative proposal for the first sector(s) is expected to be adopted by the end of 2026. The Commission is not considering more stringent verification and audit requirements for animal welfare labelling. Regulation (EU) No 1169/20114 clearly prohibits any food information, including labels or claims, that is ambiguous, not based – where appropriate – on relevant scientific data, or could confuse or mislead consumers regarding the nature, identity, properties, method of production or other characteristics of the food. The competent authorities of the Member States are responsible for the enforcement of these provisions, by conducting regular, risk-based official controls.

E-10-2026-001790.t: Age verification app, the DSA and risks to privacy and freedom of expression
qt: to the Commission Afroditi Latinopoulou (PfE) Subject:

The Commission recently announced, in the context of the Digital Services Act, that the age verification app, aimed at protecting minors, is ready for use. However, organisations such as the Electronic Frontier Foundation and European Digital Rights warn that even privacy-by-design solutions may lead to loss of anonymity, metadata leaks and mission creep, especially if integrated into the European Digital Identity Wallet (EUDI). In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
How does it ensure, in practice, that the application does not end up becoming mandatory for accessing digital services?
What specific technical and legal measures guarantee that it will not be possible to track or create user profiles through metadata?
How does it intend to prevent use of the system being extended beyond the protection of minors, so as not to undermine freedom of expression and anonymity online?
at: (English version) to the Commission Afroditi Latinopoulou (PfE) (30 April 2026) Subject: Age verification app, the DSA and risks to privacy and freedom of expression The Commission recently announced, in the context of the Digital Services Act, that the age verification app, aimed at protecting minors, is ready for use. However, organisations such as the Electronic Frontier Foundation and European Digital Rights warn that even privacy-bydesign solutions may lead to loss of anonymity, metadata leaks and mission creep, especially if integrated into the European Digital Identity Wallet (EUDI). In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
How does it ensure, in practice, that the application does not end up becoming mandatory for accessing digital services?
What specific technical and legal measures guarantee that it will not be possible to track or create user profiles through metadata?
How does it intend to prevent use of the system being extended beyond the protection of minors, so as not to undermine freedom of expression and anonymity online?

(29 June 2026) The Digital Services Act (DSA) (1) requires all providers of online platforms accessible to minors to ensure a high level of privacy, safety, and security for them. The guidelines on the protection of minors (2) under the DSA set out clear guidance on how online platforms can meet this obligation, including concrete guidance on the specific conditions under which age assurance technologies should be deployed for the effective protection of minors online. The guidelines specify that age verification should only be used where there are no less restrictive measures available to ensure the privacy, safety, and security of minors on an online platform. The Commission is enforcing the DSA on this basis. The DSA aims to make the Internet safer and more secure while preserving fundamental rights, including children’s rights and freedom of expression for all users. Furthermore, the principle of online anonymity, as established in the e-Commerce Directive (3), remains unchanged by the DSA. The EU’s Age Verification Blueprint is privacy-preserving and has been developed in line with guidance from the European Data Protection Board (4). To ensure that sensitive personal data are not exposed, stored or misused, the system uses zero-knowledge proofs, letting users prove their age without sharing their identity or personal details. Platforms receive only a cryptographic confirmation (no raw data), which ensures unlinkability and no centralised storage of data is carried out. Strict compliance with data protection rules is enforced via contractual obligations on implementers (Member States or private providers) which include mandatory data protection impact assessments.

E-10-2026-001789.t: Technical support during the formulation of financial proposals to ensure compliance with the existing fiscal discipline framework
qt: to the Commission Afroditi Latinopoulou (PfE) Subject:

Every Member State in the euro area has a duty to respect basic obligations of budgetary discipline when conducting its economic policy, in accordance with the existing institutional framework. Compliance with this framework is achieved with technical support from various national bodies, such as the budget offices and the courts of auditors. At the same time, however, the drawing up of the budget is a leading expression of national sovereignty and democratic debate. Hence, opposition parties are also involved in the process of voting national budgets. However, so far there is no institutional framework in place to give them access to technical support when drawing up their own policy proposals. The resulting risk is the expression of opinions which deviate from the existing budgetary discipline framework, and the spread of unsubstantiated and dangerous opinions in European societies. In the light of this uneven access to technical support during the process of formulating economic policies, can the Commission say: 1.

Is it prepared to introduce an obligation for Member States to provide technical support to political parties outside government in order to draft political proposals that comply with the existing budgetary discipline framework?
Is it prepared to introduce mechanisms for providing independent information to citizens on the content of the budgets voted on by the Member States?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (29.6.2026) 1. Based on proposals of the Commission, the position of independent fiscal institutions in each Member State was significantly strengthened in the 2024 review of European economic governance1. The independent fiscal institutions bring clarity and improve transparency in the national debate on public finances. For example, one of their tasks, according to Article 8a(5) of Council Directive 2011/85/EU2, is to participate in hearings of national parliaments. Member States had until the end of 2025 to transpose the corresponding amendments into national law and the Commission is currently assessing the transposition. The Commission shall publish a review of the effectiveness of this Directive by 31 December 2030 and, at the same time, shall also report on the capacity and tasks of independent fiscal institutions. 2. Providing independent information on the content of budgets to the general public is one of the core activities of the independent fiscal institutions in Member States whose institutional role was codified and strengthened by Directive 2011/85/EU on requirements for budgetary frameworks of the Member States.
1 https://economy-finance.ec.europa.eu/economic-governance-framework/what-economic-governance-
framework/evolution-eu-economic-governance/new-economic-governance-framework_en. 2 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2011/85/oj/eng.

E-10-2026-001788.t: Redistributing multiannual financial framework funds towards national security, the demographic problem and primary production
qt: to the Commission Afroditi Latinopoulou (PfE) Subject:

The new multiannual financial framework (MFF) should serve the real needs of European citizens and not be a vehicle for enforcing the woke agenda. For Greece, the priorities should be national survival and security. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

Does it intend to increase funds for the preventive guarding of the Greek border and for mass deportations, instead of wasting resources on NGOs and ‘integration’ programmes that alter European identity?
Does it intend to establish specific funds to support the traditional Greek family and incentivise births, instead of promoting population replacement through migration?

Will it stop channelling billions into ideological action, such as ‘gender budgeting’, instead directing these resources towards truly necessary action, e.g. to the European and Greek farmers and livestock breeders crushed by the costs of the ‘green’ transition?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.7.2026) The Commission proposal for the 2028–2034 multiannual financial framework (MFF)1 aims at responding to Europe’s challenges and ensuring its long-term security and prosperity. It focuses on competitiveness, security, defence, migration, food security and strategic autonomy and a reinforced commitment to the European principles and values. It includes a tripling of the funding for migration, border management, and internal security compared to the current framework. These allocations will have to be used by the Member States for addressing specific needs and challenges. The Commission proposed to significantly strengthen the European Border and Coast Guard Agency (Frontex) and the European Union Agency for Law Enforcement Cooperation (Europol) by doubling their allocations. The Commission supports Member States in addressing demographic challenges with a range of EU instruments and policies, including the European Social Fund Plus (ESF+). Under the proposal for the 2028–2034 MFF, support would be delivered through the National and Regional Partnership Plans, allowing Member States and regions to design measures providing an integrated framework for addressing economic, social and territorial challenges, by identifying and prioritising investments and reforms that respond to their specific demographic needs, in accordance with the applicable regulatory framework. The Commission recognises the vital role of farmers to ensure food security and sustaining rural economies. This is reflected in the 2028–2034 MFF proposal by including a ring-fenced amount for agricultural income support, which can be complemented based on national and regional needs, including a 10% rural target and the possibility to programme part of the flexibility amount as of 2028 to address farmers’ needs.

E-10-2026-001787.t: EU strategic autonomy and security with regard to the legal and geopolitical status of the British Sovereign Bases in Cyprus
qt: to the Commission Afroditi Latinopoulou (PfE) Subject:

The continued presence of the British Sovereign Base Areas (SBAs) in Cyprus after Brexit constitutes a unique case of non-EU sovereign military territory within an EU Member State. These areas are excluded from the sovereignty of the Republic of Cyprus on the basis of the 1960 Treaty of Establishment (Article 1), while Protocol No 3 to the Act on the Accession of Cyprus and Article 355(5)(b) TFEU state that the EU Treaties do not fully apply to SBAs. In the current context, the existence of a non-EU country’s military infrastructure outside the EU framework raises significant concerns about the EU’s security, its Common Foreign and Security Policy (Articles 21-46 TEU) and its strategic autonomy. In light of Article 3(5) and Article 21 TEU, will the Commission say: 1.
How does it assess the impact of the 1960 Pact and of Protocol No 3 on the EU’s strategic autonomy and security after Brexit?

Does it consider that such exceptions (Article 355 TFEU) justify a dialogue with the United Kingdom and Cyprus to review or phase out the military presence of a non-EU country on the territory of a Member State?
What measures does it intend to take to ensure that these arrangements do not undermine the EU’s coherence in the areas of security and external relations?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.7.2026) The Sovereign Base Areas (SBAs) of the UK in Cyprus were established under the 1960 Treaty of Establishment. Their specific status, as outside of the territory of the Republic of Cyprus, was recognised upon the accession of Cyprus to the EU through Protocol No 3 on the SBAs. Following the withdrawal of the UK from the EU, the Protocol relating to the UK SBAs in Cyprus included in the Withdrawal Agreement ensures that EU law, in the areas stipulated in Protocol No 3 on the SBAs, continues to apply in the SBAs. However, the Protocol on the SBAs does not cover matters related to the EU security architecture and strategic autonomy, nor its security or external relations. The UK is a close, trusted partner of the EU and the arrangements on the SBAs do not concern the EU’s security architecture or strategic autonomy as such. The European Council of 19 March 20261 acknowledged the intention of Cyprus to initiate discussions with the UK regarding the UK bases in Cyprus and expressed readiness to provide assistance, as appropriate. The EU has a strategic interest in a stable and secure Eastern Mediterranean.
1 https://www.consilium.europa.eu/media/lwhk3itd/en-20260319-european-council-conclusions.pdf.

E-10-2026-001786.t: Creating artificial islands in European EEZs to protect our coral reefs
qt: to the Commission Emmanouil Fragkos (ECR) Subject:

The European Union now has advanced marine monitoring tools, such as Copernicus Marine, EMODnet Seabed Habitats and the European Digital Twin Ocean, while EU law recognises reefs (habitat type 1170), including Mediterranean coral habitats. Meanwhile, the Nature Restoration Regulation entered into force in 2024, with the objective of restoring at least 20 % of the EU’s land and sea areas by 2030. At the same time, Article 60 of UNCLOS grants coastal states the exclusive right to construct and regulate artificial islands, installations and structures in their EEZ. Internationally, projects such as the Marker Wadden in the Netherlands show that artificial islands can be used to restore ecosystems, improve water quality and support scientific research, while international guidelines for artificial reefs recognise their role in protecting and regenerating marine biological resources. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

Has it assessed the legal, environmental and technical feasibility of creating artificial islands or fixed sea stations within Member States’ EEZs for the research, surveillance and protection of Mediterranean coral and related reefs?
Does it intend to support such pilot projects through LIFE, Horizon Europe or other funding tools?
How will it ensure that such infrastructure is included in the EU’s maritime policy and in the exercise of Member States’ sovereign rights to protect marine ecosystems?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (10.7.2026) The EU has not conducted a specific assessment of artificial islands or fixed sea stations for Mediterranean coral protection. However, existing EU legislation, notably the Habitats Directive1, the Marine Strategy Framework Directive2, the Environmental Impact Assessment Directive3 and the Maritime Spatial Planning Directive4, provides a framework within which Member States may consider, depending on the specific activities involved, such artificial structures in the marine environment, subject to assessment of their environmental impact before authorisation. Although artificial structures may bring certain ecological benefits, their impact on the marine environment should be carefully assessed. EU funding programmes such as the EU programme for the environment and climate action (LIFE)5, Horizon Europe6 and the European Maritime, Fisheries and Aquaculture Fund7 include possibilities for support. Concepts as those described in the question can be covered under climate adaptation, nature-based solutions or ecosystems restoration, without explicitly referring to the specificities of the case. For example, the LIFE NatuReef project8, is deploying oyster reefs. Information about current and past projects, including their results, can be found in the CORDIS database9 or in the LIFE project database10. It is for Member States to ensure that the authorisation of such infrastructure is done in accordance with applicable EU legislation.

E-10-2026-001785.t: Use of modern technology to deal with the bureaucratic nightmare faced by businesses
qt: to the Commission Emmanouil Fragkos (ECR) Subject:

Bureaucracy in Greece remains a significant limiting factor for entrepreneurship. The World Bank’s Ease of Doing Business index ranks Greece 28th out of the continent’s 39 states. According to the OECD Product Market Regulation index (2023-2024), the country is close to the average but continues to face obstacles in the professional services and retail sectors and in state involvement. The World Economic Forum gives a regulatory burden score of 3.9/7 and 66 % of businesses say bureaucracy is a barrier to investment. Regarding administrative efficiency, the figures recorded show public payment delays of 16.7 days and delays of 125 days in public procurement procedures compared to the European average of 74 days. Meanwhile, entrepreneurship figures show a predominance of very small businesses and low growth dynamics. Overall, the data confirm a clear correlation between administrative burden and limited business activity. Once a business has been founded, bureaucracy acts like a wall, stopping many before they even get started. This is the ‘mental’ index of bureaucracy and economic instability. When asked: ‘Would the fear of failure prevent you from starting a business?’, Greece recorded a rate of 55.4 %, one of the highest rates globally. In view of the above, can the Commission say: Could it work on creating a technological tool that would inform start-ups and other companies of all their obligations towards EU states?

When asked: ‘Would the fear of failure prevent you from starting a business?’, Greece recorded a rate of 55.4%, one of the highest rates globally. In view of the above, can the Commission say: Could it work on creating a technological tool that would inform start-ups and other companies of all their obligations towards EU states? (29 July 2026) The Commission is aware of the described problems and is actively working on reducing barriers that businesses may face when operating in the Single Market. One important initiative is the Single Digital Gateway (1), setting out the Your Europe portal as its user interface (2). Your Europe provides citizens and businesses with online access to information on rights, rules and obligations at EU and national level, administrative procedures and assistance services. It covers key areas linked to starting and doing business cross-border including support opportunities. It also offers the possibility to report an obstacle in the Single Market. The Your Europe portal receives around 30 million visits annually, while the linked national portals receive over 100 million. The Commission is working with Member States to ensure that the procedures covered by the Single Digital Gateway are offered fully digitally, in the same way for national and cross-border users, and applying the once-only principle. When fully rolled out the Once-Only Technical System (3) will enable public authorities across the EU to exchange documents and data upon request to reduce the burden on businesses of having to resubmit them manually when dealing with an authority in another Member State. As to starting and operating a business, the relevant EU legislation provides for fully digital procedures to set up companies, register branches and file with business registers, including through once-only principle and other measures such as abolishing apostille (4).

qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Emmanouil Fragkos (ECR) Subject:

Yazidis are an indigenous religious community of Mesopotamia with a historical presence in Iraq, Syria, Türkiye and Iran. Following the genocide committed by the Turks against 300 000 Yazidis between 1915 and 1916 (in tandem with the genocide of 3.5 million Christians), in 2014, ISIS committed crimes against the Yazidis, assisted by Türkiye. Independent investigations – including under the auspices of the UN – have found that these crimes meet the legal definition of genocide under the 1948 Convention. According to a 2017 report by the Secretary-General of the UN, attacks in areas such as Mosul, Sinjar and Nineveh were accompanied by systematic sexual violence on a mass scale, mainly against Yazidi women and girls. Thousands of women and girls in Iraq and Syria are living in conditions of slavery, with recorded cases of trafficking, forced transfers and use as human shields. The Vice-President / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy is asked: 1.
What steps has it taken to investigate and identify the states and organisations that helped target Yazidis, along with the motives behind these acts?
What specific measures has it taken or supported to ensure accountability and justice for victims, including support for international mechanisms and judicial proceedings?
How does it support the recognition of the Yazidi genocide and the strengthening of their protection, as well as that of other religious or ethnic minorities?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (30.6.2026) The Yazidis, an ancient community that forms an integral part of Iraq’s and Syria’s rich social and cultural fabric, endured unimaginable suffering as a result of the atrocities committed by Da'esh, which the EU has repeatedly and unequivocally condemned, including through the commemoration of the Yazidi tragedy of 3 August 20141. Since 2016, the EU has listed Da'esh as a terrorist organisation. The EU welcomes the commitment of the Government of Iraq to protecting and improving the situation of vulnerable communities, including the Yazidis, and reiterates its call to advance with the implementation of the 2020 Sinjar Agreement to improve living conditions in Sinjar and enable the return of displaced Yazidis. The EU stands in solidarity with the Yazidi community, providing substantial financial support, including EUR 21.1 million in 2025, focusing primarily on supporting the most vulnerable internally displaced people (IDP), IDP returnees and refugees. The EU stands firmly behind Iraq’s unity, sovereignty and territorial integrity and will continue to contribute through its EUR 165 million Multiannual Indicative Programme for Iraq (2021– 2027)2 aimed at strengthening inclusive governance with the participation of women, youth and diverse ethnic and religious communities. Similarly, in its engagement with the Syrian Transitional Authorities, the EU advocates for a sustainable and inclusive transition, that meets the aspirations of all Syrians. Victims and survivors deserve justice, including members the Yazidi community. The EU welcomes all actions undertaken by the Iraqi authorities and the international community to advance accountability and ensure that those responsible for these crimes are brought to justice.

E-10-2026-001782.t: Need for an effective European response to the new faits accomplis attempted by the occupying ‘authorities’ on the territory of the Republic of Cyprus
qt: to the Commission Loucas Fourlas (PPE) Subject:

The recent tensions witnessed in Pyla have raised serious questions about the effectiveness of the European Union. On 15 April 2026, Turkish forces violated the status quo within the buffer zone, challenging both the mandate of the UNFICYP and fundamental principles of international law. When members of the United Nations attempted to prevent ‘police officers’ of the pseudostate from illegally entering the buffer zone, the latter called for reinforcements, including tanks, triggering tensions in the region. In addition to condemnation, this development calls for decisive and meaningful EU action against the new faits accomplis being attempted on the ground. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
How does it intend to respond to these violations, bearing in mind that the Republic of Cyprus is an EU Member State?
What concrete steps will it take to ensure respect for the sovereignty of a Member State?
Does it consider the EU’s current stance towards Türkiye to be sufficient or does it intend to review it in the light of the ongoing provocations?

(10 August 2026) The Commission is aware of the matter raised by the Honourable Members of the European Parliament. The United Nations Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus (UNFICYP) is the authority mandated to operate in the buffer zone. On 13 April 2026, the Spokesperson for the UN Secretary-General reiterated that unauthorised entry, presence or activity within the buffer zone constitutes a violation of UNFICYP’s mandate and underlined that respect for UNFICYP’s mandate is essential to maintaining stability in this sensitive area (1). The EU has a strategic interest in a secure and stable environment in the Eastern Mediterranean and remains committed to defending its interests and those of its Member States as well as to upholding regional stability. A comprehensive settlement of the Cyprus issue would significantly contribute to sustainable stability and security in the Eastern Mediterranean. In this context, the EU remains fully committed to a comprehensive settlement of the Cyprus issue, within the UN framework, in accordance with the relevant UN Security Council resolutions and in line with the principles on which the EU is founded and the acquis. Unequivocal commitment to international agreements and the UN Charter, as well as abstaining from unilateral actions that violate international law and the sovereign rights of Member States, remains essential to ensure the development of a cooperative and mutually beneficial relationship between the EU and Türkiye.

E-10-2026-001781.t: ‘War-induced’ price hikes in air transport are benefiting corporations but hitting ordinary people hard
qt: to the Commission Kostas Papadakis (NI) Subject:

Air carriers were quick to take advantage of the Commission’s affirmation, so that they could pass off passenger fees as a ‘tsunami’ of price increases that had been a long time coming. The new Accelerate EU strategy is a blatant war preparation move, aiming to direct any fuel left over from military refuelling/preparations to civil aviation. Airline groups are inflating the price of already extortionately priced tickets (by 25 %-30 %) and more than 20 000 short- to mid-haul flights have been cancelled or discontinued. Meanwhile, in the period 2024 to 2025, airline profits, generously subsidised with public and EU money, reached record highs. All this, while price increases are also making life hard for the people due to crumbling incomes, with Nea Dimokratia seeking thanks for its policy of coupons, passes and scant benefits. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

What view does it take of the fact that the EU’s complicity in military involvement and preparedness is giving impetus to the new Accelerate EU strategy, which seeks to ensure the profits of air transport groups by providing a new round of aid and funding, citing the current war climate, while allowing the cost to be passed on to the people by means of price increases, extra fees, flight and network restrictions and all sorts of other burdens?

What view does the Commission take of the call for immediate measures to relieve working-class households from the unsustainable cost of air transport, such as wage increases, collective agreements, the complete abolition of excise duties on fuel, energy and air transport, and the abolition of the energy exchange and ‘green’ charges paid by passengers?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.8.2026) 1. The Commission takes note of the concerns linked to the consequences of the conflict in the Middle East, and would like to reassure the Honourable Member that the measures proposed in the AccelerateEU Communication1 are aimed at alleviating the increased costs for citizens and vulnerable consumers triggered by the crisis situation, notably those most vulnerable, while upholding the energy transition, connectivity and access to energy and transport services. 2. In light of the current situation, the AccelerateEU Communication aims to support timely, targeted and temporary measures to protect European consumers. Therefore, the Commission issued on 8 May 2026 guidance on the flexibilities available under EU aviation legislation to ensure a coordinated response across Member States2. Specifically on passenger and traveller rights, the guidance recalls strong protection under EU law, including the rules on price transparency. The aim is to safeguard the Single Market, protect passenger rights, and maintain essential air connectivity.

E-10-2026-001780.t: Greece’s ongoing criminalisation of NGOs and use of mutual recognition instruments against human rights defenders
qt: to the Commission Tineke Strik (Verts/ALE), Erik Marquardt (Verts/ALE), Saskia Bricmont (Verts/ALE), Estrella Galán (The Left) Subject:

Recent amendments to the Greek Migration Code1 make membership of a registered nongovernmental organisation (NGO) an aggravating circumstance in migration-related offences, elevating vaguely defined misdemeanours such as ‘facilitation of illegal entry’ to felonies carrying sanctions of at least 10 years’ imprisonment and hefty fines. Greece has since issued a European arrest warrant against Norwegian national Tommy Olsen, founder of the NGO Aegean Boat Report2. Both Olsen and Panayote Dimitras, director of the NGO Greek Helsinki Monitor, had already been indicted for their work in documenting serious fundamental rights violations at the EU’s borders, including pushbacks. 1.

Can the Commission provide its assessment of the compatibility of this law with the EU acquis, paying particular attention to Article 12 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the EU, the principles of legal certainty and proportionality, and life-saving obligations stemming from the international law of the sea, as recognised by the Commission’s own guidance3?
What concrete steps has the Commission taken to assess these facts and ensure compliance of the Greek law and related prosecutorial practice with the EU acquis?

What will the Commission do, concretely, to prevent mutual recognition instruments such as the European arrest warrant from being misused in retaliatory or groundless prosecutions of human rights defenders?

(29 June 2026) Saving lives at sea is a moral duty and an international law obligation. Current EU legislation on migrant smuggling (1) and the Commission’s proposal for a revised Facilitation Directive (2) target smugglers who put migrants in danger for financial or material benefit. The Commission takes note of the concerns raised regarding recent amendments to the Greek Migration Code and related prosecutorial actions. In its 2025 Rule of Law Chapter for Greece (3), the Commission recommended that Greece maintains an open framework for civil society organisations and strengthen dialogue with them. The Commission further acknowledges the crucial role of civil society organisations and human rights defenders in the firstever Strategy for Civil Society (4), adopted in November 2025 (5). The European arrest warrant (EAW) is a judicial tool enabling the surrender of individuals between Member States based on mutual recognition and trust between Member States’ legal systems. Decisions on EAWs are taken by judicial authorities and must remain free from political interference from national or other bodies. The Commission cannot directly intervene in individual cases or dictate judicial outcomes. However, judicial authorities remain bound by the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the EU when applying the EAW.

E-10-2026-001779.t: Compliance of the Sokli mining project with EU environmental law in the context of potential strategic project status under the Critical Raw Materials Act
qt: to the Commission Maria Ohisalo (Verts/ALE), Ville Niinistö (Verts/ALE) Subject:

The Sokli mining project in Finland has applied for recognition as a strategic project under the Critical Raw Materials Act1. This project previously faced the rejection of environmental and water permits by Finland’s Supreme Administrative Court in 2022 due to significant environmental risks. Recent developments indicate that the project promoter intends to proceed with test mining activities without a full environmental impact assessment, and has signalled the possibility of applying for derogations if permits are not granted. 1.

Can the Commission confirm that, prior to any designation of strategic project status, it will verify full compliance with the requirements of the Environmental Impact Assessment Directive2, in particular with regard to assessing projects as a whole and preventing circumvention of the Directive through the artificial splitting of projects3?
How does the Commission assess the compatibility of the project with the Water Framework Directive4, given the potential impacts on sensitive river systems?
Can the Commission confirm whether projects that previously failed to obtain environmental permits due to significant risks can qualify as ‘strategic projects’ under the Critical Raw Materials Act?

Regulation (EU) 2024/1252 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 11 April 2024 establishing a framework for ensuring a secure and sustainable supply of critical raw materials and amending Regulations (EU) No 168/2013, (EU) 2018/858, (EU) 2018/1724 and (EU) 2019/1020 (OJ L, 2024/1252, 3.5.2024, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1252/oj). Directive 2011/92/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 December 2011 on the assessment of the effects of certain public and private projects on the environment (OJ L 26, 28.1.2012, p. 1, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2011/92/oj). Article 2(1) and Annex III point 1(c) on cumulation https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legalcontent/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A02011L0092-20140515. Directive 2000/60/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 23 October 2000 establishing a framework for Community action in the field of water policy, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legalcontent/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A02000L0060-20141120.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.7.2026) The second selection round of Strategic Projects under the Critical Raw Materials Act (CRMA)1 is ongoing. The assessment is conducted with the help of external experts and in consultation with the Critical Raw Materials Board. The Commission cannot comment on whether projects have applied and cannot prejudge possible outcomes of the assessment. With regard to the sustainability selection criterion, the Commission conducts an overall assessment of a project’s compliance with relevant EU or national law, including the Environmental Impact Assessment Directive2 and the Water Framework Directive (WFD)3. Without prejudice to the Commission’s role as guardian of the Treaties, Member States are primarily responsible for ensuring compliance with EU law and for appointing the competent authorities for the required permitting procedures. The competent authorities are in charge of the environmental impact assessment process for raw material projects where required, and of determining the scope of such environmental impact assessments4. In the case of a risk of deterioration of water bodies under the WFD, the authorisation can only be granted subject to strict conditions5. The Strategic Project assessment focuses on the project’s fulfilment of the selection criteria defined in Article 6 of the CRMA on the basis of the project development status at the time of submission. In accordance with Article 7(8) of the CRMA, the Member State whose territory is concerned can raise its objection to a proposed project, following which a project shall not be recognised as a Strategic Project. Through this process, permitting developments at national level as well as possible project evolvement can be taken into account as part of the Strategic Project assessment.

E-10-2026-001778.t: Exhausting on-call shifts in Greek National Health Service hospitals
qt: to the Commission Konstantinos Arvanitis (The Left) Subject:

The case of a specialist doctor being forced to carry out five consecutive 24-hour on-call shifts1 once again calls into question Greece’s compliance with EU law as regards working conditions and rest periods for healthcare workers. It also highlights not only the enormous understaffing and the unfavourable and exhausting conditions prevailing in public health bodies, but also the risks that such practices pose to the protection of the health and safety of staff and patients. In light of Directive 2003/88/EC, can the Commission say: 1.
Does it consider that the practice of carrying out consecutive 24-hour on-call shifts without adequate rest is in line with EU law?
How does it assess the risk to the health and safety of both staff and patients resulting from such practices?
Does it intend to investigate a possible breach of the directive by Greece (see CJEU judgment C-180/2014)?

at: (English version) to the Commission Konstantinos Arvanitis (The Left) (30 April 2026) Subject: Exhausting on-call shifts in Greek National Health Service hospitals The case of a specialist doctor being forced to carry out five consecutive 24-hour on-call shifts (1) once again calls into question Greece’s compliance with EU law as regards working conditions and rest periods for healthcare workers. It also highlights not only the enormous understaffing and the unfavourable and exhausting conditions prevailing in public health bodies, but also the risks that such practices pose to the protection of the health and safety of staff and patients. In light of Directive 2003/88/EC, can the Commission say: 1.
Does it consider that the practice of carrying out consecutive 24-hour on-call shifts without adequate rest is in line with EU law?
How does it assess the risk to the health and safety of both staff and patients resulting from such practices?
Does it intend to investigate a possible breach of the directive by Greece (see CJEU judgment C-180/2014)?

(29 June 2026) To protect the safety and health of workers, the Working Time Directive 2003/88/EC (1) lays down minimum requirements for the organisation of working time. Every worker is entitled to a minimum daily rest period of 11 consecutive hours per 24-hour period (2). While derogations from this rule are allowed in the case of services relating to the reception, treatment and/or care provided by hospitals or similar establishments, they must be compensated for by an equivalent period of rest (3). The Court of Justice of the European Union has clarified that this compensatory rest must follow on immediately from the working time which it is supposed to counteract (4). On-call time, during which a worker is required to remain at the workplace or at another location determined by the employer, must be counted as working time (5). Assuming that, in the case described, the performance of several consecutive 24-hour periods of on-call duty was not interrupted by 11 consecutive hours of daily rest (per 24-hour period), this situation was not in line with Directive 2003/88/EC, which applies to both private and public sector employers. The responsibility for ensuring that the national legislation transposing EU directives is correctly and effectively applied lies primarily with the competent national authorities, including the courts, as only the competent national authorities can assess the state of facts in individual cases. In its role as guardian of the Treaties, the Commission monitors compliance with the directive by all Member States, including Greece.

E-10-2026-001776.t: Obligatory further training modules in rational driving for professional drivers
qt: to the Commission Pascal Arimont (PPE) Subject:

Directive (EU) 2022/2561 on the initial qualification and periodic training of drivers of certain road vehicles for the carriage of goods or passengers provides for rational and resource-efficient driving (‘eco-driving’) training, among other things, in many Member States. In individual Member States and regions, this training includes obligatory theoretical and practical driving lessons that must be retaken at regular intervals. However, from a practical standpoint, there are doubts as to whether a blanket recurrent training requirement – particularly for drivers with many years’ experience of modern vehicle technology – always provides sufficient added value. At the same time, companies and workers face increased costs and organisational effort as well as additional burdens from journeys made as part of practical training. 1.

What specific rules of EU law require Member States to implement training on rational and resource-efficient driving (‘eco-driving’), including practical driving lessons as part of regular further training?
How much flexibility do Member States have in their approach, particularly with regard to digital training or differentiated rules for experienced drivers?
Does the Commission plan to review these rules with a view to cutting red tape, bolstering competitiveness and creating real added value in terms of road safety and environmental impact?

(17 July 2026) 1. The ability to optimise fuel consumption is one of the objectives of the training under Directive (EU) 2022/2561 (hereinafter ‘the directive’) (1). In accordance with Article 6 of the directive, the courses that lead to the issuance of a certificate of professional competence (CPC) certifying the initial qualification have to cover all subjects referred to in Section 1 of Annex I to the directive, including the optimisation of fuel consumption. However, there is no such requirement for the periodic training. While, in accordance with Section 4 of Annex I to the directive, at least one of the training course periods in the periodic training has to cover a road-safety related subject, the other subjects to be covered in the periodic training are not specified as such. The directive explicitly requires the content of the periodic training to take into account training needs specific to the transport operations carried out by the driver and relevant legal and technological developments and, as far as possible, specific training needs of the driver. 2. E-learning training is currently limited to 12 hours in a 35-hour periodic training cycle. The directive does not foresee differentiated requirements for experienced drivers. 3. Well trained drivers are important for road safety and the environment. Moreover, they increase the competitiveness of the sector and the economy as a whole. While the directive already provides flexibility for Member States, in order to permit effective and targeted implementation, the Commission envisages holding an implementation dialogue in autumn 2026 in order to hear the views of stakeholders and national authorities on the way the directive is implemented, following which further possible actions may be considered.
It is listed under point 1.3 in Section 1 of Annex I to the directive. OJ L 330, 23.12.2022, p. 46, ELI : https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2022/2561/oj.

E-10-2026-001774.t: Relaxation of the rules on genetically modified organisms to the detriment of hardworking farmers
qt: to the Commission Kostas Papadakis (NI) Subject:

The Commission’s proposal for a regulation on plants obtained by new genomic techniques introduces a distinction between two categories of plant: NGT1 and NGT2. NGT1 plants are exempt from basic requirements for risk assessment, labelling and traceability of the end product. This means that consumers do not know what they are consuming and there is a risk of crops being accidentally contaminated by other adjacent crops or by the NGT1 reproductive material. The proposed framework allows for the patenting of plants obtained by such techniques, with some exceptions, and provides for mechanisms to regulate access to such genetic material. At the same time, the use of these plants in organic production is still banned. NGT2s are subject to risk assessment and authorisation procedures, in line with the current GMO framework. The proposal seeks to build a regulatory framework for the development and use of these techniques, arguing that the rules currently in force pose an obstacle to innovation and competitiveness. Can the Commission answer the following: 1.

What view does it take of the fact that by relaxing any restrictions and by not making labelling compulsory for NGT1 plants, the proposed regulatory framework will increase mass imports of such products from non-EU countries, worsening the situation farmers are facing as a result of a policy that promoted competitiveness and profits for agroindustrial groups?

What view does it take of the fact that the overall strategy being promoted in the agrifood sector, including the promotion of the EU-Mercosur free trade agreement, further concentrates production in the hands of big corporations, to the detriment of hardworking farmers and livestock farmers?

(9 July 2026) Under the proposed Regulation on plants obtained by new genomic techniques (NGTs), NGT plants equivalent to conventional plants will be subject to the provisions that apply to conventional varieties. By providing for enabling and proportionate rules, the regulation will allow EU breeders to accelerate the development of crops and EU farmers, in particular small ones, to benefit from plants offering, for example, enhanced resilience to climate change, improved nutrient use requiring fewer fertilisers, pest resistance, or traits beneficial for processors and consumers. This will help farmers to access new varieties more quickly, opening new markets and reducing dependence on inputs such as synthetic fertilisers. NGTs can also boost domestic production of protein plants, reducing supply chain vulnerabilities and enhancing food security. Furthermore, imported products from NGT plants must fulfil the same requirements as those produced in the EU. The regulation has thus the potential to strengthen the EU’s strategic autonomy and enhance the sustainability and competitiveness of the EU’s agricultural sector. The EU-Mercosur Interim Trade Agreement (ITA) (1), which has been provisionally applied by the EU and the Signatory MERCOSUR States as of 1 May 2026, will significantly reduce tariffs on EU agri-food exports to the Mercosur region, while offering safeguards to protect sensitive EU sectors such as beef and poultry. These new opportunities and safeguards will benefit EU companies of all sizes, including SME s (2). In addition, the Agreement contains a dedicated chapter for SMEs to address the specific challenges they face in trade and investment activities.

E-10-2026-001773.t: Operationalisation of the EU’s mutual assistance clause and NATO’s role and transatlantic relations
qt: to the Commission Michał Dworczyk (ECR) Subject:

The EU summit in Cyprus and the irresponsible and damaging interview which Prime Minister Donald Tusk gave to the Financial Times1 in this context confirm a worrying shift in the EU’s security thinking. Increasing importance is being attached to an expanding catalogue of political concepts, such as European strategic autonomy or a European army, which undermine the role of NATO and could lead to the United States being gradually pushed out of Europe. At a time of unprecedented threats to our continent, this is extremely dangerous and short-sighted, especially from the perspective of the eastern flank countries. I was therefore concerned to learn that the Commission had begun work on operationalising the mutual assistance clause (Article 42(7) TEU). Although the provision itself may constitute an important element of solidarity between Member States, it should not be used to redefine transatlantic relations or to diminish the role of the United States in Europe’s security system. The cornerstone of this system is NATO and its key pillar is Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty. The EU’s mutual assistance clause will not replace the deterrence guarantees provided by the Alliance, in particular through the US military presence and capabilities. I would therefore like to ask: 1.

How does the Commission intend to ensure that the work on operationalising the EU’s mutual assistance clause and the implementation plan being drawn up are not exploited or interpreted as measures which weaken the role of NATO, undermine the significance of Article 5 of the Alliance or damage transatlantic relations?
Is this work being coordinated with the North Atlantic Alliance and key allies, including the United States?
https://www.rp.pl/polityka/art44226821-donald-tusk-w-rozmowie-z-ft-czy-usa-sa-gotowe-na-lojalnoscwobec-europy?utm.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (29.7.2026) In the current volatile geopolitical environment, strengthening the EU’s crisis preparedness has become essential. The discussions on Article 42(7) of the Treaty on European Union (TEU)1 are part of the EU’s broader reflection on the future of EU security and defence. The Treaty is clear: the implementation of the mutual assistance clause is entirely the prerogative of EU Member States. Ongoing reflections focus on clarifying how Member States may invoke it, the necessary coordination and the possible support from EU institutions, if requested by the affected Member State. For the 23 Member States that are also NATO allies, NATO remains the cornerstone of collective defence. Article 42(7) of the TEU itself explicitly recognises this reality, stating that it shall not prejudge the specific security and defence policies of certain Member States, including those linked to neutrality or NATO obligations. Ongoing work will by no means replace the deterrence and defence guarantees provided by NATO, nor should it be interpreted as weakening its role or undermining the significance of the provisions of Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty2. On the contrary, discussions on the implementation of Article 42(7) of the TEU are being conducted in coordination with NATO, with the aim of ensuring coherence, complementarity and mutual reinforcement between the two frameworks, including through clear and coherent strategic communication.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=OJ:C:2008:115:FULL. 2 https://www.nato.int/en/about-us/official-texts-and-resources/official-texts/1949/04/04/the-north-atlantic-treaty.

E-10-2026-001772.t: Systemic shortcomings in food safety controls and imports in the EU
qt: to the Commission Emil Radev (PPE), Malika Sorel (NI), Georgiana Teodorescu (ECR), Ilhan Kyuchyuk (Renew), Antonín Staněk (PfE), Krzysztof Hetman (PPE), Andrey Novakov (PPE), Ilia Lazarov (PPE), Anne-Sophie Frigout (PfE), Nikola Bartůšek (NI), Volker Schnurrbusch (ESN), Ciaran Mullooly (Renew), Eva Maydell (PPE), Kosma Złotowski (ECR), Andrzej Buła (PPE), Maria Grapini (S&D), Petr Bystron (ESN), Ivaylo Valchev (ECR), Sebastian Tynkkynen (ECR) Subject:

Recent cases in several Member States have raised serious concerns about the effectiveness of controls across the food supply chain for products placed on the EU market. These cases include food products that were past their shelf life, of unclear origin, or found to contain noncompliant pesticide levels. These are not isolated cases. Data for 2025 indicate hundreds of alerts per month within the RASFF1 system, while data from early 2026 confirm weekly alerts regarding unsafe food. At the same time, a significant number of suspected food fraud cases are being recorded, including issues related to traceability, origin and the unlawful extension of shelf life. Recurring cases of excessive pesticide levels in imported products also raise concerns about whether all EU consumers benefit from equal levels of protection and whether a level playing field is ensured within the internal market. In this context: 1.
How does the Commission assess the effectiveness of existing EU-level mechanisms for controlling food imports from non-EU countries, particularly regarding risk management and traceability?
How will the Commission ensure that its new AI tool2 enhances prevention rather than merely reaction?
Does the Commission envisage additional measures to guarantee uniform standards and equal protection for all consumers in the EU?

The Rapid Alert System for Food and Feed (RASFF) was established to facilitate the exchange of information between Member States and to support swift action by food safety authorities in cases of risks to public health arising from the food chain. On 10 March 2026, the Commission presented a new artificial intelligence platform, TraceMap, aimed at accelerating the detection of food fraud, contaminated food and foodborne disease outbreaks across the EU.

(3 July 2026) 1. The EU system for import controls is a live and flexible mechanism continuously monitored by the Commission through Information Management System for Official Controls (IMSOC) (1) data and EU alert networks. It is regularly adapted where necessary through targeted risk-management measures, including intensified official controls under Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1873 (2), increased frequencies of physical checks for products of animal origin under Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/2129 (3), and reinforced border controls for certain food and feed of non-animal origin under Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1793 (4). 2. The new TraceMap is not a predictive tool but analyses existing data from the Alert and Cooperation Network and TRACES to identify suspicious patterns more efficiently. By automating traceability mapping through AI-assisted analysis, it enables proactive screening of more cases and significantly reduces response times for recalls and investigations, thereby strengthening preventive risk management and evidence-based enforcement. 3. The EU already has a robust and well-established system for food import controls, based on harmonised legislation, risk analysis, and close cooperation between the Commission and Member States. The system evolves continuously in response to emerging risks and fraud patterns. A recent example is the honey sector: following coordinated EU actions identifying suspected adulteration with sugar syrups, the EU strengthened authenticity requirements. Under the revised Honey Directive (5), the EU improved origin labelling, introduced new listing requirements for third-country establishments exporting honey to the EU, and will strengthen traceability systems.
