E-10-2026-001771.t: Concerns about the EU’s new age verification app
qt: to the Commission Fernand Kartheiser (NI), Ondřej Dostál (NI), Christine Anderson (ESN), Kateřina Konečná (NI), Hans Neuhoff (ESN), Milan Uhrík (ESN), Friedrich Pürner (NI), Petr Bystron (ESN), Marc Jongen (ESN), Nikolaos Anadiotis (NI), Diana Iovanovici Şoşoacă (NI) Subject:

On 15 April 2026, the Commission declared the EU’s age verification app ‘technically ready’ for citizens and that it met ‘the highest privacy standards in the world.’ The app was positioned as a privacy-preserving, open-source tool to help enforce age limits on ‘online platforms’ under the Digital Services Act. Shortly after the launch, critics highlighted multiple concerns around rushed deployment, security and privacy failings, and threats posed to fundamental rights12345. Can the Commission clarify: 1.

whether all EU social media users will be required to undergo mandatory passport/ID age verification via this app before accessing platforms with an age limit, and, given the Commission’s repeated use of the term ‘online platforms’, does it wish to extend this obligation beyond social media platforms?
why it stated that the app was ‘technically ready’, given its technical vulnerabilities revealed by experts and concerns raised by researchers ahead of the announcement?
how it will protect the ability of at-risk citizens to maintain online anonymity if it obliges all EU citizens to link their accounts to government-issued IDs?

https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-brussels-launched-age-checking-app-hackers-say-took-them-2-minutesbreak-it/. https://www.wired.com/story/security-news-this-week-it-takes-2-minutes-to-hack-the-eus-new-ageverification-app/. https://www.sofx.com/eu-declared-age-app-ready-while-github-flagged-it-unfit-then-hackers-bypassed-it-in2-minutes/. https://itif.org/publications/2026/04/15/eu-age-verification-app-raises-concerns-about-what-comes-next-saysitif/. https://edri.org/our-work/why-age-verification-misses-the-mark-and-puts-everyone-at-risk/.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.7.2026) There is no specific mandatory method for age checks prescribed in the Digital Services Act1. The guidelines on the protection of minors2 under the Digital Services Act set out clear guidance on the circumstances in which, depending on the level of risks, the Commission considers the use of age assurance methods, like age estimation or age verification, appropriate and proportionate measures to ensure a high level of privacy, safety, and security of minors. The blueprint presented on 15 April 20263 is feature-complete and constitutes an early reference implementation of the European age verification solution. It was released openly for scrutiny prior to public deployment. Some of the issues raised by independent experts were well founded and have been corrected by the development consortium, with an updated version made available shortly thereafter and further improvements to follow. The age verification blueprint does not require any linking of accounts to government-issued IDs. The system has been specifically designed to enable users to prove their age without sharing any identity data or personal details. Platforms receive only a cryptographic confirmation (no raw data), which ensures unlinkability and no centralised storage of data is carried out. Although a government-issued ID may be used to generate the proof of age, this process relies exclusively on local device processing. The ID is never transmitted to anyone, and any data used for the issuance is deleted once the issuance process has been performed.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/2065/oj/eng. 2 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:C_202505519. 3 https://ageverification.dev/.

E-10-2026-001770.t: Impact of the EU relinquishing management of the Mercosur meat import quota system on Europeans’ food safety
qt: to the Commission Jadwiga Wiśniewska (ECR) Subject:

A few days before the EU-Mercosur agreement came into effect, the EU changed the rules on meat imports from Mercosur countries, relinquishing management of the quota system. Instead of the procedure applied to date in which the EU determines the entities to which it issues an import permit, that decision will now be in the hands of South American countries. At the same time, tariffs have been lifted on premium beef imports. Food from Mercosur countries does not meet EU health security requirements on pesticides and hormones; for example, in November 2025, beef imported from Brazil was found to contain 17β-oestradiol – a carcinogen banned outright for food production in the EU. By handing over the tools to determine which firms are to export beef to the EU, the Commission is putting European consumers at risk of compromised food safety. Can the Commission answer the following: 1.
On what grounds or legal basis has the EU relinquished management of the quota system?
Why have the changes made to the quota management system not been made public?

Since the Commission has renounced the possibility of deciding which entities will export beef to the EU, how and under which procedure will product quality controls be carried out with respect to EU standards?
at: (English version) to the Commission Jadwiga Wiśniewska (ECR) (30 April 2026) Subject: Impact of the EU relinquishing management of the Mercosur meat import quota system on Europeans’ food safety A few days before the EU-Mercosur agreement came into effect, the EU changed the rules on meat imports from Mercosur countries, relinquishing management of the quota system. Instead of the procedure applied to date in which the EU determines the entities to which it issues an import permit, that decision will now be in the hands of South American countries. At the same time, tariffs have been lifted on premium beef imports. Food from Mercosur countries does not meet EU health security requirements on pesticides and hormones; for example, in November 2025, beef imported from Brazil was found to contain 17β-oestradiol — a carcinogen banned outright for food production in the EU. By handing over the tools to determine which firms are to export beef to the EU, the Commission is putting European consumers at risk of compromised food safety. Can the Commission answer the following: 1.
On what grounds or legal basis has the EU relinquished management of the quota system?
Why have the changes made to the quota management system not been made public?

Since the Commission has renounced the possibility of deciding which entities will export beef to the EU, how and under which procedure will product quality controls be carried out with respect to EU standards?

(29 June 2026) 1. The EU has not relinquished the management of the quota system. Import Tariff Rate Quotas (TRQ) established under the EU-Mercosur Interim Trade Agreement (ITA) are administered exclusively by the EU, as laid down by Regulation (EU) 2026/996 (1), which introduced in Implementing Regulations (EU) 2020/761 (2) and (EU) 2020/1988 (3) rules for the management of those import TRQs for agricultural products. The only element which falls under the competence of Mercosur countries is the issuance of a document which shall accompany all imports into the EU of products under the TRQs, as required by Article 3.30 of the Agreement (4). A model of the document was published in the Official Journal on 14 April 2026 (5). 2.
The Agreement, the regulations and the document referred to above were published in the Official Journal.

3. Minimum frequencies for official controls at the border on products of animal origin entering the EU from third countries are laid down in Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/2129 (6). Accordingly, documentary and identity checks are performed at a 100% frequency rate, while physical check rates vary from 15% to 30%, depending on the type of meat or product thereof. According to Article 5(3) of the same Regulation, the frequencies of physical checks are to be increased where, for specific goods from specific third countries, the level of non-compliance in the last 12 months exceeds by 30% the average rate of noncompliance for the same category of goods from all third countries. At present the frequency rate of physical checks on bovine meat from Brazil is established at 30%, while for bovine minced meat and meat preparations of the same origin it is at 50%, and for poultry meat, meat preparations and meat products it is at 100%.

E-10-2026-001769.t: Transparency and targeting of political advertising
qt: to the Commission Katri Kulmuni (Renew) Subject:

Regulation (EU) 2024/900 of the European Parliament and of the Council on the transparency and targeting of political advertising entered into force last autumn. As a result, small local branches of political parties, for example, are required to find space on their meeting notices for large QR codes costing EUR 100. They are also required to produce detailed reports. According to the feedback I have received, these rules are widely perceived as being annoying and pointless. Although the regulation does not ban political advertising, Facebook, for example, has already banned paid political advertising altogether, at least in part as a result of the regulation. Political parties are the bedrock of democracy, also in Europe. Many national parties are made up of small local branches whose activities are based on people carrying out voluntary work. They should not have to bear the burden of unnecessary bureaucracy. In general, in a democracy, party activities should not be seen as inherently suspicious, but rather as something worthy of support. In its reply of 29 January 2026 to Merja Kyllönen’s written question (E-004384/2025)1, the Commission stated that it was in contact with stakeholders as it monitors the application of the regulation. The Commission is also planning to revise the EU public procurement directives in the second quarter of 2026. With the above in mind: How does the Commission intend to assess the actual impact that the regulation will have on civil society and establish the extent to which the new rules can effectively prevent electoral interference from outside the EU?
https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/E-10-2025-004384_EN.html.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (19.6.2026) Regulation (EU) 2024/900 on the transparency and targeting of political advertising1 establishes common transparency and accountability standards of political advertising services. The guidelines2 adopted by the Commission in October 2025 to support the effective implementation of the Regulation clarify the obligations for sponsors, including political actors, as well as other entities engaging in political advertising activities. Such obligations, primarily relate to declaring political advertising and providing the information necessary for providers of political advertising services to ensure compliance with their transparency or due diligence obligations. In this regard, the guidelines clarify that reporting, labelling and record keeping obligations are only applicable to service providers, not to the political actors or entities requesting such services. The Regulation also contributes to the prevention of electoral interference from outside the EU, by introducing an obligation for third-country service providers to designate a legal representative in one of the Member States where they offer their services, and by prohibiting political advertising service providers from engaging with sponsors from third countries during the three months leading up to any election or referendum in a Member State. Under Article 27 of Regulation (EU) 2024/900, the Commission will submit a report on the evaluation and review of the Regulation to the European Parliament and to the Council within two years after the next elections to the European Parliament. The Commission will also organise, in 2026, an implementation dialogue to draw insights from the application of the rules.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=OJ:L_202400900. 2 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:C_202505514.

E-10-2026-001768.t: The administrative burden and impact of the Procurement Directive on small operators
qt: to the Commission Merja Kyllönen (The Left) Subject:

It is unclear whether it was the Commission’s intention for the EU Procurement Directive to impose a significant administrative burden and transaction costs on small operators and to divert public funds towards expensive external expertise (procurement consultants). Operators are left wondering whether Member States’ interpretations and application practices in this regard are in line with the original objectives of the directive and are in any way proportionate to the size of the operators or the authority – or lack thereof – they actually have. With the above in mind: 1.

Is the Commission intending to clarify the directive to the effect that public funding (e.g. a government grant) alone does not make an independent association or foundation a body governed by public law if the public authority does not actually exercise control?
Does the Commission see a need to reduce the administrative burden and transaction costs associated with procurement procedures, which can be disproportionate for small operators?
Can the Commission assess what impact the current rules have on competition, in particular as regards the participation of small businesses and new entrants in competitive tendering processes?

(29 July 2026) According to Article 2(4) of Directive 2014/24/EU (1) public funding alone does not subject an organisation to the directive. The Commission is committed to simplifying public procurement in the context of the modernisation of its legislative framework. Simplification is expected to further stimulate competition, including the participation of small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in public procurement. Although competition has been decreasing in some public procurement markets, participation of SMEs in public procurement contracts covered by the Public Procurement Directives (2) has increased over time. Between 2017 and 2024, SMEs accounted for the majority of bidders and were awarded 71% of the contracts (3). Overall, they secure around 55% of the value of procurement governed by the directives, estimated at around EUR 616 billion/year (4).

E-10-2026-001767.t: Mutual recognition of pilot licences between the European Union and the United Kingdom
qt: to the Commission Merja Kyllönen (The Left) Subject:

Before the Brexit process, pilot training and qualifications were mostly standardised in the EU and the United Kingdom, and consequently licences were comparable in practice. Nevertheless, the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) and the UK Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) do not currently recognise each other’s licences, even though the training requirements are still very similar. It is currently very burdensome to convert licences between the EASA and CAA systems. The process is similar to that of converting a third-country licence, and among other things it requires that the theory tests, medical examinations and additional training be repeated. This incurs substantial costs (in excess of EUR 20 000) and can delay professional progression by up to a year. This question relates not only to individual professionals but also has a wider impact on Europe’s aviation sector. For example, Member States have traditionally benefited from the expertise of British pilots in relation to helicopter operations, including fighting wildfires and mountain rescue. At the same time, the sector is suffering from an ageing workforce and a shortage of new pilots. On the basis of the above, I would like to request a response to the following questions: 1.

Is any action being taken or planned in the EU to promote the mutual recognition of pilot licences between the EASA and the United Kingdom, and how do you assess the impact of the current situation on the availability and safety of the workforce in Europe’s aviation sector?
Could the Commission promote a shorter and more cost-effective conversion process where the training requirements practically converge?
Has the Commission evaluated the option of negotiating a new agreement on the mutual recognition of pilot licences with the United Kingdom?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (25.6.2026) 1. The Trade and Cooperation Agreement signed between the United Kingdom and the EU foresees some alleviations compared to normal trade rules with third counties. In the area of aviation, alleviations to standard rules concerning third country certification were only agreed for initial airworthiness, i.e. the initial approval of new aircraft and other aviation products. 2. Pilot licences issued by states that are not part of the EU aviation safety rules, can be validated under the conditions in Regulation (EU) 2020/7231, which ensures that their training is at same level as that of EU-trained pilots and which also allows for specific short-term validations in case of need to cover sudden pilot shortages in some specialist tasks. 3. There are currently no changes foreseen to this agreement and the Commission is not aware of a particular shortage of pilots in the EU that would necessitate additional measures. The EU has a vibrant pilot training industry and has been able to cover any increase in pilot jobs.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32020R0723.

E-10-2026-001766.t: The Spanish Government’s invitation to Delcy Rodríguez, acting President of Venezuela and persona non grata in the European Union
qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Dolors Montserrat (PPE) Subject:

Since 2017, the European Union has imposed restrictive measures on Venezuela, which include individual sanctions, such as bans on entering the EU and asset freezes, against various high-ranking officials, including Delcy Rodríguez, for being responsible for human rights violations and for undermining democracy and the rule of law. According to recent reports, the Spanish Government has confirmed the invitation of Rodríguez, currently the acting President of Venezuela, to the Ibero-American Summit that will be held in Madrid in November 2026, despite the fact that she remains on the EU sanctions list. In view of the above: 1.

Do the Commission and the Vice-President / High Representative consider the invitation and possible presence in the EU of a person subject to an entry ban to be compatible with EU law and with the Council Decision concerning restrictive measures in view of the situation in Venezuela?
Has the Commission been informed of any request by Spain for an exemption or derogation, and what would be the consequences of the Common Position being violated?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (31.7.2026) EU sanctions on Venezuela provide for exemptions and derogations from the restrictions on admission established under this regime. In particular, Article 6 of Council Decision (CFSP) 2017/2074 provides for such an exemption when a Member State is bound by an obligation of international law, namely (a) as a host country to an international intergovernmental organisation; (b) as a host country to an international conference convened by, or under the auspices of, the UN; (c) under a multilateral agreement conferring privileges and immunities; or (d) under the 1929 Treaty of Conciliation concluded by the Holy See and Italy1. The Council shall be duly informed when a Member State grants such an exemption2. That Article also allows Member States to grant exemptions from the the restrictions on admission where travel of the listed person is justified on the grounds of urgent humanitarian need, or on grounds of attending intergovernmental meetings and meetings promoted by the Union, or hosted by a Member State holding the chairmanship in office of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe, where a political dialogue is conducted that directly promotes democracy, human rights and the rule of law in Venezuela3. Member States wishing to grant such exemptions have an obligation to notify the Council in writing and respect the procedure set out by that same Article4.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dec/2017/2074/oj/eng - Article 6, paragraph 3, of Council Decision (CFSP)

2017/2074 of 13 November 2017 concerning restrictive measures in view of the situation in Venezuela, OJ L 295, 14.11.2017, p. 60. 2 Article 6, paragraph 5, of Council Decision (CFSP) 2017/2074. 3 Article 6, paragraph 6, of Council Decision (CFSP) 2017/2074. 4 Article 6, paragraph 7, of Council Decision (CFSP) 2017/2074.

E-10-2026-001765.t: Internationalisation of Prüm data exchange between police forces
qt: to the Commission Özlem Demirel (The Left) Subject:

The Prüm Convention allows the automated exchange of police data (DNA profiles, fingerprints, vehicle license plates) between EU Member States for the purpose of law enforcement and counter‑terrorism. Discussions are now taking place at EU level to expand aspects of the Prüm model to include non-EU countries, such as by introducing a legal framework entitled ‘Prüm International’ or similar agreements. 1.

Which non-EU countries does the Commission currently consider to be, in principle, suited to participating in ‘Prüm International’ or a comparable automated data exchange with EU Member States, when account is taken of their institutions, legal framework and level of data protection, and which non-EU countries have already expressed interest in taking part in the scheme?
What workshops or conferences has the Commission already held on this subject, and which non-EU countries, Schengen countries and EU agencies (such as Europol and euLISA) have taken part?
Is the Commission designing the ‘Prüm International’ framework on a ‘one size fits all’ basis, or are there plans for a legal framework tailored to each non-EU country?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.7.2026) The Commission is assessing the possibility for a ‘Prüm international’ initiative. At this stage, the consultation and assessment phase for this new initiative are on-going. In that context, data protection standards, legal conditions and technical factors are being taken into account. On 5 March 2026, the Commission services organised a technical workshop with Member States, the EU Agency for the Operational Management of Large-Scale IT Systems (eu-LISA) and the EU Agency for Law Enforcement Cooperation (Europol). Schengen Associated countries joined for the final point included in the agenda of the workshop, during which the agencies presented their views and provided initial feedback on the ongoing reflections concerning the initiative. A public consultation has been launched on 12 June 2026 on the Commission’s website Have your say.

E-10-2026-001764.t: Worker deaths in Sicily and bolstering EU workplace security measures
qt: to the Commission Giuseppe Antoci (The Left) Subject:

The recent workplace deaths of two employees in Sicily (one in Palermo) are a reminder of the chronic nature of occupational fatalities. These incidents highlight the urgent need for continuous and rigorous assessments to determine the effectiveness of prevention measures, checks and mandatory worker training and the extent to which stakeholders are complying with their obligations. Enshrined in Article 153 TFEU and implemented through Framework Directive 89/391/EEC as well as secondary legislation, the protection of worker health and safety is a fundamental EU principle. In the light of the above, could the Commission answer the following questions: 1.
Is it aware of the alarming increase in workplace deaths in Sicily and in the rest of Italy?
What further steps will it take to strengthen checks on the implementation of EU directives, including as regards public procurement, subcontracting and precarious employment?

Will it push for European funds – including ESF+ and other relevant instruments – to be allocated specifically to training and prevention programmes and projects for the digitalisation of labour inspections and inspectorates in the areas most impacted by workplace fatalities?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (26.6.2026) The statistical office of the EU (Eurostat) collects statistics on accidents at work1 reported by Member States’ statistical authorities. Data on individual Italian regions such as Sicily are not published by Eurostat. EU occupational safety and health (OSH) legislation applies to all workers, including those working for subcontractors or in precarious employment. The Framework Directive 89/391/EC2 requires that employers sharing a workplace (who may be contractors or subcontractors) cooperate in implementing health and safety provisions, coordinate their actions and inform one another and their workers of the OSH risks. The EU OSH directives set obligations for all employers, including contractors and subcontractors. Member States have to transpose EU directives into national law and enforce relevant national transposing provisions. They are competent to decide on the organisation of enforcement authorities and on the nature, frequency, procedure and other characteristics of such controls. The Commission promotes better and equivalent enforcement through activities of the Senior Labour Inspectors’ Committee. In the 2021-2027 programming period, the European Social Fund Plus (ESF+) is the EU’s main financial tool to invest in people. Implemented in shared management, Member States can decide to use the ESF+ to co-finance projects. Under the specific objectives set out in Article 4(1) points (b) and (d) of the ESF+ Regulation3, Member States could use the ESF+ to support, amongst others, training and prevention programmes as well as the digitalisation of labor inspections with a view to reducing workplace fatalities.
1 Data collection implemented by the Commission Regulation (EU) No 349/2011 of 11 April 2011 implementing

Regulation (EC) No 1338/2008 of the European Parliament and of the Council on Community statistics on public health and health and safety at work, as regards statistics on accidents at work. 2 Council Directive 89/391/EEC of 12 June 1989 on the introduction of measures to encourage improvements in the safety and health of workers at work (OJ L 183, 29.6.1989, p. 1) - https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legalcontent/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A01989L0391-20081211. 3 Regulation (EU) 2021/1057 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 24 June 2021 establishing the European Social Fund Plus (ESF+) and repealing Regulation (EU) No 1296/2013.

E-10-2026-001763.t: Rising energy costs and effects on regional cohesion and freight transport in Sicily
qt: to the Commission Giuseppe Antoci (The Left) Subject:

Recent protests by road hauliers in Sicily have highlighted serious problems in the island’s logistics system, with blockades in the main ports and real risks to continuity of supply. Operators in the sector are unhappy about the rise in energy costs and sea freight rates and the shift, under the European Green Deal, of ETS1 burdens along the supply chain. Those effects disproportionately affect island regions, such as Sicily and Sardinia, which are structurally dependent on maritime transport. Given the EU’s principles on regional cohesion, if its climate policies are not equipped with proper compensatory measures, they may have regressive effects and exacerbate regional disparities. Can the Commission answer the following questions: 1.

How will it ensure that Article 174 Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU)2 is upheld in the implementation of the European Green Deal, preventing disproportionate effects for island regions?
Does it take the view that instruments such as the Cohesion Fund and the Just Transition Fund should be made available or stepped up to support islands’ freight transport sectors?
Will it take measures to prevent ETS costs being passed on to road hauliers and other more vulnerable operators in the sector?

The EU ETS (European Union Emissions Trading Scheme) is one of the EU’s main tools to cut greenhouse gas emissions in industrial sectors with the heaviest impact on climate change. Article 174 TFEU establishes that one of the purposes of the EU is to strengthen its economic, social and territorial cohesion, paying particular attention to island regions.
at: (English version) to the Commission Giuseppe Antoci (The Left) (29 April 2026) Subject: Rising energy costs and effects on regional cohesion and freight transport in Sicily Recent protests by road hauliers in Sicily have highlighted serious problems in the island’s logistics system, with blockades in the main ports and real risks to continuity of supply. Operators in the sector are unhappy about the rise in energy costs and sea freight rates and the shift, under the European Green Deal, of ETS (1) burdens along the supply chain. Those effects disproportionately affect island regions, such as Sicily and Sardinia, which are structurally dependent on maritime transport. Given the EU’s principles on regional cohesion, if its climate policies are not equipped with proper compensatory measures, they may have regressive effects and exacerbate regional disparities. Can the Commission answer the following questions: 1.

How will it ensure that Article 174 Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU) (2) is upheld in the implementation of the European Green Deal, preventing disproportionate effects for island regions?
Does it take the view that instruments such as the Cohesion Fund and the Just Transition Fund should be made available or stepped up to support islands’ freight transport sectors?
Will it take measures to prevent ETS costs being passed on to road hauliers and other more vulnerable operators in the sector?

(10 July 2026) Islands have always benefitted from cohesion policy in line with the article 174 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU, which calls for ‘particular attention’ to these territories. On this basis, the EU strategy for islands (1) was adopted on 10 June 2026. In 2021-2027 period, at least EUR 14.7 billion from cohesion policy funds (2) (3) is allocated to investments supporting island development, competitiveness, green transition and improved connectivity. Rising energy costs, which affect islands connectivity, underline the need to accelerate transport decarbonisation and reduce dependencies on fossil fuels. Cohesion policy funds support smart and sustainable mobility, with focus on transport decarbonisation, making it more resilient to volatile energy costs. For example, the European Regional Development Fund (ERDF) regional programme for Sicily has indicative allocations of around EUR 37.2 million for the reconstruction or modernisation of the Trans-European Transport Network (TEN-T) railways and around EUR 462 million for other railways (for example, acquisition of zero-emission electric rail assets), regional roads and ports. The ERDF regional programme for Sardinia 2021-2027 provides around EUR 31 million (EU contribution) to sustainable urban transport, including clean rolling stock, digitalisation and alternative fuels. The EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) recognises the challenges faced by islands and includes targeted derogations to preserve their connectivity. 1

The EU ETS (European Union Emissions Trading Scheme) is one of the EU’s main tools to cut greenhouse gas emissions in industrial sectors with the heaviest impact on climate change. Article 174 TFEU establishes that one of the purposes of the EU is to strengthen its economic, social and territorial cohesion, paying particular attention to island regions. COM(2026) 520 final: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex:52026DC0520 . Regulation (EU) 2021/1058 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 24 June 2021 on the European Regional Development Fund and on the Cohesion Fund, OJ L 231, 30.6.2021, p. 60, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2021/1058/oj. Regulation (EU) 2021/1056 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 24 June 2021 establishing the Just Transition Fund, OJ L 231, 30.6.2021, p. 1, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2021/1056/oj .

The Commission also assesses regularly the ETS social and economic impacts on their maritime sectors. While the ETS Directive (4) allows for the transfer of the ETS costs from the shipping company to another entity operating the ship, it does not regulate the pass-through of costs to shippers.

As part of such actions, some content is classified as ‘left-wing extremism’ or ‘extreme left-wing terrorism’ without there being any publicly known criteria for this. 1.

at: (English version) to the Commission Özlem Demirel (The Left) (29 April 2026) Subject: EU IRU Action Days against alleged extremist left-wing content The EU Internet Referral Unit (EU IRU) set up within Europol carries out coordinated action days where online content is reported to platforms for deletion. E-10-2026-001760.t: EU support for the Tunisian coastguard and assessment under international law of the sea
qt: to the Commission Özlem Demirel (The Left) Subject:

Since 2015, the German Federal Police has been taking part in EU projects to support the reform of the Tunisian security sector, with a particular focus on developing more efficient police structures and strengthening the coastguard. Supported projects include the construction and extension of facilities in Zarzis, Sfax and Bizerte (2023-2025) and the provision of operational assets (2024). 1.

Which authorities from which Member States and, where applicable, non-EU countries are involved in EU-funded projects to build a maritime training academy for the Tunisian National Guard, what is/was the time frame for these projects, and what are/were the arrangements for funding and delivery?

Which authorities from which Member States and, where applicable, non-EU countries are involved in EU-funded projects to build a maritime rescue coordination centre in Tunisia, what is/was the time frame for these projects, and what are/were the arrangements for funding and delivery?

Does the Commission consider Tunisia to be a safe place pursuant to international law of the sea (i.e. the rules on search and rescue, and those of the International Maritime Organization and the International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea) for the disembarkation of rescued persons and, if so, what conflicting observations have been taken into account?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (7.8.2026) The EU is supporting Tunisia to strengthen its capacities in search and rescue. Enhancing training and operational capacities is essential to save lives at sea and ensure compliance with international standards and procedures. In this context, the EU is working with the International Centre for Migration Policy Development and the German Federal Police to develop training curricula for the Tunisian Coast Guard and support the possible establishment of a maritime training academy. The programme is funded by the EU with EUR 13.5 million and has been implemented since January 2023 for a duration of 42 months. The EU is also cooperating with the French agency Civipol to strengthen the capacities of the Tunisian Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre. The project supports the development of coordination, communication and operational capabilities for maritime search and rescue activities. This activity is funded by the EU with approximately EUR 6.6 million, started in January 2023 and has a duration of 60 months. Search and rescue operations are regulated by international law and aim to ensure that people in distress at sea receive assistance and are disembarked safely and quickly at the closest safe port of disembarkation, in line with international law. The Commission has no competence to coordinate search and rescue operations, nor to indicate safe places for disembarkation, the latter task being the competence of the relevant Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre in charge of the coordination of each rescue operation.

E-10-2026-001759.t: Frontex takeover of the FADO database
qt: to the Council Özlem Demirel (The Left) Subject:

Since the adoption of Regulation (EU) 2020/493, Frontex has been legally responsible for the False and Authentic Documents Online (FADO) system, which the EU Member States use to confirm the authenticity of travel documents and to identify forgeries. The database is to be transferred to the new EBCG FADO platform in order to harmonise the systems and improve document checks at the external borders. What technical, organisational or data protection issues relating to the takeover or operation of FADO by Frontex are known to the Council as the cause of the delay, and who is responsible for this (including with regard to any potential compensation claims)?
at: Article 79 of Regulation (EU) 2019/1896 foresees that Frontex ‘shall take over and operate the False and Authentic Documents Online (FADO) system established in accordance with Joint Action 98/700/JHA’. Recital 96 of the same Regulation indicates the intention for the Agency to ‘take over the administration and the operational and technical management of the FADO system from the General Secretariat of the Council as soon as the European Parliament and the Council have adopted the relevant legal act on the FADO system replacing Joint Action 98/700/JHA’. This took place in 2020 with the adoption of Regulation (EU) 2020/493. As of June 2026, the Commission has not yet adopted the implementing act determining the date of the effective implementation of the FADO system by Frontex (Article 6(1)(d) of Regulation (EU) 2020/493) and consequently the General Secretariat of the Council is still operating the FADO system in accordance with Joint Action 98/700/JHA. The adoption by the Commission of the implementing act determining the date of the effective implementation of the FADO system is subject to the conditions listed in Article 6(2) of Regulation (EU) 2020/493, which include two notifications by Frontex to the Commission. By mid-May 2026, Frontex had not yet made these notifications. Against this background, the Honourable Member is invited to address questions regarding the takeover of the FADO system by Frontex to the European Commission.

E-10-2026-001758.t: Military mobility, maritime resilience and dual-use infrastructure in northern Germany
qt: to the Commission David McAllister (PPE) Subject:

The changing security landscape in Europe requires an efficient and resilient infrastructure for military mobility. Northern Germany serves as a central logistics hub for the deployment of troops and equipment to Eastern Europe. Ports, waterways and their hinterland connections play a key role in ensuring security of supply, economic stability and military operational capability. At the same time, significant shortcomings remain in approval procedures, infrastructure resilience and cross-border operational coordination. 1.
What is the Commission’s assessment of the capacity of transport and port infrastructure in northern Germany in terms of its suitability for military mobility?

What specific regulatory and operational measures does the Commission plan to implement as part of the military mobility package to remove existing obstacles – such as lengthy approval procedures, inconsistent national rules and regulations and infrastructural constraints – quickly and effectively?

To what extent does the Commission intend to specifically prioritise and provide financial support for infrastructure projects in northern Germany that are highly relevant in terms of their dual-use nature, and on the basis of which criteria does it ensure that these investments contribute directly to strengthening military mobility and resilience?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.8.2026) The Commission, supported by the EU Military Staff and working with Member States, is reviewing transport infrastructure against military needs to identify key chokepoints. This work focuses on the four priority military mobility corridors set out in the Council’s Military Requirements, with the aim of building a resilient and operational network. Northern Germany remains a key EU military mobility hub, including its port infrastructure. The EU Military Mobility Package1, adopted in November 2025, tackles barriers in regulation, infrastructure and capabilities. It simplifies rules and procedures, introduces a new emergency framework, promotes pooling and sharing of capabilities, advances digitalisation, supports the readiness of dual-use infrastructure, and strengthens governance and coordination. Together, these measures support the creation of an EU-wide Military Mobility Area2 by 2027, paving the way to a ‘Military Schengen’, enabling large-scale military transport of troops and equipment at speed and scale. Financial support for projects with a multinational defence dimension may be provided through the Security Action for Europe programme. For dual-use projects, funding may also be available from several instruments, in particular the Connecting Europe Facility (CEF), National and Regional Partnership Plans, and cohesion policy funds. Under the current Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF), EUR 1.69 billion has been allocated to 95 dual-use projects under CEF. For the next MFF, the Commission proposes increasing the CEF military mobility budget tenfold to EUR 17.65 billion. The European Investment Bank’s new defence lending policy can also support such projects through loans and guarantees.
1 https://transport.ec.europa.eu/transport-themes/military-mobility_en. 2 https://defence-industry-space.ec.europa.eu/eu-defence-industry/military-mobility_en.

E-10-2026-001757.t: DT Global’s implementation of the Neighbourhood, Development and International Cooperation Instrument – Global Europe (NDICI – Global Europe) programme

E-10-2026-001755.t: Risks from uncontrolled re-entry of space debris on EU territory
qt: to the Commission Giuseppe Antoci (The Left) Subject:

In recent months, there have been several sightings of things in the skies over Europe, including a recent luminous trail reported over Sicily, which can likely be traced back to space debris re‑entering the atmosphere. According to data from the European Space Agency, the number of objects in orbit is increasing, with potential risks to public safety, the environment and infrastructure. Space debris is a growing form of orbital pollution, with possible impacts also on the territory of the European Union. Currently, the European regulatory framework appears fragmented, and the EU mainly deals with monitoring and coordination, for example through the EU Space Surveillance and Tracking system, without a fully harmonised regime on prevention, mitigation and liability. However, it is encouraging that the Commission recently presented the proposal for the EU Space Act, which would be a first step towards a more coherent and binding regulatory framework on space activities and orbital sustainability. In the light of the above: 1.
Can the Commission confirm the timeline and state of play of the EU Space Act legislative initiative?
Will the Commission include legally binding obligations for the prevention and mitigation of space debris throughout the life cycle of satellites in the future EU Space Act?
Will it propose a harmonised EU liability regime for damage caused by space debris on EU territory or to EU infrastructure?

(1 July 2026) The EU Space Act (1) was tabled by the Commission on the 25 June 2025 to strengthen the competitiveness and resilience of the European space sector by establishing an internal market for space. The ordinary legislative procedure is currently ongoing and the Commission services are committed to providing all necessary support to both co-legislators. Given the disparities in national approaches to regulating space activities, the proposal for the EU Space Act lays down harmonised rules for key requirements in safety, resilience and environmental sustainability addressed in the authorisations for space activities. The safety requirements are envisaged to address the risks posed by the congestion of the orbits caused by the increasing proliferation of satellites constellations. The Act includes a set of collision avoidance measures, space debris mitigation rules, requirements to the trackability of spacecrafts and lay down key elements regarding the orbital traffic, and the coordination with air and maritime authorities to prevent and mitigate the risk of collision leading to the generation of debris both in space and on Earth. The proposal for the EU Space Act preserves the national prerogatives of Member States as regards the authorisation and supervision of space activities therefore liability aspects of space activities are outside the scope of the proposal.

E-10-2026-001754.t: The digital divide in southern Italy and its impact on the school system: the situation in Sicily
qt: to the Commission Giuseppe Antoci (The Left) Subject:

Recent studies covered by the Italian and international press highlight that Italy’s digital technology uptake and basic digital proficiency figures are below the EU average. According to ISTAT data, 54.3 % of people in Italy between the ages of 16 and 74 were equipped with basic digital skills in 2025, a far cry from the 80 % target the EU has set for 2030. Another fact of note is that around 10 % of the Italian population does not use the internet at all. These issues are further exacerbated in Italy’s southern and island regions, where a lack of infrastructure and uneven access to digital technology have resulted in persistent and substantial territorial inequalities. The country’s digital divide is also reflected in the education system: 54 % of schools in the islands have computer rooms, as opposed to 67 % in north-western Italy. Because of the shortcomings outlined above, digital skills among pupils in Sicily have fallen behind the rest of the country, a state of affairs that could undermine this demographic’s social integration and career prospects. In the light of the above: 1.
What view does the Commission take of the chronic digital divide in southern Italy and in Sicily in particular?
What impactful instruments will the Commission bolster – potentially by means of cohesion and NextGenerationEU funds – to bridge the digital divide and ensure equal access to digital education?

(7 July 2026) As a response to the gaps created by the covid crisis and the acceleration of the digital transformation of educational systems, the Recovery and Resilience Facility (1) (RRF) supported, through Member States’ approved recovery and resilience plans, digital initiatives, such as investments in school infrastructure, digital equipment, Internet coverage and digital skills. The RRF complements funding for education and skills under Erasmus+ and Cohesion policy fund s (2). The EU allocates for Sicily around 113 million EUR in open, digital and participative educational environment under the current Regional Development Programme. The Commission is aware of the challenges linked to digital skills and regional disparities in Italy, including in southern regions and the islands. The Training Monitor (3) and the Digital Decade (4) country reports monitor closely the situation in Italy. They show little progress in increasing basic digital skills in Italy and highlight the deep geographical divide in skill acquisition as one of the main obstacles to equity in education. The Commission attaches high importance to fostering digital skills as a driver of innovation, competitiveness and upward economic cohesion across the EU. This policy priority is embedded in the Union of Skills, the STEM Education Strategic Plan, Digital Decade Policy Programme (5), the Digital Education Action Plan and the upcoming Education Package (6). The funding under the next multiannual financial framework will follow these priorities, aiming to close the digital divide. The future National and Regional Partnership Plans (7) will be determine in close partnership between the Commission, the Member States, regions, local communities, thus better addressing their specific needs.

E-10-2026-001753.t: Violence against teachers and psychosocial risks in the school environment in the EU
qt: to the Commission Nikos Pappas (The Left) Subject:

Recent incidents in Greece have highlighted signs that teachers are being inadequately protected against violence and psychosocial pressures. In particular, investigations are being carried out into the death of a teacher in Thessaloniki, with reports of intimidation in the school environment, and the death of a head teacher at a school in Athens, with witnesses claiming she had been put under intense mental stress. There is also publicly available audiovisual material pointing to threatening attitudes towards teachers. Similar incidents in other Member States suggest a broader European dimension, raising questions about the adequacy of existing prevention and protection mechanisms, both at national and European level. The Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union enshrines the right to dignity and safe working conditions. Directive 89/391/EEC requires that occupational risks, including psychosocial risks, be prevented and the European Pillar of Social Rights provides for a high level of protection of workers’ health and safety. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Does it have comparative data on the extent of the violence and psychosocial risks that exist in the field of education?
What is its assessment of the existing health and safety framework in school environments?
Does it intend to take initiatives to boost prevention and teacher protection?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (20.7.2026) The 2024 European Survey of Enterprises on New and Emerging Risks1 of the European Agency on Safety and Health at Work provides data on psychosocial risks at work by sector and country. In Greece, 85% of respondents in the education sector reported having to deal with difficult customers, patients, pupils – one of the highest rates in the EU. Eurostat collects annual data on reported non-fatal and fatal accidents at work across all economic sectors. In the education sector in Greece, no fatal2 accidents were reported for 2014-2023. The number of non-fatal cases3 rose from 42 in 2021 to 54 in 2023. The Commission is working with stakeholders to find solutions for this complex topic. The Framework Directive on Safety and Health at Work4 covers all occupational risks and lays down the main principles of prevention and protection against them. This Directive applies to all sectors of activity, including education, and it is up to Member States to properly and effectively transpose it. As part of the envisaged Quality Jobs Act, the Commission is carrying out a review of the Workplace Directive5 and Display Screen Directive6. EU action, applicable also to education, would strive to reconcile the need to improve worker protection in light of the digital transition, while avoiding unnecessary burden on companies and simplifying the legislation. Issues to be addressed would include better addressing the psychosocial risks, among others. In the field of education, the Commission supports teacher safety by promoting safe, inclusive school environments and whole-school measures to prevent school violence, bullying and harassment7. The envisaged EU Teachers and Trainers Agenda announced in the Union of Skills would also cover teachers’ working conditions.

E-10-2026-001752.t: European support for the coconut industry in the outermost regions of the European Union
qt: to the Commission André Rougé (PfE) Subject:

The coconut industry is facing a global crisis, characterised by ageing plantations and the growing impact of climate change. While demand for coconut products, including cosmetics, is increasing, yields are stagnating at insufficient levels. This situation is particularly undermining small-scale producers in the outermost regions (ORs), who make up the bulk of the sector. The lack of access to agricultural innovations increases their vulnerability, while their current reliance on limited plant protection solutions raises environmental concerns. In this context, the French Agricultural Research Centre for International Development announced on 14 April 2026 the establishment of a roadmap focusing on genetic research and pest management. While this French scientific initiative is to be welcomed, it nevertheless raises questions about the role of the European Union in supporting the coconut industry in the ORs. 1.
In concrete terms, what measures is the Commission taking today to provide specific support for the coconut industry in the ORs?

Does it intend to step up its financial and technical support for research and innovation in the coconut industry (and, if so, how), while guaranteeing agricultural sovereignty and the protection of producers in the face of imbalances in global trade?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (18.6.2026) The Commission is aware of the challenges affecting coconut production globally. These challenges are particularly relevant in certain outermost regions (ORs), in particular the tropical French ORs, where coconut production may contribute to local food systems, rural diversification, agroforestry and tourism-related activities. The EU supports agriculture in the ORs through the POSEI programmes, established under Article 349 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU, which help maintain local agricultural activities, strengthen resilience and support diversification. While coconut remains a relatively minor sector compared with major OR productions such as bananas or sugar cane, producers may benefit from support for sustainable production, agroecological practices, local processing and short supply chains. Additional opportunities are available under the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) Strategic Plans (CSP) and cohesion policy instruments, including for climate adaptation, circular economy projects and small agri-food enterprises. Within the framework of EU funds under shared management with national authorities, it is the responsibility of each Member State to determine the specific interventions financed through POSEI and the national CSP. Research and innovation for agriculture remain priorities under Horizon Europe1, LIFE and regional cooperation programmes. Union support may contribute to work on climate-resilient varieties, agroforestry systems, sustainable pest management and the valorisation of coconut by-products. The Commission welcomes the roadmap announced by the French Agricultural Research Centre for International Development on 14 April 2026 and encourages synergies between national, regional and Union initiatives.

E-10-2026-001749.t: Explosion in cancer deaths among young people since 2021
qt: to the Commission Gerald Hauser (PfE) Subject:

Cancer cases have been increasing steadily for decades as a result of environmental factors and people’s lifestyles. That increase has accelerated dramatically since 2021, however, particularly among young people. Between 1980 and 2013, the number of people aged 15-49 dying from cancer slowly decreased, and between 2014 and 2020 it remained roughly constant at a low level. But between 2021 and 2023 an alarming trend emerged: for the first time in over 40 years, cancer deaths in that age group worldwide shot up: there was an increase of 8.3 % in the space of just three years. A comprehensive review of scientific literature – covering 69 studies from 27 countries – showed a close temporal relationship between cancer cases and COVID-19 vaccinations. What is more, the US Centers for Disease Control’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices has officially identified four main mechanisms of the mRNA COVID-19 vaccination that can cause cancer. 1.
In the Commission’s view, what has caused the explosion in cancer rates among young people since 2021?
What view does the Commission take of the suspicion that the rise in cancer rates among young people was caused by COVID-19 vaccinations?
What does the Commission intend to do to analyse and stop the increase in cancer cases among young people?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.7.2026) The Honourable Member refers to a scientific article describing rare, retrospective, temporally associated patterns rather than rigorous, prospective, multidisciplinary research to determine causality1. In the Commission’s replies to Parliamentary Questions E-002078/20252 and E000093/20263, it detailed that there is no scientific evidence of any increase of cancer occurrence following COVID-19 vaccination. Based on the official data from the European Cancer Information System (ECIS), there is no evidence either of an ‘explosion’ or sudden spike in cancer rates among young people since 2021. As indicated in the Commission’s reply to PQ E-000972/20264, data enabling robust analysis and conclusions from 2021 will only become available in ECIS in the second half of 2026, following the 2026 update with incidence data up to 2024. Broader evidence shows so far a gradual long-term increase in some types of early-onset cancers (typically defined as cancers under age 50), with important differences by cancer type, sex, and country/registry5. There is no evidence of sharp discontinuity around 2021 visible in the published ECIS indicators or the broader epidemiology literature. Instead, studies show a slow upward trend over many years, often beginning well before 2020. The Horizon Europe Cancer Mission6, working in synergy with Europe’s Beating Cancer Plan7, translates evidence generated through research and innovation (R&I) into concrete solutions for people at risk of or living with and beyond cancer and supports Member States in delivering efficient cancer control strategies. This includes supporting R&I to identify environmental and lifestyle risk factors8 that contribute to the development of cancer in younger age groups.

E-10-2026-001748.t: New security breach at the Commission and potential mass exposure of personal data
qt: to the Commission Alvise Pérez (NI) Subject:

On 27 March 2026, the Commission confirmed that there had been a cyberattack against the cloud infrastructure hosting part of its web presence on Europa.eu and admitted that early findings suggested that data had been taken from those websites. CERT-EU subsequently confirmed that the published dataset contained names, last names, usernames and email addresses, predominantly from the Commission’s websites but potentially also pertaining to users from multiple EU entities. In view of the above: 1.
Can the Commission say how many individuals and how many EU entities have already had their data compromised by another major security breach of systems it is responsible for?
Why did the Commission not identify and block in time a breach that, according to CERT-EU, enabled a significant volume of data to be exfiltrated?
Which political and technical decision-makers will bear consequences for this fresh demonstration of vulnerability in the Commission’s own systems?
at: (English version) to the Commission Alvise Pérez (NI) (29 April 2026) Subject: New security breach at the Commission and potential mass exposure of personal data On 27 March 2026, the Commission confirmed that there had been a cyberattack against the cloud infrastructure hosting part of its web presence on Europa.eu and admitted that early findings suggested that data had been taken from those websites. Why did the Commission not identify and block in time a breach that, according to CERT-EU, enabled a significant volume of data to be exfiltrated?
Which political and technical decision-makers will bear consequences for this fresh demonstration of vulnerability in the Commission’s own systems?

(23 June 2026) The cyberattack targeted the Commission’s Drupal cloud hosting service, affecting 39 internal clients and 18 other EU entities (1). Given that the processing activities were carried out under the responsibility of multiple independent operational controllers, risk assessments and subsequent actions for the personal data they control were carried out by those entities themselves. The Commission is working closely with affected parties to ensure appropriate measures are taken to mitigate the impact. The breach occurred outside of any Commission-monitored systems, with attackers exploiting compromised credentials from Aqua Security to deploy a malicious version of the Trivy security scanner. This allowed them to steal credentials, conduct reconnaissance, and expand their activities. The attack’s sophistication enabled threat actors to evade detection temporarily despite the Commission’s robust security measures. The Commission is continuously improving its security protocols, including account management, behavioural monitoring, and decoy techniques, while investigating the incident to identify and address vulnerabilities. The Commission takes cybersecurity incidents extremely seriously and is collaborating with the Cybersecurity Service for the Union institutions, bodies, offices and agencies (CERT-EU) and other bodies to strengthen cybersecurity. Lessons from this incident will inform future improvements to better protect systems and data.
All information included in this reply is based on the current status of the investigation, which the Commission is finalising.

qt: to the Commission Sakis Arnaoutoglou (S&D) Subject:

Illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing continues to present a serious threat to the sustainability of Mediterranean marine ecosystems as well as to the income and safety of European fishers. Repeated instances of fishing activities carried out by non-EU vessels in the maritime zones of Member States are causing particular concern. These instances raise serious questions about compliance with the international law of the sea and protection of the sovereign rights of Member States. In the Mediterranean there have been repeated complaints about fishing activities being carried out by non-EU vessels, including Turkish vessels, in areas where European fishers operate. The situation is creating conditions of unfair competition and is increasing tensions at sea. These instances undermine the effectiveness of European policy on combatting illegal fishing and test the zero tolerance policy proclaimed by the Union. In view of the above: 1.

Has the Commission recorded any instances of illegal or non-compliant fishing activities by non-EU vessels, including Turkish vessels, within the maritime zones of EU Member States in the Mediterranean?
What specific EU-wide measures does the Commission take or is it intending to take when there are repeated infringements by non-EU fishing vessels operating in areas of European interest?

Does the Commission intend to consider introducing stricter surveillance and control mechanisms and potential trade restrictions for countries that do not ensure compliance of their fishing fleets with international and European rules against illegal fishing?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (12.6.2026) 1. Member States are in charge of fisheries control in their waters. The Commission receives and assesses sightings reports transmitted by Member States on alleged non-compliant fishing activities by third-country vessels in the Mediterranean. They are examined with the support of the European Fisheries Control Agency (EFCA) where relevant. 2. The EU has a comprehensive framework to address such situations, in particular Regulation (EC) No 1224/2009 on fisheries control1 and Regulation (EC) No 1005/2008 on Illegal Unreported and Unregulated (IUU) fishing2. Member States have responsibilities as coastal States, including for surveillance, reporting and, where applicable, transmission to the flag State. Where sufficient information is available, the Commission may request the flag State to investigate and report on the outcome. 3. The Commission will continue to assess the information received and to use the tools available under EU and international rules where the legal conditions are met. The IUU Regulation already provides for cooperation with third countries and, where appropriate, for the identification of non-cooperating third countries and related trade measures. Any such step must be based on substantial evidence and its comprehensive assessment.

E-10-2026-001746.t: REACH proposal on lead in civilian ammunition – transition timeline and supply chain risks
qt: to the Commission Zala Tomašič (PPE) Subject:

Regarding the ongoing discussions on the REACH1 proposal to restrict the use of lead in gunshot, there are concerns over the industrial feasibility of the proposed transition timelines for industry and users, particularly in sectors such as hunting and sport shooting. Given that production capacities for ammunition are, to a large extent, shared across civilian and military segments, a rapid transition could risk creating supply chain disruptions and shortages. This is particularly sensitive in the current geopolitical context, marked by ongoing conflict at the EU’s borders and instability in neighbouring regions, where maintaining resilient industrial capacities is strategically important. In the light of the above: 1.

Has the Commission assessed the indirect impact of the proposed transition timeline on shared production infrastructure and the cross-financing of defence investments by civilian revenues beyond the formal military exemption?

How has the Commission assessed the potential impact of such a transition on supply chain resilience and the increased risk of dependence on non-EU suppliers, particularly given the current geopolitical tensions?
Has the Commission considered postponing further steps in this proposal or providing a longer transition period until a more stable geopolitical context allows for a balanced and secured transition?

at: (English version) to the Commission Zala Tomašič (PPE) (29 April 2026) Subject: REACH proposal on lead in civilian ammunition — transition timeline and supply chain risks Regarding the ongoing discussions on the REACH (1) proposal to restrict the use of lead in gunshot, there are concerns over the industrial feasibility of the proposed transition timelines for industry and users, particularly in sectors such as hunting and sport shooting. Given that production capacities for ammunition are, to a large extent, shared across civilian and military segments, a rapid transition could risk creating supply chain disruptions and shortages. This is particularly sensitive in the current geopolitical context, marked by ongoing conflict at the EU’s borders and instability in neighbouring regions, where maintaining resilient industrial capacities is strategically important. In the light of the above: 1.

Has the Commission assessed the indirect impact of the proposed transition timeline on shared production infrastructure and the cross-financing of defence investments by civilian revenues beyond the formal military exemption?

How has the Commission assessed the potential impact of such a transition on supply chain resilience and the increased risk of dependence on non-EU suppliers, particularly given the current geopolitical tensions?
Has the Commission considered postponing further steps in this proposal or providing a longer transition period until a more stable geopolitical context allows for a balanced and secured transition?

(29 June 2026) The Commission based its initial restriction proposal on the evidence and recommendations provided by the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA) and its scientific committees, which concluded that the restriction (as proposed by ECHA) is proportionate in term of costs and would not have impact on the EU military and defence capacity. In light of the current geopolitical context, the Commission went one step further and excluded bullets, the main ammunition used for defence purposes, from the proposed restriction. Consequently, the market demand of lead bullets will remain stable or increase after the restriction. Considering this, and the fact that use of gunshot for defence is minimal, no impact is expected on shared production infrastructure and the crossfinancing of defence investments by civilian revenues. Concerning supply chain resilience, the transition to non-lead gunshot triggered by the restriction would not significantly worsen the dependence on non-EU suppliers. While most alternatives to lead (steel, bismuth, tungsten) are imported, most lead currently used in gunshot production also comes from outside the EU. Discussions with the Member States in the Registration, Evaluation, Authorisation and Restriction of Chemicals (REACH) (1) Committee on the proposed restriction are ongoing, including on the most appropriate duration for transitional periods. The transitional periods for gunshot for hunting have already been extended to seven years to address the concerns of some Member States. While discussions with Member States in the REACH Committee continue, there remains openness for further refinements to the proposed restriction, if needed.

Regulation (EC) No 1907/2006 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 18 December 2006 concerning the Registration, Evaluation, Authorisation and Restriction of Chemicals (REACH), establishing a European Chemicals Agency, amending Directive 1999/45/EC and repealing Council Regulation (EEC) No 793/93 and Commission Regulation (EC) No 1488/94 as well as Council Directive 76/769/EEC and Commission Directives 91/155/EEC, 93/67/EEC, 93/105/EC and 2000/21/EC (OJ L 396 30.12.2006, p. 1, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2006/1907/2022-12-17). https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02006R1907-20221217 .

E-10-2026-001745.t: Preventing charter platforms and intermediaries from being used to circumvent EU aviation sanctions against Russia
qt: to the Commission Johan Danielsson (S&D) Subject:

On 23 April 2026, Swedish public broadcaster SVT1 reported allegations that Russian brokers and customers linked to the Russian elite have been using the Swedish company Avinode – a major digital marketplace for private aviation – to circumvent EU sanctions after restructuring or re-registering operations through countries such as Türkiye, Cyprus and the United Arab Emirates. 1.

How does the Commission assess the responsibilities of digital charter platforms and other intermediaries under Regulation (EU) No 833/20142 when their services may enable Russian clients or proxies to access the European private aviation market, directly or indirectly, via third countries?

Does the Commission see a need for further guidance or additional requirements for platforms, brokers and operators, particularly regarding beneficial ownership checks, complex group structures, re-registrations in high-risk jurisdictions and the reporting of suspected circumvention?

What additional EU-level measures are being considered to prevent the use of thirdcountry subsidiaries, shell companies or restructuring arrangements to bypass aviation sanctions, especially in private aviation?

https://www.svt.se/nyheter/granskning/svenskt-foretag-hjalper-ryska-eliten-att-runda-eus-sanktioner-for-attsemestra-i-europa. Council Regulation (EU) No 833/2014 of 31 July 2014 concerning restrictive measures in view of Russia’s actions destabilising the situation in Ukraine (OJ L 229, 31.7.2014, p. 1, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2014/833/oj).
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.7.2026) Digital charter platforms and other intermediaries based in Member States are bound to comply with EU restrictive measures (‘sanctions’), including Council Regulation (EU) No 833/20141, and are thus required to ensure their services do not enable Russian customers or brokers – whether directly or indirectly via third countries - to access the European private aviation market in breach of sanctions. That Regulation applies not only within the territory of the EU but also to any national of a Member State globally, to any legal entity constituted under Member State law, and to any business conducted in whole or in part within the EU. Those entities are also subject to the provisions on circumvention, which prohibit them from engaging in activities whose object or effect is to circumvent prohibitions set out in Regulation (EU) No 833/2014 – whether knowingly and intentionally or without deliberately seeking that object or effect, but being aware that the participation may have that object or effect and accepting that possibility. They should also report any attempt of circumvention to the competent authorities of Member States or to the Commission. Implementation and enforcement of EU sanctions fall under the responsibility of Member States. The Commission has issued Frequently Asked Questions to provide guidance to national authorities and operators regarding the implementation and interpretation of the relevant provisions. Question 212 notably clarifies the need for involved entities to undertake appropriate due diligence with their customers and to check with national authorities in case of doubt.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex%3A32014R0833. 2 https://finance.ec.europa.eu/publications/aviation_en.

E-10-2026-001744.t: Concerns regarding situation of Nagyváradhegyfok Premonstratensian Provostry and use of EU funds in Romania
qt: to the Commission Zsuzsanna Borvendég (ESN) Subject:

In Oradea, Romania, the local government initiated eviction proceedings against the leader of the Nagyváradhegyfok Premonstratensian Provostry, Rudolf Anzelm Fejes O. Praem., Premonstratensian provost-prelate, despite the provostry and its associated properties being recognised and registered ecclesiastical legal entities and assets by the Romanian state. The central authorities of the Romanian state officially recognise and finance the provostry, while the Oradea local government lists the building complex in its EU-funded renovation project (SMIS 316653) as a ‘former Premonstratensian monastery’, thereby challenging the institution’s legal status. This contradictory situation between the state authorities raises concerns regarding rule of law, legal certainty, respect for vested rights and the prohibition of abuse of rights, particularly concerning the lawful use of EU funding. There is a suspicion that the financing documentation does not adequately reflect the officially recognised ecclesiastical institution associated with the properties. 1.
Does this situation raise suspicion of an irregularity under Article 2(30) of Regulation (EU) 2021/1060?

Will the Commission examine whether Article 17 TFEU, as well as Articles 10 and 47 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights, have been violated, and whether the Romanian authorities’ actions justify initiating infringement proceedings under Article 258 TFEU?

Will the Commission examine whether this internal incoherence affects the proper financial management of the EU budget and whether it raises the applicability of the regime of conditionality for rule of law under Regulation (EU, Euratom) 2020/2092?
at: (English version) to the Commission Zsuzsanna Borvendég (ESN) (29 April 2026) Subject: Concerns regarding situation of Nagyváradhegyfok Premonstratensian Provostry and use of EU funds in Romania In Oradea, Romania, the local government initiated eviction proceedings against the leader of the Nagyváradhegyfok Premonstratensian Provostry, Rudolf Anzelm Fejes O. Praem., Premonstratensian provost-prelate, despite the provostry and its associated properties being recognised and registered ecclesiastical legal entities and assets by the Romanian state. The central authorities of the Romanian state officially recognise and finance the provostry, while the Oradea local government lists the building complex in its EU-funded renovation project (SMIS 316653) as a ‘former Premonstratensian monastery’, thereby challenging the institution’s legal status. This contradictory situation between the state authorities raises concerns regarding rule of law, legal certainty, respect for vested rights and the prohibition of abuse of rights, particularly concerning the lawful use of EU funding. There is a suspicion that the financing documentation does not adequately reflect the officially recognised ecclesiastical institution associated with the properties. 1.
Does this situation raise suspicion of an irregularity under Article 2(30) of Regulation (EU) 2021/1060?

2. Will the Commission examine whether Article 17 TFEU, as well as Articles 10 and 47 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights, have been violated, and whether the Romanian authorities’ actions justify initiating infringement proceedings under Article 258 TFEU? 3. Will the Commission examine whether this internal incoherence affects the proper financial management of the EU budget and whether it raises the applicability of the regime of conditionality for rule of law under Regulation (EU, Euratom) 2020/2092? (19 June 2026) 1. Under shared management, Member States should prevent and address irregularities in EU-funded projects, ensuring also compliance with the fundamental rights as enshrined in the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union (the Charter). After assessments by Romania’s Managing Authority, based on Regulation (EU) 2021/1060 (1) and national law, no financial irregularities, fraud, conflict of interest, false declarations or incomplete documentation were found in relation to the implementation of the EU-funded project concerned. 2. The EU has no general competence to regulate religious matters. Article 17(1) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union provides that the Union respects and does not prejudice the status of churches and religious associations under national law. In addition, the provisions of the Charter apply to Member States only when implementing EU law (2). In all other cases, national authorities, including national courts, bear the primary responsibility for ensuring compliance with fundamental rights in accordance with national and international legal obligations. 3. The application of the Rule of Law Conditionality Regulation (3) is subject to specific conditions, including the existence of a sufficiently direct link between the breach of rule of law principles and the EU budget, as well as the absence of more effective protection of the EU budget through other procedures established by EU legislation. Based on the information currently available, the conditions for applying the regulation do not appear to be met. The Commission nevertheless continues to monitor developments in all Member States and anyone can submit relevant information through the dedicated complaint form (4).
