E-10-2026-001743.t: Non-compliance of the Tobacco Products Directive and the Tobacco Advertising Directive with Better Regulation framework
qt: to the Commission Pietro Fiocchi (ECR) Subject:

In its 2021 application report on Directive 2014/40/EU, the Commission stated it had been ‘systematically assessing the conformity of national provisions with the Directive on the basis of six priority areas’ and that ‘this conformity check is ongoing and has been completed for a first group of Member States’. It also acknowledged ‘deficiencies and variations in the Directive’s transposition’ and noted it was ‘holding structured bilateral dialogues with Member States to ensure conformity’. The Commission’s Better Regulation framework (Tool 39, p. 346) states that compliance assessment should feed into the evidence base for effective evaluation. Therefore, the conformity check should produce a clear written document with the results. However, the evaluation of the Tobacco Products Directive and the Tobacco Advertising Directive, published on 2 April 2026, contains no summary of these outcomes nor any explanation for their absence. 1.
Has the conformity check of national transposition measures for Directive 2014/40/EU been completed for all 27 Member States? If not, which remain unassessed and what is the timeline for completion?
What were the overall findings of the conformity check, including the number and types of non-conformities identified across the six priority areas?
Why were these results not summarised or referenced in the 2026 evaluation, despite Better Regulation requirements that evaluations build on compliance checks and the best available evidence?
at: (English version) to the Commission Pietro Fiocchi (ECR) (29 April 2026) Subject: Non-compliance of the Tobacco Products Directive and the Tobacco Advertising Directive with Better Regulation framework In its 2021 application report on Directive 2014/40/EU, the Commission stated it had been ‘systematically assessing the conformity of national provisions with the directive on the basis of six priority areas’ and that ‘this conformity check is ongoing and has been completed for a first group of Member States’. It also acknowledged ‘deficiencies and variations in the directive’s transposition’ and noted it was ‘holding structured bilateral dialogues with Member States to ensure conformity’. The Commission’s Better Regulation framework (Tool 39, p. 346) states that compliance assessment should feed into the evidence base for effective evaluation. Therefore, the conformity check should produce a clear written document with the results. However, the evaluation of the Tobacco Products Directive and the Tobacco Advertising Directive, published on 2 April 2026, contains no summary of these outcomes nor any explanation for their absence. 1. Has the conformity check of national transposition measures for Directive 2014/40/EU been completed for all 27 Member States? If not, which remain unassessed and what is the timeline for completion? 2. What were the overall findings of the conformity check, including the number and types of non-conformities identified across the six priority areas? 3. Why were these results not summarised or referenced in the 2026 evaluation, despite Better Regulation requirements that evaluations build on compliance checks and the best available evidence? (28 July 2026) The compliance assessment of the national transposition measures for Directive 2014/40/EU (1) comprised several stages, including complete transposition and conformity checks. In this context, the Commission has engaged in bilateral exchanges with a number of Member States concerning specific aspects of the transposition of the directive 2014/40/EU. The internal assessment is ongoing. The findings of the conformity checks informed the Commission’s evidence base underpinning the evaluation process and contributed to identifying how the said Directive was implemented in the Member States, as described in the evaluation report.

E-10-2026-001739.t: Spain’s growing economic alignment with China and the systemic risks involved
qt: to the Commission Hermann Tertsch (PfE), Jorge Buxadé Villalba (PfE), Jorge Martín Frías (PfE) Subject:

During Pedro Sánchez’s recent visit to China, the Spanish Government and Xi Jinping’s communist regime signed three memoranda of understanding to foster a ‘closer’ economic relationship1. Greater economic alignment with Beijing would heighten strategic risks that are already an issue in Spain, such as: 1. the Spanish Port Authority’s decision to allow controlling stakes in the ports of Bilbao and Valencia to go to COSCO Shipping, a Chinese state-owned company, through its subsidiary CSP Spain – this being reminiscent of the takeover of the port of Piraeus (Greece) by the same company2; 2. the purchase of the Mula megaproject, Spain’s largest photovoltaic plant, by Three Gorges, a Chinese state‑owned energy company3; 3. the fact that data from judicial wiretaps is stored by the technology firm Huawei – something that has drawn criticism from both the Commission and the US4. Does the Commission believe that the agreements the Sánchez government has entered into with Beijing are in line with the commitment made at the European Council meeting of 30 June 2023 to reduce the EU’s critical dependencies and vulnerabilities, including in its supply chains, and to de‑risk when it comes to China5?

https://www.lamoncloa.gob.es/serviciosdeprensa/notasprensa/economia-comercioempresa/Paginas/2026/140426-acuerdos-cooperacion-espana-china.aspx https://www.europarl.europa.eu/RegData/etudes/BRIE/2018/614767/EPRS_BRI(2018)614767_EN.pdf https://forbes.es/empresas/581903/la-energetica-china-three-gorges-compra-la-mayor-planta-solar-de-espana/ https://es.euronews.com/next/2025/08/11/eeuu-exige-a-espana-cancelar-su-contrato-con-huawei-ante-elriesgo-para-la-seguridad https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-7-2023-INIT/en/pdf
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.7.2026) The Commission is aware of the recent engagements between Spain and China. Member States remain competent to pursue bilateral economic cooperation with third countries, in full respect of EU law, the EU’s common policies and the EU Economic Security Strategy1. The Commission recalls the European Council conclusions of 30 June 20232, which called for reducing critical dependencies and vulnerabilities and for pursuing de-risking, not decoupling, in relation to China. The Commission continues to work with Member States to strengthen the EU’s economic resilience, preserve open and fair trade, and address risks linked to excessive strategic dependencies. Since 2023, the EU has intensified diversification and resilience efforts through the EU Economic Security Strategy, strengthened trade defence and anti-coercion instruments, enforcement of the Foreign Subsidies Regulation3, and initiatives under the Critical Raw Materials Act4 and Net-Zero Industry Act5 to diversify supply chains and strengthen domestic capacities in strategic sectors. The EU is also advancing trade agreements and partnerships with reliable partners, including Mercosur, Mexico, Chile, New Zealand, India, Indonesia and partners in the Indo-Pacific and Africa, while expanding cooperation on raw materials, clean technologies, digital infrastructure and energy security. The Commission will continue to monitor developments closely and work with Member States to ensure that engagement with China remains consistent with the EU’s economic security objectives and long-term strategic interests.

E-10-2026-001738.t: State of the rule of law in China following statements by the Second Deputy Prime Minister of Spain
qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Hermann Tertsch (PfE), Jorge Buxadé Villalba (PfE), Jorge Martín Frías (PfE) Subject:

On 16 April 2026, coinciding with the visit of the Spanish Prime Minister, Pedro Sánchez, to China, the Second Deputy Prime Minister of Spain, Yolanda Díaz, responded to a question on whether human rights were respected in China by stating that the Asian country was ‘making gradual progress and strengthening the rule of law’1. It is worth remembering that one month earlier, on 12 March, Xi Jinping’s regime passed the Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress, which strengthens the policies of systemic repression of ethnic, cultural and religious minorities that have been implemented by Beijing for years, in particular in the regions of Xinjiang, Tibet and Inner Mongolia, as well as against Christian churches, which are subjected to a programme of forced Sinicisation conducted by the Communist Party2. In view of this: Does the Vice-President / High Representative agree with the Spanish Government’s view, expressed by its Second Deputy Prime Minister, that the rule of law is being strengthened in China?

https://www.ondacero.es/noticias/espana/yolanda-diaz-reconoce-que-china-regimen-pluripartidista-pero-queavanza-estado-derecho-actor-clave-mundo_2026041669e097729e87c91dbff67f9f.html. https://persecution.org/2026/03/16/chinas-ethnic-unity-law-deepens-repression-of-minorities/.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (11.6.2026) The EU’s position on the human rights and rule of law situation in China is well known and has been set out in its public statements and in its exchanges with the Chinese authorities, including in the framework of the EU-China Human Rights Dialogue1 and in statements at the UN Human Rights Council2. The EU has consistently expressed its concerns about the human rights situation in China and has repeatedly urged China to abide by its obligations under national and international law, to respect, protect and fulfil human rights for all, and to uphold the rule of law. These concerns include the situation in Xinjiang, Tibetan areas and Hong Kong, as well as the situation of human rights defenders, lawyers and journalists. The EU has also repeatedly called on China to respect the rights of persons belonging to ethnic, religious and linguistic minorities, including their right to freely enjoy and preserve their culture, religion or belief, language and identity. The EU will continue to engage with China on human rights and the rule of law, both bilaterally and in multilateral fora, while reiterating its long-standing position that respect for human rights, fundamental freedoms, due process and the rule of law are essential elements of EUChina relations.
1 https://www.eeas.europa.eu/eeas/china-40th-human-rights-dialogue-european-union-takes-place-brussels_en. 2 https://www.eeas.europa.eu/delegations/un-geneva/hrc61-eu-statement-item-4_en.

E-10-2026-001737.t: Efficiency and competitiveness of the European aviation certification system
qt: to the Commission Andrea Wechsler (PPE), Oliver Schenk (PPE), Wouter Beke (PPE) Subject:

The European aviation sector is a key pillar of industrial competitiveness and innovation. Recent international and European analyses, including work by the US Government Accountability Office and the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA), point to increasing complexity in certification and validation processes, as well as capacity constraints and growing demands linked to emerging technologies such as hydrogen propulsion, advanced air mobility and artificial intelligence. In this context, concerns have been raised about the efficiency, predictability and global competitiveness of the European certification framework, including the interaction between EASA and national authorities. 1.

How does the Commission assess the efficiency and coherence of the current European aviation certification framework, in particular with regard to the division of responsibilities between EASA and national authorities?
Does the Commission consider that existing measures sufficiently address capacity constraints and process complexity, including in relation to emerging technologies?
What further action is the Commission considering to ensure timely certification processes and to strengthen the global competitiveness of the European aviation sector?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (25.6.2026) Since its inception, certification of aeronautical products has been a key competence of the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA). This and the relationship with national competent authorities are defined in the EASA Basic Regulation1. 1. The overall legal and organisational framework in the certification area is fit for purpose; EASA and national authorities cooperate effectively. The most important challenge is to ensure that the Agency has the necessary resources to accomplish its related tasks in due time. The 2025 revision of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/2347 (‘EASA Fees and Charges Regulation’) is an important element in this regard. A main challenge consists in the fact that – as all EU agencies – EASA must respect its staff ceiling as defined in EASA’s establishment plan. 2. EASA already started to address challenges from emerging technologies by building up the required expertise. The Commission sees a main challenge in the Agency’s capacity to have the technical expertise available to better support EU industry’s competitiveness to ensure the timely entry into service of the next generation of more sustainable aircraft. 3. The Commission monitors closely EASA’s workload and has taken action to reinforce staff, promote further efficiencies in processes, and support digitalisation. The Commission proposed staff increases in the 2027 draft EU budget. Work is also being undertaken to identify concrete measures to simplify the EU’s regulatory framework for aviation safety, including as regards certification.
1 Regulation (EU) 2018/1139 - https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2018/1139/2025-05-25/eng.

E-10-2026-001736.t: Consequences of ending sugar quotas in the cane-sugar-rum sector in the outermost regions
qt: to the Commission Marie-Luce Brasier-Clain (PfE), Valérie Deloge (PfE), Julie Rechagneux (PfE), Nicolas Bay (ECR), Ondřej Knotek (PfE), Catherine Griset (PfE), André Rougé (PfE), Rody Tolassy (PfE) Subject:

The lifting of sugar quotas in 2017 seriously destabilised the cane-sugar-rum sector in the outermost regions of the European Union, owing in particular to increased price volatility and stronger competition from beet sugar. These regions, which face structural constraints recognised by Article 349 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, are becoming less competitive, which is putting the entire value chain from plantations to distilleries in jeopardy. 1.

With just a few days before the publication of the new strategy for the outermost regions, what operational steps is the Commission planning to take to guarantee the cane-sugar-rum sector remains economically viable?
What other specific measures does it intend to take to protect strategic sectors facing distortions of competition on the global sugar market?

Finally, and in the same vein, does it intend to respond positively to the request submitted by all overseas agricultural sectors to maintain and bolster their primary support tool – namely, the programme of specific measures for remote and island regions?
Supporter1
This question is supported by a Member other than the authors: Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE).
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (18.6.2026) Given the structural constraints recognised under Article 349 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union1 and the sector’s critical role in local employment, targeted EU support remains essential. The programme of options specifically relating to remoteness and insularity (POSEI)2 is the core stabilisation tool, ensuring continuity of support and allocated EUR 74.86 million for France’s Outermost Regions (ORs) in 2026. Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) Strategic Plans (2023–2027) direct European agricultural fund for rural development (EAFRD) towards innovation and diversification, helping producers’ adaptation while safeguarding jobs. The Commission proposal for the 2028–2034 multiannual financial framework incorporates OR support into national and regional partnership plans, ensuring an integrated framework and coordination of all resources dedicated to the ORs. EU trade policy provides tools to address unfair practices and treats sugar as a sensitive sector in all EU trade agreements, either by excluding it from concessions or limiting these to ~1% of EU consumption via quotas. However, the sector must accelerate strategic shifts, e.g. high-value speciality sugars, rums or use of renewable energy, to boost competitiveness and preserve employment. Nine years post-quota, modernisation, efficiency, and diversification must continue to be at the heart of the sugar sector’s strategy. The CAP supports this process, but producers must drive structural reforms for long-term viability. The new OR strategy will enhance competitiveness by tailoring EU policies, funding to needs, and simplifying rules.
1 http://data.europa.eu/eli/treaty/tfeu_2008/art_349/oj. 2 The programme of options specifically relating to remoteness and insularity (POSEI) - https://eur-
lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:02013R0228-20250627&qid=1780038981157.

E-10-2026-001734.t: Rising agricultural production costs and supply chain disruptions following conflict escalations in the Middle East
qt: to the Commission Şerban Dimitrie Sturdza (ECR), Claudiu-Richard Târziu (ECR), Georgiana Teodorescu (ECR), Geadis Geadi (ECR), Diana Iovanovici Şoşoacă (NI), Ciaran Mullooly (Renew), Waldemar Tomaszewski (ECR), Tobiasz Bocheński (ECR), Volker Schnurrbusch (ESN), Katarína Roth Neveďalová (NI), Nikola Bartůšek (NI), Milan Zver (PPE), Marion Maréchal (ECR), Flavio Tosi (PPE), Nikolaos Anadiotis (NI), Jessika van Leeuwen (ECR) Subject:

Food security in the European Union is under increasing pressure. Following the escalation of conflict in the Middle East, EU farmers are facing new external disruptions affecting production capacity and significantly increasing costs. This situation builds on the impact of the war in Ukraine, which drove up fertiliser prices. The introduction of the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) in 2026 led to a further price increase of 20-25 %, with urea rising from below EUR 500 per tonne to EUR 570-600 per tonne. In the context of the escalation involving Iran, prices have exceeded EUR 700 per tonne and reached up to EUR 800 per tonne in some Member States. At the same time, farmers face rising energy and fuel costs, as well as disruptions in supply chains, particularly in transport, logistics and packaging. These pressures further reduce already limited profit margins. In this context: 1.
What urgent measures is the Commission considering to stabilise fertiliser prices and address the impact of the CBAM on agriculture?
Does the Commission intend to mobilise financial support, including under the common agricultural policy or the crisis reserve, to offset rising energy and fuel costs?
What concrete actions will the Commission take to strengthen the resilience of EU agricultural supply chains and reduce external dependencies?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.6.2026) The Commission is closely monitoring fertiliser and energy markets through the EU Fertilisers Market Observatory1. Concerning fertilisers, measures already taken include the decision for temporary duty-free tariff rate quotas for ammonia, urea and several other key nitrogen fertilisers (except for imports from Russia and Belarus) for a period of one year until 31 May 2027, a reduced carbon border adjustment mechanism (CBAM) default value markup of 1%, and the adoption of a State aid Framework on the Middle East2. On 19 May 2026, the Commission adopted a Fertiliser Action Plan3, setting out short- and long-term measures to improve fertiliser availability, affordability and resilience. The Commission will deliver, ahead of the next production cycle, targeted exceptional support through the agricultural reserve to European farmers facing high fertiliser costs, and a legislative package proposal which will include a liquidity relief measure as a possibility under Member States’ Common Agricultural Policy Strategic Plans. To strengthen long term resilience, the Fertiliser Action Plan contains actions to increase EU fertiliser production capacity, support decarbonisation of the sector, diversify supply chains, improve market transparency, promote nutrient recycling, to reduce dependency on imported fossil fuels and other inputs. The Commission is also working on measures supporting strategic autonomy across the agri-food chain and the rest of the economy including energy and fertilisers.

1 https://agriculture.ec.europa.eu/data-and-analysis/markets/overviews/market-observatories/fertilisers_en. 2 https://competition-policy.ec.europa.eu/state-aid/legislation/metsaf_en. 3 https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_26_1099.

E-10-2026-001733.t: Actions to boost European resources and strengthen EU capacities in the fields of fire prevention, detection and response
qt: to the Commission Dimitris Tsiodras (PPE) Subject:

In 2025, Europe experienced the worst wildfire season on record1. Specifically, 1 079 538 hectares – equivalent to approximately the area of Cyprus – were ravaged by fire across several EU Member States. Meanwhile, the size and intensity of the fires are increasing and the likelihood of very large fires or ‘megafires’ is expected to more than double by the end of the century. This situation calls for a drastic increase in European instruments and further use of innovative technologies to prevent, detect and respond to fires and strengthen the EU’s resilience. In light of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

qt: to the Commission Sandro Ruotolo (S&D), Nicola Zingaretti (S&D) Subject:

Meta Platforms has stated that during election periods, it activates structures known as ‘elections operations centers’, dedicated to monitoring the integrity of information and combating disinformation and coordinated interference. For the Italian elections (2018, 2022) and the 2024 European elections, the company has indicated the use of interdisciplinary teams, including former members of US intelligence services, however, without making key details public such as selection criteria, the chain of command and operational procedures. At the same time, independent analyses have shown significant variations in the visibility of political content during election periods. The Commission is therefore asked: 1.

Does it possess information on the structure, functioning and oversight mechanisms of the ‘elections operations centers’ set up by Meta in the EU and whether these practices comply with the transparency obligations laid down in the Digital Services Act?
Does it intend to examine the role of staff with previous experience in security or intelligence in the definition and application of policies on political content?

Will the ongoing investigation into the visibility of political content online include a specific assessment of the impact, at Union level, of moderation and ranking systems during the 2024 European elections?

Will the ongoing investigation into the visibility of political content online include a specific assessment of the impact, at Union level, of moderation and ranking systems during the 2024 European elections?

(1 July 2026) The Commission is aware of Meta setting up election operations centres in the EU as part of its internal operational structures. According to Meta, these centres have been designed to monitor and respond to threats during election periods, including disinformation campaigns and coordinated inauthentic behaviour (1). The Digital Services Act (2) (DSA) obliges providers of very large online platforms (VLOPs) like Meta to diligently identify, assess and analyse the systemic risks stemming from their services and put in place reasonable, proportionate and effective measures to mitigate such risks. Those include any actual or foreseeable negative effects on civic discourse and electoral processes. The DSA provides a non-exhaustive list of mitigation measures that providers of VLOPs and very large online search engines may adopt. The Commission’s Election Guidelines (3) further elaborates on that list and sets out best practices and recommendations for providers, specifically for risks related to electoral processes, and also covering staff expertise. The Commission will not hesitate to use its enforcement powers under the DSA if suspicions of non-compliance arise. As mentioned, the Commission initiated proceedings against Meta in relation to the suspicion that it demotes political content in its recommender systems, including the feeds, of Facebook and Instagram (4). The investigation focuses on the compatibility of Meta’s policy concerning political content with the DSA transparency and user redress obligations, as well as the aforementioned obligations. In this context, the Commission has sent several requests for information to Meta. At this stage, the Commission cannot comment further on specific aspects of the ongoing investigation.

at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (30.7.2026) The Commission’s Small Modular Reactors (SMRs) Strategy, presented on 10 March 2026, sets out a pathway to accelerate the development and deployment of Small Modular Reactors in Europe, with the objective of bringing the first SMR projects online in the early 2030s1. The Commission works with the European Investment Bank to implement a temporary InvestEU top-up of EUR 200 million until 20282 to support innovative nuclear technologies3. The Important Projects of Common European Interest (IPCEI) on innovative nuclear technologies (including SMRs) is currently in design phase, with funding that will be provided by Member States. The Euratom Research and Training Programme supports research activities on the safety of SMRs4. The aim of public funding should be to mobilise available private capital through suitable instruments, such as guarantees for first-of-a-kind SMR projects. Public support for de-risking SMR projects as they advance towards commercialisation is essential5. The Commission also underlines continued international cooperation on SMRs with partner countries and international organisations, while maintaining strategic autonomy and avoiding new dependencies. Breakthrough Energy or TerraPower are not members of the European Industrial Alliance on SMRs, nor is the Commission aware of their involvement in any of the SMR projects in the EU with which it is engaged. To ensure transparency in interactions with external stakeholders, the Commission applies its existing rules, including on the Transparency Register and publication of meetings held with interest representatives. Citizens can access information on, and minutes of, meetings held with interest representatives on the Commission’s transparency websites.

E-10-2026-001727.t: Implementation of Article 25 on animal health visits of Regulation (EU) 2016/429
qt: to the Commission Veronika Vrecionová (ECR) Subject:

The Animal Health Law (Regulation (EU) 2016/429) came into force five years ago. Article 25 of the regulation requires operators to ensure that establishments receive animal health visits by a veterinarian when appropriate, using a risk-based approach. It also allows for the Commission to adopt implementing acts laying down minimum requirements to ensure a uniform application of this provision. To date, no such implementing act appears to have been adopted. This situation has left the implementation of animal health visits at the discretion of the Member States and has led to differences in the advancement of such measures. In this context: 1.
How does the Commission monitor and assess the implementation of Article 25 across the Member States, in particular regarding the frequency, scope and practical content of animal health visits?

What implementation support mechanisms (including non-legislative acts, guidance, exchanges of best practice or coordination tools) are available or envisaged at EU level to support a more consistent and proportionate application of this provision across the Member States?

In light of reported veterinary workforce shortages, particularly in rural areas, what measures does the Commission envisage to support Member States in ensuring the effective implementation of Article 25?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.7.2026) Animal health visits in accordance with Article 25 of Regulation (EU) 2016/429 (Animal Health Law)1 represent an intrinsic part of operators’ own surveillance. The purpose of animal health visits is to support early detection of animal diseases and to provide advice to operators on several aspects of animal health. According to Article 25, these visits can be rationalised and combined with visits for other purposes. They can also be counterbalanced with operators’ own surveillance. Member States have different structures in place to organise animal health visits, including public-private partnerships working with farmers on surveillance. For that reason, and after discussions with stakeholders and Member States, the Commission has not adopted an implementing act in particular as regards minimum frequencies of those visits also in order not to interfere with Member States organisational flexibility, and to not create unjustified administrative burdens and costs. The Commission monitors the implementation of EU food and feed safety legislation, including the Animal Health Law, in Member States by means of Commission audits2. In addition, the Commission launched an evaluation of the Animal Health Law, which is close to completion. The evaluation addresses animal health visits.
1 http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/429/2019-12-14. 2 https://food.ec.europa.eu/horizontal-topics/official-controls-and-enforcement/health-and-food-audits-and-
analysis_en.

E-10-2026-001726.t: Visit of the Commission to Türkiye
qt: to the Commission Mélissa Camara (Verts/ALE) Subject:

On 6 and 7 February 2026, there was an official visit by the Commission to Türkiye in order to discuss EU-Türkiye cooperation on regional stability and connectivity in a shifting geopolitical context. As part of this visit, meetings were held with government officials. During the visit, the Commission reiterated that respect for the rule of law, democratic standards and political pluralism remains a core element of the EU accession process. However, it appears that no specific meetings were held with representatives of the democratic opposition, which continues to face significant repression. This contrasts with other contexts, such as in Serbia, where engagement with opposition actors and protesters has been reflected in official visits. Furthermore, there were no visible expressions of solidarity regarding the situation of Ekrem İmamoğlu, the elected Mayor of Istanbul and presidential candidate, whose imprisonment has become a symbol of broader concerns about democratic standards and political freedoms in Türkiye. In this context: 1.
How does the Commission justify this approach and how does it ensure that engagement with all democratic actors is reflected in its official visits to Türkiye?
What is the position of the Commission regarding the imprisonment of politicians, journalists and intellectuals in Türkiye, including Ekrem İmamoğlu?

(27 July 2026) Türkiye is a candidate country and a key partner for the EU. Accession negotiations with Türkiye have remained at a standstill since 2018, in line with Council conclusions (1). The Commission continues to engage with Türkiye in areas of joint interest, without overlooking the deteriorating rule of law and democratic standards, as noted in the 2025 Enlargement report on Türkiye (2). During the Commissioner for Enlargement’s visit to Ankara in February 2026, she raised those concerns and met members of the Turkish Grand National Assembly, including from the opposition. The Commission remains concerned about the imprisonments of politicians, journalists and intellectuals in Türkiye, including Mr İmamoğlu’s arrest. It has urged Turkish authorities to ensure that individuals are treated in accordance with the principles of the European Convention on Human Rights. The High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy and Vice-President of the Commission and Commissioner for Enlargement issued a joint statement on 19 March 2025 on the arrest of Mr İmamoğlu (3). Following the 21 May 2026 decision annulling the 2023 People’s Republican Party’s regular congress, the European External Action Service spokesperson noted that these developments raise questions about the rule of law, democratic pluralism and judicial independence in Türkiye (4). Respect for fundamental rights and the rule of law is essential for the EU accession process and will continue to be an integral part of EU-Türkiye relations.

E-10-2026-001725.t: Recognition of historic vehicles as part of Europe’s living cultural heritage
qt: to the Commission Catherine Griset (PfE), Matthieu Valet (PfE) Subject:

Historic vehicles are an important part of Europe’s technical, industrial and cultural heritage. They attest to the know-how of several generations, play a role in craft and mechanical skills being passed on and help make many regions more attractive to tourists. However, several European regulatory developments have raised concerns among collectors, restorers, associations and professionals in the sector, who worry that standards designed for modern vehicles will be applied uniformly. 1.
Does the Commission intend to explicitly recognise historic vehicles as part of Europe’s living cultural heritage?
Does it intend to ensure that future legislation on the environment, fuel, mobility and roadworthiness tests takes into account the specific, limited and heritage use of such vehicles?
Could it support programmes promoting the transfer of know-how relating to the restoration, maintenance and conservation of historic vehicles, particularly for young Europeans?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.8.2026) The Commission considers cultural heritage to also encompass industrial and mobile heritage, together with the historic technical skills and crafts associated with it. Relevant EU legislation takes account of the specific nature and limited use of such vehicles in several areas. For example, the CO2 emission performance standards regulation for passenger cars and light commercial vehicles1 only concerns new vehicles; it does not affect heritage vehicles. To preserve Europe’s cultural heritage, vehicles of historical interest are also excluded from the scope of the Regulation on circularity requirements for vehicle design and on management of end-of-life vehicles2 in line with the Commission proposal. As regards roadworthiness testing for motor vehicles, Directive 2014/45/EU3 allows Member States to exclude vehicles of historical interest, registered in their territory, from its scope. Under that Directive, vehicles of historical interest means any vehicle that has been recognised as historical by the Member State of registration, or by one of its appointed authorising bodies, and which fulfils all the following conditions: it was manufactured or first registered at least 30 years ago, its specific type, as defined in the relevant EU or national law, is no longer in production, and it is historically preserved and maintained in its original state, without substantial changes to the technical characteristics of its main components. In its 2025 proposal to amend this Directive, the Commission did not propose any changes to these provisions. Through Erasmus+4, the Commission supports the transfer of skills and crafts towards young generations. All types of vocational crafts are eligible under the programme’s vocational education and training actions.

1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02019R0631-20231203. 2 https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-6759-2026-INIT/en/pdf. 3 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02014L0045-20140429. 4 https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/.

the fact that, wherever the lignite phase-out and the electricity interconnection of islands has been promoted, utility tariffs and surcharges have not been reduced, but instead the people continue to face additional charges?

(17 June 2026) The clean energy transition is vital for Europe’s strategic autonomy and prosperity. Renewables, storage, interconnections and energy efficiency are essential to reduce dependence on imported fossil fuels, lower exposure to volatile prices and strengthen security of supply. Greek islands have historically relied on costly oil-fired electricity generation. The Islands Decarbonisation Fund contributes to decarbonisation of the islands’ electricity supply, while interconnections aim to reduce fossil-fuel dependence, improve security of supply and lower costs. The Commission recognises that consumers should benefit from the transition. Energy poverty remains a persistent challenge for Greece with 19% (1) of Greeks unable to keep their home adequately warm in 2024. Through the European Just Transition Fund, Greece benefits of EUR 1.37 billion to support the phase-out of the fossil fuels in the most vulnerable regions and islands (2). The Social Climate Fund (3) will support the most vulnerable, including energy poor households in the island regions. The EU strategy for Islands and Communication for coastal communities will further address energy transition challenges on these territories (4). Retail prices, network tariffs, public service obligation charges and social tariffs are primarily determined at national level, subject to EU energy market rules and regulatory oversight. E-10-2026-001722.t: Significant increase in fishing pressure on squid and other unregulated species
qt: to the Commission Anja Hazekamp (The Left) Subject:

No maximum catch quotas have been set for squid within the EU, which is not the case for many other target species. As catches of traditional target species such as plaice and sole are declining, Dutch fishing vessels in the North Sea and surrounding waters are increasingly turning to squid. As a result, fishing pressure on this unregulated species has increased significantly.1 In the 2023–2024 season, more than 3.6 million squid were caught by Dutch cutters2. Scientists warn that the rapidly growing industry of squid fishing could put the species at risk3. 1.

Given their intrinsic value and their role as a food source for dolphins, whales, seals, larger fish species and seabirds, amongst others, to what extent does the Commission consider it important to protect squid from overfishing?

What is the Commission’s assessment of the significantly increased fishing pressure on unregulated species such as squid, red gurnard and mullet, and the warning that these species will become endangered unless maximum catch limits are set in the near future?

The Common Fisheries Policy dictates that the EU must apply the precautionary principle when regulating fisheries. To what extent is the absence of maximum catch limits for heavily fished species consistent with the precautionary principle, and what measures will the Commission take in the short term to prevent squid populations and other unregulated species from becoming endangered?
https://research.wur.nl/en/projects/kd-2024-056-vooronderzoek-basisgegevens-inktvis-nl-bodemvisserij-/. https://edepot.wur.nl/686793. https://esb.nu/overbevissing-blijft-gevaar-in-noordzeevisserij/.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (29.6.2026) Non-quota stocks (NQS) play a key ecological and socio-economic role, particularly for coastal communities. The Commission is committed to ensuring their sustainable exploitation in line with the objectives of the Common Fisheries Policy. The Commission acknowledges concerns regarding increasing fishing pressure on certain NQS, like squid, and works to improve both scientific knowledge and management of these stocks, like those shared with the UK. For NQS, some conservation and management measures may be applied, depending on the fishery and the available scientific evidence. Catch limits are thus not the only tool available under a precautionary approach. At EU level, squid fisheries are currently managed mainly through technical measures, complemented where appropriate by national measures. In addition, the EU and the UK are cooperating on the management of shared NQS, like scientific exchanges on species such as cuttlefish, whelks and octopus, as well as ongoing work on Channel king scallops and brown crab. The marine strategy framework directive1 requires Member States to achieve good environmental status for their marine waters. In doing so, as part of their marine strategies, they must set and comply with threshold values at species level for various species groups, like cephalopods2. These thresholds must ensure that ‘the population abundance of the species is not adversely affected due to anthropogenic pressures, such that its long-term viability is ensured’ and that ‘the population demographic characteristics (e.g. body size or age class structure, sex ratio, fecundity, and survival rates) of the species are indicative of a healthy population which is not adversely affected due to anthropogenic pressure’.

E-10-2026-001721.t: Recent investigation into the transport of calves from Ireland to the Netherlands
qt: to the Commission Anja Hazekamp (The Left) Subject:

An investigation by the Netherlands’ largest news organisation has revealed that, during transport from Ireland to the Netherlands, calves are not being given anything to drink for a period of around 24 hours. This is in breach of European regulations. Almost all of the calves tracked were unweaned animals that spent 50 to 80 hours in transit, some just two weeks old and still reliant on a milk diet1. Animal welfare organisations have been reporting for years that calves are being systematically deprived of milk for 30 to 48 hours during transport2. There have also been repeated reports of illegal transports, inadequate water systems, fabricated logbooks and mistreatment of calves345. 1.

Does the Commission agree that it is unjustifiable that, while the legislation is being revised, a process that has been ongoing for some years now, no measures are being taken to improve conditions for animals during transport?

Will you enter into discussions with the Dutch agriculture minister in the near future with a view to introducing the ban on the import of calves from Ireland to the Netherlands that has already been proposed?

Is the Commission prepared to launch infringement proceedings against Ireland due to its approval of illegal transports over many years and the failure of the Irish authorities to take action, in spite of previous requests and the Commission’s 2023 audit67?

E-10-2026-001720.t: Compatibility of the principle of ‘national priority’ with EU law
qt: to the Commission Juan Fernando López Aguilar (S&D), Javier Moreno Sánchez (S&D), Leire Pajín (S&D), Hana Jalloul Muro (S&D), César Luena (S&D), Laura Ballarín Cereza (S&D), Alicia Homs Ginel (S&D), Rosa Serrano Sierra (S&D), José Cepeda (S&D), Elena Sancho Murillo (S&D), Cristina Maestre (S&D), Idoia Mendia (S&D), Nicolás González Casares (S&D), Javi López (S&D), Marcos Ros Sempere (S&D), Jonás Fernández (S&D), Nacho Sánchez Amor (S&D), Lina Gálvez (S&D), Iratxe García Pérez (S&D), Sandra Gómez López (S&D) Subject:

In Spain, the People’s Party and Vox have recently struck deals in regional governments introducing the principle of ‘national priority’, understood as the possibility of granting preferential access to nationals over migrants and European citizens in areas such as housing, aid, benefits and public services. That proposal raises questions as to its compatibility with EU law, in particular with the principle of non-discrimination on grounds of nationality (Article 18 TFEU), the provisions on Union citizenship (Articles 20 and 21 TFEU) and the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, in particular Articles 20 (equality before the law), 21 (non-discrimination) and 34 (social security and social assistance). In view of the above: 1.

Does the Commission consider the application of that principle to access to public housing, aid, social benefits and public services to be compatible with EU law, in particular the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union and the Charter of Fundamental Rights?
If it is implemented, what action does the Commission intend to take to ensure full compliance with EU law?

(1 July 2026) The Honourable Members refer to political agreements struck between two national parties in the context of the formation of regional governments. E-10-2026-001719.t: Impact of Omnibus simplifications on ESG reporting obligations of banks
qt: to the Commission Sibylle Berg (NI) Subject:

The Omnibus initiative significantly reduces the scope of the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD). At the same time, banks will remain subject to extensive sustainability and supervisory disclosure requirements (including under the Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation (SFDR), the EU Taxonomy Regulation and Pillar 3 of the Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) criteria). If fewer corporate customers report according to the European Sustainability Reporting Standard (ESRS), banks’ access to standardised primary data will be restricted. Estimated and proxy data are becoming more common, especially for SMEs and other counterparties not subject to CSRD reporting. This can affect the relevance, comparability and implementation costs, and can increase the risk of false incentives for the allocation of capital. 1.

Has the Commission assessed the impact of the reduction of the CSRD scope on data availability and quality for financial institutions, as well as on the comparability of bank-related disclosures, and does it intend to publish the results and, if so, when?

What specific instruments does the Commission plan to put in place to improve banks’ access to standardised and verifiable sustainability data, including for SMEs and other counterparties not subject to CSRD reporting – in particular with regard to the further development and usability of the voluntary sustainability reporting standard for SMEs (VSME), common data points and templates, the European Single Access Point (ESAP) and guidelines and technical standards (in coordination with the European Banking Authority (EBA), the European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA) and the European Central Bank (ECB)) – and by when?

Pending the availability of sufficient primary data, is the Commission planning an EUwide harmonised best-effort or safe-harbour framework for verifiable estimate and proxy data (with disclosure of the estimated share and minimum documentation)?

It refers to concerns expressed by the European Central Bank and European supervisory authorities that sustainability reporting obligations had led to a complex framework causing problems for financial institutions and potentially deterring sustainable finance. The Commission is required to submit a report by April 2029 on, among other things, whether the reporting obligations should be extended to additional companies. E-10-2026-001718.t: New Democracy Government sounds death knell for municipalities’ and workers’ social structures
qt: to the Commission Lefteris Nikolaou-Alavanos (NI) Subject:

The New Democracy Government is sounding the death knell for municipalities’ social structures by way of a legal provision on the staffing of local authority nurseries, kindergartens and children’s creative activity centres. Employees will be hired from an online, general list of candidates, on part-time contracts lasting eight to 11 months. EU guidelines treat social needs as a cost, handing responsibility (for preschool education) to private individuals and NGOs. Public social services adapt their services according to costbenefit criteria. Projects qualify on performance criteria, otherwise they are not financed by EU funds, while employee salaries are linked to reciprocity through vouchers and financing is based on the number of beneficiaries. European Union funds (NSRF) are geared towards the needs of the war economy. Specifically, Greece is reallocating EUR 634 million towards defence. In view of the above: 1.

What is the Commission’s position on the fact that the new mechanism being established in municipalities imposes new unacceptable conditions on the recruitment and employment of workers as provided for in Directive (EU) 2019/1152 on ‘predictable working conditions’, i.e. flexible forms of employment without guaranteed hours?

What is the Commission’s position on municipalities' social programmes being dependent on European programmes (e.g. NSRF), making the operation and continuity of municipal services uncertain, paving the way for business activity and placing additional burdens on the backs of working-class families who are no longer able to meet their standing commitments?

What is the Commission’s position on the just demands of workers in the social structures of municipalities for permanent/stable employment and staffing with all the necessary expert and professional personnel, with full state funding, and not on fixedterm private law contracts through NSRF, as per the EU's guidelines?

(14 July 2026) 1. Directive (EU) 2019/1152 (1) sets out minimum requirements for transparent and predictable working conditions across all sectors, including flexible arrangements such as on-demand or zero-hour contracts. While EU law does not prohibit such contracts, Member States must provide for effective measures to prevent abuse, ensuring compliance with the directive’s provisions on transparency and predictability. 2. Regarding Greece’s municipal social programmes, particularly early childhood education and care services, the Commission recognises their importance in social cohesion and employment. To ensure sustainability and reduce reliance on EU funding, a sustainability roadmap was agreed with the Greek authorities in July 2025, outlining a gradual transition to full national funding by 2030, supported by an additional EUR 162 million from the European Social Fund Plus for 2025-2029, supplementing the EUR 373 million already allocated for 2022-2025. 3. While EU funding has supported temporary employment in municipal social structures, the transition to long-term sustainability must prioritise job security and adequate staffing, as highlighted in the 2025 Quality Jobs Roadmap (2).

qt: to the Commission Delara Burkhardt (S&D), Birgit Sippel (S&D) Subject:

The Norwegian Government has announced a commercial fishing quota of 1 641 minke whales for 2026 – an increase of 235 animals compared to the previous year. Whaling is portrayed as ‘sustainable ocean management’. However, this reasoning is at odds with scientific findings on the ecological role of whales and growing public opposition to whaling in Europe for ethical and ecological reasons. 1.

What diplomatic and policy instruments is the Commission already using and does it plan to use in the future, particularly in cooperation with international bodies like the International Whaling Commission or the forums for the UN Convention on Biological Diversity, and in collaboration with like-minded partners, to increase pressure on Norway and work towards ending whaling?

To what extent does the Commission take the topic of whaling into consideration in EUNorway relations, particularly within the framework of the European Economic Area (EEA) and existing trade and fisheries agreements?

Is the Commission considering taking action at EU level to prohibit the transit of whale meat through European ports, as the European Parliament called for in 2017, or is it considering other measures?
at: (English version) to the Commission Delara Burkhardt (S&D), Birgit Sippel (S&D) (28 April 2026) Subject: Measures against whaling in Norway The Norwegian Government has announced a commercial fishing quota of 1 641 minke whales for 2026 — an increase of 235 animals compared to the previous year. Whaling is portrayed as ‘sustainable ocean management’. However, this reasoning is at odds with scientific findings on the ecological role of whales and growing public opposition to whaling in Europe for ethical and ecological reasons. 1. What diplomatic and policy instruments is the Commission already using and does it plan to use in the future, particularly in cooperation with international bodies like the International Whaling Commission or the forums for the UN Convention on Biological Diversity, and in collaboration with like-minded partners, to increase pressure on Norway and work towards ending whaling? 2. To what extent does the Commission take the topic of whaling into consideration in EU-Norway relations, particularly within the framework of the European Economic Area (EEA) and existing trade and fisheries agreements? 3. Is the Commission considering taking action at EU level to prohibit the transit of whale meat through European ports, as the European Parliament called for in 2017, or is it considering other measures? (25 August 2026) Norway maintains an objection to the International Whaling Commission’s (IWC) moratorium on commercial whaling, allowing it to continue commercial whaling under international law. It also maintains reservations under the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES) (1) for certain whale species, permitting the export of whale products. The EU continues to raise its concerns regarding commercial whaling in the appropriate bilateral and multilateral fora. In 2018, the EU and its Member States conducted a Demarche with Norway to express their concerns regarding the resumption of commercial whaling and to encourage Norway to align with international conservation efforts. The EU also supports the establishment of whale sanctuaries within the framework of the IWC, including proposals aimed at strengthening the protection of whale populations. The transit of whale products through EU ports remains legal where shipments comply with CITES requirements and are accompanied by the necessary permits. The Commission is not currently considering EU legislation to prohibit such transit. Nevertheless, it has facilitated exchanges with Norway within the framework of the Enforcement Group and among Member States through the Expert Group, in order to share relevant information and support coordinated approaches.

E-10-2026-001716.t: Security and anonymity in the EU age verification app
qt: to the Commission Dick Erixon (ECR), Charlie Weimers (ECR), Beatrice Timgren (ECR) Subject:

On 15 April 2026, the Commission stated that the EU age verification solution was technically ready and enabled anonymous age checks without sharing personal data. However, according to media reports, the app could be hacked or bypassed within two minutes of its launch1. This raises questions both about its technical readiness and the protection of users’ personal data, particularly where age verification may rely on government-issued identity documents. 1.
On what grounds did the Commission conclude that the app was technically ready, despite reports that it could be hacked or bypassed almost immediately after its launch?
How does the Commission intend to ensure that sensitive personal data are not exposed, stored or misused when users may be required to use government-issued identity documents to prove their age?
How does the Commission intend to protect the possibility of online anonymity for people who have a particular need for such protection?
https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-brussels-launched-age-checking-app-hackers-say-took-them-2-minutesbreak-it/.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (29.6.2026) The application presented on 15 April 20261 is an early reference implementation of the European age verification solution, released openly for scrutiny prior to public deployment. Some of the issues raised by independent experts were well founded and have been corrected by the development consortium, with an updated version made available shortly thereafter and further improvements to be made. To ensure that data protection and security requirements are fulfilled, age verification solutions will be assessed and approved by the Commission in accordance with Commission Recommendation (EU) 2026/10352. The rules and requirements for the assessment will be established in the age verification attestation of attributes scheme based on Article 8 of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/15693, the Age Verification Blueprint4, the Electronic Identification, Authentication and Trust Services Regulation5, Directive (EU) 2022/25556, the Cyber Resilience Act7 and the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)8. The GDPR ensures that data protection rights of citizens are protected, and this applies to age verification providers. Age verification solutions must not communicate any information identifying the user. To ensure that sensitive personal data are not exposed, stored or misused, the system uses zero-knowledge proofs, letting users prove their age without sharing their identity or personal details. Platforms receive only a cryptographic confirmation (no raw data), which ensures unlinkability and no centralised storage of data is carried out. Strict compliance with data protection rules is enforced via contractual obligations on implementers (Member States or private providers), including mandatory data protection impact assessments.

E-10-2026-001712.t: Strengthening EU civil protection in view of the escalation in the Middle East
qt: to the Commission Geadis Geadi (ECR) Subject:

The ongoing and dangerously escalating instability in the Middle East, marked by the exchange of missile strikes and a heightened risk of regional instability, is deepening concerns about the safety and preparedness of the European Union. These developments highlight the need to strengthen Member States’ resilience, particularly when it comes to informing and protecting the civilian population against modern threats, including drone attacks. As civilian protection is a responsibility that lies primarily with the Member States, with the EU nevertheless playing a key support and coordination role, including through the Union Civil Protection Mechanism (UCPM), it is now necessary to evaluate and reinforce existing tools. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
What specific measures have been taken or are being planned to strengthen the UCPM, particularly as regards prevention, rapid response and protection of the civilian population in crisis situations?
Does it intend to provide targeted financial and technical support for the development or upgrade of civil protection infrastructure, especially in frontline Member States?
What concrete measures are being taken to bring about the EU-wide strengthening of citizen information, education and preparedness?
at: (English version) to the Commission Geadis Geadi (ECR) (27 April 2026) Subject: Strengthening EU civil protection in view of the escalation in the Middle East The ongoing and dangerously escalating instability in the Middle East, marked by the exchange of missile strikes and a heightened risk of regional instability, is deepening concerns about the safety and preparedness of the European Union. (6 July 2026) In the context of the Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) 2028-2034 the Commission proposed a regulation on the Union Civil Protection Mechanism (UCPM) and EU support for health emergency preparedness and response (1), with the aim to equip the EU with means to prepare for and respond to current and future crises. This will be achieved through increased situational awareness, public warning (2) and simplified operational procedures. With this, the Commission proposes to allocate EUR 10.7 billion to the future crisis management framework. The Commission introduced the concepts of ‘preparedness by design’ and ‘security by design’ to ensure that preparedness and security considerations are mainstreamed in EU legislation, policies and programmes. Within the UCPM, technical and financial assistance is available to national authorities of Member States to support the review of preparedness plans and address knowledge gaps. Population preparedness is in the core of the EU preparedness union strategy (3). The Commission works with Member States to raise public awareness of risks and threats. An example is the development of guidelines on communicating disaster risks effectively, promoting 72 hours of selfsufficiency for the population, and integrating preparedness into childhood and primary school curricula. Under Cohesion Policy, over EUR 19 billion are allocated to enhance disaster prevention and preparedness in EU regions, with investments in civil protection infrastructures. Following the mid-term review, an additional EUR 11.9 billion were reallocated to defence and civil preparedness measures and the Cohesion for Transitions (C4T) Community of Practice (4) supports managing authorities in the implementation of these investments.

E-10-2026-001711.t: The status of Imbros and Tenedos in the light of a combined examination of the Treaty of Lausanne and the Montreux Convention
qt: to the Commission Emmanouil Fragkos (ECR) Subject:

Under the Treaty of Lausanne and the Montreux Convention Regarding the Regime of the Straits, the Bosphorus and the Dardanelles were meant to stay open to international shipping. This state of affairs was established in order to ensure freedom of transit between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean Sea, maintaining stability and the international equilibrium. As a trade-off for free shipping and as part of a geopolitical compromise, Imbros and Tenedos were given to Türkiye. Article 14 of the Treaty of Lausanne provided for a special autonomous status for the Greek population of the two islands, with a view to protecting the unique identity of the local culture and community. After the ‘ethnic cleansing’ committed against the people of Imbros and Tenedos, in recent years Türkiye has been beefing up shipping control mechanisms and going ahead with projects such as Kanal Istanbul, raising objections about the strengthening of unilateral controls in what is an international sea route. In view of the above and in the context of the EU-Türkiye negotiations, can the Commission say: 1.

Does it intend to consider the combined application of the Montreux Convention and the Treaty of Lausanne, pushing for the return of Imbros and Tenedos to Greece or at least for the restored rights of the expelled people of Imbros and Tenedos, their compensation and the drafting of an autonomy plan for the islands?
Could it consider a specific funding programme for the return of the expelled people of Imbros and Tenedos to their respective homelands?
If not, does it believe that the ethnic cleansing committed by Türkiye against the Greeks of Imbros and Tenedos does not concern it?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.7.2026)

The European Commission has highlighted, including in the 2025 enlargement report1, the persistent challenges facing the Greek minority in Türkiye. The Commission recalls that the recommendations set out in Resolution 1625 (2008) of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe2 on the bicultural character of the islands of Gökçeada (Imbros) and Bozcaada (Tenedos) remain valid and unaddressed. The resolution calls for urgent action to restore minority schools, return expropriated properties and improve infrastructure, while safeguarding the rights of the Greek minority. The Commission also recalls that the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe urged the Turkish authorities to implement the rulings of the European Court of Human Rights concerning the minority and property rights of the Greek minority on these two islands. The Commission supports these objectives and will continue to urge Türkiye to fulfil its obligations. It will also continue to encourage constructive dialogue with Greece and to promote reconciliation, restitution and respect for minority rights. The Commission will continue to monitor the situation and address these concerns in its bilateral contacts with the Turkish authorities.
1 https://enlargement.ec.europa.eu/turkiye-report-2025_en. 2 https://assembly.coe.int/nw/xml/XRef/Xref-XML2HTML-en.asp?fileid=17668&lang=en.

qt: to the Commission Emmanouil Fragkos (ECR), Galato Alexandraki (ECR), Tomáš Kubín (PfE), Emil Radev (PPE), Jana Nagyová (PfE), Diana Iovanovici Şoşoacă (NI), Şerban Dimitrie Sturdza (ECR), Zala Tomašič (PPE), Maria Zacharia (NI), Nikos Pappas (The Left), Claudiu-Richard Târziu (ECR), Waldemar Tomaszewski (ECR), Bert-Jan Ruissen (ECR), Sebastian Tynkkynen (ECR), Nicolae Ștefănuță (Verts/ALE), Georgiana Teodorescu (ECR), Lukas Mandl (PPE) Subject:

The rapid expansion of digital gambling advertising, particularly through social media platforms, raises serious concerns regarding social welfare, mental health and the protection of minors. Scientific research demonstrates that online gambling is associated with increased rates of addiction, anxiety, depression, impulse control disorders and financial ruin, with long-term psychological impacts on affected players, on their families and on their social environment. Advertising through podcasts and short-form video content (reels) and, unfortunately, through the use of willing influencers, leads to the recruitment of victims from vulnerable groups in society, including minors. The constant projection of ‘successful’ role models, the normalisation of gambling as a form of entertainment, and its association with economic and social success directly affect the psychology of children and adolescents, shaping distorted perceptions of risk, chance and money. At the same time, a significant share of digital gambling advertising is disseminated through algorithmically targeted advertisements on social media, within environments that remain, to a large extent, insufficiently controlled with regard to age verification, content and frequency of exposure. The Commission is therefore asked: 1.
How does it assess the impact of digital gambling advertising on addiction and mental health, particularly with regard to minors?
Does it intend to propose stricter rules or limitations on the advertising of digital gambling on social media platforms?

(3 July 2026) The Commission recognises that minors face risks online from exposure to inappropriate or exploitative gambling-related practices (1). The Digital Services Act (DSA) (2) provides a framework for protecting minors on online platforms, including social media. Online platforms must establish measures to ensure a high level of privacy, safety and security for minors on their service (3). The DSA also prohibits advertising based on profiling using minors’ personal data. The DSA guidelines on the protection of minors (4) recommend measures to prevent access to age-inappropriate content, such as gambling, and exposure to practices that may encourage compulsive or addictive behaviour. Users can notify gambling advertisements that they believe are illegal, for example under applicable national laws or the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive (UCPD) (5) using the notice and action mechanism provided for in the DSA (6). The UCPD prohibits misleading or aggressive advertising affecting consumers’ transactional decisions, especially when it targets vulnerable consumers, such as minors. It acts as a safety net without prejudice to national laws that restrict gambling advertising. E-10-2026-001709.t: Competition law and transportation to the islands
qt: to the Commission Emmanouil Fragkos (ECR) Subject:

The connectivity of island regions by sea is a key condition for the Union’s economic, social and territorial cohesion, as is also enshrined in Article 174 TFEU. Despite this, Greek ferry services are seeing repeated complaints about excessive price increases, frequent service cancellations due to weather conditions, which are being questioned by passengers, and limited competition on specific routes where a small number of companies operate. In some cases, the market resembles an oligopoly or even a de facto monopoly. This is having a direct impact on the cost of living, tourism and the viability of local economies. The lack of transparency over the criteria used for service cancellations and pricing is increasing concerns about adequate market surveillance. Given that maritime cabotage is governed by Regulation (EEC) No 3577/92 on cabotage and that unfair business agreements and abuse of a dominant position are prohibited under Articles 101 and 102 TFEU, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Does it systematically monitor the conditions of competition among Greek ferry lines and has it assessed whether there are indications of market distortion or excessive pricing?
How is it ensured that public service obligations and related State aid do not lead to the consolidation of monopolistic situations to the detriment of the islands’ permanent residents?
Does it intend to consider further measures or guidelines to enhance competition, transparency and consumer protection in the island cabotage sector?
at: (English version) to the Commission Emmanouil Fragkos (ECR) (27 April 2026) Subject: Competition law and transportation to the islands The connectivity of island regions by sea is a key condition for the Union’s economic, social and territorial cohesion, as is also enshrined in Article 174 TFEU. Despite this, Greek ferry services are seeing repeated complaints about excessive price increases, frequent service cancellations due to weather conditions, which are being questioned by passengers, and limited competition on specific routes where a small number of companies operate. In some cases, the market resembles an oligopoly or even a de facto monopoly. This is having a direct impact on the cost of living, tourism and the viability of local economies. The lack of transparency over the criteria used for service cancellations and pricing is increasing concerns about adequate market surveillance. Given that maritime cabotage is governed by Regulation (EEC) No 3577/92 on cabotage and that unfair business agreements and abuse of a dominant position are prohibited under Articles 101 and 102 TFEU, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

(6 July 2026) The Commission monitors market developments in the maritime sector, as well as other economic sectors, to ensure compliance with EU competition rules. The Commission shares the tasks of enforcing EU competition rules with the national competition authorities of Member States, which are generally well placed to intervene when most of the effects take place within their territory. The Hellenic Competition Authority is currently investigating potential anticompetitive horizontal agreements between operators of maritime passenger transport services in Greece (1). State aid rules support competition to the benefit of passengers. First, they impose compliance with EU public procurement rules (for sizeable services), which guarantee a competitive pressure for the award of public service contracts. Second, they allow Member States to grant public service compensation only to address observed market failures, such as excessive prices for island residents or lack of regular commercial services. To support a more efficient and well-functioning EU cabotage sector, the Commission services are currently revising the interpretative guidance on Council Regulation (EEC) No 3577/92 (maritime cabotage) (2). In this context, the guidance aims to clarify how island ferry services can be promoted through public service obligations and public service contracts, while safeguarding competition, transparency and consumer protection, and ensuring that conditions for participation in tenders do not become barriers to market access.

E-10-2026-001708.t: Democratic deficit in Bangladesh and implications for GSP+ eligibility
qt: to the Commission Emmanouil Fragkos (ECR) Subject:

Recent reports by international human rights organisations indicate that the parliamentary elections scheduled for 12 February 2026 in Bangladesh are being held under conditions that may seriously undermine political pluralism, the inclusiveness of the electoral process and the rule of law. In particular, the administrative suspension of the country’s largest political party, the mass arbitrary arrests of political activists, the intimidation of lawyers and journalists, prolonged detention without trial and credible allegations of violence against religious minorities raise concerns about compliance with the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, in particular Article 25 on participation in public affairs. Given that continued access to the EU's GSP+ trade incentives depends on the effective implementation of fundamental human rights conventions and democratic principles: 1.

How does the Commission assess the credibility and inclusiveness of the upcoming elections in Bangladesh, in light of the reported exclusion of a major political party and the broader restrictions on political and civil liberties?
Is the Commission considering launching a formal review of Bangladesh's eligibility for the GSP+ scheme, should these concerns be confirmed?

What diplomatic or monitoring measures is the Commission taking, including through election observation and dialogue with the Bangladeshi authorities, to promote conditions for free, fair and inclusive elections?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (19.6.2026) The EU deployed an Election Observation Mission which presented its preliminary findings in a press conference on 14 February 2026. It noted that the elections were credible and competently managed, marking a pivotal step towards restoring democratic governance and rule of law. The mission’s final report was published on 28 April 20261. The final report confirmed the preliminary assessment on the 2026 parliamentary elections, as described above. For the first time since 2008, elections were genuinely competitive, with fundamental freedoms broadly respected. In its report, the Election Observation Mission also indicated six recommendations on priorities for further improving future electoral processes and upholding the international commitments adopted by Bangladesh. As a least developed country, Bangladesh is a beneficiary of the Everything But Arms arrangement of the EU Generalised Scheme of Preferences (GSP)2. The country is subject to the Enhanced Engagement process, which is conducted by the Commission and the European External Action Service. It aims to facilitate and incentivise Bangladesh to make progress on critical areas with regard to the core human rights and labour rights international conventions listed in the GSP Regulation3. The process focuses on the most serious issues linked to the implementation of key principles laid down in UN and International Labour Organisation reports and recommendations. It also reflects the concerns regarding the implementation status as expressed by the European Parliament and the Council, international organisations, and civil society, including trade unions.
