E-10-2026-001707.t: CBAM implementation and cost predictability for steel imports
qt: to the Commission Mariateresa Vivaldini (ECR), Stefano Cavedagna (ECR) Subject:

The entry into force of the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) in 2026 introduced new obligations for steel imports from non-EU countries. However, there is still uncertainty about the actual applicable costs. The CBAM price is currently linked to the EU ETS and for the first quarter of 2026 it was determined ex post based on an average value of around EUR 75 per tonne of CO2. This ex-post method of calculation and reporting creates uncertainty for economic operators, making industrial planning, contracting and investment evaluation difficult. The lack of preemptive cost visibility risks affecting the competitiveness of European industry and the predictability of the regulatory framework, compromising the effectiveness of the CBAM and creating potential distortions in international trade. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Does it intend to adopt measures to ensure greater transparency and predictability in determining the CBAM price, including by publishing indicative values in advance?
Can it specify precise timeframes so that economic operators are informed of CBAMrelated costs in advance?
Can it, as a matter of urgency, grant accreditation to the bodies responsible for verifying the actual CO2 emissions of individual producers in non-EU countries?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (6.7.2026) The methodology to calculate the price of Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) certificates ensures that this price reflects the average price of the EU’s Emissions Trading System (ETS) allowances, thereby maintaining consistency between the carbon cost applicable to EU producers and that applied to imports into the EU subject to the CBAM. In 2026, the Commission will calculate and publish four quarterly prices, one for each calendar quarter. Each quarterly price in 2026 will be calculated by the Commission as soon as possible following the end of the relevant quarter. This early publication aims to enhance transparency, provide stakeholders with timely information and reduce the risk of inconsistent or unofficial price estimates circulating in the market. In addition, the Commission has published a calendar for the publication of the four quarterly prices in 2026 on its website1. The first price was published on 7 April, and the next quarterly prices will be published respectively on 6 July 2026, 5 October 2026 and 4 January 2027. The published prices are based on publicly available ETS auction data; should CBAM declarants wish to obtain an even earlier indication of the quarterly price, they can access the auction clearing prices on the ETS’s common auctioning platform2. From 2027 onwards, the Commission will calculate and publish weekly prices of CBAM certificates to reflect closely the carbon price paid in the EU’s ETS. Enabling CBAM declarants to declare actual values is a priority of the Commission. Member States’ national accreditation bodies are responsible for granting accreditation to have enough verifiers in 2027. This process already started in several Member States.
1 https://taxation-customs.ec.europa.eu/carbon-border-adjustment-mechanism/price-cbam-
certificates_en#quarterly-prices-in-2026. 2 https://www.eex.com/en/market-data/market-data-hub/environmentals/eex-eua-primary-auction-spotdownload.

qt: to the Commission Angéline Furet (PfE), Pierre Pimpie (PfE), Valérie Deloge (PfE), André Rougé (PfE) Subject:

The European Parliament and the Council have protected food names (milk, cheese and steak) and reserved them for dairy and animal products, so as to prevent confusion. The Court of Justice of the European Union has confirmed that interpretation, in the TofuTown judgment, for example. However, cosmetics are still in regulatory limbo, which means terms such as ‘keratin’ can be usurped for plant-based alternatives. In light of the requirement to provide accurate information: 1.

Does the Commission consider that, under Regulation (EU) No 655/2013, the use of the term ‘keratin’ for plant-derived proteins complies with the criteria of ‘honesty’, even though keratin is, by biological definition, exclusively an animal protein, and if EU law prohibits the term ‘soya milk’ to prevent confusion, how can it permit the designation ‘plant keratin’?

Does it think that assigning the names of animal proteins to plant proteins – whose molecular structure cannot guarantee the structural effectiveness of the original – is honest or accurate, and is this not misleading as to the actual properties of the product?

Does it intend to put an end to the difference in treatment between the food and cosmetics industries by prohibiting the names of animal tissues and proteins from being used for plant products, in order to ensure full legislative consistency within the EU single market?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (29.6.2026) Under current EU law, the situations in the food and cosmetics sectors are not equivalent. In the milk and milk products sector, dairy terms such as ‘milk’ and ‘cheese’ are expressly protected under Regulation (EU) No 1308/20131, as endorsed by the Court of Justice of the European Union in its judgment in the TofuTown case2. By contrast, Regulation (EU) No 655/2013 on cosmetic claims3 does not reserve particular biological or technical terms exclusively for animal-derived substances. It instead requires that claims comply with common criteria such as truthfulness, honesty and evidence-based substantiation. Accordingly, the use of expressions such as ‘plant keratin’ is not automatically prohibited, provided that consumers are clearly informed of the plant origin and are not misled as to the ingredient’s nature, composition or efficacy. However, claims suggesting that plant-derived proteins are chemically identical to animal keratin, or provide equivalent structural performance without adequate evidence, could be considered misleading under that Regulation. The Commission notes that enforcement of these principles is primarily the responsibility of Member States’ competent authorities on a case-by-case basis. Those authorities should assess, among others, the appropriateness and relevance of the supporting evidence for justifying the use of claims.

E-10-2026-001705.t: Ukrainian children forcibly transferred and deported by Russia
qt: to the Commission Sophie Wilmès (Renew), Mika Aaltola (PPE), Marc Angel (S&D), Petras Auštrevičius (Renew), Malik Azmani (Renew), Dan Barna (Renew), Wouter Beke (PPE), Benoit Cassart (Renew), Christel Schaldemose (S&D), Olivier Chastel (Renew), Caterina Chinnici (PPE), Elio Di Rupo (S&D), Heléne Fritzon (S&D), Sandro Gozi (Renew), Elisabetta Gualmini (Renew), Maria Guzenina (S&D), Anna-Maja Henriksson (Renew), Evin Incir (S&D), Irena Joveva (Renew), Radan Kanev (PPE), Karin Karlsbro (Renew), Michał Kobosko (Renew), Rasa Juknevičienė (PPE), Katri Kulmuni (Renew), Nicolás Pascual de la Parte (PPE), Thijs Reuten (S&D), Andreas Schwab (PPE), Lukas Sieper (Renew), Krzysztof Śmiszek (S&D), Villy Søvndal (Verts/ALE), Marie-Agnes StrackZimmermann (Renew), Benedetta Scuderi (Verts/ALE), Michał Szczerba (PPE), JanChristoph Oetjen (Renew), Riho Terras (PPE), Pekka Toveri (PPE), Reinier Van Lanschot (Verts/ALE), Vlad Vasile-Voiculescu (Renew), Hilde Vautmans (Renew), Isabel Wiseler-Lima (PPE), Dainius Žalimas (Renew), Veronika Cifrová Ostrihoňová (Renew), Martin Hojsík (Renew), Ľubica Karvašová (Renew), Ľudovít Ódor (Renew), Michal Wiezik (Renew), Lucia Yar (Renew), Tomáš Zdechovský (PPE), Elisabeth Grossmann (S&D), Vytenis Povilas Andriukaitis (S&D) Subject:

In the context of the Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine, tens of thousands of Ukrainian children have been forcibly transferred and deported to Russia and Belarus or are being held in temporarily occupied Ukrainian territories, according to several international bodies, including the International Criminal Court. However, the exact numbers remain difficult to establish. On the basis of these findings: 1.

What measures is the Commission taking to facilitate the return of the children, beyond its participation in the International Coalition for the Return of Ukrainian Children and the hosting of a summit aimed at mobilising international action?
In what way does the Commission support the Ukrainian authorities, as well as international and non-governmental organisations, in their efforts to document the children?

In the light of statements made by the President of the Commission that the return of these children should form an integral part of any peace agreement, as well as the request made in this regard by the European Parliament, how does the Commission intend to concretely ensure the inclusion of this issue in future peace processes?
at: (English version) to the Commission Sophie Wilmès (Renew), Mika Aaltola (PPE), Marc Angel (S&D), Petras Auštrevičius (Renew), Malik Azmani (Renew), Dan Barna (Renew), Wouter Beke (PPE), Benoit Cassart (Renew), Christel Schaldemose (S&D), Olivier Chastel (Renew), Caterina Chinnici (PPE), Elio Di Rupo (S&D), Heléne Fritzon (S&D), Sandro Gozi (Renew), Elisabetta Gualmini (Renew), Maria Guzenina (S&D), Anna-Maja Henriksson (Renew), Evin Incir (S&D), Irena Joveva (Renew), Radan Kanev (PPE), Karin Karlsbro (Renew), Michał Kobosko (Renew), Rasa Juknevičienė (PPE), Katri Kulmuni (Renew), Nicolás Pascual de la Parte (PPE), Thijs Reuten (S&D), Andreas Schwab (PPE), Lukas Sieper (Renew), Krzysztof Śmiszek (S&D), Villy Søvndal (Verts/ALE), Marie-Agnes Strack-Zimmermann (Renew), Benedetta Scuderi (Verts/ALE), Michał Szczerba (PPE), Jan-Christoph Oetjen (Renew), Riho Terras (PPE), Pekka Toveri (PPE), Reinier Van Lanschot (Verts/ALE), Vlad Vasile-Voiculescu (Renew), Hilde Vautmans (Renew), Isabel Wiseler-Lima (PPE), Dainius Žalimas (Renew), Veronika Cifrová Ostrihoňová (Renew), Martin Hojsík (Renew), Ľubica Karvašová (Renew), Ľudovít Ódor (Renew), Michal Wiezik (Renew), Lucia Yar (Renew), Tomáš Zdechovský (PPE), Elisabeth Grossmann (S&D), Vytenis Povilas Andriukaitis (S&D) (27 April 2026) Subject: Ukrainian children forcibly transferred and deported by Russia In the context of the Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine, tens of thousands of Ukrainian children have been forcibly transferred and deported to Russia and Belarus or are being held in temporarily occupied Ukrainian territories, according to several international bodies, including the International Criminal Court. However, the exact numbers remain difficult to establish. On the basis of these findings: 1.

What measures is the Commission taking to facilitate the return of the children, beyond its participation in the International Coalition for the Return of Ukrainian Children and the hosting of a summit aimed at mobilising international action?
In what way does the Commission support the Ukrainian authorities, as well as international and non-governmental organisations, in their efforts to document the children?

In the light of statements made by the President of the Commission that the return of these children should form an integral part of any peace agreement, as well as the request made in this regard by the European Parliament, how does the Commission intend to concretely ensure the inclusion of this issue in future peace processes?

(14 July 2026) The EU remains committed to the returning of Ukrainian children unlawfully deported or forcibly transferred by Russia in its war of aggression against Ukraine. During the High-Level Meeting of the International Coalition for the Return of Ukrainian Children on 11 May 2026, the EU announced nearly EUR 50 million to reinforce Ukraine’s child protection system to ensure that every returned child has access to timely, child-centred family and community-based services and care. This will contribute to strengthening early childhood education initiatives, giving access to child-centred justice and enable citizens to submit compensation claims. The EU supports Ukraine in processing and verifying information, including as part of its broader accountability efforts. The EU also continues to support the Bring Kids Back initiative and works with international partners to condemn Russia’s actions, including through the adoption of the EU-sponsored UN General Assembly resolution on the return of Ukrainian children on 3 December 2025. The EU supports efforts to document, investigate and prosecute crimes related to child deportations and forcible transfers and has sanctioned more than 130 individuals and entities involved in deportation, forcible transfer, militarisation and indoctrination of Ukrainian children. The EU assists relevant government bodies and civil society organisations in Ukraine directly involved.

The EU supports a comprehensive, just and lasting peace in Ukraine based on the principles of the UN Charter and international law and it remains strongly committed to ensuring full accountability for all international crimes committed in connection with Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine.

E-10-2026-001704.t: Urgent measures to tackle those who take advantage of the ‘last substantial transformation’ rule to obtain the ‘Made in Italy’ label for foreign products
qt: to the Commission Fulvio Martusciello (PPE) Subject:

In the case of goods whose production involves more than one country, the principle of last substantial transformation laid down in Article 60 of the Union Customs Code establishes the non-preferential origin of these products as the country in which they underwent their last, substantial, economically justified working, in an undertaking equipped for that purpose, resulting in the manufacture of a new product or representing an important stage of manufacture. Every year, thousands of tonnes of foreign food products enter Italy through the Brenner Pass as part of a practice that deceives consumers, entails health risks and also damages agricultural businesses by squeezing prices, wages and export margins. The principle of last substantial transformation enables operators to slap the ‘Made in Italy’ label on products made from foreign raw materials that have only been in Italy long enough to undergo the final working stage. This practice concerns key products, from tomato concentrate to the 150 000 tonnes of mozzarella curd that Italy imports every year, 90 % of which enter the country through the Brenner Pass. In the light of the above, does the Commission not agree that it should revise the customs rules for agri-food products with a view to empowering and protecting farmers and consumers by preventing operators from exporting low-quality, non-EU products under the ‘Made in Italy label – a practice that is made possible by a principle that applies to all goods that undergo the final transformation stage in Italy, no matter how inconsequential this process might be?
at: (English version) to the Commission Fulvio Martusciello (PPE) (27 April 2026) Subject: Urgent measures to tackle those who take advantage of the ‘last substantial transformation’ rule to obtain the ‘Made in Italy’ label for foreign products In the case of goods whose production involves more than one country, the principle of last substantial transformation laid down in Article 60 of the Union Customs Code establishes the non-preferential origin of these products as the country in which they underwent their last, substantial, economically justified working, in an undertaking equipped for that purpose, resulting in the manufacture of a new product or representing an important stage of manufacture. Every year, thousands of tonnes of foreign food products enter Italy through the Brenner Pass as part of a practice that deceives consumers, entails health risks and also damages agricultural businesses by squeezing prices, wages and export margins. The principle of last substantial transformation enables operators to slap the ‘Made in Italy’ label on products made from foreign raw materials that have only been in Italy long enough to undergo the final working stage. This practice concerns key products, from tomato concentrate to the 150 000 tonnes of mozzarella curd that Italy imports every year, 90% of which enter the country through the Brenner Pass. In the light of the above, does the Commission not agree that it should revise the customs rules for agri-food products with a view to empowering and protecting farmers and consumers by preventing operators from exporting low-quality, non-EU products under the ‘Made in Italy label — a practice that is made possible by a principle that applies to all goods that undergo the final transformation stage in Italy, no matter how inconsequential this process might be? (3 July 2026) Under Article 26(3) of Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011 (1), where the origin of a processed food — defined as the place of its last substantial transformation — is indicated, and this differs from the origin of its primary ingredient, the origin of that ingredient must also be declared or marked as different. The aim of this provision is to ensure that consumers are not misled when the origin of the food and that of its primary ingredient does not coincide. To assist citizens, business operators and national competent authorities in applying this Article 26(3), the Commission issued a notice (2). As set out therein, this requirement applies to single-ingredient processed foods, bearing origin claims such as those referenced by the Honourable Member and where the last substantial transformation occurs in a different place than the origin of the raw material ingredient or where the ingredient was sourced from different places. The Commission services are currently evaluating the non-preferential rules of origin laid down in the Union Customs Code (UCC) (3), focusing on whether they are still fit for purpose across an increasing number of policies. The last substantial transformation as set out in Article 60(2) of the UCC is the underlying principle for the determination of the country of non-preferential origin, anchored in the WTO (4) Agreement on Rules of Origin. This principle has been confirmed by the ECJ (5) jurisprudence. The evaluation encompasses the application of the last substantial transformation concept, but not the concept as such.

E-10-2026-001703.t: Public money, private profits and the integrity of the European sports model
qt: to the Commission Nikos Pappas (The Left) Subject:

Recent reports1 have revealed that the company Qualco, which benefits from significant public contracts, many of which are co-financed by EU funds under the Recovery and Resilience Fund, is the main and exclusive sponsor of the Athinaikos WBC women's basketball team, having even acquired naming rights for the team. This case raises serious questions about the use of EU funds to create private advantages, transparency in public contracts and the distortion of balance in sport, especially when smaller clubs do not have access to similar sources of funding. In light of the above: 1.

How does the Commission ensure that funds from public contracts and EU programmes are not used, directly or indirectly, for private promotion activities, such as the sponsorship of professional sports clubs?

Under what conditions could the channelling of funds by companies that are heavily dependent on public contracts to specific sports bodies constitute indirect state aid within the meaning of Article 107 TFEU?
What measures does the Commission intend to take to enhance transparency, prevent conflicts of interest and protect the balance and social dimension of the European sports model?

at: (English version) to the Commission Nikos Pappas (The Left) (27 April 2026) Subject: Public money, private profits and the integrity of the European sports model Recent reports (1) have revealed that the company Qualco, which benefits from significant public contracts, many of which are co-financed by EU funds under the Recovery and Resilience Fund, is the main and exclusive sponsor of the Athinaikos WBC women's basketball team, having even acquired naming rights for the team. This case raises serious questions about the use of EU funds to create private advantages, transparency in public contracts and the distortion of balance in sport, especially when smaller clubs do not have access to similar sources of funding. In light of the above: 1.

How does the Commission ensure that funds from public contracts and EU programmes are not used, directly or indirectly, for private promotion activities, such as the sponsorship of professional sports clubs?

Under what conditions could the channelling of funds by companies that are heavily dependent on public contracts to specific sports bodies constitute indirect state aid within the meaning of Article 107 TFEU?
What measures does the Commission intend to take to enhance transparency, prevent conflicts of interest and protect the balance and social dimension of the European sports model?

(2 July 2026) EU funds are subject to strict rules on transparency, audit and control. As for funds provided under the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF), Member States bear primary responsibility for ensuring that the measures supported and the use of funds comply with applicable EU and national law. However, the Commission has supervisory and corrective powers under the RRF Regulation (1). The fact that a company benefiting from public contracts sponsors a sports club does not in itself imply an irregular use of EU funds. EU funds must be used for their intended purposes and in compliance with the relevant legal and contractual obligations. The Commission monitors the implementation of EU-funded programmes through reporting, audits and control mechanisms and may take appropriate action where there are indications of irregularities. A transfer of State resources by a State to an entity often has indirect economic effects on other undertakings. Establishing whether state aid is present always requires a careful, case-by-case examination. It is the responsibility of the Member State to perform this analysis. The Commission promotes good governance, transparency, integrity and solidarity in sport, through various EU programmes, such as Erasmus+. The forthcoming Communication on reinforcing the European Sport Model will further support these objectives.

E-10-2026-001700.t: Hammerbande  case and the danger of left-wing extremism
qt: to the Commission Isabella Tovaglieri (PfE), Silvia Sardone (PfE) Subject:
Hammerbande case and the danger of left-wing extremism

For years now, the German judiciary has been pursuing the case involving the Hammerbande (hammer gang) – a far-left, anti-fascist criminal organisation responsible for numerous attacks against far-right activists or alleged far-right individuals. The gang, which takes its name from its use of hammers as weapons, has attacked at least 13 people over the years, some of whom were seriously injured and suffered life-threatening injuries – which is why the charges also include attempted murder. Among the alleged attacks is one in Budapest in February 2023. The investigation files refer to MEP Ilaria Salis as many as 27 times, describing her as a ‘foreign member’ of the group. In the light of the above: 1.
Left-wing extremism is increasingly widespread and violent – what steps will the Commission take to counter it?
Does it believe it appropriate to designate Antifa groups as terrorist organisations – as the US, for example, has done?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.7.2026) The Commission condemns all forms of violent extremism. The EU takes very seriously the threat posed by extremist radical views sowing social division, polarisation and radicalisation in Europe. In close cooperation with Member States, the EU monitors the evolving risks linked to organisations that pose a threat to the stability and security of Europe. As set out in the ProtectEU agenda to prevent and counter terrorism1, the Commission, through the EU Knowledge Hub on the Prevention of Radicalisation2, is supporting Member States in their fight against all forms of radicalisation. The Knowledge Hub brings together practitioners, policy makers and researchers and supports the development and implementation of policies and strategies based on shared knowledge and expertise. It fosters collaboration among stakeholders to address the challenges of radicalisation, emphasising an integrated, policy-driven approach and a whole-of-society perspective. The legal prerequisite for the listing of new individuals, groups or entities, under Council Decision (CFSP) 2026/455 of 26 February 2026 on restrictive measures to combat terrorism, repealing Articles 2, 3 and 3a of Common Position 2001/931/CFSP on the application of specific measures to combat terrorism3, is a decision by a competent authority as defined by Articles 2(3) of the Decision. Such a decision should concern the involvement of the individual or entity in question in a ‘terrorist act’ as defined by Article 1(1) of the aforementioned Decision. The Council may decide on a listing pursuant to Decision (CFSP) 2026/455, acting by unanimity.
1 COM(2026) 101 final. 2 https://home-affairs.ec.europa.eu/networks/eu-knowledge-hub-prevention-radicalisation_en. 3 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=OJ:L_202600455.

E-10-2026-001699.t: Allegations of exhumations and desecration of cemeteries in occupied Kyrenia
qt: to the Commission Costas Mavrides (S&D) Subject:

According to recent reports and complaints, there have been repeated cases of cemeteries being desecrated in occupied Kyrenia. Specifically, the legitimate mayor of the occupied city of Kyrenia has complained about graves and religious symbols being destroyed and about sacrilegious bone exhumations. Meanwhile, according to the same allegations, foreign persons who were illegally residing in the occupied territories are being buried in spaces where graves had existed, raising serious issues of disrespect and grave robbery. Religious monuments are also being destroyed and desecrated, cases in point being the removal of symbols from historic temples and the removal of the cross from the bell tower of the historic Archangelos Michael Church in occupied Kyrenia. All this amounts to the destruction of European cultural and religious heritage. Reminiscent of jihadist behaviour, these acts are being carried out in the occupied territories of the Republic of Cyprus and constitute a flagrant violation of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Is it aware of the allegations about the desecration of cemeteries and illegal exhumations in occupied Kyrenia?
What specific actions could it take to help repair the damage, to ensure that the cemeteries are respected and to prevent similar incidents in the future?

(17 June 2026) The Commission's only prior knowledge of the matters raised by the Honourable Member comes from online news reports which it has not been able to independently verify. The Commission firmly condemns any damage to religious and cultural sites and consistently stresses the importance of both protecting sites of cultural and religious significance and respecting the religions and traditions of all Cypriot communities. Since 2012, the EU has provided EUR 35 million in funding to the bicommunal Technical Committee on Cultural Heritage (TCCH), covering around 80% of its budget. This funding comes from the EU Aid Programme for the Turkish Cypriot community (1). Thanks to the EU support, the TCCH has been able to restore or protect over 200 cultural and religious monuments across Cyprus. More recently, the EU — through the TCCH — has supported the Greek Cypriot and Turkish Cypriot communities in cleaning and restoring around 70 cemeteries island-wide. The restoration of cemeteries was one of the confidence-building measures agreed by the leaders of the two Cypriot communities with the UN Secretary-General in 2025.

E-10-2026-001698.t: Need for a joint response coordinated by the European Commission
qt: to the Commission Loucas Fourlas (PPE) Subject:

Since it is unclear whether the war in Iran is going to escalate even further and how long it will last, a number of EU countries have already started taking temporary measures in response to the price rises. We are already witnessing rapid fuel price increases affecting oil, petrol and natural gas alike. Households and businesses are already feeling the effects on electricity. Farmers and the tourism sector are also affected because of increased fertiliser and air ticket prices respectively. Therefore, the situation is having knock-on effects on the economy. Given the specificities of each Member State and the lessons learnt from the pandemic crisis, I believe that a united European response is needed. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Is it considering a set of common European measures to support sectors affected by the escalation and continuation of the war?
Is it carrying out an impact assessment for each individual Member State?
What is the tipping point it has set for deeming necessary a set of common targeted measures for mitigating the significant impact on the Member States?

Is it carrying out an impact assessment for each individual Member State?
What is the tipping point it has set for deeming necessary a set of common targeted measures for mitigating the significant impact on the Member States?

(26 June 2026) With AccelerateEU (1), the Commission set out concrete actions to support Member States in protecting the most impacted households and sectors from the price shocks triggered by the Middle East energy crisis. They include timely, targeted and temporary measures such as the new Middle East Crisis Temporary State Aid Framework (METSAF), enabling Member States to support the most exposed businesses. Moreover, a Citizens Energy implementation package, a catalogue of good practices and a digital repository of national actions will support the protection of vulnerable consumers and enhance coordination across the EU. Regarding fuels, the Commission is establishing a Fuel Observatory to monitor EU production, imports, exports and fuel stocks and help improve visibility and coordination. The Commission is conducting regular exchanges with Member States to coordinate action through the Energy Union Task Force, and the Oil and Gas Coordination Groups. Moreover, the Commission is monitoring the situation and stands ready to provide assistance to Member States in the design of targeted, timely and temporary measures. Member States should assess the expected impacts, including fiscal costs, and avoid the fragmentation of the single market. Beyond short-term relief, the Commission is also advancing the structural measures needed to lower the EU’s dependence on fossil fuel imports and achieve long-term affordability, decarbonisation and competitiveness for all Member States. Forthcoming measures such as the initiative on electrification, heating and cooling and geothermal energy, and the legislative proposal on network charges, will address horizontal barriers to electrification and accelerate the shift to homegrown clean energy.

E-10-2026-001697.t: Transparency of EU funding for the German-Austrian Digital Media Observatory (GADMO)
qt: to the Commission Mary Khan (ESN), Irmhild Boßdorf (ESN), Christine Anderson (ESN), Harald Vilimsky (PfE), Petra Steger (PfE), Elisabeth Dieringer (PfE) Subject:

The EU Digital Media Observatory (EDMO) network has received significant public funding from the Commission since the former’s creation in 2020 and has so far received over EUR 30 million in funding. In addition, the network now includes 15 regional hubs, including the German-Austrian Digital Media Observatory (GADMO). The Financial Transparency System put GADMO’s total budget for the periods from 1 November 2022 to 30 April 2025 and from 1 May 2025 to 31 October 2027 at EUR 2 704 893.66 and EUR 2 399 051.28 respectively. Despite this considerable level of funding, it remains largely unclear how these funds are being used specifically and which organizations or projects ultimately benefit from them. 1.
Exactly how were the EU funds for the GADMO network used in detail, and which organizations were supported, when, with what amount, and for what purpose or scope?

Why is detailed information on the actual use of funds and on the final beneficiaries of funding in the Financial Transparency System not publicly available and does the Commission intend to ensure more comprehensive, traceable, and citizen-friendly transparency in this area in the future?
Why are there no conservative or EU-critical organisations in the GADMO network and why are no projects being funded that critically explore, for example, internal EU disinformation narratives?

E-10-2026-001696.t: Problems with the application of Regulation (EU) 2023/2842 and simplification measures for the fisheries sector
qt: to the Commission Stefano Cavedagna (ECR), Carlo Ciccioli (ECR) Subject:

Regulation (EU) 2023/2842 imposes extensive digital traceability obligations on operators in the fisheries sector. It requires the collection, recording, and structured submission of a considerable amount of data for each batch – including vessel identifiers, catch certificates, FAO codes, fishing zones and gear, quantities, processing units, and catch or harvest dates – for both fishery and aquaculture products. These requirements are replicated at every stage of the supply chain, thus increasing red tape without cutting the total amount of data required. The system also assumes a degree of digitalisation and interoperability that does not currently exist in the sector. In the absence of harmonised infrastructure and standards among Member States, many operators are forced to re-enter data manually, increasing errors, inconsistencies and delays. Thus the supply chain has a structural digital imbalance. In the light of the above: 1.
Does the Commission intend to adopt simplification measures to make the obligations under Regulation (EU) 2023/2842 proportionate to operating conditions in the supply chain?

Will it consider a tiered approach where comprehensive data storage is restricted to upstream operators (tier 1) and the passing of data to subsequent operators only at the request of competent authorities?
What steps will it take to develop interoperable and accessible digital infrastructure for all operators in the sector?
at: (English version) to the Commission Stefano Cavedagna (ECR), Carlo Ciccioli (ECR) (24 April 2026) Subject: Problems with the application of Regulation (EU) 2023/2842 and simplification measures for the fisheries sector Regulation (EU) 2023/2842 imposes extensive digital traceability obligations on operators in the fisheries sector. It requires the collection, recording, and structured submission of a considerable amount of data for each batch — including vessel identifiers, catch certificates, FAO codes, fishing zones and gear, quantities, processing units, and catch or harvest dates — for both fishery and aquaculture products. These requirements are replicated at every stage of the supply chain, thus increasing red tape without cutting the total amount of data required. The system also assumes a degree of digitalisation and interoperability that does not currently exist in the sector. In the absence of harmonised infrastructure and standards among Member States, many operators are forced to re-enter data manually, increasing errors, inconsistencies and delays. Thus the supply chain has a structural digital imbalance. In the light of the above: 1.
Does the Commission intend to adopt simplification measures to make the obligations under Regulation (EU) 2023/2842 proportionate to operating conditions in the supply chain?

Will it consider a tiered approach where comprehensive data storage is restricted to upstream operators (tier 1) and the passing of data to subsequent operators only at the request of competent authorities?
What steps will it take to develop interoperable and accessible digital infrastructure for all operators in the sector?

(11 June 2026) The Commission has been actively working through implementation to reduce administrative and operational burdens, while preserving the rules and objectives agreed by the co-legislators in the context of the revision of the fisheries control system, which culminated with the adoption of Regulation (EU) 2023/2842 (1). Traceability obligations for lots of fishery and aquaculture products have already applied since 2011, requiring detailed information to be available throughout the supply chain. This includes the requirement for operators to identify both the immediate supplier and recipient of such products and make this information available to competent authorities upon request. Regulation (EU) 2023/2842 requires such information to be recorded and made available ‘in a digital way’, a technologically neutral formulation that allows various means of digital transmission without mandating any specific systems or tools across the supply chain. Taking into account input received from Member States and stakeholders, including through a dedicated public questionnaire, the Commission will consider making use of the delegated powers under Article 58(12) of Regulation (EC) No 1224/2009 to establish harmonised rules for marketing control across the supply chain, including, where possible, rules on simplified data formats, transfer and submission. Such harmonisation would support interoperability by default, without prejudice to international rules and standards applicable for that purpose. The Commission will continue exploring, together with operators and Member States, the need for and options to establish a balanced, interoperable, proportionate, and accessible digital system for operators.

E-10-2026-001695.t: Statements by Commissioner Dombrovskis on ‘non-standard’ methods to expedite Ukraine’s accession to the EU
qt: to the Commission Ton Diepeveen (PfE), Marieke Ehlers (PfE) Subject:

In February 2026, Commissioner Dombrovkis said that the Commission was considering ‘non-standard’ methods to accelerate Ukraine’s accession to the EU1. Commissioner Kos, who is responsible for enlargement, underlined the commitment to abide by the due process of accession under the Treaty2. 1.
Has this been discussed in the College of Commissioners in the meantime?
Are ‘non-standard methods’ for Ukraine’s accession to the EU still on the table, and if so, what are they?

https://www.euractiv.com/news/eu-looking-at-non-standard-tactics-to-get-ukraine-in-commissioner-says/. https://www.euronews.com/my-europe/2025/11/07/eu-candidate-countries-must-choose-sides-before-joiningbloc-commissioner-kos-tells-eurone.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (29.6.2026) The legal basis for the accession of new Member States to the EU is Article 49 of the Treaty on the European Union (TEU)1. It provides that any European state which respects the values referred to in Article 2 of the TEU and is committed to promoting them may apply to become a member of the EU. Article 49 of the TEU also states that ‘the conditions of eligibility for accession agreed upon by the European Council shall be taken into account’. Upon the Commission’s opinion and the European Parliament’s consent, the Council adopts a decision on the country’s accession. The conditions of accession of a new Member State to the EU and the adjustments of the EU Treaties which such accession entails are subject to an agreement between the Member States and the applicant state, and the Accession Treaty is then submitted for ratification by all Member States and the acceding state in accordance with their respective constitutional requirements. Preparing for enlargement and taking on the obligations of EU membership remains based on the merits principle for all candidate countries. The Commission supports Ukraine in this effort.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/treaty/teu_2016/art_49/oj/eng.

E-10-2026-001694.t: Construction of a repatriation centre (CPR) in Castel Volturno
qt: to the Commission Pina Picierno (S&D) Subject:

The Italian Government has recently allocated EUR 41 million for the construction of a repatriation centre (CPR) in Castel Volturno (Campania), within the La Piana Wetland Park. This area comprises 63 hectares designated as a public leisure park, intended for naturerelated and recreational use. Castel Volturno is also a municipality that is already suffering from serious structural fragility: difficulties in collecting local taxes, a lack of essential services, and a socioeconomic situation that leaves the community vulnerable. The decision to allocate this sum to the construction of a CPR in this context runs counter to the actual needs of the region, which requires investment in infrastructure, security and social cohesion. Can the Commission therefore say: 1.

Does it consider that allocating this sum to the construction of a CPR in an area with severe shortages of essential services is consistent with the territorial cohesion objectives enshrined in Articles 174 to 176 TFEU and with the principle of partnership referred to in Article 8 of Regulation (EU) 2021/1060?

Does it intend to verify that the construction of the CPR has been preceded by an environmental impact assessment (EIA) in accordance with Article 6 of the Habitats Directive (92/43/EEC), given that the chosen site is classified as a Site of Community Importance (SCI) or a Special Protection Area (SPA) within the Natura 2000 network?
at: (English version) to the Commission Pina Picierno (S&D) (24 April 2026) Subject: Construction of a repatriation centre (CPR) in Castel Volturno The Italian Government has recently allocated EUR 41 million for the construction of a repatriation centre (CPR) in Castel Volturno (Campania), within the La Piana Wetland Park. This area comprises 63 hectares designated as a public leisure park, intended for nature-related and recreational use. Castel Volturno is also a municipality that is already suffering from serious structural fragility: difficulties in collecting local taxes, a lack of essential services, and a socioeconomic situation that leaves the community vulnerable. The decision to allocate this sum to the construction of a CPR in this context runs counter to the actual needs of the region, which requires investment in infrastructure, security and social cohesion. Can the Commission therefore say: 1.

Does it consider that allocating this sum to the construction of a CPR in an area with severe shortages of essential services is consistent with the territorial cohesion objectives enshrined in Articles 174 to 176 TFEU and with the principle of partnership referred to in Article 8 of Regulation (EU) 2021/1060?

Does it intend to verify that the construction of the CPR has been preceded by an environmental impact assessment (EIA) in accordance with Article 6 of the Habitats Directive (92/43/EEC), given that the chosen site is classified as a Site of Community Importance (SCI) or a Special Protection Area (SPA) within the Natura 2000 network?

(11 June 2026) 1. The facility in question does not receive EU funding. It fully falls under the responsibility of the Member State in terms of its location, management and operation. Because of this, the principle of partnership referred to in Article 8 of Regulation (EU) 2021/1060 (1), which provides for the close involvement of relevant partners in the implementation of the programmes, does not apply in this case. 2. Any plan or project not directly connected with or necessary to the management of a Natura 2000 site but likely to have a significant effect thereon shall be subject to appropriate assessment of its implications, in line with Article 6(3) of the Habitats Directive (2). Where a plan or project has been negatively assessed but must nevertheless be carried out for imperative reasons of overriding public interest, including of social or economic nature, Article 6(4) requires Member States to take all necessary compensatory measures to ensure the overall coherence of Natura 2000 is protected. It must inform the Commission of the compensatory measures adopted, enabling the Commission to assess whether the coherence of the Natura 2000 network will be maintained in the long term. In case a priority habitat type or priority species is affected, the Member State has to request an opinion from the Commission.

E-10-2026-001693.t: Transparency, control and potential irregularities in cultural schemes in Bulgaria financed under the Recovery and Resilience Plan
qt: to the Commission Hristo Petrov (Renew), Nikola Minchev (Renew), Radan Kanev (PPE) Subject:

Reports published1 in the Bulgarian media have raised serious misgivings over the allocation of funding for cultural schemes financed through the Bulgarian Recovery and Resilience Plan. It has been broadly disclosed that several projects connected with the same person received funding through different companies, that the amounts approved or advanced for these projects significantly exceeded well-established industry practices, and that some of these decisions were taken during the latter days of the previous government. The Bulgarian authorities have since begun conducting checks2. Given that Article 22 of Regulation (EU) 2021/241 requires Member States to protect the financial interests of the Union and to take appropriate measures to prevent, detect and correct fraud, corruption, conflicts of interests and double funding, would the Commission please specify: 1.
Whether it has requested clarifications from the Bulgarian authorities on these procedures and the funding granted under them?
Whether similar suspicions of irregularities have arisen regarding other projects under the same procedures or under other schemes financed through the RRP in Bulgaria?

Whether it considers that Bulgaria’s control mechanisms under the RRP provide sufficient guarantees to ensure quality management of funding and whether it intends to take further action in response to signs of weak controls, irregularities and lack of transparency?
https://clubz.bg/172433. https://www.bta.bg/bg/news/bulgaria/1091564-razporedil-sam-proverka-po-temata-s-ivo-arakov-i-ochakvamneyniya-rezultat-kaza.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (15.6.2026) The Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF) is a performance-based instrument, where the Commission assesses the satisfactory fulfilment of milestones and targets linked to measures included in Member States’ Recovery and Resilience Plans according to the requirements of the related Council Implementing Decision. With regards to the individual projects referred to in the question, the Commission would like to clarify that as the investment is part of the fourth payment request, which is currently under assessment by the Commission, the Commission is not in position to confirm the final list of projects funded under the RRF. The Commission has been informed by the Bulgarian authorities about the ongoing internal checks related to certain projects pertaining to this investment. Member States are responsible for the implementation of measures supported by the RRF and must protect the EU financial interests and ensure that the use of funds complies with the applicable EU and national rules1. Member States shall provide an effective and efficient internal control system. The Commission evaluated the control system set out by Bulgaria in its assessment of the RRP, as reflected in the Council Implementing Decision, concluding that the arrangements are adequate to prevent, detect and correct corruption, fraud and conflicts of interest, as well as to avoid double funding. A subsequent system audit performed by Commission services supports this overall assessment.
1 European Parliament and Council. 2021. Regulation (EU) 2021/241 on the establishment of the Recovery and
Resilience Facility, February 12, Article 22(1) (‘RRF Regulation’), available at https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legalcontent/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:32021R0241.

E-10-2026-001692.t: Risk of a kerosene crisis in the EU
qt: to the Commission Mihai Tudose (S&D) Subject:

Against the backdrop of the energy blockages triggered by the war in Iran, Europe is facing a looming kerosene crisis. The measures the Commission has announced so far boil down, as regards kerosene, to the monitoring of stocks and supplies. Meanwhile, large airline companies and the European Airports Association have warned of the risk of a systemic aviation fuel crisis. If the conflict in the Middle East continues, the EU will be faced with the bleak prospect of wholesale cancellations of flights just as the summer season approaches. What concrete measures is the Commission considering to guarantee kerosene supply in the coming months, to support the aviation sector in the event of a shortage, and to protect passengers in the event of flights being cancelled owing to fuel shortages?
at: (English version) to the Commission Mihai Tudose (S&D) (24 April 2026) Subject: Risk of a kerosene crisis in the EU Against the backdrop of the energy blockages triggered by the war in Iran, Europe is facing a looming kerosene crisis. The measures the Commission has announced so far boil down, as regards kerosene, to the monitoring of stocks and supplies. Meanwhile, large airline companies and the European Airports Association have warned of the risk of a systemic aviation fuel crisis. If the conflict in the Middle East continues, the EU will be faced with the bleak prospect of wholesale cancellations of flights just as the summer season approaches. What concrete measures is the Commission considering to guarantee kerosene supply in the coming months, to support the aviation sector in the event of a shortage, and to protect passengers in the event of flights being cancelled owing to fuel shortages? (25 June 2026) The Commission is monitoring the state of jet fuel availability at the weekly meetings of the Oil Coordination Group with Member States and Industry representatives: there is no immediate threat to the security of oil supply, although stocks of jet fuels are tight in some regions in the EU. To strengthen preparedness, and as announced in the AccelerateEU Communication (1), the Commission is establishing a Fuel Observatory to monitor EU production, imports, exports and fuel stocks. This improves visibility over supply and demand, helps detect shortages, and supports targeted action, such as alternative sourcing or coordinated stock releases in the EU. The Commission also issued on 8 May 2026 guidance on the flexibilities available under EU aviation legislation to ensure a coordinated response across Member States (2). This covers airport slots (3), travellers and passenger rights (4), fuel uplift obligations under ReFuelEU Aviation (5), Public Service Obligations (PSOs) (6), and the use of alternative jet fuel sources. Specifically on passenger and traveller rights, the guidance recalls strong protection under EU law, including the rules on price transparency. The aim is to safeguard the Single Market, protect passenger rights, and maintain essential air connectivity.

E-10-2026-001691.t: Six years of unnoticed non-compliance with animal welfare requirements in Chinese slaughterhouses
qt: to the Commission Jessika van Leeuwen (ECR) Subject:

Audit CT-2025-0037, published on 12 February 2026, found that animal welfare standards are systematically not being met in Chinese slaughterhouses: not a single slaughterhouse using electronic stunning methods had the monitoring equipment which has been required since 2019; in one slaughterhouse, a water bath for stunning designed for two animals was being used for ten at a time; and there was no procedure in place to reject batches in the event of animal welfare violations. Shortcomings in traceability make it impossible to determine whether imported products meet EU standards, allowing non-compliant products to reach the EU market unhindered and at the expense of a level playing field. In the three months between the completion and publication of the report, exports appear to have continued unabated, under a certification system that the Commission itself has already deemed unreliable. 1.

The Commission concludes that the shortcomings are systematic (conclusion 90) and that the certification system does not support the declarations made in Implementing Regulation (EU) 2020/2235 (conclusion 106). On what basis have products continued to enter the EU since that finding was made?
What objective criteria does the Commission use to determine when animal welfare guarantees from a third country are inadequate, and at what threshold does this lead to the suspension of imports?

The monitoring equipment, which has been mandatory since 2019, was missing at all the slaughterhouses inspected, without this having been identified in previous audits. How does the Commission explain that this shortcoming went unnoticed for six years?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (17.7.2026) In response to the audit and the Commission’s request to ensure compliance, the Chinese competent authority committed to address shortcomings immediately and rapidly, and provided the Commission with an action plan to address the recommendations. The Honourable Member can avail of this action plan at the Commission website1. After assessing the action plan as satisfactory, the Commission services scheduled in the second semester of 2026 an on-site follow up audit to verify the implementation and effectiveness of the proposed actions. The Commission ensures through audits that the exporting country can certify and guarantee the compliance with EU import requirements, or requirements deemed equivalent. When the EU audit identifies non-compliances, the trade partner is requested to produce an action plan containing corrections addressing those non-compliances. The Commission will have to follow up and ensure the good implementation of such corrective actions, including with onsite audits, when appropriate. In case the competent authority fails to provide an adequate action plan, the Commission may take corrective actions, including suspending imports. The previous Commission audit covering poultry meat products and rabbit meat took place in 2017 and did not identify any significant shortcomings concerning animal welfare. The Commission has committed to a 50% increase in the number of audits carried out in third countries which is already reflected in the Director-General for Health and Food Safety audit programme which is publicly available2.
1 http://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/audit_reports/index.cfm. 2 Health and food audits and analysis programme https://op.europa.eu/en/publication-detail/-
/publication/5813aab4-c5bd-11f0-8da2-01aa75ed71a1/language-en.

E-10-2026-001690.t: Delays in the northern connections of the Brenner Base Tunnel and the risk for the TEN-T network’s Scandinavian-Mediterranean corridor
qt: to the Commission Carlo Fidanza (ECR), Carlo Ciccioli (ECR), Daniele Polato (ECR) Subject:

The Brenner Base Tunnel is the backbone of the TEN-T network’s ScandinavianMediterranean corridor, a strategic piece of infrastructure for the modal shift of freight from road to rail. According to recent press reports, the completion and full entry into operation of the project is seriously compromised by the possible postponement of the opening to 2034, as well as by the Bavarian Government’s rejection of the route proposed by Deutsche Bahn for the northern access line to Kufstein. Without proper connections to the north, the tunnel risks turning into a bottleneck, undermining the effectiveness of the European investments already made. In the light of the above, could the Commission answer the following questions: 1.
Does it intend to obtain official information from the German and Bavarian Governments regarding intentions, timeframes and the definitive route of the northern link;
Does it intend to promote a special steering group that would include the Italian, Austrian and German transport ministries, with a view to defining a binding roadmap;

Does it intend to verify Germany’s compliance with the commitments it made in the context of the Scandinavian-Mediterranean corridor, considering the possible use of European financial instruments subject to firmly established deadlines.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.7.2026) The Commission fully agrees with the assessment that the success of the Brenner Base tunnel hinges on the availability of access routes with sufficient capacity to the south and the north of the tunnel. Only with such infrastructures in place the tunnel can unfold its full potential, greatly improve the connectivity through the Alps for passengers and freight and help relieve the local populations from the adverse effects of road transport. Deutsche Bahn has handed in its detailed planning and preferred route alignment for the parliamentary approval process which is expected later in 2026. After the Bundestag decision there will be more clarity on the timeline for the project. The Commission and the European Coordinator are following this process closely. As foreseen in article 55.2 of the TEN-T Regulation1 the Commission may adopt implementing acts for specific cross-border sections in close cooperation with the Member States concerned. The Commission would be ready to elaborate such an act if consensus to do so can be assured amongst the three Member States. This would complement the technical work already ongoing in the framework of the Brenner Corridor Platform2. The Commission is continuously monitoring the implementation and compliance of the European Transport Corridors through the work plans of the European Coordinators. The next work plan is expected to be published by end of 2026.
1 Regulation (EU) 2024/1679, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1679/oj/eng. 2 https://www.bcplatform.eu/corridorstudies/.

E-10-2026-001689.t: Concerns regarding the termination of the Bulgarian EPPO selection procedure
qt: to the Council Emil Radev (PPE), Andrey Kovatchev (PPE), Andrey Novakov (PPE), Axel Voss (PPE), Eva Maydell (PPE), François-Xavier Bellamy (PPE), Fredis Beleris (PPE), Ilia Lazarov (PPE), Jeroen Lenaers (PPE), Tomas Tobé (PPE), Tomáš Zdechovský (PPE), Adrián Vázquez Lázara (PPE), Marion Walsmann (PPE), Lukas Mandl (PPE) Subject:

In 2025, a national selection procedure for the nomination of Bulgarian candidates for the position of European Prosecutor at the European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO) was duly completed by the former government through an open and transparent competition involving multiple candidates and evaluated by an independent panel composed of judges, prosecutors, an academic, and representatives of the Ministry of Justice. The procedure followed the same methodology as the 2020 selection procedure, which was considered to be compliant with EU standards. The process has advanced to the EU level, with candidate interviews scheduled before the competent selection panel in April. However, the interim government, appointed in February 2026 and tasked with a limited mandate to organise elections, has decided to terminate the procedure without providing clear legal grounds for its decision. In this context, the Council is asked: 1.
How does it assess the compatibility of such actions with the principles of legal certainty and sincere cooperation, and the independence of the EPPO under Regulation (EU)2017/1939?
Could this create a precedent whereby political changes within a Member State undermine ongoing EU procedures?

Does the Council consider that the procedure should continue as planned, given that it is compliant with EU standards and has advanced to the EU level, and if so, what EU measures could ensure the continuity of the current procedure?
at: (English version) to the Council Emil Radev (PPE), Andrey Kovatchev (PPE), Andrey Novakov (PPE), Axel Voss (PPE), Eva Maydell (PPE), FrançoisXavier Bellamy (PPE), Fredis Beleris (PPE), Ilia Lazarov (PPE), Jeroen Lenaers (PPE), Tomas Tobé (PPE), Tomáš Zdechovský (PPE), Adrián Vázquez Lázara (PPE), Marion Walsmann (PPE), Lukas Mandl (PPE) (24 April 2026) Subject: Concerns regarding the termination of the Bulgarian EPPO selection procedure In 2025, a national selection procedure for the nomination of Bulgarian candidates for the position of European Prosecutor at the European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO) was duly completed by the former government through an open and transparent competition involving multiple candidates and evaluated by an independent panel composed of judges, prosecutors, an academic, and representatives of the Ministry of Justice. The procedure followed the same methodology as the 2020 selection procedure, which was considered to be compliant with EU standards. The process has advanced to the EU level, with candidate interviews scheduled before the competent selection panel in April. However, the interim government, appointed in February 2026 and tasked with a limited mandate to organise elections, has decided to terminate the procedure without providing clear legal grounds for its decision. In this context, the Council is asked: 1.
How does it assess the compatibility of such actions with the principles of legal certainty and sincere cooperation, and the independence of the EPPO under Regulation (EU)2017/1939?
Could this create a precedent whereby political changes within a Member State undermine ongoing EU procedures?

Does the Council consider that the procedure should continue as planned, given that it is compliant with EU standards and has advanced to the EU level, and if so, what EU measures could ensure the continuity of the current procedure?

Reply (27 July 2026) As regards the first question, the selection procedure for the posts of European Prosecutors is governed by Regulation (EU) 2017/1939 (the ‘EPPO Regulation’), which sets out the clear roles of Member States, the selection panel and the Council. According to Article 16(1) of the EPPO Regulation, Member States are responsible for nominating three candidates, whose independence is beyond reasonable doubt, for the position of European Prosecutor. As per the Treaties, Member States are required to act in line with the principle of sincere cooperation, including when submitting and withdrawing nominations. According to Article 14(3), the selection panel is responsible for drawing up a shortlist of qualified candidates and for providing a reasoned opinion. Finally, the Council’s role is to select and appoint one of the candidates to be the European Prosecutor of the Member State in question. Under the EPPO Regulation, it is ultimately the role of the selection panel, with its operating rules (Council Implementing Decision (EU) 2018/1696) ensuring the independence and impartiality necessary to carry out its work, to assess the nominations and their withdrawal. As regards the second question, at this stage, the effects of this situation on future procedures cannot be assessed. The Council does not answer hypothetical questions. Finally, as regards the last question, for the reasons described in the first reply, it is the responsibility of the selection panel to assess the steps to be taken in the selection procedure regarding the withdrawal of the nominations. Therefore, the Council has not discussed the issue raised by the Honourable Members.
