How does it assess the compatibility of such actions with the principles of legal certainty and sincere cooperation, and the independence of the EPPO under Regulation (EU)2017/1939?
Could this create a precedent whereby political changes within a Member State undermine ongoing EU procedures?

Does the Commission consider that the procedure should continue as planned, given that it is compliant with EU standards and has advanced to the EU level, and if so, what EU measures could ensure the continuity of the current procedure?

(15 June 2026) The regulation on the European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO) (1) does not establish rules governing the conduct of national procedures for the selection of candidates for the position of European Prosecutor within the Member States. The Commission has no role in the selection procedure for European Prosecutors, which is carried out in accordance with Article 16 of the EPPO Regulation and the operating rules of the selection panel approved by Council Implementing Decision (EU) 2018/1696 (2). While the Commission fully commits to its role as guardian of the Treaties, it is the Council, acting by simple majority, which is responsible for the selection and appointment of the European Prosecutors. The Commission would add that, once the three nominees have been transmitted to the panel by the Member State, for a withdrawal to be effective under EU law, the panel would have to assess whether there were irregularities in the national procedure, including the procedure leading to the withdrawal, which undermine the integrity of the process and the independence of the selected persons.

Council Regulation (EU) 2017/1939 of 12 October 2017 implementing enhanced cooperation on the establishment of the European Public Prosecutor’s Office (‘the EPPO’), OJ L 283, 31.10.2017, pp. 1-71, http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2017/1939/oj. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dec_impl/2018/1696/oj/eng.

E-10-2026-001687.t: Fiscal guidance on the treatment of interest-subsidised loans for affordable housing in public debt
qt: to the Commission Maria Ohisalo (Verts/ALE), Ville Niinistö (Verts/ALE), Sirpa Pietikäinen (PPE), AnnaMaja Henriksson (Renew), Li Andersson (The Left), Jussi Saramo (The Left), Merja Kyllönen (The Left), Maria Guzenina (S&D), Eero Heinäluoma (S&D) Subject:

In 2022, Eurostat recommended that interest-subsidised loans for housing construction in Finland be included in the statistical calculation of public debt. The Finnish statistical authority followed this recommendation, significantly increasing the debt ratio. The intersection of affordable housing and public debt is crucial, as Member States aim to address the investment gap and the shortage of affordable and social housing without exceeding fiscal limits. High public debt often restricts the government’s ability to invest in affordable housing. Eurostat’s instructions regarding the inclusion of subsidised loans in public debt calculations are unclear and discourage investments. If all Member States were to adopt Eurostat’s recommendations, as Finland has done, debt ratios could be artificially inflated to unsustainable levels, preventing public support for affordable housing. Member States have called on the Commission to examine the impact of subsidised loans on public debt. 1.
When will the Commission publish its guidance to Member States on designing financial and legal solutions to support social and affordable housing, taking into account public debt considerations?
What measures will the Commission propose to ensure that fiscal rules will encourage, rather than hinder public investment in social and affordable housing?
Will the Commission instruct Eurostat to clarify the rules on subsidised loans for affordable housing in public debt calculations and provide guidance to enable such investments?
at: (English version) to the Commission Maria Ohisalo (Verts/ALE), Ville Niinistö (Verts/ALE), Sirpa Pietikäinen (PPE), Anna-Maja Henriksson (Renew), Li Andersson (The Left), Jussi Saramo (The Left), Merja Kyllönen (The Left), Maria Guzenina (S&D), Eero Heinäluoma (S&D) (24 April 2026) Subject: Fiscal guidance on the treatment of interest-subsidised loans for affordable housing in public debt In 2022, Eurostat recommended that interest-subsidised loans for housing construction in Finland be included in the statistical calculation of public debt. The Finnish statistical authority followed this recommendation, significantly increasing the debt ratio. The intersection of affordable housing and public debt is crucial, as Member States aim to address the investment gap and the shortage of affordable and social housing without exceeding fiscal limits. High public debt often restricts the government’s ability to invest in affordable housing. Eurostat’s instructions regarding the inclusion of subsidised loans in public debt calculations are unclear and discourage investments. If all Member States were to adopt Eurostat’s recommendations, as Finland has done, debt ratios could be artificially inflated to unsustainable levels, preventing public support for affordable housing. Member States have called on the Commission to examine the impact of subsidised loans on public debt. 1. When will the Commission publish its guidance to Member States on designing financial and legal solutions to support social and affordable housing, taking into account public debt considerations? 2. What measures will the Commission propose to ensure that fiscal rules will encourage, rather than hinder public investment in social and affordable housing? 3. Will the Commission instruct Eurostat to clarify the rules on subsidised loans for affordable housing in public debt calculations and provide guidance to enable such investments? (29 June 2026) Statistical classification is the prerogative of national statistical institutes and Eurostat, which apply the same rules across Member States, while taking duly into account differences in how the housing markets are organised across Member States. The reclassification of specific Finnish loans from private — sector to government debt reflects the application of general EU level rules. These statistical rules are rooted in international agreements and ensure that government deficit and debt are measured both comprehensively and consistently across countries, which is essential for the conduct and monitoring of sound fiscal policy. As to the fiscal rules, the 2024 economic governance reform already provides fiscal flexibility to accommodate various forms of investment, including housing, by allowing an extension of the adjustment period in exchange for additional reforms and investment. To clarify the statistical treatment of various forms of financing structures targeting social and affordable housing, the Commission has committed to providing ‘guidance to Member States on designing financial and legal solutions to support social and affordable housing taking into account public debt considerations’. This will incorporate guidance on the revised Services of General Economic Interest (SGEI) decision regarding state aid to social and affordable housing, with completion targeted by the first quarter 2027. The Commission, including Eurostat, is working to clarify rules for specific types of debt and financing models. The guidance will aim to provide blueprints for financing social and affordable housing that minimise uncertainty regarding the application of state aid and statistical frameworks.

E-10-2026-001686.t: Young Sicilians’ bleak future – OECD concerns about Italy: stagnant wages, high tax burden and fossil fuel dependence
qt: to the Commission Giuseppe Antoci (The Left) Subject:

As confirmed in the latest international reports, including those by the OECD1, Italy continues to grapple with structural challenges that are taking a heavy toll on Sicily. Three main factors stand out in that connection: stagnation of real wages, a high and imbalanced tax burden, and ongoing fossil fuel dependence. In Sicily, these challenges are reflected in an already deeply alarming picture for young people: youth unemployment rates are among the highest in Europe, the exodus of skilled workers (‘brain drain’) is growing, precarious employment conditions are widespread, and opportunities to join innovative and sustainable sectors are limited. This state of affairs may permanently undermine the region’s economic and social cohesion, further widening geographical disparities in the EU. In the light of the above, could the Commission answer the following questions: 1.

Within the framework of cohesion policies and NextGenerationEU, what specific measures does it plan to adopt or step up to combat youth unemployment and brain drain in less developed regions, particularly Sicily?

Does it consider the current EU strategies up to the task of supporting real wage growth in Italy, and what instruments will it support to deliver fairer income distribution, especially for young workers?
With a view to alleviating the burden on young people and spurring stable youth employment, are there specific recommendations for Italy on fiscal reform?
OECD (2026), OECD Economic Surveys: Italy 2026, OECD Publishing, Paris, https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/oecd-economic-surveys-italy-2026_539538b2-en.html.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (17.7.2026) 1. Improving access to employment of young people is one of the specific objectives of the European Social Fund plus (ESF+). In Sicily, the regional ESF+ programme is investing EUR 204 million1 in targeted actions supporting youth employment2. The European Regional Development Fund supports small and medium-sized enterprises’ investments in research, competitiveness and green transition; in the Regional Programme for Sicily around EUR 502 million are allocated to these purposes aiming to generate additional jobs. Also, the Italian Recovery and Resilience Plan encompasses measures specifically aimed to support youth3 aiming at long-lasting structural effects, including in Southern areas facing deeper challenges. 2. The Commission is regularly analysing the comparatively low wage growth experienced by Italy over the past decades both under the European Semester and the Social Convergence Framework. 3. In 2025, Italy, as well as other Member States, received a recommendation to ‘promote job quality and reduce labour market segmentation, also to support adequate wages’4, as well as a recommendation to ‘make the tax system more supportive to growth’5. The Commission acknowledges the efforts already made by the Italian authorities in this regard and will continue to provide technical support to Member States wishing to press ahead with tax reforms aimed at supporting stable employment, particularly for young people.

1 EU quota, programmed under Priority IV ‘Youth’, representing 19% of the ESF+ regional allocation. 2 These include strengthening active labour market policies, promoting dual learning and apprenticeships as well

consolidating and expanding vocational education and training pathways. More broadly, the programme also aims at supporting entrepreneurship and self-employment and strengthening the training offer to align it to labour market needs, with the goal to create more quality job opportunities and fight the brain drain. 3 For example, to reduce early school leaving, which undermines youth’s opportunities particularly in the South, 820 100 beneficiaries received training and mentoring and more than 44 000 minors at risk of school drop-out in the South received support from non-governmental organisations. The Garanzia Occupabilita’ Lavoratori programme reached more than 3 million beneficiaries to return to employment, including young unemployed in the South. Further targeted measures (e.g., infrastructural projects for the Special Economic Zone) support growth and competitiveness to sustain young people’s employment prospects in the South. 4 European semester, Italy Country Specific recommendation n.8, 2025; COM(2025) 212 final. 5 European semester, Italy Country Specific recommendation n.1, 2025; COM(2025) 212 final.

E-10-2026-001685.t: Performance obligations with regard to the European Innovation Partnership
qt: to the Commission Sander Smit (ECR), Jessika van Leeuwen (ECR) Subject:

On 26 February 2026, the European Court of Auditors concluded that more than half of the European Innovation Partnership projects for the agricultural sector did not yield any useful innovations, and around a third had little relevance to agricultural practice. Unlike researchers and advisers, farmers were not systematically compensated for their participation. Projects that do compensate farmers, such as those in the Netherlands, demonstrably perform better. 1.

Is the Commission prepared to set a minimum percentage, in the regulation governing the programme for the 2028–2034 period, for European Innovation Partnership projects that must demonstrably prove to be applicable in agricultural practice?

The Commission promises to strengthen the interactive innovation approach – the same promise it made at the start of the current programme period. What, specifically, is it doing differently compared to 2021?

Can the Commission specify a concrete, quantifiable target for farmer participation that it aims to achieve for the European Innovation Partnership in the 2028–2034 period, against which Parliament can hold it to account halfway through that period?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (18.6.2026) The Commission welcomes the European Court of Auditor’s special report1 and remains committed to further refining the measure for Operational Groups (OG) projects. The Commission will not propose minimum percentage targets for projects since this would conflict with the bottom-up approach of the measure. The Commission is committed to improve the focus on farmers’ innovation needs in OG projects, as recommended by the Court. Under the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) 2023-2027, the interactive innovation model became a legal requirement, whereas it was non-binding guidance during the CAP 2014-2022 (the period covered by the audit). In its legal proposal for the CAP 2028-2034, in line with the recommendations by the Court, the Commission has proposed: emphasis on the dissemination of key results and scaling-up of project outcomes, strengthening the interactive innovation model to ensure that farmers and other practitioners are actively involved in projects and proposing a new possibility for Member States to support specific actions aimed at the wider uptake of OG projects’ results. The Commission will aim to also continue supporting EIPAGRI2 under Horizon Europe 2028-2034 via the multi-actor approach, addressed in the upcoming strategic approach to Research and Innovation. OG projects must bring together partners with complementary expertise, while ensuring the active involvement of farmers and other relevant practitioners. Fixed targets are not in line with the bottom-up nature of the measure and would hinder projects in for example forestry or rural innovation. Nevertheless, the Commission encourages and already observes improved farmers’ participation, with an increase of around 30% to 40% compared to the previous period.
1 https://www.eca.europa.eu/en/publications?ref=sr-2026-09. 2 EIP-AGRI: European Innovation Partnership for agricultural productivity and sustainability.

E-10-2026-001684.t: Commission’s assessment framework for evaluating national restoration plans.
qt: to the Commission Sander Smit (ECR) Subject:

The Agrifacts Foundation has reviewed the draft of the Dutch national restoration plan (NRP). The NRP provides for 450 000 to 850 000 hectares of additional habitat, aims for 40 % protected area and opts for result-based obligations, whereas the European Parliament explicitly opted for effort-based obligations1 when adopting the Nature Restoration Regulation2. It extends the regime for habitat types to areas of the Dutch Nature Network (NNN) outside Natura 2000. 1.

What criteria will the Commission apply in its assessment under Article 17(2) to determine whether a national restoration plan goes beyond what is necessary to achieve the objectives of Articles 4 to 13, and has the Commission established an assessment framework for this purpose which it is prepared to publish prior to the formal submission of national plans?

When assessing whether a national restoration plan is adequate, in accordance with Article 17(2)(b), is an assessment also made as to whether a plan goes beyond what is necessary to achieve the objectives, or is this assessment limited to the question of adequacy?

Does the Commission intend to publish its observations pursuant to Article 17(4) in full and in a timely manner, so that stakeholders and national parliaments may take note of the Commission’s assessment before the Member States finalises their plans?
Regulation (EU) 2024/1991. https://stichtingagrifacts.nl/aanstaand-natuurplan-veel-meer-grond-nodig-voor-huisvesten-soorten/.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (25.8.2026) The Commission will assess draft National Restoration Plans (NRP) in accordance with the requirements set out in Article 17 of the Nature Restoration Regulation (NRR)1: compliance with Article 15, adequacy for meeting the targets and fulfilling the obligations set out in Articles 4 to 13, and contribution to the Union’s objectives, targets and commitment referred to in Articles 1, 9(1) and 13. These requirements will be analysed by means of defined criteria, aligned with recognised practice for evaluation, to ensure an objective and operational assessment. The assessment framework is discussed with Member States and other members of the NRR Expert Group. As public budgets are constrained, for the finalisation of the plans the Commission encouraged Member States to design measures as cost-efficiently as possible. The Commission also advised to take measures which are already being planned or carried out and financed as a starting point. Finally, the Commission suggested to consider prioritising measures that contribute to several objectives such as climate mitigation and adaptation, land degradation neutrality and disaster prevention or reducing future restoration needs by preventing deterioration. Such multipurpose measures are likely to have a high costeffectiveness and a low cost-benefits ratio. The Commission observations on the draft NRP will be made public. After receiving them, Member States will have six months to produce the final NRP. Under the NRR, Member States have large margins of appreciation when setting the measures in the NRP and must ensure that the preparation of the NRP is transparent and inclusive, giving stakeholders opportunities to participate.
1 Regulation (EU) 2024/1991 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 24 June 2024 on nature
restoration and amending Regulation (EU) 2022/869, OJ L, 2024/1991, 29.7.2024.

E-10-2026-001683.t: Nature restoration obligations based on a non-verifiable national methodology
qt: to the Commission Sander Smit (ECR) Subject:

At the end of 2025, the Netherlands submitted its report under Article 17 covering the period 2019–2024, which shows that 28 of the 52 habitat types in the Netherlands are deteriorating. The Agrifacts Foundation has reported that the Dutch methodology differs from that of other Member States, partly because approximately 1 000 typical species are used for the 52 habitat types, including rare species and species not yet found in the Netherlands1. The underlying measurement data and the assessment criteria for the 2019–2024 cycle were not publicly available at the time of submission, meaning that the report cannot be independently verified. 1.

Does the Commission regard restoration obligations under Article 14(8) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1991, which arise from a national methodology that goes beyond the minimum requirements of Directive 92/43/EEC, as obligations under EU law or as national policy choices?

Does the Commission consider the limited public access to measurement data and methodology to be compatible with Directive 2003/4/EC on public access to environmental information and with Regulation (EC) No 1049/2001?

How does the lack of a direct legal remedy for stakeholders against methodological choices made by local authorities relate to the principle of effective legal protection as referred to in Article 9(3) of the Aarhus Convention and Article 47 of the EU Charter?
https://stichtingagrifacts.nl/nederlandse-natuur-fors-verslechterd-onderbouwing-niet-beschikbaar/.
at: (English version) to the Commission Sander Smit (ECR) (24 April 2026) Subject: Nature restoration obligations based on a non-verifiable national methodology At the end of 2025, the Netherlands submitted its report under Article 17 covering the period 2019-2024, which shows that 28 of the 52 habitat types in the Netherlands are deteriorating. The Agrifacts Foundation has reported that the Dutch methodology differs from that of other Member States, partly because approximately 1 000 typical species are used for the 52 habitat types, including rare species and species not yet found in the Netherlands (1). The underlying measurement data and the assessment criteria for the 2019-2024 cycle were not publicly available at the time of submission, meaning that the report cannot be independently verified. 1. Does the Commission regard restoration obligations under Article 14(8) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1991, which arise from a national methodology that goes beyond the minimum requirements of Directive 92/43/EEC, as obligations under EU law or as national policy choices? 2. Does the Commission consider the limited public access to measurement data and methodology to be compatible with Directive 2003/4/EC on public access to environmental information and with Regulation (EC) No 1049/2001? 3. How does the lack of a direct legal remedy for stakeholders against methodological choices made by local authorities relate to the principle of effective legal protection as referred to in Article 9(3) of the Aarhus Convention and Article 47 of the EU Charter? (6 July 2026) The Commission has no indication that would lead it to consider that the methodology of the Netherlands to assess the condition of protected habitat types goes beyond the requirements of the Habitats Directive (1). It has recently published technical guidelines to improve the streamlining of condition assessments (2) among Member States. Article 14(8) (3) of the Nature Restoration Regulation (NRR) (4) requires Member States, if applicable, to determine the reduction of the extent of the rewetting of peatland under agricultural use (5). This is as such not a restoration obligation. While the NRR builds, among others, on the concepts, definitions and data of the Habitats Directive, Article 14(8) refers to drained peatlands under agricultural use, which are not necessarily (and do not have to become) habitat types of Annex I. Citizens who are interested in the underlying measurement data and methodologies used by a Member State in reporting under the Habitats Directive can ask the national authorities for information according to Article 8(2) of the directive 2003/4/EC (6). Public access to the documents held by the Commission can be requested in accordance with Regulation (EC) No 1049/2001 (7). Where the conditions of Article 9(3) of the Aarhus Convention (8), read in conjunction with Article 47 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the EU, are met, the Netherlands, as Party to the Convention, must provide adequate access to justice, in particular where an act or omission may contravene environmental law.

E-10-2026-001682.t: Risks hanging over the European steel industry and use of public funding by ArcelorMittal
qt: to the Commission Thomas Pellerin-Carlin (S&D), Raphaël Glucksmann (S&D), Aurore Lalucq (S&D), Emma Rafowicz (S&D), Eric Sargiacomo (S&D), Pierre Jouvet (S&D), Chloé Ridel (S&D), Murielle Laurent (S&D), Christophe Clergeau (S&D), François Kalfon (S&D), Jean-Marc Germain (S&D), Claire Fita (S&D), Nora Mebarek (S&D) Subject:

The European steel industry needs to successfully decarbonise its production processes, while also remaining competitive in the face of increased and sometimes unfair international competition. To help it meet this challenge, ArcelorMittal, which accounted for around 53 % of primary steel production in Europe in 2021, was granted EU and national funding to decarbonise several of its sites, including its one in Dunkirk. However, despite a positive economic performance internationally, the group has recently announced job cuts and is considering relocating some of its activities to third countries, particularly Asia. Given the strategic importance of the sector for the EU’s industrial autonomy, including in critical fields such as defence, what control and monitoring mechanisms does the Commission intend to implement to ensure that the industrial strategies of companies receiving EU aid are in line with its objectives in terms of maintaining production capacity, jobs and decarbonisation in the European Union?

E-10-2026-001681.t: New provocation by Türkiye concerning Greece’s maps for fishing in the Aegean Sea
qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Fredis Beleris (PPE) Subject:

On 21 April 2026, based on maps published by Greece’s Fisheries Control Directorate, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Türkiye issued a press release alleging that Greece had imposed fishing restrictions in maritime areas beyond its jurisdiction. However, Greece has issued directives for its territorial waters and areas of Greek jurisdiction, while, as far as international waters are concerned, the provisions of the relevant international treaties are binding for all contracting states. These claims by Türkiye undermine the sovereign rights and established maritime borders of Greece and, by extension, those of the European Union. Moreover, Greek fishers, who fully comply with EU regulations, are forced to compete for the same stocks with Turkish counterparts who are not bound by EU regulations and are often involved in illegal, unreported, and unregulated (IUU) fishing. This creates an uneven playing field and threatens the livelihoods of Greek fishers. Reports also indicate frequent harassment of Greek fishers by Turkish vessels and the Turkish coastguard and the intrusion of Turkish fishing vessels into Greek territorial waters. In the light of this: 1.
Will the Commission consider adopting and enforcing certain measures, including diplomatic measures and sanctions, to ensure compliance with the common fisheries policy and to combat IUU fishing?
How will the EU defend its maritime borders and interests in the Aegean and the eastern Mediterranean?

(26 June 2026) As regards Illegal, Unreported and Unregulated (IUU) fishing, the EU IUU Regulation (1) is primarily a cooperation framework to help third countries meet their obligations as flag, coastal, port and market States. The identification of a non-cooperating third country is a measure of last resort and requires verifiable evidence and a case-bycase assessment respecting due process and proportionality. For alleged activities in Member State waters, the Commission relies on complete and substantiated reporting and follow-up by the coastal Member State. The Commission remains ready to examine any substantiated information. The EU remains committed to defending its interests and those of its Member States as well as to upholding regional stability. In this context, the EU attaches the greatest importance to safeguarding the sovereign rights of all Member States, in full respect of international law. Unequivocal commitment to international agreements and the UN Charter, as well as abstaining from unilateral actions which violate international law and the sovereign rights of Member States, remains an essential requirement to ensure a stable and secure environment in the Eastern Mediterranean and the development of a cooperative and mutually beneficial relationship between the EU and Türkiye.

E-10-2026-001680.t: Commission action on EASA diabetes recommendations for aviation medical rules
qt: to the Commission Thomas Bajada (S&D) Subject:

In September 2025, the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) published the final report of its three-year diabetes project. The report recommends updating the implementing rules, acceptable means of compliance and guidance material. It also proposes considering certification pathways for pilots and air traffic controllers using insulin or other glucoselowering medication with a low risk of hypoglycaemia, subject to individual assessment and appropriate operational limitations. Nevertheless, Union rules still automatically treat applicants requiring insulin as unfit. For many young Europeans living with diabetes, this means that years of ambition, training and preparation continue to be blocked by an outdated framework, even as comparable systems outside the EU have already introduced safeguarded pathways back into aviation. For some, this sends a clear message that the only way to pursue the career they have worked towards is to leave Europe. 1.
What steps has the Commission taken since the report’s publication and when will it bring forward the necessary amendments to Union aircrew medical rules?
Does the Commission intend to replace this blanket exclusion with a strict, evidencebased certification framework?
Will the Commission assess the barriers currently pushing young Europeans with diabetes to look outside the EU to pursue aviation careers?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (26.6.2026) After completing the referenced project and publishing the final report1, the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) organised a workshop with stakeholders and Member States medical experts to discuss the reports’ findings. It is now in the process of setting up a rulemaking group to draft the necessary alleviations for persons with diabetes. The Commission expects the group to start work in early 2027. The objective of this rulemaking task is to develop regulatory provisions that will allow applicants with well-controlled insulin dependency to perform pilot or air traffic control duties, subject to specific mitigating measures ensuring the continued high level of aviation safety. This should contribute to reducing barriers to entry into aviation professions for persons with diabetes. At the same time, the precise mitigating measures will need to be determined by medical experts to ensure that the high level of aviation safety is maintained.

E-10-2026-001678.t: Commission investigation into French and Polish nuclear power
qt: to the Commission François-Xavier Bellamy (PPE), Christophe Gomart (PPE), Nadine Morano (PPE), Céline Imart (PPE) Subject:

On 31 March 2026, the Commission opened an investigation into the French funding of the construction of six new European Pressurised Reactors, shortly after conducting an investigation into the public support scheme for the first Polish nuclear power plant. This investigation led the Commission to order that a number of changes be made to the power plant’s financial support and operation. 1.
What aspects of the French investment decision made the Commission’s investigation necessary, and have similar investigations been conducted into variable renewable electricity projects?
In the Polish investigation, what factors justify the Commission’s order to reduce the contract for difference from 60 years to 40 years?

Does the Commission consider that requiring the Polish nuclear power plant to be funded according to its production capacity, rather than its actual output, is consistent with the subsidiarity principle and freedom of choice with regard to energy mix, and who will finance this production capacity if the power plant does not generate enough electricity?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.6.2026) 1. The reasons for opening an investigation into the support measures for the construction and operation of six new nuclear reactors in France are described in the decision to initiate the formal investigation procedure, which has been published on 7 May 20261. Under Article 4(4) of Regulation (EU) 2015/15892, the Commission is required to open a formal investigation wherever it has doubts as to the compatibility of a measure with the internal market following a preliminary examination. This obligation applies equally to all notified State aid measures, regardless of the technology concerned. 2. The Commission has explained its doubts regarding the proposed duration of the direct price support proposed by the Polish authorities in the decision to initiate the formal investigation procedure into the aid measures for the first nuclear power plant in Poland3. The shortened duration aims to ensure that the aid is appropriate, proportionate, and does not unduly distort competition in the internal market, 3. The Commission's role under Articles 107 and 108 Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU) is to assess whether public support measures are compatible with the internal market. The Commission has exclusive competence in this area, subject to review by the EU Courts. Member States retain full competence over their energy mix under Article 194 TFEU. The design, where the power plant is remunerated for its availability to generate electricity rather than for its electricity output, helps limit distortions and avoids displacing renewable generation, supporting a more efficient and decarbonised electricity system.

E-10-2026-001677.t: Waste management, landfill and environmental inspections in La Rioja
qt: to the Commission César Luena (S&D) Subject:

The recent fire at the Nájera landfill has exposed recurrent issues in waste management in La Rioja, including shortcomings in monitoring, transparency and compliance with environmental permit conditions. The fire comes after previous incidents and inspection reports containing negative findings in recent years. This state of affairs reflects extensive reliance on landfill, which is at odds with the Union’s objective of limiting municipal waste landfilling to 10 % of the total amount generated by 2035. There are also concerns about waste shipping from other countries/regions without proper recovery and a lack of effective prevention, reuse and recycling measures. In view of the above: 1.
What does the Commission make of compliance with EU waste legislation in regions – particularly the monitoring, inspection and proper management of landfill sites?
How does the Commission make sure regions use EU funds to reduce waste generation and encourage reuse and recycling over landfilling?
Does the Commission believe the current reliance on landfilling in regions such as La Rioja is in line with EU objectives, and what action does it intend to take to remedy this situation?

(10 July 2026) The competent Spanish authorities are responsible for the application of EU law, including in the area of waste legislation. In 2024, the Commission decided to refer Spain to the Court of Justice of the EU for the breach of the obligations under Articles 13 and 15 of the Waste Framework Directive (1), in relation to the persistence of illegal/uncontrolled waste landfills (2). Also in 2024, the Commission sent a letter of formal notice to Spain concerning the disposal of municipal waste in landfills across Spain without prior treatment in accordance with the requirements of EU legislation on waste (3). EU policy and legislation, including cohesion regional funding (4), aim to ensure that waste management higher up in the waste hierarchy, such as preparing for re-use and recycling, are prioritised over landfilling (5). The Commission is in close contact with the Spanish authorities as regards the reduction of reliance on landfilling and boosting waste recycling and will monitor the situation closely.

E-10-2026-001676.t: Impact of ReFuelEU Aviation on the current crisis in the aviation fuels market
qt: to the Commission Kosma Złotowski (ECR) Subject:

The disruption in the Strait of Hormuz has caused major shocks to global oil supplies. The International Energy Agency warns that the European Union has sufficient aviation fuel reserves for about six weeks and that there may be systemic shortages of aviation fuel in the near future. Member States, as well as the European Union itself, are therefore calling on individuals and businesses to save fuel and reduce travel. Airlines are already cancelling flights and grounding part of their fleets. Lufthansa has announced that it is cutting 20 000 short-haul flights over the summer on account of the sharp increase in fuel prices and the drop in profitability of many routes. Other airlines are also temporarily reducing connections or increasing ticket prices, passing on the rising costs to passengers. In light of the above: 1.

Is the Commission analysing how Regulation (EU) 2023/2405 and its implications are affecting the current crisis situation, in particular the availability and price of aviation fuel and, more broadly, the cost of airfares?

Is the Commission considering introducing flexibility mechanisms under Regulation (EU) 2023/2405, e.g. through implementing and delegated acts, enabling the suspension or adjustment of mandatory SAF blending levels in the event of serious disruptions in the fuel market?

In the event of a prolonged crisis in the availability of fuels, including aviation fuel, is the Commission considering proposing a reform of the ReFuelEU Aviation Regulation and, if so, what direction might such a reform take?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (25.6.2026) 1. The Regulation (EU) 2023/2405 (ReFuelEU Aviation)1 aims to scale-up Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) and ensure that SAF is widely available and affordable in the EU. It creates a predictable framework for producing and using SAF, while strengthening the EU’s energy resilience and reducing dependence on imported fossil fuels. As announced in AccelerateEU2, the Commission is establishing a Fuel Observatory to improve visibility over fuel supply and demand, help detect shortages, and support targeted action such as alternative sourcing or coordinated stock releases in the EU. 2. As announced in AccelerateEU, the Commission issued on 8 May 2026 guidance3 on the flexibilities available under EU aviation legislation to ensure a coordinated response across Member States. Specifically, on ReFuelEU Aviation, the guidance clarifies how airlines can be exempted from their refuelling obligation in case of fuel shortage. The crisis in the Middle East reinforces the need to accelerate the transition towards more diversified energy sources. Maintaining the ambition of ReFuelEU Aviation and implementing the Sustainable Transport Investment Plan (STIP)4 are therefore essential to strengthen Europe’s energy security, strategic autonomy and competitiveness. 3. As announced in AccelerateEU, if the situation worsens and existing flexibilities no longer suffice, the Commission will propose temporary changes to the applicable EU legislative framework, where justified.

accelerated-action_en. 3 https://transport.ec.europa.eu/news-events/news/commission-publishes-guidance-support-eu-transport-sectoraffected-middle-east-crisis-2026-05-08_en. 4 https://transport.ec.europa.eu/news-events/news/commission-unveils-sustainable-transport-investment-planstrategic-approach-boost-renewable-and-low-2025-11-05_en.

E-10-2026-001675.t: Imprisonment of Swedish publisher and EU citizen Gui Minhai by Chinese authorities
qt: to the Commission Jonas Sjöstedt (The Left), Hanna Gedin (The Left) Subject:

On 17 October 2015, Swedish publisher and EU citizen Gui Minhai was abducted by presumed Chinese intelligence agents in Thailand. China has since sentenced him to 10 years in prison for ‘illegally providing intelligence overseas’. Since his sentencing, he has been denied consular access – in violation of China’s obligations under the Vienna Convention – independent medical care and access to his family and legal representatives. On 9 October 2025, a majority of MEPs in Parliament (546 out of 593) voted in favour of a resolution calling on the European External Action Service (EEAS), the Commission and the EU Member States to urge China to release Gui Minhai. 1.
What dialogue have the Commission and the EEAS had with Chinese authorities regarding Parliament’s demand to release Gui Minhai?
What further actions are the Commission and the EEAS, together with the Member States, taking to ensure the release of Gui Minhai?
at: (English version) to the Commission Jonas Sjöstedt (The Left), Hanna Gedin (The Left) (23 April 2026) Subject: Imprisonment of Swedish publisher and EU citizen Gui Minhai by Chinese authorities On 17 October 2015, Swedish publisher and EU citizen Gui Minhai was abducted by presumed Chinese intelligence agents in Thailand. China has since sentenced him to 10 years in prison for ‘illegally providing intelligence overseas’. Since his sentencing, he has been denied consular access — in violation of China’s obligations under the Vienna Convention — independent medical care and access to his family and legal representatives. On 9 October 2025, a majority of MEPs in Parliament (546 out of 593) voted in favour of a resolution calling on the European External Action Service (EEAS), the Commission and the EU Member States to urge China to release Gui Minhai. 1. What dialogue have the Commission and the EEAS had with Chinese authorities regarding Parliament’s demand to release Gui Minhai? 2. What further actions are the Commission and the EEAS, together with the Member States, taking to ensure the release of Gui Minhai? (28 May 2026) The EU has consistently voiced its grave concern about the human rights situation in China and resolutely called for the unconditional release of all those detained for peacefully exercising their fundamental freedoms and human rights. At the 40th EU-China Human Rights Dialogue in June 2025, the European External Action Service (EEAS) raised the case of the Swedish citizen. The EEAS inquired about the political prisoner’s hereabouts and sought reassurances concerning the health conditions. The EEAS further called on the Chinese authorities to facilitate contacts between the prisoner and his family and to respect the right to consular assistance. The EU will continue to call for the immediate and unconditional release of the Swedish prisoner and to raise the case at future meetings of the EU-China Human Rights Dialogue, in high-level meetings with Chinese interlocutors and in public statements, including at the UN Human Rights Council.

E-10-2026-001674.t: Urgent need in Lesvos to address foot-and-mouth disease and its consequences for local producers and the environment
qt: to the Commission Nikolas Farantouris (NI) Subject:

The island of Lesvos is a key pillar of Greek livestock production, with a livestock population exceeding 420 000 sheep and goats and significant production of milk and cheese products1. The first case of foot-and-mouth disease was recorded in mid-March 2026. Since then, the island has been facing a serious health crisis with significant impacts on the local economy and agricultural production. The national authorities have opted to impose a lockdown on the movement of livestock products, with the aim of preventing the spread of the disease to the mainland. This, however, has effectively suspended the commercial activity of producers. During the Easter period alone, 70 000 animals were left unsold. Farmers also express serious and growing environmental concerns, as there are no adequate sites or mechanisms for the hygienic disposal of the 250 tonnes of milk produced daily and the 10 000 animals killed, risking contamination of the aquifer and the island environment2. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
In which countries has vaccination against foot-and-mouth disease been implemented and what have been its results?
Does the Commission have sufficient stocks of vaccine and does it intend to make them available for the implementation of targeted vaccinations in surveillance zones?

Does the Commission intend to activate emergency financial support mechanisms within the framework of the Common Agricultural Policy or other financial instruments to compensate affected producers immediately and prevent an environmental and health crisis?

(2 July 2026) The EU legal framework, in particular Regulation (EU) 2016/429 (1), Commission Delegated Regulations (EU) 2020/687 (2), 2020/689 (3) and 2023/361 (4) provides for the instruments to control and eradicate category A diseases such as foot and mouth disease (FMD) including vaccination. E-10-2026-001673.t: Strengthening the EU’s manufacturing capacity in critical medicines and reducing dependence on supply chains from third countries
qt: to the Commission Piotr Müller (ECR) Subject:

Given the increasing risk of shortages of critical medicines in Member States, including Poland, and the EU’s persistently high dependence on the supply of active substances and finished medicinal products from third countries, in particular from Asia, I would like to ask: 1.
Is the Commission considering introducing mandatory minimum production levels for selected medicines in the EU?
Is the Commission analysing the impact of current environmental and energy regulations on the competitiveness of medicine production in Europe?

Is the Commission considering introducing solutions that reward European production of critical medicines in public procurement in order to make health systems more resilient to geopolitical and logistical crises?
at: (English version) to the Commission Piotr Müller (ECR) (23 April 2026) Subject: Strengthening the EU’s manufacturing capacity in critical medicines and reducing dependence on supply chains from third countries Given the increasing risk of shortages of critical medicines in Member States, including Poland, and the EU’s persistently high dependence on the supply of active substances and finished medicinal products from third countries, in particular from Asia, I would like to ask: 1.
Is the Commission considering introducing mandatory minimum production levels for selected medicines in the EU?
Is the Commission analysing the impact of current environmental and energy regulations on the competitiveness of medicine production in Europe?

Is the Commission considering introducing solutions that reward European production of critical medicines in public procurement in order to make health systems more resilient to geopolitical and logistical crises?

(3 July 2026) Whilst no mandatory minimum production levels for selected medicines exist in the EU, for medicines identified as dependent and vulnerable to supply chain disruptions the Critical Medicines Act (1) (on which political agreement was reached on 12 May 2026) introduces measures to favour EU-based manufacturing in public procurement procedures. The Critical Medicines Act also includes concrete steps to support European production of critical medicines in public procurement. The measures aim to boost supply chain diversification and resilience. Contracting authorities will be able to incentivise their manufacturing in the EU, for example by rewarding suppliers proportionally to the share of medicinal products and their active pharmaceutical substances manufactured in the EU. Before adopting any new legislation, including legislation in the fields of environment and energy, the Commission analyses the possible socioeconomic impacts, in line with the principles of Better Regulation.

Proposal for a regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council laying a framework for strengthening the availability and security of supply of critical medicinal products as well as the availability of, and accessibility of, medicinal products of common interest, and amending Regulation (EU) 2024/795, COM/2025/102 final.

E-10-2026-001670.t: Addressing the fertiliser crisis and strengthening food security in the EU
qt: to the Commission Yannis Maniatis (S&D) Subject:

The geopolitical instability of recent years has serious consequences that are not just limited to energy availability and prices, but create multiple problems throughout the supply chain. Both the 2022 energy crisis and the recent blockade of the Strait of Hormuz have shown that disruptions in the supply of natural gas to the EU directly affect, among other things, the production and availability of fertilisers (in 2022, 70 % of European factories closed). The result is a surge in the cost of agricultural production but above all a threat to the EU's food security. Spain has recently taken important initiatives, calling for the formulation of a European plan to prevent future crises and investment in research into alternative forms of fertilisation. At the same time, it is supporting its farmers with financial measures of EUR 500 million to address the impact of the increased cost of fertilisers. In Greece, the measures presented by the Government are insignificant in scale and are not sufficient to address the problem effectively. In view of the above: 1.

How does the Commission assess the establishment of a European fertiliser mechanism, with strategic planning and emergency tools, such as the creation of strategic reserves, for coordinated support to EU farmers in times of crisis?
What initiatives does it intend to take to strengthen research into alternative fertilisation technologies, in order to reduce our dependence on non-EU countries?

(19 June 2026) While no dedicated EU fertiliser mechanism as described by the Honourable Member exists, the Commission relies on instruments such as the Fertiliser Market Observatory (1) to monitor fertiliser market developments. The recently adopted Fertiliser Action Plan (2) includes measures to ensure availability and affordability, address market imbalances and strengthen coordination. It includes a specific action aiming at assessing stockpiling and other preparedness options for fertilisers. It will take full account of subsidiarity, storage and safety constraints, possible effects on prices and consistency with horizontal preparedness instruments. In terms of research, Horizon Europe has financed 116 Research and Innovation (R&I) projects related to sustainable nutrient management in the last years, for a total of EUR 750 million (3). This includes projects on bio-based fertilisers. To bridge the gap between R&I and industry, the Circular Bio-based Europe Joint Undertaking (CBE-JU) was created, a EUR 2 billion partnership between the EU and the Bio-based Industries Consortium that funds projects advancing competitive circular bio-based industries.

The Great Sea Interconnector, recently included for the 7th time in the EU list of Projects of Common Interest (PCI), having received significant funding from the Connecting Europe Facility (CEF) and being one of the Energy Highways of the December 2025 European Grids Package, ‘meets the criteria of the TEN-E Regulation, including a positive cost-benefit analysis’, as the Commission acknowledges in its previous response (E004589/2025/18.2.20261). It has also received a grant of EUR 657 million under the Connecting Europe Facility for Energy (CEF). E-10-2026-001668.t: Access to sole traders’ business data
qt: to the Commission Christophe Gomart (PPE), Susana Solís Pérez (PPE), Zala Tomašič (PPE), Fernando Navarrete Rojas (PPE), François-Xavier Bellamy (PPE), Céline Imart (PPE), Isabelle Le Callennec (PPE) Subject:

The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) has delivered important protections for citizens’ personal data. However, its current interpretation regarding sole traders, who act simultaneously as individuals and business entities, is having unintended consequences. Because no distinction is made between personal and professional data, European sole traders’ business information cannot be processed by business information providers (BIPs) without significant complexity – such as conducting a legally precarious ‘legitimate interest’ balancing test or obtaining individual consent – with a wide variety of differing interpretations of the regulation across the EU. The data gap results in greater complexity or even economic exclusion of sole traders, undermining the competitiveness of European small and medium-sized enterprises in the global marketplace. In this context, can the Commission clarify: 1.
Whether it is aware of these negative effects and their impact on the functioning of the single market, competitiveness, anti-money laundering support and the cost of complexity?

What concrete steps will it take to reform GDPR enforcement, enabling proportionate and lawful processing of sole traders’ business data with a clear distinction between personal and professional data?

More generally, whether it will support BIPs through a practical, reuse-friendly framework aligned with the European Data Strategy and single market goals for fair, transparent and competitive markets?
at: (English version) to the Commission Christophe Gomart (PPE), Susana Solís Pérez (PPE), Zala Tomašič (PPE), Fernando Navarrete Rojas (PPE), FrançoisXavier Bellamy (PPE), Céline Imart (PPE), Isabelle Le Callennec (PPE) (23 April 2026) Subject: Access to sole traders’ business data The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) has delivered important protections for citizens’ personal data. However, its current interpretation regarding sole traders, who act simultaneously as individuals and business entities, is having unintended consequences. Because no distinction is made between personal and professional data, European sole traders’ business information cannot be processed by business information providers (BIPs) without significant complexity — such as conducting a legally precarious ‘legitimate interest’ balancing test or obtaining individual consent — with a wide variety of differing interpretations of the regulation across the EU. The data gap results in greater complexity or even economic exclusion of sole traders, undermining the competitiveness of European small and medium-sized enterprises in the global marketplace. In this context, can the Commission clarify: 1.
Whether it is aware of these negative effects and their impact on the functioning of the single market, competitiveness, anti-money laundering support and the cost of complexity?

What concrete steps will it take to reform GDPR enforcement, enabling proportionate and lawful processing of sole traders’ business data with a clear distinction between personal and professional data?

More generally, whether it will support BIPs through a practical, reuse-friendly framework aligned with the European Data Strategy and single market goals for fair, transparent and competitive markets?

(9 July 2026) Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)) (1) does not cover the processing of personal data concerning legal persons, such as their name, form and contact details. Nevertheless, certain information about legal persons may exceptionally constitute personal data, e.g. when the official title identifies natural persons (2). Although a sole proprietor (i.e. self-employed), carries out business activity, and is thus engaged in a form of business, a sole proprietor is owned and run by one individual (‘you are your business’). It does not constitute a separate legal entity with its own legal personality, unlike a corporation. Accordingly, it is not a company or firm (i.e. legal person) as defined by Article 54 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU (3). Personal data protection must be considered in relation to its function in society and be balanced against other fundamental rights in accordance with the principle of proportionality (4). For example, the anti-money laundering legislative package contains robust data protection safeguards, without compromising the legislative objective (5).

Regulation (EU) 2025/2518 (6) streamlines GDPR enforcement in cross-border cases. To achieve the consistent application of the GDPR, the European Data Protection Board has committed to facilitating easier GDPR compliance, including by providing ready-to-use templates (7), as also called for by the Commission (8). The GDPR implementation dialogue, which took place in July 2025, reaffirmed that the GDPR is a balanced legal framework and has met its objectives (9). Nevertheless, to boost competitiveness, increase legal certainty, reduce costs and strengthen enforcement, targeted amendments to the GDPR are proposed in the Digital Omnibus (10).

E-10-2026-001667.t: Revelations about a global network of men drugging and abusing women
qt: to the Commission Jeroen Lenaers (PPE) Subject:

A recent shocking investigation by CNN1 has uncovered a global network of men who use messaging apps and porn sites to support and encourage one another to drug and abuse their female partners. For example, the porn website Motherless features more than 20 000 videos of women who have been drugged or who are unconscious. Telegram group chats are also being used to share tips on how to drug women, sell sleeping pills and share live streams of the abuse. 1.

Is the Commission aware of the recent CNN investigation, and does it share the view that – given the cross-border nature of platforms such as Telegram and Motherless – this issue needs to be addressed at EU level?
What obligations does existing EU legislation impose on online platforms, Member States and the Commission, and how does the Commission ensure compliance with these obligations?
Given the seriousness of this issue, is the Commission prepared to take additional measures to combat this form of sexual abuse and, if so, what specific steps is it considering?
https://edition.cnn.com/interactive/2026/03/world/expose-rape-assault-online-vis-intl/index.html.
at: (English version) to the Commission Jeroen Lenaers (PPE) (22 April 2026) Subject: Revelations about a global network of men drugging and abusing women A recent shocking investigation by CNN (1) has uncovered a global network of men who use messaging apps and porn sites to support and encourage one another to drug and abuse their female partners. For example, the porn website Motherless features more than 20 000 videos of women who have been drugged or who are unconscious. Telegram group chats are also being used to share tips on how to drug women, sell sleeping pills and share live streams of the abuse. 1. Is the Commission aware of the recent CNN investigation, and does it share the view that — given the cross-border nature of platforms such as Telegram and Motherless — this issue needs to be addressed at EU level? 2. What obligations does existing EU legislation impose on online platforms, Member States and the Commission, and how does the Commission ensure compliance with these obligations? 3. Given the seriousness of this issue, is the Commission prepared to take additional measures to combat this form of sexual abuse and, if so, what specific steps is it considering? (22 June 2026) The Commission is aware of the CNN investigation in relation to ‘Motherless.com’ and the use of Telegram for sharing information on how to drug and abuse women. These practices are unacceptable. Under the Digital Services Act (DSA) (1), providers of hosting services are obliged to put in place mechanisms for users to notify suspected illegal content. If found to be illegal, the platform must act expeditiously to remove or to disable access to that content. Providers are also required to notify suspected criminal offences involving a threat to the life or safety to competent authorities. Very large online platforms and search engines must, at least annually, assess systemic risks on their service and put in place effective mitigation measures. This can include risks relating to gender-based violence, including non-consensual sharing of intimate images, and threats to fundamental rights. The Commission is continuously monitoring these platforms’ compliance with the DSA. For example, in January 2026 the Commission opened formal proceedings against X due to, inter alia, Grok’s dissemination of sexualised deepfakes. Furthermore, Directive (EU) 2024/1385 criminalises the most serious forms of cyberviolence, including the non-consensual sharing of intimate material, and requires rapid removal of illegal content. The Commission is committed to supporting Member States in transposing the directive. Telegram is not designated as a very large online platform and has appointed its legal representative in Belgium; the Digital Services Coordinator is the Belgian Institute for Postal Services and Telecommunications. The Commission is aware that the Dutch authorities opened an investigation on ‘Motherless.com’, whose servers are located in the Netherlands.

E-10-2026-001666.t: Supporting primary health and emergency pre-hospital care infrastructure in the mountainous Acheloos Valley
qt: to the Commission Sakis Arnaoutoglou (S&D) Subject:

The Acheloos Valley is a remote and inaccessible mountainous area of Greece, on the administrative border of four regional units, and serves residents from four municipalities: Georgios Karaiskakis in Arta, Argithea in Karditsa, Agrafa in Evrytania and the area of the former Municipality of Inachos in Aetolia-Acarnania. The rugged mountain terrain, the long distances from hospitals and the limited access to health services create difficulties in residents’ health coverage and the treatment of emergencies. The creation of a health centre and a national centre for emergency care [EKAB] station in the wider area could provide health coverage for the population of the four municipalities, reduce the time to access emergency care and contribute to maintaining social cohesion and keeping residents in areas facing demographic decline and desertification. Given that the European Union recognises, in Article 174 TFEU, the specific needs of mountainous areas and supports access to basic services through cohesion policy, the Commission is asked: 1.
How can cohesion policy financial instruments or other programmes be used to support primary health and emergency care infrastructure in remote areas such as the Acheloos Valley?
Does the Commission intend to support actions that improve access to basic health services in order to address demographic decline?
Can the creation or upgrading of health structures serving more mountainous municipalities be an eligible investment under regional programmes or other European funds?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (19.6.2026) 1. Cohesion Policy 2021–2027 in Greece supports healthcare under the European Regional Development Fund (ERDF)1 with some EUR 327 million and the European Social Fund Plus (ESF+)2 with some EUR 240 million with measures such as TOMYs3 and KOMYs4. For the Acheloos Valley, the programmes ‘Thessalia’, ‘Dytiki Ellada’, ‘Ipeiros’ and ‘Sterea Ellada’ have allocated under ERDF some EUR 64 million for building and upgrading health centres and essential infrastructure. The common agricultural policy, LEADER programme and Recovery and Resilience Facility fund rural health services. 2. The upcoming Right to Stay Strategy will address demographic challenges, with actions that among others will improve access to basic health services. According to Article 168(7) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union5, Member States are responsible for organising and delivering health services while the EU supports them with technical assistance and funding. The European Semester addresses challenges including in relation to the accessibility of healthcare. 3. The Cohesion Policy 2021-2027 regulatory framework6 allows investment in the creation or modernisation of health infrastructure, including to reduce territorial disparities in access to healthcare. Under shared management Member States prepare and implement programmes and select operations. Support for health must be consistent with the national7 strategic policy framework for health required under Thematic Enabling Condition 4.6.

E-10-2026-001664.t: Conflict of interest of the Prime Minister of the Czech Republic Andrej Babiš in connection with ownership of SynBiol
qt: to the Commission Tomáš Zdechovský (PPE) Subject:

According to publicly available media information, in February 2026 a document was confirmed on the basis of which the Prime Minister of the Czech Republic, Andrej Babiš, once again became the direct owner of the company SynBiol, and changes were simultaneously made to the management of this company. SynBiol had previously, similarly to the Agrofert holding, been placed in trust funds created in response to EU rules concerning conflicts of interest. In the past, the Commission concluded that there is a conflict of interest between Andrej Babiš’s public office and his business activities, particularly in relation to the drawing of European funds. In light of the new developments, questions arise regarding compliance with EU rules on conflicts of interest and the protection of the Union’s financial interests. 1.

Is the Commission aware of these recent changes in the ownership structure of SynBiol, and if so, what is its preliminary assessment in terms of a possible conflict of interest under Article 61 of the EU Financial Regulation?

Does the Commission plan to launch a new investigation or update its previous conclusions regarding the conflict of interest of the Prime Minister of the Czech Republic, Andrej Babiš, in connection with the potential drawing of EU funds by companies that he directly or indirectly controls?

What specific measures can the Commission take to ensure that, in the event a conflict of interest is confirmed, there is no undue use of European funds and that any breaches of the rules are consistently sanctioned?
at: (English version) to the Commission Tomáš Zdechovský (PPE) (22 April 2026) Subject: Conflict of interest of the Prime Minister of the Czech Republic Andrej Babiš in connection with ownership of SynBiol According to publicly available media information, in February 2026 a document was confirmed on the basis of which the Prime Minister of the Czech Republic, Andrej Babiš, once again became the direct owner of the company SynBiol, and changes were simultaneously made to the management of this company. SynBiol had previously, similarly to the Agrofert holding, been placed in trust funds created in response to EU rules concerning conflicts of interest. In the past, the Commission concluded that there is a conflict of interest between Andrej Babiš’s public office and his business activities, particularly in relation to the drawing of European funds. In light of the new developments, questions arise regarding compliance with EU rules on conflicts of interest and the protection of the Union’s financial interests. 1. Is the Commission aware of these recent changes in the ownership structure of SynBiol, and if so, what is its preliminary assessment in terms of a possible conflict of interest under Article 61 of the EU Financial Regulation? 2. (23 June 2026) The Commission is closely monitoring all developments to ensure strict compliance with EU rules on conflicts of interest taking into account inter alia the recommendations issued by the previous Commission audit. A letter requesting information on the measures taken by the Member State has been issued on 19 February 2026. A follow up letter to the Czech authorities has been issued on 20 May 2025. Pending a legal assessment of the conflict of interest by the Commission services, and to safeguard the EU’s financial interests, the Commission has requested EU programmes’ managing authorities to ensure that any payment application submitte d (1) to the Commission does not include expenditure linked to operations involving the AGROFERT Group companies or any other entities belonging to or under the control of the Czech Prime Minister, or associated to him, outside of the AGROFERT Group, including Synbiol and Hartenberg Holding, and selected as beneficiaries of EU funding as of 9 December 2025. Such measures were applied in the past in relation to the previously detected conflict of interest. A conflict of interest can also be symptomatic of a wider rule of law issue which could be addressed via the mechanisms under the General Conditionality Regulation (5).

E-10-2026-001662.t: Need to strengthen controls and ensure reciprocity of standards on imports of processed fruit, vegetables and tomato products from non-EU countries
qt: to the Commission Konstantinos Arvanitis (The Left) Subject:

The European fruit and vegetable processing industry warns of the increasing pressure on the single market from non-EU imports of products that are often produced at lower costs, as they are not subject to the same strict standards on pesticide residues, food safety and traceability, nor to the environmental and labour standards that apply to European producers, without any effective guarantee of full equivalence of production and control conditions. This situation creates conditions of unfair competition to the detriment of European processing, undermines the resilience of the EU agri-food chain, weakens strategic production sectors and raises legitimate concerns for consumer protection and the EU's strategic autonomy in the food sector. Given the Commission's stated recognition of the need for stronger alignment of the standards applied to imported products, in particular as regards pesticides: 1.

Does the Commission intend to strengthen targeted border and laboratory controls on processed fruit and vegetables from non-EU countries immediately, as well as to revise the current framework of official controls on food of non-animal origin, in order to include products and countries of origin that systematically show compliance problems in a regime of enhanced surveillance more quickly?

What specific measures does the Commission intend to take to ensure substantial equivalence of production standards in products imported from non-EU countries, as well as to protect the competitiveness of European processing and consumer safety?
at: (English version) to the Commission Konstantinos Arvanitis (The Left) (22 April 2026) Subject: Need to strengthen controls and ensure reciprocity of standards on imports of processed fruit, vegetables and tomato products from non-EU countries The European fruit and vegetable processing industry warns of the increasing pressure on the single market from non-EU imports of products that are often produced at lower costs, as they are not subject to the same strict standards on pesticide residues, food safety and traceability, nor to the environmental and labour standards that apply to European producers, without any effective guarantee of full equivalence of production and control conditions. This situation creates conditions of unfair competition to the detriment of European processing, undermines the resilience of the EU agri-food chain, weakens strategic production sectors and raises legitimate concerns for consumer protection and the EU's strategic autonomy in the food sector. Given the Commission's stated recognition of the need for stronger alignment of the standards applied to imported products, in particular as regards pesticides: 1.

Does the Commission intend to strengthen targeted border and laboratory controls on processed fruit and vegetables from non-EU countries immediately, as well as to revise the current framework of official controls on food of non-animal origin, in order to include products and countries of origin that systematically show compliance problems in a regime of enhanced surveillance more quickly?

What specific measures does the Commission intend to take to ensure substantial equivalence of production standards in products imported from non-EU countries, as well as to protect the competitiveness of European processing and consumer safety?

(3 July 2026) Food products from third countries, regardless of their origin, must comply with EU food safety requirements laid down in EU legislation. According to Regulation (EU) 2017/625 (1) official controls have to be performed on goods entering the Union. Member States must carry out risk-based official controls on processed fruit and vegetables from non-EU countries. Where food of non-animal origin from third countries poses a risk, the Commission may adopt measures through Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1793 (2). Under the Vision for Agriculture and Food (3), the Commission pursues a stronger alignment of production standards applied to imported products. The Commission announced a series of measures to strengthen import controls at EU borders and in third countries. The Commission performs audits in Member States and in third countries to ensure that their official control systems guarantee that goods intended for export to the EU comply with the applicable EU rules (4). In addition, the Commission is working to avoid that the most hazardous pesticides banned in the EU for health and environmental reasons would be imported back into the EU through imported products. The Joint Research Centre has commenced a study that will feed into an impact assessment. Pending the outcome of this impact assessment, the Commission has proposed in the Food and Feed Simplification Package (5) to establish the possibility for the Commission to lower Maximum Residues Limits (MRLs) for the most hazardous substances not approved in the EU on a case-by-case basis, if considered appropriate, in the light of the outcome of substance-specific impact assessments.

E-10-2026-001661.t: Asbestos in children’s toys and the functioning of Safety Gate
qt: to the Commission Mohammed Chahim (S&D), Kim Van Sparrentak (Verts/ALE) Subject:

According to recent research, asbestos has been found in various types of toys containing socalled play sand. Asbestos is a carcinogenic substance and poses a serious risk to public health and the environment, particularly for children. Despite the fact that the European Union has strict rules regarding toy safety1 and that the Safety Gate system is designed to identify and remove dangerous products from the market swiftly, journalistic research by the Dutch daily newspaper Algemeen Dagblad2 has revealed that reports of dangerous products do not always appear in this system in a timely or complete manner. 1.
Can the Commission explain to what extent it can guarantee that notifications from competent national authorities are published in Safety Gate in full and in a timely manner?
Is the Commission prepared, in cases involving a potentially serious risk to vulnerable groups such as children, to also include preventive or provisional warnings in Safety Gate?

What steps is the Commission taking, in cooperation with authorities in third countries, to strengthen controls on high-risk products such as play sand prior to export to the EU, so that such products do not reach the European market?

at: (English version) to the Commission Mohammed Chahim (S&D), Kim Van Sparrentak (Verts/ALE) (22 April 2026) Subject: Asbestos in children’s toys and the functioning of Safety Gate According to recent research, asbestos has been found in various types of toys containing so-called play sand. Asbestos is a carcinogenic substance and poses a serious risk to public health and the environment, particularly for children. Despite the fact that the European Union has strict rules regarding toy safety (1) and that the Safety Gate system is designed to identify and remove dangerous products from the market swiftly, journalistic research by the Dutch daily newspaper Algemeen Dagblad (2) has revealed that reports of dangerous products do not always appear in this system in a timely or complete manner. 1. Can the Commission explain to what extent it can guarantee that notifications from competent national authorities are published in Safety Gate in full and in a timely manner? 2. Is the Commission prepared, in cases involving a potentially serious risk to vulnerable groups such as children, to also include preventive or provisional warnings in Safety Gate? 3. What steps is the Commission taking, in cooperation with authorities in third countries, to strengthen controls on highrisk products such as play sand prior to export to the EU, so that such products do not reach the European market? (15 June 2026) In accordance with Articles 26(3) and (4) of the regulation on General Product Safety (1) Member States are obliged to notify any corrective measures taken by their authorities or by economic operators against producers presenting a serious risk to the health and safety of consumers to the Safety Gate Rapid Alert System within four days after the corrective measures are taken, and the Commission has also 4 days for validation. In November 2025, Australian authorities alerted the Commission about toy sands containing asbestos. This was immediately shared with Member States, urging vigilance and mandatory reporting via Safety Gate if such items were found. Early 2026, the Commission followed up, seeking feedback on voluntary business measures, safety incidents, and accidents via the Safety Business Gateway (2). The Commission also organised in parallel a discussion on a methodology for asbestos detection in toy sands with Member States. Initial tests revealed that only a limited number of samples contained asbestos posing serious risk. These cases were reported in a timely manner in Safety Gate, alongside voluntary recalls by businesses. Safety Gate itself provides information about corrective measures taken against unsafe products but its portal (3) also hosts broader product safety information. This case shows the importance for the Commission to collaborate with a wide range of international partners, both the ones with a similar market and manufacturing countries. For example, an administrative arrangement sets up a mechanism through which Chinese authorities follow up on EU alerts of dangerous products originating from China.
