qt: to the Commission Marieke Ehlers (PfE), Mieke Andriese (PfE), Sebastian Kruis (PfE) Subject:

In the Commission’s latest attack on privacy, the President introduced an age verification app, describing it as ‘technically ready’ and built to ‘the highest privacy standards’. However, independent code reviews have revealed critical security flaws. The Commission is asked to answer the following questions: 1.

Researchers claim that the app’s PIN can be bypassed in under two minutes by editing a single local configuration file, thereby granting full access to another person’s credentials. Rate limiting and biometrics can reportedly be disabled in the same way. Is this accurate and how did this pass security reviews? If so, why should EU citizens continue to trust the Commission and its digital tools?

Does the app store unencrypted facial images from passport scans and selfies on the device without reliably deleting them? If so, how is this compatible with GDPR rules on biometric data, given that a private provider was recently fined nearly EUR 1 million in a similar case1?

The app’s repository describes it as ‘not feature-complete’ and requiring ‘further integration’. Why, then, did the Commission present it as technically ready, and will an independent security audit be required before any Member State deploys it?
https://www.dataguidance.com/news/spain-aepd-fines-yoti-eu950000-unlawful-processing.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (19.6.2026) The findings concern an early development version of the EU age verification (AV) software, that experts could examine and test before any use by citizens. The consortium released a hardening update on 17 April 20261 addressing the specific issues identified, and further updates will follow as the review process continues. The behaviours described require physical access to a device that has been modified to remove its built‑in security protections. On a standard, unmodified phone, the operating system itself prevents this kind of file access. The application (app) relies on local device processing and biometric material is used only to confirm that the user is the genuine holder of an authentic identity document, and it is never transmitted to anyone. The individual solutions published will need to comply with Regulation (EU) 2016/6792, which is supervised by the national data protection authorities. The Commission’s statement3 referred to the technical readiness of the publicly available EU AV blueprint. Further integration work must be performed by an app publisher, including translation, branding, app-store submission and operational hardening. The Commission Recommendation of 29 April 20264 explicitly calls on Member States to ensure compliance with all relevant cybersecurity standards. The EU AV Scheme will set out criteria for issuers of proof‑of‑age attestations and for AV solutions and will publish a list of providers that meet the required privacy and security standards.

E-10-2026-001658.t: Support for small, island and mountain family-run farms in the post-2027 CAP
qt: to the Commission Galato Alexandraki (ECR) Subject:

The Commission has already stated that the post-2027 CAP will be central to the next EU budget, while the third amendment to the Greek Strategic Plan was adopted on 6 March 2026. It acknowledges that there are around 600 000 agricultural holdings in Greece, with an average size of only 7 hectares. In a country shaped by island and mountainous areas, the blanket application of one set of rules often favours larger and more easily organised farms, to the detriment of small family holdings that support production, employment and social cohesion in rural areas. Can the Commission answer the following: 1.

Does it intend to include a stronger mandatory redistribution of direct payments in favour of small and medium-sized family farms, particularly those in island and mountain regions, in the post-2027 CAP?
Does it intend to maintain and strengthen the possibility of coupled payments for sectors and areas with permanent natural constraints and of particular importance for food security?
Will it introduce a specific simplified scheme for small farms, with fewer administrative obligations and targeted flat-rate support?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (18.6.2026) The future Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), as proposed in July 2025, aims at improving the targeting of income support towards those farmers who need it most, particularly, smaller farmers, young farmers, and mixed farms. This would be achieved via the requirement to differentiate income support, the introduction of an increased and simple payment for small farmers and an ambitious proposal for degressivity and capping. Other interventions such as coupled income support, natural or other-specific constraints (ANC) payments, and investment support should further contribute to a better targeting. Concerning coupled support, the Commission proposes a potentially increased envelop, and to extend eligibility to more area-based sectors such as grass and other herbaceous forages including in areas at a risk of abandonment of agricultural production. The targeted sectors or related types of farming would be defined by the Member States based on the difficulties the sectors undergo and the analysis of their additional income needs. As long as certain preconditions and limits are met, Member States would have flexibility in designing their support decisions (targeting, output value, etc) in light of local needs. With regard to the proposed specific scheme for small farmers, this would be in the form of a payment per hectare or a lump sum. Farmers receiving such support would be exempted from applying the farm stewardship requirements.

E-10-2026-001657.t: Small-scale coastal fishing, insularity and disproportionate restrictions in the Mediterranean
qt: to the Commission Galato Alexandraki (ECR) Subject:

Small-scale coastal fishing is a key pillar for many island and coastal communities in Greece. The Commission itself published a specific guide (vademecum) on the allocation of fishing opportunities in November 2025, recognising that small-scale fishers are particularly vulnerable and that Member States must apply transparent and objective social, economic and environmental criteria. On 24 March 2026, in view of the Agriculture and Fisheries Council of 30 March, the Commission returned to the issue, pointing out that small-scale coastal fishing accounts for 76 % of the EU fleet, while 23 % of vessels are already operating at a loss. Nevertheless, in areas of the Mediterranean, fishers have dropped below 130 fishing days, with income losses of up to 40-50 %, which is particularly harmful to the Greek islands. In view of the above: 1.

Does the Commission intend to ask Member States to give special priority to smallscale coastal and island fisheries when implementing Article 17 of the Regulation on the Common Fisheries Policy and the allocation of fishing opportunities and fishing days?

Does the Commission intend to activate targeted financial support through the EMFAF for fishers in island and coastal areas who are disproportionately affected by the restrictions in the Mediterranean?

Will the Commission review the current system of fishing limitations in the Mediterranean on the basis of updated scientific and socio-economic data by maritime zone, in order to avoid horizontal measures that lead to the economic suffocation of the primary sector on the islands?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (8.6.2026) Through the Communication for enhanced transparency and good governance in the allocation of fishing opportunities by Member States1, published in November 2025, the Commission encouraged Member States to use the full potential of Article 17 of the Common Fisheries Policy Regulation (CFP) Regulation2 to support small-scale and coastal fishers. Nevertheless, the Commission recognised that it is Member States’ responsibility to decide on their national allocation systems and that it has no legal tool to oblige Member States to allocate fishing opportunities to small-scale coastal and island fisheries. The Greek European Maritime, Fisheries and Aquaculture Fund (EMFAF) programme provides key support for the resilience and competitiveness of the fisheries sector and coastal communities. This includes a wide range of activities, such as diversifying activities to support income, like fishing tourism, mitigating impacts from climate change, enhancing fishers' skills and income possibilities through training. Moreover, projects related to smallscale fisheries may be supported at an aid intensity of up to 100%. The conservation of marine biological resources and the management of fisheries are based on the best available scientific advice and on a consultation process with advisory bodies and Member States, both fundamental principles of the CFP. The specificities and the technical characteristics of the type of fisheries are being considered in this regard. Furthermore, at regional level within the General Fisheries Commission for the Mediterranean, a subregional approach is followed to ensure proportionate and tailor-made measures.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=OJ:C_202506227. 2 Regulation (EU) No 1380/2013 of the European Parliament and of the Council

of 11 December 2013 on the Common Fisheries Policy, amending Council Regulations (EC) No 1954/2003 and (EC) No 1224/2009 and repealing Council Regulations (EC) No 2371/2002 and (EC) No 639/2004 and Council Decision 2004/585/EC.

qt: to the Commission Marko Vešligaj (S&D) Subject:

The agricultural sector in the EU is facing a significant demographic challenge. The average age of farmers in the EU is 57 years old, while only about 12 % of farmers are under the age of 40, highlighting a clear trend of an ageing farming population. At the same time, older farmers are often less likely to adopt digital tools, which can make it more difficult for them to access agricultural support schemes, submit applications and participate in EU-funded projects. This creates an additional barrier to ensuring equal access to financial support and modernisation opportunities across the sector. In the light of these challenges, could the Commission answer the following: 1.

What specific EU financial programmes and instruments are currently available to support the digital education and upskilling of farmers, particularly older farmers, with the aim of facilitating their access to agricultural subsidies, funding schemes and project applications?
Does the Commission plan to introduce additional targeted measures within the common agricultural policy or other EU funding frameworks to improve digital accessibility for farmers?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (18.6.2026) 1. The Commission acknowledges the importance of digital education, advisory support and upskilling to ensure broad and inclusive access to digital technologies across the farming population. The Common Agricultural Policy1 supports this objective through interventions linked to Agricultural Knowledge and Innovation Systems (AKIS), including advisory services, knowledge exchange (for example, training and advice), and EIP-AGRI Operational Groups2. Horizon Europe also promotes digital skills in agriculture by involving farmers in the design of solutions tailored to their needs, notably through the multi-actor approach3. Thematic networks4 and advisory networks5 further support digital education and access to innovative digital tools by collecting and disseminating knowledge among practitioners. Several Horizon Europe projects provide farmers with learning material and recommendations on the selection and use of digital tools. Additional support is available through cohesion-policy funds - notably ESF+6 for skills - and national recovery and resilience plans7. 2. The Commission’s proposals for the 2028–2034 multiannual financial framework prioritise digital transformation, with the EU farming sector set to benefit through several instruments, including the national and regional partnership plans8 (NRPPs), the European Competitiveness Fund9 and Horizon Europe10. The NRPPs aligns with the Digital Decade11 objectives including digital skills - while leveraging tools and cross-policy synergies to drive a data-driven transition in agriculture.

E-10-2026-001655.t: Prioritising checks at Greek entry points for fruit and vegetables with residues of substances banned in the EU
qt: to the Commission Galato Alexandraki (ECR) Subject:

The Commission has announced an impact assessment and possible further legislative action to prevent the most hazardous pesticides banned in the EU from entering via imports, while measures have already been proposed for benomyl, carbendazim and thiophanate‐methyl. At the same time, it has announced a 50 % increase in audits in non-EU countries, a 33 % increase in audits at border control posts and a special task force focusing on pesticide residues, among other things. For Greece, the issue is of particular importance. There is a need for the clear prioritisation of checks at implementation level and not just a general reference to mirror clauses. Can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Will it include specific Greek entry points and categories of high-risk imported fruit and vegetables in its priorities for checks and audits for 2026-2027?
Does it intend to organise coordinated EU monitoring for residues of banned substances in fruits and vegetables entering the EU via Greece?
What interim measures will it take until the legislative change is completed, in order to prevent unfair competition to the detriment of Greek producers?

(3 July 2026) Food products from third countries, regardless of their origin, must comply with EU food safety requirements laid down in EU legislation. According to Regulation (EU) 2017/625 (1), Member States must carry out risk based official controls and enforcement activities among others at the stage of distribution, including for imports. Where food of non-animal origin from third countries poses a risk, the Commission may adopt measures through Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1793 (2). The Commission performs audits in Member States and in third countries to ensure that their official control systems guarantee that goods intended for export to the EU comply with the applicable EU rules (3). An audit on import control system in Greece is planned in late 2026 which will include the official controls on high-risk imported fruit and vegetables. The Task Force on Import Controls (4) launched in January 2026 aims to maintain and reinforce the EU's ability to ensure imports meet EU standards, with pesticide control identified as one of its priority focus areas. The general monitoring of residues in the EU coordinated multiannual control programme is operated based on a design assessment of European Food Safety Authority which identified 36 products constituting the major components of Europeans diet but doesn’t single out Greece or banned substances exclusively. Member States tailor their risk-based sampling programmes, taking into account factors like the significance of food products in trade or national diets, historically non-compliance residues and pesticide usage patterns.

E-10-2026-001654.t: OPEKEPE, European Public Prosecutor's Office and protection of genuine farmers from the consequences of EU aid fraud
qt: to the Commission Galato Alexandraki (ECR) Subject:

The European Public Prosecutor's Office announced on 1 April 2026 that it had requested the waiving of the immunity of 11 sitting MPs in the context of an investigation into an organised fraud scheme in agricultural funds through OPEKEPE, while it had already transmitted to the Parliament information about former ministers. The Commission itself reported in February 2026 that, following serious deficiencies in the management and control system, OPEKEPE had been on probation since September 2024, with an extension until 26 March 2026, and that financial corrections of EUR 415 million had already been imposed. Given that Articles 9 and 59 of Regulation (EU) 2021/2116 require a reliable paying agency and effective protection of the Union's financial interests, the Commission is asked: 1.
What is the current accreditation and Union surveillance regime for OPEKEPE as of 26 March 2026?
What specific measures will the Commission take to ensure that legitimate farmers and livestock breeders receive their aid in a timely and complete manner?
How will the Commission ensure that the recovery of improperly paid amounts and the financial consequences fall on those who are actually responsible and not on honest producers?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (12.6.2026) 1. On 12 March 2026, the Greek Competent Authority communicated to the Commission that it had reinstated the accreditation of the Greek paying agency after the completion of an action plan initiated in September 2024. In June 2026, the Directorate-General for Agriculture and Rural Development (DG AGRI) will assess the effective implementation of the action plan. 2. It is the responsibility of the Member States to ensure that payments are disbursed to the beneficiaries in full and within the payment deadlines as laid down by Union law1. Member States must ensure that the area and animal-based payments are made between 1 December and 30 June of the calendar year following the applications, after sufficient checks have been carried out by the national authorities. Payments outside the deadlines lead to proportionate reductions from EU reimbursement to Member States, without affecting payments to beneficiaries. DG AGRI is closely monitoring the execution of payments and is in contact with the Greek authorities on a regular basis, including during the monitoring committees2. 3. Under the shared management mode of the Common Agricultural Policy, Member States are responsible for the recovery of unduly paid amounts from beneficiaries who have committed irregularities3. The Commission verifies that the Member States put in place effective systems of debt management which ensure timely recoveries. The Commission intervenes if it detects system audits issues4.

E-10-2026-001653.t: Access to risk management tools for small and fragmented farms
qt: to the Commission Galato Alexandraki (ECR) Subject:

On 25 March 2026, the Commission presented a study by the World Bank, which highlights that the EU needs a more coherent approach to agricultural risk management and that small farms face serious barriers to accessing tools due to high costs, limited options and complex procedures. According to the Commission itself, Greece has around 600 000 farms with an average size of seven hectares, with more than 70 % measuring in at less than five hectares, while more than 70 % of agricultural land is located in areas with natural or particular constraints such as insularity, aridity and steep slopes. Against this background, there is a serious risk that, in practice, it is mostly larger farms that are able to access the risk management tools set out in Article 76 of Regulation (EU) 2021/2115. Can the Commission answer the following: 1.
How will it ensure effective access to risk management tools for small and fragmented farms?
Is it considering specific increased support for small contracts and cooperative structures?
Will it require earmarking for island, mountain and other areas with natural constraints?

(29 June 2026) The Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) has a robust framework allowing Member States and farmers to manage risks, including interventions stabilising income, incentivising risk transfer via, for instance, insurance companies, or providing crisis payments. These interventions are accompanied by measures, such as preventive investments or environmental payments, to build longerterm resilience and to lower risks for farmers. Member States are provided with flexibility to design measures tailored to their national and regional contexts, deciding on access to specific risk management tools or support levels, including for small farms or areas facing natural or other specific constraints. The Commission intends to include risk management in the recommendations that it intends to issue to the Member States on the future CAP and the National and Regional Partnership Plans for the period 2028-2034. To grant the necessary budget flexibility to Member States, the CAP rules do not provide for specific earmarking for island, mountain and other areas with natural constraints.

(12 June 2026) The Commission's Protein Plan to make the EU protein system more resilient and sustainable, announced in the 2025 Vision for Agriculture and Food (1), will cover the entire European Union, while recognising that its implementation will need to take into account national and regional specificities to be successful. The current common agricultural policy (CAP) already contains several instruments to support the protein crop sector and reduce dependency on imported plant-based protein, such as sectoral interventions, coupled income support, eco-schemes and rural development measures. The Commission’s legislative package for the CAP after 2027 and, in particular, the proposed amendments to the common market Organisation Regulation (2) place particular emphasis on protein crops by establishing a dedicated protein crop sector, strengthening producer organisations in this sector, making sectoral interventions for protein crops mandatory and providing the possibility to introduce marketing standards for such crops. The Commission encourages Member States to integrate tailored measures into their National and Regional Partnership Plans, as proposed by the Commission, reflecting the diversity of agricultural systems and territorial conditions across the Union. The Protein Plan will encourage farmers to cultivate protein crops, which is expected to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and enrich soil fertility through nitrogen fixation, thereby reducing the need for fertilisers. This is acknowledged by the Fertilisers Action Plan adopted by the Commission on 19 May 2026 (3).

E-10-2026-001649.t: Anti-tankering rules and risk of disruptions to flights to and from Malta due to jet fuel shortages
qt: to the Commission Peter Agius (PPE) Subject:

Industry reports indicate that in the coming weeks, certain flights around Europe may be disrupted due to a shortage in the supply of jet fuel. In this situation, EU Member States will need to use their own stockpiles of jet fuel. However, the new anti-tankering measures in the ReFuelEU Aviation Regulation1 oblige uplift 90 % of their required fuel at the departure airport. While Malta has a sufficient local supply of jet fuel, the anti-tankering rules will make the island’s connectivity dependent on fuel supplies in European hubs. In view of this: 1.
What immediate measures is the Commission taking to assess and mitigate the risk of flight disruptions in the EU caused by jet fuel shortages?
What implementing powers under the ReFuelEU Aviation Regulation could the Commission use to safeguard island connectivity in cases of shortages and emergencies?
Is the Commission ready to suspend anti-tankering rules temporarily to safeguard island connectivity, in particular air connectivity?
https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2023/2405/oj.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.7.2026) 1. To strengthen preparedness, and as announced in the AccelerateEU Communication1, the Commission has established a Fuel Observatory to monitor EU production, imports, exports and fuel stocks. This improves visibility over supply and demand, helps detect shortages, and supports targeted action, such as alternative sourcing or coordinated stock releases in the EU. Given the context, the Oil Coordination Group meets more often to review EU oil supply security and coordinate action as needed2. The Commission also issued on 8 May 2026 guidance on the flexibilities available under EU aviation legislation to ensure coordination across Member States3. This covers airport slots4, travellers and passenger rights5, fuel uplift obligations under ReFuelEU Aviation6, Public Service Obligations (PSOs)7, and the use of alternative jet fuel sources. 2 and 3. The Commission recognises the specific challenges faced by islands, where air connectivity is essential. The AccelerateEU Communication sets out measures to preserve the functioning of the Single Market while safeguarding essential air connectivity across the EU, including island regions. Regarding the ReFuelEU Aviation Regulation, the guidance on the flexibilities clarifies how airlines can uplift more aviation fuel at the departing airport for compliance with fuel safety rules under Article 5(2). Airports located in outermost regions are not considered within the Regulation. Finally, at present, there is no immediate threat to the security of supply, although stocks of some fuels are tight. If the situation worsens and the existing flexibilities no longer suffice, the Commission will propose temporary changes to the legislation, where justified.

E-10-2026-001648.t: Establishing criteria for shipments of waste for disposal
qt: to the Commission Sirpa Pietikäinen (PPE) Subject:

Regulation (EU) 2024/11571 on shipments of waste imposes a ban on intra-EU shipments of waste destined for disposal. The ban applies to all disposal operations, including shipments bound for hazardous waste incineration, which may be needed for the safe treatment of waste due to lack of national capacity. The relevant authorities may consent to shipments for disposal, if the conditions under Article 11 of the Regulation are fulfilled. These conditions state that the notifier must demonstrate that the waste cannot be recovered/disposed of in a ‘technically feasible and economically viable manner’ in the country where it was generated. By 21 May 2027, the Commission must adopt an implementing act setting out detailed criteria for uniformly applying the conditions, specifying how notifiers are to demonstrate the lack of technical feasibility and economic viability for recovery/disposal of waste in the country it originated in and how the authorities are to assess this. However, the ban will already be applied from 21 May 2026. According to European waste operators, the planned date for adopting the implementing act (May 2027) could risk differing national interpretations of the above requirements causing market distortion due to lack of clear EU rules. What actions is the Commission taking to prepare the implementing act as soon as possible to guarantee that this EU law is uniformly applied?
https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1157/oj.

The relevant authorities may consent to shipments for disposal, if the conditions under Article 11 of the regulation are fulfilled. These conditions state that the notifier must demonstrate that the waste cannot be recovered/disposed of in a ‘technically feasible and economically viable manner’ in the country where it was generated. By 21 May 2027, the Commission must adopt an implementing act setting out detailed criteria for uniformly applying the conditions, specifying how notifiers are to demonstrate the lack of technical feasibility and economic viability for recovery/disposal of waste in the country it originated in and how the authorities are to assess this. However, the ban will already be applied from 21 May 2026. According to European waste operators, the planned date for adopting the implementing act (May 2027) could risk differing national interpretations of the above requirements causing market distortion due to lack of clear EU rules. What actions is the Commission taking to prepare the implementing act as soon as possible to guarantee that this EU law is uniformly applied? (6 July 2026) The Commission has been working on this issue with authorities from the EU Member States, as well as with economic operators. The new provisions started to apply on 21 May 2026. The Commission intends to gather further information on how these new provisions are implemented in practice, and especially if there are important differences of interpretation which could disrupt the shipments of waste for disposal between EU Member States. Based on this assessment, the Commission will evaluate if there is a need for more detailed guidance on the interpretation of the conditions laid down in Article 11 of the Waste Shipment Regulation (1).

E-10-2026-001646.t: Strengthening EU security by addressing the use of Russian SIM cards in hybrid warfare activities
qt: to the Commission Krzysztof Brejza (PPE) Subject:

Recent reports indicate that Russian SIM cards are being utilised as tools for military and intelligence operations. According to Ukrainian officials, these cards enable Russian forces to guide drones and missiles with high precision by using local cellular infrastructure and roaming services, as well as EU roaming close to the EU border. Furthermore, they enable the bypassing of Western sanctions on Russian digital services and communication tracking. In the light of these security concerns: 1.
Is the Commission aware of the specific role Russian SIM cards play in coordinating military strikes and enabling hybrid warfare activities within the EU and its neighbourhood?

Does the Commission have a comprehensive strategy for countering these Russian tactics, such as implementing an EU-wide ban on Russian SIM cards or terminating all remaining roaming agreements with Russian telecommunications providers to step up collective security?
Since the Russian Federation has already blocked network access for millions of SIM cards from EU Member States, why has the EU not yet taken equivalent steps?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.9.2026) The European Commission has presented an EU Action Plan on Drone and Counter Drone Security1 for a united approach against threats posed by malicious drones. The Action plan presents practical solutions for improved prevention of incidents, detection of drones, response to malicious drone activities and strengthening Europe’s defence readiness against drone threats. Under the European Electronic Communications Code2, Member States’ authorities are able to require providers of public electronic communications networks or publicly available electronic communications services to block, but only on a case-by-case basis, access to numbers or services where this is justified by reasons of fraud or misuse and to require that in such cases providers of electronic communications services withhold relevant interconnection or other service revenues.

E-10-2026-001645.t: Potential long-term neurological effects of artificial sweeteners and the need for an updated EU risk assessment
qt: to the Commission Krzysztof Brejza (PPE) Subject:

Recent scientific evidence has raised concerns about the possible long-term cognitive and neurological effects of certain low- and no-calorie sweeteners used in the EU food supply. A large prospective study published in Neurology in 2025, involving 12 772 participants with approximately eight years of follow-up, found that higher consumption of such sweeteners was associated with faster cognitive decline, including in memory and verbal fluency, particularly among individuals under 60. While causality was not established, the authors called for further investigation. In parallel, emerging experimental evidence, notably on erythritol, suggests possible mechanisms relevant to cerebrovascular function, including oxidative stress and endothelial dysfunction in brain microvascular cells. At the same time, the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) maintains that currently authorised sweeteners are safe within established acceptable daily intake levels. In the light of the above and in line with a precautionary and science-based approach to public health: 1.
How does the Commission assess these findings in relation to existing EFSA evaluations?
Does the Commission intend to request an updated risk assessment addressing the longterm cognitive and neurological effects?
Are additional risk communication or labelling measures envisaged, particularly for vulnerable groups?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.7.2026) Under EU law, all food additives, including sweeteners, are subject to a rigorous safety assessment based on the totality of available scientific data, including studies on long-term toxicity and potential neurological effects, as evaluated by the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA). EU legislation assures that only safe and technologically justified1 food additives can be authorised. EU legislation further requires that allowed additives are kept under continuous observation and that their safety is re-evaluated whenever necessary in the light of changing conditions of use and new scientific information2. In addition, EFSA systematically considers new scientific evidence, including long-term adverse effects and neurotoxicity, in the safety re-evaluation of food additives, including sweeteners3, permitted before 20 January 20094. For sweeteners already re-evaluated by EFSA, the conclusions indicate they are safe within established acceptable daily intake levels. Findings from observational studies reporting associations with cognitive outcomes, while suggestive, do not themselves demonstrate causality and are considered in the broader weight-of-evidence approach5 applied by EFSA. Based on the outcomes of the EFSA scientific assessments, the Commission, assisted by the Member States, takes appropriate risk management measures when needed. EU labelling rules ensure that sweeteners are clearly indicated in ingredient lists6, including specific labelling requirements for polyols7. These provisions enable informed consumer 1 In addition to the general conditions for inclusion and use of food additives in Community lists outlined in

Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 1333/2008 on food additives, the legislation lays down additional specific conditions for sweeteners (Article 7) to be met to ensure their use is justified: the sweetener can only be used (1) to replace sugars for the production of energy-reduced food, noncariogenic food or food with no added sugars; or (2) to replace sugars where this permits an increase in the shelf-life of the food; or (3) to produce food intended for particular nutritional uses. 2 Recital 14 of Regulation (EC) No 1333/2008 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 16 December 2008 on food additives (OJ L 354, 31.12.2008, p. 16). 3 The list of sweeteners authorised for use in the EU and the status of EFSA’s respective safety assessments is available at https://www.efsa.europa.eu/en/topics/topic/sweeteners. For the re-evaluation of sweeteners, a protocol on hazard identification and characterisation of sweeteners has been developed, available at https://zenodo.org/records/7788969. 4 Commission Regulation (EU) No 257/2010 of 25 March 2010 setting up a programme for the re-evaluation of approved food additives in accordance with Regulation (EC) No 1333/2008 of the European Parliament and of the Council on food additives (OJ L 80, 26.3.2010, p. 19–27). 5 EFSA’s weight-of-evidence approach is a structured, transparent process for evaluating and integrating diverse scientific data from various sources to reach conclusions in risk assessments. See ‘Guidance on the use of the weight of evidence approach in scientific assessments’ available at https://efsa.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.2903/j.efsa.2017.4971. 6 Product labels have to specify both the functional class (e.g. sweetener) and the specific substance used, either by referring to the appropriate E-number or by its name. In addition to the listing of the given sweetener in the ingredient list, the label of a foodstuff containing sweeteners should indicate ‘with sweetener(s)’ and the label of a foodstuff containing sweeteners and sugars should indicate ‘with sugar(s) and sweetener(s)’. 7 Foods containing more than 10% added polyols, as well as table-top sweeteners containing polyols, should also bear the following statement: ‘excessive consumption may produce laxative effects’.
choice, including for vulnerable groups. Therefore, the Commission considers the existing framework for safety assessment, re-evaluation, and labelling to be appropriate.

E-10-2026-001644.t: Deteriorating situation in Serbia: clashes between police and students
qt: to the Commission Ilhan Kyuchyuk (Renew) Subject:

The ongoing crackdown on student-led protests in Serbia has been marked by violent clashes between security forces and demonstrators demanding institutional accountability and the rule of law. This raises serious concerns about the state of democracy, fundamental freedoms and human rights in the Western Balkans. These developments, occurring in a country formally engaged in EU accession negotiations, call into question both the credibility of Serbia’s reform commitments and the effectiveness of the EU’s conditionality framework. In this context: 1.

Does the Commission intend to issue a formal assessment of the proportionality of the Serbian authorities’ response to peaceful student protests, and to what extent will these events be reflected in Serbia’s upcoming EU progress report?

Is the Commission prepared to consider targeted measures, including the temporary suspension or recalibration of pre-accession funding, if the Serbian authorities continue to suppress civic freedoms and obstruct independent judicial oversight?

How does the Commission plan to strengthen its engagement with Serbian civil society and student movements, and what concrete steps will it take to ensure that the EU’s democratic conditionality is applied consistently and credibly?

(17 June 2026) The Commission continuously assesses whether the relevant conditions for support under the EU’s financial instruments are met. This is part of the normal implementation of these instruments and applies throughout the process, including at the stage of each payment request under the Western Balkans Reform and Growth Facility (1). The Commission expects Serbia to make progress on key reforms, notably in the area of rule of law, fundamental rights and democratic principles. The rights of peaceful demonstration, freedom of assembly and freedom of expression must be upheld and cases of violence by the police must be investigated as a matter of priority. E-10-2026-001643.t: EU engagement in the United States-Iran ceasefire negotiations
qt: to the Commission Ilhan Kyuchyuk (Renew) Subject:

The recent ceasefire negotiations between the United States and the Islamic Republic of Iran, primarily driven by bilateral diplomatic engagement, have raised fundamental questions about the EU’s role and relevance in a crisis with direct implications for regional stability, nuclear non-proliferation and European security. The EU’s exclusion from the core negotiating framework, despite its long-standing participation in the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action process and its significant economic and strategic stake in Middle Eastern stability, risks undermining both European foreign policy credibility and the coherence of the multilateral non-proliferation architecture. In this context: 1.
What concrete steps has the Commission taken to ensure EU participation in the ceasefire process and through which diplomatic channels has the Commission attempted to assert its interests?

Does the Commission consider the current EU posture adequate in the light of the EU’s exclusion from the primary negotiating framework and does it envisage a new approach to transatlantic coordination on Iran policy?
How does the Commission intend to use its existing instruments, such as sanctions policy and economic diplomacy, to maintain credibility in any post-ceasefire settlement process?

E-10-2026-001642.t: Third-country lobbying to pre-empt pending CJEU judgment on airport capacity (Case C-857/24)
qt: to the Commission Lena Schilling (Verts/ALE) Subject:

The Advocate General’s opinion of 12 February 2026 in Case C-857/24 supports the use of passenger caps as valid operational constraints under the Slot Regulation. Airlines for America has publicly lobbied the US Government to pressure Ireland into enacting the Dublin Airport (Passenger Capacity) Bill 2026 before the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) can rule, stating that it fears ‘neighbourhoods throughout Europe and potentially the world’ being treated as stakeholders in airport capacity decisions. The Commission has registered complaint CPLT(2026)00881 (led by its Directorate-General for the Environment) alleging that this Bill would permanently remove environmental constraints at Dublin Airport without the environmental impact assessment required by Directive 2011/92/EU and without the Balanced Approach assessment required by Regulation (EU) No 598/2014, in circumstances where the Commission’s own Decision C(2026)0919 found Ireland non-compliant with the latter regulation. 1.
Is the Commission aware of lobbying by third-country industry groups seeking to preempt a pending CJEU judgment through Member State legislation?
Does the Commission intend to assess the compatibility of the Dublin Airport (Passenger Capacity) Bill 2026 with Directive 2011/92/EU and Regulation (EU) No 598/2014 before its enactment?
What steps does the Commission intend to take on complaint CPLT(2026)00881?

E-10-2026-001641.t: Tasks completed as part of the pilot project: ‘Saving our Seas – Reducing danger of munitions dumped in European seas’
qt: to the Commission Kosma Złotowski (ECR) Subject:

In 2023, a group of MEPs, on the initiative of Ms Anna Fotyga, proposed a pilot project addressing the problem of seabed pollution caused by remnants from the world wars, particularly shipwrecks, dumped chemical weapons, and munitions. These pose a threat to the ecosystem and the maritime economy, especially in the Baltic Sea basin. According to the information we received at the time, the Commission assessed the project positively and it was to be implemented. In the light of this, I would like to ask the Commission: 1.
What specific tasks were commissioned and carried out as part of this pilot project, and have these tasks already been evaluated?
What budget did the Commission allocate for implementing this pilot project, and which specific private and public entities received funding?
As a result of this pilot project, has the Commission prepared its own initiatives related to funding work on technologies to be used for the safe removal of hazardous substances from the seabed?

What budget did the Commission allocate for implementing this pilot project, and which specific private and public entities received funding?
As a result of this pilot project, has the Commission prepared its own initiatives related to funding work on technologies to be used for the safe removal of hazardous substances from the seabed?

(9 June 2026) The pilot project ‘Saving our Seas — Reducing the danger of munitions dumped in European seas’ is currently under implementation and is carried out by a consortium of public and private entities under the CAMMera project (1), including research organisations, specialised industry actors and technology providers, coordinated by the GEOMAR Helmholtz Centre for Ocean Research. It will run until June 2028. The project with a budget of EUR 5.6 million supports a range of activities aimed at advancing knowledge and testing innovative approaches for the detection, monitoring, removal and environmentally sound disposal of underwater unexploded ordnance (UXO). These activities are being progressively implemented and will be assessed through the project’s monitoring and reporting framework, with results expected to inform future actions. Furthermore, the Commission is also funding the innovation project ‘MMinE-SwEEPER (2) under the topic HORIZON-CL32023-BM-01 “Identify, inspect, neutralise Unexploded Ordnance (UXO) at sea” of Horizon Europe Cluster 3 “Civil Security for Society”. MMinE-SwEEPER is developing and testing new technologies, receives EUR 5.9 million of EU grant, and will work until March 2028 with a Consortium of 18 European organisations and innovators. In parallel, the Commission has initiated consultations with Member States aiming at the development of a comprehensive EU UXO Removal Strategy, as announced under the European Ocean Pact (3). This work will build on ongoing projects addressing UXO, including CAMMera, as well as Member States’ experience, with a view to strengthening coordination and scaling up effective solutions across European sea basins.

E-10-2026-001640.t: Recent investigations revealing coercive practices in EU-funded ‘voluntary return’ programmes
qt: to the Commission Alice Kuhnke (Verts/ALE) Subject:

In April 2025, Commissioner for Internal Affairs and Migration Magnus Brunner, in a response to a question from Parliament, reiterated the position taken by the UN Refugee Agency (UNHCR) against the promotion of large-scale voluntary repatriation to Syria1. In June 2025, the Council published its Conclusions on Syria2, which reasserted the UNHCR’s position that the situation in Syria does not allow for large-scale repatriations. Meanwhile, according to Eurostat3, Cyprus has conducted some 2 285 assisted voluntary returns to Syria. According to a media report4, Cyprus’s programme has received some EUR 17.7 million in funding from the Commission’s Asylum, Migration and Integration Fund (AMIF). According to the same report, the programme relies on coercion and deceit to pressure individuals into returning. Given the above: 1.
Does the Commission find that its funding of Cyprus’s assisted voluntary returns programme contradicts its position – and the position of the Council – on large-scale repatriations to Syria?
If yes, can the Commission explain what measures it plans to take to prevent the continued use of funding under AMIF to enable large-scale repatriations from Cyprus to Syria?

The EU will continue to support the transitional authorities in building administrative capacity to ensure an inclusive transition that allows for the necessary conditions to be in place for Syrians to be able to return home. No EU funding is being used to support forced returns from Cyprus to Syria. EU funds through the Asylum, Migration and Integration Fund are used to support voluntary returns. E-10-2026-001639.t: European management of the sargassum seaweed crisis in Guadeloupe and Martinique
qt: to the Commission André Rougé (PfE) Subject:

Since mid-March 2026, huge quantities of sargassum seaweed have once again been washing up on the coasts of Guadeloupe and Martinique. According to up-to-date data from MétéoFrance, mats of seaweed are rife in the Atlantic Ocean, heralding a steady stream of sargassum strandings in the short term. Preventive measures, such as the barriers installed, appear to be insufficient to prevent the seaweed from washing ashore and piling up on the beaches. Since 2011, more and more sargassum has been washing up on shore throughout the Caribbean basin, and the strandings are now starting earlier and are becoming more unpredictable, severely affecting the environment, public health – since sargassum releases toxic gases as it decomposes – and coastal economies, particularly the tourism and fishing sectors. In light of the above: 1.
What specific action does the European Commission plan to take to strengthen sargassum research, prevention and management in its outermost regions?
Is there specific funding that can be mobilised to support local authorities?

Finally, are there plans for a coordinated European strategy for sargassum research, treatment and repurposing, in particular via anaerobic digestion, in the face of this growing and now highly destabilising ecological phenomenon?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.7.2026) Local authorities can make use of their region’s programme, which is financed by the European Regional Development Fund (ERDF)1, to mobilise funding earmarked for the issue of sargassum seaweed, both to develop research capacities and innovative solutions and to prevent risks, deal with strandings and build resilience. This support makes it possible to finance concrete measures. For example, from 2014 to 2020 in Guadeloupe, the ERDF funded research projects on sargassum amounting to EUR 1.4 million. The municipality of Petit-Bourg received EUR 374 000 in ERDF funding for the purchase of equipment to deal with sargassum strandings. The INTERREG Caribbean programme finances two projects to combat sargassum: one focusing on prevention (SARG’COOP2) and the other on exploring the possibilities for scientific and economic exploitation of sargassum (SARGOOD3). The European Maritime, Fisheries and Aquaculture Fund (EMFAF)4 can also be mobilised for projects related to sargassum. The increase in sargassum seaweed strandings throughout the Caribbean Basin also calls for a regional approach. Since 2023, the Commission has been running a Global Gateway investment initiative5 to transform sargassum into an opportunity for sustainable economic activity6. This coordinated strategy makes it possible to speed up research and the implementation of large-scale collection and recovery methods for sargassum in order to turn it into a circular economy opportunity. Through its ‘Algae Initiative’7, the EU supports innovative companies such as ‘Origin by Ocean’8 to transform sargassum into products with high added value.

cohesion policy, which aims to reduce development gaps between regions with a view to achieving economic, social and territorial cohesion. 2 https://sargcoop.org/en/accueil-en/. 3 https://interreg-caraibes.eu/sargood. 4 The EMFAF supports innovative projects that contribute to the sustainable exploitation and management of water and maritime resources. 5 https://international-partnerships.ec.europa.eu/policies/global-gateway/turning-tide-sustainable-practices-andeconomic-opportunities-sargassum-value-chain-development_en. 6 As part of the EU’s Global Gateway Investment Agenda, the EU, Team Europe and Caribbean partners are working to turn the challenge posed by sargassum into cleaner coastlines, new job opportunities and support for local businesses. 7 https://oceans-and-fisheries.ec.europa.eu/publications/communication-commission-towards-strong-andsustainable-eu-algae-sector_en. 8 www.originbyocean.com.

E-10-2026-001637.t: Unlawful killing of protected species in Tuscany and the implementation of the Habitats Directive
qt: to the Commission Ignazio Roberto Marino (Verts/ALE) Subject:

Press sources report that the headless carcass of a wolf was recently found in Cascina (Tuscany, Italy), where it had been left on display in a public space. This is only the latest in a string of similar incidents that have occurred in the area over the last few days. The Habitats Directive classifies Canis lupus as a strictly protected species, while Article 12 thereof forbids the deliberate capture and killing of specimens in the wild and requires Member States to establish strict protection systems for these animals. In addition, Article 16 of the Directive states that derogations to the above can only be issued if certain strictly defined conditions are met. Member States are also required by Directive 2008/99/EC on the protection of the environment through criminal law to provide for effective, proportionate and dissuasive penalties for offenders. In the light of the above: 1.
Is the Commission aware of the incidents described above and has it received reports of similar cases in other Member States?
What tools is the Commission using to monitor the implementation of Article 12 and ensure that any infringements thereof are sanctioned accordingly?
Does the Commission hold that the national-level implementation and monitoring framework is fit for purpose?
at: (English version) to the Commission Ignazio Roberto Marino (Verts/ALE) (22 April 2026) Subject: Unlawful killing of protected species in Tuscany and the implementation of the Habitats Directive Press sources report that the headless carcass of a wolf was recently found in Cascina (Tuscany, Italy), where it had been left on display in a public space. This is only the latest in a string of similar incidents that have occurred in the area over the last few days. In addition, Article 16 of the directive states that derogations to the above can only be issued if certain strictly defined conditions are met. Member States are also required by Directive 2008/99/EC on the protection of the environment through criminal law to provide for effective, proportionate and dissuasive penalties for offenders. In the light of the above: 1.
Is the Commission aware of the incidents described above and has it received reports of similar cases in other Member States?
What tools is the Commission using to monitor the implementation of Article 12 and ensure that any infringements thereof are sanctioned accordingly?
Does the Commission hold that the national-level implementation and monitoring framework is fit for purpose?

(6 July 2026) The Commission has learnt about these incidents through the press and letters from concerned citizens and understands that these are illegal killings, in violation of national legislation implementing the Habitats Directive (1). The Commission is aware of other such cases in several Member States. Article 16 of the Habitats Directive requires Member States to report every two years on derogations granted from the species protection requirements, including those under Article 12, which, however, no longer applies to the wolf (2). They are not required to report illegal killings or investigations or sanctions applied. The Environmental Crime Directive (3) obliges Member States to include the unlawful killing of specimens of species of wild fauna (4) in national law as a criminal offence and to introduce dissuasive criminal penalties for these offences. The Commission considers that the practical implementation of these rules (5) requires continuous attention. In this context, the Commission opened a pre-infringement dialogue with Italian authorities on the alleged failure by Italy to comply with EU law on hunting, including poaching, and is exchanging information with the authorities and assessing the next step. The Commission relies on national reports (6) and on data from academia, civil society and law enforcement to assess compliance. The data shows that the status of most species threatened by persecution has improved since the entry into force of the Nature Directives. Nevertheless, while some Member States have established robust systems (7), others face challenges in ensuring deterrent penalties and timely judicial proceedings.

Council Directive 92/43/EEC of 21 May 1992 on the conservation of natural habitats and of wild fauna and flora, OJ L 206, 22.7.1992, p. 7-50. This is due to a recent amendment of the Habitats Directive: Directive (EU) 2025/1237 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 17 June 2025 amending Council Directive 92/43/EEC as regards the protection status of the wolf (Canis lupus). The wolf is now listed in Annex V of the directive and subject to the provisions of Article 14 instead. Directive (EU) 2024/1203 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 11 April 2024 on the protection of the environment through criminal law and replacing Directives 2008/99/EC and 2009/123/EC, OJ L, 2024/1203, 30.4.2024, to be transposed into national legislation by 21 May 2026. Protected by the Habitats Directive and listed in the directive’s Annexes IV and V. Including monitoring, investigating and penalising illegal killings of protected species. Under Article 17 of the Habitats Directive. Including for example specialised environmental police units or real-time monitoring.

E-10-2026-001636.t: Situation of the coking sector in the EU
qt: to the Commission Jadwiga Wiśniewska (ECR) Subject:

The revised regulation proposed by the Commission on critical raw materials does not cover key issues such as the protection of the critical raw materials industry, and in particular the worsening situation of the coking sector, including Jastrzębska Spółka Węglowa Koks S.A., the largest coke producer in the European Union, which is currently in a very difficult financial situation. The company produces around 3.5 million tonnes of coke annually, making it a key part of the European supply chain for the steel industry and, consequently, for strategic sectors such as the defence, automotive and infrastructure industries. Increasing regulatory costs, including those arising from the EU ETS, and the competitive pressure from cheaper imports from outside the EU are putting JSW in a dire situation. In practice, this creates the risk of losing a significant part of the EU’s production capacity and of becoming more dependent on supplies from third countries, notably China and Indonesia. In light of the above: 1.
Will the Commission take action to recognise the coking industry as a strategic sector for the EU’s economic security?
Will the Commission consider reducing the burden of the EU ETS on coke producers in the EU?
Is the Commission planning to introduce market protection measures, such as quantitative limits or tariffs on imports of coke from outside the EU?

(22 June 2026) The Commission is currently conducting its assessment of the criticality of raw materials, coking coal among them. The Critical Raw Materials Act (1) already recognises coking coal as a critical raw material, and relevant provisions, such as on spatial planning and exploration, therefore apply. Furthermore, the Commission has recently adopted a proposal for an Industrial Accelerator Act (2) (IAA) to boost industrial capacities and decarbonisation in strategic sectors, including the iron and steel making sector, while strengthening the EU’s long-term resilience and prosperity. As regards the benchmarks and the CO 2 pricing mechanism of the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS), the applied methodology for the update of the benchmarks is enshrined in the ETS Directive (3). The emission intensity of the top-performing coking plants in Europe remains below the benchmark value and will continue to receive sufficient free allowances to cover their emissions. The upcoming review of the ETS Directive will examine the rules on free allocation and consider how to best support and boost investments in decarbonisation and electrification of the sectors covered by the system. On receipt of a complaint from the EU industry with evidence showing that dumped or subsidised imports are causing harm, the Commission will take appropriate action. The Complaints Office of Trade Defence Services can be contacted to discuss the procedure (4) and get guidance and assistance on how to proceed with tackling unfair competition from imports.

E-10-2026-001634.t: Immediate suspension of the EU-Israel Trade Agreement following the adoption of a death penalty law by the Israeli Parliament
qt: to the Commission Estrella Galán (The Left), Jaume Asens Llodrà (Verts/ALE), Vicent Marzà Ibáñez (Verts/ALE), Leire Pajín (S&D), Rima Hassan (The Left), Saskia Bricmont (Verts/ALE), Carolina Morace (The Left), Vladimir Prebilič (Verts/ALE), Leila Chaibi (The Left), Pernando Barrena Arza (The Left), Rudi Kennes (The Left), Rosa Serrano Sierra (S&D), Matjaž Nemec (S&D), Damien Carême (The Left), Arash Saeidi (The Left), Giorgos Georgiou (The Left), Leoluca Orlando (Verts/ALE), Michael McNamara (Renew) Subject:

On 30 March 2026, the Israeli Parliament adopted a law stipulating that Palestinians convicted by Israeli military courts of what those authorities define as ‘deadly attacks’ would be executed by hanging within 90 days. The implementation of this law is clearly discriminatory, cruel and against human rights. The law has also faced internal opposition in Israel, as well as from the Council of Europe, which considers that its adoption ‘represents a serious regression’. 1.

What is the Commission’s view of statements made by countries such as Australia, Britain, France, Spain, Germany and Italy that consider this measure to call into question Israel’s commitments to democratic principles?

The measure once again violates Article 2 of the EU-Israel Trade Agreement, which states that relations between the two sides are based on respect for human rights and democratic principles. Does the Commission intend to take appropriate measures to immediately suspend the EU trade agreement with Israel?
Does the Commission intend to take any initiative to ensure the legal protection of incarcerated Palestinians who could be victims of this measure?
Supporter1
This question is supported by a Member other than the authors: César Luena (S&D).
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.7.2026) The EU has a principled position against the death penalty in all cases and in all circumstances. The approval of the Death Penalty Law by the Israeli Parliament marks a grave regression from Israel’s long upheld moratorium and from its own commitments. The EU is deeply concerned about the de facto discriminatory character of the Law1. Consistent with the EU global efforts towards universal abolition of the death penalty, the EU urges Israel to abide by its previous principled position and with its obligations under international law, as well as its commitment to democratic principles, as reflected also in the provisions of the EU-Israel Association Agreement2. The death penalty is a violation of the right to life and cannot be executed without violation of the absolute right to be free from torture and other ill-treatment. In 2024, a review of the EU-Israel Association agreement concluded that Israel would be in breach of Article 2 (human rights clause) of the said Association Agreement. Following the review, and in light of the deteriorating humanitarian situation in Gaza, the Commission’s President announced a set of measures, including the suspension of certain trade-related provisions of the EU-Israel Association Agreement. This requires the support of the qualified majority of Member States. Discussions are ongoing in the Council. Measures ensuring the legal protection of persons incarcerated in third countries fall under the jurisdiction of the third countries in question. Nevertheless, the EU will use the tools at its disposal and urge Israel not to enforce the Death Penalty Law, which is currently under review by the Supreme Court.
1 https://www.eeas.europa.eu/eeas/israel-statement-spokesperson-death-penalty-bill_en. 2 https://eeas.europa.eu/archives/delegations/israel/documents/eu_israel/asso_agree_en.pdf.

at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (16.7.2026) 1. To determine whether goods are entitled to preferential treatment under the EU Israel Association Agreement, customs authorities apply the rules contained in that Agreement´s Protocol on Origin and in the ‘Technical Arrangement’ adopted in 2005. E-10-2026-001632.t: Green transition of heavy-duty road transport, with a focus on hydrogen infrastructure and electricity grid capacity
qt: to the Commission Asger Christensen (Renew) Subject:

In Denmark, the increasing electrification of the heavy-duty transport sector has led to such high demand for electricity connections that there is currently no capacity in the Danish power grid. Despite this, however, in Denmark electric HGVs are regarded as the only green alternative to HGVs that run on fossil fuels. The Alternative Fuels Infrastructure Regulation (AFIR) also establishes requirements for the rollout of hydrogen infrastructure, giving lorries a green alternative to diesel that does not depend on being able to connect to the electricity grid. Unfortunately, hydrogen is not a priority solution in Denmark, despite this being a requirement in the AFIR. I fear that this might also be the case in other Member States, which is why I would like to hear what the Commission thinks. 1.

Could the Commission therefore please provide an update on the rollout of hydrogen filling stations – one of the requirements Member States must meet under the AFIR. Please outline the Member States’ national policy frameworks for the rollout of the regulation’s framework for hydrogen, with a view to shedding light on Member States’ compliance with the AFIR’s requirements for the construction of hydrogen infrastructure.
Could the Commission also state how the Commission will ensure that the Member States see to it that the requirements on hydrogen refuelling for vehicles are met?
Could the Commission state whether Europe’s electricity grid has the capacity for the continent’s heavy-duty road transport sector to switch to electric lorries?

(2 September 2026) Regulation (EU) 2023/1804 on the deployment of alternative fuels infrastructure (1), mandates the deployment of hydrogen stations every 200 km along the Trans-European Transport Network (TEN-T) core network and in urban nodes by the end of 2030. E-10-2026-001631.t: Preventing circumvention of the ban on the destruction of unsold textiles
qt: to the Commission Delara Burkhardt (S&D) Subject:

Regulation (EU) 2024/17811 (Ecodesign Regulation) prohibits the destruction of unsold textiles by large companies from July 2026 and by medium-sized companies from 2030, while micro and small enterprises are exempt. In this context: 1.

What specific measures are envisaged to address the risk that unsold textiles will be exported to non-EU countries in order to circumvent this prohibition and will subsequently be destroyed there, particularly taking into account EU waste shipment rules?
How will the Commission ensure that large companies do not circumvent the prohibition by systematically channelling unsold goods through affiliated or contracted micro and small enterprises?
What criteria and data will the Commission use as the basis for assessing whether an extension of the prohibition to micro and small enterprises is necessary because of circumvention practices?

Regulation (EU) 2024/1781 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 June 2024 establishing a framework for the setting of ecodesign requirements for sustainable products, amending Directive (EU) 2020/1828 and Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 and repealing Directive 2009/125/EC (OJ L, 2024/1781, 28.6.2024, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1781/oj).
at: (English version) to the Commission Delara Burkhardt (S&D) (21 April 2026) Subject: Preventing circumvention of the ban on the destruction of unsold textiles Regulation (EU) 2024/1781 (1) (Ecodesign Regulation) prohibits the destruction of unsold textiles by large companies from July 2026 and by medium-sized companies from 2030, while micro and small enterprises are exempt. In this context: 1.

What specific measures are envisaged to address the risk that unsold textiles will be exported to non-EU countries in order to circumvent this prohibition and will subsequently be destroyed there, particularly taking into account EU waste shipment rules?
How will the Commission ensure that large companies do not circumvent the prohibition by systematically channelling unsold goods through affiliated or contracted micro and small enterprises?
What criteria and data will the Commission use as the basis for assessing whether an extension of the prohibition to micro and small enterprises is necessary because of circumvention practices?

(6 July 2026) The Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation (ESPR) (1) provisions on unsold products do not restrict the trade in products, nor do they prohibit exporting goods for sale in other markets. Such exports are not considered a circumvention of the prohibition. However, economic operators who export unsold consumer products to third countries solely for destruction must disclose the information required under Article 24 of the ESPR. They can be held liable if they circumvent the destruction prohibition. Channelling unsold consumer products subject to the prohibition through affiliated or contracted micro and small enterprises for destruction is also considered circumvention. Article 25(2) states that economic operators not subject to the prohibition must not destroy unsold consumer products supplied to them to circumvent it. The national authorities are allowed therefore to take the necessary measures to prevent circumvention via micro and small enterprises if evidence suggests they are being used to bypass the rule, including by the setting up and enforcement of penalties, in accordance with Article 74 ESPR. National competent authorities are responsible for verifying compliance with the prohibition on destruction. They may use any information, document, finding, statement, or intelligence as evidence in their investigations, following the verification principles in Annex III of the Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/2 (2). Any signals of circumvention from these authorities will be duly considered when determining if an extension of the prohibition to micro and small enterprises is necessary.

E-10-2026-001630.t: Electoral irregularities and follow-up to local elections in Serbia
qt: to the Commission Delara Burkhardt (S&D) Subject:

Following the local elections of 29 March 2026 in Serbia, concerns regarding electoral irregularities, an uneven playing field and incidents of violence have been raised by civil society organisations, election observers and international bodies. The Commission has also publicly acknowledged these issues and called for accountability and further electoral reforms. 1.

What concrete measures will the Commission take, within the framework of the accession process, to support and monitor the effective investigation of reported irregularities and violence, as well as the implementation of the necessary electoral reforms?

How will the Commission reflect the lack of tangible progress made in these areas in Serbia’s accession process, and what benchmarks will be used to assess whether upcoming elections, including those expected in 2027, meet EU democratic standards?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (13.7.2026) The Commission closely followed the local elections held on 29 March 2026 in ten municipalities in Serbia, which were observed by the Council of Europe (CoE) Congress of Local and Regional Authorities. Following reported irregularities and incidents during the elections, including acts of violence against independent observers, citizens, representatives of political parties, and media workers, the Commission called on the competent national authorities to ensure swift and transparent follow up and to hold perpetrators accountable. Building on the first positive steps taken to address concerns about the integrity of the electoral register, such as the adoption of the amendments to the Law on the Unified voters register and election of the audit commission, the Commission has continued to underline that the electoral process requires further tangible improvement and reform. Priority recommendations from the CoE and the Organisation for Security Cooperation in Europe/Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights are yet to be fully implemented. These relate to the separation of State and party, inclusiveness and comprehensiveness of the electoral reform, audit of the voter register and transparency of voter list data, greater oversight of election campaigns and their financing, and measures to enable media freedom and independence. The Commission will continue to follow developments in the rule of law including electoral reform closely, as well as the conduct of all future elections. The proper functioning of Serbia’s democratic institutions is at the core of its EU accession process, and the Commission will report on it as part of the 2026 Enlargement Package.

E-10-2026-001629.t: Bicycle delivery: promoting sustainable employment for European youth and ending immigration-linked exploitation
qt: to the Commission Catherine Griset (PfE), André Rougé (PfE), Valérie Deloge (PfE), Séverine Werbrouck (PfE), Pierre Pimpie (PfE) Subject:

Food and parcel delivery services via digital platforms such as Uber Eats and Deliveroo have become widespread in Europe’s big cities. However, a number of studies point to worrying abuses: most of the delivery workers are immigrants, who are often working on an insecure or irregular basis, exploited and exposed to significant health risks. This raises social and economic questions. At the same time, this work, which was originally done by students or active young Europeans, including cyclists, could be a lever for getting young Europeans into the labour market, while also contributing to the EU’s climate objectives. 1.

Does the Commission intend to promote a European workforce in this sector, while respecting the competences of the Member States, through programmes focusing on soft mobility, sport and youth employment?

Does the Commission plan to incorporate these issues into policies on youth, sport and the green transition, in order to promote these urban cycling-related jobs as a way to boost local and sustainable employment?
Finally, could it encourage the exchange of good practices on social and health-related conditions in order to combat economic exploitation in this sector?
Supporter1
This question is supported by a Member other than the authors: Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE).
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.6.2026) Directive (EU) 2024/28311 aims to improve working conditions in platform work and to support the opportunities the platform economy offers, including for young people. Its provisions on transparency, intermediaries and reliable identity verification, together with the minimum standards on sanctions and measures against employers of illegally staying third-country nationals set out by Directive 2009/52/EC2 should strongly contribute to address undeclared work and other illegal practices involving undocumented migrants in the delivery sector3,4. The Commission supports the sharing of good practices via its mutual learning programme. Moreover, the European Labour Authority has organised several events and published relevant reports reflecting enforcement challenges and approaches at national level, addressing in particular employment status misclassification and undeclared work in the platform economy5. The Commission’s efforts in the area of platform work are in synergy with its policies to foster quality jobs, sustainable modes of transport and health-enhancing physical activity within the green and digital transitions. The reinforced Youth Guarantee6 remains pivotal and has already enabled 63 million young Europeans to start an offer of employment, continued education, apprenticeships and traineeships, including in the green economy
