E-10-2026-001627.t: Selective penalisation of religious expression in European football and consistency with EU fundamental rights
qt: to the Commission Geadis Geadi (ECR), Nikolaos Anadiotis (NI), Jaroslav Bžoch (PfE), Branko Grims (PPE), Paolo Inselvini (ECR), Jaroslav Knot (PfE), Tomasz Froelich (ESN), Afroditi Latinopoulou (PfE), Ondřej Knotek (PfE), Mieke Andriese (PfE), Galato Alexandraki (ECR), Daniel Obajtek (ECR), Şerban Dimitrie Sturdza (ECR), Roman Haider (PfE), Diana Iovanovici Şoşoacă (NI), Jorge Martín Frías (PfE), Jorge Buxadé Villalba (PfE), Aleksandar Nikolic (PfE), Antonín Staněk (PfE), Margarita de la Pisa Carrión (PfE), Marion Maréchal (ECR) Subject:

On 25 March 2026, UEFA’s Control, Ethics and Disciplinary Body imposed a fine on FC Crvena Zvezda following a match played against LOSC Lille in the UEFA Europa League at the Rajko Mitić Stadium in Belgrade on 26 February 2026. UEFA applied the penalty with regard to a coordinated fan display (‘tifo’) depicting an Orthodox Christian icon of St Simeon, a central historical and religious figure in Serbian heritage, accompanied by the banner ‘May our faith lead you to victory’. The display was deemed to constitute ‘a message not fit for a sports event’ (Article 16(2)(e) of the UEFA Disciplinary Regulations) and to be ‘bringing the sport into disrepute’ (Article 11(2)(d) of the UEFA Disciplinary Regulations), resulting in a fine of EUR 40 000. This decision raises concerns of inconsistency when compared to cases where no penalties have been imposed, including the use of displays linked to the Turkish occupation of Cyprus by Galatasaray supporters and the use of satanic symbols in a German stadium. In the context of the application of civil liberties and fundamental rights, how does the Commission assess whether penalising such cultural expression complies with the principles of non-discrimination and equal treatment? Supporter1
This question is supported by a Member other than the authors: Emmanouil Fragkos (ECR).
at: (English version) to the Commission Geadis Geadi (ECR), Nikolaos Anadiotis (NI), Jaroslav Bžoch (PfE), Branko Grims (PPE), Paolo Inselvini (ECR), Jaroslav Knot (PfE), Tomasz Froelich (ESN), Afroditi Latinopoulou (PfE), Ondřej Knotek (PfE), Mieke Andriese (PfE), Galato Alexandraki (ECR), Daniel Obajtek (ECR), Şerban Dimitrie Sturdza (ECR), Roman Haider (PfE), Diana Iovanovici Şoşoacă (NI), Jorge Martín Frías (PfE), Jorge Buxadé Villalba (PfE), Aleksandar Nikolic (PfE), Antonín Staněk (PfE), Margarita de la Pisa Carrión (PfE), Marion Maréchal (ECR) (21 April 2026) Subject: Selective penalisation of religious expression in European football and consistency with EU fundamental rights On 25 March 2026, UEFA’s Control, Ethics and Disciplinary Body imposed a fine on FC Crvena Zvezda following a match played against LOSC Lille in the UEFA Europa League at the Rajko Mitić Stadium in Belgrade on 26 February 2026. UEFA applied the penalty with regard to a coordinated fan display (‘tifo’) depicting an Orthodox Christian icon of St Simeon, a central historical and religious figure in Serbian heritage, accompanied by the banner ‘May our faith lead you to victory’. The display was deemed to constitute ‘a message not fit for a sports event’ (Article 16(2)(e) of the UEFA Disciplinary Regulations) and to be ‘bringing the sport into disrepute’ (Article 11(2)(d) of the UEFA Disciplinary Regulations), resulting in a fine of EUR 40 000. This decision raises concerns of inconsistency when compared to cases where no penalties have been imposed, including the use of displays linked to the Turkish occupation of Cyprus by Galatasaray supporters and the use of satanic symbols in a German stadium. In the context of the application of civil liberties and fundamental rights, how does the Commission assess whether penalising such cultural expression complies with the principles of non-discrimination and equal treatment? Supporter (1) (1 July 2026) The Commission takes note of the Union of European Football Associations (UEFA) disciplinary decisions regarding cultural or religious expressions. The Commission remains committed to protecting the values and fundamental rights enshrined in Article 2 of the Treaty on European Union (1) and the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union (2) which guarantees freedom of thought, conscience and religion (Article 10), and prohibits discrimination based on various grounds, including religion (Article 21). The Commission also promotes these principles among sport stakeholders, who remain autonomous in the way they govern sport. In particular, Article 1.4 of the Arrangement for Cooperation between the European Commission and UEFA (3) states that the two sides wish to strengthen their partnership to support and promote European values focusing on Europe’s greatest challenges, and the EU’s strategic objectives, with a focus on sport and other specific areas which are of mutual interest and relevance.
This question is supported by a Member other than the authors: Emmanouil Fragkos (ECR).

E-10-2026-001624.t: Invasion and dangerous plans to partition Lebanon by the State of Israel
qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Lefteris Nikolaou-Alavanos (NI), Kostas Papadakis (NI) Subject:

Following the criminal attack by the US and Israel on Iran and the dangerous plans to transform Gaza into an American protectorate, Israel is now also promoting the partition of Lebanon. Under the pretext of eradicating Hezbollah, it has created a so-called ‘peace plan’, in which it provides for the permanent presence of Israeli troops and the creation of a buffer zone. This is reflected in the map published by the Israeli army with the occupied territories in southern Lebanon, which also extends to a corresponding maritime zone – a move that is by no means accidental, since the Israeli-Lebanese maritime border is crucial for the establishment of an EEZ in the Eastern Mediterranean, an area with significant energy reserves. In fact, the Commission defends its involvement in the creation of the spurious ‘Peace Council’, under the pretext that the US, Israel and their allies will supposedly guarantee peace! The Vice-President / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy is asked: 1.

What view does she take of the State of Israel’s unacceptable invasion of Lebanon and of Israel’s plans to split Lebanon into three by imposing an Israeli military occupation zone on the country and creating ‘buffer zones’ to the detriment of Lebanon’s territorial integrity?

What view does she take of the call for an immediate halt to the EU-Israel Association Agreement and to all forms of EU cooperation with Israel, as the peoples are urgently demanding through their struggle?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.6.2026) The EU has continuously called upon Israel to respect Lebanon’s sovereignty and territorial integrity1. The proposal to establish a buffer zone in southern Lebanon raises serious legal, political and humanitarian concerns. It also risks fuelling more sectarian tensions and displacements and to exacerbate the current crisis in Lebanon. The EU also strongly condemns Hezbollah’s attacks against Israel. Hezbollah poses an existential threat to Lebanon and its disarmament remains a priority. The EU urges Israel to stop military operations in the country which are having a dramatic humanitarian and socioeconomic impact. The EU calls on all parties to respect the recently agreed temporary ceasefire, fully supports the continuation of bilateral dialogue between Israel and Lebanon and encourages negotiations as a path toward lasting stability and de-escalation in line with UN Security Council Resolution 1701. In 2025, in light of the catastrophic situation in Gaza, the High Representative/Vice-President conducted, with the support of a majority of Member States, a review of Israel’s compliance with its obligations under Article 2 of the EU-Israel Association Agreement2. The conclusion of the review was that there are indications that Israel would be in breach of its obligations. Following the review, the Commission’s President announced a set of proposed measures, including a reinforced package of sanctions and the suspension of certain trade-related provisions of the EU-Israel Association Agreement. The Commission has also put on hold its bilateral support to Israel, with the exception of support to civil society and Yad Vashem. Discussions continue in the Council on other measures which require approval of Member States.
1https://www.eeas.europa.eu/eeas/lebanon-statement-high-representative-recent-developments_en. 2 https://eeas.europa.eu/archives/delegations/israel/documents/eu_israel/asso_agree_en.pdf.

E-10-2026-001623.t: Frontex takeover of the FADO database
qt: to the Commission Özlem Demirel (The Left) Subject:

Since the adoption of Regulation (EU) 2020/493, Frontex has been legally responsible for the ‘False and Authentic Documents Online’ (FADO) system, which EU Member States use to distinguish between forged and genuine travel documents. The database is to be transferred to the new EBCG FADO platform in order to harmonise the systems and improve document checks at the external borders. 1.
When was the full takeover of the FADO database by Frontex – including the new EBCG FADO platform – initially planned, and for when is it currently foreseen or actually taking place?

What technical, organisational or data protection issues relating to the takeover or operation of FADO by Frontex are known to the Council and Frontex as the cause of the delay, and who is responsible for this (including with regard to any potential compensation)?
Is Frontex planning or considering an interim solution, and is there also a plan to replace FADO with a completely new integrated document and identity verification system?
at: (English version) to the Commission Özlem Demirel (The Left) (21 April 2026) Subject: Frontex takeover of the FADO database Since the adoption of Regulation (EU) 2020/493, Frontex has been legally responsible for the ‘False and Authentic Documents Online’ (FADO) system, which EU Member States use to distinguish between forged and genuine travel documents. The database is to be transferred to the new EBCG FADO platform in order to harmonise the systems and improve document checks at the external borders. 1. When was the full takeover of the FADO database by Frontex — including the new EBCG FADO platform — initially planned, and for when is it currently foreseen or actually taking place? 2. What technical, organisational or data protection issues relating to the takeover or operation of FADO by Frontex are known to the Council and Frontex as the cause of the delay, and who is responsible for this (including with regard to any potential compensation)? 3. Is Frontex planning or considering an interim solution, and is there also a plan to replace FADO with a completely new integrated document and identity verification system? (5 June 2026) Regulation (EU) 2020/493 of 30 March 2020 on the False and Authentic Documents Online (FADO) system (1) does not provide a date or timeline for the takeover of the FADO system by the European Border and Coast Guard Agency (Frontex). Article 6(1) provides that the Commission is to adopt an implementing act in order to determine the date of the effective implementation of the FADO system by the Agency. This act should only be adopted by the Commission after verifying that the conditions listed in Article 6(2) have been met. To date, the Commission has not received the notifications required by Article 6(2), points (b) and (c). The Commission is not in a position to comment on behalf of the Council. With regard to Frontex, the Commission has asked the Agency to provide a response to the questions raised by the Honourable Member and will send the replies as soon as possible. Pending the reply from the Agency, more information about the creation of the new European Border and Coast Guard False and Authentic Documents Online system is available on the website of the Agency (2).

E-10-2026-001621.t: Frontex participation in Finnish pushback exercise
qt: to the Council Özlem Demirel (The Left) Subject:

In March 2026, the Finnish Border Guard carried out a four-day training exercise at three closed border crossings with Russia – an exercise in which the European Gendarmerie Force (EUROGENDFOR) was involved for the first time. The aim was to test a new border protection law that empowers authorities to push back asylum seekers and use force under certain conditions. Frontex also participated and, according to its own statements, undertook tasks such as mobile surveillance, weapons and document checks, and the securing of transports. 1.
How does the Council assess the compatibility of this with the fundamental right to asylum and the principle of non-refoulement?
Which Member States and other actors were involved in the exercise, and in what proportions were Frontex, EUROGENDFOR and Finnish and Estonian officials involved?
at: The Council has not discussed this question.

(3 June 2026) The European Border and Coast Guard Agency (Frontex) is a decentralised Agency of the Union. Accordingly, the Agency operates with a certain degree of independence from the Commission in carrying out its activities, including training courses, provided that these remain consistent with its mandate and legal framework. As an Agency of the Union, Frontex must act in compliance with EU law, including the fundamental rights enshrined in the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the EU. E-10-2026-001619.t: Need for technical assurance of security, reliability and protection of personal data in the new European Commission age verification app
qt: to the Commission Elena Kountoura (The Left) Subject:

The Commission recently announced that the new age verification app to protect minors online is technically ready.1 The provision of this app aims to create a standardised way of verifying the age of users for major technology platforms across the Union.2 However, experts who have examined the open source code of the app have identified significant weaknesses, such as insufficient protection of stored sensitive personal data and the possibility of bypassing authentication mechanisms.3 The fact that the app was presented as technically ready, while at the same time acknowledged to be a ‘demo version’ under continuous development, raises issues of personal data protection and institutional credibility. Taking into account recent FRA data, according to which the vast majority of European citizens support the imposition of age limits on the use of social media, citing risks such as exploitation, exposure to harmful content and addiction4, and that the introduction of minimum age limits for access to social networks should meet strict conditions for secure age verification that protect personal data, such as encrypted zero-knowledge proof of age, without storing identity5: 1.
How does the Commission assess the technical weaknesses identified and what specific corrective measures have already been taken to make the app fully secure?
Does the Commission intend to reassess the implementation schedule of the app until full compliance with European security, reliability and data protection standards is ensured?

https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/da/statement_26_817. The system is based on the ‘zeroknowledge proof’ method, which means that social media users will be able to verify their age without sharing personal data with the platforms. Under the EU Digital Services Act, platforms that will be required to restrict access to minors are not obliged to use the Union app. However, they will have to demonstrate that the tools they will use are equally effective, safe, reliable and protect personal data. https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-brussels-launched-age-checking-app-hackers-say-took-them-2-minutesbreak-it/. https://fra.europa.eu/en/news/2026/europeans-deeply-concerned-about-childrens-use-social-media. See European Parliament resolution of 26 November 2025 on the protection of minors online.

E-10-2026-001618.t: Aviation fuel preparedness and scaling up sustainable aviation fuel in the EU
qt: to the Commission Johan Danielsson (S&D) Subject:

In the light of recent disruptions in the Middle East, there is a need to assess the EU’s preparedness regarding the availability of aviation fuel. Air transport is critical both for the functioning of the internal market and for crisis response. At the same time, the EU remains highly dependent on imports of aviation fuels from non-EU countries. In parallel, the EU has set ambitious targets for the uptake of sustainable aviation fuels, notably through the ReFuelEU Aviation Regulation1. However, implementation remains slow and production capacity within the EU is still limited, which risks delaying both the green transition and efforts to strengthen resilience. Against this background: 1.

Does the Commission intend to propose EU-wide requirements for minimum aviation fuel stock levels, in particular at major airports and strategic transport hubs, in order to strengthen preparedness and resilience in times of crisis?

What concrete measures will the Commission take to accelerate the build-up of sustainable aviation fuel production capacity within the EU and ensure that Member States meet their obligations under the ReFuelEU Aviation Regulation?

Regulation (EU) 2023/2405 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 18 October 2023 on ensuring a level playing field for sustainable air transport (ReFuelEU Aviation) (OJ L, 2023/2405, 31.10.2023, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2023/2405/oj).
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (23.6.2026) In response to the impact of the Middle East crisis, the Commission announced the launch of a revision process for the Oil Stockholding Directive in its AccelerateEU communication1. One of the objectives of the revision is to address the challenges identified in the current crisis, considering among others whether specific stock requirements are needed for different oil products, adaptations for sustainable fuels, mitigation of emerging risks, and enhanced military mobility readiness through improved energy resilience. The Commission has also published guidance clarifying certain EU rules applicable to passengers and tourism as well as transport operators, including in light of the current reduced supply of jet fuel from the Middle East2. The Sustainable Transport Investment Plan3 aims to accelerate investment in sustainable aviation fuels (SAF) in the EU and reaffirms the commitment to ReFuelEU Aviation4 implementation. The Plan includes actions on the Commission to work with Member States to set up a pooled joint double-sided auction for synthetic aviation fuels (eSAF), while simultaneously providing valuable insights in view of establishing an EU-wide financing mechanism. To this end, the Commission launched eSAF Early Movers Coalition in December 20255 and launched a study to define auctions design and governance. Member States are responsible for enforcing the application of ReFuelEU Aviation through their respective competent authorities and imposing fines in case of non-compliance by aviation fuel suppliers, aircraft operators and EU airport managing bodies.

E-10-2026-001616.t: Inclusion of German journalist Hüseyin Doğru on EU sanctions list
qt: to the Council Siegbert Frank Droese (ESN) Subject:

How does the Council justify the inclusion of German journalist Hüseyin Doğru on the EU sanctions list without a prior hearing, without the disclosure of any evidence and without any effective opportunity for him to defend himself, and how is the Council ensuring that these measures are compatible with the fundamental rights of the European Union, in particular freedom of speech, the right to a fair trial and protection of the family?
at: The Council recalls that respect for fundamental rights, including freedom of expression and freedom of the press, is an integral part of the EU's approach to restrictive measures. Listings are based on the criteria established in the applicable legal acts and relate to the activities of the individuals concerned. The decision to include individuals and entities in the EU's list of restrictive measures is taken by the Council unanimously on the basis of the criteria established in the legal acts in question. The Council does not comment on the specific information underlying individual listing decisions, as disclosing such information could undermine the effectiveness of the measures and prejudice ongoing processes. Listed individuals retain the right to challenge their listing before the Court of Justice of the European Union. The Council reviews restrictive measures on a regular basis to ensure that listings remain justified and proportionate, and refers to the publicly available statements of reasons, which set out the basis for individual listings to the extent possible.

E-10-2026-001615.t: Geothermal energy and the need to exclusively promote technologies with a low environmental impact
qt: to the Commission Dario Tamburrano (The Left), Pasquale Tridico (The Left), Valentina Palmisano (The Left) Subject:

Enel Green Power’s Monte Amiata (Tuscany) geothermal facilities use flash technology and produce emissions that contain similar – and sometimes higher – quantities of greenhouse gases than fossil fuel-fired electrical plants1. These geothermal facilities also emit significant quantities of ammonia, hydrogen sulphide, mercury and other substances harmful to public health and the environment. A supporter of the current model of local geothermal development, the Tuscany Regional Executive recently agreed to extend the aforementioned Enel concessions by another 20 years2. However, the Regional Health Agency (ARS) has reported that male mortality rates in the local area have long outstripped normal levels by a significant margin3. Acknowledging that geothermal production is not always clean, Recital 46 of Directive (EU) 2018/2001 states that ‘the Commission should therefore facilitate only the deployment of geothermal energy with a low environmental impact and resulting in greenhouse gas emissions savings.’ There are ways of generating geothermal energy without releasing greenhouse gases or producing emissions of any kind, a case in point being Eavor’s closed-loop technology4. In the light of the situation regarding the Monte Amiata geothermal power plants, could the Commission clarify whether it will draft guidelines that can steer stakeholders towards new geothermal technologies that have a low environmental impact and whether it will allocate dedicated funds or propose legislative measures to this effect?

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0959652613007798. https://www.intoscana.it/it/geotermia-rinnovate-le-concessioni-con-enel-green-power-il-presidente-gianiintesa-storica/. Report drafted by the ARS: https://www.ars.toscana.it/images/determinanti_salute/news/2022/1.Voller_invetta_28102022.pdf. The Monte Amiata plants are located in the area designated as ‘Area Sud’ [‘South Area’]. https://eavor.de/en/technology/.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (18.6.2026) The Commission acknowledges that geothermal energy plays an important role in the decarbonisation of the EU. A Commission study1 analysed the emissions of geothermal plants across Europe and concluded that extreme values are typically linked to specific locations and older plants. Most of the systems operate in closed loops, where no relevant emissions occur. Geothermal projects are covered by EU environmental legislation. Under the Environmental Impact Assessment Directive2, geothermal projects that may significantly affect the environment must undergo an environmental assessment before approval; it requires authorities to assess impacts on air quality, climate and human health. To facilitate the environmental assessments, the Commission proposed in the European Grids Package3 that Member States set up single digital portals that ensure access to all relevant environmental and geological data for permit-granting procedures. Furthermore, as set out in the AccelerateEU Communication4, the Commission will support Member States and stakeholders in gathering detailed geological data and create an EU-level database as well as showcase best practices for clean technologies. The Commission also supports research and development in geothermal technologies to improve the environmental performance, such as the project for geothermal emissions control under Horizon 20205 that also included consortium partners from Italy. Geothermal projects reducing greenhouse gas emissions are also supported under the Innovation Fund and in general, in EU Funding calls, the inclusion of the ‘do no significant harm’ principle as an eligibility condition reinforces environmental compliance across all topics.

E-10-2026-001614.t: Cybersecurity and data protection flaws in the age identification app
qt: to the Commission Fabio De Masi (NI) Subject:

According to media reports, cybersecurity and privacy experts have demonstrated that the European age identification app could be easily hacked, finding it to be technically inadequate for ensuring security and data protection standards.1 1.
In view of the numerous criticalities and weaknesses revealed, does the Commission intend to postpone the launch of the app until the issues reported are resolved?
In light of the vulnerabilities exposed, does the EU intend to move closer to a ‘zeroknowledge’ approach to the development of the app, in order to ensure the protection of personal data?
https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-brussels-launched-age-checking-app-hackers-say-took-them-2-minutesbreak-it/?utm_source=dlvr.it&utm_medium=twitter&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (23.6.2026) The application presented on 15 April 2026 is an early reference implementation of the European age verification solution, released openly for scrutiny prior to public deployment. Some of the issues raised by independent experts were well founded and have been corrected by the development consortium, with an updated version made available shortly thereafter and further improvements to follow. The application is in its piloting phase. Member States are responsible for adapting the implementation to national circumstances and for ensuring that all applicable cybersecurity and data protection standards are met before the application is made available to citizens, in line with the Commission Recommendation of 29 April 20261 calling for independent thirdparty scrutiny prior to deployment. No postponement of the timetable is therefore required, since deployment in each Member State remains conditional on the successful completion of these checks. The privacy-preserving approach referred to by the Honourable Member is already a constitutive element of the solution's design. The architecture relies on cryptographic techniques that allow a user to demonstrate that the relevant age threshold is met without disclosing identifying information to the online service, in line with Regulation (EU) 2016/679 and the European Data Protection Board Statement 1/2025 on Age Assurance2. The Commission remains committed to strengthening these properties further as the solution matures.

E-10-2026-001613.t: Proposal for a mandatory e-permit for e-scooter and e-bike users
qt: to the Commission Cynthia Ní Mhurchú (Renew) Subject:

Will the Commission, as a matter of urgency, introduce a mandatory online safety assessment and certification system (‘e-permit’) for all e-scooter and e-bike users, in view of the clear and growing road safety risks associated with their largely unregulated use? 1.

Given that individuals as young as 16 can operate these vehicles on public roads without any formal knowledge of road safety or traffic rules, and despite the fact that the acceleration capabilities of such vehicles are comparable to motorised vehicles that require licences, what immediate steps will the Commission take to address this regulatory gap?

Will the Commission commit to implementing measures that ensure user education through a short online road safety assessment, enforce accountability via a permit system, enable the collection of anonymised usage data to better inform infrastructure planning, and decisively reduce the increasing number of accidents involving e-scooters and e-bikes, while maintaining support for these vehicles as a convenient and sustainable mode of transport?
at: (English version) to the Commission Cynthia Ní Mhurchú (Renew) (15 April 2026) Subject: Proposal for a mandatory e-permit for e-scooter and e-bike users Will the Commission, as a matter of urgency, introduce a mandatory online safety assessment and certification system (‘epermit’) for all e-scooter and e-bike users, in view of the clear and growing road safety risks associated with their largely unregulated use? 1. Given that individuals as young as 16 can operate these vehicles on public roads without any formal knowledge of road safety or traffic rules, and despite the fact that the acceleration capabilities of such vehicles are comparable to motorised vehicles that require licences, what immediate steps will the Commission take to address this regulatory gap? 2. Will the Commission commit to implementing measures that ensure user education through a short online road safety assessment, enforce accountability via a permit system, enable the collection of anonymised usage data to better inform infrastructure planning, and decisively reduce the increasing number of accidents involving e-scooters and e-bikes, while maintaining support for these vehicles as a convenient and sustainable mode of transport? (19 June 2026) While Directive (EU) 2025/2205 (1) on driving licences (DLD) does not directly address the competence of e-scooter and ebike users, nor introduces any dedicated ‘e-permit’ system or assessment system for them, the new DLD will have an impact on those users by reinforcing training and testing requirements for drivers who share the road with micro-mobility users and other vulnerable road users. These measures include updated driver testing content (Article 10(1)(a) and Annex II), enhanced hazard perception training, and new provisions on safe interaction with vulnerable users. That said, the Commission and Member States cooperate on issues beyond the directive's scope, including by exchanging best practices on road-safety awareness and education measures on micro-mobility. At present, there are no plans to modify the existing licensing requirements for these micro-mobility devices at EU level (2). The Commission recognises the importance of user education and accountability in reducing accidents involving e-scooters and e-bikes, and the revised DLD includes several measures that support these goals, such as updated training content on micromobility and a new probationary-period regime for novice drivers. In its report on the implementation of EU road safety policy (3) the Commission committed to drawing conclusions on the potential benefits of harmonising technical specifications of personal mobility devices (4) and preparing guidance to Member States and local administrations on what issues should be taken into account to ensure the safety of riders and other road users during the use of these devices (5).

E-10-2026-001612.t: Hungary’s position on Ukraine’s EU accession and the role of national referendums
qt: to the Commission Fabio De Masi (NI) Subject:

The future Prime Minister of Hungary, Péter Magyar, has expressed his opposition to an accelerated accession process for Ukraine. What is more, Magyar has made it clear that he wishes to hold a referendum in Hungary on Ukraine’s accession to the EU.1 1.
Does the Commission welcome the Hungarian Prime Minister-designate’s call for a national referendum in Hungary should the EU accession negotiations with Ukraine be successful?

What is the Commission’s view on the possibility for Member States to confirm successful EU accession negotiations through national referendums in order to give additional democratic legitimacy to a country’s accession?
https://www.reuters.com/world/europe/hungarys-election-winner-magyar-says-he-does-not-back-ukrainesfast-track-eu-2026-04-13/.
at: (English version) to the Commission Fabio De Masi (NI) (20 April 2026) Subject: Hungary’s position on Ukraine’s EU accession and the role of national referendums The future Prime Minister of Hungary, Péter Magyar, has expressed his opposition to an accelerated accession process for Ukraine. What is more, Magyar has made it clear that he wishes to hold a referendum in Hungary on Ukraine’s accession to the EU. (1) 1. Does the Commission welcome the Hungarian Prime Minister-designate’s call for a national referendum in Hungary should the EU accession negotiations with Ukraine be successful? 2. What is the Commission’s view on the possibility for Member States to confirm successful EU accession negotiations through national referendums in order to give additional democratic legitimacy to a country’s accession? (25 June 2026) The legal basis for the accession of new Member States to the EU is Article 49 of the Treaty on the European Union (TEU). Article 49 TEU states that ‘the conditions of accession of a new Member State to the EU and the adjustments of the EU Treaties is subject of an agreement between the Member States and the applicant State, which is then submitted for ratification by all Member States and the acceding State in accordance with their respective constitutional requirements’. It is thus up to the Member States, including Hungary, to ratify an accession treaty in accordance with their respective constitutional requirements.

E-10-2026-001611.t: Protecting drinking water and watercourses in mining operations – application of EU rules in Sweden
qt: to the Commission Alice Kuhnke (Verts/ALE), Isabella Lövin (Verts/ALE), Pär Holmgren (Verts/ALE) Subject:

Mining projects in the pipeline in Medelpad and Jämtland – including the extraction of alum shale containing uranium, vanadium, zinc, nickel and molybdenum in Oviken, as well as lithium mining near the river Indalsälven at Järkvissle – pose a risk to the water systems that supply drinking water to around 37 000 inhabitants of Sundsvall and Timrå. The local water authority Mittsverige Vatten has expressed serious concerns about long-term water quality. Since 2024, the Commission has been pursuing an infringement procedure (INFR(2024)2236) against Sweden regarding the country’s failure to properly implement the EU Water Framework Directive (2000/60/EC). Through its RESourceEU action plan, among other schemes, the Commission is also pushing for more mining in the EU, as well as faster permitting processes. With that in mind: 1.

Given the ongoing infringement procedure, is the Commission confident that Sweden is correctly implementing the Water Framework Directive and the EU rules on the quality of drinking water when it comes to new mining operations?
Does the Commission take the view that it is in line with EU rules to grant mining permits when there is evidence of serious risks to drinking water quality?

How does the Commission intend to ensure – in forthcoming guidance documents, for example – that an increase in mining and streamlined permitting processes do not have a negative impact on the implementation of EU environment and water rules, and are not likely to have an adverse effect on EU citizens’ access to clean drinking water?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (6.7.2026) The Commission opened an infringement case in 2024 against Sweden1 for failure to correctly transpose the Water Framework Directive (WFD)2 by not providing for periodic reviews of relevant controls and water permits. This infringement case is ongoing. It is not directly related to alleged shortcomings in the authorisation of new mining operations. The Commission is also in the process of assessing the transposition of the revised Drinking Water Directive (DWD)3 in all Member States. The process of granting mining permits must comply with, inter alia, the Environmental Impact Assessment Directive4, which ensures that any significant effects on water are integrated in the preparation and assessment of projects. An infringement case is ongoing against Sweden5 regarding incorrect transposition of that Directive. Without prejudice to the Commission’s role as guardian of the Treaties, Member States are primarily responsible to ensure compliance with EU law, including with regard to individual cases of potential breach of the water quality rules. This includes e.g. Article 4(7) WFD for new projects, Article 7(3) WFD for the protection of drinking water, as well as the DWD. The Commission has recently adopted guidance6 aiming to help reduce uncertainties regarding procedures and assessments during permitting of new or existing activities affecting water bodies, with a focus on the mining sector. The goal is to support Europe’s overall resilience, whilst keeping a high level of protection of the environment and human health.
1 INFR(2024)2236: https://ec.europa.eu/implementing-eu-law/search-infringement-

decisions/?langCode=EN&version=v1&typeOfSearch=byDecision&refId=INFR(2024)2236&page=1&size=10 &order=desc&sortColumns=decisionDate. 2 Directive 2000/60/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 23 October 2000 establishing a framework for Community action in the field of water policy, OJ L 327, 22.12.2000, p. 1–73, as amended by Commission Directive 2014/101/EU of 30 October 2014, OJ L 311, 31.10.2014, p. 32–35. 3 Directive (EU) 2020/2184 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 16 December 2020 on the quality of water intended for human consumption (recast), OJ L 435, 23.12.2020, pp. 1–62. 4 Directive 2011/92/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 December 2011 on the assessment of the effects of certain public and private projects on the environment (codification), OJ L 26, 28.1.2012, pp. 1– 21. 5 INFR(2019)2222: https://ec.europa.eu/implementing-eu-law/search-infringementdecisions/?langCode=EN&version=v1&typeOfSearch=byDecision&refId=INFR(2019)2222&page=1&size=10 &order=desc&sortColumns=decisionDate. 6 Guidance for the implementation of the Water Framework Directive during the permitting of new and existing activities with a particular focus on the mining sector: https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_26_1129.

E-10-2026-001610.t: Imminent shortage of nitrile products and helium
qt: to the Commission Gerald Hauser (PfE) Subject:

The Tyrol Medical Chamber is warning all doctors that, owing to current geopolitical tensions, a potential supply issue is looming. The message sent to all doctors on 31 March 2026 is as follows: ‘Dear Colleagues, owing to current geopolitical tensions, a potential supply issue is emerging in the manufacture and delivery of nitrile products such as single-use gloves. This could result in supply shortages and price fluctuations in the near future. It may therefore be advisable to order these products in good time. Naturally, we will keep you informed of any further developments in this matter.’ 1.
How can such shortages occur when the European Parliament and the Commission are constantly discussing the supply of medical products?
What does the Commission intend to do to ensure the supply of nitrile products?
What does the Commission intend to do to ensure the supply of helium?
at: (English version) to the Commission Gerald Hauser (PfE) (20 April 2026) Subject: Imminent shortage of nitrile products and helium The Tyrol Medical Chamber is warning all doctors that, owing to current geopolitical tensions, a potential supply issue is looming. The message sent to all doctors on 31 March 2026 is as follows: ‘Dear Colleagues, owing to current geopolitical tensions, a potential supply issue is emerging in the manufacture and delivery of nitrile products such as single-use gloves. This could result in supply shortages and price fluctuations in the near future. It may therefore be advisable to order these products in good time. Naturally, we will keep you informed of any further developments in this matter.’ 1. How can such shortages occur when the European Parliament and the Commission are constantly discussing the supply of medical products? 2.
What does the Commission intend to do to ensure the supply of nitrile products?
What does the Commission intend to do to ensure the supply of helium?

(23 June 2026) Medicine shortages are a key priority for the Commission. The European Medicines Agency (EMA) and the Medicines Shortages Steering Group monitor and address EU-level shortages. The new Pharmaceutical Regulation (1) obliges mandatory early notification of potential shortages and introduced shortage prevention plans. The framework will be further strengthened by the Critical Medicines Act (2) on which co-legislators reached a political agreement on 12 May 2026, aiming to address supply chain vulnerabilities. Regarding nitrile medical countermeasures, the Commission has engaged with industry and has not received notifications of materialised shortages in the EU. Monitoring is ongoing. To strengthen supply security during a crisis, the Commission plans to launch a tender to reserve manufacturing capacity for nitrile examination gloves (3). The Medical Countermeasures (MCM) Strategy outlines measures to boost innovation and supply of MCMs, such as the creation of RAMP UP (4) to establish manufacturing through partnerships with industry. The Commission, alongside the EMA, is monitoring helium supply risks. Helium is essential for magnetic resonance imaging systems, pharmaceutical manufacturing and quality control, and is designated a critical raw material under the Critical Raw Materials Act (CRMA) (5). According to the Commission’s analysis, the EU does not source the majority of helium from Gulf States, and a supply disruption is not imminent.

E-10-2026-001609.t: Rising fertiliser prices: what are the risks for our EU farmers?
qt: to the Commission Valérie Deloge (PfE), Tomáš Kubín (PfE), Petar Volgin (ESN), Jacek Ozdoba (ECR), Geadis Geadi (ECR), Georgiana Teodorescu (ECR), Anne-Sophie Frigout (PfE), France Jamet (PfE), Ivan David (ESN), Petr Bystron (ESN), Roman Haider (PfE), Gilles Pennelle (PfE) Subject:

For several months, EU farmers have been facing a significant and continuous increase in the price of fertilisers, particularly nitrogen fertilisers, which are heavily dependent on the price of gas and on raw material imports. The war in Ukraine, as well as tensions and conflicts in the Middle East, which directly affect global energy and agricultural input markets, are exacerbating this situation. At the same time, the guidelines adopted by the European Union impose more and more constraints without guaranteeing economically viable alternatives. This accumulation of factors directly jeopardises the profitability of farms, the stability of agricultural production and, ultimately, the EU’s ability to produce its own food. In a context where EU farmers are paying the price for both geopolitical tensions and EU policy decisions: 1.
Does the Commission have impact assessments on the cumulative effects of those factors?
Does it intend to take immediate and targeted action to protect EU farmers in the face of rising fertiliser prices?
How does it intend to boost fertiliser production in the EU?
Supporter1
This question is supported by a Member other than the authors: Catherine Griset (PfE).
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (19.6.2026) The Commission is aware of the significant pressure that farmers in the EU face due to the increased fertiliser prices, in particular nitrogen and phosphatic ones. The Commission is closely monitoring the situation and the impacts of geopolitical events through the Fertilisers Market Observatory. Internal assessment made by the Commission services shows that the crisis is likely to affect particularly the primary production of agricultural products in view of expected cost increases for fertilisers and fuel. In this context, the Commission is acting swiftly to help farmers. Several measures were taken, such as a flat 1% mark-up to the default Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) values for fertilisers, adopting a Temporary State aid framework1 on 29 April 2026, as well as the temporary suspension of import duties for ammonia, urea and other nitrogen fertilisers from countries other than Russia and Belarus, within given quotas2, for a period of one year until 31 May 2027. On 19 May 2026, the Commission adopted the Fertiliser Action Plan3, setting out short- and long-term measures to improve fertiliser availability, affordability and resilience. Short term actions include the mobilisation and possible top-up of the agricultural reserve, liquidity support under the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) and greater flexibility for advance payments. Longer term measures focus on strengthening EU production capacity, supporting the uptake of recycled nutrients and low carbon alternatives, and reducing strategic dependencies on imports.

E-10-2026-001607.t: Defending Spain’s interests in EU-Morocco relations
qt: to the Commission Jorge Buxadé Villalba (PfE) Subject:

During negotiations on a new agreement with Morocco, meetings have been held with the Moroccan Minister of Foreign Affairs, Mr Bourita, in both Brussels and Rabat. In those talks, the Commission lauded Morocco as a reliable and close ally, as well as supporting both increased cooperation in various areas and Morocco’s plan for Western Sahara. As regards relations with Spain, Morocco continues to exert pressure on the cities of Ceuta and Melilla, preventing smooth trade across land borders in order to stifle Spanish business owners, which runs counter to the 2022 bilateral agreement. Similarly, this year to date, the number of illegal immigrants arriving in Ceuta and Melilla by land has increased by 479 %. That partner that the Commission has referred to as reliable and close adopted, in 2020, two laws that unilaterally extended its exclusive economic zone, invading Spain’s exclusive economic zone around the Canary Islands, which is an intolerable threat. 1.
Has the Commission addressed those attacks on Spain with Minister Bourita?
How are Spain’s interests being defended in EU agreements with Morocco?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (7.8.2026) The EU partnership with Morocco is founded on shared objectives, including economic cooperation, migration management, and regional security. In the ongoing dialogue, the EU underscores the importance of adhering to agreed commitments and international norms, which are essential for stability and mutual trust. The EU remains firmly committed to upholding the interests of the EU and of all Member States, including Spain, in its external engagements. The EU maintains regular exchanges with the Spanish authorities to address any concerns and align approaches where useful and within the remits of respective competencies. EU negotiations on agreements with third countries are conducted in full respect of international and EU law based on the negotiation authorisation and the negotiation directives included therein as adopted by the Council, ensuring that agreements reflect shared values and legal principles. This includes due consideration for territorial integrity, international law, economic rights, and the effective management of migration flows.

E-10-2026-001606.t: Fostering the circular economy by ensuring the mutual recognition of end-of-waste schemes
qt: to the Commission Valentina Palmisano (The Left), Pasquale Tridico (The Left), Dario Tamburrano (The Left), Carolina Morace (The Left) Subject:
Fostering the circular economy by ensuring the mutual recognition of end-ofwaste schemes

Article 6 of Directive 2008/98/EC states that Member States can adopt their own end-of-waste (EoW) criteria in the absence of harmonised EU standards, and that they must then communicate these changes to the Commission. Italy complied with the above by issuing Ministerial Decree No 188/2020 (the ‘EoW paper regulation’), as a result of which standard travel documents can be used to ship EoW paper held in collection facilities. Seeing as Regulation (EU) 2024/1157 (on waste shipments) applies to waste and does not include materials that have ceased to be waste in its scope, and that EoW legislation is considered to be a central pillar of the EU circular economy: 1.

As regards the national criteria laid down by EoW regulations that have been adopted and notified in accordance with EU law, could the Commission confirm that any materials that comply with these criteria and which can be shipped as non-waste goods in the country that enacted the relevant EoW regulations cannot, when they are being exported, be made subject by other Member States to the provisions of the Waste Shipment Regulation, a process that unfairly strips these materials of their EoW status?

Does the Commission agree that it should ensure the mutual recognition of Member State EoW regulations as a means of fostering the circular economy, facilitating the free movement of goods and preventing the emerge of trade barriers within the single market?
at: (English version) to the Commission Valentina Palmisano (The Left), Pasquale Tridico (The Left), Dario Tamburrano (The Left), Carolina Morace (The Left) (20 April 2026) Subject: Fostering the circular economy by ensuring the mutual recognition of end-of-waste schemes Article 6 of Directive 2008/98/EC states that Member States can adopt their own end-of-waste (EoW) criteria in the absence of harmonised EU standards, and that they must then communicate these changes to the Commission. Does the Commission agree that it should ensure the mutual recognition of Member State EoW regulations as a means of fostering the circular economy, facilitating the free movement of goods and preventing the emerge of trade barriers within the single market?

(7 July 2026) Article 6(1) of the Waste Framework Directive (WFD) (1) sets out general conditions under which waste which has undergone a recycling or other recovery operation is considered to have reached end-of-waste (EoW) status. Whether to adopt specific EoW criteria is left to the discretion of each Member State. When Member States establish EoW criteria, they shall notify the Commission of those criteria in accordance with Directive (EU) 2015/1535 (2) where so required by that directive. In the case of shipment of material or a substance that reached EoW status in compliance with national EoW criteria, potential disagreements between Member States can still take place as to whether the status of shipped objects or substances is waste or non-waste. For such cases, Article 29(2) of the Waste Shipment Regulation (WSR) (3) introduces a procedure to resolve potential disagreements: if the competent authorities of dispatch and of destination cannot agree on the classification as regards the distinction between waste and non-waste, taking into account the provisions Article 20(1) of the WSR, and any conditions or decisions taken at EU level or by Member States pursuant to Article 5 or 6, the object or substance shall be treated as if it were waste for the purpose of the shipment. In addition to the provisions included under the WSR, the Commission is considering possible additional measures to facilitate the recognition of EoW criteria between Member States under the forthcoming Circular Economy Act (4).

E-10-2026-001604.t: Misuse of Erasmus+ funds for political bias and interference in democratic opposition
qt: to the Commission Mary Khan (ESN) Subject:

Research on Erasmus+ projects shows that taxpayers’ money has been channelled into projects that describe democratic opposition parties, such as Alternative für Deutschland (AfD), as ‘fascist’1, ‘dangerous’2 and a threat to a ‘free and democratic society’3. These projects, often aimed at young people and students, are presented under the guise of promoting ‘European values’, ‘tolerance’, and ‘democracy’. In reality, they raise serious concerns about political neutrality, ideological indoctrination and the misuse of EU funds. Considering the EU frequently warns against foreign interference in democratic processes, it is particularly ironic that EU institutions have evidently been financing activities that clearly interfere in the internal political debate of a Member State for a number of years. 1.

Does the Commission consider that the use of EU funds to support projects which explicitly criticise or delegitimise a specific political party constitutes a form of political interference in the democratic processes of a Member State?

Does the Commission consider it appropriate for EU-funded educational programmes to label democratic political parties in Member States as ‘fascist’ or ‘dangerous’, and how is this compatible with the principle of political neutrality?
Will the Commission commit to a full review of Erasmus+ projects to ensure that no further EU funds are used to interfere in the democratic process in the Member States?

https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/projects/search/details/2020-1-DE04-KA105-019058. https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/projects/search/details/2019-1-DE04-KA347-017648. https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/projects/search/details/2016-2-DE04-KA105-014409.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (30.6.2026) EU funds are not provided for political purposes and can only be used to support projects that fully respect the values enshrined in Article 2 of the Treaty on the European Union, namely human dignity, freedom, democracy, equality, the rule of law, and respect for human rights, and in the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union. These principles apply equally to every beneficiary, and thus persons and entities involved in activities incompatible with European values cannot receive EU financial support. Respect for fundamental rights means safeguarding freedom of thought, conscience, religion and association. This includes the right of EU fund beneficiaries to express their views while respecting the applicable laws. The Erasmus + projects subject to the Honourable Member’s question promoted democratic participation, which is not a political activity but rather the exercise of citizenship. They also promoted the common values of freedom, tolerance and non-discrimination through education and freedom of expression that are essential for true involvement of citizens in democratic processes. Beneficiaries in EU-funded educational programmes can exercise freedom of expression as long as they comply with the obligations set out in the Erasmus+ Grant Agreements1 and with the applicable EU, international and national laws, such as law on defamation, and prohibition of incitement to hatred or discrimination. There is however no obligation of political neutrality. National agencies systematically review all final reports submitted by EU-funded projects, with the aim to ensure that they fully comply with EU primary law and the obligations set out in the Grant Agreements.
1 https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/docs/2021-2027/erasmus/agr-contr/general-
mga_erasmus_en.pdf.

According to serious allegations that have been made public by the BBC1, refugees and migrants are being used brutally treat and abuse other refugees and migrants, and even carry out sexual assaults, robberies, etc. at the Greek-Turkish border in Evros. E-10-2026-001602.t: Growing medicines shortages and price increases: an acute problem
qt: to the Commission Lefteris Nikolaou-Alavanos (NI) Subject:

The imperialist war in the Middle East – a critical transit hub connecting Asia and Europe – is just the ‘tip of the iceberg’ when it comes to persistent medicine shortages. Even before the outbreak of the war, the policies of the EU, national governments and the pharmaceutical industry had brought about tragic consequences, through the increased commercialisation of medicine and health. The EU’s pharmaceutical strategy is based on maximising the profits of European pharmaceutical companies rather than meeting people’s pharmaceutical needs with adequate research, planning, production and stockpiling. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

What is its position on the dangerous situation faced by millions of patients who are suffering on account of the tragic shortages and high cost of medicine resulting from the US and Israel’s criminal attack on Iran, with the support of the EU, thanks to the Commission’s policies aimed at lining the pockets of European pharmaceutical monopolies at the expense of those suffering, with the risk of the further deterioration of their health?

What is its position on the urgent need to control all medicine stocks and prices for the duration of the US-Israeli war in the Middle East, in response to the profiteering games of pharmaceutical companies marked by shortages and high prices?

What is its position on the immediate need to produce the necessary quantities of medicines in short supply, at the pharmaceutical companies’ expense, at regulated prices and without further subsidies and concessions from the EU and national governments to the pharmaceuticals industry, which has amassed vast profits – not only during the pandemic but also more generally – by turning medicine into a commodity?

What is its position on the urgent need to control all medicine stocks and prices for the duration of the US-Israeli war in the Middle East, in response to the profiteering games of pharmaceutical companies marked by shortages and high prices?

(3 July 2026) The Commission, in collaboration with the European Medicines Agency and its Medicines Shortages Steering Group, is closely monitoring the situation and potential impact of the conflict in the Middle East on the supply of medicinal products. As of today, the Commission has not received any signals of critical shortages of medicines resulting from the conflict. The situation appears to be stable, with minimal disruption to transport of medicines and no impact on manufacturing capacity at present. Improving the availability, accessibility and affordability of medicines for EU citizens is an important objective for the Commission. The measures in the recently agreed revision of the general pharmaceutical legislation and the proposal for a Critical Medicines Act both aim to strengthen the supply chain resilience and prevent and mitigate medicines shortages in the EU. The Critical Medicines Act will for example support manufacturing of medicines within the Union. In accordance with Article 168(7) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU, decisions on pricing and reimbursement of medicines remain the responsibility of Member States, which need to respect Council Directive 89/105/EEC (1).

E-10-2026-001601.t: Ensuring a uniform single market for secondary raw materials through the circular economy act
qt: to the Commission Stefano Cavedagna (ECR) Subject:

The forthcoming circular economy act, due for publication in Q3 2026, is intended to make the EU a global leader in the circular economy by 2030 by establishing a fully integrated single market for secondary raw materials, increasing the supply of high-quality recycled materials, and stimulating demand for these materials within the EU. However, the 2026 Annual Single Market and Competitiveness Report highlights that, despite some progress, circularity in the EU is improving only slowly because of persistent barriers and fragmentation within the single market. It stressed that divergent national rules for waste and secondary raw materials continue to hinder the uptake of circular practices and create additional costs and barriers to cross-border trade, undermining both environmental ambition and the single market’s integrity. Given the EU’s circularity objectives and the current state of the single market for goods and waste: 1.

How will the Commission ensure that the forthcoming circular economy act effectively supports a functioning and integrated single market for secondary raw materials while accelerating progress on meeting the EU circularity targets?

Will the Commission base the upcoming act on Article 114 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union – the legal basis for establishing and ensuring the functioning of the single market – to provide a uniform regulatory framework and prevent further fragmentation?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (9.6.2026) A functioning and integrated single market for secondary raw materials is paramount to accelerate progress on meeting the EU circularity targets. Currently, the business case for circular economy is hampered by regulatory obstacles. Complex legislation, implemented differently across Member States, hinders the business case for circularity. Measures under the Circular Economy Act are being considered to ensure the regulatory framework is simplified and barriers within the Single Market are addressed1. Potential interventions may cover improving the recognition of the ‘end of waste’ status across Member States and the simplification, digitalisation and further harmonisation of extended producer responsibility schemes2. The Circular Economy Act proposal is under development, and as such, its precise legal basis has yet to be determined. The Commission is fully committed to ensuring that the Circular Economy Act establishes a well-functioning Single Market for secondary raw materials in line with broader sustainability and economic objectives. Further details on the legal framework will be provided in due course.
1 https://ec.europa.eu/info/law/better-regulation/have-your-say/initiatives/14812-Circular-Economy-Act_en. 2 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:52025DC0085.

(19 June 2026) The Commission fully supports the European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO), which is tasked with the crucial mission of investigating and prosecuting crimes affecting the EU’s financial interests. The EPPO is bound by the principle of rule of law in all its activities and is required to conduct its investigations impartially, in full respect of fundamental rights enshrined in the Charter of Fundamental Rights. The Commission values and respects the independence of the EPPO from all EU institutions, bodies, offices and agencies as well as the Member States, and recalls that the EPPO should be able to investigate all crimes affecting the EU budget, regardless of who committed them. In light of the above, the Commission therefore is always in favour of a respectful exchange with and about the EPPO, including as regards public authorities of the Member States, as they might otherwise unduly undermine the EPPO’s legitimacy and the trust of citizens in it. The Commission stands ready to engage with the national authorities to reiterate its firm support to the EPPO and its activities as outlined above.

E-10-2026-001598.t: Application of the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism in candidate countries
qt: to the Commission Željana Zovko (PPE) Subject:

In the context of discussions concerning the implementation and revision of the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), a stronger and more targeted focus is needed on candidate countries whose energy systems and regulatory frameworks are still in transition. In this regard: 1.

What is the Commission’s assessment of the need to take better account of the particular circumstances that candidate countries face in implementing CBAM, particularly in the energy sector, where the absence of monitoring, reporting and verification (MRV) systems and carbon pricing are leading to a change in assigned emission values?
What measures is it planning to take to ensure that generators that rely mainly on renewable sources are not disproportionately penalised for the lack of regulatory capacity at national level?

How does it intend to better align CBAM implementation with the goal of supporting decarbonisation in the EU’s neighbourhood, in order to recognise and incentivise clean energy producers, rather than discouraging them?
at: (English version) to the Commission Željana Zovko (PPE) (20 April 2026) Subject: Application of the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism in candidate countries In the context of discussions concerning the implementation and revision of the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), a stronger and more targeted focus is needed on candidate countries whose energy systems and regulatory frameworks are still in transition. In this regard: 1.

What is the Commission’s assessment of the need to take better account of the particular circumstances that candidate countries face in implementing CBAM, particularly in the energy sector, where the absence of monitoring, reporting and verification (MRV) systems and carbon pricing are leading to a change in assigned emission values?
What measures is it planning to take to ensure that generators that rely mainly on renewable sources are not disproportionately penalised for the lack of regulatory capacity at national level?

How does it intend to better align CBAM implementation with the goal of supporting decarbonisation in the EU’s neighbourhood, in order to recognise and incentivise clean energy producers, rather than discouraging them?

(9 July 2026) The Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (1) (CBAM) is an environmental measure designed to fully reflect the EU Emissions Trading System (2) (ETS). The adjustment is calculated on the basis of the emissions from industrial installations in third countries on a non-discriminatory basis. With respect to monitoring, reporting and verification (MRV), the CBAM does not rely on the existence of a national MRV system in third countries. The Commission is working closely with Member States to build up verification capacity and ensure that a sufficient number of accredited verifiers is available to verify actual emissions, including those of generators of renewable electricity. 22 national accreditation bodies in Member States have already indicated their availability to provide accreditation service s (3). The first accreditations are expected to be granted in September 2026, well ahead of the first deadline for submitting CBAM declarations by the end of September 2027. In December 2025, the Commission proposed amending the rules for electricity (4), (5) as a CBAM good with the aim of further incentivising decarbonisation of the electricity grid in the EU’s neighbourhood. First, the Commission suggested modifying the methodology used to derive default values, so as to reflect the average emission intensity of all electricity sources, including renewables. This would, on average, result in a reduction of the default value by 30% per country. Secondly, the proposal simplifies and clarifies the conditions for using actual values, in order to facilitate the declaration of actual emissions.

E-10-2026-001597.t: SMEs in the creative manufacturing sector: implementing the AI Act’s support measures concerning skills, sandboxes, templates and procurement
qt: to the Commission Stefano Cavedagna (ECR), Francesco Torselli (ECR) Subject:

A number of companies and stakeholders in the creative manufacturing industry have highlighted that AI uptake is being hampered by a lack of operational skills across the board, uncertainty about requirements, and difficulties in accessing the AI Act’s measures. In the EU, AI uptake among large companies (41 % in 2024) is significantly higher than among SMEs (13%). Articles 57, 62 and 96 and recitals 143 and 145 of the AI Act provide for support measures for SMEs and start-ups which include the provision of priority access to sandboxes, dedicated training and standard templates, as well as compliance cost reductions, the single information platform and best practices for public procurement procedures. Having regard for the requirements currently in force – which concern AI literacy (Article 4) and other matters – and the upcoming implementing measures: 1.

Could the Commission provide clarification as to the timeframe, format and content of the guidelines provided for in Article 96, specifically as regards the SMEs and sectors (including the creative manufacturing and cultural industries) that need the most help with AI?
What practical tools (short forms, minimum standards, examples for non-technical profiles) will be made available for manufacturing SMEs that have a strong creative component?

What actions will the Commission take in conjunction with the European AI Office and Member States to ensure that micro and small enterprises enjoy genuine access to European Digital Innovation Hubs and that the implementation of the measures referred to in Article 62 is monitored?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.7.2026) The guidelines on prohibited AI practices1 and on AI system definition2 were adopted in February 2025. The guidelines on the implementation of transparency obligations3 and on the classification of high-risk AI systems4 were opened for public consultation. Other guidelines listed in Article 96 of the AI Act5 are in preparation6. Besides, the framework for AI regulatory sandboxes as set out in the AI Act and in forthcoming implementing acts, Member States are supported in the implementation of AI regulatory sandboxes through tools developed in the context of the AI Board. These include templates (such as for the application form to access such sandboxes) and a guidebook that consider the specific needs and circumstances of small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). Workforce of SMEs will also benefit from other EU-funded projects, such as the AI Skills Academy, which will support AI upskilling and reskilling in key sectors such as cultural and creative industries by promoting on-the-job training and by gathering AI courses per sector and job-profile. The Commission underlines the important role of the European Digital Innovation Hubs (EDIHs) in supporting the digital transformation and AI uptake of micro, small and mediumsized enterprises. As AI experience centres, EDIHs are expected to serve as first points of contact for businesses to provide initial support and practical guidance on the AI Act, and to link SMEs to other initiatives such as testing and experimentation facilities and AI factories. The AI Office will, in cooperation with Member States, continue to support a coordinated approach to the implementation of the AI Act, including as regards AI regulatory sandboxes in the context of the AI Board and forthcoming implementing acts.

E-10-2026-001596.t: Forced evictions and palm oil in Guatemala: implications regarding the EU's responsibilities
qt: to the Commission Cristina Guarda (Verts/ALE), Catarina Vieira (Verts/ALE) Subject:

According to the Guatemalan Public Prosecutor’s Office, the number of requests for forced evictions in Guatemala increased sixfold between 2022 and 2025, from 22 to 94 and finally to 154. The Special Rapporteur on the right to adequate housing and the United Nations Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination have condemned the lack of safeguards for indigenous peoples’ lands, the abuse of the justice system to facilitate evictions, the excessive use of force and the failure to comply with international standards during evictions, and have called for a moratorium. Palm oil – Guatemala’s largest export to the EU – is produced in these context. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

What measures is it taking to ensure that imported palm oil is not linked to human rights abuses in the regions from which it originates, and what measures is it taking to prevent evictions in this context?
How does it ensure that people and communities defending land and territory in these regions can carry out their work in conditions of safety?
What measures is it taking to ensure that the territorial rights of indigenous peoples are respected in relation to investments and the production of goods traded with the EU?
at: (English version) to the Commission Cristina Guarda (Verts/ALE), Catarina Vieira (Verts/ALE) (20 April 2026) Subject: Forced evictions and palm oil in Guatemala: implications regarding the EU's responsibilities According to the Guatemalan Public Prosecutor’s Office, the number of requests for forced evictions in Guatemala increased sixfold between 2022 and 2025, from 22 to 94 and finally to 154. The Special Rapporteur on the right to adequate housing and the United Nations Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination have condemned the lack of safeguards for indigenous peoples’ lands, the abuse of the justice system to facilitate evictions, the excessive use of force and the failure to comply with international standards during evictions, and have called for a moratorium. Palm oil — Guatemala’s largest export to the EU — is produced in these context. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

What measures is it taking to ensure that imported palm oil is not linked to human rights abuses in the regions from which it originates, and what measures is it taking to prevent evictions in this context?
How does it ensure that people and communities defending land and territory in these regions can carry out their work in conditions of safety?
What measures is it taking to ensure that the territorial rights of indigenous peoples are respected in relation to investments and the production of goods traded with the EU?

(30 June 2026) To complement the annual institutional dialogue on trade and sustainable development under the EU-Central America Association Agreement (1) including Guatemala, several tools and actions are in place to promote a transition towards sustainable value chains including human rights protection. Upon entry into application of the EU Deforestation Regulation (2) (EUDR) in December 2026, operators placing on the EU market products produced with commodities originating from Guatemala (3) will have to carry out due diligence to ensure that they are deforestation free and produced in line with the relevant legislation of the Guatemala, including in terms of human rights protected under international law and the principle of free, prior and informed consent, including as set out in the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples. The Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (4) will require large companies to identify and address adverse human rights and environmental impacts in their own operations, those of their subsidiaries and in their (global) value chains. Noncompliance is subject to public and private enforcement. On the respect of territorial rights of indigenous peoples, the Global Gateway strategy supports sustainable and quality investments with high social, environmental and governance standards in full compliance with human rights obligations (5). The Neighbourhood, Development and International Cooperation Instrument — Global Europe Regulation (6) ensures the systematic application of the Human Rights Based Approach in all EU funded external actions.
