E-10-2026-001595.t: Adequacy of European policies on prevention, early intervention and personalised treatment for cases of substance use
qt: to the Commission Nikos Pappas (The Left) Subject:

The increasing use of psychoactive substances, especially amongst young people, combined with recent changes in the national legislative frameworks of some Member States, such as in Greece with Law 5129/2024, raises questions as to the adequacy and direction of prevention and treatment policies. The establishment of the National Organisation for Preventing and Combating Addiction (EOPAE) and the consolidation of rehabilitation structures under a single format raise concerns about maintaining the diversification of therapeutic approaches and personalised care, in line with users’ needs. The EU Charter of Fundamental Rights enshrines the right to life and health (Articles 2 and 35). In the EU drugs strategy and action plan for 2021-2025, the reduction of deaths, early intervention and personalised treatment services are set as priorities. The EUDA provides data, analysis and best practices, supporting the development of evidence-based and personalised policy approaches. 1.
How does the Commission assess the recent legislative changes in Greece in terms of their compatibility with the European principles of personalised, differentiated and evidence-based treatment?
How is the effective implementation of personalised and evidence-based approaches to treatment and rehabilitation structures ensured at European level?
How are systems for monitoring, collecting and comparing data on deaths and therapeutic outcomes related to substance use in the EU strengthened?
at: (English version) to the Commission Nikos Pappas (The Left) (20 April 2026) Subject: Adequacy of European policies on prevention, early intervention and personalised treatment for cases of substance use The increasing use of psychoactive substances, especially amongst young people, combined with recent changes in the national legislative frameworks of some Member States, such as in Greece with Law 5129/2024, raises questions as to the adequacy and direction of prevention and treatment policies. The establishment of the National Organisation for Preventing and Combating Addiction (EOPAE) and the consolidation of rehabilitation structures under a single format raise concerns about maintaining the diversification of therapeutic approaches and personalised care, in line with users’ needs. The EU Charter of Fundamental Rights enshrines the right to life and health (Articles 2 and 35). In the EU drugs strategy and action plan for 2021-2025, the reduction of deaths, early intervention and personalised treatment services are set as priorities. The EUDA provides data, analysis and best practices, supporting the development of evidence-based and personalised policy approaches. 1. How does the Commission assess the recent legislative changes in Greece in terms of their compatibility with the European principles of personalised, differentiated and evidence-based treatment? 2. How is the effective implementation of personalised and evidence-based approaches to treatment and rehabilitation structures ensured at European level? 3. How are systems for monitoring, collecting and comparing data on deaths and therapeutic outcomes related to substance use in the EU strengthened? (3 July 2026) The organisation, management and delivery of health services, including prevention, early intervention and treatment of substance use, are primarily the responsibility of the Member States. The Commission does not assess the compatibility of specific national measures with treatment models. The new EU Drugs Strategy (1) promotes a balanced, evidence-based and multidisciplinary approach covering prevention, treatment, care and rehabilitation to reduce drug-related harm and deaths. It identifies prevention as a key priority and calls for stronger implementation of minimum quality standards nationally. The Commission works closely with the European Union Drugs Agency (EUDA) (2), which provides data, analysis and best practices to support effective responses. Under the EU Drugs Strategy, the EUDA supports Member States in designing effective awareness-raising activities, developing guidance on minimum quality standards, and delivering advice on evidencebased prevention and treatment. Implementation is supported through expert networks, exchange of best practices and programmes such as EU4Healt h (3), including actions under the Comprehensive Approach to Mental Health (4). Monitoring is reinforced through cooperation between the EUDA and Member States and will be supported by the European Health Data Space (5), once operational. The Commission remains committed to supporting Member States in advancing evidence-based and person-centred approaches to substance use.

E-10-2026-001594.t: Obsolete infrastructure leaves farmers in Kopaida without water for their crops
qt: to the Commission Kostas Papadakis (NI) Subject:

Kopaida is one of Greece’s most fertile areas, with enormous production potential. Nonetheless, it faces an acute irrigation problem as a result of a chronic lack and obsolescence of infrastructure. This situation is born of a policy that treats water as a commodity. Water levels at Lake Yliki remain at historical lows, making it impossible to extract water using existing, outdated infrastructure. The failure to repair the necessary floating pumping station, which would allow pumping from greater depths, leaves farmers exposed to water scarcity. This issue is inextricably linked to the overall policy followed by the EU and the national government, which – through the Regulatory Authority for Waste, Energy and Water (RAAEY) – promotes the commercialisation of water. The dismantling of Local Land Improvement Organisations (TOEB) and the imposition of ‘cost recovery’ (as piloted through the Water Management Organisation in Thessaly) lead to excessive pricing and further deterioration of public land improvement works, sending production costs through the roof. In view of the above: 1.

What view does the Commission take of the unacceptable fact that farmers are deprived of water for their crops because irrigation infrastructure is deemed ‘ineligible’ or ‘costly’ on the basis of EU cost-benefit criteria, at a time when ‘green’ investments by corporate groups (e.g. in wind turbines and photovoltaics) are being heavily subsidised?

What view does the Commission take of the need for specific measures to fully and immediately compensate farmers in Kopaida for the loss of their income, waiving the restrictions in the ‘State aid’ regulations that prevent the effective protection of ordinary households?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (11.6.2026) 1. The Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) Strategic Plans (CSP)1 Regulation provides funding opportunities for irrigation and water saving projects. The Greek CSP supports investments in irrigation with EUR 342 million and in water saving and/or reuse at farm level with EUR 23 million2. Based on the principles of shared management applicable to the CAP, the project implementation and monitoring process falls under the responsibility of the Member States. The Commission therefore does not possess information on the cases mentioned by the Honourable Member. Moreover, the Water Framework Directive3 allows Member States broad flexibility in setting water pricing and related cost-recovery mechanisms, considering socio-economic, environmental, geographic, and climatic conditions, provided the environmental objectives are met. 2. The Agricultural Block Exemption Regulation (ABER)4 and the Agricultural state aid Guidelines5 allow aid for investments in irrigation under specific conditions. In case of severe drought, State aid can also be granted under the ABER and the Guidelines. Support to farmers for the loss of income can be granted under the Agricultural de minimis Regulation6. Under the recently adopted simplification package7, Member States may introduce interventions in their CSPs to grant crisis payments to farmers, but only following natural disasters, adverse climatic events or catastrophic events, in addition to the already existing CAP support to the restoration of the agricultural production potential.

E-10-2026-001593.t: Amendment to Slovak Act No 280/2017 on subsidies in agriculture threatens EU financial interests
qt: to the Commission Tomáš Zdechovský (PPE), Miriam Lexmann (PPE), Ľubica Karvašová (Renew), Veronika Cifrová Ostrihoňová (Renew), Lucia Yar (Renew), Michal Wiezik (Renew) Subject:
Amendment to Slovak Act No 280/2017 on subsidies in agriculture threatens EU financial interests

Recent legislative changes in Slovakia, in particular the amendment to Act No 280/2017 on the provision of support and subsidies in agriculture and for rural development1, raise serious concerns regarding the protection of the financial interests of the European Union. According to available information2, the already amended legal framework does not exclude applicants from receiving EU funds even if they are under criminal investigation, charged, or even finally convicted. The suspension of subsidy payments is intended to apply only to a limited range of criminal offences, while serious offences such as fraud reportedly do not fall among the grounds for automatic exclusion. In light of previous cases of irregularities and investigations concerning the misuse of European funds in Slovakia, this change may pose a risk of continued disbursement of funds to entities associated with fraudulent activities. 1.
Is the Commission aware of this legislative change, specifically the amendment to Act No 280/2017, and is it monitoring its impact with regard to the protection of the EU’s financial interests?
Does the Commission consider this framework, as currently set, to be compatible with EU rules on sound financial management and fraud prevention?
What specific steps does the Commission intend to take if there is a risk that EU funds may be disbursed to entities involved in fraudulent activities?

https://www.slov-lex.sk/ezbierky/pravne-predpisy/SK/ZZ/2017/280/. https://zastavmekorupciu.sk/kauzy/takacov-rezort-pustil-agrodotacie-aj-obvinenym-pomaha-to-projektomakofafokan/?fbclid=IwY2xjawRLFXRleHRuA2FlbQIxMABicmlkETF2WXFVb2VrVzJSSlVReVphc3J0YwZh cHBfaWQQMjIyMDM5MTc4ODIwMDg5M.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (10.6.2026) The Commission is aware from media reports of the legislative changes adopted by Slovak authorities. The Directorate-General for Agriculture and Rural Development (DG AGRI) has contacted the Slovak authorities asking clarifications about the changes introduced, as the media reports contain contradicting information. The reply was received on 29 April 2026. The Commission is now assessing the reply in light of the applicable EU legal framework, including rules governing the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), and will take action, where necessary, for the protection of the EU’s financial interests. The issue is also being followed up in the framework of an ongoing audit conducted by DG AGRI assessing the compliance of the Slovak paying agency responsible for the management and control of CAP payments with the applicable accreditation criteria, including those related to antifraud measures. As the audit is ongoing, the Commission is not in a position to provide further comments in order to safeguard the integrity of the audit process.

E-10-2026-001592.t: Suspension of EU funds at the Venice Biennale because of the Russian Pavilion
qt: to the Commission Anna Maria Cisint (PfE), Silvia Sardone (PfE), Isabella Tovaglieri (PfE) Subject:

The Commission has suspended some EUR 2 million for the Venice Biennale in funding allocated to the Venice Biennale, citing the Foundation’s decision to allow the Russian pavilion to participate in the International Art Exhibition. This decision, made in the name of protecting European values, intervenes in an internationally prominent cultural event and raises questions about the role of EU institutions in the artistic choices of independent entities. At the same time, an apparent inconsistency is evident, as countries with controversial political systems – such as Syria (ranked 162nd in the Democracy Index), Iran, the ‘warlord’ regime (152nd), Saudi Arabia (147th), China (142nd), and Cuba (135th) – have not been subject to similar measures or restrictions within the framework of cultural initiatives supported or allowed at EU level. In the light of the above: 1.

Does the Commission consider direct intervention in artistic and organisational decisions by an independent institution such as the Venice Biennale to be compatible with the EU’s principle of cultural neutrality?
Why are similar measures not taken against other countries involved in international disputes, thus mitigating the risk of EU funds being applied in a selective and politicised manner?

(23 June 2026) Culture promotes and safeguards democratic values, fosters open dialogue, diversity and freedom of expression, and should never be used as a platform for propaganda. The decision by Biennale to allow Russia to re-open its national pavilion is not compatible with the EU's collective response to the Kremlin's war of aggression. In particular, it is not compatible with the sanctions regime (1), which aims to safeguard the protection of the principles of rule of law, democracy and media pluralism. By not respecting EU sanctions, Biennale undermines EU values. While the Commission does not fund Biennale of Arts, Biennale benefits from a contract under Creative Europe MEDIA, under which it commits to ensure the respect of basic EU values and professional standards. As a result of the decision on Russia’s participation in Biennale of Arts, the Commission has informed Biennale of the intention to suspend or terminate the contract. In response to Russia’s military aggression against Ukraine, the EU has massively expanded its sanctions, adopting unprecedented measures with the aim of weakening Russia's economic base, depriving it of critical technologies and markets, and significantly curtailing its ability to wage war. The Commission monitors the implementation and enforcement of EU sanctions by the Member States. It is in direct contact with the Italian authorities to understand how compliance with Council Regulation (EU) No 833/2014 has been ensured.

E-10-2026-001591.t: Equal treatment of sport shooting disciplines under the proposed lead shot restrictions
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (9.6.2026) The Commission proposal for a restriction under Regulation (EC) No 1907/2006 on Registration, Evaluation, Authorisation and Restriction of Chemicals (REACH) of lead gunshot1 includes a derogation allowing the use and sale of lead shot of sizes between 1.9 mm and 2.6 mm at outdoor shooting ranges that have specific risk management measures in place to contain lead emissions. The derogation was introduced to preserve athletes’ ability to train for Olympic disciplines, and the possibility for Member States to host the Olympic Games, as the socio-economic impact of renouncing to the Olympic games was considered too high. In addition, Olympic disciplines are the most widely practiced disciplines across Europe and the world. They are also governed by strict rules, such as the Olympic Charter2 and the World Anti-Doping Code3. In general, derogations are based on evidence provided by the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA) of (1) whether, among other things, risks (lead emissions in this case) from the derogated use can be controlled through risk management measures and (2) the socioeconomic consequences of not having a derogation. The reasons behind all derogations are stated in ECHA’s restriction dossier and in the recitals of the Commission restriction proposal. The limited information concerning lead emissions from practical shooting provided during the call for evidence and the two public consultations run by ECHA while developing the restriction dossier does not provide sufficient evidence to support a derogation for this sport. Moreover, the emissions cannot be controlled through risk management measures. The factual situation for practical shooting is hence fundamentally different from the uses derogated by the restriction proposal.

1 https://ec.europa.eu/transparency/comitology-register/screen/documents/105447/6. 2 https://olympians.org/library/olympic_charter.pdf. 3 https://www.olympics.com/athlete365/articles/Anti-Doping/world-anti-doping-code.

qt: to the Commission Lynn Boylan (The Left) Subject:

Directive 2004/38/EC1 enshrines the right of freedom of movement for EU citizens, giving them the right to live and work in other Member States. Article 5 of this directive provides for a right of entry for family members who are non-EU nationals, when accompanying an EU citizen. Any visas required for these family members should be granted as quickly as possible and on the basis of an accelerated procedure. However, in Ireland visa applications and appeals for the family members of EU citizens are currently being processed with a six-month delay. This leaves EU citizens and their families in limbo for months when they are trying to avail of their right to freedom of movement. 1.
Is a six-month wait for visa decisions for the family members of EU citizens in line with the requirements of Directive 2004/38/EC to process these visas as quickly as possible?
Has the Commission identified any other ways in which Ireland is not adequately fulfilling the requirements of Directive 2004/38/EC?

Directive 2004/38/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 29 April 2004 on the right of citizens of the Union and their family members to move and reside freely within the territory of the Member States (OJ L 158, 30.4.2004, p. 77, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2004/38/oj).
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (8.6.2026) As noted in the Guidance on the right of free movement of EU citizens and their families1, the Commission considers that processing times for visa applications of non-EU family members exceeding 15 days should be exceptional and duly justified and delays of more than four weeks are not reasonable. Since 2016, the Commission has been in dialogue with the Irish authorities regarding the processing times for visas requested by family members of EU citizens. Regular meetings are held to discuss the situation. The Commission welcomes the efforts and commitment of the Irish authorities to remedy the situation. The Commission continues to monitor the correct transposition and implementation of the Free Movement Directive2 by Ireland.

E-10-2026-001589.t: Ban on the trade of shark fins
qt: to the Commission Isabella Lövin (Verts/ALE), Pär Holmgren (Verts/ALE), Alice Kuhnke (Verts/ALE) Subject:

The European Citizens’ Initiative ‘Stop Finning – Stop the Trade’ gathered over 1.1 million signatures and calls on the Commission to introduce a ban on the trade in shark fins, including import, export and transit, even when the fins are still naturally attached to the body. The Commission has announced that an impact assessment will be carried out, but no clear timeline for follow-up or a legislative proposal has yet been presented. 1.
When will the Commission present a legislative proposal to follow up on the initiative?
Will the Commission introduce a full ban on the trade in shark fins, including fins that are still naturally attached to the body?
What is the exact timeline for these measures, especially following the call for evidence in February 2024 that provided an indicative timeline until the end of 2025?1
https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=intcom:Ares(2024)1369533.
at: (English version) to the Commission Isabella Lövin (Verts/ALE), Pär Holmgren (Verts/ALE), Alice Kuhnke (Verts/ALE) (17 April 2026) Subject: Ban on the trade of shark fins The European Citizens’ Initiative ‘Stop Finning — Stop the Trade’ gathered over 1.1 million signatures and calls on the Commission to introduce a ban on the trade in shark fins, including import, export and transit, even when the fins are still naturally attached to the body. The Commission has announced that an impact assessment will be carried out, but no clear timeline for follow-up or a legislative proposal has yet been presented. 1.
When will the Commission present a legislative proposal to follow up on the initiative?

2. Will the Commission introduce a full ban on the trade in shark fins, including fins that are still naturally attached to the body? 3. What is the exact timeline for these measures, especially following the call for evidence in February 2024 that provided an indicative timeline until the end of 2025? (1) (29 May 2026) The European Citizens Initiative (ECI) ‘Stop Finning — Stop the Trade’ requested the Commission to introduce a ban on ‘export and import of loose fins within and through the EU’. The Commission responded to this initiative in a communication of 5 July 2023 (1) setting out a triple course of action. First, continue making the best use of its existing policy tools relevant to shark conservation and management, and step up its international outreach to protect endangered sharks and ensure that the commercial shark populations remain healthy. Second, increase the EU’s capacity to monitor trade in shark products at species level. Third, assess the environmental, social and economic consequences of measures suggested by the ECI and alternative policy measures. While implementation and enforcement efforts are ongoing, the introduction of new EU commodity codes in 2024 has produced the first annual data on EU trade in shark fins at species level. In line with its commitment to evidence-based decision making, the Commission organised a call for evidence and a thorough public consultation, followed by an external study to gain an overview of the state of the global shark populations, shark fishing activities, existing regulations, trade routes and markets for shark products. This study, finalised at the end of March 2026, also provides an initial assessment of a set of policy options, including an EU trade ban on detached shark fins requested by the ECI. Based on these elements, the Commission impact assessment is expected in the second half of the year. Any specific measures and relevant timelines will depend on the results of the impact assessment.

E-10-2026-001587.t: Circumvention of EU law in environmental impact assessments
qt: to the Commission Marcin Sypniewski (ESN) Subject:

Administrative measures such as changing local government boundaries are being used in many Member States to avoid obligations under EU environmental legislation, particularly Directive 2011/92/EU. In addition, some installations subject to Directives 2011/92/EU, 1999/31/EC and 2008/98/EC have not been subject to a full, up-to-date environmental impact assessment for many years, while public participation is de facto restricted, despite clear opposition from local communities. Given this: 1.

Does the Commission consider the use of changing administrative boundaries to avoid obligations under Directive 2011/92/EU and the related requirements of Directive 1999/31/EC to potentially constitute circumvention of EU law requiring intervention at EU level?

Will the Commission take action against a Member State when an installation subject to Directives 2011/92/EU, 1999/31/EC and 2008/98/EC is operating without an up-to-date environmental impact assessment and with de facto limited public participation?
What criteria does the Commission apply when assessing whether repeated cases such as these already constitute a systemic breach of EU law, justifying the initiation of infringement proceedings?

(7 July 2026) The Environmental Impact Assessment Directive (EIA Directive) (1) applies to certain public and private projects listed in its Annex I and II and provides that Member States must ensure that, before authorisation, projects likely to have significant effects on the environment by virtue, inter alia, of their nature, size or location are made subject to an assessment of the environmental effects. The Landfill Directive (2) ensures a progressive reduction of landfilling and prevents negative effects on the environment and health by requiring permits, monitoring and after-care. Changing administrative boundaries is not a triggering factor for the application of the EIA Directive. The Commission has no information showing that such changes lead to avoidance of obligations of the Landfill Directive. The EIA Directive applies before the authorisation of projects. An assessment in accordance with that directive, where required, must be carried out before the execution of any project falling within its scope. The Commission may decide to take the necessary measures, including opening infringement cases, and has taken several Member States to Court of Justice of the European Union for breaches of the Landfill and the EIA Directives. The Commission focuses and prioritises its enforcement efforts on the most important and structural breaches of EU law affecting the interests of its citizens and business (3).

qt: to the Commission Nicolás González Casares (S&D) Subject:

After analysing the content of the trade agreement negotiated by the EU and Indonesia, the European fisheries sector has discovered that the European Commission has not only established tariff-free quotas for canned tuna and tuna loins, but has also eliminated tariffs on fresh fillets and, in seven years’ time, on frozen fillets. Indonesia is the world’s leading country for tuna catches and ranks ninth for prepared or preserved tuna. It is also the largest exporter of tuna loins to the EU in the ASEAN region. At the same time, the country is facing allegations of illegal, unregulated and unreported fishing, as well as allegations of forced labour. If so, could it provide the details of that analysis and of the support measures planned to minimise the negative impacts?
Does it intend to strengthen health audits in view of the ‘major shortcomings’ identified by the Commission in the past?
What is its explanation for scrapping tariffs on tuna fillets?

(29 June 2026) The EU and Indonesia finalised negotiations on the Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreemen t (1) (CEPA) in September 2025. The Commission has shared with the co-legislators all the EU tariff offers during the negotiations and the outcome upon their finalisation. The texts were then publicly released. The EU negotiating team has also engaged regularly with stakeholders, including the EU canning and fishing industry, throughout the CEPA talks. The CEPA achieves unprecedented levels of liberalisation, opening up opportunities for EU businesses, while carefully handling EU sensitivities and potential impacts on concerned sectors. It achieves for fish products a well-balanced outcome: it ensures modalities to avoid disruptions for EU industry, through strict rules of origin for all tuna products and tariff-rate quotas calibrated on current trade flows for canned tuna (800 metric tonnes) and for tuna loins (5 000 metric tonnes). For frozen tuna fillets, the CEPA is aligned with the tariff elimination treatment granted in most Free Trade Agreements concluded by the EU, combined with a seven-year transitional period. The CEPA also secures robust commitments on fighting against illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing, and on the effective implementation of the International Labour Organisation core labour standards and ratified conventions. The report of the last audit carried out in 2020 concluded that the official control system developed by Indonesia is based on largely adequate procedures. Deficiencies were detected, to which Indonesia responded with an action plan and written guarantees that were positively assessed. The Commission plans to conduct a follow-up audit in Indonesia in the near future.

E-10-2026-001585.t: Risk of aviation fuel shortages in the European Union due to the war in the Middle East
qt: to the Commission Elena Kountoura (The Left) Subject:

The European Union is confronted with immediate risks to its energy security and the unhindered functioning of critical infrastructure, as the war in the Middle East is evolving into the most significant energy crisis of recent decades1. The head of the International Energy Agency, Fatih Birol, has warned that Europe has ‘maybe six weeks or so of jet fuel left’, highlighting the risk of imminent disruptions to aviation in the event of a prolonged disruption of energy flows2. Taking into account that the Airports Council International Europe has warned that Europe may face a systemic shortage of aviation fuel within three weeks if activity in the Strait of Hormuz is not restored, calling for urgent and coordinated action at EU level3, that the summer tourist season is approaching and that air transport – especially in countries with very high levels of tourism activity such as Greece – is expected to increase significantly, can the Commission say: 1.
Does it confirm the above, and what is its assessment of the adequacy of the aviation fuel supply and the availability of aviation fuel across the EU?

What measures does it intend to take to prevent and manage any disruptions to the functioning of the European aviation network and to safeguard the rights of air passengers in the event of flight cancellations or price increases?
What measures is it planning to ensure adequate air connectivity, in particular for island and remote areas of the EU, and for tourist destinations, in view of the summer season?

The shipping route through which around a fifth of global crude oil and liquefied natural gas supplies passed before the war has almost come to a complete standstill since its outbreak on 28 February. According to the Financial Times, around 40 % of the global supply of aviation fuel passes through the Strait of Hormuz. https://apnews.com/video/europe-has-maybe-6-weeks-of-jet-fuel-left-energy-agency-head-tells-apd78d8b0e004d45a1b6368870dcaad2a7. https://www.euronews.com/business/2026/04/10/airport-council-warns-hormuz-closure-poses-major-fuelshortage-risks.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (10.6.2026) 1. As confirmed during the weekly meetings of the Oil Coordination Group with Member States and Industry representatives, while the stock level of some fuels has decreased, there is no immediate threat to the security of supply in the EU. To strengthen preparedness, and as announced in the AccelerateEU Communication1, the Commission is establishing a fuel observatory to monitor EU production, imports, exports and fuel stocks. This will improve visibility over supply and demand, help detect shortages, and support targeted action such as alternative sourcing or coordinated stock releases in the EU. 2. As announced in the AccelerateEU Communication, the Commission also issued, on 8 May 2026, guidance on the flexibilities offered by EU aviation legislation to ensure a coordinated response across Member States2. This covers airport slots3, travellers and passenger rights4, fuel uplift obligations under ReFuelEU Aviation5, Public Service Obligations (PSOs)6, and the use of alternative jet fuel sources. Specifically on passenger and traveller rights, the guidance recalls the strong protection granted under EU law, including concerning the rules on price transparency. 3. The Commission recognises the specific challenges faced by islands, where air connectivity is essential. The AccelerateEU Communication addresses the potential impact of fuel supply disruptions and sets out measures to preserve the proper functioning of the Single Market while safeguarding essential air connectivity across the EU, including island regions.

E-10-2026-001584.t: Exclusion of stateless persons from the extraordinary regularisation process
qt: to the Commission Isabel Serra Sánchez (The Left) Subject:

On 15 April, the extraordinary regularisation process in Spain entered into force. However, the decree excludes individuals seeking the status of statelessness, a measure that primarily affects the Sahrawi population, who make up 96% of this group in Spain. Notably, this exclusion does not apply to other groups also covered by specific international protection statuses, such as asylum seekers According to the 2023 Statelessness Index, people who have applied for the status of statelessness face severe barriers when it comes to accessing basic rights such as healthcare and employment while they are awaiting a decision regarding their application, leaving them in a situation of complete vulnerability. Taking account of Article 15 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, which lays down the right to a nationality, and Articles 1, 15 and 21 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the EU, which lay down the rights to human dignity, the right to work and non-discrimination respectively: 1.
Does the Commission consider that the exclusion of people who have applied for the status of statelessness from the regularisation process could constitute discrimination?

Does it consider that the barriers to accessing basic rights currently faced by people who have applied for the status of statelessness in Spain comply with the obligations to provide special protection for this group?

E-10-2026-001583.t: Children’s online safety – from bans to proactive protection
qt: to the Commission Friedrich Pürner (NI) Subject:
Children’s online safety – from bans to proactive protection

Children’s online safety is a growing concern. EU policy remains reliant on risk frameworks, access rules, bans and other control mechanisms. There is evidence to suggest that restrictions, bans and monitoring are ineffective or even counterproductive1. Applying the same restrictions to very different technologies and to children of different ages and in different stages of development can weaken trust, limit children’s rights and agency, and push digital consumption into other online spaces. An evidence-based approach would 1) use scientific instruments to assess and improve design options, 2) anticipate risks and treat children’s safety as a proactive design challenge and 3) establish preventative guardrails that protect children while also supporting their rights, agency and well-being. 1.
Is the Commission, jointly with the Member States, considering a proactive and systematic approach, recognising children as active participants?
Is the Commission considering aligning its policy with evidence that supports the promotion of rights, safety and privacy by design, as reflected in international legal instruments?
Is the Commission considering increasing support for disciplinary and interdisciplinary research to close gaps in understanding the interplay between risks, opportunities and digital environments?
Cortesi, S., & Gasser, U. (2026). Digital child safety at the frontier: From evidence to action. Science (New York, N.Y.), 392(6793), 30-32. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aec7804.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (23.6.2026) The Commission is strengthening interdisciplinary evidence gathering. A Special Panel was established with a mandate to draw up recommendations to the President of the Commission on child safety online and potential age restrictions1. It brings together youth representatives and experts from health, neuroscience, technology and the child rights field. The panel has held two meetings thus far, assessing the evidence of risks and opportunities for minors in digital environments and how to strengthen existing rules. Building upon the EU’s toolbox for protecting minors online, and based on the independent, evidence-based input from experts, the co-chairs of the panel will submit their recommendations by July 2026. Moreover, the EU has already in place comprehensive framework for protecting, and empowering minors online. In particular, the Digital Services Act (DSA)2 requires the providers of all platforms accessible to minors to ensure a high level of privacy, safety, and security. The guidelines on the protection of minors3 under the DSA are based on the principle of respecting children’s rights, privacy, safety, and security by design. Complementing these efforts, the Better Internet for Kids strategy supports safer and more age-appropriate digital environments with the involvement of children in policymaking as one of its core pillars, including through initiatives such as the Youth Ambassadors programme. The upcoming Digital Fairness Act4 aims to strengthen consumer protection online with a particular focus on minors.

E-10-2026-001582.t: Public launch of a European age verification app for online child protection
qt: to the Commission Friedrich Pürner (NI) Subject:

On 15 April 2026, the Commission unveiled a digital app for age verification online1. The Commission President described the functioning of the EU age verification app as ‘completely anonymous’. However, there are significant doubts as to whether the complete anonymity claimed by the Commission can actually be guaranteed in practice. 1.

How will the Commission ensure that, when implementing the measure at national level, issuing authorities do not carry out any form of logging that would allow individual users to be identified, and what control and verification mechanisms will be put in place to effectively monitor compliance in the Member States with the anonymity guarantee claimed by the Commission?

What binding technical and legal requirements exist to prevent additional metadata such as IP addresses, device identifiers or timestamps from being collected, stored or analysed in the applications or the associated backend systems?
How will the Commission ensure that the age verification function is not linked to other state or private systems, thereby enabling subsequent identification or profiling?
https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/statement_26_817.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (23.6.2026) To ensure that data protection and security requirements are fulfilled, age verification solutions will be assessed and approved by the Commission in accordance with Commission Recommendation (EU) 2026/10351. The rules and requirements for the assessment will be established in the age verification attestation of attributes scheme based on Article 8 of Implementing Regulation (EU) 1569/20252, the Age Verification Blueprint3, the Electronic Identification, Authentication and Trust Services Regulation (eIDAS)4, the Network and Information Security Directive5, the Cyber Resilience Act6 and the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)7. Providers of EU age verification solutions are trust service providers under eIDAS8 and they are required to set up internal risk management processes and notify the Commission of any security breaches. Their operations are subject to supervision by national authorities. GDPR ensures that data protection rights of citizens are protected, and this applies to age verification providers. Age verification solutions must not communicate any information identifying the user. Any privacy invasive measures are prohibited, and compliance will be assessed by the Commission and national supervisory authorities. It is technically not possible to keep IP addresses, device identifiers or timestamps fully private. However, EU age verification solutions ensure that this kind of information cannot be linked to the identity of the person who uses them.

E-10-2026-001579.t: EU action to implement a whale stranding emergency plan
qt: to the Commission Sebastian Everding (The Left), Anja Hazekamp (The Left), Tilly Metz (Verts/ALE), Sigrid Friis (Renew), Villy Søvndal (Verts/ALE), Manuela Ripa (PPE), Tomáš Kubín (PfE), Rasmus Nordqvist (Verts/ALE) Subject:

Whale strandings in European waters are not isolated incidents, but can signal broader ecosystem disturbances. The recent case of ‘Timmy’ in the Baltic Sea highlights cumulative pressures such as underwater noise, bycatch, ghost nets and pollution, and underlines the need for coordinated action at EU level. Under frameworks such as the EU Habitats Directive and the Marine Strategy Framework Directive, stranded whales are protected species and important indicators of marine ecosystem health. Their deaths may point to shortcomings in mitigating human-induced pressures and gaps in monitoring, coordination and prevention. While instruments such as Council Regulation (EC) No 812/2004, the Agreement on the Conservation of Small Cetaceans of the Baltic, North East Atlantic, Irish and North Seas and the Agreement on the Conservation of Cetaceans of the Black Sea, Mediterranean Sea and contiguous Atlantic Area address bycatch, monitoring and regional cooperation, they do not provide for a comprehensive, EU-wide emergency response mechanism for strandings. By contrast, several non-EU countries have established coordinated national response systems. In the light of the increasing number of strandings and the fragmented policy landscape: 1.
What actions is the Commission taking to protect marine ecosystems, in particular cetaceans?
Does the Commission intend to propose a coordinated EU-wide emergency plan for whale and marine mammal strandings?
How does the Commission assess the effectiveness of current EU and regional frameworks in responding to and preventing whale strandings?

(7 July 2026) The long-term protection and recovery of cetaceans and marine ecosystems on which they depend is ensured through a comprehensive EU legal framework. The Habitats Directive (1) requires Member States to establish a system of strict protection for certain specie s (2) prohibiting their deliberate disturbance, capture or killing, and safeguarding their breeding and resting areas, complemented where appropriate by the designation of Natura 2000 sites. The directive also requires Member States to establish a system to monitor incidental capture and killing of cetaceans and take appropriate preventive measures. The Marine Strategy Framework Directive (MSFD) (3) requires Member States to achieve good environmental status of their marine waters, including by reducing pressures like bycatch, underwater noise and pollution.

Council Directive 92/43/EEC of 21 May 1992 on the conservation of natural habitats and of wild fauna and flora, OJ L 206, 22.7.1992, pp. 7-50. Including all cetaceans. Directive 2008/56/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 17 June 2008 establishing a framework for community action in the field of marine environmental policy, OJ L 164, 25.6.2008, pp. 19-40.

The common fisheries policy (4) aims to minimise and, where possible, eliminate incidental catches of sensitive species (5). The Commission also works with regional fisheries management organisations to protect vulnerable species from interactions with fisheries (6), promotes consistent maritime spatial planning to minimise conflicts at sea, and supports Member States with guidance documents (7), funding opportunities (8), and by taking legal action where appropriate (9). The Commission considers that, due to the specific nature of individual cases, whale and marine mammal strandings are most appropriately dealt with by national and regional authorities. Member States have sufficient tools under the existing legal framework to take such action. The Commission assesses (10) Member States’ marine strategies under the MSFD and provides guidance (11). It is currently working on reviewing (12) the directive, following its recent evaluation (13).

And in particular the Technical Measures Regulation — Regulation (EU) 2019/1241 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 20 June 2019 on the conservation of fisheries resources and the protection of marine ecosystems through technical measures, amending Council Regulations (EC) No 1967/2006, (EC) No 1224/2009 and Regulations (EU) No 1380/2013, (EU) 2016/1139, (EU) 2018/973, (EU) 2019/472 and (EU) 2019/1022 of the European Parliament and of the Council, and repealing Council Regulations (EC) No 894/97, (EC) No 850/98, (EC) No 2549/2000, (EC) No 254/2002, (EC) No 812/2004 and (EC) No 2187/2005, OJ L 198, 25.7.2019, pp. 105-201. For this endeavour, the Commission supports Member States in adopting bycatch mitigation measures through regionalisation, such as those adopted for harbour porpoises in the Baltic Sea and common dolphins in the Bay of Biscay. The latter includes a call to promote the harmonised and standardised collection of stranding data. E-10-2026-001578.t: Application of PPWR reuse targets to insulated fish boxes in the EU fresh seafood sector
qt: to the Commission Stéphanie Yon-Courtin (Renew) Subject:

The regulation on packaging and packaging waste (PPWR) will take full effect in August 2026. However, certain requirements of this regulation pose implementation challenges for operators in the fresh seafood sector, where the use of insulated fish boxes is essential to protect seafood products from contamination, bacterial growth and other hazards. These operators are particularly concerned about the reuse targets set out in Article 29 of the PPWR, which prove to be inadequate for insulated fish boxes, risk affecting the logistics chain and the viability of the sector and would pose food safety risks to consumers. Importantly, the Commission’s impact assessment underpinning the PPWR did not assess specialised temperature-controlled transport packaging such as insulated fish boxes. 1.

Given that insulated fish boxes were not included in the impact assessment’s reuse modelling (switching tables, datasets, system assumptions), can the Commission state unequivocally whether insulated fish boxes fall within or outside the scope of the reuse targets set out in Article 29?

If the Commission considers insulated fish boxes to be within the scope, will it commit to adopting a delegated act that formally exempts insulated boxes in direct contact with food from these reuse target requirements?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (10.7.2026) Under Article 29 of the Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (PPWR)1, the reuse targets apply to transport packaging or sales packaging used for transporting products, in the form of pallets, foldable-plastic boxes, boxes, trays, plastic crates, intermediate bulk containers, pails, drums and canisters of any size or material, including flexible formats or pallet wrappings or straps for stabilisation and protection of products put on pallets during transport. On that basis, insulated fish boxes fall within the scope of the reuse targets set out in Article 29 of the PPWR. The Commission is preparing the implementing act under Article 30 of the PPWR to establish a practical methodology for calculating the reuse targets, while further clarifying the packaging formats covered by Article 29. Any consideration of an exemption for insulated fish boxes in direct contact with fresh fish under Article 29(18) would require a comprehensive assessment carried out by the Commission, considering the availability of reusable alternatives at scale. In this context, the Commission is mandating the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) to issue a scientific opinion about food safety risks of reusable fish boxes, which should be delivered in 2027.

E-10-2026-001577.t: Commission’s assessment of Hungary’s announced withdrawal from the ICC Rome Statute
qt: to the Commission Tineke Strik (Verts/ALE), Birgit Sippel (S&D), Mounir Satouri (Verts/ALE), Krzysztof Śmiszek (S&D), Villy Søvndal (Verts/ALE), Rasmus Nordqvist (Verts/ALE), Catarina Vieira (Verts/ALE), Cristina Guarda (Verts/ALE), Leoluca Orlando (Verts/ALE), Daniel Freund (Verts/ALE), Kim Van Sparrentak (Verts/ALE), Manon Aubry (The Left), Per Clausen (The Left), Hanna Gedin (The Left), Brando Benifei (S&D) Subject:

On 3 April 2025, the Hungarian Government announced its withdrawal from the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court (ICC). In May 2025, Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy, Kaja Kallas, indicated that the Commission was analysing Hungary’s announced withdrawal in the light of the EU acquis1. Hungary is currently bound by the Rome Statute, and has been referred to the Assembly of States Parties for non-compliance with the ICC arrest warrant against Benjamin Netanyahu during his visit from 2 to 6 April 20252. 1.

With regard to the analysis, can the Commission clarify: (a) whether the analysis is still ongoing and, if so, whether the results will be shared with Parliament and the public; (b) whether the analysis has been terminated or paused and, if so, why; and (c) whether the Commission can commit to publishing the results, including its conclusion on the potential violation of the EU acquis, before Hungary’s withdrawal enters into force on 2 June 20263?
Does the Commission agree with Parliament’s assessment4 that withdrawal from the Rome Statute would violate the EU acquis, including Articles 2 and 4(3) of the Treaty on European Union?
Will the Commission publicly denounce Hungary’s failure to comply with the ICC arrest warrant against Benjamin Netanyahu, considering his second planned visit on 21 March 20265?

Answer to Written Question P-001396/2025, ‘Hungary’s withdrawal from the Rome Statute’, 13 May 2025, https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/P-10-2025-001396-ASW_EN.html. Vilmos, W., ‘Benjamin Netanyahu to travel to Budapest in March’, Telex, 8 February 2026, https://telex.hu/belfold/2026/02/08/netanjahu-budapest.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.7.2026) The EU remains a steadfast supporter of international criminal justice, particularly the International Criminal Court (ICC), in its mission to ensure accountability for the most serious crimes under international law. The EU has consistently called upon all States to ensure full cooperation with the ICC to comply with their obligations under international law and as State Parties to the Rome Statute, including by the prompt execution of outstanding arrest warrants, and to protect the Court’s impartiality and independence in the pursuit of accountability around the world. The EU will continue to cooperate with the ICC in the framework of their Agreement on cooperation and assistance1, including, pursuant to Article 6 of the Agreement, by adopting initiatives to promote the dissemination of the principles, values and provisions of the Statute. Article 127 of the Rome Statute allows for states to withdraw from the ICC, by written notification addressed to the Secretary-General of the UN. However, withdrawal takes effect one year after notification of the depositary. The withdrawing State is obliged to continue fulfilling its obligations (financial obligations and obligations of cooperation with the ICC). In this context, the EU notes that the government of Hungary recently announced its intention to reverse the decision to withdraw from the Rome Statute, and that Parliament voted on 27 May 2026 on a bill to revoke Hungary’s withdrawal from the ICC, which was notified by Hungary to the Secretary-General of the United Nations on 29 May 2026.

E-10-2026-001576.t: Simplification of the Pay Transparency Directive
qt: to the Commission François-Xavier Bellamy (PPE), Isabelle Le Callennec (PPE), Christophe Gomart (PPE) Subject:

Directive 2023/970 on pay transparency aims to strengthen equal pay between women and men. It must be transposed by the Member States by 7 June 2026. Some of its provisions require companies to provide information on pay levels upon request from workers and to disclose data relating to pay gaps. Several Member States have already put mechanisms in place. However, some of these preexisting national obligations differ significantly from the indicators set out in the directive, which complicates companies’ adaptation and risks generating additional compliance costs. Furthermore, in the current context, regaining competitiveness has made it essential to simplify the regulatory framework and reduce the burden on businesses. In this spirit, the Commission has presented several omnibus packages aimed at easing certain obligations affecting our economies. 1.
Is the Commission considering including the Pay Transparency Directive in a future omnibus package?

Is the Commission considering introducing certain flexibilities for companies already subject to national obligations promoting equal pay, in order to limit their costs and allow for gradual adaptation?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (23.6.2026) The Commission does not intend to include the Pay Transparency Directive1 in any future omnibus regulatory simplification package, as it considers the Directive to be essential for the full realisation of the right to equal pay between men and women. The Pay Transparency Directive introduces proportionate pay transparency obligations, with reporting dates and periods that vary depending on the size of the companies2. It also provides flexibility concerning methodologies to guide the assessment and comparison of work of equal value by employers3 and allows the use of administrative data to assist companies in fulfilling their pay reporting obligations4. To facilitate the implementation of the Directive, the Commission has held implementation workshops with Member States and social partners, covering all of its provisions. The Commission has also made funding available via the 2024 and 2026 Citizens, Equality, Rights and Values programme to support employers with pay reporting5. Furthermore, the Commission and the European Institute for Gender Equality published an EU-wide toolkit to aid employers when carrying out gender-neutral job evaluations and classifications6.

E-10-2026-001575.t: Claude Mythos and the cybersecurity risks facing the EU
qt: to the Commission Leila Chaibi (The Left), Kim Van Sparrentak (Verts/ALE), Manon Aubry (The Left), David Cormand (Verts/ALE), Damien Carême (The Left), Pernando Barrena Arza (The Left), Elena Kountoura (The Left), Emma Rafowicz (S&D), Arash Saeidi (The Left), Rima Hassan (The Left), Jussi Saramo (The Left) Subject:

On 7 April 2026, Anthropic announced that it would not be releasing its upcoming artificial intelligence model, Claude Mythos Preview, to the public. According to its developers, the model’s capabilities in detecting and exploiting software vulnerabilities are so advanced that Claude Mythos has already identified hundreds of critical flaws in programmes that had already undergone millions of tests. Anthropic also announced a private initiative, Project Glasswing, enabling a select group of US companies and organisations to have their vulnerabilities remediated ahead of any public disclosure. As the Center for AI Safety1 has noted, time is of the essence for the EU. By Anthropic’s own admission, Claude Mythos holds only a six to twelve-month lead over its open-source competitors. Without an immediate and public response, the EU’s digital ecosystem faces severe exposure to an anticipated surge in cyberattacks. 1.
What cybersecurity strategy does the Commission intend to put in place in order to avert a potential EU ‘cybergeddon’?
How will it support the development of a sovereign EU capability for advanced vulnerability research?
How does it intend to adapt the EU legislative framework to the emergence of AI models endowed with such offensive capabilities?

(19 June 2026) Recent developments in frontier AI models have not come as a surprise, yet the speed and scale at which AI can detect and identify vulnerabilities present new cybersecurity risks and opportunities. The existing EU legal framework on AI and cybersecurity provides a robust set of rules to address such risks. It is now necessary to translate this framework into operational capacity, with an urgency that reflects the threat. On 19 May 2026, the Commission announced a dedicated Action Plan on AI and Cybersecurity (1), comprising actions to step up the EU’s preparedness, bringing together the best EU expertise in AI and cybersecurity, in close cooperation with likeminded partners. It will include practical steps to help Member States, critical infrastructure operators, open-source communities and businesses manage risks, while also strengthening Europe’s advanced AI cybersecurity capabilities. E-10-2026-001574.t: The need to reinstate the section on corruption in EU institutions in the Eurobarometer
qt: to the Commission Mariusz Kamiński (ECR) Subject:

For decades, the Commission has been analysing corruption through its Eurobarometer surveys. For years, it researched the views of EU citizens on corruption at national, local and European level. For example, according to a 2006 survey, the highest proportion of Europeans (78%) believed that corruption was present in state institutions, whilst the lowest proportion (71%) believed it was present in EU institutions1. It was similar in 2012 (73%)2. However, in later editions of the corruption surveys, although they have continued to broaden in scope we find no data on the perception of corruption in the EU institutions. The latest Eurobarometer from 2024 also analyses the perception of corruption in public institutions, but only at national, regional and local level3. This is happening at a time when the EU is telling us it is taking numerous steps and dedicating significant resources to bringing its institutions closer to citizens. Importantly, there have been a number of scandals in Brussels in recent years, with serious allegations of corruption involving top officials in Parliament, the Commission and the EEAS. Even the former Commissioner for Justice has been charged with money laundering while in office. 1.
What was the reason for deciding no longer to publish research on perceptions of corruption in the European institutions?
Is the Commission carrying out such research and, if so, what are the results?

Given that the definition of a public official as set out in the Anti-Corruption Directive includes EU officials, does the Commission plan to reintroduce a section on corruption in the EU institutions in the Eurobarometer?

(13 August 2026) The Special Eurobarometer surveys, referred to by the Honorable Member, are designed to explore the level of corruption perceived and experienced by EU citizens. From 2005 to 2022, they were carried out on a biennial basis, and then annually since 2022. Data from the surveys support policy making in the area of anti-corruption, feeding notably into the European Semester cycle and annual Rule of Law Report. Accordingly, the Special Eurobarometer surveys currently mainly focus on the national level. The survey also underpinned the development of the EU Directive on combating corruption (1). Currently, the Commission does not envisage to change the scope of these Special Eurobarometer surveys. However, it reserves the right to add any relevant questions to future surveys, to respond to changing circumstances or priorities. The Commission is fully committed to upholding the highest standards of transparency, accountability, and sound financial management of EU funding.

E-10-2026-001573.t: Risk of synthetic fuel shortage and need for greater flexibility for sustainable bio-aviation fuel
qt: to the Commission Piotr Müller (ECR) Subject:
Risk of synthetic fuel shortage and need for greater flexibility for sustainable bioaviation fuel

Although the EU’s ReFuelEU Aviation regulations set out an ambitious vision for the development of synthetic fuels (eSAF), market realities show that aviation biofuels (bioSAF) currently offer the most viable and cost-effective foundation for decarbonisation. In the face of technological barriers and the high energy inputs required for eSAF production, calls are growing from those advocating a bigger role for bioSAF – and they appear to be the voice of necessary reason. In light of this: 1.

How is the Commission planning to optimise the use of mature and readily available bioSAF technologies in order to eliminate the risk of a supply gap resulting from barriers to the deployment of synthetic fuels (eSAF) by 2030?
Does it envisage introducing flexibility mechanisms in order to fully harness the potential of European biomass as a key pillar for energy independence and the stability of the aviation fuel market?
What action is it taking to prevent an excessive cost burden for passengers and carriers by promoting more cost-effective decarbonisation pathways based on proven biofuel solutions?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (12.6.2026) 1. The last European Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) report1 shows that Aviation biofuels produced from used cooking oil were the primary type of sustainable aviation fuels (SAF) supplied in the EU in 2024. Since aviation biofuels produced from waste oils are a mature production technology, fuel suppliers will rely on them to meet the ReFuelEU2 mandates in the short-term. However, due to their supply constraints, reaching future objectives ReFuelEU will require a diverse range of SAF technologies and feedstocks to ensure that SAF is widely available and affordable across the EU. Driven by energy independence and resilience priorities of the EU, the Sustainable Transport Investment Plan (STIP)3 and AccelerateEU4 aim to enhance SAF production and supply chains within the EU, specifically of synthetic aviation fuels (eSAF) and advanced aviation biofuels. 2. ReFuelEU provides a flexibility mechanism for aviation fuel suppliers to have a weighted average approach for SAF supply across Union airports. To further support the SAF market development, the Commission, with support from EASA, is studying further flexibilities including a study on potentially establishing a book and claim system for SAF. 3. ReFuelEU flexibilities seek to limit the fuel cost burden on aircraft operators associated with the ramp-up of SAF mandates and fuel logistics. In addition, the support provided under the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS)5 allows aircraft operators to reduce fuel costs, by compensating for the price difference between uplifted SAF and kerosene. While the former provision promotes a technology-neutral, cost-effective SAF rollout, the ETS SAF support scheme is designed to de-risk the uptake of less mature SAF technologies.

report-2025. 2 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2023/2405/oj. 3 https://transport.ec.europa.eu/news-events/news/commission-unveils-sustainable-transport-investment-planstrategic-approach-boost-renewable-and-low-2025-11-05_en. 4 https://energy.ec.europa.eu/publications/accelerateeu-energy-union-affordable-and-secure-energy-throughaccelerated-action_en. 5 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex%3A32023L0958.

E-10-2026-001570.t: Follow-up on Parliament’s position on cutting reporting costs and compensating companies for reporting obligations
qt: to the Commission Jörgen Warborn (PPE) Subject:

In my report on better law-making covering 2023 and 2024, adopted on 10 March 2026, Parliament highlighted that reporting obligations often generate considerable administrative costs for companies. Does the Commission intend to assess potential mechanisms to compensate companies for reporting tasks, and if so, within what time frame?

E-10-2026-001569.t: Antifa=Terrorists: zero tolerance for political violence in Europe
qt: to the Commission Tiago Moreira de Sá (PfE), Isabella Tovaglieri (PfE), Sebastian Tynkkynen (ECR), Ernő Schaller-Baross (PfE), György Hölvényi (PfE), Pál Szekeres (PfE), Irmhild Boßdorf (ESN), Volker Schnurrbusch (ESN), Viktória Ferenc (PfE), Kinga Gál (PfE), András Gyürk (PfE), András László (PfE), Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE), Siegbert Frank Droese (ESN), Jacek Ozdoba (ECR), Branko Grims (PPE), Fabrice Leggeri (PfE), Zsuzsanna Borvendég (ESN), Catherine Griset (PfE), Hermann Tertsch (PfE), Jorge Martín Frías (PfE), Diana Iovanovici Şoşoacă (NI), Tom Vandendriessche (PfE), Alexander Jungbluth (ESN), Stephen Nikola Bartulica (ECR), Arkadiusz Mularczyk (ECR), Gerolf Annemans (PfE), Mary Khan (ESN), Petr Bystron (ESN) Subject:

Following a Molotov cocktail attack in Lisbon against peaceful demonstrators, it is urgent to question Europe’s passivity toward organised political violence. Recent events in Portugal, where an individual linked to the Antifa movement threw a Molotov cocktail at peaceful prolife demonstrators (including young people and children) raise serious concerns about the consistency and resolve of European institutions in tackling political violence. This was not mere public disorder, but a potentially lethal act that, by chance alone, did not result in serious injuries. The mild judicial response and the absence of a clear European stance reinforce a perception of impunity. At a time when the European Union claims to uphold the rule of law and citizens’ security, it is legitimate to question the lack of scrutiny over movements that, under ideological cover, resort to violence as a political tool. Therefore, we ask: 1.
Does the Commission intend to reassess the legal framework surrounding movements such as Antifa, considering recent political violence?
What objective criteria distinguish radical activism from terrorist threat in the EU?
Is the Commission prepared to propose concrete measures to prevent and sanction decentralised networks that promote or carry out violence against civilians?
at: (English version) to the Commission Tiago Moreira de Sá (PfE), Isabella Tovaglieri (PfE), Sebastian Tynkkynen (ECR), Ernő Schaller-Baross (PfE), György Hölvényi (PfE), Pál Szekeres (PfE), Irmhild Boßdorf (ESN), Volker Schnurrbusch (ESN), Viktória Ferenc (PfE), Kinga Gál (PfE), András Gyürk (PfE), András László (PfE), Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE), Siegbert Frank Droese (ESN), Jacek Ozdoba (ECR), Branko Grims (PPE), Fabrice Leggeri (PfE), Zsuzsanna Borvendég (ESN), Catherine Griset (PfE), Hermann Tertsch (PfE), Jorge Martín Frías (PfE), Diana Iovanovici Şoşoacă (NI), Tom Vandendriessche (PfE), Alexander Jungbluth (ESN), Stephen Nikola Bartulica (ECR), Arkadiusz Mularczyk (ECR), Gerolf Annemans (PfE), Mary Khan (ESN), Petr Bystron (ESN) (16 April 2026) Subject: Antifa=Terrorists: zero tolerance for political violence in Europe Following a Molotov cocktail attack in Lisbon against peaceful demonstrators, it is urgent to Question Europe’s passivity toward organised political violence. Recent events in Portugal, where an individual linked to the Antifa movement threw a Molotov cocktail at peaceful pro-life demonstrators (including young people and children) raise serious concerns about the consistency and resolve of European institutions in tackling political violence. This was not mere public disorder, but a potentially lethal act that, by chance alone, did not result in serious injuries. The mild judicial response and the absence of a clear European stance reinforce a perception of impunity. At a time when the European Union claims to uphold the rule of law and citizens’ security, it is legitimate to question the lack of scrutiny over movements that, under ideological cover, resort to violence as a political tool. Therefore, we ask: 1.
Does the Commission intend to reassess the legal framework surrounding movements such as Antifa, considering recent political violence?
What objective criteria distinguish radical activism from terrorist threat in the EU?
Is the Commission prepared to propose concrete measures to prevent and sanction decentralised networks that promote or carry out violence against civilians?

(15 June 2026) The Commission condemns all forms of violence. Violent extremism poses a serious threat to social cohesion and democratic values, as highlighted in the 2025 Communication on a European Democracy Shield (1). The EU Directive (EU) 2017/541 (2) on combating terrorism establishes minimum rules concerning the definitions of offences that Member States must classify as terrorist offences in national law, and related sanctions. In addition, the February 2026 ProtectEU Agenda to prevent and counter terrorism (3) reinforces the EU's collective response to evolving terrorist and violent extremist threats. It includes measures to prevent radicalisation, notably through the EU knowledge hub (4), to tackle terrorist and extremist content online, and to reinforce law enforcement cooperation, including by enhancing the analytical capabilities of the EU Agency for Law Enforcement Cooperation (Europol). National security, public order and investigations into terrorist and extremist attacks are competences of the Member States according to the Treaties. Therefore, the incident referred to falls under national criminal law and judicial jurisdiction. It is for the Member States to apply the law, to assess whether the case in question would fall under the definition of terrorist offences, and, where appropriate, to take measures to prevent and sanction relevant entities.

E-10-2026-001568.t: Member State implementation of the EU Critical Raw Materials Act
qt: to the Commission Martin Günther (The Left) Subject:

Is the Commission aware of the communication submitted on 7 April 2026 by a group of 60 Romanian NGOs requesting the opening of an EU Pilot procedure concerning Law L143/20261 in Romania, adopted in the context of the implementation of the EU Critical Raw Materials Act, which they allege may introduce provisions granting private mining operators pre-emption rights over private property, establish expedited expropriation mechanisms for commercial mining projects, restrict judicial review, and allow the removal of forest land from Romania’s national forestry fund? Law L143/2026 is being processed under an emergency procedure, with a tacit adoption deadline set for 22 April 2026.

Given the concerns of the NGOs, does the Commission intend to initiate an EU Pilot or any other preliminary assessment regarding the compatibility of Law L143/2026 with EU law, including the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, EU environmental legislation, and property rights protections?

In the event that the law is adopted and subsequently found to be incompatible with EU law, what measures does the Commission envisage taking, including but not limited to infringement proceedings under Article 258 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union?
https://www.senat.ro/Legis/Lista.aspx?cod=27502.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (10.6.2026) The Commission is aware of and is carefully addressing the communication submitted on 7 April 2026 by a group of 60 Romanian non-governmental organisations requesting the opening of an EU Pilot procedure concerning Law L143/20261 in Romania, as referenced by the Honourable Member. The Commission is currently assessing this communication in detail. Following this assessment, the Commission will inform the authors of the communication about the most appropriate next steps to address their concerns effectively. These steps could include engaging in a pre-infringement dialogue with the Romanian authorities (formerly referred to as the EU Pilot dialogue)2. E-10-2026-001567.t: Allegations that Meta interfered with elections and influenced the visibility of political parties
qt: to the Commission Gaetano Pedulla' (The Left) Subject:

Recent journalistic investigations1 and academic studies2 have raised serious concerns by calling Meta’s impartiality in the 2022 and 2024 Italian elections into question. They posit that, while the visibility of institutional messages on Meta was systematically penalised, that of right-wing and populist posts experienced an anomalous spike, resulting in the presence of Lega Nord content increasing by 140 % and that of pro-Donald Trump content surging by as much as 400 %. In addition, the Italian Data Protection Authority3 has reported its suspicions that the ‘Election Day Information’ tool is being used for the purposes of mass profiling, a practice that could warp public debate and interfere with electoral processes. Having regard for the DSA, which requires very large online platforms to mitigate systemic risks for democratic processes and uphold the transparency of algorithms: What dedicated audit measures is the Commission carrying out or planning to implement concerning the use of Meta’s election information tools to profile users?

https://www.ilfattoquotidiano.it/2026/04/12/meta-interferenze-elezioni-reportnews/8353065/;https://www.ansa.it/sito/notizie/politica/2026/04/12/linchiesta-di-report-meta-interferi-nelleelezioni-del-2022-con-la-raccolta_d4cb1424-3048-4081-a16a-be4b570bcf85.html. 2 https://osf.io/preprints/socarxiv/8dqag_v1. 3 https://www.garanteprivacy.it/home/docweb/-/docweb-display/docweb/10112606. 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.7.2026) Free and fair elections are at the core of democracy. The conduct and organisation of elections are the competence and responsibility of the Member States, in accordance with their constitutional and legislative rules, subject to EU law and their international obligations. The integrity of elections and the civic discourse in the EU are a priority for the Commission, as set out in the Communication on the European Democracy Shield1. The Commission has opened an investigation2 into the political content approach of the provider of Facebook and Instagram in April 2024, including into the suspicion that the provider may not have diligently identified, analysed and assessed the systemic risks to any actual or foreseeable negative effects for civic discourse and electoral processes stemming from the political content, as required by Article 34 (1) (c) of the Digital Services Act (DSA)3. The Commission is determined to advance this investigation in full respect of due process. The Commission is monitoring the functioning of Meta’s services to ensure compliance with the DSA and has sent several requests for information, including on the topic of recommender systems. To support the implementation of the DSA during electoral periods, the Commission issued guidelines4 to very large online platforms (VLOPs) and very large online search engines (VLOSEs) on managing risks related to electoral processes that focus, among others, on recommender systems. Furthermore, providers of VLOPs and VLOSEs must also comply, where applicable, with the relevant obligations laid down in the Political Advertising Regulation5. Both legislations may apply in parallel to intermediary services which are involved in the dissemination of political advertising.

1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex:52025JC0791. 2 https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_24_2373. 3 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/2065/oj/eng. 4 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/C/2024/3014/oj/eng. 5 http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/900/oj.

E-10-2026-001565.t: Interference in European elections by foreign intelligence agencies
qt: to the Commission Fabio De Masi (NI) Subject:

Recent press reporting revealed extensive intelligence and interference activities by the Israeli espionage firm Black Cube, with the goal of influencing the outcome of the Slovenian national parliamentary elections1. 1.
What information is available to the Commission regarding the scope of Black Cube’s interference activities in Slovenia and other EU countries?
Is the Commission aware of other agencies operating to influence elections in the EU?
Which kind of instruments from the European Democracy Shield toolkit does the Commission plan to employ to address foreign interferences of the kind identified in the Slovenian case?

at: (English version) to the Commission Fabio De Masi (NI) (16 April 2026) Subject: Interference in European elections by foreign intelligence agencies Recent press reporting revealed extensive intelligence and interference activities by the Israeli espionage firm Black Cube, with the goal of influencing the outcome of the Slovenian national parliamentary elections (1). 1. What information is available to the Commission regarding the scope of Black Cube’s interference activities in Slovenia and other EU countries? 2.
Is the Commission aware of other agencies operating to influence elections in the EU?

3. Which kind of instruments from the European Democracy Shield toolkit does the Commission plan to employ to address foreign interferences of the kind identified in the Slovenian case? (15 June 2026) The Commission is aware of the matter described in the Honourable Member’s questions based on press reporting and as it was also brought to the attention of the President of the Commission by the Slovenian Prime Minister in a letter sent on 18 March 2026 (1). The Commission does not have any additional information. The Commission is aware of possible operations by foreign private actors aiming at influencing elections in the EU, such as the Doppelganger campaign carried out by Russian companies notably in the context of the 2024 elections to the European Parliament. The integrity of elections is essential for democracies. The conduct and organisation of elections are the responsibility of the Member States, in accordance with their constitution and national laws, in line with EU law and their international obligations. The Centre operates as a hub for cooperation with Member States and relevant EU institutions and bodies to support capacitybuilding, including for election preparedness, building on existing structures and networks, including the Rapid Alert System, the European cooperation network on elections (4), the European Board for Digital Services and the European Digital Media Observatory (5).
