E-10-2026-001564.t: Application of Article 29(18) of Regulation (EU) 2025/40 as regards beverage packaging
qt: to the Commission Niels Fuglsang (S&D), Morten Løkkegaard (Renew) Subject:

Several Member States operate deposit return systems (DRS) for beverage packaging achieving high collection rates and high-quality recycling. Available evidence, including a new life cycle assessment from the Danish Technological Institute in 2026, indicates that DRS can deliver environmental outcomes comparable to or better than reuse, while avoiding significant additional infrastructure and costs. On this basis, the Commission is invited to clarify: 1.

whether Article 29(18) of Regulation (EU) 2025/40 may be used to provide targeted exemptions for specific beverage packaging formats, in cases where it can be demonstrated that such formats are part of high-performing systems delivering environmental outcomes comparable to or better than reuse, and/or that meeting the reuse targets would entail disproportionate economic burdens and risk disrupting existing systems;

whether documented environmental performance, including life cycle assessments, as well as evidence of system performance and disproportionate economic or infrastructural impacts, may be considered relevant elements in the application of Article 29(18);
how the Commission envisages Article 29(18) being applied in practice in relation to format-specific exemptions, with a view to ensuring legal certainty for economic operators by 2030.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (7.7.2026) The Commission is empowered to adopt delegated acts under Article 29(18) of the Packaging Waste Regulation (PPWR)1, supplementing the harmonised reuse targets in the regulation. Such delegated acts can only exempt economic operators who face particular economic constraints, or specific packaging formats where achievement of the reuse targets is prevented due to hygiene and food safety or environmental issues. To ensure legal certainty for economic operators, and the integrity of the internal market, the Commission will act only when the necessity to act is demonstrated via adequate evidence, taking the applicable exemptions in the PPWR into consideration, and when it is confirmed by the Commission’s own assessment. The PPWR includes directly applicable derogations from the reuse targets and Member States can implement further exemptions to address environmental issues or economic constraints. If the exemptions are fully applied, the number of final distributors that are required to offer reuse will be limited, and the remaining obliged final distributors would enjoy a high degree of flexibility. The Commission will review the effectiveness and feasibility of the reuse targets in 2034. The Commission has recently published a guidance document2 and Frequently Asked Question document3 for the PPWR that further clarifies how the exemptions can be applied.
1 Regulation (EU) 2025/40 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 19 December 2024 on packaging

and packaging waste, amending Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 and Directive (EU) 2019/904, and repealing Directive 94/62/EC, OJ L, 2025/40, 22.1.2025. 2 https://environment.ec.europa.eu/publications/guidance-document-packaging-and-packaging-waste-regulationppwr_en. 3 https://environment.ec.europa.eu/publications/faq-packaging-and-packaging-waste-regulation-ppwr_en.

E-10-2026-001563.t: The use of Afghan paramilitaries by the Greek authorities for pushbacks
qt: to the Commission Erik Marquardt (Verts/ALE), Majdouline Sbai (Verts/ALE), Saskia Bricmont (Verts/ALE), Tineke Strik (Verts/ALE), Jan-Christoph Oetjen (Renew), Rudi Kennes (The Left), Merja Kyllönen (The Left), Cecilia Strada (S&D), Hanna Gedin (The Left), Damien Carême (The Left), Daniel Freund (Verts/ALE), Murielle Laurent (S&D), Birgit Sippel (S&D), Konstantinos Arvanitis (The Left) Subject:

A serious incident report of Frontex’s Fundamental Rights Office1 reveals that on 22 June 2023, Greek authorities used Afghan paramilitaries to violently push a group of 61 asylum seekers, including 11 children, back to Türkiye over the Evros, while subjecting them to inhuman treatment. The pushback was done by three Greek police officers and 10-20 masked, armed third-country nationals, reported to be Afghan paramilitaries. The Fundamental Rights Office concludes that they acted under the instruction and effective control of the Greek authorities, and describes the use of mercenaries in pushbacks as ‘a matter of coordinated policy’ in the Evros region. The Greek authorities have denied this incident. 1.

Is the Commission or Frontex aware of collaboration with, or use of, mercenaries or paramilitaries from Afghanistan or other third countries by the Greek authorities in the context of pushbacks? Are other cases of such collaboration known, and if so how many, and does this constitute an official or de facto policy of the Greek authorities? Please share any information at the disposal of Frontex or the Commission.

What measures will the Commission take to hold the Greek authorities accountable for these pushbacks, to ensure swift further investigation of this incident by the Greek authorities, and to eliminate the systematic practice of both Greek collaboration with foreign paramilitaries on pushbacks and of the pushbacks themselves?
SIR 13125/2023, https://prd.frontex.europa.eu/document/serious-incident-reports-cat-1-2/.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (19.6.2026) The Commission is aware of the report of the European Border and Coast Guard Agency’s (Frontex) Fundamental Rights Office concerning the referred incident of 22 June 2023. The Commission cannot confirm the existence of similar cases or the existence of an official or de facto policy involving collaboration with paramilitary or mercenary actors. The Commission considers all allegations of violations of fundamental rights at the EU’s external borders to be a matter of concern, which is subject to investigation by the competent national authorities. The Commission recalls that all border management activities need to comply with the relevant EU law, the Charter of Fundamental Rights and the principle of non-refoulement. The Commission remains in contact with the Greek authorities and with Frontex regarding these allegations.

E-10-2026-001562.t: Respecting fundamental rights in Algeria and applying Article 2 of the EU-Algeria Association Agreement
qt: to the Commission Nicolas Bay (ECR), Sebastian Tynkkynen (ECR), Arkadiusz Mularczyk (ECR), Jaroslav Knot (PfE), François-Xavier Bellamy (PPE), Laurence Trochu (ECR), Geadis Geadi (ECR) Subject:
Respecting fundamental rights in Algeria and applying Article 2 of the EUAlgeria Association Agreement

Since Algeria’s independence in 1962, the Algerian authorities have repeatedly infringed fundamental rights, particularly those of certain minorities like the Kabyles and Christians. In Kabylia, restrictions on freedom of expression and arbitrary arrests targeting political opponents are an everyday occurrence. Freedom of religion is also severely compromised: 47 protestant churches have been closed since 2017, denying tens of thousands of worshippers their freedom of religion.1 The situation has been recognised internationally, with Algeria appearing on the Special Watch List of the United States Commission on International Religious Freedom (USCIRF) since 2021. Journalists and critics of the regime are being prosecuted and imprisoned, as in the case of French journalist Christophe Gleizes.2 However, Article 2 of the Association Agreement between the European Union and Algeria lists respect for human rights and democratic principles as one of its essential elements. 1.

In this context, does the Commission intend to activate the mechanisms set out in this Agreement in the event of a breach of its principles, including by making its application conditional on tangible and verifiable progress?
What action does it plan to take to secure the freedom of political prisoners and ensure that the rights of Kabyle and Christian minorities in Algeria are properly respected?

https://www.la-croix.com/religion/algerie-les-protestants-contraints-de-se-cacher-pour-prier-20250129. https://rsf.org/en/petition-we-call-immediate-release-french-sports-journalist-christophe-gleizes.
at: (English version) to the Commission Nicolas Bay (ECR), Sebastian Tynkkynen (ECR), Arkadiusz Mularczyk (ECR), Jaroslav Knot (PfE), François-Xavier Bellamy (PPE), Laurence Trochu (ECR), Geadis Geadi (ECR) (16 April 2026) Subject: Respecting fundamental rights in Algeria and applying Article 2 of the EU-Algeria Association Agreement Since Algeria’s independence in 1962, the Algerian authorities have repeatedly infringed fundamental rights, particularly those of certain minorities like the Kabyles and Christians. In Kabylia, restrictions on freedom of expression and arbitrary arrests targeting political opponents are an everyday occurrence. Freedom of religion is also severely compromised: 47 protestant churches have been closed since 2017, denying tens of thousands of worshippers their freedom of religion. (1) The situation has been recognised internationally, with Algeria appearing on the Special Watch List of the United States Commission on International Religious Freedom (USCIRF) since 2021. Journalists and critics of the regime are being prosecuted and imprisoned, as in the case of French journalist Christophe Gleizes. (2) However, Article 2 of the Association Agreement between the European Union and Algeria lists respect for human rights and democratic principles as one of its essential elements. 1. In this context, does the Commission intend to activate the mechanisms set out in this Agreement in the event of a breach of its principles, including by making its application conditional on tangible and verifiable progress? 2. What action does it plan to take to secure the freedom of political prisoners and ensure that the rights of Kabyle and Christian minorities in Algeria are properly respected? (5 June 2026) Upholding human rights constitutes a key element of EU-Algeria relations, as enshrined in the Association Agreement (1) and reinforced in the Partnership Priorities (2). On this basis, the EU monitors developments closely and continues to have regular exchanges on human rights and the rule of law with the Algerian authorities. Freedom of religion or belief has consistently been part of these exchanges. In particular, the closure of certain Christian places of worship was specifically discussed at the most recent EU-Algeria subcommittee meeting on Political Dialogue, Security and Human Rights (3). The EU does not envisage the activation of the mechanisms set out in the Association Agreement, which could lead to the suspension of ongoing cooperation with Algeria. Instead, the EU favours frank and constructive discussions and it is committed to support the implementation of political reforms envisaged by the Algerian authorities to enhance the protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms, including freedom of religion or belief.

qt: to the Commission Elisabetta Gualmini (Renew), Giorgio Gori (S&D), Stefano Bonaccini (S&D), Letizia Moratti (PPE), Susana Solís Pérez (PPE), Vicent Marzà Ibáñez (Verts/ALE) Subject:

The Commission is planning to adopt the Emissions Trading System (ETS) benchmark update proposal very shortly. Ahead of the European Council meeting of 19-20 March 2026, Commission President von der Leyen committed to updating the ETS benchmarks to take account of the concerns expressed by industry, and even proposed ‘an ETS investment booster’. The current context of a growing energy crisis and the recurrent non-availability of the resources and infrastructure required for the energy transition make that a commitment of the utmost importance and urgency. Does the proposal in the pipeline fulfil that commitment?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (12.6.2026) The Emissions Trading System (ETS) Directive1 provides for transitional free allocation to evolve and decline in time. The reduction rates are in line with the objective of economy-wide climate neutrality by 2050 and the interim reduction targets. The 2026-2030 benchmark update exercise, including the applied methodology is set in EU law. It is a legal obligation that the Commission has no discretion to deviate from without creating uncertainty and imposing a significant delay to the process of determining and transferring the 2026 free allocation to industry. The concerns expressed by industry have been noted and taken into account by the Commission in its draft implementing act, which is currently in public consultation. The draft implementing act proposes to apply the maximum flexibilities possible within the existing legal framework set by the ETS Directive. The Commission is committed to ensuring that Europe’s climate policies support its industrial strength. The comprehensive ETS review, due in July 2026, includes the ETS Investment Booster to fast track the first phase of the Industrial Decarbonisation Bank and allow funds to be available as soon as possible to accelerate the clean energy transition of European industry. In doing so, the Commission is also looking at ways to facilitate faster deployment of projects, and targeted support for mature, high-impact technologies. This approach aims to ensure that investments translate rapidly into real emissions reductions, while reinforcing competitiveness, energy security, electrification and the efficient functioning of the energy system.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2003/87/oj.

E-10-2026-001560.t: Protecting consumers from misleading discounts and unfair practices such as hidden fees during Black Friday and Cyber Monday
qt: to the Commission Dimitris Tsiodras (PPE) Subject:

A recent sweep of 314 online sales platforms in 23 EU Member States found that 30 % displayed misleading discounts during Black Friday and Cyber Monday. Practices that may influence consumers’ purchasing decisions were also found, such as attempts to add items to consumers’ online baskets (36 % of cases) without their consent (4 in 10 cases), failure to explain the reference price so that their prices could be compared at the time of purchase and hiding additional fees such as service or delivery fees until the end of the process (10 % of cases). Can the Commission answer the following: 1.
What measures does it intend to take to protect consumers from misleading or false discounts and practices such as hidden fees?

In view also of the revision of the Consumer Protection Cooperation Regulation, what options is it considering to ensure more effective cross-border enforcement of EU consumer law, and is it considering the uniform application of sanctions across the EU rather than on a country-by-country basis, particularly in cases of infringements affecting several Member States?
How will it help strengthen the exchange of information between authorities and coordination between EU and national actions?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (14.7.2026) In line with Article 29 of Regulation (EU) 2017/2394 (the Consumer Protection Cooperation (CPC) Regulation)1, the Commission coordinates the sweeps conducted by national authorities. However, as the responsibility for enforcing consumer protection legislation lies with the Member States, it is for the national authorities to follow up on the findings of the sweep related to individual traders and demand corrective actions as appropriate. Further rules related to misleading practices are under consideration in the context of the Digital Fairness Act2. In line with the findings of the Commission’s report on the application of the CPC Regulation3, the Commission is exploring measures that enable CPC authorities to act faster and strengthen the CPC system’s deterrent effect, including when enforcing in relation to traders not established in the EU. The Commission is also assessing the need for centralised investigation and enforcement powers in specific cases at EU level. The Commission ensures swift coordination across EU enforcement systems that complement each other, for example, enforcement under the CPC Regulation and the Digital Services Act4. In preparation for the revision of the CPC Regulation, the Commission is assessing how this coordination could be further strengthened to ensure consistency, as well as how to strengthen coordination between EU and national actions.

cooperation between national authorities responsible for the enforcement of consumer protection laws and repealing Regulation (EC) No 2006/2004, OJ L 345, 27.12.2017, pp. 1-26. 2 https://ec.europa.eu/info/law/better-regulation/have-your-say/initiatives/14622-Digital-Fairness-Act_en. 3 Report from the Commission to the European Parliament and the Council on the application of Regulation (EU) 2017/2394 of the European Parliament and of the Council on cooperation between national authorities responsible for the enforcement of consumer protection laws, COM(2024)311 final, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:52024DC0311. 4 Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 19 October 2022 on a Single Market for Digital Services and amending Directive 2000/31/EC (Digital Services Act), OJ L 277, 27.10.2022, pp. 1-102.

E-10-2026-001559.t: Information flow between Frontex and the police authorities of the Member States
qt: to the Commission Jorge Buxadé Villalba (PfE) Subject:

According to Frontex data, the European Border and Coast Guard Agency has around 3 400 deployed officers performing tasks supporting Member States’ authorities in the area of immigration and border protection. One of the tasks of these officers – in support of the border police –is to interview newly arrived illegal immigrants. During such interviews, immigrants may provide information, for example, on places through which they have transited or on the criminal networks that have provided them with transport. With the regulation on screening due to come into force1, these interviews may play a more significant role in ensuring the effectiveness of any returns and in the fight against criminal networks. In this regard, in statements to Euractiv2, the Agency itself has indicated that it has serious problems sharing this data with the police, as the EDPS has established that this would be in breach of the Regulation governing its operation. 1.
Is the Commission aware of this problem?
Is an urgent amendment of the Frontex Regulation being prepared to address these limitations in the flow of key information?
Are the relevant Commission services in contact with the national authorities and Interpol to assess any initiatives that would render the fight against illegal immigration effective?

Regulation (EU) 2024/1356 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 May 2024 introducing the screening of third-country nationals at the external borders. https://www.euractiv.com/news/frontex-blocked-from-sharing-data-on-human-traffickers/.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (15.6.2026) The European Border and Coast Guard Agency (Frontex) performs its operational activities, including debriefing interviews with migrants, under the command and control of the Member States concerned. In this respect, Frontex cannot be considered precluded from sharing data obtained from these interviews with the relevant national authorities. Moreover, when these interviews produce data potentially relevant for the fight against cross-border crime, Article 90 of Regulation (EU) 2019/18961 explicitly mandates Frontex to share this operational personal data with the relevant national law enforcement authorities. The Commission is not aware of any recommendations or opinions of the European Data Protection Supervisor that would indicate that sharing operational personal data with national police authorities would be in breach of this Regulation, as long as the applicable data protection framework is respected. The Commission intends to propose a revision of Regulation (EU) 2019/1896 in 2026. The preparatory work is ongoing, including as regards the contributions that Frontex can provide to the Member States and relevant EU agencies in the fight against cross-border crime, including with regard to information exchange. To counter migrant smuggling, the Commission engages regularly with the national authorities, both through European Centre Against Migrant Smuggling2 set up by the EU Agency for Law Enforcement Cooperation (Europol) and via the EU Policy Cycle and the Operational Action Plan3 Migrant Smuggling where Member States, EU Agencies, partners and international organisations, such as the International Criminal Police Organisation (Interpol), regularly engage in targeted operational activities.
1 Regulation (EU) 2019/1896 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 November 2019 on the

European Border and Coast Guard and repealing Regulations (EU) No 1052/2013 and (EU) 2016/1624, OJ L 295, p. 1. 2 https://www.europol.europa.eu/media-press/newsroom/news/grip-migrant-smuggling-tightens-newdepartment-europol-to-step-fight. From March 2026, the activities of the European Migrant Smuggling Centre were taken over by the European Centre Against Migrant Smuggling (ECAMS; https://www.europol.europa.eu/about-europol/european-centre-against-migrant-smuggling-ecams) and the European Serious and Organised Crime Centre (ESOCC; https://www.europol.europa.eu/abouteuropol/european-serious-and-organised-crime-centre-esocc). 3 https://home-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies/internal-security/law-enforcement-cooperation/empact-fightingcrime-together_en.

E-10-2026-001558.t: Spain’s ceramic industry condemned as a result of the scaling back of free allocations of emission allowances under the Emissions Trading System
qt: to the Commission Jorge Buxadé Villalba (PfE) Subject:

The European Union plans to cut free emission allocations under the Emissions Trading System (ETS) by 34 % for the period 2026-2030. This drastic reduction in emission allowances for domestic industries will have a huge negative impact on several sectors, including Spain’s ceramic industry (concentrated in the Community of Valencia), which is expecting to be hit by additional costs of over EUR 180 million. Recently, the Commission put forward proposals designed to mitigate the adverse effects of the ETS, since the system itself proves to be incompatible with the competitiveness and productivity of Europe’s industry, as well as with maintaining and creating jobs. In light of the fact that the Commission has put forward measures to reduce the consequences of the ETS, admitting that it is not viable: 1.
What justifies maintaining and tightening measures that are known to harm EU industry and employment, and which foreign state will benefit the most?
Does the Commission intend to take specific action to mitigate the adverse effect that reducing free emission allocations by 34 % will have on the Spanish ceramic sector?
What interest groups have led the Commission to prioritise tightening the ETS, as well as to ignore the calls from Spain’s ceramic industry?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.6.2026) The legislation on the Emission Trading System (ETS) provides for transitional free allocation to evolve and decline in time. The reduction rates are in line with the objective of economy-wide climate neutrality by 2050 and the interim reduction targets. The 2026-2030 benchmark update exercise, including the applied methodology, is a legal obligation enshrined in the ETS Directive1 that the Commission has no discretion to deviate from without creating uncertainty and imposing a significant delay to the process of determining and transferring the 2026 free allocation to industry. The concerns expressed by industry have been well noted and are taken into account by the Commission. The Commission is applying all the flexibilities that are possible within the existing legal framework set by the ETS Directive. The upcoming review of the ETS Directive will review the rules on free allocation and consider how to best support and boost investments in decarbonisation and electrification of the sectors covered by the system. Commission will also propose the introduction of an empowerment to introduce further sector-specific fallback benchmarks.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A02003L0087-20240301.

E-10-2026-001557.t: Follow-up question to question E-000437/2026 on concerns about funding of the NGO ECPS
qt: to the Commission Auke Zijlstra (PfE) Subject:

On 15 April 2026, Commissioner McGrath replied to my questions regarding funding of the NGO ECPS1. Although questions 1 and 3 can be considered to have been answered, question 2, which I consider to be crucial, has not. Can the Commission now provide an answer to this question, along with a proper explanation? That question reads as follows: Can the Commission indicate whether it considers ‘confronting the rise of populism’ to be so important that it expressly wishes to finance this effort through an NGO such as ECPS?
https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/E-10-2026-000437_EN.html.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (17.7.2026) As indicated in the answer to written question E-000437/20261, the objectives of EU funding are defined in programmes established by basic acts adopted by the European Parliament and the Council. The programmes are implemented through work programmes adopted by the Commission in accordance with the committee procedure involving representatives of the Member States. Under the Horizon Europe2 programme, the Commission funds quality and excellence in research and innovation. The ENCODE3 project has been selected under the ‘Culture, Creativity and Inclusive Society’ cluster of Pillar II of Horizon Europe, in an open call for research proposals analysing the emotional dimension of politics and democracies4. The UNTOLD Europe5 project has been selected under the Citizens’ engagement and participation strand of the Citizens, Equality, Rights and Values6 (CERV) programme that aims inter alia at supporting projects aiming at raising awareness among European citizens of their common history in order to promote mutual understanding and tolerance. The project analyses the implications of the legacy of colonialism on contemporary multicultural European societies. Proposals received under Horizon Europe are evaluated solely by independent experts, and proposals submitted to the CERV programmes are evaluated by the Commission assisted by independent external experts. Only the highest ranked proposals that best align with the objectives of the programmes are selected for funding.

E-10-2026-001556.t: Extension of exemption for the use of mercury in other high-pressure sodium lamps
qt: to the Commission Ondřej Krutílek (ECR) Subject:

Commission Delegated Directive (EU) 2022/283 of 13 December 2021 amended Annex III to Directive 2011/65/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council as regards an exemption for the use of mercury in High Pressure Sodium (vapour) lamps with improved colour rendering index for general lighting purposes. Specifically, the validity of the exemption was extended for part of item 4(b)-I, which concerns lamps with a high colour rendering index above 80 and a power input of 105 W or less. Is the Commission considering a further extension of this exemption beyond 24 February 2027, given the limited availability of substitutes and the socio-economic impacts of replacing mercury?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (17.6.2026) The Commission does not intend to review the phase-out dates for the import, export and manufacture of mercury-containing lamps for general lighting purposes. Article 4(1) of the Restriction of Hazardous Substances (RoHS) Directive1 prohibits the placing on the EU market and import into the EU of certain electrical and electronic equipment containing mercury. Annex III to that Directive lists, inter alia, certain mercury-added lamps which are exempt from that prohibition until the dates set out therein. The exemptions for mercury-containing lamps for general lighting purposes expired between 13 April 2016 and 24 February 2025, in particular the exemption for most high-pressure sodium (vapour) lamps for general lighting purposes that have an improved colouring index expired on 24 February 2023. Considering the specifications of the received request for the colour rendering index and the power used per burner, the exemption in question is the remaining exemption for high-pressure sodium (vapour) lamps for general lighting purposes listed in entry 4(b) of Annex III to the RoHS Directive, which expires on 24 February 2027. According to Article 5(5) of the RoHS Directive, an application to renew an exemption must be submitted at least 18 months before the exemption expires. In this case, however, the Commission did not receive a renewal request, meaning that the exemption listed in entry 4(b) is set to expire after the above date. The Exemptions list: Validity and rolling plan February 20262 provides information on this matter.
1 Directive 2011/65/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 8 June 2011 on the restriction of the
use of certain hazardous substances in electrical and electronic equipment, OJ L 174, 1.7.2011, p. 88–110. 2 https://environment.ec.europa.eu/document/2e1f3934-a6e0-406a-9c7b-491f7a34fcb7_en.

qt: to the Commission David Cormand (Verts/ALE), Majdouline Sbai (Verts/ALE) Subject:

The European garlic industry is facing mounting pressure linked to an increase in imports from third countries, not least Egypt and China. At the same time, EU producers are confronting continuously rising production costs, in particular for energy, storage and transport. This destabilises the market and weakens an agricultural production that is important for economic activity and employment in various rural areas of the EU. In view of this: 1.
Does the Commission have a recent, public assessment of the impact that garlic imports from third countries have on the EU market equilibrium and on small producers?
Is it prepared to revise the garlic quotas allocated to China and/or mobilise trade defence instruments to protect the European sector?
Does it intend to activate the safeguard clauses relating to the import of Egyptian garlic?
at: (English version) to the Commission David Cormand (Verts/ALE), Majdouline Sbai (Verts/ALE) (15 April 2026) Subject: Protecting the European garlic industry The European garlic industry is facing mounting pressure linked to an increase in imports from third countries, not least Egypt and China. At the same time, EU producers are confronting continuously rising production costs, in particular for energy, storage and transport. This destabilises the market and weakens an agricultural production that is important for economic activity and employment in various rural areas of the EU. In view of this: 1.
Does the Commission have a recent, public assessment of the impact that garlic imports from third countries have on the EU market equilibrium and on small producers?
Is it prepared to revise the garlic quotas allocated to China and/or mobilise trade defence instruments to protect the European sector?
Does it intend to activate the safeguard clauses relating to the import of Egyptian garlic?

(1 June 2026) The Commission closely monitors the EU garlic market using data on production and trade. It has recently adopted a Commission Delegated Regulation amending Delegated Regulation (EU) 2017/891 (1) to require Member States to report producer prices for garlic, ensuring proper monitoring of domestic market prices. This regulation is under scrutiny. The Commission does not envisage to revise the garlic quotas allocated to China. Any such revision would imply a renegotiation of EU market access commitments in line with the World Trade Organisation (WTO) rules, in particular Article XXVIII of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (2). The Commission is committed to protecting EU producers from unfair and injurious trading practices by using available trade defence instruments. Such instruments may be deployed where there is evidence of practices such as dumping or subsidisation that cause injury to the EU industry. The Commission stands ready to open an investigation regarding imports of any product, if it receives a duly substantiated complaint from industry in accordance with the relevant rules. Safeguard measures for imports from Egypt are set out in Article 24 of the EU-Egypt Association Agreement (3) (reflecting the WTO Safeguards Agreement) and Regulation (EU) 2015/478 (4). Where there is sufficient evidence that increased imports are causing injury to the EU producers, the Commission may introduce Union surveillance or apply safeguard measures, but no such concerns have been reported for garlic. WTO rules require safeguards to be applied to all countries of origin of imports, not just Egypt. The Commission will continue monitoring and taking action where appropriate.

E-10-2026-001554.t: Procedure under Article 108 TFEU for notifying the Commission about an alteration to an already approved aid scheme
qt: to the Commission Pina Picierno (S&D) Subject:
Procedure under Article 108 TFEU for notifying the Commission about an alteration to an already approved aid scheme

By Decision C(2024) 3814 of 4 June 2024, the Commission approved the draft FER2 decree, which promotes the construction of plants for the production of energy from renewable sources that are not fully mature or have high operating costs. For offshore wind, there is only one incentive tariff, with no distinction made between fixed-foundation and floating technologies. Italy has announced an amendment to the FER2 decree which will distinguish between technologies, revise incentive tariffs and CfD schemes for offshore wind, introduce a mechanism for the indexation of tariffs to inflation and do away with the annual tariff percentage reduction for all technologies covered by the FER2 decree. According to Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 794/2004, ‘an alteration to existing aid shall mean any change, other than modifications of a purely formal or administrative nature (...)’, where such an alteration is considered ‘new aid’ within the meaning of Article 1(c) of Regulation (EU) 2015/1589. Can the Commission clarify whether, as an ‘alteration to existing aid’, the amendment to the FER2 decree, as described above, is to be considered ‘new aid’, requiring notification to the Commission pursuant to Article 108 TFEU and initiation of the preliminary examination by a Commission decision which is to be taken within two months pursuant to Article 4 of Regulation (EU) 2015/1589?
at: (English version) to the Commission Pina Picierno (S&D) (15 April 2026) Subject: Procedure under Article 108 TFEU for notifying the Commission about an alteration to an already approved aid scheme By Decision C(2024) 3814 of 4 June 2024, the Commission approved the draft FER2 decree, which promotes the construction of plants for the production of energy from renewable sources that are not fully mature or have high operating costs. For offshore wind, there is only one incentive tariff, with no distinction made between fixed-foundation and floating technologies. Italy has announced an amendment to the FER2 decree which will distinguish between technologies, revise incentive tariffs and CfD schemes for offshore wind, introduce a mechanism for the indexation of tariffs to inflation and do away with the annual tariff percentage reduction for all technologies covered by the FER2 decree. According to Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 794/2004, ‘an alteration to existing aid shall mean any change, other than modifications of a purely formal or administrative nature (…)’, where such an alteration is considered ‘new aid’ within the meaning of Article 1(c) of Regulation (EU) 2015/1589. Can the Commission clarify whether, as an ‘alteration to existing aid’, the amendment to the FER2 decree, as described above, is to be considered ‘new aid’, requiring notification to the Commission pursuant to Article 108 TFEU and initiation of the preliminary examination by a Commission decision which is to be taken within two months pursuant to Article 4 of Regulation (EU) 2015/1589? (17 June 2026) By state aid decision C(2024)3814 (1), the Commission approved the Italian support scheme for electricity produced from renewable energy sources that are innovative or not yet fully mature. The scheme organises distinct competitive tendering procedures for nine technology categories to achieve diversification of energy sources, each with a different reference tariff calculated based on a reference project (see recitals (33) to (37) of the decision). The decision also sets out in recitals (51), (52) and (53) the conditions under which Italy may revise reference tariffs and modify the technology categories. If the changes envisaged by Italy are in line with those provisions, or are purely administrative in nature, they may be implemented without requiring prior notification to the Commission. If they are not, they may qualify as alterations to existing aid within the meaning of Article 1(c) of Regulation (EU) 2015/1589 (2) and therefore constitute new aid. Pursuant to Article 108(3) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU, such new aid must be notified to the Commission before it is put into effect. It is therefore Italy’s obligation to respect the standstill obligation which requires that no amendment qualifying as new aid is implemented without prior notification and Commission approval.

https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A52024AS105880&qid=1780385077265. Council Regulation (EU) 2015/1589 of 13 July 2015 laying down detailed rules for the application of Article 108 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, OJ L 248.

qt: to the Commission Pär Holmgren (Verts/ALE) Subject:

Natura 2000 protects invaluable natural habitats across the EU. It is a fundamental part of the EU’s ability to protect biodiversity and a rich natural environment because environmental problems take no heed of national borders. The EU’s system is really put to the test, however, in times when there is a lot of pressure for development. In the name of competitiveness, a number of parties, including Parliament’s largest political group, the EPP, are calling for Natura 2000 to be overhauled. At the same time, more exploration permits are being granted for development in protected areas. There are several examples of this in Jämtland (Sweden), including Jänsmässholmen, Lake Näkten and Hårkan – three examples of areas with sensitive habitats that are important for reindeer herding, outdoor recreation and red‑list species. Increasing pressure for development is threatening to undermine the conservation objectives that the Member States have to meet in Natura 2000 sites. Given that a number of stakeholders are wrongly pitting nature conservation against competitiveness – something that the responsible Commissioner has repeatedly emphasised is not a real contradiction – I should like to ask: 1.
How is the Commission, alongside the Member States, intending to ensure that Europe’s biodiversity is protected?
Can the Commission confirm that there are no plans to place restrictions on Natura 2000 or on the Habitats Directive?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (17.7.2026) Biodiversity protection in the EU is firmly grounded in the implementation and enforcement of the EU Birds1 and Habitats Directives2 and the Natura 2000 network, among other legal instruments. According to Article 6(3) of the Habitats Directive, any plan or project likely to have a significant negative effect on a Natura 2000 site, either individually or in combination with other plans or projects, must be subject to an appropriate assessment of its implications for the site in view of the site’s conservation objectives and can only be approved if it will not adversely affect the integrity of the site concerned. Exceptions to this obligation may be accepted under the conditions established in Article 6(4). Building on this framework, the Nature Restoration Regulation3 delivers on the commitment taken under the EU Biodiversity Strategy for 20304 and the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework5 by setting legally binding restoration targets across ecosystems. Together with Member States, the Commission will continue to support effective implementation, financing, monitoring and enforcement measures to halt biodiversity loss, restore degraded ecosystems and strengthen the resilience of Europe’s natural capital for future generations. The Commission is currently carrying out a stress test of the Birds and Habitats Directives6 as part of its wider initiative on simplification. The stress test aims to evaluate whether the Directives remain fit to achieve their objectives in a cost-efficient way, while maintaining their ambition and high standards of nature conservation. The results – planned for end 2026 – will form the basis for the Commission to decide on the appropriate follow up.
1 Directive 2009/147/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 30 November 2009 on the

conservation of wild birds, OJ L 20, 26.1.2010, p. 7–25. 2 Council Directive 92/43/EEC of 21 May 1992 on the conservation of natural habitats and of wild fauna and flora, OJ L 206, 22.7.1992, p. 7–50. 3 Regulation (EU) 2024/1991 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 24 June 2024 on nature restoration and amending Regulation (EU) 2022/869, OJ L, 2024/1991, 29.7.2024. 4 https://environment.ec.europa.eu/strategy/biodiversity-strategy-2030_en. 5 https://www.cbd.int/article/cop15-final-text-kunming-montreal-gbf-221222. 6 https://green-forum.ec.europa.eu/nature-and-biodiversity/stress-test-birds-and-habitats-directives_en.

E-10-2026-001552.t: Application of EU sanctions against a Russian propaganda event in a Member State
qt: to the Commission Pina Picierno (S&D), Petras Auštrevičius (Renew), Giorgio Gori (S&D), Villy Søvndal (Verts/ALE), Miriam Lexmann (PPE), Elisabetta Gualmini (Renew), Ondřej Krutílek (ECR), Nathalie Loiseau (Renew), Nicola Zingaretti (S&D), Stefano Bonaccini (S&D), Sandro Gozi (Renew), Giuseppe Lupo (S&D), Vytenis Povilas Andriukaitis (S&D), Brando Benifei (S&D), Sebastian Tynkkynen (ECR), Dainius Žalimas (Renew), Rasa Juknevičienė (PPE), Alessandra Moretti (S&D) Subject:

On 11-12 April 2026, a festival organised by an Italian association linked to RT, formerly known as Russia Today, was held in Bologna, Italy. According to press reports, the festival programme included the screening of contributions from and documentaries produced by RT, (an organisation subject to European sanctions and whose operations are banned on EU territory), which faithfully reproduced the Kremlin’s narrative, in particular regarding the conflict in Ukraine and the role of the West. The festival was also praised by Margarita Simonyan, editor-in-chief of RT and one of the key figures in the Kremlin’s propaganda apparatus. Having regard to Council Regulations (EU) 2022/350 and (EU) 833/2014 and their subsequent amendments, can the Commission clarify: 1.
Whether it was aware of the organisation of such an event in a Member State’s territory?
Whether the event and its programme constitute a violation of the European sanctions imposed on the Russian Federation and certain of its media outlets operating in the EU?

What actions it can take to prevent events of this nature from continuing to take place in a Member State where, at present, there are no legislative measures in force implementing the EU’s sanctions?
at: (English version) to the Commission Pina Picierno (S&D), Petras Auštrevičius (Renew), Giorgio Gori (S&D), Villy Søvndal (Verts/ALE), Miriam Lexmann (PPE), Elisabetta Gualmini (Renew), Ondřej Krutílek (ECR), Nathalie Loiseau (Renew), Nicola Zingaretti (S&D), Stefano Bonaccini (S&D), Sandro Gozi (Renew), Giuseppe Lupo (S&D), Vytenis Povilas Andriukaitis (S&D), Brando Benifei (S&D), Sebastian Tynkkynen (ECR), Dainius Žalimas (Renew), Rasa Juknevičienė (PPE), Alessandra Moretti (S&D) (15 April 2026) Subject: Application of EU sanctions against a Russian propaganda event in a Member State On 11-12 April 2026, a festival organised by an Italian association linked to RT, formerly known as Russia Today, was held in Bologna, Italy. According to press reports, the festival programme included the screening of contributions from and documentaries produced by RT, (an organisation subject to European sanctions and whose operations are banned on EU territory), which faithfully reproduced the Kremlin’s narrative, in particular regarding the conflict in Ukraine and the role of the West. The festival was also praised by Margarita Simonyan, editor-in-chief of RT and one of the key figures in the Kremlin’s propaganda apparatus. Having regard to Council Regulations (EU) 2022/350 and (EU) 833/2014 and their subsequent amendments, can the Commission clarify: 1.
Whether it was aware of the organisation of such an event in a Member State’s territory?
Whether the event and its programme constitute a violation of the European sanctions imposed on the Russian Federation and certain of its media outlets operating in the EU?

What actions it can take to prevent events of this nature from continuing to take place in a Member State where, at present, there are no legislative measures in force implementing the EU’s sanctions?

(15 June 2026) The Commission monitors the implementation of EU restrictive measures (sanctions) across Member States. This includes the implementation of sanctions on the activities of Russian media outlets, namely the ban on the broadcasting in the EU of content of certain outlets which disseminate propaganda aligned with Kremlin narratives. RT (formerly Russia Today) is subject to a broadcasting ban in the EU and its broadcasting license(s) in the EU are suspended (1). The broadcasting ban prohibits dissemination of RT’s content via any format, including television and online media. In addition, a number of individuals linked to RT are subject to individual restrictive measures (2). The Commission is aware of reports of the organisation of an event at which content of a sanctioned media outlet may have been broadcast. The Commission is in contact with the authorities of the relevant Member State on this issue, as the implementation and enforcement of EU sanctions is, first and foremost, a competence of the Member States. Member States’ national competent authorities must ensure the full and effective implementation of EU sanctions. Where a violation of sanctions is established, Member States’ enforcement authorities must also apply appropriate and effective penalties (3). The Commission rejects efforts by Kremlin-linked media outlets to defend Russia’s illegal invasion of Ukraine in the EU and any actions taken to circumvent EU sanctions and thereby undermine EU values and security. The Commission cannot comment further on national enforcement actions, if any, at this stage.

Article 2(f) of Council Regulation (EU) No 833/2014, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2014/833/oj/eng. Annex I of Council Regulation (EU) No 269/2014, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2014/269/oj/eng. Directive (EU) 2024/1226 on the definition of criminal offences and penalties for the violation of Union restrictive measures, https://eurlex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2024/1226/oj/eng.

E-10-2026-001550.t: Urgent protection of the European citric acid sector against unfair competition and dumping
qt: to the Commission Wouter Beke (PPE) Subject:

The European citric acid sector is in a precarious situation owing to ongoing dumping practices by third countries, particularly China. European producers are facing import prices that are significantly below production costs, which seriously undermines the sector’s viability. The European market for citric acid and citrates amounts to approximately 600 kilotons per year, while the combined production capacity of the remaining European producers is in the region of 350 kilotons (roughly 58 % of demand). Nevertheless, an estimated 60 % of the market is made up of Chinese imports, which indicates that there is a structural disruption in terms of market balance. The existing anti-dumping procedure is too slow and not effective enough. Although the problem has been acute since 2023, any potential adjustment to the measures is not expected until next year at the earliest. This poses a threat to the very existence of European production capacity in a strategic sector, which would have consequences for essential value chains. Against this backdrop, questions arise regarding the need for additional and faster protective measures. 1.
Is the Commission prepared to set import quotas to prevent market disruption?
What is the Commission’s position on imposing minimum local content requirements with a view to strengthening strategic anchoring and security of supply?
Is the Commission considering reintroducing minimum import prices (MIPs) for citric acid, and within what timeframe?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (8.6.2026) The existing anti-dumping measures on citric acid from China are in force since 2008. They are currently subject to an expiry review investigation initiated on 14 April 20261. The scope of an expiry review is to assess if there is a likelihood of continuation and/or recurrence of dumping and injury and therefore, if the measures need to be renewed for further five years. No amendment of the level and form of the measures is possible in this proceeding. Therefore, imports quotas or minimum import prices will not be considered in the proceeding. The Commission has no immediate plans to impose minimum content requirements for citric acid. Nonetheless, the Commission is exploring whether minimum content requirements for bio-based products, including citric acid, should be part of the ‘Biotech Act 2’ proposal, which is scheduled for publication by the end of 2026.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=OJ:C_202602120.

E-10-2026-001549.t: Application of the European Media Freedom Act: French legislative framework
qt: to the Commission David Cormand (Verts/ALE), Anthony Smith (The Left) Subject:

In its reply Ares(2026)2687619 of 11 March 2026, the Commission said that it was liaising with the French authorities to determine the extent to which the legal and institutional framework was ready for the application of Articles 22 and 23 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1083 on media freedom. Can the Commission say: 1.
in its view, what aspects of the French system still require clarification or adjustment?
whether it believes that an existing authority, such as the Regulatory Authority for Audiovisual and Digital Communication (Arcom), could see to this implementation in relation to print media?
whether it believes that specific national legislative action is still necessary?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (15.6.2026) The Commission recalls that the European Media Freedom Act (EMFA)1 is directly applicable in all Member States since 8 August 2025. The Commission continues to monitor and analyse diligently the alignment of national legal frameworks of Member States with the EMFA. Exchanges with Member States, including the French authorities, concern in particular the application of key EMFA provisions relating to the protection of media pluralism and editorial independence, media market concentration assessments, and the safeguards applicable to public service media. While the EMFA is directly applicable, national legislative measures may still be necessary in order to designate competent authorities, confer the necessary powers, establish procedural rules and ensure effective enforcement. The need for such measures depends on the existing national legal and institutional frameworks. The EMFA does not require Member States to establish a new authority where existing structures can ensure effective implementation. It is therefore for France to determine the competent authority or authorities. In that context, the French National Regulatory Authority (Autorité de régulation de la communication audiovisuelle et numérique (ARCOM)) already exercises important regulatory responsibilities in the audiovisual and digital sectors, and any extension of its mandate to print media would be a matter for the French authorities.
1 Regulation (EU) 2024/1083 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 11 April 2024 establishing a
common framework for media services in the internal market and amending Directive 2010/13/EU (European Media Freedom Act).

E-10-2026-001548.t: Delays in boosting administrative capacity in southern Italy: impact on the implementation of the NRRP and cohesion policy
qt: to the Commission Danilo Della Valle (The Left), Valentina Palmisano (The Left) Subject:

In accordance with Regulation (EU) 2021/241 (Recovery and Resilience Facility) and Regulation (EU) 2021/1060 (Cohesion Policy Funds), boosting administrative capacity is an essential condition for the effective use of EU funding. In this context, the ‘Coesione Sud’ (‘Southern Cohesion’) competition, aimed at recruiting 2 200 experts for public authorities in southern Italy, is a key tool to support the implementation of EU-funded projects. However, despite the approval of the shortlists in May 2025, the entry into service of the successful candidates remains far from complete. This delay – also highlighted in recent findings of the Court of Auditors – risks undermining the administrative capacity of the regions concerned when they are at the crucial stage of implementing the National Recovery and Resilience Plan (NRRP), made all the more difficult by regulatory uncertainties and issues in recruitment mechanisms at national level. In light of the above: 1.

Is the Commission aware of these problems and does it believe that the failure to employ candidates who have already been selected could affect the achievement of the administrative capacity targets laid down in Regulation (EU) 2021/241?
What tools will it use to ensure that Member States ensure adequate administrative capacity for the effective use of EU funds?

Does it deem it necessary to take specific steps to prevent implementation delays at national level from undermining the full achievement of the economic, social and territorial cohesion objectives set out in Article 174 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union?

In light of the above: 1.

(19 June 2026) 1. The Commission is closely following the implementation of the competition, supported by the European Regional Development Fund under the Capacity for Cohesion National Programme (1) and designed to introduce in the Italian public administration new staff to be exclusively dedicated to the EU Cohesion Policy. According to the information in its possession, as from 14 April 2026, 987 persons had been hired and entered service, over a total of 1394 candidates shortlisted; the managing authority of the programme reports the difference is being mainly due to the high number of selected candidates withdrawing availability once called in service. 2. The Commission supports Member States through free training — both online and in person — covering public procurement, state aid and fraud prevention. E-10-2026-001547.t: Use of Horizon Europe funds 2014-2020 in the outermost regions
qt: to the Commission Sandro Gozi (Renew) Subject:

The Horizon Europe programme for 2014-2020 has now wound up, following the closure of accounting records on 31 December 2025. However, questions remain as to the actual use of the funds allocated, particularly in the outermost regions. In view of this, can the Commission answer the following question: For EU funds (ESF, EMFF, ERDF, EAFRD) under the 2014-2020 programming period – programmes that closed on 31 December 2023, with accounting operations finalised on 31 December 2025 – what amounts for each of the outermost regions were decommitted or left unused?

E-10-2026-001546.t: EU funding of Euronews – transparency, oversight and editorial independence
qt: to the Commission Markus Buchheit (ESN), Petr Bystron (ESN), Marc Jongen (ESN), Alexander Jungbluth (ESN), Mary Khan (ESN) Subject:

Media reports raise questions about the role of Euronews, inter alia owing to its noticeable reluctance to cover the trial of Azerbaijani journalists. It is well known that Euronews has received EU funding (grants/contracts) in the past. This is not without relevance with regard to the protection of media pluralism, transparency and the most economical use of funds. 1.

What specific requirements regarding quality, transparency and independence (including disclosure of ownership and funding, compliance and auditing) were or are an integral part of the contract, and how is compliance with these requirements monitored?
What consequences does the Commission draw from the current allegations (audit, special audit, suspension of current payments, adjustment of future procurements) and why?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.6.2026) Euronews is a private, independent company and the Commission has no role regarding its internal decisions. Euronews receives EU support as a result of open calls under the Multimedia Actions budget line1, which specialised in financing professional coverage of EU affairs. In line with the principle of media independence, the Commission does not interfere in the editorial decisions of financial beneficiaries, including coverage of specific topics or events. At the same time, under the grant agreements, beneficiaries must adhere to the highest editorial standards, including transparency and impartiality in coverage. The Commission actively monitors contractual compliance through regular monitoring of deliverables stipulated in the agreements, external annual content analysis of content produced, and evaluations of the Multimedia Actions line. Audits can be conducted during or after implementation using the Commission's own services or external firms, with beneficiaries required to cooperate fully. Non-compliance with contractual obligations can result in cost rejections, grant reductions, payment suspensions or termination. At present, the Commission has no evidence of contractual non-compliance. Past evaluations find that Euronews complies with the usual professional standards.
1 https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/multimedia-actions.

E-10-2026-001543.t: Employment crisis and protection of workers at the Leonardo plant in Grottaglie
qt: to the Commission Valentina Palmisano (The Left), Pasquale Tridico (The Left), Gaetano Pedulla' (The Left), Dario Tamburrano (The Left), Danilo Della Valle (The Left), Carolina Morace (The Left), Mario Furore (The Left) Subject:

The Grottaglie plant of Leonardo S.p.A. – of key importance to the Boeing 787 – is going through a period of considerable industrial uncertainty. In the wake of the wage support programme in 2024, concerns remain about the future of the site, threatened by the possible hiving-off of the aerostructures division and the entry of foreign investors, such as the Saudi Arabian PIF fund1. The trade unions are decrying the lack of an industrial plan and are concerned about the loss of skills. Civil aviation provides long-term stable employment. Conversion to military aviation, which is characterised by much lower production rates, would fail to fill the facilities designed for the high rates in civilian aviation, leading to under-utilisation and drastic job cuts. The site employs around 1 300 direct workers for the 787, supporting a local supply chain that would be at risk of collapse2. In the light of Directive 2002/14/EC, Article 27 of the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights, Directive (EU) 2019/1023 and Regulation (EU) 2019/452: 1.
Does the Commission believe that the arrangements for the potential divestment of the aerostructures division comply with EU obligations to inform and consult employees?

What tools will it use to assess the impact of these operations on employment and safeguard strategic skills in the EU’s aerospace sector, thus avoiding the loss of vital civil know-how for these areas?

https://www.tarantotoday.it/attualita/leonardo-grottaglie-assemblea-sindacati-fondo-arabo-19-03-2026.html. https://fiomcgiltaranto.it/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/DOSSIER-Aviazione-civile-e-militare-analisicomparativa-vers.-Marzo-2026.pdf.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.5.2026) Companies must respect the body of EU law, which includes Directive 2002/14 on a general framework on information and consultation of employees1. It lays down minimum requirements for the protection of workers by providing for information and consultation of workers’ representatives on a company’s activities, economic status, and changes to employment. Italy has transposed the Directive into national law2, and it is for the competent national authorities to ensure that an individual employer complies with national rules transposing it, having regard to the specific circumstances of each case. The Commission has launched work3 on an EU Aviation and Aeronautics Strategy, to set out a comprehensive framework to strengthen Europe’s aviation and aeronautical sectors at a time of heightened uncertainty. It will also strengthen the aviation sector’s capacity to respond to crises and security challenges. As for the Aerospace sector, the transition pathway4 initiative identified 53 priority actions to support the twin transitions and the long-term resilience and competitiveness of the aerospace ecosystem. As regards specifically skills, the Commission is working on the implementation of the Union of skills5, a comprehensive strategy to improve high quality education, training, and lifelong learning. The Union of skills includes a series of initiatives to step up skills intelligence and governance at EU level, including the setting up of a European Skills Intelligence Observatory providing strategic data and foresight regarding skills. Such Observatory will also inform the work of the future European Skills High-Level Board6, a newly established group which will provide comprehensive insights on skills to the EU policy makers.

framework for informing and consulting employees in the European Community, OJ L 80, 23.3.2002, p. 29–34. 2 Legislative Decree of 6 February 2007, No 25. 3 Citizens, businesses, and stakeholders were invited to share their feedback at https://ec.europa.eu/info/law/better-regulation/have-your-say/initiatives/17372-EU-aviation-strategy_en 4 https://defence-industry-space.ec.europa.eu/newsroom/transition-pathway_en . 5 https://commission.europa.eu/topics/competitiveness/union-skills_en. 6 https://employment-social-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies-and-activities/skills-and-qualifications/unionskills/european-skills-high-level-board_en.

E-10-2026-001542.t: Transmission of data in the case of cross-border movement of reproductive material
qt: to the Commission Pascal Arimont (PPE) Subject:

The application of Regulation (EC) No 1598/2002 in conjunction with Directive 1999/105/EC raises questions about the scope of the assistance provided and the exchange of information between competent authorities. Article 16(1) of Directive 1999/105/EC provides that Member States ‘shall, by an official control system set up or approved by them, ensure that reproductive material from individual units of approval or lots remains clearly identifiable through the entire process from collection to delivery to the end user’. Article 1 of Regulation (EC) No 1598/2002 provides that, when reproductive material is moved from one Member State to another, authorities are to provide each other with ‘information’. To this end, a standardised information document is established by the Regulation. 1.
Do the requirements of the Regulation include systematic reporting of all transactions?
To what extent is the transfer of personal data (e.g. name and address of the buyer) permissible or required under these rules?
Is it compatible with EU law to require economic operators to systematically submit delivery documents for all transactions?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.7.2026) The requirements of Regulation (EC) No 1598/20021 systematically cover all movements of forest reproductive material between two Member States. Based on the principle of lawfulness enshrined in Article 5(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (the ‘GDPR’)2 in conjunction with Article 6 (1)(c) and (e) thereof, the processing of personal data shall be based on Union or Member State Law, and be necessary for compliance with a legal obligation to which the controller is subject and/or for the performance of a task carried out in the public interest or in the exercise of an official authority vested in the controller. In the context of the cross-border movement of forest reproductive material, Article 16 of Council Directive 1999/105/EC3 read together with Commission Regulation (EC) No 1598/20024, provides for the administrative cooperation and the exchange of information between the competent authorities of the Member States concerned in order to ensure traceability and the proper application of the legislation in question. Furthermore, the Annex to Commission Regulation (EC) No 1598/2002 expressly establishes a standardised ‘Information Document’ for movements of forest reproductive material between Member States, including fields relating to the name and address of the supplier and of the receiver. In that context, this EU legal framework at hand imposes the legal obligation for the exchange of such personal data, thereby complying with the lawfulness requirement under Regulation (EU) 2016/679. It should nevertheless be recalled that compliance with Regulation (EU) 2016/679 remains the responsibility of the competent authorities of the Member States, acting as controllers within the meaning of Article 4(7) thereof.
1 ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2002/1598/oj. 2 General Data Protection Regulation; Regulation (EU) 2016/679 of the European Parliament and of the Council

of 27 April 2016 on the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free movement of such data, and repealing Directive 95/46/EC (General Data Protection Regulation). OJ L 119, 4.5.2016, pg. 1, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj. 3 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:31999L0105. 4 ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2002/1598/oj.

E-10-2026-001540.t: Consistency between EU climate policies and industrial strategies
qt: to the Commission Estelle Ceulemans (S&D) Subject:

The decarbonisation of the steel sector is key to achieving the European Union’s climate targets. However, there are several indications of a disconnect between the stated ambitions of certain major players in the sector and the strategies they have implemented. Notably, ArcelorMittal has delayed or scaled back certain decarbonisation projects in Europe, while remaining highly dependent on carbon-intensive production processes. Furthermore, criticism has been levelled at the lack of emission reduction targets which are aligned with international scientific standards. In view of this: 1.
How does the Commission assess the credibility of the decarbonisation pathways of major steel groups?
What tools does it plan to use to ensure that publicly funded green investments are actually carried out in Europe?
How does the Commission intend to avoid the risks of ‘carbon leakage’ associated with the offshoring of certain operations?
at: (English version) to the Commission Estelle Ceulemans (S&D) (15 April 2026) Subject: Consistency between EU climate policies and industrial strategies The decarbonisation of the steel sector is key to achieving the European Union’s climate targets. However, there are several indications of a disconnect between the stated ambitions of certain major players in the sector and the strategies they have implemented. Notably, ArcelorMittal has delayed or scaled back certain decarbonisation projects in Europe, while remaining highly dependent on carbon-intensive production processes. Furthermore, criticism has been levelled at the lack of emission reduction targets which are aligned with international scientific standards. In view of this: 1.
How does the Commission assess the credibility of the decarbonisation pathways of major steel groups?
What tools does it plan to use to ensure that publicly funded green investments are actually carried out in Europe?
How does the Commission intend to avoid the risks of ‘carbon leakage’ associated with the offshoring of certain operations?

(22 June 2026) The Commission has published a study (1) to develop EU sectoral decarbonisation pathways consistent with the objectives of the European Climate Law, covering multiple sectors including steel. These pathways may serve as a reference framework for assessing the alignment of corporate transition plans with EU climate objectives. The Commission may support undertakings by providing sector-specific guidance that illustrates and facilitates the application of European Sustainability Reporting Standards (2). A number of actions in the Clean Industrial Deal Communication (3) and the Steel and Metals Action Plan (4) concern green investments. These include lowering energy costs, cutting permitting timelines, creating lead markets for low-carbon steel, skills and workforce development and strengthening domestic supply chains. Innovation Fund rules also require projects to be developed and deployed in Europe. The proposed European Competitiveness Fund award procedures may include local production requirements or apply incentives for Union entities. The Industrial Accelerator Act (5) proposes steel lead markets for public procurement and public support. Low-carbon steel can also be used to comply with the CO2 standards for cars and vans. The ETS review foreseen before summer 2026 will ensure that the system will maintain investment certainty and signals for decarbonisation. Carbon leakage in the steel sector is addressed by targeted free allocation in the EU ETS and by the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism. Support under the proposed Temporary Decarbonisation Fund will further mitigate risks. The provisionally agreed trade measures introduce a new tariff system with reduced import quotas and higher duties for imports exceeding those quotas.

E-10-2026-001539.t: Protecting the European steel market from international distortions
qt: to the Commission Estelle Ceulemans (S&D) Subject:

The global steel market is characterised by heavy distortion, notably owing to massive subsidies granted by certain non-EU countries, and protectionist policies such as those currently in place in the United States. In this context, the EU seems particularly exposed to what is considered unfair competition, which further weakens steel as a strategic sector – causing European plant closures, job losses and increased dependence on imports. In this context: 1.
How does the Commission assess the effectiveness of the instruments currently in place, such as the carbon border adjustment mechanism and the trade defence measures?
Does it intend to bolster these tools to better protect the internal market?
What additional initiatives could be adopted to ensure the long-term viability of competitive and sustainable European steel production?
at: (English version) to the Commission Estelle Ceulemans (S&D) (15 April 2026) Subject: Protecting the European steel market from international distortions The global steel market is characterised by heavy distortion, notably owing to massive subsidies granted by certain non-EU countries, and protectionist policies such as those currently in place in the United States. In this context, the EU seems particularly exposed to what is considered unfair competition, which further weakens steel as a strategic sector — causing European plant closures, job losses and increased dependence on imports. In this context: 1.
How does the Commission assess the effectiveness of the instruments currently in place, such as the carbon border adjustment mechanism and the trade defence measures?
Does it intend to bolster these tools to better protect the internal market?
What additional initiatives could be adopted to ensure the long-term viability of competitive and sustainable European steel production?

(10 June 2026) The carbon border adjustment mechanism (CBAM) (1) is an instrument designed to prevent carbon leakage and reduce greenhouse gas emissions. The Commission considers that CBAM is effectively contributing to these aims. Under the article 30 of Regulation (EU) 2023/956 (2), the Commission was mandated to submit a review report at the end of the CBAM transitional period which was presented in December 2025 (3). On 17 December 2025, the Commission proposed measures to strengthen the CBAM. Further review reports will follow before 1 January 2028, as well as every two years thereafter to monitor the functioning of CBAM, evaluating its impacts and considering possible adjustments. Regarding steel, on 7 October 2025, the Commission published a Proposal for a regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council addressing the negative trade-related effects of global overcapacity on the Union steel market (4). Its final text was politically agreed on 13 April 2026 and, once formally approved, will enter into effect as of 1 July 2026. It will ensure, in the field of trade, highly effective protection for the EU’s steel industry against the effects of global overcapacity, contributing to its long-term viability and sustainability. The Industrial Accelerator Act (5) supports the long-term viability of European steel primarily by creating predictable demand for low-carbon steel. It introduces minimum shares of low-carbon steel in public procurement and support schemes, helping close the cost gap and unlock investment decisions that are currently stalled despite significant project pipelines. It also accelerates permitting and prioritises industrial areas to reduce delays and bring projects faster to final investment decision.

E-10-2026-001538.t: Respect for workers’ right to be informed and consulted
qt: to the Commission Estelle Ceulemans (S&D) Subject:

According to a number of trade union sources, European-level workers’ representatives have reported repeated failures by ArcelorMittal to honour information and consultation obligations as part of an ongoing restructuring process in several Member States. Those failures raise concerns about compliance with EU law, in particular the directives on European Works Councils and on informing and consulting employees. They come at a time of major industrial changes, where social dialogue is a key part of guaranteeing a fair transition. In view of this: 1.
Is the Commission aware of this situation, and has it launched, or is it planning to launch, an investigation?
How does the Commission intend to ensure that workers’ rights are actually upheld by multinational companies operating in the EU?
Does it intend to strengthen the European legal framework to ensure that employees are more involved in strategic decisions?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.7.2026) EU Directives (Directive 98/59/EC1, Directive 2001/23/EC2, Directive 2002/14/EC3, and Directive 2009/38/EC4) provide for workers’ involvement in company decision-making by laying down requirements for employers to inform and consult workers’ representatives in cases such as collective redundancies, company restructuring and reorganisations, closures, downsizing, outsourcing and relocations. Member States may adopt more protective rules. While the Commission monitors the correct implementation of EU law by Member States, the enforcement of individual undertakings’ information and consultation obligations falls with the competent national authorities, including courts, which must ensure that the legislation is correctly and effectively applied by individual employers. Should workers consider that an employer did not inform and consult workers’ representatives in accordance with the applicable legislation, they can seek redress before national authorities. The existing rights stemming from these Directives do not limit the topics on which information and consultation must be provided and therefore are flexible enough to adapt to the various challenges that the steel industry is facing, including green and digital transitions. The Commission, nonetheless, continuously screens the EU acquis to ensure that EU rules remain relevant, proportionate and fit to achieve its objectives in the most cost-efficient way. In this context, the 2025 revision of Directive 2009/38/EC5 enhances workers’ information and consultation rights in multinational companies, clarifying the timing and steps in the consultation process, improving confidentiality and access to justice.
