E-10-2026-001537.t: The offshoring and industrial strategy of ArcelorMittal in Europe
qt: to the Commission Estelle Ceulemans (S&D) Subject:

ArcelorMittal has made several announcements recently pointing to a major reorganisation of its operations in Europe, including the relocation of its back-office functions to third countries – primarily India. The moves could eventually affect several thousand jobs and all of the sections of the group. Such decisions are taking place in a context where the European steel industry has already been weakened by falling demand, high production costs and asymmetric international competition. Those decisions raise concerns about the loss of skills, the weakening of industrial value chains and the risk of becoming increasingly dependent on third countries. 1.
What is the Commission’s assessment of the impact this offshoring has on the EU’s industrial resilience?
Does it intend to introduce specific instruments to regulate or limit offshoring in strategic industrial sectors?
What action could be taken to encourage high value-added activities to remain in the EU?
at: (English version) to the Commission Estelle Ceulemans (S&D) (15 April 2026) Subject: The offshoring and industrial strategy of ArcelorMittal in Europe ArcelorMittal has made several announcements recently pointing to a major reorganisation of its operations in Europe, including the relocation of its back-office functions to third countries — primarily India. The moves could eventually affect several thousand jobs and all of the sections of the group. Such decisions are taking place in a context where the European steel industry has already been weakened by falling demand, high production costs and asymmetric international competition. Those decisions raise concerns about the loss of skills, the weakening of industrial value chains and the risk of becoming increasingly dependent on third countries. 1.
What is the Commission’s assessment of the impact this offshoring has on the EU’s industrial resilience?
Does it intend to introduce specific instruments to regulate or limit offshoring in strategic industrial sectors?
What action could be taken to encourage high value-added activities to remain in the EU?

(1 July 2026) The Commission is committed to maintaining industrial competitiveness, innovation and high industrial employment in Europe via a mix of policies. Keeping a strong workforce and high-quality jobs in the EU is essential for the EU’s industrial resilience and economic security (1). The Commission is supporting industrial capacities through measures to boost the competitiveness of EU production. In addition to funding instruments like the Innovation Fund, EU State aid rules provide possibilities for Member States to support the decarbonisation of industry, including the steel sector. The Industrial Accelerator Act (2) proposes measures to retain and attract high-value-added activities in Europe, through lowcarbon and EU origin requirements for strategic sectors and clean technologies, as well as conditions on strategic high-value foreign investments. To strengthen the business case for industry in Europe, the Commission launched the Competitiveness Compass (3) and the Clean Industrial Deal (4). These include initiatives to improve access to energy, markets, investment and skills for energy-intensive industries, such as the Steel and Metal Action Plan (5). The 2026 Annual Single Market and Competitiveness Report (6) tracks their implementation. The One Europe, One Market (7) roadmap agreed on 24 April 2026 sets clear timelines to deliver on strategic priorities. Furthermore, to protect the EU steel sector from the negative effects of global overcapacity, the EU adopted a new trade measure replacing the steel safeguards (8), which will enter into force on 1 July 2026.

E-10-2026-001536.t: Classification of products within the PAFF Committee
qt: to the Commission Tomasz Buczek (PfE) Subject:

The classification of borderline plant protection products and products not subject to this regime, undertaken within the PAFF Committee, is crucial to the functioning of the internal market and for the implementation of EU agricultural and environmental policy. Despite this, the procedure is largely based on informal working documents and practices that are not subject to uniform, binding procedural standards. The reclassification of SILTAC in January 2024 showed that the lack of clear rules on evidentiary standards, procedural transparency and stakeholder participation can lead to decisions that have significant market effects, without minimum procedural safeguards comparable to those applicable in formal administrative procedures being provided. In practice, this means that decisions of a de facto regulatory nature are being taken with no procedural framework that is adapted to the effects these decisions have. In connection with the above: 1.
Does the Commission recognise the need to establish minimum binding procedural standards for the qualification of PAFF Committee products, in particular ‘borderline’ products?
Does the Commission plan to set requirements on evidentiary standards, transparency and stakeholder participation in the process?
In what timeframe is the Commission considering possible changes in this regard?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (30.6.2026)

Article 2 of Regulation (EC) No 1107/20091 defines the scope of that Regulation and clearly sets out the definition of both ‘plant protection products’ and ‘active substances’. The role of the working document on the scope of the Regulation2 to which the Honourable Member refers is therefore not to create new legal criteria or a separate decision-making regime but rather to support a coherent and harmonised application of the existing provisions in technically complex or borderline situations. The document and the related discussions with the Member States in the Standing Committee on Plants, Animals, Food and Feed (SCoPAFF) intends to support, but not replace the decisions taken by the competent national authorities under Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009. These are in charge of the authorisation of plant protection products according to clearly established legal requirements and procedural steps. The development and update of the scope document in the SCoPAFF is a practical mechanism for exchanges between Member States and the Commission on the basis of information, comments or questions submitted by competent authorities and/or economic operators with the aim of promoting consistency in the interpretation and application of the existing regulatory framework. The Commission will continue working with Member States towards this aim. Transparency is assured via the publication of updated versions of the working document (when needed) and via the summary of discussions in the minutes of SCoPAFF, which are publicly available. In light of the above, the Commission does not consider it necessary to establish a binding procedural framework for discussions on whether ‘borderline’ products are in the scope of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 or not.

E-10-2026-001535.t: Conditionality of public aid in the European steel sector
qt: to the Commission Estelle Ceulemans (S&D) Subject:

The European steel industry is going through a severe crisis marked by global overcapacity, distorted international competition and high energy costs. Against this backdrop, ArcelorMittal is receiving significant national and EU public support, particularly under industrial and climate policies. However, several factors are raising concerns regarding the use of such aid. First, major restructuring is under way in several Member States, with job cuts and site closures. In addition, some of the decarbonisation projects announced have been delayed, scaled back or made conditional on new public measures. Moreover, in recent years, a significant portion of the group’s financial resources has been earmarked for shareholders. In light of the above: 1.
How does the Commission intend to ensure that EU public aid granted to the steel sector is made strictly conditional on maintaining industrial capacity and jobs in Europe?
Does it intend to strengthen conditionality requirements linked to decarbonisation investments?
What monitoring and sanctioning mechanisms could be put in place in the event that those commitments are not complied with?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.6.2026) While the legal basis for the Commission’s State aid control does not allow to make an aid measure dependent on conditions aimed to maintain industrial capacity and jobs in Europe. the Member State concerned may choose to impose such conditions on the aid recipient. In such a case, it is for the Member State concerned to ensure that those conditions are complied with. Under the Clean Industrial Deal State Aid Framework (CISAF), public support can incentivise the aid beneficiary to realise the investment in the European Economic Area (EEA) rather than in an alternative location outside the EEA. As regards conditions aimed to ensure that decarbonisation projects are implemented, the 2022 Guidelines on State Aid for Climate, Environmental Protection and Energy (CEEAG) provide that Member States must demonstrate that reasonable measures will be taken to ensure that State-aided projects will actually be developed (point 120 CEEAG). In this respect, the 2023 Commission Decision approving aid to ArcelorMittal under the CEEAG1 notes that the French authorities intend to closely monitor the development of the project, and have mechanisms in place under national legislation which would allow them to act, should the project not be realised or its objectives not be met.
1 https://ec.europa.eu/competition/state_aid/cases1/202436/SA_104903_131.pdf.

E-10-2026-001534.t: Google’s verification of Android developers: are we coming to the end of open-source software on our mobile phones?
qt: to the Commission Catherine Griset (PfE) Subject:
Google’s verification of Android developers: are we coming to the end of opensource software on our mobile phones?

From September 2026, all Android apps will be subject to prior registration and verification of the developer’s identity at Google, even when the app will not be distributed by the Google Play Store. Developers will have to provide an identity document, proof of address (for private individuals) or business identification documents, and make a one-off payment of USD 25. Users will nevertheless be able to install an app from an unverified developer, by going through an ‘Advanced Flow’ process that discourages installation: — manual activation of development options; — compulsory restart of telephone; — 24-hour safety period for finalising installation; — final authentication by PIN or biometrics after that period. This control boosts user protection against malware and fraud, but at the cost of subjugating open-source software to Google. In light of the above: 1.
Does the Commission consider this verification policy to be in line with competition rules, given that Google is strengthening its position as gatekeeper on the mobile market?
Does this policy not risk allowing some Member States to block applications that are otherwise legal within the EU?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (13.5.2026) The Commission is aware of Google’s announcement to introduce this verification process starting from September 2026 in some jurisdictions (not including the EU based on publicly available information). The Commission understands that, as a result of this process, Android will require that all apps are registered by verified developers in order to be installed on certified Android devices. The Commission is also aware of public campaigns such as ‘Keep Android Open’ which have emerged in reaction to Google’s announcement. Article 6(4) of the Digital Markets Act (‘DMA’)1 obliges gatekeepers like Alphabet to allow and technically enable the effective distribution of apps on their operating system through third party app stores or the web. At the same time, the DMA also permits Google to introduce strictly necessary and proportionate measures to ensure that third-party software apps or app stores do not endanger the integrity of the hardware or operating system, provided that such measures are duly justified by Alphabet. The Commission is actively engaged in a regulatory dialogue with Alphabet concerning Article 6(4) and is diligently monitoring Alphabet's compliance with the relevant legal framework to ensure that apps, including open-source apps, can be effectively distributed on Android outside Google Play.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/1925/oj/eng.

E-10-2026-001531.t: Repeated human rights violations by Israel
qt: to the Commission Sirpa Pietikäinen (PPE) Subject:

Time and again, Israel has flouted international human rights agreements, for example by introducing the death penalty for Palestinian prisoners. What is more, the crisis facing the Palestinians will deepen as Israel continues its actions in breach of international law in both Gaza and the West Bank. What steps does the Commission intend to take in response to this situation?

E-10-2026-001530.t: Interference with the sovereignty of a Member State as a requirement for the release of frozen EU funds?
qt: to the Commission Erik Kaliňák (NI), Judita Laššáková (NI) Subject:

In response to the results of the Hungarian elections, the President of the Commission stated on 13 April 2026 that ‘Hungary is coming back to the European path’. Nevertheless, the Commission continues to make the release of frozen EU funds conditional on the fulfilment of all 27 super milestones, with particular attention drawn to four judicial super milestones (Nos 213–216), which directly interfere with the organisation and functioning of the national judiciary-an area that, under the treaties, primarily falls within the competence of the Member States, while respecting the requirements of EU law. 1.

On the basis of which specific provision of the treaties does the Commission justify the requirements contained in super milestones 213–216, which regulate fundamental aspects of the organisation and functioning of the national judiciary (strengthening of the National Judicial Council, election of the President of the Curia, allocation of cases, preliminary references to the Court of Justice of the EU, and review of decisions by the Constitutional Court)?

How does the Commission reconcile making the release of duly allocated EU funds conditional on these requirements with the principle of the institutional autonomy of the Member States and respect for their national identity under Article 4(2) of the Treaty on European Union?

In what way does the Commission ensure that these four super milestones do not constitute a disproportionate and ultra vires interference with the constitutional order of a Member State, but remain strictly limited to the protection of the Union’s financial interests?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (15.6.2026) The Commission understands that the questions relate to Hungary’s Recovery and Resilience Plan (‘RRP’). The Recovery and Resilience Facility (‘RRF’) Regulation1 only allows disbursement of funds in case the Member State’s audit and control framework effectively protects the financial interest of the Union. In the Hungarian RRP, Hungary committed to implement in total 27 audit and control milestones (or ‘super milestones’) to ensure this. This includes four reforms to strengthen judicial independence which aims at addressing the underlying challenges identified by a dedicated country-specific recommendation on the independence of the judiciary. On 15 December 2022, the Council of the European Union approved Hungary’s RRP, including those milestones. Hungary is yet to submit a payment request. In line with the RRF legal framework, the Commission will assess the fulfilment of all milestones and targets, including the ‘super milestones’, only thereafter. As for all Member States, that assessment will be carried out in line with the applicable rules and the methodology specified in Annex I to the Communication published on 21 February 20232. In particular, the satisfactory fulfilment of milestones and targets is assessed on the basis of the criteria set out in the Council implementing decisions. In this context, the Commission has to base its assessment on the wording of each milestone and target, in light of its context and purpose, to determine whether, based on the justification provided by the Member State, those criteria are satisfactorily fulfilled or not.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2021/241/oj/eng. 2 https://commission.europa.eu/system/files/2023-02/COM_2023_99_1_EN.pdf.

E-10-2026-001529.t: Does the President of the Commission intend to use the Hungarian elections to abolish the veto in the EU’s foreign policy?
qt: to the Commission Erik Kaliňák (NI), Judita Laššáková (NI) Subject:

In response to the results of the Hungarian elections, the President of the Commission on 13 April 2026 called on Member States to ‘seize the momentum’ and move to qualified majority voting in the EU’s Common Foreign and Security Policy in order to prevent ‘systemic blockages.’1 With this statement, she clearly called into question the fundamental principle of unanimity, which is explicitly enshrined in the Treaty on European Union and was expressly agreed upon by the Member States. 1.

Does the Commission consider it appropriate, immediately after elections in one country, that Ursula von der Leyen calls for changing the fundamental rules of the EU Treaties, which were adopted unanimously by all Member States?

Since the activation of the passerelle clause (or any other change in voting procedures) requires the unanimous consent of all 27 Member States, how exactly does the Commission intend to achieve this change in full compliance with the Treaties?

How does the Commission assess concerns that a move to qualified majority voting would significantly weaken the influence of smaller Member States on decisions in the area of foreign and security policy?
https://www.politico.eu/article/ursula-von-der-leyen-uses-hungary-viktor-orban-defeat-to-push-for-end-ofveto-in-eu-foreign-policy/.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (28.7.2026) 1. The Commission’s longstanding position, as expressed in Communications from 20181 and 20242 and reiterated by the President of the Commission in her State of the Union address in September 2025, is that, if the EU wants to act quickly, efficiently, and therefore strategically, unanimity voting ought to be reconsidered in certain policy areas, including on aspects of the Common Foreign and Security Policy. 2. While the Commission has indicated its support for a shift from unanimity to qualified majority voting through the activation of the passerelle clauses in the EU Treaties, the decision lies, depending on the policy area, with the European Council or the Council, which need to act by unanimity. 3. The Commission is aware of the concerns of some Member States with regard to a shift from unanimity to qualified majority voting. It considers that the activation of passerelle clauses could be combined with appropriate and proportionate safeguards to accommodate strategic national interests.
1 Communication on A stronger global actor: a more efficient decision-making for EU Common Foreign and
Security Policy, COM(2018) 647 final. 2 Communication on pre-enlargement reforms and policy reviews, COM(2024) 146 final.

E-10-2026-001528.t: Protecting our sovereignty and food security following the detection of cereulide in infant formula
qt: to the Commission Laurence Trochu (ECR), Céline Imart (PPE), Marion Maréchal (ECR), Nicolas Bay (ECR), Ciaran Mullooly (Renew), Marie-Luce Brasier-Clain (PfE), Kosma Złotowski (ECR), Paolo Inselvini (ECR), Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE), Anne-Sophie Frigout (PfE), Claudiu-Richard Târziu (ECR), Isabelle Le Callennec (PPE), Piotr Müller (ECR), Petr Bystron (ESN), Sander Smit (ECR) Subject:

In a number of European countries, babies have recently had to be hospitalised after consuming formula. Their hospitalisation – some babies even died – is the result of formula products’ contamination with cereulide, which was found in abnormally high levels in one of the ingredients of these products: arachidonic acid, produced in China, which is essential for replicating breast milk. In addition to the increase in checks by the European authorities on consignments of products imported from China, the question of food sovereignty, which is essential to ensuring public safety, must be addressed. We therefore wish to address the following questions to the Commission: 1.

with a view to safeguarding the quality of the food Europeans consume, does it have the means to ensure that production standards are high in the third countries from which we import consumer products?

given that our dependence on other exporting countries, in this case China, is undermining our food sovereignty, does the Commission intend to take steps to boost European production, such as possible relocations, particularly with regard to strategic products such as infant formula?
Supporter1
This question is supported by a Member other than the authors: Catherine Griset (PfE).
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.7.2026) The EU ensures that third-country food imports meet EU food safety standards through a robust legal framework backed by a strong system of official controls which protects consumers by preventing the entry of unsafe products into the EU’s territory. The Rapid Alert System for Food and Feed (RASFF) facilitates instant information exchange, enabling swift, coordinated action across the EU whenever risks are identified. The Commission may conduct audits in third countries and suspend or even ban imports where serious deficiencies are found. Regular bilateral dialogues between the EU and key trading partners encourage closer regulatory alignment, while the EU’s active role in Codex Alimentarius helps elevate food safety standards globally. The contaminated ingredient in the infant formula products, arachidonic acid-rich oil, is produced by fermentation. Both the Life Sciences Strategy1 and Bioeconomy Strategy2 recognise the importance of advanced fermentation technologies. The Commission is pursuing activities related to their development and deployment, benefiting the EU fermentation ecosystem.
1 COM/2025/525 final. 2 COM/2025/960 final.

E-10-2026-001526.t: What steps has the Commission taken to safeguard the integrity of its actions and public trust?
qt: to the Commission Erik Kaliňák (NI) Subject:

In its reply to my Question E-000527/20261 of 9 February 2026, the Commission explicitly stated on 14 April 2026 that it firmly rejects the unfounded and unsubstantiated allegations set out in the report of the US House Judiciary Committee of 3 February 2026, including those relating to the 2023 Slovak elections. The Commission thus clearly stated that it considers these allegations to be untrue and strongly distances itself from them. 1.

I assume that, since the publication of the US report up to the present day, the Commission has already taken specific diplomatic, political and legal steps to actively safeguard the integrity of its actions and public trust; if not, why not?

Has the Commission formally approached-by diplomatic note, official letter or other official means-the United States House Judiciary Committee, its Chair, or the US Congress with a request for a public correction, retraction, or withdrawal of the false allegations concerning interference in the Slovak elections?

Beyond the brief response to my written question, what other public steps (press releases, statements, media briefings or other forms of communication) has the Commission taken vis-à-vis the European public to actively refute these allegations and defend its credibility?
https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/E-10-2026-000527_EN.html.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (12.6.2026) The Commission has repeatedly clarified its position to the US administration and the House Judiciary Committee and stands firm on its position that the latter’s Report1 of 3 February 2026 misrepresents the nature of the EU Digital Rulebook. As affirmed by the Spokespersons’ Service at the Midday press briefing on 3 February 2026, the Commission rebuts any allegation that the Digital Rulebook weakens freedom of expression. As indicated in the answer to written question E-000527/20262, freedom of expression is at the heart of the Digital Services Act (DSA3). The DSA helps protect it by giving users the right to explanations, appeals and redress when their content is removed or restricted by platforms. The Commission pursues maximum transparency in its enforcement of the DSA. All enforcement decisions are taken in an open and transparent manner and are published on a dedicated website4. The Commission engages continuously with US representatives at both political and technical level on a wide range of subjects including the EU digital rules with the objective of promoting cooperation to address shared challenges which the online world poses. Enforcing democratically adopted legislation is not up for discussion. This remains the sovereign right of the EU, and the Commission will continue to enforce the DSA fairly, in line with due process and in maximum transparency.
1 https://judiciary.house.gov/media/press-releases/new-report-exposes-european-commission-decade-long-

campaign-censor-american. 2 https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/E-10-2026-000527_EN.html. 3 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/2065/oj/eng. 4 https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/list-designated-vlops-and-vloses.

E-10-2026-001525.t: EU support to secure access to drinking water in Mayotte, Guadeloupe and Martinique
qt: to the Commission André Rougé (PfE), Rody Tolassy (PfE), Marie-Luce Brasier-Clain (PfE) Subject:

With water in short supply in Mayotte, an agreement has recently been signed between the French Geological Survey (BRGM) and the Mayotte water authority to secure access to drinking water on the island. The programme, which has a budget of EUR 1.9 million, is part of the 2024-2027 Mayotte water plan, the aim of which is to provide a sustainable response to the water shortages that are hitting the people of Mayotte very hard. The people of Mayotte are still facing major restrictions, and the water supply is often cut off completely. This raises legitimate questions about how effective the publicly funded announcements and schemes actually are. The water shortages are, after all, well on their way to turning into a humanitarian and health crisis. What is more, Mayotte is not the only outermost region of France affected by water shortages: Guadeloupe and Martinique are also having serious problems, particularly where their water supply networks are concerned. In the light of the foregoing: 1.
Can the Commission state whether direct or indirect EU funding is being deployed for the water sector in Mayotte, Guadeloupe and Martinique?
If not, what specific measures does the Commission intend to support to make sure that these outermost regions can rely on their own supplies of drinking water in the long term?
at: (English version) to the Commission André Rougé (PfE), Rody Tolassy (PfE), Marie-Luce Brasier-Clain (PfE) (15 April 2026) Subject: EU support to secure access to drinking water in Mayotte, Guadeloupe and Martinique With water in short supply in Mayotte, an agreement has recently been signed between the French Geological Survey (BRGM) and the Mayotte water authority to secure access to drinking water on the island. The programme, which has a budget of EUR 1.9 million, is part of the 2024-2027 Mayotte water plan, the aim of which is to provide a sustainable response to the water shortages that are hitting the people of Mayotte very hard. The people of Mayotte are still facing major restrictions, and the water supply is often cut off completely. This raises legitimate questions about how effective the publicly funded announcements and schemes actually are. The water shortages are, after all, well on their way to turning into a humanitarian and health crisis. What is more, Mayotte is not the only outermost region of France affected by water shortages: Guadeloupe and Martinique are also having serious problems, particularly where their water supply networks are concerned. In the light of the foregoing: 1.
Can the Commission state whether direct or indirect EU funding is being deployed for the water sector in Mayotte, Guadeloupe and Martinique?
If not, what specific measures does the Commission intend to support to make sure that these outermost regions can rely on their own supplies of drinking water in the long term?

(22 May 2026) The 2022 Communication setting out the strategy for the outermost regions (1) recognised the need to prioritise basic needs, including access to water and sanitation. In that Communication, the Commission committed to help create synergies between national budgets and the different funds and programs in order to improve the quality of life of citizens, and it will reaffirm this commitment in the new strategy for the outermost regions, due to be adopted in summer 2026. An independent study on living conditions and access to basic needs in outermost regions published by the Commission in 2024 (2) recommended devoting additional resources to improving access to drinking water. For the European Regional Development Fund water is a key priority in French outermost regions with substantial financial support that has further increased following last year’s mid-term review of regional programmes. In Guadeloupe, Martinique and Mayotte, the EU is investing EUR 183 million in water and sanitation over the 2021-2027 period, for example to strengthen the resilience of water catchments, develop drinking water production facilities and improve the efficiency of distribution networks. In Mayotte, the construction of a new seawater desalination plant is an operation of strategic importance. Furthermore, to enhance water management, the European Agricultural Fund for Rural Development supports reservoir projects for agricultural use in Réunion and Guadeloupe. The directive on the quality of water intended for human consumption (3) includes provisions to protect human health by ensuring access to safe drinking water. Member States, including France, had to transpose this directive into national law and comply with its provisions by January 2023.

E-10-2026-001524.t: Conditionality for EU support to Nigeria in view of violations of human rights and religious freedom
qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Piotr Müller (ECR) Subject:

On 23 March 2026, the Vice-President / High Representative, Kaja Kallas, announced the mobilisation of EUR 66 million in grants and EUR 221 million in low-interest loans for new EU projects in Nigeria, as well as closer cooperation on migration, research and innovation. This decision gives rise to serious misgivings in light of persistent reports of violence against Christians, impunity for perpetrators, and wider violations of human rights and religious freedom in Nigeria. EU financial support must not give the impression that the Union is prepared to turn a blind eye to persecution and poor citizen protection for the sake of maintaining political and migratory cooperation. In light of the above: 1.

What specific conditions pertaining to the protection of human rights, in particular religious freedom and the security of Christian communities, have been tied to the latest EU financial support to Nigeria?
Before this package was announced, was an assessment carried out of the action taken by the Nigerian authorities to prosecute the perpetrators of attacks on Christians and protect civilians?

Does the Vice-President / High Representative intend to make further funding and cooperation with Nigeria contingent on a measurable improvement in the human rights situation and effective action against religious violence?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (10.6.2026) The Samoa Agreement1, signed between the EU and a number of African, Caribbean and Pacific States including Nigeria, constitutes the overarching legal framework governing, among other matters, the EU-Nigeria cooperation. Article 9 of the Samoa Agreement includes protecting and ensuring the ‘freedom of thought, religion and belief’, thus obliging all signatories not to discriminate based on religion or belief in the exercise and enjoyment of fundamental rights. In addition, under the Samoa Agreement, respect for human rights, democratic principles and the rule of law is an essential element, any breach of which may trigger consultations and, ultimately, appropriate measures, including the suspension of the Agreement or financial transfers. Financial packages under instruments such as Global Gateway are subject to internal programming procedures involving the relevant EU services, as well as strategic alignment with the EU's external action priorities. The EU has consistently expressed its concern about violence affecting all communities in Nigeria, including attacks on both Christian and Muslim communities, and has advocated for accountability and swift responses where such attacks occur. Over the last decade, the EU has invested heavily to support counter-terrorism, stabilisation and rule of law in Nigeria. It is widely recognised that violence in Nigeria is a multifaceted security challenge driven by terrorism, banditry and resource-based intercommunal conflict. It cuts across religious and ethnic lines and affects communities of all faiths. In any case, the EU's cooperation and partnership with Nigeria is not structured around single-issue conditionality.
1Partnership Agreement between the European Union and its Member States, of the one part, and the Members
of the Organisation of African, Caribbean and Pacific States, of the other, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/agree_internation/2023/2862/oj.

E-10-2026-001523.t: Unofficial migrant mercenaries used by the Greek authorities in mass pushback operations
qt: to the Commission Konstantinos Arvanitis (The Left) Subject:

Today, a BBC article1 revealed that Greek law enforcement authorities have been using migrants to assist them in large-scale pushback operations targeting hundreds of other migrants each week at the country’s land border with Türkiye. Masked mercenaries are recruited from countries such as Pakistan, Syria and Afghanistan, and rewarded with cash, valuables and mobile phones looted from other migrants, as well as with papers allowing them passage through Greece. Confirming earlier (2022) allegations by Lighthouse Reports and Frontex’s Fundamental Rights Office itself, the article refers to internal police documents describing the informal recruitment of so-called migrant mercenaries as early as 2020, as ordered and overseen by senior officers. The BBC’s findings include allegations of extreme violence, with testimonies indicating that migrants and asylum seekers have been stripped, robbed, beaten until they passed out, and even sexually assaulted. Although the Greek Prime Minister claimed that he was unaware of the allegations about the use of mercenaries, the investigative team’s police sources asserted that ‘there is no soldier, police officer or Frontex officer serving here in Evros who does not know that pushbacks are taking place.’ Can the Commission therefore answer the following questions: 1.
What action does it intend to take in response to these allegations?
What measures could it take to improve early intervention and deterrence procedures in similar/related cases?

E-10-2026-001522.t: EU energy security and regulatory approach to gas and national energy resources
qt: to the Commission Piotr Müller (ECR) Subject:

In the context of increasing geopolitical tensions linked to the conflict around Iran, reflected in increased energy prices and increased supply uncertainty, the Commission’s recent recommendations for more flexibility in replenishing gas storage facilities confirm that gas remains a key pillar of the European Union’s energy security. At the same time, the restricted status of gas and coal in the EU taxonomy and the additional burdens arising from the EU ETS2 system point to a lack of regulatory consistency. In a context of continued geopolitical instability, the importance of national energy resources, including coal, as a locally accessible pillar of supply security is also growing. The current situation calls for a pragmatic energy policy based on technological neutrality and system resilience. This prompts the following questions: 1.

How does the Commission justify maintaining a restrictive approach to gas and coal in the EU regulatory framework, despite their crucial role in ensuring energy security in a context of geopolitical instability?

Has the Commission carried out an assessment of the resilience of the current regulatory framework, including the taxonomy and the ETS2 system, to repeated geopolitical shocks, and does it take into account the role of national energy resources, including coal, in ensuring security of supply?

Is the Commission considering revising its approach to gas and coal and other available energy sources in the direction of full technological neutrality and reducing the regulatory burdens to ensure stability of supply and affordable energy prices for citizens and industry?
at: (English version) to the Commission Piotr Müller (ECR) (15 April 2026) Subject: EU energy security and regulatory approach to gas and national energy resources In the context of increasing geopolitical tensions linked to the conflict around Iran, reflected in increased energy prices and increased supply uncertainty, the Commission’s recent recommendations for more flexibility in replenishing gas storage facilities confirm that gas remains a key pillar of the European Union’s energy security. At the same time, the restricted status of gas and coal in the EU taxonomy and the additional burdens arising from the EU ETS2 system point to a lack of regulatory consistency. In a context of continued geopolitical instability, the importance of national energy resources, including coal, as a locally accessible pillar of supply security is also growing. The current situation calls for a pragmatic energy policy based on technological neutrality and system resilience. This prompts the following questions: 1.

How does the Commission justify maintaining a restrictive approach to gas and coal in the EU regulatory framework, despite their crucial role in ensuring energy security in a context of geopolitical instability?

Is the Commission considering revising its approach to gas and coal and other available energy sources in the direction of full technological neutrality and reducing the regulatory burdens to ensure stability of supply and affordable energy prices for citizens and industry?

(6 July 2026) The EU’s approach to technology neutrality in the energy sector is guided by the principle of allowing the market to determine the least-cost solution to achieve policy goals. The EU’s long term strategic objective is to reduce structural dependencies on imported fossil fuels, which have proven to expose our economies to price volatility and geopolitical risks. As the EU is a net importer of fossil fuels (1), energy security and affordability can only be achieved by reducing exposure to global fossil fuel markets (2). Scaling up domestic renewable energy, electrification and energy efficiency is central to energy security, industrial competitiveness, and climate objectives. Strengthening the EU’s energy autonomy therefore requires both diversification of supply of remaining fossil fuel imports and a progressive shift towards more domestic, clean energy sources. The Emissions Trading System 2 (ETS2) contributes to the EU’s energy security and resilience by incentivizing clean transport and building heating powered by homegrown renewable electricity. ETS2 is based on a comprehensive impact assessment (3) and includes dedicated provisions to address price shocks. The introduction of ETS2 was recently postponed to 2028 in order to further strengthen the flexibilities aiming at maintaining prices stability. With regards to the EU Taxonomy, the Complementary Climate Delegated Act adopted in 2022 sets conditions under which fossil-fuel-based gas activities can be deemed as sustainable, provided it meets some specific strict conditions that are in line with EU’s long term strategic objective.

In 2025, the EU spent EUR 336.5 billion for fossil fuels imports. Fitness check to evaluate EU's security of electricity and gas supply framework (SWD(2025) 435 final). https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:52021SC0601.

qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Anthony Smith (The Left), Emma Fourreau (The Left), Leila Chaibi (The Left) Subject:

Since in early 2026, when Donald Trump announced a tightening of the embargo against Cuba, cutting off its supply of fuel, the state of affairs and humanitarian risks in the island have been deteriorating at an alarming rate. Given the continual blackouts and shortage of medicines and other medical supplies, many medical procedures have had to be cancelled and certain courses of medical treatment have had to be abandoned. Cuba’s people have thus been deliberated placed in harm’s way. The most vulnerable among them, such as children, pregnant women, the elderly or disabled, and patients with chronic illnesses, have been the first to suffer. The WHO has expressed particular concern at this emergency, stating that: ‘Health should be protected at all costs and never be at the mercies of geopolitics, energy blockades and power outages’. The UN, meanwhile has proposed a USD 94.1 million plan to meet the country’s urgent needs and keep essential services running, particularly in the heath-care sector. The European Union has yet to react. Can the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy therefore say: 1.
Whether the Commission intends to take urgent action to get the USA to lift the embargo on Cuba?
Whether it intends to contribute to international solidarity by freeing up and sending stocks of medicines, medical supplies and fuel to Cuba?

(29 June 2026) The EU is aware of the progressive tightening of the measures being adopted by the United States (US) against the government of Cuba, and on the serious impact of these measures, including the obstacles they create for the Cuban population in obtaining essential medical care. The EU has regularly expressed the views on the longstanding US embargo and connected measures against Cuba, and it has continued to alert on the adverse impact of such measures both, on the wider Cuban population and on EU interests. The EU considers that divergences between the US and Cuba should be addressed through diplomacy. Therefore, the EU has actively engaged with the authorities in Havana and Washington to encourage constructive solutions to such divergences. Preventing social collapse in Cuba remains a clear EU priority. In 2026, the EU has decided to allocate an additional EUR 6 million as humanitarian support to alleviate suffering and save lives. This figure, together with the EUR 14 million allocated in the period 2023-2025 still under implementation, is expected to contribute to address the most urgent humanitarian needs, including health-related.

E-10-2026-001519.t: Noise from wind farms, infrasound and protection of public health
qt: to the Commission Zala Tomašič (PPE) Subject:

Recent discussions at EU level, including in the Committee on Petitions (PETI), have highlighted regulatory gaps regarding noise emissions from wind farms and their potential impact on public health and quality of life. The Commission has acknowledged that noise from wind farms is not specifically regulated in EU legislation and that existing methodologies do not fully capture low-frequency noise and infrasound. In this context: 1.

Does the Commission intend to propose specific EU rules or guidelines on noise from wind farms, including harmonised methods for measuring, monitoring and assessing low-frequency noise and infrasound?
How will the Commission ensure that when EU noise policy is updated in future it will take due account of technological developments and the cumulative effects of wind farms on nearby residents?

Will the Commission consider introducing minimum protection standards for affected residents, such as mandatory acoustic studies, enhanced health impact assessments or guidelines for the precautionary siting of new projects?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (10.7.2026) As stated in the reply to written question E-000019/2026, the Environmental Noise Directive (END)1 remains the main EU legislative instrument for addressing excessive noise pollution. The END is focused on traffic noise and noise from the industrial activities listed in Annex I of the Industrial Emissions Directive (IED)2. However, the IED does not cover the generation of electricity from wind turbines. Windfarm projects can nonetheless be subject to an Environmental Impact Assessment3. In that case noise emissions must be assessed and measures identified to address possible adverse effects. In 2018, the World Health Organization (WHO) developed guidelines4 to provide recommendations for protecting human health from exposure to environmental noise originating from various sources, including wind turbines. While the WHO conditionally recommended keeping audible wind turbine noise below 45 decibel day–evening–night noise level to prevent annoyance and sleep disturbance, due to the lack of sufficient scientific evidence, it did not propose specific limits or guidelines regarding infrasound. At the current stage of scientific and policy development on noise at global and EU level, it therefore remains the primary responsibility of the Member States to secure the protection of citizens affected by the noise produced by wind turbines, by defining and enforcing, where appropriate and taking into account the local circumstances, specific noise requirements which may use the thresholds recommended by the WHO.
1 Directive 2002/49/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 25 June 2002 relating to the

assessment and management of environmental noise, OJ L 189 18.7.2002, p. 12. 2 Directive (EU) 2024/1785 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 24 April 2024 amending Directive 2010/75/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council on industrial emissions (integrated pollution Prevention and control) and Council Directive 1999/31/EC on the landfill of waste, OJ L, 2024/1785, 15.7.2024. 3 In accordance with Directive 2011/92/EU as amended by Directive 2014/52/EU. Directive 2014/52/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 16 April 2014 amending Directive 2011/92/EU on the assessment of the effects of certain public and private projects on the environment, OJ L 124, 25.4.2014. 4 https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789289053563.

qt: to the Commission César Luena (S&D) Subject:

The European Insurance and Occupational Pensions (EIOPA) and the European Stability Mechanism (ESM) have published a joint paper proposing the creation of an EU risk pooling mechanism for natural disasters: a common pool funded by insurers and, where applicable, national schemes, and a public safety net or backstop based on loans for extreme events with an estimated capacity of between EUR 10 billion and EUR 65 billion. The aim is to close the gap between economic losses and insured losses in the EU, which is considerable in some Member States. In view of the proposal: 1.
What plans does the Commission have to set up an EU mechanism of this type?

If it intends to create such a mechanism, what options is the Commission considering (voluntary pool, participation of national schemes, backstop model) and what role does it foresee for the competent European authorities?

How does the Commission intend to coordinate this potential initiative with climate adaptation and risk prevention policies to prevent broader insurance coverage replacing risk reduction or creating negative incentives?
at: (English version) to the Commission César Luena (S&D) (14 April 2026) Subject: Pooling natural disaster risks The European Insurance and Occupational Pensions (EIOPA) and the European Stability Mechanism (ESM) have published a joint paper proposing the creation of an EU risk pooling mechanism for natural disasters: a common pool funded by insurers and, where applicable, national schemes, and a public safety net or backstop based on loans for extreme events with an estimated capacity of between EUR 10 billion and EUR 65 billion. The aim is to close the gap between economic losses and insured losses in the EU, which is considerable in some Member States. In view of the proposal: 1.
What plans does the Commission have to set up an EU mechanism of this type?

If it intends to create such a mechanism, what options is the Commission considering (voluntary pool, participation of national schemes, backstop model) and what role does it foresee for the competent European authorities?

How does the Commission intend to coordinate this potential initiative with climate adaptation and risk prevention policies to prevent broader insurance coverage replacing risk reduction or creating negative incentives?

(3 July 2026) Across Europe, physical climate risks are on the rise, as the climate-related events are becoming more frequent and severe, affecting insurance markets through premiums, coverage conditions and widening protection gaps. This raises important policy questions regarding prevention, risk awareness, insurance affordability and compensation mechanisms. The Commission is closely following developments and discussions on broader insurance coverage at both national and EU level recognising that they are complementary to key measures promoting risk reduction and climate adaptation and resilience. In this context the discussion paper of the European Insurance and Occupational Pensions Authority (EIOPA) and the European Stability Mechanism provides a useful in-depth assessment. Against this background, in the context of the ongoing work on the European integrated framework for climate resilience, the Commission has launched a public consultation covering a broad range of topics, including insurance. The contributions received from stakeholders will help inform the Commission’s reflection on possible future policy initiatives. The factual summary of the feedback was published on the Have Your Say website (1):
https://ec.europa.eu/info/law/better-regulation/have-your-say/initiatives/14770-European-climate-resilience-and-risk-management-integratedframework/public-consultation_en.

E-10-2026-001515.t: The impact of oil prices, supply routes and refinery margins on fuel prices in the EU
qt: to the Commission Danuše Nerudová (PPE) Subject:

Following recent developments in global oil markets, particularly after disruptions to operations in the Strait of Hormuz at the end of February 2026, there has been a significant increase in Brent crude oil prices (from approximately USD 72 to nearly USD 120 per barrel within one month). This development is gradually being reflected in fuel prices in the EU. Analyses show, however, that the crude oil price itself accounts for only 30–35 % of the final price of diesel. Refining margins (‘crack spread’) play a significant role; in March 2026 they reached extraordinary levels of USD 60–80 per barrel, i.e. up to four times the usual level. At the same time, supply routes are changing, particularly in Central Europe, where some Member States, following the cessation of supplies from Russia, rely on a limited number of routes (e.g. the TAL pipeline), which increases vulnerability to geopolitical and logistical shocks. In light of the above, the Commission is requested to answer the following questions: 1.
How does the Commission assess the current level of refining margins in the EU and their impact on fuel prices?
To what extent are these margins the result of market factors, and to what extent might they indicate insufficient competition or market failure?
Is the Commission considering measures to increase market transparency and limit the impact of rising refining margins on fuel prices during times of crisis?

(12 June 2026) The Commission tracks energy prices and produces a weekly oil bulletin and considers other market analysis such as product specific imbalances and refining capacities, margins and constraints, with recent volatility triggered more by regional dislocation, logistical and geopolitical shocks, rather than from any weak competition or market failure. The Commission will continue monitoring the evolution of the crisis and assessing its impacts, including on refining margins. To address the impacts of the disruption of oil and gas transit, the Commission put forward on 22 April 2026 its new initiative AccelerateEU (1), proposing timely, targeted and temporary measures to bring relief to consumers, while avoiding fragmented national responses and reducing dependency on fossil fuels.

E-10-2026-001514.t: Failings in EU governance on artificial intelligence and respect for national prerogatives
qt: to the Commission Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE) Subject:

In its Special Report No 12/20261, the European Court of Auditors highlights serious shortcomings in the implementation of the European Union’s policies on artificial intelligence. In particular, it stresses the fragmented nature of initiatives, the lack of reliable performance indicators and persistent shortcomings in assessing the true impact of EU funding. This adds up to ineffectual governance of the issue and questionable use of public funds in what is, moreover, a field of the utmost strategic importance. The report also highlights the risks of overlap with national policies, revealing a worrying tendency to encroach upon the competences of Member States. Can the Commission therefore say: 1.
What specific measures it intends to take to ensure funding is no longer fragmented and truly effective?
On what grounds it justifies the proliferation of European initiatives in an area largely falling within the remit of national industrial strategies?
How it intends to comply with the principles of subsidiarity and sound financial management laid down in Article 5 of the Treaty on European Union?
https://www.eca.europa.eu/ECAPublications/SR-2026-12/SR-2026-12_EN.pdf.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (15.6.2026) The Commission would like to note that the reference to 'serious shortcomings in the implementation of the EU’s policies on artificial intelligence’ does not appear in the Court of Auditor’s report1 mentioned in the written parliamentary question. Similarly, the report does not -in the context of AI policies- stress ’the fragmented nature of initiatives, the lack of reliable performance indicators and persistent shortcomings in assessing the true impact of EU funding’. The highlighted report is about the EU’s advisory bodies -notably the European Economic and Social Committee and the Committee of the Regions- and the impact of their opinions, not about the work of the Commission in a specific policy field. That said, the Commission would like to stress that, with regards to AI policies and initiatives, it has always closely coordinated its activities with those of Member States through existing discussion fora. For instance, when preparing the Apply AI Strategy2, the Commission based its work on the implementation of AI strategies and policy initiatives established by Member States. Direct contacts with Member States were made, including through interviews with key government entities responsible for the national AI strategies and policies, as well as through specific discussions in the AI Board. These contacts serve as a basis for understanding which practical gaps needed to be addressed and what coordinated approach to adopt in the Strategy. All these activities were organised in accordance with the principle of subsidiarity.
1 https://www.eca.europa.eu/ECAPublications/SR-2026-12/SR-2026-12_EN.pdf. 2 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52025DC0723.

E-10-2026-001513.t: Swedish Government’s proposal to revoke previously issued permanent residence permits
qt: to the Commission Alice Kuhnke (Verts/ALE) Subject:

The Swedish Government has presented a national inquiry that positively assesses the legality of revoking permanent residence permits. Consequently, a legal amendment providing for the withdrawal of such permits has been proposed. If enacted, it would apply to permits held by beneficiaries of subsidiary protection, persons with long-term resident status and refugees, including quota refugees1. A coalition of lawyers recently deemed the proposal unlawful, highlighting its incompatibility with the Swedish Constitution and the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, among other texts2. EU law does not lay down any obligation for Member States to issue permanent residence permits. However, the proposal clearly concerns an area governed by EU law, meaning that the general principles of EU law apply. The Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) has repeatedly held that retroactive legislation is permissible only under very limited conditions3. Furthermore, EU law must be implemented in compliance with the Charter of Fundamental Rights and the European Convention on Human Rights. Given this: 1.
Does the Commission consider the above proposal compatible with CJEU case-law and fundamental rights, such as the right to respect for private and family life and the rights of the child?
If the proposal is enacted, would the Commission consider initiating infringement proceedings against Sweden to obtain a swift legal assessment of its compatibility with EU law?

https://www.regeringen.se/rattsliga-dokument/statens-offentliga-utredningar/2025/09/sou-202599/. https://www.svd.se/a/d4nXOw/att-aterkalla-permanenta-uppehallstillstand-ar-olagligt-skriver-jurister. e.g. Judgment of the Court of Justice of 29 June 1982, Amylum v Council, Case C-108/81, ECLI:EU:C:1982:322, paragraphs 6-8.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.6.2026) The Commission generally does not comment on draft legislation. Accordingly, it is not in a position to provide an answer to the questions submitted by the Honourable Member.

E-10-2026-001512.t: EU funding, assistance to irregular immigrants and efficiency of returns
qt: to the Commission Mathilde Androuët (PfE) Subject:

In its communication COM(2021)592 final of 29 September 2021 on the application of Directive 2009/52/EC on sanctions against employers, the Commission promoted access for irregular immigrants to complaint, aid and reporting mechanisms, including via third parties (NGOs, trade unions, associations). Whilst the fight against employers operating outside the law is essential to combat exploitation and social dumping, the effective enforcement of removal decisions is an equally essential element in ensuring the credibility of the European Union’s migration policies. In view of the above: 1.

What precise amounts, broken down by Member State and by EU financial instrument, have been allocated since 2021 to actions directly or indirectly benefitting irregular immigrants under these mechanisms?
Which measures ensure that this funding does not, in practice, contribute to keeping persons subject to a return decision on Member State territory?
Does the Commission intend to make this funding conditional on verifiable results in terms of recovered penalties and effective cooperation with supervisory and return authorities?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (12.6.2026) Funding under the Asylum, Migration and Integration Fund (AMIF)1 is mainly implemented under shared management. Information on EU spending under shared management is available on the Cohesion Open data Platform2. In May 2026, the Commission launched a EUR 10 million call for expression of interest3 for the specific action4 ‘Protecting thirdcountry workers’ rights while fighting against illegal employment of irregularly staying thirdcountry nationals. Under direct management, in 2024, the Commission launched a call for proposals on assistance, support and integration of third country national victims of trafficking in human beings5 for a value of EUR 6 million. This call also aimed to support the prevention of labour exploitation of third-country nationals as well as the awareness on the risks of labour exploitation. Member States must ensure that any actions implemented with the support of the AMIF programmes is compliant with the relevant EU acquis, including EU rules on returning illegally staying third-country nationals. The Commission regularly monitors the implementation of the Employer Sanctions Directive6 by Member States and organises regular expert group meetings on the topic of irregular migration and the Directive to exchange information and good practices. The latest implementation report was adopted in May 20267. The conditions for AMIF funding are laid down in the AMIF Regulation, the Financial Regulation and the Common Provisions Regulation.

E-10-2026-001511.t: Genetically modified organisms: prohibited from production, but authorised for import
qt: to the Commission Gilles Pennelle (PfE), Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE), Anne-Sophie Frigout (PfE), Julie Rechagneux (PfE), Pierre Pimpie (PfE), André Rougé (PfE), Julien Sanchez (PfE), Séverine Werbrouck (PfE), Valérie Deloge (PfE), Philippe Olivier (PfE), Julien Leonardelli (PfE) Subject:

In spite of the highly restrictive framework that the European Union applies for growing genetically modified organisms (GMOs), on 10 March 2026 the Commission authorised the placing on the market of genetically modified soybean DBN-09004-6 and renewed the authorisation for several GMOs, including maize T25, for human and animal consumption, without taking any steps towards allowing their cultivation in the EU. This authorisation is yet another example of what has become standard EU practice. The EU has become a major importer of soybeans and animal feed derived from GMOs, notably from Latin American countries. This situation highlights a major contradiction: for health or environmental reasons, the EU considers that the cultivation of GMOs should remain strictly regulated, even as it grants authorisation to import and place GMO products on the market, and even deems them to be safe. In view of the above: 1.
How does the Commission justify such a discrepancy between the strict rules imposed on our farmers and the EU’s leniency with regard to imported products?
Is the Commission prepared to implement genuine measures to put an end to this practice and actually protect European consumers and farmers? If so, what action will it take?
at: (English version) to the Commission Gilles Pennelle (PfE), Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE), Anne-Sophie Frigout (PfE), Julie Rechagneux (PfE), Pierre Pimpie (PfE), André Rougé (PfE), Julien Sanchez (PfE), Séverine Werbrouck (PfE), Valérie Deloge (PfE), Philippe Olivier (PfE), Julien Leonardelli (PfE) (14 April 2026) Subject: Genetically modified organisms: prohibited from production, but authorised for import In spite of the highly restrictive framework that the European Union applies for growing genetically modified organisms (GMOs), on 10 March 2026 the Commission authorised the placing on the market of genetically modified soybean DBN09004-6 and renewed the authorisation for several GMOs, including maize T25, for human and animal consumption, without taking any steps towards allowing their cultivation in the EU. This authorisation is yet another example of what has become standard EU practice. The EU has become a major importer of soybeans and animal feed derived from GMOs, notably from Latin American countries. This situation highlights a major contradiction: for health or environmental reasons, the EU considers that the cultivation of GMOs should remain strictly regulated, even as it grants authorisation to import and place GMO products on the market, and even deems them to be safe. In view of the above: 1.
How does the Commission justify such a discrepancy between the strict rules imposed on our farmers and the EU’s leniency with regard to imported products?
Is the Commission prepared to implement genuine measures to put an end to this practice and actually protect European consumers and farmers? If so, what action will it take?

(22 June 2026) EU legislation (1) imposes strict rules both for the cultivation and for the placing on the market (including imports) of genetically modified organisms (GMOs). In both cases, GMOs must undergo an authorisation process which includes a thorough and comprehensive risk assessment, adapted to the intended use. In addition, once authorised, all GMOs are subject to traceability and labelling requirements as well as environmental monitoring. Access of farmers to GMO for cultivation depends on whether applicants request an authorisation for cultivation of GMOs in the Union and whether Member States make use of the possibility in the directive 2015/412 (2) that allows them to prohibit or restrict cultivation on their territory of GMOs authorised for cultivation in the EU, for reasons other than safety. Currently, eighteen Member States prohibit the cultivation within their territory of the only genetically modified maize authorised for cultivation in the EU. The Commission grants authorisations for the import and placing on the market of GMOs for food and feed uses only when they are considered safe in a risk assessment by the European Food Safety Authority, and in accordance with the conditions and procedures of the applicable EU legislation. These authorisations enable in particular the import of genetically modified feed, responding to the high protein feed demand of EU livestock farmers.

Directive 2001/18/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 12 March 2001 on the deliberate release into the environment of genetically modified organisms and repealing Council Directive 90/220/EEC, OJ L 106, 17.4.2001, http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2001/18/oj; and Regulation (EC) No 1829/2003 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 22 September 2003 on genetically modified food and feed, OJ L 268, 18.10.2003, http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2003/1829/oj. Directive (EU) 2015/412 amending Directive 2001/18/EC as regards the possibility for the Member States to restrict or prohibit the cultivation of GMOs in their territory, OJ L 68, 13.3.2015, pp. 1-8, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2015/412/oj.

qt: to the Commission Vicent Marzà Ibáñez (Verts/ALE), Estrella Galán (The Left), Jaume Asens Llodrà (Verts/ALE) Subject:

In June 2025, the Vice-President / High Representative presented conclusions on Israel’s compliance with the EU-Israel Association Agreement to the Council, in which she indicated that Article 2 of the agreement on respect for human rights and democratic principles had been infringed. In light of intensified Israeli army operations in the West Bank and new attacks in Iran and Lebanon, the European Union should continue pushing for diplomatic measures to respond to the growing crisis in the region. Until now, the lack of unanimity among Member States has been used by the Commission to justify not adopting the proposal to suspend the association agreement, since unanimity is required for the common foreign and security policy. Given that one single Member State can block the proposal, I ask: Does the Commission intend to amend the aforementioned proposal for suspension so that it does not require unanimity in the Council, considering that a qualified majority is sufficient in areas such as trade and scientific cooperation, in order to overcome this deadlock and address the serious political and humanitarian crisis in the region?

E-10-2026-001507.t: Turkish authorities’ failure to reply to requests to visit Ekrem İmamoğlu in detention
qt: to the Commission Sandro Gozi (Renew) Subject:

In January, a number of official letters were sent to the Ministry of Justice of the Republic of Türkiye, with copies to the Turkish Embassy in the European Union, to request authorisation to visit Mayor of Istanbul Ekrem İmamoğlu, who has been imprisoned on patently unfounded charges. Despite several reminders, no answer has been provided. This raises serious concerns about Türkiye’s compliance with its rule of law obligations, procedural safeguards, the rights of detained people and democratic pluralism, even though it remains a candidate country for EU membership and is a member of the Council of Europe. 1.
What action does the Commission intend to take with the Turkish authorities to obtain a formal response to requests to visit Mr İmamoğlu in prison?

In the view of the Commission and the European External Action Service, is the lack of response from the Turkish authorities and the detention of Mr İmamoğlu compatible with Türkiye’s commitments as an EU candidate country?
Does the Commission intend to draw political conclusions from this situation concerning its relations with Türkiye?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.8.2026) The Commission is concerned about developments in Türkiye regarding the rule of law and the protection of fundamental rights. These concerns include the detention of Ekrem İmamoğlu1, as outlined in the 2025 enlargement report2. As an EU candidate country and long-standing member of the Council of Europe, Türkiye is expected to apply the highest democratic standards and practices. The Commission will continue to promote these values in its relations with Türkiye and to address these issues in all relevant contacts with the Turkish authorities, including in the relevant subcommittee established under the Association Agreement with Türkiye3. Since the end of 2024, the Turkish authorities have authorised several prison visits for the Türkiye rapporteur in the European Parliament and for the chair of the European Parliament’s Subcommittee on Human Rights. The Commission will raise the lack of response to some requests in future meetings and dialogues with Turkish officials. The criteria allowing or restricting such visits should reflect the requirements of Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights4 and of the Optional Protocol to the Convention against Torture. Difficulties in gaining access to inmates persist and in recent cases, the European Court of Human Rights5 has ruled that Türkiye violated prisoners’ rights regarding visits and telephone calls at weekends. Respect for fundamental rights and the rule of law are essential for the EU accession process. They will continue to be an integral part of EU-Türkiye relations.

qt: to the Commission Nicolás González Casares (S&D) Subject:

On 18 November 2025, the European Commission adopted Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/2351 imposing a definitive safeguard measure on imports of certain ferro-alloying elements. The Commission decided to exclude silicon metal from these measures on the grounds that the conditions were not met. However, some European silicon metal producers such as Ferroglobe, operating in countries such as Spain and France, have had to suspend production of silicon metal and take switch to producing ferrosilicon due to the significant impact of imports from China and African countries such as Angola, which have flooded the European market at dumping prices. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Will the Commission reassess the situation and take safeguard measures in relation to the production of silicon metal?

Given that, as it stands, the European Union covers only 15 % of its silicon needs, does it consider it acceptable for the production of silicon metal – i.e. a critical and strategic material as defined in Regulation (EU) 2024/125 – to collapse in the EU, thereby increasing its dependence on external sources?
at: (English version) to the Commission Nicolás González Casares (S&D) (14 April 2026) Subject: Silicon metal On 18 November 2025, the European Commission adopted Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/2351 imposing a definitive safeguard measure on imports of certain ferro-alloying elements. The Commission decided to exclude silicon metal from these measures on the grounds that the conditions were not met. However, some European silicon metal producers such as Ferroglobe, operating in countries such as Spain and France, have had to suspend production of silicon metal and take switch to producing ferrosilicon due to the significant impact of imports from China and African countries such as Angola, which have flooded the European market at dumping prices. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Will the Commission reassess the situation and take safeguard measures in relation to the production of silicon metal?

Given that, as it stands, the European Union covers only 15% of its silicon needs, does it consider it acceptable for the production of silicon metal — i.e. a critical and strategic material as defined in Regulation (EU) 2024/125 — to collapse in the EU, thereby increasing its dependence on external sources?

(21 May 2026) The Commission collects and assesses data on raw materials periodically in line with the Critical Raw Materials Act (1). The Commission frequently performs a risk assessment regarding its sourcing of raw materials, with the outcome of the fifth assessment published in 2023 (2). Regarding safeguards, safeguard measures on four alloying elements were imposed on 18 November 2025 (3). Silicon is not covered by these measures as the criteria to include it were not met at the time. However, it appears that the situation has become very difficult in the meantime. Therefore, the Commission services remain available to explore together with the industry, the availability of any possible options under the trade defence instruments. In this context it is important to point out that the industry is facing also other challenges than harmful trade practices, such as high energy costs or structural overcapacity in third countries, and that there are limits to what can be achieved with trade defence instruments. Silicon metal is an important material for different strategic applications within the EU, while the current domestic production represents around 30% of EUs overall silicon metal demand needs. The Commission is aware of the challenges, but further silicon metal production could be boosted in the EU through strategic projects under the Critical Raw Materials Act. In the last round of applications for strategic projects under the Critical Raw Materials Act, the Commission received one application from project promotors regarding silicon metal, which is currently in the assessment process.

E-10-2026-001502.t: Re-examination of EU humanitarian funding to the West Bank, Gaza and Lebanon
qt: to the Commission Bert-Jan Ruissen (ECR), Tomáš Kubín (PfE), Fernand Kartheiser (NI), Rihards Kols (ECR), Mieke Andriese (PfE), Alice Teodorescu Måwe (PPE), Tomáš Zdechovský (PPE), Geadis Geadi (ECR), Veronika Vrecionová (ECR), Charlie Weimers (ECR), Dick Erixon (ECR), Ondřej Krutílek (ECR), Beatrice Timgren (ECR), Elena Donazzan (ECR), Sander Smit (ECR), Alexandr Vondra (ECR), Jorge Martín Frías (PfE), Sebastian Tynkkynen (ECR), Antonio López-Istúriz White (PPE), Stephen Nikola Bartulica (ECR), Matej Tonin (PPE) Subject:

In recent years, and particularly following the Hamas-led atrocities of 7 October 2023, a number of EU donor governments, including the Commission, have re-examined their funding of, and cooperation with, non-governmental organisations (NGOs) active in the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. For example, in January 2026, Sweden reportedly stopped all taxpayer-funded grants to the aid organisation Islamic Relief Sweden, following concerns that individuals within the group may have links to anti-democratic or violent activities1. In 2025, the German Government reportedly defunded NGOs that denied Israel’s right to exist2. In January 2022, the Dutch Government announced that the Netherlands would cease all funding to the Union of Agricultural Work Committees (UAWC)3. On 16 March 2026, the Commission announced EUR 458 million in humanitarian assistance for the Middle East in 2026, including EUR 124 million allocated to the West Bank and Gaza and EUR 100 million to Lebanon4. In this context, and in the light of recent efforts by Member States to increase the accountability and responsibility of humanitarian aid provision, what steps is the Commission taking to update funding contracts, partner vetting and oversight mechanisms for NGOs, UN agencies and local implementing partners to ensure that the EU supports those actually furthering EU goals and does not reward entities characterised by antisemitic, antidemocratic, and/or violent activities and/or leadership?
