For example, in January 2026, Sweden reportedly stopped all taxpayer-funded grants to the aid organisation Islamic Relief Sweden, following concerns that individuals within the group may have links to anti-democratic or violent activities (1). In 2025, the German Government reportedly defunded NGOs that denied Israel’s right to exist (2). In January 2022, the Dutch Government announced that the Netherlands would cease all funding to the Union of Agricultural Work Committees (UAWC) (3). On 16 March 2026, the Commission announced EUR 458 million in humanitarian assistance for the Middle East in 2026, including EUR 124 million allocated to the West Bank and Gaza and EUR 100 million to Lebanon (4). In this context, and in the light of recent efforts by Member States to increase the accountability and responsibility of humanitarian aid provision, what steps is the Commission taking to update funding contracts, partner vetting and oversight mechanisms for NGOs, UN agencies and local implementing partners to ensure that the EU supports those actually furthering EU goals and does not reward entities characterised by antisemitic, anti-democratic, and/or violent activities and/or leadership? (23 June 2026) The Commission is committed to ensuring that EU funding is allocated effectively and responsibly to defend the dignity of those in need in line with the values and goals of the EU. The Commission is aware of the complex operational context in which EU-funded entities operate in the occupied Palestinian territory (including in the Gaza Strip) and Lebanon. This is why robust safeguards are in place, covering due diligence and risk assessments (ex-ante checks), implementation monitoring, and post-funding oversight and controls (ex-post verification). The Commission’s non-governmental partners are thoroughly assessed against their capacity to observe basic principles and obligations, including respect of the relevant EU, international and national law, as well as compliance with transparency, accountability and internal controls, including risk management mechanisms. Under the regulation (EU) 2024/2509 (1), in line with Article 138, the Commission applies strict safeguards to ensure that a person or entity is excluded from EU funding if they are involved in any criminal activity, including terrorist financing and terrorist offences. As has always been the case, the Commission will ensure that funding allocations are made in accordance with the mechanisms outlined above in the context of the EUR 458 million in humanitarian assistance announced for the Middle East in 2026 (2).

E-10-2026-001501.t: Crisis in the Middle East – risks to the EU and need for action on energy and economic policy
qt: to the Commission Letizia Moratti (PPE) Subject:

As acknowledged by the President of the European Central Bank (ECB), the global economy is facing an unprecedented shock and a return to normality may take years. We are witnessing disruptions to energy supplies, access to critical raw materials and essential goods and services, and they are clearly affecting prices. As a result, the risk of stagflation in the euro area is high: growth is declining and inflation persistent. Against this backdrop, the ECB is ready to raise interest rates. While monetary policy has limited scope to curb energy prices, economic policy can play a decisive role. The Commission must act swiftly. In the light of the above: 1.
Is the Commission assessing the effects on public debt, maturing NextGenerationEU loans and households and businesses of an interest rate hike, and will it adopt countercyclical bridging measures?

As they would be less costly in the long term than economic contraction and increased debt burdens, will it introduce, as a matter of urgency, common European tools, such as energy bonds, and temporarily suspend the Stability and Growth Pact?
With a view to safeguarding the EU’s energy security and economic stability, will it provide realistic estimates of gas demand and urgently review the current approach to climate and energy policy?

We are witnessing disruptions to energy supplies, access to critical raw materials and essential goods and services, and they are clearly affecting prices. With a view to safeguarding the EU’s energy security and economic stability, will it provide realistic estimates of gas demand and urgently review the current approach to climate and energy policy?

(19 June 2026) The escalating crisis in the Middle East has increased volatility into energy markets, exacerbating inflationary pressures and weighing on economic growth. The Commission is aware of the risks posed by persistent inflation and rising financing costs. The Commission has provided an assessment of the macroeconomic implications, in particular on general government deficit and debt, as part of its Spring 2026 Economic Forecast. The Commission announced decisive steps to mitigate these risks in the AccelerateEU Communicatio n (1). The approach aims to support vulnerable households and industries while preserving the incentives to reduce energy demand and being consistent the need to address fossil fuel dependency as well as Member States’ commitments under the EU fiscal framework. Energy support measures should be targeted and temporary. In addition, it aims to advance energy independence through domestic clean energy, electrification, and enhanced grid infrastructure. The AccelerateEU Communication includes concrete measures that allow for a coordinated EU approach, with a view to strengthen Europe's resilience. These considerations also inform the Commission’s 2026 Spring Policy Package (2), which includes country-specific recommendations. The package also includes fiscal decisions under the economic governance framework. The publicly available Commission's dashboard on security of gas supply (3) provides detailed information on gas demand. The Commission will propose a revised EU energy security framework after summer 2026.

qt: to the Commission Dan-Ştefan Motreanu (PPE) Subject:

Representatives of the European fisheries sector have recently warned that rising fuel prices are creating a severe economic situation for many fleet segments. According to industry stakeholders, in some cases fuel costs exceed the income generated by the sale of fishery products, placing certain fishing operations at risk of becoming economically unsustainable. The sector has therefore called for the rapid mobilisation of available crisis support mechanisms under the European Maritime, Fisheries and Aquaculture Fund, as well as for temporary and targeted support measures, including possible adjustments to State aid rules and exceptional market measures to mitigate the economic impact of the situation. Proposals have also been made to facilitate access to strategic fuel stocks in EU ports as part of longerterm structural solutions. Considering the strain that high energy prices place on the fisheries sector, how does the Commission evaluate the prices’ impact on economic viability, and is it prepared to revise or expand existing EU support instruments to better address the crisis and protect sustainable fishing activities?
at: (English version) to the Commission Dan-Ştefan Motreanu (PPE) (13 April 2026) Subject: European fisheries Representatives of the European fisheries sector have recently warned that rising fuel prices are creating a severe economic situation for many fleet segments. According to industry stakeholders, in some cases fuel costs exceed the income generated by the sale of fishery products, placing certain fishing operations at risk of becoming economically unsustainable. The sector has therefore called for the rapid mobilisation of available crisis support mechanisms under the European Maritime, Fisheries and Aquaculture Fund, as well as for temporary and targeted support measures, including possible adjustments to state aid rules and exceptional market measures to mitigate the economic impact of the situation. Proposals have also been made to facilitate access to strategic fuel stocks in EU ports as part of longer-term structural solutions. Considering the strain that high energy prices place on the fisheries sector, how does the Commission evaluate the prices’ impact on economic viability, and is it prepared to revise or expand existing EU support instruments to better address the crisis and protect sustainable fishing activities? (28 May 2026) The Commission is continuously monitoring and projecting potential impacts of the situation in the Middle East. While there are no immediate concerns for the EU’s security of supply, prices, particularly for refined products like diesel face significant volatility. This has direct consequences and dire economic and social implications for the EU, in particular for primary agricultural production and fisheries. As regards fisheries, pursuant to Article 26(2) of the European Maritime, Fisheries and Aquaculture Fund (EMFAF) Regulation (1), the Commission has activated a crisis support mechanism in case of an exceptional event causing a significant disruption of markets (2). The Commission invites Member States to make support available to the sectors under their national EMFAF programmes and in line with the established EU rules. The Commission is aware that the situation may require going beyond EMFAF to support as efficiently as possible undertakings whose economic activity is directly hit by this crisis. Therefore, the Commission has consulted Member States on a Temporary state aid framework, which will allow aid for the primary production of fishery products. Member States will be able to use the new Temporary Crisis Framework, in addition to the standard state aid rules applicable to the fishery sector, to support the sector. The Commission has also put forward the AccelerateEU initiative (3) to alleviate the situation for businesses and consumers. Considering the importance of learning from crisis situations, the Commission underlines that sustainable business models and energy transition remain pivotal for the resilience of the fisheries sector and its competitiveness.

E-10-2026-001499.t: Recovery and resilience plan investment at risk owing to managing authorities’ failure to act
qt: to the Commission Catarina Martins (The Left) Subject:

Despite the fact that Portugal’s investment in housing under its recovery and resilience plan was a national priority, it has been reported1 that in Porto, owing to delays in reimbursement by the Institute for Housing and Urban Regeneration, contractors will have to abandon works, putting proper implementation of EU financing at risk. Such matters come under the exclusive responsibility of the national and municipal authorities involved; however, owners and tenants have not been offered a swift way out of their predicament and will be left – through no fault of their own – with works under the scheme left unfinished owing to the managing authorities’ failure to act. What is more, owners and tenants now find themselves in a more precarious position than before the scheme. Such goings-on put EU funds at risk and seriously discourage private owners from getting involved in public regeneration schemes in the general interest. In light of the above: 1.
Is the Commission aware of the managing authorities’ failure to ensure the correct implementation of EU funds?
What action will it take to safeguard EU investments and restore stakeholder trust in these EU mechanisms?
https://www.publico.pt/2026/03/29/local/noticia/andreza-abracou-estrategia-municipal-reabilitar-ilhas-dizseabandonada-2169396.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (25.6.2026) The Recovery and Resilience Facility1 (RRF) Regulation sets out that payments to Member States are solely based on the satisfactory fulfilment of milestones and targets. It is for Member States to organise the delivery of reforms and investments and to ensure that milestones and targets are completed. The Commission will assess the evidence submitted against the requirements of the Council Implementing Decision2 (CID) endorsing the Portuguese Recovery and Resilience Plan (RRP). Member States must meet all milestones and targets by 31 August 2026. The strict deadlines of the Facility reflect its temporary nature and purpose to support recovery from the COVID19 pandemic. Any action taken after 31 August 2026 to fulfil milestones and targets cannot be taken into consideration in the assessment of payment requests. In June 2025, the Commission invited Member States to review, streamline and simplify their RRPs to ensure implementation by the deadline. The Commission provided options for amending the Plans and engaged closely with Member States. Taking into account objective circumstances affecting implementation, including the impact of storms in early 2026, Portugal submitted a revision request on 31 March 2026. This was assessed by the Commission on 18 May 2026 and is now under review by the Council. The primary responsibility for ensuring compliance with EU and national law, including public procurement and State aid rules, lies with the Member State. The Commission has put in place an effective control system to monitor implementation of the Facility in line with the RRF Regulation.

E-10-2026-001498.t: The impact of cyberbullying and online abuse
qt: to the Commission Dan-Ştefan Motreanu (PPE) Subject:

Concerns continue to be raised about the growing impact of cyberbullying and online abuse across the EU, including cases involving the non-consensual sharing of intimate images and persistent harassment on digital platforms. While some Member States have introduced specific legislation to address such behaviour, legal approaches remain fragmented at EU level. In Ireland, the adoption of legislation commonly known as ‘Coco’s Law’ has created criminal offences for the non-consensual distribution of intimate images and certain forms of online harassment. Supporters of this approach have called for the EU to consider similar measures in order to strengthen the protection of victims of cyberbullying across the Member States. Thus, what steps could be taken at EU level to reinforce the response to cyberbullying and the non-consensual sharing of intimate content, while ensuring consistent and effective protection for victims across the Member States?
at: (English version) to the Commission Dan-Ştefan Motreanu (PPE) (13 April 2026) Subject: The impact of cyberbullying and online abuse Concerns continue to be raised about the growing impact of cyberbullying and online abuse across the EU, including cases involving the non-consensual sharing of intimate images and persistent harassment on digital platforms. While some Member States have introduced specific legislation to address such behaviour, legal approaches remain fragmented at EU level. In Ireland, the adoption of legislation commonly known as ‘Coco’s Law’ has created criminal offences for the non-consensual distribution of intimate images and certain forms of online harassment. Supporters of this approach have called for the EU to consider similar measures in order to strengthen the protection of victims of cyberbullying across the Member States. Thus, what steps could be taken at EU level to reinforce the response to cyberbullying and the non-consensual sharing of intimate content, while ensuring consistent and effective protection for victims across the Member States? (9 June 2026) The EU has already a comprehensive framework to protect and empower minors online. The Digital Services Act (DSA ) (1) requires providers of online platforms to provide user friendly notice and action mechanisms to report the presence of specific illegal content. Providers made aware of such items of illegal content must remove them promptly or risk losing their liability exemption. Under the DSA very large online platforms and search engines must assess and mitigate risks to minors. Providers of online platforms accessible to minors shall implement appropriate and proportionate measures to ensure high level of privacy, safety and security of minors. The Guidelines on the protection of minors (2) provide practical guidance for providers, including recommendations to protect young users from cyberbullying, such as default settings preventing children from being contacted by strangers. The upcoming revision of the Audiovisual Media Services Directive (3) will strengthen protections for younger viewers when accessing audiovisual content online. Complementary initiatives, such as the action plan against cyberbullying (4) under the Better Internet for Kids Strategy (5), focus on prevention, education and victim support. Moreover, under the competences given by the Treaties, the EU has established rules requiring Member States to ensure certain behaviours are punishable as criminal offence, including cyberstalking, cyber harassment, the non-consensual sharing of intimate images, cyber incitement to violence and hatred based on gender under the Violence against Women Directiv e (6), as well as the public incitement to violence or hatred under the framework Decision on combating racism and xenophobia (7) which applies to online behaviours.

qt: to the Commission Dan-Ştefan Motreanu (PPE) Subject:

A complaint has recently been lodged under the Digital Services Act alleging that YouTube, as a very large online platform, imposes a profiling-based recommendation system on users by default and does not provide a sufficiently accessible alternative that avoids personalisation based on user data. According to the complainants, certain interface design practices may make it difficult for users to find or use non-personalised recommendation options, raising concerns about the potential use of deceptive or manipulative design techniques. These allegations also highlight broader concerns regarding ‘dark patterns’ in online services, which may influence users’ behaviour or limit their ability to exercise meaningful choice when interacting with digital platforms. Can the Commission indicate how it will tackle potential breaches of the Digital Services Act linked to recommendation systems and interface design, and ensure that platforms effectively provide accessible alternatives to profiling-based recommendations?
at: (English version) to the Commission Dan-Ştefan Motreanu (PPE) (13 April 2026) Subject: ‘Dark patterns’ in online services A complaint has recently been lodged under the Digital Services Act alleging that YouTube, as a very large online platform, imposes a profiling-based recommendation system on users by default and does not provide a sufficiently accessible alternative that avoids personalisation based on user data. According to the complainants, certain interface design practices may make it difficult for users to find or use non-personalised recommendation options, raising concerns about the potential use of deceptive or manipulative design techniques. These allegations also highlight broader concerns regarding ‘dark patterns’ in online services, which may influence users’ behaviour or limit their ability to exercise meaningful choice when interacting with digital platforms. Can the Commission indicate how it will tackle potential breaches of the Digital Services Act linked to recommendation systems and interface design, and ensure that platforms effectively provide accessible alternatives to profiling-based recommendations? (1 July 2026) The Digital Services Act (1) (DSA) requires providers of very large online platforms and of very large online search engines to provide at least one non-profiling-based option for each of their recommender systems. It shall be easily accessible, directly where information is recommended. The DSA also requires interface design that does not manipulate users. The Commission continuously monitors compliance with these obligations, including for YouTube and makes use of its investigative powers to address suspected non-compliance. Currently, the providers of Temu (2) and Shein (3) are being investigated for suspected non-compliance with their recommender systems obligations. The provider of AliExpress, after a similar investigation, has implemented commitments addressing the Commission’s concerns. It now offers directly accessible controls (4) that allow users to disable personalised recommendations for each major recommender system. The provider of TikTok, after an in-depth investigation, has been preliminarily found in breach of the DSA for the addictive design of its interface (5). If the preliminary findings are confirmed, TikTok’s provider will be compelled to change its interface design, including by disabling addictive features. Giving users more control over their online environment is at the core of the DSA and diligently enforced by the Commission. Regarding broader concerns about dark patterns online, EU consumer law (6) applies to traders whose practices materially impact consumers’ transactional decision-making. The upcoming Digital Fairness Act (7) could specify rules on dark patterns under EU consumer law. Deceptive design to collect personal data is also prohibited by the General Data Protection Regulation (8).

E-10-2026-001496.t: EU response to Trump’s threats to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz
qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Per Clausen (The Left) Subject:

Donald Trump’s threats that the US will now be preventing ships from sailing through the Strait of Hormuz1 are not only manifestly illegal under international law, but they also create a situation in which vessels and crew from EU countries might potentially be attacked by US forces in the area. If this happens, it is essential for the EU to be ready with a quick and clear response – one that goes beyond the usual empty, bland statements of condemnation. Could the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy therefore please answer the following questions: 1.
What concrete action will the EU take if US forces seek – including by force – to prevent ships from EU countries from sailing through the Strait of Hormuz?

Will US attempts to block EU ships – either through threats or through the actual use of military force – constitute a clear case in which the EU’s anti‑coercion mechanism should be triggered immediately?

Has the Vice-President / High Representative already made it clear to the US and the Trump administration that the threats are illegal and unacceptable and will be met with a response if they are carried out?
https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c8dl5mly2rzo
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.5.2026) The EU will continue to defend the principle of freedom of navigation, in accordance with international law (particularly UN Convention on the Law of the Sea)1. It urges all involved in the conflict to fully ensure a toll-free and safe passage through the Strait of Hormuz. The closure of the strait disrupts international trade and threatens global energy and food security. The EU is engaged in the region through operation EU Naval Force ASPIDES ensuring safe passage through the Red Sea. The operation includes the Strait of Hormuz in its area of operation and can help providing security to merchant vessels, once the war ends. On 30 March 2026, the Council extended the ASPIDES mandate until 28 February 20272.
1 https://www.eeas.europa.eu/eeas/united-nations-speech-high-representative-kaja-kallas-annual-un-security-
council-session-eu-un-0_en. 2 https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/press/press-releases/2026/03/30/maritime-security-council-updatesmandates-of-eu-naval-operations-aspides-and-atalanta/.

E-10-2026-001495.t: Impact of rising fuel prices on the EU fisheries sector and the need for coordinated EU action
qt: to the Commission Sander Smit (ECR), Bert-Jan Ruissen (ECR), Ton Diepeveen (PfE) Subject:

The ongoing conflict in the Middle East has triggered a sharp rise in global fuel prices, placing severe pressure on the EU fisheries sector, where fuel costs are critical for viability. Many vessels are operating at a loss or remain in port. Commissioner Costas Kadis has acknowledged the severity of the situation and indicated that emergency support measures may be mobilised, including the European Maritime, Fisheries and Aquaculture Fund (EMFAF) and other instruments. At the same time, several Member States have taken immediate national action, including targeted fuel tax reductions and the provision of direct financial support. The absence of comparable measures in some Member States, including under the minority government of the Netherlands, risks contributing to an uneven playing field within the internal market and underlines the need for more coordinated action at EU level. 1.

Will the Commission encourage more coordinated action by Member States, including those that have not yet introduced emergency measures, on providing immediate support, such as fuel cost compensation, to ensure a level playing field?
When will the Commission ensure the rapid activation and flexible use of EMFAF and State aid rules to complement national efforts across the EU?

Beyond long-term decarbonisation, what immediate and technologically neutral measures does the Commission envisage to reduce fuel consumption and operational costs across the EU, including accelerating the approval of innovations such as pulse fishing and other fuel-saving technologies?

(29 May 2026) The Commission is continuously monitoring and projecting impacts of the situation in the Middle East. While there are no immediate concerns for supply, prices for diesel face significant volatility. This has direct economic and social consequences for the sector. The Commission has activated the crisis support mechanism of the European Maritime, Fisheries and Aquaculture (EMFAF), due to this exceptional situation and disruption of markets (1). The Commission encourages Member States to make this support available to the sectors under their national EMFAF programmes. qt: to the Commission Catherine Griset (PfE) Subject:

On 7 April 2026, French artificial intelligence (AI) company Mistral published a white paper on AI in Europe1 which recommends a form of European sovereignty, described as a ‘European preference mechanism in public procurement for strategic sectors’ (point 17). These strategic sectors would be drawn from the list provided in Article 4 of Regulation (EU) 2019/452 of 19 March 2019 establishing a framework for the screening of foreign direct investments into the Union2: energy, transport, water, health, communications, media, data processing or storage, aerospace, defence, artificial intelligence, robotics, semiconductors, quantum and nuclear technologies, nanotechnologies, biotechnologies, agricultural inputs, etc. This European preference mechanism would benefit companies that: – have their head offices in Europe; – conduct a significant share of their business in Europe; – are run by European management; – have a turnover exceeding EUR 500 million per year. E-10-2026-001492.t: Import authorisations for genetically modified crops
qt: to the Commission Asger Christensen (Renew) Subject:

The Commission is committed to an ambitious simplification agenda, including cutting red tape in the implementation of EU legislation. The EU agencies’ authorisation procedures, however, generate a great deal of red tape, in particular when it comes to import authorisations for genetically modified crops. At the moment, individual properties (e.g. properties A and B) are assessed separately. When these are subsequently combined through standard breeding (‘stacks’), the assessment often restarts from the beginning, resulting in the duplication of work, longer processing times and unnecessary red tape for both authorities and applicants. In the light of the foregoing: 1.

How will the Commission ensure that EU agencies – and EFSA in particular – make a tangible contribution to the simplification agenda by reducing unnecessary, overlapping assessment requirements, including for GMO stacks?

Will the Commission seek to establish a more streamlined and science-based approach to the assessment of GMO stacks, where existing data and previous authorisations are more widely reused, without compromising on safety?
Is the Commission planning to give the EU agencies a specific mandate to identify and implement ‘quick wins’ for the simplification of authorisation procedures, including as regards GMO imports?

(10 June 2026) The European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) carries out risk assessments for products under its responsibility in accordance with the procedures and requirements of the applicable EU legal frameworks. The Commission is finalising its evaluation of EFSA’s performance in the period 2017-2024, with a particular focus on the potential for simplification and administrative burden reduction where relevant. Early findings of that evaluation have been addressed in the Commission proposals for a Food and Feed Safety Simplification Package (1) and a European Biotech Act (2). The requirements for risk assessment prior to the placing on the market (including imports) of genetically modified (GM) food and feed are laid down in Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) No 503/2013 (3). For stacks, this regulation requires that both the single events and their combination in a stack are assessed. On 18 February 2026, EFSA mandated its GMO panel to issue a scientific statement on the assessment of GM stack s (4). This work builds on more than 20 years of experience in risk assessment of stacked events in GM plants and aims at streamlining the risk assessment process within the boundaries of the legal requirements. In addition to the EFSA evaluation, the Commission has announced in its communication on A Simpler, Clearer and Better Enforced EU Rulebook (5) that, as part of the Regulatory Deep Cleaning, a review of the food safety regulations looking at areas for simplification and improvement will be performed, while maintaining a high level of protection of human health. Based on this review, the Commission may propose further simplification actions.

E-10-2026-001491.t: The proliferation of data centres in Sicily, resource consumption and energy colonialism concerns
qt: to the Commission Giuseppe Antoci (The Left) Subject:

Driven by international tech corporations and private operators, the proliferation of data centres and digital infrastructure in Sicily could result in the island being exploited in order to benefit the digital sector and make money for Big Tech. Compounding the issue is the fact that these facilities use a great deal of energy, water and land in a region that is bedevilled by inadequate infrastructure and social inequalities and is frequently gripped by critical water shortages. No stranger to actors who plunder its resources without providing commensurate social benefits to local residents, Sicily could end up in the thrall of digital and energy colonialism. A particular concern is that these new colonialists could power their extremely energyintensive facilities by using locally produced renewables that were meant to drive efforts to decarbonise Sicily’s public services, households and productive sector. I therefore ask the Commission: 1.

Does it hold that concentrating large data centres on an island that struggles with water and energy security to be compatible with the objectives of the Green Deal and the EU’s territorial cohesion policies?
What instruments will it leverage to prevent peripheral areas like Sicily from being exploited as energy and digital hubs by giant global operators?

What steps will it take to strengthen European digital sovereignty by ensuring that the establishment of new strategic infrastructure in the Mediterranean does not entrench the power of non-European Big Tech companies?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (29.6.2026) Data centres are vital infrastructures for the competitiveness of the EU, as they power AI and cloud computing services. New technologies for data centres can minimise their environmental impacts and generate benefits for the regions hosting them. The proposed Cloud and AI Development Act articulates1 a consolidated vision for cuttingedge cloud and AI technologies, including sustainable data centre technologies, and harmonises the conditions for investment in data centres across the EU, with a focus on highly sustainable and innovative data centres and data centres supporting essential public sector functions. The Commission is working on a Data Centre Energy Efficiency Package that will build on the solutions provided for in the Energy Efficiency Directive2 by introducing a rating scheme3 for the energy efficiency of data centres. The Commission will also launch a public consultation for possible minimum performance standards for data centres. The Cloud and AI Development Act also leverages several instruments. It supports the deployment of sustainable data centres meeting high standards of energy and water efficiency, as well as contributing to grid stability, but it does not substitute national, regional or local decisions when it comes to permitting procedures. It supports national and regional authorities in conditioning project approvals, on clear local benefits, and enables the Commission and local authorities to detect and correct imbalances early through enhanced monitoring. Finally, the Cloud and AI Development Act also includes measures to ensure equitable and non-discriminatory access to the essential resources underpinning data centre deployment across Europe, to avoid hoarding practices by some operators.

1 https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/proposal-cloud-and-ai-development-act-cada. 2 https://energy.ec.europa.eu/topics/energy-efficiency/energy-efficiency-targets-directive-and-rules/energy-
efficiency-directive/energy-performance-data-centres_en#next-steps. 3 https://energy.ec.europa.eu/news/rating-scheme-data-centres-eu-commission-launches-call-feedback-2026-0327_en.

qt: to the Commission Maciej Wąsik (ECR) Subject:

Does the Commission still maintain its position that Huawei is a high-risk supplier that poses a threat to the security of data processed within the EU?

E-10-2026-001489.t: Executive order by the Trump administration against Cuba and human rights
qt: to the Commission Estrella Galán (The Left), Rima Hassan (The Left), Ilaria Salis (The Left), Oihane Agirregoitia Martínez (Renew), Kostas Papadakis (NI), Lefteris Nikolaou-Alavanos (NI), Marc Botenga (The Left), Manon Aubry (The Left), Giorgos Georgiou (The Left), Hana Jalloul Muro (S&D), Martin Günther (The Left), Vladimir Prebilič (Verts/ALE), Leila Chaibi (The Left), Ana Miranda Paz (Verts/ALE), Damien Carême (The Left), Estelle Ceulemans (S&D), Rudi Kennes (The Left), Pernando Barrena Arza (The Left), Vicent Marzà Ibáñez (Verts/ALE), Jaume Asens Llodrà (Verts/ALE), Benedetta Scuderi (Verts/ALE) Subject:

On 29 January 2026, the Trump administration signed a new executive order reinforcing the economic, commercial and financial blockade imposed by the United States against Cuba, including measures aimed at restricting the supply of oil and other energy resources to the island. These actions intensify an extraterritorial sanctions policy that has been repeatedly condemned by the international community, including by the UN General Assembly, because of its serious economic and humanitarian effects on the Cuban population. The restriction of access to essential energy resources is affecting the functioning of hospitals, transport systems, food production and other basic services. 1.
What measures does the Commission intend to implement to mitigate the humanitarian impact of this executive order in relation to Cuba’s access to essential fuels and energy?
Does the Commission consider that measures to prevent the supply of oil to a country are compatible with international law and the humanitarian principles that the EU claims to uphold?
What concrete action does the Commission intend to take to counter the extraterritorial application of these measures and to protect European economic operators in Cuba?
Supporters1
This question is supported by Members other than the authors: Danilo Della Valle (The Left), Maria Zacharia (NI).
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (23.7.2026) Since 1994, the Commission has been actively engaged in addressing the most pressing needs of the Cuban population. In 2024-2025, it released close to EUR 10 million to provide lifesaving health services country-wide, and emergency relief to hurricane-stricken communities. As an immediate response to the steadfast deterioration of the humanitarian crisis in 2026, the Commission has allocated additional EUR 6 million for humanitarian aid actions, including the provision of logistic support to humanitarian agencies to mitigate the impact of the energy crisis on food and drinking water distribution and health services1. The implementation is closely monitored to ensure the assistance reaches the neediest, timely and effectively. The Commission stands ready to increase its support in this crisis and operates in strict compliance with the humanitarian principles of humanity, impartiality, neutrality and independence. The EU aid is channelled exclusively through vetted, specialised humanitarian partners, including UN agencies and international non-governmental organisations. The Commission and the European External Action Service are closely monitoring the impact of the announced measures on EU economic operators in Cuba. The Commission will continue to underline the important contribution that EU economic operators can make to Cuba’s economic development, irrespective of the scenario that emerges in coming months. In parallel, the Commission will continue to emphasise the need to safeguard the rights of EU economic operators’ rights and the integrity of bilateral commercial interests.

humanitarian-aid-cuban-population-2026-04-01_en.

E-10-2026-001488.t: Classification of lithium as essential – state of play
qt: to the Commission Gerald Hauser (PfE) Subject:

In its answer of 14 November 2025 to written question E-003565/20251, the Commission states that the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) does not currently classify lithium as an essential nutrient. Tests are apparently being carried out to establish whether drugs containing lithium can be used to treat Alzheimer’s disease. As far as the Commission is aware at this juncture, however, there is no proof that a diet containing lithium has a significant effect on cognitive function. The Commission also pointed out that it would consult EFSA on ‘whether further examination of the potential essentiality of lithium, based on the information in the article referred to by the Honourable Member would warrant an EFSA opinion’. 1.
Has EFSA already issued an opinion concerning lithium as a potentially essential nutrient?
What are the results or findings of EFSA studies to date?
What are the next steps that the Commission is planning to take, and when can we expect a decision or opinion?
https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/E-10-2025-003565_EN.html
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.7.2026) The Commission referred the evidence on lithium’s potential essentiality as a trace element, including the Nature publication1 and Dr Michael Nehls’ 2025 lecture to the European Parliament,2 to the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA). EFSA’s response confirms that, as for chromium3, current evidence remains insufficient to classify lithium as essential for humans or animals, or to establish dietary reference values. In particular, lithium does not meet the essentiality criteria for the following reasons: a) Lithium lacks a defined biochemical role or known homeostatic pathways in the body. b) Studies fail to demonstrate reproducible deficiencies or requirements for lithium in animal nutrition4. c) No proof links lithium absence in human diets to reversible functional/structural abnormalities, nor are there systems to regulate its uptake. d) Specific biochemical and physiological changes associated with ‘lithium deficiency’ in humans have not been identified. e) There are no known systems to ensure the acquisition, systemic regulation and utilisation of lithium in the human body or known means to prevent its excessive acquisition. The new article published in Nature suggests lithium depletion may influence brain ageing in mouse models. However, accompanying analysis5 in the same journal stresses that human trials are lacking, and lithium’s role in diets – if any – remains unproven. EFSA will continue monitoring emerging research, but no further action is planned at this stage to classify lithium as an essential nutrient in EU legislation.

1 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40770094/. 2 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ww5scYAszN8. 3 https://efsa.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/epdf/10.2903/j.efsa.2014.3845. 4 https://efsa.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/epdf/10.2903/sp.efsa.2010.EN-68. 5 https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-025-02471-4.

E-10-2026-001487.t: Institutional gap concerning the sanctioning authorities of the Regulatory Authority for Railways (RAS), the Greek national enforcement body under Regulation (EU) 2021/782
qt: to the Commission Elena Kountoura (The Left) Subject:

Under Regulation (EU) 2021/782 on rail passengers’ rights and obligations, Member States were required to designate one or more national enforcement bodies (NEBs) and to establish a system of effective, proportionate and dissuasive penalties. The RAS had been formally designated as the national enforcement body in Greece in the context of the implementation of Regulation (EC) No 1371/20071. However, since this law was amended by Regulation (EU) 2021/782, no new administrative or legislative act has been adopted by the Greek authorities explicitly redefining the RAS as a national enforcement body2. Nevertheless, in practice, the RAS continues to operate as the competent enforcement body for rail passenger rights. The lack of such an act may raise serious issues concerning legal certainty and weaken the effective exercise of the RAS’ responsibilities. In addition, it may allow rail service providers to challenge the legislative basis for penalties, effectively limiting the protection of passengers3. Given that this legal vacuum may create practical obstacles to the application of the current Regulation4, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Has the designation of the RAS as a national enforcement body been notified by the competent Greek authorities to the Commission?

Does it consider that the current national legal framework adequately ensures legal certainty and the effective enforcement of passenger rights and that it fully complies with EU law, in particular Articles 31-32 of Regulation (EU) 2021/782, as regards the designation of a national enforcement body and the framework on penalties?

In accordance with Article 28(11) and Article 33 of Law 3891/2010, which grant the explicit power to impose penalties in the event of infringement of the provisions of Regulation (EC) No 1371/2007, the RAS could, by means of a reasoned decision and after inviting the persons concerned to provide explanations, either issue a recommendation with a warning calling on the person responsible to comply in the event of a repeat infringement or issue a fine of up to EUR 1 million, taking into account the nature, gravity and duration of the infringement. As required under Article 31 of the Regulation. This is particularly important in view of ongoing passenger complaints against the rail service provider, relating to, among other things, denied compensation for train delays and cancellations, compliance with the obligation to have an effective compensation system, poor service and inadequate handling of passenger complaints. The practical application of the Regulation may become impossible nationwide due to a formal legislative omission.
at: (English version) to the Commission Elena Kountoura (The Left) (13 April 2026) Subject: Institutional gap concerning the sanctioning authorities of the Regulatory Authority for Railways (RAS), the Greek national enforcement body under Regulation (EU) 2021/782 Under Regulation (EU) 2021/782 on rail passengers’ rights and obligations, Member States were required to designate one or more national enforcement bodies (NEBs) and to establish a system of effective, proportionate and dissuasive penalties. The RAS had been formally designated as the national enforcement body in Greece in the context of the implementation of Regulation (EC) No 1371/2007 (1). However, since this law was amended by Regulation (EU) 2021/782, no new administrative or legislative act has been adopted by the Greek authorities explicitly redefining the RAS as a national enforcement body (2). Nevertheless, in practice, the RAS continues to operate as the competent enforcement body for rail passenger rights. The lack of such an act may raise serious issues concerning legal certainty and weaken the effective exercise of the RAS’ responsibilities. In addition, it may allow rail service providers to challenge the legislative basis for penalties, effectively limiting the protection of passengers (3). Given that this legal vacuum may create practical obstacles to the application of the current Regulation (4), can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Has the designation of the RAS as a national enforcement body been notified by the competent Greek authorities to the Commission?

Does it consider that the current national legal framework adequately ensures legal certainty and the effective enforcement of passenger rights and that it fully complies with EU law, in particular Articles 31-32 of Regulation (EU) 2021/782, as regards the designation of a national enforcement body and the framework on penalties?

(6 July 2026) Article 31 of Regulation (EU) 2021/782 (1) requires Member States to designate a body responsible for the enforcement of the regulation and to inform the Commission thereof. In that regard, the Commission would like to inform the Honourable Member that it was notified by the Greek authorities that the Regulatory Authority for Railways (RAS) acts as the body responsible for the enforcement of the regulation in Greece. In addition, the Commission would like to remind the Honourable Member of the transitional provisions in that regulation. In particular, it follows from Article 40 of the regulation that whereas Regulation (EC) No 1371/2007 is repealed with effect from 7 June 2023, references thereto — including in national law — shall be construed as references to Regulation (EU) 2021/782. To this end, the regulation contains a correlation table in Annex IV. These provisions aim to ensure legal certainty in the context of the passage from one legislative act to another.

In accordance with Article 28(11) and Article 33 of Law 3891/2010, which grant the explicit power to impose penalties in the event of infringement of the provisions of Regulation (EC) No 1371/2007, the RAS could, by means of a reasoned decision and after inviting the persons concerned to provide explanations, either issue a recommendation with a warning calling on the person responsible to comply in the event of a repeat infringement or issue a fine of up to EUR 1 million, taking into account the nature, gravity and duration of the infringement. As required under Article 31 of the regulation. This is particularly important in view of ongoing passenger complaints against the rail service provider, relating to, among other things, denied compensation for train delays and cancellations, compliance with the obligation to have an effective compensation system, poor service and inadequate handling of passenger complaints. The practical application of the regulation may become impossible nationwide due to a formal legislative omission. E-10-2026-001485.t: What place is there for Romance languages in the EU institutions?
qt: to the Commission Catherine Griset (PfE), Pierre Pimpie (PfE), André Rougé (PfE), Georgiana Teodorescu (ECR), Tiago Moreira de Sá (PfE), António Tânger Corrêa (PfE) Subject:

Spanish and French have become, respectively, the third and fourth most spoken languages in the world, after Mandarin and English1, while Portuguese comes in sixth. Worldwide, there are 600 million Spanish speakers2, 396 million French speakers and around 275 million Portuguese speakers3. When Italian and Romanian are added to the mix, around 210 to 215 million EU citizens – almost half of them – have a Romance language as their mother tongue or main language. However, Romance languages are being steadily marginalised within the EU institutions, where speaking English is a must despite Brexit and the gradual breakdown of transatlantic relations. This marginalisation has become the symbol of a technocratic European Union that is far removed from its citizens. 1.
What effort is the Commission making to promote Romance languages within the EU institutions?
Is the systematic translation of working documents into the 24 official languages, at every stage, still an objective?
Should the Commission and its agencies not prioritise recruitment and promotions favouring staff who speak one or more languages other than English, including Romance languages?

Spanish and French have become, respectively, the third and fourth most spoken languages in the world, after Mandarin and English (1), while Portuguese comes in sixth. Worldwide, there are 600 million Spanish speakers (2), 396 million French speakers and around 275 million Portuguese speakers (3). However, Romance languages are being steadily marginalised within the EU institutions, where speaking English is a must despite Brexit and the gradual breakdown of transatlantic relations. This marginalisation has become the symbol of a technocratic European Union that is far removed from its citizens. 1.

(17 July 2026) The Commission is committed to the active promotion of multilingualism, both within the institution and in its relations with the other institutions, Member States and the public. The Commission does not actively promote the use of any particular language. In line with Regulation No 1 from 1958 (1), EU legislation is published in all EU official and working languages. On its main website (2), the Commission provides information in all EU official languages. Practical information on citizens’ rights and administrative and legal procedures is also provided in all EU official languages (3). When information is particularly relevant for speakers of a specific language, it is usually drafted and published in that language or translated into it. In such instances, other languages may be provided through machine translation. This balanced approach ensures that the Commission’s online communication with citizens fully adheres to the principle of multilingualism. The Commission's recruitment policy aims to secure the highest standards of ability, efficiency and integrity, while recruiting from the broadest possible geographical base of Member State nationals. To be recruited, staff must provide evidence of knowledge of one EU language and satisfactory knowledge of another. Before their first promotion, EU officials are required to demonstrate the ability to work in a third language among those referred to in Article 55(1) of the Treaty on European Union.

E-10-2026-001484.t: Are EU funds supporting the CNC Talent fund?
qt: to the Commission Catherine Griset (PfE) Subject:

The streamer Ultia was removed from the committee for CNC Talent – a fund supporting video creators within the framework of the National Centre for Cinema and the Moving Image – following her revelations about favouritism displayed by committee members towards creators cut from the same ideological cloth as them. Thus it follows that the fund, which provides grants for both fictional works and documentaries on YouTube, Instagram, TikTok and Twitch, could end up being hijacked to the benefit of left-wing activists, despite the inclusion of the principles of impartiality and neutrality in the CNC’s General Framework for Funding. The fund’s yearly budget of EUR 3 million comes from the CNC’s general budget, which is financed through taxes on: - cinema tickets (10.72 % of cost price); - television services; - the dissemination of physical videos (DVD, Blu-ray) or online videos (streaming). Against this backdrop: 1.
Does the Commission fund CNC Talent, for example under the media strand of the Creative Europe programme?
If so, are the grants subject to ethical obligations, such as compliance with the principles of impartiality or neutrality?
Does the European Court of Auditors audit EU funds for online platform content creation?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (2.6.2026) The MEDIA strand of the Creative Europe programme1 does not fund the National Centre of Cinema (CNC) Talent action2. More generally, MEDIA does not include an online platform content action like the CNC Talent action, which targets content produced by online creators with a significant presence on video-sharing platforms. When it comes to funding audiovisual content creation, the targeted beneficiaries of Creative Europe MEDIA funding are European independent audiovisual production companies, in line with the Creative Europe Regulation3. The definition of eligible production companies is not linked to a presence on video-sharing platforms. Most of the works supported for content creation under the Creative Europe MEDIA programme are intended primarily for cinema, followed by content made primarily for television. In light of the above, questions 2) and 3) do not arise in this specific case.
1 Regulation (eu) 2021/818 of the European parliament and of the Council of 20 May 2021establishing the

Creative Europe Programme (2021 to 2027). 2 Information accessed on 28 April 2026 from https://www.cnc.fr/professionnels/aides-et-financements/creationnumerique/fonds-daide-aux-createurs-video-sur-internet-cnc-talent_190814. 3 See for example sub-section a) and b) of Section 2 of Annex 1, Regulation above.

qt: to the Commission Anja Hazekamp (The Left), Sebastian Everding (The Left) Subject:

It is prohibited to transport animals in a way likely to cause injury or undue suffering to them1. Nevertheless, animals are still being transported by sea from the EU to conflict zones. Events such as port closures, attacks on infrastructure or delays at sea lead to animals experiencing severe suffering or injury, and can even result in their death. Furthermore, these situations pose health and safety risks to crew members, port workers, drivers and veterinarians. Is the Commission prepared to adopt, by means of a delegated act, a list of countries outside the EU to which Member States may not export live animals for the reasons mentioned?

1. Can the Commission explain how it monitors the welfare of animals that have recently been transported by ship from the EU to conflict zones? 2. Is the Commission aware that, in order to ensure animal welfare, it is necessary for Member States to immediately suspend the export of live animals to regions with an unstable political situation? 3. Is the Commission prepared to adopt, by means of a delegated act, a list of countries outside the EU to which Member States may not export live animals for the reasons mentioned? Joint answer given by Mr Várhelyi on behalf of the European Commission (22 June 2026) The EU legislation on the protection of animals during transport (1) does not require the Commission to monitor directly the transport to conflict zones or to suspend exports to third countries. However, Member States’ competent authorities are responsible for enforcing the rules of this legislation. They can refuse approving long journeys for exports to third countries if there is no evidence that EU animal welfare rules will be respected for the entire journey to the destination. The Commission continues to audit Member States that transport animals by sea. Given the unstable situation in the Middle East, the Commission asked Member States to exceptionally issue replacement certificates for consignments when needed and reminded their obligation to ensure protection of animals during transport up to destination, including outside the EU. To improve animal welfare outside the EU, the Commission provides technical and financial support to the World Organisation for Animal Health and works to strengthen the application of its international animal welfare standards, including during transport. The Commission has no legal basis to adopt by means of delegated act a list of third countries to which animals may not be exported from Member States. The Commission’s proposal to revise EU rules on animal transport aimed at improving animal welfare during transport is currently with co-legislators.

Council Regulation (EC) No 1/2005 of 22 December 2004 on the protection of animals during transport and related operations and amending Directives 64/432/EEC and 93/119/EC and Regulation (EC) No 1255/97 (OJ L 3, 5.1.2005, p. 1, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2005/1/oj ).

Correctiv is a German media outlet founded in 2014, with the supposed goal of exposing disinformation using so-called fact-checking programmes. In addition to receiving extensive funding from the German state, at European level Correctiv is part of the European Digital Media Observatory (EDMO), which has received over EUR 30 million in support from the Commission since it was founded in 2020. What is more, in April 2025 the Commission published two further calls for the submission of applications for funding, with a total value of EUR 5 million, for programmes combating disinformation that also involve fact-checking and that are to be carried out in collaboration with the EDMO. The increase in spending for the purpose of policing critical opinions under the pretext of combating disinformation, for example through the promotion of politically biased media outlets like Correctiv, raises questions of transparency. 1.

Is the Commission planning to continue funding Correctiv within the framework of the calls for submission of applications for funding published in April 2025, which have a total value of EUR 5 million, or via any other EU funding programmes in the future?
