E-10-2026-001478.t: EU support for the Cormorant Management Advisory Group
qt: to the Commission Bert-Jan Ruissen (ECR), Carmen Crespo Díaz (PPE), Ton Diepeveen (PfE), Gabriel Mato (PPE), Francisco José Millán Mon (PPE), Stephen Nikola Bartulica (ECR), Sander Smit (ECR), Kristoffer Storm (ECR), Flavio Tosi (PPE), Niclas Herbst (PPE), Asger Christensen (Renew) Subject:

The growing great cormorant population across Europe is increasing pressure on fisheries, aquaculture and biodiversity, resulting in estimated annual losses exceeding EUR 350 million. Due to the cormorants’ migratory nature and cross-border impact, national measures to address the problem have proven insufficient. Coordinated European action is required. A framework for a European cormorant management plan, developed under the European Inland Fisheries and Aquaculture Advisory Commission (EIFAAC), provides a science-based and widely supported approach. Its development benefited from EU funding, including under the European Maritime, Fisheries and Aquaculture Fund (EMFAF), demonstrating the framework’s alignment with EU priorities. To support implementation, 24 countries have nominated experts to the Cormorant Management Advisory Group (CMAG). Establishing a dedicated secretariat for the CMAG would ensure coordination, data collection and coherent implementation, when reporting back to Member States and the European Parliament. An annual investment of EUR 500 000 (EUR 3 million over six years) would be proportionate and cost-effective given the scale of the damage. 1.
Is the Commission willing to allocate EUR 3 million over six years, including under the EMFAF, to establish and operate a CMAG secretariat?
Does the Commission intend to appoint representatives from its Directorate-General for Maritime Affairs and Fisheries and from its Directorate-General for Environment to the CMAG?
What concrete steps will the Commission take to coordinate implementation of the EIFAAC framework at European level?
at: (English version) to the Commission Bert-Jan Ruissen (ECR), Carmen Crespo Díaz (PPE), Ton Diepeveen (PfE), Gabriel Mato (PPE), Francisco José Millán Mon (PPE), Stephen Nikola Bartulica (ECR), Sander Smit (ECR), Kristoffer Storm (ECR), Flavio Tosi (PPE), Niclas Herbst (PPE), Asger Christensen (Renew) (10 April 2026) Subject: EU support for the Cormorant Management Advisory Group The growing great cormorant population across Europe is increasing pressure on fisheries, aquaculture and biodiversity, resulting in estimated annual losses exceeding EUR 350 million. Due to the cormorants’ migratory nature and cross-border impact, national measures to address the problem have proven insufficient. Coordinated European action is required. A framework for a European cormorant management plan, developed under the European Inland Fisheries and Aquaculture Advisory Commission (EIFAAC), provides a science-based and widely supported approach. Its development benefited from EU funding, including under the European Maritime, Fisheries and Aquaculture Fund (EMFAF), demonstrating the framework’s alignment with EU priorities. To support implementation, 24 countries have nominated experts to the Cormorant Management Advisory Group (CMAG). Establishing a dedicated secretariat for the CMAG would ensure coordination, data collection and coherent implementation, when reporting back to Member States and the European Parliament. An annual investment of EUR 500 000 (EUR 3 million over six years) would be proportionate and cost-effective given the scale of the damage. 1. Is the Commission willing to allocate EUR 3 million over six years, including under the EMFAF, to establish and operate a CMAG secretariat? 2. Does the Commission intend to appoint representatives from its Directorate-General for Maritime Affairs and Fisheries and from its Directorate-General for Environment to the CMAG? 3. What concrete steps will the Commission take to coordinate implementation of the EIFAAC framework at European level? (11 June 2026) 1. The Commission recognises the benefits of EU coordination in managing the cormorant fisheries conflict and encourages Member States to cooperate and coordinate their management measures. The Commission provided the European Inland Fisheries and Aquaculture Advisory Commission (EIFAAC) a grant under the European Maritime, Fisheries, and Aquaculture Fund (EMFAF) to develop a framework for a European Management Plan for the Great Cormorant. Regrettably, the Commission is unable to provide EIFAAC with further funding for the establishment and operation of the Cormorant Management Advisory Group (CMAG) Secretariat, particularly in light of significant reductions in the EMFAF’s direct expenditure budget. Moreover, the EMFAF Work Programme 2026-2027 has been approved by the EMFAF Committee and has been adopted. However, Member States have possibilities to use various funding streams to implement measures addressing cormorants-fisheries conflicts. 2. The Commission has nominated representatives from its Directorate-General for Maritime Affairs and Fisheries and Directorate-General for Environment to the CMAG to closely follow its activities and to avoid duplication of efforts. 3. The Commission will continue to carefully monitor the issue and support Member States and the aquaculture sector by promoting good practices and research and innovation, in close cooperation with experts and the affected stakeholders and communities. The Commission will continue to organise ‘Structured Dialogues on managing cormorant conflicts’ with Member States’ authorities. The Commission is also looking into possibilities to support potential pan-European counts of the wintering population and breeding colonies in 2027, as well as further research on the species impact to fisheries.

E-10-2026-001477.t: Continued abuse of SIM cards by criminals and saboteurs
qt: to the Commission Assita Kanko (ECR), Malik Azmani (Renew), Aurelijus Veryga (ECR), Jeroen Lenaers (PPE), Lena Düpont (PPE) Subject:

In recent years, EU Member States have tightened their national rules around the acquisition and use of SIM cards. However, in several Member States, identity registration is still not required. Furthermore, even in Member States where it is required, criminals get around it by paying minors to buy SIM cards and then reselling them. This situation constitutes a serious security risk for the EU. SIM cards are used for navigation by operators of drones and smuggling balloons, such as those recently detected over Lithuania. They are also used in disinformation campaigns, and they are used by criminals for scams and phishing operations. In an EU of open internal borders and fee-free roaming, SIM cards obtained in one Member State can be freely used throughout the territory of the EU. With that in mind: 1.
How does the Commission assess the internal security risks of the current situation, whereby several EU Member States do not require identity registration for the purchase of SIM cards?
Does the Commission intend to close this security gap by proposing legislation or by urging the Member States to change their national rules?
Does the Commission agree that, even with registration requirements, more needs to be done to avoid the abusive reselling of SIM cards?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (30.6.2026) The Commission is aware of the growing phenomenon of fraud perpetrated via electronic communications services. Subscriber Identity Module (SIM) cards are the enablers of these services and Member States have the discretion to impose SIM registration requirements, in particular, for pre-paid SIM cards, to counter crimes or any fraudulent activities. These requirements have to comply with EU data protection rules. Obligations on electronic communications service providers to retain subscriber information and other non-content data are currently regulated by national laws. The Commission is currently conducting an impact assessment to evaluate the need for a possible harmonised EU framework on the retention of non-content data for criminal justice purposes. In addition, the proposal for a Digital Networks Act1 requires the Body of European Regulators for Electronic Communications to issue guidelines on measures that could effectively protect end-users against fraudulent activities through interpersonal communications in the EU. National competent authorities will be required to adopt the necessary measures taking the guidelines into utmost account. The Commission will be empowered to adopt delegated acts to supplement the Digital Networks Act with provisions enhancing the effectiveness thereof. Further to the priorities outlined in the ProtectEU Internal Security Strategy2 of April 2025, the Commission intends to publish an Action Plan to counter digital fraud before the end of 2026. As currently envisaged, the Action Plan will aim to address the multifaceted nature of digital fraud through a comprehensive, cross-sectoral approach and specific actions.
1 https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/proposal-regulation-digital-networks-act-dna. 2 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A52025DC0148.

E-10-2026-001475.t: Promotion of unlicensed online gambling services by content creators
qt: to the Commission Sabine Verheyen (PPE) Subject:

A 2024 study conducted by Yield Sec on behalf of the European Casino Association found that 71 % of online gambling activity targeting European users takes place on unlicensed, and thus illegal, websites. At the same time, the overall use of online gambling in the EU has continued to increase. Recent reports further indicate that illegal gambling websites are frequently promoted by content creators, particularly on video platforms such as YouTube and Twitch. Such promotion is often carried out through affiliate links, enabling content creators to receive a percentage or fixed payment for each new player they bring on board. The users reached through such promotional activities are often young and potentially vulnerable. Content that promotes unlicensed online gambling services is illegal and should therefore be removed by online platforms in accordance with the Digital Services Act1. Nevertheless, a significant amount of such promotional content appears to remain available online. 1.
Is the Commission aware of the active promotion, by online content creators in the EU, of unlicensed online gambling services?
Does the Commission intend to investigate the issue further?
What steps is the Commission taking to ensure the more effective enforcement of the Digital Services Act?

Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 19 October 2022 on a Single Market For Digital Services and amending Directive 2000/31/EC (Digital Services Act) (OJ L 277, 27.10.2022, p. 1, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/2065/oj).
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (12.6.2026) The Commission is aware of the issue of undisclosed advertising on online platforms, as well as the promotion of illegal products online. The Digital Services Act1 (DSA) requires online platforms to provide a user-friendly notice and action mechanism ensuring users can report content, including advertisements, they consider to be illegal. Additionally, very large online platforms (VLOPs) and very large online search engines (VLOSEs) are required to diligently assess and mitigate systemic risks on their services, including risks concerning the dissemination of illegal content The guidelines on the protection of minors2 under the DSA clarify that minors should not be exposed to advertising for products that could negatively impact their privacy, safety and security, and any commercial content should be clearly labelled as such. The protection of minors as consumers is also a priority under the upcoming Digital Fairness Act, which will address issues such as unfair influencer marketing. The Commission is closely monitoring VLOPs and VLOSEs with the DSA. For example, the Commission has adopted preliminary findings against the provider of Facebook and Instagram for appearing to have failed to provide users with a user-friendly and easily accessible notice and action mechanism. The Commission also recently opened formal proceedings against the provider of Snapchat due to suspicions relating to, among other issues, the failure to address risks linked to the promotion of prohibited or age-restricted products to minors. Lastly, the Commission is looking into the app stores for, inter alia, the effectiveness of their measures to prevent minors from accessing age-restricted apps, such as gambling apps.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:32022R2065. 2 https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/commission-publishes-guidelines-protection-minors.

E-10-2026-001474.t: Traceability of rail components and integrity of accident investigations on Spain’s high-speed network
qt: to the Commission Borja Giménez Larraz (PPE) Subject:

New press reports in April 2026, based on internal emails and documents included in the judicial summary of the accident in Adamuz (Córdoba) that resulted in the deaths of 46 people on 18 January 2026, show that a rail was installed in the area that had a serial number that did not appear on the manufacturer’s invoices or delivery orders. ArcelorMittal confirmed in writing that it could not prove the traceability of this rail and recommended its immediate replacement as a preventive measure. Upon learning this information, ADIF replaced 42 metres of track and removed welds present at the time of the accident without first informing the judicial authority investigating the accident. The investigating judge has asked for explanations in relation to the replacement and to the whereabouts of the material removed. 1.
Does the Commission consider the presence of rail infrastructure components without verified traceability on the TEN-T network to be compatible with Article 10 of Directive (EU) 2016/797?
Has Spain notified the Commission and ERA of the finding of this component in accordance with Article 11 of Directive (EU) 2016/797?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (9.6.2026) The Commission has not received evidence about the presence of rail infrastructure components without verified traceability on the trans-European transport (TEN-T) network. As indicated in Article 15 of the Interoperability Directive (EU) 2016/7971, notified bodies are responsible for verifying the suitability of the components to obtain the ‘EC’ declaration and its compatibility with Article 10 of the Directive. If a Member State finds that a structural subsystem covered by the ‘EC’ declaration of verification does not fully comply with the Interoperability Directive (EU) 2016/797, it may request that additional checks be carried out and shall inform the Commission. It is also responsible for ensuring that a component is not placed on a line if it finds that the ‘EC’ declaration has been drawn up improperly, following Article 16 of the Interoperability Directive (EU) 2016/797. According to Article 11 of the Interoperability Directive (EU) 2016/797, if a Member State finds that an interoperability constituent covered by the ‘EC’ declaration fails to comply with the essential requirements, it should inform the Commission and the European Union Agency for Railway (ERA) of the measures taken and give reasons for its decision. At this moment, neither the Commission nor ERA has received such an information in relation to the Adamuz accident.
1 Directive (EU) 2016/797 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 11 May 2016 on the interoperability

of the rail system within the European Union (recast) (Text with EEA relevance). OJ L 138, 26.5.2016, pp. 44– 101 (BG, ES, CS, DA, DE, ET, EL, EN, FR, HR, IT, LV, LT, HU, MT, NL, PL, PT, RO, SK, SL, FI, SV).

E-10-2026-001473.t: Adamuz rail accident –  safety failures by the infrastructure manager
qt: to the Commission Borja Giménez Larraz (PPE) Subject:
Adamuz rail accident – safety failures by the infrastructure manager

On 18 January 2026, 46 people lost their lives in the Adamuz rail accident. A Guardia Civil report submitted to the judge has revealed three serious failures by ADIF as infrastructure manager. The rail damage detection system recorded an electrical anomaly 22 hours before the accident but was not configured to issue automatic alerts despite ADIF’s own specifications requiring such a capability. Doubts have arisen concerning the certification and minimum experience of one of the two technicians from the contractor company who performed ultrasound inspections on the 114 welds in June 2025 in the section where the accident subsequently took place. ADIF provided incorrect information to the emergency number 112 regarding the location of the second train involved, which delayed the rescue of its passengers by approximately 45 minutes. 1.

In light of Article 9 of Directive (EU) 2016/798, which requires the infrastructure manager to ensure the control of all risks associated with their activity and to coordinate emergency procedures with the emergency services, does the Commission consider that these failures reveal systemic deficiencies in safety management?
Does the Commission intend to ask ERA for an assessment of the supervision exercised by the Spanish national safety authority?
at: (English version) to the Commission Borja Giménez Larraz (PPE) (10 April 2026) Subject: Adamuz rail accident — safety failures by the infrastructure manager On 18 January 2026, 46 people lost their lives in the Adamuz rail accident. A Guardia Civil report submitted to the judge has revealed three serious failures by ADIF as infrastructure manager. The rail damage detection system recorded an electrical anomaly 22 hours before the accident but was not configured to issue automatic alerts despite ADIF’s own specifications requiring such a capability. Doubts have arisen concerning the certification and minimum experience of one of the two technicians from the contractor company who performed ultrasound inspections on the 114 welds in June 2025 in the section where the accident subsequently took place. ADIF provided incorrect information to the emergency number 112 regarding the location of the second train involved, which delayed the rescue of its passengers by approximately 45 minutes. 1. In light of Article 9 of Directive (EU) 2016/798, which requires the infrastructure manager to ensure the control of all risks associated with their activity and to coordinate emergency procedures with the emergency services, does the Commission consider that these failures reveal systemic deficiencies in safety management? 2. Does the Commission intend to ask ERA for an assessment of the supervision exercised by the Spanish national safety authority? (4 June 2026) The Commission has not received yet the report by the Spanish investigating body (CIAF), single body responsible of the investigation of the causes of the accident as well as the emergency procedures and processes applied in the aftermath of the accident. Moreover, according to Article 4(1) of Directive (EU) 2016/798 (Railway Safety Directive) (1), Member States’ rail safety authorities are responsible for ensuring that safe train operations are delivered and adjacent risk is managed by railway undertakings and infrastructure managers, by implementing risk control measures, apply relevant legislation and establish a safety management system fit for the purpose of their activities. The European Union Railway Agency (ERA) assists CIAF high-level technical expertise on general investigation methods and independence in accordance with Article 22(5) of the Railway Safety Directive. The Commission may intervene, as appropriate, in case of clear evidence of important breach of Union law.
Directive (EU) 2016/798 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 11 May 2016 on railway safety (recast) (Text with EEA relevance) — OJ L 138, 26.5.2016, pp. 102-149.

E-10-2026-001471.t: Question regarding the progress of the OPEKEPE investigation
qt: to the Commission Sandro Gozi (Renew) Subject:

According to Greek press reports, it appears that the European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO) has faced obstacles in its efforts to investigate the OPEKEPE case, including ‘deliberate delays’ related to procedural issues in the handling of investigations by the competent Greek authorities. Specifically, the following has been reported about the European prosecutors. – More than 10 requests have been sent to obtain the necessary information regarding those involved in the OPEKEPE case. It is alleged that, in certain cases, incorrect data has been deliberately provided (for example regarding tax identification numbers), which has significantly delayed the progress of the investigation. – At least three requests have been sent to the Internal Affairs Division to obtain the full content of intercepted communications. It was found that the initial material was incomplete and that communications involving political figures, namely members of parliament and ministers, had not been forwarded. Noting the competences of the EPPO, I would like to have more information on the following point: Does the Commission have any information on obstacles the EPPO may have encountered from the relevant Greek authorities when trying to investigate the OPEKEPE case?
at: (English version) to the Commission Sandro Gozi (Renew) (10 April 2026) Subject: Question regarding the progress of the OPEKEPE investigation According to Greek press reports, it appears that the European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO) has faced obstacles in its efforts to investigate the OPEKEPE case, including ‘deliberate delays’ related to procedural issues in the handling of investigations by the competent Greek authorities. Specifically, the following has been reported about the European prosecutors. — More than 10 requests have been sent to obtain the necessary information regarding those involved in the OPEKEPE case. It is alleged that, in certain cases, incorrect data has been deliberately provided (for example regarding tax identification numbers), which has significantly delayed the progress of the investigation. — At least three requests have been sent to the Internal Affairs Division to obtain the full content of intercepted communications. It was found that the initial material was incomplete and that communications involving political figures, namely members of parliament and ministers, had not been forwarded. Noting the competences of the EPPO, I would like to have more information on the following point: Does the Commission have any information on obstacles the EPPO may have encountered from the relevant Greek authorities when trying to investigate the OPEKEPE case? (1 July 2026) The European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO) is the independent Public Prosecutor’s Office of the EU and, in the performance of its duties under the EPPO Regulation (1), neither seeks nor takes instructions from any person external to the EPPO, from any Member State, or from any institution, body, office or agency of the EU. Accordingly, the EPPO does not consult the Commission on any aspect relating to its investigations, nor does the Commission have access to operational details relating thereto. Moreover, the Commission cannot comment on ongoing criminal investigations. The Commission fully supports the EPPO in its mission to protect the EU’s financial interests and recalls that Member States are under a duty of sincere cooperation with the EPPO, in accordance with the EPPO Regulation and the Treaty (2). Furthermore, pursuant to Article 5(6) of the EPPO Regulation (3), the competent national authorities are required to actively assist and support the EPPO’s investigations and prosecutions.

Council Regulation (EU) 2017/1939 of 12 October 2017 implementing enhanced cooperation on the establishment of the European Public Prosecutor’s Office (‘the EPPO’), OJ L 283, 31.10.2017, p. 1. ‘Pursuant to the principle of sincere cooperation, the Union and the Member States shall, in full mutual respect, assist each other in carrying out tasks which flow from the Treaties’, Article 4(3) of the Treaty on European Union (TEU), consolidated version, OJ C 202, 7.6.2016, p. 13. Article 5 (6) of the EPPO Regulation: ‘The competent national authorities shall actively assist and support the investigations and prosecutions of the EPPO. Any action, policy or procedure under this regulation shall be guided by the principle of sincere cooperation’.

E-10-2026-001470.t: Consumer safety and market surveillance for personal mobility devices
qt: to the Commission Stefano Cavedagna (ECR), Denis Nesci (ECR) Subject:

Millions of personal mobility devices (PMDs), such as e-scooters, are sold across the EU, yet fall outside the scope of vehicle type-approval (Regulation (EU) No 168/20131). The Machinery Directive2 governs their placement on the market, but does not address road safety requirements such as braking, lighting, speed limitation or anti-tampering. A November 2024 TRL/fka study, conducted on behalf of the Commission, documented fraudulent CE certifications and recommended a universal EU PMD approval scheme. In December 2025, 16 Member States called for an EU-wide framework. Meanwhile, the European and Italian markets face a growing influx of electric bicycles that are sold as pedalassisted cycles but function as unregistered mopeds. These have top speeds of 50-85 km/h, but are not subject to requirements concerning insurance, helmets or licences. Seizures by law enforcement in cities across Italy confirm the systemic scale of the problem. 1.

Since there are no harmonised EU technical requirements, what tools do market surveillance authorities possess, under Regulation (EU) 2019/10203, to intercept PMDs sold online that fail to meet road safety standards?
Does the Commission consider the Machinery Regulation adequate consumer protection for devices used daily on public roads by millions of Europeans, including minors?
Will the Commission include harmonisation on PMD in its 2027 work programme, given the TRL/fka study recommendation and the call made by 16 Member States in the Transport Council?

Regulation (EU) No 168/2013 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 15 January 2013 on the approval and market surveillance of two- or three-wheel vehicles and quadricycles (OJ L 60, 2.3.2013, p. 52, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2013/168/oj). Directive 2006/42/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 17 May 2006 on machinery, and amending Directive 95/16/EC (OJ L 157, 9.6.2006, p. 24, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2006/42/oj). Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 20 June 2019 on market surveillance and compliance of products and amending Directive 2004/42/EC and Regulations (EC) No 765/2008 and (EU) No 305/2011 (OJ L 169, 25.6.2019, p. 1, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2019/1020/oj).
at: (English version) to the Commission Stefano Cavedagna (ECR), Denis Nesci (ECR) (10 April 2026) Subject: Consumer safety and market surveillance for personal mobility devices Millions of personal mobility devices (PMDs), such as e-scooters, are sold across the EU, yet fall outside the scope of vehicle type-approval (Regulation (EU) No 168/2013 (1)). The Machinery Directive (2) governs their placement on the market, but does not address road safety requirements such as braking, lighting, speed limitation or anti-tampering. A November 2024 TRL/fka study, conducted on behalf of the Commission, documented fraudulent CE certifications and recommended a universal EU PMD approval scheme. In December 2025, 16 Member States called for an EU-wide framework. Meanwhile, the European and Italian markets face a growing influx of electric bicycles that are sold as pedal-assisted cycles but function as unregistered mopeds. These have top speeds of 50-85 km/h, but are not subject to requirements concerning insurance, helmets or licences. Seizures by law enforcement in cities across Italy confirm the systemic scale of the problem. 1. Since there are no harmonised EU technical requirements, what tools do market surveillance authorities possess, under Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 (3), to intercept PMDs sold online that fail to meet road safety standards? 2. Does the Commission consider the Machinery Regulation adequate consumer protection for devices used daily on public roads by millions of Europeans, including minors? 3. Will the Commission include harmonisation on PMD in its 2027 work programme, given the TRL/fka study recommendation and the call made by 16 Member States in the Transport Council? (10 June 2026) Under Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 (1), market surveillance authorities (MSAs) have a range of tools to intercept non-compliant personal mobility devices (PMDs) sold online. These include powers to do mystery shopping online, to order the removal of online listings, to suspend the release of products at the EU's external borders, and to require the withdrawal or recall of products presenting a risk to health and safety on the basis of a general safety assessment (2) or Regulation (EU) 2023/988 (3). Furthermore, Member States undertake coordinated enforcement action across the Single Market. However, the absence of harmonised road safety requirements for PMDs limits the effectiveness of these tools in practice. Although the EU machinery legislation (4) is the main safety regulatory act applying to machinery, including mobile machinery such as PMDs, and addressing safety when the machinery is at work, its essential requirements do not cover the safety aspects of that machinery when circulating on public roads. In 2024, a study (5), prepared on behalf of the Commission, examined the challenges and opportunities associated with PMDs. The mid-term report on the implementation of the EU road safety framework (6) committed to drawing conclusions on the potential benefits of harmonising technical specifications for on-road use of PMDs (7).

Regulation (EU) No 168/2013 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 15 January 2013 on the approval and market surveillance of two- or threewheel vehicles and quadricycles (OJ L 60, 2.3.2013, p. 52, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2013/168/oj). Directive 2006/42/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 17 May 2006 on machinery, and amending Directive 95/16/EC (OJ L 157, 9.6.2006, p. 24, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2006/42/oj). Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 20 June 2019 on market surveillance and compliance of products and amending Directive 2004/42/EC and Regulations (EC) No 765/2008 and (EU) No 305/2011 (OJ L 169, 25.6.2019, p. 1, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2019/1020/oj). https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2019/1020/oj/eng. Article 16 of Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 provides a residual basis for MSAs to act on general safety grounds. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2023/988/oj/eng. Until 19 January 2027, Directive 2006/42/EU (https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2006/42/oj/eng), and from 20 January 2027, Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 (https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2023/1230/oj/eng). European Commission: Directorate-General for Internal Market, Industry, Entrepreneurship and SMEs, Study on the need for harmonised rules to support the rise of micro mobility and increased road safety for personal mobility devices — Final report (1.0), Publications Office of the European Union, 2024, https://data.europa.eu/doi/10.2873/8572224. Report on the Implementation of the EU Road Safety Policy Framework at the Mid-Point, COM(2026) 77 final, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legalcontent/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:52026DC0077. As requested by Transport Ministers at the Transport, Telecom and Energy Council meeting in December 2025.

The 2024 study also showed that PMD riders’ behaviour plays a significant role for safety. Member States have an important role to play in setting out adequate traffic rules and properly enforce them. The Commission has committed to prepare guidance to Member States and regional and local administrations on what issues should be taken into account to ensure the safety of riders and other road users during the use of PMDs (8).

This should expand on the guidance set out in the 2021 Sustainable Urban Mobility Plan Topic Guide on Safe Use of Micromobility, https://urbanmobility-observatory.transport.ec.europa.eu/sustainable-urban-mobility-plans/expert-corner-sump-reference-materials_en .

E-10-2026-001469.t: EU budget and equality policy – promoting LGBTQ projects over family policy
qt: to the Commission Roman Haider (PfE), Tom Vandendriessche (PfE), Elisabeth Dieringer (PfE), Ondřej Knotek (PfE), Jaroslava Pokorná Jermanová (PfE), Antonín Staněk (PfE), Mary Khan (ESN), Tomasz Froelich (ESN), Siegbert Frank Droese (ESN), Volker Schnurrbusch (ESN), Alexander Sell (ESN), Ivan David (ESN), Irmhild Boßdorf (ESN), Zsuzsanna Borvendég (ESN), Markus Buchheit (ESN), Kosma Złotowski (ECR), Aurelijus Veryga (ECR), Adrian-George Axinia (ECR), Paolo Inselvini (ECR), Diana Iovanovici Şoşoacă (NI), Branko Grims (PPE), Christine Anderson (ESN), Alexander Jungbluth (ESN) Subject:

Year after year, the Commission pours millions into projects, campaigns and public awareness activities. Whole strategies are dedicated to increasing visibility for gender identities – underpinned by support programmes, training and EU-wide guidelines. This policy has now become ubiquitous, from educational establishments to government departments. Brussels is financing pride campaigns, while the role of families as essential pillars of society is ignored. This massive imbalance is not only unjust; it is a political warning signal. A society that neglects families politically and financially puts its own future in jeopardy. While millions are being mobilised across the EU for specific interest groups, parents, who are responsible for children, often come away empty-handed. Anyone who tries to fob mothers and fathers off with purely symbolic policies, while wholeheartedly endorsing pride initiatives, is prioritising ideology over their social responsibility. 1.
Going forward, does the Commission intend to promote the societal image of family and parenthood just as actively as that of minority groups?
Does the Commission have a dedicated strategy for promoting and showcasing family, parenthood and children as essential pillars of society, comparable to the LGBTQ equality strategy?

What criteria is the Commission using to assess the impact of LGBTQ public awareness campaigns with regard to effectiveness, reach and societal acceptance, and are these same criteria used when assessing campaigns or initiatives that promote families?

What criteria is the Commission using to assess the impact of LGBTQ public awareness campaigns with regard to effectiveness, reach and societal acceptance, and are these same criteria used when assessing campaigns or initiatives that promote families? (30 June 2026) EU policies and funding instruments aim to support and empower families across the EU with key objectives, including the promotion of equality, supporting work-life balance and conciliation, enhancing child well-being and combating poverty and social exclusion. This is reflected in initiatives like the European Pillar of Social Right s (1), the Gender Equality Strategy (2), the LGBTIQ+ equality strategy (3), the strategy for the rights of persons with disabilities (4), the European Care Strategy (5) and the EU strategy on the rights of the child (6). The responsibility for shaping family policy and broader societal choices regarding family life and parenthood rests primarily with the Member States. Within the limits of its competences and in full respect of the principle of subsidiarity, the Commission supports families through different measures. For example, via the EU Cohesion Policy funds, or the European Child Guarantee (7), the Commission provides support for home care and family care systems, for services for children, young people and families to promote their well-being, and for the participation of children in early childhood education and care for families at risk of poverty.

E-10-2026-001468.t: Proportionality of the ‘polluter pays’ principle in the extended producer responsibility scheme under the Urban Wastewater Treatment Directive
qt: to the Commission Beatrice Timgren (ECR) Subject:

In the light of the ongoing discussions1 on the implementation of the Urban Wastewater Treatment Directive2, the directive introduces an extended producer responsibility (EPR) scheme requiring, among other things, producers of medicinal and cosmetic products to cover at least 80 % of the costs for removing micropollutants from urban wastewater. The Commission has itself acknowledged significant divergences in the available figures and referred to updated and additional studies3. Therefore, questions arise as to whether attributing micropollutant loads to specific sectors fully reflects actual emissions and whether limiting the scope to two product groups is consistent with proportionality and competitiveness considerations. In this context, can the Commission clarify: 1.

the specific data and methodology on which it bases the attribution of micropollutant loads to the sectors listed in Annex III, and how it ensures that this attribution reflects actual emissions rather than product categorisation?
how it will ensure, in the context of implementing and delegated acts, that sectors with comparatively low contributions are not subject to disproportionate financial burdens?
whether it envisages a future evaluation or possible revision of Annex III should new evidence indicate that there is a mismatch between attributed and actual contributions?

https://oeil.europarl.europa.eu/oeil/en/procedure-file?reference=2026/2652(RSP). Directive (EU) 2024/3019 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 November 2024 concerning urban wastewater treatment (OJ L, 2024/3019, 12.12.2024, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2024/3019/oj). https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/CRE-10-2026-03-25-ITM-016_EN.html.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (6.7.2026) The Commission’s impact assessment1 accompanying its proposal for a recast Urban Wastewater Treatment Directive2 built on the publicly available report ‘Feasibility of an extended producer responsibility system for micropollutants’3. The methodology and its limitations, as well as all relevant sources are presented therein. The report uses the chemicals list – Total Pollution Proxy Substances4 – which is available online. In line with the Directive, the producer responsibility organisations will determine how each producer contributes to the costs of quaternary treatment according to what they place on the EU market and by taking into account the quantity and hazardousness of the substances contained in their products. Producers can be exempted from extended producer responsibility (EPR) obligations if they fulfil the conditions described in Article 9.2 of the Directive. In addition, national authorities should consider the possible impacts of the EPR on the accessibility, availability and affordability of products at national level, as well as the possible impacts on the level playing field5. The Commission will first evaluate the Directive by 2033, and then by 2040, taking into account the experience gained through its implementation, the data resulting from the monitoring obligations on micropollutants, improved knowledge on the presence of micropollutants in urban wastewater, and their impacts on the environment and public health. That evaluation will include an analysis of the possible need to adapt the list of products to be covered by EPR and to revise the conditions for exemption from the EPR system (Article 9.2.a).

urban wastewater treatment (recast), OJ L, 2024/3019, 12.12.2024. 3 Feasibility of an EPR system for micro-pollutants- Final report (070201/2020/837586/SFRA/ENV.C.2), 2022: https://op.europa.eu/en/publication-detail/-/publication/14249cbc-5f1c-11ed-92ed-01aa75ed71a1/language-en. 4 Pistocchi et al., European scale assessment of the potential of ozonation and activated carbon treatment to reduce micropollutant emissions with wastewater, 2022: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0048969722042218?via%3Dihub#s0080. 5 Recital (21) of Directive (EU) 2024/3019.

E-10-2026-001467.t: Export of live animals to war zones
qt: to the Commission Lynn Boylan (The Left) Subject:

Haifa is the main entry point for livestock vessels arriving in Israel. Haifa is located in an area directly exposed to missile attacks. During the previous escalation, missile strikes occurred close to vessels unloading animals coming from the EU. Live animal exports have continued to Israel as conflict across the region escalates, endangering animals and workers. Article 3 of Council Regulation (EC) No 1/20051 requires that no animal be transported in a way likely to cause injury or undue suffering. Continuing exports to areas where hostilities are ongoing or likely to intensify is incompatible with this obligation.2 Will the Commission: 1.

call on the Member States to suspend the export of live animals to Israel and other destinations in the Middle East affected by the current hostilities until the security situation has stabilised and compliance with EU animal welfare rules can be effectively guaranteed?
closely monitor vessels that have already departed and ensure that contingency measures are in place to prevent animals from being left in unsafe conditions?
assess systemic shortcomings that allow exports to proceed despite clearly foreseeable risks?

Council Regulation (EC) No 1/2005 of 22 December 2004 on the protection of animals during transport and related operations and amending Directives 64/432/EEC and 93/119/EC and Regulation (EC) No 1255/97 (OJ L 3, 5.1.2005, p. 1, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2005/1/oj). Eurogroup for Animals wrote to the Commission on this issue on 5 March 2026 and has not received a response.

E-10-2026-001466.t: EU institutional reform: two-speed Europe, unanimity under threat, and the rise of hidden federalism
qt: to the Commission Tiago Moreira de Sá (PfE), Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE), Georgiana Teodorescu (ECR), Jaroslav Bžoch (PfE), Jaroslava Pokorná Jermanová (PfE), Dominik Tarczyński (ECR), Antonín Staněk (PfE), Mieke Andriese (PfE), Milan Uhrík (ESN), Diana Iovanovici Şoşoacă (NI), Irmhild Boßdorf (ESN), Ewa Zajączkowska-Hernik (PfE), Gerolf Annemans (PfE), Petr Bystron (ESN) Subject:

In current EU debates, leaders such as Ursula von der Leyen have promoted mechanisms such as enhanced cooperation and a ‘two-speed Europe’ to overcome institutional deadlocks rooted in the need for unanimity, enabling coalitions of ‘willing Member States’ to advance strategic economic and policy priorities. The Commission President has also called for the reactivation of the EU’s mutual defence clause under Article 42(7) of the Treaty on European Union, warning that the absence of effective majority decision-making undermines the EU’s responsiveness. These institutional reforms, also known as the ‘castle method’ and supported by figures such as EPP leader Manfred Weber, risk fostering a form of camouflaged federalism in which authority gradually shifts from national capitals to EU institutions under the banner of ‘strategic autonomy’. Therefore, we ask the Commission: 1.

How does the idea of differentiated integration (without unanimity) reconcile with the defence of national sovereignty and full compliance with the existing Treaties, without enabling supranational integration that undermines the authority of elected national governments?
How does the Commission justify diminishing the unanimity requirement (a key safeguard for Member State consent) in foreign and defence policy?

How does the Commission distinguish between genuine ‘strategic autonomy’ and an incremental shift toward supranational federalism that reduces national accountability and transfers decision-making power away from democratically elected national parliaments?
Supporter1
This question is supported by a Member other than the authors: Ondřej Dostál (NI).
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (23.7.2026) 1. The EU Treaties provide for European integration at different speeds. The Commission considers that the ambition should always be to reach agreement among all 27 Member States. However, where a lack of progress risks undermining Europe’s capacity to act, the EU should use fully the possibilities already foreseen in the Treaties. Examples range from enhanced cooperation to the inclusion of new Member States in the Permanent Structured Cooperation. 2. The Commission’s longstanding position is that, if the EU wants to act quickly, efficiently, and therefore strategically, unanimity voting ought to be reconsidered in certain policy areas, including on aspects of the Common Foreign and Security Policy (CFSP). To that end, the Treaties foresee the possible activation by the European Council of ‘passerelle clauses’ in key areas such as the CFSP. 3. The competences conferred on the EU are laid down in the EU Treaties, which have been ratified by all Member States in accordance with their respective constitutional requirements. These competences can only be changed through a reform of the EU Treaties, which would have to follow the ordinary revision procedure laid down in Article 48(2) to (5) of the Treaty on European Union. This procedure also includes the ratification by all Member States, in accordance with their respective constitutional requirements. Furthermore, national Parliaments play an active role in safeguarding the boundaries of EU competence through the mechanisms introduced by the Lisbon Treaty: under Protocol No. 2 on the Application of the Principles of Subsidiarity and Proportionality.

E-10-2026-001465.t: Delays in the operational deployment of helicopter emergency medical services (HEMS) for mountain rescue in Greece
qt: to the Commission Sakis Arnaoutoglou (S&D) Subject:

Greece is a country with rugged mountain terrain, a large number of remote areas and many islands. In recent years, serious accidents, including fatal incidents, have occurred in mountain areas and on islands, requiring rapid and specialised airborne intervention. These incidents demonstrate that swift access and adequate aerial coverage remain matters of life and death. Despite the adoption of a national plan for airborne rescue and medical evacuations, serious concerns remain regarding full operational deployment, the availability of resources, geographical coverage and the interoperability of the relevant services. In view of this, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

How does it assess the adequacy of preparedness and capacity for airborne mountain rescue in Greece, particularly in mountainous, remote and island areas, within the framework of the EU’s goals for prevention and preparedness in civil protection?
Which EU funding instruments, technical assistance or operational support mechanisms could be used to accelerate the full deployment of an effective and interoperable HEMS system in Greece?

Does the Commission intend to promote common European guidelines or minimum standards for airborne mountain rescue, particularly as regards readiness times, crew training and coordination between civil protection, health services and aviation assets?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (11.6.2026) Member States have the primary responsibility for civil protection and for providing disastermanagement systems, including response operations. The Commission has a supporting competence in the areas of prevention and preparedness. The Union Civil Protection Mechanism finances projects, deploys experts on request to assess the risks, provides advice and supports local or national authorities1. In this context, Greece didn’t request specific support from the Commission to address their Helicopter Emergency Medical Services system. The 2021–2027 Cohesion Policy cofinances the Greek programme ‘Civil Protection’2, with EUR 237 million signed for the procurement of six medium helicopters for firefighting operations and other missions, including aerial rescue and medical evacuations, as well as specialised medical equipment for patient transport (ambulance containment units). The programme has also allocated EUR 57.5 million to support dual-use equipment and systems, including for aeromedical evacuation. Moreover, under the Recovery and Resilience Facility, the Greek Recovery and Resilience plan includes the procurement of two medium utility helicopters for medical use, supporting emergency evacuation and crisis response. In accordance with the subsidiarity principle, the Commission has defined, together with Member States, operational standards for operational capacities which are registered in the European Civil Protection Pool3 but it does not intend to promote common European guidelines or minimum standards for airborne mountain rescue.

1 https://civil-protection-humanitarian-aid.ec.europa.eu/what/civil-protection_en. 2 https://civilprotection-program.gr/en/quot-civil-protection-quot-programme-2021-2027/. 3 https://civil-protection-humanitarian-aid.ec.europa.eu/what/civil-protection/european-civil-protection-pool_en.

E-10-2026-001464.t: Unequal treatment of EU citizens under Australia’s ETA and eVisitor systems
qt: to the Commission Matjaž Nemec (S&D) Subject:

Australia’s visitor visa programme is made up of three subclasses: the Electronic Travel Authority (ETA) (subclass 601), the eVisitor visa (subclass 651) and the Visitor visa (subclass 600). While all EU citizens are eligible to travel to Australia under the eVisitor scheme, which is generally considered part of a reciprocal visa-free arrangement, it is also the case that only a subset of EU Member State citizens are eligible to apply for ETA, while citizens from Bulgaria, Croatia, Cyprus, Czech Republic, Estonia, Hungary, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Romania, Slovakia and Slovenia are not. This differentiation results in a situation where EU citizens are not treated equally. While ETA and eVisitor are both electronic travel authorisations, they are not identical in practice, particularly with regard to processing, levels of automation and user experience. 1.
How does the Commission assess the current differentiation between EU Member States with access to the ETA system in the light of the EU’s objective of achieving full visa reciprocity?

Does the Commission consider that this differentiation constitutes unequal treatment of EU citizens and a potential breach of Regulation (EU) 2018/1806 as regards the revision of the suspension mechanism, and if so, has this issue been raised with the Australian authorities?
What concrete steps does the Commission plan to take to address the matter?
at: (English version) to the Commission Matjaž Nemec (S&D) (9 April 2026) Subject: Unequal treatment of EU citizens under Australia’s ETA and eVisitor systems Australia’s visitor visa programme is made up of three subclasses: the Electronic Travel Authority (ETA) (subclass 601), the eVisitor visa (subclass 651) and the Visitor visa (subclass 600). While all EU citizens are eligible to travel to Australia under the eVisitor scheme, which is generally considered part of a reciprocal visa-free arrangement, it is also the case that only a subset of EU Member State citizens are eligible to apply for ETA, while citizens from Bulgaria, Croatia, Cyprus, Czech Republic, Estonia, Hungary, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Romania, Slovakia and Slovenia are not. This differentiation results in a situation where EU citizens are not treated equally. While ETA and eVisitor are both electronic travel authorisations, they are not identical in practice, particularly with regard to processing, levels of automation and user experience. 1. How does the Commission assess the current differentiation between EU Member States with access to the ETA system in the light of the EU’s objective of achieving full visa reciprocity? 2. Does the Commission consider that this differentiation constitutes unequal treatment of EU citizens and a potential breach of Regulation (EU) 2018/1806 as regards the revision of the suspension mechanism, and if so, has this issue been raised with the Australian authorities? 3.
What concrete steps does the Commission plan to take to address the matter?

(12 June 2026) The Commission attaches particular importance to the reciprocal visa-free travel for all EU citizens: achieving and maintaining reciprocal visa-free travel is a principle of the EU's common visa policy and an objective pursued in a proactive manner in EU external relations, including with Australia. Regarding Australia, already in 2012 (1), the Commission noted that citizens of all Member States and Schengen associated countries are entitled to use the Australian electronic travel authorisations system called eVisitor in order to benefit from visafree travel. Therefore, the Commission considered that in principle, eVisitor provides equal treatment of the citizens of all Member States and Schengen associated countries, in line with the principle of visa reciprocity enshrined in Regulation (EU) 2018/1806 (2). The conclusions of this analysis remain relevant, therefore the Commission still considers that visa-waiver reciprocity is in place with Australia.

Report from the Commission to the European Parliament and the Council — Seventh report on certain third countries' maintenance of visa requirements in breach of the principle of reciprocity (COM/2012/0681 final). Regulation (EU) 2018/1806 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 November 2018 listing the third countries whose nationals must be in possession of visas when crossing the external borders and those whose nationals are exempt from that requirement.

E-10-2026-001463.t: Abusive practices by airlines in response to rising fuel prices caused by the conflict in the Middle East
qt: to the Commission Rosa Serrano Sierra (S&D), Laura Ballarín Cereza (S&D) Subject:

Against a backdrop dominated by the conflict in the Middle East and the resultant doubling of the price of aviation fuel in recent months, various airlines are announcing potential fare increases and the introduction of new surcharges to offset their rising operating costs. In this connection, and given the fact that some airlines are informing passengers at the time of purchase, or after booking in some cases, that the final ticket price may vary in the run-up to the flight depending on fluctuations in the cost of aviation fuel, can the Commission say: 1.

Whether it considers this practice of altering the final ticket price, and adding a surcharge once the ticket has already been bought and paid for, to be in breach of the rules governing air passenger rights, consumer protection and price transparency, which are binding on airlines?
If not, whether it plans to take measures to ensure legal certainty for passengers and prevent abusive practices that entail passing fuel price increases on to consumers?
Whether it intends to address this issue in the forthcoming review of Regulation (EC) No 1008/2008 on common rules for the operation of air services?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (5.6.2026) 1. The rules on transparent pricing of air tickets in Regulation (EC) No 1008/20081 require that the final ticket price must be displayed at all times when offering or publishing air fares to the general public. As this obligation applies explicitly to the final ticket price to be paid, any retroactive change of the price is excluded. Airlines may not include terms and conditions which would allow them to increase the price of the ticket above what is advertised at the time of purchase simply because fuel was more expensive than they had accounted for. 2. The Commission adopted on 8 May 2026 guidance2 on issues relating to aviation fuel in the context of current price increases and potential supply issues, to ensure legal certainty. In the first instance, it is for the price transparency authorities in the Member States to enforce the rules. 3. The Commission is looking at several issues relating to price transparency as part of the review of Regulation (EC) No 1008/2008.

1 Article 23 of Regulation (EC) No 1008/2008: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2008/1008/oj/eng. 2 https://transport.ec.europa.eu/news-events/news/commission-publishes-guidance-support-eu-transport-sector-
affected-middle-east-crisis-2026-05-08_en.

E-10-2026-001462.t: British Sovereign Base Areas in Cyprus and EU strategic autonomy
qt: to the Commission Geadis Geadi (ECR) Subject:

The continued presence of the British Sovereign Base Areas (SBAs) in Cyprus, following the United Kingdom’s withdrawal from the EU, constitutes a unique case of sovereign military territory of a non-EU country within an EU Member State. Rooted in a colonial-era arrangement, as affirmed by UK Supreme Court decisions and relevant UN resolutions, the status of the SBAs reflects enduring vestiges of colonialism. In the current geopolitical context, marked by increased instability in the EU’s neighbourhood, such arrangements raise legitimate concerns. The existence of military infrastructure operating outside the EU’s institutional and legal framework may have implications for the EU’s strategic autonomy, security architecture and ability to act coherently in external relations. In the light of the EU’s objective of ensuring stability, sovereignty and security: 1.
How does the Commission view the implications of the continued presence of the SBAs in Cyprus for the EU’s security architecture and strategic autonomy?
Does the Commission consider that arrangements of this nature warrant a structured dialogue with the relevant parties with a view to the eventual withdrawal of such military presences?

What steps, if any, does the Commission plan to take to ensure that such arrangements do not create vulnerabilities or undermine the EU’s capacity to act coherently in security and external relations?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (24.7.2026) Following the UK’s withdrawal from the EU, the Protocol relating to the UK Sovereign Base Areas (SBAs) in Cyprus included in the Withdrawal Agreement ensures that EU law, in the areas stipulated in Protocol No 3 on the SBAs1, continues to apply in the SBAs. However, the Protocol on the SBAs does not cover matters related to the EU security architecture and strategic autonomy, nor its security or external relations. The European Council of 19 March 2026 acknowledged the intention of Cyprus to initiate a discussion with the UK on the UK bases in Cyprus and expressed readiness to provide assistance as needed. The EU has a strategic interest in a stable and secure Eastern Mediterranean.
1 Protocol 3 on the Sovereign Base Areas of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland in
Cyprus annexed to the Act concerning the conditions of accession of the Republic of Cyprus.

qt: to the Commission Siegbert Frank Droese (ESN) Subject:

At a recent event co-organised by the Long-Distance Advisory Council and the European Economic and Social Committee entitled ‘How should the next generation of EU Sustainable Fisheries Partnership Agreements (SFPAs) look like? A multistakeholder perspective’, it was mentioned that many SFPAs are actually dormant. 1.

Is it true that a total of nine SFPAs (namely those concluded with Equatorial Guinea, Liberia, Micronesia, Morocco, Mozambique, Senegal, the Solomon Islands, Seychelles and The Gambia) are now dormant?

How would the Commission describe this state of ‘dormancy’, and can it confirm whether the EU fishing fleet has completely ceased fishing operations in the waters under the jurisdictions of each partner country?
What concrete measures is the Commission undertaking to reactive these SFPAs?
at: (English version) to the Commission Siegbert Frank Droese (ESN) (9 April 2026) Subject: Dormant sustainable fisheries partnership agreements At a recent event co-organised by the Long-Distance Advisory Council and the European Economic and Social Committee entitled ‘How should the next generation of EU Sustainable Fisheries Partnership Agreements (SFPAs) look like? A multistakeholder perspective’, it was mentioned that many SFPAs are actually dormant. 1. Is it true that a total of nine SFPAs (namely those concluded with Equatorial Guinea, Liberia, Micronesia, Morocco, Mozambique, Senegal, the Solomon Islands, Seychelles and The Gambia) are now dormant? 2. How would the Commission describe this state of ‘dormancy’, and can it confirm whether the EU fishing fleet has completely ceased fishing operations in the waters under the jurisdictions of each partner country? 3.
What concrete measures is the Commission undertaking to reactive these SFPAs?

(21 May 2026) The Commission confirms that the Sustainable Fisheries Partnership Agreements (SFPAs) with Equatorial Guinea, Liberia, Micronesia, Morocco (1), Mozambique, Senegal, the Solomon Islands, Seychelles, and The Gambia are currently dormant. The reasons behind dormant SFPAs vary. In some cases, it relates to the pre-identification or identification of SFPA partner countries as non-cooperating in fighting illegal, unreported, and unregulated (IUU) fishing (yellow or red cards ) (2). In other cases, it might reflect divergent objectives and interests. It can also be caused by delays in finalising the negotiations of the next protocol, despite best efforts by the EU negotiators to avoid interruption periods (3). The EU fishing fleet is bound to cease its fishing operations in the waters subject to dormant agreements in view of the exclusivity clause. Moreover, EU vessels cannot enter into private agreements with the partner country, even if the agreement becomes dormant. The Commission intends to address the issue of dormant agreements in the context of the upcoming new generation of SFPAs, which will be part of a broader strategy expected to be presented in autumn 2026, together with the Vision 2040 for fisheries and aquaculture. It aims to find the right balance between promoting ocean governance and giving the EU fleet the opportunity to compete fairly with third countries’ fleets.

On 20 January 2026, the Council adopted the decision authorising the opening of negotiations for the agreement and its implementing protocol. The Commission is actively preparing to initiate negotiations. Any new Agreement must comply with the judgment of the European Court of Justice Judgment of 4 October 2024 in Joined Cases C-778/21 P and C-798/21 P. Liberia, Senegal. The Seychelles is one such example.

E-10-2026-001460.t: Study: ‘Excises on Tobacco products in the EU’ (PE 772.646)
qt: to the Commission Siegbert Frank Droese (ESN) Subject:
Study: ‘Excises on Tobacco products in the EU’ (PE 772.646)

How does the Commission justify the high degree of alignment of national tobacco tax rates envisaged in the planned revision of the Tobacco Taxation Directive, in view of the principle of subsidiarity and Member States’ tax sovereignty?

How does the Commission assess the significant price increases resulting from the planned minimum tax rates – particularly in Member States with lower income levels – and their regressive effect on low-income households?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (9.7.2026) The proposal to revise the Tobacco Taxation Directive1 follows the Council conclusions of June 20202, which identified that the minimum rates should provide for further traction, secure long-term revenues, protect public health, and take into account the economic conditions of Member States. The objectives of the proposal cannot be sufficiently achieved by Member States alone and can therefore be better achieved at EU level. By focusing on those areas where cross-border issues are at stake, the proposal does not go beyond what is necessary to achieve those objectives. In line with the principle of subsidiarity set out in Article 5(3) of the Treaty on European Union3, Member States remain free to set rates for different tobacco products based on their national preferences, provided that they meet the EU minima. The analysis for the proposal followed Better Regulation principles and was based on comprehensive impact assessments and stakeholder consultations, ensuring evidence-based policymaking4. The proposed approach to determining the excise duty rates is partially based on purchasing power parities to ensure that increases in minimum taxes do not disproportionately affect low-tax Member States, while also addressing Member States where nominal tobacco prices are above the EU average but remain low in practice.
1 https://taxation-customs.ec.europa.eu/taxation/excise-duties/excise-duties-tobacco/revision-tobacco-taxation-
directive-proposal_en. 2 https://www.consilium.europa.eu/media/44235/st08483-en20.pdf. 3 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/treaty/teu_2016/art_5/oj/eng. 4 See footnote 1.

E-10-2026-001458.t: Threats to media freedom in Poland: concerns over the establishment of the new TV channel Newsmax Polska
qt: to the Commission Łukasz Kohut (PPE), Krzysztof Brejza (PPE) Subject:

According to media reports, a non-EU entity is set to launch the television channel Newsmax Polska in Poland. The Serbian public company Telekom Srbija is overseeing the process as a co-owner. Notably, the media has highlighted that the Serbian company was previously cofinanced by the Russian bank Sberbank. Media freedom in Serbia has further deteriorated, as evidenced by its fall to 98th place in Reporters Without Borders’ 2024 World Press Freedom Index. Reports adopted by Parliament indicate that Serbia must improve media diversity and pluralism, and highlight numerous concerns regarding media freedom in the country. 1.

Given that media freedom and pluralism are enshrined in the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union and that legal tools are available under the European Media Freedom Act, what actions will the Commission take to prevent Russian interference in Member States?
Will the Commission monitor the situation and take action if media freedom is threatened?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (23.6.2026) The freedom and pluralism of the media are enshrined in Article 11 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, and the Commission is committed to ensuring its respect within the remit of its competences. In the context of Russia’s illegal war of aggression against Ukraine, the EU has imposed restrictive measures (sanctions) on Russian media outlets because of their role in supporting and justifying this war of aggression and disseminating Russian disinformation. Currently, 32 media outlets are subject to a broadcasting ban and have had their EU broadcasting licenses suspended, having been included in Annex XV to Regulation (EU) 833/20141 and Annex IX to Decision 2014/512/CFSP2. It is therefore prohibited to disseminate any content from these media outlets in the EU. The implementation and enforcement of EU sanctions are primarily the responsibility of the Member States. In its role as guardian of the Treaties, the Commission oversees the implementation and enforcement of EU sanctions across Member States. Moreover, the European Media Freedom Act3 allows for swift and efficient coordination of actions against rogue non-EU media service providers presenting risks to public security, entrusted to EU media regulators, gathered in the European Board for Media Services4. The Commission also continues to monitor specific developments regarding media independence and pluralism in the Member States and in four enlargement countries5 as part of the Rule of Law Report.
1 Council Regulation (EU) No 833/2014 of 31 July 2014 concerning restrictive measures in view of Russia's

actions destabilising the situation in Ukraine, OJ L 229, 31.7.2014, pp. 1–11. 2 Council Decision 2014/512/CFSP of 31 July 2014 concerning restrictive measures in view of Russia's actions destabilising the situation in Ukraine, OJ L 229, 31.7.2014, pp. 13–17. 3 Regulation (EU) 2024/1083 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 11 April 2024 establishing a common framework for media services in the internal market and amending Directive 2010/13/EU (European Media Freedom Act), OJ L, 2024/1083, 17.4.2024. 4 Article 17 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1083. 5 Montenegro, Albania, North Macedonia and Serbia.

E-10-2026-001455.t: Escalation of violence against the Christian minority in Syria and urgent need for action by the European Union
qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Elena Kountoura (The Left), Konstantinos Arvanitis (The Left) Subject:

In recent days, serious incidents of violence have been recorded against the Greek Orthodox Christian population in the city of Suqaylabiyah in central Syria.1 These events add to a long list of violent attacks targeting the country’s Christian minority2 allegedly carried out with the tolerance or even guidance of forces close to/subject to the Syrian regime. Considering that Christians are a historical, integral part of Syria’s multicultural society and deserve special protection, and that the European Parliament has called on ‘the Syrian authorities to ensure the protection and fundamental rights of all ethnic and religious communities, including Christians’ and underlines that ‘any cooperation with the Syrian authorities must be conditional on tangible and verifiable progress in the protection of civilians, respect for the ceasefire, human rights and minority rights’:3 1.

Does the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy intend to take concrete diplomatic initiatives to protect religious minorities in Syria and prevent similar attacks in the future?
Does she intend to propose a review of the Union's stance on imposing sanctions against the Syrian interim government, in light of the ongoing human rights violations?

Is she committed to ensuring that all forms of humanitarian financial support are subject to strict conditionality, linked to the effective protection of all religious and ethnic minorities, as requested by the European Parliament?

According to audio-visual material circulated on the internet, armed individuals are seen attacking the city, destroying property and carrying out widespread looting. The incidents of violence include, among others, attacks on schools, churches and public and private spaces. A typical example is the bombing last June at the Orthodox Church of the Prophet Elijah in Damascus, with dozens of victims and injuries. See resolutions of 12 February 2026 on the situation in Northeast Syria, the violence against civilians and the need to maintain a sustainable ceasefire (2026/2602(RSP)) and of 10 July 2025 on the urgent need to protect religious minorities in Syria following the recent terrorist attack on Mar Elias Church in Damascus (2025/2798(RSP)).
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (15.6.2026) Since the historic shift in the country in December 2024, the EU has actively supported Syria’s transition, emphasising that lasting peace requires an inclusive process reflecting the aspirations of Syrians from all ethnic and religious backgrounds without discrimination as reiterated in the European Council conclusions of 18 December 20251. In this context, the EU recognises the important role of Syria’s diverse communities, including its Christian population, in shaping an inclusive future for the country. The EU demands full investigations and accountability for reported incidents, stressing these as essential for national reconciliation in its discussions with Syria’s transitional authorities. During their Syria visit, the European Council and Commission Presidents announced a new EU-Syria Political Partnership to support the transition, reconciliation and economic recovery. On 11 May 2026, the EU held its first High-Level Political Dialogue with Syria in Brussels, where, inter alia, the need to ensure a genuinely inclusive process for sustainable reconciliation and restoring Syria’s rich social fabric was underscored. The Commission pledged EUR 620 million for 2026 and 2027 for humanitarian aid, early recovery, and bilateral support, ensuring assistance reaches all Syrian communities. EU humanitarian aid is channelled only through pre-certified humanitarian partners, based on needs and humanitarian principles. The EU’s support follows strict implementation parameters and extensive monitoring, including third party monitoring and risk assessments. The EU remains committed to human rights and accountability, regardless of perpetrators’ affiliations. In 2025, the EU introduced new listings for human rights violations and actions fuelling instability in Syria in the post-Assad era.
1 https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/press/press-releases/2025/12/18/european-council-conclusions-on-the-
middle-east-european-defence-and-security-next-mff-enlargement-and-reforms-migration-and-other-items/.

E-10-2026-001454.t: Hydropower project threatening biodiversity goes ahead despite local opposition and warnings from experts
qt: to the Commission Ana Miranda Paz (Verts/ALE) Subject:

Despite opposition from local residents and various social groups, the Galician Government is going ahead with the construction of a pumped-storage hydroelectric power plant on the Tambre River. The plant will affect the municipalities of Brión, Negreira, Lousame and Rois. The campaign group ‘Non á Balsa Cornanda-Tambre’ denounces that, despite the area being saturated with wind farms, the project seeks only private profit and does not take into account the general interest or the future of Galicia’s rural areas. Building the new plant would involve 36 farms being destroyed (48 % of the land affected), three cubic hectometres of earth being moved and a 35-hectare reservoir being built only 198 metres away from people’s homes – with the risk that entails, not to mention the foreseeable environmental impact on fauna, changes to the microclimate and the project’s proximity to protected Natura 2000 areas. As a member of the Committee on Petitions, I brought this case before the European Parliament on the basis that the project breaches EU directives such as the Aarhus Convention (lack of transparency and public participation) and the EU Habitats Directive. 1.
Is the Commission aware of the project, which violates the Habitats Directive and the Aarhus Convention?
What does it intend to do in the face of another instance of the right to participation being violated and EU directives being breached?
at: (English version) to the Commission Ana Miranda Paz (Verts/ALE) (9 April 2026) Subject: Hydropower project threatening biodiversity goes ahead despite local opposition and warnings from experts Despite opposition from local residents and various social groups, the Galician Government is going ahead with the construction of a pumped-storage hydroelectric power plant on the Tambre River. The plant will affect the municipalities of Brión, Negreira, Lousame and Rois. The campaign group ‘Non á Balsa Cornanda-Tambre’ denounces that, despite the area being saturated with wind farms, the project seeks only private profit and does not take into account the general interest or the future of Galicia’s rural areas. Building the new plant would involve 36 farms being destroyed (48% of the land affected), three cubic hectometres of earth being moved and a 35-hectare reservoir being built only 198 metres away from people’s homes — with the risk that entails, not to mention the foreseeable environmental impact on fauna, changes to the microclimate and the project’s proximity to protected Natura 2000 areas. As a member of the Committee on Petitions, I brought this case before the European Parliament on the basis that the project breaches EU directives such as the Aarhus Convention (lack of transparency and public participation) and the EU Habitats Directive. 1.
Is the Commission aware of the project, which violates the Habitats Directive and the Aarhus Convention?

2. What does it intend to do in the face of another instance of the right to participation being violated and EU directives being breached? (6 July 2026) The Commission does not possess information on the project in question, nor evidence indicating that the competent authorities have infringed EU law. Article 6(3) of the Habitats Directive (1) requires Member States to subject any plan or project likely to have a significant effect on a Natura 2000 site to an appropriate assessment of their implications for the site. A project can only be authorised after having ascertained that it will not adversely affect the integrity of the site concerned, or exceptionally under conditions specified in Article 6(4). Installations for hydroelectric energy production (2) fall within the scope of the Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) Directive (3), which implements the Aarhus Convention (4) requirements in relation to the projects it covers. The directive ensures that the public is informed early in the decision-making process and has the right to express opinions that must be taken into account by the competent authority. Moreover, the EIA Directive specifically requires that review procedures be available at national level allowing the members of the public to challenge the legality of the decisions, acts or omissions of the competent authority. The Commission therefore considers that the available national remedies constitute the most appropriate mechanism for the public concerned to exercise their rights and, where appropriate, seek compensation for any damages caused. This avenue is furthermore consistent with the Commission strategic approach to its enforcement policy, focused on systemic issues of non-compliance (5).

Council Directive 92/43/EEC of 21 May 1992 on the conservation of natural habitats and of wild fauna and flora. OJ L 206, 22.7.1992, pp. 7-50. The project in question may also fall under Point 15 of Annex I to the directive if it involves ‘Dams and other installations designed for the holding back or permanent storage of water, where a new or additional amount of water held back or stored exceeds 10 million cubic metres’.
