E-10-2026-001453.t: PDO feta undermined through non-EU trade agreements tolerated by the EU
qt: to the Commission Konstantinos Arvanitis (The Left) Subject:

‘Feta’ has been registered as a PDO in the EU since 2002. The Court of Justice of the European Union ruled that Member States must prevent the use of the name ‘feta’ even for exports to non-EU countries (C-159/20). At the same time, the US systematically promotes, through trade agreements (e.g. with Indonesia, Argentina or Bangladesh), ‘common name’ clauses that recognise ‘feta’ as a ‘generic term’, directly undermining the European PDO system and creating unfair competition to the detriment of Greek producers, cooperatives and consumers. Given this dual pressure, the Commission’s inaction amounts to the political acceptance of the downgrading of European Geographical Indications. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

In which non-EU countries, with which the EU negotiates or has made agreements, has legally binding protection for the PDO ‘feta’ been secured, and what is the timeline for its entry into force and implementation in each country?
How does it assess the compatibility or otherwise of such ‘common name’ clauses with commitments vis-à-vis the EU, and what specific measures will it take and by what deadline?
Will it commit to ensuring that the full protection of the ‘feta’ PDO constitutes a nonnegotiable ‘red line’ in all future agreements?

The Court of Justice of the European Union ruled that Member States must prevent the use of the name ‘feta’ even for exports to non-EU countries (C-159/20). Given this dual pressure, the Commission’s inaction amounts to the political acceptance of the downgrading of European Geographical Indications. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

How does it assess the compatibility or otherwise of such ‘common name’ clauses with commitments vis-à-vis the EU, and what specific measures will it take and by what deadline?
Will it commit to ensuring that the full protection of the ‘feta’ PDO constitutes a non-negotiable ‘red line’ in all future agreements?

(8 June 2026) The protection of EU geographical indications (GIs) for agri-food products in the markets of third countries has been — and remains — a clear priority of the EU trade agenda. The Commission is actively working towards strengthening the protection and enforcement of GI rights both at bilateral and multilateral levels. To date the EU has secured protection for the GI ‘Feta’ in 24 trade agreements (1), including those with New Zealand, Canada, Chile, China, Mercosur or the Republic of Korea. The Commission has also recently completed negotiations on the protection of ‘Feta’ with countries such as Indonesia and Australia. The timing of the entry into force of these agreements will depend on the procedures for signature and conclusion. The Commission is looking into ways to streamline procedural steps to support an expeditious entry into force of these bilateral trade agreements. The Commission expects all trading partners to respect their international obligations and is carefully analysing international developments and negotiations by third countries that may impact the protection of EU GIs. Its actions are — and will continue to be — adapted to the specific contexts.
Protection granted in the agreements, full list available through the GI-view database: https://www.tmdn.org/giview/gi/EUGI00000013179.

E-10-2026-001452.t: Customs checks at European ports and terminals operated or partly owned by Chinese operators, and the risk of under-invoicing goods entering the EU
qt: to the Commission Paolo Inselvini (ECR), Daniele Polato (ECR), Francesco Torselli (ECR) Subject:

Various studies and reports by customs authorities, OLAF1 and the Commission2 have highlighted instances of under-invoicing and inaccurate declarations of the value and quantity of goods imported into the European Union, particularly goods from third countries entering via major European logistics ports. Such practices can lead to the avoidance of customs duties and VAT on imports to the tune of several billion euros annually, with direct ramifications for the EU’s own resources and competition in the internal market. Given that some major European container terminals and pieces of port infrastructure are managed or part-owned by non-EU operators, including groups controlled by the Chinese state, we must ensure that checks of documents and customs requirements, as well as risk analyses on goods are uniform, rigorous throughout the logistics chain, and cannot be circumvented. Can the Commission therefore say: 1.
Whether it has up-to-date estimates of the losses in customs revenue caused by underinvoicing of goods entering the EU?
Whether it considers the customs checks systems3 and risk analyses4 at Europe’s principal ports, including at terminals managed by non-EU operators, to sufficiently uniform and rigorous?
Whether it intends to shore up customs controls and anti-fraud systems to prevent the avoidance of duties and VAT on containerised imports?

OLAF (European Anti-Fraud Office) annual reports on the protection of the European Union’s financial interests and the fight against fraud, European Commission, various editions (in particular 2017–2023, which highlight cases of under-invoicing fraud in imports, with significant impact on the EU’s own resources). European Commission, annual reports on the protection of the EU’s financial interests (‘PIF’ reports): data on customs and import VAT fraud and losses amounting to billions of euros. Special Report No 19/2017 of the Court of Auditors – ‘Import procedures: shortcomings in the legal framework and an ineffective implementation impact the financial interests of the EU. Regulation (EU) No 952/2013 of the European Parliament and of the Council laying down the Union Customs Code. This includes requirements for customs checks and risk management.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (8.6.2026) The Commission does not possess estimates of losses in customs revenues caused specifically by under-invoicing. Under the Union Customs Code1, customs controls are carried out by Member States’ customs authorities on the basis of risk analysis. The Commission has developed common risk criteria and standards, including for financial risks, which Member States implement in their risk-analysis systems. Under the common risk management framework, customs authorities also exchange risk information and risk-analysis results. These measures contribute to a more harmonised application of customs controls across the EU and to an equivalent level of protection, irrespective of the ports’ commercial set-up. The Commission also supports more adequate and equivalent controls through an EU funding programme supporting the purchase of customs control equipment2. Member States already use customs data and intelligence to target consignments at risk. The agreed EU Customs Reform of 26 March 20263 will further strengthen this data-driven approach through the future EU Customs Data Hub and EU Customs Authority, enhancing the EU-wide use of data analytics for risk analysis and the effectiveness of controls, thereby helping to protect the EU’s financial interests. Recent judgments4 of the Court of Justice have also clarified the legal framework for addressing undervaluation, thereby supporting the European Anti-Fraud Office and national authorities in this area.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2013/952/oj/eng. 2 https://taxation-customs.ec.europa.eu/about-us/eu-funding-customs-and-tax/customs-control-equipment-

instrument_en. 3 https://taxation-customs.ec.europa.eu/customs/eu-customs-reform_en, https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/press/press-releases/2026/03/26/eu-customs-council-and-parliament-agreeon-landmark-reform/. 4 Judgment of 29 January 2026, HF and WI v Anexartiti Archi Dimosion Esodon, Joined Cases C-72/24 and C73/24, EU:C:2026:51.

E-10-2026-001451.t: Impact of the EES on professional drivers from Bosnia and Herzegovina
qt: to the Commission Delara Burkhardt (S&D), Tineke Strik (Verts/ALE) Subject:

Since October 2025, the EU’s Entry/Exit System (EES) has been applied at land borders between the Schengen area and Bosnia and Herzegovina. It records the entry and exit of nonEU nationals staying up to 90 days within any 180-day period and applies to visa-free travellers, including professional drivers from the Western Balkans. Transport operators warn that the strict 90-day rule may hinder regular cross-border transport. Reports already indicate delays of up to two to three hours at some crossings, and professional drivers have announced possible coordinated regional blockades if no solution is found. Given that over 60 % of the region’s trade is with the EU, disruptions could affect supply chains, economic cooperation and the free movement of goods, which are key elements of EU accession. In this context: 1.
How does the Commission view the impact of the EES on professional drivers from Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Western Balkans?
What progress has been made on transitional arrangements or specific solutions for professional drivers?
How is the Commission addressing delays and the risk of disruptions, including potential blockades?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (12.6.2026) The entry into operation of the Entry/Exit System (EES) has marked a significant milestone for the Schengen area with a positive impact on the security of the EU, including by systematically detecting overstayers. The roll-out of the EES has not changed the rules for the length of stay in the Schengen area, but it has strengthened their enforcement. The Commission notes the concerns raised by freight transport operators from the countries neighbouring the EU and has engaged with stakeholders to clarify the legal framework and the functioning of the EES. Member States may, under their national legislation, issue long-stay visa or residence permits to professional drivers. The Commission remains engaged with relevant partner countries and Member States to exchange information and best practices. Moreover, the Commission has started discussing with Member States, as recently announced in the Visa Strategy1, solutions for professionals requiring a high degree of mobility within the Schengen area, such as a possible EU extended short-stay permit. The EES legal framework provides Member States with targeted flexibility to address situations of excessive waiting times, including the possibility to temporarily suspend the collection of biometric data. This mechanism remains available until September 2026 and has been designed to support Member States during periods of high passenger flows.
1 https://ec.europa.eu/transparency/documents-register/detail?ref=COM(2026)43&lang=en.

E-10-2026-001450.t: Financial crisis of Bosnia and Herzegovina’s public broadcaster BHRT and implications for media freedom
qt: to the Commission Delara Burkhardt (S&D), Tineke Strik (Verts/ALE) Subject:

Bosnia and Herzegovina’s state-level public broadcaster, Radio-Television of Bosnia and Herzegovina (BHRT), is facing a severe financial crisis that is threatening its operation. BHRT reportedly carries debts of around EUR 51 million, including EUR 11.5 million owed to the European Broadcasting Union. There is a risk that its bank accounts may be blocked, potentially leading to the suspension of broadcasting and salary payments. The situation has worsened due to disputes over licence fee revenues. Reports indicate that the broadcaster in Republika Srpska, Radio-Television of Republika Srpska, has withheld contributions, further undermining BHRT’s financial sustainability. A pluralistic and independent media system is a cornerstone of freedom of expression and a prerequisite for the rule of law and the protection of fundamental rights, which are essential for EU accession. In this context: 1.

How does the Commission view the risks to media pluralism and Bosnia and Herzegovina’s alignment with EU accession requirements, and what steps is it taking under the enlargement policy to address financing shortcomings?
Is the Commission considering additional measures within the enlargement framework to support sustainable and independent public service media?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.6.2026) The Commission shares the Honourable Members’ concerns regarding the financial situation of Bosnia and Herzegovina’s state-level public broadcaster Radio-Television of Bosnia and Herzegovina (BHRT), and its implications for media pluralism. A stable and independent public broadcasting system is essential for freedom of expression, democratic accountability and the rule of law, which are core elements of the accession process. The current situation highlights persistent shortcomings in the governance and financing model of the public broadcasting system, which the Commission has consistently called on the authorities to address as a matter of urgency. Ensuring the political independence and sustainable financing of BHRT is one of the key priorities identified in the Commission’s opinion of 2019 on the country’s application for EU membership1 and reiterated subsequently in the annual Enlargement Package2 and accompanying country reports3, including in 2025. It is also a commitment which the authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina took as part of the country’s Reform Agenda under the Growth Plan. The Commission will continue to monitor developments in this area and raise this issue in our interactions with the authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina, including through our policy dialogue.
1 https://enlargement.ec.europa.eu/system/files/2019-05/20190529-bosnia-and-herzegovina-opinion.pdf. 2 https://enlargement.ec.europa.eu/document/download/eb69a890-40d6-4696-801e-

612d51709fdd_en?filename=2025%20Communication%20on%20EU%20Enlargement%20Policy.pdf. 3 https://enlargement.ec.europa.eu/document/download/5d8fc547-f8f8-456f-84e3b38998acfafd_en?filename=bosnia-and-herzegovina-report-2025.pdf.

E-10-2026-001449.t: Practical measures relating to sanctions against individuals
qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Per Clausen (The Left) Subject:

With regard to EU sanctions against individuals in the EU who do not have the wealth and opportunities of oligarchs, concerns have been raised about how, in practical terms, the individuals concerned are supposed to pay for essentials (from food and nappies to medicine and rent) for themselves and their spouses or children, as they cannot work or access their savings. This issue raises a number of humanitarian issues that are still unclear. With this in mind, could the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy please explain what specific approaches and measures are being taken in this regard, and answer the following questions: 1.

How can individuals who are EU nationals or permanent residents of an EU country, and who are subject to sanctions, continue to be able to pay for the essentials that they need to survive, including food, medicine and a roof over their head?

How can we ensure that sanctions on individuals with dependent family members (spouses and children) residing permanently in an EU country do not unduly penalise those family members, while maintaining the primary idea behind the sanctions?
How many EU citizens and permanent residents of an EU country are currently subject to EU sanctions, and for how long have they been subject to those sanctions?
at: (English version) to the Vice-President of the Commission/High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Per Clausen (The Left) (9 April 2026) Subject: Practical measures relating to sanctions against individuals With regard to EU sanctions against individuals in the EU who do not have the wealth and opportunities of oligarchs, concerns have been raised about how, in practical terms, the individuals concerned are supposed to pay for essentials (from food and nappies to medicine and rent) for themselves and their spouses or children, as they cannot work or access their savings. This issue raises a number of humanitarian issues that are still unclear. With this in mind, could the Vice-President of the Commission/High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy please explain what specific approaches and measures are being taken in this regard, and answer the following questions: 1.

How can individuals who are EU nationals or permanent residents of an EU country, and who are subject to sanctions, continue to be able to pay for the essentials that they need to survive, including food, medicine and a roof over their head?

How can we ensure that sanctions on individuals with dependent family members (spouses and children) residing permanently in an EU country do not unduly penalise those family members, while maintaining the primary idea behind the sanctions?
How many EU citizens and permanent residents of an EU country are currently subject to EU sanctions, and for how long have they been subject to those sanctions?

(15 June 2026) Restrictive measures (sanctions) serve as one of the EU’s foreign policy instruments designed to address global challenges and crises, such as human rights violations, infringements of international law, or threats to peace and security. The EU’s restrictive measures are targeted, proportionate, temporary in nature, and of non-punitive character. The Commission is committed to mitigating any unforeseen humanitarian implications of EU restrictive measures and to ensuring that they are implemented in a manner that respects the fundamental rights of individuals and their dependents. All EU sanctions regimes include derogations for listed individuals and their dependent family members to cover basic needs such as food, medicine, rent or mortgage payments, and other essential living costs. Individuals facing difficulties, including designated EU nationals or permanent residents, may request derogations from the competent national authorities of relevant Member States to cover such necessary expenses. While Member States are responsible for the implementation and enforcement of EU restrictive measures, the Commission monitors the application of these derogations to help ensure consistency across the EU. To enhance transparency, the Commission provides the EU Sanctions Tracker tool, offering a comprehensive overview of current individual listings under EU restrictive measures (1). The tool allows for public scrutiny of designations, which remain temporary and subject to periodic review by the Council of the EU. Over 4 000 individuals are currently subject to EU restrictive measures. Out of these, only a few have the nationality of a Member State or are permanent residents of a Member State.
https://data.europa.eu/apps/eusanctionstracker/.

E-10-2026-001448.t: EU fuel prices and possible distortions of competition in the petroleum products market
qt: to the Commission Paolo Inselvini (ECR) Subject:

In recent weeks, a number of Member States have experienced a surge in fuel retail prices, which in some cases appears to be more pronounced than the rise in international crude oil prices. Data published in the Commission’s weekly Oil Bulletin, together with the ARA (Amsterdam-Rotterdam-Antwerp) refined product benchmarks, point to a non-linear passthrough of Brent oil price changes throughout the refining and distribution chain at times. The EU fuel market is subject to the competition rules laid down in Articles 101 and 102 TFEU, and to the energy market monitoring framework provided for in Regulation (EU) No 1227/2011 (REMIT), aimed at preventing market manipulation and abuse of information. Consequently, any asymmetrical price transmission or abnormal margins could create distortions that harm consumers and businesses. In view of the above: 1.
Does the Commission have up-to-date analyses of how margins have evolved throughout the oil supply chain and the extent to which current prices are consistent with global benchmarks?

Does it believe that it would be appropriate to launch checks or investigations, including through the EU Agency for the Cooperation of Energy Regulators and the national competition authorities, to identify any speculation or anti-competitive practices?
What measures will it take to increase transparency and price monitoring throughout the fuel supply chain in the EU?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (12.6.2026) The Commission tracks energy prices and produces a weekly Oil Bulletin and considers other market analysis such as product specific imbalances and refining capacities and constraints. Under the Regulation on Wholesale Energy Market Integrity and Transparency (REMIT)1 national authorities are responsible for enforcement against market abusive behaviour as regards wholesale energy products in electricity, natural gas and hydrogen. REMIT does not cover mineral oil markets. The Commission and national competition authorities may initiate a competition investigation where there are indications of either anti-competitive agreements (Article 101 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU)) or abuse of a dominant position (Article 102 TFEU) affecting trade between Member States. While atypical pricing may merit examination, a disparity between input costs and retail prices alone is not as such and taken in isolation, indicative of a potential breach of EU competition rules. However, certain national practices in pricing fuel may breach other EU rules. Against this background, the Commission launched, on 29 April 2026, infringement proceedings against Hungary and Slovakia for the introduction of measures discriminating between EU citizens when fuelling vehicles2. As a result, Slovakia has since lifted the discriminatory fuel measures. The Commission will continue monitoring the evolution of the crisis and assessing its potential impacts. To address the impacts of the disruption of oil and gas transit, the Commission put forward on 22 April 2026 its new initiative AccelerateEU3, proposing timely, targeted and temporary measures to bring relief to consumers, while avoiding fragmented national responses.
1 http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2011/1227/oj. 2 Infringement procedure INFR(2026)4008 against Hungary and INFR(2026)4009 against Slovakia:
https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/inf_26_720. 3 https://energy.ec.europa.eu/publications/accelerateeu-energy-union-affordable-and-secure-energy-throughaccelerated-action_en.

E-10-2026-001447.t: Repression of human rights advocates and politically motivated prosecutions in Vietnam
qt: to the Commission Nicolas Bay (ECR), Stephen Nikola Bartulica (ECR), Geadis Geadi (ECR), Patryk Jaki (ECR), Afroditi Latinopoulou (PfE), Sebastian Tynkkynen (ECR) Subject:

In Vietnam, the Communist Party is responsible for serious violations of fundamental rights, vigorously suppressing freedom of expression and severely punishing opponents who challenge the party’s monopoly on power, including by means of imprisonment or extraterritorial abductions. However, Article 1 of the Framework Agreement on Comprehensive Partnership and Cooperation (PCA) between the European Union and Vietnam states that respecting human rights constitutes an ‘essential element’ of the agreement. Additionally, Chapter 13 of the Free Trade Agreement between the European Union and the Socialist Republic of Vietnam (EVFTA) includes an obligation for the parties to implement international fundamental rights standards and to refrain from weakening their protection for commercial reasons. Lastly, in the event of a serious violation of an essential element of the agreement, Article 57 of the PCA allows for the adoption of appropriate measures, up to and including a suspension of the EVFTA. In light of the above: 1.
What action does the Commission intend to take to ensure that Vietnam complies with its human rights obligations?
Does it plan to use the EU Global Human Rights Sanctions Regime to target those identified as responsible for extraterritorial abductions?

Does it intend to activate the mechanisms provided for in the PCA, including suspending the EVFTA, on the grounds that respect for human rights constitutes an essential element of bilateral relations?
at: (English version) to the Commission Nicolas Bay (ECR), Stephen Nikola Bartulica (ECR), Geadis Geadi (ECR), Patryk Jaki (ECR), Afroditi Latinopoulou (PfE), Sebastian Tynkkynen (ECR) (9 April 2026) Subject: Repression of human rights advocates and politically motivated prosecutions in Vietnam In Vietnam, the Communist Party is responsible for serious violations of fundamental rights, vigorously suppressing freedom of expression and severely punishing opponents who challenge the party’s monopoly on power, including by means of imprisonment or extraterritorial abductions. However, Article 1 of the framework Agreement on Comprehensive Partnership and Cooperation (PCA) between the European Union and Vietnam states that respecting human rights constitutes an ‘essential element’ of the agreement. Additionally, Chapter 13 of the Free Trade Agreement between the European Union and the Socialist Republic of Vietnam (EVFTA) includes an obligation for the parties to implement international fundamental rights standards and to refrain from weakening their protection for commercial reasons. Lastly, in the event of a serious violation of an essential element of the agreement, Article 57 of the PCA allows for the adoption of appropriate measures, up to and including a suspension of the EVFTA. In light of the above: 1.
What action does the Commission intend to take to ensure that Vietnam complies with its human rights obligations?
Does it plan to use the EU Global Human Rights Sanctions Regime to target those identified as responsible for extraterritorial abductions?

Does it intend to activate the mechanisms provided for in the PCA, including suspending the EVFTA, on the grounds that respect for human rights constitutes an essential element of bilateral relations?

(10 July 2026) The Commission shares the European Parliament's concern about human rights violations in Viet Nam. The upgrade of EUViet Nam relations to a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership (1) in January 2026 reaffirms the importance of addressing these concerns. The EU remains committed to promoting human rights in Viet Nam through the partnership and cooperation agreement (PCA) (2) while the EU-Viet Nam Free Trade Agreement (EVFTA) (3) contributes specifically through its provisions on labour and environmental standards. The EU engages with Vietnamese authorities through high-level dialogues, including the annual EU-Viet Nam Human Rights Dialogue. The recent Domestic Advisory Group meeting under the EVFTA also discussed labour standards and broader human rights concerns (4). The EU continues to monitor progress towards International Labour Organisation Convention 87 ratification, urging Viet Nam to fulfil its commitments. The EU takes its commitments under the PCA and EVFTA seriously, and will consider the mechanisms provided therein, where necessary. The EU advocates at every opportunity, publicly and privately, for the release of political prisoners, protection of human rights defenders, and promotion of fundamental freedoms. The EU will continue to engage with Vietnamese authorities, civil society, and international partners to ensure human rights remain central to the bilateral relationship.

E-10-2026-001446.t: Structural shortcomings in food safety regarding Ukrainian animal products
qt: to the Commission Sander Smit (ECR) Subject:

Frequent RASFF food safety alerts and periodic reporting in agri-food fraud reports (AAC/FFN) point to structural shortcomings in Ukraine’s compliance with EU food safety regulations. In the second half of 2025 alone, there were seven reports regarding antibiotic residues in eggs. Earlier in 2025 and 2024, there were cases of salmonella contamination that could be traced back to Ukrainian eggs. 1.
What is the Commission’s assessment of the seven RASFF notifications regarding prohibited veterinary medicines in Ukrainian animal products in the second half of 2025?

Does the Commission intend, within the framework of the EU Task Force on Food Safety Import Controls announced in December 2025, to increase the frequency of physical food safety inspections of Ukrainian animal products and, where necessary, to temporarily suspend imports?
Does the Commission see any reason to reconsider the listing of Ukraine in Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2598 pursuant to Article 127(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.6.2026) Following notifications concerning the presence of residues of prohibited products in consignments of imported Ukrainian eggs, Ukraine has been responsive to the reported problems and has provided detailed information on these incidents which is published in the RASFF1 system. The Commission takes these findings very seriously and continues to closely monitor the situation. Under Article 5(3) of Regulation (EU) 2019/21292, the Commission increases the minimum frequency rates of physical checks for specific categories of goods from third countries where the level of non-compliance exceeds by 30% the average rate of non-compliance for the same category of goods from all third countries. At present, no category of goods from Ukraine faces increased frequency of checks due to non-compliance exceeding the 30% threshold. In 2025-26, intensified official controls (IOC) were triggered five times in accordance with Regulation 2019/18733 on Ukrainian eggs, milk and dairy products due to detection of illegal antimicrobials. These led to 61 reinforced controls, with one non-compliant case on nitrofurans in eggs. Third countries are listed in Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/25984 on the basis of guarantees that, in accordance with Article 118(1) of Regulation (EU) 2019/6 of the European Parliament and of the Council5, no antimicrobials for growth promotion or reserved for treating certain human infections6 have been used for animals and products of animal origin exported to the EU. The non-compliant findings concerning antibiotic residues fall outside the scope of Implementing Regulation 2024/2598. Therefore, Ukraine’s inclusion on the list under Implementing Regulation 2024/2598 remains valid for egg exports.
1 Rapid Alert System for Food and Feed - https://webgate.ec.europa.eu/rasff-window/screen/search. 2 Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/2129 of 25 November 2019 establishing rules for the

uniform application of frequency rates for identity checks and physical checks on certain consignments of animals and goods entering the Union (OJ L 321, 12.12.2019, pp. 122) ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg_impl/2019/2129/oj. 3 Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1873 of 7 November 2019 on the procedures at border control posts for a coordinated performance by competent authorities of intensified official controls on products of animal origin, germinal products, animal by-products and composite products (OJ L 289, 8.11.2019, pp. 50) ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg_impl/2019/1873/oj. 4 Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2598 of 4 October 2024 laying down the list of third countries or regions thereof authorised for the entry into the Union of certain animals and products of animal origin intended for human consumption in accordance with Regulation (EU) 2017/625 of the European Parliament and of the Council as regards the application of the prohibition on the use of certain antimicrobial medicinal products (OJ L, 2024/2598, 7.10.2024), ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg_impl/2024/2598/oj. 5 Regulation (EU) 2019/6 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 11 December 2018 on veterinary medicinal products and repealing Directive 2001/82/EC (OJ L 4, 7.1.2019, pp. 43, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2019/6/oj). 6 Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/1255 of 19 July 2022 designating antimicrobials or groups of antimicrobials reserved for treatment of certain infections in humans, in accordance with Regulation (EU) 2019/6 of the European Parliament and of the Council (OJ L 191, 20.7.2022, pp. 58), ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg_impl/2022/1255/oj.

E-10-2026-001445.t: Chinese chicken on European plates despite damning report
qt: to the Commission Sander Smit (ECR) Subject:

Audit CT-2025-0037, completed in November 2025 and published on 12 February 2026, found that Chinese slaughterhouses did not comply with food safety standards: carcasses with visible faecal contamination were simply rinsed, whereas under EU standards, the meat should have been disposed of immediately. Traceability requirements were found to be so poorly enforced that it could not be determined whether the poultry meat originated from one of the designated production sites. In the three months between the completion and publication of the report, exports to the EU appear to have continued unabated, under a certification system that the Commission had already deemed unreliable at that time. 1.

Why did the Commission not immediately suspend imports pursuant to Article 128 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, and why does the Commission consider the food safety risks associated with the identified deficiencies to be acceptable?

How many tons of Chinese poultry meat entered the EU between the audit and the publication of its findings, and can the Commission provide consumers with information on the Member States, the importers, and the products in which the meat ended up?
On what date did the Commission inform the Member States – in particular the Netherlands as one of the main importing countries – of the findings, and what specific measures were taken in response?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.6.2026) During the audit in China in November 2025 on poultry meat products1, significant deficiencies were identified and addressed with the authorities in a closure meeting. The audit team emphasised concerns about the safety of poultry meat products, particularly in the event of inadequate corrective measures. These concerns were reiterated in follow-up communications, alongside an urgent request to the Chinese authorities for taking prompt remedial actions to key recommendations. The risk of delisting China for these exports was also underscored should the required improvements fail to materialise within the stipulated timeframe. Whilst the Commission maintains a zero-tolerance policy toward food safety risks, the risk management procedure considered several mitigating factors. Under the current EU rules, imports of fresh poultry meat from China are not allowed2. In addition, all poultry meat products from China must be sterilised, except for poultry meat products from the province of Shandong, for which a less severe risk-mitigation treatment3 suffices. The relatively low incidence of RASFF4 notifications pertaining to imports of Chinese poultry meat products further informed the Commission’s evaluation of the risks. In response to the audit findings, China submitted a thorough action plan, detailing both immediate measures and long-term initiatives to address the shortcomings. The Commission assessed it as satisfactory, contingent upon its timely, effective, and rigorous implementation. To ensure compliance, a follow-up audit will be conducted in China in 2026. In 2025, Member States imported 73 000 tonnes of poultry meat products from China. They were informed via the publication of the audit report on 19 February 20265.

1 https://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/audit-report/details/4968. 2 http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg_impl/2021/404/oj. 3 E.g.: minimum core temperature of 70°C. 4 Rapid Alert System for Food and Feed. 5 China CT-2025-0037 - Food Audits and Analysis: https://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/audit-
report/details/4968.

E-10-2026-001444.t: Impact of the Omnibus I simplification package on requesting sustainability information from companies and business partners
qt: to the Commission Catarina Vieira (Verts/ALE) Subject:

Concerns have been raised that the ‘value chain cap’ in the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive omnibus (limiting what sustainability information companies can request from suppliers) may have a chilling effect on the sharing of information between business partners and hinder meaningful due diligence under the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive. In practice, companies request information for different purposes simultaneously. The risk is that this cap will lead to the information gathered being divided into separate categories that are subject to different rules, forcing companies to rely excessively on lawyers. Effective supplier engagement requires clarity on: (1) whether there are strict limits on what companies can ask their suppliers, and if so, what the consequences are for exceeding those limits; (2) whether information gathered through due diligence work or an impact assessment on human rights can be reported later; (3) whether it is possible, through contracting, to request information (for reporting or due diligence) beyond the voluntary sustainability reporting standard. The lack of clarity on these matters and the implications of this for due diligence may discourage companies from engaging in meaningful dialogue with business partners or conducting impact assessments on human rights. How quickly can the Commission provide clarity and thus prevent the consequences of a lack of clarity from arising?
at: (English version) to the Commission Catarina Vieira (Verts/ALE) (9 April 2026) Subject: Impact of the Omnibus I simplification package on requesting sustainability information from companies and business partners Concerns have been raised that the ‘value chain cap’ in the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive omnibus (limiting what sustainability information companies can request from suppliers) may have a chilling effect on the sharing of information between business partners and hinder meaningful due diligence under the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive. In practice, companies request information for different purposes simultaneously. The risk is that this cap will lead to the information gathered being divided into separate categories that are subject to different rules, forcing companies to rely excessively on lawyers. Effective supplier engagement requires clarity on: (1)
whether there are strict limits on what companies can ask their suppliers, and if so, what the consequences are for exceeding those limits;
whether information gathered through due diligence work or an impact assessment on human rights can be reported later;
whether it is possible, through contracting, to request information (for reporting or due diligence) beyond the voluntary sustainability reporting standard.

The lack of clarity on these matters and the implications of this for due diligence may discourage companies from engaging in meaningful dialogue with business partners or conducting impact assessments on human rights. How quickly can the Commission provide clarity and thus prevent the consequences of a lack of clarity from arising? (17 June 2026) The Omnibus I Directive (1) has introduced a new value chain cap regime for the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) (2). For the purposes of reporting sustainability information under the CSRD, the cap prohibits companies from requiring companies in their value chains with 1000 employees or less to provide information beyond the voluntary sustainability reporting standard. It nevertheless allows companies to request information beyond that standard, under certain conditions, including that they clearly indicate which requested information goes beyond. The legal text explicitly states that nothing in the CSRD’s new provisions ‘affects information requests for purposes other than the purpose of sustainability reporting as required by this directive, including requests for the purpose of complying with EU requirements on undertakings to conduct a due diligence process’. The Omnibus I Directive also aims to limit unnecessary requests for information from business partners under the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD) (3), but does not link this limitation to the CSRD’s value chain cap. Neither the CSRD’s value-chain cap, nor the CSDDD’s constraints prevent a company from including in its public reporting information it collected from its value chain partners. The Commission will consider the possible need for further clarifications of the CSRD provisions agreed by co-legislators depending on demand from stakeholders and any issues arising from the practical experience of implementation, and will issue guidelines for CSDDD, including on the identification process.

Directive (EU) 2026/470 amending Directives 2006/43/EC, 2013/34/EU, (EU) 2022/2464 and (EU) 2024/1760 as regards certain corporate sustainability reporting requirements and certain corporate sustainability due diligence requirements, OJ L, 2026/470, 26.2.2026. E-10-2026-001443.t: Increase cohesion funds for households and businesses
qt: to the Commission Georgios Aftias (PPE) Subject:

The continuation of the war in the Middle East is causing oil, gas and electricity prices to skyrocket. Day after day, these prices are taking a toll on households and businesses – particularly in Greece and the other southern European countries – owing to the failure to complete the electricity interconnection. As a result, they are facing objective difficulties, as most of their disposable income goes towards energy costs. With this in mind, and in view of the prolonged conflict in the Middle East, can the Commission say: 1.
Will it provide additional cohesion fund grants to small and medium-sized enterprises, which have been hit hard by high electricity costs?
Will it take immediate financial measures to support households, which are facing an unreasonable burden?
at: (English version) to the Commission Georgios Aftias (PPE) (9 April 2026) Subject: Increase cohesion funds for households and businesses The continuation of the war in the Middle East is causing oil, gas and electricity prices to skyrocket. Day after day, these prices are taking a toll on households and businesses — particularly in Greece and the other southern European countries — owing to the failure to complete the electricity interconnection. As a result, they are facing objective difficulties, as most of their disposable income goes towards energy costs. With this in mind, and in view of the prolonged conflict in the Middle East, can the Commission say: 1.

Will it take immediate financial measures to support households, which are facing an unreasonable burden?

(22 May 2026) The Commission prioritises tackling high energy costs. The Member States select specific projects in line with the shared management rules. The Commission incentivised the Member States under the mid-term review of the cohesion policy fund s (1) to invest more into connectivity, competitiveness as well as affordable and sustainable housing, offering greater flexibility and incentives such as increased pre-financing, higher maximum co-financing rates or extended decommitment and eligibility periods. The AccelerateEU (2) communication addresses EU’s rising energy costs on volatile fossil fuel markets and aims to accelerate the clean energy transition and strengthen energy resilience. Its core objectives are to provide immediate relief to consumers and businesses to reduce the EU’s dependence on imported fossil fuels. For households facing high energy costs, immediate financial support should be targeted, temporary and fiscally sustainable, focusing on vulnerable consumers and those most exposed to energy poverty. Primary responsibility for such support lies with Member States, while EU-level initiatives such as the Affordable Energy Action Plan (3), the Citizens Energy Package (4) and AccelerateEU (5) support complementary measures to lower energy costs, empower consumers and reduce exposure to volatile fossil fuel prices. Among the immediate actions under the communication (6), the Commission will draft a dedicated investment chapter to support and enable Member States to make full use of available EU funding and, where feasible, reallocate EU funds towards energy-related investments with the potential to alleviate the effects of rising energy prices.

E-10-2026-001441.t: The Commission is promoting Ukraine’s accession as a stabilising factor for the EU’s eastern border regions while ignoring key risks
qt: to the Commission Irmhild Boßdorf (ESN) Subject:

The Commission communication of 18 February 20261 on the EU’s eastern regions bordering Russia, Belarus and Ukraine points to a deterioration of the security environment, a reallocation of resources to defence, a standstill in cross-border activities (trade, transport, etc.) eastwards, slower GDP growth, higher inflation and strong demographic pressures compared to the EU as a whole. According to the Commission, along with a package of measures including billions of euros in investment, Ukraine’s expected future accession should ‘contribute to the stabilisation and strengthening of the EU regions along this border. However, this amounts to little more than irresponsible utopian thinking, particularly since it completely fails to mention the risks associated with Ukraine’s accession – such as the deep-rooted corruption, the failure to meet the Copenhagen criteria, or the fact that Ukraine remains embroiled in an ongoing war whose outcome is uncertain. Such an accession would expose the EU to a significant security risk, which could further destabilise the EU’s eastern border regions in particular. 1.

How does the Commission justify its questionable prediction that Ukraine’s accession will contribute to the ‘stabilisation and strengthening’ of the eastern border regions of the EU, and why are significant risks, in particular security risks, being ignored?

How does the Commission justify allocating EUR 1.36 billion to regions bordering Ukraine to strengthen integration and connectivity given that a peace deal might potentially provide for a neutral status, thus making the projected accession impossible?
https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:52026DC0082.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (16.6.2026) The EU’s accession process is merit based, and progress depends on each candidate country’s reform progress, including Ukraine. Enlargement will strengthen the EU by extending high Schengen standards to a larger number of countries, pushing strong external border control outwards, enabling more effective migration management, and wider cooperation on internal security. Enhanced and effective law enforcement cooperation in cross-border operations is indispensable to maintaining internal security. This means gradually integrating enlargement countries in the EU-wide law enforcement ecosystem and information exchange mechanisms. Regions along the EU’s eastern border stand to gain from accession of candidate neighbouring countries through increased trade, investment, infrastructure development and enhanced cooperation in security. Trade, institutional cooperation and people-to-people contacts between Ukrainian border regions and EU border regions are significant and expected to grow with Ukraine’s potential accession. EU programs, including support to cross-border infrastructure and energy and transport networks, will further strengthen economic and social resilience. Under the Connecting Europe Facility, EUR 1.36 billion were allocated to facilitate traffic flows at the EU external borders. The investments take primarily place on the territory of the EU’s Member States while strengthening cross-border connectivity with Ukraine.

E-10-2026-001440.t: Protecting European farmers and stockbreeders from the effects of the war in the Middle East
qt: to the Commission Galato Alexandraki (ECR) Subject:

The escalation of the war in the Middle East and disruptions in maritime transport are already affecting the cost of fuel, energy and agricultural inputs in the EU, as acknowledged by DG AGRI itself. At the same time, the Commission has pointed out that the EU depends on imports for 30 %, 68 % and 85 % of its consumption of inorganic nitrogen, phosphates and potash nutrients respectively, while natural gas can account for up to 90 % of the variable production cost of nitrogen fertilisers. Furthermore, the European Council stressed on 19 March 2026 that the conflict was having a direct impact on energy prices and supply chains. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

Does it intend to immediately mobilise the CAP’s agricultural reserve, which amounts to EUR 450 million per year, and other exceptional support tools to compensate for increased energy, fuel, fertiliser, feed and transport costs?
Will it allow Member States additional flexibility to provide targeted support for farmers, stockbreeders, cooperatives and processing companies in the agri-food chain?
at: (English version) to the Commission Galato Alexandraki (ECR) (9 April 2026) Subject: Protecting European farmers and stockbreeders from the effects of the war in the Middle East The escalation of the war in the Middle East and disruptions in maritime transport are already affecting the cost of fuel, energy and agricultural inputs in the EU, as acknowledged by DG AGRI itself. (22 June 2026) With the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, the Commission is working on multiple fronts to ease pressure and support farmers and operators. First, on 29 April 2026 the Commission adopted a temporary framework for state aid (1) to support the most exposed sectors, including agriculture. Additionally, duty free tariff rate quotas (2) for ammonia, urea and other nitrogen fertilisers from countries other than Russia and Belarus, have been adopted for a period of one year until 31 May 2027. Secondly, on 22 April 2026 the Commission adopted AccelerateEU (3), a communication proposing measures to achieve a more resilient EU energy system in the medium and long term, through inter alia greater coordination between Member States, support to Member States and accelerating the shift to domestic clean energy. The communication includes measures that will directly benefit EU consumers and businesses, including farmers. Furthermore, on 19 May 2026, the Commission adopted the Fertiliser Action Plan (4), which includes both short-term and longterm structural measures, aiming to reduce import dependency, boost domestic production and provide targeted support to farmers, while remaining aligned with the EU’s climate and environmental objectives. One of the short-term actions proposed in the Plan is the mobilisation and top-up of the agricultural reserve to provide fast relief to farmers. The Commission is closely monitoring the situation and will consider, if needed, additional support for farmers.

E-10-2026-001439.t: Full dismantling and recycling of offshore wind farms in Greece
qt: to the Commission Galato Alexandraki (ECR) Subject:

Greece has already established a specific framework for offshore wind farms, while the revised national energy and climate plan envisages 1.9 GW of offshore wind capacity by 2030 and the draft national offshore wind farm development plan envisages 25 marine areas with a total area of 2.712 km² and an estimated minimum capacity of 12.4 GW. However, bearing in mind that these installations have a finite life cycle, it remains unclear whether there are binding guarantees in place to uniformly ensure that the full dismantling, recycling or recovery of their materials and related costs will be the responsibility of the operators themselves. EU law already lays down obligations for the prevention and management of waste and the ‘polluter pays’ principle, for achieving good environmental status of marine waters, as well as for the environmental assessment of plans and projects. Can the Commission answer the following: 1.

Does it consider that the current EU framework is sufficient to enable Member States such as Greece to require the full dismantling of offshore wind farms, without the partial abandonment of foundations, moorings, or other infrastructure on the seabed?

Does it intend to propose binding EU rules on the recycling or recovery of blades and other composite materials, as well as mandatory financial guarantees so that end-of-life costs are not passed on to taxpayers?
at: (English version) to the Commission Galato Alexandraki (ECR) (9 April 2026) Subject: Full dismantling and recycling of offshore wind farms in Greece Greece has already established a specific framework for offshore wind farms, while the revised national energy and climate plan envisages 1.9 GW of offshore wind capacity by 2030 and the draft national offshore wind farm development plan envisages 25 marine areas with a total area of 2.712 km2 and an estimated minimum capacity of 12.4 GW. However, bearing in mind that these installations have a finite life cycle, it remains unclear whether there are binding guarantees in place to uniformly ensure that the full dismantling, recycling or recovery of their materials and related costs will be the responsibility of the operators themselves. EU law already lays down obligations for the prevention and management of waste and the ‘polluter pays’ principle, for achieving good environmental status of marine waters, as well as for the environmental assessment of plans and projects. Can the Commission answer the following: 1.

Does it consider that the current EU framework is sufficient to enable Member States such as Greece to require the full dismantling of offshore wind farms, without the partial abandonment of foundations, moorings, or other infrastructure on the seabed?

Does it intend to propose binding EU rules on the recycling or recovery of blades and other composite materials, as well as mandatory financial guarantees so that end-of-life costs are not passed on to taxpayers?

(6 July 2026) The EU acquis empowers Member States to shape decommissioning requirements for offshore infrastructure. The Net Zero Industry Act (1) allows setting higher thresholds for environmental sustainability and innovation criteria that can encompass site decommissioning obligations. The Renewable Energy Directive (2) includes procedures for repowering existing installations, which facilitate the continued use of established sites and reduce pressure to designate new ones. The Waste Framework Directive (3) (WFD) requires waste to be managed without endangering human health and harming the environment. In particular, Article 13 requires Member States to take necessary measures to manage waste without risk to water, air, soil, plants or animals. The Commission is evaluating possible aspects related to circularity which may be relevant to wind turbines in the impact assessment for the Circular Economy Act (4) planned for adoption later in 2026. Moreover, the Marine Strategy Framework Directive (MSFD) (5) requires Member States to ensure that human activities, including decommissioning, do not adversely affect the good environmental status of marine waters. Partial removal of offshore wind turbine foundations must be assessed against the directive’s requirements, inter alia relating to biodiversity, seafloor integrity, marine litter, energy and noise, to avoid any permanent harm to ecosystems. During assessment, planning or licensing procedures for renewable energy installations, Member States should take account of all EU environmental law (6). Without prejudice to the Commission’s role as guardian of the Treaties, Member States are primarily responsible to ensure that their obligations under EU law, including the WFD and the MSFD, are met.

qt: to the Commission Alice Teodorescu Måwe (PPE), Céline Imart (PPE), Assita Kanko (ECR), Antonio López-Istúriz White (PPE), Andrey Kovatchev (PPE) Subject:

In the early hours of 9 March 2026, an explosion occurred at the synagogue in Liège. Although windows were shattered, fortunately no victims were reported. A few hours after the explosion, a video circulated in which responsibility for the attack was claimed by a terrorist group called Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiyya. Three days later, a synagogue was set on fire in Rotterdam. Shortly afterwards, a video was released showing the same modus operandi used by the perpetrators of the Liège synagogue bombing. The following night, another explosion targeting a Jewish school took place in Amsterdam. Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiyya claimed responsibility for this third attack, as well as for an arson attack in the Jewish quarter of Antwerp on 24 March 2026. While intelligence services are still investigating these incidents, there are indications that the attacks may be linked to the regime in Tehran. In this context: 1.
Does the Commission intend to allocate additional funds for the protection of Jewish communities?
What role is the Commission playing in investigating the nature and activities of the organisation responsible for these attacks?
What measures does the Commission plan to take under its new internal security strategy to better counter terrorism?
at: (English version) to the Commission Alice Teodorescu Måwe (PPE), Céline Imart (PPE), Assita Kanko (ECR), Antonio López-Istúriz White (PPE), Andrey Kovatchev (PPE) (9 April 2026) Subject: Recent antisemitic incidents In the early hours of 9 March 2026, an explosion occurred at the synagogue in Liège. Although windows were shattered, fortunately no victims were reported. A few hours after the explosion, a video circulated in which responsibility for the attack was claimed by a terrorist group called Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiyya. Three days later, a synagogue was set on fire in Rotterdam. Shortly afterwards, a video was released showing the same modus operandi used by the perpetrators of the Liège synagogue bombing. The following night, another explosion targeting a Jewish school took place in Amsterdam. Harakat Ashab al-Yamin alIslamiyya claimed responsibility for this third attack, as well as for an arson attack in the Jewish quarter of Antwerp on 24 March 2026. While intelligence services are still investigating these incidents, there are indications that the attacks may be linked to the regime in Tehran. In this context: 1.
Does the Commission intend to allocate additional funds for the protection of Jewish communities?
What role is the Commission playing in investigating the nature and activities of the organisation responsible for these attacks?
What measures does the Commission plan to take under its new internal security strategy to better counter terrorism?

(19 June 2026) The Commission condemns in the strongest terms the recent attacks against Jewish communities across Europe. These heinous acts strike at European values and the European way of life. The Commission led an international coalition of antisemitism envoys calling for a coordinated and sustained effort across governments, civil society, and partners and underlining that all governments must ensure the security of Jews on their territory (1). The Commission allocated EUR 5 million specifically to the protection of Jewish places of worship under the Internal Security Fund Protect call, part of a EUR 30 million package (2). The Commission would like to continue to strengthen this support under the proposed tripling of home affairs funding in the 2028-2034 Multiannual Financial Framework. The Commission is monitoring the impact of the conflict in the Middle East on the terrorist threat in the EU, notably against Jewish communities and is in contact with Member States on additional security measures that can be taken. It is the competence of Member States to investigate terrorist and extremist attacks. The EU Agency for Law Enforcement Cooperation (Europol) supports Member States’ investigations. The ProtectEU Agenda to prevent and counter terrorism (3) sets out the EU's collective response to evolving terrorist threats and reaffirms that protecting all faith communities from hatred and violence is a core European commitment.

E-10-2026-001437.t: Alleged forced labour at the BYD construction site in Szeged (Hungary)
qt: to the Commission Raphaël Glucksmann (S&D), Kathleen Van Brempt (S&D), Klára Dobrev (S&D) Subject:

According to an investigation published on 31 March 2026 by The World (PRX), the NGO China Labor Watch interviewed 50 Chinese migrant workers at the BYD factory construction site in Szeged, Hungary. Workers reportedly faced seven-day working weeks, 14-hour days, non-payment of overtime, the withholding of 20–30 % of their wages, and recruitment fees constituting debt bondage. A local labour authority investigation is reportedly under way. These allegations follow findings by Brazil’s Ministry of Labour and Employment of similar violations at a BYD construction site in Camaçari, where investigators accused the company and its contractors of trafficking migrant workers into conditions analogous to slavery. 1.
Is the Commission aware of these allegations, and what action has it taken to date?

Does it have information on other cases within the EU where non-EU companies have imported workers from their country of origin and exercise coercive control over them? Has the European Labour Authority been involved or offered support in this case or in similar cases?
What measures does the Commission intend to take to investigate the alleged violations in Szeged and prevent such practices across the EU?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.5.2026) The co-legislators have adopted legislation inter alia to strengthen the enforcement of fundamental rights in supply chains, in particular the Forced Labour Regulation1 and the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive2. The Commission is working on their implementation to ensure that level playing field and fundamental rights are respected throughout supply chains. The Commission is aware of the allegations on labour rights violations at the BYD factory construction site in Szeged, Hungary. According to the Commission’s information, there is a case pending before the Hungarian Labour Inspectorate related to the allegations. The Hungarian Labour Inspectorate is the competent authority to investigate this matter. The Commission does not interfere in cases pending before the competent national authorities. The Commission informed the European Labour Authority (ELA) of the concerns in Hungary’s electric vehicle supply chain. ELA invited the Hungarian authorities to examine the matter offering ELA’s support, given ELA does not have investigative powers.
1 Regulation (EU) 2024/3015 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 November 2024 on

qt: to the Commission Gerald Hauser (PfE) Subject:

Food Chain Reaction was a simulation exercise on global food security that took place in Washington DC on 9 and 10 November 2015. It brought together around 65 international decision-makers, experts from the world of politics, business and academia, and multilateral institutions to explore how the world could respond to a hypothetical global food crisis. The simulation presented a scenario for the years 2020 to 2030 where factors such as population growth, urbanisation, extreme weather events, political conflicts and supply chain disruptions led to large fluctuations in food production and food prices. Participants had to develop policies and strategies and work together in teams – representing the US, the EU, China, Brazil, India, Africa, multinational institutions, private companies etc. – to address these crises. 1.

In the aforementioned simulation exercise, who represented and played the role of the EU?

(26 May 2026) The Commission acknowledges the importance of ensuring food supply and food security for European citizens at all times. Against this background the European Food Security Crisis preparedness and response Mechanism (EFSCM) has been established in 2021, bringing together all national and public key players of the food supply chain. A series of initiatives including a mapping of risks and vulnerabilities and the adoption of recommendations, have been implemented since then to improve the level of preparedness. This is being complemented by a wider preparedness framework including the Preparedness Union and the EU Stockpiling Strategies and by the recognition of production, processing and distribution of food as a vital societal function (1). In 2024, the Commission, through the EFSCM, participated in a Food Alert crisis simulation exercis e (2), organised by a consortium of partners to stress test the EU food system. In July 2025 (3), the EFSCM together with the Joint Research Centre, dedicated a full day workshop to the development of a methodology for stress testing the food sector and recently published an ‘Operational Framework for Stress Testing EU Food Security’ (4). Regarding the exercise mentioned by the Honourable Member, it was a privately organised exercise without representation of the Commission.

E-10-2026-001435.t: Transparency of EU humanitarian funding to the West Bank, Gaza and Lebanon
qt: to the Commission Bert-Jan Ruissen (ECR), Rihards Kols (ECR), Tomáš Kubín (PfE), Matej Tonin (PPE), Mieke Andriese (PfE), Fernand Kartheiser (NI), Alice Teodorescu Måwe (PPE), Tomáš Zdechovský (PPE), Geadis Geadi (ECR), Veronika Vrecionová (ECR), Ondřej Krutílek (ECR), Dick Erixon (ECR), Charlie Weimers (ECR), Beatrice Timgren (ECR), Elena Donazzan (ECR), Adrian-George Axinia (ECR), Jorge Martín Frías (PfE), Sebastian Tynkkynen (ECR), Antonio López-Istúriz White (PPE), Alexandr Vondra (ECR), François-Xavier Bellamy (PPE), Sander Smit (ECR) Subject:

On 16 March 2026, the Commission announced its provision of EUR 458 million in humanitarian assistance for the Middle East in 2026, including EUR 124 million committed to the West Bank and Gaza and EUR 100 million to Lebanon. Humanitarian assistance in these areas is delivered in highly complex environments. In Gaza, the de facto authorities are Hamas, while in large parts of southern Lebanon the armed group Hezbollah exercises significant influence. Given the risks of diversion in conflict environments, transparency regarding the channels and mechanisms through which EU funds are distributed is essential. 1.

Regarding the EUR 224 million allocated to the West Bank, Gaza and Lebanon, could the Commission specify the UN agencies and non-governmental organisations involved and the amount committed to each, including the local implementing partner organisations?
How much of these sums will be disbursed through cash-based assistance programmes, vouchers and/or direct transfers and could the Commission provide details on beneficiary lists and recommendations?

What monitoring, auditing and anti-diversion safeguards are in place, in addition to the EU restrictive measures list (which includes few Hamas and Hezbollah members), to ensure that EU funds do not directly or indirectly benefit Hamas, Hezbollah or affiliated entities?
at: (English version) to the Commission Bert-Jan Ruissen (ECR), Rihards Kols (ECR), Tomáš Kubín (PfE), Matej Tonin (PPE), Mieke Andriese (PfE), Fernand Kartheiser (NI), Alice Teodorescu Måwe (PPE), Tomáš Zdechovský (PPE), Geadis Geadi (ECR), Veronika Vrecionová (ECR), Ondřej Krutílek (ECR), Dick Erixon (ECR), Charlie Weimers (ECR), Beatrice Timgren (ECR), Elena Donazzan (ECR), Adrian-George Axinia (ECR), Jorge Martín Frías (PfE), Sebastian Tynkkynen (ECR), Antonio López-Istúriz White (PPE), Alexandr Vondra (ECR), François-Xavier Bellamy (PPE), Sander Smit (ECR) (8 April 2026) Subject: Transparency of EU humanitarian funding to the West Bank, Gaza and Lebanon On 16 March 2026, the Commission announced its provision of EUR 458 million in humanitarian assistance for the Middle East in 2026, including EUR 124 million committed to the West Bank and Gaza and EUR 100 million to Lebanon. Humanitarian assistance in these areas is delivered in highly complex environments. In Gaza, the de facto authorities are Hamas, while in large parts of southern Lebanon the armed group Hezbollah exercises significant influence. Given the risks of diversion in conflict environments, transparency regarding the channels and mechanisms through which EU funds are distributed is essential. 1. Regarding the EUR 224 million allocated to the West Bank, Gaza and Lebanon, could the Commission specify the UN agencies and non-governmental organisations involved and the amount committed to each, including the local implementing partner organisations? 2. How much of these sums will be disbursed through cash-based assistance programmes, vouchers and/or direct transfers and could the Commission provide details on beneficiary lists and recommendations? 3. What monitoring, auditing and anti-diversion safeguards are in place, in addition to the EU restrictive measures list (which includes few Hamas and Hezbollah members), to ensure that EU funds do not directly or indirectly benefit Hamas, Hezbollah or affiliated entities? (5 June 2026) The Commission is contracting the funds announced on 16 March 2026, and therefore unable to give a list of selected humanitarian partners and the amount to be disbursed through cash-based assistance. The Commission is steadfast in its commitment to supporting humanitarian aid delivery that is principled and needs based. For this reason, it also supports the UN-led humanitarian coordination system to ensure all humanitarian efforts remain guided by international humanitarian law and humanitarian principles. The compliance with the Commission policy on cash assistance (1) is verified before selecting humanitarian partners to implement cash-based assistance programmes. The Commission is very much aware of the complex operational context in which EU-funded entities operate in the occupied Palestinian territory and Lebanon. This is why robust safeguards are in place, covering pre-funding due diligence and risk assessments (ex-ante checks), implementation monitoring, and post-funding oversight and controls (ex-post verification). Humanitarian partners are thoroughly assessed on their capacity to observe basic principles and obligations, including respect of the relevant EU, international and national laws, as well as compliance with transparency, accountability and internal controls. The Commission only works with pre-approved and certified humanitarian partners (2). Under Regulation (EU) 2024/2509 (3) laying down the financial rules applicable to the general budget of the Union, and in accordance with Article 138 thereof, the Commission applies strict safeguards to ensure that any person or entity involved in criminal activity, including terrorist financing and terrorist offences, is excluded from EU funding.

E-10-2026-001433.t: Contingency framework for public support in the steel sector
qt: to the Commission Bruno Tobback (S&D), Kathleen Van Brempt (S&D) Subject:

Many European steel producers benefit from substantial support measures, at national and European level. In the first six months of 2025, subsidies for Europe’s steel industry have grown by EUR 500 million, to reach a total of EUR 15.1 billion. For example, for its Dunkirk site, ArcelorMittal received public subsidies of almost EUR 1 billion. Thyssenkrupp received around EUR 2 billion from the German government for its tkH2Steel-project. At EU level, the steel and metals action plan outlines support measures for the steel sector, such as the strengthened EU-steel-trade measures. Despite this, only a few projects have materialised, according to the sector, due to low steel prices, high energy costs and insufficient demand for low-carbon steel. Some companies benefiting from public support have already reduced, and are expected to further reduce, their presence in Europe. ArcelorMittal plans to offshore 5 600 European jobs across 20 countries, potentially leading to thousands more indirect job losses. How will the Commission ensure: 1.
sufficient capacity for EU low carbon steel production, safeguarding the EU’s strategic independence, and which concrete additional measures will be proposed?
that public support for steel producing companies is tied to investments in local employment and decarbonisation?
the introduction of claw-back procedures if companies that received public support offshore activities and cut European jobs, and where and how would such procedures be applied?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (15.6.2026) The Commission has implemented policies to support the decarbonisation and competitiveness of the European steel, namely the Clean Industrial Deal1 and the Steel and Metals Action Plan2. In addition to financial support under the Innovation Fund3, Just Transition Fund (JTF)4, inter alia, the proposal for an Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA)5 proposes mandatory requirements to use a minimum share of low-carbon steel in automotive and construction, in public procurement and support schemes. This will be complemented by the trade measure replacing the steel safeguards, to ensure the industry’s long-term viability. The Commission ensures that public support is linked to investments in decarbonisation by conditioning State aid approval to greenhouse gas emissions reductions criteria. Furthermore, the Clean Industrial Deal State Aid Framework (CISAF)6 allows Member States to include requirements related to social protection or employment conditions when designing the measure. The JTF supports investments in the steel sector, when necessary for the protection of jobs. Moreover, the legal basis for Cohesion Policy funds establishes common rules for the durability of supported operations. The legal basis for the Commission’s State aid control does not allow to make an aid measure dependent on conditions, such as claw-back of aid procedures where the beneficiaries offshore activities and cut European jobs. Under the CISAF, public support can incentivise the aid beneficiary to realise the investment in the European Economic Area (EEA) rather than in the alternative location outside the EEA (funding gap).

E-10-2026-001432.t: De facto mandatory nature of the codes of conduct on disinformation and hate speech
qt: to the Commission Tom Vandendriessche (PfE), Fabrice Leggeri (PfE), Mireia Borrás Pabón (PfE), Kinga Gál (PfE), Ernő Schaller-Baross (PfE), Mary Khan (ESN), Roman Haider (PfE), Branko Grims (PPE), Friedrich Pürner (NI), Sebastian Tynkkynen (ECR), Fernand Kartheiser (NI), Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE), András László (PfE), Jorge Martín Frías (PfE), Jana Nagyová (PfE), Hermann Tertsch (PfE), Milan Uhrík (ESN), Mieke Andriese (PfE), Markus Buchheit (ESN), Elisabeth Dieringer (PfE), Petr Bystron (ESN), Catherine Griset (PfE), Marieke Ehlers (PfE), Barbara Bonte (PfE) Subject:

Internal company emails released to the US House Judiciary Committee reveal that major platforms perceived participation in the Code of Practice on Disinformation and the Code of Conduct on Hate Speech as ‘effectively mandatory’, with agendas ‘set under strong impetus from the EU Commission’ and ‘consensus’ achieved under heavy regulatory pressure, especially once the Digital Services Act (DSA) was in sight. 1.

How does the Commission reconcile its public claim that these codes are purely voluntary self-regulatory instruments with the reality that companies understood nonparticipation as exposing them to heightened enforcement risks and future DSA sanctions of up to 6 % of their global turnover?

Does the Commission acknowledge that using the threat of future binding legislation and severe fines to steer ‘voluntary’ commitments can create a chilling effect on lawful political speech and incentivise platforms to over remove controversial but legal content, particularly on migration, COVID-19 and gender ideology?

Will the Commission publish all its guidance, instructions and meeting readouts related to these codes, so that citizens and Parliament can assess whether its conduct remained within the limits of content neutral regulation, or whether it effectively dictated substantive editorial lines for private platforms?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (15.6.2026) Codes of conduct under the Digital Services Act (DSA)1 are voluntary instruments, as explicitly stated in Article 45 of the DSA. They are developed by stakeholders, for stakeholders, including platforms and civil society. Non-compliance with commitments in codes is not sanctionable as such. However, if a signatory adheres to and complies with a code of conduct, this may be considered an appropriate risk mitigation measure2, supporting their compliance with the DSA. At the same time, the mere fact of participating in and implementing a code of conduct does not in itself presume compliance with the DSA. The Commission assesses the compliance of providers of very large online platforms (VLOPs) and very large online search engines (VLOSEs) with the DSA on a case-by-case basis as part of its potential investigations. Both the Code of Conduct on Disinformation3 and the Code of Conduct on Countering Illegal Hate Speech Online4 were established on a voluntary basis by their signatories even before the adoption of the DSA (respectively in 2018 and 2016). At the signatories’ request, both have been updated and integrated into the DSA framework. The codes aim to uphold the freedom of expression while enhancing transparency. The signatories of both codes are diverse, including providers of platforms of different sizes, civil society organisations, and other stakeholders56. The Commission respects transparency requirements by publishing key enforcement decisions on a dedicated website7. It also makes publicly available its meetings with interest representatives8. Moreover, the DSA requires Commission and European Board for Digital Services conclusions related to the assessment, monitoring and evaluation of codes of conduct to be published.
