strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/signatories-2022-strengthened-code-practice-disinformation. 6 The signatories of the Code of Conduct on Countering Illegal Hate Speech Online+ are the providers of Dailymotion, Facebook, Instagram, Jeuxvideo.com, LinkedIn, Microsoft-hosted consumer services, Snapchat, Rakuten Viber, TikTok, Twitch, X and YouTube, https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/code-conductcountering-illegal-hate-speech-online. 7 https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/list-designated-vlops-and-vloses. 8 https://ec.europa.eu/transparency-initiative/meetings/meeting.do?host=aae7124c-b839-4139-9ffead5660fe9404&page=1.

E-10-2026-001431.t: European Public Prosecutor’s Office 2025 annual report
qt: to the Commission Alexander Jungbluth (ESN) Subject:

The 2025 annual report by the European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO) indicates a significant amount of alleged fraud against the EU budget, particularly in connection with the recovery instrument NextGenerationEU. By the end of 2025, the EPPO was handling 518 active cases in connection with NextGenerationEU, with the estimated damages totalling around EUR 5.07 billion. In particular, the investigations concern procurement fraud, the provision of false or misleading information to obtain funding, corruption and misappropriation. 1.

What specific structural vulnerabilities has the Commission identified in the oversight, allocation and audit mechanisms in connection with NextGenerationEU, particularly in areas that are allocated a great deal of resources such as the green and digital transformation, and what measures will be taken in the future, compared with measures taken until now, to specifically address these vulnerabilities?

How is the Commission ensuring that programmes and projects carried out in the context of the so-called green transformation – such as those relating to renewables, energy efficiency and sustainable infrastructure – are not more vulnerable to fraud, market distortion or the inefficient use of funds owing to their political prioritisation?

To what extent does the Commission see the fraud cases described in the EPPO report as an indication that the current design of NextGenerationEU and comparable instruments is perversely incentivising the misappropriation or misuse of funds, and what conclusions does it draw from this for the future direction of the EU budget?
at: (English version) to the Commission Alexander Jungbluth (ESN) (8 April 2026) Subject: European Public Prosecutor’s Office 2025 annual report The 2025 annual report by the European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO) indicates a significant amount of alleged fraud against the EU budget, particularly in connection with the recovery instrument NextGenerationEU. By the end of 2025, the EPPO was handling 518 active cases in connection with NextGenerationEU, with the estimated damages totalling around EUR 5.07 billion. In particular, the investigations concern procurement fraud, the provision of false or misleading information to obtain funding, corruption and misappropriation. 1. What specific structural vulnerabilities has the Commission identified in the oversight, allocation and audit mechanisms in connection with NextGenerationEU, particularly in areas that are allocated a great deal of resources such as the green and digital transformation, and what measures will be taken in the future, compared with measures taken until now, to specifically address these vulnerabilities? 2. How is the Commission ensuring that programmes and projects carried out in the context of the so-called green transformation — such as those relating to renewables, energy efficiency and sustainable infrastructure — are not more vulnerable to fraud, market distortion or the inefficient use of funds owing to their political prioritisation? 3. To what extent does the Commission see the fraud cases described in the EPPO report as an indication that the current design of NextGenerationEU and comparable instruments is perversely incentivising the misappropriation or misuse of funds, and what conclusions does it draw from this for the future direction of the EU budget? (19 June 2026) Under Article 22 of the Recovery and Resilience facility (RRF) Regulation (1), Member States bear primary responsibility for safeguarding the EU’s financial interests and ensuring compliance with EU/national law. The Commission put in place a robust control framework by assessing national internal control systems during the evaluation of initial and revised national Recovery and Resilience Plans and carrying out system audits in each Member State to verify that they fulfil their obligations in this area. The Commission is also acting on serious irregularities (fraud, corruption, conflicts of interest and double funding, that have not been corrected by the Member State) identified through its audits or via other sources, including the European Anti-Fraud Office (OLAF) and the European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO) investigations. Upon detection, the Commission notifies the Member State concerned, which must correct the issues and recover any misused funds. If the issues have not been corrected by the Member States, the Commission may also recover those funds or reduce them if they have not yet been paid to the Member State in question. In addition, the Commission may also reduce or recover funds from a Member State in cases of serious breach of an obligation under the Financing/Loan Agreements2. The rise in EPPO’s 2025 reported cases reflects more advanced RRF implementation and heightened Member State vigilance, with 86% of new EPPO investigations triggered by national notifications, which is evidence of strengthened controls. The Commission remains confident in the effectiveness of RRF’s audit and control frameworks across all policy areas and investment sizes. The Commission has adopted its proposals for the next Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) in July and September 2025 (2). The Commission remains committed to fighting against fraud under the next MFF.

E-10-2026-001427.t: Rapid spread of sheep pox across Greece and unjustified delays in compensation
qt: to the Commission Afroditi Latinopoulou (PfE) Subject:

There has been a massive surge in cases of sheep pox in Greece, leaving understaffed veterinary services unable to keep up with immediate culling needs, which has led to the further spread of the disease. Can the Commission answer the following: 1.

Since veterinary services have taken a considerable amount of time (in some cases up to 30 days) to cull pox-infected animals, why is there no provision for compensation for sheep that have died of pox in the time between the positive laboratory test result and their mandatory culling?
What provisions are in place for holdings dealing with pox virus infections for the period of time that must elapse after infected animals are culled before restocking with new animals is permitted?
How long after the date of culling must compensation be paid to the farmer for the animals culled due to pox?
at: (English version) to the Commission Afroditi Latinopoulou (PfE) (8 April 2026) Subject: Rapid spread of sheep pox across Greece and unjustified delays in compensation There has been a massive surge in cases of sheep pox in Greece, leaving understaffed veterinary services unable to keep up with immediate culling needs, which has led to the further spread of the disease. Can the Commission answer the following: 1.

Since veterinary services have taken a considerable amount of time (in some cases up to 30 days) to cull pox-infected animals, why is there no provision for compensation for sheep that have died of pox in the time between the positive laboratory test result and their mandatory culling?
What provisions are in place for holdings dealing with pox virus infections for the period of time that must elapse after infected animals are culled before restocking with new animals is permitted?
How long after the date of culling must compensation be paid to the farmer for the animals culled due to pox?

(27 May 2026) At National level when an outbreak of sheep pox and goat pox is confirmed in an establishment, Member States are responsible for setting compensation rules for the death or killing of ovine and caprine animals, and for costs related to cleaning, disinfection and other control measures to ensure the rapid eradication of the disease. At EU level, financial support to Member States for those veterinary emergency measures is provided under the Single Market Programme (1). Eligible costs include costs incurred by Member States to compensate animals slaughtered or culled, the slaughtering, transport, cleaning, disinfection, and disposal activities. Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/687 (2) requires that killing of animals in affected establishments is carried out as soon as possible on the spot, to limit disease spread and reduce further losses. Y EU co-financing to Member States may, under specific conditions and verifications, include the compensation for animals that die for the disease after official suspicion has been notified to the competent authority. Following killing, establishments must remain under restriction until the cleaning and disinfection supervised by the competent authority. Restocking can be granted once the cleaning and disinfection have been completed and epidemiological conditions and control measures required by the competent authority are fulfilled. Restocking of sheep and goat establishments located within the restricted zones listed in Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2024/2207 (3) in Greece is prohibited. EU legislation does not set a fixed deadline for compensation payments, which is subject to national administrative procedures and verification processes.

E-10-2026-001426.t: Targeted attacks against the Greek Christian community in Syria
qt: to the Commission Afroditi Latinopoulou (PfE) Subject:

According to recent reports, there have been serious attacks in the Syrian city of AlSuqaylabiyah. These have mainly targeted the Greek Orthodox Christian population, and include attacks on residents and religious sites. These incidents are part of a broader trend of growing violence against religious minorities in Syria and are of great concern for the security and continuation of the Christian presence in the region. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
What specific actions does it intend to take to protect Christian communities in Syria and to safeguard religious freedom?
Does it intend to raise the issue of these targeted attacks against Christians in its diplomatic contacts with the actors involved, with a view to possible sanctions?
How does it explain the continued absence of a meaningful EU response to repeated attacks against Christians, and does it intend to take specific deterrence measures without delay?
at: (English version) to the Commission Afroditi Latinopoulou (PfE) (8 April 2026) Subject: Targeted attacks against the Greek Christian community in Syria According to recent reports, there have been serious attacks in the Syrian city of Al-Suqaylabiyah. These have mainly targeted the Greek Orthodox Christian population, and include attacks on residents and religious sites. (15 June 2026) Since the fall of the Assad regime in December 2024, the EU has played an active role in supporting Syria and its people through every stage of their challenging transition. The EU’s strategy is founded on the belief that lasting peace and stability in Syria can only be achieved through an inclusive transition, one that meets the aspirations of Syrians from all ethnic and religious backgrounds without discrimination. The EU also urges all parties to protect Syria’s rich cultural heritage and religious monuments. With regard to the incidents mentioned, EU continues to ask for thorough investigations and accountability for all perpetrators of violence in Syria. In its engagement with Syria’s transitional authorities, the EU underscores these principles as essential for a successful, inclusive transition. During their visit to Syria, the Presidents of the European Council and Commission unveiled a new EU-Syria Political Partnership, designed to support the political transition, national reconciliation, and reconstruction. On 11 May 2026, the EU held its first High-Level Political Dialogue with Syria in Brussels, where inter alia the need to ensure a genuinely inclusive process for sustainable reconciliation and restoring Syria’s rich social fabrics was underscored. The EU remains vigilant about the respect for human rights of Syrians from all ethnic and religious backgrounds without discrimination, and will continue to support comprehensive accountability efforts for all perpetrators regardless of their affiliation. In May (1) and June (2) 2025, the EU introduced new listings against human rights violators and will continue monitoring the situation on the ground and the follow up of the commitments of the transitional authorities. Protecting the rights of most vulnerable ethnic and religious communities is essential to ensuring social cohesion, preventing further sectarian divisions, and laying the foundations for a sustainable and inclusive peace, as reiterated in Council conclusions of 18 December 2025 (3).

E-10-2026-001425.t: Child recruitment in Colombia and the EU’s position in dialogue processes with armed groups
qt: to the Commission Irene Montero (The Left) Subject:

The EU has repeatedly expressed concern about the increase in the recruitment of children and adolescents in armed conflicts. In her reply1 to written question E-001758/20252, the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy stated that combating the recruitment is an EU priority, is regularly raised in bilateral dialogues, and is addressed through EU support for prevention and protection projects in Colombia. However, this crime is on the rise; according to UNICEF, it has quadrupled over the last five years, disproportionately affecting Indigenous peoples. In its report, the Regional Indigenous Council of Cauca documented 838 cases within its territories between January 2022 and December 2025, estimating that, due to a high rate of under-reporting, the actual figure is likely to be four times higher. The EU and several Member States expressed their intention to accompany and observe dialogue processes with armed groups in Colombia. In this context: 1.
How is the Commission addressing the specific demand for an immediate end to the recruitment and use of children?

Does the Commission consider that the issue of child recruitment should be a nonnegotiable condition in any dialogue and, if so, what concrete measures is it promoting to ensure that the Member States involved convey this message in a coherent and coordinated manner?
https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/E-10-2025-001758-ASW_EN.html. https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/E-10-2025-001758_EN.html.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (11.5.2026) The EU has been vocal in condemning the recruitment and use of children by armed groups in Colombia and has called on armed actors to respect international humanitarian law, most recently in response to the National Liberation Army (ELN)'s1 campaign of violence in Catatumbo in January 2025. This issue also features regularly on the agenda of the EUColombia high level Dialogue on Human Rights. As part of the Group of Friends of Resolution 1612, the EU coordinates with UN International Children’s Emergency Fund (UNICEF) and other Embassies advocacy actions aimed at protecting children in armed conflicts. Embassies engage in dialogue with state entities and issue public pronouncements condemning the practice and calling for respect for international humanitarian law. The EU supports several peace dialogues under Colombia's ‘Total Peace’ policy, promoting agreements with armed groups to end the recruitment of minors. While multiple agreements have been reached, their implementation and monitoring remain insufficient, and the EU continues to raise these concerns with Colombian authorities. EU funded projects provide child protection services, including mental health and psychosocial support, for children affected by conflict, including victims of recruitment, with a focus on Indigenous and Afro-descendant communities. The EU supports partners such as the International Committee of the Red Cross, Geneva Call and UNICEF to promote respect for International Humanitarian Law.

E-10-2026-001424.t: Death of 70 people in the central Mediterranean
qt: to the Commission Isabel Serra Sánchez (The Left) Subject:
Death of 70 people in the central Mediterranean

On 6 April 2026, at least 70 people died when a boat carrying more than 100 people capsized off the coast of Libya. The beginning of this year is shaping up to be the deadliest on record, amid a lack of rescue efforts and the impact of border externalisation. Those deaths are not inevitable. They are the direct result of political decisions that prioritise border control and security over protection of life – shifting routes towards increasingly dangerous paths and reducing the effective search and rescue capacity. Far from ensuring legal and safe pathways, the European Union continues to tighten its migration policy through agreements with third countries and the practical implementation of the Pact on Migration and Asylum, building a system that ensures that hundreds of people will die at sea. 1.
What is the Commission’s assessment of its responsibility for the increasing number of deaths on the central Mediterranean route as a result of externalisation and border control?
What urgent action will it take to ensure a fully operational European search and rescue operation and to establish legal and safe pathways that put an end to those preventable deaths?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (2.6.2026) Migrant deaths at sea are a tragic reminder of the need for a comprehensive approach to migration management and renewed efforts to combat migrant smuggling in the EU and with countries along migratory routes. Every life lost at sea is a tragedy. The Commission is committed to preventing dangerous journeys by tackling the root causes of irregular migration and strengthening measures against organised crime along migratory routes. The Commission also promotes safe and legal pathways to the EU, notably through Talent Partnerships, the EU’s new Talent Pool1 and the Union resettlement and Humanitarian admission Plan 2026-20272. As regards search and rescue3, the Commission keeps promoting reinforced information sharing, coordination and cooperation among all relevant stakeholders, including partner countries. Upon requests by Member States, the European Border and Coast Guard Agency (Frontex) provides technical and operational support to facilitate the safe and effective management of the external borders of the EU. The Agency is to act in full compliance with its EU and international law obligations in all its activities and engagements. In 2025 alone, 24 877 people were rescued at sea with Frontex support4. The Commission will continue to promote these efforts together with all relevant stakeholders, including partner countries.
1 The EU Talent Pool Regulation was adopted on 30 March 2026. The Commission is working on the

development of the IT platform to make it operational by 2027. https://homeaffairs.ec.europa.eu/policies/migration-and-asylum/legal-migration-and-resettlement/work/eu-talent-pool_en. 2 https://home-affairs.ec.europa.eu/commissions-proposal-union-resettlement-and-humanitarian-admissionplan_en. 3 https://home-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies/migration-and-asylum/migration-management/search-and-rescue_en. 4 Although, Search and rescue (SAR) is a responsibility of national authorities, Frontex, through the provision of services such as aerial surveillance, can support SAR operations and help saving lives at sea, by enabling the Member States to identify situations of potential distress earlier and respond more quickly and effectively.

E-10-2026-001422.t: EU funding for the Libyan Coast Guard and Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre in eastern Libya
qt: to the Commission Erik Marquardt (Verts/ALE), Saskia Bricmont (Verts/ALE), Tineke Strik (Verts/ALE), Cecilia Strada (S&D) Subject:

Recent reports show that the Commission plans to finance the construction of a Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre (MRCC) in Benghazi, Libya, at a cost of at least EUR 3 million1. As Benghazi is in eastern Libya, this suggests cooperation between the EU and General Khalifa Haftar, who controls the region. Considering the involvement of General Haftar and his forces in the mistreatment, exploitation and killing of refugees both on land and at sea, as well as international allegations of serious human rights violations and breaches of international law related to the Libyan Coast Guard, the following questions arise: 1.

How much funding has the EU provided since 2015 to support the Libyan Coast Guard, and for which specific purposes have these funds been allocated? Please distinguish between funding for equipment, training and direct financial support.
Through which EU projects, programmes and financial instruments has the provision of equipment, training and financial support to the Libyan Coast Guard been implemented?

What measures does the Commission plan to take in cooperation with General Khalifa Haftar in eastern Libya to support the establishment of an MRCC and/or support the Libyan Coast Guard? Please list all measures individually.
https://www.statewatch.org/news/2026/january/eu-to-increase-lethal-migration-cooperation-with-libya/.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (10.8.2026) Since 2015, EU support to migration management in Libya has been funded mainly through the EU Emergency Trust Fund for Africa (EUTF)1 and the Neighbourhood, Development and International Cooperation Instrument – Global Europe (NDICI-GE)2. Under the EUTF North Africa window, EUR 59 million were allocated to border management-related support in Libya under the ‘Support to Integrated Border and Migration Management in Libya’ programme. This included support for activities in search and rescue in the desert, implemented by International Organisation for Migration, as well as for the Libyan Coast Guard in Tripoli. EU support on the maritime side has included the provision of search and rescue vessels, rubber boats, training on international maritime law and human rights, technical assistance and support for operating procedures and coordination capacities. Under NDICI-GE, around EUR 35 million are currently contracted for border managementrelated activities, mainly focussing on land borders and technical assistance. The EU supports the establishment of Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre (MRCC) in Benghazi to respond to Libyan requests addressing maritime security challenges in the east, and to promote intra-Libyan cooperation, as well as with international search and rescue actors in the Mediterranean Sea. The project comprises the establishment of the MRCC and the training of the MRCC operators and coordinators, as well as the training of the Search and Rescue (SAR) vessel crews, for enhancing capacities and compliance with international law and human rights in border management and SAR operations. It will be implemented by the Operation EUNAVFOR MED IRINI3 and supported by the EU Border Assistance Mission in Libya4 and the UN Office on Drugs and Crime.

E-10-2026-001421.t: European MRV and ETS frameworks for offshore activities
qt: to the Commission Wouter Beke (PPE) Subject:

The extension of the EU MRV and EU ETS frameworks to offshore activities constitutes a significant step in the implementation of the European Green Deal. At the same time, stakeholders in the offshore sector note that the practical implementation of the MRV system presents challenges. In particular, the application of key concepts, such as the definition of a ‘port of call’, does not always seem to align well with the operational reality of offshore activities. This can lead to uncertainty and additional red tape. Since the MRV framework forms the basis for the operation of the EU ETS in the maritime sector, these stumbling points may also affect the correct application of the ETS. In addition, attention is drawn to the potential implications for the level playing field with non-European stakeholders. In view of the above: 1.

What is the Commission’s assessment of the applicability of the current EU MRV framework to offshore activities, taking into account the implementation challenges identified by the sector, particularly in light of the implications for the EU ETS?
Is the Commission considering further clarification or adaptation of the framework, and if so, what steps and timeline are envisaged?
How can the Commission ensure the competitiveness of the European offshore sector and a level playing field?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (18.5.2026) As noted in its replies to written questions P-001316/2026 and E-001335/2026, the Commission recognises the heterogeneous and specific nature of the offshore maritime sector. To address issues raised by operators of offshore vessels, the Commission has already included additional clarifications in the guidance document1 accompanying the Monitoring, Reporting and Verification (MRV) Regulation2 and the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) Directive3. Furthermore, an offshore workstream meets under the auspices of the European Sustainable Shipping Forum (ESSF). This workstream brings together offshore shipping operators, Member States’ authorities and the Commission to discuss practical implementation matters pertaining to the offshore sector with regards to MRV and ETS obligations. As was also indicated, the Commission is assessing, in the context of the upcoming ETS review foreseen in July 2026, what additional measures and adaptations to the legislative framework may be introduced to further facilitate compliance by offshore operators and ensure a level playing field by preventing market distortion, thus safeguarding the competitiveness of European operators in this important sector.

E-10-2026-001419.t: Google’s new Android developer verification program and compliance with the Digital Markets Act
qt: to the Commission Christel Schaldemose (S&D) Subject:

Google has announced a new Android developer verification program, which is expected to be phased in soon. The new updates mean that Android app developers – including those who distribute apps outside Google Play, including via third-party app stores and sideloading – have to register with Google, provide official identification, pay a fee and accept Google’s terms and conditions in order for their apps to be installed on Android devices. For now, Google’s promise of an ‘advanced flow’ feature specifically designed for superusers – and thus not ordinary users – is the only way to avoid this, but it requires an unnecessarily large number of steps and a total of 24 hours for individuals to complete. At the moment it can be done immediately, and is not hidden away in the developer settings. In the light of the foregoing: 1.

Does the Commission take the view that a requirement for the central registration and verification of all Android developers, especially those outside Google Play, is compatible with the Digital Markets Act?
Will the Commission consider such requirements to be a restriction on sideloading and third‑party app stores?
How will the Commission ensure that security requirements such as these are not used as a way of circumventing the Digital Markets Act?
at: (English version) to the Commission Alexandra Geese (Verts/ALE), Anna Cavazzini (Verts/ALE), Reinier Van Lanschot (Verts/ALE) (1 April 2026) Subject: Google’s developer registration decision and it’s threat to the EU’s tech sovereignty In August 2025, Google unilaterally decided (1) that Android developers will be required to register centrally with Google. In addition to demanding the payment of a registration fee and agreement to its terms and conditions, Google also requires software developers to upload documentation to confirm their identity (2), including government-issued ID, and to enumerate (3) all the unique ‘application identifiers’ for every app that is to be distributed by the registered developer. This has a drastic impact on open-source projects, competition and innovation. More importantly, this negatively impacts the EU’s ability to work towards technological sovereignty, as Google frequently complies with the demands of non-EU countries to remove perfectly legal apps that do not fit their political agenda. Is the Commission aware of this issue, and is it examining its compatibility with the Digital Markets Act? to the Commission Christel Schaldemose (S&D) (8 April 2026) Subject: Google’s new Android developer verification program and compliance with the Digital Markets Act Google has announced a new Android developer verification program, which is expected to be phased in soon. The new updates mean that Android app developers — including those who distribute apps outside Google Play, including via thirdparty app stores and sideloading — have to register with Google, provide official identification, pay a fee and accept Google’s terms and conditions in order for their apps to be installed on Android devices. For now, Google’s promise of an ‘advanced flow’ feature specifically designed for superusers — and thus not ordinary users — is the only way to avoid this, but it requires an unnecessarily large number of steps and a total of 24 hours for individuals to complete. At the moment it can be done immediately, and is not hidden away in the developer settings. In the light of the foregoing: 1.

Does the Commission take the view that a requirement for the central registration and verification of all Android developers, especially those outside Google Play, is compatible with the Digital Markets Act?
Will the Commission consider such requirements to be a restriction on sideloading and third-party app stores?
How will the Commission ensure that security requirements such as these are not used as a way of circumventing the Digital Markets Act?

Joint answer given by Executive Vice-President Virkkunen on behalf of the European Commission (15 June 2026) The Commission is aware of Google’s announcement to introduce this verification process starting from September 2026 in some jurisdictions (not including the EU based on publicly available information). The Commission understands that, as a result of this process, Android will require that all applications (apps) are registered by verified developers in order to be installed on certified Android devices. The Commission is also aware of public campaigns such as ‘Keep Android Open’ which have emerged in reaction to Google’s announcement.

Frey, S., ‘A new layer of security for certified Android devices’, Android Developers, 25 August 2025, https://androiddevelopers.googleblog.com/2025/08/elevating-android-security.html. Android Developers, ‘Elevating Android security to keep it open and safe’, https://developer.android.com/developer-verification#verify-your-identity. Android Developers, ‘Elevating Android security to keep it open and safe’, https://developer.android.com/developer-verification#register-your-apps.

Article 6(4) of the Digital Markets Act (DMA) (1) obliges gatekeepers like Alphabet to allow and technically enable the effective distribution of apps on their operating system through third party app stores or the web. At the same time, the DMA also permits Google to introduce strictly necessary and proportionate measures to ensure that thirdparty software apps or app stores do not endanger the integrity of the hardware or operating system, provided that such measures are duly justified by Alphabet. The Commission is actively engaged in a regulatory dialogue with Alphabet regarding Article 6(4) of the DMA and is also diligently monitoring Alphabet's compliance with the relevant legal framework to ensure that apps, including open-source apps, can be effectively distributed on Android outside of Google Play.

E-10-2026-001418.t: Safeguarding the competitiveness of the EU hosiery and underwear sector
qt: to the Commission Dariusz Joński (PPE) Subject:

In connection with the implementation of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/734, I would like to raise serious concerns expressed by EU manufacturers of hosiery regarding the impact of high anti-dumping duties on imports of polyamide yarn from China. According to industry representatives, these duties distort competition within the EU single market. While essential raw materials are subject to high tariffs, finished products and certain semi-finished goods remain relatively price-competitive. This weakens the position of EU producers, both vis-à-vis Chinese manufacturers and European competitors in non-EU countries. As a result, the sector risks job losses, reduced investment and long-term decline. At the same time, the rapid growth of direct-to-consumer sales via non-EU e-commerce platforms such as SHEIN, TEMU and AliExpress raises additional concerns. These platforms benefit from the preferential treatment of low-value consignments, which complicates the enforcement of EU rules on product safety, traceability and labelling, further distorting competition. In the light of this: 1.
Has the Commission assessed the impact of these duties on EU manufacturers of finished products?
Does the Commission plan measures to address the competitive advantages of non-EU e-commerce platforms?
Is the Commission considering adjustments to ensure a level playing field within the single market?

E-10-2026-001417.t: Latest report of the UN Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese on the situation in the Occupied Palestinian Territory and on human rights violations by Israel
qt: to the Commission Annalisa Corrado (S&D), Matjaž Nemec (S&D), Cecilia Strada (S&D), Sandro Ruotolo (S&D), Alessandro Zan (S&D), Benedetta Scuderi (Verts/ALE), Rima Hassan (The Left), Marc Botenga (The Left), Brando Benifei (S&D), Chloé Ridel (S&D), Georgia Tramacere (S&D) Subject:

According to the latest report1 presented on 23 March to the United Nations Human Rights Council by Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese, Israel’s use of torture against Palestinians has taken on a systematic and structural character, occurring not only within detention centres, but as a widespread practice throughout the entire Occupied Palestinian Territory, which has been transformed into a veritable ‘torturous environment’. The report documents practices such as waterboarding, beatings, burns, electric shocks, sexual violence and humiliation. Already in 2025, the UN Committee against Torture expressed grave concern over ‘the application of a de facto State policy of organised and widespread torture and ill-treatment’, while the UN Commission of Inquiry has found that Article II(b)2 grounds of the Genocide Convention are established. In addition, the Israeli Knesset has approved the application of the death penalty for Palestinians accused of terrorism, while Israeli military operations in Iran and Lebanon continue to affect civilians and innocent populations, further exacerbating instability and violations of international law. In the light of the above: 1.
Is the Commission aware of the findings contained in the above-mentioned report, and what is its assessment of them?

What is the state of play regarding the assessment of a possible suspension of the EU– Israel Association Agreement, in the light of the aforementioned persistent and documented human rights violations?

at: (English version) to the Commission Annalisa Corrado (S&D), Matjaž Nemec (S&D), Cecilia Strada (S&D), Sandro Ruotolo (S&D), Alessandro Zan (S&D), Benedetta Scuderi (Verts/ALE), Rima Hassan (The Left), Marc Botenga (The Left), Brando Benifei (S&D), Chloé Ridel (S&D), Georgia Tramacere (S&D) (8 April 2026) Subject: Latest report of the UN Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese on the situation in the Occupied Palestinian Territory and on human rights violations by Israel According to the latest report (1) presented on 23 March to the United Nations Human Rights Council by Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese, Israel’s use of torture against Palestinians has taken on a systematic and structural character, occurring not only within detention centres, but as a widespread practice throughout the entire Occupied Palestinian Territory, which has been transformed into a veritable ‘torturous environment’. The report documents practices such as waterboarding, beatings, burns, electric shocks, sexual violence and humiliation. Already in 2025, the UN Committee against Torture expressed grave concern over ‘the application of a de facto State policy of organised and widespread torture and ill-treatment’, while the UN Commission of Inquiry has found that Article II(b) (2) grounds of the Genocide Convention are established. In addition, the Israeli Knesset has approved the application of the death penalty for Palestinians accused of terrorism, while Israeli military operations in Iran and Lebanon continue to affect civilians and innocent populations, further exacerbating instability and violations of international law. In the light of the above: 1.
Is the Commission aware of the findings contained in the above-mentioned report, and what is its assessment of them?

What is the state of play regarding the assessment of a possible suspension of the EU-Israel Association Agreement, in the light of the aforementioned persistent and documented human rights violations?

(5 June 2026) The EU has taken note of the Special Rapporteur’s report. The EU condemns all acts of torture and other cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment, wherever these occur and it is steadfastly against the usage of arbitrary arrests and detention, as well as enforced disappearances. The EU underscores the essential role, independence and integrity of the UN Special Procedures mandate holders. The EU will continue to support UN special procedures, mandate holders and other independent investigations into violations and abuses of human rights and violations of international humanitarian law, including those that may amount to international crimes (1). In 2025, in light of the catastrophic situation in Gaza, the High Representative/Vice-President conducted, with the support of a majority of Member States, a review of Israel’s compliance with its obligations under Article 2 of the EU-Israel Association Agreement (2). The conclusion of the review was that there are indications that Israel would be in breach of its obligations. Following the review, and given the deteriorating humanitarian situation in Gaza, the president of the Commission announced a set of proposed measures, including a reinforced package of sanctions and the suspension of certain trade-related provisions of the EU-Israel Association Agreement. The Commission has also put on hold its bilateral support to Israel, with the exception of support to civil society and Yad Vashem. At the May 2026 Foreign Affairs Council, Foreign Ministers reached political agreement on the listings of violent extremist Israeli settlers under the EU’s Global Human Rights Sanctions Regime. Discussions continue in the Council on other measures which require approval of Member States.

E-10-2026-001416.t: Complexity of the AGRIP application process and dependence on external consultancies
qt: to the Commission Alexander Bernhuber (PPE) Subject:

Despite successive reforms, the Promotion of Agricultural Products (AGRIP) application process remains highly complex. The required documentation effectively excludes eligible organisations unless they engage costly external agencies. 1.

Is the Commission aware that many potential applicants from smaller Member States refrain from applying due to the disproportionate administrative burden and does it monitor the proportion of successful applications prepared with support from external consultancies?
What concrete measures does the Commission plan to introduce to simplify the programme and make it accessible without external professional support?
at: (English version) to the Commission Alexander Bernhuber (PPE) (8 April 2026) Subject: Complexity of the AGRIP application process and dependence on external consultancies Despite successive reforms, the Promotion of Agricultural Products (AGRIP) application process remains highly complex. The required documentation effectively excludes eligible organisations unless they engage costly external agencies. 1. Is the Commission aware that many potential applicants from smaller Member States refrain from applying due to the disproportionate administrative burden and does it monitor the proportion of successful applications prepared with support from external consultancies? 2. What concrete measures does the Commission plan to introduce to simplify the programme and make it accessible without external professional support? (4 June 2026) Simplification is a priority for the Commission that it also pursues in the field of promotion programmes for agricultural products (AGRIP). In 2024 and 2025, several activities were undertaken such as publishing new guidelines and further frequently asked questions. Additionally, the Commission has amended the relevant delegated ac t (1) and is currently working on amending the implementing act. 1. The Commission is aware that in some cases potential applicants have refrained from submitting applications on account of the perceived related burdens. As for the involvement of external consultancies in the drafting of proposals, the Commission does not monitor this, as a possible involvement is normally not disclosed. 2. The submission of proposals in response to calls for proposals under AGRIP does not require to make use of external professional support services. The Commission is, however, aware that some proposing organisations chose to make use of external consultancies to assist with the drafting of proposals. Simplification efforts undertaken by the Commission include the provision of information products and outreach activities relevant to potential applicants as described, and notably also the yearly AGRIP info days that provide advice on successful proposal-writing. Furthermore, as indicated in replies E- 1414/2026 and E-1415/2026, the Commission is considering ways to build capacity in Member States that have historically been underrepresented among AGRIP beneficiaries.
Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2025/70 of 21 November 2024 amending Delegated Regulation (EU) 2015/1829.

E-10-2026-001415.t: Absence of national budget allocations and structural disadvantages for smaller Member States
qt: to the Commission Alexander Bernhuber (PPE) Subject:

Unlike many other EU funding programmes, the programme for the promotion of agricultural products (AGRIP) operates exclusively on the basis of competitive calls for proposals without any form of national budget envelope or indicative country allocation. The evaluation criteria do not include any geographical balance component. 1.

Has the Commission considered introducing a partial national allocation or ring-fencing a share of the AGRIP budget for Member States that have historically been underrepresented – similar to Horizon Europe widening measures or mechanisms used in cohesion policy, and if not, why not?

Does the Commission acknowledge that Member States with fewer registered geographical indications (PDO/PGI/TSG) and smaller, less professionalised trade organisations are structurally disadvantaged under the current system – given that quality schemes are a central thematic priority and the representativeness threshold requires coverage of at least 50 % of producers or marketable production?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.6.2026) The Commission aims at a geographic balance among beneficiaries of promotion programmes for agricultural products (AGRIP) and undertakes significant efforts towards this goal. Among these, outreach efforts are continuous stakeholder dialogue, multilingual information provision and letters addressed to national authorities. 1. AGRIP has its general objective defined in the relevant basic act1 as enhancing the competitiveness of the Union agricultural sector. In relation to this objective, the Commission believes that effective mechanisms need to be put in place, which ensure that high-quality promotion programmes are being implemented. Competitive calls for proposals, rather than national (pre-)allocations are deemed as a suitable means to such end. However, the Commission is considering ways to build capacity in Member States that have historically been underrepresented among AGRIP beneficiaries. 2. The relevant basic act defines increasing the awareness and recognition of Union quality schemes, including geographical indications (GIs), as a specific objective for AGRIP.2 AGRIP annual work programmes include different calls for proposals. Calls focused on GIs are only one of several focus areas. In the last annual work programme for 2026, EUR 13.1 million were programmed with a focus on GIs out of a total of EUR 100 million for simple programmes, whereas EUR 7 million were programmed with an optional focus on GIs out of a total of EUR 60 million for multi programmes. As regards the eligibility criteria, the Commission points out that criteria were simplified and the requirement for agri-food sector bodies to demonstrate representativeness through membership was removed under certain conditions3.

1 Article 2 (1) of Regulation (EU) No 1144/2014 of 22 October 2014. 2 Article 2 (2) point (c) of Regulation (EU) No 1144/2014 of 22 October 2014. 3 Article 1 of Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2025/70 of 21 November 2024 amending Delegated
Regulation (EU) 2015/1829.

E-10-2026-001414.t: Geographical imbalance in the distribution of AGRIP funding
qt: to the Commission Alexander Bernhuber (PPE) Subject:

According to statistics from the European Research Executive Agency for the period 20162024, a small number of Member States received a disproportionately large share of funding under the promotion of agricultural products programme (AGRIP). In the 2025 selection round, successful applicants came from only 15 of the 27 Member States, and 74 % of the budget targeted markets in just four Member States. 1.

How does the Commission assess the fact that almost half of the Member States regularly receive no funding whatsoever under this programme, and does it consider this compatible with the Treaty objective of strengthening the competitiveness of the Union’s agricultural sector as a whole?
What concrete measures does the Commission intend to take within the current programming period to ensure a more balanced geographical distribution of AGRIP funds across all 27 Member States?
at: (English version) to the Commission Alexander Bernhuber (PPE) (8 April 2026) Subject: Geographical imbalance in the distribution of AGRIP funding According to statistics from the European Research Executive Agency for the period 2016-2024, a small number of Member States received a disproportionately large share of funding under the promotion of agricultural products programme (AGRIP). In the 2025 selection round, successful applicants came from only 15 of the 27 Member States, and 74% of the budget targeted markets in just four Member States. 1. How does the Commission assess the fact that almost half of the Member States regularly receive no funding whatsoever under this programme, and does it consider this compatible with the Treaty objective of strengthening the competitiveness of the Union’s agricultural sector as a whole? 2. What concrete measures does the Commission intend to take within the current programming period to ensure a more balanced geographical distribution of AGRIP funds across all 27 Member States? (29 May 2026) The Commission has a strong interest in improving geographic balance among beneficiaries of its promotion programmes for agricultural products (AGRIP) and puts significant efforts in pursuit of this goal: information sessions in Member States (Info Days), continuous stakeholder dialogue, multilingual information provision and letters addressed to national authorities to encourage participation. 1. AGRIP calls for proposals are open to applicants from all Member States and the annual work programmes are discussed and voted on in the Committee for the Common Organisation of the Agricultural Markets — Promotion. To strengthen the competitiveness of the Union agricultural sector the Commission believes that effective mechanisms need to be put in place, which ensure that high-quality promotion programmes are being implemented. The Commission regards competitive calls for proposals as a suitable mechanism. Having said this, the Commission is also concerned by the geographic imbalance of AGRIP beneficiaries and undertakes substantial efforts to improve this situation. 2. One of the reasons for the current geographic imbalance among AGRIP recipients is the different capacity among potential applicants from Member States to submit successful applications. The Commission is considering ways to build capacity in Member States that have historically been underrepresented among AGRIP beneficiaries. Besides this, the Commission will continue its outreach efforts and related activities and will also continue simplification efforts of AGRIP.

E-10-2026-001413.t: Targeting of import controls and public access to control data
qt: to the Commission Alexander Bernhuber (PPE) Subject:

According to the Alert and Cooperation Network’s 2024 Annual Report, 84 % of notified fruit and vegetable imports originated from non-EU countries – primarily Türkiye, Egypt, India and China. At the same time, the Commission acknowledges that Member States report their control data in inconsistent formats. 1.
To which specific countries of origin and product categories has the announced 50 % increase in non-EU audits been allocated, and what is the planned number of audits per country?
What binding measures does the Commission plan to take to ensure that all 27 Member States report the total number of controls, inspection rates and outcomes in a standardised format, and by when?

Given that high-risk products from specific non-EU countries are subject to increased physical checks under Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1793, can the Commission confirm that these prescribed check frequencies were actually met by all Member States from 2023 to 2025, and if not, which Member States fell short and for which productcountry combinations?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (14.7.2026) The Commission publishes yearly the programme of planned audits of Member States and third countries in the area of food and feed safety, animal health, animal welfare and plant health. The 2026 programme1 reflects the Commission’s commitment to increase by 50% its audits of third countries compared to 2025. The planned audits of third countries on food of non-animal origin cover microbiological risks, contaminants, pesticide residues and plant health aspects. Countries and commodities audited were prioritised on the basis of risks associated with their exports to the EU as well as past audits’ outcome. Since the application of Regulation (EU) 2017/6252, Member States are to record the results of official controls on consignments of goods at border control posts and to communicate this through the Information Management System for Official Controls3 (Article 56 of the Regulation). This enables to obtain real-time reports. Therefore, no additional binding measures are needed in this area. Where food of non-animal origin from third countries poses a contamination risk, the Commission may take measures through Regulation (EU) 2019/17934. The Commission follows implementation by Member States – and confirms that it is satisfactory –, applies close monitoring of non-compliant commodities and countries, with frequency of checks increased as required. Under the Vision for Agriculture and Food5, the Commission pursues a stronger alignment of production standards applied to imported products, including measures to strengthen import controls. This includes to establish a task force to make import controls more efficient, which will focus e.g. on pesticide residues and will consider coordinated EU action on specific imported products.
1 Health and food audits and analysis programme: https://op.europa.eu/en/publication-detail/-

/publication/5813aab4-c5bd-11f0-8da2-01aa75ed71a1/language-en. 2 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2017/625/oj. 3 A standardised format is available in the TRACES platform - https://food.ec.europa.eu/horizontaltopics/traces_en. 4 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg_impl/2019/1793/oj. 5 COM/2025/75 final.

E-10-2026-001412.t: Data basis for the announced reinforcement of food import controls
qt: to the Commission Alexander Bernhuber (PPE) Subject:

On 9 December 2025, the Commissioner for Health and Animal Welfare, Olivér Várhelyi, announced a 50 % increase in audits in non-EU countries and a 33 % increase in checks at border control posts. However, the Commission’s publicly available reports contain no consolidated overview of the actual number of checks carried out. 1.
What is the exact number of audits in non-EU countries and checks at border control posts carried out in 2025 on which the announced percentage increases are based?
When will the report under Article 114 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 for the year 2023 and subsequent years be published, and why does the delay in reporting currently stand at almost two years?
How many additional auditors and inspectors are required to deliver the announced increase, and has the necessary budget already been approved?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.6.2026) In 2025, the Commission carried out 28 export-related onsite audits of third countries, and five onsite audits of Member States on official controls at border control posts. The Commission will publish in 2026 the report under Article 114 of Regulation (EU) 2017/6251 related to the years 2023 and 2024. The timing is contingent on the availability of the annual reports to be submitted by the Member States and on the need to deliver on several competing priorities. The Commission will deliver on the announced increase by prioritising the control activities accordingly. As detailed in the 2026 Health and Food Audits and Analysis work programme2, the Commission plans to perform 47 export-related onsite audits of third countries and seven onsite audits of Member States on official controls at border control posts.

E-10-2026-001411.t: Compliance of Google’s ‘developer verification’ and ‘advanced flow’ mechanisms with the Digital Markets Act
qt: to the Commission Sigrid Friis (Renew) Subject:

Google intends to require all application developers to register with the company, provide government-issued identification, pay a fee and accept Google’s terms and conditions for their software to remain installable on Android devices. Google further outlined an ‘advanced flow’ mechanism aimed at so-called ‘power users’, which would allow the installation of applications from unverified developers. However, this process involves a burdensome steps. Moreover, it is delivered through Google Play Services, meaning it can be modified, restricted or withdrawn by Google without requiring an operating system update or user consent. These developments raise concerns regarding compliance with the Digital Markets Act (DMA), which obliges gatekeepers to permit the use of third-party apps without imposing unfair, disproportionate or technically restrictive conditions. In the light of the above: 1.
Has the Commission been in contact with Google about these specific measures?
What actions is the Commission prepared to take to ensure that gatekeepers do not introduce de facto technical or procedural barriers that undermine the openness of platforms in the EU?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (5.6.2026) The Commission is aware of Google’s announcement to introduce a developer verification process starting from September 2026 in some jurisdictions (not including the EU based on publicly available information). The Commission understands that as a result of this process, Android will require that all applications (apps) are registered by verified developers in order to be installed on certified Android devices and that apps by unverified developers will be subject to a so-called advanced flow. The Commission is also aware of public campaigns such as ‘Keep Android Open’ which have emerged in reaction to Google’s announcement. Article 6(4) of the Digital Markets Act (DMA)1 obliges gatekeepers like Alphabet to allow and technically enable the effective distribution of apps on their operating system through third party app stores or the web. At the same time, the DMA also permits Google to introduce strictly necessary and proportionate measures to ensure that third-party software apps or app stores do not endanger the integrity of the hardware or operating system, provided that such measures are duly justified by Alphabet. The Commission is actively engaged in a regulatory dialogue with Alphabet – including in relation to these measures – and is diligentlyvmonitoring Alphabet's compliance with the relevant legal framework to ensure that apps, including open-source apps, can be effectively distributed on Android outside Google Play. The Commission is prepared to take appropriate enforcement action where necessary.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-
content/EN/TXT/?uri=uriserv%3AOJ.L_.2022.265.01.0001.01.ENG&toc=OJ%3AL%3A2022%3A265%3ATO C.

E-10-2026-001410.t: Union Resettlement and Humanitarian Admission Framework Regulation
qt: to the Commission Alexander Jungbluth (ESN), Marc Jongen (ESN), Irmhild Boßdorf (ESN), Rada Laykova (ESN), Dominik Tarczyński (ECR), Geadis Geadi (ECR), Alexander Sell (ESN), Siegbert Frank Droese (ESN), Barbara Bonte (PfE), Tomasz Froelich (ESN), Petras Gražulis (ESN), Ivan David (ESN), Petar Volgin (ESN), Milan Uhrík (ESN), Milan Mazurek (ESN), Nikola Bartůšek (NI), Ondřej Knotek (PfE), Mary Khan (ESN), Volker Schnurrbusch (ESN), Jaak Madison (ECR), Branko Grims (PPE), Petr Bystron (ESN), Roman Haider (PfE), Tom Vandendriessche (PfE), Elisabeth Dieringer (PfE), Markus Buchheit (ESN) Subject:

In January 2026, in Germany, a 25-year-old South Sudanese man known to the police, who had been flown in as part of a resettlement programme, dragged an 18-year-old woman in front of a train, killing her and himself in the process. With the Union Resettlement and Humanitarian Admission Framework Regulation, the EU has, for the first time, created a permanent, harmonised EU system for resettlement and humanitarian admission within the framework of the Pact on Migration and Asylum. This raises the following question: In view of this murder, will the Commission work to have these resettlement programmes run by the EU and the UN suspended immediately throughout the European Union?
at: (English version) to the Commission Alexander Jungbluth (ESN), Marc Jongen (ESN), Irmhild Boßdorf (ESN), Rada Laykova (ESN), Dominik Tarczyński (ECR), Geadis Geadi (ECR), Alexander Sell (ESN), Siegbert Frank Droese (ESN), Barbara Bonte (PfE), Tomasz Froelich (ESN), Petras Gražulis (ESN), Ivan David (ESN), Petar Volgin (ESN), Milan Uhrík (ESN), Milan Mazurek (ESN), Nikola Bartůšek (NI), Ondřej Knotek (PfE), Mary Khan (ESN), Volker Schnurrbusch (ESN), Jaak Madison (ECR), Branko Grims (PPE), Petr Bystron (ESN), Roman Haider (PfE), Tom Vandendriessche (PfE), Elisabeth Dieringer (PfE), Markus Buchheit (ESN) (8 April 2026) Subject: Union Resettlement and Humanitarian Admission Framework Regulation In January 2026, in Germany, a 25-year-old South Sudanese man known to the police, who had been flown in as part of a resettlement programme, dragged an 18-year-old woman in front of a train, killing her and himself in the process. With the Union Resettlement and Humanitarian Admission Framework Regulation, the EU has, for the first time, created a permanent, harmonised EU system for resettlement and humanitarian admission within the framework of the Pact on Migration and Asylum. This raises the following question: In view of this murder, will the Commission work to have these resettlement programmes run by the EU and the UN suspended immediately throughout the European Union? (18 June 2026) The Commission is saddened by this tragic event and deplores any loss of life. Member States engage in resettlement and humanitarian admissions on a voluntary basis, as part of their comprehensive migration strategy. Besides their humanitarian impact, resettlement and humanitarian admissions strengthen partnerships with third countries, including to support the fight against migrant smuggling networks and cooperation on returns. In accordance with Regulation 2024/1350 (1), candidates for resettlement and humanitarian admission who represent a danger to the community, public policy, security or public health or have committed a serious crime shall be refused admission.
Regulation (EU) 2024/1350 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 May 2024 establishing a Union Resettlement and Humanitarian Admission Framework, and amending Regulation (EU) 2021/1147.

E-10-2026-001409.t: Proposed LNG depot in the port of Brindisi and lack of environmental impact assessment
qt: to the Commission Valentina Palmisano (The Left), Giuseppe Antoci (The Left), Mario Furore (The Left), Dario Tamburrano (The Left) Subject:

The Edison SpA project for a coastal LNG depot in the port of Brindisi was authorised by Ministerial Decree No 17487 of 22 August 2022 without undergoing an environmental impact assessment (EIA). The Region of Puglia had approved the project subject to the adoption of technical solutions to enable boil-off gas (BOG) to be fed into the network via a bidirectional connection to methane pipelines, a requirement accepted by Edison and incorporated into the project. This configuration would appear to qualify the depot as a regasification terminal connected to the network. It should thus be subject to an EIA under the national legislation transposing the relevant EU Directive, as confirmed by a ministerial opinion issued in 2023 on a similar plant in the port of Oristano. Moreover, the Brindisi depot is located in an area with establishments – that already exist or are in the process of being authorised – that are classified as major accident risks, yet there has been no assessment of the domino effects in accordance with Directive 2012/18/EU. In view of the above, I would ask the Commission: 1.

Is the authorisation issued by the Italian State, in the absence of a prior EIA, compatible with the EU legislation on environmental assessment for projects that constitute regasification terminals because of their connection to the grid?
Does the failure to examine the domino effects linked to the presence, in the same area, of other plants at risk of major accidents constitute a breach of Directive 2012/18/EU?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.6.2026) The construction of a coastal Liquefied Natural Gas depot in the port of Brindisi by Edison SpA may fall within the scope of Annex II, point 3(c) (Surface storage of natural gas) of the Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) Directive1. Under Article 4(2) of the Directive, ’for projects listed in Annex II, Member States shall determine whether the project shall be made subject to an assessment in accordance with Articles 5 to 10 […]’. The Seveso III Directive2 applies to establishments where dangerous substances may be present in quantities exceeding certain thresholds, thereby qualifying for upper or lower-tier requirements. Member States are required to ensure that operators of such establishments take all necessary measures to prevent major accidents and limit their consequences for human health and the environment. In addition, under Article 9 of the Directive, Member States must identify all Seveso establishments or groups of establishments where the risk or consequences of a major accident may be increased due to potential domino effects. Based on the information available, the Commission cannot confirm whether the authorisation issued by the Italian authorities is compatible with the EIA and Seveso III Directives nor whether a prior EIA was required for the project at stake. National authorities are primarily responsible to ensure compliance with the above EU legislation, particularly the competent national administrative and/or judicial authorities. Without prejudice to its role as guardian of the Treaty, the Commission’s enforcement action regarding bad implementation of EU law focuses mainly on systemic failures3 rather than on individual projects.
1 Directive 2011/92/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 December 2011 on the assessment

of the effects of certain public and private projects on the environment (codification), OJ L 26, 28.1.2012, p. 1– 21, as amended by Directive 2014/52/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 16 April 2014 amending Directive 2011/92/EU on the assessment of the effects of certain public and private projects on the environment, OJ L 124, 25.4.2014, p. 1–18. 2 Directive 2012/18/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 4 July 2012 on the control of majoraccident hazards involving dangerous substances, amending and subsequently repealing Council Directive 96/82/EC, OJ L 197, 24.7.2012, pp. 1–37. 3 Communication from the Commission, EU law: Better results through better application, C/2016/8600, OJ C 18, 19.1.2017, p. 10–20; Communication from the Commission, Enforcing EU law for a Europe that delivers, COM(2022) 518 final, 13.10.2022.

E-10-2026-001408.t: Protecting children from the aggressive promotion on social media of skincare products for adults
qt: to the Commission Giuseppe Antoci (The Left) Subject:

In recent months, a worrying phenomenon has spread across Italy and various Member States: the promotion, via social media platforms and digital marketplaces, of skincare products designed for adults and containing active ingredients, which are also portrayed as being a necessity for young girls and pre-teens. This commercial practice, which is often amplified through child content creators and microinfluencers, is helping to make unrealistic aesthetic patterns the norm at a very early age, thus fuelling the insecurities and anxieties that stem from girls assimilating commercially-induced beauty standards. In addition to the potential dermatological risks to children, this phenomenon raises serious questions in terms of compliance with EU consumer legislation, the protection of minors online and the transparency of commercial communications1. Given the responsibilities incumbent on economic operators2 who use child influencers to promote products intended for an adult public, can the Commission answer the following questions: 1.
What steps will the Commission take to strengthen the protection of minors against the aggressive marketing of cosmetics on social media (e.g. binding EU guidelines or harmonised guidelines)?
Does it not see a need to strengthen the application of the Digital Services Act and EU consumer law to platforms that amplify beauty product content targeting minors?

Will it promote, together with the Member States, specific digital education and body image literacy initiatives with a view to the prevention and monitoring of the phenomenon of aesthetic pressure being applied at an early age?

Particularly the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive (UCPD), along with the Digital Services Act (DSA) and the Audiovisual Media Services Directive (AVMSD). https://www.agcm.it/media/comunicati-stampa/2026/3/PS13110.
at: (English version) to the Commission Giuseppe Antoci (The Left) (8 April 2026) Subject: Protecting children from the aggressive promotion on social media of skincare products for adults In recent months, a worrying phenomenon has spread across Italy and various Member States: the promotion, via social media platforms and digital marketplaces, of skincare products designed for adults and containing active ingredients, which are also portrayed as being a necessity for young girls and pre-teens. This commercial practice, which is often amplified through child content creators and micro-influencers, is helping to make unrealistic aesthetic patterns the norm at a very early age, thus fuelling the insecurities and anxieties that stem from girls assimilating commercially-induced beauty standards. In addition to the potential dermatological risks to children, this phenomenon raises serious questions in terms of compliance with EU consumer legislation, the protection of minors online and the transparency of commercial communications (1). Given the responsibilities incumbent on economic operators (2) who use child influencers to promote products intended for an adult public, can the Commission answer the following questions: 1.
What steps will the Commission take to strengthen the protection of minors against the aggressive marketing of cosmetics on social media (e.g. binding EU guidelines or harmonised guidelines)?
Does it not see a need to strengthen the application of the Digital Services Act and EU consumer law to platforms that amplify beauty product content targeting minors?

Will it promote, together with the Member States, specific digital education and body image literacy initiatives with a view to the prevention and monitoring of the phenomenon of aesthetic pressure being applied at an early age?

(23 June 2026) The Unfair Commercial Practices Directive (UCPD) (1) prohibits misleading and aggressive commercial practices, particularly when they target vulnerable consumers such as minors. Direct exhortation to children to buy products or persuade their parents to buy such products for them is prohibited. Member States’ authorities and courts are responsible for the enforcement of the UCPD. The planned Digital Fairness Act (2) aims to put emphasis on the protection of children as consumers and to address the identified gaps in consumer protection rules, including regarding influencers. The Digital Services Act (3) requires online platforms accessible to minors to provide them with a high level of privacy, safety and security. The Guidelines on the protection of minors (4) serve as an enforcement benchmark regarding this obligation and include measures to shield minors from certain commercial practices. The Influencer Legal Hub (5) is an online knowledge resource for the influencer marketing sector developed by the Commission. qt: to the Commission Pernando Barrena Arza (The Left), Jaume Asens Llodrà (Verts/ALE) Subject:

In Colombia, particularly in territories, such as the Lower Atrato, which are controlled by illegal armed actors, there has been growing concern about the social and community impacts associated with the carbon credit market. Various projects are being formalised through very long-term contracts without full guarantees of free, prior and informed consent, with a lack of education and transparency, and with intermediation that concentrates economic benefits outside the territories. These dynamics are reportedly generating internal divisions in indigenous and Afro-descendant communities, weakening territorial governance and reproducing extractive logics in contexts affected by violence and armed control. Given the EU’s role in climate action and the growing participation of private actors in carbon markets, it is pertinent to clarify how the Commission assesses and manages the risk to human rights associated with these initiatives. 1.

What specific monitoring, traceability and control mechanisms are being applied by the Commission to ensure that European companies that are operating or brokering in voluntary or regulated carbon markets do not contribute directly or indirectly to land grabbing, community fragmentation or armed conflict?
How are these risks being integrated into the mandatory due diligence systems provided for by the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive and the Global Gateway investment plan?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.6.2026) There are no particular EU rules that would apply specifically to ‘companies that are operating or brokering in the voluntary or regulated carbon [credits] markets’, beyond those that apply to all companies regardless of their sector of activity. The Directive on corporate sustainability due diligence1, which will fully apply mid-2029, will require large companies to identify and address adverse human rights and environmental impacts in their own operations, those of their subsidiaries and in their (global) value chains. Non-compliance is subject to supervisory enforcement and civil liability under national law. Each Member State must designate independent supervisory authorities responsible for monitoring and enforcing compliance with the due diligence obligations. The Commission is not a supervisory authority, but it will support consistent application of the Directive, notably via the European Network of Supervisory Authorities and guidance. Under the Global Gateway strategy2, individual investment projects need to be aligned with the strategy’s scope and principles, as well as partner country policy objectives. The recently launched investment hub is a main channel to receive project proposals from the EU private sector in helping implement the strategy. Such projects must first fulfil a number of eligibility criteria3 that help cover the risks mentioned before the Commission may intervene. Through the Global Gateway’s 360 degree approach, the Commission aims to foster sustainable, high quality investment that promotes robust standards, including respect for human rights through the systematic application of a human rights-based approach.
1 Directive (EU) 2024/1760 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 June 2024 on corporate

sustainability due diligence, as amended by Directives (EU) 2025/794 and (EU) 2026/470. 2 Joint Communication ‘The Global Gateway’, JOIN/2021/30 final. 3 https://international-partnerships.ec.europa.eu/document/download/34480961-b492-483f-9e5618d76b30a7b4_en?filename=investment-hub-eligibility-criteria_en.pdf.

E-10-2026-001406.t: EU response to Knesset legislation on death penalty
qt: to the Commission Vlad Vasile-Voiculescu (Renew), Evin Incir (S&D), Cecilia Strada (S&D), Brando Benifei (S&D), Lynn Boylan (The Left), Cristina Guarda (Verts/ALE), Benedetta Scuderi (Verts/ALE), Irena Joveva (Renew), Catarina Martins (The Left), Maria Ohisalo (Verts/ALE), Saskia Bricmont (Verts/ALE), Pierre Jouvet (S&D), Daniel Attard (S&D), Mounir Satouri (Verts/ALE), Villy Søvndal (Verts/ALE), Rasmus Nordqvist (Verts/ALE), Hana Jalloul Muro (S&D), Leoluca Orlando (Verts/ALE), Lucia Annunziata (S&D), Alessandra Moretti (S&D), Matjaž Nemec (S&D), Marc Botenga (The Left), Barry Andrews (Renew), Abir Al-Sahlani (Renew), Kim Van Sparrentak (Verts/ALE) Subject:

We are writing regarding the Knesset’s adoption of the Death Penalty Bill. We note the statement of 31 March 2026 by the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy on behalf of the EU about the Knesset’s approval of the Death Penalty Bill. However, following the law’s final adoption, we believe that Parliament is entitled to clarity on the concrete steps the Commission and the European External Action Service now intend to take to uphold EU values in relations with Israel. 1.

In the light of the bill’s adoption and the 2025 review finding indications of a breach of Article 2 of the EU-Israel Association Agreement, will the Commission activate concrete follow-up measures, such as those presented during the 2025 State of the Union address?
When will the Commission propose a ban on the import of settlement goods into the EU?
Will the Commission present to Parliament, in the next three months, its assessment of whether the current framework governing EU-Israel relations remains fit for purpose?

We, Members of the European Parliament, stress that the EU must make clear that this law must not be implemented and that any move towards implementation must trigger serious consequences for EU-Israel relations.

E-10-2026-001405.t: Competitiveness implications of CO₂ standards for passenger cars and light commercial vehicles
qt: to the Commission Beatrice Timgren (ECR) Subject:

The EU’s regulatory framework for reducing CO₂ emissions in the automotive sector, notably Regulation (EU) 2019/631 as amended by Regulation (EU) 2023/8511, sets increasingly stringent targets for the share of zero-emission vehicles in new car sales. At the same time, market developments indicate that demand for electric vehicles in several Member States remains below the levels required to meet these targets. This occurs in a context of insufficient charging infrastructure, high energy prices in Europe and increasing global competition, notably from China and the United States. In this context, the Commission has presented an initiative to amend the existing framework as part of its Automotive Package2 of December 2025. Against this background: 1.
How does the Commission intend to ensure that the current targets remain achievable in practice, beyond the adjustments proposed in the Automotive Package of December 2025?
Has the Commission assessed the risk that manufacturers may be forced to reduce overall vehicle sales, and what would be the implications for employment and investment in the EU?

How does the Commission ensure that the framework, including its proposed revision, does not undermine the global competitiveness of the European automotive industry, including in the light of differing national energy mixes?

at: (English version) to the Commission Beatrice Timgren (ECR) (8 April 2026) Subject: Competitiveness implications of CO2 standards for passenger cars and light commercial vehicles The EU’s regulatory framework for reducing CO 2 emissions in the automotive sector, notably Regulation (EU) 2019/631 as amended by Regulation (EU) 2023/851 (1), sets increasingly stringent targets for the share of zero-emission vehicles in new car sales. The flexibilities will also allow for plug-in hybrids, range extenders, mild hybrids, and internal combustion engine vehicles to still play a role beyond 2035.
