qt: to the Commission Ilhan Kyuchyuk (Renew) Subject:

The continued Russian aggression against Ukraine and the EU’s sanctions regime targeting the Russian Federation, particularly in the energy sector, have fundamentally reshaped the EU’s energy landscape. At the same time, the escalating conflict in the Middle East and the disruption of maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz are exerting additional pressure on global energy markets, further exposing the EU’s structural vulnerabilities and external dependencies. These overlapping crises raise critical questions regarding the adequacy, pace and coherence of the EU’s energy transition and security policies. In the light of the above: 1.

Does the Commission envisage an accelerated and comprehensive strategy for achieving strategic autonomy in the field of energy, including a decisive diversification of supply sources and routes and a substantial scaling-up of domestic energy production capacities within the EU?

To what extent is the Commission considering a recalibration of existing policy frameworks, including the European Green Deal, in order to better reflect current geopolitical realities while ensuring energy security, affordability and industrial competitiveness?

Is the Commission prepared to adopt a more technologically neutral approach by reassessing the role of shale gas, nuclear energy and, where necessary, the temporary reactivation or extension of coal-based energy capacities, as part of a pragmatic and resilient energy mix during periods of acute external disruption?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (12.6.2026) The Commission is committed to strengthening the EU’s energy independence. The energy transition is an opportunity for the EU to reduce dependence on fossil fuel imports, shifting to homegrown energy sources. With REPowerEU1, the EU committed to end Russian fossil fuel dependency. In addition, the actions set out in AccelerateEU will help shelter EU citizens and industries from volatile global energy markets. The crisis in the Middle East highlighted once more that Europe’s dependency on fossil fuel imports creates vulnerability that comes at a price. It clearly confirms that long-term affordability depends on accelerating the clean energy transition. Scaling up domestic clean energy and energy efficiency will reduce fossil fuel imports and strengthen industrial competitiveness. The upcoming Electrification Action Plan will lay out concrete actions that serve these goals together with actions on heating and cooling and geothermal energy. The EU’s approach to technology neutrality in the energy sector is guided by the principle of allowing the market to determine the least-cost solution to achieve policy goals to achieve climate neutrality by 20502. This principle is underpinned by the right of Member States to choose their energy mix, as per Article 194 (2) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union.
1 COM(2022) 230 final and Regulation (EU) 2026/261. 2 As set out in the European Climate Law (Regulation (EU) 2021/119) and governed by the Governance
Regulation (EU) 2018/1999.

E-10-2026-001403.t: EU energy security, inflationary pressures and economic resilience in relation to the tensions in the Strait of Hormuz
qt: to the Commission Ilhan Kyuchyuk (Renew) Subject:

The escalation of tensions in the Middle East and the growing risks for shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, via which a significant proportion of the world’s oil supply transits, have raised serious concerns over the energy security of the European Union. There has already been a significant increase in oil and fuel prices, which has heightened inflationary pressures and created fresh economic problems for households and businesses. In this connection, at the initiative of the UK, around 35 countries are discussing coordinated diplomatic – and potentially military – measures to restore freedom of navigation and ensure supplies. In light of these developments and the need for a coordinated European response: 1.

Does the Commission have a comprehensive and coordinated strategy for EU participation in the international efforts to ensure freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, including through diplomatic, economic and – if necessary – other means?

What concrete extraordinary measures is the Commission contemplating in the short term to limit fuel price increases and contain rising inflationary pressures, including through the use of strategic reserves and coordinated fiscal and regulatory initiatives?

What medium-term policies is the Commission planning to protect the competitiveness of the European economy, and particularly small and medium-sized enterprises and energy-intensive industries, and to strengthen the Union’s strategic autonomy and resilience in the event of geopolitical shocks such as these?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (16.6.2026) The EU continues to urge all involved to fully respect the free and safe passage through the Strait of Hormuz, in line with international law, as reflected in the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS). The EU remains committed to safeguarding freedom of navigation and the security of global maritime trade routes. As set out in AccelerateEU1, the Commission will help Member States protect consumers from price shocks by assisting in the design of timely, targeted, and temporary measures including price intervention, income support schemes and tax incentives. It will also facilitate the coordination of national action on gas storage filling and on possible oil stock releases, including of jet fuel and diesel. The Commission's medium to long-term strategy is based on homegrown clean energy, resilient grids, flexibility, interconnections and energy efficiency which would allow further electrification in end use sectors and reduction of fossil fuel products use and imports. In line with the Competitiveness Compass2, this approach ultimately protects the competitiveness of the European economy by addressing the root cause of unaffordability, which is fossil fuels dependence, whose cost amounted to EUR 340 billion for the EU in 2025. These considerations will also inform the Commission’s 2026 European Semester Spring Package, which will address relevant fiscal decisions under the economic governance framework, ensuring that fiscal policies continue to both supporting growth and preserving medium-term debt sustainability.
1 https://energy.ec.europa.eu/strategy/accelerateeu-strengthen-eu-energy-resilience_en. 2 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:52025DC0030.

E-10-2026-001402.t: Paintball marker guns use against protesters in Iran
qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Danuše Nerudová (PPE), Daniel Attard (S&D) Subject:

Recent reports and open-source investigations indicate that Iranian security forces have used so-called paintball marker guns to identify, target and seriously injure protesters. Although these devices are marketed as recreational sporting equipment, evidence suggests that they can be modified to fire harder projectiles and are being systematically used as tools of repression by units linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and Basij forces. Furthermore, the range of models identified appears to be limited and traceable to a small number of manufacturers, including companies operating in North America and Europe, as well as hunting cartridges produced by the French-Italian ammunition manufacturer Cheddite. Concerns have also been raised about possible indirect supply chains involving intermediaries and distributors. In the light of the above: 1.
Does the Commission consider paintball marker guns and similar equipment to fall under the category of goods that might be used for internal repression under Council Regulation (EU) No 267/20121?
Is the Commission aware of any exports, direct or indirect, from EU-based companies, including through non-EU intermediaries, of such equipment to Iran since 2022?
Does the Commission intend to assess whether such equipment should be explicitly listed under the EU regime on goods used for internal repression?
Council Regulation (EU) No 267/2012 of 23 March 2012 concerning restrictive measures against Iran (OJ L 88, 24.3.2012, p. 1, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2012/267/oj).
at: (English version) to the Vice-President of the Commission/High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Danuše Nerudová (PPE), Daniel Attard (S&D) (8 April 2026) Subject: Paintball marker guns use against protesters in Iran Recent reports and open-source investigations indicate that Iranian security forces have used so-called paintball marker guns to identify, target and seriously injure protesters. Although these devices are marketed as recreational sporting equipment, evidence suggests that they can be modified to fire harder projectiles and are being systematically used as tools of repression by units linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and Basij forces. Furthermore, the range of models identified appears to be limited and traceable to a small number of manufacturers, including companies operating in North America and Europe, as well as hunting cartridges produced by the French-Italian ammunition manufacturer Cheddite. Concerns have also been raised about possible indirect supply chains involving intermediaries and distributors. In the light of the above: 1.
Does the Commission consider paintball marker guns and similar equipment to fall under the category of goods that might be used for internal repression under Council Regulation (EU) No 267/2012 (1)?
Is the Commission aware of any exports, direct or indirect, from EU-based companies, including through non-EU intermediaries, of such equipment to Iran since 2022?
Does the Commission intend to assess whether such equipment should be explicitly listed under the EU regime on goods used for internal repression?

(10 June 2026) Specific restrictions concerning the export of internal repression items to Iran are addressed within Council Regulation (EU) No 359/2011 concerning restrictive measures directed against certain persons, entities and bodies in view of the situation in Iran (1). Council Regulation (EU) 2021/821 (Dual-Use Regulation) (2) controls the export of dual-use goods as listed in Annex I of the regulation and restricts the export of items not listed in Annex I, but which Member States nevertheless suspect might be used for internal repression. Member States could therefore prevent the export of paintball marker guns should they suspect intended use for internal repression. The Commission is not aware of the export by EU-based companies of such equipment to Iran since 2022. Based on the above, the Commission does not see the immediate need to amend the framework to include an explicit mention of paintball marker guns and similar equipment.

E-10-2026-001401.t: The need to improve the EU Taxonomy Regulation in order to safeguard the competitiveness of European industry
qt: to the Commission Piotr Müller (ECR) Subject:

It is clear from the latest proposed amendments to the delegated acts for the EU Taxonomy Regulation that the Commission is effectively acknowledging that the existing technical criteria were overly complex, difficult to apply and disconnected from economic realities. At the same time, the repeated adjustments to these rules raise serious doubts about the quality of the original impact assessments and the influence of intense lobbying by certain Member States and technologically privileged sectors. As a result, the current framework not only fails to ensure technological neutrality, but also hinders the development of a broad industrial base in the EU and limits the competitiveness of European companies vis-à-vis global competitors operating in a more predictable and pragmatic regulatory environment. In light of the above: 1.

How does the Commission explain the fact that further significant adjustments are needed to a system that was supposed to be a stable and reliable tool for targeting investments, and what flaws in its original design have been identified?

How does the Commission intend to guarantee genuine technological neutrality and limit the influence of Member States’ vested interests in the design of the criteria, so that they do not favour certain industrial models over others?

Is the Commission planning to carry out a more thorough review of the taxonomy with a view to making it simpler and more realistic, so that it supports the restoration of European industry’s competitiveness and does not act as a barrier to productive investment in the EU?
at: (English version) to the Commission Piotr Müller (ECR) (8 April 2026) Subject: The need to improve the EU Taxonomy Regulation in order to safeguard the competitiveness of European industry It is clear from the latest proposed amendments to the delegated acts for the EU Taxonomy Regulation that the Commission is effectively acknowledging that the existing technical criteria were overly complex, difficult to apply and disconnected from economic realities. At the same time, the repeated adjustments to these rules raise serious doubts about the quality of the original impact assessments and the influence of intense lobbying by certain Member States and technologically privileged sectors. As a result, the current framework not only fails to ensure technological neutrality, but also hinders the development of a broad industrial base in the EU and limits the competitiveness of European companies vis-à-vis global competitors operating in a more predictable and pragmatic regulatory environment. In light of the above: 1.

How does the Commission explain the fact that further significant adjustments are needed to a system that was supposed to be a stable and reliable tool for targeting investments, and what flaws in its original design have been identified?

How does the Commission intend to guarantee genuine technological neutrality and limit the influence of Member States’ vested interests in the design of the criteria, so that they do not favour certain industrial models over others?

Is the Commission planning to carry out a more thorough review of the taxonomy with a view to making it simpler and more realistic, so that it supports the restoration of European industry’s competitiveness and does not act as a barrier to productive investment in the EU?

(9 June 2026) Regulation (EU) 2020/852 (1) (‘Taxonomy Regulation’) remained stable since 2020. The regulation itself does not need significant adjustments. One of the areas in which the Commission deemed necessary to introduce adjustments is the technical screening criteria to identify if an activity is Taxonomy-aligned. These technical screening criteria are included in Delegated Acts, which are designed to be updated when needed. Article 19(5) of the Taxonomy Regulation empowers the Commission to regularly review the technical screening criteria. For certain criteria, the regulation provides a maximum time limit of 3 years for their reviews, highlighting the evolving nature of the system. The Commission is currently reviewing the criteria, while keeping the level of environmental ambition. The simplified criteria should benefit European corporates, facilitate their access to sustainable finance and drive their competitiveness. Article 19(1)(a) of the Taxonomy Regulation requires the Commission to ensure that the criteria respect the principle of technological neutrality. In this context, the Taxonomy Regulation enables the Commission to revise or complement the criteria to take into account future innovations and environmental or economic progress. The Commission is not planning a thorough review of the Taxonomy Regulation. The Commission is currently revising the screening criteria to make them simpler and more usable and meaningful in supporting EU businesses in their access to finance. It is important to underscore that the Taxonomy framework does not impose any requirement on EU businesses to align their economic activities to the Taxonomy screening criteria.

Regulation (EU) 2020/852 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 18 June 2020 on the establishment of a framework to facilitate sustainable investment, and amending Regulation (EU) 2019/2088 (OJ L 198, 22.6.2020, p. 13, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2020/852/oj).

E-10-2026-001400.t: Non-recognition of degree from institution recognised by the European Higher Education Area
qt: to the Commission Michalis Hadjipantela (PPE) Subject:

The Cyprus Council for the Recognition of Higher Education Qualifications does not recognise a higher education qualification awarded by Staffordshire University, a university recognised by other Member States and an institution recognised by the European Higher Education Area (EHEA). The refusal is based on the fact that the programme of study is delivered, in whole or in part, through a partner institution in Cyprus. However, according to the case law of the Court of Justice of the European Union, notably in Cases C-153/02 (Neri v European School of Economics)1 and C-274/05 (Commission v Hellenic Republic)2, the decisive factor for recognition should be the awarding institution rather than the place, or mode of delivery, of the studies. In this context: 1.
Does the Commission consider that such a refusal is compatible with Articles 49 and 56 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union?
Has the Commission identified similar practices in other Member States concerning qualifications delivered through franchised or validated arrangements?
Can the Commission take action, including infringement procedures, to ensure compliance with EU law and the principles of mutual recognition within the EHEA?

Judgment of the Court of Justice of 13 November 2003, Valentina Neri v European School of Economics (ESE Insight World Education System Ltd), Case C-153/02, ECLI:EU:C:2003:614. Judgment of the Court of Justice of 23 October 2008, Commission of the European Communities v Hellenic Republic, Case C-274/05, ECLI:EU:C:2008:585.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (10.6.2026) The European Higher Education Area (EHEA) was created under the intergovernmental Bologna Process, which comprises 47 countries cooperating on a voluntary basis. Therefore, it is not regulated by EU law and falls within the exclusive sphere of competence of the signatory countries. Whilst recognition based on robust quality assurance is the core of the EHEA, it is an obligation of Member States to oversee its implementation. Moreover, Article 165(1) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU) provides that the EU shall contribute to the development of quality education by encouraging cooperation between Member States while fully respecting ‘the responsibility of the Member States for the content of teaching and the organisation of education systems’, including recognition of degrees for the purpose of further learning (academic recognition of qualifications). It also applies to cases where qualifications are delivered through franchised or validated arrangements. Finally, based on the available information, Staffordshire University is a university in the United Kingdom – a third country in relation to the EU. The initial recognition of a degree from a third country falls under the competence of the Member State in which the recognition application is submitted. The Commission has no authority to intervene in case of refusal by the Member State to recognise third country qualifications. Articles 49 and 56 TFEU do not apply in the present case.

E-10-2026-001399.t: Illegal quarrying in the occupied areas of Cyprus
qt: to the Commission Michalis Hadjipantela (PPE) Subject:

The Commission has already acknowledged that quarrying activities in the occupied areas of Cyprus do not adhere to EU environmental, health and safety regulations, resulting in serious environmental degradation. The Commission’s Directorate-General for Regional and Urban Policy further confirmed in August 2025 that neither the Republic of Cyprus nor the Commission can verify, monitor or enforce compliance with environmental and safety standards in the occupied north. Despite this, no enforcement action has been taken. The Pentadaktylos mountain range is subject to ongoing uncontrolled extraction. Quarry operators in the Republic of Cyprus bear the full burden of EU regulatory compliance, creating a distortion of competition. The imminent opening of new crossing points risks increasing the flow of non-compliant aggregates. 1.

Given the Commission’s admission that it cannot verify compliance with Article 4(1) of Regulation (EC) No 866/2004, does it consider that the legal conditions for permitting aggregates to cross the Green Line are met?
What concrete enforcement steps does the Commission intend to take to tackle the unfair competition faced by economic operators working in areas controlled by the Republic?
Does the Commission intend to make the provision of support to the Turkish Cypriot community conditional on compliance to ensure that EU rules are not violated by those receiving it?
at: on behalf of the European Commission (22.5.2026) The Commission would like to refer to its position, as already detailed in the replies to written questions E-002402/20251 E-001687/20242 and E-2244/20173. The Commission is aware of the quarrying activities in the Pentadaktylos mountains and continues to follow developments closely. It regularly engages with the Turkish Cypriot community to stress the importance of applying appropriate conservation measures and protect this environmentally sensitive area, as well as facilitating the alignment of legal frameworks with the EU environmental standards. The allegations concerning non-compliance by individual quarrying operators cannot be confirmed or refuted by the Commission. The principles of good administration preclude the adoption of restrictive measures in the absence of substantiated evidence. All goods traded across the Green Line must comply with the requirements of the EU acquis concerning their placement on the EU market4. Pursuant to Protocol 10 of the 2003 Act of Accession5, the EU acquis in the areas of the Republic of Cyprus in which the government of the Republic of Cyprus does not exercise effective control is suspended. The Commission will continue to support environmental protection and the preservation of Cyprus’ sensitive natural areas. Moreover, it remains fully committed to a comprehensive settlement of the Cyprus issue to the benefit of all Cypriots.

E-10-2026-001398.t: Protection of religious freedom and possible discrimination in the field of European sports competitions
qt: to the Commission Susanna Ceccardi (PfE), Aldo Patriciello (PfE), Silvia Sardone (PfE) Subject:

The press has recently reported the case of a penalty imposed by UEFA on a football club for its fans having created a large choreographed display (tifo) of a traditional Christian image1. According to the reports, the penalty was imposed on the grounds of this being an alleged violation of UEFA’s rules as regards ‘inappropriate messages’, which has triggered broad public debate on what could be perceived as the differential treatment of religious symbols, and of Christian symbols in particular. This episode would also appear highly controversial in view of the Judeo-Christian roots that form an integral part of Europe’s historical and cultural identity. The displaying of religious symbols of a Christian nature that are by no means offensive or violent is not an ‘inappropriate message’, but a legitimate expression of religious and cultural freedom. It follows, therefore, that the handing down of a penalty is disproportionate and potentially discriminatory. In light of the above, can the Commission answer the following questions: 1.
Is the Commission aware of the events described and has it conducted any checks into them?

Does it not feel that any penalising of Christian religious symbols may constitute a form of discrimination within the meaning of Article 10 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union?

Will the Commission promote guidelines and initiatives to ensure respect for Christian religious freedom, including in sports competitions organised by private bodies of European relevance, such as UEFA?
https://www.ilgiornale.it/news/politica/identit-cristiana-bandita-anche-dai-campi-calcio-2644785.html
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (29.6.2026) The Commission remains committed to protecting the values and fundamental rights enshrined in Article 2 of the Treaty on European Union and the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union1 which guarantees freedom of thought, conscience, and religion (Article 10), and prohibits discrimination on the grounds of religion (Article 21). The Commission also promotes these principles with sport stakeholders, who remain autonomous in how they govern sport. In particular, Article 1(3) of the Arrangement for Cooperation between the European Commission and the Union of European Football Associations2 (UEFA), states that the two sides are committed to strengthening their partnership to support and promote European values with a focus on Europe’s greatest challenges and the EU’s strategic objectives, particularly in sport and other specific areas of mutual interest and relevance.

E-10-2026-001397.t: Attacks against Orthodox Christians in Syria
qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Yannis Maniatis (S&D) Subject:

Over the last few days, there have been continuous attacks on the city of Suqaylabiyah – a city with a predominantly Orthodox population. Syria has always been a state with a rich multicultural identity, in which Muslims (Sunni and Shia), Kurds, Druze, Christians of various denominations, Armenians and other minorities have coexisted. Unfortunately, the interim government does not seem to share this conviction in practice, as in recent months we have seen a significant increase in attacks against religious and ethnic minorities, often with the support – if not the participation – of government-aligned forces. As Orthodox Christians prepare to celebrate Easter, and bearing in mind that the European Union is one of Syria’s principal donors, will the Vice-President of the Commission/High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy say: 1.
What will she do to protect Syria’s multicultural character and its religious and ethnic minorities, in particular Orthodox Christians, who face constant persecution?
Is she willing to impose new sanctions if the interim government continues to allow and support the attacks against them?
Is she committed to ensuring that any financial or other support for the regime in Syria is conditional on the protection of all religious and ethnic minorities?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (15.6.2026) Since the historic shift in the country in December 2024, the EU has actively supported Syria through every stage of their challenging transition. The EU’s strategy is founded on the belief that lasting peace and stability can only be achieved through an inclusive transition that meets the aspirations of Syrians from all ethnic and religious backgrounds without discrimination. The EU also calls upon all involved parties to safeguard Syria’s diverse cultural heritage and religious sites. In response to the documented incidents, the EU persists in calling for thorough investigations and ensuring that all those responsible for violence in Syria are held to account. Within its discussions with Syria’s transitional authorities, the EU reiterates that this is instrumental for pursuing national reconciliation and an inclusive transition. During their visit to Syria, the Presidents of the European Council and the Commission unveiled a new EU-Syria Political Partnership1, designed to support the political transition, national reconciliation and reconstruction. On 11 May 2026, the EU held its first High-Level Political Dialogue with Syria in Brussels, where inter alia the need to ensure a genuinely inclusive process for sustainable reconciliation and restoring Syria’s rich social fabric was underscored. The EU remains vigilant about the respect for human rights of all Syrians and will continue to support comprehensive accountability efforts for all perpetrators regardless of their affiliation. In May2 and June3 2025, the EU introduced new listings against human rights violators and will continue monitoring the situation on the ground and the follow up of the commitments of the transitional authorities. Protecting the rights of most vulnerable ethnic and religious communities is essential to ensuring social cohesion, preventing further sectarian divisions, and laying the foundations for a sustainable and inclusive peace, as reiterated in the Council conclusions of 18 December 20254.

E-10-2026-001396.t: Unfair practices by the US regarding PDO products
qt: to the Commission Yannis Maniatis (S&D) Subject:

According to a report by the Wall Street Journal, the Trump administration is pressuring nonEU countries—even if they have a trade agreement with the European Union that guarantees the protection of European Protected Designation of Origin (PDO) products, such as Greek feta cheese and other similar products—to allow the import of American products with the same name. Although these American products have similar names to their European counterparts, they have neither the same raw materials nor the same manufacturing method, factors that give them their special character and taste. Consequently, the use of these names would lead to a complete violation of the regime to protect them, allowing unfair competition from cheaper and lower-quality non-authentic products, leading to consumers being misled. Bearing in mind that PDO products constitute the export ‘flagship’ of the European and Greek agri-food sector: 1.
What is the Commission doing to address these unfair US trade practices, particularly with regard to countries with which we have concluded trade agreements?
Is this practice consistent with the spirit and letter of the trade agreement signed by the Commission in Turnberry, Scotland?
What sanctions will the Commission take against countries found to be violating— following pressure from the US—the protection regime for European PDO products?

(15 June 2026) The Commission is taking note of the fact that the United States have been negotiating so-called Agreements on Reciprocal Trade (ART) with some third countries which include elements related to geographical indications. The Commission is closely monitoring these agreements, the possible impact that certain provisions might have, in particular with regard to third countries with which the European Union has concluded agreements that protect EU geographical indications, and assessing, on a case-by-case basis, the solutions available in full respect of the Agreement on Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights (TRIPS) of the World Trade Organisation and bilateral commitments. E-10-2026-001395.t: Suspension of the Diakopto-Kalavryta Rack Railway
qt: to the Commission Yannis Maniatis (S&D) Subject:

The Greek Government recently suspended the operation of the Diakopto-Kalavryta Rack Railway, 130 years after its commencement. This specific choice raises serious issues of compliance with the European acquis for transport safety, the resilience of infrastructure and the protection of areas of high environmental value. Despite the recording of several incidences of landslides, especially after the fires of 2023, and related scientific warnings, no plan for anti-corrosion protection and reinforcing the line has been implemented, while a multitude of technical failures and serious safety incidents have been recorded. The complete suspension of the Odontotos railway, without a clear timetable for its restoration and without making use of existing studies and European funds, creates risks of obsolescence of this investment and significantly burdens the local economy, tourism and social cohesion. In view of the above: 1.

How does the Commission assess Greece's compliance with its European obligations for rail transport safety and infrastructure resilience, given the complete suspension of a transport infrastructure co-financed by the EU in an economically vulnerable mountainous region without a clear restoration plan?

How does the Commission ensure that the European funds, amounting to approximately EUR 45 million, spent on the upgrade of the line do not go to waste due to inadequate maintenance and risk management?

Given that the area falls under the NATURA 2000 regime, are the obligations of prevention, restoration and protection against natural hazards affecting critical infrastructures considered to have been met?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.6.2026) 1. Based on available data, the Commission understands that the Diakopto – Kalavryta rack railway is a historic or touristic railway. As foreseen by Article 2(3)(b) of Directive (EU) 2016/7981 and Article 1(4)(b) of Directive (EU) 2016/7972, most Member States, including Greece, decided not to apply measures implementing these Directives to infrastructure and vehicles reserved for strictly local, historical or tourist use. The Commission is therefore unable to take a position in relation to the question posed by the Honourable Member as the functioning of historic and touristic railways is governed by national rules. 2. The project ‘Upgrade of the Diakopto – Kalavryta Railway Line’ was co-funded under the operational programme ‘Western Greece’ 2000–2006, with an EU contribution of EUR 8 336 627. Cohesion policy funds do not cover operational and infrastructure maintenance costs. Recognising the importance of the resilience of infrastructure projects, Regulation (EU) 2021/10603 foresees that adequate mechanisms for climate proofing of infrastructure investments should be a part of implementation of the funds for the financing period 2021-2027. The Greek authorities have informed the Commission that the Region of Western Greece is to finance the preparatory studies for the reopening of the railway by its own resources. 3. To enhance the protection of critical infrastructure, the EU has adopted Directive (EU) 2022/25574, that takes all-hazards approach, accounting for both man-made and natural risks, and covers 11 sectors, including transport. By July 2026, Member States must identify their critical entities, and once identified, these entities will have to step up their resilience according to the Directive’s standards.

qt: to the Commission Yannis Maniatis (S&D) Subject:

One of the most significant consequences of the war in Iran is the disruption to fuel supply chains – affecting aviation fuel in particular. Already in the very first days of the war, fuel prices were soaring, with many airlines hiking up fares. In addition, there have also been significant problems affecting the supply of aviation fuel, forcing many airlines to cancel thousands of flights. Although at first these problems mainly affected countries in Asia, as the war went on, Europe began to experience its first problems as well, with at least six Italian airports facing significant shortages. Given that we are at the start of the tourist season, when air transport – particularly in Europe – is expected to increase significantly, can the Commission say: 1.
Is there a supply problem in Europe and what measures does it intend to take to ensure that there is no shortage in the coming months?

Has it calculated the possible impact on tourism resulting from increases in the cost of flight tickets or flight restrictions, particularly for countries such as Greece, which is heavily dependent on aviation-based tourism?
What measures does it intend to take to address the economic impact on the tourism sector?

What measures does it intend to take to address the economic impact on the tourism sector?

(12 June 2026) 1. As of today, there is no fuel shortage in the EU and the market is currently stable. The Commission is conducting an EU wide assessment concerning any potential supply issues, preparing for possible coordinated emergency stock releases in the Oil Coordination Group, and maximising EU refinery output, as outlined in the communication AccelerateEU (1). That communication also provides regulatory flexibility for airlines to manage any potential localised supply tightness without disrupting flight schedules. 2. Impacts on tourism resulting from increased cost of flight tickets or flight restrictions have thus far been limited. T he Commission is monitoring the situation together with Member States, international organisations and industry associations. Southern Europe could benefit from a tourism substitution effect, with European travelers replacing long-haul travel with internal short-haul trips. Such intra-European travel can involve lower spending and shorter stays. 3. The Commission has been in contact with Member States to discuss and coordinate an approach to address the situation. A coordinated network of Member States representatives is being set-up, as well as a crisis coordination industry group which will meet as required. Both groups together with the Commission will also aim to assess the impact on the tourism sector and possible measures to be taken, if needed.

E-10-2026-001393.t: Possible breach of the principles of impartial dissemination of, and fair access to, official statistics in Spain
qt: to the Commission Dolors Montserrat (PPE) Subject:

The EU legislation governing the European Statistical System, including Regulation (EU) 2019/2152 and the European Statistics Code of Practice, lays down fundamental principles such as professional independence, impartiality, reliability and, in particular, the simultaneous and fair dissemination of statistical information. However, on 6 April 2026, the Spanish Prime Minister publicly disseminated, through social media and other channels, social security affiliation data before its official publication scheduled in the statistical calendar. Those actions could constitute a violation of the information embargo and of the principles of impartial dissemination. In view of the above: 1.
Does the Commission consider the early dissemination of statistical data by political leaders to breach the European Statistics Code of Practice?

What monitoring and, where appropriate, sanctioning mechanisms are in place at EU level to ensure that Member States comply with those principles, as well as to prevent the politicised use of official statistics prior to their formal publication?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (2.6.2026) The Spanish social security affiliation data referred to by the Honourable Member are national administrative data. Eurostat does not have any role in overseeing the management and use of such administrative data, which falls under the sole responsibility of the Member State. Concerning European official statistics, the Commission continuously monitors compliance by Member States with Union law. The statistical principles mentioned by the Honourable Member are contained in Regulation (EC) No 223/2009 on European statistics1. Those principles are further elaborated in the European Statistics Code of Practice2, a self-regulatory quality framework under which the EU and national statistical authorities operate.

The policy paper ‘A stronger EU engagement for a peaceful, sustainable and prosperous Arctic’ of 13 October 2021 (JOIN(2021) 27 final)1 puts the focus of EU Arctic policy on sustainability and multilateral cooperation. E-10-2026-001391.t: Preventive measures against possible attacks on flotillas heading to Gaza
qt: to the Commission Jaume Asens Llodrà (Verts/ALE) Subject:

This year, 2026, the three flotilla organisations – Freedom Flotilla, Madleen Thousands, and Sumud Flotilla – will set sail once again with European citizens aboard. Operating in accordance with the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, they aim to break the Israeli blockade of the Gaza Strip, which has been in place since 2007. They will navigate peacefully in international waters, flying the flags of some EU countries, which, if attacked, would trigger the application of Article 42(7) of the Treaty on European Union. The EU authorities are aware that Israel has already hijacked numerous ships in the Mediterranean, so this should come as no surprise and steps must be taken to prevent it. U.N. Security Council Resolution 2803 does not prohibit maritime aid nor relations with the Palestinian population. In view of the above: 1.
What preventive measures will the Commission take to avert Israeli pirate attacks?
What action has it taken against Israel following the attacks in 2025 and before?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (21.5.2026) The EU shares the aim of delivering urgent humanitarian aid to Gaza and ending the suffering of its civilian population. Since the 7th of October 2023, the EU released over EUR 640 million in humanitarian assistance for Palestine, working with trusted partners to ensure aid reaches those most in need. The EU calls for the removal of all restrictions obstructing humanitarian access, in line with international humanitarian law (IHL). The EU has continued to urge Israel to ensure unimpeded aid delivery and compliance with IHL. While the EU respects the humanitarian commitment of the flotilla participants, it discourages such initiatives due to the risks to participants’ safety and the potential for escalation. The freedom of navigation under international law must be upheld, and any use of force against vessels in international waters, including seizures or attacks, is unacceptable. The EU has not received formal requests for assistance from the flotilla organisers, and it has no mandate or assets to escort private vessels. The EU Member States bear responsibility for consular protection and the security of their citizens at sea. Should incidents occur, the EU stands ready to support affected citizens via the EU Civil Protection Mechanism1, to assist member states with any medical evacuation needs.
1 https://civil-protection-humanitarian-aid.ec.europa.eu/what/civil-protection/eu-civil-protection-mechanism_en.

E-10-2026-001390.t: Flexible derogations for the agricultural sector in the light of input market disruptions due to geopolitical tensions
qt: to the Commission Barbara Bonte (PfE) Subject:

Recent geopolitical tensions in Iran are once again disrupting global supply chains and trade flows. Fertilisers, in particular nitrogen inputs, are a clear example of how such disruptions can quickly affect European agricultural production. While overall supply to the EU has not collapsed, repeated crises are exposing its structural fragility. The conflict in Ukraine has already demonstrated how geopolitical shocks can destabilise fertiliser markets and current tensions risk reinforcing this pattern. These recurring disruptions have led to renewed calls for derogations, including those related to manure application, as farmers seek greater flexibility to cope with input uncertainty and shifting market conditions. This volatility highlights the need for a regulatory framework that can respond swiftly to current and future disruptions. In this context: 1.
Does the Commission recognise that repeated geopolitical disruptions are structurally destabilising agricultural input markets, including fertilisers?
Is the Commission willing to introduce faster and more flexible derogation mechanisms to respond to such disruptions?
If not, what alternative measures does the Commission propose to address ongoing market volatility and future supply shocks affecting the agricultural sector?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (19.6.2026) The Commission is aware of the significant pressure that farmers in the EU face due to elevated fertiliser prices. The situation is exacerbated by ongoing tensions in the Middle East. On 19 May 2026, the Commission adopted the Fertiliser Action Plan1, setting out short- and long-term measures to improve fertiliser availability, affordability and resilience. Short term actions include the mobilisation and possible top-up of the agricultural reserve, liquidity support under the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) and greater flexibility for advance payments. Longer term measures focus on strengthening EU production capacity, supporting the uptake of recycled nutrients and low carbon alternatives, and reducing strategic dependencies on imports. Several measures have already been taken, such as the application of reduced flat 1% mark-up for the default Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) values for fertilisers, the adoption of a Temporary State aid framework2 on 29 April 2026, as well as the temporary suspension of duties for imports of ammonia, urea and other nitrogen fertilisers from countries other than Russia and Belarus, within given quotas3. Additionally, in February 2026, the Commission provided further flexibility under the Nitrates Directive for certain types of materials derived from manure processing (RENURE)4. Furthermore, as laid down in the Fertiliser Action Plan, the Commission will explore short term measures to facilitate the use of digestates, such as extending the RENURE Act.

qt: to the Commission Gerald Hauser (PfE) Subject:

The abstract of the study ‘Feeding Next‐Generation Nanomedicines to Europe: Regulatory and Quality Challenges’1 states that, over the past fifty years, many innovative nanomedicines have been developed and put on the market. A globally uniform regulatory definition is still lacking; generally, the term is taken to mean medicinal products developed or manufactured using nanotechnology. In 2006, the European Medicines Agency (EMA) described nanomedicine as a use of nanotechnology for diagnosing, treating or preventing diseases based on specific physical, chemical and biological properties at the nanometer scale. Unlike with conventional medicinal products, the behaviour of nanomedicines within the body is determined primarily by the nanosystem—specifically factors such as size, shape, and surface area. These properties influence uptake, distribution and possible side effects. Owing to their small size, they can penetrate deep into tissue and interact with cells, which can also pose risks that are difficult to predict. 1.
Were COVID-19 vaccines using nanotechnology classified as nanomedicines and, if not, why not?
Did these COVID-19 vaccines undergo all the tests required for nanomedicines?
Have COVID-19 vaccines that are nanomedicines – and for which not all the tests required for nanomedicines were carried out – been withdrawn from the market?
EMA, Reflection Paper on Nanotechnology‐Based Medicinal Products for Human Use, EMEA/CHMP/79769/2006, 2006.

(22 June 2026) The mRNA COVID-19 vaccines Spikevax, Comirnaty and Kostaive are considered nanotechnology-based medicinal products as they contain lipid nanoparticles (LNPs). E-10-2026-001387.t: Inadequate inclusion of women with disabilities in the Gender Equality Strategy 2026-2030
qt: to the Commission Elena Kountoura (The Left) Subject:

26.2 % of women in the EU live with some form of disability1 and experience intersectional discrimination. They are more exposed to poverty and unemployment, as only 20 % work full-time and only 16 % report good health, compared to 50 % and 83 %, respectively, of women without disabilities.2 At the same time, forced sterilisation of women with disabilities is prohibited in only nine Member States.3 However, the new Gender Equality Strategy 2026-2030 does not effectively address these multiple discriminations, as it does not include binding actions and largely ignores the situation of women and girls with disabilities. Having regard to: - the recent statement of the European Disability Forum (EDF), which condemned the fact that the new strategy is limited to a few general references to disability, without substantive measures to address the needs of people with disabilities4, - the provisions of the UNCRPD5, - Article 39 of the Istanbul Convention, which explicitly prohibits forced sterilisation, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

Does it intend to put in place additional initiatives and measures for women and girls with disabilities, with the aim of ensuring reasonable adjustments, enhancing access to health, employment and inclusive education and prohibiting the practice of forced sterilisation within the Union?
Does it intend to develop gender-disaggregated indicators of progress on the rights of persons with disabilities, in line with the UNCRPD, as requested by the European Parliament in its resolution?

Eurostat, hlth_silc_12. Gender Equality Index 2025, EIGE, employment and health sectors. EDF, Forced sterilisation of persons with disabilities in the EU, 09/2022. According to EDF, the new strategy does not address the forced sterilization of women and girls with disabilities, a serious violation of human rights and the CFTEU, which continues to exist in many European countries. Women with disabilities are mentioned only in the Strategy, mainly in general terms. A brief reference is made in the introduction, while in Principle 2 the obstacles to health are recognized, in Principle 5 the increased employment gap and in Principle 6 the difficulties in education, but without any specific measures, actions or political initiatives are foreseen. See UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, in particular Article 6 ‘Women with Disabilities’.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (16.7.2026) The Gender Equality Strategy 2026-20301 sets out measures to advance gender equality for women and men in all their diversity, including women with disabilities. In implementing the Strategy, specific barriers faced by women and girls with disabilities will be addressed. Directive (EU) 2024/1385 on combating violence against women and domestic violence2 ensures that victims of forms of violence against women criminalised under EU or national law can benefit from the support services and redress mechanisms provided for in the Directive. This also includes victims of forced sterilisation where such conduct is criminalised under national law. In the enhanced strategy for the rights of persons with disabilities3, the Commission commits to issuing guidance on the employment of women with disabilities and assessing the provision of reasonable accommodation at the workplace4. Ways to improve quality and accessibility of women’s physical and mental healthcare will be further explored with the World Health Organization5. This builds on recent initiatives, such as the EU4Health Programme project on improving access to care for people with disabilities6. The Commission will launch a study on violence against women with disabilities and will facilitate the development of guidelines on procedural accommodation for victims with disabilities. To improve the disaggregation of data on all grounds of discrimination, the Commission is preparing a Recommendation on equality data to help Member States and other stakeholders to monitor the state of equality in the EU.

E-10-2026-001386.t: Incomplete implementation of co-funded educational programmes and violation of the rights of schoolchildren with disabilities in Greece
qt: to the Commission Elena Kountoura (The Left) Subject:

The implementation of co-funded educational programmes in Greece, especially within the framework of the ESF+ 2021-2027, raises serious issues regarding the effective use of European funds, respect for fundamental rights and equal access to education, especially for pupils with disabilities. According to repeated reports, there are significant delays in the implementation of EUfunded programmes, shortages among teaching staff and support structures and a failure to provide the intended personalised support to pupils with disabilities.1 This situation leads to serious learning gaps, unequal treatment of pupils and the burden shifting to families. The above may constitute a violation of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union and the UNCRPD2, given that the European Structural Funds operate under shared management and national authorities bear the primary responsibility for the proper implementation of these programmes and are primarily responsible for ensuring their compliance with applicable EU regulations.3 In view of the above: 1.
Is the Commission aware of the systematic problems in the implementation of cofinanced educational programmes in Greece, in particular as regards the support of pupils with disabilities?
In light of the above, how does the Commission assess Greece's compliance with its obligations under EU law, European financial rules and fundamental rights in the field of education?
What measures can the Commission take to ensure the full and substantive application of the rights of pupils with disabilities?

The school year began in September, however, the implementation of the co-financed programme ‘Remedial Teaching in Secondary Education, 2025-2026’ began with a three-month delay. As a result, a significant part of the planned remedial teaching has been lost, while, in many school units, Parallel Support for pupils with disabilities is not being provided as planned. Often, the few teachers simultaneously cover pupils in large classes, without full coverage of teaching hours and without the necessary individualised support. See 20253rd Statistical Information Bulletin: Indicators for the access of children and people with disabilities to Education. Articles 14, 21, 24 and 26 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union and Article 24 of the UNCRPD. Given that these programmes are co-financed by European funds, questions arise as to their proper use, the effectiveness of national audit mechanisms and the responsibility of the competent authorities for ensuring compliance with EU law.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (12.6.2026) The Commission monitors compliance with conditionalities1 within the Cohesion Policy programmes monitoring committees2. The implementation of educational programmes cofinanced by the European Social Fund Plus3, including those supporting pupils with disabilities in Greece, are also monitored through regular reporting mechanisms, audits and meetings with national authorities. Issues like delays in programme execution, staff shortages or needs for personalised support are assessed to ensure that the rights of people with disabilities are promoted and protected, while considering Member States' shared management responsibilities for effective and inclusive programme delivery. The Commission recalls that under shared management the national authorities are responsible for ensuring compliance with applicable EU law, including with fundamental rights enshrined in the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union4 throughout the implementation of EU-funded projects. The enhanced Strategy for the rights of persons with disabilities up to 20305 further promotes independent living and accessible educational environments for the full inclusion of persons with disabilities in line with the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities to which the EU and all Member States are parties6. In line with the division of competences in the area of education set out in Article 165 of Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union7, the Commission promotes inclusive education under the European Education Area by fostering mutual learning opportunities, providing policy guidance to Member States, supporting progress towards EU-level targets, and offering funding via Erasmus+ and Cohesion policy funds, with the aim of advancing inclusive practices.

E-10-2026-001385.t: Risks facing the recycled and lead-free brass production sector in Europe
qt: to the Commission Thomas Pellerin-Carlin (S&D) Subject:

Against a backdrop of challenges for European industry, which faces unfair international competition and an unfavourable geopolitical climate, the European Union cannot abandon its industrial base, which is essential to our energy and environmental transition. Energy-intensive sectors, such as metallurgy, play a vital role in this transition. Many sectors are affected, but the Commission must be alerted to the fact that there is a real risk of the recycled and lead-free brass production sector disappearing from the European Union, owing to the economic difficulties faced by HME Brass, which is based in L’Aigle, Normandy. This is the only site within the Hailiang Metal Group producing this alloy, which is essential for certain European industrial value chains. In view of the strategic challenges the Union faces in terms of industrial sovereignty and the resilience of its supply chains: 1.
Is the Commission aware of the situation in this strategic sector?

What measures does it intend to take to support this strategic production within the Union, in particular through the use of available instruments such as State aid compatible with the internal market, public procurement or the integration of this production into major projects of common European interest?

(18 June 2026) The Commission thanks the Honourable Member for drawing its attention to the situation of the recycled and lead-free brass production sector in the EU and, in particular, to the case of HME Brass in L’Aigle, Normandy. The Commission acknowledges the importance of brass production for certain European industrial value chains, as well as more generally the strategic role of non-ferrous metal industries in supporting the EU’s clean transition. This was recognised in the 2025 Steel and Metals Action Plan (1), which includes actions on access to clean and affordable energy; active monitoring of scrap trade, notably to prevent scrap leakage and promotion of investments in high-quality recycling, sorting and treatment of scrap. The Commission is committed to supporting the competitiveness and resilience of strategic industrial sectors in the EU, as recently recognised in the proposal for an Industrial Accelerator Act (2), which promotes streamlined permitting for decarbonisation projects, including upgrades, and enabling conditions for facilities located in prospective acceleration areas. State aid may play an important role in supporting the transformation of industries. For example, the Clean Industrial Deal State Aid Framework (CISAF) (3) facilitates decarbonisation investments. Member States may also support undertakings in difficulty in line with the Rescue and Restructuring Guidelines.

E-10-2026-001384.t: Fears linked to the slowing pace of electrification in Europe
qt: to the Commission Thomas Pellerin-Carlin (S&D) Subject:

In 2009, the European Union set itself the target of reaching 20 % renewables in its energy mix, and reducing greenhouse gas emissions by the same percentage by 2020. The EU met this target thanks to a regulatory framework that was clear and stable over time, and which notably encouraged Member States to move towards decarbonisation and electrification. However, since 2024, we have witnessed the undermining of the existing regulatory framework, which is weakening its capacity to achieve the climate goals for 2030 and 2050 and creating uncertainty for some strategic sectors. For example, the relaxing of measures prohibiting the sale of new internal combustion engine vehicles has led a number of organisations, such as the French electricity transmission network, to revise their electricity demand forecasts downwards. This revision significantly affects the renewable energy sector, in particular the photovoltaic industry, which is seriously threatened by the negative outlook resulting from recent legislative developments. In view of this, what action does the Commission intend to take to protect sectors affected by the revision of the European regulatory framework, which is slowing down electrification in Europe?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (12.6.2026) On 22 April 2026, the Commission adopted AccelerateEU1, a toolbox to bring immediate relief to households and industries following the effects of the conflict in the Middle East, while putting Europe on a pathway to energy independence. The communication includes structural measures to further reduce dependency on volatile fossil fuel markets and build Europe's resilience against future risks based on homegrown clean energy and electrification. In 2024, 71% of the EU’s electricity generation came from clean energy sources, bringing cheap energy to the system. Nevertheless, electricity represents less than a quarter of the final energy consumption2. This provides a clear case to accelerate electrification. In this framework, the Commission has committed to present an Electrification Action Plan, including an ambitious electrification target and addressing horizontal barriers to electrification, as well as sector-specific issues in the industrial, transport and building sectors. Electrification is ramping up quickly in road transport, with more than 8 million battery electric vehicles on EU roads. The Automotive Package3 adopted by the Commission in December 2025 supports the sector’s transition to clean mobility by setting an ambitious yet pragmatic policy framework to ensure 2050 climate neutrality and strategic independence while providing more flexibility to manufacturers. As part of the Package, the proposal amending the CO2 standards for cars and vans Regulation4 enhances technological neutrality while maintaining a clear market signal for electrification which will support continued investment by the EU industry in the transition and safeguard its ability to remain competitive.

E-10-2026-001383.t: Questionable rules governing the application of the politicised EU rule of law conditionality mechanism under the SAFE instrument
at: (English version) to the Commission Michał Dworczyk (ECR) (7 April 2026) Subject: Questionable rules governing the application of the politicised EU rule of law conditionality mechanism under the SAFE instrument The regulation establishing the SAFE instrument (1) stipulates that it should be implemented in accordance with, among other things, Regulation 2020/2092 of the European Parliament and of the Council on a general regime of conditionality for the protection of the Union budget (including the rule of law conditionality mechanism) (2). At the same time, Article 12 of the SAFE Regulation concerning payments makes the disbursement of funds contingent upon the Member State’s ‘fulfilment of the conditions set out in this regulation’ (3), without clearly specifying their scope. This approach raises questions regarding the limits of the Commission’s discretion and the scope of application of the conditionality mechanism, which has in the past been used as a tool to exert political and institutional pressure on Member States. This is particularly objectionable in the area of security and defence, which should be explicitly excluded from any political disputes. In the light of the foregoing: 1.

Can Regulation 2020/2092 serve as a basis for suspending, limiting or withholding payments under the SAFE instrument if the Commission maintains that there has been an alleged breach of the ‘principles of the rule of law’?

If so, at what stage will the Commission assess and apply the rule of law conditionality mechanism — during the approval of the plan, the conclusion of the operational agreement, the disbursement of the advance, or the payment request?

Can operational agreements include additional conditions or monitoring mechanisms — beyond those set out in the SAFE Regulation’s eligibility rules (4) — that, if they are not complied with, will result in the suspension of payments, and if so, can they refer to Regulation 2020/2092?

(15 June 2026) Regulation (EU, Euratom) 2020/2092 on a general regime of conditionality for the protection of the Union budget (‘the Conditionality Regulation’) (1) applies to all EU funds, including Security Action for Europe (SAFE) funds (2). It sets the conditions for its application and the measures that can be adopted. Its purpose is to ensure the protection of the EU budget and the sound financial management of EU funds. The Commission continuously evaluates the situation in all Member States and stands ready to trigger the Conditionality Regulation as well as any other instrument under EU law, when all relevant conditions are fulfilled. Article 4 of the Conditionality Regulation makes clear that measures may only be adopted where breaches of the principles of the rule of law directly affect or seriously risk affecting the sound financial management of the EU budget or the protection of the EU’s financial interests, including in cases related to fraud, tax evasion, corruption or other serious irregularities. Any decision to apply measures under the Conditionality Regulation is taken by the Council, acting by qualified majority, on the basis of a proposal from the Commission. The SAFE operational arrangements set out the relationship between the implementation of the European defence industry investment plan and the corresponding financial assistance, including a tentative schedule for the disbursement of the loan instalments. 1

E-10-2026-001382.t: Equivalence of radioactive minerals to other strategic minerals for the EU’s energy security
qt: to the Commission Jorge Martín Frías (PfE) Subject:

In its communication on the Critical Raw Materials Act, the Commission highlights the strategic role of minerals such as lithium and rare earths for green transition technologies, including wind energy, photovoltaics and batteries. At the same time, the Commission itself and the Council recognise that nuclear energy is essential ‘to achieve the Union’s decarbonisation objectives’, as well as its security-of-supply objectives. However, radioactive minerals used as nuclear fuel – being the jurisdiction of the Euratom Treaty and the Euratom Supply Agency – fall outside the scope of the Critical Raw Materials Act. In view of the above: 1.
How does the Commission ensure that nuclear fuel supply chains receive equivalent regulatory treatment to critical raw materials linked to renewable energy?

Does it intend to propose, under the Euratom Treaty, a specific instrument establishing security-of-supply and diversification objectives for radioactive minerals that are similar to those set out in the Critical Raw Materials Act?
What does it assess is the impact of that regulatory asymmetry on the technological neutrality proclaimed in the European Green Deal?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (12.6.2026) The Commission has a longstanding policy of treating nuclear fuels as critical for energy security through a comprehensive and coordinated policy approach that addresses the strategic importance of nuclear energy for EU security of supply, as underlined in the Energy Union Strategy1 and the European Energy Security Strategy2. In May 2025, the Commission adopted the REPowerEU Roadmap3 towards ending Russian energy imports4. The Roadmap outlines future actions to support the gradual phasing out of nuclear material supplies from Russia, and the ramp-up of EU alternative capacity in the nuclear fuel cycle. Together with increased cooperation between the EU and reliable international partners, this is necessary to ensure a resilient EU energy system. The EU aims to ensure access to nuclear-energy materials for all countries within the European Atomic Energy Community. Uranium is not included in the Critical Raw Materials Act5, as the Commission closely monitors the supply of nuclear materials, including uranium, under the dedicated and well-established Euratom legal framework6. Consequently, the Commission has no current plans to propose a dedicated instrument mirroring the Critical Raw Materials Act for radioactive minerals. The global market for the supply of natural uranium7 is presently diversified. The Commission is also monitoring the supply of other materials used in nuclear fuel components8.

E-10-2026-001381.t: Preliminary audit report on the implementation of training, employment and work reintegration programmes in Greece
at: (English version) to the Commission Konstantinos Arvanitis (The Left) (7 April 2026) Subject: Preliminary audit report on the implementation of training, employment and work reintegration programmes in Greece A preliminary audit report by DG EMPL (1) on the implementation of training, employment and reintegration programmes in Greece identifies serious weaknesses in management and control systems, which increase the risk of distortions and fraud in public procurement. Main findings (2): Discriminatory/illegal tender criteria restricting competition and leading to a proposed financial correction of 25% (approximately EUR 1 950 000) with a possible extension to all relevant projects. Unclear contract definitions creating risks of unequal treatment and non-comparable bids. Inadequate procurement planning documentation limiting the participation of smaller specialised providers. Insufficient assessment of beneficiary capacity and direct awards without independent data verification or comparative assessment of alternative entities. Significant overestimation of objectives and budgets (deviations of up to 87% below target), unsubstantiated systematic use of maximum unit prices, inefficient use of resources. Risk of low training effectiveness due to a disproportionate emphasis on e-learning, limited practical training and insufficient monitoring of actual participation and acquisition of skills. at: (English version) to the Commission Nikolaos Anadiotis (NI) (7 April 2026) Subject: Safety of rail transport and reopening the Diakopto-Kalavryta rack railway Safety of public transport — and rail operation and interoperability in particular — is a key obligation for Member States under the current EU regulatory framework (Directives (EU) 2016/798 (1) and 2016/797, and Regulation (EU) 2016/796). (12 June 2026) On the basis of data contained in the Honourable Member’s question and the linked press article, the Commission understands that the Diakopto-Kalavryta rack railway is a historic or touristic railway. In this context, the Commission notes that most of the Member States, including Greece, decided to exclude infrastructure and vehicles reserved for strictly local, historical or tourist use from the scope of the measures implementing Directives (EU) 2016/798 (1) and 2016/797 (2), as permitted by Article 2(3)(b) of Directive (EU) 2016/798 and Article 1(4)(b) of Directive (EU) 2016/797. Therefore, the EU legal rail safety and interoperability framework, including the Common Safety Methods and Technical Specifications for Interoperability, does not apply to such railways used only for historic and touristic purpose. Consequently, the management of safety, maintenance and other aspects of the functioning of historic and touristic railways is governed solely by national rules.
