E-10-2026-001378.t: Framework for the digital data of deceased persons
qt: to the Commission Yvan Verougstraete (Renew) Subject:

The increasing digitalisation of our societies means that every European leaves behind a considerable amount of digital data, including online accounts, private correspondence, published content, photographs, digital assets and data stored on cloud services. However, the General Data Protection Regulation applies only to living natural persons. To date, there is no harmonised EU framework regulating what happens to somebody’s personal data after they pass away. This creates legal fragmentation among Member States and leaves platforms considerable room for interpretation based solely on their contractual terms. In a context marked by the rapid development of artificial intelligence and by data valorisation, the lack of framework means that the data of deceased persons is at risk of uncontrolled commercial or algorithmic exploitation. In view of the above: 1.
Does the Commission consider this lack of harmonisation to constitute a legal gap?
Is it considering a legislative initiative to regulate the storage, transfer or deletion of such data?
What action does it intend to take to prevent the uncontrolled exploitation of such data?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.7.2026) The Commission acknowledges the importance of data assets of deceased persons, which are protected under several EU laws. The AI Act1 provides for harmonised rules on artificial intelligence in the EU, which apply regardless of whether the data used refer to a living or a deceased person. Further, the rights to determine the usage of non-personal product and related services data under the Data Act2 might be passed on from the deceased user to their heirs under national succession rules. Third, as regards data considered a work of authorship under EU copyright law, Directive 2006/116/EC3 establishes a 70-year term of protection of authors’ rights following the author’s death. As regads the General Data Protection Regulation4 (GDPR), national legislation or case law may award protection. The option of creating rules on the processing of personal data of deceased persons is explicitly acknowledged in Recital 27 of the GDPR. Moreover, national contractual or succession law rules may grant heirs the right to access and control the user accounts and data of deceased persons. The Commission is not aware of any concerning fragmentation of such rules at national level that would require a harmonised approach under EU law. In light of the above, the Commission is currently not planning legislative action on the matter. However, the Commission will observe this matter closely and will consider taking further action if necessary.
1 Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 of 13 June 2024 laying down harmonised rules on artificial intelligence and

amending Regulations (EC) No 300/2008, (EU) No 167/2013, (EU) No 168/2013, (EU) 2018/858, (EU) 2018/1139 and (EU) 2019/2144 and Directives 2014/90/EU, (EU) 2016/797 and (EU) 2020/1828 (Artificial Intelligence Act). 2 Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 December 2023 on harmonised rules on fair access to and use of data and amending Regulation (EU) 2017/2394 and Directive (EU) 2020/1828 (Data Act). 3 Directive 2006/116/EC of 12 December 2006 on the term of protection of copyright and certain related rights, as amended by Directive 2011/77/EU of 27 September 2011. 4 Regulation (EU) 2016/679 of 27 April 2016 on the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free movement of such data, and repealing Directive 95/46/EC (General Data Protection Regulation).

E-10-2026-001377.t: State of Israel introduces death penalty for Palestinians
qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kostas Papadakis (NI), Lefteris Nikolaou-Alavanos (NI) Subject:

The Israeli Parliament (the Knesset) has passed a law authorising the death penalty for Palestinians convicted of committing ‘terrorist attacks’ by military tribunals. This includes, amongst others, Palestinians who have been arbitrarily held in prisons for years by Israel, without even having been charged, under the unacceptable regime of ‘administrative detention’. This appalling law represents a new escalation in Israel’s criminal policy perpetuating the genocide against Palestinians. For years, the EU and the European Parliament have systematically instrumentalised the issue of the ‘death penalty’ vis-à-vis countries that have competing interests with the EU, posing as a ‘human rights defender’ in order to advance the EU’s strategy, but when it comes to the imposition of similarly inhumane laws by their own allies – such as the monarchical regime in Saudi Arabia or the State of Israel – they limit themselves to expressing hollow concerns, thus applying a double standard. In the light of the above, what is the High Representative/Vice-President of the EU’s position on: 1.
the egregious law adopted by the Knesset that sets out the death penalty for Palestinians who resist the genocide committed by the State of Israel?

the calls for an immediate end to the EU-Israel Association Agreement and for an immediate embargo on the sale of arms and dual-use goods by EU Member States to Israel, which adopted this despicable law?
at: (English version) to the Vice-President of the Commission/High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kostas Papadakis (NI), Lefteris Nikolaou-Alavanos (NI) (3 April 2026) Subject: State of Israel introduces death penalty for Palestinians The Israeli Parliament (the Knesset) has passed a law authorising the death penalty for Palestinians convicted of committing ‘terrorist attacks’ by military tribunals. This includes, amongst others, Palestinians who have been arbitrarily held in prisons for years by Israel, without even having been charged, under the unacceptable regime of ‘administrative detention’. This appalling law represents a new escalation in Israel’s criminal policy perpetuating the genocide against Palestinians. For years, the EU and the European Parliament have systematically instrumentalised the issue of the ‘death penalty’ vis-à-vis countries that have competing interests with the EU, posing as a ‘human rights defender’ in order to advance the EU’s strategy, but when it comes to the imposition of similarly inhumane laws by their own allies — such as the monarchical regime in Saudi Arabia or the State of Israel — they limit themselves to expressing hollow concerns, thus applying a double standard. In the light of the above, what is the High Representative/Vice-President of the EU’s position on: 1.
the egregious law adopted by the Knesset that sets out the death penalty for Palestinians who resist the genocide committed by the State of Israel?

the calls for an immediate end to the EU-Israel Association Agreement and for an immediate embargo on the sale of arms and dual-use goods by EU Member States to Israel, which adopted this despicable law?

(5 June 2026) The EU has a principled position against the death penalty in all cases and in all circumstances. The approval of the Death Penalty Bill by the Israeli Parliament marks a grave regression from its long-upheld moratorium and from its own commitments. The EU is deeply concerned about the de facto discriminatory character of the Bil l (1). Consistent with the EU’s global efforts towards universal abolition of the death penalty, the EU urges Israel to abide by its previous principled position and with its obligations under international law, as well as its commitment to democratic principles, as reflected also in the provisions of the EU-Israel Association Agreement (2). The Association Agreement governs EU-Israel relations, including mechanisms to address concerns. In 2024, the High Representative/Vice-President found that Israel would be in breach of Article 2 (human rights clause). On 17 September 2025, the Commission proposed: suspending the trade-related provisions of the Agreement, new sanctions on Hamas, extremist Israeli ministers and violent settlers, putting on hold bilateral EU funding to Israel (excluding civil society, antisemitism programmes and Yad Vashem). Suspension of the entire Agreement requires unanimous approval from all 27 Member States. On 11 May 2026, EU Foreign Ministers reached a political agreement on a further package of sanctions against extremist settlers and against entities and organisations that support them. Discussions continue in the Council. Arms exports to third countries are controlled by Member States. Therefore, the competent authorities of Member States are in charge for taking the final decision whether to authorise or deny an individual export or transit licence of military equipment.

E-10-2026-001376.t: Double standards in the EU’s relationship with Israel
qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Nacho Sánchez Amor (S&D), Leire Pajín (S&D), Hana Jalloul Muro (S&D), Idoia Mendia (S&D), Juan Fernando López Aguilar (S&D) Subject:

The recent decision by the Knesset to approve the blatantly discriminatory legalisation of the death penalty for Palestinians is deeply concerning and completely at odds with the Union’s firm and long-held opposition to the death penalty under any circumstances. Similarly, Israel’s military actions in southern Lebanon – stemming from an illegal war in Iran – suggest a new protracted occupation that would violate Lebanon’s territorial integrity, with devastating consequences for the civilian population. This is all taking place against the backdrop of extremely serious violations of international law and international humanitarian law in Gaza and the West Bank. In view of this situation and the EU’s credibility as a global player committed to international law: 1.
Does the HR/VP believe that she has been consistent in her position towards Israel given its constant violations of both international law and the territorial integrity of third countries?
What measures and statements are planned to ensure that the Union does not apply flagrant double standards in its treatment of Israel in the light of these serious actions?
Will she push for the adoption of sanctions against those in the Israeli Government who are responsible for these violations or for alternative measures if there is insufficient consensus?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.5.2026) The EU has a clear and coherent position on the imperative for all States to fully respect international law and the principles of the UN Charter, including the sovereignty and territorial integrity of third countries. The EU is equally steadfast in its principled opposition to the death penalty in all cases and all circumstances. With reference to Israeli military actions in Lebanon as well as to the new death penalty law, the EU position has been clearly reflected for example in the latest European Council Conclusions of 19 March 20261 and in the statement issued on 31 March by the High Representative/Vice-President on behalf of the EU2. To ensure no double standards, the EU applies the same principles globally, including through its steadfast support for the International Criminal Court and the International Court of Justice, which are indispensable pillars of the global justice system. The fight against impunity and pursuit of justice for international crimes and violations of international law are non-negotiable cornerstones of EU foreign policy. In light of the catastrophic situation in Gaza and the West Bank, the EU’s 2025 review – with support of a majority of Member States - found indications that Israel had breached its Article 2 obligations under the EU-Israel Association Agreement. The Commission has since proposed a reinforced sanctions package and partial suspension of trade-related provisions, while halting bilateral support (excluding civil society and Yad Vashem), as announced in the Commission's President 2025 State of the Union address3. Further measures remain under Council discussion.

Following the multiple investigations it is conducting into the OPEKEPE scandal and the mismanagement of European agricultural subsidies, the European Public Prosecutor's Office forwarded yesterday (1 April 2026) a second case file on the alleged involvement in an organised fraud scheme concerning European agricultural funds of a former Minister and a Deputy Minister of Rural Development and Food, 11 current MPs and five former MPs.1 Already today (2 April 2026), a new, third case file appears to have already been forwarded indicating incitement to breach of duty of two more current MPs, with the alleged actual perpetrators being OPEKEPE executives.2 Taking into account the ongoing shock waves caused by the OPEKEPE scandal in relation to the mismanagement of European funds, the absence (since September 2024) of an accredited Greek organisation for the management of European agricultural subsidies and the multiple ongoing problems for Greek producers and livestock farmers: 1.

What measures does the Commission intend to take and propose to the Greek Government to protect Greek producers and livestock farmers from the new risk of significant delays in the payment of subsidies?
What measures does the Commission intend to take so that European funds are not lost but are channelled legally and promptly to their final recipients?
What measures does the Commission intend to take and propose to the Greek Government to speed up the investigation process into the new cases as well?

at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (21.5.2026) The Commission cooperates with the Greek authorities to support the sound management of EU funds. Under the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), it is a shared objective to ensure timely payments to genuine Greek farmers. Member States should set up the aid application system in line with the applicable rules and ensure that, following sufficient checks, payments are made in full and on time to beneficiaries1. The Commission obtains assurance on whether the Member States management and control systems effectively protect the EU financial interests through the audits of the national certification bodies. The Commission performs also its own audits of these systems. In case of deficiencies, the Commission opens a conformity procedure determining a financial risk to the EU budget. The Commission performed multiple audits of CAP funds spending in Greece and, in several cases, decided on financial corrections. Some of the issues identified remain relevant and are covered by ongoing enquiries. The Commission specifically addresses the issues concerning agricultural activity under its current audit work and the action plan presented by the Greek authorities for the Integrated Administration and Control System. E-10-2026-001374.t: Impact of the crisis in the Middle East on the European fishing sector
qt: to the Commission Fredis Beleris (PPE) Subject:

The ongoing crisis in the Middle East has led to instability and spikes in oil prices. This directly affects the European fishing sector, as it is highly dependent on fuel for the operation of fleets. However, countries such as Greece, which have a large number of fishing communities operating on a large scale at sea, are made to bear the brunt of this impact. For many fishers, and small-scale fisheries in particular, fuel costs already represented one of the biggest operating expenses. The recent price spikes could lead to further economic restriction, reduced fishing activity and additional economic pressure on coastal and island communities. With this in mind, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
What data does it use to assess the impact of recent oil price increases on the viability of the European fishing fleet?
Is it considering the possibility of activating exceptional European support measures for the fishing sector – reinforcing national initiatives?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.5.2026) The data used to assess the impact of recent oil price increases on the viability of the European fishing fleet are the scientific economic data formally submitted by Member States under the Data Collection Framework, analysed by the Scientific, Technical and Economic Committee for Fisheries (STECF). These data are also complemented by real-time marine diesel prices and market evidence collected by the European Market Observatory for Fisheries and Aquaculture products (EUMOFA). The Commission is aware that the situation in the Middle East has dire implications for the EU, including the EU fisheries and aquaculture sector. The Commission is closely monitoring the market situation of the sector since the inception of the crisis. Noting that a demonstrated and substantiated causal link between the exceptional situation in the Middle East and the significant disruption has been established, the Commission triggered the compensation mechanism provided under Article 26(2) of the European Maritime, Fisheries and Aquaculture Fund (EMFAF) Regulation with the adoption of the Commission Implementing Decision on 16 April 20261. Member States will be able to make this support immediately available to the sectors under their national EMFAF programmes, in line with the established EU rules. This exceptional EU support at EU level can reinforce national initiatives, including the use of State aid under the temporary crisis framework, adopted on 29 April 20262.

qt: to the Commission Nacho Sánchez Amor (S&D), Hana Jalloul Muro (S&D), Juan Fernando López Aguilar (S&D) Subject:

The Knesset’s recent blatantly discriminatory legalisation of the death penalty for Palestinians is deeply concerning and completely at odds with the EU’s firm and long-standing stance against the death penalty under any circumstances. At the same time, Israel’s military actions in southern Lebanon – in connection with an illegal war in Iran – suggest a new protracted occupation that would violate Lebanon’s territorial integrity and have devastating consequences for the civilian population. This all takes place against the backdrop of the known severe violations of international law and international humanitarian law in Gaza and the West Bank. Given the above and taking the EU’s credibility as a global player committed to international law into account: 1.
Does the Commission believe that it has maintained a coherent position towards Israel’s constant violations of international law and the territorial integrity of third countries?
What actions and statements are planned to ensure that the Commission does not apply blatant double standards in its treatment of Israel in the context of its extreme actions?
What further actions will the Commission take to comply with the Commission President’s statements in relation to suspending the EU-Israel agreement and adopting sanctions against Israeli ministers?

E-10-2026-001368.t: Tackling outflows of locally educated skilled workers
qt: to the Commission Sophia Kircher (PPE) Subject:

At the University of Innsbruck, the proportion of students with Austrian nationality most recently stood at 47.9 %. For new students in the winter semester 2025/26, the figure was 38.8 %. It has become apparent that a significant proportion of students in highly sought-after fields of study, such as those related to the health sector, come from other EU Member States. A substantial number of these graduates then leave Austria upon completing their studies. This therefore raises the question of what measures are appropriate for combatting the outflow of educated skilled workers. University education is largely paid for by public funding, yet none of the long-term benefits are seen domestically. Given that many regions are affected by this situation, the question arises as to what extent a common approach could provide the EU with some relief. 1.
In the Commission’s view, what possibilities exist for Member States to limit access to particularly heavily subscribed fields of study, without violating the EU law principle of non‑discrimination?
Under what conditions are quota systems, residency criteria, or other capacity-based admission models compatible with EU law?
Are there efforts at EU level to support Member States, legally or politically, in safeguarding national training capacity in critical fields of study and work?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (5.6.2026) The Commission promotes mobility in all fields of study. Measures restricting access to higher education are in principle prohibited by EU law as they may constitute direct or indirect discrimination based on nationality. They can be justified by a legitimate objective (such as protection of public health) but need to be appropriate for securing the attainment of that objective, should not go beyond what is necessary, and ensure sufficiently wide access to higher education, in line with case-law1. In line with the case-law quoted above, under EU law, quotas restricting access to higher education are in principle prohibited as they may constitute direct or indirect discrimination based on nationality, contrary to Article 18 of the Treaty on the functioning of the European Union, the Commission aims at removing obstacles to mobility in education. The Commission actively supports Member States in balancing local labour market needs with EU-wide mobility through targeted funding and policy initiatives. EU programmes such as Erasmus+, the European Social Fund+ or the European Regional Development Fund also support the development of the local economy by creating opportunities for students to contribute to the local market after graduation. A study on balanced and inclusive learning mobility (covering degree and credit mobility) is expected in 2026, following the Council Recommendation ‘Europe on the Move’2. Member States are encouraged to leverage EU tools to address skills gaps, including through collaboration, through a combination of funding incentives, policy coordination, cross-border cooperation, and structured partnerships between education providers, employers, and regional authorities.
1 Judgment of 13 April 2010, Nicolas Bressol and Others and Céline Chaverot and Others v Gouvernement de la
Communauté française, C-73/08, EU:C:2010:181. 2 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32024H03364&qid=1778245129107.

qt: to the Commission Jan-Christoph Oetjen (Renew), Hilde Vautmans (Renew), Lucia Yar (Renew), Veronika Cifrová Ostrihoňová (Renew), Malik Azmani (Renew) Subject:

Recent data indicate a shift in the modus operandi of migrant smuggling networks, with increasing reliance on high-speed boats. However, both Frontex and the Member States lack the capacity to effectively detect, intercept and prevent the use of such vessels. These ‘phantoms’ increase the profitability of smuggling operations and pose a risk to migrants’ lives. In order to minimise time in EU territorial waters and evade interception, migrants are at times forced to disembark prematurely. The high speeds of these vessels also significantly increase the likelihood of fatal accidents, as shown by the recent collision between a speedboat carrying migrants and the Hellenic Coast Guard. In view of this: 1.
Is the Commission aware of this evolving trend and what concrete steps has it taken to support Member States and Frontex in detecting, tracking and preventing the use of such ‘phantoms’?

How does the Commission intend to address this phenomenon in the upcoming revision of the Frontex Regulation, particularly with regard to operational capabilities, interagency cooperation with Europol and safeguards to prevent loss of life at sea?

Does the Commission plan to expand the deployment of drones and AI-based surveillance systems within Frontex operations to improve detection and interception and how will it ensure that such tools are effective and fully compliant with the EU’s legal framework on artificial intelligence and data protection?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.6.2026) The Commission is closely monitoring modi operandi of migrant smuggling networks and is aware of the growing trend of smugglers using high-speed boats to evade detection and apprehension by law enforcement. It recognises the operational challenges this poses for Member States. To address this issue, the Commission is taking decisive action, including through the establishment of Europol’s1 European Centre Against Migrant Smuggling23 and by funding the European Multidisciplinary Platform Against Criminal Threats Policy Cycle4. With the upcoming revision of Regulation (EU) 2019/18965, the Commission intends to ensure that the European Border and Coast Guard Agency (Frontex) remains well-equipped to support Member States in the safe and effective management of the external borders of the EU. Operationally, this includes enhancing the ability and flexibility of the European Border and Coast Guard community to deploy resources where and when needed, and maximising Frontex’s ability to cooperate with relevant EU agencies. Search and rescue obligations will remain anchored in international law. The Commission supports strengthening border surveillance capacities, including through funding under the Border Management and Visa Instrument6, by making technical equipment available to Frontex. The deployment of drones and surveillance systems is decided by Frontex in response to operational needs, in full compliance with applicable EU law. This will include, once applicable, the AI Act obligations for high-risk AI systems used in migration and border management, notably the fundamental rights safeguards and the deployer's fundamental rights impact assessment before putting the system into service.
1 European Union Agency for Law Enforcement Cooperation. 2 https://www.europol.europa.eu/media-press/newsroom/news/grip-migrant-smuggling-tightens-new-

department-europol-to-step-fight. 3 https://www.europol.europa.eu/media-press/newsroom/news/spain-24-arrested-in-crackdown-speedboatmigrant-smuggling-network. 4 https://home-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies/internal-security/law-enforcement-cooperation/empact-fightingcrime-together_en. 5 REGULATION (EU) 2019/1896 OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND OF THE COUNCIL of 13 November 2019 on the European Border and Coast Guard and repealing Regulations (EU) No 1052/2013 and (EU) 2016/1624. 6 https://home-affairs.ec.europa.eu/funding/borders-and-visa-funds/integrated-border-management-fund-bordermanagement-and-visa-instrument-2021-27_en.

E-10-2026-001365.t: Transparency of origin of food products is a consumer right
qt: to the Commission Gilles Pennelle (PfE), Virginie Joron (PfE), Anne-Sophie Frigout (PfE), Pierre Pimpie (PfE), Valérie Deloge (PfE), Philippe Olivier (PfE), Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE), André Rougé (PfE), Julien Leonardelli (PfE) Subject:

Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011 (‘the FIC Regulation’) guarantees the right of consumers to know the origin of foodstuffs. Article 3 of the FIC Regulation provides for a ‘high level of protection’ and enables consumers to make informed choices. Article 26 requires only the labelling of the origin if its omission could mislead consumers, or if the origin highlighted differs from that of the primary ingredient. For the other ingredients, the indication of origin is not mandatory. Article 2(a)(i) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2018/775 permits a simplified reference to ‘EU’, ‘non-EU’ or ‘EU and non-EU’, which can be difficult to understand on packaging. In this context: 1.

How does the Commission account for the contradiction between the ‘high level of protection’ promoted by the FIC Regulation and the lack of any general obligation to label the origin of food products?
If it is possible for manufacturers to highlight a place of processing that differs from the primary ingredient’s place of origin, is this not deceiving consumers?
Does the simplified use of ‘non-EU’ (which includes 86 % of countries in the world) enable consumers to make informed choices?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (10.6.2026) Under the current EU legal framework, mandatory origin labelling is required for beef, pork, sheep, goat and poultry, fruit and vegetables, fish, honey and olive oil, where consumers have demonstrated particular interest or where origin significantly influences purchasing decisions. As outlined in the Vision for Agriculture and Food1, the Commission will examine the potential extension of mandatory origin labelling to other products covered by sectorial legislation. The indication of the origin is furthermore mandatory where its omission might mislead consumers as to the true origin of the food. Beyond these cases, business operators may voluntarily provide origin information, provided it is not misleading, confusing or ambiguous. Article 26(3) of the FIC Regulation2 provides that, where the origin of a food i.e. the place of processing for processed food is given and differs from the one of its primary ingredient, the latter’s origin must also be declared or marked as different. The origin of the primary ingredient must appear in the same field of vision as the origin of the food and the letters must at least be 75% of the height of the letters used for the origin of the food3. The entire presentation of the label must not mislead the consumer as to the true origin of the primary ingredient. The aim of Article 26(3) is to avoid that consumers are misled about the origin of the primary ingredient where the origin of the food is given. If both origins are different, this must be clear for the consumer. The use of simplified origin indications such as ‘non-EU’ is allowed to reduce complexity for businesses while still providing consumers with the necessary information. Member States are responsible for implementing and enforcing these rules.
1 COM/2025/75 final. 2 Food Information to Consumers (FIC) Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011 of the European Parliament and of the

Council of 25 October 2011 on the provision of food information to consumers, amending Regulations (EC) No 1924/2006 and (EC) No 1925/2006 of the European Parliament and of the Council, and repealing Commission Directive 87/250/EEC, Council Directive 90/496/EEC, Commission Directive 1999/10/EC, Directive 2000/13/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council, Commission Directives 2002/67/EC and 2008/5/EC and Commission Regulation (EC) No 608/2004. 3 Article 3(2) of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2018/775 of 28 May 2018 laying down rules for the application of Article 26(3) of Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011 of the European Parliament and of the Council on the provision of food information to consumers, as regards the rules for indicating the country of origin or place of provenance of the primary ingredient of a food.

E-10-2026-001364.t: Extension of the RRF deadlines and implementation of the European Parliament resolution of 18 June 2025
qt: to the Commission Maria Grapini (S&D) Subject:

The current global context has created major obstacles for Member States in meeting the deadlines relating to projects to which they have committed under the NRRPs, hence jeopardising strategic investments and the stability of the SMEs involved. The European Parliament adopted, on 18 June 2025, the resolution on the implementation of the Recovery and Resilience Facility in which it called, in paragraph 42, for an 18-month extension of mature RRF projects through an amendment of the Regulation. This would enable ongoing projects to be completed by means of other funding schemes, hence avoiding the decommitment of funds. Given the limited time remaining for the implementation of the RRF (2026), and for a decision to implement the European Parliament resolution of 18 June 2025, what concrete measures has the Commission planned in this regard? The reforms and investments programmed through the RRF contribute directly to increasing resilience and reducing dependency in the EU, hence strengthening the Union’s strategic autonomy.
at: (English version) to the Commission Maria Grapini (S&D) (1 April 2026) Subject: Extension of the RRF deadlines and implementation of the European Parliament resolution of 18 June 2025 The current global context has created major obstacles for Member States in meeting the deadlines relating to projects to which they have committed under the NRRPs, hence jeopardising strategic investments and the stability of the SMEs involved. The European Parliament adopted, on 18 June 2025, the resolution on the implementation of the Recovery and Resilience Facility in which it called, in paragraph 42, for an 18-month extension of mature RRF projects through an amendment of the regulation. This would enable ongoing projects to be completed by means of other funding schemes, hence avoiding the decommitment of funds. Given the limited time remaining for the implementation of the RRF (2026), and for a decision to implement the European Parliament resolution of 18 June 2025, what concrete measures has the Commission planned in this regard? The reforms and investments programmed through the RRF contribute directly to increasing resilience and reducing dependency in the EU, hence strengthening the Union’s strategic autonomy. (3 June 2026) The Commission acknowledges the call in the European Parliament’s implementation report for an 18-month extension of the deadline for mature projects under the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF) (1). However, the RRF was established as a temporary instrument with a clear end date in 2026. The RRF Regulation does not allow any flexibility regarding the satisfactory fulfilment of milestones and targets beyond August 2026 (2). In line with these legal deadlines, the Commission must make all final payments by 31 December 2026 and cannot proceed to new net borrowing beyond that date. Any modification to these deadlines would require an amendment of the RRF Regulation, the European Union Recovery Instrument Regulation (3) and the Own Resources Decision (4). The latter, in particular, would require unanimity in the Council, as well as ratification by many national parliaments. Given the tight timelines, a proposal by the Commission to extend these deadlines would carry significant procedural and legal risks, alongside considerable uncertainty. The Commission remains committed to supporting Member States in addressing implementation bottlenecks. In the communication NextGenerationEU — The road to 2026 (5) and in the Commission Notice — Guidelines for Member States on operational aspects related to the final phase and closure of the Recovery and Resilience Facilit y (6), the Commission has set a clear path forward guiding Member States to take all the necessary actions to ensure a smooth implementation of the RRF in its final months. In particular, the RRF Regulation (7) allows Member States to request targeted amendments to their plans, and the Commission will support such revisions within the framework of the RRF Regulation.

European Parliament legislative initiative procedure (INI) of 18 June 2025 on the Implementation Report on the Recovery and Resilience Facility (2024/2085(INI)). Article 20(5)(d) Regulation (EU) 2021/241 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 12 February 2021 establishing the Recovery and Resilience Facility (OJ L 057, 18.2.2021, p. 17). Regulation (EU) 2020/2094 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 December 2020 establishing a European Union Recovery Instrument to support the recovery in the aftermath of the COVID-19 crisis (OJ L 433I, 22.12.2020, p. 23). Council Decision (EU, Euratom) 2020/2053 of 14 December 2020 on the system of own resources of the European Union and repealing Decision 2014/335/EU, Euratom (OJ L 424, 15.12.2020, p. 1); COM(2025) 310 final. E-10-2026-001363.t: Solar farm under construction in a Natura area in Fokida
qt: to the Commission Lefteris Nikolaou-Alavanos (NI) Subject:

The residents of Agia Efthymia – a historical village of martyrdom and special cultural significance in the region of Fokida – are opposed to the plan to build a solar farm in a Natura zone in the area. Machinery has already been brought in to clear 170 hectares of forest ahead of construction. The solar farm is being built on both public forest and private land, with landowners seeing their land cleared. Propelled by EU strategies, the Nea Demokratia Government is speeding up the roll-out of wind turbines and photovoltaics, while the policy to phase out lignite has resulted in incalculable consequences. Promises of supposedly cheaper energy are being shattered by the unaffordable cost of ‘green’ energy, while Central Greece has become an energy centre for renewables. At the same time, the ‘war-induced’ price hikes affecting energy and fuel are the other side of the same coin. In the light of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

What is its view regarding the concerns expressed by the residents of Agia Efthymia in Fokida in relation to the construction of a solar farm in the area, despite the Region’s negative opinion, as well as regarding the encroachment on private property?

What view does it take of the fact that the regulation on ‘nature restoration’ has paved the way for even Natura areas to be encroached upon when the interests of energy conglomerates are at stake, under the pretext of being in the ‘overriding public interest’, while in reality the people are paying a high price for the environmental and economic consequences of the unregulated expansion of renewable energy sources?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (6.7.2026) According to Article 6(3) of the Habitats Directive1, projects likely to have a significant impact on Natura 2000 sites must undergo an appropriate assessment and can only proceed if the integrity of the sites is safeguarded. Exceptionally, authorisation may be granted under Article 6(4) if there are imperative reasons of overriding public interest and respective compensatory measures are adopted. According to the revised Renewable Energy Directive2, renewable energy systems are presumed as being in the overriding public interest for the purpose of Article 6(4) of the Habitats Directive. Additionally, the provisions of Article 6(4) including compensatory measures, remain fully applicable. Under the Nature Restoration Regulation3, for the purposes of the derogations from the obligations of continuous improvement and non-deterioration outside Natura 2000 sites, projects for the production of energy from renewable sources are presumed as being of overriding public interest. However, this does not affect the application of the requirements under the Habitats Directive within Natura 2000 sites, where any such project remains subject to the conditions set out in Article 6(4) of the Habitats Directive. Without prejudice to the Commission’s role as guardian of the Treaties, it is primarily the responsibility of the Greek authorities to ensure compliance with EU environmental law.
1 Council Directive 92/43/EEC of 21 May 1992 on the conservation of natural habitats and of wild fauna and

flora, OJ L 206, 22.7.1992, pp. 7–50. 2 Directive (EU) 2023/2413 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 18 October 2023 amending Directive (EU) 2018/2001, Regulation (EU) 2018/1999 and Directive 98/70/EC as regards the promotion of energy from renewable sources, and repealing Council Directive (EU) 2015/652, OJ L, 2023/2413, 31.10.2023. 3 Regulation (EU) 2024/1991 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 24 June 2024 on nature restoration and amending Regulation (EU) 2022/869, OJ L, 2024/1991, 29.7.2024.

E-10-2026-001362.t: Concerns regarding the rule of law and fundamental rights in Georgia
qt: to the Commission Krzysztof Brejza (PPE), Dan Barna (Renew), Nathalie Loiseau (Renew), Dainius Žalimas (Renew), Petras Auštrevičius (Renew), Nikola Minchev (Renew), Liudas Mažylis (PPE), Veronika Cifrová Ostrihoňová (Renew), Łukasz Kohut (PPE), Rasa Juknevičienė (PPE), Leoluca Orlando (Verts/ALE), Michał Szczerba (PPE), Reinier Van Lanschot (Verts/ALE), Ondřej Krutílek (ECR), Malik Azmani (Renew), Maria Grapini (S&D), Sebastian Tynkkynen (ECR) Subject:

According to recent reports, opposition leader Elene Khoshtaria has been sentenced to 18 months’ imprisonment for writing the words ‘Russian Dream’ on a ruling party campaign poster, allegedly causing damage amounting to approximately GEL 570 (EUR 184). The applicable legal framework provides for substantially lighter penalties, such as fines or community service, raising serious concerns about the manifest disproportionality of the sentence and the selective use of criminal law against political opponents. Furthermore, credible allegations indicate that, while in detention, Elene Khoshtaria has been subjected to physical assault, forced stripping and degrading treatment. This would constitute a grave violation of human dignity and breach Georgia’s obligations under international human rights law. These developments point to a broader pattern of democratic backsliding, undermining both Georgia’s European path and the trust underpinning its status as an EU candidate country. Given this: 1.
How does the Commission view these developments in the light of Georgia’s commitments under the Association Agreement and the conditions attached to its status as a candidate country?
What steps is the Commission taking to ensure accountability for alleged ill treatment and safeguard fundamental rights?
What actions is the Commission taking to secure the release of Elene Khoshtaria and other people widely regarded as having been detained on politically motivated grounds?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (5.6.2026) The Commission is concerned by the serious democratic backsliding in Georgia. The EU has repeatedly condemned the deteriorating situation and urged Georgian authorities to respect, protect and uphold fundamental rights, refrain from using force, and ensure accountability for any violations. All arbitrarily detained persons should be released. In Georgia’s 2025 enlargement report1, the Commission noted that the actions taken by the Georgian authorities – including its policy of repression undermining basic democratic principles and shrinking civic space – fall short of the EU’s expectations of an EU candidate country. Georgia’s accession process has effectively come to a standstill. In response, the Commission has scaled down engagement with the Georgian authorities, halted financial assistance directly benefiting them, and paused meetings of Association Agreement bodies. In light of Georgia’s deliberate and persisting violations of key commitments on democracy and fundamental rights under its visa-free regime, the Commission has also temporarily suspended visa-free travel across the EU for Georgian holders of diplomatic, service and official passports2, as of 6 March 2026 and for an initial period of 12 months. The EU remains committed to supporting the Georgian people’s European aspirations and all efforts towards a democratic, stable, and European future for Georgia.
1 https://enlargement.ec.europa.eu/georgia-report-2025_en. 2 https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_26_564.

E-10-2026-001361.t: Increasing use of and investment in Palantir software
qt: to the Commission Raquel García Hermida-Van Der Walle (Renew) Subject:

In recent years, law enforcement and intelligence agencies in the EU have increasingly used software produced by the US tech company Palantir, which can analyse very large quantities of data to identify patterns and make predictions about crime. Recent media coverage revealed that investment in Palantir by European banks, asset managers, insurers and pension funds increased by almost 70 % from 2024 to 20251. Palantir is widely considered to be controversial because of its close connections to the White House and its supply of software to US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to help find irregular migrants. The company’s CEO recently stated that its technology is intentionally discriminatory and disruptive to our democratic societies2. Several Member States currently use Palantir technologies, while Europol used Palantir software between 2016 and 20213. 1.
Is any Palantir technology or product currently used by the Commission or by any of its agencies or bodies?

Does the Commission agree that the use of Palantir in the EU poses significant risks, not only by threatening fundamental rights but also by essentially giving the United States a way to pressure Member States to act to the White House’s liking?
As part of its focus on more European digital sovereignty, does the Commission plan to stimulate the development of European alternatives that comply with EU laws and values?

https://www.ftm.eu/articles/european-investors-palantir-investment. https://newrepublic.com/post/207693/palantir-ceo-karp-disrupting-democratic-power. https://www.euractiv.com/news/palantir-is-well-on-its-way-to-conquering-europe/.
at: (English version) to the Commission Raquel García Hermida-Van Der Walle (Renew) (1 April 2026) Subject: Increasing use of and investment in Palantir software In recent years, law enforcement and intelligence agencies in the EU have increasingly used software produced by the US tech company Palantir, which can analyse very large quantities of data to identify patterns and make predictions about crime. Recent media coverage revealed that investment in Palantir by European banks, asset managers, insurers and pension funds increased by almost 70% from 2024 to 2025 (1). Palantir is widely considered to be controversial because of its close connections to the White House and its supply of software to US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to help find irregular migrants. The company’s CEO recently stated that its technology is intentionally discriminatory and disruptive to our democratic societies (2). Several Member States currently use Palantir technologies, while Europol used Palantir software between 2016 and 2021 (3). 1.
Is any Palantir technology or product currently used by the Commission or by any of its agencies or bodies?

2. Does the Commission agree that the use of Palantir in the EU poses significant risks, not only by threatening fundamental rights but also by essentially giving the United States a way to pressure Member States to act to the White House’s liking? 3. As part of its focus on more European digital sovereignty, does the Commission plan to stimulate the development of European alternatives that comply with EU laws and values? (1 July 2026) The Commission does not use any Palantir technology or product. The Commission recalls that the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the EU (1) applies to EU institutions, bodies and agencies, and to Member States when they implement EU law. Regarding predictive policing, the AI Act (2) introduces safeguards to protect fundamental rights, including non-discrimination. It prohibits AI systems from assessing or predicting the risk of a person committing a criminal offence based solely on profiling or personality traits and characteristics. Other AI systems used to assess crime risks are classified as high-risk and are therefore subject to specific requirements and obligations. The same applies to AI systems used to assess risks in migration, asylum and visa applications, or to detect and identify individuals in migration contexts. As part of the adopted European technological sovereignty package (3), the Open Source (OS) Strategy (4) aims to support open, secure alternatives aligned with EU law and values. It is expected to put forward measures to help OS communities and EU companies develop, scale up, maintain and secure highquality OS components, and to accelerate their adoption by public and private actors. This includes support for existing sovereign alternatives and new solutions in strategic areas where dependencies exist. It will also aim at promoting a voluntary EU assessment framework to recognise solutions that comply with key EU rules and values, while avoiding technological isolation.

https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:12012P/TXT. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32024R1689 . https://commission.europa.eu/news-and-media/news/strengthening-europes-tech-sovereignty-2026-06-03_en . https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/communication-european-tech-sovereignty-accompanied-eu-open-sourcestrategy.

E-10-2026-001360.t: Guaranteeing affordable energy prices in view of the conflict in Iran and the limitations of the European electricity market
qt: to the Commission Marina Mesure (The Left), Arash Saeidi (The Left), Leila Chaibi (The Left), Damien Carême (The Left), Rima Hassan (The Left), Manon Aubry (The Left), Younous Omarjee (The Left), Emma Fourreau (The Left), Anthony Smith (The Left) Subject:

The recent military escalation in Iran resulting from Israeli-American strikes has led to rising oil and gas prices on international markets. This development highlights the EU’s persistent vulnerability as it remains heavily dependent on energy imports. Against a backdrop of heightened geopolitical tensions, the way the EU electricity market functions appears all the more problematic, as it heightens price volatility and leads to rising costs for households and businesses. In particular, the energy price‑setting mechanism is leading in practice to gas price indexation. In this context: 1.
How does the Commission plan to tackle the objective of energy independence for the EU, without simply replacing one dependence with another?
What specific measures does it intend to implement to guarantee affordable electricity prices for households and businesses, while preventing a major energy crisis across the EU?

Is the Commission considering structural reform to the EU electricity market and the repeal of Article 5 of Directive (EU) 2019/944 on setting regulated prices, allowing consumers to benefit from prices that reflect the average cost of production?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (26.6.2026) The Commission is committed to strengthen the EU’s energy security and access to affordable energy for citizens and industries. The transition to a decarbonised system is an opportunity for the EU to reduce dependence on fossil fuel imports, relying more on homegrown energy sources. This will improve energy security and help shelter citizens and industries from volatile global energy markets. On 22 April 2026, the Commission presented the AccelerateEU Communication1 to address the EU’s rising energy costs amid volatile fossil fuel markets in light of the escalating Middle East conflict. outlining immediate, targeted actions for Member States to deliver rapid and lasting relief to households and industry facing high energy prices It also includes structural measures to accelerate the delivery of the Energy Union in particular to improve energy efficiency and accelerate electrification by reducing the four components of energy billssupply costs, network charges, taxes, and carbon costs - also in the longer term. The internal electricity market is based on the free formation of prices by suppliers enabling competition among suppliers. Suppliers with more than 200,000 customers must offer both a fixed-term, fixed-price electricity supply contract and a dynamic electricity price contract. Member States are allowed to intervene in the price that suppliers charge their customers under specific circumstances and to implement below-cost regulated prices during an electricity price crisis, following the last electricity market reform. As part of the Citizens Energy Package implementation package, the Commission will publish a report on how those measures are implemented but does not foresee modification of the framework.
1 https://energy.ec.europa.eu/document/download/7fac9eea-5717-4182-a368-
bd68c427ff4c_en?filename=Communication.pdf.

E-10-2026-001359.t: Workshops in the application of the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive
qt: to the Commission Christine Schneider (PPE) Subject:

A series of workshops are planned for the application of the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD). However, the specific procedure, particularly the timetable for transposition into national law, as well as the objective of these workshops, remains unclear. 1.
How many transposition and implementation workshops are planned in total, and when are they due to take place?
What specific information, areas of focus and objectives are planned for these workshops?
How will Member States be involved in these workshops including, if necessary, during the preparation phase?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.6.2026) Following the recent entry into force of the Omnibus I Directive1, which amends the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive2 (CSDDD), the Commission is resuming the series of transposition workshops that was initially launched prior to the Omnibus proposal. Such workshops are organised for Member State experts – typically from the ministries responsible for the transposition – with a view to supporting them in their transposition work, particularly by addressing questions raised in advance or during the meetings on aspects they consider relevant for transposition. The workshops are scheduled to take place between June 2026 and July 2027 at intervals of two to four months, with the discussions expected to cover all the key elements of the CSDDD.

E-10-2026-001357.t: Access to cash and cash payments in Europe
qt: to the Commission Fernand Kartheiser (NI) Subject:

In a number of Member States, digital payments have become the preferred option for many EU citizens. In spite of this trend, a significant proportion of the population remains attached to cash. However, these people struggle to make transactions to public authorities, on public transport or in public places in general. In addition, an increasing number of our fellow citizens, particularly those in rural areas, do not have access to cash machines close to their homes or places of work. In view of this, in coordination with the European Central Bank and the Member states, the Commission is invited to answer the following questions: 1.
Will it promote the right of citizens to be able to make transactions in cash, as well as access to cash machines?
Is the Commission planning any initiatives that aim to encourage businesses and public authorities that have stopped accepting cash payments to start accepting them again?
Will the Commission work to safeguard the effectiveness of legal tender?
at: (English version) to the Commission Fernand Kartheiser (NI) (1 April 2026) Subject: Access to cash and cash payments in Europe In a number of Member States, digital payments have become the preferred option for many EU citizens. In spite of this trend, a significant proportion of the population remains attached to cash. However, these people struggle to make transactions to public authorities, on public transport or in public places in general. In addition, an increasing number of our fellow citizens, particularly those in rural areas, do not have access to cash machines close to their homes or places of work. In view of this, in coordination with the European Central Bank and the Member states, the Commission is invited to answer the following questions: 1.
Will it promote the right of citizens to be able to make transactions in cash, as well as access to cash machines?
Is the Commission planning any initiatives that aim to encourage businesses and public authorities that have stopped accepting cash payments to start accepting them again?
Will the Commission work to safeguard the effectiveness of legal tender?

(19 May 2026) Euro cash is granted legal tender status in the euro area by the Treaty on the Functioning of the E U (1). On 28 June 2023, the Commission put forward a legislative proposal to clarify the scope and meaning of legal tender for euro cash (2). The proposal ensures that the fundamental legal tender principle of mandatory acceptance is not undermined by widespread cash non-acceptance levels through the unilateral and ex ante exclusion of cash by enterprises. It also clarifies the exceptions to the rule of mandatory acceptance, including via prior agreement of the parties or for good faith reasons. This safeguards cash acceptance in the euro area, giving citizens the option to pay in cash if they so wish. At the same time, if people do not have access to cash they will not be able to pay with it; hence why the proposal establishes the obligation on Member States to ensure sufficient and effective access to cash. The proposal gives Member States the primary responsibility to monitor levels of both ex ante unilateral exclusions of payments in cash and access to cash throughout their territory, and to take appropriate action if needed. This is required to safeguard the effectiveness of the legal tender of euro cash in practice. To enforce the acceptance of and access to cash, Member States will set out rules on penalties for possible non-compliance cases. As a safeguard, the Commission can require a Member State to take measures if the Member State has taken no, or insufficient, action. To further improve access to cash, the Commission put forward additional measures through the 2023 proposal on the Payment Services Package, which will be soon adopted by the co-legislators. The Package aims to further increase access to cash in retail shops by allowing retailers to offer cash withdrawal services even in the absence of a purchase by a customer.

Article 128 (1) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union lays down the legal tender status of euro banknotes, and Article 11 of Regulation EC/974/98 does so with regard to euro coins. https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_23_3501

E-10-2026-001356.t: Recast of the Tobacco Excise Duty Directive
qt: to the Commission Fernand Kartheiser (NI) Subject:

In the context of the recast of the Tobacco Excise Duty Directive1, the Danish Presidency of the Council has tabled a compromise proposal introducing amendments to Article 32 of the horizontal excise duty framework2. These proposed changes would modify how authorities determine whether excise goods are intended for a private individual’s personal use and could reduce the flexibility that Member States currently have when making this assessment. The proposal would also expand the rules to cover new categories of products that were not previously included at EU level. In addition, it introduces fixed minimum quantity thresholds. If these thresholds are exceeded, it could automatically be assumed that the goods are not for personal use. Can the Commission clarify: 1.
Whether the proposed amendments are compatible with Article 34 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, particularly considering their potential impact on the free movement of goods?
Whether, in its opinion, the proposal sufficiently respects the competences of the Member States?

Council Directive 2011/64/EU of 21 June 2011 on the structure and rates of excise duty applied to manufactured tobacco (OJ L 176, 5.7.2011, p. 24, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2011/64/oj). Council Directive (EU) 2020/262 of 19 December 2019 laying down the general arrangements for excise duty (OJ L 58, 27.2.2020, p. 4, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2020/262/oj).
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.5.2026) Article 34 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU) prohibits quantitative restrictions on imports between Member States. Under Article 36 thereof, the provisions of Article 34 do not preclude restrictions on imports on grounds of public policy or the protection of human health. With regard to excise duty, if a private individual purchases excise goods in one EU Member State and transports them to another, the exemption from paying excise duty in the destination Member State applies only if the goods are for their personal use. Article 32(3) of Council Directive (EU) 2020/2621 sets criteria, including quantity of tobacco products, for assessing own use. Member States may lay down guide levels, as a form of evidence regarding the intended use of goods. Recital 41 of Directive (EU) 2020/262 notes that varying excise duty levels, driven by fiscal and public health policies, create risks of fraud and health threats. To address it Member States should be able to take proportionate measures to verify whether excise goods acquired by private individuals are for personal use. The Commission emphasises the need to balance internal market functioning, national health policies and effective excise duty collection. The competence of the EU to act in the field of excise duties is conferred by Article 113 TFEU, which empowers the Council to adopt harmonised rules, necessary to ensure the functioning of the internal market and to avoid distortions of competition.
1 Council Directive (EU) 2020/262 of 19 December 2019 laying down the general arrangements for excise duty,

qt: to the Commission Isabel Serra Sánchez (The Left) Subject:

On 24 March 2026, the Israeli defence minister, Israel Katz, announced that Israel was taking military control of southern Lebanon, up to the Litani River – that is, 10 % of Lebanese territory, which was home to more than 200 000 people. His announcement follows attacks that have killed over 1 040 Lebanese people, displaced hundreds of thousands of people and destroyed civilian infrastructure such as universities, homes and hospitals. All of that comes on the heels of over 10 000 Israeli violations – documented by the United Nations – of the 2024 ceasefire. 1.

Does the Commission consider that Israel’s military action in Lebanon and its leaders’ statements respect the principles of the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Lebanon that the Commission has said it upholds, including during the last meeting of the EUIsrael Association Council?

Does it consider Israel, in this latest assault on Lebanese territory, to have violated human rights and democratic principles, which constitute an essential element of the EU-Israel Association Agreement?

Does it consider that the act of upholding the EU-Israel Association Agreement complies with the obligations that the EU and its Member States have under their founding treaties, international law and the orders of the International Court of Justice?
at: (English version) to the Commission Isabel Serra Sánchez (The Left) (1 April 2026) Subject: Israel’s recent attacks on Lebanon On 24 March 2026, the Israeli defence minister, Israel Katz, announced that Israel was taking military control of southern Lebanon, up to the Litani River — that is, 10% of Lebanese territory, which was home to more than 200 000 people. His announcement follows attacks that have killed over 1 040 Lebanese people, displaced hundreds of thousands of people and destroyed civilian infrastructure such as universities, homes and hospitals. All of that comes on the heels of over 10 000 Israeli violations — documented by the United Nations — of the 2024 ceasefire. 1. Does the Commission consider that Israel’s military action in Lebanon and its leaders’ statements respect the principles of the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Lebanon that the Commission has said it upholds, including during the last meeting of the EU-Israel Association Council? 2. Does it consider Israel, in this latest assault on Lebanese territory, to have violated human rights and democratic principles, which constitute an essential element of the EU-Israel Association Agreement? 3. Does it consider that the act of upholding the EU-Israel Association Agreement complies with the obligations that the EU and its Member States have under their founding treaties, international law and the orders of the International Court of Justice? (1 June 2026) The EU has repeatedly expressed its deep concern regarding Israel’s offensive in Lebanon and the devastating humanitarian consequences thereof (1) and it stresses that attacks on civilians, on infrastructure, on healthcare personnel and facilities, as well as on personnel of the UN Interim Force in Lebanon are unjustified, unacceptable and in breach of International Humanitarian Law. The EU will continue to stand by Lebanon, its authorities and its people and will draw on its emergency reserves to assist the affected civilian population (2). The EU urges all external actors to fully respect Lebanon’s unity, independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity and strongly condemns Hezbollah’s attacks in support of Iran against Israel, which must cease immediately. Given the catastrophic situation in Gaza, and with the support of a majority of Member States, the High Representative/VicePresident has conducted in June 2025 a review of Israel’s compliance with its obligations under Article 2 of the EU-Israel Association Agreement (3), which concluded that there are indications that Israel would be in breach of its obligations. Following this review, the Commission proposed a package of measures (4) and it has then put on hold its bilateral support to Israel, except for its support to civil society and Yad Vashem. Discussions continue in the Council on the other measures. The fight against impunity and the pursuit of justice for international crimes and violations of international law wherever occurring are cornerstones of the EU’s foreign policy. The EU reiterates its strong and steadfast support for the International Court of Justice which is an indispensable pillar of the global justice system.

E-10-2026-001353.t: Escalation of violence and the humanitarian situation in Lebanon
qt: to the Commission Leire Pajín (S&D), Hana Jalloul Muro (S&D) Subject:

Lebanon is facing a sharp escalation of violence amid a fragile political transition. In January 2025, Joseph Aoun was elected President, ending more than two years of institutional vacuum. At the same time, Nawaf Salam formed a new government tasked with stabilising the country during a deep economic and political crisis and ongoing tensions between Hezbollah and Israel. The Lebanese authorities have begun a state-led plan to deploy the army in the south and progressively disarm non-state armed groups, although the situation remains highly fragile. In recent days, the situation has deteriorated dramatically. Beirut has reportedly been bombed for the first time since the civil war. More than 600 000 people have been forcibly displaced, an act that constitutes a war crime under the Geneva Conventions. Over 400 people have been killed, including many women and children. 1.
What is the Commission’s assessment of proposals discussed with Arab partners regarding a ceasefire, support for the Lebanese Armed Forces and negotiations between Lebanon and Israel?
How does the Commission plan to increase humanitarian support for the civilian population and displaced persons in Lebanon?
What diplomatic or restrictive measures does the Commission intend to pursue in response to the escalation of attacks and violations of international law involving both Israel and Hezbollah?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (13.7.2026) The EU remains deeply concerned by the deterioration of the situation in Lebanon and the dramatic socio-economic and humanitarian consequences of the conflict for the civilian population. The EU has consistently called for a cessation of hostilities, the protection of civilians and full respect for international humanitarian law. The EU considers that the ceasefire agreement brokered by the United States between Lebanon and Israel on 3 June 2026 represents a renewed opportunity to end the conflict and create the conditions for lasting peace and security. The EU has consistently called on all parties to fully respect the ceasefire and to fully implement the UNSCR1 1701, calling for the respect of Lebanon’s sovereignty and territorial integrity by Israel and the disarmament of non-state armed groups, including Hezbollah. The EU stands ready to support the Lebanese Government and to contribute to an agreement between Lebanon and Israel, and to supporting the Lebanese Armed Forces (LAF) to ensure the state's monopoly over the legitimate use of force across Lebanese territory. The European Peace Facility assistance measure2 will directly contribute to reinforcing the operational capacities of the LAF. To address the crisis, the Commission announced3 a package of EUR 100 million humanitarian assistance to Lebanon, targeting all vulnerable populations, including refugees, vulnerable Lebanese and those internally displaced by the conflict, both inside and outside collective shelters. The EU reiterates its strong support for the role of the UN Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL) and condemns all attacks against UN personnel. A continued UN presence in the post-UNIFIL context is essential to ensure the implementation of UNSCR 17014.
1 United Nations Security Council Resolution. 2 Measure of EUR 100 million adopted on 4 June 2026. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-

content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=OJ:L_202601218. 3 https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_26_611. 4 https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/press/press-releases/2026/06/06/statement-by-the-high-representative-onbehalf-of-the-eu-on-israel-and-lebanon/.

qt: to the Commission Krzysztof Hetman (PPE) Subject:

In the context of the ongoing negotiations for an EU-Australia trade agreement and the potential increased access for Australian beef and sheep meat to the EU market, there are concerns among producers in many Member States, including Poland, about the agreement being negotiated and legitimate fears about maintaining competitiveness. Beef production remains a particularly sensitive sector and is of key economic and social importance for rural areas in many EU countries. In connection with the above: 1.

Is the Commission envisaging protective measures for the most sensitive sectors, such as beef, what will those protective measures be, and will the agreement include an agricultural safeguard clause allowing for the swift and automatic suspension of preferential trade conditions in the event of market disruption?

Has the Commission carried out a detailed impact assessment at Member State level, including countries with a significant share of beef exports, also taking into account the cumulative impact on the beef sector of other trade agreements, such as those with the Mercosur countries?

How will the Commission ensure full equivalence of phytosanitary and production standards (‘mirror clauses’), in particular with regard to the use of growth hormones, animal welfare, traceability and veterinary checks, and environmental and climate requirements?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (12.5.2026) Throughout the negotiations on the EU-Australia Free Trade Agreement (FTA), which were ultimately concluded on 24 March 2026, the Commission has held a firm line to ensure that our most sensitive interests, notably those in the area of agriculture, were taken into account. The final outcome is balanced, with limited and carefully conditioned opening of the EU’s market in combination with new export opportunities by eliminating tariffs on EU exports to Australia and the protection of EU geographical indications. For beef, the market opening accounts for only a fraction of EU consumption and is phased in gradually. More precisely, this translates into a quota of 30 600 tonnes, representing around 0.5% of EU consumption, over 10 years. Importantly, the Commission secured a bilateral safeguard clause covering all products, including those under tariff rate quotas. This additional layer of safety will ensure swift and effective protection in the unlikely event of an unforeseen and harmful surge in imports or an undue decrease in producers’ prices. The comprehensive study on the cumulative impact of trade agreements on EU agriculture, including the trade agreements with Mercosur and Australia1, showed that FTAs have overall a positive impact on the EU agri-food sector and it validates the EU approach to protect the most sensitive sectors from possible disruptions with carefully calibrated tariff rate quotas. When it comes to imports of agricultural products to the EU, the strict EU standards to protect human, animal and plant health, including phytosanitary standards, veterinary checks, the ban on the use of growth hormones, will continue to apply.
1 https://publications.jrc.ec.europa.eu/repository/handle/JRC135540.

E-10-2026-001349.t: Google’s developer registration decision and it’s threat to the EU’s tech sovereignty
qt: to the Commission Alexandra Geese (Verts/ALE), Anna Cavazzini (Verts/ALE), Reinier Van Lanschot (Verts/ALE) Subject:

In August 2025, Google unilaterally decided1 that Android developers will be required to register centrally with Google. In addition to demanding the payment of a registration fee and agreement to its terms and conditions, Google also requires software developers to upload documentation to confirm their identity2, including government-issued ID, and to enumerate3 all the unique ‘application identifiers’ for every app that is to be distributed by the registered developer. This has a drastic impact on open-source projects, competition and innovation. More importantly, this negatively impacts the EU’s ability to work towards technological sovereignty, as Google frequently complies with the demands of non-EU countries to remove perfectly legal apps that do not fit their political agenda. Is the Commission aware of this issue, and is it examining its compatibility with the Digital Markets Act?
