E-10-2026-001310.t: Israeli death penalty bill targeting Palestinians
qt: to the Council Rima Hassan (The Left) Subject:

On 24 March 2026, the Israeli Knesset’s National Security Committee approved, for final readings, a discriminatory death penalty bill designed to apply exclusively to Palestinians, including through military legal structures in the occupied Palestinian territory. Executions would reportedly be carried out by hanging within 90 days of sentencing, with no possibility of pardon or commutation. The final vote on the proposal is imminent. UN experts have warned1 that the bill would violate the most fundamental principles of international human rights law, including the right to life, fair-trial guarantees, and the prohibition of torture and ill-treatment. It would also constitute a grave violation of international humanitarian law. Can the Council clarify: 1.
what concrete measures it will propose or support in response to these developments?
whether it will ensure that the current package of EU measures is updated, including with the addition of possible restrictive measures against those responsible?
https://www.ohchr.org/en/press-releases/2026/02/israel-un-experts-urge-withdrawal-death-penalty-bill.
at: EN Reply (1.6.2026)

The European Union takes a principled stance against the death penalty in all cases and in all circumstances. In the Statement of 31 March 20261 by the High Representative on behalf of the European Union, the EU noted that the Israeli Parliament’s approval of the Death Penalty Bill marked a serious regression from Israel’s long-held practice of a de facto moratorium on both executions and capital punishment sentencing, and expressed its deep concern over the de facto discriminatory character of the bill. In keeping with the EU’s global efforts towards universal abolition of the death penalty, the EU urged Israel to abide by its previous, principled position and by its obligations under international law, as well to honour its commitment to democratic principles, which are also reflected in the provisions of the EU-Israel Association Agreement. As regards the Commission proposals related to the EU-Israel Association Agreement, the Council recalls its reply to Written Question E-002313/2025, and that the Foreign Affairs Council has addressed the matter in the context of its discussions on the situation in the Middle East.

Will the Commission re-implement measures taken during the pandemic, such as revenue caps for distributors, a sector solidarity contribution, a market correction mechanism and fixed pricing for small and medium-sized enterprises?

(29 June 2026) The Commission presented on 22 April 2026 the AccelerateEU communication (1) with concrete measures to be taken immediately at Member State level to protect households and businesses alike — including small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) — building on the lessons learnt in the 2022 crisis. Measures should be limited to addressing the concrete circumstances that currently lead to rising energy costs and must be targeted, temporary and avoid worsening supply conditions. Measures should focus on protecting the most vulnerable and increase the efficiency of the energy system, accelerating deployment of electrification and homegrown clean energy to reduce dependency on fossil fuels as well as supporting demand flexibility for the benefit of consumers. The Commission also adopted in April 2026 a set of detailed recommendations to implement the Citizens Energy Package (2), aimed at preventing consumer disconnections, prioritising consumer protection and switching to cheaper contracts, as well as expanding support for self-consumption and energy communities. The internal energy market framework leaves margin for Member States to design the most appropriate measures adapted for their national circumstances, including by granting the state aid. The Commission stands ready to assist Member States in designing measures that comply with internal market rules as well as in implementing the Middle East crisis Temporary state aid Framework (3), adopted in April 2026. In parallel, as announced in the AccelerateEU Communication, the Commission is preparing legislative proposals to be presented in July 2026 on network charges and electricity taxes, which represent important components of the overall electricity bill.

E-10-2026-001308.t: Geo-blocking restricts the rights of linguistic minorities on the internal market
qt: to the Commission Anna-Maja Henriksson (Renew), Loránt Vincze (PPE), Raquel García Hermida-Van Der Walle (Renew), Pascal Arimont (PPE), Herbert Dorfmann (PPE), Oihane Agirregoitia Martínez (Renew) Subject:

The 2020 evaluation of Regulation (EU) 2018/3021 on addressing unjustified geo-blocking showed that an increasing number of residents, particularly young people, feel restricted on the internal market when it comes to accessing audiovisual content from other EU countries. The fact that audiovisual content is exempt from geo-blocking rules is a problem, particularly for people who belong to linguistic minorities or who live in border regions. Parliament has called on the Commission to present concrete solutions. In its 2025 report, the European Court of Auditors calls on the Commission to investigate how the regulation can be expanded. In this regard: 1.

In its work on discussing industry-led solutions, has the Commission specifically discussed solutions to enable access to audiovisual content for linguistic minorities and residents in border regions?

The Commission’s response to the Court of Auditors states that it will continue to analyse a potential extension and its effects, ‘focusing on specific categories of works and/or distribution models’. What categories and models is the Commission referring to?
Has the Commission been in direct dialogue with representatives from the border regions and linguistic minorities that are most affected by this restriction?

(3 June 2026) The Commission is committed to, within the remit of its competences, upholding fundamental rights, including the right to non-discrimination on grounds of language and respect for cultural and linguistic diversity, as enshrined under Articles 21 and 22 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union. The Commission is aware of the challenges linguistic minorities face in accessing audiovisual content in their native tongue and in cross-border regions. In 2022, the Commission organised a stakeholder dialogue to explore industry-led solutions to enhance access to audiovisual content across borders, inviting the Federal Union of European Nationalities. Different proposals were discussed, including proposals to facilitate access to audiovisual content for linguistic minorities (1). Following the recommendation of the Court of Auditors, the Commission will launch a study to further analyse the benefits, challenges and possible risks of extending the scope of the Geo-blocking Regulation (2) to audiovisual services (3), taking into account the European Parliament’s Resolution on the implementation of the 2018 Geo-blocking Regulation (4), which suggested considering a gradual approach targeting specific type and distribution models of the audiovisual sector. E-10-2026-001307.t: Money laundering risks associated with the rapid creation of companies under the 28th regime
qt: to the Commission Ton Diepeveen (PfE) Subject:

With EU Inc. the European Commission seeks to boost the competitiveness of our European innovative companies. The focus is on easing and speeding up the procedures for setting up businesses. However, by limiting the time taken to set up a company across the EU to 48 hours, without a minimum capital requirement and without the need for a bank account at the time of incorporation, the risks of money laundering are increased. Moreover, there is a risk of bulk incorporation, whereby companies are set up ‘in bulk’ and used as intermediary companies in complex money-laundering schemes. In addition, the fact that a company can be incorporated without a minimum capital requirement also opens the door to abuse. Thus, a company can be set up quickly without any assets, accumulate new debts or take on existing debts from other companies, and then quickly go bankrupt again. This is a classic pattern employed to facilitate, for example, VAT fraud, fraudulent bankruptcies, and social dumping schemes. What specifically is the Commission doing to make such abuse impossible?

This is a classic pattern employed to facilitate, for example, VAT fraud, fraudulent bankruptcies, and social dumping schemes. What specifically is the Commission doing to make such abuse impossible? (12 June 2026) The EU Inc. proposal (1) is aimed at enhancing EU competitiveness by simplifying the regulatory framework and reducing fragmentation. It aims to make it easier to set up, scale up and attract investment into EU Inc. companies, while providing necessary safeguards. Any formation of an EU Inc. is subject to judicial, administrative or notarial control, which helps prevent abusive or fraudulent letter-box companies. A director disqualified in any Member State cannot be appointed as an EU Inc. director. Identity checks must be carried out in accordance with Regulation (EU) No 910/2014 (2). The 48 hours deadline for EU Inc. registration does not apply to the verification of the beneficial ownership (BO) information or to the issuance of the tax and the value added tax identification number. The once-only principle ensures that business registers transmit to tax and social security authorities and BO registers the EU Inc. company information, including any updates. This ensures that authorities share the same information, which helps tackle abuse and fraud, thereby enhancing compliance. BO registers will verify the BO information in accordance with Directive (EU) 2024/1640 (3). Filings throughout the lifecycle of an EU Inc. are subject to preventive control and business registers must check the status of an EU Inc. where doubts exist (such as non-filing of accounting documents) and as a last resort strike off the company from the register. The proposal is coherent with and complements existing rules related to tax avoidance or evasion and the prevention of money laundering, which include cross-checking information with other registers. The forthcoming interconnection between the business registers and BO registers interconnection systems will facilitate this (4).

E-10-2026-001306.t: Zoning, external border controls and the functioning of the single market following the outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease in Greece
qt: to the Commission Nikolaos Anadiotis (NI) Subject:

The confirmed outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease in Lesvos led to the immediate activation of European protocols, including the culling of animals, the creation of control zones and the suspension of exports. At the same time, cross-border transmission through uncontrolled imports from non-EU countries is reportedly being considered1. Applying the ‘zoning’ principle is crucial in order to limit trade measures to affected regions only and avoid a disproportionate impact on national production and the single market as a whole. In light of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
How does it ensure the uniform implementation of zoning by non-EU trading partners to avoid blanket bans on exports beyond the affected areas?
How does it assess the risk of asymmetric trade restrictions distorting the single market and what mechanisms does it intend to put in place to prevent them?

(10 June 2026) The Commission assesses the regionalisation measures applied by third countries in relation to foot and mouth disease and other listed animal diseases based on international standards of the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH), and on relevant EU legislation. It includes documentary reviews and, where appropriate, on-the-spot audits of the implementation of the measures in place. On this basis, the Commission adopts legal acts (1), recognising disease-free areas and restricted zones in third countries for specific diseases and commodities. These acts ensure that trade from third countries into the EU is aligned with the zoning principle and only when the appropriate level of guarantees is met. Trade restrictions adopted by third countries are unilateral decisions. The Commission seeks to minimise the risk of disproportionate measures with transparency on the animal health situation in the EU and on the regionalisation measures applied in response to outbreaks. It does so by providing a solid EU legal framework (2) for emergency disease control measures for animal diseases, timely disease notifications (3), regular information to Member States and trading partners. In addition, the EU promotes the application of regionalisation as a trade-facilitating tool with multilateral and bilateral actions.

E-10-2026-001305.t: Unlawful police detentions and implications for the rule of law in Bulgaria
at: (English version) to the Commission Nikola Minchev (Renew) (29 March 2026) Subject: Unlawful police detentions and implications for the rule of law in Bulgaria On 25 February 2026, the Sofia District Court ruled that the 24-hour police detention of Varna’s Mayor, Blagomir Kotsev, was unlawful, finding that the measure lacked sufficient factual and legal justification. According to interior ministry data, over the past four years, nearly 640 24-hour police detentions have been declared unlawful by courts for similar reasons. The country chapter on Bulgaria of the Commission’s 2025 Rule of Law Report refers to issues concerning detention conditions and the implementation of judgments of the European Court of Human Rights but does not assess whether repeated judicial findings of unlawful police detentions may indicate broader structural deficiencies in safeguards against arbitrary deprivation of liberty. In light of Article 2 of the Treaty on European Union and the standards stemming from Articles 5 and 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights: 1.
Does the Commission consider that repeated judicial findings of unlawful short-term police detentions may point to systemic shortcomings affecting the rule of law in Bulgaria?

Does the Commission intend, in its next Rule of Law Report, to assess whether the use of short-term police detention and pre-trial measures raises structural concerns regarding proportionality, the presumption of innocence and effective judicial oversight?
Should such patterns persist, what measures does the Commission envisage to ensure that safeguards against arbitrary deprivation of liberty are effectively implemented?

(19 May 2026) The Commission does not comment on individual cases. The competence to investigate and prosecute suspected corruption cases lies with national authorities. The Commission will continue monitoring relevant developments relating to the rule of law in all Member States, including in Bulgaria, in the context of the annual Rule of Law Report process. The 2026 edition of the Rule of Law Report is expected to be published in July 2026.

E-10-2026-001304.t: Trade in and use of spyware based on the EU legislative framework and cover-up by the Greek Government
qt: to the Commission Lefteris Nikolaou-Alavanos (NI) Subject:

Statements by the founder of Intellexa about supplying Predator software to governments attest to the part played by Nea Dimokratia in the wiretapping scandal. The main culprit is EU ‘rule of law’ and the legitimacy of ‘no one [being] exempt from surveillance’, which is cofashioned/implemented by Greek governments. Part of the reactionary framework (Regulation (EU) 2021/821) is the legalisation of the conditions for the production, trade in, distribution and export of Predator-type spyware and the institutionalisation of mass surveillance for reasons of ‘national security’. Over 100 000 confidentiality of communications waivers have been approved in one decade. The headquarters of the Greek Communist Party’s central committee were bugged/wiretapped and the investigation has been buried, with capitalist parties bearing responsibility for this. Similar software is being distributed in the EU. In the current context of military preparedness/complicity, there is an intensification of repression and of the inculcation of the concept of ‘the enemy people’ aimed at silencing any popular struggle. The Greek Government is attempting to cover up mass surveillance and indiscriminate tracking. How does the Commission view the EU’s responsibilities, given that: 1.

many governments, including Nea Dimokratia, are using this framework, for instance Regulation (EU) 2021/821, to trade in and use spyware with all that this entails for the rights, freedoms and protection of the personal data of the people in each Member State?
at: EN E-001304/26 on behalf of the European Commission (22.6.2026) The Commission's position is very clear: any attempts to illegally access data of citizens, including journalists, representatives of civil society and political opponents, is unacceptable. The legal interception or surveillance of communications can take place in limited circumstances, such as the prevention, investigation, detection and prosecution of criminal offences and subject to strict conditions and safeguards. Furthermore, the data protection Law Enforcement Directive1 is also applicable when competent authorities process personal data for law enforcement purposes. National supervisory authorities have effective powers to examine any allegations of misuse, and data processed can be subject to judicial review. The European Media Freedom Act includes specific safeguards against the use of spyware against journalists and their families. The respective provisions entered into application in August 2025.

E-10-2026-001303.t: Prevention and management of foot-and-mouth disease in Cyprus
qt: to the Commission Fidias Panayiotou (NI) Subject:

In Cyprus, the foot-and-mouth disease situation poses a constant threat to the animal population and rural economy of the island. Given that the prevention and control measures in occupied northern Cyprus may be less stringent or differ from those in force in the Republic of Cyprus, can the Commission say: 1.

Does it intend to strengthen the surveillance and early detection systems for foot-andmouth disease in Cyprus, in order to ensure that any outbreaks in occupied northern Cyprus do not endanger the animal population of the Republic of Cyprus?
What measures is it monitoring and implementing to ensure that the management of the disease reduces its risk of spreading across the island?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (26.5.2026) The Commission is in close contact with the Cypriot authorities and supports them in the control of foot and mouth disease (FMD) on the island. The EU legal framework, in particular Regulation (EU) 2016/4291 and Commission Delegated Regulations (EU) 2020/6872 and 2020/6893, provides for harmonised measures across the Union, based on the principles of early detection via surveillance, regionalisation with movement restrictions of animals and products of animal origin and rapid eradication through stamping-out of confirmed outbreaks coupled with emergency vaccination. Under Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2026/5824, specific regionalisation measures (protection zones, surveillance zones, a further restricted zone, and a vaccination zone) were set up by the Commission to address the specific risks related to FMD in Cyprus. The implementation of these measures is the responsibility of the competent authority of the Member State concerned. The Commission regularly reviews the situation and the measures for FMD in its Standing Committee on Plants, Animals, Food and Feed5 and carries out audits aimed at monitoring the implementation and enforcement of EU legislation.

E-10-2026-001302.t: Non-paper outlining legal issues related to the charter of the Board of Peace and other information
qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Per Clausen (The Left) Subject:

The EU’s decision to participate as an observer in Donald Trump’s so-called Board of Peace was not only highly controversial, but it also runs counter to the policies of several EU Member States and seems to have taken place without a mandate and without sufficient consultation or briefing of the European Parliament. As a result, many questions are left unanswered. Since this controversial case clearly necessitates more scrutiny, clarity and discussion, is the Commission going to make public: 1.

A copy of its non-paper of 19 January 2026 outlining legal issues related to the charter of the Board of Peace, as well as any other analysis, assessment or similarly produced material about the Board of Peace and the EU’s participation in it?
A copy of the mandate on which its official participation was based or, in case it does not exist, a clear indication of with whom the participation was discussed prior to the event?

Can the Commission furthermore kindly provide an explanation outlining the complete legal basis for the EU’s participation as an observer in the Board of Peace, including information about any financial pledges or provisions relating to it?

(5 June 2026) The European External Action Service (EEAS) has made a legal assessment on the possibility to grant public access to the nonpaper of 19 January 2026 in the context of a request submitted under Regulation 1049/2001 (1). This showed that the document cannot be disclosed to the public as it constitutes legal advice (excluded from public disclosure by Article 4(2) second indent) and because its disclosure would undermine the EU international relations (Article 4(1)(a) third indent). At the inauguration ceremony of the Board of Peace meeting on 25 February 2026, in Washington DC, EU Commissioner for the Mediterranean participated as an observer. The Commissioner for the Mediterranean participated on behalf of the Commission in the meeting. It is within the remit of the Commission to accept invitations of this kind as a matter of international courtesy. The Commissioner attended alongside representatives of at least half of EU Member States, as well as other European partners and regional actors. It is of paramount importance to be at the table and engage with all relevant regional and international actors. The EU’s position on the Board of Peace has been very clear. There are serious doubts about a number of elements in the charter of the Board of Peace related to its scope, its governance and its compatibility with the UN Charter. The EU has signalled to the US that it is ready to work together on the implementation of the comprehensive Peace Plan for Gaza, with a Board of Peace carrying out its mission as a transitional administration, in accordance with UN Security Council Resolution 2803 (2).

E-10-2026-001301.t: EU ‘training programmes’ and mechanisms supporting employers rather than workers
qt: to the Commission Lefteris Nikolaou-Alavanos (NI) Subject:

Training programmes have long been championed as a means of tackling unemployment and supporting workers. In practice, however, they are a key tool for implementing the EU’s strategy to tailor the workforce to the needs of capital profitability. The ‘social partners’ – all kinds of unscrupulous union bosses – play a particular role in the implementation of political manipulation and worker assimilation, with substantial amounts of funding flowing their way for training and ‘labour market reintegration’ activities. In Greece, for many years, the leadership of the General Confederation of Greek Workers (GSEE) has been involved in the management of hundreds of millions for training programmes. This is a matter of a long-standing, institutionalised transaction between trade union aristocracy, employers and the bourgeois state. Management activities are primarily carried out by the GSEE’s Labour Institute and Centre for Educational Policy Development. What is the Commission’s position on the fact that: 1.

in practice, these programmes act as a mechanism for recycling unemployment, easing public discontent and legalising layoffs and flexible working arrangements, while also strengthening the role of union bosses who move in step with employers and governments, contributing to the implementation of anti-worker policies?

with the support of European funds, Greek governments and GSEE bodies have set up training mechanisms that not only fail to protect workers, but also strengthen employers’ and governments’ interference in trade union structures?
they thereby constitute a mechanism for manipulating and assimilating workers – especially the most vulnerable, such as the unemployed – and methodically orchestrate the weakening of their fight?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.5.2026) Across the EU, training and skills initiatives are crucial to enhance employability, support labour market transitions, and promote fair working conditions, in line with the European Pillar of Social Rights and the Union of Skills. At the same time, to be effective and relevant, training programmes need to respond to the actual needs of companies and workers. This can be achieved through the involvement of social partners – including trade unions. This is also a cornerstone of EU social dialogue1. The Commission remains committed to ensuring EU funds serve workers’ interests and promote social justice. In this respect, the Commission monitors implementation to prevent misuse, including through audits and evaluations under shared management with Member States. The Commission expects transparency and accountability in funds management. Allegations of mismanagement are addressed by national authorities, in line with the shared management principles and, where fraud concerning EU funds is suspected, also by European Independent Bodies2.
1 Article 154 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union. 2 OLAF (European Anti-Fraud Office) or the European Public Prosecutor’s Office.

E-10-2026-001300.t: Advertising of airline routes to non-self governing territories
qt: to the Commission Lynn Boylan (The Left), Vicent Marzà Ibáñez (Verts/ALE), Estrella Galán (The Left), Vladimir Prebilič (Verts/ALE), Per Clausen (The Left), Martin Günther (The Left), Oihane Agirregoitia Martínez (Renew), Andreas Schieder (S&D), Isabel Serra Sánchez (The Left), Irene Montero (The Left), Rudi Kennes (The Left), Kathleen Funchion (The Left), Jaume Asens Llodrà (Verts/ALE), João Oliveira (The Left) Subject:

The EU-based airline Ryanair has recently launched an email campaign advertising routes to Dakhla in the non-self governing territory of Western Sahara. The advertisement describes visiting Dakhla as part of a Moroccan adventure and on their website lists the city as ‘Morocco’s best kept secret’1. Several times the advertisement describes Dakhla as Moroccan and makes no reference to Western Sahara or the Sahrawi people. Dakhla is part of the non-self governing territory of Western Sahara, occupied by Morocco since 1975. The International Court of Justice confirmed2 that this territory does not belong to Morocco and it is listed on the United Nations list of non-self governing territories3. In response to a previous question4, the Commission informed airlines that the EuroMediterranean aviation agreement between the EU and Morocco does not apply to Western Sahara. However, Ryanair are still engaging in practices designed to deceive EU consumers. Will the Commission: 1.
Instruct airlines to not advertise a destination as belonging to an occupying power, thereby erasing the presence of the indigenous people?
Instruct Ryanair to cease these deceptive advertising practices?
Issue guidance for airlines operating in the EU regarding their obligations in respect of non-self governing territories?

https://www.ryanair.com/ie/en/lp/explore/morocco. https://www.icj-cij.org/sites/default/files/case-related/61/061-19751016-ADV-01-00-EN.pdf. https://www.un.org/dppa/decolonization/en/nsgt. https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/E-10-2024-002585_EN.html.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (25.6.2026) As mentioned in its reply to parliamentary question E-002585/2024, the Commission has already informed EU carriers that, in accordance with the case law of the Court of Justice, the Euro-Mediterranean aviation agreement between the EU and Morocco does not apply to routes to the territory of the Western Sahara. This means that carriers are not bound by the provisions of said agreement, including concerning the operation and the advertisement of routes from the EU to Western Sahara and vice versa. Furthermore: 1. The Commission cannot issue general instructions to air carriers on how to describe territorial sovereignty in commercial communications. However, EU-established airlines must comply with EU consumer-protection law, including Directives 2005/29/EC1 and 2006/114/EC2, which prohibit misleading actions or omissions likely to affect the average consumer’s transactional decision. Presenting a destination in a way that misleads consumers about a territory’s status may therefore raise issues under those rules. 2. The enforcement of EU consumer-protection law in individual cases is primarily the responsibility of national competent authorities and courts in the Member States. The Commission therefore cannot substitute itself for national enforcement authorities by ordering a specific company to cease a given practice. 3.The Commission takes note of the concerns raised and will continue to monitor the correct application of EU consumer-protection law in the aviation sector.

E-10-2026-001299.t: The content of the new European security strategy and related competences
qt: to the Commission Nacho Sánchez Amor (S&D), José Cepeda (S&D), Javi López (S&D) Subject:

The Commission President has announced a new European security strategy (ESS) – expected in the first semester of 2026 – an initiative not included in the current Commission work programme. Despite little public discussion on its content, media reports show a process led by the Commission, with the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy (VP/HR) playing a limited coordination role, which includes ‘consulting’ with Member States. This raises a question about competence: under the Treaties, foreign policy and security and defence are Member State competences and the VP/HR has the political initiative in this area. Moreover, recent VP/HR public statements about the ESS mention a ‘broad approach to security’ but omit the promotion of democracy and human rights. Besides being enshrined in the Treaties as a guiding principle of EU external action, promoting democracy and human rights is intimately linked with our security, since democracies act in a predictable and safer manner on the international stage. In this regard: 1.
What is the Commission legal service’s assessment of the legal basis of the ESS?
How does the Commission ensure that competences in the ESS are divided between it and the VP/HR?
Can the Commission confirm if promoting human rights and democracy is a structural element of the ESS?

(28 July 2026) 1. and 2. The European Security Strategy (ESS) will be a policy document presented jointly by the Commission and the High Representative/Vice-President and will fully respect the roles and competences of the EU and its Member States. This Strategy will be the first to adopt a comprehensive approach to security, addressing both its internal and external dimensions to respond to today’s rapidly deteriorating global security environment. 3. E-10-2026-001298.t: The automatic removal of a member of the armed forces from their trade union position and freedom of association in Italy
qt: to the Commission Giuseppe Antoci (The Left) Subject:

On 24 December 2025, the Italian Armed Forces General Staff announced in a memorandum that, pursuant to Article 1477b(2)(a) of the Italian Military Code, it was removing a member of the armed forces from his position as a trade union1 leader. This decision came nine days after CGARS2 Judgement No 1004 confirmed the legality of the serviceman’s two-month suspension from duty3. On 15 January, an appeal was lodged before the Regional Administrative Court of Sicily which, among other things, highlighted that the defendant had been automatically removed from his trade union role and that his case had not been individually assessed. In the light of the provisions outlined by Article 2 TEU and Articles 11, 12, 51 and 52 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union and having regard for CJEU case-law, we ask the Commission: 1.

Will it request information from the Italian authorities with a view to ensuring that any restrictions on the freedom of association and expression of armed forces members are necessary and proportionate and do not deter military personnel from exercising their fundamental rights and their right to union membership?

Which Union instruments – including rule of law dialogues and infringement proceedings – would be appropriate for dealing with cases in which restrictions akin to the above run counter to the values espoused by Article 2 TEU and the rights enshrined in the Charter?

These organisations are officially known as APCSMs (Associazione professionale a carattere sindacale tra militari). Council of Administrative Justice for the Sicily Region. These suspensions are reserved for defendants whose serious disciplinary offences make their continued service in the armed forces temporarily impossible.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (29.6.2026) 1. The Commission supports social dialogue in line with the provisions of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU). The Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union recognises the freedom of assembly and association and the right of collective bargaining and action1. However, the right of association does not fall under the EU’s legislative competence2. The functioning of national social dialogue frameworks falls therefore under the responsibility of each Member State3. At the same time, the Council Recommendation on strengthening social dialogue in the EU recommends to Member States that they ensure ‘an enabling environment for bipartite and tripartite social dialogue’ in the public and private sectors4. 2. As regards the case referred to by the Honourable Member, the Commission recalls that, according to its Article 51(1), the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union applies to Member States only when they are implementing EU law. Where an alleged violation of fundamental rights derives from a national legal measure, it is primarily the responsibility of national courts to safeguard the rights of individuals. E-10-2026-001297.t: Safeguarding the Mediterranean Sea: a public health priority
qt: to the Commission Giuseppe Antoci (The Left) Subject:

Though it is one of the world’s major biodiversity hotspots, the Mediterranean Sea is more exposed to plastic and microplastic pollution than most European marine areas1, a state of affairs that has negative consequences for marine biodiversity, ecosystems and public health. In addition, chemical pollution in the Mediterranean is one of the most serious and urgent environmental challenges on the European agenda. The Commission’s March 2025 assessment2 highlighted that Directive 2008/56/EC3 has not fully achieved its ‘good environmental status’ objective of clean, healthy and productive oceans and seas. According to the ‘One Health’ approach4, because human, animal and ecosystem health are closely intertwined, it follows that protecting marine species is also beneficial for public health and quality of life in the short and long term. In the light of the above: 1.
What further concrete measures will the Commission implement to reduce plastic and microplastic pollution in the Mediterranean Sea?
How will the Commission improve upon the implementation of Directive 2008/56/EC with a view to achieving the aforementioned ‘good environmental status’ objective?
Will it promote prevention, monitoring and marine ecosystem protection initiatives which specifically concern the Mediterranean?

https://www.wwf.it/pandanews/ambiente/inquinamento/mar-mediterraneo-inquinato//. https://environment.ec.europa.eu/news/commission-evaluates-sea-protection-and-bathing-water-quality-laws2025-03-06_en. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:02008L0056-20170607. https://www.who.int/health-topics/one-health#tab=tab_1.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (6.7.2026) The Commission recognises marine pollution, including litter, as major environmental concerns, particularly in the Mediterranean Sea. To address these challenges, it is implementing a comprehensive framework of EU legislation and initiatives focused on prevention, reduction and monitoring. These include the Marine Strategy Framework Directive (MSFD)1, the Directives on Single-Use Plastics and Fishing Gears2, on Port Reception Facilities3 and the Urban Wastewater Treatment Directive4, the Regulations on intentional use of microplastics in products5 and on the prevention of plastic pellets’ releases6; as well as the Zero Pollution Action Plan7. Through the common implementation strategy of the MSFD, the Commission supports Member States in improving implementation and progressing towards achieving good environmental status. This includes the development of harmonised threshold values for beach and seafloor litter, ongoing work on floating marine litter and microplastics, and technical guidance on monitoring. In parallel, the Commission is reviewing the Directive to strengthen its effectiveness while simplifying the legislative framework. At regional level, the EU cooperates with Mediterranean partners under the Barcelona Convention to reduce and prevent marine litter and enhance monitoring and assessment initiatives. This includes the funding of the Marine Litter Med Plus project8, which supports the implementation of the Mediterranean Plan on marine litter management. More broadly, the EU also plays a leading international role in negotiations for a Global Treaty against plastic pollution and pushes developments to prevent plastic pellet losses from shipping in relevant fora.

E-10-2026-001295.t: Urgent need to support livestock farmers due to foot-and-mouth disease
qt: to the Commission Loucas Fourlas (PPE) Subject:

Foot-and-mouth disease is a highly contagious animal disease, with serious implications for both animal health and the security of the food supply chain. Farmers are once again being asked to deal with considerable risk, often without adequate means of prevention and without the necessary economic shielding. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
What immediate measures is it taking to strengthen disease prevention and surveillance in Member States, especially in high-risk areas?
Does it intend to activate specific financial support mechanisms for affected livestock farmers, either through compensation or exceptional aid, to ensure that the profession remains viable?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.7.2026) The EU legal framework, in particular Regulation (EU) 2016/4291 and Commission Delegated Regulations (EU) 2020/6872 and 2020/6893, establishes harmonised measures across the EU to eradicate Category A diseases, such as foot and mouth disease (FMD). These include immediately setting up protection and surveillance zones, culling infected herds, restricting animal and product movements from affected zones, and, where appropriate, vaccination4. Following confirmation of the FMD by Greece and Cyprus, interim restrictions were immediately imposed5 under Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/687. Afterwards, the measures were reviewed and replaced by new measures6 better tailored to the evolving situation. The EU co-finances emergency veterinary measures via the Single Market Programme7, covering costs for culling, compensating farmers, cleaning and disinfecting the affected premises, and vaccination8. The Commission stands ready to deploy vaccines from the EU FMD antigen bank upon Greece’s request. Additionally, under the Common Agricultural Policy Strategic Plans Regulation9, Member States may support investments in biosecurity measures as well as restoring agricultural potential and introduce crisis payments for farmers affected by catastrophic events. The Commission may also adopt exceptional support measures for market losses linked to restrictions imposed to curb disease spread.

E-10-2026-001294.t: 20th sanctions package threatens European agricultural production and food security
qt: to the Commission Ondřej Dostál (NI) Subject:

Announced by President von der Leyen, the Commission’s proposed 20th sanctions package targets trade, energy, fertilisers and other essential agricultural chemicals. Presented as a tool of foreign policy, these measures risk inflicting immediate, severe and lasting harm on European farmers, producers and consumers. By restricting access to critical agricultural inputs, the package will increase prices, raise production costs, undermine competitiveness and compromise Europe’s food security. The Commission is therefore requested to provide a written response to the following points: 1.
How does the Commission assess the impact of these measures on European fertiliser and chemical prices, agricultural production costs and overall food security?

What measures does the Commission intend to take to prevent these sanctions from undermining the competitiveness and economic viability of Europe’s farmers and agribusinesses and how will it ensure that future sanctions or trade restrictions do not harm Europe’s food supply or economy while pursuing foreign policy objectives?
Does the Commission have a contingency plan to safeguard European food security in the event that disruptions to fertiliser and chemical imports significantly affect agricultural output?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.6.2026) EU sanctions are carefully calibrated to target sectors that generate revenue for the Russian budget, whilst minimising unintended effects to the EU economy and global food security. They are not aimed at the civilian population, nor at food products. On fertilisers, the quota established for potash and, in the 20th package, on ammonia were set at a level matching historical import allowing trade to continue while avoiding sanctions’ circumvention. By diversifying energy and fertiliser sources away from Russia, the EU seeks to shield its economy from politically motivated potential price manipulation. Over past years, Member States made substantial efforts to secure alternative energy supplies, improving the energy market resilience. The Commission maintains a close dialogue with Member States and stakeholders from the farming and fertiliser sectors, through mechanisms such as the European Food Security Crisis preparedness and response Mechanism1 or the Fertilisers Market Observatory2. On 19 May 2026, the Commission adopted the Fertiliser Action Plan3, setting out short- and long-term measures to improve fertiliser availability, affordability and resilience. Short term actions include the mobilisation and possible top-up of the agricultural reserve, liquidity support under the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) and greater flexibility for advance payments. Longer term measures focus on strengthening EU production capacity, supporting the uptake of recycled nutrients and low carbon alternatives, and reducing strategic dependencies on imports. Furthermore, imports of ammonia, urea and certain other nitrogen-based and mixed fertilisers from countries other than Russia and Belarus, now benefit from a tariff suspension4, within given quotas, until 31 May 2027. While there is currently no risk of shortage of fertilisers on the EU market for the upcoming 2026 harvest, the Commission continues to monitor the market and will take further appropriate measures if necessary.

E-10-2026-001292.t: Ensuring that the fight against cancer remains a priority in the next multiannual financial framework (MFF) 2028-2034
qt: to the Commission Elena Nevado del Campo (PPE) Subject:

Cancer is one of the biggest public health challenges in the European Union, with around 2.7 million people diagnosed and 1.3 million deaths per year1. Beyond its human impact, cancer entails a social and economic burden by affecting health systems, productivity and the wellbeing of millions of citizens. Inequalities between Member States in prevention, early detection and access to treatment highlight the need for coordinated European action. The EU has launched initiatives such as Europe’s Beating Cancer Plan to strengthen prevention, improve early diagnosis and ensure equitable care. However, concerns have been raised in discussions on the next MFF that integrating health policies into broader financial instruments – such as the European Competitiveness Fund – may reduce visibility and resources for the fight against cancer. I would therefore like to ask: 1.
How will the Commission ensure that the fight against cancer remains a priority in the next MFF?
What steps will the Commission take to prevent broader instruments from diluting these priorities?
Does the Commission intend to secure funding to continue Europe’s Beating Cancer Plan?
https://commission.europa.eu/topics/public-health/european-health-union/cancer-plan-europe_en.

(4 June 2026) The Commission has proposed a redesign of the EU budget (1), with more streamlined and harmonised spending programmes. The proposed European Competitiveness Fund (ECF) (2) includes a focus on healthcare and health technologies, aiming to support European competitiveness, while promoting innovation, private finance and industrial ecosystems. Within the ECF, the health, biotech, agriculture and bioeconomy window (with an indicative budget of EUR 20.4 billion) is envisaged to support public health by addressing communicable and non-communicable diseases through targeted health promotion, disease prevention strategies and continued investments, including into the pharmaceutical and medical devices sectors. Cancer is mentioned among the eligible activities under the window (Article 37, point (a), of the proposal). In addition, EUR 19.65 billion is indicatively allocated in the Horizon Europe 2028-2034 proposal for collaborative research under the same policy window. Horizon Europe and the ECF are proposed to be closely connected via joint work programmes and governance, ensuring a closer link between research and industrial deployment including for health technologies. The Commission also aims to bring together EU funds implemented by Member States and regions through National and Regional Partnership Plans (NRPP), which could be used to support health system investments and reforms in line with Article 3 of the proposed NRPP Regulation (3). Finally, the proposed single expenditure and performance monitoring system for all relevant programmes aims to increase transparency and provide an overview of where EU funds are allocated and what they deliver.

E-10-2026-001291.t: Strategic autonomy of the European Union and preparedness for health crises in the next multiannual financial framework
qt: to the Commission Elena Nevado del Campo (PPE) Subject:

The COVID-19 pandemic exposed the European Union’s dependence on third countries for the supply of critical medical products. In future health crises, this dependency could compromise the European Union’s ability to respond quickly and effectively. The European Union has taken steps to strengthen health emergency preparedness and open strategic autonomy. However, concerns remain about the European manufacturing capacity for certain critical medical products and the existence of sufficient strategic reserves. Products such as medical gloves have highlighted a structural dependence on external suppliers owing to differences in production costs. I therefore wish to ask the Commission: 1.
What measures is the Commission taking to strengthen the European Union’s strategic autonomy in the supply of essential medical products, in order to ensure preparedness for future health crises?
How does the Commission intend to ensure the availability of sufficient manufacturing capacities and strategic reserves within the European Union for these essential products?

Has the Commission carried out any assessments of the European Union’s strategic dependencies on critical medical products, and what measures does it propose with a view to reducing such dependencies?

(15 June 2026) In 2021, the Commission established the Health Emergency Preparedness and Response Authority (DG HERA) with the mandate to improve preparedness and response to serious cross-border threats to medical countermeasures. This implies strengthening the resilience of supply chains and the EU’s strategic autonomy. In 2025, the Commission adopted a new strategy (1) for medical countermeasures that explains its work so far and presents a number of key initiatives for the future. In an end-to-end approach, building from a thorough threat analysis, DG HERA supports the development of new vaccines, reserving production capacity in case a crisis hits and building critical stocks with national authorities. As part of the next Multiannual Financial Framework, the Commission proposed to continue funding this end-to-end approach through the health and biotech window of Horizon Europe and the European Competitiveness Fund, for the development of new countermeasures and the resilience of their supply chains. In addition, a new instrument for the Union Civil Protection Mechanism and Union Support for Health Emergency Preparedness and Response (2), has been proposed to support more operational activities to prevent, prepare for and respond to health emergencies, such as early warning and surveillance systems, training and exercises, stockpiling and the direct procurement and distribution of countermeasures in emergencies. This combination of instruments would contribute to strengthening the strategic autonomy of the EU for health preparedness. The new Pharmaceutical Regulation (3) and the proposed Critical Medicines Act (4) also aim at identifying and addressing vulnerabilities and excessive dependencies in the supply chain of critical medicines.

E-10-2026-001290.t: Cohesion funds diverted to defence priorities in Spain’s pluri-regional operational programme 2021-2027
qt: to the Commission Elena Nevado del Campo (PPE) Subject:

The European Commission recently published the results of the mid-term review of cohesion policy, adopted by the European Council and Parliament in September 2025. One of the pieces of information it gives is that Spain has amended the pluri-regional programme for Spain ERDF 2021-20271, which is financed through the ERDF and managed directly by the Spanish Government. According to the results published by the Commission, this programme has diverted around EUR 223 million of ERDF funds to the field of defence. Considering that the main priorities of the programme are the digital and smart transition, digital connectivity, the green transition, urban mobility, promotion of greener urban territories, social transformation and territorial and local integration: 1.
To what type of defence investment projects have the funds of this pluri-regional programme been diverted in the context of the mid-term review?

From which specific priorities and objectives have the funds been diverted and removed so that they could be reallocated to the field of defence? Which political priorities had the funds initially been earmarked for before they were reallocated to defence?
https://www.fondoseuropeos.hacienda.gob.es/sitios/dgfc/esES/ipr/fcp2020/P2127/PF/Documents/Programa_POPE.pdf.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (11.5.2026) In light of the unprecedented geopolitical instability and the need for the Union to ensure its own defence and civil preparedness, the European Parliament and the Council, following a Commission proposal, have amended Regulation 2021/10581 of the European Regional Development Fund (ERDF) and the Cohesion Fund, to enable Member States and regions to mobilise cohesion policy funding to support investments in defence capabilities, prioritising the dual use of industrial capacities, technologies and infrastructure. In the context of the mid-term review of 2021-2027 cohesion policy programmes, the Spanish authorities decided to amend the pluri-regional programme for Spain ERDF 2021-2027 to support the EU’s emerging priorities. Among others, Spain decided to support dual use investments in several ways. First, EUR 113 million were allocated to investments enhancing industrial capacities of a dual-use nature, specifically the testing facilities for enterprises to develop 5G technologies related exclusively to dual use. In addition, the programme will support with EUR 104.5 million part of the assembly of the track of the high-speed train line Murcia-Almeria, a military corridor of dual use, serving the transport of both freight and passengers. Finally, over EUR 5.5 million will foster the robustness, resilience and security of Spain’s national domain name system, a critical IT infrastructure to ensure technological sovereignty and national security. To finance these new investments, the Spanish authorities have reduced the programme’s initial allocations for digitisation and sustainable mobility. Nevertheless, these changes do not impact the overall strategy of the programme and its level of ambition.

at: (English version) to the Commission Billy Kelleher (Renew) (27 March 2026) Subject: Impact of the Mercury Regulation Under the revised Mercury Regulation, Member States will be expected to cease the importation, exportation and manufacturing of mercury-containing lamps, albeit with some exceptions to the rule as set out in the directives on batteries and the restriction of hazardous substances. (8 May 2026) The Commission does not intend to review the expired phase-out dates for the import, export and manufacture of mercurycontaining lamps for general lighting purposes. Under Directive 2011/65/EU (1) the placing on the Union market and import of electrical and electronic equipment containing mercury is prohibited, subject to time-limited exemptions listed in Annex III. The exemptions for mercury-containing lamps used for general lighting expired between 2016 and February 2025. Certain exemptions for specific lamp categories, including high-pressure sodium lamps and special-purpose lamps, remain valid until February 2027, and renewal applications are currently under assessment. The revised Regulation (EU) 2024/1849 (2) aligns the regulation (EU) 2017/852 (3) with the Restriction of Hazardous Substances (RoHS) framework. E-10-2026-001288.t: Implementation of Seveso III Directive, Industrial Emissions Directive and Environmental Liability Directive in Lavrio given a new corporate structure and the risk of a major accident – ASAP projects
at: (English version) to the Commission Maria Zacharia (NI) (26 March 2026) Subject: Implementation of Seveso III Directive, Industrial Emissions Directive and Environmental Liability Directive in Lavrio given a new corporate structure and the risk of a major accident — ASAP projects In its reply to Question P-000475/2026, the Commission states that military establishments are exempt from the Seveso III Directive and that the Environmental Liability Directive does not apply to national defence activities. At the same time, it also claims that it does not have the necessary details to assess whether EU law applies to the Lavrio site. However, an official registration in the General Commercial Register (GEMI) shows that a new company, ‘Hellenic Ammunition SA’, has been established, with its own management and full representation, which raises serious questions as to the real operator and, therefore, as to the applicable EU environmental law. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
How does it justify invoking exemptions for military establishments when it claims not to have the necessary data to identify the real operator in Lavrio?

Will it immediately request comprehensive information from the Greek authorities and ASAP beneficiaries in order to determine whether the activity falls within the scope of the Seveso III Directive, the Industrial Emissions Directive and the Environmental Liability Directive?

If it emerges that the activities are being carried out by a civilian corporate entity, what specific measures will it take to ensure the full application of EU law on the prevention of major accidents and to put a stop to activities in breach of that law?

(6 July 2026) Based on additional information provided by the Honourable Member, the Commission may have identified a corresponding upper-tier establishment (1) in the eSPIRS database (2). Based on the information reported to the Industrial Emissions Portal (3), it is not clear if it is also covered by the Industrial Emissions Directive (IED) (4). While Member States’ authorities are primarily responsible to ensure compliance with EU legislations mentioned above, the Commission will contact the Greek competent authorities to ascertain the regulatory status of the establishment. If the establishment in question is covered by the Seveso III Directive (5), the operator has to take all necessary measures to prevent major accidents and limit their consequences for human health and the environment (6) while the Greek competent authorities have to organise a system of regular (7) and non-routine (8) inspections. If it is covered by the IED, the operators have to take the necessary measures to prevent accidents and limit their consequences. The Greek competent authorities have to ensure that the installation is covered by environmental inspection plans.

The classification as Lower-tier Establishment (LTE) or Upper-Tier Establishment (UTE) under the Seveso Directive relies on ‘the maximum quantities [of hazardous substances] which are present or are likely to be present at any one time’ (Note 3 to Annex I). EU database on Seveso establishments. https://industry.eea.europa.eu/. When an installation is covered by the IED, the competent authorities have to report installation’s administrative and environmental information to the Industrial Emissions Portal on an annual basis, once the installation is operational. Directive 2012/18/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 4 July 2012 on the control of major-accident hazards involving dangerous substances, amending and subsequently repealing Council Directive 96/82/EC, OJ L 197, 24.7.2012, p. 1-37. Article 5 of the Seveso III Directive. Article 20(4) of the Seveso III Directive: for upper-tier establishments, the period between two consecutive sites visits should not exceed one year, unless the inspection programme covering the site is based on a systematic appraisal of major-accident hazards. Article 20(6) of the Seveso III Directive: non-routine inspections should be carried out to investigate serious complaints, serious accidents and ‘near misses’, incidents and occurrences of non-compliance as soon as possible.

If the operation of the establishment in question is not excluded from the scope of the Environmental Liability Directive (9), the Greek competent authorities have to investigate cases of significant environmental damage and imminent threat while interested parties (10) can require the competent national authorities to act (11). National courts are best placed for applying EU law effectively in cases of an individual nature, as well as for taking provisional measures if necessary.

E-10-2026-001287.t: Need for EU emergency measures to help the fishing sector in the face of rising fuel prices
qt: to the Commission Stéphanie Yon-Courtin (Renew), Oihane Agirregoitia Martínez (Renew) Subject:

In recent days, conflicts in the Middle East have caused a rise in global fuel prices, affecting European citizens and businesses. This crisis also has an impact on fishers, who are being hit by rising fuel prices that are driving up the operational costs for vessels and forcing some to operate at a loss. In 2022, in response to the energy crisis provoked by the Russian invasion of Ukraine, the Commission introduced a series of measures that provided relief to the fishing sector. As the current situation threatens the viability and competitiveness of the European fishing fleet, the Commission must consider similar emergency measures to support the sector. 1.
Does the Commission intend to use the crisis support mechanisms provided for by the European Maritime, Fisheries and Aquaculture Fund to support fishers affected by the sudden rise in fuel prices?
Is the Commission preparing a temporary crisis framework for State aid measures to allow Member States to introduce financial support schemes for fishers?
What other support measures is the Commission planning, such as structural measures or insurance schemes enabling fishing operators to better prepare for and respond to future crises?

E-10-2026-001286.t: Safeguard activation thresholds for highly sensitive products under the GSP revision
qt: to the Commission Andi Cristea (S&D) Subject:

The ongoing revision of the EU’s generalised scheme of preferences (GSP) proposes lowering safeguard activation thresholds for highly sensitive products. While this is a step forward, concerns remain that the lower thresholds may still fail to prevent sudden, disruptive import surges in particularly vulnerable sectors such as poultry meat. Recent developments, including increased imports from Ukraine, have shown how rapidly trade flows can shift and potentially disrupt the EU market. While support for Ukraine remains essential, these imports have intensified pressure on EU producers, who must comply with strict animal welfare, environmental and food safety standards. This is particularly relevant for Member States with significant poultry production, including Romania, where the sector contributes to rural employment and economic stability. In this context: 1.
Has the Commission assessed whether the use of an activation threshold is sufficient to prevent serious market disturbances in the poultry meat sector?
Has it evaluated the economic and social impact of such thresholds, including on Member States with significant poultry production, such as Romania?
Would it consider introducing lower thresholds or additional safeguards for products proven vulnerable to import surges, such as poultry meat?

(13 May 2026) The co-legislators agreed on the political elements of the new Generalised Scheme of Preferences (GSP) in December 2025 (1). The negotiations on the Commission legislative proposal of 2021 (2) lasted more than four years, during which the colegislators never tabled the possible introduction of automatic safeguards for the poultry meat sector. However, once the new GSP rules are in place, the EU agricultural sector, including the poultry meat sector, will have more tools to protect its interests in the GSP context, in recognition of its sensitivity and importance: (i) poultry is defined as a sensitive product, without tariff preferences for all standard GSP and GSP+ beneficiaries; (ii) there will be three safeguard mechanisms (general safeguards, special safeguards and the new special surveillance) which apply also to the poultry sector. The Commission systematically treats poultry meat as a sensitive product in trade negotiations with third countries. Currently, poultry imports under GSP are negligible, and the sector is covered by three GSP safeguard mechanisms. All these measures allow the EU to counter potential threats to domestic markets. Moreover, poultry meat may only be imported into the EU from third countries listed by the Commission. These lists ensure compliance with, among others, EU public health standards. Food businesses, both in the EU and in approved third countries, must guarantee compliance with food hygiene rules (3) to ensure food safety and protect consumers.

E-10-2026-001285.t: Evaluation of the Dual-Use Regulation and reform of the annual transparency report framework
qt: to the Commission Saskia Bricmont (Verts/ALE), Markéta Gregorová (Verts/ALE), Sandro Ruotolo (S&D), Veronika Cifrová Ostrihoňová (Renew), Raquel García Hermida-Van Der Walle (Renew), Daniel Freund (Verts/ALE), Hannah Neumann (Verts/ALE), Jaume Asens Llodrà (Verts/ALE) Subject:

Article 26 of Regulation (EU) 2021/8211 (also known as the Dual-Use Regulation) legally mandates a review of this regulation and its specific cyber-surveillance provisions (Article 5). In its 2024 white paper on export controls, the Commission explicitly recommended bringing the evaluation forward to 2025 to address shortcomings in the Regulation’s effectiveness and the urgency of current security and human rights challenges. However, significant concerns remain regarding the lack of disaggregated data in the annual transparency reports, which currently prevent meaningful oversight of spyware exports by masking destination countries and specific end-use risks under broad categories. 1.

Timeline and consultation: can the Commission provide a definitive updated timeline for the evaluation process and confirm that public interest stakeholders, including civil society and human rights defenders, will be formally and transparently consulted?

Transparency reform: does the Commission intend to use this evaluation to reform the annual transparency report framework, specifically by requiring Member States to provide disaggregated data on licences for cyber-surveillance items, as defined in Article 2(20) of the Dual-Use Regulation?

Effectiveness of Article 5 of the Dual-Use Regulation: how does the Commission plan to address the inconsistent application of the Article 5 ‘catch-all’ clause, which continues to allow varying levels of scrutiny for spyware exports across different Member States, creating a ‘race to the bottom’ within the single market?

Regulation (EU) 2021/821 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 20 May 2021 setting up a Union regime for the control of exports, brokering, technical assistance, transit and transfer of dual-use items (OJ L 206, 11.6.2021, p. 1, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2021/821/oj).
at: (English version) to the Commission Saskia Bricmont (Verts/ALE), Markéta Gregorová (Verts/ALE), Sandro Ruotolo (S&D), Veronika Cifrová Ostrihoňová (Renew), Raquel García Hermida-Van Der Walle (Renew), Daniel Freund (Verts/ALE), Hannah Neumann (Verts/ALE), Jaume Asens Llodrà (Verts/ALE) (26 March 2026) Subject: Evaluation of the Dual-Use Regulation and reform of the annual transparency report framework Article 26 of Regulation (EU) 2021/821 (1) (also known as the Dual-Use Regulation) legally mandates a review of this regulation and its specific cyber-surveillance provisions (Article 5). In its 2024 white paper on export controls, the Commission explicitly recommended bringing the evaluation forward to 2025 to address shortcomings in the regulation’s effectiveness and the urgency of current security and human rights challenges. However, significant concerns remain regarding the lack of disaggregated data in the annual transparency reports, which currently prevent meaningful oversight of spyware exports by masking destination countries and specific end-use risks under broad categories. 1. Timeline and consultation: can the Commission provide a definitive updated timeline for the evaluation process and confirm that public interest stakeholders, including civil society and human rights defenders, will be formally and transparently consulted? 2. Transparency reform: does the Commission intend to use this evaluation to reform the annual transparency report framework, specifically by requiring Member States to provide disaggregated data on licences for cyber-surveillance items, as defined in Article 2(20) of the Dual-Use Regulation? 3. Effectiveness of Article 5 of the Dual-Use Regulation: how does the Commission plan to address the inconsistent application of the article 5 ‘catch-all’ clause, which continues to allow varying levels of scrutiny for spyware exports across different Member States, creating a ‘race to the bottom’ within the single market? (13 May 2026) The Commission takes note of the concerns linked to the implementation of the Dual-Use Regulation (EU) 2021/821 (1) and notably those related to the Commission’s annual reports. The evaluation of the regulation, as mandated pursuant to its Article 26(4) will be launched in the course of May 2026, with the evaluation report to be published by early 2027 at the latest. A public consultation targeting the general public and civil society will be opened in the summer of 2026 and run for 12 weeks. Various stakeholders, including civil society and human rights defenders, will thus be formally and transparently consulted and their views appropriately reflected in the Commission’s overall assessment. As part of the exercise, the Commission will assess the annual transparency reporting framework, including for cybersurveillance items. More generally, the evaluation will review the extent to which the regulation has been effective in providing sufficiently clear information on EU export controls on dual-use items, while keeping in line with the relevant confidentiality requirements. The Commission will also examine the effectiveness of Article 5, that is, the EU ‘catch-all’ control on cyber-surveillance exports. The effectiveness of the regulation in light of evolving cyber-surveillance technology will also be considered, ensuring that the EU’s export control regime remains robust and adaptable.

Regulation (EU) 2021/821 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 20 May 2021 setting up a Union regime for the control of exports, brokering, technical assistance, transit and transfer of dual-use items (OJ L 206, 11.6.2021, p. 1, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2021/821/oj). https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2021/821/oj/eng.

Further proposals will follow, towards the target to reduce administrative burden by at least 25% for all businesses and 35% for small and medium-sized enterprises. E-10-2026-001283.t: EU dependence on imports of raw materials
qt: to the Commission Tobiasz Bocheński (ECR) Subject:

The EU remains highly dependent on imports of energy and strategic raw materials, which is a risk to its economic stability. The actions taken so far in terms of strategic autonomy have not yielded sufficient results. In light of the above: 1.
Will the Commission propose a plan to reduce dependence on imports of raw materials?
Can the Commission identify the sectors most vulnerable to disruptions in supply?

at: (English version) to the Commission Tobiasz Bocheński (ECR) (26 March 2026) Subject: EU dependence on imports of raw materials The EU remains highly dependent on imports of energy and strategic raw materials, which is a risk to its economic stability. (8 June 2026) The Commission has proposed several policy measures to reduce import dependencies in raw material supply chains. The RESourceEU Action Plan (1), adopted on 4 December 2025, is focusing on critical raw materials on which the EU relies on for clean energy, electric vehicles, digital transition and defence industries. These sectors are specifically vulnerable to supply disruptions. RESourceEU is a coordinated response aiming to rapidly diversify supply chains and boost domestic production. The forthcoming Circular Economy Act to be published in the third quarter of 2026 will also foster the recovery of secondary raw materials to strengthen Europe’s strategic autonomy. RESourceEU builds on the Critical Raw Materials Act (CRMA) (2), which sets clear objectives for EU supply security: by 2030, the EU should have the capacity to extract 10%, process 40% and recycle 25% of the 17 strategic raw materials it consumes. In parallel, the EU should diversify its supply so that it does not depend on a single country for more than 65% of its demand of a strategic raw material. To achieve the 2030 benchmarks, it is important to support the development of projects along the value chain. The CRMA puts in place the designation of Strategic Projects for this purpose. The CRMA provides benefits when it comes from streamlined and faster permitting timelines, a single point of contact to help them clear regulatory hurdles and facilitated access to finance and offtakers. In 2025, the first 47 Strategic Projects located in the EU and 13 Strategic Projects located outside the EU were designated (3). For the second cut-off date on 15 January 2026, the Commission has received 171 project applications. The second selection round is ongoing.

(12 May 2026) On 22 April 2026, the Commission presented the AccelerateEU Communication (1) to accelerate the delivery of the Energy Union, outlining immediate, targeted actions for Member States to deliver rapid and lasting relief to households and industry facing high energy prices. It also includes structural measures to improve energy efficiency and accelerate electrification by reducing the four components of energy bills-supply costs, network charges, taxes, and carbon costs — also in the longer term. European climate policy aims to reduce dependency on expensive, foreign fossil fuels, replacing them with clean, homegrown electricity. Carbon pricing is one of the core and most successful components of our climate policy. The EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) puts a price on pollution, stimulating investments in low-carbon production technologies and raising revenues that can be used to finance these investments as well as shield vulnerable households. The Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) ensures a level playing between European producers and importers, to avoid relocation of European installations to countries with less ambitious climate policies. The Commission has assessed the impact of ETS on inflation up to 2027, covering also the impact of the CBAM, in the European Economic Forecast, Autumn 2025 (2). The Commission will present a review of the ETS in July. The legislative proposal will be accompanied by a thorough impact assessment as well as an in-depth evaluation of the past functioning of the ETS, including an analysis of its economic impacts.

(English version) to the Commission Tobiasz Bocheński (ECR) (26 March 2026) Subject: EU competitiveness and regulatory burdens Despite declarations of strengthening competitiveness, businesses in the EU are reporting increasing regulatory and administrative burdens. It is estimated that administrative costs run into hundreds of billions of euros annually, and new regulations are putting further pressure on businesses. This raises the question of the actual impact of EU policy on the business environment. Will the Commission: 1.
identify specific legislative acts to be repealed in order to reduce regulatory burdens?
set out a measurable target for reducing administrative costs for businesses?
assess the impact of EU regulations on the relocation of business activities outside the EU?

(5 June 2026) The Commission Communication ‘A Simpler, Clearer and Better Enforced EU Rulebook’ (1) contains a Regulatory Deep Cleaning Action Plan with key policy areas which will be examined with the aim of modernisation and simplification. It will tackle inconsistencies, outdated, overlapping or redundant provisions, or overly complex rules that hinder competitiveness and innovation. The Commission has a target to lower the administrative burden by at least 25% for all businesses, and at least 35% for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), requiring cutting recurring administrative costs by EUR 37.5 billion by the end of the mandate. To this end it puts forward omnibus proposals and other legislative initiatives with a significant simplification dimension. In 2025, the Commission proposed ten omnibus packages and other simplification proposals, with net recurrent cost savings of EUR 15 billion. Half of the proposals for the Commission work programme 2026 are simplification proposals. Omnibuses proposals are part of the Commission’s ambitious simplification agenda. The objective is to lighten the EU regulatory burden while maintaining high standards. Burden reduction targets, a new SME check and a reinforced competitiveness check to measure the impact of Commission’s proposals, stress testing and new consultation tools (implementation dialogues and reality checks) support this goal. Many European industries are under pressure from third country overcapacities, export controls, and the weaponisation of dependencies, and, as consequence, are restructuring. The relocation of businesses is monitored through the European Restructuring Monitor, which provides a rich repository of case studies and intelligence on restructuring trends.

The current situation calls into question the effectiveness of the EU’s energy and climate policy, including the ETS, which further increases production costs amid a price shock. In light of the foregoing: 1.
Will the Commission present an up-to-date assessment of the impact of the ETS on the competitiveness of EU industry?

(11 May 2026) The geopolitical tensions in the Middle East and their impact on energy markets underline the dangers of Europe’s dependency on imported fossil fuels and on the volatility of global markets. Against this background the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) is a key instrument for reducing Europe’s dependency, enhancing resilience and ensuring long-term price stability. The Commission will present a review of the ETS by July to strengthen the carbon market and ensure it delivers a fair, costeffective contribution towards the recently agreed 2040 climate target (1), as well as addressing carbon price volatility. The impact of carbon costs on electricity prices is the smallest major component of electricity bills (11% for industry and 5% for households). On 1 April 2026, the Commission proposed an amendment to the Market Stability Reserve to enhance the stability and predictability of ETS prices (2). On 22 April 2026, the Commission presented the AccelerateEU Communication (3), outlining immediate, targeted actions for Member States to deliver rapid and lasting relief to households and industry facing high energy prices. It includes structural measures to improve energy efficiency and accelerate electrification by reducing the four components of energy bills-supply costs, network charges, taxes, and carbon costs. It also includes a state aid temporary framework to support some of the sectors most exposed to price spikes. To permanently reduce energy costs in the EU relative to its main economic competitors, the EU needs to accelerate electrification, the roll out of additional domestic clean energy production and the energy transition. The EU’s legal commitment to climate neutrality remains unchanged.
