E-10-2026-001278.t: State of play of the Rail Baltica project
qt: to the Commission Maciej Wąsik (ECR) Subject:

Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2025/1332 of 9 July 2025 on the implementation of the Rail Baltica cross-border project on the North Sea – Baltic European Transport Corridor and the Baltic Sea – Black Sea – Aegean Sea European Transport Corridor in application of Regulation (EU) 2024/1679 of the European Parliament and of the Council and repealing Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2018/1723 was adopted on 9 July 2025. It lays down the rules and deadlines for the implementation of the Commission’s flagship rail project – Rail Baltica. It is intended to connect the three Baltic States to the European rail network by 2030 and integrate them into the single European railway area and the TEN-T network. Rail Baltica is an extremely important project from a social, economic and security perspective for NATO’s north-eastern flank and the European Union. In recent days, the Polish Deputy Minister of Infrastructure responsible for railways has publicly questioned the feasibility of completing the Rail Baltica lines by 2030, saying that the Commission should cease ‘deluding itself’ regarding the deadline1. In this context I would like to ask the following questions: 1.

Is the Commission being realistic in its assessment of the progress of construction, and on the basis of what information? Or, as the Deputy Minister claims, is it ‘deluding itself’ regarding completion of the investment in line with the originally adopted plan?
Did the Member States (Estonia, Finland, Lithuania, Latvia, Poland and Sweden) participate in the process of adopting and agreeing the content of the decision, and what position did they take?
To the best of the Commission’s knowledge, what is the current state of progress of the project in each country in relation to the timetable, if one has been drawn up?
https://www.rmf24.pl/fakty/polska/news-rail-baltica-pozniej-niz-zakladano-przez-rosje-sa-inneprior,nId,8072691, (access: 24.03.2026)
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (19.5.2026) Regular exchanges with the Member States, implementing bodies and stakeholders involved in Rail Baltica give the Commission a clear overview of its progress. Additionally, the European Coordinator keeps the Commission informed and the European Climate, Infrastructure and Environment Executive Agency (CINEA) monitors the Rail Baltica activities supported through the Connecting Europe Facility1. Estonia, Finland, Latvia, Lithuania and Poland contributed to the development of the Rail Baltica Implementing Decision2 and supported its adoption. According to the Commission’s information, the works on Rail Baltica between Warsaw and Bialystok are completed except for the European Rail Traffic Management System (ERTMS). On the remaining sections in Poland, works are being tendered or project documentation is being developed. In Lithuania 114 km are under construction, in Latvia 40 km are under construction with 200 km contracted; and in Estonia more than 100 km are under construction. The Commission assesses the progress against the implementing decision. While actions are largely on track, some delays exist. It is important to recall that the overall time to completion will largely depend also on the funding that will be made available for the project from national and European sources. In order to continue supporting cross-border infrastructure projects such as Rail Baltica, the Commission proposed a Connecting Europe Facility with a budget of EUR 51.5 billion for transport as part of the proposals for the next multiannual financial framework3.

E-10-2026-001276.t: Controversy surrounding the planned revision of Europol’s mandate and its transformation into a ‘truly operational police agency’
qt: to the Commission Mariusz Kamiński (ECR) Subject:

A year ago, Commission Vice-President Henna Virkkunen announced the transformation of the European Union Agency for Law Enforcement Cooperation (Europol) into a ‘truly operational EU police agency’1. In doing so, the Commission announced not only a revision of Europol’s mandate, but also ambitions to further centralise powers in the area of security. There have been calls for the creation of a European FBI. As a former Minister of the Interior and now a Member of the European Parliament, I have had the opportunity to familiarise myself with Europol’s successes, which are based – as the agency’s name suggests – on cooperation, supporting Member States and coordinating the fight against cross-border crime. Europol’s activities are particularly important in combating drug-related crime, human trafficking and VAT fraud. This model is a good example of effective cooperation at European level. Meanwhile, the Commission intends to use the success of this agency as part of its federalist agenda. That is why the announcements regarding the transformation of Europol into a fully operational police agency arouse my opposition and have been criticised by many experts and Member States. During the LIBE meeting on 19 March 2026, Commissioner Brunner concluded his remarks by stating that this would not be a European FBI, which can be interpreted as the Commission backing away from its radical announcement. 1.
How does the Commission understand the concept of a ‘truly operational police agency’?
What safeguards does the Commission plan to put in place to ensure that Europol remains an agency supporting Member States, rather than a body exercising direct police powers?
Will the proposal to revise the mandate take into account concerns regarding the centralisation of powers and the criticism levelled at the announcement made by Commissioner Virkkunnen?

at: (English version) to the Commission Mariusz Kamiński (ECR) (26 March 2026) Subject: Controversy surrounding the planned revision of Europol’s mandate and its transformation into a ‘truly operational police agency’ A year ago, Commission Vice-President Henna Virkkunen announced the transformation of the European Union Agency for Law Enforcement Cooperation (Europol) into a ‘truly operational EU police agency’ (1). In doing so, the Commission announced not only a revision of Europol’s mandate, but also ambitions to further centralise powers in the area of security. There have been calls for the creation of a European FBI. As a former Minister of the Interior and now a Member of the European Parliament, I have had the opportunity to familiarise myself with Europol’s successes, which are based — as the agency’s name suggests — on cooperation, supporting Member States and coordinating the fight against cross-border crime. Europol’s activities are particularly important in combating drugrelated crime, human trafficking and VAT fraud. This model is a good example of effective cooperation at European level. Meanwhile, the Commission intends to use the success of this agency as part of its federalist agenda. That is why the announcements regarding the transformation of Europol into a fully operational police agency arouse my opposition and have been criticised by many experts and Member States. During the LIBE meeting on 19 March 2026, Commissioner Brunner concluded his remarks by stating that this would not be a European FBI, which can be interpreted as the Commission backing away from its radical announcement. 1.
How does the Commission understand the concept of a ‘truly operational police agency’?

2. What safeguards does the Commission plan to put in place to ensure that Europol remains an agency supporting Member States, rather than a body exercising direct police powers? 3. Will the proposal to revise the mandate take into account concerns regarding the centralisation of powers and the criticism levelled at the announcement made by Commissioner Virkkunnen? (4 June 2026) The political guidelines of the Commission’s President make clear that reinforcing the EU Agency for Law Enforcement Cooperation (Europol) is a central priority for the EU to ensure a high level of internal security. The proposal for a revision of the Europol Regulation (1) will fully respect the balance of competences established by the Treaties. Its objective will be to equip Europol to support cross-border cooperation more effectively through enhanced operational, analytical, and technical support. This requires systematically integrating Europol’s tools, expertise, and operational capabilities into cross-border investigations, while removing the remaining obstacles to seamless information exchange and the effective use of Europol’s support. It also means positioning Europol at the centre of the development of advanced European law enforcement capabilities. The proposal for a revision of the Europol Regulation will aim to make full use of the possibilities offered by Article 88 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, while fully respecting the clear limits that it sets. In light of the increased responsibilities and accompanying resources, the proposal for a revised legal framework for Europol will aim to provide a future-proof and robust framework for Europol’s role, with a well-defined scope of action and responsibilities, strengthen governance and accountability.

E-10-2026-001275.t: The EU’s anti-corruption strategy and the case of Sławomir Nowak as a prime example of high-level corruption, as well as of vindictiveness and the obstruction of investigations
qt: to the Commission Mariusz Kamiński (ECR) Subject:

The fight against corruption requires specialised, independent anti-corruption institutions and courageous officials backed by the law and state institutions. They must have certainty that the prosecution of even the highest-ranking officials and politicians will be met with genuine state support, rather than reprisals. Unfortunately, the return to power of parties tainted by corruption scandals is often accompanied by vindictiveness, the stalling of investigations and the persecution of those who had the courage to tackle corruption at the highest levels. This is what has happened following the return to power of the Civic Platform, a party which has been implicated in numerous corruption scandals throughout its history, and whose leader is a politician known for his extreme vindictiveness towards those who expose corruption within his inner circle. A prime example of Poland’s efforts in the fight against corruption is the case of Sławomir Nowak, Tusk’s chief of staff and Minister for Infrastructure, who was charged with over a dozen corruption offences. Following the change of government, the so-called ‘Polish plot’ case was discontinued, even though the evidence gathered during the investigation was not considered during the trial1. Instead, the disciplinary officer took action against the prosecutor who drafted the indictment, Jan Drelewski, and Minister Żurek issued a decree dismissing him from the special anti-corruption unit, despite the unequivocal opposition of the prosecutor in charge of that division2. 1.
As it draws up its anti-corruption strategy, is the Commission analysing examples of high-level corruption? Is the Commission familiar with the corruption case involving Sławomir Nowak?

In its strategy, will the Commission pay due attention to protecting public officials, whose courage enables the exposure and prosecution of corruption at the highest levels of government, from reprisals?

The decision prompted a wave of criticism, as the prosecution withdrew the charges against Nowak five years after the indictment had been filed and after three and a half years of the case ‘gathering dust’ in the District Court. It was taken on by a 29-year-old assistant judge from the District Court, who had been ‘handpicked’ for the case, and a surprising turn of events occurred during the hearing when both the defendants’ defence lawyers and the new case officer were in favour of the case being dismissed. https://www.rp.pl/polityka/art43960741-rzeczpospolita-ujawnia-prokurator-od-sprawy-nowaka-odsuniety-iz-dyscyplinarka-kulisy-decyzji and https://niezalezna.pl/polityka/zemsta-na-prokuratorze-ktory-oskarzylslawomira-nowaka-o-lapowkarstwo/565811.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (16.7.2026) Strengthening the rule of law and combating corruption are key priorities for the Commission. This is reflected, in particular, in its commitment to adopt an EU Anti-Corruption Strategy1. The Strategy will set out an overarching and comprehensive EU approach to prevent and fight corruption effectively. When it comes to individual cases or specific criminal investigations, Member States are solely responsible for maintaining law and order and safeguarding internal security. The Commission monitors and reports on developments regarding the fight against corruption in all Member States, including Poland, as part of the annual Rule of Law Report. Where needed, the report also includes concrete recommendations aimed at strengthening anticorruption frameworks2.
1 Commission work programme 2026. 2 2025 Rule of law report - Communication and country chapters;
https://commission.europa.eu/publications/2025-rule-law-report-communication-and-country-chapters_en.

E-10-2026-001274.t: Judgment T-235/24 and the interference by former Commission Vice-President Věra Jourová in the competences of Member States and the independence of judicial and constitutional bodies
qt: to the Commission Mariusz Kamiński (ECR) Subject:

Between 2020 and 2022, the Commission criticised the public service media situation in Slovenia. Following a change of government in 2022, the RTV Slovenia Act reform was adopted, which was challenged before the Slovenian Constitutional Court. The Court initially suspended its application, but in May 2023 it lifted the interim measure despite the lack of a ruling on the constitutionality of the Act. In March 2023, a few weeks before this decision, Commission Vice-President Věra Jourová met with the President of the Court in Slovenia. A briefing note prepared for the meeting indicated that the aim was, among other things, to ‘verify’ his position on the Act subject to constitutional review1. MEP Milan Zver requested access to documents relating to the visit. Only after a year and numerous interventions, including by the European Ombudsman, did the Commission grant partial access, withholding parts of the notes. In its judgment of 18 June 2025 in Case T235/24, the General Court of the EU ruled that the refusal to disclose the records was unlawful2. The case raises serious concerns not only regarding the lack of transparency in the Commission’s actions, but also regarding unlawful interference in the competences of Member States and the independence of judicial and constitutional bodies3. 1.

Does the Commission intend to disclose the full text of the documentation relating to the interference described above and to take action against those responsible for these unacceptable actions, including former Commissioner Jourová, who grossly exceeded her powers and exerted unlawful influence on the Constitutional Court of Slovenia?
Has the Commission taken similar unlawful actions against the independent judicial and constitutional bodies of other countries, including Poland?

The former Commission Vice-President made it clear publicly that she has not discussed the matter of RTV Slovenia with the then President of the Slovenian Constitutional Court. E-10-2026-001273.t: Windfall profits of oil companies in the German fuel market following the Iran conflict
qt: to the Commission Martin Günther (The Left) Subject:

Following the outbreak of the Iran conflict on 28 February 2026 petrol and diesel prices at German filling stations rose to their highest levels since 2022. A study commissioned by Greenpeace1 finds that while crude oil prices increased by 13.1 cent per litre (ct/l), diesel pump prices rose by 30.3 ct/l, and petrol prices by 18.5 ct/l, implying gross margin expansions of 17.2 ct/l and 5.4 ct/l respectively. The study estimates resulting windfall profits in the German fuel retail market at approximately EUR 17.9 million per day for diesel and EUR 3.2 million per day for petrol during the first two weeks of March 2026. 1.

Does the Commission consider that the pricing dynamics observed in the German and wider EU fuel retail markets since late February 2026 warrant investigation under Regulation (EU) No 1227/2011 on wholesale energy market integrity and transparency2 (REMIT) and, if not, why not?
Is the Commission monitoring margin developments across EU fuel markets in the context of the current Iran conflict, and does it intend to publish its assessment?
What threshold of margin divergence between crude oil costs and retail prices would trigger a Commission investigation under existing EU energy market or competition rules?

https://www.greenpeace.de/publikationen/Uebergewinne_im_Tankstellenmarkt.pdf?utm_campaign=ver kehr&utm_source=www.greenpeace.de&utm_medium=referral&utm_content=press-release. OJ L 326, 8.12.2011, p. 1, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2011/1227/oj.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (12.6.2026) The Regulation (EU) No 1227/2011 on wholesale energy market integrity and transparency (REMIT)1 requires national enforcement of market abusive behaviour as regards wholesale energy products in electricity, natural gas and hydrogen. It does not cover mineral oil markets. In light of ongoing geopolitical tensions in the Middle East, the Commission will continue monitoring the evolution of the crisis and assessing its potential impacts. To address the impacts of the disruption of oil and gas transit, the Commission has put forward on 22 April 2026 its new initiative AccelerateEU2, proposing timely, targeted and temporary measures to bring relief to consumers, while avoiding fragmented national responses. It recalls that Member States can also take measures on the taxation of windfall profits to ensure social fairness while the Commission stands ready to assist and provide best practices on national measures as well as assess their impact on the single market. The opening of an investigation under the EU competition rules requires indications of anticompetitive agreement between market participants (Article 101 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU)) or abusive conduct by a dominant market player (Article 102 of the TFEU) that affects trade between Member States. While unusual price developments may warrant further scrutiny, a divergence between input costs and retail prices is not as such and taken in isolation indicative of a potential breach of EU competition rules.
1 Regulation (EU) No 1227/2011 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 25 October 2011 on

wholesale energy market integrity and transparency (ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2011/1227/oj). 2 https://energy.ec.europa.eu/publications/accelerateeu-energy-union-affordable-and-secure-energy-throughaccelerated-action_en.

E-10-2026-001272.t: Compatibility of NRRP funding for the Garda cycle path (Limone-Riva section) and consideration of intermodal alternatives
qt: to the Commission Gaetano Pedulla' (The Left) Subject:

The Trentino portion of the Garda cycle path – more specifically, the stretch between Limone sul Garda and Riva del Garda – runs along cliffs of outstanding natural beauty, protected under Decree Law 42/2004. Many civic initiatives and positions taken by associations (including the WWF, Italia Nostra and Legambiente), not to mention institutional acts, have highlighted the environmental impact of suspended structures cantilevered to geologically fragile, landslide-prone slopes. The Italian Court of Auditors has decried the costs of the project (of up to EUR 28 million per kilometre along the Trentino portion) as ‘downright excessive’, flagging risks to public money. At the same time, Lombardy Region has adopted Regional Government Decision XII/5508, which proposes an intermodal navigation service (‘by water’) as an alternative to the most problematic stretches; this would be more environmentally friendly and cost less. In light of exchanges with the Member State, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Is the NRRP funding (investment 4.1) compatible with cost-effectiveness criteria and the ‘do no significant harm’ principle?
Given that greener and less costly alternatives are already on the table, can the on-land plans still be deemed acceptable?

(1 July 2026) Italy’s Recovery and Resilience Plan (RRP) includes an investment (M2C2 I4.1) supporting cycling paths in metropolitan areas and tourist cycle path, which falls within the scope of the Garda cycle path projects. At the time of submission of the Plan, the Commission assessed the investment, including compliance with the Do No Significant Harm (DNSH) principle, its contribution to the green transition and the costing (including whether the Plan as a whole is in line with the principle of cost-efficiency) and concluded on a positive assessment. The relevant commitments are reflected in milestones and targets set out in the Council Implementing Decision (CID) (1). The first target (M2C2-22) was assessed in the context of the 5th payment request and the Garda cycle path fell outside the scope of the target, which focused on the metropolitan areas. The final target (M2C2-23), which includes the completion of projects related to tourist cycle paths, will be assessed in the context of the 10th payment request. The Commission recalls that the assessment is conducted on the basis of milestones and targets, as included in the CID. As a rule, and without prejudice to its role as guardian of the Treaties, the Commission does not assess the environmental impact of specific projects nor their cost-effectiveness. This is a primary responsibility of the Member States, which are requested to ensure compliance of specific projects with EU and national law, in line with the applicable rules on cost-effectiveness criteria and with the environmental acquis. Similarly, Member States need to ensure full respect of DNSH conditions, taking into account commitments set out in the approved RRPs in accordance with the DNSH Technical Guidance (2) The Commission maintains a continuous dialogue with Italy to ensure that the national implementation complies with the provisions of the CID.

E-10-2026-001271.t: Energy crisis and our energy independence
qt: to the Commission Damien Carême (The Left), Manon Aubry (The Left), Anthony Smith (The Left), Leila Chaibi (The Left), Rima Hassan (The Left) Subject:

The United States and Israel are intensifying their unlawful military interventions against the leadership of oil-producing nations worldwide, targeting Venezuela in January and, since February, Iran. On 18 March 2026, Eurostat reported that the Union remains highly dependent on energy imports. The following day, it emerged that the majority of EU Member States generate less than 50% of their energy from renewable sources, despite the fact that only a transition to renewable energy can guarantee our independence. The consequences of war and our dependence have a direct impact on our economies and on the purchasing power of European citizens. The insecurity and risks weighing on the Strait of Hormuz are prompting oil groups to speculate, leading to a sharp surge in diesel prices at the pump across Europe. 1.
Does the Commission continue to regard the United States and Israel as allies despite their ongoing breaches of international law?
Will it take steps to freeze the price of diesel in order to prevent a spike in prices for European citizens?
What policies will it finally implement to extricate the European Union from its dependence on fossil fuels and mitigate its vulnerability to the unpredictability of President Trump's imperialism?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (26.5.2026) The US is a strategic partner of the EU. The transatlantic partnership is founded on a shared history and strong bonds. The EU will continue to work to maintain close engagement with the US as it is beneficial to EU citizens, as well as global stability and security. The EU is ready to continue engaging constructively on all issues of common interest while still defending its priorities, interests and values, including the defence of international law and the rules-based order. The EU has consistently underlined that Israel has the right to defend itself, but in line with international law, including international humanitarian law. Disproportionate use of force against civilians and civilian infrastructure is unacceptable. The AccelerateEU Communication adopted on 22 April 20261 follows a two-pronged approach to bring immediate relief to vulnerable households and industries, while advancing measures to end structural dependence on imported fossil fuels, in line with our long-term objectives. To help Member States protect consumers from price shocks, the Commission will assist in the design of immediate but targeted, temporary measures including price intervention, income support schemes and tax incentives. This will avoid market distortions while addressing the root causes of high prices and it will also facilitate the coordination of national action. The Commission’s long-term strategy is focused on electrification based on homegrown clean energy, resilient grids, flexibility, interconnections and energy efficiency reducing fossil dependence and external vulnerability. The AccelerateEU Communication calls for faster implementation of the Energy Union agenda2, with coordinated EU action and full delivery by Member States.
1 https://energy.ec.europa.eu/strategy/accelerateeu-strengthen-eu-energy-resilience_en. 2 https://energy.ec.europa.eu/strategy/energy-union_en.

E-10-2026-001269.t: Regulation is hampering the circular economy for vehicles
qt: to the Commission Katri Kulmuni (Renew) Subject:

The EU’s goal of stepping up carbon neutrality and the circular economy is the right one. When cars are scrapped, some parts can be used again. Intact parts can be fitted into other cars, meaning there is no need to manufacture new parts or send the entire car to be crushed. Today, however, more and more components are being programmed in such a way that they only work in the original car. It is of course in the manufacturers’ interest that only their spare parts can be fitted into cars. The current rules may lead to a situation in which the manufacturers can control the whole chain and divert parts for their own purposes rather than for re-use. Under the Batteries Regulation (EU 2023/1542), treatment facilities are required to hand over discarded waste batteries to producers who often want them sent directly for recycling, and vehicle dismantlers are not permitted to recondition batteries and resell them. Strict material recovery targets do not provide incentives for reuse – they only encourage recycling by crushing the battery. Another problem that has been identified is that independent dismantlers are not actually guaranteed non-discriminatory access to networks of producer responsibility organisations with a view to making it possible for the dismantlers to prioritise reuse over recycling. Dismantlers are required to assess the condition and safety of the parts, but if they do not have access to the manufacturer’s data (e.g. diagnostic data) and manufacturers are not obliged to provide it, the risks to dismantlers are high and, out of fear of liability, they might opt not to sell parts that would otherwise still be fit for re-use. With the above in mind, is the Commission aware of the regulatory issues described above and is it intending to take steps to amend the relevant legislation?

(6 July 2026) In July 2023, the Commission adopted a proposal for a new Regulation on End-of-Life Vehicles (ELVR) (1). On 12 December 2025, the European Parliament and the Council reached a provisional political agreement on the regulation. If adopted, its Articles 7 and 11, in conjunction with Annex V to that regulation, will respectively regulate the design for removal and access to information on removal and replacement of electric vehicle (EV) batteries present in vehicles with specific obligations concerning digitally coded parts and components. The battery passport established by Article 77 of the Batteries Regulation (2) will also provide remanufacturers, second-life operators and recyclers with up-to-date information for the handling of batteries. The forthcoming ELVR — Article 27(3) (3) mandates that the vehicle, its parts and components, including the EV batteries, are treated in accordance with the waste hierarchy. Article 24(2) of the forthcoming ELV Regulation allows the delivery of ELVs without its EV battery to authorised treatment facilities to remain free of charge for the last owner, to particularly enable a potential reuse, remanufacturing or repurposing option, under the condition that the battery is handled in a professional manner. EV batteries remaining in the vehicle will be removed and further treated in accordance with the Battery Regulation. The Battery Regulation’s recycling targets for recovery of materials do not disincentivise re-use as those targets apply only to waste batteries without a reuse potential that have entered a recycling facility. Together these provisions help promote carbon neutrality and circularity for vehicles. The Commission has therefore not planned any amendments to the legislation.

E-10-2026-001268.t: Urgent disbursement of EU financial support related to Ukraine
qt: to the Commission Krzysztof Brejza (PPE), Michał Kobosko (Renew), Magdalena Adamowicz (PPE), Bogdan Andrzej Zdrojewski (PPE) Subject:

Recent reports indicate that the disbursement of approximately PLN 2 billion (around EUR 470 million) to Poland under the European Peace Facility, intended as reimbursement for military assistance provided to Ukraine, is currently blocked in the Council. At the same time, broader EU support for Ukraine continues to face delays. At a time when Ukraine continues to defend its sovereignty and territorial integrity against Russia’s war of aggression, sustained, timely and predictable financial support from the European Union remains essential. This includes ensuring that Member States contributing to Ukraine’s defence are duly and swiftly reimbursed. In this context: 1.
What concrete steps is the Commission taking to facilitate the rapid disbursement of reimbursements to Member States under the European Peace Facility?
What options is the Commission considering to ensure that EU financial support for Ukraine can be delivered without undue delay, including in the absence of agreement in the Council?
What is the indicative timeline for resolving the current situation, and what contingency measures are available should the deadlock persist?
The European Union must continue to demonstrate unity, reliability and leadership in its support for Ukraine.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (29.7.2026) At the Foreign Affairs Councils in May, June and July 2026, the High Representative/VicePresident has called for a resolution of the blockage of EUR 6.6 billion dedicated to Ukraine under the European Peace Facility (EPF). All twenty-seven Member States now agree on lifting the blockage. The EU military support for Ukraine continues to flow through bilateral donations, through tailored and demand-driven support funded by the windfall profits of immobilised Russian assets channelled through the EPF, and through the unprecedented EUR 90 billion Ukraine Support Loan agreed in December 2025, two thirds of which is expected to go towards military support. The Ukraine Support Loan Regulation1 was adopted on 24 February 2026, together with an amendment to the Ukraine Facility Regulation2. The final piece of the package (an amendment to the Multiannual Financial Framework Regulation3 was adopted later, on 23 April 2026, with unanimity. The liquidity situation of Ukraine was not at risk due to this delay. Implementation of the Ukraine Support Loan is under way. The first disbursement of budget support was channelled through macrofinancial assistance at the end of June 2026 in parallel with the first disbursement to support Ukraine’s defence industrial capacities. The Ukraine Support Instrument under the European Defence Industry Programme4 will help rebuild and modernise Ukraine’s Defence Technological and Industrial Base. Ukraine’s association to the European Defence Fund will support its integration into the European Defence Technological and Industrial Base, while the BraveTechEU initiative will accelerate defence innovation to meet real operational needs and strengthen links between DefenceTech industrial bases.

E-10-2026-001267.t: Lethal autonomous weapon systems and use of artificial intelligence in defence
qt: to the Commission Joachim Streit (Renew) Subject:

The Commission is promoting the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in defence, in particular under the European Defence Fund and in the ‘White Paper for European Defence – Readiness 2030’. At the same time, military applications are expressly excluded from the scope of the AI Act. Indeed, Article 7 of the act requires that supported measures be compatible with international law and ethical principles, while Article 10 contains no specific provisions on AI or autonomous weapon systems. Meanwhile, Parliament expressly called for a ban on lethal autonomous weapon systems in its resolution of 20 January 2021 and stressed the need for rigorous human oversight. 1.

How does Commission explain the fact that military applications are excluded from the scope of the AI Act at the same time as AI-based defence technologies are being supported by the European Defence Fund?
How are Parliament’s calls for restrictions or even a ban on autonomous weapon systems being taken into account in AI advancements in defence?

What requirements are in place for EU-funded defence projects to ensure clear responsibilities, sufficient human oversight, and transparency over the allocation of EU funds, and is the Commission planning further legislation or will the existing regulatory gaps remain?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.5.2026) Recital 24 of the Artificial Intelligence (AI) Act (2024/1689)1 clarifies why military and defence applications are not included in the Act: ‘As regards military and defence purposes, such exclusion is justified both by Article 4(2) of the Treaty on the European Union (TEU)2 and by the specificities of the Member States’ and the common Union defence policy covered by Chapter 2 of Title V TEU that are subject to public international law, which is therefore the more appropriate legal framework for the regulation of AI systems in the context of the use of lethal force and other AI systems in the context of military and defence activities’. The European defence industrial programmes do not fund actions related to defence products that are prohibited by applicable international law. These programmes, moreover, lay down specific provisions regarding lethal autonomous weapons. The European Defence Fund specifically bans the EU funding of lethal autonomous weapons without the possibility of human control over the selection and engagement decisions when carrying out strikes against humans. Furthermore, as part of an ethics review, the Commission screens all proposals, with support of external ethics experts, to identify those actions raising complex or serious ethical issues. Actions which are not ethically acceptable will be rejected. In addition, the European Defence Industry Programme3 cannot fund defence products which are prohibited by applicable international law, nor lethal autonomous systems that operate outside a responsible chain of human command and control or cannot comply with the principles of International Humanitarian Law.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj/eng. 2 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/treaty/teu_2012/art_4/oj/eng. 3 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32025R2643.

E-10-2026-001266.t: Safety and labelling of citrus fruit treatments
qt: to the Commission Luke Ming Flanagan (The Left) Subject:

Regulation (EU) No 1129/20111 has been in force since 2011. This regulation prohibits the treatment of citrus fruits with certain additives (E230, E231 and E232), while the fungicide and pesticide thiabendazole (E233) and imazalil – which is sprayed onto the surface of citrus fruits to prolong their storage – are still permitted. Several studies, including some carried out by the US Environmental Protection Agency, have found this latter substance to be carcinogenic. If peel has been treated with fungicides, additives or preservatives, this must be indicated on the label. By law, producers must indicate on their labels any treatments carried out with waxes and other substances. Where imazalil is among the additives used, the law requires a mandatory warning – ‘inedible peel’ – to be provided on the label. These requirements, however, do not apply to pomelos, grapefruits and limes. Can the Commission clarify the following points: 1.
What level of enforcement is in place to ensure that the prescribed maximum residue limits (MRLs) are adhered to?
When were the MRLs last reviewed and have they taken into account the latest scientific data?
Why is the mandatory warning on the use of the peel (inedible peel) not extended to limes?

Commission Regulation (EU) No 1129/2011 of 11 November 2011 amending Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 1333/2008 of the European Parliament and of the Council by establishing a Union list of food additives (OJ L 295, 12.11.2011, p. 1, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2011/1129/oj).
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (10.6.2026) Regulation (EC) No 396/2005 on maximum residue levels (MRLs) of pesticides1 imposes Member States to carry out controls to ensure that food placed on the market is compliant with the legal limits. The European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) collects the information from national and EU-coordinated control programmes and publishes the EU report on pesticide residues in food2. In 2024, 86 449 samples were analysed. 96% contained no residues or residues below or equal to the MRLs. Non-compliant samples (1.8%) triggered sanctions or enforcement actions. Out of 38 169 samples analysed for the presence of imazalil, including fruits with their peel3, only 35 contained residues above the MRL. This confirms that the food available to EU consumers is safe. The MRLs for imazalil were last updated in 20204 considering EFSA’s opinion of 20195. Although imazalil is classified as carcinogen category 2, recent studies reviewed by EFSA6, show that it is not genotoxic. Further EFSA opinions confirmed that new MRLs for imazalil do not present a risk for consumers4,7. The Commission prepared new draft Regulations reviewing some MRLs for imazalil that are under discussion with Member States. The food additives authorised for surface treatment of citrus and/or other fruits, and their conditions of use, are laid down in Regulation (EC) No 1333/20088. Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/24299 lays down the marketing standard for citrus fruit, which lists the ‘commercial specifications’ required to appear on each package10. This includes: ‘When used, mention of the preserving agent or other chemical substances used at post-harvest stage’. E-10-2026-001265.t: Follow-up on the SOMO report by the Commission
qt: to the Commission Tilly Metz (Verts/ALE), Thomas Waitz (Verts/ALE), Cristina Guarda (Verts/ALE), David Cormand (Verts/ALE), Rasmus Nordqvist (Verts/ALE), Marie Toussaint (Verts/ALE) Subject:

In January 2025, the Centre for Research on Multinational Corporations (SOMO) published a report1 documenting how JBS, one of the world’s largest meat companies, allegedly used Luxembourg-based mailbox subsidiaries and intra-group arrangements to substantially reduce its tax liabilities. Between 2019 and 2022, JBS may have avoided approximately USD 293 million in corporate income taxes and USD 148 million in withholding taxes, relying on entities with little or no economic substance. Given that one year has passed since the publication of this report, can the Commission clarify: 1.
Whether it has formally assessed the evidence presented by SOMO and engaged with the Luxembourg authorities regarding these structures?
Whether any inquiries, investigations or corrective actions have been initiated in response to these findings?

What concrete measures it plans to adopt to curb the use of mailbox companies and aggressive tax planning within the EU, including stronger rules on withholding taxes and the prevention of mismatches between national tax systems?
Ensuring that multinational companies pay their fair share of tax is essential for public finances, fair competition and the credibility of the EU’s tax agenda.
https://www.somo.nl/jbss-global-tax-avoidance-hub-luxembourg/
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.7.2026) Compliance with tax rules falls under the responsibility of the country which adopted such rules. The Commission remains fully committed to tackling cross-border tax avoidance and evasion as well as aggressive tax planning at international level. The EU has strong tools to counteract tax avoidance practices (notably the Anti-Tax Avoidance Directive1). The Pillar Two Directive2, set out rules to ensure a minimum effective level of taxation for large multinational groups in every jurisdiction where they operate; this is applicable since 31 December 2023. With regard to Luxembourg, the Commission also introduced countryspecific recommendations on aggressive tax planning as of 2019. The 2025 country-specific recommendations on aggressive tax planning notably target the risks that arise from aggressive tax planning opportunities in the absence of sound defensive measures on outbound payments – especially interest and royalty payments – towards jurisdictions with zero or very low taxation. The Commission attaches great importance to maintaining an open and constructive dialogue with the European Parliament on these critical issues.
1 Council Directive (EU) 2016/1164 of 12 July 2016 laying down rules against tax avoidance practices that

directly affect the functioning of the internal market. 2 Council Directive (EU) 2022/2523 of 14 December 2022 on ensuring a global minimum level of taxation for multinational enterprise groups and large-scale domestic groups in the Union.

qt: to the Commission Tilly Metz (Verts/ALE), Thomas Waitz (Verts/ALE), Cristina Guarda (Verts/ALE), David Cormand (Verts/ALE), Rasmus Nordqvist (Verts/ALE), Marie Toussaint (Verts/ALE) Subject:

Brazil-based meat-processing multinational JBS has a documented history of large-scale corruption, including paying bribes to over 1 800 Brazilian politicians to access government loans, which enabled the company to acquire monopoly power in the Brazilian and the US meat markets.123 As JBS seeks to expand its presence in the EU market, these structural corruption practices, combined with aggressive tax planning through Luxembourg-based entities, raise serious concerns for fair competition, market integrity and public trust in the EU. In this context, can the Commission clarify: 1.
How it assesses the risks posed by companies with a history of large-scale corruption, such as JBS, when they enter and consolidate their presence in the EU market?
How the it ensures that EU trade and investment policies do not inadvertently support companies with records of structural corruption and monopolistic practices?

(1) (2) (3) As JBS seeks to expand its presence in the EU market, these structural corruption practices, combined with aggressive tax planning through Luxembourg-based entities, raise serious concerns for fair competition, market integrity and public trust in the EU. In this context, can the Commission clarify: 1.

(22 May 2026) The EU’s external policies, including trade and investment policies, do not support companies with records of corruption or anti-competitive practices. The EU-Mercosur Partnership Agreement (1) and the Interim Trade Agreement (2) contain provisions that will help counter corruption in cooperation with the Brazilian authorities and that protect the EU market against potential anti-competitive practices. In particular, the EU-Mercosur Partnership Agreement provides for strengthened cooperation on combating corruption, including prevention and investigation activities, the prosecution of offenders, and mutual legal assistance. The EU-Mercosur Interim Trade Agreement, which has been provisionally in effect since 1 May 2026, provides for an obligation of the Parties to adopt or maintain in force comprehensive competition law which effectively addresses the anticompetitive practices. It also protects EU producers of sensitive agricultural products (including beef and poultry) against sudden increases of imports from Mercosur by means of tariff quotas and safeguards. Also, if a company obtains particularly favourable treatment (e.g. cheap government loans), this may qualify as ‘foreign subsidies’ under the EU’s Foreign Subsidies Regulation (3). The Commission is empowered to assess whether such subsidies may ‘distort’ the EU market, especially as regards the company’s investments in the EU (through mergers and acquisitions) or EU activities with foreign funding and apply redressive measures towards the said company. These examples illustrate some of the tools the EU uses to address corruption and unfair competition. The Commission employs a range of mechanisms to ensure compliance and protect the integrity of the EU market.

qt: to the Commission Nicolás González Casares (S&D) Subject:

A recent study commissioned by DG MARE has, for the first time, put a figure on the cost of decarbonising the European fishing fleet. It is between EUR 10 billion and EUR 25.6 billion, depending on the case. These figures reflect the challenge the sector is facing, with the European Commission proposing to cut 67 % of the funds earmarked in the 2028-2034 MFF. All this is happening in a context of very low profit margins (around 3 %, according to the study), fierce external competition, increasing dependence on imports, etc. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Will it present a new comprehensive strategy for the renewal of the fleet, accompanied by a financial action plan to cover the cost indicated?
Will it remove existing obstacles to fleet renewal in the common fisheries policy and the European Maritime, Fisheries and Aquaculture Fund, relating, for example, to tonnage, length or capacity?
Does it plan to include maritime activities such as fishing within the scope of the EU emissions trading system?
at: (English version) to the Commission Nicolás González Casares (S&D) (25 March 2026) Subject: Decarbonisation A recent study commissioned by DG MARE has, for the first time, put a figure on the cost of decarbonising the European fishing fleet. (29 May 2026) The National and Regional Partnership Plans (NRPPs) — part of the proposal for the next Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) — will bring together EU funds implemented by Member States and regions under one coherent strategy. A single type of intervention, such as productive investments to improve competitiveness, training programmes, or generational renewal strategies, will now be applicable across several sectors, without needing dedicated schemes under many different funds. This will improve flexibility, and the fisheries sector will benefit from actions that are non-sector specific. The ringfenced allocation for certain aspects of the Common Fisheries Policy (CFP) is smaller than under the EMFA F (1), but it is only a minimum allocation, and it can be complemented by Member States from their non-ringfenced national allocation under their Plan, in accordance with their priorities for their fleet. This support will also be complemented with support under the European Competitiveness fund and Global Europe. The MFF proposal contains substantially fewer conditions than the EMFAF for financial support related to the fleet. Together with the Vision for fisheries and aquaculture for 2040 -in preparation based on the results of the recent evaluation of the CFP Regulation–, Member States will be able to develop an action plan and strategy for their fleet together with an accompanying financial plan, according to national priorities and the available resources. The Commission is reviewing potential EMFAF rule amendments based on implementation experience and stakeholder feedback. Without prejudging any future Commission proposal, the automatic inclusion of the fishing sector in the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) is not currently planned.

E-10-2026-001262.t: Restoring genuine academic freedom in our universities
qt: to the Commission Catherine Griset (PfE), Julie Rechagneux (PfE), Milan Uhrík (ESN), Elisabeth Dieringer (PfE), Jaroslav Bžoch (PfE), André Rougé (PfE), Pierre Pimpie (PfE), António Tânger Corrêa (PfE), Ewa Zajączkowska-Hernik (PfE), Petr Bystron (ESN), Petar Volgin (ESN), Hans Neuhoff (ESN), Markus Buchheit (ESN), Geadis Geadi (ECR), Annamária Vicsek (PfE), Séverine Werbrouck (PfE), Ernő Schaller-Baross (PfE), Enikő Győri (PfE), Dick Erixon (ECR), György Hölvényi (PfE), András Gyürk (PfE), Pál Szekeres (PfE), Gerolf Annemans (PfE), Pascale Piera (PfE), Kinga Gál (PfE), Antonín Staněk (PfE), Csaba Dömötör (PfE), András László (PfE) Subject:

A recent American study shows that nine out of ten students feel compelled to express more progressive views than those they actually hold1. They are thus attempting to escape pressure from lecturers and students with left-wing leanings, which can result in biased grading, harassment, or even violence. This has also given rise in a dramatic decline in the standards and rankings of the schools and universities most affected by the militant monopoly of the left and far left, which apply the theory of social engineering by making it too costly to express dissenting opinions. The peddlers of these ideologies, who are over-represented in academia, claim however that academic freedom is threatened by any criticism of their views. 1.
At a time when European institutions are issuing numerous communications and standards on academic freedom, can the Commission provide a precise legal definition of it?
Does this encompass only so-called progressive views, as left-wing academics and student activists claim?
Will the Commission undertake to strip universities that support the most violent far-left activists, particularly when they threaten dissident teachers or students of EU funding?

Supporter (2) (22 May 2026) The Commission participates actively to the European Higher Education Area as a full member of the Bologna Follow-Up Group (1). The Rome Communiqué (2) defined academic freedom in 2020 as freedom of academic staff and students to engage in research, teaching, learning and communication in and with society without interference nor fear of reprisal. The Tirana Communiqué (2024) reaffirmed that academic freedom is one of six fundamental academic values, next to academic integrity, institutional autonomy, student and staff participation in higher education governance, public responsibility for higher education and public responsibility of higher education, and that these values must be implemented as a coherent whole. Enshrined in Article 13 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights (3), academic freedom guarantees academics and students the freedom of thought and inquiry needed to advance knowledge through research and exchange openly. It is informed by the standards of academic disciplines and provides the condition for challenging these standards based on the results of research. Therefore, these fundamental values should be understood as foundational principles of higher education rather than as political positions. Education is a national competence. The Commission has therefore limited direct ascendancy over higher education institutions.

qt: to the Commission Aodhán Ó Ríordáin (S&D) Subject:
In the light of the EU’s competences in the field of occupational health and safety and the implementation of the European Pillar of Social Rights: 1.

What action can the Commission take to support Member States in ensuring that long COVID is recognised as an occupational disease for healthcare and social care workers where infection occurred in the workplace?

How will the Commission ensure that EU instruments are used to encourage adequate income protection, workplace adaptation and social support measures so that affected workers are not pushed into poverty or long-term labour market exclusion?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.5.2026) Matters relating to the recognition of and compensation for occupational diseases fall under the competence of the Member States. Nevertheless, with the Commission Recommendation concerning the European schedule of occupational diseases1 the Commission recommends to the Member States, inter alia, to introduce the European schedule as soon as possible into their national laws, regulations or administrative provisions concerning scientifically recognised occupational diseases liable for compensation and subject to preventive measures. Entry No 408 in the European schedule2 refers to COVID-19 caused by work in disease prevention, in health and social care and in domiciliary assistance, or, in a pandemic context, in sectors where there is an outbreak in activities in which a risk of infection has been proven. The European Social Fund Plus (ESF+) is the EU’s primary instrument for investments in people. The ESF+ can play a significant role in helping those with Long COVID by supporting vocational rehabilitation, employment reintegration and social inclusion. It can support rehabilitation programmes to help individuals regain capacity for work or workplace adaptations e.g. teleworking and digital skills trainings. Member States are obliged to programme at least 25% of their ESF+ resources to social inclusion. This can include measures to support individuals struggling with chronic illnesses e.g. mental health services. Member States are responsible for programming and implementation of the ESF+. The Commission can encourage Member States to programme in certain policy priorities if deemed necessary based on national or regional circumstances.

E-10-2026-001259.t: EU solidarity instrument to protect households from cost-of-living shock linked to Middle East instability
qt: to the Commission Aodhán Ó Ríordáin (S&D) Subject:

The escalating conflict in the Middle East, driven in part by US and Israeli military action in Iran, poses a serious risk of an inflationary shock to EU Member State economies – comparable to, and potentially worse than, the energy price surge that followed Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. EU households have not yet recovered from that crisis. Member States must be equipped to respond rapidly. 1.
Is the Commission assessing the potential impact of the Middle East conflict on EU energy prices and household costs?

Will the Commission consider preparing a dedicated solidarity instrument – modelled on the European instrument for temporary Support to mitigate Unemployment Risks in an Emergency (SURE) or the Security Action for Europe (SAFE) instrument – to support Member States in protecting workers and vulnerable households from a cost-ofliving shock of this nature?
What timeline does the Commission envisage for any such preparatory work?
at: (English version) to the Commission Aodhán Ó Ríordáin (S&D) (25 March 2026) Subject: EU solidarity instrument to protect households from cost-of-living shock linked to Middle East instability The escalating conflict in the Middle East, driven in part by US and Israeli military action in Iran, poses a serious risk of an inflationary shock to EU Member State economies — comparable to, and potentially worse than, the energy price surge that followed Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. EU households have not yet recovered from that crisis. Member States must be equipped to respond rapidly. 1.
Is the Commission assessing the potential impact of the Middle East conflict on EU energy prices and household costs?

2. Will the Commission consider preparing a dedicated solidarity instrument — modelled on the European instrument for temporary Support to mitigate Unemployment Risks in an Emergency (SURE) or the Security Action for Europe (SAFE) instrument — to support Member States in protecting workers and vulnerable households from a cost-of-living shock of this nature? 3.
What timeline does the Commission envisage for any such preparatory work?

(30 September 2026) The Commission released its Spring 2026 Economic Forecast on 21 May 2026 (1). The forecast provides an assessment of the impact of the energy shock from the conflict in the Middle East on the economies of the Member States, as well as the EU and euro area aggregates. The Commission is monitoring and assessing the situation on a continuous basis (2). The European instrument for temporary support to mitigate Unemployment Risks in an Emergency (SURE) demonstrated the value of EU support in the context of the severe shock caused by the COVID-19 pandemic, helping to prevent widespread job losses. However, the current energy shock differs significantly in both scale and nature. Consequently, a SURE-type instrument does not represent the most appropriate policy response. That being said, with its communication AccelerateEU — Energy Union (3), presented on 22 April 2026, the Commission committed to provide continued assistance to Member States in the design of targeted, timely, and temporary measures to relieve the burden of high energy costs, with a focus on small and medium-sized enterprises, energy-intensive industries, and households, while preserving the incentive to save energy and encouraging a reduction in fossil fuel use. On 3 June 2026, the Commission proposed to expand the scope of the existing National Escape Clause for defence spending to accommodate the measures undertaken since February 2026 to reduce the dependence on imported fossil fuels and thereby contribute to Europe’s energy security and defence, without raising the overall cap of 1.5% of gross domestic product (GDP). The flexibility allowed for these measures is to be capped at 0.3% per year, with a cumulative maximum of 0.6% of GDP until 2028 (4). Fiscal sustainability safeguards remain fully in place. Member States will have the opportunity to request the expansion in the scope of their existing National Escape Clause over the coming months.

E-10-2026-001258.t: Discontinuation of the Your Europe Advice legal advice service
qt: to the Commission Aodhán Ó Ríordáin (S&D) Subject:

Your Europe Advice is the only EU-funded service providing free, personalised legal advice to citizens, businesses and organisations across EU Member States. It handles more than 20 000 enquiries annually and provides essential support to SOLVIT centres and national advice organisations. It has come to my attention that the Commission’s Directorate-General for Internal Market, Industry, Entrepreneurship and SMEs intends to unilaterally discontinue this service without public consultation or any published impact assessment. 1.
Has the Commission conducted an impact assessment on the consequences of discontinuation for citizens, and if not, why?
What assessment has been made of the risks of directing citizens to AI tools for complex legal questions in the absence of this service?
Has consideration been given to the impact on SOLVIT and other directorates-general, and to transferring the service to another directorate-general rather than discontinuing it entirely?

E-10-2026-001257.t: EU funding cut puts social projects at risk in Slovakia
qt: to the Commission Tomáš Zdechovský (PPE) Subject:

A legislative proposal in Slovakia, due to be adopted in April 2026, envisages a drastic reduction, of up to 40 %, in compensation contributions for employers of persons with disabilities, reportedly linked to the end of EU funding. This coincides with a sharp increase in VAT, from 5 % to 23 %. Social enterprises play a crucial role in integrating persons with disabilities and other vulnerable groups, including minorities, into the labour market. These measures would therefore not only undermine businesses, but directly threaten the social inclusion model that the EU itself promotes and co-finances. Stakeholders warn that the combined impact of reduced support and increased taxation will be economically unsustainable and, in many cases, downright destructive, leading to closures and mass job losses among the most vulnerable. 1.
Is the Commission aware of this situation and the Slovak Government’s plans?

Does the Commission consider it acceptable and in line with EU objectives on sustainability, social inclusion and equal opportunities that support is reduced by 40 % while tax burdens are simultaneously increased?

What concrete steps does the Commission intend to take to address this situation, including engaging with Slovak authorities, to prevent the dismantling of inclusive employment structures supported by EU policies?
at: (English version) to the Commission Tomáš Zdechovský (PPE) (25 March 2026) Subject: EU funding cut puts social projects at risk in Slovakia A legislative proposal in Slovakia, due to be adopted in April 2026, envisages a drastic reduction, of up to 40%, in compensation contributions for employers of persons with disabilities, reportedly linked to the end of EU funding. This coincides with a sharp increase in VAT, from 5% to 23%. Social enterprises play a crucial role in integrating persons with disabilities and other vulnerable groups, including minorities, into the labour market. These measures would therefore not only undermine businesses, but directly threaten the social inclusion model that the EU itself promotes and co-finances. Stakeholders warn that the combined impact of reduced support and increased taxation will be economically unsustainable and, in many cases, downright destructive, leading to closures and mass job losses among the most vulnerable. 1.
Is the Commission aware of this situation and the Slovak Government’s plans?

2. Does the Commission consider it acceptable and in line with EU objectives on sustainability, social inclusion and equal opportunities that support is reduced by 40% while tax burdens are simultaneously increased? 3. What concrete steps does the Commission intend to take to address this situation, including engaging with Slovak authorities, to prevent the dismantling of inclusive employment structures supported by EU policies? (10 June 2026) The Commission is aware of the proposal to adjust compensation contributions for employers of persons with disabilities. The Commission emphasises that social inclusion and the integration of vulnerable groups into the labour market, notably through social enterprises, are core objectives of the European Social Fund Plus (1) and they are supported as such by the Programme Slovakia. The national project ‘Poskytovanie finančných príspevkov integračným podnikom’ (2) is set to last until the end of 2029. The Commission is not commenting on ongoing legislative negotiations at national level. As underlined by the mid-term review of the Social Economy Action Plan, adopted on 30 March 2026 (3), the Commission continues to encourage the Member States to develop their social economy ecosystems to fully benefit from its potential to address societal challenges and deliver a positive social impact.
