E-10-2026-001256.t: Upholding the right to study of Palestinian scholarship winners who are unable to leave Gaza
qt: to the Commission Danilo Della Valle (The Left), Carolina Morace (The Left), Mario Furore (The Left), Mimmo Lucano (The Left), Dario Tamburrano (The Left), Giuseppe Antoci (The Left), Cristina Guarda (Verts/ALE), Annalisa Corrado (S&D), Ignazio Roberto Marino (Verts/ALE), Pasquale Tridico (The Left), Ilaria Salis (The Left), Benedetta Scuderi (Verts/ALE) Subject:

At least 56 Palestinians who have been awarded IUPALS, AFAM and Erasmus+ scholarships by Bologna, Milan, Calabria, Roma Tor Vergata and other Italian universities cannot leave the Gaza Strip owing to a lack of safe corridors and stalled consular procedures. For these students – who hail from an area where all campuses have been completely destroyed – attending an EU university is the only chance they have of exercising the right to pursue an education enshrined in Article 14 of the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights. In the light of the fact that Article 2 of the EU-Israel Association Agreement makes relations between the two parties conditional on upholding human rights and that Regulation (EC) No 810/2009 (known as the Visa Code) provides for procedural derogations and emergency measures for humanitarian cases and prospective students, we ask the Commission: 1.
What urgent steps involving the EEAS and the competent authorities will it take to facilitate the issuing of visas and the opening of educational corridors for the 56 students mentioned above?

How will the Commission work with the Member States to ensure that this bureaucratic inertia does not prevent Palestinians who have already been granted scholarships from making use of them before they expire?
How will the Commission ensure that the right to pursue an education is upheld in line with the Union’s external action policy objectives for conflict areas?
Supporter1
This question is supported by a Member other than the authors: Cecilia Strada (S&D).
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.5.2026) The Commission is fully aware of the extremely difficult circumstances facing Palestinian students in Gaza, including those who have been awarded scholarships under programmes such as Erasmus+ and through bilateral arrangements with European universities and are unable to leave Gaza. The Commission is aware of evacuations of students from Gaza carried out by individual Member States, such as Spain and Italy. The Commission, in close coordination with the European External Action Service and in particular through the Office of the European Union Representative (West Bank and Gaza Strip, United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees) and the National Erasmus+ Office in Palestine, has been engaging with Member States, relevant consular authorities, and international partners present in Palestine to explore possible avenues to facilitate the departure of Palestinian students from Gaza, notably those participating in EUfunded programmes and in bilateral arrangements with European universities.

E-10-2026-001255.t: Ensuring competition and strategic autonomy in the AI gigafactory supply chain
qt: to the Commission Oliver Schenk (PPE), Matthias Ecke (S&D), Bart Groothuis (Renew), Wouter Beke (PPE), Borys Budka (PPE), Monika Hohlmeier (PPE), Marion Walsmann (PPE), Andrea Wechsler (PPE), Christine Schneider (PPE), Alexandra Mehnert (PPE), Verena Mertens (PPE), Jens Gieseke (PPE), Adam Jarubas (PPE), Krzysztof Hetman (PPE), Mirosława Nykiel (PPE), Andrzej Buła (PPE), Bogdan Andrzej Zdrojewski (PPE), Bartłomiej Sienkiewicz (PPE) Subject:

Europe is increasingly confronted with structural challenges related to economic dependence on a limited number of global suppliers in strategic sectors. This dependence creates vulnerabilities in terms of security of supply, rising costs and reduced technological sovereignty. The planned AI gigafactory initiatives are intended to strengthen Europe’s technological capacity and resilience. Today, however, data centers – and specifically GPUs and AI training – are overwhelmingly concentrated and dominated by a single supplier. In the framework of AI gigafactory public procurement decisions, Europe must avoid the mistake of exacerbating this dependency, strengthening the existing dominance and foreclosing alternatives. European procurement agencies and contracting authorities must actively avoid supplier lockin and dependence and must take reasonable steps to avoid non-competitive outcomes, even where switching is not easy. In this context: 1.
How does the Commission intend to ensure that procurement decisions related to AI gigafactory projects do not reinforce dominance and that they prevent vendor lock-in?
Will the Commission introduce measures to ensure that other players, including SMEs and emerging European suppliers, can participate meaningfully in the AI gigafactory ecosystem?
How does the Commission intend to use AI gigafactory initiatives to reduce Europe’s strategic dependencies while promoting competition and the diversification of suppliers?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (19.6.2026) The Commission acknowledges the structural risks of relying on a limited number of global suppliers for critical AI infrastructure, affecting both hardware and software. Exacerbating this dependency must be avoided. The Commission addresses this on multiple fronts. For example, initiatives like the European Chips Act aim to boost domestic capacity and foster a diversified ecosystem inclusive of small and medium-sized enterprises. As currently envisioned, the AI Gigafactory (AIGF) initiative1 intends for procurement evaluation criteria to structurally incentivise the integration of European technology, rewarding consortia that propose European hardware and sovereign software stacks. Additionally, to reduce third-country dependencies and actively prevent lock-in, the Commission’s proposal strongly encourages deploying European open-source software solutions in these procurements. AIGFs will not be experimental platforms; they must rely on currently available, state-of-theart technology to immediately deliver competitive services. However, the AIGF initiative will utilise a phased implementation strategy, allowing facilities to progressively integrate newly emerging yet mature European hardware in subsequent phases. This will diversify the supply chain and integrate European suppliers over time without compromising immediate industrial capabilities.
1 https://www.eurohpc-ju.europa.eu/ai-gigafactories_en.

E-10-2026-001254.t: Operation of tunnels on the Egnatia Odos motorway and toll collection despite traffic restrictions
qt: to the Commission Sakis Arnaoutoglou (S&D) Subject:

According to complaints from citizens and petitions and complaints lodged by users of the Egnatia Odos with the Hellenic Competition Commission, after the motorway was taken over by a private concessionaire a series of tunnels along the Igoumenitsa-Panagia section were simultaneously reduced to a single lane back in 2026 and have remained so ever since. This section, which is approximately 123 kilometres long, has numerous long twin tunnels spanning more than 33 kilometres in total. The single lane system applies to the entire length of the tunnels as well as to sections before them, involving traffic and vehicle speed restrictions. Meanwhile, motorway users continue to be charged full toll fees, raising questions about whether the price is proportional to the service provided and about whether this practice complies with EU law. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

Is the extensive and simultaneous reduction of motorway tunnels to single lane traffic for the purposes of performing checks and improving safety compatible with the European tunnel safety framework and the law on trans-European transport?
Has it examined or does it intend to examine whether these measures affect road safety or compliance with European requirements for the operation of road infrastructure?

Is the continued collection of full toll fees compatible with EU competition law and the principle of proportionality when there are significant traffic restrictions resulting from technical measures or interventions?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (20.7.2026) 1. Directive 2004/54/EC on minimum safety requirements for tunnels in the Trans-European Road Network1 does not prevent the reduction of the number of lanes on motorways in tunnels to a single lane, if the safety requirements are met. Similarly, neither Regulation (EU) 2024/1679 on Union guidelines for the development of the trans-European transport network2, nor Directive 2008/96/EC on road infrastructure safety management3, forbid the reduction to one of the number of lanes of a road. 2. The Commission did not assess and does not plan to challenge these measures which have been put in place to check and improve the safety along the motorway. Traffic organisation measures fall within the remit of the national competent authorities. 3. Directive 1999/62/EC on the charging of vehicles for the use of road infrastructures4 requires that the level of the infrastructure charge element of a toll levied upon heavy-duty vehicles is equal to, or less than, the level necessary to recover the cost of the infrastructure. There are no specific conditions in competition law on the level of the toll fees in relation to traffic restrictions.

1 OJ L 167, 30.4.2004, p. 39, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2004/54/oj. 2 OJ L 2024/1679, 28.6.2024, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1679/oj. 3 OJ L 319 29.11.2008, p. 59, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2008/96/oj. 4 OJ L 187 20.7.1999, p. 42, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/1999/62/oj.

E-10-2026-001253.t: Green transition or just a rip-off? Millions of euros from citizens’ pockets will flow into Brussels funds, but will this result in cleaner air?
qt: to the Commission Erik Kaliňák (NI), Judita Laššáková (NI), Katarína Roth Neveďalová (NI) Subject:

The Emissions Trading System (EU ETS), and in particular the new ETS2 for buildings, road transport, and small installations (postponed until 2028), are leading to a significant increase in the cost of fuel, heating and energy for ordinary citizens and households. Despite claims of a ‘green transition’, many citizens see these fees primarily as a tool to increase the cost of living, which hits the lower and middle classes the hardest. Revenues from ETS2 auctions are intended to partially finance the Social Climate Fund to the tune of some EUR 65--86 billion by 2032, but the question remains as to whether these payments will actually result in cleaner air or merely shift the burden onto families. 1.

Can the Commission demonstrate that ETS and ETS2 levies will actually ensure significantly cleaner air and reduced emissions in the buildings and transport sectors, or is this primarily an additional tax on consumers without measurable environmental benefits for ordinary people?

For which specific projects and in what proportions does the Commission plan to use the funds collected from ETS/ETS2, and how much will go directly to supporting lowincome households, how much to green investments, and how much will remain in the EU’s central budget?

Will the Commission assume full political and moral responsibility for further increases in energy and fuel prices, for the deterioration of European families’ standard of living, and for the potential rise in energy and transport poverty resulting from the introduction of ETS2?
at: (English version) to the Commission Erik Kaliňák (NI), Judita Laššáková (NI), Katarína Roth Neveďalová (NI) (25 March 2026) Subject: Green transition or just a rip-off? Millions of euros from citizens’ pockets will flow into Brussels funds, but will this result in cleaner air? The Emissions Trading System (EU ETS), and in particular the new ETS2 for buildings, road transport, and small installations (postponed until 2028), are leading to a significant increase in the cost of fuel, heating and energy for ordinary citizens and households. Despite claims of a ‘green transition’, many citizens see these fees primarily as a tool to increase the cost of living, which hits the lower and middle classes the hardest. Revenues from ETS2 auctions are intended to partially finance the Social Climate Fund to the tune of some EUR 65--86 billion by 2032, but the question remains as to whether these payments will actually result in cleaner air or merely shift the burden onto families. 1. Can the Commission demonstrate that ETS and ETS2 levies will actually ensure significantly cleaner air and reduced emissions in the buildings and transport sectors, or is this primarily an additional tax on consumers without measurable environmental benefits for ordinary people? 2. For which specific projects and in what proportions does the Commission plan to use the funds collected from ETS/ETS2, and how much will go directly to supporting low-income households, how much to green investments, and how much will remain in the EU’s central budget? 3. Will the Commission assume full political and moral responsibility for further increases in energy and fuel prices, for the deterioration of European families’ standard of living, and for the potential rise in energy and transport poverty resulting from the introduction of ETS2? (12 May 2026) The Emissions Trading System (ETS) has reduced greenhouse gas emissions from power and industry by 50% compared to 2005 (1), contributing to substantial health benefits from improved air quality (2). The revision scheduled for July 2026 will determine the cost-effective emission reductions for 2031-2040, in line with the economy-wide 2040 emission reduction target. ETS2 is scheduled to become fully operational in 2028. Its trajectory is set to bring emissions down by 42% by 2030 compared to 2005, complementing other EU and national policies to decarbonise buildings and road transport. The environmental and economic impacts were assessed in the impact assessment (3). More than three quarter of ETS auction revenue goes to national budgets and must be used for clean energy, decarbonisation and just transition activities. The Commission closely monitors this spending to ensure revenues are effectively and swiftly allocated. The remaining revenue is invested through EU-level instruments in industrial innovation, energy modernisation, energy security and — in particular from future ETS2 revenue — through the Social Climate Fund. An overview can be consulted on the Commission website (4). The Social Climate Fund, mobilising at least EUR 86.7 billion, is available to Member States to reduce energy and transport poverty through investments to reduce households’ vulnerability to increasingly volatile imported fossil energy prices and providing direct income support to mitigate short-term impacts of ETS2. Member States must also use national ETS2 revenues to fund climate action and support households through the transition. Strong safeguards are in place to ensure a smooth start to ETS2 with stable prices and support vulnerable households.

2025 Carbon Market Report: https://climate.ec.europa.eu/news-other-reads/news/2025-carbon-market-report-eu-ets-lowers-power-sector-emissions-andexpands-maritime-transport-2025-12-03_en. https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2319908121. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:52021SC0601. https://climate.ec.europa.eu/eu-action/carbon-markets/eu-emissions-trading-system-eu-ets/how-do-member-states-use-ets-revenues_en.

E-10-2026-001252.t: Does the Commission want to secretly push through ‘parenthood’ from commercial surrogacy and circumvent prohibitions in force in traditional states?
qt: to the Commission Erik Kaliňák (NI), Judita Laššáková (NI), Katarína Roth Neveďalová (NI) Subject:

The proposal for a parenthood regulation1 is yet to receive unanimous approval in the Council. In November 2025, Parliament condemned commercial surrogacy as the exploitation of women and children. In the interest of protecting the traditional family and the best interests of the child, the public policy exception must be strengthened so that Member States can protect their traditional values. 1.

How does the Commission plan to ensure that Member States can refuse to recognise parenthood arising from commercial surrogacy, given that this is unlikely to be accepted by the Court of Justice via the public policy exception2?
What specific steps will the Commission take to support Member States in combating reproductive tourism?
Will the Commission ensure that the European Certificate of Parenthood does not circumvent national bans on surrogacy?

https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex%3A52022PC0695. This assumption is based on the Court of Justice’s consistent approach and its overly restrictive interpretation of the concept of public policy, or the public policy exception.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.5.2026) The Commission is committed to upholding children’s and women’s rights within the framework of its competences. The exploitation of surrogacy is included as a form of exploitation in the Anti-Trafficking Directive1. The Directive targets those who coerce or deceive women into acting as surrogate mothers, without prejudice to national rules on surrogacy, including criminal and family law. Substantive family law, including rules on surrogacy, falls within the competence of the Member States. Each Member State thus decides its policy and legal position as regards surrogacy. However, the EU has competence under Article 81(3) TFEU to adopt measures of family law with cross-border implications. It is on this basis that the Commission adopted the proposal on the recognition of parenthood between Member States2. Given that, under international law3 and EU law (including the Treaties and the Charter of Fundamental Rights), all children without distinction have the same rights, the Commission proposal covers the recognition of parenthood established in a Member State irrespective of how the child was conceived or born and irrespective of the child’s type of family. Under the control of the Court of Justice and within the limits of the Court’s case law, Member States can invoke public policy to refuse the recognition of parenthood. The recognition of parenthood established in a third country will continue to be governed by national law. However, in applying their national law on the recognition of parenthood, Member States must respect their human rights obligations under international law, in particular the case law of the European Court of Human Rights on the recognition of the parenthood of children born abroad through surrogacy.
1 Directive 2011/36/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 5 April 2011 on preventing and

combating trafficking in human beings and protecting its victims, and replacing Council Framework Decision 2002/629/JHA (https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2011/36/oj/eng), amended by Directive (EU) 2024/1712 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 June 2024 amending Directive 2011/36/EU on preventing and combating trafficking in human beings and protecting its victims (https://eurlex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2024/1712/oj/eng). 2 COM(2022) 695 final. 3 In particular, the UN Convention on the Rights of children and the European Convention of Human Rights.

E-10-2026-001251.t: Yoti: when age verification tools put our data at risk
qt: to the Commission Catherine Griset (PfE) Subject:

In Spain, the age verification service Yoti has just been fined under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). The Spanish Data Protection Agency has charged the agechecker (used by Meta, TikTok and porn sites such as Pornhub) with the following violations: – unlawful processing of biometric data for the generation of biometric models from selfies for comparison against identity documents, since this implies storage (and therefore a risk of leakage); – excessive retention of biometric and geolocation information, in contravention of the principle of storage limitation; – non-compliance of consent mechanisms, which fall short of GDPR requirements on clarity and explicitness, particularly where pre-ticked boxes are involved. 1.
How does the Commission hope to enforce legal compliance among age verification services, particularly with regard to GDPR requirements?
Does the Commission prohibit age verification services from sharing data with non-EU countries?

Lastly, given the permanent and immutable nature of biometrics, what can be done to combat irreversible identity theft, which leaves victims forever at risk of fraudulent attempts to bypass the security systems in place at, for example, banks and government buildings?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.9.2026) Without prejudice to the Commission’s role as guardian of the Treaties, ensuring the application and enforcement of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) is the responsibility of Member States Data Protection Authorities and courts. The Commission does not have the competence to enforce GDPR compliance against individual age verification services. Any age verification app is required to comply with data protection rules, including by ensuring appropriate security measures to protect the personal data against the unauthorised or unlawful processing. The processing of biometric data for identification purposes constitutes special category of personal data and is therefore subject to additional rules. The GDPR imposes restrictions on personal data transfers to countries or international organisations outside the European Economic Area. This is to ensure that the level of protection of individuals granted by the GDPR remains equivalent when data is exported. The Commission released a blueprint for a robust EU-harmonised age verification solution that fully respects privacy and fundamental rights. It uses ‘Zero-Knowledge Proof’, a cryptographic technology which can securely prove that the owner has a valid age credential without revealing any other information. The solution does not allow identity tracking as the proof of age does not contain any identity data. The identity of the user is only checked once during the proof of age issuance. The Commission also recently made a Recommendation on establishing a common framework for EU wide Age Verification technologies1.
1 Brussels, 29.4.2026 C(2026) 4225 final; Commission Recommendation of 29.4.2026 on establishing a common
framework for EU wide Age Verification technologies https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reco/2026/1035/oj/eng.

E-10-2026-001250.t: Bringing balance to the infringement procedures launched by the Commission concerning decisions to take opposition media off the air
qt: to the Commission Catherine Griset (PfE), André Rougé (PfE), Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE), Pascale Piera (PfE) Subject:

In 2025, the French regulatory authority for audiovisual and digital communication withdrew the digital terrestrial television licence of C8, a right-wing French channel that was critical of the government. The withdrawal of its broadcast licence did not trigger a reaction from the Commission. Conversely, after the Hungarian Government withdrew the broadcast licence of left-wing radio station Klubrádió, the Commission took it to court, bringing an action for failure to fulfil obligations before the Court of Justice of the European Union. 1.
Does the Commission intend to launch an infringement procedure against the French authorities, who refused to renew C8’s digital terrestrial television licence on the grounds of minor infractions?
How does it justify the fact that its actions for failure to fulfil obligations seek to protect only left-leaning media outlets, without granting the same protection to right-wing ones?
In order to be more ‘inclusive’, are the Commission services responsible for the enforcement of the Media Freedom Act made aware of the need to defend pluralism and freedom of expression in Europe?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.6.2026) The Commission’s enforcement actions are strictly evidence-based and legally grounded in EU law, and do not target or favour media outlets based on their editorial line or political orientation. The Commission recalls that decisions concerning the granting, renewal or withdrawal of broadcasting licences fall primarily within the competence of national authorities. The majority of provisions of the European Media Freedom Act (EMFA)1 became applicable in August 2025. Under Article 21 of EMFA in conjunction with Article 30 of the Audiovisual Media Services Directive2, decisions taken by national authorities affecting media service providers must comply with the principles of transparency, objectivity, proportionality and non-discrimination, be taken by independent regulatory authorities, and remain subject to effective judicial review. The Commission is monitoring relevant developments in all Member States and will not hesitate to act where there are indications of a breach of EU law. The infringement procedure3 referred to concerning Hungary was based on different legal bases, namely the Authorisation Directive4, the Framework Directive5, the European Electronic Communications Code6 which all deal with electronic communications and services, as well as the Charter of Fundamental Rights.
1 Regulation (EU) 2024/1083 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 11 April 2024 establishing a

common framework for media services in the internal market and amending Directive 2010/13/EU (European Media Freedom Act). 2 Directive 2010/13/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 10 March 2010 on the coordination of certain provisions laid down by law, regulation or administrative action in Member States concerning the provision of audiovisual media services (Audiovisual Media Services Directive). 3 https://curia.europa.eu/site/upload/docs/application/pdf/2026-02/cp260019en.pdf. 4 Directive 2002/20/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 7 March 2002 on the authorisation of electronic communications networks and services, as amended by Directive 2009/140. 5 Directive 2002/21/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 7 March 2002 on a common regulatory framework for electronic communications networks and services, as amended by Directive 2009/140/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 25 November 2009 amending Directives 2002/21/EC, 2002/19/EC and 2002/20/EC. 6 Directive 2018/1972/EU establishing the European Electronic Communications Code, which recast Directives 2002/21/EC and 2002/20/EC.

E-10-2026-001248.t: Coal as a potential solution to the energy crisis
qt: to the Commission Ioan-Rareş Bogdan (PPE) Subject:

Over one thousand miners have protested in Bucharest against the closure of production facilities on 1 April 2026. Many are of an age at which retraining is not an option, especially given the criteria for hiring on the labour market. Romania committed in its RRP to close the coal mines by 2030, but at the time the RRP was being negotiated and agreed, Europe was not in the situation it is now as regards energy. 1.
What mechanisms do the Member States, and hence Romania, have at their disposal to mitigate the impact of mine closures?
Is the Commission considering a rethink of European mining policies?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.6.2026) The EU allocated a variety of funding to support Member States’ commitments towards the energy transition. The Just Transition Mechanism (JTM) mobilises around EUR 55 billion to support the most affected regions. Romania is the third largest recipient of the Just Transition Fund under the JTM, with an allocation of EUR 2.14 billion. The Fund promotes the economic diversification of coal regions, supporting workers who previously worked in the coal sector, among other measures, through upskilling and reskilling. Romania can also access 191 705 876 Emission Trade System (ETS) allowances from the Modernisation Fund, alongside EUR 13.6 billion in grants under the Recovery and Resilience Facility, EUR 24.8 billion from the European Regional Development Fund and EUR 8.5 billion to fund, among others, its energy transition and invest in clean industries. All these funds may be used to support just transition measures, such as worker retraining, education, energy transition and business development. The Commission also supports regions phasing out of coal, peat and oil shale through the Coal Regions in Transition Initiative1, and the Technical Assistance for regions undergoing a green energy transition (TARGET2) managed by the European Investment Bank. The current imported fossil energy crisis highlights the need to stay the course and even accelerate the clean energy transition in Europe to ensure energy security and stable energy prices and an independent competitive and sustainable EU.

qt: to the Commission Auke Zijlstra (PfE) Subject:

On 24 March, an article appeared on the government information channel Moldpres1 regarding the recent disbursement of part of the Moldova Growth Facility, which is valued at EUR 1.9 billion. The sum in question amounts to EUR 289 million, which has been spent on ‘support for paying energy bills, infrastructure investments, economic development, jobs, and higher incomes for citizens’. In addition, substantial support for farmers and entrepreneurs is mentioned. The funds are being used ‘to provide compensation for electricity and heating for citizens and social institutions, repair roads in 100 localities, modernise regional and district roads… and implement more than 200 local and regional projects across the country’. 1.
Is the financial support being distributed evenly across the country, and can the Commission provide an overview of this expenditure?

Is Transnistria also included in this round of funding, and for example, have the bridges connecting the region to Moldova – which were still found to be unsafe during the recent elections – been repaired?
Does the Commission consider that direct income support for farmers, entrepreneurs and citizens form part of the ‘growth’ required for accession?
https://www.moldpres.md/eng/economy/eu-growth-plan-for-moldova-1-9-billion-to-modernize-localcommunities-and-raise-citizens-living-standards.
at: (English version) to the Commission Auke Zijlstra (PfE) (25 March 2026) Subject: Moldova Growth Facility On 24 March, an article appeared on the government information channel Moldpres (1) regarding the recent disbursement of part of the Moldova Growth Facility, which is valued at EUR 1.9 billion. The sum in question amounts to EUR 289 million, which has been spent on ‘support for paying energy bills, infrastructure investments, economic development, jobs, and higher incomes for citizens’. In addition, substantial support for farmers and entrepreneurs is mentioned. The funds are being used ‘to provide compensation for electricity and heating for citizens and social institutions, repair roads in 100 localities, modernise regional and district roads… and implement more than 200 local and regional projects across the country’. 1. Is the financial support being distributed evenly across the country, and can the Commission provide an overview of this expenditure? 2. Is Transnistria also included in this round of funding, and for example, have the bridges connecting the region to Moldova — which were still found to be unsafe during the recent elections — been repaired? 3. Does the Commission consider that direct income support for farmers, entrepreneurs and citizens form part of the ‘growth’ required for accession? (24 July 2026) The Moldova Facility is a performance-based financial instrument. This means that the Facility rewards the Republic of Moldova for the achievement of reform commitments, as spelled out in the Moldova Reform Agenda. The payments from the EU to the Treasury of Moldova are made in line with the country’s compliance with these commitments. Related expenditure planning and execution are the responsibility of the Moldovan government. The Commission would thus like to refer the Honourable Member to the Moldovan authorities for further information on expenditure and the specific investment projects referred to in his question. The Neighbourhood Investment Platform does not finance any investment projects in the Transnistrian region. The reform steps included in Moldova’s Reform Agenda are closely aligned with Moldova’s accession process. Fulfilling the agreed reforms will not only support economic growth and economic convergence with the EU and deepen Moldova’s single market integration, but also help advance Moldova’s EU membership. Furthermore, the EU’s offer of EUR 60 million for energy support to the population on the left bank remains on the table subject to conditions and concrete steps by the de facto authorities.

E-10-2026-001246.t: Systemic flaw in the Funding & Tenders Portal and wrongly penalised organisations (Creative Europe programme)
qt: to the Commission Isilda Gomes (S&D) Subject:

Portuguese organisation Gerador has had three applications to the Creative Europe programme rejected for supposedly breaching a rule imposing a three-application limit per organisation. Gerador consented and took part in only three proposals, however. It was excluded because its participant identification code (PIC) was wrongly used in a fourth application submitted by third parties that did not have Gerador’s permission or signature. The Executive Agency (EACEA) has confirmed that the system allows other parties’ PICs to be included even if they do not confirm their involvement at the submission stage. This security flaw means reputable organisations can be ‘blocked’ or penalised for abusive actions by others. 1.
Is the Commission aware of this structural flaw in the portal, which allows organisations to be added to applications without their express consent and without a verification mechanism at the EACEA?
What urgent measures does the Commission intend to take to fix the system and make sure an organisation’s PIC can only be used in an application if the organisation confirms electronically?

Will the Commission instruct EACEA to immediately reassess the admissibility of their legitimate projects by organisations like Gerador, which have not given their permission to be included in more than the maximum number of projects?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.8.2026) The Funding and Tenders Portal1 is the main entry point for funding programmes and procurement procedures managed by the Commission and other EU institutions and agencies, enhancing transparency and accessibility. Under the CREA-CULT-2025-COOP call, the European Education and Culture Executive Agency (EACEA) has received complaints concerning alleged ‘inclusions without consent’. Any intentional inclusion without consent constitutes misrepresentation under the EU Financial Regulation and may lead to rejection and/or administrative sanctions. Responsibility for the accuracy of the information submitted, including consent to participate, lies with the coordinators. These complaints are under investigation by EACEA. The Commission acknowledges the importance of strengthening safeguards while not increasing administrative burden. For the CREA-CULT-2026-COOP call, the maximum of three applications per organisation will apply only to coordinators or partners, which can check their inclusion in applications, and will not include associated partners or affiliated entities. Coordinators must obtain from each participating organisation a written declaration confirming its consent to participate. These measures will contribute to preventing similar situations. Several organisations have submitted requests for redress, which are being examined in accordance with applicable procedures. EACEA is investigating the complaints and will reply in due course. Where justified, proposals may be re-evaluated. Any follow-up will be determined on a case-by-case basis, ensuring equal treatment and full respect of the applicable legal framework.
1 Funding and Tenders Portal https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-
tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/home?gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=23753956265&gclid=EAIaIQobCh MIm-3_6s-NlAMVD6n9BR3Q2RIuEAAYASAAEgKeb_D_BwE.

E-10-2026-001245.t: Disappearance of German journalist Eva Maria Michelmann and Kurdish journalist Ahmed Polad in Raqqa, Syria, and the EU’s efforts
qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Per Clausen (The Left), Hanna Gedin (The Left), Jonas Sjöstedt (The Left) Subject:

Two journalists have been missing since the city of Raqqa was captured by the forces of the Syrian transitional government on 18 January 20261, and it is feared that they have been forcibly ‘disappeared’. The two disappeared journalists are German journalist Eva Maria Michelmann (who was working for ETHA) and Kurdish journalist Ahmet Polad (who was working with outlets such as Kurdistana Azad and Özgür TV). Eyewitnesses reported that they were put in a vehicle belonging to Syrian transitional government forces2. The case of the two journalists also highlights the fact that thousands of civilians remain unaccounted for, or have been arbitrarily detained, following the Syrian transitional government’s January 2026 military operations in north-east Syria. In connection with this, can the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy kindly answer the following: 1.
How – if at all – have EU representatives raised this urgent matter with the Syrian transitional government?
What new action does the European External Action Service intend to take to acquire information about the two journalists and ensure their release, and when will such action be taken?
What steps is the European External Action Service taking to ensure the safety of journalists providing independent reporting from Syria, including European journalists?
https://cpj.org/2026/03/german-turkish-journalists-missing-in-syria/. https://cpj.org/data/people/eva-maria-michelmann/.

The two disappeared journalists are German journalist Eva Maria Michelmann (who was working for ETHA) and Kurdish journalist Ahmet Polad (who was working with outlets such as Kurdistana Azad and Özgür TV). Eyewitnesses reported that they were put in a vehicle belonging to Syrian transitional government forces (2). In connection with this, can the Vice-President of the Commission/High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy kindly answer the following: 1.
How — if at all — have EU representatives raised this urgent matter with the Syrian transitional government?
What new action does the European External Action Service intend to take to acquire information about the two journalists and ensure their release, and when will such action be taken?
What steps is the European External Action Service taking to ensure the safety of journalists providing independent reporting from Syria, including European journalists?

(3 June 2026) The EU is closely following developments in north-east Syria, including reports of the disappearance of two journalists in Raqqa. Consular assistance to EU citizens remains an exclusive national competence. The EU consistently recalls that all parties must respect international humanitarian law and international human rights law, including the protection of journalists and the prohibition of arbitrary detention and enforced disappearance. The reported disappearance of these two journalists underscores the broader issue of missing persons across Syria, and the need for efficient investigations. The EU calls on the Syrian transitional authorities to conduct prompt, transparent and impartial investigations into all such cases, in cooperation with the National Commission for Missing Persons as well as relevant international mechanisms, such as the International Commission on Missing Persons and the Independent Institution on Missing Persons in the Syrian Arab Republic. The EU will continue to advocate for a safe and enabling environment for independent reporting and media in Syria, in line with international standards, and to support efforts that uphold freedom of expression.

E-10-2026-001244.t: Insufficient EU sanctions against Rwanda and the murder of humanitarian worker Karine Buisset in the Democratic Republic of the Congo
qt: to the Council Rima Hassan (The Left) Subject:

The UN Group of Experts has concluded that the deployment of the Rwanda Defence Force (RDF) violates Congolese sovereignty and that Rwanda is responsible for the actions of M23. In February 2025, the European Parliament adopted by majority a resolution calling for the strengthening of sanctions, the freezing of budget support and the suspension of the memorandum of understanding on raw materials. The Council’s decision of 17 March 2025 to include nine individuals on the list of persons and entities subject to restrictive measures falls far short of meeting these demands. On 2 March 2026, the United States sanctioned the RDF as a whole, as well as four senior officials. Meanwhile, the conflict is spreading: on 11 March 2026, Karine Buisset, a French UNICEF employee, was killed by a drone strike in Goma. A war crimes investigation has been opened in France. 1.
Does the Council intend to extend its sanctions to the whole of the RDF, as the US has done?
What steps will the Council take to accelerate the peace process?
When will the Council implement the measures called for by Parliament, such as the suspension of the memorandum of understanding and the freezing of budget support for Rwanda?
at: (English version) to the Council Rima Hassan (The Left) (25 March 2026) Subject: Insufficient EU sanctions against Rwanda and the murder of humanitarian worker Karine Buisset in the Democratic Republic of the Congo The UN Group of Experts has concluded that the deployment of the Rwanda Defence Force (RDF) violates Congolese sovereignty and that Rwanda is responsible for the actions of M23. In February 2025, the European Parliament adopted by majority a resolution calling for the strengthening of sanctions, the freezing of budget support and the suspension of the memorandum of understanding on raw materials. The Council’s decision of 17 March 2025 to include nine individuals on the list of persons and entities subject to restrictive measures falls far short of meeting these demands. On 2 March 2026, the United States sanctioned the RDF as a whole, as well as four senior officials. Meanwhile, the conflict is spreading: on 11 March 2026, Karine Buisset, a French Unicef employee, was killed by a drone strike in Goma. A war crimes investigation has been opened in France. 1.
Does the Council intend to extend its sanctions to the whole of the RDF, as the US has done?
What steps will the Council take to accelerate the peace process?

3. When will the Council implement the measures called for by Parliament, such as the suspension of the memorandum of understanding and the freezing of budget support for Rwanda? Reply (8 July 2026) The Council is deeply concerned about the escalation of the conflict in the eastern part of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and continues to closely monitor the developments in the Great Lakes region (1). The situation has been regularly discussed at the Foreign Affairs Council (2) as well as in the relevant Council preparatory bodies. On 29 January 2026, the Foreign Affairs Council called for increased EU action across three key priorities: 1) political engagement, 2) humanitarian assistance and advocacy, and 3) peace support. The EU further intensified high-level political outreach to all parties involved in the conflict. The EU has also repeatedly called upon Rwanda to respect the territorial integrity of the DRC and honour its commitments — most critically by withdrawing its troops from the DRC and ending its support to the M23. The EU is the largest humanitarian donor to the region, having allocated EUR 129.5 million in 2025, and announced an initial EUR 81.5 million in EU humanitarian aid for 2026. The Council continues to support ongoing peace processes at local, regional and international levels. In addition, the Council welcomes the increasing operationalisation of the African Union-mandated mediation and stands ready to contribute to its success. In line with the EU’s renewed Strategy for the Great Lakes region (3), the Council is also working to incentivise peace and transform the root causes of conflict by promoting regional integration and economic cooperation.

As expressed for instance in an EU 27 Statement in January 2025: https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/press/press-releases/2025/01/25/democratic-republicof-the-congo-statement-by-the-high-representative-on-behalf-of-the-eu-on-the-latest-escalation-in-eastern-drc/

A renewed EU Great Lakes Strategy: Supporting the transformation of the root causes of instability into shared opportunities, adopted b Council Conclusions on 20 February 2023: https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-6631-2023-INIT/en/pdf

In response to the escalation in eastern DRC, the Council adopted additional restrictive measures in March 2025, notably against three commanders of the Rwandan Defence Force (RDF). One of these individuals, Major General Ruki Karusisi, was also sanctioned by the United States on 2 March. To date, the EU adopted and maintains restrictive measures on 31 individuals and two entities for their roles in relation to the situation in the Democratic Republic of Congo, in particular those sustaining the conflict, as well as the state of instability and insecurity in the DRC. The restrictive measures were extended on 8 December 2025 for one year (4). On 24 February 2025, the High Representative announced that the memorandum of understanding on critical raw materials with Rwanda (MoU) would be under review (5). The EU continues to actively monitor and respond to developments in the DRC and the broader Great Lakes region.

E-10-2026-001243.t: Defence of the UN rapporteurships, the mandate of Rapporteur Francesca Albanese and European citizens subject to sanctions by the Trump administration
qt: to the Commission Estrella Galán (The Left), Matjaž Nemec (S&D), Vicent Marzà Ibáñez (Verts/ALE), Saskia Bricmont (Verts/ALE), Diana Riba i Giner (Verts/ALE), Catarina Martins (The Left), Merja Kyllönen (The Left), Manon Aubry (The Left), Leila Chaibi (The Left), Cristina Guarda (Verts/ALE), Catarina Vieira (Verts/ALE), Tineke Strik (Verts/ALE), Rima Hassan (The Left), Hana Jalloul Muro (S&D), Alex Agius Saliba (S&D), Pernando Barrena Arza (The Left), Martin Günther (The Left), Danilo Della Valle (The Left), César Luena (S&D), Leire Pajín (S&D), Mounir Satouri (Verts/ALE) Subject:

Recent statements by members of the French, Czech and German governments against Francesca Albanese, UN Special Rapporteur on the situation of human rights in the Palestinian territory occupied since 1967, highlight the campaign to discredit her after she denounced the genocide in Gaza and the systematic violation of human rights in the occupied territories. These statements are in addition to the sanctions that the United States has imposed against Ms Albanese, members of the International Criminal Court (ICC) and other European citizens. These sanctions are a totally illegal and illegitimate civil conviction that affects European sovereignty. 1.
What measures is the Commission taking to safeguard the independence and legitimacy of the UN rapporteurships, and how is the Commission putting this defence into practice in the case of Ms Albanese?
How is the Commission responding to the Trump administration’s sanctions imposed against Ms Albanese, ICC members and European citizens for their professional or social activities?
What measures does the Commission plan to take to prevent interference in areas of EU competence affecting EU citizens at professional, economic and political level?
Supporter1
This question is supported by a Member other than the authors: Cecilia Strada (S&D).
at: (English version) to the Commission Estrella Galán (The Left), Matjaž Nemec (S&D), Vicent Marzà Ibáñez (Verts/ALE), Saskia Bricmont (Verts/ALE), Diana Riba i Giner (Verts/ALE), Catarina Martins (The Left), Merja Kyllönen (The Left), Manon Aubry (The Left), Leila Chaibi (The Left), Cristina Guarda (Verts/ALE), Catarina Vieira (Verts/ALE), Tineke Strik (Verts/ALE), Rima Hassan (The Left), Hana Jalloul Muro (S&D), Alex Agius Saliba (S&D), Pernando Barrena Arza (The Left), Martin Günther (The Left), Danilo Della Valle (The Left), César Luena (S&D), Leire Pajín (S&D), Mounir Satouri (Verts/ALE) (25 March 2026) Subject: Defence of the UN rapporteurships, the mandate of Rapporteur Francesca Albanese and European citizens subject to sanctions by the Trump administration Recent statements by members of the French, Czech and German governments against Francesca Albanese, UN Special Rapporteur on the situation of human rights in the Palestinian territory occupied since 1967, highlight the campaign to discredit her after she denounced the genocide in Gaza and the systematic violation of human rights in the occupied territories. These statements are in addition to the sanctions that the United States has imposed against Ms Albanese, members of the International Criminal Court (ICC) and other European citizens. What measures does the Commission plan to take to prevent interference in areas of EU competence affecting EU citizens at professional, economic and political level? Supporter (1) (5 June 2026) The EU is a firm supporter of the UN human rights system and of the independence of the UN Human Rights Council (UNHRC). The EU has a principled position of supporting the independence of special procedures mandate holders, who must be able to carry out their work effectively in an independent and impartial manner. These mandate holders work on a voluntary basis, serve in their personal capacity and are independent from any government or organisation. Special Rapporteurs and other special procedures mandate holders play an essential role in fighting impunity and ensuring accountability for serious human rights violations. Mandate holders often operate under challenging circumstances and warrant recognition and respect when discharging their functions. The EU has repeatedly called for an end to attacks and threats against mandate holders appointed by the UNHRC. This applies also to the current UN Special Rapporteur (UNSR) on the situation of human rights in the Palestinian Territory occupied since 1967. The EU cooperates with UNHRC mechanisms and fully respects their mandates, including the mandate of the UNSR on the situation of human rights in the Palestinian Territory occupied since 1967. The EU engaged with the Special Rapporteur on several occasions on matters relevant to the rapporteurs’ mandate. The EU acknowledges the difficult situation that International Criminal Court (ICC) officials and those working for or with the Court, including UN special rapporteurs and/or civil society representatives, are currently facing.
This question is supported by a Member other than the authors: Cecilia Strada (S&D).

The EU is in close dialogue with its Member States and the ICC and has engaged at key junctures with UN mechanisms and civil society, while continuing to monitor the implications of the US executive order.

E-10-2026-001242.t: EES roll-out: impact on truck drivers from the Western Balkans and implications for EU transport and Schengen rules
qt: to the Commission Tomáš Zdechovský (PPE) Subject:

The gradual roll-out of the Entry/Exit System (EES) is strengthening enforcement of the 90/180-day rule for non-EU nationals in the Schengen area. However, it is creating serious tensions, particularly for professional truck drivers from the Western Balkans, who often spend extended periods in the EU as part of cross-border logistics operations. The situation has already led to political pressure and coordinated border blockades in January 2026. At the same time, discussions are ongoing on possible solutions, such as long-stay visas or specific residence permits for professional drivers, while some Member States oppose any derogations from EES registration on security grounds. In this context: 1.
How does the Commission assess the impact of the EES roll-out on the functioning of EU freight transport and supply chains, particularly regarding drivers from the Western Balkans?
Does the Commission envisage an EU-level solution, such as long-stay visas or a specific facilitation regime, for drivers exceeding the 90/180-day limit for work purposes?
How will the Commission ensure that national measures remain compatible with EU law, preserve Schengen area integrity and avoid fragmentation across Member States?
at: (English version) to the Commission Tomáš Zdechovský (PPE) (25 March 2026) Subject: EES roll-out: impact on truck drivers from the Western Balkans and implications for EU transport and Schengen rules The gradual roll-out of the Entry/Exit System (EES) is strengthening enforcement of the 90/180-day rule for non-EU nationals in the Schengen area. However, it is creating serious tensions, particularly for professional truck drivers from the Western Balkans, who often spend extended periods in the EU as part of cross-border logistics operations. The situation has already led to political pressure and coordinated border blockades in January 2026. At the same time, discussions are ongoing on possible solutions, such as long-stay visas or specific residence permits for professional drivers, while some Member States oppose any derogations from EES registration on security grounds. In this context: 1.
How does the Commission assess the impact of the EES roll-out on the functioning of EU freight transport and supply chains, particularly regarding drivers from the Western Balkans?
Does the Commission envisage an EU-level solution, such as long-stay visas or a specific facilitation regime, for drivers exceeding the 90/180-day limit for work purposes?
How will the Commission ensure that national measures remain compatible with EU law, preserve Schengen area integrity and avoid fragmentation across Member States?

(20 May 2026) The entry into operation of the Entry/Exit System (EES) has marked a significant milestone for the Schengen area with a positive impact on the security of the EU, including by systematically detecting overstayers. The roll-out of the EES has not changed the rules for the length of stay in the Schengen area, as set out in the Schengen Borders Code, but it has strengthened the enforcement of with these rules. Therefore, economic operators within and outside the EU need to adapt their relevant business processes to be able to comply with the rules on the length of stay withing the Schengen area. The Commission notes the concerns raised by freight transport operators from the countries neighbouring the EU and has actively engaged with relevant stakeholders to clarify the current legal framework and the functioning of the EES. The Commission has announced in the Visa Strategy (1) that it will explore options to extend the limits of stay for professionals who are third-country nationals and are requiring a high degree of mobility within the Schengen area. In that context, the Commission has launched dedicated discussions with Member States on this matter. Member States may, under their national legislation, issue long stay visas, or residence permits to third-country nationals, including professional drivers. It is the nature of such national measures that they may imply a certain fragmentation in approach. The Commission remains engaged with the relevant partner countries and Member States in order to exchange information and best practices.

E-10-2026-001241.t: ECF Regulation: high costs, low chances of success
qt: to the Commission Gerald Hauser (PfE) Subject:

A new regulation on establishing the European Competitiveness Fund (ECF) is currently being prepared. According to the proposal for a regulation, in the period between 2028 and 2034, EUR 26.21 billion is to be set aside for ‘the clean transition and industrial decarbonisation’, EUR 20.393 billion for ‘health, biotech, agriculture and bioeconomy’, EUR 51.493 billion for ‘digital leadership’ and EUR 125.204 billion for ‘resilience and security, the defence industry and space’. The EU is taking on an increasing number of responsibilities in this area, but in practice it is failing miserably. The EU is no longer competitive at all. The EU’s health systems are collapsing, the EU is being deindustrialised, the economy and agriculture are being destroyed, the EU has long lagged behind China and the US digitally, and EU defence spending is being wasted pointlessly in a corrupt Ukraine. 1.
How is the Commission going to save the EU’s health systems?
How is the Commission going to provide ‘secure, affordable, efficient and clean energy for all Europeans’, as promised in the regulation?
Does the Commission guarantee that the planned ‘digital wallet’ will not be used to monitor every aspect of people’s lives (personal, health and financial data)?
at: (English version) to the Commission Gerald Hauser (PfE) (25 March 2026) Subject: ECF Regulation: high costs, low chances of success A new regulation on establishing the European Competitiveness Fund (ECF) is currently being prepared. According to the proposal for a regulation, in the period between 2028 and 2034, EUR 26.21 billion is to be set aside for ‘the clean transition and industrial decarbonisation’, EUR 20.393 billion for ‘health, biotech, agriculture and bioeconomy’, EUR 51.493 billion for ‘digital leadership’ and EUR 125.204 billion for ‘resilience and security, the defence industry and space’. The EU is taking on an increasing number of responsibilities in this area, but in practice it is failing miserably. The EU is no longer competitive at all. The EU’s health systems are collapsing, the EU is being deindustrialised, the economy and agriculture are being destroyed, the EU has long lagged behind China and the US digitally, and EU defence spending is being wasted pointlessly in a corrupt Ukraine. 1.
How is the Commission going to save the EU’s health systems?

2. How is the Commission going to provide ‘secure, affordable, efficient and clean energy for all Europeans’, as promised in the regulation? 3. Does the Commission guarantee that the planned ‘digital wallet’ will not be used to monitor every aspect of people’s lives (personal, health and financial data)? (8 June 2026) In July 2025, the Commission published its proposal for the European Competitiveness Fund (ECF) (1), which, once adopted, will mobilise an unprecedented budget for European competitiveness. The Commission supports Member States to strengthen their health systems via funding, technical assistance, knowledge sharing and policy advice. Under the ECF proposal, the Fund aims to strengthen the efficiency, innovation and resilience of health systems. Member States can also use the national and regional partnership plans (2) to facilitate access to healthcare services and associated infrastructure. The ECF is proposed to support energy projects and infrastructure that will bring down energy costs overtime, mobilising the uptake of clean energy and related technologies. The ECF aims to support the creation of a digitalised, reliable and resilient European energy system and the single energy market. Moreover, the AccelerateEU Communication (3) presented on 22 April 2026 includes immediate targeted and temporary actions to be implemented by Member States to protect households and industry from high energy prices. Data protection and privacy are cornerstones of the European Digital Identity Wallets (EUDIWs). The General Data Protection Regulation (4) fully applies to data processing under the European Digital Identity Regulation (5). The legal framework is built on the premise that EUDIWs users shall have full control of their wallet data and EUDIWs providers shall not collect information not necessary for the provision of wallet services. The use of EUDIWs will be voluntary and will offer a pseudonym function.

E-10-2026-001240.t: Commission’s participation in US Board of Peace meeting on Gaza
qt: to the Commission André Franqueira Rodrigues (S&D), Ana Catarina Mendes (S&D), Bruno Gonçalves (S&D), Sérgio Gonçalves (S&D), Isilda Gomes (S&D), Chloé Ridel (S&D), Hana Jalloul Muro (S&D), Marko Vešligaj (S&D) Subject:

On 18 February 2026, the European Commission published an official notice stating that the Commissioner for the Mediterranean, Dubravka Šuica, would travel to Washington DC to participate, on behalf of the Commission, in the meeting on Gaza held by the so-called Board of Peace, in the context of discussions on a ceasefire and post-war recovery and reconstruction. In the light of the above: 1.

Can the Commission clarify on what legal basis and with what mandate Commissioner Šuica is participating in this meeting, on whose behalf she is doing so, and what the exact purpose and status of her participation are?

The Commissioner’s participation as an observer was to help ensure coordination and complementarity between the EU and broader international efforts. It is of paramount importance to be at the table and engage with all relevant regional and international actors. E-10-2026-001239.t: EU manufacturing of net-zero technologies and trade defence
qt: to the Commission Bruno Tobback (S&D) Subject:

While the Net-Zero Industry Act1 (NZIA) identifies strategic net-zero technologies as critical to EU decarbonisation and energy security, European manufacturers face growing import pressure from heavily subsidised non-EU suppliers. This threat to European competitiveness is being compounded by delays in the Commission’s handling of trade defence submissions, due to resource constraints and a queue system that fails to prioritise strategic industries – undermining the EU’s ‘Made in EU’ ambitions for clean technology under the proposed industrial accelerator act. 1.

What steps are being taken to ensure that the Commission’s Directorate-General for Trade has sufficient staffing and operational capacity, particularly in the area of trade defence, to process time-sensitive files affecting strategic net-zero technologies (e.g. in the wind and solar power supply chain) in a timely manner?

How can the Commission remain consistent with the EU’s stated objectives on strategic autonomy, energy independence and the NZIA if it does not give strategic net-zero technology industries better access to trade defence instruments?

Given the long time frame for the deployment of net-zero technologies and the use of tenders for projects requiring certain components, will the Commission ensure that its trade defence methodology works suitably for all industries, considering the structural, temporal and operational specificities of certain sectors, particularly those that rely on tenders?

Regulation (EU) 2024/1735 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 June 2024 on establishing a framework of measures for strengthening Europe’s net-zero technology manufacturing ecosystem and amending Regulation (EU) 2018/1724 (OJ L, 2024/1735, 28.6.2024, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1735/oj).

(13 May 2026) There has been a significant increase in the demand for trade defence action to tackle unfair trade practices across many sectors. The Commission makes every effort within its resource constraints to meet this demand by adopting contingency measures and has managed to open almost three times the historical average number of new cases since January 2024. The Commission is aware of the challenges facing not only the net-zero technology industry sector but many strategic sectors in the EU and ensures that access to the trade defence instruments is open to all sectors that are facing unfair competition from imports. The Commission aims to initiate investigations as quickly as possible on the basis of complaints which meet the necessary legal standard. In this context, all potential complainants are advised on the process and all complaints received must be assessed in light of strict legal requirements, given that each step in an investigation, from initiation to the imposition of measures, can be subject to judicial review. As regards tenders, this presents technical complexities in investigations and is addressed on a case-by-case basis examining the specifics of each proceeding.

E-10-2026-001238.t: Rising memory component costs and spillover risks for consumer devices
qt: to the Commission Peter Agius (PPE) Subject:

Reports indicate sharp increases in memory (DRAM/HBM) prices and supply tightness, driven by AI-related demand, with expectations of strong demand into 2027. If these constraints persist, consumers may face higher prices not only for gaming computers but also for laptops, smartphones and other essential devices. This may also slow the deployment of EU AI infrastructure, weakening the EU’s digital competitiveness and strategic autonomy. 1.

How is the Commission monitoring DRAM/HBM supply and prices, and will it use the early warning indicators under Pillar 3 of the EU Chips Act to flag shortages and priceshock risks for downstream users in the EU?

In the light of potential impacts on the critical sectors listed in Annex IV to the Chips Act, is the Commission considering activating a ‘crisis stage’ under Article 23 of this Act and, if so, what criteria would trigger such activation?

Has the Commission assessed whether long-term supply arrangements or allocation practices could exacerbate scarcity or price pressure for non-AI buyers in the EU, and what concrete mitigation measures is it considering (including targeted competition monitoring and measures to strengthen EU capacity in the memory ecosystem), including in the context of any future revision of the Chips Act?
Supporters1
This question is supported by Members other than the author: Regina Doherty (PPE), Tomáš Zdechovský (PPE).

Supporters (1) (21 May 2026) In the context of Pillar 3 of the EU Chips Act (1), the Commission is monitoring the supply of memory chips, including prices and lead times, via regular expert reports. Early warning indicators may be used to flag shortages and price-shock risks to the Member States authorities represented in the European Semiconductor Board. Under Article 23 of the Chips Act, the activation of the ‘crisis stage’ is a prerogative of the Council. The Commission may, after consulting the European Semiconductor Board, propose to the Council the activation of a crisis. This would require evidence of serious disruptions of the supply chain affecting essential products used by critical sectors as defined in Annex IV, and evidence that the activation of the crisis stage would have a positive impact. At the moment this is not the case. The Commission has not specifically assessed whether long-term supply arrangements may have an influence on shortage of supply or pricing. The Commission welcomes proactive action from industry to manage risks of supply disruptions through commercial practices. Investment decisions under the Chips Act framework lie primarily with companies and Member States, and any public support must comply with EU competition and state aid rules. The Commission already supports, through open, competitive calls, research and innovation in embedded and specialty memories, which can serve important EU end-markets such as automotive, industrial and edge applications. The Commission recognises the strategic importance of strengthening EU capabilities in the memory ecosystem and is considering how to further reinforce this aspect in the context of the forthcoming revision of the Chips Act.

E-10-2026-001237.t: Deutsche Welle's Greek programme must not be cancelled
qt: to the Commission Georgios Aftias (PPE) Subject:

I am informed by press and online reports that Deutsche Welle’s Greek Service and corresponding broadcast (DW Griechisch, DW Greek) is to close after 62 years of continuous and uninterrupted operation, as part of the introduction of a package of measures to achieve savings. This is a journalistic programme with tradition and rich content, which has been cooperating for decades with Greece’s leading media outlets. It is also a unique bridge of communication between Greece and Germany, as it proved during the euro crisis. I consider its contribution to the coverage of European affairs to be particularly valuable. With responses from the European Parliament and the European Commission in Brussels and Strasbourg, Deutsche Welle's Greek Service contributes to a more nuanced discussion of European issues, firmly orientated towards the idea of European integration, while simultaneously promoting the value of pluralism at the national and European level. In view of the above: 1.
How does the Commission view the fact that a journalistic programme with a valuable contribution to the pluralism and diversity of the media in Europe is being cancelled?
How could the Commission help to reverse the decision to cancel Deutsche Welle’s Greek Service and protect Greek employees?
Within the framework of the regulation for the freedom of the media, will funds be allocated for multilingualism and diversity in national broadcasting networks?
to the Commission Danuše Nerudová (PPE) Subject:

The European citizens’ initiative ‘Fur Free Europe’ gathered over 1.5 million signatures in support of its call for an EU-wide ban on fur farming and on the placing of farmed fur products on the internal market. According to recent reports, the Commission is considering rejecting calls for such a ban and instead pursuing stricter animal welfare standards for fur farming. This approach appears to diverge from scientific evidence, notably the findings of the European Food Safety Authority, which concluded that current cage-based systems for fur farming cause significant welfare problems that cannot be mitigated without fundamental changes to the system. At the same time, the sector has already significantly declined within the EU, with only five countries having no plans to phase out fur farming. In the light of this: 1.

How does the Commission assess the compatibility of its approach with the objective of ensuring a level playing field in the internal market, in view of the increasing divergence of national legislation banning fur farming?

How does the Commission justify its preliminary conclusion that improved welfare standards would be sufficient, given the scientific evidence indicating that the welfare needs of animals farmed for fur cannot be met within existing farming systems?

E-10-2026-001235.t: Breach of EU environmental law due to mining waste being discharged into the Guadalquivir and the serious risk this poses to Natura 2000 protected areas
qt: to the Commission Estrella Galán (The Left) Subject:
Breach of EU environmental law due to mining waste being discharged into the Guadalquivir and the serious risk this poses to Natura 2000 protected areas

The Sanlúcar de Barrameda City Council, other riverside municipalities and collectives such as Salvemos el Guadalquivir (Protect the Guadalquivir) and Salvemos Doñana (Protect Doñana) have long been warning that mining waste discharged into the Guadalquivir is severely polluting the riverbed and estuary, threatening biodiversity and traditional economic activity such as fishing, shellfish harvesting and agriculture. The environmental deterioration of the Guadalquivir and the Doñana reserve is persistent, highlighting a structural problem of a lack of effective protection12. Mining waste discharges – the cumulative effects of which are simply being ignored by the Andalusian regional government – are in breach of the Water Framework Directive, affect the Natura 2000 network (including Doñana (ES6150009), sites of Community importance, special areas of conservation and biosphere reserves) and fail to comply with Directive 2006/21/EC and the objectives of the Nature Restoration Regulation. Given that various scientific reports warn that the volume of discharged waste could increase tenfold in the coming years – with several mining sites in operation simultaneously – and in view of the guiding principles of precaution and prevention: 1.
Is the Commission aware of mining waste currently being discharged, the effects of this and the potential for the situation to worsen due to planned projects?

Will the Commission formally request information from the Spanish authorities and demand an independent scientific investigation, as requested by platforms such as Salvemos el Guadalquivir and Salvemos Doñana?

Written question E-3692/2008 to the Commission, ‘Pollution in the river Guadalquivir’ (https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/E-6-2008-3692_EN.html). Written question E-001259/2024 to the Commission, ‘Attack on the environment in Andalusia: plan to discharge 80 billion litres of highly polluting waters into the River Guadalquivir’ (https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/E-9-2024-001259_EN.html).
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (10.7.2026) The Water Framework Directive (WFD)1 requires Member States to ensure that mining discharges do not cause deterioration of surface water status or prevent the achievement of good status. All point source discharges, such as mining waste, must receive prior authorisation with sufficiently stringent emission controls to prevent pollution and protect water-dependent Natura 2000 sites. The Extractive Waste Directive2 sets a high level of protection for the environment and human health. It includes specific provisions aimed at preventing the deterioration of water status in accordance with the WFD, while leaving competent authorities a margin of discretion when applying those rules. Under the Habitats Directive3 Member States must avoid deterioration of natural habitats and species habitats, and significant disturbance of species for which Natura 2000 sites have been designated. Any project, including mining waste discharges into rivers, likely to have a significant effect on Natura 2000 must undergo an appropriate assessment of its implications for the site. The competent authority may only approve the project after ascertaining that it will not adversely affect its integrity. In line with its enforcement strategy focusing on systemic non-compliance4, the Commission considers it is the primary responsibility of the Spanish authorities to adequately enforce the above provisions of EU law. The Commission is aware of the concerns raised by the Honourable Member and notes that, according to available information, the Spanish Environmental Prosecutor has opened an investigation5. In any event, the Commission intends to discuss bilaterally with Spain the implementation of the WFD during an upcoming structured dialogue.
1 Directive 2000/60/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 23 October 2000 establishing a

framework for Community action in the field of water policy, OJ L 327, 22.12.2000, pp. 1–73. 2 Directive 2006/21/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 15 March 2006 on the management of waste from extractive industries and amending Directive 2004/35/EC - Statement by the European Parliament, the Council and the Commission, OJ L 102, 11.4.2006, p. 15–34. 3 Council Directive 92/43/EEC of 21 May 1992 on the conservation of natural habitats and of wild fauna and flora, OJ L 206, 22.7.1992, pp. 7–50. 4 As set out in the Communication of 19 January 2017: EU law: Better results through better application C/2016/8600, OJ C 18, 19.1.2017, p. 10–20 and in the Communication of 13 October 2022: COM(2022) 518 final - Enforcing EU law for a Europe that delivers. 5 E.g. https://elpais.com/espana/2026-03-10/los-ayuntamientos-de-sanlucar-y-chipiona-denuncian-los-vertidosmineros-en-el-guadalquivir-ante-la-fiscalia.html.

E-10-2026-001233.t: Spanish Government’s failure to submit report on wolves and diversion of associated compensation funds
qt: to the Commission Carmen Crespo Díaz (PPE) Subject:

According to recent reports, the Commission has initiated proceedings against Spain for failing to submit its report on the conservation status of wolves and other protected species on time, as required by the Habitats Directive The Spanish Government justifies the delay on the grounds that the scientific basis is inadequate, despite having previously decided to increase the level of protection of wolves throughout Spain, a move that has had significant consequences on the livestock sector. In addition, it has also been reported that the government diverted around EUR 20 million intended for compensating damage caused by wolves to programmes subsidising electric vehicles, raising doubts as to whether funds were used properly and the sectors affected were tangibly supported. In light of the above: 1.
Can the Commission confirm that Spain has failed to comply with its obligations under Directive 92/43/EEC and what steps does it intend to take if this situation persists?
Did the Spanish Government have an adequate scientific basis to justify the overprotection of wolves at national level?
Is the Commission aware of any potential diversions of funds intended for compensating damage caused by wolves and, if so, does it consider this to be compatible with EU law?

In addition, it has also been reported that the government diverted around EUR 20 million intended for compensating damage caused by wolves to programmes subsidising electric vehicles, raising doubts as to whether funds were used properly and the sectors affected were tangibly supported. In light of the above: 1.
