Is the Commission aware of any potential diversions of funds intended for compensating damage caused by wolves and, if so, does it consider this to be compatible with EU law?

(7 July 2026) In view of Spain’s failure to comply with its reporting obligations under Article 17 of the Habitats Directive (1) for the period 2019-2024, the Commission initiated an infringement procedure on 30 January 2026 (2). In the previous reporting cycle, covering the period 2013-2018, Spain reported the conservation status of the wolf as ‘unfavourable’ in its three biogeographic regions. It is for national authorities to ensure that the conclusion on the conservation status of the wolf is based on the best available scientific data (3). The recent amendment of the Habitats Directive (4) has changed the protection status of the wolf from ‘strictly protected’ to ‘protected’, to align the EU legislation to the Bern Convention. This change gives additional flexibility to Member States in managing their local wolf populations, so that they can take measures that are well adapted to regional circumstances. However, Member States are still required to achieve and maintain wolf’s favourable conservation status at national and biogeographical level. Member States have discretion to maintain or introduce more stringent protective measures (5). The Commission continues to promote the use of preventive measures to facilitate coexistence with large carnivores, which can be supported by EU or national funds. EU State aid rules allow Member States to compensate up to 100% of these damages . The Commission continues to assist Member States authorities and stakeholders in the design and implementation of such measures. National authorities are, however, the ones to decide on how to allocate such funds.

E-10-2026-001232.t: Legal asymmetry of digital tachograph data and possible introduction of a ‘smart payslip’ in the road transport sector
qt: to the Commission Mario Furore (The Left) Subject:

The increasing use of certified digital systems in the implementation of Union law raises questions of legal consistency in the use and evidentiary value of data. The second-generation smart digital tachograph, as provided for in Regulation (EU) No 165/2014 and Regulation (EU) 2020/1054, records the activities of professional drivers – including driving, working and rest periods – continuously and in a certified manner, and is used by enforcement authorities as evidence to detect infringements and impose penalties. However, the same data do not automatically serve to protect workers’ rights as regards remuneration. In many cases, there is no systematic obligation to reconcile tachograph records with payslip details. Given the technologies currently available, the idea of a potential ‘smart payslip’ has been proposed, i.e. an interoperable digital system that links tachograph records to payslip details. In the light of the above, can the Commission answer the following questions: 1.
Does the Commission consider it appropriate to make greater use of tachograph data, notably for the purpose of verifying drivers’ wage entitlements?
Will it consider introducing interoperable digital tools, such as a possible ‘smart pay slip’?
What measures does it intend to take to improve the enforcement of Directive (EU) 2020/1057 and combat wage dumping in the road haulage sector?
at: (English version) to the Commission Mario Furore (The Left) (24 March 2026) Subject: Legal asymmetry of digital tachograph data and possible introduction of a ‘smart payslip’ in the road transport sector The increasing use of certified digital systems in the implementation of Union law raises questions of legal consistency in the use and evidentiary value of data. The second-generation smart digital tachograph, as provided for in Regulation (EU) No 165/2014 and Regulation (EU) 2020/1054, records the activities of professional drivers — including driving, working and rest periods — continuously and in a certified manner, and is used by enforcement authorities as evidence to detect infringements and impose penalties. In many cases, there is no systematic obligation to reconcile tachograph records with payslip details. Given the technologies currently available, the idea of a potential ‘smart payslip’ has been proposed, i.e. an interoperable digital system that links tachograph records to payslip details. (22 May 2026) The Commission considers that it is fully appropriate to make greater use of tachograph data, notably for the purpose of verifying drivers’ wage entitlements. As laid out in the relevant legislation (1), tachograph data can already be used as supporting evidence of drivers’ activities in situations where the driver has been posted. In order to contribute to the enforcement of Directive (EU) 2020/1057 (2), the Commission has set up the Road Transport Posting Declaration (RTPD) Module in the internal market Information System (IMI). This interoperable module allows enforcement authorities and operators to exchange information on posted drivers. In 2025, 1,581 checks were conducted via this IMI RTPD Module. The market may further develop tools to support, including by using tachograph data, the amounts to be paid to a posted driver in such cases, which also depends on the national legislations in the Member States. The European Labour Authority is currently working on a pilot project (3) for a ‘remuneration tool’ for the road transport sector. The Commission is continuously monitoring and improving the usage and features of the RTPD module. The Commission invests EUR 200,000 annually only on new developments in the tool, with the objective of increasing its usage and facilitate enforcement through the platform.

See in particular Article 7(1) of Regulation (EU) No 165/2014 of the European Parliament and of the Council, and indent (iii) of point (b) of Article 1(11) of Directive (EU) 2020/1057 of the European Parliament and of the Council (OJ L 60, 28.2.2014, p. 1). E-10-2026-001231.t: Flexibility of use and road safety of lane-keeping assistance
qt: to the Commission Merja Kyllönen (The Left) Subject:

The automatic activation of lane-keeping assistance in vehicles complies with EU legislation. In practice, however, these systems can cause significant safety risks, particularly in winter conditions and for professional drivers: the vehicle may suddenly turn the steering wheel on a slippery road, which frightens the driver and can result in sliding or accidents. Professional drivers end up constantly switching the system off and on again, which causes practical problems and increases risks at work. 1.

Can the Commission clarify whether enough research has been done on the safety of lane-keeping assistance in demanding driving conditions, and is it considering adapting the rules so that a driver would have the chance to take the lane-keeping assistance system permanently out of use or at least restrict its automatic activation depending on the conditions?
How does the Commission intend to ensure that automatic safety systems in vehicles support the practical experience of drivers and improve road safety in all conditions?

(22 May 2026) Regulation (EU) 2021/646 (1) does not permit the permanent deactivation of the emergency lane-keeping system (ELKS), regardless of the driving conditions or the driver's professional status. Therefore, even in winter conditions or for professional drivers, permanent deactivation is explicitly prohibited. While the regulation sets minimum safety requirements, it allows manufacturers to optimise system performance. The development of ELKS implementing regulation was informed by the impact assessment for Regulation (EU) 2019/2144 (2), which evaluated the potential safety benefits of ELKS, including its effectiveness in reducing lane-departure collisions, while also considering potential drawbacks such as annoyance caused by unnecessary system interventions. The findings of this assessment underscored the importance of designing ELKS in a way that maximises safety benefits while minimising intrusiveness. The drafting of Regulation (EU) 2021/646 involved extensive consultation with representatives from automotive manufacturers, road safety organisations and type approval authorities. These stakeholders provided critical input on the technical specifications of the regulation, ensuring that the requirements for ELKS were both effective and practical, guaranteeing that it leads to practical improvements in road safety. Furthermore, an evaluation of the General Safety Regulation (3) is foreseen for July 2027, to evaluate the effectiveness of safety measures (including ELKS).

E-10-2026-001230.t: EU self-sufficiency in the production of sustainable aviation and maritime fuels
qt: to the Commission Merja Kyllönen (The Left) Subject:

Member States are hopeful that the Commission will take action to make the EU more self‑sufficient when it comes to sustainable aviation fuels (SAF) and alternative fuels for shipping at a time when global competition for raw materials and production capacity is intensifying. The development and scaling‑up of synthetic fuels (e-SAF) are crucial for the EU’s climate goals and transport security. Europe has significant technological expertise and renewable energy potential to scale up e-SAF production, but the pace of investment is lagging behind that of key competitor countries. At the same time, the availability of bio‑based fuels (bio-SAF) may decline as China, for example, looks to divert available raw materials, such as waste oils, for its own production and also actively supports the development of synthetic fuels. There is a risk that the EU will become increasingly dependent on imported fuels, which will undermine its strategic autonomy and leave the transport sector vulnerable to disruption. Is the Commission intending to: 1.
bring in specific measures and incentives to speed up investment in e-SAF production in the EU;
ensure an adequate supply of raw materials for bio‑SAF production; and
assess how fuel self-sufficiency can be integrated into the EU’s security of supply and industrial policies?

Delegated Directive (EU) 2024/1405 (7) enlarges the list of eligible biofuel feedstocks including intermediate crops and crops grown on severely degraded land. In this context the Commission will consider whether adjusted rules on the certification of biofuel feedstocks should be modified. 3. E-10-2026-001229.t: Impact of the VECTO Regulation ((EU) 2022/1362) on the trailer industry, on emissions and on fines
qt: to the Commission Merja Kyllönen (The Left) Subject:

Shortcomings in the implementation of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/1362 are putting Finnish and other Nordic trailer manufacturers at a disadvantage compared with other operators and could increase real CO₂ emissions. The current calculation model treats structurally heavier trailers unfairly, especially side‑loading trailers, because they are classed in the same vehicle category as lighter box trailers. This results in disproportionate emission‑reduction requirements and penalises fleets that actually reduce empty runs and total emissions in practice. Equipment like this is used in the defence industry and in the transport of explosives. This raises the question as to whether any thought was given to the impact that these measures would have on critical transport operations. In practice, the emissions limits that will enter into force in 2028 cannot be achieved for this type of fleet. Consequently, the manufacture and marketing of this equipment could well come to an end. At the same time, manufacturers are being subjected to substantial fines in cases where it is not technically possible to satisfy the requirements. Will the Commission: 1.
review the VECTO classification so that side‑loading trailers are given their own sub‑category;
introduce correction factors that take account of logistical efficiency; and
reassess the use of fines in cases where it is not realistic for the requirements to be satisfied?
at: EN On behalf of the European Commission (3.6.2026) Regulation (EU) 2022/13621 sets rules to determine the performance of heavy-duty trailers with regard to their influence on the CO2 emissions, fuel consumption, energy consumption and zero-emission driving range of motor vehicles. The performance determination is done using a physics-based calculation model that considers the main trailer characteristics, such as mass, to reflect the real-world performance of the trailer. In that context, a trailer that is made heavier by features such as a side-loading doors will result in higher CO2 emissions of the towing vehicle during real-world operation compared to an identical trailer with a lower mass. The CO2 emission reduction targets for trailers and semi-trailers set in Regulation (EU) 2019/12422 will only start applying as of the reporting period of the year 2030, meaning that emission premiums do not apply until that date. The targeted amendment to the Regulation3 proposed by the Commission in December 2025 provides trailer manufacturers with an additional flexibility easing compliance with the 2030 targets by allowing them to collect more emission credits in the years before 2030. In parallel, the Commission is preparing a Delegated Act amending the Regulation to include additional reporting parameters that allow for identifying specific types of trailers, and is notably analysing the specific situation of trailers designed for the transport of explosives and ammunition. A review of the Regulation is foreseen in 2027. At this stage, the Commission cannot prejudge the outcome of the review on specific questions, including the excess CO2 emissions premium level, as it will depend on the underlying analysis.

E-10-2026-001225.t: Israel’s use of chemical weapons in Lebanon and Syria
qt: to the Commission Rima Hassan (The Left), Leila Chaibi (The Left), Damien Carême (The Left), Anthony Smith (The Left), Manon Aubry (The Left), Younous Omarjee (The Left), Arash Saeidi (The Left), Marina Mesure (The Left) Subject:

Between late January and early February 2026, Israeli aircraft sprayed chemical substances on farmland in southern Lebanon1 and Syria2, destroying dozens of hectares. According to the Lebanese authorities, the substances that were used contained extremely high concentrations of glyphosate. At the beginning of March, Human Rights Watch also documented3 the use of white phosphorous in residential areas of Lebanon. The UN has called for an international inquiry4 and Lebanon announced that it would be filing a complaint to the UN5. This ‘scorched-earth’ policy targeting resources indispensable to the survival of the local population appears to be a clear breach of international humanitarian law and an attack on state sovereignty, which runs counter to the principles of the UN Charter. 1.

These acts have been documented by independent organisations (Human Rights Watch6, Euro-Med Human Rights Monitor7 and Green Southerners8) and local authorities9. Does the Commission take the view that they constitute a clear breach of international humanitarian law?
Will this information be instrumental in the review of the human rights clause, with a view to suspending the EU‑Israel Association Agreement?
What specific action does the Commission plan to take in response to these violations to ensure that people and the environment are protected?

E-10-2026-001224.t: Europe’s direct diplomacy with Iran to protect the supply of critical raw materials
qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Vicent Marzà Ibáñez (Verts/ALE) Subject:

In the European Council conclusions of March 2026, the EU makes a commitment to ‘contribute to de-escalation’ and ‘to all diplomatic efforts’ in order to ‘bring about a lasting solution to end the hostilities’, so as to ‘ensure maritime security and respect for the freedom of navigation’ in the Strait of Hormuz. Given the EU’s reliance on the strait for more than 10 % of strategic imports such as aluminium, steel and certain hydrocarbons1: 1.
How is the EEAS engaging in direct diplomacy with Iran to restore the trade routes of EU-flagged and EU-bound vessels carrying critical raw materials for EU industry?

How is the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy coordinating with the Member States so that, as a result of that diplomacy, an illegal war the EU is not part of has as small an impact as possible on our economic interests and price stability?

Given the EU’s reliance on the strait for more than 10% of strategic imports such as aluminium, steel and certain hydrocarbons (1): 1.

(22 May 2026) Developments in Iran and the wider region threaten regional and global security. The EU has called for de-escalation, the protection of civilians and civilian infrastructure and full respect of international law by all parties, free and safe passage through the Strait of Hormuz, in line with international law, as reflected in United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (Unclos). The EU welcomes the ceasefire agreed by the United States and Iran. Now is the time to design a comprehensive strategy for lasting peace across the entire Middle East. The EU will contribute to all diplomatic efforts in this endeavour, taking into consideration its full range of interests and concerns, in coordination with partners. The EU remains committed to contributing to safeguarding freedom of navigation and the security of global maritime trade routes, including through Operation EUNAVFOR ASPIDES (1). The High Representative/Vice-President invited Member States to provide more assets to reinforce the Operation. The EU has reached the political agreement to widen the Iran sanctions framework to also be able to target those responsible for a possible prolonged closure of the Strait of Hormuz. In parallel, the EU is implementing policies to boost the domestic production of critical raw materials (such as the Critical Raw Materials Act (2) and the RESourceEU Action Plan (3)), foster access to secondary raw materials through circularity measures (including the upcoming Circular Economy Act), and to diversify its supply with trusted partners, notably via the 16 partnerships it has signed on critical raw materials. Those measures aim to increase the EU’s economic security and the resilience of its industry against external geoeconomic developments.

When will the Commission finally stop applying double standards and begin to consistently uphold the principle that a threat against any Member State is a threat against the entire European Union, regardless of who the aggressor is?
The EU is based on rules, not friendships. Citizens deserve consistency.

E-10-2026-001222.t: How is it possible for the EU to fund something that is illegal in many countries? Is the Commission openly encouraging the violation of the Treaties?
qt: to the Commission Erik Kaliňák (NI) Subject:

In response to the European Citizens’ Initiative ‘My Voice, My Choice: For Safe And Accessible Abortion’, the Commission has decided that Member States may use funds from the European Social Fund+ to cover the costs of abortions in any Member State1. This decision can also be interpreted as the Commission de facto promoting abortion as a supranational ‘right’ that should be accessible and fundable across the entire EU. However, this decision completely disregards the fact that abortion laws vary significantly from country to country and that sensitive bioethical issues, such as the protection of unborn life, fall exclusively within the competence of Member States under the Treaties. 1.
On what legal basis is the Commission intervening in an area that the EU Treaties expressly reserve as an exclusive competence of Member States, thereby undermining the principle of subsidiarity?

How can the European Social Fund+ be used to finance abortions when there is no common, generally agreed standard within the EU regarding what constitutes ‘improving health’ or ‘healthcare’ in this context, and the EU lacks the authority to establish such a standard?
How can common European funds be used for acts that are illegal or even criminal in many Member States (including abortions in the late stages of pregnancy)?
https://citizens-initiative.europa.eu/my-voice-my-choice-safe-and-accessible-abortion_en.
at: (English version) to the Commission Erik Kaliňák (NI) (24 March 2026) Subject: How is it possible for the EU to fund something that is illegal in many countries? Is the Commission openly encouraging the violation of the Treaties? In response to the European Citizens’ Initiative ‘My Voice, My Choice: For Safe And Accessible Abortion’, the Commission has decided that Member States may use funds from the European Social Fund+ to cover the costs of abortions in any Member State (1). This decision can also be interpreted as the Commission de facto promoting abortion as a supranational ‘right’ that should be accessible and fundable across the entire EU. However, this decision completely disregards the fact that abortion laws vary significantly from country to country and that sensitive bioethical issues, such as the protection of unborn life, fall exclusively within the competence of Member States under the Treaties. 1. On what legal basis is the Commission intervening in an area that the EU Treaties expressly reserve as an exclusive competence of Member States, thereby undermining the principle of subsidiarity? 2. How can the European Social Fund+ be used to finance abortions when there is no common, generally agreed standard within the EU regarding what constitutes ‘improving health’ or ‘healthcare’ in this context, and the EU lacks the authority to establish such a standard? 3. How can common European funds be used for acts that are illegal or even criminal in many Member States (including abortions in the late stages of pregnancy)? (15 June 2026) As the Commission has expressed in reply to several similar questions (1) by the Honourable Members of the Parliament, the Commission’s follow up to the Citizen’s initiative ‘My Voice, My Choice’ falls within the EU’s supportive competence. One of the specific objectives of the European Social Fund+ (ESF+), set out in Article 4(1)(k), is that of enhancing equal and timely access to quality, sustainable and affordable services, including the access to person-centred care including healthcare (2). Therefore, the ESF+ can support initiatives, that aim to ensure and enhance equal and timely access to healthcare services. The Court of Justice of the EU has held that the Treaty provisions on the freedom to provide services include the freedom for recipients of healthcare, including people in need of medical treatment (3). With regard to the legal medical termination of pregnancy, the Court has found that it constitutes a service within the meaning of Article 57 Treaty on the Functioning of the EU (4). The Commission’s reply to the Citizen’s initiative makes it clear that financial support may be provided on a voluntary basis: Member States may, if they wish, use the ESF+ to improve equal access to legally available and affordable healthcare services, including safe abortion services, in accordance with their national legislation. Any such use must respect the limits set out in Article 168(7) Treaty on Functioning of the EU.

E-10-2026-001220.t: Will the new EU contribution by large companies harm the real economy?
qt: to the Commission Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE) Subject:

The Commission is proposing to create a new EU resource based on an annual contribution paid by companies active in the EU market that have a turnover of at least EUR 100 million. The contribution could generate around EUR 6.8 billion per year. However, the European Court of Auditors has warned that the new levy could be at odds with the EU’s competitiveness objective. In view of this, can the Commission say: 1.
What is the exact legal basis for the new contribution?
How many companies located in France would be affected?
What assessments have been carried out to ensure that the measure will not have an adverse effect on investment, employment and, ultimately, consumers?
at: (English version) to the Commission Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE) (24 March 2026) Subject: Will the new EU contribution by large companies harm the real economy? The Commission is proposing to create a new EU resource based on an annual contribution paid by companies active in the EU market that have a turnover of at least EUR 100 million. In view of this, can the Commission say: 1.
What is the exact legal basis for the new contribution?
How many companies located in France would be affected?
What assessments have been carried out to ensure that the measure will not have an adverse effect on investment, employment and, ultimately, consumers?

(21 May 2026) In July 2025 the Commission put forward a new basket of own resources, including a proposal for a Corporate Resource for Europe (CORE) (1). The CORE annual lump-sum contribution would be established as an own resource for the EU based on Article 311(3) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU) (2). This provision empowers the Council to establish new categories of own resources. Article 311(3) TFEU is a self-standing legal basis enabling the direct establishment of new own resources in the Own Resources Decision (3). The Commission shared its revenue estimates per own resource and per Member State, inclusive of the underlying assumptions, with the Council and the European Parliament in the context of the ongoing interinstitutional decision-making process in relation to the EU’s future multiannual financial framework. CORE would be applicable to large companies and permanent establishments with a taxable presence in the EU with an annual net turnover above EUR 100 million. Therefore, CORE would not apply to small and medium-sized enterprises, which represent 99% of businesses in the EU. The CORE annual lump-sum contribution to be paid by large companies in scope would represent a very small fraction of their ‘net turnover’ — a maximum of 0.1%. The rather modest CORE contribution is a charge that recognises the benefits that companies operating and selling in the EU enjoy from the single market.

E-10-2026-001218.t: Information on the number of companies that have relocated from the European Union to third countries since 2020
qt: to the Commission Bogdan Rzońca (ECR) Subject:

In the context of growing global economic competitiveness, changing regulatory frameworks and recent geopolitical events, the relocation of economic activity outside the EU may have significant consequences for the single market’s economic growth and competitiveness. I therefore ask the Commission to answer the following questions relating to the scale at which companies have been relocating from the European Union to third countries since 2020. I ask the Commission: 1.
How many companies have (fully or partially) relocated outside the EU since 2020?
What are the main destinations for relocation and which sectors are most affected by this phenomenon?
What are the main reasons behind this trend and its impact on the competitiveness of the EU economy?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (10.6.2026) The European Restructuring Monitor (ERM)1 provides a repository of case studies and intelligence on restructuring trends. It has reported some 100 cases of offshoring to non-EU countries since 20202, primarily to India, China, the United States and Türkiye3. The observed trends are concentrated in the manufacturing industry, particularly electronics, textiles, transport equipment, machinery and chemicals, putting more than 30 000 jobs at risk4. The Commission closely monitors Europe’s competitiveness and analyses its underlying drivers, as presented in the 2026 Annual Single Market and Competitiveness Report5. The report underscores that barriers and administrative burden remain too high in the Single Market, including at national level. Moreover, high energy prices are weighing on industrial competitiveness and private investment momentum in the EU remains weak. Geopolitical tensions compound competitive pressures and expose vulnerabilities and strategic dependencies in Europe’s supply chains. To address these challenges, the Commission has adopted the Competitiveness Compass6 and subsequent initiatives such as the Clean Industrial Deal7, the Single Market Strategy8 and sectoral action plans9, alongside simplification packages10 to make business easier and faster in Europe. Together with the proposed Industrial Accelerator Act11, the 28th regime/’EU Inc.’12 and the forthcoming proposal for the Public Procurement Act, these measures will drive EU competitiveness and industrial renewal.

E-10-2026-001217.t: Emergency support for livestock farmers in Lesvos following the outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease and restrictive measures
qt: to the Commission Sakis Arnaoutoglou (S&D) Subject:

The recent confirmation of a case of foot-and-mouth disease on a livestock farm in Lesvos, for the first time in many years in Greece, has led to the imposition of strict restrictive measures on the island, with serious repercussions on the primary sector. Specifically, bans on the movement of animals and livestock products outside the island have entered into force and milk collection and the sale of meat have been suspended. This situation is affecting thousands of livestock farmers and is threatening the economic viability of one of Lesvos’ most important production sectors. The crisis is all the more serious given that it coincides with the run-up to Easter, when a large part of lamb and goat production is intended for sale to consumers. Given that animal diseases are a matter that concerns the whole of Europe and that the way in which they are dealt with has a direct effect on the rural economy and the security of the food supply chain, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
What emergency financial tools does it intend to deploy to support the livestock farmers in Lesvos who are affected by the foot-and-mouth disease restrictions?
Is it possible to deploy the common agricultural policy’s reserve for crises in the agricultural sector, to provide direct financial support to affected producers?

How does it intend to support Member States in preventing and responding to animal diseases so as to avoid such crises leading to the collapse of entire local economies, and will it consider specific support measures for EU island regions affected by such health crises in the primary sector?

E-10-2026-001216.t: Failure of the Mavromati customs office to function properly and impact on cross-border economic activity
qt: to the Commission Sakis Arnaoutoglou (S&D) Subject:
Failure of the Mavromati customs office to function properly and impact on crossborder economic activity

According to recent complaints from Igoumenitsa’s Traders and Craftspeople Association, the Mavromati customs office, the main gateway between Greece and Albania, has, for a long time now, faced major operational problems due to understaffing, limited opening hours and significant delays in checks. This situation has already had a negative impact on the local economy of Thesprotia, with a decrease in footfall, a loss of turnover for small businesses and difficulties in the cross-border mobility of citizens and goods, including members of the Greek minority in southern Albania. Given that the proper functioning of crossing points at the EU’s external borders is crucial for economic cohesion, regional development and trade facilitation, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

How does it rate the functioning of border posts between Member States and non-EU countries, such as the Mavromati customs office, with regard to the adequacy of staff and the effectiveness of checks?

Are there any available European funding tools (e.g. Integrated Border Management Fund, Instrument for Financial Support for Border Management and Visa Policy, or others) that can be used to reinforce staffing and modernise infrastructure and procedures?
Does it intend to examine, in cooperation with the Greek authorities, measures to improve cross-border mobility and economic activity in border regions such as Thesprotia?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.5.2026) The Commission agrees that the proper functioning of crossing points at the EU’s external borders is of crucial importance. While the organisation of customs controls and the overall performance of the border crossing points are a responsibility of EU Member States, the Commission is open to considering leveraging existing monitoring tools (such as diagnostic studies carried out by its operational customs expert teams) to collect further information. Cooperation at all levels within the EU is very important and the Commission is in regular contact with all EU Customs Administrations, including Greek Customs, to ensure a strong and performing Customs Union. The recently agreed reform of the EU Customs Union should also contribute to this goal. There are several EU programmes under the current Multiannual Financial Framework offering funding opportunities to Member States seeking to reinforce their capabilities at border crossing points. These include the Integrated Border Management Fund, which is made of two components, i.e. i) the Border Management and Visa Instrument1 (within its specific scope of border management and visa policy), and ii) the Customs Control Equipment Instrument2 providing financial support for purchasing and upgrading customs tools; as well as the Customs Programme3 supporting the development and operation of the central digital systems for customs, and the cooperation between customs authorities. Additional support is provided by the Internal Security Fund4, the Technical Support Instrument5, the Union Anti-Fraud Programme6 and the Connecting Europe Facility7. Potential beneficiaries are regularly informed of upcoming funding opportunities.

E-10-2026-001215.t: Ensuring safe and equitable access to vital treatment for dialysis patients
qt: to the Commission Sakis Arnaoutoglou (S&D) Subject:

In northern Greece, and specifically in Pieria, the closure of a chronic dialysis unit in Katerini has meant that 96 kidney patients are forced to travel outside the regional unit on a regular basis, covering hundreds of kilometres each week, to undergo dialysis. For patients who are completely reliant on stable, rigorously planned and continuous treatment, this situation entails severe physical and mental strain, long journeys, upheaval to daily life and increased stress over the consistency and quality of the care. Although treatment is provided elsewhere, long distances and the burden on patients raise serious issues relating to continuity of care, safety, equal access and dignity for people who depend on stable, uninterrupted and vital medical monitoring. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

Is it aware of the case in question and has it asked the Greek authorities for information regarding the extent to which timely, safe and equal access to treatment is ensured for dialysis patients in Pieria?

In the light of Article 35 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union and Principle 16 of the European Pillar of Social Rights, how does it view this situation, in which chronically ill people are forced to repeatedly make long journeys to receive vital treatment?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.7.2026) Safe and equitable access to treatment is an important topic for Member States and a key priority for the Commission. As per Article 168(7) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union1, Member States are responsible for the organisation and delivery of health services and medical care, including decisions on the location of facilities and the organisation of patient transport. EU tools monitor EU health systems. For example, the State of Health in the EU cycle2 includes country-specific analyses, and the European Semester provides country-specific recommendations. In 2020, 2022 and 2023, Greece received recommendations to ensure adequate and equal access to healthcare. In addition, the new Pharmaceutical Regulation3 and the Critical Medicines Act4, on which co-legislators found a political agreement respectively in December 2025 and May 2026, aim at improving access and availability of medicines for patients in the EU. The Commission recalls Article 35 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union and the Principle 16 of the European Pillar of Social Rights. However, as stated above, the organisation and delivery of health services and medical care remain the responsibility of the Member States. EU tools and initiatives support Member States to strengthen health systems via knowledge sharing, technical assistance, funding and policy guidance. EU funding instruments include the EU4Health programme, the cohesion policy funds, and the Recovery and Resilience Facility.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:12012E/TXT&from=en. 2 https://health.ec.europa.eu/state-health-eu_en. 3 COM(2023) 193 final. 4 COM(2025) 102 final.

E-10-2026-001213.t: Monitoring of pesticides in soils and coherence with the Kunming-Montreal targets
qt: to the Commission César Luena (S&D) Subject:

In its answer to question E-000426/20261, the Commission indicates that the Sustainable Use of Pesticides Directive, integrated pest management and national action plans will be used to reduce the risk from pesticides, in line with the European Union's commitment to reduce the risk from pesticides on biodiversity by at least half by 2030 under the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework. However, this answer raises questions as to the adequacy of the current framework in light of new scientific evidence on the widespread presence of pesticide residues in soils and in the context of simplifying food safety legislation. In view of this: 1.
Can the Commission guarantee that the current framework is adequate to meet the target of at least halving the risks pesticides pose to biodiversity by 2030?
How does the Commission assess the impact that initiatives to simplify regulations could have on achieving this objective?
Does the Commission intend to propose additional binding measures at EU level if the current instruments prove inadequate to meet international commitments?
https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/E-10-2026-000426_EN.html
at: (English version) to the Commission César Luena (S&D) (24 March 2026) Subject: Monitoring of pesticides in soils and coherence with the Kunming-Montreal targets In its answer to Question E-000426/2026 (1), the Commission indicates that the Sustainable Use of Pesticides Directive, integrated pest management and national action plans will be used to reduce the risk from pesticides, in line with the European Union's commitment to reduce the risk from pesticides on biodiversity by at least half by 2030 under the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework. However, this answer raises questions as to the adequacy of the current framework in light of new scientific evidence on the widespread presence of pesticide residues in soils and in the context of simplifying food safety legislation. In view of this: 1.
Can the Commission guarantee that the current framework is adequate to meet the target of at least halving the risks pesticides pose to biodiversity by 2030?
How does the Commission assess the impact that initiatives to simplify regulations could have on achieving this objective?
Does the Commission intend to propose additional binding measures at EU level if the current instruments prove inadequate to meet international commitments?

(3 July 2026) The global indicator methodology to quantify pesticide risks under the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF) (1) is due to be finalised by the fourth quarter of 2026. It will enable Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) to monitor and report on trends in pesticide risk for biodiversity. At EU level, Directive 2009/128/EC (2) on the sustainable use of pesticides (SUD) aims to reduce the risks and impacts of pesticide use on human health and the environment and therefore contributes to the objectives of the CBD. To report on trends under the SUD, Harmonised Risk Indicators (HRI) have been established. HRI 1, calculated on the basis of national pesticide sales data, shows in 2023 a 61% reduction compared to the 2011-2013 baseline period, thus exceeding a 50% reduction and a 5% decrease compared to 2022 (relative to the same baseline) (3). The Commission proposed to simplify regulations in order to reduce administrative burdens on economic operators and authorities, while fully maintaining the objectives of the legislation concerned. In particular, the Food and Feed Safety Simplification Package (4) maintains the current high protection standards and intends to facilitate the placing on the market of lower risk profile active substances and products, such as biocontrol substances. This is expected to support the substitution of more hazardous chemical active substances and to contribute to reducing the risks associated with the use of plant protection products. In view of the above, the Commission will continue to collaborate closely with Member States to ensure that this positive trend is sustained in the coming years. The Commission is currently not planning to set any additional binding measures.

E-10-2026-001211.t: Outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease on the island of Lesvos and compensation for affected farmers
qt: to the Commission Kostas Papadakis (NI) Subject:

Lesvos’ livestock farmers are under siege, as the government has imposed a full and universal lockdown due to foot-and-mouth disease, banning all livestock products from leaving the island. It is clear that the notorious ‘flexibility’ of the common agricultural policy guidelines supports the complete exclusion of Lesvos with the government stubbornly refusing to vaccinate, despite clear recommendations and guidance from EFSA. The sole criterion in both cases is that the export certificates of the four or five major dairy factories making Feta cheese should not be jeopardised in any way. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Is it true, as the Greek Government has alleged, that the European Commission itself imposed a total ban on all livestock products, even processed products, leaving the entire island of Lesvos?

Where does the Commission stand on the need for immediate and full (100 %) compensation for those affected, for the replacement of income lost by livestock farmers who cannot sell their products (milk, meat), and for effective protection measures (such as vaccination and full staffing of veterinary services with permanent staff)?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (26.5.2026) The EU legal framework, in particular Regulation (EU) 2016/4291 and Commission Delegated Regulations (EU) 2020/6872 and 2020/6893, establishes harmonised measures across the Union for eradicating Category A diseases, such as foot and mouth disease (FMD). These include culling infected herds, restricting animal and product movements from affected zones, and, where appropriate, vaccination4. Following confirmation of the FMD on Levos, restrictions were immediately imposed5 under Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/687, which permits derogations, allowing certain low-risk animal products to leave the restricted zones, provided risk-mitigation measures are applied. The EU co-finances emergency veterinary measures via the Single Market Programme6, covering costs for culling, compensating farmers, cleaning and disinfecting the affected premises, and vaccination7. The Commission stands ready to deploy vaccines from the EU FMD antigen bank upon Greece’s request. Additionally, under the Common Agricultural Policy Strategic Plans Regulation8, Member States may support investments in restoring agricultural potential and introduce crisis payments for farmers affected by catastrophic events. The Commission may also adopt exceptional support measures for market losses linked to restrictions imposed to curb disease spread.

E-10-2026-001210.t: Compliance costs of the AI Act
qt: to the Commission Michael McNamara (Renew) Subject:
The cost of compliance with the AI Act1 is estimated to be between EUR 320,000 and EUR 600,000, for entities under the high-risk classification2. 1.
What compliance costs were estimated by the 2021 study, requested by the Commission, to support the impact assessment of the regulatory requirements prior to the AI Act?
Does the Commission or European AI Office have a more recent or authoritative estimate of compliance costs regarding the high-risk provisions?

Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 June 2024 laying down harmonised rules on artificial intelligence and amending Regulations (EC) No 300/2008, (EU) No 167/2013, (EU) No 168/2013, (EU) 2018/858, (EU) 2018/1139 and (EU) 2019/2144 and Directives 2014/90/EU, (EU) 2016/797 and (EU) 2020/1828 (Artificial Intelligence Act) (OJ L, 2024/1689, 12.7.2024, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj). https://www.theparliamentmagazine.eu/partner/article/why-the-ai-act-could-cost-billions-to-europesinnovators
at: (English version) to the Commission Michael McNamara (Renew) (24 March 2026) Subject: Compliance costs of the AI Act The cost of compliance with the AI Act (1) is estimated to be between EUR 320,000 and EUR 600,000, for entities under the high-risk classification (2). 1. What compliance costs were estimated by the 2021 study, requested by the Commission, to support the impact assessment of the regulatory requirements prior to the AI Act? 2. Does the Commission or European AI Office have a more recent or authoritative estimate of compliance costs regarding the high-risk provisions? (27 April 2026) The figure of EUR 319 000, quoted from the support study to the impact assessment (1), refers to the exceptional case of a provider of a high-risk AI system without a quality management system (QMS) in place. As such, it does not provide a representative indication of costs for providers that already have a QMS in place, which will be the case for many providers as most high-risk AI systems will be covered by product legislation in Annex I of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act) and a QMS is usually already required under this existing product safety legislation (2). The figure of EUR 600 000, which is claimed to be the total cost of conformity assessment compliance under the AI Act, is based on the estimate of EUR 319 000 plus additional costs that are derived from a survey of 23 organisations’ opinions across different sectors, including defence (3). However, this study is based on a qualitative survey of perceptions and does not provide evidence on the cost of conformity assessment. Based on preliminary estimates by conformity assessment bodies, the cost of compliance with the essential requirements of the AI Act for high-risk AI systems in products in Annex I — which already undertake conformity assessment under sectorial legislation — would increase by 15-20% compared to current conformity assessment costs. Applying the figures from the support study to the AI Act impact assessment that estimate the cost for upgrading of an existing QMS for a product to cover AI Act compliance — which estimates costs in the range of EUR 159 000 — 202 000 — the resulting compliance costs that can be attributed to the AI Act would more realistically fall between EUR 23 850 and 40 400, and not EUR 600 000.

E-10-2026-001209.t: State of play of Italy’s efforts to meet EU energy transition targets
qt: to the Commission Pina Picierno (S&D) Subject:

Dramatic slowdowns in authorisation procedures for renewable energy installations could compromise Italy’s ability to achieve the targets set by the Green Deal, the ‘Fit for 55’ package, the RED III Directive and the integrated national energy and climate plan (PNIEC). Official figures indicate that Italy has a backlog of more than 1 700 ongoing environmental impact assessment (EIA) procedures and that, in 2025, the number of permit applications for renewable energy plants fell by around 70 % compared to the previous year, highlighting the scant trust that operators have in the country’s congested and unstable system. In addition to a chronically understaffed NRRP-PNIEC Technical Committee, Italy is contending with a rising number of authorisation-related lawsuits, while interministerial conflicts have brought more than 140 procedures to a complete halt. Italy’s struggles are further compounded by the energy grid’s ‘virtual saturation’ – a factor that is limiting access to connection capacity and freezing new investments – and by delays in implementing the FER2 Decree, which is supposed to incentivise state-of-the-art renewable technologies. In the light of the above: 1.
Will the Commission launch formal monitoring efforts concerning Italy’s compliance with the EU’s energy transition deadlines?
What steps will the Commission take to encourage Italy to increase its administrative capacity to an appropriate level, simplify its procedures and ensure regulatory certainty?
What corrective measures can the Commission implement to prevent slowdowns in the energy transition?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (12.6.2026) The Commission monitors the main deadlines1 applicable for energy-transition as well as the implementation of the National Energy and Climate Plans (NECP) through the bi-annually reports2. Each Member State is assessed for meeting its objectives3 and targets as set out in its NECP4. Where the progress towards meeting the targets is insufficient, the Commission issues recommendations to the Member State concerned5. The Commission also monitors the progress of the Member States towards energy transition in the framework of the European Semester annual exercise, which coordinates the EU's economic and social policies including energy policy. The Commission is aware that permitting delays for renewable energy projects are reported in most Member States, including Italy. For this reason, it has put in place a series of actions to ensure that the permitting deadlines and obligations set in the revised Renewable Energy Directive6 are respected, including launching infringement procedures against Italy7 and other Member States for lack of transposition of permitting provisions of the revised Renewable Energy Directive. Other actions aim to improve capacity building of permitting authorities, e.g. via the Technical Support Instrument which provided support to Italy to streamline permitting procedures, strengthen administrative capacities, digitalise permits, and enhance public engagement8. The Commission also works to avoid slowdowns in the energy transition, coordinates the efforts across Member States to create a robust framework that catalyses public and private investment, supports corrective measures that remove bottlenecks for faster permitting, grid and storage expansion, and de-risking of clean-energy finance. 1 A not exhaustive list of deadlines related to this framework:

- 30 June 2024 for final National Energy and Climate Plans, - 1 July 2024 for some renewables permitting rules, - 21 May 2025 for broader Renewable Energy Directive transposition (EU 2023/2413), - 11 October 2025 for the key provisions of the Energy Efficiency Directive (EU/ 2023/1791), - Commission takes action to ensure complete and timely transposition of EU directives (https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/inf_25_1842), - 29 May 2026 for the revised Energy Performance of Buildings Directive (EU/2024/1275, EPBD), - 1 March 2026 for national diversification plans under REPowerEU. 2 The next assessment of progress will be published in 2027. 3 The assessment of the updated Italian NECP is available on the Commission's website: https://commission.europa.eu/publications/commission-assessment-final-updated-national-energy-and-climateplan-italy_en. 4 Art. 29(1)b of Regulation (EU) 2018/1999 (Governance Regulation). 5 Article 34 of the Governance Regulation. 6 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2023/2413/oj/eng. 7 (INFR(2024)0232: https://ec.europa.eu/implementing-eu-law/search-infringementdecisions/?lang_code=EN&typeOfSearch=byDecision&active_only=0&noncom=0&r_dossier=&decision_date_ from=&decision_date_to=&DG=ENER&title=2023%2F2413&submit=Search&langCode=EN&version=v1&dg =ENER&page=1&size=10&order=desc&sortColumns=decisionDate&memberState=IT. 8 https://reforms-investments.ec.europa.eu/technical-support-instrument-0/green-transition/faster-permittingrenewable-energy-projects-italy_en.

E-10-2026-001208.t: ProtectEU: stronger security for Europeans or the policing of ideas and democratic dissent?
qt: to the Commission António Tânger Corrêa (PfE), Tiago Moreira de Sá (PfE), Marieke Ehlers (PfE), Petra Steger (PfE), Virginie Joron (PfE), Volker Schnurrbusch (ESN), Ondřej Knotek (PfE), Marion Maréchal (ECR), Afroditi Latinopoulou (PfE), Sebastian Tynkkynen (ECR), Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE), Tomasz Froelich (ESN) Subject:

The Commission’s new internal security strategy, ProtectEU1, aims to strengthen the EU’s capacity to address terrorism, organised crime, cyber-threats and hybrid attacks. Key measures include enhanced intelligence-sharing, expanded data access, stronger powers for EU agencies such as Europol, and a ‘whole-of-society’ approach integrating security considerations across EU legislation and policy. While the objective of protecting citizens is legitimate, these measures raise serious questions regarding proportionality, political neutrality and the protection of fundamental rights, including freedom of expression, political participation and lawful assembly. Security policies must remain focused on criminal activity and genuine threats, without encroaching on lawful civic participation or political dissent. 1.

How does the Commission ensure that ProtectEU measures focus exclusively on criminal behaviour and genuine threats, without infringing on citizens’ rights to freedom of expression, political participation and lawful assembly, as guaranteed under Articles 11, 12 and 52 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union?

What concrete legal safeguards and oversight mechanisms will the Commission implement to ensure that enhanced intelligence-sharing, data access and other security measures are strictly proportionate, limited in scope and subject to independent judicial or parliamentary scrutiny?

How will the Commission prevent the ‘whole-of-society’ security approach from inadvertently involving or monitoring lawful civic activities, associations or online expressions of opinion, and how will transparency and accountability be ensured in such cases?
Supporter2
Commission communication of 1 April 2025 on ProtectEU: a European Internal Security Strategy (COM(2025)148). This question is supported by a Member other than the authors: Christine Anderson (ESN).
at: (English version) to the Commission António Tânger Corrêa (PfE), Tiago Moreira de Sá (PfE), Marieke Ehlers (PfE), Petra Steger (PfE), Virginie Joron (PfE), Volker Schnurrbusch (ESN), Ondřej Knotek (PfE), Marion Maréchal (ECR), Afroditi Latinopoulou (PfE), Sebastian Tynkkynen (ECR), Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE), Tomasz Froelich (ESN) (23 March 2026) Subject: ProtectEU: stronger security for Europeans or the policing of ideas and democratic dissent? The Commission’s new internal security strategy, ProtectEU (1), aims to strengthen the EU’s capacity to address terrorism, organised crime, cyber-threats and hybrid attacks. Key measures include enhanced intelligence-sharing, expanded data access, stronger powers for EU agencies such as Europol, and a ‘whole-of-society’ approach integrating security considerations across EU legislation and policy. While the objective of protecting citizens is legitimate, these measures raise serious questions regarding proportionality, political neutrality and the protection of fundamental rights, including freedom of expression, political participation and lawful assembly. Security policies must remain focused on criminal activity and genuine threats, without encroaching on lawful civic participation or political dissent. 1. How does the Commission ensure that ProtectEU measures focus exclusively on criminal behaviour and genuine threats, without infringing on citizens’ rights to freedom of expression, political participation and lawful assembly, as guaranteed under Articles 11, 12 and 52 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union? 2. What concrete legal safeguards and oversight mechanisms will the Commission implement to ensure that enhanced intelligence-sharing, data access and other security measures are strictly proportionate, limited in scope and subject to independent judicial or parliamentary scrutiny? 3. How will the Commission prevent the ‘whole-of-society’ security approach from inadvertently involving or monitoring lawful civic activities, associations or online expressions of opinion, and how will transparency and accountability be ensured in such cases? Supporter (2) (19 May 2026) ProtectEU (1) embeds in its core the respect for fundamental rights, which is ultimately ensured also by the co-legislators, the Council and the European Parliament. In accordance with EU law, each proposal announced in ProtectEU needs to respect the principle of proportionality. When preparing legislative initiatives, EU Better Regulation rules (2) require the Commission to prepare impact assessments where the possible impacts of the initiatives on fundamental rights are assessed. This evidence-based approach, overseen by the independent Regulatory Scrutiny Board (3), ensures legislative initiatives are consistent with EU values and allows the co-legislators to take an informed decision. Furthermore, during the preparation for ProtectEU, the Commission consulted the EU Agency for Fundamental Rights. As one of the central principles of ProtectEU, the ‘whole of society’ approach intends to involve all stakeholders that can meaningfully contribute to the security of the EU, including citizens, civil society, academia and the private sector. Thus, public consultations made available on the Have Your Say portal accompany all impact assessments. This stakeholder engagement plays a crucial role in ensuring transparency and accountability, and in building trust in the drafting and implementation of EU security policies.

Commission communication of 1 April 2025 on ProtectEU: a European Internal Security Strategy (COM(2025)148). This question is supported by a Member other than the authors: Christine Anderson (ESN). E-10-2026-001207.t: Impact of the Middle East conflict on the EU’s food supply
qt: to the Commission Ana Miguel Pedro (PPE) Subject:

The recent escalation of the conflict in the Middle East is affecting a strategic region through which a considerable portion of the world’s fertiliser trade passes. Restrictions on shipping traffic in the Strait of Hormuz are causing significant disruptions to international supply chains, including raw materials and fertilisers. The conflict has pushed up the price of natural gas, which is an essential raw material used in the production of most nitrogen fertilisers. A number of academic studies have shown that roughly half of the world’s food production is reliant on fertilisers. Can the Commission say: 1.
Given that the current geopolitical context could lead to a considerable increase in fertiliser prices in the short term, what tangible measures are being considered to protect European farmers?

As the Commission is aware that this is a critical moment for fertilisers to be used on European farms, what urgent initiatives does the Commission intend to implement to safeguard timely access to affordable fertilisers and prevent risks to agricultural production and food supply in the European Union?
at: (English version) to the Commission Ana Miguel Pedro (PPE) (23 March 2026) Subject: Impact of the Middle East conflict on the EU’s food supply The recent escalation of the conflict in the Middle East is affecting a strategic region through which a considerable portion of the world’s fertiliser trade passes. Restrictions on shipping traffic in the Strait of Hormuz are causing significant disruptions to international supply chains, including raw materials and fertilisers. The conflict has pushed up the price of natural gas, which is an essential raw material used in the production of most nitrogen fertilisers. A number of academic studies have shown that roughly half of the world’s food production is reliant on fertilisers. Can the Commission say: 1.
Given that the current geopolitical context could lead to a considerable increase in fertiliser prices in the short term, what tangible measures are being considered to protect European farmers?

As the Commission is aware that this is a critical moment for fertilisers to be used on European farms, what urgent initiatives does the Commission intend to implement to safeguard timely access to affordable fertilisers and prevent risks to agricultural production and food supply in the European Union?

(10 June 2026) The Commission is closely monitoring the impact of the current geopolitical situation on fertiliser markets, including through the EU Fertiliser Market Observatory (1). The impact on the EU remains limited due to low direct reliance on Middle East imports, sufficient stocks and unaffected production in key supplier countries such as Egypt and Algeria. While no immediate shortages are expected for the 2026 harvest, increased global volatility is affecting fertiliser prices for farmers. To mitigate pressure, the Commission has already taken targeted measures, including a reduced 1% CBAM default value mark up for fertilisers. In addition, to support both farmers and the EU fertiliser industry, imports of ammonia, urea and other nitrogen fertilisers will benefit from duty suspension, within given quotas, for a period of one year. The Commission has also recently adopted a state aid Framework on the Middle East (2), to support both farmers and energy intensive industries. On 19 May 2026, the Commission adopted the Fertiliser Action Plan (3), setting out short- and long-term measures to improve fertiliser availability, affordability and resilience. Short term actions include the mobilisation and possible top-up of the agricultural reserve, liquidity support under the CAP and greater flexibility for advance payments. The Plan also supports biogas and biomethane projects to reduce energy and nutrient dependencies and foresees the possible activation of emergency tools under the internal market Emergency and Resilience Act (4), if necessary.

E-10-2026-001204.t: Termination of  the Your Europe Advice service
qt: to the Commission Cynthia Ní Mhurchú (Renew) Subject:
Termination of the Your Europe Advice service

The Your Europe Advice (YEA) service, which has been operating since 1996 and is currently delivered by ECAS, provides free, expert legal guidance to EU citizens and businesses, including those in Ireland. Handling over 30 000 enquiries annually and providing key support for SOLVIT, YEA is a vital source of reliable advice on EU law. Can the Commission explain why it plans to terminate the YEA service in September 2026 and what alternative measures will be put in place to ensure citizens and advice organisations continue to have access to expert information on EU rights?
at: (English version) to the Commission Cynthia Ní Mhurchú (Renew) (23 March 2026) Subject: Termination of the Your Europe Advice service The Your Europe Advice (YEA) service, which has been operating since 1996 and is currently delivered by ECAS, provides free, expert legal guidance to EU citizens and businesses, including those in Ireland. Handling over 30 000 enquiries annually and providing key support for Solvit, YEA is a vital source of reliable advice on EU law. It handles more than 20 000 enquiries annually and provides essential support to Solvit centres and national advice organisations. It has come to my attention that the Commission’s Directorate-General for Internal Market, Industry, Entrepreneurship and SMEs intends to unilaterally discontinue this service without public consultation or any published impact assessment. 1. Has the Commission conducted an impact assessment on the consequences of discontinuation for citizens, and if not, why? 2. What assessment has been made of the risks of directing citizens to AI tools for complex legal questions in the absence of this service? 3. Has consideration been given to the impact on Solvit and other directorates-general, and to transferring the service to another directorate-general rather than discontinuing it entirely? to the Commission Pina Picierno (S&D) (13 April 2026) Subject: The ‘Your Europe Advice’ service Launched in 1996, ‘Your Europe Advice’ is a Commission-funded service that provides free and tailored legal advice to citizens and businesses regarding their internal market and EU citizenship rights. On average, the service handles over 30 000 queries every year, responding by email or phone in any of the 24 official EU languages within a week. Your Europe Advice (YEA) also assists national Solvit centres, which provide Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) services. News recently broke that the European Commission’s Directorate General for Internal Market, Industry, Entrepreneurship and SMEs has decided that it will not issue a call for tenders for YEA, which will no longer be available as of 1 September 2026. In the light of the above:

Could the Commission clarify why it is discontinuing a popular service that provides direct and tailored assistance to citizens and businesses and why this decision was taken without a public consultation?
Has an assessment been carried out to assess the impact this decision will have on citizens, Solvit centres and other DGs?
Was consideration given to the possibility of transferring the management of this service to another DG?

Joint answer given by Executive Vice-President Séjourné on behalf of the European Commission (8 June 2026) Since the creation of Your Europe Advice (YEA) thirty years ago, digital advancements have significantly impacted the information services provided by the Commission to EU citizens. These changes, and the necessity to modernise the Commission’s tools, call for adaptation of support mechanisms available to citizens. The current contract for the YEA service will end on 31 August 2026. The Commission is actively reviewing options for a refreshed and modernised approach to ensure the service remains effective, user-centred, and responsive to the needs of EU citizens and businesses. The Commission remains committed to support the other existing mechanisms and information portals (e.g., Your Europe portal, Single Digital Gateway) which will continue to provide a high-quality standard of information to EU citizens and businesses. The Commission remains dedicated to support Solvit Centres, in particular via trainings, best practices and other support tools. This engagement should ensure that the Solvit network continues to deliver the best service for EU citizens.

E-10-2026-001203.t: Ireland’s compliance with EU accessibility standards
qt: to the Commission Cynthia Ní Mhurchú (Renew) Subject:

While Ireland has a strong legal framework, including the Disability Act and the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, practical implementation is inconsistent, particularly in regional areas. Public transport often requires advance notice for wheelchair users, and many town centres have narrow or uneven footpaths, inconsistent kerb cuts, and limited enforcement of universal design standards. Countries such as Sweden and the Netherlands integrate accessibility by default, exercising proactive oversight rather than relying on complaints. What measures exist to strengthen practical accessibility in rural and regional towns?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.6.2026) Directive (EU) 2019/882 (European Accessibility Act) (EAA)1 sets mandatory accessibility requirements for certain products and services, including certain elements of transport services, and optional accessibility requirements for the built environment2, for which Member States can opt-in3. The Act applies since 28 June 2025, and the Commission monitors its implementation across the EU. In 2022, the Commission issued a standardisation request4 to revise and develop standards including for Information and Communications Technology (ICT) and on the built environment5, which should support the implementation of accessibility requirements of the EAA. Moreover, the Commission launched the European resource centre AccessibleEU6, designed, inter alia, to support the implementation of EU accessibility legislation. Moreover, Article 9(3) of the Common Provisions Regulation7 states that accessibility for persons with disabilities shall be taken into account throughout the preparation and implementation of programmes in the different funds to which this Regulation applies. As regards public transport, the EU type-approval rules8 for city buses require accessibility of passengers with reduced mobility, including at least one wheelchair user. All buses and coaches designed for easy access for passengers with reduced mobility and wheelchair users must comply with requirements on accommodation for such passengers, as regards, e.g., steps, communication devices, handrails, floor slopes etc. EU passenger rights legislation requires to assist persons with reduced mobility and persons with disabilities, allowing them to request advance notification for operators to organise staff or equipment required for using their service. 1 Directive (EU) 2019/882 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 17 April 2019 on the accessibility

requirements for products and services (OJ L 151, 7.6.2019, PP.70-115, ELI:http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2019/882/oj). 2 Annex III to Directive (EU) 2019/82. 3 Ireland has not opted into the accessibility requirements for the built environment. 4C(2022) 6456 – Standardisation request M/587, https://ec.europa.eu/growth/toolsdatabases/enorm/mandate/587_en. 5 EN 17210:2021, Accessibility in the built environment, https://accessible-eu-centre.ec.europa.eu/contentcorner/digital-library/en-172102021-accessibility-and-usability-built-environment-functional-requirements_en. 6 https://accessible-eu-centre.ec.europa.eu/index_en. 7 Regulation (EU) 2021/1060 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 24 June 2021 laying down common provisions on the European Regional Development Fund, the European Social Fund Plus, the Cohesion Fund, the Just Transition Fund and the European Maritime, Fisheries and Aquaculture Fund and financial rules for those and for the Asylum, Migration and Integration Fund, the Internal Security Fund and the Instrument for Financial Support for Border Management and Visa Policy (OJ L 231, 30.6.2021, pp. 159–706) https://eurlex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2021/1060/oj/eng. 8 Regulation (EU) 2018/858 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 30 May 2018 on the approval and market surveillance of motor vehicles and their trailers, and of systems, components and separate technical units intended for such vehicles, amending Regulations (EC) No 715/2007 and (EC) No 595/2009 and repealing Directive 2007/46/EC (OJ L 151, 14.6.2018, pp. 1–218) https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2018/858/oj/eng.

E-10-2026-001202.t: Is the Commission sacrificing French agriculture in favour of an  à la carte  Common Agricultural Policy?
qt: to the Commission Mathilde Androuët (PfE) Subject:
Is the Commission sacrificing French agriculture in favour of an à la carte Common Agricultural Policy?

The European Court of Auditors points out that the reform of the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) for the period 2028–2034 would replace the two historic pillars with more flexible national and regional plans, which would create risks of fragmentation, loss of clarity, budgetary uncertainty and distortions of competition between Member States1. At the same time, a study commissioned by the Committee on Agriculture and Rural Development shows that farm incomes remain highly volatile and largely dependent on public support, the real value of which is being eroded by inflation2. 1.
How can the Commission justify a reform that allows it to pass the buck to Member States while refusing to genuinely guarantee a level playing field and stable support for farmers?

Does it acknowledge that this increased ‘flexibility’ is likely to lead, above all, to an à la carte CAP, in which French agriculture would be penalised relative to Member States that have different budgetary margins, political choices or regulatory constraints?

European Court of Auditors, Opinion No 05/2026 on the CAP for the period from 2028 to 2034. Donnellan et al., ‘Support measures for farmers’ income in different Member States in the context of inflation and rising production costs’, PE 759.349, 2026.
at: (English version) to the Commission Mathilde Androuët (PfE) (23 March 2026) Subject: Is the Commission sacrificing French agriculture in favour of an à la carte Common Agricultural Policy? The European Court of Auditors points out that the reform of the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) for the period 2028-2034 would replace the two historic pillars with more flexible national and regional plans, which would create risks of fragmentation, loss of clarity, budgetary uncertainty and distortions of competition between Member States (1). At the same time, a study commissioned by the Committee on Agriculture and Rural Development shows that farm incomes remain highly volatile and largely dependent on public support, the real value of which is being eroded by inflation (2). 1. How can the Commission justify a reform that allows it to pass the buck to Member States while refusing to genuinely guarantee a level playing field and stable support for farmers? 2. Does it acknowledge that this increased ‘flexibility’ is likely to lead, above all, to an à la carte CAP, in which French agriculture would be penalised relative to Member States that have different budgetary margins, political choices or regulatory constraints? (28 May 2026) The Commission’s proposals for the 2028-2034 multiannual financial framework (MFF) (1) reaffirm the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) as a cornerstone of EU policy, providing a cohesive and robust framework to support farmers, consumers, and the environment. Flexibility rules are designed to complement — not compromise — the Policy’s common principles. Stringent EU-wide safeguards, including common definitions and common EU rules, including farm stewardship obligations and performance monitoring continue to apply. The Commission will also issue CAP national recommendations, steering Member States’ CAP interventions to support common EU priorities while being tailored to Member States’ specific needs and challenges. These measures ensure that Member States’ tailored solutions remain aligned with common EU economic, social and environmental objectives and support a level-playing field in the EU. The Commission also advocates a collaborative approach to developing the National and Regional Partnership (NRP) Plans, incorporating early dialogues with Member State to ensure that national and local needs align with overarching EU priorities. The Commission will rigorously assess Member States’ draft NRP Plans before submitting a proposal for approval by the Council to see if the common policy objectives are met. Crucially, the budget for farmers’ income support remains secure guaranteeing predictability. The new MFF (2) introduces a new method (‘deflator’) to handle inflation challenges. It keeps the annual price adjustment at 2% if EU inflation is between 1% and 3%. If inflation falls below 1% or rises above 3%, the adjustment matches the actual forecast rate.
