E-10-2026-001201.t: Green Deal and critical raw materials – a green transition built on greater strategic dependence?
qt: to the Commission Mathilde Androuët (PfE) Subject:

The European Court of Auditors’ Special Report No 04/2026 shows that the EU’s critical raw materials policy is based on fragile data, non-binding targets for 2030 and continuous dependence – sometimes over 90 % – on a single third country. At the same time, the Green Deal and EU climate goals are driving up demand for those materials in a structural manner. In view of this: 1.

On the basis of transparent numerical analyses, how can the Commission explain that the 2030 objectives of the Critical Raw Materials Act will actually reduce strategic dependence, material by material?
What scenarios have been studied in the event that dominant countries, particularly China, place restrictions on exports?
How does the Commission square the acceleration of climate targets with the current lack of sufficient industrial and mining security in the EU?

E-10-2026-001200.t: Critical raw materials – centralised technocratic steering or Member States’ industrial sovereignty?
at: (English version) to the Commission Mathilde Androuët (PfE) (23 March 2026) Subject: Critical raw materials — centralised technocratic steering or Member States’ industrial sovereignty? The European Court of Auditors’ Special Report No 04/2026 notes a fragmentation of funding (over EUR 1.8 billion mobilised), a lack of consolidated monitoring and limited results in terms of effectively securing flows. It also highlights major internal obstacles: the slowness of permitting procedures, regulatory obstacles, high energy costs and limited processing capacity. Can the Commission state: 1.
what consolidated amount, per material and per programme, has produced effectively secured volumes since 2021?
what specific measures are planned to remove the regulatory bottlenecks identified, in particular with regard to mining and industrial permits?
how it ensures that the Critical Raw Materials Act fully respects the principle of subsidiarity and does not lead to a technocratic recentralisation of Member States’ industrial choices?

to the Commission Mathilde Androuët (PfE) (23 March 2026) Subject: Green Deal and critical raw materials — a green transition built on greater strategic dependence? The European Court of Auditors’ Special Report No 04/2026 shows that the EU’s critical raw materials policy is based on fragile data, non-binding targets for 2030 and continuous dependence — sometimes over 90% — on a single third country. At the same time, the Green Deal and EU climate goals are driving up demand for those materials in a structural manner. In view of this: 1.

On the basis of transparent numerical analyses, how can the Commission explain that the 2030 objectives of the Critical Raw Materials Act will actually reduce strategic dependence, material by material?
What scenarios have been studied in the event that dominant countries, particularly China, place restrictions on exports?
How does the Commission square the acceleration of climate targets with the current lack of sufficient industrial and mining security in the EU?

Joint answer given by Executive Vice-President Séjourné on behalf of the European Commission (22 May 2026) The Critical Raw Materials Act (CRMA) (1) establishes benchmarks for 2030 that give clear indications towards reducing and avoiding excessive dependencies. The ResourceEU Action Plan (2) aims to accelerate the implementation of the CRMA, especially for strategic projects. Most strategic projects will deliver supply by 2030, significantly strengthening the EU’s medium- and long-term resilience (3).

https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A02024R1252-20240503#tocId90. https://single-market-economy.ec.europa.eu/document/download/01c448d6-dc93-40d7-9afe-4c2af448d00c_en. https://single-market-economy.ec.europa.eu/sectors/raw-materials/areas-specific-interest/critical-raw-materials/strategic-projects-under-crma/selectedprojects_en.

The Commission regularly collects data on global production, trade and usage of raw materials. This forms the basis of the EU’s list of critical raw materials, enables the Commission to analyse the EU’s dependencies and promote risk mitigation strategies. In the CRMA, this is further enhanced by stress-testing of strategic raw materials value chains. To address current bottlenecks in the project development, the CRMA put in place single points of contact for permitting of critical raw materials projects and fast-tracked permitting timelines for strategic projects. Other enabling conditions for strategic projects include facilitation of access to finance and the support in finding off-takers. The REsourceEU Action Plan also announced the mobilisation of EUR 3 billion of EU funds within 12 months to support the raw materials value chain, of which EUR 300 million is dedicated under the Battery Booster (4). The subsidiarity principle is ensured by coordination of actions at EU level through the Critical Raw Materials Board established by the CRMA. The Board consists of the Commission, Member States representatives and the European Parliament as an observer. The funding instruments in question are not designed to secure volumes of raw materials. Their role is, for example, to develop new technological solutions and support decarbonisation measures.

E-10-2026-001199.t: Ban on euthanasia of cats and dogs except in cases of intolerable, untreatable, irreversible pain, after all other care options have been exhausted
qt: to the Commission Maria Zacharia (NI) Subject:

In 2023, the Commission presented a proposal for a Regulation on the welfare of dogs and cats and their traceability. Subsequently, the European Parliament adopted a firmer stance, stating that euthanasia in shelters must not be allowed as a population management solution and that euthanasia must be limited to cases where recovery is not possible and the animal is experiencing severe pain or suffering that cannot be alleviated. However, in some Member States the term ‘euthanasia’ is still misused to include the killing of cats and dogs for reasons such as lack of space, cost, administrative inefficiency or to generally make things easier for the competent authorities or structures. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

Does it explicitly support the inclusion, in the final text of the regulation, of a ban on the euthanasia of cats and dogs for reasons of population management, lack of places in shelters, cost or administrative inefficiency, as well as a provision explicitly stipulating that euthanasia must be allowed only in exceptional cases of proven untreatable, irreversible and severe pain or suffering that cannot be alleviated?

Does it intend to support EU-wide binding minimum guarantees, such as an expert opinion from a veterinarian, keeping a complete record of each case as well as a relevant register, and having effective control and penalty mechanisms?

Does it consider that a Member State which allows the actual killing of dogs or cats for the above reasons complies with the objective of ensuring a high level of protection of animal welfare as set out in EU law?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.5.2026) The co-legislators reached the provisional final political agreement on the Commission proposal for a Regulation on the welfare of dogs and cats and their traceability1 on 25 November 2025, hence negotiations are closed, and new elements are no longer under consideration. The agreement2 reached between co-legislators defines ‘euthanasia’3 based on the method used to end the life of a dog or cat and the outcome it brings on the animal. It requires that euthanasia is applied when the welfare of a dog or a cat is compromised and the animal experiences severe pain or suffering while its recovery is not achievable. The agreement does not limit the use of euthanasia exclusively to these specific circumstances. Where these circumstances outlined in point 1 arise, the agreement requires that a veterinarian be consulted to decide whether the dog or cat is to be euthanised to end its suffering. No record or register keeping is foreseen by the veterinarian. Member States are required to lay down rules on penalties applicable to infringements of the upcoming Regulation. Other Union legislation4 requires Member States to conduct official controls for the verification of compliance with the new rules. Those obligations also concern the issue of euthanasia. The Commission helps develop and adopt international animal health and welfare standards through the WOAH5. WOAH standards6 require dog population management programmes to be based on a national context and tailored to local circumstances. They further specify that euthanasia alone is ineffective for long-term population control and, if used, must comply with WOAH killing standards and be implemented in combination with other measures to achieve effective long-term population management.
1 COM/2023/769 final. 2 https://www.europarl.europa.eu/meetdocs/2024_2029/plmrep/COMMITTEES/AGRI/LA/2026/01-

12/1334329EN.pdf. 3 Euthanasia means the act of inducing death using a method that causes a rapid and irreversible loss of consciousness with a minimum of pain and distress, ending the life of the dog or cat. 4 Regulation (EU) 2017/625 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 15 March 2017 on official controls and other official activities performed to ensure the application of food and feed law, rules on animal health and welfare, plant health and plant protection products (Official Controls Regulation), OJ L 95, 7.4.2017, pp. 1. http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2017/625/oj. 5 World Organisation for Animal Health. 6 Terrestrial Animal Health Code, Section 7, Animal Welfare, Chapter 7.7., Dog population management, https://www.woah.org/en/what-we-do/standards/codes-andmanuals/#chapter/?rid=82&volume_no=1&ismanual=false&language=102&standard_type=5&animal_type=7.

E-10-2026-001198.t: Swift implementation of European measures to bring down energy prices
qt: to the Commission Dimitris Tsiodras (PPE) Subject:

The impact of the Middle East conflict on energy prices combined with inflationary pressures call for immediate action to ensure affordable energy for European citizens and businesses. In light of the above and following the conclusions of the summit, can the Commission say: 1.

What will be the direction taken at EU level by the targeted measures aimed at bringing down energy prices and addressing excessive price volatility, for instance increasing the Market Stability Reserve, and how soon will the measures be presented given how critical the situation is?

How does it intend to proceed with the revision of the Emissions Trading System (ETS) with a view to addressing its impact on electricity prices and reducing the risk of carbon price volatility, and what is the timeline for this revision?
How does it intend to help speed up the creation of a genuine energy union aimed at strengthening the EU’s energy security and resilience?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (11.5.2026) On 1 April 2026, the Commission announced the first concrete measure to strengthen the Emissions Trading System (ETS), proposing an amendment to the Market Stability Reserve (the ETS’s built-in stabilisation measure)1 reinforcing its role as a buffer to support market stability better equip the reserve to respond to future market developments, including supply tightness. The ETS accounts for around 11% of retail electricity prices for industry and 5% for households, remaining smaller than fuel costs, network charges, and taxes. A comprehensive ETS review, to be presented by July 2026, will strengthen the carbon market, and ensure a fair, cost-effective contribution to the 2040 climate target. On 22 April 2026, the Commission presented the AccelerateEU Communication2 outlining immediate, targeted actions for Member States to deliver rapid and lasting relief to households and industry facing high energy prices. It also includes structural measures to improve energy efficiency and accelerate electrification by reducing the four components of energy bills-supply costs, network charges, taxes, and carbon costs - also in the longer term. The crisis highlights that long-term affordability depends on accelerating the clean energy transition. Scaling up domestic clean energy and energy efficiency will reduce fossil fuel imports and strengthen Europe’s energy independence. In this context, the Commission has launched reflections on a post-2030 framework, including a revision of the Governance Regulation together with the renewable energy and energy efficiency frameworks to modernise the Energy Union and climate action.
1 https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_26_666. 2 https://energy.ec.europa.eu/strategy/accelerateeu-strengthen-eu-energy-resilience_en.

E-10-2026-001197.t: Research, potential applications and regulation of weather modification and geoengineering technologies in the European Union 8
qt: to the Commission Anja Arndt (ESN) Subject:
Does the Commission currently see a need for specific EU rules on the governance of technologies that have a large-scale influence on climate or weather processes?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.6.2026) The Commission's position on deliberate large-scale interventions in the Earth’s natural systems (referred to as ‘geoengineering’) is clearly set out in the Joint Communication of the Commission and the High Representative on the Climate-Security Nexus of 28 June 20231. It notes that such technologies are attracting more attention, and states that ‘the risks, impacts and unintended consequences that these technologies pose are poorly understood, and necessary rules, procedures and institutions have not been developed’. The Joint Communication also stresses that the EU, guided by the precautionary principle ‘will support international efforts to assess comprehensively the risks and uncertainties of climate interventions, including solar radiation modification, and promote discussions on a potential international framework for its governance, including research related aspects’. In 2024, following a Commission request for advice on solar radiation modification, the Group of Chief Scientific Advisors issued a scientific opinion2, while the European Group on Ethics delivered an ethical perspective3. Both groups stressed that these technologies are not ready to be deployed and cautioned the Commission to maintain the primary goals of its climate policy: reducing emissions and adapting to inevitable changes. The Commission’s Strategic Foresight Report 20254 also points to the need for the EU to show ethical and science-based leadership in responsible and precautionary approaches for such new controversial technologies, including by fostering global collaborative governance structures to deal with potential risks, benefits and distributional effects. In this context, the Commission is monitoring the issue.

Ethical perspectives, Publications Office of the European Union, 2024, https://data.europa.eu/doi/10.2777/951016. 4 https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/strategic-foresight/2025-strategic-foresight-report_en.

at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.6.2026) The Commission’s position on geoengineering is set out in the Joint Communication of the Commission and High Representative on the Climate-Security Nexus1, which states that ‘risks, impacts and unintended consequences that these technologies pose are poorly understood, and necessary rules, procedures and institutions have not been developed’ and stresses that the EU, guided by the precautionary principle, ‘will support international efforts to assess comprehensively the risks and uncertainties of climate interventions, including solar radiation modification and promote discussions on a potential international framework for its governance, including research related aspects’. E-10-2026-001194.t: Research into and potential applications and regulation of weather modification and geoengineering technologies in the European Union 5
qt: to the Commission Anja Arndt (ESN) Subject:

Which projects under EU research programmes (in particular Horizon Europe, Horizon 2020 or earlier framework programmes) address geoengineering concepts or technologies designed to influence atmospheric processes; which of these projects have been funded by the EU and what are their scientific objectives?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.6.2026) The EU has no legal definition for ‘geoengineering’. The Convention on Biological Diversity stated1 that ‘[…] any technologies that deliberately reduce solar insolation or increase carbon sequestration from the atmosphere on a large scale that may affect biodiversity […] should be considered as forms of geo-engineering […].’ The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) referred to geoengineering as ‘a broad set of methods and technologies that aim to deliberately alter the climate system in order to alleviate the impacts of climate change. Most, but not all, methods seek to either (1) reduce the amount of absorbed solar energy in the climate system (Solar Radiation Management) or (2) increase net carbon sinks from the atmosphere at a scale sufficiently large to alter climate (Carbon Dioxide Removal). Scale and intent are of central importance. […] Geoengineering is different from weather modification and ecological engineering, but the boundary can be fuzzy2’. Due to the rather broad scope and variable interpretation of ‘geoengineering’, it is not possible for the Commission to provide a comprehensive list of projects addressing geoengineering concepts, the entities involved in them or their scientific objectives. Depending on the scope and interpretation of ‘geoengineering’, information on specific projects funded under the Research and Innovation Framework Programmes, and the entities benefitting from them, can be extracted from the Community Research and Development Information Service (CORDIS)3.

(3 June 2026) Weather modification, most notably through cloud seeding to reduce the risk/impact of hail damage or to locally alter precipitation, has been widely practiced in many countries, including in Europe, for decades. There is no EU legislation addressing weather modification specifically. The Commission has not been monitoring cloudseeding programs or activities in a systematic manner, neither does it have information on related field trials, but any weather modification action must in all cases respect relevant EU legislation and the precautionary principle laid down in the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union. E-10-2026-001189.t: Risks for the Member States of a protracted migratory crisis
qt: to the Commission Ştefan Muşoiu (S&D) Subject:

Current geopolitical and geostrategic developments make it increasingly likely that the European Union will face renewed migratory pressure in the form of migrants from Muslim states affected by the war in the Middle East. The International Organization for Migration has drawn attention to the risk of a long-term migratory crisis and to the fact that in Lebanon over one million people have been displaced and shelter facilities are close to full capacity. Given these circumstances, the European Union should be incorporating the lessons learned from the previous migration crisis in 2015 into its current policies, and hence furnish concrete support measures for third countries and the most appropriate responses for Member States, through preventive measures and rapid response mechanisms for managing a significant influx of refugees. In this regard, can the Commission clarify what prevention plan it has decided upon for managing a foreseeable new and larger wave of refugees heading for the European Union, what updated EU-level decisions have been taken as regards a long-term migratory crisis and in what ways it intends to support frontline states and avoid a repetition of the situations that arose during the 2015 migrant crisis?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.5.2026) The Commission is closely monitoring developments in the Middle East and is supporting partner countries, including through cooperation with international organisations. There are currently no indications of increased cross-border movements towards the EU. Preparedness is ensured through the implementation of a comprehensive migration crisis response framework. Member States are responsible for contingency planning concerning border and migration management, which is complemented at EU level by coordination and support measures, including the EU Migration Preparedness and Crisis Blueprint Network1, the EU Civil Protection Mechanism, the operational and technical support of EU agencies, and flexible EU funding. The Commission recognises that Member States at EU external borders may be particularly exposed. The Commission is therefore providing targeted support, including reinforced operational deployments of EU agencies, to help ensure an effective migration management system and it is ready to step up assistance if needed. The Pact on Migration and Asylum2 offers a comprehensive approach and firm but fair rules to manage migration in a spirit of responsibility and solidarity. This includes strengthening preparedness, ensuring a coordinated crisis response and embedding migration in international partnerships, including the possibility to adapt to exceptional migration-related circumstances, as set out in the Crisis and Force Majeure Regulation3.
1 Commission Recommendation (EU) 2020/1366 of 23 September 2020 on an EU mechanism for preparedness

and management of crises related to migration, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reco/2020/1366/oj/eng. 2 https://home-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies/migration-and-asylum/pact-migration-and-asylum_en. 3 Regulation (EU) 2024/1359 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 May 2024 addressing situations of crisis and force majeure in the field of migration and asylum and amending Regulation (EU) 2021/1147, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1359/oj/eng.

E-10-2026-001188.t: EU action to prevent krill populations from collapsing
qt: to the Commission Emma Fourreau (The Left), Sebastian Everding (The Left), Leila Chaibi (The Left), Anthony Smith (The Left), Damien Carême (The Left), Anja Hazekamp (The Left), Luke Ming Flanagan (The Left), Arash Saeidi (The Left), Manon Aubry (The Left), Mélissa Camara (Verts/ALE), Lena Schilling (Verts/ALE), Jutta Paulus (Verts/ALE), Tilly Metz (Verts/ALE), Christophe Clergeau (S&D), César Luena (S&D), Eric Sargiacomo (S&D), Rima Hassan (The Left) Subject:

Krill fisheries in the Southern Ocean have drastically expanded in recent years, with the fisheries’ 620 000 metric tonne catch limit being reached for the first time during the 2024/2025 fishing season1. Such industrial fishing activities, conducted by a growing number of supertrawlers, are causing significant risks for fragile marine ecosystems. Krill are a keystone species in the Southern Ocean food chain and play a critical role in climate change mitigation. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, the scientific community and NGOs2 have raised the alarm over this dramatic situation. In November 2025, the session of the Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources (CCAMLR) concluded with no progress3 on the creation of new marine protected areas, which was vetoed by contracting parties such as China or Russia, or on the renewal of a conservation measure that allocated catches across different areas. Norway has proposed almost doubling the catch limit allowed in the Southern Ocean. Given CCAMLR’s failure to take action to protect Antarctic ecosystems: 1.
What are the Commission and the Member States doing to step up EU action to prevent krill populations from collapsing?
Will the Commission support a moratorium or a closure of krill fisheries in the Southern Ocean to protect Antarctica’s marine ecosystems?

(29 April 2026) The European Union attaches great importance to the protection of Antarctic krill and to its critical role in the Antarctic ecosystem. The Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources (CCAMLR) has generally ensured that the krill fishery in Antarctica remains at sustainable levels (1), in accordance with the precautionary principle and ecosystem approach. Following the lack of agreement during the 43rd CCAMLR annual meeting to retain a catch limit distribution mechanism, catches are increasingly concentrated in specific areas of the Antarctic Peninsula region, thereby negatively affecting these marine ecosystems, including krill-dependent predators such as penguins, seals, and whales. For this reason, the EU has strongly advocated during the 44th CCAMLR annual meeting for the reintroduction, as a matter of urgency, of a distribution of the krill catch limit in the Antarctic Peninsula region on smaller spatial and temporal scales. At the same time the EU promotes improvements to the krill fishery management approach including via regular biomass surveys, better data collection and enhanced ecosystem monitoring. The EU also supports the harmonisation of the revised krill management approach with spatial management measures through proposals to create marine protected areas, which would contribute to safeguarding key krill habitats and foraging grounds.

E-10-2026-001185.t: Long-overdue establishment of return hubs in non-EU countries
qt: to the Commission Mary Khan (ESN) Subject:

Following the meeting of the Justice and Home Affairs Council in Brussels on 5 March 2026, it was confirmed that Germany and Austria, jointly with three other Member States, are pressing ahead with the establishment of return hubs in non-EU countries.1 A long-standing political demand from right-wing European parties is finally being met – albeit much too late. Efforts must now be made to implement this plan with maximum efficiency, to ensure that nothing stands in the way of this large-scale deportation offensive. The logistical challenges relating to choice of location must on no account be underestimated. In particular, the feasibility of central African states like Uganda, which is apparently on the shortlist, needs to be thoroughly assessed. After all, it is hard to imagine that migrants who have so far been deemed ineligible for deportation could in future be removed from Europe in large numbers, if they must first be flown thousands of kilometres to a return hub and then, in due course, escorted thousands of kilometres more back to their home countries. It is therefore clear that, strategically, preference should be given to North African countries close to the EU’s external borders. 1.
Is the Commission actively supporting the countries named above in establishing return hubs in non-EU countries, and what is its specific role in this context?
How is the Commission ensuring that return hubs can be run efficiently, and which nonEU countries does it consider suitable for this purpose?
How much progress has been made in negotiations with Uganda, and what clear advantages does this location offer over North African countries close to the EU’s external borders?

(19 May 2026) The Commission proposal for a Return Regulation (1) provides the legal framework setting out the minimum conditions for the establishment of return hubs. E-10-2026-001184.t: Outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease in Lesbos and the need for immediate European assistance
qt: to the Commission Konstantinos Arvanitis (The Left) Subject:

The outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease in Lesbos highlights the vulnerability of island and border regions in the European Union in the face of health crises affecting primary production. Small and medium-sized farmers are confronted with livestock losses and restrictions on their activity, and their economic survival is at serious risk, without adequate support from the EU. The European Commission’s response seems to be limited to the implementation of preexisting protocols and assistance upon request, without a clear commitment to prompt funding or full compensation. However, this approach shifts the burden of the crisis onto Member States and producers, exacerbating regional disparities and undermining the viability of the rural economy. Protecting the health of livestock, ensuring food security and supporting rural communities cannot and should not be treated solely as technical issues, but require immediate, coordinated and adequately funded European intervention. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Why are European immediate intervention mechanisms not activated pre-emptively?
Will it immediately mobilise European funds to fully compensate livestock farmers in Lesbos and strengthen public veterinary services?
Will it cover the costs of the necessary sanitary measures?

E-10-2026-001183.t: Health and safety of transgender people in Portugal
qt: to the Commission Catarina Martins (The Left) Subject:

The Portuguese Parliament has started the process to repeal Law No 38/2018, which establishes the right to self-determination of gender identity and gender expression. If passed, the self-determination, depathologised model of gender recognition will be put to an end and access to specific healthcare will be denied. The measures run counter to the EU’s LGBTIQ+ equality strategy, breach the right to respect for private and family life laid down in the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union and go against case-law that bans discrimination based on gender reassignment, as well as international scientific recommendations accepted by the WHO. In light of the above: 1.

Does the Commission believe that the legislation, the general terms of which have been approved in Portugal, is consistent with the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, particularly Articles 1, 7 and 21, and the Court of Justice of the European Union’s case-law regarding discrimination based on gender identity?
Does the Commission intend to examine whether these measures are in line with the LGBTIQ+ equality strategy 2026-2030 and the Member States’ equality of treatment obligations?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (15.6.2026) The Commission does not comment on draft legislation or ongoing national legislative processes. Equality and non-discrimination are founding values of the EU enshrined in the Treaty on the EU and the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the EU. The Commission remains firmly committed to combating discrimination and inequalities faced by LGBTIQ+1 people, also via the LGBTIQ+ equality strategy 2026-20302, which builds on the progress achieved under the 2020-2025 strategy. The Commission will continue to closely monitor the situation of LGBTIQ+ people across the EU, within the limits of its competences, and to use all the instruments at its disposal to uphold EU law in Member States.

E-10-2026-001182.t: Acute water supply problem in Aegina
qt: to the Commission Kostas Papadakis (NI) Subject:

A new fault in Aegina’s undersea water supply pipeline, in the same place where a previous fault had occurred, has caused serious problems leading to Aegina being cut off from the EYDAP (Athens Water Supply and Sewerage Company) water network with use of the pipeline being forbidden due to the unsuitability of the water. Despite falsely reassuring promises from the Government and the local administration claiming that ‘Aegina’s water supply will be fully restored by the end of February’, the problem remains acute. This situation shows that the State, the Government and the competent bodies – referring both to the current and previous administrations – are selectively unable to ensure the proper functioning and protection of an important but also very expensive project. This policy is underpinned by the EU’s strategy of turning water into an expensive commodity, as it is managed on a commercial basis. In view of the above, where does the Commission stand on the following: 1.

the fact that Directive 2000/60/EC has led to the fragmentation of water and irrigation infrastructure and the privatisation of profitable sections, resulting in water becoming a costly commodity that is received, stored and transported in infrastructure of dubious quality, with dire consequences for Aegina and many other parts of Greece that are also deprived of access to cheap and safe water and in several cases face serious water scarcity problems, with some also affected by flooding?
the legitimate demands of the Greek people for quality and cheap water to be provided with all the necessary infrastructure in place and under the sole responsibility of the State?

(12 May 2026) The Water Framework Directive (1) is neutral regarding public or private ownership of water services and leaves full discretion to Member States as regards national governance structures. The directive also allows Member States broad flexibility in setting water pricing and related cost-recovery mechanisms, taking into account socioeconomic, environmental, geographic, and climatic conditions, provided the environmental objectives are met. Member States are hence entirely responsible for water management, including allocation decisions, prioritisation during scarcity, infrastructure investment, and compliance with the Water Framework Directive and the Drinking Water Directive (2). The latter requires ensuring access to safe drinking water, to identify and manage supply risks, and taking timely preventive and corrective action where risks are known. Particular attention must also be paid to vulnerable groups during supply disruptions. To ensure access and affordability, Member States may use tools such as subsidies, social or progressive tariffs, and cost redistribution from households to polluters and intensive users, in line with the polluter-pays principle and the ‘adequate contribution’ clause. The Water Resilience Strategy (3) recognises access to clean, affordable water as a human right and includes a flagship action to support leakage reduction and infrastructure modernisation. Under the modernised cohesion policy (4), EUR 1.3 billion (EU contribution) (5) has been allocated to Greece for 2021-2027 to strengthen water management and resilience, including drinking water systems.

E-10-2026-001179.t: Judgment in  Shipova  (C‑43/24): encroachment on competences via the Court of Justice of the European Union?
qt: to the Commission Marieke Ehlers (PfE), Sebastian Kruis (PfE), Ton Diepeveen (PfE) Subject:
Judgment in Shipova (C‑43/24): encroachment on competences via the Court of Justice of the European Union?

According to the recent judgment of the Court of Justice of the European Union in the Shipova case (C‑43/24), national rules that make a change of gender in official documents subject to specific conditions may impede the right to free movement of persons. This is particularly the case where such rules lead to discrepancies with identity data registered in another Member State. Accordingly, policy areas such as civil status and identity registration, which, pursuant to the Treaties, fall within national competence, come under the influence of EU law via the Court’s case‑law none the less. 1.

What is the Commission’s assessment of the implications of the judgment in the Shipova case for the Member States’ competence to independently establish rules on the registration of gender in national identity documents and population registers?

Does the Commission share the concern that the Court of Justice’s interpretation of the right to free movement in this case may effectively compel Member States to recognise gender changes carried out in another Member State, even where their national legislation imposes different conditions within the exclusive competence of that Member State?

In its capacity as guardian of the Treaties, what steps is the Commission prepared to consider taking to ensure that the application of EU law on freedom of movement does not lead to an indirect harmonisation of national rules on civil status and identity registration, and that the competences of the Member States in this area are thus safeguarded?
at: (English version) to the Commission Marieke Ehlers (PfE), Sebastian Kruis (PfE), Ton Diepeveen (PfE) (20 March 2026) Subject: Judgment in Shipova (C-43/24): encroachment on competences via the Court of Justice of the European Union? According to the recent judgment of the Court of Justice of the European Union in the Shipova case (C-43/24), national rules that make a change of gender in official documents subject to specific conditions may impede the right to free movement of persons. This is particularly the case where such rules lead to discrepancies with identity data registered in another Member State. Accordingly, policy areas such as civil status and identity registration, which, pursuant to the Treaties, fall within national competence, come under the influence of EU law via the Court’s case-law none the less. 1. What is the Commission’s assessment of the implications of the judgment in the Shipova case for the Member States’ competence to independently establish rules on the registration of gender in national identity documents and population registers? 2. Does the Commission share the concern that the Court of Justice’s interpretation of the right to free movement in this case may effectively compel Member States to recognise gender changes carried out in another Member State, even where their national legislation imposes different conditions within the exclusive competence of that Member State? 3. In its capacity as guardian of the Treaties, what steps is the Commission prepared to consider taking to ensure that the application of EU law on freedom of movement does not lead to an indirect harmonisation of national rules on civil status and identity registration, and that the competences of the Member States in this area are thus safeguarded? (5 June 2026) In its judgment in case Shipova (1), the Court of Justice of the European Union (the Court) recalled that as EU law currently stands, a person’s status, which is relevant to the rules on changing the family name, patronymic, first name or legal gender identity of a person, is a matter which falls within the competence of the Member States. EU law does not detract from that competence. Nevertheless, in exercising that competence, each Member State must comply with EU law, in particular the provisions of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU) on the right conferred on all EU citizens to move and reside within the territory of the Member States. In that judgment, the Court found that legislation of a Member State that does not permit, in civil registers, changes of gender data (2) of one of its nationals who has exercised the right of free movement is contrary to Article 21 TFEU and Article 4(3) of Directive 2004/38/EC (3), in light of Article 7 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the EU. The Commission is committed, as guardian of the Treaties, to ensuring the correct application of EU free movement law as interpreted by the Court.

Judgment of 12 March 20216, K. M. H. v Obshtina Stara Zagora, C-43/24, EU:C:2026:183. Data such as the sex, family name, patronymic, first name and personal identification number. Directive 2004/38/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 29 April 2004 on the right of citizens of the Union and their family members to move and reside freely within the territory of the Member States.

E-10-2026-001178.t: Statistical coverage of workplace accidents in the public sector and capacity of labour inspectorates in the EU and candidate countries
qt: to the Commission Anthony Smith (The Left) Subject:

The information available suggests that France does not have centralised, comprehensive statistics on workplace accidents throughout the public sector. This makes the data on accidents at work incomplete and difficult to compare. 1.

Is the Commission aware of this situation, and can the Commission state whether other Member States also exclude all or part of the public sector or civil service from their statistics on workplace accidents and related indicators?

What measures has it taken, or what measures is it intending to take, to improve the coverage, reliability and comparability of statistics on workplace accidents in all sectors of activity, both in the Member States and in the candidate countries?

Does it have consolidated data on the resources of labour inspectorates in the EU and in candidate countries – particularly Ukraine, Moldova and Georgia – in terms of staff numbers, the number of inspections and the ratios relative to the number of workers?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.6.2026) Statistics on accidents at work are collected in accordance with Regulation (EU) No 349/20111. As provided for in Annex II2 to that Regulation, certain categories of civil servants subject to national confidentiality rules may be excluded from the statistical coverage. Any additional limitations in coverage arising from national legislation are documented in the statistical office of the EU (Eurostat) publicly available metadata3 on national data sources. The Commission continues to support improvements in the coverage, reliability and comparability of statistics on accidents at work. Efforts are ongoing to progressively enhance the scope of data collection, within the framework set by Regulation (EU) No 349/2011. In this context, Eurostat provides methodological guidance and facilitates the exchange of best practices to promote further harmonisation of national approaches. The Senior Labour Inspectors’ Committee publishes consolidated EU data on resources of labour inspectorates in a report4. Data on labour inspectorate resources in candidate countries is limited largely to what candidate countries provide for the annual enlargement reports5 and is not consolidated.
1 Commission Regulation (EU) No 349/2011 of 11 April 2011 implementing Regulation (EC) No 1338/2008 of

the European Parliament and of the Council on Community statistics on public health and health and safety at work, as regards statistics on accidents at work, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:32011R0349. 2 List of professions subject to confidentiality for delivery on a voluntary basis. 3 https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/hsw_acc_work_esms.htm. 4 The latest version of that report can be found here: https://circabc.europa.eu/ui/group/fea534f4-2590-4490bca6-504782b47c79/library/8515c860-bdea-4f5f-9e6f-a3f132c9043f?p=1&n=10&sort=modified_DESC. 5 See, e.g., https://enlargement.ec.europa.eu/news/2025-enlargement-package-shows-progress-towards-eumembership-key-enlargement-partners-2025-11-04_en for the reports of 2025.

E-10-2026-001177.t: Possible fertiliser shortage due to disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz
qt: to the Commission Loucas Fourlas (PPE) Subject:

Instability in the Gulf region and particularly in the Strait of Hormuz raises serious concerns about the disruption of global supply chains, including for key raw materials used in fertiliser production. Agricultural production in Europe is highly dependent on the stability of international markets in these sectors. Can the Commission answer the following: 1.
What is its assessment of possible fertiliser shortages due to developments in the Strait of Hormuz?
Is there a European contingency plan to ensure the availability of sufficient fertiliser?
What measures are being considered to protect European farmers from a possible increase in production costs?
at: (English version) to the Commission Loucas Fourlas (PPE) (20 March 2026) Subject: Possible fertiliser shortage due to disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz Instability in the Gulf region and particularly in the Strait of Hormuz raises serious concerns about the disruption of global supply chains, including for key raw materials used in fertiliser production. Agricultural production in Europe is highly dependent on the stability of international markets in these sectors. Can the Commission answer the following: 1.
What is its assessment of possible fertiliser shortages due to developments in the Strait of Hormuz?
Is there a European contingency plan to ensure the availability of sufficient fertiliser?
What measures are being considered to protect European farmers from a possible increase in production costs?

(10 June 2026) In the short term, tensions in the Strait of Hormuz are unlikely to lead to shortages of fertilisers in the EU, notably due to limited direct import exposure and the existence of sufficient levels of commercial stocks. However, they have contributed to increased global price volatility for fertilisers and other inputs that will affect prices in the EU. The Commission is closely monitoring the fertiliser markets through the Fertiliser Market Observatory (1), which met on 21 May 2026 to discuss recent developments. During the meeting, participants confirmed that fertiliser availability is currently not affected. To relieve pressure, the Commission adopted the Middle East temporary state aid Framework to support farmers and energy intensive industries (2). In addition, imports of ammonia, urea and other nitrogen fertilisers will benefit from tariff suspension, within given quotas, for a period of one year. On 19 May 2026, the Commission adopted the Fertiliser Action Plan (3) to diversify import sources, reinforce EU production capacity and reduce dependencies on imported energy and feedstocks. Short term actions include the mobilisation and possible top up of the agricultural reserve, reinforced liquidity support under the CAP and flexibility for advance payments. Longer term measures focus on supporting low carbon and bio-based fertilisers, promoting circular and recycled nutrients, and supporting nutrient use efficiency, precision farming to reduce farmers’ exposure to fertiliser price volatility and production costs over time.

E-10-2026-001175.t: Increase in fuel prices due to the crisis in Iran
qt: to the Commission Loucas Fourlas (PPE) Subject:

Hostilities in Iran have already disrupted international energy markets, which has had a direct impact on fuel prices. European citizens and businesses are potentially facing a further tightening of the screw when it comes to energy in what is an already difficult economic context. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
How does it assess the impact of the conflict in Iran on fuel prices within the EU?
What measures does it intend to take to protect consumers from further increases?
Is there a plan for a coordinated energy intervention in the event of a protracted crisis?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (11.5.2026) The Commission will continue monitoring the evolution of the crisis and assessing its potential impacts across a range of plausible scenarios. While there are no immediate concerns for the EU’s security of supply, oil and gas prices, particularly for refined products like diesel and jet fuel, face significant price volatility. To address the impacts of the disruption of oil and gas transit, the Commission has put forward on 22 April 2026 its new initiative AccelerateEU1, proposing timely, targeted and temporary measures to bring relief to consumers, while avoiding fragmented national responses. This includes a set of concrete measures to save and protect consumers and promote immediate energy savings, alongside structural reforms. By scaling up homegrown, clean energy and improving energy efficiency, electrification, flexibility and interconnectivity, Europe will reduce fossil fuel imports and become more resilient. The Commission’s response includes measures for coordinated energy interventions, such as in the areas of gas storage filling, oil stock releases, scenario analysis and sharing of best practices. The Energy Union Task Force, the Oil Coordination Group, the Gas Coordination Group and other platforms will support such coordination. Among others, the Commission will also propose legislative action on network charges, taxation and carbon costs to further support lowering energy bills.
1 https://energy.ec.europa.eu/strategy/accelerateeu-strengthen-eu-energy-resilience_en.

E-10-2026-001174.t: Abolition of the CAP stand-alone fund from 2028
qt: to the Commission Gerald Hauser (PfE) Subject:

It appears that, as of 2028, the Commission will no longer provide for a standalone CAP fund – the first time this has occurred since the Common Agricultural Policy's inception. Putting the CAP into a pooled fund will turn it into some kind of political slush fund to be used for example for the war in Ukraine. The announcement of billions of euros does not replace a clear ring-fencing. If the final distribution of funds is regulated solely through national and regional partnership plans, this offers no safeguard for agriculture, instead it invites political horse trading at farmers’ expense Planning certainty is thereby destroyed, reliability eroded and the agricultural sector is reduced to a supplicant. The opposition in the European Parliament and the warnings of the European Court of Auditors are a reflection of the risks involved. 1.
How can the Commission claim that agriculture will remain a priority if, at the same time, it abolishes the stand-alone CAP fund?
What legally binding guarantees are there to stop resources intended for agriculture in a pooled fund from being redirected into other policy areas?

Why is the Commission denying European farmers a clearly defined, strictly ringfenced, legally independent agricultural fund, when that is exactly what would be required for planning certainty and trust?
at: (English version) to the Commission Gerald Hauser (PfE) (20 March 2026) Subject: Abolition of the CAP stand-alone fund from 2028 It appears that, as of 2028, the Commission will no longer provide for a standalone CAP fund — the first time this has occurred since the Common Agricultural Policy's inception. Putting the CAP into a pooled fund will turn it into some kind of political slush fund to be used for example for the war in Ukraine. The announcement of billions of euros does not replace a clear ringfencing. If the final distribution of funds is regulated solely through national and regional partnership plans, this offers no safeguard for agriculture, instead it invites political horse trading at farmers’ expense Planning certainty is thereby destroyed, reliability eroded and the agricultural sector is reduced to a supplicant. The opposition in the European Parliament and the warnings of the European Court of Auditors are a reflection of the risks involved. 1. How can the Commission claim that agriculture will remain a priority if, at the same time, it abolishes the stand-alone CAP fund? 2. What legally binding guarantees are there to stop resources intended for agriculture in a pooled fund from being redirected into other policy areas? 3. Why is the Commission denying European farmers a clearly defined, strictly ring-fenced, legally independent agricultural fund, when that is exactly what would be required for planning certainty and trust? (20 May 2026) 1. A simpler and more flexible Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) will be delivered through national and regional partnership (NRP) plans (1). In the context of multiple pressing EU priorities to address, the proposal guarantees a minimum ring-fenced amount of EUR 293.7 billion for farmers income support. This shows a recognition of the crucial role of farmers and the CAP to build an attractive, competitive and sustainable agri-food sector. 2. The guaranteed amount in the legislation ensures stability and predictability for the farming community. The amount can and will need to be complemented by Member States in accordance with their needs, by accessing the unallocated part of the NRP fund. The Commission suggested a rural target of 10% (2) to strengthen support for rural areas. In addition, to ensure further resources are accessible for Member States as of 2028 for addressing the needs of farmers and rural communities, the Commission has proposed that Member States will be able to access to up to two-thirds of the flexibility amount (3) in the plans, normally available for the stage of the midterm review. 3. The advantage of a simpler, more flexible CAP, delivered through NRP plans, is that it offers Member States increased flexibility, bringing policies together to deliver better results. The NRP plans are tailored to Member States’ needs, while ensuring predictability for long-term investment and support for farmers and regions, and increased flexibility in a fastchanging world. The NRP plans provide a harmonised planning and reporting framework that foster synergies and a leverage effect across different funding elements, while supporting EU common objectives and priorities.

E-10-2026-001173.t: Age verification procedures: risks to privacy and data security
qt: to the Commission Catherine Griset (PfE), André Rougé (PfE), Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE), Pierre Pimpie (PfE), Valérie Deloge (PfE), Julie Rechagneux (PfE) Subject:

As part of measures aiming to restrict minors’ access to social media, platforms are required to verify the age of users effectively. Some low-risk verification methods exist, such as checking how long an account has been active or whether a payment method has been registered. However, other methods rely on the transfer of sensitive data, such as proof of identity or facial recognition, often through a third-party authenticator. As a result, they pose significant risks to privacy and data security, owing to a mass rise in hacking (now facilitated by artificial intelligence). On top of this, the platforms concerned are obliged to share their information with certain states, including third countries. 1.
Will the Commission commit to not forcing platforms to adopt age verification procedures that could be hacked?

How can we protect our fellow citizens from multiple national, European and foreign public authorities seeking to use age verification and digital identification to extend their surveillance at the expense of our fundamental rights?
Why not introduce measures designed to limit time spent on social media, which would be inherently less intrusive?
at: (English version) to the Commission Catherine Griset (PfE), André Rougé (PfE), Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE), Pierre Pimpie (PfE), Valérie Deloge (PfE), Julie Rechagneux (PfE) (20 March 2026) Subject: Age verification procedures: risks to privacy and data security As part of measures aiming to restrict minors’ access to social media, platforms are required to verify the age of users effectively. Some low-risk verification methods exist, such as checking how long an account has been active or whether a payment method has been registered. However, other methods rely on the transfer of sensitive data, such as proof of identity or facial recognition, often through a third-party authenticator. As a result, they pose significant risks to privacy and data security, owing to a mass rise in hacking (now facilitated by artificial intelligence). On top of this, the platforms concerned are obliged to share their information with certain states, including third countries. 1.
Will the Commission commit to not forcing platforms to adopt age verification procedures that could be hacked?

2. How can we protect our fellow citizens from multiple national, European and foreign public authorities seeking to use age verification and digital identification to extend their surveillance at the expense of our fundamental rights? 3.
Why not introduce measures designed to limit time spent on social media, which would be inherently less intrusive?

(19 May 2026) The guidelines on the protection of minors (1) under the Digital Services Act (DSA) (2) set out guidance for where age assurance technologies should be deployed. They include minimum specifications to ensure that age assurance measures are accurate, robust, non-intrusive, reliable, and non-discriminatory. The guidelines are aligned with European Data Protection Board guidance (3), requiring platform providers to only process data that is necessary for age assurance purposes, and to ensure that data processed for this purpose is not stored or used for other purposes. The Commission developed an age verification solution (4) allowing users to prove they are 18+ online. A blueprint is available to Member States for customisation and publication. Designed to meet the highest privacy standards, it uses ‘zero-knowledge proof’ technology to securely prove that the user has a valid age credential without revealing the credential or any other information. The user’s identity is only checked once during the issuance of the proof of age. The proof does not contain any identity data, only disclosing that the user is 18+. The trusted proof provider is not informed about online services for which the proof is used. On 29 April, the Commission adopted a recommendation urging Member States to accelerate the rollout of the age verification app and make it available by the end of 2026 (5). Under the DSA, online platforms accessible to minors are required to provide them a high level of privacy, safety, and security. The aforementioned guidelines outline steps that platforms can take to do so, including to reduce addictive design.

E-10-2026-001172.t: Impact of Article 19 of COM(2025)1006 on Member States with internal grid bottlenecks
qt: to the Commission Beatrice Timgren (ECR), Dick Erixon (ECR), Charlie Weimers (ECR) Subject:

Under the EU electricity market design, certain Member States, including Sweden, have introduced internal bidding zones in line with internal market requirements, thereby ensuring the transparency of grid constraints and avoiding restrictions on cross-border electricity trade. In such systems, a substantial proportion of congestion income is generated by internal bottlenecks, notably between production and demand centres, and is ultimately borne by consumers facing persistent regional price differences. Under Article 19 of its proposed regulation on guidelines for trans-European energy infrastructure (COM(2025)1006), the Commission introduces a requirement to earmark a proportion of congestion income, including a 25 % ring-fenced component, for investments in EU-level infrastructure projects1. Against this background: 1.

Can the Commission clarify whether congestion income generated predominantly by internal bottlenecks will, in practice, remain available to address bottlenecks within the Member State concerned, or whether the 25 % ring-fencing will reduce the resources available to strengthen that country’s national grid?
Does the Commission consider that the 25 % ring-fencing of congestion income may result in a de facto redistribution of resources borne by consumers within specific Member States?
How does the Commission assess the compatibility of these provisions with the Member States’ responsibility for addressing internal grid constraints and setting investment priorities?
https://energy.ec.europa.eu/topics/infrastructure/european-grids_en.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.5.2026) The proposal in the Grids Package builds on Regulation (EU) 2019/9431, which governs the use of congestion income. The objective is to provide stronger investment signals for crossborder energy infrastructure projects. This should also improve consistency and transparency, contributing to greater predictability for investors. Furthermore, using congestion income for network investments that reduce structural congestion will provide long-term benefits for consumers and industries. First, it should be clarified that only after priority objectives a)2 and c)3 have been fulfilled, would 25% of the remaining congestion income be reserved for investments in Projects of Common Interest (PCIs) and Projects of Mutual Interest (PMIs). Second, the Commission’s proposal foresees no centralisation or EU-level pooling of congestion income. Congestion income remains nationally managed and retained within the Member State where it is generated, for PCI and PMI investments located within that same Member State, including internal infrastructure with PCI status, unless national authorities decide otherwise. Furthermore, the Commission supports the establishment of internal bidding zones where appropriate and acknowledges the specific circumstances of Member States that have implemented such systems. The Commission has already engaged with Member States to address these specificities where necessary and remains ready to continue doing so. The proposal is currently under discussion by the European Parliament and the Council. The Commission stands ready to support co-legislators in their discussions.

1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32019R0943&qid=1775155216966. 2 Guaranteeing the actual availability of allocated capacity. 3 Compensation to offshore renewable electricity generation plant operators.

E-10-2026-001171.t: Implementation of Regulation (EU) 2024/3110 and delays in the publication of European Assessment Documents
qt: to the Commission Christian Doleschal (PPE) Subject:

The timely availability of European Assessment Documents (EADs) and European Technical Assessments (ETAs) is essential for the placing on the market of innovative construction products, in particular where no harmonised standards exist. Stakeholders report that since the entry into force of Regulation (EU) 2024/31101 (Construction Products Regulation – CPR 2024), the development and publication of new EADs have been delayed because of missing implementing provisions, notably regarding sustainability and digital requirements. These delays risk slowing down construction, renovation and infrastructure projects and may negatively affect innovation and competitiveness in the European construction sector. The Commission is asked: 1.
Which legal, technical or operational prerequisites for the development and publication of EADs under CPR 2024 are not yet in place, and when does the Commission expect them to be available?
Given that not all CPR 2024 requirements are fully implemented, is the Commission considering transitional measures to allow the continued development and publication of EADs?

What measures will the Commission take to prevent a regulatory gap that could delay innovation and increase the cost of construction and infrastructure projects before CPR 2024 becomes fully operational?

Regulation (EU) 2024/3110 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 November 2024 laying down harmonised rules for the marketing of construction products and repealing Regulation (EU) No 305/2011 (OJ L, 2024/3110, 18.12.2024, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/3110/oj).
at: (English version) to the Commission Christian Doleschal (PPE) (20 March 2026) Subject: Implementation of Regulation (EU) 2024/3110 and delays in the publication of European Assessment Documents The timely availability of European Assessment Documents (EADs) and European Technical Assessments (ETAs) is essential for the placing on the market of innovative construction products, in particular where no harmonised standards exist. Stakeholders report that since the entry into force of Regulation (EU) 2024/3110 (1) (Construction Products Regulation — CPR 2024), the development and publication of new EADs have been delayed because of missing implementing provisions, notably regarding sustainability and digital requirements. These delays risk slowing down construction, renovation and infrastructure projects and may negatively affect innovation and competitiveness in the European construction sector. The Commission is asked: 1.
Which legal, technical or operational prerequisites for the development and publication of EADs under CPR 2024 are not yet in place, and when does the Commission expect them to be available?
Given that not all CPR 2024 requirements are fully implemented, is the Commission considering transitional measures to allow the continued development and publication of EADs?

What measures will the Commission take to prevent a regulatory gap that could delay innovation and increase the cost of construction and infrastructure projects before CPR 2024 becomes fully operational?

(13 May 2026) For the publication of a European Assessment Document (EAD), a delegated act for assessment and verification systems (AVS) has to be in place. The Commission is currently preparing this act. Its draft has already been discussed extensively with Member States and stakeholders, and it will be sent for Council and Parliament scrutiny soon. The format of European Technical Assessments (ETA) ((EU) 2026/387) has been published on 23 February 2026. There are no prerequisites missing for the development of EADs under Construction Products Regulation (CPR-2024) (1). The new aspects of CPR-2024 (predetermined environmental essential characteristics, machine readability and guidelines for general product information, instructions for use and safety information) will be stipulated in the process of EAD development by the European Organisation for Technical Assessment (EOTA). The Commission will assess those aspects for each draft EAD when submitted to the Commission according to Annex VI point 8 of CPR-2024. Until now EOTA has only informed the Commission about two EAD work programmes according to Annex VI point 3 (2). So far, the Commission has not received any draft EAD for assessment according to Annex VI point 8 or 9 (3). Therefore, there is no delay in the publication of EADs. Furthermore, manufacturers actively continue to use the published EADs under the CPR-2011 (4) for issuing new ETAs. This possibility will continue to be available for manufacturers until 8 January 2031. It is also important to note that during 2025 the Commission published 110 EADs which are now available for issuing ETAs. Therefore, no regulatory gap exists that would require proposing transitional measures.

E-10-2026-001170.t: Does the Commission intend to address electoral procedures, such as rules governing early voting, in its future reports on the rule of law in Slovenia?
qt: to the Commission Branko Grims (PPE) Subject:

Legal experts have long been pointing out the controversial nature of early voting in Slovenia’s National Assembly elections. Article 69 of the Slovenian Elections Act (ZVDZ) clearly states: ‘Voting shall take place at a special polling station within the district election committee’s area.’ In clear violation of this, however, in Ljubljana, for example, as many as 14 districts vote at a single location, namely Stožice. This means that voters in at least 13 districts are in violation of the law, as they are required to vote outside their district. For voters living far away, this process can be an obstacle, which effectively violates their right to participate and the constitutional principle of equality. In total, there are as many as 26 such illegal districts in Slovenia. Further doubts about the fairness of the election are raised by the coalition’s persistent refusal to release the results of early voting as they come in. Instead of counting ballots daily, recording the results and signing the minutes, ballots are kept uncounted for several days in boxes that are unsealed. They are not counted until Sunday. Security for the ballot boxes in Ljubljana is provided by Mayor Zoran Janković’s office, which, given his political prominence, raises legitimate doubts about the neutrality of the process. Can the Commission therefore answer the following question: Does it intend to address electoral procedures, such as rules governing early voting, in its future reports on the rule of law in Slovenia?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (5.6.2026) As enshrined in Articles 2 and 10 of the Treaty on European Union, democracy is a founding value on which the EU is built. Free and fair elections are at the core of democracy. The Commission does not have a general power to intervene in electoral matters of the Member States. The conduct and the organisation of elections are the competence and responsibility of the Member States, in accordance with their national constitutional and legislative rules, while respecting their international obligations and EU law. National competent authorities and courts have the primary responsibility of ensuring compliance with these rules. Electoral procedure is not specifically included in the scope of the annual Rule of Law Report. The Commission supports Member States’ efforts to ensure free and fair elections, particularly through the European Cooperation Network on Elections1, and relying on its Recommendation on inclusive and resilient electoral processes in the Union2. To address the growing and evolving challenges to democracies across the EU, the Commission adopted the European Democracy Shield in November 20253. In this context, among other initiatives, the Commission will develop a repository of common references and standards for electoral processes, based primarily on exchanges within the European Cooperation Network on Elections.
1 https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/policies/justice-and-fundamental-rights/democracy-eu-

citizenship-anti-corruption/democracy-and-electoral-rights/european-cooperation-network-elections_en. 2 Commission Recommendation (EU) 2023/2829 of 12 December 2023 on inclusive and resilient electoral processes in the Union and enhancing the European nature and efficient conduct of the elections to the European Parliament, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reco/2023/2829/oj/eng. 3 https://commission.europa.eu/document/download/2539eb53-9485-4199-bfdc97166893ff45_en?filename=JUST_template_comingsoon_standard_1.pdf.

E-10-2026-001168.t: Implementation of the CJEU judgment in Case C-461/24 concerning environmental assessments for wind power projects
qt: to the Commission Adrián Vázquez Lázara (PPE) Subject:

In August 2025, the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) delivered its judgment in case C-461/24, in response to a question for a preliminary ruling by the High Court of Justice of Galicia (TSXG), on the interpretation of Directive 2011/92/EU, as amended by Directive 2014/52/EU, on the assessment of the effects of certain projects on the environment. The CJEU stated that the law does not require that all the sectoral reports by the authorities consulted be made available to the public before the public information procedure is opened, provided that prompt and effective access to material information on the project, in particular the environmental impact assessment, is guaranteed. What is more, the CJEU stressed that to require otherwise might be unduly burdensome for national administrations. However, following this ruling, the TSXG has continued to suspend court proceedings concerning wind farm authorisations, thus maintaining legal uncertainty in the application of EU legislation. In view of the principle of primacy of EU law and the binding nature of CJEU judgments: 1.
Is the Commission monitoring compliance with the judgment in case C-461/24?
What measures could it take to ensure that it is implemented properly?

(11 May 2026) The Commission closely monitors the implementation of EU law in the Member States, including the application of the caselaw of the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU). The ruling of the CJEU mentioned by the Honourable Member is now reflected in the Commission proposal for a regulation on speeding-up environmental assessments (1) whose Article 4(4) reads: ‘Competent authorities shall consult the public concerned by the environmental decision-making procedure relating to a plan, programme or project subject to an assessment in accordance with paragraph 1 at the same time as they consult the authorities likely to be concerned by that plan, programme or project (…)’. It is worth noting that under Article 16 (6) of the Renewable Energy Directive (2) Member States are required to ensure that administrative and judicial appeals in the context of a renewable energy project and related infrastructure, including appeals related to environmental aspects, are subject to the most expeditious administrative and judicial procedure that is available at the relevant national, regional and local level.

E-10-2026-001167.t: Structural inequalities and the need for Europe to take immediate action to address the EU gender pension gap
qt: to the Commission Elena Kountoura (The Left) Subject:

In the EU, the pension gap between men and women stands at 25 %1 and is the result of structural inequalities that accumulate throughout people’s working lives2. Care-related career breaks, part-time and informal employment, and the over-representation of women in historically undervalued sectors and in jobs where they are paid less for work of equal value, exacerbate the pay gap and result in cumulative losses when women retire3. Millions of informal carers are not covered by social security systems, as well as being excluded from occupational pension schemes and being at risk of poverty in old age. Given that at the current pace it will take up to 90 years to close the pension gap in the EU4, and taking into account the new Gender Equality Strategy 2026-2030 and the European Parliament resolution calling for an action plan to tackle the gender pay and pension gap5, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

Does it intend to put forward an action plan that sets additional measurable targets with a specific timeline to reduce the pension gap, besides the process for monitoring and exchanging best practices, which has been foreseen the strategy?

Will it support the allocation of dedicated European resources in the next MFF and the inclusion in the European Semester’s country-specific recommendations of measures aimed at accessible quality care services and the elimination of the gender pension gap?
Does it intend to propose minimum European standards to allow caregiving periods to count towards pension entitlements?

In Greece, the pension gap in the 65+ age group reaches 21.5 %, accurately reflecting this accumulation (ELSTAT, Pay gap between men and women, Reference year 2024, Period 2022-2024, Piraeus, 30-01-2026). Eurostat, EU-SILC, ilc_pnp13, 2024. The gender pension gap is not only the result of accumulating pay inequalities over the course of a lifetime but also of different opportunities on the labour market, unequal distribution of informal care work at home, and gender bias in society. According to official data, there has been a modest reduction over the past decade in the average gender pay and pension gaps across the EU and the current pace of change remains insufficient to close the gaps before 2100. European Parliament resolution of 11 March 2026 on the gender pay and pension gap in the EU (2025/2038 (INI)).

Does it intend to put forward an action plan that sets additional measurable targets with a specific timeline to reduce the pension gap, besides the process for monitoring and exchanging best practices, which has been foreseen the strategy?

Will it support the allocation of dedicated European resources in the next MFF and the inclusion in the European Semester’s country-specific recommendations of measures aimed at accessible quality care services and the elimination of the gender pension gap?
Does it intend to propose minimum European standards to allow caregiving periods to count towards pension entitlements?

(22 May 2026) As outlined in the 2026-2030 Gender Equality Strategy (1), the Commission will strengthen monitoring of the gender pension gap and poverty risks among women aged 65+, analysing root causes (gender employment and pay gaps, part-time work disparities) via the social scoreboard. The Commission will also map best practices on addressing the gender pension gap and publish the 2027 report on adequate social protection in old age, detailing older women’s socioeconomic challenges and persistent pension and poverty gender gaps. Within the framework of the European Semester, the Commission systematically assesses relevant indicators to inform targeted policy responses and makes recommendations to Member States, as appropriate. The Commission proposal for the next Multiannual Financial Framework, which includes National and Regional Partnership Plans, will rely on the European Semester as one of the elements of the reference framework underpinning the programming and design of the plans. The proposal also envisages social cohesion, social inclusion, equal opportunities, access to services and associated infrastructure and supporting strong social safety nets as specific objectives. Moreover, the proposed Performance Regulation makes gender equality a horizontal principle, embedding it across EU funding through gender-disaggregated indicators and expenditure tracking to assess the performance. The Commission’s proposal is under negotiation between the Council and the Parliament.

In Greece, the pension gap in the 65+ age group reaches 21.5%, accurately reflecting this accumulation (ELSTAT, Pay gap between men and women, Reference year 2024, Period 2022-2024, Piraeus, 30-01-2026). Eurostat, EU-SILC, ilc_pnp13, 2024. The gender pension gap is not only the result of accumulating pay inequalities over the course of a lifetime but also of different opportunities on the labour market, unequal distribution of informal care work at home, and gender bias in society. According to official data, there has been a modest reduction over the past decade in the average gender pay and pension gaps across the EU and the current pace of change remains insufficient to close the gaps before 2100. Propose the full suspension of the EU-Israel Association Agreement given that Israel is clearly breaching Article 2 of that agreement?
