E-10-2026-001164.t: Geheimdienst V – issues regarding competence and the relationship between the proposed Commission ‘intelligence cell’, the Commission’s ECDR and EU INTCEN
qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Christine Anderson (ESN) Subject:

The European External Action Service (EEAS) hosts the EU Intelligence and Situation Centre (INTCEN), which analyses intelligence voluntarily shared by the Member States to support the EU’s common foreign and security policy. However, the Commission has confirmed that it is considering establishing an internal ‘intelligence cell’ to strengthen its analytical capacities1. It has already created the European Centre for Democratic Resilience (ECDR), dealing with foreign interference, which can be interpreted as a matter of security. Given that the Commission’s role in foreign policy is limited, can the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy (VP/HR) answer the following: 1.

Has the VP/HR been consulted regarding the Commission’s plans to establish such structures and can she confirm whether she or the Commission made a request to the Member States about possibly sharing intelligence or EU classified information?
In the VP/HR’s view, would creating an intelligence-analysis capability within the Commission duplicate or overlap with the analytical functions currently carried out by EU INTCEN?

Does the VP/HR consider that establishing such a structure within the Commission would be compatible with the institutional balance established by the Treaties, particularly regarding the role of the EEAS and EU INTCEN in intelligence analysis related to the EU’s foreign and security policy?
Answer to Written Question, E-004545/2025(ASW), https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/E-102025-004545-ASW_EN.html.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (10.6.2026) Plans to establish a structure such as an ‘intelligence cell’ are subject to exchanges between the Commission and the European External Action Service, in full compliance with relevant Treaty principles. Currently, the European External Action Service hosts the EU Intelligence and Situation Centre which has a specific mandate. The European Union pursues its objectives by appropriate means commensurate with the competences which are conferred upon it by the Treaties.

E-10-2026-001163.t: Madrid-Málaga high-speed rail corridor: prolonged closure, economic damage and passenger rights
qt: to the Commission Borja Giménez Larraz (PPE), Carmen Crespo Díaz (PPE), Juan Ignacio Zoido Álvarez (PPE) Subject:

Services on the Madrid-Málaga high-speed line, which is part of the trans-European transport network (TEN-T) and has been co-funded by the European Investment Bank, have been suspended since 18 January 2026, following the Adamuz accident, in which 46 people were killed, and a landslide in Álora (Málaga). Adif, Spain’s state-owned railway infrastructure manager, has postponed the line’s reopening until past Easter, which means it will be closed for over three months. Andalusia’s tourism sector is estimating EUR 2 billion in losses and some 6 000 seasonal jobs at risk, while passengers are dealing with cancellations, systematic delays, insufficient information and inadequate re-routing. In January 2025, the European Investment Bank lent Adif EUR 350 million to carry out renovation work on, and improve the resilience of, Spain’s railway infrastructure. In light of Regulation (EU) 2024/1679 and Directive (EU) 2016/798: 1.
Does the Commission consider the closure of this EU-co-funded TEN-T corridor to raise questions about Adif’s compliance with maintenance, safety and operational continuity obligations?
What action can the Commission take to ensure that Member States comply with the above obligations with regard to co-funded railway infrastructure?
What action does the Commission intend to take to ensure compliance with the obligations to inform, re-route and compensate the passengers affected (Regulation (EU) 2021/782)?
at: (English version) to the Commission Borja Giménez Larraz (PPE), Carmen Crespo Díaz (PPE), Juan Ignacio Zoido Álvarez (PPE) (19 March 2026) Subject: Madrid-Málaga high-speed rail corridor: prolonged closure, economic damage and passenger rights Services on the Madrid-Málaga high-speed line, which is part of the trans-European transport network (TEN-T) and has been co-funded by the European Investment Bank, have been suspended since 18 January 2026, following the Adamuz accident, in which 46 people were killed, and a landslide in Álora (Málaga). Adif, Spain’s state-owned railway infrastructure manager, has postponed the line’s reopening until past Easter, which means it will be closed for over three months. In light of Regulation (EU) 2024/1679 and Directive (EU) 2016/798: 1.

What action does the Commission intend to take to ensure compliance with the obligations to inform, re-route and compensate the passengers affected (Regulation (EU) 2021/782)?

(27 May 2026) According to Article 49 of the trans-European transport network (TEN-T) Regulation (1), ‘Member States’ shall make all possible efforts to ensure the TEN-T infrastructure is maintained in a way that it provides, during its lifetime, a high level of service and safety adapted to the traffic flow’, without prejudice to their responsibility for the planning, financing, and management of infrastructure maintenance. Potential and temporary disruptions of service for safety controls and other necessary works are not in contradiction with this requirement, which is why the Commission does not intend to raise questions regarding Administrador de Infraestructuras Ferroviarias’ (Adif’s) decision at this stage. The European Investment Bank (EIB) loan agreements include binding conditions, such as compliance with EU law (including EU railway safety law). If breached, the EIB can suspend disbursements or cancel or restructure the loan. EIB financing is based on a full lifecycle perspective. Loan conditions usually require that the promoter maintains the infrastructure in good condition. Failure to maintain assets can trigger suspension of disbursements. Finally, it is for the Member States and in particular their National Enforcement Bodies (NEBs) to closely monitor compliance with Regulation (EU) 2021/782 (2) and take the measures necessary to ensure that the rights of passengers are upheld. If NEBs and Member States do not correctly implement and apply the EU rules on passenger rights, the Commission may decide to take appropriate action.

E-10-2026-001160.t: Use of the ‘borderline content’ handbook promoted at the EU Internet Forum for moderating lawful political speech
qt: to the Commission Tom Vandendriessche (PfE), Barbara Bonte (PfE), Gerolf Annemans (PfE), Tomasz Froelich (ESN), György Hölvényi (PfE), Roman Haider (PfE), Enikő Győri (PfE), Pál Szekeres (PfE), Kinga Gál (PfE), András László (PfE), Annamária Vicsek (PfE), András Gyürk (PfE), Ernő Schaller-Baross (PfE), Fabrice Leggeri (PfE), Petra Steger (PfE), Mélanie Disdier (PfE), Ewa Zajączkowska-Hernik (ESN), Marc Jongen (ESN), Christine Anderson (ESN), Stephen Nikola Bartulica (ECR), Volker Schnurrbusch (ESN), Tiago Moreira de Sá (PfE), Erik Kaliňák (NI), Alexander Jungbluth (ESN), Virginie Joron (PfE), Marieke Ehlers (PfE), Petr Bystron (ESN), Markus Buchheit (ESN), Elisabeth Dieringer (PfE), Fernand Kartheiser (NI), Ondřej Knotek (PfE), Sebastian Tynkkynen (ECR) Subject:

Documents disclosed in a report from the US House Judiciary Committee show that, as part of the EU Internet Forum, the Commission promoted a handbook of borderline content in relation to violent extremism that explicitly classifies ‘populist rhetoric’, ‘anti-EU content’, ‘anti-elite content’, ‘political satire’, ‘meme subculture’ and ‘anti-LGBTIQ content’ as problematic categories to be monitored or limited by platforms, even though these are in themselves lawful forms of political or social expression. 1.

How does the Commission justify equating lawful Eurosceptic or anti-establishment speech and political satire with ‘violent extremism’ in an official handbook, and on what precise legal basis did it urge platforms to use these categories for content moderation beyond what is strictly illegal under EU or national law?

What safeguards did the Commission put in place to ensure that such guidance would not result in systematic discrimination against peaceful opposition movements, conservative viewpoints on migration and gender, or satirical criticism of EU institutions and policies?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (19.5.2026) The EU Internet Forum provides a collaborative environment to explore responses against terrorism, child sexual abuse, and other crimes online. The handbook in question provides information to support online platforms in their voluntary efforts to keep their users safe and to protect EU fundamental rights, including freedom of expression. The handbook does not equate Eurosceptic or anti-establishment speech and political satire with violent extremism. EU legislation, such as the Digital Services Act (DSA)1 and the Terrorist Content Online Regulation2, includes strong safeguards to protect fundamental rights, in particular freedom of expression and information online. For example, the DSA introduces transparency requirements and redress mechanism, empowering users to obtain explanations and redress if their content is removed or restricted. These measures aim to ensure that any content moderation aiming to remove illegal and harmful content remains lawful, non-discriminatory and fully aligned with EU values.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/2065/oj/eng. 2 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2021/784/oj/eng.

qt: to the Commission Daniel Buda (PPE) Subject:

For three decades there were no outbreaks of Newcastle disease in Germany, but the country is once again experiencing outbreaks on poultry farms, including on a large holding in Brandenburg, where over 375 000 laying hens have been infected and are about to be slaughtered1. This situation has placed additional pressure on egg production, in a context where the egg industry is already warning of an imbalance between supply and demand. The disease has spread despite the vaccination of poultry being mandatory. The competent authorities have stressed that vaccination and strict biosecurity measures continue to be essential in order contain the virus and reduce economic losses in the poultry sector. Against this backdrop: 1.
What is the Commission’s assessment of the potential impact of these outbreaks on egg production and food security in the European Union?

Does the Commission intend to make preventive vaccination mandatory across the EU and to strengthen coordination on prevention, vaccination and biosecurity in order to reduce the risk of outbreaks spreading and to safeguard the stability of the European poultry sector?

What measures is the Commission planning to support farmers affected by outbreaks of Newcastle disease, including when it comes to compensating them for economic losses and ensuring continuity of production?
https://agrointel.ro/347797/gripa-aviara-dublata-de-boala-newcastle.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (5.5.2026) The Commission is closely monitoring the evolution of the different animal product markets, focusing on the potential impact of animal disease outbreaks1. The production of eggs increased in some Member States, in particular in Germany in 2025 compared to 2024. Egg imports also increased in 2025. The EU legislative framework for animal health2 recognises and enables the use of vaccines to ensure effective prevention and control of category A diseases, including for vaccination against Newcastle disease (ND). In addition, vaccination against ND is required for certain movements within the EU3 and for entry into the EU4 from third countries or territories. In some Member States, vaccination against ND is mandatory, but certain are aiming on diseasefree status from infection with ND virus without vaccination, as granted in the EU specific legislation5. For decades well-designed and properly implemented vaccination against ND, coupled with appropriate biosecurity practices effectively prevented outbreaks. Therefore, in the current context of budget difficulties, it is essential to prioritise the use of budget available for the support of emergency measures envisaged by the Single Market Programme (SMP)6 to other category A diseases where vaccines are not available or not sufficiently effective to prevent the disease. Hence, in 2025 the Commission phased out co-financing emergency measures for ND under the SMP7.

E-10-2026-001157.t: Third-party litigation funding in the EU and the Product Liability Directive
qt: to the Commission Tobiasz Bocheński (ECR) Subject:

The European Parliament adopted its resolution of 13 September 2022 on responsible private funding of litigation1 with a large majority, calling on the Commission to introduce a harmonised regulatory framework for third-party litigation funding (TPLF). The volume of mass litigation is rising strongly and recent legislative developments, including the revised Product Liability Directive (PLD)2 and the Representative Actions Directive (RAD)3, will further increase litigation exposure for companies, including small and mediumsized enterprises, in the EU. The Commission’s study of 21 March 2025 entitled ‘Mapping Third Party Litigation Funding in the European Union’ confirms the rapid development of the multi-billion euro TPLF market and identifies transparency gaps, risks of conflicts of interest and divergent regulatory approaches in the Member States. 1.

Will the Commission issue guidance to ensure consistent PLD implementation by Member States and prevent unintended results, such as a reversal of the burden of proof, in order to protect EU competitiveness and the single market?

Despite broad support from Parliament for EU-level regulation of TPLF, why has the Commission not yet proposed any initiative on governance, transparency or financial oversight for litigation funders?

How does the Commission evaluate the combined effects of the new PLD, collective redress (RAD), and TPLF growth on legal certainty, insurance, compliance costs and EU competitiveness and simplification?

European Parliament resolution of 13 September 2022 with recommendations to the Commission on Responsible private funding of litigation (OJ C 125, 5.4.2023, p. 2). Directive (EU) 2024/2853 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 23 October 2024 on liability for defective products and repealing Council Directive 85/374/EEC (OJ L, 2024/2853, 18.11.2024, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2024/2853/oj). Directive (EU) 2020/1828 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 25 November 2020 on representative actions for the protection of the collective interests of consumers and repealing Directive 2009/22/EC (OJ L 409, 4.12.2020, p. 1, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2020/1828/oj).
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (5.5.2026) The Commission is monitoring the interaction between Directive (EU) 2024/2853 on Product Liability (PLD), the Directive (EU) 2020/1828 on Representative Actions (RAD) and developments in third-party litigation funding (TPLF), including their implications for legal certainty, costs and the internal market. The PLD strikes a careful balance between innovation and consumer protection. The Commission does not plan to issue specific guidelines but supports consistent implementation through cooperation with Member States, expert meetings, bilateral exchanges and transposition checks. In March 2025, the Commission published a study on TPLF1 which served as a basis for discussions with the European Parliament, the Member States and stakeholders in the HighLevel Forum on Justice for Growth. TPLF remains limited overall and does not reveal systemic risks. Participants expressed scepticism about the need for regulation and invited the Commission to continue monitoring developments, while assessing whether further action may be warranted. Under Article 23 of RAD, the Commission will evaluate its application by June 2028 in line with the 2030 Consumer Agenda and action plan for consumers in the single market.2 This evaluation will allow the Commission to determine whether further measures are necessary. It is therefore premature to draw conclusions on the combined effects of these legal instruments.

E-10-2026-001156.t: Draft regulation on plants obtained by certain new genomic techniques (NGT)
qt: to the Commission Tobiasz Bocheński (ECR) Subject:

In view of the forthcoming second reading of the draft Regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council on plants obtained by certain new genomic techniques and their food and feed, I am writing to the Commission to request clarification on several key issues that are causing serious concern amongst citizens, farmers and the scientific community. Under the proposal, a significant proportion of NGT plants (category 1) are to be exempted from existing GMO regulations, including requirements for risk assessment for human, animal and environmental health, traceability, monitoring and labelling. At the same time, the draft adopts the criterion of ‘equivalence’ between NGT plants and conventional plants, which – according to some experts – lacks sufficient scientific justification. Taking the above into consideration: 1.
On which specific published scientific analyses is the assumption of equivalence between NGT plants and conventional plants based?
How does the Commission intend to ensure a high level of health and environmental protection in the event that Category 1 NGT plants are exempted from a full risk assessment?
How will market transparency and consumers’ right to information be ensured where labelling requirements are reduced?
at: (English version) to the Commission Tobiasz Bocheński (ECR) (19 March 2026) Subject: Draft regulation on plants obtained by certain new genomic techniques (NGT) In view of the forthcoming second reading of the draft Regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council on plants obtained by certain new genomic techniques and their food and feed, I am writing to the Commission to request clarification on several key issues that are causing serious concern amongst citizens, farmers and the scientific community. Under the proposal, a significant proportion of NGT plants (Category c) are to be exempted from existing GMO regulations, including requirements for risk assessment for human, animal and environmental health, traceability, monitoring and labelling. At the same time, the draft adopts the criterion of ‘equivalence’ between NGT plants and conventional plants, which — according to some experts — lacks sufficient scientific justification. Taking the above into consideration: 1.
On which specific published scientific analyses is the assumption of equivalence between NGT plants and conventional plants based?
How does the Commission intend to ensure a high level of health and environmental protection in the event that Category C NGT plants are exempted from a full risk assessment?
How will market transparency and consumers’ right to information be ensured where labelling requirements are reduced?

(11 May 2026) The equivalence criteria between plants obtained by certain new genomic techniques (NGT) and conventional plants in the Commission’s proposal (1) are based on a literature study on conventional plants and on extensive work of the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) and of the Commission Joint Research Centre (2). In a scientific opinion requested by the Parliament (3), EFSA confirmed that it is scientifically justified to consider NGT plants meeting those criteria (Category c NGT plants) as equivalent to conventional plants as regards genetic modifications and potential risks. In their provisional agreement, the Parliament and the Council amended the criteria for Category c NGT plants in the Commission’s proposal but maintained that proposal’s scientific basis, which excludes from Category c modifications unlikely obtainable by conventional breeding. Scientific evidence (4), notably from EFSA, confirms that certain NGT plants do not pose new hazards and are therefore equivalent to conventional plants. This justifies exempting those plants and their products from specific risk assessment for genetically modified organism (GMO). However, Category c NGT plants remain subject to EU legislation applicable to conventional plants/products including safeguard measures to protect human, animal health and the environment, and will undergo a monitoring programme including on environmental and health impacts. Category C NGT plants will be identified in a public register and in variety catalogues. In addition, seed must be labelled, enabling supply chains to exclude NGT plants.

E-10-2026-001154.t: Revision of the Treaties in response to breaches of the rule of law in Hungary
qt: to the Commission Yvan Verougstraete (Renew), Sandro Gozi (Renew) Subject:

Recent developments in Hungary are raising serious concerns regarding the EU’s ability to ensure respect for its fundamental values, as set out in Article 2 TEU. Despite the activation of existing mechanisms, notably Article 7 TEU and the Rule of Law Conditionality Mechanism, these instruments seem insufficient to prevent institutional deadlocks and ensure a swift and credible response to persistent violations. The actions of the government led by Viktor Orbán illustrate the limitations of the current framework and fuel the debate on the need to bolster the EU’s legal and political tools. In view of this: 1.
Does the Commission feel that the current instruments are sufficient to ensure effective compliance with EU values in the event of systematic violations committed by a Member State?
Does it intend to back a revision of the Treaties (Article 48 TEU) with a view to strengthening protection of the rule of law and avoiding institutional deadlocks (Article 7 TEU)?
Does it consider that additional financial measures could be considered, in particular through broader use of existing budgetary mechanisms?
at: (English version) to the Commission Yvan Verougstraete (Renew), Sandro Gozi (Renew) (19 March 2026) Subject: Revision of the Treaties in response to breaches of the rule of law in Hungary Recent developments in Hungary are raising serious concerns regarding the EU’s ability to ensure respect for its fundamental values, as set out in Article 2 TEU. Despite the activation of existing mechanisms, notably Article 7 TEU and the Rule of Law Conditionality Mechanism, these instruments seem insufficient to prevent institutional deadlocks and ensure a swift and credible response to persistent violations. The actions of the government led by Viktor Orbán illustrate the limitations of the current framework and fuel the debate on the need to bolster the EU’s legal and political tools. In view of this: 1.
Does the Commission feel that the current instruments are sufficient to ensure effective compliance with EU values in the event of systematic violations committed by a Member State?
Does it intend to back a revision of the Treaties (Article 48 TEU) with a view to strengthening protection of the rule of law and avoiding institutional deadlocks (Article 7 TEU)?
Does it consider that additional financial measures could be considered, in particular through broader use of existing budgetary mechanisms?

(20 July 2026) The Commission considers that the Treaties provide a high level of protection of EU values and are complemented by a variety of instruments under EU law that ensure respect and protection of the EU values. Respect for the rule of law is essential for receiving and using EU funds. When implementing the EU budget, Member States and the Commission must ensure compliance with the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Unio n (1) and respect for EU values. Existing EU rules protect the EU budget against breaches of the rule of law and of the Charter. Significant amounts of funding for Hungary have been blocked under the Conditionality Regulation (2), the Charter horizontal enabling condition of the Common Provisions Regulation (3), and the Recovery and Resilience Facility (4). The Commission is engaging constructively with the new Hungarian government to help address outstanding rule of law concerns. The importance of the respect for EU values is also reflected in the Commission proposal for a regulation on national and regional partnership plans under the Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) 2028-2034, based on a combination of financial support for measures aimed at strengthening the rule of law and fundamental rights together with strong safeguards and conditionalities to ensure the protection of the EU budget. The Conditionality Regulation will remain in force under the MFF 2028-2034 and applies to breaches of the principles of the rule of law affecting the EU budget. The Commission shall use that regulation if the relevant conditions are met, unless other procedures set out in EU legislation would allow it to protect the EU budget more effectively. The Commission continuously evaluates the situation in all Member States and is prepared to use all the applicable tools.

E-10-2026-001153.t: EU rules on rail competition and the procurement of rolling stock for military mobility

at: (English version) to the Commission Bart Groothuis (Renew) (19 March 2026) Subject: EU rules on rail competition and the procurement of rolling stock for military mobility The Dutch Ministry of Defence wishes to purchase 24 decommissioned train cars from Dutch Railways (NS) to convert them into hospital trains for the transport of wounded military personnel in the event of a large-scale conflict on NATO’s eastern flank. (1) However, NS has indicated that the Ministry of Defence cannot be given priority and must participate in an open tender procedure, partly due to EU rules guaranteeing non-discriminatory access to rolling stock and competition in the rail market, such as Regulation (EC) No 1370/2007 (Article 5a) and EU competition law. (2) At the same time, the EU emphasises the importance of military mobility and civil-military cooperation, as set out in the Military Mobility Package, in order to bolster European resilience. 1. What is the Commission’s assessment of potential tensions between EU rules on rail competition and Member States’ initiatives to procure rolling stock for defence and crisis management purposes? 2. To what extent do current EU rules, including Article 346 TFEU, offer Member States flexibility to procure such equipment directly for defence purposes? 3. Does the Commission intend to amend procurement rules or issue guidelines to facilitate the procurement of civilian railway equipment for defence purposes as well as medical purposes, namely the transport of casualties? (16 June 2026) In accordance with the Treaties, EU procurement directives would require a contracting authority, like the Ministry of Defence of the Netherlands, to conduct a procurement procedure under the applicable directives when purchasing goods, such as train cars, of a value equal or higher than the applicable thresholds (1) (2). These rules would ensure, inter alia, the respect of EU primary law principles applicable to procurement, in particular those of equality of treatment, transparency, non-discrimination and proportionality. Such a procurement procedure would provide an opportunity to interested undertakings in any Member State to compete for that contract by submitting a bid for the supply of the goods in question, in conformity with the contracting authority’s technical specifications. The Commission does not see any tension that would result from the possible application of those directives to the situation described in the question. Those directives precisely apply to the purchases of, inter alia, goods by contracting authorities in Member States, including the ministries of defence. The Commission does not see any tension between the application of EU competition law and the potential purchase of decommissioned rolling stock directly from the Dutch Railways by the Ministry of Defence for the transport of wounded military personnel. In particular, the exercise of public power prerogatives such as the provision of military capabilities falls outside of the scope of EU antitrust rules. In addition, purchases by public authorities that do not provide an unfair advantage to the seller would not raise state aid issues.

E-10-2026-001152.t: Follow-up regarding the restriction of lead in gunshot: scientific basis and consistency with regard to the transitional periods
qt: to the Commission César Luena (S&D) Subject:

In its answer to question E-000171/20261, the Commission points out that ammunition and fishing tackle were split into separate files at the request of Member States. It also notes that the transitional periods for certain bullets for hunting were extended to address Member States’ concerns, given that the impact on total lead emissions would be ‘negligible’. Those developments raise questions about how consistent the current proposals are with the scientific basis underpinning the initial proposal, which identified significant impacts of lead on biodiversity and public health. The changes also raise concerns about the risk that socioeconomic considerations or industry pressure are reshaping the scope of the measure. 1.
Can the Commission clarify whether the available scientific evidence fully backs up the new transitional periods for certain bullets for hunting, and specify which studies that is based on?
What is the Commission’s justification for emissions considered ‘negligible’ overall not having a significant impact on fauna and biodiversity at local level?

How will the Commission ensure that the changes introduced neither make the proposal less ambitious than it was initially nor respond to industry pressure at the expense of protecting biodiversity and public health?
https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/E-10-2026-000171_EN.html.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.5.2026) The draft restriction proposal on lead in ammunition, like most restrictions under the Regulation on the Registration, Evaluation, Authorisation and Restriction of Chemicals (REACH)1, is based on publicly available opinions2 of the European Chemical Agency’s scientific committees, including a cost/benefit assessment and possible risk management measures. Based on the Agency’s opinion, bullets provide a minor contribution to the lead emissions targeted by the restriction. Delaying the application of the restriction to bullets by extending certain transitional periods by up to 5 years will only decrease by 0.12 % (-675 tonnes in total) the total emission savings expected from the restriction (558 000 tonnes over 20 years), as these savings mostly come from the proposed measures restricting lead gunshot. Even if, after discussions with the Member States, lead bullets would be excluded from the scope of the restriction, this would only decrease the total emission savings by 1.5% (-8 232 tonnes over 20 years). Consequently, extending the transitional periods for bullets, or even excluding bullets from the scope, would have a very limited impact on the overall effectiveness of the restriction measured as emission savings. Against this background, the proposed restriction still ensures a high level of protection of human health and the environment from exposure to lead. The Commission is discussing this proposal with the Member States in the REACH committee with the aim of reaching consensus.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02006R1907-20251023. 2 https://echa.europa.eu/registry-of-restriction-intentions/-/dislist/details/0b0236e1840159e6.

at: (English version) to the Commission Anna Bryłka (PfE) (19 March 2026) Subject: The cost of the ETS in the price of electricity 1. What percentage share does the Commission use in its own analyses, reports and documents to represent the share of ETS costs in the price of electricity in individual Member States? (19 June 2026) The geopolitical tensions in the Middle East have had an immediate impact on energy markets. Threats to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, have increased gas prices and, consequently, electricity wholesale prices across the Union. These developments underline the continued exposure of the Union to imported fossil fuels due to the volatility of global markets. They highlight the importance of accelerating the transition towards homegrown, clean energy sources. In this context, the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) remains a key instrument for reducing Europe’s dependency on imported fossil fuels, enhancing resilience and ensuring long-term price stability. Without the ETS Europe would now consume 100 billion cubic meters more gas, making Europe more vulnerable. In line with the conclusions of the European Council, the Commission is working on a toolbox of targeted, temporary measures addressing all components of electricity prices. The ETS component of the retail electricity price is around 11% for industry, and 5% for households in the EU on average, and is a smaller component than each of fuel costs, network charges and taxes and levies. The Commission will present a comprehensive review of the ETS by July 2026 to strengthen the carbon market and ensure it delivers a fair, cost-effective contribution towards the recently agreed 2040 target (1). On 1 April 2026, the Commission announced the first concrete measure to strengthen the ETS, proposing an amendment to the Market Stability Reserve (the ETS’s built-in stabilisation measure) (2). Data on electricity prices for households and non-households for the individual Member States are available on the website of Eurostat (3), (4).

E-10-2026-001150.t: Asphalt aggregates in Vilar do Colo (Cabanas, A Coruña)
qt: to the Commission Ana Miranda Paz (Verts/ALE) Subject:

An environmental problem has been affecting Cabanas since 2007. More than 290 000 tonnes of asphalt waste – brought in from the Netherlands by the now-defunct company Manmer – has been accumulating on a wooded plot in Monte dos Cocidos, near the Vilar do Colo industrial estate and the river Baa. Years of inaction on the part of the Galician Government, the competent authority, have resulted in millions of litres of water contaminated with polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons reaching the Ferrol estuary, which has polluted dozens of aquifers in the area. In light of the foregoing: 1.
Is the Commission aware of this environmental problem?
What measures does it consider necessary in this regard?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (11.5.2026) The Commission is aware of the environmental concerns raised by the Honourable Member, both through petitions submitted to the European Parliament and related correspondence. These claims have been thoroughly examined but have not led to the opening of an infringement procedure, in accordance with the principles set out below. The Waste Framework Directive1 requires Member States to ensure that waste is managed without endangering human health and without harming the environment, and in line with the waste hierarchy which prioritises waste prevention, reuse and recycling. In addition, the Directive promotes the recovery of construction and demolition waste, including through selective demolition and high-quality recycling. Where asphalt contains hazardous substances, such as tar, additional requirements under EU waste and chemicals legislation may apply. Without prejudice to the Commission’s role as the guardian of the Treaties, Member States are primarily responsible for ensuring compliance with EU law. In line with its strategic approach on enforcement action, which focuses on cases of systemic non-compliance2, the Commission considers that the means of redress available under national legislation would be the most appropriate mechanism to address individual cases of possible non-compliance such as this one. In this respect, the competent national and regional authorities are responsible for authorising, monitoring and enforcing compliance with the applicable rules and are best placed to assess the specific circumstances of the case.

repealing certain Directives, OJ L 312, 22.11.2008, p. 3–30, as amended by Directive (EU) 2018/851 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 30 May, OJ L 150, 14.6.2018, p. 109–140 and Directive (EU) 2025/1892 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 10 September 2025 amending Directive 2008/98/EC on waste, OJ L, 2025/1892, 26.9.2025. 2 Communication from the Commission - EU law: Better results through better application, OJ C 18, 19.1.2017, p. 10–20, and Communication from the Commission - Enforcing EU law for a Europe that delivers, 13.10.2022, COM(2022) 518 final.

E-10-2026-001146.t: Imposing gender budgeting and ideological priorities at the expense of the real needs of European citizens
qt: to the Commission Afroditi Latinopoulou (PfE) Subject:

In line with the recent Commission Communication on the Gender Equality Strategy 20262030, there are plans to further integrate the gender dimension into the EU budget and develop guidelines for tracking related expenditure in the next Multiannual Financial Framework. However, the concept of gender budgeting implies a reallocation of public resources based on ideological criteria and not on immediate social and economic needs. In particular at a time when European households and businesses are struggling with increased energy costs, high prices and general financial pressure. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Why does it choose to promote gender budgeting as a fiscal policy tool at a time when European citizens have immediate and pressing needs in light of the energy crisis and high prices?
What is the total estimated cost of implementing gender budgeting monitoring and integration mechanisms at Union and Member State level?
Does the Commission intend to reallocate resources from critical sectors – such as energy, industry or household support – to finance these policies?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (11.6.2026) Gender inequality causes gender gaps in employment, pay and pensions, thereby reducing the overall productivity of the EU’s economy. Gender budgeting allows to concretely address gender inequalities, thereby leading to broad societal benefits for European citizens. It also allows for a more efficient use of resources, which is particularly important in times of crisis. The Financial Regulation1 establishes that programmes and activities shall be implemented taking into account the principle of gender equality, in accordance with an appropriate gender mainstreaming methodology (Article 33). The Commission’s proposal for the Performance Regulation2 establishes that, for that purpose, activities of the budget shall be classified according to their contribution to gender equality, and that the Commission will provide specific guidance to do so (Article 7), as also committed in the Gender Equality Strategy 2026-20303. This is fully in line with the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, notably Article 84. Implementing gender budgeting bears no costs other than the use of administrative resources needed to track its progress. These costs are vastly offset by the result of having addressed gender inequality, thereby the benefits of gender equality. Implementing gender budgeting does not require a reallocation of resources from one sector to the other. It is about incorporating a gender perspective in the budgetary process, whereby gender equality strongly contributes to the EU’s overall strategic goals, including social cohesion and competitiveness, multiplying the return on investments in critical sectors.

at: (English version) to the Council Maciej Wąsik (ECR) (18 March 2026) Subject: Removal of Niels Troost from the EU sanctions list On 16 March 2026, the swissinfo.ch website reported that the EU had removed from its sanctions list Niels Troost — who is suspected of involvement in Russian oil transactions through a Dubai-based subsidiary of his company, Paramount Energy & Commodities — as well as Maya Bolotova, the daughter of Nikolay Tokarev, head of Russia’s Transneft (1). Press reports also suggest that, prior to the Council meeting scheduled for 14 March 2026, Slovakia — with the backing of some other Member States — argued that it would block the extension of the EU sanctions list targeting individuals and entities directly cooperating with Russia if the Member States did not agree at the Council meeting to remove two Russian oligarchs from the aforementioned list: Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman (2). In light of the above: 1.
Does the removal of the two individuals mentioned above from the EU sanctions list mean that they are no longer involved in aiding Russia by executing transactions on the oil and commodities markets?

Was this decision linked to press reports suggesting that Slovakia had threatened to block the Council’s decision to extend the validity of the sanctions list imposed on entities and individuals closely associated with the Russian regime by a further six months?
What are the consequences of removing the individuals in question from the sanctions list, and what were the factual circumstances that justified this decision?

Reply (1 June 2026) It is an essential principle of EU restrictive measures that the fundamental rights of targeted persons and entities must be respected. That is why EU restrictive measures are regularly reviewed and, if necessary, amended. The Council reassesses the circumstances pertaining to each listed person and entity and determines whether changes to the legal acts should be made. In the case of Niels Troost and Maya Bolotova, the Council decided as part of a review of the restrictive measures that their listings should not be maintained. A decision to include or remove individuals and entities from the EU’s list of restrictive measures in the regime concerned requires unanimity in the Council on the basis of an initiative or proposal from EU Member States or the Union’s High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy. The removal of individuals or entities from the EU’s list of restrictive measures means that the measures against these individuals and entities stop applying to them (e.g. any frozen assets are unfrozen, and/or travel restrictions are lifted).

E-10-2026-001143.t: Implementation of the SAFE programme in Poland
qt: to the Commission Maciej Wąsik (ECR) Subject:

On 13 March 2026, Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier announced the finalisation of a loan agreement with the Polish Government under the EU Security Action for Europe (SAFE) programme, with the aim of disbursing a 15% advance payment (around EUR 6.5-6.6 bn) as early as April 2026. This Commission statement came despite Polish President Karol Nawrocki vetoing, on 12 March 2026, the SAFE legislation that was to regulate national mechanisms for the management, control, audit and repayment of the loan. As a result of the veto, that legislation did not enter into force. Polish constitutional experts and lawyers argue that taking on this SAFE borrowing in spite of the veto would constitute a significant infringement of the applicable Treaty provisions and therefore a breach of the rule of law. In light of the above: 1.

On what legal basis (specific articles of the SAFE Regulation and the Treaties) does the Commission intend to conclude an agreement and disburse funds without a national law implementing the management and repayment mechanisms?
Does the Commission consider that continuing the procedure without national legislation is not an infringement of Article 4(3) TEU (principle of sincere cooperation) or the rule of law?
Is the Commission aware of the consequences of making SAFE funds available contrary to a decision by the Polish authorities?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (26.5.2026) Council Regulation (EU) 2025/1106 of 27 May 2025 establishing the Security Action for Europe (SAFE)1 is based on Article 122 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union2 which provides a legal basis for the EU to act swiftly in emergency situations. The SAFE Regulation and in particular Article 10, explicitly empowers the Commission to enter into loan agreements and operational arrangements with Member States, following the adoption of a Council implementing decision. This Regulation does not condition disbursement on the prior adoption of a specific national implementing legislation by the Member State since the instrument is directly applicable. Council Implementing Decision (EU) 2026/412 on making the financial assistance under Regulation (EU) 2025/1106 available to Poland3 fulfils the procedural requirement under Article 10(1) of the Regulation4, and the Commission’s role is to ensure compliance with the eligibility criteria set out in Article 16 of the Regulation5. To date, Polish authorities have not raised any objections regarding the availability or disbursement of SAFE funds. The Commission will act in accordance with the Treaty and the SAFE Regulation, ensuring that all procedural safeguards are respected.

1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2025/1106/oj/eng. 2 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/treaty/tfeu_2016/art_122/oj/eng. 3 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dec_impl/2026/412/oj/eng. 4 Please see footnote 1. 5 Please see footnote 1.

E-10-2026-001142.t: Prior events shaping the Action Plan on Drone and Counter Drone Security
qt: to the Commission Fabio De Masi (NI) Subject:

The Action Plan on Drone and Counter Drone Security adopted on 11 February 2026 is based on recent negative experiences in the Member States1 and provides for the following: ‘... recent incidents involving malicious or irresponsible use of drones have exposed significant and growing security challenges for the Union. Drones have been used in violation of Member States’ airspace, they have disrupted airport operations, and caused near-misses with civilian aircraft, highlighting vulnerabilities in our security architecture including in aviation safety.’ 1.
Precisely which ‘recent incidents’, in which countries, does this refer to?
Who is responsible for these incidents?
To what extent can these incidents be regarded as a threat of hybrid warfare, and what evidence is currently available to support this?
https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/action-plan-drone-and-counter-drone-security.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.5.2026) The Action Plan on Drone and Counter-Drone Security1 responds to security needs for the protection of European critical infrastructure and public spaces, covering drones as well as hybrid threats from other unmanned threat vectors such as balloons. In 2025, suspensions of flight operations due to drones, near-miss with an aircraft, violation of airspace by military drones, and the entry of unmanned balloons into national airspace were all observed in Europe. Such incidents attest to the pressing need to take measures to ensure the safe operation of drones in airspace, and to protect against threats arising from drones and other unmanned threat vectors. While incidents like these pose a security threat, attribution of responsibility for individual incidents is not within the Commission’s competence.
1 COM(2026)81 final. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52026DC0081.

E-10-2026-001141.t: Accessible and proportionate reporting requirements for recreational fisheries under Article 55 of the Fisheries Control Regulation
qt: to the Commission Sofie Eriksson (S&D) Subject:

The Commission began the gradual roll-out of the RecFishing mobile application on 9 January 2026. During the initial testing phase, stakeholders from the recreational fishing community highlighted several concerns related to the usability and practical implementation of the system, particularly regarding accessibility and enforceability. As reporting currently depends mainly on digital tools, anglers who lack suitable digital devices or sufficient digital skills may face difficulties fulfilling the obligation. The rules set out that recreational catches must be reported on a daily basis rather than immediately after each catch. This timing could create practical issues during inspections, as fishers may still be in full compliance even if catches have not yet been reported at the moment an inspection takes place. 1.

Does the Commission plan to examine the possibility of introducing an analogue reporting option in order to guarantee fair and proportionate reporting requirements for all recreational fishers, including those who are digitally excluded?

Can the Commission confirm whether the RecFishing application will be used solely for the data-collection purposes set out in Article 55 of the Regulation, and not as a tool for additional enforcement measures?

Can the Commission provide an update on the current operational status of the RecFishing application following the postponement of its launch, and explain how future developments will be communicated to stakeholders?
at: (English version) to the Commission Sofie Eriksson (S&D) (18 March 2026) Subject: Accessible and proportionate reporting requirements for recreational fisheries under Article 55 of the Fisheries Control Regulation The Commission began the gradual roll-out of the RecFishing mobile application on 9 January 2026. The rules set out that recreational catches must be reported on a daily basis rather than immediately after each catch. This timing could create practical issues during inspections, as fishers may still be in full compliance even if catches have not yet been reported at the moment an inspection takes place. 1. Does the Commission plan to examine the possibility of introducing an analogue reporting option in order to guarantee fair and proportionate reporting requirements for all recreational fishers, including those who are digitally excluded? 2. Can the Commission confirm whether the RecFishing application will be used solely for the data-collection purposes set out in Article 55 of the regulation, and not as a tool for additional enforcement measures? 3. Can the Commission provide an update on the current operational status of the RecFishing application following the postponement of its launch, and explain how future developments will be communicated to stakeholders? (13 May 2026) To facilitate implementation of the reporting obligations for recreational fisheries, and in line with Council Regulation (EC) No 1224/2009 (the Control Regulation), as amended by Regulation (EU) 2023/2842 (1), the Commission at the request of 13 Member States developed the digital system RecFishing. While the regulation requires daily reporting for certain species, Member States determine how the daily requirement is implemented and enforced nationally, including whether reporting is immediate or within 24 hours. The RecFishing mobile app accommodates these choices and allows reporting in line with Art. 55 of the Control Regulation, including offline, with data transmitted once connectivity is restored. While the Commission provides an electronic reporting system, it is the responsibility of Member States to define national rules on data collection and ensure the necessary enforcement, taking into account proportionality. During its meeting of 15 April 2026, the Working Group on Recreational Fisheries (WGRF) addressed possible challenges of a digital divide and discussed how to support fishers without mobile phone. The Commission develops, operates and maintains the RecFishing system to support data collection under Art. 55 of the Control Regulation. The current focus is to deploy core functionalities that can improve usability and acceptance, which will result in better data. It is a key objective of the Commission and Member States to develop tools to improve data quality to support future analysis. Finally, the roll-out of RecFishing was not postponed. As this is normal practice for large IT systems, it was launched progressively in the concerned Member States, following a pre-agreed schedule. Developments are discussed and agreed with Member States within the WGRF.

E-10-2026-001140.t: Discrimination and exclusion of women and girls with disabilities
qt: to the Commission Dan-Ştefan Motreanu (PPE) Subject:

Organisations representing people with disabilities have expressed concern about the persistent discrimination and exclusion of women and girls with disabilities in the EU. According to stakeholders, this group, which represents a significant proportion of both the female population and people with disabilities, continues to face persistent stereotypes, barriers to participation in public and political life and limited access to decision-making positions, due in part to insufficient accessibility measures. At the same time, serious concerns exist about the vulnerability of women with disabilities to gender-based violence, including forced sterilisation and institutionalisation. Civil society organisations have also emphasised the importance of effectively implementing existing EU legislation aimed at reducing violence against women and protecting vulnerable populations. What avenues is the Commission exploring to improve the inclusion of women and girls with disabilities, notably by enhancing their participation in public life, strengthening accessibility measures and ensuring consistent enforcement of EU legislation on violence against women?
at: (English version) to the Commission Dan-Ştefan Motreanu (PPE) (18 March 2026) Subject: Discrimination and exclusion of women and girls with disabilities Organisations representing people with disabilities have expressed concern about the persistent discrimination and exclusion of women and girls with disabilities in the EU. According to stakeholders, this group, which represents a significant proportion of both the female population and people with disabilities, continues to face persistent stereotypes, barriers to participation in public and political life and limited access to decision-making positions, due in part to insufficient accessibility measures. At the same time, serious concerns exist about the vulnerability of women with disabilities to gender-based violence, including forced sterilisation and institutionalisation. Civil society organisations have also emphasised the importance of effectively implementing existing EU legislation aimed at reducing violence against women and protecting vulnerable populations. What avenues is the Commission exploring to improve the inclusion of women and girls with disabilities, notably by enhancing their participation in public life, strengthening accessibility measures and ensuring consistent enforcement of EU legislation on violence against women? (14 July 2026) The Commission, through the strategy for the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (1) is committed to upholding the rights of persons with disabilities, including women and girls (2). Among its flagship initiatives and actions, the Guidance on independent living (3) provides recommendations on the use of EU funds for inclusion in the community, encouraging Member States to take appropriate measures to tackle unequal access and barriers faced by women in accessing social services, and to include a gender perspective in policies to support deinstitutionalisation. The communication on Enhancing the strategy for the rights of persons with disabilities up to 2030 (4) further reinforces an intersectional dimension, whereby, for instance, the Commission commits to launch a study on violence against women with disabilities in the EU. Promoting accessibility, as an enabler of rights for persons with disabilities — including women — to fully participate in society, remains a key priority. The European Accessibility Act (5) will ensure that key products and services are accessible to persons with disabilities (6). The Violence Against Women Directive (7) acknowledges that women with disabilities disproportionately experience violence. When an offence has been committed against a person with a disability, that fact alone can be regarded as an aggravating circumstance. The directive requires Member States to provide targeted support for victims with intersectional needs, and to ensure that such support (including specialist support, helplines for victims, shelters) can accommodate victims with disabilities. Member States are also required to issue guidelines for law enforcement and prosecutorial authorities, including on how to treat victims in a disability-sensitive manner.

Strategy for the Rights of Persons with Disabilities 2021-2030, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52021DC0101. The strategy promotes an intersectional perspective to address the specific needs of persons with disabilities experiencing multiple and overlapping forms of disadvantage, such as women, children, older persons and refugees, as well as those with invisible disabilities. qt: to the Commission Dan-Ştefan Motreanu (PPE) Subject:

Several European industry associations representing the digital and telecommunications sectors have raised concerns about the implementation of the AI Act, in particular regarding possible regulatory overlaps with existing EU product safety legislation and the cumulative impact of multiple digital regulations on businesses. Stakeholders contend that some sectors may be subject to double regulation, notably where AI systems are already covered by sectorspecific safety frameworks. Furthermore, industry representatives have emphasised the need for more alignment between the implementation timetable of the AI Act, the digital simplification initiatives currently under discussion, and the broader EU data protection framework, particularly with regard to the rules governing the use of data for the development and deployment of AI systems. Finally, calls have been made to consider postponing certain upcoming application deadlines of the AI Act in order to provide greater legal certainty and allow companies sufficient time to comply. Therefore, what approach is the Commission considering to address possible overlap and legal uncertainty arising from the AI Act, and could revisions to its scope or implementation timeline be envisaged to maintain consistency within the EU legal framework and to promote competitiveness?
at: (English version) to the Commission Dan-Ştefan Motreanu (PPE) (18 March 2026) Subject: AI Act Several European industry associations representing the digital and telecommunications sectors have raised concerns about the implementation of the AI Act, in particular regarding possible regulatory overlaps with existing EU product safety legislation and the cumulative impact of multiple digital regulations on businesses. Stakeholders contend that some sectors may be subject to double regulation, notably where AI systems are already covered by sector-specific safety frameworks. Furthermore, industry representatives have emphasised the need for more alignment between the implementation timetable of the AI Act, the digital simplification initiatives currently under discussion, and the broader EU data protection framework, particularly with regard to the rules governing the use of data for the development and deployment of AI systems. Finally, calls have been made to consider postponing certain upcoming application deadlines of the AI Act in order to provide greater legal certainty and allow companies sufficient time to comply. Therefore, what approach is the Commission considering to address possible overlap and legal uncertainty arising from the AI Act, and could revisions to its scope or implementation timeline be envisaged to maintain consistency within the EU legal framework and to promote competitiveness? (3 June 2026) The Artificial Intelligence (AI) Act (1) is a landmark legislation, delivering trust in AI through a single legislative framework. The AI Act complements existing product safety rules with horizontal requirements that ensure that high-risk AI systems are safe and trustworthy. The Commission acknowledges that stakeholders have questions on how to apply the new rules in practice, in particular together with existing law. To build clarity regarding the applicable rules and their practical application, the Commission has launched initiatives such as the AI Act Service Desk (2) where businesses, and especially small companies, can obtain clarification concerning any concrete questions they may have. Furthermore, the Commission is preparing guidelines and other support tools. Likewise, the AI Act complements existing EU data protection law. The Commission and the European Data Protection Board are preparing joint guidelines. To further address implementation challenges and simplify compliance with the AI Act, the Commission has proposed the Digital Omnibus on AI (3) on 19 November 2025, which builds on the lessons learned during the progressive roll-out of the AI Act. In particular, the Omnibus allows more time for the AI Act’s rules on high-risk AI systems to come into force since standards and specifications are not yet available. Moreover, targeted amendments aim to further clarify the interplay with other EU law, in particular the Machinery Regulation (4). The Digital Omnibus on AI was provisionally agreed by the co-legislators on 7 May 2026 and is expected to be adopted by July 2026.

qt: to the Commission Dan-Ştefan Motreanu (PPE) Subject:

It is anticipated that the Commission will propose an optional ‘28th regime’ for EU businesses, allowing ‘EU Inc.’ companies to operate across Member States and be established through a streamlined digital process. However, a number of the initiative’s features have drawn criticism. Concerns have been raised specifically regarding the selection of Article 114 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union as the legal foundation for a piece of business legislation, since prior court rulings have suggested that this clause might not be suitable for some company law initiatives. Additionally, the proposal calls for the establishment of a centralised EU interface for company registration and data interchange with national authorities, leaving some matters, such as social security, taxation and dispute resolution, primarily to national legislation. This calls into doubt the adequacy of safeguards against the potential misuse of simplified company formation procedures. Given this, how does the Commission justify the choice of Article 114 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union as the legal basis for the proposed regime, and what measures does it intend to take to ensure legal certainty, effective coordination with national systems, and adequate safeguards to prevent abuse while protecting employees’ rights and other stakeholder interests?
at: (English version) to the Commission Dan-Ştefan Motreanu (PPE) (18 March 2026) Subject: 28th regime It is anticipated that the Commission will propose an optional ‘28th regime’ for EU businesses, allowing ‘EU Inc.’ companies to operate across Member States and be established through a streamlined digital process. However, a number of the initiative’s features have drawn criticism. Concerns have been raised specifically regarding the selection of Article 114 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union as the legal foundation for a piece of business legislation, since prior court rulings have suggested that this clause might not be suitable for some company law initiatives. Additionally, the proposal calls for the establishment of a centralised EU interface for company registration and data interchange with national authorities, leaving some matters, such as social security, taxation and dispute resolution, primarily to national legislation. This calls into doubt the adequacy of safeguards against the potential misuse of simplified company formation procedures. Given this, how does the Commission justify the choice of Article 114 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union as the legal basis for the proposed regime, and what measures does it intend to take to ensure legal certainty, effective coordination with national systems, and adequate safeguards to prevent abuse while protecting employees’ rights and other stakeholder interests? (28 April 2026) On 18 March 2026 the Commission presented its proposal for the 28th regime corporate legal framework — ‘EU Inc.’ (1). The Commission considers Article 114 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU as the appropriate legal basis for the proposed Regulation. The proposal approximates national laws governing the activities of EU businesses throughout their lifecycle. It will improve the functioning of the internal market by creating an efficient corporate legal framework for companies and investors, also facilitating the free movement of capital. For details on the choice of legal basis, please refer to Section 2 of the explanatory memorandum accompanying the proposal. As regards the formation of EU incorporated (Inc.) companies through a centralised EU interface, any formation of an EU Inc. company will be subject to preventive control and a legality check. Effective coordination with national systems will be ensured, inter alia, through the EU central interface and the underlying Business Registers Interconnection System for making information about EU Inc. companies publicly available and for enabling the ‘once-only’ digital exchanges of information about EU Inc. companies between business registers and with other authorities. The proposal does not amend EU or national employment law. Rules protecting workers will fully apply to the EU Inc. companies. Recital 16 of the proposal recalls that regulation (EC) 593/2008 (2) also applies to individual employment relationships involving an EU Inc. company. Regarding other stakeholder interests, the proposal notably protects creditors through modern safeguards on distributions of company assets, including the requirement for balance sheet and solvency tests for such distributions.

Proposal for a regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council on the 28th regime corporate legal framework — ‘EU Inc.’, COM(2026) 321 final. Regulation (EC) No 593/2008 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 17 June 2008 on the law applicable to contractual obligations (Rome I).

qt: to the Commission Dan-Ştefan Motreanu (PPE) Subject:

In its recent opinions on the proposed Erasmus+ and AgoraEU programmes for the 2028-2034 period, the European Court of Auditors (ECA) welcomed the increased budgets but identified several shortcomings in the design and governance of these initiatives. In particular, the ECA noted the lack of clarity regarding the allocation of the overall Erasmus+ budget between its various priorities following the integration of the European Solidarity Corps, as well as insufficient information on the coordination and synergies envisaged under the new AgoraEU funding structure. It also pointed to the absence of clearly defined rules concerning the end of the eligibility period and the absence of ceilings for technical and administrative expenditure. Furthermore, the ECA warned that the planned widespread use of non-cost-related funding may reduce transparency and weaken accountability mechanisms and it considered that the proposed performance indicators were insufficient to properly evaluate programme results. Given these shortcomings, how will the Commission improve the legislative process to guarantee transparent budget allocation, stronger accountability, clearer financial rules and reliable performance indicators for monitoring and evaluating Erasmus+ and AgoraEU (in the 2028-2034 period)?
at: (English version) to the Commission Dan-Ştefan Motreanu (PPE) (18 March 2026) Subject: Erasmus+ and AgoraEU In its recent opinions on the proposed Erasmus+ and AgoraEU programmes for the 2028-2034 period, the European Court of Auditors (ECA) welcomed the increased budgets but identified several shortcomings in the design and governance of these initiatives. In particular, the ECA noted the lack of clarity regarding the allocation of the overall Erasmus+ budget between its various priorities following the integration of the European Solidarity Corps, as well as insufficient information on the coordination and synergies envisaged under the new AgoraEU funding structure. It also pointed to the absence of clearly defined rules concerning the end of the eligibility period and the absence of ceilings for technical and administrative expenditure. Furthermore, the ECA warned that the planned widespread use of non-cost-related funding may reduce transparency and weaken accountability mechanisms and it considered that the proposed performance indicators were insufficient to properly evaluate programme results. Given these shortcomings, how will the Commission improve the legislative process to guarantee transparent budget allocation, stronger accountability, clearer financial rules and reliable performance indicators for monitoring and evaluating Erasmus+ and AgoraEU (in the 2028-2034 period)? (18 May 2026) The Commission has taken careful note of European Court of Auditors’ opinions on the proposed Erasmus+ (1) and AgoraEU (2) programmes for 2028-2034, which constitute a valuable input to the ongoing negotiations of the next Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF). The next MFF is built on a streamlined budget architecture with fewer and more coherent programmes. The consolidation of existing programmes is designed to strengthen synergies, simplify access for beneficiaries and reduce administrative burden. Built-in budgetary flexibility is a deliberate feature, enabling adaptation to evolving needs over the 7-year period. The strategic steering mechanism presented in the Interinstitutional Agreement (3) accompanying the MFF Regulation (4) provides for regular guidance from the European Parliament and the Council on strategic investment priorities, thereby reinforcing transparency and democratic oversight. The use of simplified forms of financing as the default grant modality is central to the overall MFF simplification agenda and is subject to the safeguards of the Financial Regulation (5), including the ex-ante method of calculation, definition of outputs or results triggering payment and ex post checks and controls of their achievement. The proposed Performance Framework Regulation (6) establishes consistent output and result indicators across all programmes, and programme evaluations assessing effectiveness, efficiency, relevance, coherence and EU added value. Rules on the end of the eligibility period and ceilings for administrative expenditure are addressed in Financial Regulation. The Commission will continue to engage constructively with the co-legislators to ensure the timely start of the implementation as from 1 January 2028.

E-10-2026-001135.t: Competitiveness of the EU banking sector
qt: to the Commission Dan-Ştefan Motreanu (PPE) Subject:

Concerns about the competitiveness of the EU banking sector have prompted stakeholders to criticise the complexity and cumulative impact of the EU’s prudential and supervisory framework. Some stakeholders argue that the current regulatory environment imposes enormous administrative difficulties, particularly through complex reporting requirements and overlapping regulations in the EU financial services acquis. Concerns have also been raised that the EU’s implementation of international standards – including Basel III framework elements such as the output floor and the fundamental review of the trading book – may put EU banks at a competitive disadvantage compared to institutions in other major jurisdictions. At the same time, calls have been made for greater proportionality in prudential rules, particularly for smaller banking institutions, and for adjustments to certain measures in order to support financing for small and medium-sized enterprises and mid-cap companies. In addition, uncertainty remains regarding the timeline and concrete steps for further developing the banking union. What strategy is the Commission considering in order to simplify the EU prudential framework without undermining financial stability, while also maintaining proportionality and global competitiveness across diverse banking models?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (28.5.2026) As announced in the Communication on the Savings and Investments Union1, the Commission will publish in summer 2026 a report on the competitiveness of the banking sector in the Single Market. A competitive European banking sector is essential to finance Europe’s households, companies and strategic priorities. The EU banking sector is resilient and profitable. The main challenge is the fragmentation of the Single Market, including: a lack of scale, limited cross-border consolidation, national barriers and discretions, non-prudential barriers, complexities in the capital stack and an incomplete Banking Union. Banks can be competitive and contribute to the competitiveness of the EU economy only if they do business in a financially stable, well integrated, broad and deep banking market. The report is an opportunity for the Commission to develop a holistic and evidence-based assessment of what is preventing a true Single Market in banking, and, subsequently, to propose an ambitious and forward-looking banking reform agenda that simplifies the framework and caters for the needs of European markets and players. The report will look widely and openly at a broad range of issues, covering the causes of the fragmentation in the single market, the sources of regulatory and supervisory complexity, the notion of proportionality and the identification of undue reporting burdens. To inform the report, the Commission launched a consultation that ran until 19 April 20262 and organised several outreach events for a diverse group of stakeholders, including industry, analysts, academics, or industry and consumers associations.
1 COM/2025/124 final. 2 https://finance.ec.europa.eu/regulation-and-supervision/consultations-0/targeted-consultation-competitiveness-
eu-banking-sector-2026_en.

qt: to the Commission Dan-Ştefan Motreanu (PPE) Subject:

Stakeholders have voiced differing concerns regarding the suitability of current EU regulations, as well as the possibility of regulatory overlap, in the light of the upcoming proposal for a Digital Fairness Act (DFA). Civil society organisations contend that harmful online commercial practices, such as deceptive interface design, addictive features and the misuse of personal data, which may compromise consumer autonomy and result in financial or psychological harm, are not adequately addressed by current laws, such as Digital Services Act and Digital Markets Act. Business organisations caution that if a new legislative initiative overlaps with current frameworks, it may result in more regulatory layers, legal ambiguity and increased compliance costs. In view of these concerns and the repeated postponements of the DFA proposal, how does the Commission intend to overcome existing gaps in online consumer protection, notably with regard to harmful digital commercial practices, while avoiding legislative overlap and ensuring coherence with current EU digital and consumer protection frameworks?
at: (English version) to the Commission Dan-Ştefan Motreanu (PPE) (18 March 2026) Subject: Digital Fairness Act Stakeholders have voiced differing concerns regarding the suitability of current EU regulations, as well as the possibility of regulatory overlap, in the light of the upcoming proposal for a Digital Fairness Act (DFA). Civil society organisations contend that harmful online commercial practices, such as deceptive interface design, addictive features and the misuse of personal data, which may compromise consumer autonomy and result in financial or psychological harm, are not adequately addressed by current laws, such as Digital Services Act and Digital Markets Act. Business organisations caution that if a new legislative initiative overlaps with current frameworks, it may result in more regulatory layers, legal ambiguity and increased compliance costs. In view of these concerns and the repeated postponements of the DFA proposal, how does the Commission intend to overcome existing gaps in online consumer protection, notably with regard to harmful digital commercial practices, while avoiding legislative overlap and ensuring coherence with current EU digital and consumer protection frameworks? (14 July 2026) The Digital Fairness Act (DFA) is a key initiative provided in the Commission work programme for the fourth quarter 2026. The Commission is currently conducting the impact assessment. Based on the findings of the Digital Fairness Fitness Check (1), the DFA aims to address the identified gaps tackling the problems that consumers and, especially, minors often face when using online services. These may include dark patterns and addictive design, unfair personalisation targeting their vulnerabilities, problematic marketing by social media influencers, unfair marketing practices related to price and difficulties with managing contracts concluded online. The aim of the DFA is to propose targeted and proportionate measures to address the identified problems in this area, in full coherence with existing legislation, in particular the Digital Services Act (2), the Digital Markets Act (3) and the AI Act (4). Wherever relevant, the DFA will propose simplification of the existing rules without compromising consumer protection. Clearer rules lead to easier enforcement and a more level playing field for all traders, benefiting both consumers and businesses.
