E-10-2026-001133.t: European technology in Russian weapons despite sanctions
qt: to the Commission Jan Farský (PPE) Subject:

Despite extensive European Union sanctions against Russia, technological components that can be used in the military industry continue to flow from the EU to Russia. New research by the Committee for Freedom in Hong Kong Foundation (CFHK) shows that electronic components manufactured by European technology companies such as STMicroelectronics, NXP and Infineon Technologies have been found in Russian weapons used in the war in Ukraine. The analysis shows that these components reach Russia through a network of intermediaries and trading companies in Hong Kong, which act as a key transit hub for trade in dual-use technologies. The research also suggests that the current EU sanctions regime often targets individual companies, while broader trade and financial networks, including logistics companies, banks and distributors, remain outside the reach of sanctions. This allows export controls to be bypassed and enables the continued supply of technologies that may strengthen Russia’s military industrial complex. 1.
How can the Commission strengthen export controls on dual-use goods in order to prevent their circumvention through third countries such as Hong Kong?
What new tools could the Commission introduce to monitor global supply chains in semiconductors and other critical technologies?
at: (English version) to the Commission Jan Farský (PPE) (18 March 2026) Subject: European technology in Russian weapons despite sanctions Despite extensive European Union sanctions against Russia, technological components that can be used in the military industry continue to flow from the EU to Russia. New research by the Committee for Freedom in Hong Kong Foundation (CFHK) shows that electronic components manufactured by European technology companies such as STMicroelectronics, NXP and Infineon Technologies have been found in Russian weapons used in the war in Ukraine. The analysis shows that these components reach Russia through a network of intermediaries and trading companies in Hong Kong, which act as a key transit hub for trade in dual-use technologies. The research also suggests that the current EU sanctions regime often targets individual companies, while broader trade and financial networks, including logistics companies, banks and distributors, remain outside the reach of sanctions. This allows export controls to be bypassed and enables the continued supply of technologies that may strengthen Russia’s military industrial complex. 1. How can the Commission strengthen export controls on dual-use goods in order to prevent their circumvention through third countries such as Hong Kong? 2. What new tools could the Commission introduce to monitor global supply chains in semiconductors and other critical technologies? (15 June 2026) Preventing the circumvention of EU restrictive measures (sanctions) against Russia is a priority for the EU, in particular with respect to sensitive goods and technologies. The Commission takes note of the outcome of the research by the Committee for Freedom in Hong Kong Foundation and observes that the competent authorities of the Member States are actively monitoring the export of dual-use items, including semiconductors, to third countries and denying, as appropriate, exports which display risk of diversions. Over the last few years, the EU has actively deployed several new tools to counter the circumvention of EU sanctions, including the imposition of targeted export controls on entities involved in the diversion of sensitive items to Russia (1). The EU has also taken measures against banks and financial institutions in third countries as well as crypto currencies and platforms, that facilitate trade in sanctioned goods and technologies. The Commission actively supports cooperation between Member States on implementation of these measures through the exchange of licensing information and making use of the tools established by Regulation (EU) 2021/821 (2) for the exchange of information on enforcement, such as the Enforcement Coordination Mechanism.
Annex IV of Council Regulation (EU) No 833/2014, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2014/833/oj/eng. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2021/821/oj/eng.

qt: to the Commission Jan Farský (PPE) Subject:

The United States Government is planning to launch a portal that would allow Europeans to access content blocked in Europe, including possible hate speech and terrorist content. Although the freedom.gov website is not yet operational, it already shows the outline of a blue planet Earth with an animation of a distinctly American horse and rider galloping above the words ‘Freedom is coming’. The page further promises that ‘Information is power. Rediscover your human right to free speech. Get ready’. In this context: 1.

How should the Commission respond to the creation of an American portal that could allow European users to bypass EU online content regulation, to what extent could such a project undermine European legislation, in particular the Digital Services Act, and what legal tools does the EU have at its disposal to protect its regulatory framework?
What diplomatic or regulatory steps would the Commission take if such a portal actively supported the spread of content that is illegal under European law?
Could such an initiative trigger a broader dispute between the EU and the United States over the regulation of the digital space, and how would the Commission manage such a conflict?

The page further promises that ‘Information is power. Rediscover your human right to free speech. Get ready’. In this context: 1.

What diplomatic or regulatory steps would the Commission take if such a portal actively supported the spread of content that is illegal under European law?

(22 May 2026) The Commission has no specific comment to make on potential plans of the freedom.gov initiative and does not speculate on design or intent. The Commission is thus not planning to issue further comments. By law, the Commission cannot block websites in the EU. Only Member States' authorities may block a website if it is illegal under national or European law. This includes websites promoting child-sexual abuse material, terrorist content or copyrightinfringing material. The Commission remains open to engagement with the US. The enforcement of EU law, in digital like in other areas, is the EU’s sovereign right. The Commission has a responsibility to enforce its laws, including the Digital Services Act (1), effectively, fairly and without discrimination towards all companies operating in the EU.
Regulation (EU) 2022/2065, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/2065/oj/eng.

qt: to the Commission Jan Farský (PPE) Subject:

According to a report it published in February 2024, the French state organisation Viginum uncovered a network of inauthentic news websites spreading pro-Kremlin narratives. These websites used domains containing the label ‘pravda-' followed by country codes and published content translated into several European languages, including English, German, French, Portuguese and Spanish. At the same time, the Czech website Novarepublika.cz has been systematically publishing and republishing in Czech articles originating from the Russian portal Ukraina.ru, which belongs to the state media group Rossiya Segodnya. This media group was added to the European Union sanctions list on 25 February 2023. Given that EU sanctions prohibit content from certain Russian state media outlets from being distributed within EU territory, the systematic translation and republication of such content may constitute a possible circumvention of EU restrictive measures. Given this context: 1.
Is the Commission aware of cases in which content from sanctioned Russian state media is being translated and published through websites operated in EU Member States?

Does the Commission consider the systematic translation and republication of content originating from sanctioned media outlets, such as Rossiya Segodnya or Ukraina.ru, to be a possible circumvention of EU sanctions?
at: (English version) to the Commission Jan Farský (PPE) (18 March 2026) Subject: Russian disinformation According to a report it published in February 2024, the French state organisation Viginum uncovered a network of inauthentic news websites spreading pro-Kremlin narratives. These websites used domains containing the label ‘pravda-' followed by country codes and published content translated into several European languages, including English, German, French, Portuguese and Spanish. At the same time, the Czech website Novarepublika.cz has been systematically publishing and republishing in Czech articles originating from the Russian portal Ukraina.ru, which belongs to the state media group Rossiya Segodnya. This media group was added to the European Union sanctions list on 25 February 2023. Given that EU sanctions prohibit content from certain Russian state media outlets from being distributed within EU territory, the systematic translation and republication of such content may constitute a possible circumvention of EU restrictive measures. Given this context: 1.
Is the Commission aware of cases in which content from sanctioned Russian state media is being translated and published through websites operated in EU Member States?

Does the Commission consider the systematic translation and republication of content originating from sanctioned media outlets, such as Rossiya Segodnya or Ukraina.ru, to be a possible circumvention of EU sanctions?

(22 May 2026) The Commission recalls that Rossiya Segodnya International Information Agency is subject to restrictive measures (sanctions) under Regulation (EU) No 269/2014 (1), including an asset freeze and a prohibition on making funds or economic resources available to it, directly or indirectly. Moreover, several outlets of Rossiya Segodnya are also subject to restrictive measures under Article 2f of Regulation (EU) No 833/2014 (2). These measures prohibit the broadcasting or distribution of their content in the EU, regardless of the means of transmission, dissemination or distribution, including via online means. The restrictions on the broadcasting and dissemination of content by certain media outlets (designated entities), including those under the control of the Russian Federation in this sanctions regime, are justified by the designated outlets’ essential and instrumental role in the systematic disinformation and propaganda campaigns in support of the Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine. The implementation and enforcement of restrictive measures primarily fall within the competence of the Member States. The Commission monitors the application of the EU’s sanctions regime in coordination with Member States. Actions that effectively reproduce or systematically republish the above-mentioned prohibited content may, depending on the circumstances, amount to circumvention of the restrictive measures. Where indications of such conduct arise, it is for the competent national authorities to assess the facts and, where appropriate, take enforcement action in accordance with EU and national law.

E-10-2026-001130.t: Digital Services Act and the sale of risky products on online platforms
qt: to the Commission Jan Farský (PPE) Subject:

The EU adopted the Digital Services Act (DSA), which is intended to regulate large online platforms such as Shein, Instagram and Temu, particularly with regard to transparency, user safety and responsibility for the content and goods offered. However, recent investigative reports indicate that the online platform Shein offers goods that may be in breach of EU legislation, such as sex dolls resembling children and weapons. Such products fall within the category of risky and potentially illegal content, the spread of which the DSA is designed to prevent. In addition, Shein has long been criticised for using what are known as addictive design features that encourage impulsive and excessive shopping through discount codes, game-like elements and other mechanisms, with potentially negative effects, particularly on younger users. Is the Commission considering creating a specialised agency, body or coordination mechanism to oversee the production and distribution processes of large platforms, in order to detect and prevent the spread of such goods at an early stage?
at: (English version) to the Commission Jan Farský (PPE) (18 March 2026) Subject: Digital Services Act and the sale of risky products on online platforms The EU adopted the Digital Services Act (DSA), which is intended to regulate large online platforms such as Shein, Instagram and Temu, particularly with regard to transparency, user safety and responsibility for the content and goods offered. However, recent investigative reports indicate that the online platform Shein offers goods that may be in breach of EU legislation, such as sex dolls resembling children and weapons. Such products fall within the category of risky and potentially illegal content, the spread of which the DSA is designed to prevent. In addition, Shein has long been criticised for using what are known as addictive design features that encourage impulsive and excessive shopping through discount codes, game-like elements and other mechanisms, with potentially negative effects, particularly on younger users. Is the Commission considering creating a specialised agency, body or coordination mechanism to oversee the production and distribution processes of large platforms, in order to detect and prevent the spread of such goods at an early stage? (26 June 2026) At this stage the Commission is not considering establishing a new specialised EU body. The Commission is strengthening enforcement and early detection through existing EU frameworks and coordinated actions between authorities. The Digital Services Act (1) ensures that very large online platforms identify risks, including the dissemination of illegal content and serious negative consequences to the person’s physical and mental well-being and apply mitigation measures (2). The Commission opened formal investigations into Temu and Shein focusing on their assessment of risks of illegal products and those linked to the addictive design of their services. The communication on a Comprehensive EU Toolbox for Safe and Sustainable e-commerce (3) aims to create a level playing field for effective customs and safety controls through a coordinated EU and national approach. The Customs Reform (4) will enhance collaboration among customs, market surveillance and digital authorities. From July 2028 platforms intermediating in the sale of third country goods to EU consumers that are importer for distance sales will report all sales to customs authorities, allowing for an EU level customs risk analysis, early detection of documentary noncompliance, and mitigation measures at the product origin. In 2026 the Commission will adopt a proposal to revise the Market Surveillance Regulation (5) as part of a European Product Act, also reviewing the new legislative framework (6) and the Standardisation Regulation (7). It will close loopholes on market surveillance authorities’ enforcement of EU product rules ensuring that for each product placed in the EU there is an EU-based economic operator responsible for monitoring all actors involved in the products’ supply chains.

https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/2065/oj/eng. Articles 34 and 35 DSA. https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/e-commerce-communication-comprehensive-eu-toolbox-safe-and-sustainable-e-commerce. https://taxation-customs.ec.europa.eu/customs/eu-customs-reform_en. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2019/1020/oj/eng. https://single-market-economy.ec.europa.eu/single-market/goods/new-legislative-framework_en. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2012/1025/oj/eng.

qt: to the Commission Jan Farský (PPE) Subject:

Since the activation of the Temporary Protection Directive, millions of Ukrainian refugees have gained access to the labour market in the European Union. However, according to a recent analysis by the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Refugees, survey data show that 57 % of Ukrainian refugees in Europe are employed, which is a gap of 22 percentage points compared with nationals of the host countries. A serious problem remains the structural mismatch between qualifications and the jobs performed. Up to 60 % of Ukrainian refugees work below their qualification level, while those with tertiary education are five times more likely to hold low-skilled positions than local workers. This leads to significant wage gaps and at the same time limits the ability of host economies to use the available human capital and therefore also limits the potential increase in GDP, which is estimated at up to 0.7 percentage points per year. Does the Commission plan to propose additional targeted measures to prevent long-term exclusion from the labour market and skills degradation among Ukrainian refugees, especially in sectors facing persistent labour shortages?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (11.6.2026) The Commission Recommendation on the recognition of qualifications for people fleeing Russia’s invasion of Ukraine1 was adopted to ensure the swift integration of beneficiaries of temporary protection in the EU labour market. It provides guidance to Member States on the quick and fair recognition of qualifications so that professionals enjoying temporary protection can access jobs that match their potential. The Commission launched the EU Talent Pool Pilot2 for beneficiaries of temporary protection, available in Ukrainian and Russian language, to help match jobseekers benefitting from temporary protection with vacancies from EU employers. Beneficiaries of temporary protection have shown faster labour market integration rates than those of other refugee groups3. The Commission is exploring the potential of common rules to simplify the qualification recognition procedures for third-country nationals4, in order to better harness their human capital in the EU. The Erasmus+ programme has also been mobilised to contribute supporting the skills of Ukrainian pupils, students, young people and educators. The recently adopted EU Anti-Poverty Strategy5 announced the launch of the first-stage consultation of European social partners on the possible direction of EU action to support the activation of people excluded from the labour market.
1 Commission Recommendation (EU) 2022/554 of 5 April 2022 on the recognition of qualifications for people

fleeing Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, OJ L 107I, 6.4.2022, pp. 1-8: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32022H0554. 2 https://eures.europa.eu/eu-talent-pool-pilot_en. 3 https://www.oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/topics/policy-issues/migration/OECDEMN%20Inform_%20Labour-market-integration-of-beneficiaries-of-temporary-protection-from-Ukraine.pdf. 4 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX%3A52025DC0090. 5 https://employment-social-affairs.ec.europa.eu/news/commission-proposes-new-measures-fight-poverty-andimprove-lives-persons-disabilities-2026-05-06_en.

qt: to the Commission Jan Farský (PPE) Subject:

Transparent and fair financing of political parties is a key pillar of democratic systems in the European Union. Although EU rules aim to ensure transparency and accountability, a recent Transparency International analysis shows that more than 60 countries still allow anonymous political donations, and almost the same number of countries do not require political parties to report their campaign income and spending. Only seven Member States actually require the disclosure of the identity of all private donors. These gaps create unequal conditions for political competition, allow non-transparent forms of financing and may weaken public trust in democratic institutions. In this context: 1.
How does the Commission assess the effectiveness and consistent application of EU rules on political party financing and transparency across the Member States?
What measures is the Commission taking to address differences in both national oversight capacities and sanctions for illegal or non-transparent political party financing?

Does the Commission intend to strengthen EU-level tools to respond to emerging risks in political party financing, such as third-party campaigning, in order to ensure fair and transparent democratic competition?
at: (English version) to the Commission Jan Farský (PPE) (18 March 2026) Subject: Political party financing Transparent and fair financing of political parties is a key pillar of democratic systems in the European Union. Although EU rules aim to ensure transparency and accountability, a recent Transparency International analysis shows that more than 60 countries still allow anonymous political donations, and almost the same number of countries do not require political parties to report their campaign income and spending. Only seven Member States actually require the disclosure of the identity of all private donors. These gaps create unequal conditions for political competition, allow non-transparent forms of financing and may weaken public trust in democratic institutions. In this context: 1.
How does the Commission assess the effectiveness and consistent application of EU rules on political party financing and transparency across the Member States?
What measures is the Commission taking to address differences in both national oversight capacities and sanctions for illegal or non-transparent political party financing?

Does the Commission intend to strengthen EU-level tools to respond to emerging risks in political party financing, such as third-party campaigning, in order to ensure fair and transparent democratic competition?

(1 June 2026) The Commission does not have a general power to intervene in matters related to the regulation or oversight of national political party financing. Member States are competent to lay down the rules regarding the functioning and financing of national political parties, and their competent national authorities ensure compliance with national legislation, EU law and their international obligations. At the EU level, Regulation (EU, Euratom) 2025/2445 (1) has strengthened transparency and control mechanisms of the funding received by European political parties and foundations. As transparency and accountability of the party financing rules are an important factor for preventing corruption, the Commission monitors developments in Member States related to the funding of national political parties in the context of its annual Rule of Law Report (2). The Commission also supports the exchange of practices in the framework of the European cooperation network on elections (3). Regulation (EU) 2024/900 on the transparency and targeting of political advertising (4) facilitates oversight of some aspects of political party funding, including by requiring political advertising publishers to disclose essential information on political advertisements. As announced in the European Democracy Shield (5), in the framework of the European cooperation network on elections the Commission will further support common work with the Member States on the transparency and integrity of funding in politics (6), looking at issues of common interest such as anonymous donations and cryptocurrency, in full respect for the allocation of competences on electoral matters.

E-10-2026-001127.t: Peace Facility funding for drones in military operation IRINI
qt: to the Commission Özlem Demirel (The Left) Subject:

For years, Italy has supplied drones for the EU military operation IRINI. Now, these are set to be financed through the European Peace Facility (EPF), which will cover up to 60 hours of monthly flight time for US MQ-9 Reaper Block 5 drones, as well as their maintenance. 1.

How many hours of flight time and what type of drones did Italy supply over the past five years in the context of its national participation in operation IRINI, and how many are to be financed through the EPF in the future?
What has been the total cost reimbursed to Italy from EU funds for drone flights under IRINI so far, and what is the future flat rate per hour of flight time with a combatcapable ‘Reaper’?
For what reasons is the additional funding coming from the EPF, and to what extent is this also envisaged for other national contributions under IRINI?
at: (English version) to the Commission Özlem Demirel (The Left) (18 March 2026) Subject: Peace Facility funding for drones in military operation IRINI For years, Italy has supplied drones for the EU military operation IRINI. Now, these are set to be financed through the European Peace Facility (EPF), which will cover up to 60 hours of monthly flight time for US MQ-9 Reaper Block 5 drones, as well as their maintenance. 1. How many hours of flight time and what type of drones did Italy supply over the past five years in the context of its national participation in operation IRINI, and how many are to be financed through the EPF in the future? 2. What has been the total cost reimbursed to Italy from EU funds for drone flights under IRINI so far, and what is the future flat rate per hour of flight time with a combat-capable ‘Reaper’? 3. For what reasons is the additional funding coming from the EPF, and to what extent is this also envisaged for other national contributions under IRINI? (22 June 2026) The mandate of the EU Naval Force Mediterranean Operation IRINI is under the close scrutiny of Member States which exercise political control and strategic direction through the Council, more specifically the Political and Security Committee (PSC). IRINI is a Common Security and Defence Policy (CSDP) operation under the European Peace Facility (EPF) Operations pillar and as such it is managed by the Council secretariat. With regard to question 1, the European External Action Service (EEAS) is not in a position to provide information or comment on support provided to IRINI by individual Member States. Concerning questions 2 and 3, given the management modalities explained above, the EEAS considers that any request for information on funding and reimbursement should, therefore, be addressed to the relevant Council bodies. The EEAS confirms that none of the deliveries mentioned in the written parliamentary question have been financed through EPF assistance measures.

E-10-2026-001126.t: Risk of terrorist attacks in Europe due to the conflict in Iran
qt: to the Commission Loucas Fourlas (PPE) Subject:

The escalation of the conflict in Iran and the wider destabilisation in the Middle East are deepening concerns about terrorist cells or ‘lone wolves’ potentially being activated within Europe. Recent years have shown that international conflicts often act as a catalyst for radicalisation and terrorist acts within the European Union. Given the need to protect European citizens, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
How does it view the increased risk of terrorist attacks within the EU due to the escalation of the conflict in Iran?
What additional measures does it intend to take to strengthen cooperation between the security services of the Member States?
Is there an updated European plan to prevent and respond to possible terrorist threats relating to developments in the Middle East?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.6.2026) The Commission is very attentive to the impact of external conflicts and geopolitical events on EU’s internal security and is closely monitoring the evolution of the terrorist and extremist threat stemming from the conflict in the Middle East, relying on threat assessments produced by the EU Intelligence and Situation Centre and analysis from the EU Agency for Law Enforcement Cooperation (Europol). While the terrorist threat was already high in the EU, Europol has reported a heightened security threat since the beginning of the conflict in Iran, that is duly taken into account. According to the Treaties, national security remains the sole responsibility of each Member State1. The Commission is not competent for the cooperation between national security services. ProtectEU2, the European Internal Security Strategy of April 2025, encourages enhanced intelligence-sharing at EU level through the Single Intelligence Analysis Capacity, to improve EU-wide situational awareness and support informed policy work at EU level. Under the umbrella of ProtectEU, the Commission adopted on 26 February 2026 a new Agenda to prevent and combat terrorism3 that sets out a comprehensive strategic framework. It fully takes into account the importance of the external dimension and proposes specific measures to tackle the spillover effects of geopolitical developments on the EU’s terrorism threat landscape. In parallel, the initiatives foreseen under the Action Plan4 of the Pact for the Mediterranean will strengthen regional-level security cooperation with partner countries, as well as contribute to establishing new cooperation channels and hence increase situational awareness and operational preparedness in the EU and the Member States.
1 Article 4(2) of the Treaty on European Union. 2 Communication from the Commission to the European Parliament, the Council, the European Economic and

Social Committee and the Committee of the Regions on ProtectEU: a European Internal Security Strategy; COM/2025/148 final. 3 Communication from the Commission to the European Parliament, the Council, the European Economic and Social Committee of the Regions ProtectEU: Agenda to prevent and counter terrorism; COM/2026/101 final. 4 https://north-africa-middle-east-gulf.ec.europa.eu/news/eu-presents-first-action-plan-under-pact-mediterranean2026-04-17_en.

E-10-2026-001125.t: Rising cost of fuels and the impact on the fishing sector
qt: to the Commission André Franqueira Rodrigues (S&D), Thomas Bajada (S&D), Sakis Arnaoutoglou (S&D), Giuseppe Lupo (S&D), Idoia Mendia (S&D), Eric Sargiacomo (S&D), Nicolás González Casares (S&D), Sérgio Gonçalves (S&D) Subject:

As S&D members of Parliament’s Committee on Fisheries, we are greatly concerned about the continued rise in fuel costs, due to the escalation of the conflict in Iran and the Middle East, and the significant impact of the rising costs on the European fishing sector. Fishers across the EU are facing increasing operational challenges, with fuel comprising a substantial proportion of their expenses. Given this situation, we would like the Commission to clarify the actions it plans to take to address these challenges, in particular: 1.
What specific measures has the Commission taken to mitigate the impact of rising fuel prices on the fishing sector?

How will the Commission support Member States and stakeholders in ensuring that fishing activities remain financially sustainable under current market conditions, and are there any targeted financial instruments or emergency support mechanisms available or planned for the sector?
Is the Commission considering additional policy responses, including flexibility in State aid rules or market interventions?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (12.5.2026) The Commission is continuously monitoring and projecting potential impacts of the situation in the Middle East. While there are no immediate concerns for the EU’s security of supply, prices, particularly for refined products like diesel face significant volatility. This has direct consequences and dire economic and social implications for the EU, in particular for primary agricultural production and fisheries. As regards fisheries, pursuant to article 26(2) of the European Maritime Fisheries and Aquaculture Fund (EMFAF) Regulation, the Commission has activated a crisis support mechanism in case of an exceptional event causing a significant disruption of markets1. The Commission invites Member States to proceed with the relevant processes to make support available to the sectors under their national EMFAF programmes and in line with the established EU rules. The Commission is aware that the situation may require going beyond EMFAF to support as efficiently as possible undertakings whose economic activity is directly hit by this crisis. Therefore, the Commission has adopted a temporary State aid framework which will allow aid for the primary production of fishery and aquaculture products2. Member States will be able to use the new temporary crisis framework, in addition to the standard State aid rules applicable to the fishery sector, to support the sector. The Commission has also put forward the AccelerateEU initiative3 to alleviate the situation for businesses and consumers. Considering the importance of learning from crisis situations, the Commission underlines that sustainable business models and energy transition remain pivotal for the resilience of fisheries sector and its competitiveness.
1 Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2026/889 of 16 April 2026 establishing the situation in the Middle

East as of 28 February 2026 as the occurrence of an exceptional event causing a significant disruption of markets: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dec_impl/2026/889/oj. 2 https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_26_894. 3 https://energy.ec.europa.eu/strategy/accelerateeu-strengthen-eu-energy-resilience_en.

E-10-2026-001124.t: Port complex in Malcesine sul Garda and its environmental impact
qt: to the Commission Cristina Guarda (Verts/ALE) Subject:

Works are under way to expand the marinas in Retelino, Navene and Madonnina, in the municipality of Malcesine (Verona)1. Madonnina boasts an historical lakefront that still has natural and seminatural beaches – increasingly rare sights as the shores of Lake Garda are subject to extensive overdevelopment. The works include dredging, coastline management and extension of the artificial quays. Studies have been performed on sediments and swell but – as the province of Verona and Veneto Region confirmed to the Gruppo d'Intervento Giuridico (Legal Intervention Group) following an inquiry – no procedure has been initiated to screen for an environmental impact assessment (EIA)2, nor has an analysis been conducted of the lake’s ecosystem or animal and plant life, despite the dramatic decline in native fish stocks and the destruction of the lakebed. In time, the lakefront will also be affected by lot 4 of the cycle- and footpath, which will see it double in length and fully disappear under layers of concrete. In the light of the above: 1.

With a view to countering the increasing development of the Garda shoreline, which, together with overtourism, is damaging the lake ecosystem, does the Commission believe that the EIA procedure followed has been applied correctly?
Will it look into what steps need to be taken to restore the natural coastal stretches that have been artificially developed?

https://www.facebook.com/photo/?fbid=25269639972687901&set=pcb.25269653952686503. https://gruppodinterventogiuridicoweb.com/2025/11/30/lago-di-garda-malcesine-non-emergono-leautorizzazioni-ambientali-per-gli-interventi-sulla-portualita-turistica/.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (6.7.2026) Under Article 4(2) of the Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) Directive1, for projects listed in Annex II, Member States shall determine whether the project shall be made subject to an assessment. This determination must be made through a case-by-case examination or thresholds or criteria set by the Member States which may decide to apply both procedures. ‘Marinas’ and ‘any change or extension of projects listed in Annex I [or II], already authorised, executed or in the process of being executed, which may have significant adverse effects on the environment…’ fall respectively within the scope of Annex II, point 12(b) and point 13(a) of the EIA Directive. The Commission notes that local organisations have exercised their rights to access environmental information, protected under the Directive on public access to environmental information2 and the Aarhus Convention3, to obtain information on the ongoing environmental decision-making progress. In this regard, the Commission recalls that concerned citizens and environmental organisations also enjoy the right to access to justice, protected under the EIA Directive4 and the Aarhus Convention. It is for the Italian competent authorities to apply the above rules and procedures to this project and to ensure that, if damage to the environment has occurred, it is restored as appropriate. In its role as guardian of the Treaties, the Commission may decide to intervene if systemic problems arise in the application of the provisions of EU law5.

E-10-2026-001123.t: Cycle paths on the Verona side of Lake Garda and their environmental impact
qt: to the Commission Cristina Guarda (Verts/ALE) Subject:

The municipalities of Malcesine and Torri del Benaco (Province of Verona) are completing cycle paths built on entire sections of natural beaches, landscapes that are increasingly rare, as the shores of Lake Garda are subject to extensive overdevelopment. No environmental impact assessment (EIA) was carried out for those works, which have disfigured the shoreline and fish spawning grounds, nor were any studies conducted on the lake’s ecosystem or animal and plant life, against a backdrop of dramatic declines in native fish stocks and the destruction of beaches and lake beds. The routes (Lot 6 Baitone-Galleria Cantone in Malcesine, Lot 2 Ciclovia Nazionale ‘del Garda’ in Torri) also fall within and adjacent to SCI/SPA areas (IT32100391, IT32100042), further disrupting the landscape continuity between the lake and the mountains. The works were also pointless: the neighbouring municipalities of Torbole and Garda do not intend to extend the routes because they would take a heavy environmental toll. The press has already condemned the projects3. The works, which are still going on4, were financed with NRRP money. The Commission has already received a question on this matter (E-002947/2024), but work has continued in the meantime and it has had a serious impact on the environment. Can the Commission investigate the failure to assess whether the works were subject to an EIA and call for the natural stretches of shore that they have ruined to be restored, and if those steps are not taken, open an infringement procedure?

No environmental impact assessment (EIA) was carried out for those works, which have disfigured the shoreline and fish spawning grounds, nor were any studies conducted on the lake’s ecosystem or animal and plant life, against a backdrop of dramatic declines in native fish stocks and the destruction of beaches and lake beds. The routes (Lot 6 Baitone-Galleria Cantone in Malcesine, Lot 2 Ciclovia Nazionale ‘del Garda’ in Torri) also fall within and adjacent to SCI/SPA areas (IT3210039 (1), IT3210004 (2)), further disrupting the landscape continuity between the lake and the mountains. The works were also pointless: the neighbouring municipalities of Torbole and Garda do not intend to extend the routes because they would take a heavy environmental toll. The press has already condemned the projects (3). The works, which are still going on (4), were financed with NRRP money. The Commission has already received a question on this matter (E-002947/2024), but work has continued in the meantime and it has had a serious impact on the environment. Can the Commission investigate the failure to assess whether the works were subject to an EIA and call for the natural stretches of shore that they have ruined to be restored, and if those steps are not taken, open an infringement procedure? (7 May 2026) The Commission is not informed on whether an Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) was undertaken for the project at stake. The construction of cycling paths could fall within the scope of Annex II, point 10 (infrastructure projects), letter (b) of the EIA Directive (1). Under Article 4(2) of this directive, ‘Subject to Article 2(4), for projects listed in Annex II, Member States shall determine whether the project shall be made subject to an assessment in accordance with Articles 5 to 10 […]’. Furthermore, according to Article 6.3 of the Habitats Directive (2), any project not directly connected with or necessary to the management of the site but likely to have a significant effect thereon shall be subject to appropriate assessment of its implications for the site in view of the site's conservation objectives. According to Article 6.4, if, in spite of a negative assessment of the implications for the site and in the absence of alternative solutions, a project must nevertheless be carried out for imperative reasons of overriding public interest, the Member State shall take all compensatory measures necessary to ensure that the overall coherence of Natura 2000 is protected. Italy has transposed these provisions in its legislation (3) and has adopted national guidelines (4) to improve their application across its regions. Veneto has also transposed such guidelines into its regional legal order (5). It is for the Italian competent authorities to apply the above rules and procedures to this project and to ensure that, if damage to a protected sites has occurred, it is adequately restored. In its role as guardian of the Treaties, the Commission may decide to intervene if systemic issues with application of these provisions of EU law arise (6).

E-10-2026-001122.t: The Syneos Health case and relocation of clinical trials to outside the EU
qt: to the Commission Brando Benifei (S&D), Alessandra Moretti (S&D) Subject:

Syneos Health is an international contract research organisation (CRO). It provides operational services for clinical trials on behalf of sponsors – mainly pharmaceutical and biotechnology companies. After introducing a model based on process automation, digitalisation of operational activities and relocation of operations to countries outside the EU, it has announced a collective redundancy in Italy. This process would not cover activities considered ‘country-agnostic’, such as clinical research support, trial documentation management and pharmacovigilance, but could extend to branches of activities interplaying with test centres, ethics committees and national and European regulatory authorities. This would pose the risk to European clinical research of a loss of the professional expertise acquired in the EU, difficulties in coordination between operators, research centres and competent authorities, as well as increased regulatory misalignment, thus increasing dependence on third-party actors in what is a strategic sector. In the light of the above, can the Commission answer the following questions: 1.

Does the Commission not consider that significant relocation of CRO operations to third countries is liable to affect the ability of sponsors to ensure the supervision required by Regulation (EU) No 536/2014?

Does it see a need to assess the impact of these operational models on the ability of Member States’ national competent authorities and of the EMA to effectively conduct inspections and ensure compliance with good clinical practice standards?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (26.5.2026) According to the Clinical Trials Regulation (CTR)1 and the principles of good clinical practice2, the sponsor has a responsibility to ensure the safety of clinical trial participants and the reliability of data even when activities are delegated to contract research organisations, including when activities are undertaken outside of the EU. There is, however, no legal requirement for activities to be undertaken by EU-based staff. Article 71 of the CTR defines the obligations for clinical trial sponsors and investigators, including the conditions for delegation of tasks. Furthermore, under Article 74 of the CTR, sponsors established in third countries must have a legal representative in the EU. Member States are required to carry out inspections on their territory or in third countries to supervise compliance with the CTR3. The detailed arrangements for Good Clinical Practice inspection procedures are laid down in national implementing legislation, including the need for Member States to establish relevant procedures for arranging inspections outside the EU4. The European Medicines Agency also has a role in coordinating cooperation between Member States for inspections within and outside the EU. Hence, the necessary means to allow Member States to conduct inspections effectively and in a timely manner both within and outside the EU are in place.
1 Regulation (EU) No 536/2014 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 16 April 2014 on clinical trials

on medicinal products for human use, and repealing Directive 2001/20/EC. E-10-2026-001120.t: PFAS regulation in the forthcoming REACH revision
qt: to the Commission Elisabetta Gualmini (Renew), Cristina Guarda (Verts/ALE) Subject:

The REACH Regulation is due to be revised in 2026. According to some reports, the changes will also cover PFAS (a group of over 10 000 per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances), based, among other things, on the restriction proposal submitted to the European Chemicals Agency in 2023 and the 2025 technical updates. Urgent action is required in light of the various studies highlighting the harmful impact on the environment and health of many of these substances, which are particularly resistant and persistent, and accumulate in air, water, soil and living organisms. The remediation, filtration, and health, agricultural and waste management costs relating to these compounds are extremely high: a DG ENV report published on 29 January 2026 estimates that if PFAS pollution continues at current levels, the cost for the EU could amount to EUR 440 billion by 2050. At present, we can identify, precisely measure and accurately pinpoint the effects of only a small proportion of the PFAS in the Union. In view of this, can the Commission indicate how it intends to deal with PFAS in the REACH revision in order to establish a regulatory framework that respects the precautionary principle for both the environment and health?
at: (English version) to the Commission Elisabetta Gualmini (Renew), Cristina Guarda (Verts/ALE) (18 March 2026) Subject: PFAS regulation in the forthcoming REACH revision The REACH Regulation is due to be revised in 2026. According to some reports, the changes will also cover PFAS (a group of over 10 000 per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances), based, among other things, on the restriction proposal submitted to the European Chemicals Agency in 2023 and the 2025 technical updates. Urgent action is required in light of the various studies highlighting the harmful impact on the environment and health of many of these substances, which are particularly resistant and persistent, and accumulate in air, water, soil and living organisms. The remediation, filtration, and health, agricultural and waste management costs relating to these compounds are extremely high: a DG ENV report published on 29 January 2026 estimates that if PFAS pollution continues at current levels, the cost for the EU could amount to EUR 440 billion by 2050. At present, we can identify, precisely measure and accurately pinpoint the effects of only a small proportion of the PFAS in the Union. In view of this, can the Commission indicate how it intends to deal with PFAS in the REACH revision in order to establish a regulatory framework that respects the precautionary principle for both the environment and health? (26 May 2026) A restriction dossier covering all per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) has been submitted under the existing Regulation concerning the Registration, Evaluation, Authorisation and Restriction of Chemicals (REACH) (1) and is currently assessed by the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA). This restriction dossier will be processed irrespective of a potential revision of REACH. As indicated in the Chemicals Industry Action Plan (2), the Commission is committed to presenting a proposal as soon as possible after receiving the final ECHA’s opinions, with the overall objective of minimising PFAS emissions. The Commission will consider a ban on PFAS in consumer goods such as cosmetics, food contact materials and outdoor clothing. Where adequate alternatives in terms of performance and safety are not available, the continued use of PFAS in industrial applications may be allowed for critical applications, such as health, defence, semiconductors, and other strategic sector s (3), under strict conditions and until acceptable substitutes are found. Derogations for uses will need to be accompanied by requirements to reduce emissions at all lifecycle stages to limit the release of pollutants into the environment and by clear incentives to innovate. The Commission will base its restriction proposal on the ECHA’s opinions and the final restriction dossier prepared by the five national authorities, which incorporate the comments received during the two consultations. The Commission may also take into account other available, reliable information, where relevant.

E-10-2026-001119.t: Possible surge in migration from Iran
qt: to the Commission Loucas Fourlas (PPE) Subject:

The continuation of the conflict in Iran may drive a new wave of displaced populations into neighbouring regions and possibly towards Europe. We have learnt from previous crises that geopolitical upheavals in the Middle East often result in new migratory pressures at the EU’s external borders. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
What is its assessment of possible migration flows from Iran to the European Union?
Is there a specific contingency plan for dealing with mass population movement?
How does it intend to support frontline states, particularly in the Eastern Mediterranean?
at: (English version) to the Commission Loucas Fourlas (PPE) (18 March 2026) Subject: Possible surge in migration from Iran The continuation of the conflict in Iran may drive a new wave of displaced populations into neighbouring regions and possibly towards Europe. We have learnt from previous crises that geopolitical upheavals in the Middle East often result in new migratory pressures at the EU’s external borders. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
What is its assessment of possible migration flows from Iran to the European Union?
Is there a specific contingency plan for dealing with mass population movement?
How does it intend to support frontline states, particularly in the Eastern Mediterranean?

(7 May 2026) At this stage, the situation in Iran has not led to increased migratory flows towards the EU. The situation remains highly volatile. The Commission is closely monitoring developments in coordination with Member States, EU agencies, partner countries, international organisations and the European External Action Service, notably through the EU Migration Preparedness and Crisis Blueprint Network (1). This supports situational awareness, forecasting and early warning, enabling better anticipation and preparedness. Member States are responsible for contingency planning across different areas of border and migration management, enabling them to respond to a range of possible scenarios. At EU level, this is complemented by coordination and support measures, including the readiness of EU agencies to provide operational and technical assistance, and flexible EU funding, including emergency support where necessary. In the context of preparations for the Pact on Migration and Asylum (2), the Commission is supporting Member States in ensuring a well-prepared migration management system by June 2026, including coordinated crisis response. As reaffirmed by leaders during the 19-20 March 2026 European Council, the EU is ready to mobilise its diplomatic, legal, operational and financial tools to prevent uncontrolled migratory movements to the EU and preserve security in Europe.

E-10-2026-001117.t: The Gender Equality Strategy 2026-2030 and inequalities affecting men
qt: to the Commission Kosma Złotowski (ECR) Subject:

On 5 March 2026, the Commission presented its Gender Equality Strategy 2026-20301. The document states that the principle of gender equality will be mainstreamed across all areas of life, particularly in education, healthcare and the labour market. At the same time, according to generally available knowledge and data, including data published by EUROSTAT, men constitute the overwhelming majority of victims of suicide and fatal accidents at work, have a shorter average life expectancy, and struggle with an ‘education gap’ and other adverse phenomena. In this context, one might get the impression that the Commission’s Strategy, aimed at promoting equal opportunities for women and men, focuses mainly on the situation of women, overlooking areas in which men are in a significantly less favourable position or face specific problems requiring public intervention. In light of the above: 1.
Why does the Gender Equality Strategy 2026-2030 not address the issue of men’s mental health, given that they account for some 77 % of all suicides in the EU?2
Why does the Strategy not address differences in life expectancy, which, according to EUROSTAT data for 2024, stands at around 79 years for men and 84 years for women?3

Why does the Strategy not address the issue of safety in the workplace, given that, according to EUROSTAT data for 2023, a total of 2 153 161 workplace accidents were recorded, of which 1 663 598 (approximately 77 %) involved men and 488 868 (approximately 23 %) involved women?4

at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (18.5.2026) The Gender Equality Strategy 2026-20301 recognises the crucial role of men and boys, as agents and beneficiaries of gender equality. It recognises that gender inequalities significantly impact access to healthcare and that gender norms associated with traditional masculinity can adversely affect men and boys’ health, including discouraging help-seeking and increasing engagement in harmful behaviours. The Strategy refers to gender mainstreaming in health research under the Framework Programme for Research and Innovation (Horizon 2020 and Horizon Europe)2 and into the health actions of the EU, including the EU4Health programme3. The Communication on a comprehensive approach to mental health4 supports a comprehensive and inclusive life-course approach that focuses on effective prevention and access to care for all population groups, including men. Life expectancy and healthy longevity are extensively covered in the Health at a Glance 2024 report5 and informed actions under the EU4Health programme. The EU Occupational Safety and Health (OSH) acquis6, comprising the Framework Directive7 and related OSH Directives, ensures a minimum level of protection against OSH risks and requires employers to carry out a risk assessment and implement preventive and protective measures, also considering gender aspects. The EU Strategic Framework on Health and Safety at Work 2021-20278 aims to improve prevention of workplace accidents and illnesses and addresses also psychosocial risks at work. The Gender Equality Strategy refers to the upcoming Healthy Workplace Campaign on mental health and psychosocial risks at work of the European Agency for Safety and Health at Work in 20269.

E-10-2026-001115.t: Transparency over the assets of EU Member States
qt: to the Commission Markus Buchheit (ESN) Subject:

Does the Commission intend to publish the gross and net assets of the total national economy (held by companies, households and the state) of each Member State for the year 2023, broken down by asset type (tangible, financial and intangible)?

To what extent are the methodologies used by national central banks – in particular the sectoral and total economy balance sheets of the Deutsche Bundesbank – already integrated into Eurostat’s national accounting and financial account statistics?
What measures does the Commission intend to take to ensure the full comparability of such asset statistics between Member States?
at: (English version) to the Commission Markus Buchheit (ESN) (18 March 2026) Subject: Transparency over the assets of EU Member States 1. Does the Commission intend to publish the gross and net assets of the total national economy (held by companies, households and the state) of each Member State for the year 2023, broken down by asset type (tangible, financial and intangible)? 2. To what extent are the methodologies used by national central banks — in particular the sectoral and total economy balance sheets of the Deutsche Bundesbank — already integrated into Eurostat’s national accounting and financial account statistics? 3. What measures does the Commission intend to take to ensure the full comparability of such asset statistics between Member States? (22 May 2026) Eurostat publishes data on total annual financial assets and liabilities of the total econom y (1), as well as on non-financial assets by detailed asset type (2), for all Member States, starting from 1995. The data are also available by institutional sector. Annual financial accounts data are transmitted to Eurostat by all Member States, including data for Germany compiled by the Deutsche Bundesbank following the European System of National and Regional Accounts (3) (ESA 2010), and are used to compile Euro Area and EU aggregates by institutional sector. National accounts and annual financial accounts data transmitted to Eurostat by EU countries follow ESA 2010, the EU’s internationally compatible accounting framework. Eurostat issues manuals and methodological guidance to support harmonised implementation by all Member States and applies a robust quality assurance framework to the transmitted data. Since 2018, and every five years thereafter, Eurostat reports to the European Parliament and the Council on the application of ESA 2010, assessing the data quality, the effectiveness of the regulation and its monitoring process, as well as progress on contingent liabilities and data availability (the latest report was released in 2023 (4)).

E-10-2026-001114.t: The impact on SMEs of the immediate application of anti-dumping duties on ceramic imports from China
qt: to the Commission Barry Cowen (Renew) Subject:

The Commission has adopted an implementing regulation1 that increases anti-dumping duties on imports of ceramic tableware and kitchenware from China to approximately 79 %, with immediate effect. A number of EU-based importers, including small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), report that shipments already in transit at the time of entry into force of the regulation are now subject to the higher duty, resulting in significant and unforeseen costs. 1.
Why was no transitional period provided for goods that were already in transit at the time the regulation entered into force?
What assessment has the Commission made regarding the impact of this measure on EU SMEs that rely on these imports?
How were the affected importers notified in advance of the change, and will the Commission consider improved advance notice for any future trade defence measures?

at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (13.5.2026) In the case at hand, the initiation of the investigation that resulted in the increase of the applicable duties was announced on 19 December 2024. The Commission informed all interested parties on 26 November 2025 of the findings The Regulation amending the duties was published on 6 February 20261 and entered into force on the following day. This allowed for more than two months until the publication of the increased measures and more than 13 months after the initiation of the investigation. As part of the procedure, during the investigations, the Commission informs all parties that come forward about the findings in advance of any decision and invites them to comment. E-10-2026-001111.t: Foot-and-mouth disease and issues regarding practical implementation of the legislation
qt: to the Commission Michalis Hadjipantela (PPE) Subject:

Concerns expressed by farmers in Cyprus about foot-and-mouth disease highlight practical issues with the implementation of disease control measures provided for in the legislation. Pursuant to Article 12(1)(a) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/687, following the confirmation of an outbreak of a category A disease in an establishment, the competent authority orders the culling of all animals of listed species in the affected establishment. However, Article 12(4) provides for the possibility of a derogation based on a risk assessment, including when emergency vaccination is introduced, in accordance with Article 69 of Regulation (EU) 2016/429. In practice, cases may arise where most of the animals on a livestock farm have already been vaccinated and only a limited number of animals were infected prior to vaccination. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

How does it interpret the application of Article 12(1) and (4) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/687 in cases where vaccination has already been carried out and infection is confirmed only in a limited number of animals?
Under what conditions can the competent authority, following a risk assessment, limit culling to infected animals only rather than ordering the culling of all animals on the farm?
Does it intend to issue further guidelines to Member States on the proportionate application of disease control measures on vaccinated flocks?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (8.5.2026) 1. The EU’s legal framework, in particular Regulation (EU) 2016/4291 and Commission Delegated Regulations (EU) 2020/6872 and 2020/6893, provides for harmonised measures across the Union, based on the principle of rapid eradication through stamping out confirmed outbreaks of Category A diseases such as foot and mouth disease (FMD), combined with movement restrictions and, where appropriate, the use of vaccination4. 2. Under Article 12(1) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/687, the competent authority is required to order the culling of all animals of listed species in an affected establishment following the confirmation of FMD. Vaccination does not alter that requirement. Article 12(4) provides for limited derogations based on a case-by-case risk assessment, giving flexibility for performing the culling either in other locations or postponing the culling based on the context of emergency vaccination, provided that such measures do not compromise disease control. However, culling remains mandatory also in those cases. Indeed, these derogations do not alter the general principle of rapid eradication through stamping-out, which remains essential given the highly contagious nature of the disease. 3. Since the rules and guidelines remain unchanged, the Commission does not foresee issuing further guidelines.
1 Regulation (EU) 2016/429 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 9 March 2016 on transmissible

animal diseases and amending and repealing certain acts in the area of animal health (‘Animal Health Law’) (OJ L 84, 31.3.2016, pp. 1, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/429/oj). 2 Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/687 of 17 December 2019 supplementing Regulation (EU) 2016/429 of the European Parliament and the Council, as regards rules for the prevention and control of certain listed diseases (OJ L 174, 3.6.2020, pp. 64–, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg_del/2020/687/oj). 3 Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/689 of 17 December 2019 supplementing Regulation (EU) 2016/429 of the European Parliament and of the Council as regards rules for surveillance, eradication programmes, and disease-free status for certain listed and emerging diseases (OJ L 174, 3.6.2020, pp. 211–340, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg_del/2020/689/oj). 4 https://food.ec.europa.eu/animals/animal-diseases/diseases-and-control-measures/foot-and-mouth-disease_en.

E-10-2026-001110.t: Risks posed to Malta and the Italian Pelagie Islands by the drifting Russian shadow-fleet tanker vessel ‘Arctic Metagaz’
qt: to the Commission Thomas Bajada (S&D), Giuseppe Lupo (S&D) Subject:

According to notices issued by the Maltese authorities, the Russian tanker vessel ‘Arctic Metagaz’ is not under command and is damaged following an alleged attack. Public reporting has indicated that, at the time of submission of this written question, the vessel is drifting in international waters between Malta and the Italian islands of Lampedusa and Linosa. This situation raises concerns in terms of marine pollution, environmental protection, maritime safety and the resilience of critical infrastructure, including desalination-dependent water security in the Mediterranean islands. In the light of the above: 1.

What coordination, monitoring and operational support has the Commission already provided, or does it stand ready to provide, to Malta and Italy in relation to the humanitarian and ecological risks associated with the drifting damaged vessel?

How does the Commission assess the potential risks that such incidents pose to vulnerable island territories in the central Mediterranean, particularly in terms of marine pollution, environmental protection and critical infrastructure resilience?

Does the Commission intend to strengthen EU preparedness and contingency planning for similar incidents involving damaged, high-risk or sanctioned vessels drifting near coastal and island territories in the Mediterranean?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (18.6.2026) The Commission, in cooperation with the European Maritime Safety Agency (EMSA), monitored the situation of tanker Arctic Metagaz and provided satellite imagery to all parties involved from 3 March to 30 April 2026 by the Integrated Maritime Surveillance. The vessel no longer contains flammable content and no related oil spills were detected. The Commission, through its Emergency Response Coordination Centre, facilitated coordination and information exchange among authorities during the incident. This incident demonstrates the seriousness of environmental threats posed, the need for involved States to act when there is a ship in need of assistance and to provide continuous monitoring to mitigate the risks posed, including by the shadow fleet. While the vessel is not in the vicinity of Malta or the Italian Pelagie Islands, such incidents may pose risks to vulnerable coastal and island territories, sensitive marine ecosystems, fisheries and critical infrastructure1. The Commission is actively working to further enhance the maritime domain awareness and information sharing among Member States authorities, beyond the well-established and continuously refined EMSA-hosted Union Maritime Information and Exchange System2. The Commission will continue to work with Member States, EMSA and international partners to ensure preparedness and effective response. The Commission also supports coastguard cooperation, in particular in the Mediterranean area, through the Mediterranean Coast Guard Function Forum (MEDCGFF). The Commission encourages Member States to step up their efforts in the maritime domain to address the complex maritime challenges faced today.
1 Including desalination-dependent water supply systems. 2 SafeSeaNet legally mandated under Directive 2002/59/EC – Vessel Traffic Monitoring including The Union
Maritime Information and Exchange System.

E-10-2026-001109.t: Proposed marketing standards for cider and perry
qt: to the Commission Asger Christensen (Renew) Subject:

The Commission has shared with Member States draft marketing standards for cider and perry as secondary legislation to the regulation establishing a common organisation of the markets in agricultural products (Regulation (EU) No 1308/2013). The current draft of the marketing standards would have a major impact on long-standing Nordic ciders. It would re-classify them so that they could only be called ‘cider-based’ drinks, despite their long tradition and significant share of the European cider market. There is no precedent for such a standard, no equivalent rules for soft drinks or beer, and no evidence of consumer demand. Further, the draft offers no consumer benefit, adds regulatory burden and costs, and runs counter to the EU’s simplification and competitiveness agenda. It would downgrade Nordic-style ciders compared to other European styles. In light of this: 1.
Does the Commission consider the proposal to be aligned with the EU’s simplification and competitiveness agenda?
Does the Commission consider that the proposal will provide added value to the sector?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (2.6.2026) In its reply to question P-001116/2026, the Commission explained how it has been discussing different possible approaches for the establishment of marketing standards for cider and perry with national experts and representatives of the sector since 2024, after having published a report1 and an impact assessment2 on marketing standards including those for cider and perry in 2023. With the support of a large majority of Member States and of representatives of the sector, the Commission will pursue discussions with all Member States to further explore options with the objective of covering all products currently present on the market under the name of cider, in full respect of EU diversity and of providing added value to the EU cider sector as a whole, contributing to the EU competitiveness agenda, as marketing standards would equally benefit apple and pear growers as well as cider and perry producers. While the non-paper circulated up to now in different revised versions, it is not yet final and remains open to improvement, the standard envisaged by the Commission aims to harmonise rules across the whole EU market without applying to EU exports or requiring any reformulation of cider products and perry products, although some of them may need to be labelled in a way that ensure that consumers are accurately informed about the type of product they purchase and consume.
1 https://eur-
lex.europa.eu/search.html?scope=EURLEX&text=COM%282023%29200&lang=en&type=quick&qid=1774271 284377. 2 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/NL/ALL/?uri=CELEX:52023SC0097.

E-10-2026-001107.t: Investigation into irregular awarding of health equipment contracts with European funds during the COVID-19 pandemic in the Canary Islands
qt: to the Commission Elena Nevado del Campo (PPE), Isabel Benjumea Benjumea (PPE) Subject:

According to recently published information, during the COVID-19 pandemic, the Government of the Canary Islands awarded several contracts for the purchase of medical equipment worth tens of millions of euros. Some of these contracts are said to have been awarded under an emergency procedure by the current minister, Ángel Víctor Torres, to companies currently under investigation by various judicial bodies – notably the European Public Prosecutor’s Office, the Civil Guard and the Canary Islands Court of Auditors – and co-financed with ERDF funds. The information points to possible irregularities in the processing of certain dossiers, such as shortcomings in the suppliers’ technical solvency accreditation, documentary shortcomings or traceability problems regarding the use of European funds. Considering the important role of the Commission in the protection of the financial interests of the Union: 1.
Does the Commission know whether any of the health contracts awarded in the Canary Islands during the pandemic under investigation were financed, in whole or in part, by ERDF funds?

Has it requested information from the Spanish authorities or carried out verifications to ensure that said funds were used in accordance with the applicable law and the principle of sound financial management?
In the event that irregularities were to be identified in projects financed with EU funds, what measures will be taken to recover the funds?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (21.5.2026) The Commission is aware of the judicial investigations on the health equipment contracts in Canary Islands. In line with the shared management principle governing cohesion policy, the Commission has requested information to the Spanish Managing authorities on the possible support from the European Regional Development Fund (ERDF) funding to these contracts. Member States bear the primary responsibility for the implementation and control of operations funded by the ERDF, including detecting and correcting irregularities. The Spanish authorities are therefore responsible for ensuring that contracts co-financed by ERDF comply with applicable procurement rules and that funds are used correctly. The Commission’s role is supervisory ensuring that the national management and control systems provide the assurance that resources are used in compliance with EU law and the principle of sound financial management. The procurement procedures for the specific contracts in the Canary Islands were not subject to the Commission’s own verification. However, if irregularities were identified, either through national controls or investigations by the European Public Prosecutor’s Office, the Commission would expect the Spanish authorities to take corrective measures, including financial corrections where necessary1. Failing to take action at national level, the Commission would take appropriate action in order to ensure that EU funds are used in accordance with the applicable rules, including through the application of the appropriate financial corrections. The Commission remains in contact with the Spanish authorities. Should new information emerge, the Commission will assess whether further action is required.
1 in line with Article 69 of Regulation (EU) 2021/1060; ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2021/1060/oj.

E-10-2026-001106.t: Single register of leases and digital one-stop shop for rental accommodation
qt: to the Commission Borja Giménez Larraz (PPE), Elena Nevado del Campo (PPE) Subject:

In late 2024, the Spanish Government approved Royal Decree 1312/2024 of 23 December, which governs the single register of leases and establishes the digital one-stop shop for rental accommodation – for the collection and exchange of data on short-term accommodation rental services – while citing the urgent need to implement Regulation 2024/1028, due to enter into force on 20 May 2026 and the attendant obligations incumbent upon it. This was therefore done with undue haste and without justification, prior to the deadline for compliance with the requirement for a single registration procedure imposed by the Regulation. Instead of coordinating the existing registers in the autonomous communities – which are governed by principles of competence laid down in the Spanish Constitution and the statutes governing the autonomous communities – the Spanish Government has acted unilaterally and in breach of the new EU regulation by establishing a new single register. This has duplicated administrative burdens, given rise to legal uncertainty and usurped competences within the Spanish legal system. Can the Commission therefore say: 1.
What view it takes on this matter and how it intends to act if the Spanish Government fails to remedy this situation?
at: (English version) to the Commission Borja Giménez Larraz (PPE), Elena Nevado del Campo (PPE) (18 March 2026) Subject: Single register of leases and digital one-stop shop for rental accommodation In late 2024, the Spanish Government approved Royal Decree 1312/2024 of 23 December, which governs the single register of leases and establishes the digital one-stop shop for rental accommodation — for the collection and exchange of data on shortterm accommodation rental services — while citing the urgent need to implement Regulation 2024/1028, due to enter into force on 20 May 2026 and the attendant obligations incumbent upon it. This was therefore done with undue haste and without justification, prior to the deadline for compliance with the requirement for a single registration procedure imposed by the regulation. Instead of coordinating the existing registers in the autonomous communities — which are governed by principles of competence laid down in the Spanish Constitution and the statutes governing the autonomous communities — the Spanish Government has acted unilaterally and in breach of the new EU regulation by establishing a new single register. This has duplicated administrative burdens, given rise to legal uncertainty and usurped competences within the Spanish legal system. Can the Commission therefore say: 1.
What view it takes on this matter and how it intends to act if the Spanish Government fails to remedy this situation?

(27 April 2026) As indicated by the Honourable Members, the Spanish Government has adopted Royal Decree 1312/2024, which aims to implement Regulation (EU) 2024/1028 (1), the Short-Term Rental (STR) Regulation. Article 4 of the STR Regulation provides that a unit shall not be subject to more than one registration procedure. The Commission has, on several occasions, raised concerns with the Spanish authorities regarding a potential conflict between the registration procedure established by the Royal Decree and those already in place at the local level. At the same time, the STR Regulation will enter into force on 20 May 2026. Until that date, the existence of multiple registration procedures does not constitute a breach of the regulation. In the meantime, the Commission continues to monitor developments.
