E-10-2026-001105.t: Lead and the craft and heritage sectors
qt: to the Commission Céline Imart (PPE) Subject:

Lead is currently classified in the REACH Regulation as a substance of very high concern, and is already included on the restricted substances list. In 2023 the European Chemicals Agency recommended that lead be included in Annex XIV, which would make its usage subject to a system of prior authorisation. This regulatory development is raising serious concerns in a number of craft and heritage sectors, particularly in the stained glass, heritage restoration and traditional ceramics trades. In these sectors, the use of lead remains essential in certain manufacturing processes, and there are not always technical alternatives that produce equivalent results. A number of European craft enterprises, many of them operating on a small scale, fear that the costs and complexity of the authorisation processes might put their business in jeopardy, leaving them exposed to greater competition with imported products from countries subject to less strict standards. In view of this: 1.
Is the Commission planning to add lead to Annex XIV to the REACH Regulation?
If so, how does it intend to account for the specificities of the art and heritage professions, in order to preserve these traditional skilled trades?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (11.5.2026) The Commission is aware that the European Chemicals Agency proposed to include lead metal in the list of substances subject to the authorisation requirement under the Regulation for the registration, evaluation, authorisation and restriction chemicals (REACH)1. The Commission, drawing on past consultations with cultural heritage experts, is not obliged to follow this recommendation and does not intend to include lead in the authorisation list (Annex XIV to REACH). The Commission considers that lead risks are being successfully managed through other risk management measures, including existing restrictions under REACH and the recently revised occupational limits for lead. The Commission gives the utmost importance to tradition, artisanal work and preservation of cultural heritage. If ever additional measures on lead were to be considered in the more distant future, the Commission will certainly take into account the importance of lead in preserving the European cultural heritage when considering possible derogations during the decisionmaking process.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02006R1907-20251023.

E-10-2026-001104.t: Need for flexibility in the implementation of measures to combat foot-and-mouth disease in Cyprus
qt: to the Commission Geadis Geadi (ECR) Subject:

The implementation of measures to combat foot-and-mouth disease in the European Union is based on the principle of prompt eradication of the disease through strict health protocols. However, on an island such as Cyprus, with its limited livestock base, the large-scale culling of animals may have a disproportionate impact on the economy and on production. Cyprus’s situation is unique, in that the Member State is both an island and at the same time under partial occupation, with 37 % of its northern territory not under the Republic of Cyprus’s control, which poses additional challenges. In view of this, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
What is the Commission’s assessment of the proportionality of the implementation of the existing foot-and-mouth disease protocols in small island Member States such as Cyprus?

Can the Commission consider granting Cyprus specific flexibility, taking into account the country’s specific geographical and political circumstances, allowing for the implementation of alternative disease containment strategies, such as targeted vaccination policies and enhanced monitoring measures, to avoid the large-scale culling of asymptomatic animals?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (11.5.2026) The EU legal framework, in particular Regulation (EU) 2016/4291 and Commission Delegated Regulations (EU) 2020/6872 and 2020/6893, provides for harmonised measures across the Union, based on the principle of rapid eradication through the stamping-out of confirmed outbreaks, combined with movement restrictions and, where appropriate, the use of vaccination4. These measures are designed to be proportionate to the risks posed by the disease and are applied taking into account the epidemiological situation. A recent risk assessment was carried out to ensure the efficacy of those measures for Member States5. While the legal framework is harmonised, its implementation allows for a degree of flexibility in the choice and combination of measures, including the use of emergency vaccination, under the responsibility of the competent authorities of the Member States. The Commission is in close contact with the Cypriot authorities and supports them in the application of the appropriate control measures, including through technical assistance6 and access to the EU foot and mouth disease vaccine bank7. The Commission continues to monitor the situation closely in view of the evolving epidemiological situation.
1 Regulation (EU) 2016/429 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 9 March 2016 on transmissible

animal diseases and amending and repealing certain acts in the area of animal health (‘Animal Health Law’) (OJ L 84, 31.3.2016, pp. 1, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/429/oj). 2 Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/687 of 17 December 2019 supplementing Regulation (EU) 2016/429 of the European Parliament and the Council, as regards rules for the prevention and control of certain listed diseases (OJ L 174, 3.6.2020, pp. 64–, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg_del/2020/687/oj). 3 Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/689 of 17 December 2019 supplementing Regulation (EU) 2016/429 of the European Parliament and of the Council as regards rules for surveillance, eradication programmes, and disease-free status for certain listed and emerging diseases (OJ L 174, 3.6.2020, pp. 211–340, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg_del/2020/689/oj). 4 https://food.ec.europa.eu/animals/animal-diseases/diseases-and-control-measures/foot-and-mouth-disease_en. 5 Scientific Opinion on the assessment of the control measures for category A diseases of Animal Health Law: Foot and Mouth Disease, First published: 08 June 2021, https://doi.org/10.2903/j.efsa.2021.6632. 6 https://food.ec.europa.eu/animals/animal-diseases/veterinary-emergency-team_en. 7 https://food.ec.europa.eu/animals/animal-diseases/diseases-and-control-measures/foot-and-mouthdisease/support-cy_en.

E-10-2026-001103.t: Management and ownership status of EU transport capabilities within the solidarity pool
qt: to the Commission Michał Dworczyk (ECR) Subject:

In its response to my question E-004950/20251, the Commission indicated that the solidarity pool provided for in the draft regulation on military mobility2 will include registered EU transport capabilities. The Commission stressed that the capabilities procured by the Union would be hosted by Member States, and that the Member State requesting their deployment would lead the relevant support operations. However, the Commission’s response and the draft regulation leave doubts as to the division of competences between the Union and the Member States regarding decision-making on the use of EU capabilities and their ownership status. In light of the above: 1.

Which entity will be authorised to decide on the provision, deployment, redeployment or withdrawal of EU transport and logistics capabilities within the solidarity pool, and will the Member State hosting such capabilities have the right to object to their use, redeployment or withdrawal?

Which entity will be authorised to decide on the provision, deployment, redeployment or withdrawal of EU transport and logistics capabilities within the solidarity pool, and will the Member State hosting such capabilities have the right to object to their use, redeployment or withdrawal?
Does the Commission envisage that EU capabilities will constitute Union-owned assets, or will they be procured on the basis of agreements with Member States or commercial operators?

Given that the Military Mobility Transport Group is intended to play only an advisory role, which body — and on the basis of what criteria and procedures — will identify transport capability gaps, take decisions regarding the acquisition of such capabilities by the Union and determine their type, and how will Member States’ participation in this process be ensured?

(5 June 2026) The Commission recalls that, as part of its proposal for a military mobility regulation (1), the Solidarity Pool has been proposed as a framework encouraging Member States to pool and share transport and logistics capabilities. Member States may voluntarily register their own capabilities, while those that have been acquired or contracted by Member States with the financing support of any EU funding must be registered in the Solidarity Pool. Subject to the availability of EU funding, the Commission may adopt an implementing act putting into operation the Solidarity Pool which would set out the procedures to be followed to process requests by Member States for capabilities as well as any other additional rules for its functioning. The implementing act may set out more detailed rules on how EU capabilities would function under the Solidarity Pool. In addition, based on the advice of the Military Mobility Transport Group and the results of stress tests, the Commission may adopt non-binding guidelines defining the types and specifying the number of key transport capabilities required for the Solidarity Pool to address EU’s gaps. These non-binding guidelines do not constitute capability development priorities for military mobility, rather giving an indication of capabilities to be shared to support Member States’ military transport operations. As end-users, Member States have a decisive role in determining the capabilities to share. As members of the Military Mobility Transport Group, their input will aid the preparation of guidelines. Member States will also voluntarily decide what to register in the Solidarity Pool and whether to make use of possible EU financial support to procure capabilities that will then have to be registered there.

E-10-2026-001102.t: The lawfulness of return hubs under current EU law
qt: to the Commission Tineke Strik (Verts/ALE) Subject:

In an interview following the Justice and Home Affairs Council (JHA) on 5 March 2026, the Dutch Minister for Asylum and Migration, Bart van den Brink, confirmed that the Netherlands is working with Germany, Denmark, Greece and Austria to develop so-called return hubs in third countries. 1.
Is the Commission aware of the aforementioned negotiations by this group of Member States, and in what way is it involved?

If this group of Member States does conclude an agreement with a third country, what conditions must such an agreement meet, in the Commission’s view, and does the Commission intend to assess and monitor the implementation of such an agreement?

Given the lack of a legal basis for this form of forced return under Directive 2008/111, does the Commission consider that such an agreement could enter into force in accordance with EU law as the law currently stands?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.7.2026)

The Commission is aware and takes note of the ongoing discussions among a group of Member States, as it is invited to participate as observer. Member States must ensure that returns from the EU of illegally staying third country nationals comply with relevant EU law, in particular Directive 2008/115/EC1 (‘Return Directive’), and respect fundamental rights and obligations stemming from international law. This is also the case for bilateral agreements or arrangements with third countries. The Commission will continue to ensure that EU law is applied correctly across all Member States, taking to the necessary measures in case of breaches of EU law. Article 17 of the Commission’s proposal for a Return Regulation2 creates the legal framework and sets out the conditions for setting up ‘return hubs’. Among those conditions, the proposal provides for an independent body or mechanism to monitor the effective application of the agreement or arrangement. Political agreement on the Return Regulation was reached in the trilogue on 1 June 2026. It was endorsed by the European Parliament on 17 June and by Coreper on 10 June.
1 Directive 2008/115/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 16 December 2008 on common standards

and procedures in Member States for returning illegally staying third-country nationals. 2 Proposal for a Regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council establishing a common system for the return of third-country nationals staying illegally in the Union, and repealing Directive 2008/115/EC of the European Parliament and the Council, Council Directive 2001/40/EC and Council Decision 2004/191/EC.

E-10-2026-001101.t: Industrial Accelerator Act and the risk of regulatory complexity for EU industry
qt: to the Commission Fulvio Martusciello (PPE) Subject:

The Commission has brought forward a proposal for an Industrial Accelerator Act to strengthen Europe’s industrial capacity and accelerate decarbonisation in strategic sectors. The proposal includes measures such as European origin criteria in public procurement, specific conditions for certain investments and new authorisation procedures for industrial projects. This initiative is part of the Union’s recent industrial policies, alongside the Net-Zero Industry Act, the Critical Raw Materials Act and the objectives under the Clean Industrial Deal. Over the past two decades, the EU’s share of global manufacturing production has fallen from 25 % to less than 15 %, with many companies reporting that regulatory complexity and authorisation times are among the main barriers to industrial investment. Europe cannot afford complexity cloaked as ambition, especially when the aim is to strengthen industrial competitiveness and the functioning of the European single market. In the light of the above, can the Commission answer the following questions: 1.
Does it think that the measures under the proposed regulation are properly weighted against the risk of new regulatory complexity?
Have measures been envisaged to ensure realistic implementation of the regulation in the Member States?
How does it intend to define and apply the European preference in public procurement provided for in the proposal for a regulation?
at: (English version) to the Commission Fulvio Martusciello (PPE) (18 March 2026) Subject: Industrial Accelerator Act and the risk of regulatory complexity for EU industry The Commission has brought forward a proposal for an Industrial Accelerator Act to strengthen Europe’s industrial capacity and accelerate decarbonisation in strategic sectors. The proposal includes measures such as European origin criteria in public procurement, specific conditions for certain investments and new authorisation procedures for industrial projects. This initiative is part of the Union’s recent industrial policies, alongside the Net-Zero Industry Act, the Critical Raw Materials Act and the objectives under the Clean Industrial Deal. Over the past two decades, the EU’s share of global manufacturing production has fallen from 25% to less than 15%, with many companies reporting that regulatory complexity and authorisation times are among the main barriers to industrial investment. Europe cannot afford complexity cloaked as ambition, especially when the aim is to strengthen industrial competitiveness and the functioning of the European single market. In the light of the above, can the Commission answer the following questions: 1.
Does it think that the measures under the proposed regulation are properly weighted against the risk of new regulatory complexity?
Have measures been envisaged to ensure realistic implementation of the regulation in the Member States?
How does it intend to define and apply the European preference in public procurement provided for in the proposal for a regulation?

(4 May 2026) The Industrial Accelerator Act proposal (1) is designed to be targeted and proportionate, focusing only on selected strategic sectors where action is most needed for decarbonisation and resilience. It builds on existing frameworks rather than creating parallel systems, and includes safeguards to avoid disproportionate costs or administrative burden, ensuring a balanced approach between ambition and practicality. The proposal includes concrete measures to facilitate implementation in Member States, notably simplified and digitalised permitting, a ‘one project-one procedure’ approach and clear timelines. Industrial manufacturing acceleration areas further streamline procedures by addressing area-level requirements in advance, reducing complexity and increasing predictability for projects. The ‘European preference’ is implemented through EU origin requirements in specific public procurement procedures and support schemes, based on EU customs rules. It applies only in defined sectors and situations involving public funding, while fully respecting the EU’s international commitments and including safeguards to ensure competition and avoid disproportionate costs. Moreover, it will be based on self-declarations, so as to avoid administrative burden.

E-10-2026-001100.t: Compliance of the Italian law on the ‘splitting’ of cash movements with EU legislation on cash controls
qt: to the Commission Emil Radev (PPE) Subject:

Under Regulation (EU) 2018/1672 on controls on cash entering or leaving the Union, persons carrying cash are obliged to declare cash movements of EUR 10 000 or more when crossing the EU’s external borders. In Italy, national authority administrative practice and guidelines provide that when a total amount of EUR 10 000 or more is carried by two or more members of the same family, each carrying an amount below the threshold, this can be considered ‘smurfing’ and an infringement of the rules on cash declarations, on the basis of national case law, in respect of intra-Schengen cash movements. In view of the above: 1.

Does the Commission consider this national-law-based interpretation and application to be compatible with Regulation (EU) 2018/1672, particularly as regards the declaration threshold, the definition of the carrier and the fact that the amount is being carried across intra-Schengen borders?

To what extent can Member States adopt or implement national rules or practices that treat cash transfers by a family as a single operation when it comes to applying the declaration threshold within the EU?
Does the Commission not consider that national measures such as these are liable to disproportionately restrict the free movement of capital within the EU?
at: (English version) to the Commission Emil Radev (PPE) (18 March 2026) Subject: Compliance of the Italian law on the ‘splitting’ of cash movements with EU legislation on cash controls Under Regulation (EU) 2018/1672 on controls on cash entering or leaving the Union, persons carrying cash are obliged to declare cash movements of EUR 10 000 or more when crossing the EU’s external borders. In Italy, national authority administrative practice and guidelines provide that when a total amount of EUR 10 000 or more is carried by two or more members of the same family, each carrying an amount below the threshold, this can be considered ‘smurfing’ and an infringement of the rules on cash declarations, on the basis of national case law, in respect of intra-Schengen cash movements. In view of the above: 1.

Does the Commission consider this national-law-based interpretation and application to be compatible with Regulation (EU) 2018/1672, particularly as regards the declaration threshold, the definition of the carrier and the fact that the amount is being carried across intra-Schengen borders?

To what extent can Member States adopt or implement national rules or practices that treat cash transfers by a family as a single operation when it comes to applying the declaration threshold within the EU?
Does the Commission not consider that national measures such as these are liable to disproportionately restrict the free movement of capital within the EU?

(13 May 2026) Regulation (EU) 2018/1672 establishes a system of controls on cash movements of a value of EUR 10,000 or more when entering or leaving the EU, enabling their traceability. It complements the EU legal framework for the prevention of money laundering and terrorist financing. Therefore, it does not apply to movements of cash within the EU, but to movement of cash with third countries even though they are part of the Schengen area. In Regulation (EU) 2018/1672, the threshold of EUR 10,000 applies per carrier, defined as a natural person, rather than per group or family. The regulation does not prevent Member States from introducing, under their national law, additional national controls on movements of cash within the EU, provided that such controls comply with the EU’s fundamental freedoms, in particular Articles 63 and 65 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU). The Italian law seems to have introduced declaration requirements for movement of cash between Italy and other EU Member States which would be similar to the ones contained under Regulation (EU) 2018/1672 to cash movements entering or leaving the EU. The Treaty rules on free movement of capital do not preclude the export of banknotes from being made conditional on a prior declaration (1). In that context, Member States may in principle also issue guidelines seeking to address the circumvention to such declaration requirements, as well as take other appropriate measures if circumvention is established. It is for the Member State, however, to demonstrate that any such national measures comply with the requirements set out in Article 65 TFEU, and in particular that they observe the principle of proportionality (2).

Judgment of the Court of 31 May 2018. Lu Zheng v Ministerio de Economía y Competitividad, C-190/17, EU:C:2018:357, paragraph 37.

E-10-2026-001099.t: Breach of the European Media Freedom Act in Galician public media
qt: to the Commission Ana Miranda Paz (Verts/ALE) Subject:

The Commission’s response to my previous question (E-001467/2024)1, in which it stated that it would monitor compliance with the European Media Freedom Act (EMFA), is at odds with what is happening with CRTVG employees, who have been protesting for over 400 weeks against information manipulation and the use of the judicial system in employment conflicts. Article 5 of the EMFA provides that the head of management and the members of the management board of public service media ‘shall be appointed on the basis of transparent, open, effective and non-discriminatory procedures and transparent, objective, nondiscriminatory and proportionate criteria’. However, the Galician Parliament has approved a reform of the law on media to take full control of public television and radio in Galicia, despite the opposition of every parliamentary group – including the BNG – except Partido Popular, which was able to pass the law thanks to its absolute majority. The report on EMFA compliance in 2025 in Spain calls for particular attention to be paid to this reform in Galicia2. How can the Commission help put an end to Galician public media’s information manipulation?

https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/E-10-2024-001467_EN.html. Media Capture Monitoring Report: Spain – Measuring EMFA compliance, https://ipi.media/wpcontent/uploads/2025/12/SPAIN-media-Capture-Monitoring-Report-Overview-1.pdf.
at: (English version) to the Commission Ana Miranda Paz (Verts/ALE) (17 March 2026) Subject: Breach of the European Media Freedom Act in Galician public media The Commission’s response to my previous question (E-001467/2024) (1), in which it stated that it would monitor compliance with the European Media Freedom Act (EMFA), is at odds with what is happening with CRTVG employees, who have been protesting for over 400 weeks against information manipulation and the use of the judicial system in employment conflicts. Article 5 of the EMFA provides that the head of management and the members of the management board of public service media ‘shall be appointed on the basis of transparent, open, effective and non-discriminatory procedures and transparent, objective, non-discriminatory and proportionate criteria’. However, the Galician Parliament has approved a reform of the law on media to take full control of public television and radio in Galicia, despite the opposition of every parliamentary group — including the BNG — except Partido Popular, which was able to pass the law thanks to its absolute majority. The report on EMFA compliance in 2025 in Spain calls for particular attention to be paid to this reform in Galicia (2). How can the Commission help put an end to Galician public media’s information manipulation? (15 June 2026) The European Media Freedom Act (EMFA) (1), under which most provisions have applied since 8 August 2025, introduces several safeguards to ensure the independent functioning of public service media. In particular, Article 5 requires Member States to ensure that public service media providers are editorially and functionally independent and that the procedures for the appointment and dismissal of the head of management or the members of the management board of public service media providers aim to guarantee that independence. Furthermore, the article sets out requirements for transparent, open and objective procedures for appointing the heads and management boards of such providers. The enforcement of the EMFA is a matter of priority for the Commission, including with regard to ensuring the independence of public service media, to which the Commission attaches great importance. The Commission has therefore been engaging closely with the Spanish authorities regarding the preparedness of their legal and institutional framework to make sure that it complies with the EMFA. This engagement is ongoing, and the Commission will use its enforcement powers, where appropriate, to ensure such compliance, focusing on systemic issues. In addition, the Commission is monitoring relevant developments related to media freedom and pluralism in all Member States, including Spain, under the annual Rule of Law Report.

E-10-2026-001098.t: Breach of democratic principles in Argentina: approval of the Milei government’s labour reforms
qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Ana Miranda Paz (Verts/ALE) Subject:

The labour reforms recently approved by Javier Milei’s government have caused consternation in Argentina and will make life worse for working-class people in the country. Bilateral relations between Argentina and the European Union are conducted under the 1990 Framework Agreement for Trade and Economic Cooperation, which lays down the arrangements for cooperation on foreign trade, the economy, agriculture and industry. Under Article 1 of the agreement, cooperation between the EU and Argentina is based on respect for the democratic principles and human rights which underpin the internal and international policies of the EU and of Argentina. Labour Court No 3 in La Plata declared Article 55 of Law No 27.802 (the ‘labour reform’ or ‘labour modernisation’ law) unconstitutional, ruling that its application breaches workers’ constitutional rights as enshrined in Article 14a. The court’s ruling was handed down a few days after the law entered into force. It is the second time that a court has found fault with legislation championed by President Milei. Is the Commission aware of this breach of the body of law underpinning democracy, of labour standards and of respect for the democratic principles that also affect bilateral relations between the EU and Argentina?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (7.5.2026) The European External Action Service (EEAS) and the Delegation of the EU in Argentina have been following the developments related to law No. 27.802 (the ‘labour reform’ or ‘labour modernisation’ law). The EEAS and the Delegation have taken note of the recent decision of the Labour Court No. 3 to declare this law unconstitutional and of the Government’s intention to appeal against the Court’s decision. The EU uses a wide range of instruments (cooperation, investment, training and trade conditionalities) to encourage compliance with international labour standards. In addition, both the EU-Mercosur interim Trade Agreement1 and the EU-Mercosur Partnership Agreement2 link cooperation between the Parties to their mutual respect for democratic principles and human rights, and include labour-related commitments such as decent work, core labour standards, effective labour protection, social dialogue, labour inspection and nondiscrimination. The EU also provides funding for vocational training in line with international labour standards and cooperates with the International Labour Organisation (ILO), follows its recommendations and funds projects with the ILO involvement. The Framework Agreement for Cooperation of 19903 sets the legal framework for bilateral relations between the EU and Argentina. Within this framework, the Joint Committee meets regularly, with the next one scheduled for the first week of June 2026. This will be the occasion to discuss important topics in different policy areas, including this one.
1 https://policy.trade.ec.europa.eu/eu-trade-relationships-country-and-region/countries-and-regions/mercosur/eu-
mercosur-agreement/text-agreement_en. 2 https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_26_113. 3 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/agree_internation/1990/530.

E-10-2026-001097.t: Higher fuel prices in the fisheries sector
qt: to the Commission Ana Miranda Paz (Verts/ALE) Subject:

The Galician fisheries sector – the largest in Europe – is grappling with an unprecedented crisis, as fuel prices rise in response to the ongoing war in the Middle East sparked by President Trump’s imperialist invasion. Many in the sector have had to moor their boats because the cost of going out to fish is greater than the value of catches they can collect during their working day. If they moor their fleet, however, they do not receive any aid whatsoever. The resulting situation is untenable. In the light of this: 1.

Will the Commission consider measures to mitigate job losses and impact on the economy and wages, as it has done in other industrial sectors, to put fisheries on an equal footing by providing aid similar to that which other industrial sectors have received at times of crisis?
to the Commission Bert-Jan Ruissen (ECR) Subject:

To determine the actual values of embedded emissions under CBAM, verification by an accredited verifier is required. If these values cannot be verified, companies must rely on default values for the relevant types of goods. These are often significantly higher than the actual values (100 % to 600 % higher). However, the accreditation timeline for potential verifiers is ambitious and it remains unclear to them what requirements need to be meet. As a result, there are as of yet no accredited verifiers, which in turn leads to uncertainty among CBAM declarants. 1.

Does the Commission share the view that a shortage of verifiers has disproportionate consequences for authorised CBAM declarants, and how long does it expect it will take to bring the number of accredited verifiers up to the required level?
How is the Commission encouraging the registration of new accredited verifiers, and what additional measures is it taking to address this issue?

Does the Commission agree that companies which have completed all the necessary steps should not be penalised by a lack of accredited verifiers, and is it prepared to apply a more flexible default value if such companies are unable to find an accredited verifier?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (6.7.2026) The Commission adopted the implementing rules on the calculation of embedded emissions as well as on their verification and the accreditation of verifiers in end-2025. In accordance with Regulation (EU) 2023/956, Member States’ national accreditation bodies need to accredit legal persons to be Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) verifiers. The Commission is in regular contact with national accreditation bodies (NABs) as well as with the European cooperation for Accreditation (EA). 20 NABs have already indicated that they would provide CBAM accreditation services and some have opened applications for verifiers that are already accredited under the EU Emission Trading System in April 2026. The Commission is organising webinars as well as preparing a guidance document and a survey for interested applicants. Enabling authorised CBAM declarants to declare embedded emissions also on the basis of actual values – and not only on default values – is a priority of the Commission and it will follow the matter closely. It is important to ensure that there will be sufficient verification capacity in time for the submission of the first CBAM declarations by 30 September 2027. Importers of CBAM goods should ensure that third-country suppliers monitor and calculate embedded emissions in accordance with the CBAM Regulation. The mark-up on the default values is gradually phased in, from 2026 onwards. This applies for all the CBAM sectors except the fertilisers, for which the mark-up is kept lower, at 1%.

E-10-2026-001095.t: Support for national cultural heritage and respect for national identities in European cultural labels
qt: to the Commission Catherine Griset (PfE) Subject:

European cultural labels, such as the European Heritage Label or the European Capitals of Culture, are playing a larger and larger role in promoting heritage and attracting tourists. At a time when some landmarks are becoming victims of overtourism while many rural areas are struggling to attract visitors, such measures are vital tools to direct tourist flows. However, several stakeholders are questioning why the spotlight is being shone primarily on sites that already pull in a large number of visitors, as well as whether the award criteria properly take into account each nation’s unique historical and cultural characteristics. 1.
What is the Commission’s assessment of the impact of such labels on the territorial balance of tourism in the EU?
What action does it intend to take to better promote local heritage, particularly in rural areas?
Does it plan to change the criteria to better take into account the challenges of conservation and regulating tourist flows?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (5.6.2026)

1. The European Heritage Label (EHL), with 80 sites, focuses on promotion, access, and education. Although the number of sites is increasing, its impact on tourism in Europe remains limited. The latest evaluation of the European Capitals of Culture (ECoC)1 shows that it drives tourism, particularly in smaller, less-visited cities. An increasing number of small and medium-sized cities take part in the ECoC competition and hold the ECoC title. 2. Almost 50% of EHL sites are in rural settings or smaller towns, highlighting European significance in regions2. Therefore, allocation of resources for communications and capacity building for these sites is already significant, and itis continuously evaluated and used to inform future actions. The Commission is drafting the proposal for the post-2033 ECoC legal framework, considering the latest evaluation, the Call for Evidence and recommendations from stakeholders. The promotion of local heritage, also in rural areas, will be taken into consideration in the general ECoC purpose to develop cultural programmes with a strong European dimension. The Commission is also considering new actions to promote emerging and less known destinations through the upcoming European Sustainable Tourism Strategy. 3. Ongoing evaluation of the action and feedback from the open public consultation and call for evidence do not show that EHL sites face conservation challenges from unbalanced tourism. Therefore, it is not expected to adapt the criteria in that regard. The Commission is updating the selection criteria of the ECoC. It will especially consider the sustainability dimension but also the legacy dimension.
1 https://culture.ec.europa.eu/whats-new/news/european-commission-evaluates-impact-of-european-capitals-of-
culture. 2 https://op.europa.eu/en/publication-detail/-/publication/b8f452ec-fb06-11ef-b7db-01aa75ed71a1.

qt: to the Commission Joachim Streit (Renew) Subject:

The Commission’s anti-terrorism package announced on 26 February 2026 (part of ProtectEU’ the European internal security strategy) includes measures for enhanced data analysis, more comprehensive information systems and new security requirements for public spaces. It is important, both with this proposal and elsewhere, to ensure that the principle of subsidiarity is upheld by getting regional parliaments and local authorities involved. 1.

What is the Commission doing to ensure that national parliaments and regional authorities are sufficiently involved in the legislative process for new counter-terrorism measures to guarantee democratic oversight and local expertise?

The agenda provides, amongst other things, for a stronger role for EU agencies and an expansion of analytical and coordination capacities at EU level. What is the Commission doing to ensure that these measures do not impinge upon the Member States’ primary responsibility for national security and do not lead to a gradual centralisation of security competences at EU level?
How can we ensure that the centralisation of security measures does not come at the expense of data protection, fundamental rights and parliamentary scrutiny?
at: (English version) to the Commission Joachim Streit (Renew) (17 March 2026) Subject: Preventing and combating terrorism The Commission’s anti-terrorism package announced on 26 February 2026 (part of ProtectEU’ the European internal security strategy) includes measures for enhanced data analysis, more comprehensive information systems and new security requirements for public spaces. It is important, both with this proposal and elsewhere, to ensure that the principle of subsidiarity is upheld by getting regional parliaments and local authorities involved. 1. What is the Commission doing to ensure that national parliaments and regional authorities are sufficiently involved in the legislative process for new counter-terrorism measures to guarantee democratic oversight and local expertise? 2. The agenda provides, amongst other things, for a stronger role for EU agencies and an expansion of analytical and coordination capacities at EU level. What is the Commission doing to ensure that these measures do not impinge upon the Member States’ primary responsibility for national security and do not lead to a gradual centralisation of security competences at EU level? 3. How can we ensure that the centralisation of security measures does not come at the expense of data protection, fundamental rights and parliamentary scrutiny? (3 June 2026) The Commission fully respects the principles of subsidiarity and of Member States’ sole responsibility for national security pursuant to Article 4(2) of the Treaty on European Union. The measures announced under ProtectEU Agenda (1) aim to support Member States through enhanced cooperation, information exchange, analytical capacities, and a sharper legal toolbox, without altering this division of competences. The communication is a non-legislative Commission initiative. Like other Commission initiatives, it is transmitted to national parliaments, which may submit opinions under the political dialogue with the Commission. Any future legislative proposals stemming from the communication, including any reinforcement of the role of EU agencies or expansion of analytical and coordination capacities, would be prepared in accordance with the Treaties and with this division of competences, including appropriate involvement and consultation of national parliaments and regional authorities. Conditions and safeguards relating to data protection, fundamental rights and parliamentary scrutiny must be proportionate. The ProtectEU Agenda therefore also underlines that strengthened security action must go hand in hand with robust safeguards, including data protection, fundamental rights and effective oversight, in line with EU law.

Communication from the Commission to the European Parliament, the Council, the European Economic and Social Committee of the Regions ProtectEU: Agenda to prevent and counter terrorism; COM/2026/101 final.

qt: to the Commission Joachim Streit (Renew) Subject:

On 9 March 2026, the Commission announced that more than EUR 103 million would be invested in seven LIFE strategic projects in Finland, France, Greece, the Netherlands, Portugal, Slovakia and Spain. The projects aim to boost climate and water resilience, the circular economy and ecosystem restoration, and it is thought that they will mobilise additional national and private investment. 1.
How is the Commission ensuring that less developed or less prepared regions can also benefit adequately from LIFE funding in the future?
What opportunities exist for Germany and its regions to benefit more from LIFE strategic projects in the future?
How is the Commission ensuring that the administrative burden for local implementing partners is commensurate with the added value?
at: (English version) to the Commission Joachim Streit (Renew) (17 March 2026) Subject: LIFE projects On 9 March 2026, the Commission announced that more than EUR 103 million would be invested in seven LIFE strategic projects in Finland, France, Greece, the Netherlands, Portugal, Slovakia and Spain. The projects aim to boost climate and water resilience, the circular economy and ecosystem restoration, and it is thought that they will mobilise additional national and private investment. 1. 3. How is the Commission ensuring that the administrative burden for local implementing partners is commensurate with the added value? (6 July 2026) All calls for proposals under the EU programme for the environment and climate action (LIFE) (1) are equally open to applicants from all Member States and associated countries. With a view to ensuring maximum geographical coverage, the Commission, in collaboration with the LIFE Committee, has established in the Multiannual Work Programme indicative allocations for strategic integrated projects and strategic nature projects for each Member State. One proposal that had been submitted, has subsequently been withdrawn by the applicants for lack of national co-financing. The 2026 calls for proposals for strategic projects are currently open, and this represents a concrete opportunity to engage. The Commission has provided continuous support through specific technical assistance projects to develop the technical capacity of relevant authorities to participate in LIFE. The network of National Contact Points plays a crucial role in this regard, by informing potential applicants, providing guidance on policy priorities and project design. The European Climate, Infrastructure and Environment Executive Agency (2) regularly organise Info Days to assist all potential applicants and address their questions. The Commission continuously monitors and reviews administrative requirements to ensure they remain proportionate to the funds managed and commensurate with the added value delivered. This is achieved through continuous simplification of procedures, a dedicated monitoring team, and targeted capacity building activities, all of which are informed by feedback received from local implementing partners.

E-10-2026-001091.t: Security situation and carbon surcharges for European shipping companies
qt: to the Commission Marie-Luce Brasier-Clain (PfE), Philippe Olivier (PfE), Pierre Pimpie (PfE), Julie Rechagneux (PfE), Mathilde Androuët (PfE) Subject:

By forcing European shipping companies to take detours and endure delays, the war in the Strait of Hormuz is driving up their fuel and insurance costs, but also their carbon credit costs, following the inclusion of shipping in the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) in 2024. This additional cost is then passed on to customers and consumers in an already very tight economic context. According to the rules on shipping companies reporting their CO2 emissions, as laid down in Regulation (EU) 2015/757, it is not possible to exempt emissions from ships that reroute for safety reasons. The same applies to the EU ETS Directive. In 2024, shipping companies had to endure the effects of Houthi attacks in the Red Sea and the only support they were given was an assurance that the introduction of the EU ETS would be gradual, thus mitigating the potential additional costs linked to rerouting. What measures does the Commission therefore intend to take to protect European shipping from rising carbon costs under the EU ETS?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (6.5.2026) The Commission strongly condemns the disruptions brought to the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial transit for global trade, and calls for full respect of navigation rights and freedoms of merchant and commercial vessels in accordance with international law. The disruptions highlight the vulnerability of the maritime sector to geopolitical situations in critical maritime chokepoints, and the ripple effect these have on commodity markets and global supply chains. The sector will see higher transport costs due to increases in freight rates for the shipping of fuels, prices of bunker fuels and insurance premiums1. Additional impact in the form of increased costs stemming from the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) linked to the re-routing of voyages is expected to be low considering notably the relatively limited reliance of the EU on energy imports transiting through the Strait of Hormuz. It should also be noted that when ships are involved in voyages between the EU and third countries, the ETS surrender obligation only applies to 50% of relevant emissions, thus limiting possible further increase in ETS costs. The Commission continues to monitor the implementation of the ETS for maritime transport, including with regards to transport costs. Past analysis has shown that the ETS has limited impact on total transport costs or commodity prices. The Commission is working on a number of initiatives including a review of the ETS, to modernize the system in line with the 2040 emissions reduction target agreed by the colegislators. The ETS is a key tool to achieve a higher degree of energy security and independence, which in time will ensure lower, more stable energy and carbon costs, including for the maritime sector.
1 Strait of Hormuz Disruptions – Implications for Global Trade and Development; UNCTAD; 10/03/2026.

qt: to the Commission Christophe Clergeau (S&D), Jutta Paulus (Verts/ALE), Marie Toussaint (Verts/ALE), Anja Hazekamp (The Left), Martin Hojsík (Renew) Subject:

According to a recent analysis by the non-governmental organisation ChemSec1, several major European chemical companies – including AkzoNobel, Arkema, BASF, Evonik, Henkel, Solvay, Syensqo, TotalEnergies, Umicore and Yara – fail to carry out a comprehensive double materiality assessment, as required under the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive2 (CSRD). E-10-2026-001089.t: Supporting the development of leading companies in central and eastern Europe
qt: to the Commission Andi Cristea (S&D) Subject:

Over the past two decades, EU cohesion policy and structural funds have played a major role in modernising infrastructure and supporting economic convergence across central and eastern Europe. However, a structural imbalance persists within the European economy: most globally competitive European companies originate from a limited number of western European economies. At the same time, companies from central and eastern Europe often face significant barriers to accessing growth capital, scaling up internationally and competing in strategic sectors, such as technology, advanced manufacturing and green innovation. Strengthening Europe’s global competitiveness requires not only a reduction in regional disparities but also an ability to foster the emergence of strong companies across all regions of the EU. In this context: 1.
Does the Commission assess whether EU funding instruments sufficiently support the scaling-up of companies from central and eastern Europe that are capable of becoming regional or global leaders?

Does the Commission intend to develop specific financial instruments, possibly within the framework of InvestEU or other programmes, aimed at supporting high-growth companies in emerging European economies?
How does the Commission plan to ensure that companies from central and eastern Europe can better access EU innovation, investment and industrial policy instruments?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (19.5.2026) The Commission is committed to supporting Member States in central and eastern Europe through cohesion policy investments. The 2014–2020 ex post evaluation of cohesion policy funds1 showed that, while existing support in these areas has not yet been sufficiently scaled to address business growth and internationalisation, investments have laid vital foundations for growth and innovation of small and medium-sized enterprises. Smart Specialisation Strategies (S3) offer a clear path forward in the next programming period. Regions adopting S3 already demonstrate better business performance, particularly when combined with instruments such as the Innovation Investment Instrument (I3), alongside deeper synergies with Horizon Europe (HE) and InvestEU2, for example by leveraging transfer mechanisms3 or providing alternative funding for projects awarded the Seal of Excellence. Emerging European economies are among those which benefitted most4 from InvestEUsupported finance for investments and are specifically targeted by the European Innovation Council (EIC) Pre-Accelerator call5. To better target European financial support for these economies, the Commission announced the setup of the EastInvest facility, a dedicated financing platform for eastern border regions6. In the 2028-2034 Multiannual Financial Framework, renewed support is proposed to continue with investments in innovation and industrial transition via the National and Regional Partnership Plans, which will continue allowing transfer possibilities, also to the European Competitiveness Fund.
1 Commission Staff Working Document Ex post evaluation of the European Regional Development Fund

(ERDF) and the Cohesion Fund for the programming period 2014-2020: https://ec.europa.eu/transparency/documents-register/detail?ref=SWD(2025)328&lang=en. 2 The EU’s flagship research and innovation programme: https://research-andinnovation.ec.europa.eu/funding/funding-opportunities/funding-programmes-and-open-calls/horizon-europe_en. 3 The transfer mechanism gives the Member State possibility to transfer up to 5 % of their resources under shared management to any other EU directly or indirectly managed instrument. The transferred funding can be used only for the benefit of the Member State concerned. For instance, a transfer can enable excellent HE proposals from the concerned Member State/region to participate in HE when budgetary constraints would otherwise prevent them from being selected for HE support. Additionally, the InvestEU Fund currently allows the possibility for Member States to transfer resources from their shared management funds to a Member State Compartment and hence increase financing (from equity to venture debt and risk sharing loans) in their country to support high-growth companies or other investments. 4 On a gross domestic product/per capita weighted basis. 5 The Commission is supporting companies in the EU region also by the EIC Pre-Accelerator call targeting specifically small and medium sized enterprises and startups in widening countries. The goal of this initiative is to increase the business, investor and technology readiness of high potential deep-tech startups from the widening countries preparing them to successfully apply for the EIC Accelerator and secure other forms of investment. The first edition of this call was organised in 2025 with more than 1000 applications, 70 companies have been funded and 320 awarded with Seal of Excellence to help them access alternative or complementary EU and national funding sources. The next EIC Pre-Accelerator call is planned in 2027. 6 Communication on the EU's eastern regions bordering Russia, Belarus and Ukraine: https://ec.europa.eu/regional_policy/policy/themes/eastern-border-regions_en.

E-10-2026-001088.t: Non-compliance of a significant section of the Greek railway network with EU legislation
qt: to the Commission Galato Alexandraki (ECR) Subject:

According to a recent study and internal documents from the Hellenic Railways Organisation (OSE), the Tithorea-Domokos line has serious technical problems, such as flooded cable pits, a blocked drainage network, water and corrosive salt inflow into tunnels, electronic equipment exposed to intense moisture, cracked sleepers, ballast degradation and rail track subsidence. At the same time, for a long while there appear to have been no approved maintenance manuals and there were delays in dealing with problems that had been flagged during inspections. This may run counter to the requirements of Directive (EU) 2016/798 on railway safety, Directive (EU) 2016/797 on the interoperability of the rail system, Regulation (EU) No 402/2013 on a common risk assessment method, as well as the technical specifications for infrastructure and tunnels set out in Regulations (EU) 1299/2014 and 1303/2014. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

Does it consider that the above and the operation of high-speed infrastructure are compatible with the requirements of EU legislation on the safety, reliability and maintainability of rail infrastructure?

Bearing in mind that the Commission itself has launched infringement procedure INFR (2023)2036 and that Greece is implementing an action plan with a bi-monthly progress report, does it not consider that incidents such as the above prove the persistence of systemic deficiencies, which it has already identified?

In the context of the ongoing audit and ERA’s technical support to Greece, does the Commission intend to request a specific compliance assessment for this railway line, as well as to make public whether the relevant findings have been incorporated into the action plan and Greece’s bi-monthly reports?
at: (English version) to the Commission Galato Alexandraki (ECR) (17 March 2026) Subject: Non-compliance of a significant section of the Greek railway network with EU legislation According to a recent study and internal documents from the Hellenic Railways Organisation (OSE), the Tithorea-Domokos line has serious technical problems, such as flooded cable pits, a blocked drainage network, water and corrosive salt inflow into tunnels, electronic equipment exposed to intense moisture, cracked sleepers, ballast degradation and rail track subsidence. At the same time, for a long while there appear to have been no approved maintenance manuals and there were delays in dealing with problems that had been flagged during inspections. This may run counter to the requirements of Directive (EU) 2016/798 on railway safety, Directive (EU) 2016/797 on the interoperability of the rail system, Regulation (EU) No 402/2013 on a common risk assessment method, as well as the technical specifications for infrastructure and tunnels set out in Regulations (EU) 1299/2014 and 1303/2014. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

Does it consider that the above and the operation of high-speed infrastructure are compatible with the requirements of EU legislation on the safety, reliability and maintainability of rail infrastructure?

Bearing in mind that the Commission itself has launched infringement procedure INFR (2023)2036 and that Greece is implementing an action plan with a bi-monthly progress report, does it not consider that incidents such as the above prove the persistence of systemic deficiencies, which it has already identified?

In the context of the ongoing audit and ERA’s technical support to Greece, does the Commission intend to request a specific compliance assessment for this railway line, as well as to make public whether the relevant findings have been incorporated into the action plan and Greece’s bi-monthly reports?

(15 June 2026) According to Article 17(7) of Directive (EU) 2016/798 (1), national safety authorities (NSA) shall supervise the trackside, control-command and signalling, energy and infrastructure subsystems and ensure that they are in compliance with the essential requirements, including the requirements on safety, reliability and maintenance mentioned in the Honourable Member’s question, no matter if detailed in EU specifications, standards, common safety methods or not. The same article specifies that if the NSA finds that an infrastructure manager no longer satisfies the conditions for its safety authorisation in this or another respect, it shall restrict or revoke that authorisation, giving reasons for its decision. From these provisions follows the core responsibility of NSAs for supervising the rail infrastructure maintenance and to intervening in cases of non-compliance. The Commission cannot replace the NSA in these tasks, nor has it the necessary tools to investigate these findings further. The Commission notes that the infringement procedure INFR(2023)2036 (2) does not cover the issue of maintenance of railway infrastructure. The Rail Safety Action Plan established by Greece as a response to the above infringement and the technical assistance project run by the EU Agency for Railways to support the Plan’s implementation, cover training and capacity building actions addressed to national authorities, bodies and stakeholders. Neither the Plan nor the technical assistance project focuses on specific railway lines or their sections, including line TithoreaDomokos.

E-10-2026-001087.t: State of the public health system in Greece and citizens’ access to health services
qt: to the Commission Galato Alexandraki (ECR) Subject:

According to recent reports and news articles, the Greek national health system (ESY) is facing severe staff shortages and significant failures in the operation of health structures. It is estimated that there are thousands of vacant doctors’ and nurses’ posts, and in many hospitals operating theatres and clinics remain closed due to a lack of staff. Meanwhile, waiting times for planned surgeries can be as long as 6-8 months. Around 21.9 % of citizens say they are not getting the treatment they need due to costs, organisational problems or a weakness in the health system. Moreover, private health payments remain particularly high, with citizens covering around 33 % of total health expenditure. This percentage is significantly higher than the OECD average. At the same time, low wages and difficult working conditions drive many doctors to migrate, further exacerbating staff shortages. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
What is its assessment of the state of the Greek public health system and citizens’ access to health services?
Are there any European control mechanisms to verify the use of European funds in the Greek health sector?
Does it intend to look into measures to reinforce the healthcare workforce and ensure equal access to health services for citizens?

Meanwhile, waiting times for planned surgeries can be as long as 6-8 months. (11 May 2026) 1. As per Article 168(7) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (1), Member States are responsible for the organisation and delivery of health services and medical care. EU tools and initiatives support Member States to strengthen health systems via knowledge sharing, technical assistance, funding and policy guidance. For example, the State of Health in the EU cycle (2) includes country-specific analyses, and the European Semester provides country-specific recommendations: (in 2020, 2022 and 2023, Greece received recommendations to ensure adequate and equal access to healthcare which reflected, among others, the surveyed population reporting unmet medical needs for financial reasons, long waiting lists or distance (29.1% in 2025) (3)). 2. Under the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF), the Greek recovery and resilience plan (RRP) includes reforms and investments to strengthen the healthcare sector. As the Commission explained in its reply to Parliamentary Question E004260/25 (4), the implementation of RRPs falls under Member States’ responsibility (5). The Commission verifies the fulfillment of milestones and targets of measures included and funds are disbursed only after a positive preliminary assessment of payment requests (6). The Commission services regularly conduct implementation audits, so does the European Court of Auditors. During the discharge procedure, the European Parliament reviews the Commission’s management of RRF funds to ensure accountability for the performance-based disbursement of grants and loans. 3. In its replies to Parliamentary questions E-001242/25 (7) and E-000269/26 (8), the Commission explains the Commission’s work in workforce shortages and equal access to healthcare.

E-10-2026-001085.t: Infringement procedure against Italy vis-a-vis Directive (EU) 2024/1275 – possible obligations and costs for property owners
qt: to the Commission Anna Maria Cisint (PfE), Aldo Patriciello (PfE), Isabella Tovaglieri (PfE) Subject:
Infringement procedure against Italy vis-a-vis Directive (EU) 2024/1275 – possible obligations and costs for property owners

The Commission has launched an infringement procedure against Italy in connection with the requirements laid down in Directive (EU) 2024/1275 on the energy performance of buildings, which requires Member States to adopt and submit national planning instruments for gradual energy retrofits of their building stock. This regulatory approach introduces particularly ambitious targets and strict timelines for retrofitting buildings, directly affecting one of Europeans’ main assets: their homes. Italy differs significantly from other Member States, as it has one of the oldest building stocks in Europe, a high proportion of privately owned property, and a significant number of historic buildings or buildings subject to planning and landscape restrictions. Stringent, uniform application of the obligations laid down in the directive runs the risk of placing a very significant economic burden on millions of households and small-scale property owners, and could distort the housing market and property value. In the light of the above: 1.
Does the Commission consider it appropriate to continue with the infringement proceedings despite the absence of a proper assessment of the economic and social impact on the public of the directive?
Does it not consider it necessary to provide more flexibility for Member States with historic and structurally diverse building stock?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (8.5.2026) On 11 March 2026, the Commission decided to open infringement procedures by sending a letter of formal notice1 to Italy and 18 other Member States2 as they failed to submit their draft National Building Renovation Plan (NBRP) by 31 December 2025 pursuant to Article 3 of the recast Energy Performance of Buildings Directive (EPBD)3. The NBRPs are an essential tool for Member States to transform their building stock into energy-efficient, decarbonised asset by 2050. By creating predictable renovation pipelines and clear long-term trajectories, they support a cost-effective implementation of the EPBD at national level and give the necessary investment stability for national industries. The recast EPBD was preceded by an impact assessment showing that the worst-performing residential buildings are often occupied by vulnerable households and that the proposed measures will help reduce their energy bills4. Rather than imposing uniform rules, the recast EPBD already provides substantial flexibility to accommodate national specificities, especially for Member States with a significant share of historic or protected buildings such as Italy. It does not impose renovation obligations on individual homes but sets targets for reducing the energy consumption of the overall building stock. This allows Member States to determine the most appropriate and cost-effective pathways, including prioritising interventions where they are most feasible. As regards non-residential buildings, Member States can continue to exempt historic and protected ones from the renovation requirements. They can also set additional exemption criteria in light of serious hardship or an unfavourable cost-benefit assessment.

1 https://energy.ec.europa.eu/news/march-infringements-package-key-decisions-energy-2026-03-11_en. 2 Belgium, Czechia, Germany, Estonia, Ireland, Greece, France, Cyprus, Latvia, Luxembourg, Hungary, Malta,

the Netherlands, Austria, Poland, Portugal, Slovakia and Sweden. 3 EPBD - Directive EU/2024/1275. 4 SWD (2021) 453, Commission Staff Working Document, Impact Assessment Report, Accompanying the document, Directive of the European Parliament and of the Council on the energy performance of buildings.

E-10-2026-001084.t: Expansion of non-human primate breeding capacity in France and compliance with Directive 2010/63/EU
qt: to the Commission Tilly Metz (Verts/ALE), Sebastian Everding (The Left), David Cormand (Verts/ALE), Majdouline Sbai (Verts/ALE) Subject:

The French National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS) plans to expand its primate research centre in Rousset, increasing capacity from 600 to 1 800 animals by 2029 with public funding of EUR 30 million. The project would involve importing around 300 cynomolgus macaques (Macaca fascicularis) for breeding. France already uses approximately 3 500 primates annually, the highest number in EU. This expansion raises concerns regarding Directive 2010/63/EU1, which seeks to replace, reduce and refine the use of animals in science. The CNRS Ethics Committee has itself questioned the project’s strategic relevance and called for a clear roadmap to reduce the use of non-human primates. 1.

Does the Commission consider that the planned tripling of the primate population at the Rousset centre, combined with the importation of non-human primates, aligns with the objectives of Directive 2010/63/EU concerning the replacement, reduction and minimisation of animal use?
Does the Commission envisage requiring Member States to adopt time-bound roadmaps to phase out the use of non-human primates in scientific procedures?

Does the Commission consider that public national projects involving breeding or importation of non-human primates should be subject to an EU-level scientific or strategic assessment, in order to ensure they are consistent with the objectives of Directive 2010/63/EU?

Directive 2010/63/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 22 September 2010 on the protection of animals used for scientific purposes (OJ L 276, 20.10.2010, p. 33, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2010/63/oj).
at: (English version) to the Commission Tilly Metz (Verts/ALE), Sebastian Everding (The Left), David Cormand (Verts/ALE), Majdouline Sbai (Verts/ALE) (17 March 2026) Subject: Expansion of non-human primate breeding capacity in France and compliance with Directive 2010/63/EU The French National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS) plans to expand its primate research centre in Rousset, increasing capacity from 600 to 1 800 animals by 2029 with public funding of EUR 30 million. The project would involve importing around 300 cynomolgus macaques (Macaca fascicularis) for breeding. France already uses approximately 3 500 primates annually, the highest number in EU. This expansion raises concerns regarding Directive 2010/63/EU (1), which seeks to replace, reduce and refine the use of animals in science. The CNRS Ethics Committee has itself questioned the project’s strategic relevance and called for a clear roadmap to reduce the use of non-human primates. 1. Does the Commission consider that the planned tripling of the primate population at the Rousset centre, combined with the importation of non-human primates, aligns with the objectives of Directive 2010/63/EU concerning the replacement, reduction and minimisation of animal use? 2. Does the Commission envisage requiring Member States to adopt time-bound roadmaps to phase out the use of nonhuman primates in scientific procedures? 3. Does the Commission consider that public national projects involving breeding or importation of non-human primates should be subject to an EU-level scientific or strategic assessment, in order to ensure they are consistent with the objectives of Directive 2010/63/EU? (6 July 2026) The demand for non-human primates for use in science is expected to continue as they remain essential in certain research areas, such as neurosciences and immunology, and for safety testing where no viable alternatives currently exist. Their use is regulated by the directive on the protection of animals used for scientific purposes (1), which imposes stringent measures limiting their use for specific purposes. Currently, a significant proportion of non-human primates used in the EU are sourced from outside the Union. The directive aims at ending the capture of non-human primates from the wild, including for breeding purposes. It also sets out some of the highest care and accommodation standards for non-human primates globally. Increasing EU-based breeding capacity can contribute to these objectives by ensuring compliance with EU welfare standards and reducing the risks associated with long-distance transport. The directive sets out a legal framework for progressing towards their full replacement as soon as scientifically satisfactory alternatives are available. The use of non-human primates can only be authorised where a project evaluation satisfies the authorities of its compliance with the principle of the Three Rs (Replacement, Reduction and Refinement) and that the objectives cannot be met by using other species. The Commission does not have the competence to require Member States to adopt time-bound roadmaps to phase out the use of non-human primates. Similarly, the directive does not provide a legal basis for EU-level scientific or strategic assessments of national projects involving the breeding or importation of such animals.

Directive 2010/63/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 22 September 2010 on the protection of animals used for scientific purposes (OJ L 276, 20.10.2010, p. 33, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2010/63/oj). E-10-2026-001083.t: Socio-environmental conflicts and territorial rights in Chocó, Colombia
qt: to the Commission Cristina Guarda (Verts/ALE), Rima Hassan (The Left) Subject:

In Chocó, Colombia, the expansion of extensive livestock farming, legal and illegal mining, aerial spraying of monoculture and large-scale deforestation is affecting over 65 000 hectares in the Lower Atrato region1 and is having a serious impact on the territorial, environmental and cultural rights of indigenous and Afro-descendant communities. Between 2020 and 2023, over 94 % of Colombia’s wood flooring exports lacked legal certification of origin, with around 20 % directed towards markets such as the EU. In this context: 1.

How does the Commission assess the risk that EU trade and supply chains linked to Colombia may be connected to human rights and environmental violations in Chocó and what due diligence and monitoring mechanisms are in place, including under the EU Regulation on deforestation-free products2 and the EU Directive on corporate sustainability due diligence3, to prevent such impacts?

E-10-2026-001082.t: Costs of compensating informants in Europol operations
qt: to the Commission Özlem Demirel (The Left) Subject:

Europol recognises compensation for undercover agents as an eligible cost in joint investigative operations. The upper limit stands at EUR 20 000 per informant. The compensation amount is calculated using a point system with seven factors and a maximum of 300 points – taking into account the success of the investigation, the geographic scope of the criminal organisation and the personal risk taken by the informant. E-10-2026-001080.t: Pandemics – the business model laid bare in the Epstein files
at: (English version) to the Commission Gerald Hauser (PfE) (17 March 2026) Subject: Pandemics — the business model laid bare in the Epstein files The Epstein files reveal that the financial and institutional architecture to manage a pandemic — and so for private investors to profit handsomely from any outbreak — was in place long before the COVID-19 pandemic. The conceptual foundations underpinning pandemic preparedness as a managed financial and security category began to take shape as early as the 1990s. This development gained considerable traction after the 2008 financial crisis, when private capital, global health policy and risk finance increasingly converged (1). A briefing from the Gates Foundation, for example, described the Global Health Investment Fund as a vehicle targeting 5-7% returns on drugs and vaccines, backed by a 60% principal guarantee (2). The following organisations and companies are named in the files: the Gates Foundation, the World Economic Forum, J.P. Morgan, Vanguard, GAVI, CEPI, IPI, the WHO, the World Bank, senior UN and health officials, the Rockefeller Foundation, Goldman Sachs, Alibaba and MasterCard — many of which are EU partners. 1.
Which of these organisations and individuals received what sum of EU funds and when?

2. Does the Commission also regard pandemics, vaccines and drugs as a business model, and has it invested in the World Bank’s pandemic bonds, launched in 2017? 3. If it answered ‘yes’ to the previous question, how much did it invest and when, and what were the associated profits or losses? (29 May 2026) The Commission cooperates with a range of partners in Pandemic Preparedness, Prevention and Response (PPPR). All financial support is governed by the Financial Regulation (1), with strict rules on transparency, avoidance of conflicts of interest and protection of the EU’s financial interests. Information on direct beneficiaries of EU funds is published via the Financial Transparency System (2) and annual reports on the implementation of the EU budget, allowing citizens to identify the beneficiaries and the amounts received. The Commission does not regard pandemics, vaccines or medicines as a ‘business model’. EU action on PPPR is set inter alia in the EU Global Health Strategy (3), Regulation (EU) 2022/2371 on serious cross-border threats to health (4), the Medical Countermeasures Strategy (5), and the upcoming EU global health resilience initiative (6). Objectives of these policies include protecting health and wellbeing, supporting resilient health systems through equitable access to safe, effective and affordable vaccines and medicines and universal health coverage, and strengthening prevention, preparedness and response to health emergencies. The Commission has not invested in the World Bank’s pandemic bonds launched in 2017 and consequently there were no related profits or losses.

E-10-2026-001079.t: Lack of up-to-date information in Spain on wolves ( Canis lupus ) and their impact of livestock
qt: to the Commission Jorge Buxadé Villalba (PfE), Mireia Borrás Pabón (PfE) Subject:
Lack of up-to-date information in Spain on wolves (Canis lupus) and their impact of livestock

In January, the Commission opened infringement proceedings against Spain for failing to submit the six-yearly report on the conservation status of wolves by the end of 20251. According to farmers’ organisations, the report containing this data has already been drawn up and approved, but the government is not submitting it due to a lack of scientific rigour, thereby preventing a proper analysis of the current situation. Official regional data further point to an increase in attacks on livestock. In Asturias, the number of livestock killed has risen from 2 721 to 3 257 since 2021, and Castilla-León recorded 3 979 attacks and 5 985 animals killed in 2024. Given the significance of these figures and the two-month deadline the Spanish Government has been given to respond to the letter of formal notice: 1.
Has Spain responded to the letter? If so, how has it justified the delay in submitting data it already had in its possession?

If not, what does the Commission intend to do to ensure compliance on the part of the Spanish Government? If Spain’s non-compliance continues, what additional EU protection will our livestock farmers receive, particularly following the call for the provisional application of the agreement with Mercosur, which will decimate output in Spain’s livestock farming sector?
https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/es/inf_26_115.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (11.5.2026) On 30 January 2026, the Commission opened an infringement procedure by sending a letter of formal notice to Spain1 for failing to comply with the reporting obligation under Article 17 of the Habitats Directive2. The required report provides an assessment of the conservation status of the habitats and species covered by the Habitats Directive (including the Iberian wolf) based on the status and trends of species and habitats, as well as the main pressures and threats affecting them. The Commission services are assessing the reply by Spain prior to deciding on its follow-up. The Commission recalls that, under the Common Agricultural Policy3, comprehensive support is available for livestock protection measures against predators like the wolf and that EU State aid rules allow Member States to compensate up to 100% of direct and indirect costs from wolf-related damages to livestock. Regarding the provisional application of the agreement with Mercosur, the Commission does not share the negative assessment of the Honourable Members. The agreement includes an unprecedented set of measures aimed at protecting sensitive agri-food sectors. Imports of sensitive agricultural goods are subject to very limited tariff-rate quotas that will be gradually phased in.
