decisions/?langCode=EN&version=v1&typeOfSearch=byDecision&page=1&size=10&order=desc&sortColumn s=decisionDate&refId=INFR(2025)2214. 2 Council Directive 92/43/EEC of 21 May 1992 on the conservation of natural habitats and on wild fauna and flora, OJ L 206, 22.7.1992, p. 7. 3 https://agriculture.ec.europa.eu/common-agricultural-policy_en.

qt: to the Commission Nicolás González Casares (S&D) Subject:

The escalation of the conflict in Iran and volatility in energy markets have led to significant fuel price hikes in the European Union. While Brent crude oil prices have fluctuated, however, petrol prices at the pump remain high. This pattern reflects the ‘rocket and feather’ effect, when prices go up quickly but fall gradually. This state of affairs highlights serious concerns about transparency and fairness in fuel pricing in the internal market and the speed at which cost fluctuations are passed on to consumers. The Commission should safeguard transparent, competitive and fair fuel markets for European consumers. I would therefore like to ask the following questions: 1.
Is the Commission monitoring fuel price pass-through mechanisms in the Member States?
What analytical tools1 is the Commission using to detect distortions between oil prices, wholesalers and retailers?
What measures is the Commission considering to protect consumers and ensure cost reductions are reflected in the final price fairly and swiftly?
In addition to information from the Weekly Oil Bulletin.
at: (English version) to the Commission Nicolás González Casares (S&D) (16 March 2026) Subject: Fuel prices The escalation of the conflict in Iran and volatility in energy markets have led to significant fuel price hikes in the European Union. While Brent crude oil prices have fluctuated, however, petrol prices at the pump remain high. This pattern reflects the ‘rocket and feather’ effect, when prices go up quickly but fall gradually. This state of affairs highlights serious concerns about transparency and fairness in fuel pricing in the internal market and the speed at which cost fluctuations are passed on to consumers. The Commission should safeguard transparent, competitive and fair fuel markets for European consumers. I would therefore like to ask the following questions: 1.
Is the Commission monitoring fuel price pass-through mechanisms in the Member States?
What analytical tools (1) is the Commission using to detect distortions between oil prices, wholesalers and retailers?
What measures is the Commission considering to protect consumers and ensure cost reductions are reflected in the final price fairly and swiftly?

(1 June 2026) The Commission considers competitive and transparent markets as the best guarantee for fair consumer prices. It therefore pays full attention to the competitive situation in European petroleum markets on a continuous basis. The supervision of well functioning markets in the Member States is carried out by national authorities. The Commission is not aware of any general market failure or inefficiencies, including market distortions from presumed bad practices of wholesalers of petroleum products in the European market. The Commission has been taking various steps to improve transparency in energy markets and the European and global oil sector. The Commission’s Directorate-General for Energy publishes the Weekly Oil Bulletin (1) with retail fuel prices on the pump (and associated taxes) based on data provided by the individual Member State, and also monitors the wholesale prices on weekly basis. One important element of the final retail price of transport fuels, notably excise duty is subject to EU legislation. The Energy Taxation Directive (2) establishes the minimum excise duty rates that EU countries must apply to energy products for fuel and transport, and electricity. The EU legislation only sets harmonised minimum rates. Member States are free to apply excise duty rates above these minima, according to their own national needs, which allows for flexibility for situations like the current crisis. The Commission also closely monitors national measures taken by Member States to respond to fuel price increases. Where necessary, it may take action against measures violating the fundamental freedoms enshrined in the Treaties.

Under Spain’s recovery and resilience plan, financed by the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF), the health authorities of the Autonomous Community of Valencia purchased three mobile electron accelerators for intraoperative radiation therapy for public hospitals in Castellón, Valencia and Elche. This technology allows doctors to treat breast cancer patients with radiation therapy during surgery and aims to improve access to innovative cancer treatments. According to recent information, however, some of this equipment was not actually used until several years after it was purchased. E-10-2026-001076.t: Risk of rising food prices due to energy instability
qt: to the Commission Konstantinos Arvanitis (The Left) Subject:

The escalation of the conflict between the United States, Israel and Iran and the instability in the Strait of Hormuz have led to increases in international energy and fertiliser prices. Given that around 20 % of the world’s oil supply plus a significant share of raw materials for fertilisers passes through the Strait of Hormuz, there is a serious risk that production costs in agriculture will increase further. In an already strained environment where living costs are high, these developments may lead to a further increase in food prices, which will be onerous for farmers and consumers. The EU has tools, such as crisis contingency plans, to ensure farm viability and food security for European citizens. What is needed is speed and determination. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
What immediate measures does it intend to take to support farmers in the face of rising energy and fertiliser costs?
How will it prevent these increases from being passed on to food prices?
What initiatives will it take to reduce the dependence of European agriculture on volatile international energy and fertiliser markets?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.6.2026) The Commission is closely monitoring the impact of escalation in the Middle East and the situation in the Strait of Hormuz on energy and fertiliser markets. In the short term, while no physical shortages of fertilisers are expected in the EU, increased price volatility will affect input costs for farmers. No immediate risks to food availability have been identified, although cost increases for energy and inputs may exert upward pressure on food prices over time. On 19 May 2026, the Commission adopted the Fertiliser Action Plan1, setting out short and long term measures to improve fertiliser availability, affordability and resilience. Short term actions include the mobilisation and possible top-up of the agricultural reserve, liquidity support under the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) and greater flexibility for advance payments. Longer term measures focus on strengthening EU production capacity, supporting the uptake of recycled nutrients and low carbon alternatives and reducing strategic dependencies on imports. Several measures have already been taken to alleviate pressure on fertiliser prices in the EU. These include adopting a Temporary State aid framework2 on 29 April 2026, applying a reduced flat mark up of 1% to Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) default values for fertilisers, as well as the temporary duty suspension for imports of ammonia, urea and other nitrogen fertilisers from countries other than Russia and Belarus, withing given quotas3.

3 http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2026/1181/oj.

E-10-2026-001074.t: Commission pressure to privatise Azores Airlines
qt: to the Commission João Oliveira (The Left) Subject:

The Azores, an outermost region, is heavily reliant on scheduled air connections to mainland Portugal and to its large emigrant community in North America. Ryanair recently stopped flying to the Azores because its request for an increase to the public subsidies it received was turned down. TAP may also stop flying to the Azores following its privatisation and the reorientation of its activity towards profit rather than public interest. The Portuguese State spends almost EUR 100 million annually on supporting flights to the Azores, which could increase if the ‘market’ needs to be subsidised to safeguard the supply of flights. If Azores Airlines were to be destroyed and sold to TAP, serious doubts would arise about who would provide connections to the Azores and at what cost. The Commission has been pushing extremely hard for Azores Airlines to be privatised, imposing fines even though the regional government has received no acceptable purchase offers. In view of the above: 1.
How can the economic, social and territorial cohesion of the country and the region be safeguarded from the consequences if these companies are privatised?
Will the Commission drop its push for Azores Airlines to be privatised?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.5.2026) In its Decision of 2022 the Commission authorised Portugal to grant a EUR 453 million aid to bring SATA Air Açores (‘SATA')1, back to viability under its Guidelines for rescuing and restructuring undertakings in difficulty2. The Decision finds that the aid avoids the risks of disruption of an important service and of exit of an undertaking with a systemic role in the Azores. The Decision is subject to conditions to ensure a lasting financial recovery of SATA, particularly the implementation of a restructuring plan. To limit the distortions of competition brought by the aid, Portugal offered to divest at least 51% in Azores Airlines. Such divestment, committed by Portugal, does not require the sale of SATA’s operations in the Azores but only of a majority shareholding of its international business. TAP Air Portugal’s (TAP) privatisation is also a decision of the Portuguese authorities and was not imposed by the Commission decision approving restructuring aid to TAP3. The economic, social and territorial cohesion of the country and Azores can be preserved by the competition measures foreseen in the relevant decisions, which allow competitors to offer air transport services in competition with SATA/TAP, whereas all routes not economically profitable can be tendered by Portugal as Public Service Obligations4. Furthermore, the Commission approved under Article 107(2)(a) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU (TFEU) social aid schemes adopted by Portugal to support air transport for residents of remote regions, including the Azores. Under the TFEU, the Commission cannot impose any privatisation but can only assess the State aid measures notified by the Member States (Art. 107 TFEU).

qt: to the Commission Fabio De Masi (NI) Subject:

The US has imposed an import ban on Chinese drone manufacturer DJI. This came as a result of security concerns related to the deactivation of geofencing over critical security architecture. DJI has since brought an action against this decision in the US. The company has a market share of around 85 % in the US civilian sector. 1.
Has an import ban on DJI drones been discussed at EU level?
Are there plans to impose import bans on other drone suppliers?
at: (English version) to the Commission Fabio De Masi (NI) (16 March 2026) Subject: Import ban on drone manufacturers The US has imposed an import ban on Chinese drone manufacturer DJI. This came as a result of security concerns related to the deactivation of geofencing over critical security architecture. DJI has since brought an action against this decision in the US. The company has a market share of around 85% in the US civilian sector. 1.
Has an import ban on DJI drones been discussed at EU level?
Are there plans to impose import bans on other drone suppliers?

(27 May 2026) Secure use of drones and the security of drones placed in the internal market are a priority of the Commission. The action plan on Drone and Counter-Drone Security (1) (‘Action Plan’) envisages measures including a Drone Security Package to adapt the regulatory framework to new threats. In this context, the Commission will work also on establishing an EU Trusted Drone Label to further enhance trust in civil drones. The label would rely on independent third-party verification and define additional product-level trust and resilience criteria without duplicating existing EU cybersecurity legislation. The Commission has not been involved in discussion on an import ban against specific drone manufacturers, including DJI. All drones placed in the internal market must comply with the applicable regulatory framework, including Regulation (EU) 2018/1139 (2) and relevant delegated and implementing acts, such as Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/945 (3) and Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/947 (4). Based on the Cyber Resilience Act (5), a large majority of drones placed on the EU market will also be subject to mandatory cybersecurity requirements. Moreover, the proposal for revision of the Cybersecurity Act (6) sets out an objective and risk-based framework to address nontechnical cybersecurity risks in information and communications technologies (ICT) supply chains in the EU, which may also occur in relation to drones and counter-drone systems. As part of the action plan, the Commission proposed to initiate work with Member States on a coordinated risk assessment on drones and counter drone capacities. This could be followed by a Drone and Counter-Drone Security Toolbox proposing proportionate security mitigation measures.

E-10-2026-001072.t: Türkiye obstructs cable-laying project once again
qt: to the Commission Yannis Maniatis (S&D) Subject:

Turkish provocation in the Eastern Mediterranean region is growing by the day. A case in point is the Great Sea Interconnector between Greece and Cyprus. Türkiye is using military means to obstruct the laying of fibre-optic cables between Astypalaia and Amorgos. Specifically, the Turkish Navy hailed the cable-laying vessel, asking it to stop its work and leave the area. This project is part of the wider fibre optic interconnection project SEA-SPINE (High-speed Submarine Backbone for islands of the Aegean Sea) and is among the EU's priorities, receiving funding from the Connecting Europe Facility (CEF). Given that the Türkiye 2025 report states that ‘violations of Greek territorial waters continued to be reported, with a noticeable increase in incidents compared with the previous reporting period’ and that the maritime zones of EU Member States are becoming increasingly important for its green and digital transition, can the Commission say: 1.
What measures is it considering to defend the EU’s interests in the maritime zones of its Member States against illegal actions by non-EU countries?

Has the Greek Government officially informed the Commission about the above developments and, if so, have joint initiatives been taken to protect this strategic European infrastructure which is co-funded by the CEF?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (26.5.2026) The EU remains committed to defending its interests and those of its Member States as well as to upholding regional stability. In this context, the EU attaches the greatest importance to safeguarding the sovereign rights of all Member States, in full respect of international law. Unequivocal commitment to international agreements and the UN Charter, as well as abstaining from unilateral actions which violate international law and the sovereign rights of Member States, remains an essential requirement to ensure a stable and secure environment in the Eastern Mediterranean and the development of a cooperative and mutually beneficial relationship between the EU and Türkiye. The Commission is aware of reports regarding the alleged obstruction of cable-laying activities under the SEA-SPINE project co-funded by Connecting European Facility (CEF Digital)1, which aims to enhance digital connectivity between Greek islands and it is a strategic priority for the EU’s digital transition. Following inquiries via European Health and Digital Executive Agency, the consortium confirmed that the Ocean Link vessel completed its scheduled works between Amorgos and Astypalaia without disruption. While no formal notification of hailing was received, the Commission underscores that all EU-funded infrastructure projects operate in full compliance with international law (UN Convention on the Law of the Sea2). The EU rejects any unilateral actions that impede lawful activities. Given the critical role of submarine cables in securing the EU’s digital resilience, the Commission is in close cooperation with Member States to ensure the smooth completion of the project and will continue to monitor closely the situation and the project’s implementation.
1 https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/news/commission-makes-available-eu200-million-submarine-cable-and-
digital-infrastructure-projects. 2 https://www.un.org/depts/los/convention_agreements/texts/unclos/unclos_e.pdf.

E-10-2026-001071.t: ‘One Europe, One Market’ – clarification regarding Regulation (EU) 2023/988 in order to reduce the fragmentation of textile trade in the EU single market
qt: to the Commission Bruno Gonçalves (S&D) Subject:

Diverging interpretations on the applicability to textile products of Articles 9-18 of the General Product Safety Regulation (GPSR)1 have raised legal uncertainty and caused fragmentation in the single market. Article 2 provides that the regulation applies insofar as there are no specific provisions with the same objective under EU harmonisation legislation that governs the safety of such products. The Commission’s guidelines further state that where products are subject to specific safety requirements under EU law, the GPSR applies only to aspects, risks or categories of risk not covered by those requirements. Textile products are subject to Regulation (EU) No 1007/20112 on textile fibre names and related labelling and marking of the fibre composition of textile products. However, national authorities have interpreted provisions differently regarding Chapter III, Section 1 of the GPSR (Articles 9-18). Some consider that these obligations do not apply to textile products covered by EU harmonisation legislation, while others expect economic operators to comply with such legislation. In this context: 1.
Does the Commission consider that the obligations laid down in Articles 9-18 of Regulation (EU) 2023/988 apply to textile products covered by Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011?
If so, which specific obligations under Articles 9-18 apply to such products and what is the legal basis for that interpretation under Article 2 of the GPSR?

Regulation (EU) 2023/988 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 10 May 2023 on general product safety, amending Regulation (EU) No 1025/2012 of the European Parliament and of the Council and Directive (EU) 2020/1828 of the European Parliament and the Council, and repealing Directive 2001/95/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council and Council Directive 87/357/EEC (OJ L 135, 23.5.2023, p. 1, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2023/988/oj). Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 September 2011 on textile fibre names and related labelling and marking of the fibre composition of textile products and repealing Council Directive 73/44/EEC and Directives 96/73/EC and 2008/121/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council (OJ L 272, 18.10.2011, p. 1, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2011/1007/oj).
at: (English version) to the Commission Bruno Gonçalves (S&D) (16 March 2026) Subject: ‘One Europe, One Market’ — clarification regarding Regulation (EU) 2023/988 in order to reduce the fragmentation of textile trade in the EU single market Diverging interpretations on the applicability to textile products of Articles 9-18 of the General Product Safety Regulation (GPSR) (1) have raised legal uncertainty and caused fragmentation in the single market. Article 2 provides that the regulation applies insofar as there are no specific provisions with the same objective under EU harmonisation legislation that governs the safety of such products. The Commission’s guidelines further state that where products are subject to specific safety requirements under EU law, the GPSR applies only to aspects, risks or categories of risk not covered by those requirements. Textile products are subject to Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011 (2) on textile fibre names and related labelling and marking of the fibre composition of textile products. However, national authorities have interpreted provisions differently regarding Chapter III, Section 1 of the GPSR (Articles 9-18). Some consider that these obligations do not apply to textile products covered by EU harmonisation legislation, while others expect economic operators to comply with such legislation. In this context: 1.
Does the Commission consider that the obligations laid down in Articles 9-18 of Regulation (EU) 2023/988 apply to textile products covered by Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011?
If so, which specific obligations under Articles 9-18 apply to such products and what is the legal basis for that interpretation under Article 2 of the GPSR?

(18 May 2026) Economic operators are obliged to offer only safe textile products to consumers, taking into account the factors relevant for assessing safety and laid down in Article 6 of the General Product Safety Regulation (GPSR) (1). The GPSR also sets obligations for economic operators in case of distance sales as well for providers of online marketplaces that apply to textiles products. It should also be noted that there are provisions in other pieces of EU legislation that apply to textile products covered by the Textile Labelling Regulation (TLR), namely in the Market Surveillance Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 and, once ecodesign requirements are introduced for textile products, provisions in the Ecodesign for Sustainable Product Regulation (EU) 2024/1781 as well.

Regulation (EU) 2023/988 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 10 May 2023 on general product safety, amending Regulation (EU) No 1025/2012 of the European Parliament and of the Council and Directive (EU) 2020/1828 of the European Parliament and the Council, and repealing Directive 2001/95/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council and Council Directive 87/357/EEC (OJ L 135, 23.5.2023, p. 1, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2023/988/oj). Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 September 2011 on textile fibre names and related labelling and marking of the fibre composition of textile products and repealing Council Directive 73/44/EEC and Directives 96/73/EC and 2008/121/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council (OJ L 272, 18.10.2011, p. 1, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2011/1007/oj). In accordance with point b) of the last subparagraph of Article 2(1) of Regulation (EU) 2023/988 General Product Safety Regulation (EU) 2023/988 — EUR-Lex (GPSR), textile products covered by the Textile Labelling Regulation No 1007/2011 (TLR), being products subject to specific requirements imposed by Union harmonisation legislation, are not subject to certain GPSR obligations, including Section 1 of Chapter III containing Articles 9-18. Importantly, however, the GPSR provisions not mentioned in point b) of the last subparagraph of Article 2(1) of the GPSR apply to textile products covered by the TLR, notably the general safety requirement in Chapter II of the GPSR.

E-10-2026-001070.t: Misclassification of physical and rehabilitation medicine in Annex V to Directive 2005/36/EC
qt: to the Commission Alex Agius Saliba (S&D) Subject:

Annex V to Directive 2005/36/EC on the recognition of professional qualifications1 appears to list the medical speciality of physical and rehabilitation medicine under the designation ‘physiotherapy’. However, physiotherapy is an allied health profession and not a medical speciality. This apparent misclassification may undermine the proper recognition of physical and rehabilitation medicine as a medical discipline across the EU. It may also create legal uncertainty regarding the scope of professional qualifications, potentially affecting patient safety, quality of care and public health. In addition, it has been suggested that responsibility for addressing this issue lies primarily with the Member States, despite the fact that Annex V forms part of EU legislation. In this context: 1.
Is the Commission aware of the apparent misclassification of physical and rehabilitation medicine in Annex V to Directive 2005/36/EC?
Does the Commission intend to propose a correction or clarification in order to ensure accurate recognition of this medical speciality at EU level?
How does the Commission assess the potential implications of this situation for legal certainty, patient safety and the functioning of the system for recognition of professional qualifications?

Directive 2005/36/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 7 September 2005 on the recognition of professional qualifications (OJ L 255, 30.9.2005, p. 22, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2005/36/oj).
at: (English version) to the Commission Alex Agius Saliba (S&D) (16 March 2026) Subject: Misclassification of physical and rehabilitation medicine in Annex V to Directive 2005/36/EC Annex V to Directive 2005/36/EC on the recognition of professional qualifications (1) appears to list the medical speciality of physical and rehabilitation medicine under the designation ‘physiotherapy’. However, physiotherapy is an allied health profession and not a medical speciality. This apparent misclassification may undermine the proper recognition of physical and rehabilitation medicine as a medical discipline across the EU. It may also create legal uncertainty regarding the scope of professional qualifications, potentially affecting patient safety, quality of care and public health. In addition, it has been suggested that responsibility for addressing this issue lies primarily with the Member States, despite the fact that Annex V forms part of EU legislation. In this context: 1.
Is the Commission aware of the apparent misclassification of physical and rehabilitation medicine in Annex V to Directive 2005/36/EC?
Does the Commission intend to propose a correction or clarification in order to ensure accurate recognition of this medical speciality at EU level?
How does the Commission assess the potential implications of this situation for legal certainty, patient safety and the functioning of the system for recognition of professional qualifications?

(4 May 2026) The Commission has indeed received feedback from certain stakeholders indicating that a generic name ‘Physical and Rehabilitation Medicine’ would better reflect the scope of the national medical specialties currently listed in the table under the generic name ‘Physiotherapy’ in point 5.1.3 of Annex V to Directive 2005/36/EC (1). Currently, the Commission has the competence to update through delegated acts, upon notification from a Member State, the national titles listed in the table that give right to automatic recognition between Member States whose qualifications feature in the table. Any change to the generic name of the table would require legislative amendment to the directive as it falls outside the delegated powers conferred on the Commission. The Commission is currently looking into the possibility of a systemic solution to this issue as part of its evaluation of Directive 2005/36/EC. Annex V to the directive is used in the context of recognition procedures by competent authorities. Its contents and structure clearly indicate that professional qualifications of specialist doctors are recognised under the ‘automatic’ regime based on national evidence of formal qualifications expressly listed in point 5.1.3 of Annex V. Member States notify the evidence of national qualifications to the Commission and on that basis the Commission regularly updates the annex through delegated acts. Consequently, the names of national specialties in the annex reflect the current names used by Member States (e.g., Mediċina ta' Rijabilitazzjoni for Malta) (2). This system ensures legal certainty for the automatic recognition of professional qualifications in medical specialties.

Directive 2005/36/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 7 September 2005 on the recognition of professional qualifications (OJ L 255, 30.9.2005, p. 22, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2005/36/oj). Directive 2005/36/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 7 September 2005 on the recognition of professional qualifications, https://eurlex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A02005L0036-20251029. Also, e.g., Medicina fisica e riabilitativa for Italy, Physikalische und Rehabilitative Medizin for Germany, or Médecine physique et de réadaptation for France.

E-10-2026-001068.t: Threats to energy security posed by Ukraine’s attacks on the TurkStream gas pipeline
qt: to the Commission Petra Steger (PfE) Subject:

After allegedly Ukrainian operatives destroyed the Nord Stream 2 pipeline in a terrorist act of sabotage and damaged and blocked the Druzhba oil pipeline, it appears that Ukraine has also been attacking the Turkstream gas pipeline since 12 March 2026. These acts show that Ukraine is doggedly persisting with its provocations against the Member States of Hungary and Slovakia, deliberately threatening their energy security with what is in practice a total blockade simply because the two countries have repeatedly opposed self-destructive sanctions against Russia in the EU bodies. Rather than continuing to transfer billions in unilateral donations to Kyiv, it is high time the Commission took a critical look at the situation and made a decisive re-assessment. Ukraine must finally be pressured to change course to swiftly stop its attacks on infrastructure essential for individual Member States so as to safeguard the stability of the EU’s energy systems. 1.

What does the Commission make of Ukraine’s alleged attacks on the TurkStream gas pipeline and resulting threat to the energy sovereignty of Hungary and Slovakia – particularly in view of the previous destruction of Nord Stream 2 and damage to the Druzhba oil pipeline?

What real measures does the Commission plan to take to protect Hungary and Slovakia from further attacks by Ukraine on energy infrastructure, and how does it intend to effectively pressure Ukraine to comply?
Why does the Commission not explicitly and firmly condemn Ukraine’s attacks on infrastructure that is essential for individual Member States?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (12.5.2026) The EU remains committed to supporting Ukraine in the face of Russia’s ongoing war of aggression. The Commission has also actively supported EU Member States to effectively address ongoing energy disruptions in the Middle East and on the Druzhba oil pipeline following Russia’s attacks on Ukraine’s infrastructure and it continues to engage closely to ensure security of supply. At the Gas1 and Oil Coordination Group2 meetings of 26 and 27 March 2026, EU Member States, including Hungary and Slovakia, reported that there are no immediate risks to the security of their oil and gas supplies. Hungary and Slovakia also indicated that alternative crude oil supplies via Croatia and partial release of strategic stocks have prevented immediate shortages. In a joint letter of 16 March 2026, the President of the European Council and the President of the European Commission offered Ukraine technical and financial support to repair the Druzhba pipeline, which Ukraine has accepted. Discussions on implementation are ongoing. The Commission will continue close engagement with the concerned countries to ensure energy security in the region.
1 https://energy.ec.europa.eu/news/gas-coordination-group-confirms-readiness-prepare-upcoming-winter-season-
2026-03-26_en. 2 https://energy.ec.europa.eu/news/commission-and-eu-countries-discuss-latest-developments-concerningenergy-security-2026-03-27_en.

E-10-2026-001067.t: Taking account of human rights in the partnership between the European Union and Senegal
qt: to the Commission Mélissa Camara (Verts/ALE) Subject:

The European Union maintains a close partnership with Senegal which is primarily reflected in significant cooperation and EU funding that aims to support development, democratic governance and the upholding of human rights. Yet Senegal has recently passed a law which further criminalises homosexuality, including sentences of up to ten years’ imprisonment and penalties for ‘promoting’ homosexuality. This development has caused serious concern about the situation of LGBTQIA+ people in the country. In its analyses of the partnership with Senegal, the Commission has in fact noted that Senegalese legislation does not always fully meet human rights standards. 1.
What steps has the European Union taken or does it plan to take as part of its dialogue with the Senegalese authorities to promote respect for the rights of LGBTQIA+ people?

When reviewing the Multiannual Financial Framework and discussing future partnerships for the EU, how does the Commission intend to take account of this recent legal development in the continued partnership between the European Union and Senegal?
at: (English version) to the Commission Mélissa Camara (Verts/ALE) (16 March 2026) Subject: Taking account of human rights in the partnership between the European Union and Senegal The European Union maintains a close partnership with Senegal which is primarily reflected in significant cooperation and EU funding that aims to support development, democratic governance and the upholding of human rights. Yet Senegal has recently passed a law which further criminalises homosexuality, including sentences of up to 10 years’ imprisonment and penalties for ‘promoting’ homosexuality. This development has caused serious concern about the situation of LGBTQIA+ people in the country. In its analyses of the partnership with Senegal, the Commission has in fact noted that Senegalese legislation does not always fully meet human rights standards. 1. What steps has the European Union taken or does it plan to take as part of its dialogue with the Senegalese authorities to promote respect for the rights of LGBTQIA+ people? 2. When reviewing the Multiannual Financial Framework and discussing future partnerships for the EU, how does the Commission intend to take account of this recent legal development in the continued partnership between the European Union and Senegal? (12 May 2026) The EU took note of the adoption of the law amending Article 319 of the Senegalese Penal Code, which increases the penalties for consensual sexual relations between adults of the same sex. The EU is committed to promoting the full and equal enjoyment of human rights by lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer/questioning, plus (LGBTIQ+) persons internationally and reiterate its support for the universal decriminalisation of consensual same-sex relations, as stated in the Council conclusions on the EU's human rights priorities for 2026 (1). The EU does so by taking into account the local realities in which human rights defenders advance their struggle in line with the EU guidelines to promote and protect the enjoyment of all human rights by LGBTI persons (2). The EU Delegation in Dakar holds a bilateral dialogue to address human rights issues and is regularly in contact with national authorities, and other relevant stakeholders, to promote and protect the rights of vulnerable groups, including the rights of LGBTIQ people. The EU also acts in accordance with the principle of ‘do no harm’. Experience shows that public statements can sometimes increase stigmatisation and expose vulnerable communities to increased risk. The EU will continue to engage with the authorities, raise human rights issues and express concerns regarding this new legislation as part of the regular partnership dialogues and through the appropriate diplomatic channels. The partnership between the EU and Senegal is based on mutual respect, promoting protection and fulfilment of human rights, and dialogue. EU’s extensive partnership with Senegal is a leverage that enables the EU to maintain an open and frank exchange with the Senegalese authorities.

E-10-2026-001066.t: EU-Türkiye engagement and rule of law concerns
qt: to the Commission Mélissa Camara (Verts/ALE) Subject:

On 6 and 7 February 2026, the Commissioner for Enlargement, Marta Kos, visited Ankara to discuss EU-Türkiye cooperation, meeting senior Turkish officials and attending the signing of a EUR 200 million European Investment Bank (EIB) loan for small and medium-sized enterprises. The visit took place amid ongoing EU concerns about Türkiye regarding the rule of law, restrictions on freedom of expression and assembly, pressure on independent media and shrinking civic space, as reflected in recent Commission enlargement reports and Parliament resolutions. In the light of the above: 1.

How does the Commission justify the decision to prioritise high-level political and economic engagement with the Turkish authorities at a time when serious and persistent rule of law concerns remain unresolved?

What concrete benchmarks related to judicial independence, media freedom and fundamental rights were raised during the visit, and were any measurable commitments obtained from the Turkish authorities?

How does the Commission ensure that enhanced cooperation on trade, connectivity and financial instruments, including EIB-supported loans, remains fully consistent with the EU’s obligations under Article 2 of the Treaty on European Union and does not risk weakening the EU’s credibility on fundamental rights in the enlargement process?

How does the Commission ensure that enhanced cooperation on trade, connectivity and financial instruments, including EIB-supported loans, remains fully consistent with the EU’s obligations under Article 2 of the Treaty on European Union and does not risk weakening the EU’s credibility on fundamental rights in the enlargement process?

(3 August 2026) Türkiye remains a key partner for the EU and a candidate country. The Council and European Council have regularly reiterated the EU’s strategic interest in a stable and secure environment in the Eastern Mediterranean, and in the development of a cooperative and mutually beneficial relationship with Türkiye (1). The EU and Türkiye have common interests in a number of key areas, including trade, migration and regional connectivity. The Commission noted in the 2025 Enlargement Report (2) that there was backsliding in the area of rule of law and fundamental rights, including judicial independence and media freedom. During her visit to Ankara on 6 and 7 February 2026, the Commissioner for Enlargement raised those concerns and emphasised that without a reversal of this backsliding, the accession process would remain at a standstil l (3). She also met with Members of the Turkish Parliament, including from the opposition, to engage with them and hear their views. The Commission is committed to supporting projects that promote economic resilience, innovation and sustainability, while maintaining a strong stance on fundamental rights and the rule of law. The EU’s funding in support of civil society, promotion of fundamental rights and people-to-people contacts in Türkiye continues. The dialogue on rule of law remains an integral part of the EU-Türkiye relationship, and the Commission will continue to address these issues in all relevant contacts with the Turkish authorities, including within the framework of the sub-committee covering this area under the Association Agreement with Türkiye.

E-10-2026-001064.t: Possible launch of the procedure to add the Muslim Brotherhood to the EU list of terrorist organisations
qt: to the Commission Anna Maria Cisint (PfE), Aldo Patriciello (PfE), Silvia Sardone (PfE), Isabella Tovaglieri (PfE), Susanna Ceccardi (PfE), Paolo Borchia (PfE), Raffaele Stancanelli (PfE) Subject:

The May 2025 report from the French intelligence service entitled ‘Muslim Brotherhood and political Islamism in France’ fuelled widespread concern across the Member States. More recently, the report prompted the French Parliament to adopt a resolution calling on the Commission and the Council to initiate a legal assessment of the Muslim Brotherhood’s transnational network, tighten checks on EU funding, recognise the political nature of Islamic separatism and take steps, guided by EU counterterrorism criteria and backed by enhanced Member State cooperation, to potentially add the movement and its leaders to the EU list of terrorist organisations. The Muslim Brotherhood certainly poses a threat to the fundamental principles of the EU: it promotes a political and religious separatism that inherently undermines sovereignty and the constitutional order, and its European network branches throughout the Member States (even extending to Islamic centres and imams) in its pursuit of an agenda incompatible with the rule of law. In view of the above, can the Commission say whether it will consider launching the procedure, in accordance with the rule of law, to add the Muslim Brotherhood and its leaders to the EU list of terrorist organisations?
at: (English version) to the Commission Anna Maria Cisint (PfE), Aldo Patriciello (PfE), Silvia Sardone (PfE), Isabella Tovaglieri (PfE), Susanna Ceccardi (PfE), Paolo Borchia (PfE), Raffaele Stancanelli (PfE) (16 March 2026) Subject: Possible launch of the procedure to add the Muslim Brotherhood to the EU list of terrorist organisations The May 2025 report from the French intelligence service entitled ‘Muslim Brotherhood and political Islamism in France’ fuelled widespread concern across the Member States. More recently, the report prompted the French Parliament to adopt a resolution calling on the Commission and the Council to initiate a legal assessment of the Muslim Brotherhood’s transnational network, tighten checks on EU funding, recognise the political nature of Islamic separatism and take steps, guided by EU counterterrorism criteria and backed by enhanced Member State cooperation, to potentially add the movement and its leaders to the EU list of terrorist organisations. The Muslim Brotherhood certainly poses a threat to the fundamental principles of the EU: it promotes a political and religious separatism that inherently undermines sovereignty and the constitutional order, and its European network branches throughout the Member States (even extending to Islamic centres and imams) in its pursuit of an agenda incompatible with the rule of law. In view of the above, can the Commission say whether it will consider launching the procedure, in accordance with the rule of law, to add the Muslim Brotherhood and its leaders to the EU list of terrorist organisations? (27 May 2026) The EU takes very seriously the threat posed by extremist radical views sowing social division, polarisation and radicalisation in Europe. In close cooperation with Member States, the EU monitors the evolving risks linked to organisations trying to unduly influence the EU institutions, including radical and extremist non-state actors, as well as interference from third countries. The legal prerequisite for the listing of new individuals, groups or entities, under Council Decision (CFSP) 2026/455 of 26 February 2026 (1), is a decision by a competent authority as defined by Article 2(3) of the decision. Such a decision should concern the involvement of the individual or entity in question in a ‘terrorist act’ as defined by Article 1(1) of the aforementioned Decision. On that basis, the Council decides on a listing pursuant to Decision (CFSP) 2026/455 (2), acting by unanimity. The Commission remains committed to preventing and combatting all forms of radicalisation, as well as hatred, racism and discrimination, including those related to actual or perceived religion or belief.

E-10-2026-001063.t: Fertiliser costs and the impact of tariffs and the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism on the competitiveness of EU farming
qt: to the Commission Carmen Crespo Díaz (PPE) Subject:

The EU’s farmers are having to contend with increasingly challenging conditions at a time of geopolitical instability. One specific issue is fertiliser prices, which remain volatile and higher than historical levels, putting considerable strain on competitiveness and the economic viability of agriculture in the Union. It is estimated that higher fertiliser prices will lead to EUR 170 million in additional costs per year. Guaranteeing stable and affordable access to fertilisers is key to maintaining production and competitiveness in agriculture, as well as safeguarding the EU’s food security. In light of the above: 1.
Does the Commission plan to do away with the current tariffs on fertiliser imports from Trinidad and Tobago and the US?

Does the Commission intend to suspend the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism for fertilisers for a transitional period of five years to prevent further cost hikes in the EU farming sector at a time of market instability?
Has the Spanish Government requested those support measures from the EU?

E-10-2026-001062.t: Fuel costs and the impact of geopolitical instability on the primary sector
qt: to the Commission Carmen Crespo Díaz (PPE) Subject:

European farmers and fishermen are facing a sharp increase in production costs as a result, primarily, of rising fuel prices. The current geopolitical instability, particularly in the Middle East, is making oil and diesel prices highly volatile, which has a direct impact on the primary sector. In some cases, such as in Spain, the price of red diesel has risen 40 % in a matter of days, pushing costs up significantly for farmers and fishermen. As fuel is one of farms’ and fisheries’ main operating costs, this state of affairs undermines their viability and may have repercussions for food prices and security. In the light of the foregoing: 1.
Will the Commission authorise the use of the temporary crisis and transition framework to enable Member States to support fishing fleets affected by the steep escalation in fuel prices?
Will it activate further financial instruments, outside the framework of the common agricultural policy, to address the uptick in energy costs caused by the current geopolitical instability?
Has the Spanish Government requested that any of those support measures be activated?

(21 August 2026) The Commission acknowledges the significant pressure that some economic sectors face due to increased energy and fertiliser prices, exacerbated by ongoing geopolitical tensions in the Middle East. The conflict in the region has constrained global supply chains, underscoring the critical need to bolster the EU’s strategic resilience. In line with the Fertiliser Action Plan (1), the Commission proposed to mobilise the EU budget to increase the agricultural reserve to provide fast relief for farmers and will present a new liquidity scheme to help with cash flow. Concerning state aid, the Commission has adopted on 29 April 2026 a temporary framework for state aid to support the most exposed sectors including the primary production of agricultural and fisheries products and aquaculture (2). Member States may use the new Temporary Crisis Framework, in addition to the standard state aid rules applicable to the agricultural and fishery sectors, to support them. In this sense, the Commission has already approved three Spanish state aid measures (3) under the new Temporary Crisis Framework to compensate the primary producers of agricultural and fishery products for the increase of the prices of fertilisers and fuel provoked by the Middle East crisis. The Commission triggered the crisis support mechanism of the European Maritime Fisheries and Aquaculture Fund (EMFAF) Regulation on 16 April 2026 making support available to operators in the fisheries and aquaculture sector (4). The Commission remains fully committed to continuously assessing the situation and will explore whether additional support mechanisms are needed for these sectors in the short term. Regarding the measures requested by the Spanish Government, the Commission cannot comment about open state aid procedures.

E-10-2026-001061.t: Persistent imports of Russian aluminium and other strategic commodities into the EU
qt: to the Commission Bart Groothuis (Renew), Petras Auštrevičius (Renew), Karin Karlsbro (Renew), João Cotrim De Figueiredo (Renew), Ľubica Karvašová (Renew), Pascal Canfin (Renew), Dan Barna (Renew) Subject:

Following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine on 24 February 2022, the EU has imposed extensive sanctions, but imports of certain strategic commodities from Russia – such as fertilisers, nickel and especially aluminium – remain high. The importing of Russian aluminium not only undermines the effectiveness of EU sanctions but also harms European producers and erodes their competitiveness. Russian aluminium continues to enter the EU market indirectly – via Türkiye – where it is processed into semifinished products. Russian aluminium ingots are frequently sold at discounted prices, enabling non-EU producers to undercut European manufacturers and flood the market with lower-cost goods. 1.

Why do Russian fertilisers, nickel and aluminium products still constitute a significant share of direct and indirect EU imports, and what specific challenges or dependencies prevent the EU from further reducing these imports?

What concrete actions does the Commission intend to take to address these persistent imports, especially in the case of aluminium – are there plans to introduce an indirect ban on aluminium products containing Russian primary aluminium and implement mandatory smelt and cast reporting requirements?
How will the Commission ensure transparency and accountability with regard to these measures, and what follow-up mechanisms will be established with Parliament?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (29.4.2026) In response to Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine, the EU has adopted a wide range of restrictive measures, including far-reaching trade restrictions which have played a significant role in reducing imports of strategic commodities from Russia. The measures in place reflect a careful balance between the EU’s determination to impact Russia’s ability to finance its war of aggression and to limit to the extent possible negative impacts on Member States and industry, taking into account shortages of certain critical raw materials. As regards aluminium, the 16th sanctions package1 expanded the restrictions already in place to cover also primary aluminium, resulting in a ban on imports of primary aluminium from Russia as of 26 February 2026 with a remaining small quota of 50 000 metric tonnes to allow imports for contracts concluded before 25 February 2025 (i.e. one-year old contracts) still to be delivered only until the end of 2026. The Commission closely monitors the aluminium market situation, including EU imports of processed aluminium and is ready to consider appropriate actions, if necessary. EU sanctions are kept under regular review. Any decision to amend any of the existing sanctions in place or to add new sanctions is for the Council to take by unanimity.

(26 May 2026) With the new Single Market Strategy, the Commission intends to strengthen the integration and efficiency of the internal market. This initiative primarily aims to dismantle unjustified barriers, reduce the administrative burden, stimulate investment, and ensure a level playing field within the Union. With the Wine Package (1), the Commission is empowered to lay down rules for providing consumers with the list of ingredients and the nutrition declaration via electronic means on the label of wine bottles, with the aim to minimise costs and facilitate trade across the internal market. (29 April 2026) The EU financial contribution under Sustainable Fisheries Partnership Agreements (SFPAs), in line with Article 32(1) of the Common Fisheries Policy (CFP) Regulation, has two components. The first covers access to fisheries resources and is paid directly to the partner country’s government. Its use falls under national sovereignty and the Commission doesn’t monitor it and doesn’t have information on final recipients. In contrast, the second component, the sectoral support, is subject to strict monitoring and reporting. Partner countries must provide annual reports on their implementation, activities and beneficiaries. Progress is regularly assessed, including in the annual Joint Committee meetings which govern the implementation of the SFPAs, and payments depend on satisfactory implementation. More details are available in the ex-ante and ex-post evaluations, published on the website of the EU’s publication office (1). The Commission regularly assesses the impact of SFPAs, including their economic relevance for the EU fleet, through the above-mentioned evaluations carried out before each protocol is concluded or renewed. These consistently show that SFPAs support the competitiveness and viability of the EU fishing fleet, including those of Spain and Portugal. They provide access to key fishing zones and resources not available in EU waters, ensure predictable and secure operating conditions for EU vessels, support year-round continuity of fishing activities, and help sustain sectoral employment and economic activity. The Commission’s conclusion is that SFPAs remain an essential tool for supporting the external dimension of the CFP, contributing both to sustainable fisheries and the economic performance of the EU fleet.

E-10-2026-001056.t: Advertising targeting minors on TikTok and the link to the upcoming Digital Fairness Act
qt: to the Commission Veronika Cifrová Ostrihoňová (Renew) Subject:

According to research published in a paper entitled ‘The DSA’s Blind Spot: Algorithmic Audit of Advertising and Minor Profiling on TikTok’1, minors on TikTok are primarily exposed to influencer-style commercial content rather than formal platform advertisements, at levels five to eight times higher than those permitted for adults. In addition, 84 % of the advertisements seen by minors are undisclosed, compared to 51 % for adults. While the Digital Services Act (DSA) prohibits profiling-based advertising targeting minors, its definition of ‘advertisement’ focuses on content promoted in exchange for remuneration through the platform’s advertising systems. Therefore, influencer marketing, brand selfpromotion, affiliate marketing and other forms of commercial content may fall outside the scope of this definition. In this context: 1.
How does the Commission assess the risks associated with the profiling of minors through influencer-style commercial content and undisclosed advertising on platforms such as TikTok?
Does the Commission consider that existing EU legislation, including the DSA, provides sufficient tools to address this issue?
Does the Commission intend to address potential regulatory gaps related to influencer marketing and undisclosed commercial content targeting minors in the upcoming Digital Fairness Act?
https://www.researchgate.net/publication/401691760_The_DSA’s_Blind_Spot_Algorithmic_Audit_of_ Advertising_and_Minor_Profiling_on_TikTok.
at: (English version) to the Commission Veronika Cifrová Ostrihoňová (Renew) (13 March 2026) Subject: Advertising targeting minors on TikTok and the link to the upcoming Digital Fairness Act According to research published in a paper entitled ‘The DSA’s Blind Spot: Algorithmic Audit of Advertising and Minor Profiling on TikTok’ (1), minors on TikTok are primarily exposed to influencer-style commercial content rather than formal platform advertisements, at levels five to eight times higher than those permitted for adults. In addition, 84% of the advertisements seen by minors are undisclosed, compared to 51% for adults. While the Digital Services Act (DSA) prohibits profiling-based advertising targeting minors, its definition of ‘advertisement’ focuses on content promoted in exchange for remuneration through the platform’s advertising systems. Therefore, influencer marketing, brand self-promotion, affiliate marketing and other forms of commercial content may fall outside the scope of this definition. In this context: 1.
How does the Commission assess the risks associated with the profiling of minors through influencer-style commercial content and undisclosed advertising on platforms such as TikTok?
Does the Commission consider that existing EU legislation, including the DSA, provides sufficient tools to address this issue?
Does the Commission intend to address potential regulatory gaps related to influencer marketing and undisclosed commercial content targeting minors in the upcoming Digital Fairness Act?

(1 June 2026) The protection of children in the digital age is a key priority for the Commission. The existing legal framework already includes very high standards. The Digital Services Act (DSA) (1) regulates, inter alia, systemic risks posed by providers of very large online platforms like TikTok, including risks to minors (2), and on how the selection of advertisements influence such risks (3). Providers must establish appropriate measures of privacy and safety (4) for minors and ban profiling-based advertisements (5) using their personal data. In addition, the Protection of Minors guidelines (6) cover advertising on online platforms and the DSA requires establishing a functionality to flag commercial communications (7). The Unfair Commercial Practices Directive (8) ensures strict consumer protection, including shielding children from misleading commercial practices. It applies to influencers, requiring them to be clear about commercial communication. The Audiovisual Media Services Directive (9) sets minimum standards for audiovisual commercial communications (ACC), which must not cause physical, mental or moral harm to minors. Direct exhortations to acquire products or services are prohibited (applicable to influencers who qualify as audiovisual media service providers) and video-sharing platforms must ensure compliance with ACC to different degrees (10). Minors’ personal data collected for age verification or parental control may not serve commercial purposes (11). 1

qt: to the Commission Christine Anderson (ESN) Subject:

According to information provided by the German Federal Government in response to a parliamentary question (reference number 2/531, February 2026), special meetings of the European Medicines Agency’s (EMA) Pharmacovigilance Risk Assessment Committee (PRAC) were held on 18 December 2020 (on Comirnaty), on 4 January 2021 (on Spikevax) and on 22 January 2021 (on Vaxzevria) including the review of the respective riskmanagement plans for COVID-19 vaccines. 1.

What specific documents – e.g. agendas, minutes, assessment reports, memoranda on decisions or other meeting documents – exist relating to the PRAC extraordinary meetings of 18 December 2020, 4 January 2021 and 22 January 2021?

at: (English version) to the Commission Christine Anderson (ESN) (13 March 2026) Subject: Minutes of extraordinary PRAC meetings on COVID-19 vaccines According to information provided by the German Federal Government in response to a parliamentary question (reference number 2/531, February 2026), special meetings of the European Medicines Agency’s (EMA) Pharmacovigilance Risk Assessment Committee (PRAC) were held on 18 December 2020 (on Comirnaty), on 4 January 2021 (on Spikevax) and on 22 January 2021 (on Vaxzevria) including the review of the respective risk-management plans for COVID-19 vaccines. 1. (4 May 2026) The Commission would like to inform the Honourable Member that both EU citizens and healthcare professionals receive timely updates on all scientific recommendations taken by the European Medicines Agency (EMA). Following each meeting of the EMA’s safety committee (Pharmacovigilance Risk Assessment Committee — PRAC (1)), the key outcomes are communicated through the PRAC highlights (2). Furthermore, during the pandemic, the EMA implemented additional measures for COVID-19 medicinal products to maximise the transparency of its regulatory activities related to COVID-19 medicines (3). Furthermore, all three extraordinary PRAC meetings (18 December 2020, 4 January 2021 and 22 January 2021) were convened to enable the PRAC to provide advice on the Risk Management Plans (RMPs) for the respective vaccines prior the Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use (CHMP) plenary meeting on the vaccines marketing authorisation applications aiming at issuing a scientific opinion. The outcome (minutes) of these extraordinary PRAC meetings were subsequently incorporated into the minutes for the following PRAC plenaries, which are publicly available (4), (5). Additionally, the PRAC recommendations to the CHMP on the RMP are also included in the marketing authorisation assessment reports. They are therefore reflected in the respective European public assessment reports, in particular in the assessment reports for Vaxzevria (6), (7) and Spikevax (8), (9). The PRAC committee operates under EMA’s responsibility.

Are there any planned organisational, functional or reporting links between the proposed intelligence cell and the ECDR?
Will both structures operate within the same Commission services or under the authority of the same Commissioner(s) or of the President’s services?

Can the Commission confirm whether the activities of the proposed intelligence cell or the ECDR will include threat assessments, the mapping of influence networks or the systematic analysis of actors operating in the information space?

(5 May 2026) The European Centre for Democratic Resilience is a cooperation framework, under the leadership of the Commissioner responsible for democracy, justice, the rule of law and consumer protection, for exchange primarily between EU institutions, Member States and civil society to empower, protect, and promote strong and resilient democracies across the EU. The Centre is a core component of the European Democracy Shield (1), which defines a broad, whole-of-society and whole-ofgovernment approach to strengthening democracy. There are no planned organisational, functional or reporting links between the Centre and any intelligence structure. The Centre fully respects EU and national competences and the independence of existing structures at national and EU level. It will be rolled out progressively, based on Member States’ voluntary participation, and on their input and needs for support and cooperation, to ensure that it delivers the best support to national authorities and jointly at EU level. The Centre brings together expertise and resources to increase collective capacity to anticipate, detect and respond to threats to our democracies, such as foreign information manipulation and interference (FIMI) and disinformation. The Centre builds on existing networks and structures working on prevention, detection, analysis, and response to patterns of threats in the information space. The information shared via the Centre is based on open sources. The Centre will also support capacity-building activities, including trainings. It could further support response capacity.

E-10-2026-001053.t: Scientific basis for the 4.20 m threshold for incentives for ‘Small Zero-Emission Vehicles’
qt: to the Commission Andreas Schwab (PPE) Subject:
Scientific basis for the 4.20 m threshold for incentives for ‘Small Zero-Emission Vehicles’

In the automotive Omnibus package amending Regulation (EU) 2019/631 on CO2 fleet targets, the Commission proposes to introduce a new category of ‘small electric vehicles’. Vehicles in this category, if manufactured in the EU, are to be included with a factor of 1.3 in the calculation of a manufacturer’s average specific emissions of CO2. The definition included in the above-mentioned proposal provides for a maximum vehicle length of 4.20 m for this category. According to the Commission, one of the reasons for this threshold is that there are currently only 12 battery-electric models below EUR 25 000 in this size segment across the EU and that this is intended to provide targeted incentives for affordable electric vehicles. The fixed limit of 4.20 m in combination with a factor of 1.3 means that borderline cases with only minor differences in length could have a very different impact on the fleet calculation. The underlying data and the expected effect warrant further explanation. 1.

How does the Commission justify, from a methodological point of view, the discrete threshold (4.20 m), resulting in an abrupt impact on the fleet calculation instead of a continuous, proportional progression?

How will the Commission ensure that differentiation according to vehicle length adequately reflects the actual energy efficiency and environmental impact, especially given that vehicle length is not a reliable indicator of efficiency?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (20.5.2026) The Omnibus IX (Automotive)1 introduces a new sub-category for small electric passenger cars M1 (‘M1E’), based on a maximum length of 4.2 metres. This legal definition of small electric cars can be used for targeted simplification and support measures to incentivise production and uptake of small electric vehicles. The proposal to amend the Regulation setting CO2 emission standards for cars and vans2 provides that, until 2034, for the purpose of calculating a manufacturer’s average specific emissions of CO2, each new zero-emission vehicle of category M1E and made in the EU shall be counted as 1.3 vehicles. Based on stakeholder consultation and an analysis of the available electric models on the market, a maximum length of 4.2 metres is considered appropriate to boost the small cars segment, but also to serve the mobility needs of most European households. The establishment of a discrete threshold leads to inevitable edge effects irrespective of the choice of the threshold value. However, a gradual transition would cause complications in compliance and lead to a lack of transparency that the Commission considers disproportionate, in particular in the context of a simplification omnibus. Comparisons show that the most energy-efficient electric vehicles on the EU market3 have a length below 4.2 metres. In addition, a small vehicle takes less material to be built.
1 COM(2025) 993. 2 COM(2025) 995. 3 In terms of watt-hours per kilometer (Wh/km).

E-10-2026-001051.t: Belgian bank guarantee in favour of Girteka and compliance with EU rules on competition and social dumping
qt: to the Commission Estelle Ceulemans (S&D), Kathleen Van Brempt (S&D) Subject:

It has been reported that Credendo, the Belgian public export credit agency, has granted a EUR 74 million bank guarantee to the German banking consortium AKA Bank, enabling the financing of 1 200 new trucks for the Lithuanian transport company Girteka. However, Girteka has repeatedly been criticised for structural violations of EU transport rules, particularly concerning cabotage operations and the working conditions of drivers from nonEU countries. Several journalistic investigations have highlighted practices that could constitute social dumping within the internal market. In this context: 1.
Does the Commission consider that this public guarantee complies with EU rules on State aid and fair competition?
How does the Commission ensure that national public instruments, such as export credit guarantees, do not indirectly contribute to social dumping contrary to the objectives of the Mobility Package?
Is the Commission considering additional measures to ensure consistency between EU social regulations and public financial instruments?
at: (English version) to the Commission Estelle Ceulemans (S&D), Kathleen Van Brempt (S&D) (12 March 2026) Subject: Belgian bank guarantee in favour of Girteka and compliance with EU rules on competition and social dumping It has been reported that Credendo, the Belgian public export credit agency, has granted a EUR 74 million bank guarantee to the German banking consortium AKA Bank, enabling the financing of 1 200 new trucks for the Lithuanian transport company Girteka. However, Girteka has repeatedly been criticised for structural violations of EU transport rules, particularly concerning cabotage operations and the working conditions of drivers from non-EU countries. Several journalistic investigations have highlighted practices that could constitute social dumping within the internal market. In this context: 1.
Does the Commission consider that this public guarantee complies with EU rules on state aid and fair competition?
How does the Commission ensure that national public instruments, such as export credit guarantees, do not indirectly contribute to social dumping contrary to the objectives of the Mobility Package?
Is the Commission considering additional measures to ensure consistency between EU social regulations and public financial instruments?

(18 May 2026) The Commission does not possess any information on the specific guarantee issued by Credendo. If a guarantee would not have been provided on market terms and constituted state aid, Belgium would have had to notify the measure to the Commission. When it comes to the rules against social dumping, including as part of the Mobility Package (1), their enforcement is primarily ensured by the Member States’ competent authorities and the Commission monitors their correct and on time application and enforcement. If necessary, the Commission may launch infringement procedures against Member States. The Commission takes into account social objectives and regulations in several EU-level financial instruments. For instance, instruments issued under the European Social Fund Plus aim at contributing to the implementation of the European Pillar of Social Rights, to support jobs and create a fair and socially inclusive society. Further, financial instruments issued under InvestEU support financing projects in social infrastructure, social innovation, social enterprises, integration of migrants, refugees and vulnerable people, for example.

E-10-2026-001050.t: Sugar imports to the European Union from EBA beneficiary states
qt: to the Commission David McAllister (PPE) Subject:

Under the Everything but Arms (EBA) initiative, the European Union grants least developed countries tariff-free and quota-free access to the European single market. This scheme also applies to sugar. Some of the imported sugar undergoes further processing within the European Union and subsequently enters the single market. 1.
How have the annual import volumes of sugar from EBA beneficiary states to the European Union developed over the last five years, and what are the main countries of origin of these imports?

What evidence do the Commission or European customs authorities have of possible circumventions of the rules of origin – for instance, sugar from third countries being diverted through EBA beneficiary countries, additional processing stages with limited added value or other means of circumventing the preferential trade arrangements?

In this context, how does the Commission assess the effectiveness of the current control mechanisms for sugar imports under the EBA scheme, what specific possibilities for verification and tracing exist at EU level, and does it see grounds for tightening the rules of origin or control procedures for these import flows?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (5.5.2026) 1. Sugar imports of Harmonised System heading 1701 from Everything but Arms (EBA) beneficiaries have fluctuated significantly over the past five years, reflecting EU market demand. After rising from 81 000 tonnes in 2021 to nearly 190 000 tonnes in 2023 - due to low EU production - EBA imports fell sharply as EU output recovered, dropping to 60 000 tonnes in 2024 and just 11 000 tonnes in 2025. Regarding countries of origin, while their export volumes fluctuate significantly year on year, the primary suppliers are Cambodia, Mozambique, Laos, Malawi and Myanmar. 2. The Commission is not aware of possible circumvention of rules of origin for sugar imported under Generalised Scheme of Preferences (GSP) EBA scheme. No past or ongoing investigations for potential circumvention of rules of origin in relation to sugar imports from EBA countries have been conducted. Member States can use risk-based checks - verifying unusual trade routes or proofs of origin via administrative cooperation with GSP countries competent authorities - to prevent misuse of preferential tariffs. 3. The Commission monitors third countries benefiting from preferential EU tariffs under the GSP scheme - also from the perspective of compliance with the rules of origin - to ensure that the declared origin is established correctly. By 2026, 32 GSP countries (14 EBA) were monitored, with visits to 16 GSP (6 EBA) countries. No evidence has come to light of sugar exported under preference from an EBA beneficiary country having the origin of another country.

E-10-2026-001049.t: Role of drug trafficking in Mexico in the context of the modernised Global Agreement
qt: to the Commission Hermann Tertsch (PfE), Jorge Martín Frías (PfE), Juan Carlos Girauta Vidal (PfE) Subject:

The recent escalation of violence in Mexico following the operation against the leader of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel has once again highlighted the serious security crisis in the country and the growing capacity of criminal organisations to challenge the state, block infrastructure and generate instability across large areas. In this context, and while the European Union plans to move forward with the signing and implementation of the modernised Global Agreement with Mexico, it is essential to assess whether the expansion of organised crime, associated corruption and the penetration of drug trafficking into economic structures may pose risks to the security of logistics chains, customs controls and the integrity of the European internal market1. 1.
What assessment has the Commission carried out of the risks that the strengthening of organised crime in Mexico could pose to the security of supply chains and EU-Mexico trade?
Does the modernised agreement provide for concrete safeguards to prevent criminal infiltration, illicit trafficking or money laundering through bilateral trade routes?
Does the Commission consider it necessary to condition or strengthen customs, police and organised crime cooperation with Mexico before the modernised agreement is fully implemented?

See “The changing DNA of serious and organised crime. EU Serious and Organised Crime Threat Assessment 2025 (EU-SOCTA)» (https://www.europol.europa.eu/cms/sites/default/files/documents/EUSOCTA-2025.pdf), which identifies drug trafficking as one of the main criminal threats to the EU and highlights the transnational nature of the networks involved; as well as ‘Europol, Complexities and Conveniences in the International Drug Trade: The Involvement of Mexican Criminal Actors in the EU Drug Market» (https://www.europol.europa.eu/cms/sites/default/files/documents/Europol_DEA_Joint_Report.pdf), which describes the direct participation of Mexican criminal actors in the European drug market and their operational cooperation with criminal networks within the EU.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (11.5.2026) While the Commission has not conducted a specific assessment on the risks of organised crime on EU-Mexico trade, it has taken measures to address threats related to organised crime, including illegal trafficking of drugs and other goods, as part of its broader strategy to enhance security. It has also strengthened cooperation on law enforcement and judicial matters with Mexico. The EU-Mexico Modernised Global Agreement1 aims at providing a state-of-the-art legal framework for bilateral relations between the two parties. The modernised agreement includes a Protocol on the prevention of and fight against corruption in trade and investment which reaffirms the commitments under the United Nations Convention against Corruption and other relevant international agreements, including with regard to combatting bribery and moneylaundering. Within the framework of EU–Mexico cooperation, the Commission recognises Mexico’s engagement in regional security programmes such as COPOLAD III2 and EL PACCTO 2.03, as well as in platforms including the EU and the Community of Latin American and Caribbean States Coordination and Cooperation Mechanism on Drugs, la Comunidad de Policías de América (AMERIPOL)4 and the Latin American Committee on Internal Security CLASI5. This reflects a shared commitment between the EU and Mexico to strengthening the rule of law, justice and security, and to addressing transnational organised crime, illicit financial flows and drug-related challenges through evidence-based approaches and operational cooperation.

1 https://ec.europa.eu/transparency/documents-register/detail?ref=COM(2025)809&lang=en. 2 https://international-partnerships.ec.europa.eu/policies/programming/programmes/copolad-iii_en. 3 https://international-partnerships.ec.europa.eu/policies/programming/programmes/el-paccto-20_en. 4 https://ameripol.org/. 5 https://elpaccto.eu/en/el-clasi-y-sus-implicaciones-a-nivel-politico-estrategico-y-operacional/.

Reply (1 June 2026) The listing of a person, group or entity under Council Decision (CFSP) 2026/455 (4) must satisfy the conditions laid down in Article 1(1) and (2) of that Council Decision, which provides, for this purpose, definitions of persons, groups and entities ‘involved in terrorist acts’, and of ‘terrorist acts’, ‘terrorist groups’ and ‘structured groups’. Article 2(2) and (3) of the decision specifies the requirements related to the adoption of a decision by a national competent authority in respect of the persons, groups and entities concerned. Article 2(4) of Council Decision (CFSP) 2026/455 also allows the imposition of restrictive measures on persons, groups or entities associated with those listed in Annex I to the decision. The Council is not in a position to comment on any proposals that may or may not be under deliberation until the process is finalised and the decision published in the Official Journal. As regards coordination with the United States on drug-related matters, cooperation to combat transnational organised crime and drug trafficking is a central focus of the longstanding EU-US dialogue on Justice and Home Affairs held twice a year at ministerial and senior officials’ level. The EU and the United States also regularly hold a dedicated EU-US dialogue on drugs in order to exchange information, strengthen bilateral cooperation and improve the coordination of action undertaken at global level to address drug-related issues.
