E-10-2026-001047.t: Avian influenza in Italy and compliance with animal welfare legislation
qt: to the Commission Cristina Guarda (Verts/ALE), Annalisa Corrado (S&D), Niels Fuglsang (S&D), David Cormand (Verts/ALE), Thomas Waitz (Verts/ALE), Maria Noichl (S&D), Anja Hazekamp (The Left), Tilly Metz (Verts/ALE), Sebastian Everding (The Left), Günther Sidl (S&D), Maria Grapini (S&D), Diana Iovanovici Şoşoacă (NI) Subject:

In 2025, over 699 avian influenza (bird flu) outbreaks were reported in European poultry farms. In Italy, 64 outbreaks were concentrated in regions where the Commission, in 2022, had already underlined a critical health and environmental threat due to the excessive number of farms. From 2020 to 2025, the regions of Veneto, Lombardy and Emilia-Romagna allocated EUR 266 million for culls and compensation, part of which comes from the European crisis management funds, such as the agricultural reserve1. A recent television investigation carried out by RAI – the Italian national public broadcasting company – revealed that hundreds of culls were carried out in complete violation of animal welfare regulations and with serious biosecurity deficiencies2. The public health risk cannot be ignored, given the recent evidence of virus spillover. 1.
How does the Commission ensure that allocated resources are used in compliance with current animal welfare legislation?
What is the most recent data available to the Commission on the management of avian influenza in Italy?
How does the Commission plan to strengthen compliance tools for the allocation of resources within the planned revision of EU animal welfare legislation?

Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/453 of 5 February 2024 on exceptional market support measures for the eggs and poultrymeat sectors in Italy (OJ L, 2024/453, 6.2.2024, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg_impl/2024/453/oj). RAI video report of 1 February 2026, https://www.raiplay.it/video/2026/02/Febbre-alta---Report-0102202637f21f32-22cf-48c9-9c91-c13cbaae99e8.html.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (10.6.2026) The Commission continuously monitors the animal health situation and recognises the economic impact of animal diseases on the livestock sector. Considering the impact and consequences of disease outbreaks, it supports Member States through financial and technical assistance, including under the Single Market Programme and measures within the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) 1,2 3. The implementation of the measures for the control of avian influenza in the affected Member States is evaluated by the audits performed by the Commission. In the recent years, the Commission performed such audits in Italy in 20224 and 20245. The conclusions of the audits are that the competent authorities took appropriate technical and supervisory measures to ensure the protection of animal welfare during depopulation of poultry establishments to control disease outbreaks. In addition to the findings and conclusions of the audits, the measures implemented by the competent authorities of Italy to manage the outbreaks of highly pathogenic avian influenza are regularly discussed in the Standing Committee on Plants, Animals, Food and Feed (PAFF Committee)6. While the Commission recognises that there is room for improvement, Regulation (EC) No 1099/20097 provides already sufficient provisions to ensure the protection of animals at the time of killing. As a result, the modernisation of the animal welfare legislation focuses on other areas.

E-10-2026-001046.t: Continued discrimination and legal uncertainty as a result of the non-implementation of CJEU rulings
qt: to the Commission Raquel García Hermida-Van Der Walle (Renew) Subject:
Continued discrimination and legal uncertainty as a result of the nonimplementation of CJEU rulings

Over the past few years, the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) has issued landmark judgments in the areas of freedom of movement and family life1, legal recognition of transgender identity2, and the protection of the human dignity of LGBTIQ+ people3. However, Member States have often not implemented the necessary changes in national legislation. As a consequence, LGBTIQ+ people’s fundamental rights are still being violated in some Member States. Now, the CJEU has ruled on the principle of legal gender recognition for people exercising their freedom of movement in the EU4. 1.

Does the Commission agree that its role as Guardian of the Treaties requires taking action against Member States that breach EU law and do not ensure judgments are implemented effectively and promptly, rather than merely ‘monitoring the situation’ in such cases? If so, can the Commission explain why the court rulings in footnotes 1, 2 and 3 have not been fully implemented yet?
Can the Commission provide an overview of the correspondence between the Commission and relevant Member State(s) for each of the court cases?

If the latest ruling is not directly implemented in the Member States, will the Commission show less hesitation and commit to directly and fully enforcing this CJEU ruling rather than only taking selective action?

Judgment of the Court of Justice of 5 June 2018, Coman and others v Inspectoratul General pentru Imigrări and Ministerul Afacerilor Interne, C-673/16, ECLI:EU:C:2018:385; Judgment of the Court of Justice of 14 December 2021, V.M.A. v Stolichna obshtina, rayon ‘Pancharevo’, C-490/20, ECLI:EU:C:2021:1008; Judgment of the Court (Grand Chamber) of 4 October 2024, M.-A.A. v Direcția de Evidență a Persoanelor Cluj, Serviciul stare civilă, Direcția pentru Evidența Persoanelor și Administrarea Bazelor de Date din Ministerul Afacerilor Interne, Municipiul Cluj-Napoca, C-4/23, ECLI:EU:C:2024:845; Judgment of the Court (Grand Chamber) of 25 November 2025, Jakub Cupriak-Trojan, Mateusz Trojan v Wojewoda Mazowiecki, C-713/23, ECLI:EU:C:2025:917; Order of the Court (Tenth Chamber) of 24 June 2022, Rzecznik Praw Obywatelskich, C-2/21, ECLI:EU:C:2022:502. Judgment of the Court (First Chamber) of 13 March 2025, VP v Országos Idegenrendészeti Főigazgatóság, C-247/23, ECLI:EU:C:2025:172. Judgment of the Court (Fifth Chamber) of 26 June 2025, Makeleio and Zougla v Ethniko Symvoulio Radiotileorasis (ESR), Joined Cases C-555/23 and C-556/23, ECLI:EU:C:2025:484. Judgment of the Court (Second Chamber) of 12 March 2026, K. M. H. v Obshtina Stara Zagora, C-43/24, ECLI:EU:C:2026:183.
at: (English version) to the Commission Raquel García Hermida-Van Der Walle (Renew) (12 March 2026) Subject: Continued discrimination and legal uncertainty as a result of the non-implementation of CJEU rulings Over the past few years, the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) has issued landmark judgments in the areas of freedom of movement and family life (1), legal recognition of transgender identity (2), and the protection of the human dignity of LGBTIQ+ people (3). However, Member States have often not implemented the necessary changes in national legislation. As a consequence, LGBTIQ+ people’s fundamental rights are still being violated in some Member States. Now, the CJEU has ruled on the principle of legal gender recognition for people exercising their freedom of movement in the EU (4). 1. Does the Commission agree that its role as Guardian of the Treaties requires taking action against Member States that breach EU law and do not ensure judgments are implemented effectively and promptly, rather than merely ‘monitoring the situation’ in such cases? If so, can the Commission explain why the court rulings in footnotes 1, 2 and 3 have not been fully implemented yet? 2. Can the Commission provide an overview of the correspondence between the Commission and relevant Member State(s) for each of the court cases? 3. If the latest ruling is not directly implemented in the Member States, will the Commission show less hesitation and commit to directly and fully enforcing this CJEU ruling rather than only taking selective action? (3 June 2026) As established by the case-law of the Court of Justice, it is for the national courts in the national procedure that gave rise to the preliminary ruling to apply the interpretation of the Court of Justice. In the context of preliminary rulings, there is no formal correspondence comparable to Article 260 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union between the Commission and the Member States whose national court raised the question. As noted in the LGBTIQ+ (1) Strategy 2026-2030 (2), EU free movement law, particularly Directive 2004/38/EC (3) together with fundamental rights under the Charter of Fundamental Rights (4), upholds the right of all EU citizens and their family members, including same-sex spouses and partners and their children, to move and reside freely within the EU. The Commission, as guardian of the Treaties, is committed to ensuring the proper application of EU law, including EU free movement rules and relevant judgments of the Court of Justice. In addition, the Commission not only monitors the individual Member State’s compliance with the judgment but also ensures that all other Member States equally apply the standard set by the Court of Justice (5).

E-10-2026-001044.t: How does the Council ensure that, in its external dealings, the Commission does not adopt positions that fall within the Council’s exclusive competence under the CFSP?
qt: to the Council Marieke Ehlers (PfE), Mieke Andriese (PfE) Subject:

Articles 21 and 22 TEU provide that it is for the Council to define the strategic interests and objectives of the Union’s external action. Under the Common Foreign and Security Policy, implementation and external representation are, in principle, the responsibility of the VP/HR (Article 27 TEU), whilst, under Article 17 TEU, the Commission President represents the Commission in matters falling within her own competences, such as trade, development cooperation and humanitarian aid. In practice, however, there appears to be an increasingly frequent overlap or lack of clarity in the division of roles, particularly in the context of the socalled ‘Team Europe’ approach, whereby the Commission President also adopts external political positions vis-à-vis third countries. 1.

How does the Council interpret the division of competences under the Treaty between the Commission President and the VP/HR, on the one hand, and the European Council, on the other, with regard to public or diplomatic positions vis-à-vis third countries?
How does the Council ensure that the Commission President does not, in external dealings, adopt positions that fall within the Council’s exclusive competence under the CFSP?
To what extent does the ‘Team Europe’ approach influence the practical division of roles between the Commission President, the VP/HR and the Council when it comes to the Union’s external action?
at: The division of competences between the EU institutions is enshrined in the Treaties. In respect of CFSP, Article 24 TEU clearly prescribes that “the common foreign and security policy is subject to specific rules and procedures”. On the one hand, it is for the European Council to define the general political direction and priorities of the Union and for the Council to define the policy of the Union vis-à-vis third countries and international organisations. Specifically, the European Council shall provide the Union with the necessary impetus for its development and shall define the general political directions and priorities thereof (Article 15(1) TEU), while the Council shall carry out policymaking and coordinating functions (Article 16(1) TEU). Specifically regarding common foreign and security policy, this shall be defined and implemented by the European Council and the Council (Article 24(1), second subparagraph TEU, and further elaborated in Articles 26 and 29 TEU). On the other hand, it is for the Commission to ensure the external representation of the Union (Article 17(1) TEU) vis-à-vis third countries, with the exception of common foreign and security policy, for which Article 27(2) TEU provides that the High Representative shall represent the Union, and other cases provided for in the Treaties. In the exercise of their powers, the EU institutions are bound by Article 13(2) TEU. Under that provision, each EU institution is to act within the limits of the powers conferred on it by the Treaties, and in conformity with the procedures, conditions and objectives set out in them. That provision reflects the principle of institutional balance, characteristic of the institutional structure of the European Union, a principle which requires that each of the institutions must exercise its powers with due regard for the powers of the other institutions. Once a position on a foreign policy matter has been agreed in the Council, all Member States and institutional actors are bound to uphold and defend this position on the international scene.

qt: to the Commission Katri Kulmuni (Renew) Subject:

The EU Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation1 entered into force in February 2025, and its implementation with regard to food-contact packaging will start in August 2026 – for example, the restriction on per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), the conformity assessment procedure, and later requirements for recyclability, re-use and bans. However, there is no guidance on the methodology for determining possible PFAS in food-contact packaging, nor the scope and details of the conformity assessment. Without clear guidance and methodologies, it is difficult for businesses to prepare for the change, carry out their basic activities and boost competitiveness, which the Commission also aims to strengthen in Europe. In addition, some definitions, such as the ‘producer’ for transport packaging, will become available in the middle of the reporting year, in August 2026. Change during the year risks the accuracy of 2026 reporting on transport packaging. I would like to ask: 1.

When is the Commission planning to publish a Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation notice document, which was first mentioned in December 2024? After almost 15 months, the guidance is yet to be published and the first part of the implementation will start in less than six months.
In addition, has the Commission considered delaying the change of producer responsibility for transport packaging until at least the beginning of 2027, to ensure a smoother transition?

Regulation (EU) 2025/40 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 19 December 2024 on packaging and packaging waste, amending Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 and Directive (EU) 2019/904, and repealing Directive 94/62/EC (OJ L, 2025/40, 22.1.2025, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2025/40/oj).
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (7.5.2026) The Commission published the guidance document1 on the Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (PPWR)2 on 30 March 2026. The aim is to provide clarity to stakeholders ahead of the first implementation milestones. The possibility of allowing Member States to apply a transitional approach until at least the beginning of 2027 regarding the producer responsibility was examined by the Commission in cooperation with the responsible Member States’ committee on waste. The PPWR is directly applicable in Member States by 12 August 2026. However, in terms of extended producer responsibility, national implementing measures will be needed. In this context, the Member States have a margin of appreciation to take measures that accommodate for national circumstances in the implementation of the PPWR.

ppwr_en. 2 Regulation (EU) 2025/40 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 19 December 2024 on packaging and packaging waste, amending Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 and Directive (EU) 2019/904, and repealing Directive 94/62/EC, OJ L, 2025/40, 22.1.2025.

E-10-2026-001041.t: Independence of the AIReF in Spain and compliance with EU law
qt: to the Commission Dolors Montserrat (PPE) Subject:

Spain’s Independent Authority for Fiscal Responsibility (AIReF) was established in compliance with the obligations stemming from the Union’s economic governance framework and, in particular, from Directive 2011/85/EU, which requires the establishment of independent fiscal institutions tasked with monitoring compliance with budgetary rules. The Spanish Government has recently proposed a senior official in the Ministry of Finance to chair the AIReF. This has sparked public and parliamentary debate on preserving the AIReF’s independence, given that it is responsible for overseeing the government’s own fiscal policy. In the light of the foregoing: 1.

Does the Commission take the view that the procedure for appointing the AIReF chair, and the professional profile of the person proposed, are fully in line with the requirements for institutional independence provided for in Directive 2011/85/EU and the EU’s fiscal governance framework?

If the independence of the national fiscal institution were to be compromised, what tools does the Commission have to assess the situation and, if necessary, take action under the European Semester or through other mechanisms provided for in EU law?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (19.5.2026) The Commission does not comment on individual appointment procedures or candidates for membership in the board of independent fiscal institutions (IFIs). The relevant EU legislation (Article 8(a)(3) of Council Directive 2011/85/EU1 as amended by Council Directive (EU) 2024/12652) states that ‘Independent fiscal institutions shall be composed of members nominated and appointed on the basis of their experience and competence in public finances, macroeconomics or budgetary management, and by means of transparent procedures’. The Commission is in the process of assessing the national provisions transposing the amended provisions under Council Directive (EU) 2024/1265, including provisions covering independence safeguards. While the transposition deadline for Member States for the amending Directive was 31 December 2025, several Member States did not yet submit information detailing what transposition measures have been taken. The assessment will be based on formally submitted information from every Member State. The implementation of transposed provisions in practice is equally important. To safeguard the IFIs’ independence in practical terms, it is primarily the task of national actors (public authorities, elected representatives and the judiciary) to ensure a correct application of national law. The Commission follows the national debates and keeps contact with IFIs. In case of a systematic failure of national authorities to implement EU law, the Commission could take action under Article 258 of the Treaty3. In such instances, indications of measures, absence of measures, or practices of a Member State that are contrary to EU law are investigated by the Commission in cooperation with the Member State concerned in the context of an informal dialogue or an infringement procedure.

1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2011/85/oj/eng. 2 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=OJ:L_202401265. 3 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/LexUriServ/LexUriServ.do?uri=CELEX:12012E/TXT:en:PDF.

E-10-2026-001040.t: Volatility of fertiliser prices and support to European farmers in light of recent geopolitical developments
qt: to the Commission Emmanouil Kefalogiannis (PPE) Subject:

Recent geopolitical developments in the Middle East are affecting global energy markets and have led to new volatility in fertiliser prices. The price of urea recently reached USD 583.50 per metric tonne, the highest since 2022. Meanwhile, the price of ammonia imported into north-western Europe has reached a three-year high due to the increase in gas prices. Strong price volatility may significantly increase production costs for European farmers, at a time when they are already facing increased input prices and heightened geopolitical uncertainty. Farmers’ organisations have warned that persistent price volatility could undermine production and food security in the EU. 1.
How does the Commission intend to address the effects of fertiliser price volatility on European farmers?

Is the Commission considering adopting measures to ensure the availability and affordability of fertilisers for EU farmers, including possible adjustments to trade measures or targeted market support mechanisms?
What measures does the Commission intend to take to strengthen the EU’s strategic resilience and reduce its dependence on external fertiliser inputs in the medium to long term?
at: (English version) to the Commission Emmanouil Kefalogiannis (PPE) (12 March 2026) Subject: Volatility of fertiliser prices and support to European farmers in light of recent geopolitical developments Recent geopolitical developments in the Middle East are affecting global energy markets and have led to new volatility in fertiliser prices. The price of urea recently reached USD 583.50 per metric tonne, the highest since 2022. Meanwhile, the price of ammonia imported into north-western Europe has reached a three-year high due to the increase in gas prices. Strong price volatility may significantly increase production costs for European farmers, at a time when they are already facing increased input prices and heightened geopolitical uncertainty. Farmers’ organisations have warned that persistent price volatility could undermine production and food security in the EU. 1.
How does the Commission intend to address the effects of fertiliser price volatility on European farmers?

2. Is the Commission considering adopting measures to ensure the availability and affordability of fertilisers for EU farmers, including possible adjustments to trade measures or targeted market support mechanisms? 3. What measures does the Commission intend to take to strengthen the EU’s strategic resilience and reduce its dependence on external fertiliser inputs in the medium to long term? (10 June 2026) The Commission is closely monitoring developments in the Strait of Hormuz and their impact on fertiliser markets through the EU Fertiliser Market Observatory (1). While no immediate physical shortages of nitrogen fertilisers are expected in the EU, notably due to limited direct import exposure to the Gulf region and sufficient stock levels, recent geopolitical developments have increased global price volatility, which is already affecting EU fertiliser prices. To mitigate these pressures, the Commission has already taken targeted measures, including a reduced 1% Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) default value mark up for fertilisers and proposed the suspension of customs tariffs within quotas for ammonia, urea and other nitrogen fertilisers to support both farmers and the EU fertiliser industry. The Commission has also recently adopted a state aid Framework on the Middle Eas t (2) to support both farmers and energy intensive industries affected by the current situation. On 19 May 2026, the Commission adopted the Fertiliser Action Plan (3), setting out short- and long-term measures to improve fertiliser availability, affordability and resilience. Short term actions include mobilisation and possible reinforcement of the agricultural reserve, liquidity support under the Common Agricultural Policy, and flexibility for advance payments. Longer term measures focus on strengthening EU production capacity, supporting low carbon and circular fertilisers, promoting alternative nutrient sources, and reducing dependencies on imported energy and feedstocks.

E-10-2026-001039.t: Special report by the European Court of Auditors on international nuclear safety cooperation
qt: to the Commission Joachim Streit (Renew) Subject:

In its special report on international nuclear safety cooperation, the European Court of Auditors (ECA) found that while the EU was an important global player, the effectiveness of its measures was being hampered by the lack of a comprehensive strategy. In their reply, the Commission and the European External Action Service concede the need for improvement. 1.

Given the ECA’s finding that project monitoring is often focused on outputs rather than actual improvements in nuclear safety, what specific outcome indicators is the Commission thinking of using in future to ascertain whether EU-funded measures are actually delivering demonstrable improvements in nuclear safety?

What criteria is it thinking of applying in future to select projects in the area of international nuclear safety, and how is it making sure that nuclear safety risks are assigned greater weight than geopolitical or foreign policy interests, especially as certain measures might have been primarily driven by geopolitical considerations?

How is it planning on making sure in future that the cost burden of large-scale nuclear safety projects is split fairly and transparently between the EU and other international donors, particularly in view of the ECA finding that, in some cases, the EU shouldered a larger share of the financial burden than originally planned, in part replacing contributions from other international donors?
at: (English version) to the Commission Joachim Streit (Renew) (12 March 2026) Subject: Special report by the European Court of Auditors on international nuclear safety cooperation In its special report on international nuclear safety cooperation, the European Court of Auditors (ECA) found that while the EU was an important global player, the effectiveness of its measures was being hampered by the lack of a comprehensive strategy. In their reply, the Commission and the European External Action Service concede the need for improvement. 1. Given the ECA’s finding that project monitoring is often focused on outputs rather than actual improvements in nuclear safety, what specific outcome indicators is the Commission thinking of using in future to ascertain whether EU-funded measures are actually delivering demonstrable improvements in nuclear safety? 2. What criteria is it thinking of applying in future to select projects in the area of international nuclear safety, and how is it making sure that nuclear safety risks are assigned greater weight than geopolitical or foreign policy interests, especially as certain measures might have been primarily driven by geopolitical considerations? 3. How is it planning on making sure in future that the cost burden of large-scale nuclear safety projects is split fairly and transparently between the EU and other international donors, particularly in view of the ECA finding that, in some cases, the EU shouldered a larger share of the financial burden than originally planned, in part replacing contributions from other international donors? (30 April 2026) The Commission refers to its replies to recommendations 2 (a), 3 (c) and 4(c) of the Special report 08/2026 of the European Court of Auditors (1). The Multiannual Indicative Programme (2) for the European Instrument for International Nuclear Safety Cooperation (3) specifies that improvements in nuclear safety will be monitored and evaluated with performance indicators, including impact, implementation and project-specific indicators. At the design stage, the Commission checks those performance indicators for inclusion in the project’s results framework. Implementing partners report on a regular basis to the Commission on progress against indicators of the results framework during project implementation. The initial selection of cooperation proposals is informed by the assessment of criteria such as budget, duration, maturity, partnership track record, magnitude of nuclear safety risk, political priority, added value for EU policies, sustainability and urgency. Geopolitical or foreign policy interests are important and embedded in some of these criteria but are not the only ones. Each donor decides independently on the size and fairness of their contribution to multi-donor funds while all donors aim to ensure that the total of their contributions covers the full estimated project budget. However, when there is an expected shortfall in contributions from other international donors, the Commission may decide to contribute a larger share of the cost burden than originally planned due to urgency, priority, relevance for EU and to prevent additional nuclear safety risks and cost escalation linked to delayed project implementation.

European Court of Auditors, Special report 08/2026 ‘International nuclear safety cooperation — The Commission remains an important global player but lacks a comprehensive strategy and robust monitoring’, https://www.eca.europa.eu/en/publications?ref=SR-2026-08. https://international-partnerships.ec.europa.eu/document/download/7b5eaa6a-14df-4634-8677-18d51fc55c37_en?filename=insc-mip-2021-2027_en.pdf. E-10-2026-001038.t: Airport screening procedures for military personnel travelling on civil aircraft under the EU’s military mobility package
qt: to the Commission Mario Furore (The Left), Danilo Della Valle (The Left), Giuseppe Antoci (The Left) Subject:

The EU’s military mobility package addresses the strategic priority of stepping up cooperation on defence and facilitating the movement of military personnel and assets throughout the Union, including in the context of cooperation with NATO. It means that military personnel are able to travel on civil aircraft and transit through commercial airport infrastructure. However, reports have been circulating about the airport screening procedures applied to uniformed military personnel transiting through civil airports in Europe; procedures include requests to remove items of uniform and checks performed in the presence of other passengers. Although airport security requirements must be met, such practices may raise questions of proportionality and respect for the dignity and privacy of the personnel concerned. In light of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Will the transit of uniformed military personnel on civil aircraft fall within the scope of the EU’s military mobility policies?
Are there EU-wide guidelines or provisions on airport screening procedures for military personnel travelling on civil infrastructure?
Will the Commission team up with Member States and airport authorities to put forward common guidance to ensure proportionate checks that uphold the dignity of military personnel?
at: (English version) to the Commission Mario Furore (The Left), Danilo Della Valle (The Left), Giuseppe Antoci (The Left) (12 March 2026) Subject: Airport screening procedures for military personnel travelling on civil aircraft under the EU’s military mobility package The EU’s military mobility package addresses the strategic priority of stepping up cooperation on defence and facilitating the movement of military personnel and assets throughout the Union, including in the context of cooperation with NATO. It means that military personnel are able to travel on civil aircraft and transit through commercial airport infrastructure. However, reports have been circulating about the airport screening procedures applied to uniformed military personnel transiting through civil airports in Europe; procedures include requests to remove items of uniform and checks performed in the presence of other passengers. Although airport security requirements must be met, such practices may raise questions of proportionality and respect for the dignity and privacy of the personnel concerned. In light of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Will the transit of uniformed military personnel on civil aircraft fall within the scope of the EU’s military mobility policies?
Are there EU-wide guidelines or provisions on airport screening procedures for military personnel travelling on civil infrastructure?
Will the Commission team up with Member States and airport authorities to put forward common guidance to ensure proportionate checks that uphold the dignity of military personnel?

(22 May 2026) The Commission notes that the Military Mobility Package (1) adopted in November 2025 stands as a comprehensive set of measures to ensure the swift, coordinated and secure movement of military personnel and equipment across the EU. The Package includes a regulation proposal (2) aiming to strengthen Europe's defence readiness by addressing barriers to military mobility across transport regulatory, infrastructure, and capability dimensions-critical areas that currently hinder military transport across borders. The Commission takes note of the issues raised concerning airport screening procedures for military personnel travelling via civil infrastructure. However, these issues do not fall within the scope of the current legal provisions under the regulation proposal, since these do not include measures relating to security screening practices at airports. Provisions on civil aviation security such as those in Regulation (EC) 300/2008 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 11 March 2008 on common rules in the field of civil aviation security and repealing Regulation (EC) No 2320/2002 (3) stand as common rules to protect civil aviation against acts of unlawful interference that jeopardise the security of civil aviation. Consequently, the Commission does not foresee, in the context of the measures laid down in the broader Military Mobility Package, the development of additional common guidance in this area. Any such considerations would fall outside the scope of the current envisaged measures and legislative proposal.

qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Marit Maij (S&D), Saskia Bricmont (Verts/ALE), Mélissa Camara (Verts/ALE), Matjaž Nemec (S&D), Marta Temido (S&D), Marie Toussaint (Verts/ALE), Francisco Assis (S&D), Hana Jalloul Muro (S&D), Hannes Heide (S&D), Elio Di Rupo (S&D), Andreas Schieder (S&D), Tineke Strik (Verts/ALE), Erik Marquardt (Verts/ALE), Charles Goerens (Renew) Subject:

Since the capture of El Fasher in October 2025 by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), violence and human suffering in Sudan have escalated. As mass killings, systematic sexual violence and ethnically targeted attacks continue to shape everyday life, MEPs addressed the VicePresident of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy (VP/HR), calling for an inquiry into the RSF’s actions as constituting to genocidal acts. In her response, the VP/HR states that the actions of all parties to the conflict are closely monitored. This response is fundamentally inadequate given human rights organisations’ warnings of genocidal acts and the United States’ conclusion that members of the RSF and allied militias have committed genocide. There can be no delay for the people of Sudan; the Council must urgently trigger the procedure to evaluate whether the RSF fulfils the criteria for inclusion on the EU’s restrictive ‘terrorist list’, as called for by Parliament in its resolution of 25 November 20251. In view of this: 1.

Beyond sanctions on individuals involved with the RSF, does the Commission acknowledge that the RSF’s systemic killings call for a critical assessment as to whether they meet the EU’s criteria for it to be classed as a terrorist organisation?
In addition, will the VP/HR address this at the first upcoming Council of Foreign Affairs meeting on 16 March 2026?
Texts adopted, P10_TA(2025)0310 (https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/TA-10-20250310_EN.html).
at: (English version) to the Vice-President of the Commission/High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Marit Maij (S&D), Saskia Bricmont (Verts/ALE), Mélissa Camara (Verts/ALE), Matjaž Nemec (S&D), Marta Temido (S&D), Marie Toussaint (Verts/ALE), Francisco Assis (S&D), Hana Jalloul Muro (S&D), Hannes Heide (S&D), Elio Di Rupo (S&D), Andreas Schieder (S&D), Tineke Strik (Verts/ALE), Erik Marquardt (Verts/ALE), Charles Goerens (Renew) (12 March 2026) Subject: Situation in Sudan Since the capture of El Fasher in October 2025 by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), violence and human suffering in Sudan have escalated. As mass killings, systematic sexual violence and ethnically targeted attacks continue to shape everyday life, MEPs addressed the Vice-President of the Commission/High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy (VP/HR), calling for an inquiry into the RSF’s actions as constituting to genocidal acts. In her response, the VP/HR states that the actions of all parties to the conflict are closely monitored. This response is fundamentally inadequate given human rights organisations’ warnings of genocidal acts and the United States’ conclusion that members of the RSF and allied militias have committed genocide. There can be no delay for the people of Sudan; the Council must urgently trigger the procedure to evaluate whether the RSF fulfils the criteria for inclusion on the EU’s restrictive ‘terrorist list’, as called for by Parliament in its resolution of 25 November 2025 (1). In view of this: 1.

Beyond sanctions on individuals involved with the RSF, does the Commission acknowledge that the RSF’s systemic killings call for a critical assessment as to whether they meet the EU’s criteria for it to be classed as a terrorist organisation?
In addition, will the VP/HR address this at the first upcoming Council of Foreign Affairs meeting on 16 March 2026?

(30 April 2026) The EU condemned the atrocities perpetrated by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in Sudan, following the seizure of El Fasher. The EU Foreign Affairs Council adopted restrictive measures against the Deputy Commander of the RSF on 20 November 2025 and sanctioned another five RSF affiliated individuals on 29 January 2026 (1). Ensuring accountability is at the heart of the Council Conclusions on Sudan (2). The EU supports the International Criminal Court (ICC), the UN Independent International Fact-Finding Mission and their investigations of crimes including those committed by the RSF in El Fasher. The ICC recognised that war crimes and crimes against humanity have been and are continuing to be committed in Darfur (3). On 19 February 2026, the UN Fact Finding Mission published its report ‘Sudan Hallmarks of Genocide in El Fasher’ on the siege and fall of the city. On EU restrictive measures to combat terrorism, in accordance with Article 2(2) and (3) of Council Decision (CFSP) 2026/455 (4), the legal prerequisite for the listing of new entity is a competent authority decision for the involvement of that entity in terrorist acts, as defined by Article 1 of Council Decision (CFSP) 2026/455. Listing decisions are adopted by the Council, acting unanimously. The EU action should focus on those who suffered through El Fasher, to support their pursuit of justice and accountability, and to prevent perpetrators to repeat these crimes elsewhere in Sudan. E-10-2026-001035.t: Landslide emergency in Niscemi and European hydrogeological risk prevention instruments
qt: to the Commission Giuseppe Antoci (The Left) Subject:

The inertia surrounding the updating of the flood hazard maps and the implementation of risk prevention tools by the Sicilian Regional Government has already been raised in written question E-002993/20241 and corresponding answer of 21.2.20242. In January 2026, Niscemi was hit by a landslide event that left a 4-kilometre-long scar and subsidence several metres in depth. The 2024 ISPRA report3 highlights the urgent need for preventive action and the landslides in Niscemi in 1997 and 2026 are concrete proof of this. Council Decision (EU) 2019/4204 aims to strengthen Europe’s collective capacity to respond to natural disasters and to improve the effectiveness of systems for preventing, preparing for and responding to natural disasters in the EU. In the light of the above: 1.

Does the Commission feel it would be appropriate to activate the rescEU programme to furnish additional resources in response to the crisis in order to protect the citizens of Niscemi and Sicily from further similar disasters?

Would it not consider it appropriate to provide assistance, through the Technical Support Instrument, in order to strengthen local administrative capacities for the planning of risk mitigation measures?

Submitted on 17.2.2024. https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/E-10-2024-002993-ASW_EN.html Istituto Superiore per la Protezione e la Ricerca Ambientale (Higher Institute for Environmental Protection and Research), showing that 94.5 % of Italian municipalities are at risk of landslides/floods. Council Decision (EU) 2019/420 amending Decision 2009/2013/EU.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.6.2026) The Decision1 establishing the Union Civil Protection Mechanism recognises the primary responsibility of Member States for preventing, preparing for and responding to natural and man-made disasters and therefore Article 15(1) stipulates that when a disaster occurs within the EU, or is imminent, the affected Member State may request assistance through the Emergency Response Coordination Centre2. A request for assistance has not been received for the landslide in Niscemi, so the Commission cannot provide a qualitative or quantitative assessment of the question at hand. The Technical Support Instrument (TSI)3 aims to support Member States’ efforts to strengthen their institutional and administrative capacity, including at regional and local level. According to the TSI Regulation4, one objective of the instrument is to assist national authorities in improving their capacity to design, develop and implement reforms. In particular, the TSI can be used to support policies for the mitigation of climate change, the environmental pillar of sustainable development and environmental protection, and for soil protection5. The provision of support via the TSI should be initiated by a request submitted by the Member State, following a call for requests open by the Commission. In line with Article 3 of the TSI Regulation, technical support is provided to effectively address the challenges identified in the country-specific recommendations and to implement EU law.

qt: to the Commission Dan-Ştefan Motreanu (PPE) Subject:

In a recent technical brief, the World Health Organization (WHO) Regional Office for Europe warned that insufficient and inadequately skilled nursing staff are jeopardising patient safety and accelerating burnout across European healthcare systems. According to the WHO Regional Office for Europe, staff shortages, rising care demands and increasing mental health strain are creating a ‘ticking timebomb’, with a projected shortfall of nearly one million healthcare professionals in Europe by 2030. Nurses represent 56 % of the health workforce, yet inadequate nurse-to-patient ratios and poor workforce planning are heightening clinical risks and driving professionals out of the sector. The WHO calls for nursing care to be treated as safety-critical, alongside improved staffing standards, better management of care complexity and greater use of digital tools to reduce administrative burdens. Given that health workforce resilience is essential to the functioning of national health systems and to EU health security more broadly, what actions does the Commission intend to take, within its competences, to support Member States in addressing nursing shortages, promoting safe staffing standards and improving retention and working conditions across the EU?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (26.5.2026) Nurse shortages and more broadly health workforce shortages are an important challenge, requiring action in line with the division of competences in the EU. According to Article 168(7) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU1, Member States are responsible for the management of health services, which includes ensuring adequate staffing levels. The Commission supports Member States in addressing health workforce challenges, including those related to nurses, notably through knowledge sharing and technical assistance. For example, the EU4Health Programme funds initiatives addressing workforce challenges2, including the Nursing Action3 implemented in partnership with World Health Organization/Europe, which supports countries in developing effective recruitment and retention strategies. The technical brief4 referred to by the Honourable Members is a deliverable of this EU action, highlighting participating countries’ experiences. This work also adds to that of the Commission’s Expert Group on Health Systems Performance Assessment (HSPA)5. The group has mapped approaches to safe staffing levels across all health professions, including but not only nurses, and is foreseen to publish a report to further support the exchange of experiences. To facilitate mobility across the EU, the Professional Qualifications Directive6 sets out the rules on recognition of professional qualifications obtained in the EU and harmonises minimum training requirements for nurses responsible for general care. The upcoming Skills Portability Initiative7 aims at modernising and speeding up the processes for EU citizens and introducing common rules on recognition to attract talent from third countries8.

qt: to the Commission Dan-Ştefan Motreanu (PPE) Subject:

In a special report, the European Court of Auditors delivered a lukewarm assessment of Europe’s Beating Cancer Plan, launched in 2021 with a EUR 4 billion budget. While the plan has encouraged several Member States to adopt or update national cancer strategies and has supported initiatives such as the European Cancer Imaging Initiative, auditors identified significant shortcomings. They highlighted duplication of projects, insufficient Member State ownership, uneven screening rates across the EU, and weaknesses in design, including the absence of quantified targets, clear deadlines and consistent indicators. Concerns were also raised about the sustainability of certain flagship projects and future funding beyond 2027, especially following cuts to the EU4Health programme. Given these findings, how does the Commission intend to strengthen governance, eliminate duplication, introduce measurable targets and secure sustainable financing to ensure that Europe’s Beating Cancer Plan delivers tangible and lasting results after 2027?
at: (English version) to the Commission Dan-Ştefan Motreanu (PPE) (11 March 2026) Subject: Europe’s Beating Cancer Plan In a special report, the European Court of Auditors delivered a lukewarm assessment of Europe’s Beating Cancer Plan, launched in 2021 with a EUR 4 billion budget. While the plan has encouraged several Member States to adopt or update national cancer strategies and has supported initiatives such as the European Cancer Imaging Initiative, auditors identified significant shortcomings. They highlighted duplication of projects, insufficient Member State ownership, uneven screening rates across the EU, and weaknesses in design, including the absence of quantified targets, clear deadlines and consistent indicators. Concerns were also raised about the sustainability of certain flagship projects and future funding beyond 2027, especially following cuts to the EU4Health programme. Given these findings, how does the Commission intend to strengthen governance, eliminate duplication, introduce measurable targets and secure sustainable financing to ensure that Europe’s Beating Cancer Plan delivers tangible and lasting results after 2027? (7 May 2026) The Commission took note of the Court of Auditors’ Special Report, which was prepared with the full collaboration of the Commission. The identified shortcomings were raised as potential risks, rather than instances of inefficient use of funds. The finding of persisting inequalities among Member States, for example in cancer screening, is in line with the analyses from the Cancer Inequalities Registry (1). These results underline the importance of the Commission’s commitment to tackle inequalities in a cross-cutting manner, as is done through numerous Cancer Plan actions (2), (3), (4) which will need more time to evolve and show impact. The Commission has accepted the recommendations from the report to mitigate the identified risks and is currently working on follow-up actions. The Commission is continuously investing in efforts to ensure complementarity and sustainability of Cancer Plan actions and is committed to strengthening these efforts. Discussions on how to improve the governance of the Cancer Plan are ongoing with Member States. In terms of funding, the Commission cannot make any commitments going beyond the current Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF), while negotiations between the co-legislators on the next MFF are still ongoing. As the report notes, due to the complexity and varied nature of the Cancer Plan actions, there is no single end date or unified timeline. The Commission regularly publishes an Implementation Roadmap to track milestones and key deliverables for all actions. The report also acknowledged that the 2025 review (5) improved transparency on progress. The Commission is also working to establish a Cancer Plan-wide monitoring framework by the end of 2027 and will seek to evaluate the results and impact of the actions by 2030.

E-10-2026-001031.t: The EU’s dependence on seafood imports
qt: to the Commission Dan-Ştefan Motreanu (PPE) Subject:

A study commissioned by Parliament’s Committee on Fisheries shows that the EU’s dependence on seafood imports is growing. In 2022, the EU’s self-sufficiency rate stood at just 37.5 %, falling to 14.2 % when exports are excluded, meaning that more than 80 % of seafood consumed in the EU is imported. The situation varies significantly by species: self-sufficiency is only 29 % for tuna, around 20 % for groundfish such as cod and hake (with landings down 43 % since 2020) and about 12 % for shellfish. Almost all the salmon consumed in the EU is imported, while aquaculture production within the EU remains stagnant due to high energy and labour costs, regulatory complexity and limited access to sites. This growing reliance on imports raises concerns about food security, strategic autonomy, sustainability standards and the competitiveness of EU producers facing lower-cost international competition. In this context, what measures does the Commission plan to take to increase the EU’s selfsufficiency in seafood, strengthen European aquaculture and fisheries production and ensure that imported products meet equivalent sustainability and social standards?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.5.2026) In 2025, the EU’s aquatic food self-sufficiency rose to 38.1%, the first increase since 20181. The Commission works to increase food security. First, with sound fisheries management in EU waters to boost biomass and healthy marine ecosystems, optimising domestic fisheries, though the resource is finite and improvements are fragile. Second, maintaining fishing rights in third countries via Sustainable Fisheries Partnership Agreements and participation in Regional Fisheries Management Organisations. Third, and most importantly, promoting the sustainable development of EU aquaculture through a framework based on the Commission’s strategic guidelines for a more sustainable and competitive EU aquaculture2 and Member States’ multiannual national strategic plans for aquaculture. The Commission supports Member States in implementing these plans and in applying the Commission’s Strategic Guidelines, through guidance, funding and the exchange of good practices. Progress depends on effective implementation by Member States, in particular in areas such as licensing and access to space and water, which remain primarily under their competence3. Regarding imports, EU Free Trade Agreements typically include sustainability provisions, including on international labour standards, while the World Trade Organisation Agreement on Fisheries Subsidies curbs harmful subsidies. The Commission is also exploring sustainability criteria for the Autonomous Tariff Quota regime for fisheries products. Ongoing evaluations, including the Regulation on the Common Fisheries Policy4, Vision 2040 for fisheries and aquaculture5, and the EU Strategy for Fisheries External Action, integrate these efforts.

On the eve of the informal EU leaders’ retreat at Alden Biesen meeting, more than 500 European business leaders representing 1 300 companies warned that EU industry faces an existential crisis. At the European Industry Summit in Antwerp, they called on Member States and EU institutions to take urgent action to restore competitiveness, accelerate decarbonisation and prevent further industrial decline. Industry leaders highlighted electricity prices far above those in China and the United States, excessive administrative burdens and unfair global competition. They called for ‘intelligent regulation’, faster permitting, better access to finance, stronger trade defence instruments and carbon leakage protection. The ‘Antwerp Declaration’ also urged support for fair trade agreements securing raw materials and market access and promoted the idea of a ‘European preference’ in public procurement, to stimulate demand for low-carbon and circular products made in Europe. Commission President Ursula von der Leyen referred to a forthcoming reform of the Emissions Trading System (ETS), greater use of ETS revenues for industry and possible EUorigin content requirements under a proposed Industrial Accelerator Act1. However, concrete mechanisms, timelines and safeguards remain unclear. What specific legislative and financial measures does the Commission intend to propose to ensure the survival, competitiveness and decarbonisation of European industry in the short to medium term?

qt: to the Commission Dan-Ştefan Motreanu (PPE) Subject:

Energy-intensive industries across the European Union have warned that persistently high electricity prices are undermining both industrial competitiveness and the viability of electrification efforts. In a joint statement issued on 5 February 2026, an alliance of 13 major industrial players stressed that electricity costs in the EU remain significantly above levels that would enable companies to invest confidently in electrified production processes. The alliance argues that the forthcoming EU Electrification Action Plan should prioritise restoring competitive electricity prices rather than setting binding electrification targets. It supports a reference price of EUR 50/MWh, aligned with the State aid framework supporting the Clean Industrial Deal, as the maximum total electricity cost for industry. According to the signatories, the plan’s success should be measured by its ability to bring industrial power prices closer to this threshold. Given that sustained high electricity prices risk delaying industrial decarbonisation, discouraging investment and accelerating deindustrialisation, what measures does the Commission intend to take in the upcoming Electrification Action Plan to ensure that industrial electricity prices converge towards the EUR 50/MWh reference level?
at: (English version) to the Commission Dan-Ştefan Motreanu (PPE) (11 March 2026) Subject: Electricity prices Energy-intensive industries across the European Union have warned that persistently high electricity prices are undermining both industrial competitiveness and the viability of electrification efforts. In a joint statement issued on 5 February 2026, an alliance of 13 major industrial players stressed that electricity costs in the EU remain significantly above levels that would enable companies to invest confidently in electrified production processes. The alliance argues that the forthcoming EU Electrification Action Plan should prioritise restoring competitive electricity prices rather than setting binding electrification targets. It supports a reference price of EUR 50/MWh, aligned with the state aid framework supporting the Clean Industrial Deal, as the maximum total electricity cost for industry. According to the signatories, the plan’s success should be measured by its ability to bring industrial power prices closer to this threshold. Given that sustained high electricity prices risk delaying industrial decarbonisation, discouraging investment and accelerating deindustrialisation, what measures does the Commission intend to take in the upcoming Electrification Action Plan to ensure that industrial electricity prices converge towards the EUR 50/MWh reference level? (12 June 2026) The relationship between prices paid for electricity and for natural gas is a key factor influencing electrification investment decisions by industry. These prices are the results of four components: energy costs, infrastructure charges, taxes and levies, as well as carbon costs. Member States can influence all of these variables, for instance by accelerating renewable energy investments or by modifying the tax regime in favour of electricity. The Commission has committed to adopt a legal proposal on network charges and taxation, ensuring inter alia, electricity is taxed less than gas. Member States can also make use of state aid to reduce the electricity costs of certain industries. The Clean Industrial Deal State Aid Framework (1) includes the possibility of adopting temporary electricity price reliefs for energy-intensive users, with certain conditions. To support the decarbonisation of industrial heat, the Commission launched in 2025 an EUR 1 billion auction under the Innovation Fund, which serves as pilot for the upcoming Industrial Decarbonisation Bank. The auction attracted 85 bids, amounting to EUR 1.4 billion of funding requested. In the upcoming Electrification Action Plan, the Commission will put forward a set of actions to accelerate the electrification of the EU energy system. The action plan will, inter alia, set an electrification target and measures to accelerate the uptake of electrification solutions.

qt: to the Commission Dan-Ştefan Motreanu (PPE) Subject:

A recent report by the European Court of Auditors (ECA) warns that the EU is unlikely to secure a stable supply of critical raw materials by 2030, despite the adoption of the Critical Raw Materials Act in 2024. According to the ECA, EU efforts to diversify imports have produced limited tangible results, domestic extraction faces persistent obstacles and recycling remains in its early stages. Of the 26 materials needed for the energy transition, the EU is fully dependent on imports for 10. In a small number of third countries, supply chains remain highly concentrated, exceeding the 65 % dependency threshold set for 2030. Although 14 strategic partnerships have been signed, imports from partner countries decreased in many cases between 2020 and 2024. Recycling targets also appear out of reach: several materials have recycling rates of below 5 % and many are not recycled at all. Meanwhile, mining projects can take up to 20 years to become operational, casting doubt on the objective of achieving 10 % domestic extraction. In light of these findings, what additional measures does the Commission intend to propose to ensure that the 2030 targets on diversification, recycling and domestic extraction can be realistically achieved?
at: (English version) to the Commission Dan-Ştefan Motreanu (PPE) (11 March 2026) Subject: Critical raw materials A recent report by the European Court of Auditors (ECA) warns that the EU is unlikely to secure a stable supply of critical raw materials by 2030, despite the adoption of the Critical Raw Materials Act in 2024. According to the ECA, EU efforts to diversify imports have produced limited tangible results, domestic extraction faces persistent obstacles and recycling remains in its early stages. Of the 26 materials needed for the energy transition, the EU is fully dependent on imports for 10. In a small number of third countries, supply chains remain highly concentrated, exceeding the 65% dependency threshold set for 2030. Although 14 strategic partnerships have been signed, imports from partner countries decreased in many cases between 2020 and 2024. Recycling targets also appear out of reach: several materials have recycling rates of below 5% and many are not recycled at all. Meanwhile, mining projects can take up to 20 years to become operational, casting doubt on the objective of achieving 10% domestic extraction. In light of these findings, what additional measures does the Commission intend to propose to ensure that the 2030 targets on diversification, recycling and domestic extraction can be realistically achieved? (2 June 2026) The Commission welcomed the observations of the European Court of Auditors (ECA), which recognised the growing strategic importance of critical raw materials and the progress achieved so far in developing an integrated policy response in this area. The Commission is actively addressing the challenges identified by the Court by accelerating the implementation of the Critical Raw Materials Act (1) (CRMA), which entered into force only two years ago, and through the RESourceEU Action Plan (2), which was not covered by the ECA’s analysis. Both the CRMA and the action plan will help achieving the ambitious benchmarks for extraction processing and recycling. The Commission is acting on permitting acceleration, strategic project designation, access to financing instruments and diversification partnerships. Together, these elements create the conditions for investment decisions and production to materialise. RESourceEU fast-tracks delivery of the EU raw materials strategy by directly supporting strategic projects in batteries, rare earths and defence value chains, with the objective to cut single-supplier dependencies by up to 50% by 2029. The EU, as part of Team Europe (3), is mobilising EUR 3 billion to support these value chains. So far, Team Europe has already committed EUR 1.5 billion in support for strategic projects. This includes equity, loans and grants, from the European Investment Bank, Member State and EU funds. The action plan also announces the establishment of a European CRMs Centre with the mandate to help securing access to CRMs for the European industry. Strategic partnerships with resource rich countries are designed to de-risk investment and projects along the value chain.

E-10-2026-001027.t: Developments in merger control and the competitiveness of European companies
qt: to the Commission Anne-Sophie Frigout (PfE), Antonín Staněk (PfE), Pierre Pimpie (PfE), Marion Maréchal (ECR), Nicolas Bay (ECR), Fernand Kartheiser (NI), Nikola Bartůšek (NI) Subject:

The Commission has added a policy debate on revising the merger control guidelines to the agenda for the meeting of the College of Commissioners on 18 March 20261. Against a backdrop of heightened international competition, many consider the EU framework overly restrictive. While it is essential to stamp out ‘killer acquisitions’, particularly by firms from outside the EU, a number of innovative start-ups, including digital start-ups, have voiced concerns about a possible tightening of the acquisition framework. A disproportionate and insufficiently predictable approach, based on purely speculative competition scenarios, could impinge on the exit prospects at the heart of the venture capital and private equity models on which these companies may be based. In light of this: 1.
How will the Commission strike a balance between preventing killer acquisitions and ensuring greater predictability and proportionality in merger control, particularly for innovative start-ups?

Does it intend to adjust certain parameters within the merger control framework, such as notification thresholds or the assessment criteria for non-horizontal mergers, in order to promote the growth and competitiveness of EU companies, particularly in strategic technology sectors?
https://www.contexte.com/medias/pdf/medias-documents/2026/2/lpp-17-fevrier.pdf.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (5.5.2026) The main goal of the Merger Guidelines revision is to modernise EU merger policy. Mergers can have positive and negative effects for the competitiveness of the EU economy. Through this revision the Commission will provide a clear and modern assessment framework so that companies, of all sizes, have the necessary predictability when engaging in mergers. Importantly, the revised Guidelines will include positive guidance on which acquisitions involving start-ups are pro-competitive and do not warrant intervention. This ‘innovation shield’ will provide predictability and legal certainty for smaller companies when considering exit strategies. The revised Guidelines will also include clear and concrete guidance on those rare acquisitions of nascent or small innovative companies that can instead stifle innovation and merit intervention. It is critical to prevent killer acquisitions. Therefore, the Commission supports Member States’ efforts to review such mergers and will consider appropriate referrals under Article 22 of the EU Merger Regulation referred by competent Member States. The Commission will not adjust the merger control notification thresholds since the EU Merger Regulation is not subject to review. The revised Merger Guidelines will instead provide updated guidance on the Commission’s assessment criteria for all mergers, including non-horizontal ones. The fundamental objective of merger control will not change: preventing harmful mergers that lead to too much market power in the hands of too few companies – harming innovation and growth. However, there will be new guidance on pro-competitive scale and a new framework to assess dynamic efficiencies that may be pertinent to mergers in strategic technology sectors.

E-10-2026-001026.t: ProtectEU and fundamental freedoms: clarifying ideological categories under EU counter-terrorism law
qt: to the Commission Marieke Ehlers (PfE) Subject:

In its communication of 26 February 2026 entitled ‘ProtectEU: Agenda to prevent and counter terrorism’1, the Commission identifies, alongside jihadism, factors such as ‘rejection of democratic values’, ‘anti-Muslim hatred’, ‘nihilism’ and ‘anti-system ideologies’ as emerging drivers of radicalisation. Given the broad and potentially interpretative nature of these concepts, and in the light of Articles 11 and 12 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, the Commission is asked: 1.

Are the terms mentioned in the communication defined in EU law or in operational counter-terror frameworks, and do they trigger specific monitoring, risk-assessment or funding priorities, and if so, how does the Commission legally differentiate between legitimate, protected criticism of Islam and actionable ‘anti-Muslim hatred’, ensuring counter-terrorism frameworks do not infringe upon freedom of speech?

How does the Commission ensure that analytical categories, such as ‘anti-system ideologies’ or ‘rejection of democratic values’, cannot extend to peaceful political opposition, institutional reform movements or Eurosceptic positions protected under EU law?

Does the Commission confirm that only conduct involving incitement to violence or terrorist activity – and not ideological or philosophical dissent as such – can fall within the scope of EU counter-terror measures, and what specific legal safeguards exist to prevent broad philosophical classifications, such as ‘nihilism’ or ‘anti-system ideologies’, from being misused to monitor or criminalise non-violent political dissent?
Commission communication of 26 February 2026 entitled ‘ProtectEU: Agenda to prevent and counter terrorism’ (COM(2026)0101).
at: (English version) to the Commission Marieke Ehlers (PfE) (11 March 2026) Subject: ProtectEU and fundamental freedoms: clarifying ideological categories under EU counter-terrorism law In its communication of 26 February 2026 entitled ‘ProtectEU: Agenda to prevent and counter terrorism’ (1), the Commission identifies, alongside jihadism, factors such as ‘rejection of democratic values’, ‘anti-Muslim hatred’, ‘nihilism’ and ‘antisystem ideologies’ as emerging drivers of radicalisation. Given the broad and potentially interpretative nature of these concepts, and in the light of Articles 11 and 12 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, the Commission is asked: 1.

Are the terms mentioned in the communication defined in EU law or in operational counter-terror frameworks, and do they trigger specific monitoring, risk-assessment or funding priorities, and if so, how does the Commission legally differentiate between legitimate, protected criticism of Islam and actionable ‘anti-Muslim hatred’, ensuring counterterrorism frameworks do not infringe upon freedom of speech?

How does the Commission ensure that analytical categories, such as ‘anti-system ideologies’ or ‘rejection of democratic values’, cannot extend to peaceful political opposition, institutional reform movements or Eurosceptic positions protected under EU law?

Does the Commission confirm that only conduct involving incitement to violence or terrorist activity — and not ideological or philosophical dissent as such — can fall within the scope of EU counter-terror measures, and what specific legal safeguards exist to prevent broad philosophical classifications, such as ‘nihilism’ or ‘anti-system ideologies’, from being misused to monitor or criminalise non-violent political dissent?

(3 June 2026) The ‘ProtectEU: Agenda to prevent and counter terrorism’ (1) is a non-legislative policy document. The terms used in this communication are analytical descriptors reflecting trends as outlined, among others, by the EU Agency for Law Enforcement Cooperation (2), observed in Member States and practitioners’ assessments as well as research stemming from the Knowledge Hub on Prevention of Radicalisation — these do not create new legal categories or offences. References to ‘anti-system ideologies’ or ‘rejection of democratic values’ concern narratives that legitimise violence or seek to replace democratic processes by violent or terrorist means. The Commission is committed to fighting anti-Muslim hatred as defined by the European Commission against Racism and Intolerance Recommendation (3). EU action is grounded in the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the EU (4) and applicable legislation. Expressions of opinion, including criticism of religions or public policies, are protected under Articles 11 and 12 of the Charter. Intervention is justified only where conduct meets the thresholds set by law, such as incitement to violence, terrorism, hatred or discrimination, as defined in relevant EU and national legislation. Directive (EU) 2017/54 on combating terrorism (5) defines terrorist offences and offences related to terrorist activities, including the public provocation to commit a terrorist offence.

E-10-2026-001025.t: Significantly more expensive biofuel for inland waterway transport
qt: to the Commission Bert-Jan Ruissen (ECR), Kris Van Dijck (ECR) Subject:

The inland waterway transport sector is crucial for smooth and more sustainable logistics. Transport by water produces fewer emissions per tonne of freight than road transport. The sector is aiming for a 40 to 50 % reduction in CO₂ emissions by 2030 and for zero emissions by 2050. For this reason, inland waterway transport will fall under the EU ETS2 system from 2028, in addition to RED III. Essential to the 2030 targets in particular is the availability and affordability of, among other things, HVO (hydrotreated vegetable oil). However, this fuel for inland waterway transport has become significantly more expensive in 2026, with prices reaching as high as EUR 1 400 per 1 000 litres – almost three times as expensive as conventional diesel. According to media reports123, this price hike, which is partly a consequence of the new RED III Directive and the discontinuation of BIDO tickets (which previously kept prices down for inland waterway transport), makes sustainable navigation using HVO less attractive. According to RTV Noord4, some businesses, such as the ferry service to the Wadden Islands in the Netherlands, are already reverting to fossil fuels. 1.
Does the Commission share the concern that efforts to make inland waterway transport more sustainable may stall in the short term due to this sharp rise in the price of biofuel?
If so, what solution does the Commission propose?

https://www.schuttevaer.nl/nieuws/actueel/2025/12/27/prijs-hvo-gaat-door-het-dak-in2026/#:~:text=Prijs%20HVO%20gaat%20door%20het%20dak%20in%202026%20%7C%20Schuttevaer.nl. https://binnenvaartkrant.nl/kbn-slaat-alarm-over-explosieve-stijging-prijs-hvo. https://pdve.nl/stijging-prijs-hvo-voor-binnenvaart/. https://www.rtvnoord.nl/economie/1372548/wagenborg-beperkt-gebruik-biodiesel-op-veerboten-vanwegeextreme-prijsstijging.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.6.2026) The Commission would like to recall that the provisions in Article 25 of Directive (EU) 2018/20011 (as amended) set targets for the uptake of renewable energy across the transport sector, aiming at reducing overall greenhouse gas emissions. To that regard, there are no specifications per individual transport mode and Member States have flexibility in how to achieve the objectives. Accordingly, it is for the Netherlands to decide within this framework, whether to allow for the cross-subsidisation of HVO (hydrotreated vegetable oil) supplies to certain sectors through schemes such as BIDO tickets. The Commission remains committed to support the decarbonisation of the transport sector. On 5 November 2025 it adopted the Sustainable Transport Investment Plan (STIP) (COM(2025) 664 final2), which aims to de-risk investments in the production of renewable and low-carbon fuels and to increase their availability for the aviation and waterborne sectors, including the inland navigation sector. Increased supply is expected to contribute to lower costs over time for all relevant sectors.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2018/2001/oj/eng. 2 https://ec.europa.eu/transparency/documents-register/detail?ref=COM(2025)664&lang=en.

E-10-2026-001024.t: Shortage of mooring berths in inland waterway transport
qt: to the Commission Bert-Jan Ruissen (ECR), Kris Van Dijck (ECR) Subject:

The inland waterway transport sector is crucial for smooth and more sustainable logistics. The EU has 51 000 kilometres of waterways across 25 Member States, on which some 100 to 150 billion tkm of freight is transported annually. The sector produces fewer emissions per tonne of freight than road transport. The Commission supports the sector by means of initiatives such as the NAIADES action plans. However, in several countries, including the Netherlands, Germany and Belgium, the sector is facing an acute shortage of suitable mooring berths1. This problem is partly caused by the fact that ships have become longer, whilst berths have reduced in number2. This makes it more difficult for skippers to comply with working and rest periods. In addition, mooring berths near industrial estates are closed increasingly often on public holidays, meaning that skippers are unable to leave the area3. The European Union has established specific norms and standards for safe and secure truck parking areas (SSTPAs) in the road transport sector. These are intended, among other things, to meet the growing need for rest areas. Is the Commission prepared or planning to propose similar norms and standards with regard to berthing facilities for inland waterway vessels?

https://binnenvaartkrant.nl/zeeland-start-meldpunt-voor-problemen-met-ligplaatsen-en-voorzieningen. https://www.schuttevaer.nl/nieuws/actueel/2025/12/27/svs-ouderkerk-toenemende-druk-op-ligplaatsen-doortankvaart. https://eenvandaag.avrotros.nl/artikelen/binnenvaartschippers-ontevreden-over-aantal-ligplaatsen-maarrijkswaterstaat-ziet-genoeg-mogelijkheden-133935.
at: (English version) to the Commission Bert-Jan Ruissen (ECR), Kris Van Dijck (ECR) (11 March 2026) Subject: Shortage of mooring berths in inland waterway transport The inland waterway transport sector is crucial for smooth and more sustainable logistics. The EU has 51 000 kilometres of waterways across 25 Member States, on which some 100 to 150 billion tkm of freight is transported annually. The sector produces fewer emissions per tonne of freight than road transport. The Commission supports the sector by means of initiatives such as the NAIADES action plans. However, in several countries, including the Netherlands, Germany and Belgium, the sector is facing an acute shortage of suitable mooring berths (1). This problem is partly caused by the fact that ships have become longer, whilst berths have reduced in number (2). This makes it more difficult for skippers to comply with working and rest periods. In addition, mooring berths near industrial estates are closed increasingly often on public holidays, meaning that skippers are unable to leave the area (3). The European Union has established specific norms and standards for safe and secure truck parking areas (SSTPAs) in the road transport sector. These are intended, among other things, to meet the growing need for rest areas. Is the Commission prepared or planning to propose similar norms and standards with regard to berthing facilities for inland waterway vessels? (11 May 2026) The (TEN-T) Regulation 2024/1679 (1) sets out minimum requirements for the trans-European transport network, applicable to all transport modes, including inland waterways. Under Article 24, it identifies the modernisation and expansion of infrastructure capacity -specifically, mooring and rest places — as a priority, recognising that these facilities are vital for supporting multimodal transport operations, both within port areas and along waterways. However, it is important to note that the responsibility for planning, deploying, and establishing the norms and standards for mooring infrastructure remains within the jurisdiction of individual Member States. Nevertheless, the Commission has actively provided financial support to Member States for building and upgrading mooring places along TEN-T inland waterways, under the Connecting Europe Facility (CEF). Good examples can be found on the Seine-Scheldt Network or on the Danube River; in the latter case, CEF has supported several projects with EUR 47 million which also include mooring. The CEF has also supported an overnight mooring facility Spijk on the German-Dutch border with EUR 11 million.
