qt: to the Commission Fabio De Masi (NI) Subject:

As a result of the illegal attack on Iran by the US and Israel, oil and gas prices are rising. Is the Commission considering reactivating the EU energy crisis contribution, as was previously applied in 2022?
at: (English version) to the Commission Fabio De Masi (NI) (11 March 2026) Subject: EU energy crisis contribution As a result of the illegal attack on Iran by the US and Israel, oil and gas prices are rising. Is the Commission considering reactivating the EU energy crisis contribution, as was previously applied in 2022? (26 June 2026) Amid continued tensions in the Middle East and pressure on global energy markets, the Commission rapidly stepped up its coordinated response, building on the experience of the 2022 crisis and reinforced cooperation with Member States. Europe’s current energy supply remains stable, despite volatility of the global energy markets. It is also clear that Europe is more resilient when it acts together, and the Commission is now better equipped, with upgraded monitoring tools, a revised state aid framework (1) and closer coordination through dedicated energy coordination groups. Gas storage filling is progressing and the Commission invited Member States to make full use of available flexibilities in reaching sufficient levels ahead of the next winter season. On 22 April 2026, the Commission presented a comprehensive set of actions and measures as part of the communication AccelerateEU (2). This communication brings forward short- and long-term measures that shield citizens and industry from price shocks while accelerating the shift to home-grown clean energy through electrification, energy efficiency and scale-up of renewables. AccelerateEU does not include the reactivation of an emergency intervention to address high energy prices as adopted by Council Regulation (EU) 2022/1854 (3). The Commission stands ready to propose the prompt reactivation of these measures if the situation requires it.

E-10-2026-001021.t: The Commission’s next steps regarding the proposal to establish a European housing agency
qt: to the Commission Marko Vešligaj (S&D) Subject:

In its Report on the housing crisis in the European Union, adopted on 10 March 2026, Parliament called for the strengthening of European coordination on housing, including through giving consideration to the establishment of a European housing agency that would provide analytical support, collect data and assist Member States in developing affordable housing policies. In light of the growing scarcity of affordable housing in many Member States and the need for more robust Union-level instruments: 1.
How does the Commission intend to respond to the Parliament’s call for the establishment of a European housing agency?
Is the Commission considering any specific legislative or institutional measures in this regard, including the possibility of establishing a new agency or strengthening existing EU-level structures?
Within what timeframe does the Commission plan to present any initiatives on improving the coordination of housing policies at the EU level?
at: (English version) to the Commission Marko Vešligaj (S&D) (11 March 2026) Subject: The Commission’s next steps regarding the proposal to establish a European housing agency In its Report on the housing crisis in the European Union, adopted on 10 March 2026, Parliament called for the strengthening of European coordination on housing, including through giving consideration to the establishment of a European housing agency that would provide analytical support, collect data and assist Member States in developing affordable housing policies. In light of the growing scarcity of affordable housing in many Member States and the need for more robust Union-level instruments: 1.
How does the Commission intend to respond to the Parliament’s call for the establishment of a European housing agency?
Is the Commission considering any specific legislative or institutional measures in this regard, including the possibility of establishing a new agency or strengthening existing EU-level structures?
Within what timeframe does the Commission plan to present any initiatives on improving the coordination of housing policies at the EU level?

(1 June 2026) The Commission is currently not planning to establish a European Housing Agency. Wherever new EU initiatives are proposed, assignment to an existing institution, agency or body is in general favoured. In accordance with Better Regulation, any proposals to establish a new housing agency would need to be justified by an impact assessment analysing the effectiveness, efficiency, coherence, relevance, and EU added value including interaction with already existing agencies, as well as costs and financing, including the Commission’s capacity to provide for additional services. Regarding the coordination of housing policies at the EU level, the European Affordable Housing Plan (1) proposed to set up a European Housing Alliance to strengthen cooperation on housing at EU level, better coordinate actions and share best practices. This Alliance is currently being rolled out and will unite all levels of government — from cities and regions to national and European institutions, together with key housing stakeholders — to drive forward a shared commitment to ensure affordable, sustainable and quality housing for all. The Alliance complements existing tools such as the European Semester.

E-10-2026-001020.t: Internet shutdowns in Iran during regional conflict and implications for EU digital and human rights policy
qt: to the Commission Hannah Neumann (Verts/ALE) Subject:

Internet blackouts have become a recurring instrument used by the Iranian authorities during periods of unrest, protests, and now armed conflict. Such shutdowns isolate the population, prevent independent reporting and increase the risk that human rights violations will remain undocumented. At the same time, the Iranian authorities continue to expand a state-controlled national information network that allows selective connectivity for regime actors while disconnecting the broader population from the global internet. Against this backdrop: 1.

How does the Commission assess the current internet shutdown in Iran in terms of its impact on access to information, the protection of human rights and the ability of Iranian citizens to communicate with the outside world during the ongoing regional crisis?

What concrete measures is the Commission taking, together with the European External Action Service, to address internet shutdowns as a tool of repression in Iran, including through EU digital diplomacy, engagement with international partners and, where appropriate, the EU Global Human Rights Sanctions Regime?

Does the Commission intend to expand EU support for circumvention tools and secure communications infrastructure and anti-censorship technologies that allow Iranian citizens to access the global internet during shutdowns, and has it engaged with major technology companies regarding the provision of secure communication channels, inapp proxy technologies or other emergency connectivity solutions?
at: (English version) to the Commission Hannah Neumann (Verts/ALE) (11 March 2026) Subject: Internet shutdowns in Iran during regional conflict and implications for EU digital and human rights policy Internet blackouts have become a recurring instrument used by the Iranian authorities during periods of unrest, protests, and now armed conflict. Such shutdowns isolate the population, prevent independent reporting and increase the risk that human rights violations will remain undocumented. At the same time, the Iranian authorities continue to expand a state-controlled national information network that allows selective connectivity for regime actors while disconnecting the broader population from the global Internet. Against this backdrop: 1.

How does the Commission assess the current Internet shutdown in Iran in terms of its impact on access to information, the protection of human rights and the ability of Iranian citizens to communicate with the outside world during the ongoing regional crisis?

What concrete measures is the Commission taking, together with the European External Action Service, to address Internet shutdowns as a tool of repression in Iran, including through EU digital diplomacy, engagement with international partners and, where appropriate, the EU Global Human Rights Sanctions Regime?

Does the Commission intend to expand EU support for circumvention tools and secure communications infrastructure and anti-censorship technologies that allow Iranian citizens to access the global Internet during shutdowns, and has it engaged with major technology companies regarding the provision of secure communication channels, in-app proxy technologies or other emergency connectivity solutions?

(28 April 2026) In January 2026, while brutally repressing peaceful protests, the Iranian authorities had implemented a large-scale Internet shutdown following a well-known pattern observed during the periods of unrest, that became even tighter, without precedents in terms of breadth and duration, since the beginning of the conflict with US and Israel. In parallel, the so-called ‘anti-espionage law’ expanded Iranian authorities’ control over social media and online activity with harsh penalties for censorship circumvention. The EU’s response has been strong, both in statements denouncing the situation and in concrete acts. In her statement on behalf of the EU condemning the crackdown, the High Representative/Vice-President also called ‘for ensuring the right of access to information, including by restoring access to the Internet for all’. In March 2026, the Council adopted restrictive measures targeting among others the head of Tehran’s cyber police, which plays a key role in filtering the Internet, censorship, controlling the social media content and unjustly prosecuting citizens. The EU’s commitment extends to multilateral fora: At the Human Rights Council session on 16 March 2026, the EU reiterated its call for Iranian authorities to restore all communications, including full access to the Internet, and to ensure the right of free access to information for all. The EU recognises the Internet access needs of Iranian citizens and the sensitivities involved, especially in light of the ‘antiespionage law’, which increased Iranian authorities' control over social media and online activity and imposed severe penalties for censorship circumvention. The EU will therefore consider options that prioritize the safety of beneficiaries and partners.

E-10-2026-001019.t: Animal testing for cleaning products under EU law
qt: to the Commission Sebastian Everding (The Left) Subject:

Despite Parliament’s resolution of 16 September 2021 on a coordinated EU action plan to accelerate the transition to innovation without the use of animals in research, regulatory testing and education, there have been multiple reports indicating that the use of animal testing for cleaning products is continuing under the current regulatory framework. While the Cosmetic Products Regulation ((EC) No 1223/2009) establishes a clear ban on animal testing for cosmetic products and ingredients, similar protections do not appear to be applied consistently under the Detergents Regulation ((EC) No 648/2004) and the REACH Regulation ((EC) No 1907/2006) on the registration, evaluation, authorisation and restriction of chemicals. Furthermore, Directive 2010/63/EU on the protection of animals used for scientific purposes requires that animal testing be replaced wherever scientifically satisfactory alternative methods exist. In the light of the EU’s Chemicals Strategy for Sustainability, which commits to phasing out animal testing and promoting alternative methods, can the Commission clarify: 1.
How it explains that the use of animal testing for cleaning products is still permitted under the REACH Regulation and related legislation?
What concrete legislative steps and timelines are envisaged to ensure full alignment with Parliament’s resolution and Directive 2010/63/EU?
How it ensures that the European Chemicals Agency systematically prioritises validated non-animal methods and avoids unnecessary testing when evaluating dossiers?
at: (English version) to the Commission Sebastian Everding (The Left) (11 March 2026) Subject: Animal testing for cleaning products under EU law Despite Parliament’s resolution of 16 September 2021 on a coordinated EU action plan to accelerate the transition to innovation without the use of animals in research, regulatory testing and education, there have been multiple reports indicating that the use of animal testing for cleaning products is continuing under the current regulatory framework. While the Cosmetic Products Regulation ((EC) No 1223/2009) establishes a clear ban on animal testing for cosmetic products and ingredients, similar protections do not appear to be applied consistently under the Detergents Regulation ((EC) No 648/2004) and the REACH Regulation ((EC) No 1907/2006) on the registration, evaluation, authorisation and restriction of chemicals. Furthermore, Directive 2010/63/EU on the protection of animals used for scientific purposes requires that animal testing be replaced wherever scientifically satisfactory alternative methods exist. In the light of the EU’s Chemicals Strategy for Sustainability, which commits to phasing out animal testing and promoting alternative methods, can the Commission clarify: 1.
How it explains that the use of animal testing for cleaning products is still permitted under the REACH Regulation and related legislation?
What concrete legislative steps and timelines are envisaged to ensure full alignment with Parliament’s resolution and Directive 2010/63/EU?
How it ensures that the European Chemicals Agency systematically prioritises validated non-animal methods and avoids unnecessary testing when evaluating dossiers?

(29 April 2026) The revised Regulation on Detergents and Surfactants (1), which will enter into force on 23 September 2029, has introduced a general prohibition on the placing on the market of detergents and surfactants that have been subject to animal testing to meet the requirements of the regulation. At the same time, ingredients of cleaning products are subject to the provisions under the regulation on Registration, Evaluation, Authorisation and Restriction of Chemicals (REACH) (2) or the Biocidal Product Regulation (3), which might include animal testing if necessary for assessing risks to human health or the environment. Both regulations permit testing on vertebrates only as a last resort. REACH registrants are bound by the principle of last resort when submitting data to the European Chemicals Agency, which is taking this principle into account when evaluating testing proposals or the compliance of dossiers. The principle of last resort aligns these regulations with Directive 2010/63/EU (4), which requires that animal testing be replaced, reduced, or refined, if scientifically possible. The Commission roadmap towards phasing out animal testing for chemical safety assessments, planned to be published in the second quarter of 2026, will outline the steps necessary to reach the goal of phasing out animal testing for chemical safety assessments under all relevant pieces of legislation. Legislative changes, if necessary to reach the goal, will be introduced in line with the rules of the relevant pieces of legislation.

E-10-2026-001018.t: New York Times revelations on detention conditions in Bulgaria
qt: to the Commission Tineke Strik (Verts/ALE), Cecilia Strada (S&D), Estrella Galán (The Left), Murielle Laurent (S&D), Krzysztof Śmiszek (S&D), Erik Marquardt (Verts/ALE), Mélissa Camara (Verts/ALE) Subject:

On 10 February 2026, the New York Times published an article1 documenting the worrying conditions in Busmantsi detention centre in Sofia, Bulgaria. The publication describes several problematic conditions, including poor hygiene, overcrowding and a lack of medical care. Moreover, people are allegedly occasionally forced to sign ‘voluntary return’ papers by the Bulgarian police and Frontex, to countries such as Syria, Afghanistan and Iraq. The article claims that they face consequences if they refuse to sign. 1.
Does the Commission consider the conditions in Busmantsi detention centre to be in line with Directive 2013/33/EU laying down standards for the reception of applicants for international protection2?
Has the Commission received any reports of misconduct or inadequate standards at the Busmantsi detention centre?
Will the Commission launch an investigation into the allegations made in the New York Times article, and is it prepared to share the outcome with Parliament?

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/02/10/magazine/immigration-detention-europe-busmantsibulgaria.html?unlocked_article_code=1.LVA.OP_M.YTDPE6D15zjU&smid=nytcore-ios-share. OJ L 180, 29.6.2013, pp. 96, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2013/33/oj.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (26.5.2026) The Busmantsi centre operates as a pre-return detention facility. The Return Directive1 enables Member States to detain for removal purposes illegally staying third-country nationals if there is a risk of absconding or the third-country national avoids or hampers the preparation of return or the removal process. When imposing detention, Member States have to ensure compliance with the respective safeguards and the EU Charter on Fundamental Rights. The centre in question also includes a separate closed unit (places) which operates as a centre for applicants for international protection. The detention of applicants for international protection is regulated by Directive 2013/33/EU2. The Commission monitors the correct transposition and implementation of applicable EU law, including the EU Charter on Fundamental Rights. Detention conditions in Bulgaria were evaluated as part of the Schengen evaluation mission3 which took place in November 2025. The outcome of the evaluation will be reflected in the report to be adopted by the Commission in accordance with Council Regulation (EU) 2022/922 and the remedial measures subsequently put in place by Bulgaria to address the recommendations will be monitored.

E-10-2026-001017.t: Providing effective support for the European Public Prosecutor’s Office
qt: to the Commission Arash Saeidi (The Left) Subject:

In its 2025 activity report, published on 2 March 2026, the European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO) confirmed an unprecedented rise in fraud affecting the financial interests of the European Union, with figures that were even more alarming than those anticipated in December 2025. The overall estimated damage from ongoing cases has risen to EUR 67.27 billion, compared with EUR 24.8 billion in 2024. This figure almost tripled in a year as a result of a 35 % increase in the number of investigations opened, but also the increasingly prevalent and sophisticated mechanisms used in customs and VAT fraud, areas the EPPO had already expressed concerns about in December 2025. Most of the fraudulent funds will never be returned to the EU budget, however, because of worrying deficiencies in the reporting and recovery chain and a lack of support for the EPPO. In 2024, less than 1 % of reports came from the European Anti-Fraud Office and less than 13 % from the EU institutions, according to Transparency International. Furthermore, the European Court of Auditors points out that there is inadequate sharing of information to ensure that misappropriated funds are recovered and returned to the EU budget. What steps does the Commission intend to take to strengthen the EPPO’s actions and the recovery of damages relating to the EU budget?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (5.5.2026) The Commission fully supports the mission of the European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO) and remains firmly committed to further strengthening the EU’s anti-fraud architecture (AFA), of which the EPPO is a key component. Further to the adoption of its related White Paper in July 20251, the Commission is currently reviewing the EU’s AFA. In this context, the Commission is assessing the cooperation and information exchange among the relevant actors, including the EPPO, as well as the recovery of misused EU funds, with a view to identifying targeted improvements where appropriate. The Commission will also take due account of the relevant recommendations of the European Court of Auditors in this process. Furthermore, the forthcoming evaluation of the EPPO Regulation and the Directive on the fight against fraud to the Union’s financial interests by means of criminal law (the PIF Directive)2, the joint impact assessment supporting the possible revision of the EPPO and the European Anti-fraud Office (OLAF) Regulations3, as well as the ongoing consultations carried out in the context of the review of the EU’s AFA, will provide an opportunity to assess the functioning of the current EPPO’s framework, including the tools and conditions under which the EPPO operates. In that context, the Commission could consider whether any adjustments are needed to further enhance its effectiveness, including as regards the recovery of misused EU funds.

1 White Paper for the Anti-fraud Architecture Review, COM(2025) 546 final, Brussels, 16.7.2025. 2 Directive (EU) 2017/1371 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 5 July 2017 on the fight against

fraud to the Union’s financial interests by means of criminal law, OJ L 198, 28.7.2017. 3 Council Regulation (EU) 2017/1939 of 12 October 2017 implementing enhanced cooperation on the establishment of the European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO), OJ L 283, 31.10.2017 and Regulation (EU, Euratom) No 883/2013 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 11 September 2013 concerning investigations conducted by the European Anti-Fraud Office (OLAF), as amended, OJ L 248, 18.9.2013.

E-10-2026-001015.t: Interpretation of a European Commission decision
qt: to the Commission Sandra Kalniete (PPE) Subject:

A campaign is being carried out in Latvia inviting residents to enter into agreements concerning the recovery of allegedly unlawful State aid. The organisers of the campaign claim that the European Commission, in its 2017 decision in Case SA.43140, declared the aid to be ‘unlawful’ because Latvia had infringed Article 108(3) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU). Although Latvia introduced the aid prior to the Commission’s final decision, in its decision the Commission declared the aid to be compatible with the internal market pursuant to Article 107(3)(c) TFEU, and raised no objections. Similar conclusions were also reached in the Commission’s 2020 decision (SA.56310). As Latvia’s competent authorities explain, aid that is declared ‘unlawful’ (because not notified in time) but compatible with the internal market does not give rise to an obligation for the Member State to recover it. In order to provide comprehensive information to the Latvian public, could the Commission clarify the following: 1.

Does the infringement of Article 108(3) TFEU identified in the Commission’s 2017 and 2020 decisions entitle electricity consumers –businesses and households – to request the recovery of the State aid paid?

Under EU legislation and in light of the above-mentioned decisions, does Latvia have a legal duty to recover payments from aid recipients, even though the aid was declared compatible with the internal market?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (5.5.2026) 1. Where national law grants consumers (private persons or companies) standing, they can bring an action before the competent national courts in relation to unlawful aid, including asking to order its recovery. Under EU law, if aid is later approved, it does not have to be paid back. However, interest must still be paid for the time the aid was unlawful, to remove any unfair advantage obligation (Article 108(3) Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union). This interest is paid to the State budget, not to consumers. Consumers may still seek compensation separately under national law. 2. Under EU law, national authorities and courts must remove any unfair advantage gained from unlawful aid. In practice, this means beneficiaries must pay interest for the period during which they wrongly had access to the aid. The exact amount of interest is calculated under national law by the Member State concerned and the Member State must quantify the exact amount of interest to be recovered.

E-10-2026-001014.t: Availability of the list of Commission partners providing support to independent Belarusian media
qt: to the Commission Maciej Wąsik (ECR) Subject:

According to information provided by Commissioner Marta Kos on 17 February 2025, the Commission has allocated EUR 38 million to fund independent Belarusian media and journalists since 2020. The free Belarusian media sources that receive this support are an effective tool in the fight against the Lukashenka regime. In the light of the above: 1.

Could the Commission provide a list of projects, or indicate where such a list is available, which have been supported by the EUR 38 million allocated by the Commission to support free and independent Belarusian media?
Could the Commission provide a list of the implementing partners that have received funding to support independent Belarusian media?
Could the Commission indicate where reports confirming that the implementing partners have properly accounted for the expenditure of funds are available?
at: (English version) to the Commission Maciej Wąsik (ECR) (11 March 2026) Subject: Availability of the list of Commission partners providing support to independent Belarusian media According to information provided by Commissioner Marta Kos on 17 February 2025, the Commission has allocated EUR 38 million to fund independent Belarusian media and journalists since 2020. The free Belarusian media sources that receive this support are an effective tool in the fight against the Lukashenka regime. In the light of the above: 1.

Could the Commission provide a list of projects, or indicate where such a list is available, which have been supported by the EUR 38 million allocated by the Commission to support free and independent Belarusian media?
Could the Commission provide a list of the implementing partners that have received funding to support independent Belarusian media?
Could the Commission indicate where reports confirming that the implementing partners have properly accounted for the expenditure of funds are available?

(13 May 2026) The EU remains committed to assisting Belarusian journalists and independent media in providing high-quality reporting to Belarusian citizens. EU support has reached over 40 Belarusian independent outlets, helping preserve a diverse, dynamic and widely consumed Belarusian independent media ecosystem. The EU has also provided capacity-building and sector-wide support through education, training and technical assistance. Belarusian citizens, both inside the country and in exile, continue to face persecution. Public disclosure of the projects receiving EU support would expose beneficiaries to further risk. Accordingly, the Commission does not publish the names of implementing partners, in order to protect their ability to continue supporting independent media. For the same reasons, reports on implementation of EU assistance are not published. However, the Commission receives regular, comprehensive reporting from both beneficiaries and implementing partners, confirming that funding is properly accounted for. EU assistance is also subject to standard audit procedures to ensure proper use of funds and compliance with financial management rules.

E-10-2026-001013.t: Concerns regarding the Law on Internal Affairs and the Law on the National Security Agency in Montenegro
qt: to the Commission Vladimir Prebilič (Verts/ALE) Subject:

The draft Law on Internal Affairs (LIA) and the draft Law on the National Security Agency (LNSA) in Montenegro raise concerns regarding their compatibility with EU fundamental rights standards. They allow for police officers to be dismissed on the basis of so-called security obstacles, relying on classified information that the affected officer may neither access nor effectively challenge. Furthermore, the draft LNSA maintains powers allowing the National Security Agency to access citizens’ data, including location data and private databases, without prior judicial authorisation. Given this situation, can the Commission answer the following questions: 1.

In the light of the right to be heard, the rights of defence and the principle of effective judicial protection under Article 41 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, how does the Commission assess the compatibility of the draft LIA with EU fundamental rights standards, as well as with the General Data Protection Regulation and the Law Enforcement Directive?
Are provisions allowing security authorities to access citizens’ data without prior judicial authorisation compatible with EU standards?
Given the Commission’s role in monitoring compliance with the EU acquis in the accession process, how does it assess the compatibility of these draft laws with EU fundamental rights standards?
at: (English version) to the Commission Vladimir Prebilič (Verts/ALE) (11 March 2026) Subject: Concerns regarding the Law on Internal Affairs and the Law on the National Security Agency in Montenegro The draft Law on Internal Affairs (LIA) and the draft Law on the National Security Agency (LNSA) in Montenegro raise concerns regarding their compatibility with EU fundamental rights standards. They allow for police officers to be dismissed on the basis of so-called security obstacles, relying on classified information that the affected officer may neither access nor effectively challenge. Furthermore, the draft LNSA maintains powers allowing the National Security Agency to access citizens’ data, including location data and private databases, without prior judicial authorisation. Given this situation, can the Commission answer the following questions: 1.

In the light of the right to be heard, the rights of defence and the principle of effective judicial protection under Article 41 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, how does the Commission assess the compatibility of the draft LIA with EU fundamental rights standards, as well as with the General Data Protection Regulation and the Law Enforcement Directive?
Are provisions allowing security authorities to access citizens’ data without prior judicial authorisation compatible with EU standards?
Given the Commission’s role in monitoring compliance with the EU acquis in the accession process, how does it assess the compatibility of these draft laws with EU fundamental rights standards?

(4 June 2026) The Commission took note of the adoption of the law on Internal Affairs and the National Security Agency law in Montenegro. The Commission had assessed the two laws and finds that their data protection provisions are not yet fully aligned with the EU acquis, particularly the General Data Protection Regulation (1) and the Law Enforcement Directive (2). These laws require legal adjustments to align fully with the EU acquis on personal data protection. Montenegro is working on reviewing its legal framework on data protection in line with the EU acquis and as a first step has prepared a new draft law on Personal Data Protection. The Commission stands ready to assist Montenegro with its comprehensive data protection reform aimed to be finalised by the closure of accession negotiations. In the context of Montenegro’s accession, the Commission will closely monitor implementation of these laws and expects Montenegro to ensure merit-based police recruitments and strong procedural safeguards, and that any dismissals are justified and provide for access to full legal recourse. Comprehensive and inclusive reforms are essential not only for the country’s accession to the EU but for reinforcing public trust in Montenegro’s institutions.

E-10-2026-001012.t: Unclear division of competences under the Treaty in the field of foreign policy between the Commission President and the High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy
qt: to the Commission Marieke Ehlers (PfE), Mieke Andriese (PfE) Subject:

Articles 21 and 22 TEU provide that it is for the Council to define the strategic interests and objectives of the Union’s external action. As regards the Common Foreign and Security Policy (CFSP), implementation and external representation are, in principle, the responsibility of the High Representative (Article 27 TEU), whilst the Commission President, in accordance with Article 17 TEU, represents the Commission in matters falling within her own competences. In practice, there is often an overlapping or unclear division of roles, including in the context of the so-called ‘Team Europe’ approach, whereby the Commission President also adopts external political positions vis-à-vis third countries. This situation raises questions about the division of competences in the field of the Union’s external action between the Commission President, the Council and the High Representative. 1.

How does the Commission interpret the division of competences under the Treaty in the field of the CFSP between the Commission President (Article 17 TEU) and the High Representative (Article 27 TEU) when it comes to public or diplomatic positions vis-àvis third countries?

What safeguards are in place to ensure that, in external contacts, the Commission President does not adopt positions on matters falling within the exclusive competence of the Council in the field of the CFSP?
To what extent does the ‘Team Europe’ approach affect the division of roles between the Commission President, the High Representative and the Council with regard to the Union’s external action?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (19.5.2026) 1. and 2. The general provisions on the Union’s external action in the Treaty on European Union provide that the Union shall ensure consistency between the different areas of its external action1. The Council and the Commission, assisted by the High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy, cooperate to that effect. This is without prejudice to the fact that, with the exception of the Common Foreign and Security Policy, it is for the Commission to ensure the external representation of the Union2. 3. The Team Europe approach focuses on joining forces, delivering more effectively, increasing global impact and avoiding duplication of efforts, while respecting the division of competences under the Treaties. It aims at bringing together the European Union, its Member States — including their implementing agencies and public development banks — as well as the European Investment Bank and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development.
1 Article 21(3) of the Treaty on European Union. 2 Article 17(1) of the Treaty on European Union.

E-10-2026-001011.t: Energy crisis and impact on citizens and businesses
qt: to the Commission Aldo Patriciello (PfE) Subject:

Ongoing instability in Iran and rising geopolitical tensions in the Middle East have brought about a sharp increase in the cost of electricity and gas, as well as fuels such as petrol and diesel. This has had a direct effect on household energy bills and on European companies’ operating costs. These dynamics are placing a significant burden on citizens’ purchasing power and on the competitiveness of the European production system, particularly in the most energy-intensive sectors. The persistent increase in energy costs also risks having an inflationary effect on the economy as a whole, affecting the prices of goods and services and creating further difficulties for households, workers and economic activities, which have already been hit by the recent international crises. In this context, it seems necessary to consider extraordinary intervention instruments at European level. In the light of the above, can the Commission answer the following questions: 1.
Does it intend to consider setting up an extraordinary European fund to support Member States in containing the impact of price rises on households and businesses?
Does it envisage adopting specific Europe-wide measures to set a price ceiling for fuels and energy supplies, in order to soften the effects of the current geopolitical tensions on European citizens?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.5.2026) Europe is facing a serious situation when it comes to fossil fuels, which threatens to impose further costs on households and business. A united, coordinated European response is needed in order to avoid fragmented national approaches and disruptive signals to the market: solidarity, transparency, and cooperation remain critical. In response, the Commission presented on 22 April 2026 the AccelerateEU communication1 with concrete measures to be taken immediately at Member States level in order to shield families and business alike, increase coordination and accelerate phase-out from fossil fuels, building on the lessons learnt with the 2022 crisis. These measures must be targeted – protecting the most vulnerable, temporary and avoid worsening supply conditions, focusing on energy savings. They should accelerate the phasing out of fossil fuels by increasing the efficiency of the energy system and accelerating deployment of electrification and homegrown clean energy, including by better leveraging storage and demand flexibility for the benefit of consumers. No EU-wide mechanism such as price ceiling is currently envisaged. Furthermore, the Commission will adopt a set of detailed recommendations to implement the Citizens Energy Package2, to help consumers bring down their bills. These recommendations will aim at preventing consumer disconnections, prioritise consumer protection and switching to cheaper contracts, as well as expanding support for self-consumption and energy communities. EU funds can play an important role in mitigating the impact of the current situation for example to support investments on energy efficiency; the setting up of an extraordinary fund to support Member States is not currently envisaged.
1 https://energy.ec.europa.eu/strategy/accelerateeu-strengthen-eu-energy-resilience_en. 2 https://energy.ec.europa.eu/news/commission-boost-access-affordable-and-clean-energy-all-europeans-2026-

E-10-2026-001010.t: European cultural heritage and legal certainty under threat: the case of Campania’s Vesuvian Villas
qt: to the Commission Danilo Della Valle (The Left) Subject:

Littering the coastline between Naples and Torre del Greco, the 18th century Vesuvian Villas are sites of outstanding historical and artistic value for European heritage. However, Council of State Judgment No 03835/2021 authorised the construction of a base transceiver station in the gardens of Monteleone’s Villa Pignatelli, arguing that their dilapidated physical features had deprived them of their cultural value and, as a result, of their protected status. The Court used this Vesuvian site’s neglected state to justify stripping it of its legal protections, thereby paving the way for its abandonment. In addition to running counter to the conservation obligations laid down by Article 3 TEU and Article 167 TFEU and the principles of the New European Bauhaus (NEB), the Council of State’s interpretation could end up compromising the effectiveness of EU funding allocated to historical conservation projects under the ERDF and NRRP. In the light of the above: 1.
Does the Commission hold that stripping a cultural site of its protected status on the basis of its dilapidated state is an interpretation that is compatible with the standards set by the Treaties?
What steps will the Commission take to ensure that Member States fulfil their obligations to protect and restore cultural heritage?
Will the Commission check whether Villa Pignatelli is being administered in line with the conservation criteria that are applicable to projects in receipt of EU funds?
at: (English version) to the Commission Danilo Della Valle (The Left) (11 March 2026) Subject: European cultural heritage and legal certainty under threat: the case of Campania’s Vesuvian Villas Littering the coastline between Naples and Torre del Greco, the 18th century Vesuvian Villas are sites of outstanding historical and artistic value for European heritage. However, Council of State Judgment No 03835/2021 authorised the construction of a base transceiver station in the gardens of Monteleone’s Villa Pignatelli, arguing that their dilapidated physical features had deprived them of their cultural value and, as a result, of their protected status. The Court used this Vesuvian site’s neglected state to justify stripping it of its legal protections, thereby paving the way for its abandonment. In addition to running counter to the conservation obligations laid down by Article 3 TEU and Article 167 TFEU and the principles of the New European Bauhaus (NEB), the Council of State’s interpretation could end up compromising the effectiveness of EU funding allocated to historical conservation projects under the ERDF and NRRP. In the light of the above: 1.
Does the Commission hold that stripping a cultural site of its protected status on the basis of its dilapidated state is an interpretation that is compatible with the standards set by the Treaties?
What steps will the Commission take to ensure that Member States fulfil their obligations to protect and restore cultural heritage?
Will the Commission check whether Villa Pignatelli is being administered in line with the conservation criteria that are applicable to projects in receipt of EU funds?

(18 June 2026) The protection and restoration of cultural heritage remain a national responsibility. The Commission has no say on which sites are granted protected status by Member States, neither what sites are stripped from their protected status. Article 167 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union stipulates that EU action focuses on encouraging cooperation between Member States and supporting and supplementing their actions, with a view to conserving and safeguarding cultural heritage of European significance. The Commission has implemented various policies and programmes to support the safeguarding and promotion of cultural heritage in Europe. These include the designation of European Heritage Label sites, which are recognised for their symbolic value and role in European history; the European Heritage Days; and the annual European Heritage Awards. However, this does not in any way pre-empt the protection of cultural heritage at national level. In the context of the European Regional Development Fund (ERDF), the Commission encourages Member States and regions to ensure that restoration and preservation of cultural heritage is done in accordance with best practice, including the International Council on Monuments and Sites (ICOMOS) European quality principles for EU-funded interventions with potential impact on cultural heritage (1). In line with the shared management approach, national and subnational authorities may decide to incorporate such guidance in the implementation of relevant ERDF support as outlined in the respective Cohesion Policy programmes. This cultural heritage project did not receive any ERDF financing.

E-10-2026-001008.t: Abuse of temporary contracts in Spain: compliance with Directive 1999/70/EC and possible penalties
qt: to the Commission Diana Riba i Giner (Verts/ALE) Subject:

Spain is currently being investigated under infringement procedure INFR(2014)4334 for failing to correctly apply Directive 1999/70/EC on fixed-term work in the public sector. The CJEU handed down judgements on the abuse of temporary contracts on 22 February 2021 and 13 June 2024, and the judgement in Case C-418/24 is scheduled for 14 April 2026. In spite of those judgements and Law 20/2021, temporary contracts are still frequently abused in Spain, and the six-month period the Commission gave it to adopt measures ran out on 7 January 2026, without yielding any substantive results. In the light of this: 1.
In the Commission’s view, what criteria and steps are needed for Spain to comply fully with Directive 1999/70/EC and effectively reduce the abuse of fixed-term contracts in the public sector?

In view of the 2021 and 2024 judgements and the forthcoming ruling on 14 April 2026, does it intend to refer the case to the CJEU under Article 258 TFEU on the basis of Spain’s persistent failure to fulfil its obligations?

If Spain still does not fulfil its obligations following a decision by the CJEU, what criteria would the Commission use as grounds for coercive financial penalties against it, under Article 260 TFEU, and when would they be applied?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.5.2026) 1. In the framework of INFR(2014)4334, the Commission is pursuing the absence of measures to prevent and penalise the abusive use of some types of fixed-term contracts in Spain’s public administration, in breach of Directive 1999/70/EC1. The precise steps to be taken to resolve the breaches of EU law are to be decided by the Member State. 2. In October 2024, the Commission sent to Spain an additional letter of formal notice and is currently assessing the reply and subsequent information provided by Spain. If the Commission considers that the identified grievances are not solved, it could adopt a reasoned opinion and, if Spain continues to not address those issues, the Commission may decide to refer it to the Court of Justice of the European Union. 3. The principles and method used by the Commission to calculate the financial sanctions proposed to the Court can be consulted in its Communication ‘Financial sanctions in infringement proceedings’2 and subsequent revisions3. Nevertheless, it is for the Court, in the exercise of its discretion, to determine the amounts that it considers appropriate to the circumstances and proportionate both to the breach that has been established and to the capacity to pay of the Member State concerned. The penalty to be paid by the Member State is applicable from the date when the Court delivers its judgment.
1 Council Directive 1999/70/EC of 28 June 1999 concerning the framework agreement on fixed-term work

concluded by ETUC, UNICE and CEEP, http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/1999/70/oj. 2 Communication from the Commission Financial sanctions in infringement proceedings 2023/C 2/01, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=oj:JOC_2023_002_R_0001. 3 See Communication from the Commission – Modification of the calculation method for financial sanctions proposed by the Commission in infringement proceedings before the Court of Justice of the European Union , http://data.europa.eu/eli/C/2025/1481/oj, and Communication from the Commission – Annual update of data used for calculation of financial sanctions proposed by the Commission to the Court of Justice of the European Union in infringement proceedings, http://data.europa.eu/eli/C/2026/1653/oj.

E-10-2026-001007.t: Strategic protection of maritime trade routes in the Red Sea and combating systemic risks posed by digital extremism
qt: to the Commission Angelika Winzig (PPE) Subject:

The security of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait is of vital importance to European supply chains. Attacks on shipping by Houthi militias, geopolitical shifts in southern Yemen and the digital dissemination of extremist narratives are putting security of supply and competitiveness at considerable risk. 1.

How does the Commission assess the impact of the current shifts in power on the security of shipping in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, and what specific measures does it plan to take to secure European supply chains against disruptions and cost increases?

To what extent does the Commission intend to deepen its cooperation with regional partners in order to curb Houthi militia attacks and resolutely tackle extremist networks, including the Muslim Brotherhood?

What action is the Commission taking against platform operators under the Digital Services Act in order to minimise the algorithmic amplification of extremist narratives in the context of the Yemen conflict, and how are risk assessments and remedial measures being monitored?
at: (English version) to the Commission Angelika Winzig (PPE) (11 March 2026) Subject: Strategic protection of maritime trade routes in the Red Sea and combating systemic risks posed by digital extremism The security of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait is of vital importance to European supply chains. Attacks on shipping by Houthi militias, geopolitical shifts in southern Yemen and the digital dissemination of extremist narratives are putting security of supply and competitiveness at considerable risk. 1. How does the Commission assess the impact of the current shifts in power on the security of shipping in the Bab elMandeb Strait, and what specific measures does it plan to take to secure European supply chains against disruptions and cost increases? 2. To what extent does the Commission intend to deepen its cooperation with regional partners in order to curb Houthi militia attacks and resolutely tackle extremist networks, including the Muslim Brotherhood? 3. What action is the Commission taking against platform operators under the Digital Services Act in order to minimise the algorithmic amplification of extremist narratives in the context of the Yemen conflict, and how are risk assessments and remedial measures being monitored? (11 May 2026) The EU has a principled stance on freedom of navigation, in line with international law. It urges all involved in the conflict to fully ensure a toll-free and safe passage through the Strait of Hormuz. The closure of the strait disrupts the global economy and threatens global energy and food security. The EU is engaged in the region through operation EUNAVFOR ASPIDES ensuring safe passage through the Red Sea. Its extended mandate (1) until 28 February 2027 comprises strengthening links with other EU initiatives, including (CRIMARIO) (2), the EU’s critical maritime routes project, and collecting and sharing information on suspicious activities related to critical submarine infrastructure. It further contributes to capacity building by training Djiboutian maritime forces and by cooperating with the Yemeni Coast Guard. The first summit between the EU and the Gulf Cooperation Council in October 2024 highlighted the joint commitment to freedom of navigation and maritime security in the Red Sea (3). The EU implements the UN sanctions on Yemen through its Council Decision 2014/932 (4). In 2024, the EU designated individuals and entities for their support to the Houthis under its sanction regime regarding Iran’s military support to armed groups and entities in the Middle East and the Red Sea region (5). The EU monitors the evolving risks linked to organisations trying to unduly influence democratic institutions, including radical and extremist non-state actors, as well as interference from third countries. The Digital Services Act (DSA) (6) requires providers of very large online platforms and search engines to diligently identify, assess, and mitigate systemic risks on their services, including the risk of dissemination of terrorist content.

E-10-2026-001006.t: Support to women’s organisations as peacebuilders and related legislation in Colombia
qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Irene Montero (The Left), Emma Fourreau (The Left), Marta Temido (S&D), Ana Miranda Paz (Verts/ALE) Subject:

We are convinced of the importance of women’s organisations in building a country with social justice and lasting peace. We welcome the adoption in Colombia of the Comprehensive Programme of Guarantees for Women Leaders and Human Rights Defenders and of Law 2364 of 2024, known as the ‘ley de mujeres buscadoras’ or Women Searchers Law. This is a tangible, necessary and positive development. However, civil society organisations have identified significant challenges in terms of their effective implementation, as well as in their territorial approach. The European Union has repeatedly expressed its commitment to the inclusion of the gender dimension of the Peace Agreement, to the protection of women human rights defenders and to the promotion of gender equality and women’s rights in Colombia. In light of this: 1.
In its dialogues with Colombia, in what way does the Commission incorporate the monitoring and promotion of the implementation of these policies, including a territorial approach?

How does the EU plan to support women’s organisations economically and politically to enhance their capacity to influence public policy, strengthen their organisations, and develop their own prevention and protection mechanisms?
at: (English version) to the Vice-President of the Commission/High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Irene Montero (The Left), Emma Fourreau (The Left), Marta Temido (S&D), Ana Miranda Paz (Verts/ALE) (11 March 2026) Subject: Support to women’s organisations as peacebuilders and related legislation in Colombia We are convinced of the importance of women’s organisations in building a country with social justice and lasting peace. We welcome the adoption in Colombia of the Comprehensive Programme of Guarantees for Women Leaders and Human Rights Defenders and of Law 2364 of 2024, known as the ‘ley de mujeres buscadoras’ or Women Searchers Law. This is a tangible, necessary and positive development. However, civil society organisations have identified significant challenges in terms of their effective implementation, as well as in their territorial approach. The European Union has repeatedly expressed its commitment to the inclusion of the gender dimension of the Peace Agreement, to the protection of women human rights defenders and to the promotion of gender equality and women’s rights in Colombia. In light of this: 1.
In its dialogues with Colombia, in what way does the Commission incorporate the monitoring and promotion of the implementation of these policies, including a territorial approach?

How does the EU plan to support women’s organisations economically and politically to enhance their capacity to influence public policy, strengthen their organisations, and develop their own prevention and protection mechanisms?

(20 July 2026) The EU remains committed to the full implementation of the 2016 Peace Agreement in Colombia, including its gender, ethnic, and territorial transformation chapters. In its political and human rights dialogues with Colombia, the EU consistently raises the need for effective protection mechanisms for women leaders and defenders and the recognition and inclusion of women as peacebuilders. The EU Delegation in Bogotá maintains regular contact with women’s organisations, territorial platforms and civil society in conflict-affected and rural areas. EU-funded projects support local women’s organisations working on peacebuilding, political participation, transitional justice, prevention of gender-based violence, and protection of women defenders. These projects promote the participation of women and their organisations in the development of the National Action Plan on Women, Peace and Security, in the monitoring and implementation of the Comprehensive Programme of Guarantees for Women Leaders and Human Rights Defenders, and in monitoring the implementation of the gender dimension of the 2016 Peace Agreement. Initiatives provide legal and psychosocial support to women victims of sexual and gender-based violence to access the Special Jurisdiction for Peace, provide organisational and economic support to women organisations, and strengthen self-protection mechanisms for women defenders, including women searching for the disappeared. In line with EU’s human rights defender’s mechanism, ProtectDefenders.eu, and local response and protection initiatives, such as the campaign #DefendamosLavida, the EU will continue to support women’s organisation in Colombia.

E-10-2026-001005.t: EU participation in the Colombia’s national safeguard process for human rights defenders
qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Irene Montero (The Left), Pernando Barrena Arza (The Left), Jaume Asens Llodrà (Verts/ALE) Subject:

Colombia’s national safeguard process is a forum for dialogue between the state and civil society intended to ensure those working to defend human rights are protected. We welcome the resumption of discussions in the National Round Table and regional round tables under the current government. We also applaud the participation of the EU and its Member States as observers. Much, however, still needs to be done to ensure the effectiveness and sustainability of these initiatives. We were told of such drawbacks as the participation of public officials without decision-making powers, the lack of guarantees for the inclusion of the most vulnerable actors or the faltering political will of the local authorities responsible for implementation. Can the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy therefore say: 1.
What specific measures the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative plans to take for the continued support of the National Guarantee Process in the coming years?

How the EU intends to play a more prominent role, stressing the need for the participation of public officials with decision-making powers and the establishment of a clear mechanism for monitoring the commitments made, thereby making the forum more effective?
Whether the EU is considering participating in regional round tables other than the National Round Table?
at: (English version) to the Vice-President of the Commission/High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Irene Montero (The Left), Pernando Barrena Arza (The Left), Jaume Asens Llodrà (Verts/ALE) (11 March 2026) Subject: EU participation in the Colombia’s national safeguard process for human rights defenders Colombia’s national safeguard process is a forum for dialogue between the state and civil society intended to ensure those working to defend human rights are protected. We welcome the resumption of discussions in the National Round Table and regional round tables under the current government. We also applaud the participation of the EU and its Member States as observers. Much, however, still needs to be done to ensure the effectiveness and sustainability of these initiatives. We were told of such drawbacks as the participation of public officials without decision-making powers, the lack of guarantees for the inclusion of the most vulnerable actors or the faltering political will of the local authorities responsible for implementation. Can the Vice-President of the Commission/High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy therefore say: 1.
What specific measures the Vice-President of the Commission/High Representative plans to take for the continued support of the National Guarantee Process in the coming years?

How the EU intends to play a more prominent role, stressing the need for the participation of public officials with decision-making powers and the establishment of a clear mechanism for monitoring the commitments made, thereby making the forum more effective?
Whether the EU is considering participating in regional round tables other than the National Round Table?

(10 June 2026) The EU Delegation in Colombia has been engaged in the National Round Table since its inception, including at Ambassador level, and intends to maintain this engagement. Through its participation and ongoing dialogue with authorities, both bilaterally and in fora like the annual EU-Colombia Human Rights Dialogue, the EU continues to stress the importance of preserving this forum as a channel for dialogue between civil society and public institutions, with a view to improving protection for human rights defenders. In this context, the EU highlights the need for the involvement of representatives with decision-making authority and for robust follow-up to ensure that commitments lead to concrete results at the local level. Looking ahead, the EU will continue to support the National Guarantee Process. Its cooperation programmes in the field of human rights in Colombia (for example, Right to Defend Rights: Alliances for Protection and the Demand for Guarantees (1)) include measures aimed at protecting and empowering human rights defenders as well as at reinforcing the capacity of civil society actors to participate effectively in both national and regional round tables. With regard to regional round tables, the EU Delegation remains open to participating where appropriate and upon invitation. It has already contributed to the establishment of the Caquetá Territorial Round Table on Guarantees in 2024. In parallel, the Delegation maintains regular exchanges with relevant counterparts, including the Human Rights Directorate of the Ministry of the Interior, the Ombudsman’s office and civil society organisations involved in the process, in order to stay informed and to encourage follow-up on the commitments undertaken at both national and regional levels.

One of its main actions is to develop advocacy strategies and proposals to strengthen guarantees for the human rights movement and promote them within national and territorial decision-making spaces, such as the National Guarantees Roundtable and the Territorial Guarantees Roundtables.

E-10-2026-001004.t: Funding of tools to combat disinformation at EU level
qt: to the Commission Ana Catarina Mendes (S&D) Subject:

Since 2016, the Commission has funded, through the Horizon Europe programme, a series of successive projects that have helped combat disinformation: InVID, followed by WeVerify, and most recently Vera AI. These projects have enabled the development of free and opensource tools designed to help journalists, fact-checkers, and civil society groups verify the authenticity of online content. These tools allow users to detect disinformation, identify the use of deepfakes in social media posts, and uncover illegal or deceptive behaviour using artificial intelligence. They are widely recognised as a successful outcome of the Horizon Europe programme and of the Commission’s efforts to support the development of tools to combat disinformation. However, as the Vera AI project nears its conclusion, it appears that no new call for proposals has been planned to ensure that this essential work can continue. This raises concerns about the sustainability of such tools. 1.

Can the Commission explain why no new funding is currently planned to support the continued development of these tools, which have proven to be effective and are developed independently by civil society groups?
What is the Commission’s strategy to ensure the future availability of free, reliable and European-made solutions to tackle disinformation?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (20.5.2026) Safeguarding the integrity of the information space to support everyone in society to access reliable and trustworthy information and exercise their democratic rights is essential for democracy as outlined in the European Democracy Shield (EDS) Communication1. In this vein, the Commission has supported the development of technological tools that enable journalists, fact-checkers, civil society groups and all citizens to detect disinformation and foreign interference (FIMI) campaigns, including through support for consecutive projects under Horizon 20202 and Horizon Europe3 such as InVID4, WeVerify5 and vera.ai6, with around EUR 34 million through EU Horizon Europe Cluster 4 funding. Results developed under vera.ai are being further taken up by some members of the consortium in the ongoing AI-CODE project, which ensures continuity of tools and expertise supported through earlier EU funding. Furthermore, the Commission also supports other relevant projects contributing to information integrity, such as European Narrative Observatory pilots, recurring funding to foster media literacy under Creative Europe, and support to the European Digital Media Observatory (EDMO) under Digital Europe7. As part of the EDS, the Commission has also launched new initiatives, such as a call for proposals for a common research framework8 that will support technical infrastructure and research on information integrity. This is complemented by support for a European Network of Fact-Checkers. Europe must be better equipped to protect the integrity of its public debate and democratic processes. For that reason, under the new Multiannual Financial Framework, the Commission proposes to continue supporting innovation across the media sector. As part of the proposed

E-10-2026-001003.t: Digitalisation and innovation in special education
qt: to the Commission Ilhan Kyuchyuk (Renew) Subject:

How does the Commission ensure that when evaluating innovative projects under programmes such as EIC Pathfinder Open, appropriate experts with interdisciplinary expertise are included, particularly when projects combine advanced technologies with educational, psychological and social objectives, including projects aimed at individuals with neurodevelopmental needs or special educational and social needs?

To what extent do evaluations under the EIC and other programmes take into account the social and ethical impact of AI-based technological solutions on individuals with neurodevelopmental needs or special educational and social needs, and how does the Commission ensure that these evaluations are transparent and consistent?

How does the Commission assess the originality, international patent potential, and global market potential of innovations targeting neurodiversity and social innovation, and how is the risk of the EU falling behind non-EU countries in strategic AI technologies managed?
at: (English version) to the Commission Ilhan Kyuchyuk (Renew) (11 March 2026) Subject: Digitalisation and innovation in special education 1. How does the Commission ensure that when evaluating innovative projects under programmes such as EIC Pathfinder Open, appropriate experts with interdisciplinary expertise are included, particularly when projects combine advanced technologies with educational, psychological and social objectives, including projects aimed at individuals with neurodevelopmental needs or special educational and social needs? 2. To what extent do evaluations under the EIC and other programmes take into account the social and ethical impact of AIbased technological solutions on individuals with neurodevelopmental needs or special educational and social needs, and how does the Commission ensure that these evaluations are transparent and consistent? 3. How does the Commission assess the originality, international patent potential, and global market potential of innovations targeting neurodiversity and social innovation, and how is the risk of the EU falling behind non-EU countries in strategic AI technologies managed? (8 June 2026) The Commission ensures inclusion of appropriate multidisciplinary expertise in the evaluation of proposals under programmes such as the European Innovation Council (EIC) by appointing independent external experts covering the relevant scientific, technological and socioeconomic domains, including education, psychology and neurodevelopmental needs where relevant. Experts are selected from dedicated pools, trained and monitored to ensure compliance with rules and avoidance of bias. Panels are composed to ensure diversity and expertise aligned with the proposal content. Evaluation criteria are defined in the annual EIC work programme and include assessment of societal and ethical aspects, including for AI-based solutions, under the impact criterion. This covers potential benefits, risks and compliance with ethical standards. Transparency and consistency are ensured through standardised procedures like calibration of experts, quality checks and evaluation committees which review and finalise scores. Originality, intellectual property strategy and global market potential are assessed using the award criteria defined in the EIC work programme; this includes novelty, breakthrough nature, market development and scalability. Targeted calls and strategic monitoring of global trends contribute to reducing dependencies and strengthening the EU’s position in strategic AI technologies. Central to the Commission’s strategy is also the Resource for AI Science in Europe (RAISE) (1) and the European Frontier AI Initiative (2), which seek to pool resources and talent to bolster the EU's AI ecosystem through three key pillars: strategic research and innovation, expert consultation and support for the development of highly capable European AI models.

E-10-2026-001002.t: State of play of the unitary patent system, ratification of the Unified Patent Court Agreement and deadlock over the unitary supplementary protection certificate
qt: to the Commission Tsvetelina Penkova (S&D) Subject:

What concrete measures has the Commission undertaken, or intends to undertake, to encourage the remaining participating Member States to ratify the Unified Patent Court Agreement, thus ensuring the full effectiveness and geographical coverage of the unitary patent system?

What is the current state of play of negotiations in the Council on the proposed supplementary protection certificate with unitary effect, and what steps does the Commission intend to take to overcome the current deadlock and ensure that European industry can benefit from a coherent and cost-effective unitary protection framework?
at: (English version) to the Commission Tsvetelina Penkova (S&D) (11 March 2026) Subject: State of play of the unitary patent system, ratification of the Unified Patent Court Agreement and deadlock over the unitary supplementary protection certificate 1. What concrete measures has the Commission undertaken, or intends to undertake, to encourage the remaining participating Member States to ratify the Unified Patent Court Agreement, thus ensuring the full effectiveness and geographical coverage of the unitary patent system? 2. What is the current state of play of negotiations in the Council on the proposed supplementary protection certificate with unitary effect, and what steps does the Commission intend to take to overcome the current deadlock and ensure that European industry can benefit from a coherent and cost-effective unitary protection framework? (13 May 2026) 1. The Commission has taken and continues to take every opportunity to stress the importance for the remaining nine Member States (1) to join the unitary patent system as soon as possible, which has also been highlighted in the Draghi report. The Commission has underlined this objective in several of its recent Communications (for instance COM(2025)27 0 (2) and COM(2025)500 (3)). Moreover, the Commission is actively communicating the advantages of the unitary patent system for users, and its successful operation since the launch in 2023, including in terms of high uptake by EU businesses. In 2026, the Commission intends to deliver a report on the functioning of the unitary patent system, which should provide a solid basis for Member States’ reflections on joining it. 2. The Commission is actively supporting the Council in the ongoing negotiations on the reform of supplementary protection certificates (SPCs). The European Parliament has adopted its position on the reform back in February 2024. Discussions in the Council are still ongoing. The Commission remains committed to deliver on an SPC system that is effective, legally sound and ensures accountability to EU institutions.
