E-10-2026-001001.t: Implementation deadline in Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF) regions
qt: to the Commission Juan Fernando López Aguilar (S&D) Subject:

Under the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF), the implementation deadline is 31 August 2026. This instrument represents an unprecedented effort of European solidarity aimed at boosting economic recovery, social and territorial cohesion, and the green and digital transitions. As the deadline approaches, several regional governments responsible for implementing RRF-funded projects have reported insurmountable practical difficulties associated with the timelines for completing large-scale structural projects. In some cases, a significant part of the resources is already committed or at an advanced stage of implementation, but there is a risk that the implementation of all the funds will not be able to be completed within the timeframe currently foreseen. Unfortunately, and despite the efforts made, this could result in a loss of resources intended for strategic investments and for territorial cohesion in various regions. In light of this: 1.
Does the Commission intend to propose measures that would relax the deadlines for implementing the RRF or for the submission of justifications?
Does the Commission envisage any extraordinary measures under Article 349 TFEU should such a situation arise in an outermost region?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.4.2026) The Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF) was established as a temporary instrument with a clear end date in 2026. In line with the legal deadlines and the temporary nature of the Facility, the Commission must make the final payments by 31 December 2026. The RRF Regulation does not allow any flexibility regarding the satisfactory fulfilment of milestones and targets after August 20261. The Commission is working closely with Member States to address implementation bottlenecks. In the Communication ‘NextGenerationEU - The road to 2026’2, the Commission has set a clear path forward guiding Member States to take all the necessary actions to ensure a smooth implementation of the RRF in its final months. In particular, the RRF Regulation3 allows Member States to revise recovery and resilience plans if objective circumstances make it impossible for them to deliver on the previously agreed commitments. Member States can request targeted amendments to their plans and the Commission will support such revisions within the framework of the RRF Regulation. To this end, the Commission has also taken steps to simplify the process for amending the plans. If, despite the above-mentioned efforts, some of the last milestones or targets are not satisfactorily fulfilled, the corresponding disbursement will not be made. The Commission acknowledges the difficulties faced by several outermost regions in implementing RRF funds within the given deadline. However, it does not envisage proposing any extraordinary measures under article 349 Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union in this context.
1 Article 20(5)(d) Regulation (EU) 2021/241 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 12 February 2021
establishing the Recovery and Resilience Facility (OJ L 057, 18.2.2021). 2 COM(2025) 310 final. 3 Article 21 of the Recovery and Resilience Facility Regulation (please see footnote 1).

E-10-2026-000998.t: Fraud in the cultural and creative sectors through misuse of artificial intelligence
qt: to the Commission Lara Magoni (ECR) Subject:

Fraud associated with the cultural and creative content generated by artificial intelligence is a systemic challenge to the entire European creative sector, including music, the visual arts, graphic design, audiovisual works, digital publishing and podcasts. Bots, automated traffic and manipulative practices can be used to generate large-scale artificial listening, viewing and interaction, hence altering algorithms, rankings and remuneration systems. These practices deprive legitimate creators of revenue and visibility, diminish content pluralism and undermine consumer trust, leading to a distorted market. For example, in the music sector, around 10 % of the new tracks uploaded each day are generated by AI, of which 85 % are fraudulent, which goes to show the scale of the phenomenon. Such practices violate Article 50 of the AI Act, which states that AI-generated content must be clearly identifiable to ensure transparency, fairness and copyright protection. In the light of this damage to a key sector of Europe’s economy and identity, can the Commission answer the following questions: 1.
How will it ensure the transparent and uniform implementation of the obligations arising from the AI Act in the digital creative sector?
What measures is it considering to ensure economic protection, visibility and recognition for bona fide creators and to strengthen consumer trust in the EU digital market?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.7.2026) The AI Act1 includes transparency obligations to support distinguishing AI-generated content from human content. The AI Office facilitated the development of a Code of Practice2 as a voluntary tool to support compliance with those obligations; the final version of the Code was published on 10 June 2026. The AI Office will also issue guidelines on those obligations, which it intends to adopt by August 2026. Furthermore, providers placing General Purpose AI (GPAI) models on the EU market must put in place a policy to comply with EU copyright law and disclose detailed summaries of training data. To support the implementation of these provisions, a template for a public summary of training content has been developed3, together with a Code of Practice for GPAI models4, to assist providers in complying with those obligations, including identifying and respecting reservations of rights expressed by rightsholders in a machine-readable format and mitigating the risk of copyright-infringing outputs. The Commission is facilitating a process to identify technical solutions for machine readable rights reservation (beyond robot.txt). Under the Apply AI Strategy5, the commission will also launch a study on legal challenges and technological safeguards against copyright-infringing AI outputs. The Commission monitors market and technological developments affecting the cultural and creative sectors and will, if necessary, use its powers, including under EU competition law, to ensure a level playing field. Furthermore, the Commission recently published a study on the discoverability of diverse European content online6 and will present a dedicated AI strategy for the cultural and creative sectors.

1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32024R1689. 2 https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/code-practice-ai-generated-content#ecl-inpage-transparency-ofai-generated-content. 3 https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/explanatory-notice-and-template-public-summary-trainingcontent-general-purpose-ai-models. 4 https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/contents-code-gpai. 5 Communication from the Commission to the European Parliament and the Council, Apply AI Strategy, COM(2025) 723 final. 6 https://op.europa.eu/en/publication-detail/-/publication/34da2669-32b4-11f1-be39-01aa75ed71a1/language-en.

E-10-2026-000997.t: Turkish F-16 fighter jets in the illegally occupied part of Cyprus
qt: to the Commission Nikolas Farantouris (The Left) Subject:

After an Iranian drone was recently shot down in the Republic of Cyprus, Member States such as Greece, France and Spain responded by sending combat aircraft and ships to Cyprus to bolster air defence. Türkiye, in turn, sent six F-16 fighter jets to the illegally occupied part of Cyprus12. This raises legitimate concerns about military escalation and constitutes a projection of power against two EU Member States. At the same time, the deployment of US-made aircraft on the territory of an unrecognised entity raises questions as to compliance with rules on the export of defence materials. This development comes at a time when the European Union has repeatedly called on Türkiye to align itself with the principles of good neighbourliness and with the EU’s positions on the Eastern Mediterranean and the Cyprus problem3. In light of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Is the transfer and deployment of military aircraft from Türkiye to an illegally occupied EU territory compatible with the principles of the European acquis?
What is its assessment of this specific action on the basis of the principle of good neighbourliness, which is a key prerequisite for the European Union’s relations with Türkiye?
In the current context of escalation in the Eastern Mediterranean, does it consider that the political conditions for further deepening the customs union with Türkiye are being met?

https://www.kathimerini.gr/politics/564115192/i-toyrkia-esteile-exi-f-16-sta-katechomena/. https://www.fdd.org/analysis/2026/03/09/turkish-deployment-of-f-16s-in-occupied-portion-of-cyprus-raisestensions-in-eastern-mediterranean/. https://enlargement.ec.europa.eu/document/download/4bb4ddd1-4f20-4ee0-92db926996ec8dd1_en?filename=t%C3%BCrkiye-report-2025.pdf.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (8.5.2026) The EU has a strategic interest in a secure and stable environment in the Eastern Mediterranean. The Commission has repeatedly underlined, most recently in the 2025 Enlargement report1, that Türkiye is expected to make an unequivocal commitment to good neighbourly relations, international agreements and the peaceful settlement of disputes. A comprehensive settlement of the Cyprus issue would significantly contribute to sustainable stability and security in the region. The EU has welcomed the support provided by Member States through the deployment of military assets in the Eastern Mediterranean and in support of Cyprus and remains determined to defend its interests and those of its Member States. The Joint Communication on EU-Türkiye relations2 of 2023 recommends resuming Council discussions on the modernisation of the Customs Union if Türkiye keeps addressing trade irritants and circumvention of EU sanctions. It further indicates that a broader environment conducive to the resumption of Cyprus settlement talks is needed to open negotiations for the modernisation of the Customs Union.

E-10-2026-000996.t: Humanitarian situation in Cuba and implementation of the EU’s exclusion regulation
qt: to the Commission Nikolaos Anadiotis (NI) Subject:

In a recent open letter published in the European press, a Cuban citizen describes severe shortages of essential goods, medicines and electricity, attributing the worsening living conditions to the effects of, among other things, the economic embargo and secondary sanctions affecting international trade and access to humanitarian material1. This situation raises questions as to the extent to which European businesses and financial institutions avoid legitimate transactions with Cuba, despite the existence of Regulation (EC) No 2271/96 (the ‘blocking Statute’). It also raises questions as to the role of the Union in ensuring the population’s unrestricted access to essential goods. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

What is its assessment of the impact of third-country extraterritorial sanctions on Cuba’s access to medicines, medical equipment and energy infrastructure, particularly when European economic operators are involved?
What steps has it taken to fully implement the blocking statute to ensure that European businesses can carry out legitimate transactions without the risk of secondary sanctions?
Does it intend to take specific humanitarian or financial initiatives to support Cuba's civilian population in areas such as health and energy?
https://infolibre.gr/2026/02/18/anoichti-epistoli-pros-ton-kosmo-apo-tin-koyva-mia-gynaika-toy-laoykataggellei/.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (26.5.2026) The assessment of third-country extraterritorial sanctions on Cuba should be framed within the EU’s commitment to safeguarding legitimate trade and humanitarian access. The EU rejects the extraterritorial application of unilateral sanctions by third countries, as it considers such measures contrary to international law. In this context, the EU has established legislative instruments, notably the ‘Blocking Statute’1, which shields European economic operators from the legal effects of third-country sanctions and to ensure the continuity of lawful business activities, including with Cuba. Member States’ authorities are responsible for implementing the Blocking Statute, including with respect to penalties for possible breaches. EU operators whose economic and financial interests are affected by the extra-territorial application of those laws are obligated to inform the Commission. Since 1994, the Commission has been actively engaged in addressing the most pressing needs of the population in Cuba. In 2024-2025, the Commission released close to EUR 10 million to provide lifesaving health services, as well as emergency relief to hurricane-stricken communities. As an immediate response to the steadfast deterioration of the humanitarian crisis in 2026, the Commission has allocated additional EUR 6 million in humanitarian aid to support the most vulnerable with health and food assistance and potable water. Regarding support in the areas of health and energy, biotechnology and renewable energy are the priority sectors under the EU’s Global Gateway Investment Agenda in Cuba 2.
1 Council Regulation (EC) No 2271/96, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/1996/2271/oj/eng. 2 https://international-partnerships.ec.europa.eu/countries/cuba_en.

E-10-2026-000995.t: Status of the British Sovereign Base Areas in Cyprus and security of an EU Member State
qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Nikolaos Anadiotis (NI) Subject:

During the tensions in the Middle East, Greece and several other European states sent military forces to protect Cyprus, while the United Kingdom has been hesitant and slow to protect its bases12. Since 1960, Akrotiri and Dhekelia have been the sovereign territory of the United Kingdom within the Republic of Cyprus. The bases have been repeatedly described as a remnant of colonialism and recent international developments (see the decision of the International Court of Justice at The Hague on the Chagos Archipelago and the agreement for it to be returned to Mauritius) have brought the debate on the decolonisation of military territories back to the fore3. According to Protocol No 3 of the Act concerning the conditions of accession of Cyprus to the EU, the bases have a special status to which EU law applies only to a limited extent4. In view of the above, can the Vice-President / High Representative answer the following: 1.
How does she assess the status of the British Sovereign Base Areas in Cyprus in relation to the sovereignty and security of a Member State?

Does she consider that the preservation of a third country’s sovereign territory within a Member State is consistent with the principles of the Union and the modern decolonisation principles of international law?
Does she intend to consider initiatives to support Cyprus in a possible renegotiation of the status of the bases with the United Kingdom?

https://www.philenews.com/kipros/article/1689318/inomeno-vasilio-stelni-polemiko-plio-stin-kipro-giaiperaspisi-ton-vretanikon-vaseon. https://www.reuters.com/world/uk/uk-planning-send-warship-defend-cyprus-military-base-times-newspapersays-2026-03-03. https://www.reuters.com/article/world/world-court-britain-must-return-indian-ocean-islands-to-mauritiusidUSKCN1QE1WV/. http://data.europa.eu/eli/treaty/acc_2003/act_1/pro_3/sign.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.5.2026) 1. The presence of the United Kingdom (UK) Sovereign Base Areas (SBAs) in Cyprus is a matter for Cyprus. 2. The EU Treaties do not apply to the UK SBAs as these areas are the territory of the UK, except a limited application by virtue of Protocol No 31 and of the EU-UK Withdrawal Agreement2, notably the Protocol relating to the SBAs of the UK in Cyprus. 3. The European Council of 19 March 2026 acknowledged the intention of Cyprus to initiate a discussion with the UK on the UK bases in Cyprus and expressed readiness to provide assistance as needed. The EU has a strategic interest in a stable and secure Eastern Mediterranean.

E-10-2026-000994.t: Zelenskyy threatens Orbán with Ukrainian tanks: When will the EU stop tolerating these crazy threats?
qt: to the Commission Erik Kaliňák (NI), Judita Laššáková (NI), Ľuboš Blaha (NI), Branislav Ondruš (NI), Katarína Roth Neveďalová (NI), Monika Beňová (NI) Subject:

Volodymyr Zelenskyy shocked the world at a press conference: if Orbán blocks billions from the EU, he will ‘give his address to our boys so they can talk to him in their own language’. This is not just a provocative tweet – it is a direct threat of force against the leader of an EU Member State, which grossly violates Article 2(4) of the UN Charter (prohibiting the threat or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of any state). Zelenskyy, the head of a country that wants to join the EU, is blatantly escalating the conflict at a time when the EU is sending hundreds of billions of euros as well as weapons to Ukraine. This is no longer just a diplomatic faux pas – it is an open call for aggression against Member States. But that’s not all: Ukraine has halted oil transits through the Druzhba pipeline, rejected EUnominated experts, and its representatives are issuing repeated threats against Hungary and Slovakia. How far does Zelenskyy want to take this? 1.
Does the Commission consider it acceptable for the president of a candidate country to openly threaten military action against the prime minister of an EU Member State?
What immediate and resolute consequences does the Commission plan to bring to bear in order to stop this reckless behaviour?

In view of the halting of oil transits, the rejection of EU experts and the constant threats against the leaders of Member States, does the Commission still seriously claim that Ukraine is ready for membership and shares European values such as peace, respect for sovereignty and the rule of law?
at: (English version) to the Commission Erik Kaliňák (NI), Judita Laššáková (NI), Ľuboš Blaha (NI), Branislav Ondruš (NI), Katarína Roth Neveďalová (NI), Monika Beňová (NI) (10 March 2026) Subject: Zelenskyy threatens Orbán with Ukrainian tanks: When will the EU stop tolerating these crazy threats? This is not just a provocative tweet — it is a direct threat of force against the leader of an EU Member State, which grossly violates Article 2(4) of the UN Charter (prohibiting the threat or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of any state). Zelenskyy, the head of a country that wants to join the EU, is blatantly escalating the conflict at a time when the EU is sending hundreds of billions of euros as well as weapons to Ukraine. This is no longer just a diplomatic faux pas — it is an open call for aggression against Member States. But that’s not all: Ukraine has halted oil transits through the Druzhba pipeline, rejected EU-nominated experts, and its representatives are issuing repeated threats against Hungary and Slovakia. How far does Zelenskyy want to take this? 1. Does the Commission consider it acceptable for the president of a candidate country to openly threaten military action against the prime minister of an EU Member State? 2. What immediate and resolute consequences does the Commission plan to bring to bear in order to stop this reckless behaviour? 3. In view of the halting of oil transits, the rejection of EU experts and the constant threats against the leaders of Member States, does the Commission still seriously claim that Ukraine is ready for membership and shares European values such as peace, respect for sovereignty and the rule of law? (7 May 2026) The Commission expects all partners, including candidate countries, to act in line with the principles of the UN Charter and to communicate responsibly. In this sense, the Commission underlines that any suggestion of the use of force against Member States or their political leaders is incompatible with the principles of the UN Charter. The EU’s partnership with Ukraine is based on shared commitments to international law and respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity. The Commission will maintain close cooperation and trust with all Member States. At the same time, the Commission recalls that the EU remains committed to supporting Ukraine, in the face of Russia’s war of aggression, which is a clear violation of international law and of the UN Charter, and European values such as peace, respect for sovereignty and the rule of law. In addition, Russia’s unprovoked and unjustified full-scale invasion of Ukraine gravely undermines European and global security.

E-10-2026-000993.t: Use of EU funds for ‘Voices – the European Festival of Journalism and Media Freedom’
qt: to the Commission Francesco Torselli (ECR), Carlo Fidanza (ECR), Lara Magoni (ECR), Marco Squarta (ECR), Sergio Berlato (ECR), Alessandro Ciriani (ECR), Mariateresa Vivaldini (ECR), Stefano Cavedagna (ECR), Nicola Procaccini (ECR), Chiara Gemma (ECR), Pietro Fiocchi (ECR), Carlo Ciccioli (ECR) Subject:

On 10-12 March, Florence will host ‘Voices – the European Festival of Journalism and Media Freedom’. Now into its third year, the event is funded by EU funds under a Commission call that supposedly made available a total of EUR 3 million (covering up to 90 % of eligible costs) for three editions of the festival. The event boasts the patronage of the Municipality of Florence, Corecom Toscana and the Order of Journalists. The list of speakers – with Fanpage director Francesco Cancellato, La Repubblica journalist Paolo Berizzi, UN Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese and Università per Stranieri di Siena rector Tommaso Montanari topping the bill – is redolent of a startling political and cultural bias in favour of the centre-left. Guests include Sandro Ruotolo, MEP for the Partito Democratico, and Barbara Floridia, a senator for the Five Star Movement. In light of this, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
What is the total amount of public money intended for the staging of the festival?
Which individuals cherry-picked the speakers and on the basis of what criteria?
Is the Commission aware of the event line-up and the predominance of speakers of a certain political and cultural persuasion?

(22 May 2026) The Voices European Festival of Journalism and Media freedom receives co-funding from the Commission, following an open call for proposals with a maximum total contribution of EUR 3 000 000, for the duration of 27 months. This is a preparatory action initiated by the European Parliament, which are typically defined as experimental initiatives designed to test the feasibility of new actions and prepare new programmes. The festival is organised as a project carried out by a consortium of European and local organisations with strong EU-wide networks for media. As such, the choice of speakers is made by a dedicated coordinator designated by each of the organising partners. The Commission has no involvement in this process. It should also be recalled that the concerned call for proposals included strict, transparent and pre-established criteria to select projects and that the Commission does not have a role in implementation decisions taken by the beneficiaries. The Commission is committed to ensuring that projects are properly implemented in accordance with the terms of each agreement in line with the Financial Regulation (1).

E-10-2026-000992.t: Decommissioning and recycling of offshore wind turbines
qt: to the Commission Auke Zijlstra (PfE) Subject:

According to recent studies by TNO1, the costs of decommissioning offshore wind farms could be significantly higher than previously estimated. For a wind farm of approximately 2 GW, the costs could be as high as EUR 345 million. At the same time, consideration is being given to not removing the foundations of offshore wind turbines entirely, but to cutting them down to six metres below the water surface. Given the rapid expansion of offshore wind energy in the EU, the question arises as to whether such practices are compatible with European rules on waste management and recycling, in particular under the Waste Framework Directive and the objectives of the Circular Economy Action Plan. 1.
Does the Commission consider that the cutting of offshore wind turbine foundations to approximately six metres below the water surface constitutes full decommissioning?
Is the partial abandonment of such structures at sea compatible with EU rules on waste management and with the objectives in the areas of recycling and the circular economy?
Is the Commission considering EU rules or guidelines for the complete removal and recycling of offshore wind installations at the end of their life cycle?

at: (English version) to the Commission Auke Zijlstra (PfE) (10 March 2026) Subject: Decommissioning and recycling of offshore wind turbines According to recent studies by TNO (1), the costs of decommissioning offshore wind farms could be significantly higher than previously estimated. For a wind farm of approximately 2 GW, the costs could be as high as EUR 345 million. At the same time, consideration is being given to not removing the foundations of offshore wind turbines entirely, but to cutting them down to six metres below the water surface. Given the rapid expansion of offshore wind energy in the EU, the question arises as to whether such practices are compatible with European rules on waste management and recycling, in particular under the Waste Framework Directive and the objectives of the Circular Economy Action Plan. 1. Does the Commission consider that the cutting of offshore wind turbine foundations to approximately six metres below the water surface constitutes full decommissioning? 2. Is the partial abandonment of such structures at sea compatible with EU rules on waste management and with the objectives in the areas of recycling and the circular economy? 3. Is the Commission considering EU rules or guidelines for the complete removal and recycling of offshore wind installations at the end of their life cycle? (7 July 2026) EU legislation does not include a definition of offshore wind turbines decommissioning. The Waste Framework Directive (1) (WFD) requires that waste be managed without endangering human health and harming the environment. In particular, Article 13 paragraph 1(a) requires Member States to take necessary measures to manage waste without risk to water, air, soil, plants or animals. The Commission is carefully evaluating possible aspects related to circularity which may be relevant to wind turbines in the framework of the impact assessment for the Circular Economy Act (2) planned for adoption later in 2026. Moreover, the Marine Strategy Framework Directive (3) requires Member States to ensure that human activities, including decommissioning, do not adversely affect the Good Environmental Status of marine waters. Partial removal of offshore wind turbine foundations must be assessed against Descriptors 1 (4), 6 (5), 10 (6) and 11 (7), ensuring no lasting harm to ecosystems or circular economy principles. Scientific studies (8) give some insight into how foundations of offshore wind turbine foundations can function as artificial reefs, possibly enhancing biodiversity. As examples, the abundance of Atlantic cod shows that rock protections around the foundations attracted most fish, and innovative ways to incorporate European flat oyster habitats into the design of offshore wind infrastructure are being tested. Understanding and minimising environmental impacts of offshore wind, including decommissioning, was also addressed in a recent call under Horizon Europe (9).

E-10-2026-000991.t: Ethical boundaries regarding abortion policies in Member States in response to  My Voice, My Choice
qt: to the Commission Bert-Jan Ruissen (ECR), Aurelijus Veryga (ECR), Jadwiga Wiśniewska (ECR), Margarita de la Pisa Carrión (PfE) Subject:
Ethical boundaries regarding abortion policies in Member States in response to My Voice, My Choice

Given that the European Social Fund Plus (ESF+) is designed to combat poverty, could the Commission clarify how it will ensure that funds allocated to abortion-related services are used legally, what specific limits, safeguards or monitoring mechanisms are in place to prevent misuse, and how does the Commission ensure that such financing respects the diversity of ethical frameworks and legal provisions across Member States?

Considering the significant differences in abortion legislation and ethical limits among Member States, how does the Commission ensure that ESF+ funding respects national frameworks, including variations in gestational limits, medical requirements and legal definitions of abortion?

In certain Member States, including France, medical termination of pregnancy may legally be carried out until term following a diagnosis of Down syndrome. In light of the EU’s obligations under the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities and Articles 10, 21 and 26 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights, how does the Commission ensure that ESF+ funding does not contribute, directly or indirectly, to discriminatory practices on the basis of disability?
Supporter1
This question is supported by a Member other than the authors: Stephen Nikola Bartulica (ECR).
at: (English version) to the Commission Bert-Jan Ruissen (ECR), Aurelijus Veryga (ECR), Jadwiga Wiśniewska (ECR), Margarita de la Pisa Carrión (PfE) (10 March 2026) Subject: Ethical boundaries regarding abortion policies in Member States in response to My Voice, My Choice 1. Given that the European Social Fund Plus (ESF+) is designed to combat poverty, could the Commission clarify how it will ensure that funds allocated to abortion-related services are used legally, what specific limits, safeguards or monitoring mechanisms are in place to prevent misuse, and how does the Commission ensure that such financing respects the diversity of ethical frameworks and legal provisions across Member States? 2. Considering the significant differences in abortion legislation and ethical limits among Member States, how does the Commission ensure that ESF+ funding respects national frameworks, including variations in gestational limits, medical requirements and legal definitions of abortion? 3. In certain Member States, including France, medical termination of pregnancy may legally be carried out until term following a diagnosis of Down syndrome. In light of the EU’s obligations under the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities and Articles 10, 21 and 26 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights, how does the Commission ensure that ESF+ funding does not contribute, directly or indirectly, to discriminatory practices on the basis of disability? Supporter (1) (15 June 2026) In line with the principle of shared management, it is the primary responsibility of Member States to ensure compliance with the applicable laws when it comes to their national programmes under the European Social Fund+ (ESF+) (1). To this end, Member States authorities carry out management verifications and audits to ensure that the expenditure is legal and regular. The Commission also ensures that Member States have management and control systems that comply with the Common Provisions Regulation (CPR) (2) and that these systems function effectively and efficiently during the implementation of the programmes. The ESF+ strand is implemented jointly by the Commission and Member States. However, the ESF+ legislative framework leaves the responsibility for setting out the eligibility rules for support under the ESF+ to the national and regional authorities of the Member States. They have to do so within the limits set out in the regulations applicable to the ESF+ and in respect of other relevant EU legislation and Treaty principles. Therefore, it would be up to Member States, if they choose to do so, to define the conditions under which eligible women can access safe and affordable abortion care in their territory, and how such funding would be delivered, in full compliance with the relevant EU legislation and Treaty principles. When implementing the ESF +, Member States need to respect applicable law. This includes the Charter of Fundamental Rights as well as the United Nations Convention on the rights of persons with disabilities (UNCRPD).

This question is supported by a Member other than the authors: Stephen Nikola Bartulica (ECR). E-10-2026-000990.t: Contempt for EU Treaties by overstepping mandate re. ‘My Voice, My Choice’
qt: to the Commission Bert-Jan Ruissen (ECR), Aurelijus Veryga (ECR), Jadwiga Wiśniewska (ECR), Margarita de la Pisa Carrión (PfE), Laurence Trochu (ECR) Subject:

By explicitly using the European Social Fund Plus (ESF+) to pay for abortions in response to the European Citizens’ Initiative ‘My Voice, My Choice’, the Commission has shown its contempt for the EU Treaties, as abortion policies are a competence of the Member States. By circumventing the treaties and legislative process, the Commission is acting outside of its mandate. 1.
Could the Commission please clarify on what legal basis it has chosen to act outside of its mandate and what legal basis is used to fund abortions using the ESF+?

The Commission explicitly labels abortion as healthcare and refers to Article 168(7) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union and the ESF+. In many Member States, abortion is in the penal code and definitely not labelled as healthcare. How can the Commission unilaterally expand the definition of healthcare without the unanimous consent of the Member States?

Given that the ESF+ is designed to combat poverty, why has the Commission opted to divert resources towards funding abortions instead of providing comprehensive support to women facing challenging circumstances, enabling them to both choose motherhood and raise their children with dignity?
Supporter1
This question is supported by a Member other than the authors: Stephen Nikola Bartulica (ECR).
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (13.5.2026) The Commission’s follow up to the Citizen’s initiative ‘My Voice, My Choice’ falls within the EU’s supportive competence. Any support must comply with the limitations in Article 168(7) TFEU. One of the specific objectives of the of the European Social Fund Plus (ESF+), set out in Article 4(1)(k), is that of enhancing equal and timely access to quality, sustainable and affordable services, including the access to person-centred care including healthcare1. Therefore, the ESF+ can support initiatives, selected at national level, that aim to ensure and enhance equal and timely access to healthcare services. The Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) has held that the Treaty provisions on the freedom to provide services include the freedom for recipients of healthcare, including people in need of medical treatment2. With regard to medical termination of pregnancy carried out in line with the law of the country where it takes place, the CJEU has found that it ‘constitutes a service within the meaning of Article 57 TFEU3. The EU has in place ambitious legislation on maternity, paternity and non-transferable paid parental leave, through the Work-Life Balance4 and Pregnant Workers Directives5. The Commission will also contribute to combatting poverty through the upcoming EU AntiPoverty Strategy. Since ESF+ is in shared management, the Commission is not diverting any resources, as Member States define their specific objectives for the use of the ESF+ funding.
1 Regulation (EU) 2021/1057 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 24 June 2021 establishing the

European Social Fund Plus (ESF+) and repealing Regulation (EU) No 1296/2013, OJ L 231, 30.6.2021, pp. 21– 59, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2021/1057/oj. 2 See recital 26, Patients’ Rights Directive, as well as judgements of 31 January 1984, Graziana Luisi and Giuseppe Carbone v Ministero del Tesoro, C-286/82 and 26/83, ECLI:EU:C:1984:35 and judgement of 28 April 1998 Kohll, C-158/96, paragraph 29 and subsequent case law. 3 See judgement of 4 October 1991, Grogan, C-159/90, where the CJEU confirmed that abortion care is a service under internal market law, meaning that citizens can travel abroad to obtain those medical services. 4 Directive (EU) 2019/1158 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 20 June 2019 on work-life balance for parents and carers and repealing Council Directive 2010/18/EU, OJ L 188/79, ELI: https://eurlex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:32019L1158. 5 Council Directive 92/85/EEC of 19 October 1992 on the introduction of measures to encourage improvements in the safety and health at work of pregnant workers and workers who have recently given birth or are breastfeeding (tenth individual Directive within the meaning of Article 16 (1) of Directive 89/391/EEC), OJ L 348, 28.11.1992, pp. 1–7, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/1992/85/oj.

E-10-2026-000989.t: German Bundeskartellamt inquiry into Amazon pricing practices
qt: to the Commission Pascal Arimont (PPE), Andreas Schwab (PPE), Dan-Ştefan Motreanu (PPE), Olivier Chastel (Renew), Dimitris Tsiodras (PPE), Tomáš Zdechovský (PPE), Christian Doleschal (PPE), Martine Kemp (PPE), Veronika Cifrová Ostrihoňová (Renew), Rasmus Andresen (Verts/ALE), Benoit Cassart (Renew), Wouter Beke (PPE), Manuela Ripa (PPE), Sabine Verheyen (PPE), François-Xavier Bellamy (PPE), Fernand Kartheiser (NI), Liesbet Sommen (PPE), Elio Di Rupo (S&D), Leila Chaibi (The Left), Thomas Waitz (Verts/ALE), Radan Kanev (PPE), Alexandra Mehnert (PPE), Stéphanie Yon-Courtin (Renew), Branislav Ondruš (NI), Malika Sorel (NI) Subject:

After the German Bundeskartellamt launched an investigation into Amazon’s price control mechanisms in June 2025, the authority issued a ruling on 5 February 2026 stating that the US company must repay EUR 59 million in economic benefits. The authority is concerned that Amazon’s behaviour restricts the competitive process in the marketplace, hinders sellers’ economic viability and entrenches Amazon’s own dominance by blocking other online retailers from offering lower prices. This behaviour is also likely to be a violation of Article 5(3) of the Digital Markets Act1, which prohibits gatekeepers from preventing business users from offering the same products or services via different channels at prices or conditions different from those it offers via the gatekeeper. Commission Executive Vice-President Teresa Ribera has previously said that the Commission is assessing Amazon’s pricing practices and closely coordinating with the Bundeskartellamt on this investigation. 1.
What steps has the Commission taken since July 2025 to ensure that Amazon does not violate Article 5(3) of the Digital Markets Act?
Will the Commission open a formal non-compliance investigation into Amazon?

Considering the seriousness of the risks to market concentration and for the economic viability of independent sellers, will the Commission impose interim measures to ensure that Amazon immediately stops controlling independent sellers’ prices?

Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 September 2022 on contestable and fair markets in the digital sector and amending Directives (EU) 2019/1937 and (EU) 2020/1828 (Digital Markets Act) (OJ L 265, 12.10.2022, p. 1, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/1925/oj).
at: (English version) to the Commission Pascal Arimont (PPE), Andreas Schwab (PPE), Dan-Ştefan Motreanu (PPE), Olivier Chastel (Renew), Dimitris Tsiodras (PPE), Tomáš Zdechovský (PPE), Christian Doleschal (PPE), Martine Kemp (PPE), Veronika Cifrová Ostrihoňová (Renew), Rasmus Andresen (Verts/ALE), Benoit Cassart (Renew), Wouter Beke (PPE), Manuela Ripa (PPE), Sabine Verheyen (PPE), François-Xavier Bellamy (PPE), Fernand Kartheiser (NI), Liesbet Sommen (PPE), Elio Di Rupo (S&D), Leila Chaibi (The Left), Thomas Waitz (Verts/ALE), Radan Kanev (PPE), Alexandra Mehnert (PPE), Stéphanie Yon-Courtin (Renew), Branislav Ondruš (NI), Malika Sorel (NI) (10 March 2026) Subject: German Bundeskartellamt inquiry into Amazon pricing practices After the German Bundeskartellamt launched an investigation into Amazon’s price control mechanisms in June 2025, the authority issued a ruling on 5 February 2026 stating that the US company must repay EUR 59 million in economic benefits. The authority is concerned that Amazon’s behaviour restricts the competitive process in the marketplace, hinders sellers’ economic viability and entrenches Amazon’s own dominance by blocking other online retailers from offering lower prices. This behaviour is also likely to be a violation of Article 5(3) of the Digital Markets Act (1), which prohibits gatekeepers from preventing business users from offering the same products or services via different channels at prices or conditions different from those it offers via the gatekeeper. Commission Executive Vice-President Teresa Ribera has previously said that the Commission is assessing Amazon’s pricing practices and closely coordinating with the Bundeskartellamt on this investigation. 1. What steps has the Commission taken since July 2025 to ensure that Amazon does not violate Article 5(3) of the Digital Markets Act? 2.
Will the Commission open a formal non-compliance investigation into Amazon?

3. Considering the seriousness of the risks to market concentration and for the economic viability of independent sellers, will the Commission impose interim measures to ensure that Amazon immediately stops controlling independent sellers’ prices? (5 May 2026) The Commission is monitoring Amazon’s compliance with Article 5(3) of the Digital Markets Act (DMA) (1), including by investigating Amazon’s pricing practices (2). It has sent several requests for information to Amazon and is in an active regulatory dialogue both with Amazon and interested third parties. At the same time, the Commission has cooperated closely with the Bundeskartellamt within the framework of cooperation and coordination provided under the DMA and competition rules. Article 5(3) DMA does not cover all pricing practices but only those that prevent business users from offering the same products or services via different channels at prices different from those they offer via the gatekeeper. To the extent they amount to an abuse of a dominant position, pricing practices can also run afoul of Article 102 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU (TFEU) or national equivalent competition laws. For any conduct not covered by the DMA, the Bundeskartellamt can apply the stricter abuse control provisions under Section 19a of the German Competition Act in addition to Article 102 TFEU and national equivalent, which always remain applicable next to the DMA.

Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 September 2022 on contestable and fair markets in the digital sector and amending Directives (EU) 2019/1937 and (EU) 2020/1828 (Digital Markets Act) (OJ L 265, 12.10.2022, p. 1, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/1925/oj). Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 September 2022 on contestable and fair markets in the digital sector and amending Directives (EU) 2019/1937 and (EU) 2020/1828 (Digital Markets Act), OJ L 265, 12.10.2022, pp. 1-66. This includes the pricing mechanisms the Bundeskartellamt briefly explained under point 4 of the Questions and Answers accompanying the press release for its decision of 5 February 2026, available at https://www.bundeskartellamt.de/SharedDocs/Publikation/EN/Others/Amazon_QandA.pdf?__blob=publicationFile&v=8 .

The Commission remains committed to ensuring effective implementation and enforcement of the DMA. The Commission continues its supervisory and enforcement work in relation to Amazon’s compliance with the DMA, and it will not hesitate to take any measure necessary if justified by the results of an ongoing investigation.

E-10-2026-000988.t: Possible circumvention of EU public procurement law with the construction of a natural history museum in the Elbtower and a new opera house in HafenCity (Hamburg)
qt: to the Commission Fabio De Masi (NI) Subject:

According to reports, the Free and Hanseatic City of Hamburg intends to procure key construction and planning services for two major cultural projects – a natural history museum in the Elbtower and a new opera house in HafenCity – through structures involving private project companies, without conducting an open tender procedure published in the Official Journal of the European Union12. Observers and professional associations have pointed out that public works and service contracts pursuant to Directive 2014/24/EU are typically the norm with projects of this scale involving substantial public funding. This begs the question whether the chosen project structures could be a ploy to bypass EU public procurement law. 1.
When did the Commission initiate an informal examination procedure (e.g. an EU pilot) or request information from Germany and/or the relevant Hamburger authorities?
What is the status of the examination?

E-10-2026-000987.t: Illegal persecution of the red kite in the European Union
qt: to the Commission César Luena (S&D) Subject:

A report by the European LIFE EUROKITE project, based on GPS tracking of more than 3 500 birds of prey across nineteen countries over more than a decade, has revealed that poisoning and shooting are the main illegal causes of death of red kites in Europe. At least 320 illegal deaths of tagged birds have been documented, of which 293 were red kites, with poisoning being responsible for over 74 % of those deaths, often by means of banned substances such as carbofuran. Only eight cases resulted in a conviction before a court of law. Given that the red kite is a species protected under the Birds Directive (2009/147/EC) and that the illegal persecution of birds of prey continues to pose a threat to biodiversity, the following questions arise: 1.
In light of this new scientific data, how does the Commission assess the extent of the illegal persecution of the red kite and other birds of prey in the European Union?
Does the Commission plan to bolster European cooperation, monitoring and data collection mechanisms pertaining to the illegal killing of birds of prey?
What further measures does the Commission envisage to improve the implementation and enforcement of the Birds Directive when it comes to the illegal use of poisons and poaching in the European Union?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (24.4.2026) Article 5 of the Birds Directive1 requires Member States to establish the general system of protection prohibiting, among other actions, the deliberate killing or capture by any method of individuals of all wild birds in the EU, including the red kite (Milvus milvus). Also, the red kite is listed in Annex I of the Directive, which means that it must be subject to special conservation measures concerning their habitat, and Member States must classify special protection areas for its conservation. The Commission considers that the new data on illegal killing of red kites and other birds of prey provided by the LIFE EUROKITE project under the EU programme for the environment and climate action2 are important and must be given the necessary attention by the competent authorities in the affected Member States, who are primarily responsible for the correct implementation of the Directive. The Commission actively promotes cooperation, monitoring and data collection on bird protection among Member States, mainly through dialogue with national authorities, including in the framework of the Nature Directives Expert Group and its Task Force on the Recovery of Birds. In 2023, the Commission published a review of good practices on prevention in relation to combatting the illegal killing, taking of and trade in birds in the EU3. On 31 March 2026, the Commission adopted the guidance document on the general system of protection of bird species under Articles 5 and 9 of the Directive4. This interpretative guidance clarifies legal provisions and compiles the applicable case law of the Court of Justice of the European Union, to assist Member States in their implementation and enforcement actions.
1 Directive 2009/147/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 30 November 2009 on the

conservation of wild birds, OJ L 20, 26.1.2010, p. 7–25. 2 https://www.life-eurokite.eu/. 3 https://op.europa.eu/en/publication-detail/-/publication/3287d532-fdd4-11ed-a05c-01aa75ed71a1. 4 https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_26_760.

(16 June 2026) 1. Direct taxation, such as taxation of windfall or excess profits falls essentially within the competence of Member States. Every Member State remains currently fully competent to address excess profits generated by energy companies in national tax law provided it respects the fundamental freedoms laid down in the Treaties. The Italian excess profit tax but also the EU-level temporary solidarity contribution laid down in Chapter III of Council Regulation (EU) No 2022/1854, which targeted surplus profits of EU companies or permanent establishments with activities in the crude petroleum, natural gas, coal and refinery sectors, was an extraordinary emergency measure applied during the energy crisis of 2022-2023 and justified by a specific set of circumstances at that time. 2. It is the position of the Commission that the EU should stay the course on its long-term strategy of diversification, decarbonisation and Russian fossil fuels phase out. Abandoning it would make the EU more dependent, more vulnerable and weaker. In line with this, the Commission is committed to facilitating the implementation of the REPowerEU Gas Regulation. On 18 March 2026, in light of the conflict in the Middle East and its impact on global energy markets, the Commission published updated guidance (1) on the implementation of the regulation, with a view to reducing any unnecessary barriers to non-Russian gas imports into the EU.

E-10-2026-000984.t: Lack of data and of transparency regarding Moroccan tomatoes entering the EU
qt: to the Commission Mireia Borrás Pabón (PfE) Subject:

In recent months, several operators in the Spanish fruit and vegetables sector have warned that there is less and less transparency with regard to statistical data on tomato imports from Morocco. That state of affairs is making it more difficult to verify compliance with the entry price system and the applicable sanitary, phytosanitary and labour requirements at a time when the import volume is high. Considering that the EU-Morocco Association Agreement establishes tariff preferences and an entry price system to ensure fair competition, the current lack of transparent information stands in the way of checking whether those imports comply with the agreed conditions and with EU sanitary, phytosanitary and labour standards. 1.
Could the Commission explain why detailed data on those imports is not published with the relevant frequency and as required by the legislation?
What action will it take to ensure full transparency and effective compliance with both the statistical framework and the system laid down in the EU-Morocco Association Agreement?
Has the Commission analysed the cumulative impact of Moroccan tomato imports on the EU tomato market for the current season?
at: (English version) to the Commission Mireia Borrás Pabón (PfE) (10 March 2026) Subject: Lack of data and of transparency regarding Moroccan tomatoes entering the EU In recent months, several operators in the Spanish fruit and vegetables sector have warned that there is less and less transparency with regard to statistical data on tomato imports from Morocco. That state of affairs is making it more difficult to verify compliance with the entry price system and the applicable sanitary, phytosanitary and labour requirements at a time when the import volume is high. Considering that the EU-Morocco Association Agreement establishes tariff preferences and an entry price system to ensure fair competition, the current lack of transparent information stands in the way of checking whether those imports comply with the agreed conditions and with EU sanitary, phytosanitary and labour standards. 1. Could the Commission explain why detailed data on those imports is not published with the relevant frequency and as required by the legislation? 2. What action will it take to ensure full transparency and effective compliance with both the statistical framework and the system laid down in the EU-Morocco Association Agreement? 3. Has the Commission analysed the cumulative impact of Moroccan tomato imports on the EU tomato market for the current season? (4 May 2026) The information portal of the Directorate-General for Agriculture and Rural Development (DG AGRI) (1) is based on data transmitted by the EU Member States to the Commission via the Customs Surveillance system (2). The data in the Customs Surveillance system are generated in real time once transmitted by the national customs authorities. Official European statistics on imports of all goods are published by Eurosta t (3). These statistics are published with a delay of 1.5 months after the reference month. The Commission has opened infringement cases against Member States that have failed to comply with the reporting obligations related to the Customs Surveillance system (4). In addition, the Commission is working together with the authorities of the Member States to ensure that missing datasets are completed and transmitted to the Commission as soon as possible. It should be noted that this technical issue is not related to the international framework of the EU-Morocco Association Agreement. Through an analysis of official data made available by relevant national authorities, the Commission regularly monitors the market of fruit and vegetables. The Commission also conducts consultations of experts in the dedicated tomatoes market observatory, including on the import of products into the EU market.

E-10-2026-000983.t: Treatment waiting times, waiting list transparency and pressure on emergency services in Sicily
qt: to the Commission Giuseppe Antoci (The Left) Subject:

According to press reports, in the province of Syracuse, a person with a very serious disability apparently waited 13 months before they were given an appointment. The delay was due to an operational issue in the relevant medical commission1. Meanwhile, a report by the Court of Auditors in Sicily has highlighted problems with waiting lists, data governance and transparency, as well as shortcomings in the regional booking system2. At national level, the General Prosecutor's Office of the Court of Auditors points to persistently long waiting times for accessing treatment and therapies. Regarding emergencies, the SIMEU scientific association has long pointed to a structural medical staff shortage in the Sicilian emergency services. While the organisation of healthcare remains the competence of the Member States, under Article 168 TFEU, the Union contributes to the improvement of public health and, in line with Article 35 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the EU, timely access to treatment and the transparency of healthcare processes influence the effectiveness of rights. In the light of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

Does it intend to promote comparable and public minimum standards for monitoring real waiting times for services3, as well as for data quality/transparency and the interoperability of booking systems?

What support and coordination tools4does it intend to strengthen to help Member States reduce extreme waiting times and the pressure on emergency services linked partly to staff shortages, focusing on the needs of the most vulnerable?

(11 May 2026) The Commission does not envisage establishing standards to monitor waiting times. According to Article 168(7) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (1), Union action shall respect the responsibilities of the Member States for the organisation of health services. The Commission supports Member States through EU4Health projects aimed at systemic improvements of accessibility of health systems, especially for vulnerable groups (3) and actions focused on health workforce challenges (4). In addition, the Commission supports cooperation on measuring performance of health systems through the Health Systems Performance Assessment (HSPA) Expert Group. E-10-2026-000980.t: Ireland’s compliance with Article 25 of the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities
qt: to the Commission Cynthia Ní Mhurchú (Renew) Subject:
What steps is the Commission taking to ensure that Ireland is meeting its obligations under Article 25 of the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (9.6.2026) In line with the requirements of the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (UNCRPD), state parties to the Convention periodically discuss its implementation with the UN Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. In 2021 the Commission created the Disability Platform, which is an expert group composed of the Member States and civil society organisations, to discuss the implementation of the UNCRPD and the EU Strategy for the Rights of Persons with Disabilities 2021-20301. During meetings of the Platform the Member States debrief about their constructive dialogues with the UN Committee, including in relation to health, covered by Article 25 of the UNCRPD. A project funded under the EU4Health resulted in guidelines on improving access to care for people with disabilities2. Eight workshops organised within the project offered Member States practical guidance on implementing the guidelines and shared good practices in improving access to healthcare for persons with disabilities. The guidelines were presented to the Disability Forum and can be used to inform the work of the Disability Platform including experts from Member States, EU-level non-governmental organisations, and organisations representing persons with disabilities. The implementation of guidelines is in the remit of Member States, which are responsible for the design of their health policies and the management and delivery of health services in accordance with Article 168(7) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU.

E-10-2026-000978.t: Attacks on the rule of law by the Government of the Republic of Ecuador
qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Anthony Smith (The Left) Subject:

On 6 March 2026, Ecuador’s Electoral Dispute Tribunal decided to suspend the Citizen Revolution movement, the main opposition party at the head of the second largest parliamentary group in the Ecuadorian National Assembly, from the official register of political parties for a period of nine months. The decision was taken following a complaint lodged by the Ecuadorian public prosecutor’s office in the context of an investigation known as ‘Caja Chica’. That investigation concerns suspected money laundering and irregular financing of the 2023 presidential campaign. During this nine-month period, Citizen Revolution will be removed from the register of political organisations of the National Electoral Council and cannot formally act as a political party. The measure could prevent it from taking part in the local elections scheduled for 2027. The movement’s leaders accuse President Daniel Noboa of instrumentalising the country’s institutions to remove any possibility of opposition to his policies, and have announced that they will be pursuing legal remedies to challenge the suspension. Will the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy therefore: 1.
recognise and condemn this instrumentalisation of Ecuadorian institutions for political ends?
take political and diplomatic action to preserve the rule of law in the Republic of Ecuador?

(30 April 2026) The High Representative/Vice-President and the European External Action Service are following closely the recent suspension of the Revolución Ciudadana political movement. The respect for democratic principles and protection of fundamental freedoms underpin relations between the EU and Ecuador. The deployment of an EU Electoral Observation Mission (EOM) for the 2024-25 elections in Ecuador was part of the EU effort to strengthen the rule of law and electoral transparency in Ecuador (1). In its final report, the EOM noted that Ecuador’s Election Law included the possibility of suspension of political rights from six months to four years, which exceeded the period foreseen under Ecuador’s penal code (2). The EOM cautioned that such a suspension could impose disproportionate restrictions on political rights and recommended a review of the sanctions for electoral offences foreseen by the Election Law. The EU considers that dialogue and cooperation with Ecuador remain the most effective means of preserving and strengthening the country’s rule of law. The EU regularly raises its concerns through diplomatic channels and in formal dialogue mechanisms such as the EU-Ecuador High-Level Political Dialogue and EU-Ecuador Human Rights Dialogue. EU cooperation in support of the rule of law in Ecuador includes activities to fight transnational organised crime, support for human rights, strengthening the country’s judiciary, and support to independent institutions, civil society and human rights defenders that monitor, report on, and advocate for the rule of law in Ecuador.

(5 May 2026) Recital (22) of Directive (EU) 2022/2041 (1) on adequate minimum wages states that well-functioning collective bargaining on wage-setting is an important means to ensure the adequacy of minimum wages. Directive (EU) 2022/2041 contains specific obligations for Member States concerning the promotion of collective bargaining (and not merely non-binding recommendations). In particular, Article 4(2) obliges Member States where the collective bargaining coverage rate is below 80% to establish action plans to promote collective bargaining and to notify them to the Commission (2). The Commission is currently drafting its first report to the European Parliament and the Council on minimum wage protection under Article 10(3) of the directive, which will contain inter alia its analysis of these action plans. The Commission is aware of the adoption by Greece of Law 5278/2026, which has as its main objective to strengthen collective labour agreements, and will examine its compatibility with the provisions of Directive (EU) 2022/2041 in the context of the compliance assessment of the transposition that is currently being carried out. Article 1(3) and 1(4)(b) of Directive (EU) 2022/2041 indicate that this directive is without prejudice to the competence of Member States in setting the level of minimum wages (3) and that it shall not be construed as imposing an obligation on any Member State to declare collective agreements universally applicable. qt: to the Commission Catherine Griset (PfE) Subject:

YouTube, TikTok and Instagram were designated as ‘Very Large Online Platforms’ in 2023 under the Digital Services Act1. However, this designation cannot conceal what is most important here – namely the absence of any large European online video-sharing platform. Once more, we are regulating a market without generating competition against US platforms. The European Union none the less boasts many content creators who are seeking to monetise their work2. France alone is home to 150 000 of these professional creators. These creators are structurally reliant on large US platforms who reap the advertising revenue and arbitrarily set the conditions for monetisation, moderation and content promotion. In order to facilitate the emergence of European online video-sharing platforms: 1.
Will the Commission implement an economic and regulatory environment that is both open and flexible?
Would it consider following the example of X, which has committed to regularly publishing its recommendation algorithm to make it fully transparent?
Why has competition law failed to prevent this market from becoming an oligopoly?

(19 May 2026) The upcoming Audiovisual Media Services Directive (1) review will aim to streamline the regulatory framework for videosharing platforms to ease complexity as well as compliance burden for businesses. Additionally, the review will consider the emerging role of content creators in the audiovisual media landscape, to ensure that the rules applicable to them are fit for purpose, while protecting audiences and fostering creativity. In addition, the EU supports the audiovisual sector through different programmes, currently mainly via Creative Europe’s MEDIA strand (2). The Digital Services Act (3) requires providers of online platforms to set out in their terms and conditions the main parameters used in their recommender systems, including the most significant criteria in determining which content is suggested to users. Very large online platforms and very large online search engines are also required to assess and mitigate systemic risks stemming from their services, including those related to recommender systems. In January 2026, the Commission extended its investigation into X's compliance with its recommender systems’ risk management obligations. The Digital Markets Act (4) also applies to YouTube, TikTok and Instagram to ensure that these services are contestable and do not impose unfair conditions on content creators and audiences. EU competition law does not prohibit dominant positions as such. If a company acquires a strong position lawfully, this is authorised. However, once companies become dominant, they have the responsibility to avoid abusing that position.

E-10-2026-000975.t: Unacceptable deployment of Turkish fighter jets in the occupied territories of the Republic of Cyprus amid the Iranian threat
qt: to the Commission Geadis Geadi (ECR) Subject:

According to official announcements, on 8 March 2026 six Turkish F-16 fighter jets landed at the illegal airport of Tymbou in the occupied territories of the Republic of Cyprus. The deployment and presence of armed fighter jets in the occupied territory of an EU Member State can be understood as an action of military escalation and a cause of instability in the Eastern Mediterranean. Moreover, this move can be seen as an act of hostility towards Israel and towards the forces operating in the wider region. It is worth recalling that Türkiye has been repeatedly accused of lending political and diplomatic support to Iran’s authoritarian regime, as well as of tolerating or indirectly supporting extremist Islamic terrorist organisations in the region. This development may create operational difficulties for deterrence activities aimed at countering the threat posed by Iran, as well as for operations to counter terrorist organisations. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
How does it assess the move in question in the light of security and stability in the Eastern Mediterranean?
Does it intend to call on Türkiye to withdraw the fighter jets from the occupied territory of the Republic of Cyprus and, if it refuses, how does the Commission intend to react?
What measures does it intend to take to ensure that such actions do not create operational problems for the European countries that have deployed forces in the region?

(26 May 2026) The EU has a strategic interest in a secure and stable environment in the Eastern Mediterranean. A comprehensive settlement of the Republic of Cyprus issue would significantly contribute to sustainable stability and security in the region. E-10-2026-000974.t: Condemning the reinforcement of the Turkish occupation army in parts of the Republic of Cyprus
qt: to the Commission Emmanouil Fragkos (ECR) Subject:

The Republic of Cyprus is the bastion of European security in the Eastern Mediterranean. A number of EU Member States have deployed or are planning to deploy military forces, de facto implementing Article 42(7) TEU and confirming that the security of a Member State is a joint EU responsibility. Defending the Republic of Cyprus against attacks or destabilising actions by extremist regimes in the region does not only concern Nicosia; it is a matter of collective European security. Meanwhile, Türkiye continues to maintain tens of thousands of soldiers in the occupied territories of the Republic of Cyprus, i.e. on EU territory. Following the deployment of European forces in the Republic of Cyprus, Türkiye announced the deployment of additional military assets, including fighter jets and air defence systems. At the same time, the longstanding strategic military relationship between Türkiye and Iran, reflected in their numerous bilateral meetings and multilevel cooperation in recent years, cannot be understated. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Does it condemn the destabilising actions and plans of the Turkish-Iranian Islamist axis targeting the Republic of Cyprus?
Does it agree that the reinforced Turkish military presence came as a response to European support for the Republic of Cyprus?

How does it intend to ensure that the mutual defence clause set out in Article 42(7) TEU is applied effectively in order to protect the Republic of Cyprus against any threat to the sovereignty and sovereign rights of an EU Member State?

(26 May 2026) The EU stands firmly and unequivocally in support of any Member State in the face of any threat. The EU strongly condemns the indiscriminate military strikes by Iran. In the context of the overall security situation within the continent and its neighbourhood, discussions on implementing Article 42(7) of the Treaty on European Union are ongoing. Invocation of the mutual assistance clause is the sovereign prerogative of a Member State that is the victim of an armed aggression. Moreover, it is the attacked Member State that communicates the type of assistance it requires in a given situation. This could include support at EU level, whether in terms of EU instruments and tools, or coordination support, if so requested. In this context, there is a need to develop a common understanding of the article’s implementation, specifically what could be done concretely in a situation where the article is invoked, in order for a Member State to ask for and receive help and what instruments and tools can be used in such an occasion, including at EU level, should the attacked Member State(s) so request.

E-10-2026-000972.t: Comparison of new cancer cases across Member States
qt: to the Commission Gerald Hauser (PfE) Subject:

Over the last few decades, cancer cases have slowly but steadily increased. In Austria, for example, the number of new cancer cases per year increased from 37 578 in 2001 to 39 737 in 2010. From 2011 to 2020, it increased further from 40 059 to 44 520, which can be explained by general demographic and health factors. However, since 2021, there has been a clear and worrying acceleration in the rate of increase: The number of new cancer cases per year rose to 48 360 by 2024 – in just four years. Should this trend continue, some 54 000 new cancer cases per year could be expected in Austria by 2030. In addition, some oncologists and scientists report that cancer cases are becoming increasingly aggressive and developing faster. In this context, the term ‘turbo cancer’ is sometimes used. 1.
How have cancer figures evolved in each Member State up to 2020 and since 2021?
Are there Member States which are ‘outliers’ in the statistics and have particularly high or low numbers of new cancers, and what are the reasons for this?
Can the Commission rule out that there is a link between the increase in new cancers, as well as the reports of ‘turbo cancers’, and COVID-19 vaccinations?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (7.5.2026) Cancer incidence estimates and historical data for European countries are available in the European Cancer Information System (ECIS)1. The European Cancer Inequalities Registry2, a flagship of Europe’s Beating Cancer Plan3, tracks cancer disparities in the EU, Norway and Iceland. Its Data Tool integrates data from ECIS, whilst Country Cancer Profiles4 and EU Analytical Reports5 provide national analyses and EU-level comparisons. The reported number of new cancer cases grew across Member States up to 2020. This trend continued until 2022, when 2.78 million new cancer cases were estimated, a 2.4% rise from 2020. Since 2021, cancer incidence is stabilising or increasing moderately, with 2.7 million new cases estimated in 2024. However, data enabling robust analysis from 2021 will become available in the second half of 2026, following the 2026 ECIS update where incidence data for 2021–2024 will be published. Cancer incidence varies between Member States, with Central and Eastern European countries generally showing higher rates. However, in 2024 Denmark was estimated to rank highest for incidence (22% above the EU average) and Bulgaria lowest (26% below), in contrast to the general trend. These disparities likely stem from differences in prevalence of risk factors, population structures and ageing, existence and effectiveness of prevention and screening programmes, quality of diagnosis and treatment. From the data registration perspective, quality and completeness of cancer registries also play a role. Finally, the Commission refers the Honourable Member to the answer to Parliamentary Question E-002078/202576, detailing that there is no scientific evidence of any increase of cancer occurrence following COVID-19 vaccination.

E-10-2026-000971.t: Planned restrictions on the distribution of apps on mobile devices running the Android operating system
qt: to the Commission Veronika Cifrová Ostrihoňová (Renew), Martin Hojsík (Renew), Michal Wiezik (Renew), Lucia Yar (Renew), Ľubica Karvašová (Renew), Ľudovít Ódor (Renew) Subject:

According to publicly available information1, Google plans to introduce new rules for devices running Android from September 2026, according to which only apps from developers who have undergone an identity verification process directly through Google can be installed. This requirement is set to apply not only to the Google Play store, but also to alternative app stores and manual app installation. Google is justifying this move as an effort to increase user safety and limit the spread of malicious software. However, it is also raising concerns among developers, especially in the open-source community, that it could limit the distribution of apps outside the Google ecosystem and strengthen Google’s position in the mobile operating system market. This raises questions about the compatibility of such measures with EU competition rules and the obligations arising from the Digital Markets Act. 1.
In the Commission’s view, do Google’s proposed measures constitute a breach of EU rules by failing to comply with the Digital Markets Act and EU provisions on competition?

Does the Commission feel that requiring developers to undergo mandatory verification for the installation of any apps on certified Android devices may lead to restrictions on the distribution of apps beyond the Google platform and limit independent or opensource developers’ ability to access the market?
https://www.theregister.com/2025/08/26/android_developer_verification_sideloading/.
at: (English version) to the Commission Veronika Cifrová Ostrihoňová (Renew), Martin Hojsík (Renew), Michal Wiezik (Renew), Lucia Yar (Renew), Ľubica Karvašová (Renew), Ľudovít Ódor (Renew) (9 March 2026) Subject: Planned restrictions on the distribution of apps on mobile devices running the Android operating system According to publicly available information (1), Google plans to introduce new rules for devices running Android from September 2026, according to which only apps from developers who have undergone an identity verification process directly through Google can be installed. This requirement is set to apply not only to the Google Play store, but also to alternative app stores and manual app installation. Google is justifying this move as an effort to increase user safety and limit the spread of malicious software. However, it is also raising concerns among developers, especially in the open-source community, that it could limit the distribution of apps outside the Google ecosystem and strengthen Google’s position in the mobile operating system market. This raises questions about the compatibility of such measures with EU competition rules and the obligations arising from the Digital Markets Act. 1. In the Commission’s view, do Google’s proposed measures constitute a breach of EU rules by failing to comply with the Digital Markets Act and EU provisions on competition? 2. Does the Commission feel that requiring developers to undergo mandatory verification for the installation of any apps on certified Android devices may lead to restrictions on the distribution of apps beyond the Google platform and limit independent or open-source developers’ ability to access the market? (15 April 2026) The Commission is aware of Google’s announcement to introduce this verification process starting from September 2026 in some jurisdictions (not including the EU based on publicly available information). The Commission understands that, as a result of this process, Android will require that all applications (apps) are registered by verified developers in order to be installed on certified Android devices. The Commission is also aware of public campaigns such as ‘Keep Android Open’ which have emerged in reaction to Google’s announcement. Article 6(4) of the Digital Markets Act (DMA) (1) obliges gatekeepers like Alphabet to allow and technically enable the effective distribution of apps on their operating system through third party app stores or the web. At the same time, the DMA also permits Google to introduce strictly necessary and proportionate measures to ensure that thirdparty software apps or app stores do not endanger the integrity of the hardware or operating system, provided that such measures are duly justified by Alphabet. The Commission is actively engaged in a regulatory dialogue with Alphabet concerning Article 6(4) DMA and is diligently monitoring Alphabet's compliance with the relevant legal framework to ensure that apps, including open-source apps, can be effectively distributed on Android outside Google Play.
