E-10-2026-000970.t: Shortcomings in the implementation of Regulation (EU) 2016/1191 by Greek administrative and consular authorities
qt: to the Commission Sakis Arnaoutoglou (S&D) Subject:
Shortcomings in the implementation of Regulation (EU) 2016/1191 by Greek administrative and consular authorities

Regulation (EU) 2016/1191 was introduced with the aim of facilitating the free movement of citizens within the EU by abolishing legalisation or apostille requirements for certain public civil status documents, introducing multilingual standard forms and simplifying translation procedures. Greek citizens residing or active in other Member States have reported that Greek administrative or consular authorities are still demanding apostilles, certified translations or other additional paperwork. This entails financial cost, loss of working time and possible cases of unequal treatment. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

Has it verified to what extent Greece has implemented Regulation (EU) 2016/1191 with regard to ending the legalisation/apostille requirement for certain civil status documents, the mandatory acceptance of the multilingual standard forms provided for in the regulation and the envisaged translation arrangements?
If shortcomings have been identified, what specific infringements, administrative practices or differences in interpretation has it recorded, and what corrective measures does it intend to take?

In addition, has it examined whether the current practices of Greek consular or internal administrative authorities – such as demanding apostilles, certified translations or other additional paperwork – result in disproportionate costs, delays or discriminatory treatment between married parents whose marriage has already been registered in Greece, married parents whose marriage was performed abroad but has not yet been registered and unmarried parents and, if so, does it consider that such differentiation constitutes a possible breach of EU law requiring further action?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.4.2026) Regulation (EU) 2016/11911 aims to facilitate the free movement of citizens within the EU by abolishing legalisation or apostille requirements for certain public civil status documents, introducing multilingual standard forms and simplifying translation procedures. The Regulation is an important piece of legislation cutting red tape and costs for citizens, when they need to present in a Member State a public document issued in another Member State. The Commission monitors the correct application of EU legislation by Member States and may decide to take appropriate actions in cases showing a persistent failure by a Member State to apply EU law correctly. In the case of Regulation (EU) 2016/1191, there are no concrete indications of such infringements by Greece to the knowledge of the Commission. If evidence comes to light of a practice of Greek administrative or consular authorities demanding apostilles, certified translations or other additional paperwork in violation of the provisions of Regulation (EU) 2016/1191 on a general and consistent basis, the Commission would, where appropriate, take the necessary steps. Citizens who encounter problems which are allegedly caused by the misapplication of the Regulation by Greece can file a complaint to the Commission providing details of the alleged breach. On this basis the Commission is able to examine the matter and contact Greece if needed. The Commission is not able to examine the alleged breach on the basis of a general statement but would need further details.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/1191/oj/eng.

E-10-2026-000969.t: New inter-state agreement between Greece and Bulgaria on the waters of the Arda River and compliance with EU law
qt: to the Commission Sakis Arnaoutoglou (S&D) Subject:

The Arda River is a critical cross-border water resource for agricultural production in Evros. The Greek-Bulgarian water supply agreement, which was signed 60 years ago in 1964, expired in July 2024, without being replaced by a new binding inter-state agreement. Instead, in May 2025, an unpublished five-year ‘joint statement’ was presented by the foreign ministers of the two countries, without any known quantitative terms, compliance mechanisms or parliamentary ratification. This development has led to a situation of prolonged uncertainty for farmers in Evros as regards the availability of irrigation water. This directly affects the viability of the local rural economy and the management of a cross-border river basin within the EU. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Is there an obligation under EU law for an upstream Member State to ensure a predictable and sufficient flow of water across borders when the flow is regulated through dams?

Are Member States obliged, under Directive 2000/60/EC and the principle of sincere cooperation, to ensure transparency and citizens’ access to the terms of bilateral arrangements affecting cross-border waters?
Does it intend to look into whether an unpublished ‘joint statement’ without clear legally binding effects, complies with the principles of transparency, good administration and legal certainty?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (11.5.2026) Article 13 of the Water Framework Directive (WFD)1 requires Member States sharing an international river basin to ensure coordination of their management plans. Such coordination should cover measures to ensure appropriate quantity and dynamics of freshwater flow to allow the achievement of good ecological status. Moreover, as Parties to the United Nations Economic Commission for Europe Water Convention2, EU Member States must ensure ‘exchange of information on existing and planned uses of water and related installations that are likely to cause transboundary impact’. Under Article 12 of the WFD, where a Member State identifies an issue which has an impact on the management of its water, but it cannot resolve it on its own, it may report the issue to the Commission and any other Member State concerned and may make recommendations for the resolution of it. The recently amended provision3 strengthens this cooperation by making it mandatory. Neither Bulgaria nor Greece have made a notification to the Commission under Article 12. The WFD does not specify which form the cooperation between Member States should take. Article 3(4) WFD allows Member States to use existing structures stemming from international agreements. Information on cross-border cooperation should be reported in the River Basin Management Plans. Prior to their adoption, the draft plans are made subject to public consultation. Given their delay in reporting, the Commission is currently still assessing the Third River Basin Management Plans of both Bulgaria and Greece and will consider in this context the state of play in relation to transboundary cooperation.
1 Directive 2000/60/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 23 October 2000 establishing a

framework for Community action in the field of water policy, OJ L 327, 22.12.2000, p. 1–73. 2 Convention on the Protection and use of Transboundary Watercourses and International Lakes. 3 Directive (EU) 2026/805 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 30 March 2026 amending Directive 2000/60/EC establishing a framework for Community action in the field of water policy, Directive 2006/118/EC on the protection of groundwater against pollution and deterioration and Directive 2008/105/EC on environmental quality standards in the field of water policy, OJ L, 2026/805, 20.4.2026.

E-10-2026-000968.t: The need to improve monitoring of European forests and their resilience to climate change
qt: to the Commission César Luena (S&D) Subject:

A recent study published in Science warns that European forests could face unprecedented mortality as a result of increased fires, pests and other factors linked to climate change. According to the study, forest disturbances have already increased considerably in Europe and could intensify in the coming decades, especially in the Mediterranean region. Forests play an essential role in climate change mitigation and adaptation, biodiversity protection and ecosystem resilience. It is worrying, then, that the Commission has withdrawn the proposal for a regulation on a monitoring framework for resilient European forests, the aim of which was to improve data collection and scientific knowledge on the state of European forests. In view of the above: 1.
Does the Commission consider that withdrawing the aforementioned proposal for a regulation is consistent with the need to improve scientific knowledge on the state and resilience of European forests?
What measures does the Commission intend to take to improve scientific monitoring of forests in the EU?
Will the Commission specifically address forests in future European adaptation and resilience legislation in accordance with scientific criteria?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (7.5.2026) Availability of complete and reliable data on status and trends of forest health, resources and disturbances is key to support the development of a resilient and sustainable forest bioeconomy and achieving biodiversity and climate mitigation and resilience policy objectives and targets. The forest monitoring law proposal1 was intended to improve such data. However, since the European Parliament did not give this proposal the necessary support, the Commission announced its intention to withdraw the proposal. The Commission remains committed to a robust EU-wide knowledge base for effective and efficient action in response to growing pressures such as droughts, wildfires or pest outbreaks. In line with the EU Forest Strategy for 20302, the Commission will strengthen the monitoring of climate effects and other natural or human induced disturbances on forests as part of the Forest Information System for Europe3. A forest science partnership has been set up to support the development of new methods for indicator monitoring based on remote sensing, with a focus on the existing EU policy framework. Furthermore, the Commission just published new guidelines to future-proof Natura 2000 sites against climate change4, and it plans to improve in its forthcoming European climate resilience framework5 the overall monitoring of progress towards climate resilience and adaptation. Yet, it is too early to tell whether this framework will include a specific focus on forests. Under Horizon Europe6, a cofunded research and innovation partnership on Forests and Forestry for a Sustainable Future7 has been proposed which will also support the improvement and alignment of forest monitoring in Europe.

1 https://environment.ec.europa.eu/publications/proposal-regulation-forest-monitoring-framework_en. 2 https://environment.ec.europa.eu/strategy/forest-strategy_en. 3 FISE : https://forest.eea.europa.eu/. 4 https://environment.ec.europa.eu/publications/guidance-adapting-natura-2000-sites-climate-change_en. 5 https://climate.ec.europa.eu/eu-action/adaptation-and-resilience-climate-change_en. 6 https://commission.europa.eu/funding-tenders/find-funding/eu-funding-programmes/horizon-europe_en. 7 https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/opportunities/topic-details/HORIZON-

E-10-2026-000967.t: Protection of workers exposed to formaldehyde in the EU
qt: to the Commission Marianne Vind (S&D), Vilija Blinkevičiūtė (S&D), Leila Chaibi (The Left), Per Clausen (The Left), Christophe Clergeau (S&D), Anja Hazekamp (The Left), Jutta Paulus (Verts/ALE), Majdouline Sbai (Verts/ALE), Idoia Mendia (S&D), Alicia Homs Ginel (S&D), Matjaž Nemec (S&D), Lynn Boylan (The Left), Marie Toussaint (Verts/ALE), Maria Grapini (S&D), Kira Marie Peter-Hansen (Verts/ALE), Villy Søvndal (Verts/ALE), Christel Schaldemose (S&D), Niels Fuglsang (S&D), Mounir Satouri (Verts/ALE), Rudi Kennes (The Left), Johan Danielsson (S&D), Anthony Smith (The Left) Subject:

A recent documentary by the Danish Broadcasting Corporation reveals that four former young medical student assistants developed cancer after working over a prolonged period with formaldehyde. They were all under the age of 35, and three have since tragically passed away. When four young doctors fall ill after working with a known carcinogen, alarm bells should ring. Their stories raise serious concerns about the protection of workers exposed to formaldehyde. Formaldehyde is widely used across Europe – in textiles, plastics, glued wood and embalming – with many workers exposed to it daily. The documentary also exposes a concerning correlation between industry funding and research outcomes, as chemical companies and their lobby organisations have actively sought to shape the scientific basis for the EU’s occupational exposure limit. A former member of the EU scientific committee has stated that the committee’s original recommendation of an exposure limit of 0.2 ppm was likely increased to 0.3 ppm following persistent lobbying pressure. In this context: 1.
Will the Commission launch a new assessment of formaldehyde considering these revelations?
Will it ensure that any reassessment is expedited, and the limit is lowered if new evidence shows higher risks?
How does the Commission take into account industry funding and lobbying when evaluating the scientific evidence underpinning EU exposure limits?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.4.2026) The process of setting occupational exposure limits (OEL) is set out in Directive 2004/37/EC1. Directive 2019/9832 sets an occupational exposure limit for formaldehyde of 0.3 ppm (parts per million). This was based on a comprehensive evidence-based process which also took into account the views of national authorities and representatives of the employers and workers. The selection of the substances for which to possibly set new or review existing OELs includes a broad consultative approach within the tripartite Advisory Committee on Safety and Health at Work (ACSH), which includes national authorities and social partners. The ACSH regularly provides the Commission with advice for the priority chemicals for which they recommend an OEL, informing the policy-making process. This advice is provided based on the availability of new science and data as brought to the attention of the ACSH working party on ‘Chemicals at the Workplace’ (WPC). The WPC is discussing a possible updated list of chemicals for which they would advise the Commission on setting new or revising existing OEL values. Such an update is expected by mid-2026. The process of setting OELs is evidence-based. It relies on a broad consultation of stakeholders and on the scientific assessment of evidence by independent experts in the risk assessment committee of the European Chemicals Agency. Moreover, the Regulation on Registration, Evaluation, Authorisation and Restriction of Chemicals (REACH)3 restricts formaldehyde emissions into indoor air to protect consumers4.

1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2004/37/oj/eng. 2 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?qid=1576669202273&uri=CELEX%3A32019L0983. 3 OJ L 396, 30.12.2006, p. 1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-

content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ%3AL%3A2006%3A396%3ATOC. 4 Commission Regulation (EU) 2023/1464 of 14 July 2023 amending Annex XVII to Regulation (EC) No 1907/2006 of the European Parliament and of the Council as regards formaldehyde and formaldehyde releasers https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/FR/ALL/?uri=CELEX:32023R1464.

E-10-2026-000966.t: Implementation of fossil fuel phase-out commitments by EU export credit agencies
qt: to the Commission Kathleen Van Brempt (S&D) Subject:

In December 2025, the Commission published its report on export credit agencies (ECAs)1, which reviews Member States’ policies on the phase-out of fossil fuel support. The report states that ‘the Commission supports further progress in this area, including further strengthening of Member States’ commitments regarding the phase-out of fossil fuels’. In this context: 1.

What kind of support is the Commission providing to ensure further progress and strengthen Member States’ commitments to phase out export credit support for fossil fuel projects, and does this support include concrete guidance, coordination, monitoring or enforcement measures?

How does the Commission assess the compatibility of continued support by certain EU ECAs for fossil-fuel-related activities with EU climate objectives and relevant arrangements under the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development and what action is the Commission taking in this regard?

Following the recent decisions by the Atradius Dutch State Business and UK Export Finance to withdraw their support for the Mozambique liquefied natural gas project, will the Commission engage with Member States’ ECAs that may still consider supporting this project, and what steps is it taking to ensure that its export credit policies address human rights violations associated with the project and align with the EU’s climate neutrality objective?
https://ec.europa.eu/transparency/documents-register/detail?ref=COM(2025)737&lang=en.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (29.4.2026) Since the adoption of Regulation (EU) No 1233/20111, the Arrangement on Officially Supported Export Credits of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) has been an integral part of EU law. The Commission conducts an annual review for the European Parliament on the basis of the Annual Activity Reports submitted by Member States on compliance with EU standards. Starting with the 2023 reporting year, this annual review includes detailed information on Export Credit Agencies climate policies and justifications provided by Member States for any remaining fossil fuel transactions. Additionally, the Commission led efforts to create a new transparency report with other participants to the Arrangement, providing exhaustive data on all energy sector transactions since 2015. The first report was published in November 20252. Collectively, these initiatives ensure robust public scrutiny regarding Member States’ intentions to phase out export credits for fossil fuel energy projects3. Regarding the specific project mentioned, primary responsibility for due diligence lies with the individual Member State that must assess alignment with national, EU and international obligations, including the OECD Recommendation on Common Approaches for Officially Supported Export Credits and Environmental and Social Due Diligence, which is the benchmark for assessing human rights and environmental impacts. While the Commission does not intervene in individual project approvals, it pays attention to these issues when reviewing Member State reports under the Regulation, with a view to ensuring continued alignment with EU objectives.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2011/1233/oj/eng. 2 Export Finance for Future, Transparency Report 2025, Annex II;

https://www.exportkreditgarantien.de/_Resources/Persistent/b/7/1/5/b715c13f8a6fc669f97c8313d277319089595 7d8/e3f-annual-transparency-report-2025.pdf. 3 Council conclusion on export credits, 15 March 2022; https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/press/pressreleases/2022/03/15/the-council-adopted-conclusions-on-export-credits/pdf.

E-10-2026-000965.t: Planned ‘freedom.gov’ portal could result in digital interference and circumvention of EU law
qt: to the Commission Yvan Verougstraete (Renew) Subject:

According to several sources, a US platform called ‘freedom.gov’ is being developed with the stated aim of offering EU citizens a free VPN service that would enable them to circumvent the application of EU legislation, notably the Digital Services Act and the Digital Markets Act. Touted as a ‘freedom of expression’ initiative, the project would in fact make it possible to access, from EU territory, content that is regulated or banned under EU law, including hate speech and manipulative or illegal content. 1.

Does the Commission consider that a project backed by stakeholders with close ties to a foreign administration and expressly designed to neutralise the effect of EU law constitutes an attack on Europe’s regulatory sovereignty?
Does it consider that such an initiative could constitute a form of digital interference by a third country?
What specific steps will it take to ensure that EU law is implemented effectively and to prevent any organised attempt to systematically circumvent it?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (29.4.2026) The Commission has no specific comment to make on potential plans of the freedom.gov initiative and does not speculate on design or intent. The Commission does not block websites in the EU. Only Member States' authorities may block a website if it is illegal under national or European law. This includes websites promoting child-sexual abuse material, terrorist content or copyright-infringing material. The Commission has a responsibility to enforce its laws, including the Digital Services Act1, effectively, fairly and without discrimination towards all companies operating in the EU.
1 Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 19 October 2022 on a Single
Market For Digital Services and amending Directive 2000/31/EC (Digital Services Act), https://eurlex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/2065/oj/eng.

E-10-2026-000964.t: Preparation of a study on the impacts of the consumption of ultra-processed foods
qt: to the Commission David Cormand (Verts/ALE), Mélissa Camara (Verts/ALE), Majdouline Sbai (Verts/ALE), Cristina Guarda (Verts/ALE), Nikos Papandreou (S&D), Sebastian Everding (The Left), Anja Hazekamp (The Left), Elena Kountoura (The Left), Thomas Waitz (Verts/ALE), Pierre Jouvet (S&D), Danilo Della Valle (The Left), Lena Schilling (Verts/ALE), Catarina Martins (The Left) Subject:

In its Vision for Agriculture and Food, published in February 2025, the Commission announced the preparation of a study on the impact of the consumption of ultra-processed foods, intended to inform the annual food dialogues. In view of this, I ask the Commission to clarify the following: 1.
What is the planned timeline for the completion and publication of this study?
How does the Commission intend to organise the methodology and governance of the study to ensure that the most up-to-date independent scientific evidence is taken into account?

What measures will be put in place to guarantee the scientific independence of the process, and how will it both avoid any influence from actors with commercial interests in the outcome and involve relevant areas of the Commission and stakeholders with a genuine commitment to public health?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (12.5.2026) The Commission announced12,that the study on ‘ultra-processed foods’ will rely on the opinions of the Scientific Advice Mechanism (comprising the Group of Chief Scientific Advisors (GCSA)3) and the European Group on Ethics in Science and New Technologies (EGE)4. The advisory process typically spans one year from the receipt of an official request for advice. GCSA and EGE Opinions rely on scientific literature reviews, expert hearings and workshops. They are supported by the Horizon Europe-funded Science Advice for Policy by European Academies (SAPEA)5 and Support for the Activities of the European Group on Ethics by European Academia and Ethics Bodies (SAEGE)6 projects, respectively, that supply evidence review reports (ERRs) and independent expert panels. SAPEA’s reports undergo double-blind peer review, while GCSA drafts are scrutinised by experts, the Commission, and external stakeholders. Declarations of interest are available on the Register of Commission expert groups (GCSA and EGE), or the Scientific Advice Mechanism to the European Commission (SAM) website7 (SAPEA working groups) post-ERR publication, to prevent lobbying. All meetings remain closed to prevent undue influence.

1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A52025DC0525&qid=1762330863739. 2 https://health.ec.europa.eu/publications/communication-eu-cardiovascular-health-plan-safe-hearts-plan_en. 3 https://research-and-innovation.ec.europa.eu/knowledge-publications-tools-and-data/publications/all-

publications/commission-decision-setting-high-level-group-scientific-advisors_en. 4 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32024D1997. 5 https://cordis.europa.eu/project/id/101198044. 6 https://cordis.europa.eu/project/id/101256865. 7 https://scientificadvice.eu.

E-10-2026-000962.t: Removal of active substances used in farming without assuring viable alternatives
qt: to the Commission Daniel Buda (PPE) Subject:

In light of the frequent decisions on the non-renewal or withdrawal of authorisation for active substances used in agriculture under Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009, the Commission needs to clarify whether it plans, before or at the same time as removing a product from the market, to assure that equally efficient and affordable alternatives are available for farmers. EU farmers are confronted with diseases and pests on an everyday basis, and combating these cannot be ‘postponed’ until such time as new EFSA-authorised solutions emerge. In the absence of alternatives of comparable effectiveness, there is a risk of this situation directly impacting the productivity and competitiveness of EU agriculture and food security. 1.
Will the Commission apply the principle of effective substitution – i.e. only withdraw a substance when a functional alternative exists?
What measures will the Commission take, especially as regards administrative capacity, to speed up the authorisation of less toxic but equally effective products?
What impact does the Commission think these withdrawal decisions will have on the competitiveness of EU farmers?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (26.5.2026) Active substances (AS) used in plant protection products (PPPs) can, in principle, only be approved where it is demonstrated that at least one representative use of a PPP containing the AS fulfils the approval criteria set out in Regulation (EC) No 1107/20091. Alternatives are only considered to determine if AS failing approval criteria need a derogation because they're essential for controlling a serious danger to plant health that no other available method can address2. In the Vision for Agriculture and Food3, the Commission committed to carefully considering any further ban of AS if alternatives are not available, unless the AS in question represents a threat to human health or the environment that agriculture relies upon for its viability. The Food and Feed Simplification Package4 proposed by the Commission in December 2025 aims to accelerate innovation and market access for new biocontrol AS to provide more sustainable PPPs to farmers to protect their crops. To speed up Member States’ evaluation of biocontrol AS applications, the Commission proposes replacing systematic time-driven renewals for all AS with a flexible system targeting AS that may harm human or animal health or the environment5. The Commission has also proposed to allow derogations from existing approval criteria if an AS is essential to protect plant health or plant production and the possibility for Member States to grant longer grace periods to use existing stocks of nonapproved substances when no alternatives exist. The Commission receives information on alternatives provided by stakeholders. So far alternatives have always been identified where the approval of an AS has not been renewed6.
1 Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 21 October 2009 concerning

the placing of plant protection products on the market and repealing Council Directives 79/117/EEC and 91/414/EEC, OJ L 309, 24.11.2009, p. 1, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2009/1107/oj. 2 As set out in Article 4(7) of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009, such substances may be approved for 5 years 3 Communication from the Commission to the European Parliament, the Council, the European Economic and Social Committee and the Committee of the Regions A Vision for Agriculture and Food Shaping together an attractive farming and agri-food sector for future generations. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legalcontent/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52025DC0075. 4 https://food.ec.europa.eu/horizontal-topics/simplification-legislation_en. 5 The majority of Member State resources is currently occupied with the systematic renewal process for all active substances meaning that innovative companies applying for the approval of new biocontrol substances often have to wait for several years before a Member State agrees to take on the role of rapporteur (RMS) for the first risk assessment. 6 In addition, various tools to help farmers in finding solutions protecting their crops have been developed for example IPMWORKS project developed based on Horizon 2020 funds or Agrowise supported by the LIFE Program.

E-10-2026-000961.t: Need to stimulate internal sugar beet production
qt: to the Commission Daniel Buda (PPE) Subject:

The price offered to sugar beet growers has decreased by 30 % over the previous year, reflecting global market pressure. This decrease follows the record price levels recorded in the 2023-2024 season, when EU sugar production fell by around 1 million tonnes1. In an attempt to boost internal production, the Commission has decided to suspend the inward processing mechanism, which temporarily abolishes duty-free imports from third countries of sugar for processing and subsequent export outside the EU. 1.

Does the Commission think that limiting these imports will be enough to reduce pressure on the market and stabilise the EU sugar sector, while at the same time increasing the use of sugar produced in the EU?
Since 2017, 17 sugar factories have closed down in the EU2. What measures is the Commission considering to incentivise and support sugar producers in the short, medium and long term?

Romania, for example, produces only 25 % of its domestic consumption, due to the imbalance between production costs and the low sales price for sugar beet3. How will greater attractiveness of sugar beet growers’ incomes be ensured under the National and Regional Partnership Plans?

https://agrointel.ro/346380/ue-suspenda-importul-de-zahar-fara-taxe-vamale. https://agrobiznes.ro/59583-cefs-17-fabrici-de-zahar-s-au-inchis-in-uniunea-europeana-din-2017/. https://revista-ferma.ro/productia-de-zahar-in-declin-romania-mai-produce-doar-25-din-cat-consuma-restulvine-din-import/.
at: (English version) to the Commission Daniel Buda (PPE) (9 March 2026) Subject: Need to stimulate internal sugar beet production The price offered to sugar beet growers has decreased by 30% over the previous year, reflecting global market pressure. This decrease follows the record price levels recorded in the 2023-2024 season, when EU sugar production fell by around 1 million tonnes (1). In an attempt to boost internal production, the Commission has decided to suspend the inward processing mechanism, which temporarily abolishes duty-free imports from third countries of sugar for processing and subsequent export outside the EU. 1. Does the Commission think that limiting these imports will be enough to reduce pressure on the market and stabilise the EU sugar sector, while at the same time increasing the use of sugar produced in the EU? 2. Since 2017, 17 sugar factories have closed down in the EU (2). What measures is the Commission considering to incentivise and support sugar producers in the short, medium and long term? 3. Romania, for example, produces only 25% of its domestic consumption, due to the imbalance between production costs and the low sales price for sugar beet (3). How will greater attractiveness of sugar beet growers’ incomes be ensured under the National and Regional Partnership Plans? (8 May 2026) 1. The suspension of inward processing would address a short-term market disturbance. The Commission is assessing whether further action may be warranted to address potential structural challenges in the sugar sector. The Commission is conducting a ‘health check’ of the key markets, including sugar, which will inform these reflections. 2. Since the end of the quota regime in 2017, the sector has adjusted to a more market-oriented organisation by improving competitiveness and better aligning supply to demand. Without jeopardising the market-oriented nature of the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), where necessary to respond to market disturbances or imbalances, the Commission may adopt appropriate measures within the framework of the common market Organisation. To address other challenges, such as high production costs, the EU offers investment and coupled income support, which may be included in Member States’ CAP Strategic Plans to support sugar and sugar beet producers. 3. Under the future Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) 2027-2034, the proposed national and regional partnership (NRP) plans will continue to offer Member States the opportunity to support farmers depending on regional and national needs. Existing CAP policy instruments, such as income support, are maintained in the Commission proposal. In addition, the CAP and NRP Regulation proposals provide a complementary set of tools to alleviate pressure and reducing risk in farm operations. The EU facility under the NRP fund also provides a Unity Safety Net intended to help farmers cope with the impact of market disturbances.

E-10-2026-000959.t: Fairness and convergence of CAP direct payments
qt: to the Commission Daniel Buda (PPE) Subject:

Article 35(3) of the proposal for a Regulation establishing the European Fund for economic, social and territorial cohesion, agriculture and rural, fisheries and maritime, prosperity and security for the period 2028-2034, stipulates that degressive area-based income support (DABIS), which would also be the basic subsidy of the common agricultural policy, must be between EUR 130 and EUR 240 per hectare, as an average at Member State level. This translates into the possibility of a minimum difference of EUR 110 in basic subsidies between Member States, but also the possibility of majorly differentiating subsidies within a Member State. For example, a Member State that sets a subsidy of EUR 50 per hectare for a given region may compensate by granting a subsidy of EUR 430 to another region. This excessive flexibility can become a policy tool, favouring certain categories or regions. European farmers are players in the same single market, subject to the same European conditionalities and regulations, regardless of their country of origin. 1.
How does the Commission ensure a level playing field in this context?
What mechanisms are in place to ensure that certain regions are not unfairly discriminated against by the flexibility in the allocation of the DABIS amount?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (19.5.2026) The degressive area-based income support (DABIS) proposed for the 2028-2034 programming period1 builds on the experience of the current Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) 2023-2027 which already provides substantial flexibility to target the current basic income support for sustainability (BISS). Article 22(2) of EU Regulation 2115/20212 states that Member States may decide to differentiate the amount of the basic income support per hectare amongst different groups of territories in accordance with their socio-economic or agronomic conditions. Member States have to demonstrate that these differentiations by group of territories are justified on the basis of their needs. The proposed CAP Regulation for 2028-2034, in its Article 6(2), also introduces potential differentiation by geographical areas for the DABIS and by groups of farmers to those who are the most in need. A boundary is set through the obligation that ‘the planned average aid per hectare for DABIS shall not be less than EUR 130 and not more than EUR 240 for each Member State’3. Today the average payments range between EUR 110 and 640. Article 6(2) further lays down criteria that will ensure that the differentiation of the DABIS will be duly justified in the national and regional partnership plans before their approval. Indeed, it states that: ‘…the differentiation of payments shall be established based on farmers’ income from agricultural activity…’, and that the differentiation is made ‘on the basis of objective and non-discriminatory criteria’. In the Commission’s view, the proposed EUR 130-240 boundary, the clear link to income needs as well as the justification that Member States have to provide will increase the level-playing field between farmers and regions.

E-10-2026-000958.t: Violation of the democratic clause of the Trade Agreement between the European Union, of the one part, and Colombia, Peru and Ecuador, of the other part (‘the Agreement’) following the suspension of the Citizen Revolution Movement
qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Irene Montero (The Left) Subject:

On 6 March 2026, Ecuador’s Electoral Disputes Tribunal (Tribunal Contencioso Electoral, TCE) imposed an administrative suspension of nine months on the Citizen Revolution Movement (RC5), the main opposition force in the country. This administrative measure de facto prevents the political participation of a significant part of the Ecuadorian electorate. Article 23 of the American Convention on Human Rights sets strict limits as regards restrictions on political rights and protects the right of citizens to participate in public affairs and to be elected in genuine elections. Given that Article 1 of the Agreement establishes that respect for democratic principles constitutes an ‘essential element’ of the Agreement: 1.
Does the Commission consider the administrative suspension of an opposition political force in Ecuador to be compatible with the democratic commitments made in the Agreement?
Does the European External Action Service intend to activate the political dialogue with Ecuador in order to assess the impact of this measure on democratic pluralism and the rule of law?

Does the Commission intend to launch consultations with the Ecuadorian authorities in connection with the Agreement in order to assess possible measures in the event of a breach of its democratic clause?

(10 June 2026) Democratic principles, human rights and the protection of fundamental freedoms underpin EU-Ecuador relations. While the High Representative/Vice-President cannot evaluate the legitimacy of the suspension of the Revolución Ciudadana movement, the EU Electoral Observation Mission deployed for the 2024-2025 voting process recommended a review of the sanctions foreseen under Ecuador’s Election Law that could exceed those under the country’s penal code (1). The EU regularly addresses concerns with Ecuador’s authorities through diplomatic channels and formal dialogue mechanisms, such as the High-Level Political Dialogue and Human Rights Dialogue. EU cooperation with Ecuador includes joint efforts against transnational organised crime, support to human rights, and strengthening of state institutions including the judiciary. The EU also continues to support democracy, civil society and human rights defenders in Ecuador. The EU considers that dialogue, cooperation, and economic relations including trade remain the most effective means for encouraging Ecuador’s adherence to democratic principles, the rule of law and political pluralism. The EU will be monitoring developments and may consider adapting its approach based on evolving circumstances.

E-10-2026-000953.t: Urgent action for fisheries and agriculture following recent gasoil price spikes
qt: to the Commission Anna Maria Cisint (PfE) Subject:

With oil tankers blocked in the Strait of Hormuz, the war raging in Iran is steadily pushing up the price of fuels, including gasoil, which is used in the primary fisheries and agriculture sectors. In particular, the increases faced by fishers in Italy – where, for example in the Upper Adriatic Sea, the price of gasoil paid by fishers has climbed 30 % in the last 48 hours1 – are causing tremendous trouble for the already beleaguered industry. In light of this: 1.

Will the Commission take urgent action to support the primary sector in the face of surging fuel prices, perhaps by approving state aid, as it did in 2022 following price spikes triggered by the outbreak of the war in Ukraine?
Will it take measures to offset energy costs, such as co-financing the cost of gasoil shouldered by farms and fisheries?
https://www.nuovavenezia.it/cronaca/pesca-stangata-gasolio-prezzo-carburante-supera-euro-litro-lkpnv68c.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.5.2026) The Commission is aware that the situation in the Middle East has direct consequences and dire economic and social implications for the EU, in particular for primary agricultural production and fisheries. To face this crisis, the Commission acts in two directions, in close coordination with Member States to follow the most exposed sectors and assess further developments. First course of action: more flexibility for Member States mobilizing national funds. On 29 April 2026, the Commission adopted1 the Middle East crisis Temporary State aid Framework (METSAF)2 which allows for temporary limited amounts of aid for the undertakings active in primary production of agricultural, or fishery and aquaculture, products. Member States may use the METSAF, in addition to the standard State aid rules applicable to the agricultural and fishery sectors, to alleviate the consequences of exceptionally severe increases in the price of fuel and fertilisers caused by the current crisis. Second course of action: channelling existing EU funds towards affected undertakings. This is illustrated, regarding fisheries, by the activation of Article 26(2) of the European Maritime Fisheries and Aquaculture Fund (EMFAF) Regulation3. This crisis mechanism was previously activated to compensate for additional costs and income forgone arising from the disruption caused by the military aggression of Russia against Ukraine in 2022. On 16 April 2026, the Commission activated4 the compensation mechanism provided under the EMFAF Regulation.

E-10-2026-000951.t: Exclusion of Israel from Most-Favoured Nation treatment under World Trade Organization rules
qt: to the Commission Lynn Boylan (The Left), Rudi Kennes (The Left), Danilo Della Valle (The Left), Hana Jalloul Muro (S&D) Subject:

In March 2022, the EU, in collaboration with the G7 countries, stopped treating Russia as a most-favoured nation within the World Trade Organization (WTO) framework in response to the illegal invasion of Ukraine and Russia’s violations of international law. This decision was taken under Article XXI of the 1947 General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade1. The International Court of Justice (ICJ) confirmed in July 2024 that Israel is in violation of key international law peremptory norms, including the right to self-determination of the Palestinian people, the prohibition of territorial acquisition through the use of force, and the prohibition of the crimes of apartheid and racial segregation2. Given Israel is clearly breaching international law and undermining the rules-based order, the same policy response is warranted in order to ensure that the EU is consistently applying international law. Therefore, will the Commission: 1.
Stop treating Israel as a most-favoured nation within the WTO framework?
Engage with G7 colleagues to work towards the ending of Israel’s most-favoured nation treatment, as was done when Russia illegally invaded Ukraine?
Advocate at the WTO’s 14th Ministerial Conference in Cameroon for as many countries as possible to collectively stop treating Israel as a most-favoured nation?

https://www.wto.org/english/docs_e/legal_e/gatt47_e.htm#art21. International Court of Justice (ICJ), advisory opinion of 19 July 2024 on the Legal Consequences arising from the Policies and Practices of Israel in the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including East Jerusalem, para. 229, available at: https://www.icj-cij.org/sites/default/files/case-related/186/186-20240719-adv-01-00en.pdf.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (8.5.2026) Israel has been a member of the World Trade Organization (WTO) since 1995. As such, it benefits from the most favoured nation treatment (MFN), as WTO members agree to give MFN status to each other. The bilateral trade relations between the EU and Israel are governed by the free trade provisions of the EU-Israel Association Agreement1. It gives Israel preferential conditions – compared to the MFN treatment – for accessing the EU market. On 10 September 2025, the President of the Commission announced2 a set of measures the EU could take to address the catastrophic situation in Gaza and in the West Bank. These include proposals for a reinforced package of sanctions and a partial suspension of the Association Agreement on certain trade-related matters. The President also announced the decision to put on hold EU bilateral financial support to Israel, without adversely affecting work with civil society or Yad Vashem. The proposed measures on sanctions and trade have remained on the table for discussion in the Council as the number of supporting Member States is insufficient for their approval. Yet, if adopted and notified, the suspension would mean that imports from Israel would lose their preferential access to the EU market.
1 https://eeas.europa.eu/archives/delegations/israel/documents/eu_israel/asso_agree_en.pdf. 2 https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/state-union/state-union-2025_en.

E-10-2026-000950.t: Risk of losses and failures as the Commission picks winners and losers
qt: to the Commission Dick Erixon (ECR), Charlie Weimers (ECR), Beatrice Timgren (ECR) Subject:

The Commission has announced the launch of a new fund, the Scaleup Europe Fund, with the initial intention of raising EUR 5 billion from taxpayers and private investors1. The fund is to invest in European growth companies in areas such as AI and space technologies2. Situations in which governments pick the winners and losers have resulted in investment failures and the misallocation of capital. Political connections and expertise among grant applicants become more important than creating added value. For example, the European Investment Bank (EIB) has an exposure of over EUR 1 billion to the crisis‑hit firm Northvolt3. The EIB, together with Swedish pension funds, has also used hundreds of millions of euros of taxpayers’ money to support the struggling environmental startup Stegra, which has been estimated by researchers to have a societal value of minus EUR 15‑24 billion4. 1.
What proportion of the initial EUR 5 billion that the fund is to raise will consist of tax revenue contributed by the Commission?
What selection criteria need to be met in order for the fund to invest in a company, and will requirements for specific gender equality and climate policies be an investment condition?
Does the Commission see any risks in allowing politicians to choose winners and losers, rather than allowing the market to decide which projects to invest in?

at: (English version) to the Commission Dick Erixon (ECR), Charlie Weimers (ECR), Beatrice Timgren (ECR) (8 March 2026) Subject: Risk of losses and failures as the Commission picks winners and losers The Commission has announced the launch of a new fund, the Scaleup Europe Fund, with the initial intention of raising EUR 5 billion from taxpayers and private investors 1. (2 June 2026) The Scaleup Europe Fund is designed as a market-based instrument to support the scaling of innovative European companies, while mobilising substantial private investment. The EU contribution to the Scaleup Europe Fund is foreseen as EUR 1 billion, drawn from the European Innovation Council component of Pillar III of Horizon Europe (HE) (5) under the current Multiannual Financial Framework, with the target to attract EUR 4 billion from private investors (of which approximately EUR 2 billion has already been indicated by the group of private founding investors) (6). The selected private fund manager is expected to raise the remaining capital to reach the target size of EUR 5 billion. The Fund will invest high-growth scale-ups in strategic sectors, such as AI, quantum, semiconductors, robotics, energy, space, and biotechnologies/medical technologies, with selection criteria stemming from the HE Programme. The detailed investment strategy will be agreed by all founding investors, including the Commission, with the selected fund manager. Gender equality and climate considerations will be addressed in line with applicable EU legal and policy frameworks but do not constitute HE selection criteria. While the investment guidelines, agreed with all founding investors, will ensure that the Commission policy objectives are reflected in the overall mandate and investment strategy, all investment decisions will be taken by the independent private fund manager according to market standards, thus avoiding any political involvement in individual investment decisions. This ensures independent, market-based, investment decision-making, that will target Europe’s scale-up financing needs.

E-10-2026-000949.t: Hungary’s energy negotiations with Russia – implications for EU sanctions and support for Ukraine
qt: to the Commission Krzysztof Brejza (PPE) Subject:

Recent reports indicate that the Hungarian Minister of Foreign Affairs and Trade Péter Szijjártó, travelled to Moscow to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin to discuss the continuation of Russian energy supplies to Hungary. This meeting took place in the context of Russia’s ongoing war of aggression against Ukraine and the EU’s collective efforts to reduce dependence on Russian energy.1 At a time when the European Union is maintaining sanctions against the Russian Federation and providing strong political, financial and military support to Ukraine, such high-level bilateral engagements with the Russian leadership raise serious concerns regarding EU unity, the effectiveness of sanctions and the credibility of the EU’s common foreign policy. In this context: 1.
How does the Commission assess the compatibility of these bilateral negotiations with the EU’s sanctions regime and its strategy to phase out Russian fossil fuels?
Does the Commission consider that such actions risk undermining the EU’s common position towards Russia and its support for Ukraine?
What measures can the Commission take to ensure that Member States’ bilateral energy arrangements do not weaken EU sanctions or collective energy security?
https://www.euronews.com/2026/03/04/hungarian-foreign-minister-in-moscow-for-energy-talks-with-putinamid-ukraine-pipeline-row.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.4.2026) EU restrictive measures have played a significant role in reducing the EU’s energy dependency on Russia. The EU ’s share of Russian energy revenues fell to less than 9% in 2025 from almost 60% in 2022. The import of Russian crude oil and petroleum products into the EU is prohibited since June 20221. To ensure energy security during a transitional phase, certain EU Member States – including Hungary – have been granted temporary exemptions for specific pipeline imports of Russian oil. The Commission welcomes the efforts taken by a number of Member States to decouple from Russian oil, which have already allowed for the lifting of such exemptions. The latest packages of sanctions imposed further restrictions on energy imports from Russia23, and additional measures have been proposed4. Member States are required to fully respect the restrictive measures in force and ensure that any bilateral engagements do not contradict the EU’s common foreign policy objectives. Furthermore, following the REPowerEU roadmap proposed by the Commission5, in January 2026 the European Parliament and the Council adopted a permanent ban on Russian natural gas imports6. The Druzhba disruptions underscore the strategic importance of diversifying energy supplies. Hungary and Slovakia have the possibility to further reduce their dependence on Russian oil by making greater use of the Adria pipeline through Croatia. The Commission is strongly supporting Hungary’s and Slovakia’s diversification efforts and stands ready to facilitate necessary arrangements with relevant partners.

adopts-sixth-package-of-sanctions/. 2 https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/press/press-releases/2025/07/18/russia-s-war-of-aggression-againstukraine-eu-adopts-18th-package-of-economic-and-individual-measures. 3 https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/press/press-releases/2025/10/23/19th-package-of-sanctions-against-russiaeu-targets-russian-energy-third-country-banks-and-crypto-providers/. 4 https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/it/statement_26_318. 5 https://energy.ec.europa.eu/strategy/repowereu-phase-out-russian-energy-imports_en. 6 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2026/261/oj/eng.

E-10-2026-000948.t: Piñeiral da Madalena (in Cabanas, A Coruña)
qt: to the Commission Ana Miranda Paz (Verts/ALE) Subject:

The Piñeiral da Madalena pine wood is experiencing problems caused by marine erosion and pine trees growing in the sand. The conservation and regeneration project to tackle those issues is financed by EU funds earmarked for the just transition and has a budget of EUR 498 872.22. However, the local People’s Party government is attacking the conservation of the ecosystem on several fronts, indiscriminately cutting down trees to build a car park and dumping waste excavated as part of works on the sewage system on the grass. 1.
What is the Commission’s opinion of EU funds being wasted in that way, considering that those funds are intended to protect and restore the land, not put it at risk?
What action does it intend to take to improve the audit of EU-funded projects?

(6 May 2026) According to the information available to the Commission, this project was part of the Recovery and Resilience Plan Facility (RRF). The particular project referred to in the question falls under component 10 (Just Transition), investment 1 (Investment in Just Transition) of the Spanish Recovery and Resilience Plan (RRP). The relevant target (#140), which required the publication in the Official Journal of the award of at least 100 environmental, digital and social infrastructure projects in Just Transition Areas, was positively assessed under the fourth payment request (1) in June 2024. Compliance with the ‘Do No Significant Harm’ principle is a prerequisite for a measure to be included in a RRP (Article 5(2) of Regulation 2021/241) (2). Disbursements under the Facility are tied to the satisfactory fulfilment of these conditions. Member States bear primary responsibility for the management and control of EU financing provided under the RRF funds. They are required to establish robust control systems to ensure that funds are utilised effectively and appropriately. To this end, the Member States must provide details on the measures implemented, adhere to specific control requirements, and submit regular audit reports to the Commission, also for measures already assessed. The Commission, in turn, carries out its own assessments and audits to confirm that Member States are fulfilling their obligations and that funds are being appropriately implemented. The Commission utilises various tools and procedures to review and validate the information provided by Member States.

E-10-2026-000946.t: Use of Emissions Trading System revenues and Italian ‘Energy Decree’
qt: to the Commission Annalisa Corrado (S&D), Nicola Zingaretti (S&D), Brando Benifei (S&D), Giorgio Gori (S&D), Maria Grapini (S&D), Camilla Laureti (S&D), Alessandra Moretti (S&D), Sandro Ruotolo (S&D), Benedetta Scuderi (Verts/ALE), Marco Tarquinio (S&D), Bruno Tobback (S&D), Marie Toussaint (Verts/ALE), Georgia Tramacere (S&D), Alessandro Zan (S&D), Thomas Pellerin-Carlin (S&D) Subject:

Under Article 10(3) of Directive 2003/87/EC, Member States were required to use at least 50 % of EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) auction revenues for climate- and energyrelated purposes during the 2012–2023 period, and to report transparently on the allocation of such revenues. Following the 2023 revision of the EU ETS, Member States are now required to use the full amount, or an amount of equivalent financial value, for such purposes. Recent analyses indicate that Italy may have allocated only around 9 % of EU ETS auction revenues generated between 2012 and 2023 to climate-related expenditure, despite total revenues estimated to be worth approximately EUR 15.6 billion. At the same time, the recent Italian ‘Energy Decree’ introduces a mechanism that effectively sterilises the EU ETS cost component for gas-fired power plants. By neutralising the carbon price signal for fossil-fuel based energy generation, this measure risks undermining the decarbonisation objective of the EU ETS and distorting competition in the internal electricity market. In this context: 1.
Is the Commission aware of the reported gap between the required use of EU ETS revenues and their actual allocation in Italy?
Has the Commission assessed whether the recent Italian measure is compatible with EU ETS legislation, State aid rules and internal market principles?
What steps will the Commission take to ensure compliance with Article 10(3) and safeguard the integrity of the EU ETS?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (29.4.2026) Member States are encouraged to spend their Emission Trading System (ETS) revenues swiftly and effectively to maximise their impact to address the climate and energy transition. The Honourable Members note correctly that since the entry into force of Directive (EU) 2023/9591 in June 2024, Member States are obliged to spend all their auction revenues2 on the climate and energy purposes listed in Article 10(3) of ETS Directive3, except for any revenue that they spend in aid for indirect carbon costs compensation. The Commission analyses the spending by all Member States. It publishes the analysis of the Member States’ reports in the yearly Carbon Market Report4 and the Climate Action Progress Report5. In 2025, Member States reported for the first time for a full year that is subject to the new spending requirement6. These reports are available on the website of the European Environment Agency7. The Commission is closely monitoring compliance with the new spending obligation to ensure all ETS revenue is truly spent in line with the provisions of the ETS Directive. The Commission is aware that not all Member States have spent the full amount of their latest auction revenues on climate and energy purposes as of now. For Italy, on the basis of its reports not all revenues have been allocated to climate purposes. The Commission will follow up with Member States, as appropriate. On the recent Italian ‘Energy Decree’, the Commission is working very closely with the Italian government, to assess whether the decree complies with State aid rules and EU legislation.

qt: to the Commission Kathleen Funchion (The Left) Subject:

Can the Commission outline what safeguards, if any, are in place to ensure that planning permission processes and/or judicial reviews are not influenced, directly or indirectly, by the awarding of an EU Strategic Technologies for Europe Platform (STEP) award, known as the STEP Seal, to a proposed project that has yet to conclude its planning permission process or is the subject of a judicial review?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (16.4.2026) The Strategic Technologies for Europe Platform (STEP) Seal is meant to create incentives for private investors or for Member States to support the project financially. It is meant to flag the project proposal as being of interest for the European single market and of excellent quality. The STEP Seal has no connection with planning permissions or related judicial reviews unless this is specifically stated in the call for proposals. Consequently, the Commission does not track whether a project proposal is awarded the Seal prior or only after a planning permission has been granted. Should a planning permission be listed as a requirement in a STEP-relevant EU call for proposals, and the applicant project has not achieved it at the time of application, the applicant will simply not be awarded a STEP Seal.

E-10-2026-000942.t: Classification of local electricity supply facilities (‘customer facilities’) under internal market law pursuant to Directive (EU) 2019/944
qt: to the Commission Andrea Wechsler (PPE), Christian Ehler (PPE), Jens Geier (S&D), Hildegard Bentele (PPE), Jens Gieseke (PPE) Subject:
Classification of local electricity supply facilities (‘customer facilities’) under internal market law pursuant to Directive (EU) 2019/944

Following the ruling of the Court of Justice in Case C-293/23 (ENGIE Deutschland) and subsequent case-law in Germany, local electricity supply models that have been widely used to date (e.g. tenant electricity/neighbourhood solutions, business parks, shopping centres, hospitals) are being classified as distribution systems within the meaning of Directive (EU) 2019/944 much more often. This would means that operators supplying electricity to several end users via short internal lines would in many cases have obligations typically foreseen for regulated distribution system operators. The stricter classification threatens to overwhelm well-established, locally limited supply structures with significant regulatory obligations, without any measurable strengthening of competition or system security. 1.

Does the Commission agree that current EU law does not provide a proportionate exemption framework for such small-scale, geographically limited installations, where competition is not appreciably affected?

Is the Commission considering a targeted amendment of Directive (EU) 2019/944 (or accompanying legal acts) to provide Member States with a clear legal framework for ‘customer facility-like’ structures that should not be considered as networks?
at: (English version) to the Commission Andrea Wechsler (PPE), Christian Ehler (PPE), Jens Geier (S&D), Hildegard Bentele (PPE), Jens Gieseke (PPE) (6 March 2026) Subject: Classification of local electricity supply facilities (‘customer facilities’) under internal market law pursuant to Directive (EU) 2019/944 Following the ruling of the Court of Justice in Case C-293/23 (ENGIE Deutschland) and subsequent case-law in Germany, local electricity supply models that have been widely used to date (e.g. tenant electricity/neighbourhood solutions, business parks, shopping centres, hospitals) are being classified as distribution systems within the meaning of Directive (EU) 2019/944 much more often. This would means that operators supplying electricity to several end users via short internal lines would in many cases have obligations typically foreseen for regulated distribution system operators. The stricter classification threatens to overwhelm well-established, locally limited supply structures with significant regulatory obligations, without any measurable strengthening of competition or system security. 1. Does the Commission agree that current EU law does not provide a proportionate exemption framework for such smallscale, geographically limited installations, where competition is not appreciably affected? 2. Is the Commission considering a targeted amendment of Directive (EU) 2019/944 (or accompanying legal acts) to provide Member States with a clear legal framework for ‘customer facility-like’ structures that should not be considered as networks? (12 June 2026) The Commission agrees that unnecessary administrative burden for customers and small grid operators should be avoided. This is also reflected in the current rules that provide, for instance, for special regimes for Citizens Energy Communities, Renewable Energy Communities, Closed Distribution Systems, Small and Isolated Systems, energy sharing and active customers. However, as regulatory oversight over network operators can be a crucial tool to protect consumers’ interests, it is important to strike the right balance between administrative simplification and consumer protection. The Commission is working closely with national governments and regulators to assess whether there are additional cases where rules for smaller and local grids may be simplified.

E-10-2026-000940.t: Approving Solar Package I provisions on repowering photovoltaic systems under State aid rules
qt: to the Commission Joachim Streit (Renew) Subject:
Approving Solar Package I provisions on repowering photovoltaic systems under State aid rules

As part of Germany’s Solar Package I, adopted in 2024, new provisions on the so-called ‘repowering’ of photovoltaic installations were included in the country’s Renewable Energy Act (Erneuerbare-Energien-Gesetz – EEG). These provisions are intended to enable operators of older systems to replace existing modules with ones that are more modern and more efficient, without automatically losing the remuneration rate originally granted. However, according to the latest information, these provisions are still subject to the Commission’s approval under State aid rules, and can therefore not be applied yet in practice. In relevant cases, network operators are indicating that the previous arrangements will continue to apply until a decision is taken by the Commission. 1.
Is the Commission currently assessing the provisions on repowering photovoltaic systems under State aid rules?
If so, what is the status of this procedure?
Is it possible to say when a Commission decision can be expected?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.4.2026) The Commission has been in contact with the German authorities regarding the ‘Solar Package I’ amendments to the German Renewable Energy Law (EEG 2023). One of the criteria for authorising State aid is to limit aid to what is necessary to address an identified market failure and thus avoid overcompensating beneficiaries. This principle is reflected in the Climate, Energy and Environmental Aid Guidelines1, which govern the Commission’s assessment of aid. Long-term commitments to disburse aid (contract duration of up to 20 years) create considerable uncertainty about market developments and whether financial projections are being implemented in practice, and thus the possibility of undue windfall profits. For this reason, in the Commission decision of December 2022 in Case SA.1020842 approving the EEG 2023, Germany committed to introduce a claw-back clause (or similar mechanism) to limit any windfall profits. This obligation is a condition for the authorisation of the German State aid scheme. It is the responsibility of Member States to notify aid in line with the applicable legal requirements and to ensure the timeliness and quality of the information provided. Once a Member State notifies to the Commission a proposal for an aid scheme or its amendment, the Commission assesses whether the proposed scheme or amendment is in line with the State aid Guidelines and sectoral legislation. By ensuring compliance with these rules, the Commission ensures the compatibility of the proposed scheme or amendment with the internal market and its legitimacy vis-à-vis other Member States. The Commission has two months from the receipt of a complete notification to issue a decision. Given the confidential nature of discussions between the Commission and the Member States, the Commission cannot comment on the details of any particular notification.

E-10-2026-000939.t: EU Legal Gateway and its connection to the issuance of Schengen visas
qt: to the Commission Fabrice Leggeri (PfE), Tom Vandendriessche (PfE) Subject:

The EU is committed to establishing a ‘European Legal Gateway Office’ in India, with information and communication technologies (ICT) as a primary focus. This ‘one-stop hub’ will serve as a ‘digital platform and operational centre’ intended to inform potential applicants of Indian nationality about legal migration channels and support their travel to the EU as part of a pilot phase lasting approximately 26 months. It is also reported in the press that the European Union is opening this new office in New Delhi in order to accelerate the issuance of Schengen visas for ICT specialists. The office would be the first of its kind in a partner country. These commitments are part of the EU strategy to implement legal migration mechanisms with third countries. 1.

Can the Commission state whether, in the immediate or long term, this ‘gateway’ will amount to a visa office? Can it make clear the legal basis for the office, how it will be funded, who will work there and where it will be hosted?
What relationship is envisaged between this new visa office of the Commission and the consulates of EU or Schengen Member States in India and the EU Delegation to India?
at: (English version) to the Commission Fabrice Leggeri (PfE), Tom Vandendriessche (PfE) (6 March 2026) Subject: EU Legal Gateway and its connection to the issuance of Schengen visas The EU is committed to establishing a ‘European Legal Gateway Office’ in India, with information and communication technologies (ICT) as a primary focus. This ‘one-stop hub’ will serve as a ‘digital platform and operational centre’ intended to inform potential applicants of Indian nationality about legal migration channels and support their travel to the EU as part of a pilot phase lasting approximately 26 months. It is also reported in the press that the European Union is opening this new office in New Delhi in order to accelerate the issuance of Schengen visas for ICT specialists. The office would be the first of its kind in a partner country. These commitments are part of the EU strategy to implement legal migration mechanisms with third countries. 1. Can the Commission state whether, in the immediate or long term, this ‘gateway’ will amount to a visa office? Can it make clear the legal basis for the office, how it will be funded, who will work there and where it will be hosted? 2. What relationship is envisaged between this new visa office of the Commission and the consulates of EU or Schengen Member States in India and the EU Delegation to India? (22 May 2026) An EU-India memorandum of understanding on a comprehensive framework of cooperation on mobility (MoU) was signed on 27 January 2026 (1). In this context, the European Legal Gateway Office pilot in India (2) will facilitate safe, legal, and well-informed mobility from India to Member States in the Information and Communications Technology (ICT) sector. Through a dedicated office in India, a support office in the EU and an accompanying digital tool, the European Legal Gateway Office pilot will provide clear and reliable information on mobility pathways and their various skills and qualification requirements in the EU to Indian students, researchers, and professionals in the ICT sector. It will also support EU-based employers and higher education institutions to engage with Indian talent. The European Legal Gateway Office pilot will not be issuing any type of visas, as this is a competence of the Member States. To obtain a visa, third-country nationals, including those benefiting from the services of the European Legal Gateway Office pilot, will need to undergo national immigration procedures, including security checks. There is no intention for the European Legal Gateway Office pilot in India to act as a visa office; it will instead provide information about visa requirements and procedures to interested Indian nationals.
