qt: to the Commission Jörgen Warborn (PPE) Subject:

On 22 January 2026, a majority in the European Parliament voted in favour of applying the ‘one in, two out’ principle, whereby the introduction of new regulatory costs should be accompanied by the removal of at least twice the equivalent costs elsewhere. In the light of the upcoming discussions on regulatory simplification at the Council, as well as the Commission’s forthcoming communication on better regulation expected on 28 April 2026, it remains unclear how the Commission intends to reflect the position expressed by Parliament and deliver on its burden-reduction objectives. In this context: 1.
How does the Commission intend to take into account the clear support expressed by a majority in Parliament for the ‘one in, two out’ principle in its upcoming communication on better regulation?
Does the Commission plan to incorporate this principle into its broader strategy to reduce regulatory burdens and strengthen European competitiveness?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (30.4.2026) The Commission introduced the ‘one-in, one-out’ mechanism in 2022 to simplify and reduce administrative burdens for businesses1. In 2025, the Commission strengthened its efforts, going hand in hand with facilitating implementation and enforcement. The Commission has set a very ambitious target of reducing administrative burdens for companies by at least 25%, and by at least 35% for small and medium-sized enterprises. This target goes much beyond savings that could be achieved with the ‘one in, two out’ approach. During 2025, the Commission tabled Omnibus and other Simplification Proposals, which – if approved by the co-legislators, could deliver at least EUR 15 billion savings in recurring administrative costs2. This is the net result of EUR 15.25 billion in cost savings and EUR 247 million in additional costs. This result is already now significantly more ambitious than any level of savings that would result from a ‘one-in, two out’ approach. The Commission has a comprehensive agenda for regulatory efficiency and is stepping up its simplification efforts. Implementation dialogues and reality checks are helping to identify undue complexities and simplification avenues. An Action Plan on Regulatory Deep Cleaning, recently announced by the President of the Commission, will further address overlaps, duplications, inefficiencies and redundancies, as well as foster the consolidation of legislation in fragmented areas.
1 The results can be found on the website: https://commission.europa.eu/law/law-making-process/better-

regulation/simplification-and-implementation/simplification/one-one-out-approach_en. 2 https://commission.europa.eu/law/law-making-process/better-regulation/simplification-andimplementation/simplification_en.

E-10-2026-000937.t: Strengthening digital transformation programmes and facilitating SMEs’ access to them
qt: to the Commission Dimitris Tsiodras (PPE) Subject:

A number of conclusions can be drawn from the Commission’s assessment of the effectiveness of the Digital Europe Programme with regard to its successes and how to make it more effective. In particular, while small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) are a key target group of the programme’s efforts, only 17 % of funding is allocated to them. Indeed, the application process was considered challenging due to extensive administrative requirements, while many respondents pointed to issues such as obligatory double reporting to the European Commission and national authorities as well as co-financing requirements. These obstacles can have a significant impact on the programme’s effectiveness and on the EU’s ability to achieve its digital objectives. In view of the multiannual financial framework 2028-2034, can the Commission say: 1.
How does it intend to simplify the digital financing mechanisms and access thereto for SMEs, in order to boost their competitiveness and their ability to integrate into European value chains?
How will it help bridge the gap and accelerate the transition from research and innovation to the application of research results and their commercialisation?
How will it improve coordination with national funding programmes and national digital initiatives to ensure that activities at different levels support and reinforce each other?
at: (English version) to the Commission Dimitris Tsiodras (PPE) (6 March 2026) Subject: Strengthening digital transformation programmes and facilitating SMEs’ access to them A number of conclusions can be drawn from the Commission’s assessment of the effectiveness of the Digital Europe Programme with regard to its successes and how to make it more effective. In particular, while small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) are a key target group of the programme’s efforts, only 17% of funding is allocated to them. Indeed, the application process was considered challenging due to extensive administrative requirements, while many respondents pointed to issues such as obligatory double reporting to the European Commission and national authorities as well as co-financing requirements. These obstacles can have a significant impact on the programme’s effectiveness and on the EU’s ability to achieve its digital objectives. In view of the multiannual financial framework 2028-2034, can the Commission say: 1.
How does it intend to simplify the digital financing mechanisms and access thereto for SMEs, in order to boost their competitiveness and their ability to integrate into European value chains?
How will it help bridge the gap and accelerate the transition from research and innovation to the application of research results and their commercialisation?
How will it improve coordination with national funding programmes and national digital initiatives to ensure that activities at different levels support and reinforce each other?

(23 April 2026) Drawing on the learning from the programmes under the current Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF), the Commission’s proposal for the next MFF (1) foresees simpler and integrated support for stakeholders, including small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). These include the use of a single work programme for the entire digital leadership window, a single rulebook, a common set of instruments, and a coherent approach to leveraging private investments through the European Innovation Council (EIC) and the European Competitiveness Fund (2) (ECF) InvestEU Instrument. The proposal also foresees dedicated actions to increase SME participation, business support and the establishment of the ‘EU for Business’ Network. The integrated approach between the ECF and the successor of Horizon Europe (3) will ensure a comprehensive support to the entire innovation journey from research to pilots, early industrialisation, manufacturing and deployment, with the EIC playing a key role. It aims to provide key infrastructure support. The ECF will have dedicated support for scaling up, such as the scale up facility under the ECF InvestEU Instrument, and support for advanced skills development needed by SMEs to develop and deploy innovative solutions. The Digital Decade Policy Programme 2030 (4) will be a policy framework for the ECF and National and Regional Partnership Plans (NRPPs).

Communication from the Commission to the European Parliament, the European Council, the Council, the European Economic and Social Committee and the Committee of the Regions, ‘A dynamic EU Budget for the priorities of the future — The Multiannual Financial Framework 2028-2034’ (COM(2025) 570 final). Proposal for a regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council on establishing the European Competitiveness Fund (‘ECF’), including the specific programme for defence research and innovation activities, repealing Regulations (EU) 2021/522, (EU) 2021/694, (EU) 2021/697, (EU) 2021/783, repealing provisions of Regulations (EU) 2021/696, (EU) 2023/588, and amending Regulation (EU) [EDIP] (COM/2025/555 final). Proposal for a regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council establishing Horizon Europe, the framework Programme for Research and Innovation, for the period 2028-2034 laying down its rules for participation and dissemination, and repealing Regulation (EU) 2021/695 (COM/2025/543 final). Decision (EU) 2022/2481 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 December 2022 establishing the Digital Decade Policy Programme 2030 (OJ L 323, 19.12.2022, pp. 4-26, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dec/2022/2481/oj).
The State of the Digital Decade reports will ensure coordination and track progress towards the digital transformation, issuing semester-like recommendations on areas for reform and investment.

E-10-2026-000935.t: Timetable and EU framework for the Porto-Vigo high-speed rail line
qt: to the Commission Catarina Martins (The Left) Subject:

The high-speed rail line between Porto and Vigo, due to be finished by 2032, is considered strategic for cross-border travel in the north-west Iberian Peninsula. The President of the Government of Galicia, Alfonso Rueda, recently gave 2038 as the rail connection’s expected completion date. The Secretary-General of the North-West Peninsula Atlantic Corridor, Xoán Mao, meanwhile, has expressed concerns over missing or insufficient technical studies to back up Rueda’s claims, accusing him of spreading ‘nonsense and lies’. Given those contradictory statements and the urgent need to safeguard cross-border travel between Porto and Vigo, I would like to ask the Commission: 1.

What is the indicative timeline at EU level for the Porto-Vigo high-speed rail connection, which is supported by EU funds under the Connecting Europe Facility (CEF) and from the European Investment Bank (EIB)?
Is the Commission monitoring the cooperation between Portugal, the Government of Galicia and the Spanish Government on the development of this project?

What is the Commission’s assessment of the impact a possible postponement to 2038 could have on territorial cohesion, sustainable mobility and decarbonisation objectives in the Galicia-North Portugal Euroregion?

(29 June 2026) 1. Under Regulation (EU) 2024/1679, the high-speed railway line between Porto and Vigo is part of the extended core network, with a target completion date set for 2040. So far, no Connecting Europe Facility funding has been allocated to this project. 2. The EU Coordinator attends as an observer the ‘Alta Velocidad(e) España Portugal European Economic Interest Group’ (AVEP) meetings, where the cooperation for the high-speed rail cross-border projects between Portugal and Spain takes place. 3. E-10-2026-000933.t: Clarification on Child Guarantee funding: detailed disbursements per Member State
qt: to the Council Niels Geuking (PPE), Hristo Petrov (Renew), Vilija Blinkevičiūtė (S&D), Marlena Maląg (ECR), Katrin Langensiepen (Verts/ALE), Kathleen Funchion (The Left) Subject:

Biennial progress reports on the implementation of the European Child Guarantee are due by March 2026. The 2024 reports vary in quality and focus. Notably, information on budget execution within the total allocated amount of EUR 6.454 billion from the EU budget and EUR 9.284 billion from the combined EU and Member States’ budgets remains unclear. Available information provides the general allocations per country, but there is no clear and itemised breakdown for each Member State concerning the type of intervention and the result achieved regarding the key services of the Child Guarantee: early childhood education and care; education and school-based activities (including one healthy meal each school day); healthcare; healthy nutrition; and adequate housing. As detailed financial information is essential for monitoring the Child Guarantee’s implementation, we ask the Council: 1.

Will it ensure that the forthcoming biennial progress reports include the actual amounts disbursed by each Member State for the Child Guarantee, broken down by specific type of intervention (e.g. school meals), including the name or brief description of each intervention, and classified according to key services of the Child Guarantee?
Could it provide a comprehensive, comparable, EU-wide tabular overview of such payments?
What concrete steps will the Council take to improve transparency and reporting on budget execution and project-level spending under the Child Guarantee?

E-10-2026-000932.t: Air fares and protecting Europeans stranded abroad following the escalation in the Middle East
qt: to the Commission Brando Benifei (S&D), Nicola Zingaretti (S&D), Giuseppe Lupo (S&D), Alessandro Zan (S&D), Pierfrancesco Maran (S&D), Irene Tinagli (S&D), Giorgio Gori (S&D), Camilla Laureti (S&D), Alessandra Moretti (S&D), Georgia Tramacere (S&D), Marco Tarquinio (S&D) Subject:

The war that is ramping up in Iran and across the Middle East is having a dramatic effect on international and intercontinental air traffic. With scores of flight cancellations, thousands of Europeans are stranded abroad – not only in the Middle East but also in South Asia (India, Sri Lanka, the Maldives). According to consumer reports, a number of the airlines still operating are apparently charging extortionate fairs and possibly applying speculative practices and predatory pricing, putting those affected under increased economic and psychological strain. In light of this: 1.

Is the Commission aware of these goings-on, and will it check that the active European carriers are not employing speculative pricing, in violation of EU law designed to protect consumers and safeguard competition?

Does it intend to urgently adopt a guide, operational guidelines or any other resources to provide the Europeans trapped abroad with clear information on their rights, reimbursement options, consular support and protection mechanisms, so as to relieve the heavy burden currently on Member State consulates and embassies?
at: (English version) to the Commission Brando Benifei (S&D), Nicola Zingaretti (S&D), Giuseppe Lupo (S&D), Alessandro Zan (S&D), Pierfrancesco Maran (S&D), Irene Tinagli (S&D), Giorgio Gori (S&D), Camilla Laureti (S&D), Alessandra Moretti (S&D), Georgia Tramacere (S&D), Marco Tarquinio (S&D) (5 March 2026) Subject: Air fares and protecting Europeans stranded abroad following the escalation in the Middle East The war that is ramping up in Iran and across the Middle East is having a dramatic effect on international and intercontinental air traffic. With scores of flight cancellations, thousands of Europeans are stranded abroad — not only in the Middle East but also in South Asia (India, Sri Lanka, the Maldives). According to consumer reports, a number of the airlines still operating are apparently charging extortionate fairs and possibly applying speculative practices and predatory pricing, putting those affected under increased economic and psychological strain. In light of this: 1.

Is the Commission aware of these goings-on, and will it check that the active European carriers are not employing speculative pricing, in violation of EU law designed to protect consumers and safeguard competition?

Does it intend to urgently adopt a guide, operational guidelines or any other resources to provide the Europeans trapped abroad with clear information on their rights, reimbursement options, consular support and protection mechanisms, so as to relieve the heavy burden currently on Member State consulates and embassies?

(11 May 2026) 1. The Commission monitors aviation market developments on an ongoing basis, including with respect to prices. The Commission has currently no evidence that airlines operating under the EU’s jurisdiction are abusing their pricing power. Under the Air Services Regulation (1) and under many international agreements for flights to and from third countries, airlines have the freedom to set prices for air services. The Air Services Regulation also requires that the final price including all unavoidable and foreseeable elements be displayed at all times. This applies alongside general consumer law prohibiting unfair contract terms and unfair commercial practices and alongside Union competition rules. 2. The Commission provided support for the Member States’ evacuation and repatriation efforts, including through the EU Civil Protection Mechanism (2) (UCPM) and the Emergency Response Coordination Centre (ERCC), working closely with EU Delegations. The Commission has provided assistance to Member States and EU citizens with targeted information on the applicable EU passenger rights and rights of package travellers published on Your Europe website (3) and issues linked to EU passenger rights were discussed at a meeting on 12 March 2026 of the national enforcement bodies for Regulation (EC) No 261/2004 (4). The Commission has facilitated relevant exchanges between national authorities in the Consumer Protection Cooperation (CPC) Network under Regulation (EU) 2017/2394 (5), and shared relevant information with the European Consumer Centres Network (6), offering help and advice to consumers in Europe and the Europe Direct Contact Centre.

https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2008/1008/oj/eng. Between 3 and 16 March 2026, 92 flights were completed under the UCPM, repatriating over 13 400 passengers, including 12 500 EU citizens. Five repatriation flights to Romania and Poland were operated by the rescEU Transport and Logistics capacity which was mobilised for the first time. https://europa.eu/youreurope/citizens/travel/passengerrights/air/files/FAQ_Assistance_to_passengers_in_case_of_flight_disruptions_to_the_Middle_East_countries_20260305_EN.pdf (information also available in all EU languages). https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2004/261/oj/eng. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32017R2394&qid=1776269281995. E-10-2026-000931.t: Economic consequences of the carbon border adjustment mechanism for the outermost regions
qt: to the Commission Rody Tolassy (PfE), André Rougé (PfE), Marie-Luce Brasier-Clain (PfE), Valérie Deloge (PfE), Pierre Pimpie (PfE), Julie Rechagneux (PfE), Philippe Olivier (PfE) Subject:

Regulation (EU) 2023/956 establishing a carbon border adjustment mechanism (CBAM) aims to tackle carbon leakage and bring imports into line with the EU’s environmental requirements. However, the application of its environmental objectives raises concerns about its economic and social consequences in the outermost regions (ORs). The construction and fertiliser industries, which are essential for infrastructure development, housing construction and the agricultural sovereignty of the ORs, depend very heavily on imports of materials that are highly exposed to the CBAM, in particular cement, steel and fertilisers. In regions already facing geographical remoteness, narrow markets, structural additional costs and a persistent high cost of living, the potential increase of costs linked to the CBAM could exacerbate economic tensions, hinder public and private investment and undermine the development and territorial cohesion objectives. 1.

Can the Commission explain how it intends to take into account the specific characteristics of the ORs, established in Article 349 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, when implementing the CBAM?

Is it considering adaptation, compensation or exemption mechanisms to prevent the instrument from becoming an additional factor contributing to the economic and social fragility of those strategic EU territories?
Supporter1
This question is supported by a Member other than the authors: Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE).
at: (English version) to the Commission Rody Tolassy (PfE), André Rougé (PfE), Marie-Luce Brasier-Clain (PfE), Valérie Deloge (PfE), Pierre Pimpie (PfE), Julie Rechagneux (PfE), Philippe Olivier (PfE) (5 March 2026) Subject: Economic consequences of the carbon border adjustment mechanism for the outermost regions Regulation (EU) 2023/956 establishing a carbon border adjustment mechanism (CBAM) aims to tackle carbon leakage and bring imports into line with the EU’s environmental requirements. However, the application of its environmental objectives raises concerns about its economic and social consequences in the outermost regions (ORs). The construction and fertiliser industries, which are essential for infrastructure development, housing construction and the agricultural sovereignty of the ORs, depend very heavily on imports of materials that are highly exposed to the CBAM, in particular cement, steel and fertilisers. In regions already facing geographical remoteness, narrow markets, structural additional costs and a persistent high cost of living, the potential increase of costs linked to the CBAM could exacerbate economic tensions, hinder public and private investment and undermine the development and territorial cohesion objectives. 1. Can the Commission explain how it intends to take into account the specific characteristics of the ORs, established in Article 349 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, when implementing the CBAM? 2. Is it considering adaptation, compensation or exemption mechanisms to prevent the instrument from becoming an additional factor contributing to the economic and social fragility of those strategic EU territories? Supporter (1) (16 July 2026) The Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) (1) is a key instrument of the EU’s climate policy. It aims to prevent the risk of carbon leakage and support the achievement of the EU’s ambitious climate targets. Therefore, CBAM’s uniform application throughout the EU’s customs territory is essential for its coherence, environmental efficiency, and compliance with international rules. In 2027, the Commission will present its assessment of the CBAM on the basis of the results of the first year of implementation during its definitive period. It will inform measures that, where appropriate, could be taken in this regard, supported by detailed data to ensure that they do not undermine the fundamental principles of the CBAM. The Commission is fully aware of the particular challenges faced by the outermost regions and is committed to the implementation of policies adapted to their realities, in line with Article 349 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union. The Commission also recognised in the Fertilisers Action Plan (2) that farmers in the outermost regions are faced with additional costs when acquiring fertilisers and aims to address some of the specific challenges of farmers in the outermost regions as part of a new strategy for the outermost regions, and its accompanying regulatory package, to be adopted in summer 2026. In addition, the Commission will continue to mobilise instruments for economic, structural and financial support to assist the outermost regions in their green transition while preserving their economic and social development.
This question is supported by a Member other than the authors: Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE). https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A02023R0956-20251020. COM(2026) 310 final.

E-10-2026-000930.t: Safeguard measures for the European metal industry
qt: to the Commission François-Xavier Bellamy (PPE), Nadine Morano (PPE), Isabelle Le Callennec (PPE), Céline Imart (PPE), Christophe Gomart (PPE) Subject:

On 18 November 2025, the Commission imposed safeguard measures in relation to several types of ferroalloys, in response to a surge in imports that is threatening the survival of European producers. However, the safeguard measures were not applied to one specific type of ferroalloy, silicon metal, even though the silicon metal industry has been severely undermined by unfair competition from China. This material is of major strategic importance for many sectors, including semiconductors, batteries, aluminium, chemistry and defence. European producers of silicon metal face the same serious difficulties as producers of other types of ferroalloys; they are shutting off some of their furnaces, scaling back their activities or even closing down their plants entirely. 1.
Does the Commission recognise the critical situation faced by European silicon metal producers, who have alerted it on several occasions?
Is it prepared to extend the safeguard measures to silicon metal as a matter of urgency, to protect this ferroalloy in the same way as other types?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (10.4.2026) The Commission acknowledges the critical situation faced by European silicon metal producers and understands their concerns. The Commission opened a safeguard investigation on six manganese- and silicon-based alloys, including silicon metal, in December 20241. However, the conditions for safeguard measures for silicon metal were not met, as there was no increase in imports. In fact, imports of silicon decreased during the most recent period assessed. Therefore, silicon was not included in the scope of the safeguard measure imposed in November 20252. Nevertheless, the Commission remains attentive to the industry's challenges. Although the current safeguard measure in force for other ferro-alloys cannot be altered to include silicon, the Commission is committed to exploring all viable options to help the industry, including through trade defence instruments. The Commission would like to stress that it takes the difficulties of EU silicon metal producers seriously and is continuously engaging with the industry with a view to identifying the most effective way forward.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=OJ:C_202407541. 2 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=OJ:L_202502351.

E-10-2026-000928.t: Use of the European Social Fund Plus (ESF+) to finance abortion
qt: to the Commission Paolo Inselvini (ECR), Carlo Fidanza (ECR), Nicola Procaccini (ECR), Alberico Gambino (ECR), Carlo Ciccioli (ECR), Sergio Berlato (ECR), Francesco Torselli (ECR), Daniele Polato (ECR) Subject:

In its formal response to the ‘My Voice, My Choice’ European Citizens’ Initiative, the Commission stated that Member States can use national programmes co-financed by the ESF+ to support access to abortion. This position appears to be a political reinterpretation of the aims of a fund that was set up to promote employment and social inclusion and provide support for the most vulnerable. The Commissioners themselves stated in the ensuing press conference that it was the first time that a clarifying statement to this effect had been issued. Using nothing more than a communication, the EC is suggesting new funding areas that are not explicitly foreseen in the ESF+ Regulation. The Commission’s stance could also be at odds with the Treaties’ provisions establishing that bioethical choices and the organisation of public health services are Member State competences. In the light of the above, we ask the Commission: 1.
What is the legal basis for using statements to suggest new funding areas for ESF+ funds that are not specifically provided for by the relevant regulation?
How will it ensure that this interpretation does not lead to European funds being used to promote abortion tourism in the EU?

Does it consider that using ESF+ funds in this area is compatible with the safeguards provided for in the Treaties and in the specific protocols applicable to Member States like Ireland and Malta, two countries that have always claimed that abortion and upholding the dignity of human life fall within their exclusive competence?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (21.5.2026) In its formal response1 to the ‘My Voice, My Choice’ European Citizens’ Initiative, the Commission does not introduce a new funding area under the European Social Fund Plus (ESF+)2. One of the specific objectives of the ESF+, set out in Article 4(1)(k), is that of enhancing equal and timely access to quality, sustainable and affordable services, including access to person-centred care including healthcare. Therefore, the ESF+ can support initiatives, selected at national level, that aim to ensure and enhance equal and timely access to healthcare services. These efforts are part of a broader strategy to enhance social cohesion and improve the overall quality of life for everyone living in the EU. The Commission Communication3 explicitly states that any Member State action in response to this initiative would have to remain fully neutral as to where the patients come from, and could not therefore be targeted or limited to patients from other Member States. The Commission’s follow up to the initiative is fully in line with EU law and the division of competences between the EU and the Member States. In its formal response, the Commission recalls that any financial support for Member State action promoting health must comply with the limitations set out in Article 168(7) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU. Therefore, the Commission stresses that it is for Member States to decide whether they want to allocate resources received though ESF+ to abortion care, and that Member States remain competent for organising the delivery of this health service.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:52026XC01383. 2 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32021R1057. 3 See footnote 1.

E-10-2026-000927.t: Debt of public hospitals in the EU
qt: to the Commission Marcin Sypniewski (ESN) Subject:

In many Member States public hospitals are becoming increasingly indebted. Data has been published showing that more than half of hospitals in Germany are either insolvent or at the limits of solvency. In France, the total debt of public hospitals is high, with some estimates pointing to a level of EUR 30 billion. The situation is similar in Poland and other Member States. The increase in hospital debt is influenced by operating costs, including energy, heating, gas, medicines and wages. Hospital creditors often pursue claims through legal proceedings. Compensation for debt collection and interest for late payment in commercial transactions, which is significantly higher than statutory interest, is added by creditors to the amount charged for deliveries. This generates a further cost and burden for hospitals, increasing their indebtedness. 1.
In this connection, does the Commission see any possibility of taking legislative action to reduce the deficit in hospitals? If so, what kind of action?

Does the Commission see any possibility of exempting public hospitals from the application of Directive 2011/7/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 16 February 2011, so that they would not be obliged to bear the burden of additional costs?
at: (English version) to the Commission Marcin Sypniewski (ESN) (5 March 2026) Subject: Debt of public hospitals in the EU In many Member States public hospitals are becoming increasingly indebted. Data has been published showing that more than half of hospitals in Germany are either insolvent or at the limits of solvency. In France, the total debt of public hospitals is high, with some estimates pointing to a level of EUR 30 billion. The situation is similar in Poland and other Member States. The increase in hospital debt is influenced by operating costs, including energy, heating, gas, medicines and wages. Hospital creditors often pursue claims through legal proceedings. Compensation for debt collection and interest for late payment in commercial transactions, which is significantly higher than statutory interest, is added by creditors to the amount charged for deliveries. This generates a further cost and burden for hospitals, increasing their indebtedness. 1. In this connection, does the Commission see any possibility of taking legislative action to reduce the deficit in hospitals? If so, what kind of action? 2. Does the Commission see any possibility of exempting public hospitals from the application of Directive 2011/7/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 16 February 2011, so that they would not be obliged to bear the burden of additional costs? (19 May 2026) 1. Under Article 168(7) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU (1), EU action must respect Member States’ responsibilities for organising and delivering health services. The EU is therefore not competent for legislative action aimed at directly reducing hospital deficits. The EU’s economic governance framework supports Member States in strengthening debt sustainability and growth through reforms and investments, including in healthcare, where efforts are needed to improve capacity, quality and resilience. Through the European Semester, the Commission provides policy recommendations and monitors implementation. The EU also supports Member States through funding, technical assistance and knowledge sharing. 2. Directive 2011/7/EU (2) ensures suppliers are paid within a set timeframe. It recognises the specific situation of public hospitals by allowing Member States to extend the 30-day payment period up to 60 days for public entities providing healthcare. The Commission does not envisage exempting public hospitals from its scope, as this would adversely affect suppliers, in particular small and medium-sized enterprises. The directive sets minimum interest rates. Parties can negotiate other rates, if not ‘grossly unfair’. The Commission’s proposed Regulation to replace the directive puts forward a fixed interest rate and eliminates the ‘grossly unfair’ provision. While such Regulation is not approved by Council, the Commission is open to finding a negotiated solution. Meanwhile, the Commission continues to monitor the situation and prioritise enforcement, as late payments by public authorities are a priority for specific enforcement actions and horizontal investigations in the Annual Single Market Enforcement Agenda 2026 (3).

E-10-2026-000926.t: EU origin status for Turkish products
qt: to the Commission Nikolas Farantouris (The Left) Subject:

In recent hours, the Turkish press has been reporting statements by Minister of Trade Ömer Bolat, who is claiming that the European Commission’s proposed regulation on the acceleration of industrial capacity and decarbonisation in strategic sectors1 effectively recognises the customs union with Turkey, in a way that extends, in principle, the EU origin status to Turkish-made products.2 However, the EU-Türkiye customs union concluded in 1995 (the upgrading of which remains ‘frozen’) does not entail Türkiye’s participation in the single market nor equivalent access to European industrial regimes or programmes.3 Turkish industry operates in a very different regulatory environment from that of the EU. The acceptance of an equivalent regime will lead to distortions of competition, circumvention of European production rules and the transfer of industrial activity outside the EU. Furthermore, while the EU is trying to strengthen its strategic autonomy and the resilience of its production and critical infrastructures, the indirect integration of a non-EU country, which threatens the sovereignty and security of Member States, into critical industrial policies will have serious trade and geopolitical consequences. In view of the above: 1.
Is it the Commission's intention to tacitly upgrade the customs union through secondary legislation?
Is it really the case that Turkish products can be considered de facto of European origin?
What policies does the Commission intend to use to ensure the functioning of healthy and fair competition within the framework of the EU's strategic autonomy?

https://single-market-economy.ec.europa.eu/document/download/9bc8eb85-4d43-4025-be7bc86b9f3648ec_en?filename=Proposal%20establishing%20measures%20for%20industrial%20capacity%20an d%20decarbonisation%20in%20strategic%20sectors%20.pdf https://www.turkiyetoday.com/business/trade-minister-hails-turkiyes-inclusion-in-eus-made-in-euframework-as-milestone-3215620?s=2. https://taxation-customs.ec.europa.eu/turkey-customs-unions-and-preferential-arrangements_en.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (24.4.2026) The Industrial Accelerator Act1 (IAA) proposal does not amend the EU-Türkiye customs union, that remains governed by the existing legal framework agreed between the two parties, or any other international agreement. The IAA establishes internal rules governing certain public procurement procedures and public support schemes within the EU. In Article 7, ‘Union origin’ refers to content originating in the Union in accordance with the non-preferential rules of origin as laid down in Article 59 of the Union Customs Code2. Articles 8, 9 and 10 provide that, for the purposes of applying the Union-origin requirements referred to in Articles 11 and 12, content originating in countries with which the Union has concluded an agreement establishing a customs union, such as Türkiye, is deemed equivalent to Union origin. However, this equivalence applies by default and is in compliance with the EU’s international commitments. The proposal also empowers the Commission to adopt delegated acts to exclude, in whole or in part, a third country from this equivalence following set criteria such as lack of reciprocity or avoidance of dependencies. In addition, EU contracting authorities and entities shall exclude from procurement procedures tenders submitted by economic operators owned or controlled by an entity established in third countries that have not concluded an international agreement with the EU guaranteeing such access. The proposal strengthens the resilience and competitiveness of European industrial value chains while remaining consistent with the EU’s international obligations. The EU will continue to ensure healthy and fair competition within the framework of its strategic autonomy. Where necessary, the Commission will rely on the full range of instruments in the EU toolbox.

E-10-2026-000925.t: Anti-fascist movements and political violence – the real threat to democracy
qt: to the Commission Fabrice Leggeri (PfE), Jordan Bardella (PfE), Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE), Marion Maréchal (ECR), Sarah Knafo (ESN), Pierre Pimpie (PfE), Marie Dauchy (PfE), Mélanie Disdier (PfE), Séverine Werbrouck (PfE), Anne-Sophie Frigout (PfE), MarieLuce Brasier-Clain (PfE), Julie Rechagneux (PfE), André Rougé (PfE), Rody Tolassy (PfE), Aleksandar Nikolic (PfE), Pierre-Romain Thionnet (PfE), Virginie Joron (PfE), Tom Vandendriessche (PfE), Mathilde Androuët (PfE), Laurence Trochu (ECR), Guillaume Peltier (ECR), Nicolas Bay (ECR), Céline Imart (PPE), Margarita de la Pisa Carrión (PfE), Marc Jongen (ESN), Juan Carlos Girauta Vidal (PfE), Volker Schnurrbusch (ESN), Mieke Andriese (PfE), Elisabeth Dieringer (PfE), Markus Buchheit (ESN), Tomasz Froelich (ESN), Jorge Buxadé Villalba (PfE), Jorge Martín Frías (PfE), Rada Laykova (ESN), Zsuzsanna Borvendég (ESN), Petr Bystron (ESN), Mary Khan (ESN), Silvia Sardone (PfE), Sebastian Kruis (PfE), Stephen Nikola Bartulica (ECR), Tiago Moreira de Sá (PfE), Susanna Ceccardi (PfE), Jaroslav Bžoch (PfE), Milan Uhrík (ESN), András László (PfE), Milan Mazurek (ESN), Branko Grims (PPE), Petra Steger (PfE), Alexander Jungbluth (ESN), Barbara Bonte (PfE), Geadis Geadi (ECR), Marieke Ehlers (PfE), Carlo Fidanza (ECR), Gilles Pennelle (PfE), Irmhild Boßdorf (ESN), Jacek Ozdoba (ECR), Petras Gražulis (ESN), Alexander Sell (ESN), Siegbert Frank Droese (ESN), Hans Neuhoff (ESN), Mariusz Kamiński (ECR), Enikő Győri (PfE), Ewa Zajączkowska-Hernik (ESN) Subject:

The European Union plans to strengthen its ‘democratic shield’, which it presents as an instrument to protect the rule of law, pluralism and the free exercise of political activities. However, in France, numerous acts of violence attributed to groups claiming to be ‘antifascist’ have targeted activists engaged in political or metapolitical activities and participating in lawful public debate. These actions are not about a confrontation of ideas, but about intimidation aimed at silencing legitimate opinions. By targeting citizens who are peacefully expressing their opinions, this violence undermines people’s safety and the very conditions for effective democratic pluralism. On 14 February 2026, one of these assaults resulted in the death of a 23-year-old activist for the national cause. That attack raises a twofold question: about public security and about protecting democratic debate. In this regard, can the Commission: 1.
state whether such violence falls within the scope of the ‘democratic shield’?
specify what action it intends to take to guarantee protection of political activities and lawful public debate?
state whether it is specifically monitoring political violence, whatever its ideological origin?
Supporter1 1
This question is supported by a Member other than the authors: Catherine Griset (PfE).

Supporter (1) (29 April 2026) The Commission condemns all forms of political violence, which undermine the fundamental values of democracy, pluralism and the rule of law enshrined in Article 2 of the Treaty on European Union. Violent acts demonstrate the need to protect the civic space and ensure that all citizens can participate in public debate without fear of intimidation or violence. It is important to highlight that Member States are solely competent for maintaining law and order and safeguarding internal security, including as regards the protection of citizens from politically motivated violence and attacks. A priority of the European Democracy Shield (1) is to strengthen the fairness and integrity of electoral and other democratic processes and, in this context, to better ensure the safety of political candidates and elected representatives, including through a dedicated Commission recommendation and a guide of best practices, which are under preparation in the framework of the European Cooperation Network on Elections.

E-10-2026-000924.t: Imports of Chinese natural noble fibre yarns and protecting the Italian and European textile industries
qt: to the Commission Stefano Cavedagna (ECR), Francesco Torselli (ECR) Subject:

European companies involved in the production of yarns of cashmere, fine wools and other natural noble fibres have, in recent years, reported a significant increase in imports from China of products falling under certain customs codes. Data provided by sectoral operators indicate that these imports are a form of asymmetric competition – which is partly the result of the contrasting tariffs which the EU and China levy on these products – and give rise to suspicions that they are being subsidised by the PRC. The EU companies concerned are also complaining of dwindling profit margins, a state of affairs that could have a knock-on effect on investments, production capacity and jobs. In Europe, and particularly in Italy, textile hubs are a vital component of the high added-value manufacturing chain and employ thousands of people. In the light of the above: 1.

Will the Commission launch enhanced monitoring efforts on imports of products falling under the aforementioned customs codes and attempt to establish whether EU industries are indeed being harmed by dumping practices and state subsidies?
What instruments will the Commission use to ensure fair competition and trade reciprocity with China?

What guidance and technical support could the Commission provide to European industrial stakeholders in the event that they decide to issue a formal complaint under the EU’s trade defence instruments?

(8 May 2026) The EU takes robust action to protect its industries from unfairly traded imports and at present has over 230 measures in place, with almost half of those tackling unfair trade from China. Since June 2025, the Commission’s import surveillance task force (1) has been actively monitoring trade flows to identify import pressure and inform decisions and actions to protect the EU internal market. The Commission’s analysis covers all imports, including textiles, and has identified several textile codes as being potentially at risk of harmful import increases. The Commission calls on EU producers and associations to review the results and, where warranted, provide further market intelligence and data on the economic situation facing industry that will help assess whether certain products need protection through targeted, proportionate and timely action, while avoiding any unintended effects on other producers downstream. In that context, recently the Commission shared the results (2) of the Import Surveillance Task Force with the European apparel and textile confederation and is in contact with them regarding relevant market information to discuss the issues. As regards dumped or subsidised imports, the Commission takes action to defend EU industry where it receives complaints with evidence that such imports harm the particular industry in Europe. The Complaints Office of Trade Defence Services can be contacted to discuss the procedure (3) and obtain guidance on how to proceed with tackling unfair competition from imports. There is also comprehensive information regarding trade defence proceedings on the trade defence website (4) including guides on how to proceed, the evidence and information required as well as the time frame for investigations.

E-10-2026-000923.t: Commission interference: electoral processes inside the EU and political pluralism at risk?
qt: to the Commission António Tânger Corrêa (PfE), Tiago Moreira de Sá (PfE), Tom Vandendriessche (PfE), Dick Erixon (ECR), Petra Steger (PfE), Jacek Ozdoba (ECR), Diana Iovanovici Şoşoacă (NI), Hans Neuhoff (ESN), Volker Schnurrbusch (ESN), Stephen Nikola Bartulica (ECR), Alexander Jungbluth (ESN), Mieke Andriese (PfE), Erik Kaliňák (NI), Petar Volgin (ESN), Roman Haider (PfE), Friedrich Pürner (NI), Susanna Ceccardi (PfE), Milan Uhrík (ESN), Gilles Pennelle (PfE), Gerald Hauser (PfE), Antonín Staněk (PfE), Claudiu-Richard Târziu (ECR), Barbara Bonte (PfE), Gerolf Annemans (PfE), Virginie Joron (PfE), Sebastian Tynkkynen (ECR), Fabrice Leggeri (PfE), Marc Jongen (ESN), András László (PfE), Dominik Tarczyński (ECR), György Hölvényi (PfE), Kinga Gál (PfE), Pál Szekeres (PfE), András Gyürk (PfE), Csaba Dömötör (PfE), Viktória Ferenc (PfE), Ernő Schaller-Baross (PfE), Enikő Győri (PfE) Subject:

A publication by the US House Judiciary Committee reports that, in the context of Regulation (EU) 2022/20651 (the Digital Services Act – DSA) and related initiatives, Commission contacts with online platforms included requests or recommendations affecting the visibility of lawful political content, including criticism of EU migration policy, critiques of gender ideology and political satire. This raises serious concerns under Article 5(1) and (2) and Article 13(2) of the Treaty on European Union and Article 11 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, particularly during electoral periods. The Commission is asked: 1.

In the last 24 months, how many Commission-initiated contacts with platforms and search engines concerned content moderation, ranking/visibility measures (including labelling/downranking) or DSA risk-mitigation?

Can the Commission confirm that it has no competence to monitor lawful public discourse and that, under the Treaties and the DSA, its role is limited to supervising compliance procedures, not shaping the reach or visibility of lawful political opinions?

In the light of Article 15 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union and Article 42 of the Charter, when is the Commission going to publish a searchable public register of these contacts (including dates, platforms, Commission services, participants, legal basis, and whether a request/recommendation was made)?

Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 19 October 2022 on a Single Market For Digital Services and amending Directive 2000/31/EC (Digital Services Act) (OJ L 277, 27.10.2022, p. 1, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/2065/oj).
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.5.2026) The Commission rejects the report’s unsubstantiated and unfounded allegations. Freedom of expression is a fundamental right enshrined in the Charter1. The Digital Services Act (DSA)2 protects users by entitling them to explanations, appeals and redress when their content is removed or restricted. Since its application, online platforms have reversed almost 50 million decisions3, demonstrating how the DSA empowers users and effectively protects them against arbitrary platform moderation. The DSA does not prescribe which content is illegal; this is determined purely by national law or other EU laws. The Commission cannot order providers of online services to remove or amend specific content from their services. Platforms remove content based on their own policies. The DSA mandates the largest platforms4 to identify, analyse and assess systemic risks in the EU stemming from their services, and to mitigate those risks. This includes risks to electoral processes. The DSA brings accountability and transparency. For example, it requires providers of online platforms to issue statements of reasons explaining their moderation decisions in a Transparency Database5. Here, providers must specify the reason for restricting or removing content. The DSA requires the Commission and national competent authorities to publish all key enforcement decisions. This is done through a dedicated website6, with due regard to the rights and legitimate interests of providers and to the protection of confidential information concerning other persons involved, in line with established practice amongst all similar regulatory and enforcement frameworks. Moreover, the Commission’s general transparency rules apply to meetings involving Senior Managers.

E-10-2026-000922.t: Under-representation of women in the tourism industry, precarious forms of work and the need for targeted EU interventions
qt: to the Commission Elena Kountoura (The Left) Subject:

Although women make up more than half of the tourism workforce, they continue to be significantly under-represented in positions of responsibility and decision-making1. Moreover, they are disproportionately exposed to vulnerable, precarious or informal forms of work2. The combination of these factors exacerbates gender inequalities and increases the risk of poverty and social exclusion for women working in the tourism sector. In view of: — the UN's sustainable development goals3, — the need to ensure quality and stable employment in the tourism sector, including by strengthening sectoral collective bargaining, increasing wages and properly implementing the minimum wage directive, — the upcoming European strategies on gender equality and sustainable tourism, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
What measures does it intend to take to increase women’s participation in positions of responsibility and decision-making in the tourism sector?

How does it intend to address seasonal work and precarious and informal forms of work that disproportionately affect women in the tourism sector, particularly in terms of job security, social protection and equal pay?

Does it intend to develop targeted programmes or financial tools to bolster seasonal childcare services and boost training, entrepreneurship and the professional development of women in tourism, especially in regions that are highly dependent on this sector?

According to recent surveys, women working in the tourism industry hold only 33 % of management board positions and the pay gap between women and men is as high as 14.7 %. Eurostat found that, at EU level, women held around 35 % of management positions in 2024. They also occupy only 21 % of management board positions in the EU’s 100 largest travel and leisure companies. Surveys point to high levels of informal and undeclared work in the tourism industry, where women are mostly employed in low-paid, unstable or informal jobs, often without adequate social protection. According to Eurostat, one in four women (26 %) in the tourism industry work part-time, compared to around one in eight men. Notably target 5.5 on women’s full and effective participation and equal leadership opportunities, and target 8.9 on promoting sustainable tourism policies that create jobs.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.5.2026) The Commission recognises the key role of women in tourism, while noting persistent gaps in their career progression and job quality1. While tourism is primarily a Member State competence, the EU supports and complements national action, notably through its competences in employment and social policy. Under the EU Gender Equality Strategy and European Pillar of Social Rights, the Commission promotes equal opportunities, fair working conditions and work-life balance, including measures on pay transparency, adequate minimum wages and childcare2. The Women on Boards Directive3 promotes gender-balanced representation in top management positions through transparent and merit-based selection procedures. The Commission also supports actions combating stereotypes, discrimination and female leadership. The Commission supports upskilling, reskilling and career development through Erasmus+, the Pact for Skills and cohesion policy funds4. The Tourism Large-Scale Partnership under the Pact for Skills promotes skills, career pathways and the attractiveness of the sector5. Particular attention is given to disadvantaged groups, including women, and their integration into the tourism labour market. EU programmes also support entrepreneurship, including women-led small and medium enterprises, and can be mobilised to address specific needs, such as training, business development and childcare services in tourism-dependent areas6. The Commission proposal for the next Multiannual Financial Framework will continue supporting skills, social inclusion and regional resilience, including through measures relevant for tourism ecosystems. The EU Sustainable Tourism Strategy7 will further promote inclusive, resilient and quality employment across the ecosystem.

E-10-2026-000921.t: Incorporating binding measures into the upcoming Gender Equality Strategy in the areas of employment, health and education
qt: to the Commission Elena Kountoura (The Left) Subject:

According to EIGE’s new Gender Equality Index for 20251, despite some progress having been made in the EU towards achieving gender equality, this progress remains disproportionately slow and fragile. Deep-rooted gender inequalities and stereotypes continue to hinder the achievement of equality in a big way. Meanwhile, in critical areas such as employment2, health and education, there appears to be stagnation or even backsliding in many Member States3. For instance, in the health sector, progress has effectively stalled and in some Member States performance has deteriorated over the last five years4. Despite the high participation rate of women in the education sector, structural barriers persist, reinforcing gender differences in employment and in terms of their progression prospects5. Given: — the upcoming EU Gender Equality Strategy, — EIGE’s forecast that it will take at least 50 years to fully achieve gender equality in the EU, — the uneven progress seen across Member States, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

What measures does it intend to take, in the context of the new gender equality strategy, to address stagnation and regression in the areas where this is most evident, particularly in the employment, health and education sectors?
Does it intend to incorporate binding targets, specific timelines and monitoring and evaluation mechanisms to reduce gender inequalities in employment, health and education?

https://eige.europa.eu/gender-equality-index/2025/EL. Despite a modest annual increase of 0.4 points since 2015, it is estimated that it will take at least another 70 years before equality is fully achieved in employment and working life. In education, the equality index for the EU improved by a meagre 0.4 points, with 14 Member States backtracking. The equality index for the EU health sector has made no progress over five years, with 15 Member States recording negative trends. Despite the fact that more women complete higher education than men, stereotypes sustain occupational gender segregation and push many women into jobs that do not provide many opportunities for professional advancement and pay progression.

(28 May 2026) The new Gender Equality Strategy 2026-2030 (1), adopted on 5 March 2026, includes measures to advance gender equality in the employment, health and education sectors, in line with the Roadmap for Women’s Rights’ (2) principles. Measures related to employment are detailed, inter alia, in principles 3, 4 and 5 (equal pay, economic empowerment and financial independence; work-life balance and gender equality in care; equal employment opportunities and adequate working conditions). These range from the full implementation of the Pay Transparency Directive (3) to the adoption of an Action Plan for Women in Research, Innovation and Start-Ups. Measures related to health are outlined in principle 2 (the highest standards of physical and mental health), and include a new initiative with the World Health Organisation on women’s health. Measures related to education are outlined in principle 6 (high-quality inclusive education and training) and encompass a new ‘Boys in HEAL’ (Health, Education, Administration, Literacy) approach, as well as the publication of a handbook on reducing gender-based disparities in study choices and educational outcomes.

E-10-2026-000920.t: Transparency and consistency in the Commission debate on the Water Framework Directive
qt: to the Commission César Luena (S&D) Subject:

The Commission announced a roundtable discussion on the Water Framework Directive (WFD) in Stockholm, scheduled for 2 March 2026, which was subsequently cancelled. According to publicly available information prior to the event, the planned list of participants was largely dominated by representatives of the mining, metals and steel industries, while the participation of civil society organisations seemed very limited. While in the European Water Resilience Strategy of June 2025 the Commission considered the WFD to be appropriate and prioritised its implementation, in its Communication COM (2025)0980 of December 2025 it announced its intention to review it for possible obstacles to raw materials projects. In view of this: 1.
How does the Commission explain this change of approach in such a short time frame, moving from prioritising the implementation of the WFD to considering its revision?
Does the Commission consider that the discussion process with stakeholders ensures a genuine balance between industrial interests, public authorities, the scientific community and civil society?

Can the Commission guarantee that the direction of its future water initiatives is not unduly influenced by industrial and mining interests, but rather responds to the general interest and the best available scientific evidence?

(8 May 2026) Better implementation and enforcement of the Water Framework Directive (WFD) (1) is and will continue to be a priority for the Commission. The Commission is conducting Structured Water Dialogues with Member State to accelerate action on the ground. The call for evidence of the environmental omnibus highlighted possible problems in granting permits for the extractive industry, resulting from the WFD, hindering the achievement of the benchmarks for 2030 set out in the Critical Raw Materials Act (2). These possible challenges arise against a backdrop of intensifying global competition for critical raw materials and the EU’s growing reliance on single suppliers, creating systemic economic security risks. This has led to a decision to review and revise the WFD. The online Call for Evidence (3), which closed on 14 April 2026, allowed all stakeholders to provide their views on this targeted revision. This will be complemented by ad hoc consultations of experts representing all interested parties in the context of the Strategic Coordination Group under the Common Implementation Strategy of the WFD. As for the specific meeting referred to by the Honourable Member, it had to be rescheduled on short notice since the President of the Commission called an emergency Security College focused on the evolving situation in Iran and the Middle East. The Commission will be conducting an Impact Assessment for the targeted revision of the WFD that will be based on the evidence provided by all stakeholders in the Call for Evidence as well as other sources, including extensive data provided by the European Environment Agency (4).

E-10-2026-000919.t: Commission’s report on the single market and competitiveness
qt: to the Commission Dan-Ştefan Motreanu (PPE) Subject:

One year after presenting its ‘Competitiveness Compass’, the Commission’s 2026 annual report on the single market and competitiveness reports limited progress. Of 29 key performance indicators, only six have improved, while most remain unchanged and several have deteriorated. The Commission notes that single market integration has ‘reached a plateau’, with most barrier-relevant indicators showing limited progress. Fragmented national rules still make it complex and costly for companies to establish and operate across borders. Market surveillance remains weak, despite the surge in e-commerce imports, and services markets continue to face restrictive regulations. The posting of workers and the recognition of professional qualifications remain burdensome, limiting labour mobility. At the same time, research and development expenditure remains below the 3 % GDP target, private and venture capital investment lag behind global competitors, and the uptake of digital technologies such as AI and cloud computing is progressing too slowly. Strategic dependencies and persistently high energy prices further undermine EU competitiveness. In view of this stagnation and the persistence of structural barriers, what new measures does the Commission intend to take to accelerate single market integration and deliver tangible improvements in competitiveness by 2027?

E-10-2026-000917.t: Consequences for Andalusia of the agreement on Gibraltar between the United Kingdom, Spain and the European Union
qt: to the Commission Juan Ignacio Zoido Álvarez (PPE), Carmen Crespo Díaz (PPE) Subject:

We recently learned about the text of the agreement on Gibraltar between the UK, Spain and the EU. This text does not resolve many of the main disputes in the relationship between Gibraltar and the neighbouring municipalities of Campo de Gibraltar, mainly those relating to taxation or the environment. For one thing, the agreement contains no measures concerning Gibraltar’s land reclamation activities in the Eastside project, which are having negative consequences on EU Special Areas of Conservation (SAC), fishing in the area and coastal conservation. Furthermore, the text fails to address how to protect the competitiveness of neighbouring EU ports, such as Algeciras, in the face of Gibraltar’s port, which allows bunkering and external anchorage in Gibraltarian waters. It also maintains the lack of reciprocity in the right of business establishment between Gibraltar and the EU, and the emissions trading scheme remains absent in Gibraltar, all while situations of unfair competition between ports in the area persist. In view of the above: 1.
Will the Commission allow Gibraltar to continue land reclamation activities on the EU’s SACs?
Has it assessed how the environmental and taxation differences maintained by the agreement will affect the competitiveness of neighbouring EU ports?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (7.7.2026) The future EU-UK Agreement in respect of Gibraltar agreement, once applied, will not affect the issue referred to by the Honourable Members. The future EU-UK Agreement in respect of Gibraltar contains solid Level Playing Field provisions regarding State aid, taxation, labour and social standards, environment, climate and sustainable development. These provisions are aimed at preventing distortions of competition affecting EU stakeholders, including EU ports. As regards taxation, environment, climate, social and labour standards, the Agreement provides for non-regression which ensures that parties cannot weaken or reduce the level of protection in the different areas below the level in place on 31 December 2020 affecting trade or investment. Specifically, as regards emissions trading, the Agreement (Article 220(2)) provides that the UK, in respect of Gibraltar, shall ensure that such system or measures shall have an equivalent scope and effectiveness as the one in place in the EU at the time of the entry into force of the Agreement.

E-10-2026-000915.t: European Public Prosecutor's Office Annual Report (2025)
qt: to the Commission Ana Miguel Pedro (PPE) Subject:

According to data in the latest report by the European Public Prosecutor’s Office, the amount of VAT and customs duty fraud currently under investigation amounts to EUR 45.01 billion – representing 67 % of the estimated losses to the budgets of the EU and the Member States. The findings point to the consolidation of criminal networks that have taken control of significant segments of the fraud chain, exploiting global supply chains, shadow banking systems, and operational structures that have been infiltrated in European ports and trade depots, with cross-cutting impacts on strategic sectors of the economy and links to other illicit activities, including drug and human trafficking. This intensification of organised crime affecting the EU’s own revenue takes place at a particularly sensitive time, when the next multiannual financial framework (MFF) is being negotiated, with more flexibility provided for in the implementation of funds by Member States, which could amplify structural vulnerabilities to fraud, corruption and criminal infiltration. Could the Commission provide a detailed response to the following: What strategic assessment does it make of the role these criminal networks are playing in reshaping the European criminal ecosystem, including the use of clandestine banking systems, front companies, bogus logistics networks, and tax-evasion and money-laundering structures, and what geopolitical aspects does it identify in this situation?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (5.5.2026) The Commission shares the concerns about organised value added tax (VAT) and customs duty fraud and their impact on Member States and, indirectly, the EU budget, economy and security. Europol’s 2025 Serious and Organised Crime Threat Assessment confirms1 that fraud remains a serious and persistent threat. As announced in ProtectEU: a European Internal Security Strategy2, the Commission will propose to reinforce the mandates of Europol and Eurojust and modernise the rules to fight against organised crime in 2026. In addition, the European Public Prosecutor’s Office investigates and prosecutes criminal offences affecting EU’s financial interests, while the European Anti-Fraud Office conducts administrative investigations into irregularities against the EU budget. The Commission also supports the European Multidisciplinary Platform Against Criminal Threats operational action plan on VAT and Missing Trader IntraCommunity fraud3. The Commission is currently reviewing the EU’s Anti-Fraud Architecture, to strengthen the protection of the EU’s financial interests. The aim is to modernise the EU’s anti-fraud framework and, thus, strengthen the EU’s capacity to detect and combat crimes affecting the EU budget, including VAT and customs fraud. To implement the follow-the-money approach, the Commission calls for swift transposition of the Directive on asset recovery and confiscation4. Once operational, the new EU Customs Authority and EU Customs Data Hub5 will better equip customs to perform risk analysis and further improve cooperation between all law enforcement bodies. Together, these measures will better equip the EU and Member States to disrupt criminal networks and better protect Europe’s security, economy and financial system.

E-10-2026-000914.t: The scope of EU competences and the real purpose of establishing an EU forest monitoring framework
qt: to the Commission Piotr Müller (ECR) Subject:

The EU forest monitoring framework currently under discussion aims to create a harmonised system for collecting data on the state of forests across the EU in order to support climate and environmental policies. At the same time, forest management remains the competence of Member States, and the Treaties do not provide for a common EU forest policy. This raises fundamental questions about the actual purpose of creating an extensive data collection system at EU level. If the Commission does not have the competence to manage forests, there is a question as to whether this instrument will not become, to all intents and purposes, a tool for exerting regulatory pressure under the pretext of environmental protection, leading to indirect shaping of forestry policy and extending the Union’s competences beyond the scope provided for in the Treaties. This approach raises serious concerns with regard to the principles of conferral and subsidiarity, as well as the potential economic impact on sectors dependent on a stable supply of timber. 1.
What is the real purpose of establishing an EU forest monitoring system, given that forest management remains the responsibility of Member States and is not a common EU policy?
How will the Commission ensure that data from this system will not be used to exert regulatory pressure to restrict timber harvesting or to indirectly shape national forestry policies?

Can the Commission unequivocally confirm that the forest monitoring framework will not be used to extend the Union’s powers through environmental regulations, and that any potential economic impact on the timber industry will be thoroughly assessed in advance?

At the same time, forest management remains the competence of Member States, and the Treaties do not provide for a common EU forest policy. This raises fundamental questions about the actual purpose of creating an extensive data collection system at EU level. This approach raises serious concerns with regard to the principles of conferral and subsidiarity, as well as the potential economic impact on sectors dependent on a stable supply of timber. 1. What is the real purpose of establishing an EU forest monitoring system, given that forest management remains the responsibility of Member States and is not a common EU policy? 2. How will the Commission ensure that data from this system will not be used to exert regulatory pressure to restrict timber harvesting or to indirectly shape national forestry policies? 3. Can the Commission unequivocally confirm that the forest monitoring framework will not be used to extend the Union’s powers through environmental regulations, and that any potential economic impact on the timber industry will be thoroughly assessed in advance? (23 April 2026) The proposal for a regulation on a monitoring framework for resilient European forest s (1) was rejected by the European Parliament on 21 October 2025 and the Council of Ministers envisaged significant modifications affecting the objectives of the proposal. Consequently, the Commission announced its intention to withdrawal. EU action on climate, biodiversity and circular economy as well as their benefits inherently relate to natural ecosystems, including forests. The proposal aimed to set up an EU-wide forest monitoring system on forest ecosystems and resources in the EU for accurate, timely and comparable data on forests across the EU, in view of increasing pressures and stressors, and their cross-border impacts. By improving and combining national monitoring systems with satellite-based Earth observation, the system would have: (i) supported public authorities in evidence-based policymaking, (ii) provided stakeholders with accurate information for effective decision-making, (iii) supported new business models such as the certification of carbon farming schemes, (iv) supported new markets for digital monitoring services. It did not touch on forest management. The EU has a variety of competences shared with Member States that address forests and forestry, including climate, environment and agriculture policies. The Union has repeatedly exercised these competences respecting the principles of subsidiarity and proportionality. In exercising the shared competences, the Commission is working in close cooperation with Member States’ competent authorities and stakeholders, respecting subsidiarity and based on the adequate legal basis.

E-10-2026-000913.t: Feasibility of EU climate policy in the transport sector following the revision of provisions on internal combustion engine (ICE) cars and sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) obligations in aviation
qt: to the Commission Piotr Müller (ECR) Subject:

The Commission’s recent withdrawal from its original ban on the sale of ICE cars from 2035 is a de facto admission that the climate policy pursued for years in the automotive sector had become detached from industrial, technological and social realities. Instead of reducing emissions, it has led to regulatory chaos, a loss of competitiveness for European industry and increased costs for the public. The same scenario is now playing out in the aviation sector, with the Commission stubbornly defending compulsory and unrealistic thresholds for the use of SAFs, despite their limited availability, extremely high prices and lack of infrastructure, which will inevitably lead to higher ticket prices and further burdens on consumers. This policy increasingly resembles an ideological fantasy rather than a rational climate protection strategy based on real global impact. In view of this situation: 1.

Does the Commission acknowledge that the policy adjustment in respect of ICE cars was the result of flawed regulatory assumptions and an underestimation of the economic impact on the public and industry?
Why is the Commission ignoring similar warning signs from the aviation sector and continuing to push for SAF obligations that are technically and financially unrealistic?
Does the Commission intend to conduct a full review of aviation climate policy in terms of its real social costs, rather than shifting the burden of ideological ambitions onto EU citizens?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (5.6.2026) 1. The December 2025 Commission proposal amending the CO2 emission standards for cars and vans is aligned with the climate targets and objectives established in the European Climate Law1. It maintains ambitious emission reduction targets to ensure a strong market signal for zero-emission vehicles, while providing vehicle manufacturers with more flexibility to achieve their targets. 2–3. The ReFuelEU Aviation Regulation2 aims to scale up sustainable aviation fuels (SAF) to decarbonise aviation, while preserving internal market and decrease reliance on imported fossil fuels. The 2025 ReFuelEU Aviation Annual Technical Report3 shows that the sector is on track to meet its SAF obligations for 2025-2029. The Sustainable Transport Investment Plan4 aims to accelerate the transition to SAF and mobilise at least EUR 2.9 billion until the end of 2027 for production of sustainable fuels for aviation and maritime transport. In response, eight Member States launched in December 2025 an Early Movers Coalition for hydrogen-based SAF (eSAF)5. To address the EU aviation’s new pressures stemming from rapidly changing global environment, as illustrated by the supply shock caused by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, the Commission is preparing an EU Aviation Strategy. The Strategy will aim to support the EU aviation industry’s competitiveness and global leadership by embracing the sector’s green and digital transformation, boosting investments in innovation, while enhancing the EU strategic autonomy and shielding from unfair competition.

E-10-2026-000912.t: Impact of planned environmental standards for data centres on the EU’s digital competitiveness and investments in AI infrastructure
qt: to the Commission Piotr Müller (ECR) Subject:

The rapid development of artificial intelligence and the digitalisation of the economy is driving an increase in demand for data centres, which constitute critical infrastructure. Meanwhile, the Commission is considering the introduction of binding environmental standards concerning energy and water consumption, even though the sector is already struggling with high energy costs, network constraints and the scarcity of raw materials. There is a risk that, instead of promoting the digital transformation, additional regulatory and reporting obligations will lead to a slowdown in investments, the relocation of infrastructure outside the EU and an increase in the EU’s technological dependence on third countries. In light of the above: 1.

How does the Commission assess the impact of the planned binding environmental standards for data centres on the EU’s ability to attract investment in AI infrastructure and remain competitive with the US and Asia?
How does the Commission intend to prevent a situation where new regulatory obligations lead to the relocation of data centres outside the EU, which could increase the Union’s digital dependency?

Has the Commission carried out a regulatory cost-benefit analysis that takes into account the growing number of investment barriers in the energy, network and raw materials sectors, and what conclusions were reached?

Has the Commission carried out a regulatory cost-benefit analysis that takes into account the growing number of investment barriers in the energy, network and raw materials sectors, and what conclusions were reached?

(4 May 2026) The Commission has consulted the data centre industry from the outset when it drafted the Energy Efficiency Directiv e (1) and subsequent proposal delegated acts on reporting, rating scheme and minimum performance standards on water and energy usage. The introduction of these measures has not affected their investment decisions in the EU but rather the opposite: colocation data centres invested EUR 7,7 billion in 2024, and they plan to invest over EUR 26 billion in 2030 (2). The upcoming Cloud and AI Development Act will address the urgent and growing data centre capacity gap, aiming to at least triple the EU’s data centre capacity within the next five to seven years. It will do so by harmonising the conditions for investment in data centres across the EU with a focus on sustainable and innovative data centres, ensuring their operators find access to land, water, finance and energy in the EU. Additionally, through the upcoming Strategic Roadmap for Digitalisation and AI in the Energy Sector the Commission will facilitate the sustainable integration of data centres into the EU energy system. The Commission has conducted various regulatory impact assessments and cost benefit analyses related to investment barriers in the energy, network, and raw materials sectors, particularly in the context of the Green Deal Industrial Plan (3), REPowerEU (4), Critical Raw Materials Act (5) and Net-Zero Industry Act (6). It will conduct an impact assessment that will accompany any proposal for a regulation on minimum performance standards later this year.
