E-10-2026-000878.t: Circumvention of customs duties on car imports
qt: to the Commission Jan Farský (PPE) Subject:

In December 2024, following an anti-subsidy investigation, the Commission imposed countervailing duties on battery-electric vehicles imported from the People’s Republic of China in order to curb distortions of competition and protect the EU automotive industry. However, recent media reports suggest that some car manufacturers may be undermining the effectiveness of these measures through individual agreements. One example is the Cupra Tavascan model, developed in Europe and manufactured in China at a Volkswagen Group plant in cooperation with Chinese partner JAC, for which additional countervailing duties of 20.7 % were waived under an agreement with the Commission, even though it would normally be subject to them. This case raises concerns that a precedent will be set that could lead to the systematic circumvention of tariffs and to the weakening of the EU’s trade defence instruments. In this context: 1.
How does the Commission ensure that individual agreements or exemptions do not undermine the intended protective effect of countervailing duties on Chinese electric vehicles?

What specific measures is the Commission taking or planning to take to prevent the legal or economic circumvention of these duties, including the assessment of the origin of production and added value?
How will the Commission prevent the creation of precedent-setting exemptions in the future that could undermine the level playing field in the EU internal market?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (13.4.2026) Exemptions of the measures in the form of price undertakings are a statutory alternative to collection of countervailing duties, provided that the legal conditions are met. This includes that the proposed minimum import prices fully offset the effect of Chinese subsidisation in comparison to the countervailing duties, and that it is practicable and sufficiently mitigates the risk of cross compensation. Price undertakings are subject to regular monitoring, covering export and resale of each individual vehicle in the EU, and to on-site inspections. Such inspections may occur even after the end of the undertaking implementation period. Non-compliance with the terms of a price undertaking may result in the reinstatement of duties, potentially with retroactive effect, thereby imposing a significant deterrent effect. Additionally, imports from all countries are subject to both regular monitoring by the Commission and customs checks by Member States’ authorities to identify potential circumvention practices and incorrect declarations of product origin. To date, due to the complexity of the product and the diverse range of distribution channels, the Commission has only accepted a single price undertaking offer. This price undertaking includes a satisfactory minimum import price level, as well as effective measures to mitigate the risk of cross-compensation. Any price undertaking offer will be subject to the same thorough assessment and will need to meet identical legal criteria in order to be considered acceptable and practicable.

E-10-2026-000877.t: Methodological basis for the high-ILUC classification of soya under the Renewable Energy Directive
qt: to the Commission Christine Singer (Renew) Subject:

The classification of soya as a raw material with a high risk of indirect land-use change (ILUC) will effectively rule out soyabean oil as a feedstock for biofuel production. Around 20 % of soyabean oil is made as a by-product in the production of soyabean meal, which is the most important source of vegetable protein for European livestock farming. If the market for soyabean oil collapses, it will put the economic viability of domestic oilseed processing at risk, as well as being at odds with the EU’s protein strategy. Raw materials from cultivated biomass certified under the Renewable Energy Directive are already subject to strict sustainability criteria and a cap. 1.

What is the Commission’s methodological basis for the high-ILUC classification of soya, given that it is grown primarily to meet the demand for protein, and that the use of soyabean oil for energy purposes is simply maintaining the economic viability of domestic processing?

Has the Commission assessed the risks that the measure might cause the creation of value to move outside the EU and further increase dependency on soyabean meal imports, rather than boosting European security of supply?
Why is the Commission sticking to the blanket classification – which is triggering new trade conflicts, including with the US – rather than relying on precise proof of origin?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.6.2026) Emissions due to indirect land-use change (ILUC) have been found to be capable of negating some or all greenhouse gas emissions savings of individual biofuels. While the level of greenhouse gas emissions caused by ILUC cannot be unequivocally determined, the highest risks of ILUC have been identified for biofuels produced from feedstock for which a significant expansion of the production area into land with high-carbon stock is observed. Against this background, the Renewable Energy Directive1 sets out that the share of high ILUC-risk biofuels that is counted towards the targets for renewable energy must not exceed the level of consumption of such fuels in 2019 and is gradually decreased to zero by 2030 unless they are certified to be low ILUC-risk biofuels. This applies independently of the origin of the feedstock. The Directive requires the Commission to review the Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/807 as regards the determination of high ILUC-risk feedstock and the certification of low ILUC-risk biofuels based on the report on feedstock expansion2. In line with the legal base, high ILUC-risk feedstocks are determined at global level and certification of low ILUC-risk biofuels is based on precise proofs of origin. The review found that the approach set out in Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/807 is appropriate. The data in the updated report on feedstock expansion shows that both palm oil and soybeans qualify as high ILUC-risk feedstock. The production of by-products is taken into account under the applied methodology. Negative impacts on European security of supply are not expected, as the cultivation of soybeans in the EU depends only to a limited extent on the biofuel outlet and global markets are liquid.
1 Directive (EU) 2018/2001. 2 COM(2026) 36 final.

E-10-2026-000876.t: Escalation in the Middle East and urgent need to get the India-Middle East-Europe economic corridor up and running, as a strategic European corridor
qt: to the Commission Anna Maria Cisint (PfE) Subject:
Escalation in the Middle East and urgent need to get the India-Middle EastEurope economic corridor up and running, as a strategic European corridor

The military escalation involving Iran, Israel and the United States, which effectively risks spreading throughout the region, directly jeopardises the security of the Strait of Hormuz and the main global energy and trade routes, while the Suez Canal remains a further point of structural vulnerability. The European Union, which is heavily dependent on these routes, is exposed to logistical and energy shocks that require a real and timely diversification strategy. Against this backdrop, the strengthening and possible relaunch of the Abraham Accords, including with the involvement of Saudi Arabia, are of strategic importance for regional stability and the construction of new integrated economic infrastructure. The India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC), which remains merely a memorandum of understanding, can represent the logistical pillar of this architecture, with the port system of Trieste and Monfalcone as the natural gateway to Central-North-Eastern Europe. Can the Commission therefore say: 1.
What operational plan and timetable it intends to adopt to get the IMEC up and running.
Whether it has, or intends to, put in place instruments and financial resources to strengthen the infrastructure linking Trieste and Monfalcone with Central and NorthEastern Europe.

(28 April 2026) In line with its 2023 Economic Security Strategy (1), the Commission has been working steadily over recent years in ensuring resilient and diversified supply chains. The India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC) is part of these efforts, which is why the Commission has played a key role in the revival of this initiative over the last year. The current military escalation in the region and the logistical and energy shocks resulting from this disruption make such a corridor even more relevant than before. Since May 2025, the IMEC signatories have been meeting regularly at senior official level (the latest meeting organised by Italy, one of the eight initial signatories, in Trieste on 17 March 2026) and at technical level, with the establishment of five technical working groups, whose current and future work will help operationalise IMEC. All IMEC signatories are already investing in, or supporting, soft and hard infrastructure projects that contribute to the objectives of IMEC, i.e. boosting connectivity between Europe, the Midde East-Gulf region and India, be it in terms of transport, energy and digital connections. The current aim of the IMEC signatories is to identify gaps and relevant projects to address these. Infrastructure investments and accompanying soft measures are key to the success of IMEC and while the private sector will be the main engine behind IMEC, all signatories are expected to contribute to this aim, including Italy. The Commission will use its existing tools and financial instruments in this respect.

E-10-2026-000875.t: The role of batteries in the defence sector
qt: to the Commission Thomas Pellerin-Carlin (S&D) Subject:

As the war in Ukraine shows, the electrification of the battlefield is profoundly transforming the ways in which armed forces operate. The accelerated development of drones, in particular short-range and tactical drones, as well as the widespread use of on-board electronic equipment for soldiers (radios, night vision devices, GPS systems, etc.) and for ground, air and space platforms, are redefining supply constraints on armies. There is no universal battery suitable for all these uses. The technologies and chemicals used vary according to usage requirements (energy density, power, durability, etc.), as well as the operational constraints of the different theatres of operation. In this context, and in view of the strategic challenges related to industrial sovereignty and the resilience of EU supply chains: 1.
Can the Commission specify what measures have been taken at EU level to secure supply chains for military-use batteries?
Does the work done on interoperability within NATO and the European Union help to reduce these vulnerabilities, in particular through better standardisation or harmonisation of European equipment?

Can the Commission specify what measures have been taken at EU level to secure supply chains for military-use batteries?
Does the work done on interoperability within NATO and the European Union help to reduce these vulnerabilities, in particular through better standardisation or harmonisation of European equipment?

(11 May 2026) Advanced storage technologies from batteries to supercapacitors have important dual civilian and military use. Establishing a strong and resilient battery supply chain while reducing external dependencies is therefore of strategic importance for the EU, as reflected in the Battery Booster Strategy (1). The EU also supports technological innovation and innovators ecosystems in the Strategic Energy Technology Plan (2) and in the Startup and Scaleup Strategy (3). In terms of defence policy, the European Defence Fund (4) supports defence sector interoperability in energy-efficient solutions and green technologies that meet NATO and EU standards, notably energy storage systems like customised batteries, fuel cells and multi-source energy systems. The BraveTech EU initiative (5) established between EU and Ukraine will also contribute to this objective by considering the lessons learnt in the battlefield. The European Defence Industry Programme (6) supports resilient European defence supply chains through cross-border industrial cooperation, procurement actions, strategic reserves and industrial reinforcement actions. It includes measures to anticipate and mitigate serious disruptions in the supply of defence and non-defence products, which the Commission is currently implementing in consultation with Member States through the Defence Security of Supply Board. In addition, the Commission is working with Member States, industry and civilian standardisation stakeholders to prepare a landscape and gap analysis for defence and dual-use standardisation, to further reinforce the efficiency and interoperability of the EU defence market.

E-10-2026-000874.t: Global loss of biodiversity and the collapse of ecosystems and national security
qt: to the Commission Thomas Pellerin-Carlin (S&D) Subject:

As the impact of climate change and the sheer scale of the environmental challenges facing us become clearer, a recent report from the UK Government has shed light on the potential security repercussions of an ecological collapse. Such a collapse could lead to increased risks to food supplies, greater vulnerability to pandemics, opportunities for non-state actors and geopolitical instability that could intensify inter-state rivalries or even cause conflicts. The EU’s Strategic Compass for Security and Defence, established in 2022, calls for strengthening resilience to climate change, disasters and emergencies. 1.
Is the Commission aware of any similar studies carried out by one or more Member States?
Does it plan to conduct a study to analyse the security risks and repercussions of climate change for the European Union?
Could such a study also identify specific solutions to prevent or limit these risks?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (5.5.2026) The European Union continues to address climate change issues, including its security and defence implications, through various initiatives and studies. The EU regularly commissions research and reports on the security and defence risks posed by climate change. This is part of its broader strategy to integrate climate considerations into security, foreign and defence policy frameworks. The first European Climate Risk Assessment1 (EUCRA, 2024) considered the repercussions of climate change for the European Union. It identifies 36 climate risks that pose a threat to Europe’s energy and food security, ecosystems, infrastructure, water resources, financial stability, and people’s health. In the next EUCRA report, due for 2028, security may be addressed more directly. The Commission is currently preparing a comprehensive risks and threat assessment under the Preparedness Union Strategy2, foreseen for summer 2026. The EU recognises climate change as a threat multiplier that impacts resource scarcity, migration, and geopolitical stability. The Joint Communication ‘A new outlook on the climate and security nexus: Addressing the impact of climate change and environmental degradation on peace, security and defence’3 was adopted in 2023 and continues to guide the Commission work4. The focus on security and defence aspects is often reflected in the work of the European External Action Service and other relevant agencies that collaborate on assessing climate-related security threats.

E-10-2026-000871.t: Outdated environmental impact assessment and potential repercussions for the Campolattaro reservoir’s water resources
qt: to the Commission Danilo Della Valle (The Left), Valentina Palmisano (The Left), Pasquale Tridico (The Left), Mario Furore (The Left) Subject:

REC S.r.l’s plan to build a hydroelectric plant in Campania’s Benevento Province is based on an environmental impact assessment (EIA) that was carried out in 2015. The establishment of the Matese National Park in April 2025 and the launching of a major NRRP-funded project that will use the Campolattaro reservoir as a source of drinking water have drastically changed the way in which the local environment is being managed and protected, rendering the EIA obsolete. The REC S.r.l. facility is set to have an impact on the park’s Zone 1 areas (which are afforded the highest level of protection) and to draw water from the Campolattaro reservoir. According to expert reports, the planned hydroelectric plant could drain the local karst aquifers and deplete the sources that provide drinking water to around 18 000 local residents. These and other major shortcomings could constitute breaches of Directives 2011/92/EU, 2000/60/EC and 92/43/EEC – which regulate EIAs, water and habitats respectively. In view of the above: 1.

Does the Commission hold that using an outdated EIA is in line with Directive 2011/92/EU, particularly given that a national park has since been established in the area and that the project concerned clashes with a new NRRP project?

How does the Commission view the hydroelectric plant’s potential adverse repercussions for Campolattaro’s bodies of water and drinking water sources in relation to the objectives set out by Directive 2000/60/EC?
What action will the Commission take to ensure that the REC S.r.l. plant does not compromise the NextGenerationEU-funded project’s effectiveness and compliance with the DNSH principle?

(8 May 2026) The Environmental Impact Assessment Directive (EIAD) (1) requires the competent authority to be satisfied that the reasoned conclusion on the significant effects of a project is up to date when taking a decision to grant development consent. E-10-2026-000869.t: Ending the privatisation of European railways
qt: to the Commission Emma Fourreau (The Left) Subject:

Opening national rail markets to competition through the European Union’s railway packages1 is promoting the fragmentation of national railway networks into different companies and is leading to confusion among users, who are struggling to understand the changes to services and responsibilities. What is more, the benefits expected in terms of lowering prices and improvements in performance have not become a reality. In many cases, the arrival of new operators on national networks threatens the long-term stability of incumbent operators. A number of countries, including Italy, the Netherlands and Belgium, have opened their networks to competition and have demonstrated that this system does not work; on the contrary, it is weakens the rail sector at a time when we actually want to strengthen it. With this in mind: 1.

Is the Commission preparing a comprehensive assessment of the effects of liberalising the rail market on fares, quality of service, network cohesion and the financial sustainability of national railway undertakings?

Will the Commission publish updated guidance for Member States and their transport authorities, detailing all available options for organising rail services without systematically requiring competitive tendering?
Will the Commission revisit its plans to liberalise the rail network?
https://www.ecologie.gouv.fr/politiques-publiques/ouverture-concurrence-du-transport-ferroviaire-paquetsferroviaires-creation.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (6.5.2026) In July 2025 the Commission adopted a report on the implementation of Directive 2012/34/EU1 as amended by Directive (EU) 2016/2370, based among others, on market studies2 requested by the Commission and official market data. Results show that, where passengers could choose between different operators, railway services became cheaper and more frequent. Market opening encouraged railway operators to become more responsive to customer needs and improve their cost-effectiveness, enhancing the role of rail in accelerating the reduction of transport emissions and congestion. The Commission has already provided comprehensive guidance on how to apply Regulation (EC) No 1370/20073. In 2023, following extensive consultations with stakeholders, the Commission adopted revised interpretative guidelines to take account of the legislative changes introduced by the Fourth Railway Package, including exemptions from the obligation to tender competitively public service contracts in the railway sector. The Commission does not currently envisage the adoption of new interpretative guidelines concerning Regulation (EC) No 1370/2007. In 2016 the Fourth Railway Package completed the opening to competition of the rail services market by introducing mandatory tendering for public services and allowing commercial operators to offer domestic rail passenger services in other Member States. The Commission remains firmly committed to support the rail sector in reaching its growth potential working together with all the stakeholders.

E-10-2026-000867.t: Implications of the European Industrial Accelerator Act for the EU-UK strategic economic partnership
qt: to the Commission Andi Cristea (S&D) Subject:

The European Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA) is an important piece of legislation that will affect the EU’s relationship with its trading partners, including with the United Kingdom. To recall: – the EU and the UK have agreed a strategic partnership; – the UK is the EU’s third-biggest trading partner (10.1 %); – the EU’s export of goods to the UK mainly includes machinery and appliances (20.4 %), transport equipment (18.9 %), chemical products (11.5 %), foodstuffs, beverages and tobacco (9.3 %), and base metals (5.5 %). In the light of the above, could the Commission answer the following questions: 1.

Does the Commission agree that the IAA presents the EU with an opportunity to show global leadership and forge stronger economic ties with trusted partners and likeminded economies, such as those that share EU values and an openness to trade and investment?

Does the Commission agree that businesses operating across the EU and the UK are the very companies that define a ‘Made with Europe’ approach, as they facilitate trade between the EU and the UK, thus driving growth, competitiveness and security across Europe?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (21.5.2026) The proposal for the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA)1 indeed aims to reinforce the EU’s global leadership by strengthening the resilience, competitiveness and decarbonisation of its industrial base, while making the Single Market a stronger platform for secure and sustainable industrial cooperation. This also supports deeper cooperation with partners with which the EU has concluded trade agreements in full respect of the EU’s international commitments. The Commission recognises that businesses operating across the EU and the UK are part of integrated trade, investment value chains across Europe, supporting growth, competitiveness and economic security. The measures in the IAA reaffirm the EU’s openness to trade as a source of economic strength and resilience, while ensuring fair access to the Single Market and strengthening Europe’s industrial base.

E-10-2026-000866.t: EU financing and the Algeciras-Madrid-Zaragoza rail motorway
qt: to the Commission Borja Giménez Larraz (PPE) Subject:

The Algeciras–Madrid–Zaragoza rail motorway is a strategic infrastructure project that supports Spain’s industrial, logistics and export competitiveness and the EU’s freight transport decarbonisation goals. It connects southern Europe’s top port with the central and north-eastern mainland, underpinning areas such as Aragon and fostering balanced regional development. According to the information available, the project has received EU co-financing, specifically, through NextGenerationEU and transport policy-related instruments. However, the initial lead times have been pushed back significantly and the motorway is not now expected to be fully operational until 2027. In view of this state of affairs: 1.
How much EU funding in total (broken down by financial instrument) has been allocated to the rail motorway thus far and what percentage has been spent?
Does the Commission consider the Spanish Government’s current disbursement pace to be consistent with the commitments it made in order to receive those funds?
What steps will the Commission take to ensure that this strategic project is completed as soon as possible?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (23.4.2026) Several measures under the Spanish Recovery and Resilience Plan (RRP)1 partly concern actions on the Mediterranean Trans-European Transport Network Corridor, including the section Algeciras-Madrid-Zaragoza2. At this stage, the Commission does not have any information on the funds allocated to the specific rail motorway referred to by the Honourable Member, as the assessment of the satisfactory fulfilment of these railway measures is to be made under the last payment request, expected in the second half of 2026. Furthermore, under the Connecting Europe Facility, Spain has received EUR 2 426 090 of funding for one project concerning directly the development of the Algeciras–Zaragoza rail motorway3. The Commission has not yet assessed the satisfactory fulfilment of this project as its end date is set for 30 September 2026. The Spanish authorities have not informed the Commission of any delays to the implementation of these measures. The Commission is therefore not in a position to comment upon the current disbursement pace of the Spanish Government. The Commission assesses the fulfilment of milestones and targets under the Spanish RRP in line with the requirements in the respective Council Implementing Decision4. Should the Commission deem that milestones and targets associated with the railway investments are not satisfactorily fulfilled, it can suspend the payment of EU funds pursuant to Article 24 of the Recovery and Resilience Facility Regulation5.

E-10-2026-000865.t: Integration of the EU4Health programme into the European Competitiveness Fund
qt: to the Commission Friedrich Pürner (NI) Subject:

The Commission’s proposal for the next multiannual financial framework includes the establishment of a European Competitiveness Fund to invest in strategic technologies across the internal market. Union-wide digital solutions, interoperable portals and an enhanced exchange of health data are envisaged, alongside the integration of the EU4Health programme into this fund. Independent investigations1 point to the risks associated with expanding the role of private tech companies in health policy, for instance by granting them access to publicly financed medical data sets for the purpose of developing AI-powered decision-support systems that can then be sold back to the public sector. The COVID-19 pandemic demonstrated that caution must be exercised. The broad integration of health data raises issues of corporate oversight in addition to concerns relating to data protection, confidentiality and informed consent, as well as patient safety. Algorithmic tools can help to standardise diagnoses and treatments, but they can also be misleading, while large-scale systems tend to be less reliable, more unstable and susceptible to structural dependencies. 1.
Which technologies are to be prioritised and what are the risks associated with a potential dependence on big tech companies – including the scaling of other health services and medical care?
How is the Commission ensuring compliance with Article 168(7) TFEU, and how does it guarantee democratic accountability while preventing the commodification of health?
European Research Council (ERC), ID: 804985.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (9.7.2026) The European Competitiveness Fund does not favour any specific technology or provider. In line with the Apply AI Strategy1, the Commission supports the uptake of trustworthy AI, fostering innovation while mitigating risks and strengthening Europe’s technological sovereignty. This aligns with the Data Union Strategy2, which aims to scale up access to highquality data for AI and innovation, and safeguard the EU data sovereignty to strengthen the global position on international data flows. In the field of health, the Commission promotes secure and interoperable access to health data, notably through the European Health Data Space (EHDS) Regulation3. The EHDS establishes a common framework for the exchange and use of electronic health data across the EU. It strengthens individuals’ access to and control over their personal electronic health data while enabling the reuse of certain data for public interest purposes, policy-making and scientific research, subject to strict conditions and safeguards. Regarding Article 168(7) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU4, the Commission fully respects Member States’ competences for the organisation and delivery of health services. EU action focuses on supporting cooperation and facilitating cross-border data exchange, including through MyHealth@EU5. Democratic accountability is ensured through EU legislation adopted by the co-legislators and through established oversight mechanisms. Both the EHDS Regulation and General Data Protection Regulation6 provide strict safeguards governing access to and use of health data, helping prevent misuse or inappropriate commercial exploitation.

E-10-2026-000864.t: Nitrate pollution of drinking water in Denmark and scope for EU action
qt: to the Commission Per Clausen (The Left) Subject:

In Denmark, the municipality of Aalborg is suing the government1 for DKK 1.1 billion to cover a sharp increase in costs owing to the need for drinking water to be purified as a result of nitrate pollution. This action has been brought because, under the EU Nitrates Directive2, nitrate pollution (from agriculture) of drinking water must not be allowed to occur on this scale. In this case it did happen, however, and the Danish Government did nothing about it. Press reports3 stating that in Aalborg alone 74 people each year are diagnosed with bowel cancer – which has been linked to nitrate pollution – show just how serious this situation is. The situation is clearly untenable, and raises a number of questions requiring answers from the Commission. In the light of the foregoing: 1.
What is the Commission’s assessment of the Danish decision to allow more fertiliser to be used, even though it was well known that it can lead to increased nitrate levels in drinking water?

Given the problems with excessive nitrate levels stemming from the use of fertilisers in several EU countries (including Denmark, Germany, Ireland and the Netherlands), what practical action is the Commission going to take to improve the situation?
Will the Commission launch a new study on how many cases of bowel cancer in the EU can be linked to nitrate pollution, and what the social costs of this are?

https://aalborgforsyning.dk/artikelliste/28-02-2026-aalborg-forsyning-staten-skal-betale-for-vandrensning/. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:31991L0676. https://nyheder.tv2.dk/samfund/2026-02-28-aalborg-staevner-staten-for-en-milliard-for-ikke-at-sikre-rentdrikkevand.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (24.4.2026) The Nitrates Directive1 requires Member States to implement action programmes ensuring that farmers adhere to good practices for the use of fertilisers in areas vulnerable to nitrate pollution with the aim of reducing and preventing further such pollution. Pollution is defined as a situation where nitrate concentrations in surface or groundwater exceed 50 mg/l or could exceed this limit if no action is taken, or where surface waters suffer from eutrophication. The EU threshold for nitrates in drinking water remains 50 mg/l2, but Member States are free to set stricter standards to protect public health. The Commission closely follows the implementation of the Nitrates Directive in the Member States. Based on their reports for 2020-2023, an EU summary report is currently in preparation. The Commission is finalising an evaluation of the Directive, expected later in 2026. The Commission is in contact with national authorities and has over the years initiated numerous infringement proceedings to ensure effective enforcement of the Directive. Also, the Common Agricultural Policy3 provides Member States several tools to support farmers towards sustainable nutrients management. The Commission is not conducting scientific studies on individual cancer risk factors and their social costs but supports Member States in their efforts to improve cancer prevention, early detection and care through Europe’s Beating Cancer Plan4. Relevant actions addressing colorectal cancer include the European Code Against Cancer5, the EU-funded Joint Action EUCanScreen6, the development of European guidelines and a quality assurance scheme for colorectal cancer prevention, screening and treatment.

E-10-2026-000863.t: Commission’s financing of the Confederation of African Football (CAF) under the Global Gateway Strategy
qt: to the Commission Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE) Subject:

The Commission recently entered into a ‘historic’ partnership with the Confederation of African Football (CAF), in order to promote its Global Gateway initiative. According to public information, a sum of EUR 5.5 million has been paid to CAF, including for the purchase of advertising space during the Africa Cup of Nations in December 2025. There has been outrage as public funds are used to bankroll visibility for a bureaucratic programme on stadium billboards, while Europeans are caught in an ongoing economic crisis. CAF is frequently embroiled in scandals pertaining to corruption and misuse of funds. The organisation’s former president was suspended by FIFA for abuse of power and embezzlement, while the current president is facing accusations of opaque management and questionable financial practices. 1.
How does the Commission justify a financial partnership with an entity whose leadership is regularly implicated in corruption scandals?
Furthermore, how does it justify this spending in accordance with the principles of sound financial management laid out in Article 317 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union1?
What guarantees and audit mechanisms has the Commission put in place to avoid any risk of irregularity and misuse of funds?
Regulation (EU, Euratom) 2024/2509 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 23 September 2024 on the financial rules applicable to the general budget of the Union.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (13.5.2026) The Commission takes its duty to communicate about EU policies and programmes seriously. It therefore agreed a partnership with the Confederation of African Football as a means to appeal to a young adult audience that is hard to reach. The Africa Cup of Nations is watched by nearly two billion viewers worldwide, making it an impactful visibility opportunity. With increasing reach on digital platforms, the tournaments are a key platform to communicate about the EU’s investments in Africa and support for young people across the continent, including through the Global Gateway strategy1. The contract followed the standard checks and safeguards for these kinds of agreements, in line with the EU Financial Regulation2. As with all conditions for contracts for external actions financed by the EU, the agreement has robust verifications, checks, audits and reporting requirements. For this service contract, the Commission relies on a combination of (i) contractual audit and inspection clauses in the General Conditions for service contracts, (ii) record‑keeping and access obligations for contractors and contracting authorities, (iii) management checks, expenditure verifications and ex post audits, and (iv) specific anti‑fraud and irregularity mechanisms3 (suspension of implementation and payments, and recovery of unduly paid amounts) designed to prevent, detect and remedy irregularities and misuse of EU funds.

E-10-2026-000862.t: Participation of strategic partners in SAFE – status and evaluation of applications from Japan, South Korea and Türkiye to join common defence procurement
qt: to the Commission Engin Eroglu (Renew) Subject:

The industrial fragmentation of the European defence market, alongside regulatory hurdles and a lack of collective demand, have further hampered the necessary upscaling of production in the defence industry. This is causing a substantial loss of efficiency and weakening the resilience and competitiveness of the EU’s Defence Technological and Industrial Base (EDTIB). With this in mind, and given the acute threat situation associated with Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine, the Commission has devised the instrument for Security Action for Europe (SAFE) to promote common procurement and incentivise stronger collaboration in the defence industry. Japan, South Korea and Türkiye have made bids for access to common procurement under SAFE. Cooperation in the defence industry with strategic partners outside the EU is not just an option; it is a necessity for strengthening Europe’s political agency, resilience and deterrence capabilities. Partners in the Indo-Pacific currently play a vital role in robust supply chains, technological innovation and geopolitical stability. 1.
What is the current status of the applications to SAFE from Japan, South Korea and Türkiye?
How does the Commission evaluate each application’s chance of success?
What specific steps is the Commission considering in terms of further assessment and the potential opening of negotiations?

3. What specific steps is the Commission considering in terms of further assessment and the potential opening of negotiations? (28 April 2026) The Security Action for Europe (SAFE) (1) instrument provides for an open architecture that allows concluding bilateral agreements with third countries — specifically acceding, candidate and potential candidate countries or those with whom the EU has entered into a security and defence partnership. Regarding the expressions of interest submitted by Japan, South Korea, and Türkiye, the Commission is currently assessing these requests and finalising loan agreements that each Member States will sign with the EU. Once these loans agreements are established, the Commission will have a clearer picture on any possible budgetary leftover under SAFE. That also includes the possibility of certain amounts under the agreed national plans that could be re-attributed to other procurements. This would be also the right moment to discuss with Member States on the possibility to negotiate additional SAFE bilateral agreements. Any potential opening of negotiations of a bilateral agreement in the context of SAFE, needs to follow the procedure set out in Article 218 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU) (2), where the Council may authorise the Commission to negotiate the said agreements on behalf of the EU. Furthermore, Article 17 of the SAFE Regulation spells out conditions for the participation of third countries’ entities and products in SAFE, including the conditions and modalities of participation of contractors and subcontractors established in the third country in the common procurement under the SAFE instrument; the rules related to the cost of components originating in the third country; conditions of any financial contribution to be provided by the third country to the EU.

E-10-2026-000861.t: Protecting maternity, unequal treatment of fixed-term workers, infringement procedure and the demographic challenge in Greece
qt: to the Commission Elena Kountoura (The Left) Subject:

In Greece, substitute teachers on fixed-term contracts do not enjoy adequate1 and equal protection in matters of pregnancy, maternity and sick leave due to threatened miscarriage, compared to permanent teachers2. This practice constitutes discrimination against fixed-term workers and is contrary to EU law on equal treatment. On 7 May 2025, the Commission issued a reasoned opinion3 to Greece, pointing out that the current national framework does not comply with Directive 1999/70/EC concerning the prohibition of discrimination against workers on fixed-term contracts4. Meanwhile, Greece is facing an acute demographic problem, with declining births and accelerated population ageing. The insecurity of thousands of women in precarious forms of employment and the lack of maternity protection act as a disincentive to starting a family and run counter to the Union’s strategic objectives on gender equality, social cohesion and demographic sustainability. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

How does it view the compatibility of Greek legislation with the principle of equal treatment of workers and with the obligations arising from the relevant directives on maternity protection, and at what stage is the infringement procedure against Greece?
How does it view the impact of the lack of maternity protection on the country's demographic development?
What initiatives does it intend to take in the event of non-compliance of Greek legislation with EU law?

EU equality legislation sets minimum standards for the protection of pregnant workers, workers who have recently given birth or are breastfeeding, as well as for fixed-term workers. See Directive 92/85/EEC on the introduction of measures to encourage improvements in the safety and health at work of pregnant workers and workers who have recently given birth or are breastfeeding. In Greece, there is a serious issue of discrimination regarding maternity leave for substitute teachers, who are only entitled to 119 days of parental leave. Many women are forced to return to work prematurely or even resign, with negative consequences for their family, economic and professional situation. Greece had two months to reply and take measures – see reasoned opinion (INFR (2024) 4013), https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/inf_25_982. Council Directive 1999/70/EC concerning the framework agreement on fixed-term work concluded by ETUC, UNICE and CEEP.

(4 May 2026) As the Honourable Member refers in her question, a potential discrimination of fixed-term teachers contrary to Directive 1999/70 EC (1), is already being examined in the framework of an infringement procedure INFR(2024)4013 (2). Currently, the Commission is assessing the reply provided by the Greek authorities to the reasoned opinion sent in May 2025. The steps that the Commission decides to take in the infringement procedure will be made publicly available. The Greek authorities with the support of the European Social Fund Plus (ESF+), have initiated efforts to address Greece’s demographic challenges. This includes the establishment of a National Observatory of Demographic Policy to support the implementation of the National Action Plan for Demography and to strengthen the capacity of public administration to design targeted interventions at national and regional level. E-10-2026-000860.t: Vaccination against avian influenza – risks and benefits
qt: to the Commission Sergio Berlato (ECR) Subject:

In November 2025, EFSA stated that it had detected 1 443 cases of avian influenza in wild birds in the previous three months, chiefly waterfowl, from 26 EU countries, the highest number since 20161. In November 2025, the EMA authorised the use of2: five veterinary vaccines against the highly pathogenic avian influenza virus, subtype H5. seven influenza vaccines for human use in preparation for a pandemic, without a pandemic having been declared, in addition to four antivirals. The specifications for authorisations for suggest that the medicines are still in at an experimental phase: ‘medicine authorised in exceptional circumstances’, further studies ‘to obtain data on efficacy’ and ‘the benefits of the vaccine outweigh its risks’. Can the Commission therefore say: 1.

What measures it intends to take to ensure full transparency and access to information on the efficacy of authorised vaccines, including the criteria for their selection, data on their efficacy and post-vaccination surveillance protocols (DIVA strategy), also assessing the risk to humans and animals and the consequent potential damage to food safety?
what structural prevention measures, such as checking farm density and production planning, will accompany vaccination in order to reduce the risk of new outbreaks?
whether it has carried out or intends to carry out assessments of the impact of vaccination on exports to third countries and on the competitiveness of the supply chain?

In November 2025, the EMA authorised the use of (2): five veterinary vaccines against the highly pathogenic avian influenza virus, subtype H5. seven influenza vaccines for human use in preparation for a pandemic, without a pandemic having been declared, in addition to four antivirals. Can the Commission therefore say: 1.

(27 April 2026) The authorisations referred to by the Honourable Member aim to address exceptional circumstances related to animal or public health. These are only granted where the benefit of their immediate availability outweighs the risks linked to the absence of certain documentation. These authorisations are only valid for one year and subject to re-examination to confirm that i) the exceptional circumstances remain, and ii) the benefit-risk balance remains positive (1). The outcome of their assessment as regards their quality, efficacy, risks to humans, animals and food safety, is reflected in the assessment reports prepared by the European Medicines Agency. These reports are publicly available in the EU Product Database (2), ensuring full transparency. In accordance with the assessment (3) of the European Food Safety Authority, poultry holding density should be considered a major contributing factor for large highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) epidemics. Member States should consider this risk factor when designing their prevention strategy against HPAI. Vaccination may be used as a complementary tool that, added to biosecurity and other measures, can help prevention against infection and spread of HPAI in poultry. Currently, France is the only Member State implementing preventive vaccination against HPAI in poultry and only a few trading partners continue applying trade restrictions, limited to certain products of vaccinated poultry.

E-10-2026-000859.t: On the war against Iran and the need for Europe to stop submitting to the United States
qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Irene Montero (The Left) Subject:

On 28 February 2026, the United States and Israel launched a military operation against Iran, causing the death of Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, members of the Revolutionary Guard Corps and over 555 civilians. In response, Iran has attacked targets in Israel and US military bases in Persian Gulf countries. These events all constitute an illegal attack contrary to international law and to the UN Charter, with unpredictable consequences for regional and global peace. 1.

What specific measures will the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy take to promote immediate de-escalation and compliance with international law in the face of an action that constitutes illegal use of force?
Will the VP/HR propose adopting sanctions and a total arms embargo against the USA and Israel, in line with measures adopted by the EU in the context of other cases of international aggression?

Does the VP/HR consider Member States participating in integrated military structures under US leadership to compromise European autonomy and peace, and will the HR/VP promote the necessary initiatives for Member States to leave NATO and to prohibit the use of military bases and EU territory for this war?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (13.5.2026) The High Representative/Vice-President (HR/VP) has been in continuous contact with partners in the Middle East to call for maximum restraint, urge all parties to comply with international humanitarian law and to protect civilians and civilian infrastructure, as well as to ensure freedom of navigation and safe passage through the Strait of Hormuz. On 9 April 2026, the HR/VP on behalf of the European Union, welcomed the ceasefire1 agreed by the US and Iran. The statement stressed that diplomacy is key to resolve all outstanding issues and parties should continue engaging in good faith in efforts to reach a sustainable agreement on all areas of concern. The EU contributes to all diplomatic efforts in this endeavour, taking into consideration its full range of interests and concerns, in coordination with partners. EU restrictive measures (‘sanctions’) as tools of the Common Foreign and Security Policy are adopted by the Council with unanimity. The Council is empowered to decide on the possible extension of any measure, while Member States are responsible for the effective implementation and enforcement of sanctions. It is for the Member States to decide their own policies within NATO. Membership of NATO, including participation in its integrated military structures, is a national prerogative and decision. As regards the use of military bases by individual Member States, this also remains their prerogative; decisions are taken by national governments in line with their sovereign authority. NATO is a strategic partner for the EU and plays a key role in territorial defence for the 23 common members, while providing crucial deterrence against external threats to Europe’s borders.
1 https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/press/press-releases/2026/04/09/statement-by-the-high-representative-on-
behalf-of-the-eu-on-the-ceasefire-agreed-by-the-united-states-and-iran/.

E-10-2026-000858.t: Call to respect consumers when taking old video games offline
qt: to the Commission Catherine Griset (PfE) Subject:

The European citizens’ initiative ‘Stop destroying videogames’ has won the backing of 1.3 million signatories1. It takes aim at the publishers taking their video games offline without maintaining them in a playable state. Yet the publishers claim that community-led maintenance would be fraught with risks2. In the same vein, the French Court of Cassation has ruled that digital game distribution platforms are entitled to deny customers a second-hand market3, and so to prevent consumers from reselling their video games as they used to do with CD ROMs and cartridges. Therefore, while online distribution makes games more accessible, it comes at the expense of a considerable erosion of player/consumer rights. 1.
Would the Commission consider funding (under the Horizon Europe programme, for example) an EU-wide AI venture to maintain old games that have been taken offline by their publishers?

Could publishers not enter into a mutually beneficial commercial agreement with an AI company, whereby the latter is legally authorised to train on disconnected games in exchange for relieving the former of their maintenance?

E-10-2026-000857.t: Alleged favourable treatment of renewable energy projects in Spain during the term of office of current Commissioner Teresa Ribera
qt: to the Commission Dolors Montserrat (PPE), Elena Nevado del Campo (PPE) Subject:

The Public Prosecutor’s Office for the Environment in Spain is currently investigating the actions of senior officials of the Ministry for the Ecological Transition and the Demographic Challenge who are said to have authorised renewable energy projects by means of environmental impact statements which allegedly ran counter to national and European legislation, thereby arbitrarily favouring certain companies1. Those decisions are alleged to have been taken during the term of office of Teresa Ribera – now a member of the College of Commissioners – at the head of that ministry. These facts, if confirmed, could affect the correct application of Union law, in particular as regards environmental protection, the use of European funds and the principles of good administration. In light of the above: 1.

Is the Commission aware of this information and does it consider that it could entail a breach of EU law, in particular of environmental legislation and of the rules applicable to the granting of EU funding?

Does the Commission intend to verify whether, during this period, the authorisations and possible financing of renewable energy projects in Spain were fully in line with EU law and, where appropriate, to take any corresponding action?

E-10-2026-000856.t: Applying the MiCA Regulation to small operators in the crypto-asset sector
qt: to the Commission Marcin Sypniewski (ESN) Subject:

Regulation (EU) 2023/1114 on markets in crypto-assets (MiCA) introduced uniform rules across the European Union for the operation of crypto-asset service providers, including capital and organisational requirements, and the obligation to obtain a licence. However, as part of the public debate, serious doubts have been raised – including by cryptoasset market experts – as to how proportional the new rules are for smaller companies. It has been pointed out that cumulative licensing costs, capital requirements and increasing compliance obligations may in practice lead to smaller operators being eliminated from the market, paving the way for the sector to be dominated by large financial institutions. There are also indications that supervisory practices are particularly restrictive in some Member States, which may result in an uneven playing field within the single market. In connection with the above: 1.

Has the Commission carried out a separate impact assessment (SME test) on the effects of MiCA capital and licensing requirements on micro- and small enterprises, and what conclusions were drawn with regard to barriers to market entry and potential concentration in the sector?
Is the Commission analysing the risk of the activities of crypto-asset operators being relocated outside the EU owing to the regulatory costs resulting from MiCA?

Does the Commission envisage the possibility of reviewing or adapting the rules if the way in which they are applied results in a disproportionate burden being placed on small businesses and in a loss of competitiveness for the EU’s digital market?

However, as part of the public debate, serious doubts have been raised — including by crypto-asset market experts — as to how proportional the new rules are for smaller companies. It has been pointed out that cumulative licensing costs, capital requirements and increasing compliance obligations may in practice lead to smaller operators being eliminated from the market, paving the way for the sector to be dominated by large financial institutions. (24 April 2026) Regulation (EU) 2023/1114 of the European Parliament and of the Council (MiCA Regulation ) (1) was drafted based on an impact assessment, which included a dedicated section for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). That impact assessment demonstrated that the MiCA framework would likely increase non-bank sources of funding for SMEs through the development of initial coin offerings and securities token offerings, providing an opportunity for start-ups to raise substantial amounts of funding at an early stage of development. Different provisions of the MiCA Regulation aim at limiting costs for SMEs, exempting for instance, for crypto-assets other than stablecoins, small offerings below a certain threshold and crypto-assets distributed to small circles of users from publishing an information document describing the issuance of tokens (so-called ‘white paper’). The proportionality principle also applies to all minimum prudential requirements, whether quantitative or qualitative, applying to issuers of asset referenced tokens and crypto-asset service providers. It also allows adapting the content of redemption plans to be drawn up by issuers of asset referenced tokens, and the frequency of their reviews, to the size, complexity and nature of the asset-referenced token, and to the issuer’s business model. By 30 June 2027, the Commission is to issue a report on the application of the MiCA Regulation and on the latest developments with respect to crypto-assets. That report will enable the Commission to assess whether there is a risk that crypto-asset activities relocate outside the EU and whether any legislative amendment is required.

E-10-2026-000855.t: Possible breach of EU environmental legislation and use of the ERDF in a solar power project in a Natura 2000 network area in Spain
qt: to the Commission Dolors Montserrat (PPE), Elena Nevado del Campo (PPE) Subject:

The Public Prosecutor’s Office for the Environment is looking into an administrative procedure under which authorisation was granted to build a high-capacity solar power plant at Alcántara (Cáceres), in an area that is protected under the Natura 2000 network. Authorisation was apparently granted on the basis of an environmental impact statement that was allegedly in breach of national and EU legislation on the conservation of habitats and protected species and included possible adverse effects on species protected under Directive 92/43/EEC (the Habitats Directive) and Directive 2009/147/EC (the Birds Directive)1. Apparently, the project received ERDF funding, and the cross-border notification obligation required under EU legislation was not met, even though the area concerned is close to the border with Portugal. In view of this: 1.

Has the Commission carried out, or does it intend to carry out, any investigations or exchanges of information with Spain to determine whether there has been a breach of EU environmental legislation, in particular the Habitats and Birds directives?
Does the Commission take the view that all the legal conditions required for the granting of EU funding have been met?

E-10-2026-000853.t: Assessment and classification of projects submitted under the Citizens, Equality, Rights and Values (CERV) programme
qt: to the Commission Margarita de la Pisa Carrión (PfE) Subject:
Owing to the confusion that may have been generated and in order to be able to correctly understand the procedure carried out under the CERV programme: 1.

Can the Commission clarify whether the executive agency can modify or adjust the scores or ranking resulting from expert evaluations and, if so, in what cases, according to what criteria and with what guarantees of traceability and transparency?
What is the applicable procedure when a project is deemed compliant by the agency, but not by the experts, or vice versa, and which assessment prevails and on what legal and procedural basis?

How is final funding determined when experts’ scores and other programmatic or budgetary criteria differ, which criteria take precedence, and how are they reflected and justified in the event of an appeal or review?
at: (English version) to the Commission Margarita de la Pisa Carrión (PfE) (2 March 2026) Subject: Assessment and classification of projects submitted under the Citizens, Equality, Rights and Values (CERV) programme In respect of the assessment and classification of projects submitted under the Citizens, Equality, Rights and Values (CERV) programme: 1.

What criteria and procedures are being used to select and appoint specific experts from the database of experts to evaluate a call for proposals under the CERV programme, and how is the professional profile of the experts, including their public statements, interests or positions that may affect their impartiality, specifically assessed, weighted and documented as part of this process?

What arrangements are in place to guarantee the neutrality, independence and absence of conflicts of interest of the appointed experts and ensure that assessments comply with the principles of equal treatment, non-discrimination, independence, impartiality, proportionality and objectivity in accordance with the regulation establishing the Citizens, Equality, Rights and Values programme?
Specifically, what measures are there to prevent an expert's positions or interests from influencing their assessment of others or the final outcome?

to the Commission Margarita de la Pisa Carrión (PfE) (2 March 2026) Subject: Assessment and classification of projects submitted under the Citizens, Equality, Rights and Values (CERV) programme Owing to the confusion that may have been generated and in order to be able to correctly understand the procedure carried out under the CERV programme: 1.

Can the Commission clarify whether the executive agency can modify or adjust the scores or ranking resulting from expert evaluations and, if so, in what cases, according to what criteria and with what guarantees of traceability and transparency?
What is the applicable procedure when a project is deemed compliant by the agency, but not by the experts, or vice versa, and which assessment prevails and on what legal and procedural basis?

How is final funding determined when experts’ scores and other programmatic or budgetary criteria differ, which criteria take precedence, and how are they reflected and justified in the event of an appeal or review?

Joint answer given by Mr McGrath on behalf of the European Commission (29 April 2026) Experts interested in evaluating proposals register in the Commission database. When proposals need to be evaluated, the Commission searches the database using keywords linked to the relevant programme and call. The Commission then selects experts based on their relevant expertise, experience and qualifications as recorded in the database. Before selection, each expert's professional profile is thoroughly reviewed, including professional background, reputation, and potential conflicts of interest.

The corporate template of the experts’ contract used under the Citizens, Equality, Rights and Values programme (CERV) (1) requires experts to comply with the Experts Code of Conduct (2) which outlines the principles of impartiality and confidentiality that must guide the experts’ work. Various checks are performed to identify potential conflicts of interest; moreover, each proposal is independently assessed by two experts, who prepare separate evaluation reports, while a consensus report (CR) is prepared normally by a third expert. Proposals are evaluated on the basis of the pre-announced selection and award criteria. The selection and award of proposals are under the direct responsibility of an evaluation committee, which for CERV is composed exclusively of staff from the Commission and the European Education and Culture Executive Agency. External experts may assist the evaluation committee, but do not have decision-making authority. The evaluation committee analyses the proposals received and reviews all CRs. On this basis, the evaluation committee drafts the Evaluation Summary Report that documents the merits and shortcomings of each proposal, the decisions taken, and it ranks the proposals up to the available budget.

Regulation (EU) 2021/692 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 28 April 2021 establishing the Citizens, Equality, Rights and Values Programme (OJ L 156, 5.5.2021, p. 1); ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2021/692/oj. https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/docs/2021-2027/experts/code-of-conduct_en.pdf.

E-10-2026-000849.t: Fitness check of EU rules on trade in seal products
qt: to the Commission César Luena (S&D) Subject:

In May 20241, the Commission launched a fitness check of EU rules on trade in seal products. To date, only a factual summary report of the public consultation and a call for evidence have been published. This consultation found that 98 % of respondents would not purchase seal products of any kind. Only 3 % of respondents indicated that would consider buying ‘products from hunts intended to protect fishery activities’. 1.
Could the Commission explain why – more than one and a half years later – no detailed fitness check report or Commission staff working document have been forthcoming as yet?
Could the Commission confirm when these documents will be published?
https://ec.europa.eu/info/law/better-regulation/have-your-say/initiatives/14031-Trade-in-seal-productsfitness-check-of-EU-rules/public-consultation_en.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (6.7.2026) The Commission considers that the fitness check of the EU Seals regime1 should be based on a comprehensive, evidence-based assessment which requires some time. The fitness check includes a thorough collection of data, stakeholder consultations, as well as a robust analysis of the data. The Commission intends to publish the results of the fitness check in 2026.
1 https://environment.ec.europa.eu/topics/nature-and-biodiversity/trade-seal-products_en.

qt: to the Commission Jan-Peter Warnke (NI), Rudi Kennes (The Left), Michael von der Schulenburg (NI), Maria Zacharia (NI), Kateřina Konečná (NI), Fabio De Masi (NI), Thomas Geisel (NI), Ruth Firmenich (NI) Subject:

The European Commission is not only providing grants to but, through Horizon Europe and the European Innovation Council (EIC), is also investing in, holding shares of, and profiting from the activities of Israeli companies. Companies that have benefited from Horizon Europe and the EIC participated in Israel’s attack on Gaza and support the Israel Defence Forces in potential genocide, as determined by the International Court of Justice. Sightec, a manufacturer of AI navigation technology for drones, received almost EUR 2.5 million from the EU. Its CEO, Roy Shmuel, stated on LinkedIn that Sightec technology was ‘combat-proven and deployed on over 3 000 drones in critical missions’1, publicly admitting that this technology is also used for military purposes. 1.

To what extent did the Commission follow due process with respect to due diligence and the ongoing monitoring of human rights violations and the ethics of companies in which the Commission invested through Horizon 2020 and Horizon Europe?
To what extent do the background checks on company leadership assess the risks of human rights violations by individuals who are potentially implicated in violence?
To what extent is the Commission in line with Article 2 of the EU-Israel Association Agreement and the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights?
https://www.linkedin.com/posts/roy-shmuel-78324b6_gpsfree-visualnavigation-electronicwarfare-activity7362144414355374082-huua.
at: (English version) to the Commission Jan-Peter Warnke (NI), Rudi Kennes (The Left), Michael von der Schulenburg (NI), Maria Zacharia (NI), Kateřina Konečná (NI), Fabio De Masi (NI), Thomas Geisel (NI), Ruth Firmenich (NI) (2 March 2026) Subject: Breach of EU-Israel Association Agreement The European Commission is not only providing grants to but, through Horizon Europe and the European Innovation Council (EIC), is also investing in, holding shares of, and profiting from the activities of Israeli companies. Companies that have benefited from Horizon Europe and the EIC participated in Israel’s attack on Gaza and support the Israel Defence Forces in potential genocide, as determined by the International Court of Justice. Sightec, a manufacturer of AI navigation technology for drones, received almost EUR 2.5 million from the EU. Its CEO, Roy Shmuel, stated on LinkedIn that Sightec technology was ‘combat-proven and deployed on over 3 000 drones in critical missions’ (1), publicly admitting that this technology is also used for military purposes. 1. To what extent did the Commission follow due process with respect to due diligence and the ongoing monitoring of human rights violations and the ethics of companies in which the Commission invested through Horizon 2020 and Horizon Europe? 2. To what extent do the background checks on company leadership assess the risks of human rights violations by individuals who are potentially implicated in violence? 3. To what extent is the Commission in line with Article 2 of the EU-Israel Association Agreement and the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights? (1 June 2026) Under the Horizon Europe (HE) (1) legal framework, all funded actions must comply with ethical principles and applicable national, EU and international legislation (2). At the level of HE implementation, several mechanisms are in place to prevent that EU funds are used for activities that could be unethical, or contrary to international or EU law. Applicants must complete an ethics self-assessment and all proposals considered for funding undergo an ethics review carried out by independent ethics experts (3). Furthermore, for Israeli entities, specific eligibility criteria related to the place of establishment or activities apply (4). Article 2(2) of the Agreement associating Israel to HE (5) sets out the principle that Israeli entities participate in the HE programme under terms and conditions equivalent to those applicable to legal entities established in the EU. Any actions of the State of Israel cannot be considered automatically attributable to Israeli entities participating in HE. The HE Agreement is based on the Euro-Mediterranean Association Agreement (6). In the context of the events in Gaza, the Commission concluded that there are indications that Israel would be in breach of Article 2 of the Euro-Mediterranean Association Agreement. 1

https://www.linkedin.com/posts/roy-shmuel-78324b6_gpsfree-visualnavigation-electronicwarfare-activity-7362144414355374082-huua. https://research-and-innovation.ec.europa.eu/funding/funding-opportunities/funding-programmes-and-open-calls/horizon-europe_en. Article 19(1) of Regulation (EU) 2021/695 (HE Regulation) explicitly requires that: ‘Actions carried out under the Programme shall comply with ethical principles and relevant Union, national and international law, including the Charter and the European Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms and its Supplementary Protocols’. These obligations are also embedded in the HE Model Grant Agreement, Article 14, and are applicable to all beneficiaries of EU funding under HE, see https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/docs/20212027/common/guidance/aga_en.pdf. The HE ethics appraisal scheme ensures a rigorous ethical evaluation. Proposals with serious or complex ethics issues must undergo an ethics assessment and may be made subject to specific ethics requirements which become obligations in the grant agreement as ‘ethics deliverables’. Furthermore, Article 19(3) of the HE Regulation in its first sentence sets out the systematic screening of the ongoing actions regarding the observance of the ethical standards under paragraph 1. Any ethical concerns arising during implementation of a project are taken very seriously and may lead to ethics-related checks or reviews when appropriate. A non-compliance may trigger contractual measures such as reduction of the EU funding or termination of the grant or termination of the participation of the respective beneficiary. https://op.europa.eu/en/publication-detail/-/publication/044b0978-9f3f-4cdc-b0df-827d94af5c6c/language-en . https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:22022A0323(10) . https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=OJ:L:2000:147:FULL .

The Commission therefore proposed to the Council a suspension of trade-related provisions of the Association Agreement as well as a partial suspension of the application of the HE Agreement with Israel, so that legal entities established in Israel would not be eligible to participate in calls for grant and investment support under the HE European Innovation Council Accelerator. The Council has not taken a decision yet. The Commission continues to closely monitor the situation.

The European Innovation Council (EIC) Accelerator programme is the only part of Horizon Europe that supports research on nuclear technology and its use. According to the Council of the EU, the omnibus package will amend five key EU programmes, including Horizon Europe and the European Defence Fund, in order to provide ‘more support for dual-use and defence companies’1. Israel is one of the countries considered to be an ‘associated country’ in Horizon Europe and is actively participating in European Defence Fund projects. It is treated like an EU Member State as regards eligibility. Sightec, a manufacturer of AI navigation technology for drones, received almost EUR 2.5 million from the EU. Its CEO, Roy Shmuel, stated on LinkedIn that Sightec technology was ‘combat-proven and deployed on over 3 000 drones in critical missions’2, publicly admitting that this technology is also used for military purposes. Nevertheless, Israel is not a signatory to the Non-Proliferation Treaty or Euratom. Given these facts, what measures is the Commission taking to manage proliferation risks associated with Israel’s development of nuclear technology and materials?

at: (English version) to the Commission Jan-Peter Warnke (NI), Rudi Kennes (The Left), Michael von der Schulenburg (NI), Maria Zacharia (NI), Kateřina Konečná (NI), Ruth Firmenich (NI), Fabio De Masi (NI), Thomas Geisel (NI), Ľuboš Blaha (NI) (2 March 2026) Subject: Nuclear technology and Horizon Europe The European Innovation Council (EIC) Accelerator programme is the only part of Horizon Europe that supports research on nuclear technology and its use. According to the Council of the EU, the omnibus package will amend five key EU programmes, including Horizon Europe and the European Defence Fund, in order to provide ‘more support for dual-use and defence companies’ (1). Israel is one of the countries considered to be an ‘associated country’ in Horizon Europe and is actively participating in European Defence Fund projects. It is treated like an EU Member State as regards eligibility. Sightec, a manufacturer of AI navigation technology for drones, received almost EUR 2.5 million from the EU. Its CEO, Roy Shmuel, stated on LinkedIn that Sightec technology was ‘combat-proven and deployed on over 3 000 drones in critical missions’ (2), publicly admitting that this technology is also used for military purposes. Nevertheless, Israel is not a signatory to the Non-Proliferation Treaty or Euratom. Given these facts, what measures is the Commission taking to manage proliferation risks associated with Israel’s development of nuclear technology and materials? (28 May 2026) Nuclear activities that contribute to the achievement of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU) (1) objectives can be funded under the TFEU where the Euratom Treaty (2) does not lay down exhaustive or specific rules. This is the case for the European Innovation Council (EIC). As set out in Article 19(1) of the Horizon Europe (HE) Regulation (3), any action carried out under the HE programme must comply with ethical principles and relevant EU, national and international law, including the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights (4) and the European Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms and its Supplementary Protocols (5). Export control of dual use items in the EU (6) is based on a common list of dual-use items (7) that must be controlled in all Member States (8). Sightec applied successfully for EIC blended finance support in 2021 and received the grant support but was rejected for the equity investment (10), so there is no ongoing investment in the company. Regarding the statement by Sightec’s CEO pointing to dual use, it should be noted that the HE legal base, at the time, specified that activities supported had to be exclusively civilian (11).
