E-10-2026-000844.t: Tragic situation on Greek and European railways due to lack of safety measures, three years after the crime of Tempi
qt: to the Commission Kostas Papadakis (NI), Lefteris Nikolaou-Alavanos (NI) Subject:

Three years after the crime of Tempi - a foregone conclusion - there is widespread demand for it not to be covered up, for criminal and political responsibility to be assigned, and for there never to be another ‘Tempi’. The causes are still here. The competent ERTMS coordinator of DG MOVE admits in a report that ‘only 10 % of the total TEN-T and 19 % of the EU railway fleet are equipped with ETCS’ and ‘the development of ERTMS is very slow’, while a goal is set of ‘reducing the cost of ERTMS on trains’. The EU and governments’ main criterion is ‘cost-benefit’, sacrificing security for the profits of business groups, while funding for military mobility is increased tenfold in the new MFF (2028-2034) and another 100 billion euro are announced - through the CEF - for the ‘military Schengen’. In view of the above: 1.

What is the Commission’s position on the fact that, three years after the inevitable crime of Tempi, train collisions are increasing throughout Europe, with dozens of deaths and injuries, as the railway liberalisation strategy and the EU and governments’ ‘costbenefit’ policy condemn the network to tragic shortages of personnel and a lack of modern security systems, infrastructure and maintenance, with painful consequences for the safety of passengers and workers?

What is the Commission’s position on the fact that, while the recruitment of personnel and the installation of modern security systems are at a standstill and a report by a Commission official recommends new ‘cost reductions’, even ‘on trains’, the Commission is promoting a tenfold increase in funding for military mobility and war preparation, involving the people of Europe in incalculable risks?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (28.5.2026) The Commission has no data that confirms a negative impact on safety of the rail market opening to competition. On the contrary safety indicators and safety performance data collected by the European Union Agency for Railways imply a positive trend of improved safety levels in the Single European Railway Area since 2010. Despite deplorable large accidents in recent years, the number of significant accidents has dropped from 2230 in 2010 to 1565 in 2023. A similar downward trend can be observed for the number of victims of accidents (fatalities and seriously injured). Moreover, most of the reported accidents refer to accidents caused by third parties: road users at level crossings or unauthorised persons trespassing railway tracks. These two categories of accidents account also for 97,4% of all fatalities1. Finally, in respect of military mobility, the Commission promotes the concept of ‘dual-use infrastructure’ to ensure that military mobility projects will positively contribute to the development of the EU rail system and thus society as a whole. The cost reductions advocated by the European Rail Traffic Management System (ERTMS) European Coordinator’s report2 are supposed to lower the cost of ERTMS deployment on trains and therefore allow for a wider roll-out of this important safety system.
1 Safety Overview 2025, EU Agency for Railways, March 2025, see figures 2, 8 and 10. Document available at:

https://www.era.europa.eu/sites/default/files/2025-03/safety-overview-2025.pdf. 2 Work plan of the European coordinator Matthias Ruete, Publications Office of the European Union, 2026, https://data.europa.eu/doi/10.2832/9894936.

E-10-2026-000843.t: Exemptions from the reuse targets under the PPWR on environmental grounds
qt: to the Commission Jessica Polfjärd (PPE) Subject:

Article 29 of the Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (PPWR) establishes binding reuse targets for beverage packaging from 2030. Several Nordic Member States already operate well-functioning deposit return systems (DRS) for single-use containers. Independent life-cycle assessments, including a study by the RISE Research Institutes of Sweden indicate that in countries with low population density and long transport distances, such systems may have a lower overall climate impact than reusable bottle systems. Article 29(18)(c) empowers the Commission to adopt delegated acts granting exemptions for specific packaging formats where environmental considerations prevent the achievement of the reuse targets. In this context: 1.

How will the Commission ensure that implementing the reuse targets does not undermine well-functioning DRS, particularly in smaller markets, and how will it provide timely guidance and legal clarity to ensure predictability for businesses?
Will the Commission use Article 29(18)(c) to grant exemptions where independent lifecycle assessments demonstrate a lower climate impact for existing national systems?
What criteria and evidence will be required to justify such exemptions?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (11.5.2026) The Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (PPWR)1 strongly supports deposit and return systems, as they have many positive qualities including ensuring high collection rates, and less litter. The 10 % reuse target for beverage packaging in the PPWR applies as of 2030 and to larger ‘final distributors’ such as retailers and restaurants, with a sales area of more than 100 m2. All micro-enterprises are exempted from offering reuse, and Member States can implement further exemptions to consider specific local conditions, including final distributors in areas with low population density. A Member State can also introduce national exemptions for packaging of materials with high recycling rates, such as aluminium, provided that it fulfils the conditions set in Article 29(14). The Commission has recently published a guidance document2 for the PPWR that clarifies how this exemption can be applied. The Commission is empowered to adopt delegated acts under the Article 29(18) supplementing the harmonised reuse targets in the PPWR. Such delegated acts can exempt economic operators who face particular economic constraints, or specific packaging formats where achievement of the reuse targets is hindered due to hygiene and food safety or environmental issues. To ensure legal certainty for economic operators and the integrity of the internal market, the Commission will act only when the necessity to act is demonstrated via adequate evidence, also taking the applicable exemptions into considerations, and when it is confirmed by the Commission’s own impact assessment.
1 Regulation (EU) 2025/40 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 19 December 2024 on packaging

and packaging waste, amending Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 and Directive (EU) 2019/904, and repealing Directive 94/62/EC, OJ L, 2025/40, 22.1.2025. 2 https://environment.ec.europa.eu/publications/guidance-document-packaging-and-packaging-waste-regulationppwr_en.

qt: to the Commission Oihane Agirregoitia Martínez (Renew) Subject:

The alarming spread of lumpy skin disease (LSD), an insect-borne viral disease, is another example of how climate change is driving an increase in livestock illnesses. These shifts, together with endemic trends in disease transmission, are rendering disease protocols and categories obsolete. Even in cases where a single infected specimen is detected, the entire holding has to be depopulated, putting the livestock sector in a troubling position. In its reply of 12 February 2026 to my question E-004688/20251, the Commission fails to respond to two points that are of particular concern to the sector, so I reiterate below: 1.
Taking into account that LSD is not a zoonosis, does the Commission plan to update its protocol and classification?
Has the Commission carried out any analyses assessing the impact of the virus on livestock farms and the sector as a whole and, if so, is it considering taking any compensatory measures?
https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/E-10-2025-004688_EN.html.
at: EN E-00842/2026 on behalf of the European Commission (21.4.2026) As set out in the Commission’s replies to questions P-004478/20251 and P-004688/20252, infection with Lumpy Skin Disease (LSD) is categorised as a Category A disease under the Animal Health Law (AHL, Regulation (EU) 2016/4293). Therefore, it requires Union-level intervention, and immediate eradication measures must be taken upon its detection due to the seriousness of its impact on animal health, the economy, society, and the environment. The appropriateness of this categorisation has been assessed in light of the disease profile and impact criteria laid down in Articles 5 and 7 of the AHL and supported by scientific evidence from the European Food Safety Authority4, the EU Reference laboratory and the World Organisation for Animal Health. Based on this assessment, the Commission has concluded that the current categorisation is appropriate and proportionate to the identified risk. No recategorisation is deemed necessary. The Commission continuously monitors the animal health situation in the Union territory and recognises the economic impact of animal diseases on the livestock sector. E-10-2026-000840.t: Tackling the misrepresentation of products as Greek and strengthening local honey production
qt: to the Commission Emmanouil Fragkos (ECR) Subject:

In accordance with the applicable EU legislation on honey, in particular Directive 2001/110/EC, as recently amended by Directive (EU) 2024/1438, and in the context of official controls under Regulation (EU) 2017/625, in conjunction with the general principles of Regulation (EC) 178/2002 on food safety and traceability, the Union has strengthened its traceability and market control tools. However, there are increasing reports of imports of honey of dubious authenticity from nonEU countries, as well as of instances of the ‘Greekification’ of products that are either not of Greek origin or do not even meet the definition of honey. It appears that, in particular in some Member States, controls are lax, leading to easy access to the European market. In view of the above: 1.

Does the Commission systematically monitor honey imports to Greece and the EU in terms of authenticity, composition and correct labelling, and are there any recent findings from coordinated controls or from the EU agri-food fraud network?

Does the Commission intend to propose further measures to tackle illegal ‘Greekification’, such as stricter mandatory labelling of the country of origin per batch or strengthening laboratory methods for detecting adulteration?

In the context of the ‘farm to fork’ strategy, how does the Commission intend practically to strengthen short supply chains and boost the consumption of local honey, in order to support local beekeepers and restore consumer confidence?

(17 April 2026) 1. The Commission monitors the official controls performed on honey imported into the EU to verify compliance with the EU food safety legislation in general, and with Directive 2001/110/EC (1) in particular. Every consignment of honey is subject to official controls at the border control post of first arrival, including documentary and identity checks at a frequency of 100%, as well as physical checks on 15% of consignments (2). During 2025, two coordinated measures of intensified official controls were launched at EU level (3), with 22 consignments controlled under these measures, none of them related to Greece. 2. Directive (EU) 2024/1438 (4) introduced mandatory origin labelling for honey blends and new provisions on traceability and authenticity. From June 2026, the countries of origin will have to be labelled for blends, including the percentage share represented by each country. By June 2029, the Commission will adopt delegated acts laying down methods and criteria to determine the place where honey has been harvested and EU-wide traceability requirements (5). The Commission is also working to reinforce the capacity to detect honey adulterated with sugar syrups thanks to a project, running until end of 2026, that aims to harmonise analysis methods. The Commission has until June 2028 to adopt implementing acts laying down methods of analysis to detect adulterated honey (6). 3. The Commission supports efforts to strengthen short supply chains and promote the consumption of local honey through the Common Agricultural Policy, which provides funding for advisory services, technical assistance, investments and actions aimed at supporting local beekeepers to improve production and quality of honey and enhance consumer confidence in local products.

at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (10.6.2026) Members of the College are subject to strict obligations arising directly under the Treaties as well as to the ethical obligations emanating from the Code of Conduct for the Members of the Commission1. E-10-2026-000837.t: Need for a single European safety, certification and accountability framework for autonomous driving (levels 4-5)
qt: to the Commission Elena Kountoura (The Left) Subject:
Need for a single European safety, certification and accountability framework for autonomous driving (levels 4-5)

High-level and fully autonomous driving (levels 4-5), where no driver is expected to control the operational functions, is developing rapidly and the transition to a fully autonomous (driverless) road environment is creating new needs in terms of road safety1, system reliability and harmonisation of testing and certification procedures. Despite the existing EU framework2, significant gaps remain in terms of type approval, realworld testing, infrastructure interoperability, cybersecurity, post-market surveillance, remote software updates and the liability framework for autonomous vehicles. The European Parliament has called for3 a single European framework with common realworld testing standards, uniform requirements for autonomous systems, interoperable marking, signalling and digital mapping specifications, strong cybersecurity rules and a clear liability framework to ensure the protection of citizens. In view of the above: 1.
How will the Commission ensure that the rapid development of fully autonomous technologies will be accompanied by strict and uniform European safety standards?

What actions will the Commission take to establish a harmonised European framework to fill the gaps in the approval procedures for fully automated driving systems (levels 45), as well as in the certification of autonomous vehicles, with common, mandatory testing procedures in real-world conditions?

How will the Commission ensure that the operation of autonomous vehicles without a driver in control of operational functions will have a clear, specifically regulated framework of liability for the protection of citizens?

The development of unmanned vehicles can significantly contribute to improving road safety. However, since these vehicles will coexist on the same roads as conventional vehicles, as well as with pedestrians and cyclists, it is essential to establish appropriate safety measures and harmonise road traffic rules at EU level. In particular Regulation (EU) 2019/2144 and Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/1426, Regulation (EU) 2018/858 on the approval of vehicles and Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on artificial intelligence. In its resolution on autonomous driving in European transport and in its resolution on the EU road safety policy framework 2021-2030, the European Parliament called on the Commission to propose a new harmonised regulatory framework for automated cars, in order to ensure, through comprehensive testing, that they operate in a safe manner for their drivers and other road users, in particular as regards their interaction with conventional vehicles and vulnerable road users.

(24 April 2026) The Commission continues updating the EU regulatory framework for autonomous vehicles, guided by the Automotive Action Plan (1). A key aspect is the harmonisation of technical rules for automated driving systems under the United Nations framework for vehicle regulations, ensuring strict and uniform safety standards for these vehicles. A new UN Regulation for automated driving systems is expected to be adopted in June 2026 and to be integrated in the EU type-approval framework subsequently. It will be accompanied by interpretations and guidance for consistent global implementation, including real-world testing procedures and a broadened scope of mandatory monitoring and reporting of in-service safety performance, as introduced by Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/1426 (2), enhancing market surveillance. Rules on cybersecurity (3) and over-the-air updates (4) complement the new technical requirements for automated driving systems.

E-10-2026-000836.t: Flaws in the Commission’s proposal for the Multiannual Financial Framework 2028-2034 flagged by the European Court of Auditors in its Opinions 09 and 10/2026
qt: to the Commission Mihai Tudose (S&D) Subject:
Flaws in the Commission’s proposal for the Multiannual Financial Framework 2028-2034 flagged by the European Court of Auditors in its Opinions 09 and

The European Court of Auditors (ECA) has published opinions on the legislative proposals brought forward by the Commission on two key strands of the EU budget in the period 20282034: the future European Fund and the new system for measuring performance and tracking EU spending. According to the audit, the pressure on Member States to attain European objectives through national plans will increase, as the Commission wants to integrate different funds and policies. Yet, as the ECA report notes, the burden on beneficiaries will remain the same and the promised administrative simplification will only be felt in Brussels. Result indicators are lacking for a quarter of the intervention fields audited. The ECA also notes that there are accountability risks. Furthermore, the ECA stresses that there is no clear link between funding and results, which raises serious question marks over the functionality, management and control of the future multiannual financial framework. Is the Commission planning to urgently assess and remedy the vulnerabilities flagged by the auditors?

According to the audit, the pressure on Member States to attain European objectives through national plans will increase, as the Commission wants to integrate different funds and policies. Yet, as the ECA report notes, the burden on beneficiaries will remain the same and the promised administrative simplification will only be felt in Brussels. Result indicators are lacking for a quarter of the intervention fields audited. The ECA also notes that there are accountability risks. Furthermore, the ECA stresses that there is no clear link between funding and results, which raises serious question marks over the functionality, management and control of the future multiannual financial framework. Is the Commission planning to urgently assess and remedy the vulnerabilities flagged by the auditors? (15 April 2026) By bringing together EU funds under one coherent strategy, with cohesion and agricultural policies at its core, the Commission’s proposal on the National Regional and Partnership Plans (1) aims to address current and future challenges in a holistic, coordinated and consistent manner, which will bring simplification for both authorities and beneficiaries. A common set of rules will apply for shared management funds, including for programming, governance, financial implementation, assurance and transparency. Payments will be conditional upon the fulfilment of investment and reform milestones and targets linked to agreed priorities to deliver funding and results faster and more efficiently, with a focus on the results of EU spending. Furthermore, in what relates to simplification for Member States, the proposal relies on the single audit principle, striking a balance between an appropriate level of controls and simplification for stakeholders. Strong safeguards have been included to ensure the robustness of national control systems and effective action in case of issues, including where the applicable law is not respected. The Commission retains the possibility to block payments and protect the EU’s financial interests. Moreover, the Performance Regulation (2) proposal replaces the current complex and fragmented set of rules with a horizontal approach for key principles — climate and environment, ‘do no significant harm’, social policies and gender equality — applicable to all EU funding. A common framework links how funds are spent to the results delivered, using a standard set of performance indicators for each intervention field (3). When preparing the proposal for the 2028-2034 Multiannual Financial Framework (4), the Commission gave due consideration to recommendations by other EU institutions, including the European Court of Auditors.

E-10-2026-000835.t: Israel’s ongoing occupation of Gaza and the misleadingly named ‘Peace Council’
qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Lefteris Nikolaou-Alavanos (NI) Subject:

The long-suffering people of Palestine face all kinds of deprivation and bloody raids by the Israeli military. The misleadingly named ‘Peace Council’ lays the foundations for ‘rebuilding’ Gaza on the basis of the toxic plan America has announced for Gaza and the West Bank. The ‘International Stabilisation Force’ is to be set up in Gaza , turning it into an American-Israeli protectorate. By participating as an ‘observer’, Nea Dimokratia bears a great deal of responsibility for this. The EU and Member States bear the same responsibility as they are following the same policy. The Palestinian people are essentially living through the ceasefire with a gun pointed at their heads because of the criminal policy pursued by Israel and its allies. In view of the above, can the Vice-President/High Representative answer the following: 1.

What is its position regarding the fact that with the US and Israel’s plans to expand the war into the Middle East and Israel's continued pursuit of its criminal policy, despite the ceasefire, the Palestinians face bloody raids, illegal settlements and inhumane deprivations, without access to basic necessities?

What is its position regarding the so-called ‘International Stabilisation Force’ and the misleadingly named ‘Peace Council’, which imposes US and Israeli plans to ‘rebuild’ Gaza by displacing Palestinians and confiscating their property, promoting the interests of business groups in the countries responsible for the genocide, the displacement of the Palestinian people and support for these criminal plans?

What is its position regarding the call for the establishment of an independent Palestinian state based on the 1967 borders, with East Jerusalem as its capital, territorial unity without settlements and foreign troops, and with the right of refugees to return from all the structures and the grip of power of the other states?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (13.4.2026) The EU has been deeply concerned about the catastrophic humanitarian situation in Gaza. The EU has called on the Israeli authorities, including on humanitarian access, dual-use policy and international non-governmental registration, to address the enormous needs of the population. The EU is totally opposed to forced displacement of the Palestinian population or to geographical or demographic changes in Gaza. The EU strongly condemns the ongoing extremist settler violence in the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, and recalls that Israel has the duty to protect civilians and hold perpetrators accountable. The EU is not a member of the Board of Peace and its participation as an observer at the inaugural meeting of the Board of Peace in Washington, District of Columbia, focused on Gaza’s reconstruction, is to be seen as part of the EU’s commitment to the implementation of the ceasefire in Gaza and international efforts for recovery and reconstruction. The EU welcomed the adoption of UN Security Council (UNSC) Resolution 2803 and stands ready to work together with the US on the implementation of the comprehensive Peace Plan for Gaza. The EU has an important role to play in this context, being the biggest provider of external assistance to the Palestinians, including EUR 124 million in humanitarian aid confirmed for 20261. The EU is committed to lasting and sustainable peace in accordance with the relevant UNSC resolutions, on the basis of the two-state solution, with the State of Israel and an independent, democratic, contiguous, sovereign and viable State of Palestine living side-by-side in peace, security and mutual recognition, and Jerusalem serving as the future capital of both states. The EU supports the diplomatic efforts anchored in international law.

E-10-2026-000834.t: Removal of evidence and compliance with European Union Agency for Railways (ERA) preservation guidelines in the investigation of the Adamuz accident
qt: to the Commission Borja Giménez Larraz (PPE) Subject:

On 18 January 2026, a railway accident in Adamuz killed 46 people and left many injured. The technical investigation is being carried out by Spain’s Commission of Inquiry into Railway Accidents (CIAF) as an independent body (Directive (EU) 2016/798). According to published information and court testimonies, Adif – Spain’s state-owned railway infrastructure manager – removed evidence from the track before the authorities concluded their inspection. Directive (EU) 2016/798 requires the granting of immediate access to evidence in full and at the site of the incident, as well as the cooperation of the authorities and their independence. In addition, ERA1 requires there to be evidence preservation mechanisms, controlled access to the site, immediate listing of evidence and controlled removal of wreckage only under the supervision of the investigator. In light of the above: 1.

Does the Commission consider the removal of items before the CIAF compiled a listing to be in compliance with Article 21(2) of Directive (EU) 2016/798, which requires cooperation and immediate access to the accident site and evidence?
Is the principle of independence of the investigating body compromised if third parties had physical contact with the evidence beforehand?
If failures are identified, what steps will the Commission take to ensure the adequacy of the Spanish procedures, including a possible infringement procedure?

(3 June 2026) National legislation must guarantee that rail accident investigations are carried out independently, efficiently and within the shortest time. Pursuant to Article 22(1) of Directive (EU) 2016/798 (1), national investigating bodies established by the Member States must be independent in their organisation, legal structure and decision-making from any party whose interests could conflict with tasks entrusted to such bodies. Article 21 of Directive (EU) 2016/798 defines the principles and requirements to be established in national law as regards the legal status of investigations, cooperation between investigating authorities, other authorities and courts, and rights of investigators including their right to access any relevant information. The Commission has not received evidence from the Spanish investigating body suggesting that the investigation cannot be carried out independently, nor that the national legislation fails to guarantee the rights of investigators, notably the right to access any suitable evidence. Responsibility for guaranteeing that the procedures under national law pertaining to the investigation of rail accidents are adequate lies primarily with national authorities and courts. The Commission, as guardian of the Treaty, may initiate an infringement procedure, as appropriate, in case of solid evidence of breach of Union law.

E-10-2026-000833.t: Guarantees for less developed regions in the proposed European Fund for 2028-2034
qt: to the Commission Giuseppe Antoci (The Left) Subject:
Guarantees for less developed regions in the proposed European Fund for 20282034

The Commission’s proposal for a Regulation establishing the European Fund for 2028-2034 includes provisions for national and regional partnership plans (NRPs) and milestone- and target-related payments. In opinion 09/20261, the European Court of Auditors highlighted that pooling resources into a single envelope and providing for flexibility amounts that are not firmly ring-fenced ex ante will reduce the visibility and transparency of allocations and, when the ex-ante regional breakdown is not known, make it more challenging to verify compliance with minimum earmarking requirements for less developed regions. The ECA also flagged issues related to ex-ante cost estimates, the n+1 decommitment rule and the proposal that payments be made based on Member State declarations without any prior checks being required. In the light of the above: 1.
What NUTS2-related obligations will the Commission introduce to these NRP plans with a view to monitoring and ensuring compliance with the minimum earmarking requirements for less developed regions?
What are the corrective tools that can ensure full compliance with the principles of partnership and multilevel governance?

Will the Commission propose n+1-related safeguards and mandatory prior checks of milestones/targets before payments are made so as to avoid the loss of resources and protect long-term investments in the most fragile regions?
https://www.eca.europa.eu/ECAPublications/OP-2026-09/OP-2026-09_EN.pdf.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (19.5.2026) 1. As part of the requirements of the National and Regional Partnership Plans1, Member States must provide a comprehensive overview of how their plans support the different categories of regions. E-10-2026-000832.t: Serious shortcomings in access to social, health and educational services for persons with disabilities and autism spectrum disorder in Sicily
qt: to the Commission Giuseppe Antoci (The Left) Subject:

In Sicily, persons with disabilities and autism spectrum disorder still face systemic shortcomings in access to essential services: splintered division of competences among bodies, delays in diagnosis and care, shortages of specialised staff, therapy discontinuity, insufficient availability of independence and communication support assistants, along with disruptions to transport and school support services. Those shortcomings undermine individuals’ continuity of care, ability to live independently and right to educational and social inclusion. This state of affairs appears to be at odds with Article 26 of the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights and with obligations arising from the UN’s CRPD1, to which the EU is a party. It also runs counter to the objectives of the EU strategy for the rights of persons with disabilities 2021-2030 and the coordination actions planned through the disability platform and its monitoring framework. The European Parliament has pointed out the need to step up protections for individuals with autism in the EU. In the light of the above: 1.

Is the Commission aware of the problems described in the Region of Sicily and will it request information from the competent authorities2 on regional misalignments in the implementation of the rights of persons with disabilities and autism?
What steps will it take to activate the tools available at EU level, in particular the 20 November 2024 guidance3 on independent living in the context of EU funding?

Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. Within the framework of the disability platform strategy 2021-2030 and its monitoring framework. Push for investment and the reorganisation of regional services in a manner consistent with the UNCRPD and the Charter; ensure that EU resources are not financing non-inclusive action; support, including through dialogue with managing authorities and targeted checks, measures leading to continuity of care, sufficient availability of qualified staff and effective educational support (including independence and communication support assistants and transport).

(23 April 2026) The Commission supports the rights of persons with disabilities through the implementation of the EU Strategy for the rights of persons with disabilities 2021-2030 (1) (the strategy), which takes into account multiple forms of disabilities, including socalled invisible disabilities, such as intellectual disabilities or autism. The upcoming Communication on enhancing the strategy up to 2030, announced in the Commission Work Programme 2026 (2), will aim to reinforce action to guide the EU and Member States in their joint engagement to promote disability rights, including to support implementation of the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities to which the EU and all Member States are parties (3). The strategy promotes inclusive education and accessible environments and calls on Member States to implement good practices of deinstitutionalisation, transitioning from institutional care to community support services, in line with the approaches reflected in the Commission Guidance on independent living in the context of EU funding (4). The Guidance serves as a benchmark for transitioning from institutional care to community-based inclusion, providing guidance for doing so when using EU funds. The organisation of social protection, healthcare and education systems, including assessment of disability status and allocation of related benefits, are matters under the national competence of Member States.

Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. Within the framework of the disability platform strategy 2021-2030 and its monitoring framework. Push for investment and the reorganisation of regional services in a manner consistent with the UNCRPD and the Charter; ensure that EU resources are not financing non-inclusive action; support, including through dialogue with managing authorities and targeted checks, measures leading to continuity of care, sufficient availability of qualified staff and effective educational support (including independence and communication support assistants and transport).

E-10-2026-000830.t: Fertility of women vaccinated against the corona virus
qt: to the Commission Gerald Hauser (PfE) Subject:

The Commission states in its answer to my written question E-002731/20251 of 3 September 2025 that: ‘The long-term safety data of COVID-19 vaccines to date remain very reassuring, including regarding fertility.’ However, a study on which our questions are based indicates a discrepancy between the fertility of women who have been vaccinated against COVID-19 and those who have not. The results of the study are as follows: During the study period, there were approximately 1 300 000 women aged 18-39 years in the Czech Republic, and the proportion of COVID-19vaccinated women increased from January 2021 until reaching a steady level of around 70% by the end of 2021. At least from June 2021, successful conceptions per 1000 women were considerably lower for women who were vaccinated than for those who were not. Furthermore, successful conception rates for the vaccinated group were much lower than expected based on their proportion of the total population. 1.
Does the Commission intend to undertake an independent, EU-wide epidemiological investigation into the possible correlation between COVID-19 vaccination status and birth rates?
Which other countries have published similar studies?
Why is the public not being kept proactively informed about this issue?
https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/E-10-2025-002731-ASW_EN.html
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (28.4.2026) The Commission, together with the European Medicines Agency (EMA) and Member States, monitors the safety of COVID-19 vaccines, including data from the scientific literature, through a robust pharmacovigilance system1. Based on the continuous monitoring and assessment of safety data from vaccination campaigns worldwide, there is no scientific evidence of any association between COVID-19 vaccines and impaired fertility in men or women. Detailed information on the continuous safety monitoring of COVID-19 vaccines can be found on the EMA website, including the Periodic Safety Update Reports2 for each vaccine and the report on pharmacovigilance activities carried out by Member States and the EMA between 2019 and 20223. While there have been some reports about the short-term variation of fertility trends during the pandemic, this was attributed to behavioural changes, as in most of the studied countries the fertility rates returned to pre-pandemic levels and no evidence of effect of COVID-19 vaccinations on fertility trends was found4,5,6. Based on the existing scientific evidence, the Commission does not consider a specific study on this matter to be necessary. It should be noted that EU citizens and healthcare professionals are informed in a timely manner about the latest scientific decisions taken by the EMA. Following each meeting of the EMA’s safety committee (Pharmacovigilance Risk Assessment Committee - PRAC7), decisions are communicated through the PRAC highlights8. In addition, exceptional measures for COVID-19 medicines were implemented by the EMA to maximise the transparency of its regulatory activities related to COVID-19 medicinal products9.

E-10-2026-000827.t: Administrative barriers stopping public schools in Rivas-Vaciamadrid from being air-conditioned
qt: to the Commission Vicent Marzà Ibáñez (Verts/ALE) Subject:

The local council in Rivas-Vaciamadrid got the ball rolling on a plan to air-condition schools in light of temperatures exceeding 30 °C during term time. However, the regional administration responsible for educational infrastructure has opposed this, creating an administrative barrier that prevents adaptation measures from being taken. This state of affairs is set against a backdrop of more and more heatwaves and the need to adapt the public building stock. Under Directive (EU) 2024/1275, climate adaptation and indoor environmental quality must be considered, while Regulation (EU) 2021/1119, Article 168 TFEU and Articles 24 and 35 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights lay down the obligation to ensure a high level of health and well-being protection, particularly for children. 1.

Does the Commission consider the bureaucratic hurdles blocking local investment in heating and air-conditioning schools to be compatible with the Renovation Wave’s aim of increasing the rate and depth of renovations?

Given the systematic delays in the Community of Madrid, would it assess there to be potential non-compliance with the trajectory of intermediate milestones in the national renovation plans provided for in Directive (EU) 2024/1275?

Does it intend to issue specific guidance for the education sector on appropriate thermal conditions, on heat risk assessments and on prioritising the sustainable refurbishment of schools in EU funding instruments?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (11.5.2026) In line with the Renovation Wave, Directive (EU) 2024/12751 prioritises strategies that enhance buildings’ thermal performance during the summer period, with measures that avoid overheating, such as shading and passive cooling techniques that improve indoor environmental quality. The implementation of the Directive is a matter for the Member State authorities. Assessing whether a city may be deviating from the trajectory outlined in the National Building Renovation Plan (NBRP) is outside the Commission’s responsibility. In its draft NBRP2, Spain highlights that planning of interventions in the building stock should anticipate future cooling needs, mitigate the urban heat island effect and promote passive comfort solutions, through strategies such as shading or the use of materials with high thermal inertia. The Commission published guidance in 20253 on the implementation of Directive (EU) 2024/1275, including on indoor environmental quality, with indicators for resilience against heat waves.

E-10-2026-000826.t: Unfair competition resulting from unequal access to water in Israel and the occupied territories
qt: to the Commission Vicent Marzà Ibáñez (Verts/ALE) Subject:

EU trade policy is governed by the objective of stimulating competition and good business practices. In this regard, reports from the UN, the European Union and European embassies to Israel and the State of Palestine report of the asymmetric control and distribution of Palestinian water and Syrian Golan Heights water by Israel with regard to surface water, groundwater, rainwater, wastewater and treated wastewater. There is a system of exploitation that favours Israeli agriculture over agriculture in the occupied territories in terms of quantity and price, meaning that the former is propped up at the expense of the latter. The EU has instruments to prevent this unfair competition from Israeli agriculture and the illegal settlements, which also harms the competitiveness of European agriculture. In the light of this state of affairs: Will the Commission temporarily suspend imports of agricultural and livestock products from Israel and the settlements until there is an equitable distribution of water between Palestinians and Israelis, at the same price for both, and European agriculture and livestock farming is not harmed by Israel’s unfair use of water?

(29 April 2026) EU trade policy towards Israel and Palestine (1) may help address some of the issues raised in the Honourable Member’s question as far as goods exported to the EU are concerned. Trade preferences granted to Israel under the EU-Israel Association Agreement (2) do not apply to goods originating in Israeli settlements in the Occupied Palestinian Territories (OPT) or the Golan Heights. Conversely, the EU grants trade preferences to goods which are originating in Palestine in accordance with the EU-Palestine Interim Association Agreement (3). The case law of the Court of Justice of the European Union has confirmed that goods originating in Israeli settlements in the OPT do not qualify for preferential treatment under the EU-Palestine Interim Association Agreement. As regards a temporary suspension of imports, Article 23 of the EU-Israel Association Agreement allows either party to adopt safeguard measures if a product is imported in such increased quantities and under such conditions as to cause serious disturbance to a sector of the economy, or serious difficulties in a region or market of the importing side. From the information provided it is however not possible to ascertain whether imports from Israel are causing such serious sectoral disturbances or regional difficulties. On 17 September 2025, following the military intervention of Israel in the Gaza Strip, the Commission adopted a proposal for a Council Decision regarding the suspension of certain trade-related provisions of the Association Agreement (4).

E-10-2026-000823.t: Revision of PCB limits for regenerated mineral oils under Regulation (EU) 2019/1021
qt: to the Commission Annalisa Corrado (S&D), César Luena (S&D), Irene Tinagli (S&D), Nicolás González Casares (S&D), Giorgio Gori (S&D), Benedetta Scuderi (Verts/ALE), Yannis Maniatis (S&D), Matteo Ricci (S&D), Alessandra Moretti (S&D), Sakis Arnaoutoglou (S&D) Subject:
Revision of PCB limits for regenerated mineral oils under Regulation (EU)

Regulation (EU) 2019/1021 on persistent organic pollutants currently sets a polychlorinated biphenyls (PCB) limit of 50 parts per million (ppm) for used oil to be regenerated (and it is 25 ppm in some Member States). The Commission is preparing an implementing act revising Annex I to the regulation, with early drafts indicating a possible reduction of this limit to 2.5 ppm (with initial proposals having been even lower) for products resulting from the regeneration of used oil, such as base oil, bitumen and gasoil. Current standard analytical methods used across the EU for monitoring PCB content in used and regenerated oils (EN 12766 1–2) do not allow for reliable detection below 4 ppm. Setting a limit below this threshold would therefore create a gap between the legal requirements and available detection technologies. Should regeneration become technically or economically unviable for a significant share of collected waste oil, it may be diverted to combustion, which remains subject to a higher PCB limit (50 ppm). This would risk undermining the waste hierarchy principle established in Article 4 of Directive 2008/98/EC, which prioritises regeneration over energy recovery, without any clear environmental benefit. In this context: 1.

Has the Commission assessed the technical feasibility and enforceability of limits below 4 ppm and considered a gradual decrease, aligned with the declining presence of unintentional trace contaminant PCBs?
Has it assessed the impact on industrial competitiveness and circular value chains?
How will the Commission ensure compliance with the waste hierarchy principle?
at: EN on behalf of the Commission (8.5.2026) The aim of the Persistent Organic Pollutants (POPs) Regulation1 is to safeguard human health and the environment from the threats posed by POPs. This is achieved by prohibiting, swiftly phasing out, or restricting the manufacturing, placing on the market, and use of specific POPs. In this context, and to provide legal clarity and facilitate enforcement, the Commission is currently setting an unintentional trace contaminant (UTC) limit value for polychlorinated biphenyls (PCB). Pursuant to the objectives of the POPs Regulation, the Commission seeks to establish this limit value as low as is practically feasible. The Commission has analysed the impacts of the measure. When setting up a proposed UTC limit value for PCB, the Commission will take into account waste hierarchy principles, the expected decrease over time of PCB-content in input material, the technical feasibility of industrial processes to achieve such limit, the technical limitations of detection methods and the technical progress in analytical techniques. The Commission is also evaluating claims from Member States and stakeholders concerning analytical capabilities and is dedicated to ensuring that the UTC limit value matches advances in detection technologies and can be adequately enforced.
1 Regulation (EU) 2019/1021 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 20 June 2019 on persistent
organic pollutants (recast), OJ L 169, 25.6.2019, pp. 45–77.

E-10-2026-000822.t: Road safety and the fleet of vehicles and two-wheelers in Greece
qt: to the Commission Nikolaos Anadiotis (NI) Subject:

The age of fleets of vehicles and two-wheelers raises serious concerns relating to road safety, environmental impact and social cohesion, and highlights strong disparities between Member States. According to the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association1, Greece has the oldest fleet of vehicles and two-wheelers in the EU. The average age of passenger vehicles is 17.8 years, while the ages recorded by Eurostat for commercial vehicles, trucks and buses are also high2. As regards users of two-wheelers in particular, the European Road Safety Agency warns that they are among the most vulnerable groups of road users, representing a disproportionately high proportion of road fatalities in the EU3, which is particularly significant for Greece and other Member States where two-wheelers remain a key means of transport for everyday journeys. In light of the above, can the Commission say: 1.
How does it assess Greece, in terms of vehicles and two-wheelers, in the context of the EU’s road safety and sustainable mobility objectives?
Does it intend to look into targeted European financial or regulatory measures for the renewal of the fleet of vehicles and two-wheelers in Greece?
What measures are being taken to ensure that the green transition in the area of transport does not exacerbate inequalities in Member States that are lagging behind structurally, such as Greece?

(31 July 2026) Concerning two-wheelers, the Commission has published the overview of Member States’ road safety statistics in country specific profiles (1). The report assessing Greece’s road safety progress (2) was published on 13 February 2026. More detailed information is available in a thematic report (3), which also covers Greece until 2024. In 2025 Greece has achieved a significant 22% reduction in fatalities, mainly due to systematic enforcement of helmet wearing & drink-and-drive, and the adoption of the new Road Traffic Code. Under the Social Climate Fund (4), the Commission is mobilising EUR 86.7 billion between 2026 and 2032, including EUR 4.8 billion for Greece, to ensure a just transition and support vulnerable households and small businesses who are most affected by rising energy and transport costs as Europe moves towards climate neutrality, where zero- and low emission vehicles can be eligible for funding. It is for Greece to identify vulnerable groups needing support most and propose actions. E-10-2026-000820.t: Ability of passengers and workers to request independent expert's opinion on state of public transport
qt: to the Commission Afroditi Latinopoulou (PfE) Subject:

The derailments and train collisions at Tempi in the Greek regional unit of Larissa and in Adamuz in the Spanish province of Córdoba, demonstrate that the existing framework of preventive safety measures is not sufficient to avoid such tragedies, even though there had been warning signs, which unfortunately were overlooked. Similar red flags have been raised from time to time for other means of public transport too, for instance the repeated technical failures in the air navigation systems of the Greek Civil Aviation Authority. Given that, under Article 90 TEU, the Commission can put forward legislative initiatives on transport safety policies in the EU, as has repeatedly been the case with Regulations (EU) 2021/782, (EC) 261/2004, (EU) 1177/2010 and (EU) 181/2011, can the Commission answer the following: Is it prepared to establish provisions whereby passengers and public transport workers would be entitled, under certain conditions, to request an independent, non-state expert’s opinion for the purpose of assessing safety risks and informing European passengers whenever there are worrying signs of infrastructure failure or inadequate staff training that endanger the lives or safety of passengers and workers?
at: (English version) to the Commission Afroditi Latinopoulou (PfE) (26 February 2026) Subject: Ability of passengers and workers to request independent expert's opinion on state of public transport The derailments and train collisions at Tempi in the Greek regional unit of Larissa and in Adamuz in the Spanish province of Córdoba, demonstrate that the existing framework of preventive safety measures is not sufficient to avoid such tragedies, even though there had been warning signs, which unfortunately were overlooked. Similar red flags have been raised from time to time for other means of public transport too, for instance the repeated technical failures in the air navigation systems of the Greek Civil Aviation Authority. Given that, under Article 90 TEU, the Commission can put forward legislative initiatives on transport safety policies in the EU, as has repeatedly been the case with Regulations (EU) 2021/782, (EC) 261/2004, (EU) 1177/2010 and (EU) 181/2011, can the Commission answer the following: Is it prepared to establish provisions whereby passengers and public transport workers would be entitled, under certain conditions, to request an independent, non-state expert’s opinion for the purpose of assessing safety risks and informing European passengers whenever there are worrying signs of infrastructure failure or inadequate staff training that endanger the lives or safety of passengers and workers? (6 May 2026) The Commission agrees that social partners like passengers or staff of transport companies may deliver valuable insights concerning possible safety risks for the operation of the transport system. In the Commission’s view however, the existing legal framework already provides for possibilities to adequately involve such actors. In the area of railways, Regulation (EU) 2018/762 (1) requires that the safety management system (SMS) of railway undertakings and infrastructure managers covers mechanisms for consultation of staff. Additionally, in line with Article 33 and Article 35(5) of Regulation (EU) 2016/796 (2), the EU Agency for Railways (ERA) has certain monitoring powers towards national safety authorities and Member States. When preparing these assessments, ERA takes into account data coming from various sources, including from social partners. Similarly, social partners may request the Commission that it triggers an assessment according to Article 35(5) of the above Regulation. In the area of civil aviation, the EU Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) Basic Regulation (3) is the legal framework for safety. More generally, all citizens are entitled to raise complaints with the Commission if they believe an EU country has infringed EASA Basic Regulation or any other EU law. The Commission is of the view that the existing legislation allows for citizens’ complaints to be taken into account when it comes to the assessment of safety concerns and thus it has no intention to propose any further legislation on the issue at this stage.

E-10-2026-000819.t: Sustaining Horizon Europe Support for ME/CFS Research
qt: to the Commission Pascal Arimont (PPE) Subject:

The Commission is to be commended for funding the first research project on ME/CFS through the Horizon Europe call ‘Tackling high burden for patients and under-researched medical conditions’ (HORIZON-HLTH-2025-01-DISEASE-07). Funding for research projects like these is of great importance to the more than 2 million patients with myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS) and related conditions such as long covid. There is an urgent need to continue this line of research and make scientific breakthroughs possible for those stricken with these debilitating illnesses, suffering from such a severe symptom burden accompanied by a heavy social stigma. 1.

Will the Commission renew suitable calls, such as the previous calls on high-burden, under-researched conditions, that allow ME/CFS researchers to apply for funds from Horizon Europe to ensure that ME/CFS research will continue to be funded?

The call HORIZON-HLTH-2025-01-DISEASE-07 had a success rate of only 6 %, and even proposals scoring 14.5 out of 15 points, well above the funding threshold of 12, were not funded. Given that this indicates a shortage of resources rather than a lack of quality, what steps will the Commission take to provide sufficient funds for high-quality ME/CFS research proposals?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (29.5.2026) The Commission recognises the importance of tackling high-burden under-researched medical conditions like Myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS) and depending on the outcome of the negotiations on the next Multi Annual Financial Framework is considering the possibility of including in future work programmes of Horizon Europe (2028-2034) topics like the call topic: ‘Tackling high burden for patients and underresearched medical conditions’1 from the Horizon Europe Work Programme 2025. Regarding the current Health Cluster part of the Horizon Europe Work Programme 20262027, where topics are generally broad, there is an open call topic that is likely of interest for the ME/CFS research community: ‘Advancing research on the prevention, diagnosis, and management of post-infection long-term conditions’2. The Commission is committed to fund high-quality proposals in all medical fields within the limitation of budget allocations and based on strategic choices made together with Member States and associated countries. Noteworthy, the observed increase in oversubscription across all call topics can in part be attributed to the rise in the use of artificial intelligence in proposal writing.

E-10-2026-000818.t: The Sidex Galați plant – an EU strategic industrial objective
qt: to the Commission Diana Iovanovici Şoşoacă (NI) Subject:

The largest steel plant in Romania, formerly Sidex Galați, was purchased by ArcelorMittal in 2001 and taken over by the Liberty House Group (GFG Alliance) in 2019, and is the most important steel producing site in Romania. The plant is currently in an arrangement with creditors and a restructuring plan has been implemented. It is a key industrial and geostrategic pillar for Romania and South-East Europe, with even greater strategic relevance in the current geopolitical climate marked by the war in Ukraine and the need to strengthen Europe’s steel supply chains. The plant has a vital role to play for the European Union’s defence industry, infrastructure and strategic autonomy. Its location in proximity to Ukraine lends it additional importance from the perspective of the reconstruction of the region and the reconfiguration of industrial chains. Given the challenges faced by the steel industry and the dependence on external markets, rescuing and developing this industrial site constitutes a strategic priority for the European Union. 1.
Have the Romanian authorities contacted the Commission to request support for the development of this plant, given its strategic and geopolitical importance?
What tools and possibilities does the Commission have at its disposal to support the development of the plant and prevent the loss of specialists and skilled workers?
Is it possible to draw up, as a matter of urgency, an EU-level plan for the development and support of this strategic industrial objective?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.4.2026) The European Steel and Metals Action Plan1, adopted on 19 March 2025, outlines a roadmap to help secure the industry’s competitiveness and support its decarbonisation. To this end, policy instruments and initiatives available or forthcoming include: Trade defence instruments on unfair pricing, subsidies for the steel sector, and tariffrate quotas on EU steel imports. The Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism keeping carbon costs of imported steel comparable to those of EU producers; Funding for low-carbon steel technologies under the European Green Deal; The Industrial Accelerator Act2 to help boost manufacturing, grow businesses, and create jobs; Amendments to the European Social Fund Plus and the European Globalisation Adjustment Fund, as well as the Pact for Skills3 support workers, companies affected by structural change, and large-scale partnerships of energy-intensive industries; The Emissions Trading System State aid Guidelines4, the Clean Industrial Deal State aid Framework5, and the Guidelines on State aid for climate, environmental protection and energy6 support decarbonisation plant development. The General Block Exemption Regulation7 helps retain skilled staff during plant transformation. Besides, Romania listed the Liberty Galati plant under the Romanian Just Transition Programme. Its funding contributes to the steel industry’s transition towards clean and efficient technologies, including training and re-skilling of staff. These measures show the Commission's commitment to support the steel industry. Without prejudice to other EU law obligations, they can be tailored to specific strategic industrial needs. The Commission is also ready to discuss any planned measures by Romania under EU competition rules.

E-10-2026-000817.t: Modernisation of the EU-Andean Trade Agreement
qt: to the Commission Sebastian Kruis (PfE) Subject:

Since the EU-Andean Trade Agreement (EU-Colombia, Ecuador, Peru Trade Agreement) entered into force in 2013, the geopolitical and economic environment has changed fundamentally. The EU now faces increasing supply chain vulnerabilities, intensified competition over critical raw materials and a rapid digital transformation. In this context, relations with the Andean partners need to evolve from a traditional trade relationship into a mutually beneficial strategic partnership. A modernised and forward-looking framework under the EU-Andean Trade Agreement could reinforce competitiveness, resilience and longterm economic cooperation on a strategic basis. In the light of this: 1.
Does the Commission intend to launch a formal evaluation of the EU-Andean Trade Agreement with a view to transforming it into a modern strategic partnership framework?

Is the Commission considering the inclusion of new chapters covering critical raw materials, digital trade, regulatory cooperation and dedicated small and medium enterprises facilitation mechanisms to strengthen the strategic dimension of the Agreement?

Will the Commission request that the Council swiftly grant a negotiating mandate to modernise the EU-Andean Trade Agreement and align it with the EU’s current strategic, industrial and economic priorities?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.4.2026) The Trade Agreement between the EU and Colombia, Ecuador and Peru1 entered into force on 1 November 2024. The Commission agrees with the Honourable Member that it would now be appropriate to initiate a reflection on how the Agreement fits with the current geopolitical and economic environment. Regarding the transformation into a modern strategic partnership, the Commission committed in the 2022 Joint Communication ‘A New Agenda for EU-Latin America and Caribbean Relations’2 to discuss the possible upgrade of the Agreement's provisions on sustainable development. To this end, the EU and the Andean countries have established a Working Group under the relevant Committee where discussions are still ongoing. A broader modernisation of the agreement could be considered. The Commission is exploring with various partners to extend the trade and economic cooperation to new fields. Any formal request for a negotiating mandate to the Council would require further scoping to ensure alignment with the EU’s strategic priorities. The conclusions of any deliberations in this regard will be fully reported to the European Parliament.

ecuador.html. 2 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52023JC0017.

E-10-2026-000816.t: Financing Framework Programme 10 for Research and Innovation
qt: to the Commission Regina Doherty (PPE) Subject:

The Commission has presented the next iteration of Horizon Europe, called Framework Programme 10 for Research and Innovation (FP10), to Parliament and the Council as part of the legislative process1. It said that the European Competitiveness Fund (ECF) would be ‘tightly linked to FP10’, for which EUR 175 billion was earmarked. The ECF has four policy ‘windows’, with funding for FP10 coming from pillars three and four. However, Article 182 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU) may prohibit the ECF from being used to fund FP10. This issue was aired during the summer of 2025 and means that the Commission cannot now finance FP10 through the ECF. If so, this places the Commission in a serious predicament. University associations apparently expected a legal opinion and/or comment to be given during the Danish Presidency, but as yet the Commission has not issued a statement. 1.
What is the legal opinion from the Commission on whether Article 182 of TFEU prohibits the ECF from funding FP10?
If it is prohibited, how will the Commission finance FP10?

Mario Draghi had suggested that the ECF should have four policy ‘windows’. What happened to this plan? In particular, what happened to the funding that had been allocated for policies 3 and 4, which had been intended for research and innovation?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (2.6.2026) The proposal for the European Competitiveness Fund1 (ECF) and the proposed Framework Programme for research2 (FP10) will have closely coordinated programming of activities. In particular, certain actions under FP10 (those collaborative research actions under the ‘Competitiveness’ part of the FP10 Pillar II falling in a policy area also covered by an ECF policy window) will be programmed in specific dedicated parts of single work programmes. Moreover, the specific programme on defence research is integrated with the policy window covering defence as part of the ECF proposal (thus also mirroring the current setup of the European Defence Fund3 in that window). However, there is no legal issue as regards funding of the programmes as both ECF and FP10 have separate budgetary envelopes; ECF actions will be financed from ECF budget and FP10 actions will be financed from FP10 budget. Where an action contributes to objectives of both the ECF and FP10, it could be financed from both envelopes taking the form of, for example, a synergy call. The architecture proposed by the Commission for the ECF indeed foresees four policy windows. To ensure a seamless investment journey – from research to manufacturing and market deployment – the Commission has proposed to mirror the same policy windows within Pillar II of Horizon Europe (2028- 2034)4, under its ‘Competitiveness’ component. Horizon Europe will fund the research and innovation activities of the policy windows, while the ECF will focus on later stages of the investment journey, including scale-up manufacturing and market deployment. A tight connection between the two programmes will be ensured through single work programmes, in line with the proposed regulations.
1 https://commission.europa.eu/publications/european-competitiveness-fund_en. 2 See the proposal for Horizon Europe 2028-2034 - https://commission.europa.eu/publications/horizon-
europe_en. 3 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:32021R0697. 4 https://commission.europa.eu/publications/horizon-europe_en.

qt: to the Commission Regina Doherty (PPE) Subject:

The new specifications for the EU disabled parking permit are to be introduced in 2027/2028. In the new design the photograph of the permit holder is no longer required. This change will severely hinder those involved in policing disabled parking spaces as the new design does not allow the inclusion of a photograph on the permit. Disabled parking spaces are a very precious resource for disabled motorists. The removal of the photograph will certainly reduce the ability of the police and parking enforcement officials to ensure that disabled spaces are properly managed. While recognising that in the future there will be more digital enforcement of the scheme, the reality is that the digitalisation of the scheme is currently many years away and for the foreseeable future the physical permit will remain in operation. It is also worth noting that many EU countries have mandatory ID schemes which may remove the requirement for a photograph on the permit in certain locations. No such scheme is in place in Ireland. This issue has the potential to become a very significant source of concern within the disabled community. Is there a possibility of retaining the photograph on the permit?
at: (English version) to the Commission Regina Doherty (PPE) (26 February 2026) Subject: Disabled parking permits The new specifications for the EU disabled parking permit are to be introduced in 2027/2028. In the new design the photograph of the permit holder is no longer required. This change will severely hinder those involved in policing disabled parking spaces as the new design does not allow the inclusion of a photograph on the permit. Disabled parking spaces are a very precious resource for disabled motorists. The removal of the photograph will certainly reduce the ability of the police and parking enforcement officials to ensure that disabled spaces are properly managed. While recognising that in the future there will be more digital enforcement of the scheme, the reality is that the digitalisation of the scheme is currently many years away and for the foreseeable future the physical permit will remain in operation. It is also worth noting that many EU countries have mandatory ID schemes which may remove the requirement for a photograph on the permit in certain locations. No such scheme is in place in Ireland. (17 April 2026) The Commission proposal for a directive establishing the European Disability Card (EDC) and the European Parking Card for persons with disabilities (EPC) (1) provided for a photo of the cardholder on the reverse side of the EPC. However, during the negotiations of the proposal, the European Parliament and Council decided not to retain the photo on the EPC for privacy reasons. The agreed Directive (EU) 2024/2841 (2) establishes common formats for the EDC and the EPC, which must be respected. The format of the EPC does not provide for additional information to be added by the Member States other than the data fields in Annex II of the directive. The EPC will be issued in a physical version, which may be complemented by a digital version, if a Member State so decides. The physical version of the EPC will be placed inside the parked vehicle. As to enforcement checks, it should be noted that the card will be equipped with an interoperable QR code (quick response code), which will allow for verification of the card across borders by the relevant authorities. The Commission is preparing a delegated act to be adopted in accordance with Articles 7(7) and 8(7) of the directive, which will, inter alia, lay down technical specifications for the QR codes and will provide for interoperability.

E-10-2026-000814.t: Funding of Important Projects of Common European Interest
qt: to the Commission Miriam Lexmann (PPE) Subject:

Important Projects of Common European Interest (IPCEIs) are ambitious, cross-border projects that support EU objectives of competitiveness, industrial policy and decarbonisation. In recent years, the use of IPCEIs has increased significantly, which can help to harness the full potential of innovative European companies and support competitiveness. However, according to several companies across the EU, despite the lengthy and complicated procedure that is required in order to be recognised as IPCEIs, companies still face insecurity as to whether they will receive funding, because national governments often hamper access to European funds and there is no guarantee of funding actually being provided. This uncertainty discourages European companies, endangers the continuation of innovative projects, as well as jobs connected to them, and hampers European competitiveness and innovative potential. In the light of the above-mentioned points: 1.

Is the Commission aware of these problems and if so, does it plan to adopt changes to the procedures for companies to be recognised as IPCEIs, so that companies can be guaranteed to receive European funding?
Does the Commission follow-up with the companies after they are recognised as IPCEIs and does it request information from national governments regarding the funding?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (20.4.2026) Important Projects of Common European Interest (IPCEIs) are a State aid tool enabling Member States to grant national funding to bring together knowledge, expertise and economic actors throughout the EU and create positive spillover effects to the whole EU. The disbursement of State aid after the Commission approval decision is the sole responsibility of the respective Member State and creates neither a right nor a legally enforceable act for a beneficiary to receive the aid approved, even if named in the approval decision. The Commission is aware that, in some approved IPCEIs, some Member States have delayed or even abandoned their initial plans to grant aid notified to and approved by the Commission, which were also identified by the European Court of Auditors1. Aiming to prevent such potential delays, the Joint European Forum for IPCEI (JEF-IPCEI), which involves all Member States, European Economic Area countries and the Commission, agreed on and published a collection of national best practices including hands-on guidance for all national authorities when to start and how to prepare for the implementation phase of an IPCEI after the adoption of the Commission decision in an efficient manner to ensure a timely disbursal of approved aid2. The Commission follows the implementation procedures of IPCEIs, for instance, by being ready to respond to requests from Member States and by participating in exchanges within the respective IPCEI governance body meetings. Member States involved in IPCEIs need to submit annual reports, which were standardised and streamlined in 2025 to improve efficiency. Based, on these reports the JEF-IPCEI is developing a dashboard to monitor the implementation of IPCEIs3. For more information on aid granted by Member States, please see the State Aid Transparency website4.
1 See European Court of Auditors’ Special Report on ‘The EU’s industrial policy on renewable hydrogen’,

recital 76, https://www.eca.europa.eu/ECAPublications/SR-2024-11/SR-2024-11_EN.pdf. 2 See i.e. Collection of national best practices https://competitionpolicy.ec.europa.eu/document/download/4bec8fa3-ff8b-4248-8522-b0534de6f46a_en?filename=JEFIPCEI_National%20Best%20Practices%20Collection%20KPs%201%20to%208.pdf on national budgeting process available at the dedicated IPCEI website https://competition-policy.ec.europa.eu/state-aid/ipcei_en. 3 IPCEI website https://competition-policy.ec.europa.eu/state-aid/ipcei_en. 4 State Aid Transparency website https://webgate.ec.europa.eu/competition/transparency/public/search/home?lang=en.

E-10-2026-000813.t: Digital Services Act and the removal of online media content
qt: to the Commission Miriam Lexmann (PPE) Subject:

According to the report by the Judiciary Committee of the United States House of Representatives, the Commission, in the days preceding the 2023 Slovak parliamentary elections, sent TikTok a spreadsheet identifying at least 63 ‘problematic’ accounts, despite some of them being explicitly noted as complying with TikTok’s Community Guidelines. In response to this request, TikTok banned 19 of these accounts while others with few or no violations were placed on watchlists. Some of the banned accounts were flagged for alleged ‘hate speech’, containing statements like ‘there are only two genders’ or ‘I think that LGBTI ideology, gender ideology, transgender ideology are a big threat to Slovakia, just like corruption’, not considering that these topics were major political issues in Slovak political discourse. Moreover, many other statements with conservative narratives were deleted or labelled as ‘disinformation’. In this context: 1.
Is the Commission aware of the findings of this report and does it intend to provide detailed explanation?
What specific criteria did the Commission apply when labelling content as ‘hate speech’ or ‘disinformation’?
How does the Commission plan to enforce Digital Services Act without pushing the platforms to remove lawful political speech during elections?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (17.4.2026) The Commission is aware of the report and rejects its unsubstantiated and unfounded allegations. The Commission is not planning to issue further explanations. The Digital Services Act (DSA)1 aims to create a safe, predictable online environment, protecting fundamental rights, including freedom of expression, enshrined in the Charter of Fundamental Rights2. The Commission acts when providers of very large online platforms (VLOP) and very large online search engines (VLOSE) fail to meet the transparency and accountability obligations. In April 2024, the Commission opened an investigation into Meta for suspected demotion of political content through their recommender systems3. The DSA does not define illegal content, hate speech or disinformation, nor does it contain criteria for determining this. What constitutes illegal content is determined by national law or other EU laws4. The Commission cannot issue orders to act against illegal content; only national judicial or administrative authorities can issue orders to providers of intermediary services, on the basis of other EU legislation or national law in compliance with EU law. Providers must inform authorities of any effect given to the order without undue delay, if such orders fulfil the requirements stated in Article 9 of the DSA. Content moderation decisions are taken by providers themselves, while the DSA obliges them to specify the reasons for restricting or removing content and provide effective redress. 30% of appealed moderation decisions5 have been reversed since the DSA’s application. In relation to elections, the Commission has issued guidelines6 for providers of VLOPs and VLOSEs on the mitigation of systemic risks for electoral processes.

E-10-2026-000812.t: In excess of EUR 1 million of public money spent on establishing whether large carnivores – bears and wolves, in particular – can co-exist alongside human activities: to what end?
qt: to the Commission Sergio Berlato (ECR) Subject:
In excess of EUR 1 million of public money spent on establishing whether large carnivores – bears and wolves, in particular – can co-exist alongside human activities: to what end?

Through the Biodiversa+ consortium, the Commission has co-financed a number of activities intended to preserve European flora and fauna. In particular, under the 2021-2022 BiodivProtect action, with a budget of around EUR 1.2 million, the TransWILD project1 was launched with the aim of researching coexistence between humans and wild animals by analysing their interactions. Five project partners reportedly carried out an email survey of the local population, leading to ‘selection bias’. From an IT perspective, the platform they used2 could not provide a representative sample because it was not restricted to the geographical area and because users could complete the survey more than once. What is more, neither previous analyses nor local associations as promoters of the survey were taken into consideration. 1.

Given the need to prevent resources being wasted on obtaining potentially distorted results, does the Commission believe that it should check whether the research method used meets criteria on good statistical research?
Does the Commission plan to spend EUR 1.2 million to retrieve data that national authorities already have3?

Given the increasing distribution and often uncontrolled proliferation of the Canis lupus species, Parliament and the EU Council have lowered its level of protection from ‘strictly protected’ to ‘protected’ species. Why does the Commission consider it appropriate to continue unnecessarily funding research seeking a form of co-existence that has already proven unattainable?

Changing browser makes it possible to vote multiple times. https://nina.qualtrics.com/jfe/form/SV_8faSdpjpMegXFci. Press conference, Italian Senate. Presentation of scientific survey on carnivorous/human predatory cohabitation. Sample, 45 000 residents, Province of Trento. https://youtu.be/lzdNYVl9uRo?si=GS57tN7TVUFm4xN.
