(23 April 2026) The Commission does not check itself the implementation of projects funded by co-funded partnerships like Biodiversa+ (1) but ensures that mechanisms are in place to meet criteria for excellent research, including for statistics. The implementation of TransWILD (2) is being supervised by the relevant Biodiversa+ Call Steering Committee, while the Research Executive Agency (3) oversees the implementation of Biodiversa+ under the supervision of the Commission. Co-funded partnerships pool resources from different partners to achieve common objectives, avoiding duplication of efforts. Biodiversa+ is co-funded by national research funding organisations (70%) and by Horizon Europe (4) framework programme (30%). The EU contribution to the budget of TransWILD amounts to a maximum of EUR 360 000. While the Commission cannot precisely comment on the details of statistical methodologies applied, using existing data is relevant for research activities. The TransWILD project was selected through a competitive and independent process and awarded under the 2021-2022 call on ‘Supporting the protection of biodiversity and ecosystems across land and sea’. While the change to the Habitats Directive (5) entails greater flexibility for the management of the wolf, the species remains protected. Member States have to adopt the necessary measures to ensure that the wolf achieves and maintains favourable conservation status. E-10-2026-000811.t: Rule of law and financial conditionality
qt: to the Commission Marcin Sypniewski (ESN) Subject:

In recent years, the Commission has taken action against Poland in relation to the rule of law situation, including initiating a procedure under Article 7 TEU, proceedings before the CJEU, the conditionality mechanism and the blocking of funds from the Recovery and Resilience Facility. In the opinion of many citizens and Member States, the application of the rule of law criterion in the allocation of EU funds is arbitrary in nature, undermines the predictability of funding and can be perceived as a tool for the imposition of political pressure. In light of the above: 1.
Does the Commission currently consider Poland to be in full compliance with the standards of the rule of law? If so, on what basis?
Did Poland fail to meet these standards between 2015 and 2023? If so, please indicate the specific legal principles – objectively recognised throughout the EU – that were violated.
What specific legislative or institutional changes introduced after 2023 demonstrate, in the Commission’s view, an improvement in the rule of law situation?
at: (English version) to the Commission Marcin Sypniewski (ESN) (26 February 2026) Subject: Rule of law and financial conditionality In recent years, the Commission has taken action against Poland in relation to the rule of law situation, including initiating a procedure under Article 7 TEU, proceedings before the CJEU, the conditionality mechanism and the blocking of funds from the Recovery and Resilience Facility. In the opinion of many citizens and Member States, the application of the rule of law criterion in the allocation of EU funds is arbitrary in nature, undermines the predictability of funding and can be perceived as a tool for the imposition of political pressure. Did Poland fail to meet these standards between 2015 and 2023? If so, please indicate the specific legal principles — objectively recognised throughout the EU — that were violated.
What specific legislative or institutional changes introduced after 2023 demonstrate, in the Commission’s view, an improvement in the rule of law situation?

(29 April 2026) In May 2024, the Commission decided to formally close the procedure of Article 7 of the Treaty on European Union (TEU) for Poland, by withdrawing its reasoned proposal that had triggered this procedure in 2017. The decision to close the article 7 procedure followed a thorough analysis which concluded that ‘a clear risk of a serious breach’ of the rule of law no longer exists (1). The concerns regarding the situation of the rule of law in Poland between 2015 and 2023 have been clearly set out in the Commission’s reasoned proposal under the article 7 TEU procedure, in several judgments of the Court of Justice, and in the Commission’s Rule of Law Reports. The Commission continues to monitor rule of law related developments in Poland, including progress made by Poland to implement the action plan on the Rule of Law, in the annual Rule of Law Reports (2).

See the Commission press release of 6 May 2024 IP/24/2461, https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/api/files/document/print/lv/ip_24_2461/IP_24_2461_EN.pdf. https://commission.europa.eu/document/download/bac7fb6c-b5f2-4593-b62a-b9a4b87269e4_en?filename=2025%20Rule%20of%20Law%20Report%20%20Country%20Chapter%20Poland.pdf.

E-10-2026-000810.t: ‘Fair by design’ projects funded under Horizon Europe and respect for fundamental freedoms
qt: to the Commission Mathilde Androuët (PfE) Subject:

Chapter 4.3.3. (pp. 17-18) of the Commission report ‘Promoting Gender Equality and Institutional Changes through EU-Funded Research1 mentions the financing of projects aiming to develop tools to detect sexist prejudice, ‘fair by design’ systems and algorythmic correction mechanisms, notably the AEQUITAS Fair-by-Design engine of the AEQUITAS project. Taking account of articles 11 (freedom of expression and information) and 16 (freedom to conduct a business) of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union: 1.

Considering Regulation (EU) 2021/695 establishing Horizon Europe, what is the specific legal basis, which permits the funding of mechanisms that incorporate genderrelated standards in algorithmic architectures that may influence automated decisionmaking systems?
What impact assessments have been carried out on the possible effects of these tools on freedom of expression, scientific plurality and technological neutrality?
Does the Commission plan to set up a monitoring mechanism to ensure that these mechanisms do not have an indirect effect of censorship or standardisation?
Directorate-General for Research and Innovation, November 2025, ISBN 978-92-68-33291-7.
at: EN On behalf of the European Commission (1.6.2026) The respect for fundamental rights is a founding principle set out in Article 2 of the Treaty on European Union. The EU safeguards fundamental rights in research inter alia through the ethics review process that operates within the framework of Horizon Europe (HE)1. All projects undergo a rigorous ethics review process, ensuring compliance with ethical standards and respect for human rights. The gender equality provisions of HE are anchored in the legal basis of the programme, which commits to ensuring the effective promotion of equal opportunities for all and the implementation of gender mainstreaming, including the integration of the gender dimension in research and innovation content2. The project AEQUITAS3 has been funded under the topic ‘Tackling gender, race and other biases in AI’ of a HE Cluster 4 call in the 2021-2022 Work Programme4. Work programmes and most notably the HE calls are shaped through inclusive consultation with Member States, stakeholders, and experts, and are aligned with the HE general and specific objectives in the basic act and the operational objectives in the Council Decision on the Specific Programme5, including gender equality promotion.

E-10-2026-000809.t: Conditionality of Horizon Europe funding, academic freedom and the principle of subsidiarity
qt: to the Commission Mathilde Androuët (PfE) Subject:

The Commission’s report ‘Promoting Gender Equality and Institutional Changes through EUFunded Research’ states that, under Horizon Europe1, gender mainstreaming is assessed by default under the ‘excellence award criterion’ and that having a gender equality plan is an eligibility criterion for certain beneficiaries (pp. 7–9). It also specifies that approximately 11 % of Horizon Europe commitments (EUR 5.056 billion) are directly linked to gender equality-advancing efforts (p. 8). In the light of Article 13 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union (freedom of the arts and sciences) and Article 5 of the Treaty on European Union (principle of subsidiarity): 1.

What legal safeguards are in place to ensure that the requirement for gender equality plans and gender mainstreaming does not undermine the academic freedom and scientific neutrality of beneficiary institutions, particularly where making a distinction between men and women is necessary?

On what legal basis does the Commission feel that making access to European funding conditional on the adoption of internal institutional governance mechanisms is in line with the principle of subsidiarity?
Directorate-General for Research and Innovation, November 2025, ISBN 978-92-68-33291-7.
at: (English version) to the Commission Mathilde Androuët (PfE) (26 February 2026) Subject: Conditionality of Horizon Europe funding, academic freedom and the principle of subsidiarity The Commission’s report ‘Promoting Gender Equality and Institutional Changes through EU-Funded Research’ states that, under Horizon Europe (1), gender mainstreaming is assessed by default under the ‘excellence award criterion’ and that having a gender equality plan is an eligibility criterion for certain beneficiaries (pp. 7-9). It also specifies that approximately 11% of Horizon Europe commitments (EUR 5.056 billion) are directly linked to gender equality-advancing efforts (p. 8). In the light of Article 13 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union (freedom of the arts and sciences) and Article 5 of the Treaty on European Union (principle of subsidiarity): 1.

What legal safeguards are in place to ensure that the requirement for gender equality plans and gender mainstreaming does not undermine the academic freedom and scientific neutrality of beneficiary institutions, particularly where making a distinction between men and women is necessary?

On what legal basis does the Commission feel that making access to European funding conditional on the adoption of internal institutional governance mechanisms is in line with the principle of subsidiarity?

(29 May 2026) The Commission promotes and protects fundamental rights by ensuring that all legislative, policy and administrative measures falling under EU competence comply with the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights. The gender equality provisions of Horizon Europe are anchored in the legal basis of the programme, which commits to ensuring the effective promotion of equal opportunities for all and the implementation of gender mainstreaming, including the integration of the gender dimension in research and innovation content (1), (2). The Gender Equality Plan eligibility criterion is set out in the General Annexes to the Work Programmes of Horizon Europe (3), established through governance and programme design mechanisms that balance EU-level coordination with national and regional autonomy, ensuring the upholding of the principle of subsidiarity. The gender equality plans are expected to be adapted to the unique institutional contexts of organisations. The mandatory provisions are designed to accommodate the internal governance structures of diverse institutions. By enabling organisations to tailor these plans, they support inclusivity without compromising organisational autonomy. Integrating the gender dimension in research refers to the systematic incorporation of sex and/or gender differentiated analysis into the design, methodology and implementation of a research project (4). This practice ensures outcomes that benefit the society as a whole, enhancing the relevance and excellence of research. This requirement aims to enrich scientific inquiry without imposing constraints on intellectual creativity and expression, thereby fully respecting and enhancing academic freedom and integrity of scientific inquiry.

Directorate-General for Research and Innovation, November 2025, ISBN 978-92-68-33291-7. Article 7(6) of Regulation (EU) 2021/695 establishing Horizon Europe, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2021/695/oj/eng . They are direct applications of the Treaty-based principle of equality mainstreaming, Article 10 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union states: In defining and implementing its policies and activities, the Union shall aim to combat discrimination based on sex, racial or ethnic origin, religion or belief, disability, age or sexual orientation, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=OJ:C:2016:202:FULL .

E-10-2026-000807.t: Vice-President / High Representative Kallas’s hawkish turn: from experts to soldiers – Brussels putting pressure on Hungary and Slovakia
qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Erik Kaliňák (NI), Judita Laššáková (NI) Subject:

According to statements made by Hungarian Foreign Minister Péter Szijjártó in the media (source), Kaja Kallas supposedly suggested during the EU Foreign Affairs Council meeting on 23 February 2026 that Hungary and Slovakia should send soldiers to Ukraine instead of experts to inspect the damaged Druzhba oil pipeline. Szijjártó described this as a new level of pressure from Brussels1. 1.

Can the Vice-President / High Representative confirm that she suggested that Hungary and Slovakia send soldiers to Ukraine instead of experts to inspect the Druzhba pipeline during the aforementioned Council meeting?

If the above statement was indeed made, then this is an extremely serious matter, as the EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs is recommending that Member States act in violation of international law (which sending troops without a UN Security Council mandate certainly would be). E-10-2026-000805.t: The US Foreign Account Tax Compliance Act (FATCA), transfers of tax data to non-EU countries, and compliance with the General Data Protection Regulation
qt: to the Commission Saskia Bricmont (Verts/ALE), Murielle Laurent (S&D) Subject:

In its 2018 resolution on the adverse effects of FACTA on EU citizens, particularly on ‘accidental Americans’1, the European Parliament expressed serious concerns regarding respect for fundamental rights, protection of personal data, lack of reciprocity in FATCA agreements, and compliance with EU law. On 24 February 2025, the Belgian Data Protection Authority2 ruled that the data transfers carried out under FATCA are contrary to the General Data Protection Regulation. The Cour des Marchés of Brussels also referred several preliminary questions to the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU). 1.

How does the Commission intend to ensure that any initiative related to exchanging tax information with non-EU countries is fully in line with the positions expressed by Parliament and does not lead to a weakening of the existing data protection safeguards?
Does the Commission consider it appropriate to work on such instruments while a national decision requesting compliance has been taken and a preliminary ruling is pending before the CJEU?

Resolution 2018/2646(RSP) https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/TA-8-2018-0316_EN.html. Decision 79/2025, 24 April 2025, Plainte transfert par le SPF Finances de données personnelles vers autorités fiscales américaines en exécution de l’accord « FATCA » https://www.autoriteprotectiondonnees.be/publications/decision-quant-au-fond-n0-79-2025.pdf.
at: (English version) to the Commission Saskia Bricmont (Verts/ALE), Murielle Laurent (S&D) (25 February 2026) Subject: The US Foreign Account Tax Compliance Act (FATCA), transfers of tax data to non-EU countries, and compliance with the General Data Protection Regulation In its 2018 resolution on the adverse effects of FACTA on EU citizens, particularly on ‘accidental Americans’ (1), the European Parliament expressed serious concerns regarding respect for fundamental rights, protection of personal data, lack of reciprocity in FATCA agreements, and compliance with EU law. On 24 February 2025, the Belgian Data Protection Authority (2) ruled that the data transfers carried out under FATCA are contrary to the General Data Protection Regulation. The Cour des Marchés of Brussels also referred several preliminary questions to the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU). 1. How does the Commission intend to ensure that any initiative related to exchanging tax information with non-EU countries is fully in line with the positions expressed by Parliament and does not lead to a weakening of the existing data protection safeguards? 2. Does the Commission consider it appropriate to work on such instruments while a national decision requesting compliance has been taken and a preliminary ruling is pending before the CJEU? (29 April 2026) Without prejudice to the role of the Commission as guardian of the Treaties, it is for the independent data protection authorities in the Member States (DPAs), under the control of national courts, and ultimately the Court of Justice of the European Union where questions of Union law are involved, to determine whether transfers of personal data from national tax authorities to the US carried out under the bilateral agreements to improve international tax compliance and to implement the US Foreign Account Tax Compliance Act (FATCA) take place in compliance with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). The Commission closely follows developments in this regard, including in collaboration with the European Data Protection Board. The preliminary ruling in Case C-804/25 on the questions referred by the Cour des Marchés of Brussels is likely to provide important clarifications in this regard. In general, an appropriate balance must be struck between the right to protection of personal data and the legitimate objectives of general interest, such as the fight against tax avoidance and evasion, including by identifying financial assets that taxpayers may hold abroad.

E-10-2026-000802.t: Critical disparity in NDICI cushion allocations with regard to the humanitarian catastrophe in Gaza
qt: to the Commission Danilo Della Valle (The Left), Kateřina Konečná (NI), Rudi Kennes (The Left), Mimmo Lucano (The Left), Valentina Palmisano (The Left), Maria Zacharia (NI), Michael von der Schulenburg (NI), Carolina Morace (The Left), Marc Botenga (The Left), Nikos Pappas (The Left), Pernando Barrena Arza (The Left), Jan-Peter Warnke (NI), Ruth Firmenich (NI) Subject:

In a recent Commission document1, the Commission outlines the mobilisation of the Neighbourhood, Development and International Cooperation Instrument (NDICI) – Global Europe cushion. While immediate concrete allocations are earmarked for India (EUR 500 million) and Syria (EUR 150 million), support for Gaza is relegated to the ‘remaining part of the cushion’ to be mobilised at a ‘later stage’. Given the unprecedented historical gravity of the situation in Gaza, where the total collapse of infrastructure and the humanitarian toll represent a defining crisis for international law and EU values, this ‘residual’ approach is deeply concerning. The Commission itself acknowledges the needs as ‘most pressing’, yet fails to provide an immediate, quantified financial commitment. 1.

Considering that Gaza is at a critical historical juncture, why has the Commission prioritised long-term strategic partnerships and political transitions over the immediate, large-scale reconstruction required in a conflict zone of such symbolic and human importance?
Can the Commission specify the exact amount of the ‘remaining part’ and justify how these residual funds can realistically address the massive damage to infrastructure in Palestine?
Does the Commission acknowledge that delaying aid to a ‘later stage’ contradicts the EU’s commitment to being a leading humanitarian actor and exacerbates regional instability?

Supporter (2) (20 May 2026) In 2026, the Commission announced EUR 124.4 million in humanitarian funding for Palestine (1). This brings the total of EU humanitarian aid to Palestine to almost EUR 675 million. The EU is also delivering on its commitment to provide the Multiannual Comprehensive Support Programme (2025-2027) worth up to EUR 1.6 billion to foster Palestinian recovery and resilience (2) and to support the Palestinian Authority’s reform agenda. E-10-2026-000801.t: Cross-border exploitation and substandard housing of EU mobile workers
qt: to the Commission Kathleen Van Brempt (S&D), Mohammed Chahim (S&D) Subject:

Recent events in the Belgian-Dutch border region have exposed a systemic failure in protecting EU mobile workers. On 8 March 2025, a fire broke out in a former ‘rendez-vous’ hotel in Lommel, Belgium. Although officially registered as vacant, the building housed 21 Latvian workers in appalling living conditions. They were employed by a Dutch meatprocessing company but housed across the border in Belgium by a Dutch real estate agency. This is not an isolated case as similar situations have been reported involving other companies. It shows that certain actors exploit regulatory differences between Member States to circumvent housing rules and labour inspections. 1.

Is the Commission aware of this practice, whereby employers or recruitment agencies house mobile workers in a different Member State to where the workers are employed in order to circumvent certain regulations or inspections, and how can the European Labour Authority help address these abuses?

How will the Commission’s first-ever European Affordable Housing Plan ensure that ‘affordable and quality housing’ also protects mobile workers from illegal, exploitative or employment-tied arrangements?

Is the Commission considering European minimum standards for mobile workers’ housing, and will it support or fund cross-border initiatives, such as the Arrondissement Information and Expertise Centres (ARIEC) in Belgium and the Euro-regional Information and Expertise Centre (EURIEC), to tackle organised crime and human trafficking linked to labour migration?
at: (English version) to the Commission Kathleen Van Brempt (S&D), Mohammed Chahim (S&D) (25 February 2026) Subject: Cross-border exploitation and substandard housing of EU mobile workers Recent events in the Belgian-Dutch border region have exposed a systemic failure in protecting EU mobile workers. On 8 March 2025, a fire broke out in a former ‘rendez-vous’ hotel in Lommel, Belgium. Although officially registered as vacant, the building housed 21 Latvian workers in appalling living conditions. They were employed by a Dutch meat-processing company but housed across the border in Belgium by a Dutch real estate agency. This is not an isolated case as similar situations have been reported involving other companies. It shows that certain actors exploit regulatory differences between Member States to circumvent housing rules and labour inspections. 1. Is the Commission aware of this practice, whereby employers or recruitment agencies house mobile workers in a different Member State to where the workers are employed in order to circumvent certain regulations or inspections, and how can the European Labour Authority help address these abuses? 2. How will the Commission’s first-ever European Affordable Housing Plan ensure that ‘affordable and quality housing’ also protects mobile workers from illegal, exploitative or employment-tied arrangements? 3. Is the Commission considering European minimum standards for mobile workers’ housing, and will it support or fund cross-border initiatives, such as the Arrondissement Information and Expertise Centres (ARIEC) in Belgium and the Euroregional Information and Expertise Centre (EURIEC), to tackle organised crime and human trafficking linked to labour migration? (13 April 2026) The Commission is aware of concerns related to the conditions of accommodation of posted workers as noted in the Implementation report of Directive (EU) 2018/957 (1) and has suggested follow-up actions. The cooperation established between German and Dutch authorities, also involving the European Labour Authority, shows how successful inspections can be organised in that area (2). The Commission recognises that national legislation and increased attention to law enforcement on the ground constitute key elements to address these problems (3). The European Affordable Housing Plan (4) puts forward actions aiming at facilitating affordable housing to most vulnerable groups. It does not particularly envisage situations like the one described by the Honourable Members in which case employers’ obligations stem from the applicable labour laws. EU law on free movement of workers ensures that mobile workers have the same rights as national workers in housing (5). The Commission has supported the Euregional Information and Expertise Centre (6) since 2019 with grants from the EU’s Internal Security Fund — Police and, by doing so, contributes to the close cooperation of Dutch, Belgian and German authorities. Beyond that, the Commission also supports the trade-union driven fair labour mobility EU project (7); labour conditions of people working in the domain of meat processing is one of the areas of particular attention for the project team (8).

E-10-2026-000800.t: Listing the eel as ‘endangered’ in the Spanish Catalogue of Threatened Species
qt: to the Commission Isabel Serra Sánchez (The Left) Subject:

Recently (in February 2026), the Spanish autonomous communities rejected for the third time the Spanish Government’s proposal to list the eel as ‘endangered’ in the Spanish Catalogue of Threatened Species. With that refusal to protect the European eel stock, Spain not only supposedly breaches the dedicated regulation adopted in 2007, but may also violate several cross-cutting EU directives on environmental protection: - the Habitats Directive (92/43/EEC)1, - the Water Framework Directive (2000/60/EC)2, - the Environmental Liability Directive (2004/35/EC)3. In light of the above: 1.
What is the Commission’s view of the refusal to protect the eel for the third time?
What action will it take to ensure that Spain protects the eel?

https://cobio.csic.es/index.php/component/content/article/505-en-que-consiste-la-directiva-habitats?catid=68 https://www.chguadiana.es/sites/default/files/2021-06/A12_Obj_MA_Excepciones.pdf https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:52012DC0670
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (12.5.2026) The European eel1 is not protected under the Habitats Directive2. The obligation under the Environmental Liability Directive3 (ELD) to prevent and remediate significant biodiversity damage is limited to damage to habitats and species protected under the EU law. The ELD only applies to damage caused by economic activity. A potential damage resulting from the non-recognition of eel as endangered species is thus not covered by the ELD. Regarding the Water Framework Directive4, it requires Member States to implement measures to ensure that the status of water bodies, including as regards river continuity and fish communities, does not deviate, or only slightly, from undisturbed conditions. Furthermore, it is not allowed to trade eels from and to the EU5. Member States, including Spain, take various measures through their eel management plans under the Eel Regulation6 and other legal instruments. In particular, the EU sets temporary fishing closures under the Fishing Opportunities Regulation7. As there is no obligation in EU law to list the eel as ‘endangered’ in the national catalogue of threatened species, the decision on this matter is solely for the Spanish national authorities, without prejudice to the aforementioned obligations under EU law. The Nature Restoration Regulation8 requires Member States to make inventories of their artificial barriers to the connectivity of surface waters, and to plan for removals of obsolete barriers in order to reach the EU-wide objective of restoring 25 000 km of rivers to freeflowing rivers between 2020 and 2030. The Commission monitors the implementation of relevant EU legislation and continues working with Member States and stakeholders to help rebuild the eel stock. 1 Anguilla anguilla. 2 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/1992/43/oj/eng. 3 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2004/35/oj/eng. 4 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2000/60/oj/eng. 5 The competent scientific authorities of the Member States agreed unanimously that they would not be able to

issue a non-detriment finding for the export of European eel specimens, as it is critically endangered, as required under Article IV(2)(a) of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES). Therefore, since 2010, a zero-export quota has been issued and published on the CITES website. 6 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX%3A32007R1100. E-10-2026-000799.t: Adherence to the principle of multilingualism in the EU institutions’ digital communications
qt: to the Commission Željana Zovko (PPE) Subject:

Multilingualism is one of the fundamental principles of the EU and a cornerstone of its democratic legitimacy and accessibility to citizens. The aim of the multilingualism policy is to facilitate communication with citizens in their mother tongue, protect Europe’s linguistic diversity and promote language-learning. The right of EU citizens to contact the EU institutions in any of the 24 official languages and receive a reply in that language is enshrined in the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the EU. What is more, Article 342 TFEU and Regulation No 1 establish that all official and working languages of the EU institutions are equal. Despite this legal framework, in practice, content on the websites of the Commission and Parliament is often not available in Croatian, except via machine translation. This is the case not only for general information, but also for some documents of direct interest to citizens. Could the Commission therefore answer the following: 1.
What specific measures is it taking to ensure the systemic availability of official content in Croatian?
What are the most common reasons why content is made available only via machine translation for certain languages, including Croatian, while official translations are available in others?
Is it planning additional steps to ensure strict adherence to the principle of multilingualism in digital communication with citizens?
at: (English version) to the Commission Željana Zovko (PPE) (25 February 2026) Subject: Adherence to the principle of multilingualism in the EU institutions’ digital communications Multilingualism is one of the fundamental principles of the EU and a cornerstone of its democratic legitimacy and accessibility to citizens. The aim of the multilingualism policy is to facilitate communication with citizens in their mother tongue, protect Europe’s linguistic diversity and promote language-learning. The right of EU citizens to contact the EU institutions in any of the 24 official languages and receive a reply in that language is enshrined in the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the EU. What is more, Article 342 TFEU and Regulation No 1 establish that all official and working languages of the EU institutions are equal. Despite this legal framework, in practice, content on the websites of the Commission and Parliament is often not available in Croatian, except via machine translation. This is the case not only for general information, but also for some documents of direct interest to citizens. Could the Commission therefore answer the following: 1.
What specific measures is it taking to ensure the systemic availability of official content in Croatian?
What are the most common reasons why content is made available only via machine translation for certain languages, including Croatian, while official translations are available in others?
Is it planning additional steps to ensure strict adherence to the principle of multilingualism in digital communication with citizens?

(11 June 2026) In line with Regulation No 1 from 1958 (1), EU legislation is published in all EU official and working languages and natural and legal persons can write to the Commission in all of them, including Croatian, and will receive a reply in the same language. On its main website (2), the Commission provides information in all EU official languages, including Croatian. Practical information on citizens’ rights and administrative and legal procedures is also provided in all EU official languages (3), including Croatian. When information is particularly relevant for speakers of a specific language, it is usually drafted and published in that language or translated into it. In such instances, other languages may be provided through machine translation. An example of this is the website of the Commission’s Representation in Croatia (4), where the content is drafted and published in Croatian. This balanced approach ensures that the Commission’s online communication with citizens fully adheres to the principle of multilingualism.

E-10-2026-000798.t: E-money tokens backed by central bank money in the CSDR reform
qt: to the Commission Sibylle Berg (NI) Subject:

As part of the market integration package (the ‘Master Regulation’), the reform of the Central Securities Depositories Regulation (CSDR) aims to reduce the default settlement cycle to T+1 (settlement one-day after trading), while allowing for voluntary T+0 models (same-day settlement). Article 40 CSDR requires settlement in central bank money where practical. At the same time, the Regulation on a pilot regime for market infrastructures based on distributed ledger technology (the DLT pilot regime) and the Regulation on Markets in Crypto-Assets (MiCAR) govern the use of e-money tokens (EMTs) that are pegged 1:1 to a currency and fully backed. It is unclear whether EMT models whose reserves are held entirely as central bank deposits in a TARGET account (a Eurosystem payment system) held by a supervised intermediary and which effectively serve only as a tokenised access layer can qualify as settlement in central bank money within the meaning of Article 40 CSDR. 1.
Does the Commission agree with this interpretation and, if not, how does the Commission distinguish ‘settlement in central bank money’ from ‘settlement in EMTs’ in such models?

Does the Commission plan to make clarifications in the CSDR refit and/or give the European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA) a mandate to develop guidelines or regulatory technical standards, in particular on segregation, insolvency protection, transparency and the delivery-versus-payment mechanism?

How does the Commission intend to ensure that the transition to T+1 and the use of the DLT pilot regime do not hinder voluntary T+0 DLT models, and when can any clarifications or Level 2 or Level 3 measures be expected?
at: (English version) to the Commission Sibylle Berg (NI) (25 February 2026) Subject: E-money tokens backed by central bank money in the CSDR reform As part of the market integration package (the ‘Master Regulation’), the reform of the Central Securities Depositories Regulation (CSDR) aims to reduce the default settlement cycle to T+1 (settlement one-day after trading), while allowing for voluntary T+0 models (same-day settlement). Article 40 CSDR requires settlement in central bank money where practical. At the same time, the regulation on a pilot regime for market infrastructures based on distributed ledger technology (the DLT pilot regime) and the regulation on Markets in Crypto-Assets (MiCAR) govern the use of e-money tokens (EMTs) that are pegged 1:1 to a currency and fully backed. It is unclear whether EMT models whose reserves are held entirely as central bank deposits in a TARGET account (a Eurosystem payment system) held by a supervised intermediary and which effectively serve only as a tokenised access layer can qualify as settlement in central bank money within the meaning of Article 40 CSDR. 1. Does the Commission agree with this interpretation and, if not, how does the Commission distinguish ‘settlement in central bank money’ from ‘settlement in EMTs’ in such models? 2. Does the Commission plan to make clarifications in the CSDR refit and/or give the European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA) a mandate to develop guidelines or regulatory technical standards, in particular on segregation, insolvency protection, transparency and the delivery-versus-payment mechanism? 3. How does the Commission intend to ensure that the transition to T+1 and the use of the DLT pilot regime do not hinder voluntary T+0 DLT models, and when can any clarifications or Level 2 or Level 3 measures be expected? (28 April 2026) Central securities depositories (CSDs) are currently required to settle the cash leg of securities transactions through ‘accounts opened with a central bank’ or, under restrictive conditions, ‘through accounts opened with a credit institution’ pursuant to Article 40 of the Central Securities Depositories Regulation (CSDR) (1). With the aim of fostering innovation, the proposal to amend the CSDR as part of the Market Integration and Supervision Package (2) enables CSDs to settle the cash leg of securities transactions with certain electronic money tokens (EMTs) regulated under the Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (MiCAR) (3). EMTs (4) are subject to specific rules, including requirements on reserve assets and how EMTs must be issued. Holders of EMTs have a claim against the issuers which have therefore a liability towards holders. In addition, a definition of ‘central bank money’ is included in the proposal in order to further differentiate between the possible means of settling the cash leg of securities transactions including in the context of distributed ledger technology (DLT)-based settlement. The proposal is currently under negotiation in the European Parliament and Council. The proposal to amend the CSDR also includes legal empowerments (5) for the European Securities and Markets Authority to draft technical standards on how to operationalise DLT-settlement.

Regulation (EU) No 909/2014 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 23 July 2014 on improving securities settlement in the European Union and on central securities depositories and amending Directives 98/26/EC and 2014/65/EU and Regulation (EU) No 236/2012, http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2014/909/oj. COM(2025) 943 final. Regulation (EU) 2023/1114 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 31 May 2023 on markets in crypto-assets and amending Regulations (EU) No 1093/2010 and (EU) No 1095/2010 and Directives 2013/36/EU and (EU) 2019/1937, OJ L 150, 9.6.2023, pp. 40-205. EMTs are defined in Article 3(1)(7) of MiCAR as ‘a type of crypto-asset that purports to maintain a stable value by referencing the value of one official currency’. Articles 6(5) and 45a of the proposal to amend the CSDR set out the mandate for the European Securities Market Authorities to take into account the use of new technologies, including DLT, in the drafting of technical standards pertaining to communication protocols used by issuers, CSDs and other market infrastructures and the mandate to draft technical standards in relation to the mitigation of the risks stemming from the use of DLT for the provision of CSD services outside of an outsourcing arrangement.

The DLT Pilot Regulation (6) provides that Article 5 of the CSDR applies, which does not preclude same-day settlement models, as it specifies that the settlement should occur no later than two business days after the trade. Regulation (EU) 2025/2075 (7) will shorten that period to one business day from 11 October 2027.

Regulation (EU) 2022/858 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 30 May 2022 on a pilot regime for market infrastructures based on distributed ledger technology, and amending Regulations (EU) No 600/2014 and (EU) No 909/2014 and Directive 2014/65/EU, http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/858/oj. E-10-2026-000797.t: Damage caused to Lampedusa-based fishing boats by wrecked migrant smuggling vessels and the need to clean up the seabed
qt: to the Commission Giuseppe Lupo (S&D) Subject:

On 24 February 20261, the ANSA press agency revealed that a number of Lampedusan fishing boats recently found derelict migrant smuggling vessels in their nets. Sectorial operators report that hulks resting on the seabed are getting caught up in fishing nets, resulting in damaged gear and significant economic losses. The fishers involved are also losing working days, as they have to return to port to disentangle these wrecks (an operation they cannot perform at sea) and repair their equipment. Large-scale seabed clean-up operations must be carried out, seeing as these derelict ships aren’t just causing direct financial losses for businesses, but are also an obvious threat to the environment and safe navigation. In the light of the above: 1.
Is the Commission aware of this state of affairs affecting fishing vessels operating near Lampedusa?

What EU instruments – including those under EMFAF and other relevant programmes – could be activated with a view to implementing mechanisms to compensate fishers for damages caused by these sunken vessels?

Does the Commission agree that it should, in conjunction with the competent national authorities, push for the establishment of a programme to clear seabeds containing wrecked ships with a view to ensuring safe fishing conditions and protecting the marine environment?
https://www.ansa.it/amp/ansamed/it/notizie/rubriche/nazioni/2026/02/24/a-lampedusa-i-pescatori-trovano-barche-di-migranti-nelle-reti_26e1aeea-9df9-4d41-a321294b64a41a12.html.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (28.4.2026) The Commission has not been notified about the incidents mentioned by the Honourable Member and does not dispose of sufficient information to assess their impact on fishing operations around Lampedusa Island. The European Maritime, Fisheries and Aquaculture Fund (EMFAF)1 can support measures that contribute to the protection and restoration of aquatic biodiversity and ecosystems, including actions to achieve a good environmental status as set out in Article 1(1) of the Marine Strategy Framework Directive (MSFD)2. Under specific conditions, the EMFAF can also provide for compensation to fishers for the temporary cessation of fishing activities. It remains within the competence of the Italian authorities to assess and, where appropriate, mobilise the relevant EMFAF resources in line with the objectives of Italy’s EMFAF programme. The Commission remains available to support Italy in the implementation of its EMFAF programme. In implementing their marine strategies, Member States are already obliged to protect the marine environment to achieve good environmental status. No further programmes are therefore envisaged.
1 Regulation (EU) 2021/1139 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 7 July 2021 establishing the

European Maritime, Fisheries and Aquaculture Fund and amending Regulation (EU) 2017/1004. 2 Directive 2008/56/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 17 June 2008 establishing a framework for community action in the field of marine environmental policy (Marine Strategy Framework Directive).

qt: to the Commission Hanna Gedin (The Left), Jonas Sjöstedt (The Left) Subject:

The rule of law is a universal principle of governance that is fundamental to international peace, security and political stability. As part of the development of rule of law policy at EU level, in 2014, the Commission issued a communication on the new EU framework to strengthen the rule of law, recognising it as a constitutional principle and setting out a nonexhaustive list of its key elements. In 2019, the rule of law was further defined, and, in December 2020, the EU co-legislators (the European Parliament and the Council) established a legally binding definition of the rule of law under the Conditionality Regulation (Article 2). In its official report 2025:99, the Swedish Government proposed a special law allowing for the blanket revocation of permanent residence permits. The proposal would mean that previously favourable administrative decisions could be retroactively amended to the detriment of the individual. According to the principle of legality, however, public powers must be exercised in a predictable and clearly regulated manner. Several consultative bodies have rejected the proposal, arguing that it runs counter to the fundamental principles of the rule of law, international law and the principle of the best interests of the child. 1.

Does the Commission consider the retroactive blanket revocation of permanent residence permits that have already been granted to be compatible with legal certainty and the fundamental principles of the rule of law?
Does the Commission consider the proposal to be compatible with the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights and the Treaty on European Union?
Does the Commission intend to take action and, if so, what would such action entail?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (11.5.2026) The Commission generally does not comment on draft legislation. Accordingly, it is not in a position to provide an answer to the questions submitted by the Honourable Members.
